<meta>This page transitions from the historical records of the first century into the "Gnostic Century" (the second century AD), shifting the focus from the era of the Apostles to the era of the early Church Fathers, the rise of major heresies, and the Roman persecutions under Trajan and Marcus Aurelius.</meta>

# THE GNOSTIC CENTURY.

->Overview of the Century<-

<margin>2nd CENTURY AD</margin>
Despite a hatred from the Jews toward Christians that was more than Vatinian <note>A proverbial expression for extreme or unrelenting hatred, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius.</note>, and notwithstanding the arguments of philosophers and the military power of the Emperors, the Christian religion grew with miraculous strength. Many of the more distinguished Gentiles were converted to the faith, such as *Justin Martyr*, *Theophilus of Antioch*, and others, who, by offering "Apologies" <term>Apology (A formal defense of a religious or philosophical position rather than an expression of regret)</term> on behalf of the Christians and their worship, vigorously defended this most holy religion against the slanders of the pagans. The most foul heresy of the Gnostics—the *Valentinians*, *Carpocratians*, *Menandrians*, *Marcionites*, and so on—which were offshoots of the school of Simon Magus from the preceding century, began to spread more widely. These were followed by the heresies of *Tatian*, *Montanus*, and *Theodotus*, to say nothing of other most impure sects. During this time, the Holy Bible was translated more than once from Hebrew into the Greek language. After the line of the Bishops of Jerusalem (who until this time had been from the "circumcision" <note>That is, they were of Jewish descent.</note>) came to an end, the first Bishop from the Gentiles, Marcus, was appointed in the year 136 AD. A schism flourished concerning the date of Easter: on one side, Victor, the Bishop of Rome, contended that the Feast of Easter should be celebrated only on the Lord’s Day (Sunday); on the other, Polycrates and the Asian Bishops insisted it be held on the "Fourteenth Moon" <term>Quartodeciman (The practice of celebrating Easter on the 14th of the Jewish month of Nisan, regardless of which day of the week it fell upon)</term>. Because of this, Victor rashly brandished the lightning bolt of excommunication against the Asians. Various Synods were held in both the East and the West regarding this matter, which Eusebius discusses in Book 5, chapters 23, 24, and 25 of his history. Near the beginning of the century, in the year 107 AD during the reign of Trajan, the third persecution against the Christians took place. It was provoked under the pretext that their solemn assemblies were "secret societies" (*hetaeriae*) <note>original: "hetæriæ"</note> and illegal associations, which were expressly forbidden by Roman laws. *Trajan* consulted Pliny the Younger, the Proconsul of Bithynia, regarding the Christians: *Pliny* replied that they were good men, though laboring under a "depraved and immoderate superstition," but were nonetheless most ready to undergo death for their religion. Trajan wrote back that Christians were therefore not to be sought out, but if they were reported and convicted, they must be punished. Tertullian, in his *Apology* (chapter 2), argued against this decree with great wit:

> *O judgment confused by necessity; he says they must not be sought out, as if they were innocent: and yet commands they be punished, as if they were guilty. He spares and rages, he ignores and notices: Why do you cheat yourself with your own sentence? If you condemn them, why not also seek them? If you do not seek them, why not also acquit them? Therefore, a man is brought forth for condemnation whom no one wished to search for; who, I think, now deserves punishment not because he is guilty, but because he was found, despite not being sought.* <note>original: "O sententiam necessitate confusam; negat inquirendos... inventus est."</note>

Sulpitius Severus places the fourth persecution under Hadrian; however, Eusebius and others refer it to the times of Marcus Antoninus (Marcus Aurelius), around the year 163 AD, and this persecution does not seem to have lasted only a single year. Certainly, in the year 167 AD, it blazed more violently in Gaul, as evidenced by the struggles of so many illustrious martyrs who died for their piety at Lugdunum (Lyons); Eusebius treats these events at length in Book 5, chapter 1, drawing from the letters of the people of Lyons and Vienne.

# WRITERS.

<margin>
2nd CENTURY, from 101 AD.

* Homily on St. Ignatius, p. 499, Vol. I.

† Dialogue I, p. 33.
</margin>

IGNATIUS: The ancient writers are silent regarding his homeland and parents. St. Metaphrastes, Nicephorus, and others maintain—based on an entirely uncertain tradition—that he was that same young child whom Christ lifted up in his hands and presented to the Disciples, and that he earned the name *Theophoros* <note>Greek: Θεοφόρος, meaning "God-bearer" or "one carried by God."</note> from that event. Chrysostom testifies to us that he lived on familiar terms with the Apostles and drank from them spiritual streams, "sharing in both their spoken and unspoken teachings" <note>Original Greek: καὶ ῥητῶν, καὶ ἀποῤῥήτων αὐτοῖς κοινωνῆσαι</note>, and was judged by them to be worthy of the leadership of the See of Antioch. Certainly, after the death of Euodius, he was elevated to the prelacy of that Church; he received this grace "through the great right hand of Peter" <note>Original Greek: διὰ τῆς μεγάλης Πέτρου δεξιᾶς</note>, as Theodoret says †, with Peter himself laying hands upon him. He had governed this Church for more than forty years when Trajan, around the year 107 AD, came to Antioch to wage war against the Parthians. St. Ignatius was condemned by him to the wild beasts and sent in chains to Rome to undergo martyrdom. There, brought into the Amphitheater on the 13th day before the Kalends of January <note>December 20th</note> in the year 107, his body was soon ground up by the teeth of lions, and he returned his blessed soul to God. However, concerning his journey and the entire course of his martyrdom, one should consult the very ancient *Acts of his Martyrdom*; regarding which, see below.

### ->GENUINE WORKS.<-

<margin>
* Epistle to the Smyrnaeans.
</margin>

SEVEN Epistles: namely, to the Ephesians, to the Magnesians, to the Trallians, to the Romans, to the Philadelphians, to the Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp. The first four were written at Smyrna, and the last three at Troas, while he was delayed in those places while hurrying to Rome to undergo martyrdom. Behold the famous testimony of Polycarp * concerning these Epistles: "from which you will be able to derive great benefit; for they contain faith, and patience, and every edification pertaining to our Lord" <note>Original Greek: ἐξ ὧν μεγάλα ὠφεληθῆναι δυνήσεσθε· περιέχουσι γὰρ πίστιν, καὶ ὑπομονὴν, καὶ πᾶσαν οἰκοδομὴν τὴν εἰς τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν ἀνήκουσαν</note>. And they are indeed the most brilliant witnesses of primitive piety, Church doctrine, and the Episcopal <term>Episcopal (Governance of the church by bishops)</term> system flourishing in the Apostolic age itself. For this reason, the "Innovators" <note>A term used here for Protestant critics who challenged the authenticity of the letters to undermine the historical precedent for bishops.</note> rise up sharply against them, and Blondel, Saumaise, and Daillé—the most learned heads of those seeking innovations—have attacked them with all their might. To say nothing now of the writers of lesser rank, such as Owen, Voet, etc. But our own "great" Hammond <note>Henry Hammond, an influential English theologian.</note> bravely defeated their empty attacks in four dissertations published in 1651 against Blondel and others. He was followed by the most learned John Pearson, later Bishop of Chester (never to be named without a preface of honor), who brought to light the *Vindication of Ignatius* in 1672. In this work, he so utterly blew away all objections and fortified the cause of Ignatius with such strong and invincible arguments that it should seem quite a marvel if our adversaries dare to bring their so-often-defeated forces into battle again. These Epistles, which for many centuries past had been miserably interpolated <term>Interpolated (Corrupted by the insertion of fake or later text)</term>, the Reverend Archbishop of Armagh <note>James Ussher, a famous 17th-century scholar and prelate.</note> finally began to restore to their integrity. He published an ancient Latin translation alongside the Greek text, taken from the public library of Gonville and Caius College at Cambridge and the private library of the Reverend Montague, Bishop of Norwich. He distinguished the additions to the Greek with red ink so that the true might be more easily discerned from the false; he also added preliminary dissertations and notes, published at Oxford in 1644. Two years later, in 1646, the illustrious Isaac Vossius published the genuine Greek text from the Medicean Library—where it had long lain hidden—which perfectly matched Ussher’s ancient Latin version, along with that version and his own notes. Finally, in the following year, to make his edition complete, Ussher added a *Genuine Appendix* containing Vossius's text with a new version and other related matters.

### SPURIOUS WORKS.

Eight Epistles: namely, to Mary of Cassobola <note>In the 1644 edition by Ussher, a Latin version is provided; in the 1647 Appendix, the Greek. This includes a letter from Mary of Cassobola to Ignatius, apparently produced by the same impostor, though it is older than Antonius Melissa, who cites it in Book 2, Sermon 19</note>; *to the Tarsians, to the Antiochians, to the Philippians, to Hero, to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and two to John the Apostle.* These last three exist only in Latin.

Regarding the interpolation <note>the unauthorized altering or "padding" of a text</note> of the genuine Epistles of Ignatius and the plant of spurious ones, the distinguished scholars James Ussher and John Pearson offer this judgment: the genuine letters were interpolated at the beginning of the sixth century, as they were first cited by Stephen Gobar around the year 580, Anastasius of Antioch in 595, and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle in 630. Ussher adds (and attempts to prove with many arguments) that they were corrupted by the same hand that attached the last 35 chapters to the Apostolic Canons and interpolated the Apostolic Constitutions; he further argues that the interpolator, whoever he was, was a heretic. Regarding the spurious Epistles that exist in Greek, they believe these were forged at the end of the same century, as they were first cited by Anastasius the Presbyter around 650, Antiochus the Monk in 614, John of Damascus, and Antonius Melissa. Among these, Pearson excepts the Epistle to the Philippians, which he considers to be of a later age, yet older than Ado of Vienne <note>a 9th-century chronicler</note> who cites it. Finally, they judge the three Latin Epistles to be of Latin origin and of a much more recent stamp, as they are found cited for the first time by Bernard of Clairvaux, Dionysius the Carthusian, and the Pseudo-Dexter.

In almost all editions of Ignatius, there is an old Latin translator of the interpolated Epistles, whom Ussher guesses is older than Ado of Vienne (who flourished around 875). In Ussher’s own editions, there is a Latin version of the non-interpolated Epistles, mentioned above. Ussher believes the author of this version was Robert, Bishop of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste, the famous 13th-century polymath and bishop</note>.

<margin>
* Preface, chapters 2, 3, 4, 5.
† Supplement to Bellarmine's "On Writers," p. 8.
</margin>
Setting aside other editions, of which Pearson * provides an accurate list (followed recently by Oudin †), all the letters—both spurious and genuine—are available in the *Oxford* edition of 1644, together with the Appendix, *London*, 1647, in quarto; and in Cotelier’s collection of the Apostolic Fathers, *Paris*, 1672. The edition by Vossius was also reprinted in *London*, 1680, in quarto.

It seems that in former times, certain heretics forged a *Didache* <note>Greek: Διδαχὴ, meaning "Teaching"</note> or *Didascalia* <note>Greek: Διδασκαλία, meaning "Instruction"</note> under the name of Ignatius, in which they explained traditions and dogmas supposedly received from the Apostles during conversation. From various "Instructions" of this kind, as has been mentioned, the Apostolic Constitutions were patched together; and in those, the Ignatian portion holds a significant place, though it is so mixed and confused with others that no one could determine what belongs specifically to him, even by guesswork. However, John of Damascus and Antonius Melissa do present certain fragments.

<margin>107 AD.</margin>
### PHILO, a Deacon of Tarsus, and Agathopus, companions of Ignatius from the East all the way to Rome (whom Ignatius himself mentions at the end of the Epistle to the Philadelphians), wrote, as is reasonable to believe, the *Acts of the Martyrdom of Ignatius*. The Reverend Ussher was the first to retrieve two copies of the most ancient version of these, making them public in the Ignatian Appendix of 1647. Bollandus also published them in the *Lives of the Saints* under the first day of February. It must certainly seem strange that the most learned Ussher did not publish the Greek text, given that he himself testifies to having found a manuscript copy of it in the Bodleian Library.

<margin>108 AD.</margin>
### POLYCARP of Smyrna, appears to some to have been born toward the end of Nero's reign. 
<margin>* Book 3, ch. 3.</margin>
> A man, says Irenaeus *, who was not only instructed by the Apostles and lived familiarly with many who had seen the Lord, but was also ordained Bishop of the Church of Smyrna in Asia by the Apostles themselves.

He refers especially to John the Apostle, whose disciple Polycarp was, and by whom he was appointed Bishop; this must have taken place around the year 94 or 95 AD; if only...

<meta>This page continues the history of the Apostolic Fathers, shifting focus to Polycarp of Smyrna, his relationship with the apostles, his journey to Rome, his martyrdom, and his literary remains.</meta>

-># The Gnostic Century.<-

<margin>
2nd CENTURY, from 101 AD.
</margin>
If the conjecture of the most learned Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh and famous chronologist</note> were true, Polycarp is that "Angel of the Church of Smyrna" to whom Saint John wrote the Epistle in *Revelation* II. When a serious controversy arose concerning the date of Easter <note>original: *die Paschatis*</note>, he traveled to Rome, and there he lived familiarly with Bishop Anicetus (who, according to the calculations of Pearson and Dodwell derived from Eutychius, began his pontificate in 142 AD). During this time, he brought back many to the faith who had been deceived by the errors of Marcion and Valentinus <note>two prominent Gnostic leaders of the 2nd century</note>. Finally, under Marcus Antoninus—or as others say, Antoninus Pius—as persecution grew hot, Polycarp was condemned to the pyre at Smyrna and given to the flames. However, the flame, like a ship's sail billowed by the blowing winds, encircled the Martyr's body without daring to touch it; at last, he was pierced with a sword.

The Pagans reduced the dead body to ashes, fearing that the Christians might carry away his remains and honor them with divine worship. "Fools," says the Church of Smyrna, "who did not know that we can never leave Christ, nor worship anyone else: *for Him we adore as the Son of God, but the Martyrs we deservedly love as disciples and imitators of the Lord because of their extraordinary devotion which they declared toward their King and Master.*" Nevertheless, the Christians gathered the martyr's half-burnt bones, "dearer than the most precious gems" (to use their own words) "and purer than any gold," and honorably placed them in a tomb, recalling the memory of his Passion by celebrating an annual feast day. Polycarp died *at a very great age* <note>original Greek: *πάνυ γηραλέος*</note>, says Irenaeus; specifically in the 86th year of his life. For so he himself told the Proconsul: *Eighty and six years have I served Him* <note>original Greek: *ὀγδοήκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτη δουλεύω αὐτῷ*</note>. The Ancients maintain these years should be understood as his entire lifespan, rather than the duration of his Christian profession as some recent writers interpret it. Regarding the year in which he suffered martyrdom, writers vary wonderfully. Eusebius places it in 167 AD; Ussher and Bucher in 169 AD; Petitus in 175 AD; but our most learned Pearson strongly contends that he suffered in 147 AD. He demonstrates this at length with many types of argument; see his extensive and learned discussion on this matter in *Dissertations II, chapters 14 through 20.*

<margin>
* Letter to Florinus in Eusebius, Book 5, ch. 20. || Prologue to the works of St. Dionysius.
* Book 3, ch. 3 and in Eusebius Book 4, ch. 14.
† Codex 126.
* Under the entry "Polycarp." † On Illustrious Men, ch. 17.
</margin>
He wrote several Epistles, partly to neighboring Churches to strengthen them, and partly to certain brothers, admonishing and exhorting them, as Irenaeus reports \*. Saint Maximus || and Johannes Maxentius cite an *Epistle to the Athenians*; Suidas mentions another *to Dionysius the Areopagite*. However, those seem spurious. Of his works, there still exists the *Epistle to the Philippians*, often published in Latin together with the Epistles of Ignatius. It was first published in Greek and Latin by Pierre Halloix, a Jesuit, in his *Life of Polycarp* (Douai, 1633), and later in an expanded version by the Reverend Ussher in his *Ignatian Appendix* (1647). Finally, the learned Stephen Le Moyne, a theologian of Leiden, recently brought it to light among his *Varia Sacra* (*Leiden*, 1685, 4to), though whether he "adorned" or "burdened" it with his long and miscellaneous notes is a matter of opinion. It is not unworthy of note that in Le Moyne's edition, the part of the Epistle containing that most celebrated testimony for the Ignatian Epistles is missing; even though it was not in his specific manuscript codex, he could not have been ignorant that it was found in both the Halloix and Ussher editions. Irenaeus says of this Epistle \*: *There is also a most sufficient Epistle of Polycarp written to the Philippians, from which those who wish and care for their own salvation can learn both the character of his faith and the preaching of the truth.* Photius † says similarly: *Polycarp's Epistle to the Philippians was read, full of much admonition with clarity and simplicity, according to the ecclesiastical style of interpretation.* Suidas calls it *altogether wonderful* \*, and Jerome † calls it *very useful*, stating that even in his time it was customary for it to be read in the assembly of Asia. There also exist certain fragments of Polycarp translated into Latin by Victor of Capua around the year 480 from a Greek codex of the *Chapters of Responses of Blessed Polycarp*. These were first published by François Feuardent at the end of Chapter 3, Book 3 of Irenaeus, and from him by P. Halloix in *Lives of the Oriental Fathers*, Volume I, page 525. Lastly, James Ussher gave them to the public in his *Ignatian Appendix*. But whether these are genuine, one may doubt with good reason. There were circulated—

-># The Gnostic Century.<-

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ’s Birth.
</margin>
In former times, a certain *Teaching* <note>original: Διδαχή (*Didache*)</note> was cited under his name by Maximus, Bede, Ado, and others; it was of the same character as the writings of Ignatius, and it holds a place in the *Apostolic Constitutions*. I do not know if it is worth mentioning what Pierre Halloix notes in his *Life of Polycarp*, chapter 16: "Pionius," he says, "who 
> "wrote the life of Saint Polycarp in Greek, is the authority that this same Polycarp wrote many 
> "treatises, homilies, and letters. It is also said that he composed an entire book on 
> "the death of Saint John the Evangelist, his master, which survives today 
> "in manuscript form in the Library of the Abbey of Saint Flora in Gaul <note>Specifically Cisalpine Gaul, modern Northern Italy</note>. From this 
> "book, François Humblot produces several points in a sermon on Saint John the 
> "Evangelist, near the end. If this book truly belongs to Saint Polycarp, 
> "Good God, what a shameful thing it is to keep such a treasure in the dark, and to 
> "begrudge the public its use and benefit!" 
But I believe no sane person will doubt that, instead of a treasure, we would likely dig up only charcoal <note>A reference to a Latin proverb meaning something that seems valuable but turns out to be worthless</note>.

<margin>
110. * Book 3, ch. 39. † Book 5, ch. 33. * Codex 232. † Year 3 of the 235th Olympiad. * Book 3, ch. 38. * Book 5, ch. 33. * Book 3, ch. 39. † Commentary on Revelation, Sermon 12. || On chapter 27 of Matthew.
</margin>
**PAPIAS**, a man of Asia, perhaps born in Hierapolis, was a hearer of Saint John and a companion of Polycarp. Eusebius * indeed understands him to have heard not the Apostle John, but John the Presbyter <note>or "John the Elder"</note>. However, Irenaeus †, and a long line of other writers after him †, seem to indicate clearly enough that he was a disciple of John the Apostle. Whatever the case, it is certain that he lived familiarly with the Elders who had been hearers of the Apostles. He inquired of them curiously as to what the sayings of the Elders were: what Peter, what Andrew, what Philip, what the other disciples of the Lord used to say; and what Aristion and John the Presbyter preached. For he said, "I did not think that I could gain as much benefit from reading books as from the living voice of men still surviving." Having been made Bishop of the Church of Hierapolis in Phrygia, he presided over it for many years with the highest praise. Stephanus Gobarus (as cited in Photius *) testifies that he became a martyr, and the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle* † records that he suffered at Pergamum during the burning persecution under Marcus Aurelius. 

Eusebius * says he was "a man in all respects most eloquent and learned, and skilled in the scriptures" <note>original: ἀνὴρ τὰ πάντα ὅτι μάλιστα λογιώτατος, καὶ τῆς γραφῆς εἰδήμων</note>. Henri Valois suspects this eulogy was added by an unskilled scholar, because it is missing in certain manuscripts he used, and because Eusebius says elsewhere of Papias that he was "of a very small mind" <note>original: σφόδρα μικρὸν εἶναι τὸν νοῦν</note>. But these last words of Eusebius should be restricted to certain mystical senses of Scripture and the narrations of the Apostles. From these—poorly weighed and badly understood (and I would add, from the frivolous comments of the Jews)—Papias fashioned his opinion on *Chiliasm* <note>Millenarianism: the belief that the saints would reign with Christ on earth for a thousand years after the resurrection</note>. (Indeed, Eusebius is speaking only of this in the preceding words). Papias wrote five books of the *Exposition of the Oracles of the Lord* <note>original: λογίων κυριακῶν ἐξηγήσεως</note>, of which nothing remains today except certain fragments about the Millennium in Irenaeus †, and about the Apostles, the elders, and the miracles performed by them, and about the Gospels of Matthew and Mark in Eusebius *. Andreas of Caesarea † and Oecumenius || also have certain passages from him.

<margin>
112.
</margin>
**BASILIDES**, a disciple of Menander and a fellow student of Saturnilus (though he established a different sect from them), was a leader of the Gnostics. Greatly addicted to the magic arts, he propagated his heresy chiefly in Egypt. He used to boast that he had Glaucias, the interpreter of Saint Peter, as his teacher. He flourished around the year 112 AD, though according to others, somewhat later. He died under Hadrian. Concerning his age, see the most learned Pearson disputing with his usual erudition and accuracy in *Vindiciae Ignatianae*, Part 2, chapter 7. These were the main points of his heresy: that in the creation of things, a successive "ladder" is admitted, in which each being created by a prior one would create the next. Thus, only a single being owes its creation to God; and furthermore, among the 365 heavens between the highest heaven <note>the empyrean</note> and the earth, each has its own moving and creating angel assigned to it, who was created by a superior Angel. From this comes that celebrated word which occurs so often on Basilidian gems: **ABRASAX**, or **ABRAXAS**,

<meta>This page continues the biography of Polycarp of Smyrna, transitioning from his relationship with the Apostle John to his leadership in the early Church, his defense against Gnostic heresies, and his eventual martyrdom.</meta>

-># The Gnostic Century.<-

<margin>
2nd CENTURY
Year of Christ’s Birth
</margin>
...if the conjecture of the most learned James Ussher were true, he would be that "Angel of the Church of Smyrna" to whom Saint John wrote the letter in Revelation 2. When a grave controversy arose concerning the date of Easter, he traveled to Rome and there lived on familiar terms with Bishop Anicetus (who, according to the calculations of Pearson and Dodwell, drawn from Eutychius, entered the papacy in the year 142). While there, he brought many who had been deceived by the errors of Marcion and Valentinus <note>Leading Gnostic teachers who were seen as heretics by the early Church</note> back to the faith. Finally, under Marcus Antoninus (or as others say, Antoninus Pius), as persecution grew hot, Polycarp was condemned to the stake at Smyrna and handed over to the fire. However, as the flame billowed around the martyr’s body like the sail of a ship filled by the wind, and refused to touch him, he was at last pierced through with a sword.

The pagans reduced the body of the deceased to ashes, fearing that the Christians would carry off his remains and follow them with divine honors. 
> *Fools,* (said the Church of Smyrna) *who did not know that we can never abandon Christ, nor worship any other: for Him we adore as the Son of God, but the Martyrs, as disciples and imitators of the Lord, we deservedly follow with love because of their extraordinary devotion which they declared toward their own King and Master.* 

Nevertheless, the Christians gathered the martyr's bones—half-burned but more precious than the costliest gems (to use their own words) and purer than any gold—and placed them honorably in a tomb, observing the memory of his suffering by celebrating an annual festival day. Polycarp died <term>at a very advanced age <note>original: πάνυ γηραλέος</note></term> (says Irenaeus), having lived a very long life, specifically in the 86th year of his age. For he himself said to the Proconsul: <term>"Eighty and six years I have served Him" <note>original: ὀγδοήκοντα καὶ ἕξ ἔτη δουλεύω αὐτῷ</note></term>. The ancients intend these years to be understood as his entire life’s course, rather than the time since his profession of Christianity, as some more recent writers interpret it. Regarding the year in which he suffered martyrdom, writers vary wonderfully. Eusebius places it in the year of Christ 167; Ussher and Bucher in 164; Petitus in 175. However, our most learned Pearson strongly contends that he suffered in the year of Christ 147. He demonstrates this at length and with more than one kind of argument. See his own extensive and learned discussion on this matter in *Dissertations II*, chapters 14 through 20.

<margin>
* Letter to Florinus in Eusebius, book 5, ch. 20.
|| Prologue to the works of Saint Dionysius.
</margin>
He wrote several letters, partly to neighboring churches to strengthen them, and partly to certain brothers, warning and exhorting them, as Irenaeus reports. Saint Maximus and Joannes Maxentius cite a *Letter to the Athenians*; Suidas mentions another to Dionysius the Areopagite under the entry <term>Polycarp <note>original: Πολύκ.</note></term>. But those appear to be spurious. Of these, there still exists the *Letter to the Philippians*, often published in Latin along with the letters of Ignatius; first in Greek and Latin by Pierre Halloix, of the Society of Jesus, in his *Life of Polycarp* (Douai, 1633). Then it was published in an expanded Greek and Latin version by the Reverend Ussher in the *Ignatian Appendix*, 1647. Finally, the learned man Stephen Le Moyne, a theologian of Leiden, recently published it among his *Varia Sacra* (Leiden, 1685, 4to), and adorned—or shall I say, burdened—it with long and miscellaneous notes. It is worth noting, however, that the part of the letter containing that very famous testimony regarding the Ignatian letters is missing there. Although it was not in his manuscript codex, he could not have been unaware that it is found in both the Halloix and Ussher editions.

I do not know if it is worth mentioning what Pierre Halloix notes in his *Life of Polycarp*, chapter 16:

> "Pionius," he says, "who wrote the life of St. Polycarp in Greek, is the authority that the same Polycarp wrote many treatises, homilies, and letters. It is also said that he composed an entire book on the death of St. John the Evangelist, his teacher, which still exists today in manuscript in the Library of the Abbey of St. Flora in Cisalpine Gaul. From which book Francis Humblot produces some excerpts in a sermon on St. John the Evangelist, near the end. <margin>
110. * Book 3, ch. 39. † Book 5, ch. 33. * Vol. 232. † Year 3 of the 235th Olympiad. * Book 3, ch. 38. † Book 5, ch. 33. * Book 3, ch. 39. † Commentary on Revelation, Sermon 12. || On chapter 27 of Matthew.

**PAPIAS**, an Asian, perhaps born in Hierapolis, was a hearer of St. John and a companion of Polycarp. Eusebius * indeed understands him to have known not the Apostle, but John the Presbyter <term>Presbyter: a title for an "Elder" or priest, distinguishing him here from John the Apostle</term>. But Irenaeus †, and a long line of other writers after him, seem to indicate clearly enough that he was a disciple of John the Apostle. Whatever the case, it is certain that he lived familiarly with the Elders who had been hearers of the Apostles; from them, he curiously inquired what the sayings of the Elders were: what Peter, what Andrew, what Philip, and what the other Disciples of the Lord used to say; and what Aristion and John the Presbyter preached. "For I did not think," he said, "that I could receive as much benefit from reading books as from the living voice of men still surviving." Having been made Bishop of the Church of Hierapolis in Phrygia, he presided over it for many years with the highest praise. Stephen Gobar, in Photius *, testifies that he became a martyr, and the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle* † records that he suffered at Pergamum during the height of the persecution under Marcus Aurelius. Eusebius * says he was a "man in all things most eloquent, and knowledgeable in the scriptures" <note>Original Greek: *anēr ta panta hoti malista logiōtatos, kai tēs graphēs eidēmōn*</note>. Henri Valois suspects that this praise was added by some unskilled scholar, because it is missing in certain manuscripts he used, and because Eusebius says elsewhere of Papias that he was "of a very small mind" <note>Original Greek: *sphodra mikron einai ton noun*</note>. But these last words of Eusebius must be restricted to certain mystical senses of Scripture and the narrations of the Apostles; from which, having not well weighed them and having misunderstood them (I would add, and from the futile commentaries of the Jews), he fashioned his opinion on **Chiliasm** <term>Chiliasm: from the Greek word for "thousand," the belief that Christ would return to reign on earth for a literal 1,000-year period</term>—for Eusebius speaks of this alone in the preceding words—namely, that the blessed would reign corporally with Christ on earth for the space of a thousand years after the resurrection of the body. Papias wrote five books *On the Explanation of the Oracles of the Lord* <note>Original Greek: *logiōn kyriakōn exēgēseōs*</note>, of which nothing survives today except certain fragments concerning the Millennium in Irenaeus †, concerning the Apostles and elders, and concerning certain miracles performed by them, and concerning the Gospels of Matthew and Mark in Eusebius *. Andrew of Caesarea † and Oecumenius || also have certain passages from him.

<margin>112.</margin>
**BASILIDES**, a disciple of Menander and a fellow-student of Saturnilus (from whom, however, he established a different sect), was a leader of the Gnostics <term>Gnostics: a group of early religious thinkers who believed in "gnosis" or secret, salvific knowledge</term> and much addicted to magical arts; he propagated his heresy chiefly in Egypt. He was accustomed to boast that he had Glaucias, the interpreter of St. Peter, as his teacher. He flourished around the year 112, or according to others, somewhat later. He died under Hadrian. Concerning his age, see the most learned Pearson arguing learnedly and accurately, as is his custom, in *Vindic. Ignat.* Part 2, chapter 7. These were the main points of his heresy: that in the creation of things a certain successive scale is admitted, in which each being created by a prior one would create the following; thus, the only being to receive its creation directly from God is the first. Furthermore, out of the 365 heavens, the highest heaven <note>Original: *empyreum*</note> and the earth have intermediate levels, each having a motor and a creator angel attached to it, who was created by a superior angel. From this comes that famous word which occurs so often on Basilidian gems, **ABRAXAS** <note>A mystical name used by Basilides; the Greek letters of Abraxas sum to 365, representing the days of the year or the levels of heaven.</note>, or *ABRAXAS*, or...

<header>The Gnostic Century.</header>

from 120 AD.
* Heresies, 24, num. 7. p. 73.

**"Above every power and authority,"** <note>original: *hyperanō pasan dynamis kai archē*</note> says Epiphanius *, is the supreme deity of Basilides, formed from the fact that the letters of this word [Abraxas] produce the number 365. It does not seem improbable, as St. Jerome suggests elsewhere, that this "Abraxas" was none other than the Mithras or Sun of the Persians, who completes his annual course in 365 days. Furthermore, Basilides taught that Christ appeared to mortals only in appearance, and was a **"mere phantom in his appearing, but not truly a man, nor having taken on flesh"** <note>original: *phantasian en tō phainesthai, mē einai d’ anthrōpon, mēde sarka eilēphenai*</note>. He claimed that Christ did not actually suffer on the cross, but substituted a proxy, Simon of Cyrene, in his place. He taught that promiscuous intercourse between men and women was permissible; that martyrdom should not be undergone, and that faith could be rightfully renounced when occasion arose, since it is sufficient to profess it in appearance only—in the same way that Christ bore death for us [only in appearance]. He believed salvation is owed to the soul alone, and thus the body would never emerge from its state of corruption. Finally, in the manner of the Pythagoreans, he imposed a five-year silence on his followers (as witnessed by Agrippa Castor in Eusebius, Book 4, Chapter 7). Whoever wishes to know more about him should consult Epiphanius, *Heresies* XXIV, where these matters are set out at length. Basilides wrote 24 books of *Commentaries on the Gospel*. Whether he composed these expositions on the New Testament Gospel, or rather, as Valesius suggests, on his own gospel—**"The Gospel according to Basilides"** <note>original: *to kata Basileidēn euaggelion*</note>, mentioned by Origen *, Ambrose †, and others—is not entirely clear. Fragments survive in Epiphanius (*Heresies* XXIV, num. 1) and Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata*, Book 4, pp. 506, 509). Origen mentions his *Odes* in Olympiodorus’s *Commentary on Job*, edited by P. Comitolo, p. 345.

---

<margin>
120.
* Exercise 1 on Baronius, num. 10. p. 75, etc.
</margin>
**HERMES**, the Pseudo-Trismegistus <term>Trismegistus: "Thrice-Greatest," a legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth</term>, who wrote the *Poimandres* and certain other works, is considered by the illustrious Casaubon * to be a Christian, or rather, a semi-Christian. "We do not hesitate to declare," he says, "and confirm with all assurance, that the entire book which began to be circulated under the name of Mercury Trismegistus several centuries ago is **falsely attributed** <note>original: *pseudepigraphon*</note>. It is a pure fabrication of some Christian, or to put it better, a semi-Christian. Nor do we doubt that the author's aim was to prove that many dogmas of Christian piety, which were being rejected as new and previously unheard of, had been known to the wise men of the most remote antiquity, and had been recorded by that very Mercury whom not only the Egyptians but also the Greeks greatly admired for his antiquity and reputation for learning." He later argues at length that the contents of the *Poimandres* could have been written by no one other than a certain Platonizing Christian. He seems to have flourished around the year 120. His works exist in Greek and Latin, published in Paris in 1554 (4to) and Cologne in 1630 (folio).

* Book 3, ch. 4.
† Heresies 31.
</margin>
**VALENTINUS**, born, as they say, in Phrebonis in Egypt, was a follower of the Platonic school and educated in the arts of the Greeks. He was a close disciple of Theodas, an acquaintance of St. Paul—if the Valentinians are to be believed. Certainly **"he was no ordinary man,"** <note>original: *ouk eutelēs ēn anēr*</note> says Drosenius, one of his followers, in Origen's *Dialogue against Marcion*, § IV. After being rejected for a bishopric, he defected from the Catholic Church and became the author of another branch of the Gnostic heresy. He began to be famous around the year 120, or as others say, slightly later. Leaving Alexandria, he came to Rome (according to Irenaeus *) during the pontificate of Hyginus, flourished in the times of Pius, and remained until the time of Anicetus. Withdrawing from Rome to the island of Cyprus, he fell into the extreme of impiety (as Epiphanius † holds) and immersed himself deeper into that discipline of outrages which he defended. Besides those things he held in common with Basilides, he invented dogmas of this sort: He devised a legendary genealogy of Gods and <term>Aeons: In Gnosticism, these are divine emanations or beings that bridge the gap between the supreme God and the material world.</term> filled with barbaric names, very similar to the system of Hesiod. He taught that Christ brought his body down from heaven and passed through the Virgin Mary "like water through a pipe," taking nothing from her womb. He established three ranks of men: the Spiritual, the Animal, and the Carnal. He claimed that the first (namely his own followers and other Gnostics) could achieve salvation through "knowledge" <note>Greek: *gnosis*</note> alone; the second through both faith and works; and the last could in no way attain salvation. He taught that the most shameful lusts could be practiced lawfully, and even that no one could reach the highest degree of perfection unless they [aroused] a woman to love...

...never enticed him. Epiphanius * says that Valentinus denied the resurrection of the flesh; however, Tertullian † clarifies that he did not deny the resurrection of all flesh, but only of *this specific* [physical] flesh. Having approved certain books of the Law and the Prophets, he rejected others. More on these matters can be seen in Irenaeus throughout his first and second books, in Tertullian’s book *Against the Valentinians* and *On Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 49, and in Epiphanius’s *Heresies*, book 31. He wrote a *Gospel* mentioned by Tertullian *, and *Psalms*, mentioned by the same author † and also by Origen *. Clement of Alexandria mentions his *Letters* and cites certain fragments from them in the *Stromata* <note>The "Miscellanies," a major work by Clement</note>, book 2, pages 375 and 409, and book 3, page 451. He also mentions a certain *Homily*, a fragment of which he provides in book 4, page 509; likewise another from a *Homily on Friends* (unless perhaps it is the same as the former) in book 6, page 641, and another on page 635. There is a fairly long fragment of Valentinus regarding that most vexing question, **"From where does evil come?"** <note>original: *pothen ta kaka*</note>; he contends that evil is to be attributed not to God, but to matter which is co-eternal with God, as found in the author of the *Dialogue against Marcion* under the name of Origen, section 4, page 85. Furthermore, a large fragment from his book, or at least from his disciples, can be seen in Epiphanius, *Heresies* 31, numbers 5 and 6.

Clement of Alexandria, in *Stromata*, book 1, page 502, mentions a man of great name among the followers of Valentinus called Heracleon (the teacher of Cerdo and successor of Colarbasus, according to Epiphanius, *Heresies* 36, who reviews his dogmas). There, Clement adds a snippet from one of his writings in these words: *Whoever confesses me*, etc. from Matthew 10. Some of his words are also found in the *Excerpts of Theodotus*, page 804. Indeed, he is cited and refuted here and there by Origen in his commentary on John. Other details about him are not clear, so much so that it seemed less useful to assign him a separate place among the writers.

**EPIPHANES** had Carpocrates as his father *, an Alexandrian by birth and the founder of the Gnostic sect <term>properly</term> <note>original: *kyriōs*</note> so-called; his mother was Alexandria, of the Cephalonian people. He flourished around the year 120. Having been instructed by his father in the full course of studies and Platonic philosophy, he turned out to be a distinguished champion of his father’s heresy. For besides many dogmas he held in common with Basilides and Valentinus, he maintained that the world was created by angels and that Christ was born of Joseph and Mary in the ordinary way. He sponsored magical arts, love-potions, and sorcery both by word and example. He contended that wives ought to be common to all who aspire to Christian perfection, and he taught that the use of promiscuous unchastity and lust was not only permissible but necessary for all those seeking the highest peak of piety. He died at only seventeen years of age and was buried at Samos, a city of Cephalonia, where he was granted divine honors by his father's followers; a magnificent temple was built in his honor, sacrifices were offered to him, and hymns were sung in his praise every year. He wrote a book *On Justice*, in which he took it upon himself to prove that all women should be common to all men. Clement of Alexandria provides many fragments of this in *Stromata*, book 3, page 428, etc.

**QUADRATUS**, perhaps an Athenian by city or at least by education, was appointed Bishop of that see after the martyrdom of Publius, who succeeded Dionysius the Areopagite. Dionysius of Corinth * testifies that by his labor and industry, the Athenians—who had been wandering like sheep without a shepherd after Publius's death—gathered again into the Church, and the fire of faith was revived and restored in them. He was a disciple of the Apostles, as Eusebius † and Jerome || expressly record; this is to be understood chiefly of St. John, unless perhaps the word "Apostles" is to be taken in a broader sense for "Apostolic Men" who lived with the Apostles. Accordingly, elsewhere Eusebius * numbers our Quadratus among those who held the <term>first rank</term> <note>original: *tēn prōtēn taxin*</note> among the successors of the Apostles. He was a man of obvious piety and is said to have possessed the <term>prophetic gift</term> <note>original: *prophētikon charisma*</note>, which still flourished in the Church at that time. Around the year 123, while the Emperor Hadrian was spending the winter in Athens and being initiated there into the Eleusinian mysteries, a very severe persecution arose against the Christians. To oppose this, Quadratus offered the Emperor an *Apologetic Oration* for our religion, composed by himself. **"From which one can see clear evidence of both the man's intellect and his apostolic sound doctrine,"** <note>original: *Ex quâ & ingenium ejus viri, & rectam Apostolicæ fidei doctrinam perspicuè licet cognoscere*</note> says Eusebius *.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of early Christian apologists and scholars during the 2nd century, following the mention of Quadratus at the end of the previous page. It addresses the historical identity of Quadratus and introduces the apologist Aristides and the Bible translator Aquila.</meta>

<header>The Gnostic Century.</header>

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.
* Century 2, chapter 10, column 152.
† Ecclesiastical Antiquities, century 2, article 1, page 183.
* On the 26th of September.
</margin>
...to know: and he presented it with such success that he calmed the raging persecution through his excellent intellect. This *Apology* <note>A formal defense of the Christian faith</note> perished long ago; nothing of it survives today except a very brief fragment concerning some who had been healed by Christ the Lord and were still alive in that age, which Eusebius records in the place cited. Besides this, he committed nothing else to writing—at least nothing of which even the slightest mention remains. From this, the error of the Magdeburg Centuriators * <note>A group of 16th-century Protestant historians who wrote the first comprehensive history of the church</note> is more clearly evident (which the modern Strasbourg professor Balthasar Bebelius † nevertheless swallowed with his eyes closed), who claim that Eusebius mentions another book composed by Quadratus called the *Syngramma* <note>original: *Syngramma*; a Greek term for a "written treatise"</note>. However, it is apparent at first glance even to schoolboys looking at the passage in Eusebius that he is speaking there only of the aforementioned *Apology*. Regarding the death of Quadratus, nothing is certain, except what the Greeks report in their *Menaion* <note>A liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church containing the lives of saints</note> *: that he was driven far from Athens, first attacked with stones, then tested by fire and other tortures, and finally, while Hadrian was still reigning, he carried off the palm of martyrdom.

Indeed, it does not escape me that Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century classical scholar</note> and others following him contend that our Quadratus is distinct from the Bishop of Athens, relying on a twofold argument. First, that Eusebius (Book 3, chapter 37) mentions a certain Quadratus endowed with prophetic gifts while omitting the title of Bishop. But this is of no weight, since the titles of their office are not always attached to men, especially illustrious ones; and Quadratus seems not to have been made Bishop yet at the time Eusebius is discussing there. Second, they object that Quadratus the author of the *Apology* did not survive into the times of Hadrian, whereas the Bishop is praised by Dionysius of Corinth (in Eusebius, Book 4, chapter 23) as being his contemporary and recently ordained. However, whoever seriously weighs that passage of Dionysius will easily recognize that such a meaning can by no means be squeezed out of it. Add to these points that Jerome and the Greek *Menology* <note>A calendar of saints' lives</note> stand on our side, explicitly affirming that they were one and the same Quadratus.

<margin>
123.
* Letter to Magnus the Orator, page 327.
</margin>

### ARISTIDES, (of whom there is very sparse mention among the Ancients) an Athenian philosopher, professed the Christian faith while wearing his philosopher's robe. He flourished at the same time and in the same place as Quadratus, and for the same reason offered an *Apologetic* work for the Christians to the Emperor Hadrian. This work was woven together, says Jerome *, with the opinions of philosophers; it was later imitated by Justin, who was also a philosopher. This *Apology* of Aristides existed not only in the time of Eusebius and Jerome, but also in the age of Usuard and Ado of Vienne <note>9th-century chroniclers</note>; if at least the things they report from it concerning the passion of Dionysius the Areopagite are true, as we noted above regarding Dionysius.

|| On Weights and Measures, Number 14.
* Page 598.
* Letter to Pammachius, page 370.
</margin>

### AQUILA, of the nation of Pontus, originating from the most famous city of Pontus, Sinope, was a Gentile by religion and a <term>relative by marriage</term> <note>original Greek: *pentherides*</note> of the Emperor Hadrian (according to Epiphanius ||) or a <term>father-in-law</term> <note>original Greek: *pentheros*</note> (according to the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle* *); both perhaps drawing from the fabulous traditions of the Jews. He was appointed by the Emperor as the overseer of the works in building the city of Aelia, or Jerusalem. Having seen the miracles of the Christians which they frequently performed, he embraced the faith of Christ and was initiated by baptism. However, when he would not abandon the vain astrology which he had learned from boyhood—but rather devoted himself more and more to the <gloss>horoscopic art</gloss> and did not correct himself when warned by the teachers of the Church—he was finally cast out from the Church. Bearing that disgrace impatiently, he renounced Christianity, went over to the Jews, and was marked by circumcision. He became a disciple of Rabbi Akiva, a most bitter enemy of the Christians. From the Jews, he learned the Hebrew language with incredible diligence, which he cultivated to such an extent that around the year 128 or 129 AD, he undertook a new Greek translation of the Bible. He did this primarily with the intent of displacing the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> and perverting the testimonies concerning Christ brought forth in the Scriptures by publishing them differently. Regarding him, Jerome says *: "*Aquila, a proselyte and contentious interpreter, who attempted to translate not only the words but even the etymologies of words, is rightly rejected by us.*" Although elsewhere he speaks more kindly of him: namely, "*that Aquila interpreted word for word, not as contentiously as some think, but more studiously*" (Question 2 to Damasus, volume 3, page 35). He calls him "*the most diligent researcher of Hebrew words.*"

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.</margin>
...calls [him] a most meticulous explicator, in his *Letter to Marcella*, ibid. p. 96. "I compare *Aquila’s* edition with the Hebrew scrolls, lest the Synagogue might have changed anything out of hatred for Christ," etc.; "to confess with a friendly mind, I find more things that pertain to strengthening our faith." *Letter to Marcella*, Vol. ii. p. 312. Hence, he not rarely prefers *Aquila* to the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the standard Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> themselves. "I think that which is found in the Hebrew was better translated by Aquila." *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, Vol. iii. p. 216. and elsewhere, more than once. Origen preceded Jerome in his *Commentary on John*, Vol. viii. p. 131. and Vol. iii. *On Genesis* in the *Philocalia*, ch. 14. asserting that he "strived to interpret most accurately" <note>original: κυριώτατα ἑρμηνεύειν φιλοτιμώμενον</note>, having studied to interpret very aptly. Jerome testifies * <margin>* On Ezekiel, ch. 3, vol 5.</margin> that he polished his version in a second edition, which the Jews called "according to precision" <note>original: κατ᾽ ἀκρίβειαν</note>. Today, only certain fragments of this translation survive, scattered here and there in the writings of the Ancients, which Nobilius, Drusius, and Walton have edited and collected into one.

**ISIDORUS**, son of Basilides, a Gnostic by sect, was famous around the year 130. Regarding his doctrines, they were common to those of his father, whose fabulous sayings he confirmed with certain new additions. He wrote *Exegetica*, or books of *Expositions on Barcaham † and Parchor* (H. Finally, *Ethics* <note>original: Ἠθικὰ</note>, fragments of which are found in the same author, book 3, p. 427, and in Epiphanius, *Heresies* 32, No. 4.

**AGRIPPA**, called Castor, a "most well-known writer" <note>original: γνωριμώτατος συγγραφεὺς</note>, as he is called by Eusebius *; a "very learned man," as he is called by Jerome †. He flourished especially under the reign of Hadrian, around the year 132. He wrote a very accurate *refutation* † *Against Basilides*, certain fragments of which Eusebius has in the place cited, where he testifies that in it all the frauds and deceits of Basilides are detected, and all his secrets brought to light. <margin>136.</margin>
**HERMES**, who was also called the *Shepherd* <note>original: *Pastor*</note>, a Priest and brother of Pius I, Bishop of Rome, flourished in the year 136 and died in the year 150. Pseudo-Damasus, in the *Life of Pius*, and the Author of the *Poems against Marcion* (attributed to Tertullian) make him the author of that most ancient book called the *Shepherd*. However, † Bellarmine <margin>† On Writers</margin> contends rather that there were two men named Hermes, and that different men distinguished by the same title wrote *Commentaries* on Hermes. For the Apostolic Hermas was nearly a hundred years older than this man of ours; nor is that mandate of the Angel, delivered under the guise of a Shepherd concerning the celebration of Holy Easter on the Lord’s day—which the brother of Pius had stitched into his *Shepherd*—found anywhere in the book of the *Shepherd* that exists today. Add to this that Jerome says || <margin>|| On Writers, ch. 10.</margin> that although that most ancient book of the *Shepherd* was publicly read in certain churches of Greece even in his age, it was nevertheless almost unknown among the Latins. Therefore, it is probable that the book of Hermes, if indeed he ever wrote such a thing (which I would not easily dare to affirm), perished quickly. Baronius also attributes to this Hermes the *Acts of the Virgin Praxedes* and her brothers; and he presents an *Epistle* of his to Timothy, the brother of Praxedes, and another from Timothy to the Shepherd, in Volume ii, for the year 162.

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>2nd CENTURY AD</margin> ...do not seem to differ entirely from those things which immediately preceded in the letter of Clement. No one fails to see that they were fabricated, and indeed for the sake of the Christian faith; meanwhile, it cannot be denied that some things from the songs of the ancient Sibyls <note>Prophetic women of the ancient world whose verses were often imitated by later writers</note> were mixed in with the modern ones, so that they might be more plausibly foisted upon the learned world. Regarding their true age and origin, not everyone holds the same opinion. The Illustrious Isaac Vossius thinks a significant part of them was forged by Jews about 80 years before the birth of Christ, deposited by the Romans in the Capitol, and circulated through the hands of everyone before, around, and after the coming of Christ, and finally received many additions from Christians (and among them especially by the Gnostics). Hornbeck attributes them to Papias; Blondel attributes them either to Hermes (mentioned immediately preceding) or to Montanus the Heresiarch; Maresius attributes them to this latter man. Finally, a recent author, Johannes Marck, ascribes them to certain Heretics, especially those seized by the Montanist spirit: a sufficiently gross error, since it is clearer than the sun that those Oracles began to become known to the world more than 40 years before Montanus arose. But to dispute further about these things, we have neither the leisure nor the inclination; those who wish may consult those who have dealt with this matter in passing, such as Baronius, Casaubon, Montacutius, G. J. Vossius, etc.; or those who have most recently treated this matter in specific writings, such as Blondel, Isaac Vossius, Marck, and Crasset. These oracles exist, along with other things relating to this topic, comprised in eight books with the notes of Opsopæus, *Paris 1599, 1607, in octavo*, not to mention other editions here which are far inferior.

<margin>136.</margin> ### ARISTO OF PELLA,
so called because he was born in Pella in Palestine; a Jew by birth and a Hebrew by culture, though whether he was a Christian is not sufficiently clear. He seems to have flourished around the year 136, after the rebellion of the Jews under the leader Bar Kokhba <note>The leader of the second major Jewish revolt against Rome</note> had recently been crushed by Hadrian. Aristo wrote *The Siege of Bethar and the Conquest of the Jews*, from which work Eusebius produces certain things in Book 4, chapter 6. The *Disputation of Jason and Papiscus* also seems to be attributed to him: I have this on the word of Saint Maximus, who in his notes <note>Scholia</note> on Dionysius's *Mystical Theology*, ch. 1, teaches us these things: 
> <note>original Greek:</note> "I read this in the dialogue of Papiscus and Jason written by Aristo of Pella, which Clement of Alexandria says in the sixth book of the *Outlines* <note>Hypotyposeon</note> was recorded by Saint Luke."

I also read of the seven Heavens in the *Disputation of Papiscus and Jason, which was written by Aristo of Pella, which Clement of Alexandria in the sixth book of the Outlines says Saint Luke described.* Many wish this Jason to be the same as Jason of Thessalonica, of whom mention is made in Acts 17:5 and Romans 16:21, and whom the Greeks in their Menologion <note>A church calendar of saints' lives</note> hand down as having been appointed the first Bishop of Tarsus by Saint Paul. But these things are uncertain, relying on no author worthy of trust. Whoever he was, he joined a Disputation with Papiscus, an Alexandrian Jew, concerning the Truth of the Christian Religion, which had this outcome: that Papiscus, defeated by the Christian's arguments, renounced Judaism and earnestly requested baptism. There existed 
<margin>* Note in Celsus’s Preface.</margin> formerly in Greek—indeed (if trust is to be given to Rigaltius*, who cites certain words from it) there still exist—the *Acts of this contest*, whether reduced to writing by our Aristo or by someone else. 
<margin>† Against Celsus, Book 4, not far from the middle.</margin> Celsus the Epicurean <note>An early critic of Christianity</note> once mocked these as a sort of foolish work: for which reason Origen† cleared away his unfair judgment and attributed to them an excellent eulogy of learning. Jerome mentions the same in his *Questions on Genesis*. A certain Celsus translated these *Acts* into the Latin language, and expanded them with a quite long preface dedicated to Bishop Vigil; who or what sort of man he was is not established. It is only clear from many places in the preface that he wrote while the times of Persecution were still flourishing, and before the Christian faith was adopted by the Emperors. The *preface* exists among the works of Cyprian, to whose name it is usually wrongly inscribed.

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.
</margin>

...who presided over the church, was expelled by his own father, a most holy man. Nor could he be induced to restore him by any prayers or any pretense of penance, for his father was a man most observant of Ecclesiastical discipline. For this reason, when Marcion could not bear the reproaches of his fellow citizens, he secretly fled his homeland and set out for Rome around the year 140 AD, hoping not only to be admitted to communion, but also to attain a leading position there. But when his case was investigated and the firm resolve of his father became known, the Elders of the Roman Church refused to receive him, fearing lest the principles of public discipline and the bond of Catholic communion be broken. With his mind then provoked, he broke into open schism, and following in the footsteps of his master Cerdo, he began to cast new and blasphemous dogmas among the common people.

<margin>
* Irenæus, book 3, chapter 3.
</margin>

While he was at Rome *, Polycarp the Bishop of the Smyrneans happened to meet him; when Marcion said to him, *“Recognize us, Polycarp,”* Polycarp replied, *“I recognize you as the firstborn of Satan.”* <note>original: "Agnosce nos... Agnosco te, Primogenitum Satanæ." This famous encounter highlights the intense animosity between early orthodox leaders and those they deemed heretics.</note>

<margin>
On Prescription, chapter 30, page 212.
</margin>

Tertullian reports that Marcion finally repented of his errors and wished to publicly testify to his repentance; but while he was to be received back into the Church on the condition that he restore to the Church those he had led into error, he was prevented by death from completing it. It is clear that his followers honored him with the title of Bishop, as seen both from Megethius in Origen’s *Dialogue against the Marcionites* (section 1) and from Optatus (book 4, page 116). His dogmas were of this sort: That there are three supreme Gods, or principles of things: the first invisible, whom he called the Good God and the Father of our Lord; the second visible and the Creator, as well as the Judge; the third a middle between both, whom he also called the Devil. And indeed, Epiphanius recounts these principles of Marcion in this way; but Theodoret lists four unbegotten substances: 1. The good and unknown God, the Father of the Lord. 2. The Just Creator, whom he also named Evil. 3. Matter, which is evil. 4. Another Evil one, to whom Matter is subject. But strictly speaking, Marcion established only two principles, namely Good and Evil: one a Judge, fierce and warlike; the other mild, peaceful, and only good and excellent—to use the words of || Tertullian.

<margin>
|| Against Marcion, book 1, chapter 6, page 368.
</margin>
<margin>
* Preface to *The Origin of Sin* (Hamartigenia).
</margin>

Hence Prudentius calls the Marcionite sect the heresy of the *Duitæ* <note>original: "Duitarum" – derived from the Latin "duo" (two), referring to their dualistic belief in two opposing gods.</note>. That Marcion drew that dogma of his from the Stoics, no one can doubt. For it is well known that the Stoics established two principles, a Good and an Evil Spirit <note>original: "Dæmonem"</note>, which is why Marcion is called a "student of the Stoics" by † Tertullian.

<margin>
† Location cited above.
</margin>

From these, he fashioned the second God to be exceedingly severe and unjust, who both gave the harshest laws to the Jews and forbade Adam from touching the most beautiful tree of Paradise with a most unjust command. Therefore, he claimed the serpent was far better than that God, since the serpent urged our parents to eat the fruit of that tree; hence his followers even worshipped a bronze serpent kept in a small chest, as Theodoret narrates naturally <term>αὐτοφυῶς</term> <note>original: "autophuōs" – meaning spontaneously or as a natural consequence of their logic.</note>.

<margin>
* Heretical Fables, book 1, chapter 24.
</margin>

Furthermore, he claimed that Christ descended from the heavens to free those believing in him from the servitude of that unjust God; however, he did not put on true flesh, but only a visionary appearance <term>φαντασιώδη</term> <note>original: "phantasiōdē" – this is the core of "Docetism," the belief that Christ only *seemed* to have a physical body.</note>, and did not truly suffer, though he appeared to suffer. Descending to the underworld after death and preaching the Gospel there, he brought back to heaven with him the converted Cainites, Sodomites, and all others infamous for crimes and vices; but Noah, Abraham, and the rest of the Patriarchs, who relied too much on their own justice and refused to listen to his preaching, he left bound there. He taught that the resurrection is of the soul alone, not the body; that Baptism could be repeated three times for the sake of those who, after receiving the saving bath a first and second time, had fallen into a mortal sin. Finally, he held that the Law and all the Prophets were to be rejected, as they prophesied by the inspiration of that evil God, the Creator of the world. He even rejected four of Paul’s Epistles and foully corrupted the remaining ten, removing much from them and adding much; and from all the Gospels, he received only that of St. Luke, and that with the greater part of Christ’s genealogy cut away, while the rest of the Canonical Scriptures were utterly repudiated. Regarding these absurd and tasteless dogmas, one may consult Irenæus (book 1, chapter 29), Tertullian (five books *Against Marcion*), Epiphanius (Heresy 42), and Theodoret (*Heretical Fables*, book 1, chapter 24). He composed two books for the use of his disciples, which he wished to be held as of divine authority: one, a Gospel taken from the Gospel of St. Luke with some things changed or cut out; the other called the *Apostolicon*, composed from the Epistles of St. Paul to the Galatians, to...

### 140. JUSTIN, Martyr

<margin>
140.
† Book 2, ch. 13.
* In Photius, Codex 234.
|| Epistle to Diognetus, p. 501.
Eusebius, book 4, ch. 11.
</margin>
**JUSTIN**, called "Martyr" by way of excellence <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν" (kat’ exochen). A Greek term meaning pre-eminently or by way of distinction.</note>, the son of Priscus and grandson of Bachius, was born in Neapolis, a notable city of Samaria. He lived "not long after the time of the apostles," as Eusebius says †; "a man neither distant from the apostles in time, nor in virtue," says Methodius of Tyre *. Indeed, Justin speaks of himself || as having been "a disciple of the apostles," which is to be understood as him being a student of the Apostolic men, or rather, of the doctrine of the Apostles. Having curiously explored almost all the sects of the philosophers, he settled on Platonism; until, having been taught better things by a certain venerable and truly divine old man, he transitioned to a more divine and noble Philosophy—namely, Christianity—around the year 133. "In the dress of a philosopher, he served the divine Word," <note>original: "ἐν φιλοσόφου σχήματι πρεσβεύων τὸν θεῖον λόγον"</note> preaching the word of God even while wearing his philosopher’s cloak. At the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Pius, he traveled to Rome and took up residence on the Viminal Hill. In order to quench the cruelty raging against the Christians and to vindicate them from the false slanders of the Gentiles, he offered his *First Apology* for the Christians around the year 140, addressed to Antoninus Pius, his sons, and the Roman Senate. Although it is said in the *Apology* that 150 years had passed since Christ, this must be attributed to a corruption of the numeral characters, since the Edict of Emperor Antoninus Pius obtained by Justin’s *Apology* was issued during Antoninus's third Consulship, which falls in the year of Christ 140. After this, returning to Asia, he held that most famous *dialogue* with Trypho the Jew. From there he returned to Rome and wrote a second *Apology* for the Christians, dedicating it to Marcus Antoninus and the Roman Senate. Finally, while he was quite freely rebuking Crescens, a Cynic philosopher—describing him as a gluttonous man, fearful of death, and a follower of luxury and lusts, "a lover of noise and a braggart, but no lover of wisdom" <note>original: "τὸν φιλόψοφον, καὶ φιλόκομπον, οὐδὲ φιλόσοφον"</note>—he was accused by Crescens before the Emperor.

<margin>
* In Surius at June 12 & Baronius at year 165.
† History of Heresies, 46, p. 171.
† Codex 125.
</margin>
By the Emperor he was condemned and struck with a sword, as the *Acts* of his martyrdom hold; though the Greeks † in the Menaion <note>A liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church containing the services for the saints.</note> say he died by being given poison, around the year 164, the 4th year of Marcus Aurelius, or as noted in the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, the 6th year of the Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius. From this it is clear that Epiphanius * suffers from a monstrous error, as he refers Justin’s death to the reign of Hadrian and says it happened in the thirtieth year of Justin’s life. Photius † has this to say of him: "The man was raised to the highest peak of philosophy, both our own and especially that of the outsiders [secular], overflowing with multifaceted erudition and a wealth of histories. But he did not strive to imbue the beauty of his philosophy with rhetorical arts; wherefore his discourses, though otherwise powerful and preserving a scientific style, are not persuasive by means of underlying rhetorical sweetness, nor do they draw the listeners in by allurements or charms." <note>original: "Ἐστὶ δὲ φιλοσοφίας μὲν ὁ ἀνὴρ... τοὺς ἀκροατῶν ἐφελκόμενοι." Photius is praising Justin's intellect while noting that his writing style is dense and academic rather than "flowery."</note> That he was entirely unpolished and unskilled in Hebrew letters should not be turned into a fault against Justin: first, because although he was a Samaritan by country, he was born to Greek parents; second, because he spent a great part of his life in the religion of the Gentiles; and finally, because he gave himself entirely to Philosophy and Greek disciplines, which are vastly removed from the study of Hebrew letters. Thus it happened that he slipped so childishly regarding Hebrew matters. I will give an example. Everyone knows that "Satan" is derived from the word *Satan*, meaning "to be an adversary," even those who have only greeted the Hebrew language from the front doorstep. Yet behold the clearly ridiculous interpretation of our Justin: "He was addressed as Satanas, having obtained a name composed from the deeds he performed. For *Sata* in the speech of the Jews and Syrians is 'apostate'; and the name *nas* is that from which the interpretation 'serpent' is called; the same as when interpreted in the speech of the Hebrews. From both of which, when joined together, the one name Satanas was made." <note>original: "Σατανᾶς προσηγορεύθη... ἓν ὄνομα γέγονε Σατανᾶς." Justin's etymology is incorrect; he is trying to combine two different sounds to explain the name, whereas the word is actually a single Hebrew root.</note> For *Sata*...

<margin>
* Dialogue with Trypho, p. 331.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Justin Martyr's scholarship against critics like Christopher Sandius, specifically regarding linguistic knowledge, before providing a catalog of Justin's genuine works.</meta>

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.
</margin>
...among the Jews and Syrians is the word for *Apostate* and *Deserter*; however, the name *Nas* (from which the word "serpent" is also derived by interpretation) is the same as the Hebrew *Sata*, when explained in speech. From both of these combined, the name *Satanas* is formed. How much more correctly did Origen <margin>* Against Celsus, book 6, p. 306.</margin> state: <note>original: "Ὁ δ' Ἑβραίων διαλέκτῳ Σατᾶν, κ' Ἑλληνικώτερον ὑπὸ τίνων ὀνομαζεὶς Σατανᾶς, μεταλαμβανόμενος εἰς Ἑλλάδα φωνὴν ἐστὶν ἀντικείμενος."</note> "He who is called Satan in the Hebrew dialect, and named more in the Greek fashion as Satanas by some, is translated into the Greek tongue as the *Adversary*." That trifling hawker of Ecclesiastical Antiquity, Christopher Sandius <margin>† Treatise on Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 44. Question 50.</margin>, did not notice these things; he contends in his *Questions to the Orthodox* that this is not a genuine work of Justin, using the argument that this author ridiculously interprets the word *Osanna* <note>Hosanna</note> as "excellent magnificence" <note>original: "μεγαλωσύνην ὑπερκειμένην" (megalosynēn hyperkeimenēn)</note>. For, Sandius says, the true Justin, being a Samaritan, could not have been ignorant of the meaning of the word *Osanna*. Who could easily say whether the man's ignorance or his impudence was greater? For besides the fact that he relies on a false and frivolous argument, he copied that entire, quite long passage from the *Critico* of Rivet <margin>* See Rivet, book 2, ch. 5.</margin>—keeping Rivet’s name silent, indeed, with not even the slightest mention of him made except distantly and indirectly. And so, while Rivet was napping, Sandius himself slept securely. But let us return to Justin. Eusebius says <margin>* Book 4, ch. 18.</margin> that he wrote many monuments of his talent, learning, and study intent upon divine matters, which are "full of every utility" <note>original: "πάσης ὠφελειας ἔμπλεα" (pasēs opheleias empleia)</note>; those which follow are:

---

### GENUINE WORKS.

**Exhortation**, or *Admonition to the Greeks*, in which he exhorts the Gentiles to embrace the Christian faith.

**The Refutation**, or *Oration to the Greeks*, in which he chiefly describes the way by which the Greeks can arrive at the knowledge of Christian faith. In these Orations against the Gentiles, some things seem to be missing. For Jerome reveals that Justin disputed concerning the nature of Demons in one of them; yet this is found nowhere in those that survive. Indeed, Leontius of Byzantium, in his second book against Nestorius and Eutyches, brings forth a fragment from Justin’s *Oration against the Gentiles* which you would seek in vain in either of those we possess; as well as a disputation against Plato, concerning death and immortality, formerly found in them, shreds of which Stephen Gobarus cites in Photius, Codex 232.

**The First Apology for the Christians**, which is placed in the second position in all editions of Justin.

**The Second Apology for the Christians**.

**A Book on the Monarchy of God**, perhaps mutilated at the beginning, or rather the second part of a complete work. The style proves it to be a genuine work of Justin, and whatever others may say, the matter itself proclaims it.

**Dialogue with Trypho the Jew**. This Trypho was perhaps the same man whom the Jews call Rabbi Tarphon, and commonly <term>הכהן העשיר</term> <note>ha-Kohen ha-Ashir: The Wealthy Priest</note>; a colleague and fellow soldier of Rabbi Akiba; who, on account of the rebellion stirred up by Bar Kokhba, had left his fatherland and betaken himself to Greece.

**Letter to Diognetus**, not mentioned by Eusebius; but Eusebius did not see everything. Nor does the style—being a little more polished and elegant—prevent it from being Justin's. For it can be a doubt to no one that Justin, according to the occasion, was able to use a more refined and flowery style. It is not unlike the truth that this Diognetus was the same person whom Marcus Aurelius <margin>* Meditations, book 1, § 6.</margin> counts among his teachers.

**Letter to Zenas and Serenus**, which is ethical in nature and discourses accurately and learnedly on Morals. Bellarmine calls this into doubt, undeservedly in my opinion; nor does Bellarmine himself bring forward any reason for his opinion.

**The Overturning of Certain Aristotelian Dogmas**. Perionius brings forward many points in his Notes which might cause a doubt concerning this booklet; nevertheless, they are not of such weight that we should for that reason judge this booklet not to be Justin's, especially since Photius expressly ascribes it to our Martyr.
