# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.</margin> ...[the collection] of two letters to the Corinthians, one to the Romans, two to the Thessalonians, and those to the Ephesians, Colossians, Philemon, Philippians, and Laodiceans, but it was miserably corrupted and stuffed with additions. Epiphanius provides very extensive excerpts from both versions along with his own refutations in *Heresy 42*. He <note>Likely referring to Marcion or a similar Gnostic figure mentioned on the previous page</note> also wrote other volumes, the titles of which are not recorded by the ancient writers.

<margin>140.</margin> **JUSTIN**, called Martyr <term>par excellence</term> <note>original Greek: "kat' exochēn", meaning the most notable or pre-eminent example of the name.</note>, the son of Priscus and grandson of Bachius, was born in Neapolis, a well-known city of Samaria. <gloss>He lived not long after the Apostles, as Eusebius says †; a man neither far from the Apostles in time, nor in virtue,</gloss> <margin>† Book 2, Chapter 13.</margin> <margin>* In Photius, Codex 234.</margin> <margin>|| Letter to Diognetus, p. 501.</margin> says Methodius of Tyre *. Indeed, Justin even speaks of himself || as if <gloss>having become a disciple of the Apostles</gloss>, which should be understood as referring to the Apostolic Men <note>The generation of Christian leaders who personally knew the Apostles</note>, or rather to the doctrine of the Apostles. Having curiously wandered through almost all the sects of the philosophers, he settled on the Platonic school; eventually, he was taught better things by a certain venerable <margin>Eusebius, book 4, ch. 11.</margin> and truly divine old man, and he transitioned to a more divine and noble philosophy—namely, Christianity—around the year 133 AD. <gloss>In the attire of a philosopher, he acted as an ambassador for the divine Word,</gloss> even preaching the word of God while wearing the philosopher's robe. At the beginning of Antoninus Pius's reign, he traveled to Rome and stayed on the Viminal Hill. In order to quench the cruelty raging against the Christians and to vindicate them from the fabricated slanders of the Gentiles, he offered his first *Apology* for the Christians around the year 140 AD, addressed to Antoninus Pius, his sons, and the Roman Senate. Although it is said in the *Apology* that 150 years had passed since Christ, this must be attributed to a corruption of the numerical characters <note>A common occurrence where Roman numerals or Greek letter-numbers were miscopied by scribes</note>, since the Edict of the Emperor Antoninus Pius obtained by Justin's *Apology* was issued during Antoninus's third Consulship, which falls in the year 140 AD. After these events, he returned to Asia and held that most famous dialogue with Trypho the Jew. From there he returned to Rome and wrote a second *Apology* for the Christians, dedicating it to Marcus Antoninus and the Roman Senate. Finally, while he was quite freely rebuking Crescens, a Cynic philosopher—describing him as a gluttonous man, fearful of death, and a follower of luxury and lust, <gloss>the "philosopher" and "braggart" who was not even a philosopher</gloss>—he was accused by Crescens before the Emperor. <margin>* In Surius, for June 12th, and Baronius, for the year 165.</margin> <margin>† Volume II, p. 187.</margin> <margin>* Heresy 46, p. 171.</margin> <margin>† Codex 125.</margin> Condemned by the Emperor, he was struck with the sword, as the *Acts of his Martyrdom* record *; however, the Greeks † in the *Menaion* <note>A liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note> say he died by drinking poison, around the year 144, in the 4th year of Marcus Aurelius, or as noted in the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, the 6th year of the Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius. From this it is clear that Epiphanius * labors under a massive error, as he dates Justin's death to the reign of Hadrian and says it happened in the thirtieth year of Justin's life. Photius † has this to say about him: <gloss>The man was raised to the highest summit of both our philosophy and especially secular philosophy, overflowing with diverse learning and a wealth of historical knowledge; however, he did not take care to color the natural beauty of his philosophy with rhetorical arts. Therefore, his words—which are otherwise powerful and preserve a scientific quality—do not breathe forth those [rhetorical] seasonings, nor do they draw in the crowd of listeners with lures and charms.</gloss>
> *Indeed, that man was raised to the highest peak of both our philosophy and especially profane philosophy, overflowing with the abundance of multifaceted erudition and histories. But he did not make it his study to color the native beauty of his philosophy with rhetorical craftsmanship. For this reason, even his speech, which is otherwise potent and valid, breathing a scientific style, does not breathe those rhetorical seasonings, nor does it drag the common crowd of listeners with allurements or charms.*

That he was completely unrefined and unskilled in Hebrew letters ought not to be held against Justin as a fault: first, because although he was a Samaritan by birth, he was born to Greek parents; second, because he spent a large part of his life in the religion of the Gentiles; and finally, because he gave himself entirely to philosophy and Greek disciplines, which are immensely distant from the study of Hebrew letters. Hence it happened that he slipped so childishly regarding Hebrew matters. I will give an example. Everyone knows that "Satan" is derived from the word *Satan* [שטן], meaning to oppose or to hate—everyone, that is, who has greeted the Hebrew language even from the front doorstep. <margin>* Dialogue with Trypho, p. 331.</margin> Yet the interpretation of our Justin is clearly ridiculous. <gloss>* He is called Satanas, a name assigned by a combination [of words] based on the actions he performed. For "Sata" in the speech of the Jews and Syrians is "Apostate"; while the name "Nas" (from which the interpretation "serpent" is called) is the same as the word "Sata" in the common speech of the Hebrews. From both of these aforementioned words, one name is made: Satanas.</gloss>
> *He is called Satanas, having obtained a name consistent with the very things he did, and composed from them. For Sa—*

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.</margin>
<margin>* Against Celsus, book 6, p. 306.</margin>
<margin>† Treatise on Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 44. Question 50.</margin>

"Sata" in the language of the Jews and Syrians signifies "Apostate" and "Deserter"; however, the name "Satanas" (from which, by interpretation, he is also called the serpent) is the same as "Sata" explained in the Hebrew speech. From both of these, the single composite name Satanas is formed. How much more correctly Origen * states: <gloss>“Satan” in the Hebrew dialect—and named “Satanas” in a more Greek manner by some—when translated into the Greek tongue, means “the adversary.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Ὁ δ’ Ἑβραίων διαλέκτῳ Σατᾶν, καὶ Ἑλληνικώτερον ἀπὸ τίνων ὀνομασθεὶς Σατανᾶς, μεταλαμβανόμενὸς εἰς Ἑλλάδα φωνὴν ἐστὶν ἀντικείμενος."</note> Furthermore, what is called "Satan" in the Hebrew language, and named "Satanas" by some in a more Greek form, is interpreted as <term>Adversary</term> <note>The Hebrew "Satan" literally means one who opposes or obstructs.</note>. That trifling peddler of ecclesiastical antiquity, Christopher Sandius †, failed to notice these things; he contends that the *Questions to the Orthodox* is not a genuine work of Justin using this argument: because the author ridiculously interprets the word *Hosanna* as <gloss>excelling magnificence</gloss> <note>original Greek: "μεγαλοσύνην ὑπερκειμένην"</note>. Sandius claims that the true Justin, being a Samaritan, could not have been ignorant of the meaning of the word *Hosanna*. Who could easily say whether the man's ignorance or his impudence was greater? For besides the fact that he relies on a false and frivolous argument, he copied that entire long passage from Rivet's * *Critici* without acknowledging Rivet's name, making only the slightest mention of him from a distance and indirectly; and thus, while Rivet was nodding off, Sandius himself slept securely. But let us return to Justin. Eusebius * says he wrote many monuments of his talent, learning, and intense study of divine matters, <gloss>full of every utility</gloss> <note>original Greek: "πάσης ὠφελείας ἔμπλεα"</note>; which follow below.

### GENUINE WORKS.

*Exhortation to the Greeks*, in which he urges the Gentiles to embrace the Christian faith.

*The Refutation, or Oration to the Greeks*, in which he chiefly describes the way the Greeks can arrive at the knowledge of the Christian faith. In these Orations against the Gentiles, some parts seem to be missing. For Jerome reveals that in one of them, Justin disputed regarding the nature of demons; yet this is found nowhere in the extant versions. Indeed, Leontius of Byzantium, in his second book against Nestorius and Eutyches, brings forth a fragment from *Justin's Oration against the Gentiles* which you would seek in vain in either of the ones we possess; as well as a dispute against Plato regarding death and immortality, once found in them, a fragment of which Stephen Gobarus cites in Photius, Code 232.

*First Apology for the Christians*, which is placed in the second position in all editions of Justin.

*Second Apology for the Christians.*

*Book on the Monarchy of God*, perhaps mutilated at the beginning, or rather the second part of a complete work. The style argues that it is a genuine work of Justin, and whatever others may say, the matter speaks for itself.

*Dialogue with Trypho the Jew.* This Trypho was perhaps the same man whom the Jews call Rabbi Tarphon, and commonly <term>the rich priest</term> <note>original Hebrew: "הכהן העשיר" (ha-Kohen ha-Ashir)</note>; he was a colleague and fellow soldier of Rabbi Akiva; who, having left his homeland due to the rebellion stirred up by Bar Kokhba, had moved to Greece.

*Epistle to Diognetus*, which was indeed not mentioned by Eusebius; but Eusebius did not see everything. Nor does the slightly more polished and elegant style prevent it from being Justin's. For no one can doubt that Justin was capable of using a more refined and flowery style depending on the occasion. It is not unlikely that this Diognetus was the same person whom Marcus Aurelius * numbers among his teachers.
<margin>* *To Himself* (Meditations), book 1, section 6.</margin>

*Epistle to Zenas and Serenus*, which is ethical in nature and discourses accurately and learnedly on morals. Bellarmine calls this into doubt, undeservedly in my opinion; nor does Bellarmine himself bring forward any reason for his opinion.

*Overthrow of Certain Aristotelian Doctrines.* Perionius brings forward many points in his notes that raise doubts about this booklet. Nevertheless, they are not of such weight that we should strip Justin of this booklet, especially since Photius expressly ascribes it to our Martyr.

## SPURIOUS WORKS.

<margin>2nd CENTURY from the year of Christ.</margin>
*Questions and Responses to the Greeks.* In these, the Manichaeans are cited: <note>The Manichaeans followed Mani, a 3rd-century prophet; their mention proves this work was written long after Justin's death in 165 AD.</note> so I shall not bring up other evidence.

*Greek Questions regarding the Incorporeal, and God, and the Resurrection of the Dead, and Christian Responses to them*: these seem to be of the same style and author as the previous works, to which they are added as an appendix.

<margin>* Codex 125.</margin>
*The 146 Questions: Responses to the Orthodox.* Either this book is entirely not the offspring of our Justin—which seems most likely to me—or it is remarkably altered. For there are many things in it which clearly savor of several centuries after Justin, and the Arian age <note>The Arian controversy over the nature of Christ began in the 4th century.</note>, and the subsequent <note>original Greek: "μετὰ ταῦτα"</note> times of Christianity: to say nothing of Irenaeus, Origen, and the Manichaeans cited therein. Certainly, the illustrious Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), a prominent Irish scholar.</note> judges the author to have been Justin the Sicilian, who wrote as the fifth century was coming to a close. Whoever the author may be, he is surely a writer of great judgment, varied learning, and elegant talent. Meanwhile, see whether it might be the same book, though wretchedly altered, of which Photius * speaks under this title: *Summary Solutions of Doubts Against Religion* <note>original Greek: "ἀποριῶν κατὰ τῆς εὐσεβείας κεφαλαιωδεῖς ἐπιλύσεις"</note>. For the accurate judgment, sharpness, and learning of Photius do not permit us to doubt that that work was a genuine one of Justin.

*Exposition of the Faith on the Holy Trinity*: However, Leontius of Byzantium cites this as a work of Justin the Philosopher and Martyr in his first book *Against Nestorius* in Canisius's *Ancient Readings*, Volume 4, and brings forth certain things from it which are read in this exposition today.

*Commentary on the Soul.*
The book called the *Psalter*.

The book *Against All Heresies*, which Justin himself mentions in his *First Apology* to Antoninus Pius.

*Against Marcion.* Irenaeus cites some things from this book in book 4, chapter 14, and book 5, chapter 26; also Eusebius in book 4, chapter 11. It seems not so much a distinct work from the preceding one as it was a certain part of it.

*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, according to Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian.</note>, who cites many and very large fragments from that book in his *Parallels*; Father Halloix presented these extracted in Greek and Latin in his *Life of Justin*, chapter 27.

Furthermore, Tatian (Justin's disciple), in his *Oration to the Greeks*, page 157; Antony Melissa, in his *Sermons* book 1, chapter 19; book 2, chapters 6 and 43; and Damascene in *Parallels* book 1, chapter 19 and elsewhere, all possess certain fragments from Justin’s lost books.

I shall record here a single sentiment of Justin from Antony Melissa, book 2, chapter 43, most worthy of a Christian Philosopher and Martyr: *The goal for the one practicing philosophy is to become as like God as possible.* <note>original Greek: "Τέλος τῷ φιλοσοφοῦντι, ἡ πρὸς Θεὸν ὁμοίωσις κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν"</note>

Of the flaws which occur in Justin’s writings today—and in which he had at least many of the Ancients as supporters <note>original Greek: "ὁμοψήφους" (homopsēphous), meaning they cast the same vote or held the same opinion.</note>, if not all—the chief ones are: the doctrines of Millenarianism <note>The belief in a literal 1,000-year reign of Christ on Earth.</note>; the state of souls after this life; the salvation of Pagans, whom he says lived according to Reason <note>original Greek: "μετὰ λόγου βιῶν"</note> and recognized Christ in part; the cohabitation of Angels with women, arising from a bad translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament. The "bad translation" refers to interpreting "Sons of God" in Genesis 6 as angels.</note>; and concerning the excessive power of free will. Others have written on these, and we have written more extensively elsewhere. Indeed, regarding his contention that Socrates and certain other Gentiles lived according to Reason and recognized Christ in part, he was certainly of this opinion, and with him almost all the more illustrious theologians of that time...

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the year of Christ.

|| Apology 1, page 46.
* Ibid, page 51.
† Pages 46, 48.
</margin>
Christ is the true and eternal Word <note>original Greek: "λόγον" (Logos)</note> of the Father, the fountain of all reason and wisdom; from Him, just as a ray from the sun, the Word—or Reason—is naturally derived into every human being. For the Word <note>original: "λόγος"</note> which was with God, and was itself God, was that true light which enlightens every man coming into the world. Hence, according to our Martyr <note>Justin Martyr</note>, Christ is often called the "Universal Word" <note>original Greek: "τῷ παντὸς λόγῳ"</note>, and in respect to Him, human reason is called the "seminal word" <note>original Greek: "σπερματικὸς λόγος"; this refers to the "seeds" of truth planted in all people</note>. This is frequently described as a "kinship" <note>original Greek: "συγγενές"</note> with the seminal divine Word, and as a "concept innate to the sowing of the Word" <note>original Greek: "ἡ ἔννοια ἔμφυτος τῷ λόγῳ σπορᾷ"</note>. Consequently, Justin distinguishes this reason clearly enough from "the seed itself" <note>original Latin: "ab αὐτῷ τῷ σπερματι"</note>, and elsewhere affirms more than once that whatever the Poets or Philosophers taught excellently concerning morals, all of it flowed from "the seed of the Word innate to the whole race of men" <note>original Greek: "διὰ τὸ ἔμφυτον παντὶ γένει ἀνθρώπων σπέρμα τῷ λόγῳ"</note>. This, as far as I can grasp, was his opinion, and the essence of the opinion of those who followed him in the next interval; I have elsewhere detailed this at greater length by citing many testimonies from Justin himself, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen. Certainly, I do not recall observing Justin affirming anywhere that the Gentiles <note>non-Christians</note> living outside the profession of the Christian religion would be saved, nor that the bare knowledge of Philosophy suffices for this. Rather, he only meant that whoever among them rightly used the "innate Word" <note>original Greek: "τῷ λόγῳ"</note>—that is, Reason—to worship God and establish a most excellent life, approached most closely to Christ, the "eternal Word" <note>original Greek: "τῷ λόγῳ"</note>, and was to that extent conformed to Him. 

His works, as many as survive, were published in Greek by the care of Robert Stephens, Paris, 1551 and 1571 in folio; in Latin at Basel, 1528 and 1551; Paris, 1554 and 1565; Basel, 1555 and 1565; Paris, 1578. The Greek-Latin editions were published at Heidelberg by Hieronymus Commelinus, 1593 in folio; Paris, 1615 and 1636 in folio. In these newest Parisian editions, besides the notes of Sylburg, Peronius, Billius, and Lanselius, the other Apologists were added.

->**THE CHURCH OF SMYRNA**<- was widowed of its leader Polycarp in the year 167 according to common chronological accounts; however, according to the calculation of Pearson and Dodwell (whom we follow here), it was in the year 147. In that same year, they wrote a circular letter "to all the parishes of the holy catholic church in every place" <note>original Greek: "πάσαις ταῖς κατ' πάντα τόπον τῆς ἁγίας καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας παροικίαις"</note> (Eusebius * says they wrote "to the parishes in every place" <note>original Greek: "ταῖς κατ' πάντα παροικίαις"</note>), in which they set forth the whole history of the passion of Polycarp and those who suffered with him, truly elegantly and at great length. These *Acts* exist in Eusebius, but are mutilated at the beginning and the end. However, these gaps were opportunely filled by the Most Reverend Primate of Ireland, James Ussher, who in 1647 published the complete Martyrdom from the Baroccian Codex, together with an ancient Latin interpreter from a manuscript codex of the Church of Salisbury, in his *Ignatian Appendix*. This Letter of the Smyrnaeans (as is clear from the notes added to the end of Ussher's *Acts*) was transcribed by Gaius, an associate of Irenaeus, from the copy belonging to Irenaeus himself, a disciple of Polycarp; just as Socrates of Corinth transcribed his own from the copies of Gaius, whose manuscript codex Ussher used.

->**PTOLEMAEUS**<-, of the school of Valentinus and the Gnostics, a man (by the admission of Epiphanius *) by far the most learned. There exists a quite long Greek-Latin *Letter against the Law of Moses* to Flora, a woman of his flock, setting forth his impious and blasphemous dogmas, found in Epiphanius, *Heresy XXXIII*, from numbers 3 to 7; and certain fragments in Irenaeus.

By a far more accurate calculation, Pearson and Dodwell show that he sat from the year 127 to the year 142. There exist under his name two Letters to Justus of Vienne, rejected by the almost universal consensus of the learned as spurious; nor does Bellarmine * himself, who cites testimony from them, dare to defend them as being of undoubted faith. These accounts are held in the *Orthodoxographa*, Volume 2, page 3; in all editions of the *Library of the Fathers*; in Baronius under the year 166; and in Jean à Bosco’s *Library of Fleury*, part 2, pages 22 and 24.

<margin>164.</margin> **SOTER**, an Italian by nationality, from the region of Campania and born in the city of Fondi, was eventually made Bishop of Rome. Ancient and modern writers vary wonderfully regarding the order and timing of his succession. Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper place him at the year 168. Two catalogues, the Bucherian and Henschenian, place him at 161. A third catalogue published by Schelstrate cites the year 164. Onuphrius and Antonio Agustín point to 163. Baronius and Bellarmine favor 175. Petau and Labbe cite 173. According to Pearson, he was Pontiff from 161 until 170. However, by Dodwell’s calculation, he served from 153 until 175. He wrote <margin>|| On Heresies, 26 & 86.</margin> ||—according to the author of *On Heresies*, published by Sirmond under the name of *Prædestinatus*—a book *against the Cataphrygians* <note>original: "contra Cataphrygas"; these were the Montanists, an early Christian prophetic movement</note>, to which Tertullian responded while acting as a defender of Montanus; however, both works have long since perished.

<margin>164.</margin> **ABERCIUS**, of Hierapolis, born of noble and Christian parents, was created Bishop of the Church of Hierapolis around the year 164. He suffered much under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus at the hands of the Gentiles; while they were still reigning, he peacefully departed from the living. Pierre Halloix <margin>* Lives of the Oriental Fathers, vol. ii.</margin> described his life at length and even to the point of tedium, drawing from the Greek *Acts* collected by Simeon Metaphrastes and from the Greek *Menologium* <note>a church calendar containing lives of saints</note>. But anyone can easily see what kind of reliability and authority these *Acts* possess; certainly neither Eusebius nor any of the Ancients handed down to us a memory of Abercius of this sort. He is said to have written a *book on Discipline*, for the use of the order of Priests and Deacons, as well as a *Letter to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius* which (if one stands by the judgment of Baronius) "clearly breathed an Apostolic spirit." Baronius had unearthed this from a Greek <margin>* See Baronius at the Year 163, No. 15, and notes to the Roman Martyrology, Oct. 22.</margin> manuscript of Cardinal Sirleto and promised that he would present it in its entirety in his *Annals*; but by some accident it slipped from his hands and never appeared afterward.

<margin>
167.
* Basil, On the Holy Spirit, ch. 29.
|| Augustine, Against Julian, book 1, ch. 3.
† Letter to Theodoret, p. 196.
* Letter to Florinus in Eusebius, book 5, ch. 20.
</margin>
**IRENAEUS**, of Asian descent and seemingly a native of Smyrna, was "one who was near the Apostles" <note>original Greek: "ὁ ἐγγὺς τῶν ἀποστόλων γενόμενος"</note> *; Augustine says he lived "not far from the times of the Apostles" ||. According to Jerome †, he was a disciple of Papias, but by Irenaeus's own testimony *, he was a disciple of Polycarp. He diligently noted all of Polycarp's actions, his gait, and the form of his whole life; he listened most studiously to all his sayings and sermons, and stored what he heard in his mind. It is probable that he came to Rome with Polycarp under Pope Anicetus, and from there set out for Gaul, settling his household in Lyons <note>original Latin: "Lugduni"</note> and becoming a Priest of that Church. After the death of Pothinus, he obtained the bishopric of the Church of Lyons; and so that he might better adorn the province he had obtained, he spared no labor. He refuted heretics in word and writing; he worked immensely in repairing the union of the Churches, especially in settling the Paschal controversy <note>The "Easter Controversy" regarding the proper date to celebrate the holiday</note>. In that matter, when the Roman Pontiff Victor was preparing a decree of excommunication against the Asian Churches, Irenaeus—having convened a Synod of Gallic Bishops—peacefully admonished him by letter and sharply rebuked his resistance. He died by beheading, if we follow common calculations, during the Severan Persecution around the year 202, or as others say, in 208, when the Emperor Severus stayed for some time in Lyons while preparing for the British expedition. However, our singular friend, the illustrious Dodwell, in his dissertation on the *age of Irenaeus* (which he is preparing along with others for a new edition of Irenaeus), arranges the dates of Irenaeus quite differently than is commonly done. I will briefly explain his opinion, which we have decided to embrace in this place. He maintains that Irenaeus was born under Nerva in the year of Christ 97. This indeed seems able to be gathered from his own words in Book 5, Chapter 30, where he calls the end of Domitian’s reign "almost our own generation" <note>original Greek: "σχεδὸν τὴν ἡμετέραν γενεάν"</note>, or as the ancient version has it, *almost our own age*. There can be no doubt that he reckoned his "age" from his own birth. It seems that around the year 122, while he was still "in his first youth" <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ ἡλικίᾳ"</note> (Book 3, Chapter 3), he saw and heard Polycarp; and he saw Florinus with Polycarp in Lower Asia "while still a boy" <note>original Greek: "παῖς ὢν ἔτι"</note>, as noted in the *Letter to Florinus* in Eusebius.

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.</margin>
Eusebius, Book 5, chapter 20: that is, in the 25th year of his age, and certainly before his 30th year, which Epiphanius calls "a settled age" <note>original Greek: ἡλικίαν καθεστῶσαν; a term used to describe full maturity</note> in *Against Heresies*, Book 46, Number 1. At the same time, he saw Florinus living splendidly "in the royal court" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ αὐλῇ βασιλικῇ</note>, as cited in that same location; this occurred while Hadrian was active in Asia, which could hardly have happened before that year. In the year 167, as the persecution in Gaul grew heated, Irenaeus succeeded Pothinus, the Bishop of Lyons, who had suffered martyrdom. Irenaeus was an "elder" <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτερος; *presbyter*, used here to denote both his seniority in age and his ecclesiastical rank</note> by both age and office, being then 70 years old, while Eleutherus held the papacy. In the year 176, or perhaps the following year, he wrote *Against Heresies*; this work, the first of all his writings, was composed after the death of Tatian in 174, after the publication of Theodotion’s version of the Bible, and after Marcus Aurelius had admitted Commodus as co-emperor in 175. It was also written after several successions in the seat of Smyrna following the martyrdom of Polycarp. By then, Irenaeus had grown old, being nearly 80 years of age, while Eleutherus was still living. In the year 182, at the age of 85, he wrote the letters against Blastus and Florinus during the reign of Pope Victor; this seems to have occurred in this year, the third year of Commodus's reign, according to the records of Eusebius in his *Chronicle* and the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*. Blastus favored the Asians in the matter of the date of Easter <note>The "Asians" refers to the Quartodecimans of Asia Minor who celebrated Easter on the 14th of Nisan, regardless of the day of the week</note>, and for that reason, he was removed from the presbytery. From this began the dispute with the Asians themselves. In the year 189, at the age of 92, in the 10th year of Commodus under Victor, a debate was held regarding Easter, which Irenaeus survived, dying shortly thereafter. Indeed, Caius—a disciple of Irenaeus himself (if faith is to be placed in the *Acts of Polycarp*)—records him among the writers older than the end of Victor’s reign, writing under Pope Zephyrinus as recorded in Eusebius, Book 5, chapter 28.

And thus far is the opinion of very learned men regarding the years of Irenaeus, described "in outline" <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐν τύπῳ</note>, leaving a fuller explanation and confirmation to the Dissertations themselves soon to be published. As for the fact that Irenaeus is commonly said to have been a Martyr, that should be considered a fiction of later centuries. Certainly, the older writers—Tertullian, Eusebius, Augustine, and Theodoret—seem to have been ignorant of it. Almost the first to attach this title to him is the author of *Questions and Responses* under the name of Justin, a writer perhaps of only the fifth century. Jerome does call Irenaeus a Martyr once in his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 64, page 240; but it is permitted to doubt whether the word "Martyr" might have crept into the text in that place. Jerome nowhere else calls him a Martyr, not even in his book *On Famous Men* <note>original Latin: *De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis*</note>, where he treats Irenaeus specifically.

### W R I T I N G S.

<margin>* On Famous Men, chapter 35.</margin>
**Against Heresies**; or, *On the Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So-called*, in five Books. In these, he deals with all the leaders of heresies up to his own time and their cursed doctrines and deeds; he refutes their impious objections, clears up the questions they raised, and courageously defends the truth against all their weapons. Since the original Greek is lost (for those who wish to claim Irenaeus wrote in Latin do not deserve a rebuttal), there exists a Latin version of these books, which is old enough, but exceptionally barbarous, difficult, and rough. The most learned Dodwell will demonstrate in a special dissertation that this version is more recent than Tertullian, but older than the final years of St. Augustine, and was therefore made at the end of the 4th century. The Priscillianist heresy, which renewed the dogmas of the ancient Gnostics, seems to have given rise to this version. Priscillian had a certain Egyptian teacher named Marcus, whom some have rashly confused with the Marcus who was the leader of the Marcosians in Irenaeus’s work, perhaps falling into the error of thinking Irenaeus had written specifically against this later Marcus. It is truly regrettable that the original text of this work has perished. However, so that the loss might be repaired in some way, Epiphanius preserved many of Irenaeus's Greek passages for us; many were also preserved by John of Damascus in his *Parallels*. These were presented in both Greek and Latin, to the great benefit of the literary world, by Father Halloix in his *Life of Irenaeus*, chapter 15. He also wrote works which do not exist today: a short book *Against the Gentiles*, entitled *On Knowledge* or *On Discipline* (Jerome * made two volumes out of this one); the *Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching* addressed to his brother Marcianus; a book of *Various Disputations* or "discourses" <note>original Greek: διαλέξεων</note>; and a *Commentary on the Ogdoad*, at the end of which he added that solemn and most useful note or adjuration which is found in Eusebius, Book 5, chapter 20: "I adjure you, who transcribes this book, by our Lord Jesus [Christ]..."

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>2nd CENTURY AD</margin>

For those heretics had devised a most foul genealogy of certain <term>Aeons</term> <note>Aeons were divine beings or emanations in Gnostic cosmology</note>, whom they had joined together in marriages divided into various sexes, calling two Aeons joined in marriage a "Conjugation" <note>original Latin: *Conjugationem*; also known as a *syzygy* or pair</note>: and dreaming that all the rest drew their origin from the first four Conjugations, or the first eight Aeons. But he who wishes to know these things more deeply should consult Jean de Croï, who discusses the entire theology of the Gnostics most learnedly in his *Specimen of Conjectures on certain passages of Origen, etc.*

<margin>On Writings, chapter 9.</margin>
He also wrote a letter to Blastus regarding the Schism; and another to Florinus regarding the Monarchy, or that God is not the author of evils: a part of which survives in Eusebius in the place cited. He also wrote a Commentary on the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, which Jerome mentions.

<margin>* Codex 120.</margin>
Finally, he wrote a Synodic Letter to Victor, the Bishop of Rome, concerning the date of Easter, from which Eusebius preserves certain fragments in Book 5, chapter 24. Indeed, he wrote several letters to various bishops concerning the same matter. Regarding certain of his works, Photius says this *: "Even if in some of them the accurate truth of ecclesiastical dogmas seems to be adulterated by spurious reasonings." <note>original Greek: "Εἰ καὶ ἔν τισιν αὐτῶν ἡ πρὸς τὰ ἐκκλησιαστικὰ δόγματα ἀληθείας ἀκρίβεια νόθοις λογισμοῖς κιβδηλεύεται."</note> It must certainly be admitted that even in those works which survive, there are certain blemishes; which, if they cannot be defended, deserve to be excused. Among these, the most noteworthy is found in Book 2 of *Against Heresies*, chapters 39 and 40: namely, that Christ did not enter upon his prophetic office until the fiftieth year of his age. This could have arisen partly from an excessive fervor in disputing against the Gnostics, who wanted Christ to have departed from the earth after completing his thirty-first year; and partly from a poorly understood passage in Saint John 8:57 <note>"You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?"</note>; especially with the addition of a certain false tradition, which it might not be wrong to believe he received from his teacher Papias, or someone else. There is no need to note the somewhat harsh phrases and awkward expressions that occur frequently in his work, which perhaps ought to be attributed for the most part to a somewhat barbaric Latin translator; the prudent reader will easily notice them himself. He used a style that was quite simple and unrefined;

<margin>† Preface to Book 1.</margin>
For he does not show, as he admits of himself †, any artistry of words, nor force of speech, nor ornament of expression, nor faculty of persuasion: inasmuch as he neither learned nor affected such things. Add to this that he greatly corrupted his native simplicity of speech by learning the language of the Barbarians <note>The Celts/Gauls in the region of Lyons</note> among whom he lived. His works were published by Erasmus at Basel in 1526, 1534, 1548, 1560 in folio; at Paris in 1563, 1567 in octavo; at Geneva (with the notes of Gallas) 1570 in folio; at Basel (by the care of Grynæus together with various readings) 1571 in octavo; at Paris 1577 in octavo; at Cologne 1595 in folio. However, among all the editions, the most excellent is the Parisian edition of the year 1639 in folio, with Greek fragments and the very rich commentaries of François Feuardent, who nevertheless tends to drag everything "by the neck" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to force or distort an argument</note> to establish the papal cause.

<margin>168.</margin>
**THEOPHILUS** of Antioch, learned in every branch of secular literature: he was once entirely wandered through the various studies of the Gentiles and the vain labyrinths of superstitions; until, compelled by the force of truth and conquered by the strongest arguments of the Christian faith, he abandoned the worship of the Pagans and fled to the camp of Christ. He was promoted to the Bishopric of Antioch after the death of Eros, around the year 168, or at least the following year. When he had administered this province with the greatest diligence and faith for thirteen years; at the beginning of the Emperor Commodus's reign, around the year 181, he happily finished his course. He wrote to Autolycus, a most upright friend but a most bitter enemy of the Christian Religion, three books concerning the Faith of the Christians and against its detractors. These were "elementary writings" <note>original Greek: "στοιχειώδη συγγράμματα"</note>, as Eusebius calls them *, containing the instruction of the faith. They were printed in Greek and Latin among the *Orthodoxographa* at Basel, 1555, Volume 1; at the end of Justin Martyr, Paris 1615, 1636; in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* in Greek and Latin with the notes of Fronton du Duc, Paris 1624, Volume 1; and separately at Oxford, 1684, in duodecimo.

MELITO, a man of Asia <note>Specifically from Sardis in Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note>, famous for his piety no less than his learning. 170 AD.
</margin>
DIONYSIUS, a man most celebrated among the prelates of his century for the piety of his doctrine, the holiness of his life, the gravity of his character, and the eloquence of his speeches, held the bishopric of the Church of the Corinthians. He flourished around the year 170, and he looked after not only the interests of his own Church, but also served the common utility of almost all other cities and provinces by sending "Catholic" <note>In this context, "Catholic" means universal or general letters intended for the whole church.</note> letters everywhere. He died a Martyr, according to the Greek Menology <note>A calendar of the lives of saints and martyrs.</note>, struck by a sword on November 29th, perhaps around the year 178. He wrote several Letters, none of which survive today; however, Eusebius 
<margin>
* Book 4, ch. 23.
† On Illustrious Men, ch. 27.
</margin>
and after him Jerome wove an index of them:
1. *To the Lacedaemonians*: One letter which contained instruction in the right faith and arguments for peace and concord. 
2. *Another to the Athenians*, in which he stirred them to purity of faith and the evangelical life. 
3. *A third to the Nicomedians*, against the heresy of Marcion, urging them to adhere firmly to the rule of truth. 
4. *The fourth was to the Gortynians and the other Churches of Crete*, proclaiming the praises of their Bishop Philip and warning them to guard themselves against the fraud and cunning of heretics. 
5. *The fifth to the Amastrians and the other Churches of Pontus*, dealing with various passages of Scripture, *on Marriage and Chastity*, and on the need to kindly receive *Penitents* who had fallen into any grave sin or heretical depravity. 
6. *The sixth to the Gnossians*, in which he admonished their Bishop Pinytus not to impose the heavy burden of chastity on the necks of the brothers as if it were a necessity, but to take into account the weakness found in most people. 
7. *The seventh to the Romans*, addressed to their Bishop Soter, in which he discussed the great generosity of the Roman Church in liberally helping those in need, and mentioned that the Letter of Clement of Rome was customarily read in the Corinthian Church in his time. From this letter, Eusebius (Book 2, ch. 25) cites certain details about the journey of Peter and Paul to the city of Rome, and other matters regarding the customs and institutions of the Roman Church (Book 4, ch. 23). Finally, he wrote another letter *to Chrysophora*, a most faithful sister, to whom he supplied spiritual nourishment. I will only add that Dionysius himself complained that while he was still alive, certain heretics had corrupted his letters, deleting some things and adding others; *for whom,* he said, *woe is reserved,* <note>original Greek: οἷς τὸ οὐαὶ κεῖται</note> meaning that deadly "woe to you" awaits them.

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.
170 AD.
* Codex 232.
† Book 2, ch. 23.
|| On Illustrious Men, ch. 22.
</margin>

HEGESIPPUS, of Jewish origin it seems, was later converted to the faith of Christ. Stephen Gobarus, as cited in Photius <gloss>*</gloss>, calls him <gloss>an ancient and apostolic man</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀρχαῖός τε ἀνὴρ καὶ ἀποστολικός</note>, or as Eusebius <gloss>†</gloss> has it, <gloss>belonging to the first succession of the apostles</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς πρώτης τῶν ἀποστόλων γενομένος διαδοχῆς</note>, which Jerome <gloss>||</gloss> renders as *near to apostolic times*. Having been born around the beginning of the second century, he undertook a journey to Rome; during his travels through various provinces, he held conversations with "Apostolic Men" <note>Early Christian leaders who were believed to have personally known the Apostles or their immediate disciples.</note> renowned for their doctrine and piety, and from them he diligently investigated the origins of the Churches and the growth of the faith. At Rome, he eventually lived on familiar terms with Pope Anicetus, his contemporary, and remained there for nearly a decade, from approximately the year 170 until the reign of Commodus, during whose rule he passed away—as attested by the *Alexandrian Chronicle* for the first year of Commodus. He was the first who attempted to compose an Ecclesiastical History. For he wrote <gloss>Memoirs of Ecclesiastical Affairs</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὑπομνήματα τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν πράξεων</note>, or *Five Books of Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Acts*, in a simple style, as Jerome says <gloss>*</gloss>, so that he might express the character of those whose lives he followed in his own manner of speaking. To the great loss of the Church, these *Commentaries* have perished; nothing remains of them except certain illustrious fragments which Eusebius preserved for us: namely, the *History of the Martyrdom of James, the Brother of the Lord* (Book 2, ch. 23); *On the persecution of the relatives of our Savior* (Book 3, ch. 20); *On the martyrdom of Simeon son of Cleopas, and the state of the Jerusalem Church at that time* (Book 3, ch. 32); *On his own age* (Book 4, ch. 8); and *On the Journey to the City of Rome, and the Jewish Sects* (Book 4, ch. 22). There is also a rather brief fragment from the fifth book of these same Commentaries presented by Stephen Gobarus in Photius, Codex 232. While these cannot fully quench our thirst for knowledge, they can at least soothe it.

<margin>* Place cited.</margin>
->Regarding the <gloss>Memoirs</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὑπομνήμασι</note> of Hegesippus, see St. Ambrose in the 4th Century.<-

<margin>
172 AD.
† Book 4, ch. 23.
</margin>

PINYTUS, a most eloquent man and Bishop of the very ancient city of Cnossus in Crete, flourished as a contemporary of Hegesippus in the year 172; he was a most strict observer of disciplined living. Eusebius <gloss>†</gloss> mentions his only *Letter*, which was very elegant (though lost to the ravages of time); in it, he replied to the advisory letter of Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Corinth, who had written to the Cretans suggesting they not impose too heavy a burden of celibacy.</note> regarding the "yoke of chastity." While praising Dionysius warmly, Pinytus also urged him to finally impart "solid food" <note>A reference to Hebrews 5:12-14, distinguishing between basic "milk" for spiritual infants and "solid food" for the mature.</note> and asked that he nourish the people committed to his care with more advanced doctrine in future letters, lest the people, perpetually nurtured on "milky" sermons, might gradually grow old while remaining in an infantile state of discipline. From this, Eusebius infers that in this Letter, the correct faith of Pinytus, his concern for the progress of the people entrusted to him, and his eloquence and skill in divine matters are all excellently displayed, as if in a painted portrait.

---

<margin>
172 AD.
See Eusebius, Book 4, ch. 25.
</margin>

PHILIP, also of the same age—namely the year 172—was a Cretan Bishop and leader of the Church of the Gortynians. Dionysius of Corinth greatly proclaimed his praises in his letters to the Gortynians, because through Philip's care, the Church of Gortyna had won outstanding praise for its courage and noble spirit by the common testimony of all. The ancient writers have passed down nothing more about him, except that he composed a most brilliant *Book against Marcion* <note>Marcion was a major heretic who taught that the God of the Old Testament was different from and inferior to the God of the New Testament.</note>, which has not reached us.

---

<margin>
172 AD.
* In the Chronicle for the year 172.
</margin>

MONTANUS, originating from Ardaban, a village of Mysia bordering Phrygia (from which his followers were called Phrygians and Cataphrygians). Around the year 172 (by the calculation of Eusebius <gloss>*</gloss>), he founded a new Sect. Boasting that the gift of Prophecy had been divinely granted to him, he called himself the "Paraclete" <note>The "Comforter" or "Advocate," a title for the Holy Spirit in the Gospel of John.</note> sent by God. He associated with himself two most abandoned women, Priscilla and Maximilla, whom he preached had achieved the highest peak of the prophetic office by the gift of the Holy Spirit. Boasting that God the Father lived in himself and the Holy Spirit lived in his prophetesses, he spread various errors among the common people under that pretext. I will here present the summary of the errors which these Cataphrygians fostered, in the words of an ancient writer published by Sirmond under the name of *Predestinatus* (chapter 26):
> "And so these men [claimed] that the arrival of 
> "the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord was in themselves rather
> "than in the Apostles..."

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.
</margin>
"...they assert that [perfection] has been returned. They regard second marriages as fornications; and for this reason, they say that the Apostle Paul permitted them only because he knew in part, and he prophesied in part. For that which was perfect had not yet come. However, they rave that this 'perfection' has come in Montanus and in his prophetesses, whom we mentioned above. Having chosen Pepuza, a village in Phrygia, as a sort of Metropolis of their Heresy, he [Montanus] wanted all those eager for salvation to gather there as if to a New Jerusalem; together with his prophetesses, he poured out frequent prophecies wrapped in obscure and enigmatic diction. <margin>See Eusebius, book 5, ch. 16, 17, 18, 19; and Epiphanius, Heresy 48.</margin> Always seized by ecstatic movements, and appearing plainly as those placed outside of themselves, they prophesied, and among other delusions, they taught that no Prophet would arise after them. Meanwhile, gasping for profit, having scraped together silver vessels, money, and precious clothes from everywhere, they swindled the gullible common people. They were constantly boasting about the martyrs coming from their sect; yet the Catholics constantly affirmed that these were either non-existent or had been justly punished with death for crimes committed. Montanus himself, and Maximilla, are said to have finally broken their own necks with a noose. They wished to appear as the most observant of a more rigid discipline and a more severe piety; and therefore they forbade marriage and the use of certain foods: they taught the separation of marriage, and while praying—in order to display a sadness of mind and a certain affected holiness—they placed the index finger of the hand on the nose, from which they were nicknamed *Tascodrugitae*: because in their language *tascos* <term>tascos (τασκὸς)</term> means a Peg, and *degos* <term>degos (δέγγος)</term> means a nose. They are said to have used a detestable rite in celebrating their mysteries on a certain feast day: for, pricking an infant all over its body with brass needles, they used the blood they collected in their sacrifices. In other matters, they embraced almost the Catholic doctrine. He [Montanus] wrote Prophetic Books in his own name and those of his prophetesses; brief fragments of these are preserved in Epiphanius, in the place cited.

---

<margin>172.</margin> **THEMISON**, an illustrious follower of Montanus, flourished at the same time as Montanus, or a little after. At first devoted to the Catholic faith, for the profession of which he endured chains for a while, he later released himself from them by means of a large sum of money collected from Christians; and being held in hatred by the Catholics for the horror of this most shameful deed <note>Buying one's way out of martyrdom was considered a sign of weakness or betrayal in the early church.</note>, he deserted to the camp of Montanus. Relying on the title of Confessor and Martyr, he strenuously defended his Sect, to the extent that he used the authority of his name to inhibit the most pious Catholics, Zoticus of Comana and Julian of Apamea, bishops who wished to rebuke the Demon by which they believed Maximilla was driven (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V. 18). Having written a *Catholic Epistle* in the likeness of an Apostle, he dared to exhort all the Churches to receive the prophecy of Montanus; and attempting to instruct those who had stood more faithful than himself, he spoke impiously against the Lord, against the Apostles, and the most holy Church. This work does not survive.

---

<margin>172.</margin> **TATIAN**, a Syrian by birth, a Sophist by profession, a Gentile in worship, and then a Christian, had become a disciple of Justin Martyr; whom he accompanied all the way to Rome, where he experienced the hatred and enmities of Crescens. After the death of his Teacher, like a blind man deprived of a leader, he threw himself into precipices. For, puffed up with arrogance and a swelling of eloquence, he founded a certain new Heresy, <margin>See Irenaeus, book 1, ch. 31; Eusebius, book 4, ch. 29; Epiphanius, Heresy 46; Theodoret, Heretical Fables, book 1, ch. 20.</margin> condemning marriage as corruption and debauchery—indeed, calling "marriage the work of the devil" <note>original Greek: τὸν γάμον τοῦ διαβόλου</note>—introducing moreover an abstinence from wine and living things [meat], using only water even in the sacred mysteries: for which reason his followers were called *Encratites* <term>Encratites (the "Abstainers")</term> and *Hydroparastatae* <term>Hydroparastatae (the "Water-offerers")</term>. Furthermore, he denied Salvation to Adam, and with Valentinus, he devised certain invisible Aeons. Finally, in his book *Against the Gentiles*, he writes that human souls are mortal by their own nature, but made immortal by divine benefit; yet in such a way that the souls of the impious perish with the body and rise again with it to be punished with eternal pains. Returning to the East, he first opened a school in Mesopotamia around the year 172, in the 12th year of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (Epiphanius wrongly says Antoninus Pius). He preached especially at Antioch near Daphne, and also in Cilicia and Pisidia. Nothing is certain concerning his death. He wrote "a great multitude of writings" <note>original Greek: πολὺ τι πλῆθος τῶν συγγραμμάτων</note>, says Eusebius <margin>* Place cited.</margin>, infinite volumes,

# The Gnostic Century.
<page-num>47</page-num>

<margin>2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ.</margin>
...as Jerome <margin>† *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 29.</margin> states: among all the works he wrote, the most distinguished is that "most beautiful and most useful" <note>original: κάλλιστός τε, καὶ ὠφελιμώτατος</note>, at once most elegant and most beneficial book, *Address to the Greeks*. In this work, by tracing back to earlier eras, he proves that Moses and the other Prophets were more ancient than all the most celebrated figures among the Greeks. He demonstrates that the Greeks themselves received almost all the studies they boast of from the "Barbarians" <note>In this context, "Barbarian" refers to non-Greek cultures, specifically the Hebrews and their ancient traditions.</note>. This oration survives in Greek and Latin among the *Orthodoxographa* (Basel, 1551, 1555), in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* (Paris, 1624), at the end of Justin’s *Works* (Paris, 1615, 1636), and was also published in Paris in 1618. I shall pass over the Latin editions. Furthermore, he compiled a "Chain" or *Harmony of the Gospels* mentioned by Eusebius <margin>* Cited location.</margin> and Theodoret, which he named the *Diatessaron* <note>original: Διὰ τεσσάρων; literally "Through the Four." This was the first major attempt to combine the four separate Gospels into a single, continuous narrative.</note>, or "The Gospel Composed of Four." He removed from it the genealogies and all other passages that show the Lord was born from the seed of David according to the flesh <note>Tatian likely did this to support his "Encratite" or Gnostic views, which often downplayed Christ's physical, human heritage.</note>. Theodoret testifies that not only his followers but even those who followed Apostolic dogmas used this as a summary book, not noticing the deception. Indeed, there were some who called this book the *Gospel according to the Hebrews*, as is clear from Epiphanius <margin>* Cited location.</margin>. This *Gospel Harmony* exists in Latin in the *Orthodoxographa*, Volume 1, and the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 2, where it is wrongly attributed to Ammonius of Alexandria—just as Ammonius’s *Harmony* is incorrectly labeled as Tatian’s. This seems to have first arisen from an error by Victor of Capua, the translator of the Ammonian Harmony. It is easily recognized from the notes on Tatian’s *Harmony* found in Theodoret and Eusebius, which match the *Harmony* attributed to Ammonius exactly, and vice versa (but see more on this under "Ammonius"); though I would readily concede that it was much altered by the Latin translator, a man of no small elegance. He also wrote a book *On Perfection according to the Savior*, in which he condemned marriage and strove to prove it unlawful. Clement of Alexandria cites and refutes a fragment from it in the *Miscellanies* <note>original: *Stromata*</note>, book 3, page 460. Rhodon, in Eusebius (book 5, ch. 13), mentions a book of *Problems* written by Tatian. Rufinus also attributes a *Chronicle* to him <margin>*Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, ch. 11.</margin>; however, it is certain that this error arose from a misunderstanding of Eusebius’s words (book 6, ch. 13). Of his remaining works, not even the titles have reached us. I will mention one final thing about him, which Eusebius records from the tradition of some <margin>* Book 4, ch. 29.</margin>: that he dared to express the sayings of the Apostle Paul in more elegant words, as one who sought to "correct" the composition of Paul's language.

---

## <margin>172.</margin> BARDESANES

A Syrian, born at Edessa in Mesopotamia, he flourished chiefly around the year 172. A man learned in both Greek and Syriac, most eloquent in speech, and most sharp in disputation. Eusebius says <margin>† *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 6, ch. 6, p. 273.</margin> that he was "not unacquainted with Chaldean science" <note>original: οὐκ ἄπειρος δὲ καὶ Χαλδαικῆς ἐπιστήμης ἐληλακὼς</note>, having attained the highest perfection of Chaldean learning. He was especially intimate with Abgar, the prince of the Edessenes—a most holy man—and joining his studies with him, he strongly asserted the Christian faith, which he defended through his life, writings, and debates. After he had provided this service for many years, he slipped into the errors of Valentinus (from whose school he had indeed emerged). Consequently, Epiphanius <margin>* Heresy 56.</margin> compares him to a most beautiful and well-laden ship which, wrecked near the shores of the harbor, loses all its cargo and brings death to others who had boarded. However, he did not drink the final poison of that heresy: for he recognized the books of the Law and the Prophets, and thus the entire Old and New Testaments—though he denied the resurrection of the dead even more stubbornly than Valentinus himself. It is certain from Marinus <margin>† In Origen, *Dialogue against Marcion*, Section 3.</margin> that the Bardesianists departed from the Catholic Church in three main points: 1. They asserted that besides God there is another "beginning" or "root" <note>original: ἀρχὴν seu ῥίζαν</note>, namely the Devil, whom they affirmed to be "self-produced and self-born" <note>original: αὐτοφυῆ καὶ αὐτογέννητον</note>, the source and author of all evil. 2. That Christ was not born of a woman, but brought his flesh from Heaven. 3. That the body would not rise again. However, it is clear from Eusebius <margin>† Book 4, ch. 30.</margin> that Bardesanes later disapproved of Valentinian doctrine; and when he had proved most of its dogmas to be fabricated fables, he seemed to himself to have transitioned to a more correct opinion—though in such a way that he did not entirely shake off the filth of his old and deep-seated error. He wrote many dialogues in his native language, namely Syriac, along with infinite other short works, and among these, he wrote against Marcion and nearly all the Heretics who had sprouted up in his time, and many volu- <meta>catchword: volu-</meta>

<header>The Gnostic Century.</header>

<margin>2nd CENTURY AD.</margin> ...volumes composed on the occasion of the persecution raging at that time; these his disciples (of whom he had many) translated from the Syriac language into Greek. Among these, that truly most excellent *Dialogue on Fate*, which he inscribed to Antoninus, was especially prominent. Whether Eusebius means the Emperor Marcus Antoninus <note>Also known as Marcus Aurelius.</note> (as it seemed to Jerome), or rather one of Bardesanes' own friends, is not sufficiently clear. However, the former opinion will seem more likely <margin>† Loc. cit.</margin> to anyone who considers what Epiphanius † relates concerning Apollonius, a friend of Antoninus, who warned Bardesanes to deny that he was a Christian. Bardesanes opposed him manfully, even to the point of confession <note>In the early church, a "confessor" was someone who suffered for the faith but was not necessarily martyred.</note>, saying that he did not fear death, as it would necessarily happen even if the Emperor did not oppose <margin>† Ibid.</margin> it. Epiphanius † undoubtedly refers to the same *dialogue* when he says that while he argued against Abidas the Astronomer regarding Fate, he collected many points. A large enough fragment of this *dialogue* exists today in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 6, chapter 10; the greatest part of which is found word-for-word in the ninth book of the *Clementine Recognitions*: so much so that it is uncertain who received their material from the other. Indeed, we might perhaps suspect, not without reason, that Bardesanes himself was the author of these *Recognitions*, as we noted above regarding Clement. Porphyry, in *On Abstinence*, book 4, chapter 17, mentions a book *On the Indian Gymnosophists* <note>The "Gymnosophists" or "naked philosophers" were Indian ascetics known to the Greeks.</note> written by Bardesanes the Babylonian, and presents a fragment from it. It is not very difficult to believe the author was the same as our Bardesanes, especially since Porphyry distinguishes him with this note: <note>original: ὁ ἐπὶ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν γεγονὼς</note> *who lived in the times of our fathers.* N. E.

---

<margin>174. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 3.</margin> JULIUS CASSIANUS, a disciple of Valentinus, seems to have flourished around the year 174. He founded the <term>Docetic</term> <note>Docetism is the belief that Christ’s body was not real flesh and blood, but merely an appearance or phantom.</note> heresy: teaching that Christ assumed only a phantasmal body; indeed, in the matter of marriage and continence, he held the same views as Tatian. More details about him are not clear. He wrote several books of *Exegesis* (from the first of which Clement of Alexandria preserves some excerpts in *Stromata*, book 1, page 320) and a book <note>original: περὶ ἐγκρατείας, ἢ περὶ εὐνουχίας</note> *On Continence, or On Eunuchry*, from which the same Clement cites many things in *Stromata*, book 3, pages 465, 466.

---

<margin>175. † *Against Heresies*, book 3, ch. 24. * *On Weights and Measures*, no. 17. * *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, ch. 2, vol. 7. * *Treatise on the 70 Interpreters*, ch. 6, p. 58.</margin> THEODOTION, of the Pontic nation (Irenaeus † calls him an Ephesian, perhaps because he lived there). He flourished (as Epiphanius * teaches us, though he makes him later than Symmachus by a massive <term>metachronism</term> <note>A chronological error where an event is placed later than its actual date.</note>) under the second Commodus, that is, the son of Marcus Aurelius Verus, who began his rule in the year 180. But it should be noted that already in the year 175, the Emperor Marcus had admitted Commodus as a partner in the empire, and thus Theodotion could have become famous several years earlier, at least by the year 175. Having professed the Christian faith, he gave himself to the sect of Marcion of Pontus, his countryman, who had mixed some of the dogmas of Ebion with his own; hence he is sometimes called an <term>Ebionite</term> <note>A Jewish-Christian movement that emphasized Jewish law and often viewed Jesus as a human prophet rather than divine.</note>. Finally, becoming hostile even to that heresy, he utterly deserted the Christian religion, and having undergone circumcision <note>original: detracto præputio; literally "having the foreskin removed."</note>, he defected to the Jews. Having been taught Hebrew letters by them, he translated the *Old Testament* into Greek, chiefly following the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The "LXX" or standard Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translators; from whom Jerome says *, *he does not differ in the simplicity of his language.* For this reason, he was preferred over the others; so much so that Origen, when he compiled his <term>Hexapla</term> <note>A massive six-columned edition of the Bible comparing different versions.</note>, decided that those parts missing from the Septuagint but present in the Hebrew should be supplied from Theodotion, marked with asterisks. Indeed, the Church formerly read and still reads today the entire Prophecy of Daniel not from the Septuagint, but from Theodotion’s version. Hence, in a very ancient copy of the Prophets mentioned by the Illustrious Ussher *, the book of Daniel had this title prefixed: <note>original: Δανιὴλ κατὰ Θεοδοτίωνα</note> *Daniel according to Theodotion.* Theodotion is said to have published this translation, which occupied the fourth column in Origen's *Hexapla*, around the year 182, or as the *Alexandrian Chronicle* has it, in 186, the sixth year of Commodus. Certainly, it was before Irenaeus wrote his books *Against Heresies*, which were written while Eleutherus was Bishop of Rome. But since Irenaeus wrote in the year 176 or 177, as we noted above under Irenaeus, it is necessary that Theodotion not only prepared but also published his version before that time. The few fragments that remain are presented in the works of Nobilius, Drusius, and in the London edition of the Septuagint of the year 1653, and in Walton's Polyglot Bible, volume 6.

<margin>THE 2nd CENTURY, from 176 AD. * Book 4, chapters 21 & 28.</margin>
**MUSANUS**, a noteworthy writer of this age, flourished under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus around the year 176. Eusebius * numbers him among those whose books—containing the sincere doctrine of Apostolic tradition and the true faith—survived to his own day. He wrote a most elegant book addressed to certain brothers who had fallen away to the **Encratite heresy** <note>The Encratites were an ascetic Christian sect that practiced "self-control" by forbidding marriage and the eating of meat.</note>. N. E. <note>original: "N. E.", likely "Non Extant," meaning the work is now lost.</note>

<margin>176. * Book 4, ch. 25. † On Illustrious Men, ch. 32.</margin>
**MODESTUS** also gained fame at the same time, specifically in the year 176. He wrote a distinguished volume against **Marcion** <note>Marcion was a prominent 2nd-century heretic who taught that the God of the Old Testament was different from and inferior to the God of the New Testament.</note>; in this work, as Eusebius * testifies, he uncovered Marcion's errors and deceptions more remarkably than others, putting them on display for all to see. Jerome † warns that other small works are also circulated under his name, but these are rejected by the learned as **pseudepigrapha** <note>original: "pseudepigrapha", meaning works falsely attributed to an author.</note>. N. E.

<margin>177. * Cyprianic Dissertations XI, sections 37, 38.</margin>
**ATHENAGORAS**, a noble Athenian philosopher, was no less celebrated for his Christian theology than for his knowledge of Gentile learning. He flourished around the year 177. There is a deep silence regarding him in the works of Eusebius and Jerome; indeed, none of the ancient writers mention him except Methodius of Patara. In Methodius's excerpts from the book *On the Resurrection of the Dead* (which are preserved in Epiphanius, *Heresies* 64, and Photius, *Codex* 234), a passage is cited from Athenagoras that is found today word-for-word in his *Legation for the Christians*, page 27. He left behind two small works that still exist today: the *Apology*, or *Legation for the Christians*, presented to the Emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus—whom he calls "Conquerors of Armenia and Sarmatia," and what is greatest, "Philosophers." (This was offered in the year 178, as the illustrious Dodwell * contends). In this work, he petitions that Christians should enjoy the same legal rights at tribunals as other defendants; next, he vindicates them from the shameful crimes commonly attributed to them; finally, in the manner of the ancient Church, he prays from his heart for all prosperity and happiness for the Emperors. The other booklet is *On the Resurrection of the Dead*, in which he also argues the cause of Christian truth against unbelievers. Simon Grynæus was the first to bring these books to light in Greek and Latin among the *Orthodox Writers* (Basel, 1551). The booklet *On the Resurrection* was also published (Greek and Latin, Paris, 1541), and both appeared in Greek and Latin (Basel, 1555). Both were reprinted together in Greek and Latin (Paris, 1557), Greek (Leiden, 1558), Cologne (1567), and in Greek and Latin at the end of Justin’s works (Paris, 1615 and 1636). They appeared in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* (Paris, 1624), and separately (Oxford, 1682, in 12mo). The *Apology* was printed at Paris (1577, 8vo) and Leipzig (1684, 8vo) with various notes. As for the twelve books <term><note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν εἰς ἑαυτὸν</note> To Himself</term>—which some claim lay hidden in the Gesnerian Library—the title alone shows they do not belong to Athenagoras, but to the Emperor Marcus Antoninus <note>Better known today as the "Meditations" of Marcus Aurelius.</note>.

There also exists under the name of Athenagoras a work titled *Amorous Matters, or concerning True and Perfect Love: A historical work*, of the genre that people today call **Romances**. This book (if I am not mistaken) was brought from the East long ago, translated into French, and sent in 1569 to Lord de Lamané, the Secretary of the Cardinal of Armagnac, by Martin Fumée, Lord of Genillé. Finally, having been found among his papers, it was published in 1612 by Bernard de Sanforry. Where the Greek originals might now be hidden is completely unknown to me. I saw the French version in the well-stocked library of the illustrious Isaac Vossius, and because the book is in the hands of so few, I will not find it troublesome to include the full title here:

> *Of True and Perfect Love; written in Greek by Athenagoras, Athenian Philosopher: containing the honest loves of Theogone and Charide, and of Pherecides and Melangenie. At Paris, at the house of Daniel Guillemot, living on the Street of the Cordeliers behind the Jacobins, 1612.*

Whether this is a genuine work of our philosopher may be doubted with good reason. One might suspect it was written by him before he embraced the Christian faith. If that is the case, it will be easily apparent to anyone examining it that many additions have been made by a more recent hand. After these notes were written and already being sent to the press, I came across the illustrious Huet’s *Discourse on the Origin of Romances*, recently translated from French into Latin. In this, he discusses this work and its author at length, weighing everything with a marvelous sharpness of mind, turning it over and over, raising objections, and [answering] objections...

Nevertheless, he still denies the work to our Athenagoras; indeed, he goes so far as to suspect, led by the slightest conjecture, that Philander <note>Guillaume Philandrier (1505–1565), a French humanist and commentator on the Roman architect Vitruvius.</note>—the commentator on Vitruvius, a man most learned in every respect and very dear to Cardinal d’Armagnac—forged this work from his own brain. He suggests Philander did this to bolster his own opinions with some authority of antiquity and to more attractively commend the work to the Cardinal, who was intensely devoted to the art of architecture, since the book displays so many traces of architectural skill. Thus, he claims, Philander deceived the Prothonotary Lamanæus and the translator Fumée; however, this most learned man will hardly ever persuade those of "keen scent" <note>An idiom meaning "discerning" or "perceptive."</note> of this theory. Meanwhile, he extols the book itself with wonderful praise: "Whatever it may be," he says, "that work is certainly cleverly and skillfully devised, artistically composed, illuminated with excellent sentiments and distinguished moral precepts, and decorated with a great variety of most wisely arranged and delightful images. There one finds realistic events, episodes drawn from the subject matter, distinct styles of speaking, and a dignity religiously observed everywhere; there is nothing base here, nothing far-fetched, and nothing that reeks of the childishness of the Sophists."

<margin>177.</margin>
**HERMIAS**, a Christian philosopher, whose homeland, age, lineage, and manner of life I have not been able to track down with any amount of diligence. He is given a place here because he is usually joined—and perhaps not undeservedly—with the other Apologists of this century. He wrote the *Mockery of the External Philosophers* <note>original: "διασυρμὸν τῶν ἔξω φιλοσόφων" (diasyrmon tōn exō philosophōn)</note>, or a derision of the Gentile philosophers, in which he pits the conflicting opinions of the philosophers regarding God, the Soul, and other matters against each other, exposing them to ridicule with wit and elegance. It survives in Greek and Latin with Cydonius (Basel, 1552), at the end of Justin (Paris, 1615, 1636), and in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* (Paris, 1624), Volume 1. De la Bigne and other editors of the *Library of the Fathers* counted him among the writers of the fourth century, though they relied on no authority for this.

<margin>
177.
* Against Praxeas, chapter 1, page 501.
</margin>
**THE MARTYRS** of Lyons, around the year 176 AD, while the persecution was raging (of which more below), wrote various *Letters* while they were still in chains. These were written for the peace of the Church and against the **Montanists** <note>Montanism was a prophetic movement that claimed new revelations through "ecstasy"; the mainstream church grew to view it as a threat to apostolic authority.</note>, addressed partly to the brothers living in Asia and Phrygia, and partly to Eleutherus, the Bishop of the City of Rome. Eleutherus himself, according to the testimony of Tertullian \*, had been infected with the stain of the Montanist error. They wrote these letters as if they were performing an official embassy. The Martyrs gave these letters to **Irenaeus**, then still a Presbyter <note>A priest or elder.</note>, to be carried to Rome, and through them they commended him to Eleutherus. Eusebius provides a fragment of these letters in Book 5, chapter 4.

<margin>177.</margin>
**THE CHURCH** of Vienne and Lyons in Gaul: when the persecution against the Christians flared up—both in other provinces and especially in Gaul, and specifically in the City of Lyons—they sent a letter to the Churches of Asia and Phrygia. This letter contained nearly the entire history of this Lyonese persecution, in which Pothinus (the most reverend Bishop of the Church of Lyons, in the 90th year of his age), Attalus of Pergamon, Sanctus the Deacon of Vienne, Blandina a noblewoman, Alexander the physician, and many others, having suffered the most grievous torments, were crowned with the wreath of martyrdom. To this, they subjoined their religious and especially orthodox judgment concerning the prophet Montanus and his dogmas, which at that time were greatly disturbing the Phrygian churches. This survives for the most part intact in Eusebius, Book 5, chapters 1, 2, 3.

PANTÆNUS: whether he was Sicilian by birth, or Palestinian, and of Hebrew descent, as some gather from the words of Clement of Alexandria * and Eusebius †, remains entirely uncertain. Clement of Alexandria, whose teacher he was, calls him the *Sicilian Bee*, gathering the flowers of the Prophetic and Apostolic meadows—if indeed (as Eusebius maintains) his words are to be understood as referring to Pantænus. For this reason, Valesius <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a French classical scholar.</note> believes he was a native of Sicily; and perhaps it is not improbable that he was born in Alexandria to Sicilian parents. He was a Christian philosopher from the Stoic sect, and, according to the testimony of Photius *, he learned from teachers who had seen the Apostles. However, what follows deserves less credit in my view due to the long interval of time—namely, the claim that Pantænus himself was a hearer of some of the Apostles. Around the beginning of Emperor Commodus's reign, circa 181 AD, he presided over the Catechetical School of Alexandria, which had been "customary from the beginning" <note>original: ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἔθος</note> (as Eusebius says *) and had flourished since the time of Mark the Evangelist (according to Jerome †). He burned with such great zeal for the Word of God that he preached the Gospel to the nations of the East. He was sent by Demetrius, the Bishop of Alexandria, at the request of legates from that nation, as far as India <note>In the 2nd century, "India" often referred to Southern Arabia (Yemen) or Ethiopia rather than the modern Indian subcontinent.</note>. There, he found the Gospel of Saint Matthew written in Hebrew letters, which had been left there long ago by the Apostle Bartholomew among some who had been imbued with the knowledge of Christ; he brought it back with him upon his return to Alexandria. After his return, he once again directed the Academy of Alexandria and performed that duty until his death, which did not occur until the reign of Antoninus Caracalla, around 213 AD. Eusebius says * he was "a most renowned man of learning" <note>original: τῶν ἀπὸ παιδείας ἀνὴρ ἐπιδόξοτατος</note>, a man very famous for his doctrine, who set forth the treasury of Divine Dogmas partly by word of mouth and partly through writings. Indeed, he wrote many commentaries on the Holy Scriptures, from which a few small fragments, though not "word for word" <note>original: κατὰ λέξιν</note>, are cited in the Greek *Excerpts of Theodotus*. —N. ASTERIUS URBANUS: it is uncertain whether he was a Bishop or a Priest; he certainly calls Zoticus of Otrous his "fellow priest." He flourished around 188 AD. When he discovered the Church at Ancyra <note>Modern Ankara, Turkey.</note> in Galatia was being disturbed by the Cataphrygian heretics and their false prophets, he engaged in a public debate in the assembly of that local church for several days. He discussed the individual points of controversy proposed by them both extensively and eloquently; having put the heretics to flight, he greatly strengthened the Church of Ancyra. When the priests of Ancyra earnestly requested that he leave them a record of what had been said against the adversaries of the truth, he deferred it at that time. However, later, at the direction of Abercius Marcellus (scholars should consider whether this is the same as Abercius of Hierapolis, mentioned above), he compiled his arguments against the *Cataphrygians* into three books and dedicated them to Marcellus. Rufinus *, and others following him, attribute these books to Apollinaris of Hierapolis; Jerome || attributes them to Rhodon, and sometimes even to Apollonius. However, from a note by Eusebius attached to fragments of the work, it is clear that a certain Asterius Urbanus is the author of these books. Some "golden fragments" concerning Montanus and his sect are extant in Eusebius, Book 5, Chapters 16 and 17.

APELLES: called the *Old Man*, a hearer of Marcion and a fellow-student of Lucian, though he established a sect different from theirs after he was expelled by his teacher on account of committing an act of sexual immorality. He flourished in the year 188 AD. He maintained that Christ's body was neither a mere phantom nor of a coarse substance; rather, he claimed that Christ, descending from heaven, wove for himself an aerial body, which he returned to the air when he ascended. He taught that there is indeed one principle of all things, namely God, but that after He created the evil angels, He entrusted the creation of the world to one of them. He denied the resurrection of the flesh. He repudiated the Law and the Prophets. Finally, he held that the Christian faith should be subjected to whatever examination...

<margin>189 AD.</margin>
**RHODON**, a native of Asia, flourished around the year 189 AD. While he lived in Rome, he had Tatian (the disciple of Justin Martyr) as his teacher. He fought especially against the <term>Marcionites</term><note>Followers of Marcion, who believed the God of the Old Testament was a different, lesser deity than the Father of Jesus.</note> and held a dialogue with Apelles, in which he easily convicted and put to flight a man who was clearly simple and of mediocre talent. He wrote various books, and notably among the others, a work *Against the Heresy of Marcion, dedicated to Callistion*. In this work, he recounted that the Marcionite sect in his own time had split into various conflicting opinions; he identified the authors of that discord and carefully refuted the lies devised by each. Some excerpts from this work are preserved by Eusebius (Book 5, Chapter 13). He also wrote a *Commentary on the Six Days of Creation* <note>Known as a *Hexaemeron*, a common genre of early Christian writing reflecting on the Book of Genesis.</note> and promised that he would publish a separate work containing solutions to the *Questions proposed by Tatian regarding obscure and involved passages of Holy Scripture*. —Editor's Note.
