**EZEKIEL**, a poet who compiled *Jewish Histories* in tragic verse; whether he was Hebrew or Christian by religion is not clear. He flourished before 190 AD, being earlier than Clement of Alexandria *, who quotes certain passages from him. Nothing more certain can be established regarding his age. The conjecture of the most learned Le Moyne † seems not to stray far from the truth: that our Ezekiel composed his drama after the destruction of Jerusalem and the dispersion of the Jewish nation, or shortly after the times of <term>Bar Kokhba</term><note>Leader of the ill-fated Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 AD).</note>, to comfort the Jews who were overwhelmed by such great calamity. He sought to raise their spirits with the hope of a future liberation and a "new Moses" who would lead the captive Jews back to freedom—just as Moses had long ago liberated the Hebrews who were groaning under Pharaoh’s yoke. Ezekiel wove the history of this Mosaic liberation into a dramatic poem to which he gave the title <term>*The Exodus*</term><note>Original Greek: Ἐξαγωγή (Exagoge), meaning "The Leading Out."</note>, or *The Leading Out of the Hebrews*. A large fragment of this exists in Greek and Latin (Paris, 1609) and in the Bignean Appendix to the *Library of the Fathers* (Paris, 1624, p. 153).

<margin>190 AD.</margin>
**ANONYMOUS**, the author of the *Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs*, seems to have written at the end of this century around the year 190 AD; he certainly wrote before Origen, by whom he is cited in the *Homilies on Genesis and Joshua*. It is not entirely clear whether the author was a Jew or a Christian—perhaps a "Judaizing Christian," of whom there were many in that age. To be sure, the book is not free of absurdities, yet it is filled throughout with many ethical precepts of a high quality. In it, each of the twelve sons of Jacob, as they are about to die, is depicted speaking to their gathered descendants about the pursuit of a specific virtue or the avoidance of a vice; they bequeath these precepts to their grandsons as a final testament. It exists in Latin from a translation made by Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, in the year 1242. There is also a Greek manuscript in the possession of the distinguished Thomas Smith, Doctor of Divinity and Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford (and I believe others), who confirmed to me some time ago that he intended to publish a Greek-Latin edition.

He applied himself to combatting heretical depravity with no less diligence and fervor than the previous bishops of that city. He wrote a *Letter to Caricus and Ponticus*, men of the Church, *against the Heresy of Montanus*; a part of this exists in Eusebius (Book 5, Chapter 19), along with the signatures of certain Thracian bishops: Aurelius Cyrenius the Martyr, Aelius Publius Julius (Bishop of Debeltum, a colony of Thrace), and others, who sent letters to the churches of Asia and Phrygia condemning <term>Montanism</term><note>A movement emphasizing new prophecy and strict asceticism.</note>. <margin>192 AD.</margin> **APOLLONIUS**, whose lineage and fatherland the ancients have not recorded. He flourished around the year 192 AD. He composed a specific volume against the <term>Cataphrygians</term><note>Another name for the Montanists, a prophetic movement that began in Phrygia.</note>; in this work, he abundantly and most clearly refuted their most destructive errors. He did this both by examining their false prophecies word-for-word (which they were peddling as truth) and by discussing the lives and morals of those who had been the authors of that heresy. Some fragments of this are found in Eusebius, Book 5, Chapter 18. Tertullian, having by then become a Montanist himself, published six books <term>On Ecstasy</term><note>Original Greek: περὶ ἐκστάσεως (peri ekstaseos).</note> and produced a seventh specifically against Apollonius, in which he busied himself defending everything that Apollonius had criticized. 

Distinct from this man is that other Apollonius, famous for his noble birth and wealth, who was considered exceptional in the knowledge of the humanities and philosophy. Eusebius mentions him *, and he was crowned with martyrdom at Rome during the reign of Commodus. Jerome includes him among the ecclesiastical writers †, stating that he composed a distinguished volume in defense of his faith, which he read in the Senate. However, Eusebius does not say this, but only that Apollonius, when asked by the judge Perennis, delivered a most elegant speech before the Senate in defense of his faith. Whatever the case, Eusebius included that oration—whether it was read from a script by Apollonius or recorded from his speech by court reporters—along with the *Acts of his Martyrdom* in his *Collection of Ancient Martyrdoms*. Unfortunately, both works have long since perished. <margin>* Book 5, ch. 21. † On Illustrious Men, ch. 42.</margin>

---

<margin>192 AD.</margin> **VICTOR**, an African by birth, was moved to the governance of the Roman Church in the year 192 AD (according to Dodwell, 177 AD) after the death of Eleutherius. A man of a rather hot-tempered nature, consistent with his people, he was most hostile toward the Asian churches due to their different custom of celebrating Easter <note>The "Quartodeciman" controversy, where some churches celebrated Easter on the 14th of Nisan regardless of the day of the week.</note>. Consequently, regarding them as holding views contrary to the right faith, he not only attempted to cut them off from communion (as Henri Valois softens the matter), but indeed <term>openly through letters, he proclaimed all the brethren there to be utterly excommunicated</term><note>Original Greek: συλλήβδην γε διὰ γραμμάτων, ἀκοινωνήτους ἄρδην πάσας τὰς ἐκεῖσε ἀνακηρύττων ἀδελφὰς. This marks one of the earliest instances of a Bishop of Rome attempting to exercise universal authority.</note>; <margin>* Book 5, ch. 24. † On Illustrious Men, ch. 34.</margin> these are the very words of Eusebius *. Having sent these letters, he proscribed all the brethren who were there and pronounced them to be entirely alienated from the unity of the Church. For this reason, he was sharply rebuked by almost all the bishops of that age, especially by Saint Irenaeus. He died as a martyr, according to common calculation, in the year 201 AD. He wrote, as Jerome witnesses †, regarding the Easter Question, and certain other small works. —Editor's Note.

---

<margin>192 AD.</margin> **THEOPHILUS**, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a contemporary of Irenaeus and Victor. He flourished around the year 192 AD. He wrote, in the name of the Synod of Caesarea, <margin>* Book 5, ch. 23. † On Illustrious Men, ch. 43.</margin> a very useful letter regarding the Easter question, which was being most violently debated at that time. Both Eusebius * and Jerome † mention him. Found in Bede's *Book on the Equinox* and Bucherius's *Commentary on the Paschal Canon of Victorius* are the Acts of the Synod of Caesarea, held by Theophilus in the year 196 AD concerning the question of celebrating Easter, though they are listed under the name of a certain Philippus.

---

<margin>192 AD.</margin> **THEODOTUS**, a native of Byzantium, by trade a leather-tanner, but exceptionally learned in literature. He flourished in 172 AD. During a period of intense persecution, he denied Christ and, fleeing his homeland, went to Rome. There he was recognized by someone and accused of his foul defection from the faith of Christ. To excuse himself, he devised a vain dogma and began to boast that he had not denied God, but a man. When asked, "Which man?" he replied, "I denied Christ, the man." Taking this opportunity, he devised a new heresy, and for this, he was excommunicated by Pope Victor around the year 194 AD. Epiphanius and Theodoret do not have much more to say about his heresy; however, the main points of it...

(such as are found today in his *Excerpts*) the main points were roughly these: That **Christ** was created by the **Father** before the foundation of the world, so that the world might subsequently be created by him. That he was indeed the most perfect image of the Father, yet dissimilar to him in substance and inferior in dignity. That **God** the Father alone is immaterial, while the **Son** and all the **Angels** are material—composed, that is, of a certain subtle matter—such that the **Angels** are clothed in a body less refined than that of **God the Son**, and among them, some excel others in the subtlety of their bodies according to their rank of dignity. Furthermore, that both **Christ** and the **Angels** are circumscribed by certain figures and external forms, which are invisible to us but easily seen among themselves; and that among the **Angels**, a difference of sex is still found. He held that souls and **Demons** are also corporeal, for otherwise the punishments of hell could not be felt by them. He taught that **Christ** was incarnate from the first principle of things, for the <term>Spirit</term><note>Original Greek: πνεῦμα (pneuma)</note> was always present as a vehicle for the <term>Word</term><note>Original Greek: λόγῳ (logō)</note>, and when he descended to earth, a <term>soul</term><note>Original Greek: ψυχὴ (psychē)</note> and <term>body</term><note>Original Greek: σῶμα (sōma)</note> were joined to these, so that in this way he might be rendered visible to human eyes. Furthermore, that **Jesus** himself had need of redemption, which he obtained by the benefit of the dove sent down after his baptism. That **God** the Father suffered in the suffering **Christ**, insofar as the Son is a part of the Father emanating from him. Then, making a distinction between the <term>divine soul</term><note>Original Greek: θείαν ψυχὴν (theian psychēn)</note> and the <term>material soul</term><note>Original Greek: ὑλικὴν ψυχὴν (hylikēn psychēn)</note> (much like the distinction the **Platonists** make between <term>intellect</term><note>Original Greek: νοῦν (noun)</note> and <term>soul</term><note>Original Greek: ψυχὴν (psychēn)</note>), he teaches that his divinity and his spiritual or divine soul withdrew from **Christ** before the passion, as the essence with which he had been clothed when baptized in the **Jordan** departed. He claimed that the **stars**, or rather the **Angels** governing the stars, induce a certain fate upon all things and human actions by their natural power; and therefore **Christ** put on our flesh and suffered for this purpose alone: to liberate those believing in him from that fate and the necessity of their actions. At the end of the *Works of Clement of Alexandria*, there are two very large excerpts from the writings of **Theodotus**, the first of which seems to be taken from **Theodotus's** book titled *Oriental Doctrine* <note>Original Greek: Ἀνατολικὴ διδακαλία (Anatolikē didaskalia)</note>, and the other from his work *On the Law* <note>Original Greek: Περὶ τοῦ νόμου (Peri tou nomou)</note>. In these, however, are contained certain things that may be believed to have been received from elsewhere. Indeed, it might rightly be doubted whether both excerpts are by the same author, both because of the difference in style and the difference in dogmas. Whether these were compiled by **Clement** himself or by someone else is not entirely clear. See *Clement of Alexandria's Outlines* in the following article. N. E.

**T. FL. CLEMENT**, an **Alexandrian** by fatherland, or as others say, an **Athenian**; unless we should rather say he was an **Athenian** by origin and an **Alexandrian** by home. He flourished from the year 192 AD. He himself seems to indicate his age, in a broader sense, where speaking of himself \*, he testifies that he was very close to the first times of the **Apostles**. He was instructed to the highest degree in every kind of more refined literature. He had several teachers in Theological precepts, <term>blessed men, and truly worthy of esteem</term><note>Original Greek: ἄνδρας μακαρίους, καὶ τῷ ὄντι ἀξιολόγους (andras makarious, kai tō onti axiologous)</note>, from whom he was privileged to hear that living and effective doctrine of the **Apostles**. One was an **Ionian** in **Greece** (whom **Baronius** † thinks was **Dionysius of Corinth** or **Caius**), another in **Magna Graecia** <note>The coastal areas of Southern Italy</note> (whom the same author thinks was **Theophilus, Patriarch of Antioch**), this one originally from **Coelesyria**, that one from **Egypt**. In the **East**, he attached himself to a certain **Assyrian** (whom some wish to be **Bardesanes**, others **Tatian**), and in **Palestine** to a **Hebrew** (who appears to **Baronius** to be **Theophilus, Bishop of Caesarea**, but more correctly **Theodotus**). His very last teacher was **Pantaenus**, under whose discipline he applied himself to the study of the Divine Scriptures; he took his place in directing the **Catechetical School** while **Pantaenus** was occupied on a journey to **India** around the year 191, and succeeded him in that office upon his death. A Presbyter of the **Church of Alexandria**, not a Prelate (as **Jac. Gaddius** claims), he was forced to change his soil when the **Severian** persecution was raging and withdrew to the **East**, spending time in **Jerusalem**; where, as **Bishop Alexander** || testifies, he both confirmed and greatly increased the **Church of Christ**. From there he set out for **Antioch**; finally having returned to **Alexandria**, he died perhaps around the end of the reign of **Antoninus Caracalla**, or at least did not long survive his times. For **Alexander of Jerusalem** speaks of him as if he had already departed this life, in a *Letter* \* to **Origen**. ## EXTANT WORKS.

*Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>original: *Protrepticon ad Gentes*</note>, in which he refutes the pagans and urges them to embrace Christian Philosophy.

*The Instructor* <note>original: *Pædagogus*</note>, comprised of three books, in which he trains the newly converted pagan in the true Christian life and morals.

*Hymn in Praise of Our Lord Jesus Christ.* <note>original: *Hymnus in laudem D. N. J. C.*</note>

<margin>
* Book 6, chapter 13.
|| *Stromata* book 4, page 476.
* Code 111.
† Code 110.
† *Stromata* book 7, at the end. See also book 1, page 293.
</margin>
The *Miscellanies* <note>original: *Stromateon*</note>, eight books written after the death of the Emperor Commodus. They are "Full of the greatest useful knowledge," says Eusebius <note>original Greek: Πλείστης χρησιμαθείας ἔμπλεοι</note>, being packed with a wide variety of the most useful learning. In these books, he instructs adults—"those who have their senses trained" <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα ἔχοντας</note>—toward a fuller and more perfect knowledge of sacred things. He strews throughout them many "little flowers," not only from the sacred scriptures but also from the books of the pagans, should they happen to have said anything appropriately. He explains the various opinions of both the Greeks and the Barbarians <note>meaning non-Greeks</note>, refutes the false dogmas of the leaders of heresies, and recounts many histories. In this way, he provides us with "the most abundant material for a wide-ranging education" <note>original Greek: ὑπόθεσιν πολυμαθῶς παιδείας</note> through a mixture of learning. For this reason, he himself teaches us that these commentaries are called *Stromateis* <note>Greek for "tapestries" or "patchworks"</note>, or "Variegated Discourses." Photius <note>a 9th-century scholar and Patriarch</note> observed that in these books, some things are "not healthily stated." <note>original Greek: οὐχ ὑγιῶς</note> David Blondel, in his work *On the Sibyls* (book 1, chapter 6), notes several of his blemishes, whether historical, chronological, or even theological, as if "in passing." Regarding Clement's style, especially in the *Exhortation* and *The Instructor*, Photius has this to say: "The style is flowery, rising to a well-proportioned and fitting weightiness combined with sweetness, to which the extensive knowledge prominent in them is perfectly suited." <note>original Greek: Ἡ φράσις ἀνθηρὰ, καὶ εἰς ὄγκον τὸν ἡρμοσμένον σύμμετρον μετὰ τοῦ ἡδέος, καὶ ἡ πολυμάθεια ἐμπρέπουσα.</note> In the *Miscellanies*, however, Clement himself confesses that he did not strive for order, nor for ornament or elegance of speech, being content to explain matters so they might be understood. The eighth book treats certain unrelated matters and has nothing in common with the rest, being concerned primarily with the principles of Logic and Philosophy.

*Discourse* on the theme "Who is the Rich Man that is Saved?" <note>original Greek: περὶ τοῦ, τίς ὁ σωζόμενος πλούσιος</note>, from which Eusebius preserves a reasonably long fragment in book 3, chapter 23. In some manuscripts surviving in the time of Photius, this work made up the eighth book of the *Miscellanies*. François Combefis recently presented it to us in its entirety in the *Supplement to the Library of the Greek and Latin Fathers* (Paris, 1672), and a newer edition appeared in Oxford in 1683. It had actually been published before that by Michael Ghisler, but under the name of Origen, in his commentary on Jeremiah.

## LOST WORKS.

<margin>
* Code 109.
† Code 111.
</margin>
The *Outlines* <note>original: *Hypotyposeon*</note>, or *Institutions*, in eight books, in which he undertook a brief explanation of both Testaments, the Old and the New. In these, he set forth whatever he had drawn from his master Pantaenus, as it had been handed down to him by his predecessors. However, Photius once noted in these books many "impious and mythical stories" <note>original Greek: ἀσεβεῖς καὶ μυθώδεις λόγους</note>—entirely impious and legendary discourses—indeed, "monstrosities of blasphemies" <note>original Greek: βλασφήμους τερατολογίας</note>. Photius suspects that these were added by someone else assuming Clement's persona. Furthermore, he says later that many things are contained in these books which Clement attacks in his other writings. There is little doubt that the Arians foully corrupted his books, as they did those of many others; on this, see Rufinus's *Apology for Origen* among the works of Jerome, Volume 4. The fragments of these books that survive can be seen in Eusebius.

*Theodotian Fragments* (mentioned under the previous heading). If indeed these were excerpted by our Clement, they seem to have been inserted into these [lost] books by him and thus transmitted to us.

According to Cassiodorus, he also wrote *Commentaries on the Canonical Epistles*, namely, the first of St. Peter, the first and second of St. John, and St. James, in which he spoke many useful things, but some things incautiously. Of these, the last three are the best—though the very last is less correct and accurate than the others—containing the notes of Sylburgius and Daniel Heinsius, and various collections from others.

## QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS,
Born in Carthage, as it seems, a little before the middle of this century, he had a Proconsular Centurion for a father. He cultivated every branch of the humanities and especially the knowledge of Roman Law. However, he was devoted to a most profligate lifestyle, as he himself confesses, until he embraced the Christian religion around the year 185. He took a wife, though whether while still a pagan or as a Christian is not yet clear; except that a little...

# The Gnostic Century.

<margin>The 2nd Century after Christ.</margin>
...certain things seem to suggest this happened shortly before he took up the rank of the Presbyterate <note>The office of a priest or elder in the early Church.</note>. Having been made a Presbyter of the Church of Carthage around the year 192, he defended the cause of the Christian faith and the doctrine and discipline of the Church with great zeal. There are those who claim that once he was elevated to the rank of Presbyter, he renounced the duties of marriage by a solemn vow, with his wife's consent, and lived with her thereafter as if celibate; however, this cannot be proven with sufficiently strong arguments. Tertullian certainly implies the opposite quite clearly, having exhorted his wife in almost the whole of Book I <note>His treatise *Ad Uxorem* or "To His Wife."</note> that she should renounce marriage after his passing with as much continence as possible; and in the same book, chapter 7, he addressed her thus: *“Why should we not love the capacity for continence as much as we can? As soon as the opportunity arises, let us drink it in, so that what we are not strong enough to do in marriage, we may pursue in widowhood. We must embrace the occasion which has taken away what necessity used to command.”*

<margin>* Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 53.</margin>
<margin>* Cave, *Lives of the Primitive Fathers*, Vol. I, p. 208.</margin>
Around middle age, according to the testimony of Jerome <note>original: Hieronymus</note> (understanding "age" not so much as his natural life, but his Christian life—that is, around the end of this century, in the year 199, as can be reasonably guessed), he fell away into the teaching of Montanus <note>Montanism was a prophetic movement in the early church that emphasized new revelations and strict asceticism.</note>; provoked by the envy and insults of the clergy of the Roman Church. Concerning this, while respecting the judgments of others, let me briefly set forth my own conjecture here, which I once proposed in the *Life of Tertullian* written in 1675, No. 9. Specifically, that the Roman clergy, offended by his harsh nature and the excessive sternness of Tertullian’s morals, accused him of being a follower and defender of the Montanists, and cut him off from communion when he refused to condemn the Montanist decrees. Moved by this—being a man of great and fiery spirit, and not one to suffer insults well—and captivated by the still impressive <note>original: *speciosis*, meaning "fair" or "outwardly beautiful."</note> fasts and vigils of the Montanists and the rest of their more rigid discipline of life, he joined their assembly. For I would not believe that Tertullian—a man of great judgment, talent, gravity, and sincere integrity—ever drank the "dregs" of Montanism, but only that he recognized Montanus as a kind of new Prophet and Paraclete <note>The "Comforter" or "Helper"; Montanus claimed to be a mouthpiece for the Holy Spirit.</note>, equipped with the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit and sent into the world by God to more forcefully correct the lapsed morals of Christians, and to teach more fully and clearly the Gospel Doctrine once delivered by Christ the Lord, which was still partially hidden under certain veils. Having become a Montanist, he manfully defended this sect, publishing many books that were equally learned and eloquent, in which he vindicated the rigor of their discipline from contempt, as well as others in which he attacked the Catholic Church under the name of *Psychics* <note>original: *Psychicorum*. A derogatory term used by Montanists for "ordinary" Christians who they believed lacked the fullness of the Spirit.</note>. He died at a very advanced age, and if it is permitted to rely on conjectures in such an uncertain matter, around the year 220.

<margin>|| Cited location and elsewhere. * Epistle to Magnus, Vol. 2, p. 328. † *Commonitory*, chapter 24, p. 345.</margin>
He was a man, as Jerome truly said of him, *“of a sharp and vehement wit”*: and elsewhere, *“What is more learned than Tertullian? What is more acute?”* Setting others aside, I will bring forward one witness, Vincent of Lérins: *“Just as Origen is to be judged easily the first of all our people among the Greeks, so is he [Tertullian] among the Latins. For what man is more learned than this one? Who is more practiced in divine and human affairs? Indeed, he grasped all philosophy, all the sects of philosophers, the authors and defenders of those sects, all their disciplines, and the entire variety of history and studies with a certain marvelous capacity of mind. Truly, did he not excel with a genius so grave and vehement that he proposed almost nothing for himself to conquer which he did not either break into with sharpness or crush with weight? Furthermore, who could sufficiently praise his oration, which is packed with such a strange necessity of reasoning that it compels those to agree whom it could not persuade; whose words are almost as many as his sentences; whose thoughts are as many as his victories?”* Then, in what follows, Vincent mourns his fall as one who was not sufficiently tenacious of Catholic dogma and the ancient faith.

<margin>* *Divine Institutes*, book 5, chapter 1.</margin>
Regarding his style, Lactantius says this: *“Septimius [Tertullian] was also less polished and very obscure.”* Yet (if I may say so with respect to such a great man), Tertullian’s style has a certain majesty proper to itself, and a grand eloquence seasoned with much wit and sharpness, which simultaneously exercises the reader's intellect and sweetly delights the mind. Scholars raise no small dispute concerning the time and order in which Tertullian composed his writings.

<margin>* Pierre Allix, *Dissertation on the Life and Writings of Tertullian*.</margin>
Among these, since the most learned Dr. Allix <note>A prominent 17th-century French Protestant scholar.</note> seems to have come closest to the truth of the matter, I shall chiefly follow the order designated by him in listing Tertullian's Works; however, in some points, I cannot help but disagree with that famous man.

### WRITTEN AFTER HIS FALL.

<margin>
Spartianus in the *Life of Severus*, chapter 17, page 352.

† Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, chapter 1.
</margin>
**T**he *Apology against the Gentiles*, presented if not to the Roman Senate, then at least to the Governors of the Provinces (which is more likely): written at Carthage, as some believe, in the year 196, and others in 199. Others reject this, among them the distinguished Master Allix <note>Pierre Allix, a 17th-century scholar.</note> who places it in the year 217, when Scapula, the Proconsul of Africa, afflicted the Christians terribly; at which time Tertullian addressed a petition to Scapula. It is not our place to settle such great disputes. To me, indeed, it seems more likely to have been written during the sixth persecution, around the year 202, when the Emperor Severus <note>Septimius Severus.</note> forbade anyone to become a Christian under heavy penalty. And indeed, it is clear from the jurist Ulpian that Severus ordered by a rescript <note>A formal imperial legal response.</note> that those suspected of joining an illegal association (among which number no one is unaware that the Christian assembly was included) should be accused before the Prefect of the City. Indeed, this Severan persecution burned so hot that, as Eusebius reports, through all the churches everywhere, illustrious martyrdoms were completed by athletes striving for piety, who are said to have endured torments and deaths with an unconquered spirit. Furthermore, the minds of many were so vehemently disturbed that they even thought that famous, much-discussed arrival of the Antichrist was imminent. Therefore, we can assign the birth-year of this writing to no other era with a greater appearance of truth.

*To the Heathen*, in two books, of the same argument, fortified by the same reasons, and even written for the most part in the same words: so much so that it can be believed both works were composed and published at the same time, with the plan that in the *Apology* he might teach the Judges those things they needed to know, while in the books written *To the Heathen* he might inform the common people about the same matters. Concerning these (which have reached us miserably mutilated), as well as the *Apology*, Jerome <note>original: Hieronymus</note> briefly and no less truly wrote: *“They contain all the learning of the age.”*

## LOST WORKS.

On Paradise.

On the Hope of the Faithful.

*Seven Books on Ecstasy.* Of these, the last campaigned against Apollonius, and perhaps also against Pope Soter; Primasius—or another writing under the name of *Praedestinatus* published by Sirmond (Heresy 26)—records that Soter wrote a book against the Montanists and was attacked by Tertullian (who had by then become a Montanist) just as Apollonius was, as we noted above regarding Soter.

*Against the Followers of Apelles.*

*On the Vestments of Aaron.*

*On the Census of the Soul*, which, however, the illustrious Allix suspects is none other than the one which survives today under the title *On the Soul*.

Furthermore, Tertullian testifies in *On Baptism* (chapter 15) and *On Veiling Virgins* (at the beginning) that he previously treated both subjects in Greek. Indeed, in the book *On the Crown* (chapter 6), he writes that he discussed *On Spectacles* in the Greek style. Somewhere he also testifies that he published the book *On the Soldier’s Crown* in Greek.

## SPURIOUS WORKS.

The *Catalog of Heretics*, attached as an appendix to the book *On the Prescription of Heretics*: which, besides the difference in style and many other arguments, the authority of almost all manuscript codices denies to Tertullian. The illustrious Allix believes it was composed shortly after the age of Jerome.

<margin>See Gennadius, *On Writers*, ch. 67, and the Appendix to Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 6.</margin>
Various poems, namely: *Genesis, Sodom, Five Books against Marcion, On the Judgment of God, Poem to a Senator, and On Jonah and Nineveh*: which Pamelius ascribes to Tertullian while still a young man, though supported by no testimony of the ancients and no reason. Of these, the most learned Allix attributes the first two to Salvian, a Priest of Marseille, and the *Poem on the Judgment of God* to Verecundus, an African Bishop (who flourished around the middle of the sixth century), although he does not deny that in the latter case, some scraps were woven in by a man of the tenth century. The same scholar considers the *Books against Marcion* to have been born after the age of Jerome; while the *Poem to a Senator* (which is read among the Works of Cyprian, volume 3) he judges to have been written before the time of Constantine. Finally, he conjectures that the poem *On Jonah and Nineveh* (which is found inscribed to Tertullian in the Library of the Fathers) is the work of some ancient author, perhaps the same one who wrote *Sodom*.

# The Gnostic Century

His *Works* were published in *Basel* in 1521, 1525, 1528, 1539, 1550, and 1562; in *Antwerp* in 1579 and 1584; in *Paris* in 1566 (2 volumes in octavo), 1580, 1583, 1608, and 1616; in *Heidelberg* in 1596 and 1601; in *Cologne* in 1617; in *Geneva* in 1597; and in *Franeker* in 1597. In all these editions, the two books *To the Nations* <note>original: "Ad Nationes"; an apology defending Christianity against pagan charges</note> were missing; they were first published by Jacques Godefroy in *Geneva*, 1624, in quarto. Subsequently, more complete editions of Tertullian’s works appeared in *Paris* in 1624, 1630, 1634, 1641, 1644, 1646, 1650, 1658, and 1662, and in *Strasbourg* in 1657. Among these, the editions by Rigaltius are outstanding, especially that of Paris published in 1663 by Philippe Le Prieur. This edition included the complete notes of Rigaltius, selected notes from Pamelius, La Cerda, and others, and added Le Prieur's own notes at the bottom of each page where necessary.

### BACCHYLUS
Bishop of the Corinthians, who was called "Archbishop" by the author of the *Synodicon* published by Pappus. He flourished around the year 196 AD and is numbered by Eusebius * among those who left behind the doctrine of the right faith preserved in their writings. ### POLYCRATES
The leader of the Church of Ephesus, he was considered most celebrated among the bishops of this time for his learning, gravity, and the dignity of his see. He had seven bishops among his relatives, to whom he succeeded as the eighth, and he flourished around the year 196 AD. He convened a synod of a great number of Asian bishops on the occasion of the *Paschal Controversy* <note>A major dispute in the early church regarding the correct date to celebrate Easter</note>. In their name, being already sixty-five years old, he wrote a most brilliant *Epistle to Victor* and *to the Church of the City of Rome*. In this letter, he defended his opinion regarding the custom of Easter as it had been steadfastly handed down to him by his ancestors and the authority of the ancients, and he boldly resisted Victor <note>Pope Victor I</note>, who was acting fiercely against the Asians. Eusebius (Book 5, ch. 24) presents a truly golden fragment of this remarkable letter. He provides another fragment concerning the deaths of Saint *John* and Saint *Philip* in Book 3, ch. 31. This work no longer survives.

It should also be noted in passing that at nearly the same time and on the same subject, many other *Epistles* were written; namely, by the bishops of Pontus, Gaul, the province of Osrhoene, and many others. All of these, putting forward the same faith and the same doctrine as Victor of Rome, issued a single opinion. Concerning these, see Eusebius, Book 5, ch. 23. This work no longer survives.

There is circulated under the name of Polycrates of Ephesus a work titled *The Passion of Saint Timothy*, first published by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples; it is held in Greek and Latin by Bollandus under the date of January 24th. However, it is established by more than one argument that this is a forged work.

### ATHENOGENES
A most celebrated martyr, who seems to have been a <term>contemporary</term> <note>Greek: σύγχρονος (synchronos)</note> of Clement of Alexandria and to have met his martyrdom by fire. He wrote a *Morning Hymn*, which begins, <term>"Glory to God in the highest,"</term> <note>Greek: Δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις Θεῷ (Doxa en hypsistois Theo); the "Great Doxology"</note> and an *Evening Hymn*, beginning, <term>"O gladsome light of holy glory,"</term> <note>Greek: φῶς ἱλαρὸν ἁγίας δόξης (Phos hilaron hagias doxes); one of the oldest known Christian hymns</note> which Saint Basil * records that he left to his disciples as a parting gift while hastening toward martyrdom. These are wrongly ascribed by some to Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem. They can be found in Ussher's *Treatise on the Creeds* near the end, and in the *Miscellanea* of the distinguished Thomas Smith (with notes), London, 1686, octavo.

### MAXIMUS
<term>"A man equally distinguished in Christ,"</term> <note>Greek: ἐπ᾽ ἴσης ἀνὴρ ἐν Χριστῷ διαπρέπας (ep’ isēs anēr en Christō diaprepas)</note> a man of distinction among the Christians who flourished in the year 196 AD. He wrote a volume on that question most common among the philosophers, *Whence comes Evil?*, or <term>"Concerning Matter,"</term> <note>Greek: περὶ τῆς ὕλης (peri tēs hylēs)</note> or, concerning the fact that *Matter was created*, and *is not the cause of evils*. Eusebius presents a very large fragment from it in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 7, ch. 22, which is also found word-for-word in Origen's *Dialogue against the Marcionites*. This has been a harvest of disagreement for learned men. The distinguished Wetstein, in his preface to Origen's *Dialogue*, contends that Origen inserted it into his own dialogue, having taken it from Maximus’s book *On Matter*.

### Pagan Authors who attacked the Christians in this Century.

C. CORNELIUS TACITUS, a Roman by birth and Procurator of Gallia Belgica under Vespasian, held the consulship under Nerva in the year of Christ 97. Writing under Trajan after the year 100, he condemns the Christian religion as a "deadly superstition," and the Christians themselves as "hated for their shameful vices" and "convicted of hatred for the human race." *Annals*, Book 15.

<margin>* Book 10, letter 97.</margin>
C. PLINIUS SECUNDUS <note>Pliny the Younger</note>, born in Como, nephew of Pliny the Elder and student of Quintilian, was a contemporary of Tacitus. He served as Quaestor, Praetor, Prefect of the Treasury, and finally Consul in the year of Christ 100; he appears to have died near the beginning of Hadrian's reign. In a *letter* to Trajan, he brands Christianity as a "depraved and immoderate superstition," and asserts that their constancy in defending their religion is a "stubbornness and inflexible obstinacy" that should be punished by the law. Nonetheless, he otherwise provides a noble enough testimony regarding their innocent customs and sacred worship.

C. SUETONIUS TRANQUILLUS, a Roman Grammarian, flourished under Trajan around the year of Christ 112 and was made Master of Letters under Hadrian. He calls the Christians a "race of men of a new and mischievous superstition," and says they were subjected to punishments under that name in his *Life of Nero*, Chapter 16. For his remarks on the Jews "rioting at the instigation of Chrestus," see his *Life of Claudius* <note>The source text says *Vit. Tiber.*, but this famous quote is usually found in the *Life of Claudius*</note>, Chapter 25.

<margin>† Chronicles, for the year 147.</margin>
ARRIANUS, from the house of Nicomedia and a student of Epictetus, was a philosopher, orator, and great historian, called the "New Xenophon." He also held the consulship in the Republic. He is mentioned by Eusebius † for the year of Christ 147. He disparages Christians using the hateful name "Galileans," and attributes their readiness to face dangers to "insanity and habit" in his *Discourses of Epictetus*, Book 4, Chapter 7. See also what he says regarding the baptism of the Jews (or as others believe, the Christians) in Book 2, Chapter 9.

CELSUS, a philosopher of the Epicurean sect (though also well-disposed toward the school of Plato), flourished during the later years of Hadrian and thereafter. He attacked the faith and customs of the Christians in a specific book, which he titled <term>The True Word</term> <note>original Greek: *alēthē logon*</note>.

<header>The Gnostic Century</header>

<margin>2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ</margin>...he flourished. Fragments of his work exist scattered here and there in the eight books written by Origen *Against Celsus*, in which Origen powerfully refuted Celsus’s futile slanders and arguments.

MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS, surnamed "the Philosopher," son of the Praetor Annius Verus and son-in-law of Antoninus Pius, was elevated to the Roman Empire in the year of Christ 161. He died in the year 180. In Book 11 of his *Meditations* <note>original Latin: *de rebus suis*, literally "on his own affairs"</note>, section 3, he asserts that the fortitude of Christians in undergoing martyrdom was a "mere display" <note>original Greek: *psilēn parataxin*; often interpreted as a theatrical or military-style posturing</note>, a matter of mere obstinacy of mind; he further claims it did not "arise from a specific judgment" <note>original Greek: *apo idikēs kriseōs*; meaning a reasoned or rational decision</note>.

LUCIAN, a native of Samosata and an Epicurean by profession, flourished 
<margin>† Preface to the book *On the Lives of the Philosophers*</margin>around the year of Christ 176. He was "a man who took laughter seriously" (as Eunapius himself admits † <note>original Greek: *anēr spoudaios eis to gelasai*</note>). With the sharp wit of his talent, he mocked the Christians, their rituals, and their doctrines on more than one occasion, especially in these dialogues: *The False Prophet* <note>original Latin: *Pseudomantis*</note>, *On the Death of Peregrinus*, and *The Patriot* <note>original Latin: *Philopatris*</note> (if indeed it is his, or at least the work of a contemporary writer). He also seems to touch upon them once indirectly in his work *The Ass* <note>original Latin: *Asinus*</note>.

# THE NOVATIAN CENTURY

## Overview of the Century

<margin>
3rd CENTURY from the Year 200
</margin>
The Christian faith is propagated far and wide. The heresies of Sabellius arise, who confuses the three persons <note>Latin: *hypostases*</note> in the Trinity; and of Nepos, who, following Papias and his adherents, argued for a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth <note>the "millennium"</note>; and of Paul of Samosata, who affirmed that Christ was a "mere man" <note>original Greek: *psilon anthropon*</note>, for which he was condemned by the Synod of Antioch in the year 265, and by another held in the same place in the year 270. <margin>†</margin> Finally, the heresy of Mani, or the Manichaeans, emerged around the year 277. Because of excessive leniency toward the "lapsed" <note>those who renounced their faith under persecution</note>, Novatian fostered a schism that would not be extinguished for more than a century. Pope Stephen, Cyprian, Firmilian, and others argued strenuously over the baptism of heretics. Several Synods were held in Africa regarding this cause, which Cyprian mentions throughout his writings, though the *Cyprianic Annals* of the illustrious Pearson should be consulted above others.

In the year 202, shortly after the 8th day before the Ides of April, Septimius Severus—an Emperor truly "Persistent" <note>Latin: *Pertinax*</note> and truly "Severe" <note>Latin: *Severus*</note> as his names suggest, according to the common talk of the time—instigated the fifth (others say the sixth) persecution. <margin>* Eusebius, Book 6, Ch. 1</margin> "Throughout all the churches in every place, the athletes of piety achieved illustrious martyrdoms," says Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, Chapter 1 <note>original Greek: *Lampros men tōn eusebeias athlētōn...*</note>. Indeed, throughout all the churches in every place, famous martyrdoms were completed by these athletes contending for their devotion. This persecution was ennobled by the blood of Leonides (the father of Origen), Serenus, Heraclides, Heron, and Herais (disciples of Origen); Marcella and her daughter Potamiaena; Felicitas and Perpetua; and many others whose names are written in the Book of Life. The origin of this most grave and long-lasting persecution (for it lasted until the year 204) seems to have been the rebellion of the Jews, whom Severus had recently defeated in war. This can be gathered from Aelius Spartianus in his *Life of Severus*, chapter 16, who records that the Senate decreed a Jewish triumph for Severus because of his successful actions in Syria. He adds shortly after that the Emperor, while traveling through Palestine, established many laws and forbade anyone from becoming a Jew or a Christian under heavy penalty.

In the year 235, the sixth persecution broke out under Maximinus the Thracian, who vented his rage especially against Bishops and Priests. "By nature his character was as barbaric as his race," says Herodian in Book 7 <note>original Greek: *physei de ēn to ēthos hōsper kai to genos barbaros*</note>; there was no more cruel animal on earth, as Julius Capitolinus himself admits in his *Life of Maximinus*, chapter 9. At the end of the year 249, the seventh persecution occurred under Decius, having begun the previous year in Alexandria; it was indeed a heavy and truly brutal persecution, which did not subside until its third year.

In the year 257, the eighth persecution occurred under Valerian, who, "seized by a similar madness," <margin>† Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, Ch. 5</margin> (as Lactantius says in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 5) "stretched out impious hands against God, and shed much righteous blood, though in a short time." Dionysius of Alexandria and Cyprian write at length about these martyrs; Cyprian himself won the crown of martyrdom under this Valerian. Finally, the ninth persecution occurred under Aurelian in the year 275, which, as it consisted only of issued edicts, hardly deserves the name of a persecution. Indeed, (as Lactantius witnesses in the same work, chapter 6) his bloody writings had not yet reached the more distant provinces when he himself lay bloodied on the ground at Coenofrurium, a place in Thrace, killed by his own friends due to a false suspicion. Thus, he was not even allowed to complete what he had intended, as Lactantius observes in the preceding words. <margin>* Eusebius, Book 7, Ch. 30</margin> Eusebius records the same, adding this truly pious note to his narrative in Book 7, chapter 30: "Showing most clearly to all that it is never permitted for the princes of this world to act against the churches of Christ, unless the protecting right hand of God—by a secret and heavenly judgment for our chastisement and correction—permits it to happen at the times that seem fit to Him" <note>original Greek: *Lamprōs te tois pasi synoran...*</note>.

# THE GNOSTIC CENTURY

<margin>
2nd CENTURY from the Year of Christ
</margin>
[...he defended]. Fragments of this work are extant here and there in the eight books of Origen's *Against Celsus*, in which Origen powerfully refuted the futile slanders and arguments of Celsus <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and the first comprehensive intellectual critic of Christianity</note>.

**MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS**, surnamed the Philosopher, son of Annius Verus the Praetor and son-in-law of Antoninus Pius, was raised to the Roman Empire in the year of Christ 161. He died in the year 180. In Book 11 of his work *On His Own Affairs* <note>the famous *Meditations*</note>, section 3, he asserts that the fortitude of Christians in undergoing martyrdom was "sheer opposition" <note>original Greek: *psilēn parataxin*</note>, a mere obstinacy of the mind; he further asserts that it does not proceed "from a reasoned judgment" <note>original Greek: *apo tēs idikēs kriseōs*; original Latin: *à judicio particulari*</note>.

<margin>† Preface to the book *On the Lives of the Philosophers*</margin>
**LUCIAN**, a native of Samosata and an Epicurean by profession, flourished around the year of Christ 176. He was "a man earnest about being laughed at" (as Eunapius <note>a Greek sophist and historian</note> himself admits †), who, with the wit of his own talent, more than once mocked the Christians and their rituals and dogmas, especially in these dialogues: *The False Prophet*, *On the Death of Peregrinus*, and *Philopatris* (if it is his, or at least by a contemporary writer). He also seems to attack them indirectly once in his work *The Ass*.

# THE CENTURY OF NOVATIAN

## Overview of the Century

<margin>
3rd CENTURY from the Year 200
†
*
†
</margin>
The Christian faith is propagated far and wide. The heresies of Sabellius arise, who confuses the three persons <note>original: *hypostases*</note> in the Trinity; and of *Nepos*, who, following Papias and his followers, established the millennium <note>the belief in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ</note>; and of *Paul of Samosata*, who affirmed that Christ was a "mere man" <note>original Greek: *psilon anthrōpon*</note>, and was condemned for this by the Synod of Antioch in the year 265 and another held there in 270. Finally, there was *Mani* or the Manichaean around the year 277. On account of excessive leniency toward the "lapsed" <note>Christians who renounced their faith during persecution</note>, Novatian fosters a schism that would not be extinguished for more than a century. Pope Stephen, Cyprian, Firmilian, and others argue strenuously regarding the baptism of heretics. Many Synods were held in Africa on this cause; Cyprian writes of them in various places, but one should consult the *Annals of Cyprian* by the distinguished Pearson above all others. 

In the year 202, shortly after the 8th of April, the fifth persecution (according to some, the sixth) was stirred up by Septimius Severus, an Emperor truly a man of his own name—truly *Persistent* <note>original: *Pertinax*</note> and truly *Severe*, as was then commonly said. "Indeed, illustrious martyrdoms of the athletes for piety were completed in all the churches and in every place," says Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, Chapter 1 <note>original Greek: *lampros men tōn hyper eusebeias athlētōn en pasais tais ekklēsiais k’at’ panta topon apeteleito martyria*</note>. Through all the Churches in every place, illustrious martyrdoms were achieved by those athletes striving for piety. This persecution was ennobled by the blood of Leonides (the father of Origen), Serenus, Heraclides, Heron, Heraïs (disciples of Origen), Marcella and her daughter Potamiana, Felicitas and Perpetua, and many others whose names are written in the book of life. 

The cause of this most heavy and long-lasting persecution (for it lasted until the year 204) seems to have been the rebellion of the Jews, whom Severus had recently crushed in war. This can be gathered from Aelius Spartianus in his *Life of Severus*, Chapter 16, who records that the Senate decreed a Jewish triumph for Severus due to his successful actions in Syria. He soon adds that the Emperor, while traveling through Palestine, established many laws and forbade anyone from becoming a Jew or a Christian under heavy penalty. 

In the year 235, the sixth persecution arose under Maximinus the Thracian, who was especially brutal toward Bishops and Priests. "By nature his character, just as his race, was barbaric," says Herodian <note>original Greek: *physei de ēn to ēthos, hōsper ki to genos, barbaros*</note>; there was no more cruel animal on earth, as Julius Capitolinus himself admits in his *Life of Maximinus*. 

At the end of the year 249, the seventh Persecution occurred under Decius, having also arisen in Alexandria the previous year; it was indeed heavy and truly savage, and did not subside until the third year. In the year 257, the eighth persecution began under Valerian, who, seized by a similar madness (says Lactantius in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, Chapter 5), "stretched out his impious hands against God, and shed much righteous blood, though in a short time." Dionysius of Alexandria and Cyprian write at length about these martyrs; Cyprian himself received the crown of martyrdom under this Valerian. 

Finally, the ninth persecution occurred under Aurelian in the year 275, which, as it only involved the sending of edicts, scarcely deserves the name of Persecution. For his bloody writings had not yet reached the more distant provinces (according to Lactantius, Chapter 6), and he already lay bloody on the ground at Caenophrurium, a place in Thrace, slain by his own friends due to a false suspicion. Thus, he was not even allowed to complete what he had planned, as Lactantius observes in the preceding words. Eusebius records the same things, adding this truly pious note to his narrative: "Showing most clearly to all that nothing is ever permitted to the princes of this world against the Churches of Christ, unless the defending right hand of God, by a secret and heavenly judgment for our discipline and correction, permits it to happen at such times as seem good to Him" <note>original Greek: *lampros te tois pasi synoran parestōsa...*</note>.

# WRITERS.

<margin>
3rd CENTURY from the Year 201.
\* Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, § 16.
† In the place cited.
</margin>
Symmachus, a Samaritan by race, was *one of the Wise men among them* <note>original Greek: *ek tōn par' autois Sophōn*</note>, \* from the number of those held to be Sages among the Samaritans. He flourished under the Emperor Severus at the beginning of this century, around the year 201. Athanasius—or whoever was the author of the *Synopsis of Holy Scripture*—is not quite consistent with himself; in reviewing the Greek interpreters of Scripture, he places Symmachus in the third position under Severus, but puts Theodotion in the fourth position under Commodus, yet says that Theodotion translated the Holy Scripture at the same time as Symmachus. Epiphanius † is no different; he places Symmachus (flourishing under Severus) before Theodotion (who thrived under Commodus), and explicitly says, *after these things* <note>original Greek: *meta tauta de*</note> (meaning after Symmachus) *and many years in the following time* <note>original: *kai posas en tō hexēs chronō*</note>, after him, in the progress of the following time, came a certain *Theodotion of Pontus, etc.* Some, to remedy this chronological error, suspect a mistake lies in Epiphanius’s manuscript, proposing that "Lucius Verus" should be put in place of "Severus," and thus they argue Symmachus flourished during Verus's reign. Certainly, in that passage, Epiphanius does not enumerate the years or the order of the Emperors with enough accuracy. However, I am rather of the opinion that Epiphanius, when he wrote those things, as well as the author of the *Synopsis*, had Origen's *Hexapla* <note>a massive six-columned edition of the Old Testament</note> before his eyes. In that work, Symmachus occupied the second place among the versions and Theodotion the fourth, with the translation of the Seventy <note>the Septuagint</note> placed between them; and therefore they presented them in the same order in their narratives, only excepting the Seventy Interpreters, who rightly claimed the first place for themselves. But let us return to Symmachus. When he did not receive the favor and honor he deserved among his own people, but was instead held in hatred because of his ambition, he defected to the Jews and was circumcised a second time. This was the custom of those fleeing from the Jews to the Samaritans, or from the Samaritans to the Jews; they would pull back the skin of the prepuce through an instrument they called a *Spathister* <note>a surgical tool used in "epispasm" to reverse the appearance of circumcision</note> so that they might be circumcised again. Finally, he defected from the Jews to the Christians, or at least to the Ebionites <note>a Jewish-Christian sect that maintained Jewish law and viewed Jesus as a human prophet</note>. In order to subvert the interpretations of his former countrymen, and simultaneously to conceal certain passages concerning Christ—especially those regarding his Genealogy—he composed a new *Greek Translation of the Old Instrument* <note>the Old Testament</note>, which he even polished in a second edition. In this translation, he did not express the text 
<margin>
\* Preface to Job, Volume 3, page 23.
</margin>
word-for-word like Aquila, as Jerome \* seems to suggest, but rather "sense-from-sense." Fragments of this *Version* were collected by Nobilius, Drusius, Walton, and others. Besides his *Version*, Symmachus also wrote *Commentaries to defend the Ebionite Heresy*, in which he argued sharply against the Gospel of Matthew, especially attacking the Genealogy of Christ. For the Ebionites contended that Christ was born from Joseph and Mary and was a "mere man" <note>original: *nudumque hominem*</note>, and they were called "Symmachians" after him. Origen testifies \* that he received these *Commentaries* of Symmachus, along with his *Version*, from a certain woman named Juliana, to whom they had come 
<margin>
\* In Eusebius, Book 6, Chapter 17.
† Catalog of Chaldean books, page 18.
</margin>
by right of succession. N.E. <note>Translator note: possibly "Note Edited" or "New Evidence"</note> Hebediesu † reports that several books by Symmachus still exist among the Chaldeans <note>Syriac Christians</note>, one of which is titled *On the Distinction of Precepts*.

<margin>
202.
† Cyprianic Dissertations, IV, § 12, 13.
</margin>
An Anonymous Author, who wrote the *Acts of Felicity and Perpetua*. He flourished around the year 202. To some he was a follower of Montanus <note>a prophetic Christian movement often considered heretical</note>, though to the illustrious Dodwell † he was, not without some likelihood, a Catholic writer. Holstenius first brought this work to light and published it in *Paris*, 1664; and thereafter, corrected with the help of an ancient Salisbury Manuscript, the curators of the Sheldon Press added it to the end of Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, *Oxford*, 1680, in duodecimo format.

Many other *Acts of the Holy Martyrs* are circulated today, but many of these are clearly faked antiquities, and the rest claim ancient status with very doubtful right.

**JUDAS**, both a Theologian and Historian, flourished in the year 202. He wrote most extensively *On the Seventy Weeks in Daniel*; in this dissertation, he brought the calculation of time down to the tenth year of the Emperor Severus. At that time, the Sixth Persecution was raging so fiercely that our Judas believed the present end of the world and the much-heralded arrival of the Antichrist were already at hand. <note>The "Seventy Weeks" refers to a prophecy in the Book of Daniel (9:24-27) which early Christians often used to calculate the timing of the Messiah and the end of the world.</note> N. **CAIUS**, or *Gaius*, a most eloquent man, was a Priest of the Roman Church and ordained as *Bishop of the Nations*, according to the testimony of Photius *, which is to say, if I interpret it correctly, he was made a Bishop for the purpose of converting the Gentiles living in barbarian lands to the faith of Christ and presiding over the churches founded there. He flourished around the year 210. While he was active in Rome, he held a famous Disputation with Proclus, a champion of the Cataphrygian heresy <note>The Cataphrygians were more commonly known as Montanists, an early Christian movement characterized by a belief in new prophetic revelations.</note>, which he later committed to writing in the form of a *Dialogue*. From this work, Eusebius (book 2, ch. 25) quotes a passage word-for-word concerning the Tombs of the Saints Peter and Paul; another passage *concerning Cerinthus* is found in book 3, ch. 28, and others in book 6, ch. 20. He likewise wrote against the *Heresy of Artemon*, and another book called the *Labyrinth*, unless (as seems much more likely) it is the same work, which some have wrongly attributed to Origen. It appears Photius * was mistaken on this point when he stated that, in addition to the *Labyrinth*, Caius wrote another specific book against the heresy of Artemon. From this *Little Labyrinth* (for such was its title), Eusebius drew that noble fragment against the heresy of Theodotus and Artemon, which appears in his book 5, ch. 28. For besides Photius † testifying that a certain book against the Artemonite heresy and another called the *Labyrinth* were written by Caius, Nicephorus * reports that this book by an unknown author against Artemon, from which Eusebius drew his fragment, was titled the *Little Labyrinth*. Theodoret || also records that the book composed *against the Heresy of Artemon and Theodotus* was distinguished by that name, and from it he brings forward a very charming little story. Caius also wrote *On the Substance of the Universe* <note>original Greek: *peri tēs tou pantos ousias*</note>, as he himself left testimony at the end of his *Labyrinth*, according to the transcriber Photius †. However, it is uncertain whether this is the same work as the one titled *On the Universe* <note>original Greek: *peri tou pantos*</note> which is commonly included among the works of Hippolytus. On this matter, see more under Hippolytus. This Gaius seems to be no different from the one mentioned at the end of the Acts of the Blessed Polycarp in Ussher's edition, where we read that he lived with Irenaeus and transcribed the Epistle of the Smyrneans from Irenaeus’s own copies. N. E.

210.
Against the Valentinians, ch. 5.

**PROCULUS** or *Proclus*, called by Tertullian *the honor of a chaste old age and of Christian eloquence*, was a most fierce and famous defender of the Montanist doctrine. One of the two split factions of the Montanists took its name from him, being called *those according to Proclus* <note>original Greek: *hoi kata Proklon*</note>. He flourished around the year 210. At Rome, under Pope Zephyrinus, he entered into a disputation with the Priest Caius. A certain argument brought forward by him there can be seen in Eusebius, book 3, ch. 31. He wrote an excellent work against the Valentinians, according to Tertullian in the place cited, which has since been lost. Valesius contends that the Montanist Proclus is a different person from this Proculus, but his arguments are not sufficiently compelling.

Eusebius book 6, ch. 11.
</margin>
**ALEXANDER**, Bishop of the Cappadocians, first began to become famous under Severus. After the Emperor's death, being warned by a divine revelation in dreams, he set out for Jerusalem both to pray and to visit the holy sites. There, the clergy of that Church, having also been forewarned by a Revelation, went out beyond the city gates and most kindly received the Bishop destined for them by God. With the consent of the Bishops of Palestine, and especially Narcissus, the leader of the Jerusalem church who was then over 116 years old, they compelled him to remain with them from then on. And so, around the year 212, he was given to Narcissus as a Colleague and Assistant; after the latter's death, he held the see of Jerusalem alone. In that place, he built a most noble Library, and in it he stored the writings of ecclesiastical men who excelled in learning, especially their Epistles. From this source, a most rich...

Eusebius* gratefully acknowledges that he had [excellent] material for composing his Ecclesiastical History. Alexander suffered much under Severus, and likewise under Caracalla; finally, under Decius—a man conspicuous for his graceful old age and venerable gray hair—he was cast into prison at Caesarea. There, after a noble and illustrious confession of the Christian faith made during a trial before the governor, around the year 250, "he rested blessedly," as Dionysius of Alexandria* says <note>original Greek: μακαριος ἀνεπαύσατο</note>, meaning he died a blessed death; or, according to Jerome†, "he was crowned with martyrdom." He wrote *several letters* to the people of Antinoöpolis, from one of which Eusebius (book 6, ch. 11) preserves a fragment. He wrote another to the people of Antioch, from which the same author cites certain passages in the place mentioned. Likewise, he wrote another to Origen, where he mentions Clement and Pantaenus as being his close acquaintances. Eusebius (book 6, ch. 14) provides a fragment of this. He also wrote *a letter together* with Theoctistus of Caesarea to Demetrius of Alexandria, in which he defended Origen (who was not yet initiated into holy orders) for preaching in the Church in the presence of Bishops. A fragment of this exists in Eusebius (book 6, ch. 19). He wrote several others, which do not survive. <note>The abbreviation "N. E." stands for "Non Exstant," meaning these works are lost to history.</note>

* Institutes, book 5, ch. 1.
* On Illustrious Men, ch. 58.

**MARCUS MINUCIUS FELIX**, likely of African origin, held a position of no small renown among Roman lawyers, yet was far more renowned for his Christian learning and piety. Regarding the age in which he lived, I have nothing I dare affirm for certain; however, if one may venture a guess in such an obscure and doubtful matter, I would suggest he flourished around the year 220, as a contemporary of Tertullian and older than Cyprian. At *Rome*, he wrote a *small book*—an outstanding *Dialogue* titled *Octavius*—which for several centuries past was falsely attributed as the eighth book of Arnobius. This dialogue is between Caecilius Natalis, a most fierce accuser and pagan, and Octavius Januarius, a sharp defender and patron of the Christians; the good Minucius Felix sits between them as an impartial Arbiter. In this book, he tears down the entire cult of the Pagans and the lineage of their gods with as much erudition as charm and wit; he elegantly and forcefully defends the Christians and their sacred rites from all of Caecilius's slanders and objections. Finally, Caecilius gives in and boasts that while he was defeated by Octavius, he has triumphed over error. This book certainly declares, says Lactantius*, "how suitable a defender of the truth he could have been, had he devoted himself entirely to that pursuit." It is found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 3, and at the end of Arnobius in the early editions of that Father. François Baudouin first reclaimed it for Minucius and published it under his name at *Heidelberg* in 1560. Then Fulvius Ursinus, wishing to appear to have done the same thing while concealing Baudouin's prior work, published it at *Rome* in 1583. These were followed by Wower (Basel, 1603), Elmenhorst (Hamburg, 1612), Hérault (Paris, 1613), Rigault (Paris, 1643) at the end of Arnobius, and again there in 1666 at the end of Cyprian with notes and Baudouin’s introduction. Ouzel then published his own revised version, illustrated with very extensive commentaries by various scholars, at *Leiden* in 1652. Finally, it appeared together with the notes of various scholars at *Leiden* in 1672. Jerome* reports that a *book on Fate* or *against Mathematicians* existed in his time under the name of Minucius, which, although he acknowledges it to be the work of an eloquent man, he judged to differ from Minucius's style. It does not survive.

**HIPPOLYTUS** was a disciple of Irenaeus, according to Photius*. It is agreed among all that he was a bishop, but it is not yet established of which city. This seems to have escaped Eusebius, and after him, Jerome. For the former† says: "Beryllus was bishop of the Arabs at Bostra. Likewise, Hippolytus also presided over some other bishopric." <note>original Greek: Βήρυλλος ἦν ἐπίσκοπος τῶν κατὰ Βόστραν Ἀράβων. Ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ Ἱππόλυτος ἑτέρας πῶς καὶ αὐτὸς προεστὼς ἐπισκοπῆς.</note> But the latter [Jerome] says ||: "*Hippolytus, Bishop of a certain Church (for I have not been able to learn the name of the City).*" From this, material was born for the writers of later centuries to either guess or invent stories. Zonaras* and Nicephorus†, along with nearly all more recent authors, want him to be the Bishop of the Roman Port. Germanus of Constantinople|| and Leontius of Byzantium* say he was a Bishop of Rome. The Magdeburg Centuriators† call him the Bishop of Ostia. Finally, Gelasius|| writes that he was the Bishop of the Metropolis of Arabia. However, among all the opinions on this matter, the recent conjecture of the illustrious Le Moyne* seems the most likely: that Hippolytus was the Bishop of the Roman Port in Arabia, "the trading center of Arabia." <note>original Greek: ἔμποριος τῆς Ἀραβίας</note>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Hippolytus of Rome. The previous page (66) likely introduced his background and his distinction from other figures of the same name. This page focuses on his scholarly collaboration with Origen, his reputation for driving Origen's productivity, and the significant archaeological find of his statue and Paschal calendar.</meta>

# The Century of Novatian.

<margin>
3rd CENTURY from the Year 200.
* Hymn 11.
† Cited place.
* On Illustrious Men, ch. 61.
</margin>
Called Aegitias by Ptolemy, and afterwards acquiring the name *Adana* or *Adena*—which it retains even today—it was very well known to Roman merchants and frequently visited by them at that time. From here, it can be reckoned that he came to Rome as he reached maturity, and finally died and was buried there. He flourished around the year 220. Certainly, there were several men named Hippolytus in this age; that other Hippolytus, the Martyr whose passion Prudentius describes in a rather lengthy hymn*, seems to be different from our subject. For that man had been a priest among the followers of the Novatian schism. <note>The Novatianists were a rigorist sect who refused to readmit Christians who had lapsed during persecutions.</note> However, the one we are discussing was very close with Origen; he imitated him and, as Origen was often present, he delivered homilies to the people. According to Photius†, he held Origen's sermons in such high admiration that he urged and compelled him to illustrate the Divine Scriptures with a commentary. To this end, he provided at his own expense seven notaries who would quickly take down what was dictated, and as many copyists who would accurately transcribe the texts. Consequently, he used to demand any work Origen was elaborating upon without pause; for this reason, he was called a <term>Task-master <note>original Greek: ἐργοδιώκτης</note></term> by Origen. Jerome* seems to concur with this narrative. Nevertheless, both clearly fell into error by attributing to Hippolytus what was actually characteristic of Ambrose. <note>Ambrose of Alexandria was Origen's actual patron; the author is pointing out a common historical confusion between these patrons.</note> Hippolytus is said to have undergone martyrdom around the year 230; however, this is based on uncertain reports, and it is not improbable that he lived even longer.

->The works written by him, as well as those attributed to him, are these:<-

<margin>
* Book on the Correction of Time.
† Pages 140, 141.
* Commentary on Victor’s Paschal Canon, ch. 15.
</margin>
**A book on** Easter, to which he gave the title <term>Demonstration of the Times of Easter <note>original Greek: ἀπόδειξις χρόνων τοῦ πάσχα</note></term>; in which, describing the sequence of times, he concluded in the first year of Emperor Alexander <note>Alexander Severus</note>, that is, the year of Christ 222. In this work, he also inserted a Paschal Canon of a <term>sixteen-year cycle <note>original Greek: ἑκκαιδεκαετηρίδα</note></term>, beginning from the first year of the same Emperor. This Canon was finally found in the last century, inscribed in Greek on the chair of a marble statue of Hippolytus himself (as it appears) sitting in a seat. The letters on both side-panels of the seat display a sixteen-year circuit: on the right side, the cycle of the "Fourteenth Days" <note>The 'quartodeciman' calculations for the full moon of Easter.</note>, and on the left, the cycle of the Lord's Day Easters. Together, these encompass a total of 112 years, a period of years in which Hippolytus believed the same feast days would return in a circle. Furthermore, on the margin of the right panel, many of Hippolytus’s own writings are listed, knowledge of which you would seek elsewhere in vain. This noble monument of ecclesiastical antiquity was unearthed in the Veranian field, not far from the Church of St. Lawrence outside the walls of the city of Rome, in the year 1551. It was brought into the Vatican Library, published with Greek notes by Joseph Scaliger*, included by Gruter† in the *Corpus of Ancient Inscriptions*, and finally translated into Latin and illustrated with a commentary by Aegidius Bucherius*. **M. MINUCIUS FELIX**, likely of African descent, held a notable position among Roman trial lawyers, yet he was far more noble in his Christian learning and piety. Regarding the age in which he lived, I have nothing I dare to affirm as certain; however, if one may speculate on an obscure and doubtful matter, I would guess that he flourished around the year 220, as he was a contemporary of Tertullian and lived earlier than Cyprian. He wrote a small book in Rome which for several centuries was falsely considered the eighth book of Arnobius; I am speaking of that distinguished *Dialogue* called the ***Octavius***. It is a debate between Caecilius Natalis, a most fierce pagan accuser, and Octavius Januarius, a sharp defender and patron of the Christians; sitting between them as a good Arbiter is Minucius Felix. In this book, he tears down the entire pagan worship and the lineage of the gods with as much erudition as charm and wit, and he elegantly and vigorously vindicates the Christians and their sacred rites from all of Caecilius's slanders and objections. Finally, yielding his hand <note>a gesture of surrender</note>, Caecilius boasts that while he was indeed defeated by Octavius, he has triumphed over error. Jerome* records that a book titled *On Fate, or Against the Mathematicians* existed in his time under Minucius’s name, which, although he acknowledges it to be the work of an eloquent man, he judged to differ from Minucius's style. It is no longer extant.

# The Century of Novatian.

<margin>3rd CENTURY from the Year 200.</margin>
The people of Aeglae, named by Ptolemy and later given the name *Adana* or *Adena* (which it still retains today), were well known to Roman merchants and were frequently visited by them at that time. From there, as he aged, it can be considered that he came to Rome, and was finally buried there after his death. He flourished around the year 220. Certainly, there were several men named Hippolytus in this age; that famous Martyr Hippolytus, whose passion Prudentius describes in a lengthy hymn*, seems to be different from our subject. <margin>* Hymn 11.</margin> For that man had been a Priest among the followers of the Novatian schism <note>The Novatianists were a rigorist sect who refused to readmit those who had lapsed during persecutions.</note>. But the one we are discussing was a very close friend of Origen; he imitated him, and often delivered homilies to the people in Origen's presence. Indeed, according to Photius†, <margin>† In the place cited.</margin> he held Origen's sermons in such high admiration that he urged and impelled him to illustrate the Divine Scriptures with commentaries. To assist this, he provided at his own expense seven Notaries to take down what was dictated quickly, and as many copyists to transcribe them accurately. Consequently, he used to demand any work Origen was laboring on without pause, and for this reason, he was called a <term>taskmaster <note>original Greek: ἐργοδιώκτης (ergodioktēs)</note></term> by Origen. Jerome* seems to give his approval to this narrative. <margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 61.</margin> However, both men clearly erred by attributing to Hippolytus what was actually proper to Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Alexandria was Origen's wealthy patron; the author notes that historical sources often confuse him with Hippolytus.</note>. Hippolytus is said to have met his martyrdom around the year 230, though the report is uncertain, for it is not improbable that he lived a longer life.

<margin>
3rd CENTURY from the year 200.

<insert>
The right corner of this small tablet was broken off, which truncated the first five lines.

We have followed the copy of the inscription by Gruter <note>Jan Gruter (1560–1627) was a prominent scholar who compiled ancient inscriptions</note> throughout. Thus, in the word for "three volumes," the Latin 'R' is placed instead of the Greek 'P' <note>A common error in early transcriptions where the Greek rho was mistaken for a Latin R</note>; in the word for "John," the letter 'N' is missing once; in the word for "Plato," the 'L' is missing; in most places, the letter 'omega' is written in a lowercase form, and many words run together as one.
</insert>

<column-break/>

Thus far we have the Inscription of the marble Chair <note>This refers to the famous "Statue of St. Hippolytus," the oldest known Christian statue, which features a list of works and a calendar for calculating Easter</note>. Since the very learned Le Moyne has pursued its explanation most extensively, we shall dispatch it very briefly <note>original: tribus quasi verbis, literally "as if in three words"</note>.

In this inscription, the first two lines are for the most part mutilated, leaving room only for conjectures. Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a leading 16th-century scholar of ancient history</note> thinks that "...IOUS" and "...NIAS" are the remains of the words *PSALMS* and *PENITENCE*. Following him, Bucherius placed this title at the head of his Latin version of the list: ON THE PENITENTIAL PSALMS. However, since a work of Hippolytus on the Psalms appears later in the list, and the inscription clearly shows "...NIAS" rather than "...NOIAS," and the very concept of "Penitential Psalms" <note>A specific grouping of psalms used in later medieval liturgy</note> is clearly of recent origin, that conjecture must be entirely rejected. The illustrious Le Moyne suspects that these are the remains of the phrases *On the Six Days of Creation* <note>original Greek: εἰς τὴν ἑξαημέρον</note> and *On the Origin of the World* or *the Origin of Life*, which would designate Hippolytus's scholarly works *On the events following the Six Days of Creation* and *On the Six Days of Creation*. Both Eusebius <margin>† Book 6, ch. 21.</margin> and Jerome <margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 61.</margin> testify that such books were written by him, though Jerome wishes those books to be understood as commentaries on Exodus and Genesis. But in a matter so obscure, it is better to withhold our agreement than to indulge too boldly in guesswork.
