# The Age of Novatian.

### [PSALMS]
<margin>THE 3rd CENTURY, from the Year 200.</margin>
These are undoubtedly the final syllables of the word *Psalms* <note>original: ΨΑΛΜΟΥC</note>, on which Hippolytus wrote *Commentaries*, as Jerome testifies. Many excerpts from these are found in the *Catena* <note>A "chain" of interpretations or a collection of scriptural commentary from various authors</note> on the Psalms preserved in a manuscript in the Medicean Library, mentioned by Le Moyne in his *Prolegomena to Sacred Varieties*. Theodoret also provides two fragments from them in his *Unconfused Dialogues* (Volume 4, pages 89–90): the first from the Commentaries on Psalm 2, and the second from the Commentary on Psalm 23. Alexander Morus, in his *Notes on the New Testament* (page 167), provides a fragment from the Preface to the Psalms.

### [THE WITCH OF ENDOR]
<margin>* Jerome, in the place cited.</margin>
The word for "ventriloquist" or "witch" <note>original: ἐγγαστρίμυθον</note> is somewhat distorted in the inscription. Jerome writes that Hippolytus wrote a work *On Saul and the Witch of Endor*.

### [IN DEFENSE OF THE GOSPEL, etc.]
(Perhaps to be read as) *In defense of the Gospel and Revelation according to John*. Jerome mentions this work of his on the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>.

### [ON SPIRITUAL GIFTS]
The title of this work is undoubtedly taken from 1 Corinthians 12.

### [APOSTOLIC TRADITION]
<margin>* Vindications of Ignatius, part 1, pages 60, 62.</margin>
This can be believed to be the same as his *Teaching* <note>original: Διδασκαλίᾳ</note>, which is frequently mentioned in manuscript copies of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, which were woven together from the *Teachings* of Hippolytus as well as other Fathers. The illustrious Pearson testifies that the *Teachings of Hippolytus* lie hidden in a manuscript in the Oxford Library, and that they constitute the greater part of the eighth book of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. John Mill, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Principal of St. Edmund Hall at Oxford, has extracted this from the manuscript and is soon to publish it with the rest of Hippolytus’s works; we expect more certain information about Hippolytus and his writings from him.

### [CHRONICLE AGAINST THE PAGANS]
*Chronicle against the Pagans* <note>original Latin: Chronicon ad Gentes</note>. It was not unusual for Church writers of that age to weave together chronologies of historical events to refute the false antiquity claimed for the Pagan gods and heroes. That our Hippolytus was highly skilled in chronology is demonstrated by his work on the *Pascha* <note>The calculation of the date of Easter</note>.

### [AGAINST PLATO, or also ON THE UNIVERSE]
<margin>* Codex 48.</margin>
*Against Plato, or On the Universe.* David Hoeschel published a very large fragment of this book sent to him from Italy in Greek and Latin in his *Notes on Photius* (page 9), under the title: *From the Discourse of Josephus against the Greeks, titled "Against Plato: On the Cause of the Universe."* However, Hoeschel himself rejects the attribution to Josephus. And since the inscription calls it a *Discourse against the Greeks*, one might not incorrectly guess that the earlier words on the list should be joined with this title. In fact, a work once existed (according to Photius) under Josephus's name titled *On the Universe*, or *On the Cause (or Nature) of the Universe*, in which Photius nonetheless found a note at the end stating it was not by Josephus, but by Caius the Presbyter. Others ascribed it to Justin Martyr, and some to Irenaeus. The work was divided into two small books in which the author showed that Plato contradicted himself; he also refuted Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher</note> for arguing falsely and absurdly about the soul, matter, and the resurrection. He set forth his own opinions on these theses and taught that the Jewish nation was far more ancient than the Greeks. Photius cites a short passage from it in the place mentioned. However, while the ancients did not agree on the true author of this work, almost all modern scholars—relying on the authority of this inscription, the style, the subject matter, and other arguments—attribute it to Hippolytus. Among these is the very recent Stephen Le Moyne, who had the fragment originally published by Hoeschel reprinted with a Latin translation in his *Sacred Varieties* (Leiden, 1685).

### [EXHORTATION TO SEVERINA]
Le Moyne thinks this should be read as *To Severa Augusta* <note>Addressing the Empress</note>, which is a very probable conjecture. Hippolytus perhaps wrote an "Exhortation" <note>original: προτρεπτικὼ</note> as a letter to Severa, the wife of the Emperor Philip, whom...

* Eusebius, Book 6, chapter 36.
</margin>
...which Eusebius writes that he even addressed to Origen in letters *. However, if stretching the life of Hippolytus to that point seems too difficult, this Letter might not improperly be referred to the sister of Alexander Severus, or some woman of his family <note>This likely refers to Julia Mamaea, the Emperor's mother, who was known to consult Christian scholars</note>. Certainly, Theodoret expressly testifies that Hippolytus wrote a Letter *to a certain queen* <note>original: πρὸς βασιλίδα τινὰ</note>, and he cites two fragments from it in Dialogue III, and another in Dialogue II.

### [DEMONSTRATION of the times of Pascha according to the table]
<note>original: Α Π Ο Δ Ε Ι Ξ Ι Σ χρόνων τοῦ πάσχα κατὰ τὸ ἐν πίνακι</note>
Concerning which we spoke above. Its summary, or the *Paschal Canon*, was inscribed on the Chair, and is found in the works of Scaliger, Gruter, and Bucherius <note>These were prominent 16th and 17th-century scholars of ancient chronology</note>.

### [ODES upon all joys]
<note>original: Ω Δ Α Ι Ι Σ πάσας τὰς χαρὰς</note>
Using a rather unusual conjecture, Le Moyne <note>Stephen Le Moyne (1624–1689), a French theologian</note> thinks it should be read as *against all heresies* <note>original: εἰς πάσας τὰς αἱρέσεις</note>. By that reasoning, anything could be carved out of anything with no effort, and "square things could be changed for round" <note>A Latin idiom for changing things arbitrarily or attempting the impossible</note> most easily. I would prefer to confess my ignorance in this matter than to devise something new "against the grain" <note>original: invitâ Minervâ; literally 'with Minerva unwilling,' meaning without natural inspiration or against logic</note> and in defiance of reason.

### [ON GOD and the resurrection of the flesh]
<note>original: Π Ε Ρ Ι Θ Ε Ο Υ καὶ σαρκὸς ἀναστάσεως</note>
Hippolytus wrote various short works that somewhat resemble this title. For if we split the title in two: *On God and the Flesh* <note>original: Περὶ Θεοῦ καὶ σαρκὸς</note> [could refer to] Hippolytus's books either on the Triune and One God and on the Incarnation, or on Theology and the Incarnation, which survive today; and *of the resurrection* <note>original: ἀναστάσεως</note> (with *on* being understood) could designate his book *On the Resurrection* mentioned by Jerome. If we instead recognize a single title hidden under these words, it is not far from the truth that a certain work *Against Heretics* is denoted (Jerome records that Hippolytus refuted them all in writing). For almost no Heretics of that age failed to rave regarding the divine essence and the Resurrection of the flesh.

### [ON the good, and the origin of evil]
<note>original: Π Ε Ρ Ι τ’ αγαθῶ, καὶ πόθεν τὸ κακόν</note>
A most vexed question in that age, which the Doctors of the Church illustrated in many Commentaries published both against the Pagans and the Heretics. Of the former, almost all the Philosophers; of the latter, the Marcionites, Cerdonians, Hermogenians, and many others established different principles of good and evil. Jerome is the authority for the fact that Hippolytus wrote against Marcion. Perhaps this title could not improperly be understood to refer to that book. However, contenting ourselves with pointing a finger at this matter, and not relying too much on conjectures, however likely, we will subjoin the remaining works of Hippolytus, which the List <note>The list on the statue's chair</note> does not openly mention.

*Oration on the End of the World and the Antichrist and the second coming of the Lord;* which many, however, call into doubt. It appeared in Greek and Latin, *Paris, 1557.* It also appears in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers*, Volume 2, *Paris, 1624.* The Reverend Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh</note> strives to prove in many ways in his *Theological Library* (Manuscript) that this is not a genuine work of Hippolytus, finally closing his arguments with these words: *"It appears therefore both from the very nature of the Greek style, which is for the most part childish, and from the truth of the matter and weight of the book, that the author of this little book was an illiterate and unlearned man."*

*Demonstration concerning the Antichrist, and on Susanna.* Available in Greek and Latin in Combefis's *Supplement to the Fathers*, *Paris, 1672.*

*Homily on the Triune and One God, and on the Mystery of the Incarnation, against the Heresy of Noetus.* Available in Latin with Gerard Vossius as translator and editor in the *Appendix to Gregory Thaumaturgus*, *Mainz, 1604,* and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 3.

*On Theology and the Incarnation against the Heretics Beron and Helicon.* Sirmond <note>Jacques Sirmond (1559–1651), a Jesuit scholar</note> published certain excerpts from it in Greek and Latin among the collections of Anastasius the Librarian, *Paris, 1620, octavo.* These, however, are held suspect for more than one reason by Le Moyne, and they seem to him—as well as to Possevino and Canisius—to reek of Eutychianism <note>A heresy which claimed Christ had only one nature, effectively merging his divinity and humanity</note>.

*Demonstration against the Jews,* which Possevino first published in Latin translation in his *Apparatus*. Many call its authenticity into doubt. A Greek copy of this treatise was in the possession of Turrianus.

*A List concerning the Twelve Apostles, where each of them preached and was perfected <term>perfected: a common term in early hagiography for completing one's life through martyrdom</term>;* likely to be attributed to "Hippolytus the Younger." Available in Greek and Latin in Combefis's *Supplement*, *Paris, 1648,* Volume 2.

# The Age of Novatian.

<margin>THE 3rd CENTURY, from the Year 200.</margin>
Hippolytus also wrote (though they are no longer extant) various Commentaries on Scripture, which are mentioned by the Ancients. These include a commentary on **Genesis** (from which there seems to be a fairly long fragment concerning the mystical significance of Isaac, Rebecca, and Esau, produced by Jerome in his *Letter to Damasus, Question 3*); on **Exodus**; on the **Song of Songs** (Theodoret displays three fragments from this in his *Dialogue 2*); on **Proverbs**, **Ecclesiastes**, and **Isaiah** (Theodoret has something from this in *Dialogue 1*); on **Zechariah**, on certain chapters of **Ezekiel**, and on **Daniel**. Photius <margin>* Volume 202.</margin> had read the Commentary on Daniel and noted things in it to be criticized. For he writes as follows: *Furthermore, regarding the coming of the Antichrist (which will be followed by the destruction of this visible world), which the Lord did not reveal even to his requesting Disciples, this Hippolytus dared to assign to the five-hundredth year after Christ, as if its destruction were imminent after six thousand years had run their course since the first constitution of the world; this is certainly the mark of a mind more rash than is proper.* Of this exposition on Daniel, there exists to this day a short Greek manuscript commentary on the dream of Nebuchadnezzar, which the illustrious Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon (1632–1707), a Benedictine monk and founder of the study of old documents</note> saw in Rome in the Chigi Library, in a very ancient codex of the four Major Prophets written at least eight hundred years ago. Le Moyne <note>Stephen Le Moyne (1624–1689)</note> testifies that Hippolytus’s commentaries on the Song of Songs and the books of Solomon are still preserved today in the Imperial Library. Moreover, the catalog of the Escorial Library published by Barvoetius claims that Hippolytus’s treatise on Susanna, a fragment on Daniel, and many excerpts from his commentary on Proverbs exist there.

Hippolytus also wrote: *On the Praises of our Lord* and *On the Resurrection*. Anastasius Sinaïta <note>A 7th-century monk and priest at Saint Catherine's Monastery</note> has an excerpt from Hippolytus’s treatise <term>On the Resurrection and Incorruptibility</term> in his *Guidebook* <note>original: Ὁδηγ.</note>, chapter 23. He also wrote *Against Marcion* and *Against All Heresies* (as Jerome notes), which numbered thirty-two according to the testimony of Photius <margin>* Volume 121.</margin>. Beginning with the Dositheans and continuing through the thread of the argument to the Noetians, he refuted each heretic, for the most part using the reasoning of his master Irenaeus. He himself did not deny <margin>† In Photius, location cited above.</margin> that he wrote his little book by collecting a summary of Irenaeus's arguments. Gelasius <margin>* Book on the two natures in Christ.</margin> cites that work under the title <term>A Record of Heresies</term>.

Finally, Hippolytus wrote various Homilies, from which Theodoret presents several excerpts in his *Dialogues*: namely, from the *Homily on the text "The Lord feeds me"*; from the *Homily on Elkanah and Hannah*; from the *Homily on the Distribution of the Talents*; and from the *Homily on the Two Thieves*. Holstenius <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661), a German humanist and geographer</note> had intended to publish Hippolytus’s *Homily on the Holy Theophany*, along with his small work *Against the Error of Noetus* and a *Fragment on the Incarnation*, which he had in his possession; however, snatched away by death, he did not complete his proposal, as Le Moyne testifies.

From a certain book by Hippolytus <term>On the Apostles according to Knowledge</term>, Palladius presents an excerpted narrative about a certain Christian virgin in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 148.

Hebediesu <note>A 13th-century East Syriac bishop and author</note> reports that among the Chaldeans there exists Hippolytus's book *On Governance*, an *Exposition on the Minor Daniel and Susanna*, as well as chapters *Against Caius*, and an *Apology for the Apocalypse and the Gospel of Saint John*.

Regarding his style, Photius says: <term>His phrasing is clear, somewhat dignified, and concise, even if it does not lean toward Attic speech.</term> His speech is clear, quite serious, and not at all redundant, even if it does not strive for the Attic dialect <note>The prestigious dialect of classical Athens</note>. This is not at all surprising in an Arabian man <note>Some ancient traditions associated Hippolytus with the East, though he is now primarily associated with Rome</note>. Finally, I will add what Nicephorus notes concerning certain works of Hippolytus <margin>† Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 31.</margin>: that they were not free from criticism, but that he wiped away every stain of ignorance with his martyrdom.

## **AMMONIUS**, the Alexandrian Philosopher, lived at the same time as Hippolytus and was held in high regard from the reign of Commodus himself, but especially around the year 220. Having left these things behind, he gave himself entirely to philosophy and emerged as the most famous of all the philosophers of his time. He opened a Platonic school in Alexandria, in the governing of which <term>he was inspired toward the truth of philosophy</term>, to use the words of Hierocles * concerning him, while by a certain heat toward the truth of philosophy...

<margin>THE 3rd CENTURY, from the Year 200.
* Book 6, chapter 36.</margin>
Eusebius writes * that Hippolytus even addressed letters to Origen. If it seems too difficult to extend the lifespan of Hippolytus to that point, this letter might not be wrongly attributed to the sister of Alexander Severus <note>Roman Emperor from 222–235 AD</note>, or someone from his household. Certainly, Theodoret <note>A 5th-century influential theologian and bishop</note> clearly testifies that Hippolytus wrote a letter <note>original: πρὸς βασιλίδα τινὰ, "to a certain queen"</note> and provides two fragments from it in his *Dialogue 3*, and another in *Dialogue 2*.

### [Demonstration of the times of Easter according to the table]
Regarding which we spoke above. A summary of it, or the "Paschal Canon," was inscribed on his Chair <note>Refers to the famous marble statue of Hippolytus discovered in 1551, which has a list of his works and an Easter calendar carved into it</note>, and it is preserved in the works of Scaliger, Gruter, and Bucherius.

### [Songs on all the scriptures]
Using a rather bold conjecture, Moynius <note>Jean Le Moyne (1628–1689), a French scholar</note> judges that the text should read <note>original: εἰς πάσας τὰς αἱρέσεις, "Against all heresies"</note>. Indeed, by such reasoning, anyone could carve anything out of anything with no effort, and "square things could be swapped for round" with the greatest ease. In this matter, I would prefer to admit my own ignorance rather than devise something new against the will of Minerva <note>A Latin idiom meaning "against one's natural ability" or "against logic"</note> and in defiance of reason.

### [Concerning God and the resurrection of the flesh]
Hippolytus wrote various small works that align somewhat with this title. For if we divide the title in two: *Concerning God and the flesh* could designate Hippolytus’s books (still surviving today) either on the Triune God and the Incarnation, or on Theology and the Incarnation; and *the resurrection* (with the word *concerning* understood) could designate his book *On the Resurrection* mentioned by Jerome. If, however, we prefer to recognize a single title hidden under these words, it is not far from the truth that it signifies some work against the Heretics (whom Jerome records that Hippolytus refuted in writing). For there were almost no heretics of that age who did not rave concerning the divine essence and the resurrection of the flesh.

### [Concerning the Good, and the origin of evil]
This was a most vexing question in that age, which the Teachers of the Church illustrated in many commentaries published both against the Gentiles <note>non-Christians, specifically Pagans</note> and the Heretics. Of the former, almost all the Philosophers, and of the latter, the Marcionites, Cerdonians, Hermogenians, and many others established different principles for good and evil. Jerome is the authority for the fact that Hippolytus wrote against Marcion. Perhaps that title could be aptly applied to that book. However, we are content to merely point our finger at this matter, not trusting too much in conjectures, however probable, and we shall subjoin the remaining works of Hippolytus, which the short Index does not explicitly mention.

*Oration on the End of the World and the Antichrist, and the second coming of the Lord;* which, however, many call into doubt. It was published in Greek and Latin at *Paris, 1557.* It is also found in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers, Volume 2, Paris, 1624.* The Reverend Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, famous for his biblical chronology</note> strives to prove with many arguments in his *Theological Library manuscript* that this is not a genuine work of Hippolytus, finally closing his arguments with these words:

> It appears, therefore, both from the style of the Greek itself, which is for the most part childish, and from the reality and weight of the subject, that the author of this little book was an illiterate and unlearned man.

*Demonstration on the Antichrist, and on Susanna.* Available in Greek and Latin in Combefis’s *Supplement to the Fathers, Paris, 1672.*

*Homily on the Triune God, and on the Mystery of the Incarnation, against the Heresy of Noetus.* Available in Latin, translated and edited by Gerard Vossius in the *Appendix to Gregory Thaumaturgus, Mainz, 1604,* and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 3.*

*On Theology and the Incarnation against the heretics Beron and Helicon.* Sirmondus published certain excerpts from it in Greek and Latin among the *Collections of Anastasius the Librarian, Paris, 1620, in octavo.* These, however, are held as suspicious by Moynius for more than one reason, and they seem to him, as well as to Possevino and Canisius, to reek of Eutychianism <note>The belief that Christ had only one nature, which was considered a heresy by the Roman church</note>.

*Demonstration against the Jews,* which Possevino first published in a Latin translation in his *Apparatus*. Many call its authenticity into doubt. A Greek copy of this tract was in the possession of Turrianus.

*A Brief List of the Twelve Apostles, where each of them preached and met his end;* more likely to be attributed to "Hippolytus the Younger." Available in Greek and Latin in Combefis’s *Supplement, Paris, 1648, Volume 2.*

Hippolytus also wrote various commentaries on Scripture (which are no longer extant), among which the ancient writers mention: *On Genesis* (from this, it seems, comes that quite long fragment concerning the mystical significance of Isaac, Rebecca, and Esau, which Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> provides in his *Epistle to Damasus*, Question 3); *On Exodus*; *On the Song of Songs* (three fragments of which are shown by Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and historian</note> in *Dialogue 2*); *On Proverbs*; *On Ecclesiastes*; *On Isaiah* (of which Theodoret has a portion in *Dialogue 1*); *On Zechariah*; *On certain chapters of Ezekiel*; and *On Daniel*. ...he was seized by the truth, he despised the quarrelsome little disputes of the Platonists and Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle</note>; and having purified the opinions of the ancient philosophers and rejected the trifles that had grown up on both sides, he demonstrated that the judgment of Plato and Aristotle was in agreement on every principal and most necessary dogma. For this reason, Hierocles <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist</note> proclaims that he was commonly called "God-taught" <note>original: "Θεοδίδακτον"</note>. He was a Christian, born of Christian parents and educated by them, as Porphyry <note>A famous Neoplatonist critic of Christianity</note> himself admits—that distinguished adversary of the Christians. However, when Porphyry says that he crossed over from the worship of the true Deity to the rites of the Gentiles, "he clearly lies," <note>original: "ψεύδεται μὲν σαφῶς"</note> says Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History"</note>; in this, he most manifesty lied. For Ammonius wrote, among other things, *On the Harmony of Moses and Jesus*, an elegant work which no longer survives; and he devised the *Evangelical Canons* <note>A system for cross-referencing parallel passages in the four Gospels</note>, which Eusebius of Caesarea followed later. So says Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note>. Yet Jerome seems to have slipped in this matter. For besides the fact that Cassiodorus <note>A 6th-century statesman and scholar</note> explicitly attributes them to Eusebius, Eusebius himself, in his *Epistle to Carpianus* prefixed to the Canons, testifies that he devised those Canons on the occasion of the *Ammonian Monotessaron* <note>A single Gospel narrative woven from the four</note>. Perhaps Victor of Capua <note>A 6th-century bishop</note> is more correct, writing that the Canons were discovered by Ammonius with wonderful zeal and then diligently refined by Eusebius. There exists in the *Orthodoxographia* <note>A collection of early Christian writings</note> (Volume 2) and in every edition of the *Library of the Fathers* a *Harmony of the Four Holy Gospels* put together by Ammonius, but incorrectly titled by its translator, Victor of Capua, as being by Tatian. For in it are presented the Genealogies of Christ, which Eusebius and Theodoret testify were cut out by Tatian, and which are indeed missing from Tatian’s *Diatessaron* <note>meaning "through the four"</note>, though incorrectly attributed to Ammonius. Furthermore, Victor himself remains in doubt for some time as to which man—Ammonius or Tatian—it should be attributed; while Zacharias of Chrysopolis, who illustrated that Harmony with commentaries five hundred years ago, explicitly attributes it to Ammonius. There also exists (as mentioned above) Tatian’s *Diatessaron* bearing the false name of Ammonius. The *Canons of the Harmony* are usually either placed before or after it. Far different from our Ammonius was that Egyptian Ammonius, the teacher of Plutarch of Chaeronea, who lived almost a whole century earlier; concerning him, see Plutarch’s book *On the E at Delphi* (p. 385) and Eunapius in the *Prooemium to the Lives of the Sophists* (p. 11).

-> JULIUS AFRICANUS, whom some wish to have been a Palestinian, was, according to Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> (by whom he is also called Sextus), a native of Libya, and undoubtedly drew the name "Africanus" from there. Stirred by the fame of Heraclas—a disciple of Origen and a man excellent in philosophy and other Greek disciplines—he set out for Alexandria so that he might join him more closely in promoting the study of the best literature. However, he primarily fixed his home at Nicopolis in Palestine, which was called by its ancient name *Emmaus*. On its behalf, in the year 220, he undertook an embassy to Emperor Antoninus Heliogabalus so that the walls of the ruined city might be restored; indeed (if Hebediesu, the Metropolitan of Soba, is to be believed), he was the Bishop of that city. He died at an advanced age around the year 232.

He began from the creation of the world and brought the chronology down to the advent of Christ; however, he recorded more succinctly the deeds from the time of Christ up to the times of Emperor Macrinus, where he ended—or, as others prefer, in the third year of Heliogabalus (who succeeded Macrinus), which was the year of Christ 221. However, since the Greek originals of both Africanus and Eusebius have been lost, nothing remains except what George Syncellus <note>A 9th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> preserved in his *Chronographia*. From this, as well as from the *Sicilian Fasti* <note>A chronological list</note>, Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century scholar of chronology</note> assembled the Greek *Chronicle* of Eusebius—which remains quite mutilated and confused—as he presented it to us in the *Treasury of Times*. Also, that story is not recorded among the Hebrews in their sacred books. 7. Nor would a Prophet use the words of another Prophet (as this Daniel does). Finally, 8. That the style differs greatly from the true Daniel. *The work "The Cesti"*, <note>Latin: "Cestorum Opus". Whatever the number of these books was, Joseph Scaliger (*) and Henri Valois (†) attribute them to a different Africanus; thus they maintain there were two men named Africanus: one a Palestinian, our Chronographer, a Christian by religion; the other an African, a Pagan philosopher called *Sextus*, the author of the *Cesti*. **ORIGEN**, who was called "Man of Bronze Guts" <note>Greek: χαλκέντερος (chalkenteros), a nickname for his tireless work ethic</note> and "The Indestructible" <note>original: "Adamantius"</note> because of the incredible labors he endured for the sake of both study and religion, was born in Alexandria in the year 186. Born to Christian parents, he was practiced in the Divine Scriptures from his very childhood, a fact which Eusebius † proves clearly with many examples. From this, it is evident how greatly Porphyry <note>A famous Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity</note> * lies when he says that Origen, while he was a Gentile <note>a non-Christian/Pagan</note> and nourished in the disciplines of the Gentiles, turned toward "the daring ways of the barbarians" (for this is how the Gentile man insultingly attacks the Christian Religion). Under the guidance of his father, Leonides, he took his first steps in literature, drawing from him a knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. The boy cultivated this knowledge with such diligence that, not content with the simple and obvious reading of them, he sought something greater and scrutinized their deeper meanings even then. He caused his father no small trouble by asking him what the intended meaning of the divinely inspired Scripture was. From there, he was handed over to the teaching of Clement of Alexandria, and finally, he had as his teacher that famous Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas</note>, whom we mentioned above, under whom he applied himself especially to Platonic Philosophy.

<margin>
* Cited in Eusebius, Book 6, ch. 19.
† Ibid. ch. 1.
</margin>
Indeed, he daily held in his hands not only the writings of the Platonists but also those of the Pythagoreans and Stoics. As Porphyry correctly noted of him *, since he had learned the allegorical method for explaining the mysteries of the Greeks, he applied it to the Jewish Scriptures. In the year 202, during the persecution under Emperor Septimius Severus, he lost his father †, who was crowned with martyrdom. From that time, after his father's property had been confiscated by the state treasury, he supported his mother and six small children, providing the means of life for his family through his profession of the Art of Grammar. At the age of eighteen, he was placed in charge of the private instruction of the catechumens <note>students preparing for baptism</note>.

<margin>
* Ibid. ch. 3.
</margin>
Afterward, he was appointed by Bishop Demetrius to take the place of his teacher Clement in the public School of Catechesis *; in that position, he had many students, including Gentiles of great reputation.

<margin>
† Cited in Eusebius, Book 6, ch. 14.
</margin>
While Zephyrinus was still Bishop of Rome, he traveled there, "praying to see the most ancient Church of the Romans," as he himself teaches us †. However, after staying there for a short while, he returned to Alexandria to his accustomed duty of catechesis.

<margin>
† Eusebius, ibid. ch. 19.
</margin>
Some time later, after a riot broke out in Alexandria and Emperor Caracalla led an army there, Origen fled secretly and sought out Palestine, fixing his home in Caesarea †. There he was asked by the Bishops of that region—namely Theoctistus of Caesarea and Alexander of Jerusalem—to discourse publicly in the Church and explain the Holy Scriptures, even though he was still a layman. Demetrius, however, grumbled and took this very poorly, complaining sharply to the Bishops by letter about the matter. They, in turn, defended their actions by citing more than one example of where this had been done before. Demetrius did not stop urging Origen's return by sending deacons, and finally, having returned to Alexandria, Origen performed the usual duties assigned to him again by Demetrius.

<margin>
† Ibid. ch. 21.
</margin>
When war later broke out between the Persians and the Romans, Emperor Alexander Severus came to Antioch accompanied by his mother, Julia Mamaea. She was a woman of primary piety and religious devotion who, stirred by the great fame of Origen, summoned him to Antioch by sending a military escort †. From him, she drew many lessons of piety and divine knowledge.

<margin>
* Ibid. ch. 23.
</margin>
Returning then to Alexandria *, at the urging of Ambrose—who liberally supplied the necessary expenses—he girded himself to write commentaries on the Holy Scripture, sharing the care of the Catechetical School with his student Heraclas. He cultivated both duties strenuously until he was called away to Achaia for the purpose of settling some ecclesiastical business. He set out for Caesarea again, where he was ordained a Priest <note>original: "Presbyter"</note> by the Bishops Theoctistus and Alexander in the year of Christ 228, in the 43rd year of his age.

<margin>

</margin>

Indeed, having called a Synod <note>a council of church leaders</note> *, he saw to it through synodical decrees that Origen should not only be expelled from Alexandria but also stripped of his priesthood. Whether this was done by one or two Synods matters little. Therefore, having left Alexandria in the year 233...

<margin>
3rd CENTURY, from the Year 200 AD.

...andria, he migrated again to Caesarea *, where he flourished with great reputation and honor among all. From his school came men most famous for their learning and piety, including Gregory the Wonderworker <note>original: "Gregorius Thaumaturgus," a 3rd-century bishop known for his missionary work</note> and his brother Athenodorus. However, when a persecution was stirred up against the Christians by Emperor Maximinus two years later, Origen thought it best to leave Caesarea. He withdrew to Firmilian, the Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to whom he was bound by the closest friendship. While the danger still pressed, both of them remained hidden at the home of Juliana, a matron as pious as she was wealthy, until the death of Maximinus. Once he was removed and peace was restored to the Churches, Origen left Cappadocia and, after staying for some time in Nicomedia, migrated once more to Athens. (Eusebius * testifies that while Origen stayed there, he finished his *Commentaries on Ezekiel*; Epiphanius || seems to suggest this was his first arrival in that city). Soon he returned to his former seat at Caesarea in Palestine; every place he visited was made famous by the writings he had recently published. Around that time, Origen was summoned to Arabia * by the urgent pleas of the Arabs to put to rest the heresy of Beryllus, the Bishop of Bostra. Having set out for that place, he suppressed the heresy in a public dialogue, refuted Beryllus, and brought him back to the truth. Moreover, as time went on, he conquered the stubbornness and errors of the Helcesaites <term>Helcesaitae: A Jewish-Christian gnostic sect that emphasized secret revelations</term> and other heretics in a similar fashion. Finally, when the Emperor Decius * stirred up a most grievous persecution against the Christians, Origen—already over sixty years old—received the violence of that lightning bolt at Tyre (where he had stayed for nearly a year after leaving Caesarea). For the malignant Demon moved all his forces against him with great persistence; so much so that he endured chains and bodily tortures, and the miseries of an iron collar in the deepest recess of the prison. For many days, his feet were stretched in the stocks <term>nerve: A wooden torture device or stocks where the legs were distended to painful widths</term> even unto the distance of four holes. In addition to this, he bravely sustained the threats of fire and whatever else was inflicted by his enemies. Despite these things, he survived into the times of Gallus and Volusianus, who succeeded Decius. He died at Tyre and was buried there in the first year of Emperor Valerian, in the year of Christ 254, at the age of 69. Pamphilus the Martyr, and many others with him (according to the testimony of Photius *), report that Origen departed this life through a famous martyrdom during the Decian persecution. However, Photius rightly notes this as an error, since Origen lasted until the times of Gallus and Volusianus. Furthermore, although Epiphanius * admits that Origen suffered many things under Decius, he expressly records that he did not achieve the end of martyrdom <note>In the early church, a "martyr" died for the faith, while a "confessor" suffered for it but survived.</note>. The error of Pamphilus (if indeed it was his) likely flowed from no other source than the fame of that celebrated confession which Origen bore at Caesarea under Decius’s persecution, which can rightly claim the title of a "preparatory martyrdom."

<margin>
* On Famous Men, chapter 54.
* Commonitorium, chapter 23, page 342.
</margin>

His character was most blameless, and he led a life that was plainly philosophical—rigid and severe almost beyond belief. Likewise, his reading and erudition were infinite; he was most skilled in languages, especially Hebrew and Greek. He also mastered Dialectic, Geometry, Astronomy, Arithmetic, Music, Grammar, and Rhetoric (to use the words of Jerome * regarding his "immortal genius," as he calls it), as well as the sects of all the philosophers. As a result, he had followers who were students of secular literature, and he interpreted these subjects for them daily. Wondrous crowds would gather to him, whom he received for the purpose of instructing them in the faith of Christ under the pretext of secular literature. I will add what Vincent of Lérins * says—somewhat lengthy, but elegant and appropriate for this place:

> "In Origen," he says, "there were so many excellent, so many singular, and so many wonderful qualities, that anyone would easily judge from the start that faith should be placed in his assertions. For if life creates authority, he possessed great industry, great modesty, patience, and endurance. If lineage or erudition matter, what could be more noble than one born in a house illustrated by martyrdom? Furthermore, having been deprived for Christ's sake not only of his father but also of all his resources, he made such progress amidst the straits of holy poverty that he was frequently afflicted, as they say, for the sake of the confession of the Lord's name. Nor were these the only qualities in him which would later serve as a temptation; there was also such power of genius—so profound, so sharp, so elegant—that he surpassed almost everyone by a great distance. There was such magnificence in his doctrine and total erudition that there were few things in divine philosophy, and perhaps none in human philosophy, which he did not thoroughly master. When Greek science yielded to him,

# The Age of Novatian.

<margin>
3rd CENTURY, from the Year 200 AD.
</margin>

> "...were studied, and works in Hebrew were also painstakingly produced. Truly, why should I mention his eloquence? His speech was so pleasant, so milky, so sweet, that to me it seemed not so much words as a kind of honey flowed from his mouth. What difficult matters did he not clarify through the power of his persuasion? What arduous tasks did he not make to seem most easy? But perhaps he wove his assertions only with the knots of arguments? On the contrary, there was plainly never any of the teachers who made use of more examples from the divine law. But, I believe, he wrote little? No mortal wrote more; so many are his works that it seems to me they can not only not be read through, but cannot even be found. And so that nothing should be lacking to him as tools for knowledge, he even possessed a full abundance of years."

<margin>
* Cited in Eusebius, book 6, ch. 19.
Epiphanius, Heresy 64.
* Epiphanius to John, in Jerome, Vol. ii. p. 158.
† Dissertation on the Ventriloquist <note>original: "de Engastrimythos," referring to the Witch of Endor</note>, p. 384.
* Ibid. p. 403.
</margin>

He certainly attained the greatest praise, by the testimony of Porphyry * himself, for those monuments of his talent which he left behind. For the rumor was that he had written six thousand books <note>The number 6,000 was a common ancient exaggeration for Origen's massive output, counting every individual letter and sermon as a "book."</note>; in which number it is necessary to include individual Homilies and Epistles. He used a style that was clear and easy, but excessively diffuse and redundant. For this reason, it was attributed as a fault to him by his adversaries that *he multiplied infinite words*. Hence, Eustathius † of Antioch, who was older than Jerome, so often objects against him that *he repeats the same things up and down in a babbling way* <note>original Greek: "ἄνω κὶ κάτω ταυτολογεῖ γεγωδῶς"</note>; that *he fills the world with the nonsense of his complaints, not even understanding this himself* <note>original Greek: "κεφαλογίᾳ μεμψίους ἀπεριπληθεῖ τὸν κόσμον, ὑδὲ τοῦτο ξυνίνων"</note>; and that *he poured forth an immense circuit of words either with or without measure, repeating the same things again and over with much triflings* <note>original Greek: "φλυαρείᾳ δὲ πολλῇ ταυτολογήσας"</note>. But the style matters little, provided there was nothing in his dogmas <note>Theological doctrines or core beliefs</note> to which his adversaries could object. It must be confessed, however, that he was condemned by almost the entire assembly of the ancients and was pressed by very heavy errors, the traces of which appear clearly enough in his works today. For besides many grave errors which the ancients either forced upon him against his will, or which were common to ancient writers, these main points of error are found everywhere in his writings; concerning which, among others, the illustrious Huetius has written most extensively in his *Origeniana*.

Among the Persons of the Holy Trinity, he wished for an inequality and grades of dignity to intercede; so that the Son was inferior to the Father, and the Holy Spirit inferior to both—just as a ray emitted from the solar body yields in dignity to the sun itself. He held that Christ's death profited not only men, but also Angels, Demons, and even the Stars (since, in his opinion, they were endowed with a rational soul and were thus capable of sin). He dreamed that all natures participating in reason—whether Demons, or human Souls, or any others whatever (for he imagined many others were masters of reason)—were all of the same nature among themselves and were created by God at the same time, namely from eternity. He believed they were then *minds* <note>original Greek: "νόας" (noas)</note>, but later, on account of their various movements and different use of free will, they were distributed into various orders of either Angels, Men, or Demons, having put on heavier or more subtle bodies according to the mode and measure of their crimes. For he believed that Angels and other rational beings consist of a body of their own kind, subtle and ethereal indeed, but nonetheless material; so that they deserved to be called incorporeal and spiritual only when compared to the other bodies of the world and in respect to the thicker ones.

Furthermore, he believed that minds (embracing all rational beings by 그 name), in whatever state they were engaged—whether of Angels, Men, etc.—according as they used their free will well or poorly (of which they never suffer even the smallest loss), could after shedding that state either ascend to a higher grade or be thrust down to a worse one. This occurred through a certain mutual *re-embodiment* <note>original Greek: "μετενσωματώσει" (metensomatosis), a concept similar to reincarnation or transmigration</note> made into eternity, so that one and the same mind could experience all orders of rational beings successively and quite often. Hence, human souls are thrust into the prison-houses of bodies only for the sake of a sin previously committed; when released from these, they become either Angels or Demons to pay for the crimes committed with temporary punishment. For he taught that the mystery of the Resurrection consists in this: that the souls of the Just are to be clothed in lighter and ethereal bodies, while the impious, according to the magnitude of their sins, are to undergo heavier or lighter torments. Furthermore, he taught that neither the punishments of the damned, nor of the Devils themselves, nor the joys of the blessed would be everlasting; but that when the punishments were completed and the earth burned up, there would be a future conversion and *restoration* <note>original Greek: "ἀποκατάστασιν" (apokatastasis), the doctrine that all creation will eventually be returned to its original state of harmony with God</note> of all things. All things would return to their original state, the earth would be inhabited again, and minds would be in the same place they were before they fell, through virtues or sins, into the nature of Angels, Demons, or Men.

# The Age of Novatian.

<margin>3rd CENTURY, from the Year 200 AD.</margin>

...deserved to be joined to a physical nature, and to obtain once more the opportunity of experiencing their own fates. Finally, that cycles of things of this sort revolve for eternity, and follow one another in turn. <note>This refers to Origen's controversial theory regarding the pre-existence of souls and the possibility of their falling into or rising out of material bodies in cosmic cycles.</note>

These errors, and others related to them which can easily be deduced as consequences, and especially the **Allegorical method of explaining the Holy Scriptures** (which he indulged in to such an extent that he interpreted the entire History of Paradise, almost the whole Mosaic law, and even many of the commands and deeds of Christ allegorically), brought upon him the hatred and hostility of many, and eventually, formal condemnations <note>original: "anathemata"</note>. While these views can by no means be defended, they deserve to be excused for many reasons. Many authors have argued this at length. Setting aside the apologies written by others, I will briefly note only these five points:

**i.** Many prejudices were absorbed by Origen while he was still a youth in the Platonic School, which were not so easy to shake off later; much is owed to the spirit of his age, in which such dogmas and especially the Allegorical Exposition of Scripture were highly favored; much is due to excessive haste in writing, and a mind distracted by many-sided anxieties and cares; and finally, much should be forgiven because of the fervent nature of Origen as he fought against Heretics. Hence, his defender in Photius <margin>* Cod. 117.</margin> attributes his error regarding the Trinity to an excessive zeal in refuting Sabellius <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century teacher who was condemned for "Modalism"—the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct persons, but merely three different roles or "masks" worn by a single God.</note>, and many of his other errors acknowledge a similar origin.

**ii.** Many things were said and written by him not as fixed dogma, but as problems for discussion <note>original: "problematicè"</note>, and merely for the sake of exercising the minds of others. What if he brought forward the greatest part of his erroneous Dogmas with great doubt and hesitation—as if he himself were not persuaded of their truth, nor hoping that readers would place faith in them? See the *Apology for Origen and his Dogmas* in Photius (location cited above); the *Apology of Pamphilus* in Jerome, Vol. 4, p. 172; Jerome's *Letter to Avitus*, Vol. 2, p. 151; and even Origen himself in <term>On First Principles</term> <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν" (peri archon)</note> book 2, ch. 6. Certainly, although Origen possessed a mind most eager for knowledge, he seems to have restrained his ardor with a certain natural timidity and modesty. Hence (as the famous Wetstein † rightly notes) <margin>† Notes on Origen’s Letter to Africanus, p. 169.</margin> the word <term>perhaps</term> <note>original: "τάχα" (takha)</note> or *perchance* or *maybe* occurs so often in his writings, as does the phrase <term>it seems</term> <note>original: "δοκεῖ" (dokei)</note>, whenever he puts forward something unusual or new. Both were evident in his correction of the Seventy Interpreters [the Septuagint]; for when he found it corrupted in many ways (I am speaking of the <term>common</term> <note>original: "κοινῇ" (koine)</note> and vulgar edition, corrected from the original), he did indeed set out to correct it. But he did so without the bold daring and intrepid heart with which Jerome later acted. The learned man [Wetstein] pursues this point further in the place cited.

**iii.** The books of Origen which contain errors more than others were not written for the general use of the Church, but for the private use of his friends, and were brought to light not by himself, but by others. Thus, he complained to Pope Fabian about his close friend Ambrosius, *that he had brought into public what was published in secret*. See <margin>† In Jerome to Pammachius on the errors of Origen, Vol. 2, p. 193. Loc. cit.</margin> especially the *Apology of Pamphilus* on this matter, pp. 174, 177. Furthermore, Jerome † himself admitted that Origen repented of these very things.

**iv.** Many opinions condemned in Origen opposed no articles of the Catholic Church, nor Apostolic Traditions, nor decrees of Councils—at least at that time; instead, they were either obscure questions debated only in the Schools of Philosophers, or notions less conveniently invented by him in recent times. Certainly, in the very preface to the work <term>On First Principles</term> <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν"</note>, Origen explicitly lays down as a foundation that the Ecclesiastical Preaching must be preserved through the order of succession handed down from the Apostles and remaining in the Churches until that time; and that only that truth should be believed which does not disagree with Ecclesiastical Tradition.

**v.** It must be noted that many of Origen’s writings were foully corrupted by Heretics, who either distorted his opinions or inserted their own under his name. Rufinus showed this to be the case against Jerome in the entire *Apology* he composed for Origen, and in the Preface to the books <term>On First Principles</term> which he translated into Latin. Indeed, Origen himself complained while still alive that people dared to do this, not only in the writing cited by Photius, but also in the Letter he wrote to the Alexandrians, which Rufinus included in his *Apology*. From this, Rufinus † rightly concludes <margin>† Apology p. 194. Preface to the book on Hebrew Names.</margin> that it could in no way happen that *a man so learned, so prudent (whom Jerome says no one but the unskilled denies is the teacher of the Churches after the Apostles), certainly*

...which even his accusers can grant—being neither a fool nor insane—he would not write things so contrary and repugnant to his own views; so much so that at times, and in the same places, or what I might call the very next chapter, statements of a contrary sense are found inserted. Certainly, in the past, Theotimus, Bishop of the Scythians <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his holiness and long hair, who famously defended Origen's memory against the attacks of Epiphanius of Salamis.</note>, a man to be revered for his piety and holiness, responded to Epiphanius (who was pressuring him to condemn Origen's books) †, that he neither wished to treat with contempt one who had long ago died in piety, nor did he dare to attempt such an impious deed as to condemn those things which the Elders did by no means reject—especially since he knew that no evil doctrine was found in Origen's books. I will summarize everything using the words of Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt. 

> "Concerning him," he says *, "saving the faith of the Fathers, I would say either that he did not write these things at all, but they were maliciously forged by Heretics to darken his famous name and titled with his name; or, if he did write them, he did not establish them as his firm belief <note>original: "ex sententiâ"</note>, but discussed them as a matter of opinion. For as he himself says, he had learned the dogmas of the Philosophers and Heretics so that he would not be unprepared to convict them if he were ignorant of what they held; and perhaps when he touched upon their errors in his writing, he was falsely accused of saying these things from himself. But even if he did write the aforementioned heresies as his settled belief, as some believe, we must feel great compassion for a man of such an erudite heart, who provided us with such a wealth of learning. If there are any flaws in his writings, a certain luminous and heavenly splendor from those things which he wrote faithfully can overcome them."

---

->His works, the knowledge of which has reached us.<-

<margin>† *Heresies*, 64.</margin>
Epiphanius † and others testify that every single book of Scripture was illuminated by the study of Origen. This was truly done by him in a threefold manner. For he either poured out whatever his genius and learning supplied in lengthy **Commentaries**; or he illustrated all the more obscure points with only brief **Scholia** <term>Scholia: Short explanatory notes on a text, often focusing on grammar or specific difficult passages.</term>; or he lowered himself to the understanding of the common people and explained selected passages of Scripture less rigorously through **Homilies** <term>Homilies: Sermons or informal religious discourses intended for a general audience.</term>. And he who applied a triple kind of Exposition to interpreting the Scriptures was also accustomed to extract and investigate a triple sense from them: the **Historical** (which they also call the Literal sense), the **Mystical**, and the **Moral**. Generally, he proceeds from the Historical sense to the Mystical, and from the Mystical to the Moral, although he occasionally changes this order. Furthermore, whatever of these Exegetical <term>Exegetical: Relating to the critical explanation or interpretation of a text, particularly religious scripture.</term> works either survive or are mentioned by the Ancients follow next. Before we list them, however, it is worth noting that great care must be used in distinguishing Origen's Homilies. For some he published having written them thoughtfully; others he allowed to be taken down by **stenographers** <note>original: "actuariis" — these were fast-writing clerks who recorded speeches in real-time.</note> as they were delivered off-the-cuff. He labored over the former at various times; but the extemporaneous ones (those committed to writing) were all delivered after the 60th year of his age. Many of both kinds survive.

***Two books of Mystical Homilies on Genesis.***
***Thirteen books of Commentaries on Genesis.*** Certain fragments survive in Eusebius, Pamphilus, and the *Philocalia* <note>An anthology of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>.
***Seventeen Homilies*** survive in Latin (translated by Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia, whose Latin translations preserved many of Origen's works that were lost in the original Greek.</note>); these are different from the *Mystical* ones. They seem to have been delivered extemporaneously.
***Volumes of Commentaries on Exodus.*** Fragments of them can be found in the *Philocalia*, chapter 26.
***Scholia on Exodus.***
***Twelve Homilies on Exodus***, translated by Rufinus. They appear to be extemporaneous.
***Scholia on Leviticus.***
***Sixteen Homilies on Leviticus*** survive from Rufinus's translation. They seem to be extemporaneous. A fragment of ***two Homilies*** on Leviticus is presented in the *Philocalia*, chapter 1; not even a trace <note>original: "ne apicem quidem" — literally "not even a tiny point," emphasizing the total lack of similarity.</note> of this is found in the 2nd Homily of the Latin Edition, or others. From this, it is easy to understand that there were several collections of Homilies on Leviticus.
The same can be shown regarding the Homilies on other books of Scripture by similar arguments.

# The Age of Novatian.

<margin>3rd CENTURY, from 200 AD.</margin>
Twenty-eight **Homilies on Numbers** survive in the translation by Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD) was a monk and scholar who translated many Greek works into Latin, often adapting them for a Western audience.</note>, and they appear to have been delivered extemporaneously. Rufinus also reveals that Origen published *Scholia* <note>Short, technical notes explaining difficult words or grammatical points in a text.</note>; however, these were so thoroughly mixed with the Homilies by Rufinus when he set them forth in Latin that they can be regarded as a single, unified work.

Origen declares in several places that he once discussed **Deuteronomy**; and Cassiodorus <note>A 6th-century Roman statesman and monk who preserved many classical and Christian texts.</note> mentions eight of Origen's homilies on this book. Furthermore, Jerome calls these volumes on the Pentateuch Origen's *Hexaemeron* <note>original: "Hexaemeron." While this term usually refers to the "Six Days of Creation," Jerome applies it here to the collective volumes of the Pentateuch. See Epistle to Pammachius on the Errors of Origen, Volume 2, p. 192.</note>.

On the **Book of Joshua**, twenty-six Homilies survive from the translation by Rufinus. They are extemporaneous. A fragment from the 20th Homily is preserved in chapter 12 of the *Philocalia* <note>A collection of Origen's writings compiled by the famous Church Fathers Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>.

On the **Book of Judges**, nine Homilies survive in the same translation.

On the **Books of Kings**, only two Homilies remain in total. The first, on 1 Kings chapters 1 and 2, exists only in Latin from Rufinus's version; the other, on 1 Kings 28, titled *On the Ventriloquist* <note>original: "de Engastrimytho." Both appear to be extemporaneous. Furthermore, Origen testifies that he once discussed in church before the people the two prostitutes whose dispute Solomon settled. Cassiodorus moreover writes that he found four of Origen's homilies on the first book of Kings, one on the second book of Kings, and another quite lengthy one on the second book of Chronicles. He also relates that he saw single homilies by Origen on the two books of Ezra, which were explained in the Latin language <note>original: "Romanâ oratione"</note> by the priest Bellator.

Whatever survives today of the work on Isaiah is poorly divided into six Homilies; the first two were translated by Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the primary translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) and a complex admirer of Origen's scholarship.</note>, while the others have been attributed to Jerome by some, though incorrectly. In fact, they were translated by Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, once a friend and later a rival of Jerome, known for his somewhat loose translations of Greek works into Latin.</note>. A fragment from Volume 2 is preserved in Chapter 26 of the *Philocalia* <note>An anthology of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>.

In addition to these, Jerome's *Commentary on Isaiah* mentions two other books under Origen’s name regarding the "four-faced" <note>original: "τετραμόρφῳ" (tetramorpho). On **Jeremiah**, there were forty-five Homilies, according to Cassiodorus <note>A 6th-century Roman statesman and monk who founded the Vivarium monastery to preserve classical and Christian learning.</note>.

Of these, fourteen survive in a confused order in the Latin edition of Origen's works, translated by Jerome. Nineteen exist in Greek across various manuscripts; twelve of these are among those found in Latin by Jerome. From the manuscripts, Michael Ghislerius published the seven that were missing from Jerome’s collection in his *Commentary on Jeremiah* (Lyon, 1623). Later, Balthasar Corderius published the full nineteen (or rather eighteen, as the last belongs to Clement of Alexandria) in Greek under the name of Cyril (Paris, 1648). Finally, Huet published them, correctly restored to Origen. A fragment of Homily 39 is found in Chapter 12 of the *Philocalia*. Huet maintains they were delivered extemporaneously.

On **Lamentations**, there were nine Volumes, of which Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the foundational historian of the early Church.</note> records that only five reached his own age.

Regarding the Commentaries on **Hosea**, Jerome testifies that Origen wrote two *Volumes*, in which he nevertheless barely explained a third of the book, from the beginning up to the vision of the Chariots; specifically, a small book to which he gave the title *On How Ephraim is Named in Hosea* <note>original: "περὶ τοῦ πῶς ὀνομασθῆ ἐν τῷ Ωσηὲ Ἐφραιμ"</note>, in which he intended to show that whatever is said against Ephraim should be referred to the person of Heretics; also another volume that was "headless and incomplete" <note>original: "ἀκέφαλον καὶ ἀτέλεστον" (akephalon kai ateleston), meaning it lacked both its beginning and its conclusion.</note>. Of these, whatever survives in Greek—namely the portion of the Commentaries starting from Chapter 13, verse 36, and reaching Chapter 22, verse 33—was published by Huet, together with several fragments from Volumes 2 and 8 preserved by Pamphilus, Eusebius, and the *Philocalia*. Whatever survives in Latin (specifically the part of the Commentaries starting at Chapter 16, verse 33 and continuing nearly to the end of the Gospel) is found in the Latin Edition, poorly divided into thirty-five Homilies. The translator, as Huet conjectures, was either Epiphanius the Scholar or the priest Bellator, both associates of Cassiodorus.

# The Age of Novatian.

<margin>
3rd CENTURY.
From the Year 200.
</margin>

In his 30th treatise on Matthew, Origen promised an *Exposition on the Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>; whether he actually produced it remains unclear.

Whatever could be found in Greek of these exegetical works <note>original: "ἐξηγητικῶν"</note> was published in two folio volumes at Rouen in 1668 by the illustrious Pierre Daniel Huet. He added his own "Origenist Notes and Dissertations," into which he gathered everything pertaining to Origen, his doctrines, and his books, "with the whole bag" <note>original: "ὅλῳ τῷ θυλάκῳ"—a Greek idiom meaning he included every single detail or resource available</note>. We gratefully acknowledge that we have received no small amount of light from these notes while reviewing Origen’s writings. A Frankfurt edition recently reprinted Huet’s work in two folio volumes in 1686.

During his retreat at the home of the noble lady Juliana, Origen compiled and published a work that was as magnificent as it was useful, which he called the *Hexapla* <note>meaning "six-fold," a massive comparative edition of the Old Testament</note>. This work consisted of "Double Hebrew" <note>referring to the Hebrew text written in both Hebrew and Greek characters</note> and four versions of the Old Testament—namely, the Septuagint (LXX), Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus—arranged in as many columns. The layout was such that the Hebrew text written in its own letters occupied the first column; the same text written in Greek characters occupied the second; the version by Aquila the third; that of Symmachus the fourth; the Septuagint of the seventy elders the fifth; and the version by Theodotion the sixth. Among these, Origen had carefully revised and corrected the Septuagint version. Using Theodotion’s version, he filled in whatever was missing from the Septuagint that appeared in the Hebrew, marking these additions with an asterisk (*). Conversely, whatever the Septuagint had added that was not faithful to the Hebrew manuscripts, he marked with an obelus <note>a symbol (†) used in ancient manuscripts to indicate suspected or spurious text</note>. Later, when two other Greek versions were added and placed in the final positions, the work became the *Octapla* <note>meaning "eight-fold"</note>. The first of these extra versions was found in jars at Jericho during the reign of Caracalla by a scholar among those in Jerusalem; the second was found under the emperor Alexander Severus at Nicopolis near Actium by a certain disciple of Origen. With the further addition of another version of the Psalms, which had been found along with the Jericho manuscript, the *Enneapla* <note>meaning "nine-fold"</note> emerged. However, some maintain that the *Hexapla* and *Octapla* were one and the same work, named sometimes for six columns and sometimes for eight. For the anonymous versions were not complete, but contained only certain books of Holy Scripture. Thus it happened that the work was partly a *Hexapla* and partly an *Octapla*; and finally, by counting the last version of the Psalms, partly an *Enneapla*, though the name of the entire massive biblical collection was taken from the main title.

<margin>
* In *The Life of Origen*, No. 18. *Lives of the Primitive Fathers*, vol. 1.
</margin>
In time, for the sake of students who lacked either the leisure or the means to acquire the *Hexapla*, Origen published the *Tetrapla* <note>meaning "four-fold"</note>. This was compiled from the four most well-known Greek versions—namely Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion—arranged in the same order and method as in the *Hexapla*. Both works have perished. Only a specimen of the *Hexapla* from a manuscript belonging to Cardinal Barberini is presented in Volume 6 of the Walton Polyglot Bible <note>a famous 17th-century multi-language Bible edited by Brian Walton</note>, from which we once sketched a certain diagram of the *Hexapla*, a copy of which we have provided elsewhere. *

There are two books *On the Resurrection*; Eusebius mentions this many, as does Jerome when he cites them. Pamphilus, in his *Apology*, took some fragments from the first and second books. A small portion of the same work is also found in Book 2, Chapter 10 of *On First Principles* <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν"</note>.

->*Two Dialogues on the Resurrection.*<-

There are ten books of *Stromata* <note>Miscellanies</note>; the last of these consisted almost entirely of a brief commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. Jerome preserves a specimen taken from Book 6, in which Origen contends that it is sometimes permissible to use a lie. Jerome also provides a rather long fragment from Book 10 in his *Commentary on Galatians*, chapter 4, page 191.

*Exhortation to Martyrdom*, written during the reign of the Emperor Maximinus; it was dedicated to Ambrosius and Protoctetus, a priest of the Church of Caesarea. It survives in Greek and Latin, first edited with notes by Wetstein at *Basel, 1674, in quarto.*

Origen had also written a letter on the same subject to his father, who was destined for martyrdom, while Origen was still a boy; Eusebius repeats some words from this letter in Book 6, Chapter 2.

*The Acts of the Disputation of Origen held with Beryllus*, about which more is said in the section on Beryllus <note>Beryllus of Bostra was a bishop who fell into heresy regarding the nature of Christ; Origen successfully convinced him of his error at a council in 244</note>. Besides this Dialogue (for so the Acts are titled), Origen is said to have committed others to writing as well. Rufinus mentions one written by him which was corrupted by the heretic Candidus, with whom the debate had been held. At the beginning of his Letter on Susanna, Africanus praises Origen’s *Dialogue against Agnomon*.

*More than one hundred Letters*, which Eusebius records were collected by himself and organized into dedicated books; of these, some remain complete.

*The Letter to Julius Africanus regarding the History of Susanna*, written around the year 238. It was first published in Greek by Hoeschel at *Augsburg* in 1602, in quarto; later in Greek and Latin with notes by Wetstein, in the location previously cited.

*The Letter to Gregory Thaumaturgus* <note>Gregory "the Miracle-Worker," a student of Origen</note>, an exhortation to the study of the Holy Scriptures, which is presented in the 13th chapter of the *Philocalia* <note>An anthology of Origen’s writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen</note>.

*Certain fragments of other Letters* are produced here and there by the Ancient writers: by Eusebius in Book 6, chapters 2, 19, and 36; by Rufinus, Jerome, Cedrenus, Suidas, and in the *Catenae* <note>Collections of biblical commentary by various Church Fathers</note>.

*Four books <term>On First Principles</term>* <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν" (peri archōn)</note>, written before the year 233. These are truly most difficult and obscure; they exist in the Latin edition of Origen’s Works from the version by Rufinus, which was produced with very poor character <note>original: "pessimâ fide"</note>, since many things were omitted, many interpolated, and many changed for the better, as Rufinus himself does not hide. Rufinus used a similar art in the other books of Origen he translated, so much so that Origen’s true opinion can scarcely—if at all—be discerned due to the untrustworthy translator's additions, truncations, and interpolations. For this reason, Jerome prepared another version of the books *On First Principles* so that he might expose Origen's errors and Rufinus's deceit to the Latin Church. However, his version has perished through the injury of time. This work was a perpetual field of slander and insult for Origen’s adversaries. On this occasion, I may be permitted to include here Origen’s Epitaph, written by a certain scholar in Origen's own person, which the illustrious Mabillon found prefixed to the books *On First Principles* in a very old Corbie Manuscript. This inscription is placed before it:

* Analecta.

### ORIGEN’S TITLE UPON HIS TOMB, COMPOSED BY HIMSELF.

> I am that Origen, once the truest Teacher,
> Whom the bright grace of faith first brought forth.
> If you wish to believe me, I wrote so many thousands of books,
> As the number of armed men a legion sends into battle.
> No blasphemy ever touched my thoughts,
> But I was upright, and watchful, and safe from the enemy.
> Only the words of the *First Principles* <note>original: "Periarchōn"</note> brought me ruin;
> Because of these, weapons press upon me, hurl'd from every side.

*Eight books Against Celsus*, written at the request of Ambrose around the year 247, against that Epicurean philosopher who had attacked the Christian religion in a book to which he gave the title <term>The True Word</term> <note>original: "ἀληθὴς λόγος" (alēthēs logos)</note>. D. Hoeschel first published these in Greek and Latin with notes at *Augsburg* in 1605, in quarto; then together with the most learned annotations of William Spencer at *Cambridge* in 1658, in quarto. They were reprinted in the same place a few years ago.

*Interpretation of Hebrew Names and Measures of the New Testament*, in imitation of Philo’s little book on the Interpretation of Hebrew Names of the Old Testament; Origen even published his own work joined to Philo's book. The author of the *Questions to the Orthodox* mentions it. Jerome presents a likeness of it—and perhaps a freer translation—in his book *On Hebrew Names of the New Testament*.

*A book On Prayer*, produced at the urging of Ambrose and Tatiana; in which he deals accurately enough with the nature, power, and various types of praying, and other matters looking to this subject. However, he puts forward certain dogmas that are not healthy enough, and he does so <term>with a bare head</term> <note>original: "γυμνῇ τῇ κεφαλῇ" (gymnē tē kephalē) – a Greek idiom meaning openly, boldly, or without disguise</note>, and which can scarcely be excused by any gloss. For example, in Section 1, where he denies that prayers...

## SUPPOSITITIOUS WORKS.
<note>Works historically attributed to Origen but likely written by others.</note>

*A Dialogue against the Marcionites concerning the Right Faith in God*, held with Megethius, Marcus, and other heretics: Wetstein contends with several arguments that this is a genuine work of Origen, although the greater part of learned men feel the contrary. There is at least a justified reason for doubting its authenticity. The illustrious Huet <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet, a famous 17th-century scholar of Origen</note> assigns it to Maximus, as was said above under the entry for Maximus. This dialogue was first published in Greek and Latin, illustrated with notes, by the famous Wetstein in the place cited.

<margin>On Job</margin>
* Three books of Commentaries on the first three chapters of Job. These are found in the Latin edition of Origen's Works.
* Short commentaries, or Scholia, on the whole book, translated by Perionius.
* Four Homilies, which have been discovered to belong to Chrysostom.

*Huet attributes these Commentaries and Scholia to two Arian authors from the sect of the Lucianists.*

*Commentary on the Gospel of Mark*, which is said to exist in Greek in the Royal Library at Paris and at Corpus Christi, Oxford. In some manuscripts it is attributed to Origen, in others to Cyril of Alexandria, and in the rest to Victor of Antioch. Theodore Peltanus published a Latin version of it under the name of Victor.

*Nine Homilies on Various Subjects*, which we mentioned previously, to which a tenth on Mary Magdalene is usually added. They exist in the Latin edition of Origen.

*The Philosophical Investigations of Origen, or a book on the sects and dogmas of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Ὠριγένους φιλοσοφούμενα"</note>. In the preface, the author claims to have been a Bishop. Huet assigns this to Epiphanius; see more on this in Huet's *Origeniana*, book 3, chapter 4, section 9.

*The Lament or Complaint of Origen*. This is found in Latin in the Latin editions of Origen’s Works.

*Scholia on the Lord's Prayer, and on the Songs of the Blessed Virgin, Zacharias, and Simeon*, which Fedéric Morel published in Greek at Paris in 1601, in octavo, under the name of Origen (or as he himself noted, under the name of another "anonymous" <note>original: "ἀνωνύμου"</note> Doctor). However, Huet concludes from the *Library of the Fathers* that Peter of Laodicea is the legitimate author. But the *Scholia on the Lord's Prayer* seem to be by Origen himself, and are placed after the short book *On Prayer* in the Oxford edition—if indeed they are the same Scholia, for the Paris edition is not currently at hand.

*A Short Book on the Solitary Life of the Clergy*, which is found among the works of Cyprian and has been attributed to Origen by some, but wrongly; although its author is of no small antiquity, being at least no later than the age of Jerome.

The Works of Origen, as many as are held in Latin only, were published in Paris in 1512, 1522, 1530, 1536; and in Basel in 1536; a more complete version appeared there in 1545 and 1571; and then in Paris in 1574 under the care of Gilbert Genebrard, and again in 1604 and 1619.

<summary>This page concludes the bibliography of Origen's genuine writings, including the Philocalia, and begins an extensive catalog of "Supposititious Works"—texts whose authorship is debated or has been reassigned to other figures like Maximus or Peter of Laodicea.</summary>
