</margin>
Finally, the reader should be warned that there was another Origen, a contemporary of our own, who was a Pagan Philosopher. When he entered his school, Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> stood up for him and treated him with the highest veneration. He is mentioned by Longinus †, Porphyry *, Hierocles ||, Eunapius †, Proclus *, and others. Even very learned men often wrongly confuse him with our Origen.

<margin>
|| Found in Photius, codex 214.
† In the *Life of Porphyry*.
* *Platonic Theology*, book 2, chapter 4, page 90.
230.
|| *Heresies*, 36.
† Letter found in Suidas under the entry "Origenes," page 390; and in Cedrenus, page 208.
Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 56.
* In the place cited.
</margin>
AMBROSIUS of Alexandria, most noble by his distinguished lineage, his way of life (for he was "one of the prominent men in the royal courts," says Epiphanius || <note>original: "εἷς τῶν διαφανῶν ἐν αὐλαῖς βασιλικαῖς"</note>), the abundance of his resources, and no less by the sharpness of his talent and wit—and what is greater, by his piety and his public confession of the Christian name. He flourished around the year 230. He had a wife, Marcella, by whom he had several children. Having been ensnared by the deceits of the Valentinian and Marcionite sects <note>Gnostic groups that the early Church considered heretical</note>, he was brought back to the right faith and Catholic truth through the work of Origen. He was made a Deacon of the Church of Alexandria, from which time the closest bond of friendship existed between him and Origen. These most faithful friends often lived together, and with joined studies promoted literary work with such burning passion that they did not abstain from comparing copies of the Holy Volumes even while dining; nor was it permitted to walk after dinner or to relax the body in rest. Indeed, even at that time they were free for literature, with their studies prolonged deep into the night—to say nothing of their morning labors, which were dragged out to the ninth or sometimes even the tenth hour, as Origen himself † teaches us. Ambrosius daily proposed questions to Origen for the solving of doubts, and he urged him to write Commentaries on Holy Scripture with innumerable prods—not only with words, but in actual fact; for this reason he was called a "task-master" <note>original: "ἐργοδιώκτης," someone who drives another to work</note> by him. For he generously supplied the necessary expenses to support seven or more shorthand writers <note>term: Notarios</note> who would be ready in shifts while Origen dictated, and as many book-copyists <note>term: Librarios</note> along with girls skilled in elegant writing. Origen also not infrequently submitted his own writings to him to be corrected. He died after the persecution of Maximinus, while Origen was still among the living. He is worthy of blame for this one thing: that although he was wealthy, when dying he did not remember his friend and teacher, who was already an old man struggling with poverty. He wrote letters to Origen, from which—in the judgment of Jerome *—it was clearly established that he was of a not inelegant talent. N. E.

<margin>
230.
† Book 6, chapter 20.
* Annotations, page 123.
|| *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 60.
† Book 6, chapter 33.
</margin>
BERYLLUS, Bishop of Bostra in Arabia. He flourished around the year 230. After he had ruled his church prudently and faithfully for a long time, he finally slipped into new dogmas entirely foreign to the Catholic faith, daring to assert that our Lord and Savior, before He lived among men, did not exist in the distinctness of His own person; and that He did not have His own Divinity, but only the Father's Divinity residing within Him. After many conversations and disputes between bishops had been held back and forth on this matter, Origen was asked, along with the others, to confer with him. Origen, bringing forth reasons and demonstrations, took the man as if by the hand and led him back to the way of truth, recalling him to his former and sound opinion. He wrote scholarly works and letters, especially to Origen, in which he thanked him. There also exist various monuments of his elegant talent, which Eusebius † calls "various beauties" <note>original: "διαφόρους φιλοκαλίας," often used to mean an anthology of fine writings</note>, by which Henri Valois * thinks hymns and poems are meant. In the time of Jerome || there existed a *Dialogue of Origen and Beryllus*, in which those heresies were refuted. I believe this is the same work referred to by Eusebius †: "there are still carried down to this day writings both to Beryllus, etc." <note>original: "φέρεται εἰσέτι νῦν ἔγγραφα τῷ τε Βηρύλλῳ"</note> Even today, *published writings* survive concerning both Beryllus and the Synod assembled for that cause, in which are contained the questions proposed against him by Origen, the disputes held in his Church, and the individual things that were done then. N. E.

<margin>
232.
* Chronicles, year 229.
† *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 64.
</margin>
GEMINUS, or Geminianus, a Presbyter of Antioch. He flourished around the year 232 under Zebennus, Bishop of Antioch, who, as Eusebius notes *, ascended the chair of the Church of Antioch in the year 229. Jerome † testifies that he composed a few monuments of his talent. However, what those works were, neither Eusebius nor Jerome himself have passed down to posterity. N. E.

### TRYPHON

**TRYPHON**, a student of Origen, to whom Origen wrote several letters. He flourished around the year 235. Nothing else remains to be said about him other than what Jerome mentions \*: that he was highly learned in the Scriptures. This is evidenced by many of his minor works, especially the book he composed *On the Red Heifer* <note>original: "De Vaccâ Rufâ"</note> regarding Numbers chapter 19, and *On the Divided Parts* <note>original: "de Dichotomematibus" — referring to the ritual "cutting in two" of animals</note> *that were placed with Abraham’s dove and turtle-dove in Genesis.* N. E.

---

<margin>
233.
Eusebius, book 6, chapters 26, 27.
</margin>

### FIRMILIANUS

**FIRMILIANUS**, a man distinguished by his noble birth, piety, and learning, became the Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia around the year 233. He shared a close friendship with Origen, who was then serving as a teacher in Caesarea in Palestine. Indeed, he was so well-disposed toward Origen that he would sometimes invite him to his own province for the benefit of the churches, and at other times would travel as far as Judea just to visit him, staying for some time to gain a greater understanding of divine matters. He was held in such high regard by everyone that he was always present when the more serious business of the Church was debated during that time. 

He engaged in great disputes with Pope Stephen of Rome regarding the <term>Doctrine of Re-baptizing Heretics</term> <note>A 3rd-century controversy over whether people baptized by "heretical" groups needed to be baptized again to join the mainstream Church</note>. Having called a council of the bishops of Galatia, Phrygia, Cilicia, and the neighboring provinces at Iconium, he confirmed the opinion of Cyprian—who stood firmly against Stephen—that heretics must be baptized anew. For this reason, he was treated poorly by Stephen, who broke the bond of ecclesiastical peace and cut him off from communion with his church. 

In the year 265, he took part in the Eastern Synod held at Antioch against Paul of Samosata, the bishop of that city, and played a major role in it. In that council, he condemned the novelty of the doctrine introduced by Paul, but he deferred the condemnation of the man himself when Paul promised to change his views. Firmilian was deceived by a man of no faith, hoping that the matter could be resolved for the best without any loss to religion. The synodic letter from that council, rescued from obscurity by Turrianus, exists in Greek and Latin in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* (Paris, 1624, Vol. I, p. 302). However, in the year 270, while traveling to the second Synod of Antioch gathered against the same Paul, he reached Tarsus and died there at a great age, as the Fathers of that Synod testify in their encyclical letter †.

<margin>
† Found in Eusebius, book 7, chapter 30.
</margin>

Among the letters of Cyprian, there exists a *Letter to Cyprian* from Firmilian. It appears to have been translated into Latin by Cyprian, whose style it clearly reflects. In this letter, after confirming Cyprian's view on the baptism of heretics, he harshly criticizes Pope Stephen for his inhumanity, audacity, insolence, and other wicked deeds. Basil mentions the books that Firmilian left behind in *On the Holy Spirit* (chapter 29, p. 360), though he does not say how many there were or what they were about.

---

<margin>
244.
</margin>

### NEPOS

**NEPOS**, a Bishop in Egypt, perhaps of some city in the Arsinoite district. He flourished around the year 244. He maintained that the promises made to holy men in the Sacred Volumes should be understood in a "Jewish sense" <note>meaning a literal, physical fulfillment rather than a symbolic one</note>. Consequently, he taught that after the resurrection, a period of a thousand years filled with physical delights would be granted to the saints on this earth. He drew his arguments for this doctrine mostly from the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. 

While the Orthodox argued that the oracles of that book should be understood in a spiritual and allegorical sense, Nepos composed a *book on this question* which he titled *Refutation of the Allegorizers* <note>original: "ἔλεγχον ἀλληγοριστῶν"</note>. This work was received with such favor throughout Egypt that a schism occurred, and entire churches fell away from the right faith. For this reason, Dionysius of Alexandria refuted the book of the (by then deceased) Nepos in two volumes titled *On the Promises*. After calling a synod of the priests of Arsinoe and holding a debate, Dionysius brought the followers of Nepos back to sound belief. 

Nepos also wrote many psalms and hymns for the use of the Church, which were quite pious and were praised by Dionysius himself. However, these works of our Nepos seem to have been lost long ago. One might wonder if this is the same Nepos whose "apocryphal book" is condemned in the <term>Pseudo-Gelasian Decree</term> <note>A famous 5th or 6th-century list of books prohibited or approved by the Church</note>?

# The Age of Novatian.

<header>The Age of Novatian.</header>

<margin>
3RD CENTURY, from the year 200.
</margin>

**THASCIUS CÆCILIUS CYPRIANUS**, a native of Carthage, was renowned for his profession in the art of oratory. He acquired great glory, wealth, and honors for himself; he was accustomed to banquet feasts and lavish meals, conspicuous in his costly clothing, shining with gold and purple, and delighted by the <term>fasces</term> <note>The "fasces" were bundles of rods and axes carried by officials, symbolizing their legal power and social rank in Rome.</note> and high honors. He was surrounded by crowds of clients and dignified by a frequent retinue of dutiful followers—as he himself describes <margin>* *To Donatus*, page 2.</margin> his own life. He spent by far the greater part of his life among the Gentiles as an advocate of idolatry, until through the mediation of Caecilius, a Presbyter of Carthage (whose name he subsequently adopted as his own), he transitioned from secular error to the faith of Christ. Having drawn in the Holy Spirit from heaven, a fruitful second birth restored him as a new man. Led by a sound and probable conjecture, the Reverend Bishop of Chester <note>Referring to John Pearson (1633–1686), the Bishop of Chester, a renowned scholar who wrote the *Annales Cyprianici*.</note> determined in his highly accurate *Cyprianic Annals* that this occurred in the year 246.

Having become a <term>neophyte</term> <note>A person newly converted to a religion.</note>, he sold his goods and distributed the proceeds for the use of the poor. Immediately after his baptism, he seems to have written his short book *To Donatus*, and not long after, another work *On the Vanity of Idols*. In these, he was a rival of his master Tertullian and especially of Minucius Felix, from whom he translated many passages word-for-word. At the end of the year 247, he was made a Presbyter of Carthage; and in the following year, now a mature man, he was promoted to the Episcopal throne of that most celebrated Church after the death of Donatus. This happened at the insistence of the common people, who almost carried him away by force, even while he himself humbly resisted and sought a hiding place.

He had barely graced that seat for the space of a year and a little more when, the persecution under Emperor Decius having broken out, he was frequently called "to the lion" in the Circus <note>A common Roman demand for Christians to be thrown to wild animals during public games.</note>. He sought a retreat and was proscribed under this formal decree:
> IF ANYONE HOLDS OR POSSESSES ANY OF THE GOODS OF CÆCILIUS CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF THE CHRISTIANS, etc.

In this retreat, so as not to seem entirely absent from the service of his Church, he wrote the thirty surviving Epistles. Once the persecution was quieted in the year 251, he emerged from his hiding place and was restored to his Church. He held a Synod at Carthage regarding the cause of the <term>Lapsed</term> <note>The "Lapsi" were Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under threat of death during Roman persecutions.</note>. At this synod, it was decided that their penance should be long-drawn-out, so that hope of peace was not entirely denied to them, nor was ecclesiastical discipline loosened. However, a Synod held on the <term>Ides</term> <note>May 15th.</note> of May the following year dealt with them a bit more gently, decreeing that because of the impending "storms" <note>The threat of further persecution.</note>, peace should be granted to the repentant lapsed. 

A few months later, when a deadly plague and famine were raging, Cyprian provided for his people through his preaching, his own hands, and his works. On that same occasion, he composed a most elegant little book *On Mortality*. In the year 253, he celebrated a Council of 66 Bishops at Carthage, in which the *Epistle to Fidus on Infant Baptism* was written. In the year 255, a controversy arose concerning the <term>Baptism of Heretics</term> <note>A major 3rd-century debate over whether baptism performed by heretical groups was valid, or if converts needed to be re-baptized.</note>, which Cyprian attempted to settle by a decree of the Council of Carthage, ruling that the baptism of heretics was invalid and completely null. The most learned author of the *Cyprianic Annals* shows that a Synod was held for this purpose this year. A Synod of 71 Bishops held the following year confirmed that opinion with its authority. 

However, since quite a few resisted—most notably Stephen, the Bishop of Rome—Cyprian convoked a larger and more crowded Council on the <term>Kalends</term> <note>September 1st.</note> of September of that same year, in which 87 Bishops, pronouncing their votes individually, reinforced the earlier decree. In the year 257, the Emperor Valerian moved a persecution against the Christians, at which time Cyprian, having made his confession before the Proconsul Aspasius, was sent into exile. He was banished to Curubis, a small town in the province of Zeugitana on the Libyan Sea. There, he was warned by a divine vision that he would undergo his Passion <note>Meaning his martyrdom or death.</note> after one year had passed. And so it indeed happened. For in the following year, having been recalled from exile, he was condemned to death, the Proconsul reading the decree from a tablet:
> IT IS THE PLEASURE OF THE COURT THAT THASCIUS CYPRIAN BE PUNISHED BY THE SWORD. <note>original: "THASCIUM CYPRIANUM GLADIO ANIMADVERTI PLACET."</note>

This was done on the 18th day before the Kalends of October <note>September 14th.</note> in the field of Sextus in the year 258. His body was laid in the grounds of Macrobius Candidus, the Procurator, near the Fishponds on the Mappalian Way. He occupied the See of Carthage for a full decade and earned the crown of martyrdom, the first of the Bishops of that city to do so. A man clearly <gloss>divine</gloss>, a supreme cultivator of Christian piety, and a most fierce defender of ecclesiastical discipline and Episcopal power. Being exceptionally well-imbued with the liberal arts, he excelled in rhetoric and was most sharp in sacred and theological matters. The writings of Tertullian...

### Minor works falsely ascribed to Cyprian.

*The Calculation of Easter.* <note>original: "De Pascha Computus"</note> An ancient treatise, and if not by Cyprian, at least nearly equal to his age; it was first published from the Cotton Library <note>The collection of Sir Robert Cotton, now in the British Library.</note> with notes and various readings among the *Cyprianic Minor Works of Oxford*.
*On Spectacles.*
*On Discipline and the Benefit of Modesty.* Pamelius <note>Jacques de Pamele (1536–1587), a Belgian theologian and editor of patristic texts.</note> adjudges this little book, as well as the preceding one, to Cyprian. However, a vast disparity in style argues against it. Erasmus <note>The famous humanist scholar Desiderius Erasmus.</note> judges this to be by Pope Cornelius, as is the book to Novatian.
*In Praise of Martyrdom, to Moses and Maximus, and the other Confessors.* Pamelius also ascribes this little book to Cyprian, but the same reason [of style] stands in the way.
*To Novatian, that the hope of forgiveness should not be denied to the Lapsed.* <note>The "Lapsed" were Christians who had renounced their faith under Roman persecution.</note> Many judge this work not unworthy of Cyprian; others think the opposite.
*On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, which everyone now knows to be the work of Arnold, Abbot of Bonneval <note>original: "Arnoldi Abbatis Bonæ Vallis"</note>. Beyond the Preface, it comprises the following 12 Treatises, namely:
*On the Nativity of Christ.*
*On the Reason for the Circumcision.*
*On the Star and the Magi, and the Slaughter of the Innocents.*
*On the Baptism of Christ, and the Manifestation of the Trinity.*
*On the Fasting and Temptations of Christ.*
*On the Lord’s Supper.*
*On the Washing of the Feet.*
*On the Anointing of Chrism, and other Sacraments.*
*On the Passion of Christ.*
*On the Resurrection of Christ.*
*On the Ascension of Christ.*
*On the Holy Spirit.* Thus far Arnold.
*On Dice-Players.* <note>original: "De Aleatoribus"</note> Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note> guesses this is by some Roman Pontiff of a more recent age.

# The Age of Novatian.

<margin>
3RD CENTURY from the Year 200.

*The Song of Genesis.*
*The Song of Sodom.*

*Against the Jews who persecuted Christ.*

*On the Twelve Abuses of the Age.*

All of these (excepting the books *On Discipline and the Good of Chastity*, *On the Praise of Martyrdom to Moses and Maximus*, and *On Pardon for the Lapsed to Novatian*) are rejected as Cyprian's by Bellarmine and Labbe <note>Robert Bellarmine and Philippe Labbe, famous 17th-century scholars who specialized in identifying authentic patristic texts.</note>. Finally, the reader should be advised that a certain small book survives which, though it does not name Cyprian as the author, recognizes him as its restorer. I refer to the <term>tachygraphic notes</term> <note>A system of Roman shorthand, known as Tironian notes.</note> of Tiro and Seneca, which the Bishop and Martyr enriched with a quite large collection, adding vocabulary necessary for Christian use, which appear in abundance in the code edited by Gruter.

The works of Cyprian were published in *Speyer*, 1471; *Paris*, 1512; *Cologne*, 1520; *Basel*, by Erasmus, 1520, 1525, 1558; *Lyons*, 1528, 1537, 1544, 1550; *Cologne*, 1544, 1549; *Paris*, 1541, 1564; *Rome*, 1563; then by Pamelius at *Antwerp*, 1568, 1589; *Paris*, 1574, 1603, 1616, 1644; *Cologne*, 1617; *Geneva*, by Goulart, 1593; *Paris*, by Rigalt, 1648, 1666. Regarding the Paris edition of 1541, the criticism by Pamelius of the Doctors of the Sorbonne in Paris (who contaminated Cyprian with innumerable errors) is worth noting. For he writes in note 65 on Cyprian's *On the Lord's Prayer*: "Several lines are inserted here in the Paris edition by Arnoul L'Angelier in the year 1541, but they are not by Cyprian, as he himself admits in the margin with this little note [Addition of a certain person], from which the reader may easily judge the rest; seeing that however much the title boasts of a cleansing of errors, he has contaminated Cyprian with countless mistakes. Yet, to make his edition more plausible, he did not fear to change the signature of Erasmus's dedicatory letter; and though it is established it was written at *Louvain* in 1519, he himself signed it *Paris*, 1541."

Among the editions of Cyprian, those of Rigalt stand out, especially the one published in *Paris* in 1666 by Philippe le Prieur, which arranged in one view the complete notes of Rigalt, selections from others, and his own commentaries. Also notable is the recent Oxford edition of 1682, which the Reverend Father John Fell, the Bishop of Oxford <note>original: "ὁ μακαρίτης" — of blessed memory</note>, adorned with the very <note>original: "πάνυ"</note> [extensive] *Cyprianic Annals* of John Pearson, Bishop of Chester, and illustrated with most learned notes.

Before I dismiss the reader, I thought it necessary to advise that there was (as they say) another Cyprian, the Bishop of Antioch, who suffered under Diocletian at Nicomedia along with the virgin Justina, for whom he was madly in love; wonderful things are told of him, and he is rashly confused with our Cyprian by Gregory Nazianzen, Prudentius, Metaphrastes, and others. Eudocia Augusta <note>A 5th-century Empress and poet.</note> once depicted the whole narrative of this matter (according to Photius <margin>Book 184</margin>) at length in three books composed in heroic verse, based on an older history, it seems. There exists in Latin a *Penitence or Confession* of this Cyprian (if indeed it is his), in which he most abundantly laments the outrages of his former life. This was first brought to light, together with notes and variant readings, by the aid of recent works—

...of the Cyprianic works of the Oxford edition. I know that the most illustrious Editor, supported by conjectures that are not to be despised, expressly affirms that such a person as Cyprian of Antioch never existed. Rather, he argues that the entire narrative is nothing other than the history of our own Cyprian, wonderfully interpolated—or rather, built anew—by someone from that group who was eager to decorate the deeds of the Martyrs with new additions. Be that as it may: provided it is granted (as it is clearer than the sun) that this story is very ancient and was born before the time of Gregory of Nazianzus. For Gregory seems to point to this very thing—at least a confession of this kind—when he says the following concerning Cyprian <margin>3RD CENTURY from the year 200.</margin> in his † <margin>† Oration 18, page 278.</margin> eighteenth oration: <note>original Greek: "Οὐ τῇ μακρῷ στηλιτεύων τὴν προτέραν ἑαυτοῦ κακίαν, ἵνα καὶ τοῦτο Θεῷ καρποφορῇ τὴν ἐξαγόρευσιν, καὶ πολλοῖς ὁδὸς γίνηται τῆς χρηστοτέρας ἐλπίδος τῆς ἀπὸ κακίας ἐπιστρεφόντων."</note> *Not by a long discourse denouncing his former wickedness, so that he might offer even this confession as a fruit to God, and that for many it might become a path of better hope for those turning away from vice.* Here, he cuts down the foulness of his earlier life with a long speech, so that he might offer the very confession of his crimes to God as a gift, and so that a way might exist toward better hope for those who recall their minds from a wicked and shameful way of living.

## CORNELIUS

<margin>Year 251. See the Letter of the Roman Clergy to Cyprian, number 31, page 44.</margin>
<margin>|| Letter 52 (to Antonianus), page 68.</margin>
A Roman by birth, born to his father Castinus, he held the first rank among the Priests of the Roman Church. The Roman See had sat vacant after the death of the man of most noble memory, Fabian, for one year, four months, and fifteen days; the Roman Clergy deferred the election of a new Bishop on account of the difficulties of the affairs and the times. At last, as the fury of the Emperor Decius began to cool, Cornelius was made Bishop at the beginning of June in the year 251, *by the judgment of God and His Christ, by the testimony of almost all the Clergy, by the vote of the people who were then present, and by the college of ancient priests and good men,* as Cyprian speaks ||, whom Cornelius had informed of his own ordination in letters written to him. Yet he held that see peacefully for barely the space of one year. For in July of the following year, by order of the Emperor Gallus, he was exiled to Centumcellae <note>Modern-day Civitavecchia, Italy.</note>, a city of Tuscany, where he was wonderfully refreshed by letters from Cyprian sent to him. After nearly two months, specifically on the 14th of September in the year 252, he underwent Martyrdom. He wrote several *Letters* to Cyprian, of which two survive today among the Cyprianic works in the Rigaltius edition (45 and 47) and the *Oxford* edition (49 and 50). Likewise, he wrote four letters to Fabius (whom Jerome calls Flavian *) the leader of the Church of Antioch; from one of these, a notable fragment concerning Novatian survives in Eusebius, book 6, chapter 43; the rest have perished. <margin>* On Illustrious Men, chapter 66.</margin>

## NOVATIAN

<margin>Year 215.</margin>
A Christian formerly a Stoic Philosopher, while he was being cared for by exorcists as an <term>energumen</term> <note>A person believed to be possessed by a demon or evil spirit.</note> among the Catechumens, he fell into a very grave illness. In the very bed in which he lay, he received <term>Clinical Baptism</term> <note>Baptism performed on a sickbed for those in fear of death; it was often viewed as irregular if the recipient did not later complete the full rites.</note>. Having not been freed from the disease, he neither received those things which the Church rule required, nor was he confirmed by the Bishop. Although both the clergy and the people later objected to this, he was nevertheless raised to the rank of the Priesthood in the Roman Church by the singular grace of the Bishop. After the death of Fabian, while the see remained vacant for a longer time, he bound himself by fearsome oaths that he would not seek the Bishopric. Nevertheless, when in the year 251 he saw Cornelius promoted to the sublime height of the priesthood while he himself was passed over, being a man swollen with pride and envy and full of himself, he was supported by a faction of Novatus, a Priest of Carthage (Greek writers, deceived by the similarity of the names, almost constantly confuse these two) and others who had defected from Cyprian. What was greater, being adorned by the vote of the Roman Confessors—whom he had drawn to his side under the fair-sounding pretext of a more severe discipline—he gaped for the Episcopal chair with such insane zeal and such a stubborn mind that he arranged to be constituted Bishop through fraud and force. He did this by means of three Bishops—men of a rather rough and simple nature—whom he had summoned to Rome from a very small part of Italy, and having kept them shut up for some time, he detained them while they were overwhelmed by a drunken stupor. Thus, he seemed to have a certain <note>original Greek: "εἰκονικήν τινα καὶ ματαίαν χειροτονίαν"</note> *shadowy and empty ordination*, as Cornelius † speaks. Having done this, he threw insults and reproaches against Cornelius <margin>† In Eusebius, book 7, chapter 43.</margin> with a full mouth. He sent letters everywhere, as was the custom, to inform the lesser Churches of his ordination, and he delegated his companions—whom Cyprian calls "New Apostles"—who, running through villages, cities, and towns, might lead unsuspecting men into their society and into a partnership of error. Finally...

### THE AGE OF NOVATIAN

<margin>
The 3rd Century, from the year 200.
</margin>
...so that he might bind his followers to himself by a cursed seal, while he distributed the holy Eucharist to individuals, he took their hands in his own and compelled them to swear in these very words:
> Swear by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you will never desert my party, nor return to Cornelius.

But when he realized that he gained nothing by these tricks, he broke out into an open schism and boldly <note>original Greek: "γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ," literally "with a bare head," an idiom meaning shamelessly or without disguise</note> fought for his dogma concerning <term>Penance</term> <note>the practice of repentance and formal readmission to the Church after a serious sin</note>. He asserted that penitent "lapsed" Christians <note>those who had renounced their faith or sacrificed to pagan gods during Roman persecutions</note> were never to be admitted to the peace of the Church; he claimed it was not within the Church's power to grant them pardon, but rather that such people must be left to the supreme judgment of God alone. In his other dogmas, he did not withdraw from Catholic doctrine. The circumstances of his death are not certain. *Cyprian* depicts the man in his true colors as follows:
<margin>
* Letter 57.
(to Cornelius)
</margin>
> To the destruction of the brothers, he says, he makes a noise with his tongue, and hurls the arrows of poisoned eloquence; he is more harsh through the depravity of *secular philosophy* than he is peaceful through the gentleness of the *Lord’s philosophy*; a deserter of the Church, an enemy of mercy, a murderer of penance, a teacher of pride, a corrupter of truth, and a destroyer of charity.

Before he created the schism, he wrote an elegant letter to *Cyprian* in the name of the Roman Clergy, which is numbered 30 among *Cyprian’s* letters. After the schism, however, he wrote a *Book on the Trinity* (in which he mentions the Sabellian heresy, which arose around the year 257). This work is something of an epitome of *Tertullian's* work on the same subject; it was formerly wrongly attributed by some to *Tertullian* and by others to *Cyprian*. He also wrote a *Letter on Jewish Foods*, if indeed it is his; for scholars attribute it to *Novatian* led only by conjectures, though very likely ones, as it is attributed to *Tertullian* in certain manuscripts. Both short works survive and are usually printed with the works of *Tertullian*. *Novatian* wrote further, though at what time is uncertain: *On Easter*, *On the Sabbath*, *On the Priest*, *On Prayer*, and *Short Questions on Clean and Unclean Animals* (which one might rightly suspect was the same work as the one *On Jewish Foods*). He also wrote *On Perseverance*, *To Attalus*, *On Circumcision*, a small book against *Cornelius*, and many other things which do not survive; unless the book under the title *On True Circumcision*, found among the works attributed to *Jerome* (Volume 4), is his. Whether that is actually *Novatian's* work *On Circumcision* may be rightly doubted.

<margin>
Year 251.
</margin>
PONTIUS, apparently an African by birth, flourished in the year 251. He was a Deacon of *Cyprian* in the Church of Carthage, and his inseparable companion and "faithful Achates" <note>a reference to the loyal friend of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid</note> through all the struggles he endured. He especially provided faithful service during the time of Cyprian's final exile and martyrdom when, to use his own words, *his mind was divided between the joy of the passion and the pain of remaining behind, and two-fold affections burdened his narrow heart: he exulted much and very much in the glory of Cyprian, yet he grieved more that he himself remained behind.* *Trithemius* <margin> * On Ecclesiastical Writers, leaf 12.</margin> rashly asserts that this man converted the two Emperors named *Philip* to the faith of Christ; however, others constantly attribute this to Pope *Fabian* (even if the story tastes like a fable to almost all scholars). It is not clear how long *Pontius* survived *Cyprian*, except for what can be gathered <margin> † On the 8th day before the Ides of March. </margin> from his "Acts," regarding which more is said below. Ancient martyrologies † record only this: that in his own sufferings, always glorifying the Lord, he earned the crown of life. <margin> || On Famous Men, chapter 68. </margin> In a simple and unpolished style, he wrote the *Life and Passion of Cyprian*, an excellent volume, says *Jerome* ||, which is usually placed at the beginning of *Cyprian’s* works. 
In the Rigaltius edition of *Cyprian*, there are three other "Acts of the Martyrdom of Cyprian" showing great antiquity, besides those composed by *Paul the Deacon*; however, whether they are truly ancient and genuine is uncertain. 
Furthermore, *Stephen Baluze* published the *Acts of the Martyrdom of Pontius himself* (which is said to have happened on March 8, 258), said to be written by *Valerius*, a Deacon of Cyprian and a companion of *Pontius*, in the second volume of his *Miscellanea*, page 124, Paris, 1679. What their true value is, however, is not yet clear to us.

<margin>
Year 253.
</margin>
STEPHEN, a Roman by birth, had a father named *Julius*, or as others say, *Jobius*. In the year 253, after the death of *Lucius* on the 13th day of May, he was made Bishop of Rome. A man of a harsh nature and prone to anger, he waged heavy enmities with *Cyprian* and other most famous bishops of this time regarding the *Baptism of Heretics* <note>a controversy over whether people baptized by heretical groups needed to be re-baptized when joining the mainstream Church</note>; he received them in a clearly hard and unmerciful manner. It must indeed be confessed that truth stood on the side of *Stephen*, according to the sense of the Catholic Church...

<margin>
3rd CENTURY. from the Year 200.
</margin>
...truth, though not entirely. For he <note>Referring to Pope Stephen I (reigned 254–257), who disagreed with Cyprian of Carthage over whether converts from heretical sects needed to be rebaptized.</note> did not want to rebaptize any heretics at all—not even those who attacked the doctrine of the Trinity and did not use the formula prescribed by Christ in their baptism. Although his cause was eventually deemed superior, he defended his opinion with more vehemence than was proper; he burned with such anger against Cyprian that he not only refused to grant an audience to the Bishops whom Cyprian had sent to Rome as legates on this matter, but he even commanded the entire brotherhood that no one should receive them into their home. Thus, those arriving were denied not only peace and communion, but even a roof and hospitality. He died on August 2nd <note>original: "IV. Non. Augusti," the fourth day before the Nones of August</note> in the year 257 and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. As far as we can gather, he wrote *two letters* regarding that famous controversy: one to Cyprian (which Cyprian discusses in his Letter to Pompeius), and another to the Eastern Bishops against Helenus and Firmilian, but neither of these is still in existence.

<margin>
253.
</margin>
AN ANONYMOUS author wrote the *Treatise on Not Repeating Baptism*, which was first published by Rigaltius among the works of Cyprian. It is certainly ancient and dates from very near the time of Cyprian, a fact he suggests quite clearly in several places in his booklet; he wrote it while the controversy over rebaptizing heretics was still raging. Nothing more remains to be said of him, except that a certain passage in his Treatise (p. 138, Rigaltius edition, 1666) seems to suggest he was a Bishop. In this passage, the author distinguishes himself clearly enough from the <term>lesser clergy</term> <note>At this time, "lesser clergy" usually referred to anyone below the rank of Bishop, specifically Priests and Deacons</note>, and hints that he was one of those to whom the power of conferring the Baptism of the Spirit through the laying on of hands was handed down by the Lord. To bring greater light to this matter, we will not find it troublesome to include the full passage:

> *And therefore,* he says, *since our salvation is established in the baptism of the Spirit (which he had taught above more often was conferred by the laying on of Episcopal hands), which is usually joined with the baptism of water; if indeed the baptism is administered by us, let it be assigned completely, solemnly, and through all things which have been written, and let it be administered without any separation of any part: but if it has been administered by the <gloss>lesser clergy</gloss> [<gloss>that is, a Priest and Deacon, as Rigaltius rightly notes</gloss>] out of necessity, let us await the outcome, so that it may either be completed by us, or be reserved to be completed by the Lord.*

However, a recent writer (Casimir Oudin, *Supplement on Writers* in the entry for Cyprian), relying on the authority of a Vatican Manuscript and Gennadius of Marseilles, attributes that booklet to a certain African monk named Ursinus. We can hardly bring ourselves to agree with this opinion. For besides the fact that our author seems to have written while the controversy was still heated and appears to belong to the Episcopal order,

<margin>
* On Famous Men, ch. 27.
</margin>
Ursinus (according to Gennadius *) primarily labored to prove that those who were baptized either simply in the name of Christ, or in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—even if with a corrupt understanding—should not be rebaptized. This is by no means explicitly found in our Anonymous author; although it may be conceded he felt something similar, he undertook to clarify a different argument. What removes the matter from all reason for doubt is that it can be shown in countless places in the booklet that frequent persecutions were raging against the Church during our Anonymous author’s time, whereas that Ursinus is recorded by Gennadius among the writers of the already declining 4th century. Finally, the style and the whole manner of writing quite openly reveal the age and even the nationality <note>likely North African</note> of Tertullian or Cyprian. It is found among the works of Cyprian, *Paris 1648, 1666; Oxford 1682.*

<margin>
254.
</margin>
GREGORY, also called *Theodorus*, was named *Thaumaturgus* <note>meaning "Wonder-worker" or "Miracle-worker" in Greek</note> because of the gift of miracles in which he was especially powerful. He was born in Neocaesarea in Cappadocia. He had pagan parents; his father was a most diligent worshiper of pagan superstitions. After his first basic studies in his native city, and having taken up the elements of Rhetoric and Roman Law there, he went to Alexandria for the sake of his studies, then soon to Athens, then to Beirut (the most famous center of Roman law), and finally around the year 234, along with his brother Athenodorus, he committed himself to the care of Origen, who was performing the duty of public teaching in Caesarea in Palestine at that time. From Origen, he learned Logic, Physics, Mathematics, Ethics, and other parts of more refined Philosophy and the disciplines of the liberal arts with great accuracy.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Gregory Thaumaturgus (the "Miracle-Worker"), focusing on his education under Origen and his miraculous appointment as Bishop of Neocaesarea. It details his success in converting his home city from paganism, his survival through the Decian persecution and barbarian raids, and provides a bibliography of his authentic and disputed writings.</meta>

# The Age of Novatian.

<margin>3rd CENTURY. from the Year 200.</margin>
...received [instruction]; and what was of even greater importance, he was imbued by him <note>Referring to Origen, the influential but controversial Alexandrian theologian and teacher.</note> with the knowledge of the Christian faith and Gospel theology. Having spent five years under Origen’s guidance, he returned to his homeland; there, he was ordained Bishop of Neocaesarea by Phaedimus, the prelate of Amasea, in a manner quite wonderful and hitherto unheard of. For when Gregory had withdrawn into solitude so that his mind would not be distracted from his philosophical studies, and sought new hiding places to avoid Phaedimus’s plan to ordain him, Phaedimus—moved by a divine impulse—first turned in prayer to God, and then addressed a discourse to Gregory. Even though Gregory was not present, Phaedimus consecrated him to God and to that Church as Bishop, as if he were laying hands on him in person. Once God had gently disposed his mind to it, Gregory eventually accepted the province willingly, having been formally ordained later in the customary manner, as is reasonable to believe.

Once he undertook his duties, he found Neocaesarea to be <term>full of idols</term> <note>original: "κατείδωλον," a reference to how Saint Paul found Athens in Acts 17:16</note>, just as Athens had once been; yet he cultivated it with such diligence and care that, whereas at his first arrival he had found only seventeen Christians in the entire city and surrounding countryside, at his death he left behind only the same number of pagans. When the persecution was stirred up under the Emperor Decius, he looked after the interests of himself and his Church by a timely withdrawal. Finally, when the storm had calmed and he returned, he suffered much from the incursions of the Goths and barbarian nations; yet from all of these, protected by God, he escaped safe. In the year 265, he took part in the council held at Antioch against Paul of Samosata, and in that same year, his final day closed. Nicephorus <margin>* Book 6, Ch. 17.</margin>* erred foully in writing that Gregory survived until the time of Diocletian, and Suidas <margin>† In the entry for "Gregory," p. 628.</margin>† even more so, who writes that he died during the reign of Julian the Apostate. Regarding the many signs and miracles which Gregory performed, one should consult Gregory of Nyssa (who, however, seems to have drawn quite a few things from uncertain stories) in the oration he composed on his *Life and Miracles*. Regarding him, Basil the Great <margin>* On the Holy Spirit, ch. 29.</margin>* writes thus: <term>“Gregory was great, and his words are a treasure; a man who walked by the same spirit as the apostles and prophets, who followed the footsteps of the saints throughout his entire life, and who maintained the exactness of the Gospel way of life for as long as he lived.”</term> <note>original Greek: "Γρηγόριον ἦν ὁ μέγας... κατορθώσαντα."</note> Basil discusses him at length in that place, as well as in Letter 63 to the people of Neocaesarea. Furthermore, in the following letter written to the teachers of that Church, Basil attempted to soften certain things said by Gregory with a favorable interpretation—remarks that were less than accurate and seemed to favor the Sabellian heresy <note>Sabellianism was the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different "modes" or faces of one person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>; Basil says those things were said <term>not as dogma, but in the heat of debate</term> <note>original Greek: "οὐ δογματικῶς ἀλλ' ἀγωνιστικῶς"</note> during his dispute against Aelian the Gentile.

## WRITINGS.

*A Panegyric of Thanks* addressed to Origen, which he recited before a large audience of fellow students, with Origen himself present, when he was about to bid farewell to the Origenian school. It exists in Greek and Latin.

*Metaphrase on Ecclesiastes.* It exists only in Latin in the Vossian edition, and in Greek and Latin among the orations of Gregory of Nazianzus (number 53) and in the Paris edition of 1622.

*A Brief Exposition of the Faith*, which Gregory of Nyssa relates was delivered to him at night by the Blessed John the Evangelist along with the Blessed Virgin Mary, and that it was written in Gregory’s own hand and preserved in the archives of the Church of Neocaesarea in his time. It exists in Greek and Latin.

*Canonical Letter, concerning those who had fallen [from the faith] during the barbarian incursion.* It exists in Greek and Latin.

*Several other letters, chiefly concerning the Faith, which are no longer extant.*

The *Detailed Confession of Faith*, or *A More Lengthy Exposition of the Faith*, opposed chiefly to the Arians and Sabellians. It exists in Latin.

<margin>254.</margin>
**DIONYSIUS**, of Alexandrian origin as I believe, was born to Pagan parents but was distinguished by high honor and dignity. While he was subjecting the individual opinions of various sects to diligent examination and zealously seeking the truth, he was moved toward the faith of Christ; he was perhaps helped and confirmed in no small way by the teachings of Origen, whose pupil he was. Having become a Presbyter of Alexandria, he was placed in charge of the Catechetical School after Heraclas was appointed Bishop of Alexandria around the year 232; and finally, in the year 247, upon the death of Heraclas, he succeeded to the See of Alexandria. 

When the Decian persecution broke out, he was captured by soldiers and sent to Taposiris, a small town between Alexandria and Canopus; this was perhaps done so that he might be executed there at the highest penalty without noise or riot. But by God’s arrangement, he escaped from their hands; he himself tells a charming story of how this happened in an Epistle against Germanus, found in Eusebius, book 6, chapter 40. 

He was treated more harshly in the year 257. For when Valerian stirred up a very grave persecution against the Christians, after Dionysius made a glorious confession of faith before Aemilianus, the Augustal Prefect <note>The high-ranking Roman governor of Egypt.</note>, he was banished to Cephro, a most deserted and uncultivated region of Libya. The soldiers compelled him to set out immediately, even though he was gravely ill, without granting even a single day’s delay. After a three-year exile, when Gallienus’s decree granted favor to the Christians, he returned to Alexandria; there he battled not only with the Pagans but also with schismatics and leaders of heretical movements. 

He busied himself with bringing Novatian, who was stirring up a schism <note>The Novatianist schism involved a rigorist group that refused to readmit Christians who had lapsed during persecutions.</note>, back into the bosom of the Church with a very gentle letter. He also strove by every means to quiet the controversy that arose between Stephen and Cyprian regarding the rebaptism of heretics; acting as a kind of arbiter of peace, he earnestly exhorted both toward restoring harmony, though he was more inclined toward Cyprian’s side, as he was convinced that truth was with them. 

He fought strongly against the heretic Sabellius, a native of Ptolemais in Pentapolis, who had dreamed up a "single subsistence" in the Holy Trinity—that is, a single Person distinguished by three names. However, carried away by the excessive heat of the debate, Dionysius almost crashed into the opposite rock of error: in emphasizing the distinction of the Persons of the Trinity, he taught a difference of Essence and an inequality of power and glory. In this, however, he is to be excused, both because he was blinded by his intense hatred of the heretics and because in his other writings he expresses himself in an Orthodox manner; furthermore, when he was warned of his error by a Roman Synod, he defended himself by publishing an *Apology*, explaining his more careless sayings in an Orthodox sense. 

Finally, through discussion, he extinguished and defeated the schism and error of Nepos and the Egyptian Chiliasts <note>Millenarians who believed in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth.</note>. At last, in the year 265, called to the Synod of Antioch to contend with Paul of Samosata, he delayed his arrival, pleading old age and bodily infirmity; nevertheless, he indicated his opinion on that controversy by letter, but did not even deign to greet Paul himself. In this very year, finally, after seventeen years had passed in his episcopal office, [he ended his]

He wrote many works, though hardly anything remains of them except for certain fragments preserved through the kindness of Eusebius. These can be conveniently divided into two classes: *Treatises* and *Letters*.

### TREATISES.

*A Book on Penance* to Bishop Conon of Hermopolis.
*A Little Book on Martyrdom* to Origen.
*On the Promises against Nepos*, in two books. From the second of these, a substantial and famous fragment concerning the Revelation of St. John survives in Eusebius, Book 7, chapters 24 and 25. Another regarding Cerinthus <note>An early Gnostic teacher whom Dionysius discusses in the context of the authorship of the Book of Revelation.</note> is found in Book 3, chapter 28.
*To Dionysius of Rome against Sabellius*, in four books, comprised of as many letters and titled *Refutation and Defense* <term>elenchou kai apologias</term>. On the occasion of other letters—especially those to Ammon and Euphranor written against Sabellius—our Dionysius was accused before Dionysius of Rome and a Synod held at Rome of having held somewhat unorthodox views. Being warned by them, he cleared himself of the false charge with these *Apologetic Letters*, and attacked the Sabellian heresy <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons but merely different "modes" or masks of a single person.</note> even more sharply, yet more cautiously. Many fragments and excerpts from these books are presented throughout Athanasius’s book *On the Opinion of Dionysius of Alexandria*; another is found in his book *On the Synod of Ariminum*, page 707. Other fragments of the *Second Letter* still exist in Basil’s *On the Holy Spirit*, the final chapter.
*Several books on Nature*, addressed to the boy Timothy. Eusebius provides quite large excerpts from these in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 14, chapters 23 through 27.
*The Book on Temptations* to Euphranor.
*Commentary on the first part of Ecclesiastes*.

*A Short Letter to Novatian on Schism:* the whole survives in Eusebius, Book 6, chapter 45. ### DIONYSIUS, of Greek origin, as they say, *an eloquent and wonderful man* <note>original: "logios te kai thaumasios anēr"</note>, according to the testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria †, was a Presbyter of the Roman Church, and then from the year 259, its Bishop: he held that see until the end of the year 269. Regarding the illustrious Paul Colomesius, <note>Paul Colomesius (1638–1692) was a French librarian and scholar known for his works on church history.</note> I shall not deny him a place here. This man [Eusebius] was a deacon of the Church of Alexandria under Bishop Dionysius, where, during the Valerian Persecution, he strenuously performed his ministries for the martyrs, not without danger to his own life. Later, he became not the Archbishop of Alexandria in Asia, as Turrianus <note>Francisco Torres, a Spanish Jesuit and theologian.</note> would have it, but the Bishop of Laodicea in Syria, as Eusebius clearly records. \* He flourished, therefore, around the year 257 and thereafter. For this reason, it is a matter of wonder that the aforementioned Colomesius thinks him to have lived much later, since Dionysius himself † clearly mentions our Eusebius as his own deacon. Therefore, he either lived at this time, or the Eusebius whom Turrianus and Colomesius discuss must be a different person, younger than ours. Turrianus testifies that he found eighteen *Homilies* <note>Sermons or religious discourses.</note> of this man, from which he offers fragments in his *Defense of the Papal Epistles*. Colomesius affirms that even more extensive fragments of the same man are presented in the *Parallels* of John of Damascus; and indeed, rather lengthy fragments by a certain Eusebius are found there, though whether they belong to this same Eusebius or another is not clear. Holstenius <note>Lucas Holstenius, a 17th-century German scholar and Vatican librarian.</note> had undertaken to publish four of his homilies—namely, *On the Passion of Christ*, *On the Second Coming of Christ*, *On the Lord's Day after the Sermon*, and *On the Memory of the Saints*—as Lambecius testifies, \* but he was prevented by death and did not fulfill his promise. PAUL, a native of Samosata, was elevated to the chair of the Church of Antioch in the year 260 through the power of Queen Zenobia. <note>Zenobia was the famous third-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire who challenged Rome.</note> He was a man proud and arrogant to the point of madness, and infamous for his utterly depraved morals. Falling away from the truth out of pride and vanity (as Epiphanius relates †), he revived the heresy of Artemon, denying that the Word of God had a distinct existence from the Father. He claimed that when the Word descended to earth, he was a mere man; that he did not exist before Mary, and that he earned the name "Son of God" only through his good works. For this reason, at a Synod of Eastern Bishops held at Antioch in the year 265, his heresy was condemned by the unanimous consent of the Fathers. Succumbing to their vote, Paul professed the Catholic faith and, at that time, eluded the more severe censure of the Synod through clever deception. Later, however, he slid back into heresy. Consequently, in the year 270, the bishops convened at Antioch for a second time and removed him from the see of Antioch, substituting Domnus in his place. Yet, because Paul despised the decree of the Synod and refused to renounce his dignity, he was finally driven out of the church building by an edict of the Emperor Aurelian, whom the bishops had petitioned regarding the matter. He composed certain psalms containing praise for himself; these he ordered to be sung by certain women in the middle of the church on the great day of Easter, having abolished the public Psalms of the Church that were traditionally sung in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ. Circulating under his name are *Ten Questions* proposed to Dionysius of Alexandria, together with Dionysius’s *Responses*; although some suspect their authenticity, there is no certain evidence to prevent them from being attributed to Paul. They are found in the *Letter of Dionysius to Paul*, at the beginning of which Dionysius mentions letters previously written to him by Paul.

THEOGNOSTUS of Alexandria, an interpreter of the sacred books according to Photius, \* was <term>a learned man</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ λόγιος</note> according to Athanasius, † who elsewhere calls him <term>the admirable and diligent man</term>. <note>original Greek: τὸν θαυμάσιον καὶ σπουδαῖον</note> He seems to have flourished around the year 270, being a disciple of Origen, or at least very well-versed in his writings. He wrote in a very beautiful and clear style seven books of *Hypotyposeon* <note>Outlines or Sketches of Christian doctrine.</note>, the individual arguments of which Photius reviews. \* In the first book, he dealt with *God the Father* and demonstrated that matter is not co-eternal with Him. In the second, he undertook to prove the necessity of the existence of the Son, and in the third, that of the Holy Spirit; however, in both, being too much a follower of Origen, he mixed in the worst errors, feigning as many ranks of dignity as there are persons in the Holy Trinity, and likewise thrusting Christ and the Holy Spirit down into the lot of created beings. <note>This is the error of subordinationism, viewing the Son and Spirit as lesser than the Father.</note> In the fourth book, he taught things almost identical to Origen regarding Angels and Demons. In the fifth and sixth, he discussed the Incarnation of God, striving to prove that it was passible [capable of suffering]; yet there, insisting on the footsteps of Origen, he did not cease to rave, denying that Christ's body was circumscribed [limited by space]. Finally, in the last book, concerning the Creation of God, he wrote in a more pious and ortho-

# MALCHION

<margin>270.</margin>
MALCHION, a most eloquent man, flourished in the year 270. He was exceedingly learned in secular literature. He presided over the School of the Sophists <note>A professional school of rhetoric and philosophy.</note> at Antioch, where he taught rhetoric with great distinction. <margin>* Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 71.</margin> Eventually, on account of the most eminent sincerity of his Christian faith, he attained the honor of the priesthood in the Church of Antioch. He took part in the later Council of Antioch in the year 270, assembled against Paul of Samosata; <note>Paul of Samosata was a Bishop of Antioch accused of heresy for his views on the nature of Christ.</note> in which council, in a formal disputation recorded by notaries, he contended with the Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect.</note>; and he alone was able to detect the man's hidden meanings. From this *disputation* or *dialogue*, Leontius brings forward certain passages in his books *Against Nestorius*. Jerome also records <margin>* Cited above.</margin> that Malchion wrote that famous *Letter against Paul of Samosata* on behalf of the Synod of Antioch, which the Fathers of Antioch transmitted to Dionysius, Maximus, and the other bishops of the Catholic Church in all the provinces. However, I fear that Jerome may have handed this down without an authority. For regarding this matter, Eusebius—in whose work the Synodal Letter survives almost in its entirety (Book 7, Chapter 30)—has not a single word <note>original: "ne γρὺ quidem" (not even a grunt/syllable).</note> to say. Nevertheless, Malchion won such glory from the refutation of Paul that for this reason he earned a place in the Greek Menologies <note>Church calendars of saints' lives.</note> to be commemorated on the 28th of October.

# ANATOLIUS

<margin>270.</margin>
ANATOLIUS, a native of Alexandria, flourished in the year 270. He was not only wise beyond the common crowd of scholars, but was also the most skilled among all those of his time in literature and philosophy. <margin>† Book 7, chapter 32.</margin> "He carried away the first prizes among the most highly approved," says Eusebius †, "holding the first place without controversy; for he was learned to the highest degree in every branch of doctrine: Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy, Physics, and also Logic and Rhetoric." For this reason, he was asked by the Alexandrians to establish a school of the Aristotelian succession there, modeled after the Platonic School. Valesius <margin>* Annotations on Eusebius, p. 158.</margin> <margin>† In the *Life of Iamblichus*, near the beginning.</margin> considers this man to be the same as the Anatolius whom Eunapius † makes the teacher of Iamblichus, and who is said to have held the second place after Porphyry. Be that as it may, he achieved a great reputation for his name among all people, and a principal prerogative of honor among the leading men of his city. Finally, leaving Alexandria, he set out for Syria; there Theotechnus, the Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, first laid hands upon him and ordained him a bishop, designating him as the successor to his own church: and indeed for some time he provided vicarious service to Theotechnus in governing the See of Caesarea. Later, while he was traveling to Antioch and passing through Laodicea, he was detained by the Laodiceans so that he might succeed to the place of Eusebius, the bishop of that church, who had recently died. What happened to him after that is not certainly known. However, he is said by some to have been a martyr.

He wrote a *Volume on Easter*, or *Paschal Canons*. <note>Rules for calculating the date of Easter.</note> Eusebius presents an excellent fragment of this work in Book 7, Chapter 32.

The complete work, however, from a faulty version by Rufinus—perhaps made more corrupt by the errors of transcribers—was first published by Aegidius Bucherius (Antwerp, 1634), illustrated with a most learned commentary alongside the *Paschal Canon of Victorius*. That it is genuine is clearly shown both by the parts Eusebius cites from near the beginning and those Bede cites from the end. Anatolius also wrote *ten books of Arithmetical Institutions*, excerpts of which Valesius <margin>* Annotations on Eusebius, p. 160.</note> notes still exist today among the *Theological Principles of Arithmetic*. <note>original: "Θεολογούμενα τῆς Ἀριθμητικῆς"</note> He left certain other monuments of his diligence and learning in sacred literature; from all of which, says Eusebius †, "it is possible to recognize at once both his eloquence and his manifold learning" <margin>† Cited above.</margin> <note>original: "δυνατὸν ὁμοῦ τό τε λόγιον καὶ πολυμαθές"</note> in abundance: but... <note>The text likely continues "but not all survive" or similar.</note>

3rd CENTURY from the Year 200.

...of a certain Saracen, a man deeply steeped in all the disciplines and mysteries of the Gentiles, he [Scythianus] received books; which he had composed in four volumes, titled first *The Mysteries*, second *The Gospel*, third *The Treasure*, and fourth finally *The Chapters*. These were filled with heretical dogmas, especially regarding the two principles of all things; and he left them to his servant Terebinthus, also known as Buddas, whom he had as the sole follower of his heresy. I believe this Buddas was the same as that Addas whom Heraclianus mentions in Photius, Volume 85, who wrote a gospel he called <term>Modion</term> <note>Original: Μόδιον. This title likely refers to a "bushel" or "measure," perhaps suggesting a specific volume or a "measure" of truth.</note>; nor was he any other, it seems, than Adimantus, called Addas by his proper name, a disciple of Mani, of whom Augustine speaks in Book II of *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets* near the end of Volume VI. Augustine himself refuted his book in a specific work on page 124. But this is by the way. After Buddas was removed from the scene by a horrific death, the volumes of Scythianus were in the possession of the mistress of Cubricus <note>Cubricus was the original name of Mani before he adopted his more famous title.</note>, from whom he acquired them by hereditary right, and he increased the poison he drank from them almost infinitely. For he preached himself sometimes as the Paraclete and the Holy Spirit, sometimes as the Apostle of Christ, and sometimes as Christ himself. Wherefore, in the likeness of Christ, he appointed twelve chosen ones from among his followers—worthless scoundrels above all others—to act as Apostles in preaching and spreading his dogmas far and wide. He taught that there are two principles of all things, equally eternal and equal to one another, namely God and the Devil; that all good things arise from the former, and all evils from the latter; that the former is the Author of virtue and the New Testament, while the latter is the Author of sin and the Old Instrument <note>Original: *Inſtrumenti Veteris*, a common term for the Old Testament.</note>; that we owe our soul to the former and our body to the latter. He introduced Fate into human affairs by removing free will; and he denied that Christ existed in the flesh, saying he was a phantom <note>This is the doctrine of Docetism, the belief that Jesus only seemed to have a physical body.</note>. Furthermore, he devised countless and utterly absurd fables and causes for things, which Epiphanius explained at length in *Against Heresies* 66. After spreading dreams of this kind, Mani had excited a great reputation for himself in Persia, so much so that he was summoned by the King to heal his sick son. Mani undertook to accomplish this at the risk of his own head; but frustrated in his hope, and with the death of the royal boy accelerated by his reckless remedies, he was cast into chains to pay for his rashness with his life. However, having bribed a guard, he broke his chains and took flight; but being brought back by the diligence of Bishop Archelaus, he underwent the destined punishment: his skin was stripped off while he was still alive, which, filled with straw, was preserved in Persia even up to the time of Epiphanius, as he writes. <margin>† In the place cited.</margin>

Mani published many writings, mostly compiled from the books of Scythianus, which he also sold under his own name more than once.

...since they were Christians, they seemed to lean too much toward their own side; he held a formal debate with Mani, in which he powerfully threw the man down. Mani then fled to a certain obscure village and challenged the priest of that place, Diodorus (whom Epiphanius calls *Trypho*), to renew the contest of faith. Archelaus followed in swift pursuit and shut his mouth when he dared to speak again. As Mani attempted to flee once more, the royal attendants captured him and returned him to prison. Archelaus compiled the *history of this debate* in a book written by himself in Syriac; and he wrote a quite lengthy *Epistle* to Diodorus, who was troubled by Mani's audacity and seeking counsel on the matter, to arm him with arguments to be brought against Mani. Epiphanius writes that Archelaus sent two books to Diodorus, though he seems to have erred in that. Both the *Acts* and the *Epistle* were later translated into the Greek language and became famous in the age of Jerome. Cyril of Jerusalem cites many things from them in his sixth Catechesis; Socrates also mentions them in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 1, Chapter 22, where he confesses that he drew the entire history he has concerning Mani and his books from that source. Indeed, Henri Valois published a large fragment of the debate, along with the complete Epistle to Diodorus, from a manuscript in the Ambrosian Library—which had once belonged to the Monastery of Bobbio—at the end of his annotations on *Socrates and Sozomen in Latin*, from a very ancient version. Almost that entire fragment of Archelaus’s debate is found in Greek in Epiphanius, *Heresies 66, numbers 25 to 32*. Bigot, who had shared that fragment with Valois, testifies that he corrected several passages in the Greek and more in the Latin version based on a comparison of both texts. Photius <margin>* Preface to Palladius</margin> wrote against Mani. Whether Archelaus also held the name Hegemonius <note>Hegemonius is often credited as the actual author or compiler of the *Acts of Archelaus*.</note>, or whether that was a work different from ours, let others solve the knot.

## DIODORUS
called *Trypho* by Epiphanius; a man "good and wonderful in his piety" <note>Original Greek: ἀγαθὸς καὶ θαυμαστὸς τὴν θεοσέβειαν</note>, Priest of the Village of Diodoris situated in the district of the Cascharians, and an associate of Bishop Archelaus. This most mild man first received Mani as a guest when he fled to him; however, soon becoming more certain of his cunning and heresy, and instructed by Archelaus’s letter, he began a debate with the arch-heretic and remarkably beat back his insolent stubbornness. Rather brief *Acts* of this debate survive at the end of the *Epistle of Archelaus* published by Valois.

## PIERIUS
of Alexandria, whom Eusebius counts among the singular and distinguished men who lived closest to his own times. He flourished around the year 283. He was the Master of the Alexandrian School <note>The famous Catechetical School of Alexandria, a center of Christian scholarship.</note> under Bishop Heraclas, and a Priest of the same Church, famous for his voluntary poverty and philosophical disciplines. He was especially practiced in the contemplation and exposition of the sacred scriptures and in ecclesiastical sermons; for these he became so celebrated that, on account of his strict way of life, his multifaceted knowledge of both Greek and sacred disciplines, his great diligence in preaching, and the supreme eloquence he applied to speaking, he was called the *Younger Origen*. He seems to have suffered under the persecution which Diocletian stirred up in the year 303. I know that Jerome affirms that he survived the persecution and lived in Rome through the whole of his life. The Roman Martyrology adds that he rested in peace. But I agree more with Photius, who reports that he received the crown of martyrdom along with his brother Isidore, a companion in the struggle; and even that a temple and houses were built for them by pious men. Epiphanius seems to confirm this when, listing the churches that were in Alexandria, he says one was named after Pierius. He wrote twelve books, among which were a very long *Treatise on Easter* and another on the *Prophet Hosea*, delivered in an extemporaneous and eloquent speech on the day of the Vigils of the Lord’s Passion, as Jerome teaches us in the Prologue to Hosea, Volume VI. He also wrote a Commentary on the *Gospel of Luke*. In these writings Photius notes certain things that are less sound, especially that he discussed the Holy Spirit "very subordinately and impiously" <note>Original Greek: ὑποβεβηκότως λίαν καὶ δυσσεβῶς. This refers to subordinationism, the controversial view that the Holy Spirit is inferior in essence or status to the Father.</note>, and also obscurely taught the pre-existence of souls according to the opinion of Origen. And truly, it should not seem at all strange that writers of that age derived many things from the fountains of Origen into their own streams. He wrote a *Commentary*

### VICTORINUS,
if not Greek by origin, seems at least to have been born on the borders of Greece. From an orator he became a Bishop, as Cassiodorus * teaches us in more than one place. He flourished around the year 290. He was the Bishop of Pettau <note>modern Ptuj, Slovenia</note> in Upper Pannonia by the Drava River—not, as is commonly believed, the Bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine (a point which Jean de Launoy showed at length in a specific dissertation). He is said to have undergone martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian in the year 303. He was much more skilled in the Greek language than in Latin; hence, in the judgment of Jerome *,

<margin>
* On Illustrious Men, ch. 74.
† Letter to Magnus the Orator, p. 328, Vol. ii.
</margin>
*“His works are great in their meaning, but seem somewhat meaner in the arrangement of words.”* For the idiom of the Greeks, with whom he was mostly occupied, tainted his style too much while writing in Latin, as usually happens. Elsewhere, the same Jerome † says of him: *“Although Victorinus the martyr lacks erudition, he does not lack the will for erudition.”* Launoy rightly notes from the argument of that very letter that this should be understood as a lack of education in secular disciplines. He wrote, among other things, a book *Against All Heresies*, *Commentaries on Genesis, on Exodus, on Leviticus, on Isaiah, on Ezekiel, on Habakkuk, on Ecclesiastes, on the Song of Songs, on Saint Matthew*, and finally *on the Apocalypse of John*; all of which, however, have perished through the ravages of time. There is indeed a *Commentary on the Apocalypse* extant under his name in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 3; but it must either not be his, or must be strangely interpolated and changed. For in his own commentary, Jerome * expressly relates that Victorinus favored the error of the <term>Chiliasts</term> <note>from the Greek "chilioi" (thousand); those who believed in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ</note>,

<margin>
* On Illustrious Men, ch. 18.
† On Divine Learning, ch. 9.
</margin>
yet the author of *this* commentary vigorously attacks them. And certainly, Cassiodorus † clearly indicates that our Victorinus did not illustrate the entire *Apocalypse* with a commentary, but rather treated certain of its more difficult passages. There are also two poems attributed to him, which are found in Fabricius’s collection of sacred poets, one *On Jesus Christ, God and Man*, and another titled *The Tree of Life*; but this is based on a clearly uncertain and, it seems to me, false conjecture. There is indeed in my possession a hitherto unpublished *Treatise* by Victorinus *On the Fabric of the World*, which the illustrious Henry Maurice, Doctor of Sacred Theology and domestic chaplain to the Lord Archbishop, transcribed from an ancient codex in the Lambeth Library and kindly shared with me. And for a second time, the most learned and candid John Batteley, Doctor of Theology and Chaplain to the same Archbishop, reviewed it against the manuscript codex. It is not stated in the manuscript codex who this Victorinus was. But both the style and the matter itself loudly proclaim it to be ours; especially since in it the error of the Chiliasts is manifestly defended,

</margin>

Thinking to myself and conferring with my own mind regarding the construction of this world in which we are held enclosed, I find the speed of its very construction is such as is contained in the book of Moses, which he wrote concerning its origin, which is called Genesis. God expressed this whole mass from nothing in six days for the ornament of His majesty; on the seventh, He consecrated it with a blessing. Therefore, because all things both celestial and terrestrial are governed by the <term>septenary</term> <note>the number seven</note> number of days: in place of a beginning, I shall measure from this seventh day toward all the septenary regions; and as I am able, I shall endeavor to express the power of that day in its completion. In the beginning, God made light, and He divided it into the <term>duodenary</term> <note>twelvefold</note> number of hours by day and night: specifically for this purpose, so that night might bring a place of rest for the labors of men, and the day might follow upon it, and again the day might prevail; so that by this alternating turn, labor might be refreshed by rest, and rest might again be tempered by the exercise of the day. On the fourth day, He made two luminaries in the heaven, the greater and the lesser, so that one might preside over the day and the other over the night—the sun and the moon—and He placed the other stars in the heaven to shine upon the earth, and to distinguish the seasons, and years, and months, and days, and the gifts * of the hours. Now the reason of truth is shown, why the fourth day is called the <term>tetras</term> <note>the fourth, or Wednesday</note>: why we fast on the <term>stations</term> <note>mid-week fasts</note> until the ninth hour <note>3:00 PM</note> or until evening, or why a † superposition <note>an extended fast through the night</note> is made until the following day. This world, therefore, consists of four elements: fire, water, air, and earth. These four elements, then, make a tetrad of seasons; the sun and moon also produce four seasons through the span of a year: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter; and these seasons make a tetrad. And to narrate further from the † air, behold the four living creatures before the throne of God, the four Gospels, the four rivers flowing in Paradise, the four generations of people: from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, from Abraham to Moses, and from Moses to Christ the Lord, the Son of God; and the four living creatures: the man, the calf, the lion, and the eagle; and the four rivers: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates. Christ Jesus the Man, the Author of those things which we have mentioned above, was seized by the impious on the <term>tetrade</term> <note>Wednesday</note>. Therefore, on account of His captivity, we observe the tetrad; so that because of the majesty of His works, both the seasons of humanity may run their course healthfully, joyful in crops, and tranquil in storms. For this reason † we also perform the superposition. On the fifth day, the earth and water brought forth their offspring; and so God [created] man. On the sixth day, those things which were lacking were created: from the soil He fashioned the Lord of all things which He created upon the earth and water. Yet He created the Angels and Archangels before He fashioned man, placing spiritual things before earthly ones: for light was made before the heaven and the earth *: this day is called the <term>Parasceue</term> <note>the day of Preparation, or Friday</note>, namely the preparation for the kingdom. For Adam, whom He brought to completion in His own image and likeness ||. Moreover, He completed His works before He created the Angels and fashioned man, lest they should perhaps assert by false speech that they had been His helpers. Also on this day, because of the Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, we observe either a station to God or a fast. On the seventh day, He rested from all His works, and blessed it and sanctified it; † on this day we are accustomed to superpose <note>extend the fast from Friday through Saturday</note>, so that on the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> we may go out to the Bread <note>the Eucharist</note> with thanksgiving: and let the Parasceue become a superposition, lest we should seem to observe the Sabbath with the Jews—that Sabbath which Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath, says through His Prophets that His soul hated; || which Sabbaths He dissolved with His own body. Previously, however, when He Himself commanded Moses that circumcision should not pass the eighth day—which frequently falls on a Sabbath day, as we read written in the Gospel. Moses, foresighted regarding the hardness of that people, for that reason we were reading on the Sabbath day, * and He crucified himself, † and in battle by the <term>Allophylis</term> <note>foreigners or Philistines</note> on the Sabbath so that they might be captured, and might be shaped as if by the severity of the law toward avoiding [lax] discipline. And therefore David in Psalm 6 || asks the Lord, for the sake of the eighth day, that He not rebuke or judge him in His anger or His fury; for this truly is that eighth day of the future judgment, which is to exceed the order of the weekly arrangement. Joshua <note>original: Iesus Nave</note> also, the successor of Moses, himself dissolved the Sabbath; for on the Sabbath day he commanded the children of Israel to circle the walls of the city of Jericho with trumpeters, and to declare war against the Allophylis. Moreover, Matthias, the Prince of Judah, dissolved the Sabbath; for he killed the Prefect of the † ancient † King Antiochus of Syria on the Sabbath; and he subjected the Allophylis to his pursuit.
