*...as we read in the writings of Matthew, Isaiah and his other colleagues also explained <note>original: "resolverunt"</note> the Sabbath, so that the true and just Sabbath might be observed in the seventh millennium of years.*
<margin>† Perhaps: That.</margin>
*For this reason, the Lord assigned a single millennium of years to each of those seven days. For it is cautioned: "In your eyes, Lord, a thousand years are as one day"; therefore, in the eyes of God, individual thousands of years are established, for "I have seven eyes of the Lord."*
<margin>|| Perhaps: The Lord has eyes.</margin>
*Therefore, as I mentioned, that true Sabbath is the seven thousandth year, in which Christ is to reign with His elect. There are also seven heavens, which correspond to those days; for so it is cautioned: "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth." These seven spirits are the names of those spirits who rested upon Christ, as was cautioned in the Prophet Isaiah:*
<margin>* read: of the Spirits.</margin>
*"And there shall rest upon him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and it filled him with the spirit of the fear of God." <margin>† Perhaps: Lightnings.</margin>
*the rivers extend, the fires gather together, the burning beams <note>likely referring to meteors</note> appear, the stars radiate, and the dreadful tresses <note>meaning comets</note> are brandished. Sometimes even the Sun and Moon visit one another in turn, and those bodies, radiating with formidable light beyond measure, establish the authority of the whole creation by the sight of His battle-array. "Just" is the surname given to Him by the Word; for so His Father says: "My heart has brought forth a good word." John the Evangelist says thus: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made." Therefore, He is the first-born*
<margin>* Perhaps: Lord.</margin>
*of creation, and the second of the human race, as the Apostle says. This Word, therefore, when He made the light, is called Wisdom; when He made the heaven, Understanding; when the earth and sea, Counsel; when the sun and moon and other bright things, Might; when He stirs the earth and sea, Knowledge; when He formed man, Piety; when*

*the seven golden candlesticks, the seven little sheep, the seven women in Isaiah, the seven Churches in Paul,*
<margin>† Perhaps: Paul.</margin>

# METHODIUS, also called Eubulius, was first the Bishop of Olympus in Lycia, or of Patara <margin>* Under the entry "Methodius".</margin> (for Suidas * explicitly identifies these as the same Episcopal see, or if they were separate cities, he could have held the Episcopal care of both at the same time during the heat of the persecutions), and later he was the Bishop of Tyre. He flourished at the end of the third century, around the year 290. There were some, according to the testimony of Jerome <margin>† On Illustrious Men, ch. 83.</margin> †, who claimed that he was made a Martyr in Chalcis, Greece, under the emperors Decius and Valerian; and indeed, Suidas reports this after Jerome’s time, having omitted several words of Jerome (or rather, of his translator Sophronius). However, it is certain that he lived long after the times of Decius and Valerian, being a contemporary of the philosopher Porphyry, if not surviving him; and thus he died during the most recent persecution <note>The Great Persecution under Diocletian.</note>, around the year 303, crowned with the wreath of martyrdom. Epiphanius says of him <margin>* Against Heresies, 64.</margin> *, "a learned man, and one who fought very hard for the truth" <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ λόγιος, καὶ σφόδρα περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀγωνισάμενος</note>. He was a man of prime learning and a most sharp-witted Defender of the truth. He wrote many things in a polished and well-ordered style, which are as follows:

## W O R K S.

**On the Resurrection**, a book against Origen <note>Origen was a controversial early Christian scholar; Methodius disagreed with his spiritualized view of the resurrection body.</note>, from which quite long fragments exist in the work of Epiphanius cited above; Photius has even more extensive excerpts in Code 234, as does John of Damascus in his *Third Oration on Images*, and others here and there. The entire work was conducted in the form of a Dialogue, and was divided into two, or perhaps more parts, according to the number of speakers. Certainly, Damascus, in the place cited, quotes the second oration of Methodius *On the Resurrection*, and Eustratius of Constantinople, in his book on the state of the dead, alleges Methodius’s oration to Aglaophon—which, as is clear from Epiphanius, was nothing other than a part of this very work.

**On Created Things** <note>original: Περὶ Γεννητῶν / De Creatis</note>. Excerpts are held by Photius in Code 235.

**On Free Will** <note>original: Περὶ Αὐτεξουσίου / De Libero Arbitrio</note>, and "from whence come evils," a book which exists almost in its entirety in the edition by Combefis, compiled from three larger excerpts: the Photian Code 236, the Meursian, and the Sirmondian. Leo Allatius, in his *Discourse on the Writings of the Methodii* (p. 340), testifies that he had a complete copy of the work in Greek and Latin ready for the press.

**The Banquet of the Ten Virgins** <note>original: Symposium decem Virginum</note>, and **On Chastity** <note>original: περὶ τῆς Ἁγνείας / De castitate</note>. This was held in the manner of a Dialogue among ten pious and holy women, elegantly and learnedly conversing with one another about these matters. Photius provides very full selections from it in Code 237, and others were published by Allatius from Eustathius. Finally, Leo Allatius published the complete work with a translation and notes, including an attached discourse on the writings of the various men named Methodius, dedicating it to Pope Alexander VII (Rome, 1556 <note>Likely a typo for 1656, given the reign of Alexander VII.</note>, octavo). Petrus Possinus, of the Society of Jesus, was either unaware of this or, more likely, pretended not to know, even though he was living in Rome at the time. Having obtained a Greek manuscript from Lucas Holstenius, Possinus translated it into Latin, dedicated it to the same Alexander VII, and sent it to Paris. There, it was checked against another manuscript in the Mazarin Library and illustrated with certain notes (or rather, variant readings), and published by the Royal Press in Greek and Latin in 1657, folio. Finally, it is contained in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* by Combefis (Paris, 1672). Regarding this book, Photius once noted that a large part of it had been corrupted, and that Arian <note>Arianism was a belief that Jesus was a created being, later declared a heresy.</note> and vain opinions had been added to it, along with the fables of other wrong-thinkers; however, in modern copies, these are found only very sparingly—hardly at all, if ever.

**Oration on Simeon and Anna**, or for the *Feast of the Meeting and Purification of the Blessed Mary*. Published by Petrus Pantinus in Antwerp, 1598. However, Gretser, Canisius, and more recently Casimir Oudinus <margin>* Supplement on Writers.</margin> * argue with several significant points that this is not by our Methodius, but by a certain younger man of the same name who presided over the see of Constantinople in the ninth century. But Leo Allatius, by far the most learned of the Greeks in this century, vindicates it for our Methodius based on the phrasing, elocution, other stylistic formulas, and the testimony of Methodius himself; he attempts to resolve the objections raised to the contrary in his *Discourse on the Writings of the Methodii*, p. 341. For my part, I certainly believe it should be attributed to Methodius the Confessor.

This work is lost. Leo Allatius, in the aforementioned treatise (p. 331), strives to undermine Socrates' credibility on this matter with many arguments, yet he is supported by no testimony from the ancients and no suitable evidence.
All the works and fragments of Methodius that could then be found were collected into one volume, and published together with Amphilochius and Andrew of Crete in Greek and Latin by François Combefis (*Paris, 1644, Folio*), illustrated with his own notes.

### SPURIOUS WORKS.

*On the events from the creation of the world, and those which are to happen in the future* <note>original Greek: "Περὶ τῶν ἀπὸ συστάσεως κόσμου συμβάντων, καὶ τῶν μελλόντων συμβαίνειν εἰς τὸ ἑξῆς"</note>, also known as the *Revelations*. These contain many predictions about the Turks, the Antichrist, and the Last Judgment; as such, they seem more likely to be ascribed to Methodius the Confessor, the Patriarch, or perhaps to another Patriarch Methodius who flourished around the year 1240. Although the author of the Greek Synaxarion <note>A collection of hagiographies or lives of the saints.</note> attributes these to Methodius of Patara as genuine, such testimonies hold no authority among fair judges of history. These *Revelations* exist in both Greek and Latin among the *Orthodoxographa* (Basel, Vol. 1) and in the *Library of the Holy Fathers* (Vol. 3, Latin).

## PAMPHILUS

<margin>294.</margin>
A Phoenician by birth, born of a noble family in Berytus <note>Modern-day Beirut.</note>. He flourished around the year 294. After leaving his homeland, it seems he went to Alexandria, for he was a disciple of Pierius of Alexandria; afterwards he went to Caesarea in Palestine, where he was chosen for the rank of the presbytery <note>The priesthood.</note> in that Church. He burned with such zeal for the divine scriptures that he built the Library of Caesarea; in it, he stored the books of the more famous Church writers which he had collected from everywhere, as if in a most noble cabinet. He especially collected the works of Origen, most of which he transcribed with his own hand. <margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 75.</margin> Jerome* testifies that he found there twenty-five volumes of Commentaries on the Twelve Prophets written by Origen, but traced by the hand of Pamphilus; he embraced these with such joy that he boasted he had found the riches of Croesus <note>A king of Lydia legendary for his immense wealth.</note>. Among the other virtues in which he shone, the greatest were his Charity and Munificence. For if he saw any who lacked the necessities of life, he provided largely what he could; and not only that, but he also prepared many copies of the Holy Scriptures at his own expense, which he most readily bestowed upon both men and women devoted to reading. Around the end of the year 307, after the most bitter tortures and his sides being furrowed by iron claws, he was thrown into prison by the Governor Urbanus. After two years had passed, when Firmilianus had succeeded to Urbanus's place, he put Pamphilus to the ultimate punishment in the year 309, along with his servant Porphyrius and others. Their bodies were exposed for four days by order of the Governor to be torn apart by meat-eating beasts; however, when neither wild animal, nor bird, nor dog would approach them, they were finally honored with funeral rites and committed to the customary burial.

Pamphilus published a transcription of the *Greek version of the Seventy* <note>The Septuagint (LXX).</note>, aided by the help of his close associate and greatest friend Eusebius. This was copied from the original autograph of Origen’s *Hexapla* <note>A massive six-columned comparative Bible created by Origen.</note> which lay hidden in the Library of Caesarea, just as it had once been corrected and supplemented by Origen. However, due to the carelessness and rashness of scribes who disregarded the marks <note>Referring to "asterisks" and "obeli" used by Origen to mark differences between Hebrew and Greek texts.</note> placed therein, it has come to pass that countless errors daily...

...that Origenian edition of the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> might be defiled by corruptions. Purged of these stains and prepared with the greatest diligence, *Pamphilus* published his own edition separately for the use of the Palestinian churches (from which it was called the *Palestinian* edition); it was received and celebrated with the highest applause in the church of Jerusalem and other churches of the East. A clear monument of this work is still preserved today, as the illustrious *Huet* † testifies, in the Marchal Codex, which is held by the Jesuit Fathers at Clermont. While confined in prison, and with the same *Eusebius* present and assisting him, *Pamphilus* wrote five books of an *Apology for Origen*, to which *Eusebius* later added a sixth book after *Pamphilus’s* death. They sent this *Apology* as a consolation to those who had been condemned to the mines for the name of Christ. Of these, the first book was devoted to either defending or excusing the doctrines of *Origen*; the remaining books concerned the life, character, and learning of *Origen*. Therefore, *Rufinus* chose the first book in particular to translate into the Latin language; consequently, it still exists today in his version among the works of *Origen* and *Jerome*. Of the remaining books, however, only a few excerpts are preserved in *Photius*, Codex 118. To be sure, there are some who deny that *Pamphilus* wrote anything, relying on the words of *Eusebius* cited by *Jerome* || from his books on the *Life of Pamphilus*, in which he hints that Pamphilus wrote nothing and composed nothing of his own except for some *Letters* sent to *Friends*. But since *Eusebius’s* words can be understood as referring to works composed entirely by his own individual effort, and since *Eusebius* himself * and *Photius* † testify that the *Apology* was written by *Pamphilus*, which *Jerome* also acknowledges elsewhere *, there is no reason for us to dwell long on this matter.

# LUCIAN
Born of a noble lineage, his homeland was *Samosata* <note>An ancient city on the Euphrates in modern-day Turkey.</note>, a city of Syria of no small renown—the same city and name as that famous mocker of the Christian religion <note>A reference to the satirist Lucian of Samosata.</note> who lived in the time of *Trajan*. Our Lucian here was nearly a contemporary of *Paul of Samosata*, but he flourished especially around the year 290. He was a man conspicuous both for the restraint of his life and for his knowledge of the sacred scriptures †. In his youth, he listened most studiously to a certain *Macarius* of Edessa interpreting the books of Holy Scripture; having been taught all the finest points by him in a short time, he turned toward an ascetic and solitary life. Finally, having been made a priest of the church of Antioch, he established a school there. From this school came many disciples of no small reputation, among them *Eusebius of Nicomedia*, *Maris of Chalcedon*, *Theognis of Nicaea*, and others who later emerged as supporters of the *Arian* sect. These men, after their master’s name, called themselves *Lucianists*, or *Collucianists* <note>original: "Con-Lucianistas"</note>, as is clear from the *Letter of Arius to Eusebius of Nicomedia* †. It is certainly quite evident that *Alexander*, Bishop of *Alexandria* *, accused our *Lucian* of favoring the errors of *Paul of Samosata* (while *Epiphanius* † charges him with the stain of *Marcionite* heresies), and says that for this reason he withdrew from the communion of three of his own bishops who succeeded one another for many years, and celebrated his gatherings separately. *Baronius* * attempts to purge *Lucian* of the crime of unspeakable heresy, but he relies on no testimonies of the ancients. We easily concede that he eventually emerged from the schism, which the aforementioned *Alexander* also seems to indicate; however, whether he entirely set aside or retracted his errors is not sufficiently clear. Nevertheless, I cannot help but bring in here, for his sake, what *Suidas* * says of him: namely, that the purity of divine doctrines was most beautifully and with the greatest zeal preserved by this man above all others of that age, and that his opinion on divine matters is very clearly evident to anyone from the letters he wrote, which are truly excellent. In the year 311, while the Emperor *Maximinus* (who had recently renewed the persecution against the Christians) was staying at Nicomedia, *Lucian* was brought there. There, after delivering an *Apology* for his faith in the presence of the Emperor himself, he was cast into prison. And it is truly memorable what *Philostorgius* * reports concerning him: that while he was held in prison, having neither a church nor an altar, and since because of his chains and wounds he could not even move from his place, lying on his back upon his own chest, he [offered] the awe-inspiring sacrifice of the Eucharist...

...he performed the final service, and both partook of it himself and gave it to be shared by others who surrounded him on all sides like a sacred choir. He was beheaded at Nicomedia in the same year, 311. His body, as it appears, was thrown into the sea; a dolphin later carried it back to the shore, and it was buried there near the mouth of the Gulf of Nicomedia. Lucian was learned in Hebrew and compared various Greek *Versions of the Old Testament* with one another. Through the help of older codices of proven reliability, he removed many flaws that had crept in through the negligence of transcribers. Having restored the text to its original purity in this way, he further emended the interpretation of <term>the Septuagint</term> <note>original: "τῶν LXX." — the standard Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> even more accurately by using Hebrew copies. This edition of the Bible, ultimately called the *Lucianic* edition, was found at Nicomedia under Constantine the Great, hidden behind the wall of a cabinet and plastered over with lime, where it had been placed for safekeeping. It was written in Lucian's own hand, as the author of the *Synopsis of Holy Scripture* * has recorded. Jerome also testifies † that this edition was used by all the Eastern Churches from Antioch all the way to Constantinople. However, like the rest, it has long since vanished.

<margin>* Book 3, chapter 5.</margin>
Lucian also wrote *Treatises on the Faith*, and perhaps among them was that brief Exposition of Faith found in Athanasius’s *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia* (p. 693) and Socrates’s *Ecclesiastical History* (book 2, chapter 10). The Fathers of the Council of Antioch brought this forward in the year 341, asserting they had found it written in Lucian’s own hand. Regarding this formula, Sozomen * doubts whether it is truly Lucian’s work; however, he admits that in other respects it agrees with the Nicene faith, lacking only the term <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "τὸ ὁμοούσιον" (homoousion) — the key theological term defining the Father and Son as being of the same substance</note>. This is not surprising, assuming it was composed by Lucian, since that word only began to be used frequently after his time.

<margin>* Place cited above.</margin>
Lucian also composed several letters; from one of these, sent to the people of Antioch from the prison in Nicomedia, the final clause survives in the works of the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*. As for the *Apologetic Oration* mentioned by Eusebius *, I believe it was delivered orally by him in the presence of the Emperor rather than published as a written work.

* Book 8, chapter 9.
† Book 8, chapter 10.
* On Illustrious Men, chapter 78.

**PHILEAS** appears to have originated from Thmuis, a large city in Egypt at the Mendesian mouth of the Nile. He flourished at the end of this century, around the year 296. Born of a noble family and enriched with great wealth and resources, he was highly distinguished in the study of philosophy and Greek disciplines. Having performed all the honors and duties of his native city with the highest praise, he eventually served as the Bishop of his city. During the heat of the persecution under Maximinus in the year 311, he was beheaded. Eusebius * clearly indicates that he was married even at the time of his death; while describing Phileas and his companion in martyrdom, Philoromus, he relates that although their friends, relatives, and even the magistrates and the Judge himself exhorted them to have pity on themselves and to consider their wives and children, they could not be persuaded by any of these pleas to despise the divine laws regarding the confession or denial of Christ’s name for the sake of saving their lives. He wrote a *Letter to the Thmuites* concerning the martyrdoms that had occurred in Alexandria during that time, and the tortures which the martyrs endured with manly and unconquered spirits. Eusebius † preserves a noble fragment of this letter, and Jerome * undoubtedly refers to the same when he says that Phileas composed a most elegant treatise in praise of the martyrs.

<margin>
296.
Eusebius, book 8, chapter 13.
* Apology against Rufinus, Volume 2, page 225.
</margin>
**HESYCHIUS**, a Bishop of some city in Egypt, flourished toward the end of this century. He underwent martyrdom under Maximinus in the year 311. He devoted the same effort as Lucian to correcting and emending the copies of the Greek <term>Septuagint</term> <note>original: "τῶν LXX."</note> Version. The churches of Egypt and the neighboring regions embraced and used the new edition prepared by him, as Jerome testifies *.

<meta>This page transitions from the accounts of Christian martyrs and scholars like Lucian of Antioch to the prominent pagan (Gentile) intellectuals of the 3rd century who opposed the rise of Christianity through legal and philosophical means.</meta>

# The Novatian Age

<margin>
3rd CENTURY. 
From the Year 200.
</margin>

### Pagan Writers who Opposed Christianity in this Century.

<margin>* On Justice, book 5, chapter 11.</margin>
**Domitius Ulpianus**, a Syrian by nationality, hailing from Phoenicia, a disciple of Papinian, and most skilled in the law. He flourished in the year of Christ 220. Under Emperor Alexander Severus, he eventually became Master of the Sacred Records <note>A high-ranking official in charge of the imperial archives and legal petitions</note>, Prefect of Provisions, and finally Praetorian Prefect, before being killed by the Praetorians. He not only called the Christian faith a "Jewish Superstition," but in the seventh book of his work *On the Office of Proconsul*, he collected the wicked decrees <note>original: "rescripta" — official legal responses from emperors</note> of the Princes (as Lactantius testifies*) so that he might teach what punishments ought to be inflicted upon those who confessed themselves to be worshippers of God.

<margin>* Book 10, chapter 36.</margin>
<margin>* The City of God, book 10, chapter 28.</margin>
<margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, in the Preface.</margin>
<margin>† Preparation for the Gospel, book 10, chapter 9.</margin>
<margin>|| Extant in the Codex of Justinian, on the Supreme Trinity, law 3.</margin>
**Porphyry**, called by his native name *Malchus* <note>A Semitic name meaning "King"</note>, was a Tyrian by birth and a Philosopher by his way of life. He flourished in the year of Christ 270. He died, it seems, at the beginning of the following century, or shortly thereafter. I am not entirely sure whether what Nicephorus* reports deserves belief—though he cites Eusebius as a witness in this matter—that Porphyry was at first a Christian; but when he had been beaten by certain Christians at Caesarea and could not swallow that insult well, he, stirred up by "black bile" <note>An ancient medical term for a temperament of bitter anger or melancholy</note>, renounced Christianity and turned his mind to tearing apart the scriptures of Christ and the Christians with impious insults. Saint Augustine* seems to have preceded Nicephorus in this view, writing that Porphyry, swollen with the tumor of vain Knowledge, recoiled from the most healthy humility of Christ. Whether Augustine should be understood as speaking of a renounced profession of Christ, or rather that after he had read the sacred volumes, he refused to embrace the most healthy faith of Christ, is not sufficiently clear to me. 

Among the various volumes he composed, while living in Sicily at the time, he published fifteen books *Against the Christians*, in which he took it as his chief task to tear down the authority of Holy Scripture, upon which the Christian religion is supported as if on a foundation. Hence, in the first book, he dealt with contradictions and inconsistencies found in Scripture; in the third book, he mocked the explanation of Scripture then accepted among Christians, and especially the <term>allegorical</term> <note>A method of interpreting scripture where literal stories are seen as symbols for deeper spiritual truths</note> method; in the fourth, he attacked Mosaic History and the Antiquities of the Jews; in the twelfth and thirteenth, he argued against the Prophecy of Daniel; in others, he attempted to overturn the reliability of the Gospels. For which reason he is called "a rabid dog against Christ" by Jerome*. "A conspiracy against us, put forward with an onset of hatred," says Eusebius † <note>original Greek: "τὴν καθ’ ἡμῶν συσκευὴν ἐμβολῇ μίσους προβεβλημένην"</note>. These writings of Porphyry were ordered to be destroyed by fire by a law passed by Theodosius the Great ||; nevertheless, many of them—and very extensive excerpts at that—are preserved in Eusebius (*Church History*, book 6, ch. 19; *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 1, ch. 9, and others) and another in Jerome (*Preface to the Commentary on Galatians*). 

Cardinal Baronius identifies our Porphyry as the same man as Publilius Optatianus Porphyrius, the author of a completely trifling and silly poem comprising a panegyric to Constantine; Joseph Scaliger therefore mocks him for this. But from those then-recently published, most wretched records, Baronius himself readily corrected his error under the year 325. That little poem exists today, preceded by a letter from Porphyry to Constantine and Constantine's reply to Porphyry, illustrated with notes by Marcus Velser and a critical collection by Christian Daum, prefixed to the most recent edition of Velser's works.

->*End of the Third Century.*<-

# THE ARIAN AGE

## Overview of the Century

<margin>4th CENTURY, from the Year 300.</margin>
With this century begins a dire persecution—if ever there was one—namely on February 23, 303 AD. This tenth persecution was begun under Diocletian, Maximian, and others, and was dragged out even until the eleventh year. From this came the destruction of churches, the seizure of sacred records into the treasury, the plundering of goods, and a manifold and pitiful slaughter of Christians. Tortures were sought out everywhere and devised with every kind of cruelty: torches were lit and applied to feet and individual limbs until, once all the skin was cooked away, the force of the fire penetrated to the innermost vitals; bodies were burned, ground into powder, and thrown into rivers and the sea. 

Islands, prisons, and labor in the mines—as Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I</note> notes in chapter 22—were considered light punishments. Fire, the cross, and wild beasts were daily and easy occurrences. In capital cases, the punishment of the sword was granted to very few, almost as a favor, for those who had obtained a "good death" due to their past merits. Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260 – 339), often called the "Father of Church History"</note> depicts the whole series of this persecution at length; Lactantius does so no less extensively and elegantly, clearly revealing all its secrets, its origin, and its progress. From him, one may draw many things on this matter that would be sought in vain among other authors.

Finally, in the year 312, as Emperor Constantine embraced the faith of Christ, the Christian Church took on a new face. It was everywhere adorned, endowed, and protected by laws, while the superstition of the pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum" — referring to non-Christian Gentiles</note> decreased daily. Then the Arian heresy arose, which strips Christ of his Deity and reduces him to the rank of created beings, denying that the Son is of the same substance and co-eternal <note>original: "ὁμοούσιον καὶ συνάϊδιον" (homoousion kai synaidion)</note> with the Father. This was soon condemned by the Council of Nicaea, the first of the Ecumenical councils, in the year 325. 

During the reign of Constantius, the heresy gathered its strength again, and supported by his protection, it raged against Catholics everywhere. It branched out into the new sects of the Semi-Arians, Photinians, Aetians, Eunomians, Macedonians, and others, all of which the Second General Synod of Constantinople, held in the year 381, subjected to anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note>. Theodosius the Great suppressed them by his authority and the laws he passed. 

In Africa, the Donatists <note>A schismatic group in North Africa that claimed only they were the true, pure church</note> caused great disturbances, being repressed several times by both secular and ecclesiastical power. When Julian was raised to the empire, paganism <note>original: "Gentilismus"</note> broke out again, with a very heavy persecution raised against the Christians. However, this "little cloud" quickly passed; after Julian was killed in the year 363, Jovian was soon elevated to Emperor. He fostered Catholic doctrine and restored exiled bishops to their sees. But after he was removed from human affairs barely eight months later, Valens (the brother of Valentinian) was moved to the helm of the Eastern Empire. Valens openly favored the Arian heresy; he increased its followers with high offices and adorned them with honors, while Catholics were everywhere depressed and harassed until the year 379. At that time, Theodosius the Great was admitted into the partnership of the empire by Gratian. Theodosius gave peace, quiet, and protection to the Catholics; he restrained all heresies whatsoever and governed the empire successfully for sixteen years.

# WRITERS.

<margin>4th CENTURY. From the year 300. 301. * Book 9, chapter 6.</margin>
PETER, an Alexandrian if not by birth, then certainly by education and office, leads the column of all writers of this age, and rightly so. For he was, according to the testimony of Eusebius*, "a divine ornament of bishops" <note>original: θεῖον ἐπισκόπων χρῆμα</note>, a divine glory of Bishops, and an eminent Teacher of the Christian Religion; venerable both for the holiness of his entire life and for his study and expertise in the sacred scriptures. He was trained in both piety and the holy scriptures by Bishop Theonas, whom he later succeeded in the see of Alexandria in the very secular year of Christ 300. After nearly three years in his episcopal office, the Persecution stirred up by Diocletian broke out in the year 303. From that time, for the remainder of his life, Peter exercised himself with stricter discipline due to the gathering storm and looked out for the common utility of the Churches as much as he humanly could. It is likely that he was held in prison for a long time during this Persecution, if indeed the reports are true which Epiphanius† records regarding the disagreement between him and Meletius of Lycopolis, a Bishop in the Thebaid—drawn from the uncertain, or so I believe, if not fabricated, *Acts of the Meletians*.

<margin>† On Heresies, 68.</margin>
For my part, guessing at an uncertain matter, it seems probable that Peter was handed into custody under Diocletian or Galerius Maximian, later released from his chains, and finally suffered martyrdom under Maximinus. Certainly, Eusebius*—who was present in Egypt during this very storm and was even thrust into prison there—vividly records that Peter was seized for no crime, but suddenly and against all expectation, and without any probable cause, was beheaded solely by the order of Maximinus. This happened to him in the ninth year of the persecution, the twelfth of his Episcopate, in the year of Christ 311.

<margin>* Place cited.</margin>
He wrote, for the sake of those who had fallen <note>The "lapsed" were Christians who had renounced their faith or handed over scriptures under the threat of torture</note> in the aforementioned Persecution, a *Book on Penance*; from which there survive today fifteen Canons adapted to various cases of penitents. These are found in the *Greek-Latin Councils, Volume I*, and with the *Synodical Commentaries* of Balsamon and Zonaras, or the *Universal Collection of Canons, Volume II*. Likewise, he wrote another book, *On Divinity*, from which certain passages are cited in the *Acts of the Council of Ephesus* and the *Acts of the Council of Chalcedon*; though in this last one, the Greek excerpts are missing.

There is also attributed to him a *Discourse on Easter* <note>original: Diatriba de Paschate</note> which frequently appears in manuscripts and which Petavius published in his *Uranologion* <note>A 17th-century collection of ancient texts on chronology and astronomy</note>, but whether it is truly his is not without merit doubted.

ANASTASIA, a Roman woman, most noble by birth, marriage, and wealth, but especially by her profession of the Christian faith, which she had drawn from her mother Flavia. She was the wife of Publius, a most distinguished man but one poorly disposed toward the Christian Religion, and for that reason even against his wife. Diocletian sent him as an ambassador to the Persians. Anastasia is said to have undergone martyrdom in the year 303. There exist two *Letters*, if only they be genuine, written by her from prison to the most holy Confessor Chrysogonus not long before her martyrdom, together with Chrysogonus’s *Replies*, found in Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the entry "Chrysogonos."

# THE ARIAN AGE.

->Overview of the Century.<-

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>
With this century arises a dire persecution, if ever there was one elsewhere, namely in the year 303, on February 23rd. This tenth persecution was begun under Diocletian, Maximian, and others, and was prolonged until its eleventh year. From this followed the destruction of churches, the confiscation of sacred property into the public treasury, the plundering of goods, and a manifold and pitiable slaughter of Christians. Punishments were sought out from every quarter and devised with every kind of cruelty: torches were lit and applied to feet and individual limbs until, once the skin was entirely cooked away, the force of the fire penetrated to the innermost vitals; bodies were burned, ground to dust, and thrown into rivers and the sea. 

Islands, prisons, and labor in the mines—as Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> notes in chapter 22—were considered light punishments. Fire, the cross, and wild beasts were daily and "easy" occurrences. In capital cases, the punishment of the sword was granted to very few, almost as a favor, to those who, due to old merits, had obtained a "good death." Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note> depicts the whole series of this persecution extensively; no less extensively and elegantly does Lactantius, who clearly reveals all its secrets, its origin, and its progress; from him, many things on this matter may be drawn which are sought in vain among other authors. 

Finally, in the year 312, with the Emperor Constantine embracing the faith of Christ, the Christian Church put on a new face. It was everywhere adorned, endowed, and protected by laws, while the superstition of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum" (Ethnics/Gentiles)</note> decreased daily. Then arises the Arian heresy, which detracts deity from Christ and reduces Him to the rank of created beings, denying that the Son is consubstantial <note>original: "ὁμοούσιον" (homoousion) — the Greek theological term meaning 'of the same substance.'</note> with the Father; it was soon condemned by the Council of Nicaea, the first of the Ecumenical councils, in the year 325. 

During the reign of Constantius, the heresy gathered strength and, supported by his protection, it raged everywhere against the Catholics. It spread into new sects: the Semi-Arians, Photinians, Aetians, Eunomians, Macedonians, and others. These the second General Synod held at Constantinople in the year 381 subjected to anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church.</note>, and Theodosius the Great, by his authority and the laws he passed, suppressed them. 

The Donatists <note>A schismatic group in North Africa who held that the church must be a church of saints, not sinners.</note> caused great disturbances in Africa, being frequently repressed by both secular and ecclesiastical power. When Julian was raised to the empire, Paganism flared up again, with a most heavy persecution excited against the Christians. But this "little cloud" soon passed; Julian was killed in the year 363. Jovian was soon raised to Emperor; he favored Catholic doctrine and restored exiled bishops to their sees. But after he was removed from human affairs after barely eight months, Valens, brother of Valentinian, was moved to the helm of the Eastern Empire. He openly favored the Arian heresy, increased his followers with dignities, and honored them with distinctions; meanwhile, Catholics were everywhere depressed and harassed until the year 379. In that year, Theodosius the Great, admitted into the partnership of the empire by Gratian, gave peace, quiet, and protection to the Catholics; he restrained whatever heresies existed, and for 16 years administered the empire successfully.

# WRITERS.

<margin>4th CENTURY from the year 300 [301 AD]. * Book 9, chapter 6.</margin>
Peter, if not by birth, then certainly by education and office an Alexandrian, leads the ranks of all writers of this age, and deservedly so. For, as Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the historian.</note> testifies, he was "a divine ornament of bishops" <note>original Greek: θεῖον ἐπισκόπων χρῆμα</note>, an excellent teacher of the Christian Religion; venerable both for the sanctity of his entire life and for his study and expertise in the sacred scriptures. He was trained in both piety and the holy scriptures by Bishop Theonas, whom he then succeeded in the Alexandrian see in the secular year of Christ 300. After nearly three years in his episcopal duty, the Persecution stirred up by Diocletian arose in the year 303. From that time, for the remainder of his life, Peter exercised himself with stricter discipline due to the gathering storm, and looked out for the common utility of the churches as much as a man could. It is certain that he must have been held in prison for a long time during this Persecution; at least if those things are true which Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop and writer against heresies.</note> <margin>† Heresy 68.</margin> relates regarding the discord between him and Meletius of Lycopolis, a bishop in the Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt. The "Meletian Schism" was a dispute over how to treat Christians who had renounced their faith under persecution.</note>, based on what I believe are the uncertain—if not fabricated—Acts of the Meletians. To me, guessing at an uncertain matter, it seems probable that Peter was handed into custody under Diocletian or Galerius Maximian, was later released from his chains, and <margin>* Place cited.</margin> finally suffered under Maximinus. Certainly, Eusebius <note>Eusebius was a contemporary witness to these events in Egypt.</note> clearly records that Peter—who was then in Egypt during this very storm and even thrown into prison there—was arrested for no crime and, beyond everyone's expectation, was suddenly and without any probable cause beheaded by the sole command of Maximinus. This happened to him in the ninth year of the persecution, the twelfth of his episcopate, in the year of Christ 311.

For the sake of those who had fallen <note>The "lapsed" (*lapsi*) were Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under threat of death.</note> during the aforementioned Persecution, he wrote the *Book on Penance*; from which *15 Canons* survive today, adapted to various cases of penitents. These are found in Greek and Latin in the *Councils*, Volume I; and with the commentaries <note>Scholia: explanatory notes or commentaries.</note> of Balsamon and Zonaras in the *Synodikon* or *Pandects of Canons*, Volume II. Likewise, he wrote another book, *On the Divinity*, from which certain passages are cited in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus (Act 1, p. 508; Act 7, p. 836, *Councils* Vol. III) and the Council of Chalcedon (Act 1, p. 286, *Councils* Vol. IV); though the Greek text is missing for this last excerpt.

A *Discourse on Easter* is attributed to him, which frequently appears in manuscripts and which Petavius <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit scholar and expert in chronology.</note> published in his *Uranologion*, though it is reasonably doubted whether it is truly his.

ANASTASIA, a Roman woman, most noble by birth, marriage, and wealth, but especially by her profession of the Christian faith, which she had drawn from her mother Flavia. She was the wife of Publius, a most distinguished man, but one ill-disposed toward the Christian Religion and, for that reason, toward his wife as well; Diocletian sent him as an ambassador to the Persians. Anastasia is said to have met her martyrdom in the year 303. Two *Letters* exist, provided they are genuine, written by her from prison to the most holy confessor Chrysogonus not long before her martyrdom, together with Chrysogonus’s *Replies*, found in the Suda <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> under the entry "Chrysogonos."

<margin>4th CENTURY from the year 300 [301 AD].</margin> ...admitted into his assembly only Virgins, Monks, those practicing continence, and Widows. He flourished around the year 302 and died in his nineties. He wrote *Commentaries on Scripture*, works on the *Six Days of Creation* <note>original: *Hexaemeron*</note>, and other works drawn from sacred literature, to which he added many *Psalms* composed by himself. Certain fragments remain in Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 67. <note>This refers to Hieracas (or Hierax) of Leontopolis, an Egyptian scholar known for his rigorous asceticism and for denying the literal resurrection of the body.</note>

<margin>
303 AD.
See Jerome's *Chronicle* at the year 417.
† *Letter to Paulina*, p. 104.

ARNOBIUS, of African descent, flourished in the year 303. At Sicca Venerea, an inland city of Africa, he taught Rhetoric. He was a pagan <note>original: *Gentilis*</note> by religion, which he defended vigorously; at length, warned by dreams to embrace the faith of Christ, he could not obtain Baptism from the Bishop until he had testified to the sincerity of his faith by publishing a truly elegant book *Against the Pagans* <note>original: *Adversus Gentes*</note> as a most certain pledge. He himself points out the time of his conversion when he says, "it is nearly three hundred years, more or less, since we began to be Christians." He rightly says, "more or less," for these books were written in the year 303, or not long after, once the persecution had already broken out. Nothing is certain regarding his death. Jerome † criticizes his style as uneven and excessive, and his book as confused without proper division of the work; quite rigidly and undeservedly, in my own judgment. For the Arnobian style has its own eloquence and a clearly flourishing diction; nor is the work lacking a neat and well-ordered method, as will be openly clear to anyone reading attentively. He holds certain dogmas that are perhaps less than Catholic <note>meaning "unorthodox" or not in line with what became standard church doctrine</note>; these are to be forgiven in a man recently breaking out from the darkness of the pagans and not yet sufficiently instructed in the elements of the Christian faith.

Books I–VII of *Against the Pagans* are extant, printed in *Rome* 1543, *Basel* 1546, *Paris* 1580, *Antwerp* 1582 with the notes of Canter; *Geneva* (by Heraldus) 1597, *Paris* 1605, *Hamburg* (by Elmenhorst) 1610, *Douai* (by Stewart) 1634, *Leiden* 1651 in quarto with the complete commentaries of various scholars, and finally *Paris* 1666 at the end of Cyprian's works with the notes of Ph. Priorius and selected others.

There are also circulated under his name *Short Commentaries on the 150 Psalms*, which the learned have long suspected to be the work of Arnobius the Younger.

<margin>
303 AD.
* *Chronicle* at the year 318.
† *Letter to Paulina*, p. 104.
</margin>
L. CÆLIUS LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS flourished chiefly in the year 303 and thereafter. His homeland was Italy, perhaps originating from Fermo, which is a town in the Picene territory on the coast of the Adriatic Sea; it seems he took the name Firmianus from there, though this rests on conjecture alone. He had as his master Arnobius, who was then teaching at Sicca in Africa; under him, while still a youth, he gave a most elegant specimen of his precocious talent by writing the *Symposium*. From there he was summoned to Nicomedia, which Diocletian was striving to adorn excessively and make equal to the city of Rome, so that he might open a school of eloquence for the youth. But, driven by a shortage of students, especially in a Greek city, he turned himself to writing. Among other things, once the Persecution had begun, he defended the cause of the Christian Religion against any troublesome enemies with the weightiest arguments and all the strength of his eloquence—and specifically against Hierocles, the Governor of Bithynia, who had been the author and advisor for inciting the Persecution and had composed two booklets, which he titled *The Lovers of Truth*, <term>addressed "To the Christians"</term> <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς Χριστιανούς</note>. Finally, when Constantine had gained supreme power, he was called to Gaul to instruct Crispus Caesar, the firstborn son of Constantine, in Latin literature. He died in extreme old age, but in which year is not clear. He was so poor in this life that (as Jerome † relates from Eusebius *) he often lacked even the necessities. He was very strong in the Theology of the Pagans, but little practiced in the <term>more mystical</term> <note>original Greek: μυστικωτέροις; here meaning the deeper, internal theological doctrines</note> principles of the Christian faith. Whence Jerome says: "Lactantius, like a certain river of Ciceronian <note>original: *Tullianae*, referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman standard for eloquence</note> eloquence, if only he could have confirmed our doctrines as easily as he destroyed those of others." Regarding the flaws noted in his writings—concerning the divinity, the eternal existence of the Son, the pre-existence of souls and the state after this life, the end of the age and the thousand-year reign, the arrival of Elijah who would convert many to the worship of God, and other chapters about which he spoke obscurely, incautiously, and sometimes even dangerously—one should excuse them...

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>4th CENTURY from the year 300 [301 AD].</margin>
...[learned] evaluators of things attribute his errors to the ignorance of the age in which he lived concerning these matters; the dogmas were somewhat more abstract, not yet clearly explained by theologians, nor defined by the decrees of Synods, and in which many Fathers of preceding centuries held the <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: *ὁμοούσιος* (*homoousios*), the theological term meaning "of the same substance," which would eventually become the orthodox standard at the Council of Nicaea</note> view. Other factors included his diligent study of secular literature and his almost continuous struggles against the Pagans <note>original: *Gentiles*</note>, which occupied the whole man and called his mind back from a more thorough examination of Christian doctrine. His style is polished, elegant, and easy, flowing naturally from a native fountain of eloquence. He is certainly a wonderfully elegant and eloquent writer, without controversy the most eloquent of all Christians; hence he is commonly called the *Christian Cicero*, and there are those who argue he not only equaled Cicero but even excelled him. This can be said without offense: from the age of Cicero himself, in the brilliance and purity of his speech, he has had scarcely any equal and no superior.

### W R I T I N G S .

<margin>* Book 5, chapters 2, 4.</margin>
The *Divine Institutes* in seven books. The first, *On False Religion*, attacks pagan theology and asserts the unity of the Divine Power. The second investigates the origin of human error regarding divine things and the causes of the foul fall into idolatry. The third deals with *False Wisdom* and shows the vanity of pagan philosophy. The fourth proposes *True Wisdom*, namely the dogmas of the Christian religion. The fifth treats *Of Justice* and demonstrates that it is held by Christians alone, while accusing the pagans who harass them with punishments and torments of wicked cruelty. The sixth discusses *True Worship*, regarding both the internal duty of the mind and the external duty of action; it also refutes the errors of the philosophers on this subject. The seventh has *The Blessed Life* as its subject, proves the immortality of souls, depicts the future state of life and the Final Judgment, and recalls the mind from bodily and fleeting things to eternal and divine objects. These books were written during the Persecution of Diocletian, which Lactantius himself * clearly enough testifies—not, as many would have it, under Licinius. The inscriptions to Constantine the Great that appear at the beginning of books 1, 2, 4, and 5 are recognized neither by older editions nor by the better manuscript codices; therefore, they must be considered the work of another hand.

*The Epitome of the Institutes*, though mutilated, providing a summary of only the last three books.

*On the Wrath of God*.

*On the Workmanship of God*.

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Scarcely any of the ancients after Jerome mention this small book. Étienne Baluze <note>original: *Steph. Baluzius*</note> was the first to bring it to light, publishing it with extensive notes in *Miscellanea, Vol. ii, p. 1*. Afterward, it appeared separately with brief commentaries at Oxford in 1680 (12mo) and at Åbo in 1684 (8vo).

A small fragment *On the Final Judgment*, attached to the end of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and first published along with it by Baluze.

*The Grammarian* <note>original: *Grammaticus*</note>.

*The Journey* <note>original: *Ὁδοιπορικὸν* (*Hodoeporicon*)</note>, a heroic poem about his journey from Africa to Nicomedia.

*To Asclepiades*, two books.

*To Probus*, four books of letters.

Jerome, in his *Commentary on Galatians IV*, cites an eighth book of letters to Demetrianus, likely a slip of memory; for the entire volume of Lactantian letters contained only eight books, of which the letters to Demetrianus constituted the seventh and eighth. ## SPURIOUS WORKS.

The *Poem on the Phoenix* <note>original: *Carmen de Phœnice*</note>, written by a certain Pagan.

The *Works of Lactantius* were published in Rome in 1465, 1470, 1474; in Venice 1472, 1478, 1483, 1490, 1497, 1502, 1509 (folio), 1515; in *Paris* 1513 (quarto); in *Florence* 1513; in Venice 1521, 1535; in Basel 1521 (quarto), 1523, 1532, 1563 (folio); in *Antwerp* 1539, 1555, 1568; in Lyon 1532, 1553, 1556, 1567 (16mo); in *Cologne* 1544; in *Paris* 1563, 1589; in *Antwerp* 1570 (octavo), 1579, 1587; in *Geneva* (a most accurate edition by Jean de Tournes) 1613 (16mo); in Lyon 1616 (16mo); in *Rome* 1650 (folio); in *Leiden* <note>original: *Lugd. Bat.* (Lugdunum Batavorum)</note> 1652, 1660 (octavo); in Oxford 1684; and in Cambridge 1685 (octavo). The *Leiden* edition excels the others, which Servatius Gallaeus published in 1660 with the most learned notes of various scholars <note>original: *Variorum*, referring to a standard edition including commentary from multiple previous editors</note>, to which he added his own clearly most erudite notes.

303 AD.

**Dorotheus**, (entirely distinct from Dorotheus the Priest of Antioch, whom Diocletian appointed as the overseer of the dye-works at Tyre—of whom Eusebius speaks in book 7, chapter 32; and also distinct from Dorotheus the Chamberlain and Martyr of Diocletian, mentioned by the same author in book 8, chapters 1 and 6). He was, as they say, the Bishop of the city of Tyre. Indeed, more recent writers, following the *Roman Martyrology*, make him a Priest; this seems to have flowed from no other source than a poor confusion of this man with Dorotheus of Antioch. To this error no small weight was added by the Latin translator of the preface (which we shall provide shortly), who calls our subject "Priest," rendering the Greek *presbyteros* <note>original: πρεσβύτερον</note> simply as *Presbyter* <note>In the early church, "presbyter" could denote an elder or priest, but was often distinguished from the rank of Bishop</note>. Our Dorotheus is said to have flourished in the year 303, having suffered much under the persecution of Diocletian and at last being sent into exile. When the storm subsided, he returned to his Church and survived until the times of Julian <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate," r. 361–363 AD</note>, under whom he fled to the city of Odyssopolis. There, he was seized by Julian’s officials and, after various tortures, ended his life in martyrdom at the age of 107. However, it will soon be apparent that all these details are uncertain and clearly fabricated, supported by the testimony of no writer older than the sixth century. Regarding him—except for a single Anonymous author from whom the compilers of the *Roman Martyrology* and the *Greek Menology* <note>A calendar of hagiographies used in the Eastern Church</note> took their material—there is a deep silence.

Our Dorotheus is said to have written many *Ecclesiastical Commentaries*; there is circulated today under his name a *Synopsis on the Life and Death of the Prophets, Apostles, and Disciples of the Lord*, which is preserved in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: *Bibliothec. PP.* (Bibliotheca Patrum)</note>, Volume III, and at the end of Salvian's works, printed in *Rome*, 1564 (folio). No one fails to see that this is spurious and should be relegated to the category of most foul fables. Regarding this *Synopsis* and its author, I confess I was long stuck <note>original: *aquam mihi diu hæsisse*, a Latin idiom for being "stuck" or "at a loss"</note>, until a Greek fragment by a certain Anonymous author opened the scene of the whole story. This fragment was transcribed by his own hand from two Barocci Manuscripts <note>A famous collection of Greek manuscripts in the Bodleian Library, Oxford</note>—namely, one numbered 206 and another joined to the questions of Anastasius of Nicaea on Holy Scripture, number 142—and was kindly shared with me by Henry Dodwell <note>A famous 17th-century Irish scholar and theologian</note> out of his courtesy. It contains many old wives' tales supported by no antiquity and arranged in no order; nevertheless, it contains quite a few things by no means to be despised, which contribute greatly to illustrating not only this Dorothean *Synopsis* but also other chapters of Church history. Therefore, I shall subjoin here the entire fragment, adorned with a Latin version, and then illustrate it with some observations. I was not permitted, by health nor by leisure, to review the manuscript codices from which it was taken. I fear that the friend whose labor I used in transcribing the Dodwell copy may have hurried too much here and there. Certain variant readings which I received from the famous Dodwell I have either included in brackets or placed in the margin.

### An ecclesiastical composition concerning the 70 disciples of the Lord <note>original: ο’ μαθητῶν</note>, by Dorotheus, Bishop of Tyre, an ancient man, bearer of the Spirit <note>original: πνευματοφόρου (pneumatophorou)</note>, and who became a martyr in the times of the emperors Licinius and Constantine.

This aforementioned and celebrated man left behind both Roman <note>In this context, "Roman" refers to the Latin language.</note> and Greek writings, since he was skilled in both languages and was very learned by nature. After the death of Diocletian and Licinius, he returned to his own diocese <note>original: παροικίαν (paroikian); literally "parish," but here referring to his episcopal see</note> and guided the Church in Tyre with great success until the time of Julian the Tyrant <note>A reference to Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive Roman paganism</note>. Because Julian did not kill Christians openly but secretly through his governors, Dorotheus went again to the city of Odyssopolis <note>Modern-day Varna, Bulgaria</note>. There he was seized by Julian’s governors, and after enduring many tortures in extreme old age, he died from the torments for his confession of Christ, being already one hundred and seven years old. This great elder left us ecclesiastical writings, in which he recorded the history of the 70 disciples of the Savior, and where each of the Prophets and Apostles ended their lives.

In the first part, he says that there were those 70 disciples, most of whom became bishops in various dioceses, whom the divine Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> mentions in his greetings. He indicates that after the resurrection of our Savior from the dead, they all returned and were among the Apostles; he notes their names in order as follows, saying:

### Ecclesiastical Treatise on the 70 disciples of the Lord <note>original: LXX. Domini discipulis</note>, written by Dorotheus, Bishop of Tyre, a very ancient man and divinely inspired, who was a Martyr in the times of Emperors Licinius and Constantine.

The Latin version of this Preface is prefixed to the published Synopsis.
</margin>

This celebrated man left behind various scholarly works <note>original: lucubrationes; literally "works produced by lamplight"</note> in both Latin and Greek, for he was skilled in both languages and knowledgeable in many matters due to his natural talent. After the death of Diocletian and the exile of Licinius, he was freed and regained his own diocese; indeed, he ruled the Church of Tyre until the time of Julian the Tyrant. Because Julian killed Christians not through manifest command but secretly through his governors, Dorotheus came again to the city of Odyssopolis, where he was apprehended by Julian's governors. After suffering many lashes in his great old age for his confession of Christ, he died amidst the torments themselves when he was **107** years old. Therefore, in the Ecclesiastical Commentaries which this great old man left behind, he composed the history of the **70** disciples of our Savior, and [recorded] where each of the Prophets and Apostles ended his life.

Thus, he first reports that there were **70** disciples, most of whom held the office of Bishop in various places; the divine Apostle mentions these same men in his greetings. ### Following in the manuscript is the Synopsis of the Disciples, just as it is found in the published editions. At the end of the "Seventy Disciples," these things are read:

---

These things the most holy and blessed Dorotheus, while staying in Rome, left recorded in the Latin language <note>original: "Latino sermone"</note> in his Commentaries. From these we have drawn these accounts, and translating them into the Greek language, we have brought to everyone's knowledge the register of the seventy disciples, which we had received as certain and true. For the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note>, while writing, made mention of them in these words: "those who were in the Lord before us." Therefore, it should by no means be considered incredible that the seventy disciples returned after the resurrection of Christ and believed in him, having witnessed his resurrection from the death—which holds the first place among all miracles.

[A Commentary by the same Dorotheus, Bishop and Martyr, concerning the city of Byzantium and its Bishops.] This great prelate <note>original: "praesul"</note> Dorotheus recorded in writing that the venerable house of the holy and glorious martyr Euphemia was first constructed in a rocky place <note>original: "in petræo"</note> by a certain Titus. This Titus presided over the See of Byzantium, and after his death, he was laid to rest in the said house near the old walls. After Christ’s resurrection, Andrew the Apostle set foot in these places and drew many thousands of Christians to his side; so much so that in other places, such a great multitude of disciples was by no means to be found. For all the Byzantines became teachers and steadfast, and because of their humble strength, they escaped the threats of tyrants, while propagating the divine word to the Pagans and Jews—especially since Titus performed miracles of the same kind that our Savior himself used to perform. Furthermore, while the tyranny of Licinius and Diocletian still held power, the Emperor Carus was killed in that state of affairs, along with his two sons, Carinus and Numerian. Once these were removed, the tyrants laid aside their fear...

[By the same Dorotheus, bishop and martyr, concerning Byzantium and its bishops.] This great high priest <note>original: "ἀρχιερεὺς"</note> Dorotheus therefore related in writing how the August house of the holy and fair-victorious martyr Euphemia was built in the rocky district by a certain Titus for various reasons; which Titus, having become Bishop of Byzantium and having reached his end, was laid to rest in it near the old walls. <margin>
4th CENTURY from the year 300.

...they surrendered to the punishments of the Christians, killing thousands of them every day. Among these, Adrian, the son of Probus, was eager to die for the cause. While in the city of Nicomedia, following the death of Carus, he witnessed the crowds of Christians being shamelessly slaughtered by Licinius <note>Licinius was a Roman Emperor (reigned 308–324 AD) who initially co-authored the Edict of Milan but later resumed the persecution of Christians in the East</note>. Adrian approached the tribunal and said to Licinius: "Why do you so shamelessly destroy the Roman army, while the barbarians occupy most of the Roman lands?" Licinius replied to him: "Are you also a Christian?" Adrian answered: "Indeed, I prefer to be perfected <note>original: "τελειωθῆναι" - a term used in early Christianity to signify completing one's faith through martyrdom</note> in this confession than to deny Christ." Licinius subjected him to many tortures, but also many flatteries and promises, hoping he would abandon his confession of the Christian faith. However, seeing him standing firm, Licinius flew into a rage and ordered his head to be cut off. After Adrian had completed his martyrdom in that confession, Metrophanes <note>Metrophanes was the Bishop of Byzantium from 306 to 314 AD</note>, who had recently begun his episcopate, learned of the event. He traveled to Nicomedia with his companions, secretly took the remains of the victorious martyr Adrian, and brought them back. He deposited them in the church appropriate for them located near Byzantium, in a place called Argyropolis <note>meaning "Silver City," a suburb of ancient Byzantium</note>. In that same place, Titus—the first to preside as bishop of Constantinople—had also placed the remains of the Adrian who was martyred under Maximian, along with Natalia his wife and others martyred with him. These remains were placed near those of Stachys, one of the seventy disciples, who had been appointed the first bishop of Byzantium in that very place by Andrew the Apostle. For Andrew, while passing through the region, intended to preach Christ to the people of Byzantium. But because Zeuxippus, who then governed the city, was a bloodthirsty man, he questioned all strangers arriving in Byzantium about Christ before allowing them entry; if anyone confessed to knowing Christ, he immediately ordered them bound hand and foot and thrown into the sea. Avoiding his cruelty, Andrew sailed past Byzantium and stayed for two years in the Thracian region not far away, exactly one stadium <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters</note> from the city of Argyropolis. There he gathered a congregation of law-abiding and God-loving men. As if always...

<column-break/>

<margin>4th CENTURY from the year 300.</margin>
...and they subsequently turned even more boldly to the slaughter of Christians, daily murdering several thousands of them. Among these, Adrian, son of Probus, sought death by a deliberate effort. For being present at Nicomedia after the death of Carus, and having seen the multitude of Christians killed by Licinius without any shame, he approached the tribunal and addressed Licinius in this way: "For what reason is the Roman army punished by you with such madness, while in the meantime the Barbarians occupy many Roman provinces?" To which Licinius replied: "Are you also a Christian?" Adrian answered: "Indeed I am, for I would rather die for that confession than deny Christ." Licinius offered many punishments, and even many flatteries and promises; but when he saw him constantly adhering to the confession of the Christian faith, burning with anger, he ordered his head to be cut off. After he had completed his martyrdom in that confession, Metrophanes, who had recently undertaken the Episcopate, being aware of the matter, took the friends who were at hand and arrived at Nicomedia. Having stolen away the remains of the glorious martyr Adrian, he carried them back and deposited them in the primary Church of the Byzantine Christians, located near the city, which received the name Argyropolis from the place where it is situated. In the same place, Titus, the first Bishop who presided over the See of Constantinople, deposited the remains of Adrian, who died as a martyr under Maximian, and Natalia his wife, and other companions of his martyrdom. In the same place are still deposited the remains of Stachys, one of the seventy disciples, who was appointed the first Bishop of Byzantium by the Apostle Andrew in that same place. For Andrew, crossing to the location, had it in mind to preach Christ to the Byzantines. But since Zeuxippus, the governor of the city at that time—a man of a cruel nature—would not permit any strangers arriving at Byzantium to enter the city except after an examination regarding the Christian religion; and if anyone confessed that he knew Christ, he would immediately order him to be thrown into the sea with his hands and feet bound; Andrew, avoiding his cruelty, sailed past Byzantium and established his seat for two years in the parts of Thrace not so far from Byzantium, only one stadium from the city of Argyropolis; and in that place, he gathered a congregation of pious men who were students of the truth.

...he gathered them. Therefore, when he had brought together about two thousand disciples, established an altar to Christ in Argyropolis <note>Argyropolis, meaning "Silver City," was a suburb of Byzantium on the European shore of the Bosphorus</note>, and ordained Stachys as Bishop, he departed for Sinope, a city of Pontus. Stachys departed from the living in the sixteenth year of his episcopate. Onesimus succeeded him, about whom the Apostle Paul wrote to Philemon. He presided over the see for fourteen years. After him, Polycarpus held the Byzantine episcopate for three years. Eighteen years after his death, Plutarchus received the priesthood and held it for sixteen years. Sedecion was his successor, who presided for nine years. Following him was Diogenes, who died after completing fifteen years in the episcopate. After him, Eleutherius presided for seven years; then Felix for five years, and soon Polycarpus, who reached his twelfth year. In the aforementioned house of worship, the bodies of these men were deposited in a stone chest; in that same place, the bodies of Natalia and Adrian, who later suffered martyrdom, were also deposited. In another sarcophagus placed directly opposite, the remains of thirteen martyrs were enclosed; but Adrian, the husband of Natalia, was deposited separately in a lead sarcophagus. Just as they lie to this day for all to see in the subterranean cave where the Apostle Andrew placed the altar. Now, once a significant multitude of disciples had been converted to the faith of Christ, and after the tyranny in the city of Byzantium had ceased following the death of Zeuxippus <note>The text likely refers to the end of the civil wars and persecutions that preceded the rise of Constantine</note>, the overseers of the Church of Argyropolis, having acquired more space and wishing to avoid the disturbances of the vast multitude and the conflict with the Greeks <note>In this context, "Greeks" refers to practitioners of the old pagan religions</note> and Jews, built another church in the open field near Argyropolis. The Emperor Constantine the Great later made this church larger and shaped it in the form of a cross, as he wished his own body to be deposited there. However, after the affairs of Byzantium had grown, Constantine’s courtiers persuaded him that it was not at all fitting for the bodies of Emperors to be carried outside the city. For that reason, another place was established for the burial of the Emperors. This building, having been completed to its summit, was dedicated to the most brave and pious martyrs of the Mosaic law, the seven boys and Eleazar the high priest <note>These are the Maccabean martyrs from the Old Testament/Apocrypha, who were highly honored as precursors to Christian martyrs</note>. However, the church retained the ancient name of the place, for from ancient times this place was called the Olive Grove <note>original: "Olivetum"</note>...

# The Arian Century.

<margin>4th Century, from the year 300 AD</margin> ...[Pro]bus, the son of Dometius, took up the priesthood and, once undertaken, administered it for twelve full years. After him, Metrophanes, the brother of Probus and son of Dometius, was ordained Bishop of Byzantium and ruled the see for a decade. During his episcopate, Constantine—forever Augustus—occupied Byzantium to better prepare his battle-lines against Licinius <note>Licinius was Constantine’s rival and co-emperor; their conflict ended in 324 AD.</note>. Charmed by the dignity of the man [Metrophanes] and having contemplated the excellent situation of the place, after he had defeated Licinius in war through the prayers of Metrophanes, he immediately transferred the seat of the Roman Empire to Byzantium. He fortified the city with walls and laws, granted very generous gifts to the citizens, and willed that it be called Constantinople after his own name.

These things the excellent Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Tyre, a traditional figure to whom an influential list of the Seventy Disciples and Apostles is attributed.</note> left written in the Latin language. They were translated into Greek by us during the consulship of Philoxenus and Probus <note>This dates the translation to the year 525 AD.</note>, when John, the Bishop of Rome, came to Constantinople. For when he was asked by the Archbishop of Constantinople to celebrate the sacred solemnities with him on the birthday of Christ <note>Christmas</note>, he refused to do so unless he were permitted to celebrate the rites before the Bishop of Constantinople. This was because Rome had received a Bishop before Constantinople. Therefore, when this dispute arose, our people drew arguments from the writings of Saint Dorotheus, proving that the see of Constantinople and the ordination [or succession] of the holy Apostle Andrew had been older than the Roman one. Indeed, John, the Bishop of Rome, acknowledged that Dorotheus's writing was true. However, he wished to be placed before the Bishop of Constantinople because he held the place of the Prince of the Apostles <note>original: "Apostolorum Principis" — refers to Saint Peter, considered the leader of the Apostles.</note>, and for this reason alone the priority of place was granted to him, not because the Roman see was older than the Constantinopolitan one. Then, returning as if from a detour, Saint Dorotheus, at the end of his commentary, made mention of the Twelve Apostles, recounting where each of them preached.

1. Peter the Apostle, after his departure from Antioch, preached the Gospel in Galatia and the inland places of Pontus, and in all Cappadocia and Bithynia, and finally in all Italy and Rome.

2. Andrew, his brother, [traversed] Bithynia, all Thrace, and Scythia...

<column-break/>

...[Pro]bus, inheriting the priesthood until the completion of twelve years. After him, Metrophanes, the brother of Probus and son of Dometius, was established as Bishop in Byzantium, having been devoted to the priesthood for ten years. It was during his time that Constantine, the ever-venerable, having occupied Byzantium because of the dispute with Licinius, and being pleased by the dignity of the man and recognizing the orderly arrangement of the places, became master of the wars against Licinius through the prayers of Metrophanes. And immediately he transferred the palace of Rome to Byzantium; and having fortified it with walls and divine decrees <note>original: "θέσφασι" — sacred laws or oracles.</note>, and having favored the citizens with lavish provisions, he renamed it Constantinople after his own name.

The all-virtuous Dorotheus left these things in Roman <note>original: "Ῥωμαϊκοῖς" — meaning Latin.</note> writings; they were compared by us also during the consulship of Philoxenus and Probus, when John the Bishop of Rome came to Constantinople. For having been invited by the Archbishop of the city to concelebrate with him on the birthday of Christ, he forbade this to be done unless the Bishop of the city [Constantinople] preceded him in the priestly service. This was on the grounds that Rome had received a Bishop before Constantinople. A movement having arisen from this, he [the Archbishop] made his defense from the writings of the great Dorotheus, showing that the bishopric of Constantinople and the ordination of the holy Apostle Andrew were already more ancient than that of Rome. And John, the Bishop of the Romans, confirmed that the extensive writing of Dorotheus was true. But he said that the Bishop of the city [Rome] should be put forward because he held the place of the chief of the Apostles, and for this sake the precedence was granted to him, and not because the bishopric of Rome was older than that of Constantinople. Going down further in the final parts of his writing, the holy Dorotheus makes mention of those twelve Apostles, saying where each of them preached.

1. Peter the Apostle preached the Gospel in the Gauls <note>original: "Γαλλίαις" — though the Greek word is used for France/Gaul, in this context it refers to Galatia in Asia Minor.</note> and in the inland parts of Pontus, and all Cappadocia and Bithynia after he had received Antioch, and later also in all Italy and Rome.
