Under his episcopate, Constantine, forever Augustus <term>Augustus: a title for Roman emperors signifying their majesty</term>, occupied Byzantium to better prepare for battle against Licinius. Delighted by the dignity of the man and observing the excellent location, and having defeated Licinius in war through the prayers of Metrophanes, he immediately transferred the seat of the Roman Empire to Byzantium. He enclosed the city with walls, fortified it, and bestowed very generous gifts upon the citizens, decreeing that it be called Constantinople after his own name.

The most excellent Dorotheus left these accounts written in the Latin language. They were translated into Greek by us during the consulship of Philoxenus and Probus <note>c. 525 AD</note>, when John, the Bishop of Rome, came to Constantinople. For when he was asked by the Archbishop of Constantinople to celebrate the sacred solemnities of Christ's birth <note>Christmas</note> with him, he refused to do so unless he were permitted to perform the rites before the Bishop of Constantinople. This was because Rome had received a bishop before Constantinople. Therefore, when this question was raised, our people drew arguments from the writings of Master Dorotheus, proving that the see of Constantinople and the ordination [or succession] of the holy Apostle Andrew was older than that of Rome. Indeed, John, the Bishop of Rome, acknowledged that Dorotheus's writing was true. However, he wished to be placed before the Bishop of Constantinople on the grounds that he held the place of the Prince of the Apostles <note>St. Peter</note>, and for this reason alone priority of place was granted to him, not because the Roman see was older than the Constantinopolitan one. Then, returning as if from a detour, Saint Dorotheus made mention of the twelve Apostles at the end of his commentary, describing where each of them preached.

1. Peter the Apostle, after his departure from Antioch, preached the Gospel in Galatia and the inland areas of Pontus, and in all Cappadocia and Bithynia, and finally in all Italy and Rome.

2. Andrew, his brother, traveled through Bithynia and all Thrace and Scythia...

<column-break/>

...succeeded to the priesthood for a full twelve years. After him, Metrophanes, the brother of Probus and son of Dometius, was appointed Bishop of Byzantium, presiding over the priesthood for ten years. During this time, Constantine, the forever-venerated, having occupied Byzantium because of the battle against Licinius, and being pleased by the man’s holiness and recognizing the beauty of the locations, had meanwhile become victorious in the war against Licinius through the prayers of Metrophanes. For which reason, transferring the royal palace of Rome to Byzantium, fortifying it with walls and glory, and graciously bestowing abundant provisions upon the citizens, he renamed this city Constantinople after his own name.

The all-virtuous Dorotheus left these things in Roman <note>Latin</note> writings; they were compared by us in the consulship of Philoxenus and Probus, when John the Bishop of Rome came to Constantinople. For when he was invited by the Archbishop of the city to concelebrate with him on the birthday of Christ, he forbade this to be done unless he, as the officiating priest, took precedence over the Bishop of the city. This was on the grounds that Rome had received a bishop before Constantinople. A movement having then arisen from that time, they made their defense from the writings of the great Dorotheus, showing the Bishopric of Constantinople and the ordination of the holy Apostle Andrew to be older than that of Rome. John, the Bishop of the Romans, confirmed that the writing by Dorotheus was true; but he said he held the Bishopric of the city with dignity because he occupied the place of the Chief of the Apostles, and for that reason the primacy was then granted to him, and not because the bishopric of Rome existed before that of Constantinople. These things again the holy Dorotheus mentions at the end of his writing, and of those twelve Apostles, saying where each of them preached:

1. Peter the Apostle preached the Gospel in the Galatias <note>original: "Γαλλίαις" — This Greek term could mean Gaul (France) or Galatia; contextually it refers to Galatia in Asia Minor.</note> and in the inland parts of Pontus, and all Cappadocia and Bithynia after his departure from Antioch, and later also in all Italy and Rome.

2. Andrew, his brother, [preached] throughout all Bithynia and all Thrace and Scythia...

These things Dorotheus collected for us from Greek and Hebrew records and set down in Latin Commentaries; we, compiling these as useful and likely truths, have made them known, so that it might be understood what the origins of the See of Constantinople are, and from what lineage Metrophanes <note>Metrophanes (died c. 326 AD) was the Bishop of Byzantium, later known as Constantinople</note> was descended. Also that Jeremiah, being at once a priest and a Prophet, when he had foreseen by divine inspiration the future captivity of Jerusalem after the death of Josiah, the king of Judah, moved the Mosaic Tabernacle from its former place, along with the Ark of the Covenant and all the holy things that were in it, the vessels, and all the furnishings that Moses had caused to be made. From that time on, that place has escaped the notice of everyone, even of those priests who had deposited the sacred vessels there together with Jeremiah. In addition to these things mentioned before, we also found written in the same place that when Lake Gennesaret <note>The Sea of Galilee</note> was constricted by ice under the consulship of Galba and Sulla <note>The text likely refers to the years 33 or 52 AD; the freezing of this lake is a legendary or rare climate event in this context</note>, the daughter of Herodias <note>Traditionally identified as Salome</note> walked upon the ice for her own amusement; but as the ice broke, her body was submerged in the water, while her head, cut off by the ice, remained above. Herodias, placing her daughter's head upon her knees amid many tears, confessed that she suffered this misfortune because of her demand for the head of John the Baptist. Furthermore, King Herod, the Tetrarch of the Jews at that time, died after being seized by the "louse disease" <note>original: *pediculari morbo*; a common description in ancient hagiography for a gruesome, parasitic infestation seen as divine punishment</note>. Pilate was the heir to Herod, for Herod's four sons and Herodias herself—the mother of those sons—breathed their last in Pilate's sight, having been consumed by the same disease.

Therefore, a certain Procopius, distinguished by the dignity of the priesthood, as much for the holiness of his life as for his knowledge of the sacred scriptures...

### Certain Observations on the Preceding Fragment.

1. <margin>Year of Christ 525.</margin> From this fragment, one may perceive that this transcriber of Dorotheus (as he presents himself) wrote during the consulship of Probus and Philoxenus—that is, in the year 525 AD, two hundred years after Dorotheus himself. For our author explicitly reports in the preface that Dorotheus suffered martyrdom under Julian the Apostate; therefore, when it is said at the head of the work that he was made a martyr under Licinius and Constantine, it must be said either that the final clause of the title came from a later hand, or at least that the word "martyr" <note>original: "μάρτυρα"</note> should be taken in a looser sense for a "Confessor." <note>In the early church, a "Confessor" was someone who suffered for the faith but was not killed, whereas a "Martyr" was one who died for it.</note> In this sense, confessors of the truth were frequently called *Martyrs* in the writings of the ancient Fathers while they were still among the living, even before they had won the palm of martyrdom.

2. It is very probable that this anonymous writer was the actual creator of the *Dorothean Synopsis* itself. For who ever mentioned any Dorotheus, Bishop of the Tyrians, in the time of Diocletian or Julian? Indeed, who mentioned him even before the year 357 AD, when a certain Dorotheus was substituted in place of the deposed Bishop Photius of Tyre? Who ever called Dorotheus a martyr under Julian, or a confessor under Diocletian? The Roman Martyrdom for June 5th says he suffered many things under Diocletian; our anonymous author says he was punished with exile. But would this have escaped the notice of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History," who was a contemporary of these events</note>, who sought out the deeds of martyrs and confessors from every quarter, being a confessor himself under this persecution, and what is more, living in Tyre around this very time? Who among the ecclesiastical writers who flourished in these first centuries ever remembered this *Dorothean Synopsis*—even among those who professionally handed down catalogs of ecclesiastical writers? Who but a dullard, and one whose head is hardly sound, would present to us Dorotheus—a Greek man and a leader in Tyre among the Phoenicians—composing his commentaries in the Latin language? It remains, therefore, that either our anonymous author fabricated these things, or at least published things fabricated by his priest, Procopius. Hence, after the fashion of nearly all impostors, he feigns that these things lay hidden and unknown for a long time, only becoming known to the world nearly two full centuries after Dorotheus's death. This cannot be believed with any probability, especially since these commentaries contained nothing but a summary of Apostolic and Church history, which would have been clearly useful if it were genuine.

3. One may extract the origin of the entire forgery from the fragment itself: it seems to be nothing other than that much-discussed <note>original: "πολυθρύλλητος"</note> contention between the Roman See and Constantinople concerning primacy <note>original: "πρωτοκαθεδρίᾳ" - literally the "first seat" or highest authority</note>. So that the matter may shine more clearly, the history must be traced back a bit further. Once the seat of the Empire was transferred to Constantinople by Constantine the Great, the prelate of the Royal City soon began to raise his crest and extend the boundaries of his ecclesiastical dignity. In the year 381 AD, the Fathers of the second Ecumenical Council, held at Constantinople, decreed in Canon III that the Bishop of Constantinople, because it is the "New Rome," should have the "prerogatives of honor" <note>original: "τὰ πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς"</note> after the Bishop of Rome. From this point on, the prelates of the See of Constantinople daily assumed new strengths for themselves; more by deed, indeed, than by right, until the year 451 AD, when the general Council of Chalcedon...

# The Arian Century.

<margin>
THE 4th CENTURY, from the year 300 AD.
* Book 17, chapter 9. See Marcellinus in the *Chronicon* under the consulship of Philoxenus and Probus, page 61.
</margin>
...it was established in Canon IX: "But if anyone has a controversy with the Metropolitan of the province, let him go to the Exarch <note>A high-ranking regional governor or ecclesiastical official</note> of the Diocese, or to the throne of the imperial city of Constantinople." And they decreed not only this, but also in Canon XXVIII: "Since the Fathers rightly granted privileges to the throne of Old Rome because that city was the seat of empire, the 150 bishops, moved by the same consideration, have granted equal privileges <note>original: "τὰ ἴσα πρεσϐεῖα"</note> to the most holy throne of New Rome; rightly judging that the city which is honored by both the Empire and the Senate, and enjoys equal privileges with Old Rome, should also be extolled and magnified in Ecclesiastical matters no differently than she, being indeed second after her." The fathers at the Council of Chalcedon ratified this, even though the Legates of the Roman Pontiff resisted most vehemently; they subjected the dioceses of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace to the See of Constantinople. The most glorious Judges who presided over the Synod also ratified it, declaring that "above all, the primacy and extraordinary honor <note>original: "πρὸ πάντων μὲν τὰ πρωτεῖα καὶ τὴν ἐξαίρετον τιμὴν"</note> must be preserved for the Roman Archbishop according to the Canons, but the Archbishop of New Rome ought to enjoy the honor of the same privileges, and have authority of his own power <note>original: "τῶν αὐτῶν πρεσϐείων τῆς τιμῆς ἀπολαύειν, καὶ αὐτὸν ἐξ αὐθεντίας ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν"</note> to ordain the Metropolitans in the Asian, Pontic, and Thracian dioceses." And in the Synodic Letter to Pope Leo, the Holy Fathers affirm that they have done nothing else in this matter than confirm by synodal decree the custom which has prevailed for a long time <note>original: "τὸ ἐκ πολλῶ κρατῆσαν ἔθος"</note>.

Pope Leo took these things poorly; he fumed, he gnashed his teeth, and filled nearly every place with complaints and outcries, claiming that the venerable Canons of the Council of Nicaea were being trampled, Metropolitan rights violated, and therefore the decrees of Chalcedon should be held as naught. Leo's successors also took this poorly, so much so that Pope Felix struck Acacius of Constantinople with an anathema; Acacius soon returned like for like, striking the Pope’s name from the Church of Constantinople's diptychs <term>Diptychs: Lists of names of the living and dead commemorated during the liturgy; removing a name was a sign of excommunication</term>, as Basil the Cilician testifies in his *Ecclesiastical History* according to Nicephorus, Book 16, chapter 17. Finally, under Justin the Elder, a certain peace was patched up between the bishops of both seats, though the dispute was not entirely settled. For when in the year 525 AD, Pope John was sent to Constantinople by Theodoric, King of the Goths, he refused to perform sacred rites with the Bishop of Constantinople unless he himself celebrated first; nor, as Nicephorus witnesses, would he sit beside the prelate of the Royal City, but so that he might defend the prerogative of the Apostolic See, he was placed on a throne above the Bishop of Constantinople, even in the Patriarchal Church. On this occasion the controversy flared up again, with John putting forward the apostolic dignity and antiquity of his see. The Bishop of Constantinople, on the contrary, strenuously asserted the priority of his own Church, claiming it was founded by Saint Andrew the Apostle before Peter himself ever came to Rome. Therefore, when this question was raised, as our own Anonymous author testifies, these "Dorothean monuments" were brought forward; from these the Constantinopolitans drew arguments to prove the antiquity of their Church, contending that it was older than the Roman one.

Indeed, I believe no prudent person will deny that these Commentaries were first fabricated under the name of Dorotheus on this occasion, and perhaps the impostor pretended they were written in Latin for that reason: so that he might strike a stronger argument against John of Rome. Finally, this is the aim of all the splendid fables our author tells concerning the Byzantine martyrs, the translation of relics thither, and the sacred buildings—even in these first budding times of Christianity—magnificently constructed there, and other things which served to exalt the dignity of the Byzantine See.

4. From this it is clear from which records the Patriarch Nicephorus of Constantinople in his *Chronography*, and Nicephorus Callistus in Book 8, chapter 6, derived their catalogs of Byzantine prelates from Andrew the Apostle down to Metrophanes (the contemporary of Constantine the Great); namely, from our author, with whom they agree exactly, except for one or two errors in the numbering of years. Indeed, Nicephorus Callistus even transcribed a quite long, complete passage of our author word-for-word. That same succession of bishops is exhibited in that Patriarchal series which exists in Book 4, page 296 of the *Greco-Roman Law*; from these the *Catalog of the Patriarchs of Constantinople* (or *Chronicle* of the Greek Church, as it is called) by Philippus Cyprius, Prothonotary of Constantinople, departs in a few places, which was not long ago published in Greek and Latin by Nicolaus Blancardus.

He highlights how these fables were later used by major Byzantine historians like Nicephorus Callistus.</summary>

5. From this, finally, one can see from what source those well-known fables flowed—the stories of Herod, Herodias, and her daughter dancing upon the ice <note>A legendary tradition where Salome, the daughter of Herodias, fell through the ice while dancing, and the ice cut off her head; this is not found in the Gospels</note>, and so on—which can be found in no author older than our own. <margin>313 AD.</margin>
### RHETICIUS

**RHETICIUS**, Bishop of the city of Autun <note>original: "Augustoduni"</note>, formerly the capital of the Haedui in Gaul, flourished in the year 313. In that year he set out for Rome, being one of the three bishops of Gaul whom Constantine the Great appointed as judges—alongside Miltiades of Rome and other Italian bishops—to decide the case of Caecilian of Carthage against Donatus <note>The Donatists were a schismatic group in North Africa who claimed that only "pure" clergy could administer valid sacraments</note>. In the following year, he was present at the Synod of Arles, where the same case was handled by a fuller assembly, and sentence was again passed against Donatus. He wrote a large volume against *Novatian* <note>An early rigorist who taught that the church could not forgive those who lapsed during persecutions</note>, and *Commentaries on the Song of Songs*. NE.

<margin>312 AD.</margin>
### ALEXANDER

**ALEXANDER**, Bishop of Alexandria, the noble champion of ecclesiastical dogmas <note>original: "ὁ γενναῖος τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν δογμάτων πρόμαχος"</note> (an honorific with which Theodoretus distinguishes him †) <margin>† Church History, book I, chapter 2.</margin> *a most sharp defender of Church doctrine*. He succeeded Achillas in the See of Alexandria around the year 312 or 313. Under his leadership, Arius began to spread his detestable heresy and openly vomited out the venom he had hitherto brewed in his heart. He found an opportunity (if Socrates narrates the matter correctly <margin>* Church History, book I, chapter 5.</margin> *) in a somewhat overly subtle sermon by his Bishop. While Alexander was disputing a bit too ambitiously concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity, Arius, thinking the bishop was introducing the dogma of Sabellius <note>The heresy that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely three "modes" or masks of a single person, rather than three distinct persons</note>, turned toward the opposite opinion out of a zeal for contention; he asserted there was a time when the Son did not exist, and that he was therefore a created being. And indeed, Constantine the Great rebuked both Alexander on this account—because he had proposed useless questions to his Priests—and Arius, because he had impudently brought forward in response something he should never have thought, or at least should have suppressed in silence. But in truth, Theodoretus is a witness that a deeper cause of hatred against Alexander lay in Arius's soul <margin>* Cited location and Heretical Fables, book 7, chapter 1.</margin> *; he reports that Arius, taking it poorly that Alexander had been preferred over him and placed in the highest rank of Ecclesiastical dignity, and being unable to cause him trouble otherwise, began to openly contradict his doctrine, driven by the stings of envy. However the matter stood, Arius went about his business diligently. When Alexander could not recall him to a sounder mind through any warnings or advice, he called a Synod at Alexandria, condemned his impious dogmas, and cast the man out of the order of Priests. He later confirmed this same sentence in a fuller Council of nearly one hundred Bishops, writing letters so that the Arian impiety might become known to the Catholic Church. Yet a third Synod was held on this matter at Alexandria, arranged by Hosius of Corduba <note>A Spanish bishop and trusted advisor to Emperor Constantine</note>, whom Constantine had sent there with letters addressed jointly to Alexander and Arius to settle these disputes. But it was all in vain. Therefore, that great and most celebrated Council of Nicaea was convoked from the whole Christian World in the year 325, of which Alexander was a major part, being both an author and a participant in these events <note>original: "εἷς ὢν καὶ κοινωνὸς τῶν γεγονότων τυγχάνων"</note>. By his presence, he brought the greatest joy to the whole Synod; and despite his advanced age, he sustained much labor so that peace might be restored to the Alexandrians, as the Nicene Fathers themselves <margin>* Synodical Letter in Theodoret book I, chapter 9 and Socrates book I, chapter 9.</margin> * speak of him. After the errors were condemned and Arius was proscribed, Alexander died five months after the Synod was held, at the end of the year 325 or the first month of the following year. Of the letters he wrote concerning Arius and his dogmas, which numbered more than seventy <margin>† See Socrates, book I, chapter 6.</margin> †, only two survive today: one lengthy one written after the expulsion of Arius, in which he uncovers the heretic's craftiness and refutes his dogmas at length, addressed to his namesake *Alexander*, the Bishop of Byzantium <note>Constantinople</note>, which is found in Theodoret book I, chapter 4; the other is an Encyclical <note>A circular letter intended for wide distribution</note> to the Bishops of the Catholic Church established in every city, written at the same time, in which he recounts the blasphemies of Arius and asks all the Bishops to take note of both him and his followers, whom he had struck with excommunication...

# The Arian Century.

<margin>The Year 300 AD.</margin>
**4th CENTURY.** [Alexander] informs others <note>This likely refers to the circular letter sent by Bishop Alexander of Alexandria to other bishops</note> so that they do not admit these heretics to communion. This account is found in Socrates, Book 1, Chapter 6, and Gelasius of Cyzicus, *History of the Council of Nicaea*, Book 2, Chapter 3.

315. **ARIUS**, the most famous <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A founder or chief leader of a heretical sect</note> in the whole world and throughout all preceding ages, was Libyan by race—or as Photius holds, an Alexandrian by birth. He was the son of Ammonius and began (as some say) to become known as a heresiarch from the year 315; however, it seems to me that this happened a little later, only a few years before the Council of Nicaea. It is probable that he came out of the school of Lucian of Antioch, for he explicitly calls Eusebius of Nicomedia a *Fellow-Lucianist* <note>original: "Conlucianistam"</note>; the disciples of Lucian the Martyr seemed to glory in this title and addressed one another by it. 

When the Meletian schism <note>A dispute over the treatment of Christians who had lapsed during persecution</note> arose, he initially defended the side of Meletius. Later, having deserted him, he went to Peter, the Bishop of Alexandria, and was admitted into the rank of deacons by him, but was ejected again due to his turbulent nature. After the death of Peter, he feigned repentance and, having begged forgiveness from Bishop Achillas, was promoted by him to the dignity of a priest. He was entrusted with the care of one of the Alexandrian churches, which was called Baucalis. Indeed (if we are to trust an unknown writer, Patricius Ararsius, in a book called *The Ocean* cited by the author of the <margin>* Of the Synod, published by Pappus, p. 14.</margin> *Synodicon*), the governance of the Catechetical School was even demanded for him. 

He also enjoyed favor for some time from Alexander, the successor of Achillas, until he found a convenient opportunity to vigorously attack Catholic truth regarding certain primary <margin>From Arius’s *Thalia* in Athanasius, *On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia*, p. 681, etc.</margin> articles of faith. He openly taught that there was indeed a Trinity, but that it was not equal in glory and majesty, and that one person was more glorious than the other. He taught that God had made His Son the beginning of all creatures and had adopted Him as a son, but that the Son had nothing of the Father's substance. He claimed: "For he was not with [the Father], nor was he <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "ὁμοόσιῷ" (homoousios) - meaning having the same essence or being</note> with him. The Father is foreign to the Son in terms of substance, because the Father exists without a beginning." <note>original: "ἐκ ἦν γὰρ σὺν τῷ, ἀλλ’ ἐδὲ ὁμοόσιῷ αὐτῷ. — ξένῷ τῶ υἱῶ κατ’ ὐσίαν ὁ πατὴρ, ὅτι ἄναρχῷ ὑπάρχει."</note> The Father is alien to the Son as far as substance is concerned, since He lacks a beginning. For the Son is neither equal to the Father nor consubstantial, and therefore, "he is neither eternal, nor co-eternal, nor co-unbegotten with the Father, nor does he have his being together with the Father." <note>original: "ἐδὲ ἀΐδιῷ ἢ συναιδιῷ, ἢ συναγίνητῷ τῷ πατρὶ, ἐδὲ ἅμα τῷ πατρὶ ἔχει εἶναι"</note> 

And elsewhere, <margin>From the *Thalia* in Athanasius, *Oration 2 against the Arians*, p. 141.</margin> "The Son was not always; for he did not exist before he was born; nor was he from the Father, but he emerged from non-beings; nor did he have the Father's substance as his own; for he was a creature and a work; and therefore Christ is not true God, but was made God by participation." <note>original: "ἐκ ἀεὶ ἦν ὁ υἱὸς, ἐ γὰρ πρὶν γεννηθῆ, ἐκ ἐσὶν ἐκ τῶ πατρὸς, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἐκ ὄντων ὑπέση, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐκ ἐσὶν ἴδιῷ ἢ τῆς πατρὸς ὐσίας· κτίσμα γὰρ ἐσὶ καὶ πόνημα, καὶ ἐκ ἐσὶν ἀληθινὸς θεὸς ὁ χριστὸς, ἀλλὰ μετοχῇ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐθεοποιήθη."</note> We have expressed these things in Arius’s own words so that his mind might be more clearly understood. 

And although this man of versatile character used to soften, or rather cover up, such monstrous words and portentous propositions with disguised and plausible explanations as the situation required, the sum of his errors always came back to this: that the Son is inferior to the Father in time, nature, and dignity, made from things that did not exist, and clearly a creature, even if placed in a more excellent order of creatures. 

On account of these things, he was frequently warned by his Bishop, frequently rebuked, and frequently condemned by synods, yet he refused to renounce his impious opinions. He propagated these far and wide, both publicly and privately, through sermons and letters sent everywhere, to such an extent that he had many followers—not only at home, but also bishops of great name in foreign regions who favored him. They entered into communion with him and tried to restore him to his Bishop’s grace and peace by their intervention. 

But since Arius would not set aside his errors, and Alexander would not betray the Catholic faith, the Council of Nicaea was assembled. In this council, by the vote of 318 bishops, the impious doctrine of Arius was condemned. By order of Emperor Constantine, his books were burned, and Arius himself was banished to Illyricum. From there, after three years, having offered a document of repentance and professing to embrace the Nicene faith, he was recalled by a letter from the Emperor. He so thoroughly deceived the Emperor with his contrived tricks that Constantine explicitly commanded Alexander, the Bishop of Constantinople, to admit him into communion without delay. 

While Arius was proceeding there, surrounded by the henchmen of his faction, and had reached the Forum of Constantine, he sought out a latrine because of an urgent necessity of the bowels. There, like Judas, he burst open in the middle; and having collapsed, together with...

...his intestines spilled out, he breathed out his unhappy soul, around the year 336. Thus indeed that most cursed and hated head met a fatal end, not unworthy of his name which is to be execrated for eternity. I know indeed that the illustrious man Henri Valois <gloss>original: "Hen. Valesium"; a famous 17th-century scholar of church history</gloss> affirms that Arius had already died some years before, and therefore the man who was admitted to the peace of the Church at the Synod of Jerusalem in the year 335 along with Euzoius was not our Arius, but another Arius who was a follower of the <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A leader of a heretical sect</note>. But nearly all these things are said without proof, relying only on light conjectures and not on any clear testimony of the Ancients; and one must be a complete stranger to Church History who does not know that the Ancients refer all these things solely to our Arius with unanimous consent. On the contrary, Rufinus <gloss>†</gloss>, Zonaras <gloss>*</gloss>, and others <gloss>†</gloss> err when they claim that Arius lived under Constantius and died during his reign. He was a man clearly sharp and learned, with manners composed for deception, and more religious in appearance and form (as Rufinus <gloss>||</gloss> says of him) than in virtue. For what his <unclear>constitution</unclear> <note>original Greek: "τὴν... σωτὰς"</note> was like, see Epiphanius, *Heresy 69*, and Constantine’s *Letter to Arius* in Gelasius, Book 3, Chapter 1.

He wrote songs (according to Philostorgius <gloss>*</gloss>) of various kinds—namely, songs for sailors, millers, and travelers, and others of that sort, set to specific melodies as he thought suitable for each song; his goal was to gradually lead the minds of the unlearned toward his impiety through the sweetness of the song. But most celebrated of all is that book called *Thalia*, so often cited by Athanasius, written in the manner of Sotades <note>A Greek poet known for using "obscene" or coarse meters</note>, a most shameful Iambic writer from Crete (which is why he is called a *fox* by Athanasius). In this book, he discussed the most grave and venerable mysteries of the faith in the lightest and most futile rhythms. It can be doubted, however, whether the entire work consisted of verses, or if instead songs were scattered throughout it to make it more accommodating to the habits and character of the common people. Certain excerpts from it are found in Athanasius, *On the Decrees of the Nicene Synod against the Arian Heresy*, p. 413; *Against the Arians*, Oration 2, p. 137, 140, 141, etc.; and *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*, p. 680. Of the many letters he wrote, *one to Eusebius of Nicomedia* survives in Epiphanius, *Heresy 69*, and Theodoret, Book 1, Chapter 5. Athanasius has another, given in his own name and those of his followers to Alexander, the Bishop of Alexandria, in the book *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*, p. 682, and also in Epiphanius in the place cited above.

|| In Socrates, Book 1, ch. 8.
</margin>
**EUSEBIUS**, who obtained the surname *Pamphili* from the very close friendship he shared with the martyr Pamphilus, had Palestine as his homeland, and perhaps Caesarea as his birth city. For in this Church he was both instructed and dipped in the "salutary bath" <note>A poetic reference to Baptism</note>, and he seems to me to indicate obscurely at the beginning of his *Letter* <gloss>||</gloss> *to the People of Caesarea* that he held ecclesiastical offices there. He was born toward the end of the third century, around the year 270, if one may guess. As a man exceedingly learned in nearly all secular literature, he devoted himself with the greatest effort to the study of ecclesiastical antiquities. To this end, he diligently sought out the monuments of the learned who came before him, searched the archives of earlier centuries, examined the acts of civil judgments, and shook out every shelf of the libraries—especially that most noble library which Pamphilus had built at Caesarea, which he studied day and night. And indeed, it seems not to be disregarded what Jerome (or whoever is hidden under his name) relates in the *Letter to Chromatius and Heliodorus*: that when Constantine entered Caesarea, he told Eusebius to ask for some benefits for his Church. Eusebius, however, replied that his Church was sufficiently enriched with wealth and lacked nothing, but that he had one unique wish in his prayers: that the public monuments be discussed through careful scrutiny so that it might be established more certainly what was done by judges throughout the entire Roman world against the Saints of God. Specifically, he asked that the records of which martyrs won the palm of their passion, by which judgment, in which province or city, on which day, and with what perseverance, be taken from the archives and sent to him by royal order. This was done, and from that source, having become a suitable reporter, he wove together his *Ecclesiastical History* and the trophies of nearly all the martyrs.

<margin>4th CENTURY, from the Year 300.</margin> And indeed, Antipater of Bostra <note>original: "Antipater Bostrensis"; a 5th-century bishop and critic of Eusebius</note>, an adversary of Eusebius, easily concedes that these things are not far from the truth: <margin>\* Sermon 1 against the Apology for Origen by Eusebius, in the Second Council of Nicaea, Act 5.</margin>
> "For my part, I confess and acknowledge that the man was widely learned, and that nothing from the writings of the ancients escaped his knowledge. Indeed, by utilizing imperial cooperation, he was easily able to gather to himself what was scattered everywhere." <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ, ὅτι μὲν πολυΐστωρ ὁ ἀνὴρ...; original Latin: Ego vero, quod multus quidem in historiis vir fuerit...</note>

In the year 307, he followed Pamphilus, who had been thrown into prison, with his usual duties of affection, staying with him constantly; by their joined efforts, they busied themselves with strenuously advancing literary work. Two years later, after Pamphilus had completed his journey through martyrdom, Eusebius withdrew to Tyre, undoubtedly hiding with his most sincere friend, Bishop Paulinus, <margin>† Book 8, chapter 7.</margin> where he testifies that he witnessed firsthand various and most cruel struggles of the martyrs †. From there he sought Egypt, and there he found the cruelty of the persecutors even more heated, with himself also being thrown into chains. From this later arose material for his adversaries to slander him—namely, that while he was shut in prison, he had sacrificed to idols <note>Offering sacrifice to Roman gods was the standard test to identify Christians; those who did so to escape death were called "lapsi" or "fallen."</note>. Egyptian confessors <note>Those who suffered for the faith but were not killed</note>, and among them especially Potamo, Bishop of Heraclea, charged him with this in the year 335 while he was presiding, among others, at the Synod of Tyre <margin>\* In Epiphanius, Heresies 68, n. 7; see Athanasius, Apology 2, p. 567.</margin> \*. But if accusing were enough, who would be innocent? Driven by hatred and envy, they snatched up weapons against him from every side; nor do they bring forward any witness in this matter, except for a certain slight rumor, or rather a suspicion of a rumor, which Potamo himself does not deny arose from no other cause than that Eusebius escaped from prison safe and unharmed. What then? If he had sacrificed, according to the rigid discipline of that time, he would have fallen from every clerical rank, and certainly would by no means have been promoted to a higher order. Athanasius and Socrates explicitly note this regarding Asterius the Sophist, who was seeking clerical rank, specifically a bishopric <margin>† On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia, p. 684. \* Book 2, c. 36, p. 72.</margin> † \*. 

But I return to Eusebius. When the persecution ceased, he returned to Palestine, where after the death of Agapius he was appointed Bishop of Caesarea. I admit that in the Latin signatures attached to the Synod of Ancyra held in the year 315, one Agricolaus is listed as Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. But those signatures, as they now appear in the volumes of the Councils, came from the workshop of Isidore Mercator <note>Also known as Pseudo-Isidore, an 8th-century author of forged documents; the author is questioning the reliability of these records</note>. An older version published by Christophe Justel contains only <margin>\* Page 13.</margin> \* *Agricolaus of Caesarea*; whom the Greek *Synodicon* edited by Pappus \*—dealing with this very Synod—clearly teaches us was not Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, but of Cappadocia.

Not long after, the dedication of the most beautiful church which Paulinus had built at Tyre was held, around the year 316, I believe, at which time Constantine celebrated the tenth anniversary of his reign <note>The "Decennalia," a major Roman festival</note>. For it was the custom then for Christians, as for the Pagans before them, to dedicate their <term>Basilicas</term> <note>Large public buildings or churches</note> on the tenth anniversaries of Emperors, or other such solemnities, as the renowned Antoine Pagi learnedly observes in his *Dissertation on the Consular Years*, Part 2, Chapter 3. All the bishops of the neighboring churches were present at this dedication, to whom Eusebius delivered a most elegant oration, which he presents in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 10, Chapter 4. I am not unaware that it is called into doubt by some whether this oration had Eusebius as its author. Unjustly so. The oration itself breathes his talent and multifaceted learning. The <term>Panegyrical</term> <note>A speech of high praise</note> part agrees perfectly with those things he had treated in the preceding chapters, in the same sense and almost the same sentiments; his close friendship with Paulinus suggests that we should believe it could have been held by no one rather than Eusebius, who inscribed this tenth book of his *History* to Paulinus, and therefore it was fitting for this oration to be inserted here. Furthermore, if it were by another, why would he insert such a lengthy sermon in this place? Why with the author's name suppressed? He who usually cites the writers he alleges by name. You will say that Eusebius makes no mention of himself. I confess, out of modesty, he concealed his name: "And a certain person," he says, "of moderate merit among those who were praising, having composed a discourse, came forward into the midst," <margin>\* On Byzantine Writers, Part 1, ch. 1, Num. 56.</margin> \* a man of some moderate merit who had composed such an oration. And writers are generally accustomed to speak in this way whenever they speak of themselves. Nor is there any reason for someone to say, along with the renowned Hanck \*, that that oration could have been spoken by Eusebius while he was still a priest. For who is unaware that it was not then a common custom that...

# The Arian Century.

...would priests preach in the presence of Bishops, especially at such a solemn gathering and on such a splendid occasion? But enough of these matters.

<margin>
4th CENTURY, from the Year 300.
* Book 1, chapter 7.
† Treasury of Orthodox Faith, book 5, chapter 7, page 445.
|| Book 1, chapter 9.
* On the Life of Constantine, book 3, chapter 11.

In the Council of Nicaea, in the year 325, such honor was bestowed upon him that he welcomed the Emperor entering the Synod with a panegyric <note>A formal speech of high praise</note> and held the first place at the Emperor’s right hand. Theodoret * indeed attributes this to Eustathius of Antioch, and Nicetas Choniates † to Alexander of Alexandria, but both Sozomen || and a very ancient title of a chapter in Eusebius’s own work * support our Eusebius. Finally, Eusebius himself † relates that during the twentieth-anniversary celebrations of Constantine's reign—at which this Council was held—he delivered the Panegyric to the Emperor while surrounded by the assembly of the servants of God. After the case of Arius <note>Arius was a priest whose teachings—that Jesus was a created being and not eternal—led to the first major schism in the Church</note> was examined at length from all sides, Eusebius offered a Creed <note>Symbolum fidei</note> of the Catholic faith to the Fathers. This was indeed approved by everyone; however, they promulgated another formula—or rather the same one, slightly expanded and changed—as the original was not clear enough regarding the principal point of controversy. In particular, they published the <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "τῷ ὁμοουσίῳ" (homoousion); the defining term of the Nicene Creed meaning that the Son is of the very same essence as the Father</note> term, by which they might more clearly declare against Arius that the Son is of the same essence, glory, and eternity as the Father. Eusebius hesitated at this word for some time until, having weighed the matter well and fully perceiving the sense of the Fathers after a careful examination, he willingly gave his assent. He informed his people in Caesarea of this entire matter by sending them a letter.

<margin>
* Letter to Eusebius on the Life of Constantine, book 3, chapter 11.
* Book 2, chapters 4 & 5.
</margin>
Around the year 330, when the See of Antioch became vacant through the deposition of Eustathius, Eusebius was chosen for the position by common consent, with both the people and the Synod of Antioch petitioning the Emperor. But he generously rejected the offered Bishopric, even though it was grander and more sublime than that of Caesarea, knowing well that the <term>translations</term> <note>The practice of moving a bishop from one diocese to another, which was discouraged to prevent clerical ambition</note> of Bishops from one Church to another were prohibited by Ecclesiastical canons, especially by Canon 15 of the recent Synod of Nicaea. For this reason, Constantine extolled him with wondrous praise, testifying among other things * that everyone had desired to have him as their Bishop, and that he should consider himself blessed for this very reason: that by the testimony of almost the entire world, he was judged worthy to be Bishop of the universal Church. Certainly, he was uniquely dear to this most pious Prince, who often greeted him by letter when absent and heaped every honor upon him when present. At last, full of years and fame, he closed his final day around the year 340, shortly before the death of Constantine the Younger, as Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian</note> notes *.

<margin>
* To Pammachius, page 189.
Apology against Rufinus, page 499. Apology II, page 219.
* Ecclesiastical History, book 10, chapter 4.
† On the Praises of Constantine, chapter 12, pages 639, 640.
* Ibid, chapter 2, at the beginning.
</margin>
There is no need for me to discuss at length his supreme and far-reaching learning, for almost the entire literary world rises in veneration of his scholarly name both in the past and today. He was so venerable in piety that he was numbered among the Saints in many Western Churches, and earned the title of *Holy Confessor, Bishop of blessed memory, and priest of an extraordinary life.* But alas! The memory of this excellent man is burdened not only by more recent writers but by many of the ancients with the fault of heretical depravity. By these, he is commonly called an Arian, and (if it may be said so) "most Arian," the prince and standard-bearer of the Arian faction, as Jerome * writes of him in more than one place. This was surely done rashly, and with a harsher judgment than was fair. It must be admitted that he was long and deeply immersed in the writings of the Platonists and the books of Origen; from there he drew certain new ideas and introduced phrases into Christian theology that were less suitable, and sometimes even dangerous. Yet this was common to him and many doctors of past centuries, who spoke too securely and boldly about those matters on which the Church had not yet delivered its judgment. However, that he was by no means imbued with the <term>chief dogmas</term> <note>original: "κυρίαις δόξαις"</note> of the Arian heresy is clearly enough attested by many passages still extant today in his writings, which pull up the very foundations of Arianism by the roots. Such are the places where he calls Christ <term>God in himself</term> <note>original Greek: "αὐτόθεον"</note>, <term>the all-king and all-leader, and God himself</term> <note>original: "τὸν παμβασiλέα καὶ πανηγεμόνα, καὶ αὐτὸν Θεὸν"</note> \*, and <term>the living and manifest Word of the God over all, subsisting in essence</term> <note>original: "Θεοῦ δὲ τὸν ἐπὶ πάντων ζῶντα καὶ ἐναργῆ ὑπάρχοντα λόγον, κατ' οὐσίαν τε ὑφεστῶτα"</note> †; for since he is <term>the power of God and the wisdom of God, he proceeds from the Father's divinity and kingdom</term> <note>original: "Θεοῦ δύναμις, καὶ Θεοῦ σοφία, προήξει δὲ τῆς πατρικής θεότητός τε καὶ βασιλείας"</note>. He is <term>one Son, as being from one Father, one in essence</term> <note>original: "εἶναι ἕνα υἱὸν, ὡς ἂν ἐξ ἑνὸς ὄντα πατρὸς, essentia quidem unum"</note>; and <term>the only-begotten Word of God reigns with his Father from ages without beginning into infinite and endless ages</term> <note>original: "τε τοῦ Θεοῦ μονογενῆ λόγον τῷ αὐτοῦ πατρὶ συμβασιλεύειν ἐξ ἀνάρχων αἰώνων εἰς ἀπείρους καὶ ἀτελευτήτους αἰῶνας"</note> \*.

...lacking a beginning, to reign together with the Father unto infinite and unending ages. How often does he condemn Marcellus and his followers as guilty of monstrous blasphemy, because they dared <note>original: "διελεῖν τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ ἕτερον θεὸν τὸν λόγον ὀνομάσαι ὁσίᾳ, τε καὶ δυνάμει"</note> "to divide God, and to name the Word another god, differing in substance and power"? † Nor, according to them ||, would the Word have anything in common with the Father’s divinity, but would be ranked in all things with the crowd of created beings, and <note>original: "κἀξ' οὐκ ὄντων ὑπέστη"</note> "existed from things that were not," because he was procreated out of nothing. A thousand such examples are met everywhere, of which we have produced many elsewhere *. It is of no small importance to the matter that in the Council of Nicaea, he expressly condemned Arian dogmas, and—not rashly or unadvisedly (as he himself teaches us), but only after a long and accurate examination—he subscribed to its Creed sincerely and from the heart. Those who claim he subscribed craftily and deceitfully are entirely devoid of Christian charity. Let them read his *Letter to the People of Caesarea*, and see with what spirit they can maintain such an assertion. Meanwhile, we do not deny that in his writings, published both before and after the Council of Nicaea, there are certain harsher and more dangerous statements that require a fair and kind reader. In this regard, I rightly find a lack of the usual fairness and integrity in the most learned Petavius <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian known for criticizing the orthodoxy of the Ante-Nicene Fathers</note>, who is accustomed to interpreting many passages of our Eusebius too harshly and twisting them into a worse sense. Our Eusebius’s style is indeed unrefined and somewhat harsh, and in the judgment of * Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and influential scholar</note>, <note>original: "ᾧ δέ φησιν οὐκ ἔστιν ἡδὺς οὔτε λιτὸς, οὔτε λαμπρότητι χαίρων"</note> "his phrasing is nowhere pleasant, nor simple, nor delighting in brilliance." Theodorus Metochites <note>A 14th-century Byzantine statesman and scholar</note>, in the *Miscellanies* cited by Henri Valois, believes this should be attributed to his long stay in Egypt; hence <note>original: "τεχνίτην τὸ λέγειν χρώμενον"</note> "he uses a rough and harsh way of speaking." This man, most learned in every respect, wrote a great many works, a catalog of which we shall weave together here.

The **Chronicle** <note>original: "Chronicon"</note>, called a <note>original: "παντοδαπὴν ἱστορίαν"</note> "**universal history**"; a work in two parts: in the first part, which is today greatly mutilated, he followed the origins and most memorable deeds of almost all nations—Chaldeans, Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Lydians, Hebrews, Egyptians, etc.—from the creation of the world. And by far the greater part of this he took from the *Chronography* of Africanus <note>Sextus Julius Africanus, an early 3rd-century Christian traveler and historian</note>, whose cabinets he plundered remarkably. In the second part, which is called the **Chronological Canon**, he reduced the former part into a sort of compendium, dividing the entire series of time into Decades; and taking his starting era from Abraham, he assigned the memorable events of each nation to their respective years. Both parts end in the twentieth year of Constantine's reign, that is, in the year 325 AD, in which year, shortly before the Council of Nicaea, the work seems to me to have been completed. It was translated into Latin by Jerome, who nevertheless interpolated his version with additions here and there, especially regarding Roman history. The Greek originals are lost; to supply this defect, Joseph Scaliger <note>A leading 16th-century scholar of chronology</note> scraped together from everywhere whatever could be found from Syncellus, Cedrenus, and the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, though there is a just reason to doubt whether all these should be considered Eusebius's own. The work as it now exists, with Jerome’s version and extensive observations, was published by the said Scaliger in *Leiden, 1606*. It was reprinted in Amsterdam in the year *1658* in folio format, with notes expanded by a third. A truly most noble work, and "not cheap even compared to gold" <note>An idiom meaning the work is of immense value</note>, in which, even if there were nothing else, so many golden fragments of ancient authors are preserved for us. Published in Greek and Latin with notes by Fr. Viger, *Paris, 1628, folio*.

**Proof of the Gospel** <note>original: "De Demonstratione Evangelica"</note>: of the 20 books, only 10 survive today, in which he argues the Christian cause chiefly against the Jews. The ten books of **Ecclesiastical History**, containing the state of the Christian Church from its very cradle <note>Latin: "incunabulis"</note> until the death of Licinius the Elder, covering a span of 324 years. Eusebius finished this history during the peace immediately preceding the Council of Nicaea, but he did not actually publish it until several years later. In this work, he mentions not only his *Chronicle*, but also the books on the *Demonstration of the Gospel*. For everyone can see that these latter works are designated by the phrase "particular interpretations" <note>original: "οἰκείας ἑρμηνείας"</note>, special commentaries in which he says he collected the prophecies of the Prophets concerning our Lord Jesus Christ and supported them with the firmest proofs. Nor is it an objection that he makes no mention of the Council of Nicaea, since he himself testifies that his goal in composing this history was to show how the favorable and kind protection of our Savior finally shone upon His Church; he did not wish to mar the happy outcome of events—now that external enemies were destroyed—with the internal bickering of Bishops. Add to this what the Illustrious Antoine Pagi notes: that writers of those times were accustomed either to finish or publish their works during the *vicennalia* <note>The twenty-year anniversary festivals of an Emperor's reign</note> and similar festivals. He proves this with many examples, including this very history and the *Eusebian Chronicle*. Eusebius dedicated his history to Paulinus, Bishop of Tyre, the closest of his friends, whom Henri Valois <note>Valesius</note> claims was transferred from the see of Tyre to that of Antioch; indeed, moved by his authority, I was once of that opinion. But upon better consideration, although I willingly grant that Paulinus survived the Council of Nicaea by several years, I deny that he presided over Antioch. No ancient writer, with the sole exception of Philostorgius, affirms this; nor does the passage from Eusebius himself, which Valois cites from Book 1 of *Against Marcellus*, chapter 4, suggest it when correctly understood. From that passage, nothing else can be extracted except that Paulinus administered the Bishopric of Tyre with such praise that the Church of Antioch used to boast of him as their own good (for he had been a Priest of that same Church). Meanwhile, the most learned Valois is not consistent with himself: in one place * he asserts that the Eusebian history was written before the Council of Nicaea, but a few pages later, he writes it was not completed until several years after the Council. We rightly wonder at this inconsistency <note>original: "ἀσυμφωνίαν"</note> of so famous a man. But we easily forgive him, for he undertook such great labors to give us this History perfected in every detail, adorned with a most accurate translation and most learned annotations. He published it at *Paris, 1659*, and again in 1671. The Frankfurt edition of 1672 reprinted the Paris edition, though unfortunately. A very elegant and accurate Greek edition had appeared from the press of Robert Estienne, *Paris, 1544*, folio; and a Greek-Latin edition at *Geneva, 1612*, folio.

A single book **On the Martyrs of Palestine**, appended to the 8th book of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

# The Arian Century

...was absent <note>This continues the discussion of Eusebius’s work against Hierocles from the previous page.</note>, the Governor of Bithynia under Diocletian and later the Prefect of Egypt. He is not that philosopher mentioned by Photius, for he lived nearly a full century later than the man from Nicomedia. This booklet by Eusebius is extant, published in Paris in 1628 along with his books *On the Preparation for the Gospel*, and at the end of Philostratus’s *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*.

***Against Marcellus*** (who was condemned for Sabellianism <note>A 3rd-century heresy that claimed the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of a single person, rather than three distinct persons.</note> in a small council held at Constantinople in the year 336). These two books were written by order of the Synod itself.

***On Ecclesiastical Theology***, in three books. In these, he treats the same argument against Marcellus more extensively. These five books <note>The two books of "Against Marcellus" plus the three of "Ecclesiastical Theology."</note>, with the version and notes of the most learned man Richard Montagu <note>An English bishop and controversialist (1577–1641) known for his great patristic learning.</note>, our Bishop of Chichester, are appended to the books *On the Preparation for the Gospel*, Paris edition, 1628.

***Letter to the People of Caesarea*** concerning the Nicene faith. This is found in Socrates, Book I, Chapter 8, and Theodoret, Book I, Chapter 12.

***On Hebrew Places***, or a description of the cities and locations in Holy Scripture, arranged in alphabetical order and dedicated to Paulinus, Bishop of Tyre. Jerome <note>The famous 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> formerly translated and expanded this book, as he lived in those places for a long time. Although he performed the duty of a translator for the most part, he nevertheless changed some things, corrected certain errors, and added not a few things of his own. Jacques Bonfrère <note>A Jesuit scholar known for his biblical commentaries.</note> was the first to bring forth the Greek text of Eusebius's book itself from the Royal Library in Paris, along with the ancient translation of Jerome and a new one he prepared himself, and he published it with notes of significant value in Paris, 1659, to which he added commentaries on the Book of Joshua.

***Oration in Praise of Constantine***, delivered in the year 335 during the thirtieth anniversary festival <note>The "Tricennalia," a major celebration marking thirty years of an Emperor's rule.</note> of the same Emperor. It is found at the end of the *Ecclesiastical History*. In a manuscript codex at Trinity College, Cambridge, this Oration is divided into two parts: the first comprises the first ten chapters, and the second begins from Chapter 11.

***On the Life of Constantine***, in four books, which he wrote most recently. In these, he did not intend to hand down an accurate history of Constantine’s life, but rather to select the more beautiful deeds and those most worthy of the memory of posterity, especially those that seemed to pertain to piety and the worship of God. He performed this in an oratorical rather than a historical manner. Hence, as Photius notes <margin>* Codex 127.</margin> <note>original Greek: "μακράν τι πρὸς τὸ λαμπρότερον ἐκβεβιάσθαι αὐτῷ ὁ λόγος, καὶ λέξεις εἰς τὸ ἀνθηρότερον ἐνιαχοῦ συνελήφθησαν"</note> "his speech is somewhat forced toward a more splendid style, and words are elsewhere gathered into a more flowery kind." Those who would strip these books from our Eusebius are mistaken, nor are their objections so great that we should dwell on refuting them. Meanwhile, those who wish may look at Book 2, Chapters 45 and 46; Book 3, Chapter 61; Book 4, Chapters 33, 34, and 35, and elsewhere throughout. Henri Valois <note>Also known as Valesius, the preeminent 17th-century editor of the Greek ecclesiastical historians.</note> reviewed these books, illustrated them with a translation and notes, and appended them to the *Ecclesiastical History* as was his custom.

***Exposition on the Song of Songs***. This is extant in Greek together with Polychronius and Psellus, published by Meursius at Leiden, 1617, in quarto. It is not, however, the work of Eusebius alone, but is patched together <note>original: "confarcinata," meaning stuffed or compiled like a patchwork.</note> partly from his own writings and partly from those of Athanasius, Didymus, Gregory of Nyssa, Philon of Carpasia, and others.

***Lives of the Prophets***, or *On the Names in the Book of the Prophets* <note>original Greek: "περὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ Βιβλίῳ τῶν προφητῶν ὀνομασίας"</note>, are ascribed to our Eusebius in an ancient copy. Jean Courtier published them in Paris, 1580, along with the commentaries of Procopius on Isaiah, in Greek and Latin.

***The Ten Canons of the Holy Gospels***, usually placed with the prefixed *Letter to Carpianus* in the *Harmony of the Gospels* by Ammonius. They are held in Jerome's translation among the *Orthodoxographa*, the *Works of Jerome*, and in the *Library of the Fathers*. See more regarding these under "Ammonius."

***Apology for Origen***, the first book (for the remaining five have perished). It is extant in a Latin translation by Rufinus among the *Works of Jerome*.

***Sermon on that passage***, "Late on the Sabbath," and likewise ***On the Angels seen at the Tomb***, in Greek and Latin with notes in Combefis’s *New Appendix*, Volume I, page 779. However, these appear to be excerpts rather than complete treatises.

# The Arian Century

<header>*The Arian Century.*</header>

<margin>
4th CENTURY, from the Year 300.
* Mentioned by Athanasius in *On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia*, page 683.
* *Against Marcellus*, book 1, page 27.
† Ibid. page 29.
</margin>

A letter to Bishop Euphration is mentioned by the Alexandrian priests \*. A fragment remains in the source cited above (Acts of the 5th Council, page 365). In this fragment, Eusebius is said to have affirmed <term>that Christ is not the true God</term> <note>original Greek: *ὅτι ὁ χριστὸς οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς*</note>. Since these words are quoted plainly without any explanation, and because they diametrically oppose the Eusebian view expressed so clearly in many other places, it is easy to guess that Eusebius, given the occasion, was referring to that passage in John 17:3:
> that they might know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent;

and from this his adversaries seized an opportunity for slander. Eusebius himself is our witness that this was the case \*; for when Marcellus had accused him of writing that there is only one true God—as if Eusebius had invented "younger" gods who are not so truly or properly Gods—Eusebius rejects the calumny. He says he gave that most slanderous man no other occasion than that he had quoted the aforementioned words of the Lord †. Again, the same Marcellus objected that he had affirmed Christ was a mere man, for no other reason than that in a certain letter he had used that Apostolic sentence:
> There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

But these things are mentioned in passing.

<term>Archaeology</term> <note>original Greek: *Αρχαιολογία* (*Archaiologia*); here meaning "Ancient History."</note>, or <term>Ancient History</term>. Two fragments of this survive in Anastasius Sinaita, Questions 41 and 65. Whether this is perhaps the same work as the *Chronicle* or <term>Universal History</term> <note>original Greek: *παντοδαπὴ ἱστορία* (*pantodapē historia*)</note>, let the reader judge. His *Books to Marinus* are frequently cited by the same Anastasius.

<margin>* On the Holy Spirit, chapter 29.</margin>
St. Basil * mentions his <term>Treatise on the Polygamy of the Ancients</term> <note>original Greek: *τὰ ἐπιτηδεύματα περὶ τῆς ἀρχαίων πολυγαμίας*</note>: though perhaps this should be understood not as a complete work, but as a part of the preceding work.

### DOUBTFUL WORKS.

**O**n the faith against Sabellius, 2 books. On the Resurrection. On the Resurrection and Ascension of the Lord. On the incorporeal and invisible God. On the incorporeal. On the incorporeal soul. On the spiritual thought of man. That God the Father is incorporeal. On the same. On that which the Lord says, *I came not to bring peace*, etc. On the command of the Lord, *What I tell you in the ear*. On good and evil works. On good works from the 2nd Epistle to the Corinthians.

Jacques Sirmond published these Homilies in Latin only, under our Eusebius’s name, in **Paris, 1643, octavo**. He relied on no other reasoning (as he himself confesses in the preface) than that the name of Eusebius of Caesarea was prefixed to two manuscript codices; from this, Henri Valois cites them throughout as genuine works of Eusebius. I would sooner attribute them to Eusebius of Emesa <note>A later bishop and student of Eusebius of Caesarea, often confused with him in manuscript traditions.</note>.

Hebediesu <note>A 13th-century East Syrian (Chaldean) bishop and writer.</note> reports that among the Chaldeans there still exist works by Eusebius: books on the Divine Origin, on the Dissonance of the Gospels, on the Figure of the World, a History of the Western Martyrs and Panegyrics for them, a sermon on the Lack of Rain, and an Apology for Origen.

<margin>
316.
* Panegyric to Maximian and Constantine, page 3.
* Panegyric to Constantine, page 94.
</margin>

**FLAVIUS CONSTANTINUS**, surnamed the Great, of the Claudian clan, the only son of the Emperor Constantius Chlorus by his wife Helena. He is said to have ennobled our Britain by his birth: for a passage in a Panegyric \* delivered as an oration to him seems to suggest this (setting aside more recent writers for now):
> He [Chlorus] freed the Britains from slavery, but you made them noble by originating from there.

Although, to confess the truth, there is no lack of writers of no small authority who pass down the tradition that he was born in Naissus, a town of Illyrian Dardania <note>Modern Niš, Serbia.</note>. He was born on the third day before the Kalends of March, in the year 272. In the year 306, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, upon the death of his father at York <note>original: *Eboraci*</note>, he was elevated to Emperor. And although there are those who grudge our nation the glory of his birth, they cannot deny the honor of the purple assumed here, and of the empire begun here.
> O fortunate Britain, and now more blessed than all lands, who first saw Constantine as Caesar!

says the orator Eumenius Rhetor \* while the Emperor himself was listening. In the year 312, while leading his army against Maxentius, two visions were made from heaven: one of a cross glowing in the sky after midday, the other of Christ himself appearing to him as he slept at night, holding the cross in his right hand, of the victory soon to be report— <note>The text cuts off mid-word as a catchword for the next page: *repor-* (likely *reportata*, "won" or "brought back").</note>

# The Arian Century

<header>*The Arian Century.*</header>

<margin>4th CENTURY, from the Year 300.</margin>
...[to be] reported, and what is far greater, the faithful messenger of conversion and eternal salvation to be obtained through Christ crucified. Therefore, after Maxentius was defeated at the Milvian Bridge <note>A pivotal battle in 312 AD where Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius, leading to his sole rule over the Western Roman Empire.</note>, he himself submitted his head to Christ, embracing the Christian faith. From here, edicts were published in favor of the Christians; peace was restored to the Church; churches were built and increased by gifts and revenues. (Regarding the gifts granted to the Great Church of Constantinople, and the Imperial garments placed upon the sacred table—which were not to be used by the Emperor except publicly and on a great feast of our Lord—Constantine Porphyrogenneta <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Emperor and author.</note> narrates clearly wonderful and rare things <margin>* *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 13, page 24.</margin> *, and he relates that he drew these from Ancient History <term>written in secret words</term> <note>original Greek: *ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις λόγοις γεγραμμένα*</note>). Honors were bestowed upon Bishops and Clergy. In the year 316, he celebrated his ten-year jubilee, and in 325, his twenty-year jubilee. Having become the sole Monarch of the Roman Empire, and with his enemies now destroyed and peace given to the Roman World, he applied his mind with more intense zeal to managing the affairs of the Church, having summoned Bishops from everywhere, <margin>* *On the Life of Constantine*, book 1, chapter 44.</margin> * <term>as if he were a common bishop appointed by God</term> <note>original Greek: *οἷα τις κοινὸς ἐπίσκοπος ἐκ θεοῦ καθεσταμένος*</note>, as Eusebius says. In that same year, having sent letters everywhere, he summoned the Bishops to the Council of Nicaea; he graced their assembly with his presence, heard their disputes most patiently, diligently weighed the questions proposed, solved doubts with his sharp intellect, restrained quarrels and dissensions with prudence, and recalled those struggling among themselves to concord through persuasion and counsel. Finally, he fortified the most wholesome decrees with his own authority, publicly declaring that the sentence of the Synod should be freely accepted no otherwise than as <margin>Letter to the Alexandrians, in Socrates, book 1, chapter 9.</margin> <term>the will of God, which is truly a holy and divine command</term> <note>original Greek: *τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ γνώμῃ ἣν ἁγίαν κ' θείαν ὡς ἀληθῶς ἐντολὴν*</note>. And certainly, although he was later deceived by the "crafty arts" of Eusebius of Nicomedia and others, and sometimes did things that seemed to favor the Arians, he remained most tenacious of the Nicene decrees as long as he lived. This most pious Emperor died—decorated by the later Greeks with the title <term>Equal-to-the-Apostles</term> <note>original Greek: *ἰσαπόστολος* (*isapostolos*)</note>—having first requested baptism from the attending Bishops. He was baptized, as it seems, by the hand of Eusebius of Nicomedia, as he was the Bishop of that place (though neither Eusebius, Socrates, Sozomen, nor Theodoret record this), at Achyrona in the suburbs of Nicomedia during the very solemnity of Pentecost, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June <note>May 22</note>, in the year of Christ 337, at the age of 66. After a reign of 30 years and ten months, he was buried in Constantinople in the vestibule of the Basilica of the Holy Apostles, which he himself had built. Among the virtues and ornaments of his soul, by which he shone far above the imperial purple, were his Erudition, Elegance, and Affability, which—according to Aurelius Victor <margin>* *On the Caesars*, chapter 40.</margin> *, a pagan man—carried him to the stars by the prayers of all. Sextus Aurelius Victor <margin>† *Epitome*, chapter 60.</margin> † (or whoever was the author of the *Epitome*) says no differently: that he used to nurture the good arts, especially the study of letters, and he himself was accustomed to read, write, and meditate. He was certainly the greatest patron of the learned, being himself educated beyond the common level. Hence his frequent declamations or sermons, even on the gravest subjects, for which he sometimes spent entire nights awake in meditation. On these, one should consult Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book 4, chapter 29. Indeed, even on the last day of his life, with death hanging over him, he recited a certain funeral oration in his accustomed auditorium; Eusebius records its main points in book 4, chapter 55. He composed many Letters and Orations, which translators designated for that duty turned from the Latin tongue into Greek. Of these (to say nothing of the constitutions concerning ecclesiastical persons and things contained in the last book of the *Theodosian Code*), there remain today:

---

*Oration to the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea*, in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book 3, chapter 12. Gelasius of Cyzicus in *History of the Council of Nicaea*, book 2, chapter 7, presents another one, much longer than this; however, one might rightly suspect it was fashioned from the historian's own genius rather than actually delivered by Constantine.

*Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, regarding which see Eusebius, as cited above, chapter 32. It survives with the notes of Henri Valois at the end of the books on the *Life of Constantine*, where it is usually attached.

*Many Letters*. Eusebius is the authority (in the same work, chapter 24) that Constantine wrote almost innumerable letters, and that he intended to collect them in a separate volume; this he either never performed, or that collection has long since perished. So that we may, in some way at least, repair that loss, the letters which [survive]...

<margin>* Place cited.</margin>
<margin>† Ibid.</margin>
<margin>|| Where above, Chapter 11.</margin>
**HOSIUS**, Spanish by birth, Bishop in the province of Baetica at Corduba—famous as the birthplace of Seneca and Lucan—distinguished as a <term>Confessor</term> <note>A title for those who suffered for the faith during persecutions but did not die as martyrs.</note> under the persecution of Maximian. He was present at the Council of Elvira held in the year 305, or according to the calculation of Ferdinand de Mendoza ||, in 300 or 301. He flourished for many years in the highest favor with Constantine the Great and served as his advisor on sacred matters; he was summoned by him to the Council of Arles in the year 314, and in the year 324, he was sent to Alexandria with letters to settle the Arian controversy. In the following year, he held a leading position at the Council of Nicaea and was the first to subscribe to its decrees; Socrates † notes this from the *Synodicon* of Athanasius. That he held this honor as a legate of the Roman Pontiff is the empty dream of Baronius and others. Francisco de Bivar ||, though himself among the Pontiff's supporters, denies this, contending that Hosius subscribed only in the name of his own Province and performed the duties of presiding officer due to the merits of his distinguished learning and his record as a Confessor; he brings forward two other equally learned and grave Spanish writers who are in agreement <note>original: "ὁμοψήφους" (*homopsēphous*), meaning "of the same vote."</note> with him on this point. In the year 347, he presided over the Council of Sardica, and through his particular care and wisdom, twenty Canons were established. He was certainly held in such high honor by all, and possessed such great authority, that the Arians rightly judged that he must be drawn over to their side by any means, fair or foul. He was tempted by them in various ways, but in vain. At last, in the year 356, he was punished with exile to Sirmium; in the following year, weary of exile and hardships, and broken by the use of threats and tortures, being now a hundred years old and "all too fond of his own grave" <note>original: "nimiumque sepulchri sui amans"</note>—to use the words of Hilary * concerning him—he surrendered. He subscribed to the Arian formula, which was indeed blasphemous (if indeed it was the one Hilary records), and even, if the title does not deceive, composed by himself. Be that as it may, it is clearly established that Hosius entered into communion with the Arians; Philostorgius † even reports that he condemned not only the <term>Homoousion</term> <note>The doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.</note> but also Athanasius himself; however, Athanasius || himself protests and expressly denies this. I pass over what Marcellinus and Faustinus—Priests of the Luciferian schism during the time of Emperor Theodosius—and the *Appendix to Ildefonsus on Ecclesiastical Writers* say regarding his return to Spain, his madness or insane cruelty toward Catholics, and finally his unhappy end. A witness above all exception is Athanasius *, who records that as Hosius was dying, he protested the violence the Arians had used against him, condemned their heresy, and forbade it to be approved or received by anyone. That Abraham-like old man, the truly Holy One <note>original: "ὁ ἀληθῶς Ὅσιος" (*ho alēthōs Hosios*). Athanasius often used this wordplay, as 'Hosios' means 'holy' in Greek.</note> as Athanasius † calls him, seems to have died in the year 361, over a hundred years old, after he had held his Episcopal see for nearly 70 years. Indeed, he was already in the sixtieth year since his confession under Maximian when violence was brought against him by the Arians at Sirmium; Ferdinand de Mendoza || rightly observes that he was not a newly made Bishop at the time of the Council of Elvira, because in the subscriptions of that Council, his name is found not in the last place, but in the middle (that is, the eleventh) spot. Of his letters, only one survives today, written to the Emperor Constantius and found in Athanasius's *Letter to the Solitaries*; it is an illustrious monument of faith, piety, and courage. By his labor also the formula of the Nicene faith was composed, as the Arians themselves admit in the place cited in Athanasius. Isidore of Seville, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Chapter 1, mentions a letter of his to his sister in praise of Virginity, adorned with beautiful and eloquent speech, but I fear it has long since perished.
