**EUSEBIUS**, called "of Nicomedia," was related by maternal descent, I believe, to the Emperor Julian, who had been educated under him while still a boy. (See Ammianus Marcellinus, book 22). He was among the disciples of Lucian the Martyr, and from that connection was labeled a *Collicianist* <note>original: Collicianistæ. This was a term Arius used for his fellow students under Lucian of Antioch, possibly referring to a specific meeting place.</note> by Arius. At first the Bishop of Berytus in Syria, he later managed to be transferred to Nicomedia—then the seat of the Eastern Empire, a rival to Rome, and recently adorned with great splendor by Diocletian. He was a man ambitious beyond measure. He took Arius into his protection after Arius had been condemned and cast out by his own Bishop for his notorious Heresy; he cultivated friendship and communion with him and zealously championed his cause by sending letters everywhere.

<margin>
Letter in Theodoret, book 1, ch. 6.
* In Theodoret, book 1, ch. 20.
† On the Faith, book 3, ch. 7.
</margin>
He taught exactly the same as Arius: namely, that the Son was not only *created, founded, and begotten in essence* <note>original: κτιστόν & θεμελιωτόν & γεννητόν τῇ οὐσίᾳ</note>, but was truly distinct from the Unbegotten One, not made from His substance, nor in any way a participant in that nature, nor existing from His substance, but entirely different in nature and power—though created for a perfect likeness to the nature and power of his Maker. Furthermore, not content to teach these dogmas, he became the leader and standard-bearer of the entire faction, and the sole *driver* <note>original: ἐργοδιώκτης; literally a taskmaster or overseer who pushes a project forward.</note> of all the evils the Arians plotted against Athanasius. Hence, the followers of Arius were commonly called *Eusebians*, and "those around Eusebius." In the Council of Nicaea, he stood by Arius until, seeing Arius's opinion condemned by the full vote of the Fathers, he himself embraced the Synodal Faith. Notwithstanding this, three months after the Synod, when he was stirring up new troubles, publicly preaching things contrary to the Nicene faith, receiving members of the Arian faction as guests, and joining himself as a partner in their malice, he was sent into exile by the Emperor's order. Constantine was also indignant because, during the recent civil war, Eusebius had not only sent spies against him and provided almost armed assistance to Licinius, but had also been an initiate of tyrannical cruelty and the author of the slaughter of many Bishops of the Catholic Church, as Constantine openly testifies in his *Letter to the Nicomedians*. After spending three years in exile, having offered a petition of repentance and professing that he fully agreed with the Nicene faith, he was recalled from exile and restored to his see. Finally, after the death of Constantine, the Arians found his son Constantius much more favorable to them; near the beginning of his reign, in the year 338, after Paul had been forcibly driven from the see of Constantinople, Eusebius—always true to himself—left Nicomedia and immediately thrust himself onto the throne of the royal city. He died at the time of the Synod of Antioch, around the year 342. Of the many *Letters* he wrote, Theodoret (Book 1, Chapter 6) has preserved one for us concerning *Arius* and his dogmas. Ambrose mentions another read in the Council of Nicaea, in which Eusebius used an argument of this kind: *"If we call him the true and uncreated Son of God, we begin to confess him to be of the same substance* <note>original: ὁμοούσιον (homoousion)</note> *with the Father."* From this, the Nicene Fathers seized the opportunity to insert that word into their *Creed* <note>original: Symbolo</note>, because they saw it was a source of dread to their adversaries; thus, as if using a sword drawn by the Heretics themselves, they cut off the head of the abominable Heresy.

<margin>
* In Theodoret, book 1, ch. 8.
† Annotations on Theodoret, p. 10.
</margin>
Nor perhaps was that *booklet* anything other than this Letter, which Eustathius of Antioch relates Eusebius brought before the Synod, calling it a most certain proof of his blasphemy. When read openly in the hearing of all, because of the perversity of its doctrine, it caused immense grief and was torn to pieces in the sight of everyone. For it is clear that this was not the *Creed* of Eusebius of Caesarea (as the most learned Valesius <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a French classical scholar.</note> wishes), because the *Eusebian Formula*—which still exists in his Letter to the people of Caesarea—contains not even the slightest shadow of blasphemy or impiety; rather, it was approved by both the Emperor and the entire Synod, as he himself most clearly testifies in that same Letter.

**EUSTATHIUS** was born in the maritime city of Side in Pamphylia, though Nicetas Choniates, led by I know not what authority, records that he drew his origin from Philippi, a city in Macedonia. He flourished in the year 325. First Bishop of Beroea in Syria, then appointed Bishop of Antioch by the Fathers themselves in the Council of Nicaea, according to the report of the same Nicetas; this must have happened in the earlier sessions of this Synod. He was the first of all, says Theodoret, to deliver a Panegyric <note>A formal public speech of high praise.</note> to Constantine in the name of the Synod—though some attribute that duty to Eusebius of Caesarea...

...while others were present. Although Alexander of Alexandria is credited with the opening address by Nicetas, a certain Allatian Codex of Theodoret (with which the author of the *Tripartite History* <note>A famous medieval history of the church that combined the works of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret.</note> agrees) holds that both Eusebius and Eustathius greeted the Emperor with a preliminary oration. Eustathius defended the Catholic faith with every effort, being the fiercest enemy of the Arians, who for that reason would not suffer him to hold the See of Antioch for long. Once Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea were recalled from exile, they convened a Synod at Antioch and decided that Eustathius must be deposed before all else. First, with Cyrus, Bishop of Beroea, acting as the accuser, they charged him with being a supporter of Sabellian doctrine <note>Sabellianism was a heresy teaching that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different "modes" or masks of a single person, rather than three distinct Persons.</note>, a claim Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian.</note> reports from George of Laodicea. However, Socrates proves George to be inconsistent with himself on this matter. 

Next, they leveled a charge of foul lust against him, and in this way they "set the stage." They brought a common woman of ill repute into the Synod, carrying a nursing infant at her breast; she shamelessly cried out and, having taken an oath to give the "play" credibility, affirmed that she had borne this child from an affair with Eustathius. Without delay, the judges passed sentence against this most holy man. As soon as the matter was reported to the Emperor, Eustathius was banished by his order to Trajanopolis, a city in Thrace. 

To these, add a third calumny from Athanasius: namely, that Eustathius had been insulting toward the Emperor’s mother—meaning Helena, who was traveling in the East at that time. Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a cardinal and great Catholic historian.</note>, Petavius, and others report this under the year 340, relying chiefly on the testimony of Athanasius and Jerome, who write that Eustathius was sent into exile under Constantius <note>Constantine's son and successor, who favored Arianism.</note>. But in truth, Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret, and Philostorgius all testify that these things happened under Constantine, not long after the return of Eusebius of Nicomedia—specifically around the year 329 or 330—and this is confirmed by many arguments. 

1st. The letters of Constantine himself and the title of a chapter in Eusebius clearly demonstrate that the election of Eusebius of Caesarea to the See of Antioch (to replace the ousted Eustathius) took place at this time. 2nd. Flaccillus—the third, or according to others, the fourth Bishop of Antioch after Eustathius—was present at the Synod of Tyre in the year 335 while Constantine was still alive, as is plainly evident from the letters of the Egyptian Bishops to Count Dionysius. 3rd. Meletius, who is known to have succeeded to the Bishopric of Antioch in the year 360, was transferred to this see twenty years after the deposition of Eustathius, as can be gathered from Theodoret. 4th. Socrates expressly testifies that Eustathius, the "teller of falsehoods" <note>original: ψευδολόγον. This likely refers to the nature of the false charges or a textual variation in the history.</note>, ruled the Church of Antioch for only a short span of time; this would be entirely false if he had remained there from the Council of Nicaea until the time of Constantius, much less until the year 340. 

From these points, it becomes most manifest that a mistake lies in the texts of Athanasius and Jerome, and that the name "Constantius" crept in place of "Constantine." This is acknowledged by Sophronius (the translator of Jerome) and the older editions of Jerome's works. Consequently, Baronius himself is in error when he rashly declares that Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret, and those who followed them are entirely mistaken in saying Eustathius was sent into exile by Constantine Augustus. Therefore, the illustrious Valois and Jacques Gothofredus rightly rebuke Baronius and dissolve his arguments. 

But setting these matters aside, let us return to Eustathius, whose innocence and the wicked traps of his enemies were finally brought to light. For that wretched woman, falling into a most serious illness, publicly confessed that she had been hired for money to act out the "play." She admitted she had spoken falsely regarding the name "Eustathius," for a certain coppersmith named Eustathius was actually the infant's father. This most holy Confessor died in exile at Trajanopolis in Thrace, where he was also buried. There must have been another Eustathius of Antioch, distinct from ours, who was recalled by Jovian and exiled again by Valens to Bizye, a town in Thrace, of whom Socrates, Sozomen, and others speak. 

Athanasius extols our Eustathius with a distinguished tribute:

> A man of confession <note>A "Confessor" is someone who suffered for the faith but was not martyred.</note> and pious in faith, abundant in his zeal for the truth.
<note>original Greek: Ἀνὴρ ὁμολογητὴς καὶ τὴν πίστιν εὐσεβὴς, πολὺς τῷ ζηλῶν ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας.</note>

He was a man renowned for his confession, pious in religion, who fought with great zeal for the truth and pursued the Arian heresy with hatred. Sozomen also commends him, both for other reasons and because he was "justly admired for his eloquence" <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ εὐγλωττίᾳ δικαίως θαυμαζόμενος</note>; as can be learned, he says, from the books of his that survive today,

# The Arian Century

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>
4th CENTURY.
Year 300.
</margin>
...who <note>original: "ab ἀρχαιότητι φράσεως καὶ σωφροσύνῃ νοημάτων, καὶ ὀνομάτων κάλλει καὶ χάριτι ἐπαγγελίας εὐδοκιμοῦσι"</note> are highly esteemed for the antiquity of their phrasing and the sobriety of their thoughts, and for the beauty of their names and the grace of their promise; they are greatly approved both for their ancient style of eloquence and the weight of their opinions, as well as for the elegance of their words and their charm in explaining matters. Of these, the following remain:

*A Brief Oration to the Emperor Constantine at the Council of Nicaea.* This survives, if indeed it is genuine, in the work of Gregory the Priest titled *Oration on the Nicene Fathers*, which Laurentius Surius provides in Latin (July 10th, Number 6), and François Combefis in Greek and Latin (Supplement Vol. II, p. 547).

*Commentary on the <term>Hexaemeron</term>* <note>The "Hexaemeron" refers to a theological treatise on the six days of creation described in Genesis.</note>; first published in Greek and Latin with extensive notes and collected materials by Leo Allatius (Lyon, 1629, in quarto). Learned men raise no small dispute over this work, and rightly so: for although the author handles the subject he undertook quite suitably in some places, the greater part of the work is flawed. It is filled with silly fables about the Blessed Virgin and her parents (to say nothing of other things) taken from the *Protevangelium of James* <note>An early apocryphal gospel detailing the birth and life of Mary.</note>, which are entirely foreign to the doctrine, judgment, and gravity of Eustathius. Nor do I think anyone of sound judgment would affirm that the *Gospel of James* reflects the era of Eustathius, or that Eustathius—a man of such gravity and learning—would have approved it with his vote. One might perhaps suspect that the entire story of the Blessed Virgin and the fables that follow were added by a later hand. Certainly, that entire section from page 68, where he discusses the sons of the Patriarch Jacob, until page 75, where he resumes the same material, seems quite <note>original: "ἀπροσδιόνυσον"</note> irrelevant and clumsily intruded into a place where it does not belong; for if this part is removed, the rest holds together perfectly. The impostor realized this, and therefore closed the fabulous little narrative with the caution that he had only said these things <note>original: "ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ"</note> "as if in passing." Either this must be said, or the entire work must be stripped from Eustathius; and perhaps both views are not far from the truth. Certainly, no one among the ancients or the moderns has recorded that our Eustathius labored over a work of this kind. Nor does Leo Allatius himself, who first published it, speak with his usual confidence regarding its author, relying on no other testimony than the titles of the manuscript codices. Yet everyone knows how deceptive and uncertain the titles of manuscript books often are. Whoever the author was, he lived—or at least wished to appear to have lived—in the thirtieth year of Constantine (that is, the year of Christ 335) or at least the following year. However, his method of calculation is not accurate, as he says on page 55 that from the time of Christ (let us assume he means from the year of the Lord’s Passion) to the thirtieth year of Constantine, 249 years are counted. Even if the writer was a contemporary of Eustathius, the same difficulty remains regarding the alterations and the fables. Let the learned untie this knot.

<margin>* Book 6, ch. 13.</margin>
*Dissertation on the <term>Engastrimythos</term>* <note>Referring to the "ventriloquist" or medium known as the Witch of Endor from the Book of Kings.</note> *against Origen, in which he fiercely attacks Origen and his opinions.* Indeed, Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian.</note> lists Eustathius among the primary detractors of Origen. The same Allatius published this Dissertation in Greek and Latin along with a very learned treatise on the same subject at the place and year mentioned above. It is also found in the eighth volume of the *Sacred Critics* printed in London. He also wrote the following, which have been lost, or at least have not yet seen the light of day, besides infinite Letters:

*A Book on the Soul,* of which some fragments are displayed by Theodoret in his Dialogues 1, 2, and 3.

*A Sermon or Homily on that passage of Proverbs 8: "The Lord created me as the beginning, etc."* <note>A key verse in the Arian controversy regarding the nature of Christ.</note> A fragment survives in Theodoret's *Ecclesiastical History* (Book 1, ch. 8) and many others in the same author's Dialogues 1, 2, and 3; two in Facundus (Book 11, ch. 5); another in Anastasius' *Collection*.

*Interpretation of the Psalms.* Some fragments on Psalms 15 and 92 survive in the same Dialogues 1 and 3. Theodoret also cites our Eustathius in Dialogues 2 and 3 *on the inscriptions of the monuments* and *on the inscriptions of the steps* <note>Referring to the "Psalms of Ascents" or degrees.</note>, which seem to have been part of the Commentaries on the Psalms.

The city of Antioch Amygdonia (which the Syrians call Nisibis), located on the border of the Roman and Persian Empires, gave him birth. # The Arian Century

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>
4th CENTURY.
From the Year 300.
</margin>

<margin>
* Religious History, ch. 1. Works, Vol. 3, p. 768.
</margin>

...living in mountains and caves, constantly exercising himself with fasts and the harshest duties of a severe discipline. He became famous for his confession of faith during the Persecution of Maximinus, and was eventually raised to the Bishopric of his home city <note>Nisibis, an important border city in Mesopotamia, modern-day Turkey.</note>. In the year 325, he attended the Council of Nicaea as a primary champion of orthodox doctrine—<note>original: "τῶν ὀρθῶν δογμάτων, οἷά τις δεινὸς καὶ πρόμαχος ἁπάσης φάλαγγος"</note> "of the orthodox dogmas, like a formidable champion and leader of the entire rank," as Theodoret says \*, acting as *a most valiant warrior and prince of the whole line to debate on behalf of true dogmas*. Theodoret adds in that passage that James, joining his prayers to God with those of Alexander, called down that ill-fated end upon Arius; however, he makes a significant error by attributing these events to Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, and the time of the Nicene Synod. 

<margin>
* As above, and Church History, b. 1, 2. ch. 31.
</margin>

Near the beginning of the reign of Constantius, around the year 338, Sapor, the King of the Persians, surrounded Nisibis—which was then subject to the Romans—with a tight siege. All of his engines and missiles were rendered useless by the prayers of this holy man. When the city wall collapsed due to the violent force of a river passing the city (whose course Sapor had blocked with built-up mounds), it was rebuilt in a single night by the inhabitants, who were encouraged by James’s prayers. Finally, stationed in a certain tower, James prayed to God that a swarm of gnats and mosquitoes might be sent against the enemy. No sooner said than done. For the horses, elephants, and other pack animals of the Persians, unable to endure the stings of the tiny creatures, broke their ranks, threw off their riders, and took to flight. Thus, the most unhappy King, forced to retreat, brought home disgrace instead of victory. 

<margin>
† On Ecclesiastical Writers, ch. 1.
</margin>

Theodoret relates these things at length, testifying in more than one place \* that James was renowned for the Apostolic gifts of miracles, that he raised the dead, predicted the future, and performed other stupendous deeds, many examples of which he provides in the first chapter of his *Philotheus* <note>original: "φιλόθεος"; literally "Friend of God," the title of Theodoret's Religious History.</note>. He ended his life during the reign of Constantius and was buried in his native city; the Emperor Julian, upon entering the city, ordered the relics of his sacred body to be carried out, according to Gennadius †. 

<margin>
* Book 5, ch. 3.
</margin>

<margin>
† Religious History, ch. 1.
</margin>

However, Sozomen \* merely says that Julian, passing that way, threatened the people of Nisibis that he would neither bring them help nor admit their embassy, nor set foot in their city (which he considered wicked) until he learned they had converted to the religion of the Pagans. I feel we should rather believe Theodoret †, who was closer to the events; he relates that when Nisibis was handed over to the Persians by Jovian, Julian's successor, almost all the inhabitants left the city and carried the body of their Bishop with them because of their <note>original: "τῆς σπουδῆς"</note> zeal. Jerome grants him no place among the Ecclesiastical Writers because his works, as Gennadius † rightly observes, had not yet been translated from the Syriac language in Jerome’s time.

<margin>
† Location cited.
</margin>

According to the same witness, he wrote a massive work consisting of twenty-six books, namely: *On Faith against all Heresies*, *On General Charity*, *On Special Love toward one's Neighbor*, *On Fasting*, *On Prayer*, *On the Resurrection*, *On Life after Death*, *On Humility*, *On Patience*, *On Penitence*, *On Satisfaction*, *On Virginity*, *On the Perception of the Soul*, *On Circumcision*, *On the Blessed Grape-cluster*—regarding which it is read in Isaiah, "the cluster is not to be destroyed"—*On Christ, that he is the Son of God and Consubstantial with the Father*, *On Chastity*, *Against the Pagans*, *On the Construction of the Tabernacle*, *On the Conversion of the Heathen*, *On the Kingdom of the Persians*, *On the Persecution of Christians*, and also a *Chronicle* in which, by the authority of the Divine Scriptures, he silenced the mouths of those who vainly philosophize with bold suspicion regarding the Advent of our Lord. I refrain from saying more about these, however, because they are no longer extant. 

There is held in the library of Leiden, among the manuscript books brought from the East by Jacob Golius (number 87, folio), a work titled *The Six Days of Creation dedicated to Constantine*, or the *History of Creation and Created Things in Syriac* by James, Bishop of Edessa; whether this is truly the work of our James, let others judge: certainly the timeline fits very well. Indeed, those people are pleasantly trifling who claim our James was the compiler of the *84 Arabic Canons of the Council of Nicaea*. The illustrious Pearson, in his *Vindication of Ignatius* (part 1, p. 187), confirms with many arguments that those Canons were forged after the age of the Emperor Justinian.

# The Arian Century

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

From the Year 300.
</margin>

<note>original: "ἀρχαιότητι φράσεως καὶ σωφροσύνῃ νοημάτων, καὶ ὀνομάτων κάλλει καὶ χάριτι ἐπαγγελίας εὐδοκιμοῦσι"</note> They are esteemed for the antiquity of their phrasing, the sobriety of their thoughts, the beauty of their vocabulary, and the grace of their delivery; they are greatly praised both for their ancient style of eloquence and the weight of their sentiments, as well as for the elegance of their words and their charm in explaining matters. Of these, the following remain:

*A Short Speech to the Emperor Constantine at the Council of Nicaea.* This survives, if it is indeed genuine, in the priest Gregory’s *Oration on the Nicene Fathers*, which Laurentius Surius provides in Latin (July 10, No. 6), and appears in Greek and Latin in Combefis's *Supplement*, Volume 2, page 547.

*Commentary on the Hexaemeron;* <note>The "Hexaemeron" refers to the six days of creation described in Genesis.</note> first published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius (*Lyons, 1629, quarto*), who added extensive notes and collections. Scholars have raised significant doubts about this work, and rightly so. For although the author handles the subject he undertook quite capably in some places, the greater part of the work is flawed, being filled with silly fables about the Blessed Virgin and her parents (to say nothing of other issues) taken from the *Proto-evangelium of James*. Such things are foreign to the doctrine, judgment, and gravity of Eustathius. Nor do I think anyone of sound judgment would claim that the "Gospel of James" reflects the age of Eustathius, or that Eustathius—a man of such gravity and learning—would have approved of it. One might perhaps suspect that the entire fable regarding the Blessed Virgin and the things that follow were added by a later hand. Certainly, that entire section from page 68, where he discusses the sons of the Patriarch Jacob, until page 75, where he resumes the same material, seems quite <note>original: "ἀπροσδιόνυσα"</note> irrelevant and improperly thrust into a place where it does not belong; for if this part is removed, the rest holds together perfectly. The impostor realized this, and therefore closed the fabulous little narrative with the caution that he had only said these things <note>original: "ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ"</note> "in passing." Either this must be said, or the entire work must be stripped from Eustathius; and perhaps both views are not far from the truth. Certainly, none of the ancients or moderns recorded that our Eustathius labored over a work of this kind. Not even Leo Allatius, who first published it, speaks with his usual confidence regarding the author, relying on no other testimony than the titles of the manuscript codices. Yet everyone knows how deceptive and uncertain the titles of manuscript books often are. Whoever the author was, he lived—or at least wished to appear to have lived—in the thirtieth year of Constantine, that is, the year of Christ 335, or at least the following year. Yet even so, the accurate method of calculation does not hold up when he says on page 55 that from the time of Christ (taking this to mean the year of the Lord’s Passion) to the thirtieth year of Constantine, 249 years are counted. <note>The math here is inconsistent with the historical dates the author is trying to reconcile.</note> Even if the writer was a contemporary of Eustathius, the same difficulty remains regarding the interpolations and fables. Let the learned resolve this knot.

<margin>
* Book 6, ch. 13.
</margin>
*Dissertation on the Ventriloquist against Origen,* <note>The "Engastrimytho" or Ventriloquist refers to the Witch of Endor from the Book of Samuel. Eustathius argued against Origen’s view that she truly summoned the soul of the prophet.</note> in which he sharply attacks Origen and his opinions. Indeed, Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian.</note> counts Eustathius among the primary detractors of Origen \*. This dissertation was published in Greek and Latin by the same Allatius, together with a very learned treatise on the same subject, at the place and year mentioned above. It is also found in the eighth volume of the *Critici Sacri* printed in London. He also wrote works that have been lost, or at least have not yet come to light, besides infinite *Letters*:

*A Book on the Soul,* of which some fragments are presented by Theodoret in Dialogues 1, 2, and 3.

*A Sermon or Homily on that passage of Proverbs 8: "The Lord created me at the beginning,"* etc. <note>This was a central verse in the Arian controversy regarding the nature of Christ.</note> A fragment survives in Theodoret's *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 1, ch. 8, and many others in the same author's Dialogues 1, 2, and 3; two in Facundus, Book 11, ch. 5; and another in Anastasius's *Collection*.

*Interpretation of the Psalms.* Some fragments on Psalms 15 and 92 survive in the same Dialogues 1 and 3. Theodoret also cites our Eustathius in *On the Inscriptions of the Columns* and *On the Inscriptions of the Steps*, which seem to have been parts of the Commentaries on the Psalms.

# The Arian Century

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

...living in mountains and caves, constantly exercising himself in fasts and the harshest duties of a stricter discipline. <margin>4th CENTURY. From the Year 300.</margin> He became famous as a Confessor <note>In the early church, a "Confessor" was someone who suffered for the Christian faith during persecutions but was not killed.</note> during the Persecution of Maximinus; eventually, he was elevated to the Bishopric of his home city. In the year 325, he attended the Council of Nicaea as a primary champion of orthodox doctrine, <gloss>fighting for the orthodox dogmas, like a skilled foot-soldier of the entire phalanx,</gloss> as Theodoret says*, <margin>* Religious History, ch. 1. Works, Vol. 3, p. 768.</margin> like a most valiant warrior and leader of the whole army about to debate on behalf of true teachings. In that same passage, Theodoret adds that James joined with Alexander in prayers to God to call down a cursed end upon Arius; however, the author falls into a significant error by attributing these events to Alexander, the Bishop of Alexandria, and the time of the Synod of Nicaea.

Near the beginning of the reign of Constantius, around the year 338, Sapor, the King of the Persians, surrounded Nisibis (which was then subject to the Romans) in a tight siege. All of his engines of war and weapons were rendered useless by the prayers of this holy man. When a wall collapsed under the violent force of the river flowing past the city—the course of which Sapor had blocked with built-up mounds—it was rebuilt in a single night by the inhabitants, who were encouraged by James’s prayers. Finally, standing upon a certain tower, James prayed to God that a swarm of gnats and mosquitoes might be sent against the enemy. No sooner said than done. For the horses, elephants, and other pack animals of the Persians, unable to bear the stings of the tiny creatures, broke their ranks, threw off their riders, and took to flight. Thus, the most unhappy King, forced to retreat, brought home disgrace instead of victory.

Theodoret relates these things at length, testifying in more than one place* <margin>* as cited above, and Church History, Book 1, ch. 7, and Book 2, ch. 31.</margin> that James was famous for the Apostolic gift of miracles, that he raised the dead, predicted the future, and performed other stupendous deeds, many examples of which he provides in the first chapter of his <gloss>God-loving</gloss> History. James ended his life during the reign of Constantius and was buried in his native city. According to Gennadius†, when the Emperor Julian entered Nisibis, he ordered the relics of James’s holy body to be carried out of the city. <margin>† On Ecclesiastical Writers, ch. 1. * Book 5, ch. 3.</margin> Sozomen*, however, only says that Julian, while passing through, threatened the people of Nisibis that he would neither bring them aid nor admit their legation, nor set foot in their city (viewing it as wicked) until he learned they had converted to the religion of the Pagans. I feel we should rather believe Theodoret†, as he was closer to the events; he records that when Nisibis was handed over to the Persians by Jovian <margin>† Religious History, ch. 1.</margin> (Julian’s successor), nearly all the inhabitants left the city and carried the <gloss>zealously guarded</gloss> body of their Bishop with them. Jerome grants him no place among the Ecclesiastical Writers because, as Gennadius† correctly observes, his works had not yet been translated from the Syriac language in Jerome’s time. <margin>† Cited location.</margin>

According to the same witness, James wrote a massive work consisting of twenty-six books, namely: *On Faith against all Heresies*, *On General Charity*, *On Special Love toward one's Neighbor*, *On Fasting*, *On Prayer*, *On the Resurrection*, *On Life after Death*, *On Humility*, *On Patience*, *On Penance*, *On Satisfaction*, *On Virginity*, *On the Perception of the Soul*, *On Circumcision*, *On the Blessed Cluster* (regarding the passage in Isaiah which reads, *the cluster is not to be destroyed*), <note>Isaiah 65:8. This is a common patristic metaphor for Christ or the faithful remnant.</note> *On Christ, that He is the Son of God and Consubstantial with the Father*, *On Chastity*, *Against the Heathens*, *On the Construction of the Tabernacle*, *On the Conversion of the Nations*, *On the Kingdom of the Persians*, *On the Persecution of Christians*, and also a *Chronicle* in which, by the authority of the Divine Scriptures, he silenced those who vainly philosophize with bold suspicion regarding the Coming of our Lord. I shall refrain from saying more about these, however, as they are no longer extant. There is held in the library of Leiden, among the manuscript books brought from the East by Jacob Golius (No. 87, folio), a *Hexaemeron* <note>A treatise on the six days of creation.</note> addressed to Constantine by James, Bishop of Edessa, or a History of Creation and Created Things in Syriac; whether this is truly the work of our James, let others judge: certainly, the timing fits well. Truly, those who make our James the compiler of the *84 Arabic Canons of the Council of Nicaea* are merely spinning pleasant trifles. The distinguished Pearson, in *Vindiciae Ignatianae* (part 1, p. 187), confirms with many arguments that those Canons were fabricated after the age of the Emperor Justinian.

# The Arian Century

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>4th CENTURY. From the Year 300.</margin>...too credulous, and one who reports these things from hearsay alone, being himself removed from the actual events by almost an entire century. It should not be seen as a light prejudice that a matter so memorable was unknown to all the writers of that age, and that no one before Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345–410 AD) was a monk and historian known for translating Greek church fathers into Latin, though his historical accuracy is sometimes questioned.</note> heard so much as a word about it; nor are other arguments lacking that suggest the same, should I wish to dwell on them.

But let us proceed with Athanasius. Having been trained in the liberal arts, he was admitted into the household of Bishop Alexander, who subsequently employed him as a Secretary and later appointed him as the Chief of Deacons. In the Synod of Nicaea, he brought aid with wonderful skill to Alexander, who was vigorously opposing Arius; through the debate he held, he defeated the craftiness of the Heretic. Consequently, for the rest of his life, he experienced the Arians as his most bitter enemies. Five months after the Synod, upon the death of Alexander in the year 326, he was placed in charge of the Church of Alexandria by the common vote of the Catholics, being then, it appears, in the twenty-eighth year of his age.

The restless and stubborn malice of the Eusebians <note>The "Eusebians" were a political-religious faction led by Eusebius of Nicomedia who supported Arius and opposed the Nicene Creed.</note> prevented him from performing the duty entrusted to him in peace for long. After various deceptive slanders were tried in vain, he was finally summoned in the year 334 to Caesarea by a Synod of several bishops hostile to him, gathered in that place to answer for the supposed murder of a certain Meletian Bishop named Arsenius. However, Athanasius refused to attend, fearing the enmity of the bishops. The Emperor Constantine, somewhat angered, ordered another Synod to be held the following year at Tyre. There, the Eusebians began to ventilate the cause of Athanasius more openly and "with a bare head" <note>original: "γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ" – a Greek idiom meaning shamelessly or without disguise.</note>; and loading him with false charges of injury, tyranny, rape, murder committed for the sake of magic arts, a broken mystic chalice, holy books given to the fire, the Lord’s table overturned, and even an illegal ordination, they deposed him from his see. 

However, Athanasius, having left Tyre earlier, traveled to Constantinople and informed the Emperor of the foul injustice of the bishops. Therefore, in the year 336, the leaders of the Eusebians, summoned to Constantinople, charged Athanasius before the Emperor with a new crime, suggesting that he had threatened to prevent the grain supply, which was usually carried annually from Alexandria to Constantinople, from being sent. Moved by this accusation, Constantine soon banished him to Trier, a city in Belgic Gaul. 

After a full year and about six months, Constantine having passed away, Athanasius was restored to his see by a letter from Constantine the Younger dated the 15th of the Calends of July in the year 337. Yet in the year 341, the Synod of Antioch, renewing the slanders, deposed him for a second time, substituting in his place Gregory of Cappadocia, an obscure man of no reputation. But before the wolf could invade the fold, Athanasius had fled to Rome, summoned there by Bishop Julius; there, in a Synod held in the year 342, he was acquitted of the crimes alleged against him. 

He remained in this City and other parts of the West for several years, until in the year 347, having been again acquitted by the decree of the Synod of Sardica and fully restored, the Emperor Constantius—at the intervention of his brother Constans—returned him to the Church of Alexandria. But again, "clouds after the rain." In the year 353, by the decrees of the Synod of Arles, and in the year 355, by those of Milan, he was again condemned and ordered to be driven from his see. The following year, he was expelled from his Church by the Arian faction raging against the Alexandrian Catholics; and in his place, George of Cappadocia was substituted—a relative of Gregory (who had died some time before), the most wicked of two-legged creatures, surrounded by a military guard. 

At this point, allow me to note an enormous error of Dorotheus, Metropolitan of Monemvasia, who published a *Synopsis of Histories* in the common or "barbarian" Greek dialect, <margin>* Synopsis of various histories, p. 254.</margin> where he speaks of Constantius thus *: "In the fifteenth year of his reign, he exiled the great Athanasius to England, and Felix was ordained by him." <note>original: "Τῷ δὲ ιεʹ τῆς αὐτοῦ βασιλείας ἐξώρισε τὸν μέγαν Ἀθανάσιον εἰς τὴν Ἐγλιτέραν, καὶ ἐχειροτονήθη Φίλιξ ὑπ' αὐτοῦ."</note> Where it can be doubted by no one that Liberius <note>Pope Liberius (r. 352–366 AD) was indeed exiled by Constantius II, but to Thrace, not England.</note> ought to be understood in place of Athanasius, and that he was banished not to England or Britain, but to Beroea in Thrace.

Athanasius, having been put to flight, withdrew into the most deserted wilderness of the Thebaid <note>The Thebaid was a region in ancient Egypt around Thebes, famous as a retreat for early Christian hermits and monks.</note>; in which he lay safely hidden until the death of Constantius, occupying himself securely with prayers, fasts, and other duties of piety, and the composing of Letters and Apologies. During the reign of Julian, having been recalled from exile, he held a synod to establish the true meaning of the terms "essence" and "substance" <note>original: "οὐσίας & ὑποστάσεως" (ousia and hypostasis). These technical terms were central to the Trinitarian debates regarding the nature of God.</note> and regarding the reception of lapsed bishops back to their sees. Soon made an exile again in the year 362...

# The Arian Century

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>

He escaped the snares of the Pagans and Arians breathing down his neck, though not without extreme danger to his life; of these enemies he wittily said: *“Let us withdraw for a little while, O friends; it is a small cloud, which will soon vanish.”* In the year 373, he met the Emperor Jovian at Antioch and presented him with a booklet on the faith. In the early years of the reign of Valens, being sought for punishment or exile by the Augustal Prefect, he went into hiding; but as this cloud also vanished, he lived thereafter in peace and security. Finally, broken by labors, hardships, and troubles, he succumbed and returned his most holy soul to heaven in the year of Christ 371, in the 46th year of his episcopate. For thus Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD), a Greek church historian whose "Ecclesiastical History" is a primary source for this period.</note> expressly records it, although Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> and many modern writers following him postpone it to the following year; indeed, Proterius, in a letter to Pope Leo, writes that Athanasius was still alive in March of the year 373.

He was a man most abundant in every kind of virtue, possessing a constant and invincible spirit in defending Catholic truth, which knew not how to yield to hardships, dangers, or difficulties; <note>original Greek: "τοῖς μὲν παίουσιν Adamas, τοῖς δὲ στασιάζουσιν Magnes"</note> **“an Adamant <note>A term for an indestructible diamond-like stone, symbolizing his hardness against enemies.</note> to those who struck him, and a Magnet to those in disagreement.”** In other disciplines he was not unskillfully practiced, and in Theology he was most precise; of the controversies of his age, he was as knowledgeable as anyone could be, and a most sharp judge and defender of Orthodox doctrine. He was exceptionally fit for ecclesiastical assemblies and the duties of the sacred office, and as Sozomen <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), another major historian of the early Church.</note> aptly puts it, <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἐν νῷ αὐτοδίδακτος"</note> **“as if self-taught in his mind.”**

The Bishop of Sasima <note>This refers to Gregory of Nazianzus, who was appointed Bishop of Sasima.</note> spoke of him briefly and quite elegantly: <note>original Greek: "ὁ τῶν Σασίμων... ὀρθῷ μὲν ἐπισκοπῆς ὁ ἐκείνου βίος καὶ τρόπος, νόμος δ’ ὀρθοδοξίας, τὰ ἐκείνου δόγματα"</note> **“His life and character were a rule for the episcopacy, and his doctrines were the law of Orthodoxy.”** Photius <note>Photius I (c. 810–893 AD), Patriarch of Constantinople and a renowned scholar who reviewed hundreds of books in his "Bibliotheca."</note> says of his style: <note>original Greek: "κομψῶς τε καὶ λαμπρῶς καὶ ἔτι σαφῶς συντεθειμέναι... καὶ τὸ πιθανὸν καὶ τὸ χαρίεν ἀνθῆσαι"</note> **“His letters are elegantly, brilliantly, and yet clearly composed, flourishing with both the power of persuasion and with charm.”** His speech is clear in all his writings. Finally, Photius says of his books against Arius: **“The diction in these is clear, and as in all his others, it is sober, candid, vehement, and deep, driving its arguments forcefully; indeed, his abundance and fruitfulness in these works was truly wonderful.”** Moreover, the great value in which the writings of Athanasius were once held is shown by the command given by the most pious Abbot Cosmas to John Moschus: <note>John Moschus (c. 550–619 AD) was a monk and author of the "Spiritual Meadow."</note> **“When you find anything from the small works of Saint Athanasius, and you have no paper for writing, write it on your clothes.”**

*Five Disputations or Orations against the Arians.* Photius calls these the *Five-book work* against the Arians and says (in Codex 140) they are a **“Trophy against all heresies, but especially the Arian.”** (Peter Flecmannus presents this passage more completely than it appears in the published editions, in his Appendix to the Works of Athanasius, p. 6). Photius wonderfully commends their style, method, richness, and arguments; he even writes that from these, as from a fountain, Gregory the Theologian and Saint Basil derived the clear streams of their own books against the errors of Arius. 

Furthermore, it is surprising how the order of these Orations varies and is mixed up in the manuscript codices and among ancient writers. To mention just a few examples, Cyril of Alexandria cites the fourth of these under the name of *“The second discourse on the Holy Trinity,”* and again as *“The second discourse on the Consubstantial Trinity.”* The Council of Chalcedon simply calls the third one the *“Oration against Heresies.”* The fifth (which some manuscripts call the *Sixth Discourse against the Arians*, placing the *Oration against Arius and Apollinaris*—found below—in the fifth spot) contains certain things on page 322 which seem to suggest to some that it was written after the Nestorian controversies <note>The Nestorian controversy regarding the nature of Christ began in the 420s, long after Athanasius's death, implying some scholars believe this section was added or edited later.</note>.

But this reason is nothing to me, for we have already observed from Photius above that Athanasius sometimes wrote "elegantly and brilliantly"* <note>original Greek: "kompsōs te kai lamprōs"</note>. *2nd, that it confesses three "hypostases" in the Trinity, while Athanasius usually acknowledged only one. <margin>4th CENTURY. From the Year 300.</margin>
*Letter to all those everywhere leading a solitary life in a hermit's retreat, written just like the preceding Apologies.* It seems the whole work is contained in the first two pages, ending with the word "Amen" <note>original Greek: ἀμὴν</note>, and serves as a dedication for the books against the Arians. The remainder of the work, starting from the word "This" <note>original Greek: Αὐτὴ</note>, is a fragment of some other "headless" <note>original Greek: ἀκεφάλου; a manuscript missing its beginning</note> work. Certainly, below on page 652, certain premises are mentioned which are by no means found in this letter. <margin>4th CENTURY. From the Year 300.</margin>
*Synopsis of Holy Scripture;* today’s critics almost unanimously agree this was not written by Athanasius. However, even if it is not his, it is the work of a quite ancient writer.

*Testimonies from Scripture on the shared essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.* The style proves it is not Athanasius’s; furthermore, it harshly attacks Origen—whom Athanasius always praised—and mentions the Origenist heresy. It even cites certain passages from the *Questions to Antiochus* <note>The "Origenist heresy" refers to later controversies regarding the teachings of the 3rd-century scholar Origen; Athanasius lived before these disputes reached their peak.</note>.

*Sermon on the Passion and the Cross of the Lord;* this work completely forbids the taking of oaths, a practice that Athanasius frequently uses in his genuine writings.

<margin>† Supplement, p. 31.</margin>
*Disputation against Arius in the Council of Nicaea.* This appears to be the invention of some raving monk from a later age, as is evident from many clues found within the disputation itself. I do not know, however, what Casimir Oudin <note>Casimir Oudin (1638–1717) was a Premonstratensian monk and a noted bibliographer of church history.</note> means when he attributes it to Vigilius of Thapsus †.

*Sermon on the Gospel regarding the Most Holy Virgin Mother of God, and the mysteries of the Annunciation and Incarnation:* This was written after the rise of the Monothelite heresy <note>The Monothelite heresy, which concerned the "will" of Christ, did not emerge until the 7th century, long after Athanasius died in 373.</note>, as it attacks that heresy very frequently.

<margin>† Life of Athanasius, Sect. 6, Num. 10.</margin>
*The Athanasian Creed;* <note>original: Symbolum Athanasii</note> Sufficient evidence that this is not a genuine work of Athanasius is found in the fact that neither Athanasius himself, nor any writer of the following centuries before Theodulf of Orléans <note>Theodulf (c. 750–821) was a key figure in the Carolingian Renaissance.</note> (in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, p. 72), mentions it. Nor did it gain a place in the Churches before the year 1000, nor did it begin to become famous everywhere until it was produced as a testimony under Athanasius’s name by the legates of Pope Gregory IX around the year 1233, during a debate held in Constantinople. But others have said more on these matters, and we have discussed them elsewhere †. It may be believed, perhaps not wrongly, to have been composed by Vigilius of Thapsus <note>Vigilius of Thapsus was a 5th-century bishop in Africa known for writing under the names of famous fathers like Athanasius to gain authority for his anti-heretical works.</note>, later translated into the Greek language, and hidden for a long time in church archives. Regarding Vigilius, the theory is strengthened by the fact that Theodulf of Orléans cites the Creed from those books of "Athanasius" which are now certainly recognized as the work of Vigilius of Thapsus—and which, in the ancient and well-known Fleury Manuscript <note>original: Codice Floriacensi</note>, are joined with Vigilius’s books against Nestorius and Eutyches.

*Treatise on Definitions,* in which Gregory of Nyssa is found cited; it perhaps has Maximus <note>Likely Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662).</note> as its author, and it is placed among his works edited by Combefis.

*Seven Dialogues against the Arians, Apollinarists, and Macedonians.* In the Heidelberg edition, these are divided into two parts: the first five are titled *Dialogues on the Holy Trinity*, while the last two are titled *Dialogues between an Orthodox and a Macedonian*. Some attribute all these dialogues to the monk Maximus, others to Etherius of Tyana. It is more certain than certainty itself that they are not by Athanasius. For they were written after the Eutychian heresy arose <note>The Eutychian heresy arose in the mid-5th century.</note>. See more on this in the section on Theodoret.

<margin>* Codex 46.</margin>
*A Letter written as a Preface,* in which the tragedy of the ecclesiastical movements is described, along with the seventeen following chapters, are by Etherius; Photius <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893), Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople and a famous scholar.</note>, though clearly in error, attributes them to Theodoret *.

*136 Questions on the Old and New Testament to Antiochus, and the same number of Responses,* in which Athanasius himself and Dionysius the Areopagite are cited. They appear to have been collected from various writings of the Fathers by some scholar after the Monothelite era. That it is the offspring of a later age is evident even from the fact that in these texts, all Westerners are designated by the name of "Franks."

*Sayings and Interpretations of the Gospel Parables,* comprised of 133 questions and as many responses. A work of a later age.

*Twenty Other Questions* with the same number of responses; these appear to have been written after the disagreements arose between the Latin and Greek Churches.

*Disputations held with Arius at Laodicea.* It is now known to everyone that these are the work of Vigilius of Thapsus, the Bishop.

However, there are many things that suggest it is spurious: primarily the instructions found therein given to monks about renouncing possessions and paying tithes, the prohibition of marriage for Clerics, and the mention of a Monastic Rule; not to mention the total silence of the ancient writers regarding such a book. It must therefore be the work of a younger Athanasius, a fact which the Illustrious Vossius himself did not hide from me when we discussed this matter in person. Nevertheless, since the manuscript shows an age of five or six hundred years, the work is by no means to be despised, even if it is not ascribed to our Athanasius. A controversy has arisen on this matter between the Illustrious Arnold and a certain theologian of Rouen, as we recently learned from the *News of the Republic of Letters* (July, page 744) and the *Acts of the Learned of Leipzig* (1685, page 511).

*Commentary on the Psalms,* which appeared under Athanasius’s name in *Rome* (1477) and *Tübingen* (1515) among his Latin works, is actually the work of Theophylact <note>Theophylact of Ohrid, an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop.</note>.

*Furthermore, Thomas Aquinas \* mentions a chest, or Volume on John, written by Athanasius; and the First Lateran Synod mentions a Treatise by the same author on the sin against the Holy Spirit. Whether Athanasius actually wrote such things or not remains uncertain.*

The works of Athanasius exist in Greek and Latin, printed at Heidelberg in 1601, in two folio volumes with the Flecmannian Appendix, which contains many fragments and variant readings. There is also the Paris edition of 1627 in two folio volumes, which is indeed a more beautiful and polished edition; however, the Commeliana edition <note>Referring to the printer Jerome Commelin.</note> takes the prize from it because it possesses indices that are far more extensive and accurate, especially regarding historical matters. The Cologne edition of 1686 recently followed the Paris edition, adding the *Syntagma* <note>A collection of shorter works or a systematic arrangement.</note> edited by Arnold.

<margin>326.</margin>
**COMMODIANUS**, a writer almost unknown for many centuries (since, besides Gennadius and perhaps Pope Gelasius of Rome, none of the ancients mentioned him), also took the name Gazaeus. Whether this comes from *gaza* or *gazophylacium* <note>meaning "treasury."</note>, just as Commodianus comes from Commodus, or from Gaza, a city in Palestine, I confess (along with the illustrious Rigaltius <note>Nicolas Rigault (1577–1654), a French classical scholar.</note>) that I do not know. He himself indicates well enough that he was a pagan by birth and upbringing in his *Instructions to the Gentiles, 33*, addressing them thus:

->*And I, who give this warning, was once the same—ignorant and wandering.*<-

Hence, in *Instruction 61*, he says he was *lifted from the sewer*. For while he was reading the books of the Christian faith, illuminated by the rays of divine truth, he joined the Christians. Whether he was Italian is not clear; it is certain he lived in Italy, and most likely in Rome, in the age of Constantine the Great—at the time, it seems, of the Council of Nicaea, and most certainly under Pope Sylvester, to whose "stable" <note>The "manger" or "fold" of the Church.</note> he invites the wandering Gentiles in *Instruction 33*. He wrote a *Work of Instructions against the Pagans*, in which he sharply criticizes the worship and deities of the Gentiles and sternly rebukes the somewhat lapsed morals of the Christians of his century. It is, believe me, a remarkable monument of ancient piety, in which a true love for Christ and burning zeal, a singular care for the poor, and a mind prepared for martyrdom breathe throughout. His style of writing is "metro-prosaic" <note>A hybrid style that uses the rhythm of poetry without following strict classical meter.</note>, observing no laws of meter, but merely <margin>\* On Ecclesiastical Writers, ch. 15.</margin> imitating the form and character of a small poem. Thus, Gennadius \* says he wrote in a mediocre style, as if it were verse. The entire work is an acrostic <note>A poem where the first letter of each line spells out a word or name.</note> comprising 80 Instructions, which contain as many acrostics, with the exception of the 60th, which follows the order of the alphabet. In the final Instruction, by reading the initial letters of the verses backwards, he expresses his name and character in this way: **COMMODIANUS, BEGGAR OF CHRIST**. He uses words quite suitable <margin>† Preface to Commodianus.</margin> to the subject matter he treats. Yet his style, says Rigaltius †, tastes of the "rusticity of African ferocity" <note>A scholarly jab at the vigorous, unpolished Latin typical of North African writers like Tertullian.</note>; nevertheless, it frequently alludes to the sharp insights of Tertullian, Cyprian, and Minucius. He also intersperses certain uncommon findings of Greek and Latin antiquity. In that little book, one can find certain blemishes mixed in, which Commodianus shared with many...

<margin>4th CENTURY. From the year 300.</margin>
...held in common with the fathers of the preceding centuries. In *Instruction* 3, he asserts that apostate angels fell from heaven and, being ensnared by an insane love and the embraces of women, procreated a "Gigantic offspring" <note>This refers to the "Nephilim" mentioned in Genesis; the author notes this was a common early Christian interpretation influenced by Jewish apocrypha.</note>; an ancient error, indeed, but one drawn from the apocryphal *Book of Enoch* (frequently praised by the ancients) and from a poorly understood Septuagint translation of Genesis 6:2. In *Instructions* 19, 43, 44, and 80, he defends the fable of the Chiliasts <term>Chiliasts: from the Greek 'chilioi' (thousand), these were Christians who believed in a literal 1000-year earthly reign of Christ before the final judgment</term>, concerning golden ages to come hereafter, a kingdom of a thousand years, the first Resurrection, earthly happiness, the end of the age, and a world that—according to ancient tradition—would endure for six thousand years. Because of these errors, it is reasonable to believe that Pope Gelasius, in his Synodal Decree (Council Records, Volume 4), reckoned the short works of Commodianus among the Apocrypha. Yet, as the Reader should well note, in that same decree as it survives in Gratian <note>Johannes Gratian, the 12th-century compiler of canon law.</note>, the name of Commodianus is not found. Nicolaus Rigaltius was the first to publish these *Instructions* from the transcript of Sirmond, with notes appended to his edition of Cyprian (Paris, 1640, and again in 1666); finally, they are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 27, page 12.

DONATUS, an African by birth, became the Bishop of the Donatist faction in Carthage after Majorinus and gave his name to his sect. For although another Donatus, the Bishop of Casae Nigrae, had been the first leader and author of the Schism, the schismatics preferred to be named after this one, as he was more distinguished. He began to be known around the year 329: for he is placed in this year by Jerome \*, and in the previous year by Prosper †, namely during the consulship of Januarius and Justus; perhaps because he was made Bishop around this time. He was a man of singular arrogance and swollen with unbearable pride, who, with raised eyebrows, treated even the civil Prefects with ignominy. When Paul and Macarius were sent to Africa by the Emperor Constans with church ornaments and alms to relieve the poor, he received them with insults and rejected the gifts, shouting furiously: *What has the Emperor to do with the Church?* <note>original: "Quid Imperatori cum Eccleſiâ?" This became a famous slogan for those arguing for the separation of church and imperial power.</note> Moreover, having sent letters throughout the province, he warned his followers not to accept what had been brought. He used to boast of his faction, saying: *What is being done on my side among you?* And as if he alone held the leadership of Carthage, he was rarely called "Bishop," but was referred to as "Donatus of Carthage." He boasted that responses had been made to him from heaven; indeed, he reached such a point of madness that he allowed men to swear by him, as if by some deity. He was driven out of Carthage in the year 356, if Jerome marks the time correctly, though Baronius \* protests, contending that the Donatist bishops were banished by Constans and not restored until the reign of Julian. Donatus wrote many small works pertaining to his heresy, according to the testimony of Jerome †, and among these a book *On the Holy Spirit*, in which he taught doctrines consistent with Arian dogma. NE. <note>Arianism: The belief that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note>

CHALCIDIUS, *Vir Clarissimus* <term>Vir Clarissimus: "A Most Distinguished Man," a specific title of rank for the Roman senatorial aristocracy</term>, and, as some wish, Archdeacon of the Church of Carthage. He flourished perhaps around the year 330; certainly he was a contemporary of Hosius, if indeed it was Hosius of Córdoba, at whose persuasion Chalcidius translated Plato’s *Timaeus* into Latin and explained it with a learned commentary. My friend Seller <note>Abednego Seller (c. 1646–1705), an English hagiographer and friend of the author.</note> advised me of this matter long ago; and since I see certain not unlearned men leaning toward this opinion, we have not denied him a place among the ecclesiastical writers. I confess that I certainly "suspend judgment" <note>original: "ἐπέχειν" (epéchein). A technical term from Greek skepticism meaning to withhold assent.</note>, for it is not sufficiently clear whether he was merely a Platonic philosopher or also a Christian. The title "Most Distinguished Man" found at the beginning does not quite suit a Deacon; in his letter to Hosius, he never calls him "Bishop"; nor does he hint by even a little word that he himself was an ecclesiastical man, let alone a Christian. He cites the Mosaic theology of creation more than once; he cites Solomon, the Greek interpreters—the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX).</note>, Aquila, Symmachus—and even Origen; once he mentions the star showing the way to the newly born Christ, of which mention is made in the Gospel history. Nevertheless, he speaks of these things in a manner not quite fitting for a Christian writer (p. 372). Concerning Moses he has this to say: *Moses, the wisest of the Hebrews, energized not by human eloquence but by divine inspiration—AS THEY SAY—in that book which is considered to be about the Origin of the world,* etc. Would a Christian man write thus about Moses? Or a Deacon of Carthage? Truly, I decide nothing; I would prefer to hear the judgments of the more learned on this matter. Meanwhile, Chalcidius is an author of weight and prudence, with much profound...

## JUVENCUS

A poet of this time of no small renown, he was born in Spain—the most fertile soil for excellent poets—sprung from an ancient and noble lineage, and held the dignity of a Priest. He flourished under Constantine the Great, as he himself testifies near the end of his last book, in the year 330 according to Jerome \*, or slightly earlier according to Juan Vaséo in the *Chronicle of Spain*. Among other disciplines, he cultivated the study of poetic skill with no small diligence; having made no contemptible progress in this, he led the Muses to the summit of Zion <note>A metaphor for applying classical poetic forms to Christian themes.</note>. He dared to bind the majesty of the divine law and the entire life of our Lord while He lived among mortals to the laws of Meter. He encompassed the Gospel history, following the lead of St. Matthew, in four books of Heroic verse <term>Heroic verse: the dactylic hexameter, the meter used by Virgil for the Aeneid</term>. His speech is indeed simple, and his talent <note>original: "vena," literally "vein"</note> is not sufficiently rich, yet he possesses a candid mind and a pious and chaste spirit befitting one who handles sacred things. He followed the Evangelist with a "strict foot" <note>A pun on poetic "feet" or meter, meaning he stayed very close to the literal text.</note>; of whom Pietro Crinito \* truly said: *In this matter, he used greater diligence in preserving the history of events than in demonstrating the elegance of his own wit.* He also composed some works in the same meter pertaining to the order of the Sacraments, but these are now lost, as Jerome † testifies—from whom, as the sole source, almost all knowledge of this writer must be sought. Juvencus’s *Gospel History* is available in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothec. PP."</note>, Volume 4, p. 55, and in the Bigne collection (Paris, 1624, p. 629), and among Christian poets with notes by Fabricius (Basel, 1564, 4to). It was published separately (Basel, 1541, 8vo), in the complete collection of all ancient Latin poets (Lyons, 1603, Vol. 1), and elsewhere quite often.

## AMMON

Or *Ammonius*, an Egyptian by birth, the father of the Nitrian monks <note>Nitria was one of the earliest Christian monastic centers in the Egyptian desert.</note>. He flourished under Constantine around the year 330. At the age of 22, persuaded by his relatives to marry, he yielded, performed the betrothal, put on the wedding crown, and leading his bride into the bedchamber, exhorted her at length to renounce secular life and follow the monastic path; by his exhorting, he succeeded. Therefore, both remained under the same roof for eighteen years, intent on piety and prayers while preserving their virginity. When these years had passed, Ammon left his wife and retired to the Nitrian wilderness, where he established an even more severe way of life for 22 years. He passed from the living in the 62nd year of his age. It is told that Anthony saw the soul of the dead man carried into heaven by Angels. Many things regarding his piety, character, and miracles are told by Palladius \*, Socrates †, and Sozomen ||, whom the curious Reader interested in such matters should consult. There exist among the works of St. Ephrem (Volume 2) nineteen *Paraenetic Chapters* <note>Admonitions or hortatory writings.</note> inscribed with our Ammonius’s name. However, there is no argument for these being by Ammonius other than the authority of the manuscript from which Vossius drew them. Hebediesu mentions that several of his *Letters* exist among the Chaldeans.

## ANTONY

The father and prince of Monks, an Egyptian by nation, born in Coma (a village near Heraclea Minor) of a distinguished and splendid family. In the year 252, at the age of eighteen, having been orphaned of his parents, he gave his ancestral lands to his fellow villagers; after selling his remaining goods and distributing the money to the needy, he withdrew into the deserts of Egypt. He was the first inhabitant of the wilderness to intensely cultivate Monastic Philosophy <note>A common term in this period for the ascetic life of a monk.</note> through the most severe exercises and the harshest way of life, bringing it to nearly the highest perfection. His food was only bread with salt, his drink water—and these were taken only after sunset. Often he fasted for two days or more; often he kept watch through nearly entire nights intent on prayers. Content with the shortest sleep, he usually slept lying on the bare ground. Having been removed from all sight of men for twenty years, only...

# The Arian Century.

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>4th CENTURY. From the year 300. <image-desc>ornamental flourish</image-desc></margin>...he had commerce only with God and divine matters. When the persecution of Maximian broke out, he set out for Alexandria and mingled with the Martyrs; on their behalf, he daily interceded with the judges, not without danger to his own head. Certainly, despite his austere way of life, he was remarkably gentle and humane, likewise prudent and brave, pleasant and delightful in conversation, most patient in dispute, and very diligent in defending those who were treated unjustly. For their sake, he frequently came to the cities and interceded with the governors and leading men. He frequently visited the Great Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373), the chief defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> when he was nearly overwhelmed by the Arians, and wrote on his behalf to the Emperor Constantine on more than one occasion. He never wished to involve himself in the communion of schismatics or heretics. He condemned the Arians—who were using his authority to protect themselves—in public discourse and drove them from his mountain, saying that their words were much worse than serpents, and their heresy was the precursor of the Antichrist. Regarding his frequent conflicts with demons and the miracles performed by him, the *Life of Anthony* written by St. Athanasius will teach more than enough, as it exists today, though significantly altered <note>original: "haud parùm interpolata" — the author suggests the text has been modified by later hands.</note>. As he was dying, he bequeathed his sheepskin <note>term: "melotem" — a garment made of sheepskin, typical of monks.</note> and worn cloak to Athanasius in his will; he died in the year 357, in the one hundred and fifth year of his age. He was almost unlettered in formal studies, which he held far below himself, commending instead a good mind—as it is older than letters—and the contemplation of divine works. Therefore, when he was asked by a certain Philosopher how he could live deprived of the consolation of books, he replied <margin>* Evagrius in Socrates, Book 4, ch. 23.</margin>*, "My book, O Philosopher, is the nature of created things, and it is present whenever I wish to read the words of God." <note>original Greek: "Τὸ ἐμὸν βιβλίον, ὦ φιλόσοφε, ἡ φύσις τῶν γεγονότων ἐστὶ, καὶ πάρεστιν ὅτε βούλομαι τοὺς λόγους ἀναγινώσκειν τοὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ."</note> Sozomen <margin>† Book 2, ch. 31.</margin>† testifies that he wrote frequent letters to Constantine. He also wrote seven Epistles in the Apostolic spirit for the Monasteries in Egypt, which were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek; among these, Jerome <margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 88.</margin>* commends the one to the Arsenoites above the others. They exist in the version by Valerius Sarasus, published together with the commentaries of Dionysius the Carthusian on Dionysius the Areopagite at *Cologne, 1536*, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume IV, p. 85. In that same volume, *Two Books of Sermons* are also held under his name; however, the names of Basil, Chrysostom, and others found within them clearly show they belong to a much more recent author. Furthermore, Saint Anthony’s *Rule prescribed for Monks*, along with many other Rules of the first inhabitants of the desert, is found in the *Collection of Rules of Saint Benedict*, which Holstenius edited, *Paris, 1663, 4°, Part I, p. 3*; whether it is genuine, however, is quite uncertain. Of better repute is the quite lengthy *Exhortation to Monks* which appears in Athanasius’s *Life of Anthony*.

Abraham Ecchellensis <note>A Maronite scholar (1605–1664) known for translating Arabic texts into Latin.</note>, in the year 1646 at *Paris, 8°*, published the following small works of Saint Anthony, translated into Latin from Arabic. These are:
* *Rules or Canons for Monks, eighty in number.*
* *Twenty Sermons to Monks.*
* *Various Admonitions and Instructions for Monks.*
* *An Exposition of certain Maxims, and Answers to various Questions.*
To these he added a double *Life of Saint Anthony* translated from Arabic, as well as the *Path of Wisdom, or Method for Acquiring Sciences*, which he himself translated into Latin from an Arabic manuscript. Finally, in the Preface, he mentions that four years earlier he had published twenty *Epistles* of Saint Anthony dedicated to Cardinal Barberini.

<margin>330.</margin>**ASTERIUS**, a Cappadocian by birth, a Sophist <note>A professional teacher of rhetoric and public speaking.</note> by profession, and a Pagan by religion. Having abandoned his original religion along with the art of Rhetoric, "he professed to follow the Christian way," says Socrates <margin>* Book 1, ch. 36.</margin>*. Having become a Christian, he attended the school of Lucian of Antioch; Philostorgius <margin>† Book 2, ch. 14.</margin>† therefore counts him among Lucian's disciples. Under the persecution of Maximian, having denied the faith of Christ, he sacrificed to the gods of the Pagans; later, however, as his teacher promoted his repentance, he amended his lapse. Imbued with the doctrine of Lucian (who had been a follower of Paul of Samosata), he joined the Arians and was an intimate of Arius himself, whose cause he did not wish to fail. He sought the favor of the Eusebian bishops <note>The party following Eusebius of Nicomedia, who supported Arius.</note> with every form of obedience; he stayed with them constantly, frequently attended their Synods, and, recommended by their letters, he traveled through the cities of Syria and other churches, and [sought...]

# The Arian Century.

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>
4th CENTURY. From the year 300.

...having taken a seat among the Clergy—which was not at all permitted to him—he publicly recited the books he had composed in favor of the Arian faith. He turned this alone in his mind, having it as his only wish—a vain slave to ambition and glory—that through their efforts he might be raised to the rank of Bishop. However, he did not achieve this in the least; indeed, he was not even admitted to the order of the Clergy, as the discipline of this time forbade anyone who had fallen into idolatry <note>This refers to the "lapsi," Christians who had offered sacrifices to pagan gods during Roman persecutions and were subsequently barred from holding church office.</note> from being chosen for the Clergy. Indeed, those stained by that crime lost their priestly dignity, and even after performing penance, they were regarded only as laymen. Asterius flourished after the Council of Nicaea, especially around the year 330, at which time he published that famous *Syntagma* or *Syntagmation* <note>A "Syntagma" is a systematic collection or treatise.</note>, which Athanasius mentions so often. In this work, he openly asserted that besides Christ, there is another wisdom in God, which was the Creator of Christ himself and of the world; that the Son is "one among all things, but the first of created beings" <note>original: ἕνα τῶν πάντων, πρῶτον δὲ τῶν γενητῶν</note>—one from the totality of things, though the first of things founded, whom the Father made "by an energetic love of honor and unstinting power" <note>original: ἐνεργητικῇ φιλοτιμίᾳ κῂ ἀφειδίᾳ δυνάμεως</note>. "If the will of God," he said, "penetrates through all works in a continuous flow, then it is clear that the Son, being a creature, came to be and was fashioned by will" <note>original: δῆλονότι κῂ ὁ υἱὸς ποίημα ὢν, θελήσει γέγονε κῂ πεπλάται</note>; certainly the Son, when there was a need, was begotten and made by the Father's will. Nor did he wish Christ to be the "power of God" in any other sense than that in which the locust and the caterpillar are called the power of God in the writings of Moses <note>A reference to the biblical plagues where insects are described as God's "great army" or power.</note>; along with six hundred such monstrous blasphemies which that "sly and many-headed Sophist, the advocate of the godless heresy" <note>original: ὁ πανδούρῳ κῂ πολυκεφάλῳ σοφιστῇ, ὁ κῂ ἀθέου αἱρέσεως συνηγορος</note>—as Athanasius calls him—that old fox and many-headed Sophist, the patron of Heresy, spewed out against Christ. Saint Athanasius cites certain passages from this work in his *Epistle on the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*, page 684; *Oration III against the Arians*, page 217; and *Oration IV*, page 252. Some are cited by Acacius in Epiphanius, *Heresy 72*; and finally some by Marcellus in Eusebius, *Book 1 against Marcellus*, chapter 4.

### MARCELLUS

<margin>
330.
Eusebius, *Against Marcellus*, book 1, ch. 1; book 2, ch. 2. *On Ecclesiastical Theology*, book 1, ch. 17; and elsewhere throughout.
</margin>

MARCELLUS, Bishop of Ancyra (which is the Metropolis of Galatia), presided over the Council of Ancyra held in the year 315—if any faith is to be placed in the *Synodical Booklet* published by Pappus, which the signatures of this Synod generally support in this regard. At any rate, it is certain that he was present at the holy Synod of Nicaea in the year 325, in which he strenuously debated for the Catholic faith against the Arians. But afterward, while he was more vehemently refuting the impious writings of the Sophist Asterius, he incautiously fell into the opposite heresy of Sabellius, and likewise that of Paul of Samosata. He taught that the Son was the <term>logos prophorikos</term> <note>Translated as "the uttered word"; a philosophical term suggesting the Word is a temporary expression of God rather than an eternally distinct person.</note>, and was not a person distinct from the Father, being "one and the same in God" <note>original: ἓν κῂ τὸν αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ Θεῷ</note>, one and the same with God. Just as a human word is one and the same with a man—not by power or hypostasis <note>The individual reality or "personhood" of a being.</note>, nor separable in any way other than by the effect of operation alone—so he claimed the word "rested in God" <note>original: ἐν τῷ Θεῷ ἡσυχάζειν</note>, just as it usually happens in us when we fall silent. He claimed that He was not the Son of God, nor even the image of the invisible God, before He went out from the Father (that is, assumed flesh), so that all things might be made through Him. Only from that time did He have the beginning of His kingdom, which would have an end after the final judgment. The Word itself, having been separated from the body, was finally to be reunited with God, "so that the Word might be in God in the same manner as it was previously before the creation of the world" <note>original: ἵν' ὅπως ᾖ ἐν τῷ Θεῷ ὁ λόγος, ὥσπερ κῂ πρότεron ἦν πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου γενέσεως</note>. That is, as Eusebius correctly explains, "that He might again become one and the same with God, just as He was before" <note>original: Ὡς ἓv κῂ ταὐτὸν πάλιν τῷ Θεῷ γενέσθαι, καθà κῂ πρότερον ἦν</note>. On account of these and many other impieties of the same sort, the Bishops in the assembly held at Jerusalem at the Dedication in the year 335 demanded of him—though he was absent—that he give an account of the books he had written and change his opinion. Thus, overcome with shame, he promised he would burn his book (according to Socrates *), but he did not stand by his promises. Therefore, the Bishops, having gathered in a Synod shortly afterward at Constantinople, condemned his dogmas and stripped him of his Episcopate. They wrote letters to the churches of Galatia so that they might diligently seek out and destroy copies of Marcellus's book. The task of refuting him was also assigned to Eusebius of Caesarea, whom Marcellus had attacked sharply...

<margin>

</margin>
