# The Arian Century.

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>
4th CENTURY. From the year 300.
In Eusebius, *Against Marcellus*, book 2, p. 53.
Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 86.
[Epiphanius], *Against Heresies*, 72.
† In the fragments, column 413.
* Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book 2, p. 149.
|| Page 547.
* Page 630.
† Letters 52, 74, 78.
† Cited above.
</margin>

...they demanded of him that he censured [Asterius] sharply; this he accomplished in five books. Having been sent into exile, Marcellus fled to Julius, who then held the Roman See <note>Pope Julius I, reigned 337–352 AD.</note>, and remained there for a full year and three months. However, because his adversaries—whom Julius had summoned to plead their case—did not appear, he was admitted to communion after offering an apologetic discourse on his faith. In the year 347, he was acquitted by the sentence of the Council of Sardica. As is clear from the Synodical Letter, he complained that his words had not been correctly understood by the followers of Eusebius, and that those things for which they were slandering him had been proposed by him merely in the spirit of inquiry. 

In this matter, Marcellus acted in bad faith and <term>deceived the good Fathers</term> <note>original: "fucum fecit," literally "applied a dye/pretense."</note>. For the excerpts of his books found in Eusebius demonstrate more clearly than light that he taught these things not as theoretical problems, but seriously and from the heart. In these writings, he pronounces quite boldly on all matters, with the exception of that single question, *On the Immortality of the Flesh of Christ* (to which he perhaps pointed his finger at the Council of Sardica), concerning which he says: <note>original Greek: ὅτι δογματίζειν περὶ ὧν μὴ ἀκριβῶς ἐκ τῶν θείων μεμαθήκαμεν γραφῶν, οὐκ ἀσφαλὲς εἶναι νομίζομεν</note> *"We do not consider it at all safe to dogmatically determine those things which we have not learned exactly from the Holy Scriptures."* 

It is certainly evident that he remained hidden among the Catholics for a long time; when accused of <term>Sabellian dogma</term> <note>Sabellianism was the heresy that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct Persons, but merely three "modes" or "masks" of a single divine Person.</note>, he defended himself with the weapon that he was protected by the communion of Julius and Athanasius. But at last, the mask having been pulled away, he bore the mark of a Heretic branded upon him by all Catholics. 

When Athanasius was asked at one time by Epiphanius what he thought of Marcellus, he neither defended him nor attacked him severely; with only a slight smile, he indicated that the dogmas of Marcellus were not far removed from impiety, and that he regarded him as a man who found it necessary to clear himself with an apology. Consequently, the wavering Epiphanius wished neither to fully acquit the man nor to utterly condemn him. Saint Hilary † and Sulpicius Severus *, however, expressly record that when Athanasius clearly discovered Marcellus was of unsound faith, he denied him communion; and this happened before Photinus broke out into heresy, who was first condemned at the Synod of Sirmium in the year 349. 

Yet it is clear they are mistaken in their chronology, because Athanasius—both in his first *Apology* || and in his *Letter to the Solitaries* *, which were not written until the year 357 or the year following—seems to speak honorably of Marcellus as a Catholic Bishop. But a contemporary writer, Saint Basil †, is a witness that they were not mistaken about the facts themselves, for he often clearly condemns Marcellus as a heretic; not to mention Theodoret, Chrysostom, and others. For the rest of what can be said in favor of Marcellus, the reader may consult Richard Montagu’s notes at the beginning of Eusebius’s *Against Marcellus*. 

Marcellus died at a very advanced age, two years before Epiphanius wrote his work *Against Heresies* (that is, in 372 AD). He wrote many volumes of *Various Hypotheses*, says Jerome †, though he does not list them. Among these, the *Work Against Asterius* on the *subjection of Christ the Lord* was particularly prominent; Hilary identifies this as the title of the book, or at least its primary argument. Many and quite ample excerpts from it are preserved in Eusebius’s books *Against Marcellus* and *On Ecclesiastical Theology*, from which the heretical character of the man is clearly perceived. His apologetic letter to Julius of Rome also exists in Epiphanius’s *Against Heresies*, 72.

## THEODORUS, a Thracian by birth, appears to have been born in Heraclea (a city of Thrace on the Black Sea, formerly called Perinthus); hence he was called "the Heracleote." He was eventually promoted to the Bishopric of his native city. Athanasius * mentions him while he was still a Priest, but Theodoret † is the first to mention him as Bishop of Heraclea, numbering him among those who, around the year 334, persuaded Constantine to convoke the Council of Caesarea in Palestine to judge the case of Athanasius. Finally, having been summoned many times to the Council of Sardica and not appearing, he was stripped of his Bishopric. Indeed, he was held in great name among his own people and among the "front-line leaders" <note>original: "primipilos," a Roman military term for a lead centurion, used here to mean a chief proponent.</note> of the Arian sect. Wherefore, when Philostorgius places him among those who asserted the *consubstantial* <note>original: "$\tau\grave{o}$ $\acute{o}\mu o o\acute{\upsilon}\sigma\iota o\nu$" (the homoousion); the orthodox belief that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.</note>, it seems that *of similar substance* <note>original: "$\acute{o}\mu o\iota o\acute{\upsilon}\sigma\iota o\nu$" (homoiousion); the belief that the Son is of similar, but not identical, substance.</note> ought rather to be read. For Theodorus was of this opinion, as were his associates (whom Philostorgius joins with him in the same place): George of Laodicea, Eustathius of Sebaste, Basil of Ancyra, etc., all of whom it is certain were Homoiousians, or Semi-Arians. Theodorus seems to have died around the year 358, having Hypatian as his successor. According to the testimony of Theodoret ||, he was *exceptionally renowned* <note>original: "$\delta\iota\alpha\phi\epsilon\rho\acute{o}\nu\tau\omega\varsigma$ $\text{ἐ}\lambda\lambda\acute{o}\gamma\iota\mu o\varsigma$"</note>, a man of singular learning, and one who published—according to Jerome’s testimony \*—in an elegant and clear style, and with a more historical understanding, *Commentaries on Matthew, on John, on the Apostle (that is, the Epistles of St. Paul), and on the Psalter.* Theodoret mentions an *Exposition on the Gospels* †, and Jerome \* obscurely hints at *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians* written by the same man. Of these works, there exists a *Continuous Commentary on the Psalms*, in Greek and Latin, placed before the *Chain of Ancient Fathers on the Psalms*, which B. Corderius published in Greek and Latin at Antwerp, 1643, in three volumes, folio. He adds certain *Fragments* in Corderius's *Chain on Matthew*, and the *Author of the Chain on Luke, Antwerp*, 1630, folio. There was another Theodorus different from ours, or rather Dorotheus (Philostorgius once calls him Theodorus), the Arian Bishop of Heraclea, who around the year 370, by the prerogative of his see, ordained Demophilus as Bishop of Constantinople; he was later transferred to Antioch and expelled from there under Theodosius the Great. Jacques Gothofredus † wrongly confuses him with our Theodorus, for which he was rightly rebuked by the Illustrious Valesius ||.

### JULIUS
A Roman by birth, son of Rusticus, succeeded Pope Mark in the Roman See on the 8th day before the Ides of February <note>February 6th</note> in the year 337. He was a *champion* <note>original: "$\pi\rho\acute{o}\mu\alpha\chi o\varsigma$"</note> and most powerful defender of the Orthodox faith against the Arians. He received Athanasius and others exiled for the faith with hospitality, acquitted them by judicial sentence, and granted them communion; for their sake he convoked a Synod at Rome, sent Elpidius and Philoxenus as legates to the East, and summoned the Bishops of the Eusebian faction to have their cause recognized synodically. In the year 347, the Pseudo-Synod of Sardica <note>The rival council held by Eastern bishops who broke away from the main Council of Sardica.</note> condemned and deposed him as a leader and chief of evils, who first opened the door of communion to the wicked and condemned, and provided an entry for others to dissolve divine laws. Indeed, if the Author of the *Pontifical Book* \* is to be believed, Julius was in exile for ten months after many tribulations; from there he returned with glory after the death of Constantius. This is a plainly foolish and trifling fiction, supported by no pillar of antiquity. For Julius himself ended his life many years before the death of Constantius. He died on the day before the Ides of April <note>April 12th</note> in the year 352. He was buried on the Via Aurelia in the Cemetery of Callipodius.

<margin>
* On Illustrious Men, ch. 2.

* Act 1.
</margin>

*Two of his Letters* exist: one *to the Orientals* in Greek and Latin in Athanasius's *Apology regarding his flight, p. 775, and from there in the Councils, Vol. 2.* The other *to the Alexandrians* in favor of *Athanasius*, which is held in his *2nd Apology, p. 598, and in Socrates [Scholasticus], book 2, ch. 23.* Certain fragments of *Letters or Decrees* are found here and there in Gratian and Ivo of Chartres, collected in *Councils, Vol. 2*, where there are also *two Letters* falsely attributed to him: an *upbraiding letter to the Orientals*, and a *Rescript against the same*. Long ago, a *Letter to Dionysius of Corinth on the Incarnation of the Lord* was also circulated under his name, which Gennadius \* believed was truly his. But Leontius of Byzantium † proves by many arguments that it was not Julius’s letter, but that of the heretic Apollinaris; he also mentions another inserted in the *Acts of the Council of Ephesus* \*, as if written by Julius, and cited under his name by Facundus, Vincent of Lérins, Ephrem (in Photius), and Anastasius, when it was actually a letter of Timothy, a disciple of Apollinaris.

**ACACIUS**, called the "One-Eyed" <note>original: "Μονόφθαλμος" (Monophthalmos)</note> because he was cross-eyed, a disciple of Eusebius of Caesarea, attained the highest praise for eloquence and erudition, not only by his own effort but also from the fame of his Master. In the year 340, upon the death of Eusebius, he succeeded him in the Bishopric of Caesarea. to be similar to the Father by will alone. In the year 359, when the Synod of Seleucia was divided into two parts—the Semi-Arians, who approved the Council having accepted the single word "the similar" <note>original: "τὸ ὅμοιον"</note>, whose leader was George of Laodicea, and the Anti-Nicenes, who contended that the Nicene faith should be utterly abolished and another written—Acacius was the head of this latter party. Having offered a booklet of faith in the Synod, he rejected not only "the dissimilar" <note>original: "τὸ ἀνόμοιον"</note>, but also "of similar substance" <note>original: "ὁμοιούσιον"</note> and "of the same substance" <note>original: "ὁμοούσιον"</note>. ...on his journey to Constantinople, and having drawn to his side both the nobles and Emperor Constantius himself—over whom he had immense influence—he gathered a small council. In this council, he even provided support to those professing <term>the consubstantial</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ὁμοούσιον (to homoousion); the Nicene doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father</note> formula; he saw to it that Basil of Ancyra and others who opposed him were deposed. The versatile and inconstant nature of the man sufficiently shows that this is not far from the truth; for during the reign of Jovian, he presented a document composed by himself and others, signed with his own hand, to the Emperor, in which he eloquently confirmed the Nicene faith and the doctrine of consubstantiality. He departed from this life around the year 366. He was a man, according to Sozomen †, "capable in thinking and even more worthy in speaking" <note>original Greek: ἱκανὸς τὸ νοεῖν, καὶ φράζειν ἀξιώτερος</note>, rich in opinions and elegant in speech; so much so that he left behind many books that are by no means to be looked down upon. **FORTUNATIANUS**, born in Africa, was the Bishop of Aquileia in Italy. He flourished around the year 340. For many years, he fought for the Catholic faith against the <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note> with a constant mind and a sincere heart, especially at the Synod of Sardica. This lasted until the year 354; when Constantius was staying at Arles, Fortunatianus, along with the other Western Bishops, suffered extraordinary violence and heavy insults. Seduced by the tricks of the Arians, he went over to their side; from then on, he not only condemned Athanasius but also promoted the Arian cause with all his might. What is even more detestable is that in the year 357, he broke the constancy of Liberius, the Bishop of Rome—who was in exile for the faith at that time—and by his advice and warnings, he brought it about that Liberius subscribed to the condemnation of Athanasius and the Arian formulas. He composed *Commentaries* on the Gospels arranged by headings, which Jerome * says were written in a "brief and rustic style" <note>original: brevi & ruftico fermone</note>. These are <term>lost today</term> <note>original: NE (Non Extant)</note>.

**TRIPHYLLIUS**, a man most refined in all liberal learning, stayed for a long time in the city of Berytus <note>Beirut</note>, which was a very famous school of Civil Law, for the study of Roman laws. Afterward, in sacred matters, he had the great Spyridon, Bishop of Trimithus in Cyprus, as his teacher; finally, he was appointed Bishop of Ledra in Cyprus. He flourished around the year 340 and held a place in the Synod of Sardica in the year 347, as is clear from the signatures of that Synod. He was the most eloquent of all in his age, a study upon which he bestowed excessive care, for which he was sharply corrected by his teacher Spyridon. For when, in a solemn assembly of Cypriot bishops, Triphyllius was asked to deliver a sermon to the people and bring forward that saying of the Savior, "Take up your bed and walk" <note>original Greek: Ἄρον σοῦ τὸ κράββατον καὶ περιπάτει</note>, he substituted "couch" <note>original: σκίμποδα</note> in place of "bed" <note>original: κράββατον</note>, as if the word were less elegant. Stirred by this, Spyridon said, "Are you more excellent than He who said 'bed,' that you are ashamed to use His words?" With this said, in the sight of the people, Spyridon leaped from his priestly throne, teaching the man—who was carrying himself too insolently because of his eloquence—to be modest by this means. He composed many things. Jerome * testifies that he read his Commentaries on the Song of Songs. He also wrote an iambic poem on the life and miracles of his teacher Spyridon, which should be sought out as they are "exceedingly useful," says Suidas †. These are <term>lost</term> <note>original: NE</note>.

# The Arian Century.

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

<margin>
4th CENTURY. From the Year 300.
</margin>
...spent his time. He flourished especially after the year 341, when he refused the see of Alexandria offered to him (from which the Synod of Antioch had ejected Athanasius), and instead accepted Emesa in Phoenicia. However, when the people of Emesa raised a riot at his ordination, accusing him of being a student of mathematical and magical arts <note>In the 4th century, "mathematics" was often associated with astrology and the occult</note>, he moved to Laodicea. There he lived with Bishop George, whom he held as one of his few close friends. Later he returned to Emesa. He died and was buried in Antioch around the year 360. He was particularly favored by Emperor Constantius, who took Eusebius along on his journeys whenever he waged war against the Persians. Indeed, if we believe George of Laodicea, he performed not a few miracles. He was accused of a crime, as if he held the same views as Sabellius <note>Sabellianism taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of one person, rather than three distinct persons</note>, under the pressure of the envy of those who are accustomed to be burned by the virtues of others, as Sozomen rightly notes. In the eyes of Jerome <margin>* Chronicle, year 348.</margin> * he is heard of as a "standard-bearer of the Arian faction," a stain Jerome commonly burns into Eusebius of Caesarea elsewhere more than once. It is probable that our Eusebius was somewhat more inclined toward the opinion of the semi-Arians <note>A middle-ground group who believed the Son was of "similar substance" (homoiousios) to the Father, rather than "same substance" (homoousios)</note>. Jerome says <margin>† On Illustrious Men, ch. 91.</margin> † that he was of an elegant and rhetorical talent, who composed innumerable books received with much applause from the people; following history more closely, he was most studiously read by those who wished to practice public speaking. Among these, Jerome lists as the principal ones: *Against the Jews*, *To the Novatians*, *Ten Books of Hypotheses on the Epistle to the Galatians*, and *Brief Homilies on the Gospels, but very many*. Theodoret has a quite long excerpt from some of his writings in Dialogue III, p. 172, in which Eusebius's opinion regarding the Son of God is clearly found to be less than orthodox. There exist under his name *Short Homilies* on the Gospels for the whole year, and *more than fifty other Homilies* on various subjects; but by common consent they are denied to our Eusebius. Of these, some are rightly attributed to Eucherius of Lyon, others to Bruno of Asti, and other more recent authors—or at least they are patched together from their writings. Whoever desires to know the various opinions of different people on these Homilies should consult Edmund Albertin, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book 2, p. 877. Albertin offers his own opinion in these words: "I would think," he says, "that these Homilies are rhapsodies by various authors; some could be by Eucherius, some by Faustus, some by Caesarius and Maximus (either of Riez or Turin), and some even by others unknown to us. For the diversity of style evidently indicates many authors." <margin>Paris 1575. Antwerp 1602. 8º.</margin> Whether the *Thirteen Homilies* that Jacques Sirmond published in Latin under the name of Eusebius Pamphilus <note>Eusebius of Caesarea</note> (Paris, 1643) belong to this Eusebius of Emesa, <margin>Paris 1643. 8º.</margin> we leave to the learned to investigate. Certainly, Sirmond had no other basis for his opinion except the title of the manuscript codex, into which the name of Eusebius Pamphilus—better known to Latin writers—might have crept. How weak the authority of manuscript codices is, however, is evident from the fact that the short Homilies (which everyone recognizes as spurious) have the name of Eusebius of Caesarea prefixed to them in certain codices.

Of our Eusebius’s works, Ebed-Jesu <note>A 13th-century East Syrian writer and bibliographer</note> writes that there still exist among the Chaldeans: <term>A Book Against the Jews</term>, <term>Questions on the Old Law</term>, and <term>An Oration on St. Stephen</term>.

---

**GEORGE**, <margin>340.</margin> an Alexandrian by birth, nourished in philosophical disciplines, was first a Priest at Alexandria. Removed from his rank by Saint Alexander because of his misconduct <note>original: "nepotatum," suggesting a life of luxury or profligacy</note>, he turned completely to the Arians, and was substituted by them in the see of Laodicea after the death of Theodotus. He was the "most wicked" <term>πονηρότατος</term> <note>original Greek: ponerotatos</note> of all heretics, as Athanasius calls him <margin>* Apology 2.</margin> *. From then on, he took part in the Synods against Athanasius at Tyre in the year 335 and at Antioch in 341. Later, summoned to the Council of Sardica in the year 347, and not appearing out of fear, he was condemned by the common consent of all the Fathers. In the year 358, he sent a letter (found in Sozomen, Book 4, ch. 13) urging the bishops gathered at Ancyra for the dedication of the basilica built by Basil of Ancyra to meet in synod and condemn Bishop Eudoxius of Constantinople and Aetius, who were then stirring up new troubles. In the following year, at the Synod of Seleucia, he stood on the side of the Homoiousians <note>those who believed the Son is of "similar substance" to the Father</note>; although later, being a man of a versatile and inconstant character, he turned toward the Anomoeans <note>an extreme Arian sect believing the Son is "unlike" the Father</note>. This perhaps was the reason Philostorgius <margin>* Book 8, ch. 17.</margin> * [placed] George among the primary <term>homoiousians</term> <note>those of "similar substance"; the text notes this reading is likely a correction</note> [it seems this should be the reading]

He wrote a book on the *Life of Eusebius of Emesa*, an excerpt of which is found in Socrates, Book 2, Chapter 9 (compare also Book 1, Chapter 24), and another work against the Manichaeans <note>A dualist sect that believed in two opposing powers of Good and Evil</note>, which is mentioned by Theodoret * and Photius †. **NE.** <note>The initials NE. likely refer to a specific editor or source used by the author.</note>

<margin>340 AD.</margin>
**HELIODORUS**, a Presbyter, flourished around the year 340. He wrote against the Manichaeans, as it seems, a book titled *On the Nature of Initial Things*, in which he demonstrated that there is only one Creator of the world and all things, a single principle of reality, and that nothing is co-eternal with God that could create evil. **NE.**

<margin>
340 AD.
* *Letter to Principia*, page 119.
† *On Writers*, Chapter 7.
</margin>
**PACHOMIUS**, born in the Thebaid in Egypt, had parents who were followers of Gentile <note>Pagan</note> superstitions. In the twentieth year of his age—if we trust his *Life* as described by Simeon Metaphrastes <note>A 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer</note> from older Records, which themselves exist today in the version by Dionysius Exiguus <note>A 6th-century monk best known for inventing the AD/BC dating system</note> in Surius's *Lives of the Saints* for May 14th—while he was being led among other recruits to perform military service under Constantine the Great, he observed that the soldiers with whom he was sailing, who were suffering from a lack of all supplies, were relieved by the incredible kindness of the inhabitants at a certain town in the Thebaid. He marveled at such great benevolence toward strangers; and when he understood that they were Christians, he began to inquire into their faith and customs. To summarize briefly, he embraced the Christian religion, and having been dipped in the saving font <note>Baptized</note>, he withdrew to Tabbenesis, a village in the Thebaid. There he became the founder and institutor of all the Tabbenesian monks. From this source, indeed, about seven thousand monks came forth; in fact, the single monastery of Pachomius contained one thousand four hundred men. He flourished under Constantine and his sons, especially around the year 340. He was held in high regard by Athanasius, who is said to have visited him, and Jerome * testifies that Athanasius taught Pachomius’s way of life to the noble matron Marcella while he was staying in Rome. He died on the day before the Ides of May <note>May 14th</note> in the year 350, or as others say, 360. He wrote *Five Letters* to his fellow superiors, in which (says Gennadius †, who lists them one by one) he included an *Alphabet Concealed with Mystic Sacraments*, which as it were exceeds the understanding of human custom. There remains in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, Chapter 38, a *Rule of the Monks*, which an Angel is said to have delivered to Pachomius inscribed on a bronze tablet. Indeed, the same *Rule* exists in a much fuller version, written first in Egyptian <note>Coptic</note>, as they claim, then translated into Greek, and finally rendered into Latin by Jerome at the request of the monk Silvanus; this is found at the end of the works of Cassian and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 4, page 86. However, I fear these claims are made without proof. It is certainly strange that Jerome, if he had translated this, did not include Pachomius among his *Ecclesiastical Writers*. I would rather believe that the short *Rule* which Palladius presents was expanded and enriched by Pachomius's successors; at the very least, it must be said that the Palladian version is an abridgment of the other. Also under Pachomius's name, Gerard Vossius published in Latin some *Spiritual Admonitions*—brief indeed, but truly golden—in the *Appendix to the works of Gregory Thaumaturgus*, Mainz, 1606, in quarto. They are also held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 4.

<margin>344 AD.</margin>
**THEODORE**, born of a noble family, attained the dignity of a Presbyter. He was a companion and steward to Pachomius, and his successor in the government of the monastery. He flourished in the year 344. More is recorded about him in the *Life of Pachomius*; let the reader curious about these matters go there, for they are not of such importance that we should detain the reader with them any longer. He wrote *Three Exhortatory Letters* to the monasteries, composed in the language of the Holy Scriptures. **NE.** *Eleven Homilies* of a certain monk named Theodore existed in Greek in the possession of Holstenius. Whether they belong to our Theodore, or rather to a certain younger Theodore, is not sufficiently clear.

* *On Writers*, Chapter 9.
</margin>

He composed a book seasoned with divine salt, constructed with the tools of all monastic discipline, and to put it simply, in which almost the entire Old and New Testament is found explained in concise dissertations, according to the needs of monks at least. This book he [left] to the brothers <note>original: "fratribus"</note> as a testament near the day of his death...

**VITELLIUS**, an African by birth and a member of the <term>Donatist</term> <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa that argued only those who had remained "pure" during Roman persecutions could administer valid sacraments</note> sect. I believe no one among the ancient writers mentions him except for Gennadius alone. He flourished under the emperor Constans (who began his reign in 337 and died in 350); thus it is reasonable to believe Vitellius was prominent around the year 344. He wrote *On Why the Servants of God are Hated by the World*, in which he attacked the Catholics under the name of "persecutors." He also wrote *Against the Pagans* and *Against the Catholics*, whom he labeled as <term>traditores</term> <note>literally "handers-over"; a derogatory term for those who surrendered sacred scriptures to Roman authorities during times of persecution</note> of the Holy Scriptures. He also wrote many things pertaining to Church discipline. **NE.**

344 AD.
† Optatus, Book 2, ch. 5.
* Optatus, Book 2, ch. 5.
</margin>
**MACROBIUS**, apparently of African origin and holding the rank of Priest. At first he was a Catholic, but later he defected to the Donatists. Optatus mentions him frequently † and lists him among the Donatist bishops who lived in Rome. It should be known that the Donatists, seeking greater glory for their sect, sent bishops from their own party to hold a seat in the city of Rome. However, having been expelled from the city along with the few followers they had, they were forced to hold their small assemblies in the surrounding mountains; for this reason they were called *Montenses* (Mountaineers), *Rutupiani*, and *Campitæ* (Field-dwellers). I am of the opinion that Macrobius flourished around the year 344—at least while he was still a Priest in the Catholic Church—not only because Gennadius places him immediately after Vitellius the African, but also because the succession of Donatist bishops who sat in Rome, according to Optatus *, suggests this, as Macrobius is placed in the fourth position. While still a Catholic, he wrote a book addressed to Confessors and Virgins regarding moral but highly necessary doctrine, perfectly suited for guarding chastity. After becoming a Donatist, he also wrote a *Letter to the People of Carthage* regarding the passion of the Donatists Maximian and Isaac; a large fragment of this survives in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume 4 (Paris, 1685), page 119.

344 AD.
* Epiphanius, *Heresies* 71.
* Loc. cit. (In the place cited).
</margin>
**PHOTINUS** originated from Galatia Minor, though some, following Epiphanius *, wish to claim he originated from Sirmium, a town in lower Pannonia <note>modern-day Serbia</note>. Janus Cornarius, the translator of Epiphanius, interprets it this way, but Epiphanius himself wrote: "He set out from Sirmium," which should be rendered as, *“He broke forth from Sirmium, or advanced from there, to declare war against the truth.”* He was a disciple of Marcellus, the Bishop of Ancyra, and served as a deacon under him; it was from him that he drank in the seeds of his heretical character. For a time he remained a Catholic and was admitted to the Bishopric of the Church of Sirmium with great consensus from everyone. It is uncertain at what time he obtained that seat, or in what year he began to sow his weeds. However, if Epiphanius * is to be believed, this happened while Constantine was still alive. We need not spend much effort showing that the most holy father Epiphanius was mistaken in this matter, as almost all writers of Ecclesiastical History teach the opposite, and the facts themselves cry out. At first, Photinus conducted his business secretly and in private, turning over the condemned dogmas of Sabellius and Paul of Samosata in his mind. But later, he exposed his heresy openly before the eyes of all, teaching that Christ was a <term>mere man</term> <note>original Greek: "psilon anthrōpon"</note> and had His beginning from Mary only after the Holy Spirit came upon her. Because of this, he was called a "Little-Man-ist" <note>original: "Homuncionista"</note> by Vigilius of Thapsus, and his followers were called "Little-Man-ists" by Augustine. He began to teach these things publicly under the reign of Constantius, at a time when the Arians were doing everything according to their whim. Finally, as I was about to send this to the press, I came across a dissertation on *Photinus* by the most distinguished man Matthæus Larroquanus (in which he argues the case against Petavius with great learning), who dates the epoch of the Photinian heresy to the year 346. Certainly, the fact that Photinus was detected before the year 344 is indicated by the "revelation" <note>original Greek: "phanerōsin"</note> of that formula established in the Synod of Antioch...

This was also done in the Synod of Sardica in the year 347, and in the one held at Milan in the year 348. In the year 350, he was deposed in the Catholic Council of Sirmium, but he was kept in his position by the people through force. Finally, he was deposed in the second Council of Sirmium in the year 351, when he challenged the bishops to a debate. This took place on a set day in the presence of the Emperor and many of the Senatorial order, with notaries recording everything. Basil of Ancyra took up the role of debating against Photinus. The contest was fought with great effort on both sides, but Photinus was defeated and punished with exile. Afterward, however, he seems to have recovered his church, but was later driven out again by the Emperor Valentinian and sent into exile; having returned from there, he died in Galatia in the year 377. His heresy was not long-lasting, as it was already dissipated by the time of Epiphanius; nor did even small remnants of it remain by the time of Theodoret *, and not even his name was known. It is truly to be lamented that in this unhappy century, ill-fated men recalled this most pestilential heresy from the abyss <note>original: "ab Orco"; Orcus was a Roman name for the underworld or Hell</note>. Photinus was learned in both Greek and Latin; he was very powerful in the strength of his mind, the abundance of his learning, and a certain natural eloquence most suited for persuasion. Because of this, he drew many over to his opinion, a fact noted by Epiphanius \*, Sozomen †, and Vincent of Lérins ||. He wrote several volumes in both languages, including *Against All Heresies* <note>original: "adversùs omnes Hæreses"</note>, in which he tried to show all other heresies were false except his own; likewise *Against the Pagans* <note>original: "Contra Gentes"</note>; and a work *To Valentinian* <note>original: "ad Valentinianum"</note>, seemingly addressed to the Emperor.

### BASIL
**BASIL**, born in Ancyra, was first the Bishop of the Fortress of Mechea—a fact which, as far as I know, only Jerome mentions \*. Later, he was the successor to Marcellus <note>Marcellus of Ancyra, who was deposed for his controversial views on the Trinity</note> in the see of Ancyra after the Synod of Constantinople stripped Marcellus of his bishopric in the year 336. There is little mention of him before the year 347, when the Fathers at the Council of Sardica deposed him along with others. But he, relying on imperial favor and familiarity, maintained his position. Indeed, he was uniquely dear to the Emperor Constantius, who greatly favored the <term>Semi-Arians</term> <note>A group that sought a middle ground in the Arian controversy, using the term "homoiousios" (of similar substance) rather than the Nicene "homoousios" (of the same substance)</note>. Basil joined himself to these men and held the leadership of that party. In the year 351, he held a famous debate with Photinus in the Council of Sirmium before the Emperor, in which the victory remained with him. In the year 358, he took part in the Synod of Ancyra; after Eudoxius of Constantinople was deposed there, Basil himself was sent as an envoy to the Emperor in the name of the Synod, along with Eustathius of Sebaste and Eleusius of Cyzicus, to obtain the ratification of the synodic decree. In the year 359, in the Council of Seleucia, he prevailed against Acacius <note>Acacius of Caesarea, leader of the "Homoean" Arians who argued the Son was simply "like" the Father</note> and his followers, ensuring they were condemned by the Synod. But at the beginning of the following year, Acacius paid him back in kind and deposed him in the Synod of Constantinople, and he was soon banished to Illyricum by the Emperor’s command. The charges against him were various: that he had exercised tyranny over others; that he had punished some with beatings, others with chains, and others with exile; that he had manufactured slanders against many; that he had disturbed many churches; that he had been convicted of perjury and had promoted a man of shameful life <note>original: "homuncionem"; literally "a little man" or "fellow," used here dismissively</note> to Baptism and the office of the Diaconate; and that he was accustomed to making illicit pacts at the sacred table. Regarding these and other things objectified against him, one should consult Socrates \*, and especially Sozomen †. During the reign of Jovian, he and the other Semi-Arians presented a petition of prayers to the Emperor. However, in the signatures of the profession of Faith presented to Jovian, a man named Athanasius is called the Bishop of Ancyra—a most certain proof that Basil had not been restored to his see at that time. Notwithstanding the slanders of the Acacians, Theodoret \* praises the man for the exceptional holiness of his life; Sozomen † also describes him as very famous for his eloquence and erudition. He wrote several things, especially *Against Marcellus* and the *Book on Virginity*.

### SERAPION
**SERAPION**, an Egyptian by birth and an <term>Ἀσκητὴς</term> <note>original: "Asketes"; a practitioner of religious self-denial or a monk</note> by his way of life, lived for a long time among those who practiced a stricter discipline in the deserts of the Thebaid. He was the leader of many monks there, and was finally made Bishop of Thmuis, a significant city near Mendes, by Saint Athanasius. He was very dear to Blessed Anthony and joined to Athanasius by the closest bond of friendship. Indeed, Athanasius was very familiar with Serapion...

...was on the most intimate terms with him, entrusting him with the secrets of his faith, submitting his own writings to his judgment to be either expanded or corrected, and consulting him by frequent letters on the most momentous affairs, as three letters—or rather short treatises—addressed to him testify today. In the year 357, among the Fathers of the Council of Sardica <note>The Council of Sardica (c. 343 AD) was a significant gathering of bishops intended to resolve the Arian controversy and the status of Athanasius</note>, he acquitted Athanasius by his vote. Our Serapion of Thmuis <note>Thmuis was an ancient city in Lower Egypt</note> was the leader of these men, himself renowned for his confession of faith under Constantius. He died around the year 358. "A man most divine in his life, and powerful in speech," says Sozomen <note>original: "’Ανηρ εις τὰ μάλιστα τῷ βίῳ θεσπέσιος, καὶ λέγειν δεινὸς"</note>. He was famous for such great eloquence that he earned the nickname <term>Scholasticus</term> <note>A title given to those distinguished for their learning and rhetorical skill</note> because of the elegance of his intellect. Socrates † mentions a golden saying of his from Evagrius: "A mind filled with a draught of spiritual knowledge is fully purified; likewise, parts of the soul inflamed by anger are healed by charity; and base desires flowing into the mind are restrained by abstinence." <note>original Greek: "πεπωκὼς πνευματικὴν γνῶσιν τελείως καθαίρεται, ἀγαπη δὲ τὰ φλεγμαίνοντα μόρια τοῦ θυμοῦ θεραπεύει, νῆψις δὲ επιθυμίας επιρρεούσας ἵστησιν εγκράτεια"</note> He wrote useful letters to various people, a *Treatise on the Titles of the Psalms*, and an excellent *Book against the Manichaeans* <note>The Manichaeans followed Mani, teaching a dualistic universe of Light and Darkness</note>. Of these, only the *Book against the Manichaeans* survives, which Henry Canisius first published from the version by Francisco Torres in *Ancient Lessons*, Volume 5, page 1, and which was subsequently moved into the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, Volume 4, page 160.

MAGNES, a very obscure writer, lived (if Torres and Scribonius correctly place his age) around the year 350. He wrote five books in Greek *Against Theosthenes, who slanders the Gospels*. Manuscripts exist in some places, as Francisco Torres saw them and cites certain passages from them in his *Apology for the Letters of the Popes*. Coccius also has some excerpts, borrowed from Torres, though he conceals this fact. "But these are mere trappings for the common people," says the illustrious Albertinus †. "For who among the ancients—or even the moderns for nine or ten centuries—would have remembered this Magnes even by name? He is a completely fictitious author, or at least some recent and minor Greek writer <note>original: "Græculus"</note> whose certainty rests entirely with Torres, a man of small judgment and highly suspect faith. And yet our adversaries dare to bring forward such refuse as monuments of the ancients without any shame. By the faith of God and men! Surely it is better <term>to suspend judgment</term> <note>original: "ἐπέχειν"</note> concerning such writings until the authors themselves come forth into public view so that a judgment may be made about them."

CYRIL, a Deacon under Bishop Macarius of Jerusalem, was ordained a Priest by Maximus and also performed the duty of <term>Catechist</term> <note>A teacher who instructs those preparing for baptism</note>; he delivered his *Catechetical Lectures* in the same Church around the year 367 <note>The text notes this was seventy years after the rise of Mani, who began spreading his heresy in 277 AD</note>, as he himself teaches us †. After the death of Maximus around the year 350, he succeeded to the Chair of Jerusalem, having been ordained by Acacius of Caesarea by right of Metropolitan authority; indeed, as it pleases Jerome * and others †, he obtained this dignity by the help of the Arians, being an Arian himself. But Theodoret || speaks quite differently, calling him a most fierce champion of Apostolic doctrine when discussing his promotion to this see. Furthermore, long before Theodoret, the Fathers † of the Second Ecumenical Council <note>The Council of Constantinople, 381 AD</note>—at which Cyril himself was present—are witnesses more worthy of faith in this matter than a hundred Jeromes; they explicitly affirm that this most Reverend and Religious Cyril, as they call him, was canonically ordained long ago by the Bishops of the province, and that he had many struggles against the Arians in various places. Truly, it is surprising how much Ecclesiastical writers disagree in weaving the catalog of the Bishops of Jerusalem for this age, as will be clear to the eye from this diagram.

I do not have time now to dwell on explaining these various small indices. It must only be observed, as Epiphanius notes, that another Cyril, different from ours, presided over the Church of Jerusalem at roughly the same time; this could have provided an occasion for the errors and material for the slanders of other historians. In the year 351, with the wondrous sign of the cross shining splendidly in the sky at Jerusalem, Cyril informed the Emperor Constantius through a letter (which he calls *the first fruits of writings seen from Jerusalem* <note>original: "ὁράτας ἐξ Ἱεροσολύμων γραμμάτων ἀπαρχάς"</note>). Afterward, he had a great dispute with Acacius of Caesarea <note>Acacius was a leader of the Arian faction and sought to maintain the superiority of his see over Jerusalem</note> regarding metropolitan rights, which Cyril wished to assert for his own church as an Apostolic See, though custom and the seventh Canon of the Council of Nicaea itself <note>The 7th Canon of Nicaea (325 AD) granted Jerusalem an honorary priority but kept it under the jurisdiction of the Metropolitan of Caesarea</note> protested against it. Frequently summoned to trial for this reason, he did not appear; consequently, he was deposed by Acacius and a Palestinian Synod, under the pretext of another crime—that during a raging famine, he had sold the treasures of the Church for the use of the poor, and among these a sacred robe woven with gold threads, donated to this church by Constantine the Great, which was later found to have been worn by a certain stage actress. From the unjust sentence of Acacius, Cyril appealed to a higher court, with the support of Emperor Constantius himself; he was the first and only one of all who filed such an appeal contrary to the custom of Ecclesiastical Canon, if we believe Socrates †; yet students of Ecclesiastical History know that Socrates is mistaken in this matter.

<margin>
† Book 2, chapter 40; Book 3, chapter 20.
</margin>

Expelled from Jerusalem, he lived in Tarsus with Bishop Sylvanus, and in his church, he delivered frequent sermons to the people, who were greatly delighted by Cyril's preaching, despite Acacius protesting in vain by letter. In the year 359, at the Synod of Seleucia <note>A regional council that attempted to find a compromise between the Arian and Nicene factions</note>, he was superior to Acacius; but in a small council held shortly after in Constantinople, after the prior slanders were polished up and new ones added, Acacius deposed him again. Restored to his see under Julian <note>Emperor Julian the Apostate, who initially recalled exiled bishops to sow discord among Christians</note>, he mocked the Jews who were encouraged by imperial favor to rebuild the Temple of Jerusalem from its ruins and were working on it with great effort; calling to mind both the prophecy of Daniel and the oracle of the Savior, he said it would shortly come to pass that not one stone would remain upon another in that temple: which indeed happened, as we have shown at length elsewhere * <note>This refers to the 363 AD attempt to rebuild the Temple, which was reportedly stopped by fire and earthquakes</note>.

<margin>
* In the Life of Cyril.
</margin>

Finally, under Theodosius, after his adversaries were put to flight, he held his see unshaken thereafter. In the year 381, he was numbered among the *leaders* or *exarchs* <note>original: "ἡγεμόνας" or "ἐξάρχους"</note> of the Second General Council [the First Council of Constantinople], having been fully restored by that venerable council and adorned with a most honorable eulogy. Having finished his mortal life, he peacefully fell asleep in the Lord in the year 386. That he by no means acceded to the opinion of the Arians is proven by his writings which survive today; in these, he condemns the dogmas of the Arian heresy as an apostasy from the true faith and a precursor of the coming Antichrist: and in his *Letter to the Emperor Constantius* (which he wrote while already a bishop, around the time he was most accused of compliance toward the Arians), he professes that he venerates the *holy and consubstantial Trinity* <note>original: "ἁγίαν καὶ ὁμοούσion τριάδα"</note>.

<margin>
See Catechesis 11, page 234; Catechesis 15, page 369.
† Sacred Criticism, book 3, chapter 11.
</margin>

Hence one may wonder at the clearly perverse mind of Rivet † <note>André Rivet (1572–1651) was a French Protestant theologian often critical of the Church Fathers</note>, who concludes from this very letter either that it is not by Cyril, or that Cyril was an Arian heretic.

->Extant Writings.<-

<margin>* Book 4, chapter 5.</margin>
**A** Letter to the Emperor Constantius, which is mentioned by Sozomenus *.
Eighteen Catechetical Lectures to the <term>Candidates for Baptism</term> <note>Latin: *Competentes*; those in the final stage of preparation for baptism</note>, in which he explains the principal heads of the Christian faith.
Five <term>Mystagogical Catecheses</term> <note>Instructions on the "mysteries" or sacraments, given to the newly baptized</note> to the recently baptized; in which he treats the two Sacraments of the Church.

<margin>
* On Illustrious Men, chapter 112.
† Dialogue 2, page 106.
|| On Images, Oration 3, page 783.
* Cited above, chapter 10.
</margin>
Those who stir up a dispute over whether these Catecheses are genuine act in vain; for Jerome *, Theodoret †, and John of Damascus ||—not to mention others now—vindicate them for our Cyril. The objections raised by Rivetus <note>André Rivet, a French Protestant theologian known for his critical examination of patristic texts</note> and others do not deserve a response. By way of example, Rivetus objects * that they are sewn together like <term>Centos</term> <note>A poem or work made up of quotations from other authors; a patchwork</note> from various places in the Scriptures, and are prolix to the point of nausea in matters that are not so necessary. Even if this were entirely true (which it is not), those Catecheses were <note>original: "σχεδιασθεῖσαι"</note> *extemporaneous*, as the title itself conveys: that is, delivered offhand, composed with no study, polished with no art, and professedly adapted to the capacity of the listeners; they were held in his youth, when mature age and seasoned judgment were still lacking. Rivetus objects again that Cyril affirms regarding the wood of the cross: <note>original: "μέχρι σήμερον παρ' ἡμῖν φαίνεται"</note> *it appears among us even to this day*, and some say this was only twenty or a little more years after the discovery of the Cross itself, whereas that phrase "until today" is not usually used for recent things, but for things seen in the same state for many years through a long series of time. But first, that phrase in Cyril's usage does not usually designate such a long span of time. 

<margin>Page 441.</margin>
Thus in Catechesis 17, he says: *We see the Princes of this Age being ruled and instructed by Churchmen <note>original: "μέχρι σήμερον"</note> until today;* when no more than thirty-five years had passed since the conversion of Constantine the Great itself. Therefore, by this phrase, he understands nothing other than "at this time, even until today," as he speaks in the words immediately preceding. Secondly, Cyril in that passage does not have even a word about the discovery of the Cross, but says only this: that the Wood of the Cross still exists today, and together with many other things which he brings forward there, it is a witness—namely, a noble monument of the Lord's death and resurrection. 

<margin>See Catechesis 13, page 322; Catechesis 14, page 349.</margin>
Elsewhere he uses the same phrase in exactly the same argument more than once. I pass over the rest of Rivetus’s petty exceptions, which are hardly worth an empty nutshell.

His Works were published in Latin at Paris, 1589. The Catecheses in Greek at Paris, 1564, 8vo; in Greek and Latin at Cologne, 1564. Joannes Prevotius edited the Complete Works in Greek and Latin at Paris, 1608, 4to; then Dionysius Petavius in the same place, 1622, folio; as well as in the same place in folio with Synesius, 1631.

A Letter to Augustine regarding the Miracles of Jerome. Found in Latin among the Works of Augustine and Jerome.

**L**IBERIUS, a Roman by birth, son of Augustus, was elected Roman Pontiff on the 11th of the Calends of June in the year 352, after the death of Julius. Soon, having written letters, the Oriental bishops tried greatly to draw him to their side. But he, having assembled a Synod at Rome, wrote back to the Orientals that he could not agree with them; and for a long time indeed, he constantly refused to abandon the cause of Athanasius. In the year 355, having been summoned to Milan, he manfully resisted Constantius; who, when after a long conversation held with him, could not bend the man's mind by prayer or price, by any reasons or by any promises or threats,

...and overcome by the persistence of Demophilus and Fortunatianus, in a painful example of human weakness he finally yields, condemns Athanasius, and subscribes to the formula of the <term>Homoiousians</term> <note>A group that held the Son was of a "similar substance" (homoiousios) to the Father, rather than the orthodox "same substance" (homoousios)</note> which they had recently established at Sirmium in the year 358. He testified that he had done this in letters sent to the Easterners, and others to Ursacius and Valens. Having returned to Rome, he entered the city like a Conqueror, received with great joy by the Roman People, while Felix <note>Felix II, who had been installed as Pope while Liberius was in exile</note> was expelled from the City by either the Senate or the common people. He lived nine years after his return and met his final day on the 8th day before the Calends of October <note>September 24, 366</note>; he was buried on the Via Salaria in the Cemetery of Priscilla. I do not deny that he repented of his subscription at Sirmium; provided it is true, as Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a major Catholic historian of the Counter-Reformation</note> takes for granted—though supported by no evidence from antiquity—that Liberius sent that very famous *Confession of Faith* which exists today to Athanasius after his fall at Sirmium.

Of Liberius’s writings, there remain: a *Dialogue with Constantius* held at Milan, taken, it seems, from the very acts of the <term>Consistory</term> <note>The Emperor's high court</note>, found in Theodoret, book 2, chapter 16; and twelve *Letters* taken from the Fragments of Hilary, the books of Lucifer of Cagliari, and elsewhere, in the *Concilia*, Volume II, column 743. Of these, the last is a fragment of a *Letter or profession of faith*, which is also found in Athanasius, Volume I, page 396. However, the eighth letter, which is taken from Hilary’s Fragments and begins thus, *Striving for the peace and concord of the Churches*, etc., is either entirely forged or—as I rather think—it was pushed out of its place and replaced a more <term>Catholic</term> <note>In this context, meaning "orthodox" or Nicene</note> one in Hilary's work; this is very certain to me from a note added to this Letter by Hilary. For he says: *What is not holy in these letters? What does not proceed from the fear of God?* No one of sound mind can think that Hilary said these things about the Letter that appears there now <note>The author suggests the original letter was replaced by a forgery that Hilary would never have praised</note>. Furthermore, there is a *Synodical Letter of Liberius* to the Macedonian Bishops (in Greek and Latin) in Socrates, book 4, chapter 12, and in the *Concilia*, Volume II, page 760. Two quite long forgeries are attached to his name in Latin: one to all Bishops generally, the other to Athanasius and the Egyptian Bishops.

# HILARY

<margin>
See Hilary, *On the Synods*, col. 319; *Book to Constantius*, col. 306; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 100.
*Book 2, p. 163.
</margin>
HILARY, a Gaul by origin, from Poitiers (a very famous city of <term>Aquitania Secunda</term> <note>A Roman province in southwestern France</note>), was born to honorable parents of no small reputation among their people, and was nurtured in the liberal arts. He seems to have crossed over from Pagan superstition to the Christian religion, and at a slightly more advanced age, sought by public acclaim, he was appointed Bishop of Poitiers around the year 355 according to Baronius’s calculation; however, there is no compelling reason why he could not have been elevated to the see of Poitiers several years before that time. The more sensible <term>Pontificians</term> <note>Catholic scholars</note> do not deny that he was married and lived with his wife even after accepting the Bishopric. A most vigilant pastor in all parts of his duty, fervently animated toward the Catholic faith; he greatly restrained the Arian faction, which was then dominant even in the West, by presenting a petition to Constantius for that purpose. Especially at the Synod of Béziers in the year 356, he strenuously opposed the Arians; from there, the Emperor—deceived by the tricks of Saturninus, Bishop of Arles—drove him into exile, and he was banished to Phrygia. During this four-year exile, now freed from other cares and labors, he applied his mind to producing writings. From this was born his noble *Work on the Trinity* in twelve books; the *Book on the Synods*; and certain *Orations to Constantius*; to say nothing of his *Letters*, of which he wrote many. In the year 359, he was present at the Council of Seleucia, in which he publicly cleared the Gallic churches of the infamous charge of <term>Sabellianism</term> <note>The heresy that God is one person who simply acts in different "modes"</note>. What he personally heard regarding the impious and horrendous dogmas of the <term>Anomoeans</term> <note>Extreme Arians who held that the Son was "unlike" the Father</note>, you may see in his own book *Against Constantius*, which begins: *It is time to speak*, etc., column 292. Having followed the legates of the Synod to Constantinople, and noticing the extreme danger to the faith, he requested from the Emperor in three publicly delivered petitions that he be allowed to debate in the presence of the Arians; which the Heretics most greatly refused. Finally, as a "sower of discord and a disturber of the East" (to use the words of *Sulpicius Severus* <note>A contemporary Christian historian</note>), he was ordered to return to Gaul, though without a formal pardon of his exile. He therefore sought Gaul by slow journeys; and did not return home until the beginning of Julian’s reign, received with the greatest joy by his people of Poitiers. Having returned home, he [checked] the Arian heresy spreading everywhere by holding frequent Synods within Gaul...

<meta>This page continues the biography and bibliography of St. Hilary of Poitiers, a key opponent of Arianism in the 4th century, picking up from the description of his efforts to purge heresy from Gaul.</meta>

# The Arian Century

<margin>4th CENTURY from the Year 300.</margin>
...he nearly exterminated [heresy] by his authority and teaching. It was agreed among all, says Sulpicius Severus, that by the benefit of Hilary alone our Gaul was freed from the crime of Heresy. Around the year 368 or 369, he traveled to Milan so that he might expose and refute Auxentius, the Bishop of that city and the chief leader <note>original: "primipilum", literally the first rank of a Roman legion</note> of the Arians, in the presence of the Emperor Valentinian. But after much dispute, he saw that his effort was in vain; for Auxentius was turning himself into every possible shape <note>i.e., being evasive or slippery</note> and deceiving the Emperor with his cunning and feigned <note>fucatis - literally "painted" or disguised</note> professions of faith. Returning in the same year, Hilary piously returned his soul to God. He was a man long versed not only in Latin but also in Greek writings, from which, especially Origen, he drew many things; he was a close associate of the priest Heliodorus the interpreter <note>original: "ἐξηγητῆ" (exēgētē)</note>, who nevertheless sometimes misled him. From this, as well as from the custom of his nation, his style is turgid and sublime; his diction is excessively grand and laborious. It is elevated, says <margin>† Letter to Paulinus, p. 104.</margin> Jerome †, on "Gallic buskins" <note>A "cothurnus" was a thick-soled boot worn by tragic actors; Jerome means his style is high-flown and tragic</note>; it is sometimes entangled in long sentences. Elsewhere, <margin>* Preface to Book 2 of the Commentary on Galatians.</margin> Jerome calls him the "Rhône of eloquence," after the swiftest of all rivers in Gaul. As Erasmus rightly notes, <margin>† Preface to the Works of St. Hilary.</margin> having borrowed the substance from the Greeks, Hilary added Gallic grandiloquence; he frequently rises to a certain flowery and theatrical sublimity, especially when he encounters passages that shine easily when treated. And it seems very true what that Great Censor of eloquence [Jerome] observes on this matter: that hardly any provincials have successfully rendered the simplicity of the Roman tongue, except for a few who were educated in Rome from childhood. In the cited place, Erasmus shows some specimens of certain words peculiar to Hilary that fall outside the common usage of speech. Among his faults <note>original: "nævos", literally blemishes or moles</note> and singular opinions of the first rank are what he holds regarding the flesh of Christ being incapable of suffering <note>impassible</note> and exempt from pain, concerning the divinity withdrawing from the humanity of the dying Christ, regarding the corporeity of the soul, concerning the world being created all at once and lasting six thousand years, regarding the oath being entirely forbidden to Christians, and several others; concerning which, please consult Erasmus in the cited Preface, Jean Gillot in the Commentary prefixed to the works of St. Hilary, and Scultetus in *The Core of Patristic Theology* near the end.

### GENUINE WRITINGS.

<margin>* Letter to Magnus, Vol. II, p. 328.</margin>
**On** the Trinity, twelve books. Concerning this work, Jerome says: *Hilary, a Confessor of my times and a Bishop, imitated the twelve books of Quintilian in both style and number.* Let Erasmus follow Jerome. He says: <margin>† In the place cited.</margin> *He seems to have striven with all his might that he might declare and exercise in this work whatever he could by his genius, his eloquence, and his knowledge of the Holy Scriptures.*

*Book to Constantius*, which begins: *Your beneficent nature, etc.*

*Book to the same [Constantius]*, beginning: *I am not unaware, etc.*

*Book against Constantius, now deceased*, which indeed, like the preceding two, seems unfinished.

*Book against the Arians and Auxentius*: to which is added the Letter of Auxentius to the Emperor.

*Book on the Synods against the Arians*, written to the Bishops of Gaul and Britain; it is translated for the most part from the Greek [acts of] Synods, but with the freedom preserved to mix in something of his own where it was necessary.

*Fragments from the Historical Work on the Synods of Rimini and Seleucia*, and the things done after the Synods up to the year 366, contained in two books. Nicolas Le Fèvre of Paris first edited these and adorned them with a Preface in 1598.

*Commentaries on the Gospel of St. Matthew*, which others are accustomed to call a "Canon."

<margin>* Letter to Florentius, Vol. I, p. 53.</margin>
*Commentaries on the Psalms*, for the most part excerpted from the Commentaries of Origen, with harmful things pruned away here and there. Jerome reveals that he himself transcribed these Commentaries, as well as the *Book on Synods*, for Hilary with his own hand at Trier.

EUSEBIUS, a Sardinian by birth, first a Reader of the Roman Church, then Bishop of Vercelli among the Insubrians <note>A Celtic people of Northern Italy, in the region of modern Milan</note>. He flourished around the year 354, in which year he was requested by letters from Liberius, the Bishop of Rome, to travel along with his legates to the Emperor Constantius, who was then staying in Gaul. This he did, and by his own pleas to the Emperor, he arranged for the Council of Milan to meet the following year. Although he was acting in place of Liberius, he was admitted to it with difficulty, as the Arians were throwing everything into disorder through force and fraud. Our Eusebius persistently opposed their plans and schemes against Athanasius and the Nicene faith. The main point comes to this: Constantius, becoming rather hostile toward the Catholic bishops, set himself up as Athanasius's accuser and ordered them to condemn the man. When they objected that this was not according to the Church Canon <note>Ecclesiastical law</note>, he replied: "Whatever I wish, let that be considered a canon" <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ἐγὼ βούλομαι, τοῦτο κανὼν νομιζέσθω</note>. "What *I* wish, let that stand for the Canon: for thus the Bishops of Syria are accustomed to endure me when I speak." Finally, threatening sharply because of this and brandishing a sword, he ordered some of them to be led away; and among them, he banished Eusebius to Scythopolis, a city of the Decapolis in Syria, formerly called Bethshan. Joseph, a convert from Judaism to Christianity who had been honored with the title of Count by Constantine the Great, received the exiled Eusebius with great kindness; Epiphanius * testifies that he visited him there. From there he was sent to Cappadocia; indeed, if credit is given to Socrates † and others, he was exiled in the upper Thebaid <note>A region in Southern Egypt</note>. From there, under [the Emperor] Julian, after holding a Synod with Athanasius in Alexandria, he proceeded to Antioch; and when he could not settle the schism that had arisen there because of Lucifer of Cagliari, he departed. Having traveled through the Eastern Provinces, he returned to Italy; he died in the year 371, to be honored not only with the title of Confessor but even of Martyr, for he was supposedly overwhelmed by stones from the Arians—provided that the inscription found on his tomb is genuine, in which was held in acrostic verses: EUSEBIUS BISHOP AND MARTYR, and provided that several writers report the truth; though Baronius † himself acknowledges that all of these are more recent [than the events].

LUCIFER OF CAGLIARI <note>Cagliari is the capital of Sardinia</note>, bishop in Sardinia. He flourished at the same time as *Eusebius of Vercelli* and was his almost inseparable companion in labors, struggles, travels, and exile. He traveled with him to *Constantius* in Gaul, and in the year 354, he acted as the representative <term>vicar|One who acts in the place of another; here, representing the Pope</term> of *Pope Liberius* at the Synod of Milan. Together with Eusebius, he fought manfully against the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being rather than co-eternal with God the Father</note>. Finally, he was banished with Eusebius to Palestine, staying primarily in Eleutheropolis. While there, he published two books in defense of *Athanasius* addressed to *Constantius*. In these, he treated the Emperor harshly and without mercy—with very little respect, and to put it bluntly, in a manner far below the dignity of a great Prince. He soon sent these books to *Constantius* himself to be read. The Emperor ordered *Florentius*, his Master of Offices, to return the manuscript and ask Lucifer by letter if he acknowledged it as his own. Lucifer wrote back, professing that he was indeed the author and was prepared to defend his work even unto death. At the request of *Athanasius*, he also sent his writings to him while Athanasius was hiding in the desert. Athanasius praised the man wonderfully, spoke highly of his writings, and arranged for them to be translated into Greek. Lucifer was exiled not only in Palestine but also in other parts of the East, eventually being deported with his friend *Eusebius* to the Upper Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt</note>. Later, during the reign of the Emperor *Julian*, he sent his deacon to the Synod of Alexandria while he himself headed straight for Antioch. Finding the Catholics there divided among themselves, he ordained *Paulinus* as Bishop of Antioch. This was done prematurely and against the protest of a large part of the Catholic community, who refused to join with Paulinus, causing an even greater and more open <term>schism|A formal split or division within a religious body</term>. *Eusebius of Vercelli*, having left *Alexandria* and arrived in *Antioch*, disapproved of this action. When Lucifer learned of this, he burned with anger and resentment; as he was of a very fiery and vehement nature, he received his faithful and upright friend sharply and spiritedly, and broke off communion with him. He was further agitated because, against his own opinion, the Synod of Alexandria had decreed that repentant bishops who had associated with the Arians should be received back into peace. Returning at last to Sardinia, he not only condemned those defiled by Arian communion but also separated himself from those who had received such men back under satisfaction or penance. From this arose the "Luciferian Schism," though it does not seem to have lasted beyond the end of this century. Lucifer died in the same year as *Eusebius of Vercelli*, namely 371. *Marcellinus* and *Faustinus*, themselves members of the Luciferian sect, extol him with wondrous praise as an "Apostolic man" for his contempt of the world, his devotion to sacred literature, the purity of his life, his constancy in faith, and divine grace. They boast of his four exiles and the divine miracles <note>original: "virtutes"</note> performed through him, writing that he was in exile for ten years. His writing style is no less harsh and unrefined than his character. The aforementioned priests admit he was ignorant of "artful eloquence," yet they boast that he wrote in a prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic manner—which is above all human eloquence—and that he possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit.

HILARY had the island of Sardinia as his homeland. He became a deacon of the Roman Church (where he had received baptism) in the year 354. Together with the priest Eutropius (*whom Jerome calls Pancratius*) and others, he delivered the letters of Pope Liberius to the Emperor Constantius. Upon his arrival, the Arians not only received him with jeers and insults but even stripped off his clothes and lashed his back with whips. Amidst the blows, they taunted him: *“Why did you not resist Liberius, but instead brought his letters?”* The most gentle deacon praised God amidst the crack of the whips. In the following year, because he refused to condemn Athanasius, he was driven into exile. Later, he joined the Luciferian schism; indeed, he contended that the baptism performed by heretics was absolutely null and void, and therefore he insisted that those returning from heresy must be rebaptized. For this reason, he is sarcastically called the *Deucalion of the World* <note>Deucalion was the "Noah" of Greek mythology; Jerome uses this title to mock Hilary's desire to "wash" the entire world over again with his second baptism</note> by Jerome.

He wrote (as scholars have long been convinced) the *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, which are read among the works of Augustine (Volume 4, column 697), and the *Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul*, which are found among the works of Ambrose (Volume 5, page 1). The former work was written in Rome around the year 370, as is clear from Question 44; the latter was written under Pope Damasus before the year 384, as can be seen from the Commentary on the 1st Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3. Regarding the latter work, however, it should be noted that the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews* is not by the same author, but was excerpted from Chrysostom’s commentary on that epistle.

POTAMIUS, a Spaniard by birth and Bishop of the city of Lisbon <note>original: "Odyssiponæ"</note>. Initially a Catholic, he was later seduced by the lures of a government estate <term>fiscal estate|Land or property belonging to the imperial treasury, often given as a bribe</term> and went over to the Arians. In the year 357, he signed the Formula of Ariminum; indeed, he composed that confession himself. Not content with this, and burning with hatred against Hosius (who had once exposed Potamius's impious heresy among the Spaniards), he did not stop until, partly by threats and partly by force, he drew that man—broken by old age and too fond of life—into the same faction as himself. This was a crafty but impious plan, and its end was clearly ill-fated for him—if indeed Faustinus and Marcellinus tell us the truth in the petition they offered to the Emperor Theodosius. For when Potamius was returning to Spain to the government estate (the reward for his betrayed faith), he was seized by a terrible agony in his tongue and died on the road; thus, he did not even happen to see his estate from afar. There exists a *Letter to Athanasius*, which Luc d’Achery first published in the second volume of the *Spicilegium*.

PHÆBADIUS (or Phægadius), a Gaul by birth and, it seems, from the province of Aquitaine; hence Sulpicius Severus calls him “our own.” He was the Bishop of Agen <note>original: "Agenni"</note> in Aquitania Secunda. He flourished in the year 359, in which he attended the Council of Ariminum along with the other bishops of the Western Empire. There he fought for the Nicene truth with the fiercest determination. Even after the others (except for Servatius of Tongeren) had yielded to the deceits, threats, and terrors of the Prefect Taurus, he withstood all the Arian assaults with a brave and unbroken spirit. He declared that he was ready to undergo exile and every punishment, but would never accept the creed devised by the Arians. The matter finally reached the point where he was allowed to add whatever he wished to the proposed formula, which he did. However, Valens, the crafty Bishop of Mursa, eluded that explanation by inserting a clause that Phæbadius did not properly understand. In the year 384, according to the writer Pseudo-Dexter, he presided over the Council of Zaragoza <note>original: "Cæsar-Augustano"</note> held against the Priscillianists. Certainly, eight canons of this Synod (held in 380) survive, in which Phæbadius is found to have signed in the first place. Toward the end and...

His book *Against the Arians* survives (in which he subjects the Formula of Sirmium, sent to the Gauls in the year 358, to scrutiny and refutes it step-by-step <note>original: "κατὰ πόδας" (kata podas)</note>). **AETIUS** had his home in Antioch, a city of Coele-Syria. He was the son of a certain soldier who had served in the governor's office and died shortly thereafter. While still a youth, he practiced the craft of a traveling metalworker for a woman named Ampelis; Theodore of Mopsuestia claims his father had also practiced this trade in the past. It is more certain, however, that Aetius was a goldsmith; but upon his mother's death, being a man of excellent natural talent, he applied his mind to philosophical disciplines. First, he heard Paulinus of Antioch, then Athanasius of Anazarbus <note>Not the famous Athanasius of Alexandria, but an Arian bishop of the same name.</note>, then Antonius, a priest of Tarsus, and after this, Leontius, a priest of Antioch. Finally, in Alexandria, he studied under the most celebrated physician Sopolis, under whom he devoted himself to medicine. Since he excelled in this art, he provided free medical service to the needy; meanwhile, he supported his life by laboring at his goldsmith’s craft by night. Having returned to Antioch, he was ordained a deacon by Bishop Leontius, who gave him the power to teach his doctrines publicly in the Church, which Aetius performed with all his might. The most significant points of his heresy <note>This radical form of Arianism is known as Anomoeanism.</note> were: *That the Son is a created being* <note>original: "κτιστὸν" (ktiston)</note>, *and made from nothing* <note>original: "ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων" (ex ouk onton)</note>, *and in all things unlike* <note>original: "ἀνόμοιον" (anomoion)</note> *the Father*, and therefore *of a different substance* <note>original: "ἑτεροούσιον" (heteroousion)</note>, *plainly diverse in his essence*. Because of this, the nickname "The Atheist" rightly stuck to him. The rest may be sought from Epiphanius, Theodoret, and Nicetas Choniates.

He began to be especially famous around the year 359 and the year following, when he was accused before Constantius of being an accomplice and participant in the conspiracy of Gallus, and was sent into exile to Pepuza in Phrygia. Under Julian <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who often recalled exiled heretics to foster division among Christians.</note>, he received a bishopric; Philostorgius does not record of which city. Julian treated him very kindly after he was recalled from exile and gave him a farm on Lesbos near the city of Mitylene as a token of his goodwill; a letter from him to Aetius, by then a bishop, still survives. Under Valens, he retired to his Lesbian estate, <margin>Letter 31.</margin> where he came into danger of his life during the usurpation of Procopius. Fleeing from there to Constantinople, he departed this life shortly thereafter, around the year 366, with Eunomius closing his eyes and managing the funeral arrangements. 

According to Nicetas, he was rash and scurrilous, and took pleasure in the speech, gestures, and unseemly habits of mimes and theater-players. For he was accustomed to lift his garment up to his buttocks to strike his thighs, and while lifting one foot and striking his belly, he would break wind; moreover, at banquets, he would attack the Holy Trinity with blasphemous words amidst his jests. A *Small Book on the Faith* written by him survives, consisting of forty-seven chapters, found in Epiphanius’s *Heresies*, 76, who refuted his book step-by-step fully and solidly. According to Socrates †, he also composed letters, both to the <margin>† Book 2, ch. 35.</margin> Emperor Constantius and to certain others, in which he wove long disputes and proposed sophisticated arguments. A fragment of a letter of his, perhaps to Eunomius, is held along with Eunomius’s notes in Athanasius’s *Dialogue II on the Trinity*, Volume II, pages 166, 162. In this fragment, he mentions a small work he had elaborated on the "Unbegotten God" <note>original: "ἀγεννήτῳ" (agenneto)</note> and on the "Begotten God" <note>original: "γεννητῷ" (genneto)</note>, which his adversaries published in a corrupted form, with some things removed and others inserted.

I am aware that Socrates * and Sozomen † refer these events to the time of the Emperor Valens; but Philostorgius is more to be believed, as he was a most keen-eyed observer regarding Eunomian matters. Theodoret * also supports him in this regard. Under Julian and Jovian, Eunomius lived in Constantinople; under Valens, he retired to a garden in Chalcedon, until he was reported to the Emperor on the grounds that he had hidden the usurper Procopius on his estate, and was sent into exile in Mauritania. While stopping at Mursa in Illyria during the journey, he was recalled by the Emperor. Later, Theodosius the Great ordered him to be snatched away from Chalcedon and banished to Halmyris, a place in Moesia situated on the Danube. Driven from there by barbarians, he was brought to Caesarea in Cappadocia. However, being hated by the citizens because he had once written books against Basil, their Bishop, he was permitted to live at Dacora, his birthplace, on his own lands. There he died at a great age, around the year 394. For he was still among the living when Jerome was closing his *Catalogue of Writers*. The nobleman Eutropius saw to it that Eunomius's body was moved to Tyana to be kept by monks there, lest it be moved to Constantinople by his disciples and share a common tomb with his master; furthermore, he ordered Eunomius's books to be destroyed by public edicts. Philostorgius, himself a Eunomian by sect, extols him with the highest praise; indeed, almost his entire *Ecclesiastical History* should be considered little more than a panegyric <note>A formal speech of high praise.</note> for Eunomius. However, Photius *, who produced an abridgment of Philostorgius, notes that Eunomius's style of speaking was far from the beauty of a panegyric—it was obscure, redundant, swollen, and should be classified as unpleasant, ridiculous, and confused in character.

<margin>
* Code 138.
† Socrates, bk. 4, ch. 7.
</margin>
Socrates † agrees with Photius, observing that Eunomius was "wordy in his speech" <note>original: "πολυχεῖν τὴν λέξιν" (polychein tēn lexin)</note> and constantly repeated the same words. He also notes a "sophistic craftiness" <note>original: "τεχνον σοφισικὸν" (technon sophistikon)</note> in him learned from Aetius, and that being too devoted to certain empty little words, he unwittingly wove deceptive arguments, since in truth he was very little skilled in Holy Scripture and could not grasp its meaning.
