*An Exposition of Faith* <note>original: "Ἔκθεσις πίστεως" (Ekthesis pisteōs)</note>, or a small book on Faith, presented to Emperor Theodosius in the year 383. Henry Valesius was the first to bring this to light from a Florentine manuscript and published it with a version in his *Annotations on Socrates*, Book 5, Chapter 10.
*The Apology*, in which this cunning Arch-heretic argues subtly against the dogma of the Holy Trinity, especially against the eternal and consubstantial <note>The orthodox belief that the Son is of the "same substance" as the Father.</note> Deity of our Lord. ### The Apology <note>original: Ἀπολογητικὸς; here meaning a formal legal and theological defense</note> of the impious <note>The epithet "impious" was added by later orthodox editors to signal their disapproval of Eunomius's Arian views.</note> Eunomius, against which the Great Basil wrote his refutations.

-> Prologue. <- -> Translated by H. W. <-

Knowing that to slander and defame is a wicked and hateful act belonging to an unbridled tongue and an ungrateful mind, but that for wise men to strive with all diligence to turn away by evidence the falsehoods still held as opinions from slander, and to provide for the safety of many through their own good counsel—regarding many diverse matters—we prayed, having knowledge of both through reason, that we might never fall into the former lot, nor experience the latter. But since it has happened that we did not escape these plots, and a false reputation has been constructed against us in various ways and manners through both words and deeds among many—a reputation painful to us and harmful to those who believed it—orchestrated by certain wicked men who do not hesitate to say or do anything, and who measure the truth by the poorly-timed accusations of their differences, while those men have made these slanders against us, we thought it profitable for ourselves for an apology, and for the safety of those to whom things are said without scrutiny, to set forth a written confession of our own doctrine. We do this so that through this confession we might turn away the blasphemy that has gone before us, and for the future make the wicked less daring and the overly gullible more secure, by imposing on the former a fear of speaking falsely, and by showing the latter something certain that can be safely believed, while the truth on our side is demonstrated along with the punishment deserved by both; for associating with a lie brings a common punishment to both the speaker and the believer. We ask above all that you who are now listeners, and all who will read this hereafter, not to wish to judge the truth from the lie by the sheer number of votes, nor by attaching the better part to the greater number; nor should you allow your minds to be obscured by attending to the dignities or the arrogance of anyone, nor by granting more to the rank of those who first instructed you, thereby causing your ears to be prejudiced against those who come after, either because of the teaching of our Savior Jesus Christ in every part, or by providing a blind consent to those former teachers, while excluding the second—

<column-break/>

Since we are well aware that to bring calumnies and insults against someone is the mark of an unbridled tongue and an uncontrolled mind, and indeed is the behavior of the wicked and the quarrelsome; yet to strive with the greatest zeal to turn away calumnies and lies that would bring us disgrace by using arguments is the mark of a prudent man, and of one who provides equally for his own reputation and for the rectitude of many in judging; it would have been pleasant for us, holding both truths by contemplation alone, neither to have fallen into the former lot, nor ever to have experienced the latter. But since the matter did not turn out according to our wish, and a false calumny was heaped upon us by many in many different ways, both in words and deeds—a calumny mournful to us, and no less harmful to those who believe it, and that from certain very wicked little men who would blush at saying or doing nothing; since even more sincere men measured the truth of the matter by the accusations of many, and did not weigh by right reason the calumnies brought against us, we have deemed it conducive to our defense, and likely to bring light to things rashly said, to publish a confession of our dogma committed to writing. For by this method we might be able to ward off past calumny, and for the future render the wicked less bold, and the overly credulous more certain in judging, by striking into the former a fear of saying false things, and indicating to the latter something certain that can be safely believed; having demonstrated equally the justice of our cause, and the punishment which both have deserved. For to approach and assent to a lie attracts a common penalty for both those who speak and those who believe. Above all, we implore both you who are to hear this at present, and all who will read it hereafter; that you do not wish to judge the true and the false from a multitude of votes, granting the palm to the majority; nor, by caring for the dignity or the boastings of anyone, should you allow your mind to be obscured, nor finally, by offering blind assent to those teaching you in the first place, should you close your ears to the teachers who follow; of the doctrine of our Savior Jesus Christ—

<sig>Z 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: teaching [doctrinam]</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Eunomius’s "Apology," a defense of his Arian beliefs. He frames his writing as a necessary response to the widespread slander and "mob rule" of the majority of church leaders, appealing to the reader to judge his words by reason rather than by numbers or the rank of his opponents.</summary>

Having been made a Deacon by Eudoxius of Antioch, he was soon sent as an envoy by his party to the Emperor Constantius, but was captured on the journey by the followers of Basil <note>Basil of Ancyra, a leader of the semi-Arian faction</note> and banished to Midaion in Phrygia. In the year 360, he was ordained Bishop of Cyzicus by Eudoxius and Maris, but was soon after driven out by the citizens. I am aware that Socrates * and Sozomen † refer these events to the time of Valens; but Philostorgius is more to be trusted as a most keen-eyed observer of Eunomian affairs; and he is supported in this regard by Theodoret *. Under the Emperors Julian and Jovian, he lived in Constantinople; under Valens, he retired to a garden in Chalcedon, until he was denounced to the Emperor for having hidden the usurper Procopius on his land, and was sent into exile in Mauritania. While stopping at Mursa in Illyricum during the journey, he was recalled by the Emperor. However, Theodosius the Great <note>original: "Theodoritus Magnus" - likely a scribal or OCR error for Theodosius</note> ordered him to be snatched from Chalcedon and banished to Halmyris, a place in Moesia situated on the Danube. Driven from there by Barbarians, he was brought to Caesarea in Cappadocia; but because he was hated by the citizens for having once written books against Basil, their Bishop, he was permitted to live on his own lands in his native village of Dacora, where he died at a great age around the year 394. For he was still among the living when Jerome closed his *Catalog of Writers*. Eutropius the Patrician saw to it that Eunomius's body was moved to Tyana to be guarded by monks, lest it be moved to Constantinople by his disciples and share a common tomb with his master; furthermore, he ordered Eunomius's books to be destroyed by public edict. Philostorgius, himself an Eunomian by sect, extols him with the highest praise—indeed, nearly his entire *Ecclesiastical History* ought to be considered nothing other than an encomium <note>a speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly</note> of Eunomius. Nevertheless, Photius *, the abbreviator of Philostorgius, notes that his style of speaking was far from panegyric beauty, being obscure, redundant, turgid, and to be classified as an unpleasant, ridiculous, and confused style. Socrates † agrees with Photius, observing that Eunomius was "prolix in his speech" <note>original: "πολυχεῆ τὴν λέξιν"</note> and constantly repeated the same words; he also notes in him a "sophistical artifice" <note>original: "τεχνὸν σοφιστικὸν"</note> learned from Aetius, and that being devoted to certain empty little words, he unwittingly wove deceptive arguments, since in truth he was very little skilled in the Holy Scriptures and could not attain an understanding of them.

---

### W R I T I N G S.

**Seven books of Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans.** Not surviving.
**Several Letters,** which Philostorgius says "surpassed his other works even more" <note>original: "διαφέρειν τῶν ἄλλων ἔτι μᾶλλον"</note> than the rest of his writings. Not surviving.
***Exposition of Faith**, <note>original: "Ἔκθεσις πίστεως"</note> or a small book of Faith, presented to the Emperor Theodosius in the year 383. Henri Valesius was the first to bring this to light from a Florentine manuscript and published it with an added version in his annotations to Socrates, Book 5, chapter 10.
**The Apologeticus**, in which the crafty heresiarch disputes subtly against the dogma of the Holy Trinity, especially the eternal and consubstantial Deity of our Lord. St. Basil answered this book and preserved several fragments; others were preserved by Gregory of Nyssa and Epiphanius. However, the complete little work exists in Greek, both among others and in the possession of the illustrious man Thomas Tenison, Doctor of Theology, and a friend to me in few matters <note>The author is likely referring to the scholarly intimacy shared with Tenison, the future Archbishop of Canterbury</note>. I shall subjoin here the Prologue and Epilogue, along with the confession of Eunomius attached to it, which Mr. Wharton <note>Henry Wharton, a famous 17th-century scholar</note> transcribed for my use from the Tenison manuscript and translated into Latin; these constitute nearly a fifth part of the whole work, as I intend to present the rest, being more prolix, in a summary.

### Z 2

# The Apology for the Impious Eunomius, against whom Great Basil wrote his refutations. <note>original: "Ἐυνομίῳ τῷ δυσσεβεῖ Ἀπολογητικός" — The title labels Eunomius as "impious," a common practice by orthodox scribes when preserving heretical texts.</note>

### Prologue.

**K**nowing that to slander and defame others is the work of an unrestrained tongue and a mind belonging to the ungrateful, the wicked, and the quarrelsome; yet knowing also that for a man of sound mind to strive with all diligence to block lies with proof—lest he appear wicked through slander—is to look out for his own good counsel and the safety of many. We would have prayed, even while possessing the knowledge of both through reason, neither to have fallen into that former lot of falsehood, nor ever to have escaped the latter [through such a struggle]. Since, however, the outcome did not happen as we hoped, and a false infamy has been scattered among many against us in various and manifold ways through both words and lies—painful indeed to us, but harmful to those who believe them—by certain wicked men who do not hesitate to say or do anything; and since even those who are more innocent have reported the truth based on the accusations of our opponents, or have weighed the slanders cast against us poorly, we thought it beneficial both for ourselves in our defense and for the safety of those things spoken of without examination, to set forth to you in writing the confession of our own opinion. If perhaps through this we might shake off the previously existing blasphemy, and for the future make the wicked less daring and the overly gullible more secure, by restraining those who speak lies and showing those who believe them a safe path; while our truth, being heard in silence, will bring punishment upon both <note>This refers to the spiritual punishment for those who speak and those who believe falsehoods.</note>; for fellowship with a lie works a common punishment for both. Above all, we entreat you—both those who will hear us now and those who will read this in the future—not to judge truth or falsehood by the multitude of votes, joining the better side to the larger portion; nor indeed to allow your mind to be darkened by paying attention to the dignities or the arrogance of certain men; nor by granting more to the rank of those who came before to block your ears to those who come after. Rather, [hold] the teaching of our Savior Jesus Christ above all—

<column-break/>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the year 300 AD.
</margin>

### Translated by H. W.

**S**ince we are well aware that to bring calumnies and insults against anyone is the mark of an unrestrained tongue and a powerless mind, and indeed the work of the wicked and the quarrelsome; but to strive with the greatest zeal to turn away calumnies and lies—which would bring ignominy upon us—through arguments is the mark of a prudent man, and of one who consults both his own reputation and the rectitude of many in judging; it would have been pleasant for us, holding both truths by contemplation alone, neither to have fallen into the former lot, nor to have ever experienced the latter. Since, however, the matter has by no means turned out according to our wish, and in many and diverse ways, by both words and deeds, a false calumny has been heaped upon us by many—grievous indeed to us, and no less harmful to those who believe it—and this by certain most wicked men, who would blush at saying or doing nothing; and since even more sincere men measured the truth of the matter by the accusations of many, and did not weigh the calumnies brought against us with right reason, we have deemed it conducive to our defense and something that will bring light to things rashly spoken, to publish a confession of our doctrine recorded in writing. If by that method we might both avert past calumny and for the future render the wicked less bold, and the overly credulous more certain in their judging—striking fear into the former for speaking falsehoods, while indicating to the latter something certain that can be safely believed; having demonstrated equally the justice of our cause and the punishment which both have deserved. For to approach and assent to a lie draws a common punishment upon both those who speak and those who believe. Before all things, however, we protest both to you who are about to hear us now, and to all who will read us in the future; that you should not wish to judge the true and the false by the number of votes, granting the palm to the majority; nor by caring for the dignity or the boastings of anyone should you allow your mind to be obscured, nor finally, by offering blind assent to those teaching you in the first place, should you close your ears to the teachers who follow; but [holding] the teaching of our Savior Jesus Christ— <note>The text cuts off here. The catchword "ctrinam" indicates the next page begins with "doctrinam" (teaching/doctrine).</note>

...teaching above every multitude of men, every ambition or contention, even the favor of parties, and kinship, and (to put it in a word) everything that usually clouds the mind's vision. For it contributes most toward finding the truth if one, having set aside prejudices, is made like it <note>original Latin: "assimiletur illi" — the idea is that the mind must become as pure as the truth it seeks to perceive.</note>. Furthermore, I would not wish for you to be angry with me if, having set aside the care for vain glory and punishment, and having preferred a certain hope of future goods over present favor and security—judging that the threats denounced against the impious are more to be feared than any earthly punishment or temporal death—I have set forth the truth stripped of every covering. For, to use the words of the Apostle, the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared to the glory hereafter to be revealed <note>A reference to Romans 8:18.</note>, nor could the whole world, if it were subjected to the possession and dominion of one man, equal the loss of an individual's soul; for the things we expect, whether you look at the rewards or the punishments, far surpass the present. But lest we dwell on these things too long and extend the discourse more than is proper, let us now turn to the confession of our faith itself, from which an easy and very quick knowledge of our faith can be obtained by all who wish. First, however, it is necessary that those who speak on such matters and give an account of their own doctrine should not lazily surrender themselves to opinions received among the common people; but rather, taking up the sacred tradition received in the order of succession from the fathers as a judge and rule for themselves, they should use that criterion at last for judging the truth of the things spoken.

We believe in one God, Father almighty, from whom are all things; and in one only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and in one Holy Spirit, the Paraclete <note>The "Comforter" or "Advocate."</note>, in whom every distribution of grace is given to each of the saints according to the measure of his necessity. This, therefore (to speak briefly and in summary), is the simpler confession, common to all who wish to be or be considered Christians. There remain, however, certain other things of the second order, about which there has been doubt until now, etc.

<column-break/>

...number of men, preferring [truth] above all ambition or rivalry, and again familiarity and kinship, and to speak collectively, all things which are accustomed to darken the soul's criteria of judgment; for the greatest part toward the discernment of truth is the kinship with it. In addition to these things, do not be harsh with us if, having disregarded vanity and fear, and having preferred the glory of the future over immediate favor and safety—judging that the threat defined against the impious ought to be more fearful than any earthly suffering and temporary death—we set out the truth naked of every covering. For, according to the Apostle, the sufferings of the current time are not worthy to be compared to the glory that is to be revealed; nor is the whole world, even for the enjoyment and dominion of it, a balanced exchange for one's own soul, since the things expected, both in terms of enjoyment and punishment, far exceed the present. But so that we do not lengthen the discourse beyond measure by lingering further, let us now turn to the confession of our faith itself, from which a convenient and easy understanding of our opinion may be available to those who wish. Perhaps it is necessary for those making arguments about these things, and undergoing an examination of their own opinion, not to surrender themselves carelessly to the opinions held by many, but having embraced the pious tradition prevailing from above from the fathers like a certain standard and rule, to use this as an accurate criterion for the judgment of the things being said.

We believe in one God, Father almighty, from whom are all things; and in one only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and in one Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, in whom the distribution of every grace is given to each of the saints according to the proportion of what is beneficial. This simpler and common [confession] of all who care to seem or to be Christians, to speak summarily as if in a running overview, is this; there still remain things of the second rank, about which there has been dispute for a time, etc.

Then, explaining this brief Confession at length, he sharply attacks the consubstantiality <note>The "of the same substance" doctrine established at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, co-eternity, and equality of the Son, using mostly philosophical arguments drawn from the idea and nature of God. He boasts of this argument above others: that from the primary idea of God, it is clear that God is *unbegotten* <note>original Greek: *ἀγέννητον* (agennēton)</note>. Christ, however, is not *unbegotten*: therefore, he is not God. *If unbegotten, he is not a son; if a son, he is not unbegotten.* <note>original: *Αγ f. 38 ἀγέννητος, ἐχ υἱὸς· ἂν f υἱὸς, ἐκ ἀγέννητος*</note> Everywhere he mocks the Catholic <note>Here referring to the Nicene or orthodox position.</note> opinion as impious, bold, tasteless, and absurd. After the middle of the work, he attacks those Arians who hold the "of similar substance" <note>original: *ὁμοιούσιως* (homoiousios) — referring to the Semi-Arians who believed the Son was similar to, but not the same as, the Father.</note> view and disputes at length against the similarity of essence in the Father and the Son. Finally, moving to the Holy Spirit, he teaches that he is inferior to the Father and the Son in nature no less than in order. Near the end, he reduces his dogmas, established by the previous arguments, into a Summary <note>original: *Epitomen*</note>, which begins thus: *I reveal the one and only true God of all, unbegotten, without beginning, incomparable,* etc. <note>original: *φαίνω ἕνα κὶ μόνον ἀληθινὸν τ̅ π̅ πάντων Θεὸν, ἀγέννητον, ἄναρχον, ἀσύγκριτον*</note> Where it should be noted that he attributes the creation (for he uses that word) of the Holy Spirit to the Son no less than to the Father. *The Son is less than the Father as a thing made, but greater than the Holy Spirit as a maker.* <note>original: *Τ̅ μὲν υἱ̅ (Patre) ἐλάττων ἐστὶν (Filius) ὡς ποίημα, τ̅ δ̅ (Spiritus S.) κρείττων, ὡς ποιητής.*</note>

# EPILOGUE.

All these things having been clearly and more extensively demonstrated by us elsewhere, but now briefly set before you, I would ask both you who are present and all those joined to us in the society of these same sacred mysteries, that you—fearing not the reproach of men, nor led astray by fallacies, nor turned aside by flatteries—might give your vote to these words according to a true and just judgment. That is to say, let the better cause prevail among all. Preferring reason over prejudices, may you escape all the snares and nets which the Devil constructs for the human race, desiring to put many to flight or to entice them—those who do not prefer the useful to the pleasant, or who think present things are more certain than future ones. Indeed, should worse things seem better to some (may God avert this), with many conspiring on the side of falsehood and resisting the truth—whosoever values present security and glory more than things pleasing to God and truly useful—I would wish that my followers preserve that faith once delivered to Christ, firm and unshaken.

<column-break/>

They should await the judgment of our Savior Christ, from which empty pomp, and glory, and falsehood are utterly removed. There they stand naked to be judged, deprived of all power, service, and flattery; for cunning and riches are of no worth in bending the judge, however much they may be able to do among men. For if truth indeed holds its place, not even a multitude of illustrious men ought to be equaled to a single pious poor man in judgment. Otherwise, religion, according to a just retribution, stands on the side of those who [consider] death for... <note>The text cuts off here at the word "pro" (for).</note>

...they consider it a gain to encounter death for that truth; for Christ distributes the rewards of these contests both in ages past and now—to those laboring for the sake of truth, he gives true liberty and the kingdom of heaven, but to those who, out of folly, count the truth as naught <note>original: *floccifacientibus*, literally "to value at a tuft of wool," meaning to treat as worthless</note>, he gives inescapable punishments. ->The confession of faith of Eunomius, added to the end of his Apology.<-

There is one God, unbegotten <note>original Latin: *ingenitus*; Greek: *ἀγέννητος* (agennētos). This is the core of Eunomius’s theology: if God’s very essence is to be "unbegotten," then anyone "begotten" (like the Son) cannot be the same kind of being as God.</note> and lacking a beginning; He has nothing existing before Himself (for nothing can exist before the unbegotten), nor anything coexisting with Him (for the unbegotten God is one and alone), nor anything existing within Himself (for God is simple and uncompounded). Since He exists as one, and alone, and always the same, He is the God, creator, and founder of all things—primarily and especially of the only-begotten *Son*, but properly of all things founded through the Son. For He begot, created, and made the Son alone, before all things and every creature, by His own power and operation; He communicated nothing of His own substance <note>original Latin: *substantiæ*; Greek: *ὑποστάσεως* (hypostaseōs)</note> to the one begotten (for God is immortal, indivisible, and inseparable, and an immortal being never communicates His own substance to another), nor did He produce another like Himself. For He alone is unbegotten, and it is impossible for another to be generated according to His unbegotten substance. Therefore, He did not use His own substance in begetting the *Son*, but His will alone; nor did He beget him according to His own substance, but as He willed. *Once this was done*, through the Son He made the Holy Spirit, the first and greatest of all things, by His own power and command, yet by the operation and power of the Son. After the Holy Spirit, He created all other things through the Son, both in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal. For there is one God, from whom are all things (to use the words of the Apostle) and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. There is, therefore, one God: unbegotten, uncreated, not made; and one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God: the begotten of the unbegotten (yet not like one of the begotten), the creature of the uncreated (yet not like one of the creatures), the thing made of the one not made (yet not like one of the things made). As Holy Scripture says: *The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, before the ages* <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:22 in the Septuagint translation, which Arians frequently used to argue that Christ was a "created" being.</note>

<column-break/>

...giving; or Christ, who formerly and now acts as the judge of the contests, awarding to those who have toiled for the truth true liberty and the kingdom of heaven. But to those who, through malice, have dishonored this truth, he awards inescapable punishments. Let these two possibilities be spoken to you, and may the end result in the better lot.

There is one God, unbegotten and without beginning, having nothing existing alongside himself (for nothing can be alongside the state of being unbegotten), nor with him (for the unbegotten God is one and alone), nor in him (for he is simple and uncompounded). Being one, and being alone, and being always the same, he is the God and founder and creator of all things: primarily and especially of the only-begotten, and specifically of those things which came into being through him. For he begot, and created, and made the Son alone before all things and before every creature by his own power and activity, having shared nothing of his own person <note>original: *hypostasis*</note> with the one begotten; for God is incorruptible and indivisible and inseparable, and that which is incorruptible does not share anything of its own being with another, nor does it establish another like itself. For he alone is unbegotten, and it is impossible for the essence of the unbegotten to be begotten. Nor did he make use of his own essence [to beget], but only of his will; nor did he beget according to his own essence, but as he willed. And because of this, he made the Holy Spirit first of all and greater [than the rest], by his own authority and command, but by the activity and power of the Son; after which he made all other things through the Son—all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, both bodies and bodiless things. For there is "one God from whom are all things," according to the Apostle, "and one Lord Jesus Christ through whom are all things." Thus, there is one God: unbegotten, uncreated, unmade; and one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God: the offspring of the unbegotten (but not as one of the offspring), the creature of the uncreated (but not as one of the creatures), the work of the <insert>read: "unmade"</insert> [but not as one of the works. ...before all the hills, He begets me <note>Original Greek: *πρὸ δὲ πάντων βουνῶν γεννᾷ με*. This is a reference to Proverbs 8:25, a crucial text in the Arian controversy used to argue about the "birth" or "creation" of Wisdom/Christ.</note>. And there is one Holy Spirit, the first and greatest of all the works of the Only-Begotten, produced indeed by the command of the Father, but by the operation and power of the Son.

---

His *Defense of his Apology* comprised three books against Basil; he spent many Olympiads <note>An Olympiad is a four-year period; the author is emphasizing the many years Eunomius spent in seclusion writing this.</note> shut away in a small dwelling to refine this work. However, while Basil was alive, Eunomius prudently suppressed it, only publishing it after Basil's death. Fragments of this book, as well as his *Apology*, can be found scattered throughout the writings of Epiphanius, Basil, and Gregory of Nyssa in their books against Eunomius.

<margin>360.</margin>
**MELETIUS**, an Armenian by birth from the city of Melitene, was first substituted into the place of Eustathius, the Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, after Eustathius was deposed by the Synod of Gangra. However, because the common people were in an uproar, he soon withdrew to Beroea, where he lived as a private citizen. As for the historian Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian.</note> writing that he was transferred there, he seems to have been mistaken in that regard <margin>\* Book 2, ch. 44.</margin>. In the year 359, at the Synod of Seleucia, he subscribed to the Acacian formula <note>A "Homoean" creed stating the Son is "like" the Father, avoiding the controversial term "substance."</note>. In the following year, when Eudoxius had occupied the throne of Constantinople and the see of Antioch was thus vacant, Meletius was summoned from Beroea and elected Bishop by the common vote of both the Catholics and the Arians. To make this election more secure, a decree was drawn up and protected by the signatures of all; they gave it to Eusebius, the Bishop of Samosata, to keep as a mutual pact, with Emperor Constantius himself consenting in letters sent to Meletius. Certainly, both parties claimed the man as a sharer of their own opinion. Indeed, Philostorgius <margin>\* Book 5, ch. 11.</margin> did not hesitate to write that Meletius, in order to accommodate himself to the Emperor's will, feigned "different substance" <note>original Greek: *τὸ ἑτερούσιον* (to heteroousion). This was the extreme Arian position that the Son's essence is entirely different from the Father's.</note> and subscribed to the Western Tome (that is, the formula of Ariminum). As he entered Antioch, all the bishops and other ranks of the clergy, along with a crowded mass of people, came out to meet him. When he entered the city <margin>See Theodoret, Book 2, ch. 31.</margin>, the Emperor urged him to speak in the church—to be recorded by shorthand writers—on that most troubled passage of Solomon: *The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works* <note>Proverbs 8:22. This was the primary "proof text" for Arians to argue that the Son was a created being.</note>. Other bishops were also to perform this task. When George of Laodicea and Acacius of Caesarea had finished their parts in preaching, Meletius finally rose in the third place and demonstrated what the rule of right theology truly was. When this was received with great applause by the people, and everyone begged him to give them a summary of his doctrine, he held up three fingers, then closed two of them, leaving one as it was, and uttered this memorable sentence: "Three are understood, but we speak as to one" <note>original Greek: *Τρία τὰ νοούμενα, ὡς ἕν δὲ διαλεγόμεθα*. This was a clever way of affirming the Trinity—three persons but one essence—without using the forbidden technical terms that would trigger an immediate riot or arrest.</note>. Because of this, the Emperor became enraged and he was soon banished to his home city, with the Arians accusing him of the crime of perjury; there were even those who accused him of <term>Sabellianism</term> <note>The belief that Father, Son, and Spirit are not distinct persons, but just three "modes" or "faces" of one God.</note>. Under Julian, he was restored to his see; and while the Antiochian Schism was still burning, he celebrated the divine mysteries with the people who followed him in Pella (that is, the Old City). When Jovian was staying in Antioch, Meletius was the first, along with other bishops, to present a confession of faith to him. Under Valens he was banished again, and later restored by Gratian. In the year 381, when he set out for Constantinople to hold a general council, the Emperor Theodosius received him with honor. Theodosius recognized him at first sight because, when he had first taken up the government of the Roman Empire, he had seen Meletius in a dream dressing him in the imperial cloak and placing the royal crown on his head; the Emperor kissed his eyes, head, and the right hand that had crowned him. While the Synod was still in session, the venerable old man passed away; Gregory of Nyssa delivered the funeral oration in his praise before the Synod. His body was carried back to Antioch; the Emperor ordered that, contrary to the Roman custom regarding burials within cities, he should be received inside the cities while on the journey. Thus, welcomed with the singing of psalms in every place, he was honorably led all the way to Antioch and laid to rest next to the tomb of the martyr Babylas.

# The confession of faith of Eunomius, appended to the end of his Apology.

<margin>The 4th Century, from the year 300 AD.</margin>

There is one God, unbegotten <note>Greek: *agennētos*. This was a central term for Eunomius, arguing that being "unbegotten" is the very essence of God the Father, making him fundamentally different from the Son.</note> and without beginning, who has nothing existing before himself (for nothing can exist before the unbegotten), nor anything coexisting with him (for the unbegotten God is one and alone), nor existing within himself (for God is simple and uncomposed <note>A philosophical term meaning God is not made of parts.</note>); while he exists as one, and alone, and the same, always; he is the God and creator and founder of all things—first and preeminently of the only-begotten *Son*, and specifically of all things created through him. For he alone generated, created, and made the Son before all things and all creation, by his own power and operation; sharing nothing of his own substance with the one generated (for God is immortal and impartible and indivisible; and that which is immortal in no way shares its own substance with another) nor producing another similar to himself. For he alone is unbegotten; and according to his unbegotten substance, it is impossible for another to be generated. Therefore, he did not use his own substance in generating the Son, but only his will; nor did he generate him according to his own substance, but as he willed. *When this was done*, through the Son he first and foremost made the Holy Spirit, the greatest of all things, by his own authority and command, yet by the operation and power of the Son. After the Holy Spirit, he created all other things through the Son, both in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal. For there is one God, from whom are all things (to use the words of the Apostle) and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. There is, therefore, one God, unbegotten, uncreated, not made; and one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the offspring of the unbegotten, yet not as one of the offspring; the creature of the uncreated, yet not as one of the creatures; the work of the one who is not made, yet not as one of the works. Just as Holy Scripture says: "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, before the age..." <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:22, which Arians used to argue that Christ was a created being.</note>

<column-break/>

But to those who, through malice, have dishonored this, he grants inescapable punishments. Let these things be said to both of you, but may the end result in the better portion.

There is one God, unbegotten and without beginning, having nothing existing before himself (for nothing can be before the unbegotten), nor with him, for the unbegotten God is one and alone, nor in him, for he is simple and uncomposed. Being one, and alone, and the same, he is the God and creator and craftsman of all things, first and especially of the only-begotten, and particularly of those things made through him; for before all things and before every creature, he alone generated and created and made the Son by his own power and activity, sharing nothing of his own essence <note>Greek: *hypostasis*.</note> with the one generated; for God is incorruptible and undivided and indivisible, and the one who is incorruptible does not share his own essence, nor does he cause another to exist like himself. For he alone is unbegotten, and it is impossible to be generated in the essence of unbegottenness. Therefore, he did not make use of his own essence, but by his will alone, nor did he generate him according to his own essence, but as he willed. And because of this, first of all and greater [than the rest], he made the Holy Spirit, by his own authority and command, but by the activity and power of the Son; and after this, he made all other things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, both bodies and bodiless things, through the Son. For there is one God from whom are all things, according to the Apostle, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. There is therefore one God, unbegotten, uncreated, unmade, and one Lord Jesus Christ the Son of God, the offspring of the unbegotten, but not as one of the offspring, the creature of the uncreated, but not as one of the creatures, the work of the maker <insert>Read: of the unmade</insert> <note>Original Greek: *poiēma tou poiētou [lege apoiētou]*. A defense of his Apology, comprised of three books against Basil; he spent many Olympiads <term>Olympiad: A four-year period; here meaning a long duration of time.</term> shut away in a small hut working on it. However, while Basil was alive, he prudently suppressed it, only publishing it after his death. Fragments of this book, as well as the Apology, can be found here and there in the writings of Epiphanius, Basil, and [Gregory of] Nyssa in their books against Eunomius.

<margin>360.</margin>
MELETIUS, an Armenian by birth from the city of Melitene, was first substituted into the place of Eustathius of Sebaste, the Bishop of the Armenians, who had been deposed by the Council of Gangra. But with the common people rioting, he soon withdrew to Beroea <note>modern-day Aleppo, Syria</note>; and there he lived as a private citizen. <margin>* Book 2, chapter 44.</margin> In truth, Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian.</note> writes that he was transferred there; in this, he seems to have been mistaken. In the year 359, at the Council of Seleucia, he subscribed to the Acacian formula <note>A compromise creed that avoided the controversial term "substance."</note>; in the following year, when Eudoxius had occupied the throne of Constantinople, and the see of Antioch was thus vacant, he was summoned from Beroea. By the common vote of both the Catholics and the Arians, he was elected Bishop. To make this more secure, a decree was composed and protected by the signatures of everyone; they handed this over to Eusebius, the Bishop of Samosata, to be kept as a common pact, with the Emperor Constantius himself agreeing in letters sent to Meletius. Certainly, both parties claimed the man for themselves as a sharer of their own opinion. <margin>* Book 5, chapter 1.</margin> Philostorgius * indeed did not hesitate to write that Meletius, in order to accommodate himself to the Emperor's will, feigned the "heteroousian" <note>The belief that the Son is of a different substance than the Father.</note> view and signed the Western Tome (that is, the formula of Ariminum). As he entered Antioch, all the Bishops and the rest of the clergy, together with a crowded mass of people, came out to meet him. When he entered the city, the Emperor urged him to speak in the Church—to be recorded by notaries—regarding that most troubled passage of Solomon <margin>see Theodoret, book 2, chapter 31.</margin> *The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways for his works* <note>Proverbs 8:22, a central text in the Arian controversy.</note>; the same duty was to be performed by other Bishops. When George of Laodicea and Acacius of Caesarea had fulfilled their parts in preaching, Meletius finally rose in the third place and demonstrated what the rule of right Theology should be. When this was received with immense applause by the people, and everyone prayed that he would hand over to them a summary of his doctrine, he showed three fingers, and then, pressing two together and leaving one as it was, he uttered this memorable sentence: *Three are understood, but we speak as to one.* <note>Greek: Τρία τὰ νοούμενα, ὡς ἑνὶ δὲ διαλεγόμεθα. This was a clever way to affirm the Trinity (three persons) and the Unity (one God) simultaneously.</note> Because of this, the Emperor, becoming enraged, soon banished him to his native city, while the Arians charged him with the crime of perjury; nor were there those lacking who accused him of the Sabellian heresy <note>The belief that Father, Son, and Spirit are merely different "modes" or masks of one person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>. Under Julian, he was restored to his see; and while the Antiochene Schism was still burning, he celebrated the divine mysteries with the people who followed him in Pellaea (that is, the Old City). When Jovian was staying at Antioch, Meletius was the first to offer him a petition of Faith along with other Bishops. Under Valens he was banished again, and later restored by Gratian. In the year 381, when he set out for Constantinople for the celebration of the General Council, the Emperor Theodosius received him honorably and recognized him at first sight; for when he had first taken up the governance of the Roman Empire, he had seen Meletius in a dream clothing him in the Imperial cloak and placing the royal crown on his head. He kissed the eyes, the head, and the right hand that had crowned him. While the Synod was still sitting, the venerable old man reached his end. Gregory of Nyssa delivered a funeral oration in his praise before the Synod. His body was carried back to Antioch; the Emperor ordered that, despite the Roman custom against bringing bodies into cities, he should be received while on the way; and so, received with the singing of psalms alternately in every place, he was honorably led all the way to Antioch and laid to rest next to the casket of the martyr Babylas.

### AQUILIUS SEVERUS

AQUILIUS SEVERUS was an obscure and almost unknown writer, for whose notice we are indebted solely to Jerome. He was Spanish by birth, from the lineage of that Severus to whom Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325) was an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> once addressed two books of Letters. He lived around the year 360 AD and passed away during the reign of Valentinian. He wrote a *Travelogue* <note>original Greek: 'Οδοιπορικὸν (*Hodoiporikon*)</note> in both prose and verse, to which he gave the title *Calamity* <note>original Greek: Καταστροφῆς (*Katastrophēs*)</note> or *The Blow* <note>original Greek: Πλάγης (*Plagēs*)</note>; in this work, he depicted the state of his entire life.

360 AD.
* Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 14.
</margin>

### AUDENTIUS

AUDENTIUS was an author no less obscure, and he himself was also Spanish by birth. As far as I know, he is mentioned only by Gennadius. He held the rank of Bishop of some city in Spain and was a Catholic in his faith. He seems to have lived around the year 360 AD. He wrote a book *against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians*, and most especially against the Photinians <term>Photinians: Followers of Photinus, who taught that Jesus was a mere man and did not exist before his birth to Mary.</term>, which he titled *On the Faith Against All Heretics*. In this work, he showed that the Son was co-eternal with the Father and did not only begin to exist when he was conceived and born of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

360 AD.

### ZENO

ZENO was the Bishop of Verona, whom some treat as a martyr and claim suffered death around the year 260 AD; however, they are supported by neither reason nor authority. It is probable that he flourished around the year 360 AD, several years before St. Ambrose, and was the predecessor of Syagrius, Bishop of Verona. Ambrose himself mentions him in his 64th Letter. Indeed, the most learned of the modern scholars seem to hold this opinion, whose arguments on this matter were collected by Philippe Labbé. There are *90 Sermons* extant under his name concerning many passages of Holy Scripture and arguments on divine matters; these were drawn partly from St. Basil and partly from St. Hilary and others. Not even the slightest mention was ever made of these sermons until Guarinus, an orator of Verona, first published them. They were printed at *Venice in 1508, then at Verona in 1586 in quarto, and finally in the Library of the Fathers, Volume 3.*

362 AD.
Sozomen, Book 6, ch. 25.
Socrates, Book 2, ch. 46.
</margin>

### APOLLINARIUS the Elder

APOLLINARIUS the Elder was a native of Alexandria and a grammarian by profession. He first taught at Berytus <note>Modern-day Beirut, Lebanon.</note> in Phoenicia, then at Laodicea in Syria, where he was made a priest of that church. Having taken a wife there, he had a son of the same name, who was the founder of the Apollinarian heresy (whom we shall discuss in his proper place). He maintained a very close friendship with Epiphanius, a noble Sophist <term>Sophist: A teacher of rhetoric and philosophy.</term> but a Gentile <note>original Latin: *Gentili*, meaning a non-Christian or pagan.</note>. He frequently attended Epiphanius’s lecture hall, even while he was reciting profane <note>Non-religious or secular classical poetry.</note> poems. Having been warned about this by Theodotus, the Bishop of Laodicea, and failing to abstain, he was publicly convicted and cast out of the Church along with his son, who was guilty of the same crime. However, upon performing penance, Theodotus received them back again. 

He flourished around the year 362 AD, during the reign of Julian <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who attempted to revive Roman paganism.</note>. When Julian forbade Christians from using the books of the Gentiles, Apollinarius—fearing that the forms of Greek expression might be left as something new and unheard of by Christians—composed several books in imitation of the ancients. 

<margin>
* Socrates, Book 3, ch. 16.
</margin>
Socrates says that he arranged the art of grammar "in a Christian style" <note>original Greek: χριστιανικῷ τύπῳ (*christianikō typō*)</note>. He interpreted the books of Moses in heroic verse, imitating Homer. 

<margin>
* Sozomen, Book 5, ch. 18.
</margin>
Indeed, if Sozomen relates the matter correctly, he wrote the entire history of the Hebrews up to the reign of Saul in that same type of verse. Dividing the whole work into twenty-four parts, he gave each book a title according to the letters of the Greek alphabet in order. Furthermore, he expressed other historical books of the Old Testament partly in dactylic verse and partly worked them into the form of tragedies with characters. Taking his themes from Holy Scripture, he wrote comedies in the style of Menander's plays; he also imitated the tragedies of Euripides and the lyric style of Pindar. Thus, in a short time, as Sozomen says, he composed works equal in number and excellence to those which were famous among the Greeks in those genres, whether one considers the genius, the diction, the form, or the arrangement of the work. However, all these things have long since perished. Whether the *Metaphrasis of the Psalms*—which is extant today both in the appendix to the *Library of the Fathers, Paris, 1624*, and published separately in *Greek, Paris, 1580* and *Greek-Latin, Heidelberg, 1596*—belongs to him or to his son is not yet sufficiently certain. It is commonly attributed to the younger Apollinarius...

DIONYSIUS, who grandly assumes the false name of the *Areopagite* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 1st-century convert of St. Paul; the author discussed here is now known as Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>, seems to have written around this time. Many writers have long since demonstrated by many means that the Works circulating under his name are entirely spurious; most recently, following others, the most learned Daillé <note>Jean Daillé (Dallaeus), a French Protestant theologian.</note> proved this with numerous and invincible arguments in his book on the *Writings of Dionysius the Areopagite* (Geneva, 1666). It is indeed a wonder that in this midday light, after so many arguments clearer than the sun itself and after such manifest signs of forgery, some are still found today—such as Noël Alexandre, Emmanuel Schelstrate, etc.—who busy themselves defending these writings as the genuine works of Dionysius of Athens. For this reason, let me include the judgment of the most erudite Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar.</note> (which is found written in his own hand in a copy of Dionysius’s works kept in our Most Serene King’s Library): *The author,* he says, *is indeed most worthy of reading, and one who openly cuts the throat of the Papists' cause in many places. However, to believe that he was a contemporary of the Apostles is a stupor; to wish to persuade others of it is madness. They must be asses who allow themselves to be persuaded of this.* Regarding the age in which this Impostor lived, not all feel the same. Daillé and others with him push him back to the start of the Sixth Century, around the year 520 AD. The illustrious Pearson †, who refutes Daillé’s opinion on this matter at length, refers him to the final times of Eusebius of Caesarea <note>c. 339 AD.</note>. I closely agree with him and suppose he lived around this time. There is no less controversy among the Learned regarding the Author himself than there is regarding his age. Among all the opinions on this matter, the leading one—which even held sway before the age of St. Maximus—is that the Author of these books was Apollinarius, the Bishop of Laodicea; and I confess I was of this opinion for a long time. But upon reconsidering the matter, I leave it to the Learned to inquire whether the *Areopagitica* <note>The collected works of Pseudo-Dionysius.</note> should be attributed to Apollinaris the Father rather than the Son. Certainly, the Ancients classify the Son as a Heretic in other articles of faith, as well as among the proponents of the Millennium; yet this Error, as St. Maximus once noted \*, is clearly condemned in these books. The Father, however, was sound in faith; nor do the Ancients speak of him otherwise, except that Socrates † once seems to involve him in the same Heresy as the Son. The same Socrates says he was <term>a teacher of Greek learning</term> <note>original Greek: ἑλληνικῶν λόγων διδάσκαλος</note>, and according to Sozomen † he was <term>prepared for every kind of knowledge and for the practice of rhetoric</term> <note>original Greek: πρὸς παντοδαπὴν εἴδησιν καὶ λόγων παρασκευασμένος</note>; he cultivated the schools and writings of the Gentiles so intensely that he was expelled from the Church on this account. Since he was born in Alexandria and educated (it seems) in the Platonic School, he deeply drank in the dogmas of Platonic Philosophy. From this source comes that sublime and "super-celestial" Theology regarding God, the divine Names and Perfections, the Celestial Hierarchy, Angels, etc., which fill every page of the *Areopagitica*. Indeed, an egg is no more like an egg than the perplexed and enigmatic doctrine delivered in these books is like that mystical Theology which—especially around these times—Porphyry, Plotinus, Iamblichus, and later Proclus and others of the Neoplatonic school delivered to their disciples. Hence, Suidas † noted such an affinity between this Dionysius and the leaders of the Platonic school, especially Proclus, in both concepts and even in their very words, that he suspected (which is not surprising in one who believed him to be the genuine Areopagite) that the older Athenian Philosophers had stolen Dionysius’s works and claimed them as their own, suppressing his name so they might appear to be the authors. Furthermore, the man's poetic talent was perfectly suited to that affected, inflated, and turgid style of speaking, and that empty and futile grandiloquence; he knew how to vary this faculty of speaking excellently through the grammatical art in which he excelled. Finally, what wonder is it if he formed Christian Theology according to a Platonic idea, when he also composed the art of Grammar according to the form of the Christian religion? He was a man who wrote the antiquity of the Hebrews up to the reign of Saul in Heroic verse, imitating Homer, and [recounting] the rest of the history of the Old Testament...

ZENO, Bishop of Verona, is a figure whom others claim as a martyr, asserting he suffered around the year 260; however, they do so with no reasoning and no supporting authority. It is probable that he flourished around the year 360, a few years before St. Ambrose, and was the predecessor of Syagrius, Bishop of Verona. Ambrose himself mentions him in Letter 64. Indeed, the most learned of modern scholars seem to hold this opinion; Philippe Labbe \* has collected their arguments on this matter. There are *90 Sermons* extant under his name regarding many passages of Holy Scripture and arguments on divine matters, taken partly from St. Basil and partly from Hilary and others. No mention of them—not even the slightest—was ever made before Guarinus, the Orator of Verona, first published them. They appeared in *Venice in 1508*, then in *Verona in 1586* in quarto, and finally in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 3.

<margin>
362 AD.
Sozomen, book 6, ch. 25.
Socrates, book 2, ch. 46.
</margin>
APOLLINARIUS the Elder, a native of Alexandria, was a grammarian by profession. He first taught at Berytus <note>Modern-day Beirut.</note> in Phoenicia, then at Laodicea in Syria, where he was made a Priest of that church. Having taken a wife there, he had a son named after him, who became the founder of the *Apollinarian Heresy* <note>A belief that Jesus had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a human soul.</note>, about whom we shall speak in his proper place. He maintained a very close friendship with Epiphanius, a noble Sophist but a Pagan; he frequently attended Epiphanius’s lecture hall even when profane poems were being recited. For this, he was warned by Theodotus, the Bishop of Laodicea. When he did not desist, he was publicly convicted and cast out of the Church along with his son, who was guilty of the same crime. However, upon doing penance, Theodotus received them back. He flourished around the year 362. At that time, because the Emperor Julian <note>Known as Julian the Apostate, he banned Christians from teaching classical Greek literature.</note> prohibited Christians from teaching the books of the Pagans, Apollinarius composed several books in imitation of the Ancients so that the forms of Greek expression would not be left as something new and unheard of by Christians. He arranged <margin>* Book 3, ch. 16.</margin> the art of grammar *in a Christian style* <note>original: *christianskō typō*</note>, as Socrates \* says. Imitating Homer, he interpreted the books of Moses in Heroic verse. Indeed, if Sozomen \* <margin>* Book 5, ch. 18.</margin> relates the matter correctly, he wrote the entire antiquity of the Hebrews up to the reign of Saul in that same type of verse; and, dividing the whole work into twenty-four parts, he gave each book a name from the letters of the Greek alphabet in order. Furthermore, he expressed other historical books of the Old Testament partly in dactylic verse and partly crafted them into the form of Tragedies with dramatic characters. Taking his subjects from Holy Scripture, he wrote Comedies in the style of Menander's plays; he also imitated the Tragedies of Euripides and the lyric style of Pindar. He did this so well that in a short time, says Sozomen, he composed works equal in number and excellence to those famous among the Greeks in those genres, whether one considers the genius, the diction, the form, or the arrangement of the work. However, all these have long since perished. Whether the *Metaphrase of the Psalms*—which is extant today both in the Appendix to the *Library of the Fathers* (Paris, 1624) and published separately (Greek: Paris, 1580; Greek and Latin: Heidelberg, 1596)—belongs to him or his son is not yet sufficiently certain. It is commonly attributed to the younger Apollinarius.

Certainly, neither the Ancients nor the Moderns distinguish these two Apollinaris-figures with enough accuracy, making it quite easy to fall into error regarding them. To this same Apollinaris I would also attribute the tragedy titled *Christ the Suffering* <note>original: *Christus Patiens*</note>, which is usually printed among the works of Gregory of Nazianzus †.

**DIONYSIUS**, who grandly feigns the name of the *Areopagite* <note>Dionysius was a member of the Athenian council (the Areopagus) converted by St. Paul; however, the works discussed here are "spurious" or "Pseudo-Dionysian," written centuries later.</note>, seems to have written around this time. Many authors have long since demonstrated through many arguments that the works circulating under his name are entirely spurious; most recently, the highly learned Dallæus <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Protestant theologian.</note>, following others, proved this with numerous and invincible arguments in his book *On the Writings of Dionysius the Areopagite* (Geneva, 1666). It is therefore a matter of wonder that in this clear light of day, after so many arguments brighter than the sun itself and such manifest signs of falsehood, some can still be found today—such as Noël Alexandre, Emmanuel Schelstrate, etc.—who busy themselves defending these writings as the genuine works of Dionysius of Athens. For this reason, let me include the judgment of the most erudite Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar.</note> (which is found written in his own hand in a copy of Dionysius's *Works* preserved in our Most Serene King's library): *“The author,”* he says, *“is certainly most worthy of reading, and one who openly cuts the throat of the Papists’ cause in many matters. However, to believe that he was a contemporary of the Apostles is stupor; to wish to persuade others of it is madness. They must be asses who allow themselves to be persuaded of this.”*

Regarding the age in which this Impostor lived, not all scholars think the same. Dallæus and others with him push him back to the beginning of the sixth century, around the year 520 AD. The illustrious Pearson †, who refutes Dallæus's opinion on this matter with many points, refers him to the later times of Eusebius of Caesarea. I follow this view most closely and reckon that he lived around this time. There is no less controversy among the learned regarding the author himself than there is regarding his age. Among all opinions on this matter, the primary one—which even prevailed before the time of St. Maximus—is that the author of these books was Apollinaris, the Bishop of Laodicea. I confess that I held this opinion for a long time myself. But having weighed the matter better, I leave it to the learned to investigate whether these *Areopagite* writings should be attributed to Apollinaris the Father rather than the Son. Certainly, the Ancients count the Son as a heretic in other articles of faith and place him among the defenders of the Millennium <note>The belief in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ, which was later viewed as an error.</note>; yet this error, as St. Maximus \* once noted, is clearly condemned in these books. The Father, however, was sound in the faith; the Ancients speak of him in no other way, except that Socrates || once seems to involve him in the same heresy as the Son. The same Socrates says he was “a teacher of Greek literature,” <note>original Greek: ἑλληνικὸν λόγον διδάσκαλος</note> and Sozomen † describes him as “prepared for every kind of knowledge and literary form.” <note>original Greek: πρὸς παντοδαπὴν εἴδησιν καὶ λόγων ἰδέαν παρεσκευασμένος</note> He cultivated the schools and writings of the Gentiles so zealously that he was ejected from the Church on this account. Since he was born in Alexandria and educated, as it seems, in the Platonic School, he deeply drank in the dogmas of Platonic philosophy. 

From this comes that sublime and super-celestial theology concerning God, the divine Names and Perfections, the celestial Hierarchy, the Angels, etc., which fill every page in the *Areopagite* works. Indeed, an egg is not more like an egg than the perplexed and enigmatic doctrine handed down in these books is like that mystical theology which the Neoplatonists—Porphyry, Plotinus, Iamblichus, and later Proclus and others—taught to their disciples, especially around these times. Hence, Suidas † noted such an affinity between this Dionysius and the leaders of the Platonic school (chiefly Proclus), both in concepts and in the very wording, that he suspected (which is not surprising for one who believed the Areopagite was genuine) that the older Athenian philosophers had stolen Dionysius's works and claimed them as their own, suppressing his name so that they might appear to be the authors. Furthermore, the man’s poetic talent was perfectly suited to that affected, inflated, and turgid style of speaking—that empty and futile grandiloquence; and he knew how to vary this faculty of speaking excellently, according to the grammatical art in which he excelled. Finally, what wonder is it if he formed Christian theology according to the Platonic idea, when he composed the art of Grammar according to the form of the Christian religion? He was a man who wrote the history of the Hebrews' antiquity down to the reign of Saul in heroic verse, imitating Homer, and the rest of the Old Testament history...

# The Arian Century #

<margin>
4th Century, from the year 300 AD.

...did he [Apollinaris] not refine history into the form of Comedies, after the style of Menander's plays, and Tragedies, after the style of Euripides, by employing various characters? Nor was there any lack of those, especially from the school of Apollinaris the Younger, who were accustomed to forge writings under borrowed names—namely, those of Gregory Thaumaturgus <note>Gregory the "Wonder-worker," a 3rd-century bishop.</note>, Athanasius, and Julius of Rome—and to sell them to the public. Leontius discusses this at length in his book *On Sects* <note>original: "de Sectis, Act. 8. p. 527."</note>. Indeed, this was a common practice in many centuries; and no name more celebrated could be attached to a work than that of Dionysius the Areopagite, the disciple of Saint Paul and the first Bishop of Athens, who had been famous for his studies in Alexandria for many years. Regarding this conjecture which I now propose, I leave the judgment to others, for I am making no definitive claim on the matter. 

After these thoughts had remained hidden with me for a long time, and yet I was not entirely satisfied with my own conjecture, I consulted by letter the illustrious Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), a prominent Anglo-Irish scholar.</note>, whom I knew to hold the opinion that the *Areopagitica* <note>The works of the "Areopagite."</note> should be dated to the time of Gregory the Great <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604 AD).</note>, having first been forged, it seems, by a certain Latin writer. <margin>See the notes we shall include below from the illustrious Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh.</note>.</margin> I raised the objection that there are clear testimonies concerning Saint Dionysius that are nearly a full century older than Gregory. That learned man wrote back that this matter required further investigation; he suggested it is uncertain whether the "Dionysius" cited by the Severian heretics <note>A Monophysite group following Severus of Antioch.</note> for the phrase "one nature" <note>original: "μία φύσις" (mia physis). This refers to the controversial doctrine that Christ had only one nature.</note> in the conference held at Constantinople around the year 532 AD was a different person from the one whose works we possess today. 

He further suggested that in that contentious age, there was no shortage of Catholics (perhaps even Gregory himself, who lived in Constantinople for a long time) who might have forged a "Catholic" Dionysius to oppose the Easterners on the question of "one person" <note>original: "μία ὑπόστασις" (mia hypostasis). A key theological term regarding the Trinity and the nature of Christ.</note> and other controversies debated at that time. Thus, these works were placed in the archives of the Roman Church and first explicitly brought forward by Pope Gregory. The same illustrious man adds in his book *On the Priesthood of the Laity* <note>original: "de Sacerdot. Laicor. c. 8. §. 3. p. 389."</note> that no small light is shed on this matter by the letter of Anastasius the Librarian <note>A 9th-century historian and translator.</note>, which is prefixed to the *Scholia* <note>Explanatory comments or notes.</note> of Maximus and John of Scythopolis. The suspicion is increased by the fact that the Areopagite described the customs of the Romans rather than the Greeks (as Maximus himself once noted); it is hardly probable that this would be done by a Greek man, in terms of both ethnicity and language. 

He therefore advised me to examine this matter more diligently. I would have gladly obeyed according to my modest abilities, but as the printing presses could bear no further delay, and my aching eyes could no longer endure the exhaustion of poring over books, I deemed it sufficient for the present to have merely alerted the reader to these things. Meanwhile, I cannot help but notice that Ephrem of Antioch, who became Patriarch in 526 AD and wrote perhaps before the conference with the Severians, certainly around this time cited Dionysius the Areopagite as a witness for "one person" <note>original: "μία ὑπόστασις" (mia hypostasis)</note> in Christ and the union of natures—though in a sense entirely different from how the Severians cited him. Whatever the case may be, there exist under the name of this Pseudo-Dionysius:

*   **On the Celestial Hierarchy.**
*   **On the Divine Names.**
*   **On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.**
*   **On Mystical Theology.**
*   **Four Letters to Caius.**
*   **Letter to Dorotheus.**
*   **Letter to Sosipater.**
*   **Letter to Polycarp.**
*   **Letter to Demophilus.**
*   **Letter to Titus.**
*   **Letter to John the Evangelist.**
*   **Letter to Apollophanes.** (This is held only in Latin, from the version by Hilduin <note>Hilduin (d. 840), Abbot of Saint-Denis, who translated these works into Latin.</note>.)

The works of Dionysius were published in Latin together with the commentaries of Dionysius the Carthusian <note>A 15th-century mystic and theologian.</note> at **Cologne, 1536**, from the translations of Joannes Scotus <note>John Scotus Eriugena (c. 815–877), a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, Joannes Sarracenus (who flourished around the year 1170), and Thomas of Vercelli. A Greek and Latin edition was published in **Paris, 1615, folio**, and in **Antwerp, 1634, two volumes in folio**, augmented with the *Lives of Dionysius* by several writers and numerous dissertations by Halloix, Delrio, Lansselius, and Corderius. Finally, an edition was published in **Paris, 1644, two volumes in folio**, to which was added the *Defense of the Areopagite* by the most illustrious and noble Jean Chaumont.

# The Arian Century

<margin>
4th CENTURY, from 300 AD.
</margin>

"...the Steward <note>original: "nomus," likely referring to Methodius the Oeconomus</note> of the Church of Constantinople and the other legates of Emperor Michael presented [the books] to Louis the Pious on the very eve of the feast of St. Denis: as recorded by Hilduin <note>Abbot of St. Denis and chaplain to Louis the Pious.</note>, who was present then, in his *Preface to the Areopagitica*, and by Sigebert in his *Chronicle* for the year 824. Following this, in a letter to Hilduin (then Abbot of the Monastery of St. Denis near Paris), Emperor Louis commanded that he should compile the *Acts of Dionysius* from other writings as well as from the books (he said) written by Dionysius in his native tongue <note>Greek</note>, and that through our imperial command, your own diligent study, and the labor of translators, these should be explained and recorded in our own language <note>Latin</note>. Hilduin, in his response to the same, wrote: *Concerning the knowledge of the books which he wrote in his native tongue, and for whom he composed them at their request, the reading of them—which by God's grace and your command has been provided to us—satisfies us; by your dispensation, the translated works in our archives may now be offered to those who seek them.* From this it is gathered that, if not by Hilduin himself (an opinion toward which Cardinal Baronius inclines for the year 824), then at least by others at the command of Louis the Pious, the books of Dionysius were translated into Latin. From this source was drawn the translation of the *Letter to Apollophanes* (which does not survive in our Greek copies), the *Letter to John the Apostle*, and the greater part of the *Letter to Demophilus*, which is found inserted in Hilduin’s own *Areopagitica*. Around the year 1180, John the Saracen (a close friend of our own John of Salisbury) published his version of Dionysius; Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, did so around 1250; while Thomas, Abbot of Vercelli, wrote his commentaries on Dionysius around 1242." Thus far Ussher.

Anyone desiring to know more regarding the writings of Dionysius should consult the celebrated Pearson in *Vindiciae Ignatianae*, part I, chapter 10, where he treats them at length. Pearson points out several other writers of the fifth and sixth centuries who praised the writings of Dionysius: namely, Leontius (year 590), John Nesteutes (year 585), Ephrem, Patriarch of Antioch (year 526), Andrew of Caesarea (year 500), Juvenal of Jerusalem (year 431), and finally (as he himself contends), Gregory Nazianzen.

362 AD.
See Sozomen, book 5, ch. 15.
</margin>
TITUS, Bishop of the city of Bostra in Phoenicia <note>Modern-day Bosra, Syria.</note>, flourished around the year 361. In the following year, when Julian <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who attempted to revive Roman paganism.</note> had obtained the empire and was attempting to utterly extinguish the Christian religion, he used this method among others: he saw to it that the overseers and clergy of the churches were ejected from every city, so that the common people, destitute of pastors, might more easily slip into forgetfulness of their religion. However, he publicly pretended no other cause than that the clergy were exciting dissensions among the people. To this end, he exhorted the people of Bostra to expel their bishop, Titus, by a public herald's proclamation. Titus, having sent a petition to the Prince in his own name and that of his clergy, testified that the Christians in that city were no fewer in number than the Pagans; yet they remained quiet and meditated no sedition. 

<margin>Letter 52.</margin> 
Seizing upon this statement and desiring to make Titus hated by the common people, the Emperor warned the Bostrians in a rescript <note>A formal written reply to a petition; this letter still exists among Julian's correspondence.</note> that Titus was their slanderer, and that he was traducing them by claiming they abstained from sedition not of their own will, but only by his exhortation. He thereby incited the people to expel him from their city as a public enemy. After the death of Julian, Titus took part in the Synod of Antioch held under Jovian in the year 363, and he fortified the Profession of Faith offered to the Emperor with his signature. He died under Emperor Valens around the year 371.

* Jerome, On Illustrious Men, ch. 102.
</margin>

Our author must be of a more recent date, since he frequently praises Gregory Nazianzen, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom, Isidore of Pelusium, and Cyril of Alexandria. In these commentaries, the author cites his own *Exposition on Matthew*, though whether it has been published is entirely unknown to me. # FABIUS MARIUS VICTORINUS, <term>V. C.</term> <note>original: "Vir Clarissimus," an honorary title for a person of senatorial rank.</note> an African by birth, a rhetorician by profession, and a pagan in religion until his old age. During the reign of Constantius <note>Emperor Constantius II, reigned 337–361 AD.</note>, he taught rhetoric at Rome for many years; from his school emerged many men who were not only learned but also of noble and senatorial rank. He was so celebrated for his eloquence that he earned the honor of a statue dedicated to him in the Roman Forum. At last, in his extreme old age, he began to profess faith in Christ, but at first timidly and under a veil of secrecy. Simplicianus <note>A mentor to St. Augustine and later Bishop of Milan.</note>, to whom he had confided his secret, urged him to make it public, telling him he would not count him among the Christians unless he saw him in the Church of Christ. Victorinus mocked this, saying: *“So, do walls make Christians?”* Eventually, he grew ashamed of his vanity and said to Simplicianus: *“Let us go to the church; I want to become a Christian.”* Having been instructed in the elements of the Christian faith, he was reborn through baptism, to the wonder of Rome and the joy of the Church; the proud saw it and were angry, they gnashed their teeth and wasted away—to use the words of Augustine <margin>* Ibid. ch. 5.</margin> on this matter. And when the priests, respecting his modesty, allowed him to give his formal confession of faith (which was usually done from an elevated place) in private, he refused, wishing instead to pronounce it in the sight of the whole Church, while the entire crowd of bystanders applauded and shouted the name of Victorinus. In the year 362, when Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, who attempted to revive paganism and restrict Christian education.</note> passed a law forbidding Christians to teach oratory and pagan literature, Victorinus joyfully resigned his chair, preferring—as Augustine says—to desert the "talkative school" rather than Your Word [Lord]. He seems to have died around the year 370, or survived only a few years after.

While still a pagan, he translated many books of the Platonists into the Latin language, but these versions have long since been lost. In addition to his commentaries on Cicero's *Rhetoric*, his translation of Porphyry's *Isagoge*, and his three books *On the Five Voices*, *On the Pronunciation of Letters*, and *On the Theory of Verse* (which have been frequently published), there exist in the *Library of the Fathers* (Volume IV, pages 253, 294) works written by him after his conversion:

<margin>|| On Famous Men, ch. 101.</margin>

> *Four books on the Most Holy Trinity against the Arians*, of which Jerome || writes: *“He wrote very obscure books against Arius in a dialectical style, which are understood only by the learned.”*

*To Justin the Manichean against the Two Principles of the Manicheans.*
*On the Beginning of the Day, whether it starts at evening or in the morning.* These two small books were first brought to light by Jacques Sirmond <note>A French Jesuit scholar (1559–1651) and patristics editor.</note> among the *Dogmatic Works of the Ancients* (Paris, 1630, in octavo).

*On the Generation of the Divine Word against Candidus the Arian.*
*Three Hymns on accepting the Homoousion* <note>The theological term meaning "of the same substance," used to define the relationship between God the Father and God the Son.</note>.
*Poem on the Seven Maccabees.*

<margin>* Preface to the Dogmatic Works of the Ancients. * Preface to the Epistle to the Galatians, Vol. IX, p. 158.</margin>

Commentaries on several of St. Paul's Epistles, which still lie hidden as manuscripts in the library of the Monastery of Évreux <note>original: "Herevallensis," referring to the Abbey of Lyre in the Diocese of Évreux, France.</note> in France (see Sirmond's *Preface to the Dogmatic Works of the Ancients*). Regarding these, Jerome writes *: 
> *Preoccupied with the study of secular literature, he was entirely ignorant of the Holy Scriptures; and no one, however eloquent, can argue well about that which he does not know.*

Victorinus’s style was not particularly successful; in his dogmatic works, it is convoluted and unpleasant, retaining hardly any traces of his celebrated eloquence. However, the most learned Sirmond, who has read them, testifies that in the commentaries the style is plainer and clearer. Ultimately, his works require an attentive and sharp-eyed reader. Since he spent the much larger part of his life in the study of pagan literature and only embraced Christianity at an advanced age...

**CANDIDUS**, an Arian by sect (nothing more about him has been discovered by me so far), flourished around the year 364. He wrote a book *to Marius Victorinus on the Divine Generation*, which survives together with Victorinus's refutation, appended to the *Commentaries on Genesis* by Ziegler <note>Bernhard Ziegler (1496–1552), a Lutheran theologian.</note>, published in Basel, 1548, in folio.
