**ULPHILAS**, or Urphilas <note>Better known today as Wulfila (c. 311–383 AD).</note>, a Goth by birth, was descended from Christian ancestors who, during the reign of Gallienus, were taken captive by barbarians from Sadagolthina, a village in Cappadocia. After the death of Theophilus (who was present and signed at the Council of Nicaea), he became the Bishop of the Goths. At first, he served among the Catholics, but later he defected to the camp of the Arians. Historians do not entirely agree on his dates. Philostorgius \* explicitly places him under Constantine the Great, writing that he served as an ambassador <note>original: "πρεσϐευόμενον"</note> to the Emperor and was held in great honor. However, Socrates †, Sozomenus ||, and Theodoret \* more correctly, in my judgment, consistently refer him to the times of Valens, during which he most flourished, around the year 365. Indeed, one might suspect that Philostorgius—who wonderfully extols Ulphilas as an Arian—assigned him to the era and friendship of Constantine in order to more impressively show the antiquity of Arianism’s spread among the barbarians. 

The account by Sozomenus seems most likely: that Ulphilas, sent as an envoy to Constantius, imprudently attended the Council of Constantinople in the year 360, yet remained in communion with the Catholics; only later, while serving as an envoy to Valens, was he seduced by the deceits of Acacius and Eudoxius <note>Influential Arian bishops who sought to compromise the Nicene Creed.</note> and embraced the Arian heresy, which he then spread through his nation. He led many of the Goths not only to a gentler way of life but also to the Christian religion. He held such authority among them that his words, according to Theodoret, were regarded as unshakeable laws. He was the first inventor of Gothic letters and translated all the books of Holy Scripture into his native tongue. Regarding this, Philostorgius notes a detail not unworthy of mention: that in this version, Ulphilas omitted the *Books of Kings* (which includes the books of Samuel and Chronicles) because these books contain records of wars, and the Gothic people, being "war-loving" <note>original: "φιλοπόλεμῳ"</note>, had more need of a bridle than a spur to incite them to military impulses. This work of Ulphilas seems to have long since perished, unless perhaps that Gothic version of the Four Gospels is a part of it, which [Franciscus] Junius and [Thomas] Marshall published in Gothic and Anglo-Saxon with a glossary and notes at Dordrecht in 1665, in quarto. Let those skilled in these letters offer their judgment on the matter. Certainly, that version appears to be very ancient.

† Book 27.
</margin>
**DAMASUS**, the son of a certain Antonius, was Spanish by race and a Carpetanian from Mantua <note>Modern-day Madrid.</note> by birth, though some claim he was from Tarragona and others from Igedita in Lusitania. He was a Deacon under Liberius in the Roman Church, then a Priest, and finally appointed Bishop in the year 366—while in the meantime another faction ordained the Deacon Ursinus (or Ursicinus) as Bishop of Rome. The matter was conducted with great contention and much bloodshed, so much so that in a single day (as noted by Ammianus †), 137 citizens were killed. Furthermore, Damasus raged against Ursinus's party with immense cruelty for a long time, if we believe what Faustinus and Marcellinus tell in the preface they added to their *Book of Prayers*. At last, after Ursinus was defeated and put to flight, Damasus held the see in peace. Around the year 369, having held a Synod of 90 bishops at Rome, he condemned Auxentius of Milan and the acts of the Council of Ariminum, and confirmed the Nicene faith. In the year 373, he held another Synod at Rome, attended by Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, in which he deposed Apollinaris and his disciple Timothy for the heresy recently made public, and struck their followers and dogmas with anathema. In the year 381, the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople gathered for a Synod at Rome...

### SPURIOUS WORKS.

The *Book of the Popes* <note>original: "Liber Pontificalis"</note> or *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, commonly attributed to Anastasius the Librarian <note>A 9th-century historian</note>. However, manuscript copies older than Anastasius testify that it is not his; authors older than Anastasius, such as Walafrid Strabo, Rabanus Maurus, Bede, and the legates of Pope Agatho (who began his papacy around 678), cite the work under the title *The Acts of the Pontiffs*. It is a common opinion that the first part of this work should be attributed to our Damasus, but it could be shown by infinite arguments, if necessary, that this is entirely false. The style and the structure of the whole work are against it, being clearly unworthy of Damasus; the deep silence of Jerome, who listed his works after Damasus’s death, also argues against it, to say nothing of other points. Certainly, it is more than certain that the *Book of the Popes* which exists today arose and received its growth from various catalogs of Roman Pontiffs, according to the varying fortunes of the times and the talent of the editors. These catalogs are discussed by Bucherius, Labbe, Henschen, Papebroch, Schelstrate, and most recently and accurately of all, by Pearson and Dodwell.

We will compress into a few words what seems most likely to us regarding this matter: an anonymous author who wrote under the Emperor Alexander Severus laid the first foundations of such a work. The little work itself has perished, with only the title surviving, as is clear from the index of the preface to the book *On the Division and Generations of Nations* published by Labbe after Canisius in the *New Library of Manuscripts*, Vol. I, p. 309, where these words are found: *The names of the Bishops of Rome, and who presided for how many years*. The author of the Catalog that ends with Pope Liberius expressed this small index and brought it down to his own time, noting only the names of the Popes, the succession, and the dates coinciding with the Emperors and Consuls. Cuspinianus was the first to insert this into his commentaries; Aegidius Bucherius provided a slightly more complete version in his *Commentary on Victor*, p. 269; would that it had reached us in a purer state! The compiler of the Catalog who lived under Justinian increased this with some additions; it was first published by Henschen, then by Papebroch. Later, others interpolated this catalog and added not only the names and dates of the Roman Pontiffs, but also their fathers, their ethnicity, their places of burial, ordinations, and decrees, as well as the length of the vacancies of the see; and thus at last the *Book of the Popes* grew into this form which we now possess.

**E U Z O I U S**, a follower of the Arian faction <note>Arianism was the belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, rather than co-eternal</note>, yet distinct from that other Euzoio, the Bishop of Antioch, who is mentioned so often in the Church history of this period. While still a youth, he had Gregory of Nazianzus as a classmate in the School of Caesarea in Palestine; there, both applied themselves to the study of eloquence under the rhetorician Thespesius. After Acacius died in the year 366, Euzoius was appointed Bishop of the Church of Caesarea. <margin>See Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 73.</margin> Indeed, no small contention flourished regarding this see; Cyril of Jerusalem first ordained Philumenus, then his own nephew Gelasius, while Eutychius of Eleutheropolis ordained a certain old man named Cyril. However, when these men withdrew due to their mutual dispute, Euzoius held the seat undisturbed. He was a clearly learned and diligent man who, with great labor, restored and renewed the Library which the Martyr Pamphilus had collected (primarily from the books of Origen) and deposited at Caesarea, which had become corrupted by the passage of time and human neglect. Under the reign of Theodosius, as the affairs of the Arians were wavering and clearly collapsing, he himself was driven from his Church around the year 380. <margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 113.</margin> Jerome mentions only these things regarding his writings *, to which I have nothing to add; various and manifold Treatises of his are said to exist, which are very easy to recognize.

<margin>368 AD.</margin>
**E P I P H A N I U S**, a Palestinian by birth, was born in the village of Bezanduca located in the territory of Eleutheropolis, born, it seems, to Jewish parents. I pass over the details regarding his parents, education, conversion, and his entire life-course recorded by his disciples John and Polybius, the writers of the *Life of Epiphanius*; <margin>This *Life* exists in Greek and Latin in Epiphanius, Volume II, Petau's edition.</margin> for these are uncertain, not to say for the most part legendary. While still a young man he set out for Egypt, where he fell into the snares of the Gnostics, and especially into the company of certain women, from whom he learned the secrets of that detestable sect. However, he escaped their allurements; and when he had diligently examined the customs and institutions of the Egyptian ascetics <note>early Christian hermits and monks who practiced self-denial</note>, he returned to his homeland in the twentieth year of his age. He lived for some time under the discipline of the great Hilarion, the father of the Palestinian monks. Later, he founded the "Old Monastery" near his aforementioned native village, which he himself governed. Around the year 368, he was promoted to the bishopric of Salamis in Cyprus, a city later called Constantia and the metropolis of the whole island. Positioned there in the midst of a multitude of people, in a great maritime city, he attained the greatest celebrity of name through his speech, writings, and the utmost simplicity of his character. In the year 382, he was summoned to Rome by imperial letters to judge the cause of Paulinus regarding the see of Antioch; in that city, the most holy Paula, widow of Toxotius, received him with kind hospitality. After some years, great and long-lasting disputes arose between him and Bishop John <margin>Jerome, *Letter to Pammachius*, p. 166.</margin> in the Church of Jerusalem. These flared up to such an extent that John received Epiphanius with a gaping mouth, laughter, and a wrinkled nose <note>gestures of mockery and contempt</note> along with his choir; he even went so far as to send an Archdeacon to order him to be silent. And when on another occasion Epiphanius was about to deliver a sermon there, John himself stood up and, in the middle of the assembly, denounced the venerable old man as an "Anthropomorphite" <note>someone who believes God has a physical human body</note>, while Epiphanius was present and listening, pub-

# The Century of Arianism.

<margin>4th CENTURY, from 300 AD.</margin>
...exposed him <note>Referring to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, from the previous page</note> to the common people. The longer this dispute lasted, the more fiercely the flame erupted; on one side, Epiphanius was charging John with holding the dogmas of Arius and Origen <note>Origen (c. 185–253) was an early Christian scholar whose complex allegorical interpretations of the Bible became highly controversial in the 4th century</note>, while on the other, John accused Epiphanius of having torn down a veil from the Church of Anablatha <note>Epiphanius had torn a curtain because it bore an image of Christ or a saint, which he considered a violation of biblical law</note>, of violating the legal rights of the See of Jerusalem, and of ordaining Paulinianus (Jerome’s brother) in the monastery "At the Priest's." Consequently, many letters and defenses were sent back and forth; many friends frequently intervened to settle this lawsuit, but it was all in vain. John's wounded spirit could be soothed by no remedies, until several years later—once the cause was more fully understood and publicly explained through Jerome’s letters to Pammachius—shame itself finally restrained the man.

<margin>Socrates, Book 6, Ch. 10. Sozomen, Book 8, Ch. 14. Many letters of Jerome, Epiphanius, and Theophilus among Jerome's Works, Vol. II, p. 309.</margin>
But there was not yet an end to the labors and contentions for Epiphanius. For Theophilus, the Bishop of Alexandria—who had expelled certain monks from Nitria <note>The "Tall Brothers," famous ascetics in the Egyptian desert</note> for being too favorable toward Origen (whom John Chrysostom <note>The Archbishop of Constantinople, famed for his eloquence</note> had deemed worthy of hospitality and favor when they fled to Constantinople)—drew Epiphanius to his side. Epiphanius soon gathered a Council of Cypriot bishops and condemned Origen and his books, sending letters about this matter to others and to Chrysostom. Shortly after, led by the advice of Theophilus, he personally sought out Constantinople; however, he refused to meet or communicate with Chrysostom unless Origen was first condemned and the Nitrian monks were cast out. But when he made little progress and was sharply rebuked by Chrysostom (partly for other reasons and partly because he had encroached upon Chrysostom’s episcopal rights), and having been received with little kindness even by the Empress Eudoxia herself, he departed from Constantinople. It is said that as he was leaving, he said goodbye to Chrysostom with this formula: *I hope you do not die a bishop*; to which John Chrysostom replied in turn: *I hope you do not reach your homeland.* An angry divinity granted the wishes of both. Chrysostom was soon deposed from his see and died in exile; Epiphanius, having boarded a ship, met his final day in the middle of his journey in the year 402, or at least at the beginning of the next; he was indeed of extreme old age, being nearly in his hundredth year of life and his thirty-sixth of his episcopate. Indeed, if Polybius (his disciple and traveling companion) is to be believed, Epiphanius himself told the Emperor Arcadius as he was leaving Constantinople that he was 115 years and 3 months old.

<margin>* Defense 1 against Rufinus, p. 222. Defense 2, p. 233. † Codex 122. || On Illustrious Men, ch. 114.</margin>
He was a man most adorned with piety and the rest of the Christian virtues, and learned in Hebrew, Syriac, Egyptian, Greek, and Latin; for this reason he was known to Jerome as "The Five-Tongued" <note>original: Πεντάγλωττος (*Pentaglottos*)</note>. He was most skilled in ecclesiastical antiquities, yet too credulous in admitting little stories without examination, and not very accurate in distinguishing time periods—a fact to which his history of the Arian heresy alone bears witness. In the debates he undertook against impious heresies, in the judgment of Photius †, he was for the most part weak; "his language was humble" <note>original: τῶν δὲ ῥητῶν ταπεινός (*tōn de rhētōn tapeinos*)</note> and clearly such as was fitting for one who took no account of Attic elegance <note>High-style classical Greek</note>. Jerome || agreed, saying: *His writings are read by the learned for their content, and by the simpler folk also for their words.*

## W R I T I N G S.

*The Ancoratus* <note>The "Well-Anchored Man," a defense of the Trinity</note>, or *A Discourse on the Faith*, written around the year 373 at the request of the priests of Suedra (a city in Pamphylia) and the Governor Palladius, so that he might give them the Catholic doctrine regarding the Holy Trinity—and especially the Holy Spirit—and restrain by his writing the Macedonian heresy <note>The Macedonians, or Pneumatomachi ("Spirit-fighters"), denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit</note> which was spreading among them.

<margin>* In the place cited.</margin>
*The Panarion* <note>Literally "The Medicine Chest" or "The Bread Basket"</note>, or *Against Eighty Heresies*, comprised of three volumes in seven sections. It was begun in the year of Christ 374, the eleventh year of Valens and Valentinian, at the request of the Archimandrites <note>abbots or heads of monasteries</note> Acacius and Paul. Their letter sent to Epiphanius on this matter still survives, prefixed to the *Panarion*, along with Epiphanius’s letter in response. Photius says * this work is more abundant and useful than all the treatises written against heresies before him; for it gained no small increase from the writings of Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Hippolytus, and other ancients. Indeed, Epiphanius left nothing devised by them untouched, and added what he had worked out by his own effort. He composed a catalog of these heresies, beginning from "Barbarism" and running through every rank.

*Eight Orations:* namely, *On the Feast of Palms, On the Burial of Christ, On the Resurrection of Christ, On the Assumption of Christ, In Praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary, On Palm Sunday, On the Mysteries of Numbers, On the Resurrection of Christ*; these seem to belong to a certain Epiphanius the Younger. For several men named Epiphanius held the office of Bishop in Cyprus.
There exist Greek manuscripts under the name of Epiphanius in the Imperial Library [of Vienna]: *An Explanation of the verse, "The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God" [1 Cor 2:10]; and on the verse, "Of that day and hour no one knows" [Matt 24:36].* A review of 22 works on the *Hexaemeron* <note>The Six Days of Creation</note>, etc., as witnessed by Lambeck in his Commentaries, book 3, pages 163, 164, and 196.

OPTATUS, an African by birth, Bishop of the city of Milevis in Numidia, and a most fierce opponent of the Donatists <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa that argued that the validity of sacraments depended on the moral purity of the clergy</note>. He flourished around the year 368 while Damasus held the keys of the Roman Church <note>Pope Damasus I, reigned 366–384 AD</note>. As for the fact that Siricius <note>Pope Siricius, reigned 384–399 AD</note> closes the line in the catalog of Roman Pontiffs which Optatus provides in his second book, Baronius* suspects that he is much more recent and that the name of Siricius was added by a scribe who copied the book during Siricius’s time. For Jerome† explicitly records that Optatus wrote under the Emperor Valens; but Siricius did not obtain the Roman Chair until the reign of Theodosius in the year 384 or the following, as Baronius and others maintain. Furthermore, Optatus himself in two places, speaking of the persecution of Diocletian which began in the year 303, says that sixty and some odd years had passed; here Baronius rightly notes that this phrase, *"and what runs beyond,"* signifies the greater part of the current decade.
He wrote against Parmenian, the Bishop of the Donatist sect at Carthage, seven books *On the Schism of the Donatists*, in which he reveals the origin and progress of the entire schism; the puffed-up, insolent, and savage manners of the schismatics...

<header>The Century of Arianism.</header>

<margin>4th CENTURY, from 300 AD.</margin>
...he depicts [the Donatists], refutes their frauds and lies, and defends the cause of the Catholic Church against their brazen slanders with no less praise for his modesty and gentleness than for his learning and sharp wit. Jerome mentions only six books written by Optatus against the Donatists; indeed, Optatus himself, in the first book, when giving an account of his purpose, promises that he will complete the matter in six books. Furthermore, the seventh book differs greatly in style from the preceding ones and introduces contrary dogmas. Thus, one might not undeservedly suspect that the seventh book is the work of an ancient author, though different from Optatus. If it is indeed to be considered his, it must necessarily have been composed by him some time after the first six books. Among the various editions of these books, the following stand out: the *Parisian* edition of 1563, illustrated with observations and a history of the Donatists by François Baudouin; the *Parisian* edition of 1631, with the commentaries of Gabriel de l'Aubespine; and the *London* edition of the same year with the notes and emendations—certainly most learned—of Méric Casaubon in octavo. But the Parisian edition published by Philippe Le Prieur <note>original: "Philip. Priorius"</note> surpasses all others both in the elegance of its type and the sheer volume of nearly all published notes, *Paris, 1679, folio.* He placed the notes of l'Aubespine, Méric Casaubon, Barthius, and a certain learned anonymous author at the bottom of each page, to which he also prefixed his own annotations. He relegated the acts of the Conference of Carthage (first published by P. Masson), Baudouin’s history of this matter, and the more extensive annotations on Optatus by both Baudouin and l'Aubespine to an appendix; he also joined the works of Facundus of Hermiane, and finally added l'Aubespine’s two books on the ancient rites of the Church and other small works.

### PACIANUS,
a Spaniard by birth, from a noble family, and Bishop of Barcelona <note>original: "Barcelonæ sive Barcenonis"</note>, an illustrious city of Spain situated near the peaks of the Pyrenees. He flourished around the year 370. That he was married is proven by the most certain evidence: his son Flavius Dexter, a Praetorian Prefect and friend of Jerome. Francisco de Bivar <note>original: "Fr. Bivarius," a 17th-century Spanish scholar</note> concludes that Pacianus fathered him by a lawful wife before becoming a bishop because he is praised by Jerome† for his "chastity and eloquence." Bivar argues that such things could not be said of an adulterer, no matter how much he repented. As if, indeed, every marriage—especially of the clergy—however honorable, must be considered adultery! Yet the Apostle clearly pronounced that "marriage is honorable among all and the bed undefiled" <note>Hebrews 13:4</note>. Pacianus died at a very great age under the Emperor Theodosius before the year 390. He wrote various small works, including the one to which he gave the title <term>Κέρβος</term> <note>original Greek: "Kerbos," likely a corruption of "Cervus" or "The Stag." It refers to a pagan New Year's custom where people dressed as animals.</note>, according to Jerome*. I confess that I was long stuck on this word; at last, the celebrated Colomiès removed the doubt. He notes that the Greek word crept into the text from the version by Sophronius, and that it should read *Cervus* (The Stag), as is clear from Jerome’s manuscript in the Lambeth Library. This "Stag" was a type of pagan folk-play among the ancient Gentiles in Gaul, and perhaps also in Spain. To rebuke this custom, Pacianus wrote a book titled *The Stag* or *The Little Stag*, which he himself praises in his *Exhortation to Penance*, though it has been lost to the ravages of time. Those works of Pacianus which still exist include *Three Letters against the Novatians* <note>The Novatians were a rigorist sect who refused to readmit those who had lapsed during persecutions</note> (which Jerome calls a "book against the Novatians"), an *Exhortation to Penance*, and a *Booklet on Baptism for Catechumens*. These were published by Du Tillet in *Paris, 1538, in quarto*; by Paolo Manuzio in *Rome, 1564, in folio*; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 4, pages 305 and 315.

### GREGORY,
a Spaniard by nationality, from the province of Baetica, and Bishop of Illiberis <note>modern-day Elvira</note>, a town in that same province near the Pyrenean mountains. He flourished around the year 370 AD. Pseudo-Dexter and his commentator Bivar identify him as the same person as Gregory, the Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls mentioned by Sulpicius* and Pope Innocent†, and they claim he did not ascend the episcopal throne until the year 390. But Saint Jerome* is much more to be heeded; he calls him a Bishop of the Spains, makes him a contemporary of Lucifer of Cagliari <note>A bishop known for his fierce opposition to Arianism</note>, and writes that he never involved himself in Arian depravity. He was indeed an implacable enemy of the Arians, with whom—even if they returned to the Church—he [refused to share] communion...

4th CENTURY, from 300 AD.

Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 105.

† See Dissertation 14, numbers 5, 6, etc., page 716.

...did not wish to provide care <note>likely referring to providing communion to those he deemed heretical</note>. What he is said to have suffered on that account from Hosius and others can be seen in the writings of Faustinus and Marcellinus in their *Libellus Precum* <note>A "Book of Petitions" written by priests of the Luciferian schism to the Emperors</note>. Certainly, the Emperor Theodosius, having sent a rescript <note>a formal imperial response or decree</note> to Cynegius, the Pretorian Prefect (which survives at the end of the *Libellus Precum*), gave orders that he should defend and protect this praiseworthy bishop of the sacred law and other similar priests from the injuries of wicked men and heretics. In the year 392, he was already in extreme old age; however, the compiler of the *Chronicle of Dexter* (a forged work) extends his life until the year 423, which forced Francisco Bivar to claim that he died nearly a centenarian. Jerome says, "He composed various treatises in a moderate style, and among them, an elegant little book *On the Faith*." Indeed, there exists under our Gregory's name in the *Library of the Fathers* a book *On the Faith against the Arians*, inscribed to the Empress Flaccilla (some manuscripts have Galla Placidia), which is nevertheless discovered to be the work of Faustinus the Priest. However, in the *Roman Code of Canons* published by Pasquier Quesnel, three formulas of faith or booklets are found: he attributes the first to Marcellinus and the second to Faustinus (both priests) †, while the third, poorly inscribed to Gregory Nazianzen, Quesnel assigns to Gregory of Elvira, believing it to be the same book *On the Faith* mentioned by Jerome.

**EPHREM**, a Syrian by nationality, from Edessa as some wish, or more correctly from Nisibis according to others. He flourished in the year 370. From his early youth, he practiced himself in "monastic philosophy" <note>a term often used for the ascetic life of a monk</note>, and by his own effort, he progressed so far in the studies of deeper philosophy that he easily grasped even the most difficult theorems. Leaving his solitude, he went to Edessa so that he could benefit not only himself but others as well; consequently, many men of great name among the Syrians handed themselves over to his teaching. Having been made a Deacon of the Church of Edessa, he refused to ascend to higher ranks. When he was elected to the Episcopacy by common decree and men were sent to seize him, he immediately ran into the marketplace and, acting indecently, pretended to be out of his mind; fleeing from there, he remained hidden until another had been ordained. He traveled to Caesarea in Cappadocia for no other reason than to see Basil the Great and spend time with him; Basil, admiring the man, looked up to him greatly for the sake of his learning and piety. He vehemently detested the heretics who corrupted the doctrine of the Catholic Church, and he often refuted their frauds and deceits with marvelous dexterity and sharpness. He brought help to the city of Edessa when it was suffering from a most severe famine, both by his voice and example, by rebuking the rich and taking the care of the needy upon himself. The *Encomium* <note>a speech of high praise</note> written about him by Gregory of Nyssa will supply more to the curious reader, to say nothing of others. This most holy man, surnamed the "Prophet of the Syrians" (according to Hebediesu * in the catalog he published on the books of the Chaldeans), died around the year 378. When about to die, he forbade with a heavy interdict that they should praise him with a funeral oration, bury him in precious clothing, or establish a special tomb for his body. He knew no language other than his native Syrian (Syriac), in which he was considered the most eloquent of all in his time. Indeed, his discourses possessed this peculiar grace—noted by both Sozomen * and Jerome †—that even when translated into the Greek language, they retained the sharpness of his sublime genius, the splendor of his oratory, and the density of his thoughts; nor did they recede much from their domestic and native beauty. In these works, Photius * says he rightly admires "the persuasive, the pleasing, and in general how much sweetness overflows" <note>original: "τὸ πεῖθον, τὸ ἡδύνον, καὶ ὅλως εἰς ὅσον βρύει τὸ ἡδύ"</note>, how deeply the power of persuasion penetrates into the souls of men, how much pleasantness flows forth, and finally, how filled they are with an abundance of emotion.

<margin>
† Place cited.
</margin>
Ephrem wrote infinite things: more than a thousand *Orations*, according to Photius †; Sozomen says "three million lines" <note>original: "τὰς τριακοσίας μυριάδας ἐπῶν"</note>; and among these are many hymns and poems elaborated by him, which the Syrians—whom he had seen charmed by elegance of words and the harmony of modulation—would recite in the praises of the saints. Nearly all his writings were translated into Greek while he was still alive; they were once held in such honor that, according to Jerome's report, they were publicly recited in certain churches after the reading of the Scriptures. The minor objections usually raised against his writings are for the most part light and futile. If any occur which are less [worthy] of the holy Father...

...things less dignified, or which seem not to fit well in other places, should be attributed to our ignorance of the Syriac idioms <note>original: "Syriacè loquendi modorum"</note> or to poor translations made from other translations, rather than to Ephrem’s lack of refinement or knowledge. Indeed, if there were truly errors, they ought to be forgiven out of respect for the man’s great zeal, simplicity, and piety. Gerard Voss <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), the Provost of Tongeren and a Dutch scholar known for organizing patristic texts</note> collected many of Ephrem’s works, translated them into Latin, and organized them into three volumes. These were first published in Rome in the year 1593, then in Cologne in 1603, and finally in Antwerp in 1619 in folio format. I wish we could be so fortunate as to eventually enjoy, if not the Syriac originals (which are found in great numbers in the Bodleian Library <note>At Oxford University</note>, the Leiden Library <note>Lugduno-Batavâ</note>, and elsewhere), then at least the Greek versions. This would provide the opportunity to approach the sources a little more closely and to judge the translations we currently have with more certainty.

Furthermore, a Song of Ephrem concerning *Mary and the Magi*, translated from Syriac into Latin by Ecchellensis, was published in *Rome* in 1645.

</margin>
Moreover, Photius mentions 49 homilies or sermons of Ephrem seen and read by him*, whose titles he enumerates. Which of these are contained in the Vossian edition cannot be judged with certainty due to the similarity of titles and the lack of the Greek text. However, it is clear that many of them are present there. He also mentions an *Oration delivered to the monks of Metebinos regarding many Virtues and Vices*; whether this is found among the Vossian works, we can only guess with little certainty, though it seems to be found in the first volume, not far from the beginning. Indeed, it might not be unjustly considered that many small works in the Vossian edition do not have Ephrem as their author; but how many or which they are is not easy to judge for the reasons stated above. There exists a Greek manuscript, together with other prayers and hymns, in the possession of the distinguished man John Batteley, Archdeacon of Canterbury, a lengthy Prayer of our Ephrem with this title: <term>A prayer of our holy father Ephrem the Syrian, said as a confession whenever one wishes, but especially on Sundays. <note>original: "Τοῦ ὁσίου πατρὸς Ἐφραῒμ τοῦ Σύρου εὐχὴ λεγομένη εἰς ἐξομολόγησιν ὅταν θέλει, μάλιστα δ' ἐν ταῖς Κυριακαῖς."</note></term>

Furthermore, Hebediesu the Chaldean-Syrian, a writer of a later century, writes in *Among his Countrymen*, page 25, that there still exist in the Syriac language the *Commentaries of Saint Ephrem on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, the books of Kings, David [the Psalms], Isaiah, the Twelve Minor Prophets, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel; also books and letters on the faith of the Church; metrical prayers; exhortations; songs; all the offices for the dead; alphabetic arrangements; <note>This refers to acrostic poems, a signature style of Ephrem, where each verse begins with a consecutive letter of the alphabet.</note> disputes with the Jews as well as against Marcion, Bardesanes, Marcion, and the Ophites; <note>The source text repeats Marcion twice, though it likely intended Mani, another major rival of Ephrem's theology.</note> and finally, the destruction of the impiety of Julian.* <note>The Roman Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363).</note>

# The Arian Century.

<margin>
4th CENTURY, from 300 AD.

370.
† Possevin, *Apparatus on Basil*.
|| Labbe, *On Writers*, addition to Volume I, page 737.
* See *Magdeburg Centuries*, Century 4, chapter 10. <note>The *Magdeburg Centuries* was a massive 16th-century Protestant history of the church, organized by centuries.</note>
† Oration 20, page 324.
</margin>

**BASIL**, called *the Great*, was born of an illustrious and ancient lineage to most holy parents, Basil and Emmelia. Among his ancestors were those who shone with the glory of being Confessors <note>A "Confessor" was someone who suffered for the Christian faith during persecutions but was not killed.</note> under the Emperor Maximian. *Possevin* †, *Labbe* ||, and others * record that Basil’s father was a Bishop; however, this is said without the slightest authority from the ancient writers, as far as I know. *Nazianzen* † <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil's closest friend.</note> does indeed call him a <term>universal teacher of virtue</term> <note>original Greek: κοινὸν παιδευτὴν ἀρετῆς</note>, whom the region of Pontus held up at that time, but that does not refer to the episcopal office. Basil himself was a Cappadocian by birth—or to speak more precisely, from Pontus—and a citizen of Neocaesarea, if we are to go by conjectures; for what some say about Helenopontus is supported by no author.

After completing his early education at home under his father, he devoted himself to literature at Antioch under Libanius <note>Libanius was one of the most famous Greek rhetoricians of the 4th century.</note>, then at Caesarea in Palestine, then at Constantinople, and finally at Athens. He was received there with great fame attached to his name as a student of Himerius and Prohaeresius. Above all his colleagues, however, he held Gregory Nazianzen as his dearest friend, a most close companion for his whole life as well as his studies. Having finished his course of literary studies at Athens, he returned to his homeland. He was first made a Lector in the Church of Caesarea, then ordained a Deacon by Meletius of Antioch, and soon after raised to the order of the Priesthood. But since his mind inclined toward the discipline of a more rigorous life, he sought retreat. In the wilderness of Pontus, enjoying the company of his friend Gregory, he zealously promoted the monastic life both by his example and by the rules he established. Eventually recalled from the wilderness, he took up the deputy care of the Church of Caesarea under Bishop Eusebius, having by then returned to his favor. Around the year 370, when Eusebius was translated to a "higher and more blessed seat" <note>A polite way of saying the Bishop died.</note>, Basil succeeded him in the episcopal office.

Most firm for the sake of truth, he waged heavy legal and theological battles throughout his life against heretics of every sect. He nobly opposed Eustathius of Sebaste and the entire flock of Arians who were breaking in against the Catholics. He patiently listened to Modestus, the Prefect of Cappadocia, who (while the Emperor Valens himself was then staying at Caesarea) threatened him with nothing but crosses, lashes, and a thousand kinds of death. Basil bore reproaches and injuries with a level mind and avenged them with contempt. He presided over the Church of Caesarea for eight years, dying in the year 378. Having spoken these final words,

<margin>
See Nazianzen, Oration 20, page 348.
</margin>

> Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit,

he joyfully breathed out his soul and was laid in his father’s tomb. A funeral worthy of such a great man was arranged, celebrated by a gathering of the whole city, and even by the tears of Jews, Pagans, and foreigners. Indeed, there was such a crowd and such a dense throng that many, crushed by the excessive force, expired at that very moment. These were called *Blessed* by Nazianzen <note>Gregory Nazianzen</note> on this account, <term>as though they died with him and were funeral sacrifices</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐκείνῳ συνθνῆσαι, καὶ θύματα ἐπιτάφια</note>, because they had been companions of his departure and, as it were, victims of the funeral. He was eulogized, though after some time had passed, by Gregory the Theologian, who consecrated the memory of this best of men and most upright of friends to eternity with a most eloquent Oration. For this was the supreme crowning of his happiness: to have a "Most Eloquent Praiser," if I may borrow the words of Pliny the Younger *. I set aside the elegies that the Ancients heaped upon Basil. Every page is full of them; the entire chorus of Antiquity venerates him; the whole theater of the learned applauds him. Indeed, even if they were silent, his many writings which still exist today testify to the man's supreme piety, profound knowledge, and most perfected eloquence.

Let *Photius* *, <term>the most critical of judges</term>, give his opinion on Basil's style: "The great Basil," he says, "is <term>divine in all his words</term>. He knows how to use—if anyone else does—a style that is pure, distinct, proper, and altogether statesmanlike and festive. He is first, and second to none, in the order and purity of his thoughts; he loves the power of persuasion, sweetness, and indeed brilliance; and his speech flows as if a stream were gushing from a spring of its own accord." <note>This is a translation of a long Greek passage by Photius, a 9th-century scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople who reviewed hundreds of books in his *Bibliotheca*.</note> He adds that no one who correctly sets Basil before himself as a model would ever miss any other writer, not even Plato or Demosthenes themselves. Philotheus, the Patriarch of Constantinople *, followed Photius not only in his library but also in his judgment; he observes that it is unique to Basil to discuss individual matters with such vigor, <term>as if giving a soul to things without a soul</term>.

* Book 2, Epistle 1.

* Code 141. <note>Refers to the entry number in Photius's *Bibliotheca*.</note>

* Oration on St. Basil, *Library of the Greek and Latin Fathers*, Volume 2.
</margin>

Gregory of Nazianzus \* <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers" and Basil's closest friend.</note> testifies that Basil wrote the **Monastic Rules** while he was still living in the desert, and indicates † that he himself worked alongside Basil in composing them. It must certainly be admitted that many things foreign to Basil’s natural style have crept into these *Ascetic* works; however, exactly which parts those are, or who their authors might be, cannot be judged with total certainty. It is not improbable that some parts are owed to Eustathius <note>Eustathius of Sebaste, an early mentor of Basil whose radical asceticism later led to a falling out.</note>. In the time of Photius † <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and renowned scholar.</note>, who highly praises the work, the entire collection consisted of two books. The first contained those short sermons *On the Judgment of God, On Faith*, etc., which are usually placed before the *Ethics*. The second contained the *Ethics* or *Morals*, as well as the **55 Longer Ascetic Rules**, explained in a question-and-answer format. Following these were another **313 Shorter Rules**, just as they survive today, transcribed from a very ancient copy brought from Pontus and compared with another that was kept in Basil’s own <term>Ptochotrophion</term> <note>A famous hospital and complex for the poor established by Basil in Caesarea.</note> in Caesarea; this is evident from certain scholia <note>Ancient marginal comments or explanatory notes.</note> usually attached to these Rules.

The **Liturgy**, of which there is no just reason to doubt Basil was the author. Basil himself, in a letter \* to the clergy of Neocaesarea, describes a *Formula of Prayers* that was observed in his monasteries and was, as he says, in harmony with all the Churches of God. This *Liturgy*, as it exists today, has been greatly interpolated <note>Altered or expanded by later editors.</note>, increased by various additions according to the taste and conditions of the centuries in which they were made. Consequently, the older the copies found, the shorter and purer they are, as is clearly evident from the <term>Anaphora</term> <note>The most solemn part of the Eucharistic liturgy.</note> which Andreas Masius translated from the Syriac language. # The Arian Century.

<margin>4th CENTURY. From the year 300.</margin>
*The Letter of Consolation in Adversities* is in Latin and belongs to Victor of Cartenna <note>A 5th-century African bishop.</note>.
*On the Praises of the Desert, or the Solitary Life* is a Latin fragment from the work of Peter Damian <note>A 11th-century monk and reformer; this is a chronological error in earlier attributions to Basil.</note>.
*Admonition to a Spiritual Son* in Latin. A slightly more corrected version is found in the appendix to Holstenius's *Code of Rules* (Paris, 1663, 4to).
*A Prayer* which Saint Basil was accustomed to use before performing the Sacred Rites.
*Two Letters to Apollinarius* <note>Apollinarius of Laodicea, whose teachings were later declared heretical.</note>, published in Greek and Latin by Cotelerius in the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume 2. These are of very doubtful authenticity; indeed, if compared with Letters 59, 79, and 82, they are certainly spurious. The *Letter to the Emperor Theodosius* published by the same author is of no better quality.
*A Fragment of a Letter to the Emperor Julian* <note>Julian "the Apostate," the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note> is found in the Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (Acts 2 and 4) and from there placed among Basil’s letters as Number 205. Both the style and the subject matter sufficiently prove it to be forged; even the more sensible <term>Pontificii</term> <note>A term used by the author, likely a Protestant scholar, to refer to Roman Catholic theologians.</note> acknowledge this not unwillingly.

The works of Basil were published in Greek at *Venice* (1535) and *Basel* (1532—in which almost half of Basil's works are missing; and 1551). The first part of the 1551 edition (as noted by the distinguished James Ussher in his *Theological Library*, p. 303) was printed from the *Basel* edition of 1532. The second part follows from page 373, previously unpublished, from the *Venice* edition of 1535. In this part are contained: 1st, the *Ascetics* (for they are commonly titled so there), found from pages 373 to 646; 2nd, the *Five Books against Eunomius* <note>Eunomius was a leading radical Arian who argued that the nature of God was entirely comprehensible to human reason.</note> from page 646 to the end of the volume. Latin editions appeared in the same places in 1520, 1540, *Antwerp* 1568, and *Paris* 1571. A Greek-Latin edition with notes by Fronto Ducæus <note>A learned Jesuit editor.</note> and an appendix was published in *Paris*, 1618, in two volumes, folio. Then in the same city (though not keeping the same order) in 1638, in three volumes, folio; this edition was expanded by our countryman Richard Montagu, who recovered and translated into Latin more than two hundred letters, though it is less beautiful and less corrected than the former. For a more convenient understanding of the works of Saint Basil, the *Basilius Restitutus* <note>Latin: "Basil Restored."</note> of François Combefis will contribute no small amount; in this work, he corrected, expanded, and illustrated the text from the best manuscripts and revised the translations. He published this work in *Paris*, 1679, in two volumes, 8vo.

<margin>370.</margin>
GREGORY, a native of Pontus and the younger brother of Basil the Great, devoted himself entirely to the study of rhetoric in the first years of his youth. Gregory of Nazianzus, through letters sent to him, called him back to the knowledge of sacred literature. He brought it about that Gregory came to hold in contempt the "glory of the inglorious" <note>original: ἀδόξου εὐδοξίαν. This refers to the vanity of worldly fame compared to Christian humility.</note>, to use the words of the Theologian \* <margin>\* Letter 43, p. 804.</margin>, in which he previously seemed to take too much delight. At the end of the year 375, it seems, he was appointed Bishop of Nyssa on the border of Cappadocia, becoming a most fierce champion of the Nicene faith. On that account, accused by a single—and quite worthless—shabby fellow, he was soon sent into exile by the order of the Emperor Valens <note>An Arian emperor who persecuted supporters of the Nicene Creed.</note>. For about eight years he wandered as an exile in various places, suffering harsh and most grievous treatment from the Arians everywhere. Restored to his see in the year 378, he was sent as a legate by the Council of Antioch (which he attended along with certain other bishops) to visit the churches of Arabia, with the Emperor Theodosius granting him the use of the public carriage system. Proceeding through Arabia, he visited Jerusalem and contemplated the Holy Places with a pious mind; however, offended by the vices and disagreements of the people of Jerusalem, he quickly withdrew. He even wrote a letter shortly thereafter against those who travel to Jerusalem for the sake of piety. In the year 381, when he went to the Council of Constantinople, he brought with him the books he had written against Eunomius, which he read to Gregory of Nazianzus and Jerome. He was a great part of that Council; so much so that he was not only chosen by the Fathers to praise Meletius of Antioch (who died while the Council was in session) with a funeral oration, but he also had the composition of the Synodal Creed committed to his care (according to Nicephorus \*) <margin>\* Ecclesiastical History, book 12, chapter 13.</margin>, so that he might supply what was missing in the Nicene Creed and establish a perfected confession of faith. Around the same time, he was appointed as a judge of the Catholic profession for the dioceses of Pontus, together with Helladius, Bishop of Caesarea and successor to Basil. Nothing is certain regarding his death; this only is established with total certainty: that he prolonged his life until the times of the Council held in Constantinople in the year 394, at which he was present. That he was married, and had a wife named Theosebia, even called the "spouse of a priest" <note>original: τῆς ἱερέως σύζυγον</note>, is attested by witnesses beyond all exception: Gregory of Nazianzus \* (who praises her exceedingly), Nyssen himself †, <margin>\* Letter 95. † Book on Virginity, chapter 3. || Book 11, chapter 19.</margin> and Nicephorus ||. He was a man who, by the remarkable holiness of his character and his all-encompassing [learning...]

# The Arian Century.

<margin>
4th CENTURY. From the year 300.
</margin>

Euthymius of Panopolis <note>A 12th-century Byzantine monk, also known as Euthymius Zigabenus, author of the "Panoplia Dogmatica."</note> (in part 2, title 2) cites a passage from Nyssa’s book *That one should not say there are three gods*, which does not appear in the version of the book with that title that survives today.

His works are extant in Latin, published in various places and times: *Basel*, 1562; an expanded version in the same place, 1570; *Paris*, 1573; and under the care of Fronto Ducaeus in the same place, 1605. In two volumes, Greek and Latin, by the effort of Fed. Morell, *Paris*, 1615, with notes by Fronto Ducaeus. Jacob Gretser added an appendix in 1618 (folio) supplying those things which were missing in that edition, whether in Greek and Latin, or in Greek alone. Finally, the complete works appeared in Paris in 1638 in three volumes (folio), though this edition was poorly corrected and fell far short of the previous one.

<margin>370.</margin> PETER, the youngest brother of Basil and Gregory, was educated under the care and guardianship of his sister Macrina. She diligently formed this young man—who was naturally inclined toward virtue and the liberal arts—for the ascetic life and the exercises of a more rigorous piety. He was courteous and kind toward everyone, and most charitable toward the poor. He was first made a priest by Basil, and later ordained Bishop of Sebaste in Cappadocia, though it is not entirely clear in which year. Surviving Basil, he asked his brother Gregory to defend Basil’s reputation through published writings after it had been attacked by the heretic Eunomius. It is uncertain in which year he died. *A single letter to his brother Gregory survives, placed at the beginning of Nyssa’s books against Eunomius.* The reader should note, as it is not unworthy of observation, that there were three brothers who were bishops at one and the same time and in the same region, each famous for his piety and learning.

<margin>370.</margin> GREGORY, called "the Nazianzen" after Nazianzus, an obscure town in the province of Cappadocia Secunda. He was not only a "yokefellow" <note>original Greek: "syzygos"</note> to Basil, but his greatest companion and friend, joined to him in such close intimacy that, as he himself admitted, *one soul bound two bodies together in a single disposition.* <note>original Greek: "psychē mia duoin sōmatōn diathesin"</note> He was born at Arianzus on his father’s estate near Nazianzus around the time of the Council of Nicaea; God arranged it so that he was brought into the world at the very time when he would become the most powerful "hammer of the Arians." His father was Gregory, an excellent man, but miserably misled by the errors of the Hypsistarians. (This was a sect fused from Judaism and Paganism, which nevertheless uniquely worshipped that supreme and "Most High God," <note>original Greek: "hypsistō Theō"</note> from which the sect took its name.) His mother was Nonna, a most distinguished woman noted for her piety; through her mediation, her husband was recalled from his errors to the Christian religion. After being washed in the saving font of baptism, he was promoted to the Bishopric of the city of Nazianzus, which he held for 45 years, and he died nearly a centenarian. Our Gregory, a brilliant young man, devoted himself to the study of the disciplines, first at Caesarea in Cappadocia, and then attended the school of the rhetorician Thespesius at Caesarea in Palestine. After this, he set out for Alexandria, and from there, after a very dangerous voyage, sought Athens. Having successfully completed his studies there, and just as he was about to depart, at the request of the academic youth who held him back almost by force, he undertook the duty of teaching for a little while. But he soon laid down the professor's chair and returned to his homeland, where he was soon ordained a priest by his father. During the reign of Julian [the Apostate], he was almost entirely occupied with composing verses, which he wrote in nearly every kind of meter and on every most serious

<margin>* L. 21 & 25.</margin> subject, so that he might elude and repair the damage of that unpraiseworthy—and, as Ammianus himself admits *, "harsh"—edict which should be buried in eternal silence, by which the books of the Pagans were struck from the hands of Christian teachers. <note>The pagan Emperor Julian forbade Christians from teaching classical Greek literature; Gregory responded by writing new Christian literature in the classical style to ensure students didn't have to rely on pagan texts.</note> Afterward, weary of the turmoils and being more suited by nature to a more rigid life, he withdrew to his friend Basil in the solitudes of Pontus, which he skillfully called "the Islands of the Blessed." <note>original Greek: "tas tōn makarōn nēsous"</note> 

<margin>† To Basil, Ep. 7.</margin> Later, around the year 370, when Basil achieved the Archiepiscopal dignity of the churches of Cappadocia, he appointed Nazianzen as Bishop of Sasima, a mean little town in Cappadocia Secunda. Gregory was resentful, almost breaking the indissoluble bond of friendship; indeed, he did not even deign to visit his see once—an ignoble, unhealthy, and unpleasant place, full of storms and urban disturbances. At last, having been earnestly asked to take up the care of the Church of Nazianzus to relieve the weakness of his father, who was then laboring in extreme old age, he consented, on the condition that once his father had departed from this life, he would not be forced to hold the helm of that church any longer.

# The Arian Century.

<margin>
4th Century. From the year 300.
* On Famous Men, chapter 117.
† Letter 42. See also Oration 8, page 148.
</margin>

From this, the error of Jerome \* (who was actually his disciple) and others is clear, for they frequently claim that Gregory was the Bishop of Nazianzus. Gregory himself † expressly denies this, affirming that he was never made Bishop of Nazianzus, but only performed the duties of his father while the latter was still alive. Around the year 378, he was sent—quite against his will—by the Synod held at Antioch to Constantinople, so that he might raise up and sustain the Catholic cause, which was then being oppressed by the Arians <note>A group of Christians who followed the teachings of Arius, who argued that Jesus Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father; this was the central theological conflict of the 4th century.</note>. He did this vigorously and successfully. The number of Catholics increased daily; he faithfully gathered them in the house of his relative, Nicobulus, which was soon established as a church and given the name *Anastasia* <note>original: "Anastasiæ"; from the Greek word for "Resurrection."</note>, because the faith, which had previously been languishing and near death, seemed to come back to life there. Consequently, he was placed on the episcopal throne of the Imperial City by Theodosius the Great and confirmed in that position by the Ecumenical Council <note>The First Council of Constantinople, 381 AD.</note> assembled there in the year 381. However, when a significant dispute arose in the Synod regarding this matter, he voluntarily resigned from his seat and returned home. Thereafter, he lived a private and quiet life, easing the hardships of old age partly through exercises of piety and partly through his poetic labors. He exchanged this fleeting life for a better one in the year 389, at approximately 65 years of age.

<margin>\* In the entry for "Gregory."</margin>

Thus, it must be that Suidas \* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note> is incorrect when he writes that Gregory died at over ninety years old. He was a man most excellent in every branch of learning and supreme in Theology.

<margin>
† Oration on St. Basil. Library of the Greek and Latin Fathers, Volume 2.
|| Prologue to the books of Gregory translated by him.
\* Cited in Suidas under the entries for "Basil" and "Apollinaris."
</margin>

Philotheus † teaches us that the ancients noted this [Theology] as being "as if his own unique trait" <note>original: "ὥσπερ τὸ ἴδιον"</note>. For this reason, Gregory was also called *The Theologian* "par excellence" <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν"</note>; he is the only one (to use the words of Rufinus ||) about whose faith not even disagreeing parties and factions—as is usually the case—could argue. Rather, he obtained such merit with the Lord and the Churches of God that anyone who dared to oppose his doctrine in any way would, by that very fact, be proven to be a heretic. For it is a manifest judgment that a man is not of the right faith if he does not agree with Gregory in faith. Gregory used a grand and sublime style of speech, full of majesty throughout. In his manner of speaking, he followed Polemon <note>A 2nd-century Sophist orator.</note>, as Jerome observed; though he certainly also followed Isocrates, who was older than Polemon, which is why the Greek Scholiast notes his "Isocratic style" <note>original: "τὸ ἰσοκρατικὸν"</note> more clearly. Let us hear the judgment of Philostorgius \*, an Arian, who compared him with Basil and Apollinaris, saying: *The speech of Apollinaris is better suited for commentaries; Basil’s is most splendid in the panegyric style; but Gregory’s speech, when examined alongside both, has a greater foundation for writing, possessing the richness of Apollinaris and the piety of Basil* <note>original: "τῷ τοῦ Γρηγορίου καὶ παρ’ ἀμφοτέροις ἐξεταζομένῳ μείζω βάσιν εἰς συγγραφὴν ἔχει ὁ λόγος, καὶ τῷ εἰπεῖν Ἀπολλιναρείου ἁδρότης, Βασiliου ἡ εὐσέβεια."</note>. Indeed, Gregory's oratory, compared with either of them, held a more sublime place in writing; for he was more abundant in speaking than Apollinaris, and weightier than Basil. Certainly, it is established that he indulged in the oratorical faculty (in which he was especially powerful) more than was proper, particularly in his Encomiastic <note>Speeches of high praise or eulogies.</note> sermons; from this, he seems to have been among the first to pave the way for the errors of subsequent centuries regarding the invocation of Saints. It should rightly seem strange to us that Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch and scholar.</note> excerpted nothing at all from his writings; perhaps he did so in some part of his *Library* that does not survive today. Regarding his writings, two things especially must be observed by the reader: first, that very few works falsely attributed to his name are unworthy of such an erudite mind; and second, that few, or perhaps none, of his actual works are missing.

## SPURIOUS WORKS.

*A Metaphrase, or Translation of Ecclesiastes*, fifty-third among the Orations, which is established to be the work of Gregory Thaumaturgus <note>Gregory "the Miracle-Worker," a 3rd-century bishop.</note>.

*The Suffering Christ*, a *Tragedy*, which it is likely was written by Apollinaris the Elder.

The works of Nazianzen were published: Greek, Basel 1550; Latin (with the notes and commentaries of various authors) in three volumes, Basel 1571; Paris (in two volumes) 1583; Greek-Latin, Paris 1609 and 1630, 2 volumes in folio, with the commentaries of Nicetas Serronius, Psellus, Nonnus, and Elias of Crete; which Jacques de Billy translated from the Greek and added his own annotations and commentaries where necessary. Frédéric Morel expanded the later edition with several letters and also his own notes. Richard Montagu published two *Invectives against Julian* separately at Eton in 1610, in Greek, in quarto, with Greek commentaries and Nonnus’s collection of histories; to which he also added his own notes and various readings. Finally, it may be added to these, as the most learned Colomiès informed me, that a certain Basilius (who calls himself a companion, equal in rank, and kinsman of Basil the Great) wrote explanations on the *Invective Orations* <note>original: "Στηλιτευτικὰς"; these were Gregory's famous public denunciations of the Emperor Julian the Apostate.</note> of Gregory Nazianzen; he testifies that he saw these explanations in a fairly thick manuscript volume held by the illustrious Isaac Vossius. They are also extant in the libraries of the Emperor, the King of France, and of Augsburg. Seberus, in his edition of Pollux (pages 99 and 105), brings forward two fragments from a letter of David Höschel.

<margin>
See Basil, Letter 84; and Nazianzen, Oration 10.
</margin>
Caesarius, the younger brother of Gregory of Nazianzus, a young man of quick wit and great promise; having been sent to Alexandria as if to a most famous marketplace of the liberal arts, he devoted himself to philosophy, and especially to medicine. Having set out from there to Constantinople, he achieved such great fame in a short time that public honors, a noble marriage, and senatorial dignity were offered to him; and it was requested of the Emperor by legates through a common decree that the imperial city be adorned with Caesarius as both Physician and Citizen. However, overcome by the persistence of his brother, he then rejected the offered position. Under Julian, he held a post <note>original: "ἐσχημάτισεν"</note>—to the indignation of both his father and brother—as Chief Physician of the imperial household and Count of the Private Estate; he was also made Quaestor of Bithynia and Treasurer. Indeed, he was tested by Julian with both promises and arguments, but he remained steadfast in the profession of his faith, and shortly afterward withdrew himself from the palace. But after two years he returned, and having served in the same offices under Valens, he died in the year 368. About to die, he made a will, brief indeed, but truly pious: "I wish all my things to belong to the poor" <note>original: "Τὰ ἐμὰ πάντα βούλομαι γίνεσθαι τῶν πτωχῶν"</note>, "I want everything that is mine to be given to the poor."
<margin>
* Under the entry "Caesar."
</margin>
That he wrote various things, and specifically against the Pagans, is attested by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic lexicon.</note>; however, it is not clear from where he obtained this information.

<margin>
* Supplement on Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 40.
† Codex 210, at the end.
</margin>
There are extant under his name four *Dialogues*, or explanations of certain very weighty questions. Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch and scholar known for his reviews of ancient books.</note> deals with these in <term>Codex</term> 210 <note>A "Codex" in this context refers to a specific entry or volume in Photius's library catalog.</note>, mentioning that the work consisted of 220 chapters; yet today they do not solve more than 195 questions. Truly, many things suggest that these *Dialogues* are not the work of our Caesarius. First, for instance, his brother Gregory, in the oration he held at the funeral of Caesarius (where he reviews even the smallest things contributing to Caesarius’s praise), makes not even a tiny mention of these *Dialogues*, or indeed of any writing published by Caesarius. ...Nazianzen, who by this reasoning would have wished to commend the name of his brother to posterity. For beyond the fact that such a holy man should not be judged as wanting to deceive the Christian world with such a notable fraud, if he had intended any such thing, he would not have remained silent about his brother’s work in such an opportune place. Secondly, Caesarius was a young man, a physician by profession, a <term>Quaestor</term> <note>A high-ranking financial official in the Roman administration.</note> by rank, and almost entirely occupied in civil business and honors. These *Dialogues*, however, show a deeper expertise in theological matters; for they deal for the most part with the Holy Trinity and other more hidden mysteries of the Christian faith. Thus, they reveal a veteran theologian of refined judgment, for whom, in the judgment of Photius \*, <margin>\* Codex 210.</margin> <note>original: "τῶν δογμάτων ἀκρίβειαν ὀλίγων δεῖ"</note> *the precision of dogmas is a requirement for few*. Thirdly, the author of these *Dialogues* is said in the inscription itself to have remained in Constantinople for a full twenty years and to have taught there; however, Caesarius stayed in Constantinople for only a few years, and one does not read that he taught medicine there, much less theology, in a public capacity. <margin>† As cited above.</margin> It is clear from Photius that some in his age attributed this work to Gregory the Theologian. But to see how they did so without any reason, please see the argument of Jacques de Billy in his commentary on Nazianzen’s tenth Oration. Perhaps it is not the work of one and the same man; at the very least, it seems to be patched together from various writers—Gregory of Nyssa, Maximus (who are cited by name within it), and others. Whoever the author is, he uses a sufficiently clear style in the opinion of Photius, except that he frequently and with youthful excess turns toward poetic expressions.

These *Dialogues* have been published frequently in the Latin editions of Gregory Nazianzen and in the "Libraries of the Fathers." Fronto Ducæus first published them in Greek and Latin in his *Supplement* of 1624, Volume I; then Elias Ehinger published them in *Augsburg*, 1626, in quarto.

### APOLLINARIS the Younger, a native of Laodicea, son of the priest Apollinaris (mentioned above), and a disciple of the <term>Sophist</term> <note>A teacher of rhetoric and philosophy.</note> Epiphanius; he taught Rhetoric, first serving as a Reader in the Church of Laodicea, and finally as Bishop. He flourished from the beginning of Julian’s reign, but especially around the year 370. For a time a Catholic, he is said to have turned away from the straight path of the Church on this occasion: George, the Bishop of Laodicea and a member of the Arian faction, was moved to anger against him because Apollinaris cultivated a very close friendship with Athanasius the Great and refused to abstain from meeting with him. George excluded him from communion; indeed, he even reproached him for former offenses for which he had been cast out by Theodotus. Nor did he deign to receive him back into communion, though Apollinaris sought it many times. Resenting this injury, Apollinaris established his own peculiar sect, which disturbed the Church significantly for several centuries. In which year exactly he began to spread his heresy is not very clear; it is only certain that his teachings were by no means entirely new or unheard of, since the primary one among them was condemned by the Synod of Alexandria held in the year 362. At that time, Apollinaris does not yet seem to have been spreading the heresy himself, but later he more carefully refined and "re-cooked" the errors he received from others. The sum of his heresy, which he spread among the common people, was this: that Christ brought a human nature down from heaven with him; that he had an eternal soul <note>original: "ψυχὴν" (psyche)</note> joined to his own substance (though he had first denied this); but that the divinity of the Only-begotten took the place of the mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (nous)</note>. Finally, he held that Christ was mortal and suffered in his own divinity; and that in that three-day death of the body, the divinity also died with it, being finally recalled from death by the favor of the Father. See Gregory Nazianzen’s *Letter to Nectarius* and his two *Letters to Cledonius* (or Orations 51 and 52), where he most fully refutes the dogmas of Apollinaris. For these views, Apollinaris was condemned both elsewhere and in the Roman Synod <margin>\* Notes on Sozomen, p. 143.</margin> in the year 373, according to Baronius; however, Valesius \* contends it was held around the year 377 or 378. But this bold man, most tenacious in his dogmas, disregarded the judgment of the Church; nor is it at all certain that Apollinaris ever set aside his errors. He died during the reign of Theodosius, though in what year is not clear.

Socrates Scholasticus, Book 3, ch. 16.
</margin>

## AMPHILOCHIUS

If we can attain anything by conjecture, he was a Cappadocian by birth. Only after his father’s death did he embrace the monastic life, withdrawing into the solitudes of the Pontic desert, where he had Basil and Gregory as companions. Around the year 370, or perhaps a little later, he was appointed Bishop of Iconium, the metropolis of Lycaonia. Regarding the manner in which he was consecrated by angels and other deeds performed by him, Simeon Metaphrastes (or whoever the author of his *Life* \* is) tells us wondrous fables; let those whose lips love such lettuce <note>A Latin idiom meaning "people who like that sort of thing," implying the stories are hard to swallow or suited for specific tastes.</note> seek him out. In the year 381, when the Emperor Theodosius established a law appointing certain more celebrated bishops within the borders of each Eastern diocese—so that churches would be handed over only to those who communicated with them and confessed the Nicene faith—the care of the Asian diocese was committed to our Amphilochius (according to Sozomen \*); to whom the Theodosian law † joins Optimum, the Bishop of Antioch in Pisidia. Two years later, when he had asked the Emperor in vain during a Synod that the assemblies of the Arians be forbidden, he obtained it by a certain clever art. For, entering the palace, he treated Theodosius with the usual honor, but passed by Arcadius (standing by his father) without a greeting. When the Emperor took offense at the contempt shown to his son,

> "You see, Emperor," said Amphilochius, "that you cannot bear an insult to your son; believe, therefore, that God also turns away from and hates those who blaspheme His only-begotten Son."

Marveling at the saying, the Emperor immediately granted the law requested by the Bishop. Around the same time, he fought strenuously against the Messalians <note>A sect also known as Euchites, accused of believing that outward prayer was the only necessity for salvation, often leading to neglect of social norms.</note> (wretched heretics who veiled the most shameful indecencies with constant prayers). The Synod of Side, which Amphilochius presided over, condemned them by its sentence; moreover, Amphilochius refuted them in a published book. He was still among the living in the year 394, when the case of Bagadius and Agapius was being handled in the Synod of Constantinople; and he seems to have died in the following year. Saint Basil extols him with the highest praises for his tireless zeal for learning and industry, and his clearly singular humility and other excellent gifts. He was so dear to Basil that he was accustomed to consult him in all the most serious matters; Basil inscribed certain books to his name and sent letters to him so frequently that, as Basil himself admitted, they could serve as a journal <note>original: "ephemerides"</note> and set forth the daily course of his life. He was a man especially distinguished in both secular learning and the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, so much so that Jerome \* does not hesitate to compare him with his fellow countrymen, Basil and Gregory. He wrote many things; but whether those which now exist are genuine is not sufficiently clear. It is all the more difficult to pronounce anything certain about them because no writings of undisputed authenticity remain by which the others might be judged.

# DIDYMUS

<margin>
370.
Socrates, Book 4, ch. 25.
Sozomen, Book 3, ch. 15.
Theodoret, Book 4, ch. 29.
</margin>
DIDYMUS, an Alexandrian by birth, a monk by institution, head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria, and the teacher of Jerome and Rufinus. He flourished especially around the year 370, being quite celebrated from the time of Constantius himself. While still a young boy, having already learned the first elements of letters, he was afflicted by disease and utterly lost the power of sight. Notwithstanding this, he advanced so far in every branch of learning that he not only thoroughly learned Grammar, Rhetoric, Logic, Arithmetic, Music, and the other disciplines of the Philosophers, but also perceived even the most difficult theorems of Mathematics. He accurately investigated Holy Scripture and its more hidden meanings; he harbored certain errors of Origen, <note>Origen was a 3rd-century theologian whose complex views on the pre-existence of souls were later controversial.</note> but nevertheless, he disputed most powerfully against all heretics, especially the Arians. He was held in great admiration by all, so much so that when Anthony the Great <note>One of the "Desert Fathers" and a founder of Christian monasticism.</note> came to Alexandria, having seen the man's learning, he is said to have spoken these words to him: *“Let the loss of physical eyes move you not at all, O Didymus; for you are deprived of the kind of eyes with which even flies and gnats can see. Rejoice rather that you have those with which Angels see, with which God is discerned, and His light is understood.”* He was still among the living in the year 392, at which time he had exceeded the eighty-third year of his age.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*Book on the Holy Spirit*, translated by Jerome, is found among the works of St. Jerome.
Certain brief *Expositions on the Canonical Epistles*, first published in Latin by Canisius. Both works are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume IV, pages 320, 338.
*Book against the Manichaeans*, <note>A major dualistic religion that competed with Christianity, teaching a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> which, translated into Latin by Turrianus, Henricus Canisius published in his *Ancient Lessons*, Volume V, page 17. A Greek-Latin edition was published by Combefis in his *Supplement* of 1672.

*Commentaries on Proverbs*, from which the author of the *Catena on Luke* cites a certain passage. Cassiodorus mentions in his *On Divine Letters*, chapter 5, that these commentaries were translated into the Latin language by his most upright friend Epiphanius.

*Commentaries on Hosea in 3 books*, dedicated to Jerome.

PETER, Archpriest of the Church of Alexandria under Athanasius, and his inseparable companion on journeys and pilgrimages, with whom he underwent various dangers. At last, after the death of Athanasius, having been designated by him before his passing, he was made Bishop of Alexandria by the Catholic party in the year 371. He was placed upon the Pontifical throne with the people applauding and the neighboring Bishops supporting him; but soon he was violently driven from his see by the Arians and cast into chains. Escaping from these a little later, he boarded a ship and went to Rome, where he was kindly received by Damasus. Protected by Damasus’s letters, he later recovered his see and died shortly thereafter. How highly he was held by all is evident from the fact that in the year 380, the Emperor Theodosius established him, together with Pope Damasus, as the standard of orthodox truth, <margin>† On the Catholic Faith, book 2.</margin> calling him a man of Apostolic piety. While detained in prison, he wrote an *Encyclical Letter* regarding the violence brought against him, newly elevated to the Episcopate, by the Arians, and regarding the shameful ambition of Lucius, who seized the see of Alexandria for himself through right or wrong. It survives almost in its entirety, truncated only at the beginning and end, in Theodoret, Book 4, Chapter 22. Furthermore, Facundus has preserved for us two fragments of another letter to the Egyptian Bishops exiled for the sake of the faith, in Book 4, Chapter 2, and Book 11, Chapter 2.

<margin>371.</margin>
LUCIUS, whose origin is uncertain; he was first appointed Bishop of Samosata by the Arians with force and arms after Eusebius was driven out by order of Emperor Valens. There he was received with hatred by all and was infamous for many crimes. Afterward, in the year 371, he was led to Alexandria by Euzoius of Antioch and Magnus, Count of the Sacred Largesses, <term>Count of the Sacred Largesses: A high-ranking financial official in the later Roman Empire.</term> and was substituted in the place of Peter of Alexandria, who had been cast into prison by them. Having been made Bishop, surrounded by a bodyguard of Arians and Pagans, he vented his rage wonderfully against the Catholics; some of these he drove away, others he put in chains, and he tormented everyone with the greatest injuries. Some of them were tortured by being burned with iron claws and ox-hide thongs, others with burning torches. Peter of Alexandria will teach the reader more fully about this enormous tyranny in his letter in Theodoret, Book 4, Chapter 22. For some time, he afflicted the Egyptian monks who held fast to the Catholic faith with a most severe persecution; their leaders, including Macarius, Isidore, and other most holy men, were deported to a certain island dreaded for the savagery of its inhabitants. But, deterred by the miracles of Macarius, he finally abandoned that purpose. Near the end of Valens’ reign, at the start of the year 378, or shortly before, after Peter returned to Alexandria, Lucius was ejected from the Episcopal see by the <margin>Socrates, book 4, chapter 37.</margin> hostile populace. Boarding a ship, he immediately set out for Constantinople (as is reasonable to believe) to bring accusations before the Emperor. But since Valens was killed by the Goths shortly thereafter, he failed in his wish. What happened to him from then on is not clear. He was a man of a very restless and truculent disposition, who according to Gregory Nazianzen * is called: <unclear>the second plague and scourge of Egypt, the liar against the truth, the shepherd of wolves, the thief entering through the fold, the second Arius</unclear>, <note>original Greek: "δευτέρα τῆς Αἰγύπτου πληγὴ καὶ μάστιξ, ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας ψευδέτης, ὁ λύκων ποιμήν, ὁ διὰ τῆς αὐλῆς εἰσβαίνων λῃστής, ὁ δεύτερος Ἄρειος"</note> etc. He wrote a *Sermon on Easter*, of which a certain fragment is held in Greek and Latin in the Lateran Council, Volume 6, page 313. It is not known what else he wrote.

### ESAIAS

ESAIAS was, it seems, an Alexandrian by birth, though born to a Spanish father who was a merchant. He flourished around the year 371. After the death of his father, having divided his inheritance with his brother Paesius, he withdrew into the Egyptian desert. There, having established a monastery and gathered several companions of the ascetic life, he devoted himself entirely to piety, the study of sacred literature, and the receiving of guests. Palladius <note>A 4th-century bishop and historian of early monasticism.</note> provides more information about him; anyone desiring more details should consult his work. Scholars should consider whether the *Twenty-Nine Sermons to the Brothers living in the Desert*, which exist under the name of Esaias, are truly his; they were published in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers* in Cologne, Volume 2, and in the recent edition, Volume 12, page 384. Certainly, it is not sufficiently clear in what age the author of these Homilies lived.

† Letter 8.
* Letter 168.
