### PROBA FALCONIA

PROBA FALCONIA was a Roman by birth, descended from a most noble family, and the daughter of a man of consular rank. She was the wife of Anicius Probus, the Praetorian Prefect and a man illustrious in every respect (not the wife of the Proconsul Adelphus, as Isidore of Seville claims *). She flourished in the year 371, in which year her husband held the consulship along with the Emperor Gratian. She bore sons to Probus: Olybrius, Probinus, Probus, and Juliana. Of these, the first two held the consulship together in the year 395; Probus also attained the same dignity. Her daughter Juliana was married to Claudius Hermogenianus Olybrius (who held the consulship in 379) and had a daughter, the virgin Demetrias, who was praised so often and so greatly by Jerome.

Proba herself, no less distinguished for her virtue than for the nobility of her birth, earned wonderful praises from Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, Prudentius, Claudian, and Cassiodorus. Setting others aside, let Jerome † stand for them all, who extols her praises thus: <note>original Latin: "Proba illa omnium dignitatum & cunctæ nobilitatis in orbe Romano nomen illustrius..."</note> "That Proba, a name more illustrious than all honors and all nobility in the Roman world, whose holiness and goodness, poured out upon all, was venerable even among the Barbarians." Because of her outstanding piety, Augustine praises her; at her own request, he wrote for her the treatise *On Seeing God*. She was also accustomed to kindly receive the legates and friends of St. Chrysostom into her home, whether they were sent to Rome or were fleeing there. For this reason, Chrysostom * thanked her in a letter written in the year 406, in which he also commended his legates, John the Priest and Paul the Deacon, to her protection. 

In the year 410, when Rome was captured by Alaric <note>The King of the Visigoths who sacked Rome.</note> (though some falsely claim the city was surrendered by Proba's betrayal), she, having been a widow for a long time and having suffered the loss of her property, fled to Africa together with her daughter Juliana and her granddaughter Demetrias. There, after being stripped of the meager remains of her fortune by Count Heraclianus, she only with difficulty found a place to live in safety for a short time. In that place, she formed a friendship with Augustine, by whom a letter (number 179) exists written to her, in addition to the aforementioned treatise. In what year she died is uncertain; it is certain that before her death she bequeathed all her possessions to the Church.

There exists a work written by her before her husband's death (as is clear from the end of the small work) titled the *Virgilian Cento on Divine Matters* <note>original Latin: "Cento Virgilianus de Rebus Divinis." A "cento" is a poem made up of verses or phrases taken from another author, in this case using Virgil's poetry to tell the story of the Bible.</note>, found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 5 (Lyon 1516; Frankfurt 1541; Paris 1578; Cologne 1601).

She also wrote an *Epitaph for her Husband*, which was carved into his marble tomb, excavated in Rome in the previous century and presented by Baronius in his *Annals*, Volume 4, for the year 395.

### MACARIUS THE ELDER

MACARIUS the Elder was an Egyptian by birth, originating from the province of Thebaid. He was a monk of Scetis and a disciple of Anthony the Great. He flourished around the year 373. While still in his youth, he so shone with virtues and a philosophical and austere way of life that he was called <term>The Old-Young Man</term> <note>original Greek: Παιδαριο-γέρων (Paidario-geron). This title implies he possessed the wisdom of an old man despite his young age.</note> by the monks. At forty years of age, he was raised to the rank of priest; and after sixty years spent in solitude, he died as a nonagenarian in the year 391 (as they say). In character, he was both reverend and severe toward those who approached him. Renowned for miracles and prophecy, he healed so many sick and liberated so many possessed by demons that, according to the testimony of Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian.</note>, the miracles performed by him would require a work of their own. Palladius discusses these at length in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 19.

He wrote *Fifty Spiritual Homilies on the Integrity that Befits Christians*, which exist in Greek and Latin (Paris 1559; then by the care of Zacharias Palthenius, Frankfurt 1594; and finally with the works of Gregory Thaumaturgus, Paris 1622), though they were perhaps interpolated by someone of a later century. Socrates and Palladius present more of his *Responses* to monks in the places cited.

### MACARIUS THE YOUNGER

**MACARIUS**, also called the *Junior* and the *Citizen* <note>original: "Politicus"</note>, was a native of Alexandria, where in his youth he earned a living selling sweets. He was a disciple of Saint Anthony and a contemporary <note>original: "σύγχρονος" (synchronos)</note> of the other Macarius <note>Macarius the Great/the Elder</note>, whom he outlived. Having renounced both his city and his trade, he withdrew to the desert of Nitria <note>A famous early monastic center in Egypt</note> and embraced the monastic life. In his fortieth year, he received baptism and was later made a Presbyter and the Archimandrite <note>A title for a superior of a monastery or group of monasteries</note> of Nitria. He died a centenarian around the year 404. He cultivated the strict discipline of the monastic life with such zeal that, due to the extreme dryness of his skin, the hair of his beard did not grow. However, in this one respect he differed from the other Macarius: he received those who came to him with a cheerful face and delighted them with witty conversation, using a certain urbanity to draw younger men toward monastic discipline. Palladius (who was an intimate friend of his) tells wonderful things of his virtues, his abstinence, the miracles he performed, and the demons he put to flight in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 20.

A *Monastic Rule* in thirty chapters, written in Latin, is attributed to him; it was first published by the Jesuit Petrus Roverius in the *History of the Monastery of Reims*, page 24. However, it is not yet clear to me whether it is truly by our Macarius. I also have in my possession a work by Macarius of Alexandria (for so the title reads) titled *Sermon on the departure and state of Souls after this life*, transcribed from a manuscript in the Pauline Library at Leipzig. It contains many foolish and "old wives' tales," and it seems to me to be the invention of some more recent "little Greek" <note>original: "Græculi"; a term often used to dismiss later Byzantine writers</note> who reduced his dreams on this subject to the form of a dialogue between Macarius and the Angels. But because it is unpublished <note>original: "ἀνέκδοτος" (anekdotos)</note>, and perhaps will recommend itself to the reader by its novelty, I shall subjoin it here, provided with a Latin translation.

Once, when we were making a journey in the desert, I saw two Angels escorting Saint Macarius, one on his right and one on his left. As we were walking along together, a rotting and stinking corpse was found lying there. Perceiving the stench, Saint Macarius blocked his nostrils with his hand until he had passed. The Angels did the same. Seeing this, the old man said to them: "Do you also smell the stench of this world?" They answered: "Not at all; but seeing you closing your nostrils, we did the same. For we do not perceive worldly stench, but we only smell the stench of sinful souls, in the same way that you turn away from the stench of that corpse." The old man said to them: "Make it known to me, I pray, whether you perceive the stinking soul of sinners in this life or after death? And how do you distinguish the souls of sinners who believed in the Lord from those of the impious who did not believe? Tell me—"

Now indeed, acknowledge Him, being delivered over to eternal punishments." Then, leading it even unto the first heaven, they station it there, and show it from a distance the glory of the Angels and of all the heavenly powers, saying: "The Lord of all these is Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, whom you did not wish to acknowledge and adore. Depart from here, however, led away to the ungodly like yourself and their prince the Devil, into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels, whom you—while still placed among the living—adored as if they were Gods." After the Angels had said these things, having embraced the servant of God, Macarius, they vanished from our sight. But we render glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# The Age of Arianism.

<margin>
THE 4TH CENTURY, from the year 300, 373 AD.
</margin>
**MACARIUS**, an Egyptian by birth and a disciple of **Anthony the Great** <note>Saint Anthony (c. 251–356), a central figure in early Christian monasticism.</note>, at whose death he was present, flourished at the same time as those mentioned previously. However, Pierre Poussines <note>original: "Petrus Possinus"; a 17th-century Jesuit scholar.</note> proves in his *Introduction to the Ascetic Treasury* that he is entirely distinct from the others, a view echoed by Oudin in his *Supplement* (p. 29), and we concur with this opinion.

He wrote seven small works, namely: *On the Guarding of the Heart, On Perfection in the Spirit, On Prayer, On Patience and Discernment, On the Elevation of the Mind, On Charity, and On Freedom of the Mind*. These were recently published in Greek and Latin <note>original: "Gr. Lat."</note> in his *Ascetic Treasury* by Pierre Poussines of the Society of Jesus at Toulouse in 1684, in <term>quarto</term> <note>A book size where each sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>. Poussines does not hesitate to also attribute to this Macarius the fifty homilies (mentioned above).

<margin>
374. Paulinus in the Life of Ambrose.
</margin>
**AMBROSE**, Roman by heritage but born in Gaul, was born to a noble and illustrious family in the year 333. His father was also named Ambrose and was the <term>Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls</term> <note>One of the highest administrative offices in the late Roman Empire, overseeing a vast territory including modern France, Britain, and Spain.</note> at that time; it is probable that he resided in Arles, the capital of Gallia Narbonensis. While the boy was still a crying infant sleeping in the courtyard of the Prefecture with his mouth open, a swarm of bees suddenly settled on his mouth. After they had flown in and out repeatedly, they finally flew up high into the air. Seeing this, his father, who was walking nearby, said: *"If this little child lives, he will be something great."* While he was still a boy living in Rome, and saw his widowed mother and his sister, along with her companion, kissing the hand of a Bishop, he offered them his own right hand, saying playfully: *"They ought to do this for him; for he claimed he would one day be a Bishop."*

Refined in every branch of secular literature, he argued cases in the court of the Praetorian Prefecture with such eloquence and success that Probus, the Praetorian Prefect, took him as his advisor. Soon after, Probus granted him consular honors, committing the provinces of Liguria and Emilia to his governance. As Ambrose was departing, Probus gave him his orders in these words: *"Go, act not as a judge, but as a bishop."* <note>original: "Vade, age, non ut Iudex, sed ut Episcopus." This is often interpreted as a command to rule with mercy rather than strictly by the letter of the law.</note> Entering the province, he settled in Milan, until in the year 374, Auxentius—the Bishop of that city—died. When the Catholics and the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; they were the primary theological rivals of the Orthodox Catholics at this time.</note> were contending fiercely over the election of a new Bishop and the situation was on the verge of violence, Ambrose arrived to ensure public peace through his authority. Suddenly, a voice like that of a child was heard among the people: *"Ambrose for Bishop!"* The bishops and people present shouted their acclaim and approved the choice with their votes. Ambrose recoiled and, having rejected the office, sought safety in flight; however, worn down by prayers and nearly forced by the people, he surrendered. Thus, having first been baptized (for he was still a <term>catechumen</term> <note>a person receiving instruction in the Christian faith but not yet baptized</note>), he was initiated into the sacred office. The Emperor Valentinian, who was present for all these events, broke out in these words:

<margin>
Theodoret, Book 4, Chapter 7.
</margin>
> I thank you, Almighty God and our Savior, that to this man, to whom I had committed bodies, you have committed souls to be ruled, and have declared my choice to have been just. <note>original: "Gratias tibi ago, Deus omnipotens..."</note>

Having become Bishop, he divided his wealth and distributed it for the use of the poor. Entrusting the care of his family's affairs to his brother Satyrus, he devoted himself entirely to theological studies, in which he employed the Roman priest Simplicianus as his instructor. Around the year 377, when barbarian tribes were breaking into the Roman Empire, he fled to Illyricum; taking that opportunity, it seems, he also visited Rome. There, when a virgin companion of his sister kissed his hand according to the pious custom of that age, he said with a smile, *"Look, as I told you, you are kissing a priest's hand."* In the year 380, while the Arians gnashed their teeth in vain, he appointed Anemmius as Bishop of Sirmium. In the following year, he presided over the Council of Aquileia, in which he took it upon himself to debate against Palladius, the leader of the Arians, and did so successfully. In the year 383, Magnus Maximus of Britain seized the reins of the Empire and, in a battle joined at Lyon, killed the Emperor Gratian by treachery. Ambrose, sent by the Emperor Valentinian [II] to the tyrant, used his authority and eloquence to ensure that Maximus remained within the Transalpine provinces. Emboldened by these internal movements within the Empire, the Pagans took heart and gathered strength to restore their worship, with Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, the Prefect of Rome—most famous for his praise of eloquence—leading their cause. From this arose that noble contest between Symmachus himself and Ambrose concerning the restoration of the Altar of Victory; in which [Ambrose proved to be] far supe-

# The Age of Arianism.

<margin>
THE 4TH CENTURY, from the year 300.
* Prosper of Aquitaine, *On the Promises*, part 3, chapter 38.
</margin>
...Ambrose emerged victorious, so much so that Symmachus not only lost his case, but was shortly thereafter expelled from the city and, placed upon a common cart, was ordered to remain beyond the hundredth milestone from the City <note>The City refers to Rome; being sent beyond the hundredth milestone was a standard form of honorary or legal exile.</note>. While the pagans were silenced, the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> rose up, relying on the patronage of the Empress Justina and the young Emperor Valentinian II. Consequently, in the year 386, using military force, they demanded that the cathedrals be handed over to them. The most holy man [Ambrose] manfully opposed them, and he steadied the terrified hearts of the citizens both by his presence and his prayers; he caused the heretics to fail in their desire. Although provoked by so many and such great injuries from the Emperor, he nevertheless did not hesitate to undertake a second embassy to **Maximus** <note>Magnus Maximus, a usurper who had seized power in the West.</note> when he was threatening Italy. There, he dealt fearlessly with the tyrant in a long enough conversation, but he returned without having accomplished the mission. Three years after this occurred the exceedingly barbaric and cruel massacre of the **Thessalonians**, perpetrated by order of **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius the Great (r. 379–395). In response to the murder of a Roman official, he ordered the massacre of thousands in the circus of Thessalonica.</note>. For this reason, Ambrose rebuked him most sharply; nor would he admit him to the Church until he had performed a long and public penance. In the year 392, after Valentinian was removed by the treachery of Arbogast and Eugenius seized the tyranny, Ambrose left Milan and withdrew to Bologna, then set out for Faenza, and finally to Florence; from there, once Eugenius was defeated, he returned home. Four years having passed, and being aware of his own fate, he predicted that death would come to him before Easter of the year 397. God confirmed this prediction. For at sixty-four years of age, he fell into illness; and though he was confined to his bed and earnestly entreated by the nobles of the city to beg God for his life through prayer, he refused, replying: *“I have not lived among you so as to be ashamed to live: nor do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord.”* He died on the day before the Nones of April in the year 397 <note>April 4, 397 AD.</note>, and was buried with a great funeral procession in the Ambrosian Basilica. He was a man of the highest piety, venerable in every kind of virtue; a prelate of unconquerable spirit who boldly resisted Jews, Pagans, and heretics of every sort. He was most skilled in Greek as well as Latin literature; for which reason he watered his own little gardens abundantly from the writings of the Greek Fathers, such as **Origen** and **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a famous theologian of Alexandria.</note>; in this he is to be praised, that he plucked the flowers while suppressing the weeds <note>original: "loliis" (darnel or tares).</note>. He employed a style that was concise, sharp, and mosaic-like <note>original: "tessellato"; referring to a style composed of many finely joined pieces of thought or citation.</note>, which imitates the eloquence of **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher known for his pithy, sententious prose.</note>, though with a gentler flow.

contains this note: THE SECOND BEGINS. Bishop Ambrose translated this from Greek into Latin <note>original: "Ambroſius Epiſcopus è Græco tranſtulit in Latinum"</note>. The immense parity between the styles of Ambrose and Hegesippus, the same phrases frequented by both, and the same verbal subtleties delighted in by both, argue for this attribution; Johannes Gronovius, in his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, proves this most extensively by producing nearly six hundred matching passages. However that may be, it is certain that the author was a contemporary of Ambrose and flourished as this century was drawing to a close. It is clear from his own frequent hints that he lived while the Roman Empire in the West was still standing and flourishing. It is no less certain that he wrote after the times of Constantine, as he frequently mentions Constantinople and "New Rome." Indeed, the names of the provinces of Scotland and Saxony found in his work clearly date him to the end of this declining century. Furthermore, the reader should be warned that the *Summary* <note>Anacephalæoſis</note> joined to the end of this History does not belong to the same author as the History itself, but is the work of some foul and witless compiler.

This History exists comprised in five books: Paris, 1511; Cologne, 1521, in folio; with the notes of Gualther, Cologne, 1575, in octavo; and in the *Christian History* of Laurent de la Barre, page 399.

---

<margin>375.</margin>
MARTIN, a native of Sabaria in Pannonia <note>modern-day Szombathely, Hungary</note>, was born in the year 319. Born to a pagan father and a military man, he was educated at Ticinum in Italy <note>modern Pavia</note>. In the year 327, he became a catechumen; in 334, he was bound by the military oath; three years later, he was washed in the sacred bath <note>baptized</note>; and in the year 356, he obtained a discharge from Julian Caesar while he was campaigning in Gaul. In the year 375, he was ordained Bishop of Tours; he was held in such high esteem by all that even Maximus the Tyrant <note>The usurper emperor Magnus Maximus</note> considered it an honor to have him as a dinner guest. He died in the year of Christ 400, at the age of 81. His *Profession of Faith* survives, which is found in almost every edition of the *Library of the Fathers*.

---

<margin>378.</margin>
DIODORUS, noble in the splendor of his birth, a Priest and Abbot of Antioch, instructed many <term>monastics</term> <note>original: "μονάζοντας" (monazontas) — those living as monks</note> under his rule in piety and the higher disciplines. When Meletius, the Bishop of Antioch, was sent into exile under Emperor Valens, and the gathering of the Catholic flock was excluded from the city and the public churches, Diodorus fed the sheep by frequently holding religious assemblies for the celebration of the <term>Synaxis</term> <note>The liturgical assembly, particularly for the Eucharist</note> in a field by the banks of the nearby river, where soldiers were accustomed to exercise. He courageously resisted the traps and tyranny of the Arians. In the year 378, Meletius returned from exile and appointed him Bishop of Tarsus. In the year 381, Diodorus took part in the Ecumenical Council of Constantinople; by this council, the care and governance of the Eastern Churches were entrusted to him along with Pelagius of Laodicea, while still preserving the prerogative of honor they wished to grant to Meletius <margin>Socrates, Book 5, ch. 8.</margin>. How long he held his episcopal office remains uncertain to us, except that by the year 394, Phalerius had succeeded to his see, as is clear from the Acts of the Synod of Constantinople held under Nectarius in that same year. He was truly a man most learned in every respect, who, in investigating the sense of the Holy Scriptures, rejected allegories and sought only the simple and obvious understanding of the words. However, he harbored certain blemishes and errors regarding the faith; these, mixed throughout his books, were later found to favor too much the cause and heresy of Nestorius (who was his student). Regarding his style, Photius <margin>* Codex 223.</margin> gives this judgment: <note>original: "ὅτι δὲ τὴν φράσιν καθαρός τε καὶ εὐκρινὴς, ταῖς δὲ ἐνθυμήμασι καὶ τῇ τῶν ἐπιχειρημάτων διαπλάσει" — stating that his style was pure and clear, and excellent in its ideas and the structure of its arguments.</note>

Among Diodorus's short works, the most notable was the one *Against the Synousiasts*, or against the Apollinarians. Proclus of Constantinople chose excerpts from this, which both he himself in a letter to the Armenians, and Cyril in three books (now lost), took pains to refute. Besides the fragments Proclus has in that location, Marius Mercator (Garner edition, part 2, pp. 317, 318) provides others he translated; some are provided by Leontius in book 3 *Against Eutyches*, and many by Facundus of Hermiane; others are in the Acts of the Fifth Synod, Session 5, though Diodorus's name is suppressed. Often, other ancient writers also wrongly cite this work under the name of Theodore of Mopsuestia.

# The Arian Century.

<margin>THE 4th CENTURY, from the year 300.

He also wrote Interpretations of the entire Old Testament; *On the distinction between Contemplation and Allegory*; a *Chronicle*, in which the chronological errors of Eusebius are noted. He wrote on the four Gospels; on the Acts of the Apostles; and on the Epistle of Saint John. Further works include: *That there is one God in the Trinity*; *Against the Melchizedekites* <note>A sect that believed Melchizedek was a celestial power greater than Christ</note>; *Against the Jews*; *On the Resurrection of the Dead*; *On the Soul*; and *Against various sects concerning the Soul*. He wrote *Chapters to Gratian* and various arguments regarding the Holy Spirit, which were filled with incautious dogmas redolent of heresy. Photius briefly describes a treatise on this subject in volume 102. He wrote eight books *Against the Astronomers, Astrologers, and Fate*, of which Photius preserved very extensive excerpts for us in volume 223. Other titles include: *On the Sphere and the Seven Zones, and the contrary Movement of the Stars*; *On the Sphere of Hipparchus*; *On Providence*; *Against Plato*; *On God and the gods*; *On Nature, Matter, and the Just*; *On God and the false matter of the Greeks*; *That invisible Natures are not made of the Elements*; *Questions and Answers to Euphronius*; *Against Aristotle*; *On the Celestial Body*; *On the heat of the Sun*; and *Against those who say the heavens are a living animal*. Also: *How the Creator remains eternal, but his creations do not*; *How willing and unwilling exist in the eternal God, against Porphyry*; and *On Animals and Sacrifices*. From these, it might perhaps be rightly judged that many which follow the books against Fate were merely individual parts of those books, taking their titles from the specific subject matter discussed within them. This much is recorded by Suidas and Photius. Basil mentions two books written by him against the heretics. To these may also be added works which Hebediesu <note>A 13th-century East Syrian writer also known as Abdisho bar Berika</note> says still exist in Syriac, namely: *The Book of Politics*; *The Book of the Destruction of Astrologers*; *Against the Eunomians*; *Against the Contentious*; *Against the Jews*; *Against the Manichaeans*; *Against Apollinarius*; and an *Exposition on part of Matthew*. Hebediesu adds that Diodore composed sixty books in total, which the Arians burned.

<margin>378.
* Book 8, chapter 6.</margin>
**HELLADIUS**, in the year 378, succeeded Basil the Great in the see of Caesarea. In the year 381, he took part in the Council of Constantinople; and after the synod was dismissed, he was appointed by the Emperor Theodosius as a judge of Catholic communion for the Pontic province, along with Gregory of Nyssa and Otreius, Bishop of Melitene. It is clear from Sozomen that he was married, for Sozomen writes that Helladius ordained Gerontius as Bishop of Nicomedia as a favor, because Gerontius had secured a military post in the palace for Helladius's son. It is uncertain in what year he died. He wrote a *Life of Saint Basil*, his predecessor, which is cited by John of Damascus in his first *Oration on Images* near the end. However, whether that work (of which Damascus has a fragment) truly had Helladius as its author—regardless of what Damascus claims—there is a just reason for doubt.

---

<margin>378.</margin>
**JEROME**, a Dalmatian by nation, was born in the town of Stridon, which was once situated on the border of Pannonia and Dalmatia. He was born to a Christian father named Eusebius in the year 329, if those who write that he died in the ninety-first year of his age calculate correctly. Instructed in the higher disciplines from his very boyhood, he obtained the best teachers in every field: in Grammar, Donatus, a grammarian of great name in Rome (where Jerome was sent while still a boy); in Rhetoric, Victorinus, a professor of eloquence in the same city; just as later in Hebrew he studied under Bar-hanina and other Jews hired with difficulty and at no small price. In the Sacred Scriptures, he studied under Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, Apollinaris of Laodicea, Paulinus of Antioch, and—having already become gray-haired—Didymus of Alexandria. Good God, what men and how great they were! Baptized already in adulthood, he left Rome and began to travel through foreign regions. He wandered through all the Gauls on every side with his fellow student Bonosus as a companion, and diligently searched all the libraries. He stayed for some time at Trier <note>Treveris</note>, where, at the request of Hilary, he transcribed with his own hand Hilary's huge book *On the Synods*. From here he sought Aquileia, where he formed a friendship with Rufinus, a priest of Aquileia; from there, through Dalmatia, Thrace, and various provinces of Asia, he proceeded to Antioch with the very wealthy Evagrius of Antioch and his fellow student Heliodorus as companions. There he fell into a very serious illness, but through the hospitality of Evagrius...

# The Arian Century.

<margin>THE 4th CENTURY, from the year 300.</margin>
The practice of this lifestyle grew strong in him. From then on, having embraced the monastic rule of life and having tested—and soon deserted—many places of retreat, he finally settled for four years in a harsh wilderness among the Syrians and Hagarenes <note>A medieval term for Arabs, believed to be descendants of Hagar</note> at the age of thirty. There, with his necessities supplied at the expense of Evagrius, he applied himself with intense passion to the study of piety and literature; he mastered the Oriental languages and prepared himself for writing. In the year 378, he was raised to the rank of Priest by Paulinus of Antioch, from which time he became especially famous. Shortly before the Ecumenical Council <note>The First Council of Constantinople in 381</note>, he set out for Constantinople, where he diligently listened to Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> and benefited from him as a teacher. In the year 382, Paulinus and Epiphanius, summoned to Rome by imperial letters, took Jerome with them from the East as a traveling companion. Staying in Rome, he lodged for three years with Paula, a matron illustrious for her piety and the splendor of her name. He attained such a great reputation and esteem among everyone that he was chosen by Pope Damasus to be his secretary for correspondence <note>original: "ab Epistolis conscribendis"</note>, and he was acclaimed by the clergy and common people alike as worthy to fulfill the office of the High Priesthood <note>The Papacy</note>. After the death of Damasus in 385, Jerome was hounded by various slanders from the Origenists <note>Followers of the theologian Origen, whose works Jerome initially admired but later fiercely opposed</note>, who had tried in vain to draw him to their side; consequently, he felt it necessary to leave Rome. Accompanied by his brother Paulinian, he boarded a ship and was received by Epiphanius after being carried to Cyprus. From there he proceeded to Antioch and, led by Paulinus, entered Jerusalem in the middle of winter. There he declared that he saw many miracles with his own eyes which he had previously known only by reputation. In the following year, he traveled to Egypt, visited the monasteries of Nitria, and while staying for some time in Alexandria, he listened to Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind</note>. However, offended by the excessive zeal for Origenism which he found taking root among the monks, he returned to Palestine. He chose the rural district of Bethlehem as the seat for his monastic life and his old age. There he diligently pursued his studies, produced innumerable writings, and instructed many noble boys committed to his care in piety and fine literature. He provided an illustrious example of perfect piety in every respect to the holy inhabitants of those places, and he gave answers to the most distinguished men—both in rank and learning—who flocked to him from everywhere as if consulting an oracle. In this place, he engaged in great disputes for many years with his friend Rufinus (once very intimate) and John, Bishop of Jerusalem, who were defending the cause of Origenism; he also crushed the heresy of Pelagius and his followers with his writings. In the year 410, he kindly received into his monastery many refugees from the city of Rome after it was captured by the Goths, who were heading toward Jerusalem and the holy places, and he relieved them with all the help he could muster. Finally, in the year 420, full of fame and days, and heavy with old age, he was removed from human affairs in his Bethlehem retreat at the age of 91. To contract into a few words what ought to be said of such a great man, the eulogy that Prosper* <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a 5th-century Christian writer</note> once dedicated to him is sufficient, unsurpassed for his age:

<margin>* From the book "On the Ungrateful" <note>original: "Lib. de ingrat."</note>, not far from the beginning.</margin>

> ->Graced with Hebrew, Greek, and Latin<-
> ->Eloquence, a model of conduct, and teacher of the world,<-
> ->Jerome, with his most excellent books, cut through the enemy,<-
> ->And revealed by what whirlwind the darkness that had arisen<-
> ->Wished to obscure the true light.<-

<margin>
† Against Rufinus, Apology 2, page 233.
|| Letters, book 5, letter 19.
</margin>
"I am a Philosopher, Rhetorician, Grammarian, Logician, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Trilingual"; as he says of himself against Rufinus†. Add to this that he was a most accomplished Theologian, and in the judgment of Erasmus||, he was without controversy by far the most learned and eloquent of all Christians of that time, and the prince of Theologians. However—let it be said with the peace of so holy a man—he possessed a fervid and unrestrained mind that indulged too much in its own passions; once provoked, he treated his adversaries most harshly, and he hardly—if ever—restrained himself from an invective and satirical vein of writing. Sufficiently clear witnesses for us are the enmities he once had with Rufinus (his former close associate), John of Jerusalem, Jovinian, Vigilantius, and others. With hardly any restraint, he vomits forth whole wagonloads of insults, having no regard for person, dignity, or learning. And what wonder is this? Since he is accustomed to exercise an overly harsh and clearly insolent judgment even against Saint Paul the Apostle himself. How often does he anxiously weigh Paul’s words against the critical rules of Grammarians, objecting to *Solecisms* <note>Grammatical errors or improprieties</note>, *faulty delivery, and the use of common speech* * (so much so that he felt it necessary to write an apology for himself on this matter: "We," he says, "whenever we note Solecisms or anything of the sort, are not attacking the Apostle, as the malevolent claim," etc.) † *because Paul was unable to express profound meanings in a foreign tongue, nor did he care greatly for words since he kept the meaning safe*; and so || *Paul said he was unskilled in speech not out of humility, as most people think, but truly*. Finally, * *he became a fool with the foolish Galatians, using only the simplest arguments, such as fools could understand and which were almost common street-talk; so much so that if he had not prefaced it by saying 'I speak as a man' <note>original Latin: "secundùm hominem dico"</note>, he might have displeased the wise.* I pass over more harsh things said against a man who was divinely inspired <note>original Greek: θεόπνυστον (theopneuston)</note> and by far the most learned of the Apostles, lest I seem to overly disturb the spirit of a most learned man who served the Church so well. In this also Jerome is to be reproved: that while he extols virginity with altogether immoderate praise, he seems to hold views on marriage that are less than honorable or modest. Certainly, he makes those who marry twice only better than harlots, comparing them to the unclean animals and serpents of Noah's Ark; and he does not blush to compare a woman seeking a second fertile marriage to a dog returning to its vomit or a washed sow returning to the wallowing mire.

But we each suffer our own spirits. Let Erasmus alone * give his opinion on Jerome's eloquence. "In him," he says, "what phrasing! What artistry of speech! By which he has not only left all other Christians a long distance behind him, but he even seems to compete with Cicero himself. I certainly, unless my love for this most holy man deceives me, when I compare Jerome’s oratory with that of Cicero, seem to find I know not what lacking in the prince of eloquence himself. There is such variety in our Jerome, such weight of thought, such a fluency of Enthymemes <note>A type of logical argument or syllogism used in rhetoric</note>. To point out this artistry in the letters of the eloquent is as difficult as it is by far most useful."

The Psalter [Book of Psalms] was translated into Latin from the Hebrew by Jerome himself. Jerome spent a great deal of effort partly in translating Holy Scripture anew and partly in correcting it. While still a young man, he corrected the entire Latin Old Testament by comparing it with the Greek manuscripts of the *Hexapla* <note>The *Hexapla* was a massive six-column edition of the Old Testament compiled by Origen, which Jerome used to identify discrepancies between the Hebrew and Greek texts</note>, adding marks and asterisks wherever he changed anything. He also accurately translated certain books, including the Psalms, from the Greek. But that version was lost long ago; moreover, at the request of Pope Damasus, he twice corrected the Latin Psalter using the Lucianic edition of the Seventy <note>original: "τῶν ο'" (the Seventy), referring to the Septuagint, the standard Greek translation of the Old Testament used by the early Church</note>; this corrected version began to be used immediately by the Roman Church and still exists today in the Vulgate Bible, just as the New Testament was purged by him from the Greek sources in a similar manner. Furthermore, he published a corrected and emended version of the Greek Septuagint <note>original: "τῶν LXX."</note> from better-quality manuscripts for the use of students. Later in life, during his retreat in Bethlehem, he translated all the books of the Old Testament held as canonical by the Jews from the Hebrew truth <note>original: "Hebraicâ veritate", a term Jerome used to argue that the original Hebrew text was the ultimate authority for the Old Testament, rather than the later Greek translations</note> into the Latin language; to these he also added the books of Judith and Tobit, translated from the Chaldean <note>referring to Aramaic</note> language. From this translation, the Book of Psalms (which is read among his works) and the Prophets still exist today. For Jerome's version of the Prophets is preserved in the Vulgate Bible with only very slight changes, while it exists whole and pure among his Commentaries on the Prophets. Regarding the other books of the Old Testament translated by him, whatever survives of them is preserved in the Vulgate Bible, mixed and confused with the ancient Latin version made from the Greek, so that it can scarcely be distinguished which parts belong to Jerome and which to the ancient version. Finally, let me note that Jerome, just as he did for the other books of the New Testament, also prepared a new version of the Canonical Epistles. To these he added a Preface addressed to the Virgin Eustochium, which, although found in almost all manuscript copies, is rarely included in printed editions; it was even missing from the editions of Erasmus. Nicholas of Lyra placed it before his exposition on the Canonical Epistles in the final volume, folio 209. In this Preface, Jerome teaches us two things in particular. First, that in the Latin manuscripts of his time, the Epistles of Blessed Peter held the first place among the seven Canonical Epistles: *so that, because Peter was first in the order of the Apostles, his Epistles might also be first in the order of the others.* He himself, however, following the Greek manuscripts, restored them to their proper order. Second, that the most famous passage of Saint John in the First Epistle concerning the Trinity <note>This refers to the "Johannine Comma" (1 John 5:7-8), a verse explicitly mentioning the Father, Word, and Holy Spirit, which was a point of intense debate during the Arian controversy</note> had been deleted by unfaithful translators (by whom he primarily means the Arians), with the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit completely omitted. Thus, it should not seem surprising if it is missing from so many manuscript copies today.

Hebrew locations translated from Eusebius, though in a looser version, with many things added or changed from his own [knowledge].

### WORKS BY OTHERS [which are found among the Works of Jerome]

Commentaries on all the Psalms, written by many and uncertain authors; however, it cannot be doubted that many things truly belonging to Jerome are present within them. For in the explanation of Psalm 93 (to say nothing of other arguments), a fragment of Jerome’s *Exposition* is inserted word-for-word, which was cited by Augustine in his *Letter to Fortunatianus*. Furthermore, in the exposition of Psalm 50, words of Jerome are referenced that were alleged by Gregory the Great in his explanation of the 4th Penitential Psalm. <note>The Penitential Psalms are a traditional collection of seven psalms expressive of sorrow for sin.</note> Mariano Victorio <note>A 16th-century Italian bishop and scholar who edited Jerome's works.</note> strove mightily to prove this was a genuine work of Jerome through many arguments, and he busied himself with refuting the arguments brought against it; but in resolving those arguments, the matter turned out so poorly for him that he seems to have wasted his effort.

*The Letter of Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, inviting her to the Bethlehem retreat, which seems to have been dictated by Jerome.*
*The Letter of Pammachius and Oceanus to Jerome.*
*The Gospels of Luke and John, corrected from ancient copies by an uncertain author.*
*The Letter of Valerius to Rufinus on not taking a wife.* <note>This was a popular medieval text often wrongly attributed to Jerome or Valerius of Hippo; it is actually a satirical work by Walter Map.</note>
*The Rule of Monks, compiled from the writings of Jerome by Lupus of Olmedo, and approved by Pope Martin V after the year 1417.*
*A Dialogue of Jerome and Augustine on the origin of souls, collected from their own writings by an uncertain, and indeed unskilled, author.*
*A Homily on the Body and Blood of Christ, and another on the Gospel of Matthew, by an uncertain author.*

There are also found in the same place several works by Augustine, Damasus, Theophilus, Anastasius, Epiphanius, and Rufinus; regarding these, you may see more in their respective sections.

<margin>
* On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 140.
</margin>
The *Works of Jerome* were published through the care of Erasmus at Basel in 1516, 1526, and 1553 (which is a clearly beautiful and accurate edition), and in 1565. Also at Rome in 1566 and 1572 (which Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a highly influential Cardinal and Jesuit scholar of the Counter-Reformation.</note> advises has been purged of the errors of Erasmus; whether the same occurred in the subsequent editions of the Papists, the learned may judge); at Antwerp in 1580 (under the care of Mariano Victorio); at Cologne in 1578; and at Paris in 1533, 1546, 1579, 1602, and 1623 (to which various observations and corrections were added); and finally at Frankfurt in 1684, in twelve volumes. This last edition includes all the notes, scholia, <note>Grammatical or explanatory notes written in the margins of ancient manuscripts.</note> censures, indexes, and other collected materials of all scholars pertaining to Jerome's works, which are contained in the final three volumes.

GELASIUS the Elder, the nephew of Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem, was installed by his uncle in the see of Caesarea in Palestine in the year 380. In the following year, he took part in the Second Ecumenical Council, and he was still writing before this century ended. He was a man, according to the testimony of Theodoret, *distinguished in both speech and life* <note>original Greek: λόγω καὶ βίω κοσμέυενος</note>, notable for his learning as well as the holiness of his life; Jerome says he was also *of accurate and polished speech* <note>original Latin: accurati etiam limatique sermonis</note>. He translated the two books of Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History* into the Greek language, as Photius teaches us. However, as for what Photius adds from Gelasius's preface—that Cyril was the author who urged him to write these very things—and what is held elsewhere—that Cyril himself joined with Gelasius in forging that translation—it is clear from the facts that this is impossible, because Rufinus wrote his *Ecclesiastical History* almost a decade after Cyril's death. Furthermore, a fragment of a homily by our Gelasius on the Epiphany survives in Theodoret’s *Dialogue 3*, page 167.

<margin>
Year 380.
</margin>
TIMOTHY, the brother of Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, whom he succeeded in that see around the year 379. In the year 381, after the Synod had already begun, he set out for Constantinople with his bishops. There, he was indignant that Gregory Nazianzen had been confirmed in the see of Constantinople by the Fathers without waiting for his consent. He opposed Gregory with all his might, taking up the defense of Maximus's faction, and he brought it about that Gregory, weary of the outcries and troubles, abdicated his see.

# The Arian Century.
<note>The "Arian Century" refers to the 4th century, a period dominated by the theological conflicts following the rise of Arianism, which questioned the nature of Jesus Christ's divinity.</note>

<margin>
The 4th Century from the year 300.
* Sozomen, Book 6, chapter 29, page 680.
* Location cited above.
† Gerardus Vossius, *On Greek Historians*, book 2, chapter 19.
</margin>

He died in the year 385. Among other works, he wrote the **Book on the Lives of the Monks**, <note>original: *Librum De Vitis Monachorum*</note> which is mentioned by the historian Sozomen *, but which the ravages of time have stolen from us. There exist today writings by him in Greek and Latin titled **Canonical Responses to the questions proposed to him** regarding Bishops and Clerics, featuring the commentaries of Balsamon <note>Theodore Balsamon was a 12th-century canon lawyer of the Byzantine Church.</note> published in Paris, 1618, and in the *Collection of Canons*, Volume 2, Oxford, 1672. There is also a work under his name titled **Narrative of the Miracles of Saint Menas, the Egyptian Martyr**, <note>Saint Menas was one of the most famous Egyptian martyrs, often depicted with two camels.</note> available in Latin in Surius’s collection for November 10th. That Timothy indeed wrote the *Lives* of the Holy Fathers and certain monks is testified (as we have said) by Sozomen *; and the illustrious Vossius † conjectures that many of the lives currently circulating in the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>The *Vitae Patrum*, a famous collection of early monastic biographies.</note> are his. Finally, Facundus <note>A 6th-century African bishop.</note> cites his **Letter to Diodorus of Tarsus** in book 4, chapter 2.

---

<margin>
Year 380.
Sozomen, book 6, chapter 30.
Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 86.
* Location cited above.
</margin>

**EVAGRIUS**, the son of a priest, was a native of the city of the Iberians located near the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea. "Iberia" here refers to Caucasian Iberia, roughly modern-day Georgia.</note>; for this reason, Jerome called him the **Hyperborean**. <note>A term from Greek mythology for people living in the far north.</note> He was ordained as a Reader of the Church of Caesarea by Saint Basil, and after Basil’s death, he was made a Deacon by Gregory of Nyssa, flourishing from the year 380. He drank deeply from the fountain of sacred learning under Gregory Nazianzen, by whom he was promoted to the Archdiaconate of the Church of Constantinople. Since he was of elegant appearance and wore exquisite clothing, he fell under the suspicion of a certain nobleman who believed Evagrius was too familiar with his wife; thus, his life was put in danger. However, having been warned by an Angel in a dream, and feeling himself forced by an oath—after touching the Gospels—to leave the city immediately, he departed Constantinople after the year 385. He sought out Jerusalem and was welcomed into the home of Melania the Roman <note>Known as Melania the Elder, a wealthy noblewoman who founded monasteries in Jerusalem.</note>. At her urging, once he had decided to lead a monastic life, he set out for Egypt. He remained hidden for fifteen years in a certain monastery in Nitria <note>A famous desert monastic center in Egypt.</note> as a disciple of both Macarii <note>Macarius of Egypt and Macarius of Alexandria, two pillars of early desert monasticism.</note> in the ascetic life. While he stayed in that place, he completely refused the burden of the Episcopacy—which Theophilus of Alexandria had tried to impose on him by leaving no stone unturned—by withdrawing through a clever deception. He strenuously defended the cause of the Origenists <note>Followers of the teachings of Origen of Alexandria; this became a major controversy in the late 4th century.</note>, for which reason he was often lashed by the pen of Jerome. He died at an advanced age, though in what year is not clear. As Sozomen notes *, he was a man of primary learning, endowed both with a faculty for understanding and a great abundance of speech. He was most sagacious in distinguishing thoughts that tended toward either virtue or vice. His character was moderate, and he was so far removed from all pride and arrogance that he did not swell with pride when rightly praised, nor did he bear insults with an uneven mind when undeservedly criticized. His reputation for miracles and portents was in no way inferior to that of either of his teachers, and he was moreover greatly distinguished by the immense abstinence of his life. Regarding his style, Nicephorus says: *“His works are all wonderful, filled with thoughts and expressions that possess a persuasive power, and whoever reads them will know what kind of man he was.”* <note>original Greek: *Θαυμαστά γε πάντα (Opera ejus) κὰι νοήμασι κὰι φράσει μεσή τὴ ἐπαγωγήν ἐπανχουντα, κὰι δí’ ὧν γέγονεν ὁ ἀνήρ, ὁ τέτοις ἐντυχῶν εἴσεται.*</note>

### W R I T I N G S.

<margin>
See Jerome, *To Ctesiphon against the Pelagians*, page 252.
Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 42.
* *On Famous Men*, chapter 11.
</margin>

He wrote **Orations or Prayers**, **600 Gnostic Problems**, and a **Letter to Melania**. He also wrote a **Book and Sentences on Dispassion** <note>original: *περὶ ἀπαθέιας*; "Apatheia" in this context refers to freedom from disordered passions.</note>, and a **Book of 100 Sentences for the Use of Anchorites** <note>An anchorite is a monk who lives in total seclusion.</note> (whether this is the same as his practical work, let others decide). He wrote **a few very obscure brief Sentences** which Gennadius translated into Latin *. He also wrote **two books of Stichera** (for which Palladius uses the term *Sacred*), or **Elementary Books**, one addressed to monks living in communities, and the other to virgins consecrated to God. These *Stichera* are available in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, volume 27, where, although they are attributed to a writer of uncertain age, it is clearer than the sun that they belong to our Evagrius. He wrote the **Monasticum, or On Practice**, <note>original: *περὶ τῶ Πρακτικῶ*</note> consisting of 100 chapters; Socrates Scholasticus recites a fragment of this book in book 3, chapter 7, and another much longer one in book 4, chapter 23. The illustrious Cotelerius published the complete treatise in Greek and Latin with notes in the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, volume 3, page 70, preceded also by a Greek and Latin **Letter to Anatolius**, which serves as a preface to the *Practical* and *Gnostic* works. For Evagrius also wrote the **Gnosticus, or On those granted the gift of knowledge**, divided into 50 chapters; Gennadius testifies that he translated this into Latin, and a fragment exists in Socrates, book 4, chapter 23. Finally, he wrote the **Antirrheticus** <note>A work "against" or "refuting" specific temptations.</note> collected from the Holy Scriptures against tempting demons, divided into eight parts according to the number of the **eight vicious thoughts**, <note>These eight thoughts (gluttony, lust, greed, pride, etc.) were the direct ancestors of the Seven Deadly Sins.</note> dedicated to Anatolius; which he himself admits he rendered into Latin—

The most learned Émery Bigot first brought it out in Greek and Latin, and published it with Palladius's *Life of Chrysostom* (Paris, 1680, in quarto), though he doubts whether the book we have today is the same one mentioned by the historian Socrates *; as nothing regarding the Collected Holy Scriptures is read in it. Yet he is not unwilling to concede that it could be that this treatise is a small fragment <term>ἀποσπασμάτιον: a small piece or excerpt</term> of the work described by Socrates; namely, with the scriptural testimonies removed, and the words of Evagrius retained, which graphically depicted the wicked thoughts of men. Furthermore, the *Book on the Principles of Monastic Affairs, and their arrangement according to tranquility*; as it is established from the *Lives of the Fathers* that Evagrius wrote such a work, was published in Greek and Latin with notes by Cotelier in *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume III, p. 103. The same Cotelier gave a *Fragment or Scholium of Evagrius on the Tetragrammaton, the Name of God written as PIPI* <note>Because the Hebrew letters for God's name (YHWH) looked like the Greek letters ΠIΠI (PIPI), early Greek scribes sometimes wrote them that way to preserve the visual appearance of the holy name.</note> in Greek and Latin with notes in the same place, p. 116. Besides, Rufinus converted many of Evagrius's works into the Latin language; but those versions perished long ago.

<margin>

</margin>
### MAXIMUS, Egyptian by birth, Alexandrian by city, had parents of no low station, and as the report goes, they were martyrs; indeed, he himself used to boast that after the death of Athanasius, he was banished to the Oasis for the sake of the faith. By his way of life, he professed himself a Cynic philosopher; and he did not lack the cloak, the staff, the long beard, the bold and shameless manners, and the reckless audacity and biting wit characteristic of that sect. He had earned no small name for himself among foreigners; hence, letters from Basil to him survive today. He flourished especially in the year 380. Leaving Alexandria, he arrived in Constantinople. Upon his arrival, Gregory of Nazianzus welcomed him not only with an Encomiastic Oration <note>A formal speech of praise.</note> but also with hospitality; he invited him to his table, imbued him more fully with the elements of the faith, washed him in the sacred font, and finally co-opted him into the ranks of the clergy. But Maximus, forgetful of these benefits and friendship, called three bishops from Egypt during Gregory’s absence and arranged to be ordained Bishop of Constantinople. But when the people, and even the Arians themselves, were indignant at the act and burst into the church, the bishops were put to flight and forced to perform the rest of the scene in the house of a certain flute-player. Indeed, Maximus himself fled from the city as the common people raged and poured carts full of insults upon the treacherous man; he first commended his cause to be heard by the Synod of Aquileia, and then to the Emperor Theodosius. But all his efforts were in vain; condemned also by the Synod of Constantinople, he returned to Alexandria, where, having stirred up a faction against the Bishop, he was cast out of the city by the Augustal Prefect. What became of him after that is not clear. He wrote, as Jerome testifies <margin>* On Illustrious Men, chapter 127.</margin>, a distinguished *Book on the Faith against the Arians*, which he presented to the Emperor Gratian at Milan.

---

<margin>380.</margin>
### NEMESIUS, formerly a Christian philosopher and then Bishop of Emesa, as they say, flourished around the year 380. Others assign him to the fifth century. But everything is uncertain, for the ancients are entirely silent about him. There does exist among the poems of Gregory of Nazianzus a certain letter dedicated to a certain Nemesius, a legal expert; but whether he is our Nemesius is completely unproven. Whoever he certainly was, he defends Origen’s dogma regarding the pre-existence of souls, and specifically refutes the heretics Mani, Eunomius, and Apollinarius; so that no bad conjecture can be drawn that he wrote around this time. There exists in Greek and Latin the *Book on the Nature of Man* <note>original: *De Natura Hominis*</note> in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* (Paris, 1624, Vol. II, p. 466), and separately (Antwerp, 1565), and newly revised and illustrated with notes (Oxford, 1671, octavo).

A strenuous champion of Catholic truth against the Arians, he everywhere overthrew their heresy with reasons and arguments. He flourished around the year 380. He was very familiar with Ambrose when he was promoted to the see of Milan; Augustine testifies that he saw him staying with Ambrose in Milan *. <margin>* Book on Heresies, at the beginning.</margin> In the year 381, he was present at the Synod of Aquileia. He died while Ambrose was still alive, in the year 387, as some say, though this is not entirely clear.

He wrote a *Book on Heresies*; in which he everywhere breathes a love for Catholic truth, but often reveals a less accurate judgment, as he counts among heresies those dogmas which least deserve to be noted by that name. It is extant in the *Library of the Fathers*, volume 7, page 701, and separately together with Idacius Clarus *Basel, 1528; Helmstadt (edited by Fuchtenius), 1611, octavo*, to which a Supplement by an uncertain author was also added.

<margin>381. Sozomen, Book 7, chapters 8, 12.</margin> NECTARIUS, a native of Tarsus in Cilicia, was a man of senatorial rank who held high office in the city of Constantinople. When the see of Constantinople was vacant in the year 381, while he was preparing to return to his homeland, he met with Diodorus, the Bishop of Tarsus, to ask if there was anything he wanted done in Tarsus. Diodorus, respecting the man's gray hair, his countenance worthy of the priesthood, and the gravity of his character, judged that he should be placed in charge of the see. And so he arranged it that among the names of candidates to be offered to the Emperor, Nectarius's name was also written on the list, indeed at the very end of it. When the list had been read through, the Emperor stopped at Nectarius and chose him; and he could not be swayed from this decision. Everyone immediately yielded to the Emperor’s judgment and confirmed it with their votes. Thus, Nectarius was soon baptized and, by the common vote <term>calculo: literally a pebble used for voting</term> of all the bishops, was declared Bishop of Constantinople. In the year 383, when Emperor Theodosius demanded an account of their dogmas from the leaders of all the sects, Nectarius acted with the greatest prudence. He ensured that the faith of the Homousianists <note>Those who believe Christ is of the "same substance" (homoousios) as the Father.</note> was approved, and that the heretics lost both their cause and their freedom to hold assemblies. He died in the year 398. A *Homily on St. Theodore* exists in Latin under his name, printed among certain homilies of Chrysostom, *Paris, 1554, octavo*. However, whether it is genuine may rightly be doubted. His *Synodal Decree on the Bishopric of Bostra* is also preserved in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law*, Book 4.

<margin>381. Theodoret, Book 2, chapter 24; Book 4, chapter 25.</margin> FLAVIAN, born of a noble family and a native (if I am not mistaken) of Antioch, followed the monastic way of life. While still a monk, he fought vigorously against the Arians and fearlessly resisted Leontius, the Bishop of Antioch. Aided by the help and counsel of Diodorus, he took care of the Antiochene flock while Meletius was in exile. He was the first to divide the choir of singers into two parts and taught them to sing the Psalms of David <note>original: *Davidicos Hymnos*</note> alternately. <margin>* Book 6, chapter 8.</margin> Socrates the historian *, supported by no authority that I know of, traces this custom of singing back to Ignatius himself, the third Bishop of Antioch, who had once seen angels in a dream celebrating the Holy Trinity with hymns sung alternately. Later, he attained the dignity of the priesthood; and after Meletius finally died in the year 381, he was appointed Bishop of Antioch, elected by the common vote of the Council of Constantinople. Diodorus of Tarsus and Acacius, Bishop of Beroea, laid hands upon him, while the entire Church honored him with common consent and as if with one voice; as the Fathers themselves <margin>In Theodoret, Book 5, chapter 9.</margin> speak of this matter in letters sent to Damasus <note>Pope Damasus I</note>. Nevertheless, it must not be concealed that this was held as a fault against him, because he had previously bound himself by an oath that he would not consent to the election of a new bishop to be substituted for Meletius while Paulinus was still alive. Because of this act, the Antiochene Schism flared up more sharply, with bishops from almost the entire world taking different sides. For the Westerners and the Egyptians, along with the Arabians and Cypriots, adhered to Paulinus; but the Syrians, Palestinians, Phoenicians, Armenians, Cappadocians, Ponticians, and by far the largest part of the Easterners supported Flavian's cause. ...of Antioch; once the schism was extinguished, he restored the original harmony. Thus, a people who had been divided for a long time were united into one. Furthermore, through the mediation of Theophilus of Alexandria, Damasus <note>Pope Damasus I</note> and the others who had shrunk from communion with Flavian sent him letters of peace. In the year 387, or the following year, that furious sedition of the people of Antioch broke out, in which they threw down the statues of the Emperor and the Empress <note>Emperor Theodosius I and Empress Flaccilla</note> and provoked them with every kind of insult. Flavian was therefore sent to Constantinople in the name of the city’s public interest; with a humble countenance and spirit, through suppliant prayer, gravity of character, and sweet eloquence, he soothed the Emperor's boiling rage. Having accomplished this, he returned home joyful, received by the great acclaim of the people and the poured-out joy of the entire city. He died around the year 403. He wrote several letters, of which Photius * mentions one to the Bishops of Osroene and another to a certain Armenian Bishop; likewise, he wrote certain homilies. Indeed, fragments from his homilies on John the Baptist and on the text, *The Spirit of the Lord is upon me* <note>Original Latin: "Spiritus Domini super me"</note>, are presented by Theodoret in Dialogue 1, page 43; Theodoret also brings forward excerpts from Flavian’s homily on the Theophany <note>The Feast of the Epiphany</note> and from a treatise on the Gospel of Luke in Dialogue 2, page 105.

<margin>
381. Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, book 2.
</margin>
**P**RISCILLIAN, a Spaniard by birth, from a noble family and very wealthy, was led astray by a certain Marcus of Egypt, a follower of the Gnostics and Manichaeans. Around the year 381, he began to concoct a new heresy from the dogmas of both, adding some of his own. From the Gnostics, he introduced into his sect promiscuous lusts and the dissolution of marriages; from the Manichaeans, he took the belief in two principles <note>The dualist belief in a Good God and an Evil God</note> of all things, as well as the follies of astrology and fatalistic necessity. To better hide the secrets and shameful wickedness of his sect, he taught that lying and even perjury were permitted. Regarding the Trinity, he cherished the same views as Sabellius <note>The "Sabellian" heresy claimed that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three persons, but merely three modes or "masks" of one God</note>; he mixed many other monstrous heresies into his dogmas and was moreover deeply addicted to the magical arts. Meanwhile, he maintained a pretense of humility in his speech and dress, teaching a barefoot way of walking and preaching that fasts should be observed even on the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note>. He enticed many nobles and even more commoners into his society through a feigned gravity of character and the art of flattery; he also held many women bound to him, who flocked to him in troops out of a desire for new things and a license for lust. He was accustomed to leading these disciples into mountain hiding places and remote retreats to hold wicked assemblies; to hide these from the eyes and knowledge of others, he allowed his sectarians to feign communion with the Catholic Church by receiving the sacred elements <note>The Bread of the Eucharist</note> in their hands and carrying them away with them rather than consuming them. 

Among the Spanish bishops, he drew Instantius and Salvianus to his side; having been condemned by the Synod of Saragossa at the end of the year 381, they appointed Priscillian—who was a layman until then—as Bishop of Avila to strengthen their cause. However, after Bishops Idacius and Ithacius obtained an edict from the Emperor Gratian that heretics should be expelled from the cities, Instantius, Salvianus, and Priscillian, accompanied by a significant crowd of followers, felt it necessary to travel to Rome to clear themselves of the charges before Damasus. But they were not even admitted to Damasus’s presence, so they returned to Milan, where they found Ambrose equally opposed to them. Therefore, changing their plans, they elicited an edict from the Emperor through the help of Macedonius, the Master of Offices, who had been corrupted by gold, by which they were ordered to be restored to their churches. Relying on this, Instantius and Priscillian (for Salvianus had died) returned to Spain; having bribed the Proconsul, they cast Ithacius, who opposed them, into exile. 

In the year 385, Priscillian was accused by Ithacius before Maximus the Usurper <note>Magnus Maximus, who had seized power in the West</note>; he was brought from Spain to plead his case before a Synod held at Bordeaux <note>Original: "Burdigala"</note>. But when Priscillian appealed from the bishops to the Emperor, his case was committed by Maximus to the prefect Evodius for investigation. After the matter was heard, with Ithacius and Idacius accusing him vigorously and the records being delivered to the Palace, Priscillian was condemned to death by Maximus in the city of Trier <note>Original: "Treveris"</note> in the year 385 or the following year—though others say in the year 388 or 389. His body was returned to Spain and buried with the greatest veneration by his followers, who cherished his memory with such honor that swearing by Priscillian was considered the highest religious act. He was a man, says Sulpicius Severus, who was sharp, restless, eloquent, learned through much reading, and very prompt in debate and disputation.

### HELVIDIUS
HELVIDIUS, a student of Auxentius, Bishop of Milan, and a forerunner of Jovinian. He was prominent in Rome around the year 382. He seems to have held the rank of Priest. Jerome says he was a "rustic man" <note>Original Latin: "homo rusticanus" — implying he was unrefined or lacked formal education</note> and barely initiated into basic letters; seeking to make a name for himself through new dogmas, he argued in a published booklet that the Blessed Mary—after the birth of the Lord, whom she bore as a virgin—was joined to her husband Joseph and had children through their union, who were called the "Brothers of the Lord." Jerome presents certain fragments of this book here and there in his work *Against Helvidius*.

<margin>384.</margin>
### FAUSTINUS
FAUSTINUS, a Priest of the Luciferian Schism <note>A group named after Lucifer of Cagliari, who refused to reconcile with bishops who had previously compromised with Arianism</note>. He was prominent in the year 384. In that same year, it seems, he presented the *Booklet of Prayers* to the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius. This work defends the cause of Lucifer of Cagliari and the followers of the schism he started, clears away the slanders of their opponents, accuses bishops who communed with the Arians of corrupting the orthodox truth, and depicts their shameful behavior as well as their ill-fated deaths. A *Confession of Faith* prepared by Faustinus is placed before the *Booklet of Prayers*, and at its conclusion, the *Rescript* <note>An official imperial response or decree</note> of Emperor Theodosius, issued in favor of Faustinus, is added. He also wrote *On the Trinity*, or *A Book on the Faith Against the Arians*, consisting of seven chapters (or, as others call them, books), dedicated to Empress Flaccilla. These short works survive under Faustinus's name, first published by Sirmond in Paris, 1650, in octavo; then in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 5, pages 637 and 651; and finally illustrated with notes in Oxford, 1678, in octavo.

<margin>384.</margin>
### MARCELLINUS
MARCELLINUS, a Priest of the same time and schism, who presented the *Booklet of Prayers* mentioned above to Emperor Theodosius along with Faustinus. For this reason, it happened that under his name, omitting Faustinus, that booklet is cited by Baronius and others. Furthermore, of the three formulas of faith published by Paschasius Quesnel in the *Roman Code of Canons*, the second is attributed to Marcellinus by Quesnel.

<margin>385.</margin>
### THEOPHILUS
THEOPHILUS, perhaps from Alexandria by birth, became Bishop of Alexandria after the death of Timothy in the year 385. He vigorously opposed the worship of the pagans; for he not only completely overturned the shrines of the idols, but also publicly exposed the tricks of the priests who were deceiving the common people. On this matter, see what Theodoret says in Book 5, Chapter 22. He fought strongly not only against the pagans but also against the monks of Nitria who were fostering the Anthropomorphite heresy <note>The belief that God possesses a physical human body</note>, relying on the protection of Origen’s books. However, not long after, forced by rioting monks, he pretended to condemn those books himself. But soon after, in order to stir up hatred among the monks against Dioscurus and his brothers, called the "Tall Brothers" <note>Original Latin: "Longis"</note>—who held the same views as he did regarding the incorporeal form of God, but were engaged in very serious disputes—he suddenly declared himself an Anthropomorphite and ordered Origen's books to be condemned by everyone. When the Tall Brothers and their followers refused this, he seized that opportunity to drive them out of Egypt and harassed them in the worst ways. In the year 400, having held a Synod in Alexandria, he ensured that Origen and his books were condemned; and through his influence, he brought it about that they were also condemned by Epiphanius in a Synod held on the island of Cyprus. And since he took it poorly that the monks he had expelled were kindly received in Constantinople, he set out for Constantinople in 403 and, having convened a Synod <note>The infamous "Synod of the Oak"</note>, deposed John Chrysostom. But when he found the common people more favorable to Chrysostom and more hostile to himself, he secretly slipped out of the city and returned to Alexandria. <margin>* On Famous Men, chapter 33.</margin> He died in the year 412. Gennadius says * that he wrote one large volume against Origen, in which he condemned almost all his sayings and the man himself equally. Theodoret presents two fragments of this work in Dialogue 2, page 101. From the same work, it seems, is taken that quite long fragment, *The Address to those who flee the churches* <note>Original Greek: "τῷ προσφωνητικῷ πρὸς τοὺς φευγόντας τὰς ἐκκλησίας"</note>, which is found in Con-

## SIRICIUS

<margin>385.</margin> SIRICIUS, a Roman by birth, born to his father Tiburtius, was first a Priest of the Roman Church, then, upon the death of Damasus at the start of the year 385, became the Bishop of Rome. He condemned Jovinian <note>Jovinian was an opponent of Christian asceticism who argued that virgins, widows, and married women had equal merit in the eyes of God</note>, who was forging new errors, by calling a meeting of his priests; he sent letters regarding this matter to inform the Church of Milan. That censure was confirmed by a synodal sentence of the Bishops gathered in Milan in the year 390, who, in writing back to Siricius, extolled him with immense praise as one keeping the watch of a good shepherd, who diligently guarded the door committed to him, and protected the sheepfold of Christ with pious concern, being worthy of the Lord's sheep to hear and follow. He died on the twenty-sixth day of November in the year 398. *Five Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume 2, page 1017. <margin>* This differs in the 5th [letter] regarding Leo the Great.</margin> Of these, the fourth, addressed to the Bishops of Africa, is demonstrated to be a forgery by very strong arguments by Paschasius Quesnel.

---

## IDACIUS CLARUS

<margin>385.</margin> IDACIUS CLARUS, distinct from Ithacius the Bishop of Sossuba, was the Bishop of a certain city in Spain (perhaps Emerita <note>Modern-day Mérida, Spain</note>). He was prominent in the year 385. Joining his efforts with Ithacius with the greatest fervor, he attacked the Priscillianists <note>Followers of Priscillian, who were accused of a mix of Gnosticism and Manichaeism; this was the first group in Christian history to be executed for heresy by the state</note>, obtained an edict from the Emperor Gratian for the driving of heretics into exile, and stood by Ithacius when he accused them before Maximus. On that account, he was eventually removed from the communion of the Church and sent into exile, where he met his end, while the elder Theodosius was still reigning. He wrote an *Apology*, which perished long ago, in which he uncovered the execrable dogmas of Priscillian, his sorcerous arts, and detestable lusts. There remains a book *Against Verimudus the Arian Deacon* (which Chiffletius, not without justice, attributes to Vigilius of Thapsus), and an *Explanation of certain more difficult passages of Holy Scripture*, along with other *small works against Heresies*, Basel, 1528, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 5, page 726.

---

## MATRONIANUS

<margin>385. † On Famous Men, Ch. 122.</margin> MATRONIANUS, or Latronianus as he is called by Sulpicius, was Spanish by race and a follower of Priscillian. He was prominent in the year 385; condemned to death along with Priscillian by the order of Maximus, he was struck by the sword at Trier. He was a very learned man, and, in his metrical work, comparable to the ancients, says Jerome†. He published various small works in different types of meter, which do not survive today.

---

## TIBERIANUS

<margin>385. * On Famous Men, 123.</margin> TIBERIANUS, Spanish by race, from the province of Baetica, was a sectarian of the Priscillianist faction. He was prominent in the year 385, the same time Priscillian was killed; by the sentence of Maximus, he himself was stripped of his goods and banished to the island of Sylina; where, finally overcome by the weariness of exile, he changed his purpose and joined himself in marriage to a virgin devoted to Christ, as Jerome teaches us*. He wrote an *Apology* in a turgid and composed style, so that he might free himself from the suspicion of the Priscillianist Heresy. NE.
