# The Arian Century.

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
386.
Jerome, Letters 61, 62.
</margin>
**JOHN**, it is not certain from what nation or family he was born. In his youth, he followed the monastic life, and was later made a Priest. During the persecution directed against the Catholics by the Emperor Valens <note>Valens (reigned 364–378) was an Eastern Roman Emperor who famously supported Arianism and persecuted Nicene Christians.</note>, he appeared to lean toward the Arian faction, having turned away from communion with the Western Bishops who were exiles for the faith. Indeed (if Jerome, who frequently criticized him, is to be believed), he even joined in the errors of the Arians, Macedonians, Photinians, and Manichaeans; he finally became a Catholic out of the hope of attaining dignity, redeemed from heresy by the promise of a Bishopric. However, perhaps no small part of this accusation should be attributed to the fierce spirit of Jerome, who, subsequently breathing more gently, seemed to clear John of such a mark. <margin>* Letter 61.</margin> *“We grant you,”* he says \*, *“that you are never an Arian, and even more, that you never were.”* <margin>† Letter 62.</margin> In the year 386, having not much passed his thirtieth year of age according to Jerome †, he was appointed successor to Cyril in the See of Jerusalem. At that time, when the cause of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria was a prolific early Christian scholar; his complex allegorical interpretations later became the subject of intense "Origenist" controversies regarding orthodoxy.</note> was being sharply debated in the Christian world, John supported it fervently—not so much out of devotion to Origen's dogmas as out of concern for his reputation. From this grew an ample harvest of dissensions and quarrels for him.

The beginnings of the dispute raised between him and Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis, a staunch defender of orthodoxy known for his "Panarion" (a catalog of heresies).</note> were mentioned above in the entry for Epiphanius; it eventually reached the point where Epiphanius regretted holding communion with John. When Epiphanius performed the sacred rites to God, he was accustomed to say: *“Lord, grant to John that he may believe rightly.”* Indignant at this act, it is a wonder how John roared with anger. Sending letters everywhere, he accused Epiphanius of violating Christian charity. Furthermore, he most severely charged him for having elevated Paulinianus, Jerome’s brother, to the dignity of the Priesthood within the Diocese of Palestine. Epiphanius cleared himself of the crimes objected to him in a mild Letter written in the year 392, showing that he was sought after with complaints and insults not so much for laying hands on Paulinianus in a foreign jurisdiction, as for the Origenism he had once reproached John for. He furthermore exhorted John with many words to guard against the poison of Origenist doctrine, which he summarized in eight chapters.

But as John closed his ears to these warnings and burned even more fiercely, Epiphanius did not hesitate to renounce communion with him and brand him with the mark of heresy. Both the cause of his brother Paulinianus and a hatred of Origenism drew Jerome into Epiphanius’s party and into enmity with John. Indeed, joining his voice with Epiphanius, Jerome did not cease to urge John with constant prayers and terrify him with accusations, trying to drive him to pronounce an <term>anathema</term> <note>A formal curse or excommunication by a church authority.</note> against Origen. John proceeded to such a point of wrath that he separated Jerome from the communion of the Church, and even declared him an exile, though the attempt was in vain. Jerome retained his seat at Bethlehem; yet he did not immediately lay aside his hostile mind toward John. Count Archelaus and Theophilus of Alexandria busied themselves with trying to restrain the provoked spirits on both sides, but to no avail. As long as Epiphanius lived, John rejected peace, and he attacked the Palestinian monks (who, on Epiphanius’s persuasion, refused to enter into the communion of the Holy Assembly with him) with hatred and injuries as if they were public enemies. However, the wound finally seems to have closed; John’s irritated spirit cooled down somewhat, conquered partly by shame and partly by arguments.

<margin>See Orosius's *Apology on Free Will*; Augustine, Letter 106; and *On Original Sin*, book 2, chapter 11.</margin> After the Origenist dispute had been somewhat settled for many years, John began to have a bad reputation among the Westerners around the year 415, as if he favored Pelagianism <note>The theological doctrine named after Pelagius, which emphasized human free will over divine grace in achieving salvation.</note>. In that year, having called together a Council of his Priests, he lent an ear that was not at all hostile to the heretic, but was less than fair to Orosius who was accusing Pelagius, effectively leaving the matter undecided. Soon after, he was present at the **Synod of Diospolis**, where Pelagius, pretending to abjure the errors attributed to him through crafty arts, deceived John and the other Bishops; he was acquitted of the mark of heresy and admitted into the communion of the Church. In this, however, John deserves to be excused at least in that it seems to be a lack of prudence, rather than a lack of zeal for the Catholic faith, that was missing in judging Pelagius's cause. He died in the year of Christ 416, in the 30th year of his Bishopric. He was a man who, whether you look at his gifts of intellect or spirit, was by no means to be despised, except for the fact that he was too arrogant and proud in defending causes once undertaken—specifically the reputation of Origen—with stubborn and obstinate persistence. Nor should he be judged to have favored the errors of Origen; he was concerned only for his fame, for which reason he was so often pressed by Jerome and Epiphanius to subject Origen to an Anathema...

**GAUDENTIUS**, of whom there is almost no memory among the ancients, or very little; while he was traveling through the Eastern Provinces for the sake of religion, and was staying at Caesarea in Cappadocia around the year 387, Philastrius, the Bishop of Brescia, died. Gaudentius was designated as his successor while absent by Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), the influential Bishop of Milan.</note> and other bishops of the Cisalpine province. To ensure that the election of such a man did not fail through any deceit, it was confirmed by the oath of every individual. When Gaudentius heard this and refused to return to the West, a delegation was sent to him by the Bishops, and also to the Prelates of the East, asking that they compel the reluctant Gaudentius to return by ecclesiastical censures. This was done, and Gaudentius, forced to return, brought with him the relics of the 40 Holy Martyrs which he had received from the holy virgins who were nieces of St. Basil living at Caesarea. He then took up the governance of the Church of Brescia. In the year 405, he seems to have undertaken a mission on behalf of the Roman Synod and Emperor Honorius, along with certain other bishops, to make the Emperor Arcadius (who was somewhat hostile toward Chrysostom) more peaceful. In what year he was taken from the living is not very clear. Some place it in the year 410, but the illustrious Labbe * puts it in the year 427.

*The Life or Encomium of his Predecessor Philastrius.* It is found in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a German monk who compiled a famous multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints.</note> for the date of July 18th.

Furthermore, the reader must be warned that another Gaudentius, entirely different from ours, flourished at almost the same time: Bishop Gaudentius of Thamugadi of the Donatist sect <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian group in North Africa who believed the church must be a church of "saints" and that sacraments performed by "traditors" (those who had handed over scriptures during persecution) were invalid.</note>. He offered two apologetic letters to Dulcitius, the Emperor’s Tribune and legate in Africa, which were refuted by Augustine in two books. Gaudentius opposed these with a response, which was likewise overturned by Augustine in a third book. Indeed, in the same province of Italy, at the same time as the Bishop of Brescia, another Gaudentius, the Bishop of Novara, held the high priesthood; a man of no great fame, but he should not be rashly confused with the one from Brescia.

**EVAGRIUS**, a Priest of Antioch, a man of sharp and fervent intellect. In the year 388 or the following, he was made Bishop of Antioch by the followers of the recently deceased Paulinus, who detested the perjury of Flavian <note>The "Antiochene Schism" involved multiple rival claimants to the Bishopric of Antioch, which divided the Christian world for decades.</note>. He died shortly after his consecration, and by his death, the Antiochene schism was extinguished. He was very close with Jerome, to whom he read the treatises on various hypotheses he had composed. He also translated the *Life of the Blessed Anthony* written by Athanasius from the Greek language into Latin. A version of the *Life of St. Anthony* from the Greek of Athanasius does indeed exist under his name among the works of Athanasius, Volume 2, page 544; also in Surius, January 17th; and in Rosweyd’s *Lives of the Fathers*, Volume 1. However, whether it is genuine is a matter of more than one doubt.

Indeed, a *Chronicle of Universal History* is circulated today under his name, tracing events from the birth of Christ down to the year 430; it was first dedicated to Jerome (as the title states), but after Jerome had passed to the heavens, it was enlarged in many places and dedicated anew to Paulus Orosius of Tarragona <note>Orosius was a 5th-century historian and student of Augustine.</note>. **VIGILIUS**, Bishop of Trent, flourished in the year 390. While he was attempting to utterly root out the remains of idolatry, he was struck by a shower of stones from wild and barbarian men and fulfilled his martyrdom for the name of Christ, as witnessed by the *Roman Martyrology* \*. This occurred during the consulship of Stilicho <note>Stilicho was a high-ranking general and regent of the Western Roman Empire.</note>, namely in the year 400, or at least 405. Gennadius states \* that he wrote a *Small Book* <note>original: "Libellum"</note> to a certain Simplicianus in praise of the Martyrs, as well as a *Letter* containing the deeds of the Martyrs among the barbarians in his own time. There exists today a *Small Book* or *Letter on the Martyrdom of Sifinnius and His Companions* found in the works of Surius (under May 29th), Lippomanno, and others. Meanwhile, it should be noted that there were several men named Vigilius in this and the following century, and our Vigilius is often confused especially with Vigilius of Thapsus, who wrote against Eutyches.

**TICHONIUS**, an African by birth, was somewhat inclined toward the faction of the Donatists <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian group in North Africa who held rigorous views on the purity of the church.</note>, yet he also attacked them most sharply in his writings. He flourished around the year 390. He was a man learned in divine literature, not ignorant of secular letters, and a devoted student of ecclesiastical matters. He wrote three books *On the Internal War* <note>original: "de Bello intestino"</note>; *Expositions of Various Causes*, in which he mentions ancient Synods in defense of the Donatists; and a *Commentary on the Apocalypse of John*, into which Cassiodorus says \* he mixed many dregs of his "poisonous" dogma. For while he interpreted everything according to a spiritual sense, he nevertheless taught that the nature of angels was corporeal, and held certain views regarding the millennium and the resurrection that were considered less than sound at that time. This work survives, comprised of *18 Homilies*, among the works of Augustine (Volume 9), to whom it was falsely attributed. He furthermore wrote *Seven Rules* <note>These "Seven Rules" became a foundational text for medieval biblical interpretation.</note> for investigating and finding the meaning of the Holy Scriptures; Saint Augustine reviews these and subjects them to examination in the place cited above. These *Rules* are found in the *Orthodoxographa* (p. 1352) and in any edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, with the most corrected version being in the 1618 edition (Vol. 5) and the newest Lyon edition (Vol. 6, p. 49). The rest of Tichonius's works are missing.

**SOPHRONIUS**, a man described by Jerome \* as exceptionally learned and with whom Jerome himself was on intimate terms, flourished around the year 390. The ancients have handed down nothing more concerning him. While still a boy, he wrote *In Praise of Bethlehem*, and later an excellent book *On the Overthrow of Serapis* <note>Serapis was a major Greco-Egyptian deity whose temple in Alexandria was destroyed by Christians in 391.</note>, as well as a work *On Virginity* addressed to Eustochium, and a *Life of Hilarion the Monk*. I am well aware that this translation is called into doubt by many, and indeed is obstinately denied by the illustrious Isaac Vossius <note>A famous 17th-century Dutch scholar and book collector.</note>. In fact, if I remember correctly, when discussing this matter with me in person once, he said he believed that Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the great Renaissance humanist.</note> had forged that translation under the name of Sophronius for the sake of practicing the Greek language. ## RUFINUS TORANIUS,

an Italian by race, and from the homeland (it seems to me) of Aquileia; for in this Church he received both the washing of faith <note>original: "fidei lavacrum," a common metaphor for Baptism.</note> and the order of the priesthood. Before the year 360, he formed a very close friendship with Jerome while staying at Aquileia; and having entered the monastic life, he set out for the East around the year 371 together with Melania the Elder. In that same year, as is reasonable to believe—and certainly before the death of Athanasius—he sought out Egypt with Melania as his companion. There he spent some time with the monks of Nitria and with Didymus of Alexandria. After suffering many things from the Arians, he departed for Palestine after eight months (although he himself falsely boasted that he spent six years in Egypt). Once there, supported by the wealth of Melania, he built a monastery and took in fifty-two virgins to be educated under Melania's care. He spent twenty-five years there, or twenty-seven according to <margin>390.</margin> Palladius \*, intent on receiving holy men as guests who were making pilgrimages to Jerusalem for the sake of religion. <margin>\* Lausiac History, chapter 118.</margin> He flourished chiefly around the year 390. Around this time, a disagreement arose between Epiphanius and John of Jerusalem, and Rufinus joined John's side. He strenuously defended Origenism, a love for which he seems to have drawn from Didymus; for this reason, the bond of friendship was broken and he engaged in massive disputes with Jerome. Although a peace was established between them for a short time through the efforts of Theophilus of Alexandria, the wound reopened in the year 397 when Rufinus returned to Rome with Melania and published Origen’s books *On First Principles* <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν" (Peri Archon). This work was highly controversial for its speculative theology.</note>, which he had translated in bad faith. Having been accused of deception by Marcella and convicted of the translation of the *Periarchon* (which he had denied was his work), he incurred such envy and hatred from everyone that, branded as a heretic, he found it necessary to withdraw to Aquileia. In the year 400, he published three books against Jerome which he had labored over for the previous three years. The following year, called to Rome by Pope Anastasius to plead his case, he hesitated and excused himself by sending an *Apology*. Because of this, Anastasius soon condemned him and branded him with the mark of heresy. In the year 402, having received Jerome’s *Responses* to the invectives he had published two years earlier, he became so incensed that he sent a letter threatening Jerome with death at the hands of the "secular arm" <note>original: "brachio sæculari"; a reference to using civil or imperial authorities to execute punishment.</note> unless he stopped. In the year 410, after Aquileia was devastated by Alaric, he fled to Sicily, where he seems to have died in that same or the following year. Cassian says of him \*, "A man of Christian philosophy, a not insignificant portion of the Church Doctors." <margin>\* On the Incarnation, book 7, chapter 27.</margin> Palladius writes ||: "Most noble, most venerable, and most knowledgeable and most reasonable among the men he met," <margin>|| Location cited above.</margin> or as it is also put, "Most noble and strong, than whom no one more learned or mild has been found among men." Paulinus of Nola says †, "Truly holy and piously learned, rich in scholarly and salvific literature in both Greek and Latin." <margin>† Letter 9 to Severus, page 115.</margin> Jerome, however, depicts the man far differently, and others following him, as an Origenist, a Pelagian, a forger, a corrupter of others' works, a leader of heresy, and what not? Hence, various names of ignominy attached to him by Jerome are found everywhere; in Jerome's writings he is frequently called "Grunnius" <note>The Grunter.</note>, "Alecto" <note>One of the Furies from mythology.</note>, "Lucius Lavinius," "Afinius Pollio," "Calphurnius Lanarius," and "Scorpius" <note>The Scorpion.</note>. No prudent person would easily deny that he was a great admirer of Origen, and that he attributed too much to free will along with the followers of Pelagius. However, whether "excessive reaction" <note>original: "ἀμετρία τῆς ἀνθολκῆς" (amētria tēs antholkēs), a Greek phrase suggesting a lack of moderation in pulling in the opposite direction.</note> drove Jerome too far off course, or whether Rufinus deserved all the insults vomited upon him with a full mouth, is for fair judges of history to weigh. Meanwhile, it cannot be denied that Rufinus, in translating the writings of others from the Greek language, acted for the most part in very bad faith by changing, cutting, and adding to the text; so much so that they might appear to be new works rather than the work of someone else. Not even by divine inspiration could one determine which parts were by Rufinus and which belonged to the author himself.

## WORKS.

**T**wo books *On the Blessings of Judah and the remaining 11 Patriarchs* addressed to Gaudentius of Nola.
*Three books of Commentaries on Hosea with a Preface to the Twelve Minor Prophets.*
*Commentaries on the Prophets Joel and Amos.*
*Exposition of the Creed addressed to Bishop Laurentius* <note>original: "Expositio Symboli," a foundational explanation of the Apostles' Creed</note>, which is rashly attributed by many to Jerome and Cyprian and is found among their works.
*Two books of Ecclesiastical History addressed to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia,* reaching from the beginnings of the Arian heresy to the death of Theodosius the Great, or rather around the times of Alaric's first invasion of Italy. In arranging this history and organizing the chronology, it is well known that Rufinus was quite credulous, being too prone to fables and the uncertain rumors of the common people, which he was often accustomed to rashly commit to writing, having picked them up from street corners and barber shops. When Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian</note> had initially shaped the first and second books of his *Ecclesiastical History* based on Rufinus’s reliability, he later came upon better authors and determined to start those books over from the beginning <margin>* Preface to book 2.</margin> as he himself tells us.
*Commentaries on 75 of David’s Psalms,* which seem to be interpolated by certain more recent authors, with some additions from Augustine, Gregory, and others. These Commentaries exist in a form somewhat different from others in the Library of Saint Germain in Paris, no. 73, as indicated by Philippe Labbe in his *New Manuscript Library*, page 23.
*The works just listed were published at Lyon in 1570 and Paris in 1580 in folio;* the works of Rufinus were also published at Rome in 1470 in folio.
*The Apology of Pamphilus for Origen, translated by Rufinus around the year 397.*
*Apology for Origen, or on the Corruption of Origen’s books.*
*Another Apology for the same on the same subject, drawn from his own Letters.*
*A Letter or Apology to Anastasius regarding his faith.*
*A later Invective against Jerome* (for the earlier one has been lost) in two parts, as Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet, a noted 17th-century scholar</note> rightly notes, the first of which refutes the accusations cast upon him by Jerome, while the second attacks Jerome himself.
These five minor works last listed are usually found among the works of Jerome.
*A Profession of Faith made in the Bethlehem Monastery,* consisting of twelve Anathemas <note>Formal curses or denunciations of heresy</note> opposed to Origenist and Pelagian errors; which was attributed to Rufinus of Aquileia among the works of Marius Mercator in the manuscript codices found by Garnerius and published among them in part 1, page 114. However, Garnerius inclines toward the opinion—led by arguments that are certainly not weak—that this Profession is owed to Rufinus, not of Aquileia, but the Syrian, a disciple of Jerome. This Syrian Rufinus was sent by Jerome in the year 399 from Palestine to the West to incite Venerius of Milan and Anastasius of Rome against the Origenists; he seems to have offered this Profession to the Bethlehem monks around the year 414 so that he might obtain communion from them. For those monks, at the urging of Epiphanius and Jerome, had cut themselves off from communion with John of Jerusalem and all suspected Origenists.
*A very lengthy Little Book of Faith,* in which he disputes most sharply against the Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, Apollinarists, Novatians, Origenists, and especially against original sin; written in Greek by the same Rufinus (whoever he may have been), and translated into Latin, it seems, by Julian of Eclanum. Jacques Sirmond brought this to light from an uncertain author and translator nearly forty years ago, and Jean Garnerius subsequently claimed it for Rufinus the Syrian, illustrating it with notes and dissertations in the Appendix to part 1 of the Works of Marius Mercator, page 286.
*The Works of Josephus translated by him exist in many printed editions.* Regarding this translation, let us hear the <margin>* On the Annals of Baronius, Exercise 1, number 99.</margin> judgment of the most learned Casaubon.

[The misfortune of Rufi]nus in this noble undertaking was such that he happened to use books even more corrupted than our modern ones sometimes are; a fact he demonstrates there with many examples. In Milan, in the Ambrosian Library, there is preserved—according to the testimony of Jean Mabillon <note>A French Benedictine monk and scholar (1632–1707) considered the founder of paleography and diplomatics</note> who saw it (*Italian Journey*, p. 12)—a manuscript codex made of Egyptian paper <note>Papyrus</note>, of venerable antiquity, written more than eleven hundred years ago, not long after the age of Rufinus, which contains several books of Josephus’s *Antiquities* from Rufinus’s version. If only that most learned man, born to advance literary affairs, had compared it with the published version of Rufinus as he intended.

*The nine books of the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius of Caesarea.* Rufinus prepared this version with shaky reliability, contracting many parts and adding many; he omitted half of the eighth book and barely touched the tenth. He published the version shortly after the year 400. It survives along with Rufinus’s *Continuation* and the *Tripartite History* (Basel 1528, 1570, and elsewhere frequently).

*The ten books of the Recognitions of St. Clement of Rome,* with a Preface added.

*Letter to James, the brother of the Lord.* Both versions exist among the works of Clement, and in Basel (1526, folio) and in Cotelier’s *Apostolic Library*.

*Anatolius’s Book on Easter.* The version was published by Bucher along with Victorinus’s *Paschal Canon* (Antwerp 1634, folio).

*Certain works of Saints Basil of Caesarea and Gregory Nazianzen,* with Rufinus as translator, are found in the old Latin editions of their works.

*The Lives of the Fathers,* which constitute the second and third books of Rosweyd’s collection (Lyons 1617, Antwerp 1628), are believed to be either authored or translated by our Rufinus. The second book consists of Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, and the third is largely Heraclides’s *Paradise*.

*The Handbook or Sentences of Xystus (or Sextus) the Pythagorean Philosopher,* translated by Rufinus and published by him in bad faith under the name of Pope Sixtus, survive (Louvain 1518, 8vo; Basel 1520; Cologne 1522, 4to; and elsewhere).

[Theotimus] <note>Theotimus was the Bishop of Tomis in Scythia, known for his long hair and holiness</note> was held in such high regard that he was called "the God of the Romans" by the Huns. He wrote short, <term>commatic</term> <note>From the Latin 'commaticus,' referring to a style of writing composed of short, punchy sentences or fragments</note> treatises in the manner of dialogues and ancient eloquence, as well as certain other works, of which John of Damascus <note>A 7th-century Syrian monk and Church Father</note> presents a few small fragments in his *Parallels*.

### PONTIUS PAULINUS, Roman by origin, of Patrician and Consular lineage, was born in Bordeaux <note>Latin: Burdigala</note> in Gaul—or at least in the village of Paterno not far from there—in the year 353. He had Decimus Ausonius <note>A famous Roman poet and teacher</note> as his tutor, under whom he made wondrous progress in the study of poetry and rhetoric. After Ausonius was summoned to the imperial court by Emperor Valentinian to oversee the studies of his son Gratian, Paulinus left Bordeaux and moved to Rome. There, he pleaded legal cases with such success that in the year 375, while still a young man, he attained the honor of the Consulship. He was illustrious for his Senatorial dignity and was held very dear by the entire city. In the following year, preparing himself to visit foreign lands, he traveled through nearly all the Western Provinces, becoming an intimate friend of the greatest men everywhere, such as Martin <note>St. Martin of Tours</note>, Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose of Milan</note>, and others. He spent nearly fifteen years on these travels. Finally, in the year 391, he was washed in the sacred font <note>Baptized</note> by Bishop Delphinus of Bordeaux. Having sold his goods and distributed the proceeds to the poor, he set out for Spain for a second time. Residing mostly in Barcelona, he cultivated a stricter discipline of life, though Ausonius and others tried in vain to recall him to a worldly life. At the end of the year 393, on the very birthday of Christ, he was raised to the rank of the Priesthood by Bishop Eulampius of Barcelona—almost by the force of the common people. From that time on, he began to become famous among the men of the Church. He was later made Bishop of Nola in Campania, but in what year is thus far unknown to me and others. In the year 410, when Nola was captured and devastated by the Goths, and he feared he would be tortured by the barbarians on account of hidden treasures (as they might suspect), 
<margin>
Augustine, *The City of God*, Book I, ch. 10.
</margin>
he poured out these words to God:
> Lord, let me not be tortured on account of gold and silver; for where all my things are, you know. <note>original: "Domine, non excrucier propter aurum & argentum: ubi enim omnia mea sint, tu scis."</note>

This most holy Bishop died on the 10th of June <note>original: "X. Cal. Junias"</note> in the year 431, at the age of 78. He had a wife, Therasia, a most select woman and an inseparable companion of both his ecclesiastical and secular life; by her he had a single child who survived barely eight days. Those who desire to know more about him should consult his *Life* written by Francesco Sacchini, which is included in the newest editions of Paulinus’s *Works*. He was a man pious toward God, charitable toward the poor, and courteous and sincere toward all. Indeed, he burned with such singular and stupendous charity that 
<margin>
Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book 3, ch. 1.
</margin>
(if Gregory relates the truth to us) when Campania was devastated by the Goths, he spent all he had on redeeming captives. When nothing more remained to be spent, he went to Africa and gave himself into slavery as a substitute to redeem the son of a certain widow whom the Vandals had carried away captive. He delivered himself as a slave to the son-in-law of the King of the Vandals and was appointed by him to cultivate a garden. Finally, however, when it was recognized who he was, he was sent back honorably to Italy, with all the captives of his city given to him as a gift, along with many ships loaded with grain. Saint Martin <margin> * In Sulpicius [Severus], *Life of Martin*, ch. 26. </margin> often held up the example of Paulinus's piety to his students, seeing as he was almost the only one in those times who had fulfilled the Evangelical commands; Martin proclaimed that century blessed for such a testament of faith and virtue. Regarding his learning, he is made famous by the praises of the most distinguished men of that age. As for his skill in poetry, let his teacher Ausonius <margin> * Letter 20 to Paulinus. </margin> speak, who wrote to him:

> ->We yield in genius as much as we lead in age:<-
> ->Our Muse rises to honor yours.<-
<note>original: "Cedimus ingenio, quantum præcedimus ævo: Affurgit Musæ nostra Camæna tuæ."</note>

<margin>
* Letter 13 to Paulinus.
</margin>
Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> extols Paulinus's eloquence with wonderful praise, saying: "If it should happen that you were to teach Sacred Literature, and as if by hand deliver the mysteries of the Scriptures, something would be born for us that learned Greece did not possess." and shortly after: "If the final touch were to be applied to your work, we would have nothing more beautiful, nothing more learned, nothing sweeter, and nothing more 'Latin' than your volumes."

### AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, an African by nation, had his birthplace in the city of Tagaste in Numidia. He was born in the year 354 to respectable parents, though of modest standing, as they were of the rank of curials <note>Curials were local city councilors. In the late Roman Empire, this was often an exhausting and financially risky position, as they were personally responsible for tax shortfalls.</note>. His father was Patricius and his mother was Monica, both Christians; his mother, however, was most celebrated for her piety, which exceeded her common station. He applied himself so diligently to liberal studies that, while still a youth, he taught Grammar in his native city, and soon after Rhetoric in Carthage, and for some time moved among the lawyers in the forum. There, he not only tasted but deeply drank in the poison of the Manichaean errors <note>Manichaeism was a major dualistic religion that taught the world was a battlefield between Light (the soul) and Darkness (matter). Augustine was a member for nine years before his conversion.</note>. But weary of the brawls in the Gymnasium of Carthage, in the year 383 he left Africa against his mother’s wishes and set out for Rome, where he instructed several students committed to his care in liberal letters. However, things did not go according to his wishes in that place; therefore, in the following year, after a mandate was sent by the Emperor to Symmachus, the prefect of the city, requesting that a master of Rhetoric be provided for the city of Milan, he was sent by him to Milan. Upon his arrival, Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan</note> recognized him and treated him with wonderful kindness. While Augustine listened to the sermons delivered to the people by Ambrose, he began to be gradually recalled from his errors; thus, having rejected Manichaeism, he moved toward the Academics <note>At this stage, Augustine adopted the skeptical philosophy of the "New Academy," which doubted that certain knowledge was possible.</note>. Meanwhile, Monica, exceedingly anxious for her son’s salvation, came to Milan, and now experienced the truth of what a certain Bishop had said (whose ears she had worn out with daily prayers and groans, so that he might labor in bringing her son back to a better path). Being somewhat irritated, he had said: *Go away from me; as I live, it is impossible that the son of those tears should perish.* Finally, while Augustine was pouring out prayers to God alone with burning vows in his little garden, the voice of some child singing was heard: *Take up and read, take up and read.* <note>original: "Tolle, lege, tolle, lege." This famous moment in the Confessions marks his final conversion.</note> Snatching up the book, he cast his eyes upon the passage of the Apostle: *Not in revelry and drunkenness, not in lewdness and lust, etc.* <note>Romans 13:13.</note> The mind of the listener was struck with awe, and he immediately decided to embrace Christian piety. After spending two years among the Catechumens, he was baptized by Ambrose in the year 388. The following year, his mother having died, he returned to Africa and remained hidden on his father's estate for nearly three years. In the year 391, having set out for Hippo to urge a certain imperial agent <note>original: "Agentem in rebus." These were officials of the central government who served as inspectors and messengers, often acting as a secret police force.</note> toward a more perfect degree of Christian life, the people of Hippo laid hands on him. Although he resisted and wept, they dragged him to Bishop Valerius and saw to it that he was ordained a Priest by him. Having become a Priest, he applied himself to the exercise and teaching of piety in a monastery established within the Church; furthermore, despite it being contrary to the custom of the African Church, Valerius assigned him the duty of preaching in his own presence. He [combated] the Manichaeans, Donatists,

<margin>4th CENTURY from the Year 300.</margin>
He defeated the Circumcellions <note>A radical, often violent splinter group of the Donatists in North Africa.</note>, the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans could achieve salvation through free will without divine grace.</note>, and other heretics through both his writings and his voice. In the Synod of Hippo in the year 393, at the command of the bishops, he—still only a priest—debated concerning the faith and the Creed. He became so famous among all people that it became necessary for Valerius <note>The Bishop of Hippo.</note> to secretly hide the man he had designated as his successor, for fear that he might be carried off to become the bishop of another city. For this reason, Valerius pleaded by letter with the Primate bishops of Africa that Augustine might be appointed as his Co-bishop while he was still living; this was done in the year 396 by Megalius of Calama, the Primate of Numidia. Augustine initially protested and only with great difficulty gave his assent, as it was a practice that conflicted with the Church Canons <note>Church laws, specifically the Council of Nicaea, which generally forbade having two bishops in one city at the same time.</note>. Once he was made Bishop, he devoted himself even more sharply to the establishment of the Church and the protection of religion. He engaged in massive and perpetual disputes and controversies with the heretics who clamored on all sides, and more than once he faced the danger of death from their ambushes.

He refuted the Donatists <note>A schismatic group that argued the validity of sacraments depended on the moral purity of the priest.</note> in a conference held at the Synod of Carthage, and again at Caesarea. He brought Felix the Manichaean back to the Catholic truth after a second or third dialogue held at Hippo. He excellently defended the Catholic faith and refuted the delusions of the heretics in debates with Pascentius and Bishop Maximinus, the leaders of the Arians <note>Arias's followers, who denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>—the former at Carthage, the latter at Hippo. Finally, he labored for nearly ten years against the Pelagians through held debates and published writings. To better oversee the affairs of the Church, he frequently attended Synods and was a major part of them; for he was present at the fourth Synod of Carthage in 398 and, it seems, the fifth held in that same year; the third African Synod in 401; the Synod of Carthage in 403; the fourth African Synod in 407; the Conference of Carthage against the Donatists in 411; the Synod of Cirta against the same in 412; the second Synod of Milevis against the Pelagians in 416; the Synod of Carthage against the same in 418; the sixth Synod of Carthage regarding the matter of appeals in 419; and the seventh Synod of Carthage on the same matter celebrated in that same year—to say nothing of other Councils where his signatures do not survive.

Finally, with the Vandals <note>A Germanic tribe that invaded North Africa.</note> laying waste to Africa everywhere with slaughter and fire, and already pressing the siege against Hippo, he prayed to God that He would either deliver the city from the enemies or take his own life. Thus, in the third month of the siege, he fell ill with a fever and peacefully fell asleep <note>A traditional Christian euphemism for death.</note> on August 28, in the year of Christ 430, at the age of 76, having held the office of Bishop for 35 years. Possidius <note>Augustine’s friend and biographer.</note> beautifully depicts the outstanding character of this most holy man throughout the entire course of his life. He was certainly pious, modest, chaste, mild, gentle, polite, and calm; frequent in preaching, sharp in debating, tireless in writing, and diligent and assiduous in handling both civil and ecclesiastical business. He was devoted to the poor, for whom he provided either from the revenues of the Church or from the offerings of the faithful. He wore clothing that was neither splendid nor shabby, and kept a table that was indeed sparse and frugal, yet well-furnished and neat, to which he invited strangers and friends alike. However, he set a rule for all, which he even saw fit to have inscribed upon his table:

->Whoever loves to gnaw at the life of the absent with his words,<-
->Let him know this table is unworthy of him.<-

<margin>* Preface to the works of Augustine.</margin>
<margin>† Letter to Alfonso Fonseca, Archbishop of Toledo, book 19, Letter 35.</margin>
The happiness of his genius, in the judgment of Erasmus*, was altogether incomparable; whether you look at his sharpness, easily penetrating the most obscure matters, or the reliability of his capacious memory, or the certain indefatigable power of his mind. The same author elsewhere† writes: *Augustine alone provides all the gifts of a Christian writer: diligent in teaching, vigorous in refuting, fervent in exhorting, gentle in consoling, everywhere pious, and breathing a truly Christian gentleness.* To discuss his all-encompassing erudition further would be like pouring light upon the sun: one would have to be a stranger to both his writings and the writings of others not to know that Augustine stands out in the entire circle of higher learning, and holds the first place in theological questions.

<margin>|| Preface to the works of Augustine.</margin>
Regarding his style, Erasmus|| says this: *Augustine has a certain way of speaking of his own, which is sharp and involves many things in long-extended periods <note>In rhetoric, a "period" is a long, complex, but grammatically complete sentence.</note>; it requires a reader who is familiar, sharp, attentive, and possesses a good memory—in short, one of great patience and labor.*

* Epistle to Germanus of Brescia, Book 20, Epistle 2.
</margin>
...and patient in labor; such as you would not find many. Hence elsewhere*, he is heard of as a writer of both obscure subtlety and a lengthiness that is little pleasant. <note>The author is quoting a critique of Augustine's writing style, likely from Erasmus or a contemporary scholar.</note>

### Genuine Extant Works.

*Retractions*, two books, written a few years before his death and reviewed immediately before his death. <note>original: *Retractationes*; a work where Augustine reviewed and corrected his earlier writings.</note>
*Confessions, thirteen books.*
*On Grammar, one book.*
*Principles of Dialectics.*
*Ten Categories excerpted from Aristotle.*
*Principles of Rhetoric.* These last four treatises just listed were relegated to the Appendix and counted among the spurious works by the Parisian Benedictines <note>The "Maurists," a famous congregation of French monks known for their high-quality scholarly editions of the Church Fathers.</note> in their recent and truly elegant edition of Augustine’s works. This was done partly because they are foreign to Augustine's style and unworthy of his learning, and partly because they are not written in the form of dialogues, nor do they turn the mind toward incorporeal things—which Augustine’s genuine small works on these subjects are known to have done, as is clear from *Retractions, Book I, chapter 6*.
*On Music, six books.*
*Against the Academics, three books.*
*On Order, two books.*
*On the Blessed Life, one book.*
*Soliloquies, two books.*
*On the Teacher, one book.*
*On the Immortality of the Soul, one book.*
*On the Quantity of the Soul, one book.*
*On Free Will, three books*, which he began as a layman in Rome and completed as a Priest in Africa.
*On True Religion, one book.*
*On the Morals of the Catholic Church and of the Manichaeans, two books.*
*On Genesis against the Manichaeans, two books.*
The *Rule*, the last of three, which was given to women, not men, although the pronouns and adjectives have been changed from the feminine to the masculine gender. Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the great Renaissance humanist and editor of the Church Fathers.</note> doubts its authenticity, yet acknowledges it is not unworthy of Augustine.
*Letters, a book of 242 epistles*, compiled haphazardly without any order of subject or time. Augustine in his *Retractions* and Possidius <note>Augustine's friend and first biographer.</note> in his *Indiculum* <note>A catalog or list of Augustine's works.</note> designate many of these letters as treatises; however, eleven are spurious (142, 181, 182, 184, 185, 187, 189, 192, 194, 196, 198), and finally, fifty belong to other authors. In the recent Benedictine edition, the letters are arranged according to the time in which they were written. In these, three previously unpublished letters are presented: one to Alypius and two to Paulinus; to which is added a fourth to Marius Mercator, now published in full for the first time. The Benedictines prove with unanswerable arguments that the *Dispute with Pascentius*, which until now held the place of Epistle 178, is not by Augustine; they attribute it, with quite reasonable logic, to Vigilius of Thapsus.
Nearly sixty *Letters* were added in the Parisian Supplement, and twenty of those in the Louvain edition.
*On Christian Doctrine, four books.*
*On the Expressions of Holy Scripture, seven books.*
*On Faith and the Creed, one book.*
*Enchiridion to Laurentius on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, written in the year 421. <note>An *Enchiridion* is a "hand-book" or manual of Christian doctrine.</note>
*On the Trinity, fifteen books.*
*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, one unfinished book.*
*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, twelve books.*
*On the Christian Combat, one book.*
*On the Work of Monks, one book.*
*On the Spirit and the Letter to Marcellinus, one book*, written in the year 412.
*On the Divination of Demons, one book.*

# The Arian Century.

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>

*35 Sermons on the Words of the Apostle.* <note original="De verbis Apostoli">Referring to the Epistles of St. Paul.</note> Out of these, Sermon 25 is by Maximus <note>Maximus of Turin (c. 380–420), a prolific preacher whose works were often confused with those of other Fathers.</note>, found as the ninth among the works of Ambrose.

*Book of 50 Homilies;* of these, the fourth is excerpted from the writings of Ambrose. These three collections of Augustine’s Sermons mentioned above are ancient—indeed, made 800 years ago—yet they are by no means contemporary with Augustine. The following collections of Sermons *on the Liturgical Seasons* <note original="de Tempore">Sermons following the church calendar (Advent, Easter, etc.).</note> and *on the Saints* <note original="de Sanctis">Sermons for specific feast days of martyrs and saints.</note> were prepared (and this was done with the greatest carelessness) by the editors of the Amerbach edition, *Basel, 1495.*

*256 Sermons on the Liturgical Seasons,* out of which several claim other authors: indeed, Sermons 87, 215, 251, and 255 are considered spurious by Perkins, Rivet, and others. <note>William Perkins and André Rivet were prominent 16th/17th-century Protestant theologians who engaged in the textual criticism of Patristic works.</note> Labbe denies Sermon 191 to Augustine. Of these, the ninth is by Bernard; the 11th is attributed to Maximus; the 15th is ascribed to Severian as well as Fulgentius; the 33rd is by Saint Leo; the 37th by Maximus; the 48th is taken here and there from Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine; the 63rd is by Saint Leo; the 68th and 77th by Saint Ambrose; the 117th by the same; the 118th by Maximus; the 120th is attributed to Eusebius; the 125th is nearly the same as the *Creed* <note original="Symbolum">In this context, a "Symbolum" refers to a formal statement of faith or a creed.</note> inscribed to Damasus among the works of Jerome; the 128th has Maximus as its author; the 130th has Chrysostom; the 136th, 138th, 156th, and 176th are found among the works of Eusebius; the 137th is by Saint Gregory; the 171st is taken from his writings; the 226th, 228th, 229th, and 242nd are from the writings of Ambrose.

*51 Sermons on the Saints,* out of which some ascribe Sermons 1 and 18 to Fulgentius. Sermon 22 is excerpted from Peter of Ravenna <note>Peter Chrysologus, known for his short, golden homilies.</note>; the 26th is found among the works of Ambrose; the 27th is by Maximus; the 30th and 31st are spurious, the latter being found among the works of Ambrose, as is Sermon 33. Sermon 35 is by Fulbert <note>Fulbert of Chartres (died 1028).</note>; the 36th by Bishop Eusebius; the 37th by Alcuin the Priest <note>Alcuin (c. 735–804), the leading scholar of the Carolingian Renaissance.</note>, though patched together from various sources; the 47th is also attributed to Saint Leo.

*17 Other Sermons,* six of which are on the Liturgical Seasons and ten on the Saints, first published in the Parisian edition of 1531.

*Four Sermons:* namely, *on Jacob and Esau* on the Feast of Saint Vincent; *on the 13th chapter of Proverbs*; *on the Parable of the Sower*; and *on the 16th chapter of Matthew.*

*Treatise on the Lord’s Prayer.*

*43 Sermons on Various Subjects.*

*27 Fragments of the Sermons of Saint Augustine,* excerpted from the treasury of Abbot Eugippius and the Commentaries of Bede. All those small works were first produced inclusively in the Basel edition of 1569. And thus far reach the Froben editions. <note>The Froben family in Basel were famous for printing scholarly editions of the Church Fathers, notably those edited by Erasmus.</note> The genuine works which follow saw the light at various times and were collected into one volume in the Parisian supplement prepared by Jérôme Vignier in 1654.

*40 Sermons on various arguments,* first edited with notes by Sirmond in the year 1630.

*123 Sermons on various subjects,* edited by the Louvain scholars, including the 43 Sermons first published in *Basel, 1569.* The Louvain scholars themselves admit that many of these are counterfeit.

*11 Homilies* edited by the Parisians in the year 1614 from Carthusian manuscripts, and another 13 from the Pithou manuscripts.

*A Brief Explanation of the Creed.*

*On the Calends of January.* <note>Sermons against pagan New Year customs.</note>

*Regarding the Calends of January.*

*Before the altar, to the children, regarding the Sacrament.*

*Six Sermons* first published in Rome in the year 1644 by Giovanni Battista Maro.

*Treatise on the seven vices and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.*

*A book on the Proceedings of Pelagius, against the adversaries of the grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ, addressed to Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage,* written in the year 417. It first appeared in *Augsburg, 1615, in octavo.* <note>This work documents the trial of the monk Pelagius, who taught that humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace.</note>

*The Mirror of Holy Scripture.* <note original="Speculum">A common title for a compendium or summary of essential texts.</note>

*Six books of the finished work against Julian the Pelagian Heretic, or the final Response,* while finishing these, Augustine died; and therefore these books are called an "unfinished work" by Possidius <note>Possidius was Augustine’s friend and biographer who compiled the first catalog (Indiculus) of his works.</note> in the Index.

*Letter to Macrobius.*

46 Sermons previously unpublished. Furthermore, in the preceding Sermons, it should be noted that it not infrequently happens that the same Sermon is numbered twice or perhaps more often in different Collections of Sermons: very many, however, are excerpted from other writings of Augustine. We have noted in passing that some of these Sermons are spurious <note>Work falsely attributed to an author.</note>. Truly, since the Parisian Benedictines <note>The Maurists, a famous group of French scholars who produced the definitive early-modern edition of Augustine's works.</note> have performed this task far more accurately in their recent edition, we judge it profitable to exhibit a summary of the judgment passed on the Sermons by them. They have therefore reduced all the Sermons (which complete Volume IV) into four classes: *on the Scriptures, on the Liturgical Seasons, on the Saints, and on Various Subjects*; to which is added a fifth Order of *Doubtful Sermons*; while some clearly counterfeit ones have been relegated to the Appendix. These five classes encompass 394 Sermons, besides Fragments. In the Appendix, 317 Sermons are rejected as certainly spurious, selected from various places in the collections mentioned above, namely from the common Collection of *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, Sermons 3, 14, 19, 20, 22, 28, 34, 47, 52, 54, 56, 57, 58. From the *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, Sermons 21, 25, 26, 34, 35. From the *Book of 50 Homilies*, Sermons 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22, 26, 30, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 46, 47, 48. From the *Sermons on the Liturgical Seasons*, Sermons 1, 2, 3, and all the rest except 5, 12, 16, 19, 20, 23, 25, 27, 28, 30, 31, 32, 34, 39, 40, 42, 45, 49, 50, 52, 72, 74, 94, 96, 107, 109, 110, 113, 119, 135, 139, 140, 141, 143, 144, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149, 151, 155, 160, 164, 165, 170, 174, 186, 187, 196, 205, 212, 214, 220, 234, 235, 236, 237, 245, 246, 254, 256. The *Sermons on the Saints* are all spurious except 4, 12, 17, 23, 24, 42, 45, 48, 50, 51. Among the 17 Sermons added in the Paris 1531 edition, the following are spurious: 1, 2 (which is part of Sermon 51 in this new Benedictine Collection), 7 (part of Sermon 88), 15 (part of Sermon 150). Among the *Sermons on Various Subjects*, the following are spurious: 7 (part of Sermon 361), 35, 36 (part of Sermon 279), 38, 61, 96, 97, 98, 99, 118 (part of Sermon 325). Of the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert* <note original="ad Fratres in Eremo">A collection of sermons once attributed to Augustine but now universally considered to be of medieval origin.</note>, only six are presented in this Volume, the rest in the following Volume. Of these six, three are spurious, which hold a place in the common Collection of those sermons: 50, 70, and 72. Of the Sermons edited by Jerome Vignon <note original="Hier. Vignerio">Jerome Vignon (1581–1627) was a French lawyer and scholar.</note>, in Part I of the Supplement, the following are spurious: 3, 4, 5, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18. In Part II of the Supplement, the following are spurious: 1, 2, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 20, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29, 34, 36, 37, 38, 39. And thus far the Benedictines.

*Treatise on Prayer and Almsgiving.*

*Testimonies against the Pelagian Heretics, which appear to be excerpts of some rather lengthy Work.*

Certain other small works were added by the Louvain editors <note>Scholars from the University of Leuven who produced an edition of Augustine in 1577.</note> in their edition, which, because they have been rejected by all as spurious, are not of such great importance as to merit being enumerated individually here.

*The two books of Meditations.* The Parisian Benedictines maintain these are more recent than Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153).</note>.

*Book of Soliloquies of the soul to God.* The Benedictines indicate this is more recent than Hugh of St. Victor <note>Hugh of Saint Victor (c. 1096–1141), a prominent mystical theologian.</note>, whose writings it plunders abundantly, and that it is perhaps by the same Author who wrote the subsequent Work.

*The Manual.* It appears to be by Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109).</note>, among whose Works it finds a place. However, the Parisian Benedictines think it should rather be ascribed to the Author of the *Treatise on the Spirit and the Soul*, as well as the *book on loving God*.

*Thirty-three Brief Questions on the Trinity.*

*Testimonies against the Pelagian Heretics*, in the Paris Supplement.

*A brief Treatise on the Trinity*; it exists in Greek and Latin, translated by Maximus Planudes <note>A Byzantine monk and scholar (c. 1260–1305) known for translating Latin classics into Greek.</note> in the Library of the Fathers. Also the excerpts *on the freedom of the will*, which are held in the same place.

*On faith in things unseen.* Concerning these small works, almost one and the same opinion can be rendered: that they are cobbled together from the writings of Augustine; except that the Parisian Benedictines assert with the greatest confidence that the Treatise mentioned in the last place is genuine.

*On True and False Penance to a woman devoted to Christ* <note>original: "De verâ & falsâ pænitentiâ ad Christi devotam"</note>. This was transcribed almost in its entirety under Augustine's name into the *Decrees* and *Sentences* <note>Standard collections of canon law and theology in the Middle Ages.</note>; however, there is almost no reason to doubt that the work is spurious.
*On Wednesday, or the cultivation of the Lord’s field* <note>original: "De quartâ Feriâ sive culturâ agri dominici"</note>.

*On the Deluge* <note>original: "De Cataclysmo"</note>.
*On the Time of the Barbarians* <note>original: "De tempore Barbarico"</note>.
The Parisian Benedictines <note>The Maurists, a group of French scholars known for their rigorous editorial standards.</note> maintain that these three sermons or treatises are highly doubtful, and that they all share the same author as the three later works on the Creed—perhaps a certain disciple of Augustine.

*On the Utility of Penance* <note>original: "De utilitate Pænitentiæ"</note>. This is Homily 27 among the *Fifty Homilies*, and is ascribed by some to Eradius, Augustine’s successor. In some editions, there is also a *Little Book on the Medicine of Penance*, which is nearly word-for-word the same as the final homily among the fifty, and is usually ascribed to the same Eradius.

*Two Rules given to the Clergy.*
*Book on the Eremitic Life to his Sister*, which cites Saint Benedict and Saint Gregory <note>Since these saints lived after Augustine, he could not have written this.</note>. It is attributed to Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx <note>An 12th-century English Cistercian monk.</note>, according to the judgment of Holstenius, whose opinion the Parisian Benedictines embrace and confirm.
*Letter to Cyril on the Praises of Jerome.*
*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas.* This belongs to Gennadius of Marseilles <note>A 5th-century priest and historian.</note>.
*On Faith to Peter the Deacon.* This belongs to Fulgentius of Ruspe <note>A 6th-century North African bishop and theologian.</note>.
*On the Miracles of Holy Scripture* in three books. The author mentions "Cycles" <note>Systems for calculating the date of Easter.</note>, and as is evident from the calculations he provides, he wrote in the year 657 AD. The author was a certain Augustine, a monk of Canterbury, or rather of Wales—that is, an Irishman. This is what the Parisian Benedictines teach us.
*On the Spirit and the Soul.* The author cites Boethius; Trithemius attributes it to Hugh of St. Victor. In reality, however, it is owed to a certain Cistercian monk; the Parisian Benedictines indicate his name was Alcher.
*On the Blessings of the Sons of Jacob*; this is culled from Saint Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, and its author is Alcuin <note>A prominent scholar at the court of Charlemagne.</note>.
*388 Sentences*, collected from the works of Saint Augustine by Prosper of Aquitaine.
*Book of 21 Questions.*
*Dialogue of 65 Questions with Orosius asking and Augustine responding*, compiled for the most part from various passages in Augustine’s genuine works.
*Questions on the Old and New Testaments* divided into three parts: the version published by the Louvain scholars includes a fourth part, *65 Questions* covering both Testaments equally, which is spurious; it is nothing more than an interpolated repetition of the first and second parts, and thus is rightly omitted from the *Basel* editions. The work itself is commonly accused of Pelagianism <note>A theology that emphasizes human free will over divine grace, declared heretical by the Church.</note>, and is usually assigned to Hilarius the Deacon. The illustrious Garnerius extensively refutes the charge of Pelagianism in his Appendix to Part I of the *Works of Marius Mercator*, Dissertation 1, chapter 8, sections 1–4, and confirms the long-accepted opinion of Hilarius's authorship in section 5.
*On the Incarnation of the Word.* The author cites Augustine himself as a source <note>Indicating the author is not Augustine.</note>.
*Book on the Trinity and Unity of God*; with a few exceptions, this is the same as the book *Against the Sermon of the Arians*.
*Book on the Essence of the Divinity*; apparently excerpted from Eucherius of Lyon.

# The Arian Century.

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>

*On the Substance of Affection and Love* <note>original: "De substantiâ dilectionis & amoris"</note>. Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous 16th-century humanist and editor of the Church Fathers.</note> considers this to be by Hugh of Saint Victor <note>A 12th-century philosopher and mystic.</note>; the Parisian Benedictines <note>The Maurists, a group of French scholars known for their rigorous editorial standards.</note> agree with him.

*Exhortation on Wholesome Instructions to a Certain Count* <note>original: "Exhortatio de salutaribus documentis ad quendam Comitem"</note>. This is the work of Paulinus of Aquileia <note>An 8th-century theologian and advisor to Charlemagne.</note>.

*On Friendship* <note>original: "De Amicitiâ"</note>. This is merely an abridgment <note>A shortened summary.</note> of the three books by Aelred of Rievaulx <note>A 12th-century Cistercian monk famous for his writings on spiritual friendship.</note> on the same subject, produced by some idle person.

*A Dialogue on the Dispute of the Church* <note>original: "De altercatione Ecclesiæ Dialogus"</note>. Erasmus calls this work elegant and believes it to be the work of some courtier or lawyer. The author testifies to having been a contemporary of John Scotus <note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena, a 9th-century philosopher.</note>.

*Book on the Faith or Unity of the Trinity against the Manichaeans* <note>original: "De Fide seu Unitate Trinitatis contra Manichæos liber"</note>. This belongs to Evodius, Bishop of Uzalis <note>A close friend of Saint Augustine who often appears in his dialogues.</note>.

*On Predestination and Grace* <note>original: "De Prædestinatione & Gratiâ"</note>. This has Fulgentius <note>Fulgentius of Ruspe, a 6th-century North African bishop.</note> as its author.

*On the Predestination of God* <note>original: "De Prædestinatione Dei"</note>.

*Six Books of the Hypognosticon <note>A Greek-derived title meaning "Refutations" or "Reminders."</note> against the Pelagians* <note>original: "Contra Pelagianos Hypognosticon libri VI"</note>. The illustrious Garnier <note>Jean Garnier, a 17th-century Jesuit scholar.</note> published a lengthy and learned *Dissertation* on these books in the Appendix to Part I of the Works of Marius Mercator, Dissertation VI, chapter 6. The essence of his argument is roughly this: the sixth book appears to be separate from the rest of the work, being neither by the same author nor of the same style; indeed, it is absent from most manuscript codices. The first five books were written between the years 418 and 420 against Julian of Eclanum <note>The leading intellectual defender of the Pelagian heresy against Augustine.</note>, and indeed by one of the primary defenders of the Catholic faith. Garnier confirms with many arguments his opinion that they are most certainly not to be attributed to Augustine, but rather should be ascribed to Sixtus the Priest of Rome, who succeeded Pope Celestine in the Pontifical see <note>Pope Sixtus III.</note>; the reader may consult Garnier for more detail. Seraphinus Piccinardus of the Dominican Order took another path; in his *Dissertation on the Predestinated* published by himself at Padua in 1686 in quarto <note>A book format where the paper is folded twice.</note>, after weighing and rejecting Garnier's arguments, he contends that Marius Mercator <note>A 5th-century ecclesiastical writer.</note> is the author of that work.

*Exposition or Eighteen Homilies on the Apocalypse* <note>original: "In Apocalypsin Expositio seu Homiliæ XVIII"</note>. This is commonly held to be the work of Tyconius <note>A 4th-century Donatist theologian whose rules for biblical interpretation were highly influential.</note>. However, if the Parisian Benedictines judge correctly, it is not by Tyconius, but consists of certain annotations patched together from the words of Victorinus, Primasius, Bede, and perhaps Tyconius himself, and reduced into the form of homilies.

*Book on the Threefold Dwelling* <note>original: "De triplici habitaculo liber"</note>. Also ascribed to Saint Fulgentius, and by others to Saint Patrick.

*The Ladder of Paradise* <note>original: "Scala Paradisi"</note>, which is found among the works of Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>, where you will find more regarding it.

*On the Twelve Steps of Abuse* <note>original: "De duodecim abusionum gradibus"</note>. It is ascribed to Patrick in some manuscript codices. It is certainly older than Jonas of Orleans <note>A 9th-century bishop.</note>, by whom it is cited.

*Book on the Contrition of the Heart* <note>original: "De contritione cordis liber"</note>. This has indeed been patched together from the works of Anselm <note>Saint Anselm of Canterbury.</note>.

*On the Knowledge of the True Life* <note>original: "De cognitione veræ vitæ"</note>. Some adjudge this to Anselm; but the Parisian Benedictines more correctly ascribe it to Honorius of Autun <note>A 12th-century theologian.</note>.

*On the Mirror* <note>original: "De Speculo"</note>, in which Boethius <note>The 6th-century philosopher and statesman.</note> is cited.

*Book on the Christian Life* <note>original: "De Vitâ Christianâ liber"</note>. It belongs to Fastidius the Briton <note>A 5th-century British bishop.</note>; Lucas Holstenius <note>A 17th-century scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> took pains to reclaim it for him and produced a special edition of it at Rome in 1663.

*On the Assumption of the Blessed Mary* <note>original: "De Assumptione B. Mariæ"</note>.

*On the Contempt of the World* <note>original: "De contemptu mundi"</note>.

*On the Vanity of the Age* <note>original: "De vanitate Sæculi"</note>.

*On Obedience and Humility* <note>original: "De obedientiâ & humilitate"</note>.

*On the Benefit of Discipline* <note>original: "De bono disciplinæ"</note>. This belongs to Valerian of Cimiez <note>A 5th-century bishop in Gaul.</note>.

*Two Books on the Visitation of the Sick* <note>original: "De visitatione infirmorum libri II"</note>.

*Two Sermons on the Consolation of the Dead* <note>original: "De consolatione mortuorum Sermones II"</note>.

*On Sobriety and Virginity* <note>original: "De sobrietate & virginitate"</note>.

*The Sinner’s Mirror* <note>original: "Speculum Peccatoris"</note>.

*On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* <note>original: "De conflictu vitiorum & virtutum"</note>. Labbe <note>Philippe Labbe, a 17th-century Jesuit historian.</note> conjectures it to be by Isidore of Seville. The Parisian Benedictines adjudge it to Ambrose Autpert <note>An 8th-century Benedictine abbot.</note>.

*On the Rightness of Catholic Conduct* <note>original: "De rectitudine Catholicæ conversationis"</note>. This belongs to Eligius of Noyon <note>A 7th-century bishop and patron saint of goldsmiths.</note>.

*On the Creation of the First Man* <note>original: "De creatione primi hominis"</note>.

*On the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil* <note>original: "De arbore scientiæ boni & mali"</note>.

*On the Antichrist* <note>original: "De Antichristo"</note>; it mentions the empire being transferred from the Greeks to the Franks <note>This refers to the "translatio imperii," a medieval political concept regarding the transfer of imperial authority.</note>. Some attribute this to Rabanus Maurus <note>A 9th-century Benedictine monk and influential theologian.</note>. In a manuscript codex held in the library of the Most Reverend Archbishop of Canterbury, this book bears the following title: *The Epistle of a Certain Wise Man — excerpted from codices for the Queen* <margin>* It should be read, if I am not mistaken, as Gerberga, who was the daughter of Henry the Fowler.</margin> *Gerberga <note>Gerberga of Saxony (c. 913–984), daughter of King Henry the Fowler and wife of Louis IV of France.</note>, daughter of Henry, the most noble King of the Saxons, concerning the Antichrist, the wicked sorcerer, and one worthy of all wickedness.* It contains a Preface, a concluding summary, and certain other elements that do not exist in the printed versions.

*A Prayer on the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.*
*On Spurious Letters and Sermons*, which was discussed in its proper place.

### WORKS BY OTHERS, which are held among the works of Augustine.

# The Arian Century.

<margin>THE 4TH CENTURY, from the Year 300.</margin> Among the various editions of the *Works of Augustine*, the most prominent are those of *Basel, 1529, 1543, 1556, 1569; Venice, 1571, 1584,* in 9 volumes in octavo; *Antwerp* (by the Louvain Theologians <note>Theologians from the University of Leuven who produced a corrected edition of Augustine's works in the 16th century.</note>) 1577; *Cologne, 1616; Paris, 1515, 1586, 1635.* To these was added a Supplement, *Paris, 1654,* in two volumes in folio. A truly elegant edition is being prepared by the Benedictines of Paris <note>The famous "Maurist" edition, known for its high scholarly standards.</note>, of which six or seven volumes have already been published.

<margin>396.</margin>
### EUTHALIUS, a deacon of an uncertain Church, or, if Turrianus is to be believed in his *Preface to the Apostolic Constitutions*, the Bishop of Sulca. According to Turrianus, he lived in the time of Athanasius of Alexandria; however, Turrianus was mistaken in this matter. Indeed, it is clear from Euthalius’s own *Prologue to the Epistles* (as Mr. Wharton recently pointed out) that he wrote during the fourth consulship of Arcadius and the third of Honorius—that is, in the year of Christ 396. He wrote *Commentaries on the Gospel of Luke* and on the *Acts of the Apostles*, which lie hidden somewhere in libraries. The *Prologue on the Life of Saint Paul with a Prefatory Epistle* (which is missing in the commentaries of Oecumenius) was edited by the illustrious Boeler at the end of the *New Testament, Strasbourg, 1645,* in duodecimo, and in the second Curcellaean edition.

<margin>397. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 36. Augustine, *Retractations*, Book 2, ch. 1. *On the Predestination of the Saints*, Book 1, ch. 4.</margin>
### SIMPLICIANUS, perhaps a Roman by birth, or at least a Priest of the Roman Church by rank. Around the year 374, or the following year, he was sent to Milan to oversee the theological studies of Ambrose (who was by then Bishop of Milan). He spent nearly the rest of his life with him. When those standing by Ambrose’s deathbed were discussing a successor in hushed voices, and Simplicianus was mentioned among others, Ambrose, though lying some distance away, cried out three times: *An old man, but a good one.* <note>original: "Senex sed bonus."</note> Consequently, after Ambrose died in the year 397, Simplicianus succeeded him in the See of Milan. He died in the year 399 or the following year. He encouraged the Priest Augustine with many and constant exhortations to elucidate the Holy Scriptures with expositions; so much so that, just as Ambrose had once been to Origen, Simplicianus seemed to be Augustine’s <term>ἐργοδιώκτης</term> <note>original: "ergodiōktēs" — a Greek term for a "taskmaster" or "driver," someone who pushes another to complete their work.</note>. He wrote an *Epistle of Propositions to Augustine*, in which, as Gennadius says, by asking questions *as if he were about to learn, he teaches the one who is to teach.* <note>original: "quasi disciturus, docet docturum."</note>

<margin>397.</margin>
### Q. JULIUS HILARIO, of whom there is profound silence among the ancient writers. He is thought to have lived and written around the year 397. There remains a Latin *Chronicle, or a Small Book on the Duration of the World*, in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume VI, page 373. He also wrote a *Book on the Day of Easter*, which is lost. It is clear from the end of his chronicle that he was a Chiliast <note>A believer in "Chiliasm" or Millenarianism, the idea that Christ would reign on earth for a literal thousand years.</note>.

<margin>398.</margin>
### ANASTASIUS, a Roman by nation and the son of Maximus the Priest, was elected Pontiff of the Roman Church in the year 398. He died in the year 401 on the 14th of December, though according to Baronius and others, it was the 27th of April in the year 402. There exists an *Epistle to John, Bishop of Jerusalem*, who had consulted Anastasius regarding Rufinus and the books of Origen translated by him; it was written in the same year he died and is found among the *Works of Jerome*, Volume IV, and the *Councils*, Volume II. A more corrected version is held among the *Works of Marius Mercator*, Garner’s edition, part 1, page 109. The Appendix to Liberatus’s *Breviary* displays *Three Fragments of an Epistle to Ursinus on the Incarnation of Christ*. Two other *Epistles* of the same Anastasius are found in the aforementioned volume of the Councils, but anyone can see they are spurious; regarding these, see what Daniel Papebroch has in his *Historical-Chronological Endeavor on the Catalog of Pontiffs*, page 60.

<margin>398.</margin>
### JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, so named for the remarkable eloquence <note>The name "Chrysostom" means "Golden-Mouthed" in Greek.</note> which he possessed, was born of a noble lineage in Antioch on the Orontes river around the year 354. His father, Secundus, was highly distinguished among military men, and his mother, Anthusa, was a truly pious and most choice woman. Having completed the first rudiments of childhood and showing wonderful signs of a gifted nature, he was handed over to the most excellent teachers in every faculty. In Rhetoric he heard Libanius; in Philosophy, Andragathius; in Holy Scripture, Carterius and Diodore (afterward Bishop of Tarsus), the Archimandrites of Antioch, from whom he learned the literal method of explaining the Holy Scriptures. He had many fellow students and friends,

<meta>This page continues the biographical entry for John Chrysostom, likely transitioning from a discussion of his early life and education. The catchword "buit" completes the word "habuit" (had) from the previous page.</meta>

<header>The Arian Century.</header>

...[he] had no one, indeed, with whom he was on more familiar terms (with whom he also held <note>original: "Sermones de Sacerdotio"</note> *Sermons on the Priesthood*) than Basil. Socrates <margin>CENTURY IV. from the Year 300.</margin> and others maintain that this was Basil of Caesarea <margin>* Book 6, ch. 3.</margin> <note>Basil the Great, one of the three Cappadocian Fathers.</note>; Photius <margin>* Code 148.</margin> and many following him believe it was Basil, Bishop of Seleucia; but I judge it to be a third Basil, distinct from both. In matters of Theology, he also diligently listened to Meletius of Antioch, in whose household he remained for three years, receiving from him the fundamentals of Sacred Scripture (for he listened to Carterius and Diodorus later). It was by Meletius that he was washed in the <note>original: "salutari lavacro"</note> saving bath of baptism and ordained as a Lector of the Church of Antioch. While still a young man, Chrysostom had it in his mind to join the monastic life; despite the advice of his mother, who had previously persuaded him otherwise, he withdrew to the nearby mountains. He lived there with an elderly hermit for four years. Then, seeking a more secluded desert solitude, he shut himself in a cave for two full years until, wasted by vigils, fasting, and other exercises of strict discipline, and with his natural strength nearly failing, he was forced to return to Antioch. By Bishop Meletius, at the beginning of the year 381, he was appointed Deacon and applied himself to writing. He published books <note>original: "adversus Judæos, Gentiles, Anomæos, de Sacerdotio, de Providentiâ ad Stagirium Monachum"</note> *Against the Jews, the Pagans, and the Anomoeans* <note>An extreme sect of Arians who believed the Son was "unlike" the Father.</note>, *On the Priesthood*, and *On Providence to the Monk Stagirius*, along with several others. After five years in the Diaconate, he was made a Priest of the Church of Antioch in the year 386 by Flavian (for Socrates is mistaken <margin>* In the place cited.</margin> in attributing this to Evagrius). At that time, he delivered his first sermon, which survives in Volume IV, page 953. In the year 388, during the Antiochene sedition sparked by the toppling of the Emperor’s statues—when the whole city was full of tumult, noise, complaints, and groaning—he took upon himself the daily duty of preaching. He delivered those twenty-one celebrated <note>original: "Homilias εἰς τοὺς Ἀνδριάντας"</note> *Homilies on the Statues* to the people of Antioch. He had spent nearly twelve years as a Priest when, in the year 397, following the death of Nectarius, he was designated Bishop of the Royal City <note>Constantinople.</note> by the Emperor Arcadius, much against his will. Asterius, the Count of the East (to whom the Emperor had given orders to summon John to Constantinople), certainly had to use a clever ruse to snatch a man so dear to his own people away from the Antiochenes. Thus, on February 26, 398, he was placed on the see of Constantinople, despite the protests of Theophilus of Alexandria. Having become Bishop, while he pressed for the reformation of ecclesiastical morals and discipline in the following year with clearly immense zeal and the highest passion of mind, he earned the fierce hatred first of the Clergy, then the Laity—and among these especially Eutropius the Patrician and Gainas the Scythian, the Prefect of the entire military and an Arian by faith. In the year 400, he set out for Ephesus; having called a Synod, he placed his Archdeacon Heraclides over that See, following the recent death of Antoninus, whom Basil of Valentinopolis had accused of various crimes (the headings of which are shown by Palladius <margin>* Life of Chrysostom, ch. 13, p. 125.</margin>) in the presence of Chrysostom. Returning home, he suppressed the Arians, who were behaving more insolently than usual, and labored with the greatest zeal to convert the Goths to the Catholic faith and other nations to the Christian religion. Shortly thereafter, Antiochus of Ptolemais and Severian of Gabala in Coele-Syria, bishops who had been friends with Chrysostom until then, entered into a pact with others against him. They drew to their side Theophilus of Alexandria, who was most hostile to Chrysostom (partly because the see of Constantinople had been snatched away from his own deacon, Isidore, and partly because Chrysostom had kindly received the Nitrian monks whom Theophilus had driven out). To these was added the Empress Eudoxia, whom Chrysostom’s excessive <term>parrhesia<gloss>boldness or freedom of speech</gloss></term> and liberty in reproof had offended. By her counsel, Theophilus was summoned to Constantinople by royal letters and finally arrived there. Since he refused to stay with Bishop Chrysostom as was the custom, lodging was prepared for him in the royal Placidiae palace. A small gathering of forty-five bishops was soon collected from all over at Chalcedon, at the estate of Rufinus called *The Oak*. A booklet of accusations containing twenty-nine headings (which are found in Photius <margin>* Code 59.</margin>) was presented; to this, Isaac later substituted another containing seventeen articles. Cited for the fourth time to clear himself of these frivolous and most trivial charges, Chrysostom refused to appear, disregarding the authority of the judges as much as their lack of equity. Because of this, he was immediately condemned by a Synodal sentence, deposed from his see, and banished to Bithynia by Imperial Edict in the year 403 (or, as the illustrious Savile contends, in November of the preceding year). However, due to the rioting of the common people, he was immediately recalled with solemn pomp. But thus far, this was only [the beginning] of his sorrows...
