# The Arian Century.

<margin>CENTURY IV. Year 300.</margin>...from their beginnings: for at the end of that same year, his enemies rose up again, and having held another Synod, they deposed the already condemned Chrysostom once more. They did so primarily on the grounds that, although he had been deposed by a Synod, he had re-occupied his see in defiance of the 4th and 12th Canons of the Council of Antioch. Not only he, but all his supporters and followers, known as the **Joannites**, who held their gatherings separately, were harassed with force, weapons, swords, and fire; meanwhile, many Bishops pleaded Chrysostom’s cause before the Emperor Arcadius, both in person and through letters, but to no avail. Thus, in the year 404, surrounded by a military guard on a continuous seventy-day journey, he was deported to Cucusus, a city in Armenia—a place more barren, unpleasant, and inhospitable than almost any other. Nevertheless, he was received with kindness and great honor everywhere along the way. Indeed, as he crossed the borders of Cappadocia, a long procession of Bishops, Monks, and Virgins came out to meet him, pouring out these words amidst a heavy rain of tears: <margin>Chrysostom, Letter 115.</margin> *“It would be better for the sun to withhold its rays than for the mouth of John to be silenced.”* <note>original Greek: "ἥλιον συνέστειλε τὰς ἀκτῖνας αὐτοῦ, ἢ ἵνα τὸ στόμα Ἰωάννου ἐσώπησε."</note> Even Cucusus itself did not deny him friends and hospitality. However, troubled by constant illnesses and almost daily raids by the Isaurians <note>A mountain people from southern Asia Minor known for raiding Roman territories.</note>, he was frequently forced to change his place of exile.

After three years of exile had passed, his enemies, who held all power over Arcadius, saw to it that he was transferred to Pityus, the most deserted region of the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea.</note>. While being led there, he reached Comana in Pontus; there, broken by cares, hardships, injuries, and the constant weariness of a harsh exile, and warned in a dream at night of his approaching death, he laid aside his mortal remains the next day. He surrendered his most holy soul to heaven on September 14, in the year 407, having completed fifty-two years and eight months of life, in the third year and third month of his exile, and the ninth year, sixth month, and sixteenth day of his episcopate. He was buried in the martyry of Saint Basiliscus near Comana, enclosed in the same tomb as the Martyr himself. Thirty years later, his bones were moved to Constantinople in a solemn procession and interred in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles; his name was also honorably restored to the <term>Diptychs</term> <note>The official lists of names of people, living and dead, commemorated by the local church during the liturgy.</note>, from which it had been removed. Concerning such a great man, it would be better to say nothing than to say too little. His profound piety, zeal, modesty, abstinence, care for the poor, diligence in preaching, and tireless vigilance and concern in performing his Episcopal duties—his entire way of life—were described as extensively as they were accurately by Palladius, whom the curious reader may consult. Here is a brief eulogy on his character and habits <margin>* Book 8, ch. 2.</margin> **rendered** to him by Sozomen: *“One who is adorned with deeds worthy of faith is justly called capable in speech... In John’s case, he was proven in both; he practiced a straightforward and unencumbered way of life, and used a clear and brilliant style of speaking.”* <note>original Greek: "Λόγῳ ἱκανῷ περὶ ἔργων κοσμούμενον πίστεως ἀξίῳ ὠνόμασται... Τῷ δὲ (Joanni) κατ' ἀμφότερα δεδοκιμάσθαι περιττὸν· ἀγωγῇ εὐθὺ τοῦ βίου σαφηνεῖ καὶ πολιτείᾳ ἀνεκηδεῖ ἐχρῆτο, φράσει δὲ λόγων σαφεῖ καὶ λαμπρότητι."</note> Indeed, speech adorned by deeds deservedly seems worthy of trust. Furthermore, John flourished equally in both areas of praise. For his **way of life and conversation** were indeed strict; but his **diction** was both clear and splendid. Who does not praise, who does not admire the immense progress he made in Philosophy, his exquisite skill in divine matters, his peculiar dexterity in the Sacred Scriptures, and his incomparable faculty and ease in writing and pleading? Finally, concerning his singular <margin>* Book 2, Letter 42.</margin> and truly golden style of speaking, let us hear, if you please, the testimonies of a few of the ancients. If Plutarch is to be believed (says Isidore of Pelusium), *“who considers clarity and ease to be the hallmark of true Attic style, the illustrious and celebrated John surpasses all others, both in speaking like an Athenian and in employing a clarity such as I know not if any other has used.”* <note>original Greek: "πλεονεκτεῖ τὸν ἄλλως ἅπαντας ἀοίδιμον Ἰωάννην, καὶ κατὰ τὴν φωνὴν Ἀττικίσαι, καὶ σαφηνείᾳ, ὡς οὐκ οἶδ' εἴ τις ἕτερος, χρησάμενον."</note> Photius, in Code 172, writes: *“His diction, along with its usual sweetness and purity, also displays brilliance in all things, bringing with it a wealth of thoughts and an abundance of the most appropriate examples.”* <note>original Greek: "Ἡ δὲ φράσις αὐτῷ μετὰ τῆς συνήθους γλυκύτητος καὶ καθαρότητος καὶ τὸ λαμπρὸν ἐν ἅπασιν ἐνδείκνυται, τὸ πολύχουν τῶν νοημάτων, καὶ τὴν ἐν ταῖς δείγμασι τῶν προσφορωτάτων εὐπορίαν συνεισφέρουσα."</note> Suidas has more on this matter <margin>* Under the entry for 'John'.</margin> in the same place: *“His tongue flowed so much that it broke the cataracts of the Nile; he alone, in a manner quite unlike any other, inherited a name that was something golden and divine.”* <note>original Greek: "Καὶ τὴν γλῶτταν αὐτοῦ καταῤῥεῖν, ὥστε τοὺς Νείλους καταῤῥήγνυσθαι· μόνον ἀπεικὸς ὡς τὸ χρυσοῦν τι, καὶ θεῖον ἐκληρονόμησεν ὄνομα."</note> He possessed a tongue that in its flow surpassed the Cataracts of the Nile. Truly, no mortal of any age has abounded with such a great store of eloquence as he alone was enriched with, and he alone without deceit...

# The Arian Century.

<margin>4th CENTURY. From the year 300.</margin>
...he obtained that golden and divine name [**CHRYSOSTOM**] <note>Chrysostom means "Golden-mouthed" in Greek, a title given to him for his legendary eloquence.</note> as if by a hereditary right. <margin>† Oration on the Three Holy Fathers: Basil, Gregory, and Chrysostom. Works of the Holy Fathers, Volume II, Page 329.</margin> Philotheus, † Patriarch of Constantinople, wrote: *“If John seemed wonderful and supernatural for his golden tongue, he was truly thrice-greatest; for now, rivers of theology gushed forth from the body of Christ and from his theological tongue, watering the whole earth with the holy word of salvation. Moreover, the drinkable and most sweet sea of his discourses, the infinite abyss of his sublime and unspoken thoughts, the persuasiveness he offered to men, the clarity and soul-stirring nature of his words, that unspeakable pleasure and sweetness, his rhetorical power of persuasion, and the strength and force of his words joined with truth, showed that even the Greeks who were most famous for their eloquence were like children compared to him. Through these means, he explained the whole of both the Old and New Testaments.”* <note>original Greek: "Ἰωάννης εἰ ὁ τὴν γλῶτταν χρυσὸς θαυμαστὸς τὶς ἂν ἔδοξε... δι’ ὧν τὴν τε παλαιὰν ὁμοῦ, καὶ τὴν νέαν πᾶσαν γραφὴν ἐξηγήσατο."</note> Indeed, John "the golden-tongued" earned a glorious name for himself. Now, from the mouth of Christ and his theological tongue, the streams of theology have burst forth and irrigated as much of the earth as the saving discipline of Christ has embraced. The sea of his sermons is most sweet to drink, an infinite abyss of sublime and choice meanings, possessing an abundance, height, and clarity beyond human reach. He possessed an inexplicable delight and sweetness, a rhetorical efficacy in persuasion, and a vigor and drive in his speech that, when joined with the truth, showed the Greeks—otherwise famous for their eloquence—to be mere boys in comparison. By these gifts, he explained the entire Old and New Testament. Philotheus includes much more in this vein, but this is more than enough on the matter.

<margin>* Under the entry for "John".</margin>
He wrote, according to the testimony of **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>*, almost infinite things; to recount their number, he says, *“is a task for God, who knows all things, rather than for a man.”* <note>original Greek: "ἀνθρώπου, Θεοῦ δὲ μᾶλλον τὸ τὰ πάντα γινώσκοντος."</note> Indeed, both **Suidas** and <margin>† Divine Letters, Preface, p. 421. || Book 13, ch. 2.</margin> **Cassiodorus** † testify that he explained the whole of Holy Scripture with commentaries from beginning to end. **Nicephorus** || records that he himself read over a thousand of John’s "lucubrations" <note>Works produced by laborious study, often by lamplight at night.</note>, which flow with an ineffable sweetness. Nicephorus had been inflamed with love for Chrysostom since his youth and testifies that he found rest in John’s words as if they were the utterances of God Himself. Not only did he credit Chrysostom for whatever erudition he possessed, but he even persuaded many friends to leave everything else behind to make Chrysostom their intimate companion.

| <margin>D</margin> *The Liturgy.* The nature of this is the same as that of the Liturgy of Basil; it seems to have been composed for the use of the Church of Constantinople, but was altered in various centuries according to the character of each age; it is still in common use among the Greeks today. Among the many editions, you will find almost none (unless perhaps one was copied from another) that do not differ immensely. The best of all, which was first published in Greek as the shortest and simplest, was edited by Demetrius Ducas in *Rome*; then in Greek and Latin at *Venice, 1528*; soon after (with the version of Erasmus corrected) it appeared in Greek and Latin at *Paris, 1537, in 8vo*. The Latin version (from the translation by Leo Tuscus made in Constantinople around 1180) was published by Johannes Hofmeister in 1540, and by Claude de Sainctes in *Antwerp, 1560, 1562, in 8vo*; (from the version of Ambrosius Pelargus) at *Worms, 1541, in 4to*; from the common version at *Prague, 1544*; from the version of Gentian Hervet at *Venice, 1548*. It was edited again in Greek by Morel at *Paris, 1560*. Finally, the most distinguished Jacob Goar prepared the best Greek-Latin edition, augmented with notes and variant readings, in the *Euchologion of the Greeks*, published at *Paris, 1647, in folio*. | VI. | 983 |

# The Arian Century.

<margin>
4th CENTURY
from the year 300 AD.
</margin>
...in the Morell edition <note>Edited by Fedon Morell in the early 17th century</note>, the name <term>Constantius</term> <note>original Greek: Κωνσταντίῳ</note> is mistakenly recorded instead of <term>Constantine</term> <note>original Greek: Κωνσταντίνῳ</note>. Due to the similarity in style, Fronto le Duc <note>A French Jesuit scholar (1558–1624)</note> believes these were dictated by Chrysostom; however, the majority of scholars disagree with him on this point, asserting that they are the proper "offspring" <note>original Latin: "fœtum" — a common metaphor for a literary work</note> of the man whose name they bear, Constantius. There are just as many Letters in the Savile edition as in the Morell edition, though they are arranged in a different order. For after placing the 17 letters to Olympias first and subjoining the 5 letters of Constantius, the illustrious Savile saw to it that the remaining 223 were published in the middle section, arranged according to the alphabetical order of the persons to whom they were sent.

31 Florilegia <note>A "florilegium" is a collection of excerpts or "flowers" of literature, compiled here from Chrysostom's homilies by Theodore the Master.</note> excerpted from the Homilies of Chrysostom by Theodore the Master. In the Savile edition, there are 48 Florilegia, specifically including the additions of the 5th, 9th, 11th, 21st, 28th, 32nd, 33rd, 39th, 40th, 41st, 42nd, 43rd, 44th, 45th, 46th, 47th, and 48th. However, very many of these are excerpted from the surviving Homilies and are thus found elsewhere. For example, Florilegium 33 is the same as the previously mentioned Homily on the Confession of the Holy Cross.

---

->VOLUME VII.<-

<margin>II. 1</margin>
**91** Homilies of Commentaries on Matthew <note>original: "Commentariorum in Matthæum"</note> (numbered as 90 in the Savile edition). It should be noted that different divisions of the Homilies and short works are sometimes found in the various editions; for this reason, a difference in their numbering is not infrequently detected. An example is the present work, which consists of 90 homilies in the Savile edition but 91 in this one, even though the work itself is considered complete in both. Furthermore, lest any error arise from this, we have thought it necessary to warn the reader that a huge difference is often found in the titles of the short works between the two editions. For example, the Homilies which in the Savile edition have the title *On Uzziah*, in the Morell edition are called Homilies *On that passage of Isaiah: I saw the Lord*; and the work that is fourth *On Hannah* in the latter is the fifth in the former. Let it suffice to have warned of this once.

---

->VOLUME VIII.<-

<margin>*</margin>
**54** Homilies of the "Imperfect Work on Matthew" <note>original: "Operis imperfecti in Matthæum." This is a famous anonymous commentary once wrongly attributed to Chrysostom.</note> (or rather, a *Commentary wrongly divided into Homilies*). It is now recognized by everyone not to be by Chrysostom. It appears rather to be the work of a certain Latin writer, and an Arianizing one at that <note>Meaning the author held Arian views, which were considered heretical by the mainstream church.</note>; at least, it has been significantly interpolated by followers of Arius, Montanus, Manichaeus, and others. The work is indeed not unlearned, and was certainly written during the age of Chrysostom; but it hardly acknowledges a Greek author, and therefore it should by no means seem strange that the Greek original is not found today. Yet it is truly a wonder what came into Possevino's <note>Antonio Possevino (1533–1611) was a Jesuit diplomat and bibliographer.</note> mind when he wrote expressly that the 54 Homilies of this work had been published more than once in Greek and Latin (*Apparatus on John Chrysostom, p. 855*).

<margin>II. 555</margin>
87 Homilies of Commentaries on the Gospel of John, which, like the earlier ones on Matthew, he wrote while still a Priest at Antioch, according to the testimony of Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note>. It should be noted, however, that among these, Homilies 62, 63, and 64 (or as the Latin manuscripts distinguish them, 61, 62, 63) are the same as the last five Homilies among the works of Basil of Seleucia, published in Greek by Commelin in 1596, and are held under his name as translated by Theodore Peltanus in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patrum."</note>.

Nicephorus <note>referring to Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century church historian</note> is the authority that the small works contained in Volumes IX, X, & XI were written by Chrysostom after he undertook the office of Bishop. The Homilies on the Epistles of Saint Paul appeared previously in Greek (but it is surprising how corrupt they were) at *Verona*, 1532, in folio. They were translated into Latin by Wolfgang Musculus at *Basel*, 1536, in folio; then edited in Greek and Latin by Commelinus at *Heidelberg*, 1596.

Chrysostom’s *Synopsis of the Old Testament* exists in a Greek manuscript in the library of the Illustrious Isaac Vossius. But whether it is genuine, I cannot affirm for certain, as I have not yet looked through it.

Furthermore, the Reader must be warned of a few things regarding the doubtful or supposed <note>spurious or misattributed</note> works of Saint Chrysostom.

I. Sixtus of Siena, Antonius Possevinus, and other common critics have given a fairly large catalog of the doubtful and spurious writings of Saint Chrysostom, which the Reader may consult at leisure: in which, besides the *Imperfect work on Matthew*, etc., there are held the *Exposition on the Gospel of Saint Mark*, *59 Homilies to the People of Antioch*, and others, partly stuffed together from various sermons of Chrysostom, and partly received from elsewhere; these are now entirely rejected from Chrysostom’s Works.

II. Fronto Ducæus <note>a French Jesuit scholar and editor of Chrysostom</note> threw all the supposed works (which he nevertheless thinks were written by authors contemporary with Chrysostom, or at least not far removed from his age) into Volume VI, except for a few certain Sermons on the *Psalms* at the end of Volume III; as they are reviewed by us above.

III. To his own edition, the best and most corrected of all, that most learned man Henry Savile prefixed an index of Chrysostom’s works, both of those which

<margin>
* Complained of in book 12 of Anastasius on the Hexaemeron, published London, 1682, in 4to.
</margin>
The Letter to the Monk Caesarius against the heresy of Apollinaris, written during his second exile. Peter Martyr of Florence formerly transcribed an ancient Latin version of this letter—long desired for many centuries—from a Florentine manuscript. Having brought it with him to England, he deposited it in the library of Archbishop Cranmer of Canterbury: from which he produced that noble testimony (if ever there was one) against the dogma of Transubstantiation, in his *Defense of the Eucharist* against Gardiner of Winchester, part 1, pages 390, 502, Zurich edition, 1559, and in his *Common Places*, Class 4, chapter 10, page 603. But after Cranmer's martyrdom, the Archbishop's library being plundered, the Letter appeared nowhere thereafter. Hence it happened that Cardinal Perron, among others, did not hesitate to boldly assert that it was a mere fiction and that this Letter never existed. Finally, a few years ago, the Illustrious Emeric Bigot appended that same version, transcribed by himself from a Florentine manuscript preserved in the Dominican library of St. Mark, to Palladius’s *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*. However, once the printing was completed, certain censors of the Sorbonne saw to it that the Letter was torn away from the rest and suppressed: concerning which notable fraud a Parisian theologian of the Reformed party has rightly complained. In the meantime, we have published a not insignificant Greek fragment of this Letter, transcribed from an ancient manuscript in the Arundel library, in our *Treasury* <note>original: "Chartophylace"</note>, page 69.

# The Arian Century <note>original: "Sæculum Arianum." This refers to the 4th century, the era in which John Chrysostom lived, named here for the theological dominance of the Arian controversy.</note>

<margin>4th CENTURY, from the Year 300.</margin> Around the same time, Stephen Le Moyne, who deserved great credit for his work on ecclesiastical antiquity, published a complete Latin version (though one teeming with many errors) among his *Sacred Miscellany* <note>original: "Varia sua Sacra"</note>. Nor should praise be withheld from that most distinguished theologian of the Church of England <note>Likely referring to Gilbert Burnet</note>, who, having obtained the very gathering of pages <note>original: "quaternionem"</note> cut from the Bigot Codex by the Doctors of the Sorbonne, faithfully included it in his *Vindication of his Exposition against the Bishop of Meaux*, published in his native tongue in London in 1686, together with the *Bigot Preface* and as many Greek fragments as could be found, which Bigot had collected to adorn his own edition.

Furthermore, there exist in the Latin editions of Chrysostom’s works many *Short Works and Homilies* which are not found in the Greek; Sixtus of Siena and Antonio Possevino deal with these at length, and we refer the reader to them, being content here to review them only briefly.

<margin>VOLUME II.</margin> *The Imperfect Work, or Fifty-Four Homilies of Commentaries on the Gospel of Saint Matthew.* <note>The "Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum" is a famous Arian commentary long attributed to Chrysostom.</note> These are found in the *Morel* edition and in all Latin editions; they were published separately in *Cologne, 1487 in 4to* and *Antwerp, 1537 in 8vo*. This latter edition, however, suffered at unfair hands, being "purged from the dregs of the Arians" (as the title claims). Other editions appeared in *Paris in 1543, 1547*, and especially *1557 in 8vo*, which the editor also boasts has been cleansed of all filth. But under the pretext of performing a "purgation of Arian dregs," that much-discussed <note>original: "πολυθρύλλητος" (polythrylletos)</note> passage—frequently cited by us against the Papists regarding the fact that the reading of Holy Scripture should not be forbidden to the Laity—is utterly cut out from *Homily 49*. It is removed from the words [And why does he command at this time that all Christians should betake themselves to the Scriptures?] in the *Morel* edition pp. 174, 175, all the way to those words [And through this they shall fall into the abomination of desolation, which stands in the holy places of the Church], to say nothing of other frauds, such as a clear passage on the Eucharist being entirely omitted. Indeed, I remember reading once that certain people complained that this passage—concerning the Scripture being read by everyone—had been inserted into this work by some Protestants, contrary to the evidence of the manuscript codices. But truly, he is to be met with laughter who serves up such dreams; meanwhile, is he not secure in the *Cologne edition of 1487*, prepared long before the Reformation began, in which that very passage is read in so many words?
*Twenty-Seven Homilies on various passages of Saint Matthew.*
*Fourteen Homilies on the Gospel of Saint Mark.* The work of some quite witless monk.
*Six Homilies on various passages of Saint Luke*, the first of which, concerning the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, or concerning the Solstices, is certainly the work of an ancient author.

### ->LOST WORKS.<- <note>original: "OPERA DEPERDITA"</note>

Very many commentaries on the books of Holy Scripture. For Suidas and Cassiodorus <note>Historical scholars and encyclopedists</note> provide evidence that the entire Scripture was explained by Chrysostom in commentaries. And certainly, Zonaras reports (Volume 3, folio 96) that many of Chrysostom’s "gifts" <note>original: "χαρίσματα" (charismata)</note> and "expositions of divine scripture" <note>original: "ἐξηγήσεων τῆς θείας γραφῆς" (exegeseon tes theias graphes)</note>, which were kept in the Thomaite palace, perished in a fire under the emperors Constantine and Irene.

Four Orations against the *Syneisactoi* <note>original: "Συνεισάκτους." This refers to "spiritual sisters"—women who lived in the houses of celibate clergy. Chrysostom wrote strongly against this controversial practice.</note>. For the writers of his life reveal that six orations on that subject were written by Chrysostom.

An Exposition on Job, of which very large fragments exist in the *Catena on Job* edited by Patrick Young <note>original: "Patricio Junio," a 17th-century librarian to King James I.</note>.

An Exposition on the Prophet Zechariah is cited by Ephrem in Photius’s *Library*, Codex 229; unless Ephrem is rather to be understood as speaking of the explanation of some particular passage.

Several Orations against Julian <note>Referring to Emperor Julian the Apostate, who attempted to revive paganism.</note>. John of Damascus cites the first in his third book *On Images*.

A continuous Exposition of Psalm 41. Theodoret has a fragment in his second *Dialogue*.

Photius (Codex 274, 277) mentions and provides us with excerpts from: Orations on the Forty Martyrs, on the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, on that passage in Luke 1:78 ("Christ is the Orient"), on 1 Corinthians 5:17 ("If any man therefore..."), on Luke 16:24 ("Send Lazarus"), and an exhortatory speech on Repentance. He also mentions twenty-two short Orations bearing the name of Chrysostom on the death of the Lord, and another twenty-two on the ascension of the Lord, as well as seventeen on Pentecost (Codex 25). Some of these are still extant. It should be noted, however, that many spurious works of Chrysostom were incautiously cataloged by Photius.

An Epistle to the monk Acacius, fragments of which are held in the works of Theorianus (p. 75) and Euthymius’s *Panoply*, Title 15.

More treatises, sermons, and letters; which, though cited by Ecclesiastical writers (especially the more recent Greeks), have not reached us. We have neither the time nor the need to collect them all.

Beyond those things which we have observed so far to clarify the writings of Chrysostom; since the great Ussher <note>original: "ὁ πάνυ Ufferius"</note> collected and noted many things from everywhere with truly incredible diligence in his manuscript *Theological Library*, it is pleasing for the reader's sake to select a few items from there and distribute them into certain chapters.

4th Century AD from the Year 300.

## On the Ancient Interpreters of Chrysostom.

Anianus, who flourished around the year 415, or as others say, 506 (see more about him in his proper place), translated into Latin the first eight Homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew, seven homilies on the praises of Paul, and a single homily to the Neophytes. He prefixed to the former a preface to Bishop Horontius (or Oruntius); for his letter to the Priest Evangelus, which is read in the volumes of Bede’s works and is usually prefixed to the Homilies on St. Paul, shows that these translations belong to him. These versions exist in most editions of Chrysostom’s works, especially the older ones.

<margin>* Divine Lessons, chapter 8.</margin>
Mutianus Scholasticus followed closely after him around the year of salvation 550. His version of the 34 Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews was printed in Cologne in the year 1530 by Jacob Gymnicus. Marcus Aurelius Cassiodorus testifies that this translation was made in his own time and at his request, using these words <note>original: "Divin. Lect. cap. 8."</note>: *“The Epistle to the Hebrews, which Saint John, Bishop of Constantinople, treated in thirty-four homilies in the Attic tongue <note>original: "Attico sermone," referring to the Greek language.</note>, we have caused Mutianus, a most eloquent man, to translate into Latin.”* Henry Savile <note>Sir Henry Savile (1549–1622), an English scholar who produced a definitive edition of Chrysostom.</note> calls him an exceedingly learned and diligent interpreter. It should be noted, however, that the Commentaries on the Epistle to the Hebrews which are falsely attributed to Ambrose (and are cited under his name by Alger <note>Alger of Liège, an 11th-century theologian.</note>, the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, author of the Four Books of Sentences.</note>, and others) were actually excerpted from these Homilies of Chrysostom translated by Mutianus.

Burgundio of Pisa emerged next after these (at a long interval, but the next in sequence), by whom ninety Homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew were perfectly and completely translated in the year 1147 (as recorded in the works of John Boston of Bury <note>A 15th-century English monk and bibliographer.</note>). I have seen fit to add the history of that translation from Burgundio’s own Prologue:

> “Since two incomplete expositions by the Blessed John Chrysostom on the Gospel of St. Matthew are brought forward (namely, the *incomplete work* <note>original: "opus, quod extat imperfectum." This refers to the 'Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum,' an Arian commentary once wrongly attributed to Chrysostom.</note> that survives, and that part of the perfect work which was translated by Anianus) etc. [as in Boston of Bury, down to those words] I have faithfully translated the aforementioned work in its entirety from Greek into the Latin language.”

This version has not yet been printed anywhere. Eighty-eight Homilies of Chrysostom on the Gospel of John were also translated by the same man; regarding which Robert of Torigni <note>original: "Robertus Montensis," a 12th-century chronicler and Abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel.</note>, who lived at the same time, writes in the Appendix to the Chronicle of Sigebert for the year 1181: *“Alexander III held a Council at Rome, etc. (see the author himself).”* So says he. But here for you are excerpts from the Prologue of Burgundio himself, which has not yet (so far as I know) been published: *“To all the faithful in Christ, Burgundio, judge and citizen of Pisa, greetings in the Lord. When I was sent to the Emperor Manuel by my fellow citizens for the public business of my homeland, etc... the Explanation of the Gospel of St. John, etc. [as in Boston of Bury, down to that point].”* Here Saint John Chrysostom divides this book into 88 Homilies, which he delivered to the people gathered in the Church on two days of each week, namely Saturday and Sunday; in nearly every Homily he composes a Prologue at the beginning and a moral lesson <note>original: "morale," the 'ethikon' or practical application that concludes Chrysostom’s sermons.</note> at the end, taking the material from the text of each Homily.

---

## On the Various Editions of the Works of Saint Chrysostom.

The first of all editions appeared in Venice in 1503 in two volumes in folio; it was soon reprinted in Basle in 1504. Then, the works of Chrysostom appeared divided into five volumes in Basle at the press of Andreas Cratander in 1522. This was followed by the Paris edition of 1524, which was succeeded by the much richer Froben edition in Basle, 1530, in five volumes. In these editions, whatever could be found translated into Latin (especially by the ancient interpreters) bearing the name of Chrysostom was included, with no regard for order or the identity of the author. Later, the works of Chrysostom appeared arranged in a better order in Paris, 1543 and 1546. These were the work of Jean de Verly <note>original: "Joannis Eucherii Vernoliensis."</note>, and were restored to their native integrity in almost countless places, both by the comparison of Latin manuscripts and by the authority of Greek copies. They were then expanded and revised with a similar method in Basle in 1547 and 1558, under the care of Sigismund Gelenius. They were revised by the same method under the care of Philippe Montanus in Paris in 1556, and further expanded in 1576. There also appeared (but defective, and mutilated by many omissions) five vo-

# The Arian Century <note>original: "Sæculum Arianum." This refers to the 4th century, a time dominated by the theological conflicts surrounding Arianism, during which Chrysostom lived.</note>

...distinguished editions in Venice in 1574, but revised and more complete than before (with the writers of the Life of Chrysostom prefixed) in *Paris*, 1581 and 1588. However, the most complete of all editions are those that were produced in *Antwerp* in 1614, and under the care of Fronton du Duc <note>original: "Frontonis Ducæi." Du Duc (1558–1624) was a French Jesuit scholar famous for his editions of the Church Fathers.</note> in *Paris*, 1613. So much for the Latin editions.

The Greek works of Chrysostom appeared in eight volumes through the care and expense of the most illustrious Sir Henry Savile, together with notes by Savile himself, Boys, Downes, Hales, and others, at *Eton* in 1613. Greek-Latin editions with notes by Fronton du Duc were published in *Paris* in 1609 (and following years) in eleven folio volumes, and again in 1636 in the same number of volumes. There is also another edition, which is commonly available, consisting of the six earlier volumes by Morell and four by Commelin, containing the *Commentaries on the New Testament*, published in *Heidelberg* in 1603.

Furthermore, many of Chrysostom’s smaller works and sermons appeared separately in various places and times in Greek or Greek-Latin; James Ussher <note>original: "Usserius." Ussher (1581–1656) was the Archbishop of Armagh and a prolific bibliographer.</note> catalogs these editions as follows:

Chrysostom’s *Explanation of the Four Gospels*, namely the eighty-three *Homilies on Matthew*, etc., were produced in Greek and Latin from the Commelin workshop in 1591 in quarto <note>4^o refers to the book size, where each sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>. *Commentaries on all the Epistles of St. Paul*, published there in 1596 in two folio volumes. *Orations on Providence, on Avarice, on Gluttony, on the Soul, on Beauty and the Wife, on Riches and Poverty, on the Church and its Mysteries not to be Despised, on Humility of the Soul, and on Ill Health* were printed in Greek and Latin by Oporinus at *Basel* in 1552, with Martin Cromer and Vitus Amerbach serving as translators. *Ten Orations* in Greek were first edited by Cardinal Sirleto in *Rome* in 1581, and later in Greek and Latin with Johann Jakob Beurer as translator at *Basel* in 1585. *Nine Orations* were edited in octavo <note>8^o refers to a smaller book size where the sheet is folded three times.</note> in *Rome* by Hieronymus Brunellus. From the preceding edition, the *Praise of those who frequently come to Church* is inserted here. There are also *Two Orations* first printed in Rome from Vatican manuscripts, then printed in Germany in 1595 in octavo; one of these is *On Peter and Paul*, the other *On the Twelve Apostles*. Likewise, *Two Orations on Prayer* were previously published in *Basel* in 1525 and *Antwerp* in 1579. *Eleven Other Homilies* in Greek were edited by David Hoeschel <note>original: "Davide Hæschelio." Hoeschel was a German humanist and librarian.</note> in 1587 in octavo. *Two Homilies* in Greek and Latin were edited by Petrus Pantinus (namely *On the Birth of the Lord, and on the Forerunner* <note>Referring to John the Baptist.</note>) in *Antwerp*, 1601, in octavo (of which the former was previously edited by David Hoeschel at *Augsburg* in 1594). *A Homily on the Holy Passover* <note>original: "In S. Pascha."</note> in Greek and Latin was edited by Petrus Pantinus in *Antwerp*, 1598. *On the Meeting of Our Lord, likewise on the Mother of God and Simeon* <note>original: "De Deiparâ." A translation of the Greek 'Theotokos'.</note> in Greek and Latin was translated by Laurentius Sifanus, *Cologne*, 1568. *An Argument on Jeremiah and Lamentations, with a fragment on Susanna* in Greek was edited by Hoeschel at *Augsburg* in 1602. *Six books on the Priesthood* in Greek and Latin were edited by the same Hoeschel at *Augsburg* in 1599. *Six Homilies against the Jews* in Greek and Latin were edited by the same in the same place in 1602. The *Liturgy* in Greek, *Paris*, 1560, and in Greek and Latin, *Paris*, 1537. *Four Homilies on the Rich Man and Lazarus, likewise on that text, 'I would not have you ignorant, brethren, etc.'* were edited in Greek from manuscripts by John Harmar at *Oxford* in 1586. *Six Short Orations on the Providence of God* in Greek, *Basel*, 1526. *A Greek Oration on Babylas the Martyr with the Letters of Erasmus*, same place, 1527. *A Homily that no one should be pursued with anathema or dreadful curses*, in Greek and Latin, translated by Guillaume Plancy, printed at *Paris*. *A book on Virginity*, translated by Joannes Livineius, *Antwerp*, 1575. *Four Orations* in Greek and Latin, the latter two of which are now published for the first time by the study and labor of Fronton du Duc at *Ingolstadt*, 1595.

### On the Writers of the Life of Chrysostom.

The Dialogue of Palladius and Theodore on the Life of John Chrysostom was first brought to light in *Venice* in 1533, with Ambrose the Camaldolese monk as translator. The Latin version is placed in the *Appendix* of Volume II of Fronton du Duc, page 1; see the notes there on pages 54 and 55, and the Greek fragment of this work on page 56. For more on this, see Savile in the unpublished treatise which we shall subjoin shortly. [The complete work in Greek and Latin was edited by the illustrious Emery Bigot <note>original: "Emericus Bigotius." A French scholar and book collector.</note> at *Paris* in 1680. See more regarding this in its proper place.]

The *Life of Chrysostom* by George, Archbishop of Alexandria (Volume 8 of Savile’s edition, page 157, with Savile’s notes on columns 941, 943) was published in Latin by Godfrey Tilmann in the year 1557, which is also found at the beginning of the first volume of Chrysostom's *Works*, Paris edition, 1581...

# The Arian Century <note>original: "Seculum Arianum." This refers to the 4th century, a time defined by the theological struggles against Arianism, the era in which Chrysostom lived and wrote.</note>

4th Century AD from the Year 300.

### On the Ancient Translators of Chrysostom.

Anianus, who flourished around the year 415, or as others say, 506 (more on him in his proper place), translated the first eight Homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew, seven on the praises of Paul, and a single one "To the Neophytes" into Latin. He prefixed a preface to the first ones addressed to Bishop Horontius (or Oruntius); for the letter of his to the Priest Evangelus, which is read in the volumes of the works of Bede and is usually prefixed to the Homilies on St. Paul, shows it to be his. These versions exist in most editions of Chrysostom's works, especially the older ones.

<margin>
* Divine Letters <note>original: "Divin. Lect." refers to Cassiodorus's "Institutiones Divinarum et Saecularium Litterarum."</note> chapter 8.
</margin>

Mutianus Scholasticus <note>A 6th-century translator who worked at the request of Cassiodorus.</note> followed closely after him around the year of salvation 550. His version of 34 Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews was printed in Cologne in 1530 by Jacob Gymnicus. Marcus Aurelius Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and scholar who founded the Monasterium Vivariense.</note> testifies in these words that this translation was made in his time and at his request: *“The Epistle to the Hebrews, which St. John, Bishop of Constantinople, treated in 34 Homilies in the Attic speech <note>original: "Attico sermone," meaning Greek.</note>, we have caused Mutianus, a most eloquent man, to translate into Latin.”* Savile <note>Sir Henry Savile (1549–1622), an English scholar who produced the first major Greek edition of Chrysostom.</note> calls him a very learned and diligent translator. It should be noted, however, that the Commentaries on the Epistle to the Hebrews, which are falsely attributed to Ambrose (and are cited under his name by Algerus, the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, author of the famous theological "Sentences."</note>, and others), are actually excerpts from these Homilies of Chrysostom as converted by Mutianus.

Burgundio of Pisa <note>A 12th-century jurist and translator from Greek to Latin.</note> was the next after these (following at a long interval, but next in significance). By him, 90 Homilies of Chrysostom on Matthew were perfectly and completely translated in the year 1147 (as recorded in John Boston of Bury). It seemed appropriate to add the history of that translation from Burgundio’s own prologue:

> “Since two imperfect expositions by the Blessed John Chrysostom on the Gospel of St. Matthew are brought forward (namely, the work which survives as 'The Imperfect Work,' and that part of the perfect work which was translated by Anianus) etc. [as in Boston of Bury, up to those words] I have faithfully and entirely translated the aforementioned work from Greek into the Latin language.”

That version has not yet been printed anywhere. Eighty-eight Homilies of Chrysostom on the Gospel of John were also translated by the same man; concerning which matter Robert of Torigni <note>original: "Robertus Montensis," a 12th-century chronicler.</note> writes in the Appendix to the Chronicle of Sigebert under the year 1181, having lived at that same time: *“Alexander III held a Council at Rome, etc.”* (see the author himself). Thus he wrote. But look here at excerpts from Burgundio’s own Prologue, which has not yet (so far as I know) been published.

> To all the faithful in Christ, Burgundio, judge and citizen of Pisa, greetings in the Lord. When I was sent by my fellow citizens to the Emperor Manuel <note>Manuel I Komnenos, Byzantine Emperor (reigned 1143–1180).</note> at Constantinople for the public business of my country, etc. An explanation of the Gospel of St. John etc. [as in Boston of Bury, up to this point] Moreover, St. John Chrysostom divides this book into 88 Homilies, which he delivered to the people gathered in the Church on two days in each week, namely Saturday and Sunday; in almost every Homily, he composes a prologue at the beginning and a moral lesson at the end (taking the material from the text of each Homily).

---

### On the Various Editions of the Works of St. Chrysostom.

The first of all editions appeared in Venice in 1503 in two folio volumes, soon reprinted in Basel in 1504. Then the works of Chrysostom appeared divided into five volumes in Basel at the press of Andreas Cratander in 1522. A Parisian edition followed in 1524, which was followed by the much richer Froben edition in Basel in 1530 in five volumes. In these editions, whatever could be found translated into Latin (especially by the ancient translators) bearing the name of Chrysostom was included, with no regard for order or the true author. Later, the works of Chrysostom appeared in a better order in Paris in 1543 and 1546 through the labor of Jean Archer of Verneuil <note>original: "Joannis Eucherii Vernoliensis."</note>, restored to their native integrity in almost countless places, both by comparison with Latin manuscripts and by the authority of Greek copies. They were later enlarged and revised by the same method in Basel in 1547 and 1558 under the care of Sigismund Gelenius. They were revised by the same method under the care of Philippe Montanus in Paris in 1556, and enlarged in 1588. There also appeared (but lacking and mutilated, with many things omitted) five volumes...

...divided into separate volumes, was revised at *Venice in 1574*, and made more complete than before (with the inclusion of the early writers of the life of Chrysostom) at *Paris in 1581 and 1588*. Truly, the most perfect editions of all are those which were published at *Antwerp in 1614* and under the care of Fronto Ducæus <note>a learned Jesuit scholar known for his editions of the Church Fathers</note> at *Paris in 1612*. Thus far concerning the Latin editions.

The works of Chrysostom in Greek were published in eight volumes through the care and expense of that most distinguished gentleman, Sir Henry Savile <note>an English scholar and warden of Merton College, Oxford, who established a press at Eton specifically for this monumental work</note>, together with the notes of the same Savile, and those of Boys, Downes, Hales, and others, at *Eton in 1613*. The Greek-Latin editions with notes by Fronto Ducæus appeared at *Paris in 1609* (and in following years) in eleven folio volumes, and again in 1636 in just as many folio volumes. There also exists another edition, which is commonly available, consisting of the first six volumes by Morell and four by Commelin, which include commentaries on the New Testament, published at *Heidelberg* in the year 1603.

Furthermore, many of Chrysostom's smaller works and sermons appeared separately in various places and times in Greek or Greek-Latin; Ussher <note>original: "Ufferius"; referring to James Ussher, the Archbishop of Armagh and a noted chronologist</note> recounts their editions as follows:

Chrysostom's *Exposition of the Four Gospels, namely 83 Homilies on Matthew, etc.* <note>original: "Explicatio IV. Evangeliorum, viz. Homiliæ in Matthæum LXXXIII. &c."</note> These were published in Greek and Latin from the Commelin press in 1591 in quarto. *Commentaries on all the Epistles of St. Paul* were published there in 1596 in two folio volumes. *Orations on Providence, on Avarice, on Gluttony, on the Soul, on Beauty and the Wife, on Riches and Poverty, on the Church and its Mysteries not to be despised, on Humility of the soul, and on ill Health* <note>original: "Orationes de Providentiâ, de Avaritiâ, de Ingluvie, de Animâ, de Pulchritudine & Uxore, de Divitiis & Paupertate, de Ecclesiâ ejusque Mysteriis non contemnendis, de Humilitate animæ, de adversâ Valetudine"</note> were printed in Greek and Latin with Martin Cromer and Vitus Amerbach serving as translators by Oporinus at *Basel in 1552*. Ten Orations in Greek were first edited by Cardinal Sirleto at *Rome* in the year 1581, and later in Greek and Latin with Johann Jakob Beurer as translator at *Basel in 1585*. *Nine Orations* were edited at *Rome* by Hieronymus Brunello in octavo. From the preceding edition, there is inserted here the praise of those who frequently come to Church. There are also two *Orations* first printed at *Rome* from Vatican Manuscripts and thereafter printed in Germany in the year 1595 in octavo, one of which is on *Peter and Paul*, and the other on the *Twelve Apostles*. Likewise, *Two Orations on Prayer*, previously published at *Basel in 1525* and *Antwerp in 1579*. Other *Eleven Homilies* in Greek were edited by David Hoeschel in the year 1587 in octavo. *Two Homilies* in Greek and Latin were edited by Petrus Pantinus (namely, on the *Nativity of the Lord* and on the *Forerunner* <note>John the Baptist</note>) at *Antwerp in 1601* (of which the former was previously edited by David Hoeschel at *Augsburg in 1594*). *A Homily on the Holy Easter* <note>original: "In S. Pascha Homilia"</note> in Greek and Latin was edited by Petrus Pantinus at *Antwerp in 1598*. *On the Meeting of our Lord, also on the Mother of God and Simeon* in Greek and Latin was translated by Laurentius Sitanio at *Cologne in 1568*. The *Argument on Jeremiah and Lamentations* <note>original: "Argumentum in Hieremiam & Threnos"</note> with a fragment *on Susanna* in Greek was edited by Hoeschel at *Augsburg in 1602*. *Six books on the Priesthood* <note>original: "De Sacerdotio libri VI."</note> in Greek and Latin were edited by the same person at *Augsburg in 1599*. *Six Homilies against the Jews* <note>original: "Contra Judæos Homiliæ VI."</note> in Greek and Latin were edited by him in the same place in 1602. The *Liturgy* in Greek at *Paris in 1560* and in Greek-Latin at *Paris in 1537*. *Four Homilies on the Rich Man and Lazarus*, likewise that one, *I would not have you ignorant, brothers, etc.* <note>referring to 1 Thessalonians 4:13</note> were edited from manuscripts by John Harmar in Greek at *Oxford in 1586*. *Six Short Orations on the Providence of God* in Greek at *Basel in 1526*. *A Greek Oration on Babylas the Martyr with the Letters of Erasmus* <note>referring to Desiderius Erasmus, the famous humanist</note> in the same place in 1527. A *Homily that it is not right to pursue anyone with anathemas or cursed persecutions* in Greek and Latin with Guillaume Plancius as translator was printed at *Paris*. A *Book on Virginity* with Jean Livineius as translator at *Antwerp in 1575*. *Four Orations* in Greek and Latin, the latter two of which are now published for the first time by the study and labor of Fronto Ducæus at *Ingolstadt in 1595*.

The *Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom* by Palladius <note>Bishop of Helenopolis and a contemporary of Chrysostom</note> and Theodore was first brought to light at *Venice in 1533*, with Ambrose the Camaldolese monk as translator. It was placed in Latin in the *Appendix* to the second volume of Fronto Ducæus, page 1, where one may see the notes on pages 54 and 55, and a Greek fragment of this work on page 56. Concerning this, see more in Savile in the unpublished tract which we are about to subjoin shortly hereafter. ...and is found printed in the year 1588. A summary of it is contained in the *Library* of Photius <note>a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and renowned scholar</note>, entry 96. See the notes of Hoeschel on this passage, and the marginal notes of Andreas Schott; the second note discusses the age of this author, a point which Dr. Savile follows at greater length in his own notes (columns 941, 942). In the *Epilogue* of this work, two genuine <note>original: *γνήσιαι* (gnēsiai)</note> Orations of Chrysostom are interwoven: one delivered before he went into his first exile, and the second after his return from that exile, which is found nowhere else; although the historian Sozomen mentions these "genuine" ones in Book 8, chapter 18, as Savile advises in his notes (which you may consult at columns 959, 960).

To the points found in the notes (column 951, line 12) regarding the title of "Augustal" <note>original: *Augustalio*, referring to the Prefect of Egypt</note>, the following should be added. Palladius also mentions the *Augustalia* <note>festivities or administrative duties related to the Prefect</note> in the *Lausiac History* where he treats Melania; and the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicles* (for so Cujacius calls those "Barbaro-Latin" excerpts edited by Scaliger alongside the *Chronicle of Eusebius*) writes as follows near the end of his *Collectanea*, at the consulship of Lupus and Jovinus (which falls in the year of Christ 377): "In that year Tatianus entered Alexandria as the first Augustal <note>the high-ranking governor or prefect of Egypt</note> on the 6th day before the Calends of February." Likewise, Anastasius the Sinaite mentions this in his *Guide* <note>original: *Ὁδηγῷ* (Hodēgō)</note> on pages 198 and 202.

*The Panegyric on Chrysostom by Emperor Leo* (surnamed the Wise, who began to reign in the year of Christ 886) is found in Volume 8 of Savile’s edition, page 267, with Savile’s notes at columns 959, 960. It is also found in the work of Symeon Metaphrastes for the 13th day of November; and from there it is available in Latin (translated by Gentianus Hervetus) in Volume 5 of the *Lives of the Saints* by Aloysius Lipomannus, folio 114, and in Volume 1 of Surius (January 27), page 685. From these sources, the gap <note>original: *lacuna*</note> of one page or leaf in Savile’s edition at page 274, line 27, should be filled. It is, however, merely a *Breviary of George* <note>referring to George of Alexandria</note> collected with poor judgment and written in a nearly barbaric style; for Leo added nothing to George’s account except for a certain forced obscurity of style in places.

*The Anonymous Life of Chrysostom* is found in Volume 8 of Savile’s edition, page 293, with Savile’s notes at column 963. This author was later than the Emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus (that is, after the year 950), as is evident from the index of authors prefixed on page 293. Between this author and Metaphrastes (who seems to be later, as he is not recorded in that index), the meaning is almost always the same and even the words are often shared; yet this author is richer and more expansive, and much more scholarly in his grammar <note>original: *γραμματικώτερος* (grammatikōteros)</note> than George. Regarding his unexamined assumptions <note>original: *ἀνυποληψίαις* (anypolēpsiais), or perhaps historical errors</note>, see Dr. Savile at the end of his unpublished admonition concerning the writers of the history of Chrysostom.

*The Life of Chrysostom by Symeon Metaphrastes* (Volume 8 of Savile’s edition, page 331, with notes at columns 967, 968) is available in Latin (translated by Gentianus Hervetus) along with the rest of Metaphrastes’ *Lives* in Volume 5 of Aloysius Lipomannus for November 13, folio 79, and in Volume 1 of Surius (January 27), page 634. At page 337, line 35, Dr. Savile notes many additions from the manuscript of the Queen Mother (Catherine de' Medici), which the Latin translator does not recognize. Likewise, from page 386, line 16 until the end, there was such a great difference between the Royal Manuscript described at Paris (which Savile reproduced in his edition and the Latin translator followed) and the Queen's Manuscript (which agreed more with the *Anonymous Life*, which Metaphrastes usually follows), that one might reasonably doubt whether both were the work of one and the same author. This writing by Symeon is cited by Nicephorus in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 13, chapter 2, and by Gennadius Scholarius in his *Defense of the Synod of Florence*, chapter 5.

# The Arian Century <note>The 4th century is often called the "Arian Century" because of the theological dominance of Arianism—a belief that Jesus was a created being rather than co-eternal with God—which John Chrysostom and his contemporaries fought against.</note>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>

## V. THE ADMONITION OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS HENRY SAVILE
### concerning the Writers of the history of Chrysostom, and especially George and the other more recent Biographers <note>original: Βιογράφοις (Biographois)</note> who must be read with caution.

For one who is about to annotate the writers of the history of Chrysostom, it seems to me that above all else a system of chronology must be established. Once this is properly settled, other matters will become clearer, and it will not be difficult to resolve many doubts in this history and to correct many chronological errors of the historians. Nevertheless, I leave these findings, like all my work, to the judgment of readers to be either accepted or rejected. 

And first, regarding the day and the Consul <note>Roman years were traditionally named after the two Consuls who held office that year.</note> in which our John was born, none of the ancient Greeks have recorded anything, nor have any of the moderns. Thus the origins of great men, just like the sources of rivers, are obscure, while their progress and endings are conspicuous. 

Second, it is clear from his mother’s words to John in Book 1 of *On the Priesthood* that John’s father died a few days or months after his son's birth: "the death of your father followed the labor pains of your birth" <note>original: τὰς ὠδῖνας τὰς ἐπὶ σοὶ διεδέξατο ὁ θάνατος τοῦ πατρός</note>. Now, since his mother had completed twenty years of widowhood while he was still living in Antioch at the school of Libanius <note>Libanius was the most famous pagan teacher of rhetoric in the 4th century.</note>, this is apparent from Chrysostom’s own words in *Oration 1 to a Young Widow*: 

"For I myself, when I was still a youth, remember that my teacher the sophist—namely Libanius (who was the most superstitious <note>meaning "devoutly pagan" in this context</note> of all men)—marveled at my mother. For when those who were lamenting with him asked who she was and how she was, I told him (as I said) that she was a widow; he then learned from me my mother's age and the length of her widowhood. When I said that she was forty years old, and that twenty of those years had passed since she lost my father, he was struck with amazement and cried out with a loud voice, and looking to those present, he said, 'Heavens! What women there are among the Christians!'" <note>original Greek: Καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ πότε νέος ἔτι ὢν... Βαβαὶ, ἔφη, οἵαι παρὰ Χριστιανοῖς γυναῖκές εἰσι.</note>

If that number of twenty years is exact <note>original: ἀκριβὴς (akribēs)</note> and not a rounded figure (which is perhaps more likely), and assuming the father died immediately after John’s birth, it follows that John must have remained in the auditorium of Libanius until at least the age of twenty. Palladius <note>a contemporary and biographer of Chrysostom</note> testifies that he devoted himself to rhetoric in his eighteenth year. Cedrenus <note>an 11th-century Byzantine historian</note> explicitly writes that he left Libanius in his eighteenth year. George and Leo report that he returned from Athens in this same year (where, as they say, he had migrated for the sake of studies after his education in Antioch); others say his sixteenth year, wandering even further from the truth. 

Therefore, having completed his twentieth year (for the calculation of subsequent times does not allow us to place it later, nor do the words of Chrysostom allow it earlier), and having abandoned his youthful studies of eloquence and philosophy—"bidding a long farewell to the little words of the Sophist Libanius" <note>original: λεξιδίοις Sophistæ (Libanii) πολὺ χαίρειν ἐάσας</note> (as George says)—he began to adhere to Blessed Meletius, the Bishop of Antioch, and never left his side. Having been diligently instructed by him in sacred dogmas, and having been a student for NEARLY <note>original: FERME</note> three years after his Baptism, he was ordained a Reader <note>term: Lector (a minor clerical office responsible for reading scripture during the liturgy)</note>. So say Palladius, Cedrenus, and others. 

Here, then, you have him at twenty-three years of age. It is probable that his mother died around this time, and that he thereafter committed himself to the monastic life, which he had delayed rather than rejected, having been overcome by his mother's pleas. All writers, both ancient and modern, testify that he lived for four years in a monastery near Antioch, and that he devoted himself to the reading of the sacred books "and to ascetic exercises" <note>original: κἀν τοῖς ἀσκητικοῖς</note> under Carterius and Diodorus, "having then hastened to the monastery" <note>original: τότε τῷ μοναστηρίῳ προσδραμόντες</note>. So says Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian</note>. 

Among these teachers, Diodorus (later Bishop of Tarsus) wrote much, "attending to the bare letter of the divine scriptures" <note>original: ψιλῷ τῷ γράμματι τῶν θείων προσέχων γραφῶν</note>, while "shunning their deeper speculations" <note>original: τὰς θεωρίας αὐτῶν</note> (namely the allegories and anagoges in which Origen had delighted more than was fitting). Our John seems to have borrowed this method of interpretation from his master, for we see him defending allegories only with a prior apology. Cedrenus mentions only Carterius. Palladius mentions a certain Syrian elder particularly devoted to continence, to whom John gave himself as a companion in the monastery. Whether that Syrian was one of those two, or rather Hesychius (named "a Syrian by birth" by George), I cannot determine. Certainly, from George’s whole narrative, if he did not lead the monastery, he certainly led the way in all piety...

# The Arian Century <note>The 4th century is called the "Arian Century" because the church was dominated by the Arian controversy—a theological debate over whether Jesus was of the same substance as God the Father or a created being.</note>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.

to his brothers, and that he established *ascetic* rules for them, rather than appearing to have lived under another’s discipline. Having left this monastery after four years, and desiring to hide himself away, he sought a more remote desert; and there, enclosed in a cave, he spent NEARLY <note>original: FERME</note> two years. Regarding these six years, as I have said, the authors are in agreement. Returning then to the city, he was ordained a Deacon by St. Meletius (as is evident to all) who was already setting out, I believe, for Constantinople to hold the Second Synod <note>The Second Ecumenical Council of 381 AD, which refined the Nicene Creed.</note> at the beginning of the year of our Lord 381; he served at the venerable altars for five years. 

For regarding what Socrates says happened after the death of Meletius (which occurred at the very time of the Second Synod), that <note>original: ἀναχωρήσας ὁ Ἰσίδωρος τῶν Μελετιανῶν (τῆς πόλεως, inquit Georgius,) ἐπὶ τρεῖς ὅλας ἐνιαυτοὺς ἡσύχως διῆγε. ἐπειδὴ δὲ γίνεται ἐν τῷ μοναστηρίῳ, ἐν ᾧ πρώην ἦν</note> "Isidore, having withdrawn from the Meletians (of the city, says George), spent three whole years in quiet. Since he was in the monastery where he had been before," says George; I judge that this three-year period was inserted inconveniently against the logic of the timeline (as will be shown in what follows) and without the support of Palladius, and should be removed from the count of Chrysostom’s years. 

Therefore, after his deaconate, he was next ordained a Priest (which all agree upon) five years later by Flavian—not, as Socrates claims, by Evagrius the successor of Paulinus—which we shall demonstrate later. Thus we have, from the birth of John until his youthful desert studies, twenty years according to Chrysostom himself, or eighteen according to others; NEARLY three years with Meletius; then in the desert NEARLY six years; in the rank of Deacon five years; and (excluding that three-year gap mentioned by Socrates and more recent writers) twelve years in the rank of Priesthood. 

If these years were full, rather than hollow or overlapping (which I rather believe, especially in the years before the deaconate, according to the custom of almost all authors who often inflate numbers, and because the word NEARLY is repeated twice by Palladius), the years from his birth to his bishopric would total 46. But if we take away two years from his youthful studies along with Palladius and more recent authors, and one year for that twice-repeated NEARLY, the years would only be 43. 

The remaining dates are straightforward and the epochs certain, not only in terms of years but almost to the months and days. It is agreed among all, both ancient and modern, that John was summoned from Antioch (where he was a Priest) by Augustus Arcadius <note>The Eastern Roman Emperor.</note> and placed upon the episcopal throne in Constantinople during the Consulship of Honorius (for the 4th time) and Eutychianus—that is, in the year of Christ 398, as we reckon it, on February 26th. 

He was driven from the see and the city (I speak of the second exile, for we shall see regarding the first later) during the Consulship of Honorius (for the 6th time) and Aristaenetus (which is the year of our Lord 404) on the twentieth day of June, or, as others say, five days after the completion of Pentecost. Indeed, thirteen days later, that is on July 3rd, the ninth letter of our John to Olympias was sent; and on the day following that, July 4th (or the month of Panemus), another was sent to Constantius. 

In this exile, he lived at Cucusus for one year, and at Arabissus for two years, the remaining months being spent on the journey toward Pityus, which he never reached, being prevented by death at Comana during the Consulship of Honorius (7th time) and Theodosius (again)—that is, in the year of Christ 407, which is established among all. 

There is a controversy regarding the month. Socrates writes that he died on November 14th; George, and all the more recent writers after him, and the Roman Calendar (as it seems) say September 14th, on the very day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. Furthermore, it is clear that in Socrates "September" should be read, as seen in the old Latin translation in Cassiodorus's *Tripartite History*, Book 10, Chapter 18. 

Thus, the years from the beginning of his Bishopric until his death are nine years, six or eight months, and sixteen days; and from birth to death, according to the larger calculation collected above, 52 years and several months; according to the smaller calculation, 52 years and some months. Zonaras, Cedrenus, and almost all others write that he lived no more than fifty-two years. An uncertain author on page 54 of the Latin Paris edition of 1588 adds eight months, with whom I mostly agree. Thus, according to the larger calculation, the year of John’s birth falls in the Consulship of Constantius (5th time) and Gallus Caesar, in the year of our Lord 352, in the month, as it seems, of January or March. Now the relics of Chrysostom, by order of the Emperor Theodosius the Younger and at the persuasion of Proclus, then Bishop of Constantinople, were transported from Comana to the royal city and brought into the Basilica of the Holy Apostles, according to Theodoret, Book 5, Chapter 36.

It details his progression from a desert ascetic to a priest in Antioch, and finally to his embattled tenure as Bishop of Constantinople and his death in exile.</summary>

# The Arian Century <note>The "Arian Century" refers to the 4th century, dominated by the theological conflicts following the Council of Nicaea. Though this page discusses events in the early 5th century, it is part of a larger history of that era.</note>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>

5. From Chapter 36 and Socrates’ *Ecclesiastical History* (Book 7, Chapter 45), it is established that during the 16th Consulship of Theodosius—that is, in the year of Christ 438, on the 27th day of January—the following occurred: this was 33 years and 8 months after his second exile, and 30 years and 3 (or perhaps 5) months after his death. Cosmas Vestitor <note>An 8th-century official and author who wrote encomiums on Chrysostom.</note> writes: "After thirty-three years" <note>original: Μετὰ τριάκοντα καὶ τρεῖς χρόνους</note>. Socrates, in Book 7, Chapter 45, with notable inconsistency, says "in the thirty-fifth year after his deposition" <note>original: τριακοστῷ πέμπτῳ ἔτει μετὰ τὴν καθαίρεσιν</note>, and yet seven lines later, "in the thirty-fifth year after his death" <note>original: τριακοστῷ πέμπτῳ ἔτει μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν</note>; even though three years and several months intervened between these two events. And these are roughly the points in which one can note the dates, and almost the very moments of time, from the histories. The rest must be gathered "at large" <note>original: ὡς ἐν πλάτει</note>, either by logical arguments or even by conjecture.

And first, Eutropius <note>A powerful eunuch and advisor to Emperor Arcadius who eventually fell from grace.</note>, fleeing the anger of the Emperors, fled to the church while he himself and Theodore were Consuls—that is, in the year of Christ 399. He was a man not only Christian but also Orthodox; for he was the one who ordered the books of Eunomius the Heresiarch <note>Eunomius was a leader of the radical Arians who claimed the Son was unlike the Father.</note> (who had surpassed Arius himself in impiety) to be publicly burned and his corpse to be dragged out and cast away. According to Nicephorus (Book 13, Chapter 1), the business of the Asiatic Bishops began to be handled "during the thirteenth indiction" <note>original: ἐπὶ τρισκαιδεκάτης ἐπινεμήσεως</note>—that is, in the thirteenth Indiction <note>An 'Indiction' was a 15-year tax cycle used for dating in the late Roman Empire.</note> (not a "distribution," as the translator of Palladius and others wrongly have it), which is the year of our Lord 400. This lasted for two years, according to Palladius, which is to say until the end of the year 401 or even the beginning of 402.

Regarding the time of his first exile, it is not so easy to define; therefore, the truth must be drawn out by arguments and conjectures, as much as we are able. Twelve hours after his first expulsion (which Socrates and others say happened at midday, though Chrysostom’s own *Letter to Innocent* says "late in the evening" <note>original: πρὸς ἑσπέραν βαθεῖαν</note>), John was recalled by the order of the Emperors (so says Palladius). A few days later, though unwilling and resisting greatly, he was placed on the throne and delivered that sermon to the people which survives at the end of George's work: "When Sarah [was taken] from Abimelech" <note>original: Οτε τοῦ Σάρραν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀβεσὰμ. This sermon compares his return to the restoration of Sarah to Abraham.</note>, while Theophilus <note>Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, was Chrysostom’s chief antagonist.</note> was still staying in the city and not daring to open his mouth against him (Sozomen, Book 8, Chapter 18). And when, because of the judgment intended against Heraclides, Bishop of Ephesus (who was absent), frequent skirmishes occurred in the city between the people of Constantinople and the Egyptians of Theophilus’ faction, "so that many were wounded, and some even driven away" <note>original: ὡς πολλοὺς τραυματίας γενέσθαι, τινὰς δὲ καὶ ἀπελάσαι</note>; and since the city sought to throw Theophilus into the sea, Theophilus fled in fear to Egypt, "winter already beginning" <note>original: ἤδη τοῦ χειμῶνος ἀρχομένης</note>, as Sozomen says, and Nicephorus (Book 13, Chapter 17). Accordingly, the Anonymous author (Chapter 100), Metaphrastes (Chapter 36), and the Greek Menologies <note>Church calendars containing lives of the saints.</note> place the day of his return from exile on the 13th of November. The same Anonymous author and Metaphrastes write that this day was celebrated as a feast in Constantinople up to their own times, as the Greek Menologies also indicate.

Since, therefore, from their unanimous testimony he returned from exile in the month of November, we must next inquire about the year: specifically, whether he returned in November of the year 403 (when Theodosius and Rumoridus were Consuls) or in November 402 (when Arcadius and Honorius were Consuls for the 5th time). I say, and I declare clearly, that his return from exile cannot have fallen in November of the year 403; although Cardinal Baronius and others place it in that year. George (Chapter 53) says: "during this year... while others were held back in various ways [at the second Council against John], nine months passed" <note>original: τοῦτον ἔτος ... παρίππευσαν μῆνες ἐννέα</note> ("ten," says Emperor Leo in Chapter 26, while Palladius gives both numbers). "And when the feast of the birth of the Savior arrived" <note>original: ῆ δὲ ἑορτῆς τῶν γενεθλίων τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἐπελθούσης</note>, etc. From these words, it appears that the second "Council-let" <note>A derogatory term for the irregular synod held against Chrysostom.</note> against John was begun in the month of April in the year 403; thus it is necessary that the first exile falls in November of the year 402, since it could not have fallen in November 403. If the authority of George seems slight to anyone, let him at least believe Palladius, a "more trustworthy" <note>original: ἀξιοπιστέρῳ</note> witness speaking almost the same things about the same matter.

What, you will ask, was done in the meantime? I respond that John, after his first exile, remained quiet for some time and was in great favor with Eudoxia <note>The Empress, wife of Arcadius, whose relationship with Chrysostom fluctuated between support and bitter enmity.</note>, indeed having honored her with great praises in the Oration mentioned above found at the end of George’s work. The same Palladius is a witness, whose words are: "After two months again from the blow inflicted" (namely the flight of Theophilus and the Egyptian bishops), "breathing a little" (John’s enemies) "raged a second time against John." This was around the month of January in the year 403, on the occasion of the silver statue of the Empress "clothed in a robe" <note>original: χλανίδι ἐνδεδυμένης</note>, placed upon a porphyry column. This event is recorded in this year (Theodosius and Rumoridus being Consuls) not only by Socrates (Book 6, Chapter 18) but also by Prosper of Aquitaine and Marcellinus Comes in their Chronicles. At this statue, perhaps on the very Kalends of January <note>January 1st.</note> (which is the solemn day of the beginning Roman year)...

# The Arian Century <note>Though the "Arian Century" typically refers to the 4th century dominated by the Arian heresy, this section deals with the immediate aftermath and the early 5th-century conflicts involving Chrysostom.</note>

(of the recipient) having been dedicated, when public games and dances <note>original: δημοθίαις</note> were held; John, moved to anger, sharpened his tongue against those who took part in these games. Seizing this opportunity, John’s enemies—who, besides the Egyptians, were still present in the city—instigated by the Augusta <note>Empress Eudoxia</note>, set in motion clandestine plots against him. After communicating with the absent Theophilus through messengers and letters, they convened a second Council against John, beginning, I believe, in April. This Council, dragged out for various reasons until the following Christmas, and then to Lent in the year 404, and finally to Easter, became the cause of our John’s second exile five days after the completion of Pentecost. This occurred one full year, seven months, and seven days after his return from his first exile. And this is my opinion regarding the timing of the first exile. Nor does it stand in opposition to what Theodoret writes in Book 5, Chapter 34: "after a few months had passed" <note>original: ὀλίγων διελθόντων μηνῶν</note> (namely, from his return) "they gathered again and exacted penalties for his performing liturgy after his deposition" <note>original: συνήθροισαν αὖθις, κὶ δίκας εἰσέπραττον τὸν μετὰ τὴν καθαίρεσιν λειτουργίαν</note>. For they convened the Council after five months, or slightly less, which then lasted for 14 months afterward. It is not surprising that events spanning a year and a half are narrated by Theodoret in barely three words; he touches upon this whole business briefly and timidly, moved by those reasons provided at the start of the said Chapter 34. The "Anonymous" writer records that "one year" <note>original: ἕνα ἐνιαυτὸν</note> passed between the return and the Easter before the second exile; Metaphrastes calls it "a full year" <note>original: ἔτος ἐυτελές</note>. This "full year" must necessarily have been seventeen months, since both write that he returned on the 13th of November.

Having settled the record <note>original: ἀπογραφῷ</note> of Chrysostom’s years, it follows that we should add a few details regarding the substitution of Arsacius, the succession of Atticus, and the death of Eudoxia Augusta. In the place of the once-again expelled John, Arsacius was substituted, "after a few days had passed" <note>original: ὀλίγων διελθουσῶν ἡμερῶν</note>, as Socrates says in Book 6, Chapter 19. The Greek Annals (recently edited by Joseph Scaliger along with Eusebius) report that Arsacius was made Bishop "in the [Church of the] Apostles" <note>original: ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις</note> (the Cathedral of Hagia Sophia having been burned) "in the month of Daios, six days before the Kalends of July" <note>Daios is a Macedonian month corresponding to June</note>, that is, June 26th, the sixth day after John’s expulsion. Socrates, in Book 6, Chapter 20, is the authority for the fact that Arsacius died the following year around November 11th, during the second Consulship of Stilicho and Anthemius—that is, in the year of our Lord 405. Arsacius therefore lived in the Episcopacy for one year, 4 months, and 16 days. Palladius and several others attribute 14 months to him; Patriarch Nicephorus says two years. After the death of Arsacius (which, as I said, happened on November 11, 405), Atticus succeeded him; "he was proclaimed," <note>original: ἀνεκηρύξατο</note> says Socrates, "while the bishopric was sought by many, and after much time had elapsed" <note>original: πολλοῖς γινομένης τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς, κὶ πολλοῦ διαδραμόντος χρόνου</note>. Georgius says this happened "in the forty-fourth year" <note>original: Τετταρακαὶ τεσσαρακοστῷ χρόνῳ</note>: so that the creation of Atticus must fall in the month of March in the year 406, during the 6th Consulship of Arcadius and Probus. There remains the greatest question of all concerning the death of Eudoxia Augusta: in noting the time of her death, modern writers depart from all the ancients who explicitly mention it. Socrates (Book 6, Chapter 19) writes that a massive hailstorm, "in the shape of stones" <note>original: εἰς τύπον λίθων</note> ("the size of walnuts," <note>original: μεγέθους καρύων</note> says the author of the Greek Annals) fell around September 30th in the same year John was driven out, during the Consulship of Honorius (VI) and Aristaenetus—that is, 404 AD—and that Eudoxia died four days later. The Greek Annals record that she died on the day before the Nones of October <note>October 6</note> and was buried in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles on the 4th day before the Ides of October <note>October 12</note> under the same Consuls, Honorius and Aristaenetus. Count Marcellinus says Eudoxia, wife of Arcadius, died under these same Consuls; Prosper of Aquitaine likewise says Eudoxia, wife of Arcadius, closed her final day under the same Consuls. Against this phalanx of ancient writers, what can a weak handful of moderns do? Yet they all testify with one voice that she survived our John by three months—that is, she died around the middle of December in the year 407, or around the middle of February in 408. This is the opinion that I embrace as more probable. The reasons are: first, because I believe those cruelties <note>original: ἀπανθρωπίας</note> and monstrosities committed against the Bishops sent as legates from the West, against our John until his very death, and against all the Bishops, Clerics, and others of John’s party, proceeded from no other source than the implacable fury of a most powerless woman (since Arcadius himself was otherwise of a simple and mild nature, and nearly ignorant of such great evils). Nor is it credible that the Bishops and John's other enemies would have had such weight with the soldiers, port guards, and other ministers of the Empire, were it not for Eudoxia, a woman [fierce] beyond her sex...

# The Arian Century <note>This heading refers to the 4th century, which was dominated by the Arian controversy, though the text here focuses on the early 5th-century aftermath surrounding Chrysostom.</note>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
