...of a fierce woman who dominated her husband, supported by wealth and fortified by authority. But what moves me most of all to pronounce against the ancient writers in favor of more recent ones—something I do very reluctantly—is this: that our John [Chrysostom], who (if we follow the ancients) must have survived Eudoxia by three full years, never once mentions Eudoxia's death in so many letters to the Pope, to the Bishops, and to other friends written over those three years. They say she died of a long-term, agonizing, and even foul disease; John would not have been silent about such a great and remarkable vengeance of God. Indeed, he would have been encouraged by that very event toward a certain hope of return or better fortune. Palladius also, a contemporary of those times, although he recounts one by one the punishments immediately taken against John's enemies for their <term>blasphemies<note>original Greek: βλασφήμων</note></term>, is silent regarding Eudoxia, who they say died after great torments from a foul disease.

Having therefore established the chronology as far as we are able, let us proceed to the authors themselves. The chief among them is easily Palladius, or whoever is the author of that Dialogue that goes by his name (for we warned in the notes to the *Biographers* <note>original Greek: Βιογράφους (Biographous)</note> that the author's identity is not entirely clear). From him, I will propose two doubts, which perhaps seem <term>insoluble<note>original Greek: ἄλυτα (alyta)</note></term> to others, but are to me entirely <term>solvable<note>original Greek: λυτὰ (lyta)</note></term>; unless a Greek manuscript <note>original: Codex</note> <term>"whenever, God willing"<note>original Greek: ὅτε ποτὲ σὺν θεῷ</note></term> is dug out of the shadows like a <term>god from a machine<note>original Latin: deus ex machina — a plot device where a seemingly unsolvable problem is suddenly resolved by an unexpected intervention.</note></term> to untangle these knots for us, which are certainly worthy of a rescuer. The first doubt concerns Palladius the dialogist in that Dialogue translated by Ambrogio Traversari <note>Ambrogio Camaldolese (1386–1439), a famous humanist scholar who translated many Greek patristic works into Latin.</note>, and inscribed in our books to a certain "Palladius the Deacon." Is he a different person from Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, the writer of the *Lausiac History* <note>The *Historia Lausiaca* is a famous collection of the lives of the Desert Fathers.</note>, a contemporary, disciple, and traveling companion of our John? Or is he the same person? I see that this matter is not without reason doubted by the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), the great Catholic historian and author of the *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note> (year 388, number 110). These points suggest they are the same person: First, the title itself: "Palladius, disciple of Chrysostom, Bishop of Helenopolis, and Theodore, etc., converse." Then, lest anyone distrust titles and headings, the same words immediately follow in the preface of the work. Second, Palladius the dialogist professes that he did not desert John for even a moment during that journey to Asia, but remained a constant companion; everyone knows this is true of Palladius the Lausiac. Third, Palladius the dialogist mentions his own gray hair, lest anyone say another <term>namesake<note>original Greek: ὁμώνυμον (homonymon)</note></term> of a younger age was substituted for the elder Palladius in that same see. And certainly, that Lausiac writer must have lived for some years after the fall of Rome <note>The Sack of Rome in 410 AD.</note>, because in the *Lausiac History* he mentions the death of Melania, which happened after that <term>conquest<note>original Greek: ἅλωσιν (halosin)</note></term>. 

On the contrary, arguments that are, in my judgment, insurmountable and taken from no other source than the words of the Dialogue itself, prove otherwise. First, the dialogist Palladius testifies that he came from the East during the time of Pope Zosimus, and that he saw Rome then for the first time; whereas it is most certain from the very words of this dialogue that Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, came to Rome eight or ten years before Zosimus entered the Papacy, while not only Innocent but John himself was still living. Second, both Theodore and Palladius himself speak of that Bishop of Helenopolis in the third person. Regarding this question, it will not be troublesome to record here what occurred to the mind of a most talented young man, my close friend, John Hales <note>John Hales (1584–1656), an English cleric and scholar known as "the Ever-Memorable." This indicates the author of this text is likely Sir Henry Savile or a contemporary English scholar.</note>. For either the things he brings forward are true, or at least probable; or I do not think anyone will easily bring forward anything more probable.

From the *Dialogue of Theodore the Deacon* (for I am most convinced that the work which goes under Palladius's name is actually his), it is established that there were two Palladiuses, contemporaries, both bishops, and both inseparable companions of John. The first is the Bishop of Helenopolis, who converses with Theodore in the aforementioned dialogue, and who was a disciple of Chrysostom, who first came to Rome while Pope Zosimus sat in the chair. The second is Palladius, Bishop of the Blemmyes or Ethiopians <note>The Blemmyes were a nomadic people of the Nubian region.</note>, whom Palladius relates in the Dialogue was detained by military force at Athyris on the return from Rome to Constantinople and banished to Syene. Therefore, the greatest obscurity has been produced in that Dialogue by the confusion of names. For first, what Theodore relates—that Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, came to Rome after Cyriacus and Eulysius under Pope Innocent—I think is a scribal error; an error, I say, although an ancient one (for George of Alexandria reads it thus, as do the Latin manuscripts)

### The Arian Century <note>This heading refers to the 4th century, characterized by the theological conflicts following the Council of Nicaea, though the discussion here extends into the early 5th century.</note>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>

...judges) yet it is a clear error. For he was in fact Palladius, Bishop of the Blemmyes <note>The Blemmyes were a nomadic tribal group in the regions of Lower Nubia and Upper Egypt.</note>. For that Palladius, who came to Rome without letters, is the same one who, relying on the letters of the Western Bishops, returned with Eulysius and Cyriacus and was indeed detained at Athyris by military force. And yet, when Theodore asked what had happened to those detained there, Palladius, among others whom he enumerates, recounts that Palladius, Bishop of the Blemmyes, was banished to Syene <note>Modern-day Aswan, Egypt.</note>; no mention at all is made of any other Palladius. It is necessary, therefore, that the Palladius who came to Rome under Pope Innocent, and who was detained at Athyris upon his return and shortly after relegated to Syene, is one and the same Palladius—namely, the Bishop of the Blemmyes. Now, as for the fact that Palladius seems to speak of Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, as if he were an absent person in the third person; we should note that this happened by the same error as before, a <term>logical impossibility<note>original Greek: τῶν ἀδυνάτων (tōn adynatōn)</note></term>: so that those things which are told there concerning Palladius of Helenopolis being sent to Smyrna with two others to investigate Asian affairs, should rather refer to the other, the Bishop of the Blemmyes. This was likely due to the variety of names imposing upon a writer who was not sufficiently careful, or perhaps a note by a half-learned scholar written in the margin next to the name of Palladius later broke into the main text. But if this seems a bit harsh to anyone, I do not see what is absurd if we say that Palladius of Helenopolis, in narrating his own deeds, speaks of himself in the third person. For those who either write or speak of their own affairs occasionally do this.

The second <term>puzzle<note>original Greek: ἀπόρημα (aporēma)</note></term> is how it could happen that within three days after receiving the letters of Theophilus, in which he indicated that John [Chrysostom] had been deposed by him—which must necessarily have been written from the Synod of the Oak <note>An illegal provincial synod held in 403 AD that deposed Chrysostom.</note> (for Theophilus did not attend the later Council, but remained at Alexandria; nor was any head of accusation proposed in that Council, but only a bare Canon of the Council of Antioch was brought forward)—how, I say, three days after receiving the letters of Theophilus, Pope Innocent could receive John's letters (the beginning of which is, *And even before the letters...* <note>original Greek: Καὶ πρὸ τῶν γραμμάτων (Kai pro tōn grammatōn)</note>) written after the second Council, or rather after John's actual expulsion (as appears from John’s own words: *I was expelled from the church a second time* <note>original Greek: δεύτερόν τε ἐκκλησίας ἐξεβλήθην (deuteron te ekklēsias exeblēthēn)</note>, and those following). For between the two exiles, as we have fully demonstrated, nineteen months intervened. What then? **I am completely at a loss here** <note>original Latin: "Aqua mihi hîc planè hæret," a proverbial expression meaning "the water stops here," used when a writer is stuck on a problem.</note>, unless we apply a "hard wedge to a hard knot": namely, to say that this letter of John, *And even before the letters...*, was woven into this place by error instead of another sent earlier. In this matter, we shall have Nicephorus as a supporter, who alone of all men most correctly placed this letter after the later exile in Book 13, Chapter 19. Alternatively, perhaps the letters of Theophilus, although written during the first exile, were not sent until after the later one—that is, 19 months afterward, as is clear from the calculation above. This opinion seems to be favored by the words which immediately follow the letter of Innocent (*Brother Theophilus*), which I think was written shortly after the first exile once the charges were first read. A "short time," he says, had passed (unless we extend that "short time" to a span of a year and a half), when Theotechnus, a Priest of Constantinople, came to Rome with letters from 25 Bishops of John's communion, by which it was signaled that he had been banished to Cucusus. These are roughly the points that it seemed appropriate to note regarding that Dialogue.

In Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380 – after 439), a Byzantine Christian church historian.</note>, there are four or five historical errors on the same page in the narration of Chrysostom’s affairs. I will not touch upon the others, but will begin from the last: that he writes John was ordained a priest by Evagrius, the successor of Paulinus and Bishop of the Eustathian faction at Antioch. This is refuted by Palladius and all others, both ancient and modern, who with one voice attribute this to Flavian, the Bishop of the other—that is, the Meletian—faction <note>The Meletian Schism was a complex division in the Church of Antioch over several decades of the 4th century.</note>. John followed this faction in that schism from the beginning, as is clear from the above; and he remained in the same most constantly until the end. For it was not until after the death of Porphyry, who succeeded Flavian, that the discord between the Eustathians and Meletians was laid to rest through the wisdom and dexterity of Alexander, then Bishop of Antioch, according to the testimony of Theodoret, Book 5, Chapter 35. But to refute this error of Socrates, it is not necessary to borrow proofs from outside...

### The Arian Century <note>The "Arian Century" refers to the 4th century, a period dominated by the theological conflicts following the Council of Nicaea. Although Chrysostom was a champion of orthodoxy, his life is situated within this historical framework.</note>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>

...since in six hundred places <note>A common Latin idiom meaning "countless places."</note> it is clearer than light from the words of Chrysostom himself that he was ordained a Priest by Flavian, and lived under him thereafter until the time of his Episcopacy. The next point is not indeed less false, but it is one that has found at least some supporters among more recent writers (for in Palladius there is no trace of this matter), regarding that whole three-year period in which, after the death of Meletius, Socrates says **"he lived quietly,"** <note>original Greek: ἡσύχως ἔζησεν</note> and George says: **"he remained in the monastery, where he had been before"** <note>original Greek: παρέμενε δὲ ἐν τῷ μοναστηρίῳ, ἔνθα ἦν πρῴην</note>; from which he was later taken to the Priesthood. This cannot stand in any way unless, against all histories, we assign not 12, but 14 years or more to John’s Priesthood. For first, from the death of Meletius, which (as we said above) happened in the year 381 at the time of the second Synod, until the Episcopacy of John in the year 398, there are 16 full years; from which we have rightly, I believe, assigned 4 to John’s Deaconate and 12 to his Priesthood. If you take away 12 from these, during which he lived as a Priest, there will remain not three years, as they wish, but four, before John was taken to the Priesthood. Furthermore, it will be necessary for those following this opinion to say that the five-year period of the deaconate ended with the death of Meletius. But in that case, John would be nearly seventy years old at the time of his death—one of the **"blessed elders"** <note>original Greek: τῶν μακαρίων (tōn makariōn)</note>—not, as is the universally accepted opinion, one of those **"in their prime."** <note>original Greek: τῶν ἀκμαζόντων (tōn akmazontōn)</note> Therefore, along with Palladius, I will clearly remove this three-year period from the **calculation** <note>original Greek: ἐπιλογισμῷ (epilogismō)</note> of Chrysostom’s years; moved both by other reasons and so that the number of John’s years would not grow too large.

The third point is that he writes John was created an <term>Anagnostes<note>A "Reader," one of the lower orders of the early Christian clergy.</note></term> or Reader by Zeno, the Bishop of Maiuma in Palestine, upon his return from Jerusalem (for no one called him Bishop of Jerusalem, even if a "Great Man" <note>Likely referring to a specific scholar like Baronius.</note> understood it otherwise); whereas we have shown above from Palladius that this was done by Meletius; nor do the Canons allow ordinations to be made in a foreign Province. The fourth is that notable <term>anachronism<note>original Greek: ἀναχρονισμὸς (anachronismos)</note></term> regarding Basil the Great and John Chrysostom, which has been sufficiently refuted by Photius, the Anonymous author, Symeon Metaphrastes, and Cardinal Baronius. Fifth, that he seems to assert that John was made a Reader after leaving the monastic life, contrary to the express words of Palladius. 

For as to his assertion that those *Sermons against the Jews* were composed by him while a Reader, we have refuted this in the notes; as well as his affirmation that the books *On the Priesthood* to Stagarius, *On the Incomprehensible*, and *On the Co-dwelling Virgins* <note>original Greek: περὶ Συνεισάκτων (peri Syneisaktōn); these were controversial ascetic arrangements where men and women lived together in spiritual companionship.</note> were composed by him while a Deacon. Did that divine genius and "Golden Mouth" remain silent for those entire six years in solitude? Indeed, if there were room for conjectures, I would think the books *On the Priesthood* to Stagarius were written by him while he was a Reader and a Monk. For so says Symeon Metaphrastes. However, it is certain from Chrysostom's own words that the *Orations against the Jews* were delivered in the second or third year of his Deaconate; in which year that excellent *Oration on Babylas* was also spoken. 

And here, although it is outside the main point, I will weave in some things from the Histories concerning his writings after the Deaconate. Nicephorus, who writes that he burned with love for him from his youth and rested in his words as if they were the voices of God himself, records that the *Expositions on the Gospels*, *on the Psalms*, the *Demonstrative Treatise*, and *On Virginity* were composed by John as a Priest. (The *Anonymous* writer adds the *Exposition on Isaiah*). From him as Bishop came the *Expositions on the Blessed Apostle* (about which more above), *on the Acts*, and the *Panegyrics*; a good part of which, however, as we have shown in their proper places, were written at Antioch. And not to go too far afield, that *Oration on Meletius* was delivered five years after the death of Meletius—that is, in the first year of his Priesthood. 

But let us return to Socrates; whose last point you might not unjustly reproach: that in express words and without any doubt, he attributes the burning of the Temple and the Senate House to the **Joannites** (for so those who were of our John’s party were called). This he does even though cruelty had been raged against men and women with threats, confiscations of property, dire tortures, and most exquisite torments; so much so that some died under interrogation, and others expired shortly thereafter; yet no trace of that crime was ever found among the Joannites.

Now, if you please, let us move to George of Alexandria; upon whom Photius—a man of great judgment and a most sharp critic of ancient writers—fastens two crimes: a failure to observe <term>Hellenism<note>In this context, Photius refers to the purity and elegance of the Greek language and classical style.</note></term>, and <term>Bad Taste.<note>original Greek: Ἀφιλοκαλίας (Aphilokalias); literally a lack of love for the beautiful or refined.</note></term> Concerning the former, we have noted much throughout the notes, and the matter is obvious to anyone; concerning the latter, which George's History—

# The Arian Century <note>The "Arian Century" refers to the 4th century, a time of intense theological debate following the Council of Nicaea. Chrysostom lived and worked during the later half of this era.</note>

<margin>
4th CENTURY from the Year 300.

...since nothing is explicitly stated, it is difficult to determine which part [the author] intended to note. However, so that we do not seem to fail our studious readers in this matter, we shall bring forward our conjectures, supported by reasons that are, I believe, not to be looked down upon. 

First, I divide the writers of Chrysostom’s history into two classes. In the first class, I place the ancients: Palladius, Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen, who wrote either during John’s own lifetime or immediately afterward, and who drew their information from various sources. For it is not probable that any of them had seen the history written by the others. To these, for the sake of their antiquity, I add our own writers, Prosper of Aquitaine and Count Marcellinus. In the second class—that of the more recent writers—I place George alone. For since all the others speak from his mouth—including Emperor Leo, the Anonymous author, Metaphrastes, Zonaras, Glycas, Nicephorus, Cedrenus, and others—they are to be counted as only a single witness. Therefore, wherever George departs from the ancients, or adds new details of his own, I treat almost all of those accounts as either false or suspicious.

First, I must sweep away those miracles of healings and visions, and all those matters about which there is an obstinate silence among the ancients; George, however, makes neither measure nor end in recounting them. Certainly, not only George is at fault in this, but also others who followed him. Because they did not think the naked and solitary truth was magnificent enough, or perhaps they feared that saying of Thucydides, that <term>the lack of the mythical makes a story seem less pleasing? <note>original Greek: τὸ μὴ μυθῶδες ἀτερπέστερον φαίνεσθαι?</note></term>, they piled up an immense quantity of miracles. To create more room for inventing these wonders, they changed the attested truth of history itself, quite often and quite significantly. 

Therefore, I leave among the <term>doubtful matters <note>original Greek: ἀμφιβαλλομένοις</note></term> those accounts found in George concerning Anthemius, the vision of Hesychius, the nobleman of Antioch, the man suffering from a migraine, Archelaus the leper, the Christian <term>woman with a hemorrhage <note>original Greek: αἱμοῤῥοούσῃ</note></term>, Eucleus the one-eyed, Leo prostrated, the white dove sitting on John’s head when he was ordained a Priest, the son of Euclia, the wife of the Prefect of Antioch, the demoniac delivered on the day of his consecration, the Angel with a drawn sword preventing Eudoxia’s captains and soldiers from entering the Episcopal palace, the man whose hand was miraculously withered and healed, the paralytic in Armenia restored to health, the vision of Adelphius, and any others of that kind. For they are destitute of authority from even one of those ancients, or even from more recent writers like Damascene, Zonaras, Nicephorus, and Cedrenus. 

Indeed, if one looks closer, most of them seem to have been forged through a certain <term>distorted zeal <note>original Greek: κακοζηλίᾳ</note></term> to resemble the miracles in Holy Scripture. I leave that whole drama of Anthemius the Philosopher, Demosthenes the prefect, and John to be judged by the learned; it seems to have been squeezed out of an idle brain following the biblical examples of Elymas, Sergius Paulus, and the Blessed Apostle. The same is true for Archelaus, created in the image of Naaman the Syrian; the nobleman with a migraine and the Christian <term>woman with a hemorrhage</term> following the <term>woman with a hemorrhage <note>original Greek: αἱμοῤῥοοῦσαν</note></term> in the Gospel; the demoniac following the one delivered in the ninth chapter of Mark; and—what I cannot read without indignation—the dove sitting on John’s head at his ordination, following the image of the only-begotten Son of God at his Baptism. 

As for that vision of Proclus, who claimed to see St. Paul through a hole in a door whispering into the ear of John (then already a Bishop) and dictating what he should write as he meditated on the exposition of Paul’s Epistles, it lacks credibility. It is well established that most of his finest writings on the Apostle were written during his years of leisure in Antioch, and that his later works had <term>descended into a humbler style <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ ταπεινότερον ἀπενεχθῆναι</note></term>. See columns 225 and 226 of the notes. 

Regarding the transfer of John’s relics, Theodoret—a <term>trustworthy witness <note>original Greek: ἀξιόπιστος</note></term>—testifies that Emperor Theodosius pressed his eyes and forehead against the urn of the relics. But the story about the Emperor’s <term>piety <note>original Greek: ὁσιοτήτι</note></term>, and his gout in the feet and hands being healed in the presence of all there, is a later addition by George. It is not even mentioned by Cosmas Vestitor, a man who was the <term>most superstitious <note>original Greek: δεισιδαιμονεστάτῳ</note></term> of all. 

But I return to earlier matters. George reports that John was first baptized by Meletius, and then his parents followed; whereas John himself (as is clear from Palladius) was not baptized before his twentieth year—as was the custom of that age, especially for those not born to Christian parents—his father Secundus having died some years before, as shown above. That his mother was indeed a Christian, at least by the time he was twenty, is clear from Chrysostom’s own words...

...appears twice in the *Oration to a Young Widow*. Regarding his father, I would affirm nothing rashly; or if both parents were Christians from the beginning—which is perhaps more likely—the fact that the son delayed baptism until that age will not be surprising to anyone who has read the life of Gregory Nazianzen <note>A prominent 4th-century theologian and Archbishop of Constantinople</note>, who was born to two Christian parents (his father being a Bishop) and yet delayed his baptism similarly. Next, there is no mention of a journey [to Athens] among the ancients, Palladius and Socrates, nor even any trace of it, though they recorded his youthful studies with enough care. Secondly, I find no empty time in the chronological reckoning <term>epilogismos</term> <note>original: ἐπιλογισμῷ; a summing up or calculation of time</note> of Chrysostom’s years that I could assign to this journey. Thirdly, his most indulgent mother, who could not bear for him to withdraw even to the nearby mountains of Antioch, would—I say—hardly have allowed him to migrate to Athens, separated by such a great distance of land and sea. Especially since for those suspected of the monastic life, it was not considered a crime of "apostasy" <note>The abandonment of one's religious vows</note> in those times to leave a monastery and return to the city—which Chrysostom himself later did, having grown weary of that deeper solitude due to ill health. And to say what I feel, I think this whole story was fabricated after the example of Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen; it is well known that both studied in Athens. This was likely done so that our John would not seem inferior to the other "great lights" of the Eastern Church.

George, in chapter 16, writes that John was snatched from the monastery with great pomp by Flavian after that three-year withdrawal and ordained a Priest. Firstly, that three-year withdrawal has no place in the life of Chrysostom; both because of what we showed above, and because it is certain that during those very years Chrysostom delivered those Orations in the Church which are still extant—those against the Jews and on the martyr Babylas, as can be seen above. Furthermore, what applause, what shouts that "Golden Mouth" <note>The literal meaning of the name 'Chrysostom'</note> would have stirred up, if he had been sought with such effort from a monastery and granted the priesthood, rather than being taken from the midst of the group of Deacons for this ministry? Anyone who reads that Oration with judgment, *The events are true* <note>original: ἀληθῆ τὰ συμβάντα</note> (Volume 6, p. 443), will agree with me on this truth. Now, as for what George writes in chapter 32—that not only six, but six other bishops besides were deposed by John in Asia—Palladius explicitly denies this, and it is closer to the number 16 or 17 that John’s adversaries charged him with. The History of Callitrope (chapter 34) contains many circumstances, nothing like which I remember seeing in ancient Ecclesiastical History, nor do I know if they can all be defended. Cedrenus confuses this History with the widow of Theognostus (chapter 41), which is so similar to the story of Naboth and Jezebel <note>A biblical story from 1 Kings 21 where Queen Jezebel unjustly seizes a vineyard for King Ahab; the author suggests the hagiographers copied this motif</note> that one seems to be modeled on the other. Yet, this story of the widow of Theognostus is accepted by [John] Damascene, as well as by nearly all more recent biographers. For among the ancients, there is no mention of this story; nor is there any decree, as far as I know, in the entire Roman Law such as the one cited by [Empress] Eudoxia in this matter. 

To these historical errors <term>anhistoresias</term> <note>original: ἀνιστορησίας; a lack of historical accuracy or record</note> of George, I add that he writes that John was recalled from his first exile by order of [Emperor] Arcadius, due to both the cries of the people and letters from his brother Honorius. In fact, he was recalled by order of the Emperors within twelve hours of his expulsion; meanwhile, Honorius, who was staying mostly at Ravenna or Milan, could not have learned anything of his expulsion. For as to his claim that Chrysostom’s Epistle, *And regarding the letters* <note>original: καὶ περὶ τῶν γραμμάτων</note>, was written after the first exile, it is a most manifest error, though one he shares with Palladius. But this next point is his own peculiar and quite gross mistake: in chapter 61, he writes that the Bishops from John’s communion wrote letters via Theotechnus to Pope Innocent, signifying that John had been banished to Cucusus; yet the same author, in chapter 64, as if forgetting himself, narrates that Innocent first learned of this from merchants or others who happened to come to Rome "for certain needs" <note>original: διὰ τινὰς χρείας</note>. He says, "For he had not yet heard the whole story concerning his exile" <note>original: Οὕπω γὰρ τὸ πᾶν ἀκηκοώς... περὶ τε τῆς αὐτοῦ ἐξορίας</note>. As for his report (chapter 58) that a servant of Epidius was sent with a dagger <note>Latin: sica</note> to kill Chrysostom at Cucusus: that undoubtedly happened in Constantinople. As for his calling Adelphius the Bishop of Arabissus, when at that time the Bishop of Arabissus was Otreius (as witnessed by John himself in Epistle 121). As for his writing that John was received into the house of the same Adelphius at Cucusus—which office of kindness (for the Bishop of Cucusus, who I believe was Adelphius himself, provided other offices of kindness, as is clear from Epistle 13 to Olympias) no other than...

# The Arian Century <note>The 4th century is often called the "Arian Century" because of the widespread theological conflict regarding the nature of Christ, following the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD. Chrysostom’s life (c. 347–407 AD) fell within this era of transition and turmoil.</note>

4th CENTURY from the Year 300.
</margin>

...which John himself attributes to Dioscorus in Letter 12 to Olympias <note>Olympias was a wealthy widow and a close friend and deaconess of Chrysostom</note>, of which there is no mention in George’s work. As for George calling Proclus the "Bishop of Cyzicus" during the translation of the relics—when Proclus, having left Cyzicus, was by then the Archbishop of Constantinople—these are, it seems to me, clearly <term>false attributions</term> <note>original: παρεπιγραφαὶ (parepigraphai); a technical term for errors in the title or authorship of a document</note>.

There remains a first-rate and difficult question regarding the letters sent back and forth between the West and the East. On this matter, I shall open my opinion candidly and freely, after the manner of our ancestors, led by no partisan zeal and by no favor or hatred toward anyone. I divide these letters, therefore, into three classes: they were sent either after the first exile, after the second exile, or after the death of John. In the first and second classes, I have no dispute with George, except for that which he shares with Palladius <note>A contemporary biographer of Chrysostom</note>, which I discussed above regarding Palladius. We must investigate the third class, of which George writes as follows in chapter 68: "With the blessed John now dead," he says, "two Priests and one Deacon, who had been with him in exile, came to Rome and laid a complaint before Pope Innocent regarding the persecutions inflicted upon John. Innocent, moved by the atrocity of the matter, immediately hurried to the Emperor Honorius. In short, both gave letters to Arcadius: Innocent sent those beginning with *The voice of blood* <note>original: φωνὴ αἵματος (phōnē haimatos); a reference to the biblical cry of Abel's blood from the ground</note> and *cries out to the brother after John* <note>original: ἀδελφῷ μετ᾽ Ἰωάννην βοᾷ (adelphō met’ Iōannēn boa)</note>, etc., in which he excommunicates Arcadius and Eudoxia; Honorius sent those beginning *I know not what opposing power* <note>original: Οὐκ οἶδα ποία ἀντικειμένη ἐνέργεια (Ouk oida poia antikeimenē energeia)</note>." Having received these letters, Arcadius (as recorded in George, chapter 69), after taking vengeance on all the enemies of John, kept his wife Eudoxia shut in her chamber with her attendants. He even severely punished her by scourging her with rods, as an Anonymous author says. After Acacius, Severian, and the <term>opponents</term> <note>original: ἀντιψήφοις (antipsēphois); those who voted against John in the ecclesiastical trials</note> of Theophilus—and it would be a wonder if the Blessed Cyril were not among the rest—had been bound and sent to Innocent at Rome, Arcadius wrote to Innocent that letter which begins *All men know* <note>original: Πάντες ἄνθρωποι ἴσασιν (Pantes anthrōpoi isasin)</note>, etc., most humbly begging that pardon be granted to him and Eudoxia, and that both be received back into communion. Eudoxia also wrote to Innocent, and Arcadius to his brother Honorius. Innocent, having received the letters of Arcadius and Eudoxia, wrote to Proclus, Bishop of Cyzicus, to come to Constantinople and receive the Emperors into communion; and he wrote back to Arcadius with that letter, *Having received your piety toward God* <note>original: Ἀναδεξάμενος τὴν κατὰ Θεὸν εὐλάβειαν (Anadeksamenos tēn kata Theon eulabeian)</note>; and he also commanded Proclus to take up the care of the Church of Constantinople, *Until the matter concerning Atticus is investigated* <note>original: Ἄχρις ἂν ἀνακριθῇ τὰ κατ᾽ Ἀττικὸν πρᾶγμα (Achris an anakrithē ta kat’ Attikon pragma)</note>.

I say confidently that this entire business is poorly divided by time and is thus plainly <term>implausible</term> <note>original: ἀσύστατον (asystaton); logically inconsistent or without historical foundation</note>. For first, if Eudoxia died three years before the death of John—which all the ancient historians before George affirm with one voice—I think no one will be so bold-faced as to dare deny that all these letters are forgeries. But even if we grant what some more recent writers assert, that she survived John by three months, the chronological calculation still will not hold. I add also that the death of Arcadius—which, as appears from the public records and the testimony of Socrates (Book 7, chapter 1), happened on the first of May during the consulship of Philippus and Bassus, in the year 408—leaves no room for these absurdities. This was five months (or, as others say, seven) and sixteen days after the death of John. Why is this? First, those two Priests and one Deacon had to remain for some time at Comana <note>The place of Chrysostom's death in modern-day Turkey</note> while the funeral rites for so great a father were performed, while that solemn and accidental gathering of all ranks was dismissed, and while the necessities for so great a journey were prepared. I deny, therefore, that they could have reached Constantinople before the death of Eudoxia. For they first set out *through the New Rome to the Old* <note>original: διὰ νέας Ῥώμης ἐπὶ τὴν παλαιὰν (dia neas Rhōmēs epi tēn palaian); meaning from Constantinople to Rome</note>, as the Anonymous author and Nicephorus say, and as the geography of the regions suggests. For the journey from Cucusus <note>John's previous place of exile</note> to Constantinople is 70 days (according to Chrysostom’s letters to Simeon and Briso), and it cannot be said that Comana is closer than Cucusus, since it is well established that John was always deported to more distant places of exile. Then, they had to travel from Constantinople to Rome; the complaint had to be laid before the Pope; Innocent had to meet with Honorius, who was usually away from Rome; those two letters (*The voice of blood* and *I know not*) had to be drafted and sent to Constantinople; many things had to be settled by Arcadius in Constantinople first; Arcadius’s letters (*All men know*) and Eudoxia’s had to be sent to Rome; new letters had to be drafted at Rome for Proclus and sent to Cyzicus; still others to Arcadius (*Having received*, etc.); and finally, Proclus had to come from Cyzicus and receive the Emperors into communion while they were still alive and healthy—

</margin>

...to complete: for the dispatching of such business, five or seven months—not to mention three—would hardly suffice; even an entire two-year period would barely be enough. And so that we may understand how slow the aid from the West is: the first letters of *Honorius* <note>Western Roman Emperor, r. 393–423 AD</note> following the later exile of *John* <note>St. John Chrysostom</note>, which is **now for the third time** <note>original: τρίτον ἤδη (triton ēdē)</note> mentioned in the works of *Palladius* and *George*, did not reach *Constantinople* until after two years. This is true if indeed *Atticus* <note>The bishop who replaced Chrysostom's immediate successor, Arsacius</note> (as is found in *Palladius*) was already Bishop when the legates arrived at *Athyra*. Indeed, those very Bishops, *Gaudentius* and *Aemilius*, who were the **representatives** <note>original: τοποτηρηταὶ (topotērētai); official legates of the Pope</note> of the Roman See, completed that journey only once in six months, according to *Leo*—or four months, according to others. This journey would have needed to be made at least twice here, in addition to the time that must be allotted for the travel from *Comana* to *Constantinople*, and from *Cyzicus* to *Constantinople*. For as to what the *Anonymous* writer says, that **on the tenth day they arrived at the port of Constantinople** <note>original: δεκάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ πρὸς τὴν Κωνσταντινόπολιν προσσορμίσθησαν</note> (referring to the representatives of the Roman See, *Gaudentius*, *Aemilius*, etc.), I believe there is an error in the number. It is in no way to be admitted that those who spent four months on the return trip could have arrived there within ten days. Therefore, even if there were nothing else, the very calculation of the times openly refutes this falsehood. Added to this is the fact that those Letters have no other defenders than more recent writers, and even then, not all of them (for in *Photius*, *Leo*, *Zonaras*, and *Metaphrastes*, there is a deep silence concerning them). Nor do these writers agree, but rather show great variety and inconsistency. For *George*, *Glycas*, and *Nicephorus* hold one version, while the *Anonymous* writer and the *Greco-Roman Law* hold another, as will be manifest from a comparison. Among the ancients, to whom the matter ought to have been best known—such as *Palladius*, who lived in *Rome* for a long time (where he could very easily have learned all these things either by himself or from *Theodore*, a Deacon of the Roman Church); *Sozomen*, who seems to have diligently examined all letters; and others—I say confidently that there is no trace of those letters, not even a shadow. Nor was this a small or contemptible matter that should or could have been omitted: that the Emperors of the East were excommunicated by the Roman Pontiff, then absolved, etc. This is especially true when all histories are full of a much smaller matter: how the present *Theodosius* was barred from his church by the present *Ambrose* <note>A famous incident in 390 AD where St. Ambrose of Milan forced Emperor Theodosius I to do penance</note>. Furthermore, it detracts from the credibility of these Letters that they seem to have been written only in Greek (and certainly the character of the writing itself clearly tastes of some half-learned little Greek scholar), whereas *Innocent* <note>Pope Innocent I, r. 401–417 AD</note> was accustomed to compose his Letters, even those sent to the East, only in Latin, as is established by the eighth book of *Sozomen*. Now, I also believe that story is false regarding *Atticus* being stripped of his Bishopric and the administration being committed to *Proclus*. It is well established that *Atticus* held the Bishopric for twenty years and handed it down through the hands of *Sisinnius*, *Nestorius*, and *Maximian*, so that *Proclus* did not succeed to that see until the sixth place after *John*. I have spoken freely what seems probable to me in this matter: let the learned judge.

Among the **historical errors** <note>original: ἀνιστορησίας (anistorēsias); lack of historical knowledge</note> of *George*, I also count this: that he seems to make the death of *Innocent* occur before the death of *Theophilus* <note>Patriarch of Alexandria and a chief rival of Chrysostom</note>, which is openly false. For *Theophilus* died, according to *Socrates* <note>The church historian Socrates Scholasticus</note> in Book 7, Chapter 7, during the consulship of *Honorius* (for the 9th time) and *Theodosius* (for the 5th time), which is the year of our Lord 412, on the 25th of October. *Innocent*, as is clear from the **Pontifical Annals** <note>original: Fastis Pontificiis</note>, did not die until 417, or 415. If it seems strange to anyone—since *Theophilus* survived *John* by five years, and *Innocent* by eight—why it was that *Innocent* cast aside all plans for convening a Synod at *Thessalonica* (at which he had commanded *Theophilus* to be present with such severity and rigor before his death, if we are to believe the Letter of *Arcadius* <note>Eastern Roman Emperor, r. 395–408 AD</note> found in *George*, which begins: **You have occupied all the regions of the inhabited world** <note>original: Πάντα τὰ κλίματα τῆς οἰκουμένης ἐπέσχας</note>) and never spoke a word about it afterward; perhaps it happened because *Arcadius* had died shortly after *John*. It was by his effort and command, as those times required, that a Synod would be convened. Or perhaps it was because such times followed for the republic, especially in the West—with *Rome* captured <note>The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 AD</note>, *Italy* plundered, and the provinces devastated—which could turn the mind of even the most constant man from a lesser care to a greater fear.

So much for *George*. In the remaining matters I shall be briefer, because almost all of them have things in common with *George*; it would not be worth the effort to linger twice over refuting the same absurdities. *Leo* gave us a summary of *George*, except that in those Letters he follows *George*, or at least does not shorten them, just as *Photius* in the *Gregorian* Epitome, Code 96, certainly could have omitted them without loss (for he added nothing to *George*, except for an occasionally affected obscurity of style).

<summary>The author critiques George of Alexandria's historical accuracy regarding the aftermath of John Chrysostom's death, using travel logistics and chronological errors (such as the death dates of Pope Innocent I and Theophilus) to argue that certain letters claiming the Pope excommunicated the Eastern Emperors are later forgeries.</summary>

...unless it seems that a great addition was made to the rest of John’s glory from the fact that he found so great an Emperor to be the herald of his praises. The Anonymous writer has one or two errors peculiar to himself. First, a rather lofty and thick-headed lie: he claims that Libanius <note>A famous 4th-century pagan teacher of rhetoric in Antioch</note> said to Julian, who was already Augustus <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate," r. 361–363 AD</note>, that **"None of those great philosophers is superior to John, not even that great and divine Plato, nor Demosthenes in eloquence."** Even if we were to grant that this was true later on, it certainly could not have been said to Julian, who died when John had barely—if even—entered his eighth year. One is tempted to cry out:

-> —— and what does lying Greece <-
-> *not dare in history* —— <note>original: "—— & quid non Græcia mendax / *Audet in historia* ——" (Juvenal, *Satires* 10.174). A classic Roman critique of Greek historical exaggerations.</note> <-

especially these more recent writers? Similar to this, and almost a sibling to it, is the claim that Gregory of Nazianzus <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers" and a contemporary of Chrysostom</note>—specifically while he was still Patriarch of Constantinople—conversed with Theodosius the Great about John’s *Orations on the Statues*. Yet it is very well known that Gregory, having abdicated his Bishopric and left Constantinople, had withdrawn to Cappadocia during the time of the Second Synod in the year of our Lord 381. At that time, John was barely a Deacon, and it was at least seven years before the time the statues were overturned <note>The "Affair of the Statues" occurred in Antioch in 387 AD, long after Gregory left the capital.</note>. As for the miracles, although George might seem to have made a diligent collection of them, he still left a large enough gleaning for the Anonymous writer. There is the vision given to Gregory the Theologian concerning John (chapter 37); the account of St. Paul confirming John’s Expositions **in bodily form** <note>original: σωματειδῶς (sōmateidōs)</note> (chapter 59); that John predicted the succession of Proclus to the see of Constantinople (chapter 60); John’s frequent **apparitions** <note>original: ὀπτασίαι (optasiai)</note> during the celebration of **the Liturgy** <note>original: Synaxin (from Greek σύναξις)</note> (chapters 72, 73, 74); the appearance of Andrew, Stachys, and the Blessed Virgin (chapter 79); the prediction made at Nicaea concerning Emperor Maurice (chapter 107); the visions of Mark and Cyril (chapters 128, 129); the trembling of the tomb of Eudoxia <note>The Empress who was Chrysostom's primary antagonist</note> (chapter 132); and I know not what miracles performed **during the translation of the relics** <note>original: ἐν τῇ τῶν λειψάνων ἀνακομιδῇ (en tē tōn leipsanōn anakomidē)</note>, which he borrowed from the "Vestitor" <note>Cosmas the Vestitor, a 10th-century homilist</note>. All these things, I say, are of the same rank and place as those other "Georgian" tales. If that passage from Ephorus, written in Strabo’s works concerning the Delphic Oracle, had come to the minds of those who were to transmit the affairs of God and the Church to posterity—that it is "unfitting for one dealing with the truest Oracle of all to indulge in uncertain rumors and improbable narrations"—then we would not now rightly complain that the reliability of historical monuments has been corrupted by an immense lust for inventing. But enough of useless complaints; I pass on to Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer</note>, about whom there is no need to note anything. For he has nothing that you will not find either in George or the Anonymous writer, whom he almost entirely mimics. Indeed, the sense and often even the words are common to both Metaphrastes and the Anonymous writer. And so, it seemed right to note these few points from many regarding the authors of Chrysostom’s life; which things I submit to the judgment of the learned, as I do all my works.

Thus far the most noble Savile <note>Sir Henry Savile (1549–1622), who published the first complete Greek edition of Chrysostom's works</note>. Let me be permitted to add a few things to his remarks. Savile himself presents to us (Volume 8, page 293) a small index of writers who committed the affairs of Chrysostom to writing, compiled by a certain Greek. Among these are Proclus, Bishop of Constantinople; Cyril of Alexandria (whose papers George is later said to have plundered); Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem; Nicetas Sceuophylax; and Nicetas the Paphlagonian. However, whether their Discourses survive today, I have not yet learned. In addition to the four that Savile published, he testifies in the same place (page 944) that he had in his possession five other **biographers** <note>original: Βιογράφους (biographous)</note> or Panegyrists of Chrysostom in Greek—namely John of Damascus, Cosmas the Vestitor, John of Euchaita, Philotheus the Patriarch, and Matthew Camariota. Yet he judged them all unworthy of the light and thought they should be suppressed, recording only the titles of the books. He also adds that there exists in the Roman libraries a Discourse on Chrysostom by Emperor Constantine (son of Leo the Wise) beginning **"When the [relics] of the wise Chrysostom..."** <note>original: ἡνίκα τὸ τοῦ σοφοῦ Χρυσοστόμου (hēnika to tou sophou Chrysostomou)</note>; but this, perhaps no less than the others, is judged scarcely worthy of the light.

## Pagan Writers who Opposed the Christian Religion in this Century.

<margin>302.</margin>
<margin>* Divine Institutes, book 5, ch. 2.</margin>
<margin>† On the Deaths of the Persecutors, ch. 16, p. 30.</margin>
**Hierocles**, whether he was a true philosopher or merely a political official, is not clear. He flourished at the beginning of this century around the year 302 AD. He was a chief architect and a great "extirpator" <note>original Greek: ἐξολοθρευτὴς (exolothreutēs) - a destroyer or annihilator</note> of the fierce persecution under Diocletian <note>The Roman Emperor who launched the last and most severe persecution of Christians in 303 AD</note>. He served first as Deputy Governor of Bithynia, and later as the Prefect of Alexandria. In both places, he raged against the Christians with wondrous cruelty. Lactantius * encountered him while he was staying in Nicomedia; for although he suppressed his name in one work †, he names him clearly elsewhere, stating that he was the author and advisor behind the carrying out of the persecution. In the former passage, he has these words to say about him:

> Another wrote on the same subject more bitingly; he was then among the number of the Judges, and was a primary author of the persecution. Not content with this crime, he also pursued those whom he had afflicted with his writings. For he composed two short books, not *against* the Christians—lest he seem to pursue them as an enemy—but *to* the Christians, so that he might be thought to be advising them humanely and kindly. In these books, he attempted to prove the falsehood of the Sacred Scripture by showing it to be entirely contradictory to itself; for he set out certain chapters which seemed to oppose one another, listing so many intimate details that he seemed at times to have come from that same school of discipline. He titled these books *Truth-loving Discourses* <note>original Greek: λόγους φιλαλήθεις (logous philalētheis)</note>; a truly poisonous work, in which among other things he compared Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century pagan philosopher and wonder-worker often presented by pagans as a rival to Jesus</note>, a most famous magician, to Christ the Lord, contending that he had done equal or even greater things.

Only a single fragment of this work survives in Eusebius’s book *Against Hierocles*, not far from the beginning. This man is different from, and older than, that other Hierocles who wrote about fate (mentioned by Photius), as we noted above in the section on Eusebius of Caesarea.

**AN ANONYMOUS** philosopher of Nicomedia, famous at the same place and time, whom Lactantius depicts elegantly in the cited passage as infamous for his vices. This man, at the same time as Hierocles—namely during the persecution of Diocletian—insulted the prostrate and dejected Truth, I know not whether more proudly or more insolently; and against the Christian religion and name

> he vomited up three books; having professed above all, says Lactantius, that it was the duty of a philosopher to come to the aid of human errors and to recall men to the true way—that is, to the worship of the Gods; and that he had undertaken this duty, worthy of philosophy, so that he might hold out the light of wisdom to those not seeing it, so that by laying aside their stubborn obstinacy, they might avoid the tortures of the body. After much that Lactantius says concerning this work and the Author’s intent, he adds: "But this man was held in contempt for his own vanity; he did not obtain the favor he hoped for, and the glory he sought was turned into blame and reproach."

<margin>* Toward the year 302, nos. 51, 57.</margin>
Lactantius did indeed keep the name of this leader of philosophy hidden: Baronius * contends that it was Porphyry <note>A famous Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity</note>. However, what Lactantius reports about our philosopher does not fit Porphyry’s character, his age, or the number of his books. Therefore, let the name of the author perish along with the work itself, deservedly condemned to eternal darkness.

<margin>* Page 252.</margin>
**LIBANIUS**, a native of Antioch and a sophist by profession, flourished around the year 360 AD and lasted until the final days of Theodosius the Great. He was elevated by him to the dignity of Praetorian Prefect, and taught Rhetoric at Constantinople, Nicomedia, and finally Antioch. He says much about himself in the book he wrote about his own life, where he treats his own affairs to the point of nausea. He often draws his pen against the Christians, especially in three Orations. The first *, which is called the *Monody for Julian* <note>original Greek: Μονωδία εἰς Ἰουλιανὸν; a funeral lament</note>, covertly snatches at Constantine the Great (for the Scholiast notes that he is the one intended), because he had brought a vehement and unending war against the Pagans, had clearly extinguished the sacred fire, had forbidden the sweetness of animal sacrifices, and had permitted the altars to be overturned by heels; he had indeed closed some sacred places and shrines, and buried others, and pro-

...renounced these profane things and allowed them to be inhabited by common prostitutes. The second oration, titled **Funeral Oration for Julian** <note>original Greek: Επιτάφιος ἐπὶ Ἰουλιανῷ (Epitaphios epi Ioulianō)</note>, is quite long; in it, he not only disparages the Emperor Constantius and secretly sneers at the Christian religion, but also openly blames the death of Julian on the Christians (whom he calls **those who live by the laws** <note>original Greek: τοὺς ζῶντας καὶ τοὺς νόμους (tous zōntas kai tous nomous) — likely a sarcastic reference to Christians following their own 'new' laws</note>). He adds that they had long been preparing an ambush for this very purpose. Gerard Langbaine, a distinguished scholar of his time, assures us in his *Notes on Longinus, p. 53*, that an as-yet-unpublished speech by Libanius **On the Punishment of Julian** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῇ τιμωρίᾳ Ἰουλιανοῦ (epi tē timōria Ioulianou)</note>, in which he demands that the perpetrators of Julian's death be sought out for execution, exists in manuscript at the Oxford Library. Finally, the third Oration, which has been published, is *On the Temples of the Pagans*, presented to Theodosius the Great. In this work, he not only argues the case for the solemnity of the Pagan religion and its sacred buildings, but also vehemently accuses the Christians—especially the bishops and monks who were most active in destroying the temples of the Pagans—doing so "unveiled" or **with a bare head** <note>original Greek: γυμνῇ τῇ κεφαλῇ (gymnē tē kephalē) — an idiom meaning to act openly or shamelessly</note>. The first two Orations are found among the works of Lucian, Volume II; the latter was published with notes in Greek and Latin by Jacques Godefroy.

## JULIAN,
<margin>
* To the year
337.
57.
</margin>
A native of Constantinople, the younger son of Julius Constantius (the brother of Constantine the Great) and third in order of birth, born in the year 331. At the age of seven, he was assigned Mardonius the Eunuch as his tutor, whom Baronius * undeservedly renders suspect of Paganism. Later, at Nicomedia, he listened to Maximus the Philosopher; he even met secretly with the Sophist <note>A professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy</note> Libanius. In order to more plausibly elude all suspicion from the Emperor Constantius, although he intensely and from his heart favored the superstitions of the pagans, he nevertheless splendidly feigned a profession of Christianity, as Libanius himself admits. Indeed, he even wished to be enrolled in the Register of Readers <note>A 'Reader' or 'Lector' was a minor clerical office in the early church responsible for reading scriptures during services</note> in the Church of Nicomedia. Afterward, he traveled through almost all of Greece and was initiated into the sacred mysteries of the Pagans. In the year 355, honored with the title of Caesar <note>The title given to the junior emperor or designated heir</note>, he was sent to Gaul by Constantius. After five years there, having been proclaimed "Augustus" <note>The title for the senior or supreme Emperor</note> by his soldiers, he moved his camp against Constantius. When Constantius died on the journey, Julian held the empire alone. Having become Emperor, he held nothing more urgent than the total uprooting of the Christian religion and the recalling of the Pagan rites from the Underworld. To this end, among other things, he not only set the leaders of the Christian law at odds with one another and fostered all manner of heresies, but he also forbade the children of 
<margin>
See Sozomen, book
5, ch. 18. Theodoret,
book 3, ch. 8.
* Ammianus, book 22.
1626.
</margin>
Christians from frequenting the schools of the pagans to be educated in the study of Poetry, Rhetoric, or Philosophy. He said: **"For we are struck,"** as the proverb says, **"by our own feathers."** <note>original Greek: οἰκείοις γὰρ πτεροῖς... βαλλόμεθα (oikeiois gar pterois... ballometha). This refers to an Aesopic fable where an eagle is shot by an arrow feathered with its own plumage; Julian meant Christians used Greek learning to destroy Greek religion.</note> Indeed, Ammianus Marcellinus *, a pagan who served as a soldier under this very Julian, confesses that this was an unmerciful act that should be buried in eternal silence. Not content with this, Julian mocked Christians in letters sent everywhere; he treated them with taunts and insults, stripped them of honors and dignities, restrained them by laws, crushed them with punishments, and tore them apart in his writings. Even while he was still occupied with the Persian expedition, he most sharply attacked the Christian faith in three books he wrote **against the holy Gospels and against the pious religion of the Christians**, as says Cyril of Alexandria. Cyril strongly refuted these very books and wove the greater part of Julian's writings into his own work (omitting only the direct invectives against Christ and his religion), found in Volume IV of his works. The remaining works of Julian were published with the notes of Denis Pétau in Greek and Latin at Paris, 1630, in quarto. There exists in Latin a letter from Julian to the heretic Photinus (though not complete) against Diodore of Tarsus, whom he calls the "Magician of the Nazarenes." In this letter, the impious man—**the one struck by God** <note>original Greek: ὁ θεοβλάβης (ho theoblabēs) — a term used by Christian writers to describe Julian as one whose mind was ruined by divine judgment</note>—calls Christ the Lord "that new Galilean God of a trumped-up divinity" and calls His worship a "rustic religion," according to Facundus of Hermiane, book 4, ch. 2.

## HIMERIUS,
originating from Bithynia, the son of Aminias the Rhetorician, was a famous Sophist in the year 361 AD. He died at a great age, having lost his sight and being seized by the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>. He published various declamations in which (according to Photius) he barked at the Christians like a dog that bites in secret.

**AMMIANUS MARCELLINUS**, Greek by birth and apparently a native of Antioch, was a soldier by profession. He flourished around the year 380, though he had been well known long before then. He wrote a *Roman History*, of which eighteen books survive today. In these writings, he criticizes the Christians on more than one occasion, although he speaks quite fairly of the religion itself which they professed. The most excellent edition of Ammianus is the *Parisian* one, which was published in Paris in 1681 by Hadrian Valois after the death of his brother; it was enriched with the extensive notes of Lindenbrog and Henri Valois. Claude Chifflet provided a dissertation on the life and writings of Ammianus as a preface, in which he gives us hope that Marcellinus's lost books <note>Ammianus originally wrote 31 books, but the first 13, covering the era from Nerva to Constantine, are lost.</note> might be hidden away somewhere today.

**EUNAPIUS**, born at Sardis, was a student of Chrysanthius and later of Proaeresius. He was a Sophist <note>A teacher of rhetoric and philosophy.</note>, a physician, and a historian of some renown, flourishing around the year 380. How hostile he was to the Christian name is sufficiently proven by his book *On the Lives of Philosophers and Sophists*, especially in what he writes on this subject in the *Lives of Aedesius and Maximus*, and perhaps elsewhere. It is available in a Greek and Latin edition from *Geneva*, 1616, in octavo, and has been printed elsewhere more than once.

**Q. AURELIUS SYMMACHUS**, a native of Rome and a Senator and Prefect of that same city, was especially prominent in the year 384. He held the Consulship in the year 391. He reveals his hostile mind toward the Christian religion everywhere, but most notably in his *Relation for the Altar of Victory* <note>original: "Relatione pro Arâ victoriæ"</note>. He presented this petition to the Emperor Valentinian, in which he strenuously and explicitly argues the cause of the Pagans. He met an adversary in Saint Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, who elegantly and vigorously refuted Symmachus’s work. Symmachus not only lost his case, but shortly thereafter, having been accused of high treason <note>original: "reus Majestatis," likely referring to his support of the usurper Eugenius</note>, he was placed in a common carriage and sent into exile at the hundredth milestone from the city. However, he was soon restored to favor by Theodosius. This *Relation* of Symmachus exists both among the works of Ambrose and among Symmachus’s own *Letters*. These were published with the notes of Fr. Juret and Jean de Lec in *Geneva*, 1598, and again in *Paris*, 1604, with ten books of miscellaneous writings and the notes of Pareus in *Neustadt*, 1628.

# THE NESTORIAN CENTURY.

## Overview of the Century.

<margin>
5th CENTURY
from the year 400.
</margin>
While Arcadius—a sluggish man devoted to leisure and luxury—ruled in the East, ecclesiastical affairs were miserably disturbed, as the high officials of the Court held all the power. He was succeeded on May 1st, 408, by Theodosius the Younger, who possessed <term>every virtue of knowledge through God <note>original: "πᾶσαν ἐπιστήμης ἀρετὴν διὰ Θεοῦ"</note></term>, as Sozomen says in the Preface to his *Ecclesiastical History*. Certainly, few among the ranks of Princes have surpassed him in piety and humanity. He was a great patron of scholars and was himself well-versed in literature; he even poured over books by night, using a lampstand for his reading that was so mechanically crafted that it poured oil into the lamp automatically, without any servant’s assistance. Under his auspices and protection, not only did the Church flourish wonderfully, but so did the entire world of letters, which he strove to promote vigorously. He did this both through his own laws and by renewing those of previous Emperors, which can be seen in the *Theodosian Code*, Book 14, Title 9: *On the liberal studies of the cities of Rome and Constantinople.* This title deals with those who moved to Rome for the sake of their studies, their privileges, the <term>copyists <note>original: "Antiquariis"</note></term>, the Keepers of the Library of Constantinople, the public professors of Constantinople, and other related matters. To add to this, in the year 438, by the command and care of Theodosius, the *Theodosian Code* was compiled and promulgated, into which were gathered the Constitutions of all the Christian Emperors from Constantine the Great down to these times. Jacques Godefroy <note>A famous 17th-century jurist known for his work on the Theodosian Code.</note> edited this code after all others and illustrated it with very rich commentaries; it is difficult to say whether they show greater diligence or erudition. But this is mentioned in passing.

Even while the Empire of Theodosius flourished and favored the Church, its peace was nonetheless disturbed:

**I. THE DONATISTS**, who for an entire century—since the time of Diocletian—had torn the Catholic Church apart with a grave schism. Against these men, who were spreading everywhere with deceits and murders, a delegation was decreed in the year 404 by the Synod of Carthage to the Emperor Honorius; this was repeated a second time in 407. In the year 411, the Catholic Bishops even held a conference with them at Carthage, the records of which still exist today and are found both separately and in the volumes of the Councils.

**II. PELAGIUS** and his followers, who stirred up controversies regarding original sin, free will, and so on. They were frequently defeated and put to flight by various Synods—the Diospolitan, African, and Gallic—to say nothing of the Church Fathers like Augustine, Jerome, Prosper, and others.

**III. NESTORIUS**, who, by teaching that there were two Persons in Christ and consequently that Mary was not the <term>God-bearer <note>original: "Θεοτόκον"</note></term>, was condemned by the Third Ecumenical Council held at Ephesus in 431. This led to many disputes between Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret.

**IV. EUTYCHES**, who acknowledged only one nature in Christ after the Incarnation. He was subsequently condemned by the Council of Chalcedon in 451, even though the <term>Robber <note>original: "λῃστρικὴ"</note></term> Synod of Ephesus in 448 had acquitted him with an armed hand and forced signatures.

Great struggles and dissensions followed immediately. To apply a healing hand to these, the Emperor Zeno composed the <term>Act of Union <note>original: "Ἐνωτικὸν"</note></term>, which was signed by Acacius of Constantinople and—though only pretendingly—by Peter Mongus and Peter the Fuller (the author of the addition to the Trisagion hymn: <term>“who was crucified for us” <note>original: "ὁ σταυρωθεὶς δι’ ἡμᾶς"</note></term>). Meanwhile, the Bishops of the Roman See, Simplicius, Felix, and others, protested; on this matter, see the *Acts concerning the name of Acacius* and other records in the *Councils*, Volume 4, from page 1079. The See of Constantinople was greatly honored by the Council of Chalcedon, whose 28th Canon decreed to it <term>equal privileges <note>original: "τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα"</note></term> with the Bishop of old Rome. In the earlier part of this century, it seems, the <term>Sleepless Ones <note>original: "Acœmetæ"</note></term> monks were established. They were so called because they were divided into three classes and succeeded one another in turn, celebrating the divine offices day and night without any interval. Many monasteries were built in Constantinople for their use, especially the most famous one which took its name from Studius <note>The Monastery of Stoudios became the most important monastery in Constantinople.</note>, who had been Consul in the year 454.

# WRITERS.

<margin>401.</margin>

**A**STERIUS, Bishop of Amasea (which is a city of Pontus), was a disciple of a certain Scythian whom a citizen of Antioch had purchased and educated in the liberal arts. He flourished around the year 401, not far removed from the times of the Emperor Julian, by his own testimony <margin>* Homily against Avarice.</margin> *. The ancients do not have much more to say about him. The <term>lover of festivals <note>original: "ὁ φιλέορτος" (ho phileortos)</note></term> Asterius wrote much, as <margin>† Codex 271.</margin> † Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who recorded summaries of books he read.</note> reports, from which the following survive today:

> *Five Homilies: namely, On the Rich Man and Lazarus; On the Unjust Steward; Against Avarice; On the Feast of the Calends; and on the text: "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?" Published in Greek and Latin by Rubens at Antwerp, 1615, in quarto; and in the Supplement of 1624, Volume 2, page 563; and in the Supplement of 1648, Volume 1, page 1, in which the following added Homilies are held:*
> *On the Prophet Daniel and on Susanna.*
> *On the Man Blind from Birth.*
> *On the Princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul.*
> *On the Holy Martyr Phocas.*
> *A Eulogy for the Holy Martyrs.*
> *An Account of the Martyrdom of Saint Euphemia, excerpted from the 6th Act of the Second Council of Nicaea.*
> *A Eulogy for the Holy Protomartyr Stephen, which Vincent Riccardus had published under the name of Proclus, although both the style and the authority of Photius attribute it to Asterius. These are the Homilies collected thus far by Combesis: however, it is rightly doubted whether all belong to the same Asterius. Combesis added excerpts of eight other Homilies taken from Photius’s Codex 271: namely, Sermons on Repentance; on those words, "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho"; on the text, "Two men went up into the Temple"; on Zacchaeus; on the Prodigal Son; on the Centurion’s servant healed by the Lord; on Fasting; on Jairus and the woman suffering from a flow of blood.*

Seven Homilies on Psalms 5, 6, and 7, in Greek and Latin with notes, are found in Cotelier’s *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume 2, page 1.

Finally, many fragments of Asterius exist in the <term>Catena <note>original: "Catena," meaning "chain." A form of biblical commentary where various interpretations by Church Fathers are linked together following the biblical text.</note></term> on the Psalms, and others in the Catena on Luke; most of which are found nowhere else.

**M**ARCUS, called the <term>Ascetic <note>original: "Ἀσκητὴς" (Asketes)</note></term> or the <term>Practitioner par excellence <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχὴν" (kat' exochen)</note></term>, perhaps Egyptian by birth, led a solitary life among the monks of Nitria and flourished around the year 401. He was a man of remarkable mildness and supreme temperance, who, while still a youth, held the entire Old and New Testaments in his memory. As he grew older, he became so famous for sanctity that a rumor spread among the Nitrian monks that the sacred mysteries [the Eucharist] were always delivered into his hands not by a priest, but by an Angel. He lived to a decrepit old age and died after passing his hundredth year. He left behind many writings, concerning which some raise a dispute against our Marcus, doubting whether they should instead be ascribed to a certain Marcus the Younger, who flourished under the Emperor Leo around the year 900. However, that conjecture has not even the slightest <margin>|| Codex 200.</margin> shadow of truth, since Photius || not only mentions those writings but also refers to their chapters in summary. Regarding the style of Marcus, he says:

> He is clear, so far as the common usage of words and the concise expression of his style are concerned, even if the whole is not refined according to the <term>Attic tongue <note>The prestigious, classical dialect of ancient Athens; Photius notes Marcus wrote in simpler, common Greek.</note></term>; but if any obscurity is perceived, it is because these matters are naturally better understood through practice [and] it withdraws from the... <note>The sentence in the original Greek breaks off mid-word.</note>

<note>original: "λαμπρῶν ἑρμηνείας, ἀλλ' οὐ δυσκόλως ἐκφᾶσθαι"</note> "...of brilliant interpretations, yet not difficult to express." His diction is clear, insofar as he uses common words, and his discourse runs through the primary points—even if he does not compose his language with perfect accuracy according to the standards of Attic Greek. Whenever some obscurity is perceived in these writings, it is surely because he moves away from a clear explanation through words for this reason: these matters are of such a kind that they ought to be perceived primarily through action itself, rather than because they are difficult to express in speech. Photius <note>A 9th-century scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople whose "Bibliotheca" summarizes hundreds of now-lost works.</note> notes this not only regarding the writings of Marcus alone, but teaches that this kind of defect of obscurity is found in nearly all those who have treated ascetic subjects, <note>original: "τῆς ἐκ τῶν ἔργων αὐτῶν ἐπιγνώσεως, ἥ τις μάλα περιγέγονε ταῖς διὰ τῶν ῥημάτων ἐπιδηλώσεσι"</note> "because the knowledge gained from the works themselves far surpasses the descriptions made through words."

### EXTANT WRITINGS.

*On Paradise and the Spiritual Law*: A preface with these exact words is found in Macarius's 37th Homily.
*On those who think they are justified by works.*
*On Repentance.*
*On Baptism.*
*Saving Precepts to Nicholas.*
*Chapters on Temperance, or on Fasting.*
*Disputation with a Lawyer.*
*Consultation of the intellect with its own soul.* Photius mentions these eight short works, though he describes them in a different order; to these he also adds (though it is missing from our collection) *Against the Melchizedekians* <note>A sect that held unusual views about the biblical figure Melchizedek, sometimes viewing him as a divine power.</note>, in which he inveighed against his own father, who had been contaminated by the stain of this heresy.

Nicephorus reports that eight books, equaling the number of universal affections, and thirty-two others on ascetic matters from our Marcus reached his own time. It is quite likely that these eight short works we possess were included in those; thus, thirty-two are still missing.

Furthermore, among the eight extant treatises, there is an "Epistle of a certain Nicholas" that is not to be overlooked, in which he thanks Marcus for the "Saving Precepts" dedicated to him.

The short works listed above exist as translated into Latin by Joannes Picus of Paris, published in Paris, 1563; from there they were taken into the *Library of the Fathers*. They appear in Greek and Latin in the Paris *Supplement*, 1624, Volume 1, page 871.

<margin>401.</margin>
**A**NIANUS, an Egyptian Monk—different from the one who translated several of Chrysostom's writings into Latin, as we shall show below—flourished around the year 401. He wrote a *Chronology* in which he followed Eusebius, yet not infrequently proved him to be in error, as is evident from George Syncellus. <note>An 8th-9th century Byzantine chronicler.</note> Not Extant.

<margin>401.</margin>
**P**ANODORUS, likewise an Egyptian Monk and <term>contemporary <note>original: "ὁμόχρονος" (homochronos)</note></term> of Anianus, according to Syncellus, flourished under the Emperor Arcadius. He wrote a *Chronography*, <note>original: "ἐκ ἀπείρως... χρονικῆς ἀκριβείας"</note> "not without... chronological accuracy," as Syncellus says; he similarly followed Eusebius himself and corrected him in a not dissimilar manner. His *Chronography* has perished; however, Syncellus preserved many fragments for us, and from him, Scaliger presents them in his *Observations on Eusebius*.

<margin>401.</margin>
**V**ICTOR of Antioch, a contemporary of Chrysostom, seems to have flourished at the beginning of this century and thereafter. He wrote a *Commentary on the Gospel of St. Mark*, which exists in Latin from the translation of Theodore Peltanus in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 4, page 370.

<margin>401.</margin>
**M**ACARIUS, a Roman by birth (as is likely) and a Monk by profession, was quite intimate with Rufinus of Aquileia. (Miræus rightly conjectures that he is the same person to whom Rufinus dedicated his *Apology for Origen*, and whom Jerome notes in his second book *Against Rufinus*.) He flourished around the year 401. He wrote a book in the city of Rome *Against the Mathematicians* <note>In the late Roman Empire, "mathematicians" often referred specifically to astrologers and those who predicted the future by the stars.</note>, in which labor he sought the consolations of the Eastern Scriptures, as Gennadius holds in *On Famous Men*, chapter 28. Not Extant.

**SEVERUS SULPITIUS** <note>Better known today as Sulpicius Severus (c. 363–c. 425), he is most famous for writing the earliest biography of Saint Martin of Tours.</note>, a Gaul by nationality, an Aquitanian by birth, and of noble descent, was a disciple of Phaebadius, Bishop of Agen; he flourished in the year 401. That he devoted himself to secular eloquence in his youth, achieved a significant reputation in the forum, and married a woman from a family of consular rank is clearly indicated by Paulinus in his first letter to him. As for his way of life, while some believe he was a monk, he was certainly a Priest of Primuliacum <note>A site in southern France, likely modern-day Prémillac.</note>. Those who wish to claim he was a Bishop are rashly confusing him with Sulpicius Severus, the twenty-seventh Bishop of Bourges (who died at the end of the 6th century). He was very close friends with Martin, Paulinus, and Jerome. In his declining old age, having been deceived by the Pelagians <note>A theological movement that emphasized human effort over divine grace; it was eventually condemned as heretical.</note>, he later repented of his error and atoned for the rashness of his tongue with perpetual silence. Severus’s style is clear and easy, and far more refined and polished than the general spirit of his age; for this reason, he is called the "purest writer of the Churchmen" by Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), one of the greatest scholars of the Renaissance.</note>. In his *Dialogues*, he reveals the error of the Millenarians <note>Also called Chiliasts, these Christians believed Christ would establish a literal 1,000-year kingdom on Earth before the final judgment.</note>; a fact which Jerome once observed ||, numbering him among the primary defenders of the Millennium.

*Third Letter to Bassula, his mother-in-law*, concerning the death of the Blessed Martin.

*Three Dialogues*, with a Gaul and Posthumianus as speakers, and himself as mediator and judge: the first of these deals with the virtues of the Eastern Monks, and the second and third deal with the virtues of the Blessed Martin. On account of the Millenarian error found therein, Pope Gelasius (or whoever was the author of that Decree) formerly condemned these under the title *The Short Works of Posthumianus and the Gaul.*

*Two Letters to his sister Claudia*, which the distinguished John Battely, a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, transcribed from a manuscript in that college and sent to the famous Baluzius; they were published by him in the *First Volume of the Miscellany, page 329.*
