**ANTIOCHUS**, a Syrian by nationality and Bishop of Ptolemais in Phoenicia, flourished around the year 401. Renowned for his fame in eloquence, he traveled to Constantinople; there, by holding frequent assemblies for the people, composed with clear diction and pronounced with a sonorous voice, he earned such great applause that he was called "Chrysostom" <note>Meaning "Golden-Mouthed," a title usually reserved for John Chrysostom, indicating Antiochus was a rival in preaching talent.</note> by some. He also acquired so much money that he returned to his own city loaded with gold shortly before the troubles of Chrysostom arose. Later, however, he involved himself in the lawsuit brought against Chrysostom by Severianus, Acacius, and others, and is numbered among the most bitter enemies of Chrysostom by Palladius ||. He died before the year 408, while the Emperor Arcadius was still reigning. He wrote, besides *many Sermons, one long volume against avarice, and a Homily on the healing of the blind man enlightened by the Savior.* His writings are not extant: Theodoret (Dialogue 2) provides a certain short maxim from him; while the author of the *Catena on John* <note>A "Catena" (Latin for "chain") is a form of biblical commentary made up of fragments of older commentaries strung together.</note> (p. 443) provides a somewhat longer *Fragment* of the same concerning Christ pierced by the spear, and another is found in the *Acts of the Council of Ephesus*, part 1, chapter 4.

<margin>
401. Socrates, book 6, ch. 11. Sozomen, book 8, ch. 10, 18. Palladius, Dialogue, throughout.
</margin>

**SEVERIANUS**, a Syrian by nationality and Bishop of Gabala in Syria, flourished around the year 401. He was a man highly learned in the Scriptures and very famous for his eloquence. He was therefore a rival to the fame and riches acquired by Antiochus in Constantinople. After he had practiced speaking for a long time and composed many orations with great labor, he came to Constantinople, where, having found Chrysostom to be well-disposed toward him and having preached often in the Church, he excited great admiration for himself; he attained so much honor and authority that he became an intimate of the Emperor and the Augusta <note>Empress Eudoxia, who was often at odds with John Chrysostom.</note>. Indeed, he was dear to Chrysostom above others, who, when setting out for Ephesus, delegated the care of his Church to him. Severianus poorly maintained the trust committed to him, and he endeavored to make the devotion of the listeners—now taken away from John—entirely his own. Moved by rivalry, John hastily returned to Constantinople, and incited by the false accusations of the Deacon Serapion (who accused Severianus of heresy), he cast him out of the city. However, Severianus was soon recalled by the Augusta Eudoxia, and was reconciled to John—at least in appearance—with the Empress leaving no stone unturned to achieve that end. But the wound soon broke open again: for having entered into a conspiracy with Theophilus, Antiochus, and others, he labored with all his might for the deposition of John, which he indeed achieved. However, when the common people rioted and rose up against John’s enemies, he found it necessary to look to his own safety by flight. Therefore, at the end of the year 402, hurrying to Antioch, he ordained Porphyrius as Bishop of that place after receiving money; he was soon driven from the city by the people of Antioch, who were indignant at that crime. What became of him after that is not very clear.

->WORKS WHICH SURVIVE.<-

*Six Orations on the Creation of the World* <note>original: "De Creatione Mundi"</note> are extant in the Savile edition of Chrysostom, Volume 7, near the end, and in the *Supplement* of Combefis, Paris, 1672. From these are taken those many fragments which are presented in the *Catena of the Greek Fathers on Genesis*, translated into Latin and edited by Francisco Zephyro, *Cologne, 1572.*

<margin>401.</margin>
**PALLADIUS**, a Galatian by nationality, was born in the year 368. At twenty years old, he began to travel to foreign regions; and having arrived in Alexandria, he committed himself to the care of the Presbyter Isidore, to be instructed in the discipline of the monastic life. Isidore delegated this duty to Dorotheus, a very famous Theban ascetic, under whose rule Palladius spent three years. In the year 391, he withdrew to Mount Nitria <note>A major center of early Christian monasticism in the Egyptian desert.</note>; and there, among the Archimandrites <note>Superiors of monasteries; abbots.</note> Arradius, Putabastus, etc., he devoted a whole year to ascetic exercises and to visiting the more illustrious monks. He obtained Evagrius Ponticus as a teacher, from whom he drank in a love of Origenism <note>The controversial theological ideas of Origen of Alexandria, which were often debated and condemned in the 4th and 5th centuries.</note>—on which account he was sharply rebuked by Epiphanius and Jerome in more than one place. Finally, troubled by certain lustful temptations, he secretly withdrew from his teacher Evagrius into the desert of Scetis; and he lay hidden for some time with Saint Pachon. Soon he set out for the deserts of the Thebaid <note>The region around Thebes in Upper Egypt, famous for its hermits.</note> to visit Abbot John, who predicted that he would one day have a Bishopric and many afflictions. Making frequent journeys of this kind, Evagrius <note>Though the text says "Evagrius," the context refers to Palladius’s travels.</note> traversed the whole region of Egypt until, suffering from diseases of the spleen and stomach, he was sent to Alexandria by his companions. From Alexandria, for the sake of restoring his health, he set out for Palestine, where he spent many years—for example, with Abbot Innocent, a Presbyter of [the Mount of] Olives, a whole

...for a full three years. In the year 400 or 401, coming from Palestine to Bithynia, he was ordained Bishop of a certain city. These things the author of the *Lausiac History* <note>A famous collection of biographies of the desert fathers.</note> says of himself. The events that follow are not so certain as to whether they should be attributed to the same Palladius. Around the year 400, Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, was sent by Chrysostom to Ephesus along with two other bishops to investigate the case of Bishop Antoninus. In the year 404, after Chrysostom (whose party he constantly supported) was driven into exile, Palladius fled the fury of the magistrates and hastened to Rome. There, he personally exposed the unjust hatred of Emperor Arcadius and the enemies of John [Chrysostom] to Pope Innocent and the Western Bishops. Soon, having been sent back with the Latin bishops who were carrying letters from Emperor Honorius to Arcadius, he was banished into a distant exile by Arcadius. He was to be held in the town of Syene, located in the vicinity of the Blemmyes <note>A nomadic people of the Nubian region</note>; he was led there by a military escort and harassed by the most severe injuries on the journey, his servant having been taken away and his writing tablets seized. Finally, having left the see of Helenopolis, Socrates <margin>* Book 7, ch. 26.</margin> records that he was made Bishop of Aspuna. Finally, the author of the *Lausiac History* composed that work around the year 421, at the age of 53. However, the writer of the *Life of Chrysostom* committed his *Dialogue* to writing immediately after Chrysostom's death. Now, let us proceed to the writings that circulate under the name of Palladius.

## WRITINGS WHICH ARE EXTANT.

*The Lausiac History*, or *On the Lives of the Holy Fathers*, addressed to Lausus, the Prefect of the Chamber <note>A high-ranking court official, or Chamberlain</note>; hence it is called the *Lausiaca*. See more on this under Heraclides. After various Latin editions based on the ancient version by Rufinus, Johannes Meursius first published it in Greek with notes at Leiden, 1616, in quarto. A Greek-Latin edition with notes by Fronto Ducæus appeared in the *Supplement* of 1624, Volume 2, page 893. A supplement, by means of which the gaps in the Greek text can be filled, is offered by the illustrious Cotelerius in *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume 2, page 341; he also provided eleven quite extensive fragments missing from the published copies—which either expand the History or supplement the Greek text—in Greek and Latin with notes in the *Monuments*, Volume 3, pages 117 and 158. The illustrious Vossius holds a manuscript codex of this History in his very well-equipped library that is twice as long as the published versions, which one may hope will be brought to light someday.

*Dialogue on the Life of St. John Chrysostom, between Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, and Theodore, a Deacon of the Roman Church.* There is much dispute among the learned concerning the author of this *Dialogue*. The common opinion of writers is that Palladius, the author of the *Lausiac History*, was the author; yet some call this into doubt, and others flatly deny it. The primary argument of those who deny it is that in the *Dialogue*, Palladius admits he saw Rome then for the first time, whereas it is expressly stated that Palladius of Helenopolis had stayed there some years before. To this, however, it can be answered that the author of the *Dialogue*, intentionally disguising his name and persona (which is evident from elsewhere), inserted that earlier passage into his work for the purpose of better remaining hidden. Either this must be said, or it is necessary to conclude with the illustrious Bigot that there was another Palladius, who succeeded to the see of Helenopolis after the former one was transferred to Aspuna; and that it was this second Palladius who held the *Dialogue* with Theodore in Rome. Meanwhile, it is not unworthy of note that the writer of the *Lausiac History* was very familiar with Olympias, the Deaconess of Chrysostom, and a sharer in Chrysostom's calamities; and that he finally set out for Rome on her account <margin>† Lausiac History, ch. 144, 43, 121.</margin>, as he himself testifies †. Furthermore, not only do George of Alexandria and, following him, Photius call Palladius the author of the *Dialogue*, and not only do the title of the Greek codex of the *Dialogue* and the Savilian index testify that this man was the Bishop of Helenopolis (as the same Bigot rightly notes), but also Theodore, Bishop of Trimithus in Cyprus, explicitly makes the writer of the *Lausiac History* and the *Dialogue* one and the same Palladius. Truly, I willingly submit all things to the judgment of the more learned. Ambrosius Camaldulensis was the first to translate this *Dialogue* into Latin; his version, dedicated to Eugene IV, appeared separately at Venice, 1533, in octavo; it was afterwards reprinted many times with the works of Chrysostom at Paris and elsewhere. Emericus Bigot, after a long search by Fronto Ducæus and Savile, finally found the Greek text at Florence, and from an ancient codex of the Medicean Library (the same...

### HERACLIDES

<margin>
401.
Socrat. Book 6, ch. 10.
Sozom. Book 8, ch. 6.
Pallad. in the Dialogue.
|| Book 13, ch. 9.
</margin>
HERACLIDES, a Cypriot by birth, followed the monastic way of life in the Skete Desert <note>A famous center of early Christian monasticism in Egypt</note>, having had Evagrius Ponticus as his teacher. At length, having been brought to Constantinople in the year 398, or at least at the beginning of the following year, he was ordained a Deacon by John Chrysostom. Nicephorus || <note>Nicephorus Callistus, a later historian</note> calls him Archdeacon. At the beginning of the year 402, he was placed over the see of Ephesus by Chrysostom and ordained in a Synod of seventy bishops. In the following year, in the "Synod of the Oak" <note>An extra-legal synod held near Chalcedon to depose Chrysostom</note> held by Theophilus, he was accused of Origenism <note>The controversial teachings of the early theologian Origen</note> along with Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, with specific charges brought against both. Theophilus and his followers wanted Heraclides to be judged in his absence, additionally accusing him of injury and cruelty. But when John [Chrysostom] soon returned from exile and Theophilus was put to flight by the citizens, that storm vanished. Finally, however, when John was sent into exile a second time, Heraclides himself underwent a similar fate; for in the year 404, having been deposed from his see, he was thrown into prison in Nicomedia. He had spent four years there when Palladius wrote his *Dialogue*. What happened to him after that is not clear. He was a man, according to Palladius, very well instructed in secular disciplines and remarkably skilled in the Divine Scriptures.

<margin>
* On Greek History, Book 2, ch. 19.
</margin>
He wrote a book called the *Paradise*, or *On the Lives of the Holy Fathers*. This title is prefixed to the *Lausiac History* in some manuscripts; and specifically, the first edition of this History, prepared by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Fabro Stapulensi," a French Renaissance humanist</note> in Paris, 1504, does not carry the name of Palladius, but has the title *The Paradise of Heraclides*. Add to this that a double preface is prefixed to the *Lausiac History*, of which almost no one doubts that the first belongs to Heraclides. Therefore, the illustrious Vossius * <note>Gerardus Vossius, a Dutch scholar</note> suspects (whose opinion we also embrace) that the *Lausiac History* was forged from two books: one by Palladius, the other by Heraclides. Thus it happened that in manuscript codes, it bears now the name of this one, now that one.

<margin>
† Notes in Vol. 3 of the Monuments, p. 566.
</margin>
Johannes Meursius, in the Preface to the *Lausiac History* published by him, points out that another book by Heraclides existed in his possession, inscribed thus: *A Narrative concerning the Holy Fathers who shone forth in Egypt* <note>original: "Διήγησις περὶ τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ διαλαμψάντων ἁγίων πατέρων"</note>, which he had copied from the Palatine Library. Perhaps that work was either a small fragment <note>original: "ἀποσπασμάτιον"</note> or some compendium of the *Lausiac History*; at least, it was a separate book by Heraclides, not yet mixed with Palladius's work. Indeed, as I discovered later, it is the *Paradise* of Heraclides itself, which, according to Cotelier † <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, a 17th-century scholar of early Church texts</note>, is held in Greek manuscript under other names twice in the Library of the King of France, and as many times in the Colbertine Library: in the first code it is called *The History of the Monks in Egypt* <note>original: "ἡ κατ᾿ Αἴγυπτον τῶν Μοναχῶν Ἱστορία"</note>; in the second, *The History in Egypt, which others also name the Paradise of the author* <note>original: "ἡ κατ᾿ Αἴγυπτον Ἱστορία, ἣν καὶ παραδείσου ἄλλοι ὁ συγγραφεὺς ὀνομάζει"</note>; in the third, *Paradise* <note>original: "Παράδεισος"</note>; in the fourth, *A History of the Lives of the Holy Egyptian Fathers, written by Jerome, a monk and priest from Dalmatia* <note>original: "Ἱστορία εἰς τοὺς βίους τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων τῶν Αἰγυπτίων, συγγραφεῖσα παρὰ Ἱερωνύμῳ μοναχῷ καὶ πρεσβυτέρῳ τῷ ἀπὸ Δαλματίας"</note>. An inspection of these manuscripts not only confirms but demonstrates our conjecture and that of Vossius. For by far the largest part of the book is read mixed into the *Lausiac History*. The illustrious Cotelier published the remainder along with the Preface of the whole work in Greek and Latin with notes in the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume 3, page 171.

# The Nestorian Century.

<margin>
5th CENTURY
from the Year 400.
401.
</margin>
CHROMATIUS, a Roman by birth according to some, and Bishop of Aquileia, flourished in the year 401. Around that time, having been warned by Pope Anastasius regarding Rufinus (who was then living in Aquileia) whom the Pope had condemned, Chromatius called a council of his bishops and likewise condemned the books of Origen. However, he did not condemn Rufinus himself; indeed, he did not hesitate to receive him into the communion of the Church. Furthermore, being somewhat annoyed by the excessive anger of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the famous scholar and translator of the Vulgate, who was known for his sharp polemics</note>, he warned him by letter to stop attacking Rufinus with biting writings and to finally put an end to the controversy that had so greatly troubled them both by keeping silent. He was a strenuous defender of the cause of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" Archbishop of Constantinople, who was then in exile</note> in the West, for which he received high praise and many thanks from him, as can be seen in Chrysostom's *Letter 155*. He seems to have died around the year 410. His surviving writings include *Several Homilies and Treatises on the Eight Beatitudes, and on the remainder of Chapter 5 and part of Chapter 6 of Saint Matthew*, published in *Basel, 1528*, along with the *Apologetic of Symmachus*, *Louvain, 1646*, in the *Micropresbyticon* (Basel, 1551), in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 5, page 976, and in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 1191. Among several other letters he wrote, there was one to the Emperor Honorius regarding Chrysostom's case. Honorius himself testifies (in Palladius, chapter 3, page 30) that he sent this letter along with his own to the Emperor Arcadius. We spoke above of the warning letter to Jerome. Both have perished. There exists among the works of Jerome a *Letter to Jerome under the name of Chromatius and Heliodorus regarding the Nativity of the Blessed Mary*, and another to him under the same names. However, everyone acknowledges both to be forged <note>original: "supposititiam"—meaning a work falsely attributed to an author to gain authority</note>.

<margin>
402.
* Book 5.
† Book 9, ch. 7.
|| Book 7, ch. 9.
</margin>
INNOCENT <note>Pope Innocent I</note>, an Italian by nationality from the city of Albano, was made Bishop of Rome at the beginning of the year 402. Upon taking up the bishopric, he began to stir up great disputes with the Eastern bishops regarding the case of Saint John Chrysostom, whose side he had vigorously defended. While Chrysostom was alive, Innocent supported him as much as possible with his authority and consoling letters; after his death, he honored him with great respect and reverence. Furthermore (if later writers of Chrysostom's life are to be believed), upon hearing of Chrysostom's death, he struck the Emperor Arcadius and the Empress Eudoxia with anathema <note>A formal ecclesiastical curse or excommunication</note>, along with Atticus of Constantinople and other enemies of Chrysostom. But the illustrious Savile <note>Sir Henry Savile, a 16th-century English scholar known for his edition of Chrysostom</note> completely demolished this story in a treatise published by us at the end of the previous century's section. Regardless, Innocent certainly did not desert the cause of the deceased Chrysostom; instead, he stubbornly refused to enter into communion with the Eastern bishops until Chrysostom's name was restored to the <term>Diptychs</term> <note>The official lists of those recognized as being in full communion with the Church, read aloud during the liturgy</note> with full rights of recovery. In the year 409, he was sent by the Emperor Honorius as an envoy to Alaric, King of the Goths, who had moved his army toward Rome, in order to turn the barbarians away from laying siege. The embassy lacked success, yet the situation turned out well for Innocent; having been withdrawn from the City in this way, he stayed at Ravenna and witnessed the wretched ruin of his see from a distance <note>Referring to the Sack of Rome by Alaric in 410 AD</note>. He spent the rest of his life opposing the Novatians and Pelagians <note>Two groups deemed heretical: the Novatians for their rigorism regarding sinners, and the Pelagians for their views on free will and grace</note>. He accomplished this effectively, driving the former out of the City and condemning the latter through frequent letters, councils, and decrees. The claim that Innocent permitted the pagans to secretly perform their ancient rites and sacrifices while Alaric was threatening Rome is a slander invented by Zosimus *. Against Zosimus, a pagan writer, may be set Socrates † and Sozomen || <note>5th-century church historians</note>, who, in narrating the siege of Rome and the plots of the pagans, are completely silent on the matter. They would by no means have done so if Innocent had committed such a crime, as their own dislike for Innocent (due to his opposition to the Novatian sect) would have made them likely to report it. He died (not in the year 417 on July 28th, as is commonly believed) but at the end of the previous year, on December 21st, as Papebroch <note>Daniel Papebroch, a Jesuit scholar known for historical criticism</note> contends.

### WORKS.

There are 34 Letters, of which the first 23 are claimed to be spurious by the Magdeburg Centuriators, Tilemann, Osiander, Fulke, and others. They base their arguments on the barbarity of the style, the clumsy adaptations of Scripture, many errors in faith, chronological mistakes, and mentions of ecclesiastical rites that had not yet been established in the Church. Erasmus applied the same criticism to the three following letters.

Certainly, Papebroch <note>Daniel Papebroch (1628–1714), a Jesuit scholar and one of the founding Bollandists known for critical hagiography</note> himself frankly confesses that several of his letters are highly suspect of being forgeries based on chronological evidence. Letters 28 and 29—namely, those addressed to Saint John and to the Clergy of Constantinople—are preserved in Greek and Latin, taken from Nicephorus; a third letter, number 30, addressed to the Emperor Arcadius, is considered a forgery by George of Alexandria; for more on this, see the cited treatise by Savile <note>Sir Henry Savile (1549–1622), an English scholar who edited the works of John Chrysostom</note>.

<margin>402.</margin> **POLYBIUS**, a disciple of Epiphanius and his inseparable companion on his travels, and, as is reasonable to believe, his deacon. For he accompanied Epiphanius when the latter was summoned to Rome by Honorius to heal his sister who was suffering from a grave illness; and in the year 402, he remained at his side when he set out for Constantinople. He was present with Epiphanius as he died during the voyage and received his final commands. As he was about to die, Epiphanius ordered Polybius to put into port at Cyprus as soon as possible and, after boarding a ship, to seek out the upper Thebaid <note>A region in ancient Egypt, centered around Thebes</note>. Polybius obeyed, and after he had brought the body of Epiphanius into the church at Constantia and remained near the relics for nearly seven days, he hastened to the Thebaid before the final funeral honors were paid to Epiphanius. He spent a full year there; after that time was up, he was made Bishop of Rhinocorura <note>original: "Rhinocerorum"; a city on the border between Egypt and Palestine</note> by Heracleon, the Governor of Egypt, in the year 403, or at least early in the following year. Other details about him are not clear. He wrote *The Deeds of Epiphanius*, which encompasses the latter part of his life and his death, and a *Letter to Sabinus, the successor of Epiphanius, in which he asks that the description of Epiphanius’s funeral, which he himself had written, be sent to him.* That description survives in Latin at the end of Polybius's work.
The earlier part of the life of Epiphanius was written by John, who was also a disciple and companion of Epiphanius. The work of both survives, though filled with many fables; it can be found in Latin in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk and hagiographer</note> on May 12, and in Greek and Latin among the *Works of Epiphanius* in Petau’s edition, Volume 2.

<margin>402.</margin> **MARCUS**, who was at first a scribe <term>librarius: a professional copyist or secretary</term> and, as he testifies of himself, highly skilled in the art of beautiful writing; later, he was taken into the service of Porphyrius, eventually Bishop of Gaza, while Porphyrius was staying in Jerusalem for religious reasons. He lived in the year 402. He was first sent to Thessalonica by Porphyrius to divide his property, which was soon to be distributed for the use of the poor. Later, after Porphyrius had been made Bishop and the pagans <note>original: "Gentilibus"</note> were harassing the Church in Gaza, Marcus was sent as an envoy to the Emperor Arcadius in the year 398; he was also to deliver letters written to Chrysostom, in which Porphyrius requested that Chrysostom himself advance the matter. From the year 402, he accompanied Porphyrius to Constantinople when he traveled there for the same cause; he served him until the final day of his life, having been made a deacon by him. The *Life of Porphyrius* written by him survives, though augmented by the interpolations of Simeon Metaphrastes; it is found in Latin in Surius on February 26.

<margin>405.</margin> **AURELIUS PRUDENTIUS CLEMENS**, a Man of Illustrious Rank <note>original: "V. C." or "Vir Clarissimus," a title for those of senatorial status</note>. A Spaniard by nation, from the house of Tarragona according to some, or Zaragoza according to others, he was born in the year 348. As a young man, he devoted himself to the eloquence of the law courts and pleaded cases quite unfairly; he gave free rein to his vices. Having also become a court soldier, he followed the military camps. Finally, having changed his life for the better, he applied himself to sacred literature, especially to the composing of verses. He flourished in the year 405, in which he wrote the Preface to his *Daily Hymns* <note>original Greek: "Καθημερινῶν"</note>. He composed many poems in various types of meters, in a style elegant and charming enough, although there are things in them that the purity of the Roman tongue can hardly bear; these works survive today:
*Psychomachia*, or the Battle of Virtues and Vices.
*Cathemerinon*, or Hymns suitable for all daily activities.
*Apotheosis*, or On the Divinity.
*Hamartigenia*, or On the Origin of Sins. The conclusion, or Prayer to God, placed at the end of that little book, seems to be a forgery. For it contradicts Ode 7 of the *Daily Hymns* by saying, "I do not graze my household in the blessed region," etc. An impious statement, and unworthy of Prudentius.
*Against Symmachus and the ancient cult of the Pagan Gods* in two books. Isaac Grangeus of Vendôme published these books separately with learned commentaries in Paris, 1614, in octavo.

The *Diplochaion* <note>original: Διπλοχαῖον; likely meaning a "double-fold" or "two-fold" food portion, here referring to a poetic digest</note>, or the *Handbook of the Old and New Testament*, was published by Fabricius under the name of a certain Amœnus, a very obscure poet, at Basel in 1564. It is also attributed to the same author, along with a certain *Acrostic* addressed to Leontius, Bishop of Bordeaux, in the *Bignean Appendix* (Paris, 1624, p. 702). However, in addition to Gennadius *—who expressly attributes it to Prudentius—Giselinus asserts the same in many places in his notes on Prudentius.

The *Works of Prudentius* were first published through the care of Aldus Manutius (Venice, 1501); then among the *Christian Poets* (Lyons, 1603); at Antwerp in 1564, with the notes of Pulmann and Giselinus in the *Bignean Appendix* (p. 461); and in the *Library of the Fathers* (Volume 5, p. 990). A version adorned with the commentaries of all, edited by Johann Weitz (Hanover, 1613), far surpasses the earlier editions. Finally, an edition with the highly learned notes of Nicholas Heinsius was published at Amsterdam in 1667.

**PELAGIUS**, a man called by some a Gaulish-Briton, by others a Scot or Irishman, but in truth a Briton from "hither Britain," which we today call Cambria or Wales. In his native tongue, he was called *Morgan* or *Marigena* <note>Both names signify "sea-born," mirroring the Greek-derived name Pelagius</note>; hence the name Pelagius stuck to him. We readily concede that he was a monk; however, the claims that he was the Abbot of the College of Bangor (Bannonchorensis), that he had two thousand monks under his rule, that he was later driven into exile by his own people, or that he was an alumnus of the University of Cambridge—these appear to be the mere dreams of Ranulph of Chester, John of Tinmouth, Nicholas Cantilupe, Caius, Bale, and others. 

At the end of the fourth century, or at least the beginning of the fifth, he traveled to Rome, as it seems. There he became an intimate of Melania and Rufina <note>Followers of the controversial theologian Origen</note>, and drinking deeply of the dogmas of Origen which they offered, and making them even worse, he founded a new heresy. He began to disseminate this among the common people around, or rather a little before, the year 405. He employed such deceit, however, that he maintained a Catholic appearance; the heresy which he taught in fact, he denied in words. It is certainly clear that he was famous for spreading his heresy around this time, as Chrysostom †—while living as an exile at Arabissus in Armenia—vehemently deplored the "fall" of Pelagius in a letter sent to Olympias. 

In the year 408 or the following year, as the Goths were devastating Italy, he departed Rome with his disciple Cœlestius and withdrew to Sicily. Having stayed there for two or three years, he crossed over to Africa in 411 and landed at Hippo. In the following year, Augustine || testifies that he saw him present at the Conference held between the Catholics and the Donatists <note>A major schismatic movement in North Africa</note>. Hurrying on from there, he set out for Egypt to visit the monasteries located there. From Egypt, he sought Palestine, where in 415 he gained favor with John, Bishop of Jerusalem, through his veteran arts of persuasion, while Orosius accused him in vain. He also deceived the Fathers of the Synod of Diospolis <note>Modern-day Lydda</note>. By partly denying and partly softening the points of heresy objected to him by Orosius, he escaped the censure of the Synod and was pronounced worthy of Catholic communion. 

In the following year, he was condemned for heresy by the Councils of Carthage and Mileve, as well as by Pope Innocent. In 418, Pope Zosimus and the Fathers of the African Council branded him with the same mark of infamy. Furthermore, there exists a rescript of the Emperor Honorius given to the Prefect of the city in the same year, by which he ordered Pelagius, Cœlestius, and their sectaries to be expelled from Rome. Around the same time, Theodotus, Bishop of Antioch, held a Synod in the East; he summoned Pelagius to Jerusalem by the judgment of the bishops—Pelagius having long shifted ground and woven various webs of complication—and ensured he was condemned as manifestly convicted of heresy. What became of him after that, where he lived, or when or by what manner of death he passed away, is not at all certain. 

He was a man of remarkable sharpness of wit and endowed with knowledge of the better letters; moreover, he was conspicuous for the sanctity of his life and the unblemished integrity of his morals. By these "engines" especially—namely, the reputation of his learning and the appearance of his piety—he drew to himself so many and such great disciples for his dogmas. And lest anything be lacking to his frauds, whenever he was put on trial on that account, he never failed to disguise his errors; or at least he pretended that he was not putting forward his own opinion, but that of others. 

As far as his heresy is concerned, the sum of it comes to this: he fundamentally removed Original Sin, teaching that Adam's sin is not imputed to his offspring. On the contrary, he taught that everyone is born in the same perfection of will in which Adam was created; and that we undergo temporal death not because of Adam’s fall, but out of the necessity of nature...

from the Year 400.
</margin>

[...not out of] necessity: finally, he taught that baptism is not a remedy for original sin. Regarding grace, he did not always think or say the same thing. At first, he attributed everything to nature. Later, having been refuted by the Catholics, he changed his terminology but did not change his opinion. For by "grace" he understood the power of nature created by God—namely, the rational will. He maintained that the grace of Christ was nothing other than His teaching and example; and that all duties of virtue, even the very beginnings of repentance and conversion to God, could be fulfilled by us without any particular divine help. He went so far as to say that if divine grace were to be admitted at all, it should be numbered only among things that are "useful," but not "necessary." He expanded free will to such an extent that he judged a man could live without sin and satisfy the law of God perfectly <note>original: "ad amussim"; literally "by the carpenter's rule," meaning with absolute precision</note>. He contended that men—or at least most of them—are justified and predestined to eternal life not by the benefit of divine grace, but because of the merits of their own works. Finally, he taught that oaths were altogether unlawful, and he took away the hope of eternal salvation from the wealthy. His writings follow.

### EXTANT WRITINGS.

<margin>
* Commonitory, chapter 2. Noted in the Preface.
† Heresy 88.
|| Divine Lectures, chapter 8.

Fourteen books of *Expositions on the Pauline Epistles*, written before the capture of Rome by the Goths <note>Rome fell to the Goths in 410 AD</note>, which are mentioned in more than one place by Augustine, by Marius Mercator *, by the author of *The Predestined* †, and by Cassiodorus ||. Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a famous Dutch scholar</note> and many other learned men feel that these are the same works that are circulated under the name of Jerome and exist among his works. However, the Illustrious Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), the Archbishop of Armagh and a renowned scholar of early church history</note> embraced another opinion, which he pursues at length in his *Manuscript Theological Library*. It will perhaps not be useless to subjoin his words. Thus he says on page 574:

> “Three different sets of shorter annotations on the Pauline Epistles were circulated in the time of Cassiodorus; likewise, three in our own. Regarding the former, see Cassiodorus’s *Divine Lectures*, chapter 8. Similarly, in our own times (besides Haymo and more recent authors), three sets of an older character are circulated under the names of Jerome, Primasius, and Sedulius. The set currently circulated under the name of Jerome is believed by some to be the work of Pelagius the heretic; others believe it is the same as that which was formerly circulated under the name of Gelasius and is mentioned in the first place by Cassiodorus. I would rather think that the one mentioned by Cassiodorus was Pelagius's own (for it is gathered from that citation by Augustine in chapter 16 of *On the Proceedings against Pelagius* that his name was not prefixed everywhere; in which citation the word *They say* <note>original: "Dicuntur"</note> should be noted). However, this version which we have, I believe to have been patched together by some later person from the explanations of Pelagius, Jerome, and Primasius, with so little judgment that he did not notice that contrary doctrines (the *Pelagian* ones drawn from the heretic, and the *orthodox* ones drawn from Jerome and Primasius) were mixed together throughout. Hence, in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 11, we read that faith is bestowed by the goodness of God; and elsewhere very frequently (certainly nowhere more frequently in any of the Ancients) that we are justified by the free grace of God and by faith alone. Since these things are utterly abhorrent to Pelagian doctrine, they are an argument that those who think the entire work should be attributed to Pelagius are mistaken. This is also clearly proved by three passages from Pelagius’s *Commentaries* cited by Augustine in Book 3 of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapters 2, 3, and 5: none of which are found in our texts. <margin>* History of Pelagianism, p. 13.</margin> For the comparison of the passages themselves—cited by Augustine from Pelagius not just according to the sense, but according to the very words—makes it clear that the passages Vossius * produces here do not fit. To these, add that the Prefaces and Arguments of Pelagius to the Epistles are clearly absent from these Commentaries which we possess. Nevertheless, that many things from Pelagius are intermingled here is demonstrated both by the Pelagian dogmas that occur throughout (especially that one on Romans 7: *They are insane who assert that sin comes to us from Adam by transmission* <note>original: "per traducem"; referring to the doctrine of Traducianism, where the soul and its sin are passed from parent to child</note>), and by the citations from Augustine mentioned above, as well as those produced from *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* book 3, chapter 12, *On the Proceedings against Pelagius* chapter 16, and the Cottonian Book of Canons. However, the greater part seems to have been compacted from the very brief annotations of the Blessed Jerome (mentioned by Cassiodorus), as is shown by his name being prefixed in the oldest Gothic manuscripts, and by the Preface to Heliodorus—concerning which, however, there is that sharp critique by Erasmus. Someone or other had added the Preface to Heliodorus under the name of Jerome.”

Even Walafrid Strabo, in his *Ordinary Gloss*, frequently cites under Jerome’s name passages that are found here; and once, it seems, Sedulius <note>Sedulius Scotus, a 9th-century Irish teacher and commentator</note> himself does so. For we read thus in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 7:

> "Otherwise, as Jerome explains: *If anyone*, that is, whatever man, *over a virgin*, that is, his own flesh, [does] *what the man himself wills*, that is, virginity or marriage; because he has free will. Garnier <note>Jean Garnier (1612–1681), a Jesuit scholar and editor of Mercator</note> fosters an entirely different opinion from Ussher; he contends that these Commentaries are owed to Pelagius alone, and that having been purged of heretical filth long ago by Cassiodorus, they are now free from all stain of Pelagianism as they currently exist (Appendix to Dissertation 6, part 1, *Works of Marius Mercator*, p. 367).

*Letter to Demetrias on Virginity*, which begins, *If with the highest talent*, written in the year 413. It is held among the works of Jerome and Augustine, falsely ascribed to both—to the former even before the age of Bede, who detected the fraud through certain short annotations.

*Brief Book of Faith to Pope Innocent*, sent along with letters in the year 417; it was received by Zosimus, Innocent’s successor, in the same year and sent to Africa with letters. The letters themselves have perished; the *Brief Book* survives both after Pope Zosimus’s letter to the African Bishops (Councils, Vol. 2, p. 1563) and among the works of Jerome (Vol. 4, p. 98) under the title *Explanation of the Creed to Damasus*. That it was formerly ascribed to Jerome is evident from this: that by Charlemagne and the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt, the entire work (with the epilogue removed) was woven into the *Capitulary on Not Worshipping Images* (Book 3, ch. 1) under Jerome’s name. The argument and fragments of the Letter can be seen in Augustine’s *On the Grace of Christ* (chapters 30, 34, 35, etc.) and likewise in his *On Original Sin* (chapters 17, 18, 19).

## WRITINGS WHICH ARE NOT EXTANT.

*On the Faith of the Trinity*, in three books, written before his heresy was spread; that Pelagius held correct views on the Trinity is clear from his *Brief Book of Faith*.

*The Book of Blessings* <note>original: "ευλογιών" (eulogion); meaning praises or blessings</note>, *or of Honorable Sermons on Actual Conduct: or the Book of Testimonies*, in which, following the example of Cyprian, he collected chapters of maxims from the Holy Scriptures. Which chapters were used as objections against Pelagius from this book is shown both by Jerome in his *Dialogue against the Pelagians* and by Augustine in *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).

*Two Letters to a Widow*: one consolatory, the other exhortatory. Jerome presents two fragments in Book 3 *Against Pelagius*; Mercator gives as many in his *Commonitory*; Augustine gives a single one in *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (ch. 6).

*On Free Will, in four books*, written around the year 416, in opposition to Jerome’s *Letter to Ctesiphon* and his three *Dialogues against the Pelagians*. Fragments of these are brought forward in various places by Saint Augustine in *On the Grace of Christ* (chapters 4, 7, 10, 18, 28, 29, 39, 43) and *On Original Sin* (ch. 13).

*On Nature, one book*, which Augustine mentions in his *Retractions* (ch. 42); he specifically refuted it in his book *On Nature and Grace*, where many fragments of Pelagius's work can be found. Garnier provided these collected into one in his Appendix to part 1 of the *Works of Mercator*, p. 373.

*Letter to Paulinus*, and another to *Constantius*. Augustine mentions both in *On the Grace of Christ*. *Two Letters to Augustine*. A *Defense of his Faith* to the same. A *Letter to a certain Priest friend* concerning the events at Diospolis. Augustine mentions each of these four letters in *On the Proceedings in Palestine* (chapters 26, 30, 32). Pelagius certainly wrote more letters that have perished.

## VIGILANTIUS

By nation (not a Gaul, as Gennadius has it *, but) a Spaniard, born in the city of Calagurris, and eventually a priest of the Church of Barcelona; he flourished around the year 406. Leaving his homeland, he sought Italy to visit Saint Paulinus, with whom he had previously formed a friendship while Paulinus was active in Barcelona. From there he set out for Jerusalem, recommended to Jerome by letters from Paulinus. Thus, in the year 394, he was present along with Jerome during the earthquake that shook Jerusalem. Departing from Palestine, having become somewhat hostile toward Jerome, he went down into Egypt and traveled through other regions, everywhere accusing Jerome of Origenism <note>The controversial theological system of Origen of Alexandria, which Jerome had once admired but later attacked.</note>. Finally reaching Gaul, he began to spread his teachings, and having returned to Barcelona, as it seems, he died in peace. However, Jerome reports that he was condemned by the Roman Church. Regarding his heresies and the accusations against him, they were roughly these: that the relics of martyrs should not be treated with excessive worship or veneration; that the miracles usually occurring near them could be believed to be the tricks of demons; that the celibacy of the clergy is no more pleasing to God than marriage; that Christ's commands do not require someone to sell all their belongings and give everything to the poor at once; and finally, that the ritual of lighting lamps in churches and the vigils then frequently observed should be condemned. For these reasons, Jerome engaged in a sharp dispute with him; Jerome jokingly calls him *Dormitantius* <note>original: "Dormitantius." A pun on his name Vigilantius, which means "The Wakeful." Jerome mockingly calls him "The Sleepy One."</note> and pronounces him the worst of heretics. However much Jerome might rage, it is certain—even by Jerome's own admission—that even after the controversy arose, Vigilantius was considered not unworthy of Catholic communion by his own bishop. He wrote some things out of religious zeal, says Gennadius, and in these he explained the second *vision of Daniel* with a twisted mind.

<margin>† Letter 75.</margin>

Jerome perhaps refers to the same work † when he attacks Vigilantius thus:

> "Among the other blasphemies which you uttered with a sacrilegious mouth, you dared to say that the Mountain, from which the stone was cut without hands in the Book of Daniel, is the Devil, and the stone is Christ."

But whatever he wrote, nothing survives today.

## ATTICUS

Born in Sebaste, Armenia, he was trained from an early age in the monastic way of life by the Macedonians <note>A group that followed the teachings of Macedonius, often accused of denying the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>; later, upon entering adulthood, he moved to the Catholic Church. Having become a priest of the Church of Constantinople, he was among those who laid traps for John Chrysostom. Finally, after the death of Arsacius, four months later in March of the year 406, he was ordained Bishop of Constantinople while Chrysostom was still alive. On account of the unjust condemnation of Chrysostom and the seizing of his seat—and because he refused to restore the name of the now-deceased Chrysostom to the Diptychs <note>Lists of names of the living and dead commemorated during the liturgy; removal from the list was a sign of excommunication.</note>—Atticus was excluded from communion by the Western bishops. He was not admitted until, after many years, he returned the name of that most holy man to the sacred lists. He died in the year 427. A man of great learning, he was most famous for his piety and prudence; he possessed the highest dexterity in managing affairs and was very skillful at both laying and avoiding traps. In character, he was charming, mild, calm, and most ready to help the poor. He devoted much work and time to reading the writings of the ancients; he preached frequently, though his sermons were not of the sort that were received with applause by listeners or committed to writing.

There exists a quite long Letter to Cyril of Alexandria concerning his restoration of Chrysostom’s name to the Diptychs, found in Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 14, chapter 26; also another fairly short one written to Calliopius, priest of the Church of Nicaea, when he sent money for the relief of the poor of Nicaea, found in Socrates, book 7, chapter 25.

There is also a fragment of what appears to be a homily *On the Nativity of the Lord*, repeated for a third time in the Council of Ephesus, *Councils*, Volume 3, pages 116, 517, 849. Another fragment from a letter *To Eupsychius* is found in Theodoret, *Dialogue* 2, page 110.

## CÆLESTIUS

Wrongly called Celestinus by some, he was, as some claim || of the Scottish (that is, Irish) race and a relative of Solomon, Duke of Cornwall. However, both claims are uncertain. What is more certain, as established by the authority of Marius Mercator *, is that he was noble by birth, and by a rare defect of nature, a eunuch from his mother's womb. Established in the class of legal advocates in Rome, he argued cases with no little elegance. He flourished from the year 407. From the very start of the century, [he followed] Pelagius

[Pela]gius teaching at Rome, and he drank in with his whole heart the dregs of that most wretched heresy received from him. In the year 408 or 409, he accompanied Pelagius to Sicily, and then in the year 411 to Africa. Left there by Pelagius, who was hurrying to the East, Caelestius strenuously propagated the poison of the Pelagian doctrine <note>Pelagianism was a 5th-century belief that human nature is not corrupted by original sin and that mortals can choose good or evil without special divine aid.</note>. He won the favor of many clerics through his reputation for learning and piety, so much so that he did not fear to seek the dignity of the priesthood. However, in the year 412, he was accused of heresy before Aurelius, the Bishop of Carthage, by Paulinus, a deacon of the Blessed Ambrose. A Synod <note>A regional council of church leaders.</note> was assembled, and when he refused to condemn the Pelagian dogmas, he was deprived of communion. Immediately appealing to the Bishop of Rome, he left Africa and traveled to Ephesus, where by crafty arts he obtained the dignity of the priesthood. From there, as if from a citadel, he disseminated the Pelagian heresy far and wide through Asia, Rhodes, and the neighboring islands. He acted with such zeal and success that the Pelagians were even called *Caelestians* after him; and he thereafter, as if a leader of the sect, faced the same judgment as Pelagius in all Synods. At the end of the year 416, he set out for Constantinople, but his wickedness having been detected, he was soon driven out by the Patriarch Atticus. Therefore, heading straight for Rome in the year 417, he sought and obtained the favor of Pope Zosimus; so much so that the Pope, in letters sent to the African bishops, praised him greatly and ordered that the sentence passed by them in the year 412 be recalled for a more mature examination. However, in the following year, having been informed of the truth of the matter by the Africans, Zosimus held a Synod at Rome and condemned Caelestius. Around the same time, the Emperor Honorius issued an edict ordering him to be expelled from the City and the entire Western Empire. When Caelestius, taking advantage of the negligence of the City Prefects, still lingered in Rome, the Emperor renewed the decree with another rescript in the year 420. Driven into flight, Caelestius thereafter lay hidden in the East, staying sometimes with Theodore of Mopsuestia, and sometimes with Sisinnius and Nestorius, the Bishops of Constantinople, doing his utmost for the Pelagian cause. He attempted to influence the former in vain; but the latter, although publicly condemning Caelestius's errors in the Church, proved more favorable to him and even wrote intercessory letters to the Pope on his behalf. In the year 429, after Marius Mercator presented a *Commonitory* <note>original: *Commonitorio*; a formal written complaint or memorandum of charges.</note> against him to the Emperor Theodosius, he was expelled from the city of Constantinople by the Emperor's command. The following year, he was condemned by Pope Celestine in a Roman Synod. In the year 431, after the same Mercator presented a *Commonitory* at the Council of Ephesus, and after the Acts sent from Rome by Celestine against the Pelagians were read, he was struck with anathema <note>A formal curse by a council or the pope, excommunicating a person and denouncing their doctrines.</note> by the sentence of 275 bishops, along with Julian and the other accomplices of the sect. Thereafter, no mention of him is found among the ancient writers; whether he wasted away immediately from grief of mind, or withdrew into perpetual retirement.

### W R I T I N G S.

*The Profession of Faith* offered to Pope Zosimus, which for the most part contains the same opinions, and even nearly the same words, as the *Short Book of Faith* by Pelagius. It survives in its entirety among the works of Saint Augustine, dispersed in various places. The greater part is the same as the *190th Sermon on the Season*, with the preface revised; the remaining parts are found in the book *On Original Sin*, chapters 5, 6, and 23. Garnier collected these divided members into one and published the complete *Confession* in the *Appendix* to the first part of the Works of Marius Mercator, page 313.

*A Letter to the Roman Clergy of his party*, written in the year 418. Augustine wrongly conjectured that this anonymous letter circulating in Africa was by Julian; Augustine cites many fragments from it in his first book *To Boniface*. Garnier presents these collected into one, in the same place, page 318.

<margin>* *On Famous Men*, chapter 44.</margin>
*Letters to his Parents, or three short books* exhorting them to virtue; these were written by him while still a youth, from a monastery, or regarding the monastic life. Gennadius praises them greatly *.

*A short book to Pope Zosimus*, in which he denied that infants are bound by original sin. Augustine cites certain fragments of it in the book *On Original Sin*, chapters 2, 5, 6, and 23.

<margin>5th CENTURY from the Year 400.</margin>
The *Book of Definitions*, which Augustine mentions at the beginning of the book *On the Perfection of Justice against Caelestius*: he did not think it was by Caelestius himself, but by one of his disciples; it is preserved in its entirety within that book of Augustine.

A *Petition presented at the Council of Carthage*; in which, although he denied original sin, he rightly confessed that through the Baptism of Christ, the redemption of even little children takes place. The Fathers of the Council of Carthage mention this in a letter to Innocent.

The *Book against Original Sin*, written before the year 408; mentioned by the author of *Praedestinatus*, book 1, Heresy 88.

A *Letter to his followers living in Rome against the Roman Clergy*; some fragments remain in Augustine’s first book *To Boniface*.

Furthermore, Augustine, in the book *On the Proceedings in Palestine*, chapters 13, 14, 17, and 18, cites chapters 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 12, and 13 from a certain book by Caelestius, which Pelagius was forced to answer for in the Synod of Diospolis <note>A church council held in 415 AD where Pelagius was initially acquitted of heresy.</note>.

Finally, the Louvain scholars <note>original: "Lovanienfes"; referring to the influential faculty of theology at the University of Leuven.</note> attribute two letters to him which are found among the works of Jerome: one *On the Knowledge of Divine Law*, the other *On the Two Sons, the Frugal and the Luxurious*, which begins, *Of all the questions regarding the Scriptures*. It is certainly established that these letters were written by a Pelagian; however, there is no reason available to the Louvain scholars as to why they should be attributed to Caelestius specifically. There are also those who, relying on certain manuscripts, attribute Pelagius’s *Letter to Demetrias* to Caelestius.

<margin>407.</margin>

### THEODORE,
Syrian by race, perhaps born in Antioch, of noble birth: in Rhetoric he had the Sophist Libanius as his master, and in Theology, Diodore of Tarsus and Carterius. At that time, he had John Chrysostom <note>The famous "Golden-Mouthed" preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> as a companion and fellow student; by whose persuasion he first embraced the monastic and philosophical way of life. Later, however, when he had not yet reached the twentieth year of his age, led by love for a certain woman named Hermione, he returned to secular life. Yet, by writing a double *Exhortation*, Chrysostom recalled him to his former way of living. He was then made a Priest of the Church of Antioch (for Photius places it beyond all doubt that Theodore of Mopsuestia and Theodore of Antioch—who is mentioned so often in Gennadius, Photius, and in the *Catenae* <note>Collections of commentary by early Church Fathers.</note>—were the same person), and afterward Bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia; and for some time, he had Nestorius and Theodoret as his pupils. He flourished in the year 407: indeed, if I correctly track the time of his death, he held the Episcopate from the year 392. For he seems to have died in the year 428, after he had governed the Church of Mopsuestia for 36 years. Various judgments are passed on him; he is praised by some and blamed by others.

<margin>
Hesychius of Jerusalem, in the Acts of the 5th Council, Session 5.
* Sozomen, Book 8, ch. 7.
</margin>
* "A man," says Sozomen <note>A 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note> *, "skilled not moderately both in the sacred books and in the other disciplines of rhetoricians and philosophers." <note>original: "Ἀνὴρ... καὶ ἱερῶν βίβλων, καὶ τῆς ἄλλης παιδείας, ῥητόρων τε καὶ φιλοσόφων ἱκανὸς ἐπιστήμων."</note>

<margin>† Theodoret, Book 5, ch. 40.</margin>
† To Theodoret †, he was "a teacher of the whole church, and one who turned back the entire phalanx of the heretics." <note>original: "πάσης τῆς ἐκκλησίας διδάσκαλος, καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν φάλαγγα τῶν αἱρετικῶν ἀποστρέφων."</note> He adds that Theodore fought diligently during his whole life against the ranks of Arius and Eunomius <note>Prominent leaders of the Arian heresy, which denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, and put to flight the troop of Apollinaris <note>A theologian who argued Christ had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a human soul.</note> which lay in wait like robbers, while providing the best pasture for the sheep of Christ. After Theodore died, however, his doctrine and writings were not only criticized by the Acephali <note>A group of "headless" Egyptian monks who rejected the Council of Chalcedon.</note> on account of the unhealthy dogmas they seemed to foster, but he himself, along with his books, was condemned by the Fathers of the Fifth Council <note>The Second Council of Constantinople (553 AD), which posthumously condemned Theodore during the "Three Chapters" controversy.</note>: a matter that stood as the cause and seed-bed of the gravest disturbances in the Church. Vigilius <note>Pope from 537–555 AD.</note> busied himself in defending him with many arguments sought from every side, which can be seen in his *Constitution*. Facundus of Hermiane also, in the year 547, while the controversy was still burning, wrote twelve books for the defense of the *Three Chapters* and another later against Mucianus. In these, he defended Theodore with all the zeal he could as a Catholic man; having heaped up many testimonies of the Holy Fathers, he protected his reputation as if it were "tightly roofed" <note>An idiom meaning "perfectly intact."</note>, excusing some of his sayings, softening others, and explaining them in a favorable sense, showing that some had been truncated by adversaries, interpolated, or distorted into a clearly foreign meaning. Finally, he argued it was unjust that one who was held as a Catholic Bishop and died in the peace of the Church should be subjected to anathema as a heretic more than a full century after his death. Lastly, it is not unworthy of observation...

It is a matter of regret <note>original: "indignum est," implying something undeserved or shameful</note>, as Gregory the Great <margin>5th CENTURY from the Year 450. Book 6, Epistle 31.</margin> relates, that the *Ecclesiastical History* of Sozomen (for whose name Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar of church history</note> rightly advises that the name of Theodoret should be read) is not received by the Roman Church for the reason that it praised Theodore of Mopsuestia too highly, and claimed that he was a great Teacher of the Church until the day of his death.

## W R I T I N G S.

The *Creed* or *Exposition of Faith*: This exists in Greek and Latin in the sixth session of the Council of Ephesus, *Councils*, Volume 3, page 678. It exists in Latin among the works of Marius Mercator <note>A 5th-century Latin writer who opposed the teachings of Nestorius and Pelagius</note>, from his own version made before the year 440. The rest of his works have perished; however, the titles and fragments of many survive. He seems to have written *Commentaries* on all the books of Holy Scripture; as many of these as we have been able to find mentioned by ancient or more recent authors follow here.

<margin>* Codex 38.</margin>
*Commentaries on the Pentateuch* <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>; of which many fragments are held in the Greek *Catena* <note>A "Catena" (Latin for "chain") is a form of biblical commentary made up of a string of excerpts from earlier theologians.</note> on the Pentateuch, translated into Latin by Francisco Zephyro. Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note> mentions a first volume of the *Commentaries on Genesis* comprising seven books: in which he notes that Theodore followed the historical and literal sense everywhere, dismissing allegories, and scattered the seeds of the Nestorian heresy <note>The belief that there were two separate persons, one human and one divine, in Jesus Christ</note> throughout. Fifteen fragments taken from there, as it seems, survive under the title *Books on Creation* in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod.

*Commentaries on the Psalms*, fragments of which occur throughout the Greek *Catena* on the Psalms, which Daniel Barbaro published in Latin. Four excerpts from these are also found in Latin in the *Constitutum* <note>A formal decree or document</note> of Vigilius, *Councils*, Volume 5; two in the fourth session, and just as many in the fifth session of the Fifth Council; Facundus of Hermiane has three regarding Psalm 44 in Book 9, chapter 1.

<margin>* Breviary, chapter 10.</margin>
*Commentaries on Samuel, Job, Ecclesiastes, and the Four Major Prophets*; Hebediesu <note>Abdisho bar Berika, a 13th-century East Syriac writer</note> reports that these exist among his own people (as do many other Commentaries by Theodore). Indeed, Liberatus <note>A 6th-century deacon of Carthage</note> testifies that many of Theodore's volumes were translated into the Chaldean <note>Usually referring to Syriac or Aramaic</note> language.

*Commentaries on the Twelve Minor Prophets*. Three fragments are held in Latin in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod. Coccius cites a fragment of the *Commentary on Zephaniah*; where he drew it from is uncertain. However, they are said to exist in their entirety in the Imperial Library at Vienna.

*Commentaries on the Gospel according to St. Matthew*. Four fragments exist in Latin in the *Constitutum* of Vigilius; five in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod; Facundus of Hermiane presents a single one in Book 3, chapter 4, and others in Book 9, chapter 2.

*Commentary on the Gospel according to St. Luke*. A single fragment is held in the *Catena* on Luke; another in the *Constitutum* of Vigilius; a third in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod of Constantinople.

*Commentary on the Gospel according to St. John*. Very many fragments are preserved in the Greek *Catena* on John; three in the *Constitutum* of Vigilius; and five in the fourth session of the Synod of Constantinople; one in Facundus of Hermiane, Book 9, chapter 3.

*Commentary on the Acts of the Apostles*. Vigilius has two fragments in his *Constitutum*; the Fathers of the Fifth Synod have a single one in the fourth session.

<margin>* Preface to the Commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul.</margin>
*Commentary on the Fourteen Epistles of St. Paul*, all of which Theodoret is the authority for saying were explained at length by Theodore. Vigilius, in his *Constitutum*, brings forward fragments from the *Commentaries on the Epistles to the Romans* (Facundus of Hermiane has one in Book 3, chapter 6), the *First to the Corinthians*, the *First to Timothy*, and to the *Hebrews*. Others on the *Epistle to the Hebrews* are cited in the fourth session of the Synod of Constantinople.

<margin>† On Writers, chapter 12.</margin>
*On the Incarnation of the Lord, in fifteen books*, written before the year 390, regarding which see Gennadius. Twelve fragments are found in the fourth session of the Synod of Constantinople. Marius Mercator also has several excerpts translated by himself into Latin, Garner edition, Part 2, page 259; who, because the true nature of the Incarnation is not explained in those books but is instead overturned, gave them another title, namely: *Against the Lord and His Incarnation*. Leontius presents others in the book *Against the Eutychians*. Many more are found throughout Facundus of Hermiane: namely from Book 5, chapter 52; Book 9, chapter 3; from Book 6, chapter 54; in the same place, chapter 3; from Book 9; in the same place, chapter 5; from Book 10, chapter 70; in the same place, chapter 3; from Book 12; in the same place; from Book 13; in Book 3, chapter 1; from Book 14, chapter 3.

*Twenty-five (or, as Photius notes elsewhere, twenty-eight) books **Against Eunomius** on behalf of Saint Basil; in these, says Photius, he demonstrates at length that Eunomius was ignorant not only of secular disciplines but of Christian Theology as well. Perhaps the books against **Apollinarius** were no different from these; sixteen fragments of those survive in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod <note>The Second Council of Constantinople, held in 553 AD.</note>, while a preface is found in Facundus of Hermiane, Book 10, Chapter 1. ***Against those who assert that men sin by nature, not by will**, five books, written against the Westerners infected by this stain, according to Photius. Photius presents the dogmas of the Westerners that Theodore attacked in the aforementioned passage: where he also recounts Theodore's own unhealthy opinions, shared with the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who emphasized human free will over the necessity of divine grace, a view often opposed by Saint Augustine.</note>, which are revealed there. Marius Mercator confirms that these books were written against the dogma of original sin and its champion **Saint Augustine**; Mercator preserved many excerpts of them for us, translated into Latin (Garner edition, Part 1, page 97, etc.).*

<margin>

</margin>
***On the Magic of the Persians**, three books, dedicated to Mastubius, an Armenian and a Country-Bishop <term>Chorepiscopus</term><note>A "chorepiscopus" was a rural bishop in the early church who assisted the city bishop.</note>. In the first book, he explained and refuted the wicked Persian dogma introduced by Zafrades <note>likely referring to Zoroaster</note>; in the two following books, he treated the pious Doctrine of the faith from the very beginning of the world. The author of this work, says Photius, appears to be **Theodore of Mopsuestia**. However, regarding Photius's remark that Theodore "foretells the Nestorian heresy" <note>original Greek: ἀπεμφαίνοντα προαναφωνεῖν</note>, especially in the third book, it should be understood as referring to those same dogmas which Theodore secretly fostered while still alive, and which Nestorius publicly broadcast after Theodore's death.*

***Exposition of the Nicene Creed**: A fragment is held in the "Constitution of Vigilius" <note>An official decree by Pope Vigilius regarding the Three Chapters controversy.</note>; and another in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod.*

***Book for those to be Baptized**; of which eight fragments are shown in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod, and some also translated into Latin by Mercator among the fragments from Theodore's books **On the Incarnation**. A very brief fragment is held by Facundus of Hermiane, Book 9, Chapter 3.*

***Many Sermons**: From the second sermon **On Miracles**, a fragment exists in Greek in the Lateran Council (Council Records, Volume 6, page 318); and another in the same place from the sermon **On the Incarnation**. Two fragments of a certain sermon delivered at Antioch are held in the fifth session of the Fifth Synod.*

***Several Letters**: from which Photius says he was certain that **Theodore of Antioch** (whose name appears on most of the works listed above) is the same person as **Theodore of Mopsuestia**. Facundus of Hermiane presents a fragment from his second Letter to Artemius, a Presbyter of Alexandria, in Book 3, Chapter 5.*

*Furthermore, in the **Constitution of Vigilius**, forty fragments are found that have not yet been categorized, taken from the writings of Theodore (though the titles are not added). In the fifth session of the Fifth Synod, twelve other fragments of Theodore are placed, borrowed from the writings of **Cyril** <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a major opponent of Nestorianism.</note> against him. There is also a work called the **Mystic Codex**, from the twelfth book of which Facundus of Hermiane has a fragment in Book 3, Chapter 3; in it, Theodore explicitly condemns Paul of Samosata and calls him an "Angel of the Devil."*

*Finally, among the minor works of **Theodore Abu Qurrah** <note>A 9th-century theologian; the author is distinguishing between him and the earlier Theodore.</note>, several Disputations are held; these, some manuscripts attribute to **Theodore of Hagiopolis** (that is, of Antioch).*

*Photius describes his style in this way:* <note>original Greek: Ἔστι δὲ τὴν μὲν φράσιν οὐ πάνυ λαμπρός· τοῖς δὲ διανοίαις καὶ τοῖς ἐπιχειρήμασι λίαν πυκνὸς, καὶ ταῖς γεγραφικαῖς ἄδειαν πλουτῶν μαρτυρίαις.</note> **"His phrasing is not at all brilliant; yet in his thoughts and arguments he is extremely dense, and he is exceptionally rich in testimonies from Holy Scripture."** <margin>† Codex 38.</margin> *And elsewhere:* <note>original Greek: Οὐδὲ λαμπρός, οὐδὲ λίαν σαφής. φεύγων δὲ τὸ δυνατὸν αὐτῷ τρόπον τὰς ἀλληγορίας, καὶ κατὰ τινὰ ἱστορίαν τὴν ἑρμηνείαν ποιούμενος. Ταυτολογεῖ δὲ τὰ πλεῖστα, καὶ ἀχάρις πως, καὶ ἀηδὴς εἶναι δοκεῖ.</note> **"His style is neither illustrious nor very clear. Avoiding allegories as much as he can, and treating interpretation only according to the historical narrative, he repeats the same things to a tedious degree; he comes across as ungraceful and even unpleasant to the reader."** *And finally elsewhere:* <margin>|| Codex 177.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἔοικε δὲ φιλοπονώτερον περὶ τὴν ἱερὰν ἡμῶν καὶ θείαν γραφὴν διατεθῆναι, εἰ καὶ ἐν πολλοῖς παρασύρεται τῆς ἀληθείας.</note> **"It appears that he was quite industrious concerning our sacred and divine Scripture, even if in many matters he drifts away from the truth."** *And truly, Theodore [influenced] not only Nestorius, but—*

but it also cannot be denied that he clearly foreshadowed Pelagius <note>Pelagius was a monk whose followers, the Pelagians, believed humans could achieve salvation through free will without the necessity of divine grace.</note> in many respects. **POLYCHRONIUS**, a Syrian by birth and the brother of Theodore of Mopsuestia. He was a disciple and imitator of Zebinas, a very famous ascetic in the Province of Cyrrhus; he later became the Bishop of Apamea. He flourished in the year 410. He seems to have still been among the living in the year 427, the year in which Theodoret closed his *Ecclesiastical History*. Theodoret says of him that he was "gifted with the grace of speech and the brilliance of his life" <note>original Greek: "τῇ τοῦ λόγου χάριτι, καὶ τῇ τοῦ βίου λαμπρότητι χρώμενος"</note>. Elsewhere, the same Theodoret extols him with the highest praise for his outstanding virtues, his singular way of life, and the many miracles he performed. He wrote an *Exposition on the Song of Songs*, edited in Greek by Meursius along with the expositions of Eusebius and Psellus, *Leiden*, 1617, in quarto. He also wrote a *Commentary on Job*, the introduction of which was prefixed (and the much larger part inserted) by Nicetas in his *Catena on Job* <note>A "Catena" or "Chain" is a form of biblical commentary made up of fragments from various successive authors.</note>, which was published through the care of Patrick Young in Greek and Latin, *London*, 1637, in folio. He wrote a *Commentary on Ezekiel*, of which some fragments are presented by John of Damascus in his books against the Iconoclasts; other fragments appear in Latin in Villalpandus’s *Commentary on Ezekiel*. The *Introduction in Greek* was edited by David Hoeschel, *Augsburg*, 1602, in quarto, along with certain other works; it is also found among the *Sacred Critics*, Volume 2, *London*, 1660. Finally, fragments from his *Commentary on Daniel* survive in Greek at the end of Broughton’s commentaries on the same book.

**PAULINUS**, Bishop of Béziers in Gaul, flourished in the year 410. There exists a work written by him, says Miraeus, titled *Letter on Terrifying Signs*; however, he does not indicate where it is located. Rosweydus suggests in his notes that the *Martyrdom of Saint Genesius*, which is circulated under the name of Paulinus of Nola, belongs to this Paulinus.

**NONNUS**, an Egyptian by race from the city of Panopolis, lived around the year 410. He had a son named Sosenas, who transferred his father’s property to others, according to Synesius. He wrote several poems in Greek, of which the following survive today:

*A Paraphrase of the Gospel of St. John*: published in Greek (by the care of Aldus Manutius) at *Rome*, 1508; *Frankfurt*, 1541; in Greek and Latin at *Paris*, 1578, in octavo; with the notes of Nansius at *Leiden*, 1598, in octavo; then in Greek by Daniel Heinsius with his *Exercises*, *Leiden*, 1627, in octavo; and in Greek and Latin in the Bignean Appendix, *Paris*, 1624, in folio.

*A Collection and Explanation of Stories*, mentioned by Gregory Nazianzen in his two *Invectives against Julian*. Richard Montagu edited this in Greek from a manuscript in the Vienna Library, along with Nazianzen’s *Invectives*, *Eton*, 1610, in quarto. Jacques de Billy translated it into Latin in the second volume of the works of Nazianzen.

The **Dionysiaca** *in 48 books*: written by him while he was still a Pagan, as it seems. They exist in Greek with the readings of Falkenburg and Canter, *Antwerp*, 1569, in quarto; in Greek and Latin at *Hanau*, 1605, in octavo; among the *Greek Heroic Poets*, *Geneva*, 1606, in folio, part 2, page 307; and finally with the notes of Cunaeus and Scaliger, *Hanau*, 1610. His diction in the "Dionysiaca" is frequently confused <note>original Greek: "συγκεχυμένη"</note>; which is not surprising for poets, since he is there sacrificing to Bacchus <note>An idiomatic way of saying the poem's style is influenced by the god of wine/drunkenness.</note>. But I wish that his excessive obscurity did not also sometimes tire the reader in his paraphrase of John.*

**SYNESIUS**, an Egyptian by nation, from the Pentapolis region and the city of Cyrene. He was originally a Pagan by worship and a Platonic philosopher by school. Around the year 400, he was sent as an ambassador on behalf of his home city to the Emperor Arcadius; he offered the Emperor a golden crown, and at the same time delivered an *Oration on Kingship* more precious than any gold. Around the year 410, when the citizens of the city of Ptolemais asked Bishop Theophilus of Alexandria to grant them Synesius as their bishop, he refused the office. He did not hide the fact that the faith in the bodily resurrection had not yet settled in his mind; furthermore, he confessed that his wife was so dear to him that he would neither be separated from her,

to be separated from her, nor would he find it necessary to consort with her in secret; rather, he openly declared that he desired from his soul that many and excellent children be born to him. He publicly professed that he would undertake the episcopal office on no other condition, unless both his wife and his scruples were left untouched <note>Synesius was a Neoplatonist philosopher who struggled to reconcile his intellectual views, such as the pre-existence of the soul, with orthodox Christian dogma.</note>. Theophilus finally agreed to these conditions and raised the man to the dignity of the High Priesthood, having regard, says Photius <margin>* Codex 26.</margin> <note>Photius was a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who reviewed hundreds of books in his *Bibliotheca*.</note>, both to the man's general probity and the integrity of his past life, and because a man who had so ordered his life could not fail to be illuminated by the light of the resurrection. Nor did that hope fail: for quite easily, as soon as he was created Bishop, he also believed the doctrine of the resurrection. Concerning his style, Photius has this to say: "he was lofty in expression and possessed weightiness, yet inclining also toward the more political [perhaps *poetic*] style" <note>original Greek: <term>τὴν μὲν φράσιν ὑψηλός, καὶ ὄγκον ἔχων, ἀποκλίνων δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὸ πολιτικώτερον [forsan ποιητικώτερον]</term></note>. His style is indeed sublime and grand, but one which simultaneously inclines somewhat toward popular [or poetic] diction. And of his Letters, Photius says, "they flow with grace and sweetness, along with strength and density in their thoughts" <note>original Greek: <term>χάριτος καὶ ἡδονῆς ἀποστάζουσι, μετὰ τῆς ἐν τοῖς νοήμασιν ἰσχύος καὶ πυκνότητος</term></note>.

<margin>412.</margin>
**ISIDORE**, Egyptian by nation, perhaps Alexandrian by birth, a disciple of St. Chrysostom, flourished around the year 412. He led a monastic life near Pelusium—the largest of the seven mouths of the Nile—from which he is called "the Pelusiote." Indeed, if Nicephorus is to be believed, he was the Prefect of the monks living on Mount Pelusium. <margin>* Book 1, Ch. 15.</margin> In this place, as Evagrius <note>Evagrius Scholasticus was a 6th-century historian of the church.</note> witnesses, he wore down his body with labors to such an extent, and nourished his soul with secret and more sublime doctrines, that he clearly led the life of angels on earth, and was a perpetual living image of both the monastic life and divine contemplation. He was still among the living in the year 435, which is clear from Letter 311 of the first book. He zealously cherished the memory of Chrysostom; hence it happened that he always opposed Theophilus and even attacked Cyril for a long time, until Cyril, finally becoming fairer to the memory of Chrysostom, moved to Isidore's side. He wrote very many things, filled with manifold utility <margin>† Book 14, Ch. 53.</margin>. Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> says he wrote three thousand letters; according to Nicephorus, however, he wrote ten thousand letters, in which, for the most part, a question having been proposed, he usually interprets some passage of Holy Scripture. Of these, 2,012 exist printed <margin>|| Library, Book 4.</margin> divided into five books. Sixtus Senensis relates that he saw a manuscript volume in the Library of Saint Mark in Venice, containing 1,168 letters of our Isidore, the first of which begins thus: "Since time is cyclical" <note>original Greek: <term>Ἐπειδὴ κυκλικόν ἐστι χρόνος.</term></note>. Since, however, none in those published thus far begins this way, it is not unlike the truth that this and the following letters still lie hidden, not yet having seen the light. <margin>* See "Isidore".</margin> As for what Suidas relates, that our Isidore wrote three letters that interpret Holy Scripture, Sirmondus corrects the passage of Suidas from emended codices in this way: "he wrote 3,000 letters interpreting the divine Scripture, and another 7, and others more" <note>original Greek: <term>γέγραφεν ἐπιστολὰς ἑρμηνευούσας τὴν θείαν γραφὴν Γ. καὶ ἑτέρας Ζ. καὶ ἄλλας πλ.</term> Sirmondus is correcting the count of Isidore's letters by re-interpreting the Greek numerals in the manuscript.</note>.
