<header>The Nestorian Century.</header>

Furthermore, Isidore wrote works that are now lost to us, <margin>5th CENTURY from the Year 400.</margin> such as a *Book Against the Pagans*, which he himself mentions in Book 2, letters 137 and 228; an *Oration Against Fate*, mentioned in Book 3, letter 253; and a work *To, or against, Cyril*, which is discussed by Evagrius in Book 1, chapter 15, and Nicephorus in Book 15, chapter 53, and perhaps certain other works.

The first three books of his Letters (comprising 1,213 letters) were published in Greek and Latin by Jacques de Billy in *Paris, 1585*, to which he subjoined his own books of *Sacred Observations*. Conrad Rittershusius reprinted these books and added a fourth (consisting of 230 letters) together with his own extensive notes on each book, published in *Heidelberg, 1605*, in folio. Finally, a fifth book (containing 570 letters), illustrated with notes, scholia <note>Scholia are grammatical or explanatory notes written in the margins of ancient manuscripts.</note>, and arguments, was published separately in Greek and Latin from the Vatican Library by Andreas Schott in *Frankfurt, 1629*, in folio. Thus, the combined editions of Rittershusius and Schott constitute a complete edition of Isidore’s letters. Indeed, all five books were published together in Greek and Latin in *Paris, 1638*, in folio.

There was another Isidore entirely distinct from our author, whom the *Suda* <note>The Suda is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> mentions frequently under the entries *Aphtheia, Mother, and Sardon*—namely, a Pagan Philosopher whose life was written by Damascius, which may be seen in Photius <margin>* Codex 242.</margin>.

<margin>412. † Concerning the Carmelite Order, Book 2, Page 36.</margin> CYRIL, a native of Alexandria—though Trithemius † <note>Johannes Trithemius was a 15th-century German abbot and historian.</note> claims he originated from Constantinople—was the nephew of Theophilus of Alexandria by his brother, and a Priest of the Alexandrian Church. Those who count him among the Carmelites, such as Trithemius, Baronius, Allegre, and others, are merely babbling nonsense. Following the death of Theophilus in the year 412, Cyril succeeded to the See of Alexandria; and not long after beginning his episcopate—though only after much long-standing hesitation—he restored the name of John Chrysostom to the Diptychs <note>The Diptychs were lists of names of the living and dead commemorated by the church during the liturgy; removing a name was a sign of excommunication or dishonor.</note>. In the year 415, he expelled from Alexandria the Jews who were attacking the Christians. He strongly opposed heretics breaking out on every side, especially Nestorius. When Nestorius began spewing the poison of his heresy in the year 429, Cyril first warned him kindly by letter. Soon after, having informed Pope Celestine of the matter by letter and having convened a Synod at Alexandria, he summarized the truth (as opposed to Nestorius's blasphemies) in twelve chapters, or *Anathematisms* <note>Formal ecclesiastical curses or condemnations of specific doctrines.</note>. Sending four bishops as legates to Nestorius, he demanded that if he wished to preserve Catholic communion and his own see, he must subscribe to them. 

But when Nestorius refused this, yielding to no warnings or arguments, Cyril petitioned the Emperor Theodosius that an Ecumenical Synod should be gathered at Ephesus by his command. This was done, and the Synod was called for the day of Holy Pentecost in the year 431. At that time Cyril arrived, and with him nearly two hundred bishops. While John of Antioch and other Eastern prelates wove delays from day to day, the Synod was finally begun fifteen days later, namely on the 10th of the Calends of July <note>June 22nd.</note>. In this Council, 270 bishops assembled. Cyril acted as President, being the foremost Patriarch of the East. I do not deny that he acted as a representative for Pope Celestine, but it was then the custom that any bishop could delegate his own right of voting to another. He presided, therefore, not merely as a legate of the Pope, but by his own right as the leader of the Eastern Patriarchs. 

Nestorius was summoned to the Council three times, but since he refused to present himself for judgment, his case was examined by the bishops present; he was condemned as one holding impious views by the synodal sentence and cast down from his see. Meanwhile, John, Theodoret, and other Eastern bishops arrived at Ephesus, and having held a separate "conventicle" <note>An unofficial or unauthorized religious meeting.</note>, they "deposed" Cyril and Memnon of Ephesus. Winning over Irenaeus, the Imperial legate, to their side, they saw to it that Cyril and Memnon were shut up in prison. However, the fathers of the Synod soon investigated the cause, and both were restored to their sees. After the Council was finished and the Emperor had heard the dispute of both sides, Nestorius was clearly defeated and prostrate, and Cyril returned to Alexandria. In the following year, both he and the Eastern bishops were appealed to by the Emperor via letters to enter into peace. On behalf of the Easterners, therefore, Paul of Emesa came as a legate to Cyril, bringing a confession of faith to Alexandria that was sufficiently Catholic; in turn, he brought back another from Cyril to be signed by the Easterners. This covered the wound somewhat, but did not fully heal it. Indeed, disputes subsequently arose between him and the Easterners—especially Theodoret—which did not cease to be agitated until his death. He died in the year 444, a man truly as much for his piety as for his learning and zeal...

<margin>5th CENTURY from the Year 400.</margin> [Cyril was] noble and invincible in his defense of the Catholic faith. Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457) was a bishop and theologian who often clashed with Cyril during the Nestorian controversy.</note> certainly brings many accusations against him, shouting that Cyril proposed a single nature in Christ. It must be admitted that Cyril quite often affirms that <note>original: "μίαν εἶναι φύσιν λόγου"</note> "there is one nature of the Word"; but it is equally clear that in all these places he uses the word "nature" <note>original: "φύσεως" (physeos)</note> in place of "person" or "subsistence" <note>original: "ὑποστάσεως" (hypostaseos)</note>. This could be demonstrated more clearly if I wished to dwell on these matters. Furthermore, Cyril is blamed for the death of Hypatia, that most famous Alexandrian philosopher, with the claim that he, driven by hatred and envy, caused her to be torn limb from limb by the mob. However, Damascius, who levels this slander against Cyril, deserves little credit in this matter, as he was a most bitter enemy of the Christian religion. That this was done by the Alexandrians—a most volatile race of men—cannot be denied; but Cyril’s proven integrity by no means allows us to believe it happened at his instigation. Regarding his style, <margin>* Code 49.</margin> Photius <note>Photius was a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who reviewed hundreds of books in his "Bibliotheca."</note> writes the following: <note>original Greek: "Ὁ δὲ λόγος αὐτῷ πεποιμένος, καὶ εἰς ἰδιάζουσαν ἰδέαν ἐκβεβιασμένος, καὶ οἷον λελυμένην καὶ τὸ μέτρον ὑπερορῶσαν ποίησις"</note> "His speech is labored and forced into a peculiar form, and is like a loose poetry that neglects meter." His discourse is conflicted and twisted into his own particular way of speaking (indeed, Photius notes a "certain idiosyncratic quality" <note>original: "οἰκεῖόν τι"</note> in Cyril's style several times) and is, as it were, disjointed and neglecting the rhythms of "meter."

[Concerning] Cyril. Epistle 55 to Rabbula of Edessa is preserved only in Latin. Regarding the two epistles to Succensus, Bishop of Diocaesarea in Isauria (which are commonly appended to the book *On the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*), Ullerius warns in his *Manuscript Library* that nearly half of the latter epistle should be excised. This is because: 1. Eulogius, cited in Photius, and Maximus, cited in Euthymius <margin>* The Panoply, part 2, title 15.</margin> *, quote a passage from the end of the second letter to Succensus that is found in the middle of this one. 2. The second half of the epistle is found word-for-word in Cyril's 29th letter to Acacius of Melitene. 3. The narrative found at the end regarding the letter of Athanasius to Epictetus, which was corrupted by heretics, could rightly be woven into the letter to Acacius, but not into this one to Succensus; for Cyril had already recounted that same narrative at sufficient length in the previous letter.

The *Letter to his Clergy stationed at Constantinople*, which begins, *Necessity [is] laid upon me* <note>original Greek: "Ἀνάγκην τὸ ἐπ’ ἐμοὶ κείμενον"</note>, is found in a much longer and more corrected version from the translation by Marius Mercator <note>A 5th-century Latin ecclesiastical writer and translator who opposed Nestorianism.</note> among his works edited by Garnier, Part II, p. 49.

*Against Nestorius, five books. Published in Greek and Latin at Rome, 1608.*

*Explanation of the Twelve Chapters.* <note>These "Chapters" or "Anathemas" were Cyril's primary theological points against Nestorius.</note>

*Defense of the Twelve Chapters against the Eastern Bishops.*

*Defense of the same against Theodoret.* Both of these Defenses were translated into Latin by Marius Mercator, and consequently, you can find both in Latin among his works.

*Defense addressed to the Emperor Theodosius, written near the end of the year 431.*

*Against Julian, ten books, written around the year 433.* <note>Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who attempted to revive paganism.</note>

*Book against the Anthropomorphites.* <note>The "Anthropomorphites" were a group of monks who believed that God possessed a physical human form.</note>

*Book on the Holy Trinity.*

*Nineteen Homilies on Jeremiah under Cyril's name* (except the last, which is Clement of Alexandria's *Who is the Rich Man that Shall be Saved?*), published in Greek and Latin by Balthazar Corderius, Antwerp, 1648, in octavo format. These have been discovered to be the work of Origen. Corderius had previously published the *Moral Fables* under Cyril’s name; a work written by a Latin author and formerly published in Paris under the title *The Mirror of Wisdom*.

## LOST WORKS.

<margin>* The Breviary, ch. 10.</margin>
Cyril also wrote, according to Liberatus *, three books against Diodore <note>Diodore of Tarsus</note> and the excerpts of Theodore <note>Theodore of Mopsuestia</note> collected by Proclus of Constantinople. In the first of these, he refuted the views of Diodore, and in the second and third, those of Theodore, though he did not mention either man by name. Fragments of these exist in the Acts of the Fifth Synod, Session 5.

<margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 57.</margin>
Gennadius * further records works by Cyril that have perished, namely *On the Failure of the Synagogue* and *On the Faith against Heretics*; unless perhaps this latter title refers to some writing against Nestorius. Furthermore, a fragment from Cyril's *Oration against those who say offerings should not be made for those who have fallen asleep in the faith* is cited by Eustratius of Constantinople in his work *On the State of Souls after this Life* (published by Leo Allatius in the book *On Purgatory*), p. 371.

The *Works of Cyril* appeared in Latin through George of Trebizond (Basel, 1546, in 4 volumes), through Gentian Hervet (Paris, 1573 and 1605, in 2 volumes), and in Greek-Latin edited by Jean Aubert (Paris, 1638, in 7 volumes).

The *Memorandum on Nestorius* was first brought to light by Étienne Baluze, who published it in Greek and Latin in the *New Collection of Councils*, p. 377.

The *Liturgy attributed to Cyril*, translated from the Arabic language into Latin by Victorio Scialagh, was published at Augsburg, 1604, in quarto format.

ANIANUS, a native of Campania, a Deacon of Celeda, and secretary to Pelagius, was a most sharp defender of the Pelagian heresy. He flourished in the year 415, in which he attended the Synod of Diospolis <note>A council held in Palestine where Pelagius was initially cleared of heresy.</note> and handled Pelagius’s case with the greatest diligence and zeal of mind. He wrote several books against Jerome’s *Letter to Ctesiphon*, as Jerome himself testifies *, who also reveals that he intended to write a refutation of them. Garnier † contends at length that this man is the same as the Anianus who translated several of John Chrysostom's Homilies. The arguments he brings forward boil down to this: they shared the same name, rank, and sect (for [he fought for?] the Pelagian heresy...

<note>Continuing from the previous page regarding Anianus</note> It is clearly evident from his letters to Orontius and Evangelus that the translator of Chrysostom was a man infected by heresy <note>original: "refeos," likely a transcription of "haereseos"</note>; furthermore, his era is confirmed by quite clear evidence in the said letters, showing that the translator flourished while the Pelagian controversy <note>A theological dispute regarding the nature of grace and free will, named after the monk Pelagius.</note> was still burning. **TIMOTHY**, a Bishop, though of which city is not known. He flourished around the year 415. He wrote a book *On the Nativity of the Lord according to the Flesh*, in which he judged that it occurred on the day of Epiphany. The work is no longer extant.

<margin>
415.
</margin>
**LUCIAN**, a Priest of the Church of Caphargamala in the territory of Jerusalem, flourished in the year 415. In that year, he had a revelation in his dreams from Gamaliel <note>The famous Jewish teacher and Pharisee mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles.</note> regarding the relics of St. Stephen the First Martyr; he soon communicated this to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, by whom the bones of the First Martyr were translated to the Church in Jerusalem. Lucian composed the entire history of this matter in the Greek language; this was immediately translated into Latin by Avitus, a Spanish priest who was staying in those parts at the time. Having added a single letter to Balconius, the Bishop of Braga, Avitus sent the work to Spain along with a few relics of St. Stephen which he had received from Lucian, by way of Paulus Orosius, who was then returning from the Synod of Diospolis. This little book or letter, in Avitus's translation, is found among the works of Augustine, and in Surius under August 3rd; it was revised and corrected according to four manuscript codices of the Vatican Library by Baronius in his records for the year 415. Eustratius of Constantinople presents two significant fragments of this little book in Greek in his *Book on the State of the Departed*, chapter 23; Photius also cites some parts in Codex 171. Both Lucian and Avitus, as well as this letter, are mentioned by Gennadius in chapters 46 and 47.

<margin>
416.
</margin>
**PAULUS OROSIUS**, Spanish by birth and a Priest of Tarragona, flourished in the year 416. In the year 413, he was sent as a legate by the Spanish bishops Eutropius and Paul to St. Augustine in Africa, to inform him about the errors of the Priscillianists and Origenists <note>Early Christian movements deemed heretical: Priscillianism involved asceticism and mysticism, while Origenism followed certain controversial teachings of the scholar Origen.</note> then sprouting in Spain. Having stayed with Augustine for some time, he began his *History* at Augustine's urging, to which he finally put the finishing touches four years later. From Africa, in the year 415, he was sent by Augustine to St. Jerome in Palestine to seek Jerome's opinion on the origin of souls. Having set out for Palestine, he was present that same year at the Assembly of Jerusalem and the Council of Diospolis, where he busied himself with exposing the errors of Pelagius before the eyes of the Palestinian bishops by drawing back the veil of deception. Meanwhile, Orosius himself was accused of blasphemy by John of Jerusalem, as if he had said that no one could fulfill the law of God even with divine help. To clear himself of this charge, Orosius addressed his *Apology to the Palestinian Bishops*. In the following year, having obtained some relics of St. Stephen and having the letter of Avitus committed to his care, he returned to Africa. There, after he had related the craftiness of Pelagius to the Africans and shared the relics with his friends, he seems to have returned to Spain. Nothing certain is known of his death, whatever the writers of Spanish history may say. His writings follow:

*Seven Books of Histories against the Pagans*, in which he strives to refute the slander of the Gentiles who attributed the plucking of Rome by Alaric <note>The Visigothic king who sacked Rome in 410 AD.</note> to the Christian religion; he demonstrates that much greater calamities had occurred in the past while the ethnic <note>pagan</note> religion flourished. This work is called by many the *Hormesta of Orosius* <note>term: <term>Hormesta</term> — a mysterious title for Orosius's history, the origin of which remains a subject of scholarly debate.</note>, for which reason it is easier to guess than to establish anything for certain. ## ZOSIMUS

A Greek by nation, the son of Apameus or Abramius. On the 6th day of January in the year 417, he was made Pontiff of the Roman Church. When a statement of faith was offered to him—which *Pelagius* and *Cœlestius* <note>Pelagius and Cœlestius were the primary proponents of Pelagianism, which argued that humans could achieve salvation through free will without divine grace.</note> had previously intended for his predecessor Innocent—he sent two letters to the African Bishops. In these, he pronounced Pelagius and Cœlestius to be Catholics, even though they had been condemned by an African Synod. He accused the Africans themselves of having lent their ears too easily to Lazarus and Heros, the men who had informed against the heretics. Augustine himself does not deny that the "shifty heretics pulled the wool over the eyes of the good man" <note>original: "bono viro fucum fecisse," a Latin idiom for deception.</note> in this matter, writing: *When those minds, perverted by a wicked error, were treated somewhat more gently than the stricter doctrine of the Church required.* Augustine deals with this matter at length in that passage. Later, however, having been better informed by Augustine and the Africans, Zosimus changed his opinion; he issued a circular letter condemning Pelagius and his followers. 

During that same time, he received into communion *Apiarius*, a priest of Sicca in Africa, who had been excommunicated by his own Bishop, Urbanus, on account of his shameful crimes. Having sent legates to Africa, Zosimus not only demanded that Apiarius be restored (and that Urbanus be deposed if this were not done), but he also demanded that the authority of the Roman Bishop be recognized above all others. He claimed it was lawful to appeal to Rome from anywhere, and finally, that legates sent by him to Africa should judge cases arising there. He claimed all these rights for himself as if they had been sanctioned by the Canons of the Council of Nicaea. The African Fathers were stunned by these claims; they contended that they recognized no such power and that no such Nicene Canon existed. However, while this controversy was being examined, Zosimus died on September 17 in the year 418. 

There remain *13 Letters* written by him, found in the *Councils*, Volume 2, page 1556. Of these, two are to the Africans regarding the case of Pelagius; certain Roman Catholic writers would like to cast doubt on these based on slight conjectures. Yet in these letters, Zosimus—whom Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar.</note> rightly calls a <note>original: "præcox Hildebrandulus"</note> "precocious little Hildebrand" <note>Hildebrand was the birth name of Pope Gregory VII, who famously asserted supreme papal authority centuries later; the author suggests Zosimus was an early version of this ambition.</note> (to use the words of the illustrious *Vossius*)—seems to have done nothing foreign to his own character and habits. Accordingly, in the newest edition of the *Councils*, not even the slightest mark of <term>forgery</term> <note>original Greek: νοθεύσεως (notheuseōs), referring to spurious or illegitimate text.</note> is placed upon them. *Garnerius* extensively vindicates these as belonging to Zosimus in his Appendix to the works of Marius Mercator. The *Encyclical Letter* in which he condemned the Pelagians is lost; Augustine provides some fragments of it in *Letter 157* to Optatus, as does Prosper in *Against the Solicitor, chapter 10*, and the collector of testimonies of the *Apostolic See regarding grace and free will, chapters 5 and 6*, which are appended to the letters of Cœlestine I to the Gauls.

## BONIFACE

A Roman by birth, the son of Secundus the priest. He was established as Bishop in the Basilica of Julius on December 28, 418. At the same time, Eulalius the Archdeacon was ordained by another faction in the Constantinian Basilica. A significant schism arose from this, and both were ejected from the City by imperial edict. However, when Eulalius entered the City against the Emperor's command and acted as the Roman Bishop, Boniface was recalled and Eulalius was stripped of his authority. Eulalius was deposed by a Synod of 252 Bishops as one who had not been justly ordained, according to the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*. 

To Boniface, now established as Bishop, the African prelates wrote via legates returning to Rome. They stated they would observe the *Instruction* of Zosimus regarding the matter of Appeals only until they could be made more certain of the true Canons of the Council of Nicaea. For they had sent Legates to the East, who brought back with them <term>the most true and faithful copies</term> <note>original Greek: τὰ ἀληθέστατα καὶ πιστότατα ἴσα</note> of the Nicene Canons, along with letters from Cyril of Alexandria and Atticus of Constantinople. However, before their return, Boniface reached his final day on September 4, 423. There remain *3 Letters* and some fragments not found in the *Councils*, Volume 2, page 1582, and five other letters partly to Rufus of Thessalonica and partly to the Bishops established throughout Macedonia, etc., in the *Councils*, Volume 4, page 1702. These were taken from a manuscript in the Barberini Library...

<margin>418. * Cod. 35. L. 7. c. 27.</margin>
**PHILIP**, a Pamphylian by race <note>Pamphylia was a region in southern Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> and a native of Side—where he used to boast of being related to the scholar Troilus—flourished in the year 418 and thereafter. While still a Deacon, he heard the teachings of Chrysostom and was on very familiar terms with him. Having been ordained to the Priesthood, he contended with Sisinnius for the See of Constantinople <note>The "See" refers to the bishop's seat or jurisdictional authority.</note> after the death of Atticus in the year 427. Because Sisinnius was preferred over him, Philip thereafter criticized the man very sharply in his writings. He composed a *Christian History* in thirty-six books, beginning from the very creation of the world. He divided each book into several volumes, so that in total there were nearly a thousand; he prefixed an argument <note>A summary or introduction.</note> to each volume that was equal in length to the volume itself. It was indeed an immense work, filled with various learning, but it contained many useless things that were foreign to history (especially Christian history), and the subjects were treated with no order. Photius says of him: "He is abundant in words, not refined, but rather over-ornamental" <note>original Greek: πολύχους ταῖς λέξεσιν, οὐκ ἀστεῖος δε, ἀλλ' ἐπίχαρις.</note>. He pours out a great many words without any elegance or grace; indeed, he brings about satiety, or rather, annoyance: "He is more for display than for use" <note>original Greek: ἐπιδεικτικός μᾶλλον, ἢ ὠφέλιμος</note>, so much so that he possessed more ostentation than utility. Furthermore, Socrates—who lived earlier than Photius and was a contemporary <note>original Greek: σύγχρονος (synchronos).</note> of Philip himself—reports that Philip affected the "Asiatic" style of speaking <note>The "Asiatic style" was a rhetorical term for a flowery, verbose, and highly emotional way of writing, often contrasted with the more restrained Attic style.</note>. He also wrote against the Emperor Julian and refuted his books, among many other works. However, the injuries of time have snatched his writings from us, regardless of how many or of what quality they were. A fragment from his *Christian History*, seemingly excerpted by Nicephorus Callistus, is preserved in manuscript by the illustrious Mr. Dodwell.

<margin>418. † Auct. c. 72. || C. Th. lib. 16. Tit. viii. l. 25. & 26.</margin>
**SEVERUS**, Bishop of the Balearic island which today is called Minorca (or Menorca) in the Mediterranean Sea near Spain, flourished in the year 418. In that year occurred that miraculous conversion of the Jews of Minorca to the Christian faith, the history of which he himself follows at length. His *Encyclical Letter* survives, which is quite long, *concerning the conversion of the Jews on this Island, and the miracles performed there at the relics of St. Stephen*. This was recovered from the Vatican Archives by Baronius, in whose work it is found under the year 418, page 429. Miræus † writes with a rather gross error that these events took place and the Letter was given during the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus—that is, in the year of Christ 423—when it is clearly evident from the Letter itself that these things happened in the year after the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II, which is the year 418. Casimir Oudin, who recently published a supplement to Bellarmine's *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, followed the error of Miræus and transcribed his entire paragraph without changing a single word, let alone citing the author. Truly, such behavior is nothing new for this man.

<margin>418.</margin>
**HESYCHIUS**, Bishop of the city of Salona in Dalmatia <note>Modern-day Solin, Croatia.</note>, flourished in the year 418. A great intimacy existed between him and St. Augustine, whom he urged to explain the Prophets and the predictions found in Holy Scripture concerning the Last Day; he elicited two quite lengthy letters on that subject from Augustine. He died before the year 429, as St. Augustine mentions him with praise as already deceased in *The City of God*, Book 20, Chapter 5. A *Letter to Augustine* survives among the Augustinian works, number 79. It is not certain whether he wrote other things.

He flourished from the year 418, when he consulted Augustine on certain questions regarding the Pelagians <note>Pelagianism was a 5th-century belief system that denied original sin and emphasized human free will over divine grace.</note>. It is by no means clear whether he was a member of the clergy; rather, it is established that in the year 446 he was not yet either a Bishop or a Priest: thus, if he was ever initiated into Holy Orders, it must have happened at an advanced age. Garnerius <margin>* Prolegomena to the Works of Marius Mercator.</margin> * argues, with several points—not entirely certain, yet not to be dismissed—that he once served among the legal clerks <note>original: "Auditoriales Scholasticos," referring to administrative or legal assistants in the Roman imperial service.</note> in Rome. In the year 449 or the following year, he wrote against Theodoret. He either did not live until the year 451, or wrote nothing after that time. He was a most valiant champion of the Catholic faith against the Pelagians and Nestorians, and was learned in both Greek and Latin. He composed not many works by his own hand <note>original: "proprio Marte," a Latin idiom meaning "by his own effort/warfare."</note>. For the works of his that survive are almost entirely a patchwork of excerpts from elsewhere, especially taken from the writings of heretics. Certainly, the works he translated from Greek into Latin are far more numerous than those he produced by his own labor: although he himself usually added prefaces to his translations that are quite useful for the study of Church history. His writings follow, listed in order as they are arranged in the most accurate edition by Garnerius.

<margin>418.</margin>**PHILIP**, a Pamphylian by race and a native of Side—where he used to boast of being related to the family of Troilus—flourished in the year 418. While still a long-serving Deacon, he listened to [John] Chrysostom and was on very familiar terms with him. Having been ordained to the priesthood, after the death of Atticus in the year 425, he contended with Sisinnius for the See of Constantinople. However, when Sisinnius was preferred over him, he sharply attacked the man in his writings regarding the circus. He composed a work called *Christian History* in thirty-six books, starting from the very beginning. He divided each book into <unclear>several</unclear> volumes, so that in total there were nearly a thousand of them. He assigned a specific topic to each volume, and the volume itself was as long as its introductory summary. The work was indeed filled with varied learning, but it contained many things foreign to history, especially Christian history, and treated matters without any <note>original: "ratione," meaning methodical reasoning or logic</note> logical order. Photius <margin>* Codex 35.</margin> says of him, <note>original Greek: πολύχους ταῖς λέξεσιν, ἐν ἀστείοις δὲ, οὐδὲ</note> *“He uses a great abundance of words, yet without any refinement or grace;* <margin>Book 7, chapter 27.</margin> *indeed, he brings about satiety, or rather, annoyance.”* He was <note>original Greek: ἐπιδεικτικὸς μᾶλλον, ἢ ὠφέλιμος</note> more for show than for use, to the point that he possessed more ostentation than utility. Furthermore, Photius reveals that like the ancient Philostratus, Philip’s *muddle* <note>original Greek: σύγχυσιν (synchysis), referring to a confused or disordered style</note> betrays an affected Asiatic style of speaking. He also wrote *Against Emperor Julian* and refuted his books, among other works. However, the passage of time has snatched away most of his writings, regardless of their quantity or quality. A fragment from his *Christian History*, seemingly excerpted by Nicephorus Callistus, is preserved in manuscript by the illustrious Dodwell.

<margin>418.</margin>**SEVERUS**, Bishop of the Balearic island which is today called Minorca (or Menorca) in the Mediterranean Sea near Spain, flourished in the year 418. In that year, there occurred that remarkable conversion of the Jews of Minorca to the faith of Christ, the history of which he himself follows in great detail. There exists an *Encyclical Letter of his, quite lengthy, concerning the conversion of the Jews on this Island, and concerning the miracles performed there at the relics of Saint Stephen* <note>The discovery of St. Stephen’s relics in 415 caused a surge of religious fervor across the Mediterranean.</note>. This was first published by Baronius from the Vatican Archives <margin>† Author, chapter 72.</margin> where it is found under the year 418, page 429. Miraeus † fell into a thick error by dating these events and the letter to the year 423, during the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus; yet it is clearly evident from the letter itself that it happened in the year after the 11th consulship of Honorius and the 2nd of Constantius—that is, the year 418. <margin>|| Theodosian Code, book 16, title viii, laws 25 & 26.</margin> Baronius, therefore, correctly records these events. There do exist || two laws of Theodosius the Younger *Concerning Synagogues and the Offerings of Jews*, given during the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus (the year 423); Baronius attached the first of these to the end of the Letter to illustrate it, which perhaps led a man who was otherwise not diligent into error. Casimir Oudin followed Miraeus's error and copied his entire paragraph—changing only a single word and failing to cite the author—in the supplement to Bellarmine's *On Ecclesiastical Writers* which he recently published. Truly, such behavior is nothing new for this man.

<margin>418.</margin>**HESYCHIUS**, Bishop of the city of Salona in Dalmatia, flourished in the year 418. He died before the year 433, as Saint Augustine mentions him with praise as already deceased in *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 5. A *Letter to Augustine* survives among the Augustinian collection, numbered 79. It is not certain whether he wrote other works.

## W R I T I N G S.

**The first part**, containing those short works which concern the Pelagian heresy.

✥ *A Memorandum on the name of Caelestius*, composed in the Greek language in the year 429 and presented to the Emperor Theodosius and other men of great reputation, and later rendered into the Latin language by Marius. It was first published by Labbe in the *Collection of Councils, Volume 2, page 1512.*

✥ *A book of critical notes on certain sayings of Julian, addressed to the Priest Pientius.* The first part of this short work (for it is divided into two) is titled, *A Memorandum to the Reader against the heresy of Pelagius and Caelestius, or even the writings of Julian.*

+ *A Letter of Nestorius to Caelestius the Pelagian*, translated into Latin by Marius.

+ *Four Sermons or Treatises of Nestorius against the heresy of Pelagius or Caelestius*, translated into Latin with a Preface added.

+ *The Creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia* <note>Theodore was a prominent theologian whose ideas were seen as the precursor to Nestorianism</note> translated into Latin, preceded by a *Memorandum* or *Prologue* by Marius; it is followed by a *Refutation* of the creed composed by Marius.

+ *Excerpts from five books of Theodore against Saint Augustine*, collected and translated into Latin by Marius.

**The second part**, containing those short works which concern the Nestorian cause.

✥ *A Preface to various Sermons of Nestorius*, translated into Latin by himself.

+ *Thirteen Sermons of Nestorius on the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, translated into Latin.

+ *A Letter on the distinction between the heresy of Nestorius and the dogmas of Paul of Samosata, Ebion, Photinus, and Marcellus* <note>These were earlier heretics who held various views on the nature of Christ deemed unorthodox by the Church</note>.

+ *The Protest of Eusebius against the errors of Nestorius*, translated into Latin.

✥ *A Homily of Proclus against Nestorius*, translated, it seems, by Marius.

✥ *The fourth Letter of Saint Cyril, and the second of Nestorius*, translated by Marius.

✥ *Eighty-five Excerpts from the writings of Nestorius*, collected by Cyril and translated by Marius.

✥ *The twelve Anathemas of Nestorius, set against the same number from Cyril*, translated into Latin by Marius, with a *Refutation* or *Contradiction* added to each.

✥ *Cyril's Response against the Objections of the Orientals written by Andrew of Samosata*, translated by Marius.

✥ *Cyril's Response to the Reproofs of Theodoret*, translated by the same.

✥ *Cyril's Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten Word* (much more complete than in the Greek edition of Cyril), translated by Marius.

✥ *Excerpts from the book of Theodore of Mopsuestia on the Incarnation of Christ*, collected and translated by Marius.

✥ *Excerpts from the "Pantalegium" of Theodoret, three Letters by the same, and Fragments from his letter to Himerius, Bishop of Nicomedia, and from a Sermon delivered at Antioch after the death of Cyril*, translated into Latin by Marius.

*The Epilogue of Marius Mercator.*

The reader should note that the *Small Works marked with a cross* were illustrated with most learned notes by Rigberius and published in Brussels, 1673, in duodecimo format; in this work, they are frequently cited by us under the title of the *Acts of Marius Mercator*. The *Nestorian Treatise of a certain person*, which begins with the words <note>original: "Contumelias quidem in me Hæreticorum arbitror"</note> "I indeed consider the insults of the heretics against me," was translated into Latin by Marius and placed at the end of his edition by Rigberius; I have not yet been able to find this in the edition by Garnier.

The Works of Marius Mercator were published, adorned with very extensive and most learned commentaries by Jean Garnier, in Paris, 1673, in folio; thereafter in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 27, page 129; and finally edited with notes by Stephen Baluze, Paris, 1684, in octavo.

The sixth Action of the Council of Ephesus, translated into Latin by Marius, was first provided by Baluze in the *New Collection of Councils*, Paris, 1683, in folio.

## NICEAS,
Of Romatiana <note>This likely refers to Remesiana in modern Serbia, though the text notes an alternative identification.</note> (that is, as Baronius <margin>*</margin> rightly interprets, of Aquileia), was a Subdeacon under Bishop Chromatius, and the successor to the see of Aquileia after his death: he flourished around the year 420 and thereafter. While still a young man, he was very familiar with Jerome, whom he accompanied for a long time as he traveled through foreign regions; Jerome himself testifies to this in a letter written to him while he was still a subdeacon, which is found in Volume 1. He survived the destruction of his city by the Huns, and he consulted Pope Leo regarding certain Church Canons that had been violated during the Hunnic invasion; Leo's response, given in the year 458, survives among his letters as number 79.

<margin>
* Concerning Church Writers, chapter 22.
</margin>

Gennadius says <margin>*</margin> that he composed, in simple and clear language, *Six small books of instruction for Neophytes* <note>newly baptized Christians</note>; in the first he instructed the neophytes, in the second he attacked the errors of Paganism, in the third he treated the faith of the "unique Majesty" <note>referring to the Trinity</note>, in the fourth he argued against Astrology <term>Genethlologiam; the practice of casting horoscopes based on birth</term>, in the fifth he discussed the Creed, and in the sixth the Paschal Lamb. He also wrote a small book to a fallen Virgin, urging her to perform penance.

## JULIANUS,
An Italian by race and an Apulian by country, he was commonly held to be the son of Memorius, Bishop of Capua, and Juliana, a woman of high rank (Augustine <margin>*</margin> and Marius Mercator <margin>†</margin> both praise both parents exceedingly). However, Marius Mercator hints that a well-known rumor once held that he had been substituted for such parents by a nurse, and was in truth the offspring of a common house-slave. He was born before the year 386. In theological matters, he had as teachers first Pelagius (either in Rome or Sicily), and then Theodore of Mopsuestia. He served as a Deacon under his father; and while still a youth, after undertaking the office of Lector, he married a most choice woman named Ia <note>The OCR "Jam" is a likely error for "Ia," the known name of Julian's wife.</note>, the daughter of Bishop Aemilius of Benevento; Paulinus of Nola wrote a wedding song <term>epithalamium; a poem or song written specifically for a bride and groom</term> for their marriage <margin>||</margin>, which is still extant.

<margin>
|| Poem number 14.
* The first Memorandum.
</margin>

Finally (which Marius Mercator <margin>*</margin> records was done by Pope Innocent), he was appointed Bishop of the city of Eclanum, located among the Hirpini between Campania and Apulia; the name of this city is found strangely corrupted among writers. For it is sometimes called Celanensis, or Edanensis, or Actenellensis, or Atelensis or Attellenensis. On account of the Pelagian dogmas, which he began to defend vigorously around the year 417, he was stripped of his see. In the year (it seems) 420, he soon set out for the East, and being expelled from Constantinople in the year 421, he lay hidden for a long time in Cilicia with Theodore of Mopsuestia; there he gave himself entirely to the labor of writing books to defend his heresy. In the year 423, after a Synod of Cilician Bishops was held, he was condemned for heresy, with Theodore himself consenting to the condemnation, at least in appearance. In the year 424, after the death of Pope Boniface, having been enticed from the East to the West by the vain hope of recovering his bishopric, he seems to have returned. Driven out of Italy, in the year 426 he set out again for Constantinople, and hoping for the advancement of Nestorius, he appealed to the Emperor Theodosius with frequent prayers regarding the restoration of his bishopric. Concerning this matter, Nestorius informed Pope Celestine by two letters, which survive in Latin in Volume 3 of the *Councils*. In the year 429, after a memorandum was presented by Mercator... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Mercatore" for the next page.</note>

<margin>
† Works of Mercator, Part 1.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the biography and bibliography of Julian of Eclanum, a major figure in the Pelagian controversy. The previous page ended with the beginning of the entry for Julian (following Niceas), and this page details his later life, character, and written works.</meta>

<page-num>309</page-num>
<header>The Nestorian Age.</header>

<margin>
THE 5th CENTURY
from the Year 400.
</margin>

<margin>
* Pelagian History, book 1, chapter 6.
</margin>

<margin>
† Acts, page 20. Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, chapter 45.
</margin>

By a memorandum <note>original: "Commonitorio"</note> sent by Marius Mercator <note>A layman and staunch defender of orthodoxy against Pelagianism.</note> to the Emperor Theodosius regarding Julian's errors, Julian was again expelled from the City <note>Rome</note>. He was condemned by Pope Celestine the following year in a Roman Synod, as well as in the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus in the year 431. At that time, Theodoret and other delegates of the Ephesian assembly, in a letter sent to Rufus of Thessalonica, make mention of a certain Julian, Bishop of Eridica. The illustrious Vossius * identifies this man as the same as our Julian, and conjectures that after being ejected from Campania, he held the see of Eridica. Consequently, there are those who suspect that this "Eridica" is actually Ericusa or Ericodes (commonly called Alicur), an island in the Sicilian sea where Julian might have fled. However, I can hardly persuade myself that this Julian, Bishop of Eridica, is the same as ours. Holstenius confirms our opinion; he corrects an error in the common manuscript of the said Letter, and in the place of "the Erican church" <note>original Greek: "Ἐρικάνης ἐκκλησίας"</note>, he reads "the Sardinian church" <note>original Greek: "τ. Σαρδινῆς ἐκκλησίας"</note>.

In the year 439, pretending to have abandoned his unusual errors, Julian pleaded at length with Pope Sixtus <note>Xystus III</note> for the recovery of his see at Eclanum. But his effort was in vain, and he died, as some believe, in the following year. Yet, if we prefer to follow the calculations of Garnier, he extended his life at least until the year 454. However, what the illustrious Vignier claims in the preface to the supplement of St. Augustine exceeds all belief: that Julian reached the beginning of the following century, specifically the time of Fulgentius. He adds that after Julian had served for some time as a schoolmaster among the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who taught that humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace.</note>, he finally died in an obscure village in Sicily. A tomb was placed over him when he died with this inscription, which was still being read in the ninth century: **HERE RESTS IN PEACE JULIAN, A CATHOLIC BISHOP.**

He was a bold man of sharp intellect, learned in both Greek and Latin, and very well-versed in the Holy Scriptures. He possessed a marvelous power of eloquence and fluency, so much so that he was commonly regarded as the "Roman Demosthenes" <note>Demosthenes was the greatest of the ancient Greek orators; this is high praise for Julian's speaking skills.</note>. He knew how to perfectly disguise the heresy he cherished with ambiguous words and phrases; for this reason, he is called "Pyrrhus" and "Loxias" <note>Loxias is a title for Apollo meaning "the Ambiguous One," referring to the cryptic nature of his oracles.</note> by Marius Mercator †. He was also considered not without fame for his piety, and was especially conspicuous for his extraordinary charity toward the poor. During a time of famine and distress, he spent all his own resources to relieve the destitute; by this appearance of virtue, he held many people captive to his errors. Nevertheless, he was quite infamous for his slanderous tongue, so much so that Marius Mercator accuses him of having vomited forth innumerable insults and reproaches against Augustine throughout his writings—something Augustine himself laments in many places. For this reason, Julian is also openly condemned in the Decree of Pseudo-Gelasius.

### WRITINGS.

**Two Letters to Pope Zosimus:** which St. Augustine refutes in four books addressed to Boniface; fragments of these letters can be found scattered there, as well as in Mercator’s *Commonitorium*, chapters 7, 6, and 9. Of these, the second, which is quite lengthy and is also titled the **Statement of Faith** <note>original: "Libellus Fidei"</note>, was written in the year 418 in the name of eighteen bishops of Sicily who refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius. In this small work, he first treats the Supreme Trinity, the Incarnation of the Word, and the other articles of the Creed; then he discusses his own dogma and the Pelagian questions, namely, concerning the grace of God, Free Will, etc. Soon after, he condemns the dogmas of the heretics (and among them, secretly, those of the Catholics). Finally, he gives various reasons why the bishops of his party refused to sign the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius, and having quietly rebuked the Roman Pontiff, he appeals to a plenary Synod. Jean Garnier of Paris first brought this *Statement of Faith* to light, attributed it to Julian, and published it in 1668 in octavo, illustrated with notes and three long dissertations. It was published again among the works of Marius Mercator, Part I, page 320. Although Julian himself admits to having written two letters to Zosimus, he says a third was directed to Rome in his name, though he strenuously denied it was his own work (as seen in Augustine's *Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapter 17).

**A Letter to Rufus, Bishop of Thessalonica**, written in the name of eighteen Pelagian bishops. See Augustine’s *Unfinished Work*, book 2, chapter 178. Many fragments of this Letter survive in St. Augustine’s books against Boniface. Garnier presents these collected into one in the Appendix to Part I of Marius Mercator.

*Eight books to Florus (Gennadius incorrectly records seven) against Augustine's second book on Marriages.* For those who think these eight books were opposed to the aforementioned six books of Augustine are mistaken. For although this work of Julian followed that of Augustine by nearly eight years, Julian either did not know of those six books of Augustine or pretended not to know of them. They were written in Cilicia in the year 422, while he lay in hiding for a long time with Theodore of Mopsuestia, but they were not published until the year 426. Augustine refuted them in eight books published shortly before his death; where fragments from Julian's books are cited throughout. Very many excerpts from these same works are cited by Marius Mercator in his book of *Subnotations*.

FASTIDIUS, called Priscus, a Briton by nationality, and according to Gennadius \*, a Bishop of the Britains: hence more recent authors, who love to encrust genuine antiquity with new fictions, claim he was the Metropolitan [Archbishop] of London. He flourished in the year 420. He wrote *To Fatalis*, a pious and most excellent widow, *a golden little book on the Christian life and the cultivation of widowhood*. It exists, without the author's name, among the works of Augustine, Volume 9, page 888; Lucas Holstenius <note>A 17th-century German humanist and Vatican librarian.</note> edited it in Rome in 1663, restored to the credit of a manuscript codex and assigned to Fastidius. From this one book, Gennadius (who alone among the ancients, as far as I know, mentions Fastidius) made two: <margin>† Century 1, chapter 41. || Age 5, page 86.</margin> *one on the Christian Life, and another on Preserving Widowhood*. Bale † <note>John Bale, a 16th-century English historian.</note> listed four, namely: *On the Christian Life, book 1; On the Doctrine of the Spirit, book 1; On Preserving Widowhood, book 1; and On Pious Admonitions, book 1.* John Pits || <note>An English Catholic biographer often criticized for copying Bale's errors.</note> did even worse, adding his own error to Bale’s: what Gennadius said regarding the aforementioned booklet—namely, that it was *sound doctrine worthy of God*—Pits transformed into a book title: *On Doctrine Worthy of God and Spiritual, book 1.* Johannes <margin>\* On Illustrious Writers, folio 37, face 2.</margin> Trithemius \* was much more accurate, recording only this regarding Fastidius’s book: *Content to interpret Gennadius, he wrote a certain volume with sound doctrine.* As for what [Thomas] Dempster <note>A Scottish scholar notorious for claiming English or Irish figures as Scottish.</note> affirms in his *History of the Scots*, book 6, number 536—that our Fastidius wrote a *Chronicle of the Scots*—that must be forgiven as the work of a peddler of trifles who is almost always foolish regarding the history of his own people.

<margin>420.</margin>
LEPORIUS, formerly a monk of Marseille (or as others say, of Aix), and a Priest, flourished around the year 420. At first he followed the camp of Pelagius <note>Pelagianism was a heresy that denied original sin and emphasized human effort over divine grace.</note>: then, warned by the Gallic bishops, and more fully instructed by Augustine after he had crossed over into Africa, he was restored to a sounder mind around the year 425. He wrote a *Little Book of Correction, or Satisfaction, to the Bishops of Gaul*; in which he corrected his errors and gave thanks for the cure they provided him. He also revoked a perverse opinion on the Incarnation of Christ which he had rashly imbibed in the past, confessing a single person in two natures. Jacques Sirmond <note>A famous French Jesuit scholar and editor of church councils.</note> was the first to bring this booklet to light from a manuscript of Hérivaux, and published it with other *Dogmatic Works* of the ancients in Paris, 1630, in octavo. It is also found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 7, page 14; and in the *Councils*, Volume 2, page 1678; and a more corrected version was edited by Garnier in the *Appendix* to part 1 of the works of Marius Mercator, Dissertation 2, chapter 20, page 225. The reader should be warned that this booklet is sometimes cited by the ancients under the name of Saint *Augustine*: perhaps because it was written at his urging and approved by him. On this basis, Pasquier Quesnel <note>A French theologian known for his Jansenist views.</note>, in his notes on the 134th letter of Saint Leo (page 906), attempts to assert that Augustine was the genuine author—relying on the authority of a German manuscript and the second Act of the Council of Chalcedon, where a passage from this booklet is placed among the testimonies of Blessed Augustine; he also brings forward certain conjectures of no great weight to strengthen his opinion. Of this Lepo- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the name Leporius on the next page.</note>

**PAULINUS**, a Deacon and Notary of Saint Ambrose of Milan, later elevated to the dignity of the priesthood. The author known as *Praedestinatus* (in the edition by Sirmond) calls him the procurator and defender of the Church of Milan. He flourished in the year 420; indeed, he began to be known as early as 412, when, while serving in Carthage, he accused Caelestius of heresy before Bishop Aurelius and vigorously defeated him at the Council of Carthage. There exists a *Life of the Blessed Ambrose*, composed at the urging of Saint Augustine, though written perhaps too sparingly and meagerly; it is usually placed at the beginning of Ambrose's works. *There is also a small book giving thanks to Pope Zosimus for the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius (Collection of Councils, Vol. ii, p. 1578).* Although Isidore of Seville attributes a book on the *Blessings of the Patriarchs* to our Paulinus, it is known to everyone everywhere that it should be assigned to Rufinus of Aquileia.

<margin>420.</margin>
**EUODIUS**, by nation an African, it seems, and Bishop of Uzalis in Africa. A close friend of Saint Augustine, he flourished in the year 420. Having obtained a small portion of the relics of Saint Stephen from Orosius (who was bringing them from Palestine to Africa), he erected a Basilica in memory of the Holy Martyr; after observing many miracles performed there, he saw to it that their history was committed to writing (as can be believed). Indeed, in the Antwerp edition of Saint Augustine’s works (1577) and several others, there are two books addressed to our Euodius *On the Miracles of Saint Stephen*. Since these do not bear the author’s name, they are commonly attributed to Euodius and seem to have been composed at his command. He wrote several *Letters* to Augustine, four of which survive among Augustine's correspondence (numbers 98, 246, 247, and 249), not to mention a fifth to Pope Innocent, which he penned along with four other bishops. He is also said to have written a *Book on Faith, or on the Unity of the Trinity against the Manichaeans*, which is found in Volume 6 of Saint Augustine’s works. This man was distinct from that other Euodius, an African bishop, who in the year 404 was sent as an envoy by the Synod of Carthage to the Emperor Honorius (along with Bishop Theasius) to expose the injuries and audacity of the Donatists, and who was killed by the Donatists in 408 along with the same Theasius.

<margin>
420.
* On Famous Men, ch. 51.
</margin>
**VIGILIUS**, a Deacon, flourished around the year 420. According to Gennadius, he wrote in brief and clear language a *Rule for Monks*, containing the discipline of the entire monastic life. That Rule exists, edited by Lucas Holstenius in the *Code of Rules*, page 89 (Paris, 1663, quarto).

<margin>420.</margin>
**ISIDORUS**, likely of Spanish origin, Bishop of Córdoba, seems to have flourished in the year 420. He is said to have died in the year 430. Pseudo-Dexter <note>A 16th-century forgery of a late antique chronicle, which the author here treats as a source.</note>, in his *Chronicle* for the year 423, asserts (along with Sigebert of Gembloux and Trithemius) that he wrote *Four books of Allegories or Commentaries on all the books of Kings* and dedicated them to Paul Orosius of Tarragona. There are indeed *Allegories* among the works of Isidore of Seville which likely belong to our Isidore, because they were written to Orosius, who was his <term>contemporary <note>original: "σύγχρονος" (synchronos)</note></term>. Certainly, allegorical commentaries of this kind are listed among the works of Isidore of Seville neither by Braulio nor by Ildefonsus. Pseudo-Dexter also reports in more than one place that Isidore explained the Gospel of Luke with *Commentaries*. Francisco de Bivar discusses the various Isidores and Spanish writers at length in his notes on Dexter’s *Chronicle* for the year 423.

<margin>420.</margin>
**SEVERUS**, an African, Bishop of Milevis, and an intimate friend of Augustine, whose writings he read studiously. He flourished in the year 420. He died while Augustine was still living. At his death, he designated a successor bishop to the clergy alone, without waiting for the consent of the common people. After he died, when a suspicion of a riot being stirred up arose, Augustine hurried to Milevis at the request of the clergy. Through his intervention, peace was established, and the bishop whom Severus had designated was ordained—as is clear from the records of Augustine regarding the designation of Erradius as his own successor, which [are found] among Augustine's letters...

**EUDOCIA**, named *Athenais* while she was still a Pagan, was the daughter of Leontius, an Athenian Sophist and Philosopher. She was instructed by him in every branch of fine literature, so much so that she emerged remarkably learned. In the year 421, in the twentieth year of her age, when the Emperor Theodosius <note>Theodosius II, reigned 402–450</note> was about to take her as his wife, she embraced the Christian faith and was washed in the saving bath <note>original: *salutari lavacro tincta est* — she was baptized</note> by Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople. In the year 432, she was proclaimed *Augusta* <note>Empress</note> by Theodosius. In the year 445, for a slight cause regarding her unstained marital fidelity—driven by a suspicion of her being too fond of Paulinus—she undeservedly fell into the Emperor's indignation. For this reason, she withdrew to Jerusalem, where she devoted herself entirely for many years to building and decorating churches and relieving the poor. Finally restored to her husband's favor, she returned to Constantinople and lived with him until his death. After he died, she returned to Palestine and dedicated the remainder of her life to pious leisure, dying there in the year 459. As she lay dying, she bound herself with an oath that she was entirely innocent of any crime of violated chastity. She wrote several poems in Greek, the style of which Photius describes as follows:

* Code 183.
</margin>
> This poem is worthy of wonder, both because it is by a woman, and one raised in royalty, and because it is so beautiful. Indeed, the labor is illustrious, composed in heroic meter as well as any other ever was. <note>original: "ὅπερ (Poema) ὅτι κὴ γυναικὸς... admiratione sanè dignum iudicatur."</note>

->W R I T I N G S.<-

|| Addition, chapter 307.

*Homeric Centos* <note>A "cento" is a poem made up of lines or phrases borrowed from another author, in this case, Homer</note>, begun by a certain Patrician named Pelagius (whence they are often attributed to him) but completed and organized by Eudocia; as Zonaras † expressly relates and as the inscription of the work itself makes clear. They survive in Latin in almost every edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, and in Greek and Latin in the Bignean collection of *Christian Poets*, *Paris 1624, p. 95.* Aubertus Miraeus || errs immensely in attributing these Centos to Eudocia Augusta, the wife of Constantine XI (surnamed *Ducas*), who died in the year 1067.

*A Metaphrasis of the Octateuch* <note>A poetic retelling of the first eight books of the Bible</note> composed in heroic verse, in eight books.

*A Metaphrasis of the Prophecies of Zechariah and Daniel:* In these retellings, Photius testifies that Eudocia expressed the sacred text religiously and "foot by foot" <note>original: *κατὰ πόδας* — meaning word-for-word or very closely</note>, adding nothing and changing nothing, so much so that they could be considered legitimate versions of the sacred books.

*The History of the Blessed Martyr Cyprian and the Virgin Justina*, contained in three books written in heroic verse. This Cyprian was distinct from Cyprian of Carthage; he is said to have suffered at Rome under Diocletian along with Justina. Photius, in Code 184, provides a summary of the whole history of both, excerpted from this poem. The diligent reader will discover a wonderful agreement between this History by Eudocia and the *Penitence of Cyprian* (which holds a place in the Oxford edition of Cyprian’s works) if they compare the Photius summary with that other small work.

*A Heroic Poem on the victory reported by her husband Theodosius over the Persians*; which Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian</note> mentions in book 7, chapter 21.

**MAXIMUS**, whose place of origin is uncertain, was the Bishop of Turin <note>original: *Augustæ Taurinorum*</note> in Subalpine Gaul, the region which today is called Piedmont. He was also present in 451 at the Synod of Milan, when the provincial bishops were assembled to confirm with their own judgment what Pope Leo had written to Flavian against Eutyches. ...our Maximus <note>Maximus of Turin (died c. 423), a prominent bishop and preacher.</note> signed his name after the Roman Pontiff, and according to the opinion of Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a cardinal and ecclesiastical historian.</note>, this was due to the seniority of his age as an active Bishop. <margin>423.</margin>
**T**HEODORET <note>c. 393–457 AD, a prolific author and influential bishop of Cyrus.</note>, Syrian by nation and a native of Antioch, was born toward the close of the fourth century. The exact year is not entirely certain, though Garnerius <note>Jean Garnier (1612–1681), a Jesuit scholar and editor of Theodoret’s works.</note> dates it to the year 386. His parents were distinguished both for their piety and their wealth. His mother, a most pious woman, had remained childless for thirteen years of marriage; at her husband's encouragement, she asked Macedonius, a most holy ascetic, to obtain a son for her from God through his prayers. After three years, he did so, but on the condition that she consecrate the child to God. Thus, being "given by God" and "returned to God" by his parents, he seems to have rightly received the name Theodoret <note>From the Greek *Theodoros*, meaning "Gift of God."</note>. He had not yet completed his seventh year when he was sent to the Monastery of St. Euprepius, located not far from Antioch, to be educated in both literature and virtue. In that place, he formed a very close friendship with Nestorius and John (later Bishops of Constantinople and Antioch, respectively). He had as teachers Theodore of Mopsuestia and John Chrysostom <note>Two of the most famous theologians of the Antiochene school, known for literal and historical biblical interpretation.</note>, from whom he learned both great eloquence and the best method for explaining the Holy Scriptures. While still a young man, he was ordained a Lector by Porphyrius, Bishop of Antioch, and a Deacon by Alexander, Porphyrius’s successor; yet he did not leave his monastic way of life. In the year 423 according to Baronius, but 420 according to Garnerius (who relies on more certain chronological accounts), he was appointed Bishop of Cyrus, a notable city in the Syrian province of Euphratensis, taking the place of the recently deceased Isidore. He found the region of Cyrus miserably overgrown with the unlucky weeds of heresy; Arians, Macedonians, Apollinarists, and especially Marcionites <note>Followers of Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament and the God of the Jews.</note> were rampant everywhere. He immediately prepared himself to drive them out as the worst plague of the Church, doing so at frequent risk to his own life. Meanwhile, he met with such success that he himself boasts that ten thousand Marcionites were washed in the waters of bap-
<margin>* Epistle 145. compare Epistle 81.</margin>
tism by him. In this work, he had as "fellow workers" <note>original: *synergous* (συνεργούς)</note> many anchorites <note>Hermits or religious recluses.</note>, including Maras, Jacob, and others, who had long ago chosen the territory of Cyrus as the seat of their ascetic life. Around the year 429, Nestorius began to offer certain unhealthy doctrines concerning Christ the Lord and His Blessed Mother. After the matter was first debated in the Synod of Alexandria, Cyril proposed twelve "Chapters" <note>Also known as the Twelve Anathemas of Cyril of Alexandria.</note> for an examination of the faith. Theodoret, having been asked by Nestorius (his former close friend and fellow student), drew his pen against Cyril; and those Chapters...

<page-num>315</page-num>

...or the Anathemas, he attempted to strike out Apollinarianism <note>The heresy which claimed Christ had a divine mind rather than a human soul.</note> from them, and refuted them in a book that was quite bitter and virulent. Meanwhile, carried away by the heat of the dispute, he did not hesitate to assert—at least in careless and highly dangerous words—that the Blessed Mary did not give birth to the Word made flesh, that the natures in Christ were not united *according to hypostasis* <gloss>hypostatically</gloss>, and that there was not a single *hypostasis* <gloss>person or individual existence</gloss>. Finally, he claimed that God the Word could not be said to have died. Lest he leave anything untried, he sent letters on this matter everywhere to the Monks, and charging Cyril with even graver things, he portrayed his Chapters <note>Cyril of Alexandria's 12 Anathemas</note> as a "Lerna of ancient heresies" <note>original: "hæreseωn antiquarum Lernam." A reference to the Hydra of Lerna; a source of many evils.</note>. In the year 431, having been summoned to the Council of Ephesus, he withdrew into a secret gathering separately with John of Antioch and other Eastern Bishops. After nearly two months, having six Bishops of his faction joined with him, he was sent to Constantinople as a legate from this "Conciliabulum" <note>An unofficial or illicit council.</note> in the name of the Easterners. However, ordered by the Emperor to stay at Chalcedon and excluded from the Church by the Bishop of the city, he gave frequent sermons to the people in a great hall, which were received everywhere with immense applause from the listeners. Admitted to the Emperor, he dealt with him with great *parrhesia* <gloss>boldness of speech</gloss>, but he "lost both labor and oil" <note>A Latin idiom, "operam & oleum perdidit," meaning to waste one's time and effort.</note>. For the Emperor, having finally approved Cyril’s cause and condemned Nestorius, sent the Eastern legates back, each to his own province.

<margin>* In the Excerpts of his Works, Part 2.</margin>
Returning home, therefore, Theodoret published five books against the Synod of Ephesus, which Marius Mercator <note>A Latin ecclesiastical writer and contemporary of the events.</note> says were written at the instigation of the devil. A little later, through the mediation of the Emperor, a peace was made between Cyril and John of Antioch, Theodoret, and the other Easterners; but the "badly healed ulcer" broke open again later. In the year 444, when Cyril had died, he treated him even more harshly; indeed, he could not contain himself from publicly expressing the joy of his soul. The Emperor, finally more moved by all these things, ordered him in the year 445 to stay at his own home and did not allow him to leave the borders of the region of Cyrrhus. In the year 449, a second Synod was assembled at Ephesus (to which the name "Latrocinalis" <note>The "Robber Synod," known for the use of military force to coerce the bishops.</note> has stuck), in which, with Dioscorus presiding and holding all laws in contempt, and extorting the votes of the Bishops by force and arms, Theodoret—whom the Emperor himself had expressly commanded to be absent from the Council—was deposed; he had already been struck with anathema by Dioscorus at Alexandria. Where was Theodoret to turn now? Should he appeal to a Synod? He had been condemned by one. Should he flee to the Emperor? He had recently found him most hostile, both for other reasons and specifically because he had ordained Count Irenaeus as Bishop of Tyre, even though Irenaeus had been expelled from the court and was a *digamus* <gloss>married twice</gloss> <note>At the time, a second marriage often disqualified a man from the episcopate under canon law.</note>. He therefore called upon Rome to defend his cause, sending two *Chorepiscopi* <gloss>country bishops</gloss>, Abramius and Hypatius, along with the Abbot Alypius. Pope Leo, therefore, having reviewed the case and approved his faith, absolved Theodoret and, as far as was in his power, restored him to his see.

In the year 450, after the death of the Emperor Theodosius, Theodoret was recalled from exile by his successor Marcian (for he had retreated to the Monastery of Apamea after being driven from the Province of Cyrrhus) and was restored to his see. In the following year, the Fourth General Council <note>The Council of Chalcedon, 451.</note> was held, in which Theodoret, specifically summoned by the Emperor, took his place despite the protests of the Egyptians. He expressly professed the Catholic faith, though he hesitated for a long time to condemn Nestorius. Finally, in the eighth session, his case was more fully examined; and after he struck Nestorius with anathema, he was at last restored with full rights by the solemn acclamation of everyone, and he condemned Eutyches by his synodal vote. Returning home from Chalcedon, he gave himself entirely to writing books and honorable leisure, leaving the episcopal duties mostly to the care of Hypatius. He died in the year 457, or at least the following year, over seventy years old (though there are some who extend his life for several more years), and was placed in an urn with James the Thaumaturge <gloss>the Wonder-worker</gloss>, a most loyal friend who died shortly after. After death, his reputation experienced varied fortunes. During the reign of Justin, his image was carried into the church with solemn pomp by certain clerics of the Church of Cyrrhus, placed upon the episcopal throne, and a sacred assembly was celebrated in his honor. He had been condemned shortly before by the Emperor Anastasius and his followers, a condemnation that was carried out even more sharply and clearly by the Fifth Council held at Constantinople under Justinian.

Theodoret was truly worthy of a better fate and a gentler judgment. He preserved the greatest purity of soul and the discipline of a strict life, which he had learned from childhood under the best masters of true and primitive *askesis* <gloss>ascetic discipline</gloss>, throughout the entire course of his life...

### THEODORET,

a Syrian by nationality and a resident of Antioch, was born as the fourth century was drawing to a close. The exact year is not entirely certain, although **Garnier** <note>Jean Garnier (1612–1681), a Jesuit scholar and editor of Theodoret's works.</note> attributes it to the year 386. He had parents who were distinguished both for their piety and their wealth. His mother, a truly most pious woman, had already passed thirteen years in a childless marriage when, at the encouragement of her husband, she asked **Macedonius**, a most holy Ascetic <note>A monk living a life of extreme self-denial.</note>, to obtain a son for her from God through his prayers. After three years, he finally did so, but on the condition that she dedicate the child to God. Thus, as one "given by God" and "returned to God by his parents," he seems to have rightly taken the name **Theodoret** <note>The name Theodoret translates from Greek as "Gift of God."</note> from that time forward.

He had not yet reached his seventh year when he was sent to the Monastery of Saint Euprepius, located not far from Antioch, to be educated in both literature and good character. In that place, he entered into a very close friendship with **Nestorius** of Constantinople and **John** of Antioch, both of whom later became Bishops. He had as teachers **Theodore of Mopsuestia** and **John Chrysostom**, from whom he learned both the height of eloquence and the best method for explaining the Holy Scriptures. While still a young man, he was ordained a Reader by **Porphyry**, the Bishop of Antioch, and a Deacon by **Alexander**, Porphyry's successor; nevertheless, he did not yet abandon his monastic lifestyle. 

In the year 423 according to **Baronius** <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius, a major 16th-century church historian.</note>, or in 420 according to Garnier (who relies on more certain chronological reasoning), he was appointed Bishop of Cyrrhus—a city of some renown in the province of Euphratensis in Syria—by **Theodotus**, the successor of Alexander of Antioch, taking the place of the recently deceased Isidore. He found the region of Cyrrhus miserably overgrown with the unlucky weeds of heresy; Arians, Macedonians, Apollinarians, and especially **Marcionites** <note>A radical sect that rejected the Old Testament and the physical nature of Christ.</note> were rampant everywhere. He immediately prepared himself to drive them out as the worst plague of the Church, and he did this not without frequent danger to his own life. Meanwhile, he performed this work with such success that he himself boasted that ten thousand Marcionites were washed by him in the waters of baptism. 

<margin>
* Letter 145. 
Compare Letter 81.
</margin>

In this work, he had many "fellow-workers" <note>original: "συνεργους" (synergous)</note> among the Hermits, such as Marinus, Jacob, and others who had long ago chosen the territory of Cyrrhus as a seat for the ascetic life. Around the year 429, **Nestorius** began to offer certain ill-omened dogmas regarding Christ the Lord and His Blessed Mother. After the matter was first debated in the Synod of Alexandria, **Cyril** proposed twelve "Chapters" <note>Also known as the Twelve Anathemas of Cyril of Alexandria.</note> for an examination of the faith. Theodoret, having been asked by Nestorius—his former close friend and classmate—took up his pen against Cyril and his Chapters...
