...or five Anathemas, attempting to hammer out <term>Apollinarianism</term> <note>A heresy suggesting Christ had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a full human soul.</note> from them, he refuted them in a book that was sufficiently sharp and virulent. In the meantime, swept away by the heat of the dispute, he did not hesitate to assert—at least in incautious and overly dangerous words—that the Blessed Mary did not give birth to the Word made flesh; that the natures in Christ were not united <gloss>according to hypostasis</gloss> <note>original: "καθ' ὑπόστασιν"; meaning a personal, substantial union of the divine and human</note>, and that there was not a single <gloss>unconfused</gloss> <note>original: "ἀσύγχυτον"</note> nature. Finally, he claimed that God the Word could not be said to have died. Lest he leave any stone unturned, he sent letters regarding this matter everywhere to the Monks, and by raising more grave objections against **Cyril**, he traduced his Chapters as a "Lerna" <note>A reference to the Hydra’s swamp; he meant Cyril’s writings were a breeding ground for ancient heresies.</note> of old errors. 

In the year 431, having been summoned to the **Council of Ephesus**, he went off into a secret assembly apart from the others with **John of Antioch** and other Eastern Bishops. After nearly two months, having six bishops of his own faction joined to him, he was sent to Constantinople as a legate from this "Conciliabulum" <note>An unofficial or illegal church assembly</note> in the name of the Easterners. However, he was ordered by the Emperor to remain at Chalcedon. Excluded from the church by the Bishop of the city, he delivered frequent sermons to the people in the Great Hall, which were received everywhere with the immense applause of his listeners. When admitted to the Emperor, he truly dealt with him with great <gloss>boldness of speech</gloss> <note>original: "παῤῥησίᾳ" (parrhesia)</note>, but he "lost his work and his oil" <note>A Latin idiom meaning he wasted his time and effort.</note>. For the Emperor, having finally approved **Cyril's** cause and condemned **Nestorius**, sent the Eastern legates back, each to his own province. 

Therefore, having returned home, **Theodoret** published five books against the Synod of Ephesus; **Marius Mercator** says these were written at the instigation of the devil <margin>* In the Excerpts of his Works, Part 2.</margin>. A little later, through the mediation of the Emperor, a concord was reached between **Cyril** and **John of Antioch**, **Theodoret**, and the other Easterners; but the poorly healed ulcer later broke open again. In the year 444, after **Cyril** had died, he treated him even more harshly; indeed, he could not restrain himself from openly expressing his joy of spirit. Finally, the Emperor, being quite moved by all these things, ordered him in the year 445 to remain in his own home and did not permit him to leave the borders of the region of Cyrrhus. 

In the year 449, a second Synod was gathered at Ephesus (to which the name "Robber Synod" <note>original: "Latrocinalis"</note> has stuck), in which **Dioscorus** presided. Holding all law and divine right as naught, and extorting the votes of the Bishops by force and arms, he deposed **Theodoret** (whom the Emperor himself had expressly commanded to be absent from the Council). Even before this, he had been struck with an anathema by **Dioscorus** at Alexandria. Where could **Theodoret** turn now? Should he appeal to a Synod? He had been condemned by one. Should he flee to the Emperor? He had recently found him to be most hostile, both for other reasons and specifically because he had ordained **Irenaeus** (a Count who had been expelled from the court and was twice-married) as Bishop of Tyre. 

Therefore, having sent two rural bishops, **Abramius** and **Hypatius**, along with the Abbot **Alypius**, he called upon Rome to defend his cause. **Pope Leo**, having reviewed the case and approved his faith, absolved **Theodoret** and, as much as was in his power, restored him to his see. In the year 450, after the death of Emperor **Theodosius**, **Theodoret** was recalled from exile by his successor **Marcian** (for he had been driven from the Province of Cyrrhus and had retired to a monastery in Apamea) and was restored to his see. In the following year, the Fourth General Council <note>The Council of Chalcedon</note> was held, in which **Theodoret**, summoned by name by the Emperor, took his place despite the protests of the Egyptians. He expressly professed the Catholic faith, though for a long time he hesitated to condemn **Nestorius**. Finally, in the eighth session, his cause was more fully recognized; and after an anathema was struck against **Nestorius**, he himself was finally restored with full rights by the solemn acclamation of all. He also condemned **Eutyches** with his synodal vote. 

Returning home from Chalcedon, he gave himself entirely to the writing of books and honorable leisure, leaving the episcopal duties mostly to the care of **Hypatius**. He died in the year 457, or at least the following year, being over seventy years old (though there are some who extend his life for several more years). He was enclosed in the same tomb as his most upright friend **James the Wonder-worker**, who died shortly thereafter. After his death, he experienced varied fortunes. Under the reign of **Justin**, certain clerics of the Church of Cyrrhus brought his image into the temple with solemn pomp, placed it on the Episcopal throne, and celebrated a sacred assembly in his honor. However, he had been condemned shortly before by the Emperor **Anastasius** and his followers, and this was done even more sharply and clearly by the Fifth Council held at Constantinople under **Justinian**. Truly, **Theodoret** was worthy of a better fate and a gentler judgment. He maintained a supreme purity of soul and a discipline of the strict life—which he had learned from childhood under the best masters of true and primitive <gloss>asceticism</gloss> <note>original: "ἀσκήσεως"</note>—throughout the entire course of his life...

<header>The Nestorian Age.</header>

<margin>
5th CENTURY,
from the Year 400.
</margin>

...[his life] he kept whole and unsullied; he burned with great zeal for God and devotion to the Catholic Church. In relieving the poor, he was kind and liberal almost beyond measure; the very large estate he had received from his parents was sold and distributed for their use, and he was never afterwards lacking in his care for their needs. He also spent an immense sum of money on the construction and decoration of public buildings. He possessed a lofty and elevated spirit, but was most tenacious in any opinion he had once formed, and was not sufficiently patient of insults and contradictions. If he fell into any errors, they are to be attributed not so much to his will or a perverse judgment, but rather to his fervent nature, the intemperance of disputes, and an <gloss>immoderate reaction</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἀμετρίᾳ τῆς ἀνθολκῆς"; a phrase referring to the tendency of a debater to pull too hard in the opposite direction when countering an opponent, thereby falling into a different error.</note>. By nature, he possessed a noble intellect, which he cultivated with equal care and study. He was renowned for his all-encompassing learning and was, beyond controversy, by far the most learned man of his century. Regarding his style, let **Photius** <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar known for his "Bibliotheca," a collection of reviews of hundreds of books.</note> be heard: <margin>* Code 46, 203, etc.</margin> <gloss>He is clear in all his phrasing, as it is well-tempered and pure, and not devoid of pleasure, being directed appropriately to the thoughts.</gloss> <note>original: "Σαφής δ’ ἐστὶν ἐν ἅπασι τὴν φράσιν, ὡς εὐκρατής τε καὶ καθαρά, καὶ οὐκ ἀμοίρου τοῦ ἡδέος, καταλλήλως τε τοῖς νοήμασιν εὐθυνόμενος."</note> His style is perspicuous in all things (for it is distinct and pure) nor is it lacking in pleasantness, but it overflows with a sense of proportion. <gloss>His diction is, if anyone’s is, most suited for interpretation. For by the purity and clarity of his words, he reveals everything that was hidden and obscure, and by a certain delight, as if by a soothing ointment, he invites one to read him with a sweet charm, preparing the reader more cheerfully for the task.</gloss> <note>original: "Ἔστι δὲ τὴν φράσιν, εἴτις ἄλλος, ἑρμηνείαις πρέπων, τῷ τε καθαρῷ καὶ εὐσήμῳ τῶν ῥημάτων ἀνακαλλύνων τὰ συνεσκιασμένα καὶ τῷ ἡδύνοντι ἅτε δὴ διαγλυκαίνων, φαιδρωτέρως πρὸς τὴν ἀνάγνωσιν παρασκευάζων."</note> In the following passages, Photius pursues even more praises of his style, drawing arguments from the ease of his method, his choice and elegance of words—which deserve to be called Attic—his exceptional sagacity and diligence in interpreting and explaining the Holy Scriptures, his unadorned simplicity of speech, and the all-encompassing utility of his subject matter; and finally, from his avoidance of digressions and ambiguities, and other gifts which are able to render a writer perfect in every respect.

...[concerning his style, Evagrius] <note>Evagrius Scholasticus was a 6th-century church historian who assessed Theodoret's work.</note> <gloss>He established a style more suited to history; for he is clear, lofty, and concise—except that he sometimes used metaphors too daringly and, as it were, with a lack of refinement.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "κατάλληλον φράσιν τῇ ἱστορίᾳ μᾶλλον ἔθος ἐπέθηκε· σαφής τε γὰρ καὶ ὑψηλὸς καὶ ἀπερίττος· πλὴν ὅτι ἐνίοτε ταῖς μεταφοραῖς παραβόλως καὶ ὥσπερ ἀπειροκάλως ἐχρήσατο"</note> *Of all those I have most recently named, he employs a style more appropriate to history. For he is clear, grand, and by no means redundant: except that he occasionally uses metaphors somewhat audaciously, almost ineptly. It was published in Greek at Basel in 1535; then from the workshop of **Robert Stephanus** <note>A famous Parisian printer known for his high-quality editions of the Bible and classics.</note> among other Ecclesiastical Writers, Paris 1544 in folio, Greek and Latin; Geneva 1612; and finally, most accurately adorned with the notes and translation of **Henri Valesius**, Paris 1673 in folio, which the Cologne editors have recently reproduced.*

*The **Religious History**, or **Philotheus**, containing the eulogies of thirty most holy ascetics, written in the year 444.*

*One hundred and forty-six **Letters**, written after he was elevated to the Episcopacy.*

*The **Eranistes**, or **The Beggar** <note>The title "Eranistes" means "one who collects contributions," implying the heretic in the dialogue has begged or scavenged various errors from past heresies to create a "multiform" (Polymorphus) new error.</note>, comprised of four books, the first three of which take the form of a Dialogue; the fourth is titled "Demonstration by Syllogisms." In the first, he teaches that God the Word is immutable; in the second, he asserts the unconfused union of the natures of Christ; in the third, he demonstrates that God is impassible <note>Meaning God is incapable of suffering or being affected by external forces</note>; in the fourth, he contracts the arguments he had discussed more diffusely and in an oratorical manner in the earlier books into **syllogisms** <note>Formal logical arguments consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note>, so that the force of the arguments may be clearer and more effective. This work was written in the year 446 and, not long after, was consigned to the flames by a double decree of Emperor Theodosius, one given in 447 and the other in 449. It appeared separately in Greek at Rome in 1547; in Greek and Latin with the notes of Beumler at Zurich, 1593 in octavo; and in Greek at Leipzig in 1568.*

*Five books on the **Compendium of Heretical Fables**, written in the year 453. In Book IV, chapter 12, titled "On Nestorius," the text is spurious <note>False or fake; not written by the original author.</note>; it was fabricated by some lover of Theodoret's name around the time of the Fifth Council. The work appeared separately in Greek at Rome in 1545.*

*Ten **Orations on Providence**, delivered at Antioch around the year 430; they appeared separately in Greek at Rome 1545, Zurich 1546, and Paris 1630.*

*The **Oration on Charity**, which is usually appended to the Religious History, written in the year 449. It was first published at Rome in 1580 in Greek and Latin by Gerard Vossius with notes and variant readings.*

*Twelve books **On Healing Greek Maladies** <note>Also known as "The Cure of Pagan Maladies," a defense of Christianity against Greek philosophy and religion.</note>, written in the year 427 against Emperor Julian. They were published in Greek and Latin with the very learned notes of Sylburg at Heidelberg, 1592 in folio. **Jean Garnier** <note>A 17th-century Jesuit scholar and editor of Theodoret's works.</note> recently published many emendations by Fulvio Orsini and variant readings from a Vatican Library manuscript in his Supplement, page 393.*

*A **Letter to John**, Bishop of Germanicia, written toward the end of the year 449.*

*The **Reprehension of the Twelve Anathemas**, or Chapters of Cyril, written in the year 439, together with a preceding letter to John of Antioch.*

*The book **Against Nestorius** addressed to Sporacius: it is spurious, and for the most part is identical to chapter 11 of the fourth book of Heretical Fables.*

THE 5th CENTURY,
from the Year 400.

...[this] age <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "se-culum" (century/age) from the previous page.</note> he kept whole and unstained; he burned with great zeal for God and devotion to the Catholic Church. He spent an immense sum of money on constructing and decorating public buildings. ...and finally, that he was the author of all of them, though this was long uncertain. These Dialogues should not be attributed to St. Athanasius <note>A 4th-century champion of orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> nor to the monk Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor, a 7th-century theologian.</note> (among whose works they are usually found), but are to be ascribed solely to our Theodoret. He proves this to be the case with clearly probable arguments.

### LOST WORKS.

<margin>
* Ecclesiastical History, book 14, chapter 54.
</margin>
**Very many Letters:** For Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopulus, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note> testifies that over five hundred of Theodoret's letters have perished.

***Pentalogium*** <note>From the Greek for a "five-part work."</note>**, or five books on the Incarnation of the Word, against Cyril and the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus.** The fragments of this work mentioned above are also found among the *Works of Marius Mercator* <note>A 5th-century Latin ecclesiastical writer who opposed Nestorianism.</note> edited by Garnier, part 2, page 267.

***The Mystical Work*****, or twelve books on the exposition of the mysteries of the faith.**

**Several books *On Theology and the Incarnation*:** Garnier believes these are the same as the *Three Dialogues against the Macedonians* <note>A heretical group that denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note> and the *Two Dialogues against the Apollinarists* <note>Followers of Apollinaris, who taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind.</note> which circulate under the name of Athanasius. Garnier presents a fragment of the second book *On the Incarnation* in Greek in his Supplement, and Marius Mercator provides a Latin version of the same, though more than half of it is cut off.

***Work against Marcion*** <note>Marcion was a 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament and its God.</note>.

***Work against the Jews***, which could perhaps be considered the same as his *Commentaries on Daniel*.

**Hebediesu** <note>Also known as Abdisho bar Berika, a 13th-14th century Syriac writer and scholar.</note> **reports that a *Work against Origen* exists among his countrymen.** However, it is quite improbable that Theodoret wrote such a thing.

***Responses to the Inquiries of the Persian Magi***.

***Five books or Sermons in praise of St. John Chrysostom*** <note>The famous "Golden-Mouthed" preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, of which Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and renowned scholar.</note> gives excerpts in *Codex 273*.

***Two Speeches delivered at Chalcedon against Cyril in the year 431***. Two fragments survive in Latin in the *Acts of the Fifth Synod*.

***A Sermon delivered at Antioch in the presence of Domnus in the year 444***, mocking the death of Cyril. A single fragment survives in Latin among the *Acts of the Fifth Synod*, and another version exists in Marius Mercator.

**Two rather long fragments of Theodoret, one against Sabellius** <note>A 3rd-century heretic who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different modes of one person.</note> **and the other *On the Trinity***, are presented in Latin by Etienne Baluze in his *Miscellany*, Volume 4; it is uncertain from which books these were primarily taken.

<margin>
On Famous Men, chapter 89.
</margin>
In the time of **Gennadius** <note>Gennadius of Massilia, a 5th-century priest and biographer.</note>, five other books of *Ecclesiastical History* were circulating under Theodoret's name, covering the years 427 to 517. Theodore Lector cites these twice under the same name in his *Collections*, as does John of Damascus twice in his third book *On Images*. It seems most likely, as Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century Cardinal and church historian.</note> suspects, that there were two Theodorets: one the elder, and another younger one; and that the latter continued the five books of the *Ecclesiastical History of Cyrrhus*. Garnier is of the opinion that this younger one is none other than the Bishop of Alinda in Caria, who was present at the Council of Constantinople under Menna in the year 536. The time, name, and level of learning all match.

Furthermore, Photius was in error in *Codex 46* when he ascribed twenty-seven books against various propositions of heretics, and especially against the Eutychians <note>Followers of Eutyches, who taught that Christ had only one divine nature.</note>, to Theodoret; he provides a summary of their arguments. On the authority of Marius Mercator, it is clear that the last twenty-one of these belong to Eutherius, Bishop of Tyana. It is well known that the first six are by Theodoret. For they are the same as the *Pentalogium*, with one of those books being poorly divided into two.

Finally, a **Sermon or Ascetic book**, consisting of questions and answers (which is often published under the name of Maximus the Confessor, and indeed seems to be his), is ascribed to Theodoret in many manuscripts.

Besides the Latin editions of Theodoret's works by Paolo Manuzio (*Rome 1556, Cologne 1567, 1573; Paris 1608; Cologne 1617*), there appeared a Greek and Latin edition organized by the efforts of Jacques Sirmond, *Paris 1642*, in four volumes in folio. To these, Jean Garnier—the most learned and upright of the Jesuits after Sirmond and Fronton du Duc—added a fifth volume, collected partly from manuscript codes and partly from those works circulating under the names of others. ### CELESTINE
a native of Campania, son of Priscus, was elevated to the Pontificate of the Roman Church on September 16, in the year 423. In order that the controversy started some years earlier might finally be ended, the legates having returned from the East bringing with them copies of the Nicene Canons, the Fathers of the African Synod sent letters <note>original: "literas"</note> to Celestine, now Bishop, in which they defended the rights of their churches against appeals to the Roman See. They described these as *impious refuges of Priests and Clerics* (as they call them), supporting their case with the firmest arguments and a clearly unconquerable spirit; they sharply criticized the *smoky pride of the world* <note>original: "fumosum saeculi typhum" — a metaphor for worldly arrogance or vanity</note> which the Prelates of the City of Rome were attempting to introduce into the Church of Christ in the year 428. 

Regarding Nestorius <note>Archbishop of Constantinople whose teachings on the nature of Christ led to the Nestorian controversy.</note>, who still pretended to be Catholic, Celestine congratulated him on his dignity in the See of Constantinople. The cunning Nestorius indeed deceived the good Celestine, and did not fear to offer him the poison of his heresy through plausible letters and other writings, thinking it would be no small advantage if he could draw the Prelate of so great a city to his side. However, having been informed of the whole matter by Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, the chief opponent of Nestorianism.</note> in the year 430, Celestine condemned the dogmas of Nestorius at a Synod held in Rome; sending letters, he announced that Nestorius was to be cast out from the communion of the Roman Church unless he publicly corrected his error within ten days. 

In the year 431, he sent legates to the Council of Ephesus to vigorously promote the condemnation of Nestorius. In the following year, he congratulated the Ephesine Fathers on the actions taken against Nestorius; at the same time, he gave letters of communion to Maximian, who had been substituted in Nestorius's place. He died on August 1, in the year 432. *Fourteen Letters are extant in the Councils, Volume 2, page 1611*, five of which are held in Greek among the Acts of the Council of Ephesus. Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopulus, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note> indeed mentions three other letters of his given to Cyril, John of Antioch, and Rufus of Thessalonica, by which he is said to have approved the transfer of Proclus from the see of Cyzicus to Constantinople. However, since that transfer occurred two years after Celestine's death, it is clearly evident that these letters are spurious. Nor should Celestine's *Book of Secrets* be considered of any better quality; Nicephorus cites two fragments of it in the place mentioned. It seems to have been forged by certain supporters of the Roman see at the time when controversies between the Greek and Roman Churches were being debated.

<margin>* Dissertations of M.P. 394.</margin>
A *brief Memorandum* <note>original: "Commonitorium breve"</note> given by Celestine to the Bishops and Priests going to the Council of Ephesus was published by Christian Lupus at the end of the Ephesine Letters, page 470; and from another manuscript by Baluzius in the *New Collection of Councils, Paris, 1683, folio*. Finally, it should be noted that to the first letter of Celestine to the Gauls are subjoined the *Authorities of the Apostolic See regarding the Grace of God and the Free Choice of the Will*. And indeed, Dionysius Exiguus <note>A 6th-century monk known for his collection of church canons.</note> subjoined them in this way long ago. Fulgentius, Cresconius, Florus the Master, Johannes Scotus, Hincmar of Reims, Ivo, and others attribute them to Celestine. The illustrious Pasquier Quesnel <note>A famous 17th-century French theologian.</note>, who is accustomed to drawing almost everything toward increasing the glory of Pope Leo, takes them away from Celestine and claims them for Leo I in his edition of Leo's works—by his own admission, without the authority of any manuscript, without the example of previous editions, and without the supporting conjecture of any author, whether recent or ancient. But perhaps more will be said on this matter under Leo the Great. Meanwhile, as long as the matter is conducted by conjectures alone, what if, while the Pelagian controversy <note>A theological dispute concerning human nature, sin, and the necessity of divine grace.</note> was raging, some private person collected these testimonies and offered them to Celestine, whence they were found in his archives and subjoined to his letters? Let the learned judge.

### JOHN CASSIAN
a Scythian by race, originating from the Tauric Chersonese <note>The modern-day Crimean Peninsula.</note>, was born in Athens; although Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar.</note> reports that his homeland was Rome. While still a boy, he was nurtured in the studies of the monastic life in the countryside of Bethlehem. Later he visited the Nitrian monks <note>Early Christian ascetics living in the Nitrian Desert of Egypt.</note>; from there, having entered Constantinople, he was ordained a Deacon by Saint John Chrysostom, and served at the altar in the Church of Constantinople.

<margin>

</margin>

...served. In the year 404, after Saint John <note>John Chrysostom, the Archbishop of Constantinople</note> was sent into exile, Cassian was sent as a legate by the Clergy of Constantinople—who were devoted to John’s cause—to Pope Innocent, together with Germanus the Priest. His mission was to plead John’s case and to obtain a remedy from the Western Bishops against the monstrous wickedness of his enemies. Having been raised to the dignity of Priest at Rome by Innocent, he moved to Marseille <note>original: "Massiliam"</note> after the city of Rome was captured by the Goths in the year 410. There he founded two monasteries, one for men and another for women. He began to write from the year 424 and died in the year 448 at the age of ninety-seven. He held the primary place among the <term>Semi-Pelagians</term> <note>A theological movement that sought a middle ground between Pelagianism (which emphasized human will) and the strict Augustinian view of grace. They were also known as the "Massilians" due to Cassian's influence in Marseille.</note>, for whom he seems to have carried the torch; nevertheless, he remained a most bitter enemy of the Pelagians. Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a disciple of St. Augustine</note> praises him greatly for his knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and his sharp mind for disputation, while Cassiodorus praises him for his eloquence. 

The doctrines he taught which diverged from the Orthodox faith, and which were called Semi-Pelagian <note>original Greek: μείως, meaning "in a diminished sense" or "to a lesser degree"</note>, were roughly of this sort: That original sin must indeed be admitted, as well as the necessity of divine grace—not only as a helper and promoter of works once begun, but as a precursor to all good works. However, he held that in most people, the beginning of faith, the good will, and the desire for conversion are excited by the powers of nature alone; these would precede divine help and prepare the mind to receive it. He taught that these first efforts of nature do not strictly "merit" the grace of God, but they do provide the occasion by which God is moved to grant His grace, rewarding such a tiny start of good with so brilliant a prize. Cassian championed other errors peculiar to himself, arising mostly from an excessive zeal in attacking the Pelagians. For example, in *Conference 23*, he asserts that all the "justices" of the righteous are sins. In *Conference 17*, he claims it is sometimes permitted to tell a lie. In *Conference 4*, he says it is a good thing that the flesh lusts against the spirit, and that it would be an evil thing if the will adhered entirely to the spirit and completely conquered the flesh. I remain silent on other errors of the same sort which occur throughout his writings and were attacked by Prosper. Therefore, Cassiodorus <margin>* *Divine Letters*, chapter 29.</margin> advises not without reason that Cassian must be read with caution; he even reports that Cassian's writings were purged of errors by Victor, the African Bishop of Martyritani.

->S C R I P T A.<-
<note>WRITINGS</note>

<margin>
* Code 197.
</margin>

**A** work consisting of twelve books; the first four of these deal with the *Institutes of the Coenobia* <note>The rules and communal life of monks</note>, and the last eight deal with the *Eight Principal Vices*, addressed to Castor, the Bishop of Apt. <note>original Greek: "Χρήσιμα δ' εἴπερ τι ἄλλο, τὰ λόγια ταῦτα τοῖς αἱρουμένοις· ἢ ἀσκητικὸν ἀναδέχεσθαι ἀγῶνα. ἢ ὑπὸ τούτων αὐτοῖς ἡ οδὸς μελετᾶται."</note> *“These words,”* says Photius, *“are as useful as any others to those who choose to undertake the ascetic struggle; for by these, the path is meditated upon by them.”* Or: *“These pronouncements are most useful to those desiring to enter the religious life. And indeed, such power exists in them, a sort of divinity, etc.”* Here Photius pursues the praises of this work at length, as if it were perfect in every respect.

*The Conferences of the Fathers* <note>original: "Collationes Patrum"</note>, twenty-four in number. The first ten are dedicated to Bishop Leontius of Fréjus and Helladius, Abbot of Saint Castor; the seven that follow were sent to Honoratus (not yet Bishop of Arles) and Eucherius; the last seven were inscribed to Jovinian, Minervius, and other monks.

*On the Incarnation of Christ Against Nestorius*, in seven books, written at the urging of Leo (then a Roman Deacon) around the year 430. In these books, he testifies to a great affection for Saint John Chrysostom, sharply attacks Nestorius, and closes the work with a similarly vehement and elegant address <note>original: "apostrophe"</note> to the citizens of Constantinople.

The Works of Cassian were published in *Basel*, 1575; *Antwerp*, 1578, with notes by Henricus Cucquius; *Rome* (by the care of Petrus Ciacconius), 1580, 1611 in octavo; with the notes of Alardus Gazæus, *Douai*, 1616, in two volumes; and adorned with longer commentaries by the same and others, *Arras*, 1628, in folio. They are finally found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 7, pages 17, 69, 102.

...daughter. In the twentieth year of his age, he set out for Constantinople to be educated in fine literature; and it is clearly evident that he was excellently trained in the liberal arts. From this education, he brought many things into his *History* which reflect a knowledge of Philosophy, natural history, Geography, Astronomy, Poetry, and Medicine that is far from common.

<margin>
THE 5th CENTURY, from the Year 400.
</margin>
By sect, he was not so much an <term>Arian</term><note>A follower of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> as he was an Eunomian and an <term>Anomoean</term><note>A radical branch of Arianism that held that the Son was "unlike" the Father in substance.</note>; he contended that the Son was of a different substance <note>original Greek: ἑτερόσιον (*heteroousion*)</note> and inferior to the Father, which is clear from six hundred passages in his *History*. For this reason, he also earned the nickname "the Atheist." He wrote around the year 425. Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and renowned scholar who preserved summaries of many lost ancient works.</note> describes his style thus:

<margin>* Code 40.</margin>
> He is elegant in expression and poetic, yet he uses these words without satiety or unpleasantness. His use of metaphors and emphatic words draws the reader in with a certain sweetness and pleasure. However, he sometimes uses them too boldly or in an excessively distorted way, falling into a style that is cold and ill-timed. His discourse is varied in many ways and with great ornament; yet it is done so that the listener is secretly drawn into an obscurity that is not always pleasing or pure. Nevertheless, in many places, he speaks with fitting and wise maxims. <note>Translated from the original Greek quote provided in the text.</note>

His style is quite elegant, and he uses poetic vocabulary without causing weariness or displeasure. His metaphors and expressive words win him favor and delight, except when he occasionally uses them recklessly or twists them too much, falling into a cold and inconvenient manner of speech. His oratory is varied and decorated, even to the point of excess, such that the listener is subtly led into an obscurity that is not always pleasant. Yet in many instances, he expresses his views quite appropriately.

<margin>* Code 40.</margin>
He composed twelve books of *Ecclesiastical History* (which Photius says should not be called a History, but rather an "encomium of heretics" <note>original: "ἐγκώμιον μετ’ αἱρετικῶν"</note>). This work covers the period from the rise of Arius to the death of the Emperor Honorius. The books were arranged in such an order that the initial letters of each book, if joined together, would spell out the name of the writer, Philostorgius. This was noted long ago by Photius, who selected longer extracts <note>known as "Eclogues"</note> than usual from these books. These extracts, rescued from the Bongarsian Library, were first published with his own translation by Jacques Godefroy <note>original: "Jac. Gothofredus"</note> at Geneva in 1643. In his *Prolegomena* <note>preliminary remarks</note>, Godefroy discusses this History at length, as is his custom, and adds very rich annotations, though they were not always approved by the most learned Henri Valois <note>original: "Valesio"</note>. However, Valois should have remembered the arguments Godefroy brought forward at the end of his *Prolegomena* regarding the mildness of the judgment to be passed on his edition. Valois himself published the same extracts of Philostorgius in Paris in 1673, slightly corrected and illustrated with his own notes, along with the works of Theodoret, Evagrius, and others. He also appended other fragments of Philostorgius—which do not appear in the Photian extracts—collected from Suidas and other sources, by way of a supplement at the end.

Furthermore, Philostorgius himself testifies in Book 10, Chapter 10, that he wrote certain things against Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and famous critic of Christianity.</note> on behalf of the Christians, or to use his own words, "set down contests" <note>original: "ἀγῶνας καταθέσθαι"</note>.

<margin>425.</margin>
SABINUS, Bishop of Heraclea, a city in Thrace, of the Macedonian sect <note>A group that denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>, flourished in the year 425. He published a *Collection* <note>original: "συναγωγὴν"</note> of synodal acts, or a gathering of the deeds of Synods from the Council of Nicaea down to his own times. In this collection, he suppressed other records and gathered everything that seemed to contribute to the glory of his own sect. In this book, as Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian who is a primary source for this period.</note> notes:

<margin>* Book 1, ch. 8.</margin>
He mocked the leaders of the Council of Nicaea as if they were unlearned and destitute of all knowledge. He intentionally omitted some things, perverted others, and changed others still; finally, he twisted everything to suit his own purpose and meaning.

<margin>† Book 2, ch. 15.</margin>
Elsewhere, Socrates also writes that Sabinus did not even mention the name of Macedonius, the leader of his heresy, anywhere in his work—acting, of course, to completely hide his tragic crimes. From that book, Socrates takes what he presents regarding the Council of Seleucia in Book 2, chapter 39 and Book 3, chapter 10, as well as that small confession of faith which the Eastern Bishops offered to the Emperor Jovian at Antioch, which appears in Socrates, Book 3, chapter 22.

In the year 426, he entered the monastery of Lérins with his brother Vincent and committed himself to the cultivation of fine literature and character under the Abbot Saint Honoratus.

Two years later, when his uncle Germanus was sent to Britain to root out the Pelagian heresy <note>A belief that humans can achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace.</note>, Lupus was given to him as a companion by the Gallic bishops. Having set out for Britain, and working together with Germanus, he refuted the Pelagians in a conference held at the shrine of Saint Alban. He also assisted the Britons against the Picts and Saxons...

...having miserably harassed the Saxons, he obtained a memorable victory through his prayers. In the following year, he returned to Gaul. Those who claim that Lupus joined Saint Germanus as a companion on his second journey to Britain in the year 448 are in error. He died in the year 479, after he had held the <term>Episcopate</term><note>The office or term of a bishop.</note> for fifty-two years, as Bede, Usuard, and the ancient writer of his *Life* in Surius’s collection clearly testify. Certainly, Sidonius Apollinaris, in Book 9, Epistle 2, reveals that he had completed ten <term>quinquennia</term><note>Periods of five years; thus, fifty years.</note> in the Episcopate at that time. He was in every respect a most great man. Sidonius Apollinaris calls him:
> "The Father of Fathers, the Bishop of Bishops, another James of his age, undoubtedly the first among all the <term>Pontiffs</term><note>A general term for high-ranking bishops at this time.</note> throughout the whole world, a rule of conduct, and a pillar of virtues" <margin>* Book 6, Epistle 1.</margin> <note>original: "Patrem Patrum, Episcopum Episcoporum, alterum sui sæculi Jacobum, omnium toto, qua patet, orbe Pontificum proculdubio primum, normam morum, & columnam virtutum"</note>.

A letter exists in his and Euphronius of Autun’s name addressed to Thalassius, Bishop of Angers, regarding <term>bigamous</term><note>In this context, clerics who had married twice, which was prohibited by church law.</note> clerics, etc., found in the *Councils*, Volume 4, page 1048. Another letter to Sidonius Apollinaris is held in D’Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, Volume 5.

<margin>427.</margin>
**JOHN**, nurtured from his early youth in the study of sacred matters in the Monastery of Saint Euprepius located near Antioch, had Nestorius and Theodoret as classmates. In the year 427, after the death of Theodotus <note>The Latin text reads "Theodoreto," but this is a historical error in the source; John succeeded Theodotus of Antioch.</note>, he was appointed to the <term>See</term><note>The seat of authority or jurisdiction of a bishop.</note> of Antioch. In the year 429, carried away by his affection for Nestorius, he began to sharply oppose the "Chapters" of Cyril <note>The Twelve Anathemas issued by Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius.</note>, giving orders to Theodoret and Andrew of Samosata to publish books accusing them of <term>Apollinarism</term><note>The heresy that Christ had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a full human soul.</note>. Meanwhile, he himself condemned them everywhere by sending frequent <term>Synodical</term><note>Related to a church council or assembly.</note> letters; however, for a long time, he made a show of being convinced that they were not actually Cyril's work. In the year 431, when the Council of Ephesus was convoked by the Emperor, he strove with all his might to ensure that no other confession of faith besides the <term>Nicene Creed</term> would be proposed for signature, leaving Nestorius's dogmas untouched, and that Cyril's Chapters should be judged contrary to it. Having therefore sent two legates in his name to the Council—Alexander of Apamea and Alexander of Hierapolis—he continued to weave delays. But finally arriving at Ephesus on the fifth day after the Council had begun, and finding Nestorius already condemned by the Fathers, he held a <term>conciliabulum</term><note>An unofficial or rival "little council" not recognized as legitimate by the main body.</note> in his lodgings on that same day and deposed Cyril and Memnon. When he was called to judgment by the Fathers to give an account of such audacity, and since he refused to present himself, he was removed from the communion of the Church. After the Council ended, hurrying to the Emperor, among other signs of a mind embittered against Cyril, he swore he would never communicate with him, even if Cyril repented of his error and <term>anathematized</term><note>Formally cursed or denounced as heretical.</note> his own Chapters. In a sermon delivered to the people at Chalcedon, he exhorted the common folk to persist in the ancestral faith. Returning to Antioch, he persisted for a long time in constantly protecting Nestorius; however, he seems to have by no means embraced Nestorius's opinions. He refused to condemn him because he believed he had only spoken incautiously, while in the meantime holding the true faith. But later, being urged by the Emperor and made more peaceful by the explanation of the Chapters published by Cyril, he embraced the conditions of peace proposed by Cyril—sending Paul of Emesa to Alexandria—and condemned Nestorius. He then busied himself to ensure that both were done by all the bishops subject to his jurisdiction, which he finally achieved after much time and labor, persuading some and ejecting others from their churches by calling upon the civil arm. He died in the year 441. There exist six letters written by him in Greek and Latin in the *Councils*, Volume 3, and fifteen others in Latin among the letters pertaining to the Council of Ephesus published by Christianus Lupus (Louvain, 1682). I omit the very many letters existing in both places which have the name of our John prefixed among the names of other bishops.

<margin>
428.
Socrates, Book 7,
ch. 29, etc.
</margin>
**NESTORIUS**, a Syrian by nation, born in the city of Germaniciana in Syria Euphratensis, was educated in the Monastery of Saint Euprepius and later had Diodore of Tarsus as his teacher. He then became a Priest of the Church of Antioch. After the death of Sisinnius, Bishop of Constantinople, since it seemed best to the Emperor to promote no one from that church to the Episcopate, Nestorius—celebrated for his ready eloquence and temperance—was summoned from Antioch and placed on the Episcopal throne on the 10th of April in the year 428. On that very day, addressing the Emperor in a sermon before all the people, he said: "Give me, O Emperor, the earth pur-" <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the full historical quote is: "Give me, O Emperor, the earth purged of heretics, and I will give you heaven in return."</note>

# The Nestorian Age
<page-num>323</page-num>
<header>The Nestorian Century</header>

<margin>
5th CENTURY, from the Year 400.
</margin>
...cleansed <note>original: "purgatam"; completing the sentence from the previous page where Nestorius promises to "purge" the empire of heresy</note>; and I will give you heaven in return; fight the heretics with me, and I will fight the Persians with you. His efforts did not fail his words: for on the fifth day after his ordination, he expelled the Arians from their churches; he began to harass the Novatians; he inflicted many evils upon the <term>Quartodecimans</term><note>A group who celebrated Easter on the 14th of the Hebrew month of Nisan, regardless of which day of the week it fell upon.</note> throughout Asia, Lydia, and Caria; he bitterly persecuted the Macedonians in the Hellespont through Bishop Anthony of Germa; and he condemned the Manichaeans at a Synod held in Constantinople in the year 430. Yet he himself soon became a <term>Heresiarch</term><note>The founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note> second to none. For when his Presbyter, Anastasius, uttered these words in a sermon: *“Let no one call Mary the Mother of God <note>original Greek: θεοτόκον (Theotokos)</note>; for Mary was a human being, and it is impossible for God to be born of a human being,”* Nestorius not only protected the babbling Anastasius as if he were speaking piously, but he himself repeatedly lectured on this controversy in the Church, stubbornly proposing questions on the matter and perpetually rejecting the term *“Mother of God.”* To put it briefly, the sum of that heresy came to this: that the natures in Christ, the divine and the human, were united not <term>hypostatically</term><note>A theological term referring to the union of divine and human natures in the single person of Christ.</note> but only by a shared relation; and that in the God-man Mediator, two persons are to be admitted; and consequently, the Blessed Virgin cannot be called the mother of the divine person, but only of the human person (whom alone Nestorius called “Christ”). Thus, she was to be called the *“Mother of Christ”* <note>original Greek: χριστοτόκον (Christotokos)</note> and not the *“Mother of God.”* When Nestorius refused to renounce such insane dogmas after frequent warnings, Cyril and Celestine <note>Cyril of Alexandria and Pope Celestine I.</note> declared he must be removed from the Church and the Episcopate. Nor did Nestorius fail his own cause, vigorously pursuing his interests through letters to other bishops and through cunning with the Emperor and the people. But when the Council of Ephesus was called in the year 431, he was among the first to hurry to Ephesus for the celebration of the Council. While the Synod was delayed for sixteen days due to the absence of the Eastern bishops, he did not hesitate to vomit the poison of his mind in daily skirmishes with many bishops, and especially with Cyril. He broke out into these blasphemous words: *“I cannot call him God who was two or three months old; and therefore I am clean of your blood, and I will not come to you anymore.”* Once the Synod began, when Nestorius refused to appear despite being summoned three times, his case was examined, and a sentence of condemnation was passed against him, which was confirmed by the Emperor not long after. The Emperor first ordered the man to be relegated to Petra, a city of Arabia; but soon moved by his prayers and those of his friends, the Emperor softened the sentence and permitted him to withdraw to the Monastery of Saint Euprepius, located in the suburbs of Antioch. After staying there for four years, he was finally exiled by Imperial edict to the Oasis, a city in Libya also called Ibis. In that place, he was captured by the <term>Blemmyes</term><note>A nomadic tribe from the Nubian region.</note> who were devastating the city, but was soon released; he then went to Panopolis, a town in the <term>Thebaid</term><note>The region of ancient Upper Egypt centered around Thebes.</note>. From Panopolis, he was led away by soldiers to Elephantine, a town in the same province. While he was still on the journey, he was recalled by the Governor and ordered to return to Panopolis. Then, by the Governor's command, he was deported to another place near Panopolis, and finally sent to a fourth place of exile by a new Imperial edict.

<margin>
* Book 1, ch. 7.
</margin>
Regarding his death, Evagrius <note>Evagrius Scholasticus, a 6th-century church historian.</note> writes that while wandering around the borders of the Thebaid, he was finally *dashed upon the earth*, and like another Arius, met an end worthy of his life. Indeed, at the end of the chapter, he cites an older writer who recounted that Nestorius died with his tongue consumed by worms. He died, as some wish, in the year 436; however, Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a contemporary historian of the 5th century.</note> expressly testifies <margin>† Book 7, ch. 34.</margin> that he was living in the Oasis in the year 449, when he closed his *History*. He was a man <margin>|| Book 7, ch. 32.</margin> by no means learned, if Socrates is to be believed, who attributes his heresy to ignorance. For, he says, although he was endowed with natural eloquence, he seemed learned, yet in truth he was uneducated. He did not even deign to read the books of the ancient interpreters. Elevated by arrogance because of his speaking ability, he did not give enough accurate attention to reading the ancients, but thought himself superior to all others. Socrates has more on the same subject in that place, which the reader who wants more may consult. There exist in Greek and Latin two *Epistles* in the *Collection of Councils, Vol. 3, pp. 316, 321* (the latter of which is quite long and is found translated by Marius Mercator among his works). There are also two others in Latin (*from a very ancient version*) in the same place, p. 349. *Epistle*...

From these I have drawn not a few things to illustrate the history of this time. <margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, ch. 52.</margin> Furthermore, Gennadius testifies that Nestorius composed infinite treatises on various subjects.* Of these, by far the greatest part has been consumed either by the injury of time or by the vengeful flames of the Emperors. Nevertheless, the famous Garnerius suspects that many homilies circulated under the names of Chrysostom, Amphilochius, Asterius, Basil of Seleucia, and others, are actually owed to Nestorius; and specifically two homilies *On the Resurrection and Ascension of Christ*, which François Combefis published in Greek and Latin under the name of Athanasius in his *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers*, 1648, Volume 1, page 479.

<margin>428.</margin>
MELETIUS, Bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia Secunda, succeeded Theodore in the year 428. He cherished the memory of his predecessor [Theodore] exceedingly and was very devoted to the name of Nestorius. For this reason, he stubbornly refused communion with Cyril and John <note>John of Antioch</note> (after John had been reconciled to Cyril); indeed, he was so incensed against John that he threw the letters of peace sent by him into the face of the bearer. Consequently, he was driven from his see by the Emperor, yet he did not cease to hold clandestine assemblies and perform his priestly office in the territory of Mopsuestia. On this account, he was accused by John before the Emperor and banished to Melitene in Armenia Secunda, to be guarded by Bishop Acacius. Having suffered many injuries from Acacius, he finally died, remaining tenacious of the Nestorian faction until his death. Eleven of his Letters survive in Latin among the Ephesian Letters edited by Lupus, numbers 82, 119, 124, 141, 145, 155, 158, 163, 171, 174, and 177.

He was present at the Conference of Carthage in the year 411 and at the Council of Milevis in the year 416. **EUTROPIUS**, a Priest and disciple of Augustine, flourished in the year 430. He wrote, says Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Massilia, a 5th-century historian who continued Jerome's biographies of famous Christians.</note>, to two sisters, handmaidens of Christ, who were disinherited by their parents for their devotion to chastity and love of religion, two consolatory letters in the form of books, written in elegant and clear language, supported not only by reason but also by the testimony of the Scriptures. <note>The abbreviation N.E. stands for 'Non Exstant', indicating these works have since been lost.</note> N. E. This man was entirely different from the Eutropius who was the author of the *Summary of Roman History*, who served as a soldier under Emperor Julian and seems to have been of the Gentile <note>Pagan</note> religion. Hence it should be seen as surprising that Ptolemy of Lucca, Volaterranus, Philippus Bergomas, Gesner, Possevin, and others confused him with our Eutropius.

<margin>430. * On Illustrious Men, ch. 75.</margin>
**PAULUS**, a Priest of the Pannonian nation <note>Modern-day Hungary and surrounding regions.</note>, flourished in the year 430. He wrote to the virgin Constantia in a modest style, but one seasoned with divine salt (as Gennadius says), two books on *Preserving Virginity and Contempt for the World*, and on the *Rule of Life or the Correction of Morals*. N. E.

<margin>430.</margin>
**OLYMPIUS**, a Spaniard by birth and a Bishop by rank, flourished around the year 430. He wrote a book on the faith against those who blame nature rather than free will for sin; showing that evil was inserted into nature not through creation, but through disobedience <note>This was a defense against Manichaean or early Pelagian ideas regarding the origin of sin.</note>. So says Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 23. N. E.

<margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 50.</margin>
**EUAGRIUS**, a different man from Evagrius Ponticus: nothing more can be known about him, except that he seems to have flourished around 430, and that he wrote the *Dispute between Simon the Jew and Theophilus the Christian*, which was greatly celebrated in the time of Gennadius, but is now lost.

<margin>430. * On Illustrious Men, ch. 55. * On Images, book 2, ch. 5.</margin>
**THEODOTUS**, incorrectly called "Theodorus" by Gennadius, was Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia <note>Modern Ankara, Turkey.</note>. In the year 431, he was present at the Council of Ephesus, where he vigorously opposed Nestorius and diligently supported the side of Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, the primary opponent of the Nestorian doctrine.</note>. There survive, in Greek and Latin, *Two Homilies on the Birth of Christ* delivered at the Council (found in the *Collection of Councils*, Vol. 3, pp. 988, 1008) and a *Homily against Nestorius* delivered on the feast day of St. John the Evangelist at Ephesus (ibid., p. 1024). Also, a *Discourse on the Holy Mother of God and Simeon*, published among the works of Amphilochius by Combefis (*Paris*, 1644), which Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, confirms in his *Antirrhetics* is by our Theodotus. Also, *An Exposition of the Nicene Creed, or a Confutation of Nestorius*, first published by Cardinal Barbarino in *Rome*, 1669, and later by Combefis among other works in *Paris*, 1675. This same book could be considered the *little book of refutation and confutation, arranged with dialectic skill*, which Gennadius mentions Theodotus wrote against Nestorius while still at Ephesus. The Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea <note>The council in 787 AD that restored the use of icons.</note> affirm that Theodotus published six books against Nestorius dedicated to Lausus; indeed, they mention his *Homilies on the Lights [Epiphany], on Elijah and the Widow, on Saints Peter and John, on the Lame Man who sat at the Beautiful Gate*, on those who received the talents, and on the two blind men. He also wrote three books on the *Holy Spirit*, which he himself mentions at the end of the *Exposition of the Nicene Creed*. There exists in the sixth session of the Second Council of Nicaea a testimony taken from a certain book of Theodotus against holy and venerable images, which Theodotus called a vain invention—<gloss>a discovery of diabolical trickery</gloss> <note>original Greek: τῇ διαβολικῇ μεθοδείᾳ εὕρημα</note>. The Nicene Fathers contend with rather slight conjectures that this testimony is false and falsely attributed to Theodotus; although we might agree with the famous Daillé <note>Jean Daillé, a prominent 17th-century Protestant scholar.</note> that the latter part of the testimony consists of the words of the Fathers of Constantinople, not Theodotus himself.

**HILARY**, a Gaul by nation, was born around the year 301 <note>The text reads 301 (ccci), though historical records usually place his birth around 401; this may be a printer's error in the source.</note>. At the encouragement of Honoratus, the first Abbot of Lérins <note>A famous monastery on the Île Saint-Honorat off the French Riviera, a major center for 5th-century Christian thought.</note>, he devoted himself to the study of the monastic life; and having set out for Lérins, he gave himself over to be shaped by that discipline. In the year 426, when Honoratus was made Bishop of Arles, Hilary accompanied him out of respect. Soon after, however, led by his love for the solitary life, he returned to Lérins. From this it is clear that Miræus is mistaken when he writes that Hilary returned to Lérins only after several years in the Episcopacy because he missed his former life. For Hilary returned to Lérins from Arles while Bishop Honoratus of Arles was still living and surviving, as Sidonius 
<margin>
* Poem 16, p. 161.
</margin>
Apollinaris once noted, and as Jean Savaro has demonstrated at length *. In the year 429, or as others say 430, he succeeded the deceased Honoratus in the see of Arles. In the year 439, he presided over the Council of Riez, and then in 441 over the Council of Orange. When, in the year 445, he was strenuously asserting the rights of his see over the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne (for Arles had formerly been the seat of the Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls and was enriched with many privileges from the Emperors) and had recently deposed Bishop Celidonius in the province of Vienne, substituting another in place of the ejected man: a complaint about this matter was brought to Pope Leo. Leo flared up against Hilary, and having obtained a decree from Emperor Valentinian III, he forced Hilary to remain within the limits of his own province. Nor could Leo’s mind be easily appeased, even though Hilary himself traveled to Rome on foot to argue his cause before the Pontiff. Returning to Arles without having settled the case, he sent the priests Ravennius, Nectarius, and Constantius to Leo for the same reason, even calling upon the aid of the City Prefect. But the effort fell through in vain. Leo retained his original harshness; Hilary retained his constancy. He died in the year 449, as is most clearly evident from two letters of Leo given to the Bishops of Gaul in that year. The memory of this most holy man is spoken of poorly by almost all writers of the Roman Church; indeed, even those who lived under a freer sky, such as de Marca, Morinus, Filesacus, and others, call him:
> “a man of stubborn defiance, unbridled rashness and insolence, who did everything according to his own whim, and turned his vicariate granted by the Pontiff into a tyranny; who, like Diotrephes, refused to receive the Pontiff himself; and who had broken out into such arrogance and pride in his Apostolic legation and primacy that he already designed for himself the supreme pontificate, and if I may say so, the papacy in Gaul.” 

These are indeed heavy crimes, to be expiated by no small penalty.

It is no wonder, then, if there were those who lacked the courage to speak for his cause. At last, a most learned man arose, Paschasius Quesnel *, who in a very extensive 
<margin>
* Dissertation 5, Apologia to the Works of Leo, p. 431, Vol ii.
† Year 464, num. viii.
</margin>
Dissertation consisting of three parts, argues Hilary's cause freely and learnedly, vindicating him from these and other slanders and reproaches, and gathered everything pertaining to this matter into a single collection <note>Original Greek: "ἐν τῷ θυλάκῳ" (en tō thulakō), literally 'in the bag' or 'in the pouch.'</note>. In fact, not even Baronius † denies that Leo the Great was most sharply incensed against Saint Hilary due to a misunderstanding <note>Original Greek: "ἀνεκδοχῆς" (anekdochēs), meaning a misinterpretation or taking things in the wrong sense.</note>, and because of false accusations and subreptions.

# The Nestorian Century.

<margin>5th CENTURY from the year 400.</margin>
...usually placed before the *Predestination of the Saints* and *The Gift of Perseverance* <note>Two famous works by St. Augustine, which were often bound with Hilary's letters.</note>.

*The Narrative of the Miracles of Saint Genesius*: concerning which the aforementioned Quesnel <note>Pasquier Quesnel (1634–1719), a French theologian and expert on the works of Leo the Great.</note> says: The narrative of the miracles of Saint Genesius, which is read in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a 16th-century hagiographer who compiled the "Lives of the Saints."</note> (August 25) adorned with the name of Hilary, is foreign to his eloquence and rather tastes of the style of Honoratus of Marseille, whom Gennadius also testifies wrote several things pertaining to the lives of the Holy Fathers.

All the minor works of Hilary that are extant are found collected in one volume in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patr."</note>, Volume 7, page 1228.

Furthermore, the author of his Life, which is found in Surius under April 5, mentions other works of Hilary—namely, *Homilies for each festival of the year*, an *Exposition of the Creed*, *many Letters*, and a *Poem <note>original: "Carnem," likely a typo for "Carmen," meaning poem or song.</note> concerning a certain burning spring*; these have not come down to us.

<margin>430.</margin>
## ACACIUS,
a Syrian by birth, it seems, was trained in monastic discipline from his early youth and lived a most blameless life in the monastery of Gindarus (a village located near Antioch) under the rule of Asterius. While he was still a Priest, he strenuously promoted the Catholic cause against the Arians (at whose hands he suffered much); for this reason, around the year 378, he was promoted to the Bishopric of Beroea by Eusebius of Samosata. He is placed here, however, because whatever of his writings survive were written during the time of the Council of Ephesus. After the year 381, Acacius—who, according to Theodoret <margin>* Book 5, ch. 23.</margin>, was even then **"the thorn that sprouted in every land"** <note>original: "ὁ πανταχῷ ἧς γῆς ἡ ἀκάνθης ἐξέφυε." This is a pun on his name, Acacius, and the Greek word "akantha," meaning thorn.</note>—was sent to Rome by Flavian <note>Bishop of Antioch.</note> to obtain the communion of the Western Bishops for Flavian and to finally extinguish the Schism of Antioch, which he successfully accomplished. At the beginning of the fifth century, he joined with Antiochus, Severian, and others conspiring against John Chrysostom, and at the Synod held "at the Oak" <note>An 11th-century council held near Chalcedon to depose Chrysostom.</note>, he voted that Chrysostom should be deposed. Finally, when the controversy arose between Cyril and Nestorius (at which time, because of the man's remarkable white hair and virtue, he began to be called the father and master of all Bishops in every quarter), he contended in letters sent to Cyril that the dispute was merely a question of names and attempted to excuse Nestorius. He did not attend the Council of Ephesus, but delegated his synodal vote against Cyril to Paul of Emesa and warned the Eastern Bishops by letter to charge Cyril with Apollinarianism <note>A heresy suggesting that Christ had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a human soul.</note>. Soon, once the Synod was finished, he pleaded with the Emperor by letter to confirm the condemnation not only of Nestorius, but also of Cyril and Memnon. Theodosius at first complied with this advice (as is clear from the Acts and Letters of Ephesus) and, having given the command to Count John, ordered them each to be deposed; however, having eventually been better informed, he issued fairer edicts. In the year 432, he took part in the Synod held by John of Antioch at Beroea and persuaded the Easterners in every way to enter into peace with Cyril; he did not hesitate to promote this peace to the best of his ability through letters written to Cyril and Celestine. He died at a very advanced age around the year 436. Of the many letters he wrote, three survive: *two to Alexander of Hierapolis, his Primate, among the Ephesian Letters (numbers 129 and 143), and one to Cyril, in Greek and Latin, Council Records, Vol. 3, p. 382.*

## ALYPIUS,
a Priest, as he calls himself, *of the Apostles*—that is (if I am not mistaken), of the Great Church of Constantinople <note>Likely referring to the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.</note>—flourished in the year 430. There exists an *Exhortatory Letter written by him to Cyril, urging him to proceed manfully against heresy, Council Records, Vol. 3, p. 785.*

Priest and Steward <note><term>Oeconomus</term>: the officer in charge of a diocese's or church's finances and property.</note> of the Church of Philadelphia, flourished in the year 431. Not long before the Council of Ephesus, two Priests of Constantinople, Anastasius and Photius, followers of Nestorius’s dogma, came to Philadelphia together with a certain Bishop of the same stripe named James. They craftily induced some of the clergy and laity, who had recently converted from the Quartodeciman heresy <note>Early Christians who insisted on celebrating Easter on the 14th day of the Jewish month of Nisan, regardless of which day of the week it fell upon.</note>, to subscribe to a rather lengthy Exposition of Faith that was not free from Nestorius's blasphemies. Charisius boldly resisted them; for this reason, they prohibited him from communion and the sacred ministry as if he were a heretic. Therefore, in the year 431, Charisius set out for Ephesus and, having presented his accusations against Anastasius, Photius, and James...

# The Nestorian Century.

<margin>5th CENTURY from the year 400.</margin>

<margin>* Dissertation 5. Apology to the works of Leo, page 431, Volume 2. † Year 464, number 8.</margin>
**HILARY**, a Gaul by birth, was born around the year 400. At the encouragement of Honoratus, the first Abbot of Lérins, he devoted himself to the studies of the monastic life; and having traveled to Lérins <note>original: "Lirinum," a famous Mediterranean monastery and center of learning</note>, he gave himself over to be shaped by its discipline. In the year 426, he accompanied Honoratus, who had been made Bishop of Arles <note>original: "Arelates"</note>, as a mark of honor; however, led by a love for the solitary life, he soon returned to Lérins. From this it is clear that Miraeus is mistaken, as he writes that Hilary returned to Lérins after several years in the episcopate, touched by a longing for his former life. For Hilary returned to Lérins from Arles while Honoratus, the Bishop of Arles, was still alive and well, as Jean Savaro once noted to Sidonius Apollinaris and demonstrated with many proofs. In the year 429, or as others say 430, he succeeded Honoratus in the see of Arles upon the latter's death. In the year 439, he presided over the Synod of Riez <note>original: "Regensi"</note>, and then in 441, the Synod of Orange <note>original: "Arausicanæ"</note>. And when, in the year 445, he was strenuously asserting the rights of his see over the Provinces of Vienne and Narbonne (for Arles had formerly been the seat of the Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls and was enriched by many privileges from the Emperors), and had recently deposed Bishop Celidonius in the Province of Vienne, substituting another in the place of the ejected man: a complaint about this matter was brought to Pope Leo. Leo flared up against Hilary and, having obtained a rescript from the Emperor Valentinian that he should keep himself within the boundaries of his own province, he achieved his goal. Nor could Leo’s mind be easily pacified, even though Hilary himself hastened to Rome on foot to argue his case before the Pontiff. Having returned to Arles without success, he sent the priests Ravennius, Nectarius, and Constantius to Leo for the same reason, even calling upon the help of the City Prefect. But the matter fell through in vain. Leo retained his former harshness, while Hilary retained his constancy. He died in the year 449, as is very clearly established from two of Leo’s letters given to the bishops of Gaul in that year. The memory of this most holy man is poorly regarded by almost all writers of the Roman Church; indeed, even those who lived under a freer sky—de Marca, Morinus, Filesacus, and others—call him "a man of stubborn defiance, unbridled rashness, and insolence, who did everything according to his own whims and turned his vicariate granted by the Pontiff into a tyranny, who like Diotrephes <note>A biblical figure mentioned in 3rd John 1:9 as one who loves to be first and refuses to acknowledge authority.</note> refused to receive the Pontiff himself, and who had broken out into such arrogance and pride through his apostolic legation and primacy that he was already designing the supreme pontificate, or so to speak, the papacy in Gaul for himself." These are heavy crimes indeed, to be atoned for by no small penance. It is no wonder, then, if there were those who would speak in his defense. At last, a most learned man arose, Pasquier Quesnel, who in a very long Dissertation consisting of three parts, freely and learnedly argues Hilary's case, vindicates him from these and other slanders and reproaches, and gathered everything pertaining to this matter "with the whole bag" <note>original: "ὅλῳ τῷ θυλάκῳ" – a Greek idiom meaning "in one great heap" or "exhaustively."</note>. Indeed, even Baronius himself does not deny that Leo the Great was incited to lash out most sharply against Saint Hilary due to complaints of non-compliance, false accusations, and deception.

*Heroic Poem on the history of Genesis* addressed to Pope Leo, which is usually found among the works of Hilary of Poitiers.
*A short letter to Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon*. Pasquier Quesnel published these three minor works, revised according to the printed codes and the reliability of the Arles manuscript, at the end of the first volume of Leo the Great, page 731; to these he also prefixed the life of Saint Hilary written by Honoratus of Marseille, his disciple.
*Two Letters to Augustine* among the works of Augustine. However, this Hilary seems to be someone other than ours, likely a layman, who informed Augustine about the heresy of the people of Marseille <note>Refers to the Semi-Pelagian controversy involving the monks of southern Gaul.</note> by sending him a fairly long letter, which [is placed] in Augustine’s books on *Predestination*...

**ACACIUS**, a Syrian by birth as it seems, trained in monastic discipline from an early age, lived a most blameless life in the Monastery of Gindarus, a village situated near Antioch, under the rule of Asterius. While still a Priest, he strenuously promoted the Catholic cause against the Arians (from whom he suffered much); for this reason, he was promoted to the Bishopric of Beroea <note>modern-day Aleppo</note> by Eusebius of Samosata around the year 378. He is placed here, however, because whatever writings of his survive were composed at the time of the Council of Ephesus. After the year 381, Acacius—who was even then, as Theodoret says <margin>* Book 5, ch. 23.</margin>, **"famed everywhere on earth"** <note>original Greek: "ὁ πανταχοῦ τῆς γῆς ἀδομένῳ"</note>—was sent to Rome by Flavian to obtain the communion of the Western Bishops for Flavian and finally extinguish the Antiochene Schism <note>A long-standing dispute over the rightful Bishop of Antioch</note>, which he successfully accomplished. At the beginning of the fifth century, he joined with Antiochus, Severian, and others conspiring against Chrysostom; and in the **Synod of the Oak** <note>An informal synod held in 403 to depose John Chrysostom</note> he voted for his deposition. When the controversy finally arose between Cyril and Nestorius (at which time, because of the man’s remarkable gray hair and virtue, he began to be heard everywhere as the "father and teacher of all bishops"), he contended in letters sent to Cyril that this dispute was a mere question of names and attempted to excuse Nestorius. He did not attend the Council of Ephesus; but he delegated his synodal vote against Cyril to Paul of Emesa and advised the Eastern Bishops through letters to charge Cyril with Apollinarianism <note>A heresy suggesting Jesus had a human body but a divine mind</note>. Soon, after the Council ended, he pleaded with the Emperor by letter to confirm the condemnation not only of Nestorius, but also of Cyril and Memnon; Theodosius initially followed his advice (as is clear from the Acts and Letters of Ephesus) and, having given the order to Count John, commanded that each be deposed; but eventually, being better informed, he issued fairer decrees. In the year 432, he took part in the Synod held by John of Antioch at Beroea and urged peace between the Easterners and Cyril by all means, which he did not hesitate to promote to the best of his ability through letters written to Cyril and Pope Celestine. He died at a very advanced age around the year 436. Out of many letters he wrote, three remain: two to Alexander of Hierapolis, his Metropolitan <note>the presiding bishop of the province</note>, among the Ephesine Letters, numbers 129 and 143; and one to Cyril in Greek and Latin, in the *Councils* Volume 3, page 382.

5th CENTURY from the year 400.

...[he] accused [them] before the Fathers of the Council by means of a petition of accusation, a confession of faith imposed by those Quartodecimans <note>a group that celebrated Easter on the 14th of Nisan, regardless of the day of the week</note>, and copies of their signatures. But to purge himself of the charge of heresy, he offered a brief Confession of Faith, sufficiently in harmony with the Nicene Creed. Each of these is extant in Greek and Latin in the *History of the Councils*, Volume 3, page 673.

<margin>431.</margin>

### ACACIUS
ACACIUS, Bishop of the city of Melitene in Armenia Secunda <note>a Roman province in modern-day Turkey</note>, flourished in the year 431. A most fierce opponent of Nestorius and defender of Cyril; although he did no small harm to that cause when he contended before the Emperor that the deity was capable of suffering <note>original: "deitatem esse passibilem"</note>; on which account Theodosius [the Emperor], being somewhat moved, long turned away from Cyril and his supporters. He was present at the Council of Ephesus, where he held a private conversation with Nestorius shortly before the Synod began; the errors he detected there he soon exposed to the Fathers of the Council. Upon returning home, he most constantly defended the authority of the Synod as long as he lived; and he strove with all his might to see that peace was established between the Easterners and Cyril, and that once established, it was preserved. There is extant in Greek and Latin a *Homily delivered at the Synod of Ephesus, in which he strenuously asserts the Catholic faith against Nestorius*; in the *History of the Councils*, Volume 3, page 983. In Latin, there is a *Letter to Cyril* among the Ephesian Letters edited by Lupus, number 172.

<margin>431.</margin>

### MEMNON
MEMNON, Bishop of Ephesus, flourished in the year 431. In the Council of Ephesus, he championed the Catholic faith as strongly as anyone; and he excluded John [of Antioch], Theodoret, and their followers from his church, by no means permitting them to be present at the holy assembly <note>original: "sacræ synaxi"</note>. In the Council, he underwent a fate equal to Cyril's: deposed by John’s "Conciliabulum" <note>a term for an irregular or unauthorized council</note>, restored by the [true] Council, first condemned by the Emperor, and soon received back into favor. There is extant in Greek and Latin a *Letter to the Clergy of Constantinople, in which he recounts the evils which he and the Ephesian Fathers suffered daily from the Nestorian faction at Ephesus*; in the *History of the Councils*, Volume 3, page 762.

<margin>
431.
See the Letter of Cyril to Acacius of Beroea.
</margin>

### DOROTHEUS
DOROTHEUS, Bishop of Marcianopolis and Metropolitan of Moesia Secunda <note>a province in the northern Balkans</note>, flourished in the year 431. He was a most persistent follower of Nestorius, not only of his party but also of his heresy; so much so that not long before the Synod of Ephesus, while speaking in the Church of Constantinople, he did not blush to pronounce: *If anyone says Mary is the Mother of God <note>original: "Deiparam"</note>, let him be anathema*. He was present at the Council of Ephesus and held a place in the Nestorian assembly. He was therefore deposed by the Catholic Synod, and soon ordered to be expelled from his city and his throne by the Synod of Maximian of Constantinople. When the people of Marcianopolis, at his instigation, drove away Saturninus (the successor designated for him) in a popular riot, he was ejected by an edict of the Emperor and banished to Caesarea in Cappadocia. There are extant in Latin *four Letters* among the Ephesian Letters of Lupus, numbers 46, 78, 115, and 137.

<margin>431.</margin>

### ALEXANDER
ALEXANDER, Bishop of Hierapolis and Primate of the Province of Euphratesia, flourished in the year 431. He was sent ahead by John of Antioch to the Synod of Ephesus in the name of the Easterners to champion the cause of Nestorius, which indeed he did diligently, though in vain; and in John’s "Conciliabulum" <note>irregular council</note> he soon subscribed to the condemnation of Cyril. He was a most devoted friend to Nestorius, but a most bitter enemy to Cyril, and never wished to accept conditions for entering into peace with him, shouting that Cyril was a manifest Apollinarian <note>a follower of Apollinaris, who was accused of denying that Christ had a human soul</note>, that his Chapters savored of the worst heresy, and that communion should be denied to him in every way. Indeed, he fostered such persistent hatred toward Cyril that [he preferred] <note>The Latin text seems to skip a word here, likely "maluerit" (preferred)</note> to renounce communion with John, Theodoret, and the other Easterners on account of the peace they made with Cyril. Fearing, therefore, to be thrust from his see, he implored the help of the Roman Pontiff, but was rejected by him; and as he did not cease to rail against Cyril and to attack the term "Mother of God" <note>original: "Deiparæ"</note>, he was finally expelled from his see by an edict of the Emperor and sent into exile to Famocho in Egypt. There are extant in Latin *twenty-three Letters* among the Ephesian Letters of Lupus, numbers 57, 58, 64, 65, 69, 93, 94, 96, 100, 102, 104, 105, 127, 136, 147, 149, 154, 156, 165, 167, 169, 178, and 182.

<margin>In the entry for Alexander, p. 164.</margin>
He also wrote, according to Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note>, a *discourse full of monotony* <note>original: "Sermonem μονότον γέμοντα"</note>, comprising nine chapters, in which he taught *what new things Christ brought into the world*. There was another Alexander, distinct from ours, the Bishop of Apamea, sent as a legate to the Synod of Ephesus along with him by John of Antioch.
