### MAXIMINUS
MAXIMINUS, Bishop of Anazarbus and Metropolitan of the province of Cilicia Secunda <note>an area in modern-day southern Turkey</note>, flourished in the year 431. He was a high-ranking follower of Nestorius and a most bitter enemy to Cyril of Alexandria, whom he condemned by his vote in the rival assembly <note>original: "Conciliabulo," referring to the counter-synod held by the Eastern bishops who supported Nestorius</note> at Ephesus. After a Synod was later called at Anazarbus, he decreed again that Cyril should be removed from his see and from Catholic communion, and he struck Cyril’s "Chapters" <note>Cyril’s twelve anathemas against Nestorius</note> with an anathema. Finally, however, he returned to favor with Cyril and his own Patriarch, John of Antioch (whom he had long avoided after John reconciled with Cyril), and he ceased to disturb the Church. There are extant three *Letters* in Latin among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, numbers 67, 109, and 112, in addition to two synodal letters which he signed in the first place, numbers 113 and 119.

<margin>
431.
* Philotheus, chapter 10.
</margin>

### HELLADIUS
HELLADIUS was first a monk and, according to the testimony of Theodoret, was to be admired for the exceptional holiness of his life. He was a disciple of Abbot Theodosius, and after the Abbot’s death, he took up the governance of the monastery founded by him near Antioch, which he led for sixty years; he was finally made Bishop of Tarsus. He flourished in the year 431. He maintained the closest friendship with Nestorius and signed the condemnation of Cyril in the rival assembly at Ephesus. Because he stubbornly refused to consent to the deposition of Nestorius and the substitution of Maximianus, he was ordered to be ejected from his see by the Synod of Maximianus of Constantinople, and he was specifically excluded from peace by Cyril. In response, when Maximianus’s officials arrived at Tarsus to carry out the Synod’s mandates, Helladius had them chased away by the common people. At a Synod held in Tarsus, he decreed the same things Maximinus had at the Synod of Anazarbus, and he consoled Nestorius by letter, promising that he would always defend his cause. Eventually, however, moved by fear, he appealed to Pope Sixtus; through his mediation, the sentence passed against him and three other Metropolitans in the Synod of Constantinople was repealed, and he himself was restored to the peace of the Church. Having then gathered a Synod of the bishops of Cilicia, he anathematized Nestorius; at last, he died a pious death in his own church. There are extant six *Letters* in Latin among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, numbers 68, 111, 114, 144, 154, and 193.

<margin>
431.
</margin>

### EUTHERIUS
EUTHERIUS, Metropolitan of Tyana, flourished in the year 431. He was a persistent enemy of Cyril, whose condemnation in the rival assembly of Ephesus he ratified by his vote. He was a unique friend to Nestorius, though he seems not to have followed his heresy at all, but only to have supported his party because he believed Nestorius had been falsely accused of heresy. Deposed in the Synod of Maximianus at Constantinople, he was excluded by Cyril and the Egyptian bishops from any hope of entering into peace. Therefore, after he had fought long and hard for the cause of Nestorius and against Cyril, he was cast out of his church and exiled to Scythopolis <note>modern-day Beit She'an, Israel</note>; driven even from there, he finally died at Tyre. There are extant five *Letters* in Latin among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, numbers 73, 74, 116, 117, and 201. In Greek and Latin, there are *Seventeen Sermons on various heresies, together with a preceding Letter describing the tragedy of the ecclesiastical upheavals,* which are ascribed by some to Athanasius (and are therefore usually found among his works), by others to the monk Maximus, and finally by Photius <margin>* Codex 46.</margin> to Theodoret. However, relying on the authority of Marius Mercator, the most learned Garnier rightly claims these for Eutherius, having promised a more full dissertation on this matter which he did not complete, being snatched away by death. They are found among the *Works of St. Athanasius*, Volume 2, page 245 (Commelin edition) and at the end of the *Supplement to Theodoret* edited by Garnier, *Paris, 1684.*

<margin>
431.
</margin>

### MAXIMIANUS
MAXIMIANUS, a monk by his way of life and a Priest of the Church of Constantinople, was indeed unrefined and unskilled in speech, yet famous for the holiness of his life. In the year 431, four months after Nestorius was deposed, he was made Bishop of the Church of Constantinople. Immediately, having held two Synods at Constantinople, he deposed the primary patrons of the Nestorian party; he ordered his own name to be inscribed in the <term>diptychs</term> <note>liturgical tablets or lists of those officially recognized and prayed for by the church</note> in place of Nestorius’s, and in many places he ensured this was done by using military force. He died in the year 434, after he had sat for two years and five months. There is extant a single *Letter* in Greek and Latin to Cyril, in which he honors him with both praise and consolation for the evils he had suffered for the sake of the faith; *History of the Councils, Volume 3, page 1061.*

# The Nestorian Century. 329

<margin>
5th CENTURY
from the year 400.
---
431.
</margin>
**PAUL**, Bishop of Emesa <note>modern-day Homs, Syria</note>, was present at the Council of Ephesus in the year 431. There, he acted as a patron for the cause of Nestorius, and in the rival assembly <note>original: "Conciliabulo," referring to the counter-council held by Nestorius's supporters</note>, he signed the decree for the condemnation of Cyril. In the following year, he was sent as a legate to Alexandria by John of Antioch, Acacius of Beroea, and other Eastern bishops who were eager for peace, in order to enter into a peace agreement with Cyril. John recommends him to Cyril in this way: *he who has always stood out as distinguished among churchmen, knowing how to meet circumstances with both deeds and words, and possessing a reverence toward the Lord which, being used most excellently, has often benefited the common good.* Paul labored with great cunning at Alexandria, but he could not obtain peace from Cyril until he offered a booklet of faith, confessing that Mary is the <term>Theotokos</term> <note>original: "θεοτόκον"; literally "God-bearer" or Mother of God</note>, and anathematized <note>formally cursed or denounced</note> Nestorius. He confirmed both of these points by speaking aloud in the Church of Alexandria. Having done this, in the name of John and the others by whom he was sent, he struck a peace with Cyril and returned to Asia. There survive in Greek and Latin his *Booklet on Faith* and *Two Sermons delivered at Alexandria*, in the Councils, Volume 3, pages 1089 and 1096. In Latin, there is his *Letter to Anatolius, Prefect of the Military*, among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, number 107.

<margin>431.</margin>
**RHEGINUS**, Bishop of Constantia, a city of Cyprus, was present at the Council of Ephesus in the year 431 and confirmed the condemnation of Nestorius with his vote. In the seventh session of the Synod, he accused the leaders of Antioch of an ambitious attempt to invade the rights of the Cypriot Church. He petitioned for, and obtained, a decree from the Fathers confirming the <term>autocephaly</term> <note>original: "ἀυτοκεφαλίαν"; the right of a church to head itself rather than being subject to a foreign patriarch</note> of his church. There survives in Greek and Latin his *Sermon delivered in the Synod of Ephesus after the deposition of Nestorius*, in the Councils, Volume 3, page 577.

<margin>431.</margin>
**JUVENAL**, first Bishop of Ephesus and later of Jerusalem, flourished in the year 431. He was present at the Council of Ephesus and stood for Cyril against Nestorius, using Cyril's help to protect his own ambitions against John of Antioch. For he had unjustly claimed the rights of the Patriarchate for himself; not content with that, he attempted to bring Arabia and the two Phoenicias under his jurisdiction, after having withdrawn them from the governance of the Church of Antioch. Because of this, it also happened that in the "Robber Synod" <note>original: "Latrocinio Ephesino," an 449 AD council that was later declared invalid</note> of Ephesus in the year 449 and the Council of Chalcedon in 451, he fought for Eutyches and Dioscorus against Flavian of Constantinople. Indeed, in the Council of Chalcedon, he obtained the rights of the Patriarchate for himself, but he was forced to let go of Phoenicia and Arabia. There survives in Latin his *Synodal Letter to the Priests, Archimandrites, and remaining Monks of Palestine*, by which he confirms the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon in his own name and that of his bishops: Councils, Volume 4, page 889.

<margin>431.</margin>
**ANDREW**, Bishop of the Samosatenes <note>Samosata, in modern-day Turkey</note>, flourished in the year 431. Around the year 429, by the mandate of John of Antioch, he attacked the "Chapters" <note>the twelve anathemas</note> of Cyril in a published writing. At first, he did this rather mildly and as if unwillingly; but later, having been offended by Cyril’s sharp response against Theodoret (who had struggled in the same arena as himself), he attacked the same points in a very poisonous booklet. He refused to attend the Council of Ephesus, citing illness as an excuse; nevertheless, he defended the cause of Nestorius with as much authority as he could, and he did not set aside his deep-seated hostility toward Cyril for several years. Finally, however, around the year 436, moved by the authority of John of Antioch, he entered into peace with Cyril. He spent a great deal of effort—though it was in vain—to persuade his Metropolitan, Alexander, to do the same. Yet Andrew himself could never be led to approve Cyril’s "Chapters" or to confess that God had suffered <note>referring to the controversy over whether God the Word suffered in the flesh</note>. He died before the time of the Robber Synod of Ephesus; Theophanes writes incorrectly that he was present there, for a man named Rusticus, the successor to our Andrew, is numbered among the bishops of the Robber Synod in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon. There survive in Latin *Eight Letters* among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, numbers 43, 59, 62, 90, 98, 101, 103, and 106. A fragment of his second book against Cyril’s Anathemas is provided by Anastasius in *The Guide* <note>original: "Ὁδηγ." (Hodegos)</note>, chapter 22. Many fragments of his first book are found in Cyril’s *Apology for the Twelve Anathemas against the objections of the Easterners, or that book itself*: for the Synod of the Easterners, held at Antioch before the year 431, had approved it and sent it to Alexandria via the Deacon Possidonius in the name of all, fortified by everyone's signatures.

# The Nestorian Century. 331

<margin>5th CENTURY from the year 400.</margin>
**RABBULAS**, Bishop of Edessa <note>a major center of Syriac Christianity, now Şanlıurfa, Turkey</note>, was indeed blind in his eyes, but not at all lacking in his mind. He flourished in the year 431. At the Council of Ephesus, he originally judged that Cyril and Memnon should be deposed because of the [Twelve] Chapters <note>Cyril’s twelve propositions against Nestorius</note>; and he turned away from all the Egyptian bishops as if they were heretics. Later, however, having changed his opinion, he favored Cyril's cause with such ardor of soul that, having gathered a Synod at Edessa, he struck with anathema <note>a formal curse or excommunication</note> all the writings of Theodore [of Mopsuestia], and whatever was written by Theodoret and Andrew of Samosata against Cyril's Chapters, and decreed they should be burned. He bound with the same sentence anyone who either read the said books or henceforth resisted Cyril's Chapters; he even renounced communion with John [of Antioch] and all the Eastern bishops. John tried to restrain the man's excesses at a Synod held in Antioch in the year 436, ordering him to be removed from ecclesiastical communion and his see. But it was in vain: Rabbulas retained both as long as he lived, and died in peace some time later. There exists a Latin *Letter, mutilated at the beginning and end, among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, number 200.* Almost the same thing is held entire in the Latin *Councils*, Volume 5, page 469. Furthermore, Theodore Lector <margin>* Collection, Book 2, page 565.</margin> mentions that he was accused by Andrew of Samosata as if he had written against Theodoret’s Chapters; unless perhaps the conjecture of Valesius is truer, that *Anthimus* should be put in place of "Andrew," and *Cyril* should be read instead of "Theodoret," since it is well known that Andrew wrote against Cyril’s Chapters. However that may be, it can hardly be doubted that Rabbulas wrote many things in that quarrelsome century, of which he was so great a part.

---

<margin>431.</margin>
**CAPREOLUS**, by nation, as is likely, an African, succeeded Quodvultdeus (who had succeeded Aurelius) as Bishop of Carthage, and flourished in the year 431. Emperor Theodosius had written to Augustine the previous year, requesting that he grace the Synod summoned at Ephesus with his presence; but Augustine being already dead, the letters were delivered to Capreolus, who did what he could. Having sent his deacon Bessula to Ephesus, he gave letters to the Synod, in which, having testified to his greatest care and zeal for the Catholic faith, he excused the less formal embassy because the bishops of the African Church could not meet in a Synod at this time—partly because of the short interval of time, and partly because all the approaches of the roads were besieged on all sides by the Vandals <note>a Germanic tribe then ravaging North Africa</note>. Capreolus's letter was read in the Synod, with Cyril of Alexandria also asking that it be inserted into the Synodal acts. For he wishes, he says, that the ancient dogmas of the faith be confirmed, while new and absurdly devised and impiously publicized ones be rejected and proscribed. Soon all the bishops cried out together, *These are the voices of all: this we all assert: this is the wish of all.* This *Letter* exists in Latin in Baronius at the year 431, and in Greek and Latin together in the *Councils*, Volume 3, page 533. He also wrote to Vitalis and Constantius, two Spaniards, a *Little book or Letter on the one person of Christ, true God and Man, against the recently condemned heresy of Nestorius*—a new and unspeakable destruction, as he calls it, crushed in the entrance-hall with its author and advocate, and extinguished by the ray of Apostolic light. Baronius inserted this letter (mutilated by half) into his *Annals* at the year 431. Jacques Sirmond published it entire from the Herévall Manuscript, and placed the letter of Vitalis and Constantius to Capreolus before it, among the *Little Works of the Ancients, Paris 1630, 8vo.* It is also held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 7, page 5. In this letter, Capreolus himself mentions the embassy he sent to Ephesus; as noted by Casimir Oudin, who described what he has about this writer from Miraeus (just as Miraeus himself almost did from Sirmond), having copied the author's name word for word, adding not even a peep <note>original: "ne γρῦ quidem"; a Greek idiom meaning "not even a grunt/peep"</note> of his own. But I would be infinite if I wished to note everything which this recent compiler—otherwise a fairly candid man—is accustomed to copy from others.

**URANIUS**, a Priest and a disciple of Paulinus of Nola, whom he served in his final moments in the year 431. He wrote a *narrative on the death of St. Paulinus*, which is found in Surius, June 22nd, and in all recent editions of Paulinus.

# The Nestorian Century. 330

<margin>
5th CENTURY
from the Year 400.
---
431.
</margin>
**PAUL**, Bishop of Emesa <note>modern-day Homs, Syria</note>, was present at the Council of Ephesus in the year 431; there, he championed the cause of Nestorius and, in the rival assembly <note>the *Conciliabulum*, a separate meeting of bishops who opposed Cyril of Alexandria</note>, he signed the condemnation of Cyril. In the following year, he was sent as an envoy to Alexandria by John of Antioch, Acacius of Beroea, and other Eastern bishops who were eager for peace, in order to enter into a peace agreement with Cyril. John recommended him to Cyril in this way:
> *who has always stood out as distinguished among ecclesiastics, knowing how to be competent in both deeds and words, and possessing a reverence toward the Lord which, by employing it, he has very often and most excellently served the common good.*

Though Paul managed matters at Alexandria with the greatest subtlety, he could not obtain peace from Cyril until he had offered a document of faith, confessed that Mary is the <term>Theotokos <note>Greek: "God-bearer" or Mother of God</note></term>, anathematized <note>formally cursed or denounced</note> Nestorius, and confirmed both articles by speaking aloud in the Church of Alexandria. Having done these things in the name of John and the others by whom he was sent, he struck a peace with Cyril and returned to Asia. There exist, in Greek and Latin, his *Document of Faith* and *Two Homilies* delivered at Alexandria (Council Collections, Vol. 3, pp. 1089, 1096). In Latin, there is a *Letter to Anatolius, Prefect of the Military*, among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, number 107.

<margin>
431.
</margin>
**RHEGINUS**, Bishop of Constantia in Cyprus <note>the ancient city of Salamis</note>, was present at the Council of Ephesus in the year 431 and confirmed the condemnation of Nestorius with his vote. In the seventh session of the Synod, he accused the leaders of Antioch of trying to seize the rights of the Cypriot Church through ambition, and he sought and obtained a decree from the Fathers confirming the <term>autokephalia <note>Greek: "self-heading" or ecclesiastical independence; the right of a church to appoint its own leaders without outside interference</note></term> of his church. There exists, in Greek and Latin, a *Homily in the Synod of Ephesus* delivered after the deposition of Nestorius (Council Collections, Vol. 3, p. 577).

<margin>
431.
</margin>
**JUVENAL**, Bishop first of Ephesus and then of Jerusalem, flourished in the year 431. He attended the Council of Ephesus and stood with Cyril against Nestorius, so that with Cyril's help he might protect his own ambitions against John of Antioch. Indeed, he had unjustly claimed the rights of a Patriarchate for himself; not content with that, he attempted to bring Arabia and the two Phoenicias under his own jurisdiction, having removed them from the governance of the Church of Antioch. It also happened that in the "Robber Synod" <note>the *Latrocinium*, an unauthorized council</note> of Ephesus in the year 449 and the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451, he fought for Eutyches and Dioscorus against Flavian of Constantinople. In the Council of Chalcedon, he finally obtained the rights of the Patriarchate for himself, but he was forced to relinquish Phoenicia and Arabia. There exists in Latin a *Synodical Letter to the Priests, Archimandrites <note>superiors of monasteries</note>, and other Monks of Palestine*, in which he confirms the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon in his own name and that of his bishops (Council Collections, Vol. 4, p. 889).

<margin>
431.
</margin>
**ANDREW**, Bishop of Samosata, flourished in the year 431. Around the year 429, at the command of John of Antioch, he attacked Cyril’s [Twelve] Chapters in writing; at first, he did this somewhat half-heartedly and as if against his will. Later, however, he was offended by Cyril’s sharp response to Theodoret (who had labored in the same arena as himself), and he attacked the same Chapters with a very venomous book. He refused to attend the Council of Ephesus, citing illness; nevertheless, he defended Nestorius's cause with all the authority he could muster, and did not set aside his deep-seated hostility toward Cyril for several years. Finally, around the year 436, moved by the authority of John of Antioch, he entered into peace with Cyril. He spent much effort—though it was in vain—trying to persuade Alexander, his Metropolitan <note>the chief bishop of a province</note>, to do the same. Yet Andrew himself could never be brought to approve Cyril’s Chapters or to confess that God had suffered. He died before the time of the "Robber Synod" of Ephesus; Theophanes writes incorrectly that he was present there, since Rusticus, Andrew's successor, is listed among the bishops of that Synod in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon. There exist in Latin *Eight Letters* among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus (numbers 42, 59, 62, 90, 98, 101, 103, 106). A fragment of his second book against Cyril’s Anathemas is presented by Anastasius in the *<term>Guide <note>Greek: "Hodegos," a theological handbook</note></term>*, chapter 22. Numerous fragments of his first book are found in Cyril's *Apology for the Twelve Anathemas against the Objections of the Easterners* (or Andrew's book); for that work had been approved by the Synod of the Easterners held at Antioch before the year 431, fortified with everyone's signatures, and sent to Alexandria through the deacon Possidonius in the common name of all.

## RABBULAS

Bishop of Edessa, though blind in his eyes <note>original: "oculis quidem captus" - Rabbulas was known for his physical blindness but intense intellectual and spiritual vigor</note>, he was by no means lacking in spirit. He flourished in the year 431. At the Council of Ephesus, he initially judged that Cyril and Memnon should be deposed because of their Chapters <note>The "Twelve Anathemas" or theological points proposed by Cyril of Alexandria</note>; and he turned away from all the Egyptian bishops as if they were heretics. Later, however, having changed his opinion, he championed Cyril’s cause with such a burning passion of soul that, having assembled a Synod at Edessa, he struck with anathema <note>a formal ecclesiastical curse</note> and decreed the burning of all the writings of Theodore <note>Theodore of Mopsuestia</note>, and whatever works of Theodoret and Andrew of Samosata had been written against Cyril’s Chapters. He bound by the same sentence anyone who would either read the said books or henceforth resist Cyril’s Chapters; he even renounced communion with John <note>John of Antioch</note> and all the Easterners. John attempted to restrain the man’s excesses at a Synod held in Antioch in the year 436, ordering him to be removed from Church communion and his see. But it was in vain: Rabbulas retained both as long as he lived, and he passed away in peace some time later. 

There exists in Latin a *Letter*, mutilated at the beginning and the end, among the Ephesine Letters of Lupus, number 200; almost the entire letter is held in Latin in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume 5, page 469. Furthermore, Theodore the Reader <margin>* Collection, book 2, p. 555.</margin> records that he was accused by Andrew of Samosata as if he had written against the Chapters of Theodoret—unless perhaps the conjecture of Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar</note> is more true, that "Ardericus" should be substituted for *'Ἀνδρέᾳ* <note>Andrew</note> and "Cyril" should be read for *Θεοδωρίτῳ* <note>Theodoret</note>; for it is well enough established that Andrew wrote against Cyril’s Chapters. Be that as it may, it can hardly be doubted that Rabbulas wrote many things in that quarrelsome century, of which he was such a large part.

<margin>
431.
</margin>

## CAPREOLUS

Of the African race, as is likely, the Bishop of Carthage who succeeded Quodvultdeus (who himself succeeded Aurelius), he flourished in the year 431. In the previous year, the Emperor Theodosius had written to Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo</note> so that he might honor the Council summoned at Ephesus with his presence; but as Augustine was already dead, the letters were delivered to Capreolus, who did what he could. For he sent a letter to the Synod at Ephesus via his deacon, Bessula; in this, having testified to his greatest care and zeal for the Catholic faith, he excused the less-than-formal delegation because the Bishops of the African Church were unable to meet in a Synod at that time. This was partly due to the short interval of time, and partly because all the approaches to the roads were besieged on all sides by the Vandals <note>A Germanic tribe then invading North Africa</note>. 

The Letter of Capreolus was read in the Synod, with Cyril of Alexandria also requesting that it be entered into the Synodal acts. For he wished, he said, the ancient dogmas of the faith to be confirmed, and the new ones—absurdly devised and impiously spread—to be rejected and proscribed. Immediately all the Bishops cried out together, *These are the voices of everyone! We all assert these things! This is the wish of all!* This Letter exists in Latin in Baronius under the year 431, and in both Greek and Latin in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume 3, page 533. He also wrote to Vitalis and Constantius, Spaniards, a *Treatise* or *Letter on the one person of Christ, true God and Man, against the recently condemned heresy of Nestorius*—a new and unspeakable destruction, as he calls it, crushed in the foyer along with its author and champion, and extinguished by a ray of Apostolic light. Baronius inserted this Letter (mutilated by half) into his *Annals* under the year 431; Jacques Sirmond published it in its entirety from the Herivall Codices, and prefixed the letter of Vitalis and Constantius to Capreolus, among the *Opuscula of the Ancients, Paris 1630, 8vo*. It is also found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 7, page 5. In this Letter, Capreolus himself mentions the delegation he sent to Ephesus, as noted by Casimir Oudin; Oudin, however, described what he has on this writer word-for-word from Miraeus (just as Miraeus himself did almost entirely from Sirmond) while suppressing the name of the author, adding not even a "grunt" <note>original: "ne γρυ quidem" - a Greek idiom meaning not a single syllable or the slightest bit</note> of his own. But I would be infinite if I wished to note all the things which this recent compiler <note>Oudin</note>—otherwise a sufficiently honest man—is accustomed to transcribe from others.

431.
</margin>

## URANIUS

A Priest and a disciple of Paulinus of Nola, whom he served as he was dying in the year 431. At the urging of Pacatus, he wrote a narrative regarding the death of Saint Paulinus, which is found in Surius on June 22nd, and in all recent editions of Paulinus’s works.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ecclesiastical figures from the 5th century. The previous page concluded the entry for Rabbulas of Edessa; this page focuses primarily on the life and writings of Saint Patrick, the Apostle of Ireland, before beginning the entry for Pope Sixtus III.</meta>

# The Nestorian Century. 332

<margin>
5th CENTURY
from the Year 400.
</margin>
Born near Dumbarton and the city of Glasgow around the year 371, Patrick's parents were Calphurnius, a deacon, and Concessa. After his childhood and youth—about which his biographers tell many tales—he was sent to Rome in the year 432 by Germanus of Auxerre <note>A prominent bishop in Gaul known for combating heresy in Britain</note>. There, as some maintain, he was appointed by Pope Celestine as the Apostle and Archbishop of the Irish. Returning to his homeland, he prepared himself for the conversion of Ireland; he purified nearly all the petty kings of the island with holy baptism once they had converted to the faith of Christ. In the year 447, he crossed the sea to Britain, and having gathered fellow-workers from all sides, he returned to Ireland. He propagated the Christian religion far and wide: he founded churches, established episcopal sees, held synods, and performed miracles. Full of days, labors, and glory, he finally died in the year 493 on the 17th of March, at the age of 122. It is said that he founded 365 churches and ordained as many bishops, along with three thousand priests; he is also said to have raised 60 from the dead and baptized 12,000 people. However, the Reverend Archbishop of Armagh <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), a famous Irish scholar and prelate</note> treats Saint Patrick and his deeds extensively after Probus and Jocelin in his work *On the Origins of the British Churches*, chapter 17.

## W R I T I N G S.

*The Confession*, explained in a *Letter to the Irish*, in which he gives an account of his whole life and preaching.

*A Letter to Coroticus*, a petty king of the Welsh-Britons; in this, he pursues the cruelty of that king, who had killed many of the Irish whom Patrick had converted. These two small works are written in a quite rough and semi-barbaric style, yet they are ancient. Indeed, they reflect the *Itala* version <note>The "Old Latin" Bible translation used before Jerome's Vulgate became standard</note> throughout.

*The Synod of Saint Patrick*, containing 31 chapters or canons, previously published by Spelman among the *British Councils*.

*Nine Canons*, previously unpublished.

*The Synod of Bishops Patrick, Auxilius, and Iserninus*, containing 34 canons, found in the *British Councils*.

*Several other Canons.*

*Some Proverbs.*

The book *On the Three Habitations* is found among the works of St. Augustine, but some manuscripts attribute it to Patrick; Sir James Ware <note>An Irish historian and antiquarian</note> judges it belongs to neither.

*The Charter of Saint Patrick, or the Letter on the Antiquity of Avalon* <note>Glastonbury</note>, taken from William of Malmesbury's manuscript book *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury*, is spurious <note>fake or forged</note> if ever a work was.

The book *On the Abuses of the World* is found among the localized works of Cyprian and Augustine; in it are found several sentences cited under Patrick's name in an ancient manuscript at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and by Cathwulph in a *Letter to Charlemagne* found in Duchesne's *French Writers*, Volume 2, pages 666–667. However, Ware believes it is not by Patrick due to the difference in style and the use of Jerome's translation, unless one suspects it was written by Patrick in Irish and translated into Latin by a later hand.

All these were collected and partly revised, and partly published for the first time with notes, by the illustrious Sir James Ware, *London, 1656, octavo.*

Richard Stanihurst composed a *Sermon* under Patrick’s name, which he published in his *Life of St. Patrick*, Book 2, at *Antwerp* in 1587; Messingham gave a reprint of the same at the end of his *Irish Florilegium*, *Paris, 1624*. However, Ware refused to grant it a place among Patrick’s works.

The *Letter on the Embassy or Mission to the Irish* was first published by Gerard Vossius, then in the *Library of the Fathers*, *Cologne, 1618*. The year of the Christian era, which appears immediately at the head of the letter, proves it is spurious, as Miraeus rightly notes. For in that century, the Era of Christ <note>Anno Domini dating</note> had not yet begun to be used in calculating years.

Bale, Pits, and Ware mention several other works; one may doubt whether they exist anywhere, or indeed, whether they ever existed at all.

# The Nestorian Century. 333

<margin>
5th CENTURY
from the Year 400.
</margin>
<margin>
* Appendix to part 1 of the Works of Marius Mercator, Dissertation vi, chapter 6.
</margin>
Provoked by this slander, he began to attack the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who emphasized human free will over divine grace</note> more sharply; so much so that in the Council of Rome held in the year 428 regarding the case of Caelestius, he was the first of all to judge that anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication</note> should be struck against them; and he refuted their heresy in a published book. On August 7, 432, he was ordained Bishop of the Roman see. He diligently protected the authority of the Council of Ephesus; meanwhile, he was not unmindful of the need to foster peace between the Eastern bishops and the Egyptians; he took care to initiate this peace by all means and finally obtained it happily. Furthermore, having sent letters to Nestorius <note>The former Archbishop of Constantinople, accused of heresy</note> while he was in exile in the Monastery of Euprepius, he attempted to bring him back to the confession of Catholic truth, but it was in vain. Nestorius did not cease to cherish his former error. Sixtus himself contracted a stain of suspicion from the literary correspondence he established with the heresiarch <note>A leader of a heretical sect</note>, being accused on that account of having a mind not shrinking from Nestorianism—to such an extent that he found it necessary to dispel the charge by writing a letter to Cyril. Near the end of his pontificate, he firmly excluded from the Church Julian and other leaders of the Pelagians who were craftily seeking Catholic communion. He died in the year 440, on the 24th or 25th of July. There exist in Latin *two Letters: one to Cyril, another to John of Antioch, in the Councils, Volume iii, p. 1175.* A writer of that age, Vincent of Lérins, cites the latter in his *Commonitory*, p. 368. In Greek and Latin, there is a *second Letter to Cyril*, found in Cotelier's *Monuments of the Greek Church, Volume i, and Baluze in the New Collection of Councils, p. 657.* There is also a Latin *Letter to the Eastern Bishops* under his name in the *Councils, Volume iii, p. 1263*, which is rejected by everyone as being of no credibility. Finally, three books are falsely attributed to Sixtus, namely: *On Riches; On Chastity; On Evil Teachers, Works of Faith, and the Future Judgment*; these were published in *Rome, 1573, in octavo; Antwerp, 1575, in sixteen-mo*; and subsequently in more than one edition of the Library of the Fathers. Everyone now agrees with one voice that these small works are supposititious <note>Spurious or fake</note> and tainted with Pelagian errors, with the single exception of Jean Garnier*, who contends at length that Sixtus was indeed imbued with Pelagian error before the year 418 and had composed those small works; but after the year 418, being stirred by the warnings of Augustine and others, he shook off the error and held sounder views; and to redeem both his reputation and his fault, he composed the books of the *Hypognosticon*, which are held among the supposititious works of Augustine.

* Codex 2.
</margin>
ADRIANUS, author of the *Isagoge* <note>An "Isagoge" is an introductory manual or textbook</note>, flourished (if the famous James Ussher correctly marks his age) around the year 433. To me, the matter is quite uncertain. He was certainly older than Cassiodorus, being mentioned by him in chapter 10 of his *Divine Lectures*. His *Introduction to Holy Scripture* is extant, illustrated with brief scholarly notes by Hoeschel, and published in Greek along with other such writings at *Augsburg, 1602, in quarto, and in the Critici Sacri of London, Volume viii*. Regarding this book, Photius writes*: <note>original Greek: ’Aδριανοῦ εἰσαγωγὴ τὴ γραφῆς χρησίμὴ τοῖς εἰσαγομένοις ἡ βίβλος.</note> *Adrian’s Introduction to the Holy Scripture is a useful book for those who are first approaching it.*

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, an Italian by nation and distinguished by nobility, was born at Forum Cornelii <note>Modern-day Imola</note>. He was instructed in both good character and letters by Cornelius, the Bishop of that place, and was finally brought to the sacred altar by him. In the year 433, he was made Bishop of Ravenna, and he died before the year 451. For those who drag his life into the beginning of the following century are wandering in error; indeed, there exists a letter from Pope Leo* given to Leo, Bishop of Ravenna, during the consulship of Marcian and Adelphius (that is, in the year 451). He was a man, besides other gifts of mind, quite remarkable for eloquence, from which he drew the name *Chrysologus* <note>Meaning "Golden-worded" or "Golden-speech" in Greek</note>.

### W R I T I N G S.

One hundred and seventy-six Homilies or Sermons; these were published at *Cologne, 1541, 1618; Paris, 1614*; together with the works of Leo and Maximus at *Paris, 1623, and Lyon, 1633* in the Library of the Fathers, Volume vii; *Bologna, 1643, in quarto; Cologne, 1678, in quarto.*

A Letter to Eutyches the Archimandrite <note>A superior of a monastery or group of monasteries</note>, in which he labors to bring him back to the Catholic faith. It is extant in Greek and Latin by Gerard Vossius at the end of the Works of Gregory Thaumaturgus, *Mainz, 1603, p. 205, and in the Councils, Volume iv, p. 35.*

<page-num>332</page-num>
# The Nestorian Century.

<margin>
5th CENTURY
from the Year 400.
</margin>

Born near Dumbarton and the city of Glasgow around the year 371, Patrick had for his parents Calphurnius, a Deacon, and Concessa. Passing over the years of his childhood and youth, about which his biographers tell many fables, he was sent to Rome in the year 432 by Germanus of Auxerre <note>St. Germanus, a prominent Gallic bishop who combatting the Pelagian heresy</note>; and there, as some maintain, he was appointed Apostle and Archbishop of the Irish by Celestine <note>Pope Celestine I</note>. Returning to his homeland, he prepared to convert Ireland; and he purified with holy baptism nearly all the petty kings <note>original: "regulos"</note> of the island, who were converted to the faith of Christ. In the year 447, he crossed over to Britain; and having gathered fellow-workers from all sides, he returned to Ireland. He spread the Christian religion far and wide: founded churches: established episcopal seats: celebrated synods: and performed miracles. Full of days, labors, and glory, he finally died in the year 493, on March 17th, at the age of 122. It is said that he founded 365 churches, and ordained just as many bishops, along with three thousand priests, raised 60 dead people to life, and baptized 12,000 men. However, concerning Saint Patrick and his deeds, the Reverend Archbishop of Armagh <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), a famous Irish scholar and archbishop</note> deals extensively after Probus and Jocelin in his *Antiquities of the British Churches* <note>original: "de Britann. Eccles. Primord."</note>, chapter 17.

### W R I T I N G S.

The *Confession*, explained in a *Letter to the Irish*, in which he gives an account of his whole life and preaching.

*Letter to Coroticus*, a Welsh-British petty king; in which he pursues the cruelty of that king, who had killed many of the Irish converted by Patrick. These small works are written in a very rough and semi-barbaric style, yet they are ancient. For they exhibit the *Itala* <note>The Old Latin version of the Bible used before St. Jerome’s Vulgate</note> translation everywhere.

*The Synod of Saint Patrick*, containing 31 chapters or canons, previously published by Spelman <note>Sir Henry Spelman, an English antiquary</note> among the British Councils.

*Nine Canons*, previously unpublished.

*The Synod of the Bishops Patrick, Auxilius, and Iserninus*, containing 34 canons, preserved in the British Councils.

Several other canons.

A number of proverbs.

The book *On the Three Dwellings* <note>original: "De tribus habitaculis"</note> is found among the works of Saint Augustine, but some manuscripts ascribe it to Patrick; Ware <note>Sir James Ware, a prominent Irish historian</note> rejects this attribution.

*The Charter of Saint Patrick*, or the letter on the antiquity of Avalon <note>Glastonbury</note>, taken from William of Malmesbury's manuscript book on the antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury; it is spurious if anything ever was.

The book *On the Abuses of the World* <note>original: "De Abusionibus Seculi"</note> is found among the pseudo-works of Cyprian and Augustine; in it are found some sentences cited under Patrick's name in an ancient manuscript at St. Benedict’s College, Cambridge, and by Cathwulf in a *Letter to Charlemagne* found in Duchesne's *French Historians* <note>original: "Script. Francic."</note>, Volume 2, pages 666, 667. Ware, however, judges it is not Patrick's due to the difference in style and the use of Jerome's version <note>the Vulgate Bible</note>, unless he suspects it was written by Patrick in Irish and translated into Latin by a later hand.

All these were collected and partly revised, and partly then first published with notes by the illustrious Sir James Ware, London, 1656, in octavo.

Richard Stanihurst composed a *Sermon* under Patrick's name, which he published in his *Life of Saint Patrick*, Book 2, Antwerp, 1587; Messingham gave a reprinted version of it at the end of his *Irish Anthology* <note>original: "Florilegii sui Hibernici"</note>, Paris, 1624; but Ware did not want to grant it a place among Patrick's works.

*Letter on the Legation or Mission to the Irish*, first published by Gerard Vossius, then in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliotheca Patrum"</note>, Cologne, 1618. The year of the Christian era, which immediately occurs at the front of the letter, proves it is spurious: as Aubert Miraeus rightly notes. For in that century, the era of Christ had not yet begun to be used in calculating years.

Bale, Pits, and Ware mention many other things; whether they exist anywhere, or indeed whether they ever existed, one may doubt.

Stirred up by this slander, he began to attack the **Pelagians** <note>Followers of Pelagius, who taught that humans could achieve salvation through free will without divine grace</note> more sharply; so much so that in the Roman Council held in the year 428 regarding the case of **Coelestius**, he was the first of all to judge that anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note> should be struck against them; and he refuted their heresy in a published book. In the year 432, on August 7th, he was ordained Bishop of the Roman see. He diligently protected the authority of the **Council of Ephesus** <note>Held in 431, it condemned the teachings of Nestorius</note>; meanwhile, not forgetful of reconciling peace between the Easterners and the Egyptians, he took care that it should be entered into by all means, and at last happily obtained it. Moreover, by sending letters to **Nestorius**, who was living in exile at the Monastery of Euprepius, he tried to lead him back to the confession of Catholic truth; but it was in vain. Nestorius did not cease to cherish his former error: Sixtus contracted a stain upon himself from the literary correspondence established with the Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect</note>, being accused on that account of having a mind not shrinking from **Nestorianism** <note>The belief that Christ existed as two separate persons, one divine and one human</note>: so much so that he found it necessary to clear himself of that crime in a letter written to Cyril. Toward the end of his Pontificate, he firmly excluded **Julian** and other leaders of the Pelagians from Catholic communion when they were craftily seeking it. He died in the year 440, on the 24th or 25th of July. There survive in Latin: *Two Letters, one to Cyril, the other to John of Antioch, Council Vol. iii. p. 1175.* The later one is cited by a writer of that age, Vincent of Lérins, in his *Commonitory*, p. 368. In Greek-Latin: *Two Letters to Cyril,* in Cotelerius’s *Monuments of the Greek Church, Vol. i. and Baluzius in the New Collection of Councils, p. 657.* There is also held in Latin under his name a *Letter to the Eastern Bishops, Council Vol. iii. p. 1263,* which is rejected by everyone as being of no credibility. Finally, three books are falsely attributed to Sixtus, *namely: On Riches; On Chastity; On Bad Teachers, Works of Faith, and the Future Judgment;* which were published *at Rome in 1573 in octavo, and at Antwerp in 1575 in sixteen-mo;* and then in more than one edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. Everyone now agrees that these small works are spurious and tainted with Pelagian errors, with the sole exception of **Garnier** <margin>* Appendix to part 1 of the Works of Marius Mercator, Dissertation vi. chapter 6.</margin> who contends at length that Sixtus had been imbued with the Pelagian error before the year 428 and had written those works; but after the year 428, stirred by the warnings of Augustine and others, he shook off the error and held sounder views; and that to redeem his reputation and his guilt at the same time, he composed the *Hypomnesticon* books, which are held among the spurious works of Augustine.

**MAXIMUS**, a Gaul by birth, was a monk of the Monastery of Lérins <note>A famous island monastery off the French Riviera, a center of 5th-century Christian thought</note>, and eventually its Abbot, having succeeded St. Honoratus in the year 426. In the year 433, he was made Bishop of Riez <note>original: "Regensis sive Regiensis"</note> in Narbonnese Gaul: and in the year 439 he took part in the Council of Riez, and in 452 in the Council of Orange. More about him is not clear. There exist several Homilies written by him, which hold a place among the Homilies of Eusebius of Emesa or Eucherius of Lyons: for it is established that the fourth of these is by Maximus; whose title further indicates that the three preceding ones are by the same author: as the most learned man Jean Savaro rightly notes in his remarks on Sidonius Apollinaris, Book 4, Work 3, page 232.

<margin>
434.
Socrates, Book 7,
chapters 28, 41, 45.
</margin>

**PROCLUS**, having been imbued from an early age with the study of good literature, especially Rhetoric, closely assisted Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople</note> while still a youth, serving as his amanuensis <note>A personal secretary or literary assistant</note>; and when he was made a Reader, he served him in the writing of books. He was constantly in the company of Atticus, who was later Bishop of Constantinople, and was his notary; he was raised by him to the rank of the Diaconate. Around the year 427, he was appointed Bishop of Cyzicus by Sisinnius; while he was preparing for his journey there, the people of Cyzicus, anticipating him, chose a certain monk named Dalmatius as their Bishop. Proclus therefore remained in Constantinople, where he achieved the greatest glory by preaching in the churches. In the year 434, after the death of Maximianus, he was promoted by the Emperor Theodosius to the Bishopric of the royal City <note>Constantinople</note>. In the year 435, in a letter given to the Armenians, he condemned the errors of Nestorius and Theodore of Mopsuestia, yet without touching the name of Theodore, so as not to offend the Armenians too much, to whom his memory was dear. In the year 438, he recalled the Johannites <note>Followers of John Chrysostom who had separated from the main church after his exile</note> to the unity of the Church; with the Emperor's consent, he brought the body of Chrysostom, which had been buried at Comana, to Constantinople; and having carried it through the city in a solemn procession, he deposited it with great honor in the Church of the Holy Apostles. He died in the year 446.

<margin>
* Book 7, chapter 41.
</margin>

*He was a man of excellent character*, says Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian</note> <note>original Greek: "Ἦν δ’ ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς τὰ ἤθη"</note>, *if ever there was one*. He was a man endowed with the best of morals, if anyone else was: but he was most distinguished for his patience and *forbearance* <note>original Greek: "ἀνεξικακίᾳ"</note>; inasmuch as he judged that heretics should be recalled to the bosom of the Church by gentleness and mercy, rather than by calling upon the imperial power for aid.

<margin>* Letter 10.</margin>
The Works of Proclus were published in Greek and Latin from the Elmenhorst library at *Leiden*, 1617, in duodecimo. (However, that edition contains hardly half of Proclus's works). They were later published much more fully, with notes by Vincent Riccardi, at *Rome*, 1630, in quarto, as we have listed them above. François Combefis collected all of Proclus’s *Homilies*, twenty in number (excluding the one falsely attributed to *St. Stephen*), and published them in Greek and Latin with notes in the Supplement, *Paris*, 1648, Volume 1, page 301.
Furthermore, Proclus wrote many Homilies which are no longer extant; Nicephorus, in his *Ecclesiastical History* (Book 14, chapter 38), provides a fragment of one delivered on the occasion of the Romans' defeat of the Barbarians.

**EUCHERIUS**, a Gaul by birth and of illustrious parentage, led a monastic life on a certain island situated near Lérins; <note>The island of Saint-Honorat, part of the Lérins Islands off the French Riviera, famous for its monastery.</note> where, it seems, he lived until the <margin>* year 434.</margin> year 434, when he was made Bishop of Lyon. In the year 444, he took part in the Council of Orange. He died around the year 454, during the reigns of Valentinian and Marcian. It is well established that he was married. From this marriage, he fathered Salonius and Veranius, who later attained the dignity of the Episcopate. There was another Eucherius, also Bishop of Lyon, who was distinct from ours and flourished in the following century; he participated in the second Council of Orange in the year 529, as Théophile Raynaud proves at length in his *Index of the Saints of Lyon*, page 227, etc.

->WRITINGS.<-

**A Parenetic Letter** <note>A letter of advice or exhortation.</note> on the contempt of the world and of secular philosophy, addressed to his kinsman Valerian; written from his retreat near Lérins in the year 432. Erasmus follows this letter with wonderful praise. "If you grant any weight to my judgment," he says, <note>original: "Si quid meo suffragio tribuis..."</note> "I see nothing produced by men of our religion, who also flourished in the glory of eloquence, which can be compared with his phrasing. So much so that he everywhere proves himself an excellent craftsman: whether in the appearance of the order, or, etc." It was published separately with the scholarly notes of Erasmus at *Basel* in 1520 and 1531, and with notes by Rosweyde at *Antwerp* in 1620.
*A Letter in Praise of the Desert*, or on the solitary life, written to Hilary of Arles from his retreat. Genebrard published it separately at *Paris* in 1578, and Rosweyde published it together with the Letter to Valerian at *Antwerp* in 1620.
*A book on the formulas of spiritual intelligence, addressed to his son Veranius.*
*Two books of Instructions for his son Salonius*, one of which deals with the more difficult questions of Holy Scripture, while the other provides an interpretation of the Hebrew names occurring therein.
Several *Homilies* among those circulated under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, published at *Antwerp* in 1602 and elsewhere quite often. There are those who attribute all the Homilies of the Emesan to Eucherius; but it is sufficiently established that some of them are owed to Bruno of Asti, others to Maximus of Riez, and others to various authors. Meanwhile, Claudianus Mamertus <margin>* Book on the state of the soul, ch. 2.</margin> testifies that Eucherius published some very eloquent sermons.
*The History of the Passion of St. Maurice and his companions, the Martyrs of the Theban Legion;* which many people ascribe to the younger Eucherius, and rightly so. For near the end of the History, the author relates that it was established that hymns should be sung day and night in honor of those Martyrs in the Church of Agaunum by the command of the holy and illustrious martyr of Christ, the Blessed King Sigismund, and that this custom is preserved even to this day. However, that Sigismund died a martyr's death in the year 524. It is found in Surius under the date of *September 22nd*. It was published separately with notes by Peter Stevart at *Ingolstadt* in 1617.
*Commentaries on Genesis and the books of Kings;* which can be ascribed to neither Eucherius, since they cite Gregory the Great and Cassiodorus <note>Because Gregory the Great and Cassiodorus lived after both Eucheriuses, they could not have been cited by them.</note>.

Furthermore, Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Marseille, a 5th-century historian who continued Jerome's work on Christian authors.</note> reveals that **Eucherius** compiled certain minor works of Cassian into a single volume, cutting out errors and shortening the language. Hence, there are those who contend that our Eucherius is the author of the fourth book of the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "Vitis Patrum"</note>—which was composed from the writings of Sulpicius Severus and Cassian, as will be easily apparent to those inspecting the book.

## CLAUDIUS MARIUS VICTOR, or Victorinus, a Rhetorician <note>A teacher of oratory and public speaking.</note> of Marseille and a poet, flourished in the year 434. He died before the year 450. Sidonius <note>Sidonius Apollinaris, a Gallo-Roman poet and bishop.</note> says of him that he was as excellent a man as he was learned in every respect; while he composed other works powerfully, he wrote his verses most powerfully of all. He wrote the following poems:

*Three Books of Poems or Commentaries on Genesis*, spanning from the beginning of the book until the death of Abraham, dedicated to his son Aetherius. In these books, says Gennadius *, he expressed his thoughts with a Christian and pious sentiment, but—being a man occupied with secular literature and trained by no master in the Divine Scriptures—his opinions are of lighter weight <note>Gennadius suggests Victor lacked formal theological training despite his piety.</note>.
<margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 60.</margin>

*A Letter to Abbot Solomon on the Perverse Morals of His Age*, written in heroic verse <note>The meter used for epic poetry, such as the works of Homer or Virgil.</note>.

The poems of Victor are contained in the Fabrician Collection of Poets, in Bigne’s Appendix on page 580, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 417; they were published separately at *Paris, 1560, in octavo.*

<margin>434.</margin>
## CAELIUS SEDULIUS, a Scot by nation (if trust is to be placed in Trithemius, Dempster, and Bale), is said to have flourished around the year 434. While he was still a layman, he studied philosophy in Italy. He later became a Priest, according to Isidore; moreover, the poets Liberatus and Belisarius call him a Prelate (in the acrostics dedicated to Sedulius, which are found in Bigne’s Appendix, page 680). Sigebert calls him a Bishop, and the "Pseudo-Dexter" calls him the Bishop of Oreto in Spain. Whoever he may have been, he flourished in this era: for his poems were collected and published by Turcius Rufus Asterius, who held the Consulship in the year 494, and who was praised by Arator, Cassiodorus, and Venantius Fortunatus. The small notes added to two very ancient manuscripts (the Thorne and Pithou manuscripts mentioned by Ussher and Labbe) provide evidence that he wrote his books in Achaia <note>A province in Greece.</note> during the time of the Emperors Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian. Regarding the style of Sedulius, Olaus Borrichius writes:
<margin>* Dissertation 2 on the Latin Poets.</margin>
> *His diction is easy, ingenious, rhythmic, clear, and sufficiently pure—if you excuse certain faults in meter—and above all, it serves as a recommendation for Christian piety.*

### WORKS

*The Paschal Poem* <note>original: "Carmen Paschale"</note>, or *Five Books on the Miracles of Christ*, together with a dedicatory letter to the Priest Macedonius, which is missing from most editions. In it, mention is made of the Deaconess Syncletica, to whom Eustathius dedicated his Latin translation of St. Basil’s *The Six Days of Creation* <note>original: "Hexaemeron," a work describing the creation of the world.</note>. In some editions, certain dedicatory verses to Theodosius the Elder are prefixed; these seem to have been stitched on from the work of some other, older poet. Certainly, they do not have Sedulius as their author.

*A Comparison of the Old and New Testaments*, written in elegiac verse. Turcius Rufus Asterius published it after the death of Sedulius; consequently, it is sometimes incorrectly attributed to him.

*An Alphabetic Hymn to Christ* <note>original: "Pæan Alphabeticus"</note>, written in iambic verse, which briefly encompasses the deeds of Christ <note>This hymn is the source of the famous Christmas hymn "A solis ortus cardine."</note>.

*The Paschal Work in Five Books*, described in prose, together with a second letter to the Priest Macedonius; it was he who had urged Sedulius to express the *Paschal Poem* in a prose version. François Juret published this work from the Pithou manuscript, *Paris, 1585.*

The *Collection, or Explanation of all the Epistles of St. Paul*, compiled from the writings of the Holy Fathers, is consistently attributed to Sedulius the Scot of Ireland. That this is not the work of Sedulius the Poet is sufficiently indicated by the fact that passages excerpted from Gregory the Great (*Morals on Job*, book 19, chapter 21) are read therein <note>Gregory the Great lived in the 6th century, much later than the famous poet Sedulius, proving the author must be a later namesake.</note>. Indeed, a certain Sedulius, a Bishop of Britain of the Scots race, together with Fergus, Bishop of the Scots Picts, subscribed to the Roman Council held in the year 721. This man could reasonably be believed to be the author of the *Collection*; although Labbe <note>Philippe Labbe, a 17th-century Jesuit scholar.</note> thinks it should be ascribed to a certain Sedulius the Scot who (according to the Monk Hepidannus in the *Annals* edited by Duchesne) was held to be famous in the year 818. To this later Sedulius he also adjudges certain *Grammatical Works* which existed in the *Library of De Thou* under the name of Sedulius.

The Works of Sedulius were published, printed by Aldus Manutius in the year 1502; then at *Basel in 1528, 1534*; and with the notes of Antonio de Nebrija <note>A famous Spanish Renaissance scholar.</note> in the same place in *1541*; in the Fabrician Collection in 1564; and finally in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 6, page 458; and in the Bignean Appendix, pages 658 and 911, which is considered an accurate edition.

---

<margin>434.</margin>
**VINCENT**, a Gaul by nation, born at Toul (a town of Belgica Prima <note>A province of the Roman Empire in what is now northeastern France and Luxembourg.</note>), sprung from a splendid and noble family, had Epirochius as his father and Lupus, Bishop of Troyes, as his brother. In the first years of his youth, he followed a secular military career; having abandoned this, he betook himself to Lérins <note>A famous island monastery off the French Riviera.</note> and led a monastic life, soon being elevated to the dignity of the Priesthood. He flourished in the year 434—namely, three years after the Synod of Ephesus—at which time he wrote his *Commonitorium* <note>A "Reminder" or manual on the Catholic faith.</note>, as he himself testifies <margin>* Chapter 41.</margin>. He died before the year 450, while Theodosius and Valentinian were still reigning. There are those who count Vincent among the Semi-Pelagians <note>Those who sought a middle ground in the debate between Augustine’s views on grace and Pelagius’s views on free will.</note>; there are others who deem him free from that stain. To the authors of the first opinion, the *Objections against the doctrine and writings of Augustine* supply a very strong argument; it is very likely that these were written by our Vincent, but we shall speak of this shortly. Added to this are two marks of Semi-Pelagianism, formerly noted by Blessed Prosper, which Vossius <margin>* Pelagian History, book 1, ch. 9.</margin> detects in the *Commonitorium*: the first is the display of the letters of Popes Celestine and Sixtus; the second is a hidden accusation of "novelty" struck against the later writings of St. Augustine. Furthermore, what Prosper writes about Honoratus proves that the inhabitants of the Monastery of Lérins favored the Semi-Pelagians at that time; and everyone knows what he wrote about Faustus (who presided over the Monastery in the year Vincent wrote). 

Vincent wrote—with his own name suppressed and having assumed the name of "Peregrinus" <note>Latin for "The Pilgrim" or "The Stranger."</note>—in a sufficiently polished and open style (as Gennadius <margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 64.</margin> rightly says) against the Heretics a *Double Commonitorium*. He lost the second part after it was stolen from him; hence he subjoined a certain recapitulation to the first part to take its place. This small work appeared in *Basel, 1528*; *Cologne, 1569* with the commentaries of Costerus; *Paris, 1569* in octavo; in 1586 edited by Pithou with certain others; *Cologne* (with notes by Colterius), 1613, in duodecimo; with the commentaries of Jean Filezac, *Paris, 1619*, in quarto; finally, with the notes of Baluze, joined to the works of Salvian, *Paris, 1669*, in octavo; in the *Library of the Fathers, Vol. 7, p. 249*; and at *Cambridge, 1687*, in duodecimo.

Vincent also wrote *Objections against the writings and doctrine of Augustine on predestination and free will*; these, summarized in sixteen chapters, Prosper presents in the book in which he refutes them. That these objections are due to our Vincent is sufficiently indicated both by what I have already brought forward regarding his zeal for Semi-Pelagianism, and by the striking convenience of the timeframe. For Prosper refuted those objections while Pope Sixtus was still sitting, namely between the years 432 and 440. Indeed, it does not escape me that Baronius and others attribute them to a certain Vincent the Younger, who <margin>Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, ch. 88.</margin> was an associate of Gennadius and commented on the Psalms. But the chronology does not allow for this. For that Vincent could hardly have emerged from his youth when the Vincentian objections had already been circulating in everyone's hands for a long time. Vossius <margin>* In the place cited.</note> has more arguments, which the reader may consult.

...he had not blushed to openly blurt out such blasphemies: <note>original: "Οὐ φθονῶ τῷ Χριστῷ γενομένῳ Θεῷ· ἐφ᾿ ὅσον γὰρ αὐτὸς ἐγένετο, κἀγὼ ἐγενόμην."</note> **"I do not envy Christ having become God; for insofar as he was made [God], I too was made [God]."** The Emperor committed his case to be judged by Uranius of Himeria, Photius of Tyre, and Eustathius of Berytus <note>modern Beirut</note>, joined by the prefect Damascius. They held two synods on the matter, one at Tyre and the other at Berytus in the year 448, and pronounced **Ibas** free from the crimes charged against him. For he strenuously denied the second head of the accusation; as for the first, he confessed it had been done by him before the peace was established between the Easterners and Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note>, but affirmed that from that time forward he had cherished an unviolated concord with Cyril. In the year 449, he was accused again in the "Robber Council" of Ephesus <note>term: <term>Latrocinio Ephesino</term>—a name given by later historians to the Second Council of Ephesus because of its violent and irregular proceedings</note> and was deposed by Dioscorus of Alexandria. Driven from his see, and as Facundus of Hermiane * testifies, dragged through forty stopping-places across various provinces, he changed prisons twenty times or more. He eventually withdrew to the Monastery of Apamea, where he remained in hiding together with Theodoret, until he was restored to his former dignity by the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451. Finally, many years after his death, he was condemned by the Fathers of the Fifth Council in the year 536 <note>The Fifth Ecumenical Council was actually in 553; 536 may refer to a local synod or a typo in the original text</note> as a cultivator of the Nestorian name and dogma, despite the resistance of Pope Vigilius, who brought forward many arguments for his cause—the defense of which is handled by Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century cardinal and historian</note>. Ibas wrote a famous **Letter to Maris the Persian**; the much larger part of it, which deals with Cyril and the Acts of Ephesus, the restoration of peace to the Church, and the praises of Theodore of Mopsuestia, is extant in Greek and Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 661.

**SYAGRIUS**, whom only Gennadius * mentions. His homeland, age, and way of life are entirely hidden from us. However, he can be conveniently assigned to the year 437. He wrote a small book *On the Faith against certain Heretics*, who refused to allow the persons of the Holy Trinity to be expressed by names indicating their mutual relationship <note>referring to the internal relations of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>. There were also circulated under his name, in the time of Gennadius, seven books *On Faith and the Rules of Faith*; Gennadius judged that all of these were not his, due to the dissonance of style. **ANTONINUS**, called *Honoratus* by Gennadius * (for I have no doubt he is the same person), Bishop of Constantine in Africa, flourished in the year 437. At that time (as we learn from the *Chronicle* of Prosper), Gaiseric, King of the Vandals, was stirring up a persecution against the Catholics. Among others who then experienced the cruelty of the barbarian king, Arcadius—a Spaniard by birth and formerly a man of noble standing—was driven into exile because he refused to embrace the Arian impiety; indeed, he at last carried off the palm of martyrdom. To this Arcadius, while already in exile, our Antoninus wrote a **Consolatory and Exhortatory Letter to bear labors for Christ**, strengthened, says Gennadius, both by contemporary examples and by the reasonings of the Scriptures. It is a clearly pious and elegant letter; and one which, as Baronius * rightly notes, smells of that ancient Apostolic character. It is extant both in Baronius at the year 437, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 665.

<margin>439.</margin>
**VALERIAN**, a Gaul by nation, as is probable, Bishop of Cimiez <note>then called Cemelium, near modern Nice</note> across the Var in the Maritime Alps, flourished in the year 439, at which time he was present at the Synod of Riez in Gallia Narbonensis. Around the year 451, among other Bishops of Gaul, he subscribed to the Synodal Letter sent to Pope Leo. In the year 455, at the third Council of Arles, together with Bishop Theodore, he brought a charge against Faustus, Abbot of Lérins, for usurping the Episcopal office in the Monastery of Lérins; and having brought him back into line, he caused him to be confined within his ancient limits. When our Valerian was accused by a certain obscure scoundrel of the Semi-Pelagian dogma, he was vindicated by Theophilus Raynaud *, who published a lengthy **Apology**. Raynaud rightly contends that this blame should be cast upon a certain Valerian—a "belly-speaker" and gluttonous slave mentioned by a certain Eusebius in a letter to Cyril of Alexandria, published by Baronius at the year 417. There are extant **20 Homilies** written by Valerian on various subjects, together with a **Parenetic Letter to Monks**; these were first brought to light by Jacques Sirmond at *Paris, 1612, in octavo.* They were afterwards published with the *Works* of Leo, Chrysologus, etc., at *Lyon, 1633, in folio*, edited by Theophilus Raynaud together with his Apology...

<margin>439.</margin>
**SOCRATES**, a native of Constantinople, was born, it seems, at the beginning of the reign of Theodosius the Younger. In grammar, he had as teachers Helladius and Ammonius, who had opened schools in Constantinople after fleeing from Alexandria; in rhetoric, according to the judgment of Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar and editor of church historians</note>, he studied under Troilus the Sophist. Having entered his adult years, he practiced law in the courts; hence he was called **Scholasticus** <note>term: <term>Scholasticus</term>—a title for a professional lawyer or advocate</note>. Almost all writers declare that he was a follower of the **Novatian** sect <note>term: <term>Novatians</term>—a rigorist Christian group that refused to readmit those who had renounced their faith during Roman persecutions</note>; however, the illustrious Valesius clears him of this fault. Certainly, although he is somewhat more favorable toward the Novatians, it cannot be concluded from this that he was a member of that sect. Furthermore, does he not himself count the Novatians among the heretics in more than one place? <margin>Book 6, chapters 19, 20, 23.</margin> He flourished in the year 440, when he set himself to write his *Ecclesiastical History*, which he brought down from the beginning of the reign of Constantine the Great to the year 439. In composing this work, as Valesius rightly observes, he used singular judgment and diligence. His judgment is demonstrated by the excellent observations woven in here and there; his diligence by the mostly accurate notations of time and the best monuments of church history sought out from all sides: letters of bishops, acts of synods, and the books of the ecclesiastical writers of that age, from which he fashioned his work. Since he had first begun his history based on the reliability of **Rufinus**, having later found better authors, he corrected his errors and rewrote the first two books entirely from the very beginning. Photius * discusses him briefly; concerning his style, he has only this to say: <margin>* Code 28.</margin> <note>original: "ἡ δὲ φράσις αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔχει ἀξιόλογον, ἀλλὰ κῂ ἐν τοῖς δόγμασιν οὐ λίαν ἐστὶν ἀκριβής."</note> **"His style is not especially remarkable, nor is he very accurate in matters of dogma."** His style is not particularly splendid, nor is he very precise in doctrine; he indicates an affection for the Novatians. Regarding his style, Socrates himself * frankly confesses that he was **"proceeding with a sparing step"** <note>original: "ὁ φειδωλὸς βῆμα φέρειν"</note>, being little concerned with the empty pomp of words. There exists the *Ecclesiastical History of Socrates*, comprised of seven books, published in Greek along with other authors of ecclesiastical history by Robert <margin>* Book 1, ch. 1.</margin> Stephanus <note>Estienne</note> in *Paris, 1544, folio.* Greek and Latin in *Geneva, 1612*; with a new translation and the most learned annotations of Henri Valesius in *Paris, 1668*, and thereafter in *Mainz, 1677, folio.*

<margin>440.</margin>
**HERMIAS SOZOMENUS**, apparently a Palestinian by birth, was born to parents of no low status; he certainly traced his lineage to Bethelia, a village in Palestine near Gaza. As Valesius believes, he seems to have taken the name of Salaminius from a certain Salamanes, a relative of his (whom he mentions in Book 6, chapter 32), and not from Salamis, a city in Cyprus, as Nicephorus thought. Educated in Palestine, he applied himself to the study of law in Berytus <note>modern Beirut</note>, a city of Phoenicia; afterward, having set out for Constantinople, he was engaged in legal practice. However, he turned his mind to the labor of writing church history above all else. At first, he wrote a *Compendium of Ecclesiastical History* from the ascension of Christ to the year 323, containing the most notable events in two books, which have been lost. Then, starting from the year 324, he wove together a history of 115 years with greater effort and diligence, finishing the work in nine books dedicated to the Emperor Theodosius around the year 440. <note>original: "Ἔστι δὲ Σωκράτους ἐν τῇ φράσει βελτίων, διαφωνεῖ δὲ αὐτῷ κῂ κατὰ τίνας ἱστορίας."</note> **"He is better than Socrates in style,"** says Photius *, **"but he disagrees with him on certain historical accounts."** <margin>* Code 30.</margin> To this judgment, Valesius says, "we gladly agree; but as much as Sozomen surpasses him in elegance of speech, so much does Socrates surpass him in judgment." For Socrates judges best both concerning men and concerning ecclesiastical affairs and business. There is nothing in him that is not grave and serious, nothing that you could strike out as superfluous. In Sozomen, on the contrary, some light and childish things occur, which could be demonstrated by many examples. It is gathered that he wrote after Socrates because he occasionally adds certain things to Socrates' accounts, corrects others, and disagrees in many. His *History* was issued in Greek, printed by Robert Stephanus in *Paris, 1544, folio.* Greek and Latin in *Geneva, 1612*, with the translation and notes of Valesius in *Paris, 1668*, and thereafter in *Mainz, 1677, folio*; however, that edition falls far below the Parisian one.

**EUSTATHIUS**, whom Cassiodorus \* calls a *most eloquent* man, and whom Sigebert † also mentions, flourished around the year 440. He was a contemporary of the poet Sedulius. He translated nine Homilies on the Hexaemeron <note>term: <term>Hexaemeron</term>—a theological treatise or series of sermons on the six days of creation</note> by Saint Basil from the Greek language into *Latin* with such grace that, according to Cassiodorus, he seems to have matched the genius of that most learned man with the strength of his own eloquence. He dedicated that translation to his sister, Syncletica. It is extant in the *Paris* edition of the Works of Saint Basil (1603), the *Antwerp* edition (1616), and published elsewhere. Miræus will teach you more about Eustathius and his sister Syncletica in his notes on Sigebert, as will Casimir Oudin (who, according to his custom, copies Miræus in full while rarely naming him) in his *Supplement*, page 87.

**NILUS**, a native of Constantinople, was illustrious for the nobility of his family and his wealth; so much so that he was granted the Prefecture <note>the high office of city governor</note> of the City of Constantinople. Joined in marriage, he had two children by his wife—a male and a female, if the Greek Menology <note>term: <term>Menology</term>—a liturgical book containing lives of the saints arranged by their feast days</note> is to be believed; though if Nilus himself is rather to be heard, both were male. He flourished in the year 440. After he had spent several years in secular life, he desired to pursue more zealously the piety whose foundations he had once drawn from his teacher, John Chrysostom. He with difficulty persuaded his wife that, after dividing the children between them, he might be permitted to withdraw to the solitudes of Egypt and lead a monastic life from then on. Taking his son Theodulus with him, he sought out Egypt and established his desired way of life. However, while he was enjoying the most pleasant company of the Nitrian monks <note>monks from the Nitrian Desert, a major center of early Christian monasticism in Egypt</note>, Barbarians suddenly rushed in and carried off his son Theodulus as a captive along with many others. While he was anxiously searching for him, he himself was captured by the Barbarians; however, he was soon liberated by them and found his son in Elusa at the home of the city's Bishop, by whom Nilus himself was ordained a Priest, though unwillingly. He died while Marcian was still reigning. Many years after his death, his body was translated to Constantinople by Justin the Younger and placed in the Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul. He wrote many *short works, "which," says Photius \*, "witness not only to a remarkable perfection in his deeds, but also to his power in speaking."* <note>original Greek: "τὴν τε χζῑ τὰ ἔργα τελειότητα... κ; τὴν ἐν λόγοις μαρτυρεῦσι δύναμιν"</note> Those which have come to our knowledge have a place here:

*Exposition on the Song of Songs*, which is found mixed with the commentaries of Gregory of Nyssa, Maximus, and Psellus on the same book; Greek and Latin, in the Ducæan Supplement, *Paris*, 1624, Volume 2.

*Seven Narrations on the Slaughter of the Monks on Mount Sinai, and the Captivity of his son Theodulus.* Extant in Greek and Latin with the translation and notes of Petrus Possinus, *Paris*, 1639, quarto.

*Oration on Albianus, a Nitrian Monk*, Greek and Latin, joined to the *Narrations*.

*229 Hortatory Chapters:* These are found in Greek and Latin in the *Orthodoxographi* <note>a collection of "writers of right doctrine"</note>, Volume 1, and in the Supplement of 1624, Volume 2. They also appeared in Greek and Latin with the commentaries of Michael Neander, *Leipzig*, 1577, and with the notes of Peter Schoning, *Franeker*, 1608, octavo.

*A Book on the Eight Vicious Thoughts*, which Bigotius published in Greek and Latin at the end of the works of Palladius, together with an ancient translation made a thousand years ago. Combefis had previously published the Greek text in the *Latest Supplement* (1672), as did Joseph Maria Suares in the *Collection of the Works of Saint Nilus*, *Rome*, 1673.

*Another Treatise on the same subject*, which Jacques de Billy provided in a Latin translation among the works of Damascene; Jean Baptiste Cotelerius exhibits it in Greek and Latin with notes in *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume 3, page 185.

*153 Chapters on Prayer*, in which the form of praying is explained: Photius mentions the same number in Codex 201, and the Suaresian edition contains them along with a Prologue. For the Latin edition published by Francisco Torres at *Florence* in 1578, octavo, which is also found in the *Library of the Fathers*, exhibits only 147 or 150 chapters.

*355 Letters*, published in Greek and Latin by Possinus, *Paris*, 1657, quarto. Leo Allatius had these reprinted, enlarged by many other letters, in Greek and Latin, adding a dissertation on Nilus, *Rome*, 1668, folio.

*Treatise on the Ascetic Life.*

*To the Monk Agathius, on Cultivating Virtue and Fleeing Vice.*

*To Magna, Deaconess of Ancyra, on Voluntary Poverty.*

**DRACONTIUS**, Spanish by birth and a Priest <note>term: <term>Presbyter</term>—an early Christian title for a priest or elder</note> by rank, flourished around the year 440 during the reign of Theodosius the Younger, to whom he wrote an *Elegy*.
