**BACHIARIUS**, called Maccaus; according to Miræus he was Irish, and according to Bale and Pits he was British. A disciple of Saint Patrick, as they claim, and educated in the Monastery of Bangor, he applied himself especially to the mathematical disciplines. More certain are the things Gennadius \* says of him. "A man," he says, "unencumbered and ready in Christian philosophy, intending to devote his time to God, he chose a life of pilgrimage for the sake of preserving his integrity." He flourished in the year 440. According to the same Gennadius, he wrote an *Apologetic Defense of the Faith* to the Bishop of the City of Rome (Leo, as one may suspect), in which he proved against his detractors that his pilgrimage was undertaken solely for the sake of religion. That book is lost. However, his *Letter to Januarius on Receiving the Lapsed* <note>term: <term>The Lapsed</term>—Christians who had renounced their faith under Roman persecution but wished to return to the Church</note> is extant among the *Orthodoxographa*, page 485, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Vol. 6, page 1174. Concerning other things he is said to have written, one may consult Bale and Pits.

### **URSINUS**

**URSINUS**, African by birth, and a Monk by his way of life. He was prominent around the year 440. According to the testimony of Gennadius \*, he wrote *against those who decree that heretics ought to be rebaptized*, teaching that those who are baptized in the name of Christ, or simply in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, ought not to be rebaptized, even if the sense in which they were baptized was perverse. He argued that after a simple confession of the Trinity, the imposition of the Bishop’s hands was sufficient for their salvation. Philippe Labbe, and following him Casimir Oudin, argue on the evidence of a Vatican Manuscript that this small book by Ursinus is the same as the anonymous treatise published by Rigaltius among the works of Cyprian. For reasons that are not to be disregarded, I cannot grant my assent to them, and therefore I have left that work to the "Anonymous" author elsewhere. Thus, it perhaps proceeded not so much from ignorance (as Casimir Oudin would have it) that the most learned Bishop of Oxford—the one now among the saints <note>original: "ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις"</note>—left this work as anonymous in his edition of Cyprian; rather, it was because he believed, along with the illustrious Rigaltius and others, that the author was nearly a contemporary of Cyprian. Certainly, the only argument in favor of Ursinus is the title in the Vatican Manuscript, which would have been easy for any scribe who had read Gennadius to add to any anonymous treatise.

---

<margin>440.</margin>

### **LEO I.**

**LEO I**, surnamed the Great, Roman by birth (though the author of the *Book of the Popes* <note>term: <term>libri Pontificalis</term>—the 'Liber Pontificalis', a medieval biographical history of the popes</note> calls him a Tuscan, despite the protests of certain manuscripts), was born to his father Quintianus. While still an Acolyte <note>term: <term>Acolyte</term>—a minor clerical rank in the early church</note> of the Roman Church around the year 418, he was sent to Africa with letters to Aurelius, the Bishop of Carthage—provided that this was the same Leo mentioned by Augustine in letter 104. Under Pope Celestine, he served as a Deacon, and around the year 430, he urged John Cassian, a Deacon of the Church of Constantinople (who, having lived long among the Easterners, best knew the customs and character of heretics), to write against Nestorius, who had then recently emerged. Cassian performed this by publishing seven books *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, which, as is clear from the end of the letter prefixed to the work, he dedicated to our Leo. In the year 439, when a discord arose between Aetius and Albinus, the leaders of the Roman army in Gaul, Leo was sent to restore harmony, which he successfully accomplished. While he was still delayed on this legation, Pope Sixtus died, and our Leo was elected to his place by common consensus, though he was absent, on July 28 in the year 440. He was elevated to the Pontifical Throne on September 8. It was a time of little joy; due to the encroaching incursions of the Barbarians and the surrounding noise of the Nestorian, Pelagian, and Arian heresies, the face of both the Church and the State was most sorrowful. Notwithstanding these things, Leo proceeded in the execution of his duty with a manly spirit. In the year 443, many Manichaeans, having fled from the Vandals in Africa, sought hiding places in Rome; and so that they might hide more safely, they mingled themselves in the mysteries of the Catholics. However, they betrayed themselves like thieves by this sign: though they took the bread, they rejected the Eucharistic cup. Leo soon warned the common people of this, and by what mark the execrable heretics were to be discerned. Here are his own words:

<margin>In Sermon 4 on Lent, p. 217.</margin>

> *When they dare to be present at our mysteries to hide their infidelity, they so temper themselves in the communion of the Sacraments that sometimes, lest they be unable to remain entirely hidden, they receive the body of Christ with an unworthy mouth, but they altogether decline to drink the Blood of our redemption. We make this known to your holiness for this reason: so that such men may be made manifest to you by these signs, and so that those whose sacrilegious simulation is detected may be driven from the society of the Saints by priestly authority.*

At this time, therefore, in the Roman Church, the faithful were accustomed to receive the Eucharist under both species <note>note: This refers to receiving both the consecrated bread and wine, a practice later restricted in the Roman Catholic Church but defended by Protestants during the era this manuscript was likely written.</note>, and those who did otherwise were publicly marked with the infamous sign of heresy. If the decrees and customs of the Roman Church are now different, let those whom it concerns look to it.

In the year 445, on account of the metropolitical rights of the Church of Arles being rescinded by Leo, a dispute arose between him and Hilary; Hilary defended his rights until his death, a matter we have discussed under the entry for Hilary. In the year 448, Eutyches, not yet known in the West, sought Leo's favor through letters. Leo wrote, both to the Emperor,

<margin>
The 5th Century
from the Year 400.

...the Emperor, and then interceded for the man with Flavian. Once he was better informed of the whole matter, Leo condemned the heretic <note>This refers to Eutyches, who argued that Christ had only one nature.</note> and sent a lengthy letter to Flavian, in which he discussed Eutyches and his errors in a sprawling and learned manner. In the following year, he sent Legates to the Council of Ephesus—which has been called the *Robber Council* <note>original: "Latrocinalis." This council was infamous for its violence and procedural irregularities.</note>—but as soon as he learned that everything there was being done by Dioscorus through force and fraud in favor of Eutyches, he quickly assembled a Synod at Rome, annulled the Acts of Ephesus, and condemned both Dioscorus and Eutyches. In turn, Leo himself was removed from the communion of the Church by Dioscorus and ten others associated with him. 

As these disturbances broke out into a greater flame day by day, an Ecumenical Council was decreed. Leo labored in vain with both the Emperor and the Empress Pulcheria to have it held within Italy. It was instead summoned to Chalcedon in the year 451 and began on the 8th of the Ides of October. The Pope’s legates, Bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius and the Priest Boniface, arrived there; in the fifth Session, they strenuously contended that Leo’s letter to Flavian, written two years earlier, should be included in the Council’s definition regarding the faith. The Fathers responded that they were prepared to confirm the Letter with their own signatures, but they would never allow it to be woven into the Synodal decree itself. When the Legates insisted even more sharply, and the Emperor himself urged it, the Bishops said: <term>οἱ ἀντιλέγοντες εἰς Ῥώμην ἀπελθέτωσαν</term>, which means *let those who speak against it travel to Rome*. 

Finally, when they came to the establishing of the Canons, it was established by Synodal Decree that the Overseer of the See of Constantinople should be allotted <term>τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα</term>, or *equal privileges*, with the Bishop of Elder Rome. The Papal Legates protested vehemently, arguing that the Canons of Nicaea were being violated in this way, that they would admit nothing that opposed the dignity of the Roman Church, and that the Apostolic See must not be humbled—noting they had received instructions to this effect from Leo. Nevertheless, after a most diligent examination of the case, by the common vote of the Bishops and with the assent of the Emperor’s judges, the decree was sanctioned and confirmed. 

When the matter was reported to the Pope, he dissolved into total rage; Leo truly roared, but he especially fumed against Anatolius, the Bishop of Constantinople. He accused him of injury, arrogance, ambition, trampling the statutes of the Council of Nicaea, invading the rights of others—in short, what did he not accuse him of? He almost never returned to good terms with him after this. While he ratified the faith defined at Chalcedon, he utterly rejected that specific decree. *We declare it void, and by the authority of the Blessed Apostle Peter, we annul it by a general definition*, to use his own *words on this matter. These things are mentioned briefly here, for I have explained the whole history of this affair more extensively elsewhere. †

<margin>
* Letter 79 to Pulcheria, chapter 3, page 598.
† Dissertation on the Ancient Government of the Church, chapter 6, sections 3, 4, 5.
</margin>

In the year 452, as Attila, King of the Huns, was moving his arms against Italy, Pope Leo was sent to him as an envoy by the Emperor Valentinian. By his eloquence and prayers, Leo so softened the man's fierce spirit that he abandoned Italy and led his army across the Danube. In the year 453, Leo delegated his duties at the imperial court to Julian, Bishop of Cos; this was a new development, as the scholar Quesnel correctly notes for this year, and was not practiced by earlier Popes. From this point forward, it became the custom for them to have *Apocrisiarii* <note>A term for a high-ranking ecclesiastical representative or legate at the imperial court.</note> in the Royal Palace to manage their affairs at Court. 

In the year 455, the City of Rome was plundered by the Vandals under the leadership of Genseric; however, through Leo's intervention, it was saved from slaughter and fire. Afterward, he primarily turned his mind to settling the disturbances of the East and the Church of Alexandria. While he was almost entirely occupied with these things, he laid aside his mortal remains on the 3rd of the Kalends of November in the year 461. Regarding the year of his death, the scholars Quesnel and Papebroch treat the subject more extensively than others, whom the curious may consult. This distinguished prelate is deservedly commended for his piety, erudition, eloquence, prudence, pastoral vigilance, and great zeal against heretics, as well as his constant and perpetual concern for the Catholic faith. However, he was not equally praised for his pride, his rather lofty spirit, and his immense study of increasing the Papal dignity. He was indeed a strenuous amplifier of Papal power and a spirited defender of the privileges he claimed for his See, which was clearer than daylight in his contentions against the Decree of Chalcedon.

Among these letters, many by others also find a place—namely by Flavian, Ravennius, Rusticus, Eusebius, Paschasinus, etc.—which are by no means counted as Leo's own epistles. Leo's letters are found in almost any edition of the Councils; however, depending on the time, place, and the editor's diligence, there may be more or fewer, and they may be more or less corrected. ### WORKS ATTRIBUTED TO LEO.

*On the Calling of All Nations* <note>original: "De Vocatione Omnium Gentium"</note> in two books. These have been ascribed by some to Saint Ambrose, by others to Eucherius of Lyon, and by others to a certain Hilary—either of Arles, or the Syracusan companion of Prosper—or even to Prosper of Orléans. However, by the common opinion of the learned, they are attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine <note>A 5th-century Christian writer and disciple of Saint Augustine.</note>, supported by all manuscript codices for the last eight hundred years and by the consensus of all France. This is not denied by Pasquier Quesnel <note>A prominent 17th-century French theologian and editor of Leo's works.</note> himself, who nevertheless attempts to claim them for Leo in a special dissertation. He does this with a long line of conjectures rather than arguments, which essentially amount to this: that against Prosper’s authorship militate various ways of speaking on the same subject, a disparity of style, the method of the work, and the calculation of time; while in favor of Leo stand the phrasing and character of speech, the age, the homeland, the familiar use of Scripture, the peculiar citation of certain scriptural passages, and finally, a similarity of doctrine. This learned man expands on these points at length; but since such things tend to vary according to any man’s ingenuity and can be found more or less in others, they do not seem to provide a sufficiently firm foundation for this opinion.

The *Letter to Demetrias on Christian Humility* is commonly judged to belong to Prosper. The same Quesnel claims it for Leo using almost the same arguments: namely, from the similarity of style, doctrine, and concepts, and from the cited version of Jerome and the Vulgate, to say nothing of other matters of lesser weight. Consequently, the same judgment must be passed on this as on the previous dissertation.

The *Chapters*, or *Authorities of the Past Bishops of the Apostolic See regarding Grace and the Free Choice of the Will* <note>original: "De Gratia & libero Voluntatis arbitrio," a central topic in the Pelagian controversy over how much human will contributes to salvation versus divine grace.</note>, which are usually attached to Pope Celestine’s Letter to the Gauls. Quesnel argues Leo’s case for these chapters in a prolix dissertation divided into two parts. In the first part, he assesses the claim for Prosper but asserts they belong to Leo, using almost the same conjectures he used above. In the second part, he discusses the necessity and importance of the dogmas contained in the final part of the *Chapters*. He places these three small works at the front of the *Works of Saint Leo*, although supported by no compelling reason, no testimony of the ancients, and no faith in an ancient codex. Certainly, if they had Leo—a man most celebrated in his time—as their author, would that have remained hidden from Cassian, Prosper, Eucherius of Lyon, Vincent of Lérins, and others? Indeed, would it have remained hidden from his own successors in the Roman See, who seem not to have thought of Leo in this regard even in their dreams? Furthermore, would Leo himself, who had ample opportunity in so many letters dealing with the Pelagian controversies, have failed to mention these works? Meanwhile, the points produced by this learned man to confirm his opinion merit no common praise for ingenuity and diligence.

The complete *Works of Leo* have been published—to pass over other less accurate editions—at Paris in 1614 and 1618 in folio; at Lyon in 1633, 1651, and 1671; and elsewhere quite often, with the works of Chrysologus and Fulgentius joined to them. Finally, Pasquier Quesnel collected and revised all of Leo's works, drew some out anew, and published them in Paris in 1675 in two volumes in quarto. Besides other merits, he adorned and illustrated his quite elegant edition with the ancient *Code of Canons of the Roman Church*, a more ancient Dionysian version, sixteen dissertations, and very learned notes.

*On Governance*
book 7, p. 139.
</margin>

SALVIAN, not indeed an African by nation, as some wish to claim, but a Gaul <note>From the region of modern-day France.</note>, since he himself calls Gaul his native soil. Baluzius <note>Étienne Baluze (1630–1718), a French scholar.</note> correctly gathers from Salvian's first letter that he was born in Cologne <note>original: "Coloniæ Agrippinæ"</note>, although he also lived for a long time in Trier. He flourished from the year 440, and thereafter began to become more and more famous. He married Palladia, the daughter of Hypatius (who was still a pagan <note>original: "Gentilis"</note>) and Quieta. She herself was a pagan in religion, but he later led her to the Christian faith. From her, he had a single child named Auspiciola. At last, having left his homeland, he set out for the province of Vienne and was soon made a Priest <note>term: "Presbyter," an elder or priest in the early church.</note> of Marseille. The fact that he is called a "Bishop" in several editions of Salvian is quite a serious error, since Gennadius <margin>* *On Famous Men*, ch. 67. † *Commentary on Salvian*, p. 1</margin> expressly calls him a Priest. To meet this objection, Conrad Rittershusius †, a most learned man, thinks it could be said that at the time when Gennadius wrote those things,

Gennadius believed that Salvian had reached the rank of Bishop, not noticing that in the year 495, when Gennadius was writing, Salvian was already weighed down by age and near death. However, by no means relying on that weak argument, he seeks <note>original: "ouden"</note> nothing else to apply here except one far weaker: namely, that there was a time in the Christian Church when the same men were called both Presbyters <note>Priests</note> and Bishops. According to the scholar Baluze, the error regarding his status as a bishop arose from certain editions of Gennadius stating that "having been made a Bishop, he composed many homilies," whereas the text should be read as "homilies made for Bishops" or "to Bishops." For this eloquent and learned man used to write homilies which were then recited in the Church by the Bishops. He died at a great age at the close of the century, as it seems.

->EXTANT WRITINGS.<-

In the year 1640, the Pithou edition was reprinted at Paris. Finally, Étienne Baluze edited the works, revised against manuscript codices and illustrated with notes, at Paris, 1663, in octavo; and a second, enlarged edition at Paris, 1669, in octavo.

**CONSTANTIUS**, a Gaul by birth and of high nobility, was a Presbyter of Lyon (Isidore of Seville wrongly calls him a Bishop*), and was thereafter held in religious veneration by Sidonius; he flourished in the year 440 and following. After the church of that city was built by Patiens, the Bishop of Lyon, Constantius himself celebrated the walls near the altar of the Basilica in hexameter verses. Between the years 475 and 480, when the city of the Arverni <note>Modern Clermont-Ferrand</note> was pressed by a long siege by Euric, King of the Goths, Constantius overcame all difficulties—the length of the journey, the shortness of the days, the lack of fodder, and other impediments—and traveled from Lyon to Arvernum by a path quite impassable and steep. There, he called the rioting citizens back to harmony and led others, who were fleeing in fear of the attacking Goths, back into the city. We have excerpted these facts mostly from Sidonius Apollinaris, who everywhere marvels at Constantius as a man of singular genius and saving counsel. Certainly in public discourses,

<margin>440.</margin>
### PETRONIUS
<margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 41.</margin>
PETRONIUS, Italian by birth, was born of an illustrious family. He was the son of Sextus Anicius Petronius Probus, a Praetorian Prefect <note>a high-ranking administrative official in the Roman Empire</note> who held the consulship in the year 406 along with the Emperor Arcadius. The historian Baronius conjectures from the words of Gennadius and Eucherius that Petronius himself held the office of Praetorian Prefect just as his father had. Certainly, Eucherius, in his book *On Contempt for the World* <note>original: "de contemptu mundi"</note> written in the year 432, mentions a Petronius who was then a Bishop <note>original: "Antistitis"</note> in Italy; one who ascended to the title of the priesthood from the highest seat of worldly power. However that may be, it is established by the testimony of Gennadius * that our Petronius was the Bishop of Bologna and was eminent for the holiness of his life. He flourished around the year 440. He died before the year 450, while Theodosius was still reigning. He wrote a book *On the Ordination of a Bishop* <note>original: "de Ordinatione Episcopi"</note>, which Gennadius notes was attributed by some to his father. Even in the time of Gennadius, it was commonly held that he had written the *Lives of the Desert Fathers of Egypt* <note>original: "Vitas Patrum Monachorum Ægypti"</note>. Whether that title refers to the book currently circulated under that name, or rather to some other specific work, is not entirely certain.

### PHILIPPUS
<margin>440.</margin>
<margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 62.</margin>
PHILIP, a Priest <note>Presbyter</note> and a disciple of Jerome, flourished chiefly around the year 440. He died during the reigns of Marcian and Avitus, which is to say in the year 455, or at the very beginning of the following year. For Avitus, who was made Emperor on July 10, 455, laid down the purple <note>resigned the imperial office</note> around May of the following year, after holding power for ten months. Besides personal *Letters*, which were very eloquent <note>original: "vafra," perhaps meaning clever or subtle</note>, and specifically written to exhort the endurance of poverty and pain—which have long since perished—Gennadius * testifies that our Philip wrote a *Commentary on Job*. Indeed, three books of *Commentaries on Job addressed to Bishop Nectarius* were published under Philip's name at Basel in 1527, both in quarto and in folio. The scholar Bede, in his book *On the System of Ounces* <note>original: "de Ratione unciarum"</note>, cites a passage from Philip’s *Exposition on Job* which is found in these Commentaries today, proving they are indeed Philip's work, <margin>* Book 4, p. 293.</margin> as Sixtus of Siena * noted some time ago. Casimir Oudin also affirms that he saw these Commentaries in manuscript in a very ancient codex in the Library of Igny in the region of Reims, which had the authority of Gennadius prefixed to them. These Commentaries are also commonly included among the works of Bede and Jerome.

### ISAAC
<margin>440.</margin>
<margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 66.</margin>
ISAAC, a Syrian by birth, was a monk and later a Priest of the Church of Antioch; he flourished in the year 440. He died around the year 456. He composed many things in the Syriac language, especially against the Nestorians and Eutychians <note>two groups deemed heretical for their views on the nature of Christ</note>. He also lamented the ruin of Antioch in a long poem. Gennadius * mentions these as having been written by him, though none of them survive today. There is indeed a *Book on the Contempt of the World* <note>original: "Liber de Contemptu mundi"</note> extant in Latin under Isaac's name in the eleventh volume of the *Library of the Fathers*, which some—not without reason—attribute to a younger Isaac who flourished at the end of the sixth century. Since neither Gennadius nor Trithemius, who list the writings of our Isaac, make any mention of this book, it seems no less probable (as Miraeus rightly observes) that the book belongs to the younger Isaac.

### ASCLEPIUS
<margin>440?</margin>
<margin>* On Illustrious Men, ch. 73.</margin>
ASCLEPIUS, an African by birth, flourished in the year 440 and was still among the living in the year 485. Among the ancient writers, only Gennadius * records these facts about him: *A Bishop of a small village in the territory of Baia <note>likely in North Africa</note>, he wrote against the Arians: and is said to be writing now against the Donatists. He is celebrated for a great reputation in extemporaneous teaching.* N. E.

### PASCHASINUS
<margin>443.</margin>
PASCHASINUS, Bishop of Lilybaeum <note>modern Marsala</note> in Sicily, was a friend to Saint Cyril, Pope Leo, and other men of great name. He flourished chiefly around the year 443. He seems to have suffered much for his confession of the Catholic faith during the persecution by Genseric <note>King of the Vandals</note>. He himself complains in his letter of the exile and many evils inflicted upon him. Whether he was the same person as the Paschasius who was driven from the court by Genseric in the year 437, and who finally underwent a brave martyrdom after many tortures—

...Prosper mentions his death in his *Chronicle* <note>original: "Chronico"</note>; I leave it to the reader to investigate this more accurately. In the year 451, he was sent as a legate by Pope Leo to the Council of Chalcedon, alongside Bishop Lucentius of Asculum and the priest Boniface, to attend the Synod in the Pope’s name. Paschasinus held the primary position in this delegation and was the first of all the bishops to sign the decrees of the Synod in Leo's name. He wrote a *Letter on the Observation of Easter to Pope Leo*, which survives among Leo's letters; a more corrected version is found in Bucherius’s *On the Doctrine of Times* <note>original: "de Doctr. Temp."</note>, page 75. He also wrote a letter to the same Pope, in his own name and those of his fellow legates, *concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus*, which is contained in the volumes of the Councils. Trithemius attributes the *Acts of the Council of Chalcedon* to him, though the authority for this is unclear, except for the fact that Paschasinus attended and presided over the Council.

<margin>444.</margin> TIRO PROSPER, a native of Aquitaine, was a layman, it seems, and a notary <note>a secretary or legal scribe</note> to Pope Leo. He flourished in the year 444. It is commonly believed that he was a Bishop of Riez <note>original: "Regensis"</note> in Aquitaine, or as others say, of Reggio in Italy; however, I can hardly agree with this opinion. The scholar Labbe <margin>* Vol. 2. p. 247.</margin> rightly notes that none of the ancient writers before Honorius of Autun assigned him even the lowest rank in the clergy, much less the dignity of a Bishop. He especially devoted himself to the name and teachings of Augustine. In the year 426, he sent letters to Augustine informing him of the <term>Massalian errors</term> <note>often called Semi-Pelagianism; a movement in southern Gaul that emphasized human effort alongside divine grace</note> budding in Gaul; he succeeded in getting Augustine to oppose them by writing his treatises on perseverance and predestination. After Augustine's death, Prosper defended his memory against the slanders of the Massalians with great passion and diligence. In the year 431, he and his fellow student Hilary traveled to Rome to accuse those who attacked Augustine's name of slander and heresy before Pope Celestine. He obtained a letter from the Pope to the Bishops of Gaul, which strengthened him to resist the plots of the Massalians more firmly. Upon returning to Gaul, he continued to tirelessly oppose the <term>Pelagians</term> <note>followers of Pelagius, who taught that humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace</note> through both his writings and his example. In 433, he published a particularly noble work against Cassian, whom he calls "the Collator" <note>referring to John Cassian's famous book, the 'Collationes' or Conferences</note>. After the year 440, he seems to have been called to Rome by Pope Leo to serve as his secretary and to fight against the Pelagians who were disturbing Italy. In 443, he was sent to Campania by Leo to perform this duty and to counter the deceits and audacity of Julian <note>Julian of Eclanum, a major Pelagian theorist</note>. He was still alive in 455, for he brought his *Chronicle* up to that year. Furthermore, Count Marcellinus mentions him in his own *Chronicle* as late as the year 460. He was certainly a man of great learning and no less zeal for the Catholic faith; so much so that Photius <margin>* Code 54.</margin> attributes the ruin of the Pelagian heresy to him more than to others. That he was married is evidenced by the *Verses to his Wife*, which are cited by Bede at the end of his small book on metrics.

-> EXTANT WORKS. <-

*The Book on the Promises and Predictions of God*, divided into three parts, with accompanying booklets titled *Half of the Time* <note>original: "Dimidium temporis"</note>, which contains much concerning the Antichrist and the glory and kingdom of the Saints. Ussher, in his manuscript *Theological Library*, contends that this work is not by Prosper of Aquitaine, using this chief argument: Prosper never saw Africa, at least not while Augustine was alive. However, the author of this work writes that he saw Bishop Aurelius (who died not long after Saint Augustine) at Carthage. Moreover, he reveals that he suffered much in the Vandal persecution, was driven out of Africa, and was finally brought to Italy—details which do not fit our Prosper at all. To these points, add the enormous difference in style, which is so great that it alone could disqualify the work from being Prosper’s. The scholar Quesnel recently added his own judgment in his *Dissertation on the Life of St. Leo* (at year 444, no. 4). "For that work," he says, "is not by Prosper, but by some unknown anonymous African, whose style and character of speech is so far removed from that of Prosper that any fair judge of matters can easily see it. Indeed, the speech of this author is humble, meager, and simple; Prosper’s manner of speaking is abundant, rich, powerful, vigorous, and full of great thoughts." It would be in vain for someone to say that this work was written by Prosper as a young man, since it is the work of a man advanced in age, as the author himself testifies and as is clear from many passages. Add to this that Gennadius, while listing the works of Prosper,

Jacques Sirmond first published this from manuscript codices, followed by Pierre-François Chifflet in Volume I of the *Contemporary Historians of France*.

*The Pithou* or *Imperial edition* <note>original: "Pithæana seu Imperatoria"</note>, which begins from the year 379 and proceeds not by the names of Consuls, but by the years of the Emperors noted in the margin, ending in the year 455. Pierre Pithou published this edition in *Paris, 1588*; Philippe Labbe, with the help of a manuscript copy, revised and reprinted it in the *New Library of Manuscripts (Paris, 1657)*, Volume I, page 56.

*The Labbe edition* <note>original: "Labbeana"</note>, which finally presents the complete Chronicle of Prosper as described by Gennadius. Starting from the beginning of the world, it reaches the year 455. After the year 379, a supplement concerning various heresies is inserted. The part that narrates the events from 379 to 455—commonly called the *Consular* part—is more corrected and expanded than what was previously published. Philippe Labbe was the first to provide this long-desired edition in the *New Library of Manuscripts*, Volume I, page 16.

In these four editions, it is surprising how much the part of the Chronicle called "Consular" varies; covering the years 379 to 445 or 455, it is nearly twice as long in some as in others. In several, it is quite diluted and meager, while in others, it is sufficiently accurate. Truly, this difference, which is indeed enormous, must be attributed to the audacity and ignorance of the scribes and interpolators.

The Works of the Blessed Prosper have been published (excluding the Chronicle and the Confession of Faith, which have no place in some editions) at *Lyon, 1539 in folio; Cologne, 1565 in quarto; Louvain, 1566 in quarto; Douai, 1577 in octavo; Cologne, 1609 in octavo, and 1618; Lyon, 1639 in octavo* in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume VIII, page 1.

<margin>
444.
</margin>

IRENAEUS, a Syrian by birth, it seems, and a Count of the Holy Empire by rank, was sent to Ephesus by the Emperor Theodosius in the year 431 to attend the Ecumenical Council <note>The Council of Ephesus</note> in the Emperor's stead. Having arrived at Ephesus, he openly favored the side of Nestorius <note>A bishop whose teachings on the separation of Christ's natures were deemed heretical</note> and harassed the Orthodox bishops with various injuries. When the Council ended, he was entreated by the Eastern bishops and hurried to Constantinople to deceive the Emperor with lies and tricks, and to block access for Cyril <note>Saint Cyril of Alexandria</note> and the truth. In the year 435, when Nestorius was again stirring up trouble from his retreat at St. Euprepius, Irenaeus was present at Antioch and again openly patronized him. For this reason, the angered Emperor reduced him to the ranks and expelled him from the court; indeed, he ordered him to be deported into exile as far as Petra, a town in Arabia, though accompanied by a sufficiently honorable retinue. However, it seems Irenaeus never actually went there, having escaped either by flight or by petitions. Stripped of his former rank, he withdrew to Syria, where by a decree of the bishops of Phoenicia in the year 444, he was ordained Bishop of Tyre by Theodoret, even though he had been twice-married <term>digamus<gloss>a man who has married twice, which usually disqualified one from the priesthood under early Church law</gloss></term>. Yet he did not hold the see for long. For the Emperor, taking the matter poorly, ordered him to be deposed by edict after two years unless he confessed that Mary was the Mother of God <note>original: "Deiparam"</note> and anathematized Nestorius. Since Irenaeus stubbornly refused these terms, he was finally driven from his bishopric by force in the year 448, or rather the following year. Cast out from his see, he turned to writing his *Tragedy* <note>original: "Tragœdiam," the title of his history of the Nestorian conflict</note>, so that in that way at least he might take vengeance for the loss of both his secular and ecclesiastical dignities. It is not clear how long he survived his bishopric. He wrote a commentary on the events of the Council of Ephesus and the deeds throughout the whole East during the twenty years or so following the Nestorian controversy. That work was divided into several books (one of which, for example, was titled *On History*). It was not so much a perfect History as a hodgepodge of Synodal Acts, letters, Imperial rescripts, and other such writings regarding the Ephesian cause; to these, he added historical notes here and there as the occasion arose, mocking Cyril and the Orthodox while praising Nestorius and his sectaries. That work has indeed perished; however, a not-insignificant part of it, translated from Greek into Latin, has been preserved for us by the compiler of the Ephesian Letters (whoever he was, certainly an ancient author), which Christianus Lupus published at *Louvain, 1682 in quarto*. For that entire collection of letters and Synodal Acts, in its entirety, was taken from the larger work of Irenaeus

<margin>445.</margin>
IDATIUS, or Hydatius, a Spaniard by race, a Gallaecian <note>from Gallaecia, modern-day Northwest Spain and Northern Portugal</note> by country, and a native of Lemicis. He is called "of Lemicis" by Sigebert, but more correctly "of Aquae Flaviae" <note>modern Chaves, Portugal</note>, where he served as Bishop. He flourished around the year 445, at which time Pope Leo mentioned him as a Gallaecian Bishop in his 91st Epistle. Idatius himself records that he, in alliance with Bishop Turibius of Astorga, detected certain Manichaeans <note>followers of a dualistic religion that the Church deemed heretical</note> hiding in Gallaecia. However, he had already attained the Episcopate before the year 431, when he undertook a journey to Gaul as a legate for his people to meet with Aetius, the Commander of Both Services <note>original: "utriusque militiæ Ducem," a high-ranking Roman military official</note>. In the year 461, he was captured in the church of Aquae Flaviae by the Suebi <note>a Germanic people</note> who were then devastating Gallaecia; he was carried off but returned home after three months of captivity. He died in the year 468 or the following year at a very advanced age. He wrote a *Chronicle* from the year 379 (where Jerome’s work ended) to the year 428, the third year of Valentinian III, as he himself testifies in his Preface; he later extended it to the year 467. Joseph Scaliger published only some excerpts of it at the end of the *Eusebian Chronicle*, and Canisius included it in his *Ancient Readings*. The full text was provided by Jacques Sirmond (*Paris, 1619, 8°*), and from that, it was included in the Amsterdam edition of the *Eusebian Chronicle* (1658). He also compiled the *Consular Fasti* <note>chronological lists of Roman consuls</note>, beginning from the first consuls Brutus and Collatinus and continuing the catalog down to the year 468. Sirmond published an imperfect version (*Paris, 1619*) covering the years 270 to 423 AD, but the complete version was published by Philippe Labbe in the *New Library of Manuscripts*, Volume 1, page 3. Both works are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 7, page 1231. Regarding the *Chronicle*, it should be noted that some people continued it after Idatius's death down to the year 500 or 490. This led to an error by Boston of Bury <note>a medieval English bibliographer</note> and Sigebert in his Chronicle, who wrote that the *Chronicle* was carried through to those years by Idatius himself. Indeed, the version of Idatius's *Chronicle* found in Canisius and that published by Andreas Schott in Volume 4 of *Illustrated Spain* extends beyond the time of Emperor Leo. Scaliger notes that Idatius's diction is barbarous and contains not a few errors in Roman history; nevertheless, he contains several details concerning the Goths and Suebi that are not found elsewhere.

<margin>
447.
* letter 11.
</margin>
FLAVIAN, a Priest of the Great Church of Constantinople and the keeper of the sacred vessels and offerings <note>the skeuophylax</note>. After the death of Proclus in late October 447 (though others, following Baronius, refer this to the previous year), he was made the Bishop of Constantinople. Accordingly, Theodoret, in a letter * addressed to him, congratulated him on his appointment to the bishopric of the Royal City. However, he had not held the seat for long when Eutyches began more openly broadcasting his heresy <note>Eutychianism, the belief that Christ had only one nature</note>; Flavian then convened a <term>Home Synod</term> <note>original: "ενδημούση" (endemousē), a local council of bishops present in the capital</note> of forty provincial bishops in Constantinople and condemned the obstinate man. But Eutyches, relying on the power and favor of Chrysaphius—the primary Eunuch among the Imperial Chamberlains, who held total power in the Palace and pursued Flavian with the greatest hatred—appealed to a more general Synod. This council was called by the Emperor (who was deceived by Chrysaphius's schemes) to be held at Ephesus. Therefore, in the year 449, with Dioscorus presiding over the Synod and conducting everything through violence, the acts of the Constantinople synod were rescinded, Eutyches was acquitted, and Flavian was condemned, deposed, and badly treated by Barsumas and other monks of that faction. 
<margin>
* Annals Vol. 3, p. 36.
† Book 14, ch. 47.
</margin>
Furthermore, if we listen to Zonaras * and Nicephorus †, he was so severely beaten with fists and kicks to the chest and face by Dioscorus, Chrysaphius, and other enemies of piety and truth, that he died three days later. Nicephorus adds that Dioscorus even jumped with his heels onto the belly of the deceased Flavian. Others, however, report that Flavian was driven into exile by this "Robber Synod" <note>original: "Latrocinali Synodo", the Second Council of Ephesus, infamous for its violence</note> and reached the city of Hypæpa in Lydia, where he died on February 18th of the following year, broken by calamities and miseries. On this matter, see the learned Jean Garnier, who disputes this accurately, as is his custom, in his *Dissertation on the Books of Theodoret*, page 208. There remain two letters written by Flavian to Pope Leo in the *Councils*, Volume 4, page 13; the first is in Latin, the second in Greek and Latin. The latter was also published in Greek and Latin by Cotelerius in *Monuments*, Volume 1, page 50, and by Baluze in the *New Collection of Councils*.

<margin>448. Theodoret's *Philotheus*, ch. 26.</margin>
SYMEON, called the Stylite <note>from the Greek 'stylos,' meaning column</note>, and to distinguish him from the Younger Symeon who emulated his life, *the Elder*; a Syrian by race, born in the village of Sisan, he was most famous around the year 448. In his early youth, he worked as a shepherd of sheep; later, after being warned by a divine dream, he betook himself to a certain Heliodorus, a hermit most celebrated for his holiness of life. He spent ten years there (Evagrius says nine) intent on fasting and other disciplines of a severe life. From there, he was enclosed for three years in a narrow cell <note>original: "aede," likely a small chapel or hut</note> at the base of a mountain in Palestine, where he so wasted himself with fasting that he is said to have tasted food only at intervals of forty days. Having left the small house, he bound himself with a massive iron chain twenty cubits long to a rock on the very summit of the mountain. He is thought to have lived this way of life for a full seven years; unless we prefer to follow the calculations of Evagrius <margin>* Book 1, ch. 12.</margin>, who, omitting the story of the chain, records that he lived hidden in the small house for ten years. At last, persuaded by a certain Bishop Meletius, he removed the chain and sought out a high column located in a place called Mandra near Antioch; he spent seven years on the lower part of the column and thirty years on the top, and for this reason, he was called a *Stylite*. In this place, he practiced hardships of life that were truly astonishing and surpassed the human lot by a long distance; indeed, if the Greeks are to be believed, he performed countless miracles. Finally, after passing 56 years in the ascetic life, he met his final day during the reign of Leo, appearing to be between the years 460 and 467. *He wrote many Epistles*: one to the Emperor Theodosius, an *exhortation* that he should take away the churches granted to the Jews of Antioch, which Evagrius mentions in Book 1, ch. 12; *a second* in support of the Council of Chalcedon to the Emperor Leo, mentioned by the same author in Book 2, ch. 10; *a third* for the same Council to Basil, Bishop of Antioch, which Evagrius displays in full in the place cited, as does Nicephorus in Book 15, ch. 19; *a fourth* to the Empress Eudocia on the same cause, fragments of which Nicephorus records in Book 15, ch. 13; fifthly, a *Profession of the Catholic Faith* to the Emperor Leo, mentioned by Eulogius of Alexandria in Photius’s *Library*, Codex 230, which however might rightly be considered the same as the second epistle just listed. Furthermore, there exists in Latin under the name of our Symeon a *Sermon on always embracing in the mind one’s own departure*, in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 7. Antonius, his disciple and servant who provided him with necessities while he lived on the column, wrote the *Life of Symeon the Stylite*. This *Life* exists in Latin in the *History of the Fathers*, Volume 1 of the Plantin edition.

<margin>448.</margin>
POLEMIUS, or P. ANNEUS SYLVIUS; where he originated or what kind of life he followed I have not yet learned; he seems to have lived in Rome and flourished in the year 448. For he wrote under the Emperors Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian, after the usurper John had been killed, and as he himself testifies even more clearly, during the consulship of Flavius Zeno and Posthumianus, that is, in the year of Christ 448 and the beginning of the following year when Asterius entered the consulship. He composed a *Laterculus* <note>a register or calendar</note> containing the Christian and Pagan festivals for every month of the year, which he dedicated to the Most Blessed Lord Bishop Eucherius. The illustrious Bollandus testifies in his *General Preface to the Acts of the Saints*, Volume 1, ch. 4, § 3, p. 43, that he had almost the entire work in his possession; he published the month of January as a specimen, promising that he would publish the rest with observations: whether he fulfilled this promise, or others performed it in his name in that laborious collection of the *Acts*, <term>I have not found it</term> <note>original: "οὐκ εὗρον"</note>.

<margin>448.</margin>
EUTYCHES, a Priest and Archimandrite <note>an abbot or superior of a monastery</note> of Constantinople, fought strenuously against Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus and gained no small reputation for himself. Around the year 448, when he was quite an old man, he began to spread a wicked heresy among the people. For he admitted only a single nature in Christ; so that he conceded there had been two natures in Christ before the union of the divine and human natures, but contended that after the union, one was made. Hence he also denied that the flesh of Christ was consubstantial <note>of the same essence or substance</note> with ours, though confessing He was born from Mary—who was consubstantial with us—but that the flesh taken from her was not consubstantial with us...

<margin>THE 5TH CENTURY, from the year 400.</margin>
...denying that He had received [His body from His mother Mary]. He cast dogmas of this sort into a certain Creed and circulated them through the monasteries, ordering that they be signed by all the monks. On this account, he was privately warned by *Eusebius, Bishop of Dorylaeum*, but when he refused to repent, he was accused of heresy by the same Eusebius before *Bishop Flavian*. Therefore, at the end of the year 448, *Flavian* convoked a Synod at Constantinople and saw to it that *Eutyches* was summoned three times. Eutyches shut himself in his monastery, pretending to be ill; however, soon after, rushing from his home, he went to the Emperor and obtained a military escort for himself. Surrounded by this guard, he entered the Synod, thinking he would dispel the accusation intended for him by the terror of arms. However, his hope failed him. For when he refused to confess the Catholic faith and the two natures in Christ, despite being frequently challenged by Flavian, he was removed from his priestly office, the communion of the Church, and the leadership of his monastery. Condemned by the Synod as a heretic, he complained that the acts of the Council had been falsified by the fraud of his enemies. Using the authority of *Chrysaphius* <note>A powerful eunuch and chief minister to Emperor Theodosius II who supported Eutyches</note>, who was very friendly to him, he asked and obtained a mandate from the Emperor that a Synod be gathered and certain courtiers be admitted to the assembly so that the case might be re-examined. No sooner said than done. The Synod was immediately reconvoked, the acts of the previous Synod were re-read, the matters were debated on both sides, and *Eutyches* was condemned again. However, this bold scoundrel did not yet rest; drawing *Dioscorus* to his side, he obtained from the Emperor—with the help of Chrysaphius—that a more general Synod should be announced for the following year at Ephesus under the presidency of Dioscorus to hear his case. Having set out for that place and pretending to protect the Nicene faith unsullied, he was fully restored through the wicked arts of Dioscorus and an unheard-of tyranny over the bishops; conversely, he saw to it that *Flavian* and *Eusebius* were deposed. However, in the year 451, when the freedom of the Church was returned to the bishops themselves by the Emperor Marcian, his cause was duly judged in the Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon by 630 bishops. His deceitful Confession of Faith, which he had offered at the "Robbery of Ephesus" <note>original: "Latrocinio Ephesino"; a common historical name for the Second Council of Ephesus (449) due to its violence and irregularity</note>, was re-read; he had claimed it was in harmony with the Nicene Creed. But when the Fathers of Chalcedon discovered that this article—**[Who descended, and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary]**—had been omitted, and when they received his blasphemies confirmed by countless testimonies, he was struck down with anathema <note>a formal curse and excommunication</note> by the unanimous voice of all. 
<margin>Letters 45, 70.</margin>
What happened to him after that is not very clear, except that *Pope Leo*, in two letters, earnestly requested of *Empress Pulcheria* and *Emperor Marcian* that he be expelled from the monastery in Constantinople (where he was living to the danger of the faithful) and sent into exile. However, it is not certain with what outcome or success Leo achieved this. There exists a Greek and Latin *Booklet or Confession of Faith* offered at the request <note>original: "αἰτήσει"</note> of the Synod of Ephesus, *Council Records, Vol. IV, p. 134. Two Supplications to the August Emperor Theodosius, ibid. p. 241, 250. A Latin Letter to Pope Leo, with a fragment of the Confession, among the Epistles of Lupus of Ephesus, nos. 222, 223.*

<margin>448.</margin>
*EUSEBIUS*, his place of birth is uncertain; while he was still a layman, he was a man of high rank, serving as an Imperial Agent <note>original: "Agens in rebus"</note> and a Legal Advisor <note>original: "Scholasticus"</note> to the Empress, and was illustrious for his reputation for learning. At that time, around the year 430, when *Nestorius* was preaching in the Church of Constantinople and babbling his blasphemies, Eusebius publicly opposed him. Soon after, he put forward a *Protestation* <margin>Evagrius, book 1, ch. 9.</margin> *against the Clerics of Constantinople* who were followers of Nestorius, in which he demonstrated that the heresy of Paul of Samosata <note>An earlier 3rd-century heretic who taught that Jesus was a mere man who became divine</note> had been revived by Nestorius. At last, having been co-opted into the clergy, he was made Bishop of the Church of Dorylaeum in Phrygia Salutaris. He was especially famous from the year 448, when he presented a Booklet of Accusation against *Eutyches*, whom he had frequently and kindly warned of his error before. In that same year, after the Synod ended, he could rightly be considered an envoy from Flavian to Pope Leo (if only some authority of the ancients were added). For he himself testifies in the 16th session of the Council of Chalcedon that he was once at Rome with Pope Leo. Be that as it may, having set out for the Synod of Ephesus in the year 449, he was excluded by Dioscorus with the greatest injustice, and was soon condemned and deposed, and finally badly mistreated with beatings. In the year 451, at the Council of Chalcedon, having offered a booklet of accusation, he prosecuted Dioscorus for injury and Eutyches for heresy; and he was a major part of the Synod. Besides the many things which he then discussed remarkably as the occasion required, both in the Synod of Constantinople and that of Chalcedon, there exists a Latin *Protestation against Nestorius* among the works of Marius Mercator, part 2, p. 18, translated into Latin by him. *Greek and Latin.*

# The Nestorian Century. 354

<margin>THE 5TH CENTURY, from the year 400.</margin>
A petition against Eutyches <note>original: "Libellus adversùs Eutycheten"</note> presented to the Synod of Constantinople; Council Records, Volume IV, page 151. A petition against Dioscorus <note>original: "Libellus adversùs Dioscorum"</note> presented to the Council of Chalcedon; ibid., page 380. A letter to Emperor Marcian; Council Records, Volume IV, page 95.

<margin>448. * Code 168.</margin>
**BASIL**, Metropolitan <note>A bishop with authority over other bishops in a province</note> of Seleucia in Isauria, flourished in the year 448. Photius \* identifies this man as the same Basil who was a friend and companion of Chrysostom, to whom the *Six Books on the Priesthood* were written (and after him, the manuscript Code of Suidas, mentioned by Dosquius from the Antwerp Library), and quite a few more recent authors follow this. This seems highly improbable due to the very long interval of time: for if that were the case, our Basil would have already held his see for more than seventy years by the time of the Council of Chalcedon. Furthermore, Photius does not explicitly say they were the same person, but speaks only from conjecture. In the year 448, he took part in the Synod of Constantinople, where he delivered a very orthodox opinion on the natures of Christ and was not unwilling to sign the condemnation of Eutyches. However, in the following year, at the "Robber Synod" <note>original: "Latrocinio," referring to the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 AD, notorious for its violence and corruption</note> of Ephesus, moved either by the force of Dioscorus or by an innate fickleness of mind, he publicly revoked his former opinion, condemned Flavian with his vote, and anathematized <note>Formally cursed or excommunicated</note> those who confessed two natures in Christ. For this reason, when he attended the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451, he was removed from his episcopal office by the Fathers of the Council in the first session, along with the primary leaders of the "Robber Synod," having unsuccessfully pleaded that Dioscorus had used force against him at Ephesus. Nevertheless, in the fourth session, since it was found that he held Catholic views both then and previously, he was admitted back into the Council and restored to his former dignity. It is not clear how long he survived these events, except that in the year 458, he wrote back to Emperor Leo from his own Synod held in Isauria. Regarding his style, Photius \* has this to say:
<margin>* Cited location.</margin> <note>original Greek: "In his writings, one can see a certain delight, freshness, and antiquity... it is clear and sweet... but the overly colored charm, full of pigments—or rather the constant and unmixed use of them—arouses a sense of disgust and criticism... as if the writer were unable to regulate his nature with art."</note> He is a great master, if ever there was one, of figurative and excited speech, and of balanced phrases. Nevertheless, he retains clarity and sweetness. But because he is excessive in his metaphors and excited figures of speech, he produces a sense of over-saturation; or rather, because he is so constant and completely immersed in these things—to the point that nothing else occurs without end—he gives the listener a sense of loathing and an opportunity for criticism. This incites blame against the writer himself, as if he could neither moderate his nature through art, nor organize what was disordered by a rule.

### W R I T I N G S.

**43 Orations**, namely 17 on the Old Testament and 26 on the New Testament. These were published in Greek at Heidelberg in 1596, in octavo. The Jesuit Claudius Dosquius produced a Latin translation and published them with very learned notes in Greek and Latin at Heidelberg in 1604, in octavo; he added at the end an *Oration on the Transfiguration of the Lord* in both Greek and Latin, which had not been published before.
**A Demonstration against the Jews concerning the coming of Christ**, published in Latin by Turrianus at Ingolstadt, 1616, in quarto. It is also available in Greek in the Heidelberg edition of 1596.
**Two books on the life and miracles of Saint Thecla, Virgin and Martyr.** I have never been able to convince myself that these are by our Basil. The style and the legends—unknown in that age and entirely foreign to Basil’s gravity—argue against it. Photius does indeed report that Basil wrote of the famous deeds of the martyr Thecla, but he composed them in verse. From this arises a just suspicion that some Greek monk of a more recent age stuffed these books with legends from elsewhere, basing them on Basil's metrical history, if he did not rather devise them by his own labor. Published in Greek and Latin by Petrus Pantinus at Antwerp, 1608.
**All these Works of Basil** were published in Greek and Latin at Paris in 1622, in folio, with the notes of Dosquius, appended to the works of Gregory Thaumaturgus.
**A Praise of Saint Stephen the First Martyr**, published in Greek and Latin by François Combefis along with several homilies of Chrysostom at Paris, 1656, in octavo.

# The Nestorian Century. 355

<margin>THE 5TH CENTURY, from the year 400.</margin>
The *Oration on the Holy Mother of God and on the Incarnation of the Lord* <note>original: "S. Deiparam & in Domini incarnationem"</note> was published in Greek and Latin, and the gaps previously found in it were filled by the same [Frans] Combefis in his *Supplement* <note>original: "Auctuario"</note> of 1648, Volume I, page 569.

---

<margin>448.</margin>
**BASSIANUS**, a Priest of the Church of Ephesus, was ordained Bishop of Evaza against his will by Memnon, the Bishop of Ephesus. However, after the death of Basil (who succeeded Memnon), he became the Prelate of Ephesus around the year 443, four years before the death of Proclus of Constantinople. For that many years he held his see securely, confirmed by Proclus. However, when Flavian attained the see of Constantinople, he revoked Bassianus’s episcopate and substituted a certain Stephen in his place. Regarding this matter, Bassianus presented a petition <note>original: "libellum," a formal legal appeal</note> to Emperor Marcian in the year 451, and was referred by him to the Council of Chalcedon. The Fathers of the Council, therefore, having heard the case from both sides, stripped both men of the see of Ephesus and substituted another in their place. The *Petition presented to the Emperor* exists in Greek and Latin; Council Records, Volume IV, page 685.

---

<margin>449.</margin>
**ANATOLIUS**, the legate <note>original: "Apocrisiarius," an envoy representing a patriarch</note> of Dioscorus of Alexandria at Constantinople, was appointed as Bishop of Constantinople in the year 449 by Dioscorus at the "Robber Synod" <note>original: "Latrocinio," referring to the Second Council of Ephesus, notorious for its violence</note> of Ephesus, following the deposition of Patriarch Flavian, though Flavian was not yet dead. To more securely retain his see and to win the favor of Emperor Theodosius and Pope Leo, he gathered a Synod in Constantinople in 450, condemned the errors of Eutyches and Nestorius, and approved Pope Leo's letter to Flavian with his own signature. In the year 451, he was present at the Council of Chalcedon, where, in the final session, <unclear>iæ</unclear> <term>primacy</term> <note>original: "πρεσβεῖα" (presbeia), referring to the rights of seniority and rank</note> for his see was decreed by the Fathers, equal to that of Old Rome. For this reason, Leo conceived a great mass of anger and did not cease to oppose him with as much skill as possible for as long as he lived. Anatolius died in the year 458, after having held the see of Constantinople for eight years and as many months. A Latin *Letter written in the year 457 to Emperor Leo, concerning the Council of Chalcedon and the wicked deeds of Timothy Aelurus at Alexandria* exists; Council Records, Volume IV, page 905.

---

<margin>
450.
Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, chapter 74.
</margin>
**PETER**, a Syrian by birth and a Priest of the Church of Edessa, distinguished for his eloquence, flourished in the year 450. He wrote *treatises on various causes* and, following the manner of Saint Ephrem, composed *Psalms* in meter.

<margin>
450.

**DIADOCHUS**, Bishop of Photice (which was a city of Old Epirus), flourished in the year 450. Victor Vitensis praises him extensively and boasts of being his disciple. He wrote *One Hundred Chapters on Spiritual Perfection* and *Ten Definitions on as many virtues*, which serve as a preface to the Chapters. Regarding these, Photius says: <unclear>Οὗτος ὁ λόγος εἰς τὸ ἄριστον τοῖς ἀσκητικοῖς συγκείμενος, καὶ τοῖς ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐγγεγυμνασμένοις ταῖς τελειοποιοῖς πράξεσιν, οὐδ᾽ ἀσαφὴς ἢ ἐμπαρεσχόμενος.</unclear> <note>The author provides a Latin translation of this Greek passage immediately following</note> "This book is especially useful for those who practice for perfection; indeed, even for those already experienced in those very actions that perfect; meanwhile, it introduces nothing that is even slightly obscure." And again: <unclear>ὁ γε μὴ λόγος αὐτῷ εἰς τὸ ἀμώμητον συγκείται, καὶ ὁ νοῦς τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν πράξεων σοφίαν περιβάλλεται.</unclear> "For the diction is so composed that it cannot be criticized; and the meaning displays a wisdom born from actions." These *Chapters and Definitions* exist in Latin, published separately in Antwerp by the Plantin Press, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 5, page 884. They were published in Greek at Florence in 1578, according to Casimir Oudin. I have not yet happened to see that edition myself. Certainly, Greek manuscripts exist in the Imperial Library, according to Lambecius. Furthermore, a *Homily of Diadochus on the Ascension of Christ* <note>original: "de Assumptione Christi"</note> lay hidden in Greek in the possession of Holstenius.

---

<margin>451.</margin>
**ATHANASIUS**, an Alexandrian by birth and the nephew of Isidora (the sister of Cyril of Alexandria), was a Priest of the Church of Alexandria. He was stripped of his wealth by the newly-appointed Bishop Dioscorus, cast down from his rank and dignity, expelled from Alexandria and all of Egypt, subjected to various tortures, and frequently cast into prison. Thus destitute, needy, and wandering, he roamed until the year 451, when he brought his case before the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon. A Greek and Latin *Petition against Dioscorus presented to the Council of Chalcedon* exists, in which he vividly explains the evils he suffered from Dioscorus; Council Records, Volume IV, page 405.

# The Nestorian Century. 356

<margin>
5TH CENTURY.
from the Year 400.
---
451.
</margin>

**ISCHYRION**, a Deacon of the Church of Alexandria, was held in high regard by Cyril, by whom he was frequently sent as an envoy to the Emperor and to other Bishops to manage ecclesiastical affairs. After Cyril's death, he was removed from the sacred office of the diaconate by Dioscorus and stripped of his possessions, which Dioscorus burned. He was snatched away by the deacon Harpacration and imprisoned in a hospital for the diseased <note>original: "tabidorum Xenodochio," a hospice for those suffering from wasting illnesses</note>; assassins were sent more than once to kill the man. He was not released from these unjust chains until he had complied with Dioscorus’s commands. In the year 451, he presented a *Petition of Accusation* <note>original: "Libellum accusationis," a formal legal complaint</note> against Dioscorus to the Council of Chalcedon; this is found in the Greek-Latin Council Records, Volume IV, page 400.

<margin>
451.
</margin>

**THEODORE**, of the Alexandrian School of the Master of Offices <note>original: "Scholâ Magistrianorum," referring to the staff of the *Magister Officiorum*, a high-ranking administrative official</note>, served as an agent <note>original: "Agens in rebus," a term for a member of the late Roman imperial civil service who often acted as a courier or inspector</note> for Cyril of Alexandria from about the year 431. He was honored with the rank of the diaconate in the year 436. After Cyril's death, he was hated by Dioscorus because of his great intimacy with Cyril and was deprived of his clerical status; he was threatened with even greater punishments unless he departed from Alexandria more quickly. In the year 451, he presented a *Petition against Dioscorus* to the Council of Chalcedon, which survives in the Greek-Latin Council Records, Volume IV, page 396. To these may be added the *Petition* of Sophronius, a layman, presented to the same Council for the same cause against Dioscorus, found in the Council Records, Volume IV, page 411.

<margin>
451.
</margin>

**PHOTIUS**, Metropolitan of the city of Tyre, was appointed by the Emperor in the year 448 as a judge for Ibas of Edessa, alongside Eustathius, the Bishop of Berytus <note>modern Beirut</note>. In the same or the following year, he pursued a legal dispute with the same Eustathius regarding his metropolitan rights. For while the see of Berytus was subject to the metropolis of Tyre according to ancient Canons, Eustathius denied Photius his due obedience and arranged to be made a Metropolitan himself by an imperial decree and a mandate from Anatolius of Constantinople; he also obtained six cities of Phoenicia, which were taken from Tyre and placed under the jurisdiction of his own see. Therefore, to recover his former authority, Photius presented a *Petition of Supplication* to Emperor Marcian in 451. Referred by the Emperor to the Council of Chalcedon, he won his case and forced Eustathius to be restricted within his usual boundaries. This *Petition* <note>original: "Libellus"</note> exists in the Greek-Latin Council Records, Volume IV, page 541.

<margin>
451.
---
Evagrius, Book 2, ch. 8.
</margin>

**PROTERIUS**, in the year 451, was substituted in the See of Alexandria by the common vote of the Fathers after Dioscorus had been deposed by the Council of Chalcedon. As soon as he had taken up the Bishopric conferred upon him, a huge and intolerable riot broke out in the city, with some demanding Dioscorus and others constantly defending Proterius. Evagrius accurately describes this sedition in Book 2, Chapter 5, from the history of Priscus the Rhetorician, who was present during the events. Indeed, the violence of the Alexandrian commoners did not subside, so that Proterius required a military guard as long as he lived. Around the year 453, having held a Synod at Alexandria, he admitted to communion those Eutychians <note>followers of Eutyches, who emphasized a single nature in Christ</note> who renounced their error; however, he deposed the stubborn ones, including Timothy the Cat <note>original: "Timotheum Ælurus," a nickname meaning 'the Cat' or 'the Weasel'</note>, then a Priest, and saw that they were punished with exile. In 457, after the death of Emperor Marcian, the citizens of Alexandria renewed their long-held anger against Proterius more sharply and violently; they brought Timothy the Cat into the church with an armed force, after he had been ordained as the Bishop of Alexandria by two bishops of his faction. Not content with this, they cruelly murdered Proterius—who had fled to the venerable baptistery as if to a sanctuary—on Easter day itself. Respecting neither the holiness of the place, nor the time, nor the dignity of the priesthood, they drove a sword into his bowels and killed him along with six others. They dragged the dead body through the city, hounded it with insults and mockery, cut it limb from limb, tasted the flesh <note>original: "carnes degustârunt," a claim of ritual desecration found in historical accounts of the murder</note>, burned the remains, and scattered the ashes of the pyre to the wind. In 455, he wrote a *Letter to Pope Leo*, in which, defending the calculation of his predecessor Theophilus, he argued that the feast of Easter that year should be delayed to the 8th day before the Kalends of May <note>April 24th</note>. It exists in Latin in Bucherius’s *Of the Doctrine of Times*, page 82, and in Quesnel’s edition of the Works of Leo. He also wrote another *Letter to Leo containing his Profession of Faith*, which has been lost. However, Pope Leo mentions it in a letter to Julian of Cos.

**LEO**, Bishop of Bourges in Gaul, was present at the Council of Angers in the year 453 and the Council of Tours in the year 461. In the year 454, together with Bishops Victorius and Eustathius, he wrote a Letter to the Bishops—not of Thrace (as the title incorrectly states), but of the Third Lugdunensis, which was the Province of Tours, as Sirmond <note>Jacques Sirmond (1559–1651) was a distinguished French Jesuit scholar and editor of ancient church texts.</note> correctly notes. In this letter, he declares as excommunicated those clerics who, bypassing the judgment of the church, approach secular authorities for power. It is found among the letters of Pope Leo (to whom it was long attributed) as number 96, and in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume III, page 1420.

453.
</margin>

<margin>
* Letter to Eucherius.

**SALONIUS**, a Gaul by birth and the son of Bishop Eucherius of Lyon, was sent to the island of Lérins <note>The monastery of Lérins was a famous center of learning and asceticism in southern Gaul.</note> by his father when he was barely ten years old. He was educated there under the care and discipline of Honoratus, Hilary, Salvian, Vincent, and other great men. He flourished in the year 453. Salvian testifies that he and his brother Veranus were already "Masters of the Churches" while their father was still living. It is well established that he was a Bishop; indeed, Salvian and Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Marseille, an early church historian who continued Jerome's work on famous authors.</note> explicitly call him such. However, it is uncertain of which city: some believe he was Bishop of Geneva, others of Genoa, and others of Vienne. To me, however, he seems more likely to be called Bishop because he was appointed as a coadjutor <note>An assistant bishop who often has the right of succession.</note> to his father in the Bishopric of Lyon. For this reason, he can be considered to have signed at the First Council of Orange in the year 441 in his father's stead. It is not clear when he died. He wrote an *Exposition on the Proverbs of Solomon* and another mystical work on *Ecclesiastes*, written in the form of a dialogue with himself and his brother Veranus as the speakers. Both are found in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 1010, and the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 401. He also wrote a letter together with Bishops Ceretius and Veranus to Pope Leo, which is found among Leo’s letters after epistle 51.

<margin>
454.
</margin>

**RUSTICUS**, Bishop of some city in Gaul, either Narbonne (as some believe) or Bourges (as others prefer); the matter is quite uncertain. He certainly performed the duties of a Bishop in the year 449, when he was among the 47 Bishops of the Province of Narbonne who signed the synodal letter sent to Pope Leo; he is also among the first greeted in Leo’s reply given that same year. He was most prominent around the year 454, at which time it seems he wrote a letter to Eucherius of Lyon, which was published by Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris, Book 2.

<margin>
455.
</margin>

**CHRYSIPPUS**, a Cappadocian by birth, was educated in Syria along with his brothers Cosmas and Gabriel. Later, with the same brothers, he entrusted himself to the Palestinian Abbot Euthymius to be instructed in the perfection of character and the knowledge of literature. He flourished around the year 455. He served first as the Steward <note>original: "Oeconomus," the officer in charge of a monastery's finances and temporal affairs.</note> of the Great Laura <note>A "Laura" was a type of monastery consisting of a cluster of individual cells for hermits.</note>, then was appointed prefect of the Church of the Holy Resurrection <note>The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.</note>, and soon after became a Presbyter of Jerusalem and the Guardian of the Holy Cross, a duty he served for ten years. Those who wish to know more about him should consult the *Life of Euthymius* written by Cyril of Scythopolis. He left behind many monuments of his talent, composed in a florid style and concise in the manner of the Sophists <note>The "Second Sophistic" was a rhetorical style characterized by elaborate, polished, and often brief phrasing.</note>. Of these, only one has reached us: the *Homily on the Holy Mother of God* <note>original: "Deipara," or Theotokos.</note>, which exists in Greek and Latin in the *Duceano Supplement*, Volume 2, page 424. He also wrote, among other things now lost, a *Praise for Theodore the Martyr*, from which Eustratius of Constantinople provides two fairly long fragments in his book on the state of the deceased, chapter 22.

**TIMOTHY**, nicknamed Aelurus <note>original: "Aelurus," meaning "the Cat" or "the Weasel," a name given to him because of his small stature or his habit of sneaking into monks' cells at night to spread his teachings.</note>, was a monk by vocation and later a Presbyter of Alexandria. In the year 453, he was deposed from his rank by Proterius of Alexandria due to his devotion to Eutychianism <note>The belief that Christ had only one divine nature, rather than being both fully human and fully divine.</note>. In the year 457, having associated himself with Bishops Eusebius of Pelusium and Peter of Majuma, he saw to it that he was ordained Bishop of Alexandria and that Proterius was murdered. In the year 460 (as Baronius has it), or perhaps more correctly in the year 457 before the death of Anatolius, he was deposed from the see he had occupied by violence and wickedness by the Emperor Leo. He was relegated into exile, first to Gangra in Paphlagonia and later to Chersonesus, with Timothy Salophaciolus <note>Nicknamed "Wobble-cap" or "the White," known for his moderation.</note> substituted for him in the Bishopric. He spent eighteen years in exile (as Evagrius clearly testifies), and toward the end of the year 475 or the beginning

<margin>
5TH CENTURY.
from the Year 400.
</margin>
At the beginning of the following year, Timothy <note>Timothy II of Alexandria, known as "Aelurus" (the Cat), was a leader of the Miaphysite faction who opposed the Council of Chalcedon.</note> returned to Alexandria, having been recalled by the usurper Basiliscus, and recovered his former dignity after expelling Solofaciolus. In the same year, having set out for Constantinople and entered the city with the greatest pomp, he persuaded Basiliscus to condemn the Council of Chalcedon by sending encyclical letters everywhere. In the year 477, after Emperor Zeno recovered the Empire, he intended to expel Timothy from Alexandria; but, advised by certain people that the man was already elderly and would soon perish by the law of nature, he changed his mind, and Timothy soon closed his final day. So says Evagrius. But if we prefer to listen to Liberatus <margin>* Breviarium, chapter 16.</margin> *, Timothy, fearing the wrath and vengeance of Emperor Zeno once Basiliscus was defeated, committed suicide by drinking poison. Gennadius <margin>† chapter 72.</margin> † takes a different path from both, reporting that he lived as an exile in the year 495. He wrote to Emperor Leo *A very elegant and persuasive Apology for his own ordination*; Gennadius reveals that he himself translated this into the Latin language. He testifies that in this work, the Chalcedonian Fathers, Pope Leo, and almost all the Western Bishops were accused by Timothy of the rankest Nestorianism <note>The theological doctrine that there were two distinct persons in the Incarnate Christ, which the Council of Chalcedon was often accused of by its opponents.</note>. That *Apology* once had a place in the Collection of Encyclical Letters mentioned by Evagrius (Book 2, chapter 10), but today it is missing.

<margin>
457.
Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, chapter 71.
</margin>
**MOSCHIMUS**, Mesopotamian by birth and a Priest of the Church of Antioch: he seems to have flourished around the year 457. He wrote *an excellent little book against Eutyches <note>Eutyches was a monk whose teachings led to the Monophysite controversy; he argued that Christ had only one nature.</note>, and certain other things which no longer exist.*

<margin>457.</margin>
**VICTORIUS**, or as others have it, *Victorinus*, of Aquitanian birth from the house of Limoges, was extremely skilled in mathematical calculations and flourished in the year 457. In that year, he wrote to Hilarius, Archdeacon of the Roman Church, the *Paschal Canon* <note>A table or set of rules used to determine the date of Easter, which was a frequent point of contention in the early church.</note> consisting of two parts: in the first, he hand over an accurate method for computing Easter; in the second, he presents a computation of 439 years in tables, from the year of Christ 28 to the year 457, with the Consuls for each year added. The Western Church held this *Canon* in such high regard that in the Fourth Synod of Orléans in the year 541, it was decreed that the holy Easter should henceforth be celebrated by all priests according to his calculations. Aegidius Bucherius <note>Gilles Bouchier (1576–1665), a Jesuit scholar and historian.</note> of the Society of Jesus first brought this *Canon* to light and published it illustrated with extensive commentaries in Antwerp, 1634, in folio. Let the reader note well that the Paschal calculations for 111 years were added to the Victorian Canon by a certain writer of the sixth century, and these are found printed in the Bucherian edition.

<margin>457.</margin>
**AGAPETUS**, Metropolitan of the island of Rhodes, flourished in the year 457. When the Emperor Leo Augustus inquired of him by letter what he and the Bishops of his Province thought concerning the holy and universal Council of Chalcedon; *he wrote back a letter to the Emperor in which he strenuously defended the cause of the Council against Timothy Aelurus.* This Letter survives in Latin in Part 3, chapter 45, page 940 of the Council of Chalcedon.

<margin>457.</margin>
**JULIAN**, Bishop of Cos, flourished chiefly around the year 457, although he had attained the episcopal dignity many years before, as it seems. He enjoyed a great deal of familiarity with Pope Leo, as is clear from Leo’s letters, in which Julian is highly praised for his piety, erudition, and invincible zeal for the Catholic faith. There survives a *Letter to Emperor Leo against Timothy Aelurus and for the confirmation of the Synod of Chalcedon*, written by him in the year 457, in the Latin Collections of the Councils, Volume IV, page 942.

<margin>457.</margin>
**LUCIAN**, Metropolitan of Bizye, flourished in the year 457, in which year *he wrote a Letter to Emperor Leo on the same subject.* It survives in the Latin Collections of the Councils, Volume IV, page 908.

<margin>457.</margin>
**THEOTIMUS**, Bishop of the region of Scythia, flourished in the year 457. There survives a Latin *Letter to Emperor Leo concerning Timothy Aelurus and the Synod of Chalcedon*, in the Collections of the Councils, Volume IV, page 911.
