**VALENTINUS**, the Metropolitan <note>A bishop with authority over an entire ecclesiastical province.</note> of Philippopolis, flourished in the year 457. He wrote, in his own name and that of his fellow bishops, a letter on the same subject <note>Refers to the defense of the Council of Chalcedon and the petition to Emperor Leo I regarding Church peace.</note> to Emperor Leo the Great, which is found in Latin in the *History of the Councils*, Volume 4, page 909. The learned reader should note that many such letters were offered to Emperor Leo by provincial synods, and these are found in the same work in Latin.

See Theodore Lector, Book 1, page 554.
* On Famous Men, chapter 90.

**GENNADIUS**, initially a Presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, succeeded Anatolius in the see of the Royal City <note>Constantinople.</note> in the year 458. He immediately began to restore the collapsed discipline of his church with great zeal. In the year 459, having held a Synod of seventy-three bishops at Constantinople, he established, among other things, a Canon against <term>Simony</term> <note>The practice of buying or selling sacred church offices or ordinations.</note>; he issued circular letters regarding this matter. He also refused to admit anyone to Holy Orders who did not know the Psalter <note>The Book of Psalms.</note> by heart. Having appointed Marcian—who had converted from the Novatians <note>A rigorous sect that refused to readmit those who had lapsed during persecutions.</note> to the Catholics—as the Steward, he decreed that the offerings of the faithful, which the Great Church <note>Hagia Sophia.</note> had previously seized for itself, should be retained by the clergy of each individual church. According to the account of Theodore Lector, Gennadius restored the withered hand of a certain painter who had dared to depict Christ in the likeness of Jupiter, doing so through his prayers. 

One night, while intent on prayer in the church, he saw a phantom; after he rebuked the demon, it cried out that it would remain quiet while he lived, but after his death, it would utterly lay waste to the Church. Disturbed by this, Gennadius poured out most fervent prayers to God for the peace of the Church and passed away shortly thereafter. This occurred in the year 471. The other Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Marseille, a historian of the same era.</note> says of him \* that he was a man of polished speech and sharp intellect. He explained the Prophet Daniel in a complete commentary; he also published many homilies, which have since been lost. A circular letter against simony exists in Greek and Latin, written in his name and that of his Synod, in the *History of the Councils*, Volume 4, page 1025, and in the *Pandects of Canons*, Volume 2, page 181. It should be noted that in the Oxford and certain other editions, the greater part of this letter is wrongly relegated to the commentaries of Balsamon; however, the entire letter flows from beginning to end with one and the same spirit. Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, the great Catholic historian.</note> partially recognized this, and this letter can be found in Latin in his work under the year 459. He also wrote *Against the Anathemas of Cyril*; from this treatise, Facundus of Hermiane provides a fragment in Book 2, chapter 4. <note>original: "contra Cyrilli Anathematismos." This work attacked the twelve propositions of Cyril of Alexandria, showing Gennadius's leanings toward the Antiochene or "Nestorian" school of thought.</note>

---

<margin>
458.
Gennadius, On Famous Men, chapter 76.
</margin>
**PASTOR**, a Bishop, perhaps Spanish, flourished around the year 458. He wrote a small booklet in the manner of a Creed, encompassing almost the entire Christian faith in short sentences; in this work, while omitting the names of other leaders of heresy, he specifically condemned the Priscillianists <note>A gnostic-leaning sect in Spain and Gaul that emphasized asceticism and secret knowledge.</note>. NE.

<margin>
458.
Died around the year 461.
Gennadius, On Famous Men, chapter 79.
</margin>
**MUSÆUS**, a Presbyter of the Church of Marseille, a man greatly distinguished for his knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and the eloquence of his tongue, flourished in the year 458. At the encouragement of Bishop Venerius of Marseille, he selected from the Holy Scriptures *Readings suitable for the festive days of the entire year*; he also selected *Chapters of the Psalms for Responsories*, matching the seasons and the readings. Furthermore, at the encouragement of Eustathius, the successor to Venerius, he composed an *Excellent Volume of Sacraments* <note>A Sacramentary, or book of liturgical prayers and rites.</note> distributed into its various parts according to the requirements of the offices, seasons, and readings. He also wrote *many homilies*, which, along with his other works, have perished—except that Aubertus Miræus notes that the *Readings* for the whole year collected by him are preserved by Bernard Gui.

---

<margin>460.</margin>
**ANTIPATER**, Bishop of Bostra in Arabia, flourished around the year 460. He wrote a <term>Refutation</term> <note>original: "Αντίῤῥησιν" (Antirrhēsis).</note> of Eusebius of Caesarea’s Apology for Origen. The Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea, in their fifth session, provide certain fragments from the first book of this work. There exists an unpublished *Sermon on St. John the Baptist, the silence of Zacharias, and the salutation of the Blessed Virgin* in Greek; this work lies hidden among others falsely attributed to Simeon Metaphrastes <note>A famous Byzantine compiler of saint's lives.</note>, according to the testimony of Leo Allatius in his *Discourse on the Writings of Simeon*, page 89.

### CYRUS

**CYRUS** (whom the printed versions of Gennadius incorrectly call "Syrus"), a physician by trade and later a monk converted from philosophy, flourished in the year 460. Gennadius describes him as a man skilled in speaking. He wrote *Against Nestorius* with strength and elegance; however, carried away by the excessive heat of the dispute, he fell into the <term>Eutychian heresy</term> <note>The belief that Christ had only a divine nature, rather than being both fully human and fully divine—a view condemned by the Council of Chalcedon.</note> and rejected the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. **NE.** <note>The initials "NE." likely refer to a specific source or annotator used by the author.</note> It seems that another Cyrus, distinct from ours, was an Egyptian by birth from the city of Panopolis. This man was distinguished in the poetic arts and was particularly dear to the Empress Eudocia for that reason. Under Theodosius the Younger, he served as the <term>Praetorian Prefect</term> <note>One of the highest administrative officials in the Roman Empire.</note> and was eventually made Prefect of the City, a Consul, and a Patrician. When Eudocia retired to Jerusalem in the year 443, he obtained power and, according to Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note>, was made <gloss>Bishop of the holy church in Cotyaeum in Phrygia</gloss> <note>original: "ἐπίσκοπος τῆς ἱερᾶς ἐν Κοτυαείᾳ τῆς Φρυγίας"</note> and lived until the time of Emperor Leo.

---

<margin>
460.
Gennadius, *On Famous Men*, chapter 77.
</margin>

### VICTOR

**VICTOR**, an African by birth and Bishop of the city of Cartenna in Mauritania, flourished around the year 460. He wrote a lengthy book *Against the Arians* addressed to **Genseric**, the King of the Vandals, which is now lost. He also wrote a *Book on the Penance of the Publican*, in which he prescribed rules of living for penitents drawn from the Holy Scriptures. That book still exists among the works of **Ambrose**, though it is incorrectly attributed to him. Finally, he wrote a *Consolatory Book to Basil on the Death of His Son*, which is usually found among the works of **Basil** but is wrongly attributed to him. Gennadius mentions many other works of his that are now missing.

---

<margin>
460.
Gennadius, *On Famous Men*, chapter 78.
</margin>

### VOCONIUS

**VOCONIUS**, an African by birth and Bishop of the town of Castellum in Mauritania, flourished around the year 460. He wrote *Against the Jews, Arians*, and *other Heretics*. He also composed an excellent *Volume of Sacraments* <note>Likely a collection of liturgical prayers or rites.</note>. **NE.**

---

<margin>
461.
</margin>

### HILARUS

**HILARUS**, a Sardinian by birth and son of Crispinianus, was the Archdeacon of the Roman Church. In the year 449, he was sent as a legate by Pope Leo to the <term>Robber Council of Ephesus</term> <note>An infamous church council known for its violence and the dominance of the Eutychian faction; its acts were later annulled.</note> along with Bishop Julian and the priest Renatus. When he realized that everything was being conducted through foul means and that both divine and human laws were being trampled by Dioscorus, he escaped by flight with his fellow legates to warn Leo about the whole affair. On November 12, 461, he was ordained Bishop of Rome (Pope). In that same year, he sent <term>encyclical letters</term> <note>General letters intended for wide circulation among many churches.</note> everywhere condemning Nestorius and Eutyches, while approving the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon. He died on February 21, 467. Two *Letters* written while he was still a deacon survive: the first, *to Empress Pulcheria*, is found in the *History of the Councils*, Volume 4, page 51; the second, *to Victorius of Aquitaine*, is placed at the beginning of his *Paschal Canon*. Ten *Letters* written while he was Bishop exist in the *History of the Councils*, Volume 4, page 1035, and some others are found in the works of Christian Lupus at the end of the *Ephesian Letters*, page 471.

---

<margin>
461.
</margin>

### ARNOBIUS

**ARNOBIUS**, commonly called "the Younger" to distinguish him from Arnobius the African, appears to have been a Gaul. He flourished around the year 460, as inferred from the dedication of his *Commentary on the Psalms* to Bishops Leontius of Arles and Rusticus of Narbonne. He certainly lived slightly after Pope Leo, whom he praises throughout his work. The following exist under his name:

*   A *Commentary on the Psalms of David*, which was wrongly attributed to the famous Arnobius the African. It was published separately in Basel in 1522, then edited by Erasmus in Cologne in 1532, and finally corrected by Laurentius de la Barre in Paris in 1639. It is also found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 203.
*   *Annotations on certain passages of the Evangelists*, which were published in Basel in 1543 and revised by Schott in Paris in 1639.
*   *The Altercation or Conflict with Serapion the Egyptian*, a work in two books regarding the Triune and One God, the two substances in Christ and the single Person, and the harmony between grace and free will. Casimir Oudin, based on unknown authority, places this small work among the writings of Vigilius of Thapsus. However, Alcuin cited it under the name of Arnobius eight hundred years ago, even beyond the evidence of the manuscripts. It was first published by François Feuardent at the end of Irenaeus's works in Cologne in 1596. It is included in all subsequent editions of Irenaeus and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 236.

## LEONTIUS,
Gaulish by birth and Bishop of Arles, flourished in the year 461. At the end of that year, or at least the beginning of the next, he received a letter addressed to him by Pope Hilarus. Hilarus subsequently wrote several more letters to him concerning matters involving the Province of Arles; in one of these, he sharply rebukes Leontius for performing his duties as <term>Metropolitan</term> <note>The bishop of a provincial capital who has authority over other bishops in the region.</note> with insufficient diligence, and for failing to bring Hermes—an intruder into the see of Narbonne—back into proper order. He presided over the Council of Arles in the year 475. A single letter written by him to Hilarus survives in D’Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, Volume 5.

<margin>
461.
</margin>

## PERPETUUS,
Gaulish by birth and of the Senatorial class, born to a very wealthy father, succeeded Eutochius (to whom he was related by blood) in the see of Tours in the year 461 or the year prior. In that same year, he took part in the First Council of Tours, and in 465, the Council of Vannes. In the year 482, after constructing a truly splendid and magnificent Basilica over the tomb of St. Martin, he gathered the provincial bishops to celebrate its <term>Encaenia</term> <note>A dedication ceremony for a new church.</note>. He died in 490 or 491. His Testament and Epitaph survive in D’Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, Volume 5. For the use of the Church of Tours, he established fasts and vigils and how they should be observed throughout the cycle of the entire year. *Gregory of Tours presents the order established by him, transcribed from the public records of the Church of Tours, in the History of the Franks, Book 10, Chapter 30.*

## PAULINUS,
Gaulish by birth, from the house of Périgueux (alternatively *Petricordius* or *Vesunnicus*, if Sirmond’s conjecture is trusted). He flourished in the year 461. Indeed, he dedicated his work *On the Life of St. Martin* to Perpetuus, Bishop of Tours, who presided over the first Council of Tours in the year 461—not 480, as Labbe and his transcriber Oudin wrongly state. Paulinus wrote six books *On the Life of St. Martin* in heroic verse <note>Dactylic hexameter, the formal meter used in epic poetry like the Iliad or Aeneid.</note>; in these, he did little more than render into rough and unpolished verse what Sulpicius Severus had expressed in charming and elegant prose, omitting only a few details. Almost all writers of a later age attributed this work to Paulinus, the Bishop of Nola; however, even among the ancients, Gregory of Tours * especially, and Venantius Fortunatus † quite clearly, do the same. Because of this, the work frequently appeared under the name of Paulinus of Nola, first edited by Juret in Paris, 1585; then in the *Libraries of the Fathers* in Paris and Cologne, in Bigne’s Appendix on page 852, and in other collections of ancient Christian poets. Finally, restored to Paulinus of Périgueux, it appeared in the newest *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 6, page 297, and was published separately by Christian Daum along with the commentaries of Fr. Juret, the observations of Caspar Barth, the notes of Jo. Fr. Gronovius, and his own *Spicilegium* of notes in Leipzig, 1686, in octavo. Furthermore, there exists a *very brief poem* by our Paulinus regarding the visit of his little nephew, which is usually attached to the *Life of St. Martin*; and certain other fragments of lost minor works are found in the same place. Moreover, Gennadius * frequently mentions a certain Paulinus of Périgueux who composed several *Treatises* regarding *The Beginning of Lent*, *On the Lord's Day of Easter*, *On Obedience*, *On Penitence*, and *On Neophytes* <note>Recent converts to Christianity.</note>. Of those minor works, whichever Paulinus they may have belonged to, nothing survives today.

Gennadius, On Writers, chapter 83.

## CLAUDIANUS MAMERTUS,
Gaulish by birth, a priest of Vienne, and the assistant or <term>Chorepiscopus</term> <note>A "country bishop" who assisted the city bishop with rural districts.</note> to his brother Mamertus, the Archbishop of that church. He was thereafter called a "leader of the second rank" by Sidonius [Apollinaris] and the Bishop Gennadius *. He flourished around the year 462. I have not yet been able to discover the time of his death by any certain evidence. Although Sidonius † was unable to attend his funeral, he dedicated this clearly elegant Epitaph to the memory of his most upright friend:

> The glory and the grief of his brother Mamertus,
> The unique jewel of wondering bishops,
> Claudianus gives his limbs to this sod.
> Under whose mastery a triple library
> Shone forth: Roman, Greek, and Christian;
> Which he, a monk throughout his flourishing youth...

The rest may be sought from the author himself <note>Sidonius Apollinaris</note>, who further honors Claudianus with this eulogy: *He was a man of foresight, prudent, learned, eloquent, sharp, and the most ingenious of the men of his age, his place, and his people; one who philosophized unceasingly while keeping his religion intact.* <note>original: "Vir fuit providus, prudens... quique indefinenter salvâ religione philosopharetur."</note> It would take too long to transcribe all the praises with which Sidonius honors him throughout his writings.

## HIS WRITINGS FOLLOW.

<margin>* Book 4, Letter 3.</margin>
**Three books on the Nature of the Soul**, addressed to Sidonius Apollinaris. In praising this work extensively, Sidonius* remarks, among other things: *Now, if he were compared to the holy Fathers, he instructs like Jerome, destroys error like Lactantius, builds foundations like Augustine, rises to heights like Hilary, humbles himself like John <note>John Chrysostom</note>, rebukes like Basil, consoles like Gregory, flows like Orosius, is concise like Rufinus, narrates like Eusebius, stirs the soul like Eucherius, provokes like Paulinus, and perseveres like Ambrose.* This work was published separately with notes by Barth in *Zwickau*, 1655; it is also found in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 1247, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 6, page 1050.

**A Letter to Sidonius Apollinaris**, which is found among Sidonius's own letters in Book 4, Letter 2 (in addition to two other letters to the same man: one serving as a preface to the books *On the Nature of the Soul*, and another which appears to be an epilogue).

**A Poem Against Various Errors, or Vain Poets**, which is commonly found in the *Library of the Fathers*.

**A Hymn on the Passion of the Lord**, which begins, *Sing, my tongue, the Savior’s glory* <note>original: "Pange lingua gloriosi"</note>. This is commonly attributed to Venantius Fortunatus. However, that it belongs to our Claudianus is argued not only by the authority of an ancient manuscript of Gennadius used by Miraeus, but also by its extraordinary elegance—which is inconsistent with the unrefined style of Venantius—and the description of a certain poem composed by Claudianus found in the aforementioned passage of Sidonius, which fits this hymn perfectly. For Sidonius, addressing Claudianus, says: *Truly, if you ask what I think of your Hymn, it is concise, abundant, sweet, and lofty; it surpasses any lyrical dithyrambs in its poetic beauty and historical truth. This is your particular gift: while preserving the metric feet, the syllables of the feet, and the nature of the syllables, it includes many words within a few verses in its limited space. Nor does the brevity of the constrained poem crowd out the richness of your adorned speech. It was easy for you, using small <term>trochees</term> and even smaller <term>pyrrhics</term>, to overcome not only the triple rhythms of <term>molossics</term> and <term>anapaests</term>, but even the quadruple junctions of <term>epitrites</term> and <term>paeons</term>.* <note>These are technical terms for rhythmic patterns in classical poetry.</note> It is found in the Breviaries and Antiphonaries of the Roman Church, for Passion Sunday.

Sidonius also clearly indicates in Claudianus’s epitaph that he arranged the **Hymns, Psalms, and Readings** appropriate for each feast day of the year for the use of the Church of Vienne.

<margin>467.</margin>
## SIMPLICIUS
**SIMPLICIUS**, a native of Tivoli and son of Castinus, became the Roman Pontiff on March 6, 467. He engaged in a long and protracted struggle with Acacius of Constantinople, Timothy "the Cat" <note>Timothy Aelurus, a Miaphysite patriarch</note>, Peter Mongus, and Peter the Fuller. He accused the latter three of the <term>Eutychian heresy</term> <note>The belief that Christ had only one nature, rather than being both fully human and fully divine</note> and of wrongly seizing the sees of Alexandria and Antioch. He accused Acacius of seeking excessive power and of harboring a hidden favor for heretics. He rightly harassed those others as the most wicked of men and eventually brought about their removal from the sees they had wrongly occupied. However, he pursued Acacius—a man who was otherwise particularly tenacious in the Catholic faith—primarily because Acacius constantly defended and maintained the dignity granted to the See of Constantinople by the Council of Chalcedon. Simplicius died on February 10, 483. Nineteen of his letters survive in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume 4, page 1068.

**SERVUS DEI**, a Bishop, though it is not clear of which city: for many Bishops of the same name flourished in Italy and Africa in that age. He was prominent around the year 467. He wrote against those who asserted that Christ, while living on earth before his resurrection, had not seen the Father with physical eyes. He endeavored to show from the Scriptures that from the time Christ was born of the Blessed Virgin, by virtue of the **hypostatic union** <note>The theological doctrine that in the person of Jesus, a human nature and a divine nature are perfectly joined in one single "hypostasis" or individual existence.</note>, he always saw God the Father and the Holy Spirit with the eyes of his flesh. **NE.**

Gennadius, *On Writers*, ch. 82.

**SAMUEL**, of Syrian origin and a Priest of the Church of Edessa, was prominent in the year 468. He eventually moved to Constantinople and was still living there in the year 495, when Gennadius closed his Catalog. He wrote many works in the Syrian language against heretics, especially the Nestorians, Eutychians, and Timotheans; these works have since perished.

**GREGENTIUS**, of Arabian origin and Archbishop of Tephra (or Tephar), which was the royal city of the Himyarites in *Arabia Felix* <note>original: "Arabia Felice" — refers to the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen.</note>. He was prominent, it seems, around the year 470. He certainly held a dialogue with the Jews while the Roman Empire was still flourishing and active in Asia, though after the Nestorian heresy had arisen. It must be admitted, however, that his Disputation contains some elements that smack of the fables favored by later centuries—particularly regarding Christ appearing in the clouds, and the 5,500,000 people converted and baptized by Gregentius. Be that as it may, the *Acts of this Disputation held with Herbanus, the most learned of the Jews*, in the presence of the King of the Himyarites and innumerable Jews, and continued over four days, survive in Greek and Latin, edited with brief scholia by Nicolas Goulu, *Paris 1586, octavo*, and thereafter in the *Auctarium Ducæanum, Paris 1624, Volume I.*

**RURICIUS**, called *the Elder* to distinguish him from his grandson (also a Bishop of Limoges); he was the twenty-fourth Bishop of Limoges, as they say, counting from St. Martial, and was prominent in the year 470. That he had a wife named Iberia is clearly evident from the wedding poem dedicated to them by Sidonius. I grant very little credit to what Bernard Gui* reports: that he founded a monastery in honor of St. Augustine in the common cemetery of Limoges above the Vienne river and established Regular Canons there. He is said to have been buried in this monastery with his successors. In the year 506, he was summoned to the Council of Agde, and having been rebuked by Caesarius of Arles for his absence, he wrote a letter to Caesarius pleading his advanced age and bodily infirmity as the reason for his absence. He seems to have died at a great age not long afterward. Sidonius* greatly extols his erudition and supreme eloquence, adding what is even more to his praise: that his life was even more beautiful than his beautiful speech. There survive *two books of Letters*, first unearthed by Henricus Canisius in *Antiquae Lectiones, Vol. 5, p. 428*, and since reprinted in the *Library of the Fathers, Vol. 8, p. 557.*

**REMIGIUS** <note>Commonly known as Saint Remi.</note>, of Gallic origin and distinguished by his noble birth, was born in the district of Laon to parents named Aemilius and Cilinia, who were already old and advanced in years; his conception was divinely predicted by the monk Montanus. Sent to school to be imbued with higher learning, he soon surpassed all his fellow students in talent, character, and doctrine. In the year 471 (according to Hincmar, Flodoard, and Sigebert†) or 459 (according to the more accurate Le Cointe||), at the age of 22, he was substituted into the See of Reims upon the death of Bennadius. In the year 496, he baptized **Clovis**, King of the Franks, together with the primary nobles of the kingdom, after their conversion to the faith; for this reason, he is called the *Apostle of the Franks*. The vast possessions he earned from Clovis as a reward for his sacred office he himself bestowed upon the poor and the churches, which he enriched abundantly. In the year 511, he obtained from King Clovis that the First Council of Orléans be convened, where many very useful laws for the Gallican Church were enacted. In the year 517, he presided over the Council of Reims, where by his presence he struck a certain Arian Bishop into silence who was disputing most fiercely against the Orthodox, and by a miracle he restored the astonished heretic to the Catholic faith. He died at the age of 96, in the 74th year of his episcopate—this much is agreed upon by all; the year of the Christian era is uncertain. But if we follow Hincmar, Flodoard, and Sige—

# The Nestorian Century. 364

<margin>
5TH CENTURY.
from the Year 400.
</margin>
...if we follow the calculations of Sigebert <note>likely Sigebert of Gembloux, a medieval chronicler</note>, the death of Remigius should be dated to the year 545. However, this cannot be established at all. In the year 535, his successor Flavius is found to have signed the decrees of the Synod of Clermont <note>original: "Synodi Arvernensis"</note>. Therefore, the calculation of Charles Le Cointe <note>a 17th-century French historian</note> (which he confirmed with several points) seems preferable; he places the death of Remigius in the year 533. He died on the Ides of January <note>January 13th</note>, having been forewarned by heaven of his approaching death, and was buried in his church with a very solemn procession. Flodoard <note>a 10th-century historian of the church of Reims</note> provides a noble eulogy of him in Book 1, Chapter 11, which the learned reader may consult. Regarding his style and manner of writing, see the letter addressed to him by Sidonius <note>Sidonius Apollinaris, a famous Gallo-Roman poet and bishop</note> in Book 9, Letter 7.

### WORKS.

**Five Letters**, which are contained in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, pages 1268, 1401, 1608. The **Will** <note>original: "Testamentum"</note>, of which two editions exist: one longer and increased by many interpolations from a more recent age, found in Flodoard’s *History of Reims*, Book 1, Chapter 18; the other shorter and more genuine, found in Philippe Labbe's *New Library of Manuscripts*, Volume 2, page 806; in Charles Le Cointe's *Annals of the Franks*, Volume 1, at the year 533, number 50, page 407; and in Guillaume Marlot's *History of the Metropolis of Reims*, Volume 1, Book 2, Chapter 11.

**Explanations of the Epistles of St. Paul**, published under the name of our Remigius by Juan Bautista Villalpando <note>a Spanish Jesuit scholar</note> at Rome in 1598 and Mainz in 1614. In these, St. Benedict, Cassiodorus, Pope Gregory, and Bede are cited. Since this would seem at first glance to disqualify the work from being by Remigius of Reims, Villalpando busies himself with several arguments to meet this objection. However, the illustrious Le Cointe, in the passage cited above (number 49), dilutes Villalpando’s responses with far stronger arguments. The work had previously appeared under the name of Haymo of Halberstadt (Paris, 1556, in octavo) and is expressly ascribed to Haymo by Fulbert of Chartres. Nevertheless, the very learned Albertinus, in his book *On the Eucharist* (pages 886, 926, 937, etc.), claims it for Remigius of Auxerre <note>a 9th-century scholar often confused with Remigius of Reims</note> with arguments that are by no means to be despised.

His **Declamations or Orations** are praised by Sidonius Apollinaris in Book 9, Letter 7. However, these are lost.

<margin>
471.
Evagrius, Book 3, Chapter 4.
</margin>
**ACACIUS**, prefect of the Orphanage of Constantinople, and then from the year 471, Bishop of Constantinople. In the year 476, when the tyrant Basiliscus had promulgated an edict against the Council of Chalcedon <note>The Council of 451 that defined Christ as having two natures, divine and human</note> and had forced more than five hundred bishops—mostly from Asia—to sign it, Acacius defended the Catholic faith with invincible constancy of soul. By his authority among the common people of Constantinople and the monks, he ensured that Basiliscus, fearing a very serious riot, revoked his previous anti-encyclical letters <note>original: "antencyclicis literis"</note> and confirmed the Council of Chalcedon. Indeed, even the bishops of Asia who had yielded to Basiliscus’s attack on the faith, terrified by the bold zeal of Acacius, offered him a book of repentance; they claimed that the necessity had been imposed upon them by Basiliscus and professed that they held to the Chalcedonian faith. 

After a long skirmish with Pope Simplicius regarding the authority of his see, he was accused before the same Pope in 483 by John Talaia <note>a rival candidate for the see of Alexandria</note> on the grounds that he favored Peter Mongus <note>a Monophysite leader</note> and blocked Talaia’s own access to his see. Simplicius, having meditated on a punishment to be inflicted on Acacius, died exhausted by these cares after his efforts in frequently sending letters to the Emperor had proved useless. Felix, the successor of Simplicius, took up the cause and urged it more sharply. Incited by the constant complaints of John Talaia, he sent a legation to Constantinople in 483 which failed. The following year, having held a Synod at Rome, he condemned Acacius and struck him with anathema <note>A formal curse by the church, excommunicating a person</note>. He delayed publishing the sentence for a short time, until, moved by the recent deeds of Acacius—who drove Calendio from the see of Antioch in that same year—he brandished the sentence of anathema again at another Synod held in Rome at the end of the year. Acacius, however, so disregarded the Pope’s "thunderbolt" <note>a metaphor for the excommunication</note> that he removed the Pope’s name

<margin>* Book 16, Chapter 17.</margin>
from the sacred tables <note>The Diptychs; lists of those for whom the church prayed during the liturgy</note>, as Nicephorus reports from Basil the Cilician. Nevertheless, Acacius held his see in peace as long as he lived and died in peace in the year 488. His name was later removed from the Sacred Diptychs <note>original: "sacris Diptychis"</note> by Emperor Justin in the year 519 at the demand of Pope Hormisdas. Two letters written by him survive: one in Greek and Latin to Peter the Fuller regarding the Trisagion <note>The "Thrice-Holy" hymn; there was a controversy over adding the phrase "who was crucified for us" to it</note> in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 1108; and another in Latin to Simplicius regarding the state of the Church of Alexandria, ibid., page 1080.

# The Nestorian Century. 365

<margin>
5TH CENTURY
from the year 400
472
</margin>
**GAIUS SOLLIUS APOLLINARIS SIDONIUS**, a Gaul by birth, from a home in Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunensis"</note>, was born of an illustrious family. His father was Apollinaris and his grandfather shared the same name; both served as Praetorian Prefects of the Gallic provinces. He was born, it appears, in the year 431. He had Eusebius as his master in Philosophy and Oenus in Poetry. After leaving school, he entered military service. He married Papianilla, the daughter of Flavius Avitus—who was a Consul and eventually Emperor—and had three children with her. In the year 457, he was captured during the siege of Lyon by Emperor Majorian (who had stripped Sidonius's father-in-law, Avitus, of his empire), but he was not only spared but also treated with the greatest honor. At the beginning of the following year, he delivered a Panegyric <note>a formal public speech of high praise</note> to Emperor Majorian. Shortly thereafter, at the request of the Senate, he was honored by Majorian with a laurel-crowned statue placed in the Forum of Trajan and was further distinguished with the rank of Count <note>original: "Comitis"</note>. In the year 467, he was summoned to Rome by Emperor Anthemius as an envoy of the Arverni <note>the people of the Auvergne region, centered around Clermont-Ferrand</note>. There, after celebrating the praises of Anthemius in a Panegyric, he obtained the Urban Prefecture of Rome. Having served excellently in this office, he was again honored with a statue and later elevated to patrician and senatorial dignity. Finally, in the year 472, he was snatched—almost against his will—from the legal tribunal to the Bishopric of the Arverni. Leaving his inheritance and honors to his son Apollinaris and setting aside his secular studies, he thereafter devoted himself entirely to the cultivation of sacred literature. He was held in such high esteem by the provincials and his fellow bishops that he was consulted everywhere on matters of greater importance, even in theology. At the very start of his episcopate, when a dispute arose over the see of Bourges <note>original: "Bituricensi"</note>, the election of the prelate was committed to his sole judgment. He was not only a Bishop to the Arverni, but also a leader; for many years, he bravely defended their liberty against the Goths. Around the year 480, after Clermont was captured by the Goths following a long siege, he withdrew to the fortress of Livianum with his brother-in-law Ecdicius; however, he was later restored to his church by Euric <note>original: "Evarige"</note>, the King of the Goths. Shortly before his death, according to Gregory of Tours <margin>History of the Franks, Book 2, Chapter 23.</margin>, he was stripped of his church by two rebellious priests and reduced to extreme poverty. However, he recovered his see after one of those priests was struck by divine power and died the same death as Arius <note>Arius was a 4th-century heretic who, according to tradition, died a shameful and sudden death in a public latrine</note>. He is said to have died in the year 482, on the 12th day before the Kalends of September <note>August 21st</note>, although he himself writes clearly in Letter 12 of Book 9 that he had completed three Olympiads <note>a period of four years; thus, twelve years</note> in the episcopate. We have written these things briefly concerning Sidonius; if anyone desires more, let him consult Jean Savaro and Jacques Sirmond, who have studiously and accurately collected the deeds of our Sidonius.

### SURVIVING WRITINGS.

**Nine books of Letters**, arranged by Sidonius himself before his death, of which the first seven were dedicated to the Priest Constantius, the eighth to Petronius, and the ninth to Firminus.
*In Letter 9 of Book 7, a certain Sermon by Sidonius can be found attached.*
*Twenty-four Poems, besides many others interspersed within the Letters.*

### LOST WORKS.

<margin>Book 8, Letter 15.</margin>
**A History of King Attila** and the siege of Orleans, undertaken and begun at the persuasion of Leo, the advisor to King Euric, but interrupted immediately due to weariness of the labor.
<margin>Book 8, Letter 3.</margin>
*The Life of Apollonius of Tyana, translated from Greek into Latin.*
<margin>Book 5, Letter 17.</margin>
*A Treatise against a certain person who celebrated good days in an evil manner.*
<margin>Book 7, Letter 3.</margin>
*A Brief Liturgical Preface <note>original: "Contestatiuncula"</note> dedicated to Bishop Migecius.*
<margin>Book 1, last Letter.</margin>
*A Satire against Peonius, the leader of the Marcellian conspiracy.*
*A Book of Masses.*
*A Book of Legal Cases.*
*Two Panegyrics, one to Majorian and the other to Anthemius, the Emperors.*
*Many more Letters.*

The Works of Sidonius were published with the commentaries of Giovanni Battista Pio, *Basel, 1542, in quarto*; revised by the efforts of Elias Vviti, *Lyon, 1552, in octavo*; with the commentaries of Jean Savaro, *Paris, 1599, in quarto* and *Hanau, 1617, in octavo*; with the notes of Sirmond, *Paris, 1614, in octavo*; and with his expanded notes, *Paris, 1652, in octavo*. They are also held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 6, page 1075.

# The Nestorian Century. 368

<margin>
5TH CENTURY
from the year 400
Liberatus, *Breviarium* chapter 18.
* Photius, *Codex* 54.
</margin>
...of Alexandria <note>original: "drinus," likely referring to John Talaia, Patriarch of Alexandria</note> was ordained by the Catholics—though some say certain people were corrupted by bribes—and was subsequently deposed from his see by an imperial edict. In the year 483, fleeing to Rome, he sought the protection of his cause from Popes Simplicius and Felix. Indeed, they left nothing untried, using both letters and dire threats sent far and wide to diligently protect John. But all was in vain. He never recovered his lost see; however, he was eventually appointed to the see of Nola in Campania by Pope Felix, and he died in peace after the year 492. According to the testimony of Photius, he wrote an *Apology to Pope Gelasius*, in which he openly condemned not only the Pelagian heresy <note>a theological movement that denied original sin</note>, but also Pelagius himself, along with Caelestius and Julian. Sadly, the ravages of time have snatched this work from us.

<margin>
480.
* Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book 2, chapter 3.
* Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 97.
</margin>
**EUGENIUS**, of African descent, was appointed Bishop of Carthage in the year 480. He was chosen by the Catholics after Hunneric, the King of the Vandals—having been moved by the prayers of Emperor Zeno and Placidia—granted permission to elect a bishop. This followed a twenty-four-year vacancy in the faith caused by the cruelty of the Arians <note>a sect that believed Christ was a created being, not equal to God the Father</note>. In the year 484, Hunneric gathered a mob of Arian bishops at Carthage to engage in a dispute with the Catholics. Eugenius presented a brilliant *Profession of Faith* to the king, fortified with such force of reason that it drove the heretics to both silence and rage. Shortly thereafter, he was exiled by Hunneric to the city of Tamalluma, located on the border of Tripoli, and was handed over to be tortured by Antonius, the local bishop and a most ferocious heretic. Later, if we believe Gregory of Tours, he was moved to the city of Albi in Gaul, where he seems to have ended his life around the year 495 or shortly thereafter. Indeed, Gennadius speaks of him as if he were still living in his *Catalogue of Writers*, which he compiled in that same year. There exists a *Pamphlet*, or a lengthy *Confession of Faith*, offered to King Hunneric in the name of the African bishops, found in the works of Victor Vitensis on the Vandal persecution (of which it constitutes the entire third book). Gennadius, in the place cited above, places it beyond all controversy that this work belongs to Eugenius, even though Victor does not explicitly say so. It can be found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 1128, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 683. According to the same Gennadius, he also wrote other works which have perished: letters to the people committed to his care sent shortly before his exile; the *Disputations* <note>original: "Altercationes"</note> which he held with the Arian leaders through intermediaries, dedicated to King Hunneric; and finally, petitions for the peace of the Catholics, written in the style of apologies, offered to the same king.

<margin>
480.
* Chapter 90.
† *On Writers*, chapter 91.
* Chapter 134.
* *Sacred Library*, book 4, page 306.
</margin>
**THEODULUS**, whom Honorius of Autun calls "Theodorus," was a priest in Coele-Syria. According to Sixtus of Siena, he was a bishop and flourished around the year 480. He died in the year 492, three years before Gennadius closed his *Catalogue*. He wrote a book *On the Harmony of Divine Scripture* against the ancient heretics, in which he showed that one and the same God is the author of both Scriptures <note>the Old and New Testaments</note> and both dispensations. But this work has long since perished. A work titled *A Brief Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans* is circulated in Latin under his name in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 1124, and the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8. However, it falsely bears the name of Theodulus. It is actually a "Catena" <note>a string of interpretations</note> woven together not only from Basil, Chrysostom, Severian, etc., but also from Photius and Oecumenius, who lived long after Theodulus. Quite distinct from our subject is that other Theodulus, a writer of uncertain age mentioned by Sigebert of Gembloux; he was an Italian by birth, learned in Greek and Latin. While studying at Athens, he heard pagans disputing with Christians; collecting their arguments, he compiled them into a work he called the *Eclogue*, divided into three parts: the first called *The Lie* <note>original Greek: Ψεῦσιν</note>, the second *The Truth* <note>original Greek: Ἀλήθειαν</note>, and the third *Wisdom* <note>original Greek: Φρόνησιν</note>. Sixtus of Siena rashly confuses this man with our Theodulus. Possevinus not only made the same error as Sixtus, but with truly remarkable negligence, he turned one writer into three different people, calling the first two "Theodorus."

* *On Greek History*, book 2, chapter 21.
</margin>

In the opinion of the most learned Vossius, he flourished under Zeno, around the year 483. I fear, however, that he may be several years later, since he extended his history by five more books after the deposition of Peter the Fuller <note>a controversial Patriarch of Antioch</note>. -># The Nestorian Century. 369<-

<margin>5th Century from the year 400 <note>The Latin 'dccc' appears to be a typographic error for 'cccc' (400), as the text pertains to the 5th century.</note></margin>
<margin>* Codex 41.</margin>
**JOHN** <note>likely John of Aegae, a 5th-century Monophysite historian</note> wrote ten books of *Ecclesiastical History*. The first five began from the reign of Theodosius and the very start of the Nestorian heresy <note>the belief that Christ existed as two separate persons, one divine and one human</note>, and continued until the deposition of Peter the Fuller in the year 479. Photius* confesses that he has not read the five later books. In this History, John revealed manifest signs of his own heresy, criticized the Council of Chalcedon, and pursued it with slanders. A fragment of this work exists in the 5th action of the Second Council of Nicaea (Council Tom. vii. p. 369). Theodorus Lector also includes some parts from the later section in his *Collection*, book 2, p. 563. John likewise wrote a specific work against the Council of Chalcedon, which was filled with reproaches and slanders. <margin>* Codex 41, 55.</margin> Regarding his style, Photius* says: <note>original Greek: ἐστὶ δὲ τὴν φράσιν σαφής τε καὶ ἀπέριττος, καὶ λεκτικῶς τε καὶ ἡδέως μετὰ τοῦ σαφηνείας καὶ λαμπρότητος κεκοσμημένος</note> "His phrasing is clear and simple, and he is adorned in both expression and pleasantness, along with clarity and brilliance." His style is clear and flowery; he used a splendor and sweetness of words, along with perspicuity and clarity.

<margin>483. Theodorus Lector book 2. p. 566.</margin>
**FELIX**, a Roman by birth and the son of Felix the Priest, attained the Pontificate of the Roman See on the 13th day of February in the year 483. Having been made Bishop, he immediately and openly rejected the *Henoticon* <note>the "Act of Union," an imperial document intended to reconcile theological factions</note> published by Emperor Zeno the previous year. He harassed Acacius of Constantinople, who refused to renounce communion with Peter Mongus, by sending letters everywhere; indeed, he finally struck him with an excommunication in 484. In the same year, he condemned Peter the Fuller—an invader of the see of Antioch who taught that God was crucified—at a Synod of 42 bishops held in Rome. For a clearer understanding of this matter, it should be noted that Peter, a fuller by trade and a monk of the Acoemetae monastery <note>the "Sleepless Monks" known for continuous prayer</note>, was expelled from there for his devotion to Eutychianism <note>the belief that Christ had only one nature</note>. Soon after, acting as a priest of St. Bassa at Chalcedon and supported by the favor of Zeno in the year 471, he stirred up great riots in Antioch. Joining himself to the sect of the Theopaschites <note>those who believed the divine nature suffered on the cross</note>, he taught that God was crucified, adding this clause to the solemn formula of the Trisagion <note>the "Thrice-Holy" hymn: Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal</note>: >[*Who was crucified for us.*]< Martyrius, the Bishop of Antioch, became weary of the riots and resigned his see in 472, which Peter the Fuller soon after invaded like a tyrant. Peter, however, was immediately cast out by an edict of Emperor Leo and banished to an oasis, with Julian substituted in his place. In the year 476, he was restored to the see of Antioch by Basiliscus, while Julian died of a broken heart. In the following year, he was driven out by John (whom he had ordained Bishop of Apamea) and was condemned by a clandestine synod. In the year 478, he was condemned by a legitimate Council of Eastern Bishops at Antioch, by Acacius at Constantinople, and by Simplicius at Rome; he was even ordered by Zeno to be deported to Pityus. In the year 484, he was restored to his see by the Emperor through the efforts of Acacius, though he was condemned by Felix at the same time; he held the see until the year 486, when he died. But to return to Felix: he died on the 30th day of January in the year 492. Fifteen of his letters survive (two of which are addressed to Peter the Fuller, and one to Emperor Zeno, preserved in Greek and Latin) in Council Tom. iv. p. 1049.

<margin>484.</margin>
**QUINTIANUS**, Bishop of Ascoli, was prominent in the year 484. He wrote a letter to Peter the Fuller against the clause he added to the Trisagion, which he sharply contended was heretical and blasphemous, and he condemned it with twelve attached Anathemas. This letter exists in Greek and Latin in Council Tom. iv. p. 1097.

<margin>484.</margin>
**ANTHEON**, Bishop of Arsinoe, was prominent around the year 484, at which time he wrote a letter to Peter the Fuller on the same subject, which is found in Council Tom. iv. p. 1112.

<margin>484.</margin>
**FAUSTUS**, Bishop of Apollonias, was prominent in the year 484. For the same reason, he wrote a letter to Peter the Fuller, which is found in Greek and Latin in Council Tom. iv. p. 1113.

<margin>484.</margin>
**PAMPHILUS**, Bishop of Abydos, was prominent in the year 484. He wrote a letter to the Fuller on the same subject, which is found in Greek and Latin in Council Tom. iv. p. 1117.

# The Nestorian Century. 370

<margin>
5TH CENTURY.
from the year 400.
484.
</margin>
**ASCLEPIADES**, Bishop of Tralles <note>an ancient city in Lydia, modern-day Turkey</note>, flourished in the year 484. In a nearly identical letter, he attacked the *Trisagion* <note>a standard hymn in the liturgy: "Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us."</note> of Peter the Fuller, and struck him with ten Anathemas <note>formal ecclesiastical curses or excommunications</note>. The collection of the Councils, Volume IV, page 1120, presents both the letter and the Anathemas in Greek and Latin.

<margin>
484.
</margin>
**JUSTINUS**, Bishop of a certain city in Sicily, flourished in the year 484. He wrote a letter to Peter the Fuller very similar to the previous ones, which can be seen in Greek and Latin in Volume IV of the Councils, page 1103.

Flaccianus (or Flavian), Bishop of Rhodope <note>a Roman province in modern-day Greece/Bulgaria</note>, wrote a letter on the same subject to Peter the Fuller. Baronius published a significant Latin fragment of it from a Vatican Manuscript in his *Annals* for the year 483, and Volume IV of the Councils, page 1105, represents a version taken from there.

<margin>
* Dissertation on Peter the Fuller, chapter 4, page 177, at the end of volume 3 of the *Ecclesiastical History*.
</margin>
It by no means escapes my notice that the illustrious Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a renowned 17th-century French scholar</note> * not only calls these seven letters to Peter the Fuller into question but regards them as counterfeit; this he attempts to show with more than one argument. But to speak of the matter as it truly is, his reasons seem rather weak to me, and hardly worthy of so great a man’s reputation. He says, first, that none of these Bishops are found named in the history of those times. What of it? Hundreds of Bishops occur in the volumes of the Councils who are mentioned only once, and of whom not the slightest mention is found among the writers of that age. In Volume IV of the Councils, there are letters from sixty-one Bishops or Synods to the Emperor Leo for the confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon: one would look in vain elsewhere for the names of the vast majority of these Bishops. He says, secondly, that Bishops of small cities, such as these were, endowed with no authority, could not have rebuked the Patriarch of Antioch in written letters without the greatest audacity. But one must be a complete stranger to Church History not to know that such examples are found everywhere. Who is not aware of the letters of Irenaeus to Victor of Rome regarding the day of Easter, or the letters of Cyprian and Firmilian to Pope Stephen regarding the baptism of heretics, to say nothing of others? How much more was this permitted when a matter of faith was at stake, and against a Bishop who was an invader of another’s see <note>referring to Peter the Fuller's irregular seizure of the Patriarchate of Antioch</note> and who had been noted for heresy in numerous Synods, both Western and Eastern. He says, thirdly, that all these letters were written in one and the same style, quite barbaric and coarse—a manifest sign of forgery. However, one must be a most precise master of criticism to dare to assert that all came from a single hand based on a certain similarity of style. Added to this is what Valesius himself noticed, though he offers no reply to it: that these letters were translated not from Greek into Latin, but vice versa. Finally, I confess I do not know what hope or argument could induce someone to deceive the Christian world by putting forward such letters under the names of others. Nevertheless, I would not wish to hide from the reader that I shall by no means undertake the defense of the fragment of Flaccianus's letter.

<margin>
484.
</margin>
**VIGILIUS**, of African origin, Bishop of Thapsus (or Thapsitanus) in the Province of Byzacena <note>in modern-day Tunisia</note>, flourished in the year 484. In that year, having been summoned to Carthage by the decree of King Huneric <note>the Vandal king who persecuted Nicene Christians</note> to give an account of his faith, he signed the Profession of Faith of Eugenius of Carthage and fought steadfastly with him for the Catholic faith. While the Arian Vandals <note>a Germanic people who followed Arianism, which denied the full divinity of Christ</note> were enslaving the Catholics, he seems to have fled his homeland. Theodulph of Orleans and Aeneas of Paris record that he set out for Constantinople and there composed books against Eutyches <note>the monk whose teachings led to Monophysitism</note>. That Vigilius indeed lived among the Greeks is gathered clearly enough from the first book of that work. He has been wrongly confused with Vigilius of Trent; knowledge of this writer and those of the preceding age long escaped notice. Certainly, his writings lay hidden among the works of others, perhaps published and put forward by Vigilius himself under other names—at least for this reason, as Chifflet <note>Pierre François Chifflet, a Jesuit scholar</note> shrewdly conjectures: to escape the hatred and envy of the Arians, and by using great names as a pretext, to gain support for himself and authority for his writings. At last, his works were sought out from all sides and restored to their author; the aforementioned François Chifflet collected them and arranged them in the following order.

# The Nestorian Century. 371
### M m m 2

<margin>
5TH CENTURY.
from the year 400.
</margin>

*Five books against Nestorius and Eutyches in defense of the Council of Chalcedon* <note>original title: "Adversus Nestorium & Eutychem libri V. pro defensione Synodi Chalcedonensis"</note>, which were published several times under the name of Vigilius of Trent: at Zurich in 1539; then edited by Cassander at Cologne in 1575 in octavo; and among the *Works of Cassander* on page 514. A more corrected and expanded edition was published by Josias Simler at Basel in 1571, and elsewhere.

*A Disputation under the name of Athanasius against Arius, or two Dialogues held in the Council of Nicaea between Athanasius and Arius with Probus as judge.*

Three Dialogues or Disputations held by Athanasius against Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus in the presence of Probus as judge. This is to be considered the same work as the previous one, distinguished only by this difference: that the first was written in Africa by Vigilius while he still feared the Vandals <note>a Germanic tribe that practiced Arianism and persecuted orthodox Christians in North Africa</note> and did not wish to be recognized by them; after leaving Africa, it was finally revised, the preface was trimmed, many passages were polished, and it was expanded with an entire third book containing the verdict of the judge Probus. George Cassander published both versions joined into a single work under the name of Vigilius of Trent, together with the books against Eutyches, at Cologne in 1575, and among his own *Works* on page 460. The first two Dialogues are often wrongly placed among the works of Athanasius.

*Twelve books on the Trinity, or on the unified Trinity of the deity against Marivadus the Arian* <note>original: "De Trinitate, sive de unitâ Trinitate deitatis contra Marivadus Arianum"</note>. These were written at Naples in Campania and attributed to Athanasius; the first seven books appeared under his name in the Heidelberg edition of Athanasius, but all twelve appeared in the Paris edition—though poorly divided into eleven, as the last two books were fused into one.

The book *On the Unity of the Trinity to Optatus*, or a Dialogue between St. Augustine and Felicianus the Arian composed by Vigilius, is usually included among the works of Augustine.

*Three books on the Trinity against Varimadus* (or, by a transposition of letters, Marivadus), a Deacon of the Arian sect and very much in favor with King Hunneric <note>King of the Vandals, known for his late 5th-century persecutions</note>. These were formerly published by Vigilius under the name of Idacius Clarus, and have been frequently printed under that same name.

A book against *Palladius the Arian Bishop*, consisting of two parts; the first of which, presented as the **Acts** of the Council of Aquileia held in the year 381, is found in the Collections of the Councils that appeared after the year 1550. The second part has two editions, both of which, it seems, were published by Vigilius. The first is the same as Ambrose’s book *On Faith* or *On the Consubstantiality of the Son with the Father*; the second, which is more complete, is the same as Gregory Nazianzen’s 59th Oration. Subjoined to the work are two letters of the Council of Aquileia, one to the Bishops of Gaul, the other to the Emperors Gratian and Valentinian, which are to be counted among the Acts of the Council. Regarding the first part, Chifflet contends with a long line of conjectures rather than arguments that this dispute was fabricated by Vigilius under the name of the *Acts of the Synod of Aquileia*. This does not seem likely to me at all; nor are the minor reasons he brings forward so significant that we should linger in refuting them. Certainly, no one will raise a dispute against these genuine Acts of the Council of Aquileia, lest by the same reasoning and nearly the same arguments they might call the Acts of other Synods into doubt.

*Solutions to the Objections of the Arians*, which Chifflet conjectures were added by Vigilius to the first Dialogue against the Arians (under the name of Athanasius) before he undertook the second edition of those Dialogues.

Pierre François Chifflet collected these works listed above into one volume and published them, illustrated with notes and dissertations, at Dijon in 1664 in quarto. From there they are held in Volume 8 of the *Library of the Fathers* <note>Bibliotheca Patrum</note>, page 722.

*A Disputation or Dialogue of St. Augustine with Pascentius the Arian before the judge Laurentius*, fabricated by Vigilius and first brought to light by the Benedictine Fathers, the curators of the most recent edition of the works of St. Augustine, and attached to the **Appendix** of his letters.

The *Creed* <note>term: Symbolum Fidei; likely referring here to the "Athanasian Creed" (Quicunque Vult)</note> circulated under the name of Athanasius and published among his works. We believe, truth permitting, that this should be ascribed to Vigilius. See more under Athanasius.

Furthermore, it is recorded that a certain Vigilius, an African Bishop, composed an excellent *Treatise on the understanding of the thousand years prophesied in the Apocalypse*...

VICTOR, an African by birth and Bishop of Vita in the province of Byzacena, subscribed to the profession of the Catholic faith by Eugenius of Carthage in the year 484; in that same year, or at least the following one, he was sent into exile by King Hunneric <note>Hunneric was the King of the Vandals who famously persecuted those who did not follow the Arian version of Christianity</note>. Having traveled to Constantinople, he wrote in the year 487 the *History of the African or Vandal Persecution under Geiseric and Hunneric, Kings of the Vandals* <note>original: "Historiam Persecutionis Africanæ sive Vandalicæ sub Geiserico & Hunnerico Vandalorum regibus"</note>, to which he attached, by way of an appendix, the *Acts of the Seven Monk-Martyrs of the territory of Capsa*. It is not clear in what year he died. The aforementioned history exists divided sometimes into three books, sometimes into four, elsewhere into five, and occasionally into six; published at Cologne in 1535; then by the care of Beatus Rhenanus at Paris in 1541; with the notes of Baldwin attached to Optatus of Milevis at Paris in 1569 in octavo; with the notes and dissertations of Chifflet placed before the works of Vigilius of Thapsus at Dijon in 1664 in quarto; in the *Orthodoxographia* <note>a collection of early Christian writings</note> on page 799; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 675.

HONORATUS, a Gaul by birth and Bishop of Marseille, flourished in the year 490. He was an eloquent man, most celebrated for his abundance of speech and fluency, as Gennadius describes him. He published *very many homilies, both those delivered extemporaneously and those composed in leisure*, in which he both exhorted his readers to piety and refuted the ravings of the heretics. He also composed the *Lives of many Holy Fathers*; and among these, he committed to writing the deeds of his teacher, Hilary, Bishop of Arles. Of these works, nothing survives today except the *Life of Hilary of Arles*, which is found in the collection of Surius under the date of May 5th.

The same man later brought King Sigismund, the son of Gundobald, back from the same heresy to the Catholic Church. GELASIUS, an African by birth and the son of Valerius, was elevated to the Bishopric of the City of Rome <note>The Papacy</note> on February 7, 492. Gelasius, therefore, defended the sentence of his predecessor and the condemnation of Acacius in many very long letters sent to Euphemius, the Emperor Anastasius, and others. As long as he lived, he denied communion to Euphemius and the Eastern Bishops who were in communion with Euphemius. A decree in a Roman Council of 70 Bishops in the year 494 concerning Canonical, Ecclesiastical, and Apocryphal books. This most celebrated decree of Gelasius is in everyone's mouth and hands. However, I am hardly persuaded that it is actually his, or that it possesses the age and authority it claims, led by these arguments: 1st. Older manuscripts attribute it to no certain author. Hence, as the illustrious Baluze notes in ancient manuscripts of better quality, it is sometimes ascribed to Damasus, sometimes to Gelasius, and occasionally to Pope Hormisdas—a most certain sign that the genuine author of this Decree was once unknown. 2nd. Books are cited in this Decree that in the year 494 were either not yet written or were entirely unknown. For example, the *Paschal Work* of Sedulius is praised, which was first extracted from Sedulius's desks and published to the public by Turcius Rufus Asterius, a former consul. But Asterius himself held the consulship in this very year, 494. A treatise on the *Revelation of the Head of St. John the Baptist* is condemned, which was written after the time of Count Marcellinus, who is explicitly cited in it. Furthermore, the author of the Decree seems clearly to confirm the fifth, and perhaps even the sixth, general council. For those words ["But also if there are any Councils, etc."] could not be understood in any other sense; no one who reads them attentively will easily deny this. 3rd. It contains many absurdities, <term>inconsistencies</term> <note>original: "ἀσύστατα" (asystata)</note>, and things plainly foreign to the learning and judgment of Gelasius and the Roman Synod. Who would believe that Gelasius, a man of primary erudition, supported by a Council of 70 Bishops, would relegate the works of Clement of Alexandria—whom the whole world venerated—to the category of apocrypha, and place the writings of Africanus, Arnobius, Lactantius, and Commodian in the same class? Who with a sound mind would believe that the Pope and the Synodal fathers, in the same decree, would receive the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius among approved authors and then reject it with the condemned? I pass over the fact that the true Gelasius speaks excellently of Eusebius in his work *On the Two Natures*. 4th. The Decree condemns the *Apostolic Canons*; yet Dionysius Exiguus, who deeply cherished the memory of Gelasius, translated them into Latin shortly after without any such censure added; and the Roman Church accepted them and used them as a most certain norm of Ecclesiastical discipline (as is clear from Cassiodorus, and the epistle of John II to Caesarius of Arles), which it would by no means have done if they had been condemned by Gelasius shortly before. And what hits even harder: Gelasius himself seems to have admitted the Apostolic Canons and used them in his Decretal Epistles, as the most learned Pearson proves with several examples. 5th. The author of the Decree professes to follow St. Jerome in all things. "We think those things," he says, "which we know Blessed Jerome thinks; and not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom the man frequently mentioned rebuked out of zeal for God and the religion of the faith." Yet he is diametrically opposed to Jerome in defining the Canon of the books of Holy Scripture. He numbers the works of Tertullian, the *Shepherd* <note>The Shepherd of Hermas, an early Christian literary work</note>, Clement of Alexandria, Novatian, Arnobius, Apollinaris, and others among the apocrypha and forbids them to be read by Catholics; which Jerome, on the contrary, greatly praises and declares to be worthy of reading and useful. *The Book against Eutyches and Nestorius on the two natures in Christ*, once mentioned by Gennadius \*, by Saint Fulgentius in his book on the 5 Questions to Ferrandus the Deacon chapter 18, and explicitly cited under the name of our Gelasius by Pope John II in a letter to Avienus; it was also attributed to him by Anastasius the Librarian †. In this work, Gelasius provides a most powerful testimony against the substantial conversion <note>This refers to the doctrine of Transubstantiation; the author notes that Gelasius seems to argue the elements remain bread and wine in their nature</note> of the Eucharistic bread and wine into the body and blood of our Lord ||. For this reason, the Papal writers—Baronius, Bellarmine, Gregory of Valentia, Suarez, and others—strive with all their might to take this work away from Pope Gelasius, some attributing it to Gelasius of Cyzicus, others to Gelasius of Caesarea. This work of Gelasius seems once to have been divided into five books, for the *Book of the Popes* mentions that many. *The Sacramentary.* That Gelasius wrote formulas for prayers and sacraments is attested to by clear witnesses: Anastasius in his *Life*, John the Deacon in the *Life* \* of Gregory the Great, and an ancient book nearly eight hundred years old on the *Office of the Mass*, cited first by Cassander † and then by Morin ||, called the "Toulouse" manuscript by the latter—to say nothing of Hugh of Saint Victor, Rupert of Deutz, and others. Gelasius certainly collected, as is reasonable to believe, the solemn formulas of prayers and sacraments which were still in use in the Roman Church in his own time; and having arranged them in a new order and added several of his own, he compiled them into a single book. Gregory the Great later reduced this to a compendium after changing some parts and adding some of his own. The Gelasian codex consists of three books: namely, on the Circle of the Year, on the Birthdays of the Saints <note>That is, their feast days, marking their "birth" into heaven</note>, and on Sundays and various causes. The venerable age of this Order is clearly proven by the fact that the word *and from the Son* <note>original: "Filioque" – the controversial addition to the Nicene Creed regarding the Holy Spirit</note> is not contained in the Creed, a phrase first born only in the seventh century and not received in Rome until the ninth; also by the fact that many masses used in the seventh and eighth centuries are missing; and finally, that fewer saint’s feast days are celebrated than in other liturgies, and those only of martyrs. This Codex lay hidden for a long time, known to few, until in the year 1562, after the Library of Fleury was ransacked and scattered, a copy about nine hundred years old, written in square and uncial letters, finally fell into the hands of Paul Petau, a Senator of Paris. By his kindness, Jean Morin used it; he testifies that it was the oldest of all the Codices he happened to have seen. Purchased from Petau's son, it passed into the library of Christina, Queen of the Swedes; from her, Giuseppe Maria Tommasi received it and published it in Rome, 1680, in quarto. pretending to be one of them <note>The "them" refers to orthodox Christians</note>, so much so that they did not fear to attend the holy assembly and receive the most holy bread of the Eucharist in their mouths; however, they carefully and intentionally avoided the chalice. Gelasius investigated this with great diligence; and to strip the mask from these heretics, he confirmed by decree a custom received in the Church from its very beginnings: that no one should participate in the holy Gatherings unless they communicated under both kinds <note>original: "sub utrâque specie" – receiving both the bread and the wine during Communion</note>. Having detected the Manichaeans by this law, he condemned them and had them expelled from the city. No less bravely did he oppose the Pelagians and Eutychians on every given occasion, whether through his writings or his authority, acting as a most fierce enemy of heretics. He died on the 8th day of September, in the year 496.

->He wrote many things, which follow.<-

Sixteen letters, the last of which, addressed to Rusticus of Lyon, was first published by D’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, Volume 5, page 581.
*Fragments of ten other letters.*
*A volume or book on the bond of Anathema.*
*Against the Senator Andromachus and other Romans, who determined that the Lupercalia <note>An ancient, often rowdy Roman festival involving fertility rites</note> should be observed according to the ancient custom.*
*Statements against the Pelagian heresy.*
*A Decree in the Roman Council of 70 Bishops in the year 494, concerning Canonical, Ecclesiastical, and Apocryphal books.* This most celebrated decree of Gelasius is on everyone's lips and in everyone's hands. However, I can hardly persuade myself that it belongs to him, or that it possesses the age and authority it claims, led by these arguments:

1st. The older manuscripts attribute it to no certain author. Hence, as noted by the illustrious 
<margin>* Note to Gratian, p. 444.</margin>
Baluze *, in ancient manuscripts—and those of the better sort—it is ascribed sometimes to Damasus, sometimes to Gelasius, and occasionally to Pope Hormisdas: a most certain sign that the genuine author of this Decree was once unknown. 2nd. Books are cited in this Decree that in the year 494 were either not yet written or were entirely unknown. For example, the *Paschal Work* of Sedulius is praised, which was first extracted from Sedulius’s desks and published to the common people by Turcius Rufus Asterius, a former consul. Yet Asterius held the consulship in this very year, 494. A treatise on the *Revelation of the Head of St. John the Baptist* is condemned, which was only written after the age of Marcellinus Comes, who is explicitly cited in it. Furthermore, the author of the Decree seems clearly to confirm the fifth, and perhaps even the sixth, general Council. These words ["But also if there are any Councils, etc."] could not be understood in any other sense, as no one who reads them attentively could easily deny. 3rd. It contains many absurdities, <term>inconsistencies</term> <note>original: "asysta" – things that are logically incoherent or do not hold together</note>, and things plainly foreign to the learning and judgment of Gelasius and the Roman Synod. Who would believe that Gelasius, a man of the highest erudition, supported by a Council of 70 Bishops, would have relegated the works of Clement of Alexandria—whom the whole world venerated—to the rank of the apocryphal, and returned the writings of Africanus, Arnobius, Lactantius, and Commodian to the same class? Who with a sound mind would believe that the Pope and the Synodal fathers, in the same decree, would receive Eusebius's *Church History* among approved authors and then reject it with those condemned? I pass over the fact that the true Gelasius speaks excellently of Eusebius in his work *On the Two Natures*. 4th. The Decree condemns the *Apostolic Canons*; yet Dionysius Exiguus, who greatly cherished the memory of Gelasius, translated them into Latin shortly thereafter without adding any such censure; and the Roman Church accepted them and used them as a most certain norm of Church discipline (as is clear from Cassiodorus * and the letter of John II to Caesarius of Arles),
<margin>* Divine Readings, ch. 23.</margin>
which it would by no means have done if they had been condemned shortly before by Gelasius. And what hits even harder: Gelasius himself seems to have admitted the *Apostolic Canons* and used them in his Decretal Letters, which the most learned Pearson † proves with several examples. 
<margin>† Vindication of Ignatius, part 1, ch. 4.</margin>
5th. The author of the Decree professes to follow St. Jerome in all things. "We feel," he says, "those things which we know Blessed Jerome feels; and not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom the man frequently mentioned rebuked with the zeal of God and the religion of faith." Yet now, in defining the Canon of the books of Holy Scripture, he is diametrically opposed to Jerome. He numbers the works of Tertullian, the *Shepherd* <note>The Shepherd of Hermas</note>, Clement of Alexandria, Novatian, Arnobius, Apollinaris, and others among the apocryphal, and forbids them to be read by Catholics—works which Jerome, on the contrary, greatly praises and proclaims to be useful and worthy of reading. Finally, no one before the year...

...mentions the year 840; however, those who wrote specifically on Church Authors do not mention it—not Gennadius, Ildefonsus, Isidore of Seville, nor even Sigebert of Gembloux or Honorius of Autun. Neither do those who treated the controversies born in every age, in which a suitable opportunity for bringing forward this Decree could not have been lacking. Dionysius Exiguus, nearly a contemporary of Gelasius himself, collected the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs not long after the Pope's death; and while he presents the Decrees of Gelasius given in this very year, he completely omits this one. Indeed, not even the slightest memory of a Roman Synod in the year 494 remains among Church writers. Lupus of Ferrières, Hincmar of Reims, and Nicholas I—who flourished when the ninth century was already well advanced—were the first to mention this decree. Having weighed these facts properly, I conclude with good reason that this Decree of Gelasius is a fiction and a forgery, of the same sort as the Decretal Letters of the first Popes, and that it issued from the same workshop of Isidore the Merchant <note>Isidore Mercator is the pseudonym associated with the "False Decretals," a famous set of forged documents intended to bolster papal authority</note>.

*The Sacramentary.* That Gelasius wrote formulas for prayers and sacraments is confirmed by clear witnesses: Anastasius in his *Life*, John the Deacon in the *Life of Gregory the Great* *, and an ancient book nearly eight hundred years old on the *Office of the Mass*, cited first by Cassander † and then by Morin || (who called it the *Toulouse* book), not to mention Hugh of Saint Victor, Rupert of Deutz, and others. Gelasius certainly collected, as it is reasonable to believe, the solemn formulas of prayers and sacraments which were still in use in the Roman Church in his time; and having arranged them in a new order and added several of his own, he bound them into one volume. This was later reduced into a compendium by Gregory the Great, who changed and added some things himself. The Gelasian volume consists of three books: namely, on the Cycle of the Year, on the Birthdays of the Saints, and on Sundays and various occasions. The venerable antiquity of this arrangement is clearly proven by the fact that the word *Filioque* <note>The phrase "and from the Son," which became a point of major theological dispute between the Western and Eastern Churches</note> is not found in the Creed, as it first arose only in the seventh century and was not received at Rome until the ninth. Furthermore, several masses are missing that were commonly used in the seventh and eighth centuries; and finally, fewer birthdays of saints are celebrated than in other Liturgies, and those are only of Martyrs. This Volume lay hidden for a long time, known to few, until in the year 1562, when the Library of Fleury was looted and dispersed, a copy about nine hundred years old—written in square and uncial letters <note>Large, rounded script used in early medieval manuscripts</note>—finally fell into the hands of Paul Petau, a Senator of Paris. Through his kindness, Jean Morin made use of it, testifying that of all the Volumes he happened to see, this was the oldest. It was purchased from Petau's son and passed into the Library of Queen Christina of Sweden; from her, Giuseppe Maria Tommasi received it and published it in *Rome, 1680, in quarto.* A few things, especially in the third book,

### TURCIUS RUFUS ASTERIUS, of Patrician rank, held the Consulship in the year 494 together with Flavius Praesidius. He is clearly a different person from Flavius Asturius who served as Consul with Protogenes in the year 449, with whom our author is often wrongly confused. Having already become an Ex-consul, he extracted several of Sedulius’s poems from the deceased's archives, rescued them from moths and beetles, and published them to the public: as is clear from his own Epigram to Macedonius, which is prefixed to Sedulius’s *Paschal Work* in certain very ancient manuscript codices, as witnessed by Ussher* and Sirmond†. Among those works which Asterius published, namely the poems of Sedulius, there is a place for the *Comparison of the Old and New Testaments* <note>original: "Collatio Veteris & Novi Testamenti"</note>, written in elegiac verse, which begins "Let us sing, companions." From this, it can be believed that an error occurred, so that in some manuscripts it is attributed to Asterius himself, and has several times appeared under his name, namely in the *Bignean Appendix* page 701, and the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patr."</note> Volume 9, page 464, and elsewhere. However, there are some who defend that poem for Asterius as a genuine work.
