### GENNADIUS, a Gaul by birth, was a priest of Marseilles <note>original: "Presbyter Massiliensis"</note>; not, as Giacomo Gaddio* and the much older Sigebert† and Platina|| wrongly state, a priest and then Bishop of Marseilles. He flourished in the year 495, in which he closed his Catalogue and sent his book *On the Faith* <note>original: "de Fide"</note> to Pope Gelasius. Regarding his zeal for the Catholic faith, the judgments of both ancients and moderns differ. Pope Hadrian* counts him among the most holy men; the Church of Lyons† placed him among the Pelagians eight hundred years ago. It is certainly established that he was an enemy to the Predestinarians <note>Those who believed in strict predestination, a view sometimes associated with extreme interpretations of Augustine</note>, and for that reason, he seems to have thought less well of Saint Augustine and Prosper||, since he wrongly judged that the predestinarian dogma was being championed by them. However, he is cleared of the mark of Pelagianism by the books written by him against Pelagius: nor is it clearly evident that the necessity of prevenient grace <note>Divine grace that precedes human decision or merit</note> (which was the specific mark of Semipelagianism) was removed by him; so much so that he can rightly be numbered among Catholic writers.

---

-> EXTANT WRITINGS. <-

The book *On Church Writers* <note>original: "De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis"</note>, or the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, continued from the time where Jerome left off until the year 495. It was published together with the Catalogues of Jerome, etc., at *Basel, 1528, in quarto*; among the Works of Jerome, Vol. 1, with notes by Suffridus Petrus, *Cologne, 1580, in octavo*; *Helmstedt, 1612, in quarto*; and finally with the scholia of Aubert Le Mire in the *Ecclesiastical Library, part 1, Antwerp, 1639, in folio*. A much more complete version exists in a manuscript codex of the Corbie Library, of which Mabillon gave a specimen in *Analecta Volume 2, page 42*. Indeed, the printed codices differ immensely.

The book *On the Faith*, or *On Church Dogmas* <note>original: "De Fide, seu de Dogmatibus Ecclesiasticis"</note>, sent to Pope Gelasius; which, wrongly ascribed to Augustine, is usually found among his works. Thirty chapters of the work itself—namely from chapter 22 to 51 inclusive—seem to have been stuffed and woven in by another hand after the death of Gennadius, taken from the decretal letter of Pope Celestine to the Gauls and the canons of the Councils of Milevis, Africa, and the Second Council of Orange <note>The Council of Orange, 529 AD, which settled the Semipelagian controversy</note>. For Gennadius did not live to the time of the Council of Orange held in the year 529; certainly, that treatise was written by him 34 years earlier. It appeared separately with the most learned notes of Elmenhorst at *Hamburg, 1614, in quarto*.

MALCHUS, a native of Philadelphia <note>Amman, Jordan</note> and by profession a Byzantine Sophist <note>A teacher of rhetoric or philosophy</note>, flourished in the year 496. He wrote a *History of the Romans* from the reign of Constantine the Great down to Emperor Anastasius, according to the witness of Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note>*. Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note> saw only seven books of this history, in which Malchus had encompassed the deeds of Emperor Zeno from the start of his reign to the death of Emperor Nepos. Regarding this history, Photius says†: *“The author is, if any other, the best in writing history, being pure, concise, clear, and using graceful speech.”* <note>original Greek: Ἐστὶ δ᾽ ὁ συγγραφεὺς, εἴπερ ἄλλος, κατὰ τὴν συγγραφὴν ἱστορίας ἄριστος, καθαρός τε, ἀπέριττος, εὐκρινής τε, καὶ κεχαρισμένῳ ἐστὶ κεχρημένος λόγῳ.</note> This writer is, if anyone is, most excellent in the writing of history; being pure, not at all redundant, and not confused.
—Indeed, in every respect, he is the standard for historical prose. Two very large fragments of this history exist among the *Selections on Embassies* published in Greek by Hoeschel at *Augsburg*, 1603, in quarto; then in Latin, translated by Charles Cantoclarus with notes, *Paris*, 1609, in octavo; and finally in Greek and Latin with his and Valesius's notes, *Paris*, 1648, in folio.

ANASTASIUS II, a Roman by birth and the son of Peter, was created Roman Pontiff <note>Pope</note> on September 15th, in the year 496. In the following year, he sent Bishop Germanus of Capua and Cresconius of Todi—along with whom the Senator of the City of Rome, Festus, set out on civil business—to Emperor Anastasius. They were sent so that they might discuss with him the removal of Acacius’s name from the Diptychs <note>List of names read during the liturgy; removal signified excommunication</note>, and the return of the Church of Alexandria to the Catholic Church and faith. But they were singing their story to a deaf man <note>original: "surdo canebant fabulam" - a Latin idiom meaning their plea was ignored</note>. The representatives of the Alexandrian Church did indeed present a petition to Festus and the other legates (which exists in the *Records of the Councils*, Vol. 4, p. 1283), in which they opened their faith and declared they were ready to restore concord with the Roman Church. However, the Emperor constantly defended the cause of Acacius; indeed, according to Theodore Lector*, Festus himself promised the Emperor that he would persuade the Roman Bishop to subscribe to Zeno’s *Henoticon* <note>An "Act of Union" intended to reconcile theological factions, which Rome viewed as compromising the faith</note>. And though he did not succeed in inducing Anastasius to do so—for upon returning to Rome, he found him dead—Festus nevertheless took pains to draw Laurentius (who had been elected Pope by another faction of the Clergy) over to his side. Certainly, from the author of the *Book of the Popes* <note>the "Liber Pontificalis"</note>, whom Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina, a 15th-century papal historian</note> echoes in this matter, it is established that many Priests and Clergy of the Roman Church withdrew themselves from communion with Pope Anastasius. This was because he had communicated with Photinus, a Deacon of Thessalonica who stood on the side of Acacius, and because he had secretly labored to restore Acacius's name to the Roman Diptychs. They add that Anastasius was struck down by divine will: Platina even adds that there were those who said that while he was obeying the necessity of nature <note>a euphemism for using the toilet</note>, his intestines spilled out into the latrine. Be that as it may, Anastasius died on the 8th of September in the year 498. Two *Letters* survive: one *to Emperor Anastasius*, and *another to Clovis, King of the Franks*, in which he congratulates him on his recent conversion (found in *Records of the Councils*, Vol. 4, p. 1278), as well as certain fragments in Baluze’s *New Collection of Councils*, p. 1457. He also wrote, if any faith is to be placed in Platina, books on the Trinity, on Free Will, and on the Rules of Faith,

## EUSTATHIUS
**EUSTATHIUS**, a Syrian by birth, from the city of Epiphania, flourished under Emperor Anastasius around the year 496. He wrote a *Compendium of Chronicles* in nine books, stretching from the time of Aeneas to the Emperor Anastasius, as well as several other works. According to Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian</note>, he also described—likely in his *Chronicle*—the siege of Amida, which occurred in the year 503. He is discussed by Nicephorus in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 14, Chapter 57, and by Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> under the entry for "Epiphanios."

## BASILIUS
**BASILIUS**, a Cilician by birth and a Priest of the Church of Antioch around the year 497, during the papacy of Anastasius; he eventually became the Bishop of Irenopolis in Cilicia. I have no doubt that he is the same man mentioned by Suidas*, as all the details—name, time, and homeland—align perfectly. He died after the year 518. He wrote three books of *Ecclesiastical History*: the first begins in the year 450 and ends with the death of Pope Simplicius in 483; the second continues the narrative thread from there to the death of Emperor Anastasius in 518; and the third covered the deeds of Emperor Justin. He also wrote sixteen books against John of Scythopolis, whom he attempted to accuse of the Manichaean heresy; these were mostly composed in the form of a dialogue addressed to a certain Leontius, at whose urging he undertook the work. Brief excerpts of this are provided by Photius in *Codex 107*, from which it is clear that Basilius openly defended the cause of the Nestorian heresy in this massive work. However, Photius notes that Basilius did not explicitly champion Nestorius himself, but rather frequently praised Diodore <note>Diodore of Tarsus</note> and Theodore <note>Theodore of Mopsuestia</note> as the authors of his doctrine. Finally, Basilius of Irenopolis wrote against Archelaus, a priest of Coloneia, according to Suidas in the place cited above, who says that Basilius <note>original Greek: τὴν φρένα καὶ τὴν ἄσκησιν τῷ ὁμωνύμῳ Βασιλείῳ Καισαρείας ἐοικότα</note> "was similar in mind and ascetic practice to his namesake, Basil of Caesarea." Photius mentions certain other works of his that are full of heresy in *Codex 95*.

* On Latin History, Book 2, Chapter 21.
† Codex 79.

## CANDIDUS
**CANDIDUS**, a native of Isauria from the region called Trachea, was a clerk <note>term: tabellio; a notary or registrar</note> to the provincial governors and flourished around the year 496, if the distinguished Vossius has correctly calculated his age. He wrote three books of *Histories* from the election of Emperor Leo in 457 until the death of Zeno in 491. In these books, he showed himself to be not only a Christian but an Orthodox one, for he praised the Council of Chalcedon and rightly criticized its detractors. Regarding his style, Photius† writes: <note>original Greek: Τὴν δὲ φράσιν ἐκ ἔχει πρέπουσαν λόγῳ ἱςορικῷ. Ταῖς τε γὰρ ποιητικαῖς λέξεσιν ἀπειροκάλως τε κέχρηται καὶ μειρακιωδῶς. Καὶ ἡ συνθήκη αὐτῷ εἰς τὸ τραχύτερον καὶ ἀνηγμένον ἐκδεδιαιτημένηται.</note> "His phrasing is not suitable for historical writing. He uses poetic words without taste and in a childish manner. His composition is distorted into something harsh and forced, in the style of Dithyrambs <note>wild, emotional hymns</note>, and at other times it collapses into a loose and clumsy style." Excerpts of this *History* exist in Photius, *Codex 79*, and were published with notes by Philippe Labbe among the *Excerpts on Embassies* (Paris, 1648, folio).

<margin>498.</margin>
## RUSTICUS ELPIDIUS
**RUSTICUS ELPIDIUS**, or Helpidius, a nobleman of the rank of Ex-Quaestor and Ex-Illustris, and physician to Theodoric, King of the Goths, flourished around the year 498. He wrote *Twenty-four Epigrams* on as many stories from the Old and New Testaments, as well as a *Hexameter Poem on the Blessings of Jesus Christ*. These are available with notes in the *Fabrician Collection*, page 754; in the *Bignean Appendix*, page 706; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 9, page 462. He also wrote a *Poem for the Consolation of His Own Grief*, which he mentions himself, though it has since been lost.

<margin>
498.
Gennadius, On Illustrious Men, Ch. 98.
Isidore, On Illustrious Men, Ch. 12.
</margin>
## JULIANUS POMERIUS
**JULIANUS POMERIUS**, of Moorish origin, traveled to Gaul and opened a school of rhetoric in the city of Arles, eventually being ordained as a priest. He flourished around the year 498. Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Marseilles</note> testifies that he was eminent for his holiness of life and for the writings he published daily at the time Gennadius concluded his catalog. He wrote eight books *On the Soul*; the subjects of these are listed individually by Gennadius and Isidore, who note that in the second book he argued regarding whether the soul has a bodily form.

He <note>Julianus Pomerius, a priest of Arles</note> also wrote a treatise *On the Contempt of the World and Transitory Things* addressed to a prince, and another *On Vices and Virtues*, as well as a small book *On the Instruction of Virgins*, which have since perished. His only surviving work is *On the Contemplative Life*, or *On the Contemplation of the Future Life*, or *On Actual Conversation*, divided into three books; this work is commonly and incorrectly attributed to Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine</note> and is usually found among his works. It was published separately under Prosper's name in the year 1487, and again at Cologne in 1536 in octavo. D'Achéry <note>Jean Luc d'Achéry, a Benedictine scholar</note> was the first to publish the prologue of the second book of this work in the *Spicilegium*, Volume 13.

<margin>498.</margin>
**SYMMACHUS**, a Sardinian by birth and son of Fortunatus, became the Bishop of Rome <note>Pope Symmachus, reigned 498–514</note> on September 13th in the year 498. He was ordained in the Constantinian Basilica, while on the same day, the Deacon Laurentius was consecrated by an opposing faction in the Basilica of St. Mary. Because of this, both the Clergy and the Senate were divided. The matter was brought by both parties before King Theodoric <note>Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths</note>, who was then at Ravenna. He delivered the sentence that whoever was ordained first, or whoever had the largest following, should hold the Apostolic See. Once the matter was settled by royal decree, the Bishopric remained in the hands of Symmachus. In the year 499, he held a Synod in which he issued canons to eliminate bribery <note>term: *ambitus*; the illegal pursuit of office through bribery or influence</note> in Papal elections. In the year 502, having assembled a Synod in Rome called the *Palmaris* <note>The "Palm Synod," named either for the location "ad Palmaria" or because it vindicated the Pope (bearing the palm of victory)</note>, he and the bishops by common consent placed an anathema upon the Emperor Anastasius, who was a constant supporter of the Acacian cause <note>A schism between Eastern and Western churches regarding the Monophysite controversy</note>. The Emperor, moved by a grave and justified anger, published a pamphlet in which he sharply criticized the Pope for the sentence passed against him; Symmachus responded with no less ferocity by publishing an *Apology*. In that same Synod, the controversy over the Roman See between him and Laurentius was debated again, as it had recently flared up and been brought back to King Theodoric. The King had delegated the matter to Peter, Bishop of Altinum; however, Peter favored Laurentius more than was fair and had stripped Symmachus of the Church's properties. The cause was finally returned to Theodoric's royal judgment. In that Synod, Symmachus was restored to his full rights, while Peter of Altinum and the Roman clerics who followed Laurentius were removed from their positions. Symmachus died on April 6th in the year 514. Twelve *Letters* written by him are extant in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 1291.

<margin>500.</margin>
**ANDREAS**, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, seems to have lived near the end of this century and flourished around the year 500. His actual age is entirely uncertain, and there is no mention of him among the ancient writers. This much alone is certain: he wrote after Basil and Cyril of Alexandria, and before Arethas of Caesarea. He wrote *Commentaries on the Apocalypse to a certain Macarius*, which Theodore Peltanus translated into Latin. They are extant in Greek and Latin at the end of Chrysostom’s *Commentaries on St. John* in the Morellian edition, Volume 8.

## PAGAN WRITERS

### Those condemning the Christian faith in this Century.

<margin>425.</margin>
**OLYMPIODORUS**, a native of Egyptian Thebes, a poet, historian, and ambassador to the King of the Huns, flourished around the year 425. He wrote twenty-two books of *Histories* dedicated to the Emperor Theodosius the Younger, in which he covered the deeds of the Roman Empire, especially in the West, from the year 407 to 425. He gave his work the title *Sylvae* <note>original: "Sylvæ"; meaning "The Woods" or "Raw Material"</note>, as he did not wish it to be considered a finished history so much as a simple commentary on events. Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note> says of him <margin>* Codex 80.</margin>: <note>original Greek: "Σαφὴς δὲ τὴν φράσιν, ἄτονός τε καὶ ἐκλελυμένος, καὶ πρὸς τὴν πεπατημένην κατενηνεγμένος χυδαιολογίαν, ὥστ' μηδ' ἀξίως εἰς συγγραφὴν ἀναγράφεσθαι ὁ λόγος· ὃ καὶ αὐτὸς ἴσως συνιδὼν οὐ συγγραφὴν, &c."</note> "His phrasing is clear, yet it is weak and loose, and has descended into the well-trodden vulgarity of common speech, so that the style is not even worthy of being recorded as a formal history; a fact which he himself perhaps realized, [calling it] not a history..."

425.

**ZOSIMUS**, a Count <note>The title *Comes* was a high-ranking imperial official</note> and former Advocate of the Treasury, flourished around the year 425, as he cites Olympiodorus in the fifth book of his History. He wrote six books of Histories, in which he briefly recounts Roman affairs from the time of Augustus to the time of Diocletian in a single book; thereafter, he treats the history of events more extensively in the remaining five books up to the second capture of Rome by Alaric, and the elevation of Attalus to the imperial honors and his subsequent deposition in the year 410. In this, he primarily produced a condensed version of the History of Eunapius. In these books, whenever he deals with Christian affairs, he sharply criticizes their religion; for that reason, he violently rages against nearly all the Christian Princes, especially Constantine the Great and Theodosius the Elder. I am not unaware that Joannes Leunclavius, a most learned man, published a lengthy *Apology* in favor of Zosimus, in which he uses all the mental sharpness he can muster to defend him from the injuries and false slanders against the Christians, and from the stain of spite and malice with which he was most heavily inflamed. But while he tries to purge this pagan man and most bitter enemy of the Christian name, "he is washing a brick" and "attempting to whiten an Ethiopian" <note>Both are ancient idioms for attempting a futile or impossible task</note>. In acting as the advocate for a malevolent and—if ever there were one—virulent writer, he reveals himself to be unfair, and indeed toward some plainly bitter and shameless, not only against Eusebius, Chrysostom, Innocent, Theodoret, Photius, and other leaders of the Christian religion, but also against Constantine the Great and his sons, Jovian, Valentinian, Theodosius, and the entire lineage of the succeeding Emperors. Otherwise, Evagrius (Book 3, chapters 40 and 41) and Nicephorus Callistus (Book 16, chapters 41, 42, 43, 44) formerly defended Constantine and other Christians against the malice of Zosimus with deliberate effort and a more extensive defense.

<margin>
* Codex 98.
</margin>
Regarding his style, Photius says*: "He is brief, clear and pure in expression, and not lacking in sweetness... and he uses figures of speech only rarely" <note>original Greek: Σύντομος δέ, καὶ τὴν φράσιν εὐκρινής τε καὶ καθαρός, οὐδέ τι ἡδέως ἀπαλλόμενος— καὶ ταῖς τροπαῖς, εἰ μὴ σπάνιον, οὐ κεχρημένος</note>. Henry Stephens <note>Henricus Stephanus</note> published the first two books of this history in Greek and Latin, appended to Herodian, in 1581 in quarto, and they were reprinted at Lyon in 1611 in octavo. The complete six books, however, with a translation and the *Apology* prefixed, were published by Joannes Leunclavius among the minor writers of Roman History at Frankfurt in 1590 in folio; finally, they appeared separately at Oxford in 1680 in octavo.

# THE EUTYCHIAN CENTURY.

## Overview of the Century.

Emperor Anastasius launched a most cruel persecution against the orthodox defenders of the Council of Chalcedon; for this reason, he was soon after subjected to anathema <note>A formal curse by a church authority, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine.</note> by Pope Symmachus. The Eutychians <note>Followers of Eutyches, who taught that Christ had only one nature (Divine), rather than being both fully God and fully man.</note>, who arose around the middle of the previous century and were previously known by the common name "Acephali" <note>original: *Acephalorum*, meaning "The Headless," because they had broken away from their patriarch and lacked a clear leader.</note>, now split into various factions and opinions. From this were born the names of the Severians, Theodosians, Jacobites, Theopaschites, Tritheites, Aphthartodocitae, Corrupticolae, and Agnoetae—titles derived partly from their founders and partly from their specific dogmas. Although most of them disagreed with one another on many points, they all agreed with one voice in defending and spreading the general doctrine of Eutyches; for this reason, we have called this the EUTYCHIAN Century. The Arians <note>Those who believed that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> also experienced a revival, dominating in Italy, Spain, and Africa under the rule of the Goths. Consequently, the peace of the Church was broken, and the Christian faith was wretchedly undermined. Finally, in the year 522, Hilderic—son of Hunneric and King of the Vandals—restored the African bishops to their sees after recalling them from exile; they had been granted the kingdom by Thrasamund, an undying enemy of the Catholics, even as he lay on the brink of death. Around the year 520, peace was restored between the Eastern churches and the Roman See regarding the case of Acacius, through the mediation of the Emperor Justin I; Acacius’s name was struck out, and the Pope’s name was returned to the <term>diptychs</term> <note>Diptychs: Liturgical lists of names of the living and the dead to be commemorated during the Mass. Removing a name was a sign of broken communion.</note>. In the year 525, Pope John was sent to Constantinople by Theodoric, King of the Goths, to obtain churches for the Arians in the East. Although he was received with honors by Justin, he returned home without accomplishing the mission and was soon cast into chains by Theodoric.

Around the year 546, a very fierce struggle began over the **Three Chapters**, namely: *The condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia, the writings of Theodoret against Cyril, and the letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian.* This was a cunning scheme devised by Theodore, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. In order to shield the errors of the Origenists <note>Followers of Origen’s more controversial cosmic theories, then resurfacing in Palestine.</note> from an imminent sentence of condemnation, he diligently stirred up this new dispute regarding three chapters of the Council of Chalcedon. The gist of the matter was this: they accused Theodore of Mopsuestia and his writings <note>original Greek: συγγράμματα (*syngrammata*)</note> of having opened the way for the Nestorian heresy with his doctrines. They accused Ibas, Bishop of Edessa, because in a certain letter to Maris the Persian—which had been read and approved at the Council of Chalcedon—he had mentioned Theodore with praise. Finally, they accused Theodoret because he had most sharply attacked certain writings of Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius. This was done despite the fact that Theodoret himself had proven his faith to Pope Leo of Rome, and after a solemn clearing of his name and a public anathema against Nestorius, he had been received by the Council of Chalcedon both back to his See and into communion. Nevertheless, they contended that these three must be condemned; they foresaw that the "Acephali" could not be brought back to the approval of the Council of Chalcedon and church communion by any other law, knowing well that these things could not be condemned without some level of condemnation of the Council of Chalcedon itself. Caught by these deceptions, the Emperor [Justinian] first condemned the Three Chapters himself along with the Origenists, and then the Fifth General Council was held at Constantinople in the year 553. Pope Vigilius, then staying in Constantinople, resisted strenuously with his Western bishops—though he had previously condemned them himself, being a man of wondrous levity and inconsistent character. At last, changing his course, he approved the sentence of the Council, writing a letter on this matter to Eutychius of Constantinople, which Peter de Marca first published in Greek and Latin; a longer decree sent to the Emperor was recently rescued from obscurity by Baluze.

Around the year 520 (or 529 according to others), St. Benedict, the Patriarch of monks in the West, established his order under certain laws and rules. From his institute, as if from a Trojan horse, the remaining crowds of religious orders have emerged.

In the year <term>580</term> <note>original: "DLXXX"</note>, the <term>Bavarians</term> <note>original: "Boiarii," a Germanic people</note>, through the preaching of <term>Rupert</term>, Bishop of <term>Worms</term>, were converted to the Christian faith. Toward the end of the century, the Christian religion was successfully advanced in <term>Britain</term>, with <term>Columba</term> working among the <term>Picts</term> <note>A tribal people living in what is now eastern and northern Scotland.</note>, and soon after, the monk <term>Augustine</term> <note>Known as Augustine of Canterbury, sent by Pope Gregory the Great.</note> among the <term>Anglo-Saxons</term> devoting his efforts to that cause.

<margin>6TH CENTURY from the Year of the Lord.</margin>
<margin>502.</margin>
<margin>* Chapter 86.</margin>
**CAESARIUS**, a Gaul by birth, was born to honorable parents in the Province of <term>Chalon</term> <note>original: "Cabilonensi"</note> in the year 469. While still a young man, seized by a zeal for a stricter discipline, he withdrew from his father's house in secret to the **Monastery of Lérins** <note>A famous island monastery off the French Riviera known for its rigor.</note>. Having become dear to Abbot **Porcharius** on account of his excellent character, he performed the duties of **Cellarer** <note>The person in charge of a monastery's food and drink supplies.</note> for some time. Afterward, forced to leave the monastery due to failing health, he traveled to **Arles** <note>original: "Arelaten"</note>, where he was received into the home of Bishop **Aeonius** and entered into a very close friendship with him. As Caesarius recovered, Aeonius placed him in charge of a monastery of monks located on a suburban island of Arles, and three years later, as Aeonius lay dying, he designated Caesarius as his successor. Therefore, in the year 502, Caesarius was elevated to the Bishopric of Arles by the common vote of all the clergy.

I am not unaware that the commonly published copies of the *Catalog of Gennadius* <note>A 5th-century biographical dictionary of Christian writers.</note>, written in the year 395, speak of Caesarius as if he were already governing the see of Arles then, and as the author of many books approved by **Pope Felix**. However, the timeline of events is completely inconsistent; nor is the **Index of Gennadius** <note>original: "Indiculus Gennadianus"</note> of such great authority—having suffered from the worst sort of interpolations <note>Unauthorized additions or changes to the text.</note> at the end—that it should command belief in this matter. In the year 506, he attended the **Council of Agde** <note>original: "Concilio Agathensi"</note>; and shortly after, having been falsely accused of treason before **Alaric**, King of the Visigoths, he was exiled to **Bordeaux**. Soon, however, once his innocence was discovered, he was recalled with the greatest honor. In the year 508, he was accused of the same crime before **Theodoric**, King of the Goths, who at that time held supreme power in <term>Narbonnese Gaul</term> after the death of Alaric; he was summoned to **Ravenna** to either clear himself of the charge or face punishment. Caesarius easily proved his innocence; and having been dismissed with the immense respect of the King and all the Goths, he proceeded to Rome to see **Pope Symmachus**. In the year 524, he presided over the Fourth Council of Arles. Around the year 529, because suspicion had arisen regarding his doctrine <note>This refers to the controversy over Semi-Pelagianism, which questioned how much human will vs. divine grace contributes to salvation.</note>, he arranged for a Synod of Bishops to be held at **Valence**. When he could not attend due to bodily infirmity, he sent legates—**Cyprian**, Bishop of Toulon, and others—and most powerfully demonstrated that a man cannot attain salvation without the prevenient grace of God <note>The concept that God's grace moves a person even before they have the will to seek Him.</note>. He died in the year 542, on the 6th day before the Kalends of September <note>August 27th.</note>, at the age of 73, and was buried in the Basilica of Saint Mary, which he had built during his life.

---

### EXTANT WORKS.

**Forty-six Homilies** on various subjects, some of which **Labbe** <note>Philippe Labbe, a 17th-century Jesuit editor.</note> does not deny are falsely attributed to Caesarius; in the forty-second, **Gregory the Great** and **Isidore of Seville** are cited; the twenty-first bears the title of a *Sermon of Saint Augustine*, and the twenty-ninth the title of an *Admonition of Saint Ephrem on Prayer*. The 19th is said to be taken from the teachings of **Macarius**; and perhaps there are others which either do not have our Caesarius as their author or have been altered with parts from elsewhere.

*Exhortation to Preserve Charity.*

*Letter to certain young men leading a monastic life.*

*Treatise on the Ten Virgins.*

*Rules for Nuns*, written for the benefit of his sister, **Saint Caesaria**; this was published with the observations of Friar Minard by Stephen Morquot at Poitiers, 1621.

*Rule for Monks*, which exists inscribed to **Tetradius** (or Terridius), the nephew of Saint Caesarius, in the *Library of the Fathers*. We shall say more of this under the entry for Tetradius.

*A Testament* (Will), which is found in Baronius under the year 508, and in Le Cointe under the year 542, number 43.

Caesarius also wrote a book *On Grace and Free Will* against **Faustus**, which has been lost. The *Catalog of Gennadius* mentions it; but as for its addition that it was sent by Caesarius to Pope Felix and approved by Felix, the chronology of the times does not allow it.

Forty Homilies by **Caesarius** were published by Gilbertus Cognatus at *Basel, 1558, in quarto,* and in the *Orthodoxographia, page 1861.*

Fourteen homilies, previously unpublished, were recovered from a manuscript in the Royal Library and published with explanatory notes by Etienne Baluze in *Paris, 1669, in octavo.*

Indeed, all of his minor works appeared in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patrum," a massive collection of early Christian writings</note>, Volume 8, pages 819 and 860, and Volume 27, page 324.

**LAURENTIUS**, called *Mellifluus* <note>meaning "the Honey-tongued"</note> on account of his eloquence, was the Bishop of Novara among the **Insubrians** <note>A people of Northern Italy, in the region of modern Milan.</note>. He seems to have flourished around the year 507. According to Sigebert \*, he wrote a book titled *On the Two Times*—specifically from Adam to Christ, and from Christ to the end of the age—but this work has been lost. Two of his homilies, on penance and almsgiving, survive in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 9, page 465, as well as a *Homily on the Canaanite Woman* in Mabillon's *Analecta*, Volume 2, page 18.

<margin>
507.
* Chapter 70.
</margin>
**ANIANUS**, a **Notable Man** <note>original: "Vir Spectabilis," a specific title for high-ranking officials in the late Roman Empire</note> under Athalaric, King of the Goths, flourished around the year 507. Sigebert of Gembloux \* reports that he wrote the *Abridgment of the Theodosian Code* <note>original: "Codicis Theodosiani Breviarium," a collection of Roman laws</note> at the command of King Athalaric. However, it is clearly established from his own signature, which survives today, that Anianus was neither the abridger nor even the translator of this Code, but merely the reviewer and the one who signed it. See the annotations of the distinguished Gothofredus on the *Theodosian Code, chapter 5.* To this same Anianus, Sigebert and others attribute a Latin translation of fifteen homilies by **Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom, a famous Greek preacher</note>; however, Garnerius attempts to prove at length that this translation belongs to Anianus, a Deacon of Celeda, as we have noted in the appropriate place. Let the learned weigh their own judgment on this controversy.

<margin>
507.
Ferrandus the Deacon in the Life of Fulgentius.
</margin>
**FULGENTIUS**, African by birth and from the city of Leptis, was born into a distinguished family around the year 468. His grandfather was Gordianus, a Senator of Carthage; his father was Claudius, and his mother was Marriana. Having lost his father at a tender age, he was entrusted by his mother's care to teachers of both languages to be educated in both Greek and Latin literature. Fulgentius progressed marvelously in both, so much so that while still a boy he could recite the whole of **Homer** from memory and spoke Greek with the utmost purity and ease. On account of his excellent character and natural gifts, he was appointed **Procurator** <note>A high-ranking financial official or governor</note> of his home city while barely past his youth. 

However, growing weary of the troubles of secular life, he meditated on a monastic vocation. He approached Bishop Faustus—who had built a monastery for himself after being driven from his see for his profession of the **Catholic faith** <note>Here referring to the Nicene creed, in opposition to Arianism</note>—and bound himself by a vow. In the year 490, as the **Arian persecution** <note>The Arians were a Christian sect favored by the Vandal kings who denied the full divinity of Christ and often persecuted those who held to the Nicene/Catholic view.</note> flared up again and struck at the head of Faustus, Fulgentius sought out a neighboring monastery. There, his exceptional virtues being immediately recognized, he was appointed colleague or co-abbot to Abbot Felix. 

Soon harassed by frequent raids by the Moors, he departed for the territory of Sicca; there he was seized by a certain Arian priest named Felix and underwent the most severe torments, being beaten with clubs and mangled with whips. Having returned to his monastery, he was touched by a desire to visit the Egyptian monks and began his journey by boarding a ship at Carthage. However, having been brought to Syracuse during the journey, he was dissuaded from his original purpose by Bishop Eulalius and settled with him. After spending the winter in Syracuse, in the following year (around 500 AD), he set out for Rome. Soon determined to return to his former monastery, he sailed to Africa by way of Sardinia; moving the location of his monastery, he refounded it in a better place in the Province of **Byzacena** <note>A Roman province in what is now Tunisia.</note>. 

Yet, soon weary of the governance committed to him, he secretly left his monastery and, seeking another located near the shore of Vennetium, subjected himself to the command of others. He was soon recalled to his former duty against his will by his co-abbot Felix and Bishop Faustus, who threatened him with the "bolt of excommunication" <note>original: "anathematis fulmine," a formal religious ban</note> if he did not return, and he was raised to the rank of the Priesthood. In the year 507, sought out by the Catholic people to take up the Bishopric of Vintium, he avoided the dignity by taking flight; nevertheless, having been unexpectedly discovered shortly thereafter, he was ordained Bishop of Ruspe. Baronius places this in the year 504. After a short stay in his Bishopric, he was taken to Carthage by order of **Thrasamund**, King of the Vandals, and banished to Sardinia. There, in the city of Cagliari <note>original: "Caralitanâ"</note>, he led a monastic and truly holy life among sixty fellow exiled bishops; [he was held in such high regard] by all...

<header># The Eutychian Century</header>

<margin>The 6th Century from the Year of our Lord.</margin>
Fulgentius was held in such high regard by everyone for his learning that the duty of writing communal letters in the name of all the bishops was entrusted to him alone. In the same year, as it seems, he was summoned from Sardinia to Carthage by King Thrasamund <note>The Vandal King of North Africa, who was an Arian</note> to engage in a debate concerning the Catholic faith. There, he vigorously dismantled the futile objections of the **Arians** <note>A group that denied the full divinity of Christ, maintaining he was a created being</note> and excellently confirmed the orthodox truth in three books written to the king, and in another work regarding the Holy Spirit. Having been sent back to Sardinia, he returned to the established practices of his former monastic life, founding a monastery outside the city and gathering more than forty brothers. Around the year 523, after the death of Thrasamund, he was recalled from exile by King Hilderic. Received in Carthage with great honor, he was sent back to his own see at Ruspe, which he governed until his death. During this time, he attended many synods of the African bishops, such as those at Byzacena, Junca <note>original: Vincensi</note>, Sufetula, and others; in these, he almost always held the first rank due to the excellence of his virtue. He died in the year 533, on the very Kalends of January <note>January 1st</note>, at the age of 65. Baronius <note>A prominent Catholic historian</note> places his death four years earlier, and we have previously noted that he followed a different path in dating the beginning of his episcopate. He was a man easily the foremost among the bishops of his age, both in exceptional learning and remarkable piety. Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville</note> praises his doctrine thus:
<gloss>renowned in his confession of faith, copiously learned in the divine Scriptures, sweet in speech, and subtle in teaching and debate.</gloss>
<margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 14.</margin>

->### EXISTING WORKS<-

*Three books to Monimus*: 1. *On Double Predestination: one of the good to glory, the other of the wicked to punishment*. 2. *On the offering of the sacrifice, the mission of the Holy Spirit, and the "extra works" of Saint Paul* <note>original: supererogatione</note>. 3. *On the exposition of that saying, "And the Word was with God."*

*A book against the Arians*, containing ten responses to their objections, which were strangely deformed by barbarity and obscurity.

*Three books to King Thrasamund*, written in the year 507: 1. *On the mystery of Christ the mediator, retaining two natures in one person*. 2. *On the immensity of the divinity of the Son of God*. 3. *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Passion*.

*Ten sermons on various subjects.*

*A book to Donatus on the Orthodox Faith and the various errors of Heretics*, seemingly written during his exile.

*A book on Faith to Peter the Deacon*; which is also often wrongly attributed to Augustine and included among his works.

*Twelve letters to various people on various subjects*, the last of which was written by Fulgentius in the name of all the African bishops exiled in Sardinia.

*A book on the Trinity to Felix the Notary.*

*A sermon on that saying of Micah: "I will show thee, O man, what is good."*

*A book to Victor against the sermon of Fastidiosus the Arian*: which is preceded by the sermon of Fastidiosus and a letter from Victor to Fulgentius earnestly requesting a refutation of Fastidiosus.

*Three books on the truth of predestination and the grace of God*, written after the year 523; the third of these was first published in its entirety by Chifflet, along with the works of Ferrandus the Deacon, at Dijon in 1649.

*Two books on the Remission of Sins to Euthymius*, written in exile.

*A book on the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ to Peter the Deacon*, written in the name of the exiled African bishops. All the minor works listed from the book *On the Trinity to Felix* inclusive, along with the five later letters, were first published by Jacques Sirmond at Paris in 1612.

*A book on Predestination and Grace*, which is also attributed to Augustine and usually kept among his works. Some judge it to be as unworthy of Fulgentius as it is of Augustine; Theophilus Raynaud, on the contrary, defends it as belonging to Fulgentius in a lengthy dissertation.

*Eighty new Homilies*, together with a preface by Fulgentius, some of which are found among the homilies of St. Augustine. These were first published by Theophilus Raynaud at Lyon in 1633. Recent Parisian editors of Fulgentius's works consider them spurious and have therefore moved them to an appendix.

JULIAN, Bishop of the city of Halicarnassus in Caria, a member of the Eutychian sect <note>Eutychians, or Monophysites, believed that Christ had only one divine nature rather than being both fully human and fully divine</note>, flourished in the year 510. At the instigation of Emperor Anastasius, he joined the schismatic monks who were attacking Macedonius, the Bishop of Constantinople, with insults and outcries. When Justin took power and declared himself <unclear>one of the well-aligned</unclear> <note>original: σὲ ἐῦ συνοδευτῶν; this refers to those who accepted the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon</note>, Julian was driven from his see in the year 419 <note>likely a typo in the original for 519</note> along with Severus, the Bishop of Antioch, and fled to Alexandria. There, a question arose between them concerning the corruptibility of the body of Christ; Julian argued fiercely against his associate Severus and, having published books against him, refuted him. He thus gave rise to the new sect of the <term>Aphthartodocetae</term> <note>From the Greek for "believers in incorruptibility," they held that Christ's body was not subject to decay or human frailty</note> or <term>Phantasiasts</term> <note>So called because their opponents argued they made Christ's human body a mere "phantasm" or appearance</note>. Among other things, he wrote a *Commentary on Job*, part of the Preface of which, along with several fragments, is presented by the author of the *Greek Chain on Job*, published in London, 1637. Perhaps he is the same person cited once under the name of Julius by the author of the *Greek Chain on John*, chapter 17.

# The Eutychian Century

<margin>
The 6th Century from the Year of Our Lord 510.
Cassiodorus, Preface to the *Tripartite History*; *Divine Letters*, ch. 17. 5, 8, 11.
</margin>
EPIPHANIUS SCHOLASTICUS, an Italian by birth and distinguished by his skill in the Greek and Latin languages, flourished around the year 510. At the urging of Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and monk who founded the Vivarium monastery</note>, he translated the Ecclesiastical Histories of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret into Latin. Weaving them into a single body of history, he distributed them into twelve books; after Epiphanius later reduced these into a compendium, Cassiodorus gave them the title of the *Tripartite History*. He also provided Latin translations for the *Commentaries on the Proverbs of Solomon* and on the *Seven Canonical Epistles* by Didymus [the Blind], as well as Saint Epiphanius of Cyprus on the *Song of Songs*, and perhaps many others. However, those versions have perished. There does survive, however, a *Version* which he prepared by order of Cassiodorus of the *Encyclical Code* <note>original: "Codices encyclici"</note>, or the Collection of Synodal Letters to Emperor Leo in defense of the Council of Chalcedon (found in the *Records of the Councils*, Vol. 4, p. 891). Baluze published a corrected edition in his *New Collection of Councils*, Paris, 1683, folio.

<margin>510.</margin>
ANICIUS MANLIUS TORQUATUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS, or Boetius, a Roman by birth, born from the most illustrious family of all Rome, had as his father Anicius Manlius Flavius Boethius. While still a boy to be instructed in liberal arts, he was sent to Athens; staying there for eighteen years, he thoroughly absorbed not only the basic elements but also the more hidden mysteries of all arts and disciplines, so much so that he was easily heard of as the prince of all the learned men of his age. Having returned to Rome, he was immediately heaped with the greatest honors of the city and empire, made a Patrician, and co-opted into the Senate. In the year 487, he held the consulship alone, although Onuphrius Panvinius and others with him assign the consulship of that year to his father. He had a wife named Helpis, who is said herself to have excelled in literature, especially poetry. After Helpis died, he married Rusticiana, the daughter of Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (who died as Consul in the year 485); from her he had two sons, Patricius and Hypatius, both of whom attained consular dignity. In the year 500, he received King Theodoric upon his entry into Rome with a panegyric oration in the name of the Senate. Soon he was admitted to more secret councils by Theodoric and appointed Master of the Palace and Offices. In the year 510 (when he especially flourished), he again held the consulship alone. In the year 522, he was made Consul for the third time; though some attribute that year to one of his sons. In the year 523, since he did not fear to sharply rebuke the tyranny of Theodoric—which was rushing daily toward worse things—he experienced the king's enmity. Soon he was accused of attempted treason and a conspiracy entered into with Emperor Justin for the ruin of the Goths by Trigilla, Congiastus, and Cyprian, the most wicked of mortals. Indeed, that Boethius secretly sent letters to the Greeks and attempted to rescue the city and Senate from the impious hands of Theodoric and subject them to the defense of the Greeks, is openly related by a very ancient Prologue written in Saxon characters <note>This likely refers to "Insular" or early medieval script which the author identified as Saxon</note> prefixed to the books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, which the famous Mabillon brings forth from a very old codex in the Ambrosian Library in Milan (*Italian Journey*, p. 221). Theodoric brought the case to the Senate. The accusers were present at the trial, surrounded by witnesses hired with money, and displaying forged documents under Boethius's name addressed to Justin. With testimonies produced for appearance, a vote was taken. The Senators, struck with terror, judged that Boethius should be punished with exile. Boethius was therefore led away to Pavia <note>original: "Ticinum"</note> and handed over to a tight prison. Amid the weariness and squalor of long imprisonment, neither his spirit nor his tireless study of literature failed. For besides several *Philosophical Opuscules*, we owe the books *On the Consolation of Philosophy* and *On the Trinity* to this leisure. In the following year—or, as others say, somewhat later—with suspicions growing along with Theodoric's tyranny, he was beheaded in prison by an executioner sent in. Cardinal <margin>* To the year 526, p. 114.</margin> Baronius trifles plainly below the gravity of a wise man and the dignity of his purple <note>A reference to the red robes of a Cardinal</note> when he seriously reports—from a life of Boethius "learnedly" written (as he says) by Julius Marcianus—as if it were a most wonderful thing: that after the royal guardsman had inflicted the lethal wound, Boethius held up his head with both his hands after it had been torn off, and when asked by whom he thought he had been struck, he replied "by the impious," and thus, when he had come into a nearby temple and received the Holy Sacraments on bended knees before the Altar, he expired a little later. "For he who in skill of literature," says the Cardinal, "equaled that great Dionysius the Areopagite..."

<meta>This page continues the biography of the philosopher Boethius, focusing on his reputation among later scholars and a comprehensive bibliography of his logical, philosophical, and theological writings.</meta>

<header>The Eutychian Century.</header>

<margin>THE 6TH CENTURY from the Year of Our Lord</margin>He was to be compared, justly and without envy, to Dionysius the Areopagite of Athens, and he received this from God: that both in the manner of his death and in the performance of a remarkable miracle, he was made equal to him. This was the work of the supreme power of God, who is rich toward all who call upon him. Truly he was "worthy of God" <note>original: "ἄξιος θεῷ"</note>. Regarding the extraordinary learning of Boethius, let Cassiodorus <note>A contemporary statesman and scholar</note> bear witness. <margin>* Various Letters, book 1, ep. 45.</margin> "You," he says, "saturated with much learning, have so mingled the Roman toga with the choruses of those wearing the *pallium* <note>The Greek philosopher's cloak; original: "palliatorum"</note> that you have turned the dogmas of the Greeks into Roman doctrine. You have brought to the senators of Romulus's line whatever unique thing the descendants of Cecrops <note>The Athenians</note> had given to the world. For through your translations, Pythagoras the musician and Ptolemy the astronomer are read by Italians; Nicomachus the mathematician, etc." — And whatever disciplines or arts fruitful Greece produced through individual men, Rome has received in her native tongue with you as the sole author. You have rendered them so clear with such brilliance of words and so conspicuous with such propriety of language, that even those original authors might have preferred your work to their own, had they known both. From more recent scholars, I will subjoin only two: Julius Scaliger and the illustrious Vossius. <margin>* Hypercritic, book 6, p. 825.</margin> "The genius of Severinus Boethius," says Scaliger, "his erudition, art, and wisdom, easily challenge all authors, whether they be Greek or Latin. Due to the barbarism of his age, his prose is found to be somewhat diminished; but what he chose to play with in poetry is truly divine. Nothing is more refined than those verses, nothing more weighty; neither the density of his thoughts nor their sharpness has taken away their charm. Indeed, I judge that few can be compared with him." Thus says Scaliger. <margin>† On the Latin Poets, ch. 5.</margin> And so says Vossius: "Boethius, a man most learned in Latin and Greek, excelled in every kind of discipline; Rome has not had anyone more learned in every respect since the time of Varro. Truly, that age—and even the one immediately preceding it—had nothing more lovely in poetry."

# WORKS.

Two Dialogues on Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century philosopher whose "Introduction" became a standard textbook</note> as translated by Victorinus.
Five Books on Porphyry, translated into Latin by himself.
Four books on Aristotle’s *Categories*. Two books of Minor Commentaries and six books of Major Commentaries on Aristotle’s book *On Interpretation*.
Four books of Aristotle’s *Analytics*, translated by Boethius.
*Introduction to Categorical Syllogisms*. Two books on the *Categorical Syllogism*. Two books on the *Hypothetical Syllogism*. A book *On Division*. A book *On Definition*. Eight books of Aristotle’s *Topics*, translated by Boethius. Two books of *Sophistical Refutations*, by the same translator. Six books on Cicero’s *Topics*. Four books on *Topical Differences*.

Five books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, composed in both prose and verse. Concerning these books, that very ancient Prologue (which we mentioned above from Mabillon) has this to say:
> After he was convicted of high treason by the King, he was ordered to be thrust into prison; being placed there, he published these books in the form of a Satire <note>Meaning a mixture of prose and various meters, or "Menippean satire"</note>, imitating Martianus Felix Capella, who first wrote books on the *Marriage of Philology and Mercury* in the same style of poetry.

But this work excels by far in its noble subject matter and eloquence, for he is not unequal to Cicero, nor did he flourish as an inferior to Virgil in meter. They were published separately with the annotations of Badius Ascensius at *Lyon, 1502, in quarto*; also with the commentaries of Thomas Aquinas at the same place, *1514, in quarto*; with the commentaries of Johannes Murmellius, *Basel, 1536, in octavo*; with the commentaries of Johannes Bernartius, *Antwerp, 1607, in octavo*; with the notes of Bertius, *Leiden, 1633*; and with the notes of Renatus Vallinus at the same place, *1656, in octavo*.

A book *Against Eutyches and Nestorius on the Two Natures and One Person of Christ*, addressed to John, Deacon of the Roman Church.
*That the Trinity is One God and Not Three Gods*, addressed to his father-in-law Symmachus.
A book *On Unity and the One*. Published separately at *Louvain, 1633, in quarto*.

## EUGYPPIUS
Whether he was born in Noricum <note>A Roman province roughly encompassing modern Austria and Slovenia</note> is uncertain; he certainly stayed there for some time. As the Abbot of Lucullanum in Italy, near Naples, he was prominent in the year 511. He wrote the *Life of Saint Severinus, Apostle of the Noricans*, addressed to Deacon Paschasius. Surius published it for the eighth day of January, but in a mutilated form. However, Marcus Velserus, having obtained a more authentic manuscript, published it in its entirety, illustrated with his own scholarly notes; it is therefore found in his *Works*, page 629. Henricus Canisius was the first to bring to light the letter from Eugyppius to Paschasius in his *Ancient Lessons*, Volume VI, page 453; from there it was transferred into the second edition of Surius and is today placed at the beginning of the *Life of Saint Severinus*. Eugyppius also wrote, according to Isidore of Seville <margin>* On Famous Men, chapter 13.</margin>, a *Rule for Monks living in the Monastery of Saint Severinus*, which he left to them at his death in place of a testament, though it is now lost. Johannes Trithemius, Cardinal Baronius, and others rashly confuse our Eugyppius with another abbot of the same name (whom we shall discuss below); as the most noble Velserus correctly observed some time ago.

---

<margin>511.</margin>
## MAGNUS FELIX ENNODIUS
An Italian by country, of Gaulish stock, and from a Ligurian home, he was born to an illustrious and proconsular family around the year 473. He himself testifies <margin>* In the account of his own affairs.</margin> that he was sixteen years old at the time when Theodoric <note>Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths</note> entered Italy; thus Philippe Labbe wandered into a dense error when he wrote that Ennodius obtained the Bishopric of Ticinum <note>Modern Pavia</note> in the year 490. At the time of Theodoric's arrival, having been deprived of the comfort of the aunt who had raised him, he repaired his loss by marrying a most noble and very wealthy maiden. Enrolled into the "sacred militia" <note>The clergy</note> by Saint Epiphanius, Bishop of Pavia, and promoted to the office of Deacon, he thereafter remained his inseparable companion in life and travels. Yet he by no means abandoned the studies of Poetry and Oratory begun in his youth; indeed, he cultivated them with such diligence that he earned a great name for himself, appearing to hold the first rank in both arts. After the death of Epiphanius, he appears to have been chosen among the Deacons of the Roman Church. Certainly in the year 503, having presented an *Apologetic Book* to the Roman Synod, he brilliantly defended the cause of Pope Symmachus and the "Palm Synod" <note>A council held in 502 to resolve accusations against Pope Symmachus</note> held the previous year against the detractors of both. He was received with such favor by the Fathers of the Synod that his Book was ordered by common decree to take a place among the Synodical Acts. In the year 511, or shortly after, he was ordained Bishop of Pavia. In the year 514 or the following year, and again in 517, he was sent by Pope Hormisdas as a legate to the Emperor Anastasius for the sake of defending the Orthodox faith. Both embassies fell through in vain due to the deceitful and insane persistence of Anastasius; nevertheless, in both, the respected virtue of Ennodius shone forth. Since he could be bent to the Emperor's will by neither threats nor promises, he was placed upon a rotting ship and—like an exile—he was not so much dismissed as sent away back to Italy with the greatest mockery. Having returned home, he survived only a few years, departing this life in the year 521, on the 17th of July <note>original: "xvi. Cal. Augusti"</note>.

---

SEVERUS, born in Pisidia <note>A region in ancient Asia Minor, in modern-day Turkey</note> and a native of Sozopolis, first applied himself to the work of a legal advocate. Having left this career after receiving holy Baptism, he lived a monastic life between Gaza and Maiuma in Palestine. But because he too greatly favored the Eutychian heresy <note>The belief that Christ had only one nature—the divine—rather than being both fully human and fully divine</note>, he was expelled from his monastery and acted as the <term>Apocrisiarius</term> <note>A representative or legate of a high-ranking cleric at the imperial court</note> for the monks of his sect in Constantinople, where he gained the favor of Emperor Anastasius. From the year 513, in the month of November, he was substituted into the place of Flavian, the Bishop of Antioch, who had been driven from his see. Having obtained the patriarchal throne, he immediately struck the Council of Chalcedon <note>The 451 AD council that defined the two natures of Christ; Severus rejected its findings</note> with anathema; and having sent synodal letters everywhere to spread his impiety, he drew in other bishops through both threats and prayers. However, Cosmas of Epiphania and Severianus of Arethusa, being bishops, not only cut themselves off from communion with him but also sent him a formal document of deposition. In the year 519, he was cast down from the see of Antioch by Emperor Justin I and withdrew to Alexandria; there he acted as the leader of the sect of the <term>Corrupticolae</term> <note>original: "Corrupticolarum"; a group that argued Christ's body was naturally subject to corruption until the resurrection</note> against the <term>Aphthartodocetae</term> <note>A group claiming Christ's body was incorruptible from the moment of the Incarnation</note>. From there he sought Constantinople, where he persuaded Anthimus, the Patriarch and a follower of the Eutychian sect, to renounce his throne. Finally, by an edict of Emperor Justinian, he was struck with anathema along with Anthimus and others, with the severest punishments established for those who preached their doctrines.

He wrote almost infinite *Letters*, including *Synodal, Enthronement, and Personal letters*. A memory of some of these remains, namely: *Letters to Soterichus, to the citizens of Antioch, to Theodosius of Alexandria, and to the August Emperors Justinian and Theodora*. Evagrius mentions these. Those which follow are cited in the Church Councils, with fragments brought forth from them: namely the *Letter to Eleusius, to Sergius the Grammarian, to Oecumenius (the first)*, and the *Treatise against John, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine* (Council Records, Vol. 6, p. 315). Also the *Second Letter to Count Oecumenius, to Paul the Heretic, to Anthimus, and to Theodosius* (Council Records, Vol. 6, p. 834-835). A fragment from the *Letter to John the Tribune* is presented in the *Catena* <note>A "chain" of scriptural interpretations by various authors</note> *on the Songs of the Old Testament* translated by Caraffa.

He also published many *Homilies and Treatises*. You can find a fragment of a public address delivered at Daphne in the Shrine of Saint Euphemia in the Council Records, Vol. 6, p. 316. Fragments of his books *Against the Grammarian* are found in the *Catena on the Songs of the Old Testament* translated into Latin by Antonio Caraffa, p. 253.

Finally, he wrote many *Commentaries* on Holy Scripture. His *Commentaries* on John, Luke, and Job are cited on almost every page in the Greek "Chains." In the aforementioned Caraffa "Chain," fragments are brought forth from his *Commentaries on the Song of Moses* (p. 245), the *Song of Hannah* (p. 249), the *Song of Habakkuk* (p. 258), the *Prayer of Isaiah* (p. 268), and the *Song of Zechariah* from Luke 2 (p. 291). In the *Chain on the Psalms* translated by Daniele Barbaro, he is cited only once, specifically on Psalm 50, p. 534. Compare these with the things we noted above regarding Severianus of Gabala.

<meta>This page transitions from the entry on Severus of Antioch (which began on the previous page) to a detailed biography and bibliography of Cassiodorus, here referred to by his family name, Bruttius. It covers his political career under the Ostrogothic kings and his later monastic retreat at Vivarium.</meta>

<header>The Eutychian Age.</header>

<margin>THE 6TH CENTURY from the Year of the Lord.</margin>
Bruttius <note>Better known to history as Cassiodorus (Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator)</note>, Roman by descent and born of an illustrious and Senatorial family, was born after the year 463. After successfully completing his literary studies and gaining a great reputation for himself through his eloquence, prudence, and the utmost gravity of character, he was appointed Governor of Sicily at the beginning of King Theodoric's reign. He suppressed the rebellious spirits of the Sicilians, who were impatient with the yoke of rule, using wisdom no less than arms. His virtue having been recognized by Theodoric, he was admitted to the inner councils around the year 490, placed in charge of drafting the royal correspondence, and effectively co-opted into the partnership of governing the realm, being showered with immense honors. First, he was made Count of Private Property, then Count of the Sacred Largesses <note>The official in charge of the imperial treasury and finances</note>; soon after, he was appointed <term>Corrector</term> <note>A high-ranking administrative governor</note> of both Sicily, Bruttium, and Lucania. Having also performed the duties of the Palatine Quaestorship, he was named Master of Offices; then he was granted the rank of Praetorian Prefect. He attained the dignity of the Patriciate before the year 500; finally, in the year 514, he was elevated to the honor of the Consulship, which he held alone that year. Having performed such great and distinguished services for Theodoric, he held the highest place in the court as long as the king lived. After Theodoric's death, he was not so much moved into as placed at the head of the supreme councils of the kingdom by King Athalaric and his mother Amalasuntha; by them, he was further honored with the Praetorian Prefecture again in the year 534. In the year 537, having been removed from office by King Witiges, he renounced secular life. Seeking a life of quiet reflection, he founded and inhabited the Monastery of Vivarium (also called the *Castellense*) near the city of Scyllacium in the furthest part of Calabria. Living in this place, he devoted himself to cultivating piety, delighted his mind with mechanical inventions and philosophical matters, collected books by ancient authors gathered from everywhere, and composed others himself. Around the year 556, he wrote the books *On Divine Readings*, certainly after the holding of the Fifth Council <note>The Second Council of Constantinople in 553 AD</note>, which he did not entirely approve of. After those, he published a book *On Orthography*, in the preface of which he testifies that he is in the ninety-third year of his age. In the year 562, he wrote the *Paschal Calculation*; it is not clear how many years he lived after completing this work. For I do not know what authority guides those who push his death as late as the year 575.

## GENUINE WRITINGS.

*Twelve Books of Various Letters*, of which the first ten contain letters written in the names of Kings Theodoric and Athalaric, and the last two contain letters written in his own name. These were published separately at *Augsburg* in 1533, and with the notes of Brosseus and Fornerius at *Lyon* in 1595, in octavo.

*The Tripartite Ecclesiastical History in Twelve Books, collected and reduced into a compendium by Cassiodorus from three Greek authors—Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret—who were translated into Latin by Epiphanius the Scholastic.* Published separately at *Basel* in 1528 and 1568, and at *Frankfurt* in 1588.

<margin>* On Latin History, Book 2, chapter 19.</margin>
*A Chronicle dedicated to King Theodoric, from Adam down to the year 519:* which Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a renowned 17th-century humanist scholar</note> rightly notes was woven together with the greatest carelessness and is a pure and simple jumble of things. Published separately with the commentaries of Joannes Cuspinianus at *Basel* in 1552, *Heidelberg* in 1588, and *Leiden* in 1632, in octavo.

*The Paschal Calculation, or a Treatise for finding Easter, the Indiction, the Epact, etc.*

*Twelve Books on the Deeds of the Goths*, which he himself mentions in the Preface to the *Various Letters*, and which Jordanes reduced into an *Epitome* <note>A summary or abridgment</note>. The *Epitome* by Jordanes survives; the more extensive work by Cassiodorus has perished.

*An Exposition or Commentary on the Psalms of David*, mostly taken from Augustine. Published separately at *Basel* in 1491 and *Paris* in 1519.

*Two Books of Institutes for Divine Readings.* Published separately at *Paris* in 1575 and *Antwerp* in 1566, in octavo.

*A Book on Orthography, compiled from twelve ancient Grammarians.* Published separately at *Hanover* in 1605 and *Antwerp* in 1579, in octavo.

*A Book on the Seven Disciplines, namely Grammar, Rhetoric, etc.*

*A Book on the Soul.* Published separately at *Paris* in 1500.

*A Book on Speech, and the Eight Parts of Speech.*

### SPURIOUS WORKS.

*An Exposition on the Song of Songs*, in which Pope Gregory is cited. It was published separately at *Freiburg in 1538.* <note>original: "Expositio in Cantica Canticorum"</note>

*A book on Figures and Tropes*, as well as certain rhetorical passages of Holy Scripture, which are found here and there in Cassiodorus’s *Commentaries on the Psalms*; this work should instead be ascribed to Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar</note>.

The *Works* of Cassiodorus appeared with the notes of Guillaume Fournier, *Paris, 1588*, and again in the same place, *1600, in 2 volumes, octavo*; with the notes of Pierre de Brosses, *Geneva, 1601, quarto; 1609, octavo; and 1650, quarto.* Finally, Jean Garet, a Benedictine monk, collected, reviewed, corrected, and illustrated all the works of Cassiodorus with notes and dissertations, publishing them arranged in two volumes at *Rouen, 1679, folio.* They are also found (excluding the *Tripartite History* and the *Commentaries on the Psalms and the Song of Songs*) in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 11, page 1094.*

<margin>514.</margin>

## HORMISDAS,

A native of Campania, from the city of Frosinone, son of Justus, a Deacon of the Roman Church, and Bishop from April 13, 514. Having attained the Pontificate, he immediately entered into a plan for repairing the concord between the Western and Eastern Church; he acted with all his might in the matter through various letters to the Emperor Anastasius and the Eastern Bishops; he, in turn, was sought after by Anastasius and the Easterners with various schemes. However, on both sides, the matter lacked a result. Both preserved their previous state, whether it was constancy or unyielding stubbornness. Anastasius and the Easterners wanted to enter into communion with no change made and no guarantee applied. Hormisdas, on the contrary, wanted the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and the Letter of Pope Leo to Flavian of Constantinople to be approved by Imperial edict and the signature of the Bishops; he also wanted the names of Acacius, Euphemius, Macedonius, and others devoted to their cause to be struck from the <term>Diptychs</term> <note>The official lists of names read during the liturgy; to be removed from the diptychs was a form of posthumous excommunication</note>. The Easterners bore such harsh and unfair laws with difficulty. Nevertheless, Hormisdas, enticed by the vain hope of reconciling peace, sent Ennodius, Bishop of Pavia, along with certain others as legates to Emperor Anastasius in the year 515 and again in 517. But he labored in vain. The conditions of peace were rejected, and the legates were dismissed with the greatest insult. Finally, after Anastasius was removed from human affairs and Justin—who favored the Orthodox faith—was raised to the empire, Hormisdas prepared a third legation to the Easterners. Therefore, in the year 519, having sent Germanus, Bishop of Capua, he obtained without difficulty from the Catholic Emperor the confirmation of the Synod of Chalcedon; however, he did not so easily obtain that the names of Acacius and others be removed from the Diptychs. Yet, he did obtain it. The Emperor granted this for the sake of peace, so that the long-standing schism might finally be put to rest at last. Hormisdas died on April 30, 523. There exist 80 *Letters* and certain *Decrees* in the *Collection of Councils, Volume 4*; of these, the first to Remigius of Reims, in which he delegates his duties to be performed in Gaul, is clearly spurious; for in it, Hormisdas [mentions] King Clovis having been recently baptized by Remigius <note>Clovis died in 511, before Hormisdas became Pope, making the letter historically impossible</note>

**ORENTIUS**, of Spanish origin, from a home in Tarragona and Bishop of Elvira <note>original: "Eliberitanus"</note>, flourished in the year 516, at which time he attended and signed the acts of the Synod of Tarragona. He wrote a *Commonitorium* <note>A book of reminders or admonitions</note> for the faithful in heroic meter, intended to *soothe the reader with sweet brevity*, as Sigebert <note>Sigebert of Gembloux, a medieval chronicler</note> records. This *Commonitorium* survives, edited with notes by Martin Delrio in Antwerp, 1600; likewise with notes in Salamanca, 1644, in quarto; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 875.

---

<margin>517.</margin>
**JOHN**, a Cappadocian by birth, was made Patriarch of Constantinople in the year 517. In 518, after the death of Anastasius and the elevation of Justin to the empire, he was compelled—though not unwillingly—by the Catholic commoners rioting in the Great Church <note>The Hagia Sophia</note> to anathematize <note>Formally curse or excommunicate</note> Severus of Antioch. He was also forced to insert the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon into the Diptychs <note>term: Diptychs <gloss>Ecclesiastical tablets or lists where the names of those to be commemorated during the liturgy were inscribed</gloss></note> with a solemn commemoration, and to restore the names of Euphemius and Macedonius to the same. Soon, in the month of July, a Synod of forty bishops was held at Constantinople, which the people had extorted through violent prayers, and he sanctioned these actions with legitimate decrees. In the year 519, at the persuasion and almost the command of the Emperor Justin, he prepared himself to repair the union with the Roman Church. Embracing the conditions offered by Hormisdas, he anathematized the detractors of the Council of Chalcedon and removed the names of Acacius, Euphemius, and Macedonius from the Diptychs, replacing them with the names of Pope Leo and Hormisdas. For this reason, Hormisdas sent him letters of congratulation that same year and exhorted him to procure peace for the churches of Alexandria and Antioch. Three *Letters to Hormisdas* survive in Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, pages 1486, 1491, and 1521. There are two other *very brief letters*, one *to John of Jerusalem* and the other *to Epiphanius, Bishop of Tyre*, in Greek and Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 5, page 185.

* Supplement, chapter 427.
† Book 3, On Images.
</margin>
**THEODORE**, whose place of origin is not entirely clear. There are those who argue he was a Paphlagonian, though these arguments are not strong enough to command assent. He was a Lector <note>A "Reader," a minor clerical rank</note> of the Great Church of Constantinople and flourished around the year 518. Indeed, who can keep from laughing when reading the following in Aubertus Miræus? *Theodore the Reader lived around the year 1320. He adds that he wrote* a *Collection of Ecclesiastical History* excerpted from the mouth of Nicephorus Callistus. He who could write such things must be dreaming—no, he must be snoring—heedless of both his own reputation and the truth! <note>The author is mocking Miræus for a 1,000-year chronological error; Theodore lived in the 500s, not the 1300s</note>. Our Theodore compiled from Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret a *Three-Part History* <note>original: "Historiam Tripartitam"</note> comprised of two books, reaching from the twentieth year of Constantine to the reign of Julian. This History also exists in a Greek manuscript in the Venetian Library of St. Mark. Leo Allatius also possessed a copy, from which Henri Valois took his variant readings of the histories of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret. To this work, Theodore later added two other books of *Ecclesiastical History*, written by his own effort <note>original: "proprio Marte"</note>, from the time where Socrates left off until the beginning of the reign of Justin the Elder, namely to the year 518. For this reason, John of Damascus cites the fourth book of his Ecclesiastical History. From these latter books, Nicephorus Callistus excerpted very extensive collections, which are the only parts that survive to us today. They are available in Greek along with the other Greek Ecclesiastical historians...

...of the Church, edited by Robert Estienne, *Paris* 1544; in Greek and Latin, *Geneva* 1612; with the version and notes of Henri Valois, *Paris* 1673.
