520.
Photius, Code 160
* Code 160, 206.
</margin>
**PROCOPIUS OF GAZA**, named after the city in which he lived, a Sophist <note>A professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy</note> by profession, flourished around the year 520, during the reign of Emperor Justin I and thereafter. He was the teacher of Choricius of Gaza, the Sophist, who flourished during the reign of Justinian and whom Procopius saw as the successor to his school in his old age. Regarding him, Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and renowned scholar</note> says thus *: "Of this man, many and varied discourses are in circulation, a thing worthy of zeal and imitation." <margin>decorum</margin> "Their decorum <note>original: "prepeia"</note> is practiced to the highest degree, even if it possesses a style somewhat more elegant than is usual for an explanatory treatise." Many books of his, of various learning, are in circulation, worthy of reading and imitation. — His diction is most excellently refined, but somewhat more elegant than befits the simpler form of a commentary.

-> W O R K S. <-

<margin>
* Code 206.
notes
</margin>
**Commentaries** or (to use the words of Photius *, who praises them highly) *notes* <note>original: "hypomnemata"</note> on the *Octateuch* <note>The first eight books of the Bible</note> or rather the *Heptateuch* <note>The first seven books of the Bible</note>, excerpted with the greatest judgment from the writings and commentaries of the Orthodox Fathers, and woven together with the utmost elegance. They exist only in Latin, printed in *Zurich*, 1555, with Conrad Clauser <note>original: "Conrado Clusero"</note> as translator.

Scholia <note>Brief explanatory notes</note> on the four books of Kings and the two books of Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomenon"</note>. They exist in Greek and Latin, edited by Joannes Meursius, *Leiden*, 1620, in quarto.

<margin>* Code 207.</margin>
*A Summary of Various Commentaries on the Prophet Isaiah*, praised by Photius *, and edited in Greek and Latin by Jean de Courcelles <note>original: "Joanne Curterio"</note>, *Paris*, 1580.

A Commentary on Proverbs is cited by Turrianus in *Defense of the Papal Epistles*, book 4, chapters 6 and 17. Jean de Courcelles mentions commentaries on *Proverbs* and the *Song of Songs* in his preface to Isaiah, but perhaps they still lie hidden in manuscript form.

Some letters of Procopius the Sophist to his brother Philip, Jerome, Macarius, Sozomen, Pancratius, Castor, Zacharias, Bishop Elias, etc., which are very elegant, were printed by Aldus in a volume of Greek Epistles. Whether they should be ascribed to Procopius of Gaza or Procopius of Caesarea cannot be determined with certainty, as the title of "Sophist" fits both. However, more than one reason suggests they belong to the Gazan.

*Paraphrases of Homeric Verses transformed into various styles of speech*, which Photius mentions and praises in Code 160, and which we grieve to have lost.

<margin>520.</margin>
**EPIPHANIUS**, Priest of the Church of Constantinople and Syncellus <note>A confidential secretary or advisor to a Patriarch</note> of Patriarch John. In the year 519, he was sent to Thessaloniki along with Count Licinius and the legates of Pope Hormisdas so that, having held a Synod of Bishops, he might pass judgment in the name of his Patriarch concerning the case of Bishop Dorotheus of Thessaloniki, who had driven from their sees the suffragan bishops who were fleeing communion with him. In the year 520, upon the death of John, he was elevated to the throne of Constantinople. Having immediately held a Synod of Bishops, he ratified by his own authority the peace entered into between Hormisdas and his predecessor, and confirmed the Council of Chalcedon. He died in the year 535. There exist *Five Letters to Pope Hormisdas* written by him, in Latin, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, pages 1535, 1537, 1545, 1555.

<margin>520.</margin>
**PETER**, Greek by birth, or at least Asian, a Deacon by rank. In the year 520, he joined the legates of the Scythian Monks <note>A group of monks from modern-day Romania/Ukraine who were active in theological debates in Rome</note> who had set out from the East for Rome, and he supported the cause of the Monks with the greatest zeal of spirit. To secure greater authority for this cause from the support of great men, in the same year while staying in Rome, he wrote a book *On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ* addressed to Fulgentius and the other Catholic bishops exiled in Sardinia, in his own name and that of his companions. In this work, he brought to light the orthodox faith of the Scythian Monks, confirmed it with arguments, and sought out the opinion of the African bishops regarding those controversies. This book exists among the *Works of Fulgentius*, usually placed before Fulgentius's *Response*, and in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 1241, and the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 9. See more under Maxentius.

<meta>This page continues the chronological catalogue of ecclesiastical writers during the 6th century, specifically the year 520. It follows the entry for Procopius of Gaza and maintains the focus on theological controversies surrounding the Council of Chalcedon and the nature of Christ.</meta>

<header>The Eutychian Age.</header>

<margin>6TH CENTURY from the Year of Our Lord 520.</margin>
<margin>Code 36.</margin>
The **ANONYMOUS** Author of certain Christian books mentioned by Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople whose "Bibliotheca" or "Code" summarizes hundreds of works now lost to history</note> in Code 36 flourished around the year 520. He dedicated his first six books to a certain Pamphilus, who flourished under the Emperor Justin I. This work was nothing other than an *Exposition of the Octateuch* <note>The first eight books of the Old Testament</note> distributed into twelve books, and it was filled with the most trivial nonsense and absurd dogmas. As a sample of these: he claimed that neither heaven nor earth consists of a spherical shape, but that the earth is longer in one direction and joined at its extremities with the boundaries of heaven, and that the heaven serves as a vault <note>or arch</note> for the earth. He further claimed that the stars are moved by attending Angels; and that Christ, ascending from the earth, took up his seat between the heaven and the firmament, and that the kingdom of heaven is located only there. This work has perished; Photius preserved only certain very brief excerpts in the place cited. The same author illustrated the *Song of Songs* with a *Commentary*, of which not the smallest scrap survives.

---

<margin>520;</margin>
**POSSESSOR**, a Bishop in Africa—though of which city is uncertain—was driven out by the Arians <note>A heretical sect that denied the full divinity of Christ, which was dominant among the Vandal rulers of North Africa at this time</note> and traveled to Constantinople. By constantly fighting against heretics, he greatly strengthened the Catholic faith and flourished in the year 520. There exists a Letter of his written from Constantinople to Pope Hormisdas, in which he consults the Pontiff regarding the dogmas of Faustus of Riez concerning grace and free will. It is held together with the response of Hormisdas in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 1529; although there is no shortage of men of no small rank among the followers of Jansenius <note>Jansenists, a 17th-century theological movement often in conflict with Papal authority</note> who do not hesitate to strip Hormisdas of the authorship of that responding Letter.

---

<margin>520.</margin>
**JOHN MAXENTIUS**, a Scythian by birth, as they say, and also a Monk and Priest of Antioch; there are those who contend that he is the same person as John of Antioch, whom Gennadius discusses in chapter 93. There was also, according to the testimony of Sophronius of Jerusalem <margin>* Code 231.</margin> in Photius *, a certain John, Bishop of Scythopolis <note>A city in modern-day Israel, then part of the province of Palestine</note>, who wrote learnedly and piously concerning the Council of Chalcedon; it is well established that our John produced a similar work. Whether Sophronius intended to designate our John, I would not dare to affirm with certainty. Nevertheless, our author is commonly called "the Scythopolitan" <margin>† Code 95.</margin> both here and elsewhere by Photius †. He flourished in the year 520. In that year—or at least shortly before—a controversy arose between certain Scythian monks (among whose number was Maxentius, appearing to be their Archimandrite <note>The superior or abbot of a monastery</note>) and a certain Deacon named Victor concerning that manner of speaking: *One of the Trinity was crucified for us*. The monks deemed this phrase to be pious and Orthodox, while Victor argued the opposite. Furthermore, a rumor spread in the East regarding the books of Bishop Faustus of Gaul <note>Faustus of Riez</note>, which were clearly teaching Pelagianism <note>A heresy that overemphasized human free will at the expense of divine grace</note>. The monks sent four chosen men from their group—including Maxentius, if we trust Baronius—from Antioch to Constantinople to see Germanus of Capua and other papal legates then acting there. Their goal was to ensure that Faustus’s books were condemned and that their own opinion concerning "One of the Trinity being crucified" was confirmed by the legates. The papal legates refused both requests; indeed, they openly condemned the opinion of the Scythians. Therefore, proceeding to Rome, the monkish legates went to Pope Hormisdas. However, having been informed by his legates and by the African Possessor through letters, the Pope ratified the decision of his legates. Having given a letter to Possessor, he condemned the opinion of the monks as heretical and a "wicked seed of the devil," and expelled their legates from the city. To avoid failing their own cause, the monks published twelve anathemas <note>Formal curses or excommunications</note> opposed to the Nestorian heresy <note>The belief that Christ had two distinct persons, human and divine</note>, for which Hormisdas’s judgment had certainly paved too wide a path. Moreover, John Maxentius defended the Scythian opinion by writing an *Apology*, and he sharply refuted Hormisdas’s letter to Possessor, openly crying out that the author of that letter—whether it was Hormisdas (for he wished to seem to doubt it) or someone else—was a heretic and an enemy of Catholic truth. For this reason, Maxentius is treated poorly by Papal writers; nevertheless, the illustrious Forbes, in his *Historico-Theological Instructions*, book 3, chapter 21, vindicates him extensively and learnedly against the calumnies of Baronius, Binius, and others. Regarding his style, Photius * says: <margin>* Code 95.</margin> <note>original: "Ἔστι δὲ ἡ λόγον σαφὴς τε καὶ καθαρός..."</note> "His style of speech is both clear and pure, using words appropriate for a historical writer; moreover, he fights against heresy with no little strength, and makes sufficient use of scriptural testimonies, etc."

# EXTANT WORKS.

Letter to the Legates of the Roman Pontiff serving in Constantinople. <note>original: "Epistola ad Legatos Pontificis Romani Constantinopoli agentes"</note>
A Catholic profession concerning Christ in the confession of faith.
Twelve Chapters or Anathemas against the Nestorians <note>Followers of Nestorius, who emphasized the distinction between Christ’s human and divine natures to a degree the Church found heretical</note>.
Another shorter profession of faith.
The account of the union of the Word of God with His own flesh.
An Apologetic Response to the Letter of Hormisdas <note>Pope Hormisdas, reigned 514–523</note>.
A short book against the Acephali <note>A radical sect of Monophysites "without a head" or leader</note>.
Two books of Dialogues against the Nestorians, addressed to Theophilus.
All these short works are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 9, page 533.
*Scholia <note>Explanatory comments or annotations</note> on the Works of Dionysius the Areopagite*, concerning which the famous Ussher <note>James Ussher, 17th-century Archbishop and scholar</note> has this to say in his *Theological Library manuscript*: “John of Scythopolis wrote scholia on Dionysius the Areopagite, just as Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor</note> did. However, in the books of Dionysius published from the year 1561 inclusive, the Scholia of John and Maximus have been confused together. These were distinct not only in the older editions, which were circulated around the time of Cyparissiotes <note>A 14th-century Byzantine theologian</note>, but also in both manuscripts used by Morellius <note>Guillaume Morel, a 16th-century French printer</note> himself. In one of these, the Scholia (of John of Scythopolis) were placed in the margin without a name; in the other, however, the Scholia were marked separately (after the complete text of Dionysius was finished) under the name of Maximus. These were shorter because they had been separated from the more extensive notes of John, with which Morellius had joined them. Furthermore, those common Scholia of the Scythopolitan are the very same ones attributed by others to Dionysius of Alexandria; this is evident from a passage cited by Cyparissiotes from the Scholia of Dionysius, which is found word-for-word in those Scholia. That this passage belongs to the Scythopolitan, and not to Maximus, is clear from the Latin version of the Scholia of the Scythopolitan made by Robert, Bishop of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste, the famous 13th-century scholar</note>, which is preserved in a manuscript in the Library of Corpus Christi College at Oxford. Thus far Ussher.” Whether the author of these Scholia was our Maxentius, or John, Bishop of Scythopolis, whom we mentioned above—if indeed he was distinct from Maxentius—or a certain John of Scythopolis who was younger than both, we do not decide in the least: let the Learned judge.

# LOST WORKS.

Twelve books *Against the deserters of the Church, or against Eutyches, Dioscorus, and the followers of the same sect*, written at the request of a certain Archbishop Julian and praised by Photius in Code 95. A fairly large fragment taken from Book 8 is found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 6, page 830.
*A letter written in his own name and that of Deacon Venerius to Fulgentius and the other African bishops exiled in Sardinia*, in which he sought their opinion on Predestination and Grace; to which the African bishops replied with a synodal letter (found among the works of Fulgentius), and Fulgentius himself replied with three published books.

520.
</margin>

**TRIFOLIUS**, a Priest by rank—but of what place, who can guess? He flourished in the year 520. Faustus, a Roman Senator and Praetorian Prefect, had asked him whether anything could be found in the writings of the Fathers concerning the doctrine of the Scythian Monks. Trifolius replied to Faustus through a Letter; in which he argues from the decrees of the four General Councils against John the Scythian and his Monks, who had recently arrived in Rome. This Letter, though mutilated at the end, was retrieved from the papers of Sirmond by Labbe, and published in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 1590.

**JOHN**, a Tuscan by nation, son of Constantius, succeeded Hormisdas in the Roman See on the 7th of May, 523. In the year 525, having been summoned to Ravenna by King Theodoric, he was sent as an unwilling legate to the Emperor Justin, so that he might preserve by his prayers the churches for the Arians <note>Theodoric was an Arian, while the Emperor was a staunch Catholic; this was a period of high tension between the two</note>, which Justin intended to take away from them. 6TH CENTURY from the Year of Our Lord 518.
* Book 7, chapter 9.
</margin>
While in Constantinople, acting alongside Patriarch Epiphanius (whom Nicephorus* wrongly calls Euphemius <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine historian</note>), he refused to sit beside him in the Great Church. Instead, he demanded a more sublime throne be erected for himself above the seat of Epiphanius; concerning this, see what we noted above in the observations on the *Dorothean Fragment*. Having failed to achieve his business with the Emperor, he returned to Rome, was taken to Ravenna by Theodoric <note>Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths</note>, and was placed in custody. He died in prison on May 18th in the year 526. Two *Letters* survive (Volume 4 of the *Councils*, page 1603), but the most recent editors of the Councils admit these are forged, despite what Binnius <note>Severin Binius, a compiler of ecclesiastical records</note> imagines.

<margin>526.</margin>
EPHRÆMIUS <note>Ephrem of Antioch, Patriarch from 527–545</note>, a Syrian by birth, after holding other secular offices, was appointed Count of the East by the Emperor Justin. In the year 525, when Antioch was nearly destroyed by fires and a massive earthquake, and Bishop Euphrasius was buried under the ruins of the buildings, Ephræmius relieved the needs of the wretched common people with the greatest diligence and piety. Consequently, the citizens of Antioch sought him as Euphrasius's successor. In the following year, he was ordained Patriarch of Antioch and administered the office entrusted to him with remarkable piety and invincible constancy against heretics. In the year 546, at the request of the Emperor Justinian—though he resisted for some time—he condemned the *Three Chapters* <note>The Three Chapters were a series of writings by three bishops that Justinian condemned to appease the Monophysites, sparking a major schism</note>. This occurred, says Facundus of Hermiane <note>A 6th-century North African bishop who defended the Three Chapters</note>, who was then present in Constantinople, *after he was told he would be excluded unless he did so; he was found to be a lover of his own honor rather than the truth.* He did not long survive his signature, for he appears to have died that same year.
<margin>* Book 4, chapter 4.</margin>

->He wrote many works, which follow:<-

<margin>228, 229.</margin>
*Three Books* in defense of Church dogmas and the Council of Chalcedon <note>The Council of 451 AD which defined Christ as having two natures, divine and human</note>. Photius <note>The 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note> describes the first two at length and provides very ample excerpts from them in his *Bibliotheca* (Codices 228 and 229). He is entirely silent regarding the third. Of the earlier books, the
First contained: 1. *A long letter to Zenobius the Scholar of Emesa, who was infected with the heresy of the Acephali <note>A radical splinter group of the Monophysites "without a head" or leader</note>, regarding the authority of the Council of Chalcedon, Pope Leo's Letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the clause added to the Trisagion <note>The "Thrice-Holy" hymn; the addition was "who was crucified for us"</note> by the Fuller and thereafter used in the Eastern Churches, and on the two natures in Christ.* 2. *Three letters to the Emperor Justinian.* 3. *A letter to Anthimus, Bishop of Constantinople.* 4. *A letter to Domitian.* 5. *A letter to Syncleticus of Tarsus against the dogmas of the Acephali.* 6. *A letter to Anthimus, while he was still Bishop of Trebizond.* 7. *A letter to Brasem the Persian on various theological dogmas.* 8. *A letter to certain schismatic monks.* 9. *A letter to the deserters of Callinicus.* 10. *Acts of the Synod held by Ephræmius regarding the case of Syncleticus, Bishop of Tarsus.* 11. *A letter to Magnus, Bishop of Beroea, on the two natures in Christ.* 12. *A letter to the monk Eunoius on corruption and incorruption.* 13. *Six panegyric orations for as many feast days celebrated in the Church.* 14. *Two catechetical orations for the newly baptized.*

The second book contained: 1. *An apology for Cyril’s letter to Succensus, which the heretics were accustomed to use for their own slanders.* 2. *A response to the questions of Anatolius the Scholar, regarding Christ as known even now in the flesh; how Adam, if he was created as a composite being, could have been immortal; regarding John the Evangelist still surviving; how, if Adam was known to be immortal, he was ignorant of what was useful, and what that saying means: "Adam has become like one of us."* 3. *A book to the Cilician monks John and Domnus regarding the Council of Chalcedon, the two natures in Christ, and the opinion of Cyril.* 4. *To the monks of the East infected with the heresy of the Theopaschites <note>Heretics who claimed that God suffered on the Cross</note>.*

<margin>526.</margin>
FELIX <note>Pope Felix IV, reigned 526–530</note>, of the Samnite nation, son of Castorius. After Pope John died in prison, he was named as successor by King Theodoric and was thus placed in the Pontifical seat on July 12th, 526. Everyone acknowledges that he was a man of the highest character among the Roman clergy; the only fault found with him is that he was elected by Theodoric. To see what mournful and tragic outcries Baronius <note>Cardinal Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century church historian</note> pours out against Theodoric on this occasion, see his *Annals* for the year 526. Felix died on September 25th in the year 530. *Three letters* survive in Volume 4 of the *Councils*, page 1650.

...of which the first two are admitted to be spurious by Labbe <note>Philippe Labbe (1607–1667), a Jesuit editor of the "Collection of Councils"</note> himself, and after him by Papebroch <note>Daniel Papebroch (1628–1714), a Bollandist hagiographer</note>; indeed, the facts themselves cry out that this is so.

**SIMEON**, called **the Stylite** <note>From the Greek "stylos," meaning pillar; a type of ascetic who lived on top of a column</note> from his dwelling, **the Younger** due to the age in which he lived, and finally **Thaumastoria** (that is, *the one on the Marvelous Mountain* <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐν τῷ θαυμαστῷ ὄρει</note>) from his way of life; a Syrian by birth, he followed the monastic life from his tenderest years. They say that even as a boy he was distinguished by miracles. Certainly while still a boy—before he had even changed his teeth, or could distinguish a leopard from a cat—he was received onto his pillar located near Antioch in the year 527, chosen as a companion in life by a certain most holy old hermit. From that time on, Simeon spent his life partly on that pillar and partly on another positioned on the peak of a nearby mountain, devoting himself to prayers, vigils, and the most severe rules of hermit-like **ascetic practice** <note>original Greek: ἀσκήσεως (askeseos)</note>. He was a most bitter enemy of the Eutychians and Nestorians <note>Two major heretical groups of the time: Eutychians believed Christ had only one nature; Nestorians emphasized the distinction between His human and divine natures</note>, whom he hated more than a snake or a dog. Writers tell marvelous things about him. <margin>Ibid. & book 5, ch. 21.</margin> Evagrius <note>Evagrius Scholasticus, a 6th-century church historian</note>, to whom he was very well known, writes that it was **possible** <note>original Greek: οἷόν τε (hoion te)</note> for him to put demons to flight, heal diseases, search the innermost thoughts of men, and predict the future; he presents himself, for the most part, as an eyewitness. Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus, 14th-century historian</note> (book 18, ch. 14) relates the same miracles after Evagrius. Truly, many more things were invented by Arcadius, Archbishop of Cyprus, who wrote a very long *Life* of Simeon, which was cited in the **Second Council of Nicaea** <margin>* Act 4. † Oration 3 on Images.</margin> and by John of Damascus. Simeon died in the year 595, after he had spent 68 years on his pillar. He wrote several *Letters*. The fifth, addressed to the Emperor Justin, is cited and presented in full in Greek and Latin by the Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea (Action 5, Councils, Volume 7, page 349). However, Charlemagne and the Fathers of the Frankfurt Council <margin>* On not worshipping images, book 4, ch. 5. † Dissertation on the writings of the Simeons, p. 20. || Code 231.</margin> formerly suspected it to be spurious and strove to prove it with many arguments. Pope Hadrian formerly defended it for Simeon, and recently Leo Allatius <note>A 17th-century Greek-Catholic scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note> did the same. Sophronius of Jerusalem mentions a *Letter* of Simeon to the Emperor Justinian against the Eutychians and Nestorians in Photius's *Library*. A fragment of the same regarding *Images* is provided by Damascus in his *Third Oration on Images*, page 789. Finally, Leo Allatius mentions various unpublished treatises of his preserved in the Vatican Library and elsewhere, namely: 1. *Short Hymns for Saint Demetrius the Martyr.* 2. *An Oration or prayer to the Son for repelling disturbing thoughts.* 3. *An Oration to Christ to be recited when thoughts of fornication arise.* 4. *An Oration to the Holy Mother of God against evil thoughts*; the title itself proclaims this last one to be the product of a more recent age.

***

<margin>
527.
</margin>
**FLAVIUS JUSTINIANUS**, an Illyrian by birth, son of Sabbatius and Vigilantia (Bigliniza), was born at Tauresium (today Ohrid in Dardania) in the year 483. His uncle was the Emperor Justin I, by whom he was educated with the greatest care in the fortress of Bederiana and adopted as a son. Before he was Emperor, he married **Theodora**, a Cypriot by birth, a woman of insolent character and desperately devoted to the Eutychian heresy. In the year 519, he was made Master of Soldiers by the Emperor Justin; sent to the East with an army, he conducted the campaign against the Persians successfully. In 521, he held the Consulship; soon after he became a Patrician, then Most Noble, and finally on April 1st, 527, he was declared Augustus, and thereafter held sole power with his uncle. In 528, he promulgated an edict by which he decreed that Nestorians and Eutychians, as heretics, were to be punished with civil penalties; he renewed this five years later. In 541, he personally condemned Origen <note>An early Christian theologian whose speculative views on the soul and universal salvation became controversial</note> by edict, and after a Synod was held in Constantinople under Menas, he ensured that Origen and his followers were struck with anathema. In 545, having published a constitution, he condemned the **Three Chapters** <note>A complex theological dispute involving the condemnation of three 5th-century writers suspected of Nestorianism</note>; the Synod of Constantinople did the same at the end of the following year. In 553, he called for an Ecumenical Council to be held at Constantinople, in which he demanded and obtained from the Fathers the condemnation of the Three Chapters. <margin>Evagrius, book 4, ch. 39.</margin> In 563, as his mental strength failed along with his body, he was deceived by certain heretics and established an edict in which he taught that the body of Christ, in the same way both before and after the resurrection, was free from corruption and natural passions <note>This controversial view is known as Aphthartodocetism</note>; he commanded that all Bishops subscribe to his opinion. He most severely afflicted the Eastern Bishops who appealed to the opinion of Anastasius of Antioch; indeed, he drove Anastasius himself and Eutychius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, from their sees because they constantly resisted him, and sent them into exile to be **deported**...

...he ordered them to be deported. Intent on such follies, he was removed from human affairs <note>meaning he died</note> in the year 565, on the 14th of November, full of days, glory, and triumphs. There were not lacking in the past, nor are there lacking today, those who unload whole wagonloads of slanders and insults upon this most sacred prince—a man no less distinguished by learning and piety than by power and the glory of his deeds. Truly, no one ever raged against the most august remains of Justinian with a more unjust judgment and a shamelessness far below the status of a supreme prince than Cardinal Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a Catholic historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici"</note>, straining every nerve of his eloquence in this task to present the Emperor to us not as a man, but as a devil. To prove this, I will place some of his words before the reader's eyes.

<margin>
Annals for the year 551, no. 3, 4, 528, no. 20, 553, no. 21.
</margin>
> *He was,* he says, *a man entirely illiterate; so much so that he had never even learned the alphabet. A sacrilegious Emperor, who stirred up no light persecution; seized by madness, moved from his mind, seized by a malignant spirit, driven by Satan, and one who dissolved all order in the Church, and made the kingdom of heaven into a dungeon of hell.*

I would be endless if I ran through everything. It is not my intention, after Guinetus, Giphanius, Trivorius, our own Rivius, and others, to undertake the defense of the excellent prince. Concerning the distinguished virtues of Justinian, I will bring forward one or two testimonies of the Ancients. Regarding his learning and piety, Procopius <note>Procopius of Caesarea, a prominent 6th-century historian</note> wrote the following, while he was still fair toward Justinian:
<margin>
* On the Gothic Wars, book 3; on the Buildings of Justinian, book 1.
</margin>
> *He was accustomed both to pore over books dealing with divine matters himself, and to draw out conversations about them with Bishops and Priests late into the night: it was always his habit, many weeks before Easter, to macerate his body with vigils and fastings more than ascetic <note>original: "plusquam asceticis"</note>, to take food once every two days, and to completely abstain from wine, bread, and other foodstuffs, content only with herbs seasoned with salt and vinegar, and with water.*

Regarding his outstanding zeal for the Catholic faith, let us hear Pope Agatho <note>Pope from 678–681 AD</note> bearing witness from a Synod of 125 Bishops:
> *And before all,* he says, *the imitator of the true Apostolic faith, Justinian Augustus of pious memory, whose rectitude of faith, just as much as it pleased God for its sincere confession, so much did it exalt the Christian republic: and even now his religious memory is judged worthy of veneration by all nations: the rectitude of whose faith is praised throughout the whole world through his most august edicts.*

### WORKS.

Besides the **Body of Civil Law** <term>Corpus Juris Civilis; the fundamental collection of Roman law</term> (namely, the four books of the *Institutes*, the fifty books of the *Pandects* or *Digests*, and the twelve books of the *Code* (into which many things concerning Religion are mixed)), which, using Tribonian and other assistants, he began to establish in the year 528 and brought to a conclusion in 535: and the *Novels* <note>New laws issued after the Code</note> published after the year 535, many of which concern the Ecclesiastical court, printed separately in Greek by Haloander in Paris, 1553, in octavo; by Schringer in the same place, 1558, in Greek and Latin; and in Antwerp, 1575. Justinian wrote very many things regarding Ecclesiastical matters, of which the following survive today:

**Constitution against Anthimus, Severus, Peter, and Zoara**, made in the year 536; which, taken from the *Novels*, is found in Greek and Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume V, page 264.

**Letter to the Fathers of the 5th General Council**, written in the year 553: it exists in Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume V, page 419.

**Treatise or Edict against Origen**, and his errors, sent to Menas, Patriarch of Constantinople, in the year 541: it exists in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume V, page 635.

**Letter to the Synod of Constantinople**, held by Menas in the year 541 against Origen and his followers: it is found in Greek and Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume V, page 679.

**Confession of the Right Faith** (or the *Edict against the Three Chapters* <note>The "Three Chapters" were a series of writings condemned during a major 6th-century theological controversy</note>), written in the year 545: it exists in Greek and Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume V, page 684.

**Letter to the Fathers of the Synod of Constantinople**, held in the year 546 against the Three Chapters: it exists in Greek and Latin in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume V, page 724.

If Justinian used the advice and industry of his theologians in arranging these writings, it should seem neither new nor strange to anyone: nor for that reason should he be said any less to have written these by his own effort <note>original: "proprio Marte," a Latin idiom meaning "by one's own skill/strength"</note>.

AGAPETUS, a Deacon of the Great Church of Constantinople, flourished in the year 527. At that time, he wrote to Justinian, who had recently been adorned with the purple <note>meaning he had just been crowned Emperor</note>, his *Admonitions* on how one ought to conduct oneself in power. These are truly golden instructions, worthy of a supreme prince, and contain *72 exhortatory chapters.* They exist in Greek and Latin, published in *Venice, 1509, in octavo; Basel, 1518, in octavo;* by Matthæus Martinius at *Herborn, 1603, in octavo;* with the notes of Stephanus Schoningius at *Franeker, 1608, in octavo; Frankfurt, 1659, in quarto; Leipzig, 1669, in octavo;* in the *Orthodoxographa* page 180; and in the Supplement to the *Library of the Fathers* by Ducæus, Volume 2, page 362.

PROCOPIUS, a Palestinian by birth from the house of Caesarea, was by profession a Rhetorician and Sophist <note>a teacher of rhetoric and philosophy</note>, and finally a Senator of Constantinople. In the year 527, when Belisarius was made commander of the army by Emperor Justin, Procopius was assigned to him as a companion, secretary, and counselor. In the year 533, he followed Belisarius to Africa to defeat the Vandals; during the journey, he was sent to Syracuse and successfully fulfilled his orders. Left in Africa by Belisarius to settle affairs after the victory, he returned to him in Sicily in 536 due to a mutiny of the soldiers. In that same year, he accompanied him to Italy as he moved his arms against the Goths, to the point that he was entrusted with the care of the <term>annona</term> <note>the grain supply and military provisions</note>. Before the year 542, he returned to Constantinople with Belisarius, where he seems to have spent the remainder of his life. He was still among the living in the year 562, at which time he had not yet finished the *Secret History*. Several things in his works seem to show a spirit less than favorable to the Christian faith and far more partial to Paganism; so much so that there are those who stubbornly contend that he was imbued with the superstition of the Gentiles <note>Paganism</note>. See, among others, Joannes Eichelius in his Preface to Procopius’s *Anecdota*, numbers 17 to 22, where he argues this point using many passages from Procopius’s own writings. On the other hand, not a few things suggest that Procopius did not at all abhor Christian worship, at least in appearance—especially what he writes in *The Buildings of Justinian* book 5, chapter 7; *The Persian War* book 1, chapter 25, and book 2, chapter 12; *The Vandal War* book 1, chapter 21, and elsewhere. Certainly, as far as can be seen from his writings, it seems to me not unlikely that Procopius was neither entirely a Pagan nor entirely a Christian. With the Pagans, he believed the Christian religion was not the true and only one; with the Christians, he held the rites and superstitions of the Pagans up to ridicule; with both, he acknowledged a supreme deity as the founder of heaven and earth. Whatever the case may be, he was at least a Christian by profession and name; and so that he might more easily win the favor of Justinian, he outwardly displayed Christian worship regardless of what he cherished secretly in his heart. For this reason, we have given him his place here among the Ecclesiastical Writers. He wrote <margin>* Book 4, chapter 12.</margin> "most industriously, elegantly, and eloquently," as Evagrius says <note>original Greek: "φιλοπονώτατα κομψῶς τε κ) λογίως"</note>, the various books of Histories which follow:

*On the Persian War*, in two books, encompassing the history of the deeds between the Romans and Persians from the year 407 to 549.

*On the Vandal War*, in two books, presenting the history of the deeds between the Romans and Vandals in Africa from the year 395 to 545.

*On the Gothic War*, in four books, narrating the military matters conducted by the Emperors of Constantinople against the Goths in Italy from the year 487 to 554. Hugo Grotius published these together with the books on the *Vandal War*, expanded from manuscripts and translated into Latin by himself, at *Amsterdam, 1655, in octavo.*

These eight books were published in Latin at *Basel, 1531 and 1566, in folio;* and in Greek, edited by David Hoeschel, at *Augsburg, 1607, in folio.*

The *Anecdota*, or *Secret History*, describing the outrages of the Emperors Justinian and Theodora, and of Belisarius and Antonina, was begun in the year 549 and brought to completion in 562. In this work, Procopius—I will not say with great boldness, but rather with a most foul and unheard-of itch for lying and slandering—attributes the most disgraceful crimes to Emperor Justinian and others. It appears he wrote it for no other purpose than to make the court of an excellent prince seem like a "Lerna of Devils" <note>Lerna was a mythological swamp inhabited by the Hydra; here it means a sinkhole of monsters</note>, hateful to the world. Furthermore, such a lust for forceful feasting <note>excessive indulgence</note> and such a shamelessness of lies abounds everywhere in it—so foreign to the usual gravity of Procopius—that very learned men have been of the opinion that it is a counterfeit work falsely inscribed with Procopius’s name. In the printed copies, several pages describe the horrendous impudicities and lusts of Empress Theodora

**NICETIUS**, of Gaulish descent, first a monk and later an Abbot, became most famous for his reputation for holiness: so much so that he did not fear to freely rebuke King Theodoric of the Mediomatrici <note>The people of the region around modern-day Metz</note> and his son Theodebert for their vices. On account of this, Theodoric, moved by the highest veneration for the man, ensured he was given as successor to the deceased Aprunculus, Archbishop of Trier, in the year 527. Nicetius took part in the First Council of Auvergne in 535, the Fifth Council of Orleans and the Second Council of Auvergne in 549, and the Second Council of Paris in 551. Always maintaining an unbending rigor of mind in preserving Church discipline, he frequently excommunicated King Clotaire on account of his incestuous marriage. For this reason, he was sent into exile by Clotaire, but was finally restored to his see in the year 565 by Sigebert, Clotaire's son, after his father's death. He died in the year 568 on the Nones of December <note>December 5th</note>, or as others maintain, on the Calends of October <note>October 1st</note>.

**DACIUS**, Archbishop of the Church of Milan, flourished in the year 527. While the elder Justin was still Emperor, as Dacius was traveling to Constantinople for the sake of the faith, Gregory the Great tells what was done by him at Corinth regarding a certain deserted lodging inhabited by a demon in *Dialogues, book 3, chapter 4.* <margin>Variae, book 12, letter 27.</margin> There exists a *Letter from Cassiodorus* to him regarding the distribution of the grain supply to the starving people, given around the year 537. He died around the year 555. A *Chronicle of Milanese Affairs* is attributed to him, which has remained unpublished until now and is kept in the Milanese Library. So that the famous Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon, a renowned Benedictine scholar</note> might more certainly explore the reliability and authority of this Chronicle, he sent certain inquiries to Milan through Claudio Castellano. <margin>Analecta Vetera, Volume I, page 8, etc.</margin> He received a response from Antonio Maria Pustula, the Librarian of the Metropolitan Church, stating that the Chronicle is six hundred years old, written on parchment, though not by the same hand; it bears the name of Dacius, Archbishop of Milan, but the title is more recent. It narrates the affairs of the Milanese Church from the eighth century down to the time of Pope Alexander II, and ends in the year 1067; from this it is sufficiently clear that it is not the work of our Dacius. The true authors were Landulph the Elder, who wrote the first part; Arnulph, who wrote the second; and finally Landulph the Younger, who wrote the third.

**JUSTUS**, brother of Justinian <note>Justinian of Valencia, mentioned on the previous page, not the Emperor</note>, Bishop of Urgell <note>also called Orgellia</note> in Catalonia, flourished in the year 529 and was present at the Second Council of Toledo in 531. He died around the year 540. He wrote a *Commentary on the Song of Songs*; which Menrad Molther first brought to light in *Haguenau, 1529*. From there it was included in the *Orthodoxographa* <note>A collection of "orthodox" writings</note> p. 1038, and the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 9, p. 731. Georg Rost caused the same to be reprinted in *Halle, Saxony, 1617*, preceded by two letters from Justus: one to Pope Sergius (which the title itself proclaims to be spurious) and the other to Justus the Deacon (at whose urging he had composed the Commentary). Dacherius published two other letters by Justus in his *Spicilegium*, Volume 3. Furthermore, his remaining two brothers, Nebridius (Bishop of Egara <note>modern Terrassa</note>, who signed the Second Council of Toledo) and Elpidius, wrote several works; however, these escaped the notice of Isidore of Seville, and even more so, our own.

<margin>530.</margin>

**BONIFACE II**, Roman by birth, son of Sigisbald, was ordained Roman Pontiff in the Basilica of Julius on September 22, in the year 530. At the same time, the Deacon Dioscorus was ordained in the Constantinian Basilica by another faction of the Roman clergy. However, as Dioscorus was removed from the living <note>i.e., died</note> shortly thereafter, Boniface held the see peacefully and anathematized <note>formally cursed or excommunicated</note> Dioscorus after his death. In the year 531, in order to block the path of the Gothic kings' ambition in designating popes, he held a Synod in Rome and appointed the Deacon Vigilius as his successor; he had the Synodal decree on this matter confirmed by the signature of the entire clergy. Soon, however, having been sharply rebuked on that account by King Athalaric and struck with terror, he confessed himself guilty of high treason <note>original: "reum se majestatis"</note>; and in the presence of all the priests, the clergy, and the Senate, he consumed the Synodal decree in a fire. He died on October 24, 532. *Two Letters* survive: the first to Eulalius, Bishop of Alexandria, which everyone recognizes as spurious; the second to Caesarius of Arles, which contains poorly recorded Consuls. They are found in the *Councils, Volume 4, p. 1684.*

530.

* Eulogy of the Abbots of Monte Cassino, p. 25.

**BENEDICT**, Italian by race, from the province of Umbria and the house of Nursia, was born to Euprepius and Abundantia from the ancient and most noble Anician family <note>One of the most prestigious families of the later Roman Empire</note> in the year 480. After his childhood, he was sent to Rome by his parents to be instructed in liberal arts. However, soon weary of that place, he withdrew to the wilderness of Subiaco in the year 494, at the age of 14, and began to enter the ascetic life. Living in this place for several years, he founded twelve monasteries and placed twelve monks in each. At last, in the year 528, leaving Subiaco, he went to Monte Cassino, where, having first cut down the grove of Apollo, he built a monastery for himself. In 531, he was summoned to Rome for a Synod by Boniface II, intended to win greater authority for the Synod by his presence; this is reported from a manuscript of the Vatican Library by Antonius Scipio, a monk of Monte Cassino*. When close to death, he arranged to be carried into the Oratory of St. John the Baptist: where, intent upon sacred matters, standing and upright, he returned his soul to heaven in the year 542 or 543. Whoever wishes to know the virtues and astounding miracles of Benedict should consult Book 2 of the *Dialogues* of Gregory the Great, which is entirely spent in enumerating them even to the point of tedium.

<margin>530. * Codex 222.</margin>
**JOBIUS, an Eastern Monk**, <note>original Greek: ὁ θεοσεβὴς, καὶ φροντίσιν ἱεραῖς ἀναλωμένος ὁ ἀνὴρ</note> "a man god-fearing and consumed by sacred concerns," according to the testimony of Photius *. I would assign him to this sixth century, both because he wrote against Severus <note>Severus of Antioch, a leader of the Miaphysite movement</note> (who was condemned more than once during the reign of Emperor Justinian), and because he lived after Pseudo-Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, whose mystical writings appeared in the early 5th century but gained fame in the 6th</note> had become publicly known to the world and had begun to be considered the genuine Areopagite. Thus, he seems to have flourished around the year 530. He wrote a book against the heretic Severus, of which no traces remain today. Likewise, he wrote *On the Economy of the Incarnation* <note>original Greek: περὶ οἰκονομικῆς πραγματείας</note>, or *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, in nine books. From nearly every one of these books, Photius took excellent and quite extensive excerpts, which are found in his work under Codex 222. In handling controversies, as Photius notes, he is neither ignoble nor lax, though he does not always resolve the knots of the objections so successfully. In both of his works, <note>original Greek: ἡ μέντοιγε εὐσεβεία... οὐκ ἄπειρον</note> "his piety indeed, as far as I can tell, is consistently praiseworthy, his diligence is not to be looked down upon, and he is remarkably well-practiced in the study of the Holy Scriptures."

<margin>530.</margin>
**TETRADIUS**, or **Teridius**, Gaulish by birth, nephew of Saint Caesarius of Arles, and a Priest by rank. He flourished in the year 530. He wrote down from the mouth of Saint Caesarius, and transmitted to many monasteries of Gaul, the *Rule for Monks*; which is commonly attributed to Saint Caesarius and is found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Holstenius’s *Codex of Rules*, and elsewhere.

<margin>530.</margin>
**COGITOSUS**, Irish by nation, and apparently the nephew of Saint Brigid, is thought to have lived around the year 530 or shortly thereafter. He wrote the *Life of Saint Brigid*, which is found in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume 5, part 2, page 625, and in Surius and the Bollandists <note>Reference to the *Acta Sanctorum*</note> under February 1st.

<margin>531. * On Writers, ch. 3.</margin>
**MONTANUS**, Spanish by birth, Archbishop of the City of Toledo after Celsus, flourished in the year 531. In that year, he presided over the Council of Toledo and saw to it that a synodal decree was made: that no priest henceforth should prepare the chrism <note>the consecrated oil used in baptism and other sacraments</note>, nor should a bishop consecrate churches in another's diocese. He held the episcopate for nine years. Ildefonsus of Toledo * praises him greatly for his learning and the holiness of his life; those who wish to know more about him should consult Ildefonsus. Two letters are extant: *the first to the brothers of the territory of Palencia, the second to Theoribius, Bishop of Palencia*, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 1735. This Turibius appears to be a different person from the Bishop Turibius whom our Montanus mentions in his first letter as having written books against the Priscillianist heresy to Pope Leo.

6th CENTURY from the Year of Our Lord 532.

**JOHN II**, nicknamed *Mercurius*, a Roman by birth and the son of Projectus, was a Priest of the Roman Church at the Title of Saint Clement <note>The "Titles" were the ancient parish churches of Rome that gave rise to the cardinalate</note>. He was raised to the Papacy on December 19, 532. In 533, Emperor Justinian sent letters and legates—Hypatius of Ephesus and Demetrius of Caesarea—asking him to confirm with his apostolic support the phrase, "*One of the Trinity suffered in the flesh*" <note>original: "Unus de Trinitate passus est"</note>. He was also asked to condemn the "Sleepless Monks" <term>Acæmetas</term> <note>A group of monks in Constantinople known for keeping perpetual prayer services; they were condemned here for leaning toward Nestorianism, which over-separated Christ’s divine and human natures</note>. These monks had used a decree issued about thirteen years earlier by Pope Hormisdas to support Nestorian teachings, but John II stripped them of that argument. He accomplished both tasks: in a letter to Justinian, he decreed that the phrase (which Maxentius had once defended and Hormisdas had previously condemned in its specific wording) was indeed Catholic and could be used rightly, striking those who taught otherwise with an excommunication <note>original: "anathemate"</note>. He died on April 21, 535. Six of his *Letters* are extant in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 4, page 1741, though the *first* (addressed to Bishop Valerius) is rejected as a forgery by Labbe and others.

<margin>533.</margin>
**DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS** <note>His name literally means "Dionysius the Small" or "the Humble," a title he likely took himself</note>, a Scythian by nationality and a Monk and Roman Abbot by profession. He was a close associate of Cassiodorus <note>A famous Roman statesman and writer who founded a monastery</note> and his pupil in the study of logic. He flourished before the year 533 and died before 556, the year Cassiodorus wrote his book *On Divine Readings* <note>original: "de Divinis Lectionibus"</note>; in that work, Cassiodorus highly praises Dionysius as recently deceased. <margin>\* Chapter 23.</margin> *“The Catholic Church,”* he says \*, *“even today produces illustrious men shining with the beauty of worthy doctrines. For in our times there was the monk Dionysius... most learned in both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note>, reflecting in his actions the justice he had read about in the Lord’s books. He had examined and understood the Divine Scriptures with such diligence that... He possessed great wisdom joined with simplicity, humility with learning, and restraint in his eloquent speech... He was entirely Catholic, perseveringly attached to the rules of the Fathers; whatever readers might seek through various sources could be found shining in his knowledge.”*

->W O R K S.<-

**A** Collection or Code of Ecclesiastical Canons, translated into Latin and compiled by Dionysius at the request of Bishop Stephen of Salona. It consists of the first 50 Apostolic Canons and the canons from the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica, and certain African councils. It appears in all collections of the Councils and was edited by Justellus in Paris, 1628, and in the *Library of Canon Law*, Volume 1, page 97.

*A Collection of the Decrees of the Roman Popes* from Siricius to Anastasius II—as many as could be found—along with a dedicatory letter to the Roman Priest Julian, who signed the Synods held in Rome in 488 and 499. This appears in every edition of the Councils and was edited by Justellus with the *Code of Canons* in Paris, 1628.

*The Synodal Letter of Saint Cyril and the Council of Alexandria* against Nestorius, translated into Latin. This appears in various places and was edited by Justellus with the previous short works.

*The Paschal Letter of Proterius to Leo*, translated into Latin, along with two of Exiguus's own *Letters on Easter to Petronius and Boniface*; found in the appendix of Petavius’s work *On the Doctrine of Time* <note>Dionysius is most famous for creating the "Anno Domini" (A.D.) dating system as part of these Easter calculations</note>.

*The Life of Saint Pachomius the Abbot*, translated into Latin, and published among the *Lives of the Fathers* by Heribert Rosweyde in Antwerp, 1615 and 1628.

*The Oration of Proclus in Praise of the Mother of God* <note>original: "de laudibus Deiparæ"</note>. (Garnerius, however, contends this was translated not by Exiguus but by Marius Mercator, and thus published the version among the latter's works with the Greek text). Also, his *Letter on the Faith to the Armenians* and *another to Domnus on behalf of Athanasius, Bishop of Perrhe*, translated into Latin, are found in the edition of Proclus’s works prepared by V. Riccardi in Rome, 1630.

*Gregory of Nyssa’s book "On the Making of Man,"* divided into two sermons, translated into Latin. This version exists (printed in Basel, 1562, and Cologne, 1573) but without Dionysius's dedicatory letter.

**FULGENTIUS FERRANDUS**, an African by birth, was a disciple of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe, under whose guidance he entered and lived the monastic life while in exile in Sardinia. Finally returning to Africa, he was made a Deacon of the Church of Carthage. He flourished in the year 533 and thereafter. In that year, having been asked by letter by Anatolius, a Deacon of the Roman Church, and Severus, a Scholastic <note>A "Scholasticus" was typically a legal advisor or a highly educated scholar attached to a court</note> of Constantinople, *whether it can be rightly said that one of the Trinity suffered*; he issued an opinion by letter to both, stating that the formula was true and Catholic. In the year 546, consulted by the Roman Deacons Pelagius and Anatolius regarding the condemnation of the "Three Chapters" <note>The "Three Chapters" controversy was a complex theological dispute where Emperor Justinian tried to condemn three 5th-century writers to appease critics of the Council of Chalcedon. Ferrandus was a staunch defender of these writers' memory</note>, he replied that to strike the memory of long-dead writers with an excommunication was neither pious nor useful to the Church. Furthermore, when the African Bishops were asked by letter by Emperor Justinian to condemn the chapters, he was the authority who advised them to withhold their judgment on the matter and deny such obedience to the Emperor. He died before the year 551.

Besides the edition by Antonius Sconhovius, this *Chronicle* was published in *Paris (1546 in octavo, 1575), Heidelberg (1588)*, and at the end of the Chronicle of Eusebius in *Leiden (1606)* and *Amsterdam (1658)*. Finally, Jacques Sirmond, using a very ancient Tilian manuscript, produced a much more emended version of the *Chronicle* itself, as well as a far more augmented *Appendix* by an ancient writer (Paris, 1619, in octavo); from there it was included in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 9, page 517*. Marcellinus also wrote, according to the testimony of <margin>* Divine Letters, chapters 17, 25.</margin> *Cassiodorus*, four books on the "qualities of times and the positions of places," and another four books on the cities of Constantinople and Jerusalem. Both of these works have long since perished.

<margin>535.</margin>
**ANTHIMUS**, first the Bishop of Trebizond in Pontus, was then elevated to the Patriarchate of Constantinople in the year 535 through the favor of the Empress Theodora. He wished to remain hidden under a mask of false piety and Orthodoxy, professing that he venerated the four holy Councils, included them in the Diptychs <note>original: "Diptychis" — tablets used in the liturgy to record the names of those in communion with the Church; to be "in the diptychs" meant one was recognized as Orthodox</note>, and followed the Apostolic See in all things. Meanwhile, however, he harbored the Eutychian <note>Eutychianism was the belief that Christ had only one nature, a blend of the human and divine, rather than two distinct natures</note> poison in his heart. Therefore, in the following year, after a petition of accusation was presented by the Eastern Archimandrites <note>Superiors of monasteries</note>, he was deposed from the See of Constantinople—and soon after also from Trebizond—by Pope Agapetus, because, having been led astray by Severus, he refused to confess two natures in Christ. A Synod held in Constantinople under Menas in that same year ratified this sentence, and he was subsequently condemned many times by Emperor Justinian, Pope Vigilius, and many Synods. Some fragments exist of a *Prophetic Sermon to the Emperor Justinian* in the *Acts of the Councils, Volume 6, pages 831, 906, 907*. Evagrius mentions his letters to *Theodosius of Alexandria* in Book 4, Chapter 11.

<margin>535*</margin>
**THEODOSIUS**, a native of Alexandria and a teacher of rhetoric by profession, was later admitted into the Alexandrian clergy. He was a disciple of Severus (who lived in Alexandria after being driven from the See of Antioch) and became the leader of the sect of the *Corrupticolae* <term>Corrupticolae: Literally 'worshippers of the corruptible'; a faction that argued Christ's human body was subject to natural decay and corruption before his Resurrection, just like any other human</term> of Alexandria, who were named "Theodosians" after him. In the year 535, upon the death of Bishop Timothy, he was elected Patriarch of Alexandria by the Alexandrian clergy and duly installed. However, at the same time, Gaianus the Archdeacon, leader of the *Aphthartodocitae* <term>Aphthartodocitae: Also known as Phantasiasts, they believed Christ's body was incorruptible from the moment of the Incarnation, making his human suffering appear to be an illusion (phantasia)</term>, was elevated to the episcopate by the monks and a large majority of the common people. Gaianus drove Theodosius from his see and held it for 103 days, until Count Narses, by order of Emperor Justinian and after a sharp battle with the Alexandrian populace, expelled him and restored the position to Theodosius. The following year, Theodosius was accused of Eutychianism before the Emperor; after holding the Alexandrian see for sixteen months, he was summoned to Constantinople. Stubbornly refusing to subscribe to the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, he was deposed and banished to the sixth mile-marker outside Constantinople. While living in Thrace, he soon after became the leader of another faction of the *Corrupticolae*. For the *Corrupticolae* split into two factions, fighting over Christ’s human knowledge. Theodosius and his followers held separate assemblies for those who denied that Christ, by the power of his human nature, knew the Day of Judgment <note>This subgroup is known historically as the Agnoetae</note>. Liberatus was writing his *Breviarium* while Theodosius was still alive. Some fragments exist of a *Petition to the Empress Theodora* in the *Acts of the Councils, Volume 6, pages 320, 835*. He also wrote letters to *Anthimus* and *Severus*, mentioned by Evagrius in Book 4, Chapter 11.

<margin>535.</margin>
**AGAPETUS**, a Roman by nationality and son of the Priest Gordianus, took up the governance of the Roman Church on April 29, 535. He immediately rescinded the acts designating Vigilius for the Papacy—which had been made in a Roman Synod under Boniface—and he absolved Dioscorus, who had been condemned by Boniface after his death. The following year, he was forced by Theodatus, King of the Goths, to undertake an embassy to Constantinople to turn away Emperor Justinian’s armies from Italy with prayers. However, he did not achieve this. Nevertheless, he accomplished matters of greater importance. He deposed Anthimus, who was addicted to the Eutychian heresy, from the See of Constantinople, and ordained Menas as his replacement. He died in Constantinople on the 17th day of...

<margin>536.</margin>
### MENNAS
A native of Alexandria and former Superintendent <note>original: "Præposito"</note> of the Great Hospital <note>original: "Xenodochii" — a charitable institution for travelers or the sick</note> called "of Sampson." After Anthimus was deposed in the year 536, he was elected Patriarch of Constantinople by the clergy of the city and ordained by Pope Agapetus. Having immediately convened a Synod, he condemned Anthimus, Severus, and their other sectarians. In the year 541, at the request—and virtually the compulsion—of the Emperor Justinian, he condemned Origen in a Synod held at Constantinople; he did the same for the *Three Chapters* <note>A famous controversy involving the condemnation of three 5th-century bishops and their writings to appease Monophysites</note> in the year 546. Because of this, he was removed from communion by Pope Vigilius, who arrived in Constantinople the following year; however, after a period of three months, harmony was reached and he was fully restored. He died in the year 552. Besides the matters he discussed during the Synod of Constantinople regarding the case of Anthimus as the situation required, there is an extant *Letter in Greek and Latin to Peter, Patriarch of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, regarding the deposition of Anthimus*, found among the *Acts of the Synod of Jerusalem*, *Collection of Councils*, Volume 5, page 277.

->10.<-

<margin>536.</margin>
### SYLVERIUS
The son of Pope Hormisdas and a subdeacon of the Roman Church, he was finally made Pope on June 6, 536, through the power of King Theodahad. At the end of that same year (not at a later date, as Anastasius wrongly claims), by order of the Empress Theodora and through the wicked ambition of Vigilius, he was driven from his see by the General Belisarius. A false charge of treason <note>original: "perduellionis" — specifically, the crime of betraying one's country to an enemy</note> was leveled against him, and he was exiled to Patara, a city in Lycia. There, having held a Synod of several friendly bishops, he pronounced curses upon Vigilius. Eventually sent back to Italy by the Emperor Justinian so that his case might be properly judged in a Synod, he was—through the excessive compliance of Belisarius—handed over to the custody of Vigilius. Vigilius deported him to the island of Palmaria, where he wasted away for a long time from hunger and lack of food, and finally, on June 20, 540, was murdered by two assassins sent for that purpose. Two letters exist under his name: one to Vigilius and another to Amator. However, Labbe, Papebroch, and—what is more surprising—Binius himself judge them to be spurious, both from chronological markers and the barbarity of the style.

<margin>536.</margin>
### ZACHARIAS, THE SCHOLAR
Called "The Scholar" <note>original: "Scholasticus" — a title for a lawyer or a professional rhetorician</note> because of his profession, he first applied himself to the study of literature at Alexandria, where he had the philosopher Ammonius as a fellow student. Later, he devoted his efforts to the study of Jurisprudence at Beirut, and eventually became the Metropolitan of the Church of Mitylene. He flourished in the year 536, when he participated in the Synod of Constantinople held under Mennas; he was sent by that Synod along with others as an envoy to the recently deposed Anthimus to prevent the man from weaving delays and to draw him into the Synod to give satisfaction by offering a libellus <note>a formal written statement</note> of repentance. It is not certain in what year he died. While he was still staying in Beirut, he wrote a *Dissertation or Dialogue against the Philosophers who assert the eternity of the world*. It is extant in *Greek and Latin* with the notes of Turrianus and Barthius (Leipzig, 1654, in quarto), in the *Ducaean Supplement*, Volume 1, page 331, and with the *Philocalia* of Origen (Paris, 1619, in quarto). He also wrote a *Disputation on the Two Principles against the Manichaeans*. This is extant in Latin from the translation by Turrianus (for the Greek has not yet been published) in Canisius’ *Ancient Lessons*, Volume 5, page 143. Both short works are held in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 9.

<margin>540.</margin>
### NONNOSUS
The son of Abraham the Priest, he was sent as an envoy by the Emperor Justinian to Caisus, the prefect of the Saracens, then to Elasbaas, king of the Axumites <note>The Aksumite Empire in modern-day Ethiopia and Eritrea</note>, and likewise to the Homerites <note>The Himyarite Kingdom in modern-day Yemen</note>. Having overcome many dangers from foreign peoples and wild beasts, and having successfully completed his mission, he was returned safely to his homeland. He flourished in the year 540, or at least during the reign of Justinian, who died in the year 565. He wrote a *History of the Embassies*, which has perished. Excerpts are found in Photius, *Codex 3*.

However, he would be much more recent if it were true—as Casimir Oudin <note>A 17th-century French bibliographer and former monk</note> claims—that our subject was the same person as Arethas, the Presbyter of Caesarea, who wrote around the year 920 the *Translation of Euthymius, Patriarch of Constantinople*, which is found in Lippomannus, Volume 3. FACUNDUS, African by birth and Bishop of Hermiane in Africa. He was a strenuous and most fierce *Defender of the Three Chapters* <note>A major 6th-century theological dispute regarding the condemnation of three deceased bishops and their writings to appease Monophysite Christians</note>, and—to use the words of Cassiodorus—a *destroyer of heretics with piercing subtlety*. He flourished in the year 540. He lived for the most part in Constantinople, where he managed the affairs of the African Church before the Emperor. In the year 546, he withdrew from communion with Mennas, who had condemned the *Three Chapters*, and at the request of many bishops, he undertook a laborious *Defense of the Chapters*. In the following year, he participated in a Council of 70 bishops convened in Constantinople by Pope Vigilius; there he defended the cause of the Chapters with the greatest constancy of mind and strongly resisted Vigilius. Shortly thereafter, he completed his work (begun the previous year) and presented it to the Emperor Justinian. It is uncertain in what year he died, but it is certain that, having once undertaken the patronage of the Chapters, he performed this duty most constantly until death, and never returned to the communion of Vigilius once he had renounced it. Finally, upon leaving Constantinople, he was sent into exile. While staying in Constantinople in the year 547—the very time Pope Vigilius arrived there—he wrote to the Emperor Justinian *Twelve Books in Defense of the Three Chapters*. In these, he argues above all for the cause of Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom he clears of every stain of heretical depravity; he also inveighs sharply against the Acephali <note>A radical Monophysite sect "without a head"</note> and those he calls "Semi-Eutychians." He contends that "One of the Trinity suffered for us," though in a Catholic sense. Finally, to note this in passing, in Book 9, Chapter 5, he provides a remarkable testimony regarding the Holy Eucharist; I will present the entire passage here:

> *Christ deigned to receive the sacrament of adoption both when he was circumcised and when he was baptized; and it can be called the Sacrament of adoption. Just as we call the Sacrament of his body and blood—which is in the consecrated bread and cup—his body and blood, not because the bread is properly his body and the cup his blood, but because they contain within themselves the mystery of his body and blood. Hence the Lord himself called the blessed bread and chalice, which he handed to his disciples, his body and blood. Therefore, just as those receiving the sacrament of Christ's body and blood are rightly said to receive the body and blood of Christ, so Christ himself, when he had received the sacrament of the adoption of sons, could rightly be said to have received the adoption of sons.*

Jacques Sirmond <note>A 17th-century Jesuit scholar and editor</note>, in his notes, explains this passage with a rather cold interpretation quite alien to the author’s intent, and not with his usual candor; namely, that the consecrated bread is not bread, yet it is called bread because it was bread once, and retains the appearance of bread, and because the body and blood of Christ are contained in the Sacrament under the appearance of bread and wine. But Sirmond, realizing this interpretation was hardly reliable, immediately adds:

> "If perhaps anything spoken here seems a bit harsh or obscure, he is worthy of pardon, and should receive from a kind interpreter the same courtesy that he himself zealously showed more than once to others whose words were being criticized."

He also wrote against *Mutianus the Scholastic*, who had attacked the African bishops for denying communion to Vigilius—though the work is actually *A Single Book Against Vigilius*. Both works, illustrated with notes, were first published by Jacques Sirmond, Paris, 1629, in octavo. Then, by the care of Philip le Prieur, it appeared with Sirmond's notes joined to Optatus of Milevis, Paris, 1675, folio. To this edition was also added Facundus’s *Letter of the Catholic Faith in Defense of the Three Chapters*, which Luc d'Achery had previously published in the *Spicilegium*, Volume 4, page 106. The works of Facundus are also found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 10, pages 1 and 109.

# **APRIGIUS**, Bishop of the Church of Pace <note>The Roman "Pax Julia," modern-day Beja in Portugal</note> in Spain, a man eloquent of tongue and learned in knowledge, flourished around the year 540. Isidore says * that he wrote an *Explanation of the Apocalypse* of Blessed John, with subtle meaning and illustrious language, appearing to have explained it better than almost all the ancient churchmen. That work has perished <note>original: "Interiit Opus istud"</note>. However, Garcia de Loaysa, in his notes to Isidore’s Catalog, testifies that he saw a massive manuscript work on the Apocalypse in Spain, written in Gothic letters and compiled from the books of Victorinus, Isidore, and Aprigius, as the Preface claimed. According to Isidore, Aprigius also wrote certain other things, but not even their titles survive.

<margin>540.</margin>

# **VIGILIUS**, Roman by birth and the son of John the Scythian (who held the consulship in the year 498), was the Archdeacon of the Roman Church. He was designated as successor by Pope Boniface II in the year 531 at a Roman Synod, though he was soon excluded from that hope by the same Pope. In the year 535, he was sent as an *Apocrisiarius* <term>an ecclesiastical legate or ambassador</term> to Constantinople by Pope Agapetus. The following year, after Agapetus died, he purchased the papacy from Empress Theodora through wicked ambition. He promised, under oath and with a signed document, that as soon as he obtained the Roman See, he would restore Anthimus to the See of Constantinople, enter into communion with Severus, and condemn the Council of Chalcedon; for this reward of treachery, he received from Theodora seven hundred bags of gold <note>original: "auri septenariis centum"</note>. Certainly, <margin>* Book against Mucianus, p. 573.</margin> * Facundus of Hermiane clearly objects to this very document, noting that Vigilius was first driven by the impulse of ambition when he burned to become Bishop, and later turned to the other side through bribery. Thus, armed with the Empress’s commands, he hastened to Rome, drew the general Belisarius to his side, and saw to it that Pope Silverius was driven into exile on a fabricated charge of treason. He fulfilled his promises through letters given to the Empress; he condemned the Council of Chalcedon and confessed a single nature in Christ <note>the Monophysite position</note>, yet he forbade his letter from being made public. <margin>This is clearly testified by Liberatus, Victor of Tunnuna, and Facundus of Hermiane.</margin> Later, having obtained Silverius (who had been brought back to Italy by Belisarius) for two hundred pounds of gold, he banished him to the island of Palmaria, wasted him away with hunger and lack of food, and finally killed him in the year 540 by sending assassins. Around the year 544, complying with Emperor Justinian, he condemned Origen. But when in the year 546 he was asked by the same Emperor to condemn the *Three Chapters* <note>A series of controversial writings by three 5th-century bishops that Justinian wanted condemned to appease Monophysite Christians</note>, he stubbornly refused; nor did he openly fulfill the oath he had long ago given to the Empress about condemning the Council of Chalcedon. This made Theodora his enemy. Moved by her flatteries, Justinian called for a Council to be held at Constantinople. He summoned Vigilius from Rome. Vigilius stalled; the Emperor then gave orders to Belisarius that he be sent even against his will. Therefore, in the month of November, he was forced to begin the journey, weighed down by the curses and insults of the Roman citizens (whom he had made his enemies through murders and tyranny). In December, he reached Sicily; there he performed some ordinations and humbly petitioned the Emperor via letter that the Synod be held in Sicily rather than Constantinople. With his prayers rejected by the Emperor, he proceeded to Constantinople, entering at the start of the following year. He found Origen already condemned by the Patriarch Menas and removed Menas from communion. Theodora seized the occasion of this grudge to pressure Vigilius to restore Anthimus. Vigilius resisted, and to strip the Empress of all hope, he entered into communion with Menas after a few months. Moreover, in the month of March, he convened a Synod of Bishops and brought the case of the Three Chapters under examination. With the dispute raging fiercely among the Fathers, it was decided that each should deliver his opinion in writing. This was done. Vigilius wrote that famous *Judicatum* <term>a formal theological ruling</term> and offered it to the Emperor, in which he struck the Three Chapters with anathema. When the news of this act was spread, the Western world roared; the Roman clergy and people renounced communion with Vigilius and (if any faith is to be placed in the conjectures of Papebroch <note>A famous 17th-century Jesuit hagiographer</note>) they erased his name from the Diptychs <term>the official lists of those remembered in the liturgy</term> and appointed Pelagius the Deacon as Pope. The Africans, having called a Synod, excluded him synodally from Catholic communion, though they reserved a place for repentance. Terrified by such uprisings in the West, Vigilius revoked his sentence. Justinian became furious and attacked the Pope with insults. Vigilius fled into the Basilica of St. Euphemia and clung to a pillar of the altar. He was dragged from there by the Emperor’s order, led through the city with a rope around his neck, and thrown into prison, where he suffered the greatest hardships. This—
