...he undergoes everything with a wonderful constancy of mind. To return the favor, he excommunicates Theodore of Caesarea—who was then all-powerful with the Emperor—and other bishops, along with the Roman clergy. In the year 552, the rift is healed; Vigilius is set free, while Theodore and Mennas ask for pardon by offering a petition. The case of the "Three Chapters" <note>A major theological dispute involving the condemnation of three 5th-century bishops and their writings, which Justinian pressured the Church to denounce to appease Monophysites</note> is left entirely to be decided by an Ecumenical Council. Therefore, Justinian orders a Council to be held at Constantinople; it finally begins on May 5, in the year 553. Vigilius could be led to attend by no prayers of the Fathers and no warnings of the Emperor. Finally, in the sixth month after the start of the Synod, on December 7, having changed his mind and revoked his previous Decree regarding this part, he sent letters to Eutychius of Constantinople and soon published a more extensive Decree. In these, he anathematized <note>formally cursed or condemned</note> the Three Chapters and confirmed the decrees of the Synod. This having been done, a mollified Justinian dismissed the man and his followers from Constantinople. He withdrew to Syracuse in Sicily, where, worn down by the pains of the stone <note>likely kidney or bladder stones</note>, he died on May 7, in the year 555. His surviving writings include: *18 Letters (in the Councils, Vol. V, p. 311); a very lengthy Decree against the Three Chapters published in the year 555 (ibid., p. 337); a Decretal Letter to Eutychius of Constantinople for the confirmation of the Fifth Synod in Greek and Latin (first published by Pierre de Marca along with a very learned dissertation in 1644, ibid., p. 596); and finally, a Decree even longer than the first against the Three Chapters given in 554, recently published from the Colbert Library in the New Collection of Councils, Vol. I, p. 1551, etc. Two letters to Justinian and Theodora, once corrupted by the Monothelites and for that reason rejected by the Sixth Synod, are found there as well, together with a letter to Profuturus, Bishop of Braga.*

<margin>540.</margin>
**GORDIANUS**, a Roman by birth, a disciple of St. Benedict, and later a companion of St. Placidus, serving as a monk under his rule at Messina in Sicily. When Placidus was captured in the year 539 along with others by Mammuca, a general of Abdallah, the king of the Saracens, and thrown into chains, Gordianus ministered to him in prison. He committed the bodies of Placidus and his companions, who were crowned with martyrdom, to burial. In the following year he fled to Constantinople, where he lived for a long time; by order of the Emperor Justinian, he committed the struggles of Placidus and his companions to writing in Greek. Finally, leaving Constantinople, he returned to Sicily, and died shortly thereafter. There exists in Latin that *Life and Passion of St. Placidus the Martyr*, though it has been interpolated <note>altered or expanded by later editors</note>, found in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Ages*, Vol. I, p. 45, and in Surius for October 5.

<margin>544.</margin>
**ARATOR**, a Ligurian by birth, an Advocate <term>lawyer</term> by profession, and later made Count of the Domestics and Private Affairs by King Athalaric around the year 534. He flourished in the year 544, though he was distinguished long before that, seeing as he performed a successful embassy on behalf of the Dalmatians to King Theodoric before the year 527. Having eventually left the court, he was initiated into holy orders and chosen among the Subdeacons of the Roman Church. He was especially dear to Pope Vigilius, to whom he dedicated his poem at the beginning of the year 544. Athalaric praises his eloquence and fluency with wonderful honors in the Rescript <note>an official royal decree</note> by which he granted him the dignity of the Countship.
<margin>In Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book 8, letter 12.</margin>
> "You are aided," he says, "by the eloquence and character of your father; his speech could have instructed you even if you had no time for the books of the ancients. For he was, as we know, excellently learned in literature. — O blessed teacher, and most fortunate disciple, who learned out of affection what the terror of other teachers extorted. Finally, you found Roman eloquence not in its own regions; and there the reading of Tully <note>Cicero</note> rendered you eloquent, where once the Gallic tongue resounded. Where are those who assert that Latin letters must be learned in Rome, and not elsewhere? — For that forceful opinion is dissolved: Liguria also sends its own Tullys."

But he excelled greatly not only in eloquence, but also in poetic ability. Regarding his poem
<margin>* Dissertation 2 on Latin Poets, p. 81.</margin>
*On the Acts of the Apostles*, the illustrious Borrichius says \*: "We rightly venerate his piety and ready eloquence. But there is no doubt that certain things from the dregs of the times <note>original: "fæcibus temporum," referring to the decline of classical Latin purity</note> crept into his style. Yet in these matters, everything is pure." He wrote the *Apostolic History* in Heroic verse, expressed from the text of Luke and comprised of two books. That *History* appeared with the commentaries of Arius Mendoza at Salamanca in 1516, in the Bignean Appendix (Paris, 1624, p. 681), and in the Library of the Fathers, Vol. X, p. 125. He also wrote an *Epistle to Parthenius* in Elegiac verse, at whose urging [he wrote] in poems...

**VICTOR**, Bishop of Capua, a man learned in both Greek and Latin, was prominent around the year 545. He wrote several small works, which follow:
*Ammonius’s Gospel Harmony, translated into Latin*, with a Preface provided, and the Eusebian Canons <note>a system of cross-referencing the four Gospels</note> appended and rearranged into a better order. Victor incorrectly attributed this work to Tatian <note>an early Christian writer known for the "Diatessaron," a similar harmony</note>. It is found in almost every edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, and in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 780.
<margin>Sigebert, On Writers, chapter 20.</margin>
*Paschal Cycles*, in which Victor attacked the Easter Canon of Victorius and demonstrated that the Easter of the year 455 should have been celebrated on the 7th day before the Kalends of May <note>April 25</note>, rather than the 15th day before the Kalends of May <note>April 17</note> as Victorius had calculated. Some fragments are held in Bede’s book *On Times*, chapter 49, and *On the Vernal Equinox*, Volume 2.
*A Chain of Commentary on the Four Gospels* <note>original: "Catena," a collection of interconnected interpretations from various authors</note>, stuffed with the writings of the Ancients, which was among the manuscripts owned by Feuardentius. He published certain fragments of Polycarp from it, translated into Latin by Victor, which we discussed above under Polycarp.

<margin>546.</margin>
**CYPRIAN**, of Gaulish descent and a disciple of Saint Caesarius of Arles, was prominent around the year 546. At the request of Caesaria, the sister of Saint Caesarius, he wrote the *Life and Deeds of Caesarius* up to the year 530 in a single book. To this, at his own encouragement, Messianus the Priest and Stephanus the Deacon—likewise disciples of Caesarius—added a second book *on his miracles, virtues, and death*. Stephanus's book was published in the first edition of Surius. Vincentius Barralis published both in the *Chronology of Lérins*, Lyon, 1613, in quarto. Since then, both are held in the newest edition of Surius for August 27, and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Ages*, Volume 1, page 659.

**VERECUNDUS**, or Vergundus, Bishop of Junca in the African Province of Byzacena, was prominent in the year 546. Having been made an exile for his defense of the "Three Chapters" <note>a major theological dispute involving the condemnation of three 5th-century authors to appease Monophysites</note>, he died at Chalcedon in the year 552. According to the author of the *Appendix* to <margin>* Chapter 6.</margin> Isidore, he wrote two short books in dactylic verse: the first *on the Resurrection and Judgment*, the other *on Penitence*, in which he lamented his own sins in a mournful poem. Garsias Loisa records that he read this latter work in a manuscript codex. See Miræus on this passage.

**MUTIANUS SCHOLASTICUS**, called a most eloquent man by Cassiodorus, was prominent around the year 550. At the request of Cassiodorus, he translated 34 Homilies of Saint Chrysostom on the *Epistle to the Hebrews* into the Latin language. This version exists <margin>* Divine Readings, chapter 8.</margin> printed at Cologne in 1530. See more under Chrysostom. Mutianus also wrote against the Western bishops who withdrew themselves from the communion of Pope Vigilius after he had condemned the Three Chapters; Facundus of Hermiane wrote a specific book in opposition to this work.

---

<margin>550.</margin>
**BELLATOR**, holding the rank of Priest and a friend of Cassiodorus, was prominent in the year 550. He wrote many commentaries on Holy Scripture. For he explained the book of *Esther* in 6 books, *Tobit* in 5 books, *Judith* in 7 books, *Wisdom* in 8 books, and *Maccabees* in 10 books. Furthermore, he translated two of Origen's *Homilies on Ezra*, and perhaps certain other things, into Latin. Of so many writings, nothing survives today; unless trust is given to the conjectures of Huet, who ascribes the translation of several of Origen’s minor works to Bellator; concerning which, see more under Origen.

**PRIMASIUS**, an African by birth, was the Bishop of the city of Adrumetum <note>modern Sousse, Tunisia</note>, which was also called *Justinianopolis*, in the Province of Byzacena. He was one of those sent to Constantinople around the year 550 to manage the affairs of the African Church. There, in the following year, he took part in the assembly of Bishops in which Vigilius directed a sentence of excommunication against Theodore of Caesarea, the leader of the Acephali. In the year 553, although summoned several times, he refused to take part in the Ecumenical Synod <note>The Second Council of Constantinople</note>; but together with others, he signed Vigilius's *Constitutum* <note>a formal decree</note> in favor of the "Three Chapters" <note>a controversial imperial edict condemning three specific theologians/texts</note>, which the Pope offered to the Emperor during the time of the Synod.

### WRITINGS.

*Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul*, for the most part gleaned <note>original: "delibata"</note> from the writings of Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and other ancients. Haymo <note>a later 9th-century commentator</note> subsequently transferred many things from this work into his own commentaries; for this reason, some have mistakenly concluded that Primasius’s *Commentaries* should be attributed to Haymo. They were published separately at Paris, 1543, in octavo.
*Mystical Commentaries of exposition on the Apocalypse*, dedicated to Castorius and divided into five books. They were published separately at Basel, 1544, in octavo.
Both of Primasius's *Commentaries* are available as edited by Gagnæus, Lyon, 1543, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 10.

<margin>
Isidore, On
Writers, ch. 5.
</margin>
*On Heresies, in three books*, addressed to Bishop Fortunatus, in which he explained what Augustine had once left unfinished in his book *On Heresies*. In the first book, he shows what makes a heretic; in the second and third, he demonstrates what a heretic is. This work has long since perished.

<margin>
*German Journey,
p. 83. Analecta,
Vol. 4.
</margin>
There exist today, published under the name *Praedestinatus*, three books *On Heresies*, specifically the heresy of the "Predestinarians." In the first part, the author (whoever he may be) deals with every heresy, ninety in number, from Simon Magus up to the Predestinarian heresy; he briefly reviews their authors, tenets, and customs. The second part consists of a book *On Predestination* formerly composed under Augustine’s name. In the third part, he provides a refutation of this pseudo-Augustinian book. Scholars do not quite agree on who the true parent of these books was. By Hincmar of Reims, they are cited under the name of Hyginus—a quite manifest error, perhaps arising from no other source than that he had found the name of Hyginus in the index of authors prefixed to the work. Sirmondus, due to the affinity of style and thought, suspected they should be assigned to Arnobius the Younger. Recently, Piccinardus, a theologian from Brescia, determined the author to be a certain Vincentius, namely the one to whose sixteen objections Prosper of Aquitaine opposed as many responses. But as to who that Vincentius might be—whether that Gallic priest who commented on the Psalms, of whom Gennadius speaks in chapter 80, or Vincentius Victor, against whom Augustine wrote *On the Origin of the Soul*—he does not quite know; for he completely rejects Vincent of Lérins. He attributes the book composed under Augustine’s name to Evodius of Uzalis, whom he suspects prefixed this title to his booklet: *An Exposition of the Doctrine of Augustine*, and thus it was held to be the offspring of Augustine himself. But what Piccinardus holds regarding this whole matter rests on such uncertain and slight conjectures that he is likely to draw few into his opinion. With far better right, these works seem attributable to our Primasius, and this on the authority of an ancient manuscript codex written eight hundred years ago, which the famous Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon, a pioneering Benedictine scholar of manuscripts</note> saw in the Library at Reichenau <note>original: "Augiensi"</note>. In that manuscript, this title appeared, written in a paler ink but by an ancient hand: THE WORK OF SAINT PRIMASIUS, DISCIPLE OF AUGUSTINE, ON NINETY HERESIES <note>original: "Opus Sancti Primasii Discipuli Augustini de Haeresibus Numero XC"</note>. Certainly, the author seems to hint in more than one place that he is an African; but to speak freely what I suspect, whoever added that little note to the Reichenau codex was perhaps mistaken...

...and when he <note>the editor Jacques Sirmond</note> had read in the works of Isidore that Primasius had written three books *On Heresies*, and he had found three anonymous books on that subject, he soon assigned the name of Primasius to them. Add to this that since our author mentions almost no heresy more recent than the Nestorian heresy <note>The 5th-century belief that Christ had two distinct natures and persons</note>, Primasius—living later—would hardly have omitted so many heresies that were born and condemned after that time. However, we leave this entire matter to be discussed by the learned. Jacques Sirmond first brought these books to light from a manuscript of Hincmar of Reims at *Paris*, 1643, in octavo. In the following year, Jean Auray, a theologian of the Sorbonne, published a quite sharp critique of the whole work in French, in which he contended that the author was a Pelagian <note>A follower of Pelagius, who emphasized human free will over divine grace</note>, and charged him with errors, heresies, lies, fables, and foul ignorance. Soon the work was reprinted in Holland at *Amsterdam*, if I am not mistaken, in 1645, in octavo, to which the editor added a Latin translation of Auray’s critique. In the year 1677, it found a place in the *Library of the Fathers* at Lyon, Volume 27. Finally, Serafino Piccinardi, of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note> and a theologian in the Academy of Padua, brought it to light again at *Padua*, 1686, in quarto, adding various dissertations on the author, the work, and the entire controversy.

</margin>
### JUNILIUS, an African Bishop, lived around the year 550. He wrote to Primasius two books *On the Parts of the Divine Law* in the form of Questions and Responses. These were issued in print edited by Johann Gast at *Basel*, 1545, in octavo; at *Frankfurt on the Oder*, 1603, in octavo; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 10, page 339. *Commentaries on the first three chapters of Genesis* are circulated under his name, printed at *Cologne*, 1535, in octavo; at *Basel*, 1538, in the *Orthodoxographia*, page 925; and among the works of Bede, to whom it is now known by everyone that they actually belong.

Jornand. On the Gothic Deeds. chapter 51.

### JORNANDES, or Jordanes, a Goth by race and son of Alanovamuthis, was first a secretary <term>Notarius</term> to the Goths. Afterward, having converted either to the Christian faith or to a more rigorous way of life, he finally became Bishop of Ravenna—or rather, acting as a Bishop of the Goths while residing at Ravenna. He flourished in the year 552, in which he wrote his book on the history of the Goths. Further details about him are not clear. There remain two small works written by him, namely:

> The book *On the Deeds of the Goths* <note>original: "De Rebus Geticis"</note>, or the *History of the Goths*, from the very cradle of the race down to King Vitiges, who was defeated by Belisarius. In this work, Jordanes summarizes what Cassiodorus had treated at length in twelve books on the same subject. It has been printed frequently; a more corrected version from a manuscript belonging to Pierre Pithou was edited by Fornerius among the works of Cassiodorus at *Paris*, 1588; with notes by Lindenbrog at *Hamburg*, 1611; and with other writers on similar subjects edited by Bonaventura Vulcanius at *Leiden*, 1618; and finally by Grotius in the *History of the Goths*, *Amsterdam*, 1655, in octavo.

<margin>
* On Latin History. book 2. chapter 20.
</margin>
> The book *On the Succession of Kingdoms and Times*, or on the origin of the world and the acts of the Romans and other nations: in which Vossius notes * that almost the entire *History* of Florus was copied without his name being mentioned. It was published at *Frankfurt*, 1588; *Paris*, 1588; *Leiden*, 1595, in octavo; and *Hamburg*, 1611. Both works were edited with notes by Jan Gruter at *Hanau*, 1611.

Evagr. book 4. chapter 38.
</margin>
### EUTYCHIUS, a monk by vocation, spent his life in the monastery of the city of Amasea. From there, he was sent to Constantinople as the representative <term>Apocrisiarius</term> of the Bishop of the Amaseans. When a controversy arose shortly before the Fifth Synod <note>The Second Council of Constantinople, 553 AD</note> as to whether it was lawful to subject the dead to anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication</note>, he, being exceptionally well-versed in the Scriptures, immediately untied the knot using the precedent of King Josiah <note>Who defiled the bones of dead idolatrous priests</note>. The Emperor <note>Justinian I</note>, admiring the man’s skill, promoted him to the pontifical seat of the Royal City <note>Constantinople</note> shortly thereafter, following the death of Menas at the beginning of the year 553. In the same year, he presided over the Ecumenical Synod of Constantinople. In the year 564, when he refused to consent to Emperor Justinian’s edict regarding the incorruptibility of Christ’s body before the resurrection <note>A doctrine known as Aphthartodocetism</note>, he was expelled from his see and confined in the Monastery of Choracudis <note>original: "Hofiae"</note>. After John Scholasticus was substituted for him, he was deposed by a certain assembly eight days later, and from there deported to an island called Princepo, and soon to his own monastery in Amasea. In the year 578, he was restored to his see by Tiberius Caesar (to whom he himself had once predicted his rule). He died in the year 585, at the age of 73. There remains a single *Letter* sent to Pope Vigilius immediately after he took up the bishopric, in which he asks that the case of the "Three Chapters" be discussed in the Synod with his consent, and exhorts them to concord.

Gr.

PRIMASIUS, African by birth, Bishop of the city of Hadrumetum <note>modern Sousse, Tunisia</note>, which was also called Justinianopolis, in the Province of Byzacena. He was one of those who were sent to Constantinople around the year 550 to manage the affairs of the African Church. There, in the following year, he took part in a meeting of bishops where Vigilius hurled a sentence of excommunication against Theodore of Caesarea, the leader of the Acephali. In the year 553, although summoned many times, he refused to take part in the Ecumenical Synod <note>The Second Council of Constantinople</note>; but together with others, he signed Vigilius's *Constitutum* <note>A formal decree or constitution</note> in favor of the Three Chapters <note>A controversial imperial decree condemning three 5th-century theologians, which many Western bishops resisted</note>, which the Pope offered to the Emperor during the time of the Synod.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul*, mostly gleaned from the writings of Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and <unclear>o</unclear>thers of the Ancients. From these, Haymo <note>Haymo of Halberstadt, a 9th-century Benedictine monk</note> transferred many things into his own Commentaries; as a result, some people, through a mistake, have been accustomed to think that the Commentaries of Primasius belong to Haymo. They were published separately in *Paris, 1543, in octavo.*

*Mystical Commentaries of exposition on the Apocalypse*, dedicated to Castorius and divided into five books. Published separately in *Basel, 1544, in octavo.*

Both of Primasius’s Commentaries are available as edited by Gagnæus <note>Jean de Gaigny, a 16th-century French theologian</note>, *Lyon, 1543*, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Vol. 10.

<margin>Isidore, *On Writers*, chapter 5.</margin>
*Three books On Heresies, addressed to Bishop Fortunatus*, in which he explained what Augustine had once left unfinished in his book on heresies: in the first book showing what makes a heretic, and in the 2nd and 3rd, what demonstrates a heretic. That work perished long ago.

<margin>*German Journey, p. 83. Analecta, Vol. 4.*</margin>
Today there exist three books on heresies, especially the heresy of the Predestinarians <note>A controversial 5th-century group accused of teaching that God predestined some to sin</note>, published under the name of *Praedestinatus*. In the first part, the author—whoever he may be—deals with ninety different heresies, from Simon Magus down to the Predestinarian heresy, briefly reviewing their authors, beliefs, and customs. The second part consists of a book on Predestination formerly forged under Augustine's name; in the third part, he undertakes a refutation of this pseudo-Augustinian book. Scholars do not quite agree on who the true parent of these books was. By Hincmar of Reims, they are cited under the name of Hyginus <note>Pope Hyginus</note>; quite a manifest error, perhaps arising from no other source than that he had found the name of Hyginus in the Index of Authors prefixed to the work. Sirmond <note>Jacques Sirmond, a Jesuit scholar</note>, because of the affinity of style and thoughts, suspected they should be assigned to Arnobius the Younger. Recently, Piccinardi, a theologian from Brescia, decided a certain Vincentius was the author—namely, that one against whose sixteen objections Prosper of Aquitaine set an equal number of responses. Whether that Vincentius is the French Priest who commented on the Psalms (of whom Gennadius speaks in chapter 80) or Vincentius Victor (against whom Augustine wrote *On the Origin of the Soul*), he does not quite know; for he completely rejects Vincent of Lérins. He attributes the book forged under Augustine's name to Evodius of Uzalis, whom he suspects gave his booklet this title: *Exposition of the Doctrine of Augustine*, and was thereafter considered Augustine's own offspring. Truly, the things Piccinardi holds regarding this whole matter rely on such uncertain and slight conjectures that he will perhaps draw few people to his opinion. By much stronger right, they seem to be attributed to our Primasius, and that on the evidence of an ancient manuscript codex written eight hundred years ago, which the famous Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon, a 17th-century Benedictine scholar</note> saw in the Library of Reichenau <note>original: "Augiensi"</note>. In it, this title appeared, written in a thinner ink but by an ancient hand: **THE WORK OF SAINT PRIMASIUS, DISCIPLE OF AUGUSTINE, ON NINETY HERESIES.** Certainly, the Author seems to hint in more than one place that he is African; but to speak freely what I suspect, whoever added this little note to the Reichenau Codex may perhaps have been mistaken,

**JORDANES**, or Jornandes, a Goth by race and the son of Alanovamuthis, was first a secretary <note>term: "Notarius"</note> to the Goths; then, having been converted either to the Christian faith or to a more rigorous way of life, he finally became the Bishop of Ravenna, or rather, acting at Ravenna, he was made Bishop of the Goths. He flourished in the year 552, in which he wrote his book on Gothic affairs. Further details about him are not clear. There exist two small works written by him, namely:

*A book on Gothic Affairs, or a History of the Goths from the very origin of the nation to King Vitiges, defeated by Belisarius* <note>Belisarius was the famed general of Emperor Justinian</note>, in which Jordanes summarizes what Cassiodorus <note>a Roman statesman and contemporary</note> had treated at length in twelve books on the same subject. **EUTYCHIUS**, a monk by his way of life, spent his time in a monastery in the city of Amasea; from there, he was sent to Constantinople as the <term>Apocrisiarius</term> <note>an ecclesiastical representative or legate</note> of the Bishop of Amasea. When a controversy arose shortly before the Fifth Synod <note>The Second Council of Constantinople, 553 AD</note> as to whether it was permissible to subject the dead to anathema <note>to formally curse or excommunicate them after death</note>, he, being exceptionally well-versed in the Scriptures, immediately solved the difficulty <note>original: "nodum solvit," literally "untied the knot"</note> using the example of King Josiah. The Emperor, admiring the man's skill, promoted him shortly thereafter—once Menas had been removed from the living—at the beginning of the year 553, to the Pontifical seat of the Royal City <note>Constantinople</note>. In the same year, he presided over the Ecumenical Synod of Constantinople. ### EUGYPPIUS,
by rank a Priest and an African Abbot; Cassiodorus says he was a man not so much learned in secular letters, but most full of the reading of the divine Scriptures. He flourished in the year 553. At the urging of Rendux, Bishop of Naples, he culled <note>original: "defloravit", meaning to pick the best parts or "flowers" of a text</note> questions, opinions, and various matters from the writings of Saint Augustine, and collected them into one body arranged in 338 chapters. He gave this work the name *Treasury* <note>original: *Thesaurus*</note> and dedicated it to the holy virgin Proba. This *Treasury* exists in editions from Basel, 1542, in folio, and Venice, 1543.

### FERREOLUS,
a Gaul by race, from the region of Narbonne, distinguished by the nobility of his family. His father was the Senator Ansbert, and his mother was Blitildis, daughter of King Chlothar; he was born in the year 521. While still a boy of seven, he left Narbonne for Uzès <note>original: "Ucecia"</note> and entrusted himself to the care of his great-uncle Ruricius to be imbued with fine literature. In the year 553, he succeeded his paternal uncle Firminus in the Bishopric of Uzès, where he built a magnificent church in memory of Saint Paul and founded a monastery named Ferriolacense after himself. But because he associated familiarly with the Jews out of a desire to win their souls, he was brought under suspicion of plotting an uprising <note>original: "rerum novarum cudendarum", literally "forging new things" or revolution</note> before King Childebert. In the year 555, he was banished to Paris, where he lived in exile for three years, though he was held in the greatest honor by the King. In the year 558, permitted to return, he went back to Uzès; and to remove every handle of suspicion, he expelled from his city all Jews whom he could not bring to the Christian faith. He died in the year 581, in the 28th year of his episcopate. He composed a *Rule for Monks* for the use of his monastery, which is preserved in full in the *Code of Rules* edited by Holstenius, Paris, 1663. He also wrote, according to Gregory of Tours *, several books of letters in imitation of Sidonius, which have perished. Whether the *Sentences* found under the name of Ferreolus the Priest in the booklet *On the Office of the Rector of the Church* (Cologne, 1531, octavo) belong to our Ferreolus is completely unknown to me.
<margin>* History, Book 6, chapter 7.</margin>

<margin>
553.
* *Breviary*, chapter 20.
</margin>
### LIBERATUS,
Archdeacon of the Church of Carthage and a most fierce defender of the *Three Chapters* <term>Three Chapters: a major 6th-century theological controversy regarding the condemnation of certain writings and authors deemed Nestorian</term>. In the year 534, or early the following year, he was sent to Rome by a Council of 217 African Bishops at Carthage to consult Pope John regarding certain doubts, along with the priests Caius and Peter. Although he did not reach the City before John’s death, he himself * testifies that he spent time in Rome while John was still living; so it seems he traveled to Rome twice before the year 536. He flourished especially in the year 553, around which time—though before the Fifth Council was held—he concluded his *Breviary* <note>original: *Breviarium*, meaning a summary or historical abstract</note>. He undertook many journeys on behalf of the cause of the *Three Chapters*. Having obtained a sufficiently rich supply of knowledge of events—partly from the accounts of very serious men, partly from histories, synodal acts, and the letters of bishops—he wove together a *History of the Nestorian and Eutychian Controversies*. In this, he encompassed events spanning nearly fifty years specifically looking at this controversy, containing things that can hardly be found elsewhere. It was written in a humble and pedestrian style, which, due to the variety of both Greek and Latin authors he follows, moves unevenly almost everywhere. That *Breviary*—for so he wished his history to be called—exists in the *Councils*, Volume 5, page 740, and with notes and dissertations by Garnier, Paris, 1675, in octavo. In the first edition of the *Councils* prepared by P. Crabbé, there is an Appendix to Liberatus's *Breviary* in Volume 2, from page 121 to 128, which is sought in vain in recent volumes of the *Councils*.

## VICTOR, African by birth, of Tununa <note>original: "Tununensis", a city in modern-day Tunisia</note> (erroneously called Cemmensis or Cummenensis by others), a Bishop in Africa, flourished in the year 555. He was a most steadfast patron of the *Three Chapters* <term>Three Chapters: a major 6th-century theological controversy involving the condemnation of three authors (Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and Ibas of Edessa) to reconcile with Monophysites, which many Westerners resisted</term>, and endured many very grave hardships for the sake of defending them. Summoned from Africa to Constantinople by the Emperor Justinian along with certain other bishops, he was afflicted with various exiles when he refused to condemn the Three Chapters. Indeed, after enduring guards and beatings at Salla and Valerici, as well as being relegated once and again to the Monastery of Mandra on the island of Egum in Mauritania, he was thereafter deported to Alexandria and cast into the prison of the Castle of Diocletian. Shortly thereafter, having been led out of that prison in the year 557, following continuous disputations in the Praetorium for fifteen days, he was sent to another custody in the Monastery of the Tabennesiotans at Canopus. In the year 564, having been summoned again from Egypt to Constantinople, and because he by no means feared to still defend the Three Chapters in the presence of the Emperor Justinian and Eutychius of Constantinople, he was again placed in custody in a certain monastery of the Royal City: where, after the year 565, he met his final day. He wrote a *Chronicle of events from the foundation of the world until the year 565*, in which year Justin the Younger began his reign. The first part of this Chronicle has perished; the latter part survives, which begins from the year 444 (where Prosper left off) and proceeds to the year 566. It is found edited by Canisius, *Ingolstadt, 1600, in quarto*; a more corrected version, however, appears in both Scaligerian editions of the Chronicle of Eusebius.

<margin>
555.
</margin>

## GERMANUS, a Gaul by birth, son of Eleutherius, born in the territory of Autun <note>original: "Augustodunensi"</note>, was ordained a Deacon in the year 533 by Agrippinus, Bishop of Autun, and thereafter a Priest in the year 536. He was appointed Abbot of Saint Symphorian by Nectarius, the successor of Agrippinus, and was finally created Bishop of Paris in the year 555. In 557, he subscribed to the third Council of Paris; in 560, he was present at the ordination of Siagrius, Bishop of Autun. He died at eighty years of age in the year 576. He wrote, in the year 573, a *Letter to Queen Brunhilde*, demanding that she recall King Sigebert from his plan for war, which he was about to bring against his brother Chilperic. This letter is extant in the Councils, Volume 5, page 923.

<margin>
555.
</margin>

## PELAGIUS, a Roman by birth, son of John Vicarianus, a Deacon of the Roman Church, served as the *Apocrisiarius* <term>Apocrisiarius: a high-ranking diplomatic representative or legate of the Pope</term> of Popes Agapetus, Silverius, and Vigilius at Constantinople before the Emperor. First sent by Agapetus in 535, he immediately entered into the greatest favor with Justinian and the entire Imperial court. Around the year 539, along with the Patriarchs Ephrem of Antioch and Peter of Jerusalem, he was appointed by the Emperor Justinian as a judge for Paul, Patriarch of Alexandria, who had been banished to Gaza shortly before on account of the murder of a deacon. Pelagius, therefore, making his journey through Antioch and Jerusalem, removed Paul from his see at Gaza. Returning to Constantinople, he encountered on the road certain Palestinian monks who were approaching Justinian to suppress the audacity of the rioting Origenists <note>original: "Origenistarum", followers of the controversial theologian Origen</note> by obtaining an edict. Earnestly requested by them, he freely promised to place his efforts at the disposal of the court: which he indeed accomplished so successfully that in the year 541 he obtained from the Emperor an edict condemning the Origenists. Around the year 545 he returned to Rome, whether recalled by Vigilius or sent back by Justinian, so that—having brought with him a great weight of money—he might come to the aid of Rome, which was then in peril, as he indeed did. In 547, he was sent as an envoy by the Roman citizens to Totila, King of the Goths, that he might turn away the arms of the barbarian king from the City with his prayers. Pelagius indeed failed in his wish in this matter, yet shortly after the City was captured by Totila, he obtained the gift of the lives and liberty of many citizens for himself; and in the same year, he was sent by Totila as an envoy to Constantinople to establish peace between the Goths and the Romans. In the year 553, he subscribed to the first *Constitution* <note>original: "Constitutum"</note> of Pope Vigilius; as well as to the second, by which the Fifth Synod was confirmed. Finally, in the month of April in the year 555 (556 according to the Catalog of Anastasius), he was ordained Roman Pontiff, after he had purged himself of the crime of the death of Vigilius brought against him <note>Pelagius was accused by some of being involved in the death of his predecessor, Pope Vigilius, who died in Sicily</note>. Once made Pope, he confirmed the Fifth Synod: and he fought strenuously until death with the Western bishops, who had fallen into schism because of the Three Chapters being condemned by the Roman See. He died in the year 559 (561 accord-

<margin>555.</margin>
CYRIL, a Palestinian by birth and a citizen of Scythopolis, began to profess the monastic life in his home city in the sixteenth year of his age. Later, led by a desire to visit the holy places, he traveled to Jerusalem and, by his mother's command, entrusted himself to the direction of John the Silent <term>John the Silent: a saintly bishop who resigned his see to live as a simple monk in total silence</term>; by whom he was finally sent to the very famous Great Laura Monastery and was admitted among the monks by Abbot Leontius, who took charge of the monastery in the year 542. He flourished in the year 557, when he wrote the *Life of Saint John the Silent*. It is not clear when he died. He wrote the *Life of Saint Euthymius the Abbot*, who died in the year 472. This *Life* exists, but was altered by Metaphrastes <note>original: "Metaphraste"; Simeon Metaphrastes was a 10th-century Byzantine author who rewrote older saint lives in a more polished style, often losing original details</note>, in Greek and Latin in Cotelerius's *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume 2, page 200; in Latin in Surius, January 20th. There also exists the *Life of Saint John the Silent* written by him, in Greek and Latin, edited by Henschen and Papebroch for May 13th; in Latin in Surius, May 13th. Finally, he wrote the *Life of Saint Sabas*, which still lies hidden in Greek among the *Lives* of Simeon Metaphrastes, but is found in Latin (altered by him) in Surius, December 5th. Bollandus provided an ancient Latin version of that *Life*, not yet corrupted by Metaphrastes, for January 20th. Having finally obtained the complete and authentic Greek text, the distinguished Cotelerius published it with a translation and notes in his *Monuments*, Volume 3, page 220.

<margin>* Concerning the deeds of Justinian, book 5.</margin>
PAUL CYRUS FLORUS, son of Cyrus, illustrious by the nobility of his family, called *The Silentiary* <term>Silentiarius: a high-ranking court official in Byzantium responsible for maintaining order and silence in the imperial palace</term> from the office he held, flourished around the year 555. He excelled in the art of poetry and described the Temple of *Saint Sophia* <note>Hagia Sophia in Constantinople</note>, recently founded by Justinian, in a lengthy poem. Charles Du Fresne <note>also known as Du Cange, a pioneering 17th-century scholar of Byzantine history</note> first brought it to light in Greek and Latin and illustrated it with very rich annotations in *Paris, 1670, folio*, at the end of the *History of Cinnamus*. Agathias says *, "He also wrote very many other poems worthy of mention and praise. However, it seems to me that those he wrote about the Temple are filled with all the more labor and knowledge as the subject itself is more wonderful." The distinguished Du Fresne echoes Agathias, judging that Paul approached the description of the Sophian building with such accuracy that whoever reads it immediately grasps the entire structure and its individual parts with their eyes, so to speak, as well as their mind.

<margin>555.</margin>
AGNELLUS, born of a noble house and wealthy in status; after the death of his wife, he was made a Deacon by the Archbishop of the People of Ravenna (who died in the year 542) and was placed in charge of the Temple of Saint Agatha. Finally, after the death of Maximian in the year 555, he was appointed Archbishop of the People of Ravenna. Through the mediation of Narses, Justinian's general, he obtained all the goods of the Goths for the use of the Church of Ravenna; he purged the temples built by the Arians <term>Arians: a Christian sect that disagreed with the orthodox view of the Trinity; they were prominent among the Gothic rulers of Italy</term> and defiled by their rites, and converted them to the true worship of God. He died on the first day of August <note>original: "Calendis Sextilibus"</note> in the year 556, at the age of 94. Girolamo Rossi <note>original: "Hieronymus Rubeus"</note> has many things to say about him in his *History of Ravenna*, book 3, page 169. He wrote an *Epistle to Arminius on the Nature of the Faith*, which is found in the *Antidote against Heresies*, *Basel, 1528*, in the *Heresiology of Basel*, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 8, page 666.

<margin>The great Eutychius, Archbishop of Constantinople, my whole honor and sacred head. <note>original Greek: Ὁ μέγας Εὐτύχιος ὁ ἀρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, ἡ μοὶ πᾶσα τιμὴ καὶ ἱερὰ κεφαλή.</note></margin>
<margin>6th Century from the Year of Our Lord</margin>
...began to be known. 3rd: He seems to have flourished under Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople. For he speaks of him thus: *The great Eutychius, Archbishop of Constantinople, a sacred head to be revered by me in all things.* <note>original: "Ὁ μέγας Εὐτύχιος Ἀρχιεπίσκοπος CP. venerandum mihi in omnibus, sacrumq; caput."</note> He flourished, therefore, around the year 560, or at least not long thereafter; and accordingly, Casimir Oudin <note>A French bibliographer and former monk known for his history of ecclesiastical writers.</note> is mistaken, for in his brief chronology of Labbe, he places him nearly a whole century later. He wrote a book *On the State of the Departed*, in order to refute those who say that human souls do not act as soon as they are released from their own bodies. Photius <note>The 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and author of the *Bibliotheca*, a collection of summaries of books he had read.</note> once read this and took some excerpts from it. Leo Allatius was the first to bring it out of the shadows and adorn it with a Latin version—though the end is mutilated—and he included it in his book *On the Perpetual Consensus of the Western and Eastern Churches on the Dogma of Purgatory, Rome 1655, in octavo,* from page 319 to 581. Mireus and his copyist Oudin are in error, however, when they affirm from Photius that our Eustratius wrote three treatises on the souls of the departed; for Photius says nothing else <margin>Codex 171.</margin> than that Eustratius had three primary intentions in mind for this work, about which he informs the reader in the same place. Regarding his style, Photius says this: *Careful in his condensed phrasing, with very imaginative reasoning, yet his speech is clear.* <note>original Greek: Φράσει δὲ συγκεκλεισμένῃ ἐπιμελὴς λογισμοῖς δὲ λίαν φαντοῖς, σαφὴς δ᾽ ὁ λόγος.</note> He used a style that was not at all praiseworthy, but arguments that were not much to be blamed; nevertheless, the diction itself is clear. Furthermore, Oudin ascribes to our Eustratius the *Commentaries on Aristotle's Posterior Analytics* (published in Greek at Venice in 1534) and those on *Aristotle's Ethics* (published in Greek there in 1536); he could have learned from the title of the books alone that they belong to Eustratius, Metropolitan of Nicaea, and do not pertain to our author. Not to mention what Gesner suggests: that in some titles of books of this kind, the name of Eustathius should be substituted for Eustratius.

<margin>560.</margin>
SIMPLICIUS, a disciple of Saint Benedict, was appointed the third Abbot of the Monastery of Monte Cassino after the death of Constantinus in the year 560. A most shining exemplar of piety and all virtues, he died in the year 576. He handed down the Rule of his Master to be read and kept everywhere in the dwellings of the religious; moreover, excelling in poetic skill himself, he explained its wider promulgation in verse. Lucas Holstenius published these poems together with various Monastic Rules in *Paris, 1663.*

<margin>560. Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 3, Chapter 4.</margin>
COLUMBA, Irish by birth, flourished in the year 560, in which he founded the Monastery of Dearmach <note>Now known as Durrow.</note> in the midlands of Ireland. In the year 565, however, to avoid the danger that threatened his life from King Dermitius, he crossed over to Britain and preached the word of God to the Northern Picts; and on the island of Iona, called *Hu* and *Y-Columb-kill*, he established a monastery, over which he himself presided as Abbot. He died on the 5th day before the Ides of June <note>June 9th.</note> in the year 597, at the age of 77, and was buried in his church at Iona. <margin>* On Irish Writers, Book 1, page 15.</margin> The distinguished Ware * catalogs his writings in this manner: namely, the *Monastic Rule*, which survives and is commonly called *Columb-kill*; a *Hymn in praise of Saint Kieran the Abbot*; and three other *Hymns*, the first of which begins *Altus Prosator* <note>"High Creator."</note>. There was another Columbanus, also Irish, who flourished at the end of this century, whom we shall discuss below.

VENANTIUS HONORIUS CLEMENTIANUS FORTUNATUS, an Italian by birth, was born in the village called Duplabilis, not far from the city of Treviso, but was nurtured in the study of fine letters at Ravenna. Before the year 560, having been delivered from severe eye pains by the aid of Blessed Martin, he left Italy and set out for Gaul to show a sign of his gratitude, visiting the relics of Saint Martin deposited in the city of Tours. In the year 565, he offered his prayers for every blessing on the marriage of King Sigebert and Brunhilda in an elegiac poem. ### WORKS.

Eleven books of poems, with a dedicatory letter to Gregory of Tours prefixed.

*Hodæporicon* <note>original: "Hodæporicon", a Greek-derived term for a poem describing a journey.</note> to the Emperor Justin the Younger and Empress Sophia Augusta.

There is a just reason to doubt whether the latter two *Lives* have Fortunatus as their author, though it cannot be doubted that he wrote Lives of that kind. But these seem to have been substituted for the genuine ones, which have perished. D’Achery <note>A French Benedictine scholar.</note> published the *Life of St. Medard* written in prose in *Spicilegium, Vol. VIII*.

**MARTIN**, a Pannonian by birth, as a young man sought out Jerusalem to visit the holy places. Sailing from there, he arrived in Galicia, a province of Hither Spain; there, after many of the Suebi <note>A Germanic people who had established a kingdom in the Iberian Peninsula.</note> people were converted to the Catholic faith, he founded various monasteries. He himself presided over the one at Dumio, which he founded, until about the year 560, when he was elevated to the Bishopric of the Church of Braga. In the year 563, he took part in the Second Council of Braga; he presided over the Third Council of Braga.

* Gregory of Tours, *History*, book 3, ch. 37.

He died, according to Baronius <note>A 16th-century cardinal and historian.</note>, in the year 583. However, since it is clear from Gregory of Tours that he held the see for thirty years, more or less, it must be that he either became Bishop earlier or lived longer. But in the year 589, his successor Pantidus signed the Third Council of Toledo; thus, either Gregory must be thought to have calculated the number of years in a round and loose sense, or Martin's episcopate must be placed a little before the year 560. He was indeed a very learned man, who had so steeped himself in literature—as witnessed by Gregory of Tours, his <term>contemporary <note>original Greek: συγχρόνῳ (synchrōnō)</note></term>—that he was considered second to none in his time. Venantius Fortunatus fills both pages with his praises in book 5.

In this collection, it is not unworthy of note that the *Apostolic Canons* are not cited by Martin. ANASTASIUS, called "Sinaita" from the monastic life he led on Mount Sinai, was promoted to the dignity of the Patriarchate of Antioch in the year 561. He strenuously and constantly defended orthodox doctrine and most strongly fought against the delusions of the Emperor Justinian regarding the "incorruptibility" of Christ's body. <note>Justinian, in his later years, fell into the heresy of Aphthartodocetism, which claimed Christ's body was incapable of decay or suffering from the moment of conception.</note> For this reason, Justinian intended to send him into exile, which he was unable to carry out, being snatched away by a sudden death. At that time, such great zeal for untainted religion and such fame shone in Anastasius that all the Eastern Bishops, ordered by Justinian's decree to subscribe to his heresy, responded with one voice that they were waiting for Anastasius's opinion and would follow in his footsteps. Truly, Anastasius himself could be led by no threats and no prayers to betray the faith even slightly. In the year 570, the Emperor Justin accused Anastasius of pouring out sacred money for profane uses, of insulting him, and finally of criticizing John Scholasticus for unjustly seizing the see of Eutychius of Constantinople; he cast him down from the throne of Antioch. He was only restored to his see 23 years later, in 592, after the death of Gregory, who had been substituted in his place. He died in the year 599. <margin>* Book 4, chapter 40.</margin> Evagrius says \*, "He was a man most learned in divine matters, precise in his conduct and way of life, so as to reprove even the slightest faults, and never let a profane thought pass by, nor fail to bridle his tongue, so that his speech was measured and his silence was better than speech." <note>original Greek: τὰ θεῖα εἰς τὸ μάλιστα λογιθ., ἀκριβὴς ἧ τῆς τεζῶτος κὶ τῶ δίαιταν, ὡς κὶ τοῖς λίαν ψιλοῖς ἐπισκήπτειν, κὶ μηδαμῶ ἢ ἐννοίας ἐκ βεβήλω παρεξιέναι, μήτη ἢ γλώσσαν χαλινῶς ἐπείχειν, ὡς κὶ ἳ λόγον ῥυθμίζεσθαι, κὶ τώ σιωπιώ κρείττονα λόγε καθεσάναι.</note> And indeed, in serious conversations, he had open ears and a flowing tongue, and he solved proposed questions prudently and sharply; but in foolish and superfluous talk, he kept his ears entirely closed and restrained his tongue as if by a bridle, so that reason measured his speech, and silence was more excellent than any speech.

*The Guide* (or *Hodegos*) against the <term>Acephali</term> <note>literally "the headless ones"; a sect of Monophysites who rejected the Council of Chalcedon.</note>. That work seems to be patched together from various short works of Anastasius himself as well as some of the Ancients, as will be clear to anyone who reads the first four chapters attentively; not only that, but it has been significantly altered by some more recent hand. There, he asks pardon from his readers for the various corrections applied here and there, and for the tautologies <note>repetitive phrasing</note> often committed, since the frequency of his illnesses did not allow him to work on them according to his own mind's judgment. *Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron, in 11 books.* <note>The "Hexaemeron" refers to the six days of creation; "anagogical" refers to a spiritual or mystical interpretation.</note> Published in Latin in 1609. Because the twelfth book had been suppressed until now—either due to the rarity of manuscript copies or through the deceit of the Papists—<unclear>Allix</unclear> saw to its publication in Greek and Latin in London, 1682, in quarto.

*Five Dogmatic Orations, namely: On the Holy Trinity. On the Uncircumscribed. On the Divine Incarnation.* (A book *On the Economy of Christ* survives in a Greek manuscript in the Arundel Library, now transferred to Gresham College.) *On the Passion and Impassibility of Christ. On His Resurrection.* These were issued in Latin, translated by Godefroy Tilmann, *Paris 1556, in octavo*, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Paris 1575, 1589. Translated by Turrianus, *Ingolstadt 1616, in quarto*. All the works of Anastasius enumerated so far are included in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 9, at the end.

*Two Homilies on the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary*, which Joannes Meursius published in Greek among his *Sacred Miscellany*, *Leiden 1619, in quarto*.

*Homily on the Holy Communion, and on Not Judging.* Greek and Latin, with the *Hodegos* <note>original: "Ὁδηγῷ" — The "Guide" or "Manual," Anastasius's most famous polemical work against heresies.</note> 16...

*Homily on the Sixth Psalm.* These two homilies were issued in Greek and Latin, *Ingolstadt 1603, in quarto*.

*Another Homily on the same [Psalm].*

*Homily on the Transfiguration of Our Lord Jesus Christ.* These six homilies are available in Latin, edited by François Combefis in the *New Addition, 1648, Volume 1, page 850.*

*Treatise on the Three Holy Lents*, regarding how they are to be observed and that those who transgress them violate the law. It exists in Greek and Latin with <unclear>notes</unclear> among Cotelier’s *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume 3, page 425.

## LOST WORKS.

<margin>* Book 4, ch. 40.</margin>
*A Valedictory Oration to the People of Antioch*, delivered when he had received Emperor Justinian’s mandate for his exile; *which one rightly loves*, says Evagrius <note>Evagrius Scholasticus, a 6th-century church historian.</note>, <note>original: "ὃς ἔτη δικαίως ἀγαπᾷ"</note> *for its beauty of expression, the strength of its thoughts, or the richness of the sacred words, and its lack of anything unbefitting or mediocre.* <note>original: "τῇ τε καλλιεπείᾳ, τῇ τε ῥώμῃ τῶν νοημάτων, ἢ τῇ εὐπορίᾳ τῶν ἱερῶν ῥήσεων, καὶ τὸ ἀπρόσφορον ἢ ἰσοκλεές."</note>

*An Oration delivered to the same people when he inaugurated his Episcopal duties.*

*An Oration delivered to the same people when he returned from exile.* Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century historian who summarized earlier works.</note> praises both in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, ch. 44.

*A Dissertation on the Sabbath addressed to Simeon, Bishop of Bostra*, of which some fragments are found in the Second Council of Nicaea, Action 4, Council Volume 7, p. 248.

*A Letter to a certain Scholar* <note>original: "Scholasticum" — likely a lawyer or a highly educated official.</note>, in which he answered a question beginning with, *“If wisdom shall be reckoned to one who only makes a show of wisdom.”* <note>original: "Ἐὶ τῷ μόνον ἐπιφαίνοντι σοφίαν σοφία λογισθήσεται"</note> Several excerpts are held in the same place.

*A Book to Emperor Justinian against the dogma proposed by him concerning the incorruptibility of Christ’s body*, <note>This refers to Aphthartodocetism, the belief that Christ's body was immune to decay from the moment of conception, a doctrine Justinian attempted to enforce late in his reign.</note> mentioned by Evagrius in the place cited above.

*Against the book of John Philoponus called "The Arbiter"*, <note>original: "Διαιτητὴν" — John Philoponus was a Christian philosopher and scientist often accused of Tritheism (belief in three gods).</note> a short work, of which an excerpt translated into Latin by Turrianus was provided by Gretser in the preface to the *Guide* <note>original: "Ὁδηγὸν" (Hodegos)</note> edited by him.

<margin>564.</margin>
### JOHN SCHOLASTICUS,

called *Climacus* <note>From the Greek "Klimax," meaning ladder.</note> from the book he wrote, and *Sinaita* from the mountain where he lived; he flourished around the year 564. He lived the monastic life and shone among the leading ascetics of that age in learning and piety. At last, having become the Abbot of the monks dwelling on Mount Sinai—perhaps also of the monastery which Emperor Justinian placed at the foot of the mountain <note>Now known as Saint Catherine's Monastery.</note>—he reached extreme old age, and (if the Greek Menalogion <note>A liturgical book containing biographies of saints.</note> is to be believed) died at nearly a hundred years old on the 30th of day of March.

---

## WRITINGS.

*The Ladder of Paradise*, addressed to John, Abbot of the Monastery of Raithu; it consists of 30 chapters, which serve as steps or ladders by which one ascends to the peak of religious perfection. It was published in Latin from the version by Ambrogio Traversari <note>original: "Ambrosii Camaldulensis"</note> at *Venice*, 1531, 1569; *Cologne*, 1583; with the commentaries of Denis the Carthusian, *Cologne*, 1540. Also in Latin in the same place, 1601, in octavo. Finally, Matthäus Rader published it in Greek and Latin, along with the Greek-Latin Scholia <note>explanatory notes</note> of Elias, Metropolitan of Crete, at *Paris*, 1633, in folio.

*The Book to the Pastor*, frequently printed from the Latin version of Ambrogio Traversari, and given in Greek and Latin with the Scholia of Elias of Crete by the same Rader at the end of the *Ladder of Paradise*. Both works, translated into the vulgar or "Barbaric-Greek" language <note>Early Modern Greek.</note> by Maximos Margunios, Bishop of Kythira, were published at *Venice*, 1590.

<margin>564.</margin>
### JOHN SCHOLASTICUS,

a Syrian by birth, born in the village of Sirimis in the region of Cynegica within the territory of Antioch; he was first a Priest of Antioch and handled business in Constantinople as the <term>Apocrisiarius<note>An ecclesiastical envoy or representative, acting as a liaison between a bishop and the imperial court.</note></term> of that church. In the year 564, after Eutychius was deposed, he was made Patriarch of the Royal City <note>Constantinople.</note>. In the year 578, a little before the return of Eutychius, he passed away.

---

## WRITINGS.

*A Collection of Canons*, digested into 50 titles, arranged solely by subject matter. The 85 Canons of the Apostles are inserted into this collection. John completed this while he was still a Priest of Antioch. There are some, however, who attribute it to Theodoret, though they are supported by not even the slightest shadow of a reason.

The *Nomocanon* <term>Nomocanon: A collection of ecclesiastical laws (canons) and imperial civil laws (nomos) arranged by subject.</term>, which, in addition to a certain summary of the Collection of Canons, notes civil laws that are in agreement with the canons. It is not unlikely that this *Nomocanon* was composed by John while he was already Patriarch.

### Ecclesiastical Chapters.

These small works are available in Greek and Latin, first published by Henri Justel and Guillaume Voël in the *Library of Canon Law* (Paris, 1662), Volume II, pages 499, 603, and 660.

<margin>* Codex 75.</margin>
John moreover wrote a *Catechetical Oration on the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity*, mentioned by Photius <note>Photius (c. 810–893), Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who cataloged hundreds of ancient books.</note> in his *Codex*, which John Philoponus <note>A Christian Neoplatonist philosopher often accused of "Tritheism" (the belief in three distinct gods).</note> refuted in a specific work. That Oration has long since perished.

<margin>570.</margin>
GREGORY, first a monk, then a Byzantine Abbot, and later, during the reign of Justin, appointed head of the Monastery of Mount Sinai; finally, after Anastasius was deposed by the Emperor in the year 570, he was elevated to the Patriarchate of Antioch. In the year 589, he was falsely accused of incest and other crimes by certain citizens of Antioch, and was summoned to Constantinople to plead his case before a Synod, where he was acquitted after the facts were examined. Shortly after his return, he restrained and brought back to order the Roman army which was rioting in the East, having delivered a speech to the soldiers, with whom he was very popular. He died in the year 592.

<margin>* Book 5, ch. 6.</margin>
He was a man <note>original: "τὴν γνώμην κὶ ἀρετὴν ψυχῆς πάντα ἐν πᾶσι κράτιςος, κὶ εἴ τις ὅτι ὁσιώτατος, ἐξαιρετικώτατός"</note> "who in his judgment and the virtue of his soul was best in all things and among all, and if anyone was most holy, he was most excellent," says Evagrius <note>Evagrius Scholasticus, the 6th-century historian who served as Gregory's legal advisor.</note>, who pursues his praises at length. The *Oration delivered to the rebellious soldiers* is extant in Evagrius, Book 6, ch. 12; and with the words changed but the meaning mostly preserved, in Nicephorus, Book 18, ch. 15. There is also a *Homily on the Women Bearing Ointments* (the Myrrh-bearers) under his name, in Greek and Latin, in Combefis’s *New Supplement* (Paris, 1648), Volume I. Finally, Evagrius himself reveals in Book 6, ch. 24, that in two lost volumes of his own letters, reports, and speeches, almost all the small works were written in the name of our Gregory.

---

<margin>573.</margin>
GEORGE FLORENTIUS GREGORY <note>Better known to history as Gregory of Tours.</note>, a native of Auvergne of noble birth—his father being Florentius and his mother Armentaria, the niece of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Langres—was born in the year 544. Educated in fine literature by Gallus, Bishop of Auvergne, he moved to Tours in 566; he was ordained a Deacon in 569, and at last, on August 23, 573, he became Archbishop of Tours, having been designated as successor by Bishop Euphronius before his death. In the following year, he dedicated an Oratory in the city of Tours, in which he placed the relics of many saints. In 577, he took part in the Council of Paris and bravely defended Praetextatus, Bishop of Rouen, who had been accused by King Chilperic. In 580, he was falsely informed against to Chilperic on the charge that he had said Queen Fredegund was accustomed to have illicit relations with Bertram, Bishop of Bordeaux; he was summoned to the Synod of Berny, and after he had cleared himself by oath, he was acquitted. In that same Synod, he brought King Chilperic—who was leaning toward Sabellianism <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different "modes" or masks of a single person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>—back to a sound mind by the force of his arguments. Furthermore, in that same year, being challenged by Agilan, an Arian <note>Arianism: The belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal or of the same substance as God the Father.</note> and envoy of Leuvigild, King of the Goths in Spain, to King Chilperic, he entered into a debate and remarkably rebuffed the heretic’s insolence. He undertook a similar contest with Oppila, an envoy of the same King passing through Tours, on Easter Sunday in 584. In 585, he steadfastly defended Theodore, Bishop of Marseille, who was insulted by King Guntram on account of the death inflicted upon Chilperic, in the city of Orléans. In 588, he was sent by King Childebert to Guntram at Metz to treat with him on various matters, both civil and ecclesiastical. In 590, he held a debate with one of his own priests who denied the resurrection, and freed the poor little fellow from that most wretched error. In 594, he set out for Rome to visit Pope Gregory and the thresholds of the Apostles. Having returned home, he died on November 17, 595, at the age of 52, in the 22nd year of his episcopate. He was a man not unlearned for the age in which he lived, but one in whom you might not undeservedly find judgment and sharp insight lacking. His simplicity was noted long ago by

<margin>* Letter to Emperor Louis.</margin>
Abbot Hilduin. <note>Hilduin (c. 775–840), Abbot of Saint-Denis.</note> "We must be indulgent," he says, <note>original: "Parcendum est... fimplicitati viri religiofi; quis multa aliter, quàm fe veritas habeat, æftimans, non calliditatis aftu, fed benignitate fimplicitatis voto, literis commendavit."</note> "toward the simplicity of this religious man; for he, judging many things to be otherwise than the truth holds them, committed them to writing not out of crafty deceit, but out of a devoutly kind simplicity."

## EXTANT WORKS.

<note>Gregory of Tours (c. 538–594) was a Gallo-Roman historian and the Bishop of Tours, whose writings are the primary source for Merovingian history.</note>

*Ten Books of History or Annals of the Franks*, covering events very briefly from the beginning of the world to the founding of the Frankish Monarchy, and then describing events copiously up to the year of Christ 591. Gregory died while still engaged in this work <note>original: "immortuus"</note>, leaving it unfinished at the end. Charles Le Cointe <note>An 17th-century French ecclesiastical historian.</note> (*Annals of the Franks*, Vol. I, at the years 417, 544, 545, 567, 572, 576, 580, and elsewhere) not only frequently complains that the common copies of this work are remarkably corrupted, but proves it with infinite examples; after André Du Chesne and Adrien de Valois, Le Cointe diligently compared these books against five manuscript codices of better quality. This *History* was published in Paris, 1552; Basel, 1568 in octavo; and Paris, 1610 in octavo. However, André Du Chesne labored to ensure it appeared in its most corrected form, including it in the first volume of the *Frankish Writers* (Paris, 1636).

*Eight Books of Miracles, namely:*

*Four books On the Virtues and Miracles of Saint Martin, begun before the year 590 and finally completed in the year 595.*

*Two books On the Glory of the Martyrs, written around the year 590.*

*A book On the Glory of the Confessors, written in the year 595.*

*These seven books were published at Cologne, 1583, in octavo.*

*A book On the Lives of the Fathers, or on the lives of certain most blessed men, begun around the year 590 and completed in 595. It is available together with the History (Paris, 1522).*

*A small book on the life and death of the Seven Sleepers, addressed to Sulpitius, Archbishop of Bourges. It was published in Paris, 1501 and 1640.*

<margin>* On Writers, chapter 49.</margin>
*An Epitome of the deeds of the Franks, prepared before the more detailed History was written, according to the testimony of Sigebert \*. It is contained in the Body of Ancient Frankish History (Hanau, 1613).*

*All the works of Gregory were published in the Library of the Fathers, Vol. XI, pages 707, 831, 896, 932, 959.*

### LOST WORKS.

A *Commentary on the Psalms*, of which two fragments are presented by Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon (1632–1707), a Benedictine monk and founder of the disciplines of palaeography and diplomatics.</note> in his *Analecta*, Vol. I, page 7.

A book *On Ecclesiastical Courses* <note>A work describing how to determine the times for prayer and liturgy by observing the stars.</note>.

---

<margin>579.</margin>

PELAGIUS II, a Roman by birth and son of Winigild, was ordained Roman Pontiff on the 26th day of November in the year 579. He was allotted a truly difficult province to govern, with a schism consuming the Church from within and the hand of barbarians devastating it from without. For the Lombards were plundering all of Italy and even surrounding Rome itself in a tight siege; moreover, the greatest part of the Western Bishops had separated themselves from communion with the Roman Church because of the "Three Chapters" <term>Three Chapters: A major theological controversy involving the condemnation of three 5th-century authors; many Western bishops viewed this condemnation as an attack on the Council of Chalcedon.</term> condemned by the popes. 

To restrain the former, he sent Gregory the Deacon <note>The future Pope Gregory the Great.</note> as an envoy in the year 583 to the Emperor Tiberius to beg for reinforcements; to bring back the latter, he acted first with arguments and writings, and then with force and arms. After he had fruitlessly attempted to reach Elias and Severus of Aquileia and other bishops of Istria with frequent letters, he turned to the "civil sword." Drawing Smaragdus, the Exarch of Ravenna, to his side around the year 586, he caused Severus and the leading bishops of Istria to be seized by an armed force and compelled to enter into communion. 

In the year 589, when John of Constantinople <note>Known as John the Faster.</note> had arranged for the title of "Ecumenical Patriarch" <term>Ecumenical Patriarch: A title implying universal jurisdiction, which the Popes in Rome saw as a challenge to their own authority.</term> (which he had seized for himself) to be confirmed by a synodal decree at a Synod held in Constantinople at the start of the year, Pelagius roared in protest. He sent letters decreeing that the acts of the Synod be nullified by his authority, and threatened John with anathema unless he relinquished the haughty title. He died of the "groin-wasting" plague <note>original: "tabe inguinari"—referring to the bubonic plague which caused swellings (buboes) in the groin.</note> on the 4th day of February in the year 590. There exist under his name ten Letters and six Decrees (taken from Gratian) in the *Collection of Councils*, Vol. V, page 931. The editors of the Councils themselves acknowledge that the 1st letter (to Archbishop Benignus), the 2nd (to the Bishops of Italy), the 8th (to the Fathers of the Synod of Constantinople held under John), and the 9th (to the Bishops of Germany and Gaul) are spurious.

# 424 The Eutychian Age.
<header>The Eutychian Age.</header>

<margin>6th CENTURY from the Year of Our Lord 580.</margin> **THEOPHANES**, a Byzantine by birth, seems to have flourished around the year 580, if indeed he lived at the time when he concluded his History; unless we should rather conclude that he was the same person as Theophanes the Confessor (who flourished in the year 780), though this seems unlikely. He wrote an account of the wars waged between the Romans and the Persians from the year 567 to 573, encompassing the history of that time in ten books. Furthermore, he narrated the deeds done under Justinian and even after the year 573 in certain other books of History which Photius <note>Photius (c. 810–893) was the Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar whose "Bibliotheca" or "Myriobiblos" preserves summaries of many lost ancient works.</note> did not see, though he mentioned them. Of the ten books mentioned above, Photius preserved certain excerpts for us in Code 64, which are also found with the notes of Labbe among the *Excerpts of Embassies* (Paris, 1647, folio).

<margin>581.</margin> **MARIUS**, Bishop of the see of Aventicum <note>Modern Avenches, Switzerland.</note> among the Helvetians (which was later transferred to Lausanne), flourished around the year 581. He was present at the Second Council of Mâcon held in the year 585. He spent twenty years and eight months in his Bishopric and died in the 64th year of his age, as noted by Casimir Oudin; who, as is his habit, suppresses the author's name and copies everything he has regarding this author from Miraeus. Marius composed a *Chronicle* from the year 455, where Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a 5th-century Christian writer and disciple of St. Augustine.</note> left off, up to the year 581. It is extant in André Du Chesne’s *Frankish Writers*, Volume I, page 210.

<margin>581.</margin> **EULOGIUS**, a primary Priest of the Church of Antioch and head of the sanctuary of the Holy Mother of God <note>original: "S. Deiparæ"</note>, and finally Patriarch of Alexandria from the year 581. He was a most bitter enemy of Heretics and a most valiant champion of the Catholic faith. He died in the year 608. He wrote many things, namely:
*A Homily on Palm Sunday*, also attributed to Saint Cyril of Alexandria; it is extant in Greek and Latin with notes by Combefis in the *New Supplement*, Volume I, page 652.
*Six books against the Heresiarch Novatus regarding ecclesiastical administration*, excerpts of which Photius provides in Code 182 and 208.
*Two books against the heretics Timothy and Severus*, in defense of the Letter of Pope Leo to Flavian of Constantinople. Photius displays very extensive portions of these in Code 225.
*A book against Theodosius and Severus, who attacked Saint Leo with insults and slanders*, of which you may find excerpts in Photius, Code 226.
*An Invective Oration or "Pillorying Speech"* <note>original: "Λόγον Στηλιτευτικὸν" — a formal speech intended to publicly denounce or shame an opponent.</note>, *divided into three parts, against the peace entered into between the Theodosians and Gaianites so that they might more fiercely oppose the Catholics*. Fairly ample fragments are extant in Photius, Code 227.
*A Letter to Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople, containing the certainty of piety and the Orthodox faith, which he wrote while still a Priest and inserted into the work mentioned immediately above.*

<margin>* Code 182.</margin> Regarding the style of Eulogius, Photius offers a judgment of this kind: "This man's style, as far as vocabulary is concerned, is somewhat moderately polished, but as for syntax, he often comes close to solecisms <note>grammatical errors or improprieties</note>. Yet he is not unpracticed in the Divine Scriptures, but uses them with insight; he is persuasive for such a style, and is both instructive and sharp-witted." <note>original Greek: "Ἔστι δὲ οὖτος ὁ ἀνὴρ, ὅσα μὲ εἰς λέξιν ἥκει, τὸ μετρίως πως ἐπ' ἔλαττον ἠπεικωσμένος, ὅσα δ' εἰς σύνταξιν, ἐγγύς πολλάκις τῶν σολοικιζόντων ἀφιγμένος· τῇ δὲ θείων οὐκ ἀμελετήτῳ γραφῶν, ἀλλὰ διανοίᾳ αὐταῖς κεχρημένος, πιθανὸς δὲ, ὡς ἐν τοιαύτῃ φράσει, διδασκαλικός τε, καὶ ἀγχίνους."</note> The man's diction, regarding the words, is generally moderately accurate, but in construction it is often not far from a solecism. Nevertheless, he is not unskillful in the Divine Scriptures, whose testimonies he applies successfully and appropriately. He is likewise persuasive, as far as his style allows, and he teaches and pleases.

<margin>581.</margin> **GILDAS**, surnamed *the Wise*, and called *Badonicus* to distinguish him from Gildas Albanius. He was British by race, born in the year 520, a year made famous by the Battle of Badon <note>A legendary battle between the Britons and Anglo-Saxons, often associated in later tradition with King Arthur.</note> (hence his name). He was a disciple of Illtud of Glamorgan and a monk of Bangor, where, after first drinking in the elements of good literature, he devoted himself entirely to the study of Holy Scripture for the sake of teaching the people. Afterwards, having been requested by messengers sent by Americus, King of Ireland (the author of his life, published by Jean du Bois from the Fleury Library, adds—though he is prone to recklessly confusing our Gildas with Gildas Albanius—and by Saint Brigid), he crossed over to Ireland. And (if faith is to be placed in the said Author) he restored the wavering Christian faith in that place to its integrity by converting Pagans, convicting Heretics, and founding Monasteries everywhere, and by restoring piety and good morals...

<summary>This page catalogs four significant 6th-century figures: the Byzantine historian Theophanes, the Swiss chronicler Marius of Avenches, the anti-heretical Patriarch Eulogius of Alexandria, and the British monk Gildas the Wise.</summary>
