# 425 The Eutychian Age.
<header>The Eutychian Age.</header>

<margin>
6th CENTURY
from the Year of Our Lord
</margin>
...preceded others in restoring [monastic life] as much by his voice as by his example. Having finally returned from Ireland, he visited the Monastery of Llancarfan <note>Lancarvanæ; a famous Welsh monastery founded in the 6th century</note>, which had been founded by **Cadoc Ventolugius** <note>Saint Cadoc the Wise, a celebrated Welsh abbot</note>, a man illustrious for the nobility of his lineage and the sanctity of his character; by his own example, he inspired many others renowned for learning to do the same. He wrote in the year 581, according to the testimony of *Radulphus de Diceto* <note>Ralph de Diceto (c. 1120–1202), an English archdeacon and chronicler</note> *, to say nothing now of *Polydore [Vergil], Bale, etc.*, who claim that he died at the age of ninety at Bangor <note>Bannochori; specifically Bangor Is-y-Coed in Wales</note>: although others, including the Reverend *Ussher* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh and a famous chronologist</note> †, date his book to the year 564 and maintain that he died in the year 570. He wrote the *Epistle on the Ruin of Britain, and the Correction of the Ecclesiastical Order*; regarding these works, *John Price* <note>Joannes Prifeus; Sir John Price (1502–1555), a Welsh lawyer and historian who defended the legends of King Arthur</note> has roughly this to say in the final chapter of his *Defense of the History of Britain*: It can be doubted, not without merit, whether these works have *Gildas* as their author or not, partly because he renders British names poorly, and partly because he addresses the kings of the Britons as if they were reigning at one and the same time and were contemporaries; when, however, it is clearly established from history that they succeeded one another in turn. Furthermore, doubt arises from the thick ignorance of British affairs which he betrays everywhere. For it is not to be believed that this is the work of that *Gildas* who is celebrated everywhere by the ancients for having illustrated British affairs in a proper volume, and for having written individual books on the Molmutine laws <note>Legendary laws attributed to the British King Dunvallo Molmutius</note>, on the praises of *Aurelius Ambrosius* <note>A 5th-century leader of the Romano-British against the Saxons</note>, and on the lives of several saints of Britain. For in that book which we have in print, hardly even the smallest part of those matters is presented, and moreover, many things are missing which are cited from *Gildas* by several older historians. Add to this the affected eloquence of this little book, and its often empty chatter, which is utterly foreign to *Gildas*, who was certainly a most serious man; and furthermore, the wagons-full of insults heaped upon the British nation everywhere betray the worst malice of the writer. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that some things from this book are cited under the name of *Gildas* by both *Bede* and *Geoffrey [of Monmouth], and others*; and that this book has long circulated under the name of *Gildas*. However, these points can be conveniently countered by the hostile mind of *Gildas*—which all historians confirm with one voice—on account of the murder of his brother *Hoel* or *Huelinus* perpetrated by King *Arthur*, and his wonderful, yet not pointless, plan to call the Britons back to virtue through the shame of their misdeeds, since he could not do so through teachings: which, if they do not remove the difficulties first raised, certainly lighten them considerably. And indeed (says *Ussher* in his *Theological Library MS, p. 113*), *Bede* confirms that *Gildas*, the historian of the Britons, described their crimes in a mournful speech; from whose work he even inserted entire pages into his own history. Whence *Price* himself, near the end of the cited book, giving the reason why *Arthur* was passed over by *Bede*, says: "From this Gildas he had drawn that error, since he seemed to have read nothing of British affairs himself except what he received from this man." This book of *Gildas* is also cited by *Alcuin* in *Epistle 1 to Æthelhard, Archbishop of Canterbury (volume 1 of the Ancient Readings edited by Henry Canisius, p. 5)*, or to the monks of *Wearmouth*, as it is alleged by *William of Malmesbury* in *book 1 of the Deeds of the Kings of the English, chapter 3*. Therefore, the *Gildas* published by *Polydore* is undoubtedly a fragment of the ancient *Gildas* (says *Leland* <note>John Leland (1503–1552), an English antiquary</note>), but as he adds, "maimed, disjointed, and mutilated"; so much so that if the parent were now restored to life, he would hardly recognize his offspring. These things *Leland* wrote in his *Assertion of Arthur, folio 32*. Forty-two years after *Polydore’s* edition, *John Josselin* <note>Jo. Josselinus (1529–1603), secretary to Archbishop Matthew Parker and an Anglo-Saxon scholar</note> came across two old manuscripts of *Gildas*, one of which formerly belonged to the *Augustinian Library at Canterbury*, written in very strange characters long out of use (having been written more than six hundred years ago); the other was much more recent and written with less care (which nevertheless differed very little from the former), and once belonged to the *Monastery of Glastonbury*. When he compared these with the *Gildas* published by *Polydore*, he found many things that were missing in the printed *Gildas*, both of those which are the author's own, and especially the sacred testimonies which are brought forward here by the author himself for the correction of his nation. He also discovered that *Polydore* had inserted certain small portions of his own sentences; and that he did not replace the sacred testimonies of the Scriptures, which he retained, in the same words in which he found them, but placed some of them taken from the Vulgate version of the Scriptures, even though it appears that *Gildas* used an older edition <note>Original: "vetustiore editione"; referring to the Vetus Latina or Old Latin Bible used before the Vulgate became standard</note>. Therefore, *Josselin*, aided by the authority of the ancient copies, produced *Gildas* so corrected, with the faults removed, in the year 1568, so that not only true, but clearly complete...

The writings of **Gildas** still survive: the *Epistle on the Ruin of Britain* and the *Correction of the Ecclesiastical Order*, found in the *Orthodoxographa* <note>A collection of early Christian writings published in Basel</note> p. 487; in the *Library of the Fathers* Vol. 8, pp. 707, 715; and among the *Minor British Writers* published at Heidelberg, 1587, in folio. Furthermore, **Henry of Huntingdon**, Bale, Price, and several manuscripts attribute to Gildas a *History of the Deeds of the Britons*, which has since been discovered to belong to **Nennius** (about whom see more below under Nennius). **Leland** <note>John Leland (1503–1552), the "father of English local history"</note> believes there was another Gildas, a poet, distinct from ours, who rendered the poetic book of *Merlin of the Woods* into verse and wrote several books of *Epigrams* which were, in the judgment of **Giraldus** [Cambrensis], not without elegance. **Geoffrey of Monmouth** <note>Galfridus Cambrensis; the text likely refers to Geoffrey of Monmouth, author of the "History of the Kings of Britain"</note> wove many of his verses into the first book of the *History of Britain*, though the author's name was either unknown or suppressed. Perhaps he could reasonably be considered the same as **Gildas Albanius**, who became famous for many writings, and among them poems, at the beginning of this century, and who is discussed by Bale in Century 1, Chapter 50.

**EVANTUS**, or **Evantius**, first an Abbot, and then—according to **Christopher Brower** <note>A Jesuit historian (1559–1617)</note> and others (though I would not rashly assert it as certain)—Bishop of Vienne in Gaul, flourished around the year 581. **JOHN**, a Cappadocian by birth, called the **"Faster"** <note>original Greek: νηστευτὴς (Nēsteutēs)</note> because of the astounding abstinence to which he accustomed himself; at first he lived a private life and worked in a respectable trade, but later, on account of the outstanding virtues for which he shone—"a man who was a dwelling-place of virtue" <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ ἀρετῆς οἰκετήριον (anēr aretēs oikētērion); cited from Sophronius in Photius</note>—he was promoted to higher things. In the year 589, at a Synod held in Constantinople regarding the case of **Gregory of Antioch** (at which all the Eastern Patriarchs were present either in person or through legates), John assumed for himself the title of **Ecumenical Patriarch**. Even if we grant, along with the most recent editors of the Councils, that the letter of Pelagius found in the *Volumes of the Councils* is a forgery, it is nonetheless attested to us beyond controversy by **Gregory the Great** <note>original: *L. 4. ep. 36. & alibi paſſim* (Book 4, Letter 36 and elsewhere throughout)</note> that Pelagius did indeed send letters of this kind, in which he cancelled the Acts of the Synod and most sharply rebuked John for having usurped for himself the proud and pestiferous title of "Ecumenical." <header>The Age of Eutychius <note>This period is named after Eutychius, a Patriarch of Constantinople, though the text here focuses on his successors and contemporaries.</note>.</header>

...once he was appointed, [Pope Gregory the Great] raged almost to the point of hoarseness in nearly every letter against this unspeakable, proud, and Antichristian title. Despite this, John constantly retained the title once he had seized it; and as is clear from Gregory's letter to Sabinian <note>Sabinian was Gregory's representative in Constantinople and later succeeded him as Pope</note>, in the records concerning John the Presbyter sent to Rome, John named himself "Ecumenical Patriarch" <note>original: "Oecumenicum Patriarcham"; a title implying universal authority that deeply offended the Roman papacy</note> in almost every line. He died around the year 596 and was enrolled in the number of the Saints by the Greeks.

->He wrote several works, which follow.<-

*Homily on Repentance, Continence, and Virginity*, which is quite lengthy, or rather, a *Parænetic <note>An advisory or exhortatory letter</note> Letter to a certain Virgin devoted to God*. It exists in Greek and Latin among the works of *Chrysostom*, Volume 5 of Morell’s edition, and Volume 7 of Savile’s edition.

*Homily on False Prophets and False Teachers*, which is commonly ascribed to Chrysostom and held among his works in Volume 5 of Morell’s edition and Volume 7 of Savile’s edition. However, Vossius and Pearson <note>Gerhard Johann Vossius and John Pearson, prominent 17th-century scholars</note> believe it belongs to our John.

*The Penitential Book, or the Order to be observed toward those who confess their sins*, in Greek and Latin, edited by Morin <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French theologian</note> in the Appendix to his book *On Repentance*, page 77.

*Tractate or Sermon on Confession and Repentance*, in Greek and Latin, ibid. page 91. Morin seems to doubt somewhat whether this is truly by our John, or rather extracted from his *Penitential*. However, the title of the manuscript codex bears the name of *John the Faster*; nor could any righteous suspicion of forgery be found in it.

Morin also collected in the same place various excerpts from our John’s *Penitential* which are found among the ancients, ibid. page 98. His *Canon* regarding various disturbances that can occur, which indeed seems to be part of the *Penitential*, is held in a Greek manuscript in the Augsburg Library, Shelf 2, Codex 30, according to Anton Reifer in the *Index of the Augsburg Library*, page 29.

*A book on the Sacrament of Baptism to Leander, Bishop of Seville*, in which he collected the opinions of the Fathers regarding triple immersion. This minor work has perished; the memory of it survives only in Isidore's *On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "de Script[oribus]"; specifically Isidore of Seville's biographical catalog</note>, chapter 26.

**LEANDER**, Spanish by nation, from the house of Carthage, was the son of Severianus (whose sister Sanctia was taken as a wife by Theodoric, King of the Ostrogoths) and Turtura. He was the elder brother of Isidore of Seville, and after a long profession of the monastic life, he was made Archbishop of the Church of Seville. He flourished in the year 583, at which time he was sent as an ambassador to Emperor Tiberius in Constantinople by Prince Hermenigild—who was being pursued with an armed hand by his father Leovigild, King of the Goths in Spain, on account of his zeal for the Catholic faith—to obtain reinforcements. He accomplished this successfully, and there he entered into a great friendship with Gregory the Deacon, the legate <note>original: "Apocrisiario"</note> of Pope Pelagius. Returning to Spain in the year 584, he was punished with exile by King Leovigild. However, in the following year, when the king was near death, he was moved by repentance for his deed and commended his son Reccared to Leander's care. Having obtained such a pupil, Leander cultivated him diligently; he converted him first from the Arian heresy <note>Arianism taught that Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father; it was the dominant faith of the Goths at the time</note>, then with his help the Gothic nobles, and finally almost the entire Gothic nation to the Catholic faith. He so succeeded that he deserved to be called the *Apostle of the Goths*. At the Third Council of Toledo held in the year 589, in which he played a major part, he admitted the Goths he had converted into the bosom of the Church, and he saw to it that the orthodox faith was confirmed by the signature of everyone. He died in the year 595. According to his brother Isidore *, he was a man of sweet eloquence, most excellent talent, and no less famous for his life than for his learning. He wrote to his sister Florentia a *Rule for the Instruction of Virgins and Contempt for the World*, which Lucas Holstenius first published in the *Collection of Rules*, Paris, 1663, part 3, page 89; from there it was transferred into the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 12, page 999. There also exists his *Homily in Praise of the Church for the Conversion of the Goths* delivered at Toledo after the conclusion of the Council, *Councils*, Volume 5, page 1018. He furthermore wrote, as mentioned by Isidore but now lost: two books *Against the Dogmas of Heretics*; a minor work *Against the Customs of the Arians*; *Many letters to Pope Gregory*, one regarding baptism, another *to his brother on not fearing death*, and many familiar *Letters* to other fellow bishops. "Finally," says Isidore, "he labored with no small zeal in the Ecclesiastical Offices. In..."

*A book on the Sacrament of Baptism to Leander, Bishop of Seville*, in which he collected the opinions of the Fathers on triple immersion <note>The practice of dipping a person in water three times during baptism to represent the Trinity.</note>. This small work has perished; the memory of it survives only in Isidore's *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 26.

***

<margin>585.</margin>
LEANDER, Spanish by birth, from a Carthaginian family, was the son of Severianus (whose sister Sanctia was taken as a wife by Theodoric, King of the Ostrogoths) and Turtura. He was the older brother of Isidore of Seville. After a long profession of the monastic life, he was made Archbishop of the Church of Seville. He flourished in the year 583, at which time he was sent as an envoy to Emperor Tiberius in Constantinople by Prince Hermenigild—who was being persecuted with an armed force by his father Leuvigild, the Gothic King in Spain, because of his zeal for the Catholic faith. Leander went to seek reinforcements, which he successfully achieved, and there he entered into a great friendship with Gregory the Deacon, who was the *Apocrisiarius* <note>An "Apocrisiarius" was a high-ranking diplomatic representative or legate, in this case representing the Pope at the Byzantine court.</note> of Pope Pelagius.

Returning to Spain in the year 584, he was punished with exile by King Leuvigild. However, in the following year, when the King was near death, he was led by repentance for his deed and commended the care of his son Reccared to Leander. Having gained such a student, Leander diligently cultivated him and converted him from the Arian heresy <note>Arianism was a theological belief that held that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father. It was the dominant faith of the Germanic Goths before their conversion to Catholicism.</note> first, then the Gothic nobles by his help, and finally almost the entire Gothic nation to the Catholic faith; so much so that he deserved to be called the *Apostle of the Goths*. Having held the Third Council of Toledo in 589, of which he was a major part, he admitted the Goths he had converted into the bosom of the Church and saw to it that the orthodox faith was confirmed by the signatures of all. He died in the year 595. According to his brother Isidore, he was—
<margin>* Chapter 28.</margin>
—a man of sweet eloquence, most outstanding talent, and no less famous for his life than for his teaching. He wrote to his sister Florentia the *Rule for the Education of Virgins and Contempt for the World*, which Lucas Holstenius first published in his *Collection of Rules, Paris 1663, part 3, page 89*; from there it was transferred into the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 12, page 999. His *Homily in Praise of the Church on the Conversion of the Goths*, delivered at Toledo after the synod had ended, is also extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume 5, page 1018. He wrote besides, as mentioned by Isidore but now lost: *Two books against the dogmas of heretics*, a *Short Work against the institutions of the Arians*, *Many letters to Pope Gregory*, *One on baptism*, *Another to his brother on not fearing death*, and *Very many personal letters to other fellow bishops.*

...for he composed prayers for the entire Psalter in a double edition. In the praises of the sacrifice <note>This refers to the prayers used during the Mass or Eucharist.</note> and the Psalms, he composed many things with a sweet sound. From this passage, some conclude—not incorrectly—that our Leander was the author of the *Mozarabic Mass*. It is reasonable to believe that Leander composed a liturgy for the use of the Goths, which was subsequently used in the Spanish Church for several centuries and eventually began to be called the *Mass of the Mozarabs* or rather the *Mixtarabs* <note>original: "Mixtarabum"</note>; this name was adopted after the Christians had become intermingled with the Arabs <note>The term "Mozarab" refers to Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule after the 8th-century conquest, preserving their Christian faith and Latin liturgy.</note>. His brother Isidore expanded this Mass, which had been first arranged by Leander. As time went on, it was modified by the additions of various Bishops and is still used today in certain churches in the city of Toledo. Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros published it in 1504, having revived it from the Gothic ruins and dressed it in new characters <note>This refers to the printing of the Mozarabic Missal in modern typeface to preserve the ancient rite.</note>. It is also found, though not in its entirety, in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 27.

**LICINIANUS**, Bishop of Cartagena <note>original: "Carthaginis Spartariæ," a Roman name for the city in southeastern Spain</note> in Spain, flourished in the year 584. Because of his zeal for the Catholic faith, he was driven into exile by King Leovigild <note>Leovigild was a powerful Visigothic king who sought to unify Spain under Arianism, a version of Christianity that the Catholic Church considered a heresy.</note> and traveled to Constantinople. It is said that he finally met his end there, killed by poison from his rivals. He wrote several *Letters*, including one on the Sacrament of Baptism, and many to Abbot Eutropius (who later became Bishop of Valencia). A single letter to Pope Gregory remains in the books of the *Morals*. However, García de Loaysa possessed other manuscript letters by the same author. See the notes by Miræus on Isidore, chapter 29.

**SEVERUS**, Bishop of Malaga in Spain, flourished in the year 584, at which time he was punished with exile by King Leovigild on account of his Catholic faith. He wrote a book against Vincent, the Bishop of Zaragoza, who had defected from the Catholics to the camp of the Arians. He also composed another short book on Virginity addressed to his sister, to which he gave the title *The Rings*. Both works have perished.

584.
Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 31.
</margin>
**JOHN**, a Goth by birth, was born in Scalabis in Lusitania <note>Modern-day Santarém, Portugal.</note>. While still a youth, he went to Constantinople; for many years he devoted his efforts to the study of fine literature and both languages <note>Meaning Latin and Greek.</note>. Returning to Spain in 584, when he refused to consent to the Arian heresy, he was banished to Barcelona by Leovigild. There, for a full decade, he suffered many plots and persecutions from the Arians. Later, he founded the Monastery of Biclaro at the foot of the Pyrenees mountains and presided over it. At last, having been made Bishop of Gerona, he passed away at the beginning of the seventh century. He wrote a *Chronicle* from the year 565 (where Victor of Tunnuna left off) to the year 590, and for the use of his monastery, he wrote a *Rule*, along with many other things according to the testimony of Isidore. Of these, only the *Chronicle* survives, first published by Henricus Canisius along with the Chronicle of Victor in Ingolstadt, 1600; then by Scaliger in the *Eusebian Chronicle* in Leiden, 1606, and elsewhere.

589.
* 14th Century, chapter 12.
</margin>
**COLUMBANUS**, Irish by race and a native of Leinster <note>original: "Lageniensis"</note>, was a disciple of Abbot Comgall of the Bangor Monastery in eastern Ireland (not the Bangor in Britain, as Baleus <note>John Bale, a 16th-century English historian.</note> claims). After crossing over to Britain and staying there for some time, he moved to Burgundy in the year 589, where he established and governed the Monastery of Luxeuil. After presiding over it for nearly twenty years, he was driven into exile by Theuderic, King of the Austrasians, because he had rebuked the king's immoralities with more than usual boldness. Having wandered through all of Gaul, he withdrew to Italy, where, having obtained a suitable place from Agilulf, King of the Lombards, he built the Monastery of Bobbio near Naples <note>The author is mistaken here; Bobbio is in northern Italy, near Piacenza, not Naples.</note>. After fulfilling the governance of this house for a single year, he met his final day on the 23rd of November <note>original: "ix. Cal. Decembr."</note> in the year 615.

Saint Columbanus, while still a young man, also wrote a *Book of Psalms* in polished language, which is mentioned and praised by Sigebert. Ware enumerates other works from the *Life* written by his disciple Jonas: a *Commentary on the Psalter*, a *Book against the Arians*, and—as Ware learned from an eyewitness—two letters to *Pope Boniface* which were still extant in France, as well as a *Modest Apology* presented to the fathers of the Council of Mâcon when he was called to judgment because of his unconventional observation of Easter. For Columbanus constantly maintained the "Quartodeciman" custom of observing Easter <note>The practice of celebrating Easter on the 14th of the lunar month of Nisan, regardless of the day of the week, which was the tradition in the British and Irish churches but differed from the Roman practice.</note>, which he had drawn from Britain, even in foreign regions. He was certainly a man of ancient virtue and plain, primitive simplicity; how much freedom, and with what immense and noble zeal he treated even the leaders of the Christian religion, is testified by his single letter to Pope Boniface IV, in which he argues against the acceptance of the "Three Chapters" <note>A major 6th-century theological dispute involving the condemnation of certain texts. Columbanus urged the Pope to clear the Church of suspicion of heresy.</note> and approaches the Pope on this matter, setting aside all <term>partiality</term> <note>original: "$\pi\rho\omicron\sigma\omega\pi\omicron\lambda\eta\psi\acute{\iota}\alpha$"; refers to favoritism or showing bias based on a person's status.</note>. Certainly, the current customs of the Roman Court would find such <term>frankness</term> <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\rho\rho\eta\sigma\acute{\iota}\alpha\nu$"; bold, direct, and uninhibited speech.</note> difficult to endure.

<margin>590.</margin>
**LEONTIUS**, called **THE BYZANTINE** by birth or office, was first a lawyer; then, having left secular business, he became a monk in the monastery of the Great Laura in Palestine <note>Mar Saba, one of the oldest inhabited monasteries in the world.</note>. He flourished in the year 590 and thereafter. To the very learned Vossius <margin>* From *On Greek Historians*, book 4, chapter 8.</margin> he seems the same as Leontius of Cyprus, of whom we speak below at the end of this century: namely, that he was Byzantine by homeland, a lawyer by profession, and later the Bishop of Cyprus. Certainly, the dates do not conflict. Leontius of Cyprus flourished under Emperor Maurice and extended his life until the year 620; and our Leontius mentions not only Eulogius of Alexandria, but also John Philoponus. But I make no determination on this matter.

**GREGORY I, called "The Great"** for his achievements, was Roman by birth, the great-great-grandson of Pope Felix III, and the son of Gordian and Silvia. Deeply imbued in his youth with the elements of grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric, he began to earn a great reputation for his name in legal service. Having reached manhood, he was chosen as one of the Senators of the City. In the year 581, he held the office of Urban Prefect. Though heaped with so many honors, he nevertheless cultivated such great holiness of life that he was in no way inferior to the most famous monks of his age. He himself longed entirely for the monastic life; so much so that while he could not yet extricate himself from secular affairs, he founded six monasteries in Sicily and a seventh within the city walls with his own resources. Over his Roman monastery, he placed Valentius, whom he had summoned from the Monastery of Saint Equitius in the province of Valeria; eventually, he entered the monastery himself and subjected himself to the rule of Valentius.

However, he was not permitted to enjoy his desired leisure for long. For in the year 583, Pope Pelagius drew him out of the monastery, ordained him a Deacon, and sent him to the Emperor Tiberius as an *Apocrisiarius* <term>Apocrisiarius: A high-ranking diplomatic representative or legate, specifically the representative of the Pope to the Byzantine court in Constantinople.</term>. In the year 586, while still active in Constantinople, he entered into a dispute with Eutychius, the Patriarch of Constantinople. Eutychius had fallen into the error of Origen <note>An early Christian theologian whose views on the nature of the resurrected body were later condemned as heretical.</note> and had denied that the body would rise again clothed in palpable flesh; Gregory outstandingly defended the truth of the resurrection. In the same year, upon the death of Emperor Tiberius, Gregory—after managing the affairs of the Roman Church in Constantinople with the greatest loyalty and diligence for three years, and having either completed or begun many volumes in that place—returned to Rome and gave up his post to another *Apocrisiarius* sent according to custom to the newly-made Emperor Maurice.

Having found leisure, he withdrew again into his monastery and brought to completion <note>original: "ad umbilicum," literally "to the navel," a Roman idiom for finishing a scroll.</note> the writings he had begun in Constantinople. Furthermore, at the urging of Pelagius, he composed other works against the Western bishops who had separated from the communion of the Roman Church. In the year 590, after the death of Pelagius, he was elevated to the Roman Pontificate by the conspiring prayers of all good men. After he himself had woven many and varied delays and attempted to flee in vain, he was finally ordained on the 3rd of September. In the same year, when a most grievous plague was raging in the City, he instituted that famous "Sevenfold Litany" <note>A massive penitential procession involving seven groups of the Roman population.</note> for the purpose of appeasing the Divine Will.

Once made Pontiff, he held frequent Synods and sent letters everywhere to issue a profession of faith, restore the shaken affairs of the Church, recall the clergy and monks to the ancient standard of discipline, and bring the resistant—including Archdeacon Laurence—back into order. He set out with the greatest constancy of mind and an invincible zeal for religion to extinguish the schism born in the West, to drive stubborn bishops from their seats (including Demetrius, Bishop of Naples) by invoking the secular sword <note>That is, calling upon the civil authorities to enforce church rulings.</note>, to protect the Catholic faith, and to defeat heretics. In particular, he took care to crush the pride of John of Constantinople, who arrogated to himself the ambitious title of "Ecumenical" <note>Meaning "Universal." Gregory argued this title was an affront to the equality of bishops and the primacy of Rome.</note>; Gregory cried out that the title John had seized was proud, heretical, blasphemous, Antichristian, and Diabolical. In the year 593, he took very poorly the edict of Emperor Maurice concerning the non-admission of soldiers into monasteries; however, so as not to fail in his duty and obedience, he promulgated it quite unwillingly. In the year 594, through letters to Emperor Maurice, the Empress Constantina, and the Eastern Patriarchs, he acted strenuously to bring John of Constantinople back into order. In the meantime, he forbade his *Apocrisiarius* Sabinian to communicate with John. Having held a Synod in Rome that same year, he acquitted John, a priest of Chalcedon, who had been condemned by John [the Faster] on account of the Marcianite heresy; he also decreed several canons regarding ecclesiastical matters. In the year 596, drawing an omen from the "angelic" appearance of the English captives <note>Refers to the famous story where Gregory saw blonde English slaves and remarked, "Not Angles, but Angels."</note>, he applied his mind to converting the English nation to the Christian faith, sending Augustine of the Mo-

Once this praiseworthy work had begun, he did not cease to promote it through his advice and authority. In the year 601, he sent Justus, Paulinus, Lawrence, and others to propagate the faith in England. In the year 603, he wrote letters to the tyrant Phocas, congratulating him on an empire seized through the most wicked crimes. Indeed, if the truth be told, Gregory slipped so shamefully in this matter that he did not blush to flatter a most wicked murderer with the most calculated arts of adulation, while raging most bitterly against the ghost of the most pious Prince Maurice. He died in the year 604, on the 12th of March. He was a man of remarkable piety and, considering the standards of that age, of significant learning. Indeed, if we listen to Isidore of Seville: *he was endowed with such a light of knowledge through the grace of the Holy Spirit, that not only was no teacher of the present times equal to him, but no one in the past was ever his peer.* <note>original: "tanto per gratiam S. Spiritus scientiæ lumine præditus..."</note> Thus says Isidore; however, the reader should remember that his words in this matter are to be taken with a grain of salt. While the praise for his piety and erudition should by no means be denied him, he is rightly and deservedly blamed for the fact that, according to John of Salisbury in *The Statesman's Book* <term>original: "De Nugis Curialium," a work of political philosophy and courtly critique</term>, book 2, chapter 26, and book 8, chapter 19, he not only ordered Mathematics <note>In this context, "Mathesis" often referred to astrology or divination, which were viewed as pagan superstitions.</note> to be removed from the Court, but, so that the authority of Holy Scripture might be greater and more diligently studied, he applied fire to the most noble Palatine Library out of a premature and frankly burning zeal. In that fire, many venerable monuments of antiquity, which were stored in its archives, perished.

> *Whatever writings Palatine Apollo once held.* <note>A poetic reference to the library founded by Augustus near the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine Hill.</note>

## WORKS.

**Six books of Exposition on the first book of Kings**, which is also called the Book of Samuel.

**The Morals on Job, or 35 books of Moralia.** A work begun in the year 583 and finished in 590. It was published separately during the first "cradle-days" of printing <term>original: "incunabilis," referring to books printed before 1501</term> in *Rome, 1475; Paris, 1495, in folio.*

**Exposition on the Seven Penitential Psalms.** There are those who believe that many things are found in it that relate to the times of Emperor Henry IV; therefore, they think it should instead be attributed to Pope Gregory VII.

**Exposition on the Song of Songs.** Basel, 1496, in quarto; Paris, 1498.

**Two books of Homilies on Ezekiel**, written around the year 595.

**Forty Homilies on various readings of the Gospels**, addressed to Secundinus, Bishop of Taormina, completed in the year 592.

**The Book of Pastoral Care**, addressed to John, Bishop of Ravenna, written at the beginning of his papacy, and later translated into the Greek language by Anastasius of Antioch around the year 602. That translation has perished. The book itself was published separately in *Strasbourg, 1496; Paris, 1498, in quarto.*

**Four books of Dialogues on the life and miracles of the Italian Fathers, and on the eternity of souls**, written around the year 593. Not a few of the Reformers have brought a dispute against these Dialogues, while the writers of the Roman Church strenuously reclaim them. Various arguments are brought forward on both sides. On the side of those denying their authenticity, there is first the massive difference in style, which deviates immensely from Gregory’s usually elegant, steady, and not ungraceful style. Indeed, it must be admitted that many expressions used in these Dialogues belong to a man only moderately skilled in the Latin language, to say nothing more severe. Second, the "old wives' tales" and silly fables that occur everywhere are entirely unworthy of Gregory the Great, or indeed of any prudent man. Consequently, Melchior Cano, a man of the Roman Church and famous for his learning and piety, severely criticized the author of these tales <margin>* Commonplaces, book 11, chapter 6, p. 658.</margin>. Third, things are found in these Dialogues that clearly oppose the doctrine Gregory handed down in his undisputed works, of which our own Robert Cooke provides more than one example in his *Censure of Ancient Writers*, page 209. ...the suspicion remains that these *Dialogues* should be attributed to Pope Gregory II, who entered the Pontificate in the year 716, and that he derived the name of the *Dialogue* from them. On the other hand, first, it is most certainly established that our Gregory had a work of this kind in mind, and that he collected reports from everywhere for that purpose, as is evident from his letter to Maximian of Syracuse in book 2, chapter 89. Second, John the Deacon, who flourished in the year 875 and wrote four books on the life of the Blessed Gregory, clearly testifies that Gregory the Great composed these four books of *Dialogues*, and that Pope Zacharias translated them into the Greek language nearly 175 years later; here *Baronius* <note>Cardinal Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a prominent Vatican historian</note> corrects the error in the number, saying there were only 118 years. To this is added the testimony of † *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note>, who adjudges these *Dialogues* to our Gregory and asserts that they were written 165 years before they were translated into Greek by Pope Zacharias. Having weighed the arguments from both sides, it remains that these *Dialogues* are at least of doubtful authenticity; written, as it seems, by Gregory the Great, but expanded and <term>interpolated</term> <note>meaning later editors added their own words into the original text</note> by more recent authors. Therefore, I would not deny they are his. Meanwhile, in the composing of this work, no one who reads it with a calm mind and free from prejudice will easily deny that he indulged his credulity too much, and was more inclined toward fables than was proper.

They have appeared separately quite often, for example in *Venice 1475, Paris 1499, Venice 1561, Cologne 1610,* and elsewhere. Pope Zacharias once translated them into Greek. That version was published in *Rome in 1591,* but it was mutilated, with six and a half chapters missing from the third book. Canisius restored these from manuscript codices and brought them to light in *Ancient Readings, Volume III.* <note>original: "Antiq. Lect. Tom. iii."</note> Consequently, the complete version is presented in the edition of Gregory's *Works* printed in *Paris, 1640.*

*Twelve Books of Letters,* in which not a few <term>supposititious</term> <note>forged or falsely attributed</note> ones are mixed. Indeed, the editors of the *Councils* themselves admit that the Privilege of the Monastery of Saint Medard subjoined to letter 77 of book 2, and letter 32 of book 12 to Felix, Bishop of Messina, are spurious. Letter 42 of book 2 is missing from seven manuscript codices found here in England, one of which is nearly contemporary with the age of *Gregory* himself. Our own illustrious Thomas James, in his vernacular book *On the Corruption of the Fathers,* part 2, notes certain corrupted places in letter 38 of book 4, and letters 54 and 64 of book 7, based on manuscript codices. The same James, in his *Gregorian Vindication* <note>original: "Vindiciis Gregorianis," published in Geneva, 1625</note>, shows more fully with what license the monks in the past raged <note>meaning they took great liberties or were reckless</note> in transcribing Gregory’s books, and more recent Papists in printing them. The *Letters* of *Gregory* are also held in the *Councils, Volume V, page 1028.*

*The Antiphonary, or Gradual Book,* arranged throughout the cycle of the year.

*The Book of Sacraments for the Yearly Cycle.* These two small works appeared together among the *Liturgies* of Pamelius, *Volume II, Cologne 1571,* and the latter separately in *Paris, 1642,* with the notes of *Menard*.

*Several Hymns.*

*A Concordance of Certain Testimonies of Holy Scripture,* first published in the *Paris edition of 1571.*

The *Works* of Saint Gregory appeared in *Paris 1523; Rome 1588, 1593 in 2 volumes; Basel 1564 in 2 volumes; Paris 1571; Antwerp 1572, 1615; Paris 1605, 1640 in folio; and Rome 1613 in 5 volumes, octavo.*

*The Book of Blessings, or a Collection of Solemn Blessings* used by Saint Gregory in sacred matters; previously thought to be unpublished by Lambecius, he published it in its entirety from a codex in the Vienna Library in his *Commentaries, book 2, chapter 5, page 300.* However, he later corrected his error, discovering it had been published by *Menard* in *Paris, 1642,* in Gregory the Great’s *Book of Sacraments*; yet it was not in the place of an appendix or a specific work, but was inserted and mixed throughout according to the time and subject of the individual blessings.

**DYNAMIUS**, a Patrician of Gaul and a manager of the Roman Church's revenues within Gaul, as is established from a letter of Gregory the Great * addressed to him. He flourished in the year 593. Two years later, when he retired from his duty, he was succeeded by the priest Candidus. Dynamius wrote the *Life of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Riez*, addressed to Urbicus, the successor of Faustus (who had followed Maximus in the Bishopric); this work is held—though with the author's style "improved" by Surius—in Surius’s collection for November 27th. **EVAGRIUS SCHOLASTICUS**, of Syrian descent from the city of Epiphania, was born in the year 536 or 537. At the age of four, he began attending the schools of the grammarians; he was taken by his parents to Apamea to witness the precious wood of the Cross shown in a solemn procession by Bishop Thomas. Leaving the schools of the grammarians, he attended those of the Rhetoricians; and when he had been fully imbued with that knowledge, he was admitted among the Advocates and began to plead cases in the forum of Antioch—from which he drew the name *Scholasticus* <note>a title for a lawyer or scholar</note>. He gained great favor with Gregory, the Patriarch of Antioch, whom he assisted in judging cases and served in writing letters and sermons. Indeed, he seems to have held a place among the primary citizens of the city of Antioch; for the whole city in the year 592, when he entered into marriage for the second time, celebrated with holidays and solemn games to wish him well. From Emperor Tiberius he earned the rank of Quaestor, and from Maurice the dignity of an honorary Prefecture. In the year 589, he accompanied Gregory of Antioch (who was burdened with various accusations and summoned to Constantinople to plead his case) to serve as his legal assessor and counselor. In the year 594, the year in which he was most prominent, he concluded his *History*. It is not clear how many years he survived after that. Regarding his style, Photius * says:
<margin>
* Codex 29.
</margin>
> *His style is not without grace, even if he seems somewhat hesitant at times; in the orthodoxy of his doctrines, he is purer than most other historians.* <note>original Greek: Ἔστι δὲ τὴν φράσιν οὐκ ἀχάρις, εἰ καὶ πὼς ὀκνηρότερός ἐνίοτε δοκεῖ· ἐν δὲ τῇ τῶν δογμάτων ὀρθότητι ἀκραιφνής ἢ ἄλλων μᾶλλον ἱστορικῶν.</note>

His style is unpleasing <note>The author here contradicts Photius's "not without grace"</note>, although it seems to overflow somewhat at times; certainly, in the truth of his doctrine, he is more accurate than other historians. While this praise should not be denied him, it will be clearly evident to anyone not blinded by prejudice that in recounting many events he was too credulous and prone to fables, judging from what he reports on every given occasion concerning the cross, relics, and fabricated miracles (which had already begun to be held in higher esteem).

*Two books of letters, reports, decrees, orations, and disputes*, most of which were written in the name of Gregory of Antioch, which have been lost.

**ISIDORE**, called *the Younger* to distinguish him from Isidore of Córdoba; a Spaniard by birth, the son of Severianus, Prefect of Carthage in Spain, and Turtura. He had two bishops as brothers: Fulgentius of Cartagena and Leander of Seville, whom he himself succeeded in the Archiepiscopal see in the year 595. In the year 610, he signed the edict of King Gunthemar regarding the <term>Prerogative</term> <note>the leading status or jurisdictional rights</note> of the see of Toledo. In 619, he presided over the Second Council of Seville, in which he saw to the decreeing of many canons regarding ecclesiastical matters; and after holding a debate with a certain Syrian 
<margin>See Session 12.</margin>
bishop who was infected with the <term>Acephali</term> heresy <note>a branch of Monophysitism that "lacked a head" or leader and rejected the Council of Chalcedon</note>, he refuted the man's error by bringing forth abundant testimony from Holy Scripture and restored him to the Catholic faith. In 633, he presided over the Fourth National Council of Toledo, where he restored the fallen state of the Spanish Church by passing a great many canons. In 636, being near death, he had himself carried into the Church of Saint Vincent; there, on the third day of April, after receiving the <term>viaticum</term> <note>the final reception of the Eucharist before death</note>, he peacefully fell asleep in the Lord. The Fathers of the Eighth Council of Toledo praise Isidore most highly. They say: *The eminent doctor of our century, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last in time among those preceding him, but not the lowest in comparison of learning, and what is more, the most learned at the end of the ages, and to be named with reverence: Isidore.*

# 436 The Age of Eutychius <note>Eutychius was the Patriarch of Constantinople in the late 6th century; this heading identifies the era by his patriarchate.</note>

<margin>
6th CENTURY
from the Year of Our Lord 596.
</margin>
PHOTINUS, a Priest of Constantinople and a defender of the Great Church <note>original: "Ecclesiæ Magnæ"; this refers to the Hagia Sophia</note>, was prominent in the year 596. He wrote the *Life of John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople.* A lengthy fragment of this work is presented in the Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea, Volume 7, page 272, where one may see a certain dramatic and utterly foul <note>original: "putidissimam"; literally "stinking," used here to mean absurd or distasteful</note> story in which Photinus himself played a major part.

---

<margin>596.</margin>
AUGUSTINE, a Roman by birth, was a monk by training and a disciple of Gregory the Great. He served as the Superior <note>original: "Præfectus"</note> of a monastery established by Gregory in the city of Rome. Since Pope Gregory desired the conversion of the Anglo-Saxon people, he turned the matter over in his mind and, in the year 596, sent Augustine to England for this purpose, accompanied by about forty companions. When Augustine wavered while already on his journey, the Pope strengthened his spirit with counsel and provided him with letters of authority. Augustine landed on the Isle of Thanet and, having obtained permission from Æthelbert, King of Kent, prepared himself to preach the Gospel. He drew many to the faith, and soon King Æthelbert himself, along with his entire household, embraced the religion of Christ. In the year 598, he traveled to Gaul and was consecrated as the Archbishop of the English nation by Etherius, the Bishop of Arles. He immediately transferred the Archiepiscopal seat—which London claimed for itself as the metropolis of the island—to <margin>See Bede's *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, chapter 2.</margin> *Dorobernia*, or Canterbury, in honor of Æthelbert.

To promote the conversion of the Saxons more successfully, he invited the bishops of Britain to this harvest, arranging a conference with them on the borders of Wales. However, the Britons were offended by the pride of his manners, and especially because he demanded that they abandon their own customs and adopt Roman rites. They responded that they would do none of these things, nor would they accept him as their Archbishop. To them, Augustine is said to have foretold threateningly that if they refused to accept peace with their brothers, they would receive war from their enemies; and if they would not preach the way of life to the English nation, they would suffer the vengeance of death at their hands. Nor did the event fail his prediction, for Æthelbert incited Æthelfrith, the petty king of the Northumbrians, who gathered an army and committed a horrific slaughter of 1,200 monks of Bangor <note>original: "Banchorensium"; referring to the monastery of Bangor-is-y-Coed</note>. It is highly likely that this was done at the persuasion and instigation of Augustine. 

Some object that before this slaughter took place, Augustine had already been taken up to the heavenly kingdoms long before, according to the testimony of Bede himself. However, there are not a few of our better-known historians—and among them Bede himself—who extend his life beyond the slaughter at Bangor to the year 608, or even to 614, which could also be supported by other arguments. From this arises a significant suspicion that the passage concerning Augustine's death was added to Bede's *History* at a later time, especially since it is missing from King Alfred's Saxon translation, made only a century and a half after Bede's death. But even if he were dead before the slaughter was carried out, who does not know that he could have given the advice which was only brought to its conclusion after his death? 

Augustine was of a tall and upright stature, with a rather haughty mind and harsh manners; he was religious rather than learned, and more devoted to superstition than to true piety. There exist *Eleven Questions* written by him to Pope Gregory, together with *Gregory's Responses*, found at the end of Saint Gregory's letters and with a Saxon version in Bede's *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 1, chapter 27. He also wrote a fairly long book on the *Conversation of Novices*, which begins: "Will is understood in three ways," and ends with these words: "These things concerning the characters and manners of men we have spoken through comparisons inserted in their proper place, so that they might be held longer in memory. For just as a kernel is preserved longer within its shell, so something said through a comparison is held longer in memory," because it recurs more tenaciously to the memory. This manuscript book is held among other miscellanies in the public library at Cambridge, Class 4, fig. 5, in octavo. This is noted by Mr. Wharton, who himself handled and inspected the volume. It should seem quite remarkable not only that it remains unpublished to this day, but that neither the ancients nor the moderns, as far as I know, have made mention of it. Bale <note>John Bale (1495–1563), an English historian and playwright</note> indeed reports that Augustine, immediately after his arrival in Britain, wrote to Gregory himself via his messengers Laurence and Peter: one book on his prosperous success and one book on the statutes of his churches—works which perhaps Bale himself never saw, and it may be doubted whether they ever existed.

<margin>599.</margin>
**ANASTASIUS**, called the *Sinaite* <note>original: "Saniata" (likely an error for "Sinaita"); he is named for Mount Sinai, where he lived as a monk</note>, also known as *the Younger* to distinguish him from his predecessor, succeeded to the Patriarchate of Antioch in the year 599. After holding the see for nearly ten years, in the year 608 (or at the very start of the following year), a massive riot broke out between Christians and Jews. The Jews, who had been superior in the struggle, dragged him from his throne. They bound his feet with a rope and dragged him through the city; after his private parts <note>original: "αἰδοίοις" (Greek: aidoiois)</note> had been cut off and stuffed into his mouth, he was finally committed to the fire, thus winning the palm of martyrdom. There exists in Greek and Latin under his name a *Brief Instruction on the Faith* <note>original: "Compendiaria fidei Institutio"</note> in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 11; however, some attribute this to Anastasius the Elder. In truth, it belongs to neither, as it is the offspring <note>original: "foetus"</note> of Saint Maximus. See more under Anastasius the Elder. Furthermore, our Anastasius was the author of the *Greek Version of Gregory the Great’s book on Pastoral Care*; Gregory himself praises this in Book 10, Letter 22. However, that work has not come down to us.

Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 32.
</margin>
**EUTROPIUS**, a Spaniard by birth, first an Abbot of the Servitan monastery and later Bishop of the Church of Valencia, flourished in the year 599. He wrote a very useful, though now lost, *Letter to Licinianus, Bishop of Carthage, in which he consulted Licinianus regarding the anointing with chrism granted to baptized infants.* He also wrote to *Peter, Bishop of Ittabica, on the Distinction of Monks*, a salutary letter very necessary for monks; this was published by Lucas Holstenius in the *Code of Rules*, Paris, 1663, Appendix, page 82.

<margin>
599.
Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 33.
</margin>
**MAXIMUS**, a Spaniard by nation and Bishop of Zaragoza <note>original: "Cæsaraugustæ"</note>, flourished in the year 599, in which year he signed the Council of Barcelona. He was present at the Council of Toledo in 610 and the Council of Egara in 614. He wrote in a brief style a *History of the deeds of the Goths in Spain*, as well as many other things which are no longer extant.

At the end of this century, it is pleasing to set down several writers of entirely uncertain age, yet older than Photius <note>Photius was a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople whose "Bibliotheca" preserves summaries of many lost ancient books</note>; these are placed here until their true, or at least probable, age can be fished out from elsewhere.

**ANDRONICIANUS**, a man greatly devoted to the study of philosophy. He wrote *two small books against the Eunomians* <note>a radical Arian sect that claimed the Son was "unlike" the Father</note>, in which he promised great things but delivered only mediocre results. See Photius, Codex 45.

**LUCIUS CHARINUS** <note>Also known as Leucius Charinus</note>, at once the worst and the most foolish of heretics, produced a work under this title: *The Travels of the Apostles*, comprising the *Acts of Peter, John, Andrew, Thomas, and Paul*. He used an uneven and unlovely style, and his doctrines were truly monstrous. For in that book, he offered to the reader a mixture of the most tasteless delusions of the Ebionites, Marcionites, Valentinians, Encratites, and other heretics of the worst sort, all melted into one. It overflowed everywhere with things most absurd, childish, unexpected, and maliciously fabricated and false—indeed, foolish, self-contradictory, and finally impious and detestable. See Photius, Codex 114.

**HERACLIANUS**, Bishop of Chalcedon, a man as pious as he was learned. He wrote *against the Manichaeans in twenty books*, addressed to a certain Achilius, in a clear and elegant style. In these, he most powerfully defeated their impiety; he refuted the most celebrated books of the Manichaeans—the *Gospel*, the *Book of Giants*, and the *Treasures*—and he pressed the arguments of all those who had labored in that same wrestling-ground <note>original: "Palæstra"</note> before him more strongly, established them firmly, and piously supplied what had been omitted. See Photius, Codex 85.

<margin>6th CENTURY from the Year of Our Lord</margin>

**LEONTIUS**, Bishop of Arabissus <note>Arabissus was a city in the Roman province of Cappadocia, modern-day Turkey</note>. He wrote a *Sermon on the Creation* and another *On Lazarus Brought Back to Life*. Photius provides quite long excerpts of these in his Codex 272.

**HESYCHIUS**, a Priest of Constantinople. He wrote four books *On the Bronze Serpent of Moses*, which Photius mentions and briefly describes in Codex 51.

**SOPHRONIUS** wrote, in an elegant and vigorous style, a *Book for Basil against Eunomius* <note>original: "pro Basilio adversus Eunomium"; this refers to a defense of Basil the Great’s theology against the Arian teachings of Eunomius</note>. In this work, Photius (Codex 5) judges that Sophronius surpassed Theodore of Mopsuestia, who had labored in that same arena.

**METRODORUS** compiled a *Calculation of the Easter Feasts* from nineteen-year cycles multiplied by twenty-eight <note>This refers to the calculation of the "Great Paschal Cycle" of 532 years, used to determine the date of Easter</note>. He followed the custom of the <term>Quartodecimans</term> <note>Christian groups who celebrated Easter on the 14th day of the Hebrew month of Nisan, regardless of which day of the week it fell upon</note> in fixing the dates of Easter; he began his calculation from the time of Diocletian and extended it for 533 years. From this, one might perhaps rightly conjecture that this Metrodorus flourished around the end of the third century. However, that remains uncertain. See Photius, Codex 115.

**ANONYMOUS** Author, who wrote several volumes *On the Holy Feast of Easter* in a clear style. Photius read the third of these, which consists of eight books and is dedicated to a certain Theodore. Many matters pertaining to theology are included regarding the <term>Hexaemeron</term> <note>original: "Hexaemero"; refers to the six days of Biblical creation</note>; and in this work, Metrodorus is criticized in several places. See more in Photius, Codex 116.

**ANONYMOUS**, Author of a book titled *A Disputation against the Jews and Heretics of the Same Mind, and the Quartodecimans*, who do not celebrate the holy feast of Easter in the first month of the Hebrews. Photius contains some very short fragments of this work in Codex 115.

**ANONYMOUS** various writers who committed to writing the *Lives or Martyrdoms of certain Saints*, namely: the *Martyrdom of the Seven Sleeping Youths*, who, fleeing the *Decian Persecution*, entered a cave near Ephesus in the year 250 and, having fallen into a deep sleep, finally woke up in the year 445. You can find excerpts of this story <note>original: "fabulæ istius"; the author uses 'fabula' here in the sense of a narrative or account</note> in Photius, Codex 253. Also, the *Martyrdom of Timothy the Apostle*, of which fragments are shown in Photius, Codex 254. The *Martyrdom of the Great Martyr Demetrius*, who suffered under Maximian; a summary of it can be seen in Photius, Codex 255. The *Lives of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander*, in which the *Life of Constantine the Great* is narrated at length; Photius gives very extensive excerpts in Codex 256. The *Life of Paul, Bishop of Constantinople and Confessor*; quite long fragments of it are extant in Photius, Codex 257. Finally, the *Life of Saint Athanasius*, of which Photius provides very extensive excerpts in Codex 258.

# 439 The Age of Eutychius

<header>The Age of Eutychius.</header>

<margin>6th CENTURY from the Year of Our Lord</margin>
<margin>* Under the entry "Proclus"</margin>
<note>This entry continues the biography of the philosopher Proclus (412–485 AD), though his life spans the late 5th century, his influence and the school he led define the start of this period</note> [Proclus] studied under a Rhetorician, Orion the Grammarian, Olympiodorus the Philosopher, and Hero the Mathematician. Having left Alexandria, he set out for Athens; where, in the study of philosophy, he found teachers in Plutarch the younger and, after his death, Syrianus. Finally, having been made Rector of the Platonic School among the Athenians at the beginning of this century, he grew old in that place, and departed from the living at the age of 75. Among the many and famous volumes he published on Philosophy and Gentile <note>Pagan</note> Theology, he wrote eighteen *arguments* <note>original: *ἐπιχειρήματα* (epicheirēmata)</note> against the Christians: he was the second after Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century philosopher famous for his "Against the Christians"</note>, says Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, who sharpened his impure and insulting tongue against the Christians. Against this man's pen, John Philoponus <note>A Christian Neoplatonist and scientist who famously refuted Proclus’s arguments for the eternity of the world</note> successfully took up arms.

<margin>540.</margin>
<margin>* Codex 181.</margin>
**DAMASCIUS**, a native of Damascus, a Stoic by sect (according to others, a Peripatetic), flourished around the year 540. He studied Rhetoric under Theo, dialectics under Isidore, Geometry and Arithmetic under Marinus (the successor of Proclus in the Athenian school), Philosophy under Zenodotus (the successor of Marinus), and Platonic studies and Mathematics under Ammonius, the son of Hermias. He himself eventually presided over the school of Rhetoric for nine years after Theo; and after Isidore, he governed the Athenian Philosophical school. As far as religion is concerned, he was "impious to the extreme" <note>original: *εἰς ἄκρον δυσεβής* (eis akron dysebēs)</note>, says Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note>, exceedingly ungodly, carrying both a mind and a discourse filled with strange and old wives' tales. Wherefore he not infrequently barks at our holy faith—albeit timidly and with hidden malevolence—in his *Life of Isidore*, his teacher. For Damascius wrote, among other works, the *Life of Isidore the Philosopher*, which Photius tastes of briefly <note>original: "strictim delibat"</note> in Codex 181, though Codex 242 provides very extensive excerpts from it.

# 440 The Monothelite Age

<header>THE MONOTHELITE AGE.</header>
<meta>catchword: WRIT-</meta>

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year 600.
</margin>

### Overview of the Century.

The title of "Universal Bishop" was obtained from the tyrant Phocas—the most wicked of two-legged creatures, who was as well-disposed toward the Pope as he was hostile in mind toward Cyriacus, the Patriarch of Constantinople—by Pope Boniface III around the year 606. This occurred despite the fact that Boniface's predecessor, Gregory the Great, had recently, clearly, and openly condemned this title in the Bishops of the See of Constantinople as *a new name, blasphemous, singular, a swelling of empty glory, a new pride, an evil of pride and confusion, a temptation of diabolical usurpation, a superstitious, rash, and unspeakable term of haughtiness, the invention of the first Apostate, and the precursor of the Antichrist*. 

In the year 622, from which the *Hegira* <note>The migration of Muhammad from Mecca to Medina</note> or Era of the Muhammadans begins, there arose Muhammad, a cunning as well as fortunate Arabian impostor—certainly a heavy scourge for the heresies and dissensions among Christians. Having joined to himself Sergius, a Nestorian monk, Phineas, a Jew, and Abdalla, an Arabian, he composed the Quran <note>original: *Alcoranum*</note>, which he hawked everywhere as if it had fallen to him from heaven. From this, he emerged as a new Prophet and a supreme Prince; regarding his origin, false prophecy, dogmas, Hegira, battles, successors, death, and the entire worship and religion of the Orientals, the celebrated Hottinger <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian</note> treats at length, beyond others, in his *Oriental History*. 

The heresy of the **MONOTHELITES**, who asserted a single will in Christ <note>from the Greek *monos* (one) and *thelema* (will)</note>—a new offspring of the Eutychians—arose around the year 630. Through the efforts of Sergius of Constantinople and Cyrus of Alexandria, it pervaded the East, with its poison spreading even through the West, Pope Honorius himself being stained by this blight. In the year 639, the Emperor Heraclius promulgated his *Ecthesis* <note>original Greek: *ἔκθεσις* (Ekthesis), meaning an exposition or statement of faith</note>, by which he confirmed the Monothelite dogma. This was strenuously defended by Sergius, Cyrus, and others, but was condemned at Rome and by the Westerners. As the harvest of dissensions grew daily from this, in the year 658, the Emperor Constans <note>referred to here as Constantinus Augustus</note> issued the *Type* <note>original: *Typum*; an imperial edict</note> or decree, by which he imposed silence on both parties regarding this controversy. 

Finally, in the year 680 and the following year, the Sixth General Council was held at Constantinople, in which this question was aired. The heresy was condemned, and its supporters—Paul, Sergius, Cyrus, etc.—together with Pope Honorius, were struck with anathema. A few years later, an Ecumenical Synod was convoked in the *Trullo* <note>A domed hall</note> of the Imperial Palace, by which 102 canons were established. Since it is, as it were, an appendix and supplement to the two preceding councils, it is commonly called the **Penthekte** <note>original Greek: *Πενθέκτη* (Penthektē); meaning "Fifth-Sixth"</note>, or *Quini-sexta*; however, the Roman Church accepts its canons with difficulty. 

The Christian faith in this century was propagated further and wider through the various kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxons; indeed, from this nation, as if from a perennial spring, many rivers were diverted into foreign nations. Hence, by the labors of Suitbert, Wigbert, Wilfrid, Willibrord, and other Englishmen, the Frisians, Germans, and other northern peoples were converted to the faith of Christ.

<meta>This page continues the ecclesiastical history of the 7th century, shifting from the general political and religious upheavals (the rise of the Papacy and Islam) to the lives and works of significant writers of the period, starting with the controversial philosopher-theologian John Philoponus.</meta>

<header>The Monothelite Age.</header>

# W R I T E R S .

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year 601.
</margin>
John, called **PHILOPONUS** <note>literally "lover of labor"</note> due to his tireless dedication to his studies, was an Alexandrian by birth and a Grammarian by profession. He was deeply well-versed in both Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy. As Tertullian once rightly noted that philosophers were often the "patriarchs" of heretics, so too did our John, emerging from the school of philosophers, soon stumble in his faith once he turned his mind to handling theological questions. He flourished at the beginning of this century around the year 601, having already been famous in the preceding century. Indeed, he had published his heresy during the time of John Scholasticus, who held the patriarchal throne of the Royal City <note>Constantinople</note> from 564 to 578. This is evidenced by the *Acts of the Disputation* held before Patriarch John between the Tritheites <note>those accused of believing in three gods</note> Conon and Eugenius, and the "Hesitators" <note>original: *Diacrinomenos*, a term for those who hesitated to accept the Council of Chalcedon</note> Paul and Stephen, regarding the excommunication of Philoponus, as recorded by Photius in Volume 24. John lived beyond the year 608, for he undertook his work on the *Hexaemeron* <note>The Six Days of Creation</note> at the urging of Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople, and dedicated it to him upon completion.

He published many dogmas that were out of harmony with the truth of the faith. Because his mind was so thoroughly imbued with Aristotelian philosophy, he remained fixed on the idea that "person" <term>hypostasis</term> and "nature" <term>natura</term> were the same thing. Because of this, he first asserted that there was only a single nature in Christ and rejected the Council of Chalcedon. Later, when Catholics countered him by pointing out that there are three persons in the Trinity but only one nature, he tried to extricate himself from the objection by daring to teach that three natures or substances exist in the Trinity. However, he always consistently denied that there were "three Gods" or three deities. Because of this, he was considered—and is still considered today—the leader and standard-bearer of the sect of the **Tritheists**. Furthermore, placing no restraint on his philosophical cravings, he taught that the bodies of the dead would perish entirely in both matter and form, and that other bodies, formed by God in their place at the resurrection, would stand for divine judgment. For this reason, he is said by some to have denied the resurrection. He scattered other errors among the common people as well, which can be gathered either from his own writings or from contemporary authors.

<margin>* Vol. 75.<br/>† Vol. 215.</margin> Regarding his style, Photius writes: *His phrasing is consistent with itself: clear, but possessing nothing of intensity or majesty.* (Elsewhere: *For he turns away from distinct and pure expression, yet he nonetheless adorns himself with a select and Attic-style <note>imitating classical Athenian Greek</note> phrasing.*) *In his arguments, however, he is not only impious, but also excessively unsound and weak, such that he cannot even color his own sophisms against the pious with a superficial appearance of truth or piety.*

## EXTANT WORKS.

**Book on the Hexaemeron**, or a Commentary on the first chapter of Genesis, dedicated to Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople.

**Disputation on Easter**. These two small works were published in Greek and Latin by Balthasar Corderius in Vienna, 1630, in quarto.

**Book on the Eternity of the World against Proclus**. Published in Greek in Venice, 1535.

**Book on the Dialects of the Greeks**, printed in Greek and Latin in Basel, 1532; Paris, 1521; and Venice, 1525.

**Commentary on Aristotle's Analytics**. Available in Greek, Venice, 1534.

**Commentary on the book "On Generation and Corruption"**. Greek, Venice, 1527.

**Commentary on the books "On the Soul"**. Published in Greek in Venice, 1535.

**Commentary on the five books "On the Generation of Animals"**. Greek, Venice, 1526.

**Commentary on the first book of "Meteorologics"**. Available in Greek, Venice, 1551.

**Commentary on the first four books of "Physics"**. In Greek, Venice, 1555.

## LOST WORKS.

A work *On the Resurrection*, mentioned by Photius in Volume 21.
A book *Against the Council of Chalcedon*, which Photius touches upon briefly in Volume 55.
A book *Against those things which John Scholasticus, Archbishop of Constantinople, handed down concerning the Holy Trinity* in his *Catechetical Oration*. Photius describes it briefly in Volume 75.

A book *Against Proclus's work "Against the Christians,"* in which Philoponus, meeting Proclus’s arguments to the great admiration of all readers, refuted them most excellently. He demonstrated that Proclus was ignorant and senseless even in those Greek disciplines for which he held himself in such high regard. So says Suidas <note>the *Suda*, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the entry "The Peplum" <note>original: *Πέπλῳ* (Peplo), a title of a work</note>.

A book *On the Union*, called *The Arbiter* or *The Mediator* <note>original: *Διαιτητής* (Diaitētēs)</note>, written at the request of Sergius of Constantinople, which Nicephorus discusses at length in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 18, Chapter 47, where he also includes some fragments of it.

601.

* Under the name "Tiberius."
</margin>
**JOHN MALALAS**, a native of Antioch, flourished at the beginning of this century around the year 601. John Tzetzes <note>a 12th-century poet and grammarian</note> mentions him and cites certain passages from him in his *Chiliads* (5. History 29, 30). He was also one of the fourteen historians from whom Constantine Porphyrogenitus <note>the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII</note> compiled his collection *On Virtues and Vices*. He composed a *Chronicle* from the birth of Christ down to his own times; he was immensely devoted to fables, and we rightly find him lacking in both judgment and reliability. The illustrious Valesius <note>Henri Valois, a French scholar</note> chose not to include excerpts of Malalas with the rest of his Constantinian collection, as he informs us in his Preface, because—aside from three or four myths about Minos, Antiope, and Bellerophon, and those woven in an ungraceful style—they contained nothing of real value. We have seen the complete *Chronicle*, preserved today in the archives of the Bodleian Library; Edmund Chilmead, Chaplain of Christ Church, who died in 1653, translated it into Latin and prepared it for the press with notes in Greek and Latin. However, the Curators of the Sheldon Press have deferred printing it until now, as they judged it not quite worthy of public light. I wish, nonetheless, that they would not begrudge the world of scholars this work, such as it is. Meanwhile, Selden cites some items from this Chronicle in his work *On the Sanhedrin* (Book 1, Chapter 8), as does the great Ussher <note>James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh</note> both in his notes on the *Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians* and in his *Ignatian Appendix* (p. 9). Furthermore, I have no doubt that what Suidas records concerning Tiberianus is taken from this source.

<margin>
601.

* Dissertation on Writers, Vol. I, p. 632 and in the Appendix, p. 820.
† On the Sacred Eucharist, Book 1. 2. p. 846.
</margin>
**HESYCHIUS**, or Isychius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, is thought to have lived around the year 601, as there exists a letter from Gregory the Great to him (Book 9, Letter 40). There were certainly several men named Hesychius among both the Greeks and the Latins; regarding them and the writings attributed to them, Philippe Labbe (*) and, before him, Edm. Albertinus (†) accurately review various opinions; the curious may consult them. We have neither the leisure nor the inclination to copy out their observations. The sum of the conjecture (which indeed seems most likely to me; let others enjoy their own judgment) comes to this: that Hesychius wrote much while he was still a Priest of the Church of Jerusalem, and other things after he had ascended the Patriarchal throne of that Church; finally, that some of these works were translated into Latin, with many additions of his own, by a certain Hesychius—perhaps the younger one of Salona, who is said to have lived around or shortly after the time of Gregory the Great. Truly, this matter requires a "Delian diver" <note>A Greek proverb meaning a problem so deep it requires a master to solve it without drowning</note>; for in a matter so obscure, nothing else...
