<meta>This page continues the discussion of 7th-century authors, moving from the historian John Malalas to a detailed examination of the works attributed to Hesychius. There is a debate over whether the author is Hesychius of Jerusalem or Hesychius of Salona.</meta>

# The Monothelite Age.

<note>The "Monothelite Age" refers to the 7th-century controversy over whether Christ had one will or two.</note>

...is more obscure than we are permitted to guess. Now, let us proceed to the works which circulate under the name of *Hesychius*.

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year 600.
</margin>

*Seven Books of Explanations on Leviticus*, which were published in Latin at *Basel, 1527* and *Paris, 1581, in octavo.* Concerning the author of this work, there are as many opinions as there are men. Some manuscript codices attribute it to *Isychius, a Priest of Salona* <note>modern-day Solin, Croatia</note>. However, the author of the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>the standard medieval biblical commentary</note> on Leviticus and *Boston of Bury* (as noted by *Ussher* in his *Theological Library Manuscript, page 229*) attribute it to *Isychius, Bishop of Jerusalem*. But Ussher says in that same place that there was only one Bishop of Jerusalem of that name, who held that see for 8 years after Amos (as *Nicephorus* records in his *Chronicle*) from the year 601, the year in which *Pope Gregory* writes that he had recently attained the Episcopate. *Bellarmine* further concludes that the author of these commentaries did not flourish before that time based on the argument that he explains Jerome’s version as the common and received version in the Church, when it is well-established that it was not so commonly received until a long time after Jerome's own death. Indeed, the edition explained here is so balanced that it agrees with the Septuagint <note>original: LXX</note> and does not disagree with the Latin Vulgate; yet it remains to be seen whether this balance is due to the author or rather to his Latin translator. For other writings attributed to *Hesychius*, a Priest of Jerusalem, are published in the Greek language. 

However, whoever wrote the *Commentary on Leviticus* frequently assumes the persona of a Latin man, such as when he writes in Book 1: *“What we call a sacrifice, is called in Greek* κάρπωμα <note>original: karpōma, literally 'fruit' or 'burnt offering'</note>;” and in Chapter 4: *“The Septuagint in the Greek version record this such that they say a* χίμαρον <note>chimaron</note> *and a* χίμαιραν <note>chimairan</note> *ought to be offered, which the Latins have translated from that same edition as a male kid from the goats, and a female goat from the kids.”* And in Book 2: *“Moses did as the Lord had commanded, and with the whole crowd gathered before the doors, he said—which is translated more expressively in the Greek language of the Septuagint as* ἐκκλησίασας τὴν συναγωγήν <note>ekklēsiasas tēn synagōgēn, meaning 'having called the assembly together'</note>.” These are Ussher's points. Truly, to say briefly what I think: it seems the author of this work is Hesychius of Jerusalem; certainly, the time and place agree best. In that specific work, Nestorius and Eutyches <note>theological opponents concerning the nature of Christ</note> are often refuted, and the work is seen cited by *Amalarius*, *Rabanus Maurus*, and other writers of that age. Furthermore, many passages found therein clearly argue for his being from Jerusalem. Nevertheless, the Latin translator—whom I would readily believe to be *Hesychius of Salona*—changed and added many things, and among other things, seems to have adapted these commentaries to the Vulgate version.

*Verse-arrangement* <note>original: Στιχηρὸν (Stichēron)</note> or *Chapters on the 12 Minor Prophets and Isaiah*, published in Greek together with the Introduction of Adrian by *David Hoeschel at Augsburg, 1602, in quarto*; it is also found in the *Critici Sacri, Volume 8, page 26*.

*Refutations and Prayers, or Two Centuries of Sentences to Theodulus on Temperance and Virtue*, which teach the method by which one must struggle against passions and vices, and how to pray. These were published in Greek together with the short works of *Mark the Hermit* at *Paris, 1563, in octavo*, and in the same year and place in Latin, translated by *Jean Pic*. Also in the *Parisian Supplement of 1624, Volume 1, page 985*. These "Centuries" <note>collections of 100 sayings</note> contain many sentences transcribed word-for-word from the ascetic works of Mark, and as *Photius* notes in his *Library, Code 198*, they closed the book of the lives of the Saints who were contemporaries of St. Anthony.

*Two Sermons on the Blessed Virgin.* Found in Greek and Latin in the *Supplement of 1624, Volume 2, page 417*.

*A Demonstrative Oration on St. Andrew the Apostle.* Extant in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 12, page 190*. *Labbe* considers the excerpt found in *Photius, Code 269*, to be from this work, where it will be easily apparent to anyone inspecting the passage that *Thomas* was wrongly substituted for *Andrew* by the scribes.

*Homily on the Resurrection of Christ*, which some codices attribute to *Gregory of Nyssa*.

*At Which Hour the Lord was Crucified.* These *two Homilies* were published by *François Combefis* in the *Supplement of 1648, Volume 1*.

Otherwise, besides the *Verse-arrangement* and these latter two *Homilies*, the rest of the works of Hesychius are extant in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 12*.

*An epigram of Hesychius the Priest, Isaiah on the Psalter, or a rather lengthy Introduction to the Psalms.* <note>original: Ἡσυχίου πρεσβυτέρου ἐπίγραμμα Ἡσαΐας εἰς ψαλτήριον</note>

DOROTHEUS, a Palestinian Archimandrite <note>a head of a monastery</note>, a disciple and servant of the most celebrated monk John, called the "Prophet," whom he served for many years while John was bedridden due to poor health. I confess I do not know his true age; however, led by a not entirely improbable conjecture, I think he flourished at the beginning of this century. For since that John was a disciple of Barsanuphius (who flourished around the year 550 according to the testimony of Evagrius †), and our Dorotheus was the servant of John when he was already in his extreme old age, he could not be more conveniently placed in any other period. Dorotheus mentions many things about himself here and there, which are not of such importance as to be transferred here. I will only say this: after the death of John and his departure from the monastery of Abbot Seridus, he was able to establish and govern a monastery of his own. He wrote *Instructions on leading a right and pious life*, or *Twenty-four Ethical and Ascetical Dissertations, and certain short letters on the same subject*. These *Instructions* (the last of which lacks the Greek text) are extant with the *Letters* added at the end; published in Greek and Latin in the *Orthodoxographia*, page 195, and in the Ducean Supplement, Volume 1, page 743.

He flourished in the year 601 and thereafter; finally, if Arnold Wion * is to be believed, he was created Bishop of Brescia because of his great reputation for learning. He wrote *three books of Explanations on the more obscure passages of both Testaments, excerpted from the works of Gregory the Great*; or, as Sigebert † has it, collecting all the testimonies of Holy Scripture through which Gregory clarified the obscurities of his own Exposition. He published three books: two *concerning the testimonies of the Old Testament* and one *concerning the testimonies of the New Testament*; and he called the volume itself the *Book of Testimonies*. This work by Paterius appeared at *Rome*, 1553 in folio, and among the works of Saint Gregory there in 1591 and subsequent editions. But in all the printed versions and some of its manuscript codices, the second book is missing, which Casimir Oudin, in his *Supplement*, page 156, reports having seen complete along with the other two in a manuscript in the Library of the Celestines in Paris.

# The Monothelite Age.
<note>The "Monothelite Age" refers to the 7th-century theological controversy regarding whether Christ possessed one will or two. This period was marked by intense debate over the nature of Christ's divinity and humanity.</note>

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year 600.
</margin>
<margin>* Book 9, Letter 69.</margin>
...our [Eusebius] (whom Gregory the Great* discusses) having been challenged by him through letters, wrote a *Response*, refuted the trifles of Andrew, and thoroughly overturned the dogmas of the Aphthartodocitae <note>The Aphthartodocitae held that Christ's body was incorruptible from the moment of the Incarnation, making his suffering and death appear a matter of choice rather than human necessity.</note>. But when Andrew issued another work to confirm his opinion with greater effort, Eusebius composed ten books treating the matter more extensively and accurately, and excellently established the Catholic truth. *Excerpts* of both works are preserved in Photius’s *Library*, Code 162.

<margin>601.</margin>
**CONON**, at first a disciple of John Philoponus <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570) was a Christian philosopher whose "Tritheist" views—treating the three persons of the Trinity as three distinct substances—were highly controversial.</note>, whose side he strenuously defended in a dispute he held along with Eugenius against the Eutychians <note>Followers of Eutyches, who believed Christ had only one nature (Monophysitism).</note> Paul and Stephen in the presence of John, Patriarch of Constantinople. He flourished around the year 601. Eventually, he became hostile to Philoponus because Philoponus would not admit that the three natures or substances he placed in the Trinity were equal in all respects and varying in nothing. Conon established a sect different from him, to which he gave his own name, and presided over it as a Bishop; he even struck Philoponus’s writings with anathema and wrote an *Invective Oration* against his delusions concerning the Resurrection of the Flesh. Eugenius did the same, himself once a notable follower of Philoponus who had gained fame in the aforementioned dispute. The works of both have perished. Besides the *Invective Orations*, the *Acts of the Dispute* against Paul and Stephen were committed to writing and read by Photius. See Code 23, 24.

<margin>601.</margin>
**THEODOSIUS**, a monk, flourished, it seems, around the year 601. He wrote a fairly accurate *Refutation of the Testimonies* that were brought forward by John Philoponus against the Resurrection of bodies, whether from Holy Scripture or from the writings of the holy Fathers. That book, mentioned by Photius in Code 22, has now perished. As for the unhealthy dogmas of the same Philoponus regarding the Holy Trinity, Gregory—whom Nicephorus* calls "the chief in theology" <note>original: ἐξάρχας ἐν θεολογίᾳ (exarchas en theologia)</note>—most clearly refuted them in his book to Evagrius the monk on the Divinity. 

<margin>601. † Book 48, ch. 5 || Code 108.</margin>
**THEMISTIUS**, called by the adopted surname Calonymus (whom Nicephorus Callistus † very poorly confuses with the philosopher Themistius who flourished under Emperor Valens), was a follower of the Severians <note>A Miaphysite group following Severus of Antioch.</note>, Theopaschites <note>Those who believed that God the Son suffered on the cross in his divine nature.</note>, and Agnoetae <note>A sect that argued Christ's human nature was subject to ignorance, such as not knowing the time of the Last Judgment.</note>. He flourished in the year 601. A man not unlearned, says Photius ||, who knew best how to combine clarity of speech with the strength of arguments. He wrote an *Invective Oration* against the delusions of Philoponus concerning the Resurrection. For the sect of the Agnoetae, however, he composed a small book to which he gave the title *Apology for Saint Theobaptius*, in which book he did not hesitate to criticize Severus himself. Theodorus † opposed this booklet with a volume; to repay him, Themistius wrote a specific work against Theodorus. Themistius also wrote several other things, of which the memory and some fragments survive in the *Acts of the Lateran Council and the Third Council of Constantinople*, namely: *Several books to the Empress Theodora, some Sermons against Colluthus, in favor of the Tome of Theodosius. A Letter on behalf of the people of Salamis. A Sermon to Charisius the monk. A Book to Constantine, Bishop of Laodicea. Books on satisfaction, for the Agnoetae, to Marcellus the Priest and Stephen the Deacon* (Council Records Volume 6, pages 316, 320). Finally, *contradictory books against the Tome of Theodosius*, from the second of which you have a fragment in the Council Records Volume 6, page 831.

<margin>601. Photius Code 108.</margin>
**THEODORUS**, an Alexandrian monk, followed the heresy of the Severians, Theopaschites, and Theodosians. He flourished in the year 601. He wrote a *Brief Refutation of the Repeated*, rash, and most absurd contention of Themistius against the Fathers, or of that Apologetic book for the sect of the Agnoetae. When Themistius had objected to this Refutation with a *Response*, Theodorus published three other books on the same argument to defend his work. 

<margin>601.</margin>
**NICIAS**, a monk, flourished around the same time, it seems, namely in the year 601. He wrote against the seven chapters of Philoponus, which Philoponus himself had mentioned in his *Arbiter* <note>original: Διατητῇ (Diaitete). This refers to Philoponus's work "The Arbiter," which sought to reconcile different views on Christ's nature.</note>. He also attacked Severus in his writings and refuted the Pagans in two books. See Photius, Code 50.

# The Monothelite Age.
<note>The "Monothelite Age" refers to the 7th-century theological controversy regarding whether Christ possessed one will (Monotheletism) or two. This debate significantly divided the Eastern and Western Churches.</note>

<margin>7th CENTURY from the Year 600. 606.</margin>
**FAUSTUS**, an Italian by birth, was entrusted as a boy of only seven years to Saint Benedict by his parents to be instructed in good character. He was educated under Benedict’s rule at the Monastery of Monte Cassino <note>original: "Monasterio Cassinensi"</note> and was assigned as a companion to Saint Maurus when the latter was sent to Gaul. Following Maurus into Gaul, he spent forty-two years in the monastery built by Maurus on the banks of the Loire. Two years after Maurus's death, he returned to Italy and sought out Monte Cassino again. There, at the request of the monks and especially at the command of Abbot Theodore, he wrote *The Life and Deeds of Saint Maurus* <note>original: "Vitam & res gestas S. Mauri"</note> and dedicated it to Pope Boniface III in the year 606. This *Life* still exists, though it was altered by Abbot Odo of Glanfeuil; it can be found in the works of Surius and the Bollandists for January 15th, and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Ages*, volume 1, page 274. He likewise wrote a *Life of Saint Severinus the Abbot*, which is found in Mabillon’s work on page 568.

<margin>606.</margin>
<margin>* On the illustrious men of Monte Cassino, chapter 3.</margin>
<margin>* Abac. Patr. Page 301.</margin>
**MARCUS**, a monk of the Benedictine Order and a disciple and close friend of Saint Benedict, flourished in the year 606. He recounted the *Life of Saint Benedict* (originally described in prose by Gregory the Great) in quite elegant verse, adding some details of his own. His style was so charming and superior to the spirit of his age that, according to the testimony of Peter the Deacon*, he composed most elegant verses concerning the arrival of the most holy Benedict at Monte Cassino, the site’s location, and the construction of the monastery. This *Life* was published by Prospero Martinengo in Rome (along with other poets) in 1590 in the third volume of his *Collection*. However, the *Maxims* <note>original: "Gnomæ"</note> printed at Hagenau in 1531 and certain other small works published in Paris in 1563—which Gottfried Olearius* attributes to our Marcus—almost certainly belong to Marcus the Hermit, who flourished at the beginning of the 5th century. It was perhaps J.B. Marus, in his notes to Peter the Deacon (page 8), who led Olearius into this error.

<margin>606.</margin>
<margin>† Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 4.</margin>
**BONIFACE IV**, a native of Valeria from the Marsi people and son of John the physician, was elected Pope from the rank of Priest of the Roman Church after the start of November in the year 606, and was ordained on August 26th of the following year. He obtained the *Roman Pantheon* from Emperor Phocas and converted it into a church (which is today called Saint Mary of the Martyrs, commonly known as the *Rotunda*), just as his predecessor Boniface III had obtained the title of *Ecumenical* <note>Universal</note> from the same tyrant. In the year 610, Mellitus, the Bishop of London, having built a monastery outside the city walls, traveled to Rome to consult the Pope regarding the life and rules of monks and other affairs of the English Church. A Synod was held on this matter in which Mellitus himself sat; as Bede says†, he confirmed what had been decreed by subscribing with his own authority, and he carried the Canons back to Britain along with *letters from Boniface*. Boniface died on May 8th, 615. There survives a *Letter to Ethelbert, King of the English*, and a *Decree issued in the Roman Synod concerning monks administering the priestly office*, found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 5, page 1618.

<margin>608.</margin>
**SERGIUS**, Patriarch of Constantinople from the year 608. In the year 629, having been consulted by the Emperor Heraclius who was of an uncertain mind, he decreed in a Synod and wrote back that there was only a single will and operation in Christ, revealing then for the first time the poison that had long been hiding in his mind. In the year 633, he negotiated by letter with Pope Honorius so that the Synod of Alexandria might be confirmed by the decree of all Patriarchs. That Synod, at the expense of the Orthodox faith, had brokered an unfaithful peace between the Catholics and the Eutychians <note>followers of Eutyches, who denied the distinct human nature of Christ</note> by teaching a single will in Christ. In the year 639, after publishing the *Ecthesis* <note>a formal statement of faith</note> and holding a Synod at Constantinople, he confirmed the Monothelite heresy; he died on the same day. There are *three letters* written by him: one to Cyrus, Patriarch of Alexandria (in Greek and Latin, *Councils* Vol. 6, p. 176); another to Cyrus, Bishop of Phasis (Greek and Latin, among the Acts of the Third Council of Constantinople, Session 12, *Councils* Vol. 6, p. 915); and a third to Pope Honorius (Greek and Latin, ibid., p. 918). The *Acts of the Synod* which he held in 639 to confirm the Emperor’s heretical *Ecthesis* are extant in Greek and Latin (*Lateran Council*, Act 3, *Councils* Vol. 6, p. 201).

# The Monothelite Age.
<note>The "Monothelite Age" refers to the 7th-century theological crisis regarding the nature of Christ's will. The term "Seculum Monotheleticum" marks a period where this debate dominated Church politics and literature.</note>

<margin>7th CENTURY from the Year 600. 610.</margin>

### TIMOTHEUS
<margin>610.</margin>
**TIMOTHEUS**, a writer of uncertain age. A Priest of the Great Church of Constantinople and the keeper of the vessels of the Temple of the Holy Mother of God <note>original: "S. Deiparæ"</note> in the Copper-market <note>original: "Chalcopratiis"</note>; he was younger than Philoponus, Conon, and Theodore, whom he mentions, yet he seems to be earlier than the Monothelites, of whom he makes no mention. He therefore likely flourished around the year 610. He wrote to *John, Priest of Constantinople, a notable Epistle or booklet* <margin>concerning those who approach our most holy faith <note>original Greek: "περὶ προσερχομένων τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ ἡμῶν πίστει"</note></margin>, *or on various Heretics, and their diverse dogmas, and the various formulas for receiving them into the Church*. It exists in Latin in the earlier editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, and in Greek among the *Various Divine Matters* of Joannes Meursius, Leiden, 1619, in quarto. A Greek-Latin version is in Combefis’s *New Appendix, Volume 2*. Finally, having found a manuscript significantly different from the published ones, Cotelerius deemed it worthy to publish in Greek and Latin with notes in the *Monuments of the Greek Church, Volume 3, page 377*. It is no wonder that the manuscript copies of this booklet vary so much, for as it was received into the Rituals of the Churches, it was changed, increased, or diminished according to the custom of each place.

### EUSTASIUS
<margin>610.</margin>
**EUSTASIUS**, or Eustathius, a disciple of Saint Columbanus, whom he succeeded in the government of the Monastery of Luxeuil <note>original: "Luxoviensis"</note> among the Burgundians in the year 610. In the year 627, he saw to it that the Synod of Mâcon was held; in this synod, he strenuously defended the *Rule* given to the monks by Saint Columbanus, which had been rashly criticized by Agrestius (a former notary of King Theodoric of the Franks who became a monk at Luxeuil). He silenced that troublesome man and his followers, and earned a distinguished eulogy for piety and learning from the fathers of the Synod. He wrote the *Itinerary of Saint Columbanus*, which Jonas appears to have used in composing the *Life of Columbanus*, and which perhaps still lies hidden and unpublished somewhere.

### THEOPHYLACTUS
<margin>611.</margin>
**THEOPHYLACTUS**, called Simocatta, an Egyptian by race but a Locrian by country; from being a Sophist or Scholastic <note>a professional teacher of rhetoric or law</note>, he became a prefect and *Antigrapheus* (that is, perhaps, a Chancellor). He flourished in the year 611. He lived after the year 628, in which year he records in his *History*, book 8, chapter 12, that Khosrow, King of the Persians, was killed by Heraclius. He wrote the *Deeds of the Emperor Maurice in 8 books*, which he composed for the most part before the year 610. For immediately after the death of Phocas, while reading his History from a high place, when he came to the murder of Maurice, he drew tears from the standing people. However, he did not put the finishing touch <note>original: "coronidem"</note> on his work before the year 629. Concerning his style, Photius says this:

<margin>* Code 65. <br> "Indeed his phraseology has some grace, except that his excessive use of figurative words and allegorical meanings ends in a certain 'chilliness' <note>a technical term in rhetoric for a style that is over-labored or 'stiff'</note> and youthful lack of taste; nonetheless, the poorly-timed insertion of maxims is a proof of his ambition and vanity, though in other respects he is persuasive in sound." <note>original Greek: "ἡ μὲντοι φράσις αὐτῷ ἔχει μέν τι χάριτος..."</note></margin>

> *His style has some charm, except that by using figurative words and allegorical meanings too distastefully and frequently to the point of satiety, he slides into a certain coldness and juvenile follies. Nevertheless, that poorly-timed insertion of maxims proves a diligence that is both painstaking and superfluous; in other respects he is good and does not incur censure.* <note>This is a Latin translation of the Greek note provided by Photius.</note>

---

->W R I T I N G S.<-

**T**he eight books of the *History of the deeds of Maurice*, reaching from the year 582 to the year 602, reduced into an Epitome <note>summary</note> by Photius in Code 65. They were published in full in Greek and Latin together with Photius’s Epitome, with Pontanus’s version and notes, *Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto*; and with the same plus Fabrotus’s *Greco-Barbarian Glossary*, *Paris, 1648, in folio*. There is no reason to dwell on the *Excerpts on Embassies*, as they are taken from that same history.

*85 Epistles*, very brief and on various subjects, published in Greek by Aldus, *Venice, 1499*; in Greek and Latin by Cujacius among the *Greek Epistles*, *Geneva, 1606, in folio*.

*Physical Problems*. These appeared in Greek, published by Vulcaneus along with the Epistles, *Leiden, 1596, in octavo*; then in Greek and Latin with the same, translated by Jacob Kimedoncius, *Heidelberg, 1598, in octavo*; a fuller version edited by Schott, *Antwerp, 1599, in octavo*; finally published by Rivinus, *Leipzig, 1653*.

# The Monothelite Age.
<note>The "Monothelite Age" refers to the 7th-century theological crisis regarding whether Christ had one will (Monothelitism) or two. This period was marked by significant imperial intervention in Church doctrine.</note>

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year 600.
614.
</margin>

### ANTIOCHUS
**ANTIOCHUS**, a Palestinian monk, lived his life in the most celebrated monastery of Saint Sabas, called the *Laura* <note>original: "Laurâ". A "Laura" is a type of monastery consisting of a cluster of individual cells for hermits.</note>. He flourished in the year 614, the year in which Jerusalem was captured by the Persians, the precious wood of the Cross was carried away, and the monks of the Laura were killed or driven into flight. Among these, Antiochus suffered many evils. He was still living in the year 629, for in his final Homily he expresses indignation at the aforementioned Athanasius of Jerusalem being promoted to the see of Antioch. 

At the request of a certain Eustathius, he wrote the *Pandects of Divine Scripture, or a Compendium of the entire Christian religion and the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures, comprised of 130 Homilies*. These are preceded by a *Prayer and a Dedicatory Letter to Eustathius*, and followed by a *Confession to God* <note>original: "Exomologesis ad Deum"</note>. These Homilies were first published in a Latin translation by Godefridus Tilmannus in the *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, 1575. Fronto Ducaeus provided the Greek text along with Tilmannus’s version in the *Supplement*, Paris, 1624, Volume 1, page 1. Furthermore, Antiochus’s book *On Vicious Thoughts* <note>original: "de Vitiosis Cogitationibus"</note> survives in Latin, interpreted by Petrus Pantinus, in the *Library of the Fathers*, Cologne, 1618, and elsewhere.

### JOANNES
**JOANNES**, of Spanish descent, was first the Abbot of a certain monastery, then made the Prelate of the Church of Zaragoza <note>original: "Cæsaraugustanæ"</note> after Maximus, around the year 615. He died around the year 627. Regarding ecclesiastical Offices, he composed certain works with elegance in both sound and speech; he also wrote a small book on investigating the cycles of the Easter festival. <note>NE likely refers to a source or "Notate" - mark.</note>

<margin>
620.
</margin>

### BONIFACE V
**BONIFACE V**, of the Campanian region and a citizen of Naples, son of John, was first the Archpriest of the title of St. Xystus; then, on April 21 in the year 620 (according to the Anastasian Catalogue), he ascended to the summit of the Roman Church. In the year 624, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, Justus of Rochester succeeded to the see of Canterbury upon the death of Mellitus. Boniface sent the *Pallium* <note>A wool garment worn by bishops as a symbol of jurisdictional authority granted by the Pope.</note> as a gift to him, along with letters by which he granted him the power to ordain bishops. 

But what authority does this good Pope imagine for himself here? Neither Eadbald nor Justus himself had requested it from him; and it is clearer than the midday light that the ancient Canons of the Church long ago granted the right to ordain to any Bishop within his own Province. Boniface died on March 11 in the year 626. There exists his *Letter to Justus on the use of the Pallium*, another *to Edwin, King of the Northumbrians*, in which he exhorts him to the Christian faith, and a *third to Ethelburga* <note>original: "Edilburgam"</note>, the wife of Edwin, in which he congratulates her on her faith and advises her to provide the same benefit of faith to her husband. These Letters are found both in Baronius under the years 625 and 628, and in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 5, page 1658.

620.
* Cod. 278.

### MODESTUS
**MODESTUS**, Patriarch of Jerusalem, as he is expressly called by Photius, flourished in the year 620. After Patriarch Zacharias was led away into captivity by the Persians in the year 616, Modestus governed the see of Jerusalem. He restored the destroyed churches, recalled and reorganized the monks who had scattered in flight, and finally managed all the affairs of the Palestinian Church with the greatest diligence until the year 628, when the return of Zacharias occurred. He wrote *three Homilies, namely: on the women bearing ointments* <note>The "Myrrh-bearers" who visited Christ's tomb.</note>, *on the Meeting of the Lord and Simeon* <note>The Presentation in the Temple.</note> (of which Photius gives excerpts in Code 275), and finally an *Encomium on the Dormition of the Virgin Mother of God*; which Photius notes was quite long, but of little use.

620.

### CYRUS
**CYRUS** was first the Bishop of Phasis, or of the Lazica <note>original: "Lazorum", a region in modern-day Georgia.</note>, from around the year 620. Afterward, having sought the favor of Emperor Heraclius in the year 630, he was appointed to the see of Alexandria in that same year. In the previous year, he had learned that Heraclius, uncertain of what should be felt concerning the two natures in Christ, had consulted Sergius of Constantinople. Cyrus himself, feigning doubt so that he might more easily move away from Catholic truth, had asked Sergius to hold a torch before him in what was an entirely obscure matter. In the year 633, under the pretext of mending a seven-year peace among Catholics, he convened a Synod at Alexandria; in it, he subjected to anathema all those who did not confess a single "God-manly" operation <note>original: "Deivirilem operationem", referring to the Monothelite "Theandric" energy.</note> in Christ. In the year 639, he strengthened the *Ecthesis* <note>An imperial decree by Heraclius defining Monothelitism as official doctrine.</note> of the Emperor Heraclius with his signature...

# The Monothelite Age.
<note>The "Monothelite Age" refers to a 7th-century theological crisis centered on the question of whether Jesus Christ possessed one will (Monothelitism) or two wills (Diathelitism). It was a major point of contention between the Byzantine Emperors and the Papacy.</note>

He ordered it to be signed by the followers of Theodosius or Severus <note>These were "Non-Chalcedonian" or Monophysite groups that the Emperor was trying to reunite with the Imperial Church</note> who were to be received back into the bosom of the Church. It consists of nine chapters, the seventh of which confirmed the Monothelite heresy in no obscure terms: found in *The Councils*, Volume VI, page 954. (2.) *Three Letters* to Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople: *The Councils*, Volume VI, pages 207, 950, 952.

<margin>620.</margin>
**GEORGE**, succeeded John the Almsgiver in the see of Alexandria around the year 620. He died in the year 630, or slightly later. He wrote the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*; which Gerard Vossius <margin>* On the Greek Historians, Book 2, chapter 20.</margin> asserts he took from a book on the same subject by Cyril of Alexandria. Vossius relied, I believe, on the authority of an anonymous writer of a *Life of Chrysostom*, which [Henry] Savile published in Greek at the end of Chrysostom's *Works*. Truly, of what trustworthiness, authority, or even age that Anonymous writer was is entirely unknown to me, except that he flourished after the year 950. Nor is it established from any other source that the deeds of Chrysostom were committed to writing by Cyril. Meanwhile, it is most certainly established from Palladius’s *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom* that George described his own materials, for the most part interwoven with fables; <margin>† Codex 96.</margin> which Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and renowned scholar who reviewed hundreds of books in his "Bibliotheca"</note> † noted long ago. Furthermore, the most noble Savile treats George and his *History* accurately in the treatise on the writers of Chrysostom’s life published above, which we were the first to bring to light. Regarding his style, however, let Photius be heard: <gloss>original Greek: "Indeed, he says that the speech is simple and has fallen into great commonness; he does not even follow the construction of names and verbs used by grammarians."</gloss> <gloss>*His diction is certainly simple, sliding into an extremely humble style; nor does he at least apply the accurate construction of names and verbs that is readily available even to teachers.*</gloss> Godefridus Tilmannus first published this *Life* in Latin in Paris, 1557; and thereafter Surius on January 27th. It appeared in Greek with the notes of the celebrated Savile among the *Works of Chrysostom*, Volume VIII. Photius has very extensive excerpts in his *Codex XCVI*.

---

<margin>620.</margin>
**JOHN**, a Monk of Antioch, flourished around the year 620. He wrote a *Chronological History* from the beginning of the world down to his own times, which still lies hidden, unpublished, on library shelves. However, Constantine Porphyrogenitus <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Emperor who compiled massive encyclopedias of historical excerpts</note> inserted very large excerpts of it into his *Collections on Virtues and Vices*. Henri Valois published these in Greek and Latin with explanatory notes from the Peiresc Manuscript in Paris, 1634, in quarto.

---

<margin>620.</margin>
**NENNIUS**, a Briton by birth, a disciple of Elvodugus, Probus, and Beulanus the Priest; first a monk of the monastery of Bangor <note>original: "Bannochorensis"</note>, then its Abbot. He flourished, according to Bale, Vossius, and others, around the year 620. Bale and others believe that this man was the same as that famous Abbot Dinoth, who became well-known in the dispute held with Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Canterbury, the missionary to the English</note> in the year 613 and narrowly escaped the slaughter at Bangor—let the learned judge if they are correct. Certainly, the timeline and circumstances agree remarkably well. For Nennius is said to have spread the Gospel far and wide, not only through the borders of the Welsh <note>original: "Cambrorum"</note> but also the neighboring islands of the Scots <note>likely referring to the Irish or northern Britons</note> by preaching. This, one might rightly believe, he did after the monks were killed and the Bangor monastery was destroyed. While spending time among the Scots, he had Finan, the Bishop of Lindisfarne, committed to his care to be instructed in higher learning. There exists a book written by him *On the Deeds of the Britons*, or a *Brief Summary or History of the Britons*, in manuscript in the Royal Library at Westminster, in the Cambridge University Library, in the Cottonian Library, and in more than one other place; in some manuscripts, it is attributed to Gildas the Irishman. Since [James] Ussher <note>The famous 17th-century Irish Archbishop and chronologist</note> collected many things from everywhere that are not unworthy of being known in his *Theological Library* manuscript, we shall take some portions from there. Regarding a very ancient manuscript found by him, Priseus says: "It seems this little book was first composed by Nennius, but later strangely corrupted by several scholars who happened upon it. For immediately after the beginning, it reads: 'From Adam until the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ are 5,228 years; but from the passion of Christ there have passed...' Here a gap <note>original: "lab-" likely for "labes" or "lacuna"</note> appears..."

# The Monothelite Age.

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year 600.
</margin>

...a gap, where the old writing having been erased, this number 796 is supplied in new characters; namely, by the scribe himself bringing the calculation of time down to his own period, whereas previously it had only been applied to the era of the Author. Next, in the context of the History where the Author of the booklet records the inhabitants of this Island who were there in his time, he had these words: "And in it dwell <gloss>4</gloss> Nations, the Scots, Picts, Saxons, and Britons." This new Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace was a famous Greek grammarian; here used sarcastically to describe a critical editor who alters texts</note> wrote "previously dwelt" for "dwell": (which is clearly established to have been recently added beyond the context of the old copy, from the more recent appearance of both the characters and the ink) no account having been taken of the time in which the earlier parts were written, but only of his own period. And in that manner, while he wished to correct very many places of that booklet, he spoiled and corrupted them. Although those things which seem to have been added to it by some later sciolists <note>People who pretend to have knowledge but are actually superficial</note>, which do not at all fit the time of Gildas <note>A 6th-century British monk and historian</note>, I could easily believe that this work was taken from the *Commentaries of Gildas*. For it is not a new thing to add more recent events of things as they emerge to the Chronicles of the ancients, the inscription of the first Author being by no means abolished. 

John Priseus <note>Sir John Price (1502–1555), a Welsh historian and manuscript collector</note> brings forward more examples of the interpolated volume in the same place, and adds those things which William of Malmesbury says he read in the *Acts of the Britons* regarding Vortigern, and what he has concerning Vortimer, and he writes that Arthur performed wonders at the siege of Badon Hill relying on an image of the Mother of the Lord; it must be believed that he took them from here. For those things are recorded in this booklet, and he could not take them from the Gildas which Polydore [Vergil] took care to publish, since he makes no mention specifically of Vortigern, much less of Vortimer or Arthur. Furthermore, he could not take those things from Geoffrey of Monmouth; for he had not yet published the *British History* when Malmesbury published his own. Henry of Huntingdon also has entire clauses taken word-for-word from this booklet in his description of Britain; when he had not yet seen Geoffrey's History. There are others also, among whom is John the Englishman, who cite certain things from this booklet under the name of Gildas. Leland thinks some Nennius or other is the author of this booklet. So says Priseus. Indeed, Leland in the *Assertion of Arthur* reveals that from his speech it can be gathered that Nennius is the author; and in the *Commentaries on the Swan Song* he cites certain things from there under the name of Nennius: but Camden calls him the Pseudo-Gildas. 

However, those err if any think this is the work of that scoundrel who, a few years before (as Polydore Vergil reports in the Preface to Gildas), had composed a *Breviary* from Geoffrey's writings, and had falsely inscribed it as the *Compendium of Gildas the Wise*, or that fictional Gildas, whom Leland in the *Assertion of Arthur* says was exposed as prey to cockroaches and moths at the ford of the Isis <note>The River Thames at Oxford</note> in the Merton Library. For I take this to be about the work of Pseudo-Gildas Albanius (concerning whom Bale writes in the *Centuries*), not concerning this more recent one of ours. For Nennius, to whom this work is attributed by Leland, may be seen commended by him above, and he himself as well as Camden cites a passage by his name; which Priseus repeats from this booklet of Gildas in the *Defense of British History*, page 50. Thus says Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh and a noted scholar of early church history</note>.

Nennius or Gildas the Irishman (for it is not unlikely that the same man is designated by two names) wrote still more things, which Bale testifies at the end of the 13th *Century* that he left in Ireland when fleeing from there: a very ancient <term>Chronicle of the Origin of the Britons</term> <note>original: "De origine Britannorum Chronicon"</note>, (Pitseus writes that it is held in manuscript at the College of St. Benedict in Cambridge), the <term>Eulogy of Britain</term> <note>original: "Eulogium Britanniae"</note>, and a book <term>On the Wonders of Britain</term> <note>original: "de Mirabilibus Britanniae"</note>. This *Eulogy* is held in manuscript in an ancient Codex in the College of St. Benedict, vol. 338, in quarto; but it proceeds all the way to the year 840. From which it is clear either that our Nennius was two entire centuries more recent, or at least that the *Eulogy* was continued by a more recent hand. There also exists a manuscript in the Library of Trinity College, Cambridge, with this title: <term>Eulogy of a Benedictine Monk</term> <note>original: "Eulogium Monachi Benedictini"</note>, with the book <term>On the Wonders</term> added, etc. In the 1st *Century*, chapter 74, Bale records other books of Nennius, namely: <term>On the Cities of the Britons</term> <note>original: "De Urbibus Britannorum"</note>, <term>A Certain Apology</term> <note>original: "Apologiam quandam"</note>, <term>A Cosmography of the History of the World</term> <note>original: "Cosmographiam historiae mundi"</note>, and the <term>Additions of Gildas</term> <note>original: "Additiones Gildae"</note>; whether these still lie hidden anywhere is not clear. It must be noted, however, that there was a certain older Nennius, the brother of King Lud, about whom they tell amazing stories, and who is said to have composed a history of British affairs in the native tongue from the songs of the Bards and the writings of the Flamens <note>Ancient Roman priests, here used to refer to pagan religious officials</note>. Nennius of Bangor translated his history into Latin, and brought the thread of the narrative down to his own times.

# The Monothelite Age.

<margin>
7th CENTURY,
from the Year
624.
</margin>
**SULPITIUS**, called *the Pious*, a Gaul by birth, born in the territory of Bourges <note>original: "agro Bituricensi"</note>, was ordained a priest in the year 612. Shortly after, he was made Abbot of Castres, and finally, in the year 624, upon the death of Austregisilus, he was appointed to the see of Bourges. The following year he attended the Council of Reims. Three of his *Letters* are extant in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume V, among the letters to Desiderius of Cahors.

<margin>625.</margin>
**VERUS**, Bishop of Rodez in Gaul, was prominent in the year 625, at which time he attended the Council of Reims. Two *Letters* written by him are extant in Canisius, Volume V, as cited above.

<margin>626.</margin>
**HONORIUS**, a Campanian by birth and son of the consular official Petronius, was ordained Roman Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> on September 28, in the year 626. In the year 633, when Cyrus of Alexandria had confirmed the confession of a single will in Christ <term>Monothelitism: the theological claim that Christ had two natures but only one will, later declared a heresy</term> by a synodic decree; and when Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, being present in Alexandria, publicly accused Cyrus of error and withdrew from his communion: Sergius of Constantinople informed Honorius of the whole matter by letter. Honorius, in his response, approved of Cyrus’s action and disapproved of Sophronius’s. He confessed that there was a single will and operation in Christ, and he endeavored to prove this with arguments drawn from the Holy Scriptures and the authority of the Fathers. He established these same dogmas in other letters on more than one occasion by his authority, as much as he was able. They labor in vain <note>original: "Laterem lavant," literally "they are washing a brick"—a Latin idiom for a useless task</note>, and clearly waste their time and effort, who struggle to exempt Honorius from this stain—he who was expressly anathematized <note>formally cursed or excommunicated</note> for the Monothelite heresy by the Sixth General Council, and held as a Monothelite by more than one Roman Pontiff. The arguments of all those defenders, or rather their frivolous and empty evasions, were most fully refuted by the illustrious John Forbes, a distinguished ornament of our Northern Britain <note>Scotland</note>, in his *Historical Theological Instructions*, Book 5, where he treats this matter accurately through nearly the entire book. See what we shall say below regarding the *Diurnal Book* <note>The "Liber Diurnus Romanorum Pontificum," a collection of formulaic papal documents</note>. Honorius died on September 13, in the year 638. Eight *Letters* written by him are extant in the *Councils*, Volume V, page 1681, as well as an *Epigram on the Apostles being awestruck by Christ’s ascension into heaven*, in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XII, page 214.

<margin>627.</margin>
**BRAULIO**, brother of John, Bishop of Zaragoza <note>original: "Cæsaraugustani"</note>, whom he succeeded in the episcopal see in the year 627. He attended the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, the Fifth in 636, and the Sixth in 638. He died in 656. He wrote the *Life of Saint Emilian the Monk*, which is extant in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Age*, Volume I, page 205; two *Letters* to Isidore of Seville, which are usually found among the works of Isidore; and a brief *Eulogy of Isidore*, which is found in Surius under the date of April 3, and is frequently prefixed to Isidore's works.

<margin>629.</margin>
**SOPHRONIUS**, born in Damascus, was first a Sophist <note>a teacher of rhetoric</note>, then a monk, a close friend of John the Almsgiver, and finally, in the year 629, Patriarch of Jerusalem. He was a tireless champion of Orthodox truth: being present in Alexandria in the year 633, he strenuously cried out that Cyrus, under the pretext of entering into peace, had introduced heresy into the Church, and he renounced communion with him. Furthermore, he pleaded in letters to Sergius of Constantinople that the Seventh Chapter of the *Document of Satisfaction* prescribed by Cyrus to the Severians should be quashed; he even sent Stephen as a legate to Pope Honorius to manage the same matter. In the year 636, after Jerusalem was captured by Umar <note>original: "Haumare"</note>, leader of the Saracens, he negotiated a pact that the free profession of religion be granted to Christians; he ended his life that same year.

### SURVIVING WRITINGS.

An Encyclical **Letter**, written immediately after undertaking his Bishopric to Honorius, Sergius, and perhaps the other Patriarchs. That letter is indeed prolific, if any ever was, so much so that it could equal the bulk of a proper book. It is extant in Greek and Latin in the *Third Council of Constantinople*, Act XI, Volume VI, page 851.

Furthermore, John Moschus’s *Limonarium* <note>original: "Limonarium," also known as the "Spiritual Meadow," a collection of anecdotes about desert monks</note> or *Spiritual Meadow* is cited under Sophronius’s name both by Damascene in his first "Oration on Images," and by the Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea in Act 4. From this, the distinguished Vossius \*—using a quite probable conjecture that can also be confirmed from other sources—is of the opinion that Sophronius worked together with Moschus in weaving together the *Limonarium*; indeed, that he took the primary role in that work, although out of love and modesty he yielded the glory of it to his friend.

---

629. **DESIDERIUS**, a Gaul by birth, born in the town of Albi in the furthest reaches of Aquitaine, the son of Silvius and Herchenefreda. Around the year 614, he performed the duties of Treasurer in the court of King Chlothar II. In the year 629, after his brother Rusticus was killed by rioting citizens, he was appointed as the successor to the Bishopric of Cahors <note>original: "Cadurcensi"</note>. He died in the year 652, in the 23rd year of his episcopate. Two *Books of Letters* are extant, the first of which contains letters from Desiderius to his friends, and the second letters from others to Desiderius; these are found in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume V, p. 526, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume VIII, p. 579.

---

630. **JONAS**, an Irishman by birth, as he himself testifies in the Preface to the *Life of Saint Columban*. However, a passage found in the *Life of Attala* clearly shows that he was actually Italian, born not far from Piacenza. So much so that the author of the former work may be different from the author of the latter; or the words in the *Preface to the Life of Saint Columban* must be understood in another sense (which perhaps can be done without much trouble). A student of both the monasteries of Bobbio and Luxeuil, and finally Abbot of Luxeuil, he was prominent around the year 630 and thereafter. He survived until the year 665. He wrote the *Life of Saint Columban*, which is found in Surius, November 21st, and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Age*, Volume II, p. 5; the *Life of Eustace, Abbot of Luxeuil* in Surius, March 29th, and Mabillon, same volume, p. 115; the *Life of Attala, Abbot of Bobbio* in Surius, March 10th; the *Life of Bertulf, Abbot and successor to Attala* in Surius, August 19th, and Mabillon, same volume, p. 160; and the *Life of Saint John of Reomaus, founder and first Abbot of the monastery*, which was published with notes by Roverius in Paris, 1637, in the *History of the Abbots of Reomaus*.

---

<margin>\* On Irish Writers, book 1, chapter 3, p. 20. † Century 14, p. 190.</margin>
630. <note>The original text repeats the number 630 for the next entry.</note> **GALLUS**, an Irishman by birth, committed by his parents to the care of Saint Columban at a very tender age; he established his monastic life under him. He crossed the sea with him to Britain and then to Gaul, and was a companion in life and labors in the monastery of Luxeuil. Around the year 610, following Columban as he prepared for a journey to Italy, he remained in Rhaetia <note>a Roman province in the central Alps</note> at Columban's command, to drench the local people in the light of the Gospel; this he did vigorously after building himself a separate cell. When he was designated for the Bishopric of Constance by the votes of neighboring prelates, he saw to it that his disciple John was put in charge instead. Around the year 615, he founded the very famous monastery named after him in Switzerland <note>The Abbey of Saint Gall</note>. He was especially prominent in the year 620, and having reached the age of 95, he was seized by a fever and died in the year 635 according to Ware \*, or in 650 according to Bale †, Baronius, and others. There is an extant *Sermon delivered at Constance in the Church of Saint Stephen at the Consecration of John, Bishop of Constance*, found in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume V, p. 896, and a *Letter to Desiderius, Bishop of Cahors*,

<margin>630.</margin>
JOHN MOSCHUS, also called *the Castrate* <note>original: "Eviratus"</note>, by others *Eucrates*, flourished in the year 630. He led a monastic life, first in the Monastery of Saint Theodosius, then in the desert near the Jordan, and in the "New Laura" <term>a cluster of caves or cells for hermits</term> of Saint Sabas. Afterward, for the purpose of visiting illustrious monks, he began to travel to foreign regions, reaching the shores of Antioch, Alexandria, and the nearby desert; having been carried as far as the Oasis, he finally set out for Rome and the Western regions. When he had gathered from all quarters the famous deeds of the most distinguished monks of that century—partly witnessed by himself and partly accepted through the reports of others—he composed a *Historical Work*. He dedicated this to Sophronius the Sophist (who was later the Patriarch of Jerusalem), his nearly inseparable companion on his travels and his helper in arranging the work. This book is extant, called the *Spiritual Meadow*, the *New Little Garden*, the *Meadow-land*, and the *Orchard*. It was translated into Latin by Ambrogio Traversari <note>a 15th-century monk of the Camaldolese order</note> and published among the *Lives of the Fathers* (of which it constitutes the 10th book) by Rosweyde at Lyon, 1617, page 647, and elsewhere. Fronto Ducaeus added the Greek text (though mutilated by frequent gaps) to Ambrogio's Latin version in the *Supplement*, 1624, Volume II, page 1057. Cotelerius filled these gaps from a more complete manuscript in the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume II, page 341. Photius <margin>\* Codex 199.</margin> once noted that Moschus's style <gloss>tends toward the humbler and less learned</gloss>, being unrefined and simple.

633.

CONANTIUS, who followed Murila as Bishop of Palencia in Spain, flourished in the year 633, in which he signed the acts of the Fourth Council of Toledo. He was present at the Fifth Council of Toledo in 636 and the Sixth Council of Toledo in 638. He died after he had held the episcopal see for thirty years. He wrote a *Little Book of Prayers on the Universal Property of the Psalms* and published *many melodies or hymns*. NE. <note>"NE" likely indicates the work is "Not Extant" or lost.</note>

<margin>
633. 
Ildefonsus, *On Famous Men*, chapter 8.
</margin>
JUSTUS, trained in the monastic life under Helladius, succeeded him first in the rule of the Monastery of Agali and then in the governance of the See of Toledo; he flourished in the year 633, when he was present at the Fourth Council of Toledo. He held the episcopal see for three years and died nineteen days before King Sisenand in the year 635. He wrote a *Letter to Richila, Abbot of Agali*, in which he demonstrated clearly and forcefully that a flock, once undertaken, must never be abandoned. NE.

<margin>635.</margin>
ANDREW, a native of Damascus, was first a monk at Jerusalem, then a Deacon and *Orphanotrophos* <term>an official in charge of an orphanage</term> at Constantinople, and finally the Archbishop of Crete; he flourished around the year 635 and for a long time thereafter. Certainly, scholars do not agree well on his dates. Some wrongly refer him to the year 550 or 570. Others, including Casimir Oudin, led by I know not what authority, push him down to the year 720. But the authority of the Greek *Triodion* <term>a liturgical book for the season of Lent</term> supports our assigning the year 635 to him, in which he is said to have been <gloss>a contemporary</gloss> of Sophronius, the Patriarch of Jerusalem. However, it is clear that he extended his life beyond the year 680 from his *Eucharistic Iambics* <note>poems of gratitude written in iambic meter</note> addressed to Agatho, the Deacon and scribe of the Sixth Council, for the Synodal Acts which had been lent to him for copying.

### GEORGE PISIDES,
<margin>640.</margin>
Deacon and Archivist <term>Chartophylax</term> of the Church of Constantinople; he flourished around the year 640. He wrote many things, of which some survive, while many have perished.

*Cosmopoeia*, or an Iambic Poem on the Six Days of Creation <note>the Hexaemeron</note>, dedicated to Sergius of Constantinople. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> records that it formerly consisted of 3,000 verses, though in the poem we now have, you will find barely two thousand. In it, under the cover of Proclus’s name, John Philoponus is argued against, so much so that it may rightly be believed to be the same poem <margin>* Book 18, ch. 48.</margin> against Philoponus which Nicephorus reports was composed by George <term>εἰς τοὺς ἀθέους ὥσπερ εἰς γῆν φερομένους</term> <note>original Greek: "against the godless who are carried along like the earth"</note>.

An iambic poem *On the Vanity of Human Life*, incomplete at the end. Both poems, together with the remaining fragments collected from Suidas and elsewhere, appeared in Greek and Latin, *Paris, 1585, octavo, and in the Bignian Appendix, Paris, 1624, folio, p. 387.*

History of the deeds of Heraclius, and of the Persian War.

The *Avarica*, or History of the Avars.

<margin>† Under the entry "George."</margin>
Praise <note>original: "Encomium"</note> of Anastasius the Martyr. Suidas mentions that these works were written by George in prose, but they have not reached us.

Before we dismiss the reader, it must be noted that the *Sicilian Fasti*, or the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, is attributed to our George by most. This is a chronicle in which the times of the world are arranged through every age up to the tenth consulship of Heraclius, that is, up to the year of Christ 628. It is called "Alexandrian" because Peter of Alexandria had recommended it in a note placed on the frontispiece of the manuscript. This Chronicle was first found in an ancient library in Sicily by Girolamo Zurita, from whom Antonio Agustín received it. Agustín first brought the manuscript with him to Italy, where Sigonio and Panvinio used it, and then to Spain. From Antonio's copy, Andreas Darmarios—a "little Greek" from Crete—transcribed a copy; around the year 1573, he sold his manuscript along with nearly three hundred other valuable <note>original: "aureis," literally golden</note> manuscripts to Isaac Casaubon. Casaubon handed it over under fair conditions into the hands of Friedrich Sylburg, <margin>Letter 437; compare Letters 252 and 440.</margin> as he himself informs us in a letter to Scaliger. Finally, redeemed from Sylburg for 36 gold coins, David Hoeschel placed it in the library of Augsburg. From this, a small index of Roman Consuls was first published in Greek by Sylburg under the name of the *Sicilian Fasti*, and placed before the Greek writers of Roman history, set opposite the *Capitoline Fasti* of Panvinio, Frankfurt, 1590. Scaliger inserted the brilliant excerpts <note>original: "Eclogas"</note> which Casaubon had selected for his own use into his *Eusebian Chronicle*. Finally, the complete Chronicle, transcribed from the Augsburg library, was published in Greek and Latin by Matthäus Rader of the Society of Jesus, Munich, 1615, quarto. But the author's name is found neither in the manuscript itself, nor elsewhere...

He was led to think this chiefly by the argument that the author follows Alexandrian affairs most closely, and extending down even to these times, is commended by Peter, the successor of George. Whoever he may finally be, the author is certainly not to be looked down upon, for he not only provides a continuous series of Consuls, but has also woven into his work many "patches of better purple" <note>A literary metaphor meaning passages of high quality or distinction</note>—monuments of venerable antiquity that would be sought in vain elsewhere.

## ELIGIUS
A Frank by birth, born in the village of Chaptelat <note>original: "Catalacensi"</note> near the city of Limoges <note>original: "Lemovicum"</note> to his father Eutherius and mother Terrigia; he practiced the craft of goldsmithing for some time in the city of Limoges. In the year 635, sent as an envoy by King Dagobert into Little Brittany, he negotiated a truce with Duke Judicael <note>original: "Clippiaco"</note>. While he was still a layman, he founded many monasteries and basilicas, and was finally ordained Bishop of Noyon <note>original: "Noviomensis"</note> in the year 640 (not in the year 646, as is commonly calculated), as Charles le Cointe demonstrates in the *Annals of the Franks*, Volume II, at the year 640, number 20, etc. Once made Bishop, he devoted his efforts to building churches and instructing the Flemish, Frisians, and Swabians in the Christian faith. In the year 644, he took part in the Third Council of Chalon <note>original: "Concilio Cabilonensi III"</note>. In the year 650, he founded a monastery for men at Tournai, one for girls at Noyon, and dedicated the Church of Courtrai to the memory of Saint Martin. He died on the Calends of December <note>December 1st</note> in the year 659 according to le Cointe; in 665 by the common calculation; or according to others in 663.

*Letter to Desiderius of Cahors*, found among the letters of others to the same man in Canisius, Volume V.

And certainly, if not all the Homilies, at least most of them must be stripped from our Eligius.

## CUMMIANUS

## JOHN IV
A Dalmatian by birth, son of Venantius the Scholastic, a Deacon of the Roman Church, and finally elected Roman Pontiff in the year 640 before the 2nd day of August; he was ordained on the 3rd day of December after the death of Heraclius. Having held a Synod at Rome in that same year, he condemned the *Ecthesis* <term>an imperial edict defining the Monothelite faith</term> of Heraclius and the <term>Monothelite</term> heresy <note>The belief that Christ had two natures but only one will</note>; however, he defended the memory of Pope Honorius—who had been accused of that same heresy—in an *Apology* issued to the Emperor Constantine. The following year, having sent legates through Dalmatia and Istria, he asserted the freedom of many Christians led away into captivity by the Slavs, paying a great sum of money for their release. He died in the year 642 on the 20th day of September. There remain writings by him: a *Letter to the Scottish Bishops on celebrating Easter according to the Roman custom*, and *on rooting out the Pelagian heresy*...

### THALASSIUS

THALASSIUS, the Abbot of a certain monastery in the Libyan deserts, is assigned by some to the year 640 with a great appearance of probability, especially since Blessed Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662)</note> addresses him in a letter; others refer him to the year 465. Suidas * mentions a certain Thalassius who was very familiar with Theophilus, the most celebrated Bishop of the Churches <note>likely Theophilus of Alexandria</note>, and who recorded one of his miracles. However, it is not entirely clear whether that was our Thalassius. Thalassius wrote to Paul the Priest on sincere Charity, continence of life, and the governance of the mind, titled *Four Centuries of Sentences* <note>original: "Sententiarum Hecatontadas IV"; these were collections of 100 short wisdom statements</note>. These were published in Latin from the translation of Oecolampadius at Augsburg in 1520, and with other short works of the ancient theologians there in 1551, page 106; in the *Orthodoxographia* <note>A collection of "orthodox" writings</note>, page 897; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XII, page 337. ### AUDOENUS

AUDOENUS, also known as *Dado* <note>Saint Ouen (c. 609–684)</note>, a Frank by birth from the region of Soissons, was a Referendary <note>a high-ranking administrative official or chancellor</note> to King Dagobert; later, having left the secular world, he sought entry into the clergy. In the year 640, on the same day as Eligius of Noyon, he was ordained Archbishop of Rouen. In the year 644, he signed the acts of the Third Council of Chalon-sur-Saône <note>original: "Cabilonensi III"</note>. In the year 672, he wrote the *Life of Saint Eligius*. In the year 676, he set out for Rome for the sake of religion, returning the following year. In the year 683, after he had mediated peace between the Eastern and Western Franks, he was seized by a fever at the villa of Clichy <note>original: "Clippiacum"</note> and passed to the Lord in his ninetieth year, in the 44th year of his episcopate. He wrote the *Life of Saint Eligius of Noyon* in two books for Robert, Bishop of Paris; a third book, containing a summary of the previous ones, was added later. The first two are found in Surius, December 2nd. However, Luc d'Achery, having obtained a better manuscript, published three complete books in the *Spicilegium*, Volume V. A *Letter to Desiderius of Cahors* by the same author exists among the letters of that name in Canisius, Volume V, page 542.

### THEODORE

THEODORE, Bishop of the city of Pharan in Arabia Petraea near the border of Egypt, was most ruinously devoted to the heresies of the Eutychians and Monothelites. He flourished in the year 640. ### THEODORE

THEODORE, a Greek by nation, the son of a certain Bishop Theodore who seems to have been a native of Jerusalem, was ordained Pontiff of the Roman Church on the 3rd day of November in the year 642. # The Monothelite Age.
<note>Monothelitism was a 7th-century theological doctrine which taught that Christ had only one "will" (thelema). It was promoted by emperors to unify the empire but was rejected by the Roman Church as heresy, as it was seen to undermine Christ's full humanity.</note>

<margin>
7th CENTURY, from the Year 600.
</margin>
...and he struck Pyrrhus <note>Pyrrhus was the Patriarch of Constantinople who briefly recanted his Monothelite views before returning to them</note> with anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication</note> after he relapsed into his former errors. Theodore died on April 20, in the year 649. His extant works include: *A Synodic Letter to Paul of Constantinople; A copy of the proposal sent to Constantinople concerning the anathematization of the Ecthesis* <note>The 'Ecthesis' was an imperial edict issued by Heraclius in 638 that officially promoted Monothelitism</note>; and a *Letter to the Bishops who had consecrated Paul*, found among the collections of Anastasius edited by Sirmond, Paris, 1620, page 47; and thereafter in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume V, page 1777.

---

<margin>642.</margin>
**PAULUS**, a follower of the Monothelites, was substituted into the Patriarchate of Constantinople in the year 642 in place of Pyrrhus, who had withdrawn to Africa due to the Emperor’s irritated mind. In the year 648, through deception, he elicited an edict from Emperor Constans <note>Constans II, reigned 641–668</note> known as the *Typos* <note>original: "edictum"; the 'Typos' or 'Type' forbade all discussion of whether Christ had one or two wills or energies</note>, by which silence was commanded on the Monothelite controversy for everyone, whether they asserted one or two wills in Christ. For this reason, he was condemned by Pope Theodore in the same year in a Roman Synod, and was struck again with anathema by Pope Martin in the Lateran Council of 649. Paul himself, to pay back the favor, brought about by his crafty schemes with the Emperor that Pope Martin was summoned to Constantinople in 651 and afflicted with most grave evils. Paul died that same year, having been touched by repentance before his death. There remains: *A Letter to Pope Theodore written in 648 about receiving the Imperial Edict*, in Greek and Latin, in the *Lateran Council, Act 4, Collection of Councils, Volume VI, page 221*; and a *fragment of a letter to Theodore of Pharan*, in the *Sixth Council, Act 10, Collection of Councils, Volume VI, page 839*.

<margin>
645.
Life of St. Maximus, Greek/Latin Works, prefixed page 2.
</margin>
<margin>
* Letter 2 to John the Priest, Volume 2, page 250.

<margin>
See the Acts of St. Maximus, Greek/Latin, page 29, etc. Works, Volume I, where these things are narrated at great length.
</margin>
**MAXIMUS**, a native of Constantinople born of ancient nobility, was born in the year 580. After being exceptionally educated in every kind of discipline, he was called to the Court by Emperor Heraclius and worked on writing the Royal Commentaries, having been made *Proto-a-secretis* <term>Head Secretary</term>. When Heraclius eventually fell into the Monothelite heresy, Maximus, indignant at the situation—as the author of his biography says (though see the notes by Fr. Combefis regarding this)—or rather led by an immense love for solitude, deserted the Court and withdrew to the monastery called Chrysopolis near Constantinople. Shortly after, he was forced by the monks to take up its leadership. However, when he saw the Monothelite heresy triumphing everywhere in the East and groaned as Catholic truth went to ruin daily—and especially terrified by the fear of the Persians * who were rushing through nearly all parts of the East—he decided to withdraw to Western regions. Therefore, before the year 640, having set out for Africa, he urged the African Bishops to fight strenuously against the Monothelites, leading them by both word and example. In the year 645, after holding a disputation in Africa with the former Patriarch Pyrrhus of Constantinople in the presence of bishops and Gregory the praetorian prefect, he convicted the man of error and solidly demonstrated that there are two wills in Christ. In the same year, he hastened to Rome to oppose the Monothelites everywhere. In 649, he urged Pope Martin, with whom he was on familiar terms, to hold the Lateran Council, and he himself participated in that Council. Because Maximus so actively resisted the heretical error with which Emperor Constans was laboring, he was abducted from Rome by a military force in 655 and taken to Constantinople along with his disciple Anastasius, and cast into prison. After a few days, he was led to the palace to be tried on trumped-up charges of treason and slander against the Emperor, injury to Pyrrhus, and the crime of Origenism; when he had very clearly refuted these, he was ordered to subscribe to the imperial edict issued in 648 <note>The Typos</note> concerning the observance of silence on the Monothelite controversy by both sides. Refusing this, he was exiled to Bizya, a small town in Thrace, where in the following year on August 24 <note>original: "IX. cal. Septembr."</note>, a disputation was held between him and Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia. But when Maximus's adversaries made no progress at all in their cause by such artifice, the consul Paul was sent to lead him to a monastery near Rhegium, where the same cause was debated again. Since the holiest man could be bent by no deceits and no threats, he was immediately deported to Perberis by order of the Emperor, there to be afflicted with continuous harassments. From there, on June 8 <note>original: "VI. Id. Jun."</note>, 662, he was banished to the region of the Lazicans and thrust into the fortress of Schemre on the border of the Alans, where, after he had predicted that death would come to him within a few days,

<margin>7th CENTURY from the Year 600.</margin>
<margin>* Code 192.</margin>
On the 13th of August, he returned his soul—which had been harassed by so many evils—to heaven. Regarding his style, Photius * has this to say <note>original Greek: "Ἔστὶ δὲ τὴν φράσιν χιονωπὸς..."</note>: "His phrasing is as white as snow and pleasing to the ears; it shines with brilliant insights and uses authoritative language without being forced. However, where his writing is spread thin by obscurity and difficulty, it is due to a certain ruggedness and bulk. In those parts where he lowers his tone for the sake of clarity and repose, he strives to be pleasant to the ear. His use of metaphors does not lean toward grace or ornamentation, but is adopted simply and without affectation." His speech is continuously drawn out in complex periods, and he delights in *hyperbaton* <note>the inversion of normal word order</note>, gaining strength through long-windedness, even if he does not strictly avoid speaking plainly. Consequently, obscurity and difficulty run throughout his discourse. Furthermore, he sought a certain roughness of turgid diction (in terms of composition and pacing) in his oratory, such that he did not even strive to be pleasant to hear. Moreover, his use of figurative language was by no means composed to win favor or entice the reader, but was taken up simply and without care.

---

## W R I T I N G S.

**I**n response to difficult passages of Scripture, he wrote *Sixty-Five Questions to the Monk Thalassius* <note>Thalassius was an African abbot and friend of Maximus</note>. In this work, he is almost entirely an allegorist, bypassing the literal sense to dwell mostly on the mystical and spiritual meaning. Photius describes this work at length in Code 191.

*Seventy-Nine Questions and Answers on Various Doubts.* In resolving these questions, Saint Maximus does not apply the same precision as in the former works; hence, the illustrious Combefis <note>François Combefis, a 17th-century Dominican scholar and editor of Maximus’s works</note> willingly admits that the work was either begun by Maximus and finished by others, or at the very least, significantly altered by later hands.

*An Exposition on Psalm 59*, in which he clings stubbornly to the allegorical method of explanation.

*An Exposition on the Lord's Prayer.*

*An Ascetic Book*, composed in the form of a dialogue through questions and answers regarding the leading of a pious life. It was published in Latin along with some small works of Chrysostom and Basil by Fl. Nobilius at Rome in 1578.

*On Perfect Charity, and other Christian Virtues*, addressed to the Presbyter Elpidius in four "Centuries" <note>A 'Century' refers to a collection of 100 short theological or moral aphorisms</note>. These were published in Greek and Latin at Hanau in 1631, in octavo. The editor of this edition, Vincent Obsopoeus, foolishly attributed these chapters to Maximus of Turin. They appeared with the sentences of Antonius through the care of Conrad Gesner at Zurich in 1546; in the *Micropresbyticon* at Basel in 1555; and separately at Helmstädt in 1616.

*On Theology, and on the Dispensation of the Son in the Flesh*, in two hundred chapters. In this work, he treats the subject in almost the same manner as in the questions to Thalassius, but with slightly more refined arguments. Photius mentions these sentences in Code 191.

*Various Theological and Economic Chapters, and five hundred chapters on virtue and vice.* John Picus <note>Jean Picard, a legal official in the Parlement of Paris</note>, President of the inquisitorial classes in the Parisian Senate, first published these chapters in Greek and Latin, Paris, 1560, in octavo.

*To Theopemptus the Scholastic*, concerning the judge of iniquity.

*Another 213 Chapters* taken from a Vatican manuscript, which are very similar to the chapters on Charity.

*Excerpts from the work of 63 doubts.* These are not unworthy of Maximus, even if the ancient writers are silent about them.

*A Letter to the Presbyter Marinus.*

*To the same Marinus*, from the treatise on the operations and wills <note>Refers to the two "energies" and "wills" of Christ, the core of the Monothelite debate</note>, Chapters 50 and 51.

*To the Presbyter Gregory*, on the mystery of Christ.

*On the passage: "If it be possible, let this cup pass from me."*

*A Dogmatic Tome*, sent to the Deacon Marinus in Sicily.

*To Bishop Nicandrus*, on the two operations in Christ.

*A Letter to the Bishops of Sicily*, etc.

*To the Presbyter Marinus*, on the Procession of the Holy Spirit.

*Selections from the Letter to the Illustrious Peter*, concerning Pyrrhus, Sophronius, etc. In Latin.

*A Treatise on the Two Natures of Christ*, divided into ten chapters. Francois Combefis published it in Greek and Latin in his *Supplement* of 1648, Volume II, page 443; however, he thinks this book should rather be ascribed to Timothy the Presbyter of Constantinople.
