Various definitions appeared in Greek at Heidelberg in 1561, in octavo. They were also published in Greek and Latin by Hoeschel along with the *Mystagogy* <term>Mystagogy: an explanation of the Divine Liturgy and its symbolic meanings</term> at Augsburg in 1599, in octavo.

A Dogmatic Volume against the *Ekthesis* of Heraclius <note>The *Ekthesis* was an imperial edict issued in 638 by Emperor Heraclius that attempted to resolve theological conflicts by asserting that Christ had only one will.</note>.

A book on the two wills of the one Christ.

Definitions of Distinctions by which matters are settled.

Responses to Theodore, and the questions of Paul to Marinus the Presbyter.

A Dogmatic Volume addressed to Marinus the Presbyter.

On Quality, property, and difference, addressed to Theodore the Presbyter.

On Substance, or Essence and Nature; on the Hypostasis <term>Hypostasis: the distinct personhood of Christ as opposed to his nature</term> and nature.

That it is impossible to say there is only one will in Christ, and on the double will of Christ. From the questions proposed to him by the monk Theodore.

Definitions of the Holy Fathers regarding the two operations of Christ.

The Acts of the dispute regarding the two wills of Christ held with Pyrrhus in Africa. Photius <note>original: "Photius Cod. CXCV"</note> noted long ago in *Code 195* that these were written in a humbler style and did not sufficiently observe the laws of logic, nor the purity of speech; this may indeed be attributed to the ignorance of the notaries who recorded the acts of the dispute. Cardinal Baronius first published this dispute in Greek, adding the version by Turrianus, in the *Appendix to Volume VIII of the Ecclesiastical Annals*. From there, it is available in Greek and Latin in the *Councils, Volume V, page 1784.*

A book on the Soul.

Forty-six Epistles, of which the earlier ones may rightly be considered complete sermons or treatises.

Five Dialogues on the Holy Trinity, which are usually included among the works of *St. Athanasius*. Although Garnerius claimed them for Theodoret in his supplement to Theodoret's works, they are adjudged to *Maximus* by the authority of many manuscript codices and scholars.

The *Mystagogy*, or an Exposition of the Liturgy, published in Greek and Latin by *David Hoeschel* at Augsburg in 1599; thereafter in the *Ducaean Supplement, Volume II, page 166.*

Theological Chapters, or Sermons through excerpts from various writings, both Christian and Gentile or secular. *Conrad Gesner* published these maxims or commonplaces together with the Sermons of *Antony Melissa* in Greek and Latin at Zurich in 1546, in folio. They later appeared at the end of *Stobaeus* at Frankfurt in 1581 and Geneva in 1609, in folio. Regarding these editions, in which the sermons of *Maximus* and *Antony* are mixed together, see the observations in the notes by the *Illustrious Combefis*.

All these works of *St. Maximus*—partly published previously, and partly unearthed for the first time from various Roman, Italian, and French libraries and sought out from every quarter—were collected, revised, and illustrated with a Latin version and Greek notes and scholia <term>Scholia: ancient or medieval marginal commentaries on a text</term> by *François Combefis*. He published them in Greek and Latin in two volumes at Paris in 1675, in folio. He also included in his edition the *Life and Struggle of St. Maximus* written by a certain Greek author, the *Acts of the Collation with the Princes in the Secretariat*, the *Dispute with Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia*, an *Invective against the People of Constantinople on behalf of St. Maximus*, and the *Double Office of the Greek Church for St. Maximus* (to say nothing of other items), providing these in Greek and Latin with notes.

An Ecclesiastical Computation comprised of two books, or an explanation of the Christian Passover, with a brief reckoning of times, published in Greek and Latin by *Dionysius Petavius* in his *Uranology*, Paris, 1630, in folio.

*The Ambigua of St. Maximus, or Scholia on difficult passages of Gregory the Theologian.* A long work, which *John Scottus Eriugena* once translated for the most part into Latin. The complete work, together with the same *Scottus's books on the Division of Nature*, appeared in Greek and Latin at Oxford in 1681, in folio.

Scholia on the works of Dionysius the Areopagite, which exist in Greek (Paris, 1562, in octavo) and in Greek and Latin among the works of *Dionysius* (Antwerp, 1615; Paris, 1633 and 1644).

An Exposition on the Song of Songs, which *Michael Psellus* collected from the commentaries of *St. Maximus, Gregory of Nyssa, and Nilus*. It is available in Greek and Latin in the *Ducaean Supplement, Volume II, page 681.*

**VICTOR**, African by nation, Bishop of Carthage from the year 646. Immediately after undertaking the Episcopate, he wrote a letter to *Pope Theodore*, in which he informed him of his appointment and declared the Orthodox faith regarding the two wills in Christ. It is extant in Greek and Latin in the *History of the Councils*, Volume VI, page 151.

646.

**THEODORE**, a Priest in the Monastery of the Laura <term>Laura: a type of monastery consisting of a cluster of individual cells for hermits</term> called Raithu; he was a contemporary and close friend of Saint Maximus, who wrote a Letter to him regarding the wills and Operations in Christ. He flourished in the year 646. *Theodore of Raithu* wrote a *Commentary on the Incarnation of Christ* against the heresies of Mani, Apollinaris, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Nestorius, Eutyches, Julian of Halicarnassus, Severus, and others: Godefridus Tilmannus published this work in his own Latin translation under the title *Introduction to the Five Dogmatic Orations of Anastasius Sinaita* (Paris, 1556, octavo). Theodore Beza also translated this same commentary into Latin and published it in Greek and Latin at Geneva (1576, quarto); it was thereafter reprinted among the *Theological Works of Beza*, Volume 3, page 390. It appeared later in Greek and Latin edited by Robert Balfour at the end of the works of Gelasius of Cyzicus (Paris, 1599, octavo); and finally in the *Ducean Supplement*, Volume I, page 319. According to the Illustrious Pearson <margin>* Vindications of Ignatius, Part 1, page 18.</margin>, our Theodore seems to be that Priest Theodore mentioned by Photius in *Codex 1* <note>Photius was a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople whose "Bibliotheca" or "Codex" summarizes hundreds of books from antiquity.</note>, who composed a specific book written expressly to show—though unsuccessfully, no doubt, to use the words of that most learned man—that the work of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite is genuine <note>These works are now known to be by a "Pseudo-Dionysius," but their authenticity was a major debate in church history.</note>; he responded as best he could to the arguments brought against it. Four of the arguments remain in Photius’s summary, but the solutions to them are missing.

<margin>
646.
</margin>

**EUGENIUS**, Spanish by birth, a Priest of the Church of Toledo. Upon the death of the previous Eugenius, he was designated Archbishop of the See of Toledo, but he fled to Zaragoza [Caesaraugusta]; repairing to the tombs of the Martyrs, he requested that he be allowed to lead a monastic life. However, by the king's command, he was brought back to Toledo and ordained Bishop in the year 646. He presided over the Ninth Council of Toledo in 655 and the Tenth Council of Toledo in 656. He held the bishopric for nearly twelve years; and having died at last in the year 657, he had Ildefonsus as his successor. He reviewed, expanded, and polished the small books of Dracontius on the *Hexaemeron* <term>Hexaemeron: a theological treatise on the six days of creation</term>, and completed them by adding a Heroic Poem on the Work of the Seventh Day, which Dracontius had left unfinished. He also wrote certain *Epigrams*, which were published with the aforementioned Poem by Jacques Sirmond (Paris, 1619, octavo) and are contained in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XII, page 344. He also wrote a small book *On the Holy Trinity*, which has perished, and various other works in both verse and prose, which Ildefonsus mentions in *On Writers*, chapter 14.

646.
</margin>

**TAIO** or **TAGO**, surnamed Samuel, Spanish by birth, Bishop of Zaragoza, flourished in the year 646. At the command of King Chindasuinth and with the approval of the Seventh Synod of Toledo, he undertook a journey to Rome to obtain the books of Saint Gregory’s *Moralia* <note>Saint Gregory the Great's influential commentary on the Book of Job.</note>, which were much desired in Spain. After he had made a long and fruitless stay there, and had been mocked by the Roman Pontiffs who were occupied with other matters, he is said to have found the books—which he had previously sought in vain in Rome—in the temple of the Apostles, through a vision granted to him while sleeping. Having retrieved the books from the cabinets by the grace of this vision, he obtained them without difficulty from Pope Martin and brought them back with him to Spain. He was present at the Eighth Council of Toledo in 653 and the Ninth in 655. From the books of Blessed Gregory, he compiled *Five Books of Sentences*, preserving Gregory's own words and supplementing them with a few passages from Saint Augustine where Gregory's were lacking. They exist today among the Thuanus Manuscripts in folio. See the *Library of Thuanus*, Volume II, page 424. Mabillon published the Preface of that work addressed to Quiricus of Barcelona, along with Quiricus’s response, in *Analecta*, Volume II, page 68. His *Letter* to Eugenius of Toledo is also found in Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Volume IV, page 397.

...called the Lateran Council, which he began at Rome; in this council, he condemned the *Type* <note>original: "Typum"; an imperial edict issued by Constans II in 648 that forbade discussion of whether Christ had one or two wills</note> issued by Emperor Constans the previous year, and also condemned the leaders of the Monothelites: the Patriarchs of Constantinople, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul; Cyrus of Alexandria; and Theodore of Pharan. He fortified the Catholic faith regarding the two wills in Christ by passing Canons, and struck the Monothelite heresy with anathema. In the year 651, Olympius, the Exarch of the Emperor, came from Ravenna to Rome by imperial command and unsuccessfully attempted to set snares for the Pope. In the year 653, Calliopas, who had succeeded Olympius in the Exarchate, came to Rome escorted by the army of Ravenna; on June 19, he seized Martin with an armed hand. After spending three months in navigation, Martin was deported to the island of Naxos. After staying there for an entire year and being treated poorly, the Pontiff was brought to Constantinople on September 17, 654, and placed into custody. After 93 days, he was led to the tribunal of judges and, burdened with many criminal charges, was forced to plead his case. But since he would neither approve the Emperor’s *Type* nor enter into communion with the Patriarch of Constantinople, he was sent back to prison, laden with chains and vexed on all sides with dire punishments. After 85 days had passed, he was deported to Cherson <note>A city on the Crimean Peninsula</note>, arriving there on May 15, 655. He died an exile in the same year on September 16, and was buried near Cherson in the church of the Blessed Mary called Blachernae. Seventeen of his *Letters* are extant, of which eleven are preserved in Greek and Latin in the *History of the Councils, Volume VI, page 5.*

---

<margin>649.</margin>
**MAURUS**, Bishop of Ravenna, flourished in the year 649. He wrote a *Letter to Pope Martin against the Monothelites*, which was read and approved at the Lateran Council and ordered to be inserted into the Synodal Acts; it is found there in Greek and Latin in *Session 1, History of the Councils, Volume VI, page 96.* Furthermore, let no one wonder why so many letters from Western Bishops exist in Greek and Latin in the Acts of the Lateran Council: one should know that the Acts of the Council, and thus the Letters and Petitions mixed within them, were later translated into the Greek language, as they still survive today.

---

<margin>655.</margin>
**ANASTASIUS**, at first a Monk and later an Abbot, born in the year 618. A disciple of Saint Maximus and an inseparable companion of his travels, calamities, and exiles for an entire decade, he flourished in the year 655. In that year, by order of the Emperor, he was taken from Rome to Constantinople along with Saint Maximus; there he was brought to trial, harassed in terrible ways, and finally banished to Perberis. In the year 662, he was deported to Lazica <note>A region in modern-day Georgia</note> with the Blessed Maximus, where he was imprisoned first in a castle called Scotorus in Apsilia near Abasgia, and then in Suania. Due to the many tortures and lashings he had endured in Byzantium, as well as the afflictions and hardships brought upon him in this place, he fell asleep in the Lord while barely half-alive on July 24, 664. He wrote a *Letter to the Community of Monks established at Cagliari* in 655, which is extant in Latin among the *Collected Works of Anastasius* edited by Sirmond (Paris, 1620, octavo, page 142) and among the *Works of Maximus, Volume I, page 43.*

---

<margin>655.</margin>
**ANASTASIUS**, a Priest and Apocrisiarius <note>A permanent diplomatic representative or legate</note> of the Roman Church and a disciple of Blessed Maximus, flourished in the year 655. In that year, because of the cause of his teacher Maximus and his confession of the Orthodox truth, he was sent into exile to Mesembria, a city in Thrace, and later banished to Trebizond. In the year 662, he was deported with Blessed Maximus to the region of the Lazi; there, torn away from Maximus and his fellow exile of the same name, Anastasius, he was cast into a fortress called Buculus in the Mesimian region near the borders of the Alans. After a few days, he was sent away to the castle of Thacyria near Iberia, and from there to the fortress of Phustas, and soon to Schemaris. He died on October 11, 666. While an exile in Lazica in 665, he wrote a *lengthy Letter to Theodosius, a Priest of Gangra*, in which, besides narrating the exiles of himself, Blessed Maximus, and Anastasius of Constantinople, he wove in many testimonies drawn from the writings of Saint Hippolytus concerning the two operations of Christ; from these, we too have borrowed certain things that shed light on these matters. This *Letter* is extant in Latin among the *Collected Works of Anastasius* edited by Sirmond (Paris, 1620, page 193) and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XII, page 858.*

<margin>656.</margin>
FRUCTUOSUS, of Spanish origin, born from the royal blood of the Goths <note>The Visigoths, who ruled the Iberian Peninsula at this time</note>, was a disciple of Conantius, the Bishop of Palencia. He founded many monasteries, among them the Complutense <note>Located in modern-day Alcalá de Henares</note>, which he himself governed. Later, he was made Bishop of Dumio, and finally, in the year 656, by a decree of the Tenth Council of Toledo, he was substituted into the place of Potamius, the Archbishop of Braga, who had recently been deposed. He died before the year 675. He wrote a double *Rule of Monks* <note>original: "Regulam Monachorum"</note>, one consisting of 23 chapters, the other of 20. Lucas Holstenius published both in the *Code of Rules* (Paris, 1663, part 2, page 133).

<margin>
657.
* On the affairs of Spain, Book 6, chapter 10.
</margin>
ILDEFONSUS, of Spanish origin, was born in Toledo to a noble family; his father was Stephen and his mother Lucia. The historian Mariana* records that the house made famous by his birth is still pointed out there. Having been taught the first elements of letters by Eugenius, the Archbishop of Toledo, he was sent to Seville to be further polished by Bishop Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville, the great encyclopedist of the Middle Ages</note>. This being done, he spurned all the honors of secular life which his father had intended for him and took the monk’s cowl in the Monastery of Agali. In a short time, on account of his piety and exceptional learning, he gained such a high reputation that upon the death of Abbot Adeodatus, the governance of the monastery was entrusted to his care. During that time, he founded a college for virgins at his own expense on the Debiensi estate; and finally, in the year 657, he succeeded Eugenius in the See of Toledo. Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a prominent church historian</note> pushes this back to the year 662. Having been made Bishop, he suppressed with much labor the boldness of Pelagius and Helladius, who were striving to revive the error of Helvidius <note>Helvidius was a 4th-century writer who argued that Mary had other children after Jesus; Ildefonsus was famous for defending her perpetual virginity</note>, which had long been obsolete; he earnestly defended the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Mary. He died in the year 667, after completing almost nine years and two months of his episcopate. He became so famous through his many writings after his death that he is often called the *Chrysostom* <note>meaning "Golden-Mouthed," after the famous Greek orator</note> and the *Anchor of Faith* by those who cite him.

->Writings which are extant.<-

*Book on the unblemished virginity of the Blessed Virgin against the Infidels.* <note>original: "Liber de illibatâ virginitate B. Virginis contra Infideles"</note>
*Book against those who argue about the perpetual virginity of Blessed Mary, and about her labor.* <note>original: "Liber contra eos qui disputant de perpetuâ virginitate B. Mariæ, & de ejus parturitione"</note> Boston of Bury warns that these two books are ascribed by some to Radulfus Flaviacensis. Dacherius more correctly adjudges them to Paschasius Radbertus.
*Homily against those who falsely claim that the Virgin Mary gave birth to the Lord against the law.*
*Six Sermons on the Assumption of Blessed Mary*, of which Boston attributes the 2nd and 3rd to Ansbert, Abbot of Fontanelle.
*Double Sermon on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary.*
*Sermon on her Purification.*
Father Feuardentius published these treatises (Paris, 1576); with the exception of the single book on the unblemished virginity of the Blessed Virgin, Joannes Poza contends in the *Elucidation of the Mother of God* (Book 4, track 4, chapter 6) that these are spurious, both because of the style and the doctrine contained within them. To these, add those which Father Combefis has in the *Library of Preachers* (Volume 7) and Lucas Dacherius in the *Spicilegium* (Volume 1, page 12), with the learned Oudinus noting (*Supplement*, page 182) that quite a few things in these Homilies were taken partly from the *Homilies of Saint Bernard*, and partly from the *Commentary on the Penitential Psalms* attributed by some to Gregory VII and by others to Anselm of Lucca. Furthermore, these treatises are also held in the *Library of the Fathers* (Volume 12).
*Book on Fourteen Ecclesiastical Writers*, or an Appendix to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men* after Jerome and Gennadius. This was published by Miraeus in the *Ecclesiastical Library* (page 93, Antwerp, 1639) with notes, and elsewhere quite often.
*Two Letters* found in Dacherius's *Spicilegium* (Volume 1, page 308). Trithemius and Possevinus testify that Ildefonsus wrote an entire volume of letters: whether this still lies hidden somewhere is not certain.

*Prosopopoeia of his own weakness.* <note>original: "Prosopopoeiam imbecillitatis propriæ"; a prosopopoeia is a rhetorical device where an abstract thing is personified.</note>

Furthermore, Ildefonsus extended Isidore’s *History of the Origin of the Goths* <note>Saint Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose history of the Goths was a foundational text for Spanish identity.</note> from the fifth year of King Swinthila, where Isidore stopped, up to the eighteenth year of King Recceswinth. For the most learned Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> very likely conjectures that this historian, whatever he provides concerning that period of time which Ildefonsus pursued, copied from Ildefonsus’s Chronicle with only a few changes.

<margin>657.</margin>
VITALIAN, a native of Campania from the city of Segni, son of Anastasius, was ordained Pontiff of the Roman Church on July 30, in the year 657. In the year 663, he received the Emperor Constans <note>Constans II, the last Eastern Emperor to visit Rome.</note> arriving in Rome with the greatest humility and obedience. Around the year 668, he excommunicated Maurus, the Bishop of Ravenna, because, having been summoned many times to Rome to state his case, he refused to attend. Maurus held the <term>brutum fulmen|a "senseless thunderbolt," meaning an empty or ineffective threat</term> in such low regard that he, in turn, struck Vitalian with anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication from the Church.</note>; and being close to death, he bound the bishops of his province by oath that they would never yield to the Roman Pontiff. Vitalian died on December 30, in the year 671. *Six Letters* are extant in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 6, page 445.

<margin>657.</margin>
SYRICIUS, Bishop of Barcelona, flourished in the year 657. There are *Two Letters* written by him, which Luc d’Achery first published in his *Spicilegium*, Volume 1.

<margin>660.</margin>
MARCULF, a monk, if I am not mistaken, from Paris, already seventy years old, wrote around the year 660. He collected *Two books of Ecclesiastical Formulas* <note>A collection of legal templates used for administrative and church business in the Frankish kingdom.</note>; which he dedicated to Landry, the Bishop of Paris. Jérôme Bignon first rescued these from the shadows and published them with most learned notes (Paris, 1613, octavo). However, an enlarged edition, prepared by the very erudite Bignon, appeared again in the same place in 1666, in quarto. They are also found among the *Capitularies* <note>Administrative or legislative decrees of the Frankish kings.</note> published by Baluze, Volume 2, page 369, who added his own notes to those of Bignon; from there they also appear in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 12, page 767.

<margin>660.</margin>
CUMMENEUS, called "the White" <note>Cumméne Find (d. 669), the seventh abbot of Iona.</note>, an Irishman by birth—a different man from the Cummian mentioned above—was made Abbot of Hy <note>Iona, the famous monastery off the coast of Scotland founded by St. Columba.</note> in the year 657. He flourished in the year 660 and died in the year 669. He wrote the *Life of Saint Columba, the first Abbot of Hy in Britain*, which is published by Mabillon in the *Benedictine Century*, Volume 1, page 361.

<margin>668.</margin>
THEODOSIUS and THEODORE, Eastern monks, companions of the Blessed Maximus, Pope Martin, and the Anastasiuses, flourished in the year 668. In that year, returning from Lazica <note>A region on the Black Sea where Maximus the Confessor was exiled.</note>—which they had sought out for the sake of visiting the Holy Confessors Maximus and his companions—they received from the monk Gregory a copy of the letters of Anastasius the <term>apocrisiarius|a high-ranking representative or legate of a bishop or the Pope</term> concerning the death of Maximus and the other Anastasius. They wrote a *Scholion or Memorandum concerning the exile and death of Maximus and his companions, and especially of Anastasius the Apocrisiarius*; which Jacques Sirmond published in Latin among the *Miscellany of Anastasius* (Paris, 1620, page 251). The Greek and Latin version appeared in the *Combefis Apparatus* to the works of Saint Maximus, page 80.

...also those of *St. Maximus* <note>Saint Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), a monk and theologian who was a leading opponent of Monothelitism.</note> not long ago published by *Combefis* <note>François Combefis (1605–1679), a French Dominican scholar who edited many patristic works.</note>, p. 67.

<margin>656.</margin> **FRUCTUOSUS**, a Spaniard by birth, descended from the royal blood of the Goths, was a disciple of Conantius, Bishop of Palencia. He founded many monasteries, among them the Complutense <note>The monastery of San Cosme y Damián de Compluto in the region of El Bierzo.</note>, over which he himself presided. Later he was made Bishop of Dumium, and finally in the year 656, by a decree of the Tenth Council of Toledo, he was substituted into the place of Potamius, the recently deposed Archbishop of Braga. He died before the year 675. He wrote a double *Rule for Monks* <note>original: "Regula Monachorum"</note>, one consisting of 23 chapters, the other of 20. Lucas Holstenius published both in the *Codex of Rules* <note>original: "Codice Regularum"</note>, Paris, 1663, part 2, p. 133.

<margin>657. * On Spanish Affairs, book 6, ch. 10.</margin> **ILDEFONSUS**, a Spaniard by birth, was born in Toledo to a noble family; his father was Stephen and his mother Lucia. *Mariana* <note>Juan de Mariana (1536–1624), a famous Spanish Jesuit historian.</note> records that the house made famous by his birth is still pointed out there. Having been instructed in the first elements of letters by Eugenius, Archbishop of Toledo, he was sent to Seville to be further polished by Bishop Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), the great encyclopedist of the early Middle Ages.</note>. This being done, he spurned all the honors of secular life which his father offered him and took the cowl <note>original: "cucullum induit"; became a monk.</note> in the Agali Monastery. In a short time, on account of his piety and exceptional learning, he obtained such a great reputation that upon the death of Abbot Adeodatus, he had the prefecture of the monastery committed to his trust. During that time, he founded a college of virgins at the Deibi estate at his own expense; and finally, in the year 657, he succeeded Eugenius in the See of Toledo. *Baronius* <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), known for his ecclesiastical annals.</note> rejects this date, moving it to the year 662. Having been made Bishop, he suppressed with much labor the audacity of Pelagius and Helladius, who were striving to revive the long-obsolete error of Helvidius <note>Helvidius was a 4th-century writer who argued that Mary had other children after Jesus; Ildefonsus was famous for defending her perpetual virginity.</note>, and he strenuously vindicated the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Mary. He died in the year 667, after completing almost nine years and two months since undertaking the Episcopate. He became so famous through his many writings even after death that he is often called "Chrysostom" <note>Greek for "Golden-mouthed," a title usually reserved for St. John Chrysostom.</note> and the "Anchor of Faith" <note>original: "Ancora fidei"</note> by those who cite him.

->*Extant Works.*<-

**B**ook *on the unstained virginity of the Blessed Virgin against Unbelievers.*
*Book against those who dispute the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Mary, and her childbirth.* *Boston of Bury* <note>John Boston of Bury, a 15th-century English monk and bibliographer.</note> advises that these two books are ascribed by some to *Radulfus Flaviacensis* <note>Raoul of Flaix, a 12th-century Benedictine.</note>. *D'Achery* <note>Jean-Luc d'Achery (1609–1685), a Benedictine scholar.</note> more correctly adjudges them to *Paschasius Radbertus* <note>A 9th-century theologian.</note>.
*Homily against those who falsely affirm that the Virgin Mary gave birth to the Lord against the law.*
*Six Sermons on the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, of which Boston attributes the 2nd and 3rd to Ansbert, Abbot of Fontenelle.*
*A double sermon on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary.*
*Sermon on her Purification.*

Brother *Feuardentius* published these treatises in Paris, 1576. *Juan Poza*, in the *Elucidarium of the Mother of God* <note>original: "Elucidario Deiparæ"</note> book 4, tract 4, chapter 6, contends that—with the exception of the single book *on the unstained virginity of the Blessed Virgin*—these are supposititious <note>term: supposititious (spurious or forged)</note> both because of the style and because of the doctrine contained in them. To these add those which *Fr. Combefis* has in the *Preacher’s Library* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Concionat."</note> Vol. 7, and *Lucas D'Achery* in the *Spicilegium* Vol. I, p. 12. *Cl. Oudin* warns in his *Supplement* p. 182 that not a few things in these Homilies are taken partly from the Homilies of *St. Bernard*, and partly from the Commentary on the Penitential Psalms attributed by some to *Gregory VII* and by others to *Anselm of Lucca*. Furthermore, these treatises are also found in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Biblioth. Patr."</note> Vol. XII.
*Book on Fourteen Ecclesiastical Writers, or an Appendix to Isidore’s book On Illustrious Men after Jerome and Gennadius.* This was published by *Miraeus* in the *Ecclesiastical Library* p. 93, Antwerp, 1639, with notes, and often elsewhere.
*Two Letters in D'Achery’s Spicilegium Vol. I, p. 308.* *Trithemius* and *Possevinus* testify that *Ildefonsus* wrote an entire volume of Letters: whether it still lies hidden somewhere is not certain.

**VITALIAN**, a Campanian by birth from the city of Segni and son of Anastasius, was ordained Pontiff of the Roman Church on July 30 in the year 657. # The Monothelite Century.
<note>The 7th century is termed "Monothelite" due to the intense theological debate over whether Jesus Christ possessed one will (Monothelitism) or two (Dyothelitism).</note>

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year
600.
668.
</margin>

**THEODORE**, a Cilician by birth, from the city of Tarsus—a fellow countryman of Saint Paul—and a monk by training, was residing in Rome in the year 668. After he had first received the tonsure <note>The practice of shaving the top of the head as a sign of clerical or monastic status; Theodore, coming from the East, had to adopt the Roman style of tonsure before his appointment.</note> in the Roman fashion, he was elevated to the Archbishopric of Canterbury by Pope Vitalian and consecrated by the Pontiff himself on April 1. While he set out on his journey to England, he was delayed for a long time in Gaul <note>Modern-day France.</note> and finally arrived in Canterbury eighteen months later. His first concern was to bestow a more beautiful appearance upon the English Church; his second was to revive the study of literature, a task he accomplished successfully. To this end, he brought with him to England a copious library furnished with both Greek and Latin books. Some of these, according to the author of the *Antiquities of Britain* <margin>$\dagger$ *Antiquities of Britain*, p. 53.</margin>—whether that was Parker <note>Matthew Parker (1504–1575), Archbishop of Canterbury.</note> or Josselin <note>John Josselin (1529–1603), Parker’s secretary and a noted Anglo-Saxon scholar.</note>—written in the Greek language, remain among us. These include the *Works of Homer*, written so elegantly and exquisitely in Greek characters that they surpass the accuracy of printed books (a large volume on very ancient paper); the *Homilies of Chrysostom* on parchment leaves; the *Psalms of David*; and the *Hypomnesticon* <note>A "commemorative summary" or "memorandum."</note> of Joseph in the same language. These works are truly rare in our century due to the excellence of their script and deserve to be held in perpetual memory. What wonder is it, then, if the English Church should lower its fasces <note>A Roman symbol of authority; here meaning the church submitted its leadership and customs.</note> to such a grave Prelate and so learned a head, and, having abandoned the old custom of celebrating Easter, should pass almost everywhere without difficulty into Roman rites?

In the year 673, on the 24th of September, he held the Synod of Hertford; in this meeting, those things which had been canonically decreed in ancient times by the fathers across the sea were decreed to be observed by the English. Ten of its chapters may be seen in Bede, Book 4, Chapter 3. In the year 680, a second Synod was held by him at Hatfield in the county of Kent; in this synod, to declare the faith of the British Churches against the heresies of Eutyches <note>The Eutychian heresy claimed Christ had only one nature.</note> and the Monothelites, five Ecumenical Councils were accepted. See Bede, Book 4, Chapter 17. Theodore died on the 19th of September in the year 690, at the age of 88; he used to predict he would live to this age, and no further, having been warned in a dream. 

Theodore wrote a *Penitential* <note>A manual for priests containing a list of sins and the corresponding penances to be assigned.</note>, a sufficiently large work adapted to nearly all cases of penance. The most famous Spelman, in the first volume of the *English Councils*, presented to us the titles or summary chapters—seventy-eight in number—of the complete work, which in his time was still surviving in the Benedictine Library at Cambridge <note>The Parker Library at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.</note>. What happened to it thereafter is not quite clear; I fear it may not be found anywhere among us. For the portions that remain in the Benedictine Library today, and those published in Paris, are only excerpts from a much longer work. Casimir Oudin <margin>\* *Supplement*, p. 185.</margin> wishes that Spelman had offered the entire *Penitential* to the Christian world, making no mention of the Parisian edition in the meantime. Could he, who was so sharp-sighted regarding foreign matters, be blind at home? That is, was he unaware that Theodore’s *Penitential*—enlarged with all the chapters that could be found and other distinguished monuments of ecclesiastical discipline, and adorned with the very rich annotations of Jacques Petit—was published in Paris in 1677, in two volumes? 

Petit indeed confesses that he gave the name *Penitential* to his collection, not as if he were presenting the complete book of penance, but because he seemed to omit nothing of importance. Meanwhile, he deserved no small thanks from the Christian commonwealth for having sought out from all sides, with laudable zeal and the greatest diligence, everything that could be obtained. Since, however, Petit constantly boasts of the manuscript codices he used and praises their owners as is fitting, I have heard more than once from the Fellows of the Benedictine College at Cambridge <note>Corpus Christi College.</note> that they had taken care to have the very ancient codex of Theodore’s *Penitential* (which is kept in that College’s library) beautifully transcribed with the greatest care, and sent the transcript to Paris—a fact which the editor suppressed with entirely ungrateful silence. 

The entire collection published by Petit is divided into two volumes. In the first are presented Theodore’s *Penitential* containing 14 chapters; his *60 Chapters*; the 10 Chapters offered by Theodore as president to the Synod of Hertford; *other chapters* from fragments published by D’Achery; *others from Canons, from penitential books, from collections of Canons*, collected from certain manuscript codices; the *Titles of the Penitential Book* published by Spelman; the *Theodorian Penitential* compared with certain chapters and Canons excerpted from it; *Selected Canons* from a very ancient collection of Canons; the *Hérouval Codices* <note>Manuscripts owned by the French magistrate and scholar Hérouval.</note> regarding Ecclesiastical doctrine and Discipline; and excerpts...

# The Monothelite Century. 465
<note>The 7th century is called the "Monothelite" century because of the theological conflict regarding whether Christ had one will (Monothelitism) or two (Dyothelitism).</note>

<margin>
7th CENTURY
from the Year
of Our Lord
</margin>

...from other manuscript codices concerning certain principal matters treated in Theodore’s *Penitential* and *Chapters*. These are followed by many excellent monuments of ecclesiastical discipline, gathered from all sides and distributed into various classes and articles. In Volume II, there is a first *Dissertation*, in which he defends Theodore’s pastoral vigilance against slanderers—namely [John] Bale and the Magdeburg Centuriators <note>The Magdeburg Centuriators were a group of Lutheran scholars who wrote a massive history of the Church from a Protestant perspective; John Bale was a contemporary English polemicist.</note>—using the traditions of the ancients and testimonies of the Fathers drawn in a long line from Ignatius of Antioch down to Theodore’s own times. To this, he adds his observations on examples of this pastoral vigilance. In the second *Dissertation*, he extensively vindicates Theodore’s doctrine on *Penance* from any suspicion of innovation against Jean Morin <note>A 17th-century French theologian and scholar of liturgy.</note>. Finally, in the last place, there are notes which, to use his own words, are like so many dissertations in themselves, in which the lies of malicious men are refuted—those who dare to rashly call the most holy and learned prelate of the Church of Canterbury a teacher of a "novel and superstitious religion." Lastly, it must be noted that our Theodore, who borrowed this custom from his fellow Greeks, was the first to write a penitential book for the Westerners, which others later imitated; thus, he should rightly and deservedly be considered the source and origin of all penitential formulas in the Latin Church. *Theodore’s 120 Ecclesiastical Chapters* are also found in d'Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, Volume IX, and in the Appendix to the *Councils*, Volume VI, page 1875. There also exists a *Letter* from Theodore to Æthelred, King of the Mercians, regarding the restoration of friendship between himself and Wilfrid, Bishop of York, whom Theodore had unjustly caused to be deposed; this is found in William of Malmesbury’s *On the Deeds of the Bishops*, Book 3, folio 151, and the *Councils*, Volume VI, page 1383.

---

<margin>672.</margin>
**ADEODATUS**, a Roman by birth and the son of Jovinianus, was a monk by profession and finally became the Roman Pontiff from March 14, 672. He died on May 18, 677. He wrote *A Letter to All the Bishops of Gaul*, by which he granted a privilege to the Monastery of Saint Martin. It is found in the *Councils*, Volume VI, page 523.

<margin>679.</margin>
**AGATHO**, a Sicilian by birth, was ordained Pope of Rome from being a monk on May 29, 679. In the year 680, after an Ecumenical Council was summoned at Constantinople by Emperor Constantine <note>Constantine IV, who oversaw the Third Council of Constantinople.</note>, Agatho himself held a Synod at Rome to prepare the way for the successful management of the affairs of the Western Church at the Constantinopolitan Council. He earnestly invited Theodore of Canterbury from England by urgent prayers; however, the weight of old age prevented Theodore from complying with the Pontiff’s wishes. From the Roman Synod, Agatho sent as legates to Constantinople the bishops Abundantius of Paterno and John of Reggio, the priests Theodore and George, John the Deacon, and Constantine the Subdeacon, to act in his place at the General Council. He died on December 1, 681. *Three Letters* written by him exist: one, which is quite lengthy, addressed to Emperor Constantine, found in Greek and Latin in the 4th action of the 6th Synod (*Councils*, Vol. VI, p. 629); a second in his own name and that of the Roman Synod to the Emperor and the Council of Constantinople regarding the legates sent to the Synod (ibid., p. 678); and a third *to Æthelred, King of the Mercians*, and another regarding the delegated authority granted to the Abbot of Medeshamstede <note>Now known as Peterborough.</note> (ibid., p. 576).

<margin>679.</margin>
**ADAMNAN** (or **ADOMNÁN**), of the Scots-Irish people, a monk and priest, succeeded to the government of the monastery of Iona after the death of Failbe in 679. In the year 701, sent as an ambassador by his people to Aldfrith, King of the Northumbrians, he learned and approved the Roman custom of celebrating Easter in England; upon returning home, he unsuccessfully tried to get his own people to observe it. Later, crossing over into Ireland, he brought many, indeed nearly all, to the English custom of celebrating Easter. Finally, having returned to Iona, and after he had again recommended the rite of the Roman Church to his monks with fruitless labor, he departed from this life before the year was out, on October 23, 704, at the age of 74 (or according to others, 80). He published *The Life of Saint Columba in Three Books*, which are found in Canisius, Volume V, part 2, page 562, and in Surius on June 9. Also *On the Places of the Holy Land in Three Books*, which he [wrote] from the mouth of Arculf... <note>Arculf was a Frankish bishop who was shipwrecked in Britain after a pilgrimage to the Levant; his stories became the basis for Adamnan's famous geographical work.</note>

<margin>680.</margin>
### CEOLFRID
An Englishman by nation, from the region of Bernicia <note>An early Anglo-Saxon kingdom in what is now northern England and south-east Scotland</note>, he was the Abbot of the Monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow after Benedict Biscop. The teacher of the Venerable Bede, he flourished in the year 680. He set out for Rome—though in which year is not sufficiently clear—from which he brought back many books with which he adorned the Library he built in both Monasteries; regarding these, see Bede’s *Lives of the Abbots of Wearmouth*, book 2, page 46. By sending monks to Rome, he also obtained a privilege for his monastery from Pope Sergius, which was confirmed by the subscription of King Aldfrith and all the Bishops in a gathered English Synod. Having been asked by envoys sent by Nechtan, King of the Picts <note>Nechtan mac Der-Ilei, ruler of a confederation of peoples in what is now Scotland</note>, to teach him more fully concerning the method of celebrating Easter and the Roman clerical tonsure <note>The practice of shaving the top of the head as a sign of religious devotion; different traditions used different shapes</note>, he wrote a lengthy Letter on these arguments. Nechtan received this with such joy that, rising from the midst of his nobles and kneeling on the ground, he gave thanks to God that he had been worthy to receive such a small gift from the land of the English; he soon after decreed by edict that the Roman rites in these matters should be observed throughout all the provinces of the Picts. At last, nearly broken by old age and labors, and to the great grief of his followers, he resigned his rule and prepared to undertake a second journey to Rome. However, reaching Langres in Gallia Narbonensis <note>Modern-day France</note>, heavy with disease and age, he yielded to nature and died in the Monastery of the Twins <note>The Monastery of Saint-Geosmes</note> on the 7th day before the Kalends of October <note>September 25</note>. He was buried there, aged 74; having spent 47 years in the priesthood and 35 in monastic rule. He was a man industrious in all things, sharp in wit, tireless in action, mature in mind, and fervent in religious zeal, as Bede says of his master in the place cited on page 47. His *Letter to Nechtan on Easter and the Tonsure* is extant in Bede’s history, book 5, chapter 22, and in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume VI, page 1423. Other writings of his—namely, *Solemn Homilies; Letters to Monks; A Book on His Pilgrimage;* and his *Will to Hwenberht*—are mentioned by [John] Bale and [John] Pits.

<margin>680.</margin>
### ALDHELM
An Englishman by nation, son of Kenten, and nephew of Ina, King of the West Saxons, he traveled through Gaul and Italy while still a young man. He applied himself to both sacred and secular literature with such ardor of mind that he far surpassed all the theologians of his time. Having returned home, he was first a monk and then made Abbot of Bladun, or Malmesbury, in the year 671. He flourished especially around the year 680. After spending 34 years in monastic rule, he was consecrated Bishop of the Church of Sherborne in the year 705. He died on the 25th of May in the year 709. While he was still performing the duties of Abbot, he wrote, at the command of a Synod of his people, against the neighboring Britons, because they stubbornly <note>original: "mordicùs," literally "with their teeth"</note> retained the Quartodeciman <note>A term for those who celebrated Easter on the Jewish Passover date, the 14th of Nisan, rather than the following Sunday</note> custom of celebrating Easter. He was the first of the English nation, 
<margin>
* Camden’s *Britannia* in Wiltshire, p. 116.
† [Bede] Book 5, ch. 19.
</margin>
according to Camden*, who wrote in Latin, and the first who taught his countrymen the method of composing Latin verse. He was a man, by Bede’s testimony†, most learned in every respect; for he was polished in speech and marvelous in his knowledge of both liberal and ecclesiastical Scriptures. Besides the *Work on Easter*, now lost, he wrote (by the same testimony) an excellent book *In Praise of Virginity*, which he composed following the example of Sedulius in both hexameter verse and prose <note>This style of writing the same work in both prose and poetry is known as an *opus geminatum* or "twin work"</note>. That book is extant, published at *Paris, 1576*, in Canisius, Volume 5, part 2, page 798, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 13, page 1. He also wrote several other things which are extant: a book *On the Eight Principal Vices*, which is found in the aforementioned places in Canisius and the *Library of the Fathers*; and *A Thousand Lines of Riddles*, which Martin Delrio published with other small metrical works of Aldhelm at *Mainz, 1601, in octavo*. His prosaic *Treatise on Virginity* is held in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 1677. He wrote furthermore *On the Life of Monks, On the Praise of Saints, On the Kinds of Meters, On Riddles*, and many other things which are cataloged by Bale and Pits.

<note>The 7th century is often called the "Monothelite Century" due to the theological debate over whether Jesus Christ had one will (Monothelitism) or two wills, divine and human (Dyothelitism).</note>

**APONIUS**, whoever he may be, was a man not unlearned; he flourished, according to the calculation of [Philippe] Labbe, around the year 680. He is certainly older than Bede, by whom he is cited <margin>* Commentary on the Song of Songs, book 4, chapter 2.</margin> *. There are extant six books of a *Commentary on the Song of Songs* written by him to the Priest Armenius, which were published at *Freiburg* in 1538, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 14, page 98.

<margin>680.</margin>
**MANSUETUS**, Archbishop of Milan; he flourished in the year 680. Around this time, on the occasion of the Ecumenical Council summoned in the East by Emperor Constantine [IV], he held a Synod in Milan; from that assembly, he wrote letters to the Emperor, advising him on matters regarding the Catholic faith, and declared that the faith in two wills in Christ <note>The orthodox "Dyothelite" position</note> was dear to his heart. In the same year, he took part in a Roman Synod and signed the synodal letters regarding the legates sent to Constantinople. His *Letter to Emperor Constantine on the Catholic Faith*, written from the Synod of Milan, is extant among the Acts of the 6th Council, part 1, chapter 3, *Councils*, Volume 6, page 601.

<margin>680.</margin>
**THEODORE**, called *of Kempten* from the small cell in which he first led the monastic life, was later a monk of St. Gall and a disciple of St. Magnus. He flourished in the year 680. By order of Bishop Tozzo, the teacher of St. Magnus, he wrote the *Life* [of Magnus], which is found in Canisius’ *Ancient Readings*, Volume 5, page 911.

<margin>680.</margin>
**MACARIUS**, Patriarch of Antioch, a *Monothelite* heretic; he flourished in the year 680, in which he participated in the Sixth General Council. Besides a brief *Confession of Faith* which he gave orally in the Council, he offered to the fathers a more extensive *Exposition or Confession* recorded in writing; but since he refused to condemn the dogma of a single will in Christ and a "theandric" <note>original: "deivirili", meaning "God-manly". This was a key term in the debate over Christ's divine-human actions.</note> operation, and professed that he would never acknowledge two natural wills or operations in Christ, even if he were torn limb from limb and cast into the sea, he was condemned by the Synod and sent into exile by the Emperor. Both of his *Expositions or Confessions of Faith* are extant in the *Councils*, Volume 6, page 743. He also wrote a book *to Luke, a Monk and Priest of Africa*, who had written about the new heresy of the Maximians, and a *congratulatory address* <note>original: "προσφωνητικὸν" [prosphōnētikos]</note> to the Emperor, and a certain other book; fragments of which are contained in the *Councils*, Volume 6, page 906.

<margin>680.</margin>
**PETER**, Metropolitan of Nicomedia; he flourished in the year 680. Brought under suspicion of the Monothelite heresy, he presented himself at the Sixth Council, and having touched the Gospels, he confessed the Orthodox faith of two wills in Christ, which he further confirmed by offering a small book of confession. His example was followed by Bishops Theodore, Solomon, and Anthony, together with certain monks who had been accused of the same crime; they cleared themselves of the charge by offering books in the same form. This *Book of Confession* is extant in Greek and Latin in the *Councils*, Volume 6, page 842.

<margin>680.</margin>
**JULIAN**, also called **POMERIUS**, a Spaniard by race and a citizen of Toledo, was a disciple of Eugenius II, Bishop of Toledo. In the year 676, at the request of King Ervigius, he wrote books *On the Coming of Christ against the Jews*. At the beginning of the year 680, after Quiricus, he was ordained Archbishop of the Church of Toledo. In the year 681, he presided over the 12th Council of Toledo; in 683, the 13th; in 684, the 14th; and in 688, the 15th. In this last Synod, he laboriously conducted a defense of his book *On the Three Substances* <note>Referring to the body, soul, and divinity of Christ</note>, which Pope Benedict [II] had judged less than orthodox when it was brought to Italy; he presented Benedict to the fathers of the Council as a laughingstock, like some stupid, common teacher, and demonstrated that the frivolous quibbles of the unlearned Pope ought to be disregarded. He died on the 6th of March in the year 690. Felix of Toledo composed a distinguished eulogy of his virtues and learning in the Appendix to Ildefonsus' *On Illustrious Writers*, which the reader may consult. We shall pursue [the list of] Julian’s writings:

**AGATHO**, first a Reader of the Great Church of Constantinople, later Librarian, Patriarchal Chief Notary <note>term: "Protonotarius"; a high-ranking legal officer in the Byzantine church</note>, and second Chancellor; he flourished from the year 680, in which, while still holding the rank of Reader, he was a Notary to the holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod. # The Monothelite Century. 469
<note>The "Monothelite Century" (7th century) was defined by the Monothelite controversy—a debate over whether Christ possessed one divine-human will or two distinct wills (divine and human).</note>

<margin>7th CENTURY from the Year 600.</margin>
...writes that he was born, as [Cesare] Baronius <note>A famous 16th-century Italian cardinal and church historian</note> himself does not deny. Daniel Papebroch <note>A Jesuit scholar and hagiographer</note> published a sermon delivered on the day of his Ordination under the same name from the papers of [Lucas] Holstenius in his *Chronological Attempt at a Catalog of Roman Pontiffs*, page 107. Papebroch acknowledges it is not entirely clear whether that sermon should be ascribed to Leo or to his successor Benedict, though he himself leans toward the opinion that it is the offspring of our Leo.

<margin>684.</margin>
**BENEDICT II**, by birth a Roman and the son of John, was elected to the Pontificate on June 28, 684, and ordained on May 14, 685. If we believe Anastasius <note>likely Anastasius the Librarian, a 9th-century historian of the Popes</note>, he obtained an edict from the Emperor Constantine [IV] stating that henceforth the person elected to the Roman See should be consecrated immediately without waiting for the Emperor’s mandate. However, it is clearly evident from the formulas in the *Daily Book* <note>original: "Libri diurni"; a collection of standard forms and letters used by the papal administration</note> that the imperial right to confirm Popes continued to hold its place for some time longer. Benedict died on March 25, 686. Two of his letters survive in the *Collections of the Councils, Volume 6, page 1277*, which the Papal authorities themselves consider to be forged.

<margin>688.</margin>
**SERGIUS**, by birth a Syrian from a family in Antioch, and son of Tiberius (who lived at Palermo in Sicily), was ordained Pope of the Roman Church on November 22, 688. In the following year, he baptized Caedwalla, King of the West Saxons, who had come to Rome. In 692, the Quinisext Synod <note>original: "Synodus Quini-sexta"; also known as the Council in Trullo, intended to complete the work of the 5th and 6th ecumenical councils</note> was held at Constantinople; the Pope's legates attended and signed the decrees of the Synod. Emperor Justinian [II] ordered Sergius to confirm these same decrees with a formal signature, and when the Pope resisted, the Emperor ordered him to be deported to Constantinople by the envoy Zacharias the Protospatharios <note>original: "Protospatharius"; a high-ranking Byzantine court official</note>. However, the Italian militia would not allow Sergius to be taken away and drove Zacharias out. Sergius died on August 14, 702. An incomplete letter survives, addressed to Abbot Ceolfrith regarding the sending of Bede <note>The "Venerable Bede," the famous Anglo-Saxon scholar</note> to Rome, found in the *Collections of the Councils, Volume 6, page 1294*, and in William of Malmesbury’s *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English, book 1, page 11*.

<margin>690.</margin>
**ARCULPHUS**, a Bishop of a certain city in Gaul; he flourished in the year 690. Having undertaken a journey to the East for religious reasons and surveyed the holy sites, he also visited Damascus, Constantinople, Alexandria, and other places. At last, while returning to Gaul, he was carried by the force of a storm to the western shores of Britain and was kindly received as a guest by Adamnan, the Abbot of Iona <note>original: "Hyensi"; referring to the island of Iona off the coast of Scotland</note>. Adamnan committed to writing the history of this pilgrimage and the description of the holy places as he heard it from Arculph's own mouth, encompassing the work in three volumes. These books exist under the title *On the Location of the Holy Land* <note>original: "de situ Terræ sanctæ"</note>, published by Serarius at Ingolstadt in 1619, and later by Mabillon in the *Benedictine Centuries, volume 3, part 2, page 502*, as we noted above under the entry for Adamnan.

<margin>690.</margin>
**CRESCONIUS**, a Bishop of a certain city in Africa; he flourished around the year 690. He composed two works concerning Canon Law <note>original: "Jus Canonicum"</note>: namely, the *Abridgment of Canons* <note>original: "Breviarium Canonum"</note>, in which he reduced the Canons of the Councils and the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs to 300 chapters, citing only the places where they could be found; and the *Concordance*, or book of Canons, in which he compensated for the brevity of the former work by reciting the actual words of the Canons and Decrees under the same titles. Recent editors, however, warn that the beginning of this *Concordance* was added by another hand. The *Abridgment* was first brought to light by Pierre Pithou at Paris in 1588, and was thereafter reprinted through the care of [Gabriel] Altafarani at Poitiers in 1630, by François Chifflet at Dijon in 1649, and in Justel’s *Library of Canon Law*, with an ancient index added, *Volume 1, page 456*. Justel and Voell first published the *Concordance* from a manuscript in the Clermont and De Thou libraries, *ibid., in the Appendix, page 33*. Furthermore, Cresconius described in hexameter verse the wars and victories over the Saracens achieved by John the Patrician, who was sent to Africa by the Emperor Leontius; but that work has perished.

<margin>693.</margin>

# The Monothelite Century. 470
<note>The "Monothelite Century" refers to the 7th century, dominated by the theological debate over whether Christ had one will (Monothelitism) or two (Dyothelitism).</note>

<header>The Monothelite Century.</header>

<margin>7th CENTURY from the Year 600.</margin>
<note>This first paragraph refers to Felix of Toledo, who is not named in this specific snippet but is identified by the reference to the 16th Council of Toledo.</note>
Having been substituted into his place after the previous bishop was deposed from his see and dignity by the 16th Synod of Toledo and relegated to perpetual exile, he presided over that Council as the Bishop of the royal city and Metropolitan of the province. He died in the year 702. He wrote the *Life or Eulogy of Julian, Bishop of Toledo*, which is usually added as an appendix to the catalog of writers by Ildefonsus <note>Ildefonsus of Toledo was a prominent 7th-century bishop and writer</note>.

<margin>699.</margin>
**ANGRADUS**, a Monk of Fontenelle in Normandy; he flourished around the year 699. He wrote to Hilbert, his Abbot (who died in the year 700), the *Life of Saint Ansbert, Archbishop of Rouen*, who died in the year 695. This biography is found in the works of [Laurentius] Surius <note>A 16th-century German monk famous for his multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints</note> under the date of February 9th.

**ANONYMOUS** Author, commemorated by Photius <note>Photius the Great was a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople whose "Bibliotheca" preserves summaries of many lost ancient books</note>, a Theban by birth and from the house of Panopolis. Though the exact time he wrote is uncertain, he should seemingly be assigned to this century, as he lived not long after the times of the Emperor Heraclius and resided in Constantinople with his wife and children. He composed a voluminous work <note>original: "πολυβίβλιον" (polybiblion)</note> in fifteen books, in which he collected testimonies and entire passages from pagan <note>original: "Gentilium"</note> writings—not only Greek, but also Persian, Thracian, Egyptian, Babylonian, Chaldean, and even Italian—for the sake of the favor and confirmation of the Christian religion. Photius touches upon certain main headings of the work in Code 170 [of his *Bibliotheca*]. In these books, the author chiefly treated the Holy Trinity, the Incarnation of the Word, the Miracles, Crucifixion, Burial, Resurrection, Ascension, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit poured out upon the disciples; the second coming of the Lord, the resurrection of the dead, the judgment, and the future life; the structure of the universe, providence, and Paradise; the specific virtues of Christians, and other subjects of this kind. He did not neglect historical matters fitting for his purpose, mixing them in where necessary—for example, in which places the individual Apostles preached the salvific doctrine, and in what manner they departed from human cares and labors. This was truly an immense work, and no less useful, elaborated by the author with the goal of showing that Christian doctrine had been foretold among all nations and preached by the most eloquent men in every nation; he sought to prove that all those among the Gentiles who did not assent to this sacred doctrine were without excuse. Meanwhile, although Photius praises the man’s zeal, piety, and industry, he seems—not without reason—to find his judgment and eloquence lacking.

# THE CENTURY OF ICONOCLASM.

## General View of the Century.

<margin>THE 8TH CENTURY from the Year 700.</margin>
The Saracens <note>A term used by medieval writers for Arab Muslims</note> heavily afflict the Christians in Spain, as do the Lombards in Italy. In the East, the face of affairs is quite mournful; with the strength of the Empire declining, the Saracens occupy almost everything, with three Patriarchs <note>The leaders of the churches in Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem</note> subjected to the tyranny of barbarians, and the "abomination of desolation" <note>A biblical reference (Daniel 9:27, Matthew 24:15) used here to describe Islamic rule over Jerusalem</note> placed even in the holy place. Within the Church, all things are confused: disputes, disagreements, heresies, schisms, superstitions, the ambition of the clergy, ignorance, luxury, and the bickering and contentions of the Bishops. The famous controversy regarding the veneration of Images occupies almost the entire century. In the one or two preceding centuries, pictures and images of the Holy Martyrs, illustrious bishops, and sometimes Secular Princes had begun to be placed in temples and the vestibules of temples, for the sake of decoration or history, so that by looking at them, the minds of men might be stirred to recall their deeds and imitate their virtues; yet no sign of veneration was yet introduced, at least not from the common practice of the Church. But around this time, certain sacred rites were applied, namely: salutation, kneeling, lighting of candles, burning of incense, and other such things; over which a sharp conflict soon began. 

The Emperor Philippicus was the first to "break the ice," and with him John, the Patriarch of Constantinople. Rejecting the Fathers of the Sixth Council and others who condemned the Monothelite <note>The belief that Christ had only one will</note> and similar dogmas, they banished their images from the Church of Hagia Sophia, issuing an edict on this matter in the year 713. Meanwhile, Pope Constantine did the exact opposite at Rome, even excommunicating Philippicus Bardanes for this reason. In the year 723, a Provincial Synod of Nakoleia, presided over by Metropolitan Theophilus, condemned the veneration of images. Leo III the Isaurian <note>Reigned 717–741; a famous iconoclast emperor</note> did the same in the tenth year of his reign; once the law concerning Images was published at Constantinople in the year 726, he was excommunicated for that reason by Pope Gregory III. Constantine Copronymus <note>Constantine V, nicknamed "Copronymus" or "Dung-named" by his enemies</note>, by an edict promulgated at Constantinople in the year 741, removed images, even demanding an oath from his subjects that no one should worship images. 

Finally, the 7th Ecumenical Synod <note>This refers to the Council of Hieria, which iconoclasts considered the 7th Council, though it was later overturned</note> was held at Constantinople in the Church of the Virgin Mary <gloss>the Mother of God</gloss> in Blachernae in the year 754. In this council, 338 bishops gathered from all parts of the eastern empire; after holding an examination of the case for nearly six months—drawing from Holy Scripture, reason, and the testimonies of the Holy Fathers—they finally decreed with unanimous consent that images should not be constructed for the sake of <gloss>iconoclasm</gloss> <note>original: "εἰκονοκλάσεως" – the author likely means "to prevent the breaking of images" or refers to the controversy itself</note>, nor should they be placed for that purpose in a Church or a private home; they expressly called this a vain thing and a <gloss>diabolical scheme</gloss> more than once. The Acts of this Council (would that they were complete!) are inserted into the Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea, though these should be called the excerpts of their adversaries rather than the true Acts. 

Finally, in the year 787—after first removing her husband with poison and while her son Constantine was still a minor—the Empress Irene (a clearly headstrong and unrestrained woman, to say nothing worse, and quite prone to the worship of images) called a Synod at Nicaea. She took into her counsel Tarasius, who had recently been made Patriarch from being a layman. There assembled at this council (if the gods permit!) the <gloss>representatives</gloss> <note>original: "τοποτηρηταὶ" (topoteretai)</note> of the prelates of the three Eastern Patriarchs—wretched monks, indeed, who splendidly feigned the names and persons of the Patriarchs. For the Patriarchs themselves, oppressed by the yoke of the Saracens, had perhaps not heard even a single word about this Synod at that time. In this Council, the decrees of the previous Synod of Constantinople were abolished, and it was decreed that the life-giving cross, and images of Christ and the Blessed Virgin...

# THE MONOTHELITE CENTURY.
<note>While the header reads "Monothelite," the content describes the 8th-century Iconoclasm and the Council of Frankfurt.</note>

<margin>THE 8TH CENTURY from the Year 700.</margin> [The council decreed] that images of Angels and Saints were to be displayed in churches and houses, to be venerated, worshipped, and honored with candles, incense, and other signs of prostration <note>original: προσκυνήσεως (proskynesis); a gesture of bowing or falling low in respect</note>. Meanwhile, they stubbornly denied that images of the divine nature or of the Holy Trinity should be manufactured or worshipped; in this part at least they remained "sane," though they were soon to produce a more corrupt offspring <note>The author suggests that while they initially avoided depicting God the Father, this restraint would eventually fail</note>. 

After the Acts of this Council <note>The Second Council of Nicaea, 787 AD</note> were transmitted to the West, Charles the Great <note>Charlemagne</note> convened a Synod of 300 bishops at Frankfurt in the year 794. At this meeting, it was decreed that images are not to be worshipped; indeed, the Acts of the Nicene Synod were condemned, rescinded, and refuted, with the four *Carolingian Books* <note>The *Libri Carolini*, a massive theological rebuttal of image-worship</note> published for that purpose. How successfully the Nicene decrees were received in other parts of the West, let others relate. 

Regarding our own England, Roger of Hoveden—hardly the least among the leaders of our history—has this to say in his *Annals*, part 1, page 232: 

*In the year 792, Charles, King of the Franks, sent to Britain a synodal book directed to him from Constantinople; in which book (alas, for shame!) many inconvenient things and things contrary to the true faith were found; especially that it was confirmed by the unanimous assertion of almost all oriental doctors—no less than three hundred or more bishops—that images ought to be worshipped, a practice which the Church of God altogether detests. Against which Albinus <note>Also known as Alcuin of York, a famous scholar and advisor to Charlemagne</note> wrote an epistle, marvelously supported by the authority of the divine Scriptures; and he brought that letter, along with the same book, in the name of our bishops and princes to the King of the Franks.* 

In the same Synod of Frankfurt, Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo, Spanish bishops who taught that Christ according to the flesh was only the "adoptive" son of God, were expressly condemned by canons established for this matter <note>This refers to the heresy of Adoptionism</note>. Finally, the pride and power of the Roman Pontiffs grew wonderfully in this age, especially after the Empire of the West was transferred from the Greeks to the Franks, and the Exarchate of Ravenna <note>The center of Byzantine power in Italy</note> was extinguished, which had long acted as a bridle upon their ambition.

# WRITERS.

<margin>
THE 8TH CENTURY
from the Year 700.
</margin>
JOHN, Bishop of the island of Carpathos <note>John of Carpathos, an ascetic writer whose works were popular in Eastern monasticism</note>, of whom Photius makes mention in Codex 202; it is not entirely clear to me whether he should be assigned to this century or the previous one. Having been requested by the monks of India, he wrote for them a *Consolatory Work* completed in one hundred chapters, according to the testimony of Photius. Today there survive in Latin, from the version by Jacobus Pontanus, ninety-seven *Exhortatory Chapters or Spiritual Documents*, found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 12.

<margin>701.</margin>
BEDE, called "the Venerable," English by nation, was born in the year 672 in the territory of the Monastery of Jarrow <note>original: Ingyrvensis</note>, in the region of Durham, not far from the mouth of the river Tyne. As a boy of seven years, he was given by the care of his relatives to be educated by Benedict [Biscop], Abbot of the Monastery of St. Peter at Wearmouth <note>original: Weremutham</note> and the Monastery of St. Paul at Jarrow <note>original: Ingyrvum or Girvicum</note>. In these monasteries, under the rule of the Abbots Benedict and later Ceolfrid—which were situated about five miles apart—he grew up and lived. With Bede's own consent, at the age of 19 he received the rank of Deacon, and at age 30 the rank of Priest, from John of Beverley, the Bishop of Hexham <note>original: Hagulstadensi</note>, who had formerly been his teacher of fine letters. In the year 701, he was summoned to Rome by a letter from Pope Sergius to treat and judge very serious religious matters. However, it is by no means certain that he ever undertook the journey to Rome; rather, it appears he never left the boundaries of his monastery. Around the year 702, having been made a Priest and now equipped with a most excellent supply of all kinds of learning, and a deeper knowledge of both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note> and the best sciences, he set himself to writing. In the year 731, he placed the finishing touch <note>original: coronidem imposuit</note> on his *Ecclesiastical History*. In the year 735, shortly before the feast of Easter, he began to suffer from a slight <unclear>rheum</unclear> <note>Likely a printer's error for "reumate" (rheum/catarrh), which matches historical accounts of Bede's final illness.</note>; as this illness increased daily, he prolonged his life through reading, singing, and praying until the 26th of May—the day on which the memory of the Lord's Ascension happened to be celebrated that year. At that time, having just finished the translation of the *Gospel according to John* into the common language <note>Old English</note>, upon which he had worked most diligently, he calmly and piously returned his spirit—which had long been gasping for the dwellings of the blessed—into the hands of the Lord. Regarding the year of his death, there are various opinions among the learned. Some place it in 729, others in 731, others in 732, and many in 734. There are even those who refer his death to the year 762, and some to 766. Roger of Hoveden—the founder of the Saxon Chronology appended to Bede's *Ecclesiastical History*—Simeon of Durham, and Thomas Stubbs write much more correctly that Bede died in the year 735. To these is added the testimony of Cuthbert, who was present at Bede's death and recorded it in letters. For he reveals that Bede died on the 7th of the Calends of June [May 26th], on the day of the Lord's Ascension, which is also certain from other sources. This date agrees exactly with the year 735 and does not harmonize at all with the calculations of others. Bede was buried in his monastery at Jarrow; from there his bones were later translated to Durham and placed in the same casket as those of St. Cuthbert. Concerning his praises, let William of Malmesbury alone be heard:

<margin>* On the Deeds of the English, book 3, chapter 3, folio 10.</margin>
> "A man," he says \*, "whom you could more easily admire than worthily praise; who, born in the furthest corner of the world, struck all lands with the brilliance of his learning." And a little later: "Here talent fails, eloquence yields, not knowing what I should praise more: the vast number of his books or the sobriety of his sermons. Divine wisdom had undoubtedly poured into him with no meager draft, so that he produced such great volumes in so short a span of life." And having added the letters of Pope Sergius summoning him to Rome, he says: "He was already so famous that the Roman highness required him for unraveling difficult questions. Nor indeed did Gallic pride <note>original: Gallicanus tumor; referring to the intellectual rivalry between the English and Frankish/Gallic scholars</note> ever find anything in this Englishman to justly criticize: so much did all Latinity grant the palm to his faith and mastery." To these I might add many more things concerning his erudition and holiness which he accumulates in that place, but I will let them pass for now.

### Here Begins the Prologue to the Seven Canonical Epistles.

<margin>* Missing: from Jerusalem.</margin>
<margin>† Missing: of James.</margin>
James, Peter, John, and Jude published seven Epistles, which ecclesiastical custom calls "Catholic"—that is, universal. In these, the Epistle of James is placed first because he undertook the governance of the Church in Jerusalem. In the catalog of the Apostles, Peter and John are usually named first; however, the fount and origin of Gospel preaching, beginning * [at Jerusalem], was diffused throughout the entire world. Honoring the dignity of his seat, the Apostle Paul also mentions him with respect, saying: *James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be columns of the Church* <note>Galatians 2:9. "Cephas" is the Aramaic name for Peter</note>. Or perhaps, because James sent his Epistle to the twelve tribes of Israel, who were the first to believe, it rightly deserved to be placed first.

The Second Epistle is rightly that of Peter, because he wrote to the "chosen strangers" who are called *Proselytes* <note>original: "Proselyti." Converts to Judaism, here referring to those who converted from Paganism to Judaism and then to Christianity</note> in Greek; that is, he wrote to those who were converted from Gentility to Judaism, and from Judaism to the grace of the Gospel election.

John’s Epistles are rightly placed in the third position, because he wrote to those who believed from among the Gentiles, though they had not previously been so by nature or profession. Furthermore, many Ecclesiastical writers, among whom is Saint Athanasius, the leader of the Church of Alexandria, testify that his first Epistle was written to the Parthians <note>original: "ad Parthos." The Parthian Empire was located in what is now modern-day Iran</note>.

The Epistle of Jude is rightly placed last; for although he himself is great, he is nonetheless lesser than the three preceding Apostles. Or perhaps, because James's Epistle was written first, then Peter's, and after those, John's; thus they retain until now the order † [of James] in which they were written. For it is established that the Blessed James completed his martyrdom in the thirtieth year after the Passion of the Lord. Peter suffered in the thirty-eighth year—that is, the last year of Nero—and he himself wrote in his second Epistle: *I am certain that the laying away of my tabernacle is at hand, according as our Lord Jesus Christ also hath signified to me by revelation* <note>2 Peter 1:14. "Tabernacle" here refers to the physical body</note>. From this it is clear that he wrote this Epistle when his suffering was imminent, whereas James had departed to Christ much earlier. Nor was it fitting for Peter's Epistles to be separated from one another, since he wrote them to the same Churches. Furthermore, John wrote his Epistles and his Gospel much later in time; having returned from exile after the killing of the Lord's people <note>original: "dominicam occisionem," likely referring to the persecution of Christians</note>, he found the Church disturbed in his absence by heretics, whom he strikes out at in his Epistles, often calling them "Antichrists." The Prologue ends.

### Retractions and Questions on the Acts of the Apostles.

<margin>* For the year 562.</margin>
Commentaries on all the Epistles of St. Paul, mostly excerpted from the works of St. Augustine. Regarding this work, Baronius * <note>Caesar Baronius, a 16th-century Cardinal and historian</note> raises a dispute, thinking it should be ascribed to Peter, Abbot of Tripoli (whom Cassiodorus mentions in *Divine Teachings*, chapter 8). This dispute was brilliantly cleared up by the illustrious Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon, a 17th-century Benedictine scholar</note>, who demonstrates in a special dissertation (*Analecta*, Vol. 1, p. 12) that these commentaries are owed neither to Bede nor to Peter, but to Florus the Master <note>Florus of Lyon, a 9th-century deacon and scholar</note>. Meanwhile, Bede’s true Commentary remains hidden in manuscript form in Mabillon’s possession (for Bede himself gives evidence in his list of works that he explained the Epistles of St. Paul, and Lupus of Ferrières <note>A 9th-century Carolingian abbot and humanist</note> testifies in Letter 76 to Hincmar that he possessed a large volume of Bede's collection on the Apostle, gathered from Augustine's works). See the notes by Baluze <note>Étienne Baluze, a 17th-century French scholar</note> on Lupus of Ferrières, p. 405.

Homilies according to the season: 33 for Summer; 15 for Winter; 22 for Lent; 32 for the Saints in Summer; 16 for the Saints in Winter; and various sermons to the people. These were published separately in *Cologne, 1534*.

A book on the *Strong Woman* <note>A commentary on the poem of the virtuous woman in Proverbs 31</note>.

A book on *Offices* <note>Referring to liturgical or ecclesiastical duties</note>.

*Scintillæ* <note>original: "Scintillæ," meaning "Sparks"</note> or *Commonplaces*.

Fragments on the Sapiential books <note>The "Wisdom" books of the Bible, like Proverbs and Ecclesiastes</note>, and verses from the Psalter.

A book on *Solomon’s Temple*.

Questions on the *Octateuch* <note>The first eight books of the Bible</note> and the four books of Kings.

Various Questions.

Commentaries on the Psalms.
