<margin>705.</margin>
**ACCA**, an Englishman by birth, was a disciple of Bosa, Archbishop of York, and of Saint Wilfrid, with whom he traveled to Rome. He devotedly pursued the monastic life according to the custom of his age and was very close to the Venerable Bede. He flourished in the year 705 and thereafter, eventually being honored with the episcopal miter. <note>original: "Episcopali infulâ." This refers to his promotion to the office of Bishop.</note> Although in certain printed books he is called only an Abbot, it is clear from the Lambeth manuscript that he was the Bishop of Hexham <note>original: "Hagulstadensis."</note> and he enriched and adorned his see with a magnificent library. He outlived Bede and died around the year 740. Bale and Pits record several of his writings, namely: *On the lives and passions of the Saints* whose relics were kept in his church; *On the Ecclesiastical offices of his Choir*; *Various Poems*; and *Letters to various people*. There remains among the works of Bede a *Letter from Acca to Bede*, in which he urges him to explain the Holy Scriptures, specifically the Gospel of Saint Luke.

<margin>705.</margin>
**JOHN VII**, a Greek by birth and the son of Plato, was ordained Roman Pontiff on the 8th day of February in the year 705. In the same year, requested by the Emperor Justinian to confirm the canons of the Quinisext Council, <note>A church council held in 692, also called the Council in Trullo, which dealt with administrative and disciplinary matters.</note> he held a Synod in Rome. In this synod, he made no ruling regarding the canons, which he sent back to the Emperor marked with "neither a white nor a black pebble." <note>original: "nec albo, nec nigro lapillo." A classical idiom meaning he neither approved (white) nor condemned (black) them; he remained neutral or indecisive.</note> However, he did acquit Wilfrid, the Archbishop of York, who was present at the Synod, of the crimes charged against him. He died on the 24th day of September in the year 707. A single *Letter to Ethelred, King of the Mercians, and Alfrid, King of the Deirans, concerning the case of Wilfrid of York* is extant in the Collections of the Councils, Volume VI, page 1390.

# The Iconoclastic Century.

<margin>THE 8TH CENTURY. from the Year 700.</margin>
<note>This paragraph refers to Pope Constantine (708–715), mentioned on the preceding page.</note> received with great honor by Justinian <note>Emperor Justinian II</note>, although the matter was nevertheless left undecided, he returned to Rome in the year 711. He died on the 18th day of March in the year 715. A single letter of his remains, addressed to Berhtwald, Archbishop of Canterbury, found in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume VI, page 1397.

JOHN, Patriarch of Constantinople, was appointed by the Emperor Philippicus Bardanes in the year 712. He supported the <term>Monothelite heresy</term> <note>The belief that Christ had only one will, rather than a human and a divine will.</note>, whether out of personal conviction or fear. When Bardanes was stripped of his power, John was also reduced in rank and fell from the Patriarchal see in the year 715. A letter of his remains, addressed to Pope Constantine and written after the death of Bardanes, in which he rejects any zeal for or favor toward Monothelitism, claiming it was a force imposed upon him by Bardanes. <note>original: "Monothelismi seu studium, seu favorem in vim sibi à Bardane illatam rejicit"</note> Found in the Greek and Latin *Collections of the Councils*, Volume VI, page 1410.

<margin>715.</margin>
GREGORY II, a Roman by birth and the son of Marcellus, served as Subdeacon and Treasurer under Pope Sergius and had charge of the Pontifical Library. Later promoted to the order of Deacon, he set out for Constantinople with Pope Constantine, where his intellect became greatly renowned during the debates concerning the Canons of the <term>Quinisext Council</term> <note>Also known as the Council in Trullo (692), which issued disciplinary canons not recognized by Rome.</note>. Finally, after the death of Constantine on the 28th day of April in the year 715, he succeeded to the Roman see. In the year 721, having held a Synod at Rome, he passed many canons concerning illicit marriages. 

In the year 726, the Emperor Leo <note>Leo III, the Isaurian</note>, in order to place a barrier against the spreading <term>Iconodule</term> <note>Venerators of icons.</note> superstition and to take away the pretext for terrible scandals from the Muslims and Jews, decided by a prudent counsel in a Council of Bishops called at Constantinople that images should be removed from the Churches, or at least moved to higher places out of sight. He wished this decree, when sent to Italy, to be confirmed by the authority of Pope Gregory. Gregory, instead of complying, held a Synod at Rome at the end of 726 or the beginning of 727 (Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century ecclesiastical historian.</note> places this in the year 730), where he subjected the Emperor to an <term>anathema</term> <note>Formal excommunication.</note>, condemned the Iconoclasts, and decreed that the worship of images of Christ and the Apostles was consistent with established practice. 

Furthermore, having sent letters everywhere, he assailed the Emperor with the harshest insults as one guilty of impiety and an enemy of Christians. He cried out that the Emperor was unworthy of rule, forbade the payment of taxes to him under a most severe interdict, sounded the trumpet for the revolt of the Italians, and supported them in every way. He prohibited images from being removed from the temples and caused the statues of the Emperor to be trampled underfoot with the most foul mockery. He bound Paul the Patrician and Exarch <note>The Byzantine governor in Italy.</note>, who had been sent by Leo to seize the Pope and lead him to Constantinople, with an anathema. He appealed to the faith of the Italians and the barbarians occupying Italy, solicited their aid, and pounced upon the Emperor’s territories as if they were certain prey. Having sent a splendid embassy to Gaul along with the chains and keys of Saint Peter, he implored Charles Martel to come to the aid of the struggling Church, to remove Italy from the Emperor’s dominion, and to protect it with arms. 

To hide nothing, however, some scholars ascribe this embassy to Gregory III without violating the truth. But concerning his prior deeds, all who possess even a small amount of honesty are in agreement. Cardinal Baronius even goes so far as to not deny that the Emperor's power was stripped from him, but rather glories in it as a distinguished deed.

<margin>* For the year 730, Number 5.</margin>
> *When,* Baronius says, *Pope Gregory could by no words or writings recall the Emperor from his undertakings, thinking that the time had now come to put the ax to the root of the unhappy tree, he cried out by Apostolic authority: "Cut it down." Roused by this thunder, the Western faithful soon defected entirely from Leo’s empire, clinging to the Apostolic Pontiff. Thus, the same Gregory left a worthy example to posterity, so that heretical Princes should not be permitted to reign in the Church of Christ if, having been often warned, they were found to persist in their error with an obstinate mind.*

He so broke the spirit of Liutprand, King of the Lombards, when he came to Rome with an army, and so softened the man’s fierce mind with prayers, that (according to the witness of Anastasius) he stripped off the arms he had been wearing—namely, his *mantum* (or short cloak reaching only to the hands), his *armilausa* (a military garment reaching from the shoulders to the knees), his belt, his *spatha* (longsword), and a gilded sword, as well as a golden crown and a silver cross. All of these he laid before the altar of Saint Peter. Gre- <meta>catchword: -gory</meta>

[Gre]gory <note>Gregory II</note> died on the 17th day of January in the year 731. Fifteen of his letters survive, along with a *Capitulary* <note>A set of ecclesiastical instructions or decrees</note> given to the legates sent to Bavaria, found in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume VI, page 1437. Two of his letters are preserved in Greek and Latin among the Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea, session 2, *Councils*, Volume VII, page 824, and in Baronius's *Annals* for the year 726; however, Labbe <note>Philippe Labbe, a Jesuit scholar</note> considers these should be attributed to Gregory III.

Furthermore, the Liturgy of our Gregory—or the *Order of the Mass*—was published along with the Greek version by George Kodinos by Morel in Paris, 1595; it was later included in the *Supplement to Duc* <note>The Auctuarium Duceanum</note>, Volume II, page 125.

<margin>715.</margin>
### THE DAILY BOOK

**THE DAILY BOOK** <note>original: "Liber Diurnus"</note>, in which are contained the solemn formulas for letters and other ecclesiastical matters anciently used by the Roman Pontiffs. It comprises nine chapters, with each chapter containing several titles. To this day, it remains unknown who first collected and arranged these formulas. The book itself seems to have been compiled under Gregory II around the year 715, as Jean Garnier suggests with great probability; this is supported not only by the antiquity of the manuscript (which is about nine hundred years old) but by many internal clues. This work, long suppressed and long desired, was finally brought to light and illustrated with very learned notes—as is his custom—by **Jean Garnier** in *Paris, 1680, in quarto.* In these *Formulas*, two things especially deserve notice. First: even in the eighth century, it was the custom that when a Pope died, the <term>Exarch of Ravenna</term> <note>The Byzantine governor in Italy</note> was notified by those acting as caretakers of the Apostolic See. Once a successor was elected by the agreement of not only the clergy but also the nobles and the people, a report was made to the Emperor in Constantinople, humbly requesting approval of the election. Letters were also sent to the nobles in both Ravenna and Constantinople, and especially to the Exarch, so that he might either confirm the election in the name of the Prince or see that it was confirmed. It was not permitted for a Pope to be ordained until this confirmation had been received. All these facts are clearer than the sun from the Formulas themselves. Second: the Pope-to-be, about to be ordained at the tomb of St. Peter, was accustomed to make a solemn profession of faith. In this, he not only explicitly approved the six holy Ecumenical Councils, but he also struck with the condemnation of anathema the <term>authors of the new heretical doctrine</term> <note>The Monothelite heresy</note>—specifically naming Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople, along with Honorius, *who bestowed encouragement upon their wicked assertions* (to use the words of the Formula itself). From this, the futility of Baronius, Bellarmine, and more recent <term>vain babblers</term> <note>original: "κενοφώνου" (kenophonou)</note> is clearly established; they imagine, without even the slightest shadow of probability, that the name of Honorius was intruded into the Acts of the Sixth Synod by some "little Greek." The reading of the *Daily Book* itself will supply other matters well worth noting for the reader curious about ecclesiastical antiquity. Leo Allatius once received an ancient manuscript of this *Daily Book* from Hilarion Rancatus, a Cistercian, and intended to publish a transcript of it; however, since the printing was prohibited, he was not allowed to bring it to light. The famous Mabillon inspected this same manuscript and excerpted many things from it, which he provides to us as a supplement to Garnier’s edition in the *Italian Museum*, Volume I, page 32; see also what he has in the *Italian Journey*, Section 31, page 77.

<margin>715.</margin>
### FELIX

**FELIX**, an Englishman by birth, was born in the province of the Mercians. He led the monastic life in the Abbey of Crowland, which had been recently founded by King Ethelbald in honor of St. Guthlac the Confessor. He flourished around the year 715 and was considered a noble rhetorician and poet among his contemporaries. He wrote the *Life of St. Guthlac*, the anchorite of Crowland, which is found in Surius under April 12th, and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Centuries*, Volume III, part I, page 263.

<margin>715.</margin>
### GERMANUS

**GERMANUS** was the son of Justinian the Patrician (who was killed by Constantine Pogonatus <note>Constantine IV</note>) and was himself castrated as a youth by the same Emperor. He was first the Bishop of Cyzicus, and then, in the year 715, was elevated to the Patriarchate of Constantinople following the deposition of John. In the year 726, he stubbornly resisted the edict of Emperor Leo and the decrees of the Synod of Constantinople regarding the removal of images. In doing so, he foolishly offered the authority and example of seven centuries as a defense, bringing up stories of icons of the Mother of God painted by St. Luke, the image of Christ sent to King Abgar, and similar trifles...

For four full years, the most merciful Emperor <note>Leo III, the Isaurian</note> patiently bore the man's stubbornness; however, when he could be brought to a sound mind by no warnings or evidence, nor to show obedience to the Imperial and Synodical decrees, he was finally removed from the Patriarchal see in the year 730 after a Synod was held. ### SURVIVING WORKS.

Three Letters: namely, *to John, Bishop of Synnada; to Constantine, Bishop of Nacolia; and to Thomas, Bishop of Claudiopolis*. These appear in Greek and Latin in the Second Council of Nicaea, act 4; *Collections of the Councils*, Volume VII, page 289.

*A Treatise on the Six Ecumenical Synods*, first published by Stephen le Moyne in Greek and Latin among the *Various Sacred Works* <note>original: "Varia Sacra"</note>, Volume I, page 68.

*The Retribution* or *The Substitute* <note>original Greek: Ἀνταποδοτικὸς ἢ Ἀνθύπωτος</note>, or an *Apology for Gregory of Nyssa* and his writings, which had been wrongly accused of Origenism <note>The controversial teachings of the 3rd-century scholar Origen</note>. In this work, besides the defense of Gregory of Nyssa, he also solidly refuted the errors of Origen. This book, which the injury of time has snatched from us, is praised at length by Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch and scholar</note> in Code 233, who says of Germanus's style: <note>original Greek: ὅτι τῷ λόγῳ καθαρός τε καὶ διειδής...</note> "His style is pure and clear, successfully employing pleasing turns of phrase; he is more powerful because of this, not sinking into coldness; he is noble in the character of his expression, and equally capable in conducting arguments; he introduces nothing unnecessary and neglects nothing that ought to be said, whether in his arguments or his reflections."

There are also available in Greek and Latin in the *Supplement to Duc* <note>Auctuario Duceano</note>, and in Combefis's *Origins of Constantinople*, and in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>Bibliotheca Patrum</note> under the name of Germanus: *A Theory of Ecclesiastical Matters*, *Three Orations in Praise of the Birth and Dormition of the Mother of God*, an *Oration on the Dedication of the Venerable Church of the Blessed Mary and on the Swaddling Clothes of the Lord*, a *Fragment of an Oration against Heresies*, and others; we shall deal with these under Germanus the Younger at the year 1222, to whom they seem more likely to belong.

</margin>**HEDDIUS**, surnamed *Stephen*, an Englishman by birth, a Priest and Monk of Canterbury, flourished in the year 720. Since he was highly skilled in music and ecclesiastical chanting, he was summoned by Wilfrid, Archbishop of York, to the kingdom of the Northumbrians, to teach the provincial people who were ignorant of music until that time. He was a man, says Bale <note>John Bale, a 16th-century historian</note>*, learned in literary actions—as appears from his speech—if we rightly consider the times: terse, neat, and elegantly refined. His *Life of Wilfrid*, written at the urging of Acca, Bishop of Hexham, still exists in the archives of the Church of Salisbury and in the *Cottonian Library*; Jean Mabillon published a version taken from this in the *Benedictine Century* IV, part 1, page 671. Heddius also wrote the *Lives of Eata and Tumbert*, and several other works; whether these still exist today is not clear.

</margin>**BONIFACE**, called *Winifred* in his native tongue, an Englishman by nation, was born at Crediton in the county of Devon in the year 670. As a youth of thirteen years, he retired to the Monastery at Exeter, from which he later moved to the Monastery at Nursling <note>original: "Nutsicellense"</note> and committed himself to the discipline of Abbot Wimbert (or Wigbert). Being instructed by him in more refined literature, he held a place among the foremost learned men of his age. Around the thirtieth year of his age, he was ordained a Priest—that is, in the year 700—and he joined Abbot Wigbert as a companion when he set out for the National Council held by Berhtwald, Archbishop of Canterbury. Shortly after, around the year 704, touched by a pious desire to preach the Gospel among heathen regions, he crossed the sea to Frisia <note>The coastal Netherlands/Germany</note> after with difficulty obtaining permission from his Abbot. Having stayed for some time in the territory of Utrecht <note>original: "Ultrajectensi"</note>, and finding he had little success with Radbod, Duke of the Frisians...

...having progressed in his mission to those desperately addicted to heathen superstitions, he returned to England in the year 716, and refused the position of Abbot <note>original: "præfecturam"</note> offered to him by the monks of the monastery. Around the year 718, protected by letters of recommendation from Daniel, Bishop of Winchester, he resumed his interrupted duty of preaching. After traveling to Rome and obtaining certain relics and letters of commission from Pope Gregory, he spread the light of the Gospel far and wide through Bavaria, Thuringia, and other territories of Germany. Then, hearing of the death of Radbod <note>A pagan King of the Frisians who had resisted Christian missions</note>, he went into Frisia and stayed for three years with Willibrord, the Apostle of the Frisians, providing him with outstanding assistance in performing his sacred duties. 

After three years, he returned to Germany and disseminated the Christian faith among the Hessians. In the year 723, he was summoned to Rome by Pope Gregory and, on the day before the Calends of December <note>November 30th</note>, was ordained Bishop of the Germans; setting aside the name Winifrid, he began thereafter to be called Boniface. Returning to Germany, he vigorously carried out the task entrusted to him, baptizing <note>original: "sacro lavacro tinxit" — literally, "dipped in the sacred font"</note> many thousands of pagans converted to the faith. He founded monasteries and churches everywhere, appointed superiors for those he founded, and called many clerics from England to share in his labor and office, diligently performing all the duties of both an Apostle and a Bishop. 

In the year 732, he earned the Archbishop’s Pallium <note>A woolen vestment symbolizing high archepiscopal authority</note> from Gregory III. In the year 738, he traveled to Rome for a third time to consult Pope Gregory on the most serious matters of the Church. In the year 742, he presided over the German Council, and in 743, the Council of Les Estinnes <note>original: "Leptinensi"</note>. He continued to celebrate frequent councils, visited the churches he had previously established, suppressed sprouting heresies, and diligently devised remedies for the corruptions that occasionally arose. In the year 754, having entrusted the care of the Church of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinæ"</note>, which he had governed until then, to his disciple Lullus, he hastened to Frisia to lead the people who had relapsed into paganism back to the faith. 

At first, the matter succeeded happily for him, with many thousands of men baptized and Eoban appointed Bishop of Utrecht <note>original: "Trajecti"</note>. Soon after, however, he was killed by pagans rushing in with a sudden violent force at Dokkum, a village in what was once East Frisia. On the 5th of June that same year, he won the Palm of Martyrdom. He wrote the *Life of Saint Livinus* and many *Letters*, which Nicolaus Serarius first brought to light and published with notes at Mainz in 1605, reprinted there in 1629. Some *Letters* are found here and there in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume VI, but all of them are in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XIII, page 70. The *Life of Saint Livinus* also appears in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Centuries*, Volume II, page 449, though it is ascribed by him to a certain older Boniface who is said to have flourished in the previous century. Lucas D’Achery published certain *Statutes of Saint Boniface* in his *Spicilegium*, Volume IX, page 63. Boniface is said to have written many other things, which Bale \* and Arnold Wion † enumerate individually. Pope Zachary praises that *Book on the Unity of the Faith* in the 2nd book of his life, chapter 10.

<margin>
\* Century 2, chapter 13.
† Tree of Life, book 5, pages 688, 729.
</margin>

**JONAS**, a Frenchman by birth and a monk of Fontenelle, flourished in the year 729. At the command of his Abbot Bainus, he wrote the *Life of Saint Wulfram*, Bishop of Sens, who died in the year 710. This Life is found in Surius under March 20th, and in Mabillon, *Century III*, part 1.

**COSMAS OF JERUSALEM**, called by some "the Holy-Citier" <note>original: "Hagiopolites"</note>, was born in Italy and was a man highly refined in every kind of elegant literature; he flourished in the year 730. Captured by Saracen pirates, he was carried off to Damascus; received into the household by the father of John of Damascus, he was appointed as a tutor to John while he was still a youth. Eventually, he became the Bishop of Maiuma. He wrote thirteen *Hymns* for the principal festivals of the year, composed with such art that the initial letters of all the sentences of which each Hymn consisted, when collected together, formed a short sentence prefixed to the Hymn <note>This refers to an acrostic format</note>. These Hymns survive in Latin only in Bigne’s *Appendix to the Library of the Fathers*, Paris, 1624, page 716, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XII, page 734. <margin>\* In the Life of John of Damascus.</margin> Suidas \* says of him: "A man most gifted, and breathing forth music and harmony in every way" <note>original Greek: ᾿Ανήρ εὐφυέστατος, καί πνέων μουσικήν ὅλως καί ἐναρμόνιον</note>. He is a most talented man, and his whole being breathes musical melody. Witnesses to this, besides the *Hymns* mentioned above, are the *Poetic Canons*, regarding which Suidas adds that they admit no comparison, nor ever will. Among these, the *Triodion*—or *Canticle consisting of three Odes*—deserves no low place; it is contained in the sacred Office of the Greeks...

...sacred, and usually recited from Septuagesima <note>The third Sunday before Lent</note> to Holy Saturday. Our Cosmas devised the first part of it—I mean the three Odes—to represent the holy and life-giving Trinity, for the Great and Holy Week of the Lord, composing the songs according to the acrostics of nearly every day. Theodore and Joseph the Studite added the remainder for the other weeks, as we learn from the *Synaxarium* <note>A collection of hagiographies and liturgical readings</note> of Nicephorus Callistus. Later, after many additions were made by Mark the Monk, it began to be called the *Tetraodion* <note>A liturgical book containing four odes</note>. Leo Allatius, in his first dissertation on the books of the Greek Church (p. 69), best informs us from the more recent Greek writers which parts of this book belong to our Cosmas and which to others.

<margin>730.</margin>
# JOHN, called *Damascene* from his homeland, *Chrysorrhoas* <note>meaning "Gold-streaming," a reference to his eloquence</note> for his speech, and *Mansur* or *Manseron* by the Arabs, was born in Damascus to a father who was a leader among his citizens and a member of the secret council of the Saracen Prince <note>The Umayyad Caliph</note>. John himself was educated in liberal disciplines in his father's house by Cosmas, and in a short time he acquired a distinguished reputation for learning and eloquence. Upon his father's death, he was summoned to the court by the Saracen Caliph and held his father's place in the inner council. Around the year 738, while the Iconoclastic controversy was raging, he himself intensely favored the cause of images and sent letters to friends everywhere against the efforts of Emperor Leo, intended to be published openly and spread far and wide. It is said that Emperor Leo, provoked by this, forged a letter under John's name to make the Prince of Damascus lose faith in John’s loyalty and cut off his right hand. Lest a miracle be lacking for this outstanding Confessor of the Iconodules <note>Venerators of icons</note>, it is reported that his hand was restored to wholeness through the intercession of the Mother of God <note>original: "Deiparæ"</note>. But, to speak truly, this entire story, as great as it is, tastes of a most foul fable; it has no other author than that most trifling writer of the *Life of Damascene*, namely John of Jerusalem. The celebrated Spanheim most abundantly demonstrates the futility and silliness of this entire fable in his *History of Restored Images* (Section II, number 13). Around the same time, John with difficulty obtained a dismissal from the Caliph; and having found Cosmas as a companion for his purpose and journey, he sold off his possessions, distributed them among the poor, and set out for Jerusalem. There he was distinguished with the dignity of the Priesthood; and from then on, having long meditated on the Monastic life, he withdrew to the Monastery <note>original: "Lauram"</note> of Saint Sabas, to spend the remainder of his life there in honorable leisure. In the year 730, he applied himself to writing and published his *Orations on Images*. In the year 749, he opposed in writing and speech Anastasius, the Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Euthymius, who was reviving the extinct heresy of Peter the Fuller regarding the *Trisagion* <note>A standard hymn in the Eastern liturgy; Peter the Fuller had added "who was crucified for us," implying the Trinity suffered</note>. Around the year 750, he met his final day. No one with a sound mind <note>original: "sanum sinciput" — literally "a healthy skull"</note> will deny him a reputation for doctrine and erudition. John of Jerusalem greatly celebrates his exceptional knowledge of Philosophy and Mathematical disciplines. Indeed, everyone knows his outstanding skill in Theology. However, in historical matters, it is shocking how gullible he was; hence Baronius candidly enough notes that *in many of his writings, his reliability wavers, and he abounds in several lies*; which indeed Casaubon shows with more than one example in his *Exercise XIII* (number 38, page 305).

## W O R K S.

<margin>* To year 31, num. 75.</margin>
**On the Orthodox Faith**, in 4 books. They appeared separately in Latin, *Paris 1507, 4to*; in Greek, *Verona 1531, 4to*; in Greek and Latin among other works of Damascene, *Basel 1548, 1575.*

**The Work of Parallels**, or selections or collections taken from Holy Scripture and the holy Fathers, and arranged into Commonplace headings. They are held only in Latin among the Works of Damascene, first edited by Jacques de Billy. The Greek text, however, survives in various libraries in France.

**Book on those who have fallen asleep in the faith**, which is rejected as being by Damascene by almost everyone on account of its most silly fables. It appeared in Greek together with the books *On the Orthodox Faith*, *Verona 1531, 4to*; in Greek and Latin separately, *Venice 1541, 8vo*; and among the other works of Damascene in both *Basel* editions.

*Three Orations on the Sacred Images* <note>original: "De sacris Imaginibus Orationes III." These are John’s famous defenses of icons against the Emperor's decrees</note> were published separately in Greek in *Rome, 1553, in octavo.* In Latin in *Antwerp, 1556.* In Greek and Latin in the *Basel edition of 1575,* and in Latin in the remaining editions.

*Oration: How We Are Created in the Image of God.* Available in Greek and Latin in the *Basel edition of 1575.*

*A Book on the Two Wills and Actions of Christ, and Other Natural Properties.* <note>A theological defense of the orthodox position that Christ possesses both a fully human and a fully divine will</note> It exists in Greek and Latin in the *Basel edition of 1575.*

*On the Composite Nature, Against the Acephali Heretics or Monophysites.* <note>The "Acephali" or "Headless ones" were a faction of Monophysites who rejected the Council of Chalcedon but lacked a clear leader</note> It exists in Greek and Latin in the *Basel edition of 1575.*

Another *Incomplete Little Work* <note>original: "Opusculum ἀκέφαλον"</note> by Damascene on the same subject was published in Latin by Henricus Canisius in the *Ancient Readings, Volume IV.*

*Book Against the Nestorians,* <note>The Nestorians followed the teachings of Nestorius, who emphasized a strict separation between Christ's human and divine natures</note> published in Latin by the same author in the same place.

*Arguments against the Nestorians with questions and answers on the faith,* published with notes in Greek and Latin by Johannes Wegelin at *Augsburg, 1611, in octavo.*

*Letter on the Trisagion.* <note>The "Trisagion" is the ancient hymn: "Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us"</note> Available in Greek and Latin in the *Basel edition of 1575.*

*Book Against the Manichaeans, or a Dialogue between an Orthodox and a Manichaean on the Principles of Two Realities.* <note>Manichaeism was a dualistic religion that taught a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness</note> It was published separately in Greek and Latin at *Basel, 1578, in octavo; Padua, 1572, in octavo; and in the Basel edition of 1575.*

*Book on Heresies, or a Catalog of Heresies,* which existed up to his time. The latter part, beginning with the Nestorians—which is the only part actually attributable to Damascene—is available in Greek in the *Paris edition of 1619.* For the first part is nothing other than the *Anacephalaeosis* <note>A summary or "re-heading"</note> of Epiphanius. However, Cotelerius provided the complete work in Greek and Latin in *Monuments of the Greek Church, Volume I, page 278.*

*Dispute between a Christian and a Saracen,* <note>The medieval term for a Muslim. This records an early theological dialogue between Christianity and Islam</note> thus far printed only in Latin.

*Fragment of Sayings on the Eight Passions, or Capital Vices;* printed only in Latin. The Greek text exists in the Royal Library of Paris.

*Homily on the Day of Judgment, or a brief treatise,* in Latin only. Labbe considers this to be the work of a different author.

*Letter to Zacharias, Bishop of the Doari, on the body and blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ,* together with another longer chapter on the same subject, published in Greek and Latin by Petrus Pantinus at *Antwerp, 1601,* and from there taken into the *Paris edition of 1619.*

*Short book on the Resurrection and Paradise.* Published in Greek at *Paris, 1541, in sixteen-mo.*

*Oration on the Transfiguration of the Lord.* Exists in Greek and Latin in the *Paris editions.*

*Oration on Holy Saturday,* published in Greek and Latin by Petrus Pantinus at *Antwerp, 1601.*

*Three Orations on the Nativity of the Mother of God,* <term>Deipara: A Greek-derived term meaning "God-bearer" or Mother of God</term> first published in Greek and Latin by Jacques de Billy in the *Paris edition of 1577.* Of these, the latter two are attributed to *Andrew of Crete* in several manuscript codices.

*Two Orations on the Dormition or Assumption of the Blessed Mary,* of which the latter is clearly spurious. In that work, *Euthymius* is cited, who lived under the Emperor Alexios. They exist printed only in Latin, but the Greek text remains in the Gallic <note>French</note> libraries.

*Iambic Pentastichs and Acrostics on Christ's Nativity, His Epiphany, and the Feast of Pentecost,* <note>These are complex poetic forms where the first letters of lines spell out a message</note> first published in Greek and Latin by Aldus Manutius along with other Christian poets at *Venice, 1501, in quarto,* and thereafter in almost all editions of Damascene’s works.

*Oration to Christ composed in Anacreontic verses.* <note>A poetic meter named after the Greek poet Anacreon, usually used for light or lyrical themes</note> Exists in Greek and Latin in the *Paris editions.*

*Various Songs in free verse, on the Ascension of Christ, on the Transfiguration, and for the Annunciation of the Mother of God.* Available in Greek and Latin in the *Basel edition of 1575.*

*Certain short prayers to the Lord, the Mother of God, and the Archangel, etc.* These exist in Latin only.

*Octoechos, or Eight Tones, or Ecclesiastical Songs of the Greeks,* titled *Octosoni* <note>The system of eight musical modes that governs much of Eastern Orthodox liturgical music</note>, by authors Damascene, Metrophanes of Smyrna, and other Doctors of the Eastern Church. They exist in Latin in the *Paris editions;* the Greek text is found in the Gallic libraries.

*Book on Dialectics, addressed to Cosmas, Bishop of Maiuma.* Exists in Greek in the *Basel edition of 1575.*

*First Instructions on the Decrees and Opinions [addressed] to John, Bishop of Laodicea.* These are available in Greek and Latin in the *Basel edition of 1575.*

*Physics, or a certain compendium of Aristotelian Philosophy.* It exists in Latin only in the *Paris* editions.

*Indian History, or the Life and Conversation of Saints Barlaam and Josaphat,* or of two soldiers of Christ; regarding which two things primarily must be asked: 1st. Whether the History is true or fictional; that it is a fable, not a true History, could be demonstrated by many points from the work itself, nor can it be a doubt to anyone who has read the History itself attentively. That there perhaps were a certain Barlaam and Josaphat, and certain general foundations of the work, is not unlike the truth, the rest being fashioned from the author's genius: 

<margin>
* On the Origin of Romance Fables, p. 60.
</margin>
And indeed I see the Illustrious Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721) was a renowned French scholar and bishop known for his work on the history of the novel</note> descending into this opinion, setting aside others; *that fable,* he says, *is indeed a Romance, but a pious one; it deals with love, but divine love; much blood is shed here, but that of martyrs; this work was labored over according to the norm of history and from the laws of Romance fables; nevertheless, even if verisimilitude is observed there accurately enough, it still presents so many signs of fiction that whoever reads the work with serious mental reflection will never go so far as to deny it was fabricated.* 2nd. Whether it belongs to Damascene. For besides the fact that it teaches the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son <note>The "Filioque" doctrine, which was a point of contention between the Western and Eastern Churches; its presence here suggests a later Western influence or a different author</note>, in some Manuscript Codices it is inscribed to John of Sinai (namely, as I suppose, John Climacus), which indeed Jacques de Billy openly enough refutes in several points in the Preface to the new version prepared by himself. It exists in Latin from an old version by a certain Monk (not George of Trebizond, as the title wrongly claims) in the *Basel* editions, and separately in *Cologne, 1593, in octavo* and *Antwerp, 1602, in octavo;* and from the version of Jacques de Billy in the *Paris* editions. It is held in Greek as a manuscript in the *Royal Library of Paris.*

*Life of Stephen the Younger,* who met death because of the worship of images; he was punished with the ultimate penalty by Constantine Copronymus in the year 767 <note>Constantine V, nicknamed "Copronymus" or "Dung-named" by his iconodule enemies, was a fierce opponent of religious icons</note>. So much so that it must be said either that this *Life* is falsely attributed to Damascene, or Damascene did not die before the year 767. It is found in Latin in the *Paris* editions and in Surius on November 28th. In Greek, however, it is a manuscript in the *Royal Library of Paris.*

The works of John of Damascus appeared, partly in Greek and partly in Latin, in *Basel, 1539, 1548, 1575,* and by the care of Jacques de Billy, *Paris, 1577, 1603, 1619, in folio.* In this, however, the third Basel edition far surpasses the Parisian ones, because it presents many more of Damascene's treatises in Greek.

*Epistle on the Sacred Images* published under the name of Damascene in Greek and Latin by François Combefis in *Origins of Constantinople, p. 110;* which, however, Combefis clearly proves in the same place to actually be a Synodical letter of the Eastern Bishops, written long after the death of Damascene.

*Demonstrative Oration on the Holy and Venerable Images against the Emperor Copronymus.* It exists in Greek and Latin, published with notes by Combefis in the *New Supplement, Vol. ii, p. 663.* It does not, however, seem to be the offspring of Damascene.

Almost innumerable Troparia [short hymns].*

*Scholia <note>Explanatory notes or commentaries</note> on Aristotle’s Categories*. *On the Months of the Macedonians*. A collection of various *Theses*. *On the Divine Commandments. On the Three Faculties of the Soul. On Free Will. A Compendium of Logic.* A collection of *Testimonies from the Writings of the Holy Fathers; regarding the Trinity, the two natures in Christ, the divine economy <note>The plan of God for the salvation of humanity</note>*, and other ecclesiastical dogmas, distributed into forty-one chapters. However, Labbe <note>Philippe Labbe (1607–1667), a French Jesuit bibliographer</note> acknowledges that it is not entirely certain whether this is a genuine work of Damascus.

Perhaps many other works could be found hidden here and there. Regarding the unpublished works of Damascus, anyone wishing to know more should consult the *Overview of all the works of St. Damascus*, which Philippe Labbe published in *Paris, 1652, in quarto*, at which time he intended to produce a new edition of Damascus's works. Jean Aubert had also planned this before him; accordingly, Leo Allatius <note>A Greek scholar and librarian at the Vatican</note> had sent several works of Damascus and others relating to this subject to Aubert, which had been recovered in Greek from manuscript codices, some of which Allatius himself had translated into Latin. On this account, Allatius even accuses Labbe of plagiarism, claiming that after Aubert’s death, Labbe plundered the papers sent from Rome. 
> "We have lost both our effort and our oil," <note>original: "Operam, inquit, & oleam perdidimus" — a Latin idiom meaning to waste time and labor, specifically "burning the midnight oil."</note> he says, "and some jackdaw or other, stealing the labors of others, wraps himself in them." 
Indeed, so that everyone might know what he himself contributed to Damascus, Allatius saw to it that a catalog of the works sent to Aubert was attached to the end of his *Symmicta* <note>A collection of shorter miscellaneous works</note> on page 445. Meanwhile, this new edition, promised so many times, has never appeared to this day.

<margin>730.</margin>
### THE ROMAN ORDER, regarding the divine Offices and Ministries through the circle of the entire year. 
It seems to have been written in this century, and thus, following the illustrious Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh and a famous chronologist</note>, we place it around the year 730. Certainly, neither the author nor the age of this work is sufficiently established. The author himself is entirely unknown, although it is not improbable that it was someone of no small reputation among the clergy of the Roman Church. As for its age, there are those who maintain it was sent into Gaul <note>Modern-day France</note> around the same time that **Divine Offices** with Roman chant were introduced there through the efforts of Charlemagne. However, things can be detected within the work itself that argue the author was older than Charlemagne. Meanwhile, it is not improbable that the book, having been sent to Gaul, was expanded and edited by Alcuin <note>A leading scholar and advisor to Charlemagne</note>; indeed, a few things can be observed that clearly taste of the times following the Carolingian era. As for Melchior Hittorp's conjecture that this book was the *Gelasian Code* <note>The Gelasian Sacramentary, a book of liturgy</note>, he was certainly "as wrong as the heavens are wide," <note>original: "toto erravit cælo" — an idiom for being completely mistaken</note> as is immediately clear from the recently published Gelasian code itself. This book is found among the *Writers on Divine Offices* edited by Melchior Hittorp, *Paris, 1610, p. 1, and in almost any edition of the Library of the Fathers*: it was also published elsewhere by Cassander and others.

<margin>731.</margin>
### GREGORY III, a Syrian by nation, son of John, made Pope from being a Priest of the Roman Church in the year 731, on the 22nd day of February. 
He followed diligently in the footsteps of his predecessor Gregory; he strenuously defended the cause of images, overwhelmed the Iconoclasts <note>Those who opposed and destroyed religious icons</note> with the lightning-bolts of excommunication, proceeded to withdraw Italy from the rule of the Greek [Byzantine] Emperors, and began to claim and seize the surrounding territories of Rome in the name of St. Peter—"if the gods please" <note>original: "si Diis placet" — a sarcastic Roman expression used here to critique the Pope's worldly territorial claims</note>—for the dominion of the Church. Immediately upon entering the Papacy, he sent a letter of warning to the Emperor Leo regarding the restoration of images. However, since Gregory the Priest, to whom the letter was entrusted, was afraid to put it into the Emperor's hands, the matter came to nothing. Therefore, having returned to Rome, Gregory was forced to plead his case in a Synod, and having narrowly escaped a sentence of deposition, he was sent as a legate to Constantinople again, armed with other letters on that subject. But by the Emperor's command, he was seized in Sicily, stripped of the letters, and sent into exile. When news of this reached the city, Pope Gregory, having gathered a Synod of Italian bishops from all sides, raged with lightning-bolts and devoted the enemies of images to dire curses, a notable decree having been passed on that matter. Constantine the Defender, who was sent from the Synod to carry the warning letters to the Emperor, as well as Peter the Defender in the following year, experienced the same fortune as Gregory the Priest. In the year 739, with Rome besieged by Liutprand, King of the Lombards, Pope Gregory as a suppliant sought aid from Charles Martel <note>The Frankish leader and grandfather of Charlemagne</note>, sending legates to Gaul who carried letters and keys,

**EGBERT**, of the English nation, born of the royal blood of the Northumbrians, being the brother of King Eadberht. After the death of Wilfrid in the year 732, he was made Archbishop of York (not of Canterbury, as Oudin <note>Casimir Oudin (1638–1717), a French bibliographer and former monk</note> mistakenly has it). Relying on the power and wealth of his brother, he raised the Church of York to a far more illustrious state; and since he was a man of superior intellect, he obtained the pallium <note>A liturgical vestment sent by the Pope to symbolize the authority of an archbishop</note> from the Roman Pontiff for his see. He was a man born to promote studies and was the finest patron of all learned men; for this reason, he established a most noble library at York, as Malmesbury <note>William of Malmesbury, a 12th-century historian</note> testifies. Alcuin speaks of this library famously in a letter to Charlemagne: *“Give me,”* he says, *“books of more exquisite scholarly learning, such as I had in my homeland through the good and most devoted industry of my master, Archbishop Egbert; and if it pleases, I shall send back some of our boys to your Excellence, who may select everything necessary and carry back the flower of Britain into France.”* <note>original: "Date mihi... exquisitioris eruditionis scholasticae libros... et revehant in Franciam florem Britanniae."</note> Egbert died in the year 767, in the 36th year of his episcopate. He wrote the *Dialogue on Ecclesiastical Institution*, which the distinguished Ware <note>Sir James Ware (1594–1666), an Irish historian</note> first brought to light from the Cottonian Library and published along with some of Bede’s minor works in Dublin, 1664, in octavo; it was later transferred into the *Collection of Councils, Volume VI, page 1604.* There exist 144 *Excerpts* from the sayings and Canons of the Holy Fathers, compiled by Egbert and contributing to the constitution of ecclesiastical governance, first published by Henry Spelman in the first volume of the *British Councils*, London, 1639; and thereafter in the *Collection of Councils, Volume VI, page 1586.* Egbert also wrote a *Penitential* <note>A manual for priests determining penance for specific sins</note> divided into four books, which is preserved today in manuscript in many libraries at both Cambridge and Oxford Universities. From the second book, the same Spelman published thirty-five Canons, which are also found in the *Collection of Councils, Volume VI, page 1601.* Morinus <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French theologian</note> published a larger portion of the *Penitential* in the Appendix to his book *On Penance*, page 11. I wish that the entire work might someday be published. Many of these excerpts, and those of Gregory III, have things in common with Bede's little book, or *Canons on the Remedies for Sins*. Furthermore, I should like it noted that these Canons of Bede, in the edition by Antonio Agustín attached to the *Roman Penitential*, bear the name of Archbishop Egbert.

<margin>
740.

* Commentaries, Book 2, chapter 8, page 850.
</margin>
**FREDEGARIUS SCHOLASTICUS**, of the Frankish nation, as it seems; he flourished in the year 740. At the command of Count Childebrand, the uncle of King Pippin, he wrote a *History*, or *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Franks*, beginning from the year 596, where Gregory of Tours left off, and continuing to the year 739. That history is usually attached to Gregory of Tours as an appendix, but it was first published under the name of Fredegarius by Marquard Freher in his collection of ancient Frankish historians (who also annexed an *Anonymous Appendix* reaching from the year 739 to 768), and thereafter in an expanded form by André du Chesne in *Frankish Writers, Volume I, page 740*, and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XI, page 740.* He also wrote a *Miscellaneous History*, or five books of *Chronicles*, following the example of Jerome’s *Chronicle*, in which he had reduced almost all of Gregory’s history into a compendium. However, that work has long since perished. But if the distinguished Lambecius <note>Peter Lambeck (1628–1680), a German historian and librarian</note> conjectures correctly, the whole work survives. For there is an anonymous manuscript in the Imperial Library, a *Chronicle* written in very barbaric style, from the creation of the world to the death of Belisarius. Lambecius (who presents its Prologue and Epilogue) thinks it is by Fredegarius, and wants it to comprise the first three books of the aforementioned work; so that the fourth book is that part of the published Chronicle which, excerpted from the History of Gregory of Tours, progresses from the Hunnish invasion of Gaul up to the death of King Chilperic; while the fifth book is nothing else than the remaining part of the published Chronicle, which continues Gregory’s history up to the death of Charles Martel.

<margin>THE 8TH CENTURY, from the Year 700.</margin>
<margin>Life of Bede</margin>
<margin>Letter on the death of Bede</margin>
<margin>* Writers of England, Century 2, chapter 7. & † Defense of the History of Britain, chapter 12, page 112.</margin>
...he made wonderful progress in scholarly learning. He flourished in the year 740. He served as a scribe to his teacher [Bede] when the latter was already struggling in extreme old age, and he took down his dictations with a pen; he also stood by him as he was dying and diligently listened to his final words. He wrote *a book on the life and death of Bede dedicated to his peer Cuthwin, in which he records that Bede's death occurred on the 8th Calends of June <note>original: "VIII. Cal. Junii"; this corresponds to May 25th</note> on a Wednesday, which immediately preceded Ascension Day.* A *Life of Bede* without an author's name is held in Volume VIII of the works of Bede, Basel edition, as well as the *Letter on the Death of Bede*. However, it appears that that *Life* was taken from Peter de Natalibus's *Catalog of Saints*, Book 5, chapter 55; but I am persuaded (says Ussher in his *Theological Library*, page 128) that the letter regarding the death of Bede (also recorded by Surius in Volume VII on May 10th) is by Cuthbert. For besides the fact that it is expressly ascribed to him in many manuscript codices, the author testifies that he himself was present at Bede's death, and those things which Florence of Worcester has from Cuthbert’s book in his *Chronicle* for the year 734 are found in this Letter in the exact same words. Here it should be noted that the date [May 9th] <note>original: "VII. Idus Maii"</note> which is incorrectly held in the Letter should be corrected and read as [May 25th] <note>original: "VII. Cal. Junii"</note> according to Florence and Matthew of Westminster <note>referred to here as "Florilegus"</note>; both the calculation of the dates requires this, and the illustrious Ussher proves it with several points in the place cited. Abraham Wheelock provided this Letter under Cuthbert’s name in the *Life of Bede* prefixed to his edition of the *Ecclesiastical History*, Cambridge, 1644. Furthermore, according to Bale*, Cuthbert wrote *a book of familiar Letters*, and several other works which are now lost. John Fries† mentions a "Closing" <note>original: "Coronis," literally a curved line or flourish at the end of a book, here meaning a concluding supplement</note> added by him to Bede’s *History*, which he says he has seen in his own collection.

<margin>741.</margin>
**ANASTASIUS**, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Euthymius in Palestine. He flourished in the year 741. Finally, in the year 749, when he began to hold erroneous views regarding the <term>Trisagion</term> <note>A standard hymn in the liturgy: "Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us." Anastasius was accused of applying the whole hymn only to the Son, rather than the Trinity</note>, referring the whole of it to the Son, he gave John of Damascus an occasion for writing the Letter *On the Trisagion* to Jordan the Coenobiarch <note>The head of a monastic community</note> against his error. Anastasius himself wrote *A Book Against the Jews*, which was first published in Latin by Canisius in the *Ancient Readings*, Volume III, from the version by Turrianus; from there it is held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XIII. The Greek text still survives in manuscript in Rome and elsewhere.

<margin>741.</margin>
<margin>* Codex 252.</margin>
**ZACHARIAS**, a Syrian by nation, son of Polychronius, a monk by profession, and finally Roman Pontiff in the year 741 on the 19th of November. He immediately entered into peace with King Liutprand, from whom (having set out the following year for Terni <note>original: "Interamnam"</note> on the borders of Spoleto) he obtained by his prayers four cities that had been snatched from the Roman Duchy three years earlier; likewise, in the year 743, traveling to Pavia <note>original: "Ticinum"</note>, he obtained from the same king that peace be granted to the people of Ravenna. In the year 742, having held a Synod at Rome, he ratified the German Council of Boniface of Mainz. In the year 745, having gathered a Council of Bishops at Rome, he subjected to anathema Adelbert and Clement, and in the year 748, Samson the Scot <note>In this period, "Scot" often referred to the Irish</note>—certain crude heresiarchs who had been condemned by Boniface shortly before. In the year 750, having set out for Perugia, he moved Ratchis, King of the Lombards, away from the siege of that city through prayers and gifts. In the year 752, he is said to have transferred the kingdom of France from the Merovingian line to Pepin, the son of Charles Martel, by Apostolic authority, and to have stripped King Childeric of his sovereign power. However, the more prudent writers on the "Transfer of the Empire" <note>The *translatio imperii*, the political concept of the linear succession of imperial power</note> constantly deny this entire matter; the reader may consult them. Zacharias died on the 3rd of March in the year 752. *Eighteen Letters* are extant in the *Councils*, Volume VI, page 1498. A *Letter to Theodore, Bishop of Pavia* is found in D'Achéry’s *Gleanings* <note>original: "Spicilegium"</note>, Volume VIII, page 120, and in Baluze’s *Appendix to Regino*, page 601. Furthermore, there are his Greek translations of the *Dialogues of Saint Gregory*, with the Latin text joined to them, in the edition of Gregory's works, *Rome, 1590*, where six chapters are missing, to be supplied from Canisius, *Volume III, page 24*. Consequently, the complete Greek version is found in the *Parisian 1640* edition of Gregory’s works. Moreover, Photius* informs us that Zacharias translated certain other small works of Saint Gregory into Greek, which are no longer extant.

...born from a family of the primary nobility of the Franks, he was raised in the court of Charles the Great <note>Refers here to Charles Martel, "the Elder," mayor of the palace, rather than his grandson Charlemagne</note>, and was later made his Referendary <note>A high-ranking administrative official or chancellor</note>. Upon the death of Sigebald, on the 1st of October in the year 742, he was created the prelate of the Church of Metz. In the year 749, he founded the Monastery of Gorze. In 753, he was sent to Rome by Pepin along with Duke Autcharius to escort Pope Stephen into the lands of the Franks <note>Gaul</note>. In the year 757, he prescribed a *Rule* <note>original: "Regulam"</note> for the Clergy of his Diocese, whom he wished to cultivate a shared life in the manner of monastics, so that instructions would be ready for them by which they might best restrain themselves within the boundaries of the Ecclesiastical life. In the year 764, he sought Rome again to obtain from the Pope the relics of Saints which had been moved from the cemeteries into the city; consequently, bringing back with him the bodies of Saints Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius, he placed them in his Monastery of Gorze. He died on the day before the Calends of March <note>February 28th</note> in the year 766. *He was a man*, according to the testimony of Paul the Deacon, *distinguished in every respect, handsome in form, most eloquent in speech, learned in both his native and the Latin tongue, a nourisher of the servants of God, and not only a provider for orphans and widows, but also their most merciful protector.* Furthermore, he was a strenuous champion of Pontifical authority, who, <margin>* On the Bishops of Metz.</margin> <margin>† On Illustrious Men, part 1, page 262.</margin> as Heinrich Pantaleon † rightly notes, extolled beyond measure the celibacy of Priests, voluntary poverty, the monastic life, fasts, feasts, masses, and other things of this sort. His *Rule prescribed for the Clergy of Metz* <note>original: "Regula Clericis Metensibus"</note> survives, first published by Luc d'Achéry in the *Spicilegium*, Volume I; however, it was significantly altered and changed for the general use of the whole Church. Philippe Labbe provided the pure and genuine version in *Councils*, Volume VII, page 1444. Having obtained even more accurate Codices, the celebrated Cointius compared both editions with his own copy, and added variant readings and his own observations to almost every chapter in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, Volume V, for the year 757. The Reader should also note that another Rule, compiled from Chrodegang and others, is presented by Labbe in the same work cited above, page 1464.

742.
Life of Saint Willibald in Canisius, Ancient Lessons, Vol. 4, p. 695. Pantaleon on Illustrious Men, part 2, p. 263.

WILLIBALD, English by race, from Devon by birth, from the illustrious families of the English, and—as some would have it—born of royal stock; he was a disciple and nephew of Saint Boniface, under whose guidance he gave himself entirely to the study of literature. As a five-year-old boy, he was given by his parents to the Monastery of Waldheim to be educated by Abbot Egviwald. Having reached adulthood, led by a desire to visit holy places, he began to travel in foreign regions; and having set out for Rome and from there to Jerusalem, after seven years spent in pilgrimage, he settled in the Monastery of Monte Cassino. In the year 738, while hurrying to Rome again, he met Boniface, by whom (through the mediation of the Pope) he was persuaded to gird himself to bring auxiliary help to him in the German Apostleship. Therefore, entering Germany, he applied himself strenuously to preaching the Gospel, and having been made Bishop of Eichstätt by Boniface in the year 742, he took part in the German Council. He died near the Baltic <note>possibly referencing the region or a specific locality</note> in the year 781 at the age of 77. At the request of Lullus, Archbishop of Mainz, he wrote the *Life of Saint Boniface* <note>original: "Vitam S. Bonifacii"</note>, which is held in Canisius, Volume IV, part II, page 341, and was published with the Letters of Boniface by Serarius at *Mainz*, 1605; it is also found in Surius on the 5th of June, and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Century* III, part II, page 1. He is also said to have written the *Life of Saint Walpurga*, his sister, and several *Letters* to Monks. However, whether these survive today is not clear.

<margin>750.</margin>
MARCUS, Bishop of Otranto <note>original: "Hydruntinus"</note>; he flourished, as some hold, in the year 750. He wrote in Greek a short acrostic *Hymn for Holy Saturday* <note>original: "Hymnum... in Magnum Sabbatum"</note>, which exists translated into Latin in the Bignean Appendix, page 725, and in the *Library of the Fathers*.

<margin>750.</margin>
PIRMINIUS, Abbot, and also, as it seems, a Bishop or Rural Bishop <note>term: Chorepiscopus; a rank of bishop who assisted the primary bishop in rural areas</note>, though of what place is unknown to me. He flourished around the year 750. He wrote a *Booklet on the individual Canonical books* <note>original: "Libellum de singulis libris Canonicis"</note>, into which he also mixed many things against the wicked customs of his age. That Booklet exists as edited by Mabillon in the *Analecta*, Volume IV, page 569.

<margin>8TH CENTURY. from the Year 700.</margin>
...ordained Pope on the 19th of March. At the beginning of his Pontificate, the city <note>Rome</note> was besieged by Aistulf, King of the Lombards. Although the Pope had long and fruitlessly pleaded through prayers and letters for the conciliation of peace and the restoration of the Exarchate of Ravenna to the jurisdiction of St. Peter <note>original: "S. Petri ditioni," referring to the Papal lands</note>, and had petitioned Emperor Constantine <note>Byzantine Emperor Constantine V</note> by sending legates—though without success—he himself in the following year undertook a journey into Gaul to obtain aid from King Pepin. Therefore, an army having been sent by Pepin against the Lombards, Aistulf was driven to the peace conditions desired by Stephen. However, when the fear of Frankish arms ceased in the year 755, Aistulf violated these terms and again surrounded the city of Rome with a siege. Stephen sought help from Pepin a second time, threatening him with excommunication if he did not come to the aid of the Roman Church. Thus, Pepin flying into Italy with his army forced Aistulf to abandon the siege, enter into peace, and restore the territory of Ravenna to the jurisdiction of the City of Rome. He died on the 16th day of April in the year 757. There survive *six Letters* and other *Precepts and Responses*, found in the *Collection of Councils, Volume 6, page 1630*.

<margin>755.</margin>
## MARCELLINUS, an Englishman by nation, a Brigantian by birth <note>Refers to the region of the Brigantes in Northern England</note>, a Priest and Monk of York, was prominent around the year 755, having been famous long before; for he was one of twelve Englishmen whom Egbert, later Archbishop of York, sent into Frisia <note>A coastal region in the modern-day Netherlands and Germany</note> to spread the light of the Gospel among the pagan people. In this work he is said to have labored for 70 years, and he had the care of the Transisalania province <note>Modern Overijssel in the Netherlands</note> committed to him. He died almost a centenarian around the year 770. There exist under his name the *Acts or Life of St. Swithbert*, first Bishop of Werden, who died in the year 717 (found in Surius, March 1st); but as they exist today, they are either falsely attributed to our Marcellinus or significantly altered <note>interpolated</note>. He also wrote a *Life of St. Willibrord*, whom he had accompanied from England to Frisia while still a youth. But that work is missing.

<margin>757.</margin>
## PAUL I, a Roman by nation, son of Constantine, full brother of Stephen II, and a Deacon of the Roman Church, was sent as a legate by his brother Stephen to King Aistulf in the year 752 to demand peace. In the year 757, on the 22nd of May, he succeeded his brother in the Roman see. He wearied Emperor Constantine and King Pepin with frequent letters and embassies, imploring the latter to protect the Roman Church against the injuries of the Lombards, and the former to restore the [sacred] images <note>Referring to the Iconoclastic controversy where the Byzantine Emperor Constantine V opposed the use of religious icons</note>. He died in the year 767, on the 21st of June. There survive *twelve Letters*, [in] *Councils, Volume 6, page 1672*. Of these, as Papebroch correctly observes, ten lack any date; the remaining two, because they do have one, are rendered suspect, since one was dated two years, and the other four years, after Paul had departed from the living.

<margin>760.</margin>
## AMBROSE AUTPERT, a Frank by birth, a Monk and eventually Abbot of the Monastery of St. Vincent in Samnium <note>An ancient region of south-central Italy</note> at the source of the Volturno, flourished in the year 760, in the time of Pope Paul and Desiderius, King of the Lombards, as the distinguished Labbe correctly notes from Autpert's own words at the conclusion of his *Commentary on the Apocalypse* and from other sources. There was no real reason for Labbe to wonder why Trithemius, Gesner, Simler, Possevino, Bellarmine, and others referred to him among the writers of the ninth century,

But I shall speak freely about what I think regarding this matter. That monk *Autpert* who flourished during the reign of Emperor Lothair and died in the year 837 was clearly someone else than our subject; it is he of whom Sigebert (chapter 91), Peter the Deacon, Ant. Scipio, and others speak. This [later] Autpert, according to the testimony of Peter the Deacon, composed a *Sermon in praise of St. Matthias the Apostle*, a work *On the Purification of the Holy Mother of God*, and other very beautiful homilies of Saints, which either no longer exist or are preserved in the library of Monte Cassino. Our Autpert died in the year 778. He wrote *ten books of Commentaries on the Apocalypse of John*, which were published in print at Cologne in 1536, and thereafter included in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 13, page 403*. There are those who find the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, located among the works of Ambrose and Augustine,

760.

* Preface to the 
Martyrology.
</margin>
**FLORUS**, a Monk of St. Trudo <note>The Abbey of Saint-Trond in modern-day Belgium</note>, in the diocese of Liège, of the Gallican congregation, flourished around the year 760. He wrote the *Acts and Passions of the Holy Martyrs*, or, as Usuard states*, he supplemented, increased, and enriched the previously brief and concise *Martyrology of Bede*. Achard also testifies to this in the Preface to his own Martyrology, saying: "the Martyrology, which by the study of the Venerable Florus had grown through labor in the Lord from that of Bede." See what the most recent editors of the *Acts of the Saints* <note>The Bollandists</note> note on this matter in the Prologue to the Month of March, Volume II. That Martyrology exists under Bede's name, though enriched by the additions of Florus as well as others, among the Works of Bede and elsewhere quite frequently. We judge that the remaining small works ascribed to Florus the Martyrologist belong to Florus of Lyons, where we shall note more concerning them.

768.
</margin>
**STEPHEN III**, a Sicilian by nation, son of Olivus, Priest of St. Cecilia, was elected in the year 767 and ordained Roman Pope on the 7th day of August in the year 768. In the year 769, having summoned Bishops from Gaul and all of Italy, he celebrated a Council at Rome, in which he condemned the Antipope Constantine—who, after the death of Paul, had violently seized the Pontifical seat and held it for an entire year—and he struck him with fists and slaps in the full assembly of the Fathers <note>original: "pugnis & alapis in pleno Patrum consessu cecidit"</note>. He removed the clerics ordained by Constantine from their rank and ordered that the decrees made at Constantinople regarding the removal of images be voided <note>A rejection of Byzantine Iconoclasm</note>. He died on the 3rd day of February in the year 772. There survive *three Letters* and certain *Decrees* in the *Collection of Councils, Volume VI, page 1714*.

**CHARLES THE GREAT** <note>Charlemagne</note>, son of King Pepin, was born near Ingelheim <note>near Mainz</note> in the year 767. He had the most famous men of that age as his teachers: Peter of Pisa in Grammar, and in other disciplines, Alcuin the Englishman, a man most learned in every respect. Primarily through Alcuin's labor, he emerged as remarkably well-educated in every kind of refined literature, and no less illustrious in piety. We shall set aside those things which concern his secular life and his deeds in war, content to briefly note those things which touch upon the Church.

Therefore, in the year 768, upon the death of Pepin, he took up the divided Empire of the Franks with his brother Carloman; and after Carloman died in 771, he thereafter held the kingdom alone. In the year 774, after Pavia was taken by storm and Desiderius, King of the Lombards, was captured, he began to be called King of Italy as well; and as a sign of his lordship, he proceeded to Rome and obtained from Pope Hadrian the right of electing the Roman Pontiffs. In the year 775, he held the Assembly of Düren, where he decided to pursue the Saxons who were invading Gaul with war, until they were either conquered and subjected to the Christian religion or utterly destroyed. This was successfully achieved in the following year, with peace granted to the defeated people on the condition that they embrace the Christian faith. In the year 777, after celebrating a Council at Paderborn, he saw to the baptism of many thousands of Saxons and prepared himself to wage war in Spain against the Saracens on behalf of the Christian religion. In the year 780, penetrating as far as the Elbe <note>original: "Albin"</note>, he took care to send Bishops and Abbots to instruct the Saxons, along with the Slavs and Frisians. In the year 781, seeking Rome again, he bestowed the territory of Sabina upon the Roman Church. In the year 785, to promote the conversion of the Saxons, he again visited their province, saw to the baptism of the nobles, and bestowed gifts upon those baptized. In the year 787, he celebrated Easter in the city of Rome and enriched the Apostolic Church with a new donation. In the year 789, he labored strenuously so that the Monastic Order in Gaul might be reformed according to the Rule of St. Benedict. In the year 790...

<margin>8TH CENTURY from the Year 700.</margin> He saw to it that the letters of the Roman Pontiffs written to Gaul, which had been nearly destroyed by age, were transcribed. In the year 792, he sent the Greek Synodal book concerning the adoration of Images <note>This refers to the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which Charlemagne opposed</note>, which had been sent to him from the East, to Britain to be refuted by Alcuin. In the year 794, having gathered a Council of more than three hundred Bishops from the entire West, which he attended himself along with the legates of Pope Hadrian, he ensured the rejection and condemnation of the heresy of Elipandus of Toledo and Felix of Urgell—who had taught that Christ, in respect to his humanity, was the son of God only by right of adoption <note>This heresy is known as Adoptionism</note>—and even the decrees of the Council of Nicaea concerning the adoration of images. Returning to Saxony in the same year, he brought many to the faith through his authority and kindness. In the year 796, he received the Keys of Saint Peter and the Banner of the City of Rome sent by Pope Leo as symbols of submission; and with Abbot Angilbert as his legate to Italy, he bound the Roman people to his loyalty by an oath. In the same year, he labored for the conversion of the Huns, and through instruction and gifts, he brought about the baptism of Theodo, their ruler. In the year 797, he employed Alcuin to revise and explain the Holy Scripture, and Paul the Deacon to compile a *Homiliary* <note>A collection of sermons or "homilies" to be read in church</note> for every festival. In the year 800, making a journey to Rome, he convoked a Synod there, and after investigating the case, he declared Pope Leo innocent (who had been cast out of the city two years earlier for various crimes) and restored him to his see. At the end of that year, he was acclaimed Emperor by the Romans, and was anointed and crowned by Pope Leo in the Basilica of St. Peter on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord. In the year 805, he began to publish his Ecclesiastical <term>Capitularies</term> <note>A series of legislative or administrative acts divided into "capitula" (chapters)</note>. In the year 809, he held the Synod of Aachen, in which the question of the Procession of the Holy Spirit was debated and strengthened against the opinion of the Greeks <note>The "Filioque" controversy regarding whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son</note>; legates were sent from the Synod to Pope Leo to consult with him on that matter for the common good. In the year 812, after entering into peace with Emperor Michael of Constantinople, he began to be called **Emperor** <note>original: Βασιλεύς (Basileus)</note> by the Greeks; and in the same year, through encyclical letters, he demanded a response from the Archbishops to questions concerning the entire method of administering Baptism, and the ceremonies, formulas, rites, and symbols used during baptism. In the year 813, having announced a meeting at Aachen, he ordered Synods of Bishops to be held at Reims, Mainz, Arles, Tours, and Châlons at roughly the same time, and commanded that the synodal decrees be brought to him. This was done: and with a Council held again at Aachen in the month of September, he accurately weighed the canons of the individual Synods, and from them composed a Capitulary divided into twenty-six chapters. He died in the year 814, on the fifth day before the Calends of February <note>January 28</note>, at the age of 67. He was buried at Aachen. A prince not so much by title as in truth, he was great, worthy of a better age and a longer life; it is doubtful whether he was more illustrious for his piety or his majesty. He had made no small progress in fine literature, being learned in Greek and Latin; he was so eloquent, says Einhard <note>Charlemagne's biographer</note>, that it seemed he could even have fulfilled the office of a teacher. He cultivated the liberal arts most studiously, and greatly venerated their teachers, bestowing high honors upon them. He redeemed whatever time he could from his duties for the study of better literature, so much so that he would hold small debates or readings even while dining. History and the deeds of ancient kings were most often read to him: he took delight in the books of Saint Augustine, especially those he titled *The City of God*. Yet it is a singular thing which Einhard relates of him: that so learned a prince did not know how to write. *He used to try,* he says, *to write; and for this purpose he was accustomed to keep tablets and notebooks under his pillows in bed, so that when he had free time, he might accustom his hand to forming letters. But the poorly timed labor, begun too late in life, met with little success.*

*The Capitularies <note>A series of legislative or administrative acts organized into chapters</note>, for the most part Ecclesiastical, collected by Abbot Ansegis in the year 827 from the chapters of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, and distributed into four books; to which Benedict the Levite later added three other books, extracted from the archives of churches, especially that of Mainz, and from ancient chests of charters. Pierre Pithou saw to the separate publication of the first four books in Paris, 1588, reprinted in Mainz, 1602, in quarto. The complete seven books were issued in Venice, 1537, in octavo, with a Glossary, and the Capitularies of Charles the Bald and others added at the end in Paris, 1603, in octavo; an enlarged and improved edition appeared in the same city, 1640, in octavo. Finally, they were revised with the greatest care by Baluze, and illustrated with notes and dissertations among his Capitularia, Paris, 1677, in two volumes in folio.*

*The lengthy Capitulary containing four books—or the "Carolingian Books" <note>Libri Carolini</note> as they are commonly called—concerning the non-adoration of Images, written against the decree of Emperor Constantine VII of Constantinople and his mother Irene, and against the Second Council of Nicaea (the "Pseudo-Seventh" Ecumenical or Universal Council), issued in the year 794 at the Council of Frankfurt. It matters little whose labor Charlemagne eventually used in composing these books—whether it was Angelramnus (or Ingelramnus), or Angilbert, or what seems far more likely (also witnessed, if I am not mistaken, by Roger of Hoveden), Alcuin. It is only established that they were composed shortly before the Council of Frankfurt and issued in the name of Charlemagne while the Synod was in session; he clearly testifies in the Preface that he undertook this work out of zeal for God and a study of the truth, with the agreement of the priests of his kingdom. And indeed, Pope Hadrian (in his response to this very work given shortly after), Hincmar of Reims, the Council of Paris under Louis the Pious, the monk Althelmus, Ado of Vienne, Walafrid Strabo, and the monk of Angoulême place this fact beyond all doubt, not to call upon a long line of other witnesses. However, to avoid the blow of these books, the "defenders of image-worship" <note>original Greek: εικονοδουλιας προμαχοι (eikonodulias promachoi)</note> turn themselves into almost every shape; and although the more sensible papists, driven by the force of truth, surrender, there are those who "with bare heads" <note>original Greek: γυμνη τη κεφαλη (gymnē tē kephalē); a Greek idiom meaning shamelessly or with open audacity</note> stubbornly contend that it is not a genuine work. They have progressed to such madness that they do not blush to assert it was forged either by Karlstadt or by some other Lutheran or Calvinist, even though Jean du Tillet (himself a papist and Bishop of Meaux in France) first brought it to light from a very ancient manuscript. An ancient copy from the Vatican Library, written in elegant and old Lombardic characters, corresponded to it in every detail; not to mention that the diction and style itself sufficiently claim the book's antiquity. Against these books, Possevino fights with what is clearly a "leaden weapon" <note>an ineffective or weak argument</note>, claiming they are not by Charlemagne because Pope Hadrian wrote to Charles against them: from which it is clearly understood, he says, that those books were written by some heretic and sent by Charles to the Pope so that he might respond to them. How weak, or rather how false this is, is abundantly clear from Hadrian’s own response. Charles Cointius, a recent author of Ecclesiastical Annals, also denies the work to Charles, but he argues the case too coldly for a man otherwise most learned. The "winning" argument he uses comes down to this: that the modern books do not match well with the excerpts found in Hincmar, which he tries to show by a comparison of a single chapter; from which nothing else can be hammered out than that the same sense, with two or three different words or rather syllables of words, con-*

And who is now of such a hardened brow <note>original: "perfrictæ frontis," a Roman idiom for shamelessness</note> as to reject these books, which Noel Alexandre <note>A famous Dominican historian</note> and even Maimbourg himself <note>Louis Maimbourg, a Jesuit historian known for his defense of the papacy</note> did not dare to deny were genuine?
