<margin>772.</margin>

### HADRIAN I
A Roman by birth, born of a noble family, the son of Theodore the Consul and Duke; he was made a Regional Notary <note>A high-ranking administrative official in the Roman church</note> by Pope Paul, and a Deacon by Stephen III. After the death of Stephen, he obtained the Pontifical seat in the year 772, ordained on the 9th of February. At the beginning of his Pontificate, when he had sought peace through repeated embassies in vain from Desiderius, King of the Lombards—who had invaded the Exarchate of Ravenna and devastated the Roman territory with fire and sword—he sent legates to Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolum M."</note> in Gaul to beg for aid. He obtained this aid by sending legates again the following year. In the year 774, he received Charlemagne as he arrived in Rome with the highest submission and honor, and he obtained from him the donation of many cities to the Roman See which had been seized from Desiderius. In the year 781, he again received Charlemagne in the city of Rome and purified his son Pippin with the washing of baptism; at the same time, he anointed as kings both him and his brother Louis, who had been taken into the partnership of the kingdom by their father Charlemagne. In the year 785, when Tarasius had been elevated from a layman to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, Hadrian was asked to approve the election with letters of communion <note>formal letters acknowledging shared faith</note> given according to custom, but he refused unless Tarasius would rise up sharply against the Iconoclasts <note>Those who destroyed or opposed the use of religious images</note> and see that their heresy was condemned by a Synod. He even gave a lengthy letter to the Emperors Constantine and Irene, in which he pleaded the cause of images to the best of his ability, though with the foulest arguments <note>original: "putidissimis," suggesting the author finds the reasoning absurd or distasteful</note>, scraping together fables and nonsense from everywhere, and most shamefully distorting the testimonies of the *Holy Scriptures and the Fathers* for his own purpose. In the year 786, he gave an elaborate *Collection of 80 Canons* to Ingilram, Bishop of Metz, with which he might defend his cause against accusers. In the year 787, he threatened Tassilo, Duke of Bavaria, with the lightning bolt of excommunication unless he complied with Charlemagne. In the year 794, having sent letters to the Bishops of Spain, he condemned the errors of Elipandus of Toledo; and having given a small book to the Emperor Charlemagne, he defended the cause of the *Second Council of Nicaea* and of images. He died on the 25th of December in the year 795. There exist written by him: *18 Letters in the Councils, Volume VI, page 1762; an Epitome of Canons offered to Charlemagne at Rome in the year 774, ibid. page 1800; Chapters collected from Greek and Latin Canons and decrees of the Popes for the use of Ingilram, Bishop of Metz, ibid. page 1828; and a Letter or Responsive Book to Charlemagne on behalf of the Second Council of Nicaea, opposed to the Carolingian books, Councils, Vol. VII, page 915.* He wrote many other *Letters* lost by the injury of time, the arguments of which remain in the *Volumes of the Councils*, prefixed to the *18 Letters*.

### PAUL THE DEACON
A Lombard by race, he flourished around the year 774. Vossius, in his *On the Latin Historians*, book 2, chapter 30, narrates his birth and deeds no less succinctly than elegantly in these words:

> "Paul, the son of Warnefrid and Theodelinda, known by the
> "surname Winfrid, was a Lombard: who was first a Deacon of Aquileia,
> "and Chancellor to Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. After his king

> "of the Franks: and on account of his prudence and excellent erudition, he was
> "held in great honor for some time: but being later held more suspect, he was
> "banished to the Diomedean island <note>Now known as the Tremiti Islands</note>: from there he fled to Arichis,
> "Prince of Benevento, the son-in-law of King Desiderius. After he died,
> "Paul was made a monk of the Monastery of Cassino <note>Monte Cassino</note>."

The king <note>Charlemagne</note>, breaking out in a rage, ordered his hands to be cut off; but soon coming to himself, he said: "If we cut off his hands, where shall we find so elegant a writer?" Having survived for a long time into a good old age, he exchanged life for death—not without the highest praise for his innocence, humility, and all other virtues. It is now appropriate that we review the books written by him.

## WORKS.

*Six Books on the History of the Lombards.* These were published in print at *Augsburg* in 1515, *Basel* in 1532, and *Leiden* in 1595, in octavo. In these editions, the work ended with these words: *preserving the peace of the Franks and the Avars.* <note>original: "Francorum, Avarumque pacem custodiens"</note> However, Friedrich Lindenbrog, in the *Hamburg* edition of 1611, appended a brilliant fragment; which Freher also presents among the *Frankish Historians*, *Hanau*, 1613. Finally, they exist revised according to the authority of manuscript codices (though lacking the aforementioned fragment) at the end of the *History of the Goths* edited by Grotius, *Amsterdam*, 1655, in octavo, and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 13*, page 160.

<margin>* In the place cited.</margin>
*Twenty-four Books of Miscellaneous History.* Of these, Vossius says that the first eleven books are the same as the ten books of Eutropius <note>A 4th-century Roman historian</note>, except that Paul occasionally adds something of his own; this was done by him at the command of Adelperga, the wife of Arichis and daughter of Desiderius. From that point, Paul continues Eutropius, and the following five books are his. The remaining eight were added by Landulphus Sagax, primarily from Theophanes, or at least from Anastasius the Librarian, who translated Theophanes into Latin. They were published at *Basel* in 1569, and with variant readings by Henricus Canisius of Nijmegen at *Ingolstadt* in 1603, in octavo; with corrections and notes by Janus Gruter at *Hanau* in 1611; and with observations by Lindenbrog at *Hamburg* in 1611.

*Four Books on the Life of Pope St. Gregory.* Published by Jean Mabillon in the *Benedictine Century* I, page 385.

*The Life or Passion of St. Cyprian*, which is usually placed at the beginning of his Works.

*The Lives of Saints Benedict, Maurus, and the virgin Scholastica*, printed at *Rome* in 1590.

*Verses on the same St. Scholastica*, published by Arnold Wion in the *Tree of Life* <note>original: "Ligno Vitæ"</note> on the 10th of February.

*Certain Excerpts on the first Bishops of Metz*, written at the request of Bishop Angilramnus; published by Marquard Freher among the *Frankish Historians* and by André Duchesne among the *Contemporary Historians*, Volume II. They are also found in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XIII*, page 329.

*The Life of St. Arnulf, Bishop of Metz*, found among the Works of Bede and in Surius on the day of August 24th.

*A Hymn in honor of St. John the Baptist*, which begins, *So that [your servants] may with loosened [voices]* <note>original: "Ut queant laxis." This famous hymn is the source of the musical syllables Ut (Do), Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La.</note>, still commonly sung in the Roman Church today.

*Certain Fragments of Letters* in Baluze’s *Miscellany, Volume I*, page 362.

*A Homiliary, or Homilies, Lessons, and Postils* <note>Short commentaries on scripture</note>, suitable for every feast of the entire year, distributed into two volumes, taken from the works of Saints Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Origen, Leo, Gregory, Maximus, Bede, and others. This Homiliary was published at *Speyer* in 1482, in folio; at *Cologne* in 1517 and 1539; and at *Paris* in 1535 and 1569, in folio. Certain other small works by our Paul, still unpublished, are preserved today in the library of Monte Cassino; regarding these, see what J. B. Marus has in his notes to Peter the Deacon, chapter 8.

Furthermore, there was another Paul the Deacon, distinct from our own, who belonged to the Church of Naples. He translated the *Life of Saint Mary of Egypt*—originally written in Greek by Sophronius, the Bishop of Jerusalem—into Latin. This version, including a Preface to the Emperor Charlemagne, can be found in the works of Laurentius Surius <note>A 16th-century hagiographer</note> under the date of April 9th. In that preface, Paul testifies that he translated certain other works which are now lost.

<margin>776.</margin>
**PAULINUS**, of the Austrian nation according to some, was a master of the grammatical arts. On account of his distinguished erudition, he was gifted with various estates and possessions by the Emperor Charlemagne in the year 776; and at the end of that same year, he was elevated to the Patriarchate of Aquileia (also known as Friuli). In the year 793, he published a short book on the Holy Trinity called the *Sacrosyllabus* <note>meaning "The Sacred Collection of Words"</note> against the heretical letters of Elipandus of Toledo <note>Elipandus was a leader of the Adoptionist heresy, which claimed Christ was the "adopted" rather than natural son of God</note>. In the year 794, he was present at the Council of Frankfurt, where he opposed Elipandus and Felix; and having held a Synod at Friuli in the following year, he condemned them both. In the year 797, Alcuin requested from Emperor Charlemagne that Paulinus be given to him as an assistant to oppose the writings and heresy of Felix of Urgel. This was done: and Paulinus, advised by the Emperor, wrote and published three books against Felix in the year 798. In the year 803, moved by the brutal death of John, the Patriarch of Grado—who had been thrown headlong from a very high tower by John, the Duke of the Venetians—he celebrated the Council of Altinum. From this council, he sent letters to the Emperor Charlemagne, seeking that such a horrendous crime be restrained with worthy punishment. He died in the year 804, on the 11th of January.

**FLACCUS ALCUIN**, also known as **ALBINUS**, was of the English nation. He was born in the region of York according to some, or not far from London according to others. He was first a disciple of Bede, and then of Egbert of York. He was a Deacon of the Church of York and Abbot of the Monastery of Canterbury. He became famous in the year 780. In 793, he was summoned by Charlemagne to assist him in opposing the heresy of Felix of Urgel and the canons of the "False Synod" of Nicaea <note>referring to the Second Council of Nicaea regarding the use of icons</note>; he crossed the sea to Gaul, and having been received into the closest friendship with Charlemagne, he was appointed head of the Palace School. In the following year, he accompanied Charlemagne to the Council of Frankfurt, and by Canon 56, having been commended to the Synod by the King, he was admitted into the fellowship and friendship of the Fathers. <margin>8th CENTURY from the Year 700.</margin>
...the Emperor <note>original: "peratore"</note> with frequent and earnest prayers, seeking permission to bid farewell to secular affairs, he at first met with a refusal; nevertheless, he was granted the governorship of the Monasteries of Saint Martin <note>at Tours</note> and Cormery. In the year 798, he took up his pen against Felix of Urgell <note>A Spanish bishop and leader of the Adoptionist heresy</note>, whom he had previously addressed many times with kind letters but to no effect, and he refuted his errors in seven books. In the year 799, when invited by Charles <note>Charlemagne</note> to undertake a journey to Rome with him, he pleaded for excuse, citing his infirmities and old age. In the year 801, having congratulated Charles upon his return from Italy, he finally obtained his desired end through his oft-repeated prayers and secured his dismissal from the court and from secular business. Having been granted his discharge <note>term: "Rudi donatus" — a reference to the wooden sword given to Roman gladiators upon their retirement</note>, he withdrew to his Monastery of Saint Martin at Tours, and spent the remainder of his life in honorable leisure, devoted to the instruction of students in the literary arts at the school he founded at Tours. He was several times recalled to the court by letters from the Emperor, but in vain. He died at Tours, not in the year 790 as Pits <note>John Pits, an English biographer</note> incorrectly states, but in 804, on the 14th day before the Kalends of June <note>May 19th</note>, on the very day of Pentecost. He was a man everywhere known for being pious, learned, and grave; and as Bale <note>John Bale, a 16th-century historian</note> rightly says of him <margin>* Century 2, chapter 17.</margin>, he was indeed the most learned of all Englishmen from the beginning after Bede and Aldhelm, being skilled in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. Whatever deeper learning or more polished literature France displayed in that and the following centuries must be credited entirely to him. The Academies of Paris, Tours, Fulda, Soissons, and many others owe their origin and growth to him; for if he did not preside over them in person or lay their very foundations, he at least lit the way with his teaching, led by example, and increased them through the favors he obtained from Charles.

*Letter of Elipandus to Felix, recently converted.* <note>original: "Epistola Elipandi ad Felicem nuper conversum"</note> This man <note>Felix, Bishop of Urgell</note> abjured his heresy in the Synod of Aachen at the end of the year 799; however, having been deposed from his see, he was relegated to perpetual exile at Lyon. He did this somewhat later, and Elipandus himself, having been convinced by Alcuin’s books, died piously in the year 808. <note>Elipandus of Toledo and Felix of Urgell were the primary proponents of Adoptionism, the belief that Christ was the son of God only by adoption.</note>

*Confession of Faith by Felix, Bishop of the See of Urgell, sent to the Clergy and People of Urgell after renouncing his heresy in the Synod of Aachen.*

*Letter to a most dear Daughter in Christ.*

*Book on Divine Offices, or an exposition of the Roman Order.* <note>original: "De divinis Officiis liber, sive expositio Romani Ordinis"</note> This is held under Alcuin’s name among other writers on the same subject and has been frequently published; however, in Du-Chesne's edition of Alcuin’s works, it was increased by twelve entire chapters. It is certain beyond a doubt, however, that it is not by Alcuin and was written after the year 1000.

*Letter on the reasoning of Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima.* <note>These are the names for the three Sundays preceding the start of Lent.</note>

*Letter to the Priest Odwin on the ceremonies of Baptism.*

*Another Letter on the same ceremonies*, which Sirmond <note>Jacques Sirmond, a Jesuit scholar</note> rightly judges not to be by Alcuin; for it belongs to Amalarius of Trier.

*Letter to the boys of Saint Martin on the Confession of sins.* <note>Saint Martin refers to the monastery at Tours where Alcuin was Abbot.</note>

*Book of Sacraments.* Published in Cologne, 1571.

*Three Homilies. 1. On Silence, in which the incarnate Word was sent. 2. On the Nativity of the Blessed Mary. 3. On the Feast of All Saints.* These are spurious, taken from the collection of sermons by Paul the Deacon. The third holds the 37th place among the sermons of Augustine "On the Saints."

*The Life of the Antichrist, addressed to Charlemagne.*

*Book on Virtues and Vices, addressed to Count Wido.*

*An incomplete book on the seven Arts*, <note>Referring to the Seven Liberal Arts: Grammar, Rhetoric, Dialectic, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note> of which only two chapters remain, namely on Grammar and Rhetoric, with a transition to Dialectic.

*Grammar.* Published separately in Hanau, 1605.

*Dialogue on Rhetoric and the Virtues.* Published in Paris, 1599, in quarto.

*Dialectic, with Charlemagne and Alcuin as speakers.* Published together with the Grammar, Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto.

*A Royal Disputation between the most noble youth Pepin (afterward King of Italy) and Albinus the Scholar.* <note>Albinus was the scholarly name Alcuin used at court.</note>

*Sermon on the Passing of Saint Martin.*

*Life of Saint Vedast, Bishop of Arras*, written in the year 795.

*Life of the most blessed Priest Richarius.* It is found in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a hagiographer</note> under April 26th.

*Two books on the Life of Saint Willibrord, Bishop of Utrecht*; one composed in prose, the other in verse, with a Homily on the same and an Elegiac poem. These are found in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Centuries*, Volume 3, part 1, page 601, and in Surius under November 7th.

*115 Letters*, 67 of which are found in Canisius.

*Poems and Verses concerning several Saints.*

*Other Verses collected from various places, which with the former make 272 Poems.* These works of Alcuin listed above were published by the care of André Du Chesne <note>original: "Andreæ Quercetani"</note>, Paris 1617, in folio.

*The four Caroline Books on Images*; Roger of Hoveden <note>A 12th-century English chronicler</note> records that Alcuin wrote these under the name of Charles; we have dealt with them extensively under Charlemagne, whose name they bear as author, and therefore they are not found among Alcuin’s works.

*Confession of Faith, or a small collection of excerpts collected from the writings of Augustine and other Fathers, and divided into four parts; it was published under Alcuin’s name by Chifflet in Dijon, 1654, in quarto*, among other short works by different authors. The most learned Daillé <note>Jean Daillé, a Huguenot minister</note> attempted to prove this Confession was a work falsely attributed to Alcuin in a posthumous treatise published in Rouen in the year 1675. Jean Mabillon strives no less extensively to claim it for Alcuin in a long dissertation found in his *Analecta*, Volume 1, page 178, etc. Let the truth stand between both parties; let the learned judge. I would wish it noted, however, that Mabillon quite candidly admits that he has not so much settled the matter as rendered it probable.

*A short Commentary on the Song of Songs*, published by Patrick Young <note>original: "Patricio Junio"</note> with the Commentary of Gilbert Foliot, London 1638, in quarto.

<margin>783. See Juan de Mariana, *History of Spain*, Book 7, Ch. 8, p. 408.</margin>
ETHERIUS (or HETERIUS), Bishop of Osma in Spain, and BEATUS, a Priest in the province of Asturias—inferior in rank, yet greater in learning and zeal for the faith—flourished around the year 783. At this time, they began to fiercely oppose the heresy of Elipandus of Toledo <note>Adoptionism, which claimed Christ was only the "adopted" son of God in his humanity</note> which was then sprouting in Spain. They were then accused by Elipandus, in letters sent to Abbot Fidelis, of arrogance, pride, and even heresy on that account. However, such a false accusation in no way stopped Etherius and Beatus from pressing on with the work they had begun. When they realized they could not call Elipandus back to a sound mind by any warnings, they published a proper volume divided into two books, in which they refuted the errors of Elipandus and defended the Catholic faith. These books exist, titled *On the Adoption of Christ the Son of God*, first published by Peter Stevart from the Toledo Library in the *Canisian Supplement*, Ingolstadt, 1604, page 17; and later included in Volume 13 of the *Library of the Fathers*, page 353. A fragment of some book written by Etherius and Beatus against Folmarus is also held in the said Stevart supplement, page 243.

<margin>785. Life of Tarasius by Ignatius the Deacon, found in Surius and Bolland, February 25.</margin>
TARASIUS, a native of Constantinople born of an illustrious family, the son of George the Prefect of the City and Encrantia, and the great-uncle of Photius. Admitted to the court, he was the Emperor’s secretary until the year 785 (or the end of 784). After the Patriarch Paul, a most holy man, was ousted by Irene Augusta <note>Empress Irene (r. 797–802), who favored the restoration of icons</note>—the most wicked of women—Tarasius was substituted from the rank of layman onto the Throne of Constantinople. Pretending a piety and zeal for religion, he feigned that he did not wish to take up that dignity unless icons were restored and an ecumenical synod were called for that purpose. Therefore, a synod was called for the year 786, and the stage was meanwhile prepared by Tarasius through both force and flattery. It began in the year 786, on the first of July, in Constantino... <note>The word is cut off and continues on the next page as "Constantinople."</note>

...at the Synod of Constantinople, since he feared that the Bishops who were opponents of <term>Iconodulia</term> <note>The veneration of sacred images</note> would prevail, he saw to it that a riot was stirred up. Under that pretext, he managed to have the Synod postponed until the following year and transferred to the city of Nicaea. The following year, with affairs arranged according to his wishes, he began the Council of Nicaea on September 24th <note>original: "VIII. Cal. Octobr."</note>. In the year 795, he courageously resisted for some time when Emperor Constantine [VI] intended to repudiate his lawful wife, the Empress Maria, and take his mistress Theodote as his wife, threatening excommunication unless he desisted from the crime he had begun. Soon, however, failing shamefully in his resolve, he permitted the wicked nuptials to be consecrated by Joseph, the Abbot of Constantinople, and allowed Maria to be tonsured and shut away in a monastery. He died on February 25th in the year 806. His surviving writings include an *Encyclical Letter to the Eastern Patriarchs* sent immediately after he undertook the Episcopacy (published in Greek and Latin in the *Councils*, Volume 7, page 161); a *Second Letter to Pope Hadrian* (Greek and Latin, ibid. page 624); a *Letter to John the Anchorite* (Greek and Latin, ibid. page 637); an *Apologetic speech delivered to the people* on the day he was elected to the dignity of the Patriarchate (Greek and Latin, ibid. page 33); and a *Sermon on the Blessed Virgin*, <unclear>to be contained in the temple</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ ναῷ περιέχεσθαι</unclear>, which begins, <unclear>“Bright is our festival, or rather the festival of the heavens.”</unclear> <note>original Greek: Φαιδρὰ ἡ παρ᾽ ἡμῖν ἢ παρ᾽ οὐρανοῖς πανήγυρις</note>. ### THEOPHANES

<margin>
792.
Life of Theophanes in Surius & Henschenius.
March 12.
Greek Menologion on the same day.
</margin>
**THEOPHANES**, called Isaacius after his father, and the "Confessor" because of the evils he suffered, was a native of Constantinople. The son of Isaacius, governor of the Aegean Islands, and Theodota, he was born in the year 758. After his father was taken from the living, he received the Emperor Constantine Copronymus as his guardian. While still a young man, he was compelled by the Imperial authority to marry the daughter of Leo the Patrician; however, on the very day of the wedding, he entered into a singular pact with his wife regarding the mutual observance of continence <note>This refers to a "chaste marriage," where the couple remains celibate for religious purposes</note>. Called to the court by Emperor Leo [IV], he served in the office of <term>Strator</term> <note>originally an official in charge of the stables, but by this time an honorary court title</note>; and being sent to the fortress of Cyzicus, he took charge of public buildings near Sigriana in Lesser Mysia. Upon returning to Constantinople, he was admitted into the rank of the <term>Spatharii</term> <note>literally "sword-bearers," a class of high-ranking Imperial dignitaries</note>. In the year 780, after his wife was sent away to a monastery on the Prince’s Island near Constantinople, he himself sought out the Polychronium Monastery near Sigriana, and from then on cultivated the monastic life. From Polychronium, he departed for the island of Calonymus, where he spent six years after converting his father’s estate into a monastery. Returning then to the region of Sigriana, he acquired an estate which was called "The Field" (*Ager*), and having built a monastery, he himself took on the role of Abbot. In the year 787, summoned to the Council of Nicaea, he strenuously defended the cause of <term>Iconodulia</term> <note>the veneration of sacred images</note>. After the year 813, he was ordered by Leo the Armenian to condemn the worship of images; steadily refusing, he was brought to Constantinople in chains, even though he had been ill and bedridden since the year 808. When he could be conquered by no arguments to abandon the veneration of images, he was cast into prison in the year 815 (or the beginning of the next), and after two years was banished to the island of Samothrace. There, after twenty-three days had passed, broken by hardships and miseries, he met his final day. He obtained the title of "Confessor" and the honors of a Saint after death from the followers of Iconodulia. He wrote a *Chronography*, which encompasses the ecclesiastical and civil deeds performed in the Empire of Constantinople arranged according to a series of years, from the first year of the Emperor Diocletian (285 AD) to the first year of Leo the Armenian (813 AD). In this work, it should be noted that Theophanes employs the Alexandrian chronology, which, in calculating the years of the Christian Era, falls eight years short of the calculation accepted among the Latins. Almost everything that Anastasius the Librarian contains in his history from the year 285 to 813 was also translated into Latin from this work. Theophanes composed this *Chronography* in a concise style, but one that is quite rough and common; the illustrious Goar frequently noted entirely useless repetitions, transpositions of events, contradictory narrations, and foul errors in the arrangement of dates. Prefixed to the part of the history arranged by years are Chronological Tables, divided by cells—that is, the years of the World, of Christ, of the Emperors, of the five Patriarchs, and so on. It is clearly evident to anyone inspecting them that these were written most erroneously: they are often prefixed to the wrong years, many cells are left blank, and they teem with monstrous calculations, especially regarding the years of the Patriarchs. For this reason, Henschenius <margin>* Chapter 1, Section 4.</margin> and Papebrochius suspect that they did not originate from Theophanes himself but rather from another hand in their *Exegesis on the Chronography of Theophanes*, which they placed before the third volume of the *Acts of the Saints* for March. The complete *Chronography of Theophanes* was published in Greek and Latin with notes by Jacques Goar and François Combefis in Paris, 1655, in folio. There also exists his *Triumphal Hymn* for the first Sunday of Lent, consisting of nine Odes, in the Greek *Triodion*, and in Baronius in Greek and Latin among the *Ecclesiastical Annals* at the year 842.

### THEODULPHUS

<margin>
794.
Life by Sirmond.
Notes by Le Cointe at years 781, 786, 796, etc.
</margin>
**THEODULPHUS**, Italian by birth, born among the Cisalpine Gauls <note>Northern Italy</note>, was first the Abbot of Fleury and a dear friend of Charlemagne, by whom he was promoted to the see of Orléans around the year 794 or shortly before. Under Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, he flourished in great favor at the court, being sent by Louis to honorably receive Pope Stephen [IV] when he arrived in Gaul in the year 816. <margin>795.</margin>
**LEO III.** A Roman by birth and the son of Asuppius, he was a Priest of the Roman Church and was finally ordained Pope on December 27, 795. In 796, he sent the keys of St. Peter and the Banner of the City of Rome to Charlemagne as symbols of his submission. In 799, he began to be harassed by the envious nephews of the late Pope Hadrian with false slanders and, soon after, physical injuries. In the middle of the city, in full view of all the people, he was seized, beaten with fists and clubs, and thrown into prison. I pass over the most foul fables about his eyes being plucked out and his tongue cut off—and both being divinely restored—which Anastasius and his followers (those purveyors of trifles) chatter about. <note>The author is skeptical of the miraculous accounts of Leo's recovery found in the "Liber Pontificalis" attributed to Anastasius the Librarian.</note> Rescued from prison by the Roman people, he traveled to Charlemagne in Gaul to seek protection and patronage. Envoys sent by Charlemagne to Rome brought Leo back to Italy; after examining the case, they cleared him of the charges and restored him to his see, while the seditious clerics were disciplined and punished with exile. Some scholars move this judgment to the year 800 and claim it was performed by Charlemagne himself while present in Rome. For in the year 800, Charlemagne came to Rome and, having held a Synod, either judged Leo's cause (which had remained untouched until then) or confirmed the judgment previously made by the envoys. At the end of that year, by the order of the Roman people, Leo crowned Charlemagne as Emperor. In 804, Leo traveled again to meet Emperor Charlemagne in Germany. In 809, he raised a dispute with the Spanish bishops because they had added the word *Filioque* <note>Latin for "and from the Son," referring to the Holy Spirit's origin</note> to the Nicene Creed, forbidding it to be sung openly in the churches. To transmit a lasting monument of his judgment to posterity, he had two silver tablets affixed in the Basilica of St. Peter, on one of which the Creed was written in Latin and on the other in Greek, without the addition of that word *Filioque*. He died on June 11, 816. *Thirteen Letters* survive in the *Council Collection, Vol. VII, p. 1111.*

Therefore, in the year 800, Charlemagne sent Leidradus to Spain again, along with several co-workers, to preach sound doctrine to the Christians who had been led astray by Felix's error. **JESSE**, also known as Jesseus or Jesse, was made Bishop of Amiens in the year 799: and in that same year he was appointed by Charlemagne as a companion to Pope Leo III upon his return to Italy, so that he might investigate the Pope's cause and take action against the rebellious Romans. In the year 802, he was sent by Emperor Charlemagne to Constantinople to enter into a peace treaty with the Empress Irene. The following year, having returned from the East, he led the legates of Emperor Nicephorus, who were his traveling companions, to Charlemagne at Mainz. Around the year 808, having been sent to Italy by Charlemagne to manage affairs, he incurred the enmity of Pope Leo. In the year 811, he was present as a witness to Charlemagne’s Will. In the year 812, he published a **Response** to the circular letters of Charlemagne regarding the ceremonies of Baptism. He took part in the Council of Noyon in 814, and the Council of Paris in 829. In the year 830, he followed the camp of Lothair <note>Lothair I, son of Louis the Pious</note> against the Emperor Louis: for this reason, he was soon rightfully deposed at the Assembly of Nijmegen. Three years later, having been restored by force by Lothair, he was driven out again in the year 834, and joined Lothair as a companion as he fled to Italy. He died in the year 836. There exists a **fairly long Letter to the Priests and people of his Diocese on the Exposition of the church rites, especially those used in Baptism**, which Jean Cordes published with the works of Hincmar (Paris, 1615, in quarto, p. 664); and from there it was included in the *Library of the Fathers, Vol. XIV, p. 67.*

**DACRIANUS**, an Abbot of the Benedictine Order, is assigned to this eighth Century by Marguerin de la Bigne in the Chronological Index which he placed at the beginning of his edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. There exist under his name the *Mirror of Monks* and *Documents of the Spiritual Life* in the *Library of the Fathers, Cologne edition, Vol. VIII*. However, Théophile Raynaud argues * that no such writer exists, nor was there ever an "Abbot Dacrianus" in the nature of things; and that the true author of these small works is none other than Louis de Blois <note>also known as Ludovicus Blosius</note>, Abbot of Liessies, who (as Possevino notes †) died in the year 1566. He named himself "Dacrianus"—that is, the one groaning and weeping <note>Derived from the Greek "dakry," meaning a tear</note>—so that he might restore the collapsed morals of those he wished to properly instruct with less resentment. It is perhaps for this reason that this writer does not appear in the most recent edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. We retain him here for this reason alone: so that when students find him mentioned in De la Bigne and others, they do not search for him in our work in vain.

# THE PHOTIAN CENTURY.

### Overview of the Century.

<margin>
9TH CENTURY from the Year 800.
</margin>

<margin>
...young people were educated in the finer letters. Of this kind were the *Italian* Monasteries, such as Monte Cassino and Farfa; the *German* ones, Fulda, St. Gall, Reichenau, and Lobbes; the *French*, Corbie, Reims, Orbais, and Fleury; and the *English*, St. Albans, Malmesbury, Worcester, Westminster, Glastonbury, etc. Regarding the state of the Church, the veneration of Images in the Eastern Church was again abolished by Leo the Armenian in the year 814 and by Theophilus Augustus in 830, but was restored by Michael III in 842. In the West, it was also condemned by synods, to say nothing of the views of Agobard, Claudius of Turin, and others. In the year 824, Emperor Michael the Stammerer <note>Michael II, "the Balbus"</note> of Constantinople sent legates to Louis the Pious, along with letters in which he explicitly condemned all veneration of images and "mad superstition." On this occasion, a synod of the more famous bishops of all Gaul was assembled in the Royal Palace at Paris; in this meeting, the most learned and holy prelates, having first rejected the Iconoclasts <term>Iconoclasts: those who destroy religious images</term> and tolerated the historical use of paintings, condemned those who, with undue superstitious worship, honor them, adore them, call them holy, and claim to attain holiness through them. They responded at length with arguments to the contrary, all of which they explicitly proved by bringing forth testimonies from the ancient Fathers and Councils. The Acts of this synod were published from the library of Pierre Pithou and inserted by Melchior Goldast in his book on the worship of images, p. 623. However, the "Photian cause" eventually pushed aside and almost absorbed all other controversies. In the year 858, after Ignatius was ejected, Photius was elevated to the Patriarchate of Constantinople; this was confirmed by the synod which the Greeks call Ecumenical, assembled at Constantinople in 861. In the year 869, after Photius was deposed, Ignatius was restored by the synod commonly called the *Eighth*. When Ignatius finally died, Photius was restored to his see, and he convened a synod of 183 bishops, which the Greeks maintain was the *Eighth Ecumenical Council*, in which everything was decided in favor of Photius. The Roman Pontiffs involved themselves no small amount in these disturbances of the Eastern Church, sometimes favoring the cause of Photius, but most often that of Ignatius, railing against Photius until they were hoarse. From this arose an incurable dissent between the Eastern and Western Churches, born primarily from three causes—to say nothing of the various rituals and ceremonies of each. I. From the habitual desire for dominance of the Roman Pontiffs, who wanted the Eastern Church to sail in the wake of the Roman See's prerogative, which Photius and his successors obstinately and constantly denied. II. From the addition made by the Latins to the Creed concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit with the word *FILIOQUE* <gloss>and from the Son</gloss>, which was condemned by the Greeks. Photius objects to this in his encyclical letter, p. 51, "as the crown of all evils" <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ κακῶν κορωνίδα</note>, and charges that they had the supreme audacity to adulterate the Holy and Sacred Creed—confirmed by the votes of all the Ecumenical Councils—"with spurious reasonings and interpolated words" <note>original Greek: νόθοις λογισμοῖς καὶ παρεγγράπτοις λόγοις</note>.
</margin>

Literacy and learning flourished more and more in this age under the auspices of Charlemagne <note>Carolus Magnus</note>, at the urging and promotion of Alcuin the Englishman, Charlemagne’s tutor, by whose advice the Academies of Paris, Pavia, Bologna, and Osnabrück were established. Closely following these were the colleges of Canons, and in many monasteries, even more famous schools of the liberal arts, in which young...

The Roman Pontiffs involved themselves in these turmoils of the Eastern Church to no small degree—sometimes favoring Photius's cause, but mostly supporting Ignatius, raging against Photius even to the point of exhaustion. From this arose an incurable dissension between the Eastern and Western Churches, born chiefly from three causes (to say nothing of the various rites and ceremonies of each). 
I. From the habitual lust for power of the Roman Pontiffs, who wanted the Eastern Church to be subservient to the prerogative of the Roman See—which Photius and his successors stubbornly and constantly denied. 
II. From the addition made by the Latins to the Creed regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit in the word **FILIOQUE** <term>Filioque: "and the Son," a phrase added to the Nicene Creed by the Western Church but rejected by the East</term>, which was condemned by the Greeks. # The Photian Century

<margin>9th CENTURY, from the Year 800.</margin>
...they were attempting to corrupt [the faith], *“Oh, what wicked schemes!”* <note>original Greek: ὢ τῶν πονηρῶν μηχανημάτων</note> Oh, Devilish Machinations! etc., where he most sharply attacks the Latins at length for this reason.

Indeed, he attacked the matter itself in more than one published book. This arose from the case of the **Bulgarians**, whom **Pope Nicholas** wished to assert under Papal jurisdiction, while **Photius** protested and the Greeks contended that Bulgaria had been part of the Eastern Empire, that the nation was first converted by Greek priests, and that it had voluntarily submitted to the Patriarchate of Constantinople. It is well enough known to those not entirely ignorant of the history of this century how much turmoil this Bulgarian controversy stirred up. From this, concord was subsequently broken entirely, and a **Schism** <note>The "Photian Schism," a precursor to the Great Schism of 1054 between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches</note> was born that perhaps no century will ever extinguish. At the beginning of this century, a certain power over the city of Rome and the Pope remained with the Emperor; however, as time gradually progressed, this power became weaker, until finally under **Pope John IX** <note>Though the text says John IX (r. 898–900), the date 875 and the reference to Charles the Bald suggest the author may have intended Pope John VIII</note>, around the year 875, the yoke was almost entirely shaken off, as **Charles the Bald** transferred the Imperial rights over Rome and its territories to the Pope. Moreover, from then on, the Popes claimed for themselves the right to choose the Emperor.

In this age, the controversy regarding the supernatural change made in the **Eucharist** began to seethe. The first who dared to publicly propose and boldly defend a fleshly and physical presence of Christ in the Sacrament was **Paschasius Radbertus of Corbie**, who did not blush to assert in a published booklet that, after the consecration is performed, the substance of bread and wine is changed into the true flesh of Christ and His true blood—namely, that very same flesh which the Lord took from the womb of the Virgin, and in which He suffered and rose again. **Rabanus Maurus**, **Bertram** (also known as **Ratramnus of Corbie**), and **Johannes Scotus Eriugena** immediately opposed him, to say nothing of others.

</margin>
**Benedict**, a Frenchman by birth, was born in Septimania <note>A historical region in southern France, roughly equivalent to modern Languedoc-Roussillon</note> in the year 751. He was of Gothic origin, the son of the Count of Maguelonne, and was educated in the court of King Pepin the Short, where he held the office of **Cupbearer** <note>A high-ranking position of trust in a royal household</note>. He also served for some time as a soldier under Charlemagne, until in the year 774, he abandoned secular life and withdrew to the Monastery of Saint-Seine in Burgundy. He was appointed the monastery’s **Cellarer** <note>The officer in charge of a monastery's food, drink, and worldly stores</note> in 777. To avoid being elected Abbot, he returned to Septimania in 780 and established a small cell for himself near the Aniane River, where he lived for several years in great poverty. After the year 793, he fiercely opposed the heresy of Felix of Urgell <note>Felix of Urgell was a leader of Adoptionism, the belief that Christ was the son of God only by adoption</note> which was spreading in Septimania. In 797, he built the Monastery of Saint Savior near the Aniane River and, once it was completed, he presided over it as Abbot. In 799, he was sent as an envoy by Charlemagne, along with Leidrad of Lyon, to Spain to recall Felix from his errors; he returned to those same places the following year with Leidrad to preach sound doctrine to the people. At the beginning of the ninth century—the period in which he was most prominent—he was the leader and guide for the founding and reform of many monasteries. He personally governed many of them in succession. After ruling eleven monasteries, which would be tedious to list, he finally took charge of the Abbey of Inde <note>Also known as Kornelimünster Abbey, near Aachen</note> in 814. He died there at the age of seventy on February 11, 821.

->WORKS<-

*The **Codex of Rules** <note>original: "Codex Regularum"</note>, which the Holy Fathers prescribed to be observed by Monks and Holy Virgins, divided into three parts. The first part comprises the Rules for Monks from the Eastern Fathers: Anthony, Isaiah, Serapion, Macarius, etc. The second comprises the Rules for the same from the Western Fathers: Benedict, Caesarius, Ferreolus, Columban, etc. The third comprises the Rules for Virgins from the Holy Fathers: Augustine, Caesarius, Aurelian, Leander, etc. Lucas Holstenius first brought this Codex to light with added notes in Rome, 1661; it was reprinted soon after in Paris, 1664, in quarto.*

*The **Harmony of Rules** <note>original: "Concordia Regularum"</note>, in which the Rule of Saint Benedict is compared with twenty-five Rules of other Fathers. Hugh Ménard published it in Paris, 1638.*

*A **Book composed of Exhortatory Sermons of the Holy Fathers to Monks** <note>original: "Liber ex SS. Patrum Sermonibus Paræneticis ad Monachos"</note>, which Holstenius published as an appendix following the Codex of Rules.*

*A **System of Various Penances** <note>original: "Modus diversarum Pœnitentiarum"</note> organized by our Benedict from the Rule of Saint Benedict of Cassino, published by Baluze at the end of the Carolingian Capitularies, and thereafter in Cointius's Annals at the year 821, number 36.*

*A **Letter to Abbot George of Aniane**, and another to Nebridius, Archbishop of Narbonne, which are found in Ardo’s "Life of Benedict."*

<margin>801.</margin>
## NICEPHORUS, Chartophylax, flourished perhaps around the year 801.

His exact dates are quite uncertain. Having been consulted by a certain monk named Theodosius, a recluse in Corinth, concerning difficult questions or cases of conscience, he wrote to him two *Letters of Solutions*. These survive in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law, Book V, page 341*; and in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XII*. A fragment is also found in Latin in the *Orthodoxographis, page 74*. This fragment of a certain letter from our Nicephorus to the same Theodosius seems to have served as a preface, either to the two mentioned letters or to another letter on the same subject that is now lost.

# The Photian Century

<margin>
9th CENTURY, from the Year 800.
802.
Life in Surius, March 26. Crantz, *Metropolis of the Saxons*, book 1, chapter 5, page 12.
</margin>
**LIUDGER**, the son of Thiadgrim and Liafburga, was born at Wierum near Dokkum in Nearer Frisia <note>A coastal region spanning the modern Netherlands and Germany</note>. Sent to Utrecht while still a boy, he was fortunate to have the Priest Gregory as his teacher. In the year 760, he took the monastic habit in the Monastery of Utrecht. In 767, traveling to England, he was ordained a Deacon by Ethelbert, the Archbishop of York. After a year, he returned to Utrecht; and in 769, he returned to England to study under Alcuin <note>A famous scholar and advisor to Charlemagne</note>. In 773, leaving York, he returned again to the Monastery of Utrecht. In 777, he was ordained a Priest by Albric, Bishop of Utrecht, and was placed in charge of the Church in the district of Oftergo, where Boniface <note>The "Apostle of the Germans" who was martyred in 754</note> had been crowned with martyrdom; meanwhile, he was chosen for the four-part government of the Monastery of Utrecht according to the four seasons of the year. In 784, driven out of Oftergo by the cruelty of Wittekind, Duke of the Frisians, he set out for Rome, and from there retired to the Monastery of Monte Cassino. In 787, with Wittekind now converted to the faith, he was sent back to Frisia by Charlemagne, and in 796 he founded the Monastery of Werden, where he himself presided as Abbot. In 802, he was made Bishop of Münster <note>Original: Mimigardevordensis</note> and Abbot of Leuze <note>Original: Lutofæ</note> by Charlemagne. He died on March 26, 809. He wrote the *Life of his Teacher, St. Gregory*, Bishop of Utrecht, which was edited by Christopher Brower (Mainz, 1615) and is found in Surius under August 25, and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Centuries*, Part 3, vol. 2, page 319. He also wrote a *Letter* to Rixfrid, Bishop of Utrecht, concerning the *Life and Miracles of St. Suitbert*, which appears in Surius and Bollandus under the Calends of March. However, that Letter is judged not to be by Liudger based on several arguments by Charles Cointe in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* at the years 779 (num. 31), 749 (num. 52), and 754 (num. 78); the reader who desires more should consult him.

<margin>
806.
*Life of Nicephorus* written by Ignatius the Deacon. Greek and Latin in Henschenius under March 13. Compare Hanckius on Byzantine Writers, page 223.
</margin>
**NICEPHORUS**, a native of Constantinople, was the son of Theodore (a notary to Constantine Copronymus <note>Emperor Constantine V, an intense Iconoclast; the name "Copronymus" or "Dung-named" was a derogatory nickname given by his religious enemies</note> who was twice driven into exile for his devotion to images) and Eudocia. Having received from nature a sublime intellect capable of great things, he cultivated it diligently with every kind of discipline. Consequently, he served as secretary to Emperor Constantine and his mother Irene; and in 787, at the second Council of Nicaea, he strenuously promoted the veneration of images. However, growing weary of court life, he retired to a monastic lifestyle in a certain monastery situated in the region of the Thracian Bosphorus. Finally, in 806, upon the death of Tarasius, he himself was raised to the height of Patriarchal dignity on April 12. In 811, he sent letters to Pope Leo III in accordance with church custom; a custom which Emperor Nicephorus suppressed as long as he lived. At the end of 814, Leo the Armenian prohibited the cult of images by public edict. Patriarch Nicephorus resisted Leo in this matter as much as he was able; when the Emperor could bend him by no warnings or advice, he deposed him from the Patriarchal see on March 13 of the following year and drove him into exile. First, he went to the monastery he himself had founded and called *The Good*; soon he was deported to another monastery, likewise built by him, on the island of Proconnesus in the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>. There he remained hidden until his final day, which occurred on June 2, 828, although the Latins usually celebrate his memory on March 13. Regarding his style, here is the judgment of Photius <note>A later Patriarch of Constantinople and famous literary critic</note>: 
<margin>* Code 66.</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἔστι δὲ ἡ φράσις ἀπέριττός τε καὶ σαφής...</note> "His style is unadorned and clear; in its choice of words and composition of speech, it is neither loose nor, on the other hand, too compressed, but flows smoothly. It is the kind of style a truly rhetorical and perfect man would use. For he avoids modern innovations and does not overlook the ancient and refined style. Furthermore, a certain pleasantness combined with grace seasons his words." <note>The translation continues, blending Photius's critique and the Latin commentary:</note> *His style has nothing superfluous or obscure; he used a careful selection of words and a composition of speech that was neither too relaxed nor too restricted, but such as any orator, even the most accomplished, would employ. For he avoids recently invented words, yet does not pass over those approved by antiquity. A certain sweetness still wins him favor in his speaking. Finally, Photius adds that he obscures most who preceded him by surpassing them in the writing of history, except that in his excessive brevity he does not seem to have fulfilled all the parts of elegance.*

# The Photian Century

<margin>
9th CENTURY, from the Year 800.
</margin>

### WRITINGS

**A Brief History**, tracing events from the murder of Emperor Maurice <note>Reigned 582–602 AD</note> down to the year 769. Dionysius Petavius first brought this to light and published it with his own translation and notes in Greek and Latin (*Paris, 1616, octavo*). He also added a **Fragment on the Life and Death of Constantine Copronymus** <note>Emperor Constantine V, a fierce opponent of religious icons</note>, which he found in the Greek-Latin manuscript of Cardinal Joyse. Although the style of this fragment appears different from the style of the *Brief History*, it may still be considered a <note>original: Ἀπόσπασμάτιον</note> "small fragment" of another work by the same author. Both works were published again in Greek and Latin, appended to the history by Theophylact Simocatta (*Paris, 1648, folio*).

**Tripartite Chronology**, or a list of Kings, Patriarchs, etc. A Latin version translated by Anastasius <note>Anastasius the Librarian, a 9th-century scholar</note> is available, woven into his own history. The Greek was first published by Scaliger at the end of the *Chronicle of Eusebius*. A Greek-Latin version with notes by Jacob Goar was also attached to the *Chronicle of Syncellus* (*Paris, 1652, folio*).

**A very long Letter** to Pope Leo, containing a confession of faith. It exists in Greek and Latin, published by Commelin with the *Acts of the Council of Ephesus* (*Heidelberg, 1591*), together with the works of Zonaras (*Paris, 1620*), and finally in the *Collections of the Councils, Volume VII, page 1205*.

**Four Small Works against the Iconoclasts** <note>Literally "image-breakers"; those who opposed the use of religious icons</note>. Published in Latin by Canisius in *Ancient Readings, Volume IV, page 253*, and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XIV*.

**Seventeen Short Canons**. These exist in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law, Book 3, page 195*, in the works of Zonaras, and in the *Collections of the Councils, Volume VII, page 1297*.

**Thirty-Seven Other Canons**. Published in Greek and Latin with notes in Cotelerius’s *Monuments of the Greek Church, Volume III, page 445*.

**A Letter containing Seventeen Questions on Canon Law** and as many responses. In Greek and Latin, in the same volume, page 453.

<margin>
* Vindication of Ignatius, part I.
</margin>

**Stichometry**, or a <note>original: Στιχημερία</note> **Short List of Canonical, Ecclesiastical, and Apocryphal Books**, with the <note>original: στίχοις</note> "number of verses" or lines appended to show how long each book is. However, the <term>great Pearson<note>referring to John Pearson, a famous 17th-century English theologian and scholar of the early Church</note></term> proves that this is not actually the work of our Nicephorus. He argues that although it is frequently attached to Nicephorus’s *Chronography*, it is not explicitly attributed to him in any manuscript or by any ancient testimony. Nevertheless, it is clear the author was a contemporary of Nicephorus, as it was translated into Latin by Anastasius the Roman. It exists in Greek at the end of the *Chronography* in all editions.

**Three Books of Refutations against the Iconoclasts**. A thick and lengthy work, of which ample fragments were published in Greek and Latin by François Combefis in his *Addition to the Library of the Fathers* (*Paris, 1648*). These include: a vindication of the testimony of St. Asterius from Book 2 (*Volume I, page 267*); another piece against the Iconoclasts from Book 3 (*ibid. page 277*); and another concerning the Six Councils from Book 2 (*ibid. Volume II, page 603*).

<margin>
808.
</margin>

**JOSEPH**, brother of Theodore the Studite <note>A famous abbot and defender of icons</note>, and a sharer in those same studies and labors for the cause of <term>Iconodulia<note>The veneration of religious images or icons</term></note>. For this reason, he is also called a "Confessor" <note>One who suffers for the faith but is not martyred</note>. He was made Archbishop of Thessalonica before the year 808. When he followed his brother's lead in stirring up sedition in Constantinople and insolently refused communion with Patriarch Nicephorus, he was removed from his see in the year 809 and sent into exile. He died after the year 816. We have his **Sermon on the Exaltation of the Venerable and Life-Giving Cross** in Greek and Latin in Gretser’s *On the Cross, Volume II, page 1200*, and a **Letter to Simeon the Monk** in Latin in Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 808, number 22. The **Iambic verses against the Iconoclasts** composed by him have been lost.

<margin>
810.
</margin>

**IGNATIUS**, a grammarian by profession, Deacon and <term>Sceuophylax<note>The official keeper of the sacred vessels and liturgical equipment</note></term> of the Great Church of Constantinople. He was a disciple of Patriarch Tarasius and eventually became the Metropolitan of Nicaea. He flourished in the year 810. He lived until at least the year 828, in which he delivered the funeral oration for Patriarch Nicephorus. He wrote the **Life of Patriarch Tarasius**, which exists in Latin in the collections of Surius and the Bollandists (*February 25*). He also wrote the **Life of Patriarch Nicephorus**, which is available in Greek and Latin in the works of Henschenius and Papebroch with notes from both (*March 13*). Also, according to Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>, he wrote **Epitaph Elegies**, iambic verses against Thomas Entarten, letters, and many other things which have been lost.

# The Photian Century

<margin>
9th CENTURY, from the Year 800.
810.
</margin>

### SMARAGDUS, Abbot of Saint Michael on the Meuse in the Diocese of Verdun, succeeded Abbot Hermengaud after the year 805, but before 810. I am well aware that he is commonly pushed back to the year 980, and the works of our Smaragdus are attributed to a certain younger Smaragdus who was Abbot of Saint Michael in Saxony and flourished under the Ottonian Emperors. However, besides the fact that it is well-established that our Smaragdus was a shining light of learning and devoted himself to writing books—whereas nothing certain is known of the Saxon Smaragdus—and besides the fact that all of Smaragdus's writings clearly taste of the spirit and studies of this 9th century: it is perfectly clear that the *Royal Way* published by D’Achéry <note>Luc d'Achéry (1609–1685), a Benedictine scholar</note> is owed to our Smaragdus. This is true both because it is dedicated to King Louis (later Emperor) <note>Louis the Pious</note>, and because the manuscript mentioned by Holstenius <note>Lucas Holstenius, a 17th-century Vatican librarian</note> in letters to D’Achéry was written before the age of the Saxon Smaragdus. Furthermore, there is such a great similarity of style, method, subject matter, and even wording between the *Royal Way* and the *Diadem of Monks* that it is easily apparent that both works are the offspring of one and the same author. Our Smaragdus was present in Rome in the year 810 at the Conference held between Pope Leo and the legates of Charlemagne regarding the **Procession of the Holy Spirit** <note>The "Filioque" debate concerning whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son</note>, and he recorded its Acts in writing. In the year 824, together with Frotharius, Bishop of Toul, he was appointed by Emperor Louis as a judge for Halmund, Abbot of Milan, and his hostile monks. It is not clear when he died.

->WRITINGS<-

*   **Commentary (or Postil) on the Gospels and Epistles** to be read in the Divine Offices throughout the circle of the year, collected from the Holy Fathers. Published at *Strasbourg* <note>original: "Argentoratum"</note> in 1536, folio.
*   **The Diadem of Monks**, woven from the sayings of the Fathers. Published at *Antwerp* in 1540.
*   **Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict**. Published at *Cologne* in 1575.
*   **The Royal Way**, divided into 32 chapters. Published by D’Achéry in Volume V [of the *Spicilegium*].
*   **Letter of Charlemagne to Pope Leo III regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit**, which is held to have been written by Smaragdus. It is found in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume VIII, page 1199.
*   **Acts of the Roman Conference on the Procession of the Holy Spirit in the year 810**. Found in the same work, page 1194.
*   **The Major Grammar**, or 14 books of commentaries on Donatus <note>Aelius Donatus, the standard Latin grammarian of late antiquity</note>. Manuscripts exist in the Corbie Library. The prologue can be seen in Le Cointe <note>Charles Le Cointe, author of ecclesiastical annals</note> under the year 824, number 75.

<margin>810.</margin>

### AMALARIUS, or Amalharius, called Fortunatus, obtained the Archbishopric of Trier in the year 810. In 811, he was sent as a legate by Emperor Charlemagne to instruct the Saxons across the Elbe in the Christian faith; there, having founded the Church of Hamburg, he returned to Gaul the following year and gave a written response to Charlemagne's circular letter regarding Baptism. In the year 813, he was sent to Constantinople to confirm peace with the Emperor of the Greeks. Having returned from the East in 814, he died shortly thereafter. There exists among the works of Alcuin a **Book on the Rationale of the Rites of Holy Baptism**, falsely ascribed to Alcuin, as it was written a full eight years after his death and by a certain Bishop; it is established by the authority of the Petavian Manuscript <note>A manuscript from the collection of Alexandre Petau</note> that this author was indeed Amalarius.

<margin>811.</margin>

### HATTO, a German by birth, was educated in the Monastery of Reichenau <note>original: "Augia major"</note> and served as Abbot of the same monastery; finally becoming Bishop of Basel, he was distinguished in the year 811. In that year, he was sent as a legate by Charlemagne to Nicephorus, Emperor of the Greeks, together with Hugh of Tours and others; he established peace with him and defined certain borders for both Empires. In 812, he returned to the West to Charlemagne together with the legates of Emperor Michael. He died in the year 836; however, while still living but burdened by old age, he handed over the Bishopric to Huldric. There exists a **Capitulary for the Priests** prescribed for his diocese, teaching how they should rule the people committed to them chastely and justly, containing 25 Canons; found in D’Achéry’s *Spicilegium* Volume VI and the *Councils* Volume VII, page 1522. Also, a **Book of Visions, or on the Life of Wetti**...

<margin>812.</margin>
AMALARIUS, a Deacon of Metz and, as some would have it, eventually granted the episcopal mitre, though he is more correctly identified as the Rural Bishop <note>term: "Chorepiscopus" — a "country bishop" who assisted the main bishop in rural areas</note> of Metz. Certainly, in the year 825, a certain Amalarius, a bishop of an uncertain see, was sent by the Synod of Paris to Emperor Louis at Aachen <note>original: "Aquisgranum"</note> to deliver collections of writings from the Fathers regarding Images. In any case, Amalarius the Deacon flourished from about the year 812 until 836, and perhaps longer. After the year 827, he was sent as a legate by Emperor Louis to Pope Gregory IV; nothing further is clear concerning him.

### W R I T I N G S

*Four Books on Divine or Ecclesiastical Offices*, written to Emperor Louis around the year 827, certainly after 819. Regarding this work, Boston of Bury <note>John Boston, a 15th-century English bibliographer</note> writes: "Amalarius wrote four books to King Louis on the Ecclesiastical Offices, the beginning of which is [*Most Glorious*] and the end [*Prayers*]." From this, it is clear that the last two chapters of the fourth book are additions, just as they do not appear in the Table of Chapters prefixed to the fourth book. From this it is also evident that the very long *Supplement* published by Mabillon in *Analecta* Volume II, page 96, and in the *Library of the Fathers* Volume XIV, page 934, belongs to someone else. William of Malmesbury <note>12th-century English historian</note> reduced these books of Amalarius into a compendium, an abbreviation of which exists today in manuscript; at the end of it, he offered this judgment on these books:

> "If you wish to know from a compendium the significations of the Mass, you should first read the verses of Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans and later Archbishop of Tours. If you seek the significations of the Holy Vestments and other things of that kind, read the sermons of Ivo of Chartres. For these men seem to have understood such matters more clearly and woven them together more beautifully. But concerning the varieties of the Offices, you will seek another in vain besides Amalarius. There might perhaps have been someone who wrote more eloquently, but certainly no one wrote more skillfully."

*Book on the Order of the Antiphonary*, written after the year 827. It exists together with the four books *On Divine Offices* among other writers on the same subject, Paris, 1610, folio, pages 305 and 503; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XIV, page 1032.

*Eclogue on the Canon of the Mass*, published by Baluze in *Capitularies*, Volume II, page 1352.

*Several Letters* to Bishops, published by D'Achéry in *Spicilegium*, Volume VI, page 164.

*The Rule or Institution of Canons*, collected from the writings and decrees of the ancient Fathers and Councils by the command of Emperor Louis (who also supplied him with a wealth of books from the Palace at Aachen). It was arranged for the use of the Western Churches and was read, approved, and confirmed by synodal authority at the Council of Aachen in the year 817. It consists of 113 chapters, to which the Fathers of Aachen themselves added another 32. It is found in *Councils*, Volume VII, page 1313.

<margin>813. Life of Theodore the Studite by Michael the Monk, and the Letters of Theodore in Baronius, Vol. IX, throughout.</margin>
THEODORE, called "Studite" from the Monastery over which he presided, was a native of Constantinople, born in the year 759. In the year 781, withdrawing to the Monastery of Saccudion located in the suburbs of Constantinople, he submitted himself to the discipline of Abbot Plato. In the year 794, when Plato voluntarily resigned his authority, Theodore took up the leadership of the Monastery. Recklessly devoted to "Icon-mania" <note>The author uses "Iconomania" to describe the intense devotion to the use of religious images, likely reflecting a skeptical or critical historical perspective</note>, he strenuously busied himself with the cause of images—paying no regard to piety toward God or obedience toward Princes. He quickly acquired a great name for himself in a City eager for revolution, and the highest veneration among the Greek monks, who were at that time the most insolent of two-legged creatures <note>original: "bipedum... procacissimos"</note>. Swollen with pride from this, he began to meddle in ecclesiastical government and matters of the greatest importance with "unwashed hands" <note>original: "illotis manibus" — a metaphor for approaching sacred or serious matters without proper preparation or authority</note>. # The Photian Century
<note>Named after Photius (c. 810–893), the influential Patriarch of Constantinople whose scholarship and conflicts with Rome defined this era.</note>

<margin>
9th CENTURY, from the Year 800.
</margin>

When *Emperor Constantine* repudiated *Mary the Empress* and brought in a mistress, *Patriarch Tarasius* was seen to act too leniently. Theodore, however, dared to strike the Emperor with the lightning bolt of excommunication <note>original: "anathematis fulmen"</note> and to attack him with the gravest insults. He even renounced communion with *Tarasius* and was the primary instigator among the monks for inciting and fostering a horrific schism <note>term: schism — a formal split or division within a church</note> in the Church of *Constantinople*. Thus, in the following year, he was banished to *Thessaloniki* by *Emperor Constantine*, paying for his insolence with exile. In the year 797, after *Emperor Constantine* was removed by the plots of his mother *Irene*, *Theodore* was brought back to *Constantinople* with a solemn procession. He gained the highest favor with that most wicked woman <note>Irene, who had her own son blinded to take power, was nonetheless a supporter of the icons Theodore championed</note>, for he—a man entirely composed of the most foul arts of flattery—did not blush to fawn over her in every way and extol her with almost divine praises.

In the year 798, he was appointed head of the *Stoudios* Monastery <note>original: "Studio"; one of the most important monasteries in the Byzantine Empire</note> located within the city. In the year 806, when *Nicephorus* was elevated to the Patriarchate of *Constantinople* from the status of a layman, and *Abbot Joseph* (who had once blessed *Constantine’s* illicit marriage) was restored to Church communion by the Synod of *Constantinople* after nine years of penance, *Theodore* was again driven by his outbursts. Using both matters as an excuse, he threw heaven and earth into confusion <note>original: "coelum terra miscuit," a Latin idiom meaning to cause a total uproar</note>. He cursed the Synod, the Patriarch, and *Emperor Nicephorus* with dire threats, sounded the trumpet of sedition everywhere, and, separating himself from the Patriarch's communion, dragged more than seven hundred monks into schism with him. Indeed, when he was rebuked by *Pope Leo* for his unbridled lack of self-control, he wrote back letters full of pride and anger. "What is it to us," he said <note>original: "inquit"</note>, "whether the Pope does this or that?" He then proceeded to attack *Leo* with the most severe taunts.

*Emperor Nicephorus* decided that such surges of fury should be restrained by exile; and so, in the year 809, he sent him, along with his brother *Joseph* and *Abbot Plato*, to a certain island near *Byzantium*. In the year 811, he obtained freedom from prison from *Michael Rangabe*, after he had reached an agreement and returned to favor with Patriarch *Nicephorus*. In the year 813, he began to suffer hardships for the cause of *Iconodulia* <note>term: Iconodulia — the veneration of religious images or icons</note>, and was consequently honored by his followers with the glorious title of Confessor. For when *Emperor Leo the Armenian* sought to suppress the "impious superstition of the Icon-worshipers" by public edict, *Theodore*, immediately surrounded by a whirlwind of monks, began to turn everything upside down: slandering the excellent Prince, celebrating public processions of images, openly singing Icon-venerating hymns in the forums and crossroads, renouncing his obedience to the Emperor, and stirring the people to sedition with the fans of turmoil.

The most merciful Emperor punished such madness only with exile; and when he noticed that the man's insolence could be restrained by no reasoning, he ordered him to be led to a prison in *Mesopa* near *Apollonium*—though a mild and not overly confined one. While placed in this location, he did not cease to send out "Encyclical" letters (as it were) against *Emperor Leo*, full of threats, defiance, and curses in every direction. Consequently, he was moved from place to place through various prisons; finally, in the year 819, he was taken to *Smyrna* and committed to a stricter custody. In the year 821, released from exile by *Emperor Michael the Stammerer* <note>original: "Michael Balbo"</note>, he returned to the leadership of his monastery and his usual arts of madness. In the year 824, since *Emperor Michael* intended nothing harsh against the *Iconomachi* <note>term: Iconomachi — "Icon-fighters" or Iconoclasts, those who opposed the use of religious images</note>, the indignant *Theodore* openly favored the tyrant *Thomas*, who was taking up rebel arms against the Emperor. However, after *Thomas* was unexpectedly brought to heel by *Michael*, Theodore found it necessary to leave *Constantinople*. After wandering through various places like an exile, he finally settled on the island of *Chalcitis*. There at last, on the 11th day of November in the year 826, he reached his final day at the age of 67.

He was a man learned beyond the common lot of scholars, and well-versed in almost every branch of science. However, carried away by an utterly immoderate zeal for the cult of images, he raved against all Iconoclasts—even the Emperors themselves—until he was hoarse. *Michael the Monk*, who loves to weave fables upon fables, relates much about him and his struggles and miracles, as is abundantly clear to anyone not blinded by prejudice from the accounts found in *Baronius* <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian whose "Annales Ecclesiastici" the author here views as biased</note>.

# The Photian Century
<note>Named after Photius (c. 810–893), the Patriarch of Constantinople. This era was marked by the final resolution of the Iconoclast controversy and growing tensions between the Eastern and Western Churches.</note>

9th CENTURY, from the Year 800.

### W O R K S.

**134 Catechetical Sermons** <note>Instructional lectures given to monks or candidates for baptism</note> were published in Latin from the translation by Joannes Livineius, *Antwerp, 1602, in octavo.* Greek manuscripts are held among the Barocci Codices in the Bodleian Library <note>At Oxford University</note>, and in the Pauline Library at Leipzig (Theological Repository, Series 3, folio number 31). There are **220 Catechetical Sermons of Theodore.**

***Testament to the Disciples;*** In this work, the prudent reader will note the man's devoted mind toward the images of the Saints. He includes the veneration of these images within the same Confession of Faith as the most sacred mysteries of the faith. He professes that by one and the same Spirit, he believes in the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity and also embraces and adores the sacred and venerable images, while honoring the relics of the Saints. According to the spirit of his age, he extols the monastic state more than is proper. For the rest, he provides many pious teachings that are most useful to all, especially to those consecrated to the Ascetic Order. Jacques Sirmond once translated this into Latin; Cardinal Baronius inserted this version into his *Annals* for the year 826. It was also published from the translation by Joannes Livineius together with the *Sermons, Antwerp, 1602.* From there, it was transferred into the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patrum"</note>, Volume 14. I possess a Greek version transcribed from the Leipzig manuscript, which I had intended to publish here alongside Sirmond's translation. However, seeing that the work I have in hand is growing to an excessive size, I decided it was better to refrain, especially since the Latin can be found in the cited locations.

***Sermon for the Fourth Sunday of Lent.*** Latin.

***Fragment from the Fourth Letter to Naucratius, regarding Heresies and Schism.*** Latin.

***Fragment of a Letter to Gelasius, a fugitive from the Monastery.*** Available in Latin in Turrianus, book 2, *On Monastic Vows.* The small works listed so far are found in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 14, page 830.

***Canon or Hymn, consisting of nine Odes, which is sung during the Restoration of the Holy Images.*** Taken from the Greek *Triodion* <note>A liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, it exists in Greek and Latin in Baronius for the year 842, and in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, page 830. However, the mention found therein of the restoration of images—which only happened after Theodore's death—is evidence that it is not by Theodore, unless we suspect that these parts about the restored images were added by others after Theodore had passed.

***On the Honor and Adoration to be shown to the Holy Images.*** Published together with the Orations of John of Damascus on the same subject, *Latin, Antwerp, 1556*; Greek, *Rome, 1553.*

***Oration on the Adoration and Exaltation of the Precious and Life-giving Cross, delivered in Mid-Lent.*** Exists in Greek and Latin in Gretser, Volume 2, *On the Cross*, page 1403.

***Praise of the Life and Works of St. Plato the Confessor.*** Available in Latin in Surius, December 16th.

***Praise of Bartholomew the Apostle,*** edited in Latin by D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, Volume 3.

***Letter to Naucratius regarding the Twice-Married*** <note>original: "de digamis"; addressing the church's stance on remarriage</note>, held in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius, *On Consent*, book 3, chapter 13, section 13.

***Letter to Gregory his son,*** Greek and Latin, ibid., book 3, chapter 16, section 10.

***Fragment of a Letter to Arsenius, containing an objection against the Second Council of Nicaea.*** <note>The council that restored icon veneration in 787</note> Exists in Baronius for the year 787, number 91.

***Fragment of a Letter to Peter of Nicaea,*** Latin, ibid., number 98.

***Letter to Stephen the Secretary,*** Latin, ibid., for the year 795, number 86.

***Letter to Nicephorus his Cousin,*** Latin, ibid., number 88.

***Letter to Stephen the Reader,*** Latin, ibid., for the year 787, number 92.

***Two Letters to Plato on his Exile,*** Latin, for the year 796, numbers 5 and 6.

***Panegyric Letter to Empress Irene,*** <note>original: "ad Irenen Aug."</note> Latin, for the year 801, number 24.

# The Photian Century
<note>This era is named after Photius the Great, a key figure in the 9th-century Byzantine Church, though the text here focuses on the earlier generation of the Iconoclast struggle.</note>

<margin>9th CENTURY, from 800 AD.</margin>

*Letter to Emperor Nicephorus regarding the appointment of a successor to Patriarch Tarasius,* in Latin, for the year 806, number 4.

*Letter to Patriarch Nicephorus,* in Latin, same location, number 18.

*Letter to the brothers of the Monastery of Saccudion,* in Latin, for the year 808, number 8.

Baronius presents many other of his letters inserted into his *Annals* in Latin (Volume IX), from the year 808 to the year 826.

Michael the Monk, in Baronius for the year 798, enumerates many small works, homilies, letters, poems, and treatises by Theodore. Since these no longer appear anywhere today, they may be considered lost—except for the fact that a fairly thick book of letters was in the possession of Baronius. From this volume, he took the above-mentioned letters, translated into Latin by Sirmond, and presented them in his *Annals*.
