<margin>813.</margin>
**NAUCRATIUS**, a monk of Constantinople, an alumnus of the Stoudios Monastery <note>The most influential monastery in Constantinople, known for its strict rule and defense of icons</note> and a disciple of Theodore the Studite, was a most devoted "Iconolatra" <note>An "image-worshiper" or Iconodule; one who defended the use of religious icons</note> who flourished around the year 813. Because of his extreme stubbornness in defending the veneration of images, he was thrown into prison on more than one occasion and suffered beatings and other hardships. He frequently complained of these to his teacher, from whom he received several letters of consolation that can be found in Baronius. In the year 816, he was still held in prison, from which he was released three years later; the exact date of his death is not known. It is certain that he survived Theodore. He wrote to the spiritual brothers scattered here and there a fairly long **Letter or Treatise**, in which he discusses the "perfections" <note>A term often used by Naucratius to describe the sufferings or "completion" of the path of a confessor or martyr</note> endured by the Iconodules <note>Servants/venerators of icons</note>. In this work, he continues at nauseating length with the highest praises and encomiums for the recently deceased Theodore—praises far beyond the reach of human status. I have in my possession a manuscript of this little book, copied from a volume in the Pauline Library of Leipzig <note>The library of the University of Leipzig</note>. I will refrain from including the entire letter here (as it is not of such great value). I will present to the reader only the beginning and a few specimens of this most foolish praise in English <note>original: "Gr. Lat." (Greek and Latin)</note>, from which the prudent reader may judge the rest.

->To the spiritual brothers and fathers who endure "perfection" for the sake of the Lord and are scattered everywhere, Naucratius the Sinner sends greetings.<-

Until now, most honored and dearest brothers and fathers, I have delayed my humble and lowly letter, as day after day passed, keeping my sadness to myself. I did this for many reasons, which I do not think your honored Charity is unaware of. But primarily, I did so because I could not bear to be the messenger of a troublesome and bitter event for you: namely, the "falling asleep" <note>A traditional Christian term for death</note> of our blessed and illustrious Father. But after this news disturbed not only those here but also those situated further away, as I see—so that it seems difficult for most to believe that the servant of the Lord has truly been translated from human affairs—I certainly do not think that what we ourselves kept silent out of a certain reverence and fear has not reached you. I have proceeded to write out of necessity; now more clearly, although you have already heard it known by report: and clearly not without plaintive lamentations and tears. For who, though having a heart <note>The Latin text ends here and continues in the next column's translation</note>

->To the spiritual brothers and fathers who are persecuted for the sake of the Lord and are scattered everywhere, Naucratius the sinful monk sends greetings.<-

Until yesterday and the day before, most honored brothers and fathers, I postponed my humble letter, letting day after day pass and keeping the sorrow to myself. I did this for many reasons, which I believe your honors are not unaware of—especially, and above all else, because I could not bear to be the messenger to you of a sorrowful occurrence: I mean, the falling asleep of our blessed and celebrated father. Since, as I see, not only the people here but also those far away have been shaken by the shock of the news, so that it is hard for many to believe whether the servant of the Lord has really departed from here—and I do not think that what we kept silent has failed to reach you—I have necessarily come to write this letter to you more clearly, even if I am reporting what you have already heard from others. ## AGOBARDUS, a Gaul by birth

<margin>813.</margin>

**AGOBARDUS**, a Gaul by birth, was born (as we are taught by *Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon (1632–1707), a famous Benedictine monk and scholar who founded the study of paleography</note> from a brief Martyrology in which Agobard seems to have noted a few things in his own hand) in the year 779 or 782. He came from Spain to Gallia Narbonensis <note>A region in Southern France</note>: in the year 813, he was substituted as Co-Bishop for Leidradus, the Archbishop of Lyon, who was weighed down by old age; and after Leidradus retired a little later to the Monastery of Soissons in the year 816, Agobard thereafter held the throne of Lyon alone. But woe is me, wretched man: for what unhappy time have I been saved? Indeed, what was reserved for my afflicted life, that I should be the one to announce the death of him who lived not for himself, but for Christ? Truly, our common Father has fallen asleep — — — He was entirely both a disciple and imitator of Christ; that mouth of the Church; the honor of priests; the pillar of faith; the Rule of Monks; the Evangelical Pastor; the Apostolic Heart; an outstanding Confessor; a Martyr in Purpose; the Sun of the orthodox faith; the Teacher of the world; — — — that most vocal Herald of the truth; a perpetual spring of doctrine; for whom there was, as it were, an immeasurable intellect for governing toward the end of the divine purpose; that admirable counselor; the faithful dispenser of the Sacraments of God; a Citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem; a purged mind; a golden soul; the gate of penance; the fountain of dogmas; the well-tuned lyre of the Spirit; the Residence of the blessed and sovereign Trinity; — — — that earthly Angel, and heavenly man; that most pure temple of virginity; that manifold and multiform man; a most intense perceiver of the shifting wisdom of the Spirit; a true servant of Christ; the eye with the beautiful brow of the Body of Christ; the champion of patience; and the victor over the heretical Iconoclasts; the armor of justice; the fountain of alms; the diligent guardian of the Lord’s laws; the storehouse of the treasury of virtues; sweet in speech, and easy to greet.

Thus speaks this most inept Panegyrist <note>An "Encomiastes" or panegyrist is someone who writes a specialized speech of high praise. The author here clearly finds the style overly flowery or "sappy".</note>. What follows is of almost the same grain, plainly unworthy to be published in Latin, much less in Greek. Meanwhile, if any lips love such "lettuces" <note>original: *similes amant lactucas*. This is a Latin idiom meaning "to each their own taste," usually implying the taste is poor or the material is intellectual "junk food."</note>, they may satisfy their hunger from this Letter recently rendered into Latin by Father Combefis, and inserted by the most recent curators of the Library of the Fathers, Volume 14, page 903.

## AGOBARDUS

<margin>813.</margin>
<margin>* See *Italian Journey*, Section 14, page 68.</margin>
AGOBARDUS, French by birth, born (as Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon (1632–1707) was a Benedictine monk and scholar, considered the founder of paleography and diplomatics.</note> teaches us from a brief Martyrology to which Agobard seems to have noted a few things in his own hand) in the year 779. In the year 782, he came from Spain into Gallia Narbonensis <note>A Roman province in what is now southern France.</note>. In the year 813, he was appointed as co-bishop to Leidrad, Archbishop of Lyon, who was burdened by old age; and after Leidrad withdrew shortly thereafter to the Monastery of Soissons in the year 816, Agobard subsequently held the throne of Lyon alone. Around the year 818, having found among the papers of Felix of Urgel <note>Felix was a leader of the "Adoptionist" heresy, which claimed Christ was the "adopted" son of God in his humanity.</note>, who had relapsed into error at Lyon...

# The Photian Century
<note>Historians often refer to the 9th century as the "Photian Century," named after Photius the Great, the Patriarch of Constantinople, whose scholarship and conflicts with Rome defined the era's ecclesiastical politics.</note>

### THE NINTH CENTURY

<margin>The 9th Century. The Year 800.</margin>
In the 9th century, after <note>Felix of Urgell, a proponent of the Adoptionist heresy which claimed Christ was the "adopted" rather than natural son of God.</note> Felix died having relapsed into heresy, Agobard published a heretical treatise <note>The Latin here implies Agobard exposed the heretical nature of Felix's work for all to criticize.</note> so that he might be rebuked by all; at the same time, he issued a book to Emperor Louis <note>Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne.</note> in which he refuted the "Felician" errors and writings. In the year 822, he took part in the Council of Attigny, having previously been present at the beginning of the year for the election of Tructesindus as Abbot of Aniane and Gellone in Septimania. In the year 828, he used various writings to suppress the "insolence" of the Jews, who had obtained an edict from the Emperor forbidding any Jewish-owned slave from being baptized without the owner’s consent. Following a Council held at Lyon the next year, he earnestly petitioned Louis in a letter from the Synod, asking that the audacity of the Jews be restrained by Imperial authority. 

In the year 833, the Emperor’s sons, Lothar and Pippin, took up impious arms against their father, Louis the Pious; they captured their father, removed him from power, and thrust him into a monastery. Agobard joined them as a companion, among others, and fostered this execrable rebellion with such passion that he published an *Apology* <note>A formal written defense.</note> in which he strained every nerve of his talent and eloquence to protect and promote this cause. Though he was otherwise an excellent man, this was a most wicked deed, which can be excused by no skill or rhetorical coloring. Consequently, in the following year, when Lothar was driven out of Gaul by his father, Agobard was forced to join him as a companion in flight. In the year 835, at a Council held at Thionville, when he refused to appear after being summoned three times to plead his case, he was removed from his high office, though no one was substituted in his place. In the year 837, having left Lothar’s company, he returned to Gaul, was received back into the favor of Emperor Louis, and recovered his see. In the year 840, while following Louis on an expedition to protect the eastern bank of the Rhine river, he died at Saintes on the 8th of June. He possessed a sharp mind and no common erudition; he was most skilled in theological questions and a most learned judge and fierce defender of Church discipline and ancient Canons. He was most tenacious in any opinion he had once imbibed, and constant and brave in asserting it. <margin>* Notes on Agobard, page 5.</margin> Truly did the famous * Baluze say of him:

> *He was, above all, a perpetual and constant defender of the Canons, as one who knew them well; so much so that he even severely criticized the Romans of his time for looking down upon the Gallican <note>French/Gaulish.</note> Canons—for the reason, if it please the powers above, that the modern Romans had not condemned them, or because Roman legates had not been present at their establishment. It is a wonder if a man so composed would not have incurred the envy of the men of his age.* 

One could not easily say whether this man was more famous for his learning or his integrity.

---

### W R I T I N G S.

The works of Agobard lay buried in darkness for several centuries past, and indeed would have remained so forever, had not Papirius Massonus by chance entered the shop of a certain bookbinder in Lyon and discovered a manuscript copy of them—the only one, it seems, that had survived the injuries of time—in his possession. Indeed, the bookbinder himself, ignorant of such a treasure, had intended to tear it apart shortly thereafter. Massonus seized the codex and brought it to light in the following order:

*Against the Dogma of Felix, addressed to Emperor Louis.*

*On the Insolence of the Jews, addressed to the same.* The Jews, who by the Emperor's favor had established their homes in Gaul, especially in Lyon, began to behave quite insolently toward Christians; Agobard therefore strongly breaks and suppresses their audacity and impiety in this and the following few small works.

*On Jewish Superstitions.*

*A Book on the Baptism of Jewish Slaves.*

*An Exhortatory Letter to Nibridius, Bishop of Narbonne, on avoiding social life and society with Jews.*

*A Book against the Law of Gundobad, and the impious combats carried out under it.* <note>Agobard argued against the "Law of Gundobad," which permitted judicial duels—trial by combat—to settle legal disputes, viewing it as unchristian.</note>

*To Bishop Bernard, on the privilege and right of the Priesthood.*

*A book On Hail and Thunder*, in which he sharply refutes the silly and execrable superstition of the common people in this matter, using arguments drawn both from Holy Scripture and from the nature of the thing. <note>In this work, Agobard famously debunked the belief that "weather-makers" could cause storms or hail to destroy crops.</note>

# The Photian Century.
<note>The 9th century is named here for Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, whose scholarship and eventual schism with Rome dominated the era's intellectual landscape.</note>

<margin>The 9th Century, from the year 800.</margin>

**Book against the objections of Abbot Fredegisus**, who had peddled certain perverse and tasteless opinions concerning Christ our Lord and several other articles of faith. <note>Fredegisus was an Anglo-Saxon scholar and successor to Alcuin as Abbot of Saint-Martin at Tours; he and Agobard clashed over the nature of the soul and the divine inspiration of the Bible's grammar.</note>

**Letter to the Nobles of the Palace against the impious Decree regarding the baptism of Jewish slaves.** For the Jews, partly through deceit and partly through money, had obtained many favors from the Emperor to the prejudice of Christians; among others, that their slaves should not be baptized into the Christian faith without the consent of their masters. Agobard rightly rebukes the impiety of this edict.

**Letter to Bartholomew, Bishop of Narbonne**, regarding the illusion of certain signs, written on the occasion of an epidemic of epilepsy and other unusual diseases then spreading, the cause of which Bartholomew was seeking from Agobard.

**Letter to Matfred, Noble of the Palace**, in which he deplores and depicts the miseries of that time stirred up by the Jews out of hatred for the Christian religion, and seeks a remedy from the Emperor.

**Letter to the people of Lyon, on the method of Ecclesiastical governance**, written on the occasion of quarrels that arose among the clergy of the Church of Lyon regarding the administration of the Church.

**Book on Pictures and Images.** Here the Papal writers sweat and twist themselves strangely in an attempt to make Agobard appear favorable to them, or at least not opposing them in this matter. But no sought-after colors and no seductive words can obscure what he so often and eloquently asserts: that images are to be pursued with no veneration and no worship. As is his custom, *Papirius Masson* <note>A 16th-century French historian who first edited Agobard's works.</note> candidly states in his *Preface to Agobard*: "Manifestly uncovering the errors of the Greeks concerning images and pictures, he denies that they ought to be adored; a sentiment which all we Catholics approve, following the testimony of *Gregory* the Great concerning them." *Stephen Baluze* is a little more cautious in his notes, yet he does not dare to oppose the plain truth and willingly admits that Agobard wrote nothing else on this matter than what everyone in Gaul then felt. *Charles Le Cointe*, writing for the year 840 (no. 14), brings forward much on this subject from *Theophilus Raynaud* and *Jean Mabillon* (who try to soothe rather than remove the difficulty with long-winded evasions and futile explanations), without adding even a <term>γρυ</term> <note>original: γρυ (gry). A Greek term meaning "a grunt" or "a peep," used here to mean "not even a syllable" or "nothing at all."</note> of his own opinion.

**Book on the Management of Ecclesiastical Property**, in which he deals with the reform of collapsed Church discipline, especially against the sacrilegious seizure of church revenues by laymen; he strongly refutes this practice using the custom of primitive antiquity and Ecclesiastical rules and sanctions.

**Book against the Judgment of God, or on divine sentences**, with very brief annotations, against the damnable opinion of those who think the truth of divine judgment is revealed by fire, or water, or armed conflict. <note>Agobard was a pioneer in opposing "trials by ordeal," arguing that they were superstitious and had no basis in scripture.</note>

**Exhortatory Sermon to the people**, on the truth of the faith and the institution of all good things.

**A Lamentable Letter on the Division of the Frankish Empire among the sons of Emperor Louis.**

**On the Comparison of both Ecclesiastical and Political rule**, and in which ways the dignity of the Church outshines the majesty of Empires. To this booklet is subjoined the *Letter of Pope Gregory IV to the Bishops of the Kingdom of the Franks*.

**Apologetic Book for the sons of Louis the Pious against their father.** <note>This refers to the civil wars between Louis the Pious and his sons, where Agobard sided with the sons (Lothar, Pippin, and Louis the German) against the Emperor.</note>

**A document presented to Augustus Lothar in the Synod of Compiègne, in the year 833**, which he presented to Emperor Lothar to approve the deposition of his father Louis, having secured it in his own name and by his own hand (a task which the rest of the bishops also performed, each in his own name).

**Letter to Ebbo, Bishop of Reims, On hope and fear.**

**Book on Divine Psalmody**, in which he learnedly defends the custom of the Church of Lyon in singing against the recent minor objections of a certain pretender to knowledge (whom Baluze maintains was *Amalarius the Deacon*).

**Book on the Correction of the Antiphonary.** <note>An antiphonary is a liturgical book containing the chants (antiphons) sung during the Divine Office.</note>

**Book against the four books of Amalarius.** *Stephen Baluze* was the first to rescue this book from the shadows and publish it, using an old manuscript codex belonging to *Pierre de Marca, Senator of Grenoble*, and also performing a collation with the *Chiffletian* codex.

### HILDUIN

<margin>814. See Le Cointe for the years 814, 817, 818, etc.</margin>
HILDUIN succeeded Abbot Waldo in the leadership of the Monastery of Saint-Denis around the year 814; later he was made Abbot of Saint Medard near Soissons, and Saint Germain near Paris. In the year 818, he was named Arch-chaplain of the Palace. In 824, he followed Emperor Lothair to Rome, who had set out to settle the seditions of the citizens; in the following year he returned to Gaul and devoted himself entirely to gathering the relics of the Saints from everywhere, sending a double embassy to Rome for that purpose. Meanwhile, he flourished with the greatest favor in the court of Louis the Pious, being admitted almost into a share of the government: he was worthy of all the greater punishment because, bound by so many ties, he dared to give his name among the conspirators and enemies of Louis in 830 and follow the party of the rebel Lothair. Therefore, deservedly stripped of his abbeys and dignities, he was banished to Saxony. Yet in the following year, received back into favor through the prayers of Hincmar, he recovered the Abbeys of Saint-Denis and Saint-Germain, and two years later, that of Soissons. In 835, by the command of Emperor Louis, he set himself to writing the *Areopagitica*. He died in the Monastery of Saint Medard around 842. He wrote the *Areopagitica, or on the deeds, Passion, and Writings of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite* <note>original: "Areopagitica seu de rebus gestis, Passione, & Scriptis S. Dionysii Areopagitae"</note>; as they exist today, they consist of these parts:

A *Dedicatory letter to Emperor Louis* <note>original: "Epistola nuncupatoria ad Ludovicum Imp."</note>, quite lengthy, in which he discusses the authors from whom he scraped together his work: he strives to assert the reliability of the entire history and, as best he can, dilutes contrary arguments.

A *Short prefatory letter to the Reader* <note>original: "Epistola brevis Praefatoria ad Lectorem"</note>, in which he notes certain things regarding the authors, especially Greek and Latin, from whom he drew his material.

The *Life and Passion of Saint Dionysius*, collected and organized from Greek and Latin monuments, as the title claims and Hilduin’s faith asserts. But in truth, Hilduin’s authority is not so great. For it is clearly established that Hilduin—besides admitting the most foul fables without any discernment and ascribing whatever he found written about several different men named Dionysius to the single "Areopagite"—also invented and mixed in many things of his own of no better quality. <note>Hilduin is famously responsible for the historical error of merging Dionysius the Areopagite (a 1st-century convert of St. Paul) with Saint Denis of Paris (a 3rd-century martyr), a confusion that lasted for centuries.</note>

To these were added, although written after Hilduin's death, a *Letter of Hincmar of Reims*, and another by *Anastasius the Librarian, regarding Saint Dionysius the Areopagite*, and even a *revelation* regarding the same, formerly made to Pope Stephen III; with the *Rescript of Emperor Louis to Hilduin on the composing of the Areopagitica* still prefixed to the whole work.

The *Areopagitica* are extant in the Cologne edition of 1562 and in Surius, October 9th. Furthermore, Hilduin also wrote four books *on the Life of Saint Dionysius* in verse <note>original: "oratione ligatâ", literally "bound speech"</note>, which Miraeus testifies are still preserved as manuscripts in the Monastery of Gembloux.

### EINHARD

<margin>814. See Einhard himself, *On the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter*, in Surius, June 2nd.</margin>
EINHARD, a German by nation, was secretary to Charlemagne (who died in 814) and very dear to his Emperor; therefore, in 806, he was sent as the leader of an Embassy to Rome, so that Charlemagne's Testament—which he had established regarding the partition of the kingdom among his sons—might be signed by the hand of Pope Leo among others. In 816, after a mutual agreement was made between him and his wife Emma to abstain from the custom of the marriage bed, he became Abbot of Fontenelle; he held that rule for seven years. In 817, Emperor Louis handed over his son Lothair, a partner in the Imperial dignity, to Einhard to be educated, so that he might diligently advise him both on other matters and on correcting fallen morals. In 819, he was created Abbot of Ghent, and immediately upon his arrival he restored that monastery, which had been miserably defaced by fire, and recalled the monks scattered here and there. In 826, [he brought] the relics of the Saints into the monastery...

...after he obtained the use <note>of the relics</note> for himself from Rome; and he himself committed their translation and miracles to writing. In the year 829, after the Monastery of Seligenstadt <note>original: "Selingstadii"</note> was built, he was the first to undertake the duty of Abbot. In the year 836, he lost his wife Emma, whose death he bitterly lamented; as is clearly evident from the consolatory letters from Lupus of Ferrières to him: however, in what year he himself died is not yet known to me.

### W O R K S

*The Life of Charlemagne* <note>original: "Vita Caroli Magni"</note>, written in a very elegant and florid style. It was published separately in Leipzig, 1616, in quarto; and in Strasbourg, 1644, in quarto; among the German writers of Reuber at Frankfurt, 1584, folio, page 1; among the Frankish writers of Du Chesne <note>original: "Quercetani"</note> Volume II; and elsewhere.

*On the Translation and Miracles of the Saints Marcellinus and Peter, in four books written in prose, and one in verse.* These are found in Surius under the date of June 2nd.

*Annals of the deeds of King Pepin, Charlemagne, and Louis the Pious from the year 741 to the year 829.* Men of the most unquestionable erudition, Pierre de Marca, André du Chesne, and Peter Lambeck <note>original: "Lambecius"</note>—who found them attached to the *Life of Charlemagne* in a Vienna manuscript—attribute these to our Einhard. They were edited by the care of Hermann von Neuenahr <note>original: "Nevenarii"</note> together with the *Life of Charlemagne*, Cologne, 1521, in quarto; by Justus Reuber together with others, Frankfurt, 1584, folio, page 15; by Pithou among the contemporary writers, Frankfurt, 1594, octavo; and finally by Du Chesne in the *Frankish Historians*, Volume II.

*62 Letters* published by Du Chesne in the Appendix to Volume II.

*Letter to Abbot Lupus of Ferrières*, which holds the third place among the letters of Lupus.

<margin>Letter 4.</margin>
*A Booklet on the Adoration of the Cross*, which Lupus of Ferrières testifies was dedicated to him by Einhard, has been lost.

André du Chesne ascribes the *Chronicle of Lorsch* <note>original: "Chronicon Laurishamense"</note> to Einhard. However, Charles le Cointe <note>original: "Carolus Cointius"</note> shows with several arguments against Du Chesne that it is incorrectly attributed to him, at the year 774, number 127, etc., and at the year 792, number 3.

Finally, a *Chronological Breviary* from the creation of the world to the year 809 was published by Lambeck in his *Commentary*, book 2, chapter 5, page 395, which he contends was written by Einhard, though led only by bare conjectures.

### HETTIUS, or Hetto, or Hectus,
after administering the leadership of the Monastery of Mettlach <note>original: "Mediolacensis"</note> for a decade, was made Archbishop of Trier <note>original: "Trevirensis"</note> in the year 814. ### FROTHARIUS, formerly Abbot of Saint Aper,

### EBBO, or Ebo, a German by nation,
a foster-brother and classmate of Emperor Louis, nourished in the Palace, served in the Royal Treasury <note>term: Fisco (The state or royal treasury of the Frankish Empire)</note>; later honored with sacred orders, he became the Chaplain and Librarian to Louis, then Abbot of Saint-Remi, and finally in the year 816, Archbishop of Reims. In the year 821, he took part in the Council of Thionville. In 822, having set out for Rome, he obtained permission from Pope Paschal to preach the Gospel to the Northern peoples; and in the following year, having undertaken a journey as far as the borders of the Danes, he converted many thousands of pagans to the faith and purified them with baptism. Returning to Gaul at the end of the year to be present at the Assembly of Compiègne <note>original: "Conventui Compendiensi"</note>, he soon returned to the North and applied himself diligently to the work he had begun. In the year 829 he was present at the Council of Paris, and in 830 at the Assembly of Aachen <note>original: "Conventui Aquisgranensi"</note>. In the year 833, by Louis...

# The Age of Photius

After Lothair's flight, he was stripped of the Abbey and sent away to the Monastery of Fulda. In the year 835, having been brought to the Synod at Thionville <note>original: "Theodonis villam"</note>, he confessed himself guilty of treason <term>treason; original: "læsæ majestatis," literally 'injured majesty'</term>; and, having been deposed from his seat, he was sent back to be guarded in the Monastery of Fulda. <margin>816.</margin>
**HALITGARIUS**, made Bishop of Cambrai <note>original: "Cameracensis"</note> and Arras <note>original: "Atrebatensis"</note> in the year 816. In the year 823, he set out with Ebbo of Reims to the borders of the Danes for the sake of preaching the Gospel, and in November of that same year, he took part in the Assembly of Compiègne <note>original: "Compendiensi"</note>. In the year 825, he was sent by the Synod of Paris to the Emperor Louis to deliver a collection of opinions <note>original: "Sententiarum"</note> gathered from the writings of the Fathers regarding Holy Images, which had been prepared at the Synod. In the year 828, he was sent as a legate by the Emperor Louis to Michael the Stammerer <note>original: "Michaelem Balbum"</note> at Constantinople. In the year 829, he returned from the East laden with the relics of saints, and was present to sign the decrees of the Council of Paris. He died in the year 831. He wrote a *Work on Vices and Virtues, the remedies for sins, and the order or judgments of penance, completed in six books*. The first five of these were published by both H. Canisius (Vol. V, part 2, p. 227) and the curators of the Library of the Fathers (Vol. XIV, p. 906). The sixth book, however—which is nothing other than the *Penitential Book* of the Roman Church, copied by Halitgarius from the archives of that same church—was first published by Steuart in the Supplement to Canisius, page 693; then by Hugues Ménard in the notes to the Sacramentary of Gregory (Paris, 1642); and by Jean Morin in the Appendix to his book *On Penance*, page 5. Halitgarius's preface to this Roman Penitential can be seen in Steuart, ibid., page 713.

<margin>817.</margin>
**PASCHAL I**, a Roman by birth and the son of Bonosus, was a Priest of the Roman Church and Abbot of the Monastery of St. Stephen next to the Church of St. Peter. He obtained the Papal throne on January 25th, in the year 817. He vigorously supported the Greek monks in the controversy over images <note>original: "Iconomaniam"</note> and honored Theodore <note>Theodore the Studite</note>, their primary leader, with the highest respect; so much so that he prohibited the envoys <term>envoys; original: "Apocrisiarios"</term> sent by the Patriarch of Constantinople to Theodore from entering Rome in 817. In the following year, he established a monastery at St. Praxedes in Rome for the refugee Greek Iconodules <term>Iconodules; those who venerate icons</term>. In the year 823, on Easter day itself, he placed the Imperial crown upon the Emperor Lothair in the Basilica of St. Peter; in that same year, he sent Archbishop Ebbo of Reims and Halitgarius to imbue the Danes with the Christian faith. He died on May 11th, in the year 824. *Three Letters* survive in the Collection of Councils, Volume VII, pages 1502 and 1869.

**SEDULIUS**, an Irishman <note>original: "natione Scotus"</note> by birth, was the author of the *Collections or Explanations of the Epistles of St. Paul*, compiled from the writings of the Fathers. He is said by the monk Hepidannus to have been famous in the year 818, and thus he is placed by us in this chronological position. However, this is not entirely certain. It is established, though, that he flourished after Bede, or was at least his contemporary. Thus he would have been nearly an entire century older than this present time if he were indeed the same <margin>p. 418</margin> *Sedulius, Bishop of Britain of the Irish race*, who together with Fergust the Pict, Bishop of Scotland, took part in and signed the Council of Rome under Gregory II in the year 721. See the brief notes we made regarding Sedulius the Poet, and the extensive discussion by Labbe in his *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, Volume II, page 324. That *Collection* was published in Basel in 1528 and 1534, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume VI, page 494.

Theodore, surnamed *Graptus* <note>original: "Graptus," meaning "the Inscribed." He and his brother were branded on their faces with verses by the Iconoclast Emperor</note>, a Palestinian by birth, was first steeped in the liberal arts; while still a youth, he was given by his parents to the monks of St. Sabas to be educated, and eventually took up the dignity of the priesthood in that monastery. Around the year 818, he was sent to Constantinople by Thomas, Patriarch of Jerusalem, to defend the cause of the holy images. He attempted this boldly enough, sharply and impudently rebuking Emperor Leo the Armenian to his face; on that account, he was beaten with whips by the Emperor and banished to the mouth of the Pontus <note>the Black Sea</note>. After Leo was removed <note>assassinated</note> in the year 821, he returned to Constantinople and pursued the same cause with Emperor Michael <note>Michael II</note> with the same outcome: he was handed over to prison, cast out from the city, and sent away to Sosthenis. In the year 833, as he would not yet cease his "folly" <note>original: "ineptire"; the author likely uses this term to reflect the Emperor's view of Theodore's persistence</note>, he was beaten with lashes by Emperor Theophilus and ordered to be deported to the island of Aphusia. Two years later, summoned back to Constantinople, when he would yield to no warnings or arguments, he was again tortured with various punishments by the angry Emperor and sent to Apamea in Bithynia, where, shut in prison, he met his final day. He committed to writing a *Disputation on the Worship of Images*, which Patriarch Nicephorus of Constantinople held with Emperor Leo the Armenian around the year 815. François Combefis published this in Greek and Latin with notes in *Origins of Constantinople*, page 159. He also wrote a *Letter to John, Bishop of Cyzicus* concerning the penalties and tortures inflicted on him and his brother by Emperor Theophilus; this is found in Greek and Latin in the work of his biographer, edited by Combefis, ibid., page 204. A book *On the Orthodox Faith against the Iconoclasts* <note>original: "Iconomachos"</note> survives in Greek manuscript in the Royal Library at Paris, Codices 134 and 195. From this work, a *Fragment on the Symbols of the Eucharist* was provided to us in Greek and Latin by the same Combefis, ibid., page 221.

There exists a Greek *Canon or Hymn consisting of nine Odes* written by him in honor of his brother Theodore, found in the Greek Menaiion <note>a liturgical book containing the services for the month</note> for December 27th, and from there, with an added Latin version, in Combefis, *Origins of Constantinople*, page 224.

...[Clau]dius, therefore, preparing himself to undertake that pastoral duty, increased the Christian cause among his people with all the zeal he could muster. However, when he discovered many in his diocese following the images of saints with clearly unlawful honor, he not only expressly condemned their worship and veneration (as the entire Gallican Church <note>The "Gallican Church" refers to the church in the Frankish Empire, which at this time held a moderate view on images, opposing both their worship and their total destruction.</note> did at that time), but he also passionately contended that they, and all material crosses, should be erased, overturned, and utterly discarded from all the basilicas of his parish; and so it was done. On this occasion, Theodemir, a French Abbot of the Benedictine Order with whom Claudius had previously been on familiar terms, sent a sharp letter against him. Claudius responded to him, and having published an *Apologia* <note>A formal written defense.</note>, he strenuously defended not only himself but also the purity of Christian doctrine. As for the report by Jonas of Orléans that Claudius was a follower not only of Felix of Urgell <note>A Spanish bishop who promoted "Adoptionism," the idea that Jesus was the adopted son of God.</note> but also of the Arian heresy <note>Arianism was an early Christian belief that denied the full divinity of Jesus.</note>, I would believe that this arose from envy or the heat of dispute. Certainly, Jonas himself professes that he did not draw this from his own knowledge, but from hearsay. Claudius died around the year 839.

*Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, written in the year 816, dedicated to Dructerannus, Abbot of Solignac. It appeared separately in *Paris, 1542, octavo*, and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XIV, page 134.*

*Three books of Commentaries on Genesis*, written in 814, and *four books on Exodus*, written in 821. Whether these works lie hidden anywhere is entirely unknown to me. Certainly, they have not yet been published.

*Commentaries on Leviticus*, written in 823. The illustrious Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon, a famous 17th-century Benedictine scholar.</note> has these in a manuscript in the Remigius Codex; he published both the preface and the end of the work in *Analecta, Volume I, page 30.*

*Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew*, written to Justus, Abbot of Charroux, in the year 815. It exists as a manuscript in the Library of the Church of Laon, according to the same Mabillon.

Besides the *Epistle to the Galatians*, he wrote *Commentaries on the remaining Epistles of Blessed Paul*, which are held as manuscripts in the Library of Fleury. Mabillon published the preface to the *Epistle to the Ephesians*, dedicated to Louis the Pious <note>Emperor of the Romans and King of the Franks, son of Charlemagne.</note>, in the same work, page 40.

*A Short Chronology* according to the Hebrew truth of the Holy Books, which Philippe Labbe—who first brought it to light—not without merit suspected to be by our Claudius (*New Library of Manuscripts, Volume I, page 309*).

*The Apology and Reply against Abbot Theodemir concerning the worship of Images and Saints*, written in the year 828. Certain excerpts from this book, made by order of Emperor Louis, were inserted here and there into his own books by Jonas of Orléans; Melchior Goldast presented these to the reader, collected into a single bundle, at the end of his *Collection on the Worship of Images, page 764.* From these excerpts, a prudent and pious reader can judge the whole work—as they say, "recognizing the lion by its claw" <note>original: "quasi ex ungue leonem," a Latin proverb meaning one can judge the scale of a thing from a small sample.</note>.

<margin>821.</margin>
**DUNGAL**, a monk of St. Denis in Paris and a Deacon by rank, flourished in the year 821. He lived until the year 830; it is not clear when he died. Around the year 828, he published a *Book of Responses* against the opinions of Claudius of Turin concerning the worship of images, which is found in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XIV, page 196.* He also wrote a *Letter to Charlemagne concerning the Solar Eclipse*, published by D’Achery in *Spicilegium, Volume X.*

<margin>821.</margin>
**JONAS**, made Bishop of Orléans in the year 821. In the year 826, he was sent to Rome to Pope Eugenius, carrying the "Opinions of the Fathers on Images" collected at the Council of Paris. In the year 829, he took part in the Council of Paris; in 833, at Sens; and in 835, at Thionville. In the year 836, he obtained the government of the Monastery of Micy from Emperor Louis; and in the following year, he was assigned to settle a revolt of the monks of Saint-Calais and was present at the Assembly of Crecy. In 839, he signed the Agreement of Aachen. In 840, he presented his books on images to King Charles. He died in the year 843.

<margin>* To the year 825, number 74.</margin>
Three books **Against the Defense of Claudius of Turin**, in which he receives the writing of Claudius—or rather an excerpt of the writing, for he testifies that he never saw the complete book—with considerable sharpness. Meanwhile, in this entire work, Jonas <note>Jonas was the Bishop of Orléans from 818 to 843 AD.</note> defends the cause of Images with no other sentiment than that they should not be smashed or cast out of the temples; he contends that they are to be placed in churches for decoration only, and for the memory and instruction of the faithful, but are by no means to be worshipped with any form of cult. He expressly calls that superstitious, and indeed a "destructive adoration of images" <note>original: "perniciosum Imaginum adorationem"</note> that is worthy of correction. Thus, it is not without reason that Baronius*, Bellarmine, Petavius, Mabillon, and others warn their readers that our Jonas is "to be read with caution" <note>original: "cautè legendum"</note>; for although he fought against the Iconoclasts <note>Those who sought to destroy religious images.</note>, as Baronius says, he did not fight from the camp of the Orthodox Church, from which he partially disagreed due to an old error. And indeed, one must judge this way when the cause of superstition, rather than truth itself, is at stake. This work was published at Cologne in 1554; in the *Hæresiologia* <note>A collection of writings on heresies.</note> at Basel in 1556; in the *Orthodoxographa* Volume II, page 1526; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Paris 2nd edition, Volume IV, page 688. It should be noted that in the newest edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, these books by Jonas are sought in vain.

**On the Instruction of the Laity** in three books, published by D'Achéry in the *Spicilegium* Volume I.

<margin>822.</margin>
**ADALHARD**, of Frankish origin and born of a royal lineage—being the son of Count Bernard, who was the brother of King Pippin—and Abbot of Corbie, was prominent in the year 822. In that year, he was restored to his Abbey after having been banished to Aquitaine for a conspiracy entered into with King Bernard against Louis the Pious. He established the **Statutes of the Church of Corbie**, which are found in D'Achéry’s *Spicilegium* Volume IV.

<margin>824.</margin>
**EUGENIUS II**, son of Boemund, Archpriest of the Roman Church, and finally ordained Pope on June 5, 824. In the year 826, he celebrated a Council of 63 Bishops at Rome, in which 38 Canons concerning ecclesiastical matters were enacted. He died on August 27, 827. Two of his **Letters** exist in the *Councils* Volume VII, pages 1542 and 1869, along with eleven **Decrees** (some of which are actually owed to Eugenius III) on page 1543.

<margin>824.</margin>
**FRECULFUS**, formerly a monk of Fulda, was made Bishop of Lisieux <note>original: "Lexoviensis"</note> before the year 824, when he was sent as a legate to Pope Eugenius by Emperor Louis to obtain permission for a conference to be held regarding Images. The following year, he gave an account of his mission in person at the Assembly of Paris. He was present at the Council of Paris in 829, at Thionville <note>original: "Theodonis villa"</note> in 835, and at Quierzy <note>original: "Carisiacensi"</note> in 837, at which time he also had Ebbo, the Archbishop of Reims—who had been condemned for treason—committed to his custody. He attended the Council of Paris in 846 and the fourth Council of Tours in 849. He died before the year 853. He wrote a ***Chronicle*** divided into two volumes: the first pursues history from the creation of the world until the birth of our Lord in seven books; the second, containing five books, proceeds from the birth of Christ until Pope Boniface, the successor of Gregory the Great. This Chronicle is available in the Cologne edition of 1539 (folio), Heidelberg 1597 (octavo), and in the *Library of the Fathers* Volume XIV, page 1061. His **Letter** to Rabanus Maurus is prefixed to Rabanus's *Commentaries on Genesis*.

<margin>828.</margin>
**GREGORY IV**, son of John, a Priest with the title of Confessor of Saint Mark, and finally consecrated Pope of Rome on January 5, 828, after having resisted for a long time. In the year 830, he set out for Gaul to reconcile Emperor Louis and his rebellious sons, but his efforts were in vain <note>original: "operam lusit," literally "he played with his effort."</note>. He died on January 11, 844. Anastasius, in his ***Life***, recounts his various gifts, and also the monasteries and basilicas constructed by him, to the point of boredom.

<margin>9th CENTURY from 800 AD.</margin> There remain *Three Letters of the Councils, Volume VII, pages 1571, 1870* and a *Letter concerning the Monastery of Fleury* found in Baluze's *Miscellanea*, Volume II, page 145.

<margin>828.</margin> **ANSEGISUS**, the son of Anastasius and Himilrada, was educated in the Monastery of Fontenelle under Abbot Gervold, his kinsman. Later admitted to the Royal Court, he was granted the Monasteries of St. Sixtus at Reims and St. Memmius at Châlons by the Emperor Charles <note>Charlemagne</note>; and in the year 807, he was further gifted the Monastery of Saint-Germer-de-Fly, where he soon restored the ruined affairs of the community. In the year 817, he was even appointed the Overseer of Royal Works at the palace of Aachen. He was made Abbot of Luxeuil in <gloss>823</gloss> and of Fontenelle in 823 by the Emperor Louis <note>Louis the Pious</note>; in the year 827, for which he is especially famous, he compiled the *Capitularies* <term>Capitularia: A collection of royal ordinances or laws divided into short chapters (capitula)</term> of Charlemagne. In the year 831, falling into a very grave illness, he bestowed his possessions upon the monasteries. He died in the year 833, on the 13th day before the Kalends of August <note>July 20</note>, and was buried in the Monastery of Fontenelle.

He collected the *Capitularies of Charlemagne, especially concerning Ecclesiastical matters*, and arranged them into four books; into these, however, he carelessly mixed several ordinances of Louis the Pious. These were published by Pithou at *Paris, 1588* and *Mainz, 1602*; by Sirmond at *Paris, 1640*; and, to pass over other editions in silence, they were revised and illustrated with notes by Baluze at *Paris, 1677, in two volumes, folio.* Concerning Baluze’s edition, however, one may observe that <margin>* To the year 827, number 7.</margin> it agrees very little with the earlier ones. Even Charles le Cointe states * that we must admit the newest edition contradicts the ancient ones. For besides innumerable differing readings, in the Baluzian edition, Chapters 67, 68, 74, 79, 39, and 52 of the first book are missing; Chapters 89 and 90 are added to the third book, as well as Chapters 76 and 77 to the fourth book—which Cointe long ago observed were the same as Chapters 23 and 24. In all editions, three Appendices are attached to the four books of Capitularies; in the old editions, the first consists of 33 chapters, in Baluze’s 35; the second in the old editions has 36 chapters, in Baluze’s 38; the third contains 10 chapters. Not a few Capitularies of the Emperors Lothar and Charles the Bald are also mixed into these Appendices.

<margin>828.</margin> **SERGIUS**, a Historian, who suffered much for his defense of the cult of images and was therefore called a *Confessor* by Photius, flourished in the year 828. Those are entirely mistaken who wish to identify him with Sergius the Confessor mentioned in the Greek Menology <note>A church calendar with short biographies of saints</note> on May 13, who was tortured for the defense of images, stripped of his fortune, and died in exile under Leo the Isaurian around the year 735. This Sergius wrote a *Denunciatory History* <note>original: στηλιτευτικὴν / stêliteutikên</note> against the Iconoclasts <note>Those who opposed and destroyed religious images</note>, beginning from the deeds of Michael the Stammerer (namely, in the year 821) and then returning to the times of Constantine Copronymus, finally bringing the thread of his history down to the eighth year of Michael, the year of Christ <margin>* Code 67.</margin> 828. According to the judgment of Photius *, he used a style that was clear and most elegant, yet so unaffected that his speech seemed in some way to flow forth spontaneously: to put it in a word, he employed the language most suited to Ecclesiastical history. However, of the entire work, however excellent and polished, not even the smallest fragment survives today.

<margin>828.</margin> **THEOSTERICTUS**, a monk of the Monastery of Medikion in Bithynia <note>A region in modern-day Turkey</note> and a disciple of Abbot Nicetas (himself a Confessor for the cult of Images), flourished in the year 828. He wrote the *Life of his Master Nicetas*, or a *Panegyric Oration for him*, which is available in Latin in Surius, and in Greek and Latin in Henschen’s *Acts of the Saints* for April 3.

Though designated Patriarch of Constantinople by the Empress Theodora, he refused that dignity. He flourished in the year 830. He had endured many labors and hardships for the cause of images while Theodore the Studite and the Patriarch Nicephorus were still living, as <margin>To the year 835, number 70.</margin> is clear from Theodore's letter to him in Baronius; he suffered more and greater trials after the death of both under the Emperor Theophilus around the year 835, being cast into prison and tortured. He wrote a *Eulogy for Saint Dionysius the Areopagite...*

<margin>9th CENTURY. 800 AD.</margin>
<margin>830.</margin>
**ANSGAR**, a German by birth, was a student of the New Corbie Monastery <note>Corvey Abbey</note> in Saxony. Around the year 826, he set his mind toward converting the Northern nations—the Danes and the Swedes—to the faith; he pursued this diligently and successfully for many years, for which he is called the "Apostle of the Danes and the North." In the year 830 (though others record this in the year 832 or the following year), after Hamburg was elevated to a Metropolis <term>Metropolis: A primary city or see that serves as the seat of an archbishop having jurisdiction over other bishops.</term> by Emperor Louis, Ansgar was appointed the first Archbishop of Hamburg at the Diet of Aachen; he was consecrated by Drogo, the Bishop of Metz, to add to his honors. Shortly thereafter, he obtained the pallium <term>Pallium: A circular band of white wool worn by archbishops, symbolizing their authority and bond with the Holy See.</term> from Rome, having been named Legate of the Apostolic See in the Northern regions by Gregory IV. After seven years in Hamburg, he was driven out by barbarians; he then lived in a monastery he built at his estate in Ramshola, three miles from Hamburg. In the year 846, when the See of Bremen became vacant, he was also placed in charge of that church, and after twelve years, he finally obtained the union of the churches of Hamburg and Bremen. In the year 864, or at least the following year, in the 34th year of his episcopate, he passed away. He wrote the *Life of Saint Willehad, Bishop of Bremen*, comprised of two books. It is extant in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Ages*, Part III, volume 2, page 401. In the time of Albert Krantz <margin>* Metropolis, Book 1, Chapter 42, page 75.</margin> (who discusses Ansgar at length throughout his first book), there existed a small book or Psalter, containing a summary of the Psalms in a compendium—a brief but very clear monument to Ansgar’s devotion. He also wrote several letters, which have perished, or at least have not yet seen the light of day.

<margin>830.</margin>
**LUPUS**, surnamed Servatus, was a Frenchman by birth, born in the fourth province of Lyon. A Benedictine monk of Ferrières, he was sent as a deacon around the year 828 by Abbot Aldric (who became Archbishop of Sens around 829) to Rabanus, the Abbot of Fulda, so that he might draw knowledge of the Holy Scriptures from him. After spending nearly eight years among the people of Fulda, and a short stay in the Monastery of Seligenstadt with Abbot Einhard <note>Eginhard, the biographer of Charlemagne</note>, a most loyal friend, he was called to the Court by Emperor Louis and returned with him to France in the year 836. In the year 838, he was placed in charge of the Cell of Saint Josse, and in the year 842, on the 10th day before the Kalends of December <note>November 22</note>, he was named Abbot of Ferrières by the Emperor in place of Odo, who had been removed from the position for atrocious crimes. However, as Odo would by no means step down, Lupus found it necessary to drive him from the place by order of the Emperor; he discusses this at length in Letter 20 to Jonas of Orléans, in which he clearly refutes the slander that arose against him because of it. At the end of the year 844, a Synod of bishops was gathered at Vern-sur-Brenne, a royal palace: our Lupus was present, and he alone was chosen from all of them to draft the Canons <note>Church laws or decrees</note> of this Synod, a matter he discusses in Letter 42 to Hincmar, page 83. The Canons themselves are attached to the end of his letters. In the year 853, he participated in the Council of Soissons. Before the year 855, he performed a legation to Pope Leo. He departed from the living after the year 861; for Letter 125 to Bishop Folcric of Troyes provides us evidence that he was alive at that time, as the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* testify that Folcric's predecessor, Prudentius, did not die until the year 861. Many more things concerning our Lupus can be gathered conveniently and with profit to the reader from his letters. I admit there are those who write that Lupus Servatus was a different person from Lupus of Ferrières, relying on the authority of Trithemius, who records that Lupus Servatus the Priest (to whom Rabanus Maurus wrote eight books on the *Epistle to the Romans*) died in the year 851. However, since this rests on the testimony of Trithemius alone, and none of the ancients clearly distinguish two Lupuses, and all other facts agree wonderfully with our Lupus of Ferrières, it could easily be that Trithemius was mistaken in this part—especially in matters of chronology—just as he was in others. Thus, I would prefer to side with those who hold they were one and the same. Certainly, the illustrious Baluze notes such a similarity of style and phrasing between the letters of Lupus and his book and collection on the *Three Questions* that he did not hesitate to declare they were as alike as one egg to another.

# The Photian Age
<note>Named after Photius the Great, the 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople, this era is marked by significant developments in church law and the Carolingian Renaissance.</note>

<margin>
9th CENTURY from 800 AD.
</margin>

## WRITINGS.

*A Book on Three Questions*, namely: on Free Will, on the Predestination of the good and the bad, and on the "superfluous taxation" <note>original: "superfluâ taxatione"; referring to the theological debate over whether Christ's blood was shed only for the elect or for all humanity</note> of Christ’s blood—or redemption even unto the salvation of the ungodly.

*A Collection on these same Three Questions.*

*Two Letters*: one to Charles the Bald, the other to Hincmar of Reims. These short works were prepared for the press in the year 1602 by Antonius Grimbertus, a monk and librarian of the Monastery of Saint-Amand <note>original: "Elnonensis"; the Abbey of Saint-Amand on the Elnon river</note>, from an ancient manuscript. However, they were suppressed for a long time until they were finally published in 1648 through the efforts of Jacques Sirmond under the pseudonym "Donatus Candidus." In 1650, they were reprinted somewhere in Holland with a new preface added. They are also included among the 9th-century writers on Predestination and Grace, collected and edited by Gilbert Mauguin, President of the High Court of Monies, in Volume I, Part II, page 9. However, Mauguin attributes the book on the *Three Questions* to a certain Lupus Servatus, a priest of Mainz, whom he considers distinct from our Lupus of Ferrières.

*A Book of 130 Letters*, first edited by Papire Masson (Paris, 1588, in octavo). Étienne Baluze sharply criticizes this edition as being quite faulty; it was subsequently edited by Duchesne in the *Historians of France*, Volume III.

*The Life of Saint Wigbert, Abbot of Fritzlar*, written in the year 836 for Buno, Abbot of Hersfeld. Joannes Busæus published this along with the letters of Hincmar (Mainz, 1602, in quarto).

*The Life of Saint Maximin, Bishop of Trier*, written in the year 839. This is found in Surius’s collection under May 29th. In the preface, the author claims he will omit fabulous stories lest they undermine the credibility of the rest of the work. However, he did not keep his promises; for, as Baluze correctly notes, he added so many notable fables to this book that it is truly a wonder an educated man struck such obvious reefs—unless he believed that collecting fables and delighting the minds of readers with fictions was not beneath the dignity of a historian, and thus did not dare to remove what had been handed down. In that same place, the learned scholar [Baluze] discusses with just indignation and his usual honesty the many delusions of storytellers that have defiled the *Acts of the Saints*.

The works of Lupus were published, revised, and edited with notes by Baluze (Paris, 1664, in octavo), and thereafter in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XIV, page 1.

Two sermons still exist in manuscript: *A Sermon to the English on the Incursion of the Danes*, in the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge (MS 284, no. 19), and *A Sermon on the Feast of Saint Judoc* in the Lumley Library (Vol. 165). Whether these truly belong to our Lupus, let those who have the opportunity to inspect them decide.

<margin>
830.
</margin>

**ISIDORE MERCATOR**, or (as he is called in certain manuscripts following the custom of later centuries) **ISIDORE THE SINNER** <note>original: "Peccator"; a common humble epithet used by medieval clerics</note>, the "patcher-together" <note>original: "Confarcinator"; a compiler who stuffs or crams things together</note> of the Decretal Letters, seems to have lived around the year 830. Under the names of the Roman Pontiffs, from Clement of Rome down to Deusdedit (who held the papacy in the year 614), he brought to light more than eighty letters—some composed by others (though these are few) and some compiled by himself—adding several letters from bishops and synods.

<margin>
* On Liturgical Matters, Book 1, Ch. 3, § 1.
</margin>

That these letters are spurious—and fabricated not so much by "pious fraud" (as Cardinal Bona suggests in the margin note*) but by a clearly astounding imposture—was demonstrated by David Blondel in his *Pseudo-Isidore* against Turrianus. He used a long line of arguments and invincible reasons drawn from the depths of antiquity, chronology, and sacred criticism, so that to add anything further to this matter would be "to write the Iliad after Homer" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to do something that has already been done perfectly</note>. And that this is indeed the case is now acknowledged by nearly all the more sensible Papalists. I will provide one witness among many: Étienne Baluze, a great ornament of the Gallican Church. He states: "To the ancient law, which had been in force for seven hundred years or more, succeeded a 'new law' compacted from the forged letters of the most holy Bishops of the city of Rome, brought forth by that most impudent scoundrel Pseudo-Isidore, and from the new constitutions of those who occupied the Apostolic See after the time of Charlemagne." It was therefore introduced in the favorable era of Charlemagne...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous entry regarding the intellectual climate of the 9th century and the rise of significant ecclesiastical documents. # The Photian Age
<note>This era is named after Photius the Great (c. 810–893), the Patriarch of Constantinople, whose scholarship and conflicts with Rome defined 9th-century church politics.</note>

<margin>
9th CENTURY from 800 AD.
</margin>

...namely, if at any other time, due to the great confusion that had been introduced into Church governance from the astounding and miserable ignorance of the Bishops and the rest of the Clergy, and their lack of knowledge of the ancient Canons. In this turmoil of affairs, those famous and noble Letters emerged, which are attributed to the early Roman Pontiffs. They struck the minds of all by their "new antiquity" <note>original: "nova antiquitate"; a paradoxical phrase suggesting they were newly discovered but claimed to be ancient</note> and because they bore the names of the most holy Bishops. From this, a religious scruple arose in men's minds that it was not right to doubt the law contained in these sacred monuments of antiquity. Thus he [Antonio Agustín] says, and more, in his *Preface to Antonio Agustín on the Emendation of Gratian, sections 1, 2.* He had noted almost the same things earlier in his *Preface to Regino on Ecclesiastical Disciplines, sections 3, 8.*

But as to who was the first architect of this "Isidorian" collection, or at what time this masked scoundrel <note>original: "larvatus nebulo"; referring to the anonymous forger of the False Decretals</note> lived, not everyone holds the same opinion. There are those who want it to have been Isidore, Bishop of Seville, a man indeed learned and well-versed in ecclesiastical antiquity. But the timeline is inconsistent, since certain parts of this hodgepodge <note>original: "farraginis"</note> were culled from writings a full century more recent than Isidore of Seville. Moreover, it is not likely he was Spanish by birth; for at that time, Spain was oppressed under the yoke of the Saracens <note>The Muslim Umayyad conquest of the Iberian Peninsula</note> and higher learning had almost entirely gone into exile. Nor is it reasonable to believe that a Spaniard, in inventing monuments of such venerable antiquity, would not have wished to take greater care of his own homeland, since in the entire collection of Letters, only five were addressed to Spaniards. Others attribute them to Riculphus, the Prelate of Mainz, who died around the year 814.

Certainly, the man was a German-Frank, as [David] Blondel correctly notes from the Gallo-Frankish and Lombard idioms used. Benedict Levita and Hincmar of Reims, writers of almost this same time, expressly testify that they first came from the archives of the Church of Mainz through Riculphus's care; though Hincmar reports they were brought from Spain, having been deceived, it seems, by the fraud of the imposter. But the timeline again prevents the entire collection from being attributed to Riculphus; for in the Letters of Urban and John III, passages are found taken from the Council of Paris held in the year 829—fifteen years after Riculphus's death.

Hence the illustrious Blondel conjectures that this mass of letters should rather be attributed to Benedict Levita, who, when he added the three later books of *Capitularies* <note>collections of Carolingian royal and ecclesiastical laws</note> around the year 850, inserted these Letters, cut into fragments, into his capitularies. But perhaps it seems closer to the truth that the Letters were either forged or collected by Riculphus, and later revised, expanded, and reduced into this hodgepodge we now have by Benedict Levita. And since he was a strenuous advocate for the Papal Court, he seems to have undertaken the work with the intention of more plausibly defending the authority of the Roman See under the deceptive testimonies of primeval antiquity.

As for the fact that the imposter took the name "Isidore Mercator" <note>Isidore the Merchant</note> for himself, I do not know whether Blondel's conjecture should be put forward—an ingenious one, certainly, if solid enough—namely, that there was a certain Isidore, Spanish by birth and the brother of Eulogius of Córdoba, who lived in Mainz at this very time as an exile due to civil unrest in his homeland, where he actively practiced trade. The "Letter-Imposter" seems to have abused this man's name so that the unskilled might believe the Letters were brought from Spain by our "Merchant," who, as a refugee for the sake of piety, brought this most precious treasure with him to Germany, having rescued it from "barbaric lust" <note>original: "barbaricae libidini"; referring to the perceived threat of Muslim rule</note>. 

Whatever the case, one may wonder why the compiler did not extend his Letters beyond the time of Pope Deusdedit, or the year 614. This seems to me to have been done for two reasons: first, so that they might more plausibly be believed to have been collected by Isidore of Seville, who died in 636; second, lest the mask of the forgery be more easily torn off if he reached closer to his own times. Finally, it should be noted that the entire Isidorian collection, besides the Papal Letters, contains the order for celebrating a Council, a translation of the Apostolic Canons, and the Decrees of many Synods, both Greek and Latin, which are found in almost all editions of the Councils.

**ARDO**, also called **SMARAGDUS**, was a monk of the Benedictine Order at Aniane <note>Aniane was a powerful monastery in southern France</note>; he was active around the year 836. He was a disciple of Benedict of Aniane <note>Benedict of Aniane (c. 750–821) was a monastic reformer who standardized the Rule of Saint Benedict across Europe</note>, whom he attended at his death; at the request of the monks of Inden, he wrote his *Life* <note>original: "Vitam"</note>. He passed away at the age of sixty in the year 843. Several works exist under the name of Smaragdus, and there is much debate among scholars as to whether they should be attributed to this man or another <note>specifically Smaragdus of Saint-Mihiel</note>. Meanwhile, the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane* seems to belong entirely to our subject, as it was written by an eyewitness to Benedict's death. This *Life* can be found both in Menard’s second book of observations on the Benedictine Martyrology, and in Mabillon’s Benedictine ages, volume 4, part 1, page 191.

**FLORUS**, known as the *Master* <note>original: "Magister"</note>, was a Deacon of Lyons; he was active around the year 837, the year in which he attended the Council of Quierzy <note>original: "Carisiacensi"</note>, as Margarinus de la Bigne notes he read in an ancient manuscript. On account of his excellent learning and tireless persistence in reading and writing, he is highly praised by Walafrid Strabo \* and Wandalbert †; the latter adds that he gathered a library remarkable for both the number and the quality of its books. Indeed, he excelled in his reputation for doctrine among his peers to such an extent that he was chosen by the Church of Lyons above all others to refute the work on *Predestination* by John Scotus <note>John Scotus Erigena (c. 810–877), a famous Irish philosopher whose views on predestination were controversial</note>. To the illustrious Mauguin \*, it seems he was selected for this task even more because he had previously issued a certain sermon (mentioned by Hincmar in his work on Predestination, chapter 11) in which he had published a brilliant example of his teaching on Divine Foreknowledge and Predestination. He wrote this work in the name of his Church around the year 852. How long he lived after that, I have not yet discovered.

*A Commentary on all the Epistles of Saint Paul*, composed from the writings of Saint Augustine. It is found among the works of Bede, though falsely attributed to him. Elsewhere, however, he observes that in three manuscripts in the Library of Saint Gall dating back 800 years, this same exposition of Bede is contained under the name of **FLORUS THE PRESBYTER**. **THEGANUS**, a Frank by nation, a noble and learned man, was the Country Bishop <note>original: "Chorepiscopus"</note> and Suffragan <note>An assistant or subordinate bishop</note> of Bishops Amalarius and Hetti of Trier. He flourished in the year 837, according to Walafrid Strabo; he wrote, briefly and truthfully rather than elegantly, the *Annals of the Deeds of Emperor Louis* <note>Louis the Pious (reigned 814–840), the son of Charlemagne</note> from the year 813 to 837. Petrus Pithoeus was the first to publish these, along with Walafrid’s preface and chapters, among the *Frankish Writers of the Same Period* at Frankfurt in 1594, p. 291; later they were published by André Duchesne in *Frankish Writers*, Volume 2. A manuscript copy much more extensive than the published editions is kept in the Vienna Library, as attested by the famous Peter Lambeck <note>original: "Cl. Lambecius"</note> in his work *On the Vienna Library*, Book 2, Chapter 5, p. 391, which provides a two-year appendix missing from Pithoeus’s edition.

**CHRISTIANUS DRUTHMARUS**, nicknamed *The Grammarian*, a native of Aquitaine, was a monk of the Benedictine Order at the Monastery of Corvey. He seems to have flourished around the year 840, or at least shortly thereafter, since he mentions the conversion of the Bulgarians to the Christian faith, which occurred in the year 845. According to Sigebert*, he wrote a *Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew*, which was produced through the care of Joannes Secerius at Hagenau in the year 1530, chapter 72. In this Commentary, there is more than one passage that so strongly refutes the modern dogma of Transubstantiation that the Catholic <note>original: "Pontificii"</note> writers Sixtus of Siena, Cardinal Perron, de la Bigne, and others rave almost to the point of hoarseness, shouting that Secerius, a Lutheran, corrupted Druthmarus, and that this is clear from the evidence of the manuscript codex. To ensure that the mouth of such unbridled passion for slander might be stopped forever, and at the same time to vindicate the reliability and integrity of the Secerian edition, Edmond Albertinus* brought forward a Strasbourg edition from the year 1514—three years before the rise of Luther—with a privilege from Emperor Maximilian and the insignia of Pope Leo X placed on the first page, unearthed from manuscript codices by the care of Jacob Wimpfeling. In this edition, the same passages are found word-for-word as in the Hagenau edition. Yet, there is still no end to the dispute. For Philippe Labbe*, not knowing where to turn, attacks Albertinus because he did not add where he saw that edition or in what library he found it; Labbe says he himself had never come across it until now—which is no wonder, since it was unknown to the diligent Germans Gesner, Simler, and Fries, as well as to Miraeus and other more recent authors. Finally, he says that the reliability of Albertinus, a heretical man and an <term>apostate</term> <note>original: "ἀποστάτου"; one who has abandoned their religious faith</note> from the faith and religion of his ancestors, is highly suspect to him. However, so that every opportunity for doubting or slandering this matter may be removed in the future, we advise the fair reader that this very edition by Wimpfeling is in the possession of that distinguished man Thomas Tenison, a famous theologian of the Church of England...

**GOTTSCHALK**, also called Fulgentius, a Frank by nation—born, it seems, in Belgica Secunda—was educated in the Monastery of Reichenau <note>original: "Augiæ divitis"</note> under Abbot Tato in the finer letters, in which he excelled to such an extent that he is said to have drawn the name Fulgentius from them. Later, having become a Benedictine monk of Orbais, he flourished in the year 840. While the see of Reims was vacant due to the deposition of Ebbo, he was ordained a priest by Ricbold, the chorepiscopus <term>chorepiscopus: a "country bishop" who assisted the main bishop in rural areas</term>, though Rothad, the Bishop of Soissons, in whose diocese the Monastery of Orbais was located, took this badly. To avoid ill-will, Gottschalk, led by a zeal for travel, went to Rome in 847 and journeyed through Italy, Dalmatia, and Pannonia, returning to his homeland the following year. Upon his return, Count Eberhard in Cisalpine Gaul received him kindly as a guest, with whom he stayed for some time; and he now began to bring forth more openly the doctrines he had been suppressing in his heart. 

He was most devoted to the teachings of St. Augustine, and first began to raise questions about the manner of seeing God in the future life. Having been warned in vain about this matter by Lupus of Ferrières, he disputed too inquisitively about Predestination and the absolute decree of Reprobation <term>reprobation: the theological concept that God predestines some souls to damnation</term>, about the grace of God, and other matters pertaining to this. From this, he stirred up grave controversies over these doctrines at that time, with almost the entire chorus of Gallic scholars splitting into different sides: on one side, Remigius of Lyon, Prudentius of Troyes, and Ratramnus of Corbie defended Gottschalk; on the other, Hincmar of Reims, Amalarius of Lyon, Rabanus Maurus, and John Scotus <note>John Scotus Eriugena</note> attacked him most fiercely. 

The opinion which he held regarding double Predestination and other chapters annexed to it, I shall record here in his own words, as they are found in <margin>* *On Predestination* ch. 5, p. 26.</margin> * Hincmar: *“I, Gottschalk, believe and confess, etc., that there is a double Predestination, whether of the Elect to rest or of the Reprobate to death: because just as the immutable God, before the foundation of the world, immutably predestined all His Elect to eternal life through His free grace; likewise, all the Reprobate, who will be condemned on the day of judgment because of their own evil merits, the same immutable God, through His just judgment, immutably predestined to a deserved everlasting death.”* He later explained these views more broadly in more than one booklet and more than one published confession. 

Indeed, he spoke even more harshly and dangerously on these matters, if we listen to Rabanus, Hincmar, and other writers of this time. Regarding the doctrine of Free <margin>* Cited in Hincm. ibid. ch. 21, p. 118.</margin> Will, he professed that he felt entirely one with Blessed Augustine, *“expressly damning the erroneous opinions of Gennadius of Marseilles and the ruinous doctrine of the unfortunate Cassian.”* <note>These figures were associated with Semi-Pelagianism, which Gottschalk viewed as a heresy against Augustine's total reliance on grace.</note> <margin>† Ibid. ch. 24, p. 149, 150.</margin> Regarding the Will of God, he speaks † thus: *“All those,”* he says, *“whom God wills to be saved are saved without doubt, nor can any be saved except those whom God wills to be saved; nor is there anyone whom God wills to be saved who is not saved: because our God has done whatever He willed; thus all those are saved whom He wills to be saved, and those whom God does not will to be saved are not saved.”* 

Finally, regarding the death of Christ <margin>† Ibid. ch. 27, p. 211. Ch. 29, p. 226.</margin>, he holds these views †: *“that for all those impious people and sinners whom the Son of God came to redeem by shedding His own blood, the omnipotent goodness of God wills only those predestined to life to be saved irrevocably... but for all those impious people and sinners for whom the same Son of God neither took on a body, nor offered prayer, nor, I say, shed His blood, nor was He in any way crucified for them—since He foreknew they would be the most wicked and pre-ordained them most justly to be cast into eternal torments—He does not at all wish them to be saved in any way... He willed to be the Savior of none of the reprobate, the Redeemer of none, and the Crowner of none.”* 

These are excerpts from the booklet which Gottschalk offered to Rabanus Maurus at the Synod of Mainz, who had recently refuted his opinion in a treatise on Pre- <margin>Rabanus, *Synodal Letter to Hincmar*; *Annals of Fulda* & *Chronicle of Hirsau* at the year 848; *Annals of St. Bertin* year 849.</margin> destination written to Bishop Nothingus. Therefore, in the year 848, around the Calends of October <note>October 1st</note>, a Synod was held at Mainz, attended by many Gallic prelates, abbots, and very famous monks. Gottschalk was condemned by them and sent back to his Archbishop, Hincmar of Reims, after first taking an oath that he would not return to the kingdom of Louis hereafter. In the year 849, on the occasion of a royal assembly, a meeting of several bishops was held at Quierzy <note>original: "Carisiacum"</note>; in which, regarding the case of Gottschalk...

...regarding Gottschalk and the examination of his case, they decreed by a Synodal Sentence that he was to be deposed from the priestly rank. Furthermore, lest he spread his dogmas more widely, he was to be confined in a prison cell <term>ergastulo: a Roman-style prison or workhouse, here used for monastic confinement</term> among the monks of the Abbey of Hautvillers. Finally, according to the Rule of his order, he was to be punished with the harshest floggings; this was carried out until he delivered the book he had written against Rabanus to the flames with his own hands. In the year 855, the Synod of Valence was convened, presided over by Remigius of Lyons and several others. In this assembly, canons were established in favor of Gottschalk, opposing the chapters of the Synod of Quierzy <note>original: "Cariifacensis"</note>.

Meanwhile, Hincmar <note>Hincmar of Reims, Gottschalk's primary theological opponent</note> attempted by every possible means to recall Gottschalk to a sounder mind, but it was in vain. Indeed, Gottschalk remained unmoved in defending his opinion. To more plausibly demonstrate his innocence, following the impious and perverse custom of that age, he declared himself ready to undergo the "Judgment of God," as they called it: † specifically, he offered to enter one by one into four vats of boiling water, oil, and burning pitch. He boldly challenged his adversaries to undergo the same trial. He died in the year 870, or at least did not long survive after that date, having experienced the hardships of prison for twenty-one years.

**BERTRAMUS**, or more correctly **RATRAMNUS**, a Frank by nation, it seems, was a monk and priest in the old Monastery of Corbie. Eventually, with the favor of Charles the Bald <note>King of West Francia and later Holy Roman Emperor</note>, he became the Provost of the Abbey of Orbais in the Diocese of Soissons. He flourished in the year 840, at which time, or shortly before, he prepared himself for writing. He composed a work *On the Virgin Giving Birth to the Lord*, against which Paschasius Radbertus is said to have written two books. In the year 849, while the controversy surrounding Gottschalk was burning, he published his books *On Predestination*; and shortly thereafter, he seems to have released that most celebrated little book *On the Eucharist*. In the year 866, when the controversy between the Latins and the Greeks was intensifying, the teachers of the Gallican Church were asked by Pope Nicholas to maintain the cause of the Westerners against the Greeks. Among these, at the urging of Hincmar, our Ratramnus also took up his part, which he performed strenuously and vigorously. He was still among the living in the year 870, provided that he is the same Ratramnus, a ninety-year-old priest, whom Hincmar mentions in chapter 1 of his *Chapters to his Nephew*. He was a pious and modest man, and undoubtedly learned, held in high regard by all the most learned men of his century. Indeed, with the exception of the Eucharistic dispute, he has been adorned with the highest praise even by Roman Catholic writers.
