**GOTTSCHALK**, also called Fulgentius <note>He was likely named after Fulgentius of Ruspe, a 6th-century theologian whose views on grace he championed</note>, a Frank by nationality, having been born, it seems, in Belgica Secunda <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day northern France and Belgium</note>. He was educated in the liberal arts at the Abbey of Reichenau <note>original: "Augiâ divitis"</note> under Abbot Tato, in which he so excelled that he is said to have earned the name *Fulgentius* <note>meaning "the shining" or "bright one"</note> from his skill. Afterwards, having become a Benedictine monk at Orbais, he became famous around the year 840. While the See of Reims was vacant due to the deposition of Ebbo, he was ordained a priest by Ricbold, the Rural Bishop <term>Chorepiscopo: a "country bishop" who assisted the regional bishop but had limited powers</term>, much to the annoyance of Rothad, the Bishop of Soissons, in whose diocese the monastery of Orbais was located. To avoid resentment, Gottschalk, led by a desire for travel, went to Rome in the year 847 and journeyed through Italy, Dalmatia, and Pannonia, returning to his homeland the following year. Upon his return, he was kindly received as a guest by Count Eberhard in Cisalpine Gaul, with whom he stayed for some time; it was then that he began to more openly bring forth the doctrines he had been suppressing in his heart. He was a most devoted student of the teachings of St. Augustine, and at first began to raise questions about the manner of seeing God in the future life. Having been warned in vain about this matter by Lupus of Ferrières, he began to dispute all too curiously concerning Predestination, the absolute decree of Reprobation <note>The theological concept that God eternally condemns some to hell just as he chooses others for heaven</note>, the grace of God, and other matters relating to this. From this, he stirred up grave controversies regarding these doctrines at that time, with almost the entire choir of Gallican <note>French</note> scholars splitting into different factions: on one side, Remigius of Lyons, Prudentius of Troyes, and Ratramnus of Corbie defended Gottschalk; on the other, Hincmar of Reims, Amalarius of Lyons, Rabanus Maurus, and John Scotus [Eriugena] attacked him most fiercely. The opinion which he held regarding "double predestination" and the other points annexed to it, I shall set down here in his own words, just as they are recorded in <margin>* On Predestination, chapter 5, page 26.</margin> * Hincmar:

> **I, Gottschalk,** believe and confess, etc., that there is a double Predestination <note>original: "gemina Praedestinatio"</note>, namely of the Elect to rest, and of the Reprobate to death: because just as the unchangeable God, before the foundation of the world, unchangeably predestined all His Elect to eternal life through His free grace; likewise, the very same unchangeable God unchangeably predestined all the Reprobate—who will be condemned on the day of judgment because of their own evil merits—to a death they deserved for eternity through His just judgment.

### WORKS.

<margin>9th CENTURY from 800 AD.</margin>
*On the Virgin's Birth, or on the Nativity of Christ*, a book edited by d’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, Volume I, page 218.

*Two Books on Predestination*. These are extant in Gilbert Mauguin’s *Collection of Writers on Grace, etc.*, Volume I, page 29, and in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patr."</note>, Volume XV, page 442.

*Four Books Against the Errors of the Greeks*, first edited by Luc d'Achery in the *Spicilegium*, Volume II, page 1.

*A Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord*. How openly and eloquently he discusses the matter of the Eucharist here, and how clearly he refutes the dogma of Transubstantiation <term>Transubstantiation: the belief that the bread and wine literally become the physical body and blood of Christ</term> as it is explained in the Papal schools, is known to anyone who has even begun the most basic study of theology. Consequently, in order to banish this small work to the madhouse <note>original: "Anticyras," a classical reference to a place where madness was treated</note>, or rather to the underworld, the Papists have attacked it with every possible engine of war. It was marked with a "black coal" <note>An idiom meaning to be officially condemned or blacklisted</note> by the Censors of Trent, the scholars of Louvain, Sixtus of Siena, Bellarmine, Genebrard, Possevino, Gregory of Valentia, Gretser, and others. There are those who strive to diminish the author’s reputation; others slander him as a heretic, a lover of novelty, and a monk rebelling against his superiors—charges clearly contradicted by the man’s orderly character and his untainted reputation throughout so many centuries. Others cry out that the work is corrupt and tampered with; however, the many ancient manuscripts provide evidence against them, as does the *Paschal Homily* of our own Ælfric <note>Ælfric of Eynsham (c. 955–1010), an Anglo-Saxon abbot whose writings on the Eucharist were rediscovered by Reformation scholars</note>, who flourished in the year 960 and took his text almost word-for-word from Ratramnus's booklet. Finally, others wish to claim that John Scotus Eriugena, rather than Ratramnus, is the author. What of it? As if John the Scot were not equal in both age and learning. But the honest confession of Jean Mabillon <margin>* Benedictine Annals, Century IV, part 2, Preface, number 83.</margin> easily refutes these people; he admits that he found the name of Ratramnus at both the beginning and the end of a very old, eight-hundred-year-old manuscript from the Monastery of Lobbes. Indeed, Antonius Sanderus had mentioned this Lobbes manuscript long ago in his *Library of Belgian Manuscripts, part I, page 303*. Truly, these men—otherwise serious and learned—labor over trifles when they recently took it upon themselves to prove that Ratramnus, in this little work, favors the Roman dogma of the Eucharist, or at least does not oppose it. In reality, he is as far from that dogma as the East is from the West. What will these promisers bring forth that is worthy of such a great gap? As far as I am concerned, these new defenders of transubstantiation may go their own way; they might as well transform Ratramnus into Paschasius <note>Paschasius Radbertus was Ratramnus’s contemporary and rival who argued for a more literal physical presence in the Eucharist</note> himself, for I would find it no harder to believe they were one and the same person than to believe Ratramnus held the same doctrine on this matter as Paschasius and the modern Roman Church.

This book was published at *Cologne in 1532; Geneva in 1541 in octavo;* in the *Micropresbyticon at Basel, 1550, page 513;* together with Paschasius Radbertus at *Cologne, 1551 in octavo;* among the *Small Works* of Feuguereus at *Leiden, 1579 in octavo;* in the *Catalog of Witnesses to the Truth, Geneva, 1608 in folio;* and in Latin and French in the year 1672. Finally, to say nothing of the many editions of English translations, a Latin-English edition recently appeared in *London, 1686 in octavo*, to which the editor prefixed a dissertation in our native tongue, in which he copiously and learnedly vindicates Ratramnus against all the objections and slanders of the Papists.

*Book on the Soul*. This exists in manuscript in the Lambeth Library, the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge (Code 301, number 4), the Church of Salisbury, and in the possession of Mabillon.

A book written by Ratramnus in defense of a certain ancient hymn has been lost. Hincmar <note>Hincmar (c. 806–882), the powerful Archbishop of Reims</note> had ordered this verse to be erased: [*We ask you, O Triple and One Deity*], commanding that [*O Highest Deity*] be sung in his church thereafter.

<margin>841.</margin>

<margin>841.</margin>
**AMULO**, or **Amulus**, or **Amularius**, likely a Gaul by birth, was first a Deacon of Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunensis"</note>, and then, after the death of Agobard, was ordained Archbishop of that same Church on January 15 <note>original: "XVIII. Kal. Februarii"</note>, 841. Consulted in the year 844 by Bishop Theobold of Langres <note>original: "Theoboldo Lingonensi"</note> concerning uncertain relics of Saints, and concerning the miracles which were said to happen because of them, he wrote a grave letter to him against the rashness of certain monks, whom he calls "vile and worthless little men" <note>original: "viles & nequam homunculos"</note> (to use the words of the illustrious Baluze) who were selling those relics. He stood with Hincmar against Gottschalk <note>A monk famous for his controversial views on "double predestination," which argued that God predestined some to hell just as he predestined others to heaven</note>, and was still living in the year 852. If indeed he wrote against Gottschalk in that year, otherwise nothing is clear regarding the time of his death. Certainly, it can be gathered that he wrote around this time, both because on page 169 he says that Gottschalk *for several years now has remained cut off from the Body of the Church by a just sentence of severity, and deprived of all fellowship and comfort of the Good*; and because not far from the beginning of the letter he seems to indicate that the letters of the three bishops—namely Hincmar, Pardulus, and Rabanus—had not yet been delivered to him, which were nonetheless written at the end of the year 852.

->WRITINGS.<-

*A Letter to Bishop Theobold of Langres*, the occasion of which we related above.
*A Letter to Gottschalk*, written, as we said, around the year 852, in which he deals with this wretched monk with great sincerity and gentleness of mind; nevertheless, he not only studiously refutes his erroneous opinions, but also justly reproves him for his perverse and insolent behavior and the obstinate persistence of his mind. Sirmond was the first to bring it to light, and others after him, including the illustrious Mauguin in the *Collection of 9th-Century Writers, Volume II,* who presents it divided into sections and illustrated with his own notes, in the *Historical Dissertation, chapter 23, page 195.*
*Response to a certain person's question on divine Foreknowledge, or Predestination, and on free will.*
*On the Grace and Foreknowledge of God, and on predestination and free will, also on the hope and trust of salvation, and on the opinion of Saint Augustine.*

*Opinions of Blessed Augustine, taken from his books on the aforementioned matters, and organized into a single series of distinct chapters.* The reader should note that these last three small works in the Trier Manuscript—from which Sirmond took them—were anonymous, placed after the letter of Amulo to Gottschalk; so much so that it was uncertain whether they should be attributed to him. Baluze agrees with the illustrious Mauguin that the first, or the *Response of Florus, Deacon of Lyon, concerning Predestination*, is a sermon. Mauguin, in his *Dissertation chapter 22, page 169*, contends that the second work, which is missing its beginning, is nothing other than Amulo’s letter to Hincmar, sent together with the letter to Gottschalk. Whether they have seen this correctly, others may judge. Jacques Sirmond, who first published it, attributed the third work, or the *Collection of Opinions*, to our Amulo, though only by conjecture.

Stephen Baluze published these works of Amulo with notes at the end of *Agobard, Volume II, page 135.* From there they were transferred into the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XIV, page 329.*

*Against the Jews, Book I, addressed to King Charles <note>Charles the Bald</note>, brother of Emperor Lothar.* Pierre Chifflet published this in *Dijon, 1656*, under the name of Rabanus Maurus along with the works of Fulgentius, etc.; this was entirely in error, as Trithemius <margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, folio 56.</margin> explicitly attributes it to our Amulo, an opinion which certain manuscript codices clearly confirm.

### 842. JOHN

Patriarch of Jerusalem, who flourished around the year 842, specifically after images were finally restored in the Greek Church and obtained a fixed and unmovable place, and after image-veneration <note>original: "Iconodulia"</note> began to be held in high esteem among all Greeks. He wrote—or rather translated into Greek from a version written in Arabic—the *Life of St. John of Damascus*, which is monstrously full of fables and absurdities. This *Life* exists in Latin in almost all editions of Damascus's works and in Surius, May 6; in Greek, at *Rome, 1553, in octavo*, and in the *Basel edition of Damascus, 1575.*

### 842. GEORGE

Called the Sinner <note>original: "Hamartolus"</note>, a Greek by nationality and an Archimandrite <note>a superior of a monastery or group of monasteries</note> by rank. He flourished around the year 842, to which he brought his history. Men who are otherwise very learned mistakenly confuse him with George Syncellus, a writer from the end of the previous century; Leo Allatius deals with this matter learnedly and at length in his *Discourse on the Georges and their writings, page 323.* Our George wrote a *Chronicle* from the creation of the world to Michael, the son of Emperor Theophilus, woven together from various and diverse chroniclers and sacred interpreters. As Allatius notes on *page 320*, it is not particularly rich in historical facts, but rather long in its discussions and authorities of the Holy Fathers used to strengthen the points of faith. Most of the content is described in Cedrenus, Theophanes, Glycas, and others, in almost the same words and opinions, with very few exceptions. No one would doubt that those authors drew their material from this work as if from a fountain, since they are later writers. This history is especially necessary for explaining obscure and difficult passages in other writers. This *Chronicle* exists as a Greek manuscript in various libraries: the Bavarian, the Royal Library in Paris, and especially the Imperial Library in Vienna, from which Lambecius provided an excerpt in his *Commentary, book 2, chapter 7, page 588.* Also by our George is a *Homily, or Fragment on the Finding of the Cross*, which Gretser published in *On the Cross, Volume II*, as it was taken from this very *Chronicle*.

### 842. METHODIUS

<margin>
See the Greek Menology and the Anonymous author in Allatius on Methodius, p. 361.
</margin>

Called the Confessor <note>original: "Homologeta"</note>, a Sicilian by nationality, born to noble and wealthy parents at Syracuse. Polished by a domestic education, he set out for Constantinople, and having embraced the monastic way of life there, he established his seat in a monastery built on the island of Chios. After this, having been made a Legate <note>original: "Apocrisiarius"</note> and stationed at Rome, he was falsely accused of adultery; he cleared himself of the crime by openly revealing a physical defect of nature <note>The text suggests he proved his innocence by demonstrating a physical inability to have committed the act</note>. Having returned to Greece, he was thrown into the prison at Acrita by Michael the Stammerer <note>original: "Michaele Balbo"</note> before the year 829 for defending the veneration of images. In the year 834, Emperor Theophilus, fearing that Methodius would stir up rebellions, took him along in the army against the Saracens, and after the return...

In the year 842, he was appointed Patriarch of Constantinople by Michael III "the Porphyrogenitus" <note>original: "Porphyrogenne"; a title meaning "born in the purple," referring to a child born to a reigning Emperor</note>. ->W R I T I N G S.<-

*Eulogy for Saint Dionysius the Areopagite.* Published separately in Greek at *Florence, 1516*, in octavo; *Paris, 1562*, in octavo; and in Greek and Latin among the *Works of Dionysius* at *Antwerp, 1634*, Volume II, page 242. Everything that Methodius includes in this Eulogy regarding Dionysius seems to me clearly taken from Hilduin’s *Areopagitica* <note>Hilduin was a Frankish abbot who conflated Dionysius the Areopagite with Denis, the first bishop of Paris</note>. Indeed, he could easily have obtained those writings from Rome, where he had lived for a long time. This is especially likely since Hilduin, at the time he was collecting the *Areopagitica* from all quarters, testified in his *Rescript to Emperor Louis* (number 10) that the Greek writers had said nothing about the death of Dionysius, because his passage into Gaul was entirely unknown to them due to the great distance of those lands. Nevertheless, there is no small controversy among the learned on this matter. Jacques Sirmond, Jean de Launoy, and other more discerning critics explicitly affirm that he took his material from Hilduin’s collections and demonstrate this with a long series of arguments. Leo Allatius, in his *Discourse on the Writings of the Methodiuses*, does not dare to stubbornly deny this, although after presenting arguments for both sides, he seems to lean toward the opinion that Methodius and Syncellus drew their material not from Hilduin’s *Areopagitica*, but from older Greek records.

*Sermon against those who say: What did the crucified Son of God profit us?* This survives in Greek and Latin in Gretser’s *On the Cross*, Volume II, page 1667. It contains two fragments which Gretser retrieved from the Augsburg Library. He contends they should not be attributed to Methodius the Elder <note>Methodius of Olympus, d. 311</note> because they mention Imperial Standards <note>term: "Vexillorum Imperialium"; likely referring to the Labarum</note> being changed into the form of the Cross. Leo Allatius, in his *Discourse on the Writings of the Methodiuses*, page 348, attempts to solve this objection, though quite weakly; there he also presents a third fragment on the suffering of Christ from the same library in Greek and Latin.

*Sermon on the Meeting of Simeon and Anna in the Temple, and on the Mother of God.*
*Sermon for Palm Sunday.* These two sermons exist in Greek and Latin among the works of Methodius of Patara edited by François Combefis, *Paris, 1644*, in folio, where they are discussed.

*Eulogy for Saint Agatha, Virgin and Martyr.* Found in Latin in the *Preacher’s Library of the Holy Fathers* by François Combefis. Leo Allatius possessed the Greek version, though it was mutilated, as noted in his work on *Methodius*, page 365. Leonardus Pate—an alumnus of the Greek College and primary professor of Greek Letters at the University of Messina—possessed the complete version; whether they have been published, I have not yet learned.

*The Penitential Canons of Methodius* are found in Balsamon’s Greek volume of Canons, which Gentian Hervet published in a Latin translation. See what Baronius says about them under the year 842, number 26, etc. Constantine Harmenopulus, in his *Epitome of Canons, Section IV*, cites them under the name "Distinctions" <note>original: "διαγνώσεως" (diagnōseōs)</note>. Arcudius contends they belong to Methodius the Junior, the Patriarch, though Leo Allatius, led by better reasoning, was unwilling to support him in this matter.

<margin>842.</margin>
## **WALAFRID, called STRABO or STRABUS**,
German by birth and a Benedictine monk by vocation, was a disciple of Rabanus Maurus of Fulda. He was the Dean of the Monastery of St. Gall and was finally created Abbot of Reichenau <note>original: "Augiæ majoris"; the "Greater Island," referring to the monastery on Reichenau island</note> in the Diocese of Constance in the year 842. He died in the year 849. He was a learned and wise man, distinguished above others in the knowledge of literature, to use the words of the monk Iso of St. Gall regarding him.

<margin>843.</margin>
**NITHARD**, son of Angilbert (later Abbot of Saint-Riquier <note>original: "Centulensis"</note>, who departed this life on **February 18, 814**) and grandson of Charlemagne <note>original: "Caroli M."</note> through his daughter Bertha. After he had fulfilled many embassies at Court and commands in the army, he renounced secular life and followed the monastic path, being made Abbot of Saint-Riquier. Lupus of Ferrières mentions Nithard’s arrival at Silvacus, sent by Abbot Marcward of Prüm, in Letter 55. The illustrious Baluze suspects, not without merit, that this was our Nithard, and conjectures that he was educated in the Monastery of Saint-Riquier and lived for some time as a guest with Marcward of Prüm; finally returning to his own people, he was made Abbot of Saint-Riquier in the Diocese of Amiens. He flourished in the year 843, at which time he composed his work. He died, so they say, in the year 853. He wrote *four books on the Discord of the sons of Emperor Louis the Pious, beginning from the year 814 and progressing to the year 843*. Pierre Pithou was the first to publish these among contemporary writers at *Paris, 1588, in octavo*; *Frankfurt, 1594, in octavo, page 433*; and then Duchesne among the Frankish writers, Volume II, page 259.

<margin>844.</margin>
**SERGIUS II**, son of Sergius, of noble birth, Archpriest of the Roman Church, and Pope from the year 844, ordained on **January 27**. Immediately at the start of his Pontificate, Louis <note>Louis II, later Holy Roman Emperor</note>, sent by his father Emperor Lothair, rushed to Rome to command the Romans that they should no longer dare to ordain an elected Pope before the Emperor had approved the election. Soon the Emperor himself arrived, and he had his son Louis anointed as King of the Lombards by the Pope. Sergius died on **January 27**, 847. There exists a single *Letter to the Transalpine Bishops regarding the precedence of Drogo of Metz* <note>original: "Metomaricensis"</note>, Vicar of the Apostolic See, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume VII, page 1799.

<margin>844.</margin>
**PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS**, a Frank <note>original: "gente Gallus"</note> by birth, was born around the year 786. He placed his first apprenticeships in piety and learning among the monks who served the larger community of the Nuns of Soissons. Having become an adult, he took the monastic habit in the old Monastery of Corbie under Abbot Adalard. In the year 844, he obtained the leadership of the Monastery of Corbie. He took part in the Synod of Quierzy <note>original: "Carisiacensi"</note> against Gottschalk in the year 848. He died in the year 851, on **April 26.**

<meta>This page continues the discussion of 9th-century ecclesiastical writers, focusing on Paschasius Radbertus, a Benedictine monk and theologian whose work on the Eucharist became a cornerstone of later medieval doctrine. It follows the entry for Walafrid Strabo and others of the mid-800s.</meta>

April. He was indeed a man not without learning, but one who relied too much on the strength of his own intellect. He was the first author—as [Robert] Bellarmine <margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 266.</margin> himself admits—who wrote seriously and at great length concerning the reality of the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Eucharist. Jacques Sirmond <note>A 17th-century Jesuit scholar and historian</note> agrees with this quite frankly, saying: *“He was the first to explain the genuine sense of the Catholic Church in such a way that he opened the path for others,”* who later wrote much on the same subject. Indeed, Paschasius's own words and his manner of speaking, which had been unheard of through all previous ages, confirm this to be the case. He says, “All things that the Lord willed, He did in heaven and on earth; <margin>† On the Body and Blood of the Lord, ch. 1.</margin> and because He willed it, [the bread] and blood are to be believed after the consecration.” Hence, Truth itself said to the disciples: “This is my flesh for the life of the world.” And to speak even more wonderfully: it is clearly none other than that very flesh which was born of Mary, suffered on the cross <note>original: "passa in carne", literally 'suffered in the flesh'</note>, and rose from the tomb. This, I say, is that very same flesh, and therefore it is the flesh of Christ which is still offered today for the life of the world, and when it is received worthily, eternal life is surely renewed within us. From these words, Paschasius's mind is sufficiently clear, so I shall set aside other testimonies for now.

-># W R I T I N G S.<-

**Twelve books of Commentaries on the Gospel of Saint Matthew.**
**Three books of Exposition on Psalm 44.**
**Five books of Exposition on the Lamentations of Jeremiah.** These were published separately in *Basel, 1502*, and *Cologne, 1532*.
**A book on the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ, addressed to Placidus.** According to the common calculation of scholars, this was written in the year 818; however, Charles Le Cointe <note>A French ecclesiastical historian</note> argues sharply and at length that it was written after 826, specifically around 831. See his notes on this matter for the years 818, 826, and 831. A dispute has arisen among the learned regarding this book (Number XXXVIII), which is not easily resolved. Certainly, many manuscript codices explicitly attribute it to Rabanus Maurus <note>A contemporary of Paschasius and Archbishop of Mainz</note>—namely one in the library of St. John's College, another in the Benedictine library at Cambridge, and others elsewhere. It was published under Rabanus's name at the end of Bertram's work in *Cologne, 1551*. Indeed, evidence can be sought from the work itself to suggest it is not by Paschasius, especially what it says regarding the "threefold body of Christ," which does not quite harmonize with other passages by Paschasius. On the other hand, there are very ancient manuscript codices that clearly vindicate Paschasius Radbertus as the author. The illustrious Mr. [Pierre] Allix <note>A prominent French Protestant theologian</note> recently affirmed in person that he possessed a very old one, written not long after the age of Paschasius himself. If I remember correctly, it is cited under Paschasius's name by Odo of Cluny, who was famous at the beginning of the following century. It is placed among his works by Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a German Benedictine abbot and polymath</note> and is considered his offspring by a far greater number of scholars. As for the passages concerning the threefold body of Christ that seem to conflict, perhaps they are not to be understood in the same sense everywhere. However, I do not take it upon myself to settle this dispute; nevertheless, I confess I lean toward the opinion that the book should be attributed to Paschasius. Meanwhile, it may be noted that in this very work Paschasius teaches several things that by no means agree with the accepted doctrine of the Roman Church regarding the Eucharist, especially in chapters 3, 4, and 15. Consequently, Jacques Sirmond found it necessary to apply certain <term>sharp medicines</term> <note>original Greek: "oxea pharmaka"; a metaphor for harsh interpretive corrections or explanations</note> to them, which are hardly worthy of the candor and genius of so great a man. It was published separately by the care of Jean de Gagny at *Haguenau, 1528*; under the name of Rabanus Maurus at *Cologne, 1551*; restored to its true author in an octavo edition at *Louvain, 1561*; and finally, based on the authority of four manuscript codices, by the care of Johannes Fuchtenius at *Helmstedt, 1616*.

**A Letter to Frudegard on the Body and Blood of the Lord**, to which is attached an **Exposition** on the text *“While they were eating,”* etc., from the Commentaries on Matthew.
**The Life of Saint Adelhard, Abbot of Corbie.** This is found in Surius and Bollandus <note>Authors of major hagiographical collections</note> under **January 2**.
**The Passion of the Martyr Saints Rufinus and Valerius**, which Paschasius polished in a more elegant style, as it had become corrupted and debased in his own age.

<margin>9th CENTURY from 800 AD.</margin> The works of Paschasius listed above were collected into a single volume by Jacques Sirmond <note>A renowned Jesuit scholar (1559–1651) known for editing works of the Church Fathers</note> and published in *Paris*, 1618, in folio; they were subsequently included in the *Library of the Fathers* [Bibliotheca Patrum], Volume 14, page 356.

*The Life of Saint Wala, Abbot*, written after that of his brother Adelhard of Corbie, under the title *The Epitaph of Arsenius* <note>original: "Epitaphii Arsenii"; Arsenius was a pseudonym used for Wala in this biographical dialogue</note>. It was first published by Jean Mabillon in the *Benedictine Age* [Sæc. Benedict.], Volume 4, part 1, page 453.

Two books *On the Birth of the Virgin*, which were previously attributed to Ildefonsus of Toledo and frequently published under his name, were finally restored to Paschasius Radbertus by Luc d'Achéry <note>A Benedictine scholar of the Congregation of Saint Maur</note> based on the evidence of manuscript codices, and published under his name in the *Spicilegium*, Volume 12, page 1.

<margin>
845.
Flodoard, History of Reims, Book 3, throughout.
</margin>
**HINCMAR**, born of a noble family among the Franks, was educated from childhood in the Monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris under Abbot Hilduin. There, he made wonderful progress in both literature and piety; and since he was endowed with a fortunate and sharp intellect, he earned no small favor in the court of Emperor Louis <note>Louis the Pious (reigned 814–840)</note>. When Hilduin was banished to Saxony in the year 830, Hincmar himself, with the Bishop's permission, accompanied him into exile and brought no unwelcome assistance to the exiled abbot. After Ebbo <note>Hincmar's predecessor, who was deposed for his role in a rebellion against Louis the Pious</note> was deposed in the year 835 for the crime of high treason, the see of Reims had remained vacant for nearly a decade. However, at the start of the year 845, at the Synod of Beauvais—with the combined wishes of both the clergy and the people, and with the favor of King Charles <note>Charles the Bald</note>—Hincmar was ordained Archbishop of Reims. His election was confirmed again the following year by the votes of the Bishops assembled at the Council of Paris, at which time King Charles also restored the possessions of the Church of Reims, which the palace officials had plundered while the see was vacant. In the year 848, he took part in the Synod of Quierzy, and in the synodal decrees made either there or elsewhere against Gottschalk <note>A monk who advocated for a strict doctrine of "double predestination," which Hincmar fiercely opposed</note>, Hincmar almost everywhere played the leading role.

<margin>Councils, Vol. 8, p. 79.</margin>
In the year 853, the Synod of Soissons was held, as the Acts of the Synod itself testify, although Flodoard reports it as being held in the seventh year of Hincmar’s episcopate. In this Synod, Hincmar had his own ordination confirmed once more, and he succeeded in having Wulfad and the other priests who had been ordained by Ebbo after his deposition in 840 removed from their positions.

<margin>Ibid. p. 137.</margin>
In the year 855, the decrees enacted seven years earlier at the Council of Quierzy through Hincmar's efforts were annulled at the Synod of Valence. The Synods of Langres and Toul confirmed the decrees of the Synod of Valence in 859; the chapters of these synods were presented to King Charles, and the King gave them to Hincmar to be refuted.

<margin>Loc. cit. pp. 673, 674.</margin>
He accomplished this in a distinguished written work. In the year 860, he attended the double Synod of Aachen, where Teutberga—having confessed to having had a sexual relationship with her brother Hucbert, whether forced or by the power of truth—was sentenced by the Fathers to be divorced by King Lothar and submitted to public penance <note>This refers to the famous and scandalous divorce case of Lothar II, which dominated Frankish politics for years</note>.

<margin>Ibid. p. 696.</margin>
This provided Hincmar with an excellent opportunity for much action and writing. In the same year, he signed the Second Council of Toul and, in the following year, the Third Council of Aachen.

<margin>Ibid. p. 764.</margin>
In the year 863, he was present at the Council of Metz, in which King Lothar’s marriage to Waldrada, entered into after the repudiation of Teutberga, was ratified. However, that Council was soon condemned by Pope Nicholas in a Roman Synod. In the same year, Hincmar, having obtained a confirmation of the privileges of the Church of Reims, saw to it that Rothad, the Bishop of Soissons—who was refusing to yield—was deposed at the Council of Senlis and thrust into a monastery, with another substituted in his place. When Rothad appealed to the Apostolic See (the *petition of appeal* survives in Baronius at the year 863, number 81, and in the Councils, Vol. 8, page 785), Hincmar condemned him again. Although Hincmar did release Rothad from prison at the intercession of Pope Nicholas, he by no means permitted him to go to Rome, where the Pope had commanded him to be sent for a renewal of the judgment. Not even when warned a third time by Nicholas was Hincmar willing to depart from his purpose. Although daily threats were made concerning letters of excommunication to be sent from Rome, he disregarded them all and defended himself by the authority of the Canons <note>Church laws</note>, as is abundantly clear from his own *Apologetic Letter* to Nicholas. In the year 865, at a Council in Rome, Rothad was restored to his see, and Hincmar's double judgment was rescinded.

<margin>Councils, ibid. p. 808 etc.</margin>
In the year 866, he presided over the Third Council of Soissons, in which Wulfad and his fellow priests recovered their former dignity by order of Pope Nicholas.

<margin>
9th CENTURY from 800 AD.

* Letter 42, p. 82.
† For the year 882, number 17.
</margin>

In the following year, at the Council of Troyes <note>original: "Concilio Trecassino"</note>, over which he presided, he examined the same cause more accurately. In the year 869, at the Synod of Verberie <note>original: "Synodo Vermeriensi"</note>, he himself, being more hostile toward him than others, condemned with his own vote Hincmar, Bishop of Laon, his own nephew, who had been accused of many crimes. From this arose grave enmities between the uncle and the nephew, and a vast amount of material for the great men of the realm; about which we shall perhaps say more under Hincmar of Laon. In the year 882, when the Northmen <note>The Vikings, who frequently raided the Frankish interior during this period</note> were breaking into Gaul, Hincmar abandoned Reims and, taking the body of Saint Remigius with him, sought out wooded places across the river Marne <note>original: "Matronam"</note>; there, in the villa of Épernay <note>original: "Sparnaco"</note>, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 21</note>, he breathed his last, and was buried in the Monastery of Saint Remigius. It is not for me to pass judgment on so great a man, whom Rabanus Maurus, who knew him best, calls a most reverend and most desired man, rightly to be venerated by all Catholics for the merit of his correct faith and sound profession. Lupus of Ferrières says *: "A beneficial education adorns the nobility of his lineage, and the religion of his profession commends the height of his office." In the theological faculties, as even Baronius † concedes, he was most highly accomplished, and many consulted him on various questions; he was most learned in the science of the Canons <note>Church laws</note>, although sometimes, favoring them too much, he elevated them above the decrees of the Apostolic See. And indeed, no one understood the laws and rights of the Church better, and no one defended them more spiritedly. Finally, let us come to his works, which are filled with much erudition, doctrine, and piety, and which wonderfully illuminate the history of the Gallican Church; regarding which Jacques Sirmond correctly says that there is none among them lacking in utility, and in which the author’s excellent judgment does not shine forth alongside his abundance of knowledge.

Finally, Flodoard reviews a catalog of nearly everything Hincmar ever wrote, itemizing them through fifteen entire chapters; among these are many that have either been consumed by time or remain buried in darkness. These can be better reviewed in Flodoard’s own work than transferred here by me.

<margin>846.</margin>
**PRUDENS**, or Prudentius; Spanish by birth, Bishop of Troyes <note>original: "Trecarum"</note> in Gaul; he flourished in the year 846, at which time he took part in the Synod of Paris. In 849, he was present at the Fourth Council of Tours, as well as the Second Council of Soissons in 853, in which Wulfad and other priests, who had been ordained by Ebbo after his synodical deposition, lost their offices. It is established from that time that he favored the party of Gottschalk <note>A monk who advocated for "double predestination," the idea that God predestines some to heaven and others to hell</note>, because he wrote against the "Chapters" of John Scotus Eriugena <note>A famous Irish philosopher and theologian</note> regarding these very questions. For this reason, one should not be surprised that he withdrew his presence when Hincmar consulted him about the status and suppression of Gottschalk. Hincmar complains about this matter in Flodoard, Book 3, Chapter 20. Prudentius died in the year 861.

->WRITINGS.<-

A Treatise on Predestination against John Scotus Eriugena, written in the year 852 to Wenilo, Archbishop of Sens (who had sent him nineteen "Chapters" extracted from Scotus’s book); or, the book *of John Scotus on Predestination, refuted and corrected by the presented testimonies of the ancient Fathers.* Gilbert Mauguin first edited this book in *Vindications of Grace*, Volume II, pages 191 to 562; a *Recapitulation* of the same is on page 563.

*A Collection regarding three letters to Hincmar of Reims and Pardulus, Bishop of Laon*, edited by Louis Cellot at the end of his *History of Gottschalk, Paris*, 1655, in folio. Mauguin had edited the letter, or Preface, in Volume I, part II, page 6.

*A formal letter of notification <note>original: "Tractoria Epistola"</note> against the four Chapters of the Assembly of Quierzy*, edited by Mauguin, ibid., page 176.

*A short letter to a certain Bishop, his brother*, edited by Mabillon in the *Analecta*, Volume IV, page 324.

The small works of Prudentius are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XV, page 598. Compare what the illustrious Ussher has in his *History of Gottschalk*, Chapter 8, page 130, and Chapter 11, page 247.

# The Age of Photius <note>This era, covering the 9th century, is named for the influential and controversial Patriarch of Constantinople, whose tenure marked a significant period of theological and political tension between the Eastern and Western Churches.</note>

<margin>
9th CENTURY
from 800 AD.
</margin>

A very long bill of indictment against his nephew Hincmar <note>Hincmar of Laon</note>, presented at the Council of Douzy.

Booklets presented to King Charles <note>Charles the Bald</note> for the defense of ecclesiastical liberty at Pîtres in the year 867, concerning the case of his nephew Hincmar, who had not yet fallen from grace.

A scroll <note>original: "Rotula"</note> presented to the same king when he delayed reading the aforementioned booklets.

An extemporaneous warning given to the king at the time the scroll was presented.

A letter to King Charles concerning the same case.

These five small works regarding Hincmar of Laon, together with the acts of the Council of Douzy and his own learned notes, were published by Louis Cellot (*Paris, 1658, in quarto*). These works contribute greatly to vindicating the innocence of our Hincmar <note>Hincmar of Reims, the author’s uncle and primary subject</note>. They are also contained in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume VIII, pages 1552 and 1732.

Eight quite long letters to Hincmar of Laon, transcribed from the Vatican Codex, have been published in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume VIII, page 1789.

The Life of Remigius <note>Saint Remigius, the 5th-century "Apostle of the Franks" who baptized Clovis I</note>, Archbishop of Reims. It is found in Surius, under *January 13*. Appended to this "Life" is a Eulogy of Remigius, likewise written by the same Hincmar. Flodoard certainly confirms that Hincmar wrote about the life and virtues of Saint Remigius (*History of the Church of Reims, book 3, chapter 20, page 224*). See also what Sigebert writes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 99*.

Finally, Flodoard recounts a catalog of almost everything Hincmar ever wrote across fifteen full chapters, listing them one by one. Among these are very many works that have either been consumed by time or remain buried in darkness; these can be better surveyed in Flodoard’s own work than transferred here by me.

---

<margin>846.</margin>
**PRUDENTIUS** (or Prudens); a Spaniard by birth, Bishop of Troyes in Gaul; he flourished in the year 846, when he participated in the Synod of Paris. In the year 849, he attended the Fourth Council of Tours, as well as the Second Council of Soissons in 853, in which Wulfad and other priests—who had been ordained by Ebbo after his synodal deposition—lost their clerical offices. It is established that he favored the side of Gottschalk <note>A monk who promoted the controversial doctrine of "double predestination," asserting that God predestined some to salvation and others to damnation</note>, because he wrote against the "Chapters" of John Scotus Eriugena regarding these very questions. For this reason, it should seem less surprising that he withdrew his presence when Hincmar consulted him about the status and suppression of Gottschalk. Hincmar complains about this matter in Flodoard, book 3, chapter 25. Prudentius died in the year 861.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

A Treatise on Predestination against John Scotus Eriugena, written in the year 852 to Wenilo, Archbishop of Sens (who had sent him nineteen chapters excerpted from Scotus's book); or, the book of John Scotus on Predestination refuted and corrected by the testimonies of the reasonings of the ancient Fathers. Gilbert Mauguin first published this book in *Vindications of Grace, Volume II, pages 191 to 562*; a summary <note>original: "Recapitulatio"</note> of the same is on page 563.

A collection regarding three letters to Hincmar of Reims and Pardulus, Bishop of Laon, published by Louis Cellot at the end of his *History of Gottschalk* (*Paris, 1655, folio*). Mauguin had previously published the letter, or preface, in *Volume I, part II, page 6*.

A formal letter <note>term: "Tractoria Epistola" — a circular or official letter used in the early church to communicate synodal decisions</note> against the four chapters of the Council of Quierzy, published by Mauguin, *ibid. page 176*.

A short letter to a certain bishop, his brother, published by Mabillon in *Analecta, Volume IV, page 324*.

The small works of Prudentius are held in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XV, page 598*. Compare what the famous Ussher <note>James Ussher, the 17th-century Archbishop and scholar</note> has in the *History of Gottschalk, chapter 8, page 130, and chapter 11, page 247*.

# The Photian Century <note>This era is named after Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, whose scholarship and ecclesiastical conflicts defined much of the 9th-century intellectual landscape.</note>

<margin>
9th CENTURY
from 800 AD.
</margin>

...present at the councils of Meaux (845), Paris (846), Soissons (853), and the second council of Verberie. He died around the year 856. A single letter to Hincmar of Reims survives among Hincmar's works, Volume II, page 838.

<margin>
847 AD.
The Life of Rabanus by Rodulf the Priest is prefixed to his works. See also Serrarius, *History of Mainz*, Book 4, page 625.
</margin>

**RABANUS MAURUS**, a Frank by birth (although Riccobaldus of Ferrara, Ptolemy of Lucca, and several others claim he was English), was born in Fulda in the year 785. He had **Alcuin** <note>The famous English scholar and advisor to Charlemagne</note> as his teacher in both theology and the secular arts. Thoroughly steeped in these studies, he began his monastic life in the Abbey of Fulda. In the year 810, he was appointed head of the School of Fulda by Abbot Ratgar; he led this school with such a reputation for learning and glory that countless bishops and abbots—the primary ornaments of that century—emerged from it. In 815, he was elevated to the priesthood by Haistulph, the Archbishop of Mainz. In 822, he was made Abbot of Fulda. Around the year 830, when the sons of Emperor Louis <note>Louis the Pious</note> were conspiring against their father, Rabanus conducted himself so prudently in such a dangerous state of affairs that he retained the goodwill of both sides and acted as a much-desired mediator <note>original: "sequestrum"</note> for peace between father and sons. In 834, he was given custody of Ebbo, the Archbishop of Reims, who had been condemned for high treason <note>original: "laesae majestatis"</note>. In 835, he received the relics of saints donated to the Abbey of Fulda by Deusdona, a Roman deacon, with great religious devotion and a solemn procession; likewise, in the following year, he received relics given by Sabbatinus, a Roman layman. In 838, he sent a "colony" of Fulda monks to Count Erlafrid to establish the monastery at Hirsau, which the Count had recently founded. At that same time, so that he might pursue his studies more easily and without interruption, he handed over the burden of governing the monastery to Hatto. Content with the title of Abbot, he devoted himself entirely to reading and writing books. In the following year, he was ejected from the monastery by the monks, who complained that he was too intent on literary studies, managed the common business of the Abbey less than successfully, and was nearly exhausting the monastery’s estates through his negligence. Expelled by these ungrateful monks, he is said to have retired to the Court, and there he remained—frequently recalled by the monks in vain—until he took up the bishopric. Be that as it may, in the year 847, upon the death of Archbishop Otgar, Rabanus was elevated to the see of Mainz. That same year, having held a Synod at Mainz, he consulted his fellow bishops regarding the restoration of Church property and privileges that had been seized and trampled by the injuries of the laity. In 848, having again gathered a Synod at Mainz, he reduced **Gottschalk** <note>A monk famous for his controversial teachings on "double predestination"</note>, who was present, to a standstill by the invincible force of his logic and arguments; he refuted him and sent him, condemned, to Hincmar of Reims to be shut in prison. Shortly thereafter, he strenuously attacked Gottschalk's errors in various published pamphlets. This most holy man died in the year 856, on the 4th of February.

Aside from what could be said of his piety, modesty, humility, liberality, and other virtues, he was most highly instructed in every branch of knowledge. "To speak without envy," says Trithemius, "Italy produced no one like him, nor did Germany bear his equal." To be sure, our own **William of Malmesbury** <note>A famous 12th-century English historian</note> was somewhat more unfair toward him, as is clear from his Preface to the *Abbreviation of Amalarius*, which Dr. Allix recently brought to light from the Lambeth Library in his work on John of Paris. In this, William not only marks Rabanus's opinion on the Eucharist as less than sound—indeed, dangerous—but also traduces his books as being of little use. Furthermore, he accuses him of a certain notable plagiarism <note>original: "plagii"</note>, as if he had transcribed his two books on *Ecclesiastical Offices* word-for-word from Isidore, Augustine, and Gregory’s *Pastoral Care*, and had compiled other small works from Isidore and Bede. "For that man," he says, "was peculiarly diligent in this vice, as if he entirely despaired that his readers would have no memory by which they could detect his thefts." However, these charges should be ascribed less to the truth of the matter than to the envy of the learned and a particular hatred for Rabanus’s opinions. For Rabanus was, beyond controversy, easily the leader among the men of his century distinguished for learning. Nor was he merely highly learned himself, but like the sun, he scattered the rays of doctrine in every direction. Under him, the Abbey of Fulda was a public school of virtue and erudition. He had 270 monks, whom he instructed not only in the Holy Scriptures but also in secular literature. Disciples also flocked to him from elsewhere, so that from his school there emerged men who would soon rise to the highest...

**Rabanus Maurus**: A 9th-century polymath, teacher, and Archbishop of Mainz; often called "The Teacher of Germany."
**Alcuin**: The Anglo-Saxon scholar who led Charlemagne's palace school.
**Fulda**: A prominent monastery in modern-day Hesse, Germany, founded by Saint Boniface.
**Gottschalk**: A monk whose teachings on predestination sparked a major 9th-century theological crisis.
**Eucharist**: The Christian sacrament of the Lord's Supper; its nature was a subject of early medieval debate.
</vocab>

In 835, he received the relics of saints given to the Monastery of Fulda by the Roman deacon Deusdona with great religious devotion and solemn ceremony; he did the same the following year with relics given by the Roman layman Sabbatinus. In 838, he sent a "colony" of monks from Fulda to Count Erlafidus for the monastery of Hirsau, which the Count had recently founded; at the same time, so that he might pursue his studies more easily and without interruption, he transferred the burden of governing the monastery to Hatto. Contenting himself with the title of Abbot, he devoted himself entirely to reading and writing books. The following year, he was ejected from the monastery by rebellious monks who complained that he was too intent on literary studies and was managing the common affairs of the monastery less successfully, nearly bankrupting the monastery's estates through his perceived negligence. Driven out by these ungrateful monks, he is said to have retired to the Court, where he remained until he was appointed Bishop, having several times refused the monks' attempts to recall him. However that may be, in 847, upon the death of Archbishop Otgar, Rabanus was elevated to the see of Mainz. That same year, at a synod held in Mainz, he consulted the bishops regarding the restoration of Church property and privileges that had been seized and trampled by the injuries of laymen. In 848, having again convened a synod at Mainz, he brought Gottschalk <note>Gottschalk of Orbais was a monk famous for his controversial teachings on double predestination.</note> to a standstill <note>original: *ad incitas redegit*, an idiom from games meaning to checkmate or leave without a move.</note> and refuted him through the invincible force of his logic and arguments; he then sent the condemned man to Hincmar of Reims to be imprisoned. Shortly thereafter, he strenuously attacked Gottschalk's errors in several published treatises. This most holy man died in the year 856, on the 4th of February. Setting aside what could be said of his piety, modesty, humility, and other virtues, he was most highly trained in every branch of knowledge. "To speak without envy," says Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot and polymath.</note>, "neither did Italy produce his like, nor Germany his equal." Our own William of Malmesbury <note>A famous 12th-century English historian.</note> was somewhat more unfair toward him, as is clear from his Preface to the *Abbreviation of Amalarius* (which Dr. Allix recently brought to light from the Lambeth Library), in which he not only marks Rabanus's opinion on the Eucharist as unsound and dangerous, but also traduces his books as being of little use; he even accuses him of a notable act of plagiarism, claiming he transcribed two books on *Ecclesiastical Offices* word-for-word from Isidore, Augustine, and Gregory's *Pastoral Care*, and compiled other small works from Isidore and Bede. "For that man," he says, "was particularly persistent in this vice, as if he entirely despaired that his readers would have a memory to detect his thefts." These charges, however, are to be ascribed not so much to the truth of the matter as to the envy of the learned and a peculiar hatred for Rabanus’s views. For Rabanus was, beyond controversy, easily the prince among the scholars of his age. Not only was he himself most learned, but like the sun, he scattered the rays of his teaching in every direction. Under him, the Monastery of Fulda was a public school of virtue and erudition. He had 270 monks, whom he instructed not only in the Holy Scriptures but also in secular literature. Students also flocked to him from elsewhere, so many that from his school emerged those who soon [would rise] to the highest...

**EULOGIUS**, Spanish by birth, from the city of Córdoba, a priest by rank, and shortly before his death elected Archbishop of Toledo. He flourished in the year 847. In the year 844, having been made an exile from his home by the cruelty of the Arabs, he traveled through various places in Spain, especially for the sake of religion: the Monastery of Saint Zachary <note>An "asceterium" refers to a place of ascetic practice or a monastery.</note> at the foot of the Pyrenees mountains, Pamplona, Zaragoza, and Toledo. As the tyranny of the Arabs began to cool, he returned to Córdoba; from there, in the year 851, he sent the relics of Saint Zoilus the Martyr as a gift to Wilifind, the Bishop of Pamplona, a most loyal friend. In the same year, a very heavy persecution was stirred up by the Saracens <note>A term used by medieval writers to refer to Muslims.</note> of Córdoba against the Christians; in this, Eulogius stood bravely by the martyrs, urged them to constancy with his advice, and consoled them with his writings. Soon he himself, while contemplating a journey to Rome, was seized and cast into prison. While placed in prison, he gave himself entirely to composing writings, defending the cause of the martyrs against their detractors, and recounting and praising their passions. In the year 859, when he had imbued a Muslim virgin named Leocritia with the Christian faith, the Saracens, driven into a rage, dragged Eulogius to the tribunal. There, as he refused to yield to their threats and uttered a noble confession of faith, they ordered him to be punished by the sword. This most holy man met his martyrdom on March 11 <note>original: "V. Id. Martii"</note>, and was buried by pious Christians in the Basilica of Saint Zoilus.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Memorial of the Saints* <note>original: "Memoriale Sanctorum"</note>, or three books *On the Martyrs of Córdoba*. Ambrosio de Morales, who first published these books, cut many things from the first and second books concerning Muhammad <note>original: "Muhammede"</note> and his teachings; Thomas Malvenda rightly complained of this long ago in book 1 of *On the Antichrist*, chapter 24. Consequently, in the Roman edition of this book, that passage of Malvenda does not appear.

*Apology for the Martyrs against Detractors.*

*Exhortation to Martyrdom*, or *Martyrial Instruction addressed to the virgins and Confessors Flora and Mary.*

*Several Epistles* to Wilifind, Bishop of Pamplona, to Alvarus, and to others.

The works of Eulogius were published through the efforts of P. Ponce de León, and with the notes of Ambrosio de Morales, at Alcalá de Henares <note>original: "Compluti"</note> in 1574; and among the *Spanish Historical Writers*, Volume IV, page 213; and finally in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XV, page 242.

**ALVARUS**, Spanish by nationality, from Córdoba, the companion and closest friend of Saint Eulogius of Córdoba, as is evident from the *Life* of the same written by himself. He flourished in the year 847. Surviving Eulogius, he committed the *Life* and *Martyrdom* to writing; this *Life* is found prefixed to the works of Eulogius both in the Alcalá edition and in the *Library of the Fathers*, as well as in Surius on March 11. He also wrote *Several Epistles* to Eulogius, which have a place among the letters of Eulogius and are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XV, pages 89, 303, and 306. This was published in Basel, but in a mutilated form and without the name of the author, as noted by Vossius *.

**LEO IV**, Roman by nationality, son of Rodoald, educated in the Monastery of Saint Martin. He was ordained a subdeacon by Gregory IV, and a priest with the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs by Sergius II; finally, he was elevated to the height of the Pontificate in the year 847, on the 12th day of April. The ordination had been delayed since the month of January, when Sergius died, because, as Anastasius <note>Anastasius the Librarian (c. 810–879), a scholar and historian of the Roman Church.</note> has it, they did not dare to consecrate the Pope without imperial authority. In the same year, or as others say, in the year 854, he received Ethelwulf, King of England, who arrived in Rome, with the highest honor. He devoted almost his entire Pontificate to building basilicas and other public buildings; to surrounding the city with walls and fortifying it against the attacks of the Saracens; and to enlisting military and naval forces against the same barbarians, and [providing] aid...

## EULOGIUS, Spanish by birth, from the city of Cordoba, a Priest by rank, and shortly before his death elected Archbishop of Toledo. He flourished in the year 847. In the year 844, having been made an exile from his home by the cruelty of the Arabs, he traveled through various places in Spain, especially for the sake of religion, to the Monastery of Saint Zacharias at the foot of the Pyrenees mountains, to Pamplona, Zaragoza, and Toledo. As the tyranny of the Arabs began to subside, he returned to Cordoba: and from there, in the year 851, he sent the relics of Saint Zoilus the Martyr as a gift to Wilifind, the Bishop of Pamplona, a most loyal friend. In the same year, a very heavy persecution was stirred up by the Saracens of Cordoba against the Christians; in this, Eulogius stood bravely by the Martyrs, urged them to constancy with his advice, and consoled them with his writings. Soon he himself, while contemplating a journey to Rome, was seized and thrown into prison. While placed in prison, he gave himself entirely to the painstaking production of writings, defending the cause of the Martyrs against their detractors, and narrating and praising their sufferings. In the year 859, when he had imbued the Muslim virgin Leocritia with the Christian faith, the Saracens, driven into a rage, dragged Eulogius to the tribunal. When he refused to yield to their threats and gave a noble confession of faith, they ordered him to be punished by the sword. This most holy man underwent martyrdom on March 11 <note>Original: "V. Id. Martii," the fifth day before the Ides of March.</note>, and was buried by pious Christians in the Basilica of Saint Zoilus.

### WRITINGS.

*Memorial of the Saints, or three books on the Martyrs of Cordoba.* Ambrose Morales, who first published these books, cut out many things from the first and second books concerning Muhammad and his dogmas; about which Thomas Malvenda rightly complained long ago in book I *On the Antichrist*, chapter 24. Consequently, in the Roman edition of this book, that passage of Malvenda’s does not appear.

*Apologia for the Martyrs against Detractors.*

*Exhortation to Martyrdom, or a Martyrdom Manual for the virgins and Confessors Flora and Mary.*

*Several Letters to Bishop Wilifind of Pamplona, to Alvarus, and others.*

The works of Eulogius were published through the efforts of P. Ponce de León, with the scholarly notes of Ambrose Morales, at Alcalá de Henares <note>Original: "Compluti," the Latin name for the city of Alcalá.</note> in 1574; and among the *Spanish Historians*, Volume IV, page 213; and finally in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XV, page 242.

<margin>847.</margin>

## ALVARUS, Spanish by nation, from a home in Cordoba, the companion and greatest friend of Saint Eulogius of Cordoba, as is clear from the *Life* of Eulogius written by him. He flourished in the year 847. Outliving Eulogius, he committed his *Life and Martyrdom* to writing; this biography is found prefixed to the Works of Eulogius both in the Alcalá edition and in the *Library of the Fathers*, as well as in Surius on March 11. He also wrote several *Letters* to Eulogius, which have a place among Eulogius's letters and are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XV, pages 89, 302, and 306. He also composed a book called *Sparks of the Fathers* <note>Original: "Scintillas Patrum."</note>, in which he collected the sayings of the Fathers and arranged them according to the common headings of virtues and vices. This was published in Basel, but in a mutilated form and without the author's name, as noted by Vossius <margin>* On the Latin Historians, book 3, chapter 4.</margin>.

<margin>847.</margin>

## LEO IV, Roman by nation, son of Rodoald, educated in the Monastery of Saint Martin. He was ordained a subdeacon by Gregory IV, and a Priest with the title of the Holy Four Crowned Saints by Sergius II; finally he was raised to the height of the Pontificate in the year 847 on the 12th day of April. The ordination had been delayed since the month of January, when Sergius died, because, as Anastasius has it, they did not dare to consecrate a Pope without imperial authority. In the same year, or as others say, in the year 854, he received King Ethelwulf of England with the highest honor when he arrived in Rome. He devoted almost his entire Pontificate to building basilicas and other public buildings; to encircling the city with walls and strengthening it against the attacks of the Saracens; and to raising military and naval forces against those same Barbarians, and to reinforcements

**IGNATIUS**, a native of Constantinople, was the son of Emperor Michael I <term>Curopalates</term> <note>A high Byzantine court title</note>, also called Rangabe, and Procopia. After his father was stripped of the empire, he was castrated by order of Leo the Armenian <note>A common practice in Byzantium to prevent royal sons from claiming the throne</note> and relegated to the Prince’s Islands while still a boy of fourteen. There he took the habit of a monk and lived for about thirty years, being ordained in due time as a Reader, Subdeacon, Deacon, and Priest by Basil, the Bishop of Parium, and eventually appointed head of the Monastery of Satyrus. In the year 847, upon the death of Methodius, he was promoted to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, despite the protest of Gregory, the Bishop of Syracuse, and others. Ignatius held Gregory in such contempt that he forbade him from attending his consecration. When Gregory caused a disturbance, Ignatius soon held a synod, reduced him to the ranks, and decreed him unworthy of the priesthood; however, he sought in vain to have his sentence confirmed by the Roman Pontiffs Leo and Benedict. 

Ignatius experienced even more severe enmities with Bardas, the uncle of Emperor Michael III. When Ignatius rebuked Bardas for unjustly divorcing his wife and entering into a relationship with his daughter-in-law, and subsequently barred him from the sacred rites, Bardas flew into a rage. Joining in a faction with Gregory of Syracuse, he saw to it that Ignatius was stripped of his see in 858 on charges of <term>treason</term> <note>Latin: *laesae majestatis*</note> and exiled to the island of Terebinthos. There, loaded with chains and held under strict guard, he was tortured with hunger and starvation, moved from place to place, and treated poorly everywhere. In the year 861, Photius, who had been substituted in Ignatius's place, called a synod at Constantinople and deposed the present Ignatius from both his see and his rank, soon sending him back into exile. In 867, when Basil I seized the empire, he revoked Photius's patriarchate and restored Ignatius to his see upon his recall from exile. Ignatius soon gathered a synod and condemned and deposed the followers of Photius. He died at the age of eighty in the year 878. There remains his *Letter to Pope Nicholas* written in 867 in Latin (the first part of which is held in Greek and Latin among the *Acts of the Fourth Council of Constantinople*, session 3), found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 8, page 1009. A *Sermon or Acclamation to the Fourth Council of Constantinople* is kept in Latin in the same volume, page 1097; and finally, a *Letter to Pope Hadrian* in Latin, page 1171.

**ERMENRICUS**, a monk of Reichenau <note>Latin: *Augiensis*</note>, flourished around the year 850. There remains his *Booklet to Grimold the Arch-chaplain*, in which he discusses the illustrious men of the Monastery of Saint Gall; found in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume 4, page 329.

<margin>850.</margin>
**WANDELBERT**, a Deacon and Monk of Prüm of the Benedictine Order, flourished in the year 850. By order of Abbot Marquard, he wrote one book on the *Life of Saint Goar* and another on the *Miracles* of the same saint, the narrative of which he brought up to the year 839. Both books are found in Surius (July 6th) and Mabillon’s *Benedictine Ages*, Volume 2, page 275. He also wrote a *Martyrology* in heroic verse, which was published as an addition to the *Martyrology of Usuard* through the care of Johannes Molanus of Louvain in 1568; it is found among the works of Bede, Volume 1, under the title *Bede’s Calendar*.

He was present at the Synod of Toul in 859, the first Council of Pîtres in 862, Soissons in 866, Troyes in 867, and the second Council of Pîtres and Verberie in 869. <margin>855.</margin>
### BENEDICT III, a Roman by birth and son of Peter. He was ordained a <term>Subdeacon</term> <note>A minor clerical rank below a deacon</note> by Gregory IV, and a Priest of the <term>titulus</term> <note>A parish church in Rome</note> of Saint Callistus by Leo IV. He was eventually made Pope on September 1, 855. However, he struggled to wrest the papal throne from the <term>Antipope</term> Anastasius, who was supported by the favor of Emperor Louis. Benedict was stripped of his pontifical robes, beaten, and cast into prison; yet, through the unyielding constancy of the Roman people and their stubbornness of spirit, he finally secured the <term>Patriarchal</term> throne. Not long after obtaining the papacy, he confirmed the <term>Synod of Soissons</term> <note>A church meeting overseen by Hincmar of Reims</note>. He died on March 10, 858. Four of his Letters survive in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 8, page 232.

<margin>855.</margin>
### HERARD, a Gaul by birth, and Archbishop of Tours from the year 855. In 859, at the first Council of Toul, he was appointed as judge for Wenilo, the Archbishop of Sens, who had been accused of <term>treason</term> <note>original: "perduellionis"</note> by King Charles <note>Charles the Bald</note>. In the following years, he participated in the second Council of Toul (860), the third Council of Aachen (862), the third Council of Soissons and the Council of Verberie (866), and the Council of Troyes (867). He died in the year 871. There remain 140 *Chapters* excerpted from the body of holy <term>Canons</term> <note>Church laws</note>, which were given to his priests assembled in a Synod in 858; these are found in the *Collection of Councils*, Vol. 8, p. 627, and among Baluze's *Capitularies*, Vol. 2, p. 1285. Also extant is a *Commonitorium* <note>A letter of instruction or reminder</note> given to Wenilo of Sens at the Synod of Toul, and an *Announcement regarding the case of Wulfadus and the coronation of Queen Ermentrude* made at the third Council of Soissons.

<margin>855.</margin>
### REMIGIUS, apparently a Gaul by birth, served as the Grand Master of the Sacred Palace for Emperor Lothar, or President of the Royal Chapel. Subsequently, through the favor of Lothar and following the death of Amulo, he became Archbishop of Lyon; however, it is not entirely certain in which year he obtained that dignity. In 855, he presided over the Council of Valence, in which he brought about the restoration of the failed cause of Gottschalk <note>Gottschalk of Orbais, a monk famous for his controversial views on "double predestination"—that God predestines some to heaven and others to hell</note> via synodal decrees. He had always defended Gottschalk with great zeal and ensured that the canons of the Council of Quierzy, which had been passed against Gottschalk six years earlier, were condemned. In 859, he presided over a Synod of bishops gathered at Langres, where he ensured the approval of the Valence canons and the condemnation of the nineteen *Chapters* of John Scotus <note>John Scotus Eriugena, a philosopher whose views on predestination were often at odds with church authorities</note>. Fifteen days later, Remigius and his fellow bishops brought these synodal decrees to the Council of Toul at Savonnières. He succeeded in having them read again before the three kings—Charles the Bald and his nephews Charles and Lothar. This gave rise to a serious dispute between Remigius and Hincmar <note>Archbishop of Reims and a rival to Remigius</note>, who also insisted on the reading of the canons of Quierzy. Nothing was decreed by the synod, and the matter was deferred to another council. Our Remigius was present at the councils of Soissons (866), Verberie (869), Attigny (870), Douzy (871), Chalon I (873), and Chalon II (875). He died on October 28th, though the exact year is not sufficiently established for me.

<margin>856.</margin>
### HINCMAR OF LAON
**HINCMAR**, a Gaul by birth, was born in the territory of Boulogne. He was the nephew of Hincmar of Reims <note>The powerful Archbishop of Reims and a central figure in Carolingian politics</note> through his sister; as a boy, he was given to his uncle to be instructed in literature and virtuous character. Once he reached maturity, he was assigned to business, sent as an envoy by his uncle to the King, and by the King into Gothia <note>A region in Southern France/Northern Spain</note>. Around the year 856, after the death of Pardulus, he was appointed to the see of Laon through the favor of his uncle, and he was ordained in the Church of Reims, as it was the <term>Metropolitan</term> <note>The primary cathedral city of an ecclesiastical province</note> see. Having been made Bishop, he initially complied with Hincmar of Reims, both as his uncle and as his metropolitan; he stood by him in the frequent <term>Synods</term> <note>Formal councils of church leaders</note> held against Rothad of Soissons. 

Later, however, inflated by pride and ambition, he denied the metropolitan's established rights. He accepted the administration of the Palace and an Abbey located outside his province without consulting his uncle. Though frequently summoned to Synods, he refused to come; he received into communion those who had been excommunicated by his uncle and other Bishops, and he excommunicated the subjects of other Bishops. Proceeding further from there, he began to tear at his uncle's reputation; he would not even greet or look at him when present. He pursued him with slanders, demanded that his uncle burn his own writings, cried out that he was worthy of <term>degradation</term> <note>The formal stripping of a cleric's rank and office</note>, and threatened that he would bring it about. In short, he did everything possible to harass his uncle and shake off the yoke of the Metropolitan. 

Nor did his unbridled audacity stop within these limits. He was also injurious to the King, whose power he held in mockery; he even contemplated defecting to the King's nephew, Lothair. Furthermore, having seized the <term>civil sword</term> <note>The use of secular or military force rather than spiritual authority</note>, he was accustomed to executing his insane decrees with an armed hand, and he despoiled of their goods those whom he had removed from the sacred rites. I shall say it in a word: he acted as a most powerless tyrant in both the church and the state—a torch of war and a herald of discord. A man endowed with such a nature could not rest from causing disturbances. 

The estate of Pouilly <note>Original: "Pauliacum"</note> provided a more immediate occasion for trouble; it had formerly been taken from the see of Laon, returned by King Charles to Hincmar upon his entry as Bishop, and later handed back to the King by Hincmar so that it might be given as a <term>benefice</term> <note>An endowment of land or income given to a member of the court or church</note> to a certain courtier named Norman. In the year 868, this most fickle man demanded the estate back from Norman; when Norman refused to return it, Hincmar excommunicated him. Then, with his own armed household, he stripped Norman not only of that estate but of all his goods. Not yet satisfied, he accused Norman before the Pope as a robber and a perpetrator of sacrilege. From this, he obtained letters from the Pope to the Metropolitan of Reims, by which the Metropolitan was ordered to excommunicate Count Norman. Hincmar of Reims, who well knew the injustice of the cause, refused to do so. King Charles also did not want it to happen, being more inclined toward the side of Norman and justice. 

Hincmar of Laon fumed; he simultaneously accused his uncle and the King of sacrilege and of contempt for the Apostolic See <note>The papacy in Rome</note> before the Pope. Around the same time, a greater harvest of evils arrived. For some trivial reason, Hincmar excommunicated all the clergy of his diocese. The clergy appealed to Hincmar of Reims as their Metropolitan. The latter released the clergy from the censure and restored them to communion and their ministry. The Bishop of Laon immediately caught fire: he stirred up massive heaps of rage and scattered threats everywhere. King Charles decided that such furies had to be restrained by a Synod. 

Therefore, in the year 869, the matter was brought before a Synod. Charles proclaimed the **Synod of Pîtres**; he summoned Hincmar. Hincmar stubbornly refused to go; indeed, he publicly excommunicated the King and many Bishops and nobles. Nevertheless, at the Conference of Pîtres, his uncle used his own authority to obtain a pardon for Hincmar's actions from the King and the nobles, and he arranged for the whole matter to be committed to a Synod for judgment. A Synod was called to be held at Verberie on the 8th day before the <term>Kalends</term> of May <note>April 24</note>. Hincmar was present, and when he could not wash away the crimes leveled against him, he sought an escape by interposing an appeal to Rome. He evaded the censure of the Synod by that trick; however, he was detained by the King as if in prison near Sissonne <note>Original: "Silvacum"</note> in the parish of Laon.

In the following year, a well-attended Synod convened for the same reason in the palace at Attigny. <margin>9th CENTURY, from 800 AD.</margin>
Our Hincmar <note>Hincmar of Laon</note> was present (although he had previously attempted in vain to confirm his appeal to Rome through a double pamphlet, one dull and the other more elegant). He was accused of rebellion by the King <note>Charles the Bald</note>, of obstinacy by his uncle <note>Hincmar of Reims</note>, of injury by the Norseman, of unjust excommunication by his own clergy, and of tyranny by his lay subjects. He did settle the matter with the King and his uncle by taking a new oath of loyalty to both; for the termination of the remaining cases, he accepted three bishops designated as judges by his uncle. Soon, however, rejecting their judgment, he appealed again to the Roman Pontiff. Meanwhile, Pope Hadrian <note>Hadrian II</note>, with the greatest heat of spirit, championed him before the King and his uncle through both prayers and threats. In the year 871, he clearly followed the party of Carloman <note>The son of Charles the Bald who rebelled against his father</note> as he took up rebellious arms against the King; he also refused to subscribe to the excommunication brought against Carloman by his uncle. In the same year, the Synod of Douzy was held, in which he was sharply accused by King Charles and his uncle Hincmar. Brought to the Synod, questioned in person, heard, and convicted—and despite his appeal to Rome and refusal of the judges—he was condemned by the unanimous vote of the Bishops and deposed from his see. Cast out from his see, as he continued to pursue uprisings daily, he was sent into exile around the year 876 by Charles the Bald (now made Emperor), bound in chains, and given into custody; two years later, he was blinded. In the year 878, after the death of Charles, he was released from excommunication by Pope John VIII, who had traveled to Gaul, during the Council held at Troyes. He was then admitted to sing the mass and granted some portion of the revenues of the Church of Laon. He died before the year 882, while his uncle was still alive. We have collected almost all these details to illustrate the history of this time, partly from the works of Hincmar of Reims and partly from the small works edited by Louis Cellot, not without diligence.

He indeed undertook a difficult task, as Saracen pirates <note>Refers to Muslim raiders from North Africa and Spain who frequently raided the Italian coast in this period</note> were at that time devastating Italy with fire and sword. To ensure the safety of Monte Cassino from their incursions, he surrounded the monastery with a wall, fortified it with towers and battlements, and at the foot of Mount Cassino, he built the city of Saint Germanus <note>Now known as the city of Cassino</note>. In the year 879, he traveled to Rome and, using his influence with Pope John VIII, championed the cause of Landulph, the Bishop of Capua, who had been driven out by his citizens during a rebellion; he did this for fear that the strength of Italy would be torn apart by internal discord. In the year 884, the Saracens captured Monte Cassino and murdered Abbot Bertharius at the altar while he was celebrating Mass on October 22nd.

Marus in his notes on Peter the Deacon, p. 22; there he also mentions a sermon on Saint Matthias the Apostle, and another on Saint Romanus the Abbot, though he does not say where they are currently hidden.
