### JOHN, called ERIGENA and SCOTUS,
whom some
claim was born in England at Ergene on the borders of Wales, while others say he was a Scot from the town of Ayr, and still others contend he was a native of Ireland (anciently called Eri or Erin). He flourished in the year 858. Having left his homeland, he crossed over into Gaul; because of the immense fame of his learning, he was received with the highest honor by Charles the Bald <note>King of West Francia and later Holy Roman Emperor</note>. He was chosen as one of the King’s close companions, becoming an inseparable associate at both table and bed in matters both serious and lighthearted. Around the year 850, while the controversy over Predestination was raging against Gottschalk, he took up his pen sharply, writing a small book *On Predestination* addressed to Hincmar of Reims and Pardulus of Laon; this work was immediately attacked by Prudentius of Troyes and Florus of Lyon. Although Gottschalk’s dogma was condemned, John himself suffered great hostility, which he largely brought upon himself through his many paradoxical philosophical teachings and his immense favor with the king. Therefore, either to escape this resentment or because he was summoned by King Alfred to restore learning in England, he certainly moved to England in the year 877 after the death of his great patron, Charles the Bald. He is said to have been appointed by King Alfred to oversee the study of the liberal arts—especially Geometry and Astronomy—at the University of Oxford, which the King had either newly founded or restored. After three years, following a discord that arose among the Oxford scholars, he withdrew to Malmesbury and opened a school in that famous monastery; there, finally, in the year 883 (though others date this to 886)...

(In the year 886) he died, stabbed to death on November 10th by his own students, who could hardly bear the rigid harshness and gravity of his character, using their writing styli and pens <note>original: "stylis & graphiis." A "stylus" was a sharp metal tool used for writing on wax tablets; legend says Erigena was stabbed to death with these by his pupils.</note>. According to Matthew of Westminster <note>referred to as "Matthew the Flower-gatherer" or "Florilegus"</note>, his body was buried in a humble place in the Basilica of Saint Lawrence. However, when a ray of heavenly fire miraculously fell upon his grave, the monks—warned by these revelations—transferred his remains to the Great Church and entombed them in a more honorable place to the left of the altar. Indeed, he was numbered among the martyrs and saints after his death and held a place in the Roman Martyrology for many centuries; until at last—alas, how unfortunate!—he was removed, his name being deleted after more "sharp-eyed" Papists <note>The author likely refers to Counter-Reformation censors who scrutinized medieval texts for heresy.</note> discovered that he held views contrary to Transubstantiation <note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ; Erigena was often cited by later reformers as holding a more symbolic view.</note>. Anastasius the Librarian, in a letter to Charles the Bald, remarkably praises his doctrine and piety:

> *It is a thing to be wondered at,* he says, *how that barbarian man (who, living at the very ends of the earth, was as far removed from the conversation of men as he was, I believe, from the speech of another tongue) was able to grasp such things <note>namely, the works of Dionysius</note> with his intellect and translate them into another language. I refer to John the Irish-born, a man whom I have heard is holy in all respects. But this was the work of that Master Spirit, who made him both burning with zeal and eloquent in speech. For unless he had burned with the fire of charity by the Spirit's grace, he surely would not have received the gift of speaking in tongues.*

**On the Division of Nature, or five books on the Natures of things.** Regarding this work, our own Roger of Hoveden <note>A 12th-century English chronicler.</note> once noted the following, whose words Matthew of Westminster later borrowed:
> “He composed a book which he titled *On the Division of Natures* <note>original Greek: περι φυσεών μερισμου (peri physeon merismou)</note>, which is very useful for solving certain complex questions; provided, however, that he is forgiven in certain matters where he strayed from the path of the Latins while keeping his eyes fixed sharply on the Greeks; for which reason he was even thought a heretic by some. There are indeed many things in this book which, unless they are diligently discussed, might seem abhorrent to the Catholic faith.”

**The Ambiguities of Saint Maximus**, or his scholia <note>Explanatory notes or commentaries.</note> on difficult passages of Saint Gregory Nazianzen, translated into Latin. These two works were published together in print at *Oxford*, 1681, in folio.

**A book on the Predestination of God against Gottschalk**, published by Gilbert Mauguin in the *Vindication of Predestination and Grace*, Volume I, page 103. From this book, a summary of nineteen chapters was once collected by order of Emperor Lothair and sent to his brother Charles via Ebbo, the Bishop of Grenoble. These were delivered at the Palace of Verberie in the year 853, and were later refuted by Prudentius of Troyes and Florus of Lyon; they are contained in James Ussher’s *History of Gottschalk*, chapter 19.

**The four works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite** (namely, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, *On the Divine Names*, and *On Mystical Theology*), translated into the Latin language, with the version dedicated to Emperor Charles the Bald. The aforementioned Matthew of Westminster long ago observed that this translation was flawed by an excessive affection for Greek phrasing, and was thus not sufficiently intelligible to Latin readers. Some of these appeared in the edition of the works of Saint Dionysius at *Cologne*, 1536. However, all of them are held in the manuscripts of the Library of the College of the Society of Jesus at Bourges, according to Philippe Labbe. The famous James Ussher published two prefaces to this translation addressed to Charles the Bald—one shorter in verse and the other longer in prose—in his *Collection of Irish Letters*, page 57.

**Excerpts on the Differences and Affinities of the Greek and Latin Verb**, which are circulated among the writings of Macrobius; Ussher and Pithou believe these were extracted from the more extensive writings of Macrobius by our John.

**The book On the Body and Blood of the Lord** has been lost; he wrote it at the command of Charles the Bald, and it was entirely consistent with the opinion of Ratramnus <note>Ratramnus argued for a spiritual, rather than physical, presence in the Eucharist.</note>. For that reason, it was condemned by the Synod of Vercelli in the year 1050, as is evident from the letter of Berengar to Richard, published by Luc d'Achery.

**NICHOLAS**, a Roman by birth and the son of Theodore the Regionary <term>Regionarius</term> <note>A high-ranking official in the Roman administration responsible for one of the city's ecclesiastical districts.</note>, was ordained Subdeacon by Pope Sergius and Deacon by Leo. After the death of Benedict in the year 858, he was elected Pontiff of the Roman Church and was consecrated on March 25th in the presence of Emperor Louis. In the following year, having been appealed to in writing by Photius, the recently appointed Patriarch of Constantinople, he sent legates to Constantinople in the year 860 to investigate the matter. In 861, he began to publicly criticize Photius and the Council of Constantinople held by him, while openly championing the cause of Ignatius <note>Ignatius was the previous Patriarch who had been deposed to make room for Photius, sparking a major schism.</note>. In the same year, having held a Synod at the Lateran, he summoned John, the Archbishop of Ravenna, to trial on charges of injury and robbery brought by his own citizens; when John refused to come, Nicholas deprived him of communion. Soon after, at the pleading of the people of Ravenna, the Pope traveled to Ravenna and compelled John—who had long been stalling—to satisfy the citizens, perform penance for his stubbornness, and beg for forgiveness; once he repented, Nicholas restored him to communion.

In the year 862, he rose up more sharply against Photius, and at a Synod held in Rome, he condemned the burgeoning heresy of the **Theopaschites** <note>original: "Theopaschitarum." A group holding the belief that the divine nature of God suffered on the cross, which was considered heretical.</note>. In that same year, outled by the divorce of King Lothair <note>Lothair II of Lotharingia, who sought to divorce his wife Teutberga to marry his mistress Waldrada.</note>—which the King wished to be believed was a legal repudiation of Queen Teutberga—the Pope "threw everything into confusion" <note>original: "summa imis miscuit," a classical idiom meaning to turn the world upside down or leave no stone unturned.</note>. He left nothing untried in his efforts to either defend Teutberga’s cause or lead King Lothair away from his purpose; so much so that in the following year he condemned the Synod of Metz and excommunicated Archbishops Theutgaud of Trier and Gunthar of Cologne, who had been sent to Rome as legates from that Synod.

In the same year, 863, having gathered a Council at Rome, he excommunicated and condemned Photius; he also commanded through frequent letters that Rothad, the Bishop of Soissons, who had been deposed by Hincmar of Reims, be restored to his see and sent to Rome for judgment. In 864, after holding a Synod in Rome, he removed Rodoald, the Bishop of Porto (who was his legate in both the East and in Gaul), from his faith and communion. He also called another Synod to settle the matter of King Lothair’s divorce, though in vain. In the year 865, having convened a Synod in Rome, he restored the present Rothad to communion, decreed his restoration to the see of Soissons, and sent him back to Gaul protected by the synodic decree and his own letters, threatening anathema <note>A formal curse by the church leading to excommunication.</note> against anyone who opposed him thereafter.

At this same time, he flared up more fiercely against Emperor Michael and Photius, and ordered the Emperor's writings to be publicly committed to the flames. In 866, he congratulated Michael, the King of the Bulgarians, on his recent acceptance of the Christian faith, answered 106 questions proposed by him, and sent Bishops Paul of Populonia and Formosus of Porto as legates to confirm the faith among the Bulgarians. In the same year, he excommunicated Waldrada, the mistress of Lothair; he ordered Wulfad and his associates, who had been deposed at the Council of Soissons, to be restored to their dignity; and he himself was struck by an anathema from Photius. He died in the year 867, on November 12th. His surviving works include 70 *Letters* (found in the Councils, Volume VIII, p. 268), another 24 (ibid., p. 480), six *Fragments of other Letters* (ibid., p. 514), *Responses to the Consultations of the Bulgarians in 106 Chapters* (ibid., p. 516), and *Decrees or Rescripts on various matters divided into 22 titles* (ibid., p. 550). <margin>*</margin> A *Second Appendix of Letters* containing four letters is found in the same volume, p. 563. Furthermore, the letters of our Nicholas were published separately in *Rome*, 1542, in folio.

**PHOTIUS**, born, it seems, in Constantinople and the nephew of Patriarch Tarasius, had parents distinguished by the splendor of their lineage, whom Nicetas says were made famous by suffering martyrdom (perhaps on account of the cause of the holy images <note>This refers to the Iconoclast controversy, where supporters of religious icons were often persecuted.</note>). Distinguished by birth, learning, and virtue, he ascended to the highest dignities of the state as soon as he reached maturity. He was made *Protospatharius* <term>the leader of the imperial guards</term>, *Protosecretarius* <term>Chief Secretary</term>, and Prince of the Senate of Constantinople; he even performed an embassy to the Assyrians <note>In this context, usually referring to the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad.</note> in the name of the Emperor. In the year 858, after Ignatius had been cast down and a document of abdication had been offered by him—whether voluntarily or out of fear—when the succession was being discussed, they chose Photius, **the one much talked about for both ignorance and knowledge** <note>original Greek: τὸν ἐν ἀμαθείᾳ & γνώσει πολλὰ φημiζόμενον. This phrase highlights how Photius was a polarizing figure; his enemies called him a fraud, while his admirers saw him as a polymath.</note>, according to the monk Michael, who otherwise supported the Photian cause...

# The Photian Century.

...hardly favoring the choice, both court officials and clergy raised Photius—who was greatly reluctant—to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, and he was consecrated on the very day of the Lord’s birth <note>Christmas Day, 858 AD.</note>. Certainly, regarding his acceptance of this office, whatever the followers of Ignatius may invent, he himself seriously complained—not only in a letter to Pope Hadrian but also in private letters to Bardas <note>Bardas was a powerful Byzantine regent and Photius's uncle.</note>—that he was driven to it by a kind of force.
<margin>See Photius's Letter 6, p. 69.</margin>
Notwithstanding this, the followers of Ignatius gathered in the Church of St. Irene and condemned Photius and his followers; the Photians, soon gathered in a synod, repaid them in kind. In the year 861, a Synod of 318 bishops was held at Constantinople, in which Ignatius was deposed by a solemn sentence. The papal legates, Rodoald, Bishop of Porto, and Zachary, Bishop of Anagni, were present and gave their consent. Although later Pope Nicholas himself denied this consent, daily hurling the worst insults and threats against Photius. To these was added a new reason for Nicholas’s hatred toward Photius: the cause of the Bulgarians. Nicholas had attempted to seize them for the Roman See by sending preachers there in the year 866. Meanwhile, Photius strenuously reclaimed them for his own see, as they were subjects of his see to which they had recently submitted of their own accord. In the year 867, Basil the Macedonian was raised to the imperial throne. He was not slightly hostile toward Photius, because he had been sharply rebuked by him for the murder of Emperor Michael and removed from holy communion. Having recalled Ignatius, he cast Photius 
<margin>See Leo the Grammarian in his *Chronography*, and Joel in his *Compendium of History*.</margin>
down from the Patriarchal throne. In the year 869, a Council of 102 bishops was called at Constantinople—which the Roman Catholics <note>original: *Pontificii*</note> consider the 8th Ecumenical Council. The Ignatians condemned and deposed Photius and his followers; and, to ensure the matter was conducted in an insolent manner, they signed the synodal sentence using pens dipped not in bare ink, but in the very sacramental blood <note>A dramatic and controversial claim that the bishops mixed the consecrated wine of the Eucharist with their ink to sign the decree against Photius.</note>. After this, Photius was driven into exile, stripped of his relatives, family, friends, and finally all human service, and even his books—which he held dearer than life itself. "This is new," he said, "and strange: the new punishment devised against us." <note>original: *Καινὸν τοῦτο καὶ παράδοξον, ἡ νέα παρ’ ἡμῖν ἐπινοηθεῖσα τιμωρία*</note> And this was certainly a new and strange punishment recently devised against me.
<margin>Leo the Grammarian: in his *Chronography*. John Curopalates: in his *Compendium*. Zonaras: *Annals*, Vol. III.</margin>
At last, Basil, mindful of their old friendship, began to return to Photius’s favor. After Ignatius died shortly thereafter, he restored Photius to his see in the year 878. Not content with this, he reconciled Pope John VIII to him. Accordingly, the Pope received Photius into communion and voided all decrees against him and his followers. He sent legates, Paul of Ancona and Eugene of Ostia, to Constantinople, where they took part in a council of 383 bishops gathered in the year 879. Everything here turned in Photius’s favor. He was recognized by all as the legitimate Patriarch, the contrary decrees were rescinded, and the ancient privileges of the See of Constantinople were confirmed. A Canon was even established that all those condemned by Pope John of Rome should also be condemned by Photius, and those condemned by Photius should be subject to anathema by John. The Greeks recognize only this Photian Synod as the 8th Ecumenical Council. William Beveridge <note>William Beveridge (1637–1708) was a prominent English bishop and scholar of church law.</note> was the first to publish its Acts in Greek and Latin, transcribed from the manuscript of Patriarch John Beccus of Constantinople, in his *Pandects of the Canons*, Vol. II. In the year 886, Photius was falsely accused of a plot against Leo the Augustus (the son of Basil), alongside Theodore Santabarenus. He was soon driven from his see by the Emperor and relegated to the Monastery of the Harmonians, where it seems he died not long after. He was buried in the Monastery of Jeremiah at Merdosagares. He was a man—to say nothing of his other qualities—of infinite reading and stupendous erudition, the most learned of almost all ages, not just his own; a most voracious devourer of books and a most critical judge <note>original: *κριτικώτατος*</note>. No one could look into his *Library* <note>Known as the *Bibliotheca*, this work contains summaries and reviews of 279 books, many of which are now lost.</note> even once without immediately discovering a supreme historian, a most well-equipped philologist, and a most clear-sighted critic. His many skillful answers to proposed questions testify to his accurate expertise in Law; his political wisdom is shown in his book *On the Office of a Prince*, to say nothing of his actual deeds. Let his letters be read; you will see that he possessed a perfect mastery of Philosophy, Medicine, Mathematics, and Theology. Indeed, this is acknowledged by everyone, and perhaps Philippe Briet <note>Philippe Briet (1601–1668) was a French Jesuit scholar.</note> is the only one who asserted that Photius was famous for secular letters but ignorant of divine ones. The entire assembly of scholars cries out against this, as do so many of Photius’s writings, which are filled with the highest expertise in the Sacred Scriptures and theological matters. Regarding his genius and external knowledge, let us hear only Nicetas David, who is otherwise not quite fair toward Photius.
<margin>\* *Annals*, year 858. / † *Life of Ignatius*, p. 1198.</margin>
"Finally," he says, "they designated Photius as Patriarch: now this Photius, who [occupied] the field and the..." <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; it refers to Photius's vast intellectual or social standing.</note>

Meanwhile, Photius strenuously reclaimed them for his own see, as they were subjects of his see, to which they had recently submitted themselves of their own accord.

In the year 867, Basil the Macedonian was raised to the empire. He was not slightly hostile toward Photius because Photius had sharply rebuked him for the murder of Emperor Michael and had removed him from Holy Communion. Having recalled Ignatius, Basil cast Photius down from the Patriarchal throne. In the year 869, a Council of 102 bishops was called at Constantinople—which the Roman Catholics regard as the 8th Ecumenical Council—where the Ignatians condemned and deposed Photius and the Photians. And, to ensure the matter was handled in an unusually insolent manner, they signed the Synodical sentence with pens dipped not in bare ink, but in the very sacramental blood <note>original: "ipsi sanguine sacramentali"; referring to the wine of the Eucharist—a shocking and rare practice in church history</note>. <margin>See Leo the Grammarian in his *Chronography*, and Joel in his *Compendious History*.</margin> <margin>Emperor Basil.</margin> After this act, Photius was driven into exile, stripped of his relatives, family, friends, and finally all human service, and even his books, which he held dearer than life itself. <margin>Letter 97 to Emperor Basil, p. 137. Leo the Grammarian in the *Chronography*. John Curopalates in the *Compendium*. Zonaras, *Annals*, Volume III.</margin> "What is being devised," he says, "is a new thing, or some new punishment invented for certain people," <note>original: "Kainon esti to methodeuomenon..."</note> and this was certainly a new and paradoxical punishment, recently devised against me. Finally, Basil, mindful of their old friendship, began to return to favor with Photius, whom he restored to his see in the year 878, shortly after the death of Ignatius. Not content with this, he reconciled Pope John VIII to him. Accordingly, the Pope received Photius into communion and voided all decrees against him and his followers. He sent legates, Paul of Ancona and Eugenius of Ostia, to Constantinople, where they were present at a Council of 383 bishops gathered in the year 879. Here, everything turned in favor of Photius; he was recognized by all as the legitimate Patriarch, the contrary decrees were rescinded, and the ancient privileges of the See of Constantinople were confirmed. A Canon was even established that all those condemned by Pope John of Rome should also be condemned by Photius, and those condemned by Photius should also be subject to anathema by John. The Greeks recognize only this Photian Synod as the 8th Ecumenical Council; its Acts, transcribed from the codex of Patriarch John Beccus of Constantinople, were first published in Greek and Latin by William Beveridge in his *Pandects of Canons, Volume II*.

In the year 886, Photius was falsely accused of a conspiracy entered into with Theodore Santabarenus against the Emperor Leo <note>Leo VI, known as the Wise</note>, the son of Basil. He was soon driven from his see by the Emperor and relegated to the Monastery of the Harmonians, where he seems to have died not long after. He was buried in the Monastery of Jeremiah at Merdosagaris. He was a man—to say nothing of his other qualities—of infinite reading and astounding erudition, the most learned of almost all ages, not just his own; a most voracious "glutton for books" and a most critical judge <note>original: "kritikōtatos"</note>. No one could look into his *Library* <note>The *Bibliotheca* or *Myriobiblon*, Photius's famous collection of summaries and reviews of 280 books</note> even once without immediately discovering a supreme historian, a most highly instructed philologist, and a most clear-sighted critic. His many skillful answers to proposed questions testify to his accurate expertise in Law; his book *On the Office of a Prince* shows his political prudence, to say nothing of his achievements. Let his *Letters* be read; you will see that he held a perfect grasp of Philosophy, Medicine, Mathematics, and Theology. Indeed, this is acknowledged by all, and perhaps Philippus Brietius is the only one who affirmed that Photius was famous in secular letters but ignorant of divine ones <margin>\* Annals, at the year 858.</margin>—against the protest of the entire assembly of Doctors and so many of his writings which are filled with the highest expertise in the sacred scriptures and theological matters. Regarding his talent and external knowledge, let us hear only Nicetas David, who was otherwise not very fair to Photius. <margin>† Life of Ignatius, p. 1198.</margin> Finally, he says, *they designate Photius as Patriarch*: <margin>whom [they call] the external and the internal and of the pure... <note>The margin cuts off a Greek passage praising Photius's comprehensive knowledge of both secular ("external") and sacred ("internal") wisdom.</note> p. 1198.</margin>

---

\* Brietius, *Annals* at the year 858.
† Nicetas David, *Life of Ignatius*, p. 1198.

# The Photian Century.

<margin>
9th CENTURY from 800 AD.
</margin>
<note>The Greek text here is fragmentary, but describes Photius as coming from noble stock.</note> <note>original: "ἀνωνύμων, ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐκ ἐξ ἀγενῶν καὶ σάρκα καὶ δαπανῶν"</note> He was indeed a man not at all obscure or low-born, but descended from famous and illustrious ancestors; in the practice of civil and political affairs, and in his wisdom and knowledge of all things, he was the most celebrated of his time. For he flourished so greatly in the study and knowledge of grammar, the composition of poetry, and the art of public speaking—not to mention Philosophy, Medicine, and nearly all the external liberal disciplines—that he was easily considered the foremost man of his age; indeed, he could even compete with the ancients. <note>original: "Πάντα γὰρ συνέτρεχεν ἐπ' αὐτῷ, ἡ ἐπιτηδειότης τῆς φύσεως, ἡ σπουδή, ὁ πλοῦτος, δι' ὃν καὶ βιβλία ἐπ' αὐτὸν ἔῤῥεε πάντα, πλέον δὲ πάντων ὁ τῆς δόξας ἔρως, δι' ὃν αὐτῷ καὶ νύκτας ἄϋπνοι περὶ τὴν ἀνάγνωσιν ἐμμελῶς ἐσχόλαζον."</note> For all things converged in him: a certain natural fitness and power, great diligence, and wealth, by which he acquired for himself the greatest abundance of all books; and above all else, a desire for glory and praise, by which he was so inflamed that he spent whole nights without sleep in order to devote himself assiduously to reading. I omit the praises of more recent writers, which are infinite in number and weight; Daniel Heinsius, who knew best how to judge such matters, attributed a most well-deserved eulogy to him in his *Dissertation on the Criticism of the Ancients, page 166*, which I will not transcribe here lest I be too wordy.

## PUBLISHED WORKS.

**Myriobiblon**, or the **Library** (*Bibliotheca*), written by Photius while he was still a layman, in which are contained 280 small works of the ancients—read, excerpted, and accurately judged. This is a noble storehouse of learned antiquity, if ever there was one; by it, so many "planks after a shipwreck" <note>A metaphor for surviving fragments of lost ancient texts</note> and so many golden monuments of a better age are preserved for us, at least in part. It is a work in which I could hardly say whether one should more admire the sharpness of his genius, the weight of his judgment, the industry of his reading, or the variety of the works he read. Meanwhile, it deserves to be noted that this *Library* which we possess seems to be only a part of a much larger work—specifically, only those parts which had been read aloud while his brother Tarasius was absent, as Photius himself indicates quite clearly in the Letter to Tarasius prefixed to the *Library*. This most learned man certainly read and excerpted infinite other works at other times when Tarasius was present; hence it is no wonder that in this work Ignatius, Papias, Aristides, Theophilus, Hegesippus, Athenagoras, Julius Africanus, Gregory Thaumaturgus, Dionysius of Alexandria, Gregory Nazianzen, and other writers of the greatest name—both sacred and secular—have no place; they were reviewed, it seems, in another collection, of which those Philostorgian Selections (which Gothofredus finally published in this century) were perhaps a <term>ἀποσπασμάτιον</term> <note>original: "apospasmation" - a small fragment or extract</note>. David Hoeschel first published this *Library* in Greek with notes at *Augsburg, 1601, folio, Greek and Latin*; then it appeared with Hoeschel's notes and the version and notes of Schott at *Geneva, 1613, folio*, and *Rouen, 1653, folio*. However, the reader must be warned that the Latin translation attached to these editions, although it bears the name of Andreas Schott, is poor, deceptive, and entirely unworthy of Schott’s reputation.

**268 Letters**, together with an **Appendix** of five others regarding doubtful matters in Eastern Canon Law; these were published from the translation and with the notes of our countryman Richard Montagu at *London, 1651, folio, Greek and Latin*.

**Letter to the Archbishop of Aquileia**, found in Greek and Latin in the newest *Appendix* of Combefis, *Paris, 1672*; and in Latin in Baronius under the year 883.

**Letter to Theophanes the Monk**, which Francisco Scorso inserted in Greek and Latin in his *Prolegomena* to the *Homilies of Theophanes Cerameus*, *Preface 2, Section 3*.

**Letter to Pope Nicholas**, written immediately after entering the Patriarchate and containing his profession of faith. It exists in Latin in Baronius under the year 859, number 71.

**Letter to the same Pope**, written three years later, in Latin in Baronius under the year 861, number 39.

**Encyclical Letter to the Eastern Patriarchs**, in Latin in Baronius under the year 863, number 41; but in Greek and Latin it holds the second place among the Photian Letters published by Montagu.

# The Photian Century.

<margin>
9th CENTURY from 800 AD.
</margin>
**Nomocanon**, or the *Reconciliation of Ecclesiastical Canons and Imperial Laws regarding Ecclesiastical Discipline*, distributed into 14 titles. <note>A "Nomocanon" is a collection of ecclesiastical law (canons) and civil law (nomos) pertaining to the church.</note> It was published with the commentaries of Theodore Balsamon in both Greek and Latin, first edited by Christophe Justel from the Palatine Library *Paris, 1615, in quarto*, then at the end of Balsamon’s Commentaries *Paris, 1620, in folio*, and finally in the *Library of Canon Law* by the younger Justel *Paris, 1662, Volume II, page 789*.

*Homily on the Birthday of the Blessed Virgin Mary.* Extant in Greek and Latin in the *New Supplement* of Combefis *Paris, 1648, Volume I, page 1583*.

*Description of the New Church of the Blessed Virgin in the Palace* built by Basil the Macedonian, <note>Basil I, Byzantine Emperor from 867 to 886.</note> in Greek and Latin, brought to light by the illustrious Lambecius and attached to Codinus *Paris, 1655, in folio*, and with the notes of Combefis in *Origins of Constantinople, page 296*.

*Book on the Wills, which in Christ are called Gnomic*, <note>original: "De Voluntatibus, quæ in Christo dicuntur Gnomica liber"</note> <note>The term "gnomic will" refers to a theological debate about whether Christ possessed a deliberative human will or only a natural human will.</note> extant in Latin from the translation by Torres in the *Steuartian Supplement* of Canisius, *page 437*.

*A Single Letter, and a Brief Treatise*, in Greek and Latin, edited by Cotelier in *Monuments of the Greek Church, Volume II, page 104*.

*Six Dissertations on the Divinity and the Incarnation.* Held in Latin from the translation of Torres in the *Ancient Readings* of Canisius, *Volume V, page 183*.

*Arguments of Photius against the Latins*, cited and examined by John Bekkos in *Oration I: On the Union of the Church, page 154*.

*The Little Book on Synods*, so often published, is nothing other than part of the letter he wrote to Michael, Prince of Bulgaria, *On the Duty of a Prince*; and therefore it holds the first place among the Photian letters edited by Richard Montagu. There is held in Greek in the library of the illustrious Vossius a *Synopsis of the Councils of Photius*: but it is the work not of our Photius, but of Photius, Bishop of Tyre. From this *Synopsis*, Ussher provides a fragment in *Dissertation on the Creeds, page 23*.

### UNPUBLISHED WORKS. <note>original: "OPERA Ἀνέκδοτα"</note>

Commentary <gloss>Unpublished</gloss> on the Epistles of St. Paul, from which Oecumenius took most of his own material. It survives as a Greek manuscript in the Cambridge Public Library, class 4, sign 9, folio. The codex is indeed quite ancient, but mutilated at the beginning and end; certainly, the entire Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans is missing.

*Questions and Doubts addressed to Amphilochius, Metropolitan of Cyzicus* regarding various passages of Holy Scripture. They exist as manuscripts in a large volume, but without Photius’s name, in the library of the illustrious Séguier, Chancellor of France; likewise in the Vatican, Barberini, and Bavarian libraries, and perhaps elsewhere. Combefis edited two fragments of this work: one at the end of the works of Amphilochius, *page 226*, the other in the *Supplement, Volume I*. Torres once published other fragments; Colomiès happily conjectures that the pieces found in the author of the *Catena on John* are taken from this same work.

*Collection on Bishops and Metropolitans*, formerly existed as a manuscript in the Naudean library.

*Work against the Latins*; from which a fragment on the procession of the Holy Spirit, in Greek and Latin, is presented by the illustrious Ussher in *Dissertation on the Creeds, page 25*; but it was not taken immediately from Photius's own work, but rather from the manuscript codex of Euthymius Zigabenus, *Panoply, title 12*. This passage was deliberately omitted in the Latin translation of Euthymius prepared by Francesco Zino.

*Nine Odes*, extant as manuscripts in the Clermont library.

*Book of the Prophets with Exposition.* Extant as a manuscript in the Vatican Library, as Possevino informs us.

*Lexicon*, a fairly thick volume, is currently preserved as a manuscript in the possession of Marquard Gude of Hamburg. It is truly an excellent book, and one that would be of great benefit to literature to have published, as Joseph Scaliger once noted in a letter to Thompson.

*A book on Aristotle’s Categories* is held as a manuscript in the library of the King of France.

We owe our knowledge of these manuscripts in part to the care of the illustrious Colomiès, who discusses them in his *Additions to the Ecclesiastical Archive*.

<margin>* In the entry for "Asytos."</margin> Photius also wrote, according to Suidas*, against Leontius the heretic, formerly Bishop of Antioch. But this work seems to have perished long ago.

From Theognostus’s *Booklet on Ignatius*.

**THEOGNOSTUS**, a Monk, and Exarch (or Legate) of the Patriarch of Constantinople. He flourished in the year 858. Three years after Ignatius had been deposed from the patriarchal seat in a Synod of Constantinople, Theognostus, being distressed by this turn of events, fled to Rome disguised in lay clothing. There, he advocated for Ignatius’s affairs as well as his own before the Pope. Having been summoned by Emperor Michael to return to Constantinople to stand trial, he found Pope Nicholas to be not only a most fierce protector but also a generous patron; he was granted the oversight of the monasteries of Old Rome and the title of Archimandrite <note>Archimandrite: a high-ranking title for an abbot or superior of a group of monasteries in the Eastern Church.</note> by the Pope. Once Ignatius was restored to his see, Theognostus returned to Constantinople in the year 868, protected by letters from Pope Hadrian, in which he was highly commended to Emperor Basil and Patriarch Ignatius. He was subsequently made the Hegumen <note>Hegumen: the head or abbot of an Eastern Orthodox monastery.</note> (or Abbot) of the Monastery of the Spring and the Skeuophylax <note>Skeuophylax: a high-ranking ecclesiastical official responsible for the sacred vessels and treasury of a cathedral.</note> of the Great Church. In the year 870, he was sent back to Hadrian by his emperor and patriarch to negotiate the most serious matters of the Church on behalf of both, and to obtain a place of penance for the bishops and clergy who had followed Photius. He returned to Constantinople the following year without having accomplished his purpose. Nothing further is known of him. He wrote a *Booklet on the Cause of Ignatius*, in which he used a historical style to depict the miseries and injuries inflicted upon Patriarch Ignatius from 858 to 861, and presented it to Pope Nicholas for inspection. That booklet exists in Greek and Latin in *Councils, Volume VIII, page 1263*.

<margin>
858.
Metrophanes' *Letter to Manuel the Patrician*.
Acts of the 4th Council of Constantinople, Actions III, IV, and VI.
</margin>

**METROPHANES**, a native of Constantinople, was born to a mother of somewhat tarnished reputation who once accused Patriarch Methodius of sexual immorality. He was made Metropolitan <note>Metropolitan: a senior bishop with authority over a provincial capital and its surrounding bishops.</note> of Smyrna before the year 858. In that year, he defended the cause of Ignatius of Constantinople (who had been deposed by Bardas) as much as he could; nevertheless, he eventually accepted Photius as patriarch. In the following year, when the discord broke out again, Metrophanes became more defiant; he was deposed in a Synod of Constantinople and made a companion to Ignatius in prison. In the year 867, after Photius was deposed, Metrophanes recovered his see, and in the Council of Constantinople in 870, he stood out among the primary persecutors of Photius. When Photius was restored in 878, Metrophanes stubbornly refused to acknowledge him as patriarch; although he was warned and commanded by Pope John in 879 to comply with Photius, he tenaciously maintained his defiance. For this reason, in a Council of Constantinople at the beginning of the year 880, he was removed from both his bishopric and from Communion as an obstinate schismatic. He wrote a *Letter to Manuel the Patrician*, in which he narrates the deeds of Photius in order from the year 858 to 870. This letter is extant in Latin in Baronius’s *Annals* (at the year 870, number 453) and in Greek and Latin together with the *Acts of the Fourth Council of Constantinople* (Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto) and in *Councils, Volume VIII, page 1385*.

<margin>
858.
</margin>

**PATRICIUS ARARSIUS**, a writer of unknown nationality, status, and age, placed here by me because he was older than the author of the *Synodical Booklet* edited by Pappus. Otherwise, both ancient and modern authors are completely silent regarding him. He wrote a book called *The Ocean*; from this, the author of the aforementioned *Synodical Booklet* provides a notable fragment concerning Meletius and Arius (page 14). If one may "measure the lion by its claw," <note>original: "ex ungue... Leonem metiri" — a Latin proverb meaning to judge the quality of a whole work by a small sample.</note> his style of writing must have been excellent.

</margin>

**ADO**, a Frank by birth, was made Archbishop of Vienne in the year 859. He was present at the Council of Toul in 860, the Council of Chalon in 873, and the Assembly of Chalon in 875. He died in the year 875 and earned a place in the *Roman Martyrology* on the 16th day of December.

**ULRICH** <note>original: "Huldericus"</note>, a German by birth, born of the illustrious family of the Counts of Kyburg and Dillingen, was the son of Hupald and Dietpurg, Duchess of Swabia. He was born around the year 817 in the community of St. Gall, then educated under Adalbert, the Bishop of Augsburg, who sent him to Rome. Upon Adalbert's death in the meantime, Ulrich would have been named Bishop of Augsburg had he not pleaded his immature age as an excuse. Finally, after the death of Hiltin, by the consensus of both the Emperor and the Canons, he was made the Prelate of that church around the year 860. He governed his church with great praise for 40 years; and by his authority and learning, he strongly resisted the Roman Pontiff when he attempted to impose the "yoke of celibacy" upon his priests. He died around the year 900. He wrote *A Letter to Pope Nicholas on the Continency of Clerics*, in which he freely and sharply rebukes the Pope for urging the law of celibacy too rigidly, using Scripture and ecclesiastical antiquity as his evidence. This letter was published by Johannes Wolf in *Memorable Readings*, Volume I, page 241, having previously been printed among the *Orthodoxographa* <note>Orthodoxographa: a 16th-century collection of writings by early and medieval authors deemed "orthodox" by Protestant reformers.</note> on page 481, and in Foxe’s *Acts and Monuments of the Church* <note>Commonly known as "Foxe’s Book of Martyrs."</note>, Volume 2, page 456, and at the end of Calixtus’s *On the Marriage of Clerics*. This work was once held in high regard by the defenders of clerical marriage;

<margin>
* Appendix to Hermann for the year 1079, p. 349.
</margin>
so much so that, according to Berthold of Constance \*, Gregory VII found it necessary in the year 1079 to specifically condemn that writing of Ulrich’s in a Synod assembled at Rome. From this, it is clear that certain manuscript copies of this Letter in England are false, as they bear the name of Bishop Volusianus of Carthage—especially that ancient copy given as a gift to Matthew Parker, Archbishop of Canterbury, by John Bale. Our martyrologist John Foxe testifies in the place cited that he received this from Parker; there he added another quite elegant letter on this subject, also under the name of Volusianus, in which married clerics strenuously and forcefully plead their cause against Pope Nicholas. However, let the reader note that there was another Ulrich (or Hulric), also a Bishop of Augsburg, who entered the episcopacy in 924 and died in 973 or shortly thereafter, as the German Annals clearly testify. Hence, it is no wonder that many have rashly confused this man with our Ulrich.

He was present at the Synod of Troyes in 867, Verberie in 869, Pîtres in 870, and Douzy in 871. He died in the year 875 on the 6th day before the Nones of October <note>October 2nd.</note>. **BASIL**, called "the Macedonian" after his homeland, was born of the illustrious lineage of the Arsacids <note>The Arsacids were a dynasty of Armenian origin that claimed descent from the ancient kings of Persia.</note>, the grandson of Maiectes the Arsacid, though on his mother’s side he was related to Constantine the Great. While still a boy, he was led away into captivity by the Bulgarians and spent many years in Bulgaria. Finally attaining freedom, he joined the retinue of Theophilus (or Theophilitzes), a kinsman of Emperor Michael, by whom he was designated as his *Protostrator* <note>Protostrator: originally the "first groom," this became a high-ranking military and court title in the Byzantine Empire.</note>. He was soon enrolled by the Emperor among his own *Stratores* <note>Stratores: imperial equerries or attendants.</note> and elevated to the dignity of Protostrator, then *Accubitor* <note>Accubitor: a high official of the imperial guard, literally "the one who lies near" the emperor's bedchamber.</note>, and finally the rank of Patrician. In the year 867, after the Caesar Bardas was killed, Basil earned the even deeper favor of Emperor Michael through that deed; he was declared Master of Offices, adopted as a son, and finally, on the very day of Pentecost, named Caesar. At the end of the year, Basil arranged for Michael to be removed by assassins; once Michael was out of the way, he seized the reins of the Empire. Whatever he did in ecclesiastical matters relates primarily to Photius, and thus has been narrated by us above in the entry for Photius. He died in the year 886, having administered the Empire for 18 years. He would be numbered among the best of Princes, were it not for the fact that he advanced to power through such a wicked crime.

In the year 871, the old controversy regarding the Bulgarians was revived, and he complained—though in vain—to Ignatius, the Patriarch of Constantinople. Ignatius was determined to protect the rights of the Patriarchate of Constantinople; he had expelled the bishops and priests sent from Rome to Bulgaria from the province, and having seized it from the jurisdiction of the Roman See, he reclaimed it for Constantinople. Hadrian died on November 25, 872. **THEODORE**, called **ABUCARA**, Archbishop of Caria, and if not actually transferred, at least designated by the Patriarch Photius of Constantinople for the See of Laodicea. His mission was to deliver a book he had written against Pope Nicholas and to incite Louis to shake off the "papal yoke." However, he had barely begun his journey when he was recalled by Basil the Macedonian—who had seized the imperial purple after the murder of Emperor Michael—and ordered to stay at home. In the year 869, at the Council of Constantinople, he offered a "booklet of repentance," in which he claimed that Photius had forced him, and declaring that he had been drawn into the Photian faction by trickery and snares, he asked for and obtained forgiveness for his actions; he was admitted into communion and the assembly of the Council by Patriarch Ignatius.

BASIL, called THE MACEDONIAN from his homeland, born of the illustrious lineage of the Arsacids <note>A royal dynasty of Armenian/Parthian origin</note>, grandson of Maictes the Arsacid, and on his mother’s side related to Constantine the Great. As a boy, he was carried off into captivity by the Bulgarians and spent many years in Bulgaria. Finally obtaining his freedom, he joined the retinue of Theophilus (or Theophilitzes), a kinsman of Emperor Michael, where he was appointed *Prostrator* <note>An official who assisted the emperor in mounting his horse</note>. Soon after, he was chosen by the Emperor among his *Stratores* <note>Grooms or equerries</note>, and promoted to the ranks of *Protostrator* <note>First Groom</note>, then *Accubitor* <note>Chief of the imperial bedchamber</note>, and finally *Patrician* <note>A high honorary title</note>. In the year 867, after Caesar Bardas was killed, he earned the even greater favor of Emperor Michael through that deed, being named Master of Offices, adopted son, and lastly, on the day of Pentecost itself, Caesar. At the end of the year, Basil arranged to have Michael removed by sending assassins; once he was gone, he seized the reins of the Empire. Whatever he did in ecclesiastical matters primarily concerns Photius; thus, it has been narrated by us above under the entry for Photius. He died in the year 886, having administered the Empire for 18 years, and would be counted among the best princes were it not for the fact that he advanced to power through a most wicked crime.

# The Photian Century.

<margin>9th CENTURY from the birth of Christ.</margin>
<margin>The year 800.</margin>
...delegated [them]; so that they might take part in the Council of Constantinople recently announced in his name <note>This likely refers to Theodosius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, whose entry began on the preceding page</note>. His *Letter to Ignatius* is extant in the Latin *Collections of the Councils*, Vol. VIII, p. 986.

<margin>869.</margin>
**MICHAEL**, Patriarch of Alexandria, was prominent in the year 869. In that year, he delegated his Archdeacon Joseph to take his place at the Council of Constantinople and wrote a *Letter to Emperor Basil* regarding the Unity of the Church. That *Letter* is extant in Latin in the *Collections of the Councils*, Vol. VIII, p. 1111. A Greek-Latin version (though much shorter, perhaps reduced to a summary by the Greek editors of the Council’s Acts) is found in the same volume, p. 1361.

<margin>869.</margin>
**JOSEPH**, a Monk by his way of life and Archdeacon of the Church of Alexandria, was prominent in the year 869, when he served as the representative for Patriarch Michael at the Council of Constantinople. A short Latin *Panegyric Speech to the Synod* is extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Vol. VIII, p. 1114.

<margin>870.</margin>
**PETER THE SICILIAN**, a learned and noble man, was sent as an ambassador by Emperor Basil to the Armenians around the year 870 to arrange an exchange of prisoners. He completed the mission successfully after spending nine months in the Armenian city of Tephrike <note>original: "Tibricam," a stronghold of the Paulician sect</note>. Among more recent authors following Baronius and Vossius, Miraeus and his transcriber Oudin discuss him. Peter wrote a *History of the Rise, Progress, and Fall of the Manichaeans* <note>The author refers here to the Paulicians, whom Peter Siculus identified as Manichaeans</note> addressed to the Archbishop of Bulgaria. Matthew Rader of the Society of Jesus first published this in Greek and Latin in Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto, having received it from Marcus Velser. It is also available in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Vol. XVI.

<margin>870.</margin>
**MICHAEL PSELLUS**, a most learned man and a supreme Philosopher, lived for a long time on the island of Antrus <note>likely Andros</note>. From him, Leo of Byzantium—nicknamed "the Philosopher," though not the Emperor of that name—drew the elements of the liberal arts; he learned Rhetoric, Philosophy, and other sciences. He flourished around the year 870 and thereafter. However, take care not to mistakenly confuse him (as it is known many have done) with that other Michael Psellus, the tutor of Michael Ducas and a writer of the eleventh century, about whom we will speak in his proper place. It is not entirely clear whether our Michael committed anything to writing. Yet it is likely that some treatises written by him lie hidden under the name of the later Psellus, especially the *Paraphrase of most of Aristotle's books*, the *Dialogue on the Operations of Demons*, a *Treatise on Demons* not yet published in Greek, and other works which, neither in their method of treatment nor in their sharpness of invention, nor in their style, savor of the younger Psellus. Concerning these, you may consult Leo Allatius in his *Discourse on the Pselli*, p. 12, etc., and we have written more on them elsewhere.

<margin>870.</margin>
**STYLIANUS**, nicknamed *Mapas*, Metropolitan of Neocaesarea in the province of Euphratesia, was prominent in the year 870, when he signed the Fourth Council of Constantinople. Desperately devoted to the party of Ignatius, he suffered much under Photius, being removed from his see and punished with exile. Finally, after Photius was cast down from the Patriarchal see, he recovered his see in the year 886. In that same year, and again in 889, he consulted Pope Stephen by letter regarding the reception of the "Photians" <note>the followers of Photius</note> into communion. He declaimed loudly on both sides against Photius, yet contended that the peace of the Church should be granted to his followers if they performed penance. After the year 899, he consulted Pope John IX on the same cause, and in the meantime, he himself entered into communion with the Photians. Five *Letters to Pope Stephen* are extant in Greek and Latin in the *Collections of the Councils*, Vol. VIII, p. 1397 and 1410; they were previously published by Rader together with the Acts of the Eighth Council in Greek and Latin (Ingolstadt, 1604, 4°). A work by a certain Stylianus *On the Properties of the Holy Trinity* exists in a Greek manuscript in the Royal Library at Paris, according to Labbe (*New Library of Manuscripts, p. 90*); whether it truly belongs to our Stylianus, let those who have been granted the chance to inspect the manuscript tell us.

<margin>870.</margin>
<margin>Anastasius in the Acts of the Councils translated by him. Baronius, scattered through Vol. X.</margin>
**ANASTASIUS**, a Roman Abbot and Priest of the Roman Church...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of significant figures from the 9th century, known as the "Photian Century." The previous page concluded with Peter the Sicilian, a diplomat and historian. We now move to one of the most important scholars and translators of the era, Anastasius "the Librarian," whose work bridged the linguistic and political gap between the Latin West and the Greek East.</meta>

# The Photian Century.

<header>The Photian Century.</header>
<meta>catchword: Life</meta>

<margin>9th CENTURY from the year 850.</margin>
**Anastasius** the Librarian <note>Latin: *Bibliothecarius*; a high-ranking official of the Roman Curia in charge of the archives and library</note> was prominent in the year 870. In the preceding year, he had been sent as an ambassador by Emperor Louis to Constantinople, along with Counts Suppo and Everhard, to arrange a marriage between Louis's daughter and the eldest son of Basil the Macedonian. He arrived there at the conclusion of the so-called Eighth Council <note>original: *Pseudo-Octavi*; referring to the Fourth Council of Constantinople (869–870), which the Roman Church recognizes as the eighth ecumenical council, though it was later contested</note> and was present for its final session. Soon after, he succeeded in having the "Books of Penance" <note>statements of repentance offered by the followers of Photius to the Roman See</note>—which had been surreptitiously taken from the Roman Legates with the Emperor's knowledge—restored to them. Upon returning to the West, he brought with him a copy of the Acts of the Ignatian Council, which he later translated into Latin. In the year 871, he was sent as a legate to Naples by Pope Hadrian, along with Abbot Caesarius, to ensure that Bishop Athanasius of Naples, who had been driven from the city by Duke Sergius of Naples (his own nephew), was restored to his see by any means necessary. Anastasius applied himself to this task with great diligence, yet his efforts were in vain. When the Neapolitans paid little heed to the papal threats and warnings, he used the authority delegated to him by Hadrian to bind both the clergy and the people with a sentence of excommunication. In the year 876, he sent a Latin translation he had made of the *Life of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite* to Emperor Charles the Bald. Few other facts about him are certain, though some claim he lived until the year 886. For the character of his age, he was by no means unlearned; he possessed a command of both the Latin and Greek languages and maintained a sufficiently close friendship with the leading men of the century, Photius and Hincmar.

*The Acts of the Fourth Council of Constantinople (or the so-called Eighth General Council)* held in the year 869. These were partly written in Latin and partly translated from Greek into Latin, with many additions of his own. They are found in the *Collection of Councils, Vol. VIII, p. 961.*

*The Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (or the so-called Seventh General Council)* held in the year 787, translated into Latin. They are found in the *Collection of Councils, Vol. VII, p. 29.*

*Ecclesiastical History, or the Tripartite Chronicle*, which is largely drawn from the chronicles of Patriarch Nicephorus of Constantinople, George Syncellus, and Theophanes the Confessor, and translated into the Latin language. It was published with notes by Fabrotus in Paris, 1649, folio edition.

<margin>* Vol. I, p. 252.</margin>
*The History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, or the Pontifical Book* <note>The *Liber Pontificalis*</note>, reaching from Saint Peter down to Nicholas. Labbe proves that Anastasius was not the author of the first part of this book (stretching from Saint Peter to Liberius) by the fact that he had seen a manuscript code of excellent quality written in the time of Charlemagne; in that manuscript, those *Lives* were already attributed to Damasus before Anastasius was even born, or at least before he had emerged from the "rattles of early infancy" <note>original: *infantiæ crepundiis*; a metaphorical way of saying he was still a baby</note>. Lambecius testifies in his *Commentaries* (Book 2, p. 927) that such a manuscript is held without difficulty in the Imperial Library. However, we have already dealt extensively with this *Pontifical* work above under the entry for Damasus. That History exists in every edition of the Councils, and was also published at Mainz in 1602, and at the end of the *Ecclesiastical History* with notes by Charles Fabrotus, Paris, 1649, folio.

*Collectanea* <note>A Miscellany or Collection</note> concerning those matters that pertain to the history of the Monothelites <note>A 7th-century heresy claiming Christ had only one will</note>; a medley of various short works partly written by Anastasius, partly translated into Latin, and partly inserted from other sources, namely:

> *Two Letters of Anastasius the Librarian.*

> *An Account of the Dispute between Saint Maximus and Theodosius of Caesarea.*
> *A Letter of Anastasius the Envoy <note>original: *Apocrisiarii*</note> to Theodosius of Gangra.*
> *A Memorial <note>original: *Hypomnesticon*</note> of the deeds of the Saints Maximus, both the Anastasiuses, Martin, etc.*

These *Collected Works* were published by Jacques Sirmond in Paris, 1620, octavo; and thereafter in the *Library of the Fathers, Vol. XII, p. 831.*

*The Life or Passion of Saint Demetrius the Martyr.* This can be found in Mabillon’s *Analecta* <note>A collection of shorter historical or theological works</note>, Volume 1, page 65.

*The Life of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite*, translated from the Greek of Methodius into Latin, has been lost, except for the Preface, which is contained in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a 16th-century German monk and hagiographer</note> under the entry for October 3.

<margin>870.</margin>
**EPIPHANIUS**, Archbishop of Cyprus, was prominent in the year 870. Around this time, he wrote to congratulate Ignatius on his restoration to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, professing that he wholeheartedly accepted the decrees of the Synod held the previous year. This *Letter* is extant in Greek and Latin in the prolegomena to the Eighth General Council, Volume 8, page 1276.

<margin>871.</margin>
**ALFRED**, also written as **AELFRID** or **ALURED**, called **the Great** for his many achievements, was English by birth, born at Wantage in Berkshire in the year 849. He was the youngest son of Ethelwulf, King of the West Saxons, and Osburh. At the age of twelve, he was still illiterate, but he possessed a faithful memory for the Saxon poems which he listened to day and night. As he grew older, he redeemed his lost childhood years with such zeal and diligence that he earned a place among the most learned men of his century. In the year 871, he obtained the Monarchy of England and held it for nearly thirty years. He was tested by frequent Danish invasions, whom he overcame in many battles, though he himself was often reduced by them to great straits and was once even stripped of his kingdom. Setting these matters aside, let us turn to others. He built monasteries, constructed churches, and founded schools and the University of Oxford <note>This was a common historical claim in the 17th century, though modern historians consider the "founding" of Oxford by Alfred to be a later medieval legend</note>; in these, he took particular care that the children of the nobility were imbued with fine literature. Furthermore, he led others by his own example; he spent eight hours every day reading, writing, dictating, and praying, such that he was considered a grammarian, philosopher, rhetorician, historian, musician, and no mean poet. This most learned, wise, and pious Prince died on the 7th of the Calends of November <note>October 26</note> in the year 900, in the 29th year of his reign and the 51st of his life, and was buried in the city of Winchester. His life was recorded by Asser of St. Davids, his own domestic and familiar companion, from whom the curious reader may more deeply quench their thirst for knowledge.

### WRITINGS.

*A Saxon Paraphrase of the Ecclesiastical History of the Venerable Bede*, which Abraham Wheelocke saw to the publication of, alongside Bede’s original history, at Cambridge in 1644, folio.

*Numerous Laws*, the vast majority of which concern the Church. These are extant in Latin and Saxon in the same volume, in the Appendix on page 15.

*His Will.* This can be found in Asser of St. Davids’ *Life of Alfred*, page 22.

He translated the *Pastoral Care of Saint Gregory* into the Saxon language. The Preface to this translation was published in Saxon, English, and Latin in the same volume, page 25. The *Pastoral* translation itself is kept in the library of Trinity College, Cambridge. A very ancient copy, which was once the codex of Archbishop Plegmund (who flourished in the year 890) and is written in an elegant, beautiful, and very old hand, is held in the *Cotton Library* <note>The famous collection of Sir Robert Cotton</note> under the reference *Tiberius B. 11. N. 1.*, and another codex is in the same library under *Otho B. 2. N. 1.*

He translated the *Psalter of David*, at least in part, into Saxon. This version was published along with the Latin text by John Spelman, son of Henry, in London in 1640, quarto.

He translated the *History of Paulus Orosius*, or the *Hormesta* <note>A title sometimes given to Orosius's "History Against the Pagans" in early medieval contexts</note>, into the Saxon language. The Preface to this translation is found in Sir Henry Spelman’s Appendix to the *Life of King Alfred*, page 205. The Saxon translation itself exists in manuscript in the *Cotton Library* under *Tiberius B. 1. N. 1.*

# AIMOINUS
A Frenchman by birth and a Benedictine by order, he was a monk of the Monastery of Saint Vincent in Paris (which is now called Saint-Germain-des-Prés); he flourished in the year 872. This is established from a certain ancient charter edited by Jacques du Breul in the preface to the *History of Aimoinus* in 1602, which concludes as follows: *In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Gozlin, Abbot of the Monastery of the Blessed Vincent the Martyr, where the venerable Confessor of Christ, Germain, rests in body, etc., in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 872, and in the 32nd year of the reign of Charles.* — Aimoinus, the Notary and Monk, wrote and signed this on the day before the Nones of October. He was still among the living in the year 892, when he wrote concerning the *Miracles of Saint Germain*. This Aimoinus is distinct from the famous Aimoin of Fleury, who lived in the eleventh century and wrote books on the *Deeds of the Franks* <note>original: "de gestis Francorum"</note>, though many writers rashly confuse the two. Regarding this, see the distinguished Labbe in his *Dissertation on Writers*, Volume 1, page 16. The extant writings by our Aimoinus include:

*Two Books on the Finding and Translation of the Body of the Blessed Vincent, Deacon <note>original: "Levitæ"</note> and Martyr, from Spain to the Monastery of Castres in the Diocese of Albi, performed in the year 855.* These were written to Berno, the Abbot of that monastery, together with a letter to the monk Theotgern on the same subject, consisting of 60 verses. Jacques du Breul first published these at the end of the *History of Aimoinus of Fleury*, Paris, 1603, in folio. They are also found in Mabillon’s <note>Jean Mabillon, a 17th-century Benedictine scholar and founder of paleography</note> *Acts of the Benedictine Order*, Century IV, part 1, page 643.

*Two Books on the Miracles of Saint Germain, Bishop of Paris*, written by order of Abbot Gozlin. These are found in Surius <note>A 16th-century hagiographer</note> under July 25, and in Mabillon’s *Acts of the Benedictine Order*, Century III, part 2, page 104.

*A Book on the Translation of the Holy Martyrs George the Monk, Aurelius, and Natalia; and Two Books on the Miracles of the same.* These three books were published by Jean Mabillon in the *Acts of the Benedictine Order*, Century IV, Volume 2, page 45.

<margin>872.</margin>
# JOHN VIII
A Roman by birth and the son of Gundo, he was Archdeacon of the Roman Church and was ordained Pope on December 14, 872, following the death of Hadrian. In the year 873, when Emperor Louis arrived in Rome, John absolved him from the oaths he had sworn to Adelchis, the Duke of Benevento. In 874, he traveled to Verona to begin a conference with Louis, King of Germany. In 875, he summoned Charles the Bald <note>King of West Francia and future Emperor</note> to Rome, anointed him, and crowned him with the imperial crown. In 876, at the Synod held at Ticino <note>Modern-day Pavia</note>, he ensured that the election of Charles was confirmed and that all his enemies were excommunicated <note>original: "anathematizari"</note>. In 877, as the Saracens <note>Medieval term for Muslim forces</note> were devastating Italy and even the Roman countryside, he begged for aid from Emperor Charles with most fervent prayers; he threatened the people of Naples, Benevento, and others who had entered into peace treaties with the Saracens with excommunication unless they dissolved their alliances. For this reason, he himself traveled to the crossing near Gaeta. However, since the Emperor provided very little support, he was forced to bow his neck, submit to the yoke, and purchase peace from the Saracens with an annual tribute. In 878, having sent Paul of Ancona and Eugene of Ostia as bishops and legates to Constantinople, he negotiated with Emperor Basil and Patriarch Ignatius regarding the recovery of Bulgaria for the Roman See; he threatened the Patriarch with excommunication unless he withdrew from that province. In the same year, after Rome was plundered by Lambert, Count of Spoleto, the Pope fled to Gaul to seek help. There, having held a general Synod of the Gallic bishops at Troyes <note>original: "Trecis"</note>, he excommunicated all enemies of the Roman Church, restored Hincmar of Laon <note>A bishop who had been in a long legal dispute with his uncle, Hincmar of Reims</note> (who had been deposed seven years earlier) to his clerical office, and crowned Emperor Louis <note>Louis the Stammerer</note> during that same Synod.

## HARTMUTUS

**HARTMUT**, wrongly called Hartmann or Hartmun by Canisius, was a kinsman of King Rudolph of Burgundy. He was first a monk of the Monastery of Saint Gall <note>A famous Benedictine monastery in modern-day Switzerland</note> and then elected the 14th Abbot after the death of Grimoald in the year 872. In the year 883, he voluntarily abdicated the government of the Monastery. There exist several of his writings, including *Various Poems and Hymns*, in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume V, page 728. The *Life of Saint Wiborada, virgin and martyr*, a recluse of Saint Gall, is attributed to his name in Henschenius’s work for May 2nd and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Centuries*, Volume V, page 42.

## JOANNES

**JOHN**, a Deacon of the Roman Church and an associate of Anastasius the Librarian; he flourished around the year 875. He wrote the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great, Pope of Rome* in four books, which he dedicated to Pope John VIII. This *Life* appears in Surius on March 12th, and at the beginning of all editions of Gregory the Great’s works. Sigebert records that at the urging of Gauderich, Bishop of Velletri, he also committed the deeds of Pope Clement to writing. However, those works have perished. Furthermore, a manuscript is said to exist in the Library of Saint-Germain in Paris under the name of John the Deacon entitled *Commentary, or a Brief Exposition on the Heptateuch* <note>The first seven books of the Bible</note>; however, scholars do not entirely agree whether it is truly the work of our John.

876.

## USUARDUS

**USUARD**, a Frenchman by nationality and a monk of Saint-Germain in Paris; he is commonly said to have been the Abbot of Saint Savior. He flourished around the year 876. Offended by the brevity of the *Martyrologies* <note>A list or catalog of martyrs and saints arranged by their feast days</note> compiled by Jerome and Bede, and encouraged by the command of Emperor Charles the Bald, he himself wove together a more extensive *Martyrology* from the writings of Florus and others of that kind, dedicating it to Emperor Charles. This *Martyrology* was published in *Louvain* in 1568, in octavo, with additions and annotations by Jan Molan, and was reprinted in *Antwerp, 1583, in octavo* with a critique by Johannes Heffels regarding certain legends of the Saints. However, in the Antwerp edition, those parts which displeased the Papal authorities were omitted, along with the full critique by Johannes Heffels, as the illustrious Ussher correctly noted in his *Manuscript Theological Library*, page 499.

## MICHAEL, MONACHUS

**MICHAEL THE MONK**, so called from his way of life, was a Priest of the Church of Constantinople and a <term>Syncellus</term> <note>A high-ranking administrative assistant or confidential secretary to a Patriarch</note> to Patriarch Ignatius; he flourished in the year 878. He wrote an *Encomium of Patriarch Ignatius*, which survives in a fragmented state in Greek and Latin, edited by Rader along with the Acts of the Eighth Council (*Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto*), and thereafter in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume VIII, page 1260. He also wrote a *Life of Theodore the Studite*, of which many excerpts are found here and there in Latin in Baronius’s *Annals*, Volume IX. As a writer, he is almost foolishly prone to fables, especially regarding the affairs of Theodore, and burns with a blind, pious zeal and love for images <note>Referring to the Iconodule position in the controversy over religious icons</note>. See what we have briefly noted about him above under Theodore the Studite.

**THE SYNODICAL BOOKLET** <note>original: *Libellus Synodicus*, also known as the *Synodicon Vetus*</note>, the author of which encompasses the history of all councils, both general and provincial, in a brief compendium; he seems to have flourished around the year 880. **REMIGIUS**, a monk of the Benedictine Order in the Monastery of St. Germain at Auxerre; he flourished in the year 880. After the year 882, he was summoned to Reims by Archbishop Fulk to preside over the literary school <note>original: *gymnasio literario*</note> established there by him, as Flodoard testifies *. Those who wish for our Remigius to have been the Bishop of Reims are in error. Those who confuse him with Remigius, the Bishop of Lyon, are even more grossly delusional. Indeed, our Remigius seems never to have attained the episcopal mitre <note>original: *infulas*, a reference to the insignia of a bishop</note>. Certainly, Flodoard and Sigebert †, who write about him, are silent on that matter. Remigius died around the year 900.

**ERRICUS**, or **HERRICUS** <note>Heiric of Auxerre (841–876)</note>, born in the district of Auxerre in a village named *Hery* after him, became a monk of the Benedictine Order at Auxerre from an early age. He wrote **Six Books of poems on the Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, dedicated to the Emperor Charles the Bald.** These were published separately in Paris, 1543, in octavo. He also wrote **Two Prose Books on the Miracles of the same Saint**, which Philippe Labbe first edited in the *New Collection of Manuscripts*, Volume I. He wrote **very many Homilies**, some of which have a place in the Homiliary <note>A collection of sermons</note> of Alcuin or Paul the Deacon, inserted by a later hand—namely, a **Homily on that text, "When the Comforter shall come," etc.** <note>original: "Cùm venerit Paracletus"</note>; **on that text from Luke, "When Jesus went into Jerusalem"**; and a **third on that text from Matthew, "No one can serve two masters"** <note>original: "Nemo potest duobus dominis servire"</note>. Finally, he compiled a **Miscellany of various excerpts primarily regarding morals from the writings of ancient authors and Fathers**, which he dedicated to Hildebald, the Bishop of Auxerre. This Miscellany exists as a manuscript in the Library of Saint-Germain in Paris. Mabillon presents a metrical preface to Hildebald and the beginning of the work in the *Analecta*, Volume I, page 413.

<margin>880.</margin>
**ABBO**, called *Cernuus* <note>The "Bowed" or "Crooked"</note>, a Neustrian <note>From Neustria, the western part of the Frankish Empire</note> by birth and a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; he flourished around the year 880. He was present at the siege of Paris <note>Lutetia</note> which was conducted by the Normans <note>Vikings</note> around the year 887; he sang its **History** in rough, harsh, and unpolished verse, completing the whole matter in three books. Pierre Pithou (who nevertheless seems to confuse this man with Abbo, Abbot of Fleury, who flourished near the end of the following century) edited the first two books of this poem among the *Writers of Frankish History*, Volume II; and from there, Jacques du Breul added them to the *History of Aimoin* (Paris, 1603, folio). They decided to omit the **Third book, written for the clergy**, because it pertained nothing at all to History and was excessively foolish. Furthermore, there exist under Abbo’s name **Five Sermons**, first edited by Luc d'Achery in the *Spicilegium*, Volume IX, page 79.

<margin>880.</margin>
**GEORGIUS** <note>George of Nicomedia</note>, the *Cartophylax* <note>term: Cartophylax — An official responsible for the archives and ecclesiastical records</note> of the Great Church of Constantinople, and later Archbishop of Nicomedia; he flourished around the year 880. He was an intimate friend of Photius, who addressed him in many letters. To him, it seems, should be attributed the Homilies which Combefis published, though he conjectured they should be assigned to a certain George who is said to have flourished under Heraclius. But in this, Combefis seems to have slipped, because he incautiously confused George the Pisidian with George of Nicomedia.

**Two Homilies on the Conception of the Holy Mother of God.**
**A Homily on the Conception of Saint Anne, mother of the Mother of God.**
**A Homily on the Presentation of Saint Mary in the Temple.**
**Two Orations on the Entrance of the Holy Mother of God into the Temple.**
**On that text, "There stood by the cross of Jesus his mother," etc.** <note>original: "Stabant juxta crucem Jesu mater ejus"</note>
**On the presence of Saint Mary at the sepulcher, and a thanksgiving for the glorious Resurrection.**
**An Oration on Saints Cosmas and Damian.**
**Three Idiomela** <note>term: Idiomela — Short, independent Byzantine hymns with their own unique melodies</note>, **namely: for the Feast of the Presentation of Saint Mary; for Saint John Chrysostom; and for the Nicene Fathers.**
François Combefis brought these small works to light and published them in Greek and Latin in the *New Supplement*, Paris, 1648, Volume I, page 995.

<margin>881.</margin>
**HELIAS**, Patriarch of Jerusalem, or rather the *Syncellus* <note>A "Syncellus" was a high-ranking cleric who served as a confidential secretary and advisor to a patriarch, often living in the same cell</note> of Patriarch Theodosius, whose place he took in the Councils of Constantinople—the Ignatian Council in the year 869 and the Photian Council in 879. He flourished especially around the year 881. He wrote a *Letter to the Bishops of Gaul*, which survives in Latin in [Luc d']Achery’s *Spicilegium*, Volume II. His *Encyclical Letter on behalf of the Bishop of Málaga* is found in [Jean] Mabillon's *Analecta*, Volume III, page 434.

<margin>882.</margin>
**MARINUS**, or as he is called by others, **MARTIN II**, a Frenchman by birth and the son of the priest Alumbus, was a Deacon of the Roman Church. In the year 866, he was sent as a legate <term>an official representative of the Pope</term> to Bulgaria and Constantinople by Pope Nicholas. In 869, he was sent again to Constantinople by Pope Hadrian and took part in the Ignatian Council. Ordained a Bishop by Pope John—though without a specific diocese to govern—he was sent to the regions of the Bulgarians to convert the pagans. He was sent to Constantinople for a third time, where he was imprisoned by order of Emperor Basil. Finally, upon the death of Pope John, he was made Roman Pontiff on December 23rd, 882. He died on February 23rd, 884. There survives a *Decree on the Privileges granted to the Monastery of Solignac* in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume IX, page 357.

<margin>885.</margin>
**STEPHAN V**, a Roman by birth from the Via Lata district and the son of Hadrian, was a Priest of the Roman Church with the title of the Four Holy Crowned Ones. He was ordained Roman Pope on July 25th, 885. In that same year, in letters sent to Emperor Basil, he defended his predecessor Marinus and rebuked the Emperor for the injuries inflicted upon him; he also attacked Photius with insults and requested that aid be given to him against the Saracens. He died on August 7th, 891. Three *Letters* and a *Fragment* of another survive in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume IX, page 366.

<margin>886. Zonaras, *Annals*, Vol. 3, pp. 133, 141. See Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Life of Basil the Macedonian*, ch. 31, 50, 53, 70.</margin>
**LEO**, surnamed *the Philosopher* and *the Wise*, was born in Constantinople, the son of Emperor Basil and his wife Eudocia; although some Byzantine historians suggest he was actually the son of Michael [III] the "Porphyrogenitus" from a secret union with Eudocia shortly before she was given in marriage to Basil. He had Patriarch Photius as his tutor, a master most worthy of a prince. Under him, Leo drank in an immense knowledge of fine literature, becoming highly skilled in philosophy, history, and law; however, he was more devoted than most to judicial astrology <note>The practice of casting horoscopes to predict future events</note>. While still a youth, he was cast into custody by his father due to suspicion of a plot, brought about by Theodore Santabarenos, the Bishop of Euchaita, whom Leo hated for his wicked deeds. Later, he was freed by Basil at the pleading of the Senate. Basil, having been struck by a stag while hunting, appointed Leo as his heir and successor. Thus, in the year 886, upon Basil's death, Leo took up the reins of empire on the first of March. Once he had attained power, he immediately drove Photius from the patriarchal see, substituting his own brother Stephen in his place, and recalled the bishops whom Photius had sent into exile. Around the year 901, since he had no children from his first three wives, he married a fourth named Zoe, surnamed *Carbonopsina* <note>original: "Carbonopsinam", a Greek epithet meaning "with coal-black eyes"</note>, the sister of Saint Epiphanius, Abbot of Great Agros. Because these nuptials were contrary to the Church Canons and even to Leo's own laws, Patriarch Nicholas Mysticus of Constantinople not only refused to bless them, but also deposed the priest who did perform the blessing, and interdicted Leo himself from sacred rites. Because the Patriarch would not back down from this judgment, Leo banished him to a monastery. However, what the Patriarch of Constantinople refused to do, Pope Sergius did, for as [Cardinal] Baronius admits, the Pope granted the Emperor a dispensation in this matter. Leo died in May of 911, or as others say, on July 11th. [George] Codinus records that he reigned twenty-seven years and eight months. See Charles du Fresne, *Byzantine Families*, page 141.
