*Two Orations: On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist and On All Saints.* These nine orations <note>original: "Orationes istas IX"</note> were published in Greek and Latin by Jacob Gretser at Ingolstadt in 1600.

*Oration on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross*, which was published along with the two orations mentioned last in Greek and Latin by the same Gretser in his work *On the Cross*, Volume II, page 1219.

*Three Orations: On the Nativity, the Presentation, and the Purification of the Blessed Mary*, which were published together with the seven orations listed first in Greek and Latin by François Combefis in his *New Supplement*, Volume I, page 1605.

*Oration on Saint Nicholas, Bishop of Myra*, published in Greek and Latin by Pierre Poussin at Toulouse, 1644.

*Panegyric Oration on Saint John Chrysostom.* This exists in Latin in [Laurentius] Surius's collection for January 27th, and in Greek in [Henry] Savile’s edition of the *Works of Chrysostom*, Volume VIII, page 267.

*Paraenetic Oration <note>A "paraenetic" work is an address intended to provide moral advice or exhortation</note>, or an Encyclical Letter of Encouragement to all the faithful of Christ for living well.* Baronius published it in Latin under the year 911, number 5.

*Letter to Omar, King of the Saracens, on the mysteries and truth of the Christian faith, and the impiety and blasphemies of the Saracens.* This exists in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVII.

*Song of Compunction <note>remorse or spiritual sorrow for sins</note> from the meditation on the Last Judgment*, published in Latin by Jacob Pontanus at Ingolstadt, 1603.

*Seventeen Oracles and Prophecies regarding the future state of Constantinople.* Of these, the last appeared in Greek and Latin at the end of the *Annals* of Constantine Manasses, Basel, 1573, in octavo. The first sixteen were published in Greek and Latin with the notes of [Janus] Rutgers among his *Various Readings*, Leiden, 1618, in quarto. Finally, all seventeen are found in Greek and Latin at the end of Codinus’s *Antiquities*, Paris, 1655, in folio.

*The Arrangement of the Order to be held by the thrones of the Churches subject to the Patriarchate of Constantinople*, published in Greek and Latin by [Johannes] Leunclavius in *Greco-Roman Law*, book 2, page 88.

*The Legal Manual* <note>original: "Πρόχειρον Νομικόν" (Procheiron Nomikon)</note>, or *A Concise Selection of Laws*, comprising sixty titles. Leunclavius presents the first twenty-eight titles in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law*, Volume II, page 79. Emperor Leo later undertook a work of immense labor, arranging for all the laws and constitutions of the Greek Emperors to be gathered into one body and distributed into sixty books, giving them the title of the *Basilica* <note>Imperial laws; named after the Emperor (Basileus) Basil I, Leo's father, who began the project</note> and the *Hexabiblos* <note>original: "Ἐξαβίβλων" (Six Books)</note>. Johannes Leunclavius published an ancient Greek-Latin synopsis of these *Basilica* at Basel, 1575, in folio. Charles Annibal Fabrot published the complete work, divided into seven volumes, in Greek and Latin at Paris, 1647, in folio.

*Three New Constitutions* <note>original: "Novellæ Constitutiones"</note> issued by the Augusti <term>Emperors</term> Leo and his brother Constantine; these survive in Greek and Latin at the end of Leunclavius’s *Synopsis*, page 32, and elsewhere.

*Tactics, or a Work on Military Affairs*, published in Latin by John Cheke at Basel, 1554, in duodecimo; then in Greek and Latin by [Johannes] Meursius with notes at Leiden, 1618, in quarto; and later with the translation and notes of Sixtus Arcerius at the same location, 1613.

Furthermore, Baronius reports under the year 911, number 3, that more or less eighteen orations of Emperor Leo remain unpublished in the manuscript collection of the Vatican Library, where he also provides a list of them.

<margin>886.</margin> **WOLFHARD**, a Priest and Monk of the Monastery of Hasenried <note>Hasenried was a Benedictine monastery in the Diocese of Eichstätt</note>, flourished in the year 886. At the command of Erkenwald, Bishop of Eichstätt, he wrote four books *On the Life of Saint Walpurga* (or Waltpurgis), Virgin. The first two of these survive in [Henricus] Canisius's *Ancient Readings*, Volume IV. The complete four books, though with the style altered and many parts revised, appear in Surius on February 25th; finally, they appear in their original form in the Bollandists <note>The Bollandists are a group of Jesuit scholars who publish the "Acta Sanctorum" (Lives of the Saints)</note> for February 25th and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Century* III, part 2, page 287.

<margin>887.</margin> **HEREMBERT**, or **ERCHEMPERT**, a Lombard by nation, born of a noble lineage—specifically tracing his family from the Dukes of Benevento—was a Monk and Deacon of the Monastery of Monte Cassino. He flourished in the year 887, at which time he was sent to Rome to Pope Stephen by Angelarius, the Abbot of Monte Cassino, and obtained a privilege granted to his monastery by the Pontiff. He wrote a more extensive *Chronicle, or History of the Lombards*, which he brought down to the year 888.

<margin>889.</margin>
**RICULPHUS**, Bishop of Soissons <note>original: "Suessionensis"</note>, flourished in the year 889. He was present at the Council of Reims in the year 900. There exists a Constitution containing 22 Chapters concerning matters pertaining to his Diocese, found in *The Councils*, Volume IX, page 416, and among the *Small Works of Hincmar* edited by Cordesius, Paris, 1615, page 685.

<margin>890.</margin>
**ADREVALD**, also known as **ALBERT**, a Benedictine Monk of Fleury <note>original: "Floriacensis"</note>, flourished in the year 890. He wrote the *History of the Translation of the bodies of Saints Benedict and Scholastica* from the ruins of the Monastery of Monte Cassino to the Monastery of Fleury <note>A "translation" is the ceremonial movement of a saint's remains to a new shrine</note>. Jean à Bosco first published it in the *Library of Fleury*, page 1; then Henschen in the *Acts of the Saints* for March 21st; and finally Mabillon in the *Benedictine Century*, Volume II, page 253. He also wrote a *Book on the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, to which Adelarius added two chapters as an appendix, and Aimoin, fellow monks of Fleury, added three other books. All four books remain intact in the locations cited above. Finally, he published a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* against the "follies" of John Scotus Erigena, which is held in D'Achery’s *Spicilegium*, Volume XII.

**ASSER**, a Briton by nation, born in St. Davids <note>original: "Menevensis"</note>, a relative and Chancellor of Asser, Archbishop of St. Davids, and a disciple of John Scotus Erigena, flourished in the year 890. Much harassed by Hyfaidd <note>original: "Hemydo"</note>, a petty king of his people, and summoned by Alfred, the Monarch of England, he established his home in the King's court for some time. He was gifted by the King with the leadership of the monasteries of Amesbury <note>original: "Ambresberiensis"</note> and Banwell <note>original: "Banvillensis"</note>. Finally, he obtained the Bishopric of Sherborne <note>original: "Schireburnensem"</note>; he was the advisor who prompted King Alfred to establish the University of Oxford and to enrich the professors of liberal arts with annual salaries. He died in the year 909. He wrote the *History of the Deeds of King Alfred*, which appeared together with other Histories of England at Frankfurt, 1602, in folio, page 1. In the judgment of Twyne*, he is a writer of such faith and authority that he is known to have never been suspected of falsehood by anyone. He is said by Bale to have also written the *Annals of Britain*, Homilies, and many other works.

<margin>890.</margin>
**WILLIAM**, Librarian of the Roman Church, flourished in the year 890 and thereafter. He wrote the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* starting from Pope Nicholas (where the work of Anastasius the Librarian ended) up to Stephen V inclusive—that is, from the year 867 to the year 891. These *Lives* are published along with the *Lives* by Anastasius in the Mainz edition of 1602, the Paris edition of 1649, and in every edition of the *Councils*. However, some scholars, including Baronius, believe that all those *Lives of the Pontiffs* should be attributed to one and the same author, whether to Anastasius or someone else.

<margin>891.</margin>
<margin>* On Illustrious Men of Germany, part 2, page 105.</margin>
**SOLOMON**, German by nation, born in the town of Thurgau <note>original: "Tergoviâ"</note> of a noble family, was instructed in higher learning at the school of Saint Gall under the monk Iso. Serving as Chaplain and Counselor to Emperor Louis the Stammerer <note>original: "Ludovici Balbi"</note>, he was appointed first as Abbot of Ellwangen, then of Kempten, later of Pfäfers, then of Saint Gall, and finally, in the year 891, Bishop of Constance on the Rhine. In his declining years, he traveled to Rome and was received kindly and honorably by Pope John X. Returning from there, he brought back many relics of Saints Constantius and Pelagius, which he deposited in the Monasteries of Saint Gall and Constance, the body of Constantius being placed in the former and Pelagius in the latter. He died in the year 920, in the 30th year of his episcopate. Various poems of his exist in Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, Volume I, in the Appendix, page 15, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVI, page 1300. Heinrich Pantaleon* mentions an elegant Dictionary written by Solomon while still a youth, which was preserved in his own time on parchment at the Monastery of Saint Gall. Whether it still exists today is unknown to me.

### FORMOSUS

An Italian by birth, he was first the Bishop of Porto <note>original: "Episcopus Portuensis"</note>. He was sent by Pope Nicholas to the Bulgarians to instruct them in the Christian faith, later deposed by John VIII, and then restored by Marinus. Finally, on September 19, 891, he was ordained as the Pope of the Roman Church. After suffering many injustices inflicted upon him by the citizens of Rome, to whom he was quite hateful, he died on April 4, 896. After his death, he was dragged from his tomb by his successor Stephen <note>This refers to the infamous "Cadaver Synod," where the deceased Formosus was put on trial</note>. He was first placed on the Papal throne, then stripped of his sacred vestments, and after three of his fingers were cut off, he was thrown into the Tiber. The ordinations he had conferred were also declared void. Two of his Letters remain in *The Councils*, Volume IX, page 428; the latter of these, addressed to the Bishops of England, is argued by Papebrochius* to be a mere forgery of the eleventh century.

<margin>* *An Attempt at a Chronology of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 156.</margin>

Another letter concerning the Monastery of Gigny <note>original: "Monasterio Gigniacensi"</note> was published by Baluzius in his *Miscellanies*, Volume II, page 159. Flodoardus, in his *History of Reims*, book 4, chapters 2 and 3, lists many of his letters to Fulco, Archbishop of Reims, and to Kings Charles and Otto, where he provides short summaries of their main points and arguments.

### NICHOLAS, THE MYSTIC

Called by this surname because, as some interpret it, he was a Senator of the "Secret Council" <note>The "Mystikos" was a high-ranking judicial or secretarial official in the Byzantine court</note>. Around the year 892, he was created Patriarch of the Church of Constantinople. After nine years had passed, Emperor Leo <note>Leo VI, known as "the Wise"</note>, who was still childless, took a fourth wife. Offended by this act, Nicholas threw himself at Leo’s feet and earnestly begged him to refrain. When the Emperor refused to comply, Nicholas convened a Synod in the year 901 and condemned the Emperor's marriage; he deposed Thomas, the priest who had blessed the marriage with ecclesiastical rites, and barred the Emperor himself from the sacred services. When he could not be moved from his decision by any pleas, he was driven from his see in 903, placed on a ship, and banished to the Monastery of Galacrane. No friend, servant, or even a book to comfort him with reading accompanied him into exile. The great evils he suffered are clearly set forth by Nicholas himself in a letter to the Pope. In 911, after the death of Leo, Alexander gained the empire; he ejected Euthymius, who had been substituted in Nicholas's place, and restored Nicholas to his see upon his recall from exile. He presided over it for the next 13 years and died in 924. Two Letters exist: one to Pope Anastasius and another to John X, in the Latin *Councils*, Volume IX, page 1264. A decree regarding the granting of Patriarchal letters free of charge exists in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law*, book 4, page 249. A letter to Simeon, Prince of Bulgaria, is held in Greek and Latin by Baronius under the year 917, along with five others to the princes of the Armenians, Saracens, Lombards, and Amalfians, and to Bishops living outside of communion.

---

<margin>892.</margin>

### REGINO

A German by birth, he was first a monk of Prüm <note>original: "Prumiensis," a Benedictine abbey in Germany</note>. Then, in the year 892, when Abbot Farabert resigned his rule, Regino was elected as his successor by the unanimous consent of the monks. However, he did not hold the leadership for long; after seven years, he was forced to step down due to the envy of certain rival monks. Regarding this matter, he himself wrote in his *Chronicle* for the year 899: "In the same year, Richard was appointed Abbot of Prüm;

> but how it was acted toward me, I have deferred noting in this place, lest perhaps, provoked by injustices, I might seem to have exaggerated the causes of my persecution beyond what Christian patience allows."

He died around the year 908. He wrote a *Chronicle* <note>original: "Chronicon"</note> for Adalbero I, Bishop of Metz, covering the period from the birth of Christ to the year 907 in two books, in which he chiefly encompassed the deeds of the Franks and the Germans. For the *Appendix*, which proceeds from the year 907 to 972, was added by a more recent writer. This *Chronicle* appeared among other writers of German affairs in Frankfurt, 1583, together with the *Chronicle of Ursberg* in Strasbourg, 1609, in folio. Regino also wrote two books *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines and the Christian Religion*, containing nearly 900 chapters. In the first book, he deals with ecclesiastical matters and persons; in the second, with the life and conduct of the Laity. He began this work around 806 at the urging of Rathbod, Archbishop of Trier, especially for the use of the Diocese of Trier, drawing from the canons of ancient Synods and the letters of Roman Pontiffs...

# The Photian Century
<note>This era is named after Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, whose conflict with the Papacy in the 9th century laid the groundwork for the Great Schism between the Eastern and Western Churches.</note>

...collected chiefly from genuine letters, the sermons of the Holy Fathers, the Theodosian Code <note>The *Codex Theodosianus* was a compilation of Roman laws under the Christian emperors</note>, and the Capitularies <note>legal decrees</note> of the Frankish Emperors. Joachim Hildebrand of Helmstedt first brought this to light in 1659, expanded with an appendix assembled from elsewhere. Later, Étienne Baluze published a revised edition in *Paris, 1671, octavo*, adorned with a larger Helmstedt appendix, a new one added by himself, highly learned notes and a preface, and an appendix of ancient Acts.

---

9th CENTURY

**AUXILIUS**, though it is not clear who he was or to whom he belonged, rose to prominence around the year 894. *He wrote two books On the Ordinations of Pope Formosus, or against the internal discord of the Roman Church*, or, to use the words of Sigebert*, *On the Ordinations, De-ordinations, and Super-ordinations of the Roman Pontiffs.* <note>Auxilius was a champion for the validity of ordinations performed by the controversial Pope Formosus, which were being declared void by rival factions.</note> Jean Morin first published these books at the end of his work *On Holy Ordinations, part 2, page 348*; from there they were recorded in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVII, page 1. Jean Mabillon presents another of his books, or rather a *Dialogue on the cause and business of Pope Formosus*, in the *Analecta*, Volume IV, page 610.

<margin>895.</margin>
**NICEPHORUS**, a Philosopher and Orator of the Patriarch of Constantinople, was prominent in the year 895. He wrote a *Panegyric Oration, or the Life of Anthony Cauleas, Patriarch of Constantinople*, who died in the year 891. It exists in Latin in the works of Surius and the Bollandists <note>groups of scholars who compiled lives of the saints</note> under the date of February 12th.

<margin>895.</margin>
**WALDRAMNUS**, Bishop of Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratensis"</note>, was prominent in the year 895, at which time he took part in the Council of Tribur; in the Acts of that council, he is called Baltrannus, Bishop of Strasbourg. He died in the year 905. He wrote *Several Poems to Solomon, Bishop of Constance*, which can be found in Canisius, Volume I, in the Appendix, page 31, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVI, page 1304.

<margin>896.</margin>
**STEPHANUS VI**, a Roman by birth and the son of John the Priest, seized the Pontifical seat in the year 896, having driven out Boniface (who had succeeded Pope Formosus) by force of arms; he was ordained on May 2nd. Having immediately held a Synod in Rome, he rescinded the Acts of Pope Formosus, dragged his body from the tomb and mutilated it, and deposed the clergy ordained by him. <note>This refers to the "Cadaver Synod," one of the most gruesome episodes in papal history, where a deceased pope was put on trial.</note> In the year 897, he himself was cast into prison and was strangled on August 3rd. Two of his *Letters* remain in *The Councils*, Volume IX, page 476.

<margin>898.</margin>
**JOANNES IX**, a Roman by birth from Tivoli and the son of Rampaldus, was ordained as Roman Pontiff on March 12th, 898. At the start of his pontificate, he called a Synod in Rome to discuss the election and coronation of Berengar and Lambert as Emperors of Italy, and he rescinded the Acts of the Roman Synod held by Stephen. In the same year, or early the next, he celebrated a Council of 74 Bishops at Ravenna in the presence of Emperor Lambert; in this council, Lambert confirmed his royal rights, Stephen VI and his Roman "council" <note>original: "Conciliabulum," implying an illegitimate council</note> were condemned, the priests deposed by Stephen were restored, those ordained by Stephen were deposed, and the debt of veneration was returned to the memory of Pope Formosus. He died on March 26th, 900. Four of his *Letters* remain in *The Councils*, Volume IX, page 483.

<margin>900.</margin>
**BENEDICTUS IV**, a Roman by birth and the son of Mammolus, obtained the Pontifical throne in the year 900, being ordained on April 6th. He died on October 20th, 904. Two *Letters* remain regarding the restoration of Argrinus, Bishop of Langres, to the rights of his church, in *The Councils*, Volume IX, page 511; another regarding the Bishop of Malaga is found in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume III, page 436.

<margin>900.</margin>

On the same day, at the beginning of the Council of Reims which he himself presided over, he struck the murderers of his predecessor Fulk with an anathema <note>a formal curse or excommunication</note>. # The Photian Century
<note>The 9th century is often called the "Photian Century" by Western historians, named after Photius the Great, the Patriarch of Constantinople. This period was defined by the growing theological and political rift between the Latin West and the Greek East.</note>

from the
Year 800.

...celebrated a provincial [synod] at Trosly-Loire <note>original: Trosleii</note> in the district of Soissons <note>original: Suessoniensi</note>; in which he restored the collapsed discipline of the Church; he restored the state of the Monasteries which were falling into worse condition daily; he forbade the clergy from the company of women; and he condemned the opinion of the Greeks regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit. <note>This refers to the "Filioque" controversy, a dispute over whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from both the Father and the Son.</note> In the year 921, having held a Synod at Trosly again, he excommunicated Count Erlebald on account of the church lands of Rheims <note>original: Remensis</note> which had been unjustly seized. He died in the year 922, on July 2nd <note>original: VI. Non. Julii</note>, the third day after the coronation of King Robert. He wrote to Guy <note>Wido</note>, Archbishop of Rouen <note>original: Rothomagensem</note>, a *Statute excerpted from the opinions of the Fathers and the Canons*, containing 23 Chapters, regarding what kind of penance ought to be enjoined upon unbaptized Pagans <note>Gentilibus</note>, the baptized, the rebaptized, and those who afterwards fell away from the Christian faith. It is found in the *Councils*, Volume IX, page 484, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVII, page 246, and among the *Short Works of Hincmar* edited by Cordesius, page 697. Also, by his guidance and counsel, the fifteen lengthy *Chapters* of the Synod of Trosly held in the year 909 were established, which are found in the *Councils*, Volume IX, page 521.

# THE DARK AGE.
<note>original: "Sæculum Obscurum." This term was coined by Cardinal Baronius to describe the 10th-century Papacy, a period marked by political instability and moral crisis in Rome.</note>

## Overview of the Century.

<margin>
10th CENTURY
from the
Year 900.
</margin>
**A**ll those who have committed the history of this time to writing graphically depict the mournful state of the Christian Church in this century; and the facts themselves cry out clearly enough; so confused, disjointed, foul, and shameful was everything. Few learned writers adorned this century, and there were almost no Councils worthy of mention. Detestable schisms <note>splits within the church</note> even in the very heart of the Roman See, the most shameful lives of the Popes, and abominable outrages—previously unheard of in the Christian commonwealth—deformed the age. For this reason, it is commonly called **UNFORTUNATE** and **DARK**; as even [Cardinal] Baronius himself confesses and laments at the year 900, Number 1. He says: "A new century begins, which by its harshness and lack of good is called 'iron'; by the deformity of its overflowing evil, 'leaden'; and by its poverty of writers, 'dark'." In Number 3 he says: "All that the Church suffered under the Gentile <note>Pagan</note> Emperors, or from heretics, schismatics, and any other persecutors, are to be considered somehow like children's games in comparison to these evils; indeed, they should be counted as profit and gain." At the year 912, Number 14, he asks: "How foul was the face of the Roman Church when most powerful and equally most sordid harlots dominated Rome? At whose will sees were changed, bishops were appointed, and—what is horrific and unspeakable to hear—their lovers, pseudo-pontiffs, were intruded into the seat of Peter, who are written in the catalog of Roman Pontiffs only for the purpose of marking the dates. For who could say that those intruded without law by whores of this kind were legitimate Roman Pontiffs?" These things and many more are said there by that most eminent and learned Cardinal; and at the end of the century in the year 1000, Number 22, he says it is a miracle that the Roman Church itself did not fall and utterly perish with so many wicked, criminal, unchaste, thieving, invading, bloody, and predatory men invading the Apostolic See, defiling it with depraved morals, and with such a vicious entry followed by a detestable example of evil conduct.

Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine scholar and historian.</note> says nearly the same thing, but briefly, at the entry of the 10th Century, page 552: "This century is called unfortunate, exhausted of men distinguished in genius and learning, or even of distinguished Princes and Pontiffs, in which almost nothing worthy of memory was performed for posterity." He even reports that a certain monster was found then with a dog's head and the rest of its limbs human, which wonderfully reflected the state of that time. And shortly after: "This was indeed unfortunate, because for nearly 150 years, about 50 Pontiffs—from John VIII, who succeeded the holy Pontiffs Nicholas and Adrian II, all the way to Leo IX, who was the first called by God like another Aaron—utterly failed from the virtues of their ancestors; they were apostates rather than apostolics." In these evils, the Roman Pontiffs were the "bow and the stern" <note>a Latin idiom meaning the beginning and the end, or the entirety of the matter</note>, the monstrous heads of the Catholic Church; and if things were so in the head, what wickedness, you might ask, pervaded the members? Hence, to say nothing of the laity, the morals of the Bishops, Priests, and the whole clerical order were most depraved; discipline collapsed, and there was pride, ambition, greed, fraud, perjury, luxury, lust, and almost an entire <term>Lerna of vices</term> <note>Lerna refers to the swamp where the mythical Hydra lived; here it means a "bottomless pit" or "breeding ground" of sin.</note>. It is no wonder if, in such a corrupt state of the Church, many errors arose regarding the Canonization of Saints, the Baptism of Bells <note>The practice of blessing bells with water, oil, and salt, which critics sometimes likened to the sacrament of baptism.</note>, the Celibacy of Priests, the relics of saints, and visions...

# THE DARK AGE.

<margin>
10th CENTURY
from the
Year 900.
</margin>

...visions, apparitions, the ordeal by hot iron, and other portents of superstition are brought in with all their bag and baggage <note>original Greek: ὅλῳ τῷ θυλάκῳ (holō tō thylakō), an idiom meaning "lock, stock, and barrel" or "with the whole sack."</note>. *“Christ was then clearly sleeping,”* (to use the words of [Cardinal] Baronius again at the year 912, number 14), *“in a deep sleep, as it appears, in the ship, when, with these strong winds blowing, the ship itself was being covered by the waves. He who, by pretending not to see those things, allowed it to happen so long as He did not arise as an avenger, was teaching us [a lesson].”* Nevertheless, there were not entirely lacking in this very age—even in the midst of the Papacy—those who manfully resisted Papal tyranny, the yoke of clerical celibacy <note>the requirement that priests remain unmarried</note>, the doctrine of not having the Holy Scriptures and Sacred Rites in the common language, and [doctrines] concerning Purgatory, the worship of Images, the Corporal <note>physical</note> presence in the Eucharist, and so forth. These figures are recorded in the **Catalog of the Witnesses of Truth**, by Mornay <note>Philippe de Mornay, a French Protestant writer</note>, and Heidegger in his *History of the Papacy*, as well as by whichever of the Reformed <note>Protestant</note> authors have composed a History of the Church. 

Indeed, even this unhappy age did not lack the conversions of certain barbarian peoples to the faith of Christ: the **Normans**, under their leader **Rollo**, who was washed in the sacred font <note>baptized</note> in the year 912; the **Ruthenians** <note>peoples of the Kievan Rus'</note> or **Muscovites** around the year 969; and soon after the **Poles**, **Danes**, **Hungarians**, and other Northern peoples who, abandoning Paganism, crossed over into the camps of Christ. Finally, toward the year 996 at the close of the century, the transfer of the Empire from the Franks to the Germans and the institution of the Electoral Order <note>the system of princes who elected the Holy Roman Emperor</note> is commonly reported. Whether this is recorded correctly or otherwise is for those interested to see; a large enough number of writers on the **transfer of the Empire**—whose factions do not concern us here—dispute this matter sufficiently and most fiercely.

# WRITERS.

<margin>
10th CENTURY from the Year 901.
Michael Psellus, Eulogy for Saint Metaphrastes, in Greek and Latin, found in Leo Allatius’s *On the Writings of Simeon*, p. 221.
</margin>

SYMEON, called the METAPHRASTES <note>from the Greek *metaphrasis*, meaning "paraphraser" or "translator," referring to his work rewriting older saints' lives into a more polished style</note> because of the style of writing he used, was a native of Constantinople. Born of a noble and illustrious family, he was a man destined to advance the cause of literature in an unfortunate century. He was himself endowed with an excellent intellect and adorned with all the more refined learning, through which he easily attained the highest honors of the state. Indeed, he was appointed by the Emperor Leo <note>Emperor Leo VI, "the Wise"</note> as Chief Secretary, Patrician, and, it seems, Great Logothete <note>a high-ranking administrative official</note>, or "Grand Chancellor" as we would call it. He was certainly the Logothete of the Course <note>originally the head of the imperial postal system, but by this time a role equivalent to a Foreign Minister</note>, and finally, he was named Master of the Palace, an office that stood out among the highest dignities of the Court of Constantinople. 

He flourished at the beginning of this century, around the year 901. Regarding his age, the opinions of scholars vary strangely, placing him at different times from the beginning of the third century all the way to the fourteenth. This ought to seem all the more surprising since, setting aside evidence from other sources, he himself indicates his own era quite clearly, both elsewhere and in his *Life of Saint Theoctista*, which Michael Psellus the Younger testifies was written by Metaphrastes. For in that *Life*, he testifies in more than one place that he lived under Leo the Wise and his son Constantine [Porphyrogennetus]. There he further reveals that he was sent as an ambassador by the Emperor Leo to the Arabs in Crete in the company of General Himerius, to whom he served as a counselor in military affairs. He sailed to the island of Paros, and there held a conversation with a certain aged hermit, by whom he was encouraged to write the *Life of Theoctista*. From this, the notable error of those who confuse him with Symeon Logothetes the Younger (who was famous around the year 1170) is evident—to say nothing of those who place Metaphrastes before the tenth century. Indeed, even Blondel <note>David Blondel, a French Protestant scholar</note>, who is otherwise quite accurate in chronological matters, is no less deluded in thinking that he died after the year 1080.

<margin>
* Full Assertion of the Genealogy of the French, p. 126.
† Chronology, book 4, p. 631.
* Epitome of Gesner, p. 641.
† Anthropologium, book 19, p. 707.
* Supplement, p. 592.
</margin>

Genebrard and Simler wander even further from the truth, referring him to the year 1200; Volaterranus, by an even worse error, pushes him down to the year 1300; and the worst of all is Casimir Oudin, who writes that Metaphrastes flourished from the year 1314 to 1330. Oudin claims he was convinced of this by the mind and arguments of Leo Allatius <note>a Greek scholar and librarian at the Vatican</note>. He says: "In that little work on the 'Simeons,' Allatius examines most accurately everything pertaining to the writings and the age of our Simeon Metaphrastes; whom he finally binds by certain arguments, contrary to the opinion of all the ancient writers of this century, to the year of Christ 1314. I gladly embrace his opinion because of the weight of the reasons he brings forward." 

I must confess I was stunned when I read this, marveling at the man's extreme negligence, as he piles a worse error upon a bad one. For Metaphrastes did not flourish in the year 1314, nor does the most learned Allatius say so. It is clearer than the sun itself that Leo Allatius, both in his *Discourse on the Pselli* (p. 19) and in his *Dissertation on the Writings of the Simeons*, refers our Simeon to the times of Leo the Wise, and provides proof of this with many arguments beyond all controversy. 

But to return to the deeds of Simeon: in the year 904, by his wise and sagacious counsel, he softened the heart of Leo of Tripoli, the leader of the Saracens who was threatening the destruction of the city of Thessaloniki which he had recently captured, and turned him from his purpose. Around the year 912, he turned his attention to committing the *Lives of the Saints* to writing, beginning with Theoctista. How long he lived, I have not yet learned; however, it is certain that he wrote during the reign of Constantine Porphyrogennetus, when Constantine had already reached a more advanced age.

The time that Metaphrastes had free from public business, he spent in the study of literature; he was particularly devoted to illustrating the antiquities of the Church. For, at the command of the Emperor Constantine, he searched everywhere for the *Lives of the Saints* written before his time. Once collected, he reviewed them: the more elegant ones he approved with his vote as worthy of the readers' sight, and published them without any changes. Those that were less elegant, however, he partly dressed in a more polished style, and partly 

<meta>The catchword "novâ" (new) suggests the next page will describe him rewriting these lives in a "new" or fresh form.</meta>

<margin>10th CENTURY from the Year 901.</margin> He arranged and organized into order, using a new form and method, even those works received from the tradition of his predecessors, which he himself composed by his own effort <note>original: "proprio Marte," a Latin idiom meaning "by one’s own hand" or "by one's own prowess"</note>. Therefore, a most learned man <note>referring to Leo Allatius, the scholar mentioned previously who specialized in Metaphrastes</note> took upon himself the task of distinguishing the genuine lives written by Metaphrastes from those that were falsely added, which he performed with great accuracy. We shall briefly follow his guidance regarding those Lives which have been published in print either in Greek or Latin, which Martin Hank noted with clearly praiseworthy diligence in his *On Byzantine Writers*, page 436.

Leo Allatius judges the 122 Lives just numbered to be the genuine offspring <note>original: "foetus," meaning the products or creations</note> of Simeon Metaphrastes, based on arguments drawn from both style and title. He reports that these exist in Greek, both published and unpublished, in the Vatican Library and elsewhere in manuscripts, providing the opening sentences for each in his *Dissertation on the Writings of the Simeons*, page 124.

### SPURIOUS LIVES.

In addition to those, the same Allatius (in the same work, page 119) enumerates another 95 Lives which falsely display the name of Metaphrastes in manuscript codices, also including the opening lines of each. However, the true authors of these could not be discovered despite diligent investigation.

Finally, Allatius (on page 80 of the same work) lists another 444 Lives of Saints and panegyric praises <note>formal speeches of high praise</note> which falsely claimed Metaphrastes' name in some manuscript codices, listing the openings of each in alphabetical order and identifying the true authors of many of them.

It should be noted that of these 539 spurious Lives, many could have been reviewed by Metaphrastes, and perhaps some even felt his "healing hand" <note>original: "manum medicam," a metaphor for his work as an editor who smoothed out or "cured" rough older prose</note>; however, they cannot be considered his work for that reason, since he added little or nothing to them. Furthermore, very many of them were written after Metaphrastes' death.

### OTHER MINOR WORKS.

Four Poems, which Leo Allatius <note>Leo Allatius (1586–1669) was a Greek scholar and librarian at the Vatican who worked extensively on Eastern Christian texts.</note> published in Greek in his *Essay on the Simeons*, page 132.
*An Oration on the Lamentation of the Blessed Mary, while she embraced the lifeless body of Christ.*
This survives in Greek and Latin in the same work, page 245.
*Nine Letters* are found in Greek and Latin in the same work, page 254.
*Twenty-four Orations on Morals*, selected from the writings of Saint Basil. These appeared separately in Greek at Paris, 1556, in octavo; and also in both Greek and Latin among the works of Saint Basil.
*Several Prayers and Hymns*, composed by the Metaphrast <note>The "Metaphrast" refers to Simeon Metaphrastes, famous for his "metaphrasis" or rewriting of saints' lives.</note>, survive in the Greek Ritual books and Troparia <note>A troparion is a short hymn of one stanza, or one of a series of stanzas, in Byzantine music.</note>, which Allatius enumerates individually in the same work, page 131.

<margin>902.</margin> **VALERIUS**, Archpriest of Astorga <note>Astorga is a city in northwest Spain.</note>; he flourished in the year 902. He collected many *Lives of the Eastern Fathers*, which differ significantly from those already published, into a single volume. This volume, written in Gothic letters <note>This refers to the Visigothic script used in medieval Spain.</note>, still exists in the Library of the Church of Toledo, according to the reliability of Rosweyde as cited by Aubertus Miraeus in his *Supplement on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 279.

<margin>903.</margin> **STEPHANUS** (Stephen), a German by birth, son of the Count of Salm, a cleric of Metz, Abbot of Lobbes, and finally from the year 903, Bishop of Liège. He died in the year 920, on the 14th day before the Calends of June <note>May 19th.</note>. He wrote the *Life and Passion of Saint Lambert*, which Jean Chapeauville first brought to light in Volume I of his *History of Liège*, Liège, 1612. It also exists, with the style somewhat altered, in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a German monk who published a massive collection of saints' lives.</note> for September 17th. <margin>* On Writers, chapter 125.</margin> Stephen also wrote, according to Sigebert*, a *Song on the Holy Trinity*, and another *on the Finding of Stephen the First Martyr*. Durandus, in his *Rationale*, book 6, chapter 114, cites these under the names of the *Histories of the Holy Trinity* and *on the Finding of Saint Stephen the First Martyr*; indeed, they seem to have perished not so much by the neglect of others as because they were condemned by the Roman See. For a note in a manuscript codex in the Lambeth Library states: *Stephen of Liège is said to have composed an Office of the Trinity just as he did on the Finding of Saint Stephen, both of which are rejected by the Apostolic See.* Furthermore, he wrote a *capitulary* <note>A book of liturgical chapters or rules.</note> to Robert, Bishop of Metz, in which he arranged the Chapters, Responses, Verses, and Collects for every hour of the night and day throughout the entire year. However, this minor work no longer survives.

<margin>904.</margin> <margin>* On the Destruction of Thessaloniki, chapter 30.</margin> **JOANNES** (John), surnamed **CAMENIATA**, a native of Thessaloniki, the son of a certain cleric. He himself was also a cleric, and a married man, a Reader of the Church of Thessaloniki, and a Chamberlain of the Imperial palace, as is evident from his own words*. He wrote in the year 904, the year in which Thessaloniki was captured and plundered by the Saracens. He was then led away as a captive by the Saracens, placed on a ship, and carried from island to island, and finally led to Tarsus, where he composed his *History* while living in that place. At the request of a certain very learned man named Gregory, he wrote the *History of the Destruction of Thessaloniki*, in which he explains at length and elegantly not only the miserable and mournful state of the captured city, but also his own fate and that of his entire family. Leo Allatius published this in Greek and Latin in his *Symmicta*, part II, page 180.

<margin>911.</margin> **CONSTANTINUS** (Constantine VII), called ***Porphyrogenitus*** <note>Translated as "Born in the Purple," a title for children born to a reigning emperor in the purple chamber of the palace.</note> perhaps by the luck of his birth, the son of Leo the Wise by Zoe, his fourth wife. A native of Byzantium, he succeeded his father in the empire in the year 911 while still a boy of seven years; first his uncle Alexander, then his mother Zoe, administered the empire on behalf of him before he reached adulthood. In the year 919, he took the reins of empire upon himself, having taken Romanos Lekapenos—whose daughter he married—as a partner in the empire. In the year 944, having ejected the Patriarch Tryphon, he raised Theophylact, the son of the Emperor Lekapenos, to the throne of the See of Constantinople. In the following year, after Lekapenos was removed, he held the empire alone, and

When Romanus reached adulthood, growing impatient with his father’s long reign, he removed him from his path by offering him a lethal draft <note>A reference to the tradition that Constantine VII was poisoned by his son Romanus II and his daughter-in-law Theophano.</note>. Constantine died on the 9th of November in the year 959, in the 49th year of his reign and the 55th year of his life. Concerning his eulogy, let us hear Zonaras*: <margin>* Annals, Volume III, page 155.</margin>
> *Constantine was pious toward God and devoted to the study of letters, as can be learned from his writings and also from his letters; though these were not polished according to the precise art of rhetoric, they nonetheless abound in various words and ideas.* <note>original: "Ἦν δὲ Κωνσταντῖνος τὰ πρὸς Θεὸν εὐσεβὴς, κὰ λόγοις πεπαιδευμένὸς, ὡς ἐστὶ καταμαθεῖν ἐκ τῶν συγγραμμάτων αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ μέντοι κἀ ἐξ ἐπιστολῶν, αἳ ἐαν μὴ πρὸς τέχνην ἀκριβῶντο τὴν ῥητορικὴν, ἀλλά γε ῥήμασι ταύταις καὶ ποίᾳ ἰδέαις ποικίλλονται."</note>

Constantine was religious toward God and dedicated to literary studies, as is apparent from his writings and letters, which, although not polished to the level of oratorical art, nonetheless overflow with rhetorical ornaments and certain figures of speech. He also applied himself to rhythm and every kind of verse; this is seen in those writings in which he mourned the death of his wife. He even took account of Philosophy, which had almost fallen into oblivion, and other disciplines, which were failing until he revived them by appointing more learned men. Thus far Zonaras, who in the following passages did not hide the Emperor's vices. Certainly, Constantine restored the liberal arts with all the zeal he could, searching everywhere for the best professors of the sciences, as he himself was greatly devoted to letters, especially History. Indeed, he was highly skilled in Arithmetic, Music, Astronomy, Geometry, Philosophy, and Medicine, but above all others, he excelled in History. He promoted not only the humanities but also the mechanical arts, which had long been neglected, and he himself applied such effort to the art of Painting that he excelled greatly in it, as the illustrious and most learned Du Fresne notes from Liutprand in *Byzantine Families, page 142.*

### W R I T I N G S.

*Narrative of the Image of Christ*, sent by the Savior Himself to Abgar, King of Edessa, and brought from Edessa to Constantinople in the year 944. It survives in Greek and Latin, edited by Combefis in *Origins of Constantinople, page 75.* <note>King Abgar V of Edessa was said to have received a miraculous image of Christ's face, known as the Mandylion.</note>

*Life of the Emperor Basil the Macedonian, his grandfather*, published in Greek and Latin by Allatius in *Miscellany, part II, page 1.*

*A Book on Administering the Empire*, addressed to his son Romanus. <note>Known by its Latin title "De Administrando Imperio," it is a key source for the geography and politics of the neighbors of the Byzantine Empire.</note>

*A Book of Tactics.*

*Two Books on the Themes of the Eastern Empire.* <note>The "Themes" were the military-administrative districts of the Byzantine Empire.</note>

*Seventeen New Constitutions.* These political works, illustrated with his own notes and those of various others, were published together in Greek and Latin by Joannes Meursius at *Leiden, 1617, in octavo.*

*Historical and Political Pandects*, excerpted from the entire body of historians and redacted into 53 titles. Of this magnificent work, most worthy of a prince, only two titles survive today: namely the 27th, containing excerpts on embassies, edited in Greek by David Hoeschel at *Augsburg, 1603, in quarto*, and in Latin by Charles Cantoclarus with notes at *Paris, 1609, in octavo*; and the 50th, *comprising a collection on virtues and vices excerpted from 14 ancient historians*, which Henri Valois edited from the Peiresc Manuscript in Greek and Latin with notes at *Paris, 1634, in quarto.*

<margin>915.</margin>
**JOHN**, an Italian by nation and a native of Capua, born of the illustrious lineage of Princes Landulf I and Atenulph II; he was first the Archdeacon of his native church, then he joined the monks of Monte Cassino; finally, having been made Abbot of the Monastery of Monte Cassino in the year 915, he led his monks, who had been driven from their own seats by the Saracens <note>Arab raiders who frequently attacked southern Italy in the 9th and 10th centuries.</note>, to Capua. He died in the year 934. He wrote a *Brief Chronicle of the Persecutions of the Monastery of Monte Cassino and of the miracles performed therein*; Leo of Ostia testifies in his *Preface, folio 2* that he used this work in composing the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*. It is said to still exist unpublished. Under our John's name (which was nonetheless missing in the autograph manuscript), Camillo Pellegrino published a *Chronicle of the last Counts of Capua* in *History of the Lombard Princes, folio 122*, according to the testimony of J. B. Maro in his notes on Peter the Deacon, chapter 15.

<margin>916.</margin>
HUBALDUS, or *Hucbaldus*, a monk of the Monastery of Saint Amand at Elnone <note>Located in modern-day northern France.</note> of the Order of Saint Benedict. He was the nephew of the monk Milo, also of Elnone, and the teacher of Abbot Bodulf of Stavelot, by whom he was summoned to his monastery and endowed with various estates. He flourished before many others in the year 916; however, he was already well-known many years earlier during the reign of Charles the Bald. He died in the year 930.

<margin>
926.
Life of Odo by his disciple John, in Surius, Nov. 18.
</margin>
ODO, a Frank by nation, was educated in the court of William, Duke of Aquitaine. In the nineteenth year of his age, he received the tonsure at Tours and entered the clergy; he was made a musician and Archcantor of the Church of Tours in the year 901, where he drank in the elements of grammar. Later, having set out for Paris, he learned music and dialectic <note>logic</note> from Remigius. Returning then to Tours, he shut himself in a cell and devoted himself entirely to the harsher exercises of piety. In the year 912, seeking Burgundy, he took up the monastic life in the Monastery of Baume, recently founded by Abbot Berno, and was placed in charge of the monastery school. Around the year 926, he was ordained a priest by Turpio, Bishop of Limoges. In the year 927, after the death of Berno, he was elected Abbot. Soon, however, troubled by the envy and wickedness of certain monks, he laid down his office; withdrawing to Cluny, he completed the monastery he had long ago begun. In the year 936, summoned to Rome by Pope Leo VII, he brokered peace between Alberic, the prince of the Roman city, and King Hugh. Two years later, having set out for Rome again, he drew Hugh away from the siege of the city through his prayers. Shortly before his death, he was designated Abbot of Fleury but was rejected by the monks. In the year 942, he undertook a journey to Rome for a third time for the sake of religion. While staying in Rome, he began to suffer from a sharp illness. Returning in haste to France, he breathed his last at Saint Martin's in Reims—whose memory he had cherished intensely—on the fourth day after the feast of Saint Martin.

<margin>928.</margin>
**RATHERIUS**, a monk of Lobbes <note>A Benedictine monastery in modern-day Belgium, then a major center of learning.</note>, set out for Italy to King Hugh in the year 928, and was appointed Bishop of Verona by him. In the year 934, having been falsely accused of treason before Hugh, he was ejected from his seat and from Italy. He was subsequently taken under the protection of Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne <note>The brother of Holy Roman Emperor Otto the Great and a powerful political figure.</note>, and was placed by him in charge of the See of Liège, which was then vacant. However, as the clergy of Liège took poorly to his austere ways and rigid discipline, he was forced to yield the Bishopric and withdrew again to Bruno’s patronage. Soon, through Bruno's efforts, he regained his former seat at Verona; however, he fell from it again, having become hated by King Hugh because of his sharp rebukes of the King’s wicked behavior. Now an exile for the third time, he retired to his own Monastery of Lobbes; and there he met his final day in the year 973 or the following.

<margin>932.</margin>
GERARD, a monk, and as it seems, the Dean or Provost of the Monastery of Saint Medard in Soissons from around the year 932. He was still living in the year 950. He wrote the *Life of Saint Romanus*, in both verse and prose. The version written in an oratorical style was published by Nicolas Rigault (according to Mabillon, who nevertheless notes neither the year nor the place of publication). Mabillon himself published the Prologue in *Analecta*, Volume I, p. 107.

---

<margin>933.</margin>
HIPPOLYTUS, a native of Thebes, whom some wrongly confuse with Hippolytus of Portus <note>Hippolytus of Portus was a much earlier 3rd-century martyr; this Hippolytus is a medieval chronicler.</note>; he flourished around the year 933, certainly a little younger than Simeon Metaphrastes, whom he cites. A *Chronicle*, or rather a *Fragment of a Chronicle*, exists in Greek and Latin in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume III, p. 35. This man also seems to be the author of the *Short List of the Twelve Apostles*, published under the name of Hippolytus the Elder in Greek and Latin by Combefis in the *Paris Supplement*, 1648, Volume II, as we noted above under Hippolytus of Portus. To these it is permitted to add what Father Colomiès advised me: namely, that Sirmond testifies in his notes to Sidonius, p. 57, that in the ancient collections he had read a <gloss>fragment</gloss> <note>original: "αποσπασμα"</note> concerning the city of Constantinople (understand these as excerpts from Codinus) which occur in many libraries; that Constantine—after his son Crispus had been killed by him, and having been struck with grief for the deed and the error—set up a silver statue overlaid with gold, with a golden head, with this inscription: <term>MY INJURED SON</term> <note>original: "ΗΔΙΚΗΜΕΝΟΣ ΥΙΟΣ ΜΟΥ"</note>. For this matter, he says, the witnesses praise the chroniclers Herodotus and Hippolytus. I know of no one who mentions Herodotus [in this context]. Glycas praises Hippolytus in his *Annals*, as does Nicephorus Callistus in his *Ecclesiastical History*, book 2. Lambecius thinks that instead of <term>Herodotus</term> <note>original: "Ηρωδοτω"</note> one should read <term>Herodian</term> <note>original: "Ηρωδιανω"</note>, because naturally an anonymous author cites Herodian, a contemporary author, in the *Collection on the Antiquities of Constantinople*, no. 202. You can find other fragments of Hippolytus in Cotelier’s work on the *Apostolic Fathers*.

<margin>933.</margin>
<margin>Climate 3, part 3, p. 97.</margin>
EUTYCHIUS, son of Batriq, called in Arabic *Sa'id ibn Batriq*, Egyptian by nationality, originating from the city of Fostat (which the author of the *Nubian Geography*, whose name was *Sharif al-Idrisi*, relates was the old city of *Misr* [Cairo]). An eminent physician, and from the year 933 the Patriarch of Alexandria, he held the see for seventeen years and six months, and died in the year 950. In his time there occurred a great discord and continuous dispute between him and his flock, as Ibn Abi Usaibi'a testifies in his *Life*, which the illustrious Pococke placed before the Eutychian book in Arabic and Latin. He wrote to his brother Isa in the Arabic language *Annals from the Creation of the World to the Year 940*, collected from the Law and the Gospel (as he says in the Preface) and other books old and new, to which he gave the title *The String of Pearls* <note>original Latin: "Contextionis Gemmarum"; Arabic: "Nazm al-Jauhar"</note>. In these many things occur most worthy of note which are sought elsewhere in vain; certainly many are very similar to old wives' tales, which if he did not invent from his own brain, he at least drew from the frivolous records of his Church. An <gloss>excerpt</gloss> <note>original: "αποσπασματι"</note> of these *Annals*, illustrated with notes under the title *Alexandrian Origins*, was published in Arabic and Latin by the illustrious Selden, *London 1642, in quarto*. The complete *Annals* with Selden's Preface and notes in Arabic and Latin were brought to light by the most learned...

The most learned Pococke <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), a renowned English Orientalist and professor at Oxford.</note> at Oxford in 1659, in quarto, testifies that Abu'l-Abbas (or Ahmed Ben Casem) in his *Lives of Physicians* states that our Eutychius wrote a "Compendious Manual" <note>original: *Syntagma compendiosum*</note> called *Netmolgheubar* <note>original: *Netmolgheubar*; likely a transcription of the Arabic *Nazm al-Jawhar*, meaning "The String of Pearls."</note>, completed in three discourses. In these, he dealt with the knowledge of Christian fasting, their Easter, festivals, the Caliphs, the Patriarchs, and so on. John Selden <note>A famous English jurist and scholar.</note> maintained that this work was the same as the *Annals*, but Hottinger <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger, a Swiss philologist and theologian.</note> concludes it is a different work, both from the title of the book and from the distribution of its contents.

In addition to these, Eutychius wrote a book *On the Affairs of Sicily* after it was captured by the Saracens. A manuscript of this exists in the public library at Cambridge, attached to the volume of his *Annals*. He also wrote a *Disputation between Heterodox and Christians* directed against the Jacobites <note>The Jacobites were a Syrian Monophysite Christian sect; "heterodox" here refers to those not following the Council of Chalcedon.</note>, which is held in manuscript, as well as certain medical *Short Works* by the same author; concerning these, see what the celebrated Hottinger has in his *Oriental Library*, chapter 2, pages 71 and 84, and his *Ecclesiastical History of the 10th Century*, page 37.

<margin>936.</margin>
## LEO VII
A Roman by birth, he was Pope from the year 936, ordained on the 14th day of February. In that same year, he summoned Odo, the Abbot of Cluny, to Rome, so that he might restore the fallen morals and discipline of the monks with his help. He died in the year 939, on the 23rd day of August. Three of his *Letters* survive in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume IX, page 594.

<margin>940.</margin>
## FLODOARD
(called Flauvaldus by Sigebert), a Priest of Culminiac and Canon of Reims, flourished in the year 940. Count Herbert, who had plundered all ecclesiastical rights and had forced the promotion of his seven-year-old son Hugh to the Archbishopric of Reims several years earlier, deprived our Flodoard of the Church of Culminiac because he opposed his son's election. He was deprived *along with the land of the benefice <note>A "benefice" was a grant of land or income given to a member of the clergy in exchange for their spiritual services.</note> which he held at that time, to use his own words*; and not only that, but when some suggested to the Count that he was involved in plots, he held him in loose custody. He was released after five months, and later Hugh (having now reached adulthood) gave him the Church of Saint Mary located in Colrid; he restored the land that his father had taken away and granted him another in the aforementioned village. He died on March 28th, 966, at the age of 73.

### WORKS.

*Chronicle of Affairs Conducted among the Franks* from the year 919 up to the year 966. It is found among the contemporary writers edited by Pithou, Paris, 1588, in octavo, and Frankfurt, 1594, in octavo, page 109.

*History of the Church of Reims in Four Books.* These were published along with an Appendix by an anonymous (though ancient) author, edited by Sirmond, Paris, 1611, in octavo; with the notes of Colvenerius, Douai, 1617, in octavo; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVII, page 500.

<margin>* On Latin History, Book 2, chapter 40.</margin>
Joannes Bonderius, in his *Index of Manuscript Books throughout Belgium*, as the celebrated Vossius* informs us, reports that fifteen books by the Priest Flodoard *On the Italian Triumphs of the Martyrs and Confessors*, written in meter, are preserved in the High Church at Trier. Also, three books in meter *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Saints of Palestine*. Also, two books in meter *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Deeds at Antioch*. Whether this is so, let those who are granted the opportunity of inspecting the manuscripts see for themselves.

<margin>940.</margin>
## GREGORY
A Priest, perhaps of Caesarea, flourished around the year 940. He wrote a *Life of Saint Gregory Nazianzus*, composed for the most part from Nazianzus's own iambic verses, which he wrote *On His Own Life*, and from his *Orations*. It exists in Greek and Latin, prefixed to the *Works of Nazianzus*. He also wrote a *Historical Oration on the 318 Holy Fathers of the Council of Nicaea* and on *Constantine the Great*, which is found in Latin in Surius, July 10th, and in Greek and Latin in Combefis, *New Addition*, Volume II, page 547, with notes.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Three books on the deeds of the Saxons* <note>original: *De rebus Saxonum gestis*</note>, or on the achievements of Emperors Henry the Fowler <note>Henry I, King of East Francia (919–936).</note> and Otto I. These were dedicated to Queen Matilda, the daughter of Emperor Otto. They were published in Basel in 1532, in Frankfurt in 1577, and among the *Writers of German Affairs* in the same city in 1580.

*Several verses, which were found transcribed in a Manuscript of the four Gospels in the Monastery of Corvey, were published through the care of Heinrich Meibom along with the books on Saxon affairs, illustrated with notes, in Frankfurt, 1621, in folio, among certain other writers of the same century.*

The following works have been lost: *The Passion of the Virgin Thecla in verse*, and the *Life of Paul the Hermit in both prose and verse*, written by Witikind, according to the testimony of Sigebert in his *On Writers, chapter 129*.

---

<margin>945.</margin> ATTO, called "the Second," son of Aldegarius, was Bishop of Vercelli <note>A city in the Piedmont region of Northern Italy.</note> from the year 945. He died after the year 960.

### W R I T I N G S.

*The Capitulary* (or the Canons and Statutes given to the Church of Vercelli), woven together from Councils and Decretal Letters <note>Letters from popes that formulated church law.</note>, and distributed into one hundred chapters.

*A Work on Ecclesiastical Oppressions* <note>original: *De Pressuris Ecclesiasticis Opus*</note>, divided into three parts: the first deals with the Judgments of Bishops, the second with their Ordinations, and the third with the Property of Churches.

*Various Letters.*

These small works were transcribed from a Vatican Manuscript—which was quite faulty and full of many gaps—under the care of Cardinal Bona. They were brought to light by Luc d'Achery in his *Spicilegium, Volume VIII, page 1.*

*Seventeen Sermons of Atto on various subjects, and the "Political Book" or "The Plumb-line"* <note>original: *Liber Polyticus seu Perpendiculum*; the title refers to a tool used to ensure a wall is perfectly vertical, here used as a metaphor for moral rectitude.</note> *intended for the rebuke of vices and the establishment of virtues, were contained in the same Vatican Manuscript; however, they were so disfigured by bookworms and decay that they could not be read.*

---

<margin>946.</margin> AGAPETUS II, a Roman by birth, was ordained Pope of the Roman Church on August 9, 946. In the year 947, he confirmed the bishopric of Hugh, whose claim to the see of Reims had been challenged by the French bishops. Nevertheless, in the following year, the French bishops condemned Hugh in the Synod of Ingelheim and drove him from the throne of Reims; Agapetus himself ratified their sentence in a Synod held at Rome in the year 948. He died on March 18, 956. *Two Letters* survive in the *History of the Councils, Volume IX, page 618.* Another letter to Gerhard, Archbishop of Lorch <note>original: *Laureacensem*</note>, in which he confirms his metropolitan rights, is found in Lambecius’s *Commentaries, book 2, page 651.*

---

<margin>946.</margin> LIUTPRAND, an Italian by nation and from Pavia by home (if indeed Johannes Trithemius is to be believed); however, Francisco de Bivar, in a critique prefixed to the works of Liutprand, contends with conjectures that are not entirely to be dismissed that he was Spanish by race, from Cordoba by home (or at least from Andalusia), and that he settled in Italy after being put to flight along with his parents by the Saracens <note>Arab/Muslim forces then in control of much of the Mediterranean.</note>. Whatever the case may be, he was a Deacon of the Church of Pavia, and in the year 946, he was sent as an ambassador by King Berengar of Italy to Emperor Constantine <note>Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, the Byzantine Emperor.</note> for the sake of confirming friendship on both sides. Having been received very honorably and kindly by Constantine, he returned home and was gifted with the Bishopric of Cremona as a reward for his skillfully managed embassy; this occurred (if it is permitted to guess in such an obscure matter) in that same year, or at least the following one. Before the year 963 (exactly when is not sufficiently clear), having become hated by Berengar by some unknown stroke of fate, he was ejected from his see. He therefore betook himself to Germany and established his home at Frankfurt. There he composed his *History*, in which he depicts the tyranny of King Berengar of Italy to the life, nor does he keep silent about the evils which he himself suffered from him and his wife Willa, especially at the beginning of Book III, to which he gave the title *Antidosis* or *Antapodosis* <note>A Greek-derived term meaning "The Retribution" or "Tit-for-Tat."</note>: "

"For in this way," he says, "they have launched against me, my house, my kin, and my family such darts of lies, such losses from robberies, and such schemes of impiety—all without cause—that neither tongue can utter nor pen has the power to write them. Let this present page, therefore, be an *Antidosis* <note>original: *Antidofis*; a Greek term meaning 'giving in return' or 'retribution.'</note> for them; that is, a repayment, while for my calamities I have <gloss>grieved</gloss> <note>original: *dolebat*</note> for their impiety, I shall strip it bare before present and future mortals. Nor shall there be any less of an *Antidosis* for those most holy and fortunate men, in return for the benefits they have bestowed upon me." In the year 963, he was present at the Synod of Rome and acted as an interpreter for Emperor Otto I; for whatever the Emperor spoke in the Saxon <note>Old Saxon or early German.</note> language, he himself rendered into Latin for the Bishops. In the year 968, he was sent as an ambassador by Otto to Constantinople to see Nicephorus Phocas, for the purpose of arranging a marriage between Otto’s son and Anna, the daughter of the Roman Emperor Romanus II and stepdaughter of Nicephorus. However, held in mockery by Nicephorus, treated with insults, and harassed by countless injuries, he returned home with the business unfinished. He also suffered many injuries inflicted by Greek Bishops and Governors while retracing his journey; these he himself narrates and exaggerates quite extensively in his *History*. He was still living in the year 970. In such a rude and unlearned Age, he was clearly a man not uneducated, equally skilled in Greek and Latin, and distinguished in the art of Poetry, traces of which—along with the other liberal arts—are found everywhere in his works; for this reason, Sigebert <note>Sigebert of Gembloux, a 12th-century chronicler.</note> affirms in his *On Writers, chapter 127*, that he wrote in a clear and varied style.

*Six books of the History of affairs handled in Europe in his own time* <note>original: *Historia rerum in Europâ suo tempore gestarum*</note>, addressed to Raymond, Bishop of **Elne** <note>original: *Liberitanum*; referring to the ancient city of Illiberis/Elne in Spain.</note> in Spain; beginning from Emperor Arnulf and ending at his own first Legation to Constantinople. Those things which follow that Legation—namely the last six chapters of the sixth book—do not have Liutprand as their author, but were added by someone more recent. To Book III (*though not, as Sigebert once thought and Trithemius after him, to the whole work*), he gave the name *Antidosis* or *Antapodosis* <note>Greek: 'Repayment' or 'Tit-for-Tat.'</note>, the reason for which we have provided above from the Author himself.

*The Legation undertaken to the Emperor Nicephorus Phocas in the year 968.* Canisius first published it in Ingolstadt, 1600. "A clearly curious writing," says Erycius Puteanus, "although imperfect."

<margin>* Philippe Labbe)</margin>
<margin>* Vossius (in his *Latin Writers*, book 2, chapter 40; *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Vol. II, p. 35.)</margin>
*A book on the deeds of the Roman Pontiffs from St. Peter to Pope Formosus*, mostly excerpted from Anastasius <note>Anastasius the Librarian.</note>. It is well established that this work is spurious and should be rejected from Liutprand's authorship. Not against the truth, Vossius guesses (*supported in this part by Philippe Labbe*) that it should be attributed to a certain German, likely a monk of Corvey or Hersfeld, who flourished toward the end of the previous century. It was published along with the *Lives* by Anastasius through the care of Joannes Busaeus at Mainz, 1602.

*A Chronicle inscribed to a certain fictitious Liutprand, Subdeacon of the Church of Toledo*, filled with old wives' tales and monstrous lies. Francisco Bivarius <note>A Spanish scholar (1585–1634) known for defending controversial or forged Spanish chronicles.</note> marvelously proclaims the praises of this Chronicle in his *Censure, p. 28.* "I have noted," he says, "every detail; everything pleased me." He says the work corresponds to the Author, the phrasing, the style, and the matters written; it corresponds to his all-encompassing erudition, and finally to his patron, Raymund; in one word, it is as if it were the completion of the Chronicle of Dexter <note>A famous 17th-century forgery of Spanish history.</note>. And certainly, the credibility of both writers is equal, having the same weight and authority among the learned <note>The author is being sarcastic here; neither has any authority.</note>. Nor does Bivarius himself dare to hide that this Author gave credit to Pseudo-Turpin of Reims regarding the deeds of Charlemagne and many others. Finally, he was seized by such a love for this Chronicle that he promised he would bring it to light illustrated with very rich commentaries. Truly, a man selling trifles, worthy of wasting his effort and oil in fanning such rubbish.

*Adversaria* <note>A collection of miscellaneous notes or 'commonplace book.'</note> *by the same Author and of the same sort.* In these, says the same Bivarius, "the spirit of the same Liutprand shines, always adorned in both languages and both styles, everywhere rejoicing in the gravity and rarity of the matters written; and Liutprand is not unlike himself." Truly, <note>Greek phrase: ὁμοῖ- τῷ ὁμοίῳ φιλεῖ</note> *like loves like*, and as the proverb says, "like lips love like lettuces" <note>Latin: *similesque amant labra lactucas*; a proverb meaning 'like will to like' or 'bad food for bad mouths.'</note>.

*These works, collected into one and illustrated with notes, were published by Jerónimo de la Higuera and Lorenzo Ramirez at Antwerp, 1640, in folio.* Also in this edition are letters of certain Spanish Prelates collected by Julian the Arch-presbyter,

**JOHN XII**, a Roman by birth, son of Alberic the Patrician, and himself a Patrician and Cleric of the City, attained the Pontifical see after the death of Agapetus with the favor of the Roman people. He was ordained on the 23rd day of March in the year 956, before he had completed his eighteenth year of age. He was previously called Octavian, and was the first (if faith is to be placed in the *Writer of his Life*) who, having been made Pontiff, changed his name for himself. A man infamous for crimes and wickedness, he left nothing unattempted by his ambition or lust; in his debaucheries, adulteries, murders, and tyranny, he is worthily to be compared to Nero or Caligula. Moreover, hated by God for the crimes of treason, perfidy, and perjury, and having become a burden to Italy, he was accused of unspeakable crimes in a Roman Synod in the year 963 by Emperor Otto I, against whom he had raised rebellious arms; he was deposed, and Leo was substituted in his place. However, in the following year, having recovered his former see and power, he gathered a Council at Rome, expelled Leo, and excommunicated him. He died on the 13th day of May in the year 964, having been struck by the devil in the temples <note>original: *in temporibus percussus*; likely referring to the anatomical temples of the head, suggesting a sudden blow or stroke.</note> and lethally wounded while he was amusing himself one night with a certain man's wife outside the City—as Baronius relates on the authority of Liutprand *. There remains an *Epistle* to Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the *Pallium* <note>A liturgical vestment worn by archbishops, symbolizing their authority and bond with the papacy.</note>, and a *Rescript* for the excommunication of Isuard and his companions, who had been struck with anathema by a Synod in the borders of Burgundy in the year 955 for the fields belonging to the Monastery of St. Symphorian which they had unjustly withheld, Council Vol. IX. p. 641.

**FRIDEGOD**, an Englishman by birth, a Benedictine Monk of the Monastery of St. Saviour at Canterbury, and a Deacon in rank, was a man learned in both Greek and Latin who flourished in the year 960. He wrote the *Lives of Saints Wilfrid and Ouen* at the request of Archbishop Odo, who had translated <note>Moved the holy relics of.</note> the bodies of both to Canterbury in the year 956. *Indeed, he composed the Life of St. Wilfrid, Archbishop of York, in heroic verse in a sufficiently lengthy poem.* Mabillon first published it in the *Benedictine Ages*, Part III, Vol. I, p. 169. The *Life of St. Ouen*, written in prose <note>original: *solutâ oratione*</note> by a certain anonymous author, is held today; it was ascribed to Fridegod by Surius and appears in his work under the date of August 24th. Fridegod did indeed write the *Life of Ouen* in meter, but whether he did so in prose is entirely uncertain. Bale * mentions other works, namely: *On the Sinner in the Gospel*, *On Jerusalem*, *On the Vision of the Blessed*, and *Various Contemplations*, which I believe have perished. Concerning his style, William of Malmesbury || notes this: *He wrote in verses that are not so much to be condemned, except that, loathing Latinity, he loves Greekness and frequently uses "Greekish" words; so that the saying of Plautus may rightly be applied to his words: "Indeed, no one shall read these except a Sibyl."* <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses whose oracles were notoriously difficult to decipher.</note>

961.
British Antiquities p. 79. Godwin on the English Prelates p. 73.
</margin>
**DUNSTAN**, an Englishman by race, from Somerset by birth, son of Herstan and Kinedcida, nephew of Archbishop Athelm of Canterbury, was educated in the Monastery of Glastonbury and imbued with fine letters, and especially in the art of engraving and painting. Brought into the court of King Athelstan through the favor of his uncle Athelm, he lived for a long time in the royal service. Finally ejected from the court, he went to Elphege, Bishop of Winchester (who was also his maternal uncle), and at his urging he retired to the Monastery of Glastonbury and took the cowl. Shortly thereafter he was made Abbot of Glastonbury. As his reputation for holiness grew, he was again brought into courtly service by King Edmund; and under two princes, Edmund and Eadred, he ruled everything at his nod as he pleased. Around the year 955, he was driven from the court by King Eadwig and driven into exile. Thus, after a year's stay in Gaul, he was recalled by King Edgar and attained the Bishopric of Worcester. In the year 958 he obtained the see of London, and in the year 961 he was elevated to the Archbishopric of Canterbury. He died on the 19th day of May in the year 988. He was a great champion of Monasticism and the celibacy of the Clergy in England; for that reason he earned the greatest favor among the Monks, who tell marvelous tales about him. Besides other works enumerated by Bale, which I have not learned whether they survive today, he wrote for the use of the Monks and Nuns of the English nation the *Agreement of the Rules*...

<margin>961.</margin>
**NIKON**, an Armenian by race, born of very honorable parents in Pontus Polemoniacus <note>A province on the southern coast of the Black Sea.</note>: while still a boy, he fled secretly from his parents to the Monastery of the Golden Rock <note>original: *Aurea Petra*</note> located on the borders of Pontus and Paphlagonia, and there for many years he diligently practiced the monastic life. He flourished around the year 961, when he was sent by his Archimandrite <note>The superior or abbot of a monastery in the Eastern Church.</note> to convert nations and recall the Christian people to a better harvest of faith. Accordingly, after traveling through Armenia and various regions of the East, he arrived on the island of Crete, recently liberated from the yoke of the Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims; Crete had been under the Emirate of Crete until 961.</note>, which he purged of the remnants of Saracen superstition, leading the inhabitants back to the Catholic Church. In the year 981, he was summoned from Sparta to Corinth so that he might repel by his prayers the Bulgarians rushing into Greece. He died around the year 998; his memory is honored in the Calendars <note>original: *Tabulis*</note> of both the Greeks and the Latins on the 26th of November. An Abbot who was a native of Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> wrote his life and deeds in the year 1150, which Jacques Sirmond translated into Latin; from these, Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a major ecclesiastical historian.</note> extracted many details, especially concerning the miracles performed by him, under the years 961, 969, 981, 982, 986, and 998. He wrote a book *On the most wicked religion of the Armenians* <note>original: *de pessimâ religione Armenorum*; this refers to the theological disputes between the Byzantine Church and the Armenian Church regarding the nature of Christ.</note>, which is commonly available in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: *Bibliothecâ PP.* (Bibliotheca Patrum).</note>.

<margin>963.</margin>
**JOHN XIII**, a Roman by nation, son of Bishop John, was Bishop of Narni before the year 963, at which time he was present at the Roman Synod as a legate from John XII to Emperor Otto; he testified there that he had seen a Deacon ordained by Pope John in a stable. In the year 965, he was elected Roman Pontiff and ordained on the 1st day of October. He had not held the see for long when he was cast out of the city by Rotfred, the Prefect of the City, and delivered into prison in Campania. Having escaped from prison, he was received with hospitality by Pandulph, Prince of Capua: at whose request he granted the rights of an Archbishopric to the see of Capua. Around the year 969, he was restored by Emperor Otto. In the year 971, having held a general Council at Rome, he confirmed the privileges granted to Glastonbury Monastery by King Edgar. He died in the year 972, on the 6th day of September. Four of his Letters survive in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume IX, page 663.

**FULCUINUS**, or Folquin, first a monk of Saint-Bertin, then of Lobbes; after the death of Alatranus, while still a young man, he was made Abbot of the Monastery of Lobbes in the year 965. He died in the year 990.

# The Dark Age. 586

<header>The Dark Age.</header>

<margin>10th CENTURY from the Year 900.</margin>
In the year 996, he [Abbo] sought out Rome again, so that he might advocate before Pope Gregory V on behalf of Arnulf, Archbishop of Reims, who had been wrongfully despoiled of his see; he also obtained an exemption for the Monastery of Fleury <note>original: *Monasterium Floriacense*</note> from the jurisdiction of the Bishops of Orléans by papal authority. In the year 1004, having undertaken a journey to Gascony to the Monastery of Squirs—now called La Réole <note>A town in southwestern France.</note>—to settle the affairs of that monastery, which was by ancient right subject to the monks of Fleury, a riot broke out between his companions and the Gascon monks. He died on the Ides of November <note>November 13</note> after being pierced through the stomach with a spear, and was numbered among the martyrs by his followers.
