# The Dark Age.

<margin>Year 900.</margin>
**The Life of Saint Remaclus, Bishop of Utrecht**, addressed to Abbot Weinfrid. This is found in the records of the 10th Century in the works of Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a German Carthusian monk and hagiographer known for his collection of saints' lives.</note> under September 3rd; the style was originally somewhat rough but was smoothed out by Surius for the sake of the reader.

**Two books on the Miracles of Saint Remaclus**, which claim the same author, are appended to the *Life of Remaclus* in the same volume by Surius. However, they were reduced into a summary by Surius, with many miracles omitted to avoid tiring the reader. Truly, they cannot have Notger, the Bishop of Liège, as their author, since the author testifies that he was present at the burning of the Monastery of Stavelot (which occurred in the year 883). They might not be wrongly attributed to Notger the Elder.

For there was another Notger, distinct from the one in Liège: **Notger, a Monk of Saint Gall**, who flourished in the previous century and died in the year 912. He was the author of a *Martyrology* <note>A catalog or list of martyrs and saints arranged by their feast days.</note> and *Sequences* <note>A type of liturgical hymn used in the Mass.</note>. His *Martyrology* is extant in the works of Canisius, Volume IV, page 761.

<margin>972.</margin>
### BENEDICT VI, a Roman by birth and son of Hildebrand, was Pontiff of the Roman Church from September 12th in the year 972. Thrust into the Castel Sant'Angelo by the Deacon Boniface and strangled there, he ended his days at the close of March in the year 974. A single letter remains, in which he grants Apostolic authority in Noricum and Pannonia to the Bishops of Salzburg, found in the *Councils*, Volume IX, page 711.

---

<margin>975.</margin>
### BENEDICT VII, a Roman by birth from the noble family of the Alberici and son of David, was first the Bishop of Sutri, and then ordained Roman Pontiff from December 19th in the year 975. In the year 983, having held a Synod at Rome, he judged the case of Giselher, Bishop of Magdeburg, who had obtained that dignity from the Emperor through wicked arts. He died on July 10th, 984. A letter to the Gauls and Germans exists, in which he decrees the Church of Lorch <note>original: *Laureacensem*</note> to be a Metropolitan see and entrusts its Archbishop with Apostolic authority; this is found in the *Councils*, Volume IX, page 718. It was first published by Lambeck in his *Commentaries*, book 2, chapter 8, page 645, who also presents a decree of Benedict regarding the privileges of the Monastery of Gembloux, promulgated in the year 983, on page 901 of the same work.

<margin>980.</margin>
<margin>Ethelwerd;</margin>
### ETHELWERD, or Elfward, or as he titles himself at the beginning of his letter to his cousin Matilda, *Patrician Consul Fabius Quaestor Ethelwerd* <note>Ethelwerd used these grand, classicizing Roman titles to describe his high-ranking position as an ealdorman in Anglo-Saxon England.</note>; an Englishman by birth, descended from the royal lineage of English monarchs—specifically, he was the great-great-great-grandson of King Ethelred, son of Ethelwulf. He flourished in the year 980. He wrote a *Short History in four books* for his cousin Matilda, covering from the beginning of the world to the death of King Edgar, which occurred in the year 974. In these books, after he has enumerated rather than described the times before Christ, and then touched upon events with remarkable brevity up to the year of Christ 449, he thereafter devotes his effort to narrating solely the affairs of the English from the year the Saxons or Angles first landed in Britain. This *History* was published by the most noble Savile among the *English Writers*, London 1596, folio 472.

...from that time, those of Sebastea excelled in Philosophy; they came out of the school of Eustathius, whom we know as the Bishop and leader of the Monks of that place. Shortly after, he adds that from these words of **Suidas** <note>The *Suda*, or Suidas, is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek-language encyclopedic lexicon of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>, the age of Suidas himself can seemingly be gathered; for he says that he knew Eustathius, the Bishop of Sebastea and teacher of Atticus, which Atticus ceased to live around the year of Christ 425. Yet, who—even a schoolboy—does not know that Suidas is acting in this place not from personal knowledge, but from historical research? Suidas compiled an extensive Lexicon, in which he has a great many things regarding Theology and Church History, and not a few fragments of the ancients, often even where the name of the author is not provided. It was published in Greek at Milan in 1499 in folio; at Basel in 1544 in folio; and in a Latin translation by Henry Wolf at Basel in 1581. A Greek-Latin version, or rather a Paraphrase by Aemilius Portus of Crete <note>original: "Cretensis"</note> with his notes added here and there, was published at Geneva <note>original: "Coloniæ Allobrogum"</note> in 1619 in two folio volumes.

**ROSWIDA**, or Rosvitis <note>Known today as Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim (c. 935–1002), she was a secular canoness and the first known female playwright in the West.</note>, a German by nation, was a nun in the Monastery of Gandersheim. She flourished in the year 980, distinguished no less by her piety than by the nobility of her birth, but most famous for her knowledge of fine letters. These she cultivated beyond the common lot of her century and the capacity of her sex; she was learned in both Greek and Latin, and was equally skilled in prose and meter. By the command of Emperor Otto II and Abbess Gerberga, she wrote a History or Panegyric on the deeds of Otto I in heroic verse. She likewise composed eight sacred histories in verse: namely, the *Passion of Saint Denis the Martyr*, the *Passion of Saint Pelagius the Martyr*, and others. In prose, she wrote six sacred comedies <note>These plays were modeled on the Roman playwright Terence but replaced his worldly themes with stories of Christian virtue.</note> on various subjects, but chiefly in praise of the Saints. Conrad Celtes, the first poet laureate of Germany, collected and published all these small works together at Nuremberg in 1501. The Panegyric of Emperor Otto is also found among the *German Writers* edited by Reuber.

**ÆLFRIC**, or ALFRIC, an Englishman by birth, was a disciple of Æthelwold, Bishop of Winchester, and his successor in the rule of the Monastery of Abingdon (if Bale is to be believed). In William of Malmesbury† there is a charter of King Edgar granted to the Monastery of Malmesbury, in which he testifies that he placed Ælfric, a man skilled in all ecclesiastical matters, over that monastery in the 14th year of his reign and the 974th of the Incarnation of the Lord. There are many who maintain that he was first the Bishop of Wilton (Bale calls it Wells), and then Archbishop of Canterbury from the year 995; they say he died in 1006, was first buried at Abingdon, and then translated to Canterbury. However, the letter of our Ælfric to Wulfstan, Bishop of York <note>original: "Eboracensem"</note>, seems to suggest he was a different person from the Archbishop of Canterbury, for in it he honors himself with the sole title of Abbot; yet from Simeon of Durham, Roger Hoveden, and others, it is clear that Ælfric of Canterbury held that see for six whole years before Wulfstan was promoted to York—unless, with William of Malmesbury and Matthew of Westminster <note>original: "Matthæo Florilego"</note>, we place Ælfric in the see of Canterbury before Sigeric, in which case the times would align perfectly. # The Dark Age.

<margin>
10th CENTURY.
from Year 900.
</margin>

"...He left his disciple **Ordgar** as his successor at Abingdon Abbey. 2. He succeeded his fellow disciple Ordgar in the Prefecture of Abingdon Monastery. 3. Around the year 969, he was appointed Abbot of **St. Albans** (which is indeed a larger Abbey than that of Abingdon) by Oswald, Bishop of Worcester. 4. Around the year 974, he was appointed Abbot of the famous monastery of **Malmesbury** by King Edgar (as the words of that charter state). 5. From the year 978 to the year 981, he was Bishop of **Crediton** <note>original: "Cridiatunensis"</note> among the people of Devon. For historians testify that Alfric, Bishop of Crediton, was previously Abbot of Malmesbury and was considered a learned man, and that he wrote two books: one on the affairs of his monastery, the other on the natures of things; this strongly suggests that this Alfric was the same person as ours. 6. Also from the year 990 to 995, he was Bishop of the people of **Wilton** after Sigeric, just as he was also Bishop of the Devonians at the same time after Sidemann. 7. From the year 995 to 1006 (the year he died), he was **Archbishop of Canterbury** after Sigeric. Certainly, in the year 1001, Ælfric, Archbishop of Canterbury, signed a document granted by King Æthelred to the monks of Shaftesbury <note>original: "Septoniensibus"</note> (which is found in Harpsfield, p. 197)." Thus far the conjecture of the illustrious **James Ussher** <note>Ussher (1581–1656) was the Archbishop of Armagh and a famous scholar of church history and chronology.</note>. And that Ælfric held the Archbishop’s seat at this time is made most certain to me by that privilege of King Æthelred granted to Christ Church, Canterbury, which **Henry Spelman** <note>Sir Henry Spelman (c. 1562–1641) was an English antiquarian known for his collections of church councils.</note> published in both *Old English* and *Latin* in *British Councils* <note>original: "Concil. Brit."</note> Vol. I, p. 507. In this document, Ælfric signs in the place immediately after Æthelred with these words translated from *Old English* into *Latin*: *I, Ælfric, Archbishop of Christ Church, have confirmed the generosity of this King with the wood of the cross forever;* or as it is held in the old Latin copy published in the same place on p. 509: *I, Ælfric, Arch-prelate of Canterbury <note>original: "Dorobernensis"</note>, have confirmed this prerogative with the holy banner.* This privilege was granted, according to the ancient Latin copy, in the year 1006; the illustrious Spelman suspects, not without cause, that this number is an error of the scribe and thinks it should rather be referred to the year 1002. And certainly, since it shows among the witnesses **Godwin**, who came to the seat of Rochester in 1001, and **Wulfstan**, Bishop of London, who according to the Savile Fasti <note>A chronological list of officials or events.</note> died in the year 1003 or the following (that is, the 25th or 26th year of Æthelred), no other year can be given. Our Ælfric was certainly a man learned in Theology beyond the common lot of his age, and especially in Grammar (from which he was called *The Grammarian* <note>original: "Grammaticus"</note>). He gained such fame among his countrymen from this that the Sermons written by him, or translated into *Old English*, were ordered to be read publicly in the churches; and not a few of his letters were adopted into the ancient Book of Canons <note>original: "Synodicon"</note> of the English Church.

## W R I T I N G S.

**A Treatise on the Old and New Testament**, in which, having listed the volumes of each book individually and narrated the events performed under both covenants in order, he brings the sacred history down to the capture of Jerusalem by Titus. Written in *Old English*.

**The Paschal Homily on the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ**, which was once ordered by a wide-ranging Canon to be recited to the people at every Easter. In that homily, Ælfric attacks the dogma of **Transubstantiation** <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note> then slowly creeping into the Church; and having brought forth very many arguments, mostly taken from the book of **Ratramnus** <note>A 9th-century monk who wrote against the literal interpretation of the Eucharist.</note>, he utterly tears it down, so that the faith of the English Church regarding the **Eucharist** <note>The sacrament of Holy Communion.</note> in that age is clearly revealed by these most lucid signs. It was published in *Old English* and *Latin* types by **John Day** <note>A prominent English Protestant printer (c. 1522–1584).</note> in London, 1566, protected by the signatures of fifteen bishops and other dignitaries, testifying that it was faithfully transcribed from the Old English archives. It is preceded by a very learned Preface about Ælfric and his writings, composed by the Most Reverend **Matthew Parker**, Archbishop of Canterbury. Finally, it was published in *Old English* by **Abraham Wheelocke** <note>The first professor of Arabic and Anglo-Saxon at Cambridge.</note>, with a Latin version added, in his very accurate edition of Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 462.

<margin>10th CENTURY. Year 900.</margin>
...from that time those of Sebastea <note>An ancient city in Pontus, now Sivas, Turkey.</note> excelled in Philosophy, having come out of the school of Eustathius, whom we have known as the Bishop and leader of the monks of this place; he adds soon after, that from these words of **Suidas** it seems the age of Suidas himself can be gathered; for he says that he knew Eustathius, Bishop of Sebastea, the teacher of Atticus, which Atticus died around the year of Christ 420. For to whom, even as a boy, is it not known that Suidas in this place is dealing not with his own personal knowledge, but with historical knowledge? Suidas composed a lengthy *Lexicon*, in which he has very many things regarding theological matters and ecclesiastical history, and not a few fragments of the ancients, often even where the name of the author is not applied. It was published in Greek at Milan, 1499, folio; at Basel, 1544, folio; in Latin with the translator Henry Wolff at Basel, 1581; and in Greek and Latin with the version, or rather paraphrase, of Aemilius Portus of Crete with his notes added here and there, at Geneva <note>original: "Coloniæ Allobrogum"</note> 1619, 2 volumes, folio.

<margin>980.</margin>
**ROSWIDA**, or Rosvitis <note>Known today as Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim (c. 935–973), a secular canoness and the first known female playwright of the German lands.</note>, a German by nation, a nun in the Abbey of Gandersheim; she flourished in the year 980, distinguished no less by her piety than by the nobility of her lineage, but especially illustrious for her knowledge of fine letters, which she cultivated beyond the common lot of her century and the capacity of her sex; she was learned in both Greek and Latin, and was equally skilled in prose and meter. By the order of Emperor Otto II and Abbess Gerberga, she wrote the *History or Panegyric on the Deeds of Otto I* in heroic verse. Likewise, she composed eight *Sacred Histories* in verse, namely: *The Passion of St. Denis the Martyr*, *The Passion of St. Pelagius the Martyr*, etc. In prose, however, she composed six *Sacred Comedies* on various subjects, but especially in praise of the Saints. Conrad Celtes <note>A prominent German Renaissance humanist and poet (1459–1508).</note>, the first poet laureate of Germany, collected all these small works and published them together at Nuremberg in 1501. The *Panegyric of Emperor Otto* is also found among the German writers edited by Reuber.

**ÆLFRICUS**, or **ALFRIC**, an Englishman by nation, a disciple of Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester, and his successor in the government of the Abbey of Abingdon (if faith is given to Bale <note>John Bale (1495–1563), a controversial English historian and bibliographer.</note>.) However, according to William of Malmesbury*, he was made Abbot of Malmesbury by King Edgar; and indeed (if John Capgrave is to be believed) he was appointed the first Abbot of the recently restored Monastery of St. Albans by Oswald, Bishop of Worcester, around the year 969. There is indeed found in William of Malmesbury† a charter of King Edgar granted to the Abbey of Malmesbury, by which he testifies that he placed Ælfric, a man ecclesiastical in all things, over that monastery in the 14th year of his reign and the 974th year of the Lord’s Incarnation. There are very many who wish him to have been first the Bishop of Wilton (Bale calls it "Welense") and then Archbishop of Canterbury from the year 995; having met his fate in 1006, buried first at Abingdon, then translated to Canterbury. But that our Ælfric was someone other than the Archbishop of Canterbury seems to be suggested by his own letter to Wulfstan of York, in which he honors himself with the title of Abbot alone; although it is clear from Simeon of Durham, Roger Hoveden, and others, that Ælfric of Canterbury held that see for a full six years before Wulfstan was promoted to York; unless we rather place Ælfric in the see of Canterbury before Sigeric, along with William of Malmesbury and Matthew of Westminster <note>original: "Matthæo Florilego"</note>, and then indeed the times will fit best. Meanwhile, it must not be hidden that some historians report that Wulfstan did not obtain the see of York before the year 1002; which being granted, it can in no way be that our Ælfric holds a place among the Archbishops of Canterbury. There was indeed another Wulfstan, Archbishop of York. But since it is established that he died in the year 956, before the times of King Edgar, he perhaps should be judged to contribute little to our matter. However, the most learned conjecture of Ussher in his *Theological Library manuscript* will perhaps settle the dispute, which I will not be burdened to place here:

# The Dark Age.

<margin>10th CENTURY, from the Year 900.</margin>

> "Ethelwold left his disciple Ordgar as his successor at Abingdon Abbey. 2nd: He <note>Ælfric</note> succeeded his fellow disciple Ordgar in the leadership of the Abingdon monastery. 3rd: Around the year 969, he was appointed Abbot of St. Albans by Oswald, Bishop of Worcester (which Abbey is indeed larger than that of Abingdon). 4th: Around the year 974, he was appointed Abbot of the most famous monastery of Malmesbury by King Edgar (as the words of that charter state). 5th: From the year 978 to 981, he was Bishop of Crediton among the Devonians.
> "For historians testify that Ælfric, Bishop of Crediton, was previously Abbot of Malmesbury, and was considered a learned man, and wrote two books—one on the affairs of his monastery and another on the natures of things;
> "which truly argues strongly that this Ælfric was the same as our own. 6th: Also from the year 990 to 995, he was Bishop of the people of Wilton <note>The Bishopric of Ramsbury or Wilton, later moved to Salisbury.</note> 
> "after Siric, just as he was also Bishop of the Devonians at the same time after Sideman.
> "7th: From the year 995 to 1006 (in which he died), he was the Archbishop of Canterbury after Siric."

Certainly, in the year 1001, **Ælfric, Archbishop of Canterbury**, signed a charter granted by King **Ethelred** to the monks of Shaftesbury (which is found in *Harpsfield*, page 197). Indeed, that **Ælfric** held the Archiepiscopal see at this time is made most certain to me by that privilege of King **Ethelred** granted to Christ Church, Canterbury, which **Henry Spelman** published in both Saxon <note>Old English</note> and Latin in *Councils of Britain, Vol. I, page 507*; in which, in the place immediately after **Ethelred**, **Ælfric** signs with these words translated from the Saxon-Latin: *I, Ælfric, Archbishop of Christ Church, have confirmed the generosity of this good King with the wood of the cross forever;* or, as it is held in the old Latin copy published in the same place on page 509: *I, Ælfric, Archbishop of Canterbury <note>original: "Doroberniensis Archipræful"</note>, have confirmed this prerogative with the holy standard.* This privilege was granted according to the ancient Latin copy in the year 1006, in which the illustrious **Spelman** suspects, not without cause, that the number is false due to a scribe's error; he thinks it should rather be referred to the year 1002. And certainly, since it shows among other witnesses **Godwin**, who came to the see of **Rochester** in 1001, and **Wulfstan**, Bishop of **London**, who according to the *Savilian Fasti* died in 1003 or the following year (that is, the 25th or 26th year of **Ethelred**), no other year can be given. Our **Ælfric** was certainly a man learned in theology beyond the common lot of his century, and especially in Grammar (whence he was called *the Grammarian* <note>original: "Grammaticus"</note>); he achieved such fame among his countrymen from this that the Sermons written by him, or translated into Saxon, were ordered to be read publicly in the churches; and not a few of his letters were adopted into the ancient *Synodicon* <note>A collection of church decrees or canons.</note> of the English Church.

---

### W R I T I N G S.

*Treatise on the Old and New Testament*, in which, having enumerated the volumes of each one by one, and narrated in order the things done under both covenants, he brings the sacred history down to the capture of Jerusalem by Titus. *In Saxon.*

*Easter Homily on the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ*, which was once ordered by a broad Canon to be recited to the people at every Easter. In that Homily, **Ælfric** attacks the dogma of Transubstantiation <term>Transubstantiation: the doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual substance of the body and blood of Christ.</term> then creeping gradually into the Church, and having produced very many arguments, mostly taken from the book of **Ratramnus**, he utterly tears it down; so much so, that from this the faith of the English Church in that age concerning the Eucharist is revealed by the most brilliant evidence. It was published in Saxon and Latin types by **John Day** in London, 1566, protected by the signatures of fifteen Prelates and other Great Men, testifying that it was faithfully transcribed from the Saxon Archives. A most learned Preface concerning **Ælfric** and his writings, composed by the Most Reverend **Matthew Parker**, Archbishop of Canterbury, is placed before it. Finally, it was published in Saxon with a Latin version added by **Abraham Wheloc** in his most accurate edition of Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, page 462.

*Two Letters: one to Wulfsige, Bishop of Sherborne, the other to Wulfstan, Archbishop of York.* In these, many things from the Easter Homily concerning the Eucharist...

# The Dark Age.

<margin>10th CENTURY, from the Year 900.</margin>

...are repeated concerning the Eucharist and the only spiritual presence of the body and blood of Christ. Both Epistles, by order of Wulffstan, were afterwards translated by Ælfric into the Latin language and were formerly inserted into the Synodal and Penitential books of the English Church; and it was provided, by a widely applicable ecclesiastical law, that these writings of spiritual instruction and doctrine should be read by the Bishop, on any given occasion, to the Clergy and Priests.

The small works listed above were unearthed from the archives of the Churches of Exeter, Hereford, and Worcester, and published in Saxon <note>The author uses "Saxon" to refer to what we now call Old English.</note> with an added English version (except for a single Epistle to Wulffstan, Bishop of York, which he finished in Latin and gave in Saxon) by the esteemed gentleman William L'isle, *London 1623, 1638.* They had been published previously (except for the first Treatise) in both Saxon and English by John Foxe <note>Famous for 'Foxe’s Book of Martyrs'.</note>, in *Acts and Monuments of the Church, Vol. II, for the year 1538.*

*The Penitential Book, formerly given to the Church of Worcester by Bishop Wulffstan (who flourished under William the Norman), in which these Epistles hold a place among other Canons; it is still preserved in the Library of Corpus Christi College <note>original: "Collegii Benedicti"</note>, Cambridge. They also exist in both Saxon and Latin in the book of canons given to the Church of Exeter by Bishop Leofric, who held that see from the year 1046. That book is kept in the public library at Oxford.*

*The Epistle on Canons to Bishop Wulsin consists of 35 Chapters. It is found in Latin in the Councils, Vol. IX, p. 1003.*

->UNPUBLISHED WORKS.<-

Two books of eighty Sermons in the Saxon language, which he afterwards translated into Saxon for the use of the common people at the request of the Bishops, having previously written them partly himself and partly by others in Latin. Several collections of Ælfric’s Saxon Sermons are held today, which are preserved here and there in England, partly in private hands and partly in public libraries. Of these, two are extant at Cambridge: one in the University Public Library, the other in the Library of St. Benedict <note>Corpus Christi College</note>. The first consists of 60 Sermons, the second of 24. In both, however, is found the Paschal Sermon, titled *Sermon on the Sacrifice on Easter Day*. Indeed, from Ælfric’s sermons, 24 were selected above the others to be read publicly to the people, in such an order that the first 12, dealing with general matters (*such as On the beginning of creation, On auguries, On the day of judgment, On idle talk and negligence, On avarice, On false Gods, etc.*), might be read whenever it seemed fit to the Priest. The latter 12, however, are assigned to specific Feasts (*namely, On the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary, On the Nativity of the Lord, On the Circumcision of the Lord, On the Epiphany, On the Purification of Saint Mary, on the first Sunday in Lent, on Palm Sunday, on Easter Day, etc.*)

*Epistle on the custom of Monks.* Extant in manuscript in St. Benedict’s College, Cambridge.

*Epistle to Sigferth against the marriage of Clergy.* Its beginning is shown in William L'isle’s Preface to the Paschal Homilies.

*Canons of the Council of Nicaea translated into Saxon, manuscripts in the aforementioned College.*

*A Saxon Chronicle, chiefly concerning the Church of Canterbury, written in Saxon by Ælfric in the 23rd year of his age, manuscripts in the same place.*

*The Passions and Lives of the Saints,* translated from Latin into the Saxon language by Ælfric. They are held in the Cotton Library under *Julius E. 7. n. I.*

*The Life of Saint Guthlac,* written in Saxon to Ælfwald, King of the East Angles, manuscript in the same place under *Vespasiano D. 21. n. 2.*

*A Grammar of the Latin Language,* Saxon-Latin with a Latin Preface prefixed, a manuscript exists somewhere. For William L'isle has several passages from it in his Preface to the Paschal Homilies; indeed (as I discovered later), it was published in print (together with a Glossary of the same kind) at *Oxford, 1659.*

*Excerpts from Priscian Minor <note>A standard medieval grammatical textbook</note>, and translated into Saxon,* several manuscripts at Cambridge.

# The Dark Age.

<margin>10th Century, from the Year 900.</margin>

*   *A Latin-Old English Dictionary.*
*   *Certain works of Donatus <note>A famous Roman grammarian whose work was the standard textbook for Latin in the Middle Ages.</note> translated into Old English.*
*   *The Four Dialogues of St. Gregory the Great translated into Old English.*

The above are Manuscripts held at Cambridge and in the Lumley Library.

*William of Malmesbury, in his "Life of Aldhelm" (Manuscript), records that Ælfric also wrote a biography of his teacher, Æthelwold. However, it is not certain whether that work still survives.*

*Furthermore, the Latin Sermons of Ælfric have perished through the ravages of time. It is hardly surprising that the Bishops who followed Lanfranc <note>The first Norman Archbishop of Canterbury after the conquest in 1066.</note>—who were devoted followers of the doctrine of Transubstantiation <note>The belief that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual substance of Christ's body and blood.</note>—were offended by the brilliance of the truth discovered throughout Ælfric's writings. Consequently, they likely removed and suppressed them from the Archives of the Cathedral Churches where they were stored. Meanwhile, his Old English Sermons survived unharmed, largely because they were veiled in a language unknown to the Norman occupiers. Indeed, the Old English language vanished almost entirely shortly after the Norman invasion.*

---

<margin>986.</margin>
**JOHN XV**, a Roman by birth and the son of Leo the Priest, was ordained as Pope on April 25, 986. At the beginning of his papacy, he was driven out of Rome by the Consul Crescentius and fled to Tuscany, but he was soon recalled by the Romans out of fear of Emperor Otto, whom the Pope had petitioned for help. In the year 989, having held a Synod at Rome, he compelled Adalbert, Bishop of Prague—who had abandoned his duties out of a desire for the monastic life—to return to the care of his flock. In 992, he condemned the acts of the Synod of Reims, in which Bishop Arnulf of Reims had been deposed; having sent legates to Gaul in 995, he restored Arnulf to his see. He died on April 30, 996. Three of his *Letters* survive in the "Collection of Councils," Volume IX, page 731.

*A Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord, which Jean Cellot published anonymously at the end of the "History of Gottschalk," Paris, 1655, folio.*

# The Dark Age.

<margin>
The 10th CENTURY, from the Year 900.
</margin>

...tenth [century], place him. We place him at this point in the year 990, until someone emerges who can provide more certain information. There exists a *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, in Greek and Latin, in the *Duceano Supplement to the Fathers*, Volume II, page 602. It was published in Latin in 1511 and 1551, and in quarto at Basel in 1552, and is also found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVIII. A nearly complete *Commentary on Job* is found in the author of the *Catena on Job* <note>A "Catena" (Latin for "chain") is a form of biblical commentary made up of fragments of successive authors.</note>, edited in Latin by Paul Comitolus at Venice, 1587, in quarto; and in Greek and Latin by Patrick Young in London, 1637, in folio. There are some who count among the works of Olympiodorus a *Commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah*, which was published in Latin along with Origen's *Commentary* at Rome in 1598, in quarto. I have not yet seen that particular edition. Many fragments of Olympiodorus are shown to us in the Ghisleriana Catena on Jeremiah—so many, in fact, that they can almost serve as a full commentary.

<margin>990.</margin>
**OECUMENIUS**, likewise a writer of a very uncertain age, regarding whom there is deep silence among the ancient authors; it is only established that he flourished after the year 800. We join him here to Olympiodorus at the year 990, until it is possible to search out his true age. He explained a great part of the New Testament using the commentaries of the ancients, especially from John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note>, who was his "prow and stern" <note>original: "prora ac puppis" — a Latin idiom meaning the most important part or the guiding force.</note>. He did so clearly, lucidly, and concisely; for this reason, he is commonly considered the *Greek Scholiast* <note>A "scholiast" is an ancient or medieval commentator on a classic text.</note> of the New Testament. Today there exist:
> *Narrations on the Acts of the Apostles.*
> *Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul.*
> *Commentaries on the Epistle of St. James, and other Canonical Epistles.*

The works of Oecumenius were produced in Greek at *Verona* in 1532; in Latin at *Venice* in 1556, in octavo; and in Greek and Latin at *Paris* in 1631, in two volumes, folio.

<margin>994.</margin>
**SISINNIUS**, called "The Master," was made Patriarch of Constantinople after the death of Nicholas Chrysoberges in the year 994 or the following year. He settled the disputes that had long been stirred up in the Eastern Church regarding fourth marriages. He held the see for three years. There exists a treatise written by him, *A Treatise on the Marriage of Relatives, or* <term>On the prohibition of marrying two sisters who are cousins</term> <note>original: "Περὶ τοῦ μὴ λαμβάνειν δύο ἀδελφὰς ἐξαδέλφας δύο." This reflects medieval Canon Law concerns regarding "degrees of affinity" or how closely related people could be while still being allowed to marry.</note>, found in Leunclavius’s *Greco-Roman Law*, book 3, page 197.

<margin>994.</margin>
**ODILO**, a native of Auvergne born of a knightly family, was made a cleric at St. Julian in the town of Brioude. Having taken up the monastic habit in the Monastery of Cluny, he was appointed Abbot after the death of his teacher Maiolus in the year 994, having been designated as successor by Maiolus while he was still living. Distinguished for his piety and his charity toward the poor, he won immense favor and authority for himself with Robert, King of the Franks, and Henry, the German Emperor—so much so that he was presented by Henry with his own golden crown. During a time of famine, Odilo sold that crown along with other ornaments of his church to feed the poor. Around the year 1022, he traveled to Italy to visit the thresholds of the Apostles <note>A traditional phrase for visiting the tombs of St. Peter and St. Paul in Rome.</note> and the monks of Monte Cassino. In 1034, having been elected Archbishop of Lyon, he rejected that dignity. He reformed many monasteries in Gaul and founded many more. While visiting these, he met his end at Souvigny in the year 1048, on the Calends of January <note>January 1st.</note>, at the age of 87, in the 56th year of his ordination. He is said to have been the first to institute the Feast of All Saints; for he commanded his monks that on the day following the Calends of November <note>November 2nd.</note> they should celebrate the memory of all the faithful departed. This example soon passed to other churches and was finally approved by the authority of the Roman Pontiff. <note>While the text says "All Saints" (omnium Sanctorum), the date of November 2nd and the context of Odilo's life refer to the establishment of "All Souls' Day."</note>

*Several Letters to Fulbert* <note>Fulbert of Chartres, a famous 11th-century bishop and scholar.</note>.
*The Life of St. Adelaide the Empress*, wife of Emperor Otto I, who died in the year 999. It was edited by Canisius, Volume V, part 2, page 398.

<margin>996.</margin>
**GREGORY V**, formerly called *Bruno*, German by nationality, son of Marquis Otto of Verona, grandson—or at least a relative—of Emperor Otto. He was elected Roman Pontiff in the year 996 through the influence of Emperor Otto and ordained on the 17th of May. Immediately upon beginning his papacy, he was driven from the city by Crescentius the Consul and forced to flee first into Tuscany and then into Germany; however, before leaving, he gathered a Council of Bishops at Pavia <note>original: "Ticini"</note> and bound Crescentius with an anathema <note>A formal curse by the church, excommunicating a person.</note>. A little later, he was restored by Otto at the head of an armed force and placed the imperial crown upon him. Having held a Synod at Rome, he devoted his efforts to restoring the collapsed discipline of the Church and commanded Adalbert of Prague <note>A missionary and martyr, also known as Saint Vojtěch.</note> to return to his see under the threat of a thunderbolt of excommunication. In the year 998, at the request of Abbo of Fleury, he threatened the entire kingdom of France with excommunication unless Arnulf, the Archbishop of Reims, who had previously been unjustly deposed, was restored to his see. He died in the year 999, on the 18th of February. Four of his *Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume IX, page 752, along with a *Letter on the Privileges of the Abbots of Montmajour* in Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Volume IV, page 431.

See his Life, written by an anonymous author, prefixed to the "Decrees."
</margin>
**BURCHARD**, German by birth and from the region of Hesse, was a student of Olbert (later Abbot of Gembloux) and a monk of Lobbes. Finally, in the year 996, he succeeded his biological brother Franco in the See of Worms. In the year 1022, he took part in the Council of Seligenstadt. After nearly twenty years spent faithfully in his pastoral office, he closed his final day in the year 1025, or at least the year following. Many years before his death, having built a cell for himself and a nearby oratory in the woods two miles distant from Worms—far removed from all noise and secular business—he gave himself entirely to piety and literary leisure. It was in this place, at the encouragement of Brunicho, the provost of Worms, and with the collaboration of his master Olbert, that he undertook that great volume of *Decrees* <note>original: "Decretorum"</note>. It is distributed into twenty books, which he collected from Holy Scripture, from the so-called Apostolic Canons, from the rules of both Eastern and Western Synods, from the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, the sayings of the Holy Fathers, and certain penitential books. Not content with these, he gathered up with a full hand splendid "trifles" <note>original: "quisquilias," here referring to the "False Decretals," a famous set of forged documents.</note> from the forged letters of the Popes, almost innumerable examples of which David Blondel places before the reader’s eyes in his *Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore*, chapter 18, page 98. This work was published at Cologne in 1548 in folio, and at Paris in 1549 in octavo, and perhaps more than once elsewhere.

---

<margin>999.</margin>
**SYLVESTER II**, formerly called *Gerbert*, an Auvergnat by nationality, of the region of Aurillac. He was born of no lowly rank and from boyhood was excellently nourished in the noble arts, being more than commonly versed in the study of Philosophy and Astrology. Having embraced the monastic life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, he was a little later made the tutor of Robert, King of the Franks, and of his son Hugh. On this occasion, since he held great power at court, he saw to it in the year 991 that a Synod was called to eject Arnulf, the Archbishop of Reims, from his see, and to substitute himself in his place. However, having been deposed by Pope John XV in the year 995, and with the favor of Emperor Otto and the support of the people, he was appointed Archbishop of Ravenna. Up to this point, he had been a most fierce attacker of the Papal See; finally, upon the death of Gregory, and through the patronage of Otto III, he was declared Pontiff of the Roman Church and enthroned on the 11th of April, 999. He obtained many benefits and territories for the Roman Church from Emperor Otto and successfully put to rest many heresies that had recently arisen in the Church. He died on the 12th of May, 1003. As for the stories regarding the manner in which he reached the Papal See—namely, through magical incantations—and regarding his soul being pledged to the devil as a reward and finally snatched away from him...

# The Dark Age.

<margin>
The 10th CENTURY, from the Year 900.
</margin>

...seized, as Cardinal Benno—a writer of the following century—relates; these accounts can be read in the works of Benno himself in his *Life of Hildebrand* <note>Cardinal Benno was a notable 11th-century critic of the papacy; Hildebrand is the birth name of Pope Gregory VII.</note>.

### WRITINGS.

**160 Letters** written by him while he still held the see of Reims; these were published by Papire Masson (Paris, 1611, in quarto) and by André Duchesne <note>A foundational French historian often called the "father of French history."</note> in *French Historical Writers* <note>original: "Scriptor. Francic."</note>, Volume II, page 787; from there they were recorded in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVII, page 669.

**3 Letters** written after he took up the Papacy. These are found in *The Councils* <note>original: "Concil." referring to a collection of acts from church synods</note>, Volume IX, page 777.

*A Book on the Sphere.* <note>original: "Liber de Sphærâ." This work concerns the celestial sphere, used in astronomy and geometry.</note>

*A Sermon on the Instruction of Bishops.* Both of these treatises were brought to light by Jean Mabillon in the *Analecta*, Volume II, page 212.

*The Life of Saint Adalbert, Archbishop of Prague*, published in Rome by Abraham Bzovius, as attested by Louis Jacob de Saint-Charles <note>A 17th-century bibliographer and member of the Order of Minims.</note> in the *Pontifical Library*, Book I, page 214.

*A most elegant epigram* on an image of Severinus Boethius <note>original: "Sever. Boetii." Boethius was a 6th-century philosopher whom Gerbert greatly admired.</note>: it is contained in Baronius’s *Appendix*, Volume VII, page 4.

### UNPUBLISHED WORKS.

**On Arithmetic**, or on Numbers, addressed to Constantine, a monk of Fleury. A manuscript used to exist in the possession of Jean Masson, the brother of Papire.

**A manuscript book on Geometry**, formerly held in the Farnese Library. Other small works of his are mentioned, namely: *A most beautiful dialogue between himself and Leo, the Apostolic messenger*; a book *On the Construction of the Astrolabe* <note>A complex instrument used for navigation and astronomical observations; Gerbert was famous for introducing such Arabic-influenced science to Europe.</note>; one book *On Rhetoric*; and an *Oration delivered at the Synod of Mouzon* in the year 995. Whether these still lie hidden anywhere, I have not yet discovered.

11th CENTURY, from the Year 1000.

# THE HILDEBRANDINE AGE.

## Overview of the Century.

<margin>Year 1004.</margin>
<margin>Berengarius of Angers.</margin>
<margin>Year 1055.</margin>
<margin>Year 1059.</margin>
<margin>Years 1078 and 1079.</margin>
At the beginning of the Century, in the year 1004, the Sacramentarian Controversy <note>A long-standing theological debate regarding the nature of the bread and wine in the Eucharist.</note> began to seethe again, with Leutheric, Archbishop of Sens, reviving the dispute. A few years later, Berengarius of Angers <note>Often known as Berengar of Tours, a theologian who challenged the literal interpretation of the Real Presence.</note> made this cause his own; in the year 1035, he publicly attacked the carnal presence of Christ in the Eucharist, asserting that the body and blood of the Lord were present only in a certain sacramental manner. He even drew Bruno, the Bishop of Angers, into his way of thinking. For this reason, he was condemned in the Synods of Rome and Vercelli in 1054, and again at Tours in 1055. In the year 1059, at a Synod in Rome, he was compelled to renounce his opinion, which occurred a second and third time in the years 1078 and 1079; he took an oath in these words:

> *I, Berengar, believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the bread and wine which are placed upon the altar are, through the mystery of the sacred prayer and the words of our Redeemer, substantially converted into the true, proper, and life-giving flesh and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord; and that after consecration, it is the true body of Christ which was born of the Virgin, which hung upon the cross offered for the salvation of the world, and which sits at the right hand of the Father; and it is the true blood of Christ which was poured out from His side, not merely through a sign and the power of the Sacrament, but in the property of nature and the truth of substance, just as is contained in this Brief, which I have read and you understand. Thus I believe, and I will not teach further against this faith. So help me God and these holy gospels of God.*

<margin>Henry IV, Emperor.</margin>
<margin>Gregory VII, called Hildebrand.</margin>
<margin>Rudolf, Duke of Swabia.</margin>
However, it is said that he later felt remorse and returned to his earlier opinion. A sharper conflict broke out between Emperor Henry IV and Gregory VII (called Hildebrand) concerning Investitures <term>Investitures: The practice of secular monarchs appointing bishops and granting them the symbols of their spiritual office, such as the ring and staff.</term> and other royal rights. Gregory extorted these rights from the Emperor, partly by force and partly through ecclesiastical censures and his doctrine (henceforth called the Hildebrandine doctrine) regarding the supreme authority of the Apostolic See over everyone, even Kings. This was asserted by him with a bare head <note>original: "γυμνῇ τῇ κεφαλῇ" (gymnē tē kephalē), a Greek idiom meaning openly or without disguise.</note> and defended with all his might, raising the prerogative of the Roman Chair far above the imperial height. Because of this, turmoils were stirred up everywhere against Henry; he and his supporters were excommunicated by Gregory in a Roman Synod in 1076. Soon after Henry was deposed, Rudolf, Duke of Swabia, was substituted in his place, to whom Gregory sent a golden crown inscribed with these words:

->The Rock gave to Peter, Peter gives the Crown to Rudolf.<-
<note>original: "Petra dedit Petro, Petrus Diadema Rudolpho." This is a pun on the name Peter/Petrus, which means "rock." Christ (the Rock) gave authority to Peter, and the Pope (Peter's successor) now gives the crown to Rudolf.</note>

<margin>Primate of Canterbury and York.</margin>
<margin>Year 1072.</margin>
<margin>Cardinals.</margin>
With no less zeal did the Roman Pontiffs and the Patriarchs of Constantinople litigate over the right of primacy. A controversy also arose between the Archbishops of Canterbury and York regarding the primacy of their sees; in 1072, it was judged in favor of Lanfranc of Canterbury. To the middle of this century is traced the institution of "Cardinals" properly so-called. There had indeed been Cardinals in the Roman Church before—namely, clerics fixed and titled in the more famous churches of the city—nor were Cardinals lacking in other major churches. But at about this time, they were formed into the Apostolic College as the Pope's advisors and fellow judges, the Senators of the City and the World,

<margin>11th CENTURY, from the Year 1000.</margin>
...so that they might be the true hinges of the world <note>original: *veri mundi Cardines*. The word "Cardinal" is derived from the Latin word for "hinge," signifying their pivotal role in the Church.</note>, they were received into their rank. From that point on, the prerogatives of the Cardinals grew immensely, especially after Innocent IV granted them the red hat <note>original: *pileo rubro*</note> around the year 1243. This was intended as a sign that they must be prepared to shed their own blood for the liberty of the Church if the need should arise. In the year 1074, many disturbances were stirred up, as witnessed by Philippe Briet <note>A 17th-century Jesuit historian known for his works on chronology.</note>, because of the married clergy who were condemned by the Roman Council; the good Jesuit calls these men "lustful" and "most impure little sacrificers." 

The Monastic state acquired new strength and great growth in this era, with the founding of the orders of the Vallumbrosians <note>A Benedictine reform group founded in the "Shady Valley" near Florence.</note>, the Carthusians, and the Cistercians. Around the end of the century in the year 1096, at the persuasion of Pope Urban and with the approval of the Council of Clermont held the previous year, the most famous expedition of the Crusaders <note>original: *Cruce-Signatorum*, literally "those signed with the cross."</note> took place. They were so named because a cross was placed upon their garments as a token of Christian military service, and their goal was to rescue the Holy Land from the hands of the infidels. This expedition was led by Godfrey of Bouillon, who, after Jerusalem was occupied in the year 1099, was declared the first King of Jerusalem by common vote. However, he refused to be crowned with gold or to sit upon a throne in the place where the Lord of the world had lain in the hay and been crowned with thorns. Regarding him, Philippe Briet truly said: *“Great for having won the kingdom, greater for having administered it, and greatest for having most holily left it; he is to be preferred even to the Caesars and the Alexanders.”*

**AIMOIN**, a native of Aquitaine and a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict <note>original: *O. B.* or *Ordo Sancti Benedicti*</note> at Fleury <note>A famous abbey on the Loire in France, known for housing the relics of St. Benedict.</note>, flourished before 1001. He became a monk while still a young man, during the time Oylbold held the prefecture of the monastery. He later lived under the Abbots Abbo and Gauzlin; in the year 1004, he accompanied Abbo to the Monastery of La Réole <note>original: *Squirs*</note> and was present at his murder.

In the following year, he committed the *Life of Abbo* to writing. Nothing more about him is certain.

->WORKS.<-

*The History of the Franks in 4 books, dedicated to Abbo, Abbot of Fleury; from the destruction of Troy to the coronation of King Pippin, or the year of Christ 752.* <note>Like many medieval chroniclers, Aimoin links the origins of the French to the legendary refugees of the Trojan War.</note> For the parts that follow, which constitute the fifth book and the latter part of the fourth, were added by a more recent writer. This *History* exists among the *Frankish Writers* published in Frankfurt, 1613, and the *Historians of France* edited by Duchesne, Paris, 1641, Volume III.

**GODEHARD** <note>Better known today as Saint Gotthard of Hildesheim.</note>, first the Abbot of Tegernsee and then Bishop of Hildesheim, flourished around the year 1002. *Five Letters* of his survive in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume IV, page 349.

**GOZBERT**, Abbot of Tegernsee from the beginning of this century. Nothing is certain regarding his death. *Four Letters* of his survive in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume IV, page 347.

<margin>
1007.
</margin>
**FULBERT**, Abbot of Ferrières before the year 1004, was very dear to William, Count of Poitou, by whom he was granted the office of Treasurer of Saint Hilary. He was also among the most beloved by Robert, King of the Franks, and served as his Chancellor (as is commonly reported). In the year 1007, he was made Bishop of Chartres. He is said to have worshipped the Blessed Virgin with clearly immoderate honor; not only did he build the magnificent Church of Chartres in her honor—with Canute, King of the English <note>Cnut the Great, who sent a donation from England to help rebuild the cathedral after a fire.</note>, supplying the funds for it—but he also composed hymns to be sung in her praise, and is said to have been the first to celebrate the Feast of her Nativity in the regions of France. As for what William of Malmesbury and others (who are far too prone to such fables) report—that the Blessed Virgin visited him while he lay ill and healed <note>original: *sanante*</note> him with her own milk—let those who take delight in such trifles <note>original: *nugæ*</note> look into it. Fulbert died in the year 1028, on the 10th day of April.

## ->WRITINGS.<-

**H**is letters, both his own and those of certain others, numbering **134.** *Sermons, Canons, Prose pieces, Hymns, and some verses.* A fragment of a sermon on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary is kept by Jean à Bosco in the *Library of Fleury*, page 516. Certainly, this sermon is found almost word-for-word in Volume IX of the works attributed to Jerome <note>original: *Hieronymo adfictis*; St. Jerome was a prolific early Church Father, and many later works were falsely attributed to him to give them authority</note> on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary.

*The Life of Saint Autbert, Bishop of Cambrai.* This appears in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius was a 16th-century monk famous for compiling a massive collection of lives of the saints.</note> under December 13th.

The *Works of Fulbert* (excluding the *Life of St. Autbert*) were published through the care of Charles de Villiers, a Doctor of Theology of Paris, *Paris, 1608*, and thereafter in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: *Bibliotheca Patrum*; a standard multi-volume reference collection of early Christian authors.</note>, Volume XVIII, page 1. What sort of good faith that Parisian Doctor applied in publishing those Works is abundantly clear from this single example: Fulbert, on page 168, transcribes these words from Saint Augustine <margin>* *On Christian Teaching*, Book 3, Chapter 16.</margin>: "Unless you eat," he says, "the flesh of the Son of Man, and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. He seems to command a crime or a shameful act. It is therefore a figure <note>original: *Figura ergo est*; in medieval theology, a "figure" refers to a symbolic or metaphorical interpretation rather than a literal one.</note>, commanding that one must only communicate in the Passion of the Lord," etc.
At this point, the poor editor—intent on refuting the heretics of this time (as he boasts on the front of the edition)—had inserted this gloss: "*so says the Heretic*," after the phrase *It is therefore a figure*. Finally, however, when the book had been sent to the press, he was warned that the entire period <note>A "period" here refers to a complete rhetorical sentence or thought.</note> exists in the Works of Saint Augustine and was transcribed from there by Fulbert; he then moved those two words, "*so says the Heretic*," to the typographical errors, confessing they had been added against the evidence of the Manuscript he had used.

*The Letter of Fulbert of Chartres on the religious and cautious dispensing of Church matters* appears in Dacherius's *Spicilegium*, Volume II, page 827.

1008.
</margin>
**ADELBOLD**, a nobleman, counselor to Emperor Henry II, and a leader of armies. When military affairs were succeeding poorly for him, he renounced the world and took up the monastic habit in the Monastery of Lobbes in the year of Christ 1008; after the death of Anfrid, he was made Bishop of Utrecht. He died in the year 1027, on the 27th of November. There exist *Two Books on the Life of St. Henry the Emperor* in Canisius, Volume VI, page 383; in Surius under July 14th; and in Gretser among the *Writers of Bamberg, Ingolstadt, 1611, in quarto.* In these editions, Adelbold's name is not prefixed at the top; however, certain Manuscript codices attribute it to him; others, endowed with authority, allow us to place the matter beyond all controversy...

**ARNOLD**, Bishop of Halberstadt, flourished around the year 1011. He wrote a *Letter on the institution of the Bishopric of Bamberg*, which appears in Baluze in the *Miscellany*, Volume IV, page 435.

1012.
</margin>
**BENEDICT VIII**, formerly called John, a native of Tusculum, son of Gregory, Count of Tusculum. He was first Bishop of Porto, then Pope in the year 1012. As Roman Pontiff, placed in the Chair on July 20th, he was soon driven from his see and the city at the start of his Pontificate; he fled to King Henry in Saxony. Brought back to Rome by the King, he designated Henry as Emperor by placing the crown upon him. In the year 1019, summoned to Germany by Emperor Henry, he traveled there again to confirm the recently established Bishopric of Bamberg and to consecrate the Church. He died in the year 1024, on the 10th of July, having his brother John as his successor. There exists a *Single Letter against the invaders of Church property* in the *Councils*, Volume IX, page 810, and in Duchesne's *Frankish Writers*, Volume IV.

**LEO THE GRAMMARIAN**, so called, was a Prefect and leader of the Cibyrraeots <note>The Cibyrraeots were a major naval district or "theme" of the Byzantine Empire located on the southern coast of modern-day Turkey.</note> known as *the Shoemaker* <note>original: *ho Tzangarios* (ὁ Τζαγγάριος)</note>, as he is called in a note attached to his *Chronography*. There are those who maintain that he lived in the Court during the final years of Constantine Porphyrogenitus <note>Constantine VII "the Purple-born," a scholar-emperor who ruled in the mid-10th century.</note>. However that may be, it is certain that he was writing in the year 1013. He wrote a *Chronography* <note>A chronological history or timeline of events.</note> from the year 813, where Theophanes stopped, until the year 1013. This work survives in Greek and Latin, illustrated with notes by François Combefis, and was published as a supplement to Theophanes, *Paris, 1655, folio.*

<margin>
1014.
</margin>
**BERNO**, a monk of Saint Gall and later the Abbot of "Rich Augia" <note>original: *Augia dives*; modern-day Reichenau Island on Lake Constance</note> near Constance on the Rhine, flourished in the year 1014. In that year, he was present at the coronation of Emperor Henry II, which was performed by Pope Benedict VIII. He died on January 7, 1045, after presiding over the Monastery of Reichenau for 39 years. He wrote the *Book on the Office of the Mass, or on matters pertaining to the Office of the Mass*, published separately in *Venice, 1572, octavo*; it also appears among other writers of the same kind in editions from *Cologne, 1568*, and *Paris, 1610, folio*, as well as in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVIII, page 56. He also wrote the *Life of Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg*, found in Surius’s collection under July 4th.

<margin>

</margin>

**HUGO**, Archdeacon of Tours, flourished in the year 1020. His *Dialogue to Fulbert, Bishop of Chartres* survives in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume II, page 349.

</margin>
**ALEXIUS**, the leader of the Studion Monastery <note>The most important monastery in Byzantine Constantinople, known for its strict rule and influence on liturgy.</note> and later, from the year 1025 after the death of Eustathius, the Patriarch of Constantinople. In the year 1034, corrupted equally by gold and by fear, he dressed Michael the Paphlagonian—who had murdered Emperor Romanus—in the imperial crown and joined him in marriage to the adulterous Empress Zoe. In 1036, he used a clever plan to elude and render useless the traps set by the Emperor’s brother John, who was seeking the Patriarchal seat, and the bishops who conspired with him. He died in the year 1043. Several of his *Decrees on various Ecclesiastical causes* survive in the *Graeco-Roman Law*, book 4, page 230.

**JOHN**, called *Johannellinus* <note>A nickname meaning "Little John."</note> because of his small stature, was a monk of Saint Benignus, then appointed Prior of the Monastery of Fécamp by Abbot William; later, when William resigned, John was made Abbot in the year 1028. In 1052, he received the Abbey of Herbrechtingen as a gift from Emperor Henry III. He died in the year 1078. He wrote a *Little Book of Prayers collected from the writings of the Fathers* for Empress Agnes, the wife of Henry; Mabillon published this together with its prologue, though not in its entirety, in the *Analecta*, Volume I, page 133. He wrote many other things, including a *Little Book on Divine Contemplation*, of which the same author provides several fragments on page 151. He also wrote *Numerous Orations or Prayers*, eleven of which can be seen on page 153, and *Several Letters*, three of which survive on page 221. Furthermore, he wrote a *Book on the Instruction of a Widow*, *On the Life and Character of Virgins*, *On the Distribution of Alms*, and perhaps many others that no longer survive. Regarding him and his writings, please see the most learned annotations of the famous Mabillon on pages 161 and 223.

* Chronicle of Monte Cassino, Book 3, Chapter 33.</margin>
**BERENGAR**, a Frenchman from Tours and Archdeacon of Angers, became prominent in the year 1035. At this time, he began to promote his opinion regarding the Eucharist, which he claimed was consistent not only with the teachings of Ratramnus <note>original: *Bertrami*; a 9th-century monk who wrote on the Eucharist.</note> and Eriugena <note>original: *Scoti*; referring to John Scottus Eriugena.</note>, but even with the doctrine of the entire ancient Church. He asserted that the bread and wine in the Lord's sacrifice are not truly or essentially converted into the body and blood of the Lord, but only figuratively. Many monks and other defenders of "carnal doctrine" <note>The traditional view of the real, physical presence of Christ in the bread and wine.</note> immediately and sharply opposed Berengar for teaching such things. Despite them, Berengar continued to confirm his opinion through both speech and writing. Finally, in the year 1050 (as is clear from the writings of Hermann the Lame <note>original: *Hermannus Contractus*</note>, and not the year 1053 as held by Durand of Troarn in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*), Pope Leo IX condemned the man for heresy in a Roman Synod after reading Berengar's letter to Lanfranc. He deprived him of Church communion, which was also done that same year at the Synod of Vercelli, where Berengar himself did not appear, but sent two representatives. At about the same time, he was condemned at Brionne in Normandy in the presence of Duke William <note>William the Conqueror.</note>, and also in his absence at Paris before King Henry I, as Durand informs us. In 1055, a council was held against him at Florence; that same year, Pope Victor II sent his chaplain Hildebrand <note>The future Pope Gregory VII, for whom this century is named in the header.</note> to France, who, having convened a Synod at Tours, forced Berengar to a recantation <note>original: *palinodiam*; a formal statement retracting an earlier opinion.</note>. In the year 1059, he argued his case in person at a Roman Synod before Pope Nicholas II; and when no one was able to resist him (according to Leo of Ostia*), Alberic, a deacon of Monte Cassino and a most learned man, was summoned to the Synod. After many verbal conflicts where neither side yielded, Alberic was granted a week's truce and published a book against Berengar. Berengar, however, terrified by threats and weary of insults, renounced his opinion using a prescribed formula. This is the very well-known form that begins: *I, Berengar, unworthy deacon, etc.* In the year 1063, Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, held a Synod in which he condemned Berengar and his followers, opposing a confession of faith to the Berengarian dogma...

In the year 1075, another Synod was assembled against Berengar at Poitiers, presided over by Giraud, the Pope's legate, as the same Mabillon notes from the *Chronicle of Saint-Maixent*. In the year 1078, on the feast of All Saints, Gregory VII convened a Council at Rome, in which Berengar produced a short confession of faith, which Mabillon brought to light in the same location, page 487. However, to delay matters for a short while, Berengar requested and obtained a truce until the next upcoming Synod. Therefore, in the following year, during Lent <note>original: *Quadragesima*</note>, another Synod was held, in which a new formula of confession was proposed to him: *“I, Berengar, believe in my heart, etc.”* <note>original: *Ego Berengarius corde credo, &c.*</note> which he signed and confirmed. Certainly, it can be proven from many testimonies of writers contemporary to him—such as Lanfranc, the anonymous author published by Chifflet, and others—that he returned to his prior opinion. And what puts the matter beyond all doubt is that Mabillon confesses to having read a manuscript treatise by Berengar himself, in which he utterly rescinds this third profession of faith and tears it apart with many arguments; he adds how he was induced to sign the final profession of faith, namely by the fear of death certainly hanging over him, and in what sense he had asserted it. Mabillon contends with more than one argument that Berengar did indeed eventually return to a sound mind, as he calls it, and adhered to the Catholic faith until his very last breath. Whether he has fully proven this, let others judge. This much is certain: Berengar, departing from Rome, came to Tours and retired to the island of Saint Cosmas in the suburbs of the city, and there, having taken the monastic habit, he served for eight years. He died in that place on the 6th of January, in the year 1088. Even his adversaries do not deny that he was a man distinguished for his skill in the liberal arts and dialectic <note>The art of logical argumentation</note>, and illustrious for the sanctity of his life and character. William of Malmesbury <margin>*On the Deeds of the Kings, book 3, folio 63.*</margin> praises him marvelously for his humility, almsgiving, modesty, chastity, zeal, and abstinence; in his writing, there exists a noble epitaph in his praise by Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, who was a disciple of Berengar himself. From this, setting others aside, allow me to transfer a few lines here:

> He whom the world now wonders at, it shall always wonder at;
> That Berengar, not destined to die, has died;
> Whom, while he held the highest peaks of the sacred faith,
> The fifth day of January took away—a daring crime.
> That day, a ruinous day, and treacherous to the world,
> On which there was grief and the total ruin of things.
> On which the status of the Church, the hope and glory of the Clergy,
> And the cultivator of justice fell, as justice itself collapsed.
> Whatever the Philosophers, whatever the Poets sang,
> yielded to his genius and his eloquence.
> A holier and greater wisdom, having undertaken a greater task,
> Filled his sacred heart and mouth with God.

Finally, at the end:

> A man truly wise, and blessed in every part;
> Who enriches the heavens with his soul, and the earth with his body.
> After death may I live with him, with him may I rest:
> Nor may my lot become better than his own.

Finally, in the year 1050 (as is clear from Hermannus Contractus, not as Durand of Troarn has it in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, the year 1053), Pope Leo IX, in a Roman Synod, after reading Berengar's letter to Lanfranc, condemned the man for heresy and deprived him of the communion of the Church. This was also done in the same year in the Synod of Vercelli, in which Berengar himself did not appear, but two of his representatives did. At about the same time, he was condemned at Brionne in Normandy in the presence of Duke William, and also at Paris (though absent) in the presence of King Henry, as Durand informs us. In the year 1055, a council was held against him at Florence, and in the same year Pope Victor sent his chaplain Hildebrand <note>The future Pope Gregory VII</note> into Gaul, who, having convened a Synod at Tours, forced Berengar to a recantation <note>original: *palinodiam*</note>. In the year 1059, in a Roman Synod, he argued in favor of his opinion before Pope Nicholas; and since no one was able to resist him, as Leo of Ostia reports*, 
<margin>* Chronicle of Monte Cassino, book 3, chapter 33.</margin>
Alberic, a Deacon of Monte Cassino and a most learned man, was summoned to the Synod. When neither would yield after many conflicts of words, Alberic, having received a one-week truce, published a book against Berengar. Berengar himself, terrified by threats and weary of insults, abjured his opinion according to a formula prescribed to him; namely, that most well-known form which begins thus: *I Berengar, an unworthy Deacon, etc.* In the year 1063, Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, held a Synod in which he condemned Berengar and his followers, [proposing] a confession of faith opposed to the Berengarian dogma...

# ->The Age of Hildebrand.<-

<margin>11th CENTURY. Year 1000.</margin>
...he established. The Acts of this Synod were unearthed by the Illustrious Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon, a famous 17th-century Benedictine scholar</note> in *Analecta*, Volume II, p. 457. In the year 1075, another Synod was assembled at Poitiers against Berengar, presided over by Gerald, the Pope’s legate, as the same Mabillon notes from the *Chronicle of Maillezais*. In the year 1078, on the feast of All Saints, Gregory VII gathered a Council at Rome, in which Berengar produced a brief confession of faith, which Mabillon brought to light in the place cited above, p. 487. However, so that he might delay the matter for a little while, he sought and obtained a truce until the next upcoming Synod. Therefore, in the following year during Lent, another Synod was held, in which a new formula of confession was proposed to him—*I, Berengar, believe in my heart* <note>original: "Ego Berengarius corde credo"</note>, etc.—which he subscribed to and confirmed. That he did this under compulsion cannot be doubted. Certainly, that he returned to his earlier opinion can be proved from many testimonies of writers contemporary to him, such as Lanfranc, the Anonymous Chiffletian, and others. And what places the matter beyond all doubt is that Mabillon confesses he read a manuscript treatise by Berengar himself, in which he utterly rescinded that third profession of faith and tore it apart with many arguments, adding how he was induced to sign the final profession of faith: namely, by the fear of death which certainly loomed over him; and in what sense he had asserted it. Mabillon contends with more than one argument that Berengar did indeed return to a "sound mind," as he calls it, and adhered to the Catholic faith until his very last breath. Whether he has fully proven this, let others judge. This much is certain: Berengar, departing from Rome, came to Tours and withdrew to the island of St. Cosmas in the suburbs of the city, and there, having taken up the monastic habit, he served for eight years. He died in that place on the 6th of January, in the year 1088. That he was a man distinguished by his skill in the liberal arts and dialectics <note>the art of logical argument</note>, and illustrious for the holiness of his life and character, even his adversaries do not deny. William of Malmesbury* praises him wonderfully for his humility, almsgiving, modesty, chastity, zeal, and abstinence; in whose work there exists a noble Epitaph in his praise by Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, a disciple of Berengar himself: from which, setting aside the rest, let me be permitted to transfer a few lines here.

<margin>* On the Deeds of the Kings, book 3, folio 63.</margin>

> The world which just now wondered at him, will always wonder;
> That Berengar, though dying, shall not die;
> Whom, while he held the highest peaks of the sacred faith,
> Now the fifth day has carried off—having dared a wicked deed.
> That day, a ruinous day, and treacherous to the world,
> In which there was grief and the total collapse of affairs.
> In which the state of the Church, the hope and glory of the Clergy,
> In which the cultivator of the law fell, while the law itself was falling.
> Whatever the Philosophers, whatever the Poets sang,
> Yielded to his genius and his eloquence.
> A holier and greater wisdom, having attempted greater things,
> Filled his sacred breast and his mouth with God.

Finally, at the end:

> A man truly wise, and blessed in every part;
> Who enriches the heavens with his soul, and the earth with his body.
> After death may I live with him, with him may I rest:
> Nor may my lot become better than his own.

There exist two Letters to Ascelin and Richard, along with Ascelin’s letters, first published by D’Achery among the *Works of Lanfranc*, and then in *The Councils*, Volume IX, p. 1056. D’Achery presents another to Abbot Richard in *Spicilegium*, Volume II. Mabillon has three of his Formulas of faith concerning the Eucharist in *Analecta*, Volume II, p. 486. Manuscript *Disputations with Lanfranc on the presence of Christ in the Supper* are preserved in the Library of Brasenose College <note>original: "Collegii Æneonas"</note> at Oxford, Code 4, number 1. Sigebert* informs us <margin>* On Writers, chapter 154.</margin> that he published several other short works on the matter of the Eucharist. Boston of Bury testifies that he wrote on the Apocalypse. Certainly his exposition of the Apocalypse—

**HERMANN**, called **THE LAME** <note>Latin: *Contractus*, meaning "drawn together" or "contracted"</note> from his contracted limbs; noble by birth, son of Count Wolferad of Veringen and Hiltrud. Educated in the Monastery of Saint Gall, then a monk of Reichenau <note>Latin: *Augia major*</note>, of the Order of Saint Benedict. He flourished in the year 1040. With all his limbs so contracted by paralysis that he had to be carried from place to place, he nevertheless applied himself so diligently to his studies that he easily surpassed his peers in learning and intellect; for he was learned in Latin, Greek, and Arabic, and highly skilled in theology, history, philosophy, astronomy, rhetoric, and poetry. 
<margin>\* On Illustrious Men of Germany, part 2, p. 113.</margin>
In this way, he beautifully repaired with the virtues of the mind that which nature had denied to his body, as Heinrich Pantaleon correctly observes \*. He died in the year 1054. He wrote a *Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World*, from the beginning of the world to the year 1054. It was published in Frankfurt in 1583; a more complete and corrected version was edited by Urstisius among the *German Writers*, published in the same place in 1585 and 1670, Volume I, p. 231. Another edition of the same work, different from the previous ones, was provided by Canisius in *Ancient Readings*, Volume I, p. 433. It also exists among the *German Writers* edited by Pistorius, Volume I, p. 89, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVIII, p. 348.

**DOMINIC**, a Venetian by birth as it seems, Patriarch of Grado (or Venice) and Aquileia; he flourished in the year 1040 and thereafter. He flourished in the year 1040; the year in which he attained the Patriarchal dignity is not sufficiently clear, but it was at least before the year 1053, when he sent his profession of faith to Pope Leo IX. There exists, in Greek and Latin, a fairly long *Responsive Letter* to Dominic of Grado, in Cotelier, ibid., p. 112. Also a *Second Letter to Michael Cerularius* <note>The Patriarch of Constantinople during the Great Schism of 1054</note>, ibid., p. 145. Leo Allatius had previously published almost one of these in its entirety in *On the Agreement of the Eastern and Western Churches*, book 3, chapter 12, section 4; in which our Antiochian [Peter] most fiercely attacks the customs and dogmas of the Latins—especially that "evil of evils, the worst of all" <note>Greek: *kakon ek kakon kakiston*</note>, as he calls it—the addition of the **FILIOQUE** <note>The phrase "and the Son," added by the Western Church to the Nicene Creed, a major point of contention with the Eastern Church</note> to the Creed.

But since it is most clearly established from his own homilies that he was younger than Simeon Metaphrastes, whom he cites; and since the homily for Palm Sunday is said in almost innumerable manuscripts to have been delivered in the presence of King Roger <note>Roger II of Sicily, who reigned in the 12th century; this creates a chronological difficulty the author is attempting to resolve</note>, we believe with much greater probability, along with Leo Allatius, that he flourished around this time. The arguments devised by Francisco Scorso to diminish the authority of these inscriptions are plainly trivial and of no weight, nor are they worth a more diligent examination by me in this place, especially since Leo Allatius has performed this abundantly in *On the Writings of Simeon*, p. 63. Let there be a letter from Photius to Theophanes: that Theophanes should not immediately be considered our man, especially since it is said to be written not to Theophanes Cerameus, Bishop of Taormina, but only to Theophanes the Monk. Theophanes; the most learned Allatius <note>Leone Allacci (1586–1669), a Greek-Catholic scholar and librarian at the Vatican</note> demonstrates with many arguments in the cited passage that all these matters can be quite suitably attributed to Roger, King of Sicily. Miræus* and, following him, Olearius†, very poorly confuse this man with Theophanes the Confessor, the founder of the *Chronographia* <note>Theophanes the Confessor was a 9th-century Byzantine monk; the author discussed here is the 11th-century Theophanes Cerameus</note>. Our author wrote *Sixty-two Homilies on the Sunday Gospels and the Feasts of the Entire Year*, which Francisco Scorsus published with notes and very extensive prolegomena in Greek and Latin at *Paris, 1644, in folio.* Gretser had previously published two orations *On the Sunday before the Exaltation of the Cross*, in Greek and Latin, in his work *On the Cross, Volume II, p. 1207.* In certain manuscript codices, these Sunday homilies are attributed to Gregory Cerameus, Archbishop of Taormina; Scorsus untangles this knot at length and finally determines that the author had two names, being the same Theophanes and Gregory Cerameus, Archbishop of Taormina. Whether this is sufficiently solid, I will not raise a dispute with the most learned editor in this place. In his preaching, our Theophanes uses a method well-suited and elegant for explaining Gospel history; he first explains the literal sense, yet does not neglect the allegorical and moral senses. His style is not unpleasing—not ornate or flowery, to be sure, but simple, clear according to the standard of didactic speech, and flowing naturally. It is no wonder if, in this declining age of the Greek language, he lacks certain ornaments that might be expected from Basil or Chrysostom <note>Referring to the "Golden Age" Church Fathers known for their high rhetoric</note>.

<margin>1043.</margin>
NILUS, surnamed Doxopatrius, an Archimandrite <note>A superior of a group of monasteries in the Eastern Church</note> of the Greek Church. His origin is uncertain; if there is room for conjecture, I would think he originated from Magna Graecia <note>The Greek-speaking regions of Southern Italy</note>; certainly, he himself testifies to us that he lived for some time in Palermo, Sicily. He flourished in the year 1043. Being asked by letter by Roger, King of Sicily, he wrote *Briefly on the Seats of the Major Patriarchs*, which he later followed up in the aforementioned year with a more extensive work, in which he treated clearly of the five Patriarchal thrones and the Archbishops, Metropolitans, and Bishops subject to them, as well as the institution, order, and proper names of the Patriarchal seats. From this notice of the Patriarchates, Leo Allatius presents many very full and truly excellent fragments in *On the Agreement of the Eastern and Western Churches, book I, chapters 2, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 16, 17, 24.* Indeed, Stephen Le Moyne published the entire book from a more recent manuscript codex transcribed in 1611, in Greek and Latin, in *Various Sacred Matters, Volume I, p. 211.*

He wrote *To Odilo, Abbot of Cluny, Five Books of Histories, from the year 900 to the year 1045*, although he has very little to say concerning the tenth century. > “diocese than other bishops, whose diocese is defined by 
> “certain limits; and that he could do nothing at all 
> “outside of it.
Glaber puts forward his own opinion on this matter, which Baronius singles out, in *Book 2, Chapter 4 of his History.*
