<note>This entry refers to Pope Clement II</note> Having been elevated to the Roman Pontificate by Henry, King of the Germans, he was enthroned on Christmas Day, on which very day he invested Henry and his wife Agnes with the imperial crown. In the following year, he convened a Council at Rome against the Simoniacs <note>Those who buy or sell church offices</note>; and having followed Emperor Henry into Germany, he ended his days in the year 1047, on the 9th or 10th of October, and was buried in his own church at Bamberg. There exists a *Rescript* <note>An official written answer to a legal or dogmatic question</note> in favor of the Archbishop of Ravenna in Ferdinando Ughelli's *Sacred Italy, Volume II*, and a *Decretal Letter* concerning the elevation of the see of Salerno to an Archbishopric in *The Councils, Volume IX, page 945.*

ADELMANN, a disciple of Fulbert of Chartres and a fellow student of Berengar <note>Berengar of Tours, known for his controversial views on the Eucharist</note>, formerly a Scholastic <note>Head of a cathedral school</note> at Liège, became Bishop of Brescia from the year 1048. He died around the year 1061. He wrote a *Letter to Berengar on the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist*, which was published in print together with other short works on the same subject by the care of Jean Ulimmer at *Louvain in 1551, 1561, and in the Library of the Fathers, Volume XVIII, page 438.* He also wrote, according to the testimony of Sigebert <margin>* On Script. chapter 153.</margin> \*, a letter on the same subject *to Paul, the Primicerius of Metz* <note>A senior official, often the head of the cathedral school or choir</note>, in which he attempted to call him back from his opinion on the Eucharist, just as he had done for their common friend Berengar. That letter seems to have perished.

GISLEBERT, a monk of Auxerre; he flourished in the year 1048. He wrote the *Life of Saint Romanus*, which is found in Mabillon, *Century 1, page 81.*

<margin>
1048.
</margin>
HUGO, a Burgundian by country and of noble birth, the son of Dalmatius, Lord of Semur, and Aremburga, was born in the year 1023. While still a youth of fifteen, he entered the monastic life in the Monastery of Cluny, having obtained Abbot Odilo as his teacher. After some years he became Prior of the monastery, and upon the death of Odilo, he was created Abbot in the year 1048. In the year 1058, he was present with Pope Stephen as he lay dying at Florence. In the year 1074, he traveled to Rome for the sake of religion. He died in the year 1108, or as others say, 1109, on the 3rd day before the Kalends of May <note>April 29</note>, at the age of 85. Several of his *Letters* are extant in D'Achery’s *Spicilegium, Volume II.*

<margin>
1049.
</margin>
LEO IX, *previously called Bruno*, a German by nation, son of Hugh and cousin of Emperor Conrad, himself the Count of Dagsburg. From being Bishop of Toul, he was designated Roman Pontiff by Henry at Worms in the year 1048. He was elected at Rome in the year 1049 on the 2nd of February, and enthroned on the 12th. In the same year, having held Synods at Rome and Pavia, he confirmed the decree of Clement II against the Simoniacs; having also set out for Gaul and Germany, he celebrated the Synods of Reims and Mainz. In the latter, several ecclesiastical Canons were passed, especially against the Simoniacs; in the former, the new Basilica of Saint Remigius was dedicated, and his relics were translated into it. In the year 1050, he convened the Synods of Rome and Vercelli against Berengar; and in this latter synod he also excommunicated the rebellious inhabitants of Benevento and Humphrey, Archbishop of Ravenna. In the year 1051, after he had made a journey into Germany, he celebrated a Council at Rome where he excommunicated Gregory, Bishop of Vercelli, on account of adultery. In the following year, he made another journey into Germany to broker peace between Emperor Henry and Andrew, King of Hungary. In the year 1053, leading an army against the Normans, he was defeated by them in battle, captured, and soon released. In the year 1054, he sent a legation to Constantinople to Constantine Monomachus, so that peace might be entered into between the Eastern and Western Churches, and to stir up the Emperor’s mind against the Patriarch Michael Cerularius <note>This event led to the Great Schism of 1054</note>. In the same year he died, on the 19th of April. Nineteen of his *Letters* are extant in *The Councils, Volume IX, page 949*; the first of these, which is to Michael Cerularius and which most vehemently rebukes his arrogance and that of Leo of Ohrid, as well as the errors of the Greeks, should be considered a *Treatise* rather than a Letter, as it comprises forty-one chapters. Many of his *Homilies or Sermons* are also extant, published at *Louvain 1565, Cologne 1568, and Antwerp 1583.*

# ->The Hildebrandine Century.<-

<margin>

1049.
</margin>

## ANSELM, Canon of Liège and Scholastic <note>The head of a cathedral school</note> of the Church of St. Lambert, and later the Dean of Namur; he flourished in the year 1049. At the request of Ida, the Abbess of Cologne, he wrote the *History of the Bishops of Liège* from approximately the year 666 to 1048. This work was first brought to light, along with four other writers of similar subject matter, by Jean Chapeauville at *Liège in 1612, in quarto format.*

---

<margin>1050.</margin>

## NIKETAS STETHATOS, also known as "Pectoratus" <note>meaning "the stout-hearted" or "one with a broad chest"</note>, a Monk and Priest of Constantinople in the Monastery of Stoudios; he flourished around the year 1050. He was a chief enemy of the Latins <note>the Western Roman Church</note>, against whom Humbert and other legates of the Roman Church argued vigorously in Constantinople. Indeed, if Humbert is to be believed, Niketas yielded to the legates' arguments, burned his own writings, and anathematized <note>formally cursed or excommunicated</note> all enemies of the Roman Church in the year 1054. In this matter, either the good envoys <note>original: "Apocrisiarii"</note> are deceiving us—being quite concerned for their own reputation—or Stethatos did so merely to suit the times; for the Greek writers never, as far as I know, even slightly acknowledge that he defected from the Greeks themselves. His *Book against the Latins on Unleavened Bread, on Sabbath Fasts, and on the Marriage of Priests* exists in Latin, published by Canisius in *Volume VI, page 4*, and by Baronius in the Appendix to *Volume XI*. Certain fragments of this book are preserved in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius’s work *On the Presanctified Mass, section 2.16*. From the same Niketas's *Canon on Saint Nicholas*, Allatius cites certain parts in his book *Against Hottinger, chapter 11, page 208*. He also mentions Niketas's *Treatise on the Soul*, and provides a fragment from the 14th chapter in his book *On the Eighth Photian Synod, chapter 14, page 545*. His *Iambic Poem on Symeon the Younger* (his teacher) is presented in its entirety in Greek by the same author in the *Discourse on the Writings of Symeon, page 168*. From his *Preface to Symeon's book on Divine Praises*, Allatius cites certain portions in the same work, *pages 152 and 172*.

---

<margin>1050.</margin>

## MICHAEL PSELLUS was a native of Constantinople, born of an ancient and noble lineage of both consular and patrician rank. Entrusted to a teacher at the age of five, he progressed so far in every branch of literature that he became the greatest glory of his century—"most wise" <note>original Greek: "sophōtatos"</note> and "Prince of Philosophers" <note>original Greek: "tōn philosophōn hypatos"</note>, as Zonaras and Cedrenus call him, to say nothing of the praise from more recent authors. He flourished in the year 1050 and thereafter, holding the highest honors and offices in the state. He was a Senator of Constantinople and was sent as an envoy by Michael VI Stratiotikos, along with other leading men, to Isaac Comnenus. That same Comnenus utilized Psellus's help especially in deposing Michael Keroularios. Michael VII Doukas was specifically entrusted to his care to be imbued with fine literature and good morals; Psellus accordingly shaped him accurately in every kind of discipline. Indeed, by his help and advice, Doukas himself was raised to the imperial throne in the year 1071. But six years later, after Michael Doukas was removed from power, Psellus himself was stripped of his dignities, his hair was shorn, and he took on the monastic habit. Leaving the royal city, he seems to have exchanged life for death not long afterward. He was a truly admirable man, who left almost all the learned men of his age far behind him in his eloquence, sharpness of wit, and depth of learning. Joseph, Bishop of Methone, counts him among those who were rather hostile to the Latin Church—whom he calls schismatics <margin>* Apology against Mark of Ephesus</margin>—and Allatius himself admits in more than one place that Psellus, in his exposition of the faith to Michael Doukas, affirmed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. He wrote an almost infinite number of works: philosophical, mathematical, medical, historical, and theological. This Psellus, therefore, as he was most outstanding in learning, so was he the "most prolific writer" <note>original Greek: "polygraphōtatos"</note> of all. I would dare to say that no one in that or the following age either discovered things more sharply in Greek, or ordered them more fitly, or spoke more eloquently, or treated matters more profoundly. "There was no science which he did not either illustrate with notes, or attempt in a summary, or explain with the best method," says Leo Allatius in the *Discourse* he published on the Pselli and their writings, page 42; I gladly admit that this work provided no small light to me in reviewing Psellus's works, especially for the "unlearned" <note>original Greek: "tois amathesi," referring to those unfamiliar with the breadth of Psellus's bibliography</note>.

**Poems, or a Metrical Paraphrase of the Song of Songs**, dedicated to Emperor Nicephorus Botoniates. Published in Latin at Venice, 1573, in quarto; Antwerp, 1615, in octavo. Published in Greek by the care of Joannes Meursius, Leiden, 1617, in quarto.

**Iambic verses on vices and virtues**, an *Anagoge* <note>an interpretation leading to a higher spiritual meaning</note> on Tantalus and Circe, and an **Allegory on the Sphinx**. In Greek and Latin, Basel, 1544, in octavo.

**Dialogue on the Operation of Demons**. In Latin, Paris, 1577. In Greek and Latin with the notes of Gilbert Gaulmin, Paris, 1615, in octavo. Excerpts of this work collected and translated into Latin by Marsilio Ficino have been published several times.

**Book on the faculties of the soul**. In Greek and Latin, with Origen’s *Philocalia*, Paris, 1624, in quarto.

**Annotations on several passages of Gregory of Nazianzus**. In Latin, edited by Jacques de Billy with the works of Gregory of Nazianzus.

**Panegyric Oration for Simeon Metaphrastes** <note>the famous Byzantine hagiographer</note>. In Latin, in the works of Surius, November 27. In Greek and Latin, in Leo Allatius’s *On the Writings of Simeon*, page 221.

**A Liturgical Office for his commemoration**, composed by Psellus. In Greek and Latin, in the same volume, page 236.

**Synopsis of Laws** in iambic and "political" <note>original: "politicis" — a common 15-syllable accentual verse used in Middle Greek</note> verses.
**Political poems on Dogma.**
**Poems on the Nomocanon** <note>a collection of ecclesiastical law</note>.
**A small book on the Seven Sacred Ecumenical Synods.** These four small works were published in Greek and Latin with notes by François Bosquet, Paris, 1632, in octavo.

**A Compendium on the property, utility, and harm of Foods**, collected from medical books, to which Simeon Seth, Master of Antioch, added a few things. This work, interpolated by Seth, was published under his name in Greek and Latin, Basel, 1538, in octavo.

**Book on Gout**, written by an anonymous author during the time of Michael Palaeologus, and erroneously published under the name of Psellus. In Greek, Paris, 1558, in octavo; frequently in Latin.

**On the Making of Gold** <note>original: "Περὶ χρυσοποιΐας" (Peri chrysopoiias)</note>, or the method of manufacturing gold, addressed to Patriarch Michael Cerularius. In Latin, together with other writers on the same subject, Padua, 1572, in octavo.

**Book on the Four Mathematical Sciences**: Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astronomy. In Greek and Latin, Wittenberg, 1560; and with the annotations of Xylander, Basel, 1556. In Greek, Paris, 1545; in Latin, ibid., 1557; Tournon, 1592.

**Introduction to the Six Modes of Philosophy**. In Greek, Paris, 1540; in Latin, ibid., 1541.

**Two books on the regulation of diet**, and on the properties and quality of the juices of the elements, addressed to Emperor Constantine. In Latin, Basel, 1529, in octavo.

**Paraphrase of Aristotle’s book *On Interpretation*** <note>original: "περὶ Ἑρμηνείας" (Peri Hermeneias)</note>. In Greek, Venice, 1503, in folio; in Latin, Basel, 1542.

**Compendium of the *Five Voices* of Porphyry** <note>an introduction to logic</note> and the **Categories of Aristotle**. In Greek, Paris, 1540; in Latin, Basel, 1542.

<margin>1051.</margin>

### MICHAEL CERULARIUS,
Patriarch of Constantinople from the year 1051 according to Freher, but more correctly 1043 according to Baronius and Curopalates. He was a most bitter enemy of the Latins and the Roman Pontiffs, whom he attacked in speech and writing on account of their pride and ambition, for the practice of fasting on Saturdays, and for the use of unleavened bread <term>Azyma: the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, a major point of contention between the Eastern and Western Churches</term> in the sacred rites, for the word *"and the Son"* <note>original: "Filioque"</note> inserted into the Creed, and for the seized primacy of the entire Christian world. Finally, in the year 1053, after some hope of entering into peace had dawned on both sides through the exchange of conciliatory letters, Pope Leo IX sent Cardinals Humbert and Frederick and Archbishop Peter of Amalfi to Constantinople for that purpose. After attempts to reach an agreement were tried by both sides without success, Humbert excommunicated Michael; Michael in turn removed the Pope's name from the Diptychs <term>Diptychs: official lists of names of living and dead Christians commemorated by a local church; removal signifies a break in communion</term>, and he was the authority behind the other Oriental Patriarchs doing the same. In the year 1057, being more inclined toward the faction of Isaac I Komnenos, he cunningly persuaded Michael VI Stratioticus to yield the empire. In the following year, having become hated by Emperor Isaac himself due to a suspicion of a desire for revolution, and while the Emperor was meditating on bringing him to heel and stripping him of the Patriarchal seat, Michael met a timely death in the 15th year of his Patriarchate. There remains his *Synodic Decision on marriages in the seventh degree* in Greek and Latin in the *Graeco-Roman Law*, Book 3, page 206; *Certain fragments on prohibited marriage*, ibid., Book 4, page 263; *Two Letters to Peter of Antioch* in Greek and Latin in Cotelerius’s *Monuments*, Volume II, page 135; and the *Synodic Edict against the Latins concerning the Pittacia* <note>original: "Pittacia" - here referring to the document or "ticket" of excommunication</note>, *or concerning the excommunication hurled by the Latin Legates against him, and by him against the Legates*, enacted on June 9, 1054, in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius’s *On the Ecclesiastical Books of the Greeks*, page 161.

**LEO**, Archbishop of Ohrid <note>original: "Achridiæ"</note> and Metropolitan of the Bulgarians, flourished at the same time as Cerularius, as a partner in the same studies and deeds. Leo also wrote several other *Letters*; Leo Allatius quotes certain parts of the first of these in his work *On the Harmony of the Eastern and Western Church, book 3, chapter 14, section 4.* <note>original: "de Consensu Eccles. **SYMEON**, called *the Younger* <note>Known today as Symeon the New Theologian (949–1022). "Younger" distinguishes him from Symeon the Metaphrast or Gregory of Nazianzus, also called "the Theologian."</note> to distinguish him from the Metaphrast or from Gregory of Nazianzus the Theologian; a Priest of Constantinople and Superior of St. Mamas in Xerokerkos <note>A monastery in Constantinople</note>, he flourished around the year 1051. <margin>1055.</margin>
**VICTOR II**, previously called Gebhard, a Norican <note>from the region of modern Bavaria and Austria</note> by birth, counselor to Emperor Henry [III] and Bishop of Eichstätt. After the death of Leo, he was appointed to the Roman see by Emperor Henry, to whom he was very closely related by blood; he was installed in the chair on the 13th of April in the year 1055. In 1056, having been summoned to Germany by Henry, he was present at the Emperor's death and took into his guardianship the son, Henry [IV], who had been commended to him by the father. Returning to Italy the following year, he died at Florence on the 28th of July. There exists a *Letter to Humbert, Bishop of Silva Candida*, in which he expands the privileges of that church; found in the *Collections of the Councils*, Vol. IX, page 1077.

**STEPHEN IX**, previously called *Junianus Frederick Gozzelo*, a Lotharingian <note>from Lorraine</note> by nation and brother to Duke Godfrey of Lotharingia. He was Archdeacon of the Roman Church, Librarian, Chancellor, and Cardinal of the title of St. Chrysogonus. In the year 1054, he was sent as a legate to Constantinople by Leo IX together with Humbert, where he deposed Patriarch Michael and struck him with anathema <note>a formal curse or excommunication</note>. Having returned to Italy, he experienced the enmity of Emperor Henry because he had supported the interests of his brother Godfrey; it reached the point where he found it necessary to set aside his marks of honor and put on the monk’s cowl in the Monastery of Cassino. There, in the year 1057, through the influence of Victor II, he was declared Abbot. In the same year, having set out for Florence to consult the Pope, he was again declared a Cardinal-Priest by him; soon after Victor's death, he attained the Roman Pontificate. He was consecrated on the 3rd of August, so unwillingly and reluctantly that he had to be led by force from his lodging to the Basilica of St. Peter in Chains. He held frequent Councils, in which he pursued nothing with greater zeal than stripping the clergy and priests of the permission to marry. At the start of the year 1058, he prepared a legation to Constantinople for the sake of uniting the Churches, sending Abbot Desiderius of Cassino, Cardinal Stephen, and others; those who set out for the East, however, labored in vain. Stephen himself, remaining at home, thought of transferring the Empire to his brother Godfrey. To achieve this more easily—if faith is to be placed in Papebroch* and his ancient manuscript—he declared the Empress <note>original: "vindicatam," likely referring to the Empress-Regent Agnes</note> a Heretic, and announced it by sending the Deacon Hildebrand to Germany. He died at Florence in the year 1058, on the 29th of March. *Two Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Vol. IX, page 1088. He wrote, together with Cardinal Humbert, a *Book on the Body of the Lord against Michael Cerularius*, about which...

### THE AGE OF HILDEBRAND

<margin>
11th CENTURY from the Year 1000.
</margin>
...dealing with Humbert; likewise, another work on the same subject against a monk of Constantinople, as witnessed by Peter the Deacon in chapter 17.

<margin>
1057.
Life of Damian by John the Disciple, prefixed to his works. Dittrich, History of the Cardinals, Vol. 1, p. 16.
</margin>
**PETER DAMIAN** <note>original: "Petrus de Honestis," but more commonly known as Peter Damian</note>, named after his brother Damian (whom he always regarded as a father), was an Italian by birth and a native of Ravenna. He began his monastic life in the Monastery of St. Andrew at Fonte Avellana. On account of the excellent reputation of his virtue and learning, he was summoned some years later by Abbot Guido of Pomposia to his own monastery, so that he might lead the monks of Pomposia by the example of his virtue and teaching. After he had spent two years there, he returned to Avellana and was declared Prior of the monastery, and finally Abbot. Having been made Abbot, he diligently cultivated the province entrusted to him, enlarged the monastery buildings, and incited the monks to piety and the study of fine literature by his example, instructing them through his writings. Furthermore, which increases his heap of merits immensely in the eyes of the Popes, he was the first of all to prescribe the Office of the Blessed Virgin <note>a specific cycle of prayers and psalms dedicated to Mary</note> to be recited by his monks. In the year 1057 or the following year, he was created a Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia by Pope Stephen, though against his will. In the year 1059, he was sent as a legate to Milan by Pope Nicholas II, in order to root out simony <note>the buying or selling of church offices</note> and clerical marriage from the Milanese Church; and under that pretext, to subject the Milanese See to the Roman See. Peter was indeed assigned a difficult task <note>original: "duram provinciam," a hard province or duty</note>.

<margin>
See Peter’s Letter to Hildebrand and John in the Life of Damian.
</margin>
Upon his arrival in the City, the Milanese clergy were in an uproar; they shouted that they were entirely innocent of the crime of simony; that the law of celibacy was impious and intolerable; but above all, that it was unworthy for the Ambrosian Church <note>The Church of Milan, which followed its own ancient traditions and rite dating back to St. Ambrose</note> to be subject to the Roman Church. They argued that the Roman Pontiff had no power of judging or arranging matters within that See; that the equality of authority received from their ancestors must be strongly preserved; and that they should not have to undergo the Papal yoke after the long-standing liberty of their Church. Not content with words, the clergy prepared for violence, and having formed a mob, they brought the Legate into danger of his life. Nevertheless, Peter suppressed these great storms of trouble with wonderful skill, and having drawn Archbishop Guido over to his side, he brought the clergy into order, finished the business, and brought a triumph back to Rome. In the year 1061, being indignant at the loose morals of the Roman clergy, since—to use his own words—he did not know how to live with those from whom he differed so much in character, he resigned his bishopric and withdrew into solitude. However, he was not granted a long indulgence in rest. For in the following year, he was snatched from his solitude at Avellana by Pope Alexander II and forced to undertake a legation to France to reform the state of the Monastery of Cluny. In the year 1063, he was sent by the same Pope to Florence to settle a very serious schism that had arisen between Bishop Peter and the citizens and monks of Florence. In the year 1069, he was sent by Alexander to Henry, King of the Germans, who intended to divorce his wife Bertha; he prevented this crime partly through his wholesome teachings and partly through his invincible strength of mind. In the year 1072, after the death of Archbishop Henry of Ravenna (who had been excommunicated eight years earlier by Pope Alexander for constantly refusing obedience to the Roman Church), Peter was sent as a legate to his native city to reconcile the citizens of Ravenna to the Roman Church and to release them from the bond of the anathema <note>the formal curse of excommunication</note>. Having finished this business, he went to Faenza, where he was seized by a fever and breathed forth his soul in the Monastery of St. Mary on the 23rd day of February, in the 66th year of his age. Brietius says he was a man plainly pious, and one who instilled religion into the minds of many, a most sharp defender of the Church, and worthy to have been set over it if he had fallen upon better times. I do not know if it deserves notice what is read in more than one Register of the Monastery of St. Edmund <note>Bury St. Edmunds in England</note> in these words: *Where (namely, in the Church founded by Abbot Baldwin) among the chief clergy was Peter Damian, whose most beautiful book, which is called "The Lord be with you," <note>original: "Dominus vobiscum"</note> exists to this day.* Whether our Damian had been here, let others investigate; certainly no one, as far as I know, mentions his arrival in England; otherwise, the calculation of the times fits well enough, as that Church of Bury was founded around the year 1065.

It also notes his literary contributions and a possible historical connection to the Abbey of Bury St. Edmunds in England.</summary>

### THE AGE OF HILDEBRAND <note>Referring to the era of Pope Gregory VII, formerly Hildebrand, characterized by significant Church reforms.</note>

### WORKS.

<margin>11th CENTURY from the Year 1000.</margin>
**Eight books of Letters.** Of these: I. to the Popes, II. to the Cardinals, III. to the Patriarchs and Archbishops, IV. to the Bishops, V. to the Clergy, VI. to the Abbots and Monks, VII. to secular Princes, VIII. to private Laypeople. These were published separately with notes by *Constantine Cajetan of Syracuse, Paris 1610, in quarto.*

**Sermons distributed according to the order of the months.** Among these, *Theophilus Raynaud* notes in his *Inquiries* <note>original: "Erotematis"</note> that those *on the Nativity of the Lord, on St. Martin, on the Streams of the River, on St. Stephen, on St. Andrew, and on St. Nicholas* are spurious <note>false or forged</note>.

***The Life of St. Odilo, Abbot of Cluny.*** Found in the collections of *Surius* and *Bollandus* under January 1st.

***The Life of St. Maurus, Bishop of Cesena,*** found in the same, under January 20th.

***The Life of St. Romuald, founder of the Camaldolese.*** Contained in *Surius* under June 19th.

***The Life of St. Rudolf, Bishop of Gubbio,*** found in the same, under October 14th.

***The Passion of the Holy Virgins and Martyrs Flora and Lucilla.***

***An Exposition of the visions of the Holy Martyrs Marianus and James.***

Many other ***Lives of Saints*** written by Damian are found in the collection by Surius; however, these already have their place within his Letters and Sermons, and thus have been enumerated by us above.

***A Work on the Catholic Faith, addressed to Ambrosia.***

***Counter-argument against the Jews.*** <note>original: "Antilogus contra Judæos"</note>

***A Dialogue between a Jew and a Christian.***

***The book called "The Most Gracious."*** <note>original: "Gratissimus"</note>

On various miraculous stories. On the Portraits of the Princes of the Apostles* <note>St. Peter and St. Paul</note>. *On Divine Omnipotence. On various sacred questions. On bearing correction with equanimity. On Chastity. On spiritual delights. On the perfect formation of a Monk. Instruction for a Nun. On the eremitic life. On the benefit of the religious state. On patience during the persecution of the wicked. On the Saturday fast. On celebrating Vigils. On despising the glory of the world. On the duties of a Prince in restraining the wicked. On true happiness and wisdom. On the Last Things and the Antichrist. A mystical exposition of the Book of Genesis.*

The **Works of Damian**, collected into one, were published with notes and observations by *Constantine Cajetan in Rome* in three volumes in the years 1606, 1608, and 1615. *Cajetan* also promised a fourth volume containing Prayers, Poems, and Rhythms. The Roman edition was reprinted in Lyon in 1623 in three volumes, folio; and a fourth volume was added in the Paris editions of 1642 and 1663. In these volumes, no place is held by—

### THE AGE OF HILDEBRAND

<margin>11th CENTURY from the Year 1000.</margin>
***A Book on the Correction of the Pope and the Bishop***, which was published in print at Strasbourg in 1562, and among other works at Frankfurt in 1614 and 1621, and in Goldast’s *Monarchy*, Volume II, page 43.

***Five Sermons on the Lord’s Prayer***, published by D’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, Volume VII. However, the same D’Achery, at the end of the Preface to Volume VIII, attributes these to Peter of Ravenna (also known as Chrysologus) <note>Peter Chrysologus was a 5th-century bishop known for his short, inspired sermons; the editor D'Achery corrected his earlier attribution to Damian</note>.

---

<margin>1057.</margin>
**ALBERIC**, perhaps an Italian by nation, a Monk and Deacon of Monte Cassino, and a Cardinal with the title of the Church of the Four Holy Crowned Saints. He was appointed by Pope Stephen IX or, according to others, by Alexander II. He flourished in the year 1057. In the year 1059, a Synod was held at Rome against Berengarius <note>Berengarius of Tours was a theologian whose views on the Eucharist—denying the real presence—were condemned as heretical</note>. To this meeting, or at least to the subsequent Synod held under Gregory VII in 1079, our Alberic was summoned so that he might take up the role of disputing against Berengarius. He thereafter opposed him both in person and in writing, having composed in the space of barely one week his ***Book on the Body of the Lord.***

<margin>On Illustrious Men, Chapter 21.</margin>
He wrote furthermore, according to the testimony of Peter the Deacon, ***A Book of Dictations and Salutations*** <note>A manual on the "Ars Dictaminis," the medieval art of formal letter-writing</note>; ***Hymns to St. Nicholas***; ***A Dialogue on Music***; ***On the Virginity of St. Mary***; ***Against Emperor Henry on the Election of the Roman Pontiff***; ***Hymns for Easter***; ***On the Ascension***; ***On the Cross***; ***On the Day of Judgment***; ***On the Pains of Hell***; ***On the Joy of Paradise***; ***On the Assumption of the Blessed Mary***; ***On St. Paul***; ***On St. Apollinaris***; ***The Passion of St. Modestus and St. Caesarius***; ***The Life of St. Dominic the Abbot***; ***[The Life] of St. Scholastica, and a Homily on the same***; ***On Death***; ***On Monks***; ***On Astronomy***; ***On Dialectic***; and also several letters. J. B. Marus, in his notes to Peter the Deacon (p. 43), testifies that all of Alberic’s manuscript works are held in Florence in the Library of the Friars Minor of the Holy Cross. The *Life of St. Dominic* is found in Bollandus <note>The "Acta Sanctorum" collection of saints' lives</note>, Volume II, for January 22nd. Bollandus, however, rashly confuses our Alberic with another Alberic, likewise a monk of Monte Cassino, who flourished in the year 1123 and wrote a *Book on his Vision*; this error is also made by Possevinus, Arnold Wion, Ciaconius, and others.

---

<margin>1057.</margin>
**GEORGE CEDRENUS**, a Greek Monk, flourished in the year 1057. A writer of quite obscure fame, regarding whom those who have handed down the history of subsequent times report nothing at all. He wrote ***Annals, or a Compendium of Histories from the Creation of the World up to the times of Isaac Komnenos and the year of Christ 1057.***

<margin>Notes on the Chronicle of Eusebius.</margin>
"His writings cry out that he was an unlearned man," <note>original: "idiotam"</note> says Scaliger. He gathered the jumble of his history from many authors, whom he himself mentions in his Preface; among these are three to whom he owes almost everything. From the beginning of the world until Diocletian, he transcribed almost everything from the *Chronography* of George Syncellus; from Diocletian until Michael Curopalates, he compiled the *Chronicle* of Theophanes; from then until Isaac Komnenos (where the work ends), he transcribed almost everything word-for-word from the *History* of John Thracestes Scylitzes. Indeed, he seems to have borrowed from John, rather than John from him, because he himself mentioned the history of John the Lord High Steward <term>Protovestiarius: a high-ranking court official in the Byzantine palace</term> surnamed Thracestes in his own Preface. Leo Allatius gave the following judgment of him:

<margin>Discourse on the Georges and their Writings, p. 334.</margin>
> *He completed a work stitched together from various histories, not only in sentiment but word-for-word. If these were reclaimed by their original authors, he himself would remain naked, just like that little crow <note>A reference to Aesop's fable of the jackdaw who dressed in borrowed feathers to look grander than he was</note>. I do not know with what face <note>with what audacity</note> he sold what he copied as his own, so much so that you will find scarcely one or two sentences in so vast a volume of Cedrenus that are his own and legitimate; however, thanks must be given to him because he preserved for us, through his own theft, authors who are excellent and rare.*

<margin>On Greek Historians, Book 2, Chapter 26.</margin>
Regarding his *History*, the distinguished Vossius writes: "In Byzantine matters, he is a little more diligent than Zonaras; however, in those things that precede the Emperors of Constantinople, he yields to Zonaras, by whom he is also surpassed in style, as he is also by Nicetas, Gregoras, and others."

<margin>Excursus 2, ch. 17, p. 195. Miscellaneous Letters, 61, p. 466.</margin>
To the illustrious Casaubon, he is known as a writer of almost no judgment and most unskilled in ancient history; and no less to Justus Lipsius, he is "frequently a writer of old wives' tales, and either indifferent to or ignorant of the truth. Yet," he says, "let him be read with judgment, and he will provide something helpful."

Wilhelm Xylander first published this work of Cedrenus with notes in Greek and Latin at Basel, 1566, in folio; later, it appeared far more complete with the notes and observations of Xylander, Charles Fabrot, Jacques Goar, and a "mixed-barbarian" glossary <note>A glossary of medieval or non-classical Greek terms commonly found in Byzantine texts</note>, Paris, 1647, in folio.

<keywords>Alberic of Monte Cassino, George Cedrenus, Berengarius of Tours, Byzantine history, Monte Cassino, medieval historiography, plagiarism, Joseph Scaliger, Leo Allatius, ecclesiastical bibliography</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ecclesiastical writers from the mid-11th century, specifically the "Age of Hildebrand" (the era of Pope Gregory VII’s reforms). ### THE AGE OF HILDEBRAND

<margin>11th CENTURY from the Year 1057.</margin>
**ALPHANUS**, an Italian by birth as it seems, was first a student at the Monastery of Monte Cassino, then Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Benedict in Salerno. Finally, in the year 1057, he was made Archbishop of Salerno. In the year 1059, under Pope Nicholas II, he took part in the Synod of Benevento, where he signed his name in the second place immediately following Nicholas himself. He died in the year 1086, in the twenty-ninth year of his prelacy. He wrote very many works, mostly composed in verse, which Peter the Deacon enumerates in chapter 19: namely, *The Passion of Saint Christina and Hymns about her; on Saint Benedict; Verses on Saint Sabina; Saint Christina; Saint Peter the Apostle; In Praise of the Monks of Monte Cassino; On the Site, Construction, and Renovation of that same Monastery; On Saint Maurus; Hymns on Saint Matthew; On Saint Fortunatus; On Saint Nicholas; A Metrical Confession; On the Church of Saint John the Baptist at Monte Cassino; and finally, very many Epitaphs and other poems.* Ferdinando Ughelli published almost all of these at the end of Volume II of *Sacred Italy* <note>original: *Italia Sacra*, a massive 17th-century work on the history of Italian dioceses</note>, as witnessed by J. B. Marus in his notes on Peter the Deacon, page 38. Others were published by Prosper Martinenus in *Poems*, Volume III, Rome, 1589, in quarto. His *Verses in praise of Romuald, the Advocate of Salerno* and *Sigismund, a Monk of Monte Cassino* are preserved in the library of Monte Cassino in manuscript. *The Passion of the Twelve Holy Martyrs and Brothers of Benevento*, written in heroic meter, is found in Surius’s *Lives of the Saints* for September 1st. However, the aforementioned Marus, in the place cited, promises that he will publish a version that is much longer, perfect in all its rhythms, and corrected according to the reliability of the manuscripts; there he mentions four other small works by our Alphanus which no longer appear in the library at Monte Cassino. Finally, he corrects an error by Falco in his *Chronicle*, who attributed the aforementioned poems not to our Alphanus but to a younger Alphanus, also Archbishop of Salerno, who died in the year 1121.

<margin>1058.</margin>
**NICHOLAS II**, previously called Gerard, a Burgundian by nation, was designated Roman Pontiff by King Henry while already a very old man, following the death of Stephen IX. He was promoted from the Bishopric of Florence after the removal of Benedict <note>Benedict X, now considered an antipope</note>, who had usurped the priesthood relying only on the votes of the Clergy without the command of the king and the princes. Nicholas was declared Pontiff by the king in the year 1058, on the 9th day of September, but was actually enthroned at Rome on the 21st day of January in the year 1059, at which time he excommunicated the Antipape Benedict. Soon after, however, having become more merciful, he admitted him to lay communion <note>This means Benedict was allowed to receive the Eucharist as a common person, but was no longer recognized as a member of the clergy</note>. In the same year, at a Council held in Rome, he compelled Berengarius to a recantation <note>original: *Palinodia*; Berengarius had sparked controversy by denying the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist</note>. Furthermore, by a Synodal decree, he confirmed the right of the King of Germany, Henry, to elect Roman Pontiffs—a right received from his imperial predecessors—threatening all violators of the decree with excommunication and the most severe curses. In the same Synod, at the request of Peter Damian, he issued a Constitution against the marriage and concubinage of the Clergy. He died at Florence in the year 1061, on the 24th day of June. *Eight Letters* are extant in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume IX, page 1091.

<margin>1058.</margin>
**CONSTANTINE LICHUDES**, or Licudex, holding the dignity of *Protovestiarius* <note>A high-ranking Byzantine court official, literally the 'First Vestiary' or keeper of the imperial wardrobe</note>, was elevated to the Patriarchate of Constantinople after the death of Michael Cerularius in the year 1058 or the following year. He died in the year 1066. There exist, in Greek and Latin, *Two Synodal Decrees*: namely, concerning a slave guilty of a crime, and concerning a priest guilty of murder and deposed from office, found in *Greco-Roman Law*, book 4, page 264.

<margin>1059. * Anthology for the year 1083.</margin>
**MARIANUS**, called **THE SCOT** from his homeland (being born in Ireland in the year 1028), was a blood relative in a direct line to the Venerable Bede, as Matthew of Westminster notes *. In the year 1052, Marianus left the secular world and took the habit of a Monk. In the year 1058, he set out for Germany and settled in the Monastery of Saint Martin at Cologne for three years. In the year 1059, having set out for the Monastery of Fulda with Abbot Siegfried, he was ordained a Priest at Würzburg on the 13th of March, and having entered the Monastery of Fulda on the 14th of May, he spent ten years there as a recluse <note>An 'inclusus' was a monk who lived in solitary confinement within a cell for spiritual reasons</note>. In the year 1069, by order of the Archbishop of Mainz, he moved from his seclusion at Fulda to one at Mainz; he died there in the year of Christ 1086, at the age of 58, with a reputation for holiness and was buried in the Monastery of Saint Martin. There are some who wish to believe that before his death he traveled through Germany and taught mathematical disciplines at Regensburg in Bavaria, and that he interpreted the Holy Scriptures.

...desired. <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page.</note> He wrote a *Chronicle* from the beginning of the world to the year of Christ 1083, following Cassiodorus <note>a 6th-century Roman statesman and scholar</note> above all others. <margin>1059.</margin>
### OSMUNDUS
**OSMUNDUS**, Bishop of Astorga <note>original: *Asturicensis*, in Spain</note>, flourished in the year 1059. This is known because the wife of Eustace, Count of Boulogne, built a church in honor of the Blessed Virgin in the district of Lens; when relics were being sought from all over to adorn it, Osmund wrote a letter to Countess Ida regarding the *Hair of the Blessed Mary*, which can be found in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume I, page 287.

<margin>1060.</margin>
### METELLUS
**METELLUS**, a Benedictine monk of Tegernsee in Germany, flourished around the year 1060. He wrote several poems, namely the *Quirinalia* in praise of Saint Quirinus the Martyr in Horatian meters, as well as other *Eclogues* *. These are extant and were published by Canisius in the Appendix to Volume I, page 37.

<margin>1060.</margin>
### GAUFERIUS
**GAUFERIUS**, also called Benedict, a native of Salerno and a monk of Monte Cassino, flourished in the year 1060. He wrote *Homilies for Advent and the Nativity of the Lord; for Epiphany; Septuagesima; Palm Sunday; and the Lord's Supper <note>Maundy Thursday</note>; the Passion of Saint Lucius the Pope; the Life of Saint Secundinus* addressed to the Bishop of Troia; and various poems, namely *In Praise of the Psalter; On the Miracle of the One who Killed Himself*, etc. All of these are held in manuscript in the Library of Monte Cassino, Number 280, and in the possession of the distinguished gentleman * J. B. Marus, who promised he would eventually publish them.
<margin>* *Notes on Peter the Deacon*, page 52.</margin>

---

<margin>1061.</margin>
### ALEXANDER II.
**ALEXANDER II**, previously named Anselm, a native of Milan and son of Anselm, was Bishop of Lucca. In the year 1059, he was sent as a legate to the Milanese by Nicholas II along with Peter Damian. In the year 1061, he was elected Roman Pontiff and enthroned on the 30th of September. In the year 1063, he celebrated the Lateran Council of one hundred bishops, in which he issued canons against <term>Simony</term> <note>the buying or selling of church offices</note> and clerical concubinage. He himself was accused of simony by Cadalous the Antipope <note>a rival claimant to the Papacy</note>, who was Bishop of Parma. In the year 1064, at a council called at Mantua, Alexander pleaded the cause of his election before the bishops and cleared himself of the crime of simony by oath. Having returned to Rome, he eventually defeated Cadalous—who had been besieged for two whole years in the Mole of Hadrian <note>now known as the Castel Sant'Angelo</note>—and drove him from the city. In the year 1065, he convened two synods against the "heresy of the incestuous," which was being defended by legal experts. In the year 1071, he sent Peter, Bishop of Anagni, on an unsuccessful legation to Michael, the Duke and Emperor at Constantinople. He died on April 20, 1073. Forty-five of his letters and some fragments are extant in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume IX, page 1115.

<margin>1066.</margin>
### BERTHOLDUS
**BERTHOLDUS**, a German by nationality, a Priest of Constance and an Apostolic Penitentiary, flourished in the year 1066. He was a most desperate enemy of his prince, Henry IV, against whom he did not hesitate to draw both the sword and the pen. Devoted to the party of Gregory VII, he received the duty from the Pontiff to receive back into the bosom of the Church all those who defected from the Imperial to the Papal side. He even fought against the Emperor in the battle joined at Ostrostrada in the year 1086. In his *History*, he attacked Henry most viciously with lies and slanders, showing no regard for truth or shame. He died around the year 1100. He wrote a *History of his Time* from...

# THE AGE OF HILDEBRAND <note>This period, roughly the late 11th century, is named for Hildebrand, who became Pope Gregory VII and initiated significant church reforms.</note>

<header>The Eleventh Century.</header>

...from 1053 to the year 1100. He also added an appendix of eleven years—specifically from the year 1055 to 1066 inclusive—to the *Chronicle* of Hermann the Lame. <note>Hermannus Contractus, a famous 11th-century polymath and chronicler.</note> Both works were published by Christian Urstisius among the *Writers of German Affairs*, on pages 341 and 336. He also wrote several small works in support of Gregory VII, which were published by Jacob Gretser along with his *Defense of Cardinal Bellarmine* at Ingolstadt in 1609, in folio. Sebastian Tengnagel published his treatise on *Avoiding the Company of Excommunicated Persons* among other ancient monuments supporting Gregory VII at Ingolstadt in 1612, in quarto.

<margin>1066. 11th Century from the Year 1000.</margin> **GUITMUND**, first a monk of the Benedictine Order in the Monastery of Saint Leufroy in Normandy, was later appointed Archbishop of Aversa in Italy, and, as some believe, a Cardinal. Although his name does not appear in Louis Dattichy’s *History of the Cardinals*, he is nonetheless listed among the Cardinals on page 8 of the *Nomenclature of Cardinals*, which Louis Castaigner, Bishop of Poitiers, published under a pseudonym <note>literally "with his own name suppressed"</note> in *Paris, 1615*. He flourished around the year 1066 and died in the year 1080. His surviving writings include: *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist* in three books; *A Confession regarding the Holy Trinity, the Humanity of Christ, and the Truth of the Body and Blood of the Lord*; and an *Oration to William I, King of England*, delivered when he refused a bishopric. These can be found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVIII, page 440.

<margin>1066. Zonaras, Annals, Vol. 3, p. 218.</margin> **JOHN XIPHILINUS**, a native of Trebizond <note>modern Trabzon, Turkey</note>, was a man of no low status, having been counted among the leading Senators. However, having voluntarily abandoned all worldly things, he shaved his head and embraced the solitary life among the monasteries of Mount Olympus. There he lived for a long time devoted to religious exercises, until, upon the death of Constantine Lichoudes in the year 1066, he was promoted to the Patriarchal see of the city of Constantinople. He died in the year 1078. There exists, in Greek and Latin, his *Oration on the Cross, or for the Third Week of Lent*, in Gretser’s *On the Cross*, Volume II, page 1449. Also, *Two Decrees on Betrothals* in *Greco-Roman Law*, Book 3, page 211, and a *Decree on Prohibited Marriages* in the same work, Book 4, page 266. His *Homilies on the Sunday Gospels for the Whole Year* are also said to be held in manuscript in the Bavarian and Palatine libraries—the latter now transferred to the Vatican—though they have not yet been published.

<margin>
† Prolegomena to Photius's Library.
† At the year 1066.
|| Sacred Adversaria, ch. 151, § 7.
* Annals at the year 1066.
† History of Constantinople under Constantine Ducas.
</margin>
There is a common opinion held by nearly all learned men that the John Xiphilinus who reduced the *History* of Dio Cassius into an *Epitome* <note>an abridged version or summary</note> was our Patriarch of Constantinople. Andreas Schott \*, Baronius †, and his abridgers Spondanus \* and Bzovius † support this view with all their might <note>literally "with hands and feet"</note>; as do Luis de la Cerda ||, Philippe Briet \*, Christoph Besold †, and, what is even more surprising, the most learned Gerardus Vossius in *On the Greek Historians*, Book 2, chapter 26. Indeed, even Henri Estienne, who edited Xiphilinus and corrected previous editions, hardly dares to oppose this popular opinion. Yet, despite these many great names, it is more certain than certain that John the Abridger was not the Patriarch, but rather his nephew. As a witness, I bring forward Xiphilinus himself, whose words—which as far as I know have been noticed by no one before, though I have cited them elsewhere—I will not find it burdensome to transcribe here. In his *Life of Augustus Caesar*, giving the reason why he says the events he recounts there are very remote from his own memory, he has these words to say about himself:

> I say this not as Dio of Prusa, who lived in the times of the Emperors Severus and Alexander, but as John Xiphilinus, the nephew <note>literally "the brother's son"</note> of John the Patriarch, who composed this abridgment during the time of the Emperor Michael Ducas. <note>original Greek: Λέγω δὲ τοῦτο ἐπεὶ οὐχ ὁ Δίων ὁ Προυσαεὺς, ὃς ἐπὶ τοῦ Σεβήρου καὶ Ἀλεξάνδρου αὐτοκρατόρων ἐγένετο, ἀλλ’ ὡς Ἰωάννης ὁ Ξιφιλῖνος ὁ ἀδελφόπαις ὢν Ἰωάννου τοῦ πατριάρχου, ἐπὶ τοῦ Μιχαὴλ αὐτοκράτορος τοῦ Δούκα τὴν ἐπιτομὴν ταύτην συνεταξάμην.</note>

In the year 1068, he seized the Archbishopric of Reims for himself through evil arts, and held it for several years with poor conduct. Certainly, he was accused of simoniacal intrusion <note>obtaining a church office through bribery</note>, the plundering of his church's furnishings, and the mistreatment of the clergy and abbeys...

**SIEGFRIED**, Archbishop of Mainz, rose to prominence in the year 1069, when he assisted King Henry, who was attempting to divorce his wife Bertha, with his voice and authority at the Synod of Mainz. In the year 1064, he had been the leader of seven thousand Germans on an ill-fated journey to Jerusalem and the holy places. In 1074, he convoked a Synod at Erfurt, and another the following year at Mainz, in order to either separate the priests of his diocese from their wives or remove them from the ministry of the altar <note>This refers to the controversial enforcement of clerical celibacy during the Gregorian Reform era.</note>. However, in both Synods, he was defeated by the arguments of the priests and, terrified by their threats, he surrendered and abandoned the undertaking. In 1076, he was excommunicated by Gregory VII for the loyalty he showed to his Emperor, Henry. Yet in the following year, he himself defected from his loyalty and crowned Rudolf, Duke of Swabia, with the imperial crown at Mainz. He died in the year 1084. There exist *Three Letters to Pope Alexander II, Council Collection Vol. IX, p. 1200, 1205, 1233, and a fourth to Hildebrand <note>Pope Gregory VII</note>, ibid. p. 1233.*

**LANFRANC**, an Italian by nationality and a native of Pavia, was educated from an early age in the higher branches of literature. Leaving his homeland while still a youth, he came to Normandy and became a monk in the Monastery of Bec; to relieve his poverty, he taught logic <term>dialectica</term> for a salary. Called by Duke William <note>William the Conqueror</note> to the sacred service of the Court, he was named Prior of his monastery and soon after, Abbot. Finally, in the year 1070, he was elevated by William (now King of England) to the dignity of the Archbishopric of Canterbury, with the consent not only of the Canterbury clergy but also of the court nobles and all the people. He had a great controversy with Thomas, Archbishop of York, concerning the "precedence" (as they call it) and prerogative of his see. In 1071, he set out for Rome to seek the pallium <note>A woolen vestment given by the Pope to archbishops as a symbol of their shared authority.</note> and, meeting Thomas there, he obtained a judgment from the Pope that confirmed the primary rank for the Church of Canterbury. Since Thomas contended that this primacy should not extend to Lanfranc’s successors, a general Council was held in England in 1072, where Lanfranc thoroughly crushed Thomas's pride and ensured the rights of his church were fortified by a synodal decree. In 1087, overcome by the deceits and promises of William Rufus, he placed the royal crown upon him—against what was right and lawful <note>Because Rufus's elder brother, Robert Curthose, was still alive and the rightful heir.</note>—though he later found Rufus to be ungrateful. He died on June 4, 1088.

<margin>1072.</margin>
**CONSTANTINE**, an African by nation and from a Carthaginian house, was a Physician and Philosopher; he flourished in the year 1072. He traveled through various places in the East, and staying especially in Babylon <note>The author likely refers to Baghdad, which was often called Babylon in this period.</note>, he cultivated his genius in all the disciplines of the Chaldeans, Arabs, Persians, and Saracens. Departing from Babylon, he went to India; from there he sought Ethiopia, and finally Egypt. Bringing back with him the spoils and treasures of every nation, and having spent nearly forty years in this manner learning the studies and languages of various peoples, he returned home. There, having narrowly escaped treachery, he withdrew to the Monastery of Monte Cassino; there he took the habit of a monk and, at a great age, fell asleep in the Lord. He partly wrote and partly translated various works from the books of ancient physicians, namely: *On the Recognition and Cure of Diseases* in seven books; *On Melancholy* in two books; *On the Distinction between the Soul and the Spirit* in one book; and many other things published at *Basel, 1536, in folio.* Others were published in the same place in 1539; however, since these relate very little to our purpose <note>The author's "purpose" is the history of the Church and theology, rather than medicine.</note>, we shall refrain from reviewing them. <meta>This page transitions from the general list of 11th-century figures to a focused and highly critical biography of Pope Gregory VII, also known as Hildebrand, whose reign defined the ecclesiastical and political conflicts of the era.</meta>

# THE AGE OF HILDEBRAND

<header>The Hildebrandine Century.</header>

<margin>11th CENTURY, from the Year 1000.</margin>
**GREGORY VII**, formerly called **Hildebrand**, was raised to the Pontificate in the year 1073 and consecrated on the 30th of June. For approximately twenty years prior, he had already claimed a power that was almost greater than the Pope’s, governing everything in the Roman See according to his own whim. He was a man of vast and fiercely bold spirit, swelling with vanity and pride—a true fury of his age and a most insolent tyrant of the Christian world. He dreamed of nothing but scepters and crowns, the infinite power of the "keys," <note>The "Power of the Keys" refers to the spiritual authority granted to St. Peter, which the Popes claimed gave them power over both heaven and earth.</note> and the royal rights of Peter. It was his greatest wish to see kings and princes subjected to these; indeed, he was the first of all Roman Pontiffs who dared to attempt such a thing. 

From this arose so many thunderbolts of anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church.</note> and dire threats struck against the heads of Emperors; so many shameful slaughters and murders of kin; and such great and horrific outrages that past ages have wept for them, and the present age either blushes for them or stands in wonder. Content to touch upon a few of these in summary, I shall run through the man's chief deeds in the briefest order. 

In the year 1073, he threatened Philip I, King of France, with anathema and the loss of his kingdom, citing the crime of Simony. <note>Simony is the act of buying or selling church offices or roles.</note> In 1074, having held frequent Synods in Italy, he forbade the clergy from marriage—or, as his followers did not blush to call it, "concubinage." Meanwhile, he himself was suspected and widely accused of an actual concubinage committed with the Countess Matilda. In the same year, he excommunicated **Robert Guiscard**, the Norman prince and Duke of Apulia and Calabria, for injuries inflicted upon the royal rights of St. Peter, and he attacked him with arms. He also sent letters to **Solomon**, King of Hungary, sharply rebuking him because he had dared to receive the kingdom of Hungary as a fief from the German Emperor, whereas Gregory claimed it was the property of the Roman Church and the peculiar domain of St. Peter. 

In 1075, he summoned the Emperor **Henry IV** to Rome to plead his case because Henry had received and favored those excommunicated by the Pope; when Henry refused, Gregory stirred up the Saxons to rebellion. For this, Gregory was ordered to be deposed from the Pontifical see at the Synod of Worms. However, the following year, having gathered a Council in Rome, Gregory excommunicated Emperor Henry, decreed that he should be stripped of his kingdom, and forbade his subjects from obeying him under pain of anathema. Eventually, Henry was forced to come to Rome and prostrate himself as a suppliant at the Pope's feet; only then was Gregory—with great difficulty—persuaded to release him from the anathema, though he refused to restore him to his kingdom. 

In 1077, Gregory sent an imperial crown to **Rudolf**, Duke of Swabia; and when Henry prepared for vengeance, Gregory subjected him to anathema a second time. In 1084, he was chased from Rome by Henry, and he died in exile at Salerno the following year, on the 25th of May. He was buried there in the Church of St. Matthew.

These few things we have selected from so many that could be said about this most celebrated leader of the Roman Church. Although recent Papal writers study how to skillfully smear his life and character with deceptive colors, he is depicted quite differently—to say nothing of others—by **Cardinal Benno**, a contemporary of Gregory, whom the curious may consult. He is also depicted quite differently by the **Senate and People of Rome**, and by the Bishops of nearly all **Italy, France, and Germany** who gathered at Brixia, a city of Bavaria, on the 25th of June. I will select a few of their words:

<margin>* Found in Aventinus, *Annals of Bavaria*, book 5, p. 569.</margin>
> "He is a deserting monk," says the decree* of the Senate, "he adulterates holy Philosophy with new dogmas; he tears apart the harmony of the College; he mingles the sacred with the profane and the divine with the human, polluting both alike. He is at once the Witness, the Judge, the Accuser, and the Enemy. He separates husbands from wives; he prefers harlots to modest spouses, and debauchery, incest, and adultery to chaste marriage. He incites the commoners against the Priests and the rabble against the Bishops. He teaches that no one is rightly initiated into the priesthood unless they have begged for it from him or purchased it from his gold-seeking merchants. In a little senate of petty women, he treats the most sacred mysteries of religion; he looses and binds the law of the Supreme Deity as if he were God himself."

<margin>* Ibid. p. 579.</margin>
In the Synodal decree,* he is called "a false Monk, a Sorcerer, a Diviner, an interpreter of dreams and omens, and one who thinks poorly of the Christian religion," to pass over infinite other charges. 

There exist **ten books of his Letters** (Council Records, Vol. X, p. 6, with a double Appendix on pages 306 and 410). The **Exposition on the Seven Penitential Psalms**, which is circulated under the name of Gregory the Great, is ascribed by some to our Gregory; we mentioned this in passing above under Gregory the Great.

The **Exposition on Matthew**, written while he was still Hildebrand, exists in manuscript in the Library of the Most Reverend Archbishop at Lambeth, from which the famous **Allix** produced a fragment in his *Preface to John of Paris*, p. 7.

# THE AGE OF HILDEBRAND

<header>The Hildebrandine Century.</header>

<margin>11th CENTURY, from the Year 1073.</margin>
**WILLIAM**, Abbot of Metz, a close associate of Gregory VII, whom he congratulated on his election to the Pontificate in a letter sent in the year 1073. He was also elected Abbot of the Monastery of St. Remigius at Rheims; however, being a truly modest man, he refused to take up that office. There exist *Seven Letters along with an Oration* to be recited on the Feast of St. Augustine, found in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume I, page 247.

<margin>1076. See Ingulf’s History, p. 75.</margin>
**INGULF**, an Englishman by nation, a Londoner by home, born in the year 1030 to a father who served in the Court of King Edward <note>Edward the Confessor, the last king of the House of Wessex.</note>. He himself was dear to Queen Edith for his learning. He first applied himself diligently to the liberal arts <note>The "good letters" or classical education.</note> at the Westminster School, and then at the University of Oxford, taking Aristotle as his guide in Philosophy and Tully <note>The common name for Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note> in Rhetoric. In the year 1051, he came to the attention of William, Duke of Normandy, who had crossed over to England to confer with King Edward. He accompanied William back to Normandy and was appointed as his Secretary <note>original: "ab Epistolis ascitus"</note>, rising to the highest power, if not dignity, at Court—so much so that he directed everything according to his will. In 1064, fearing the envy born from such great favor from the prince, he joined Siegfried, Duke of Mainz, and other Germans on a journey to the Holy Places <note>A pilgrimage to Jerusalem.</note>. Returning home after a thousand dangers on the road, he withdrew to the Monastery of Fontenelle to lead a monastic life, soon becoming Prior of the Monastery. In 1076, summoned to England by King William <note>William the Conqueror</note>, he was placed in charge of the Monastery of Crowland. After some years, through earnest prayers, he obtained royal mercy for Wulfketel, his predecessor who had been deposed by the king in 1075 and exiled to Glastonbury, and saw to it that he was brought back to Crowland with great honor. He himself was always among the first in the favor of King William and Archbishop Lanfranc, obtaining many benefits and privileges for his monastery; he restored its fallen state and rebuilt the structures that had been destroyed by fire. He died in the year 1109. He wrote the *History of the Monastery of Crowland* from the year 664 to approximately 1091. This History was published by the most noble Savile among the *Five English Writers* (London, 1596, folio), and later among the *Writers of English Affairs* (Oxford, 1684, folio), which is by far the better and more complete edition, with gaps filled and the entire later part added, which was missing in Savile's edition.

<margin>1077.</margin>
<margin>* On the Emendation of Time.</margin>
<margin>* Adversaria, book 49, ch. 4.</margin>
**LAMBERT**, called *of Aschaffenburg* from his homeland, entered the monastic life in the year 1058 in the Monastery of Hersfeld under Abbot Meginher, taking the cowl on the 15th of March <note>original: "idibus Martiis"</note>. At the end of that same year, he was ordained a Priest by Luitpold, Archbishop of Mainz, and immediately undertook a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Having completed this, he returned to his fellow monks at Hersfeld near the end of the following year. He was writing in the year 1077; it is not certain when he died. He wrote a *History from the creation of the world until the year 1077*, in which he runs through events before the year 1050 in chronological order, and very briefly; but thereafter he narrates German affairs up to 1077 in great detail. Concerning his style, the judgment of the great Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar of history and chronology.</note> should be added. *“Indeed,” he says, “I marvel that in such a barbarous age there was such purity in a man’s speech, and such skill in the calculation of time, that he could make the chronologists of our own time feel some shame, provided they had any sense of these matters.”* Barthius <note>Caspar Barthius, a noted German philologist.</note> agrees with Scaliger: *“No writer,” he says, “among the ancients recorded the affairs of Germany more elegantly.”* This History appeared separately in *Tübingen* (1533, octavo), in Pistorius’s collection (*Frankfurt*, 1583, folio), and among other German writers (*Strasbourg*, 1609, folio).

<margin>1077.</margin>
**THEOPHYLACT**, a native of Constantinople and Archbishop of Ohrid, the primary Church of the Bulgarians. He was truly assigned a harsh province, the miseries and difficulties of which he frequently laments in his letters. He was still among the living in the year 1077, and had perhaps been Archbishop for several years by then.

It focuses on their ecclesiastical roles, their writings, and their relationships with the political powers of England and Germany.</summary>

### WORKS.

**Commentaries on the Four Gospels**, drawn mostly from the works of Chrysostom, as are his other commentaries. Published in Latin at *Antwerp*, 1564, octavo. In Greek at *Rome*, 1542, 1568. In Greek and Latin with various readings at *Paris*, 1631, folio.

**Commentaries on the Acts of the Apostles**, Greek and Latin, together with certain *Orations* of the Holy Fathers, *Cologne*, 1568.

**Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul**, Latin, *Rome*, 1469; *Antwerp*, 1564, octavo; *Cologne*, 1531; *Paris*, 1552. In Greek and Latin, edited by Augustine Lindsell, Bishop of Peterborough, *London*, 1636, folio.

**Commentaries on the Four Minor Prophets**, namely *Habakkuk, Jonah, Nahum, and Hosea*, Latin, *Paris*, 1549, octavo. The complete commentaries of Theophylact on the *Twelve Minor Prophets* are said to exist in Greek in the Augsburg Library.

**Seventy-Five Letters.** Published in Greek with notes by Joannes Meursius at *Leiden*, 1617, quarto. In Latin, translated by Vincent Mariner of Valencia, *Cologne*, 1622; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVIII.

**Oration on the adoration of the venerable Cross** in the middle of the fasting season <note>Lent</note>, Greek and Latin, in Gretser’s *On the Cross*, Volume II, page 1499.

**Royal Instruction to Constantine Porphyrogenitus**, son of Michael Doukas <note>A "Mirror for Princes" written by Theophylact for the young Byzantine emperor</note>, Greek and Latin, edited by Pierre Poussines, *Paris*, 1651, quarto.

**A Fragment** (uncertain whether by our Theophylact or another) regarding laughter and shouting at the festivals of the Saints, and regarding Nicephorus the Confessor; Latin, in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XVIII.

**Arguments against the Latins on the Procession of the Holy Spirit** <note>Addressing the "Filioque" controversy regarding the Creed</note>, found in John Beccus, *Oration 1 on the Union of the Churches*, in *Orthodox Greece*, Volume I, page 215. A **Discourse** of Theophylact with a certain person regarding the accusations of the Latins, and an **Oration** to Emperor Alexios Komnenos, are reported by Oudin in his *Supplement*, page 345, to exist in Greek manuscript in the Bavarian Library.

All of Theophylact’s **Commentaries** were published in Latin at *Paris*, 1554; *Basel*, 1570; and elsewhere.

<margin>* Dissertation on the Pselli, p. 17.</margin>
**NICETAS**, surnamed **SERRON**, a Deacon and Master <note>original: "Magister," a title for a teacher or official</note> of the Great Church of Constantinople, later Archbishop of Heraclea. He was a contemporary of Theophylact, whose ninth letter is addressed to him. He flourished in the year 1077. Leo Allatius reveals * that he is wrongly confused with Nicetas David the Paphlagonian in certain manuscript codices. He wrote a **Commentary on the Orations of Nazianzen** <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, published in Latin among the works of Nazianzen. He also compiled from various expositions of the Greek Fathers a **Catena on Job** <note>A "Catena" or "chain" is a biblical commentary made of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers strung together</note>, which was published in Latin by Paolo Comitolo (though it seems it should rather be attributed to Olympiodorus), *Venice*, 1587, quarto; and in Greek and Latin by Patrick Young, *London*, 1637, folio. The same author seems to have written the *Catenas* that exist for Luke, Matthew, etc. His **Commentary** on Nazianzen’s Four-Line Verses, One-Line Verses, and Epigrams appeared in Greek under the name of Nicetas David the Paphlagonian, *Venice*, 1563, quarto.

<margin>1077.</margin>
**HUGO**, Bishop of Die; he flourished in the year 1077, when he was appointed legate by Gregory VII to investigate the case of the Bishop of Dol in Brittany, and he presided over the Synod of Langres, in which he ensured that the investiture of the clergy by laymen <note>The practice of kings or lords appointing bishops, which the Church was then fighting to reclaim</note> was condemned. In the year 1080, he presided over the Council of Lyons. In that same year, having been made Archbishop of Lyons, he celebrated the Councils of Avignon and Meaux. In the year 1087, he was excommunicated by Victor III, but was fully restored by Urban II and honored with a legation. In the year 1094, he excommunicated King Philip <note>Philip I of France</note> due to his unlawful marriage, at the Council of Ostia <note>Though the text says Ostia, this event is more famously associated with the Council of Autun</note>. He died after the year 1099. There exist **Two Letters to Gregory VII**, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume X, page 364; and **Two others to Countess Matilda** <note>Matilda of Tuscany, the powerful supporter of the Papacy during the Investiture Controversy</note>, ibid. page 414.

<margin>
11th CENTURY.
Year 1000.
</margin>
...whoever may finally be hidden under this name <note>original: "quisquis tandem sub hoc nomine lateat"; referring to the author of the *Micrologus*, usually identified as Bernold of Constance</note>, he certainly lived after the year 1080. Indeed, he wrote after the death of Gregory VII, following the year 1085. Furthermore, if he is the same person as the author of the *Life of Charlemagne*, he lived nearly a full century later, as a contemporary of Emperor Frederick I. He wrote a book called *Micrologus* <note>meaning "Short Explanation"</note>, titled *On Ecclesiastical Observations, or on the Proper Celebration of the Mass*. This work is available in an edition from *Venice, 1572, octavo*; among the *Writers on Divine Offices, Paris, 1610, folio*; and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XVIII, page 469*. His *Life of Charlemagne*, comprised of three books, exists in many manuscript libraries; the author testifies in his prologue that he wrote the *Micrologus*. Bollandus published that prologue on the 28th of January.

<margin>
1080.
* Under the year 1067.
</margin>
**ADAM**, called the Master, a native of Meissen and a Canon of the Church of Bremen from the year 1077, flourished in the year 1080. He was a man, as Philippe Briet rightly notes, "Most sincere, and one than whom the Church can produce hardly any more truthful historian." While still a young man, he wrote for Liemar, Archbishop of Bremen, *Four Books of Ecclesiastical History, especially of Bremen*. In these, he discusses the propagation of the Christian religion through the Dioceses of Bremen and Hamburg, and thus through the entire North, from the arrival of Willehad to Archbishop Liemar—that is, from the times of Charlemagne to the Emperor Henry IV. To these he added, as an appendix, a small book *On the Situation of Denmark and the nature, customs, and religion of the remaining regions beyond Denmark*. This history, together with an anonymous history of the Kings of Denmark and another anonymous history of the Archbishops of Bremen, was published by Erpold Lindenbrog at *Leiden, 1595, quarto*. The same was recently released with notes at *Helmstedt, 1670, quarto*. It had previously appeared at *Copenhagen, 1579, quarto*, though lacking the appendix.

<margin>
1081.
</margin>
**JOHN SKYLITZES**, called by the title **CUROPALATES** <term>Curopalates: A high-ranking Byzantine court title, originally the "guardian of the palace"</term>, was a Thracian by birth, or originating from Asia Minor near the Aegean Sea. He held the dignity of Protovestiary <note>head of the imperial wardrobe</note>, then Great Drungary of the Watch <note>a high military and judicial official</note>, and finally Curopalates. He flourished around the year 1081. He wrote a *History of Eastern Affairs* from the death of Emperor Nicephorus Phocas to the deposition of Nicephorus Botaniates, or from the year of Christ 811 (around the time the historian Theophanes ended his work) to the year 1081. He wrote the latter part of the history, covering twenty-four years, many years after the first part was published. Because of this, the earlier part—up to the year 1057—was transcribed in its entirety into the compilation of George Kedrenos (Cedrenus), with very few omissions. The remaining portion of the history, which proceeds from 1057 to 1081, appeared in Greek and Latin with the notes of Fabrot and Goar, joined to the work of Cedrenus, *Paris, 1648, folio*. The complete *History* appeared in Latin, translated by Giambattista Gabio, *Venice, 1670, folio*. There also exists his *Suggestion* <note>a formal proposal or legal advice</note> to Emperor Alexios Komnenos regarding the removal of a certain ambiguity in a recently promulgated edict on betrothals, found in Leunclavius’s *Greek-Roman Law, Volume I, page 132*.

<margin>
1084.
</margin>
**NICHOLAS**, called the Grammarian, was appointed Patriarch of Constantinople from the monastic life in the year 1084—or as Baronius has it, 1089. He was a man not unlearned in letters, says Zonaras, yet not exceptionally skilled. He died in 1111, or by Baronius's calculation, 1117. There exist, in Greek and Latin, two of his *Synodal Decrees regarding the marriages of a paternal or maternal uncle* in Leunclavius’s *Greek-Roman Law, book 3, page 215*; another *On the Payment of Canons, book 4, page 269*; and a very lengthy *Synodal Letter* to Emperor Alexios Komnenos proving from the sacred Canons and laws that it is not right for bishoprics to be taken away from their metropolitan sees, *ibid. page 271*.

<margin>
1085.
</margin>
**BENNO**, German by nationality, was an Archpriest and Cardinal of the Roman Church. He was appointed by the Antipope Clement III to replace those deposed in the synodal sentence against Gregory VII by the Council of Brixen in 1080; he flourished in 1085. He adhered most constantly to the party of Clement (previously called Guibert of Ravenna) and was a most bitter enemy to Gregory VII. For this reason, he is overwhelmed with "wagon-loads" of insults and calumnies by Baronius and other pro-papal writers. In 1098, he signed the Council of Rome among the other Cardinals.
