<margin>11th CENTURY. from the Year 1000.</margin>
What happened to him from then on is not clear. He wrote *Two Books on the Life and Deeds of Pope Hildebrand* <note>Hildebrand was the birth name of Pope Gregory VII</note>. These are extant in the works of Orthuinus Gratius in the *Bundle of Things to be Sought*, and in Illyricus’s *Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth*, page 220. They were published separately at *Frankfurt an der Oder* in 1581; and finally among the *Various Anti-Gregorian Minor Works* edited by Melchior Goldast, *Hanau, 1611, quarto, page 1.*

<margin>1086.</margin>
**VICTOR III**, a native of Benevento and the only son of the Prince of Benevento, was born around the year 1027. While he lived a secular life, he was called *Dauferius*; later, having taken the name *Desiderius*, he entered the monastic life in the Monastery of Monte Cassino and was elected Abbot in the year 1056 at the age of 30. In the following year, he was appointed <term>Apocrisiarius</term> <note>a high-ranking diplomatic representative or legate</note> to the Emperor Michael Stratioticus by Pope Stephen X. However, the Pope was removed from the living shortly thereafter, and Desiderius returned to Monte Cassino from his journey. In the year 1059, he was ordained a Priest and named a Cardinal by Nicholas II. In the year 1084, he honorably received Gregory VII into his monastery as the Pope was fleeing Rome; and in the following year, Gregory, on his deathbed, designated Desiderius as his successor. Although he was elected Pope by the Roman clergy on May 24, 1086, he could not be persuaded by any arguments to take up the burden of the Papacy; instead, withdrawing to Monte Cassino, he remained hidden there for nearly an entire year. Finally, in the following year at the Council of Capua, he yielded after being overcome by the earnest prayers of the bishops, and he was ordained on May 9. In the month of August, he held a Synod at Benevento, where he struck the Antipope Guibert with an <term>anathema</term> <note>a formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note>, commanded that fellowship with excommunicated persons be avoided, and decreed that bishops and abbots who received <term>investitures</term> <note>the act of a lay person, like a King, appointing someone to a church office</note> from laymen should be deposed. Falling ill in the month of September, he ordered himself to be carried to Monte Cassino, where he died on the 16th day before the Calends of October <note>September 16</note>, having been poisoned by venom placed in the chalice during the sacred mysteries <note>during the celebration of the Mass</note>. 

Following the example of Gregory the Great, he wrote *Four Books of Dialogues on the Miracles performed by St. Benedict and other Monks of Monte Cassino*. In these, you will find more than a few things so absurd, fabulous, and unworthy of the majesty and gravity of the Christian religion that, regardless of the spirit in which they were written, they will provoke those of a discerning nose <note>meaning readers with a sharp or critical sense of judgment</note>. Certainly, in these works, you will rightfully find both the judgment of the writer and the reliability of the events described to be lacking. The end of the third book and the entire fourth book (for both the author himself and Peter the Deacon testify that Victor wrote that many) were missing from the Vatican autograph; it is not clear whether they are still hidden elsewhere, nor is the matter of such great importance that we should investigate too curiously. J. B. Marus was the first to extract these three books of Dialogues from a Vatican manuscript and publish them at *Rome* with added notes. They were later published with the same notes at *Paris, 1666, octavo*; then in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Century IV, part 2, page 425*; in Henschenius under March 21, and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XVIII, page 837*. His speech to the bishops held at the Synod of Benevento is found in Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicle of Monte Cassino, book 3, chapter 71*, and in Baronius under the year 1087.

<margin>1086.</margin>
**BRUNO**, a German by nationality and from a house in Cologne, was born to parents of some distinction. He was first made a Canon of Reims and a master of the schools; then, in the year 1086, he withdrew to the wilderness of the Chartreuse <note>Carthusia</note>, where he first established the Order of Carthusian Monks and presided over the institution. Many writers report a story about a certain famous Parisian Doctor, long renowned for his learning and upright life, who, while his corpse lay on a bier, revived from the dead. Sitting up in his coffin, he cried out the first time that he was "accused by the just judgment of God," the next day that he was "judged," and on the third day that he was "damned by the just judgment of God." The story goes that Bruno, who was present with others, was terrified by this occasion and fled into the wilderness. This story smells entirely of a foul fable, even though it once held a place in the Roman Breviary <note>the book of daily prayers for the Catholic clergy</note>. Indeed, the celebrated Launoy, in a singular booklet titled *Dissertation on the True Cause of St. Bruno's Withdrawal into the Wilderness*, refuted the entire stage-setting of this fable with learned and candid reasoning and a full weight of evidence, as is his custom. But let us return to our Bruno. After seven years in this duty, he was summoned to Rome in 1092 by Pope Urban II, who had once used him as a teacher, so that Bruno might serve as his advisor in Church business. However, soon weary of the disturbances and the manners of the court, he left the Roman court in 1095 and rejected the Archbishopric of Reggio, which Urban of... <note>original catchword: "ob-", likely continuing "offered" or "obtained"</note>

**BRUNO**, a Lombard by birth, was born in the village of Solero among the Insubres <note>a region in Lombardy, northern Italy</note> from the illustrious Asti family, the son of Andrew and Villa. He spent his early years of piety and study in the Monastery of Asti; from there, passing into Tuscany, he was chosen among the Canons of Siena. From here he came to Rome, and in the presence of Gregory VII, he debated against Berengarius in the Roman Synod in the year 1079. Soon after, he was designated Bishop of Segni by the Pope; and although he strongly and actively resisted the Pontiff in this matter, he was circumvented by Gregory through a certain "pious deception" and forced to take up the burden imposed on him. He was especially prominent around the year 1087. In 1092, he was present at the Council of Tours. After many years spent in the Bishopric, overcome by a desire for solitude, he fled to Monte Cassino in 1104. The people of Segni, having offered earnest prayers to Pope Paschal, sought their Bishop back. Compelled by the authority of the Pope, he returned to his see. In the same year, he was sent as a legate by the Pontiff, first to Roger, Count of Apulia, and then with Bohemond, Prince of Antioch, into Gaul, where he celebrated the Council of Tours. In 1107, having returned to Monte Cassino, he was elected Abbot of that same monastery, with Pope Paschal approving the election and offering him this praise: that he was most worthy to have the government of the Christian commonwealth handed to him after the Pope's death. In 1108, he accompanied Paschal to the Synod of Benevento. In 1111, by order of the Pope, he resigned from the office of Abbot; and having returned to his people at Segni, he finally fell asleep in the Lord in the year 1125, on the day before the Kalends of September <note>August 31</note>, in the 44th year of his episcopate.

### WORKS.

Commentaries on the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>.
A Commentary on Job.
A Commentary on the Psalter.
A Commentary on the Song of Songs.
A Commentary on the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>.

**URBAN II**, previously named Otto (or Odo), was French by birth, from the town of Châtillon in the Archdiocese of Reims. He served as a Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia. In the year 1083, he was sent as a legate by Gregory VII to Emperor Henry IV, who was then active in Italy; he was captured by the Emperor and placed in custody. In 1084, he promulgated throughout Germany the sentence of excommunication <note>original: "anathematis"</note> against Henry and his supporters, which had recently been renewed in a Roman Synod. In 1085, after holding the Council of Quedlinburg in Germany—composed of "Hildebrandine" bishops <note>referring to those loyal to the reforms of Gregory VII, also known as Hildebrand</note>—he condemned Wezilo, the archbishop-elect of Mainz, for heresy. Wezilo had taught that a prince excommunicated by the Pope should not lose his kingdom, but only be excluded from communion. 

In 1087, he was designated as successor by the dying Victor III, and having been elected by the Cardinals, he was created Roman Pontiff at Terracina on March 12, 1088. In 1089, he excommunicated King Henry and all those who showed him obedience. In 1090, he held the Council of Melfi against married clergy. In 1091, having held the Council of Benevento, he subjected the Antipope Guibert to excommunication. In 1093, he excommunicated Emperor Henry again and persuaded Henry's son, Conrad, to take up rebel arms against his father. 

In 1095, at the Council of Piacenza, he condemned the Berengarians <note>followers of Berengar of Tours regarding the Eucharist</note>, the Guibertines <note>followers of the Antipope</note>, and clergy who were Simoniacs <note>those who bought church offices</note> or married. In the same year, having traveled to France, he held the Council of Clermont, in which he excommunicated King Philip of France and raised a vast army of Christians to fight against the infidels who held the Holy Places <note>The call for the First Crusade</note>. In 1096, at the Council of Tours, he absolved the repentant King Philip. In 1097, he summoned the Council of Bari to unite the Greeks with the Latins in faith; there, he gave Anselm of Canterbury the role of debating against the Greeks regarding the "Procession of the Holy Spirit" <note>The *Filioque* controversy regarding whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son</note>. In 1099, at a Roman Synod, he again excommunicated the Antipope Guibert and clergy who kept concubines. He died that same year, on July 29. 

Fifty-nine of his **Letters** are extant in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume X, page 422, and four others on page 1839. Two **Sermons** delivered at the Council of Clermont are in the same volume, page 511; and two other **Letters** are found in Baluze's *Miscellany*, Volume II, page 177.

---

<margin>
1090.
</margin>
**NICHOLAS**, Metropolitan of Methone, appears to have flourished around the year 1090, although others refer him to the end of the following century; on this matter, I establish nothing as certain. He wrote a **Small Book on the Body and Blood of Christ** against those who say that the consecrated bread and wine are not the body and blood of the Lord; however, the Papal editors themselves warn that there are things in it which must be read with caution. It is extant in Greek and Latin in Ducæus’s *Supplement* <note>original: "Auctuario Duceano"</note>, Volume II, page 272. **Three Treatises** by the same author regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit against the Latins exist in manuscript in the Vatican Library; Leo Allatius testifies to having read them in his work *On the Consent of the Churches*, book 2.

# THE HILDEBRANDINE CENTURY

### 11th Century, from approximately Section 10, § 2.
Concerning the third work, however, he <note>Referring to the author or a cited critic</note> seems to doubt whether it should be attributed to a certain younger Nicholas of Methone.

<margin>
The Year 
1092.
</margin>

**IVO**, or **YVO**, a Frenchman by birth and a native of the region of Beauvais, was born to Hugo and Hiltemburga. He was a student of Lanfranc <note>Lanfranc was the influential teacher at Bec and later Archbishop of Canterbury under William the Conqueror</note> while the latter was still the Prior of Bec. Ivo served as the Abbot of Saint Quentin in Beauvais, and finally, in the year 1092, he was ordained Bishop of Chartres by Pope Urban II. In the following year, he was accused of high treason by the bishops in the Court of Étampes because he had accepted his ordination from the Pope; however, by interposing an appeal to the Roman See, he escaped their censure. In the year 1098, when he sharply rebuked King Philip—who had dismissed his lawful wife Bertha and brought in a mistress <note>This mistress was Bertrada de Montfort; the scandal caused a major rift between the French crown and the Church</note>—he suffered many injuries from the king, was fined his property, and cast into prison. Soon, however, he was freed through the intercession of Hoël, the Bishop of Le Mans. In the year 1104, having been ordered by the Roman Pontiff to excommunicate Rotrou, the Count of Perche, he steadfastly refused, contending that no one should be excommunicated without their cause first being heard. He died in the year 1115, on the 23rd day of December.

->WORKS.<-

**The Book of Decrees** <note>original: "Decretorum liber"; also known as the *Decretum*</note>, distributed into 17 parts, the greatest portion of which was taken from the collection of Burchard of Worms. It was published in *Basel, 1499, in quarto; Louvain, 1550;* and along with his Letters in *1561, in folio.*

**Panormia** <note>The title comes from the Greek for "all-law" or "universal law"</note>, which is a kind of summary of ecclesiastical decrees, divided into 8 parts. I am well aware that there are many who deny this *Panormia* to our Ivo and attribute it to a certain Hugh of Châlons; among others, Gerard von Mastricht campaigns vigorously for this opinion in his *Ecclesiastical Law, numbers 267, 268, 269.* However, Étienne Baluze claims this work for Ivo and contends that a very ancient manuscript codex from Saint Victor in Paris is much older than Hugh of Châlons. Indeed, he argues at length in his preface to Antonio Agustín’s *On the Amendment of Gratian*, number 21, etc., that the *Panormia* was composed before the *Book of Decrees*. This *Panormia* is usually printed together with the *Book of Decrees*.

**287 Letters.** These were published with the notes of François Juret and Jean Baptiste Souchet in *Paris, 1585, in quarto, and 1610, in octavo.* Among these, the last letter, which is addressed to Haymeric under the title *A Little Book on the Body of the Lord*, is usually read in the *Libraries of the Fathers*.

**22 Sermons** on the Sacraments and Offices of the Church, and especially on the *Festivals* throughout the year. These are found among the *Writers on Divine Offices, Cologne, 1568, in folio, and 1610.*

**A Short Chronicle** concerning the Kings of the Franks from Pharamond down to King Philip of France and King William Rufus of England. For the entries concerning King Henry of England were added by another hand.

Jean Baptiste Souchet collected all these works of Ivo into one volume and published a corrected edition in *Paris, 1647, in folio.*

**A Letter to Bernerius**, Abbot of Bonneval, and certain other pieces, published by D'Achery in his *Appendix to the Works of Guibert, pages 664, 668.*

In the Monastery of Saint-Amand <note>original: "Elnonensi"</note> is held a manuscript of Ivo of Chartres titled *A Treatise on those excommunicated, who are not to be avoided unless they have been publicly renounced*; also a little book on the *Sacrament of the Dedication and Building of a Church, and on the Ordination and Dignity of Holy Orders*, as noted by Antoon Sanders in the *Manuscript Library of Belgium, part 1, pages 50, 51.* These latter small works are also held in the Monastery of Lobbes <note>original: "Lætiensi"</note>, as noted by the same Sanders in Part 2, page 28, where there are also books by the same Ivo on the *Sacraments, on the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, on the Harmony of the Old and New Testaments, and on the Meanings of Sacerdotal Vestments*. Whether these are part of the *Decretal Work* or a part of all his works, let those who have had the chance to inspect them tell us.

<margin>* On Latin History, book 2, chapter 47.</margin> Furthermore, that extensive **Chronicle** from Ninus, King of the Assyrians, until Emperor Louis the Pious, which Gerhard Johann Vossius <note>original: "Vossius"</note> (in the place cited) and others claim exists in manuscript under Ivo’s name, was published in a mutilated form under his name by Freher.

# THE HILDEBRANDINE CENTURY

### 11th Century, from the year 1091.

1611 <note>This likely refers to a numbered entry or bibliography reference in the source text</note>. This entry is credited to Hugh, a monk of Fleury; as we shall note in more detail below. <margin>11th Century, from the year 1091.</margin>

**PETER**, a Deacon and <term>Chartophylax</term> <note>The official archivist and record-keeper of the patriarchate</note> of the Great Church of Constantinople, flourished in the year 1092. His *Brief responses to questions on various cases* are extant in Greek and Latin in the *Graeco-Roman Law*, Book 6, page 395. <margin>1092.</margin>

**ANSELM**, a Burgundian by birth, was born in Aosta in the Alps. His parents were of noble descent: his father, Gundulph, and his mother, Hemmemburga. Drawn by the fame of Lanfranc <note>Lanfranc was a celebrated scholar and Anselm's predecessor as Archbishop of Canterbury</note>, he hurried to the Monastery of Bec and entered the Benedictine order at the age of twenty-seven. After Lanfranc, he was first appointed Prior, and then, fifteen years later, he was made Abbot of Bec, succeeding him in both offices. After another fifteen years spent in this duty, he was summoned to England by Hugh, the Earl of Chester. While he was attending to certain business with King William Rufus <note>William II of England</note>, who was then ill, Anselm provided him with sound advice, especially regarding the many vacant episcopal seats. He himself was designated Bishop among others, and although he resisted vehemently for a long time, he was appointed to the see of Canterbury by the King and consecrated by the bishops who were present on December 4, 1093. 

From the very start of his <term>pontificate</term> <note>In this context, his term as Archbishop</note>, frequent and massive disputes were stirred up against him by the excessively angry and fierce King. First, they argued over receiving the <term>Pallium</term> <note>A white wool vestment sent by the Pope to an archbishop as a sign of their authority and bond with Rome</note>; Anselm sought it from Pope Urban II. William was unwilling, being more inclined toward the side of Guibert <note>Guibert of Ravenna, the Antipope known as Clement III</note>. Although a truce was eventually reached and the Pallium was received at Canterbury in 1095, a sharper conflict broke out shortly after. Anselm sharply rebuked the King, who was acting with unrestrained lust, overturning temples, devastating churches, and committing outrages against both God and men. The King ordered Anselm to swear an oath that he would never appeal to the Pope. Neither gave way to the other. 

In 1097, Anselm went into exile in foreign lands and withdrew to Lyon. From there, he was summoned to Rome by Pope Urban and received with great honor; at the Council of Bari, he debated against the Greeks. He even used his prayers to prevent the Pope from carrying out a decree of excommunication against King William. In 1100, he was recalled to England by King Henry I and returned. Upon his return, other controversies immediately met him regarding the swearing of <term>homage</term> to the King and the ordaining of bishops whom Henry and his brother William had "invested" with the ring and staff <note>The Investiture Controversy: a power struggle over whether kings or the Pope had the right to appoint and install bishops</note>. Henry commanded both to be done; Anselm refused. 

In 1102, a General Council was held in London where he condemned <term>lay investiture</term> <note>The appointment of church officials by secular rulers</note> and clerical marriage. In 1103, at the King's request, he set out for Rome to consult the Pope, to whom the full knowledge of the matter had been entrusted by both parties. Since Pope Paschal II rendered a judgment in favor of Anselm, the latter, fearing to return to England, stayed in Lyon for sixteen months. In 1107, Henry was reconciled with Anselm at the request of his sister Adela, the Countess of Blois. With peace established on both sides, the King gave up the investiture of bishops and abbots. The Archbishop then ordained the prelates who had previously been invested by the King. Having returned to Canterbury, he thereafter held his see in peace and worked strenuously to remove clerical marriage from the English Church. He died in 1109, on April 21, at the age of 76, in the 19th year of his archbishopric. <margin>1093. *Antiquities of Britain*, p. 115. *Life of Anselm* by Eadmer, in Surius, April 21, p. 207. Baronius, Vol. 11, from the year 1093.</margin>

## SPURIOUS WORKS. <note>original: "OPERA SUPPOSITITIA." These are works once attributed to Anselm but now believed to be by other authors.</note>

The Book *on Similitudes commonly attributed to Blessed Anselm.* It belongs to Eadmer.

# THE HILDEBRANDINE CENTURY.

<note>original: "Seculum Hildebrandinum." This refers to the era of Gregorian Reform influenced by Pope Gregory VII.</note>

D'Achery brought eight other *Letters* to light in the *Spicilegium, Volume IX.* <note>Luc d'Achery was a 17th-century Benedictine scholar known for publishing previously unedited medieval documents.</note>

<margin>11th CENTURY, from the Year 1094.</margin>
**LAMBERT**, a Frenchman by nationality, as I believe, was the Bishop-elect of Arras; but since Rainald, the Archbishop of Reims, refused to ordain him, Lambert set out for Rome and was consecrated by the hands of Pope Urban II himself on March 19, 1094. <note>original: "XIV. Cal. April." using the Roman calendar system.</note> Nevertheless, Rainald did not cease to cause him trouble until 1095, when the Council of Clermont was held. There, the privilege which the Pope had recently granted to the Church of Arras was read aloud and soon praised and confirmed by the entire Council. Two *Letters* of Lambert survive in the *Collection of Councils, Volume X, page 468,* where many other letters to him and about him are also found. Another letter by him to Pope Paschal II, given in the year 1105 concerning the absolution of King Philip of France, is found in the same volume on page 742. <note>King Philip I had been excommunicated for his controversial marriage to Bertrade de Montfort.</note>

<margin>1095.</margin>
**RAYMOND D'AGUILERS**, <note>original: "Raimundus de Ageles"</note> a Canon of Puy and chaplain to the Count of Toulouse (who was likewise the Bishop of Puy), flourished in the year 1095, when he followed the aforementioned Count as he led an army to the Holy Land. While he was attached to this journey, he was promoted to holy orders; and having entered Palestine, he saw with his own eyes (by his own testimony) the Lord’s Spear <note>The Holy Lance, believed to be the spear that pierced the side of Jesus.</note> while it was being dug out of the earth: indeed, he even carried it in his own hands during the Siege of Antioch. At the urging of Pons of Balazuc, he wrote the *History of Jerusalem*, in which he follows the deeds accomplished over five years, chiefly under the leadership of the Count of Toulouse—namely, from the time the Christian army entered Slavonia until the victory reported over the Emir of Babylon. <note>The "Emir of Babylon" refers to the Fatimid vizier of Egypt, as "Babylon" was a common medieval name for Cairo.</note> We can learn how much sincere faith he put into this work from his own solemn oath: <margin>* Page 163.</margin> *“I pray, therefore,”* he says, *“and I entreat all who are to hear these things, that they believe these events were so. For if I have added anything through zeal or out of hatred for anyone, beyond what I believed and saw, may God add to me all the plagues of hell and erase me from the book of life.”* This *History* is found in the Bongars collection, *The Deeds of God through the Franks, Volume I, page 139.*

<margin>1096.</margin>
**GOSCELIN**, <note>original: "Gotselinus"</note> a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, first at Saint-Bertin in Artois and then at Saint Augustine's in Canterbury, flourished in the year 1096. He wrote the *Life of Saint Augustine*, the first Archbishop of Canterbury, in a two-part work: one a history, the other a shorter version. D'Achery published the shorter version in the Appendix to the Works of Lanfranc without the author's name (Paris, 1648). Mabillon published the more extensive work in the *Benedictine Centuries, Volume I, page 498.* He also wrote *Two Books on the Translation of Saint Augustine* addressed to Anselm; these are held as manuscripts by Mabillon. <note>"Translation" here refers to the ceremonial moving of a saint's relics from one place to another.</note>

<margin>1097.
* At the year 1088.
† Letter 279.</margin>
**HILDEBERT OF LAVARDIN**, a monk of Cluny and later a disciple of Berengar, was the Bishop of Le Mans from the year 1097 (or according to others, after 1099). Baronius* is clearly unjust to him, for he attributes to Hildebert those things which Ivo of Chartres† wrote concerning the unbridled sexual immorality of a certain Archdeacon named Adalbert. Around the year 1107, Hildebert was harassed by the injuries of King Henry I of England (who was also Duke of Normandy) and traveled to Rome to pray for support from Pope Paschal II. Having returned home, he was cast into prison; he was accused of various crimes, with King Henry demanding that he prove his innocence through an ordeal by fire. However, being warned by Ivo, he refused to undergo such a condition. After 22 years (or 29 according to others), he was transferred to the Archbishopric of Tours, holding that see for about six years, and died in the year 1136 (or according to others, 1132).

<margin>1097.</margin>
**BALDERIC**, Belgian by nationality, was the Secretary and Chaplain to Gerard I (who died in the year 1049), then to Blessed Liedbert, and from the year 1076, to Gerard II, the Bishops of Cambrai and Arras. Thereafter, he was a Canon and Cantor of the Church of Thérouanne. At last, he was created Bishop of Noyon and Tournai in the year 1097. He died in the city of Thérouanne on May 31, 1112. <note>original: "Prid. Cal. Junii," the day before the Calends of June.</note> He wrote a *History or Chronicle of the Churches of Cambrai and Arras* in three books, which Georgius Colvenerius published under the title *The Chronicle of Cambrai* at *Douai, 1615.* Vossius reports in *On Latin Historians, book 2, chapter 47,* that a *Chronicle of the Church of Thérouanne* written by the same man exists in manuscript in the Benedictine Monastery at Le Mans.

<margin>1099.</margin>
**PASCHAL II**, previously called Rainerius or Ragingerius, Tuscan by nationality, from the province of Flaminia and the town of Bieda, the son of Crescentius and Alfatia. He was educated in the Monastery of Cluny until the twentieth year of his age: then, having set out for Rome, he was created Priest and Cardinal with the title of *Saint Clement* by Pope Gregory. He was afterwards named Abbot of the Monastery of Saints Lawrence and Stephen. After the death of Urban in the year 1099, he was elevated to the Roman Pontificate, ordained on August 14th. In the year 1101, he excommunicated Gerard, the Archbishop of York, and other Legates of King Henry of England, because they had craftily concealed his decrees regarding the rejection of lay investiture. <note>term: <term>lay investiture</term> (the practice of secular rulers, like kings, appointing bishops and abbots by presenting them with the symbols of their spiritual office).</note> In the year 1102, having held a general Council at Rome, he struck Emperor Henry [IV] with anathema on account of his plundering and sacrilege. In the year 1106, having set out for Cisalpine Gaul, he celebrated the Synod of Guastalla, in which he condemned lay investitures and restored the state of the Church, which had been disturbed by long-lasting war. In the following year, having made a journey into France, he held another Council against lay investitures at Troyes. In the year 1111, when he had dared to bring the princes of Italy into his allegiance, and stubbornly denied the privilege of sacred burial to the remains of the deceased Emperor Henry IV, he was made a captive by Henry V, who arrived in Rome for the sake of receiving the imperial crown, and was led away to Sutri. # THE HILDEBRANDINE CENTURY.

<margin>
11th CENTURY, from the Year 1000.
</margin>
He <note>Pope Paschal II, whose biography began on the previous page.</note> renounced the rights of investiture <note>The "Investiture Controversy" was a power struggle between the Church and the State over who had the right to appoint and install (invest) bishops and abbots with the symbols of their office.</note> to Henry <note>Holy Roman Emperor Henry V.</note> by a solemn oath and anointed him Emperor. After Henry's departure, a Lateran Council was held in the year 1112; claiming that force had been used against him <note>Paschal had been taken prisoner by Henry V prior to the agreement.</note>, he revoked his concession. When the Council was reconvened in 1116, he performed public penance for having surrendered the investitures to the Emperor; and, condemning the privilege granted to him, he simultaneously excommunicated him <note>original: "anathematizavit." This is the formal act of casting someone out of the Church.</note>. Henry pursued the treacherous Pope with arms and drove him from the city in the year 1117. But the Pope, having raised a massive army of Normans <note>The Normans of Southern Italy were frequent military allies and protectors of the Papacy against the German Emperors.</note>, acted vigorously, capturing many towns in Campania; he was so certain of victory that he haughtily denied absolution to Henry when he humbly requested it. He died in the year 1118 on the 18th day of January. There remain *107 Letters* and several *Fragments of the Decrees of Councils* in Volume X, page 622; six other *Letters* are in Étienne Baluze's *Miscellanea*, Volume II; and a *Letter to Norigaud, Bishop of Autun* <note>original: "Epistola ad Norigaudum Episcopum Augustodunensem."</note> is in the same author's *Appendix to Regino*, page 651. <note>Regino of Prüm was a medieval chronicler whose work was often supplemented by later historians.</note>

<header>12TH CENTURY.</header>

# THE WALDENSIAN CENTURY.

## Overview of the Century.

<margin>12th CENTURY, from the Year 1100.</margin>
After the death of Henry IV in the year 1106, his son Henry V succeeded him. In 1111, he came to Rome and received the crown from the hand of Pope Paschal II. The Pope granted him the right of investiture <note>The power of a monarch to appoint bishops and abbots by presenting them with the symbols of their spiritual office.</note> and confirmed the rights of the German Electors to choose the Emperor. Nevertheless, in a Synod held at Rome the following year, the Pope declared these concessions void; this was done even more solemnly in 1116. This gave rise to a new harvest of troubles, and in 1117 Henry was subjected to anathema <note>A formal curse by the Church, effectively excommunicating the Emperor.</note>. Finally, in 1122, weary of the injuries and hardships, Henry renounced the right of investiture at the Synod of Worms before the legates sent from the First Lateran Council, and returned his obedience to the Pope. Throughout this entire century, several expeditions <note>The Crusades.</note> were launched into the Holy Land by almost the entire West, with varying success and ultimately an unhappy outcome.

In the year 1163, Thomas of Canterbury <note>Thomas Becket, the Archbishop of Canterbury.</note> stirred up great unrest in England and other territories of his King against Henry II. When he could be swayed by no counsel and continued to obstinately challenge the King's authority and the customs of the realm in an utterly intolerable manner, he was banished from the kingdom by common decree. Returning to his see after six years, he was slaughtered by assassins at the very altar in the year 1170. Shortly after, in 1173, he was enrolled in the list of martyrs and saints by Alexander III.

Around the year 1160, or as others say, 1170, the *Waldensians, Albigensians, Patarines, and the Poor Men of Lyon*—or by whatever other name they might be called—began to become famous, having arisen on this occasion: It happened in Lyon, amidst a large crowd of citizens, that one of them was seized by a sudden death. The others were terrified, but especially Peter Waldo, a man originating from the town of Waldo <note>Often identified as Vaud or Vaux.</note> located in the March of France. He immediately sold all his goods and distributed the money to the poor. As an immense multitude flocked to him, being somewhat literate, he explained the New Testament to them in the common language and delivered sound doctrine on faith and morals. 

As the number of disciples grew immensely, this sect prevailed everywhere. Reinerius <note>Reinerius Sachonus (c. 1200–1259), a former Waldensian who became a Dominican friar and Grand Inquisitor.</note> himself admits that there were those who claimed the sect had lasted since the time of Pope Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (reigned 314–335). The Waldensians claimed the Church became corrupt when it accepted the "Donation of Constantine" during his reign.</note>, or rather from the time of the Apostles themselves, and that there was no land in which it had not taken deep root. How sound and how harmless for the most part their dogmas, life, and morals were, is clearly evident from the accounts of Enea Silvio <note>Enea Silvio Piccolomini, who later became Pope Pius II (1405–1464).</note> in his *History of Bohemia*, chapter 35, and from Reinerius Sachonus, who was older than Enea and himself a Grand Inquisitor. Reinerius flourished in the year 1254 and wrote a book against the Waldensians, where in the fifth chapter he lists their errors and "blasphemies," as he calls them, one by one. Whether they deserve such an execrable name, let an impartial judge of facts first read and then decide. 

Meanwhile, in his fourth chapter, Reinerius admits that this *sect has a great appearance of piety, because they live justly before men, believe all things well concerning God, and hold all the articles contained in the Creed; they only blaspheme the Roman Church and the Clergy.* This was the stain of the whole evil; this was the source and spring of all the storms against them: namely, that they rejected the accepted dogmas of the Roman Church and sharply rebuked its corrupt rites, superstitions, and tyranny. For this reason, the Prelates, Nobles, Kings, and almost all of G... <note>original: "G..." likely refers to Gallia (France) or Germania (Germany).</note>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the late 12th century, specifically the aftermath of the conflict between Henry II and Thomas Becket, before pivoting to the suppression of the Waldensians and the proliferation of new religious and military orders.</meta>

<page-num>633</page-num>
<header>THE WALDENSIAN CENTURY.</header>

England rushed to arms. In the year 1179, under Alexander III, in the Third Lateran Council, they <note>The Waldensians, a medieval spiritual movement often seen as precursors to the Reformation.</note> were expressly condemned, along with 
<margin>12TH CENTURY, from the Year 1100.</margin>
*their supporters and protectors* (I refer here to the very words of the Canon, *Canon XXVII*): *Those subjected to excommunication are prohibited under anathema <note>A formal curse or ban by the Church.</note> from presuming to keep or cherish them in their houses or on their lands, or from carrying on trade with them.* Thereafter, oppressed everywhere by force and arms, they were forced to spread out into various regions. During this time, Scholastic theology <note>A method of critical thought which dominated teaching in the medieval universities, combining religious dogma with Aristotelian logic.</note> delivered in a new method, and the profession of Canon Law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority.</note> were introduced into the Church, to be propagated more widely in the following century. Around the year 1120, the Premonstratensian Order <note>Also known as the "White Canons," founded for a life of preaching and service.</note> laid its foundations in the Diocese of Laon under the Rule of Saint Augustine, by the author Saint Norbert; in 1126, the Order of Grandmont was founded by Stephen of Auvergne. In the year 1117, the knights of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem <note>The Knights Hospitaller, who originally cared for sick pilgrims.</note> began to observe their institution more strictly and to organize themselves to more successfully take up arms for the Christian faith against the infidels. In the year 1181, the Carmelite Order had its beginning, under the author Americus, Patriarch of Antioch, who settled certain monks on Mount Carmel so that they might be safe from the assaults of the Saracens. At the close of the century, around the year 1198, the Teutonic Order, which had begun a little earlier, was confirmed by Celestine III—to say nothing of the Orders of Saint James, Calatrava, the Holy Trinity, and others.

### WRITERS.

<margin>
12th CENTURY, from the Year 1100.
</margin>
<margin>
1101.
</margin>
GILBERT, or Gislebert, surnamed Crispin, a Norman by birth as it appears, lived the monastic life in the Abbey of Bec <note>A highly influential Benedictine monastery in Normandy, known as a center of 11th-century learning.</note> together with Anselm; having been instructed in letters by him, he emerged exceptionally learned in both divine and secular knowledge. He was famous at the beginning of this century, around the year 1101. After completing his studies under Anselm, he made a pilgrimage to Rome, and during his return, he engaged in a celebrated dispute concerning the truth of the Christian religion with a certain Jew of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiacensi"</note>, a man of great name among his own people. Having finally been made Abbot of Westminster in England, he committed his dispute to writing, and having reduced it to the form of a dialogue, he dedicated it to Anselm (at whose urging he had undertaken this labor), adding to it the title, *On the Faith of the Church against the Jews* <note>original: "De Fide Ecclesiæ contra Judæos"</note>. He died in the year 1117, or as the Manuscript History of the Abbots of Westminster holds (as noted by the Illustrious Ussher), in the year 1114. He was buried in the southern part of the Cloister at the feet of Abbot Vitalis, honored with this Epitaph:

->*Here lies the distinguished father, of noble birth, a virgin and an elder,*<-
->*Gilbert, you lie here—light, way, and leader for your own.*<-
->*You were gentle, just, prudent, brave, and moderate;*<-
->*Learned in the quadrivium, and no less in the trivium.* <note>The seven liberal arts: the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy).</note><-
->*Thus adorned, on the sixth day of December,*<-
->*You return your spirit to heaven, and your bones to the earth.*<-

Besides the book *against the Jews* (plainly a different work from that which is usually found among the works of Augustine under the title, *The Altercation of the Synagogue and the Church*, with which it is not infrequently confused), the Prologue of which was published by Joannes Picardus at *Cologne, 1612, in the notes to Book 2, Letter 16 of Anselm*, and the whole work by Gabriel Gerberon *among the works of Saint Anselm, Paris, 1675, page 512*; besides that book, I say, there exist manuscripts of his *Homilies on the Song of Solomon* in the Library of St. Peter's at Cambridge; likewise on the *Prologues of Saint Jerome over the Bible*, in the same place. Also *Against the sins of thought, word, and deed*, in the private library of Walter Cope. Other small works of his are mentioned by Bale <note>John Bale, an English historian and controversialist.</note> (*Century 2, chapter 63*) and Pits (*at the year 1117*); whether these still lie hidden somewhere is entirely unknown to me. As for what they hold regarding a *Book of Letters*, that seems to have arisen from the fact that in the Manuscript Codex of the Letters of Saint Anselm in the Cottonian Library, there is a single, and quite brief, letter from Gilbert to Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, which begins, *To Anselm, by the grace of God, of the English*; however, this belongs to Gilbert, Bishop of Limerick <note>original: "Lunicensis"</note>, to whom also belongs the *Little Book on the State of the Church*, which those same authors attribute to our Gilbert.

<margin>
1101.
</margin>
LEO, a Campanian by birth, perhaps called Marsicanus from his homeland <note>The Marsi were a people of central Italy.</note>, was first a monk and Librarian of the Abbey of Monte Cassino, then created a Cardinal Deacon of the Roman Church by Pope Paschal II in the year 1101. In the year 1111, when Pope Paschal was captured by Emperor Henry V and given into custody, Leo himself escaped from Rome in a disguised habit along with John, Bishop of Tusculum, traveled through Italy, and implored the people to take up arms to avenge the injury inflicted upon the Pope. He died on the 12th day of May, but in what year is entirely hidden, though certainly after the year 1115, in which he subscribed to a Bull of Paschal II. He wrote the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Cassino in three books, from the time of Saint Benedict up to Abbot Desiderius*, who was later elected Roman Pontiff and called Victor III. This was published.
This Chronicle was published separately at *Venice, 1513*; together with the History of Aimoin at *Paris, 1602*; with the notes of Lauretus at Naples, 1616, in quarto; and with the annotations of Agostino della Noce at *Paris, 1668, in folio*. Perhaps other small works of his still lie in the shadows, namely: *Sermons for Easter, and for the Nativity, the History of Pilgrims, and the Life of Saint...*

There was also another Leo around this time, a monk of Monte Cassino <note>The famous Benedictine mother-house in Italy.</note> and created a Cardinal Deacon of the Roman Church, as some say, in the year 1105 by Paschal II, or as others say, by Urban II. ### GUIBERT, or Gilbert, of the French nation, a Norman by birth, of noble origin, brother of William of Grandmesnil; first a monk of Flavigny, then Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Mary of Nogent in the district of Laon; he was prominent in the year 1101. He died on August 1st, 1124.

*A Treatise on how a Sermon should be composed.* <note>original: "Tractatus quomodo Sermo fieri debeat"</note>
*Ten books of Moralia on Job; one book on Amos;* and *one book on the Lamentations of Jeremiah.*

In composing this history, he used, by his own admission, a laborious elegance of words, quite different from that which he employed in his other short works. *His own Life, or three books of Monodies.* <note>One of the first significant autobiographies of the Middle Ages.</note>
The works of Guibert reviewed here were collected, extracted from manuscripts, and first published with his own notes, observations, and many additions by Luc d'Achery, *Paris, 1651, in folio.*
*A lengthy Sermon on that passage: "Wisdom conquers malice,"* which is usually included among the works of Bernard, is claimed for Guibert by himself in *His Life, book 1, chapter 16.*
Casimir Oudin, in his *Supplement, page 388,* reports that he saw manuscripts of *Guibert's Commentaries on the Prophet Obadiah, on Jonah, on Micah (two books), on Zechariah (three books), on Joel, on Nahum, on Habakkuk, and on Zephaniah* in the libraries of Val-Clair and Igny of the Cistercian Order.
Guibert himself provides evidence that *he also wrote Expositions on Genesis* in a *Letter to Lisiard, Bishop of Soissons, prefixed to the History of Jerusalem*; however, whether these survive today is not clear.

<margin>1101.</margin>
### ROBERT, of the French nation, a monk of Saint-Remi in the Diocese of Rheims, of the Order of Saint Benedict. He was prominent in the year 1101; he was present at the Council of Clermont in the year 1095, at which time he joined the first expedition to the Holy Land. Having returned, at the command of Abbot Bernard, he composed *nine books of the History of Jerusalem* (or as others count them, *eight books*), in which he narrates the deeds of the Franks in the East from the year 1095 until the victory reported over the Admiral <note>original: "Ammiravizo," likely referring to the Vizier of the Fatimids at the Battle of Ascalon.</note> around the year 1099. He himself modestly enough excuses his style as unpolished in the Preface of the work. A very corrupt edition of this history was produced in *Basel, 1533*; and finally it was published among the *German Writers of Reuber, page 217*, and in the *Deeds of God through the Franks, Volume I, page 30.*

### HUGH, formerly a monk of Verdun and later Abbot of Flavigny in the Duchy of Burgundy; he was prominent in the year 1101. He wrote the *Verdun Chronicle* <note>original: "Chronicon Virdunense"</note> divided into two parts: the first from the birth of Christ up to the year 1002, and the second from the year 1002 to 1102. Philippe Labbe <note>A prolific 17th-century Jesuit editor and bibliographer.</note> calls this work an incomparable treasure, especially for the history of the eleventh century; he published it from the author's own original manuscript preserved in the Library of the Jesuits of Clermont in *New Collection of Manuscripts, Volume 1, page 75.* In the meantime, he deliberately excluded several common and useless fragments from the first part that had been copied from elsewhere, which, he says, "no sensible and industrious researcher of Church History will ever rightly miss."

At last, having been forced to resign the Abbey of Saint Trudo and go into exile, he retired to the Monastery of Saint Peter in Ghent, where he died on the 7th of the Calends of May <note>April 25th</note> in the year 1107.

<margin>1101.</margin>
### SIGEBERT, apparently a Gallo-Brabantine <note>From the border region of modern France and Belgium.</note> by birth and a monk of Gembloux; he was prominent in the year 1101. While still in his youth, he opened a school at the Monastery of Saint Vincent among the people of Metz, and he imbued the monks and clergy who came to him with the finest literature. Later, he returned to his own Gembloux and devoted himself chiefly to writing books. When very grave disputes were raging everywhere between Emperor Henry IV and his son Henry V, and Popes Gregory VII and his successors Urban II and Paschal, our Sigebert constantly defended the cause of the Henries. He stood manfully on the side of the Emperor against the unjust and violent efforts of the Roman Pontiff; indeed, he openly condemned the decrees of the Roman court regarding the prohibition of clerical marriage <note>Sigebert was a rare medieval voice opposing the mandatory celibacy enforced during the Gregorian Reforms.</note>. Consequently, he was marked by the sharp censorship of Baronius, Bellarmine, and others—or rather, he was loaded down with wagonloads of their insults. Sigebert died on the 3rd of the Nones of October <note>October 5th</note> in the year 1113. Regarding him, Francis Sweert says in his *Belgian Library, page 674*: "When he had spent many years among his own people in a religious and pious old age, he returned his soul to his Creator. Would that that age had produced many such men: certainly we would not have such a fragmented history of those times."

### PUBLISHED WORKS.

**A Chronicle** from the year 381 (where Jerome’s account ends) up to the year 1112; it was published among the *German Writers* in Frankfurt, 1583, folio edition, page 477. At last, after all other editions, it was revised according to the authority of a manuscript codex and purged of the trifles of Geoffrey of Monmouth <note>original: "Galfridi Monumentensis quisquiliis repurgatum." Geoffrey of Monmouth was a British chronicler often accused by later historians of inventing legends, such as those of King Arthur.</note> by Aubert Miræus, Antwerp, 1608. Although Miræus boasts that his edition is the only genuine one and free from nonsense, there are nonetheless those who accuse it of being corrupt and distorted. Others continued Sigebert’s *Chronicle*, such as Anselm of Gembloux, etc.; see these figures in their respective places.

**A Book on Ecclesiastical Writers**, joined with other writers of this kind, with notes by Suffridus Petrus, Cologne, 1580, octavo; later published with the commentaries of Miræus in his *Ecclesiastical Library*, Antwerp, 1639, folio.

**A Letter on behalf of the Churches of Liège and Cambrai** against the Letter of Pope Paschal. This is found in Melchior Goldast’s "Anti-Gregorian" collection, page 188, Hanau, 1611. <note>This refers to the Investiture Controversy, where Sigebert defended the rights of the Holy Roman Emperor against the claims of the Papacy.</note>
*The Life of Sigebert, King of the Franks*, found in Laurentius Surius, February 1st.
*The Life of Saint Guibert the Confessor, founder of the Monastery of Gembloux*, in Surius, May 23rd.
*The Life of Saint Maclovius* <note>Saint Malo.</note>. This is found in Surius, November 15th. *The Life of Saint Theodard* formerly joined to this seems to have been lost.

---

### UNPUBLISHED WORKS.

**A Sermon in praise of Saint Lucy**, preserved as a manuscript at Gembloux, according to the testimony of Franciscus Sweertius in the location cited above.
**The Passion of the Thebans** <note>The story of the martyrdom of the Theban Legion.</note> written in verse in three books, located in the Monastery of Gembloux.
**The Life of Saint Lambert**, as well as a record of his *Translation* <note>The ceremonial movement of a saint's relics.</note>, are said to survive today in manuscript.
**On the Fast of the Four Seasons** <note>The Ember Days, which are traditional quarterly days of fasting and prayer in the Western Church.</note> addressed to the people of Liège; Sweertius testifies that this exists in manuscript. Sigebert himself lists other works written by him at the end of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he discusses his own works with precision; these either lie suppressed in darkness or have perished entirely. These are: *The Life of Bishop Theodoric* and a record of his *translation*; *The Passion of Saint Lucy* in verse; *An Apology for the Prophecy of Saint Lucy*; *The Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux*; *A Response to the Letter of Pope Hildebrand* <note>Pope Gregory VII.</note>, which he wrote against the Pope's slandering of royal power; *An Apology to Emperor Henry* against those who slander the masses of married priests; and *Ecclesiastes*, described literally, allegorically, and mythologically in heroic meter.

---

### ANSELM, Scholar and Dean of the Church of Laon;

<margin>1103.</margin>
He flourished around the year 1103. A man of great reputation among his peers, he had many disciples committed to his care, and among these was Peter Abelard—who, however, testifies that he found the man to be far inferior to his fame.
<margin>* History of his Calamities, ch. 3, p. 7.</margin>
> "I approached this old man," Abelard says, "to whom long usage, rather than genius or memory, had gained him a name. If anyone approached him to knock at his door for a question on some uncertainty, they returned even more uncertain. He was indeed wonderful in the eyes of his listeners, but a nobody in the sight of those who questioned him. He possessed a wonderful facility with words, but his sense was contemptible and void of reason. When he lit a fire, he filled his house with smoke rather than illuminating it with light. His tree seemed entirely conspicuous with leaves to those looking from afar, but to those drawing near and looking more closely, it was found to be fruitless."

Having gathered opinions from the writings of the Fathers from here and there, he illustrated the entire Old and New Testament with interlinear and marginal glosses. This **Interlinear Gloss** <note>A famous 12th-century biblical commentary where explanations were written between the lines of the text.</note> exists and has been published frequently together with the additions of Nicholas of Lyra and others, for example, at Lyon in 1528, Antwerp in 1634, etc. Furthermore, the **Commentaries on Matthew**, **Readings or Explanations** on various places in the Gospels, and **Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul, the Apocalypse, and the Song of Songs**, were published under the name of Anselm of Canterbury at Cologne in 1612. Very many manuscript codices attribute these to our Anselm of Laon, although there are some who claim those works for William of Paris, and others for Herveus the Monk of Dol.

**WALTER**, perhaps a Frenchman by birth and a relative of Robert, the Provost of Lille, was made Bishop of Maguelone and an Apostolic legate in the year 1103. He died in the year 1129. <margin>
1105.
</margin>

**PHILIP THE SOLITARY**, so named perhaps from his monastic life, was a Greek by nation, though it is not clear who he was or where he came from. He flourished in the year 1105, in which he composed his *Dioptra* <note>original: "Dioptram," meaning 'The Mirror'; a work of spiritual reflection.</note>. Indeed, he wrote the work called *Dioptra*, or the *Rule of Christian Affairs*, to his companion Callinicus, in four books or sermons in which the soul and the body engage in a dispute. It is believed that Michael Psellus <note>A famous 11th-century Byzantine scholar and historian.</note> illustrated it with added notes and a preface. It was published in Latin from the translation of Jacobus Pontanus with the Preface and Notes of Psellus at Ingolstadt in 1604, in quarto; and thereafter in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXI, page 553.

<margin>
1105.
</margin>

**ELNOTH**, whether of Danish or English origin is not entirely certain, but he surely spent the greater part of his life in Denmark, where he stayed for twenty-four years; he was a monk of Saint Augustine of Canterbury. He flourished in the year 1105. He wrote the *Life and Passion of Saint Canute, King of Denmark*, first edited by Arnold Huitfeld at Copenhagen in 1602, and then with the notes of Johannes Meursius at the same location in 1631, in quarto.

<margin>
1105.
</margin>

**ODO**, first a teacher <term>Scholasticus: the head of a cathedral school</term> at Orléans, then Abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, and finally made Bishop of Cambrai around the year 1105. Since he refused to receive his episcopal investiture <note>The formal ceremony where a lord presented a bishop with the symbols of his office; Odo refused to receive this from the Emperor, siding with the Pope during the Investiture Controversy.</note> from Emperor Henry IV, he was driven from his see and withdrew to the Monastery of Anchin near Douai, where he died on June 19th <note>original: "XIII. Cal. Julii," the 13th day before the Kalends of July.</note> in the year 1113. He wrote a brief *Exposition on the Canon of the Mass* divided into four distinctions, which appeared separately with Frans Titelmans’ book on the same subject at Antwerp in 1530, and thereafter in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXI, where other small works of his are also held, namely: *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*, *A Dialogue against Leo the Jew*, *A Book on Original Sin*, *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*, *A Homily on the Steward of Iniquity*, *A Book of Collations* <note>original: "Collationum liber," likely a collection of spiritual lectures.</note>, etc.

**ODO**, a monk of Asti of the Order of Saint Benedict, flourished in the year 1106. He wrote an *Exposition on the Psalms* composed through contemplation for Bruno, Bishop of Segni, which is found at the end of the works of Bruno of Segni, Venice, 1651.

**PETER ALPHONSE**, an illustrious man, formerly called Moses; a Spaniard, it seems, by nation and a Jew by birth. Having converted to the faith of Christ, he was baptized (by his own testimony in the prologue) by Stephen, the Bishop of the city of Huesca, in the year of Christ 1106—according to the Spanish Era, 1144 <note>The "Spanish Era" was a dating system used in the Iberian peninsula that began in 38 BC.</note>—in the month of July, on the feast day of the Apostles Peter and Paul. He was received from the sacred font by the Spanish Emperor Alfonso, whom he thereafter called his spiritual father, and from whom he took the name Alphonse. He wrote under the name of Peter and Moses a *Dialogue against the Jews*, distributed into twelve titles or parts, which is held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXI, page 172.

**ANONYMOUS Author**, who wrote the *Life of Emperor Henry IV*. He flourished in the year 1106, in which that most illustrious prince ended his life. He is a historian of ancient reliability and elegant talent, who seems to have hidden his name out of fear of envy and persecution because of his sincere and unblemished faith in narrating the affairs of Henry. It appeared in the *Bundle of Things to be Sought* <note>original: "Fasciculo rerum expetendarum," a collection of documents concerning church reform.</note> edited by Orthuinus Gratius, then among other *Writers of German Affairs* published by Justus Reuber at Frankfurt in 1584. In this little book, I know not what to admire first: the elegance of the speech*

**STEPHEN HARDING**, an Englishman by nation, born of a noble family, embraced the monastic life in the Monastery of Sherborne; from there, girding himself for travel, he journeyed through Scotland, France, Italy, and as far as Rome. Making his way back to Burgundy, he joined the Benedictine Monks at the Monastery of Molesme in the territory of Langres. Having eventually left these, he withdrew to the Cistercian Order <note>A reformed branch of Benedictines emphasizing austerity and manual labor.</note>, and after ten years had passed, he was elected Abbot of Cîteaux in the year 1109. After founding thirteen monasteries of his Order, he abdicated the governance of his Cistercians in the year 1133, and died the following year on April 17th. At the general chapter of the Cistercians convened in 1116, and again in 1119, he promulgated certain constitutions for the union of the Cistercian monasteries among themselves, which he wished to be called the *Charter of Charity* <note>original: "Chartam Charitatis"; the foundational constitutional document of the Cistercian Order.</note>. That Charter exists in the *Cistercian Menology, Antwerp 1635*, for the day of July 5th, and in the *Cistercian Annals* of Angelus Manriquez, *Lyon 1642, Volume I, at the year 1119*. Also extant are *two Letters* by him among the Letters of Saint Bernard to Louis, King of France; the *Little Beginning of his Order* <note>original: "Exordium parvum Ordinis sui"; a history of the founding of Cîteaux.</note>, published in the *Cistercian Library* by Bertrand Tissier, *Paris 1660*; and a *Sermon delivered on the death of Saint Alberic*, in Manriquez, Volume I of the *Annals* at the year 1109. An illustrious sermon delivered in 1113, when he clothed Saint Bernard and thirty companions in the habit of the Cistercian Order, is found in Britus, Book I, chapter 22, as noted by Carolus de Visch in the *Library of Cistercian Writers, page 301*. To the same man is commonly ascribed the *Book of Usages, or Rites of the Cistercian Order*, published in *Paris, 1628*, and elsewhere.

1110.

**PETER GROSOLANUS**, also called *Chrysolanus*, was first the prelate of a smaller city, and then the Archbishop of the Church of Milan; he flourished in the year 1110. Sent by Pope Paschal to the Emperor Alexios Komnenos in Constantinople, he fought strenuously against the Greeks, both in speech and in writing, regarding the burning controversy of the "procession of the Holy Spirit" <note>The "Filioque" dispute: a central theological disagreement where the West argued the Holy Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son, while the East argued the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone.</note>. Having returned home, a lawsuit arose between him and Jordan over the See of Milan; in 1116, by a decree of the Lateran Council, he was forced to abdicate the Archbishopric and return to his former see. There exists an *Oration to Alexios Komnenos on the Procession of the Holy Spirit* in Latin in Baronius at the year 1116, and in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius, *Orthodox Greece, Volume I, page 379*.

**EUSTRATIUS**, Metropolitan of Nicaea; he flourished around the year 1110. He was among those who sharpened their pens against Chrysolanus. He was certainly a weighty author, and celebrated for the merit of his other writings even among the Latins, as Leo Allatius admits in *On Consent, book 2, chapter 10*. Anna Comnena <note>A Byzantine princess and historian, author of the *Alexiad*.</note>, a contemporary witness, offers such a tribute to him:
> A man wise in things both divine and external, excelling in debates even more than those who spent their time in the Portico and the Academy. <note>original Greek: 'Ανὴρ τά τε θεῖα σοφὸς κ’ τὰ θύραθεν αὐτῶν ἐπὶ ταῖς διαλέξεσι μᾶλλον, ἢ οἱ περὶ τὴν στοὰν κ’ ἀκαδημίαν ἐνδιατρίβοντες. The "Portico" (Stoa) and "Academy" refer to the ancient Stoic and Platonic schools of philosophy.</note>
He wrote against Chrysolanus a *Work on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which is preserved today as a manuscript in the Vallicellian Library. Leo Allatius, in the place cited above, lists five other *Treatises* on the same subject which he himself saw. Furthermore, our Eustratius’s *Commentaries on the Posterior Analytics of Aristotle* were published in Greek at *Venice, 1534*. His *Commentaries on Aristotle’s Ethics* were published in Greek there in 1536, and in Latin at *Paris, 1543*.

He died in 1129. A letter to the aforementioned Robert regarding the *Flowers of the Psalms*—a collection of commentaries gathered by Lietbert, Abbot of Saint-Ruf—is extant in Mabillon's *Analecta*, Volume I, page 289.

...stupendous for those times, whether for the weight of its insights or for the piety which clearly appears to have been immense in that author. <margin>1109</margin>

### STEPHANUS HARDINGUS
**Stephen Harding**, an Englishman by birth and born of a noble family, embraced the monastic life in the Abbey of Sherborne. From there, preparing himself for travel, he journeyed through Scotland, France, Italy, and as far as Rome. Making his way back to Burgundy, he entered the Benedictine Order among the monks at the Abbey of Molesme in the territory of Langres. Having eventually left these, he withdrew to the Cistercian Order, and ten years later, in the year 1109, he was elected Abbot of Cîteaux. After founding thirteen monasteries of his Order, he resigned from the government of his Cistercians in 1133 and died the following year on April 17th. Having assembled a general chapter of the Cistercians in 1116 and again in 1119, he promulgated certain constitutions for the union of the Cistercian monasteries with one another, which he wished to be called the *Charter of Charity* <term>Charta Charitatis: The foundational document of the Cistercian Order, establishing a framework for unity and mutual oversight between monasteries.</term>. That Charter is found in the *Cistercian Menology*, Antwerp 1635, under the day of July 5th, and in the *Cistercian Annals* of Angelus Manriquez, Lyon 1642, Volume I, under the year 1119. Two of his letters are extant among the letters of St. Bernard to King Louis of France. His *Exordium Parvum* <note>The "Little Beginning," a narrative of the founding of the Cistercian Order.</note> of his Order was published in the *Cistercian Library* by Bertrand Tissier, Paris 1660. A sermon delivered at the death of St. Alberic is found in Manriquez, Volume I of the *Annals* under the year 1109. A notable sermon delivered in 1113, when he clothed St. Bernard and thirty companions in the habit of the Cistercian Order, is found in Britus, book 1, chapter 22, as noted by Charles de Visch in the *Library of Cistercian Writers*, page 301. To him is also commonly ascribed the *Book of Usages, or Rites of the Cistercian Order*, published at Paris in 1628 and elsewhere.

### PETRUS GROSOLANUS
**Peter Grossolano**, or called *Chrysolanus*, was first the prelate of a smaller city and then the Archbishop of the Church of Milan; he flourished in the year 1110. Sent by Pope Paschal to the Emperor Alexios Komnenos in Constantinople, he fought vigorously against the Greeks, both in speech and in writing, regarding the heated controversy of the procession of the Holy Spirit <note>The "Filioque" controversy, a major theological dispute between the Western (Latin) and Eastern (Greek) churches over whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from both the Father and the Son.</note>. Having returned home, a dispute arose between him and Jordan over the See of Milan; in 1116, by a decree of the Lateran Council, he was forced to abdicate the Archbishopric and return to his former see. His *Oration to Alexios Komnenos on the Procession of the Holy Spirit* is extant in Latin in Baronius under the year 1116, and in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius's *Orthodox Greece*, Volume I, page 379.

<margin>1110.</margin>

### EUSTRATIUS
The Metropolitan of Nicaea; he flourished around the year 1110. He was among those who sharpened their pens against Chrysolanus. He was certainly a weighty author, celebrated even among the Latins with the praise of other writings, as Leo Allatius admits in *On Consent*, book 2, chapter 10. Anna Comnena, a contemporary witness, offers such a eulogy of him:

> A man wise in things divine and especially in external logic, more so than those who have studied in the Stoa and the Academy. <note>original: "Ἀνὴρ τά τε θεῖα σοφὸς καὶ τὰ ἔξωθεν ἐπὶ ταῖς διαλέξεσι μᾶλλον, ἢ οἱ περὶ τὴν στοὰν καὶ ἀκαδημίαν ἐσπουδακότες." The Stoa and Academy refer to the famous philosophical schools of ancient Athens.</note>

He wrote against Chrysolanus a *Work on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which is preserved today as a manuscript in the Vallicellian Library. Leo Allatius, in the place cited above, lists five other *Treatises* on the same subject which he himself saw. Furthermore, our Eustratius's *Commentaries on the Posterior Analytics of Aristotle* <note>A work of Aristotle focusing on demonstration, definition, and scientific knowledge.</note> were published in Greek at Venice in 1534; his *Commentaries on the Ethics of Aristotle* were published in Greek at the same place in 1536, and in Latin at Paris in 1543.

When he noticed the Latins commending their dogmas and rites by the antiquity of the Roman Church, he published a small work against them on this theme: *Not simply ancient things...*

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ecclesiastical writers of the early 12th century. The previous entries discussed figures like Stephen Harding and the beginnings of the Cistercian order. # The Waldensian Century.

<margin>12th CENTURY, from the Year 1103.</margin> **WALTER** <note>original: "Galterus"</note>, perhaps of French origin and a relative of Robert, the Provost of Lille, was made Bishop of Maguelone <note>An ancient diocese on the coast of southern France</note> and an Apostolic Legate in the year 1103. He died in the year 1129. There exists a *Letter to the aforementioned Robert concerning the Flower of the Psalms*, which was collected by Lietbert, the Abbot of Saint-Ruf, found in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume I, page 289.

<margin>1105.</margin> **PHILIP THE SOLITARY** <note>original: "Philippus Solitarius"</note>, so named perhaps from his monastic life, was Greek in his speech, though it is not clear who he was or where he came from. He flourished in the year 1105, when he composed his *Mirror* <note>original: "Dioptra"</note>. He wrote this work, titled the *Mirror*, or *The Rule of the Christian Life*, to his companion Callinicus; it is comprised of four books or sermons in which the soul and the body engage in a dispute. Michael Psellus is believed to have illustrated the work with added notes and a preface. It was published in Latin from the translation by Jacob Pontanus, including the preface and notes by Psellus, at *Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto*, and later in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XXI, page 553.*

<margin>1105.</margin> **AELNOTH**, it is not entirely certain whether he was Danish or English by birth, but he certainly spent the better part of his life in Denmark, where he stayed for twenty-four years; he was a monk of Saint Augustine’s in Canterbury. He flourished in the year 1105. He wrote *The Life and Passion of Saint Canute, King of Denmark*, which was first edited by Arild Huitfeldt in *Copenhagen, 1602*, and later with notes by Johannes Meursius in the same city, *1631, in quarto.*

<margin>1105.</margin> **ODO**, first a teacher <term>Scholasticus; a master of a cathedral school</term> at Orléans, then Abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, and finally made Bishop of Cambrai around the year 1105. Because he refused to receive his episcopal investiture <note>The formal symbolic act of being granted office</note> from Emperor Henry IV, he was driven from his see and withdrew to the Abbey of Anchin near Douai, where he met his end on June 19th, 1113. He wrote a brief *Exposition on the Canon of the Mass* divided into four distinctions, which appeared separately with Frans Titelmans’ book on the same subject at *Antwerp, 1530*, and from there in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XXI*. Other small works of his are also found there, namely: *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*, *Dialogue against Leo the Jew*, *Book on Original Sin*, *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*, *Homily on the Unjust Steward*, *Book of Conferences*, and others.

<margin>1106.</margin> **ODO**, a monk of Asti of the Order of Saint Benedict, flourished in the year 1106. He wrote to Bruno, the Bishop of Segni, an *Exposition on the Psalms drawn out through contemplation*, which is kept at the end of the works of Bruno of Segni, *Venice, 1651.*

<margin>1106.</margin> **PETER ALPHONSO**, an illustrious man previously called Moses, was by nation apparently Spanish and by birth a Jew. Having converted to the faith of Christ, he was baptized (by his own testimony in his prologue) by Stephen, the Bishop of the city of Huesca, in the year of Christ 1106—the 1144th year of the Spanish Era—in the month of July, on the feast day of the Apostles Peter and Paul. He was taken from the sacred font <note>sponsored at baptism</note> by the Spanish Emperor Alfonso, whom he thereafter called his spiritual father and from whom he took the name *Alphonso*. Under the names of Peter and Moses, he wrote a *Dialogue against the Jews*, distributed into twelve titles or parts, which is found in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XXI, page 172.*

<margin>1106.</margin> **ANONYMOUS** author, who wrote the *Life of Emperor Henry IV*. He flourished in 1106, the year that most illustrious prince ended his life. He is a historian of ancient reliability and elegant talent, who seems to have hidden his name for fear of envy and persecution because of his sincere and untarnished loyalty in narrating the affairs of Henry. His work appeared in the *Collection of Desirable Things* <note>original: "Fasciculo rerum expetendarum"</note> edited by Orthuinus Gratius, and later among other writers of German history published by Justus Reuber at *Frankfurt, 1584*. From that edition, the book which I once possessed belonged to the great man Isaac Casaubon, who noted this in his own hand on the flyleaf of the volume: *Of all the writers contained in this volume, none is to be compared in any way with the one who described the life of that greatest Prince, Emperor Henry IV. In which booklet, I know not what I should admire first; the elegance of the language...*

# The Waldensian Century.

<margin>12th CENTURY, from the Year 1100.</margin>
...whether one considers the stupendous quality for those times, the weight of his opinions, or the piety which clearly was immense in that author. Indeed, if he had lived in more fortunate ages, I believe he would be second to none of the ancients, whether Latin or Greek; nor would I rank that little work of his below Tacitus’s book *On the Life of Agricola*. Thus far from the manuscript notes of Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar</note>. Baronius, however, delivered a completely opposite opinion regarding him in his records for the year 1106, Volume XII, page 50.

<margin>1109.</margin>
**STEPHEN HARDING** <note>original: "Stephanus Hardingus"</note>, an Englishman by birth, born to a noble family, embraced the monastic life in the Monastery of Sherborne. From there, preparing himself for travel, he journeyed through Scotland, France, Italy, and as far as Rome. Making his way back to Burgundy, he entered the ranks of the Benedictine monks at the Monastery of Molesme in the territory of Langres. Having finally left these, he withdrew to the Cistercian Order <note>A stricter offshoot of the Benedictines founded at Cîteaux</note>, and after ten years had passed, he was elected Abbot of Cîteaux in the year 1109. After founding thirteen monasteries of his Order, he resigned from the governance of his Cistercians in 1133 and died the following year on April 17th. Having convened a general chapter of the Cistercians in 1116 and again in 1119, he promulgated certain constitutions for the union of the Cistercian monasteries with one another, which he wished to be called the **Charter of Charity** <note>original: "Charta Charitatis"</note>. This Charter is found in the *Cistercian Menology* (Antwerp, 1635) for July 5th, and in the *Cistercian Annals* of Angelus Manriquez (Lyons, 1642), Volume I, at the year 1119. There also exist two of his Letters among the letters of Saint Bernard to King Louis of France; the *Little Beginning of His Order* <note>original: "Exordium parvum Ordinis sui"</note>, published in the *Cistercian Library* by Bertrand Tissier (Paris, 1660); and a *Sermon Delivered on the Death of Saint Alberic*, found in Manriquez, Volume I of the *Annals* at the year 1109. A notable sermon was delivered in 1113 when he invested Saint Bernard—who arrived with thirty companions—with the habit of the Cistercian Order, as recorded by Britus in Book 1, Chapter 22, and noted by Carolus du Visch in the *Library of Cistercian Writers*, page 301. To him is also commonly ascribed the *Book of Customs, or Rites of the Cistercian Order*, published in Paris in 1628 and elsewhere.

<margin>1110.</margin>
**PETER GROSOLANO** <note>original: "Petrus Grosolanus"</note>, also called Chrysolanus, was first the prelate of a smaller city and then the Archbishop of the Church of Milan; he flourished in the year 1110. He was sent by Pope Paschal to the Emperor Alexios Komnenos in Constantinople. While the controversy over the <term>Procession of the Holy Spirit</term> <note>The theological dispute over whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, or from the Father and the Son (Filioque)</note> was raging, he fought vigorously against the Greeks both in speech and in writing. Upon returning home, a dispute arose between him and Jordan regarding the See of Milan; in 1116, by a decree of the Lateran Council, he was forced to abdicate the Archbishopric and return to his former see. There exists his *Oration to Alexios Komnenos on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, in Latin in Baronius at the year 1116, and in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius’s *Orthodox Greece*, Volume I, page 379.

<margin>1110.</margin>
**EUSTRATIUS**, Metropolitan of Nicaea; he flourished around the year 1110. He was among those who sharpened their pens against Grosolano. He was certainly a weighty author, and celebrated with praise for his other writings even among the Latins, as Leo Allatius admits in *On the Agreement*, Book 2, Chapter 10. A contemporary witness, Anna Komnena, offers this eulogy for him: <note>original Greek: "Ἄνηρ τὰ τε θεῖα σοφὸς καὶ τὰ θύραθεν αὐτῷ ἐπὶ ταῖς διαλέξεσι μᾶλλον, ἢ οἱ περὶ τὴν στοὰν καὶ ἀκαδημίαν ἐνδιατρίβοντες"</note> "A man exceptionally learned in things divine and external, claiming for himself a greater place in debates than those who were trained in the Stoa and the Academy" <note>References to the major schools of ancient Greek philosophy</note>. Against Grosolano, he wrote a *Work on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which is preserved today as a manuscript in the Vallicellan Library. Leo Allatius, in the place cited above, lists five other *Treatises* on the same subject which he himself saw. Furthermore, our Eustratius’s *Commentaries on Aristotle’s Posterior Analytics* were published in Greek at Venice in 1534; his *Commentaries on Aristotle’s Ethics* in Greek at the same place in 1536, and in Latin at Paris in 1543.

<margin>1110.</margin>
**NICETAS SEIDUS**, a Greek writer and adversary of the Latins; he flourished (if I conjecture correctly in an obscure matter) around the year 1110. When he noticed that the Latins recommended their dogmas and rites based on the antiquity of the Roman Church, he published a small work against them on this theme: *Not everything ancient is simply...*

**GILLE**, or **GILLEBERTUS**, by race or nation an "Eastman" <note>original: "Ostmannus"; referring to the Norse-Irish or Vikings settled in Ireland</note>, flourished in the year 1110 as the Bishop of Limerick in Ireland <note>original: "Lunicensis" or "Lumnicensis"</note> (see the works of James Ware * and James Ussher †). **GODFREY**, born in Anjou <note>original: "Andegavensis"</note> to a noble family, joined the monks of Vendôme in his early years. While still a novice, a youth, and only a deacon, he was created the fifth Abbot of that monastery, being installed by Ivo of Chartres. In 1093, having traveled to Italy, he brought financial assistance to Pope Urban II, who was then in hiding for fear of the Guibertine faction <note>Supporters of the Antipope Clement III, also known as Guibert of Ravenna</note>. Bound by such a great favor, the Pope ordained him a priest and named him Cardinal with the title of Saint Prisca. In 1095, summoned by Urban, he attended the Council of Clermont; he was especially dear not only to Urban but also to his successor, Paschal, both of whom he hosted at his monastery in Vendôme. He flourished in the year 1110. He was a vigorous champion for the Roman Church; to defend and expand its authority, he crossed the Alps twelve times and was even taken captive three times by the Pope’s adversaries. He was still among the living in the year 1129.
