<margin>1111.</margin>
**RUPERT**, called *of Deutz* <note>original: "Tuitiensis"</note>, was first a monk of *St. Lawrence* in *Oesbrovic* near *Liège* under Abbot *Berenger* (or *Berengarius*). During Berenger's lifetime, Rupert wrote his *Commentaries on the Divine Offices* in the year 1111. As Berenger was dying, he recommended Rupert to *Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg*. Under Cuno's patronage, Rupert was freed from the "persecution of false brothers wasting away with envy" (as he himself puts it) and began to publish his *Commentaries on Holy Scripture* in 1117. Finally, because of his outstanding reputation for learning, he was summoned by *Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne*, and appointed Abbot of the *Monastery of Deutz*, situated across from *Cologne*. He died on March 4, 1135 <note>original: "IV. Non. Mart."</note>. *Baronius* * will explain what Rupert's opinion was regarding the Eucharist.
<margin>* Under the year 1111, at the end.</margin>
"He fell," says Baronius, "incautiously into that error in which he asserted that in the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist, the entire body and blood of Christ are truly present in such a way that the substance of the bread and wine also remains intact." This error was condemned in the *Lateran Council* under *Pope Innocent IV*; or, as *Bellarmine* † perhaps explains Rupert's view more clearly:
<margin>† On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Rupert.</margin>
"Rupert's error," he says, "lies in the fact that he thought the bread is not converted into the body of Christ when the Eucharist is consecrated, but is assumed by the Divine Word in the same way that his humanity was assumed." <note>This theological position is known as "impanation," which differs from the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation.</note>

*Commentaries on the most Holy Trinity and its works*, in 42 books, on both Testaments, dedicated to *Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg*: namely, 3 books on the works of the *Father*, 30 on the *Son*, and 9 on the *Holy Spirit*.

*Commentaries on the 12 Minor Prophets*, in 31 books, dedicated to *Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne*. Published separately at *Nuremberg* in 1524 and *Louvain* in 1551.

*Commentaries on the Song of Songs regarding the Incarnation of Christ and the praises of the Virgin Mother of God*, in 7 books.

*Commentary on Job*, excerpted from the writings of *Gregory the Great*.

*Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, in 5 books, dedicated to *Gregory*.

*On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man: a Commentary on Matthew*, in 13 books, dedicated to *Cuno*, who had moved from being Abbot of Siegburg to *Bishop of Regensburg*. Published separately at *Cologne* in 1533.

*On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, in 9 books, preceded by a *Hymn to the Holy Spirit*, a *Letter to the Roman Pontiff*, and a *Prologue to Cuno of Regensburg*. Published together with the preceding work at *Cologne* in 1533.

*Commentaries on the Gospel of St. John*, in 14 books.

<margin>1112.</margin>
**JOHN**, Archbishop of Lyon, flourished in the year 1112. He called a synod of his assistant bishops <term>suffragan: bishops who are subordinate to an archbishop within a specific province</term> and condemned the practice of lay investiture <term>lay investiture: the appointment of church officials, such as bishops, by secular rulers like kings or lords rather than by the church</term>. The bishops of the province of Sens, who were summoned to this synod, refused to go; instead, they sent a letter to John declaring that lay investitures were not only lawful but necessary in the present state of the Church. John replied to them with a sharp letter, criticizing them harshly and contending that their opinion was undoubtedly a heresy. This *Letter* survives, together with the letters of the bishops of Sens, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 10, page 786.

---

<margin>1113.</margin>
**STEPHAN I**, Bishop of Autun <note>original: "Aeduensis" or "Augustodunensis"</note>, was appointed in the year 1113. After the year 1129, he resigned his episcopal dignity and became a monk at Cluny under Peter Maurice <note>better known as Peter the Venerable</note>, and he reached the end of his life in Peter's presence. He wrote *A Book on the Sacrament of the Altar, and on those things which pertain to the various ministers of the Church in relation to it*, which is held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 20, page 187. There was another, younger Stephen of Autun, who died in the year 1189.

<margin>1114.</margin>
**BALDRIC**, a native of Orléans, was first a monk and then Abbot of Bourgueil in Anjou. In the year 1095, he took part in the Council of Clermont <note>the council where the First Crusade was called</note>. In the year 1114, he was made Archbishop of Dol in Brittany <note>original: "Aremorica"</note>. He died at a great age on January 27, 1131. He wrote a *History of Jerusalem in four books* <note>original: "Historiam Hierosolymitanam"</note>, in which he truthfully and elegantly described the deeds of the Western Christians in the East from the first year the pilgrimage was undertaken in 1095 until the capture of Jerusalem and the death of King Godfrey in 1100. This is the judgment of Orderic Vitalis <margin>*</margin>, who took many details from him. This history is found among the *Deeds of God through the Franks* <note>original: "Gesta Dei per Francos"</note>, Volume 1, page 81, and among the *French Historians* edited by Duchesne, Volume 4.

Likewise, the *Translation and Miracles of the head of Saint Valentine the Martyr* is in Bollandus under February 14. Vossius, in his *On Latin Historians*, book 3, part 2, chapter 6, mentions a *Life of the Blessed Samson, Bishop of Dol*, marked as being written by the same man. His small book *On the Visitation of the Sick* is held as a manuscript in the Lambeth Library.

...[Peter]borough <note>original: "burienfis"</note> *, because he could not save his soul there, he crossed over into England. Here he was first made a monk, then under Anselm he became the Prior of Canterbury, and finally the Abbot of Peterborough. At last, when Ralph was moved to Canterbury in the year 1115, on the 26th day of December, Ernulf was appointed Bishop of Rochester. He left behind many monuments of his piety, generosity, and integrity everywhere. He died in the month of March in the year 1124, at the age of 84. His works still exist: *A Small Treatise, or Letter, on Incestuous Marriages* <note>In the medieval church, this referred to marriages within prohibited degrees of kinship</note>, and another *Letter containing certain solutions to various questions of Lambert, Abbot of Saint-Bertin*, chiefly concerning the *Body and Blood of the Lord*, found in D'Achery’s *Spicilegium* <note>A famous 17th-century collection of ecclesiastical documents</note>, Volume II, pages 420 and 431. His *Small Treatise* is also kept in the Lambeth Library.

**BERNARD**, French by race and Burgundian by homeland, was of noble birth, born in the Castle of Fontaines near Dijon in the year 1091. He was the son of the knight Tescelin and Aleth. In the year 1113, having long meditated on leaving the secular world, he went to Abbot Stephen <note>Stephen Harding, one of the founders of the Cistercian Order</note> and gave his name among the Cistercian monks, bringing with him more than thirty companions of his own purpose, whom he himself had persuaded to renounce the world through his advice. In the year 1115, when he won the prize by the common vote of all for his piety and learning among the Cistercian monks, he led out a colony, as it were, of monks to Clairvaux in the territory of Langres by the order of Abbot Stephen; there, having built a monastery, he undertook the duty of Abbot, being ordained by William of Champeaux, the Bishop of Châlons. After the Monastery of Clairvaux was built, he ordered a small hut to be placed for himself outside the monastery walls; there, having set aside all the worry of governing the monastery, he devoted himself entirely to the stricter discipline of piety and literary leisure. 

In the year 1127, having been with difficulty pulled away from the boundaries of his monastery by Matthew, Bishop of Albano and the Pope’s legate throughout France, he went to the Council of Troyes. There, by the authority which his astounding piety and rare learning had won for him among all, he brought about the confirmation of the Order of the Templars, and at the urging of the bishops, he prescribed a certain Rule for them to observe. In the year 1129, he began to become famous in the Roman Court; he undertook to advocate for the cause of the good, and thereafter, through letters sent to the Popes, he began to consult on the affairs of almost the entire Western Church. In the year 1130, he pleaded the cause of Pope Innocent II in the Council of Étampes; he afterwards contended with great constancy of mind that Innocent should be held as the legitimate Pope; he even went on an embassy to William, Duke of Aquitaine, for the same cause. 

In the year 1131, he sat beside Pope Innocent in the frequent councils celebrated throughout France. In the year 1134, called by the earnest prayers of the citizens of Milan and sent as a legate by Innocent, he set out for Milan; there, received with immense veneration, he reconciled the citizens to the Roman Church and was the author of their decision to shake off the reins of Conrad and receive Lothair as Emperor. It would be a long task to list every single journey of Saint Bernard and the labors he undertook for the restoration and expansion of the Church's affairs. Three times he crossed the Alps; very often he went on embassies to Christian Princes; among all people, he worked with untiring zeal of mind through letters and speech for the sake of religion and piety. 

In the year 1138, while staying in Rome, he successfully extinguished the schism that had long since arisen between two Popes <note>The conflict between Innocent II and the Antipope Anacletus II</note>, and he prevailed so much by the force of his arguments with the Antipope Victor that the latter, having laid aside his papal robes, went to Pope Innocent to seek peace, which he obtained. Bound by such a great favor, the Romans decreed a triumph, as it were, for Bernard; they sent him back to France with a great procession, acknowledging him by public acclaim as the *Father of his Country* and the *Restorer of the Church*. 

In the year 1140, he fiercely attacked the errors of Peter Abelard, whom he refuted both in person and in openly published writings. Around the year 1146, with letters sent everywhere and sermons held for princes and the people, he applied himself to raising a huge force of soldiers to be sent to the Holy Land for the aid of the Christians; he used such authority that he himself, with his own hand, marked with the cross <note>The ceremony of "taking the cross" to become a crusader</note> Conrad, Emperor of the Romans, Louis, King of France, Theodoric, Count of Flanders, Henry of Blois, and other great men of the Christian world who had been stirred by his warnings. In the year 1147, he drove Gilbert, Bishop of Poitiers <note>Gilbert de la Porrée</note>—who rashly separated the divinity from God and published other discordant fictions about the Trinity—to a recantation by his arguments; he [condemned] his heresy in the Councils of Auxerre, Paris, and Rhe-

# The Century of the Waldensians. 644

<margin>12th CENTURY, from the Year 1100.</margin>
<margin>Letter 290.</margin>
...[Bernard] ensured he was condemned. In the same year, sent by Alberic, Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia, he prepared himself to bring Henry, the disciple of Peter of Bruys, and his followers—the Petrobrusians <note>A 12th-century religious movement that rejected infant baptism, the veneration of the cross, and the authority of the Church hierarchy</note>—back into the bosom of the Roman Church. Having set out for Toulouse, the birthplace of the Petrobrusians, he called back a countless multitude of common people from Henry’s faction through preaching, debating, and advising. Once the Petrobrusians were restored to some semblance of order, another labor awaited Bernard. At that time, a certain class of unlettered men were veiling the gravest errors under the pretentious title of ***Apostolics*** <note>original: "Apostolicorum"; a group that sought to imitate the poverty of the first Apostles but was often viewed as heretical for rejecting Church sacraments</note>. Among other things which they maintained as orthodox dogmas, they held absurdities regarding the total avoidance of oaths and abstaining from the eating of meat. Bernard, having attacked them, drew some back from their errors and silenced others. Yet Bernard was not so perceptive abroad as to be blind at home. He saw (and groaned at) the errors, corruptions, and filth of the Roman Church; he did not hesitate to chastise these as much as he could. Especially as his life was drawing to a close, he seriously urged that the discipline of the Church itself be reformed. Indeed, in letters sent in the year 1151 to the Cardinal of Ostia, after he had lamented the degenerate state of the Church and the conduct of a certain Pontiff, he added these words:

> *Read these letters to my Lord (the Pope): let him see for himself what must be done with such a man. I have delivered my own soul. Yet I speak with my usual impulsiveness. It is good for him if he himself considers his own Court, and if he clears his own conscience.*

Furthermore, in the following year, having published his *Books on Consideration*, he pursued the same matter more extensively and urged it more strongly. This excellent man died on the 13th day before the Kalends of September <note>August 20th</note>, in the year 1153, at the age of 63, after he had established 160 monasteries for his Cluniacs <note>Though Bernard was a Cistercian, his influence and the spread of his monastic reforms affected the wider Benedictine and Cluniac world</note>. He was a man of plainly sincere and unfeigned piety, burning with a remarkable love for God and a great zeal against the corrupt morals of Christians—destined to be much better if the times in which it was his lot to live had not prevented it. He was more than lightly touched by the study of the humanities, most highly instructed in theological science, and in elegance and erudition, he was far above the grasp of the century in which he lived. He was *Christianly learned, holily eloquent*, and *piously pleasant*, to use the words of Erasmus concerning him. I shall add what David Chytraeus said of him in his *Oration on Philipp Melanchthon*, page 509:

> *Bernard,* he says, *with an admirable study of religion and skill in the sacred scriptures—whose words and sentiments offer themselves spontaneously to him as he speaks—is neither slow nor ineffective in moving pious affections. At the same time, he is so pleasant and joyful that the surname "Mellifluous" <note>original: "Melliflui"; meaning "honey-flowing," a title commonly given to St. Bernard for his sweet eloquence</note> seems deservedly attributed to him; whereas many others are dry <note>original: αὔχμηροι (aukhmeroi)</note>, and more recent writers of Scholastic theology are cold and impassive <note>original: ἀπαθεῖς (apatheis)</note> in their speaking, making it their only goal to instruct the reader.*

From the very many editions of the Works of Saint Bernard, almost all of which had their own additions, we especially note the following: *Venice, 1515, 2 volumes in quarto; Paris, 1517, in folio; Lyon, 1530, in folio; 1544; 1558; Venice, 1549; Basel, 1552, 2 volumes; also there in 1566; Antwerp, 1576; Paris, 1586; with the notes of Picart, Paris, 1609; Antwerp, 1620 (to which, among other things, four short works edited by Gretser at Ingolstadt in 1617 in quarto were added); then amended through the care of Jacob Merlo Horst according to manuscript codices, and increased with many of Bernard’s previously unpublished works and an appendix of external works, Paris, 1645, 5 volumes in folio (which edition we have followed in reviewing these Works); finally, there appeared in Paris in 1666, 2 volumes in folio and in octavo.* 

*This last edition was prepared by Jean Mabillon <note>The famous Benedictine scholar of the Congregation of Saint Maur, often considered the founder of the study of paleography.</note> and his fellow Benedictine monks, who not only strove to make it exact and corrected, but also published for the first time several Letters and Treatises drawn from manuscript codices; Mabillon added most learned observations according to his custom. He excellently separated the counterfeit works from the genuine ones, and no one has ever distinguished them with greater certainty or judged them more learnedly.*

*Four Hymns on the Contempt of the World* are found in the work of Charles de Visch in his *Library of Authors of the Cistercian Order*, page 45, who lists many manuscript works of Saint Bernard not yet published on page 39 of the same book.

*Two parts of Moral Expositions; of which the first contains 13 expositions, and the second 4.*
*A Book on Music.*
*Several Parables, but manifestly spurious.*
*A brief Treatise on the Body of the Lord.*
*A continuation of the Commentaries on the Song of Songs by Abbot G., whose* name is hidden.
*A Letter on Divine Love.*
*A Metrical Book on the praises of the Virgin, consisting of 18 odes.* The second part was often published under the name of Saint Casimir; but Jacques Hommey <note>A 17th-century Augustinian scholar.</note> vindicates them all for Bernard in an introductory dissertation, and he also brought to light the other aforementioned short works in his *Supplement to the Fathers, Paris, 1684.*

HERMANN, a German by nation, from a house in Cologne, a Jew by birth and a Levite by tribe, the son of David and Sephora; finally, won over by the sermons of Egbert, Bishop of Münster, and by conversation with Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, he renounced Judaism and gave his name to Christ. Having been harassed with many injuries by the Jews on that account, he finally embraced the Canonical order in the Monastery of Kappenberg. He flourished around the year 1116 or shortly thereafter, a contemporary of Bernard and an intimate friend of Rupert of Deutz. He wrote *a short work on his conversion*, which Benedict Carpzov, having rescued it from the Paulina Library in Leipzig, added to the latest edition of Raymond Martini’s *Dagger of Faith* <note>original: "Pugionis"; a famous 13th-century polemical work against Judaism and Islam.</note>, *Leipzig, 1687, folio.*

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*The Dogmatic Panoply of the Orthodox Faith against all Heresies* <note>original: "Orthodoxæ fidei dogmatica Panoplia adversùs omnes Hæreses"</note>, woven together from various writings of the Holy Fathers, divided into two parts, the first of which contains 11 chapters, and the latter 13. Some most excellent theologians, to whom the Emperor Alexius had given this in their mandates, had collected these *Excerpts* <note>original: "Eclogas"</note> from the writings of the Fathers; afterwards, our Euthymius reduced them into order, arranged them fitly and concisely, and distributed them into their own classes. Truly, the Fathers from whose armory this *Panoply* was taken are mostly these: Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory of Nazianzus, Dionysius the Areopagite, John Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Saint Maximus, Anastasius of Sinai, Leontius of Cyprus, Leontius of Byzantium, John of Damascus, and Photius. This *Panoply* exists in a Latin translation by Francesco Zino, published in Lyon, 1556, in octavo; Paris, 1556, in octavo; and Venice, 1575. The Greek versions still survive today in various libraries. The final chapter, titled the "Armory" <note>original: "ὁπλοθήκης" (hoplothēkēs)</note>, was published in Greek and Latin from a codex, formerly in the Palatine and now in the Vatican library, with notes by Friedrich Sylburg in his *On Saracen Matters* <note>original: "Saracenicis"</note> from page 1 to page 54, and thereafter by Fronto Ducæus in his *Supplement* <note>original: "Auctuario"</note>, Volume II, page 292.

*Commentaries on all the Psalms of David, and the Ten Canticles of Holy Scripture*. These appeared in Greek in Verona, 1530; and in Latin, translated by Filippo Saulio, in Paris, 1543, in octavo; 1547, in octavo; and Venice, 1568. Etienne le Moyne was the first to bring to light a very long preface to the Psalms in Greek and Latin in his *Sacred Varieties* <note>original: "Var. Sacr."</note>, Volume I, page 150, in which the author treats accurately the nature, origin, use, goal, the manifold kinds of Psalms, their obscurity, and various Greek versions.

*Commentaries on the Four Gospels*. These appeared in Latin, translated by Johannes Hentenius, in Louvain, 1544, in octavo; and Paris, 1544, 1560, 1602. They appeared in Greek in Verona, 1530, in folio. Simler reports that his *Commentary on the Catholic Epistles* exists in Greek in the Sambucus Library.

Furthermore, all the works of Euthymius, except for the recently reviewed *Commentary*, are available in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patr."</note>, Volume XIX, pages 1, 235, and 475.

## NICEPHORUS BRYENNIUS
A Macedonian by birth, born in the city of Orestias, he was the eldest son of Nicephorus Bryennius—who, according to Zonaras, was deprived of his sight for aspiring to the empire—though according to Anna Komnene, his wife, he was the grandson. He flourished in the year 1118. He married Anna Komnene, the daughter of Emperor Alexius Komnenos; and therefore by his father-in-law, who was accustomed to forge new titles and new dignities daily, he was created first *Panhypersebastos* <note>A high Byzantine title meaning "Honored above all."</note>, and then *Caesar*. In the year 1096, while Alexius was opposing the Latins who had entered Thrace, our Nicephorus defended Constantinople against Godfrey of Bouillon <note>A leader of the First Crusade.</note>. In 1108, he brokered the peace between Alexius and Bohemond, the Prince of Antioch. In 1118, while Alexius Komnenos was ill, all things in the Court were conducted at the nod of Bryennius; and certainly, he came very close to obtaining the empire after the death of Alexius through the counsels of Anna Komnene and her mother Irene. In the year 1137, he accompanied the Emperor John Komnenos as he moved his arms into Syria; from there, having been brought back sick from the siege of Antioch, he ended his days in the same year, as it seems. <margin>* Annals, book 3.</margin> He was a man, according to the testimony of Zonaras, who was eloquent <note>original: "λόγιος" (logios)</note> and excellently instructed in learning, of which he left an illustrious monument in the *History* he composed. For he wrote a History of Byzantine affairs in four books from the year 1057 to the year 1081. It was published in Greek and Latin with a translation and notes by Pierre Poussin in Paris, 1661, in folio. Charles du Fresne <note>Also known as Du Cange, a famous philologist.</note> wrote historical and philological notes on the same books and published them at the end of Cinnamus in the same place, 1670, in folio.

<margin>* Annals Vol. 3 near the end.</margin>
zeal <note>original: "τὸ ἐν λόγοις παιδείας ἀντείχετο... καὶ τὴν γλῶτταν εἶχεν ἀκριβῶς ἀττικίζουσαν, καὶ τὸ τῶν πρὸς ὕψος θεωρημάτων ὀξύτατον· ταῦτά γε αὐτῇ προσέγενετο φύσεως τινη καὶ σπουδῇ· προσετέθησαν γὰρ ταῖς βίβλοις καὶ λογίοις ἀνδράσι, καὶ οὐ παρέργως ὡμίλει αὐ-" (as Zonaras holds *)</note> "held fast to education in letters, and her tongue spoke accurate Attic Greek <note>Attic Greek refers to the prestigious, classical dialect of ancient Athens, which Byzantine elites tried to emulate.</note>, and she possessed the sharpest insight into the loftiest contemplations; these qualities she acquired through a certain natural gift and through diligence; for she was devoted to books and to learned men, and her conversations with them were not superficial." She applied the greatest effort to the study of doctrines, Atticizing exquisitely, and was gifted with a very sharp intellect for even the most abstruse contemplations; she achieved this faculty partly by the goodness of her nature and partly by industry. For she was attached to her books and enjoyed the company of the learned not just in passing. She wrote fifteen books of Histories concerning the deeds performed by her father, Alexius, which she titled the *Alexiad*. In these, she completed the historical work that had been interrupted by the untimely death of her husband, and she narrates the deeds of Alexius from the year 1081 until his death in 1118 in a most extensive and elegant manner. The first eight books of this History were published in Greek with the notes of Hoeschel <note>David Hoeschel, a German humanist and editor of Greek texts.</note> at Augsburg, 1610, in quarto; all fifteen books in Greek and Latin with Hoeschel’s notes and the glossary of Possinus at Paris, 1651, in folio. Charles du Fresne <note>Also known as Du Cange, a foundational scholar of Byzantine history.</note> composed historical and philological notes on her work and appended them to the *History of Cinnamus*, Paris, 1670, in folio.

<margin>1118.</margin>
JOHANNES ZONARAS, a native of Constantinople, holding the rank of Great Drungary of the Watch <term>Magnus Drungarius Biglæ</term> <note>A high-ranking judicial and military official in the Byzantine court.</note> and Chief Secretary <term>Protoasecretis</term>, flourished in the year 1118. Later, after his dearest ones—namely his wife and children—were snatched from him by sudden death, he entered the monastic life. To soothe his grief and to drive away sordid and useless cares from his mind, he applied himself studiously to the investigation and treatment of the affairs of ancient times, especially those of the Church.

## W R I T I N G S.

*The Annals, or a Compendium of Histories* in 3 volumes. The first deals with Jewish affairs from the Creation of the World to the destruction of Jerusalem. The second with Roman affairs from the founding of the city to Constantine the Great, mostly transcribing Dio. The third with Byzantine affairs from Constantine the Great to the death of Alexius Comnenus, which occurred in the year of Christ 1118. Regarding the events, especially of his own time,
<margin>* On the Greek Historians, book 2, chapter 27.</margin>
the illustrious Vossius <note>Gerhard Johann Vossius, a prominent Dutch scholar and bibliographer.</note> * finds a lack of greater care and industry in him. Concerning the style he used in composing the *Annals*, he himself || pronounces, or rather excuses it:
<margin>|| Annals Vol. 1, p. 3.</margin>
<note>original: "εἴ τις τὸν λόγον αἰτιῷτο, ἢ ὅτι ὁ χαρακτὴρ τοῦ λόγου ποικίλλεται, καὶ μὴ δι᾿ ὅλου ὅμοιος ἐστὶν ἑαυτῷ, θαυμαζέτω μηδείς, μήτε..."</note> "Let no one wonder or find fault with the discourse, or me as its author, if the diction is varied and not entirely consistent with itself throughout. For since it is necessary for me to collect history from various authors like a beggar's alms, I must use the diction and composition of many of them. If, however, I should interpose and insert something of my own, the style will be adapted to the form of that author whom I am following, so that the writing does not seem to disagree with itself." Hieronymus Wolf published these *Annals* illustrated with notes in Greek and Latin at Basel, 1557, in folio. The illustrious Charles Du Fresne, a man born to assist the advancement of letters, recently prepared a new and clearly most elegant edition. He criticizes Wolf for distributing Zonaras's *Annals* into three volumes, since they were distributed into only two by the author himself: the first ending at Augustus Caesar, and the second proceeding from there to the death of Alexius Comnenus. Nevertheless, he himself took another approach, distributing the whole work into eighteen books. In the preface, he defends Zonaras from the unfair censures of other critics, and at the end, he added historical notes and a dissertation on the Hebdomon of Constantinople. Finally, he appended a short *Chronicle* by an anonymous author from the creation of the world to Alexius Comnenus, formerly published by Petau along with the *Breviary* of Nicephorus. This edition appeared in Greek and Latin at Paris, 1686, in 2 volumes, folio.

*Commentaries on the Canons of the Holy Apostles*. These appeared separately in Latin at Paris, 1558.

All these *Commentaries* were published together in Greek and Latin in Paris, 1618, and with the annotations of the Illustrious William Beveridge in the *Pandects of Canons*, Oxford, 1672, folio. In manuscript codices, they are sometimes attributed to Johannes Zonaras and sometimes to Michael Glycas; they are frequently cited by Leone Allacci <note>A famous 17th-century scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note> sometimes under the name of the former and sometimes the latter, but they seem more likely to be attributed to Glycas.

**GELASIUS II.** Previously named John, a native of Campania from the city of Gaeta, born of a noble family. He was educated in fine letters and morals in the Monastery of Monte Cassino under Abbot Oderisius. In time, he was created Chancellor of the Roman Church by Urban II, and a Cardinal Deacon with the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin by Paschal II. Finally, in the year 1118, he was elected Pope by the unanimous vote of the Cardinals in Rome on the 31st of January, and ordained at Gaeta on the 24th of February. For he had been seized in Rome by Cencio Frangipane, a leader for Emperor Henry [V], and cast into chains; soon after, he was freed by a gathering of the people, but was immediately driven from the City by the Emperor himself upon his arrival in Rome, and so he retreated to Gaeta. The Emperor, having taken control of the City, appointed Maurice Bourdin, the Archbishop of Braga, to the Papal seat <note>Bourdin reigned as Antipope Gregory VIII</note>; Gelasius immediately excommunicated him by sending letters everywhere. After Henry's departure, having gathered an army of Normans and Capuans, Gelasius besieged Rome. However, having suffered a repulse, he fled to Gaul [France]; where in the following year, on the 29th of January, in the Monastery of Cluny—

A most holy man, says **Joannes Stella**, and most worthy of all praise, whether you consider his very continent life, his character, or his singular doctrine. 1118.

**FLORENCE**, called **BRAVONIUS**, an English monk of Worcester. He wrote in the year 1118, in which he also died, or perhaps in the following year. He had a talent, says **Baleus** \*, that was clearly open and conspicuous to whatever he wished, a splendid and happy memory, and was so nobly instructed from his tender years, and so inclined toward deserving well, that he allowed no day to pass without drawing some line for the splendor of his fatherland. He wrote a *Chronicle from the Foundation of the World until the year 1118*, mostly taken from Marianus Scotus. In arranging the calculation of times, he used a double <term>Epoch</term> <note>A starting point for a calendar system.</note> from the birth of Christ: one according to the Gospel, the other according to **Dionysius Exiguus**, with a discrepancy of 22 years between them. This *Chronicle* was continued to the year 1141 by a certain anonymous monk of Worcester. The most noble man **William Howard**, later Earl of Northampton, first brought this *Chronicle* to light and published it in *London, 1592, quarto*; thereafter it was printed with Matthew of Westminster in *Frankfurt, 1601*. He also wrote a book *On the Royal Lineage of the English, or the Genealogies of the English Kings*, which is found at the end of the *Chronicle* in the London edition.

<margin>1119.</margin>
**CALLISTUS II**, previously named *Guido*, a Burgundian by birth, son of Count William, related by blood to the kings of Germany, England, and France. He was Archbishop of Vienne and a legate of the Apostolic See before the year 1112, in which, having celebrated a Council at Vienne, he decreed that <term>investiture</term> <note>The act of a secular ruler appointing a church official, a major point of conflict in the Middle Ages.</note> of Bishoprics and Abbeys received from Laymen was a heresy; he annulled the privilege regarding investitures recently granted to Emperor Henry by Pope Paschal, and bound the Emperor himself under <term>anathema</term> <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the church.</note>. In the year 1119, after the death of Gelasius, he was elected Roman Pontiff at Cluny on the 4th of February by the Cardinals who had fled to Gaul, and was crowned there at the end of the month of March. In the month of November, he celebrated a general Council at Reims, in which he excommunicated Emperor Henry, condemned lay investitures, and forbade wives to the Clergy. In the year 1120, he set out for Italy and was received everywhere with such a great gathering and applause of the people that the **Antipope Burdinus**, driven by terror, fled from Rome and retreated to Sutri. In the following year, Callistus—having raised an army of Normans with the help of William, Duke of Calabria and Apulia—captured Sutri by storm and punished the captured Burdinus with perpetual imprisonment. In the year 1122, he held the **Lateran Council**, in which he voided the ordinations made by Burdinus and decreed that peace should be entered into with Emperor Henry, as the Imperial legates were seeking it. This peace was concluded at the **Diet of Worms**, with the Emperor renouncing the investiture of Bishops and Abbots, and the Pope granting the election of both to the Emperor. He died in the year 1124, on the 12th of December. There exist 35 of his *Letters* in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 10, page 827; five other *Letters* in Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Volume 2, page 192. Four *Sermons on Saint James the Apostle* are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 20, page 1278. Baronius gave a mutilated version of his *Life* written by Pandulfus of Alatri in his *Annals*, and Papebroch gave the full version in his *Attempt*, part 2, page 14.

<meta>This page continues the biography of the philosopher and theologian Peter Abelard, which began at the bottom of the previous page.</meta>

# The Waldensian Century #

<margin>12th Century. From the Year 1100.</margin>
...noble by ancestry, he was born around the year 1080. Having completed his early education at home, he sought out teachers: in <term>Dialectic</term> <note>The art of logical argument.</note> he studied under Roscellinus; in Philosophy under William of Champeaux, the Archdeacon of Paris (who later became a <term>Canon Regular</term> <note>A priest living under a community rule.</note> and finally the Bishop of Châlons), with whom he had more than one dispute at the University of Paris; and in Theology under Anselm, the Dean of the Church of Laon. There, his fellow students included Alberic of Rheims and Lotulf of Lombardy, who were rivals of his glory and lifelong detractors of his reputation. Returning to Paris, and now flourishing as the head of a school of philosophy, he fell in love with Heloise, a most accomplished young woman and the niece of Fulbert, a Canon of Paris. <margin>* In the same work, chapters 6 and 7, page 10.</margin> From this secret union, he fathered a son named Peter Astrolabe; soon after, however, he honored both the mother and the child through a legitimate marriage. Nevertheless, shortly thereafter, his wife was placed among the nuns in the convent near Paris called Argenteuil—where she had been educated as a young girl—in order to escape the insults and outrages of her kinsmen.

<margin>* In the same work, chapter 9, page 20.</margin>
The relatives of Heloise took all of this very poorly. One night, they broke into Peter’s bedroom and <term>castrated him</term> <note>original: "virilia ei execuerunt"</note>. Following this example <note>of withdrawal from the world</note>, he retreated to the Monastery of Saint-Denis and took up the monastic habit. There, he devoted himself ardently to his studies and to the instruction of his many disciples. It was around this time that he published his book on *Theology*, in which he discussed the Holy Trinity and the Divine Unity with excessive sharpness and subtlety.

<margin>* In the same work, chapter 10.</margin>
Because of this, great outcries were raised against him, and he was charged with more than one count of heresy. Consequently, in the year 1120, he was summoned to a certain Synod in the city of Soissons, presided over by Conan, Bishop of Palestrina and the Pope's legate in France at that time. Although he was not convicted of any specific error, and without even a formal examination of his case, he was nevertheless compelled to hand over his book to be burned in the vengeful flames with his own hands. Returning to the Monastery of Saint-Denis, he found Abbot Adam and the other monks to be most hostile toward him, both because he had quite freely rebuked their shameful morals, and even more so because he denied that Saint Denis—the patron saint not only of that monastery but of all France—was the famous Dionysius the Areopagite of Athens. Therefore, leaving the monastery, he went to the territory of Troyes. There, on a piece of donated land and with the consent of the Bishop, he built an oratory with a few adjoining monks' cells. Having founded it in the name of the Holy Trinity, he later called it the *Paraclete* <note>meaning "The Comforter" or "The Holy Spirit"</note> for the sake of the consolation he found there.

<margin>* Cited above, chapter 13, page 32.</margin>
It happened after this that his homeland claimed its man, for he was elected Abbot of Saint Gildas de Rhuys in Brittany, which is said to have been founded long ago by our countryman Gildas. However, the barren soil, the nearly barbarous people, and what was even worse, the foul behavior of his own monks, denied him peace and solace even in this place. Indeed, the hatred of the monks boiled over to the point that they hired bandits to intercept him as he traveled on the road, and they saw to it that poison was mixed into his food. Although Abelard himself happened to abstain from it, a fellow monk ate it and died soon after. Even more horrifying, they did not fear to plot against his life during the very sacrifice of the altar, by placing poison in the holy chalice.

<margin>* Otto of Freising, book 1, chapter 48. Geoffrey, Life of St. Bernard, book 3, chapter 5.</margin>
Thus, having abandoned his leadership at Saint Gildas, it is not entirely clear where he retreated. Wherever he was, behold, a storm broke out again—"clouds again after the rain"—and the old charge of heresy was renewed, chiefly by Bernard of Clairvaux, a man of the highest reputation in France at that time. In the year 1140, the Synod of Sens was held. Peter was summoned, and Bernard finally appeared; he entered the arena, produced the writings, and pointed out the chapters of error. But when Abelard perceived that everything was being conducted according to the opinion of his adversaries, and that he was to argue his case before judges who were hardly impartial, he appealed to the Apostolic See <note>the Pope in Rome</note>.

<margin>* See the Letters of Peter of Cluny in the works of Abelard, pages 335, 337, 344.</margin>
The Synod having ended, while he was making his journey toward Rome, he came to Cluny, where he was kindly received by the Abbot Peter Maurice, called "the Venerable." Abelard candidly explained his mind to him and submitted himself entirely to his judgment. He was admitted into the monastery by the Abbot, and through his mediation, peace was restored between Abelard and Saint Bernard; he even obtained absolution from the Pope himself. Finally, having retired to Chalon-sur-Saône for the sake of his health, he reached the end of his days at the monastery of Saint Marcellinus (of the Cluniac Order), leaving with a great reputation for holiness, on April 21st.

# The Waldensian Century #

<margin>
12th CENTURY. From the year 1100.
</margin>
...in the year 1142, at the age of 63. The body of the deceased, just as he himself had requested by letter while he was still alive, was handed over to his wife, Heloise, and buried by her in her own Convent of the Paraclete. Peter the Venerable <note>Peter the Venerable (c. 1092–1156) was the Abbot of Cluny and a friend to both Abelard and Heloise in their later years.</note> composed a double epitaph for him; I will add only the concluding part of the second one here:

-> It is enough for the tomb: here lies Peter Abelard, <-
-> To whom alone all that was knowable lay open. <-
<note>original: "Est satis in tumulo, Petrus hic jacet Abailardus, / Cui soli patuit scibile quicquid erat."</note>

<margin>
* History of his Calamities, ch. 1.
</margin>
He was indeed of a very sharp mind and singular learning—a prince in Philosophy, supreme in <term>Logic</term> <note>original: "in Logicis"</note>, and called "The Dialectician" because of his extraordinary skill in disputation. *I preferred,* he said, *the armor of logical reasoning to all the teachings of philosophy.* In theological matters, he had few equals. The errors attributed to him were numerous, and if his adversaries are to be believed, they were most dangerous. These include: *That the Father is full power; the Son a certain power; the Holy Spirit no power, and not of the substance of the Father or the Son; that Christ did not take on flesh to free us from the yoke of the Devil; that God neither can nor should prevent evils; that those who crucified Christ out of ignorance did not sin; that the Spirit of the fear of the Lord was not in Christ; that the power of binding and loosing <note>The authority to forgive or withhold forgiveness of sins.</note> was given only to the Apostles and not to their successors; that a person is made neither better nor worse by their works; that neither the deed, nor the will, nor lust, nor pleasure (when it moves a person) is a sin; nor should we wish to extinguish it.*

<margin>
* To Cardinal Guy, Letter 192, p. 1561.
</margin>
Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, Abelard's primary intellectual and theological opponent.</note> says this briefly of him: *When he speaks of the Trinity, he tastes of Arius; when of Grace, he tastes of Pelagius; when of the Person of Christ, he tastes of Nestorius.* <note>Bernard is accusing Abelard of smelling like three famous heretics: Arius (who denied Christ's full divinity), Pelagius (who denied original sin), and Nestorius (who over-emphasized the distinction between Christ's human and divine natures).</note> These and more were charged against him, things which could hardly apply to a man of even moderate talent or one imbued with any knowledge of religion; and which Peter himself constantly denied. His surviving books free him from these charges—especially that *Apology*, or confession of faith, in which he clearly explains his mind and completely dissolves such objections. The points noted by the Parisian censors in his works are quite trivial, and were spoken incautiously or rather harshly rather than falsely or heterodoxly. In a word: Abelard seems to have sinned most in that he tried to reduce theological dogmas and the highest mysteries of the Catholic faith to logical subtleties and certain unusual philosophical terms. Finally, it should be noted that many unsound dogmas attributed to him were drawn from the books of others, which he himself never acknowledged as his own.

## W R I T I N G S.

*Four Letters to Heloise*, which can be considered treatises rather than letters. In the penultimate one, he deals learnedly with the origin of nuns and monastic religion; in the last, he provides the Instruction or Rule for Heloise and the nuns of the Paraclete.

*Seven other Letters to various people.*

*Letter to a friend, or History of his Calamities*, which André du Chesne <note>original: "Andreas Quercetanus", a 17th-century French historian.</note> illustrated with learned notes.

*Apology, or Confession of Faith.*

*Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer.*

*Exposition of the Apostles' Creed.*

*Exposition of the Athanasian Creed.*

*Solutions to the Problems of Heloise.*

*Book against Heresies.*

*Five books of Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans.*

*Thirty-two Sermons to be read on feast days throughout the year.*

*To Heloise and her Virgins of the Paraclete.*

<margin>
* To Geoffrey of Paris, Letter 21, p. 334.
</margin>
*Three books of Introduction to Theology*, or as he calls it elsewhere, *Short Works on the Faith of the Holy Trinity.* Peter Lombard <note>A famous medieval theologian known for his "Sentences," the standard textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> used to handle this work frequently, and in composing his own books of Sentences, he almost always had it before his eyes, as admitted by John of Cornwall, a disciple of Lombard himself, in the notes of Du Chesne to Abelard, page 1159.

# The Waldensian Century #

<margin>12th CENTURY. From the year 1100.</margin>
The works of Abelard were gathered from everywhere, collected, and reviewed by François d'Amboise <note>original: "Fr. Amboesius"</note>, Knight and Counselor to the King in the Privy Council. He also provided an *Apologetic Preface for Peter Abelard*. They were published, however, with a censorship review by the Doctors of Paris, by André Duchesne <note>original: "Andreas Quercetanus"</note> in Paris, 1616, in quarto. This edition also includes several letters to and about Abelard, as well as constitutions, decrees, and poems.

### UNPUBLISHED WORKS.

The *Book of Sentences* called *Yes and No* <note>original: "Sic & Non"</note>. A manuscript exists in the Library of Corpus Christi, Cambridge <note>original: "S. Benedict. Cantabrig."</note>, number 390, and in the Public Library, Code 168.
The *Dialectica*, or Logic, which André Duchesne kept in his own manuscript collection and promised to publish separately in his notes on page 1160.
*Expositions on the Epistles of Paul, the Psalter, and Genesis* are said to still exist in manuscript. He denied more than once while he was still alive that the book called *Know Thyself* <note>original: "Nosce teipsum"</note> was his. He himself mentions *Glosses* that he wrote on *Ezekiel*, which I believe have perished. His verses *To his son Astrolabe* are held in manuscript in the Cotton Library, under Vitellius, C. 8. N. 3. It remains for us to add a few details concerning HELOISE, whom Peter had first as a lover, then as a wife, and finally as a sister in the monastic state. She was of noble birth, the niece of Fulbert, a Canon of Paris. After her marriage, she first became a nun at Argenteuil and was made Prioress, as they call it. However, when this convent of nuns was dissolved in the year 1130, she moved to the Paraclete, where Abelard appointed her as Abbess over the others who followed her. She died more than twenty years after her husband, on the 16th of the Calends of June <note>May 17th</note> in the year 1163 or 1164. She was an altogether most excellent woman, of extraordinary character and elegant wit, educated in every kind of discipline, and learned in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. Among Abelard's works, there survive Heloise’s *42 Problems* addressed to Peter Abelard, a Letter to Peter, Abbot of Cluny, and *3 Letters* to Peter Abelard. These clearly display her admirable sharp-wittedness and uncommon learning; if there are things within them that betray an immoderate affection for Abelard, they should be softened by a kind interpretation.

<margin>1120.</margin>
GUIGO (or *Guido*), a native of Dauphiné, a Monk of the Carthusian Order, and the fifth Prior of the Grande Chartreuse <note>original: "Carthusiæ majoris"</note>. He flourished around the year 1120 or shortly thereafter; he was certainly a contemporary of Saint Bernard, with whom he was intimate. He died on July 27th, 1137, in the 50th year of his age, his 30th year as a monk, and his 27th as Prior.

### WRITINGS.

*The Ladder of Monks* <note>original: "Scala Claustralium"</note>, or *Meditations on the Method of Praying*, addressed to Brother Gervase. It is found among the works of Saint Augustine under the title *The Ladder of Paradise*, and also among the works of Saint Bernard, to whom it was falsely attributed. Finally, it was restored to its true author in the Paris edition of Bernard in 1666 and in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patr."</note>, Volume XXII, page 1163.
*Treatise on the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell*. Found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXIV, page 1463.
*Three Letters: 1. To Cardinal Haymeric, 2. To Hugh, Prior of the Holy Knighthood <note>Likely referring to the Knights Templar</note>, 3. To Pope Innocent II.* These are found in the Paris editions of Saint Bernard’s works from 1645 and 1666.
*Letter to the Brothers of Durbon concerning the forged Letters of Saint Jerome*, published by Mabillon in *Analecta*, Volume I, page 331.
*Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, found in Surius and Bollandus under the date of April 1st.
*The First Statutes of the Carthusians*, formerly published in Basel, 1510.

<margin>12th CENTURY. From the year 1100.</margin>
<margin>From the year 1138.</margin> ...from the year 1138. He wrote the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Saint-Trond* <note>original: "Chronicon Monasterii Trudonensis"</note> in thirteen books, which Luc d'Achéry <note>original: "Lucas Dacherius," a pioneering Benedictine scholar</note> published in the *Spicilegium*, Volume VII. He also wrote the *Life of Saint Lietbert, Bishop of Cambrai*, published by the same editor in Volume IX. Additionally, he wrote a *Letter to Sigebert on the Reception of Boys into Monasteries*, which is found along with Sigebert's letters to Rodulphus in Jean Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume II, page 495.

<margin>1120.</margin> **ALBERT**, or Albric, Canon of the Church of Aachen, and its custodian or sacristan <note>original: "aedituus"</note>. He flourished in the year 1120. Based on hearsay and the accounts of others, he wrote the *History of the Jerusalem Expedition* <note>original: "Historiam Hierosolymitane Expeditionis"</note> under Godfrey of Bouillon and other princes, in twelve books. In these, he accurately follows the deeds performed by Christians in the Orient from the year 1095 to the second year of Baldwin II, roughly the year of Christ 1120. This history was first published anonymously under the title *The Jerusalem Chronicle* by Reiner Reineccius at Helmstedt in 1584; later, it was restored to its true author by Jacques Bongars in *God’s Deeds through the Franks* <note>original: "Gesta Dei per Francos," a famous collection of Crusade chronicles</note>, Volume I, page 184.

<margin>1120.</margin> **WALTER**, called "the Chancellor" from his office, of French origin; he flourished in the year 1120. He wrote the *History of events successfully conducted by Christians at Antioch in the year 1115, and unsuccessfully in 1119*, in which he himself took part. Having been led away as a captive, he endured a long imprisonment, by the force of which he <margin>* Page 249.</margin> * complains that his own wit was dulled. This *History of the Antiochene Wars* is extant in *God’s Deeds through the Franks*, Volume I, page 441.

<margin>1120.</margin> **HUGH**, a Benedictine monk of Fleury; flourished in the year 1120. He wrote a *Chronicle* in six books dedicated to Ivo of Chartres (to whom it is wrongly attributed by some). It begins with Ninus, King of the Assyrians, and ends with the death of the Emperor Louis the Pious in the year of Christ 840. Bernhard Rottendorp first published it with notes at Münster in 1638, though it was mutilated, containing only the first part up to the time of Constantine the Great. The complete work exists in the Imperial Library. Its *Epilogue*, which embraces the deeds of Louis the Pious, is presented by Peter Lambeck in his *Commentaries*, book 2, chapter 8, page 857. Two complete manuscript copies of this Chronicle exist in the Lambeth Library. Hugh also wrote *Two Books on Royal Power and Priestly Dignity* <note>original: "de regia potestate, & sacerdotali dignitate"</note> addressed to King Henry of England, which Étienne Baluze brought to light in his *Miscellany*, Volume IV, page 9.

<margin>1120.</margin> **MICHAEL GLYCAS**, Sicilian by nationality; flourished in the year 1120. He wrote many things on various subjects, which follow here:
*The Four-Part Annals* <note>original: "Annales Quadripartiti"</note>, a work not only of history, but also of natural science and theology. In the first part, he discusses the works of the six days of creation; in the second, he narrates events from the creation of the world to the birth of Christ; in the third, he proceeds from the birth of Christ to Constantine the Great; in the fourth, he treats the events from then on, ending with the death of Alexios Komnenos in the year of Christ 1118. These appeared in Latin from the translation of Johannes Leunclavius (Basel, 1572); later in Greek and Latin with the translation and notes of Philippe Labbe (Paris, 1660, folio).
*Two Small Disputes* <note>original: "Disputatiuncula II"</note>, published in Latin by Jacob Pontanus together with the *Dioptra* of Philippus Solitarius (Ingolstadt, 1604).
Glycas wrote many *Letters*, from which Leo Allatius cites several fragments—by no means to be ignored—in more than one place, namely in *On Consensus*, and in his books *On Purgatory*, *Against Hottinger*, and *On the Books of the Greek Churches*. It should be noted that he cites some of these letters under the name of either Zonaras or Glycas.
Leo Allatius reviews several *Treatises* hitherto unpublished in *On Consensus*, namely: *A Book to Maximus Smeniotes on the Procession of the Holy Spirit* (a fragment of which is held in the same volume); *To the same, on whether Christ used Unleavened Bread at the Last Supper* <note>original: "an Christus Azymis in suprema caena usus sit?"</note>; and *To the Monk Isaiah on souls separated from the body*. Antonio Possevino also reports in his *Sacred Apparatus* that certain of Glycas’s interpretive works on Holy Scripture exist in the Imperial Library in Vienna.

**NICETAS**, a Byzantine by citizenship and a Philosopher by his way of life—that is, if I am not mistaken, a Monk; he seems to have flourished around the year 1120. He wrote the *Apologetic Treatise for the Council of Chalcedon against the Prince of Armenia*. Fragments of his work exist in Leo Allatius’s *On the Consensus* [of the Western and Eastern Churches], Book 1, chapter 5, section 3, page 72; in the book *On Purgatory*, page 4; and in *On the Books of the Greek Churches*, page 314. The complete work is available in Greek and Latin in *Orthodox Greece* <note>original: "Græc. Orthod.," referring to a collection of Greek theological texts</note>, Volume I, page 663.

<margin>1120. * On Famous Interpreters, page 141.</margin>
**ROBERT**, called of Ketton <note>original: "Retenensis"</note>, an Englishman by birth; he flourished in the year 1120. After tasting the first elements of letters in his homeland, he traveled to foreign regions. Having journeyed through France, Italy, Dalmatia, and Greece, he finally reached Syria, where he lived for a long time among the Saracens and acquired an accurate knowledge of the Arabic language. Returning home, he settled in Spain, where he devoted himself to the study of Astrology and was appointed Archdeacon of Pamplona. He died in the year 1143. He produced a summary of Muhammad’s *Koran* <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> and translated it into Latin. That version was published in Nuremberg in 1543, and in Basel in 1543 and 1550, in folio format. Regarding this version, the illustrious Huet <note>original: "Cl. Huetius," the scholar Pierre Daniel Huet</note> offers this criticism: *“To put it simply, this translation of the Koran is most inept, wretchedly subverting the meaning; moreover, it is thin and always meager, yet it immediately swells into an excessive mass, so that no one can hope to understand the Koran from it. We might hope for that if the complete translation of this other interpreter had been published, whose first Surah <note>original: "Suratta"</note> was edited with the translations of Robert and Hermann; whether it belongs to Juan of Segovia or another remains to be judged.”*

---

<margin>1120. * On Ecclesiastical Writers, folio 82. † On Illustrious Men, part 2, page 171.</margin>
**HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR**, called “The Teacher” <note>original: "Didascalus," a Greek-derived title for a head of a school</note> by some; a Saxon by birth as some claim, though more correctly from Ypres. He was a Canon and (if one trusts Trithemius* and Pantaleon†) Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Victor in Paris, of the Order of Saint Augustine; from this he took the name *Victorine* or *of Saint Victor*. He flourished in the year 1120. He was a man of great learning, as the character of his age allowed, and most well-versed in the writings of Blessed Augustine. He emulated Augustine so greatly in his own works that he was nicknamed the "second Augustine" or the "tongue of Augustine." He died on February 11, 1140, at the age of 44.

*Introductory Notes on the Scriptures and Sacred Writers.*

*Explanatory Annotations on the Pentateuch, Judges, the Books of Kings, several Psalms, Lamentations <note>original: "Threnos"</note>, Joel, and Obadiah.*

*Nineteen Homilies on Ecclesiastes.*

*Explanatory Annotations of Allegories on the entire Old Testament, except for the Prophets and the Wisdom books.*

*Explanatory Annotations of Allegories on the four Gospels.*

*Literal Annotations and questions on the Epistles of Saint Paul, which Casimir Oudin <note>original: "Oudinus," a noted bibliographer</note> attributes to a certain scholastic writer, judging them to be wrongly attributed to Hugh.*

*Explanatory Annotations on Dionysius the Areopagite.*

*Ten books of the first "Exceptions."* The famous work of twenty-four books of *Exceptions* <note>original: "Exceptionum," a title for a collection of excerpts or summaries of doctrine</note> is found scattered among our Hugh’s works: namely, the first ten books here (the first four of which also appear among the works of Richard of Saint Victor in the Rouen edition of 1650); the next nine books up to the twentieth (exclusive) are the same as the *Explanatory Annotations of Allegories on the entire Old Testament* listed above; the twentieth book is the same as the *Collected Homilies on Ecclesiastes*; and the remaining four books are the same as the *Explanatory Annotations on the four Gospels*. <margin>which</margin> Furthermore, this work of *Exceptions* bears the name of Richard of Saint Victor in some manuscripts, our Hugh in others, and no author in many. It can belong to neither Hugh nor Richard, since the author mentions King Philip Augustus of France (who began to reign in 1180) in the tenth book, and reveals that he composed his work under Philip. This is roughly the conclusion of Oudin’s very extensive discussion of this work in his *Supplement*, page 403, etc.

...a disciple of the bishop, and the inseparable companion of all his labors and journeys; indeed, he was even requested by Anselm to be the corrector of his life, a role granted to him by Pope Urban II. Finally, as witnessed by Simeon of Durham, he was made Bishop of St. Andrews in Scotland. However, the claim made by Bale, Pits, and others following them, that he was the Abbot of the Monastery of St. Albans, is completely mistaken <note>original: "planè hallucinantur"</note>. This is because that Eadmer, the head of the St. Albans community, lived more than a full century before our subject and died around the year 980. Furthermore, after Eadmer obtained his see in Scotland, he remained more mindful of his monastic obedience—by which he was bound to the Church of Canterbury—than of his episcopal dignity. He would boast of the great authority of the See of Canterbury on every given occasion and wished for it to be consulted on the difficult affairs of the Scottish Church. Because of this, he began to be viewed unfavorably by King Alexander; he suffered various insults on that account. Eventually weary of these troubles, and realizing that he could in no way benefit the Church of St. Andrews without the desired royal favor, he returned the pastoral ring and staff to the King around the year 1124. He abdicated the bishopric and returned to Canterbury, where he grew old in his original monastery.

### W R I T I N G S .

**H**istory of Recent Events, or six books of his own century <note>original: "Historia novorum, sive sui sæculi libri VI."</note>, from the year 1066 until the year 1122. Selden highly commends the excellence of this work, both for the subject matter itself and for the author's exceptional judgment in narration, combined with equal reliability and a standard of polished prose that is not to be looked down upon; of all these qualities, he provides admirable examples.

> 'In his prose,' he says, 'there is found such a polish that if you carefully examine all the ancient writers of our history to a man, this author would be incomparable. He displays a sufficiently steady and grave style, worthy of a historian of that age, with vocabulary that is pure almost everywhere. The others whom we witness, whether contemporaries, predecessors, or those more recent, are for the most part defiled by barbarism, neglect, and a heap of filth compared to Eadmer. Even Malmesbury <note>William of Malmesbury, a famous 12th-century chronicler</note> is at least equaled in style by our author here, while in other matters Eadmer clearly surpasses him by a long interval.'

The same Selden was the first to publish this *History* from the Cotton Library <note>A famous collection of manuscripts formed by Sir Robert Cotton</note>, with very learned notes and a collection of records from the public archives, printed in London in 1623. It was thereafter reprinted at the end of the *Works of Anselm* (Paris, 1675).

*On the Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in two books.* These are found in the editions of the *Works of Anselm* (Cologne, 1612; Paris, 1630, 1675) and in Surius’s *Lives of the Saints* for February 21st.

*The Life of Saint Wilfrid, Archbishop of York*, edited by Mabillon in the *Benedictine Century* III, part 1, page 196.

*On the Excellence of the Blessed Virgin Mary.*

**PETER MAURICE** <note>Better known to history as Peter the Venerable (c. 1092–1156).</note>, a Frenchman by birth and a native of Auvergne, was born from the noble lineage of the Lords of Montboissier, the son of Maurice and Raingarde. After serving with distinction in military affairs for several years, he renounced the world and joined the Cluniac monks. Following the death of Hugh the Younger in the year 1123, on the day of the Assumption of the Virgin into Heaven, he was elected Abbot of Cluny. He was commonly called the *Venerable Abbot* because of the gravity of his character.

At the very start of his leadership, he suffered serious injuries from Pontius, the former Abbot of Cluny. Pontius had resigned three years earlier to go to Jerusalem, but upon his return, he sought to reclaim his lost office. However, the timely death of Pontius soon put an end to these troubles. In the year 1126, Peter began to oppose the doctrines of Peter of Bruis <note>A popular heretical preacher who rejected infant baptism and the veneration of the cross.</note> through both speech and writing. In 1140, he happened upon Peter Abelard <note>A famous philosopher and theologian who had been condemned for heresy.</note> while the latter was traveling; Peter Maurice brought him back from his errors to a sounder mind and persuaded him to spend his old age at the Monastery of Cluny, where Abelard took up the monastic life. In 1145, he was summoned to Italy by Pope Eugene to reconcile the cities of Tuscany, which were then at each other's throats in an implacable war. Peter attempted this with great diligence, but the stubborn persistence of the Tuscans made a mockery of his pious efforts. In 1150, he undertook a journey to Rome to handle the business of the Cluniac Order, where he was received with great honor by Pope Eugene and the Roman citizens. He died at the end of the year 1156, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 25th.</note>.

**FULCHER**, of Chartres, whether a monk or a priest is uncertain. He followed Robert, Duke of Normandy, when he set out with an army for the Holy Land in the year 1095. As soon as he arrived in Syria, he served as the chaplain to King Baldwin, the brother of Duke Godfrey of Bouillon. He was still active in the year 1124. He wrote a history which he titled *The Deeds of the Franks Pilgrimaging to Jerusalem* <note>original: "Gesta Francorum Hierusalem peregrinantium"</note> from the year 1095 until the year 1124. Bongars testifies that he once used a complete manuscript in which the work itself was divided into three books; the second book beginning with King Baldwin I, and the third with Baldwin II. Thus, André Duchesne published the complete history of Fulcher in *French Writers...*

### HONORIUS II, 
previously named Lambert, was a native of Bologna born to a humble family. He was created Bishop of Velletri by Pope Paschal and eventually named Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia. In the year 1124, after displacing Cardinal Theodulph (the Priest of St. Anastasia), who had been canonically elected Pope after the death of Callixtus, Honorius seized the papal throne on December 16th. A few days later—if Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century ecclesiastical historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> is to be believed—he was duly confirmed by the Roman clergy and crowned on either December 28th or January 4th of the following year. 

In the year 1125, he excommunicated Frederick and Conrad, the nephews of Emperor Henry V, who were seeking to reclaim the empire after their uncle’s death and were pursuing King Lothar with arms. Furthermore, he subjected Anselm, the Archbishop of Milan, to the same sentence for having granted the crown of Lombardy to the same Conrad. In 1127, he waged war against Roger, Count of Sicily, for having taken the Dukedom of Calabria and Apulia without his authority, generously promising a full remission of sins <term>plenary indulgence: the complete removal of temporal punishment for sins</term> to all those who might die in that expedition. In the following year, he struck the same Roger with an <term>anathema: a formal curse or excommunication by the Church</term> because he had seized the Dukedom without consulting the Roman See and had forbidden the Bishops of Sicily from traveling to Rome. He died on February 14, 1130. Eleven of his letters survive in the tenth volume of the *Collection of Councils*, page 908, with a twelfth on page 1843.

<margin>
1127.
Life of Norbert by Hugo, in Surius, June 6.
</margin>
### NORBERT, 
a native of Cleves and the son of Heribert and Hadewig, was educated in the court of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne. He was later called to the imperial court and finally retired to the Monastery of Siegburg. In the year 1118, having obtained permission from Pope Gelasius, he devoted himself to the duty of preaching. In 1120, undertaking the observance of the Rule of Saint Augustine, he founded the **Order of Premonstratensians** <note>Also known as the Norbertines, a religious order of canons regular.</note>; five years later, he traveled to Rome and obtained confirmation for his Order from Pope Honorius. 

In 1126, called upon by the people of Antwerp, he vigorously opposed a certain Tanchelm, a most abandoned <term>heresiarch: the founder or leader of a heretical sect</term>. In 1127, he was created Archbishop of Magdeburg. In 1131, he took part in the Council of Reims. In 1133, he acted as a companion to Pope Innocent and King Lothar when they traveled from Germany to Rome. Returning to his homeland the following year, he passed away. An *Exhortatory Sermon to the Brothers* survives in the *Library of the Fathers*, Vol. XXI, page 118.

<margin>1128.</margin>
### DROGO, 
first a Prior of the Monastery of St. Nicaise at Reims, then Abbot of Laon; finally, having been called to Rome by Innocent II, he was consecrated Bishop of Ostia. He flourished in the year 1128, the year he attained his Abbacy. He died around the year 1138. He wrote a book (or sermon) *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Passion*. It is preserved in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 1388.

### HERVEUS, 
a Frenchman by birth and a native of Le Mans, was a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict at Bourg-Dieu (Dol). He flourished around the year 1130. He wrote a *Commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul*, which is falsely attributed to Anselm among his works in the Cologne edition of 1612. He also wrote a massive *Commentary on the Prophet Isaiah* dedicated to Abbot John of Bourg-Dieu, which is preserved in manuscript at the Clermont Library, according to Labbe *. Finally, he wrote short *Postils* <note>Brief marginal or interlinear notes on scripture.</note> on Deuteronomy, which Oudin || reports are held at Saint-Germain in Paris. D’Achery published an encyclical letter from the monks of Bourg-Dieu containing the life and writings of this Herveus in the *Spicilegium*, Vol. 2, page 514.

</margin>

Honorius carries the name of "the Solitary" <note>Honorius Augustodunensis, also known as Honorius of Autun, a popular 12th-century theologian and philosopher</note>, as noted by Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon, a 17th-century Benedictine monk and founder of the study of old documents</note> in *Italian Journey*, page 14. He wrote many works on various subjects, which are as follows:

->WORKS<-

*Book of the Luminaries of the Church*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, compiled mostly from the writings of Jerome, Gennadius, Isidore, and Bede. It was published with notes by Suffridus Petri at Cologne in 1580, in octavo. Aubertus Miraeus divided the same work into four small books and published it with illustrative notes in his *Ecclesiastical Library* (Antwerp, 1639, folio).

*Commentaries on the Three Books of Solomon* <note>Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon</note>. Published at Cologne, 1540.

*The Inevitable*, or *A Dialogue on Predestination and Free Will*. Published at Cologne, 1552; also among the works of Cassander (Paris, 1616; Antwerp, 1620, 1624, in octavo).

*Gem of the Soul, on the Office of the Mass and its Ceremonies*, distributed in four parts. Published at Leipzig, 1514; and among the *Writers on Divine Offices* (Paris, 1610, page 1179).

*Synopsis of the World, or On the Image of the World, in 3 books* (Speyer, 1583). The first two books are usually kept among the works of Anselm.

*The Elucidarium* <note>A popular handbook of Christian theology in dialogue form</note>, also attributed to Anselm and consequently found among his works.

*Little Book on Heresies* (Basel, 1544).

*On the Philosophy of the World, in 4 books*.

*Book on the Influences of the Sun*.

*Series of Roman Pontiffs from Saint Peter to Innocent II*.

All these works by Honorius were published together in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XX, pages 963–1226.

Honorius wrote many other things that remain unpublished to this day, namely: *A Little Book of Sermons*, *On the Incontinence of Priests*, *On Universal History*, etc., which are enumerated individually in the Appendix to his book on writers.

1130.
</margin>

### INNOCENT II, 
previously named Gregory, was born of a noble family in Rome, the son of John. He was a monk of the Lateran, then Abbot of the Monastery of Saints Nicholas and Benedict near Burano. Later, he was named Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Angelo by Urban II. In the year 1118, he followed Callixtus II as he fled to France; and finally, after the death of Honorius II in 1130, he was elected Roman Pontiff by one faction of the Cardinals on February 17th and ordained on the 23rd. Meanwhile, another faction of Cardinals placed Cardinal Peter of Saint Mary—distinguished by the name Anacletus II—upon the papal throne. 

Innocent, ejected and excommunicated by Anacletus, fled to France, where he was recognized as the legitimate Pope by the French, English, and Germans, and was confirmed the following year at the Council of Reims. In the year 1133, having been restored to his seat by Lothair, King of Germany, he in turn surrendered the investitures <term>investiture: the formal ceremony where a king or lord presented a bishop with the symbols of spiritual office, a major point of conflict between Church and State</term> to him, and 

<margin>
Peter the Deacon, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book 4, Chapter 99.
</margin>

crowned him Emperor at Rome in the year 1137. Drawing Emperor Lothair to his cause, he waged war against Roger, King of Sicily, and seized Campania and Apulia from him. In 1139, having held a Council at Rome of about a thousand Bishops <note>This was the Second Lateran Council</note>, he excommunicated King Roger and the followers of Anacletus (who had died two years earlier), condemned the marriage of clerics, and enacted other ecclesiastical canons. In the same year, while leading an army against Roger, things went poorly; he was captured by the enemies and forced into unjust peace conditions. He died in the year 1143, on September 24th. There exist 43 Letters in the *Councils*, Volume X, page 946; five others in the same, page 1843; and two Letters in Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Volume II, page 198. Thirty-eight letters of the Antipope Anacletus, edited by Christianus Lupus, are found at the end of the *Ephesine Letters*, page 491.

### W R I T I N G S.

*History of the Church of Durham*, written on the authority of the elders, from King Oswald to the death of Bishop William—specifically from the year 635 to 1096. The illustrious <note>original: "Cl." for "Clarissimus"</note> [Roger] Twysden first brought this history to light among the *Ten English Writers* (London, 1652, p. 1). The illustrious [John] Selden, who provided the dissertation for this collection, attributes the work to Turgot, Prior of Durham. Certainly, our Simeon seems to have transcribed Turgot’s history in almost the same words, with very few changes; for this reason, the manuscript in the Cottonian Library <note>A famous collection of manuscripts now part of the British Library</note> bears Turgot’s name on the front. A continuation of this history from 1096 to 1154 is found in the same volume (p. 59), added by a later hand.

*Letter to Hugh, Dean of York, concerning the Archbishops of York*. It appears in the same volume (p. 75) and in Labbe's *New Library of Manuscripts*, Vol. I, p. 322, where the preface is missing in its entirety.

*A Brief Narrative on the Siege of Durham*, found in Twysden, as cited above, p. 79.

*History of the Kings of the English and Danes, in 2 books*, from the year 731 (where Bede's history ended) to the year 1130—namely, the end of the reign of Henry I. Roger Hoveden took almost everything from this work. It appears in the same volume (p. 85). John of Hexham, the Prior of Hexham <note>original: "Hagulstadiensis"</note> and a writer of the same period, continued this history for twenty-five years; it is published in the same work.

ALGER <note>Known as Alger of Liège</note>, first a deacon and schoolmaster <note>term: "Scholasticus" / a master of a cathedral school</note> of the Church of St. Bartholomew in Liège; then transferred to the Church of St. Lambert by Bishop Otbert. He devoted his efforts to ecclesiastical affairs for nearly twenty years until the death of Bishop Frederick. Finally, he embraced the monastic life in the Monastery of Cluny under Abbot Peter the Venerable. He flourished in 1130. He wrote: *Three Books on the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord* against Berengar <note>Berengar of Tours, whose views on the Eucharist were considered heretical by the medieval church</note>, which are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Vol. XXI, p. 251. *Three Books on Mercy and Justice*, of which Mabillon published the preface in the *Analecta*, Vol. I, p. 307, having promised to see to a new edition of the full work. *A Book on the Dignity or Antiquity of the Church of Liège*, of which only the memory remains.

WILLIAM, English by nation and from Somerset by country (hence called "Somerset" or "of Somerset"), a monk of the Order of St. Benedict at the Monastery of Malmesbury, librarian, and precentor. He flourished around the year 1130. He died in the year 1143. Concerning him, the most noble [Henry] Savile <note>A 16th-century English scholar and editor</note>—than whom no one could judge better—wrote: *"Among the oldest authors of our history, William of Malmesbury holds the chief place for both the reliability of his narrative and the maturity of his judgment; a man, for those times, literarily learned, who wove together the remaining seven hundred years, more or less, with such faith and diligence that he alone among our people seems to have fulfilled the duty of a historian."*

### W R I T I N G S.

*Five Books on the Deeds of the Kings of the English* from the first arrival of the Saxons to the twenty-eighth year of King Henry I, namely from 449 to 1127. Dedicated to Robert, Earl of Gloucester, the illegitimate son of Henry I.

*Two Books of Recent History* <note>original: "Historiae Novellae"</note> from 1127 to 1143, added later and dedicated to the same Robert.

*Four Books on the Deeds of the English Bishops* from the first arrival of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Canterbury</note> to his own time.

The most noble Savile collected these histories into one and saw to their publication (London, 1596, folio; reprinted at Frankfurt, 1601).
