<margin>1131.</margin>
**GRATIANUS**, a Tuscan by nationality from the city of Chiusi, was a Benedictine monk <note>original: "O. B." for Ordo Benedictinus</note> at the monastery of St. Felix in Bologna. He was a most learned interpreter of ecclesiastical law, for which reason he was called *Magister* <note>Master</note>. He flourished from the year 1131. There is no shortage of writers who claim that Gratian was the biological brother of Peter Lombard and Peter Comestor, and that their mother gave birth to these three brothers at once, having conceived them through an illicit affair; however, this claim is supported by no testimony from a sufficiently serious author.

Around the year 1151, Gratian wrote the *Collection of Canonical Decrees*, or the *Concord of Discordant Canons*. This was compiled from the sayings of the Holy Fathers, the canons of Synods, the forged Decretals of the Roman Pontiffs, and other pseudepigrapha <note>falsely attributed writings</note>, and was illustrated by him with brief scholarly notes. It is well known to everyone that he drew a great deal from the works of Ivo [of Chartres] and Burchard [of Worms]. 

The entire *Work* is completed in three parts. The first encompasses 101 *Distinctions*; the second contains 36 *Causes* <note>legal cases</note>, each cause containing various questions, and each question various chapters. To the 3rd question of the 33rd Cause is added a quite extensive *Treatise on Penance* containing seven Distinctions. The third part deals *with Consecration*, divided into five Distinctions—to say nothing of the *Palea* <note>literally "chaff"; these were later additions to Gratian's text</note> and other matters pertaining to this. 

Pope Eugene III immediately approved this work published by Gratian in 1151 and ordered it to be read publicly in the Universities. Various judgments regarding this work and its use by editors are provided by, among others, Gerhard von Mastricht in his *History of Ecclesiastical Law*, numbers 318, 319. Certainly, although it has been "purged" so many times by the Papists, Gratian still stands with the Reformers on many points of controversy; for this reason, he is often lashed <note>original: "vapulat," meaning criticized or attacked</note> by the theologians of the Roman Church. 

However, nothing contributes more to a useful understanding of Gratian’s work than the two books by Antonio Agustín *On the Emendation of Gratian*, especially the edition with the notes of [Etienne] Baluze (Paris, 1676, octavo). The first edition of Gratian’s Decrees appeared without the name of either Gratian or the location in 1472, folio; then at *Venice in 1479* and *Paris in 1508* (which was the first to bear Gratian's name). Since that time, it has been printed in countless places and instances in every edition of Canon Law, notably at *Rome in 1580, Paris in 1612, and Lyons in 1661, 2 volumes.*

<margin>History of Civil Law, Book 3, chapter 7, page 472.</margin> I will add only what Valentin Forster notes: that this work was compiled in the Church of Saint Felix, the memory of which is preserved to this day in Bologna at the Detronium near the Chapel of St. Sebastian with this inscription:

# The Waldensian Century #

->To God, the Best and Greatest<-
<margin>12th CENTURY from the year 1100.</margin>

The monument of **Gratian** of Chiusi, a nearly divine interpreter of Imperial and Pontifical Law, who was a monk in the monastery of the martyrs Saints Felix and Nabor. There, in the year of Grace 1152, he compiled that most perfect work, the *Decretum*. His memorial, which had grown filthy with decay and rubble, was here magnificently renewed and restored at public expense by Joannes Franciscus Aldobrandus of Bologna, the Fourth Dictator, on the Ides of June in the year of salvation 1498, while Giovanni Bentivoglio II, Father of the Fatherland, was happily governing the Republic.
<note>Gratian is considered the father of the study of Canon Law; his "Decretum" was the standard legal textbook for the Church for centuries.</note>

<margin>1132.</margin>
**STEPHEN**, Bishop of Paris; he flourished in the year 1132. Four years later, he was present at the deathbed of Louis the Fat, King of the Franks, and received his confession. Several of his letters are extant in [Luc d']Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, Volume III.

<margin>1134.</margin>
**MALACHY**, Irish by birth, called *Máel Máedóc Ua Morgair* in Irish, was born in the northern region of Ireland. He was a disciple of Imar, Abbot of Armagh, and later of Malchus, Bishop of Lismore. He restored the Monastery of Bangor in Ulster and presided over it after its restoration; soon he became Bishop of Connor, and then, in the year 1134, he was made Archbishop of Armagh. In the year 1137, he voluntarily resigned his see and set out for Rome, where he was appointed legate for Ireland by the Pope. In 1148, he traveled to Rome a second time, but having been seized by a fever, he died that same year on the 2nd of November in the Monastery of Clairvaux. He was very close with Saint Bernard, who wrote a biography of his life. There exists a *Prophecy regarding the future Roman Pontiffs*, with an exposition by [Alfonso] Chacón, found in Arnold Wion’s *Tree of Life*, Book 2, chapter 40. Regarding other writings of Malachy, please see the illustrious [James] Ware, *On Irish Writers*, Book 1, page 55, who has nearly the same information in his *Commentary on Irish Prelates*, page 14; see also [John] Bale, Century 14, page 239.
<note>Saint Malachy is famous for his friendship with St. Bernard of Clairvaux. The "Prophecy of the Popes" mentioned here is now widely considered by historians to be a late 16th-century forgery attributed to him.</note>

<margin>1135.</margin>
**ODDO**, Abbot of Saint-Remi at Reims; he flourished in the year 1135. The following year he returned from Italy, where he had traveled, and gave the land for the construction of the Carthusian house of Mont-Dieu. A letter exists regarding a certain miracle of Saint Thomas the Apostle in [Jean] Mabillon’s *Analecta*, Volume I, page 334.

<margin>1136.</margin>
**ULGERIUS**, Bishop of Angers; he flourished in the year 1136. His *Account to Pope Innocent II* on behalf of the Monastery of Roë is extant in [Étienne] Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Volume II, page 200.

<margin>1136.</margin>
**GEORGE**, Metropolitan of Corfu; he flourished around the year 1136. He was sent to Rome by Emperor Manuel Comnenus to celebrate a Council; however, hindered by illness, he stopped during the journey and stayed at Brindisi for six months. Soon he was recalled by the Emperor to participate in the Patriarchal Synod held at Constantinople. Leo Allatius deals more fully with him and his books against the Latins, both in his *Discourse on the Georges and their writings*, page 339, and in *On Consent*, Book 2, chapter 11, section 6. For he wrote a *Compendium against the Latins on the fire of Purgatory*, a fragment of which is cited by the same Allatius in *Dissertation II on the books of the Greek Churches*, page 134. Also a *Commentary against the Latins*, in which he strove to prove that the Apostles and the primitive Church used only leavened bread for the Eucharist. Both works exist in Greek in the Barberini Library. There is also a *Monody* <note>a funeral lament</note> on the death of Nectarius, Abbot of the Monastery of Casole, available in Latin in [Caesar] Baronius under the year 1180. He also wrote many letters, which Federico Muzi, Bishop of Termoli, translated into Latin; Baronius published some of these in Volume XII, specifically for the years 1176, 1178, 1179, 1180, and 1188—though many were suppressed which would undoubtedly illustrate the history of this century in no small measure.

In the year 1150, he was appointed Prior of that same monastery, and six years later, he was made Abbot of the Convent of L'Aumône <note>original: "Eleemosyna" — a Cistercian monastery in the Diocese of Chartres</note>, a house of the Cistercians <term>Cistercians</term> <note>a Catholic religious order of monks and nuns that branched off from the Benedictines, emphasizing manual labor and self-sufficiency</note> in the Diocese of Chartres. <margin>1137.</margin>
**PETER**, a Roman by birth and son of Aegidius, was born in the year 1110. As a boy of only five years, he was committed to the discipline of the monks of Monte Cassino <note>the famous hilltop monastery in Italy founded by St. Benedict</note>. For eight years, he was educated by Abbot Girard, from whom he had received the Benedictine habit. He later became a Deacon of the Church of Ostia and the Librarian of the monastery of Monte Cassino. He flourished in the year 1137, when he was sent as a legate <note>original: "legatus" — an official representative or messenger</note> by Emperor Lothair to the monks of Monte Cassino to remind them to conduct themselves with modesty. Later, sent back to Lothair by the monks of Monte Cassino, he was admitted into the imperial court, employed in secret affairs, and made Chaplain to the Roman Emperor. He was also appointed Logothete <term>Logothete</term> <note>a title for a high-ranking administrative official, often acting as a secretary or chancellor</note>, as well as a notary and auditor of the same court. It is not clear in what year he died.

->WRITINGS.<-

*A book on the illustrious men of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*. It was published together with the supplement by Placidus of Rome, likewise a monk and deacon of Monte Cassino, with notes by J. Bapt. Marus, Rome 1655; and in the *Library of the Fathers* [Bibliotheca Patrum], Volume XXI, page 347, Paris 1666, in octavo format.

*The fourth book of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, containing the history of the monastery from the year 1086 (where Leo of Ostia left off) to the year 1138. It has been printed many times along with the first three books of the Chronicle.

*A book on Roman shorthand* <term>notis literarum Romanarum</term> <note>These "notes" refer to Tironian notes, an ancient system of shorthand used by Roman scribes and revived in the Middle Ages.</note> dedicated to Emperor Conrad, first published in Venice in 1525, and later in Hanau among the authors of ancient grammar edited by Elias Putsch.

Peter lists countless other small works he composed in chapter 68 of book 4 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, namely: *Miracles of the Monks of Monte Cassino. Which of these survive, and which—along with other works of our Peter that remain unpublished—are kept today in the library of Monte Cassino, J. B. Marus will demonstrate in a long series of notes. Generally, they consist of letters, festival sermons, lives, scholia, consular records, and records of emperors and popes, etc. The *Book on the Origin and Life of the Just of Monte Cassino*, and several other things which the aforementioned Marus lists individually.

## LUKE

## GUERRIC
Guerric was a disciple of Saint Bernard. He was formerly a Canon of Tournai and a schoolmaster before becoming the Abbot of the Monastery of Igny in the Diocese of Reims, of the Cistercian Order. Twenty-one Letters.

**PETER**, called **LOMBARD** from his homeland, a native of the city of Novara, commonly called the "Master of the Sentences," a Doctor of Paris in the School of Saint Genevieve, and a Canon of Chartres. He flourished in the year 1141. From being the President of the Parisian Schools, he was created Bishop of Paris in the year 1159; and he died on the 20th day of July in the year 1164. He is buried in the Church of Saint Marcellus, where his epitaph is read to this day:

->*Here lies Master Peter Lombard, Bishop of Paris, who composed the Book of Sentences, the Glosses on the Psalms, and the Epistles; his death occurred on the thirteenth day before the Calends of August.* <note>July 20th.</note><-

<margin>* These are found in Matthew Paris, *History of England*, page 138.</margin>
Against him, as if he were a heretic and a madman, Abbot Joachim of Fiore wrote a small book, as if Peter had handed down certain unsound teachings in his dogma concerning the Holy Trinity. Certainly, among other things, he asserted that Christ, *according to the fact that he is man, is not anything*; <note>This is the doctrine of "Christological Nihilianism," the idea that Christ’s humanity was a garment or instrument rather than a "thing" in the same way human persons are. It was a major point of 12th-century theological debate.</note> for which reason Pope Alexander III * issued letters from the Lateran Council held in the year 1179 to William, the Archbishop of Sens, so that, having called together the Bishops of his province, he might diligently inquire into this doctrine of Peter’s, ensure it was utterly abolished, and see to it that Christ—just as he is perfect God, so also perfect man, consisting of soul and body—be taught by the Masters and Scholars studying Theology in Paris.

### WRITINGS.

*The Four Books of Sentences*, in which the sum of Theology, collected from the writings of the Fathers and arranged into a scholastic method, is handed down. These appeared in Nuremberg, 1474; Venice, 1480, in folio; and with the conclusions of Henry of Gorkum, Basel, 1492, 1498, in folio; Nuremberg 1478, 1499, 1528 in octavo; Basel 1513; Paris 1564 in octavo; Louvain 1576 in quarto; Paris 1577 in octavo; and elsewhere very frequently. In composing this work of the *Sentences*, we are informed by John of Cornwall, a disciple of Lombard himself, that Lombard was significantly aided by the books of sentences of Peter Abelard. Others add that Lombard notably compiled the notebooks of a certain Master Bandinus, an obscure and almost unknown theologian. Bandinus wrote *Four Books of Theological Sentences*, which appeared through the care of Benedict Chelidonius at Vienna in 1519. An egg is not more like an egg than Lombard's *Sentences* are to Bandinus's work, except that Lombard is much more wordy. Which of the two copied the other is uncertain, nor is the dispute easily settled, even if there are those who would argue that Lombard took his material from Bandinus. See the things that the Famous Jacob Thomasius diligently collected on this matter of <term>literary plagiarism</term> <note>original: "Plagio literario"</note> from Section 493 to 502.

*Glosses, or Commentary on the Psalms of David*, Paris, 1541, in folio.

*Collectanea on all the Epistles of Saint Paul*, woven together from Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and other writers, Paris, 1535. All his works appeared in Nuremberg, 1478; Basel, 1486.

# The Waldensian Century #
<note>original: "Seculum Waldense" — A term used by the author to categorize the 12th century, named after the Waldensians, a reform movement that began in this era, though the figures listed here are largely part of the orthodox Church hierarchy.</note>

<margin>
12th Century
from the
year 1100.
</margin>
...or as others say, in 1180. Having become suspected by King Henry <note>Henry II of England</note> for defending the cause of <term>Becket</term> <note>Thomas Becket, the Archbishop of Canterbury who clashed with the King</note>, he retired to the monastery of Saint Victor near Paris; he died there on August 10, 1182. He wrote many sermons, letters, and epigrams, first published by Odo, son of Hadrian, in *Paris, 1585, 8vo*, and thereafter in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XXII, page 1304.* A short treatise of his addressed to Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, concerning the <term>Schism</term> <note>A split in the Church between rival claimants to the Papacy</note> between Innocent II and Peter Leone <note>the antipope Anacletus II</note> was published by D’Achéry in the *Spicilegium, Volume II.* His sermon in the Synod of Tours (where the antipope Victor and his supporters were excommunicated in the year 1163) is found in the *Councils, Volume X, page 1411.* Three of his letters to Philip, Abbot of Bonneval, are found among the works of Arnold at the end of the Oxford edition of *Cyprian*.

## CELESTINE II.
<margin>1143.</margin>
**CELESTINE II**, previously called Guido del Castello, a Tuscan by birth, was a Cardinal Priest of the Roman Church with the title of Saint Mark. In the year 1140, he was sent as a legate to Gaul by Innocent II, where he was sharply rebuked by Saint Bernard for granting protection to the heretic <term>Arnold of Brescia</term> <note>A radical reformer who called for the Church to renounce all property and political power</note>. In the year 1143, he was elected Roman Pontiff on September 26 and consecrated the following Sunday. He died on March 9, 1144. Three of his letters survive in the *Councils, Volume X, page 1031.*

## LUCIUS II.
<margin>1144.</margin>
**LUCIUS II**, previously called Gerard, a native of Bologna and son of Albert, was made Cardinal Priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem by Honorius II. He served as the Librarian of the Roman Church and was created Chancellor by Innocent II. In 1127, and again in 1135, he undertook a legation to Germany. In 1132, he was appointed governor of the city of Benevento by Innocent II, where he vigorously defended the city against the hostile attacks of King Roger of Sicily. He was elected Pope on March 12, 1144, and ordained on the 12th. He was greatly distressed by the citizens of Rome, who had completely cast off the "papal yoke" <note>This refers to the Roman Commune, which sought to strip the Pope of his temporal/political power over the city</note>; he most humbly sought military aid from Emperor Conrad via letters. He died on February 15, 1145. Ten of his letters survive in the *Councils, Volume X, page 1035*, and two others in Baluze’s *Miscellany, Volume II, page 218.*

## THOMAS, Abbot of Morigny
<margin>1144.</margin>
**THOMAS**, Abbot of Morigny, flourished in the year 1144. A single letter of his to Saint Bernard survives in Baluze’s *Miscellany, Volume IV, page 459.*

## AMEDEUS
<margin>1144.</margin>
**AMEDEUS**, of the Allobrogian people <note>From the region of Savoy</note>, was born to an illustrious family in the castle of Costa, not far from Vienne. He was a monk of the Cistercian monastery of Hautecombe, and later its Abbot. In the year 1144, he was appointed Bishop of the Church of Lausanne and named Chancellor of the Empire to Emperor Frederick. He died in 1158. There survive *Eight Homilies in Praise of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God* <note>original: "Deiparae" — literally "God-bearer"</note>, published through the care of Richard Gibbon at *Saint-Omer, 1613*; then at the end of the works of Saint Leo, *Lyon, 1633, folio*; and finally in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XX, page 1262.*

## OTHO, or OTTO
<margin>

**OTHO**, or **OTTO**, an Austrian by birth, was the son of Leopold, Margrave of Austria, and Agnes, the daughter of Emperor Henry IV. He was the maternal brother of Emperor Conrad III and Frederick, Duke of Swabia, and the full brother of Leopold of Bavaria and Henry of Austria. He was the paternal uncle of Emperor Frederick <term>Barbarossa</term> <note>original: "Aenobarbi" — Red-beard</note>. He was placed by his father Leopold in charge of the College of Klosterneuburg, which his father had recently built. However, he soon left that post and traveled to Paris to more fully study the elements of literature. Soon after, he was admitted into the Cistercian Order at the monastery of Morimond in Burgundy, serving first as a monk and then as Abbot. In 1138, he was recalled to Germany by his brother, Emperor Conrad, and was created Bishop of Freising in Bavaria; he was further named Chancellor and Prefect of the Archives. He flourished in the year 1144. In 1147, he took up the sign of the cross <note>meaning he joined the Crusades</note> and in the following year accompanied Conrad as he led an army into Palestine. After the year 1156, having set aside his episcopal duties, he retired again to the monastery of Morimond; he died there on September 21, 1158.
<margin>* On Eccl. Writers, folio 107.</margin>

## ROBERT PULLEYN, otherwise called PULLUS, an Englishman by nation,
was highly accomplished in every branch of literary knowledge and held a great reputation not only among his own people but also among foreigners. There are those who maintain he was the Archdeacon of the Church of Rochester, a fact which Richard Tillesley—himself an Archdeacon of Rochester—concludes with certainty both from the Register of the Church of Rochester and from a letter of Saint Bernard to be praised below. While a civil war was raging in England <note>The period of civil war between King Stephen and Empress Matilda, often called "The Anarchy" (1135–1153)</note>, he withdrew to France to escape the military clamor so hostile to the Muses <note>A poetic way of saying the war was bad for scholarly study</note>. At the University of Paris, he applied himself diligently to the study of literature for a long time. On this occasion, he entered into a friendship with Saint Bernard †, who extolled the man with wonderful praise and, through a letter sent to Ascelin, Bishop of Rochester, earnestly requested that Pulleyn might stay longer in Paris. 

Returning to his fatherland, he landed at Exeter and from there came to Oxford (to use the words of a certain anonymous writer * who continued the *Chronicle of Bede*). There, for five years, he lectured on the Holy Scriptures, which had fallen into neglect in England at that time because they had been disregarded by the scholars. Every Sunday, he preached the word of God to the people, and many profited from his teaching. He flourished especially around the year 1144. Our own writers, both published and in manuscript, consistently assign him to this age and time, regardless of what the French say, who refer him to the beginning of the following century. The French claim he was promoted to the Archbishopric of Rouen in 1208, that he took part in the expedition against the Albigensians in 1209, and finally died in 1221. Truly, I believe our own historians are far more safely trusted regarding English affairs and men than foreigners, to say nothing of the testimony of Bernard. Therefore, either the French are telling us dreams, or, as I consider more probable, this "Pullus" of whom they frequently speak must be a different person.

<margin>‡ Nomenclature of Cardinals, page 15.</margin>
<margin>† On the Bishops of England, part 2, page 162.</margin>
Meanwhile, two leading Frenchmen, * Louis Chasteigner de la Rochepozay and Jean Morin, support our side and place Pulleyn near the middle of this century. On account of the immense fame of his talent and learning, he was eventually summoned to Rome by Pope Innocent II, and in 1144 he was decorated with the dignity of Cardinal of the title of Saint Eusebius by Celestine II, Innocent's successor. Others add that he was made Chancellor of the Roman Church by Lucius II. Finally, mindful of his own university, he obtained from the Pope many charters and privileges for the protection and decoration of the University of Oxford. It is uncertain how long he lived; Francis † Godwin writes that he died around the year 1150, though whether he is correct is entirely unknown to me. 

He wrote *Eight Books of Sentences on the Trinity* <note>A "Book of Sentences" was a common medieval format for organizing theological topics and authorities</note>. A manuscript codex exists from the same century in which the author lived—that is, written more than 450 years ago—in the Library of Saint-Germain in the suburbs of Paris, from which Jean Morin produced several excerpts in his *On the Sacrament of Penance*, book 1, chapter 18. Our countryman James <note>Thomas James, the first librarian of the Bodleian</note> teaches us in his *Eclogues*, part 2, page 52, that it also existed in the private library of the Englishman Walter Cope. Finally, the entire work was published together with Peter of Poitiers by Hugo Mathout, a Benedictine of Paris, 1655, in folio. His sermons on the *Common of the Saints* <note>Standard liturgical readings for categories of saints</note> exist in manuscript in the Putean Codex, as Philippe Labbe testifies in his *New Library of Manuscripts*, page 28. About twenty sermons exist in manuscript in the Lambeth Library under this title: *Sermons of Robert Pulleyn, Chancellor of Rome*. The codex is very old and seems to have been written not long after the author’s lifetime. Other works are listed by Bale, Pits, and Rochepozay, the mere titles of which I do not have time to transfer here now.

...this disciple of <note>St. Bernard of</note> Clairvaux was elected Roman Pontiff on February 14, 1145, and ordained in the Monastery of Farfa on the 18th day of that month. Having been elected by Roman citizens who detested the papal rule (whom they call *Arnaldists* <note>Followers of Arnold of Brescia, a reformer who called for the Church to renounce political power and property</note>), he was immediately driven out of the City. By the end of the year, he regained the City and excommunicated Jordan, the Patrician of the Romans. Soon, however, he was put to flight again by Arnold and retreated to France. In the year 1148, at a Council held in Reims, he condemned <unclear>Eon</unclear> <note>Eon de l'Étoile</note>, a certain delusional heretic, as well as the errors of Gilbert de la Porrée. In the same year, he struck King Stephen of England with an anathema <note>an official exclusion or excommunication</note> because the King had harassed Theobald, the Archbishop of Canterbury, for having set out for the Council of Reims without his permission. In the year 1152, having entered into a peace agreement with the Romans, he returned to the City. He died at Tivoli on July 8, 1153. Sixty-six of his *Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils, Vol. X, p. 1046; five others ibid. p. 1846; and a single letter in Baluze’s Miscellany, Vol. II, p. 222.*

<margin>
1145.
</margin>
**GILBERT DE LA PORRÉE** <note>original: "Gilbertus Porretanus"</note>, an Aquitanian by birth and later from Poitiers, flourished in the year 1145. First the Rector of the School of Paris and a Canon of Poitiers, then from the year 1141 the Bishop of his home city of Poitiers, he was indeed a philosopher and a supreme theologian. However, he was accustomed—according to the testimony of <margin>* On the Deeds of Frederick, Book 1, ch. 46.</margin> Otto of Freising—to speak in a manner far beyond the common custom of men, owing to the greatness of his subtle intellect and the sharpness of his reasoning. Hence, in a certain assembly of the clergy of his diocese, when he mixed certain unsound dogmas regarding the Trinity into the sermon he was delivering, he was reported to Rome by two of his archdeacons, Arnaldus and Calo, on the grounds that his views were contrary to the doctrine of the Catholic Church, an appeal having been lodged. However, since Pope Eugenius was arriving in France at this very time, a Synod was held at Paris; in which, with Pope Eugenius presiding, Gilbert was accused of heresy but escaped censure through a cautious and orthodox interpretation of his own words. The following year, at the Council of Reims, the same case was argued again. Gilbert's dogmas were rejected, but he himself remained untouched <note>He was not personally condemned after agreeing to the Council's corrections</note>. He died on September 4, 1154. There exists a *Letter to Matthew, Abbot of St. Florentius*, in D'Achery’s appendix to the works of Guibert, p. 564. Gilbert wrote other things as well, namely a *Gloss on the Psalter*, which survives as a manuscript in Oxford in the Balliol College Library, Codex 35. At the end of the book, this note is added: *“Here ends the glossing of Master de la Porrée on the Psalter, which he himself recited before his Master, Anselm, in the land of Laon <note>original: "Emerderonis," likely referring to Anselm of Laon's school</note>.”* He also produced a brief *Commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul* and a *Work on the Trinity*, which <term>Oudin</term> <note>Casimir Oudin, a bibliographer of ecclesiastical writers</note> reports in his *Supplement, p. 421*, are extant as manuscripts in French libraries.

1148.
</margin>
**GEOFFREY** <note>original: "Gaufredus"</note>, a Monk of Clairvaux of the Cistercian Order, flourished in the year 1148, in which year he took part in the Council of Reims. After the passage of many years, having been requested by the Cardinal of Albano, he wrote a letter to him concerning the events that took place at the Council of Reims regarding the case of Gilbert de la Porrée; this letter is found among the Acts of the Council of Reims, *Collections of the Councils, Vol. X, p. 1121.*

**BURGUNDIO OF PISA** <note>original: "Joannes Burgundio"</note>, a citizen of Pisa, about whom we have said more above in the Appendix to Chrysostom. He flourished in the year 1148. In the year 1150, he took part in a Council at Rome. He died in the year 1194. Besides those writings we mentioned in the aforementioned place, in the year 1150 he translated from the Greek into the Latin language *John of Damascus’s Work on the Orthodox Faith*. That version exists in the Library of St. Benedict <note>Corpus Christi College</note> in Cambridge, Codex 135; at Merton College, Oxford, Codex 109; and at Elizabeth College. He also translated into Latin *eight books by Gregory of Emesa, or rather Nemesius, On Philosophy or On Man*; however, he did so so inelegantly, in the judgment of Beatus Rhenanus, that the version can be read but not understood. Nevertheless, that work was published at *Strasbourg in 1512 and elsewhere quite often*, after it had been purged of the unrefined and foul barbarity <note>referring to poor translation style</note> by Johannes Canon of Nuremberg and Beatus Rhenanus.

### GILBERT FOLIOT, English by nationality, formerly Abbot of Leicester; from the year 1149, Bishop of Hereford, and then from 1161, Bishop of London. In the year 1162, upon the death of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, he himself sought the Metropolitan see. When he failed in his wish—as <note>Thomas</note> Becket was preferred over him—he refused to promise canonical obedience to Becket by oath. Indeed, (if faith is to be placed in John of Salisbury, * who was too inclined toward Becket's cause), he even attempted to seize the primacy of England for the See of London, arguing that the dignity of the <term>Archflamen<note>In medieval legend, it was believed that Roman Britain had 'Archflamens' (high priests) whose seats became the centers of the Christian archdioceses; Foliot used this to claim London should be equal to Canterbury.</note></term> formerly placed in London belonged to him by hereditary right. This skirmish was followed by a more serious battle two years later, when Becket struggled to exempt the entire English Clergy from royal authority, while Gilbert adhered to the King's side with the greatest loyalty and constancy. Therefore, at the end of the year, sent as an ambassador to Rome by King Henry <note>Henry II</note>, he charged Becket with sedition before Pope Alexander <note>Alexander III</note>, strenuously defending his King’s cause. Having returned home, he was appointed to collect and manage the revenues of the Church of Canterbury. For this reason, he was immediately excommunicated by Becket, but he appealed to the Pope. Even when the censure was confirmed by the Pontiff, he cared for the "thunderbolt" <note>a metaphorical term for the power of excommunication</note> of neither man; and having called a Synod in London, he declared the sentence of both to be void. However, before the year 1170, having taken an oath before the Papal Legates, he was absolved from the <term>anathema<note>A formal curse by a pope or council, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine.</note></term>; shortly thereafter, he was again entangled by Becket because he had assisted at the coronation of the younger King Henry performed by the Archbishop of York. He was absolved a little later from the same by the prayers of King Henry upon the King's arrival in England. Finally, when he was falsely accused of entering a plan with the King to bring about the death of Becket, he again experienced the Papal anathema after Becket’s death. Nevertheless, having been absolved before his passing, he closed his final day on February 18, 1187. I shall only add the eulogy given to him by the Abbot of Ramsey in a letter written to Pope Alexander at the very time when the disputes in England were most fervent:

> *Our venerable Father Gilbert, Bishop of London, a man distinguished in merit and name among the chosen persons of our land, shines forth remarkably with a prerogative of virtues. Indeed, being perfectly educated <note>original: "ad unguem," a Latin idiom meaning "to the fingernail," implying high polish or precision</note> in secular literature and divine law, he is known to have reached and ascended almost every rank of both Religious life and Ecclesiastical order and dignity. Faithfully and prudently managing the governance of pastoral care, he passed with sufficient merit from the Monastery to the Cathedral, first of Hereford, then of London, illustrating and honoring both by his life and his teaching alike.*

He wrote a *Commentary on the Song of Songs*, which was published through the care of Patrick Young in London, 1638, in quarto format. *Seven Letters* of his are found among the letters of Thomas Becket, edited by Christian Lupus in Brussels, 1682.

### HENRY OF HUNTINGDON, English by birth, son of Nicholas, a married priest, a disciple of Albinus of Angers, Canon of Lincoln; he was himself also a Canon of Lincoln, and finally made Archdeacon of Huntingdon by Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln, whom he had accompanied as far as Rome. He flourished in the year 1150. It is not clear how long he extended his life. He wrote to Alexander of Lincoln a *History of the English* from the very origins of the nation until the death of King Stephen in the year 1154, in *eight books*; or as others distribute the work, ten. This history was published among the English Writers by the illustrious Savile in London, 1596, in folio, and was reprinted from there in Frankfurt in 1601. D’Achéry published *Henry's Letter, or the Booklet on the Contempt of the World*, in his *Spicilegium*, Vol. VIII, p. 178. Henry composed other works as well, namely: the *Letter to Warin on the Kings of the Britons*, and a *Small Work on the Provinces of Britain*, preserved in the public library of Cambridge, Code 251, numbers 9 and 10. The *Book on the Image of the World*, in the College of Saint Benedict, Cambridge, Code 367, num. 1; and in Magdalen College, Oxford, Code 17, num. 1; and Trinity College, Oxford, Code 7, num. 2. The *Book on the Saints of England*, in the Jesuit College at Antwerp, as Heribert Rosweyde testified in letters given to Pits. Certain *other* works are listed by Bale and Pits, though it is not established whether they survive today.

**JOHN**, a former monk of the island of Oxia who became the Patriarch of Antioch, flourished around the year 1150, according to the judgment of Cotelerius. **AILRED**, or Ealred, or Ælred, an Englishman—or was he Scottish? ## RICHARD, a Scot by nationality, a Canon Regular of Saint Victor near the walls of Paris, and finally Prior; a close friend of Saint Bernard and Hugh of Saint Victor. He flourished in the year 1150. He died in the year 1173, on the 10th of March <note>original: "VI. Id. Mart.", the sixth day before the Ides of March.</note>, after he had performed the office of Prior for nine years.

### WORKS.

*Treatise on the extermination of evil and the promotion of good.*

*Three Treatises on the state of the inner man.*

*Three books on the instruction of the inner man.*

Richard also wrote *one book of mystical explanation on the whole of Daniel*, a large part of which Godefridus Tilmannus appended to his compendium of *Allegories on Daniel*.

<margin>1151.</margin>
### ALAIN DE LILLE, <note>original: "Alanus de Insulis," also known as the "Universal Doctor."</note> a Gallo-Flemish man by birth and a citizen of Lille, led a monastic life in the Monastery of Clairvaux, and was soon made Abbot of the newly founded Monastery of Ripé in the Diocese of Troyes. In the year 1151, he was created Bishop of Auxerre, but growing weary of the labors, he resigned his see in the year 1167. Returning to Clairvaux, he died there in the year 1182. He wrote a brief *Life of St. Bernard*, which Jean Mabillon praised and placed at the beginning of his edition of Bernard’s works (*Paris, 1666*). We shall deal with Alain de Lille the younger in his proper place.

---

<margin>
1151.
* Annals, latter part, folio 311.
</margin>
### GEOFFREY, also called ARTHUR, <note>original: "Galfridus, Arthurus cognomento dictus." He is the primary source for the legends of King Arthur.</note> a Briton by birth, and of the house of Monmouth, as it appears, being certainly the Archdeacon of that same Church. In the year 1151, he was appointed Bishop of St. Asaph. Due to the disturbances in Wales, so that he might better provide for himself elsewhere (if indeed this is the same Geoffrey, Bishop of St. Asaph, of whom Roger of Hoveden speaks, which seems entirely probable), he withdrew into England. He was kindly received by King Henry, who handed over to his custody the Monastery of Abingdon, which was then without an abbot. In the year 1175, at a Synod held in London, the clergy of the Church of St. Asaph petitioned the Archbishop of Canterbury that either Geoffrey be restored to his church or another be substituted in his place. Constrained by that dilemma, Geoffrey voluntarily resigned the Bishopric, hoping that he would retain the governance of his Monastery; but he lost both. For Master Adam received the See of St. Asaph, and the Monastery of Abingdon was given to a certain monk. The exact time of his death is not certain. Many authors, both ancient and modern, have attacked Geoffrey’s credibility as a historian, and they weigh him down with a rather unfair judgment. Many things in his work seem unbelievable to us, as they are most distant from our own times and foreign to the customs of our age and nation; yet even if many things are conceded to be fabulous, he did not immediately devise them out of his own wit, but drew them from more ancient monuments of British affairs. While presiding under Robert, Duke of Gloucester, he wrote the *History of Britain in twelve books*, from the very first beginnings of the race down to his own times. This *History* was published at *Paris, 1517, in quarto*, and among the minor writers of Britain at *Heidelberg, 1587, in folio*. Furthermore, he translated from the British tongue into Latin—though adding many things of his own, if William of Newburgh is to be believed—the *ancient Prophecies of the British Merlin*. This version was published together with the explanations of Alain de Lille at *Frankfurt, 1603, in quarto*. A Letter to *Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln, regarding the Prophecies of Merlin* is held in manuscript in the Cottonian Library under Cleopatra c. 10. n. 2. There is also a *Life of Merlin* in not unpolished heroic verse addressed to Robert, Bishop of Lincoln, in manuscript under Vespasian E. 4. n. 5.

<margin>* Century 2, chapter 86.</margin>
Bale mentions other writings of Geoffrey still, namely: *A book on the exile of ecclesiastics; On the body and blood of the Lord; A book of Poems*, etc., which seem to have perished.

# The Waldensian Century #

<margin>
12th CENTURY from the year 1100.
1152.
</margin>
**POTHO**, a Priest and Monk of the Order of Saint Benedict <note>original: "O. B."</note> at the Monastery of Prüm in the Diocese of Trier, was prominent in the year 1152. Five of his books survive *On the State of the House of God*, as well as a single volume *On the House of Wisdom*, published at Hagenau in 1532 in octavo, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 21, page 489.

<margin>
1152.
</margin>
**NICHOLAS**, a Monk of Clairvaux of the Cistercian Order, whose elegant style so recommended him to Saint Bernard that he served as his secretary <note>original: "ab Epistolis," literally "for the letters."</note>; however, when it was discovered that he had forged letters under Bernard’s name and protected them with Bernard's own seal—and being not innocent of other crimes—he fled from Bernard’s company and went to Italy. There, he did not blush to attack Saint Bernard most bitterly. He was most prominent around the year 1152 and is said to have lived a long life thereafter. He wrote a *Book of Letters*, which is held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 21, page 517, and a *Book of Sermons* dedicated to Henry, Count of Champagne, which is found in the *Cistercian Library*, Volume 3, page 193. Two of his letters, previously unpublished, were provided by Baluze in his *Miscellany*, Volume 2, page 234.

<margin>
1153.
</margin>
**ANASTASIUS IV**, previously called Conrad, a Roman by birth from the Saburra district and son of Benedict, was a Canon Regular and Abbot of the Monastery of St. Anastasius in the Diocese of Velletri. A member of the Order of Saint Augustine <note>original: "O. A."</note>, he was a Cardinal and Bishop of Sabina before the year 1130, at which time Pope Innocent, fleeing Rome, appointed him Vicar of the city. On July 9, 1153, he was elected Roman Pontiff and crowned on the 12th. He died the following year on December 2. Thirteen of his letters survive in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 10, pages 1133 and 1851.

<margin>
1154.
* Chronicle, p. 221.
</margin>
**ADRIAN IV**, previously named Nicholas Breakspear, was English by nationality and a native of Hertfordshire, born in Langley not far from the shrine of Saint Alban, the son of Robert, a monk and priest. Having reached adulthood, he sought a place for himself in the Monastery of St. Albans but was rejected by Abbot Richard. Failing in his wish, he went to France and for some time applied himself to the study of literature in Paris. Later, in the Monastery of Saint Rufus near the city of Valence, he joined the Augustinian Monks, soon becoming Prior and finally being appointed Abbot of the monastery. In time, having traveled to Rome to manage the affairs of the monastery, he was created Cardinal and Bishop of Albano by Eugenius III. In the year 1148, sent as Apostolic Legate to the regions of Norway and Denmark, he honored the Church of Uppsala with archiepiscopal rights. On December 4, 1154, he was elected Roman Pontiff and enthroned on the 5th. In the year 1155, he excommunicated the Roman "Arnoldists" <note>Followers of the reformer Arnold of Brescia.</note> and expelled them from the city, after Arnold, the Bishop of Brescia himself, was executed on a cross; he also struck William, King of Sicily, with anathema for devastating the borders of Campania. That same year, meeting Frederick, King of the Romans <note>The Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I "Barbarossa."</note>, as he arrived in Italy, Adrian denied him the kiss of peace until Frederick performed the customary duty of a groom <note>original: "stratoris officium," the ceremonial act of holding the Pope's stirrup.</note> for him; shortly thereafter, having led him to Rome, he invested him with the imperial crown. In 1156, besieged by King William in the city of Benevento, he was forced to submit to unfair peace conditions. He died of a throat infection <note>original: "anginae morbo."</note>, or as others say, choked by a fly, at Anagni on September 1, 1159, shortly after he had—if Urspergensis* is to be believed—just excommunicated Emperor Frederick. Dying with a rare example of self-denial, he recommended his mother be supported by the alms of the Church of Canterbury. Forty-two of his letters survive in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 10, pages 1143 and 1853, and two letters in Baluze's *Miscellany*, Volume 2, page 223.

<margin>
1154.
</margin>
**ELIZABETH**, German by nationality, was the Abbess of Schönau of the Order of Saint Benedict <note>original: "O. B."</note> near the Monastery of St. Florin (where Elizabeth’s brother, Ecbert, presided) in the Diocese of Trier. She was renowned for her revelations and visions. She was prominent in the year 1154 and died on June 18 in the year of Christ 1165, at the age of 36. Three books of her *Visions* or *Revelations* exist, along with one book of *Letters*, printed in Cologne in 1628.

**ECBERT**, a German by birth and brother of the aforementioned Elizabeth <note>Elizabeth of Schönau, a famous mystic mentioned on the previous page.</note>, was a Monk and Priest of Bonn, and later the second Abbot of Saint Florin of Schönau. He flourished in the year 1154 and thereafter, surviving his sister. There survive thirteen *Sermons against the Cathars* <note>The Cathars were a dualist Christian sect prominent in the 12th and 13th centuries, often targeted by the Church as heretics.</note> along with an excerpt from Saint Augustine *Against the Manichaeans*, found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 23, pages 600 and 631. The *Life and Death of his sister Elizabeth*, which he described, is prefixed to the edition of Elizabeth’s small works published in Cologne in 1628. He also wrote several *Letters*, from which certain excerpts are held in the *Catalog of the Witnesses of Truth* <note>original: "catalogus testium veritatis"</note> on page 393. Simler mentions other works which can be seen in his own writing on page 177.

---

<margin>1155.</margin>

**LUKE**, surnamed Chrysoberges, formerly a monk, became the Patriarch of Constantinople from the year 1155 according to the succession of Freher, though according to Baronius it was from 1148. In the year 1166, he held a Synod in Constantinople. He died the following year. Twelve *Synodal Decrees* survive in Greek and Latin, namely: *That marriages of the seventh degree of kinship should not occur; Concerning Clergy involving themselves in secular business; That an irregular oath should not be kept; Concerning the baptism of captive infants; Concerning the Hagarenes* <note>original: "De Agarenis." A medieval term for Muslims, referring to the descendants of Hagar.</note>, etc., found in Leunclavius’s *Greco-Roman Law*, book 3, page 217.

---

<margin>1155.</margin>

**BASIL OF ACHRIDA**, Metropolitan of Thessalonica, flourished in the year 1155. In that year, when Pope Hadrian [IV] urged him by letter to renounce the Greek schism and submit himself to the authority of the Roman Church, he responded that the Greek Church was not schismatic, nor was the Roman Church its superior. His *Letter to Hadrian* survives (along with Hadrian's letter) in Latin in Baronius under the year 1155, and in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law*, book 5, page 307. Also found is his *Response to questions regarding certain marriages*, Greek and Latin, in the same work, page 309; see also page 408, where the same response is held, though not in the exact same words.

---

<margin>1156.</margin>

**ANDRONICUS CAMATERUS**, Prefect of the city of Constantinople and Grand Drungary of the Watch <note>original: "magnus Viglæ Drungarius," a high-ranking Byzantine official in charge of the judicial and military guard.</note>, a *Sebastos* <note>A high Byzantine court title meaning 'Venerable.'</note>, and a relative of the Emperor Manuel himself. He was an "admirable man," as Veccus himself admits, and "one displaying no small strength of speech" <note>original: "θαυμαστὸς ἀνὴρ... καὶ λόγων ἰσχὺν ἐπιδεικνύμενος ὅτε μικρὸν"</note>. He flourished around the year 1156, which makes me wonder what Casimir Oudin was thinking when he pushed him down to the year 1330 and claimed he wrote against Veccus. On the contrary, it is abundantly clear that John Veccus, who only flourished in the year 1274, wrote *against* our Andronicus, speaking of him as someone much older than himself. He wrote a book against the Latins under the character of the Emperor Manuel, or rather a *Dialogue*—with the Emperor and the Roman Cardinals then staying in Constantinople as the speakers—concerning the *Procession of the Holy Spirit* <note>The "Filioque" controversy regarding whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son.</note>, to which Veccus later responded. He also wrote on the *Dispute of the Emperor with Peter, the teacher of the Armenians*, and a small book on the *Two Natures in Christ*, as well as other chapters. These books are said to exist as manuscripts in the Bavarian Library, Codex 120.

**RALPH THE BLACK** <note>original: "Radulphus Niger"</note>, a Monk of Saint-Germer-de-Fly <note>original: "Flaviacenfis, feu Flaicenfis"</note> in the territory of Beauvais, of the Order of Saint Benedict, flourished not in the tenth century as has been believed until now, but in the year 1157, as Labbé proves at greater length in a dissertation against Maresius *. He wrote *Twenty books of Commentaries on Leviticus* with great eloquence and erudition. These are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 17, page 48. The *Commentaries on the Song of Songs* (wrongly attributed to Saint Gregory) were restored to Ralph and published under his name by Jacques Hommey in the *Supplement of the Fathers*, Paris, 1684. He is also said to have written *Fourteen books of Commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul*, a *History of the Franks*, a *Brief Chronicle*, and several other works which no longer survive.

<margin>1159.</margin>
## ALEXANDER III

Formerly named Rolando, a Tuscan by nationality from the city of Siena, the son of Rainuitius. He was first a Canon of the Church of Pisa, then called to Rome by Eugene III and made Cardinal Deacon with the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, soon after a Priest with the title of Saint Mark, and finally made Chancellor of the Apostolic See. In the year 1156, he was sent as a legate by Hadrian to William, King of Sicily, an enemy of the Pope, and arranged a peace of sorts. In the year 1157, he was sent by the same Pope to Emperor Frederick <note>Frederick I, known as "Barbarossa"</note> to deliver most insolent letters; he risked his life and was sent away with ignominy. In the year 1159, on the 7th day of September, he was elected Roman Pontiff, but was driven out of Rome by Cardinal Octavian, the Antipope <note>A person who claims the papacy in opposition to the one canonically chosen</note> called *Victor*, and was ordained at Nympha on the 20th of the same month. With the bolt of excommunication hurled by both sides, and the Christian world split into schisms, the Emperor called the Council of Pisa <note>Historically the Council of Pavia, though "Pisanum" is written here</note> in the year 1160 to judge the cause. In that council, by the common consent of the Bishops, Victor was confirmed, while Alexander was rejected and excommunicated. Alexander, in turn, excommunicated both the Emperor and the Fathers of the Council. In the year 1162, fleeing Italy because of Emperor Frederick, he withdrew to France, invited by King Henry of England and King Louis of France; in the following year, he presided over the Council of Tours. In the year 1165, after the death of Victor, he returned to Rome, but was driven out again by the Emperor in 1167. In the following year he regained Rome, and having gathered the Lateran Council, he struck the Emperor with another bolt of excommunication. In the year 1177, with the help of the Venetians, he forced the Emperor into harsh conditions for peace and absolved him from censure—but only after first placing his feet upon the neck of the Emperor as he prostrated himself on the ground, adding those words from the Psalter: *You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.* <note>Psalm 91:13. This famous scene in Venice symbolized the triumph of papal authority over imperial power.</note> In the year 1179, having convened a General Council in Rome, he decreed that full remission of sins be granted to the persecutors of heretics. He died in the year 1181, on the 25th of August. There survive *337 Letters, Council Volume 10, page 1188; four others in the same, page 1854; you may find his constitutions in the same, page 1135; four Letters in Baluze's Miscellany, Volume 2, page 227; two Letters in the same, Volume 4, page 466; and a Letter to Athalaudus concerning the Schism of that time, in the Library of the Fathers, Volume 24, page 1519.*

<margin>1160.</margin>
## GERVASIUS,

English by birth, from the house of Chichester, and a Priest by rank. He flourished in the year 1160, a man most celebrated in his time for learning; he also stirred up a great reputation for himself at the University of Paris. He had Archbishop Thomas Becket as a friend and patron, who treated him with great familiarity. He wrote, among other things, *Commentaries on Malachi*, which were kept privately in the Lumley Library, according to the testimony of James in *Eclogues, book 2, page 32.*

<margin>
1160.
* Concerning English Writers, page 226.
</margin>
## ODO,

English by nationality, a native of Kent, and Prior of the Monastery of Canterbury, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and (if Pits * is to be believed) eventually Abbot of the Monastery of Battle. He flourished (he did not die, as Pits says) in the year 1160. There survives a *Letter to Adam of Igny, a certain novice brother* (in which he holds certain absurd and almost blasphemous views concerning Saint Benedict and his order, attributing to him things that are said specifically <note>original: "ἰδικῶς"</note> of Christ in Holy Scripture), found in Mabillon's *Analects, Volume 1, page 349.* Some letters by this Odo, it seems, are found in D'Achery's *Spicilegium, Volume 2.*

## BERTRANDUS,

A monk, it seems, of Chaise-Dieu in the mountains of Auvergne; he flourished in the year 1160. There survives a *three-part book on the life, conduct, and miracles of Saint Robert, Abbot and first founder of Chaise-Dieu*, in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts, Volume 2, page 637.*

## PETER OF BLOIS,

Called such from his place of birth, a Frenchman by nationality. From being a Canon of Bourges, he became Archdeacon of Bath, and later Archdeacon of London in England

<margin>1160.</margin>JOHN OF HEXHAM, an Englishman by nation, born at Hexham in the territory of the Northumbrians, a Monk of the Augustinian Order, and Prior of the Monastery of Hexham <note>original: "Hagulstadensis"; the ancient name for Hexham</note>; he flourished in the year 1160. Severe in countenance, honest in character, an eminent lecturer on the arts and history in his Monastery. He continued the *History* of Simeon of Durham for 25 years, from the year 1129 to the year 1154. That *Continuation* exists among the *Ten English Writers* edited by Twysden in London, 1652, page 257. Bale <margin>* Century 3, chapter 31.</margin> recounts other writings of John, namely: *A Book on signs and Comets, a Description of the Scottish war, and several Sermons*, which today are found nowhere.

<margin>1160.</margin>FOLMAR, Prior, as I believe, of the Monastery of "Stone-Dripping" <note>original: "Petra Stillante"</note>, or Triefenstein in Franconia below Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipolim"</note>; he flourished (if it be permitted to guess in an obscure matter) around the year 1160. He attacked the common doctrine of the Church in this century regarding the body and blood of the Lord. There exists on this matter a *Letter to Eberhard, Bishop of Salzburg*; also another in which he revokes his opinion, along with several others addressed to Folmar, or given concerning him, by Jacob Gret- <note>The text cuts off mid-name, likely referring to the Jesuit scholar Jacob Gretser</note>

<margin>THE 12TH CENTURY, from the Year 1100.</margin>

**ADAM**, a Scot by nationality, a Canon Regular of the Premonstratensian Order <note>The Premonstratensians, or Norbertines, are a religious order of canons regular founded in 1120</note>; he flourished around the year 1160. He is said to have died around the year 1180.

### W O R K S.

Commentary on the Rule of Saint Augustine.
*Treatise on the Triple Tabernacle of Moses.*
*Book on the three types of contemplation.*
*47 Sermons on various subjects.*

These minor works were published in *Antwerp, 1659, in folio.* Previously, the two middle treatises and 14 sermons regarding the order and habit of the Premonstratensians were published in *Paris, 1518, in folio.*

Casimir Oudin, himself a Premonstratensian, confirms in his *Supplement, p. 442*, that 53 other sermons and a *Soliloquy on the Soul* exist in manuscript at the Celestines of Mantes.

---

<margin>1160.</margin>
**MICHAEL**, a native of Thessalonica, Master of Rhetoricians, and *Protecdicus* <note>original: "Protecdicus"; a high-ranking legal and administrative official in the Byzantine Church</note> of the Great Church; he flourished around the year 1160. Condemned for the Bogomil heresy <note>The Bogomils were a dualist sect in the Byzantine Empire that rejected the material world and much of the church hierarchy</note>, he renounced it toward the end of his life. Indeed, this heresy was almost identical to that of the Messalians, except that he added many absurdities and delusions; for example, that only seven books of Holy Scripture were to be received; and that the use of churches, the Eucharist, the Cross, and prayers (except for that single one, the *Our Father*) should be abolished. He claimed that the baptism of Catholics was imperfect, and that the followers of his sect could be called "God-bearers" <note>original: "Deiparos"</note>. He also taught that the persons of the Holy Trinity were unequal, and that they frequently revealed themselves to him to be seen. A brief confession of our Michael exists in Leo Allatius’s *On Consent, book 2, chapter 12, final section.*

---

<margin>1160.</margin>
**JOHN KINNAMOS**, so named by surname, Grammarian or notary of the Emperor Manuel [I Komnenos]; he flourished in the year 1160. Under Manuel Komnenos, he enlisted in military service from his very youth and, as he testifies of himself in the Preface, took part in various expeditions both to Europe and the East. He was still among the living in the year 1183, when Andronicus Komnenos—having killed Alexios and seized power—besieged Lopadium in Bithynia. After the death of Manuel, he applied his mind to writing and composed the *History* of the two Komnenoi, John and his son Manuel; narrating the deeds of the former briefly and summarily, but those of the latter at length and in detail, covering the actions of both from the year 1118 to 1176. <margin>* Dissertation on the writings of Simeon, p. 150.</margin> "An elegant author," says Leo Allatius*, "if ever there was one; in his manner of speaking he often uses foreign terms and figures from the storehouse of the Sophists. His periods are concise and full, unless they are made harsh and obscure by novelty of composition. In a word, to summarize, he models himself entirely after Procopius <note>A prominent 6th-century Byzantine historian</note>. And it is a wonder that among so many other writers of a later age, who rave haphazardly in speaking and writing, this man alone possessed such taste." <margin>† On Greek Historians, book 4, chapter 19.</margin> G. J. Vossius† says likewise: "His diction is purer and more polished than that of other Greek writers <note>original: "Græculorum"; literally "little Greeks," a term used here by Vossius to contrast Kinnamos's high style with the perceived decay of other medieval Greek writers</note>; indeed, he is a rival of Xenophon himself, whom he praises in the Preface. He is faulted for having exceeded moderation in praising Manuel. He praises him, certainly, but within the limits of modesty, and does not flatter; surely he removes all suspicion of flattery from himself when he declares that, from his infinite character and the very guidance of nature, he cannot utter even a word voluntarily or knowingly unless it be as true as it is free." <margin>* History, book 5, chapter 1.</margin> Cornelius Tollius first published this history, divided into four books, from Isaac Vossius's copy with Greek and Latin notes at *Utrecht in 1652, in quarto.* Charles du Fresne [Du Cange] published the same divided into six books with a translation and historical and philological notes at *Paris in 1670, in folio.*

---

<margin>1161.</margin>
**FASTRED**, Abbot of Clairvaux; he flourished in the year 1161, during which he attended the Synod of Toulouse. At this council, the antipope Victor [IV] was rejected, and Alexander [III] was recognized as the rightful pope.

<margin>1162.</margin> ### JOHN BELETH,
Rector of the Parisian School of Theology, appears to have flourished around the year 1162. There are others, namely Claude Joly, Canon of Paris, and Casimir Oudin, who trace him back to the year 1124: which indeed must seem strange, since Henry of Ghent, who wrote in the year 1280, listed him among the first writers in his Catalog. There exists his *Rationale of Divine Offices* <note>original: "Rationale Divinorum Officiorum"; a standard medieval reference for the symbolic meaning of church rituals</note>, published in *Antwerp, 1553, 1570, in octavo; Lyon 1583;* and with Durandus <note>William Durandus was another influential liturgical writer whose works were often bundled with Beleth's</note> *in the same place, 1592, in octavo, p. 922.*

---

<margin>1162.</margin> ### ARNOLD,
or Ernald, Abbot of Bonneval of the Order of St. Benedict <note>O.B. stands for "Ordo Benedictinus"</note> in the Diocese of Chartres, hence called "the Chartresian." He was still living in the year 1162. He was an intimate friend of Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux, the influential Cistercian leader</note> while he was still alive.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

<margin>1162.</margin> **T**reatise on the Seven Words spoken by the Lord on the Cross. Published separately with the commentaries of Fr. Titelmann, *Antwerp, 1532, in octavo.*

*Treatise on the Works of the Six Days*, edited by the care of Denis Perronet, published at *Geneva <note>original: "Aureliæ Allobrogum"</note> 1609, in octavo.*

*Sermon on the praises of the Holy Virgin Mary.* These three short works are contained in the *Library of the Fathers <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patrum"</note> Vol. XXII. p. 1280.*

*Treatise on the Principal Works of Christ*, which is usually placed among the works of Cyprian, having been attributed to him.

*Various Meditations.* All the works enumerated so far, collected into one and restored to their true author, were published at the end of the Works of St. Cyprian, *Oxford 1682, in folio.*

Of the five books on the *Life of St. Bernard*, which are usually added to his collected works, Arnold is the author of the second and <unclear>fourth</unclear> books.

His *Brief Commentary on Psalm 44* and a *Short Work on the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit* exist in manuscript in the possession of Jean Mabillon <note>A famous Benedictine scholar and monk of the 17th century</note>.

<margin>1162.</margin> ### THOMAS BECKET,
an Englishman by birth, from the city of London, the son of Gilbert the merchant and a mother of Syrian nationality. Having been educated in the first elements of letters by the Prior of Merton, he further pursued his literary studies first at Oxford, then at Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note>. Having returned to England, he was admitted into the household of Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury; soon after, he was sent by the Archbishop to Bologna, so that he might learn the science of Canon Law there. Returning again, he was gifted with the Archdeaconry of Canterbury, the provostship of Beverley, the Rectories of Bromfield and St. Mary’s Mount, and likewise two prebends, one at St. Paul’s and the other at Lincoln. Soon admitted to the Court, he was created High Chancellor of England, and after the death of Theobald, he was elevated to the throne of Canterbury in the year 1162, consecrated on the very day of Pentecost. 

Having attained the highest dignity of the English Church, this man—ambitious and defiant even to the point of wonder—dreamed of nothing except ecclesiastical liberties and the authority of the Roman See; so much so that he strove with all zeal to exempt the whole English clergy from any royal power whatsoever and to subject them to the Pope. For since the clerics were everywhere committing homicides and other outrages of that kind, the King wished for the ancient customs of the kingdom to be maintained, so that all the guilty, of whatever rank, might be restrained and punished by the royal judges. Thomas, on the contrary, contended that clerics were free from all royal power and subject to the Roman Pontiff alone. Nevertheless, at the Synod of Clarendon indicted the following year, he himself, having hesitated for a long time, finally yielded to the truth and confirmed the royal customs with his signature and appended seal. But a little later, the most fickle man, repenting of his deed, obtained absolution for himself from the Pope as if he had been entangled in the gravest crime; and having planned a flight and being brought back from it in vain, he was accused of embezzlement <note>original: "peculii"</note>, perjury, and treason at the Council of Northampton; and he was condemned by the bishops, although he appealed to the Pope.

<header>The Waldensian Century.</header>

Dismissed from the council, he once again attempted flight; and crossing over into Belgium, he retreated from there to Pope Alexander, who was then staying at Sens. There, he immediately launched an excommunication <note>original: "anathema confestim vibravit"; literally "brandished a curse"</note> against all observers of the *Constitutions of Clarendon* <note>term: Constitutions of Clarendon; a set of 16 procedures passed by King Henry II in 1164 to limit church privileges and papal authority in England</note>. It would be a long task to recount all the wicked, bold deeds of this most defiant man; how often he conspired against the life of his Prince; how often he accused the same before the Pope and foreign kings; and finally, how often he excommunicated the King of England, the Bishops, the Nobles, and the Clergy, only to absolve them and then strike them with the curse again. Meanwhile, having found most powerful patrons in Pope Innocent and King Louis of France, he remained safely hidden in France and Italy. Finally, in the year 1170, with peace settled on both sides, he returned to England and recovered his see. But since the restless man did not cease to weave new troubles, becoming a burden once more to the King and the realm, he was killed at Canterbury by four royal attendants—though without a royal command—at the end of that same year on the 28th of December, in the 52nd year of his age. There exist *six books of his Letters*, formerly collected and arranged by John of Salisbury, with many *Letters* from others to Thomas, and about him, interspersed throughout. Christian Lupus brought this collection to light and oversaw its publication in *Brussels, 1682, in quarto*, together with the *Quadrilogus* <note>term: Quadrilogus; a "four-part" biography of Becket compiled from four contemporary authors</note>, or the Life of Thomas woven together from four authors: namely, his clerk Herbert, William of Canterbury, Abbot Alan of Tewkesbury <note>original: "Deoche", likely referring to Dieulacres or Tewkesbury</note>, and John of Salisbury.

The 12th Century, from the Year 1100.

<margin>1163.</margin>
**BONACURSUS**, a native of Milan and once a Master of the Cathars <note>The Cathars were a dualist heretical movement in Southern Europe that the Church sought to suppress</note>, rose to prominence around the year 1163. There exists a *Life of the Cathar Heretics* written by him, found in D’Achéry’s *Spicilegium, Vol. XIII.*

<margin>1164.</margin>
**HUGO**, a Frenchman and monk of Silvanès <note>original: "Salvanicnsis"</note>, flourished around the year 1164. There exists his *Narrative of the Conversion of Pontius of Larazio* in Baluze’s *Miscellany, Vol. III, p. 205.*

<margin>1165.</margin>
**HELMOLDUS**, a Priest of Lübeck and Canon of Bosau near Lübeck, was a disciple of Gerold (who later became the first Bishop of Lübeck) and flourished around the year 1165. He died in the year 1170. He wrote the *Chronicle of the Slavs* <note>original: "Chronicon Sclavorum"</note> from the times of Charlemagne down to the year 1168, in which he treats the conversion of the Slavs or Vandals to the Christian faith, and the geography and history of the regions and peoples along the Baltic Sea. Sigismund Schorckelius first published it in *Frankfurt, 1556, in quarto*, with a preface by Melanchthon; then Reiner Reineccius published it in the same place in 1581; and finally, Heinrich Bangert published it with notes and observations in *Lübeck, 1659, in quarto.*

<margin>1166.</margin>
**ALEXIUS ARISTENUS**, holding the rank of Guardian of the Laws <note>term: Nomophylax; a high-ranking Byzantine legal official</note> and Steward of the Great Church of Constantinople, whom Balsamon calls "that most honorable lord" <note>original Greek: ὑπέρtiμον ἐκεῖνον κύριον</note> in more than one place. He flourished in the year 1166, when he was present at the Synod of Constantinople; being consulted there on Canon Law against Patriarch Nicephorus of Jerusalem, he brought forward the 37th Canon of the Quinisext Council <note>original: "Concilii Trullani"</note>. There exists a *Synopsis of Canons* illustrated with commentaries <note>original: "Scholiis"</note> by our Aristenus; while the Synopsis itself seems to be much older, Aristenus provided the interpretation. The *Synopsis* was published in Greek and Latin, but lacking the commentaries, under Aristenus’s name by Christophe Justel in the *Library of Canon Law, Vol. II, p. 673.* The illustrious Beveridge added the commentaries to the Synopsis and provided both in Greek and Latin, illustrated with notes, in the *Collection of Canons, Oxford, 1672, in folio.*

<margin>1167.</margin>
**MICHAEL ANCHIALUS**, Patriarch of Constantinople from around the year 1167. A learned man, and in the judgment of Balsamon, the greatest of philosophers, but a most bitter enemy of the Latins. He held the Patriarchal see for eight years. There exist *five Synodal Decrees* by him; namely, *That Readers should not undertake worldly duties*, *That Clergy should not be ordained from another Diocese*, etc., in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law, book 3, p. 227.* He also wrote a *Dialogue* which he held with the Emperor Manuel Comnenus at the time when the Pope’s Legates arrived in Constantinople to negotiate the union of the Churches, demanding nothing else from the Greeks but;

<margin>1170.</margin>
**JOHN**, an Englishman by birth from the county of Cornwall (and thus called **John of Cornwall**), was famous in the year 1170. In France, he had Peter Lombard as his teacher, with whom he later engaged in many disputes; he also lived in Rome for a long time devoted to his studies, and was very dear to Pope Alexander III.

**PETER OF RIGA**, a Frenchman by nation and the Cantor and Canon of the Church of Reims, flourished around the year 1170 or shortly thereafter. Ambrosius de Altamura <note>A Dominican historian</note> places him in the year 1263 and writes that he was promoted from a schoolmaster in France to the Church of Agen in Aquitaine; however, it is clear from his writings that he is the same Peter of Reims. Peter wrote the *Heptateuch* <note>term: Heptateuch; the first seven books of the Bible (Genesis through Judges)</note>, which he titled *Aurora* <note>meaning "The Dawn"</note>, as well as two books of *Kings* and the four *Gospels*, rendering them into verse. In this work, according to the testimony of Henry of Ghent, he briefly expressed not only the historical meaning but also the allegorical meaning as much as he was able. This *Aurora* exists in manuscript form in various libraries; Casimir Oudin recently testified that he has an edition ready for publication compared against various manuscripts, and it is hoped he will not withhold it from the public.

---

<margin>1170.</margin>
**PETER COMESTOR**, also called *the Eater* <note>original: "Manducator"; a nickname earned because he "devoured" books through intensive study</note>, was French by birth from the city of Troyes, where he was a Priest and Dean of St. Peter’s. The Parisians, stirred by the fame of this celebrated man, called him to themselves and appointed him Chancellor of the University of Paris. He flourished in the year 1170. Eventually, being a lover of solitude and quiet, he retired to the Canons of St. Victor in the suburbs of Paris, where he devoted his whole soul to the study of piety and literature. He died and was buried there on October 21, 1198, as the Victorine Canons prove from their internal records and commentaries. From this, the error of Vincent of Beauvais and others—who write that Peter died in 1160—is evident. He was a man not unlearned for the age in which he lived, nor one who entirely approved of the superstitions and tyranny of the Roman Church that were rushing in daily.

It is certainly worth remembering what his pupil, Gerald of Wales <note>original: "Gyraldus Cambrensis"; a famous Welsh archdeacon and chronicler</note>, reports of him in the *Jewel of the Church* (which is kept today as a manuscript in the Lambeth Library), distinction 2, chapter 6, in these words: "I heard the Great Peter the Eater saying this in the hearing of his whole school, which was filled with so many and such great learned men: 'That ancient enemy [the Devil] never so deceived the Church of God in any matter as he did in the requirement of that vow' (meaning the celibacy of priests)."

He wrote for William, the Archbishop of Sens, for the use of his brothers, the **Scholastic History in 16 books**, in which he reduced the Sacred History from the beginning of Genesis to the end of the Acts of the Apostles into a compendium. He interspersed many uncertain, if not fabulous, stories here and there; he also inserted certain events from the histories of the Pagans according to the timeline, like a small stream that fills the side-channels it finds along its bed, yet does not cease to flow onward, as he himself says in the preface. It first appeared in print in 1473 at *Reutlingen* by Guiternus Zainer; at *Strasbourg* in 1483; *Basel* 1486; and *Lyons* 1543, to say nothing of more recent editions.

<margin>12th CENTURY, from the year 1100.</margin>
<margin>* On the Academy of Paris, p. 113.</margin>
Eighty of his manuscript Sermons are preserved in the Monastery of Saint Victor, fifty of which he wrote while still a Priest; the other thirty as a Canon of Saint Victor, as Claude Héméré <note>original: "Claudius Hemeræus"; a 17th-century French theologian and historian of the University of Paris</note> informs us from a Victorine manuscript. Forty-four are held at Lambeth in the Archbishop's Library, Number 176, folio. More are in Cambridge in the Pembroke Library, Codex 48, Numbers 1 and 3, and Codex 76, Number 1; however, the famous [Thomas] James, who compiled the catalog, does not state how many there are in total. One hundred and fourteen are said to exist in the Cistercian monastery of Longpont. Finally, the most recent editor of the works of Peter of Blois advises that various Sermons published under Peter of Blois' name should be attributed to our Peter; others may judge how correctly.
