<margin>1170.</margin>
**THEORIANUS**, a Greek by nation and perhaps a native of Constantinople, was the Ambassador of Emperor Manuel Comnenus sent to the Armenians in the year 1170 to debate in defense of the orthodox faith. When he arrived in Armenia, he delivered the letters of his Emperor to Lord Nerses <note>original: "Naufesi"; referring to Nerses IV the Gracious, the Catholicos or head of the Armenian Church</note> the Catholicos; and he entered into a long dispute with him concerning various articles of faith and Ecclesiastical customs. At length, this was the outcome of the conference: the Catholicos, overcome by the arguments of Theorianus, yielded. He promised that he would assemble a Synod of his Bishops and propose the arguments that Theorianus had brought forward to them; that he would yield in all things to the opinion of the Catholic Church, and speak on behalf of the Greeks—indeed, on behalf of the truth against the Armenians. Finally, he promised that he and all those agreeing with him would send the orthodox faith, comprised in writing and confirmed by the signatures of himself and his Bishops, to the Emperor and the Patriarch of Constantinople. He committed this *Dialogue* held with the Catholicos of the Armenians to writing; in it, he primarily aims to refute the Eutychians and Monophysites <note>Groups who believed Christ had only one nature, rather than being both fully human and fully divine</note> by the authority of the Holy Fathers, and to establish the Catholic doctrine concerning the two natures in Christ and the authority of the Council of Chalcedon. Johannes Leunclavius published this in Greek and Latin at Basel, 1578, in octavo; it was later reprinted in the *Ducæan Supplement*, Paris, 1624, Volume 1, page 439.

---

<margin>1170.</margin>
**EUSTATHIUS**, a Greek by birth and Archbishop of Thessalonica, flourished under the Comneni [emperors]—Manuel, his son Alexios, and his cousin Andronikos—around the year 1170. Consequently, Marquard Freher wrongly confuses him in his chronology with Eustathius, the Archpriest of the Great Church, who succeeded Eulogius or Sergius in the See of Constantinople in the year 1017. He was, beyond dispute, a most learned man and a most famous writer; yet one may not unfairly doubt whether he should be placed among Ecclesiastical writers. For although he was a Bishop, and was honored with more than one tribute by Niketas Choniates (noting that he was gifted with secular learning as much as sacred letters, "far above all others" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πολὺ τῶν ἄλλων</note>, which was "his most characteristic and exceptional gift" <note>original Greek: τὸ οἰκειότατον ἐκείνῳ καὶ ἐξαίρετον ἦν χάρις ἐγχείρισμα</note>), nevertheless, nothing of an Ecclesiastical nature exists published by him as far as I know. Indeed, it is hardly clear whether anything was ever published, except that Caspar Suicer in the *Ecclesiastical Treasury*, Volume 2, under the word "Mother-Virgin" <note>original: μητροπάρθενος (metropathenos)</note>, notes that Eustathius of Thessalonica and Gregory, Metropolitan of Corinth, explained certain poems of John of Damascus for Pentecost, which are read in the Greek *Pentecostarion*. He wrote other things which, although they do not strictly belong here, should not be overlooked, namely: *Commentaries on Homer*; these appeared in Greek in 4 volumes, Rome, 1550, folio, and Basel, 3 volumes, 1560, folio. *Commentary on Dionysius Periegetes, or Description of the World*, Greek, Paris, 1577. *Six books on the Loves of Ismenias and Ismene*, Greek and Latin with notes by Gaulmin, Paris, 1647, octavo. Indeed, he is removed from [authorship of] these books primarily on the grounds that some manuscripts suggest a certain Eumathius as the author. See what the famous [Gerard] Vossius has on this matter in *On the Greek Historians*, book 4, chapter 19.

---

<margin>1170.</margin>
**SYMEON**, Master and Logothete <note>A high-ranking administrative and judicial official in the Byzantine Empire</note>, almost contemporary with Alexios Aristenos, flourished around the year 1170. An *Epitome of Canons* exists in Greek and Latin, published by Henri Justel in the *Library of Canon Law*, Volume 2, page 710. Certainly, this Canonical Synopsis seems older than both Symeon and Aristenos, though it is attributed to both here and there; it appears he transcribed it with the order slightly changed and adapted it for his own use...

# The Waldensian Century. 684

<margin>
12th Century.
Year 1100.
* Supplement p. 413.
</margin>
...our Symeon <note>Symeon Magister, a 10th-century Byzantine chronicler whose works were being rediscovered and debated by 17th-century scholars</note> seems to have adapted; and as the Illustrious [William] Beveridge <note>An English bishop and scholar of canon law</note> aptly conjectures, he had illustrated it with scholarly commentaries (scholia) which have long since perished. Casimir Oudin <note>A French librarian and ecclesiastical historian</note> records that a work of Symeon the Master Logothete <note>A high-ranking administrative title in the Byzantine Empire</note> titled *The Creation of the World from Genesis and Chronicles* <note>original: "Mundi Opificium ex Genesi & Chronicis"</note>, compiled in series, exists in manuscript in the collection of the Illustrious Du Fresne Du Cange and elsewhere. However, let those who possess the manuscript codices tell us what sort of work it is, or whose it might be—whether by our Symeon or by an older Logothete.

<margin>1170.</margin>
**GODFREY**, or Gotefridus, called "of Viterbo" from his homeland, was born an Italian and held the rank of Priest. He served three Emperors—namely Conrad III, Frederick I [Barbarossa], and Henry VI—as both a chaplain and a secretary. He flourished in the year 1170. He is said to have spent forty years traveling in foreign regions, from which he returned home filled with various observations, the spoils of libraries, and a knowledge not only of Latin, but also of Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldean <note>A term often used historically for Aramaic</note>. He died in the year 1186. He wrote for Pope Urban III a *Universal Chronicle* <note>original: "Chronicon Universale"</note>, written in both prose and verse, which he called the *Pantheon* because of its extensive history of events, eras, and nations from the creation of the world down to the year 1186. This *Chronicle* is found among the *Writers of German Affairs* edited by Johann Pistorius at Frankfurt in 1584, page 6. There also exists his *Mirror of Kings, or on the Genealogy of All Kings and Emperors from the Time of the Flood to Emperor Henry VI* <note>original: "Speculum Regum, seu de Genealogia omnium Regum & Imperatorum à Diluvii tempore ad Henricum VI. Imp."</note>, distinct from the Chronicle, preserved in manuscript in the Imperial Library at Vienna, as witnessed by Peter Lambeck in his *Commentary on the Vienna Library, Book 2, Chapter 8, page 774*.

<margin>
1170.
* In "The Ciceronian".
</margin>
**SAXO**, called **GRAMMATICUS** <note>Meaning "The Lettered" or "The Scholar"</note> because of the elegance of the style he used, was a Dane by nation and a native of Zealand, born of a knightly family and appointed Provost of the Cathedral Church of Roskilde. He flourished in the year 1170. Nine years earlier, he had been sent to Paris to the Church of Saint Genevieve by Absalon, the Archbishop of Lund—in whose household he mostly lived and served as a chaplain—so that he might bring back several religious men from there to Denmark. Around the year 1177, at the command of Absalon, he set himself to the task of composing the annals of his fatherland. He died in the year 1204. He wrote, in a style indeed beautiful and, beyond the standard of his age, florid and elegant, the *Sixteen Books of Danish History* <note>original: "Historiæ Danicæ libros XVI."</note> from the very origins of the nation down to the year 1186. Erasmus <note>The famous Renaissance humanist</note> vehemently praises his vivid and burning genius, his never-slackening or stumbling speech, his wonderful wealth of words, his frequent pithy sayings, and the admirable variety of his figures of speech; "so that," he says, "I cannot sufficiently wonder whence a Danish man of that age obtained such power of eloquence." In this opinion, as far as I know, all learned men are in agreement. Certainly, regarding his style, he seems to have held Valerius Maximus before his eyes above all others, which the Illustrious [Johannes] Stephanius demonstrates with almost infinite examples. This *History* was first published by Christian Petri, Canon of Lund, at Paris in 1514; then by Johannes Bebelius at Basel in 1534; by Philipp Lonicer and Johannes Fichard at Frankfurt in 1576; and finally, far more complete and adorned with very full introductory treatises and richer notes, by Stephen Johannes Stephanius at Sorø in 1644, in folio. And would that more beautiful type had accompanied the diligence of that most learned editor.

<margin>1170.</margin>
**HENRY**, Archbishop of Reims, flourished in the year 1170. Two of his *Letters concerning the case of Drago of Noyon* <note>original: "Epistolæ II. de causâ Dragonis Noviomagensis"</note> are found in Baluze's *Miscellany, Volume II, page 228*.

<margin>1170.</margin>
**HILDEGARD**, German by nation and a native of Sponheim, was the daughter of Hildebert and Mechtild, born in the year 1098. Given to God from her earliest infancy, she took the nun's habit at the age of eight under Abbess Jutta, the sister of Count Megenhard of Sponheim; she herself finally became the Abbess of the Monastery of Saint Rupert on the mountain at Bingen near the Rhine river. She flourished in the year 1170. Endowed with rare gifts of mind and distinguished by extraordinary piety toward God and zeal for religion, she began to become famous for divinely granted visions and prophecies when she was already in her forties. Stirred by the fame of this, Pope Eugenius III and the leading Bishops and Abbots of France and Germany—and among them Saint Bernard—subjected her prophetic visions to a sharper examination in the year 1148; and...

Later, Popes Anastasius IV and Hadrian IV ratified the same judgment: they sent letters to her and commended both themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. Hildegard died in the year 1180, on the 17th of September.

<margin>* Library p. 301.</margin>
*Four books on Physics, or on the Nature of Things.* Some wrongly attribute these to our Hildegard. Indeed, Josias Simler <note>A 16th-century Swiss scholar</note> teaches us that it is the work of a Hildegard of Bingen <note>The text here suggests a distinction was being made between the Saint and another author from the same place regarding these scientific texts</note>. Published in Strasbourg, 1533.

<margin>1172.</margin>
**JOHN**, called "of Salisbury" from his place of birth, English by nationality, a native of Wiltshire, the glory and ornament of his race and century. He was exceptionally dear to Popes Eugenius III, Hadrian IV, and Alexander III, as well as to Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury (whom he served as chaplain). He was most intimate with Archbishop Thomas Becket, and from the year 1163, he was his companion throughout his entire exile and all his hardships. Although he was often urged to desert Thomas and to promise by oath his loyalty to the King and obedience to the royal customs, he preferred to remain in exile rather than to earn peace and the King's favor on those conditions. Eventually, he left Thomas’s company, but not his cause, and was consulted by him more than others in doubtful matters. After seven years spent in exile, having obtained a pardon from the Pope and peace being made with the King, he returned to England. He found his mother (to whose wishes he had deferred by undertaking the journey) on her deathbed. In the year 1172, after Thomas had been killed, he set out again for France and was appointed Bishop of Chartres <note>original: "Carnotensis"</note> in the Province of Sens <note>original: "Senonensi"</note>. In 1179, he took part in the Lateran Council. He died in the year 1182. Many things truly worthy of memory concerning him can be sought from the collection of Thomas Becket’s letters, not without benefit to the reader. He was the most eloquent man of his age and most highly trained in every kind of more profound knowledge. He was a most severe critic of morals and, if ever there was one, a rigid preserver of integrity. In plucking out the vices of others—even those of Kings or Popes—he employed equal eloquence and freedom. He spared neither friends nor enemies. Indeed, he did not hesitate to frequently confront even Thomas himself, his lord and friend, regarding his obstinate and stubborn spirit toward a most merciful King.

## W O R K S.

<margin>* Notes on Tacitus, Annals XII.</margin>
*The Policraticus, or Eight books on the Trifles of Courtiers and the Footsteps of Philosophers.* Dedicated to Archbishop Theobald. In this patchwork <note>original: "centone"</note>, Justus Lipsius <note>A famous Renaissance humanist scholar</note> recognizes many purple patches and fragments of higher quality. Published in Paris, 1513, in quarto; Leiden, 1595, in octavo; Paris, 1610, in octavo; Leiden, 1639, in octavo; and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXIII.
*Four books of the Metalogicon*, in which he treats acutely and eruditely of every logical, philological, and even philosophical matter. Published with the *Policraticus*, Paris, 1610, and Leiden, 1639.
*The Life of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.* Published in its entirety with the *Letters of John of Salisbury*, Paris, 1611, in quarto. A fragmented and incomplete version appears in the *Quadrilogus* <note>A 15th-century composite biography of Becket using four primary sources</note> regarding the Life of St. Thomas, compiled long ago by order of Gregory XI from four authors; it was printed in Paris, 1495, in quarto, and with the *Letters of St. Thomas*, Brussels, 1682, in quarto.

1174.
* On Latin History, book 2, chapter 53.

**WILLIAM**, either a Frenchman or a German by birth, or what is more likely, a Syrian, and perhaps born in Jerusalem; indeed, as some would have it, he was related by blood to the Kings of Jerusalem. Around the year 1167, at the request of King Amalric, he was granted the Archdeaconry of the Church of Tyre by Archbishop Frederick, and shortly thereafter, as an ambassador to the Emperor of Constantinople, he conducted his business successfully. Around the year 1169, as his Archbishop’s health was failing, he undertook a journey to the West. Upon his return, Baldwin, the son of King Amalric, was entrusted to him to be instructed in literature and good character. Soon he was honored by the King with the Chancellorship of the Sacred Palace; and finally, in May of the year 1174, he was elected Archbishop of Tyre and consecrated on the 10th of June <note>original: "IV. Id. Jun."</note>. In 1177, having been summoned to the Lateran Synod, he set out for Rome, and the following year he took part in the Council, the acts and canons of which he himself committed to writing at the request of the other bishops. Returning home, he stayed for seven months at Constantinople with the Emperor Manuel, and carried out an embassy entrusted to him by the Emperor to the Princes and the Patriarch of Antioch. Thus, after a year and ten months, he returned to Tyre. In the year 1188, after Jerusalem was captured by the Saracens <note>Muslim forces under Saladin</note> and the affairs of the Eastern Christians became desperate, he himself was sent to the West to seek aid, and he was present at the conference between the Kings of England <note>Henry II</note> and France <note>Philip II Augustus</note> between Gisors and Trie. Finally, having strenuously opposed the election of Heraclius as Patriarch of Jerusalem, he began a journey toward Rome to block his path to the patriarchal seat, but he was removed by poison by Heraclius; it is not clear in what year this happened. He wrote in 23 books the *History of the war waged by the Christian Princes of the West in Palestine and the East*, from the year 1095 to the year 1180. It is clear enough from this work—to use the words of the great Vossius * regarding him—that the writer is modest, prudent, of sharp judgment, a great lover of truth, and, for the age in which he lived, learned and elegant. That *History* first appeared through the care of Philippe Poyssenot in Basel, 1549; then through the efforts of Heinrich Pantaleon in Basel, 1560; and finally in the Bongarsian collection *God’s Deeds through the Franks* <note>original: "Gestorum Dei per Francos"</note>, Volume I, page 625. He also wrote the *Deeds of the Western Princes*, or a history of the princes of the West in the East and their actions from the year 614 to the year 1184; and the *Acts of the Lateran Council*. Both works, however, appear to have perished.

---

<margin>1177.</margin>
**HUGO ETHERIANUS**, a Tuscan by nation, traveled to Constantinople under the Emperor Manuel and earned the highest favor with the Emperor; thereafter, supported by his patronage, he fought strenuously against the Greeks both in writing and in speech. He was famous in the year 1177, at which time he sent books he had polished against the dogmas of the Greeks to Pope Alexander III, and earned letters of high praise from him. There exist his book *On the Soul Divested of the Body*, or *On the Return of Souls*, in the *Orthodoxographa* <note>A collection of early Christian writings</note> page 1309, and separately in Cologne, 1540. Also, *On the Heresies which the Greeks cast upon the Latins*, or *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son*, against the errors of the Greeks, in 3 books; these appeared separately with the preceding short work in Basel, 1543, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXII, page 11.

---

...founded by Empress Pulcheria <note>original: "didit Pulcheria Augusta"</note>, he served as Provost. He flourished in the year 1180. Eventually, he was made the Patriarch of Antioch; however, since Antioch had long been occupied by the Latins <note>The city was held by Crusaders at this time</note>, he never saw his see. Instead, residing in Constantinople, he managed his affairs as best he could. Indeed, the Emperor Isaac <note>Isaac II Angelos</note> long teased him with the vain and deceptive hope of being promoted to the throne of Constantinople itself; regarding this, Nicetas Choniates <note>A significant Byzantine historian</note> tells a rather witty story in his *History*. <margin>* In *Isaac*, book 2, chapter 4.</margin> He lived until the year 1203, when Constantinople was captured by the Latins. Nothing certain is known regarding his death. He was, without envy, the most learned of the Greeks of his time, and the most skilled in Eastern Law and Ecclesiastical Canons of all those whom fruitful Greece ever produced. John, Bishop of Kitros, truly said of him: <gloss>† Response to Constantine Cabasilas.</gloss> † "That holy man, the Patriarch of Antioch, was expertly skilled in the precise civil and canonical laws, and was celebrated by everyone for his knowledge of these divinely-taught decrees." <note>original Greek: ὁ ἱερὸς ἐκεῖνος ἀνὴρ... πάντων ἐκ τῶν ἐν τοῖς θεοδιδάκτοις θεσμοῖς.</note> Furthermore, he was a most fierce champion of the Eastern Churches against the Latins, for which reason Baronius <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Catholic historian often critical of Eastern Orthodox figures</note> and other followers of the Papal cause pour out insults against him with a full mouth.

->W O R K S.<-

**C**ommentary on the Canons of the Holy Apostles, and the Holy Ecumenical and particular Councils, and on the Canonical Epistles of the Holy Fathers. Balsamon began this work by order of Emperor Manuel and Patriarch Michael Anchialus; however, he did not finish it until the time of George Xiphilinus, who ascended the Patriarchal throne around the year 1194; at the very least, he revised and dedicated it to him during his reign. This work was published in Greek and Latin, though mutilated here and there, in Paris, 1620, in folio; but it is far more enlarged and complete with the notes of William Beveridge <note>An English bishop and scholar of canon law</note> in the *Pandects of Canons* <note>original: "Pandectae Canonum"</note>, Oxford, 1672, in folio.

*Commentary on the Nomocanon of Photius.* Published in Greek and Latin, edited by Christopher Justel, Paris, 1615, in quarto; and in the *Library of Canon Law*, Volume II, page 789.

*Collection of Ecclesiastical Constitutions, called 'Paratitla' by Leunclavius and others.* It survives with the notes of Leunclavius and Fabrot in Justel’s *Library of Canon Law*, Volume II, page 1223.

*Responses to various questions regarding Canon Law, namely: on the elevation of Bishoprics into Metropolises; on those elected to the Eastern Churches; on the court of the Clergy; on Patriarchal Right over Monasteries; on Feast Days, and many other matters which are found scattered in Greek and Latin in Leunclavius’s 'Greco-Roman Law', book 2.*

*Responses to the Inquiries of Mark, Patriarch of Alexandria*, in Greek and Latin, in the same work, book 5, page 361.

*Meditations, or responses to various cases*, in Greek and Latin, in the same work, book 7, almost throughout.

*Letter to Abbot Theodosius regarding the 'Rasophoros' Monks, or those clothed in the cassock*, published by the same author in Greek and Latin, Volume III, page 473.

PETER, a Frenchman by birth, was first the Abbot of the Monastery of Celle in the suburbs of Troyes, then Abbot of St. Remigius at Reims; finally, in the year 1182, he succeeded John of Salisbury in the Bishopric of Chartres. He died on the 9th day before the Kalends of March <note>February 21</note> in the year 1187. Regarding him, Nicholas of Clairvaux wrote *: *The Abbot of Celle, a religious man fearing God, a good man having a good testimony from good men; at once conspicuous for his literature, and bound to us by such great familiarity that he is not merely one of the others, but one above the others.*

GEOFFREY, a Frenchman by birth, son of Geoffrey and Lucia, was first a monk of the Monastery of St. Martial at Limoges, and then Prior of Vigeois in the same diocese. In the year 1167, on the eve of St. Matthew the Apostle, he was ordained a priest by Gerald, Bishop of Cahors, at Benevento. JOHN PHOCAS, a native of Crete, son of Matthew (who was later a monk <note>original Greek: μοναζόν</note> on the island of Patmos), was a married priest who had an only son by his wife. He himself testifies that he once served as a soldier under Emperor Manuel Comnenus. Finally becoming a monk, he traveled to Jerusalem and visited the holy places in the year 1185. Having returned home, he briefly and accurately committed to writing all that he had observed. There exists a *compendium description of places from the city of Antioch all the way to Jerusalem, as well as of Syria and Phoenicia*, published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius in the *Miscellany, part 1, page 1, Cologne, 1653, in octavo.*

* Supplement p. 453.

BALDWIN, English by birth, from Devon, born in Exeter to parents of humble condition. He first served as a schoolmaster <note>original: "Ludi-magistrum"</note> and then became an Archdeacon; but abandoning this office, he joined the Cistercians and was thereafter created Abbot of Forde. In the year 1181, he was announced as the Bishop of Worcester. After three years, when the See of Canterbury was vacant and the electors were contending—the monks on one side and the suffragan bishops on the other—Baldwin was finally elected by common vote with the king's consent. On June 14, 1185, he was installed in the Archiepiscopal See. Thus, Oudin * is mistaken in both the timing and the order of succession when he writes that Baldwin succeeded Thomas Becket in the See of Canterbury in the year 1171; for Thomas had Richard, Prior of Dover, as his successor. Although the monks had given their assent to Baldwin's election, they nonetheless by no means acquiesced to it, especially since from the College of Secular Canons at Hackington...

<margin>1185.</margin>
**URBAN III.** Formerly called Lambert, a Lombard by nationality and a Milanese by birth, from the Crivelli family; he was created Roman Pontiff from the Archbishopric of Milan on November 26, 1185, and crowned on December 8. In the year 1186, while contending with Emperor Frederick <note>Frederick I "Barbarossa"</note> regarding the inheritance of Countess Matilda, he intended to excommunicate him, but ceased, overcome by the pleas of the people of Verona. In the same year, at the request of King Henry II of England, he confirmed the kingdom of Ireland for his son Henry <note>likely referring to John "Lackland", who was Lord of Ireland</note>, and as a token of confirmation, he sent him a gift of a crown woven from gold and peacock feathers. He died at Ferrara on October 20, 1187, consumed by grief over the disasters suffered by the Christians in the East. *Five of his Letters are extant in the Tomes of the Councils,* Volume 10, page 1742.

<margin>1187.</margin>
**GREGORY VIII.** Previously called Albert, born in Benevento, a Cardinal-Priest of the Roman Church under the title of St. Lawrence, and Chancellor. In the year 1172, he was sent as a legate by Alexander III to King Henry of England to inquire into the death of Becket; after holding a Council at Avranches in Normandy, he established many ecclesiastical canons. He was created Roman Pontiff on October 21, 1187, and consecrated on the 25th. He immediately promised full remission of sins and proclaimed a five-year fast for the recovery of the Holy Land, which had recently been snatched from the Christians by the Saracens. He died at Pisa in the same year, on December 17. *Three of his Letters are extant in the Tomes of the Councils,* Volume 10, page 1748.

<margin>1187.</margin>
**CLEMENT III.** Formerly called *Paulinus*, a Roman by birth, Cardinal and Bishop of Palestrina, he was created Roman Pontiff at Pisa on December 19, 1187, and inaugurated there on January 6 of the following year. In the same year, at the request of William, King of Scots, he exempted the Scottish Church from the jurisdiction of the Archbishop of York and ordered it to be subject henceforth only to the Apostolic See. He died on April 5, 1191. *Seven of his Letters are extant in the Tomes of the Councils,* Volume 10, page 1753.

By his eloquence and authority, he held great influence with Leopold, Duke of Austria; so much so that through his mediation—though even more through the power of English money, specifically an immense ransom price—Richard, King of England, was released from custody. <note>King Richard the Lionheart was captured by Leopold V of Austria in 1192 while returning from the Third Crusade and was held until a massive ransom was paid in 1194.</note> Elias died on August 16, 1195. <margin>1191.</margin> <margin>* Regarding the year 1191.</margin> CELESTINE III, formerly called *Hyacinthus* <note>Giacinto Bobone</note>, a Roman by nation, son of Petrus Bobo. From the year 1126, he was a Cardinal Deacon of the Roman Church with the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. In the year 1158, he was sent by Adrian III <note>Historically Adrian IV</note> to the Emperor Frederick I; on the journey, he was captured and thrown into prison, though he was soon released. In 1177, as a legate of Alexander III, he absolved Frederick and his nobles from excommunication. In 1191, on April 12, he was elected Pope, and ordained on the 14th. In the same year, he placed the imperial crown on Henry [VI], King of Germany, who had come to Rome, and once placed, he immediately kicked it off with his foot; by this rite, says Baronius*, he signified that he had the power to cast him out from the empire if he should prove unworthy. <note>Baronius was a 16th-century cardinal and historian who recorded this dramatic assertion of papal supremacy over secular rulers.</note> Furthermore, in that same year, he excommunicated Alfonso, King of Galicia <note>Alfonso IX of León and Galicia</note>, along with his whole kingdom, because of an illicit marriage; and he also struck John, Count of Mortain—the brother of King Richard—with anathema <note>excommunication</note> for stirring up revolution in England. In 1193, he cursed Leopold, Duke of Austria, with dire imprecations for having captured Richard, King of England, and he renewed the sentence two years later, at which time he also bound the Emperor Henry under the same anathema. He died on January 8, 1198. Seventeen *Letters* are extant in the *Councils*, Volume 10, page 1768. A *single Letter* is found in Baluze's *Miscellanea*, Volume 2, page 241.

<margin>1192.</margin> STEPHEN, a Frenchman by nation, from the city of Orléans, was born in the year 1135. Having successfully completed his course in the humanities, he turned his mind to the study of Theology and Civil Law. Around the year 1165, he became a regular canon <note>A priest living under a community rule, specifically the Rule of St. Augustine</note> in the Monastery of Saint Euvert at Orléans, and after the death of Albert, he became Abbot of the same monastery, being especially dear to many famous men. In 1177, he was called to the government of the Monastery of Saint Genevieve in Paris, where he established private schools in which those about to be initiated into holy orders might be imbued with both letters and religion. In 1190, when Philip Augustus was undertaking his expedition to the Holy Land, William, Archbishop of Reims—to whom the King had entrusted the government of the realm—called our Stephen to share in these cares and soon sent him to Rome as a legate to the Pope. In 1192, he was made Bishop of Tournai, consecrated by William of Reims, though the clergy resisted and Pope Celestine did not initially approve. After ten years in this office, carried out with great diligence and praise for his fidelity, his strength failed; heavy with age, this most holy man died on September 9, in the year 1200, at the age of 68.

**WILLIAM**, called by the surname **THE SMALL** <note>original: "Parvus"; he is more commonly known today as William of Newburgh.</note>, an Englishman by nation, from the district of York, born at Bridlington in the year 1136. After completing his early education at home, he was sent by his parents to the Monastery of Newburgh near the Cuckney Forest (hence he is called *of Newburgh* or *of Neubridge*) to draw from there the elements of both religion and learning; thus he became a Canon Regular of the Augustinian Order in that same monastery. He flourished in the year 1195. He died, as some claim, in 1208 at the age of 72. William’s style is quite Latinate and clear, far purer than that used by our contemporary writers. It adds no small credit to the reliability of his history that the events he records he either saw with his own eyes or received from trustworthy men. He wrote *Five Books on English Affairs of His Time* covering the years 1066 to 1197. This *History* was published in Antwerp in 1567 in octavo, and in Heidelberg in 1587; however, a version expanded by many passages and 11 full chapters, and illustrated with excellent notes by Jean Picard, was published in Paris in 1610 in octavo.

Bale lists thirteen other minor works by Ralph, partly historical and partly theological, which have not yet been published.

<margin>1198.</margin>
## ROGER OF HOVEDEN
An Englishman by nation, from the district of York, born of an illustrious family, and a member of the household of King Henry II of England. He was later the primary professor of Theology at the University of Oxford and flourished around the year 1198. He wrote two books of *Annals of the English* covering the period from the year 731 (where Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, the famous 8th-century Anglo-Saxon historian.</note> left off) until the year 1202. These *Annals* were published by the distinguished Savile among other English historians in London, 1595, in folio, and later reprinted in Frankfurt in 1601.

<margin>1198.</margin>
## INNOCENT III
Previously named Lothair, he was from the region of Campania, born in Anagni, the son of Trasimund, Count of Segni, and Clarina. In his early youth, he was sent to Paris <note>Original: "Lutetiam"</note>, where he gained great renown for his wide-ranging learning. Having returned home, he was made a Canon of Anagni and was soon enrolled by Clement III into the college of Cardinals with the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. In the year 1198, on the 8th of January, he was elected Roman Pontiff and consecrated on the 22nd of February at the age of 37. In that same year, he decreed that the son of King Philip of France, born of his mistress Mary, should be considered legitimate. He excommunicated Philip, Duke of Swabia (brother of the recently deceased Emperor Henry), who had been elected King of the Romans by the German princes, in order to render him unfit for the imperial crown; he also stirred up Christian princes to wage war against the Saracens in Asia and heretics in Europe, distributing indulgences with a lavish hand. 

In the year 1199, he forbade the people of Metz from reading the Holy Scriptures translated into the vernacular <note>This refers to an early papal suppression of lay Bible reading in local languages.</note>; he excommunicated Markward <note>Original: "Marcobaldum"</note> of Sicily and, by Apostolic authority, stripped Philip of Swabia of his empire. In the year 1203, he struck with anathema Enrico Dandolo, the Doge of Venice, the Counts of Flanders, Hainaut, and Saint Pol, and other Christian princes, along with the entire army of Crusaders <note>Original: "Cruce signatorum"</note>, because of the capture of Zara <note>Original: "Jadera," a Christian city captured during the Fourth Crusade.</note>. In the year 1206, he excommunicated King John of England for his steadfast defense of royal rights, and likewise the entire kingdom. In the year 1208, he ordered the crusade against the Albigensians to be preached everywhere. 

In the year 1209, he anointed Otto IV as Emperor in Rome (whom he himself had previously substituted for Philip of Swabia), and soon after renewed the anathema against him for defending the rights of the empire. In the year 1210, he threatened the kings of France, England, Bohemia, Sicily, Portugal, and Poland with the same "thunderbolt" <note>A common metaphor for excommunication.</note> unless they immediately satisfied the Church. In the year 1211, he devoted Emperor Otto, King Peter of Aragon, and King John of England to dire curses and placed the kingdom of France under interdict. In 1213, he excommunicated the King of Portugal and the German princes adhering to Emperor Otto. In the year 1215, he celebrated the Fourth Lateran Council, in which he placed the monstrous fiction of Transubstantiation <note>The author reveals a Protestant bias here by calling the doctrine of the Eucharist a "fiction."</note> among the articles of faith and decreed that any Christian princes corrupted by heresy or disobedient to the Roman Church were to be deposed from their dignity. In the same year, lured by certain most foolish visions, he confirmed the monastic orders of Saint Dominic and Saint Francis. He died at Perugia in the year 1216, on the 16th of July. 

Much more could be said of him; he was a man not unlearned, but immoderately proud, of a vast spirit that was entirely itching with the lust for ruling, treating emperors, kings, and all princes with clearly intolerable arrogance. It is enough to consider what Matthew Paris says of him regarding the year 1213 on page 245, where he speaks concerning King John of England:

> *He knew,* he says, *and had learned by manifold experience, that the Pope was more ambitious and proud than all mortals, an insatiable thirster for money, and as pliable as wax and inclined to all crimes for the sake of rewards given or promised.* <note>original: "Noverat, inquit, & multiplici didicerat experientia, quod Papa super omnes mortales ambitiosus erat & superbus, pecuniæque sititor insatiabilis, & ad omnia scelera pro præmiis datis vel promissis cereus & proclivis."</note>

Eleven books of Letters (with an anonymous contemporary author's account of the deeds of Pope Innocent prefixed), which Étienne Baluze <note>Stephanus Baluzius (1630–1718) was a famous French scholar and librarian to Colbert; he was a pioneer in publishing primary historical documents.</note> collected into one, published a large portion for the first time, and corrected the rest, Paris 1682, 2 volumes, folio. The first two books of this collection were published by Guglielmo Sirleto in Rome, 1543, and subsequently appeared in Cologne 1575, Venice 1578, and were transferred by Binius <note>Severin Binius, an editor of the collections of Church Councils.</note> into his volumes of the Councils. Select Letters, especially historical ones, from the Codex of the College of Foix <note>original: "Collegii Fuxensis"</note>, were released and illustrated with notes by Paul du May, royal counselor in the court of Burgundy, Paris 1625, in 8vo. François Bosquet published four previously unedited books from the same Codex in Toulouse, 1635. However, the diligence of Baluze far surpassed the efforts of everyone else; for this reason, and for his other merits in ecclesiastical matters, it is right that gratitude be returned to him by all the learned. Certainly, no one fails to see how much Innocent's letters contribute to illuminating the Church History of this time and to refining Canon Law. The most learned editors of the *Acts of Leipzig* <note>The "Acta Eruditorum," the first scientific journal of the German-speaking lands.</note> in the year 1682, page 371—to whom the literary world clearly owes much—noted many specimens regarding this matter.

A Letter for the Church of Albi, first published by Baluze in *Miscellanies*, Volume IV, page 467.

Commentaries on the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of medieval theology.</note>, Short Works on the Education of Princes, On the Sacrament of Baptism, On the Cloister of the Soul, On Purgatory, etc., are listed by Louis Jacob <note>A 17th-century French bibliographer.</note> in the *Pontifical Library*, book 1, page 118, which are said to still lie hidden in various manuscript libraries.

He wrote many things both in prose and in verse <note>original: "tum soluta, tum ligatâ oratione"</note> with charm and, surpassing the lot of the century in which he lived, with elegance.

## W R I T I N G S.

**O**n the New Poetics <note>original: "De nova Poëtria"</note>. A work in hexameter verse dedicated to Innocent III; it is the same as the book *On the Art of Speaking* <note>original: "de Arte dicendi"</note>, although others consider them to be distinct works. It exists as a manuscript in various libraries, including the Balliol, Arundel, Cottonian, and Seldenian collections, from which the renowned Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a famous English jurist and polymath</note> presents certain excerpts in the Preface to the *Ten Writers* <note>original: "X. Scriptores"</note>.

*A Treatise on the Planting of Trees and the Preservation of Fruits*, containing briefly within itself every method of grafting aromatic trees, preserving fruits, identifying vines and wines, and restoring spoiled or deteriorating wines, etc. It is held as a manuscript in the library of Gonville and Caius, Cambridge, Code 74. It is right for no one to doubt that this belongs to our Geoffrey <note>Galfridus de Vino Salvo</note>.

*History, or the Itinerary of Richard, King of the English, to the Holy Land*, attributed by some to Richard the Canon, or Richard of Devizes, and by others to Robert the Monk. It was recently restored to its true author by the most learned Oxford editor, who identifies our Geoffrey with Walter of Coutances <note>also known as Walter of Oxford</note>. This history appeared, though mutilated and anonymous, in the Bongars Collection, *God's Deeds through the Franks* <note>original: "Gestorum Dei per Francos"</note>; more recently it appeared in full among the *Writers of English History*, Oxford, 1687, Volume II, page 247.

*Two Poems on the Glorious King Richard*, in the same work, page 430.

Regarding other works, for which it is uncertain whether they survive, consult Bale and Pits <note>John Bale and John Pits were prominent 16th and 17th-century English bibliographers who cataloged the works of British authors</note>.

# THE SCHOLASTIC AGE.

->Overview of the Century.<-

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200</margin>
Scholastic Theology <note>A method of critical thought which dominated teaching by the academics ("scholastics") of medieval universities</note>, introduced in the previous age, took deep roots in this century; therefore, according to the plan of our work, a few things must be dealt with in this place. In the first centuries of the Church, the Apostles and Apostolic men handed down to posterity the doctrine which they had received pure and simple from Christ the Lord, in a certain easy and clear way, and one most adapted to the grasp of the common people. Nor did they ever turn aside to perplexed and thorny methods of disputation, unless the necessity of defending the faith against Gentiles and heretics demanded it. <margin>A pattern of sound words <note>original Greek: ὑποτύπωσιν των λόγων των ὑγιαινόντων</note></margin> In instructing catechumens <note>those preparing for baptism</note>, they used a "pattern" <note>original: *hypotyposin*, a Greek term used by St. Paul in 2 Timothy 1:13</note>, a certain brief formula of the faith to be professed, encompassing the primary heads of the evangelical doctrine; this they explained more fully in sermons delivered to the catechumens and candidates. Of this kind were the *Catechetical Lectures to the Enlightened* by Cyril of Jerusalem, and the *Catechetical Orations* of Gregory of Nyssa. Otherwise, in ordinary homilies to the people, they explained either some book of Holy Scripture, or a part of the Gospel then read in the Church, or finally, some moral doctrine in a didactic discourse.

But when this old and simple Ecclesiastical method of teaching began gradually to fall into disuse, they devised a more subtle and sublime way of explaining things: a fact which is clearly evident from the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, born in either the fourth, fifth, or sixth century. Around the middle of the 8th Century, John of Damascus was the first among the Greeks to recall Theology to a more accurate method, and he distributed its dogmas into proper classes, publishing *Four Books on the Orthodox Faith*. In the *first* of these, he treats of God as One and Triune, and of His Nature and properties; in the *second*, of Creation and the various kinds of created things; in the *third*, of the Incarnation of the Word and the hypostatic union of Natures <note>The union of divine and human natures in the one person of Jesus</note>, and of Christ’s Life, Death, and descent into hell; in the *fourth*, he treats of Christ’s Resurrection and Ascension, of faith, of the Sacraments, of the relics and Images of the saints, of the law of God and of sin, of the Sabbath, Circumcision, Antichrist, and the resurrection of the flesh. 

In the Latin church, no one is found to have "rolled this stone" <note>An idiom for undertaking a difficult task</note> before Lanfranc of Canterbury, the adversary of Berengar, who was famous in the middle of the 11th century; he is said to have substituted a new form of Theology for the older one, though this can hardly be gathered from his works that survive today. At the beginning of the following century, Peter Abelard published *Three Books of Introduction to Theology*: in the *first*, he treats of Faith, Hope, Charity, and the Sacraments, especially of faith regarding the Trinity; in the *second*, he handles those things which concern the Trinity more extensively; in the *third*, he discourses more perfectly on the Power, Wisdom, and Goodness of God, in which the Trinity consists. Notably equipped with the help of this work, Peter Lombard, around the middle of the century, compiled the *Four Books of Sentences* (from which he is commonly called the "Master of the Sentences") from the writings of the Holy Fathers, especially Saint Augustine. 

And now, theological matters began to take on a completely new face, reduced to an elenctic <note>a style of argument aiming to refute an opponent's position</note> form and serving doubts that recurred in cycles. It was restricted to a philosophical and acroamatic <note>esoteric or intended for advanced students</note> style of speaking, carved up into infinite questions, with arguments tossed about on both sides, and aired with excessive curiosity almost to the point of silliness. It was, nevertheless, a brief method, and not entirely unpolished, and suited for subtle and sharp discussion regarding...

# THE SCHOLASTIC AGE.

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200</margin> ...was sufficiently aptly composed for a method of disputing theological questions. A long line followed this leader in a dense ranks: *Alexander of Hales*, *Thomas Aquinas*, *Bonaventure*, *Albert the Great*, *Peter of Tarentaise* <note>Later Pope Innocent V</note>, *Henry of Ghent*, *Ulrich of Strasbourg* <note>original: Udalricus de Argentina</note>, *William Durandus*, *Agostino Trionfo*, *Richard of Middleton*, *Giles of Rome*, *John Duns Scotus*, *Raymond Lull*, *Hervaeus Natalis*, *Francis of Mayrone*, *John of Naples*, *Albert of Padua*, *Durandus of Saint-Pourçain*, *Peter Auriol*, *John Bassolis*, *John Baconthorpe*, *William of Ockham*, *Adam Goddam*, to say nothing of the almost infinite number of later followers. And, as usually happens in these matters, they soon split into various factions and sects. From this arose the families of the Nominalists and Realists; the Thomists and Scotists; the Sententiaries and Quodlibetarians <note>Groups named after their preferred philosophical methods or their focus on Peter Lombard's "Sentences" and "Quodlibetal" (spontaneous) debates</note>; for the most part fighting amongst themselves with mutual brawls. At last, having abandoned the simple and purer doctrine of the ancients, Scholastic Theology reigned almost alone in the Christian schools. The philosophy of Aristotle was called in for support; and that was drawn not from Greek sources, but from the muddy pools of the Arabs, and from versions poorly made and poorly understood. Nevertheless, it extended its boundaries far and wide; indeed, it even exercised command over Theology itself, which resulted in Aristotle holding the academic chairs almost alone in place of Saint Paul for several centuries. How much this new Scholastic Theology contributed to establishing many points of the Roman Church, one would have to be blind not to see. Certainly, it promoted the authority of the Papal Majesty no less than the Canon Law, which was born at almost the same time and grew by the same increments. But perhaps enough on these matters; let us move on to others.

In the year 1204, on the day before the Ides of April <note>April 12</note>, after Constantinople was captured by the Latins <note>The Fourth Crusade</note>, the republic of the Greeks, and at the same time their Church, was miserably scattered. The seat of the Empire and the Patriarchate was transferred to Nicaea in Bithynia, with Theodore Lascaris seizing the insignia of empire. At the same time, Alexius Comnenus chose Trebizond as the seat of his empire, having obtained the provinces of Cappadocia, Paphlagonia, Pontus, and Colchis; from which the Empire of Trebizond had its birth. Nor was the status of the Greeks more fortunate before the year 1260, when, the Royal City having been snatched back from the Latins, they were restored to their own seats.

At the beginning of this century, Pope Innocent III unleashed his furies. He deprived Philip Augustus <note>Philip II of France</note> of his empire, released his subjects from their Oath of Allegiance, and devoted them to dire curses unless they obeyed. He deposed John, King of the English, because Stephen Langton was not admitted to the see of Canterbury; he subjected the kingdom to an interdict; and finally, when John submitted his authority, the Pope received him as a vassal. He struck with anathema Louis, the eldest son of Philip, King of the Franks (to whom he had handed over the kingdom of England), when Louis continued to cause trouble for John.

In the year 1215, the Lateran Council was held at Rome, which more than a thousand prelates are said to have attended. By these men, the dogma of Transubstantiation was expressly established; namely, that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly contained in the Sacrament of the Altar under the species of Bread and Wine, the bread being **TRANSUBSTANTIATED** into the Body and the wine into the Blood by divine power. Abbot Joachim and Almaric of Bène, a Doctor of Paris, were condemned (the latter indeed was exhumed and burned after his death), and other decrees were made against heretics and their supporters, even to the point of absolving their subjects from the bond of fidelity and transferring the right of their domains to those who occupied them. I shall now pass over the canons concerning Auricular Confession <note>Private confession to a priest</note> to be performed annually, the reservation of the Chrism and the Host, the immunity of the Church, the putting to death of those condemned by the Roman Church, and others. Indeed, there is no lack of significant arguments that detract from all faith and authority of the decrees of this Synod; they seem to have no other shadow of Synodal authority than that, having been composed by Innocent III, they were merely proposed in the Council, but were strengthened by no vote of the Fathers. On this matter, see what the most learned *Du Pin* has recently disputed after others in his *Dissertation 7 on the Ancient Discipline of the Church*. Also present at this Synod was Dominic the Spaniard, a regular Canon of the Church of Osma, received with no small honor and reverence by the Pope, from whom he also obtained the confirmation of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note> recently founded by him; specifically with the intent that disciples coming out of this school should labor perpetually in converting the Albigensians and other heretics. But since they knew for certain that heretics were not easily to be brought back <note>original: reducen-</note> to the bosom of the Church by mere words...

In a matter so overly serious and severe, *Ludovicus à Paramo* (himself an Inquisitor of heretical depravity) acts foolishly in his *On the Origin of the Office of the Holy Inquisition, Book 1, Title 2, Chapter 1 and following*. He traces its origin from the very cradle of the world, presenting God himself to us as the first inquisitor of heretical depravity, calling our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note> to court as guilty of infidelity, heresy, blasphemy, and idolatry, and delivering a sentence of damnation against them from his tribunal. And, lest anything be missing from such a charming fable, he shows us our first parents already performing penance, dressed in leather garments as if in a small habit or "Blessed Sack" (which the Spaniards call the *Sanbenito* <note>The yellow penitential garment worn by those condemned by the Inquisition</note>); he treats all these matters diligently and at length, according to his custom. But I have no time now to pursue such laborious nonsense, for *toil over trifles is a foolish labor.* In the year 1253, *Robert de Sorbon*, a Frenchman by birth—a man indeed born of humble station but distinguished for his wealth and piety, and not entirely unlearned or ignorant of letters—founded the *Sorbonne College* in Paris for the use of Masters of Theology. This college has flourished through all subsequent centuries even to this day, famous for men of great judgment, erudition, letters, and integrity. In the year 1254, or at least the following year, a dispute arose between the University of Paris and the Dominican and Franciscan Monks. The Mendicant Friars published a certain new book which they called the *Eternal Gospel*, or the *Gospel of the Holy Spirit*. It was composed, so they say, by *John of Parma*, the General of the Minorites <note>The Franciscans</note>. In this book (according to the testimony of <margin>* On the Dangers of the Last Times, ch. 8, p. 8.</margin> *William of Saint-Amour*, who published a book in Paris at this very time against these same Monks), they taught that *the Gospel of Christ would be more perfect, better, and worthier than the Eternal Gospel, or the Gospel of the Holy Spirit* <note>The text suggests the radical friars believed their new "spiritual" gospel would eventually supersede the traditional Gospel of Christ</note>, and that upon its arrival, the *Gospel of Christ* would be voided. Specifically, as is clear from *Eymeric* <note>Nicholas Eymeric, author of a famous manual for inquisitors</note> and others, that book contained among other blasphemous dogmas: *that the Eternal Gospel is superior to the Doctrine of Christ and the entire Old and New Testaments; that the Gospel of Christ is not the Gospel of the kingdom, and thus not for the building up of the Church; that the New Testament, like the Old, is to be voided; that it would not last in its power except until the year 1260; that thereafter everyone would be in the state of the perfect; that only those who walk barefoot are fit to instruct men on spiritual and eternal matters; that Christ and the Holy Apostles were not perfect in the contemplative life; but that the contemplative life began to bear fruit from Abbot Joachim himself <note>Joachim of Fiore, a mystic whose apocalyptic "three ages" theory deeply influenced radical Franciscans</note>, and would henceforth remain more perfectly in his perfect successors.* These are but a few points out of many. Much more will be taught to you by *Nicholas Eymeric* in his *Directory for Inquisitors, part 2, Question 9, Section 4*; *Du Boulay* in his *History of the University of Paris, Vol. III, Section 5, p. 330*; *Ussher* in *The Succession of Christian Churches, ch. 9, Sections 19, 20, 21, etc.* The Parisian theologians, indignant at such execrable blasphemies, condemned the book and refuted it in opposing writings. Delegates were chosen and <margin>Matthew Paris, for the year 1257, p. 939.</margin> sent to the Pope regarding this matter. They finally obtained from the Pontiff, with difficulty, that the *Eternal Gospel* should be condemned—but secretly, and if possible, burned without scandal to the friars. So tenderly did the Pontiff treat his necessary allies, though they were the most wicked of all two-legged creatures and raved like madmen against the Christian religion. Yet the same Pontiff had recently adjudged to the flames, both at Anagni and Paris, the book by *William of Saint-Amour* titled *On the Dangers of the Last Times*, which had been written against these Monks on this very subject. But enough of these things for our purpose. As the strength of the Byzantine Empire in the East was faltering, and the forces of the Muslims <note>original: Muhammedanorum</note> were pressing more tightly from all sides, help was hoped for from the Latins. To that end, a concord between the Greeks and Latins was attempted at the *Second General Council of Lyon*, held in the year 1274, which they claim was attended by 1,500 Bishops, Abbots, and other Prelates. While the previous page discussed the internal horrors of the Inquisition, this page transitions to the failed attempts at church union with the Greeks, the persecution of Jewish populations across Europe, and the final loss of the Holy Land to Islamic forces.</meta>

# THE SCHOLASTIC AGE.

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200.</margin>
...it <note>The Second Council of Lyons (1274)</note> held its sessions, and finally a certain union of the Greeks with the Latins was entered into, especially regarding the doctrine of the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritu Sancto." This refers to the "Filioque" controversy regarding whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.</note>. However, as soon as the synod was concluded, the Greeks rejected this union. This happened despite the Emperor **Michael Palaeologus** <note>Michael VIII (1223–1282), who sought union with Rome for political protection against Western invaders.</note> struggling against them to no avail, and raging against many with threats, beatings, blindings, and exiles. Even his associate **John Bekkos** <note>John XI Bekkos, a Greek theologian who became Patriarch of Constantinople and was the primary advocate for the union.</note>, whom he had elevated to the Patriarchate, labored alongside him in vain.

During this time, the **Jews** were held in infamy and hatred almost everywhere. On account of their greed and "execrable usury," and because of children who were rumored to have been circumcised or even crucified—along with other unspeakable crimes <note>The author refers to "blood libel" accusations, which were common antisemitic myths used to justify persecutions in the Middle Ages.</note>—they were expelled from several provinces of the West. They were driven out from **England** in the year 1290; from **France** in the year 1295; and from several cities of **Germany** in the year 1298. 

Finally, the many expeditions undertaken for the recovery of the **Holy Land** <note>The Crusades</note>—which had thus far been frustrated by the mutual disagreements of Christian Princes—came to a complete end as this century drew to a close. Those very places which our Lord had consecrated by His birth, His life, His miracles, and His blood, were left thereafter as a peaceful inheritance to the barbarians and the most bitter enemies of the Christian name.

# WRITERS.

<margin>
13th CENTURY
from the Year 1200.
</margin>
**SYLVESTER GERALD** <note>Also known as Giraldus Cambrensis or Gerald of Wales (c. 1146 – c. 1223).</note>, called "the Welshman" <note>original: "Cambrensis"</note> from his homeland, and called "de Barri" after his father, was a Welsh-Briton by birth. He was born in the southern part of **Wales** <note>original: "Cambriæ"</note>, on the coastal borders of **Dyfed** <note>original: "Demetiæ," an ancient kingdom in southwest Wales.</note>, not far from the city of **Pembroke**, in the noble castle of **Manorbier** <note>original: "Mainarpu."</note>. He was the son of William de Barri and Angareth, the granddaughter of **Rhys**, Prince of South Wales. Once he reached adulthood, he was appointed Archdeacon of **Brecon** by his maternal uncle David, the Bishop of **St. Davids** <note>original: "Menevenfi," the Latin name for the See of St. Davids.</note>. Dedicating himself to travel, he completed his literary studies at the **University of Paris**, where he lectured on Theology in the English College for three full years. Upon returning home, he was highly influential in the court of King **Henry II**. In the year 1185, he was appointed as a companion to **John**, Earl of Mortain <note>The future King John.</note>, who was leading an army into **Ireland**. Although John offered him the Bishoprics of **Wexford** and **Leighlin**, Gerald refused them both. When John returned to England toward the end of the year, Gerald remained in Ireland for some time to search everywhere for the historical records of the people and their deeds, and to draft a topography of the kingdom. The following year he crossed over into Wales; there, remaining in seclusion for several years, he applied himself with the greatest zeal to composing and refining his *History*. When the work was brought to completion <note>original: "ad umbilicum perductâ," a Latin idiom meaning "brought to the end" or "finished."</note>, he traveled to **Oxford**, and having gathered a massive assembly of Doctors, Scholars, and Townsmen, he recited his *History* over the course of three full days. Once the reading was finished, he hosted a banquet for his listeners. Afterward, he joined **Baldwin**, the Archbishop of Canterbury, as a traveling companion on his journey to the Holy Land. In the year 1198, he was elected Bishop of St. Davids, but a controversy was raised regarding the see. In the year 1200, he sought out **Rome** to obtain the Pope as a judge; there, although he demanded that the long-lost Metropolitan rights <note>Rights of an archbishopric, which would have made the Welsh church independent of Canterbury.</note> be restored to the See of St. Davids, he was defeated by the power of **Hubert**, Archbishop of Canterbury, and was completely removed from his Episcopal office. He lived beyond the seventieth year of his age, but it is not clear in what year he died.

## WORKS.

*Topography of Ireland, or a book on the Wonders of Ireland.*
*The Conquest of Ireland, or a Prophetic History of the Conquest of Ireland by the English*, for which Gerald prepared two editions, dedicating the latter to King John.
*An Itinerary of Wales, contained in two books.*
*A Description of Wales, dedicated to Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury.* These two small works were published together with notes by David Powell in *London, 1585, octavo.*
All these works were published among the *English and Norman Historians* at *Frankfurt, 1602, folio, page 692.*
*A Short Letter to William de Vere, Bishop of Hereford*, published by Ussher in the *Collection of Irish Letters, page 114.*
*The Jewel of the Church* <note>original: "Gemma Ecclesiastica."</note> exists as a manuscript in the **Lambeth Library**, and at the end of it is a letter that gives an account of both his life and his writings, which is certainly worthy of seeing the light of day.
*Dialogue on the Church of St. Davids.*
*A Dialogue of Two, or a mutual discourse between a questioner and a solver, in seven books.* Both *Dialogues* are held as manuscripts in **St. Benedict’s College, Cambridge** <note>Now known as Corpus Christi College.</note>, volume 99, numbers 3 and 4.
*A Book on the Instruction of a Prince*, divided into three sections; he spends two of these attacking the Norman princes, so that under the treacherous pretext of Religion, he might return all the British Isles to the French Monarchy—a mystery that continues to operate today in the political maneuvers of the **Spaniards**. This work is held as a manuscript in the **Cotton Library** under *Julius B. 13, No. 2.*

<margin>1201.</margin>
**GERVASE**, an Englishman by birth and a monk of **Christ Church** <note>original: "Fani Servatoris," the Church of the Savior.</note> in Canterbury, flourished in the year 1201. Beyond other studies in the liberal arts, he dedicated his mind to investigating the more ancient monuments of his nation, especially those regarding British and Saxon history; having collected a massive abundance of these records, he set himself to writing.

### WRITINGS.

*Treatise on the Burning and Repair of the Church of Canterbury*, published among the *Ten English Writers, London 1652, folio page 1289.*

*Images of the Discords between the Monks of Canterbury and Archbishop Baldwin, ibid. page 1303.*

*Chronicle of deeds done in England from the year 1122 to the year 1199, ibid. page 1334.*

*Acts or Lives of the Bishops of the Church of Canterbury from Augustine down to Hubert inclusive, ibid. page 1629.*

<margin>1201.</margin>
**HERVARD**, Archdeacon of **Liège**, flourished around the year 1201. There exists a *Letter concerning Guibert of Gembloux and on the writing of the Life of Saint Martin* in Mabillon's *Analecta, Volume II, page 536.*

<margin>1201.</margin>
**MATTHEW OF VENDÔME**, concerning whose era there is no small controversy among the learned: for some claim he died in the year 1203, others that he flourished in 1215; some contend he was elected Abbot of **St. Denis** in Paris in the year 1260 and died on September 25, 1286. The opinion of those who place him at the beginning of this century seems stronger, since he dedicated his work to **Bartholomew of Tours**, who was Bishop from 1175 to 1206. The Sainte-Marthe brothers <note>original: "Samarthrani Fratres," authors of the famous historical work *Gallia Christiana*.</note> add in *Gallia Christiana, Volume I, page 773*, that our Matthew refused the Bishopric of Tours while he was Abbot of St. Denis. He wrote in elegiac verse, which was quite elegant for the standards of that age, the *Tobiad* <note>original: "Tobiadem"</note>, or the *History of Tobias the Elder and the Younger*; which was printed in **Lyons** in 1505, edited by Johannes Herold in **Basel** in 1563, and edited by Johannes Hering in **Bremen** in 1642.

<margin>1201.</margin>
**JOACHIM**, a native of **Calabria**, was a monk of the Cistercian Order in the Monastery of Sambucina in the Diocese of Anglona in Lucania, then Abbot of the Monastery of Corazzo in Calabria, and finally the founder and first Abbot of the Monastery of **Fiore** <note>original: "Florenfis"</note>, and the founder of the Florensian Congregation. He flourished in the year 1201. Eleven years earlier, because of the immense fame of the "prophecy" granted to him by God, he was summoned by **Richard, King of England** <note>Richard the Lionheart.</note>, who was then staying at Messina in **Sicily**. Joachim prophesied that the Antichrist was already born in the city of **Rome** and would soon be raised to the Apostolic See, along with many other trifles of that sort. He died before the year 1215, when his book against certain opinions of **Peter Lombard** was condemned in the **Lateran Synod**.

**THOMAS**, a Monk of the Cistercian Order, flourished around the year 1201. He wrote *Commentaries on the Song of Songs* to Pons, the Bishop of Clermont, *printed in Paris, 1521, and Lyon, 1571.* Our Thomas is the true author of these Commentaries. There are, however, others to whom they are attributed; there is much dispute among the learned on this matter, which, if it be of interest, can be found in Casimir Oudin, who treated the subject quite laboriously.

<margin>1201.</margin>
**NICOLAUS**, from the city of Otranto <note>original: "Patriâ Hydruntinus."</note>, called *Master Hydrus* by some, flourished in the year 1201. When Cardinal Benedict was sent to Constantinople by Pope Innocent III to repair the union between the Eastern and Western Churches, our Nicolaus served as the interpreter in all the disputations held then in the Royal City <note>Constantinople</note>, as well as in Thessaloniki and Athens. He wrote various *Treatises against the Latins* in Greek, namely: 1st, *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* <note>The "Filioque" controversy regarding whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father only, or from the Father and the Son.</note>, *in which he attempts to refute Hugh Etherian.* Fragments of this book are held by Leo Allatius in *On Consensus, book 1, chapter 22, section 3, and against Hottinger, chapter 19, page 421.* 2nd, *On the leavened bread handed to the Disciples by Christ at the Last Supper* <note>The "Azymes" controversy regarding whether the bread for the Eucharist should be leavened or unleavened.</note>: Leo Allatius presents two fragments in *Against Hottinger, chapter 1, page 13, and On Consensus, book 2, chapter 13, section 4.* 3rd, *On the Fasting of the Latins on Saturday, the Marriage of Priests, and other arguments.* He is cited by Allatius in the place just mentioned.

**NICETAS** of Maroneia, who rose from being the Archivist <note>original: "Chartophylace."</note> of the Great Church of Constantinople to become the Archbishop of Thessaloniki; he was somewhat more favorable toward the Latins, as he uniquely desired the union between the Greek and Roman Churches. He flourished in the year 1201. He wrote *six books of Dialogues on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, in which he introduces a Greek and a Latin speaker in conversation; he addresses the arguments of Hugh Etherian as best he can. Leo Allatius provides certain fragments from these in *Against Hottinger, chapter 19, page 467.* His *Response to the questions of the Monk Basil* is available in Greek and Latin in *Greco-Roman Law, book 5, page 345.*

## NICETAS ACOMINATUS, CHONIATES

Named after his homeland <note>Choniates refers to his birthplace, Chonae</note>, he was the brother of the aforementioned Michael. While still a boy of nine, he went to Constantinople to join his brother Michael, by whom he was instructed in character and learning. Eventually, he was enrolled among the ministers of the Court of Constantinople, made Secretary to Alexios Komnenos and later to Isaac Angelos; then a Senator of Constantinople, Grand Logothete of the Secrets <note>A high-ranking administrative official similar to a Secretary of State</note>, Inspector and Judge of the Veil, and Prefect of the Sacred Bedchamber. In the year 1204, when Constantinople was captured by the Latins <note>The Western European forces of the Fourth Crusade</note>, he went into exile with his pregnant wife and children, and having set out for Nicaea in Bithynia, he established his home there. He died at Nicaea after the year 1206. Regarding his historical work, Justus Lipsius offered this judgment: <margin>\* Politics, book 1, chapter 9, section 12.</margin> *Among the lower Greeks <note>Byzantine authors of the later period</note> there are two whom I do not despise. The first is Nicetas Choniates. He is as yet little known to the public, I confess; but he is most worthy of notice: a pure and upright mind, if there ever was one in that age. His style is elaborate, often savoring of the Poets and Homer; just as the matter and the narration itself is distinct, composed, without vanity, without nonsense, grave enough, and faithful. His warnings are frequent and timely: his judgments are not only free but sound.* Nicetas wrote a *History* of the deeds of the Emperors of Constantinople in his own century, in twenty-one books, distributed into ten smaller works. It begins with the death of Alexios Komnenos in the year of Christ 1118 and ends with the entry of Henry of Flanders in the year of Christ 1206. That *History* was published in Latin at *Paris*, 1550; at *Frankfurt*, 1568; and in Greek and Latin with the translation and notes of Hieronymus Wolf at *Basel*, 1557, in folio; at *Geneva*, 1593, in quarto; and with Fabrot’s *Glossary of Medieval Greek* <note>original: "Glossario Græco-barbaro"</note> at *Paris*, 1647, in folio. He also wrote the *Treasury of the Orthodox Faith* in twenty-seven books, which I once saw beautifully transcribed in Greek in the Bodleian Library. Of these, the first five were translated and published in Latin with notes by the most learned Peter Morell at *Paris*, 1580; *Geneva*, 1592, in octavo; and in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume 25, page 54.* A fragment from the twentieth book, concerning the order observed by those who pass from "Saracen" <note>Muslim</note> superstition to the Christian faith, is found in Greek and Latin (with Nicetas's name suppressed) among Sylburg’s *Saracenica*, *Heidelberg*, 1595, in octavo, page 74.

<margin>1204.</margin>

## JOEL, Greek Chronographer;

Who he was, or from where, I would more gladly learn from others. He flourished around the year 1204. He wrote a *Compendious Chronography* <note>original Greek: "Χρονογραφίαν ἐν συνόψει"</note>, or a summary history from the Foundation of the World down to the death of Alexios Doukas Mourtzouphlos—that is, the year 1204, at which time Constantinople was captured by the Latins. From this event, he closes his history with these words: *Alas, even these things Christians do to Christians! And how was justice to be at rest, if it did not cast us into captivity or destruction? Which indeed happened; and the royal city, on account of such unholy deeds, was handed over to the Italians.* <note>The Greek text laments the sack of Constantinople by the Crusaders, whom he identifies as Italians/Latins.</note> Leo Allatius brought this *Chronography* to light and, having added his own Greek-Latin translation, published it together with the *History* of George Acropolites at the *Royal Press in Paris*, 1651, in folio.

<margin>1206.</margin>

## WILLIAM OF SEIGNELAY,

Or Seligniaco, Bishop of Auxerre from the year 1206, later transferred to the see of Paris; he died at Saint-Cloud on the Seine on November 23, 1223. There exists a *Summa Theologica* <note>A comprehensive summary of theological knowledge</note> written by him, which was published in print at *Paris*, 1500.

<meta>This page continues the biographical entry for Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, whose career was previously introduced. It details his rise through the ecclesiastical ranks in Paris and Rome, his contentious relationship with King John of England, and his extensive theological writings.</meta>

<page-num>703</page-num>
<header>The Scholastic Century.</header>

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200</margin>
...earned him such favor that he was created Chancellor of the University of Paris, a Canon of Paris, and Dean of Reims. Finally, he was called to Rome by Pope Innocent III and chosen to be among the Cardinals. At last, in the year 1206, when a controversy arose regarding the see of Canterbury following the death of Archbishop Hubert, he was appointed as his successor—even against the wishes of King John and the monks of Canterbury—and was consecrated by the Pope himself at Viterbo on the 17th day of June. King John immediately forbade the consecrated man from entering the kingdom. Because of this, the Pope ordered the King to be excommunicated, which was carried out. Finally, in the year 1212, the King, bound by inescapable difficulties, yielded to the Pope's will: he resigned his crown, received the kingdom of England back from him as a feudal tenant of the Roman See, and called Archbishop Stephen to England, admitting him to his see. Around the year 1215, Stephen, being harassed again by the King, incited a wicked rebellion <note>original Latin: "nefariam concivit rebellionem"; this refers to the political unrest involving the Magna Carta and the Barons' War</note> and persuaded the nobles of England to defect from John and surrender themselves to Louis, the son of the King of France. In the year 1218, after the death of John and the expulsion of the French, Langton found it necessary to redeem his crime of treason with a massive monetary fine. In the year 1222, he held a general Synod in the Church at Oxford, where the reform of the English Church and monastic life was addressed. During this synod, two most wicked scoundrels—one of whom is said to have been an androgyne <note>a person of indeterminate gender or "hermaphrodite" in the language of the time</note>—who boasted of assuming the persona of Christ and of having false wounds of the divine body, were condemned and shortly thereafter fixed to a cross. Regarding this, see what Matthew Paris and the *Antiquities of Oxford* have for the year 1222. He died at his estate of Slindon in Sussex on the 9th of July, 1228. He is buried at Canterbury.

## W R I T I N G S.

*A Booklet on the Translation of the Body of the Blessed Thomas of Canterbury* <note>The "Translation" refers to the ritual moving of Thomas Becket's remains to a new shrine in 1220</note>, edited at the end of the *Letters of Thomas Becket*, Brussels, 1682, in quarto, page 885.
*Letter to King John*, found in D'Achery’s *Spicilegium*, Volume III.
*Forty-Eight Constitutions*, in Lyndwood’s *Provinciale of England*.
*Commentaries on the Octateuch* <note>The first eight books of the Bible</note>, manuscript in the Library of St. Peter, Cambridge, Codex 241.
*His Moral Exposition on Exodus* was held as a manuscript in the Naudean Codex, mentioned by Labbe in his *New Collection of Manuscript Libraries*, page 22.
*Commentaries on Tobit, Judith, Esther, Ezra, and the Books of Maccabees.* Manuscript in the same place, and in the College of St. Benedict, Codex 151.
*Commentaries on Isaiah*, manuscript in the College of St. Benedict, Codex 375.
*Commentaries on Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Ezra, and Nehemiah*, manuscript in the same place, Codex 145.
*Commentary on Job in 33 books.* Manuscript in the Oriel Library at Oxford, Codex 12.
*Tropology or Moral Interpretation of the 12 Minor Prophets*, manuscript in the public library at Cambridge, Codex 151; and at St. Benedict’s, Codex 148.
*Commentaries on the Gospels and Epistles for Sundays throughout the year*: these exist along with the *Commentaries on Isaiah and the Minor Prophets* as manuscripts in the Lambeth Library.
*Commentary on Ecclesiasticus*, manuscript in the public library at Cambridge, Codex 60; and at St. Benedict’s, Cambridge, Codex 75.
*The Life of St. Thomas, and his Passion*, woven together from various authors. Manuscript in the College of St. Benedict, Codex 150.
These small works of Langton exist as manuscripts in many other libraries in England; for these, you may consult James’s *Catalogue*.
*Various Sermons* are held as manuscripts in the Dunes Library, according to Sander’s *Belgian Library of Manuscripts*, page 183.
*A Summa on Various Topics*, beginning with "On Crimes"; in the Library of the Cambron Monastery, page 365 of the same work.
*Two Sermons on the Blessed Mary.* Manuscripts in the Paulina Library at Leipzig, Theological Repository, Series 5, octavo, Number 24. See Feller’s *Catalogue of Manuscript Codices*, page 97.
