<margin>1207.</margin> HUGOLINUS, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri <note>The future Pope Gregory IX, a central figure in medieval law and the patron of the Franciscans</note>, was prominent in 1207. There exists a Letter to the people of Velletri, etc., for the preservation of peace with the Nymphs <note>referring to the inhabitants of the town of Ninfa</note> in Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Volume II, page 248.

<margin>1208.</margin> <margin>Mariana, *History*, book 13, chapter 5.</margin> RODERIC XIMENES, a Basque or <unclear>Navarrese</unclear> by birth, was Archbishop of Toledo from the year 1208. In the year 1215, he set out for Rome and took part in the Lateran Council, where he spoke in the assembly of the Fathers with the highest praise for his eloquence. In his extreme old age, he again approached Pope Innocent IV, who was celebrating a Council at Lyon, so that he might submit to the Pope’s judgment a dispute brought against him by Peter of <unclear>Tarragona</unclear> concerning the primacy <note>the ecclesiastical leadership</note> of all Spain. On his return, while being carried by boat on the Rhone River, he died in the year 1245, on the 9th of August.

->W O R K S.<-

**N**ine books of *Spanish History*, from the first arrival of Hercules in Spain to the year of Christ 1243; published by Andreas Schott in *Spain Illustrated*, Volume II, page 26.
*History of the Ostrogoths*, from the year of Christ 453 to the year 555. Ibid, page 148.
*History of the Huns, Vandals, etc.*, from their first origin to the year 585. Ibid, page 151.
*History of the Arabs*, from the year of Christ 570 to the year 1150. Ibid, page 163.
*History of the Romans*, from King Janus to the year of the City 708. Ibid, page 194.

<margin>1208.</margin> ST. FRANCIS, an Italian by birth, was born at Assisi in Umbria in the year 1182, the son of Peter Bernardone and Pica. In his adult years, he practiced the trade of a merchant; indeed, if Walsingham <note>Thomas Walsingham, an English chronicler known for his occasionally sharp critiques</note> is to be believed, he was for a long time <unclear>enslaved</unclear> to unrestrained luxury <note>original Latin: "effræni lasciviæ diu mancipatus"</note>. In the year 1208, either improved by the <unclear>captivity</unclear> that befell him and the reading of the Sacred Book, or led back to a better way of life, he dedicated himself entirely to the study of piety, and having professed Evangelical poverty, he cultivated a new <unclear>way of life</unclear>. Then, wandering like a vagabond through all of Italy, he began to turn the faces and eyes of everyone toward himself with a <unclear>great</unclear> appearance of piety and humility. For, covered in rags and filth, girded with a thick and knotted rope, and descending to every sordid task as long as it presented a show of humility, he acted out a kind of theatrical performance <note>original: "histrioniam"; the author here views Francis’s public displays of humility with skepticism</note> in the streets and crossroads everywhere. Fearfully shunning the <unclear>harmful</unclear> touch of coins and wasting away his body with fasts and vigils, he wished to be considered a truly Apostolic man. Furthermore, he sought the name of a Prophet through <unclear>rashly</unclear> uttered predictions; and despising the human lot, he took on the persona of some divine being, more than a man, through a profane and no less <unclear>ridiculous</unclear> imitation of the things done by Christ on earth. Through follies of this kind, he won <unclear>admiration</unclear> for himself among some; but by the greater part of the common people, he was received only with sneers and taunts, and was often soundly punished with blows. He certainly did not flee from these, but rather considered them a great honor; and in every way, he sought out the <unclear>breaking of his back</unclear> <note>original: "lumbifragium"; a term for severe physical suffering or mortification</unclear>. At last, in the year 1215, he conceived greater ambitions, and having <unclear>gathered</unclear> disciples from all sides, he established a new Order of Monks, whom he wished to <unclear>zealously</unclear> emulate his own studies and character. He himself went to Rome and obtained confirmation of his fellowship and brotherhood (for thus he wished it to be called) from Innocent III. In the year 1219, he undertook a journey to the East to visit the holy places, and before his return, having met with the Sultan of the Saracens, he attempted to convert him to the Christian faith. He died in the year 1226, on the 4th day before the Nones of <unclear>October</unclear> <note>October 4th</note>; after his death, he was numbered among the Saints. The writers of his life will provide more details, and especially Luke Wadding in the *Annals of the Minors, Volume I*.

**A**RNOLD, first Provost of the Church of Hildesheim, then Abbot of Lübeck, was prominent in the year 1209. He supplemented the Chronicle of Helmold from the year 1171 up to the year 1209. In Slavic matters, he especially deserves trust, as noted by the illustrious Vossius <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius, a renowned 17th-century scholar of history and linguistics</note>; in other matters, he showed no small amount of diligence. This Continuation exists alongside Helmold’s *Chronicle*, notably illustrated by the notes of Heinrich Bangert, Lübeck 1659, in quarto. In the first edition of Helmold, Frankfurt 1556, only the first nine chapters were included. Other chapters were added in subsequent editions. Finally, the last four chapters, along with the Epilogue, were published from a manuscript codex among the historical works of Heinrich Meibom, Helmstedt 1660, in quarto, page 568.

**G**ERVASE OF TILBURY, English by nation, born in the county of Essex at Tilbury on the banks of the Thames, nephew of King Henry II of England, and eventually made Marshal <note>a high-ranking administrative and military official</note> of the region of Arles in Gaul by him; he was especially dear not only to his King but also to Emperor Otto IV. He was prominent in the year 1210. A *Commentary on the kingdoms of the Roman Emperors, Goths, Lombards, Britons, Franks, and English* by our Gervase was published by the illustrious Mader in the year 1673, according to Christopher Sand <note>original: *Christophoro Sandio*</note>; for I have not seen the edition so far. Whether this is the same work as the *Three Books of Imperial Leisure* <note>original: *Otiorum Imperialium*</note> which are held in the library of St. Benedict at Cambridge, Manuscript Code 237, number 1, let those see who have the opportunity to compare both works. Our Gervase’s book on the description of the world dedicated to Emperor Otto exists in the Cottonian Library, under Vespasian E. I. N. I.; I believe it is the same as the book *On the Wonders of the World* <note>original: *Mirabilibus Mundi*</note>, which is found in the Benedictine library at the place cited. His dialogue *on the rights and customs of the Exchequer* <note>The medieval office responsible for royal revenues</note> exists in manuscript among the Fiscal Archives of the Kingdom, and in Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. Bale, Pits, and others list other historical writings of Gervase, namely, *Illustrations of Geoffrey, History of the Holy Land, The Three Columns of England* <note>original: *Tricolumnium Angliæ*</note>, etc.

**GUNTHER**, first a Scholastic <note>a teacher or head of a cathedral school</note>, then a Cistercian monk at the Monastery of Pairis in the Diocese of Basel. He was prominent in the year 1200. He wrote, from the mouth of a certain Abbot Martin who was present at the events, a *History of the Capture of Constantinople by the Latins*. This was published by Henricus Canisius in *Ancient Lessons*, Volume 5, p. 358. The same Gunther (though I do not state this as certain) seems to be the author of a truly elegant Heroic Song comprised of ten books, called *The Ligurian Poem* <note>original: "Ligurinum"</note>; this was published among the German Writers with notes by Jakob Spiegel by Justus Reuber at Frankfurt, 1584, in folio, p. 307. It had appeared previously on its own in Basel, 1569, and with Spiegel's notes at Strasbourg, 1531; indeed, as early as 1500 in folio. In this poem, he mentions another work he wrote about the Holy War, which he calls *The Solymarian Poem* <note>original: "Solymarium," referring to Solyma/Jerusalem</note>. Certainly, this Gunther—whoever he may have been—is highly commended as a poet of no common spirit and talent, with a style that is marvelous for that age and very elegant for the capacity of a barbaric century, by *Lipsius, Casaubon †, and Vossius ||. Good God! What judges! Indeed, he described the deeds bravely and wisely performed at home and abroad in his own time (in which he depicts that most praised Emperor Frederick I) in a poem more elegant, good, and learned than his century might typically produce.

He is mentioned by Caesarius of Heisterbach in book 4, chapter 90 of his *Miracles of His Own Time*. There exist fifty-one *Festival Sermons* printed through the care of Daniel Schilling at Cologne, 1534, in folio.

**ROBERT DE MONTE**, or Robert of Torigni, a Norman by birth and Abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel in the Diocese of Avranches, was prominent in the year 1210, as is commonly claimed; this is because the *Continuation of Sigebert* ascribed to him is brought down to this year. However, it is more correctly reported that our Robert was promoted from Prior of Bec to Abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel and finally died in the year 1186; thus, the *Chronicle of Sigebert* was continued from the year 1158 (where Robert left off) to the year 1210 by some later writer. Certainly, in the catalog of the Abbots of Saint Michael presented by Du Monstier *, no other Robert appears at this time.

### W O R K S

*A Continuation of the Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux* from the year 1112 to 1210; perhaps no part of this is genuine except that which ends at the year 1158, or at least at the year 1182. It exists published with the *Chronicle of Sigebert* at Antwerp, 1608, in quarto, and frequently elsewhere.

> He arranged a *Chronicle* from the beginning of the world until his own time in a certain very large volume; and this work was so scattered and dispersed that it is nowhere found in its entirety. <margin>1215.</margin>
### **CONRAD OF LICHTENAU**, of German race and noble birth; having been made a Priest in the year 1202, then a monk of the Premonstratensian Order in 1207, and finally Abbot of the Monastery of Ursberg on the Mindel in the Diocese of Augsburg from the year 1215 until 1240, in which year he died. From various histories by others, he composed a *Chronicle* from Belus, King of the Assyrians, to the year of Christ 1229. He deserves very well of German History, since he studiously collected many things concerning our Emperors. Moreover, he applied the "notation of time"—the other eye of History—more diligently than others, says Heinrich Meibom in that very *Apology* which he wrote for Emperor Otto against the criticism of our Conrad. * This *Chronicle* appeared in Strasbourg in 1537, 1540, and 1609, in folio. <margin>* Historical Works, p. 329.</margin>

*On the Natures of Things* <note>original: "De Naturis rerum," his most famous encyclopedic work on science and natural history</note>, in the Library of G. Cope, an English nobleman, Vol. 62.
*The Library Elucidator*. It begins, *Of the individual books of the Library*, according to Bale. It exists as a manuscript in duodecimo, but without the author's name, in the Library of Gonville & Caius College, Cambridge, written in a quite ancient hand. The book contains explanations of various difficult passages of Holy Scripture, including, among others, that famous passage in John 6: *If any man eat*, etc. It contains these words not unworthy of note: *If any man eats of this bread he shall live forever; that is, whoever perseveres in Ecclesiastical unity, which is the reality of his Sacrament, which is the body of the Lord. This bread is called the flesh of Christ, and the bread itself is Christ, who refreshes his own here spiritually, intending to refresh them eternally in Glory. But whoever eats of this bread, which is Christ—that is, takes delight in faith, in works, and in the love of Christ. For "to eat" is often understood to mean "to take delight." Unless he eats, specifically in interpretation. For he truly eats the flesh of Christ who is in the unity of the Church, which, as I said, is the reality of that Sacrament.* The manuscript volume ends with these words: *...that [Christ] is more excellent than the Angels.* To doubt that this is the work of our Alexander is the height of madness. Mr. Wharton <note>Henry Wharton (1664–1695), an English writer and librarian</note> transcribed the passage and identified the author. Many other monuments which he left behind, or at least their titles, are presented by Bale and Pits <note>John Pits (1560–1616), a Catholic bibliographer</note>; let studious readers seek them from those sources if they take pleasure in lists of names.

<margin>1215.</margin>
## ALAN OF LILLE

ALAN OF LILLE <note>original: "Alanus de Insulis"</note>, a Fleming by nation, called the *Universal Doctor* <note>original: "Doctor Universalis," a title reflecting his vast knowledge</note> on account of his distinguished and most widespread erudition, was a Parisian theologian and moderator of that same Academy. Finally, he became a Cistercian *Conversus* <term>Conversus: A lay brother who focused on manual labor rather than the liturgical duties of a choir monk</term>, or Lay Brother. He was prominent in the year 1215, in which he most skillfully disputed against the disciples of Amalric of Bène <note>original: "Almerici Carnotensis," a theologian whose followers were condemned for pantheistic heresy</note> at the Lateran Council.
Regarding the age of our Alan, there is a dispute among writers not easily reconciled. For in the *Commentaries on the Prophecies of Merlin*, p. 198, he says he was a boy when Theodoric was elected Count of Flanders, which happened around the year 11[?]. Yet in his epitaph at the Cistercian Cloister, he is said to have died in the year 1294. Charles Visch <note>A Cistercian historian (1596–1666)</note> thinks the former can be resolved by claiming the *Commentaries on Merlin* are a forgery. Be that as it may: what shall become of the Epitaph? Certainly, it must be said that either an error lies in the Epitaph, or our Alan died a centenarian—if not older than a hundred years.

<margin>1216.</margin>
**HONORIUS III.** Previously named Cencio Savelli, a Roman by birth and son of Aimerico. He was made Cardinal Deacon and Chamberlain by Celestine III, and Cardinal Priest by Innocent III. He was elected Supreme Pontiff at Perugia on July 18, 1216, and consecrated on the 24th. His greatest desire and effort was to crush the Saracens in Asia and the Albigensians in Gaul with powerful forces of Crusaders. He pursued this with such momentum of spirit that he commanded Emperor Frederick II, under pain of excommunication, to assemble an army and lead it to the East once and again; when Frederick continued to weave delays, the Pope finally excommunicated him in the year 1226. In 1217, he confirmed the newly established religious order of the Carmelites. He died on March 18, 1227. Six of his letters exist in the *Collection of Councils*, Vol. XI, p. 242. Three others are found in Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Vol. II, p. 252. Seven more in Waddington’s *Annals of the Minors*, Vol. I, for the year 1219, etc. Three others are in the same location in the *Register of the Popes*, p. 1.

<margin>1216.</margin>
<margin>* Library, p. 631.</margin>
<margin>† Century 3, chapter 47.</margin>
**SIMON OF TOURNAI,** a Priest by rank and a Master at Paris, distinguished for his learning and erudition as one of the primary lights of the University of Paris; he flourished around the year 1216. His existing writings include a *Summary of Questions on the Sentences*, in manuscript at the Balliol Library, Oxford, Codices 58 and 188; and *Instructions on the Sacred Page*, in manuscript at Merton College, Oxford, Codex 36, number 2. Simler* lists other works of his: a book on the Athanasian Creed; a book on Boethius’s *On the Trinity*; and *Scholastic Lectures*, though it is not clear if these remain hidden in manuscript somewhere. Various questions of his and an *Exposition of the Creed of Saint Athanasius* are held in a manuscript at Saint-Victor, according to Labbe in his *New Library of Manuscripts*, p. 25. Furthermore, Bale† contends that this Simon was English, a native of Cornwall with the surname Thervai; he relates that Simon, eventually swelling with excessive pride in his own learning against divine law, was divinely deprived of all knowledge and rendered speechless, and Bale provides a more extensive catalog of his short works.

**JAMES OF VITRY**, of French origin, born in the village of Argenteuil near Paris and educated at the University of Paris, first served as a priest in his native town. Having left his parochial duties, he became a Canon Regular at the Monastery of Mary of Oignies in the Diocese of Namur. From there, he traveled to the region of Toulouse, where he spoke out powerfully against the Albigensians <note>A dualist religious sect in southern France considered heretical by the Catholic Church.</note>. Driven by no less zeal against the Saracens <note>A common medieval term for Muslims, particularly those fighting in the Crusades.</note>, he crossed over to Palestine, where he was appointed Bishop of Acre <note>original: "Aconensis, (quæ olim Ptolemaïs)"; Acre was a key Crusader port in modern-day Israel.</note>. He flourished in the year 1220. Eventually summoned to Rome by Pope Honorius III, he was named Bishop and Cardinal of Tusculum. Armed with the authority of a Papal Legate, he was sent through France and neighboring regions to preach the Crusade and to overthrow the Albigensians. Returning to Rome, he spent the rest of his life in peace until the year 1244, when he died. His body was brought back to Brabant and laid to rest in the Monastery of Oignies. See what Louis d’Attichy writes of him in the *History of Cardinals, Volume I, page 289.*

### W R I T I N G S.

*Three Books of Oriental and Occidental History.* In the first book, he describes the affairs of the East, the customs of the peoples, and the geography of the regions, weaving the history from the time of Muhammad to the year 1210. In the second, he narrates the Western affairs of his own time. In the third, returning to the East, he continues his history to the year 1218. This *History* was published at Douai in 1597 in octavo; and, with the second book omitted, it appeared in Bongars' collection, *God’s Deeds through the Franks* <note>original: "Gestorum Dei per Francos"</note>, Volume II, page 1047. This Bongarsian edition is in many ways more expanded and corrected than the Douai edition.

*Letter to his Friends in Lorraine regarding the capture of Damietta*, found in the same volume of Bongars, page 1146. <note>Damietta was a strategic port in Egypt captured during the Fifth Crusade.</note>

*Letter to Pope Honorius III*, found in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium, Volume VIII, page 373.*

*Sermons on the Gospels and Epistles for the whole year.* These were published at Antwerp, 1575, in folio. However, the fifth and sixth parts of these sermons are missing, which are said to exist in manuscript in various libraries.

*The Life of Blessed Mary of Oignies, in two books.* This is found in Surius’s collection under the date of June 23rd. Compare what Antonius Sanderus writes in the *Bibliography of Belgian Manuscripts, part 1, page 93.*

<margin>1220.</margin>

**ANTHONY OF PADUA**, of Portuguese origin and a citizen of Lisbon, later migrated to Italy and settled in Padua. Giving his name to the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans; original: "Minorum Ordini"</note> recently founded by Francis, he earned an immense reputation among his peers. He is said to be the first of all the Friars Minor to have held the office of Professor of Theology. He flourished in the year 1220. Ordained a priest two years later, he was sent by Francis to the Monastery of Vercelli to be further instructed in the liberal arts. In the year 1227, as he began to become increasingly famous through his strenuous efforts, he was called to Rome and received with the greatest honor by the Pope and the Cardinals. He died at Padua on June 13, 1231.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Sermons for Sundays, Advent, Lent, and other seasons. Also, Sermons on the Saints.* These were published as *The Sermons of Saint Anthony* at Paris, 1521, and Venice, 1575.

*Interpretation, or mystical exposition, of Holy Scripture.*

*Five books of Moral Concordances of the Holy Bible.*

Jean de la Haye collected these minor works and published them together with the works of Saint Francis at *Paris, 1641, in folio.*

*Other Sermons on particular Saints and various subjects*, which Antoine Pagi published as a supplement at *Avignon, 1684, in octavo.* These sermons altogether...

# GERMANUS II.
<margin>1222.
* Roman History, book 3, p. 39.</margin>
Born in Anaplous on the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara near Constantinople.</note>, a monk by vocation, "a man accustomed to adorn his life with both virtue and speech," <note>original: "aretê & logô ton bion kosmêfas"</note> says Nicephorus Gregoras. From about the year 1222, he served as the Patriarch of Constantinople, establishing his residence at Nicaea, where the Patriarchate of Constantinople had been transferred as long as the royal city was held by the Latins <note>Following the Fourth Crusade's capture of Constantinople in 1204, the Byzantine government and church went into exile in Nicaea.</note>. He was deposed from his seat in 1240 and restored again in 1254; he died in that same year, or at least the following one. Certainly, the Patriarchal seat was vacant due to his death at the time when Theodore Lascaris the Younger came to power—that is, according to Freher, in the year 1255.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*An Account on the Dedication of the venerable shrine of the Blessed Mary, and on the Swaddling Clothes of our Lord.* Published in Greek and Latin by Combefis in *Origins of Constantinople*, page 231.

<margin>* Notes to page 287.</margin>
*A Theory of Ecclesiastical Matters, or an Exposition on the Liturgy*, in Greek and Latin in the *Ducean Supplement*, Volume II, page 131. Father Simon * complains that this *Theory*, as it is currently published, is so miserably tampered with that nothing of its ancient appearance remains; it can hardly be distinguished what originated from Germanus and what from the interpolators such as Gabriel Severus. He adds that he has obtained a much more complete manuscript (noted under the title of *St. Basil’s Ecclesiastical History*), appended to the *Catena on John* by Nicetas of Heraclea, which he intends to make public someday.

*Three Orations*: namely, a Praise, a Sermon on the Nativity, and one on the Dormition <note>The "falling asleep" or passing of the Virgin Mary.</note> of the Blessed Virgin; Greek and Latin, in the same work, page 450. Of these, the second, which is on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin and begins "If the earth is measured," does not seem to belong to our Germanus; for the most ancient manuscripts, the style, and the method argue against it, and attribute it to George of Nicomedia, or the "Keeper of the Records," according to the testimony of Leo Allatius in his *Discourse on the Georges and their writings*, page 313.

*Five Homilies*: namely, on the Beheading of St. John the Baptist, on the Presentation of St. Mary, two on her Dormition, and on the burial of the Lord’s body; Greek and Latin, in Combefis’s *New Supplement*, Paris, 1648, Volume I, page 1464.

*An Idiomelon* <note>A type of Byzantine hymn with its own unique melody.</note> for the Feast of the Annunciation, Greek and Latin, in the same work.

*Oration on the Exaltation of the venerable Cross, and against the Bogomils* <note>A medieval Gnostic-Manichaean religious sect in the Balkans considered heretical by the Orthodox Church.</note>. Published in Greek and Latin by Gretser, *On the Cross*, Volume II, page 1237.

*Oration on the Life-giving Cross* for the third Sunday of the fast, ibid. page 1413.

*Another Oration* for the time of Mid-Lent, ibid. page 1427.

*Oration for the first Sunday of the fast, and on the Restoration of the Holy Images*. For the author of these homilies lived not only after the birth of the Bogomil heresy, but also after the schism arose between the Greeks and the Latins, and after the wars began between the Italians and the Emperors of Constantinople, as Gretser correctly notes. *
<margin>* In the Annotations, ibid. page 272.</margin>

*A certain fragment from the Oration against Heresies to Anthimus*, found in Canisius and in nearly every *Library of the Fathers*.

*Two Letters to the Cypriots*, Greek and Latin, published by Cotelerius in *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume II, page 462.

*Two Letters to Pope Gregory IX and the Cardinals*, in Latin, in Matthew Paris under the year 1237, and in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume XI, page 318.

*Three Decrees*, chiefly concerning Patriarchal Monasteries, found in Greek and Latin in Leunclavius, *Greco-Roman Law*, book 3, page 232.

Germanus also wrote a work *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* against the Latins, filled with carefully sought-out testimonies from both Latin and Greek Fathers; a *Synodic Response* to the delegate Franciscan Friars and others; and *Small Works on Unleavened Bread* <term>Azymes: the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, a major theological dispute between the Eastern and Western Churches</term>, on *Purgatory*, and on the *three ways of administering Baptism*, according to Leo Allatius, *On Consensus*, book 2, chapter 14, section 3, who reveals that the first two treatises exist in Greek manuscript in the Vatican Library.

<header>The Scholastic Age</header>

<margin>
13th CENTURY
From the year 1200.
1223.
</margin>
**JORDANUS**, a Saxon by birth, from the town of Borrentrick <note>original: "Borterge"</note> in the Diocese of Mainz. Around the year 1220, he became a monk of the Dominican Order <note>The Order of Preachers</note>. He served as the Provincial of Lombardy for two years, and after the death of St. Dominic around 1223, he was declared the second Master General of the entire Order of Preachers. He died around the year 1236. His extant works include *The Crown of the Virgin Mary*, published in Piacenza in 1599 among other places, and the *Book on the Origin of His Order*, with notes by Antonio Maffei (Rome, 1606), also found in Bzovius’s *Annals* at the year 1233, number 5. Ambrosius de Altamura lists several more works in his *Dominican Library*, page 6; however, he does not say where they may be found, or if they even survive today.

<margin>1225.</margin>
**CÆSARIUS**, a German by birth, became a monk of the Cistercian Order in 1199 at the Heisterbach Monastery in the Diocese of Cologne. He later became the Master of Novices in that same monastery, and finally the Prior of the Monastery of St. Peter’s Valley near Bonn. He flourished in the year 1225. His *Twelve Books (or Dialogues) on the Miracles and Visions of His Time* are extant, focusing primarily on events in Germany. In composing these, being an excessively credulous man, he deals plainly in trifles and scrapes together fables from every possible source. They were published in Cologne in 1591. He also wrote the *Life of St. Engelbert, Archbishop of Cologne* (who died in 1225), dedicated to Henry, Engelbert’s successor; it was written in three books in 1227 and published separately with notes by Aegidius Gelenius in Cologne, 1633, and also by Surius under November 7th. His *Homilies, or Moral Sermons for all Sundays and Festivals of the Year*, are divided into four parts, which Andreas Coppenstein published under the title *The Bundle of Morality* <note>original: "Fasciculus Moralitatis"</note> in Cologne, 1615. Caesarius himself diligently lists the many works he wrote in the preface to the *Bundle of Morality*, which Carolus Vischius displays in the *Cistercian Library*, page 57; whether they survive today, let others seek them out.

<margin>1227.</margin>
**GREGORY IX**, previously named Ugolino, was from the Campagna region and the city of Anagni, descending from the Counts of Segni. He was the nephew of Pope Innocent III, by whom he was chosen as a Cardinal. In the year 1227, he was elected Roman Pontiff on March 19th and ordained on the 21st. At the beginning of his papacy, he commanded Emperor Frederick II to lead an army into Asia under penalty of excommunication <note>original: "anathema"</note>. When the Emperor delayed slightly to recover from an illness, Gregory excommunicated him. Frederick, having recovered, set out for Palestine without first seeking absolution from the Pope. While he was away, Gregory invaded Frederick's territories in Lombardy and Italy and seized them. Furthermore, moved by envy over the victories the Emperor achieved in the East, Gregory conspired with the Knights Templar to bring about Frederick's death. He wrote letters to the Sultan of the Saracens, urging him to ambush Frederick unexpectedly at the Jordan River. Horrified by such treachery, the Sultan handed the papal letters over to the Emperor. Upon returning to the West, Frederick earned his absolution from Gregory in 1230 only through the terror of his arms. In 1239, Gregory excommunicated Frederick again and advised his son, Henry, to take up arms against his father. Soon, however, the Pope was defeated in battle by the Emperor and forced to enter into fair peace conditions. Yet as soon as Frederick departed, Gregory immediately recoiled from the agreements, excommunicated him again, and released his subjects from their oath of fidelity. When the war continued to turn in the Emperor's favor, and the German Bishops proclaimed that the Pope had no rights in Germany and absolved Frederick of the excommunication, Gregory, worn out by grief, died on August 21, 1241.

*Thirty-one Letters*. *Councils, Volume XI, page 310.*
*Fragments of Decrees* (191 entries). *Ibid, page 368.*
*Two Letters*. *Ibid, page 2345.*
*Forty-three Letters*. Found in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* <note>The Franciscan Annals</note>, *Volume I*, at the year 1228, etc.
*Ninety-seven Letters*. *Ibid, in the Papal Register, page 3.*

His *Decretal Letters* <note>The *Decretales Gregorii IX* were a major collection of canon law</note> were published in Basel (1511), Paris (1541), Venice (1591, in quarto), Lyon (1572 and 1606), and Paris (1601, in folio).

The *Letter for the Canonization of Blessed Elizabeth* <note>St. Elizabeth of Hungary</note> was edited by Lambecius in his *Commentaries*, book 2, page 880.

<margin>1227.</margin>
**JOHN ALGRINUS**, a Frenchman by birth and a native of Abbeville, laid the first foundations of his theological training <note>original: "tyrocinia"</note> at the University of Paris. In the conclusion of the commentaries he wrote on the Song of Songs, he is said to have been the Dean of Amiens and the Cantor of Abbeville. Around the year 1225, he was made the Archbishop of Besançon <note>Latin: "Bifontinus"</note>, and in 1227, a Cardinal and the Bishop of Sabina. He was later sent to Spain to preach the Crusade <note>original: "prædicandam... Crucem," literally "to preach the Cross"</note> against the Saracens. He died on the 4th day before the Calends of October <note>September 28</note> in the year 1236. In 1233, he wrote a *Commentary on the Song of Songs*, printed in Paris (1521, folio). Henry of Ghent <margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 38.</margin> mentions that he also composed *Sermons for the Seasons and for the Saints*, which are said to exist in various manuscript libraries.

<margin>1228.</margin>
**WILLIAM**, a Frenchman by birth from the region of Auvergne, was a man most highly educated in every branch of letters. He was a supreme theologian as well as a philosopher and mathematician; furthermore, he was renowned for his exceptional piety. In 1228, he was created the Bishop of Paris. In that same year, having gathered several most excellent Doctors <note>learned professors of the university</note>, he established a very famous disputation. In this debate, it was determined that no one could hold two sacred offices <note>original: "ministeria sacra," referring to pluralism, or holding multiple church positions</note> without the loss of their salvation, if one of those offices was worth an annual income of 15 Parisian pounds. In the year 1240, he condemned the dogmas of certain theologians that were poorly in tune with the Orthodox faith <note>This refers to the "Condemnations of 1240" regarding various philosophical and theological errors</note>. He died in the year 1249, on the 3rd day before the Calends of April <note>March 30</note>.

### The Scholastic Age.

<header>The Scholastic Age.</header>

<margin>13th CENTURY from the year 1200.</margin> *Sermons for the Seasons and for the Saints*. These appeared separately in Paris (1494, octavo), and in expanded editions in Tübingen (1499, quarto), Lyon (1567, octavo), Cologne (1629, quarto), and finally a much larger edition in Paris (1638, folio).

The *Complete Works* of William of Paris enumerated thus far were collected into one set and edited by Barthélemy Ferron, Orléans (1674), in two volumes, folio.

The *Censure of several detestable errors against Catholic truth* <note>A formal condemnation of specific theological propositions</note> made in the year 1240 is usually found in the *Libraries of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecis Patrum," a standard collection of early and medieval Christian writings</note>.

<margin>* On Good and Bad Books, Question 10, page 141.</margin> The *Dialogue on the Seven Sacraments*, which appeared under the name of William of Paris in Leipzig (1512) and Lyon (1567), is not by our man from Auvergne <note>William of Auvergne was the Bishop of Paris; the text distinguishes him from a later author of the same name</note>, but is correctly noted by Théophile Raynaud* to be by William of Paris the Younger from the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>. Certainly, his style is quite different from that of our author; furthermore, at the end of the work, he cites Thomas Aquinas and Peter of Tarentaise, both of whom were younger than our William.

<margin>* Supplement, page 520.</margin> Casimir Oudin* contends that the *Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew*, which is found among the works of Saint Anselm in the Cologne edition, belongs to our William; Oudin also testifies to having seen his extensive manuscripts of commentaries on the *Song of Songs* and on *Ecclesiastes*.

<margin>1228.</margin> **RAYMOND OF PENYAFORT** (or de Rupe-Forti), a Catalan by nation and a native of Barcelona, was born in the year 1175 from the ancient lineage of the Kings of Aragon and the Counts of Barcelona. He taught Canon Law <note>The internal religious law governing the Catholic Church</note> at the University of Bologna, eventually becoming a Canon and Archdeacon of Barcelona, and was made a monk of the Dominican Order. He flourished in the year 1228. Appointed as confessor and personal chaplain to Pope Gregory IX in 1238, he was established as the Master General of his Order at the Convent of Bologna. Having completed two years in this office, he resigned, and—according to Ambrogio de Altamura*—he most steadfastly refused the Archbishopric of Tarragona offered by Pope Gregory, <margin>* Page 41.</margin> as well as the see of Braga in Portugal and finally that of Barcelona in his own homeland. He died at the age of one hundred on January 6, 1275.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*Summa on Cases of Penance* in four books, or the *Summa on Penance and Marriage*. It was published with the explanatory notes of John of Freiburg at Rome in 1603, and in an abridged version at Cologne in 1502.

He compiled five books of *Decretals*, known as the "Extravagantes" <note>Decrees of the Pope that 'wandered' outside of earlier official collections</note>, from the ancient collections of the Decretals of the Roman Pontiffs, cutting out many things here and there; these were approved by Gregory IX in 1230. They have appeared in every collection of Canon Law.

<margin>1230.</margin> **ALEXANDER OF HALES**, an Englishman by nation and a native of Gloucestershire. As a youth, he went to the University of Paris and devoted himself to the study of Scholastic Theology and Canon Law. In both fields, he eventually became so famous that he was commonly called the "Irrefragable Doctor" <note>original: "Doctor Irrefragabilis," a title meaning his arguments were considered impossible to refute</note>. He flourished in the year 1230, having embraced the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> eight years prior. He died in Paris on August 27, 1245, and was buried among his fellow Franciscans.

->W O R K S.<-

*Commentaries on the Psalms of David*, which are attributed by some to Bonaventure and by others to Hugh of Saint-Cher. They were published in Venice (1496, folio).

*Commentaries on the Apocalypse*. They were published through the care of Jean de la Haye in Paris (1647, folio).

The *Summa of All Theology*, divided into four parts. It was published in Basel (1481), Nuremberg (1482, folio), Venice (1576), and Cologne (1622).

<meta>This page continues the catalog of works attributed to Alexander of Hales, discussing issues of authorship and locations of manuscripts, before moving on to other significant 13th-century figures including Philip the Chancellor, Conrad of Marburg, Peter de Vinea, and Edmund Rich.</meta>

<page-num>715</page-num>
<header>The Scholastic Age.</header>

<margin>13th Century from the year 1200.</margin>
*Questions, or Commentaries on the Four Books of the Sentences* <note>original: "Sententiarum." The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard textbook for medieval theology students.</note>. These were published in Lyon in 1515 in four volumes. However, they seem to be wrongly attributed to Alexander. For he wrote no other *Commentaries on the Books of the Sentences* than his *Summa of Theology*; indeed, in several manuscript codices, that work bears this title.

*The Summary on the Virtues*, from which Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a famous medieval encyclopedist</note> transcribed many parts into his *Mirror*. It was published in Paris in 1509.

*Commentaries on Aristotle’s Metaphysics.* These are extant in a Venice edition of 1572.

*Commentaries on Aristotle’s Three Books "On the Soul"* <note>original: "de Animâ"</note>. These were printed in Oxford in 1481, if the location and date are correctly noted by the man who compiled the Catalog of the Oxford Library, the illustrious Mr. Thomas Hyde, the Chief Librarian.

*The Destroyer of Vices* <note>original: "Destructorium vitiorum"</note>, which was published in Nuremberg in 1496 (folio) and in Venice in 1582. It is ascribed to Alexander of Hales by the consistent testimony of manuscript codices. Some, however, prefer to strip him of the authorship because at the end of the Nuremberg edition, it is read that this work was composed by a certain "son of a carpenter" <note>original: "Fabri Lignarii filio"</note> who, out of humility, wished his name to remain hidden. See more on this under the year 1429.

A *Mariale* <note>A work in praise of the Virgin Mary</note> survives in manuscript in the Lambeth Library.

Furthermore, Alexander of Hales' commentaries on all the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Epistles of Saint Paul are said to exist in manuscript, partly in the Ambrosian Library <note>in Milan</note> and partly in the Bodleian Library <note>in Oxford</note>.

## PETER DE VINEA,

<margin>* On good and bad books, Question 10, page 141.</margin>
The *Dialogue on the Seven Sacraments*, which appeared under the name of William of Paris in Leipzig, 1512, and Lyon, 1567, is not by our man from Auvergne, but rather by William of Paris the younger, of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, as Théophile Raynaud <note>A 17th-century Jesuit bibliographer</note> correctly notes *. Certainly, its style is far removed from our author's; and at the end of the work, it cites Thomas Aquinas and Peter of Tarentaise <note>Pope Innocent V</note>, who were younger than our William.

<margin>* Supplement, page 520.</margin>
Casimir Oudin * contends that the *Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew*, which is contained among the works of Saint Anselm in the Cologne edition, belongs to our William; Oudin also testifies to having seen his extensive *Commentaries on the Song of Songs* and on *Ecclesiastes* in manuscript.

<margin>1228.</margin>
## RAYMOND OF PEÑAFORT, or of Rochefort, Catalan by nationality, born in Barcelona from the ancient lineage of the Kings of Aragon and the Counts of Barcelona, born in the year 1175. He taught Canon Law in the University of Bologna, eventually became a Canon and Archdeacon of Barcelona, and was made a Monk of the Dominican Order. He flourished in the year 1228. He was employed by Pope Gregory IX as a confessor and for sacred matters; in the year 1238, he was appointed General of his Order at the Bologna Chapter. Having completed two years in this duty, he resigned, and—as Ambrose of Altamura reports *—refused the Archbishopric of <margin>* Page 41.</margin> Tarragona offered by Pope Gregory. He died a centenarian in the year 1275, on the 6th of January.

### W R I T I N G S.

*The Summary of Penitential Cases* <note>original: "Summa de Casibus Pœnitentialibus," a handbook for confessors</note> in four books, or *The Summary on Penance and Marriage*. It appeared with the glosses <note>explanatory annotations</note> of John of Freiburg in Rome, 1603; and was published in an abridged form in Cologne, 1502.

*Five Books of Decretals*, called the *Extravagantes* <note>original: "Extravagantium," referring to papal decrees that "wandered" outside earlier standard collections</note>, compiled from ancient collections of the Decretals of the Roman Pontiffs, with many parts cut from here and there, and approved by Gregory IX in the year 1230. These have appeared in every collection of Canon Law.

<margin>1230.</margin>
## ALEXANDER OF HALES, English by nationality, from Gloucester, traveled as a youth to the University of Paris and devoted himself to the study of Scholastic Theology and Canon Law: he eventually became very famous in both, so much so that he was commonly called the "Irrefragable Doctor" <note>original: "Doctor Irrefragabilis," meaning the teacher whose arguments are impossible to refute</note>. He flourished in the year 1230, having embraced the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> eight years prior. He died in Paris on August 27, 1245, and was buried among the Franciscans.

### W O R K S.

*Commentaries on the Psalms of David*, which are attributed by some to Bonaventure and by others to Hugh of Saint-Cher. They appeared in Venice, 1496, in folio.

*Commentaries on the Apocalypse.* They appeared through the care of Jean de la Haye in Paris, 1647, in folio.

*The Summary of Universal Theology* <note>original: "Summa universæ Theologiæ"</note>, distributed into four parts. It appeared in Basel in 1481; Nuremberg in 1482, in folio; Venice in 1576; and Cologne in 1622.

...by Pope Gregory [IX] <note>original: "gorio Papâ"</note> he was elected Archbishop by the Monks of Canterbury and consecrated in April. He was a sharp corrector of the corruptions that were then most foully staining the Church, and a strenuous restorer of collapsed discipline. On this account, being harassed by the injustices of King Henry III of England and by Otho, the Pope's Legate in England, he sought out Rome. There, when he did not hesitate to rebuke the corrupt morals of the Roman Court, he began to be hated by the Pope; having been fined a great sum of money, he was sent back to England. Broken by so many injuries, Edmund at last declared a voluntary exile for himself and, having set out for France, settled at Pontigny. From there, in the year 1242, he moved to Soisy, where, worn out by fever and sorrow, he died on the 16th of November. He was eventually enrolled among the Saints by Callixtus III around the year 1456. His *Mirror of the Church* <note>original: "Speculum Ecclesiæ"</note> is extant in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ PP."</note>, Volume XXV, page 316. His *Twelve Constitutions* are found in Lyndwood’s *Provinciale* of England <note>A famous collection of English canon law compiled by William Lyndwood.</note>.

<margin>1235.</margin>
### ROBERT GROSSETESTE, or called Capito [Big-Head],

An Englishman by nation, from the county of Suffolk, born in the village of Stradbrook. After he had applied himself to studies for some time at the University of Oxford, he moved to Paris. Having returned home, he became first the Archdeacon of Leicester, and then on June 10, 1235, was ordained Bishop of Lincoln. In order to more strongly restrain the excessive tyranny of the Roman Court in England, and the illicit "provisions" and "reservations" <note>term: provisions|A papal practice of appointing a successor to a church office before it was vacant, often used to install foreign favorites and divert English church revenues to Rome.</note>—which he found quite unbearable—he traveled to Rome himself to plead this cause before the Pope. Although dismissed with the greatest politeness, the matter remained unsettled, and he returned home. From there, he wrote back a sufficiently sharp and biting Letter regarding this business. When the Pope saw it, he was driven into a rage, conceived the greatest anger against him, and spewed forth threats. But when the Pope’s madness was slightly restrained, the Cardinals said:

> *It would not be expedient, Lord, for us to decree anything harsh against this man. For to confess the truth, the things he says are true. We cannot condemn him; he is a Catholic, and indeed a most holy man; more religious than us, holier than us, and of a more excellent life; so much so that it is believed there is no greater prelate in the entire Christian world, nor even his equal.*

And even if it is true, as some maintain, that he was not excommunicated by the Pope, he was nevertheless harassed by him with more than one kind of trouble. Nonetheless, he continued with an unmoved and undaunted spirit in rebuking the tyranny and greed of the Pope. He died at Buckden on October 9, 1253, with a notable reputation for holiness, even if he has not been recorded in the register of the Roman Church. Regarding him, besides our historians of this time, Francis Godwin treats of him in *On the Prelates of England* <note>original: "de Præsul. Angliæ"</note> under the Bishops of Lincoln, page 348. He was clearly a man (to pass over his piety, the sanctity of his life, and other virtues worthy of a Christian Bishop) of immense spirit and sharp wit. In the study of literature, as far as those times allowed, he was raised almost to the very peak, having mastered the entire circle of the encyclopedia <note>In the medieval context, this refers to the full curriculum of the seven liberal arts.</note>. He was so learned in both sacred and secular letters, in the knowledge of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages, and in Astronomy and all of Philosophy far above the common lot of scholars, that he was accused by the ignorant masses of the magic arts and of an execrable partnership with a "Cacodæmon" <note>original: "Cacodæmone" | An evil spirit or demon.</note>. This is not at all surprising in such a crude and barbaric age.

### WORKS.

Various minor works, published in *Venice, 1514.*
*Compendium of the Sphere of the World.* Venice, 1508.
*Commentary on Aristotle’s Posterior Analytics.* Venice, 1504, 1537, 1552.
*Letter to Pope Innocent IV.* This is extant in the works of Matthew Paris under the year 1253, where his mournful dying dissertations against the oppressions of the Church inflicted by the Roman Pope are also found.
*The Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs*, translated by him into Latin. It was published in *Paris, 1549, in duodecimo*, and in the *Orthodoxographa*, page 861, as well as the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume II.
*The Book on the Cessation of the Legal Ceremonies.* <note>original: "Liber de Cessatione Legalium." A work arguing that the Old Testament laws were fulfilled and ended by Christ.</note> Published in *London, 1652, in quarto.*

While still a deacon of St. Isidore, he wrote a clear account of the *Life and Miracles of St. Isidore* at the command of Queen Berengaria <note>Queen of León and Castile</note>. This work survives in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Centuries*, Volume II, and in the Bollandists' *Acts of the Saints* for April 4th. <margin>1237.</margin>
GODFREY, a German by birth and a monk of the Monastery of St. Pantaleon within the city of Cologne. He flourished in the year 1237. He wrote *Annals* from the year 1162 to 1237, which were first brought to light by Marquard Freher among the *German Writers*, Volume I, page 239.

<margin>1238.</margin>
GEORGE ELMACIN, called *Abnol-Amdi and Amda* <note>original: "Abnol-Amdi & Amda," likely a Latinization of Ibn al-`Amid</note>, an Arab by birth and the son of the scribe Abuliafiri Elamidi, flourished around the year 1238. For he declares that his father was snatched away by death in the year of the Hegira 646 <note>The Islamic calendar</note>, or the year of Christ 1238. That he was a Christian is clearly evidenced by his name, his diligent recording of Christian affairs, the immense reverence he shows in citing the books of Holy Scripture, and his clear application of prophetic oracles to Christ the Lord—not to mention other evidence that can be gathered from his work. It must be admitted, of course, that he frequently speaks too kindly of Muhammad and his law; this should certainly be forgiven as a matter of prudence or fear for a man writing and living among Muslims. He wrote a *History of the Saracens from the first rise of Muhammad to the beginning of the Atabeg Empire* in 49 books. It records the succession of emperors, also inserting Christian history and the most significant events of the Eastern Churches during that same time. This *History* was published in the translation by Thomas Erpenius in both Latin and Arabic at *Leiden, 1625*, in quarto. Elmacin had begun his history from the very beginning of the world. The first part, from the creation of the world to the flight of Muhammad <note>the Hijra</note>, existed in manuscript in the possession of Hottinger, who testifies to having seen a copy of it written in Syriac letters in the public library of Cambridge <note>original: "Biblioth. Orient. c. 2. p. 75."</note>.

<margin>1240.</margin>
MANUEL CHARITOPULUS, called "the Philosopher," seems to have held the Patriarchate of Constantinople after Germanus was removed, starting from the year 1240—provided one trusts the date on his *Decree on the Transfer of Bishops*. That decree is said to have been given in the Year of the World 6758, which by the Greek calculation <note>The Byzantine calendar</note> falls in the year of Christ 1250. He perhaps died, or at least was removed from his seat, before the year 1254. There exist *Solutions to Certain Questions* in Greek and Latin in Leunclavius’s *Greco-Roman Law*, book 3, page 238. The *Decree on the Transfer of Bishops* is found in the same work on page 240, and the *Decree on the Right of Patronage* on page 242.

<margin>1240.</margin>
MATTHEW PARIS, English by birth and a monk of the Benedictine Order, took the habit of his religion in the year 1217 at the Monastery of St. Albans near ancient Verulamium <note>modern St Albans, Hertfordshire</note>. He flourished in the year 1240. Because of his outstanding learning and the holiness of his character, he earned such a great reputation that in 1248 he was specifically requested by name by the Norwegians to reform the monks of Holm, and was sent there by Pope Innocent. There, he restored the Benedictine rule to its original purity. Returning to his homeland, he was not only warmly received by his own people but was also especially dear to King Henry III. Matthew himself testifies in several places to the great favor he enjoyed at the King's table, in the palace, and in the private chambers. This truly great man died in the year 1259. Among all the writers of English history, he easily takes the prize for both reliability and his prudent, free handling of subjects; according to Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon, a renowned 16th-century scholar</note> <margin>* Prolegomena to the Exercises</margin>, no more faithful witness or narrator of English affairs ever lived. Thus says Casaubon, who using the best manuscript codices, unbeatably refuted the foolish conjectures of Baronius and Bellarmine <note>Catholic historians</note> who believed Matthew’s history had been corrupted or altered by Protestants.

# The Scholastic Age.

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200.</margin>

## W O R K S.

The *Greater History* <note>original: "Historia Major"</note>, or the *History of English Affairs* from the arrival of William the Conqueror to the 43rd year of Henry III, King of England—specifically from the year of Christ 1066 to 1259. Matthew transcribed the first part of this history, up to the year 1235, almost word-for-word from the *Chronicle* of Roger of Wendover (a monk of St. Albans and Prior of Belvoir Cell in the district of Lincoln, who died in 1237), removing a few passages and adding others. The *Appendix* covering the years 1260 to 1273, found at the end of the History, is attributed to William Rishanger, likewise a monk of St. Albans and the historian for King Edward I.

*The Lives of the two Offas*, Kings of Mercia and founders of the Monastery of St. Albans.

*The Lives of the 23 Abbots of St. Albans*, who governed the monastery from its first foundation until the time of Matthew Paris.

*Additions to the Greater History* <note>original: "Additamenta"</note>, comprising nearly everything cited or referenced in the *History* to more fully clarify a narrative. Matthew bound these *Additions* together with the preceding *Lives* into a single volume, intending it to serve as a second volume to his history.

Matthew’s *Greater History* was published in London in 1571; in Zurich in 1606; and along with the *Lives of the Offas*, the *Abbots of St. Albans*, and the *Additions*, under the editorship of William Watts (who added a glossary, notes, and various readings) in London, 1640, in folio format; and a second time in 1684, in folio. The edition of 1640 is significantly superior.

The *Lesser History* <note>original: "Historia Minor"</note>, from the year 1066 to 1250, in which he briefly and succinctly runs through the events he narrates more extensively in the *Greater History*. However, it contains many details worth knowing that are sought in vain in the *Greater History*. It exists in manuscript form in the Arundel Library and at the College of St. Benedict <note>Corpus Christi College</note> in Cambridge.

A history from Adam to the beginning of the reign of William the Conqueror was also prepared by Matthew Paris; Matthew of Westminster transcribed nearly the whole of this into the first part of his *Flowers of History* <note>original: "Florilegium"</note>.

---

<margin>1243.</margin>
<margin>* History of Civil Law, book 3, ch. 14, p. 482.</margin>

**INNOCENT IV**, previously named Sinibaldo; a Genoese by birth, from the Fieschi family and the Counts of Lavagna. Formerly a Cardinal Priest with the title of St. Laurence in Lucina, he was elected Roman Pontiff on June 24, 1243, and consecrated on June 29. He held nothing more urgent than to nurture the deadly hatred of his predecessors against Emperor Frederick II. Consequently, he set out for France in 1244 and called for a general council to be held at Lyon the following year. At this Council, he publicly excommunicated the Emperor, stripped him of his imperial authority, forbade his subjects from obeying him under penalty of excommunication <note>original: "anathematis"</note>, and ordered the Crusade <note>original: "Crucem," literally "the Cross"</note> to be preached against him throughout the Christian world, granting full remission of sins to all who fought against him.

In 1246, he placed James, King of Aragon, and his entire kingdom under an interdict <note>a decree excluding them from church rites</note>. In 1251, after the death of Emperor Frederick, he pursued Frederick's sons Conrad and Manfred with the bitterest hatred; when they sought their hereditary rights, he attacked them with a standing army of Crusaders. When force of arms made little progress, he brandished the excommunication against them both. He died on December 7, 1254. He possessed such authority and veneration (according to Foster*) that he was called the "Father and Organ of Truth" by many of those most skilled in both Civil and Canon Law. He is said to be the first to have granted the Red Hat to Cardinals as a mark of dignity and ornament. He ordered the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin to be celebrated with an eight-day festival <note>an "Octave"</note>, and he deprived Bologna of its university status, transferring it to Padua.

There exists his *Commentary on the Five Books of Decretals* <note>papal decrees</note>, published in Venice (1570, 1578), Trino (1611), and Lyon (1578), in folio.

Twenty *Letters* are in the *Collection of Councils*, Vol. XI, p. 598. A *Letter on the Translation of the Body of Blessed Elizabeth* was published by Lambecius in his *Commentaries*, book 2, p. 883. Forty-six other letters are in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors*, Vol. I, for the year 1243, etc.; sixty-one others in the same work in the *Pontifical Register*, p. 55; and eighteen others in the *Register Appendix* of Vol. I, p. 10. The *Apologetic Book on Ecclesiastical Power and the Jurisdiction of the Empire against Peter de Vinea*, and many other small works, exist in manuscript in the Vatican Library; see Louis Jacob de Saint Charles, *Pontifical Library*, p. 121.

# The Scholastic Age.

<margin>
13th CENTURY

{
1244.
</margin>
**JOHN OF SAN GIMIGNANO**, a monk of the Dominican Order <note>original: "Ordinis Dominiciani Monachus"</note>, was active around the year 1244; however, others place him in the years 1210 or 1319. He was a preeminent theologian and preacher, and was particularly close with Thomas Aquinas. It is said that when Thomas was held in prison by his mother and brothers to prevent him from joining the Dominican Order, John rescued him by a clever trick. He was appointed by Pope Gregory IX as a legate to preach the Crusade <note>original: "Crucem", literally "the Cross"</note> against Emperor Frederick in the regions around Naples. His surviving writings include:

*The Compendium of Examples and Likenesses of Things* <note>original: "Summa de Exemplis & Rerum Similitudinibus"</note> in ten books. It was published in *Basel*, 1499; *Venice*, 1497 (in quarto), 1577, 1582; *Antwerp*, 1583 (in octavo), 1599; *Lyon*, 1585; and *Cologne*, 1670 (in quarto).

*Funeral Orations*. *Lyon*, 1510 (in quarto); *Paris*, 1611 (in octavo).

*Lenten Sermons*. *Venice*, 1584 (in octavo); *Cologne*, 1612 (in octavo).

Other writings by John of San Gimignano are listed by Ambrosius de Altamura in the *Dominican Library, Century 1, page 10.*

<margin>1244.</margin>
**VINCENT**, commonly called **OF BEAUVAIS**, French by nationality and Burgundian by birth, of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>. Some claim he was the Bishop of Beauvais, but this is incorrect; he was actually known as "of Beauvais" for no other reason than that he settled his home there. He was active in the year 1244. He died in 1256, or as others (perhaps more correctly) suggest, in 1264. He wrote the *Fourfold Mirror* <note>original: "Speculum quadruplex", a massive medieval encyclopedia</note>:
The *Historical Mirror* <note>original: "Historicum"</note>, dealing with histories from the creation of the world to the year 1254. This appeared separately in *Nuremberg*, 1473 and *Mainz*, 1474.
The *Natural Mirror* <note>original: "Naturale"</note> in twenty-two books, concerning herbs, birds, etc.
The *Moral Mirror* <note>original: "Morale"</note> in three books, concerning the emotions of the soul; published in *Nuremberg*, 1485 and *Venice*, 1493.
The *Doctrinal Mirror* <note>original: "Doctrinale"</note> in seventeen books, concerning the sciences in almost every category; published in *Nuremberg*, 1486.
This immense and lengthy *Work* was published in *Basel*, 1481; *Venice*, 1484, 1591 (in folio); and *Douai*, 1624 (in folio). Ambrosius de Altamura provides more information on Vincent and his *Mirror* in the <margin>* Dominican Library, page 21.</margin> *Dominican Library*; however, Philippe Labbe discusses both with a more accurate judgment. Labbe mentions that several other minor works by Vincent were published in *Basel* in 1481, namely: *A Consolation on the Death of a Friend*, *Four Books on the Grace of God*, *A Book on the Deeds and Life of the Blessed Mary*, and *A Book on the Education of Royal Children*, though he acknowledges that he has not seen that specific edition himself.

<margin>1245.</margin>
**HUGH OF SAINT-CHER** <note>original: "Hugo de S. Caro"</note>, or of Saint-Thierry, born in the Dauphiné region in a valley named *Barcelonnette*. He applied himself to the study of literature at the University of Paris and earned the rank of Doctor; shortly thereafter, he was admitted into the Dominican Order by Blessed Jordan. He was sent to Constantinople by Gregory IX to negotiate the union of the churches. Upon returning home, he was elected Provincial of the French friars. In the year 1245, he was named Cardinal of Saint Sabina of the Roman Church by Innocent IV at the Council of Lyon. He was subsequently employed in various diplomatic missions, most notably in 1251, when he was sent to Germany and vigorously opposed the faction of Conrad. Later, while serving as a Papal Legate in the region of Liège, he was inspired by the confusing visions of a certain very superstitious woman named Juliana <note>Juliana of Liège, whose mystical experiences led to the devotion to the Eucharist</note> and was the first of all to institute the *Feast of Corpus Christi*; this was gradually adopted thereafter throughout almost the entire Western Church. He died in the year 1260, on the 14th day before the Kalends of April <note>March 19</note>. He was buried among the Dominicans at Lyon.

->W O R K S.<-

The *Postillae* <note>original: "Postillæ", brief commentaries explaining the Biblical text</note>, or short commentaries following the fourfold sense <note>the literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical meanings</note> for the whole Old and New Testament (though many attribute the commentary on the Psalms to Alexander of Hales). These were published divided into seven volumes in *Basel*, 1504; *Paris*, 1548; and *Venice*, 1600. To the Venice edition, an eighth volume consisting of a new and very extensive index was added.

<margin>1247.</margin>
**JOHN of GOD** <note>original: "Joannes de Deo"</note>, Spanish by nationality, Doctor of Decrees <note>a doctor of canon law</note>, and Canon of the Church of Bologna; he flourished, as he himself testifies at the end of his work, in 1247. He wrote for the Bishop and Chapter of Bologna *The Penitentiary Book* <note>original: "Librum Pœnitentiarium"</note>, in which he treats generally the vices of every state of life and confession, and then specifically the penance and confession of Prelates—namely, the Supreme Pontiff, the Cardinals, etc. A manuscript exists in the public library at Cambridge, volume 118, number 2; and in Petau's library in the Monastery of *St. John in the Garden* <note>original: "S. Joannis Viridario"</note>, Shelf 10, on the left. See Philippe Thomassin’s *Catalog of the Petau Manuscripts, page 31*. Dr. Theron, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, also possessed a copy, from whose codex Jacques Petyt provided us with very extensive excerpts at the end of the *Penitential* of Theodore of Canterbury, Paris, 1677. The *Summary for Judges* <note>original: "Summa Judicum"</note>, and *On the Duty of Advocates* <note>original: "de Officio Advocatorum"</note>; likewise the *Cases on the Decretals* <note>legal rulings on papal letters</note> composed by him are preserved in manuscript in the library of the Monastery of the Dunes, according to Sander’s *Belgian Manuscript Library, part 1, page 177.* By the same author, if I am not mistaken, is the *Treatise on Excommunications*, with an exposition in verse, found in the work by Thomassin cited above.

<margin>1250.</margin>
**PETER, son of CASSIODORUS**, English by nationality and a knight by rank; he flourished around the year 1250. There exists a *Letter to the English Church on shaking off the tyranny of the Roman Pontiff in England*, found in the *Catalog of Witnesses to the Truth* <note>a famous Protestant collection of anti-papal writings</note>, page 365, and in Goldast's *Monarchy, Volume I, page 11.*

**THEOBALD OF ÉTAMPES** <note>original: "Theobaldus Stampensis"</note>, English by nationality, a secular priest; he flourished, according to the opinion of D’Achery, in the year 1108, but according to Baluze, in the year 1250. The latter is entirely more correct, provided he was a contemporary of Robert Grosseteste <note>Bishop of Lincoln and famous scholar</note>, to whom he dedicated the *Book on certain matters wavering in the divine page*, as Bale also notes *. Five of his Letters are extant in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium, Volume III*. Meanwhile, we must not remain silent about what Brian Twyne reports †, and after him the recent author of the *History of Oxford* ‡, that our Theobald published a small book against the Regulars <note>monks living under a rule</note>, which he dedicated to Thurston, Archbishop of York, who held that see from the year 1119 until 1140. Whether the chronology of Twyne or Bale holds more weight, let the skilled reader judge; it is enough for me to have noted the discrepancy.

<margin>1250.</margin>
**DAVID, called OF AUGSBURG**, because he was born in Augsburg <note>original: "Augustæ Vindelicorum"</note>, a monk of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>; he flourished around 1250 and was buried in his native city, though in what year is not clear. He wrote the *Formula for Novices on the reformation of the outer man*, the *Formula for the inner man*, and the *Mirror of the Seven Steps of the Religious*. The first two short works were published separately in *Augsburg, 1593*; but the latter appeared under the name of Bonaventure in *Antwerp, 1591*. All have been restored to David, the true author, in the *Library of the Fathers, Volume XXV, page 867.*

<margin>1250.</margin>
**JOHN SEMECA**, German by nationality (and thus also called "the German" <note>original: "Teutonicus"</note>), a disciple of Azo and a most accomplished legal scholar, Provost of the Church of St. Stephen in Halberstadt; he flourished in the year 1250. In the year 1265, when Pope Clement IV was demanding tithes from the clergy throughout Germany and France for the recovery of the Holy Land, Semeca was indignant that the clergy were being plundered, Germany was being drained, and money scraped together by unjust means was being converted to wicked uses; he bravely opposed the Pope's greed by interposing an appeal. For this reason, he was excommunicated by Clement and stripped of his provostship at Halberstadt. He died in the year 1267. He wrote the *Gloss on the Decree of Gratian* <note>the standard commentary on the foundational text of canon law</note>, which has been frequently printed alongside the *Decree* itself.

# The Scholastic Age.

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200. 1251.</margin>
**GERTRUDE**, German by nationality and of noble birth, was a nun of the Benedictine order. She lived her life in the Monastery of Rodersdorf, where she was made Abbess. In the following year, however, when the nuns were moved to the Monastery of Helfta <note>original: "Heldesensem"</note> for holy virgins, Gertrude went there as well, where she had her sister Mechtild as a companion. She died in the year 1290. She wrote small works in German, or *Spiritual Exercises* <note>original: "Exercitia spiritualia"</note>, which were translated into Latin and published together with the small works of her sister, concerning whom more is written below.

---

<margin>1252.</margin>
**ROBERT DE SORBON**, named after his birthplace, was the confessor <note>original: "pœnitentiarius"</note>, or at least the chaplain, of King Louis IX of France <note>Saint Louis</note>. He was first a Canon of Soissons and later of St. Mary of Paris <note>Notre Dame</note>. He flourished in the year 1252, in which he laid the foundations for the Sorbonne College in the University of Paris. He died after the year 1270. He wrote three small, pious, and devoted works, namely: *On Conscience* <note>original: "De Conscientiâ"</note>, *On Confession* <note>original: "De Confessione"</note>, and *The Road to Paradise* <note>original: "Iter Paradisi"</note>; these are found in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patrum"</note>, Volume 25.

---

<margin>1253. Matthew Paris for the years 1255, 1257. Nicholas Trivet for the year 1256. History of the University of Paris, Vol. 3. Preface to the works of William of St. Amour, 1632.</margin>
**WILLIAM OF SAINT-AMOUR**, originating from the town of the same name in the county of Burgundy, was a Doctor of Paris. He flourished in the year 1253 as a most sharp critic of the orders of Preachers <note>Dominicans</note> and Minors <note>Franciscans</note>. 

Since both orders—despising the Canons and ecclesiastical rules—were everywhere seizing for themselves the duty of hearing confessions and preaching without consulting the Bishops, and while professing voluntary poverty and a hatred of riches, they nevertheless performed no manual labor, but wandered about like charlatans <note>original: "agyrtarum," referring to vagabond beggars</note> under a false appearance of piety to cheat the common people out of money; and furthermore, while opening schools for the youth in the University, they refused to observe the University statutes; the University of Paris took this poorly. Led by our William, the University went to meet the bold attempts of these "petty friars" <note>original: "Fraterculorum," a diminutive and often derogatory term for the mendicant brothers</note> and, as they were insolently resisting, expelled them from the Parisian school. 

The petty friars raised an outcry: the matter was referred to the Pope. In letters sent in 1256, the Pope sharply rebuked the members of the University, and William by name. When the University members persisted in their efforts, the Pope ordered William, along with three other Doctors, to be deprived of their doctoral degrees and all ecclesiastical benefits, and to be exiled from the kingdom. Angered by these injuries, William published a biting booklet against the petty friars, in which he exposed their deceptions and wickedness to the eyes of all and criticized the excessive authority of the Pope. 

The friars immediately accused the book and its author of heresy; having brought it to Rome, they brought it about that the Pope condemned it and had it burned by public sentence in that same year. Yet William, not yet terrified, did not rest; he continued to sprinkle the petty friars with sharp wit as long as he lived. He boldly contended that it is not meritorious before God for strong and religious monks to beg for alms from door to door, nor should injury be done to parish priests through the rashly usurped duty of preaching and hearing confession. For this reason, he was ordered by Pope Alexander IV in 1257 to withdraw from the entire kingdom of France and to henceforth abstain from the duty of teaching and writing, under the penalty of the most heavy excommunication <note>original: "anathematis"</note>. 

He died several years later. After his death, he was listed among the heretics by the friars and was thoroughly assaulted with slanders and insults. However, his memory was excellently defended against the follies of certain babblers by Lawrence of England, an Abbot and Master of Paris, who, as a successor to William of Saint-Amour, sharply corrected the petty friars in his own writings. See more about him in the *Overview of this Century*.

# The Scholastic Age.

<sig>Kkkkk 2</sig>
<margin>13th CENTURY from the year 1200–1220.</margin>
*The cases and articles upon which Master William of Saint-Amour was accused by the Preaching Friars <note>The Dominicans</note>.*

*Catholic and Canonical Collections sent to the Supreme Pontiff Clement IV in the year 1266, for the defense of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, and for the instruction and preparation of the simple faithful of Christ against the dangers threatening the Universal Church from hypocrites, false preachers, those who "creep into houses" <note>A biblical reference to 2 Timothy 3:6, often used to criticize mendicant friars</note>, the idle, the meddlesome, and the wanderers.*

*A table of signs by which false preachers can be distinguished from true ones.*

*A sermon for the feast day of the Holy Apostles James and Philip.*

These works were published at *Constance on the Rhine* (as the title claims, though in truth at *Paris*) in 1632, in quarto format; I had not yet seen this edition when I published my *Cartophylax* <note>A "Keeper of the Records" or bibliography</note> in the year 1685, but I was soon informed of it by a friend.

<margin>1254.</margin>
### REINERIUS SACHONUS,
a native of Piacenza, was a most skilled philosopher and theologian. He was first a leader of the Waldensians <note>A medieval sect that emphasized poverty and lay preaching, later declared heretical</note>, but after abandoning them, he joined the family of the Preaching Friars and was made General Inquisitor of heretics. He flourished in the year 1254. However, after he destroyed the castle of Gatta, a Waldensian stronghold, and sentenced many of them to the fire, he was expelled from the city of Milan in 1259 and died in exile. There exists his *Comprehensive Treatise on the Cathars and Leonists* <note>original: "Summa de Catharis & Leonistis"</note>, published by Claude Cousford at *Paris in 1548*. Flaccius Illyricus had published a large part of the book in his *Catalog of Witnesses to the Truth* <note>original: "Catal. Test. Verit."</note> on page 431. Finally, Jacob Gretser published the *complete book of Reinerius against the Waldensians, comprising ten chapters* (in which he deals with the causes of heresies, the sects of ancient and modern heretics, and their marks, customs, examination, and punishment) with extensive introductory notes and varying readings at *Ingolstadt in 1613* in quarto; it was subsequently included in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecæ Patr."</note>, Volume 25, page 262. Attached at the end is an *Appendix on the Hypocrites who are called Stertzer* <note>A Germanic term for wandering beggars or vagabonds</note>, which contains the follies of various heretics; Gretser, supported by no sound reasoning, contends that this is not the work of Reinerius.

<margin>1254.</margin>
### ALEXANDER IV,
formerly called Raynaldus or Roland, was a native of Campania, from the Castle of Genna in the Diocese of Anagni. Born of the Counts of Segni and son of Philip of Anagni, he was the nephew of Gregory IX, a Cardinal of the Roman Church, and Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. He was elected Roman Pontiff on Christmas Day in the year 1254 and crowned two days later. In 1255, he excommunicated <note>original: "anathematizavit"</note> Manfred, the King of Sicily and Apulia, decreed he should be deposed from his kingdom, attacked him with arms, and ordered the cross <note>a crusade</note> to be preached against him everywhere. In 1256, he forbade Conradin, the grandson of Emperor Frederick, from being elected Emperor, and he excommunicated the electors leaning toward his side. In the same year, having been brought into straits by Manfred, he commanded Henry III, King of England, under pain of excommunication, to fly to Sicily with a subsidiary army on a set day, and he condemned King Alfonso of Portugal and his whole kingdom with dire curses. In 1258, he struck the Florentines and Genoese with excommunication for refusing to break the treaty they had previously made with Manfred. He died at Viterbo on May 25 in the year 1261. Three of his *Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils* <note>original: "Concil."</note>, Volume 11, page 716; fifty-one other *Letters* in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* for the year 1256, etc.; and 124 others in the same work, Volume 2, in the *Papal Register*, page 18. Also, his *Cypriot Constitution* is in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume 11, page 2352.

### HUMBERT OF ROMANS,
a Burgundian by nationality, born in the village of Romans. While he was intent on his studies in Paris, he joined the family of Saint Dominic in the year 1225. In 1254, he was made Master General of his Order. He resigned from this dignity in 1263 and died in 1274.

*Six Books of Spiritual Institutions, or the Mirror of the Religious.* These were published at *Louvain in 1575* and *Paris in 1622*.
