### THEODORE LASCARIS, Junior,

Also called Ducas, a native of Nicaea. He was the grandson of Theodore the Elder (who had moved the seat of the empire to Nicaea after Constantinople was captured by the Latins <note>Referring to the Fourth Crusade in 1204</note>) through his daughter Irene. He was the eldest son of John Ducas and his wife, and the successor of Theodore. He succeeded his father in the empire in the year 1255. He successfully conducted affairs against the Bulgarians, Thessalians, and other enemies of the empire for nearly three years; however, broken by weak health and disease, he took up the monastic habit. According to Dorotheus of Monemvasia in his *Synopsis of Various Histories* <margin>* *Synopsis of Various Histories*, p. 525.</margin>, he retired to the Monastery of Sydandronum (located in Magnesia). There he consecrated the short remainder of his life to completing his penance in pious and literary leisure. He reigned for three years and died in the year 1259 at the age of 36. He was a prince of thorough erudition, worthy of a better age. Certainly, his great devotion both to piety and to literary pursuits is clearly evident from his coins and imperial insignia, in which he is depicted holding a cross in his right hand and a book in his left. See the illustrious and noble scholar Monsieur du Fresne in *Byzantine Families*, page 223. This monk-emperor wrote a long enough *Treatise against the Latins on the Procession of the Holy Spirit* addressed to John, Bishop of Koroni. It exists in manuscript, though faultily transcribed and mutilated at the end, in the library of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. I shall subjoin here the Title and Prologue, which Mr. Wharton transcribed for my use, translated from the Greek:

->An apologetic discourse of the monk Theodore Lascaris to the Bishop of Koroni concerning the Italians, or rather concerning the Latins, regarding the Holy Spirit.<-

<margin>* Perhaps "consists of."</margin>
Since my Majesty <note>A formal Byzantine imperial self-reference</note> addressed a question to you, O Most Holy Bishop of Koroni—a question regarding my Majesty's concern as to why the most holy Great Church of God <note>The Patriarchate of Constantinople</note> does not dogmatize falsely concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit—and you gave your smooth defense to me: that the most holy Great Church of God thus understands <margin>* "consists" or "stands together"</margin> the procession of the Holy Spirit as having its procession from the Father alone, yet also being in the Son. My Majesty declares to you that our most holy Great Church of God, as you may know from the written testimonies and Gospel sayings cited below, dogmatizes that the same Spirit proceeds from the Father and from Him alone, and does not proceed from the Son; but He is bestowed upon us through the Son for purification, sanctification, and for the faithful and for glory. My Majesty, delighting in these uses, will briefly set them before you for your knowledge. *The beginning of the Truth itself. For it is good to begin from God and to rest in God. ... when the Counselor comes, whom I will send to you.* The most illustrious author then proceeds to bring forth many passages of Holy Scripture and many testimonies from the Holy Fathers, with which he is accustomed to press his points quite sharply.

In addition to what he wrote on the procession of the Holy Spirit, which he encompassed in two orations, Leontius <margin>* *On Consent*, book 2, ch. 14, sect. 4, p. 722.</margin> mentions several more *Theological Orations* in which he treats of *The One and the Deity, That the Three are One, On Divine Unions, On the Most Holy Trinity, and On the Incarnation of Christ.* Freher, in his *Chronology*, says that his book *On Natural Communication*, translated by the famous Alberi, is extant, but I have not yet seen it.

*His treatises: On the Trinity; On Virtue; On Fasting; An Epitome of Ethics; An Encomium of Wisdom; On Saint Euthymius and the Holy Unmercenaries <note>Saints Cosmas and Damian, who healed without taking payment</note>, etc.* These are extant.

# NICEPHORUS BLEMMIDA,
A Priest and Monk of the Monastery in Emathia <note>A region in northern Greece/Macedonia</note>, which he entered while still a young man. There he led a truly ascetic life worthy of a Christian Philosopher, daily wearing himself down with a harsh regime of diet and exercise. He built a church at his own expense and presided over it once completed. When Marchesina—the mistress of Emperor John Ducas—wished to frequent the church for the sake of religion, Nicephorus cast her headlong from the doors. For that divine man (as Gregoras relates) judged it a sin for that wicked and shameless woman to tread upon the sacred pavement with her profane and criminal feet. Finally, in the year 1255, after the death of Germanus, Theodore Lascaris (the successor of John Ducas) wished to promote our Nicephorus, who had been his teacher, to the position of Patriarch of Constantinople. However, he steadfastly refused the offered dignity. It is not clear in what year he died.
<margin>* *History*, book 2, page 33.</margin>
*“This man”* (says the historian Gregoras *) *“was adorned with many virtues and practiced in much wisdom—as much as the children of the Greeks know, and as much as the leaders and orators of our Church have brought forth for our benefit.”* <note>original: ᾿Ανὴρ δὲ οὗτος... εἰς ἡμετέραν ὠφέλειαν προῆλθον.</note> He was distinguished by many virtues and equipped with diverse wisdom, both that which is valued among the Gentiles <note>meaning secular or classical Greek philosophy</note> and that which the bishops and orators of the Church have produced for our profit. He was very favorable toward the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note> and even defended their dogmas against his own people. Meanwhile, some short works survive today in which he argues strongly against the opinion of the Latins, especially concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit <note>The "Filioque" controversy regarding whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son</note>. Leo Allatius, in his work *On Consent* (book 2, chapter 14, section 4), attempts to resolve this discrepancy by saying either that Blemmida poured these thoughts out as a young man before the cause had been fully discussed and revoked them after more diligent examination, or rather that these were the fabrications of Schismatics thrust out under Nicephorus’s name; for one does not observe the same weight of argument, doctrine, or style in them as in his other short works. How correct these claims are, let those who have been granted the chance to inspect the original manuscripts decide.

---

->W R I T I N G S.<-

**On the Procession of the Holy Spirit, in two books.** One addressed to Theodore Lascaris, the other to Jacob, the Archbishop of Bulgaria. They were published in Greek and Latin by Odoricus Raynaldus in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, Volume I, in the *Appendix*, and by Leo Allatius among the *Orthodox Greek Writers*, Volume I, page 1.

*An Epistle given to many, after he had ejected Marchesina from the temple.* It survives in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius’s *On Consent*, book 2, chapter 14, section 4.

*A Logical and Physical Epitome.* Published in Greek and Latin at Augsburg, 1605, in octavo.

*A Eulogy for John the Evangelist, an Oration on the Soul, another on the Body; Commentaries on several Psalms, short works on Faith, on Virtue, and on Religion;* these are said to exist as manuscripts in the Bavarian and Vatican Libraries. *His Oration on Faith, along with a short work by St. Thomas of the Order of Preachers <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> on the procession of the Holy Spirit and excerpts on various questions, is held in manuscript in the Royal Library at Paris,* as Labbé testifies in the *New Library of Manuscripts*, page 88.

*Two short works under the same name against the dogma of the Latins concerning the Procession of the Holy Spirit;* Leo Allatius mentions in the place cited above that he has seen these in manuscript. Regarding the short works of Blemmida, see also what the same Allatius has in his notes to Georgius Acropolites, page 244.

# ARSENIUS,
Called Autorianus, a native of Constantinople and a student of a certain monastery in Nicaea, over which he also presided. Later, having resigned this office, he cultivated a more private life in the ascetic retreats of Apollonias; it seems he also spent time in the monastic life on Mount Athos. Finally, around the year 1255, when Nicephorus Blemmida refused the office, he was elevated to the Patriarchate of Constantinople by the younger Emperor Theodore Lascaris, who had recently obtained power. In the year 1259, as Emperor Theodore was dying, he appointed Arsenius, along with George Muzalon, as guardian for his son John. Arsenius...

Arsenius, however, taking very poorly the treachery and snares of Muzalon <note>George Mouzalon, regent for the young Emperor John IV Laskaris</note> against the royal boy, abdicated the Patriarchate and withdrew into a monastery. In the year 1261, after Constantinople was recovered by the Greeks under the leadership of Michael Palaeologus, he was summoned back to the royal city to receive his former dignity and the seat that the Greek Patriarchs had longed for for more than half a century. In the year 1262, Emperor Michael deprived John, the ten-year-old son of Theodore Laskaris and a ward of Patriarch Arsenius, of his sight <note>a common Byzantine method of disqualifying a rival from the throne</note>. Arsenius punished such a wicked deed with ecclesiastical censures and interdicted Michael from the sacred rites. The Emperor, full of rage, called a Council of Bishops, burdened Arsenius with accusations, saw to it that he was deposed from the Patriarchate, and exiled him to Proconnesus. 
<margin>* History, book 4, page 60.</margin>
Arsenius survived for many years in exile, though it is not clear when he died. Regarding him, Gregoras * writes thus: <note>original Greek: ἦν μὲν γὰρ τὰ πρὸς ἀρετὴν φέρων... The text provides a Latin translation which I have rendered into English below.</note> "For as far as virtue and the cultivation of piety were concerned, that man was little short of the highest; but in the handling of affairs and the administration of the Empire, not even laborers <note>literally 'diggers' or 'trench-workers'</note> were less skilled than he." While still a monk, he wrote a *Synopsis of Divine Canons*, collected from the statutes of the Fathers and Synods and arranged into 142 titles, with certain chapters of imperial laws added to each title. It exists in Greek and Latin, edited by Henri Justellus in the *Library of Canon Law*, Volume II, page 749. The *Testament* of Arsenius was published in Greek and Latin by the illustrious Cotelerius in *Monuments of the Greek Church*, Volume II, page 168.

# THOMAS AQUINAS, the Angelic Doctor, Italian by birth, descended from the most noble blood of the Counts of Aquino and the Kings of Sicily and Aragon, was born in the castle of Aquino in the year 1224. While still a boy of five, he was entrusted to the discipline of the monks of Monte Cassino; when he had given excellent proof of his talent and precocious character there, he was sent to the Academy of Naples. There he had Peter of Ireland as his teacher in Logic <term>Dialectics</term> and Martin in the humanities. In the year 1241, having taken counsel with John of San Geminiano, he secretly took the habit of the Dominican Order in the monastery at Naples, without the knowledge of his parents. Upon hearing the news, his mother was stunned and left no stone unturned to recall him from his purpose. To elude these snares, his Dominican companions sent Thomas secretly to Terracina, then to Anagni, and finally to Rome. His mother followed her son everywhere so that she might be admitted to his sight, but she could in no way obtain this from the monks. Therefore, having soon called three of her elder sons to her aid, she had Thomas seized on his journey while he was being sent to Paris by his companions, and had him safely guarded in her own castle. Thomas, shut in this prison, gave himself entirely to the reading of the Holy Scriptures. Although he was provoked by the repeated prayers, tears, and entreaties of his mother, brothers, and sister to withdraw from his chosen way of life, he could be conquered by no flatteries and no threats. After two years, having escaped from the prison through a window, he sought Naples and from there Rome. In the year 1244, he was led to Paris by John, the Master of the Teutonic Order <note>Johannes von Wildeshausen</note>. After staying a short time in Paris, he went to Cologne to hear Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great</note> teaching in that place. He was summoned back from Cologne to Paris to publicly interpret the *Books of the Sentences* <note>The standard theological textbook by Peter Lombard</note>, which he performed with a great reputation and a wonderful gathering of students. He became famous in the year 1255, when he was created a Doctor of Theology in the faculty of Paris at the same time as Bonaventure. Before the year 1263, having returned to Italy, he was appointed a Definitor of his Order in the Roman Province, and in that capacity, he was present at the General Chapter of the Order held in London in 1263. Meanwhile, he by no means abandoned his scholastic duties. For he taught Theology publicly in the primary academies of Italy: Bologna, Rome, Fondi, Foggia in Apulia, and Pisa. Finally, he settled in Naples, where, honored with a salary from King Charles, he spent the remaining time of his life teaching. He was so far from being devoted to the care of worldly things that when he was called to the Archbishopric of Naples by Clement IV, he refused the offered office. Finally, in the year 1274, he was summoned by Pope Gregory X to the Second Council of Lyon, so that he might [write] a book against the errors of the Greeks, at the command of...
<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "Urba-" (likely referring to Pope Urban). The narrative describes the life of Thomas Aquinas from his noble birth through his education and imprisonment by his own family, to his professional heights as a master in Paris alongside Bonaventure.</meta>

After he [Thomas] had departed from Naples to read what he had composed for Urban IV at the Council, he died on the Nones of March <note>March 7th</note> in the 50th year of his age, at the Monastery of Fossanova, not far from Terracina. As he was nearing his end and about to receive the Eucharist, he tearfully begged the Lord Jesus that if he had written anything regarding His mysteries or the universal Church through the prompting of the Holy Spirit that was less than correct, He might grant him pardon; he submitted all his work to the most holy judgment of the Church. Concerning him, Sixtus of Siena * writes this among other things: *In the sacred studies of a more sincere Theology, he walked so closely to the most wise* Augustine, *and so thoroughly looked into and drew out his mind and all his hidden meanings, that according to the* Pythagorean Metempsychosis <note>the ancient Greek concept of the transmigration of souls</note> *it was a common proverb among all the most learned men that the soul of* Augustine *had migrated into* Thomas. Indeed, the doctrine of Thomas was always held in great esteem by everyone in the Papal Schools, yet it was not of such authority that theological dogmas were required to follow his standard; rather, one is permitted to judge freely on the questions determined by him and to challenge his doctrine, a point which Dermicius Thaddæi argues at length against Bzovius in the* Splendor of the Franciscan Religion, *page 35, etc.*

### BONAVENTURA,

<margin>1255. See Wadding, *Annals of the Minors* <note>the official history of the Franciscan Order</note> for the years 1221, 1232, 1243, 1253, 1256, 1260, 1265, 1271, 1274, and elsewhere.</margin>
John—or as others say, Peter—named Fidanza at his baptism; called by the Greeks **Eustachius** and **Eutychius**; known as the <term>**Seraphic Doctor**|A title given to St. Bonaventura, reflecting the fiery love and devotion found in his writings, similar to the Seraphim angels</term>. He was Italian by nation and Tuscan by birth, born at Bagnoregio, a city in Tuscany, to honorable parents—his father being John and his mother Ritella—in the year 1221 or around 1242. He gave his name to the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>, and having obtained Alexander of Hales <note>original: "Alexandrum Halensem"</note> as his teacher, as they say, he applied himself to theological studies at the University of Paris. He performed this with such happy success that after seven years he was considered worthy to publicly lecture on and explain the books of the *Sentences* <note>The standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages, written by Peter Lombard</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the extensive bibliography of St. Thomas Aquinas, noting which works are considered authentic or spurious, and begins the biography of St. Bonaventura, the "Seraphic Doctor" of the Franciscan Order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the history of the Scholastic Age, moving from the works of Thomas Aquinas to a detailed biography and bibliography of St. Bonaventure (1221–1274), the "Seraphic Doctor" and Minister General of the Franciscan Order.</meta>

<page-num>729</page-num>
<header>The Scholastic Age.</header>

<margin>13th Century from the year 1200.</margin>
In the year 1255, he was honored with the insignia of the doctorate. The following year, after the death of John of Parma, he accepted the leadership or Generalate of the entire Franciscan Order by the unanimous vote of all the Brothers. Having become General, he corrected the faltering discipline of the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> and excellently defended the whole Order against Gerard of Abbeville and William of Saint-Amour <note>Critics of the mendicant orders at the University of Paris</note>. Wholly devoted to the cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary with a clearly immoderate and superstitious affection <note>The author of this text displays a critical bias common in early modern Protestant scholarship</note>, having gathered a General Chapter of his Order at Pisa, he decreed among other things: That the Friars Minor should everywhere encourage the common people in their sermons to pray to and venerate her upon hearing the sound of the bell rung after Compline <note>The final prayer service of the day; this practice contributed to the development of the Angelus</note>. Indeed, he was the first of all to introduce religious societies or Confraternities of laypeople into the Christian world, establishing at Rome in the year 1270 the Confraternity called the *Gonfalone* <note>original: "Confalonis"; a prestigious Roman lay society</note>. In the year 1272, when after a long interregnum <note>A period without a Pope</note> the Cardinals could not agree on choosing a Pope, Bonaventure was chosen as arbiter by the common vote of all, to name the Pope-elect according to his own pleasure. Having accepted this power, he designated Theobald, the Archdeacon of Liège, later called *Gregory X*, as Pope. By him, Bonaventure was in turn created a Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Albano in the year 1274, shortly before the Second Council of Lyon, the first session of which he attended. He died at Lyon before the end of the Council in the year 1274, on the 15th of July, at the age of 53, and was carried out in a most honorable funeral, with the entire Synod celebrating the funeral rites with great devotion.

The works of St. Bonaventure enumerated so far were published, arranged in eight volumes, at Rome in 1588, in folio.

<margin>1255.</margin>
**THOMAS**, called of Cantimpré <note>original: "Cantipratensis"</note>, a Belgian by nation, born of noble stock in the village of Leeuw near Brussels. He was first a Canon at Cantimpré near Cambrai; then, passing over to the camp of the Preachers <note>The Dominican Order</note>, he heard Albert the Great teaching at Cologne, where he had Thomas Aquinas as a fellow student. He flourished in the year 1255. At length, having been made Subprior and Lector in the Convent of the Brothers of his Order at Louvain, he was finally consecrated Bishop of Lousentinus and performed duties as a suffragan <note>An assistant bishop</note> to the Bishop of Cambrai. He is said to have died on May 15, in the year 1263.

->WORKS.<-

**The Universal Good** *of Bees* <note>An allegorical work comparing the life of bees to the duties of humans and religious communities</note>*, addressed to Humbert, General of the Order of Preachers. Published at Douai in 1597 and 1605, and with the notes of George Colvener in 1627, in octavo.*
*The Life of Blessed Christina, called "The Astonishing," of Hesbaye. Found in Surius’s collection under June 23.*
*The Life of Blessed Mary of Oignies, found in Surius, ibid.*
*The Life of Blessed Lutgardis, a nun of Aywières, found in Surius under June 16.*

<margin>1256.</margin>
**ALBERT**, a German by nation, as I believe, although others make him a Belgian, was a monk of the Monastery of Stade in the Archbishopric of Bremen. From the year 1232, he was an Abbot of the Benedictine Order. In the year 1236, he set out for Rome and obtained a bull from Pope Gregory so that the Monastery of Stade might leave the Benedictine Order and transition to the Cistercians. However, since the monks constantly resisted, Albert, weary of the troubles, resigned his leadership of the monastery in the year 1240 and gave his name to the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>, eventually being made General Master of the entire Franciscan Order. He flourished in the year 1256. He wrote a *Chronicle from the Creation of the World to the Year of Christ 1256*, in which he illustrates the history of ancient times, but especially German affairs. In composing this work, he follows authors of better repute and retains their words almost everywhere; he includes things hardly found elsewhere, for the most part omitting the dreams and trifles of monks which the writers of his age were accustomed to peddle. Reinerus Reineccius first published this *Chronicle* from the Rantzovian Library with notes and a Genealogical Appendix at Helmstädt in 1587, in quarto; it was reprinted at Wittenberg in 1608, in quarto.

<margin>1260.</margin>
**JOHN OF WALES** <note>original: "Joannes Guallensis"</note>, an Englishman by birth, was a Franciscan monk at Worcester. He learned Philosophy and Theology at Oxford and taught at Paris; he was nicknamed the *Arbor Vitæ* <note>Tree of Life</note> on account of his exceptional learning. He flourished in the year 1260. It is not certain when he died. He died in Paris and was buried among the Franciscans. He possessed such a character, as was then commonly said,

<margin>† Manuscript Collection, Vol. 4, p. 232, in Antiquities of Oxford, p. 72.</margin>
> that (says our countryman † Leland concerning him) he had such eloquence, such readiness of wit, such harmony, and even such success, that he was able to discourse upon any matter—I will not say ornately, eloquently, or splendidly—but acutely, weightily, and learnedly. If these virtues were joined with a full abundance, I do not see why they should not rightly have a place, even in this age of ours, among the flowers of eloquence, however wonderfully varied they may be.

<margin>1260.</margin>
**BONAVENTURE BROCARDUS**, a native of Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratensis"</note>, a monk of Mount Sion of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, flourished in the year 1260. Ambrogio de Altamura places him at the year 1238, and says that he took the habit in 1218, and having been sent to the Holy Land before the year 1227, he made a long stay there. There exists his *Description of the Places in the Holy Land* <note>original: "Descriptio locorum Terræ Sanctæ"</note>, published at Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto; at Cologne, 1624, in octavo; and elsewhere.

<margin>1260. Doctor, page 15.</margin>
**ALBERT, called THE GREAT** <note>original: "MAGNUS"</note>, (indeed, according to the testimony of † Jovio, the consensus of all the universities conferred upon him the title of **THE GREATEST**, had not Christian modesty resisted the public wish), a German by nation, a Swabian by country, from the house of Lauingen, descended from the most noble line of the Lords of Bollstädt, was born in the year 1205. While still a youth, he was sent to Padua by his parents to be instructed in fine letters; in the year 1221, he joined the Brothers Preachers and received the habit of the Order from Jordan <note>Jordan of Saxony</note> himself, the Master General of the Dominicans. I omit the trifles the Dominicans tell about his innate dullness of mind and the resulting unhappiness in his studies, his despaired-of progress in learning and his consequently planned flight; and how memory and genius were divinely granted to him by the Blessed Virgin so that Albert would not flee; and how both were taken away again three years before his death; and how Albert was suddenly changed from an Ass into a Philosopher, and from a Philosopher back into an Ass.
<margin>Years 1227, 1248, 1260, and elsewhere. See Bzovius at these years.</margin>
This much is certain: Albert applied such great and successful effort in every branch of literature and science that he was considered the greatest theologian, philosopher, and mathematician of his age. He was so capable, especially in mathematics, that he was widely accused of Magic by the unlearned common folk who were stunned by his marvelous mechanical inventions. In the year 1236, after the death of Jordan, the General Master of the Dominicans, Albert governed the entire Order as Vicar for two years. In 1238, at the general chapter of the Order held at Bologna, he himself was sought for the Generalate along with Hugh of Saint-Cher. However, both missed out on the dignity. Having been made Provincial of his Order throughout Germany, he established his seat at Cologne, and there he lectured publicly on Theology, celebrated by a great gathering and applause of listeners. For from that school came forth Thomas Aquinas, Ambrose of Siena, Thomas of Cantimpré, and a long line of other leading men of this century. At the beginning of the year 1260, Albert was named Bishop of Regensburg <note>original: "Ratisponensis"</note> on the Danube by Pope Alexander IV, and although he was unwilling, he was compelled to undertake the duty. But in the year 1263, weary of the episcopal burden, he resigned his dignity; and having returned to the monastery at Cologne, he delighted his old age with literary leisure. He died in the year 1280, on the 15th day of November, at the age of 75, or as others would have it, 87.
<margin>|| Cited above.</margin>
Concerning him, P. Jovio says ||, *by teaching and writing, [he covered] all the topics of theology and philosophy*

The complete works of Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and "Universal Doctor" known for his work in the natural sciences</note> enumerated thus far were collected and edited in 21 volumes by Pierre Jammy, a theologian of the Dominican Order, in Lyon, 1651.

<margin>1261.</margin>
**G E O R G E**, called **Acropolita**, a native of Constantinople. Having already been thoroughly instructed in the liberal arts in the schools of the Grammarians, he was sent while still a youth (after the year 1228) by his father to the court of Emperor John Ducas <note>John III Doukas Vatatzes, Emperor of Nicaea</note> at Nicaea. At the age of 17, he left the court and studied mathematics, poetry, and rhetoric under Theodore Exapterygus, and logic under Nikephoros Blemmydes. At 21, he held a learned dispute regarding a solar eclipse in the presence of Emperor John and the physician Nicholas. Finally, having been made the Grand Logothete <note>a high administrative official in the Byzantine Empire, similar to a chancellor</note> of the Emperor, he flourished in the year 1261. He undertook frequent embassies for the Emperors of Constantinople and was employed in the most difficult affairs of the realm. He was sent from John Ducas to the Despot Michael to confirm a peace at Larissa; he was appointed as a judge by the same emperor for Michael Comnenus, who was suspected of treachery. Having been placed in charge of all the governors of the Western provinces by Theodore Lascaris, the son of John (whom George had instructed in logic), he fought strenuously around the year 1255 against Michael Angelos the Despot, who had revolted against Theodore. Eventually, he was besieged in the city of Prilep and, after a most brave defense, was captured through betrayal and led through the province in chains. In the year 1260, he was freed by Emperor Michael Palaiologos and sent as an ambassador to the Prince of Constantinople. In 1267, after he had instructed the church youth in literature and morals for many years as the Church Rhetor, he grew weary of the burden and was succeeded by Holobolus. In the year 1272, George presided as a judge—among the lay officials added to the clergy—at the Synod gathered to decide the case of John Veccus, the Patriarch of Constantinople. In the following year, he was sent as an ambassador by Emperor Michael to Pope Gregory X along with several others, where he helped negotiate the ecclesiastical peace between the Greeks and the Latins. In 1274, having set out for the Second Council of Lyon, he confirmed the recently established peace on behalf of the Emperor by taking an oath before the Church Fathers. In 1282, he was sent to John, the prince of the Bulgarians; after returning home, he died that same year. Gregory of Cyprus, Patriarch of Constantinople, in a eulogy prefixed to George’s *History*, extols him with immoderate praise, as if he were the only man who had united every kind of discipline and held the first place in all of them, "so that in no way could anyone be compared to him" <note>original Greek: ὡς ἂν οὐδενὶ πρὸς ἕνα καταδέχεσθαι σύγκρισιν</note>; indeed, that he followed in the footsteps of Aristotle himself in philosophy, and Plato in theology and Attic elegance. However, it will be more than enough if we grant him even half of this eulogy. He may be a learned, diligent, prudent, and faithful writer; nevertheless, to pour such praise upon men of this century is to leap over all bounds of modesty and truth in one's lauding. Certainly, Ephraemius, in a manuscript Chronicle cited by Leo Allatius, calls our Acropolita the "ruler and president of all" <note>original Greek: ἄρχοντα πάντων καὶ πρόεδρον</note>. George Acropolita composed the *History or Chronicle of Constantinople* from the time the City was captured by the Latins <note>during the Fourth Crusade in 1204</note> until its recovery by Michael Palaiologos—namely, from the year 1203 to 1261. George Douza brought this work to Constantinople, where it was found in Pera and redeemed by George Cantacuzene. It was translated into Latin and published with notes in Greek and Latin by Theodore, the brother of George Douza, at *Leiden, 1614, in octavo*. The following year, the *Genevans* added it (in Greek and Latin but without notes) to the work of Laonikos Chalkokondyles, *Geneva 1615, in folio*. Finally, a much more complete version, from the translation and with the notes of Leo Allatius—with his lengthy *Discourse on the various Georges and their writings* added at the end—was published in Greek and Latin at *Paris, 1651, in folio*. Meanwhile, it should be noted that Leo Allatius identifies a twofold "edition" or version of this Chronicle: one shorter, with many parts cut out by someone, and this is the very one which George Douza... <meta>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page with the discussion of the different editions of the Chronicle of Acropolita.</meta>

<page-num>734</page-num>

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200.</margin>
Douza first edited [these works]; another version, lengthy and detailed, and perfect in all its parts, was translated into Latin by himself and published by the Parisian printers. Finally, his work *On Faith, Virtue, and the Soul* <note>original: "Forma de fide, de virtute, & anima"</note> was held in the Library of Saint Augustine; likewise his *Exposition on the Maxims of Gregory Nazianzen regarding Psalm 43* <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390) was an influential Archbishop of Constantinople and theologian</note> and his *Prayers to God*, which were used after the Greeks recovered Constantinople and which he himself mentions in his *History*; also his *Oration on the Recovery of Constantinople to Emperor Michael* <note>Michael VIII Palaiologos, who reclaimed the city from the Latins in 1261</note>, which he mentions at the end of his *History*.

<margin>1261.</margin>
**URBAN IV**, previously called **Jacques Pantaléon**, was French by birth, born in Troyes to a humble family; indeed, he was the son of a cobbler. He was first a Canon of Troyes, then Archdeacon of Laon, later Bishop of Verdun, and served as the legate of Alexander IV in Pomerania, Prussia, Livonia, and throughout Germany. He soon became the Patriarch of Jerusalem and was finally elected Roman Pontiff at Viterbo on August 29, 1261, and crowned on September 4. In the year 1262, he excommunicated King Manfred, promising the remission of sins to all those who fought against him. In 1264, he instituted the Feast of Corpus Christi <note>The "Body of Christ," a major feast day celebrating the Real Presence of the Eucharist</note> to be celebrated henceforth in the Church. He died in Perugia on October 2 of that same year. Regarding him, Johannes Stella <note>An Italian priest and historian (c. 15th century)</note> records this:
> "Although he was born in a humble place, he possessed a distinguished and elegant tongue. Once, when he was provoked because he was born of a low-born father, he replied: *'A noble man is not born, but made; it is a matter of virtue and nobility.'*"

Two of his *Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume XI, page 817. His *Metaphrase on Psalm 50* is found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXIV, page 335. Eleven other *Letters* are found in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* for the year 1261, and thirteen others in Volume II of the *Pontifical Registry*, page 86.

<margin>1262.</margin>
**HENRICUS DE SEGUSIO**, French by nation and from Susa <note>A town in the Piedmont region</note> by birth, was born in the sub-Alpine region. Before the year 1258, he was made Bishop of Embrun in Narbonese Gaul. In 1262, he became a Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia <note>Because of this title, he is famously known in legal history as "Hostiensis"</note>. He had Guillaume Durand, the author of the *Speculum*, among his disciples. He attained such great knowledge in both branches of law <note>Canon and Civil law</note> that he was called the *Source and Splendor of Law*. He died in the year 1271, though others claim he lived until 1281. He wrote the *Summary of Both Laws*, which is commonly called the *Golden Summary of Hostiensis*. This was published with annotations by Guarini in Basel, 1573, and in Lyon, 1588 and 1597. He also wrote an *Exposition on the Six Books of the Decretals*, printed in Rome, apparently in 1470 and 1473, and in Venice in 1496 and 1581.

<margin>1265.</margin>
**CLEMENT IV**, previously called **Guido Fulcodii** (or Guy Foulques), and sometimes **Guido Greffus**, was French by birth. He was first a distinguished lawyer and a counselor to the King of France, during which time he married and had two daughters. After the death of his wife, he renounced the world; because of the holiness of his character, he was first made Bishop of Le Puy, then Archbishop of Narbonne, and finally Cardinal and Bishop of Sabina. Having been sent as a legate to England by Urban IV, he was elected Roman Pontiff by the Cardinals in his absence after Urban’s death in 1265. He gave his assent to this election at Perugia on February 6 and was crowned on the 22nd. Immediately upon entering the Papacy, he gave a rare sign of his contempt for worldly things: he gave only thirty Tours pounds <note>original: "libris Turonenfibus," the standard currency of the French crown</note> to each of his daughters, marrying one to a common man and sending the other to a monastery. To his sister’s son, who held three canonries, he gave the choice to keep whichever one he wished but required him to resign the other two immediately. In that same year, by Apostolic right, he granted the Kingdom of Sicily to Charles of Anjou, the brother of King Louis of France, since it had been taken away from Manfred due to his defiance. He ordered a Crusade to be preached against Manfred and decreed that a tenth of all ecclesiastical revenues be paid to support the costs of the war. In 1267, he struck with excommunication King Conradin (the son of Emperor Frederick), who was pursuing his ancestral rights in Italy, along with all the cities siding with him. He also decreed that King Peter of Aragon, having been devoted to dire curses, should be stripped of his <unclear>kingdom</unclear> by Apostolic authority. He died in Viterbo on November 29, 1268. Three of his *Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Volume XI.

Thirteen other letters are in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* <note>The "Minors" refers to the Franciscan Order</note> for the year 1265, etc. Thirty-four more are in the same work, Volume II, in the *Papal Register* <note>original: "Regesto Pontif."</note> on page 100. Furthermore, those who attribute massive legal works to our Clement are most disgracefully mistaken—for instance, the *Decisions* (Frankfurt, 1575), the *Golden Lecture on the Decretals* <note>The Decretals were papal letters that formed part of Canon Law</note> (Lyon 1517, Frankfurt 1580), the *Treatise on Appeals* (Cologne 1573), the *Commentaries on the Pandects* <note>The Pandects, or Digest, was a compendium of Roman law</note>, three volumes of *Counsels*, etc. For all these are actually the work of Guy, surnamed Pape, a Counselor of the Dauphiné <note>A province in southeastern France</note>, who flourished from the year 1427 to 1483.

<margin>1270.</margin>
## GILBERT,
or Guibert, called Wibert by Henry of Ghent, born in Tournai <note>A city in modern-day Belgium</note>, a monk of the Franciscan Order and Professor of Sacred Theology at the University of Paris, flourished in the year 1270. There exists his *Treatise on the Duty of a Bishop and the Ceremonies of the Church*, and another *On Peace and Tranquility of Mind*, both in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliothecâ Patr."</note>, Volume XXV, page 378. Also his *Life of Saint Eleutherius*, the first Apostle of the people of Tournai, found in Bollandus’s collection under February 20. His *Sermons for the Seasons and for the Saints* were published in Paris, 1518, in octavo format. He also wrote a *Travelogue of the First Expedition of Saint Louis the King to the East* <note>St. Louis IX of France; "Hodæporicon" is a Greek-derived term for a travel journal</note>, according to Henry of Ghent <margin>|| *On Illustrious Writers*, Chapter 54.</margin>, which is said to exist in manuscript form in Belgian libraries.

<margin>1270.</margin>
## NICHOLAS HANAPUS,
a Frenchman by nation, born in the village of the same name in the Diocese of Reims, a monk of the Dominican Order. He served as the Penitentiary of the Apostolic See in the city of Rome and flourished around the year 1270. While performing his duties with the highest praise, he was named Patriarch of Jerusalem by Pope Martin [IV] in 1281; he had also previously been appointed the first Censor of the Faith in Syria and Palestine by Nicholas III. He died at Ptolemais <note>Modern-day Acre in Israel</note> in the year 1288. Extant is his *Bible of the Poor* <note>original: "Biblia Pauperum"</note> in 134 chapters (falsely attributed to Bonaventure), or *Examples of Virtues and Vices* gathered from the entire treasury of both laws <note>Referring to the Old and New Testaments</note>, published in Venice (1537), Tübingen (1533), Paris (1547), and Basel (1555).

<margin>1271.</margin>
## GREGORY X,
previously called Theobald, an Italian by birth from Piacenza, Archdeacon of Liège. In the year 1270, he joined Edward, Prince of Wales <note>Later King Edward I of England</note>, as a companion while the Prince was leading an army to Palestine. While he was staying there, he was elected Roman Pontiff by the Cardinals at Viterbo on September 1, 1271. He gave his consent to the election on October 27 and was crowned in Rome the following year on March 27. In the year 1274, he presided over the Second Council of Lyon, in which he entered into peace with the Greek Church, as Emperor Michael [Palaiologos] accepted every condition in order to turn the weapons of the Westerners away from his still-shaky empire and to obtain the removal of Baldwin’s imperial status <note>The Latin Emperor Baldwin II's claim was suppressed to favor the Byzantine union</note> by synodic authority. Returning to Italy in 1275, he subjected the Florentines to anathema. He died on January 10, 1276, and was buried at Arezzo. Nine of his letters exist in the *Council Records*, Volume XI, page 929; ten other letters in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* for the year 1272, etc.; and six others in Volume II of the *Papal Register*, page 116.

<margin>1272.</margin>
## ROBERT KILWARDBY,
an Englishman by nation, after devoting himself to studies at Oxford, he moved to the University of Paris and there obtained the degree of Master of Arts. Returning home, he joined the brotherhood of Saint Francis [the Franciscans], and shortly after was made Provincial of his order. In the year 1272, he was promoted to Archbishop of Canterbury by Gregory X. The monks of Canterbury declared him to have been legitimately elected by their votes so that they might appear to protect their rights (even though they had recently elected their Sub-prior, William Chillinden); and thus he was consecrated on February 26. The following year, when Thomas de Cantilupe was receiving his degree at the Oxford Vespers <note>A formal academic ceremony involving public debates held the day before graduation</note>, the Archbishop did not disdain to act as the President and Moderator of the Disputation, as witnessed by Walsingham <margin>† *English History*, page 50.</margin>, despite his high office. In the year 1278, by...

<margin>1272.</margin>
**WILLIAM PERALDUS**, or "of the High Rock" <note>original: "de Petrâ altâ"</note>, a Frenchman by nation from the Province of Vienne, took the habit of the Dominican Order at the Royal Convent in the year 1219. He flourished in the year 1272, at which time (if you believe Ambrosio Altamurano) he was made Archbishop of Lyon. It is perhaps more correct to consider him as having performed only the vicarious care of Lyon by right of a suffragan <note>A suffragan is a subordinate bishop who assists a diocesan bishop; "vicarious care" implies he was acting on behalf of another</note>. He died in the year 1275. His *Summa of Virtues and Vices* is available (Venice 1492, 1497, octavo; Basel 1497; Lyon 1551, sextodecimo; Paris 1629, quarto; and often elsewhere). There are those who attribute the *Sermons for the Seasons and Saints* <note>original: "Sermones de Tempore & Sanctis"</note>, commonly ascribed to William of Paris, to this man. These sermons were published in Lyon in 1575 and elsewhere.

<margin>1276.</margin>
**INNOCENT V**, previously called Peter of Tarentaise, a Burgundian by nation, born in Tarentaise near the Maurienne valley in the year 1225. He entered the Dominican Order as a boy of ten and devoted himself to theological studies at the University of Paris, where at last, because of his rare learning, he earned the right to preside over the Chair of Theology. In the year 1263, at the general chapter of the Dominicans held in Lyon, he was declared Vicar General of the Order and Provincial of France. In the year 1271, he was created Archbishop of Lyon, and in the following year, he was transferred to the Church of Tarentaise and the Bishopric of Ostia and Velletri. He was also made a Cardinal. In the year 1273, he was appointed Grand Penitentiary <term>Grand Penitentiary: The high official in the Roman Curia responsible for matters of conscience, confessions, and dispensations</term> of the Roman Church, and in the following year, he participated in the Council of Lyon. In the year 1276, he was elected Roman Pontiff at Arezzo on the 21st of January and crowned in Rome on the 23rd of February. He absolved the Florentines, who had been excommunicated by his predecessors, on the condition that they expel all Ghibellines <note>The Ghibellines were a political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor, often in conflict with the Pro-Papal Guelphs</note> from the city. He died after five months on the 22nd of June. His *Compendium of Theology* (Paris 1551, duodecimo) and *Commentary on the Four Books of Sentences* (Toulouse 1652) are extant. Ambrosio de Altamura lists several other of his writings of quite substantial volume in the *Dominican Library* on pages 43 and 444.

<margin>1276.</margin>
**JOHN BECCUS** or **VECCUS**, a Greek by birth, Chartophylax <term>Chartophylax: The official archivist and librarian of the Patriarchate in Constantinople, a position of great power</term> of the Great Church of Constantinople, a man most celebrated in his time for both genius and erudition. At first, he strenuously opposed Emperor Michael when he was contemplating union with the Latins <note>This refers to the attempt to reconcile the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches</note>. The Emperor tried to soften him and draw him to his side in every way, both personally and through others. However, when he could achieve this by no amount of advice, he cast the man along with his associates into a most foul prison and sent him the writings of Nicephorus Blemmydes. Having read these during his leisure and weighed the sayings of the Fathers, and having considered the whole matter more diligently, Beccos changed his opinion and stood for the Emperor and the Latins against

...stood among the Greeks. Thus, in the year 1274, according to Freher <note>Marquard Freher, a German jurist and historian</note>, after Joseph Galsio was deposed, Beccus himself ascended the patriarchal throne through the favor of Emperor Michael <note>Michael VIII Palaeologus, who sought union with the Roman Church</note>. To use the words of Nicephorus Gregoras <note>A Byzantine historian and scholar</note>: *He was everything to the Emperor: his tongue, his hand, and the pen of a swift writer; speaking, writing, and establishing dogmas.* <note>original Greek: πάντα ἦν αὐτῷ τῷ βασιλεῖ, καὶ γλῶττα, καὶ χεὶρ, καὶ καλαμὸς γραμματίως ὀξυγράφοι, καὶ λέγων, καὶ γράφων, καὶ δογματίζων.</note> After he had held the Patriarchate for eight years, upon the death of Emperor Michael, and fearing he might be torn apart by the common people, he secretly left his seat and fled to the Monastery of the Panachrantos around the year 1283, with Joseph being reinstated once again. After Joseph’s death around 1284, George of Cyprus attained the Patriarchate and saw to it that Beccus was banished to the foothills of Mount Olympus. However, when Beccus complained bitterly about the injustice done to him, he was brought back to Constantinople and ordered to argue his case before a sacred council. This he did with great sharpness and eloquence; but since he continued to fiercely defend the cause of the Latins, he was banished to Bithynia along with Meliteniota and Metochita <note>Constantine Meliteniotes and George Metochites, fellow supporters of Church union</note>, to be kept in custody in the castle of St. George, where at last, broken by hardships and miseries, he died. He was a man, in the judgment of Gregoras <margin>* History, Book 5.</margin>, *singularly intelligent, nurtured in speech and learning from an early age; moreover, he was adorned with such natural gifts as no other man of that time possessed.* <note>original Greek: συνετὸς ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα, καὶ λόγου καὶ παιδείας τρόφιμος· τοσοῦτος δὲ καὶ δόξῃ τῇ φύσεως συγκρεκραμένῃ χαρίσμασιν, ὅσοις τῶν τότε ἀνθρώπων οὐδεὶς</note> *For though there were those in that day who surpassed him in the study of Greek literature, in sharpness of mind, strength of tongue, and the practice of ecclesiastical dogmas, all others seemed like children compared to him.* <note>original Greek: Ἐκλεκτικῆς γὰρ παιδείας ἕνεκα ἤσαν οἱ τότε περιοδεύοντες αὐτῷ, φύσεως δὲ ὀξύτητι καὶ γλώττης ῥώμῃ καὶ ἀσκήσει δογμάτων ἐκκλησιαστικῶν, παῖδες ἀνδρὶ ἀντιβαλλόμενοι πάντες ἐδόκουν ἐς αὐτὸν.</note>

**GEORGE METOCHITA**, Deacon of the Great Church of Constantinople, an ally of Beccus <note>original Latin: "Becci Symmysta," implying a fellow initiate or close partner in his ecclesiastical policies</note>, and the focal point of nearly all the troubles carried out under Emperor Andronicus; he flourished in the year 1276. He most zealously promoted the entry into Union with the Latins; and since he could in no way be moved from his opinion, he was frequently thrown into prison. He died in exile, though I have not discovered in which year, though he certainly outlived Beccus. *His style of speaking, in the judgment of Allatius* <note>Leo Allatius, a 17th-century scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note>, is a rough composition in all respects, unsoftened by any pigment or charm; his thoughts are grave and his arguments firm for proving what he wished, but his elocution and his application of names are rugged and jarring. So says Allatius, who repeats nearly the same things in his *Dissertation on the Georges and Their Writings*, p. 345. In both places, he enumerates the short works of Metochita: a work on the *Procession of the Holy Spirit* <note>The theological debate over whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from both the Father and the Son (Filioque)</note> divided into five parts or orations; *On the Union of the Churches*; and works against Maximus Planudes, Manuel the Nephew, and Gregory of Cyprus. Of these, there survive: a refutation of three chapters by Maximus Planudes, published by the same Allatius in Greek and Latin in *Orthodox Greece*, Volume II, p. 922; a *Response to Manuel the Nephew of Crete*, ibid. p. 959; a substantial fragment from Book V on the *Procession of the Holy Spirit* in Greek and Latin is presented by the same Allatius in his book *On Purgatory*, p. 883; a fragment from a historical oration *On the Union of the Churches* in his book against Hottinger, p. 429; two fragments from a historical oration *On the Discord of the Churches*, ibid. p. 458, 462; another fragment from Book V on the *Procession of the Holy Spirit*, ibid. p. 511; and a fragment of Book IV on the *Procession of the Holy Spirit* dealing with the Letter of Saint Maximus, published in Greek and Latin by François Combefis in the *New Addition*, Volume II, p. 1017.

<margin>1276.</margin>
**CONSTANTINE MELITENIOTA**, the Chartophylax <note>The official archivist and legal officer of the patriarchate</note> of John Beccus, Archdeacon of the archives, and an associate of Metochita and favorer of the Latins; he flourished at the same time as Beccus and Metochita and suffered the same trials with them. He died an exile in a small town in Bithynia and was buried in a hasty funeral on the island of Plata. He wrote a *Treatise on the Ecclesiastical Union of the Latins and Greeks*, and another quite lengthy one on the *Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which were published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius in *Orthodox Greece*, Volume II, p. 642, 765.

<margin>1276.</margin>
**GEORGE MOSCHAMPER**, Chartophylax of the Great Church of Constantinople; he flourished around the year 1276. He was most hostile to the Latins, whom he openly refuted and argued against in his writings. John Beccus responded to several of his writings against the Latins, as is clear from Beccus’s own short works; however, Leo Allatius confesses that he has seen neither the writings of Moschamper nor the responses of Beccus in his *On the Consensus*, book 2, chapter 15, section 13, and in his *Dissertation on the Georges*, p. 349, where he deals more extensively with him and his small works.

**SIMON**, a Constantinopolitan by kin, it seems, but born in Crete; a Hieromonachus <note>A monk who is also a priest</note> on the side of the Latins, and indeed of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>. He flourished, as I conjecture, around the year 1276 and thereafter, a friend of Olobolus the Rhetorician. If he lived at this time, he is either the same as Simon Jacumæus, who was once Bishop of Syracuse and then of Thebes (as Leo Allatius seems to believe *), or else Sixtus of Siena erred † when he wrote that Jacumæus flourished in the year 1400. There exists a long (though incomplete) Letter in Greek and Latin to John Nomophylax concerning the Councils that defined the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, found in L. Allatius’s book against Hottinger, p. 324. The same Allatius reveals in *On the Consensus*, book 2, chapter 15, section 11, that he has seen two other treatises of nearly the same subject, one addressed to Manuel Olobolus and the other to Saphonias.

Martinus Polonus in his Chron. near the end. Siffrid, Epitome, book 2.
</margin>
**JOHN XXI**, called by others XIX, named Petrus Juliani, was born in Lisbon in Portugal. Famous in every branch of knowledge, he gave his attention especially to medicine; having finally renounced this, he took holy orders upon himself and was made Cardinal and Bishop of Tusculum. Upon the death of Adrian V on the 20th of September 1276, he was declared Roman Pontiff. Even at the highest peak of pontifical dignity, he did not shrink from literature, and he provided aid to the poor, especially if he perceived them to be led by a love of letters, whom to the Chur<unclear>ch...</unclear>

Deceived by the rules of the Art of Astrology and the casting of horoscopes <note>original: "Genethliacæ," the practice of predicting a person's life based on their birth chart</note>, he had predicted a long life for himself; but suddenly a new chamber which he had built in the Palace of Viterbo collapsed to the ground upon him. <margin>1277.</margin>
### MARTIN, a POLE by nation, called by his paternal name Strempus, born of the noble Strempus family, a native of Opava <note>original: "Carfulanus," referring to Troppau/Opava in modern-day Czechia, then part of the Polish ecclesiastical province</note>. In his youth, he was exceptionally well-educated in the humanities, and he excelled especially in the knowledge of Imperial and Canon Law, and in the study of History and Theology. He joined the Monks of the Dominican Order, although Charles Visch—following Possevino and Jongelinus—attempts to claim him for the Cistercians, though with little success. At length, having set out for Rome, he was appointed Apostolic Chaplain and Grand Penitentiary <note>A high-ranking official in the Roman Curia responsible for matters of conscience and the granting of absolutions</note> by Nicholas III in the year 1277. The following year, when the See of Gniezno <note>original: "Gnesnensi," the primary archbishopric of Poland</note> became vacant and a controversy arose regarding the election, the Pope, moved by the prayers of the Chapter, Duke Bolesław, and others, promoted our Martin to the Archbishopric of Gniezno. Charles Visch errs monstrously in this part, as in others <margin>* Library of Cistercian Writers, p. 238.</margin>*, by making him Archbishop of Cosenza in the Kingdom of Naples, thus creating several "Martin the Poles" for us. I return to our man. While he was beginning his journey to Poland, he fell ill at Bologna, where he died shortly after. He was buried in the Church of St. Dominic, before the high altar, near the chapel of St. Thomas. He was honored with this funeral epitaph, which Abraham Bzovius testifies he had read in his own time (around the year 1278, no. 32):

> Here lies Brother Martin the Pole, of the Order of Preachers, Archbishop of Gniezno.

->W R I T I N G S .<-

### Chronicle, called the Martinian, which he brought from the birth of Christ first down to the year 1271, and then to 1277; those events which follow until the year 1285 were added by another hand. In this Chronicle, he briefly follows the deeds of the Emperors and Popes, arranged in columns on either side <note>Martin's layout was innovative, using a "graphic" history where one page or column represented a fixed number of years to keep the histories of popes and emperors synchronized</note>. However, nothing has made this work more famous than that most celebrated tale of **Pope Joan** <note>original: "Joanna Papissa"</note>, whether it be a fable or a mere anecdote. Truly, I have no doubt that it is a fable and was thrust into Martin’s Chronicle, especially since it is missing from most of the ancient manuscript codices. In four manuscript codices...

**JOHN PECKHAM**, an Englishman by birth, born in the county of Sussex of humble stock near Chichester; after completing the first stages of his education, he was sent to the University of Oxford, where he successfully advanced his affairs and joined the fellowship of the Franciscans <note>The Order of Friars Minor</note>. He was eventually created Minister Provincial of the Order, though this happened later. For Leland says*, *seeing that which happens quite frequently—that few are illustrious in their own country even if merit is present, while many abroad have become most famous through both letters and many other virtues—under a lucky star he sought out Paris. There he applied himself to those studies which he had rightly begun in England for so long that he was both considered learned and became a great philosopher as well as a theologian.* Returning to England, he lectured publicly at the University of Oxford, not without the applause and admiration of the entire University. But he did not remain long among his own people; for having been summoned to Paris to adorn that University as well, he set out for that place. Leaving Paris, he went to Lyon, so that he might more conveniently devote himself to the study of Civil and Canon Law. In this Church he obtained a Canonry, which he never afterwards wished to relinquish, but held until his death. As the man's fame grew daily, he sought out Italy and finally Rome, where he was so pleasing to the Pope and the entire Roman court that he was appointed an Auditor of Causes in the very palace of the Pope. Meanwhile, it happened that Robert Kilwardby, the Archbishop of Canterbury, resigned his office; the Pope soon conferred that dignity upon our Peckham, who was accordingly consecrated at Rome on March 6, in the year 1278. Having returned to England, he had scarcely occupied his see <note>original: "cathedram"</note> when the Pope demanded a huge sum of 4,000 Marks from him through letters, threatening that unless he paid, he would be excommunicated with solemn ceremonies in his own Cathedral church on any given Sunday. Peckham tried to deflect the blow in every way he could; in vain, for he was forced to pay. He had a great dispute with Giffard, the Archbishop of York, who allowed a golden cross to be carried high before him in the province of Canterbury. The Archbishop of Canterbury, being indignant, forbade all commerce with the Archbishop of York and his associates throughout the entire province under the threat of excommunication <note>original: "anathematis fulmine," the lightning-bolt of anathema</note>. To such an extent was this enforced that the Archbishop of York, destitute of lodging and all necessities, found it necessary to lower his cross. Peckham died around the year 1291, a very wealthy man, having founded a most richly endowed College and having enriched his relatives to such a degree that, as Godwin says*, *our age has seen their descendants flourishing in knightly dignity and living in great power and authority, abounding in riches.*

<margin>
* On the Prelates of England, page 142.
</margin>

*Common Perspective <note>A treatise on optics</note>, published with figures, corrected and distinguished by L. Gauricus (according to Pits).*

# UNPUBLISHED WORKS.

<margin>13th CENTURY from the Year 1200.</margin>

A book **O**n the Holy Trinity, which James <note>Thomas James, first librarian of the Bodleian</note> informs us once existed in the Lumley Library.
*Conferences on all Sundays throughout the year*, manuscripts in the Pembroke Library, Cambridge, Codex 175, no. 1.
*Meditation on the Body of Christ*, manuscript in the Library of St. Benedict, Cambridge, Codex 392, no. 34, where this note is added: *in this is contained a work by Alcuin the Englishman, disciple of Bede, a rare work*.
*Disputations of Saint Thomas and Peckham*, manuscript in Merton Library, Oxford, Codex 12.
*Treatise on the mystical interpretation of numbers in Holy Scripture* is held as a manuscript in Lincoln Library, Oxford, Codex 16, no. 9. However, whether it is by our John <note>John Peckham</note>, one may doubt, both because it is not listed by Bale among Peckham's works, and because in the Lincoln Codex the author is said to have been from the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>. Many more works are mentioned by Bale and Pits, but it is not certain whether they survive.

<margin>1278.</margin>

**ROGER BACON**, commonly called the *Wonderful Doctor* <note>original: "Doctor mirabilis"</note>, English by race, from the county of Somerset, born of a sufficiently distinguished family at Ilchester (which is *Ischalis* to Ptolemy). While placed at Oxford, he made immense progress in Grammar and Logic, and then in all of Philosophy, having Edmund Rich (later Archbishop of Canterbury) and Richard Fishacre as teachers. Equipped with these aids (as was then the custom for the English), he flew to Paris <note>original: "Luteriam"</note>, where he added a knowledge of languages, and the science of History, Jurisprudence, Mathematics, and Medicine, and finally a supreme skill in Theological matters, and brought back the insignia of a doctorate. Having returned to his fatherland, he established the seat of both his studies and his life at Oxford, and at the persuasion, it seems, of Robert of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste</note>, he took the Franciscan habit upon himself. He flourished especially around the year 1278; indeed, he had already begun to be famous many years before; even in the year 1259, before Henry III, then staying at Oxford, he delivered a sermon in which he freely rebuked the king because of the Poitevins and other foreigners—by whose counsels he acted almost exclusively—who were not only admitted into the court but even employed in the highest offices of the state.

But, immersed in Philosophical studies, he gave himself entirely to the investigation of hidden things, penetrated the secret recesses of nature, searched out every curiosity, tracked down the latent causes of things, and produced certain wonderful effects far above the common grasp of men, using machines for this purpose, devised with no small skill of intellect. Hence the name of "Magician" was so often struck against him, and so often the crime of a secret association with evil spirits was charged, and that not only among the common people, but even with Pope Clement IV, whose rescript <note>official reply</note> to our Roger you have in Wadding <note>Luke Wadding, the Franciscan historian</note> at the year 1266, no. 15; though whether it regards this calumny is not sufficiently clear. It is certain that in the following year, Bacon sent John of London, his disciple, to Rome with apologetic pamphlets and mathematical instruments he had composed. * In the year 1278, the accusation was renewed against him before Jerome of Ascoli, General of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>, then staying in France, who condemned Bacon’s doctrine and forbade them to read his books, and decreed that the author himself should be committed to prison. Certainly, almost everyone agrees that he was thrown into prison for at least some time, and that by the order of Pope Nicholas IV himself; but whether he remained there until death is entirely unknown to me. This man of deepest knowledge and most sharp intellect, greater than his age, died in the year 1284, at about 78 years of age, and was buried in the church of the Franciscans at Oxford.
<margin>* See Wadding at the year 1278, no. 26.</margin>

## PUBLISHED WRITINGS.

*Letters illustrated with notes*, Hamburg 1618. Octavo <note>8vo: a book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves</note>.
*Mathematical and Perspective Mirrors* <note>original: "Specula mathematica & perspectiva"</note>, Frankfurt 1614. Quarto <note>4to: a book size where each sheet is folded into four leaves</note>.

## UNPUBLISHED WORKS.

*Compendium of Theological Study*, in 5 books. It existed with his other small works, according to James <note>Thomas James, librarian</note>, as a manuscript in 2 volumes in the Lumley Library, Codex 251.
*Grammar*, Manuscript in Peterhouse College, Cambridge, Codex 3. *Book on Location* <note>original: "Liber de situ"</note> in the Benedictine Library, Codex 192. *Geomancy* in the Lumley Library, Codex 132. *The Greater and Lesser Rogerina* <note>medical manuals attributed to Bacon</note>, Manuscript at Cambridge in the Archives, no. 22, in the collection of G. Cope, Codex 3. *Book on the Utility of the Sciences*, in which he discusses the four obstacles to truth. It exists as a manuscript in the Cotton Library, under Julius D. 5, no. 4. *On Burning Mirrors*, in the same collection under Tiberius, B. 9, no. 5. *On the Hindrances to Wisdom*; in which treatise he also discusses the grammatical basics of the Greek language, in the same collection, Manuscript under Galba, A. 8, no. 1. 

I would be endless if I reviewed every single work which Bale (Century 4, ch. 55) and Pits (Age 13, no. 367) enumerate; since they are for the most part Grammatical, Philosophical, and Mathematical, it matters little to transfer their titles here. The most diligent collector of Oxford Antiquities <note>Anthony Wood</note> treats our Bacon’s distinguished career at length on page 136 and following. He also notes a few things in general regarding his writings, to be presented by me in this place in summary form: 

I. One may suspect that of all the books he composed, not even the titles remain; also, that copies of those which do remain are to be sought out with the greatest difficulty. For those that lie hidden in manuscripts are suppressed either by the envy or the ignorance of their owners. 

II. The works of Bacon that are commonly used by scholars are deficient in many places, or even redundant, which must also be said of those which are considered perfect; it is uncertain whether this happened through the negligence of monks or by design. 

III. Of the books of which he is commonly considered the author, several are attributed to other writers; for example, the *Book on the ebb and flow of the British sea* to Walter Burley; the *Book on the utility of Astronomy* to William Buttoner; the *Greater and Lesser Rogerina* are adjudged to a certain unnamed author. 

IV. Nor is he to be considered the author of all things assigned to him. Thus the *Treatise on the Psalter* and the *Life of Saint Edmund* Archbishop of Canterbury, which Leland attributes to our Roger, actually belong to Robert Bacon; to whom also the *Syncategoremata* <note>a logic text regarding terms that cannot stand as subjects or predicates on their own</note> are ascribed. Likewise, the *Treatise on the Magnet* is attributed by most to Peter Peregrinus <note>Pierre de Maricourt, a pioneer in magnetism study</note>.

## RAYMOND MARTINI,

Or Des Martins, a Catalan by nation, from the house of Subirats (others wrongly wish him to have been from Barcelona), a most famous monk of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>. He flourished in the year 1278. Most skilled in Oriental languages, so that he might pave an easier way for the conversion of the Jews and Saracens (who were frequent in Spain at that time), at the persuasion of Raymond of Penyafort, the master general of his Order, he wrote the *Dagger of Faith* <note>original: "Pugionem fidei"</note>, divided into three parts, in which he successfully argued the cause against the Jews and Moors from the very monuments of the Jewish people; from this work Porchetus Salvaticus took almost all his material in the book called *Victory against the Jews*, as did Peter Galatinus from Porchetus in his work *On the Secrets of Ca...* <note>The text cuts off here as it moves to the next page; the work mentioned is likely "De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis"</note>

<margin>1280.</margin>
## HENRY, nicknamed Goethals, or Bonicollius, of Flemish stock, called OF GHENT from his homeland, born in the village of Muda near Ghent, whence he is called *Henry of Muda* by many. He flourished in the year 1280 and taught Philosophy and Theology in the College of the Sorbonne for a long time with such great praise that, by the vote of the entire University of Paris, he earned the title *Solemn Doctor* <note>original: "Doctor solemnis"; a formal title granted to high-ranking medieval theologians</note>. Having eventually been made Archdeacon of the Church of Tournai, he died in Tournai on the very feast of Saints Peter and Paul in the year 1293.

### W R I T I N G S.

*The Summary of Theology*, or *Ordinary Questions* <note>original: "Quæftiones ordinariæ"</note> edited by Badius Ascensius, *Paris, 1520*.
*Theological Quodlibets on the four books of the Sentences* <note>Quodlibets were open-topic public debates common in medieval universities</note>, *Paris, 1518, folio*, and 2 volumes, *Venice, 1615*.
*A Book on Illustrious Men, or on Ecclesiastical Writers*, which continues from where Sigebert of Gembloux left off, brought down to his own times; published together with other writers on the same subject, with notes by Petrus Suffridus, *Cologne, 1580, octavo*, and with the scholarly commentary of Aubert Miraeus in the *Ecclesiastical Library, Antwerp, 1639, folio*.
Manuscripts are held of the following: *A book on maintaining Virginity*; *A book on Penance*; *Quodlibets on various matters arranged in Alphabetical order*; *A Quodlibet on commerce and business*; *Various Sermons*; *The Life of Saint Eleutherius, Bishop of Tournai*; regarding these, as well as certain *Commentaries* on *Aristotle*, please see Valerius Andreas in the *Belgian Library*, and Valerius Andrea and Franciscus Sweertius in the *Belgian Athena, page 328*.

<margin>1280.</margin>
## UDALRICUS, or ULRICH of Strasbourg, a German by nationality, native of Strasbourg, a listener and disciple of Albertus Magnus, and a Dominican Monk. He flourished in the year 1280. He was distinguished for his literary fame in Paris, where he was snatched away by a premature death before he had obtained the rank of master. The *Compendium of Theology*, which is held among the works of Thomas Aquinas, is more rightly attributed to our Ulrich by others. He also wrote *On the Forum of Conscience, and on Cases of Law*; *Commentary on the four books of the Sentences*; likewise a *Summary of Theology*, and *On the Soul*; not to mention the *Commentaries on the Metaphysics and Meteorology of Aristotle*, which are discussed by Altamura, Miraeus, and Simler (page 675). However, they do not inform us whether these have been published.

## GEORGE PACHYMERES, of Constantinopolitan origin, born in Nicaea, was born in the year 1242. Being remarkably learned in both sacred and secular literature, he was chosen for the ranks of the clergy of Constantinople. Soon advanced with honors, he was made the *Protecdicus* <note>A Byzantine official who served as a judge for legal and forensic cases</note> of the Patriarch of Constantinople, and a *Hieromnemon* <note>A high-ranking deacon who assisted the Patriarch in managing ordinations and liturgical books</note>, who, standing beside the Patriarch, took care of the duties of *Ordination, the Euchologion* <note>The prayer book containing the rites of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, and other matters that directly concerned the Patriarch. Having also been appointed the Imperial *Dicaeophylax* <note>literally "Guardian of the Law"; a high judicial officer</note>, he obtained such a reputation for judgment and integrity that in the year 1267, he was appointed by the Emperor and the Synod of Constantinople to examine the case of Arsenius, who had been removed from the Patriarchate on a charge of high treason,

...together with three others, he was appointed as a judge and sent for this purpose to the island where Arsenius <note>Arsenios Autoreianos, the Patriarch of Constantinople who had been exiled</note> was living in exile at that time. The judges not only acquitted him of the charges from his homeland but also restored the Emperor’s favor and generosity to him at the same time. Pachymeres himself tells us the whole history of this matter at length in book 4, chapters 15 and 16. In the year 1273, when Emperor Michael Palaeologus <note>Michael VIII Palaiologos, who sought to end the Great Schism</note> was contemplating a union with the Latin Church <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>—intending to draw the Latins away from the stain of heresy—he sent a booklet written for this purpose to the Patriarch. The Patriarch took care to oppose this with another "light" <note>original: "lumen," here meaning a clarifying or opposing text</note>, and our George [Pachymeres] does not deny in book 5, chapter 14, that he himself took the leading role in composing it. For he was an extremely sharp opponent of the dogmas of the Roman Church. He flourished especially around the year 1280. He lived a long life which, if one recounts the calculation of the celebrated || Lambecius, he extended to about the year 1340, dying
<margin>|| Index 3, Commentary on the Library of Vienna, book 3, appended.</margin>
as a centenarian; certainly it is established that he died after the year 1308. He was a man of no small rank among the Greeks of his time, famous for both sacred and secular learning. *His style, in the judgment of Leo Allatius, was accurate, shaped by the ancient sock <note>original: "soccum," a reference to the footwear of ancient comic actors, implying a classical or theatrical style</note> and blood, yet more swollen than the grasp of history allows, and ambiguous and obscure due to a tangled connection of speech; however, for that age, his softness and prudence would seem to run wild.* The author, while desiring to appear as a seeker of truth (says Allatius), sharpens his tongue against churchmen, and especially against the supporters of the Latin name, being far too partial to the Greeks.

### W R I T I N G S.

**A** *History of the affairs of Constantinople* under Michael and Andronicus Palaeologus, from the year 1258 to the year 1308, covering 49 years of deeds in 13 books. Certain very brief excerpts of individual books were published at the end of the Latin edition of Nicephorus Gregoras by Hieronymus Wolf (*Basel, 1562*). Denis Pétau subjoined certain fragments to the *Breviary* of Nicephorus in Greek (*Paris, 1616, 8vo*). Finally, the complete *History*, with a version, Glossary, Notes, and Chronology by Father Poussines in Greek and Latin, was produced in two volumes. The first at *Rome, 1666*; the second in the same place, *1669, folio*.
*A Paraphrase on the works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite* <note>A collection of mystical theological texts formerly attributed to a contemporary of St. Paul</note> has a place among the works of Dionysius in Greek (*Paris, 1541, 8vo*); in Greek and Latin (*ibid. 1615, folio; Antwerp, 1633; Paris, 1644, folio*).
*A Booklet on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which Leo Allatius brought to light in *Latin-Greek Orthodoxy*, volume 1, page 390.
*An Epitome of Aristotle’s Logic* in Greek (*Paris, 1548*); in Latin (*Basel, 1560*); in Greek and Latin (*Oxford, 1666, 8vo*).
He wrote almost infinite monuments on Rhetoric, which are preserved in the library of the King of France, of which Leo Allatius provides a sufficiently long index in the *Dissertation* cited above.

<margin>1280.</margin>
**MECHTILD**, of the German nation, born from a noble and splendid family, lived her life as a nun of the Benedictine Order in the Monastery of Helfta. She flourished in the year 1280 and died before the year 1290. She wrote a *Relating*, or five books of *Spiritual Grace*, which were published along with other small works of the same sort at *Paris, 1513*. Separately at *Cologne, 1536*, and elsewhere more than once. It should be noted that these books were first written in German and later translated into the Latin language.
Possevino will inform you of other editions that appeared in both Latin and Italian in his *Apparatus, Vol. II, p. 100.*

He was promoted by Urban IV to the dignity of Cardinal with the title of Priest of Saint Cecilia, and was then sent by him into France, where he performed the duty of Papal Legate for several years. After the death of Nicholas III in the year 1281, he was elected Pope at Viterbo on February 22. However, leaving Viterbo, he wished to be consecrated in Orvieto <note>original: "Urbe veteri"</note>, which occurred on March 23...

...was done for the learned. <note>original: "eruditii factum est"</note> He <note>Pope Martin IV</note> received Charles, King of Sicily, with kindness when he came to him, supported him vigorously, and restored to him the Senatorial dignity in the city of Rome, which he had lost. He excommunicated Emperor Michael Palaeologus because he had not stood by the agreements for restoring union with the Latins, as well as Peter, King of Aragon, who was occupying the kingdom of Sicily and refusing to return it to Charles. He died at Perugia, where he had moved due to the riots that had broken out between the Guelphs and Ghibellines <note>factions supporting the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor, respectively</note>, on March 28, 1285. <margin>1283.</margin>
### **GUIDO DE BAISIO**, a native of Reggio, citizen and Archdeacon of Bologna, and an eminent legal consultant. He flourished in the year 1283. He wrote three books of *Commentaries* under the title *The Rosary*, and a work *on the five books of the Decretals* <note>The Decretals of Gregory IX, a major collection of canon law</note>. These were published with notes by Nicolaus Superantius and Petrus Tretius, *Venice, 1580.*
