<margin>1284.</margin>
### **GREGORY ABUL-FARAJ**, called **IBN HAKIMA**, son of Aaron the Physician of Malatya (commonly called *Ibn Koph*); he was a physician by profession and belonged to the Jacobite <note>The Syriac Orthodox Church</note> or Melkite sect. He wrote around the year 683 of the Hegira, which is the year 1284 of the Christian Era, the year in which he concluded his History. In various copies of his work (as noted by the distinguished Hottinger*), he is honored with the following praises:
<margin>* Oriental Library, chapter 2, page 81.</margin>

> Our Lord Holy Father, the distinguished lord, renowned for learning, King of teachers, most excellent of the excellent, the model of his times, the Phoenix of the Age, the glory of the Wise, a Teacher supported by divine aid — the Crown of men preeminent in virtue, the <term>solver</term> <note>original Greek: λύτης (lytēs), meaning one who unties or solves</note> of hidden theological doubts, the foremost Prince of Christians, the marrow of the Jacobite Sect, Lord Father Mar Gregory, the unique ornament of the age, and the Phoenix of the Century.

Furthermore, he is highly commended by Muhammadan <note>Muslim</note> writers themselves as a man of great reading, instructed and thoroughly steeped in various sciences, and especially famous in his century for the glory of medicine, such that many people from Western regions flocked to him; many of the most learned Muslims confess to having learned much from him. As for the claim they add that he abandoned the Christian faith when near death, there can be no doubt that this is a calumny forged from hatred of Christians, intended to claim a man of such great reputation for themselves. He composed a *Compendium of the Ten Dynasties*, drawn from various monuments of different nations, which our distinguished Pococke published in Arabic and Latin, *Oxford, 1663, in quarto.*

---

<margin>1284. Nicephorus Gregoras, History, book 6, page 116.</margin>
### **GREGORY**, previously called George, born in Cyprus to Latin parents, and accordingly educated among the followers of the Roman Church until his twentieth year, receiving from them the rank of reader. Afterward, he went to Constantinople, where "with sails turned" <note>meaning he changed his course or loyalties</note> he adapted himself to the customs and dogmas of the Greeks, took the monastic habit, and was even enrolled in the Palatine Clergy. In the year 1284, after the death of the Patriarch Joseph, our Gregory was elevated to the Patriarchal throne with the support of the Emperor (though not without some difficulty in managing it). In this office, he not only opposed Veccus <note>John XI Bekkos, a pro-union Patriarch</note> but also vehemently persecuted him. At this time, the Church of Constantinople was suffering from the factions of the Arseniates and the Josephites <note>internal schismatic groups within the Byzantine Church</note>; thus, it is no wonder that ill-wishers conspired against Gregory. He was accused of approving the institutions of the Latins and was charged with blasphemy and impiety. The bishops rose up against him, and the Emperor abandoned his client; harassed on all sides by these evils, he resigned the patriarchate around the year 1289. He first retired to the Monastery of the Holy Mother of God called *Hodegon*, and then withdrew to the Monastery of St. Andrew, where he died shortly thereafter, having held the Patriarchal see for five years. He was a sharp adversary of the Latins; nevertheless, Leo Allatius said of him: *He was a man of the sharpest intellect, eloquent, and I might almost say [possessed of] every...*

...imbued with learning. Nicephorus Gregoras, in the place cited, calls him <note>original: "ἀνὴρ ἐν λόγοις ἐλλόγιμος, ὃς τῇ ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς εὐγενεῖ τὴν ἑλλάδα ῥυθμὸν, καὶ τὴν ἀττικίζουσαν γλῶσσαν, &c."</note> "a man distinguished in eloquence, who restored to Greece its noble rhythm in writing and the Atticizing tongue," etc., signifying a man of great fluency who, by the dexterity of his talent and singular zeal, brought to light the elegant meters of Greek literature and the Attic language—which had for a long time been submerged in the whirlpool of oblivion—recalling them, as it were, from the underworld. That he wrote several works against the Latins, especially against Beccus (or Veccus) <note>John XI Bekkos, a Patriarch of Constantinople who favored union with the Roman Church</note>, the greatest supporter of the Latins, is testified by Nicephorus Gregoras in Book 6 and Pachymeres in Book 8, chapter 1. Chief among these is the *Synodic Volume*, which, because of the dogmas of faith sincerely handed down within it, he named the *Shield of Orthodoxy*. His *Sermons against the Blasphemies of Veccus* are preserved in manuscript in the Imperial Library of Vienna (according to Gesner in his *Epitome*). See what Leo Allatius has to say in *On Consensus*, Book 2, chapter 15, number 12. Various *Encomiums* <note>formal speeches of praise</note>, especially regarding St. George and Dionysius the Areopagite, are held in the Manuscript Library of the King of France, codices 16 and 1922, and elsewhere. See Labbe, *New Library of Manuscripts*, pages 73, 74.

<margin>1285.</margin>
**HONORIUS IV**, previously called Giacomo Savelli, was Roman by birth, born from the illustrious Savelli family, and as some maintain, a Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. He succeeded Martin IV in the Pontificate, being elected at Perugia on the 4th of the Nones of April in the year 1285, and was crowned at Rome on the 20th of May. He renewed the bolt of excommunication <note>original: "Anathematis fulmen," literally the lightning bolt of anathema</note> hurled by his predecessor against Peter of Aragon; he ordered that Ladislaus, King of Hungary, who was wavering in the Christian faith, be excommunicated and deposed; and he confirmed the Order of the Carmelites, which had been attacked by others, fortifying it with new privileges. He was so afflicted by gout in the feet and hands <note>original: "Podagrâ & chiragrâ"</note> that he could only celebrate the sacred rites if supported by instruments skillfully constructed for that purpose; finally worn down by continuous pains, he paid his debt to nature <note>a common idiom for dying</note> at his residence on the Aventine Hill on April 3, 1287. He was buried in the Vatican. Two of his *letters* are extant in Bzovius under the years 1285 and 1286. Four *letters* are in Wadding, Volume II, for the same years, and ten others in the same work in the Appendix, page 558. A manuscript volume of his *Letters* is in the Vatican Library; likewise, his *Testament* is preserved in the Barberini Library, as mentioned by Louis Jacob in the *Library of the Popes*, Book 1, page 113.

<margin>
1286.
† Author, ch. 410.
</margin>
**WILLIAM DURAND**, called "The Speculator" <note>a nickname derived from his famous legal work, the *Speculum Iudiciale* or "Mirror of Law"</note>, was French by nation, from the district of Narbonne, born of a noble family in Puimisson, which is a town in that province (according to Miraeus †). While still a youth, he devoted himself to the study of Civil and Canon Law, in which pursuit he had as his leaders and masters Bernard of Compostella and Henry of Susa (later known as Cardinal Hostiensis). He began his first academic trials at Bologna; having obtained the laurel of the doctorate, he taught publicly first there and then at Modena. He excelled so greatly in legal practice that he was called the "Father of Practice." He was appointed Chaplain by Clement IV (his kinsman) and General Auditor of the Apostolic Palace; he was also made a Canon of Beauvais, Narbonne, and Chartres. In the year 1274, he was sent by Gregory X to the Second General Council of Lyon, in which he acted as the Pope’s Proctor, and in whose name he promulgated several constitutions. By Nicholas III, he was placed in charge of the Patrimony of St. Peter, distinguished with the title of Rector and Count of the Patrimony. Being no less suited for Mars than for Mercury <note>meaning he was as skilled in war as he was in administration/eloquence</note>, he was appointed General of the military forces in the Italian territories subject to the Roman See. On more than one occasion, he managed his affairs well and successfully while leading wars against the cities of Romagna, Flaminia, and Forlì, which were rebelling against the Apostolic See. In the year 1286, he was made Bishop of Mende in Aquitaine, France; and when Boniface VIII later offered him the Archbishopric of Ravenna, he refused it with a steadfast mind. In the year 1296, while serving as an envoy from Boniface to the Sultan of the Saracens, he died at Nicosia, the capital of Cyprus, on the day before the Nones of July. His body was brought to Rome and buried with great honor in the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in the Chapel of All Saints. Simon Maiolus deals with our William at greater length in the *Life of Durand* prefixed to his *Commentary on the Council of Lyon* (1569); see also Pichard in the *Lives of Jurists* and Ambrose de Altamura in the *Dominican Library*, page 72.

For the time in which he lived, he strove for a learning that was far from common, possessing an exceptional knowledge of Theology and Holy Scripture, and especially an accurate expertise in law. His famous opinion on the matter of the Sacrament <note>Referring to the Eucharist and the nature of Christ's presence</note> is reported as follows:

### WRITINGS.

*Speculum Juris* <note>The Mirror of Law</note>, divided into three volumes, written in the year 1261 and dedicated to Cardinal Ottobono. It was published in Basel in 1574 and Frankfurt in 1592.

*Repertorium Juris* <note>A legal index or repertory</note>, mostly excerpted from the *Speculum*, with which it was published in Frankfurt in 1592 and Lyon in 1516 and 1551; it was also printed in Venice in 1496.

*Rationale divinorum officiorum* <note>The Rationale of Divine Offices, a fundamental work on the symbolism of church architecture and liturgy</note>, divided into eight books and completed in the year 1286. See Book 8, chapter 9. It is available with the *Speculum* and *Repertorium* from Lyon in 1516 and 1551. Published separately in Mainz 1459, Reutlingen 1473, Venice 1485, Strasbourg 1486, Basel 1488, Nuremberg 1493, folio, Venice 1519, Lyon 1565, 1568, 1584, 1592 in octavo, and Antwerp 1570.

*Commentary on the Canons of the Council of Lyon*, published with his *Life* edited by Simone Maiolo at Fano in 1569, in quarto.

*Breviary of Glosses and Texts of Canon Law*, Paris 1519, in octavo. He likewise wrote on the *Decretals* <note>Papal decrees used as legal precedents</note> of Gregory IX and Nicholas III, and on Gratian’s *Decree*; however, either these commentaries have perished, or they are still "struggling in the darkness with the moths and bookworms." <note>A poetic way of saying the manuscripts are neglected and decaying in some unknown library.</note>

There was another man distinct from our subject (as Philip Tomasini noted long ago †) who was also a William Durand, likewise Bishop of Mende, namely the nephew and successor in the See of our subject. He was present at the Council of Vienne under Clement V in the year 1311, where he published a small book on the *Reformation of the Church*. It was published in Paris in 1545, Lyon 1635 in quarto, and with certain short works by Clémanges and Pierre d'Ailly in Paris 1671, in octavo.

### NICHOLAS IV. <margin>1288.</margin>

**Jerome**, as he was previously called, was born in Picenum at Ascoli. His father was Arminilaus Tineus, a man of honorable status. From a Franciscan monk, Jerome became the Bishop of Palestrina and Cardinal Priest of Santa Sabina. After the death of Honorius, he was created Pontiff of the Roman Church, being elected on the 22nd and crowned on the 25th of February in the year 1288. Because of riots breaking out in Rome, he set out for Rieti, but once matters were settled, he soon returned to Rome and brokered a peace between the Kings of Aragon and Naples. He was deeply concerned about propagating the Christian religion among the barbarians <note>A term often used for non-Christians outside the former Roman Empire</note>; in the same year he became Pope, he received envoys from a certain King and Queen of the Tartars <note>The Mongols</note>, whose conversion he celebrated. Furthermore, he did not cease to urge the Great Khan of Tartary to embrace the faith of Christ. In the following year, he wrote on the same matter to the Armenians and their King, as well as to the Emperor of Ethiopia. He vehemently pleaded the cause of the Christians in Syria with the Christian Princes. Moreover, he himself sent many soldiers at his own expense to protect Ptolemais <note>The city of Acre, the last major Crusader stronghold in the Levant</note>. He died in Rome on April 14, 1292, and was buried at Saint Mary Major. Luke Wadding, under the year 1292, entry number 6, preserves his epitaph written in rough and unpolished verse. However, Sixtus V, while still a Cardinal, built a far more magnificent mausoleum for him and honored him with a more noble inscription, which is likewise found in the place cited. Joannes Stella says this of him: *A man indeed exceptionally learned in both divine and human letters; and beyond his learning, he was a Pope of great goodness and integrity, loving all equally. He believed he owed no more to relatives or kin than to other good men, and therefore created excellent and learned Cardinals from almost every region, and adorned the city of Rome with very beautiful buildings.*

# The Scholastic Age. 748

### WRITINGS.

*Constitution for the Benedictines*, *Paris 1519, octavo.*
*Letters*, of which three volumes are preserved in the Vatican Library. From these, Bzovius presents eighteen for the year 1288. Wadding presents a great many for the year 1288 and the following years. In the Appendix to Volume II, page 168, he published sixty-eight others.
*Commentaries on several books of Holy Scripture*; on the *Master of the Sentences* <note>Peter Lombard’s "Sentences" was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>; *Sermons for the Saints and for the Liturgical Seasons*; *Ecclesiastical Constitutions against Heretics*, and certain other works are mentioned by Ludovicus Jacob in *The Pontifical Library, p. 165*; however, I have not learned whether they have been published, or indeed if they survive today.

<margin>1289.</margin>
### DIETRICH OF APOLDA,
<note>original: "Theodericus de Apoldia"</note>
A Thuringian by birth, born in Erfurt, he was educated among the Dominican monks and joined their ranks. He flourished in the year 1289, already more than sixty years old. He wrote *On the Life and Deeds of Saint Elizabeth*, daughter of King Andrew of Hungary and widow of Ludwig, Landgrave of Thuringia, in eight books. These are available in Canisius’s *Ancient Readings, Volume V.*
<margin>† On Latin History, book 2, chapter 6, 62.</margin>
On page 147, the † illustrious Vossius judges that these works should be attributed to another Dietrich of Thuringia, a countryman of ours. But since he offers no argument for his opinion, I do not believe they should be taken away from our Dietrich. He also composed *On the Life of Saint Dominic*, founder of the Order, in seven books, which Surius published for August 5th, though with the style slightly corrected.

<margin>1290.</margin>
### AGOSTINO TRIONFO,
<note>original: "Augustinus Triumphus"</note>
A native of Ancona and a hermit of the Augustinian Order, he flourished in the year 1290. While still a youth in 1274, he took part in the Council of Lyon. He lived for some time at the University of Paris, and for many years in Venice at the house of Saint Mary of Nazareth of his order, where he composed several short works in praise of the Blessed Virgin. He primarily made his home in Naples, being especially dear to Kings Charles and Robert. He died there in the year 1328, at the age of eighty-five.

---

### WRITINGS.

*Summary on Ecclesiastical Power*, addressed to Pope John XXII, *Augsburg 1473, folio; Rome 1479, quarto; 1582, folio.*
*Commentary on the Lord’s Prayer; the Angelic Salutation <note>The Hail Mary</note>; and the Song of the Blessed Virgin <note>The Magnificat</note>, Rome 1590, 1592, quarto.*
*On the Song of the Mother of God separately, same place, 1603. On the Lord's Prayer, same place, Rome 1587.*
*The Thousand-Word Collection from the Writings of Saint Augustine* <note>original: "Milleloquium," a massive alphabetical anthology of Augustine's thoughts</note>, which Trionfo left unfinished; it was completed by Bartolomeo of Urbino, a theologian of the same order. *It was published in Lyon in 1555, and perhaps elsewhere.*

---

### UNPUBLISHED WORKS.

*On the Four Books of Sentences; On the Holy Spirit against the Greeks; On the Spiritual Song, or on the Ten Strings; On the Entry into the Promised Land; On the Knowledge and Power of the Soul; Theorems on the Resurrection of the Dead; Exposition on Ezekiel; and on all the books of the New Testament, to some of which a double exposition is added; Sunday Sermons; likewise on the Saints for the Clergy; a Table or Index for the Moralia of Saint Gregory.* These, as well as certain *Commentaries* on Aristotle, show that they are recently discovered and hidden in various places, according to Giuseppe Panfilo, Bishop of Segni, in *Chronicle of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, p. 46.* There, he also reports that all these works of our Agostino were transcribed from the original manuscripts at the expense of the citizens of Ancona and are preserved in the Vatican Library in Rome in large and very beautiful volumes.

# The Scholastic Age. 749

<margin>
13th CENTURY.
From the year 1200.
1290.
</margin>

### JOHN OF PARIS, whether by birth or education a Parisian, was highly distinguished among the Dominican monks and the theologians of Paris. He flourished in the year 1290. When the discord arose between Pope Boniface VIII and King Philip the Fair of France, he took up the cause of his King and vigorously defended the royal rights against the Pope. He brought great honor to the Dominican assemblies through his preaching and to the theological schools through his lectures; however, while he was putting forward a certain new proposition concerning the manner of Christ’s Body in the Eucharist—namely, *that it was possible for this to occur through the "assumption" of the substance of the bread, or "paneity," into the Word* <note>original: "assumptionem substantiæ panis, vel paneitatis in Verbo." John proposed a theory called "Impanation," suggesting the bread and Christ coexist, rather than the bread's substance being entirely replaced, as in Transubstantiation.</note>, and that this was more reasonable and suited to the truth of the Sacrament—he soon provoked the Parisian Masters to great anger. He especially offended the bishops William of Paris, Giles of Bourges, Bertrand of Orléans, and William of Albi, who summoned the man for examination. When he refused to retract his dogma, they issued a decree from the theological faculty, condemned his opinion, and forbade him from both the office of preaching and lecturing under penalty of excommunication. Taking this poorly, our John appealed from the Parisian Decree to the Apostolic See <note>The Papacy</note>. Therefore, to argue his case, he traveled to Rome, where shortly thereafter he exchanged life for death, around the year 1304. Compare what Dr. Allix noted about him from the continuation of the *Chronicle of William of Nangis* and others in the preface soon to be cited, page 54.

### WRITINGS.

*A Treatise on Royal and Papal Power* <note>original: "Tractatus de Regia Potestate & Papali"</note>, written in favor of his King against Pope Boniface. It appeared with several small works of the Dominicans in *Paris, 1506, quarto*, and in *Goldast’s Monarchia, Volume II, page 107.*

*A Determination on the Manner of the Existence of the Body of Christ in the Sacrament of the Altar*, in a way other than that held by the Church. The celebrated Dr. P. Allix recently recovered this from a manuscript codex of St. Victor in Paris and published it with a long and clearly learned historical dissertation *on the dogma of Transubstantiation*, *London, 1686, octavo.*

*A Correction of the Doctrine of St. Thomas* <note>original: "Correctorium Doctrinæ S. Thomæ"</note>, attributed to Giles of Rome <note>original: "Ægidio Columnæ"</note> and published under his name, *Venice 1501, Cologne 1624, octavo.*

*A Determination on the Christian Sect through the Testimony of the Gentiles*; and others concerning the *Confessions of the Brothers*: These are held in manuscript (as James assures us) in the Lincoln Library at Oxford, Codex 16, No. 1, 2. He is also said to have written on the *Unity of Being and Essence in God*; *On the Coming of Christ, or Against the Antichrist*; *A Defense against Henry of Ghent*; and certain *Philosophical works*, which I have not found to still survive.

There were several named "John of Paris" around this time, and among them was *John of Paris the Englishman*, a Canon Regular of St. Victor in Paris, whose *Memorial, or Flowers of History* survive in manuscript both elsewhere and in the Benedictine Library at Cambridge, Codex 20. Miræus admits in his *Addition, chapter 403*, that he transferred many things from these into his own *Belgian Chronicle*.

---

<margin>1290.</margin>

### RALPH OF COLUMNA, Canon of Chartres. He flourished in the year 1290. He wrote to Lambert of Castello *A Treatise on the Transfer of the Empire from the Greeks to the Latins* <note>original: "Tractatum de Translatione Imperii à Græcis ad Latinos"</note>, which is found in Goldast, *Monarchia, Volume II, page 88*. I have nothing more to say about him.

<margin>1290.</margin>

### JAMES OF VORAGINE, more correctly "of Varazze," a native of that maritime city of the Ligurians, gave his name to the family of St. Dominic <note>He joined the Dominican Order</note>. He was made Provincial of that order in Lombardy, then General of the whole order, and finally Archbishop of Genoa, consecrated by Cardinal Orsini, Bishop of Ostia (the Roman see being vacant at the time). He is said to have favored the factions of the Emperor <note>The Ghibellines</note>; for this reason, when on Ash Wednesday Pope Boniface VIII was supposed to pronounce the customary sentence over him as he prostrated at his feet—*“Dust thou art, and unto dust thou shalt return”*—the Pope is said to have thrown the ashes into his eyes and said: *"You are a Ghibelline, and with the Ghibellines [you shall return to dust]"* <note>original: "Ghibellinus es, & cum Ghibellinis in cinerem reverteris." This is a famous historical pun playing on the liturgical words for Ash Wednesday.</note>

<margin>13th CENTURY. from the year 1200.</margin>
...by your [actions] you shall return to nothingness. So indeed Blondus and Philip of Bergamo hold, though their reliability in this matter seems to waver, as the credit should rather be given to his successor, Porchetus. He flourished in the year 1290. He died in the year 1318, although there are those who extend his life as far as the year 1314. He was a man truly devoted to God and generous to the poor, among whom he distributed almost the entire income of his bishopric; he was more pious than learned, even though he read the works of Augustine diligently and is said to have held nearly all of them in his memory. In historical matters, especially those he compiled concerning the *Lives of the Saints*, he was far too credulous, and in gathering fables from every side, he was foolish to the point of being a mockery.

## WORKS.

<margin>
* On the causes of the corruption of the arts, book 2, p. 91.
† Commonplaces, book 11, ch. 6, p. 658.
See Thuanus at the year 1555, p. 489.
</margin>
The *Lombard History*, or the *Golden Legend* regarding the lives of the Saints <note>original: "Historia Lombardica, seu Legenda aurea." This became one of the most famous books of the Middle Ages, though later scholars criticized its historical accuracy.</note>. A legend indeed "written by a man with a mouth of iron and a heart of lead," as Ludovicus Vives sharply remarked of it *. "What can be said that is more foul than that book?" Vives continues. "How shameful it is for us Christians that the most excellent deeds of our holy ones have not been committed to memory more truly and accurately, whether for the sake of knowledge, etc." Melchior Cano followed Vives' lead †; in that book, he says, "you may read monsters of miracles more often than true miracles." This [Golden Legend] was written by "a man of an iron mouth, a leaden heart, and a mind certainly lacking in gravity and prudence." The celebrated Espencæus reached exactly the same judgment, and that in a public sermon, so much so that he was forced to publicly recant his opinion. Is this work to be numbered among Christian histories, or rather dismissed as Romantical fables? As we see, it was condemned even by more sensible Papists with heavy stomach. Certainly, it is stuffed with the most trifling nonsense and with fictional and foolish narrations, which cannot be read—much less defended—without immense scandal to the Christian religion. This *History* was published in Nuremberg in 1478 and 1493; Deventer in 1479 and 1483; Venice in 1483; Basel in 1486; Strasbourg in 1496 and 1518; and Lyon in 1510. In the edition which I have in my possession (Strasbourg, 1496), our James's *Legend* ends at chapter 177. The 38 chapters which follow to the end of the book were added by others. This *Legend* was also published in an abbreviated form in Venice, 1478, in folio.

*Lenten Sermons* <note>original: "Quadragesimale"</note> Venice, 1575, 1579, 1602, in quarto.
*Sermons on the Lamentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, same location, 1602.
*Most beautiful Sermons for the seasons throughout the entire cycle of the year*, Venice, 1544, in quarto.
*Sermons on the Saints through the orbit of the whole year*, Pavia, 1500; Venice, 1602, in quarto.
*The Golden Mariale, concerning the praises of the Mother of God, arranged in alphabetical order*, and divided into 160 Sermons, Venice, 1497; Paris, 1503; Mainz, 1616, in quarto.
*Chronicle of the city of Genoa, and of its Pastors from its foundation until the year 1213.*
He mentions a *Book on the Minor Works of St. Augustine*; a *Defense of his order* against attackers who claimed they did not live according to the Apostolic Rule; likewise a *Summary of Vices and Virtues*; but Ambrose de Altamura, at the year 1290, does not say whether these still exist. Finally, he is said to have been the first to translate the most Holy Bible into the Italian language, and to have published it in the year 1270. Among his writings, some list a work called the *Catholicon*, or a *Grammar and Dictionary* (Venice, 1483); let those who have seen it judge if this is correct.

In the year 1311, he was present at and subscribed to the Council of Vienne, held under Clement V, in which the business of the extirpation of the Templars was handled. He died in the year 1314. He wrote the deeds of his episcopate from the time he was made bishop until the year 1323 <note>The text notes the record continues after his death, likely by another hand</note>. These were first brought to light by D'Achery, *Spicilegium* Vol. X, p. 247. The same D'Achery published his *Synodal Statutes* in Vol. XI.

## RICHARD MIDDLETON, 

<note>Original: "Richardus de Mediavilla."</note> Known as the "Solid and Copious Doctor," and also called the "Most Well-Founded and Authoritative Doctor," he was an Englishman by birth and a theologian of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>. As for the claim by Marianus that he was the Archbishop of Reims, it earns little credit among the learned. He flourished in the year 1290. After he had attained no common knowledge of Philosophy, Jurisprudence, and especially Scholastic Theology at the Oxford Academy, he moved to Paris <note>Original: "Lutetia."</note>—following the custom accepted among the English at that time—where he acquired a celebrated name for himself. In the year 1282, † Peter John Olivi, a Franciscan, was accused of having written several things full of heresy and error; in truth, for no other reason than that he had publicly corrected the soft and collapsed morals of his own people; and because he had attacked, with great zeal in both voice and writing, the brothers of both higher and lower orders who were living softly, and even the overly delicate Prelates of the Church.
<margin>
See Wadding at the years 1282, No. 2; 1283, No. 1; 1297, No. 23, etc.
</margin>
Hence, outcries and riots were stirred up against him, and the examination of his case was committed the following year by Bonagratia, the General of the Order, to our Richard (who was then a Bachelor of Theology) and certain others. To put it briefly: they marked certain propositions extracted from his writings with censure as being dangerous and "evil-sounding" <note>A technical term in canon law for statements that might lead to heresy even if not strictly heretical.</note>; indeed, even after his death, he was condemned as a heretic and his books were prohibited. Bale adds that his corpse was dug up and burned by the command of Pope Clement. A full defense of this Peter against Bzovius is conducted by Dermot Thaddeus, himself a Franciscan, in the *Franciscan Religious Polishing*, page 331, etc. But I return to the subject. Our Richard, having returned to his homeland, spent the remainder of his life at Oxford in the public office of teaching, with the highest reputation for erudition. He died around the year 1300.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Four books of Questions on the Master of the Sentences. Venice 1509; Brescia 1591.* <note>The "Sentences" by Peter Lombard was the standard textbook for medieval theology students.</note>
*Theological Quodlibeta containing 80 questions, appended to his Commentaries on the Sentences.*
*Regarding the Commentaries on the Gospels and the Epistles of Paul; a book on the Conception of Mary; a tract against Peter John; and others, see Bale, Century 4, page 359, and Pits, English Writers, page 386.*

<margin>1290.</margin>

## GUIDO, 

a Burgundian by nation, born of a noble family from the village of Meix <note>Original: "Villa de Mimo."</note> in the Diocese of Autun, was shaped for the monastic life in the Monastery of Auxerre under Abbot John Josnual, his kinsman (as is clear from the Appendix attached to his small work). In the Academies of Orleans and Paris, he devoted no small effort to Theology and Canon Law for nine years. He flourished in the year 1290. Having returned home, he underwent various duties, being made Almoner in the Monastery in Puisaye <note>Original: "Puscia."</note>, and Vice-Prior of the same, Dean of Reigny <note>Original: "Recognito."</note>, and then Prior of the Monastery of Auxerre. In the year 1277, upon the death of John, he was elected Abbot of his monastery. But soon, a faction of the other side having arisen, the monks brought in a certain John of Thianges, an Englishman, as Abbot for themselves. This dispute lasted a long time, with Guido traveling to Rome twice, and it was not settled in favor of our Guido until after eight years. In the year 1309, he abdicated his rule and, withdrawing into a certain private cell, died on February 24th <note>Original: "VI. Kal. Martii."</note> in the year 1313, after he had governed his monastery for nearly 24 whole years. Aymo de Bordis, a monk of the same monastery, will teach you more in that Appendix we just cited. Guido wrote concerning the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Germain of Auxerre*, from the year 1189 until the year 1277. Philippe Labbe first brought this to light in the *New Manuscript Library*, Volume I, page 570.

# RICHARD OF MIDDLETON,
## The Solid and Copious Doctor, also most deeply grounded and authoritative <note>Original Latin: "Doctor solidus & copiosus, fundatissimus etiam & authoratus." Medieval theologians were often given such honorific titles to describe their teaching style.</note>

<margin>† See Wadding, at the year 1282, No. 2; 1283, No. 1; 1297, No. 23, etc.</margin>

so-called, an Englishman by birth and a theologian of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>; however, the claim by Marianus that he was the Archbishop of Reims deserves little credit among the learned. **HENRY**, otherwise called **AMANDUS SUSO**, a Swabian <note>Original: "Suevus," referring to the region of Swabia in modern-day southwestern Germany.</note>, born from the noble lineage of the Counts of Berg <note>Original: "Comitum Montensium."</note>, a distinguished theologian of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>, and a Lector at Constance. He flourished around 1290. He seems to have died at the close of this century, or, as others say, in the year 1300. There are indeed men, and those of no small reputation, who date his death to 1365 or 1366, which can in no way be reconciled <margin>† Dominican Library, p. 77.</margin> if indeed it is true what † Ambrose de Altamura handed down to us: that Suso, together with St. Thomas Aquinas (who was enrolled among the saints in 1323), was proposed to the Supreme Pontiff to be co-opted into the number of the Saints. His body was buried in the Convent of Ulm in the province of Germany <note>Original: "Allemannia."</note> before the Altar of St. Peter.

### WRITINGS.

**T**he Clock of Wisdom <note>Original: *Horologium Sapientiæ*. This was one of the most popular devotional works of the Middle Ages.</note>, *Venice 1492, 1539; Naples 1658, 12°, and frequently elsewhere.*
*Meditations on the Passion of the Lord, with as many petitions addressed to Him.*
*The Book of the Nine Rocks.* <note>Original: *Liber de novem rupibus*.</note>
*Sermons for the Seasons; for the Saints; and for Lent.*
*The Dialogue of Truth.*
*Various Letters, filled with learning, holiness, and spirit.* Lawrence Surius translated these minor works from the German language into Latin, and they were published in Cologne, 1588, in octavo.
*The Daily Office of Eternal Wisdom*, published many times, though the years are not known to me, except perhaps *Paris, 1578, 8°.*

<margin>1294.</margin>
**BONIFACE VIII.** Previously called Benedict Gaetani, a Campanian by birth from the city of Anagni, Cardinal-Priest of St. Sylvester and St. Martin in the Mountains. In the place of Celestine V (whose simplicity he abused through a very notable trick, when, by a feigned voice at night as if sent from heaven, he persuaded him to resign the Papacy), he saw to it that he was elected Pope at Naples in December 1294. He was crowned at Rome on January 23, 1295. At his solemn <margin>† Wadding, at the year 1294, No. 8; Spondanus at the year 1295.</margin> inauguration, two bad omens † occurred, which seemed to foretell the man's turbulent character and fierce deeds. First, that while the coronation was proceeding, a very thick darkness came over them, and a violent storm arose that extinguished the candles and lamps in the Church. Second, as he was leaving the temple, a riot broke out among the people, and more than 40 men were killed. In the first year of his Pontificate, he exempted the Clergy from secular taxes; he struck the citizens of Lucca with anathema and forbade all holy offices when they refused to restore certain places which he claimed for the Church. On the occasion of the Abbey of [Citeaux?] in France, the close necessity that existed between him and King Philip of France almost collapsed; a slight disagreement indeed, but one which, after a few years with other causes added, erupted into a greater flame. In the year 1296, he saw to it that clergy in France infamous for crimes were either corrected or deposed, also enacting a censure of excommunication against the supporters of dissolute clergy. He subjected James and Peter, the Colonna Cardinals, to anathema, having stripped them of the purple and all offices at a Council of bishops held in Rome, regarding them as being addicted to the party of Celestine, more favorable to the Ghibelline faction, and secretly plotting against him. In the following year, he ordered the city of Palestrina to be destroyed as a punishment for the violated majesty of the Colonnas. In the year 1298, he haughtily commanded James, King of Aragon, to move his arms against his brother Frederick, who was tenaciously defending his right to the Kingdom of Sicily; and after three years, when neither Frederick nor the nobles of Sicily would lay down their arms, he cursed them and placed the entire kingdom of Sicily under interdict. ## WRITINGS.

**Letters:** Two are found in the *Councils*, Volume XI, part 2, page 1398. *Twenty-four Letters and Constitutions* in Bzovius for the year 1294 and following years. Four in Wadding for the years 1296, 1297. Forty-seven in the same, in the *Pontifical Registers XXII*, in the same [author], Volume III, p. 1.

*The Sixth Book of Decretals, or the Code of Pontifical Law*, which he ordered to be compiled by three most learned men from certain new decrees issued by himself, and commanded to be read publicly in the Schools, although it has not yet been received in France; it was published in *Paris, 1503, 1541; Venice, 1591, in octavo;* with the Glosses at *Lyons, 1581, in folio; Frankfurt, 1586, in octavo;* and in almost every edition of Canon Law. Ludovicus Jacobus, in his *Pontifical Library, p. 32*, enumerates a very few unpublished items, which may be sought from him.

1296.

**GILES OF ROME** <note>Original: "Egidius de Columna."</note>, called the "Most Well-Founded Doctor" <note>Original: "Doctor fundatissimus," his traditional Scholastic title.</note>, a Roman by birth, descended from a splendid and illustrious stock, namely the noble family of the Colonna. In his home city he laid the first foundations of his studies, which he later cultivated to the highest degree in other places. In Philosophy and Theology, he had Thomas Aquinas as his teacher, in whose doctrine he made such great progress and to which he adhered so tenaciously <note>Original: "mordicùs," literally "with his teeth."</note> that he took upon himself the defense of him and of Saint Bonaventure against William [de la Mare], a Professor of Sacred Theology at Oxford, publishing for this purpose twin booklets, one of which he named *A Reprimand of Saint Thomas* <note>Referring to a critique of those who criticized Thomas.</note>, and the other *A Defense of Saint Bonaventure*.

<margin>13th CENTURY. from the Year 1200.</margin>
He joined the Hermit Brothers of the Augustinian Order <note>A mendicant order following the Rule of St. Augustine.</note>, where, through his <unclear>innocence</unclear> of life and the gravity of his doctrine and character, he gained no common fame. Sought after by various universities and princes, he went to France, summoned by Philip the Bold to educate his son Philip, surnamed the Fair, in letters and morals. From there, he taught Philosophy and Theology at the University of Paris for many years with the highest praise. In 1292, at a full assembly of his Order held in Rome, he was named Prior General <note>The highest-ranking official of the religious order.</note> of the same Order by common vote; however, he voluntarily resigned from this office after one year. In the year 1296, he was very dear to Boniface VIII, whose election to the Papacy he defended in a published *Apology on the Resignation of the Pope* <note>Giles wrote this to defend the legality of Boniface’s succession after Pope Celestine V abdicated.</note>. He was appointed Archbishop of Bourges and Primate of Aquitaine; King Philip also urged this, both because of the man’s great fame and because he had once been his teacher. Most record that he was honored with the Cardinal’s hat; however, because the Pope intervened, it was never publicly announced. And the reason why Clement V, Boniface's successor, did not grant it was that King Philip and the nobles of France were not slightly offended by the commentary Giles had written in favor of Boniface. There are those, however, who stubbornly deny he was a Cardinal. The very learned Louis Ellies Du Pin weighs arguments on both sides and favors the view of his Cardinalate in the appendix to his *History of Cardinals*, Volume 1, page 372. He died in Avignon on December 22, 1316, at the age of 69. In his final will, he bequeathed vessels and ornaments for divine worship to the churches of his Order in Rome and Bourges; but his books he left to the monastery in Paris. His body was moved to Paris and buried in the church of the Augustinians, with this epitaph inscribed on the tombstone:

->*Here lies the hall of morals, the purity of life, the most clear-sighted Commentator on the Supreme Philosophy <note>Original: "Archiphilosophiae." Referring to Aristotle's Metaphysics.</note> of Aristotle, the Key and Doctor of Sacred Theology, a light leading doubts into the light, Brother Giles of Rome of the Order of Hermit Brothers of Saint Augustine, Archbishop of Bourges, who died in the year of our Lord 1316, on the 22nd of December.*<-

Abraham Bzovius grants him extraordinary praise under the year 1316, number 7; I do not investigate whether he deserved them in every respect. He was certainly, for the age in which he lived, not unlearned, and especially practiced in Aristotelian Philosophy and Scholastic Theology; hence he was called the **Prince of Theologians**. Indeed, as early as 1287, the Augustinian Hermits gathered in general assembly at Florence decreed that the doctrine of Brother Giles (*which illustrates the whole world*, to use their words) was to be accepted and inviolably observed by all lecturers and students of his Order. His style was less than elegant, a fact which Bzovius himself admits; nor did he use a Ciceronian <note>Refined, classical Latin style.</note> vocabulary, both because such was the custom of the School <note>The Scholastic method emphasized logic and technical precision over literary style.</note>, and because he remembered that common saying, *the subject itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught* <note>Original: "ornari res ipsa negat, contenta doceri." A quote from the Roman poet Manilius.</note>; and because he knew best that matters naturally difficult for the intellect cannot be explained by the allurements of words. 
<margin>* On the Writers, Volume 1, p. 13.</margin>
He wrote very many works, both Philosophical and Theological, a great part of which are still buried in darkness <note>Meaning unpublished or forgotten in archives.</note>, others published in various places, formats, and years. Philippe Labbe promised to publish an index of these printed works, but whether he stood by his promises, I have not yet discovered. We shall weave a catalog here of such as we have been able to obtain.

**ARMAND DE BELVEZER**, <note>original: "Armandus de Bellovisu"</note> an Italian by nationality, from the city of Bologna, a Monk of the Dominican Order and Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace. <note>The official theologian of the Papal household.</note> He flourished around the year 1296, though others place him much later, moving him to the year 1496. Ambrose of Altamura presents us with three Armands of Belvezer: first, our Bolognese; second, a Spaniard, famous in the year 1235 and died around 1340. However, being inconsistent with himself, he attributes almost the same works to both. Finally, a third, also of Spanish nationality, a Monk of Barcelona and Regent at the Dominican school in the University of Bologna, who flourished in the year 1530 and to whom he ascribes the *Treatise on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin*. Yet, Nicolás Antonio, in his recent *Library of Spanish Writers*, is completely silent about any writer of this name. I confess I do not know Armand's true age. There exist by him: *Writings, a Postil <note>A series of short notes or a commentary on Scripture.</note> on the Psalms, Meditations, and Prayers*, Mainz 1503; *Sermons*, Brescia 1610, in quarto; *An explanation of difficult terms in both Philosophy and Theology*, Venice 1586, Wittenberg 1623, in octavo.

**ENGELBERT**, a German by birth, a monk of the Benedictine Order, and from the year 1297 the Abbot of the Admont Monastery in Styria <note>Admont Abbey in modern-day Austria, famous for its massive monastic library</note>. He was already renowned in the year 1273, though Corvinus <note>referring to a later historian or bibliographer</note> places him at the year 1340, which is somewhat later than is accurate. There exists his *Book on the Rise, Progress, and End of the Roman Empire* <note>original title: "liber ejus de ortu, progressu & fine Imperii Romani"</note>, in which certain philosophical points are interspersed throughout. It was edited by Kaspar Brusch and published in Basel, 1553, in octavo; and with other writers of similar subjects, under the care of Joachim Cluten, at Offenbach, 1610, in octavo; it is also found in the *Library of the Fathers* <note>Bibliotheca Patrum</note>, Volume 25, page 362.

His *Epic Poem, or Panegyric on the Coronation of Rudolf of Habsburg, written in the year 1273*, is found in almost every collection of German historians. <note>Rudolf I was the first member of the Habsburg dynasty to become King of the Romans.</note>

<margin>1299.</margin>
**THOMAS WYKES** (or Wiccius), of the English people, an Augustinian monk—specifically a Canon Regular in the Monastery of Osney <note>Osney Abbey was a significant house of Augustinian canons near Oxford</note>. He flourished in the year 1299. Having been steeped in the liberal arts from his childhood and benefiting from the proximity of the University of Oxford, he acquired no small reputation for himself in literature. He especially devoted his mind to the study of illustrating the history of his homeland. He wrote a *Chronicle of England* <note>original: "Chronicon Angliæ"</note> from the arrival of the Conqueror—that is, from the year 1066—up until his own old age and the death of Edward I in the year 1304. In this work, he set out to imitate the style of William of Newburgh <note>a famous 12th-century English historian</note>. These annals were recently brought out from the shadows by the most learned man who has served literature well, T.G. <note>Thomas Gale (c. 1635–1702), who published "Historiæ Anglicanæ Scriptores" in 1687</note>, and published among the *Writers of English History*, Volume 2, Oxford, 1687, in folio. Wykes also composed a *Book on the Abbots of Osney* from the foundation of the monastery (the year 1129) until the year 1290. He was known in the time of Bale <note>John Bale (1495–1563), a controversial historian and bibliographer</note>, who also mentions his poems *In Praise of Wine* and *On the Rebuking of Gluttony*; however, whether these still survive is unknown to me.

### A few things to be added and clarified.

**Page 3.** Regarding the Letter of *Jesus Christ* to *Abgar* <note>Abgar V was a King of Edessa who, according to legend, exchanged letters with Jesus</note>, my singular friend *D. P. A.* <note>likely Pierre Allix, a prominent 17th-century scholar</note> objects in a private letter to me that in the *Acts of Edessa*, in which it is inserted (as seen in *Eusebius, Book 1, Chapter 13*), *Thaddeus* confessed the Article of the descent of *Christ* into the Underworld <note>original: "descensu Christi ad Inferos"</note>, which nonetheless does not seem to taste of such antiquity. But 1. the opinion of the descent of *Christ* into Hades <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὴν ᾅδην"</note> seems to be most ancient; it is established that it obtained a place as an article in the Creed later, but what forbids the doctrine itself from being far older? For in the proposition itself all agree (*"who but an infidel,"* says *Augustine* in Letter 99, page 437, *"would deny that Christ was among those in the Underworld?"*); they only dispute over the meaning and the manner of explaining it. 2. The Letter and the *Acts of Edessa* do not rely on equal authority for me; for the Acts were only composed after *Christ's* ascension, and perhaps by notaries who understood the matter they received by hearsay with too little accuracy, or at least could easily have been mistaken; and who show us only the main headings of *Thaddeus’s* oration, but do not explain in what sense he delivered them; truly, in this matter, let everyone enjoy his own judgment.

**Page 9, line 38.** By the *Sixth Council in Trullo* <note>The Council in Trullo (692 AD) settled matters of church discipline</note>, the *Quinisext Council* is understood, called *Trullan*, an Appendix to the *Sixth Council* properly so-called, which was likewise held in the *Trullus* <note>The "Trullus" was the domed hall of the imperial palace in Constantinople</note>.

**Page 53, line 45.** After the word *held*, add: *Bucherius* <note>Jean-Baptiste Boucher, a Jesuit scholar</note> professes that it is unknown to him who this *Philip* was; but it is probable that a mistake lay hidden in the *Bucherian* Codex, and instead of *Letter of Philip*, one should read *Letter of Theophilus*. And indeed, the Illustrious *Allix* recently advised me that it is so held in the *Oxford* Manuscript Code.

**Page 90, line 6.** For *of Poitiers* <note>original: "Pictaviensi"</note>, read *of Pettau* <note>original: "Petavionienſi"; referring to Victorinus of Pettau, modern Ptuj, Slovenia</note>; for that poem seems to be his.

**Page 143, line 37.** Regarding two Orations of *Athanasius*, namely *Against the Heathen* and *On the Incarnation of the Word*, *D. Allix* raises a dispute, and thinks the author lived at the end of the second century: 1. Because he refutes the doctrine of *Marcion* <note>Marcion was a 2nd-century dualist heretic</note>: 2. Because he attacks *Antinous*, the lover of the Emperor *Hadrian*, as a "recent" deity: 3. Because he indicates that <term>apotheosis</term> <note>the deification of emperors</note> was still flourishing. I have chosen to bring these objections of that most celebrated man into the open, to be further examined by the learned. Meanwhile, let it be noted: 1. The author nowhere explicitly mentions *Marcion*: he does indeed refute the doctrine of the origin of evil and the dual principle; but that belonged to many of the pagan philosophers, no less than to *Valentinus*, *Marcion*, *Mani*, etc., among the heretics. And even if it were conceded that he refuted *Marcionite* doctrine, it does not follow from this that he lived in the age of *Marcion*. 2. As for his saying that *Antinous* was "now" <note>original Greek: "τὸν νῦν"</note> numbered among the deities, perhaps it should be understood in no other sense than that he was still held as a God in his own time. 3. Regarding the consecrations of the Romans, he has this to say: "And do not wonder, nor think that what is said is far from belief, since not long ago, or perhaps even until now, the Roman Senate [consecrates] everyone..." etc. <note>original Greek: "Καὶ μή τι θαυμάσης..."</note> that is, as interpreted by *P. Nannio*: *"Do not hesitate here in doubt, nor believe the matter is far from the truth, because of what I say; not long ago, and perhaps even now, the Roman Senate dedicates its emperors from their origin—either all of them, or at least those they pleased—to heaven and the altars, and they command them to be gods by laws and decrees of the Senate."* These things could conveniently be said regarding the times of *Athanasius*, or those immediately preceding *Athanasius*, when a far greater part of the Roman Senate still clung tenaciously to the sacred rites of the Heathens; but they could hardly be said of the second century, when the Roman <term>apotheosis</term> was performed with a full apparatus of ceremonies. However it may be, it is certain that the Oration *Against the Heathen*—besides the fact that the Manuscript Codices attribute it to *Athanasius* with constant faith—is cited under the name of *Athanasius* by the Synod of Constantinople assembled against the worship of Images in the year 754; to which the Fathers of the *Second Council of Nicaea* do not return even a whisper in this matter (Act 6, page 481). Truly, the Oration *On the Incarnation*, which no one can doubt is by the same author, is cited as being by *Athanasius* by *Theodoret*.

...rightly in Dialogue III, pages 161, 162, where he brings forward many passages from it, not to mention Pope Hadrian, Photius, and others.

**Page 176, line 25.** After *of Verona*, add: Most recently, however, upon the advice of Mr. Allix <note>referring to Pierre Allix, a scholar often cited by the author</note>, I have learned that a sermon by Zeno, Bishop of Verona, is praised by Ratherius of Verona, a writer of the tenth century, found in D'Achéry’s *Spicilegium, Volume II*. Whether it is among those that currently circulate under his name, one must inquire.

**Page 214, line 39.** Regarding the book *On Those to be Initiated* <note>original: "de initiandis"</note>, as well as another *On the Priestly Dignity* <note>original: "de sacerdotali dignitate"</note>: whether they belong to *Ambrose* can be rightly doubted, seeing as they seem to contain none of the Ambrosian "juice or marrow" <note>original: "nil succi & tus Ambrosiani"; a metaphor for Ambrose's specific prose style and theological depth</note>. Certainly, regarding the latter work, Theophilus Raynaud says in *Erot. X. on good and bad books, page 124*, that it smacks of Anselm <note>likely Anselm of Canterbury or Anselm of Lucca</note> rather than Ambrose. **Ibid. page 215, line 18.** The book *To a Fallen Virgin* <note>original: "ad Virginem lapsam"</note> appears to be by Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia; concerning this, see Gennadius *On Church Writers*. As for the *Books on Widows*, Ambrose himself mentions them in his *Commentary on Luke, chapter 21, page 121*; they are therefore to be placed among his genuine works.

<margin>
*The Ambrosian Mass*
</margin>
**Page 216, line 13.** Since we took no account of the *Mass* when reviewing the works of Saint Ambrose, it is better to discuss it here in a few words. No one who is not a complete stranger to the monuments of the ancient Church can doubt that the Church of Milan once had its own formulas for prayers and its own peculiar rites, as was also the custom for others at that time. Indeed, there are some who wish to persuade us that the Ambrosian Missal was arranged by Saint Barnabas, the first (as they claim) Archbishop of the Milanese and founder of that Church, then expanded by Saint Mirocles, and finally reduced to its current form by Saint Ambrose, from whom it took its name. But those who tell us such dreams are dealing in nonsense, nor can they bring forward even the lightest testimony from the ancients. The first, as far as I know, who mentions it expressly is Walafrid Strabo around the year 842, who in his book *On Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 22*, reports that Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, arranged the order of the Mass and other offices for his own Church and for other Ligurians. These (he says) are held in the Milanese Church even to this day. 

However, if we do not establish Ambrose himself as the author (which is entirely uncertain and relies on no ancient testimony), it is probable that the compiler, whoever he may have been, took many things from the writings of Ambrose himself, which were then wonderfully expanded and altered by the Archbishops of following centuries (as is usually the case in these matters). The Ambrosian Mass, as it is held today, differs greatly from the Roman and others, both in the order of the rites and in the rites themselves and the arrangement of the parts. In the Psalms and the Lessons taken from Holy Scripture, it uses the ancient Italic version <note>the *Vetus Latina*, the Latin translation used before Jerome's Vulgate became standard</note>, not the Vulgate which prevails today. In length, it exceeds the Roman Mass, being more in harmony with the Greeks in this regard, because the Milanese clung more firmly to the ancient tracks of the Greeks—a point which Lindanus notes regarding the Liturgy of Saint Peter, and from him Gavantus in *Treasury of Sacred Rites, Volume I, Part II, Title xv, page 188*. Joseph Vicecomes, himself a Doctor of the Ambrosian College, depicts the order of the Ambrosian Liturgy for us in *On the Rites of the Mass, book 2*; as does Cardinal Bona in *On Liturgical Matters, book 1, chapter 10, page 89*; and Mabillon both in *On the Gallican Liturgy, book 1, chapter 2, number vii*, and in his *Italian Journey, page 15*, to name but a few others. Pamelius published this Ambrosian Missal in *Liturgies of the Latin Church, Volume I, page 293*. Mabillon records two other editions, one from 1560 and another from 1669, but they differ significantly both from the Pamelian edition and from each other; however, he does not indicate in which places they were produced.

**Page 284, line 39.** From the five letters of Sulpitius Severus published by D'Achéry, the last is not by our Severus, but by another Severus, an African by nationality, as is clear from Letter IV, page 535.

**Page 298, line 14.** After the words *Garner's Edition, Part 1, page 97, etc.*, add: It is, however, far more probable that in these books Theodore was attacking Jerome rather than Augustine. Certainly, Photius, dealing with these very books of Theodore in *Codex 177*, relates things that can apply almost exclusively to Jerome. He says, for instance, that Theodore indeed labeled his adversary with the name "The Aram" <note>original Greek: "τῆς Ἀράμ", meaning "The Syrian" or "The Aramean." This was a common nickname for Jerome because he lived in Bethlehem and studied Hebrew and Syriac</note>. Who might be hidden under the cloak of this word is a knot not so easily untied. Regarding the ill-omened meaning of "The Aram," Andreas Schottus, the translator of Photius, offers an explanation, but it is a clearly weak conjecture. It is perhaps an error of a too-hasty scribe...

### A few things to be added, etc.

...to be, <gloss>equivalent to "iseqv."</gloss> <note>original: "æqu. pro iseqv."</note> namely, an abbreviation for the name of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymiani"</note> being restored, as Mr. Allix <note>Pierre Allix, a French Protestant theologian</note> quite ingeniously conjectures. But since the most diligent Hoeschel <note>David Hoeschel, a German humanist scholar</note> noted nothing regarding the variant readings of the manuscripts in this part, and since I am almost certain that Theodore <note>Theodore of Mopsuestia</note> wished to translate his own adverb into a fictional name in this passage, it seems far more likely to me that some "little man" <note>original: "homunculum"</note> hiding in some corner of Syria is denoted by this word. For *Aram* properly signifies *Syria*, which fits Jerome quite well, as he spent by far the largest part of his life in Syria, and in those places he composed almost all his writings against the Pelagians <note>followers of Pelagius, who debated Jerome and Augustine over free will and grace</note>. Theodore indicates this clearly enough when he says that the man was indeed a native of the West but lived only in the regions of the East, and from there sent books written about a heresy he had recently devised to his fellow countrymen in his homeland, by which he drew many over to his opinion and imbued entire churches with those absurd ideas. 

Indeed, what Theodore adds about this man, whom he calls a heretic, seems to settle the matter most clearly: namely, that he fabricated a "fifth Gospel" found in the libraries of Eusebius of Palestine <note>this refers to the *Gospel according to the Hebrews*, which Jerome famously translated from Hebrew into Greek and Latin; see Jerome's *On Illustrious Men*, chapters 2 and 3</note>. As everyone can see, he rejected the versions of the Septuagint <note>the "LXX," the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> and other Greek interpreters, substituting a new one of his own making in their place. Finally, he adds that the man was a disciple of certain Hebrews of low social standing and had not been accustomed to the Hebrew language from his youth. All these things fit Jerome perfectly, but not Augustine. Read carefully, learned Reader, what Photius <note>a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar</note> has in this passage, and you will agree with me that no one other than Jerome can be intended here.

# THE AGE OF WYCLIFFE.

## Overview of the Century.

The Church experienced a century no less unfortunate since the birth of Christ—if one excludes the tenth century <note>The 10th century was traditionally known as the "Dark Age" or *saeculum obscurum* due to its lack of intellectual output</note>. The study of better literature was neglected and piety was trampled down; because of this, the Christian world was torn apart—on one side by the unrestrained excess of the Mendicant Orders <note>The "begging" orders, such as the Franciscans and Dominicans, who lived by alms rather than monastery land</note>, and on the other by futile controversies. The study of a purer theology had long been exiled from the Church, giving way to the rugged trifles of the Schools <note>Scholasticism, the medieval method of academic philosophy and logic</note>. Furthermore, few among the clergy even cultivated those. For the <term>secular priests</term> <note>Priests who lived in the world among the people, rather than under a monastic rule</note>, knowledge of Canon and Civil Law was their primary desire, as it offered a shortcut to the highest dignities of the Church. The glory of cultivating the study of divine matters was left almost entirely to the Mendicant Orders. Yet they, by no means content with having obtained immense authority among the common people, greedily flew into the university chairs; breaking the barriers of ecclesiastical discipline, they snatched for themselves the ancient duties of the secular clergy. From this was born a deadly hatred between the Seculars and the "Little Brothers" <note>original: *Fraterculorum*, a diminutive and often derogatory term for the friars</note>. The former were deeply resentful of the duties of preaching and hearing confessions—tasks rashly usurped by the Mendicants—while the latter, boasting of a more "perfect" state of life to the gullible commoners, preached that the order of Seculars was a burden and useless to the Church. This dispute was waged with the greatest zeal by both parties throughout nearly the entire century; on one side, the clergy fought for the cause of truth and ancient privileges, while on the other, the Mendicants were protected by the favor of the Roman See, of which they were for the most part the most sworn followers.

<margin>Eymeric, *Directory of the Inquisitors*, part 2, question 15.</margin>
Yet not even the Mendicants themselves agreed perfectly among one another. For at the beginning of the century, Peter John Olivi <note>original: *Petrus Joannis de Oliva* (1248–1298), a controversial Franciscan theologian</note> of the Franciscan Order arose; claiming to be divinely inspired, he taught that a "Spiritual state" had recently been introduced to the Christian world by Francis, to which the laws of the New Testament—being less perfect—must yield. He claimed the Gospel of Christ and the Apostles led no one to perfection and thus had to be abolished once the Rule of Francis was introduced. He argued the order of the Secular Clergy should be eliminated, and the governance of the Church committed to a certain Religious order; he also taught that evangelical poverty should be observed so religiously by all that it would not be permitted to possess anything as one's own, nor even in common.

By pouring out these kinds of dogmas among the common people, Peter John drew a huge crowd of Franciscans to his side; they were given the name *Spirituals*. John XXII and other subsequent Popes most sharply opposed the Spirituals; they condemned their dogmas and pronounced anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note> upon the sectarians.

But Michael of Cesena, Ockham <note>William of Ockham, the famous English philosopher and theologian</note>, and the other *Spirituals* cared little for this; they publicly proclaimed that countless heresies were contained within the Papal Bulls <note>Official decrees issued by the Pope</note>. Having scorned the authority of the Bulls, the Popes committed the matter of the Faith to the Inquisitors to be handled with iron and fire. These *Spirituals*, who had long been called *Beghards*, *Beguines*, and *Fratricelli* <note>Various names for lay and semi-monastic groups often associated with radical poverty</note>, were everywhere consigned to the pyre, and sometimes even attacked by military forces; however, they were unable to crush the defiant sect so completely that significant remnants of it did not survive until the beginning of the Reformation. So much for the quarrels of the Mendicants.

At the beginning of the century, Clement V had moved the Papal See to Avignon <note>The "Babylonian Captivity of the Papacy" (1309–1376) where the Popes resided in France</note> to repay a favor to Philip the Fair, King of France, through whose authority he had obtained the Papacy. The Council of Vienne was held in the year 1311 for much the same reason, which Clement indeed called so that he might, in that manner, evade the promise given to Philip regarding the condemnation of the heresies of Boniface VIII. In this Council, the Order of the Knights Templar was abolished, the men themselves condemned to the flames, and their property given to the Knights Hospitallers; the Feast of Corpus Christi was confirmed, and the Rule of St. Francis was declared. For, since the freedom of the Council had been taken away, the Pope decreed everything according to his own whim, neither asking for nor waiting for the votes of the Fathers. Furthermore, [concerning] the Roman See...

<summary>This page introduces the 14th century as a period of theological decline and intense conflict between the established secular clergy and the rising Mendicant orders. It details the internal Franciscan split involving the "Spirituals" and the political maneuvering of the Avignon Papacy and the Council of Vienne.</summary>
<keywords>Age of Wycliffe, Mendicant Orders, Secular Priests, Peter John Olivi, Spirituals, Pope John XXII, Michael of Cesena, William of Ockham, Beghards, Beguines, Fratricelli, Pope Clement V, Philip the Fair, Council of Vienne, Knights Templar</keywords>

--- Page 938 ---
<meta>The previous page established the decline of ecclesiastical authority and the rise of the Mendicant Orders (friars) who competed with the established secular clergy. This page continues that narrative, focusing on the relocation of the Papacy to Avignon and the Great Western Schism, as well as the life of the influential philosopher John Duns Scotus.</meta>

By this transfer <note>The "Babylonian Captivity" or the removal of the Papal court from Rome to Avignon (1309–1376)</note>, the majesty of the Pope was diminished in no small part; from that time it began to gradually fail and ceased to be a terror to Kings. After Emperor Louis of Bavaria had successfully blown away the excommunication <note>original: *anathema*</note> struck against him by John XXII, and by calling the pens of the most learned men to his aid, he taught others by what means the thunderbolts of the Popes might best be repelled. However, the authority of the Roman See received a far more serious blow from the Great Schism <note>The Western Schism (1378–1417), a period where multiple rival popes claimed the throne</note>, which began after the death of Gregory XI in the year 1378 and lasted more or less forty years. The Schism was so difficult that famous historians of that age complain that it was almost impossible to know on which side the truth stood. With the Papacy divided among several men, it happened that they conceded everything to their followers to earn their favor, until finally they were forced to surrender the Papal insignia <note>original: *fasces Pontificios*</note> by the judgment of a General Council.

After the middle of the century, Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe, an English reformer who translated the Bible into the common tongue</note> strenuously attacked the errors of the Roman Church with both his voice and his pen; having gathered countless disciples for himself through England, Bohemia, and other nations, he propagated his doctrine far and wide. As for the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, whatever leisure they had left from internal rebellions they spent on futile controversies over "goat's wool" <note>An ancient idiom meaning a pointless or trivial argument</note>. For in the middle of the century, a question arose between the Barlaamites and Palamites concerning the "Light of Mount Tabor" <note>The Hesychast controversy regarding the nature of the light seen by the Apostles at the Transfiguration of Jesus</note>, which was agitated by Synods, excommunications, and biting pamphlets with such heat of spirit as if they were fighting over the primary articles of faith—as if the beginning and end <note>original: *prora ac puppis*, literally "the prow and the stern"</note> of religion stood upon such trifles.

---

# A U T H O R S .

<margin>1301.</margin>
<margin>* The Conformity of St. Francis.</margin>
JOHN DUNS, surnamed SCOTUS, the *Subtle Doctor*, was an Englishman by nation, born at Dunston in the Parish of Emildon near Alnwick in Northumberland; though according to others he was a Scot by birth, originating from the village of Duns eight miles from England; finally, in the opinion of Wadding and others, he was Irish, born at Down in Ulster. For the Scots and Irish both stubbornly claim him as their own, yet without any reason. For besides the fact that all writers before the 16th century who mention him—among them Bartholomew Albicius*—count him among the English, there are still preserved several manuscript copies of his works written after his own time in which his name, country, and birthplace are clearly found. While still a youth, he joined the <term>Minorites</term> <note>The Franciscans, or "Friars Minor"</note> at Newcastle; sent by them to Oxford, he drank in a deeper knowledge of letters at Merton College, of which he eventually became a Fellow. He was easily the leader of all in <term>Scholastic Theology</term> <note>A method of critical thought used in medieval universities</note> in that age, and most skilled in both Civil and Canon Law; he was also highly proficient in Logic, Physics, Metaphysics, Mathematics, and Astronomy. 

He flourished around the year 1301, at which time, William Varro (his teacher) having been called from the University of Oxford to Paris, Scotus was appointed to the Chair of Theology. He managed this position with such glory to his name that thirty thousand scholars <note>This figure was likely a medieval exaggeration of the university's population</note> are said to have flocked from all sides to Oxford for the sake of hearing him. After lecturing on the *Sentences* at Oxford, he was called to Paris by his fellow Franciscan priests around the year 1304. First honored with the distinctions of the Baccalaureate and the Doctorate, he was finally created Regent by his order at the meeting at Toulouse in 1307, and he took up the direction of the Theological Schools in the University of Paris. It was at this time that he first began to publish the previously unheard-of dogma concerning the <term>Immaculate Conception</term> of the Blessed Virgin; in a formal debate, he set out to demonstrate it by presenting two hundred arguments in order. So great indeed was the fame of this learned man among the Parisian academics that they supported his opinion "with hands and feet" <note>An idiom meaning they supported it completely and enthusiastically</note>; they established the Feast of the Immaculate Conception and provided by edict that no one should be admitted to academic degrees unless they held this same opinion. # The Century of Wycliffe.

Ordered by Gonzalo, the General of the Minorites <note>The Franciscans or Friars Minor</note>, to transfer to Cologne, he departed from Paris; and he was received by the entire city of Cologne, which came out to meet him in a solemn procession. Soon after, however, in the Franciscan friary, he was seized by a stroke <note>original: *apoplexia*</note> and, having been carried out for burial with excessive haste as they say, he died in the same year on November 8th, at the age of 43—or as others hold, 34. He left behind almost countless monuments of his intellect, in which, by accurately debating and refining <note>original: *ad limam revocans*, literally "bringing back to the file"</note> the definitions of Saint Thomas [Aquinas] and Saint Bonaventure, he took a different path in most matters and an opposite path in some. From this were born the sects of the **Thomists** and the **Scotists** (also known as the **Realists**), which filled the benches of the schools with constant disputes and quarrelsome shouting for several centuries; and they still fill them today, wherever a place is given to such intricacies—not to say trifles.

<margin>1301.</margin> **RAYNERIUS**, an Italian by birth and a native of Pisa, was a monk of the Dominican Order. He was a most accomplished theologian and legal expert, though a writer of somewhat uncertain date; indeed, some refer him to the year 1333, and others to 1410. Along with Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a German Benedictine abbot and polymath</note>, we place him around the year 1301, so that his history may shine with more certain light. His surviving work is the *Pantheologia*, or the *Summa of Universal Theology* <note>A 'Summa' is a comprehensive compendium of knowledge on a subject</note> arranged alphabetically. James of Florence, a Franciscan <note>original: *Minorita*</note>, published this work in Nuremberg in 1473, though he added much, removed much, and changed it everywhere. This corrupted edition was reprinted in Venice in 1486, Lyon in 1519, and Brescia in 1580 in two quarto volumes. More recently, it was printed in Paris in three folio volumes.

<margin>1301.</margin> **THEODORE METOCHITES**, a Greek by nation, was the Grand Logothete of the Course <note>original: *Magnus Logotheta Dromi*; a high-ranking official in the Byzantine Empire responsible for the postal service and diplomacy</note> and was joined by marriage to Emperor Andronicus [II] himself. He was the father-in-law of John, the former *Panhypersebastos* <note>A high Byzantine court title</note> and grandson of Andronicus. At the end of the previous century, he was sent as an ambassador to the West with John Glycas; he brought back Maria, the sister of the German Emperor <note>Maria of Armenia, who married Michael IX Palaeologus</note>, to Constantinople, where she was betrothed to Michael, the eldest son of Emperor Andronicus. He flourished in the year 1301. Around the year 1314, having been made General Logothete, he held all power under the Emperor and governed the affairs of the Empire as he pleased, yet with the greatest loyalty and diligence. Around the year 1328, the Elder Andronicus was defeated in war by his rebellious grandson, the Younger Andronicus, and the city of Constantinople was captured. Consequently, Metochites, who had always defended the grandfather's side with unshakeable loyalty, was exiled to Didymoteicho, a coastal town in Bithynia. His magnificent house was leveled to the ground by a raging mob after his wealth had first been plundered. After some time, when the Turks were devastating Bithynia, he was brought back to Constantinople and permitted to live in the Monastery of Chora <note>The Church of the Holy Saviour in Chora, famous for its mosaics</note>, which had once been founded by Emperor Justinian; it had fallen into ruins, but Metochites himself had restored it. However, he was denied favor and deprived of conversation or any kind of correspondence with the Elder Andronicus, whom he held dearer than his own soul. He died on March 13, 1332, thirty days after the death of Andronicus. He was praised in a funeral oration by Nicephorus Gregoras <margin>* Hist. book 8. 7. p. 190.</margin>, his disciple and dearest friend. This man, in the judgment of Gregoras, was *the wisest of all men under the sun, who, by a happy natural gift for words, endurance in labor, and a healthy and pure memory, reached the very summit of all wisdom.* <note>original Greek: Τῶν ὑφ' ἡλίῳ σοφώτατος...</note> Gregoras also called him *a Living Library and a ready oracle for those seeking knowledge.* He surpassed all who ever engaged in studies by a vast distance. The illustrious Vossius <margin>† On the Greek Historians, book 2. ch. 29.</margin> †, by a massive error, confuses him with George Metochites (a companion of Beccus), and thus, by a significant mistake in dating <note>original: *Parachronismo*</note>, he adds Beccus and Meliteniotes as companions in exile to Theodore Metochites.

# The Century of Wyclif

<margin>
