...born in the Balearic Islands in the village of St. Michael in the year 1236. He flourished <note>original: *claruit*; a term used to denote a person's peak period of activity</note> in the year 1301. As a young man, he pursued trade in the hope of profit; or, as others tell it, he served in the court of the King of Majorca, having been made Seneschal <note>A high-ranking administrative officer in a royal household</note> to King James. He was infamous for his lust and mad love affairs, until at last, by an unexpected event, he was converted to a better life. Leaving the court at forty years of age, he joined the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> and began to breathe a spirit of total piety. He burned with a great desire to convert Muslims <note>original: *Mahumetanos*</note> to the faith of Christ, and thus he diligently applied himself to the study of letters, which he had once considered worthless. 

In particular, he wished to investigate and master the deeper secrets of Medicine and Chemistry <note>original: *Chemiæ*; here referring to alchemy</note>: although Luke Wadding* <note>A 17th-century Irish Franciscan historian</note> and others with him contend that the study of the Alchemical art belongs not to our Raymond, but to a younger man named Raymond of Tarrega, a so-called "New Christian" who converted from Judaism. However that may be, Lull was schooled in the first elements of the Latin language in Paris <note>original: *Lutetia*</note>. He was taught the Arabic language by a purchased Muslim slave (by whom he was soon after treacherously wounded and brought to the point of death). He then set his mind to publishing almost countless books in the Spanish, Latin, and Arabic languages. 

Thereafter, withdrawing to a mountain, he devoted seven entire months to prayer and contemplation; it is said that he received there a new light of knowledge infused by God. Soon after, around the year 1287, he set out for Rome to visit Pope Honorius IV, requesting that monasteries be ordered to be built across the world where the study of Oriental languages might flourish. To promote this same cause, he traveled to Paris, Montpellier, and Genoa in turn; in every place, he taught with great zeal his "General Art," which he called "The Inventive Art" <note>Lull's *Ars Magna*, a logical system intended to prove the truths of Christianity through reason</note>. The following year, he requested permission to lecture on this same art in Rome, but in vain. 

Returning to Genoa, he prepared himself for the work he had long meditated upon: preaching the Gospel among the Muslims. Crossing over to Tunis in Africa, he entered into a debate with the Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims</note> and faced a grave danger of execution. He was barely freed by the pleas of an Arab priest, though a law was passed that if he returned to Africa, he would be put to death. From Africa, he came to Naples, where he lectured on his art until the year 1290. Later, seeking permission from Pope Boniface VIII to teach it in Rome, he was rejected. 

Soon after, traveling to Genoa, he wrote many books; he visited the King in Majorca; he lectured on his art again in Paris; returning to Majorca, he debated with Jews and Saracens; in Cyprus, he vocally opposed the Jacobites and Nestorians <note>Eastern Christian sects deemed heretical by the Roman Church</note> and narrowly escaped being poisoned by them. Returning to Genoa and Paris, he taught his art; but when he appealed to Pope Clement V to teach the same in Rome, he was rejected. 

Then, moving to Lyon and soon to Majorca, he sailed across from there to Bugia <note>Modern-day Béjaïa, Algeria</note> in Africa and began to preach the faith of Christ. He was attacked with stones by the Saracens, and when their priest, Alfasinus, demanded an account of his faith, Lull attempted to demonstrate it using philosophical arguments. For this, he was thrown into a squalid prison. Finally freed by the pleas of Genoese merchants, he sailed from Africa; having lost his entire collection of books in a shipwreck, he landed at Pisa. Some, however, date this journey to Bugia to around the year 1313. 

Next, turning his mind to the recovery of the Holy Land, he began to strenuously urge everyone toward a Holy War <note>A Crusade</note>; under the pretext—or perhaps the genuine intent—of undertaking this, he collected a vast sum of money from Italian matrons. He then went to Clement V in Avignon to request that a Holy War be decreed. Held in ridicule by the Pope, he withdrew to Paris and devoted himself to teaching his art until the Council of Vienne in 1311. Before the Fathers of the Council, he tried every means to ensure that schools for languages were established everywhere, that all military orders were merged into one, that a Holy War was declared, and that the writings of Averroes <note>An influential Islamic philosopher whose interpretations of Aristotle were often seen as a threat to Christian doctrine</note> were condemned; however, he obtained nothing. 

Rejected by the Council, he turned to the Christian Kings, whom he did not cease to solicit to undertake the Holy War. Having wandered through the royal courts of France and Spain, he finally arrived in England, where he practiced the Alchemical art. However, little credit should be given to the report of John Imperialis* <note>A 17th-century Italian physician and writer</note>—who was himself doubtful—citing the authority of others, that *certain bronze spheres were turned into the substance of gold by Lull's work and are preserved in the courtyard of the British King to this day.* Indeed, Luke Wadding|| renders this English journey doubtful, bringing forward many arguments. Around the year 1314, Raymond, having left his wife...

# The Century of Wyclif
<meta>catchword: Art</meta>

...[leaving his] wife (for he was married), he took up the third order of the Franciscans <note>The "Third Order" allowed laypeople to follow Franciscan spirituality while living in the world</note> and, burning with an immense desire for Martyrdom, he resolved to die for Christ. After staying for a short time in Sicily and Majorca, he crossed over again into Africa. There, after he had brought some to the faith of Christ at Tunis—or as others say, at Bugia <note>Modern Béjaïa, Algeria</note>—he was thrown into prison and tortured by the Saracens <note>A common medieval term for Muslims</note> with the most severe wounds. Carried out half-dead by Genoese merchants and brought onto a ship, he breathed his last in sight of his native island on the 29th day of June in the year 1315, at the age of 80.

There is a huge controversy concerning him among writers. For some, including Bzovius <note>Abraham Bzowski, a Dominican historian</note>, number him among the heretics, stage-actors, and wandering charlatans <note>original: *nugivendulis*; literally "sellers of trifles"</note>; they reproach his insane study of Chemistry <note>original: *Chemiæ*; referring here to alchemy</note> and his thirst for making gold. They report that nearly five hundred errors taken from his books were marked with anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication</note> by Gregory XI at Avignon in the year 1372. Others, on the contrary, place him in the catalog of Saints and Martyrs, and praise his piety, zeal, and learning. They maintain that the entire hodgepodge of Chemical and Medical books should be attributed to "Raymond the Neophyte" <note>A supposed later convert from Judaism with the same name</note>. They contend, finally, that Lull was so far removed from such trifles and follies that in his genuine writings he very often mocks the stupidity of the Alchemists. With arguments of this kind, his cause is laboriously defended by Luke Wadding <note>An Irish Franciscan scholar</note> in the *Annals of the Friars Minor* <note>original: *Annal. Minor.*</note> for the years 1275, 1287, 1290, 1293, and 1295; but especially for the year 1312, throughout almost the entire entry.

### WILLIAM OF NANGIS,

<margin>1301.</margin> GUILLAUME DE MANDAGOUT, a Frenchman by birth, formerly Archdeacon of Nîmes and Uzès, Chaplain to the Roman Pontiff, and Provost of the Church of Toulouse <note>The OCR reads "Tsanæ," likely a transcription error for "Tolosanæ"</note>. In the year 1295, he was created Archbishop of Embrun by Boniface VIII. He flourished in the year 1301. In 1312, he was declared a Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Palestrina by Clement V on December 14th. He died in Avignon in the year 1321, or, as others say, 1324. Besides the labor he performed at the command of Boniface VIII in compiling the *Sixth Book of Decretals* <note>The 'Liber Sextus' is a major collection of Canon Law</note>, he wrote a *Treatise on the Elections of New Prelates, which was published in print at Cologne, 1573, with the additions of Nicolas Boër.*

<margin>1301.</margin> HEINRICH STERO, a German by nationality, a monk of the Benedictine Order at the Lower Altaich Abbey <note>Niederaltaich in Bavaria</note>, chaplain to Abbot Hermann, and finally, as some believe, Abbot of Piburg; he flourished in the year 1301. He wrote *Annals from the first year of the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa to the first year of Rudolph of Habsburg, or from the year of Christ 1152 to 1273.* Marquard Freher was the first to publish these annals among other German writers; a more complete version was provided by Henricus Canisius in *Ancient Lectures*, Volume 1, page 229. Stero also wrote a *History of the Deeds of the Emperors Rudolph of Habsburg, Adolf of Nassau, and Albert of Austria from the year 1266 to 1300*, which the brothers Ulrich and Conrad Welling—monks of the Benedictine Abbey of Saints Ulrich and Afra in Augsburg—continued until the year 1335. This history exists with the Welling brothers' continuation in Freher’s *German Writers*, Frankfurt, 1600, Volume 1, page 384.

<margin>1301.</margin> DINO DEL MUGELLO, an Italian by birth, originating from the village of Mugello in the territory of Florence, most learned in both laws <note>Civil and Canon Law</note>, and a primary professor among the Bolognese; he flourished in the year 1301. Summoned to Rome by Boniface VIII with the promise of a Cardinalship, he provided diligent labor in compiling the *Sixth Book of Decretals*. However, through the treachery of the Pope, he was deprived of his reward. Cast down by the loss of hope in attaining the dignity of a Cardinal, he is said to have died of excessive grief in the year 1303, though not without suspicion of poison.

<margin>1301.</margin> JACOPONE DA TODI <note>Latin: Jacobus de Benedictis</note>, called "Jacopone" on account of his immense self-contempt, an Italian by nationality, born in Todi of noble stock. Leaving the secular world, he joined the Franciscan family; and remarkable for his extraordinary holiness of life (as those times allowed), he flourished in the year 1301. Above other duties of piety, he shone with a wonderful contempt for himself. For, thinking that he should follow as closely as possible in the footsteps of the patriarch Francis, he greatly desired to bring mockery upon himself; this he considered most meritorious and the highest [form] of perfection...

...believing it to be a degree of Christian perfection. Nor did he fail in his vow. For while he threw unrefined Revelations to the common people, having taken up a prophetic duty, and rebuked the morals and deeds of Pope Boniface (with whom he had been familiar before his elevation to the Papacy), he suffered mockery, being cast into chains by Boniface in the city of Palestrina <note>original: "in urbe Prænestinâ"</note>. Nevertheless, that new artifice of showing piety earned a title of this sort inscribed on his tomb:

->THE BONES OF BLESSED JACOPONE DA TODI,<-
->A BROTHER OF THE ORDER OF FRIARS MINOR FROM TODI,<-
->WHO, A FOOL FOR CHRIST’S SAKE,<-
->DECEIVED THE WORLD WITH A NEW ART,<-
->AND SEIZED HEAVEN.<-
->HE FELL ASLEEP IN THE LORD<-
->ON THE 25TH DAY OF DECEMBER, IN THE YEAR 1306.<-

He wrote many *Rhymes* and *Poems* in a crude Italian tongue, into which he deliberately mixed coarser words from the dialects of Todi, Calabria, Sicily, and Naples; he did this so that he might provoke laughter in his readers and mockery for himself. Francesco Freffato, a member of the Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>, arranged these into seven books and saw them published with explanatory notes at *Rome, 1558*, and an expanded edition at *Venice, 1617, in quarto*. By the same author is the *Rhyme to the Blessed Virgin Mary standing near the cross of the Suffering Christ*, which begins, *The Mother stood grieving* <note>original: "Stabat Mater dolorosa"; this is the world-famous hymn still used in the Catholic liturgy</note>, found in the Office of the Blessed Virgin. His *Maxims and Salutary Admonitions* are found in the work of Matthäus Rader in the *Garden of Saints*. His *Song on Contempt for the World*, which begins, *Why does the world wage war under vain glory?* <note>original: "Cur Mundus militat sub vanâ gloriâ?"</note>, is well known to all. Finally, a *Prophecy in Manuscript* is held in the Vatican Library.

<margin>1302.</margin>
**JOHN OF FREIBURG**, called by some *Joannes de Uriburgo*, with the surname *Runsic*, a German by nationality, originating from Freiburg in Breisgau, of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, and finally Bishop of Ossuna in Hungary, flourished in the year 1302. He was so powerful in his sermons that while he was once railing against usury at Bologna, the citizens started a riot and drove the usurers out of the city. He died in the year 1314, after he had resigned his Bishopric and spent some time leading a quiet life among his fellow Dominicans.

*His Commentaries on the Books of Sentences*, *Glosses on the Decree*, *Letters*, and certain other works are mentioned by Ambrogio de Altamura in the *Library of Preachers*, pages 95 and 468.

<margin>1303.</margin>
**PTOLEMY OF LUCCA**, an Italian by birth, from the city of Lucca, a disciple of Saint Thomas Aquinas and a monk of the Dominican Order, flourished in the year 1303. He eventually served as the private Confessor to Pope John XXII; and in the year 1318, having been created Bishop of Torcello in the Venetian territory, he died in the year 1321. He wrote *Annals* of both sacred and civil events conducted from the year 1060 to the year 1303; likewise a *Chronicle of Popes and Emperors*. Both works appeared at *Lyon, 1619*. The *Annals* are held in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 25, page 949. He also wrote to Guillaume Pierre Godin, later a Cardinal, an *Ecclesiastical History* in 24 books, which is preserved in manuscript in the Vatican, Barberini, Colbert, and Navarre libraries. An excerpt of his regarding the *Genealogy of Robert Guiscard* is found in Volume 3 of *Illustrious Spain*. Another regarding the *Genealogy and posterity of Charles, King of Sicily* is found in the *Collection of French History*, Volume 5, page 893.

**EBERARD**, a German by nationality, a monk of the Benedictine Order at the Altaich Monastery <note>Niederaltaich Abbey</note>, and Archdeacon of the Church of Regensburg, flourished in the year 1303.

# CLEMENT V.

Formerly named Bertrand de Got, a Gascon by nationality, born in the village of Villandraut in the Diocese of Bordeaux. He was the son of Bertrand, a knight, but became a clergyman, serving first as the Bishop of Comminges <note>original: "Episcopus Convenarum"</note>, then created Archbishop of Bordeaux in 1299 by Boniface VIII. Finally, in the year 1305, he was elected Pope in absentia at Perugia on the 5th of June, and crowned at Lyons on the 14th of November. Having attained the Pontificate, he transferred the seat of the Papacy from the city of Rome to France, staying at times in Lyons, at times in Bordeaux, but most frequently in Avignon. As a token of his gratitude to the French kingdom, he declared that no prejudice had been done to the Catholic Church by the Bull of Boniface VIII titled *Unam Sanctam* <note>A famous decree asserting the Pope's absolute spiritual and temporal power; Clement sought to ease tensions between the Papacy and the French King Philip the Fair</note>. In the year 1307, he excommunicated Andronicus, the Emperor of the Greeks, for the crime of Schism. After taking counsel with the Kings of England and France, he ordered all the Knights Templar to be seized on one and the same night and thrown into prison. Their wealthy revenues had stirred up envy against them, and they were charged with crimes of idolatry and blasphemy. In the year 1309, he struck the Venetians with an excommunication <note>original: "anathemate"</note> for their occupation of Ferrara, and granted their persons and property to any who wished to seize them. Shortly after, he imposed the same censure on the people of Florence and Lucca. In the year 1311, in the month of November, having held a General Council at Vienne, he confirmed the Order of Franciscans and ordered the Templars to be condemned for heresy, proscribed, and stripped of their property. Consequently, the Templars were seized everywhere for punishment and perished in the flames; their wealth was given to the Hospitallers <note>The Knights of the Order of Saint John</note>. In the year 1313, he arranged for the removal of Emperor Henry VII, who had set out for Rome to receive his crown but had refused to provide an oath of allegiance to the Pope's cardinal-vicars, and had gone to recover his rights by force of arms. The Emperor was taken out by a poisoned host given to him while he was besieging Florence by Bernard of Poliziano, a Dominican and his confessor, who had been suborned for that purpose. Clement died at Roquemaure on the Rhône in the year 1314, on the 20th of April. Extant are his *Letters and Decrees* in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 11, page 1499. Another 16 are in Bzovius’s *Annals* for the year 1307, etc.; another 11 in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors*, Volume 3, for the year 1306, etc.; and another 46 in the same work in the *Papal Register*, page 28. The *Clementine Constitutions*, or the *Seventh Book of Decretals*, was collected into five books by order of Clement V from various constitutions of his own and of the Council of Vienne, and was published after his death by John XXII in the year 1317. It was printed in Paris, 1512, in duodecimo; again there in 1541; in Rouen, 1519; Venice, 1591; Lyons, 1582; and Frankfurt, 1586. Finally, nine volumes of the *Registers of Letters* are preserved as manuscripts in the Vatican Library.

<margin>1305.</margin>

# THOMAS JORSIUS, or JOYCE,
## An Englishman, also called the Welshman,

English by nation, a Londoner by birth, and perhaps of Welsh-British origin. A disciple of Albertus Magnus and a monk of the Dominican Order, he was distinguished with the laurel of a Doctorate and taught theology at Paris, London, and elsewhere. Later, he served as the Provincial of the Dominicans in England for seven years and was admitted as a confessor and secret advisor to King Edward. He flourished in the year 1305, when he was named Cardinal and Bishop of Sabina by Clement V on the 18th of December—having purchased that dignity for a large sum of money, if Bale is to be believed. There are indeed some, including Trithemius and Oudinus, who refer our Thomas to the year 1400. Furthermore, with a truly charming fabrication, Ambrose of Altamura, in an effort to expand the *Catalog of Dominican Writers* by hook or by crook, deliberately dissects him into four different writers and distributes them through as many parts of this century. Although he wishes it to be believed they were different men, it is obvious at first glance from the writings attributed to them that they are one and the same. Finally, in the year 1311, our Thomas died at Lyons while on a journey as a legate from Clement to Emperor Henry VII. His body was carried to Oxford and buried among the Dominicans. Certainly, the similarity of his name to "Thomas the Angelic" <note>Thomas Aquinas, known as the Doctor Angelicus</note> did no small injury to our English Thomas, since it happened as a result that a vast part of the English writer's works...

<margin>1305.</margin>
WILLIAM OF PARIS, French by nation, a monk of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, and appointed General Censor of the faith throughout France in the year 1305 by Clement V. In the year 1308, by order of the same Pope, he investigated the case and crimes of the Knights Templar along with other Preachers. It seems that this William is the author of the *Seven Dialogues on the Sacraments*, which are falsely attributed to William of Auvergne (the Bishop of Paris) and published under his name at *Leipzig, 1512* and *Paris, 1587*; we have discussed these a little more extensively above.

<margin>1305.</margin>
PHILIP OF EICHSTÄTT, German by nationality and Alsatian by birth, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Abbot of the Cistercian monastery at Paris, flourished in the year 1305. In that year, he was sent to Rome by the Emperor Albert of Austria and was created the 39th Bishop of Eichstätt (or Aichstadt) by Clement V. He died on the 25th of February, 1322. At the request of Anna, Queen of Hungary and daughter of Emperor Albert, he wrote the *Life of Saint Walpurga*, Abbess of Heidenheim; he compiled this largely from the more extensive commentaries of Wolfhard. It is extant in Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, Volume 4, page 560.

<margin>1307.</margin>
SIEGFRIED, German by nation, a Priest of the Church of Meissen in Saxony, flourished in the year 1307. Some mistakenly confuse him with Siegfried, a member of the Order of Preachers and Bishop of Cyrene, who was a suffragan to the Archbishop of Mainz around the year 1470. Our Siegfried wrote a *Chronicle from the Creation of the World to the year 1307*. Georg Fabricius of Chemnitz published this in *Leipzig, 1569* and *Jena, 1598* (folio), after omitting the first part up to the year of Christ 457 and removing many useless passages from the remainder; he appended it to the end of his *Saxon History*. From there, it was placed by Pistorius among his *German Writers* (Frankfurt, 1583, Volume 1).

<margin>1307.</margin>
HAYTON, or AITON, Armenian by nation, nephew of King Hayton of Armenia and a minor prince of a certain small province in Georgia. After performing distinguished service in the Crusades <note>original: "Sacræ militiæ"</note> under his uncle Hayton and waging a long war against the Saracens who held Palestine, he laid aside his soldier’s belt and took up the cowl. He became a monk of the Premonstratensian Order <note>Also known as the Norbertines</note> in Cyprus around the year 1290, as he himself indicates in the 46th chapter of his *History*.
<margin>*Library of the Order of Preachers, p. 87.</margin>

Hayton, having taken the name Anthony, thereafter led a quiet life, as distinguished by his piety as he once was by his noble birth. He flourished in the year 1307. While staying in Poitiers, he dictated a *History of the Tartars* <note>The Mongols</note> and their customs and deeds by order of Pope Clement V, by no means concealing the brave deeds he himself had performed. **NICHOLAS TRIVET**, or Trivettus, English by nation and from Norfolk by country, was born of a distinguished family, being the son of Thomas Trivet, a knight and royal Justice. From his childhood in London, he lived among the Dominicans <note>The Order of Preachers</note> and followed their institutes. Having laid the foundations of his learning in London, he set out for Oxford where he brought it to the summit, being honored there with the Doctor’s cap. Afterwards, traveling to Paris, he acquired for himself even greater knowledge and fame. Finally returning to London, he was elected Superior or Prior of the Dominican monastery. He flourished in the year 1310. He died nearly seventy years old in the year 1328 and was buried among the Dominicans.

<margin>1310. * On the Irish Writers, book 1, p. 65. † Century 14, p. 242.</margin>
**MALACHY**, Irish by birth, a monk of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> and a theologian at Oxford, served as a preacher to King Edward II of England. He flourished in the year 1310 and, if James Ware * correctly conjectures, later moved to Naples. *Ranked among the more distinguished leaders of his Order* (says John Bale †), *he earned great praise for his learning both at home and abroad.* There exists his *Book on the Poison of Mortal Sins and their Remedies* <note>original: "Liber de Veneno Peccatorum mortalium, deq; remediis ipsorum"</note>, issued from the press of Henri Estienne in *Paris*, 1518. A volume of his sermons, which Bale mentions he wrote, has not yet emerged from the shadows of obscurity.

<margin>1311.</margin>
**WILLIAM DURAND**, French by birth, the nephew of Durand "the Speculator" <note>William Durand the Elder, a famous jurist</note> and his successor in the See of Mende, was the fourth bishop of that name. Under the fortunate guidance of his uncle, he had devoted extraordinary effort to the study of literature and had acquired a truly remarkable knowledge of Theology, Philosophy, and especially Canon Law. He was made a Canon and eventually Archdeacon of the Church of Mende by his uncle. Upon his uncle’s death, by the mandate of Pope Boniface VIII, he was named his successor in the year 1296. In the following year, with the consent of the Chapter of Canons of Mende, he decreed that no one should be admitted among the Canons whose relatives or kin, up to the third generation, had in any way harassed the Church of Mende. He flourished in the year 1311, at which time the Council of Pope Clement V was soon to be held. By command, he wrote the *Treatise on the Manner of Celebrating a General Council and on Reforming Corruptions in the Church* <note>original: "Tractatum, De modo celebrandi Generalis Concilii, & corruptelis in Ecclesiâ reformandis"</note>, which he read at the Council of Vienne. In the year 1312, after the Jews were expelled from the city of Mende and their houses demolished, he built the College of All Saints on that same site. In the year 1316, he was sent as an ambassador by King Philip to Robert, Count of Flanders, for the sake of brokering a peace. He died around the year 1328. His *Treatise on the Manner of Celebrating a General Council* survives, in which he depicts all the vices of every rank of the Church; he especially and extensively attacks the shameful laziness, filth, and luxury of the priests and monks, and warns that a swift remedy must be applied to their corrupt morals. Philippe Probus, a lawyer of Bourges, first published it in *Paris*, 1545, under the name of Durand "the Speculator." Indeed, many wrongly confuse the "Speculator" with his nephew of the same name. It was afterwards published restored to its true author in *Paris*, 1635, in quarto, and among other works of a similar subject in *Paris*, 1671, in octavo.

<margin>1312.</margin>
**MARINO SANUDO**, or Sanuto, nicknamed *Torsello*, a Venetian patrician and son of Marco, was born in Venice in the parish of San Severo in the city of Rialto. He was a familiar and a member of the household of Richard, Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Eustace. Using the help of a certain German craftsman, he was the first of all people to introduce into the Church those pneumatic organs which are used today, called *Torsellos* in Italian; hence the name *Torsello* was given to him. He flourished in the year 1312. Devoted to the business of the Holy Land from infancy, he spent almost his entire life traveling through foreign regions, emulating the diligence of Sallust in this regard, so that he might produce the work he had planned more accurately. For he crossed the sea five times: to Cyprus, Armenia, Alexandria, Rhodes, and Palestine. Having completed his work, he spent much time in the courts of the Emperor, the Pope, the King of France, and other Princes. He died after the year 1329. He wrote *Secrets of the Faithful of the Cross regarding the Recovery and Preservation of the Holy Land* <note>original: "Secreta Fidelium Crucis super terræ Sanctæ recuperatione & conservatione"</note> in three books. In the first, he proposes means for weakening the Saracens <note>A common medieval term for Muslims</note> and bringing them to order; in the second, he describes the order which Christian leaders ought to observe in conducting a holy war; in the third, he shows the manner of preserving and holding the Holy Land once it has been recovered. He traces its history from its first inhabitants down to his own times, with a chorographic description of it and neighboring places added, illustrated by several maps or geographic charts. Marino began this work in the year 1306 and presented it to Pope John XXII in 1322. It was published, edited by Jacques Bongars, in *Hanau*, 1611, in folio, among the *Deeds of God through the Franks* <note>original: "Gesta Dei per Francos"</note>, of which it makes up almost the entire second volume. Attached at the end are twenty-two *Letters of Marino to Pope John, the Emperor Andronicus of Constantinople, and various Cardinals and Bishops; by which [he urged] them...*

<margin>1312.</margin> **ALEXANDER OF SAN ELPIDIO**, an Italian by birth, originating from the town of that name in Umbria, was a Doctor of Sacred Theology and an Augustinian Hermit <note>A member of the Order of Saint Augustine</note> from the Province of Picenum. He flourished in the year 1312, at which time, following the death of James of Orta, he was elected Prior General of his Order at the assembly in Viterbo. In the year 1315, at a meeting of his Order held in Padua, his leadership was extended for another three years; indeed, he was appointed General for a third time in 1318 at the assembly in Rimini, a fourth time in 1321, and finally a fifth time at Montpellier in 1324. In 1325, he was created Archbishop of Ravenna. It is uncertain when he died. By the command of Pope John XXII, he wrote the *Treatise on the Jurisdiction of the Empire and the Authority of the Supreme Pontiff* <note>original: "Tractatum de Jurisdictione Imperii & auctoritate summi Pontificis"</note>, divided into two books, which appeared in print at Lyon in 1498 and Rimini in 1624. Joseph Pamphilus, in his *Chronicle of the Order of Hermits* (p. 46), mentions his books *On Evangelical Liberty and Ecclesiastical Unity* <note>original: "De Libertate Evangelicâ, & Ecclesiasticâ unitate"</note>, as well as certain written *Commentaries on Aristotle* preserved as manuscripts in the Augustinian Hermit Convent at Bologna.

<margin>1312.</margin> **VITAL DU FOUR**, a native of Aquitaine from the house of Bazas, was a Professor of Sacred Theology, a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>, and prefect of the Province of Aquitaine. He flourished in the year 1312, when he was named Cardinal of Saints Sylvester and Martin by Clement V. Under John XXII, he wrote to oppose the opinion of Michael of Cesena and the "Spiritual Brethren" <note>A radical faction of Franciscans who advocated for absolute poverty</note> regarding the poverty of Christ and the Apostles; it was primarily by this labor that he earned his promotion by the Pope to Cardinal-Bishop of Albano. He died at Avignon on August 16, 1327, and was buried among his fellow friars.

*Commentaries on the Proverbs of Solomon.*

<margin>1312.</margin> **HERVÉ DE NÉDELLEC**, a Breton by nation, was a Regent Doctor of Theology in the Academy of Paris. ### HUGO PRATENSIS
also known as Hugo de Prato Florido, an Italian by birth, born in Prato near Florence, was a monk of the Dominican Order <note>The Order of Preachers</note> and a most celebrated preacher. He flourished in the year 1313 and died in 1322. There exist his *Sunday Sermons on the Gospels and Epistles for the Entire Year, Lyon, 1528, in quarto*. *Sermons on the Saints for the Entire Year, ibid., 1528, in octavo*. *Lenten Sermons, Venice, 1578, in octavo; 1584, in octavo*.

<margin>1315.</margin>
### PORCHETUS SALVATICUS
Italian by nationality and a native of Genoa, born of the illustrious Salvatici family, he was a monk of the Carthusian Order. He is a writer of quite uncertain age, of whom no one, as far as I know, made mention before Agostino Giustiniani. Nor did Giustiniani himself, who brought his writings to light, indicate his age. Indeed, the distinguished William Cave placed him around the year 1512 in his *Historical Archive*, moved by no other reason (as he himself affirmed to me in person) than that his book against the Jews was published from the press a few years later. Truly, it seems hardly credible that Pietro Galatino, whose work first appeared in 1518, would have been able or dared to plagiarize the writings of Porchetus so signally, had Porchetus written only a few years earlier and perhaps still been among the living to expose the ungrateful man’s plagiarism—especially since Galatino seems to have finished his work before the end of 1512. Furthermore, Agostino Giustiniani, although he by no means indicates a certain age for Porchetus, speaks of him as a writer of a former era. <margin>* On the Writers of the 16th Century, p. 13.</margin> Miraeus <note>original: "Mirum", likely referring to the historian Aubert Miraeus</note>, I know not by what authority, records that he lived in the year 1315. This calculation certainly seems not unlike the truth, provided that the authority of some older writer were added. Porchetus himself, equipped with no common knowledge of the Hebrew language and most well-versed in the writings of the Hebrews, wrote a distinguished work against the Jews to which he gave the title *The Victory* <note>original: "Victoriæ"</note>, *for the subversion of Jewish perfidy and so that the truth of the Christian faith might shine more excellently*, as he himself says in the Preface. In composing this work, he transcribed a great many things from Raymond Martini's *Dagger of Faith* <note>original: "Pugione fidei"</note>, yet he was not so ungrateful as to deny it, for he freely acknowledges in most places that he took the material for this booklet from that source by compiling it. Finally brought out of the shadows, Agostino Giustiniani, Bishop of Nebbio—himself most skilled in Hebrew matters—revised, expanded, and published it at *Paris, 1520, in folio*. It was preceded by a dedicatory letter to Guillaume Parvi, Bishop of Troyes, in which he vouches for the passages from Hebrew monuments cited by Raymond and Porchetus, testifying that he had read the greatest part of them in the same books, nearly all of which he had acquired for himself.

Around that time, he was the first of all to introduce the "Sorbonic Act" to the University. In this exercise, on every Friday during the summer, from sunrise to sunset without any rest, without any food or drink, and without any help from a presiding officer, a single Respondent disputes against many opponents. In the year 1323, by the letters of John XXII...

<margin>1315.</margin>
UBERTIN OF CASALE, also called "of Ilia," an Italian by nationality from the region of Casale, and a monk of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>, flourished in the year 1315. A heavy controversy arose among the Franciscans over a "matter of goat’s wool" <note>original: "de lanâ caprinâ"; a Latin idiom for a trivial or pointless dispute, though here it refers to the bitter split over the nature of Franciscan poverty</note>, and from this a schism began. On one side were the *Spirituals*, who contended that Christ and the Apostles owned nothing, neither personally nor in common; on the other side were the *Fraticelli* <note>original: "Fraterculis"; literally "little brothers"</note> of the "Community," who asserted that while they owned nothing personally, they did possess some things in common. Ubertin presented himself as a leader to the *Spirituals*. He spiritedly defended their side until the year 1312, when Pope John [XXII], his adversary, more forcefully struck down his cause. Moved by indignation, he requested of the Pope that he and his followers be allowed to live separately. Having suffered a rejection, he stirred up troubles. Therefore, fearing a more severe storm, in the year 1317 he requested and obtained the power to leave the Friars Minor and transfer to the Benedictines; he was assigned the Monastery of St. Peter of Gembloux in Brabant to which he might withdraw. At last, however, he withdrew to the Carthusians,

...it is said. In the year 1321, having been consulted by Pope John [XXII] on that most vexing question concerning the poverty of Christ, he <note>Ubertinus of Casale</note> defined it as a heretical opinion that Christ possessed anything as his own or in common in a worldly manner, but that it could be said quite Orthodoxy that he held something in common in a spiritual manner. This opinion of Ubertinus pleased the Pope and Cardinals marvelously, and it seemed to have hit the mark <note>Latin: *rem acu tetigisse* — literally "to have touched the thing with a needle," an idiom for hitting the nail on the head</note>. There exists his *Response concerning the question of the Poverty of Christ and the Apostles* <note>original: *Responsio circa quæstionem de Paupertate Christi & Apostolorum*</note> delivered in the Consistory at Avignon before John XXII; an abbreviated version is found in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors, Vol. III for the year 1321*, and a more complete version, along with the articles brought against him by brother Bonagratia, is in Baluze’s *Miscellanea, Vol. I, pp. 293, 307*. His lengthy work titled *The Tree of the Crucified Life* <note>original: *Arbor Vitæ Crucifixæ*</note> was printed in Venice, 1485, in quarto. The work *On the Seven States of the Church* <note>original: *de septem statibus Ecclesiæ*</note>, Venice, 1516, in quarto.

Furthermore, there are some who believe that the first three of the four books *On the Imitation of Christ* are owed to our Ubertinus.

<margin>1315.</margin>
**JOHN OF NAPLES**, Italian by birth, a Neapolitan citizen, descended from the most noble Sicola stock, a theologian of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, a studious reader and strenuous defender of St. Thomas Aquinas, and a Solemn Doctor of the Academy of Paris, flourished in the year 1315. In the Neapolitan school of St. Dominic, he performed the office of Regent and presided over the master's chair for many years with the highest praise. He died after the year 1323. There exist *Various Philosophical and Theological Questions, 42 in number* <note>original: *Quæstiones variæ Philosophicæ & Theologicæ*</note>, debated at Paris, published by Domenico Gravina at Naples in 1618, in folio. His other writings, namely *On the Four Books of the Sentences, Thirteen Quodlibets, Sermons for the Seasons, for the Saints, and for the Dead*, etc., are recorded by Ambrosius de Altamura in the *Library of the Preachers, p. 105*.

<margin>1316.</margin>
**JOHN XXII**, previously called *Jacques Duèze* <note>Latin: *Jacobus Ossa* or *Deusa*</note>, French by birth, from Aquitaine, of the city of Cahors, the son of Arnaud Duèze, a cobbler. Having served as Chancellor to King Charles of Sicily and Vice-Chancellor to King Robert, he was first Bishop of Fréjus <note>Latin: *Foroliviensis*</note>, then Archbishop of Avignon, soon Cardinal-Bishop of Porto, and finally elected Roman Pontiff at Lyon on August 7, 1316. He was crowned there on September 5, after he had confirmed by oath to the Cardinals—who were distressed that Clement V had moved the Roman see to Avignon—that he would never mount a horse or mule except to travel to Rome. In the year 1317, he added Louis, Bishop of Toulouse, in 1320, Thomas, Bishop of Hereford, and in 1323, Thomas Aquinas to the Catalogue of Saints. At the beginning of his pontificate, when asked by Louis the Bavarian and Frederick of Austria—whom discordant Electors had simultaneously raised to Imperial dignity—about receiving the Imperial crown, he rejected both. But in the year 1320, when Louis sought his right by arms, the Pope confirmed Frederick and opposed him to Louis’s forces. After Frederick was defeated, the Pope cited Louis in a public document to present himself at Avignon to give an account of his actions, and meanwhile to lay down the empire. The Emperor refused this and appealed to a General Council. John took this indignantly and excommunicated Louis in 1323, deposed him from the empire, and ordered the Electors to choose another. Furthermore, he subjected the Emperor’s most faithful defenders, Matteo Visconti of Milan and Marsilius of Padua, to anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication from the Church</note>. Louis, invited by the Romans (who had waited in vain for the Pope’s return), entered Italy in 1327. He received the imperial crown at Rome, and having held a Council of Cardinals, he cited John. When John refused to appear, Louis condemned him as an Antichrist, Satan, and Heresiarch <note>A leader of a heretical sect</note>, cast him down from the Pontificate, and having burned his image in public in 1328, he appointed Nicholas V (previously called Pietro Rainalducci of Corvaro) as Antipope. Meanwhile, John hid safely at Avignon and laughed at Louis's threats and schemes; and using the help of the Pisans, he reduced the Antipope to submission in 1333. But to pass to other matters, a sharp controversy was stirred up for John with the Franciscans on two counts. For they taught that Christ and the Apostles possessed nothing either as their own or in common, and that Christ hung naked on the cross; and they boasted that not the ownership <note>Latin: *dominium*</note>, but only the use of things belonged to them as well as to Christians who were in any way perfect, [holding] the contrary...

# The Wyclif Century
<header>The Wyclif Century.</header>

...accusing the former opinion of heresy. John <note>Pope John XXII</note>, who held money dearer than his soul and left an immense wealth heaped up in his coffers when he died, calling the Dominicans <note>original: *nicanos*, likely referring to the *Predicantes* or Preachers</note> to his side, condemned both articles of the Minorites <note>Franciscans</note> as vain, foolish, and heretical. He defined that Christ hung on the cross clothed with a crown, purple, a scepter, and a divided garment <note>original: *didâq; veste*</note>, and that the use of things cannot be separated from ownership <note>This was a central theological dispute: the Franciscans claimed they only "used" items without "owning" them, following the poverty of Christ</note>. He excommunicated the Franciscans who opposed him, and calling them *Fratricelli* <note>term meaning "Little Brothers," often used derogatorily for radical Franciscans</note>, he burned several of them in the flames. These were trifles; but of greater importance was that doctrine which John openly taught and preached around the year 1331—which the Sorbonne condemned and many refuted as a most false heresy—namely, that the souls of the faithful departed are not admitted to the blessed vision of God before the Resurrection <note>This is known as the "Beatific Vision" controversy</note>. John died at Avignon on December 4, 1334.

*A Register of Letters divided into five parts. Manuscript in the Vatican Library, the Barberini Library, etc. The arguments and opening lines of each letter are held in the Council Records, Vol. 11, p. 1643.*

*Two Sermons on the text, "Remember the works of the fathers which they did in their generations" <note>1 Maccabees 2:51</note>. Manuscripts in the Cambridge Public Library, Code 179, numbers 1 and 2.*

*A Retraction of the question: "Whether the souls of the Saints do not enjoy the vision of God before the Last Judgment." It exists in Giovanni Villani’s History of Florence, book 10, chapter 225, as noted by L. J. of St. Charles in the Pontifical Library, book 1, p. 139.*

*A little book "On the Contempt of the World"; I have not yet discovered if it has appeared in print. Leo Allatius testifies in "The Bees of Urban," p. 209, that Patrizio Fattorio of Turritanum meditated spiritual labors upon this little book.*

*The Art of Transmuting Metals <note>An alchemical work attributed to John XXII, though its authenticity is often debated</note>. Published translated from Latin into the French language at Lyon, 1557, in 8vo.*

<margin>1316.</margin>
## ALBERT OF PADUA, an Italian by nation, an Augustinian Hermit, and a disciple of Giles of Rome; having attained the degree of Doctor at the University of Paris, he interpreted the Holy Scriptures publicly for a great crowd of students. He flourished in the year 1316. He died at Paris <note>original: *Lutetiæ*</note> in the year 1328, or according to others, 1325, at the age of 46, and was buried in the monastery of the Augustinians. A marble statue was erected to him after his death in the Town Hall of Padua above the northern doors, with this eulogy inscribed in golden letters. Above the statue: *To Albert, most singular brother of the Hermits, most continent in life, a Paduan by birth, a foster-son of studies, and the highest splendor of the public Christian faith.* Below the statue: *Albert, the splendor of the liberal arts and of our city, having professed the rule in the Order of Hermits, was most continent; he was renowned for his intellect, first imbued with letters under the most celebrated Giles of Rome of the same Order; having taken the doctoral cap <note>original: *insulâ magistrali*</note> at Paris, he became so famous that he unlocked the Apostle Paul, Moses, the Gospels, and the book of Sentences with a splendid exposition; he was also the most eloquent preacher before all men of his age; for which reason he is most justly given this memorial here.* He wrote very many things; from which have appeared from the printing press the *Sermons for the Seasons, On the Saints, and Lenten Sermons, Lyon...*

# The Wyclif Century.

Manuscripts still exist of his *Commentaries on the Pentateuch, on the four Gospels, on the Epistles of St. Paul, and on the Master of Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" by Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, which are still preserved today in Padua, according to the testimony of Joseph Pamphilus in his *Chronicle of the Order of Hermits of St. Augustine*, page 45.

<margin>1316.</margin>
**MICHAEL OF CESENA**, an Italian by nationality, Doctor of Sacred Theology, and a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>, was a product of the Province of Bologna. He was elected Minister General of his Order at the assembly in Naples in the year 1316, on the day before the Kalends of June <note>May 31st</note>, and he immediately set himself vigorously to the task of restoring Franciscan discipline. In the year 1322, while the controversy between the Pope and the Friars Minor was raging regarding the poverty of Christ and the use and ownership of goods, Michael held a general chapter of his Order at Perugia. There, he declared that the Franciscan position was free from the mark of heresy which Pope John <note>John XXII</note> had branded upon it. As the dispute grew more bitter, Michael joined the faction of Emperor Ludwig of Bavaria. For this reason, he was summoned to Avignon by the Pope in 1327 to plead his case and was placed into custody. In the following year, after the Pope had grown more hostile toward the entire Franciscan order due to the substitution of Peter of Corbara <note>a Franciscan friar</note> as Anti-pope, he accused Michael at the excommunication in Perugia, assigned judges, and ordered the case to proceed. Michael appealed the Pope's sentence; and fearing the outcome, he fled secretly from Avignon. Upon his flight, John excommunicated him and stripped him of his rank, entrusting the leadership of the Franciscans to Cardinal Bertrand. Michael appealed to a General Council and, joining himself with Emperor Ludwig, Pope Nicholas <note>the Anti-pope</note>, William of Ockham, and the greater part of his Order, he pursued his cause boldly and mocked the Pope's threats. In June 1329, Bertrand, having gathered the Franciscan followers of the Pope at Paris, removed Michael from the Generalship of the Order and substituted Gerard Odonis in his place. Nevertheless, Michael, supported by the favor of the Emperor, did not yield in the slightest; instead, he openly accused John of heresy. Consequently, in 1330, he was again cursed with dire pronouncements by the Pope, and in 1331, he was condemned for heresy by Gerard at the Franciscan Convention in Perpignan. He died in Munich, Bavaria, in the year 1343, on the eve of St. Andrew, holding fast to his title of Minister General until his very last breath. There exist *Three Treatises against various errors and heresies of Pope John XXII, specifically regarding the beneficial ownership of Church property and the renunciation of temporal goods in the perfection of the state of Monks and Clergy*, found in Goldast’s *Monarchia*, Volume 2, page 1236. A *Letter* can be found in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* for the year 1317, and two others for the year 1322. His *Letters and Protests against John XXII* were published in Lyon in 1495. Furthermore, Luke Wadding reports in his *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*, page 259, that Michael labored over *Commentaries on the Prophet Ezekiel, On the four books of Sentences, and Sermons for the Seasons and for the Saints*.

<margin>1317.</margin>
**ASTESANUS**, or the Astensian, an Italian by birth from the Subalpine city of Asti, was a member of the Order of Friars Minor and a product of the Province of Genoa. He became famous around the year 1317 and died around 1330. At the urging of Cardinal John Gaetano Orsini of St. Theodore, he wrote the *Summa on Cases of Conscience* <note>A "Summa" was a comprehensive manual; this one served as a guide for confessors</note>, commonly called the *Astesana*, in eight books. It was published through the care of Bellatus and Gometius in Nuremberg, 1482. It was later revised and brought to light by Bartholomew de Bellatis of Feltre and Gometius of Lisbon, both Franciscans, in Venice, 1519, in folio. From this work, Antonio Agustí extracted the *Penitential Canons* and published them with explanatory notes along with other works in Venice, 1584, in quarto.

<margin>1317.</margin>
**JAMES OF LAUSANNE**, a Frenchman by nationality, a member of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, and a theologian of the University of Paris, became famous in the year 1317, when he received the rank of Licentiate <note>an advanced academic degree</note>, being granted the doctoral cap shortly thereafter. After he had taught theology publicly in Paris for a long time, he was appointed Provincial of his Order for all of France, and was eventually elevated to rule the See of Lausanne. He wrote almost innumerable works, and in particular, he illustrated many books of Holy Scripture with very extensive *Commentaries*. From these, a massive *Work of Moralities* <note>symbolic or moral interpretations of scripture</note>, divided into twelve books, was published in Limoges in 1528. Also, his *Sermons for the Seasons, for the Saints, and...*

1319.

* On the Writers of the Order of Friars Minor, page 60.
</margin>
**BERTRAND DE LA TOUR**, a native of Aquitaine, born in Camboulit in the Diocese of Cahors, commonly called the **"Famous Doctor"** <note>original: "Doctor Famosus," a traditional title given to distinguished Scholastic theologians</note>. He was a member of the Franciscan Order and Minister of the Province of Aquitaine. He flourished in the year 1319, at which time he was elevated to the Archbishopric of Salerno. Having been chosen as a Cardinal the following year, he eventually obtained the Bishopric of Frascati <note>original: "Tusculanum"</note>. Both before and after receiving the Cardinal’s hat <note>original: "Galerum"</note>, he undertook many embassies for the Roman Popes. He died in the year 1328. He was appointed as the Administrator of the entire Franciscan Order by Pope John XXII until Michael of Cesena could be brought back into line or removed from his rank. This removal was carried out by Bertrand the following year at a meeting of the Pope’s Franciscan followers held in Lyon, where Cesena’s authority was revoked. Bertrand died around the year 1334. He wrote *Epistolary Sermons, or sermons on the Epistles usually read during the Mass*, printed in Strasbourg in 1501; *Sermons for the Seasons from Advent to Easter*; *Sermons on the Saints, for Sundays, for Lent, and for Weekdays*; *Commentaries on the four books of the Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" by Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>; and *On the Gospels and Epistles of the entire year*. According to the testimony of Wadding, these are in manuscript in the Vatican Library, as are his *Treatise on the Poverty of Christ and the Apostles* and his *Theological Collations*, which I shall pass over for now.

<margin>1320.</margin>
**DURAND OF SAINT-POURÇAIN**, a Frenchman by nationality, born in the town near the Abbey of Saint-Pourçain from which he takes his name, in the region of the Auvergne. He was called the **"Most Resolute Doctor"** <note>original: "Doctor Resolutissimus"</note>. An eminent theologian of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, he flourished in the year 1320, having been declared a Doctor at Paris seven years prior. Afterwards, he traveled to Italy and was appointed Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace in 1323 by Pope John XXII; there he explained the sacred scriptures for some time. On January 13, 1326, he was created Bishop of Meaux by the Pope, and the following year he was promoted to the see of Le Puy <note>original: "Anicienfem seu Podienfem"</note>. He died on September 13, 1333, and was buried in the cathedral church at Meaux. His extant works include *Commentaries on the four books of the Sentences* (which he began as a young man and finished in old age), published in more than one edition, but notably at Venice, 1571, in folio. Also, his *Book on the Origin of Jurisdictions, or on Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction*, and his *Treatise on Laws*, were published in print at Paris, 1501. Altamura lists several more of his writings that remain unpublished in the *Dominican Library*, page 113. Those who confuse our author with Durand of Troarn, Durand of Liège, or "the Speculator" <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain is often confused with other famous men named Durand, such as the canonist Guillaume Durand</note> are mistaken, as are those who attribute to him the *Letter of Deoduin to King Henry regarding the Body of the Lord against Berengar*.

<margin>1320.</margin>
**THOMAS DE LA MORE**, an Englishman by birth, a Knight <note>original: "Eques Auratus," literally a "Golden Knight"</note>, and a servant of King Edward II of England. Under the King's auspices and leadership, he saw military service against the Scots; afterwards, he defended the King's cause with the greatest loyalty and constancy possible when Edward was unjustly driven from the throne. He flourished in the year 1320. He wrote *The Life and Deeds of Edward II from the year 1307, when he began his reign, to the year 1326, when he was murdered by wicked regicides.* He wrote his history in French; therefore, at his request, Walter Baker, a Canon of Osney, translated it into Latin. It survives in Latin among the *English and Norman Writers* edited by William Camden under the auspices of the Most Reverend Prelate Matthew Parker, Archbishop of Canterbury, published in London, 1574, folio, and Frankfurt, 1602, folio.

<margin>1320.</margin>
**NICHOLAS OF LYRA**, or Lyranus, considered English by Trithemius and Bale, but more correctly a Norman, born in Lyre in the Diocese of Évreux. He was called the **"Plain and Useful Doctor"** <note>original: "Doctor Planus & utilis"</note>. He had Jewish parents and laid the foundations of his early education among the Rabbis in Jewish letters. Afterward, having converted to the Christian faith, he took the habit of the Friars Minor in the monastery of Verneuil, in the Custody of Normandy...

# The Century of Wyclif.
<header>The Century of Wyclif.</header>

...taking [the religious habit] around the year 1292. He was created a Master of Theology at the University of Paris. He flourished in the year 1320. After he had spent several years in the Convent of Verneuil, he returned to the University of Paris; and in the Great Franciscan Convent, he interpreted Holy Scripture for many years. Finally, having undertaken a taxing and difficult work, he illustrated the entire Bible with a double commentary: one literal, the other moral. In the year 1325, he was designated by Joan, Queen of France, among other most celebrated men, to carry out the execution of her will. He died in the year 1340, on the 23rd day of October.

### WORKS.

*Perpetual Postills, or brief Commentaries on the entire Bible in 85 books. A taxing and learned work, begun in the year 1293 and completed in the year 1330. After several imperfect and less accurate editions—Basel 1508, Lyon 1529 in 6 volumes in folio, and elsewhere—it was produced more correctly through the care of Francis Feuardent, Jean Dadre, and Jacques de Cuilly at Lyon in 1590; then in the Glossed Bibles at Douai 1617, Antwerp 1634, and in the "Great Bibles" at Paris in 1660.* <note>A "Postill" is a term for a marginal or biblical commentary, derived from the Latin "post illa verba" (after those words).</note>

*Greater Postills, or Narrations on the Epistles and Sunday Gospels for the whole year. Venice 1516, 1588 in octavo.*

*A Treatise on the fit person administering and receiving the Most Holy Sacrament of the Altar. Published together with a small book by Saint Thomas Aquinas on the same subject in Germany in quarto, without mention of place or time.*

*A Disputation against the perfidy of the Jews, which is said by Miræus to have been published along with his "Preceptory" at Lyon and Paris. It certainly appeared at Venice in 1483 at the end of the Postills on all the books of both Testaments.* <note>The term "perfidy" (perfidia) was a standard, albeit polemical, theological term in this era referring to the rejection of the Christian faith.</note>

*A Treatise against a certain Jew, who attacked Christ and his doctrine using the very words of the Gospel. It appeared together with the preceding short work at the end of the Postill at Lyon in 1529.*

*A Contemplation on the life and deeds of Saint Francis, published by Luke Wadding along with the small works of Saint Francis at Antwerp in 1623 in quarto.*

*Bellarmine enumerates several other writings by Lyra in "On Ecclesiastical Writers," page 369; Bale lists more in "Centuria" 5, chapter 12; and Wadding lists several in "On the Writers of the Minorite Order," page 266, where he indicates the locations where certain manuscripts of those treatises are preserved.*

<margin>1320.</margin>
**ALBERTINO MUSSATO**, an Italian by nation and a Paduan by birth, was a poet and historian of no small renown for the standards of his age. He died an exile at Chioggia <note>original: "Clodii"</note> in the year 1329, but was buried in his native city. He wrote *Sixteen books on the Deeds of Henry VII, Emperor of the Germans, the Priapeia, the Eccerinis, a Book on Fate, and certain other things*, which were published with the notes and emendations of Lorenzo Pignoria, Osio, and Villani, printed at *Venice in 1635 in folio.*

<margin>1320. *Century 12, chapter 41.</margin>
**ANDREW HORNE**, an Englishman by nation, and—unless Bale has guessed incorrectly—a native of Gloucester, was most devoted to the study of English municipal law. He flourished in the year 1320. Bale acknowledges that Horne's exact age was unknown to him, nor does he hand down anything else about him except that he was very well-versed in history and, having gathered the "Flowers of Histories" from various sources, he composed the *Chronicle of Gloucester*. That chronicle has long since perished. However, another small work survives which entirely escaped Bale’s notice, from which the author's age can be certainly defined. For Andrew wrote a summary of English forensic law <note>Common Law</note>, which he wished to be called the *Mirror of Justices* <note>original: "Speculum Justiciariorum"</note>, in the French language—which is accustomed to be used in the English courts according to ancient custom. <note>This refers to "Law French," the Anglo-Norman dialect used in English legal proceedings for centuries.</note> From this work, it is clear that the author composed it under King Edward II, but before the year 1324. He died after the year 1343, in which year he argued the case of the Abbot of Waltham in court, as shown by testimony drawn from the forensic archives and placed at the beginning of the work. A man no less skilled in sacred literature than in jurisprudence, he wished for no laws to be used in the English courts unless they were consistent with Holy Scripture and natural law; accordingly, in the final part of the work, he enumerates English customs contrary to either and urges their abolition. The *Mirror of Justices* was published in French at *London in 1642 in octavo*, and was translated into English...

# The Century of Wyclif.

...translated in London, 1646, in octavo. Furthermore, Andrew <note>Andrew Horne (c. 1270–1328), an English legal writer and Chamberlain of London.</note> deservedly holds a place in our catalog; not only because he establishes Holy Scripture as the sole norm of jurisprudence, but also because he presented an illustrious testimony of the English Church's faith concerning the Canonical books of Scripture. Indeed, since the book is unknown to foreigners and little known even to our own countrymen (excepting legal scholars), I believe it will not be unpleasant to the reader to place the full text here. After he had prefaced that the entire forensic law was founded in Holy Scripture, and had divided the whole of Scripture into the Old and New Testaments, he reviewed the twenty-two books of the Old Testament according to the Hebrew tradition, and then added*: <note>original: "Et outre ceux sont autre liures en l' viel Testament, tout soit ne soient elles authoritez Canon, sicome, Tobie, Judith, Maccabes, Ecclesiasticus."</note> *And besides those, there are other books in the Old Testament, even though they may not be of canonical authority; for example, Tobias, Judith, the books of Maccabees, and Ecclesiasticus.* <note>Ecclesiasticus is also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note>

<margin>1321.</margin>
**PETER AURIOL**, a Frenchman by birth, born at Verberie on the Oise River, called the **Eloquent Doctor** <note>original: "Doctor Facundus." Medieval scholars were often given "epithets" or nicknames that described their intellectual style.</note>, entered the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>. He strenuously opposed the election of Michael of Cesena as General of the Order in 1316 at the assembly in Naples. In the year 1318, by papal mandate, he received a license to teach publicly at the University of Paris, having been granted the highest rank of Master. He lectured on the *Master of the Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard textbook for medieval theology students.</note> until the year 1321, on the 3rd day before the Calends of March, when he was elevated to the Archbishopric of Aix in France. He died on the 27th of April, but in which year is not certain—certainly after the year 1345, in which he wrote the *Compendium of the Bible*. Those who enroll him in the list of Cardinals are surely mistaken, as are perhaps those who wish him to have been a disciple of John Duns Scotus.

->W O R K S .<-

*Commentaries on the four books of the Sentences*, of which those on the first book were published through the care of Cardinal Sarnanus at *Rome, 1595, in folio*; those on the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th books appeared in the *same place, 1605, in folio*.
*Various Quodlibets* <note>A "Quodlibet" was a formal academic debate where a teacher answered "any question" posed by students.</note>, published with the 2nd volume of the *Commentaries* at *Rome, 1605*.
*Compendium of the Bible*, or an Epitome of the entire Holy Scripture according to the literal sense. Published at *Venice 1507, Strasbourg 1514, Paris 1565, Venice 1571*; and by the care of Étienne Noellet at *Paris, 1585*.
*Treatise on the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin*, which is said to have been published at *Toulouse in 1514*.

<margin>1322.</margin>
**JOHN BASSOLIS**, a Scot by nation, as it is said, called the **Most Orderly Doctor** <note>original: "Doctor Ordinatissimus."</note>, a fellow of the Order of Friars Minor and a disciple of John Duns Scotus. He was beloved by Scotus above all others for his talent, so much so that Scotus used to say that if Bassolis alone were present, there was a sufficient audience. In 1313 at Reims, and in 1322 (the year in which he was most famous), he lectured as a Master on the *Sentences* at Mechelen. It is not clear when he died. His *Commentaries or Lectures on the four books of the Sentences* exist, published by the care of Oronce Finé of Dauphiné at *Paris, 1517, in folio*. *His Philosophical and Medical Miscellanies were published in the same place.*

<margin>1323.</margin>
**BERNARD GUI**, a Frenchman by birth from the Limousin region, originating from the village of Royères near Roche-l'Abeille, was born of humble status in the year 1260. In 1280, he joined the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>. In 1294, having been a Lecturer at the monastery of Albi, he was made Prior; in 1297 he was appointed Prior of Carcassonne, in 1299 of Castres, and in 1301 of Limoges. In 1305, he was named Inquisitor against the Albigensians <note>A dualist religious movement in Southern France targeted by the Catholic Church.</note> of Toulouse, and in 1317 he was elected Procurator of his Order at the Roman Court. Four years later, he was sent to Italy by Pope John XXII to conciliate and confirm peace between cities. In 1323, he received the Bishopric of Tuy in Galicia as a reward for his long service; the following year he was moved to the see of Lodève...

...transferred to Narbonne Gaul <note>Narbonne is a city in Southern France; at the time, this referred to a specific ecclesiastical province.</note>. He died in the year 1331, on the 13th day of November, and was buried among the Dominicans of Limoges.

->WRITINGS.<-

A brief history *On the Foundation of the Orders of Grandmont and Artige, and of the Monastery of St. Augustine at Limoges*, brought down to the year 1313. It is found in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*, Volume 2, page 275.

*The Deeds of the Counts of Toulouse*, published by Catel at Toulouse, 1623, in folio.

*The Life of St. Fulcran, Bishop of Lodève*. It is contained in Bollandus’s collection under February 13th.

*The Life of St. Glodefidis the Virgin*, written by a certain Abbot Bernard, perhaps our author; it is found in Surius’s collection under July 25th.

*The Mirror of the Saints* <note>original: "Speculum Sanctorale"</note>, dedicated to Pope John XXII, which treats the lives of Christ, all the Saints, and the Martyrs in four books, or rather volumes. The manuscript exists in the Library of the Preachers <note>The "Preachers" refers to the Dominican Order.</note> at Avignon. Labbe provided his dedicatory letter and Preface in the same work, page 513, and he presents the names and deeds of the Bishops of Limoges from St. Martial down to the year 1273, excerpted from this work, on page 265. He also includes the *History of St. Thomas of Canterbury* on page 515, and various other *Lives of Saints* scattered elsewhere. From this same work, Fr. Bosquet published the *Lives of Popes Clement V and John XX* <note>Usually John XXII; the numbering of the Popes named John was historically inconsistent.</note>, and others have published other parts.

*The Historical Mirror of the Roman Popes, and the Emperors and Kings of France* up to the year 1322. It was written by the command of his General, Berengar, and dedicated to John XXII. The manuscript exists in the Colbert Library and among the Preachers at Avignon.

*The Acts of all the General Chapters of the Dominican Order* from the founding of the Order to his own times, collected and arranged by order of General Aymeric. The manuscripts are held by the Dominicans at Toulouse.

*The Practice of the Inquisition* <note>original: "Practica Inquisitionis." This is Bernard Gui's most famous work, serving as a manual for inquisitors in identifying and questioning heretics.</note>. A manuscript in the same location.

*A brief Treatise on the times and years of general and particular Councils*. *A Treatise on the Office of the Mass*, *On the Precepts of the Decalogue*, *On the Apostles and the Seventy-Two Disciples*, *On the Bishops of Toulouse*, *Sayings of the Holy Fathers and Doctors on original sin*, *On the Articles of Faith and the Sacraments of the Church*, and certain other works in manuscript in the Colbert Library, according to the testimony of the famous Casimir Oudin in his *Supplement*, page 595.

<margin>
1324.

* Defense of the Peace, Book 2, chapter 18.
</margin>
**MARSILIUS OF PADUA**, also called **MENANDRINUS**, an Italian by nationality and a citizen of Padua. He was educated in the elements of jurisprudence at the Academy of Orléans, as he himself reveals *; a most celebrated philosopher and jurist of his time and a counselor to Emperor Louis the Bavarian. He flourished in the year 1324, at which time, being indignant that the Imperial Majesty was being trampled upon by papal tyranny, he published that noble work, *The Defender of Peace* <note>original: "Defensorem Pacis." This work was revolutionary for arguing that the state should be independent of the church.</note>. In this book, he proves with sharp intellect and erudition that the Emperor is so far from being subject to the Pope, that the Pope ought to be subject to the Emperor—not only in temporal matters, but even in spiritual matters regarding the regulation of the external discipline of the Church. He brilliantly depicts the pride, ambition, and luxury of the Roman court; he demonstrates at length that the Roman Pope possesses not even the slightest prerogative of power or preeminence over other bishops by divine right. Driven to a frenzy by such boldness from Marsilius, John XXII issued a lengthy decree in 1327, in which he devoted him to dire curses and plucked apart his arguments as best he could. Hence it is no wonder that he is still numbered among the condemned authors in the Roman *Index of Prohibited Books*. Marsilius died at Montemalto in mid-September, 1328. His extant works include: *The Defender of Peace, or Three Books on Imperial and Papal Power against the usurped jurisdiction of the Roman Pope*, published at Basel, 1522, in folio; at Frankfurt, 1612 and 1623, in octavo; and in Goldast’s *Monarchia*, Volume 2, page 154. *On Imperial Jurisdiction in Matrimonial Causes*, in the same work, page 1383. *A Treatise on the Transfer of the Empire*, in the same work, page 147; and in the *Antilogia of the Pope* edited by Weissenburg at Basel, 1555, in octavo, which that most learned man and my very dear friend, Edward Brown, saw fit to reprint in his Appendix to the *Collection of Things to be Sought* <note>original: "Fasciculum Rerum Expetendarum." This was a famous collection of documents highlighting the need for Church reform.</note>, London, 1688, in folio, page 55.

# The Century of Wyclif.

<margin>1325.</margin>
PETER BERTRAND, of the French nation, a citizen of the town of Annonay in the jurisdiction of Viviers, son of Matthias Bertrand and brother of William, Bishop of Noyon. He was a professor of Canon and Civil Law <note>original: "Juris Pontificii ac Cæsarei"</note> in the Universities of Avignon, Montpellier, Orléans, and Paris; a Royal Councilor, and eventually Chancellor to Joan, Queen of the Franks. Originally the Dean of the Church of Le Puy, he first became Bishop of Nevers, and then, in the year 1325, was made Bishop of Autun. In the year 1329, along with William, Archbishop of Sens, and other Prelates, he argued vigorously before King Philip of Valois for ecclesiastical immunity against Peter de Cugnières, the Royal Advocate. On December 20, 1331, he was named a Cardinal of the Roman Church with the title of Saint Clement by Pope John XXII. In 1341, he founded the College of Autun at his own expense. He died in Avignon on June 24, 1349. There exists his *Short Book on Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction, or the Acts of the dispute against Peter de Cugnières for the liberty of the Gallican Church* <note>The "Gallican Church" refers to the Roman Catholic Church in France, which often sought a degree of independence from papal interference.</note>, published separately in *Paris, 1495, in quarto*, and in Goldast’s *Monarchy*, Volume 2, page 1361. Also, his *Treatise on the Origin and Use of Jurisdictions, or on Spiritual and Temporal Jurisdiction*, was published among other legal treatises in *Venice, 1584*, Volume 12, page 408. Both works are contained in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26.

---

<margin>1326.</margin>
PETER OF DUISBURG, likely a native of Duisburg, a brother and Priest of the Teutonic Order. He flourished in the year 1326, at which time he testifies to having completed his history in a dedicatory letter to Werner von Orseln, the Master of the Teutonic Knights, who was elected in 1325 and killed in 1330. Thus, Oudin is most foully mistaken in assigning Peter to the year 1420. Peter wrote the *Chronicle of Prussia, or the History of the Teutonic Order*, from its first institution in 1190 up to the year 1326, which was continued by a certain unknown author to the year 1435. Christoph Hartknoch was the first to rescue it from obscurity, illustrating it with notes and expanding it with nineteen dissertations on *Prussian Antiquities*, publishing it at *Jena, 1679, in quarto*.

---

<margin>1327.</margin>
<margin>against the Jews</margin>
ANDRONICUS, a native of Constantinople, descended from the Imperial lineage of the Comneni. He flourished around the year 1327. There exists his *Dialogue against the Jews* in Latin, from the version by Jean de Livineu, in Steuart’s *Supplement to the Council of Ingolstadt, 1616, in quarto*, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26, page 38. The following also seem to have Andronicus as their author: *A Dialogue against the Latins on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, *A Disputation of the Emperor with the Doctor of the Armenians, Peter, on the two natures in Christ and other matters*, and *A Writing against John Veccus*. These are preserved as manuscripts in the Bavarian Library, Codex 120, according to Possevino’s *Catalogue*, page 62.

---

<margin>1329.</margin>
JOHN BACON, or Baconthorpe, of the English nation, arising from the humble village of Baconsthorpe in the territory of Norfolk; he was called the *Resolute Doctor*. In his early youth, he joined the Carmelites of the monastery at Blakeney near Walsingham. He was sent by them first to Oxford and then to Paris, obtaining doctorates in both and in Holy Theology. He achieved such great fame that he was commonly regarded as the "Prince of the Averroists" <note>Averroists were followers of the philosopher Averroes, who attempted to harmonize Aristotle's philosophy with religious faith, sometimes leading to controversial views on the soul and creation.</note>. Having returned home, after several years he was elected the twelfth Provincial of the Carmelites in England at a general meeting of the Brothers held in London in the year 1329. Summoned to Rome for four years to offer his opinion on very serious questions regarding marriage, he was met with hisses during the dispute when he attributed too much authority to the Pope regarding the divine laws of marriage and the granting of dispensations. Being warned of his error, Bacon investigated the truth of the matter more sharply; he acknowledged his fault and modestly sang his recantation <note>original: "Palinodiam," a poem or song retracting a previous statement.</note>. He then contended that the power to dispense within degrees of kinship prohibited by divine law does not exist, and from that point on, he began to detest sophistry as being most ruinous to the Christian faith. He died in the year 1346 and was buried in London.
