->WRITINGS.<-

<margin>1329.</margin>
**GERARD ODONIS**, of the French nation, from the district of Rouergue, born in Châteauroux, called the *Moral Doctor*. He was a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>, and finally, in the year 1329, he was made Minister General at the Assembly in Paris, substituted in place of Michael of Cesena. This was done through the favor of Pope John XXII, to whom he was very close. I will pass over the many embassies committed to him by the Pope—two to Sicily, one to England, and another to Bosnia in Croatia; he was eventually appointed the Latin Patriarch of Antioch <note>original: "Pseudo-Patriarcha"</note> and the perpetual Administrator of the Church of Catania in Sicily. He died in Catania in the year 1349. His extant works include *Commentaries on the ten books of Aristotle's Ethics*, Venice, 1500; the *Office of the Stigmata of St. Francis*, which is still recited by Franciscans today; a *Treatise on Biblical Figures*, in manuscript at the Monastery of Mirepoix; *Two Philosophical Questions on Light and the divisibility of matter*, in manuscript in the Vatican Library; *Commentaries on the four books of the Sentences*; and *on various books of Holy Scripture*; as well as certain other works, according to Wadding in his *Library of the Order of Friars Minor, page 145.*

<margin>1329.</margin>
**JOHN CANON**, called by others "the Canonist," an Englishman by birth, a member of the Franciscan Order, highly skilled in theological matters and not ignorant of Canon Law. He was prominent in the year 1329. Having laid the first foundations of theology at Oxford, he moved to Paris to hear his countryman John Duns Scotus, who was teaching there with great glory. Having obtained the Master’s degree <note>original: "Pileum Magistralem"</note>, he taught theology in Paris for some time; but upon returning to England, he lectured at Oxford until his death. He wrote *Commentaries on the Master of the Sentences; Masterly Lectures; Disputed Questions; and on the eight books of Aristotle’s Physics.* These were published in Venice in 1492, and again in 1516 under the care of Francesco of Montefeltro, a professor of philosophy among the Franciscans in Venice.

<margin>1330.

* On Non-Ecclesiastical Writers, Vol. ii. p. 122.</margin>
**WILLIAM OF OCKHAM**, or **OCCAM**, an Englishman, born in the village of that name in the county of Surrey, called the *Singular Doctor* and the *Venerable Inceptor* <note>This title indicates he had completed all requirements for a doctorate except the formal inception or "commencement."</note>. A member of the Order of Friars Minor, he is to be numbered among the greatest and most prodigious minds, according to Jacopo Gaddi*. He was a disciple of John Duns Scotus, though he later became his sharpest critic, to the point that he either established or restored a different sect known as the *Nominalists* <note>A philosophical school arguing that universal concepts (like "humanity") are merely names, not real things.</note>. He was prominent in the year 1330, though he had been famous for his writings long before. At the start of the century, he held the chair of Theology at the University of Paris; he brilliantly defended the side of King Philip the Fair of France against Pope Boniface [VIII] by publishing a book *On Ecclesiastical and Secular Power*. Having been made the Provincial of the Franciscans in England, he was present in the year 1322 at the General Chapter of his Order held in Perugia; there, by the unanimous vote of the Franciscans, it was defined that to assert that Christ and the Apostles possessed nothing, either individually or in common, was not heretical (as Pope John [XXII] wished it to be believed) but sound and orthodox. Once the Chapter was dissolved, Ockham preached this same doctrine everywhere, and especially in Bologna; until in the following year...

# PETER OF LA PALUD, <margin>1330.</margin>
a Burgundian by birth, son of Gerard of Varembon, Lord <term>Toparch: a local ruler or governor</term> of Bresse; a monk of the Dominican Order, distinguished in the knowledge of Theology and Canon Law, and a most powerful champion of the doctrine of St. Thomas Aquinas. In the year 1314, he earned the rank of Licentiate <note>A degree between a Bachelor's and a Doctorate, granting the license to teach.</note> at the University of Paris. In 1325, he was appointed among others by Joan, Queen of France, to manage her last will and testament. He flourished around the year 1330, at which time he was appointed Patriarch of Jerusalem. He died on the last day of January, 1342, in Paris; or, as others say, on the island of Cyprus, with his body being brought back to Paris after death.

**ADAM GODDAM**, or Woodham, an Englishman by birth, often simply <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς</note> called "The Englishman," apparently from Norwich (for he spent the greatest part of his life in Norwich). He was a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>, a Doctor of Sacred Theology, and a Professor at Oxford. A disciple of William of Ockham, he flourished in the year 1330. He died in the year 1358 and was buried at Babwell near Bury St. Edmunds. He wrote *Commentaries on the Four Books of Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences*, which were published in print in *Paris*, 1512. Bale lists many other works in Century 5, chapter 98, which still lie hidden and unpublished.

<margin>1330.</margin>
**WALTER OF HEMINGFORD**, an Englishman by birth, and a Canon Regular of the Augustinian Order at the Monastery of Gisburn, near Cleveland in the county of Yorkshire. He flourished in the year 1330. He died at Gisburn in the year 1347 and was buried in his monastery. He wrote a *History of the Deeds of the Kings of England from William the Bastard* <note>William the Conqueror</note> to the times of King Edward II; namely, from the year 1066 to the year 1308, if we trust Bale <margin>* Century 5, chapter 71.</margin> and Vossius <margin>† On the Latin Historians, book 2, chapter 65.</margin> †. The illustrious Gale used a shorter copy, and in a small note prefixed to that History recently published by him, he mentions that the History produced by Walter only reached the year 1066. However, I have seen another manuscript copy of the same at Cambridge, in Corpus Christi College, which proceeds until the year 1313 and ends with these words: *The land was silent and at rest.* <note>original: "Terra siluit & quievit."</note> There also exists a manuscript of the same author’s *History of Edward II*, which, however—if I do not misremember—is nothing other than the final part of the aforementioned History, which, having progressed to the year 1308, narrates the deeds performed in the first six years of Edward II. Furthermore, the illustrious Gale took care to publish the first part of that History (namely from 1066 to 1273) among the *Five Writers of English History*, *Oxford* 1687, folio; promising that he would publish the rest shortly. Besides these annals, there are manuscripts held in the Cotton Library <margin>* Under the image of Nero, D. 2. number 19.</margin> * of the *Deeds of Edward III* written by our Walter; however, it is necessary that they only touch upon the early years of Edward III, since Walter died approximately thirty years before that King.

<margin>1330.</margin>
**LUDOLPH OF SAXONY**, called Landulph by some, a Saxon by birth. After completing 26 or 30 years in the Dominican profession, he joined the Carthusian Order in the Monastery of Mainz, and was later made Prior of the Carthusians of Strasbourg. He flourished in the year 1330. He was a truly pious writer, and elegant beyond the standard of his age. In what year he died is uncertain.

<margin>1331.</margin>
**BARTHOLOMEW OF SAN CONCORDIO**, an Italian by nationality from the city of Pisa and a monk of the Dominican Order <note>The Order of Preachers</note>, flourished in the year 1331. He died in the year 1347. He must be carefully distinguished from Bartholomew Albizzi, a Franciscan from the same home city of Pisa, about whom more is written below. There exists his *Summary of Cases of Conscience*, called the *Pisanella* or the *Magistruccia* <note>meaning "The Little Master" or "The Little Pisan"</note>, which he completed in the year 1338; and his *Lenten Sermons*; both published together in Lyon, 1519, in octavo.

<margin>1332.</margin>
**THOMAS WALLEIS**, called "the Welshman" and "the Englishman" (being English by nationality and, as it seems, a Welsh-Briton by birth), was an Oxford theologian and a monk of the Dominican Order. He flourished in the year 1332, at which time, while delivering a sermon at Avignon <note>The seat of the Papacy at the time</note> before the entire Papal court on the feast of St. John the Evangelist, he strongly asserted the doctrine of the immediate vision of God <note>The "Beatific Vision"—the belief that souls see God immediately after death rather than waiting until the Last Judgment</note> and accused the presiding Pope John XXII of heresy. Consequently, he was committed to prison by the Pope, but was soon released at the request of the King of France and the University of Paris. This Thomas is distinct from our other Thomas Jorz, an Englishman and Cardinal of Sabina who died in 1311; however, his writings are so often confused with the writings of Jorz that it is impossible to distinguish which belong to Jorz and which to our Thomas. It is only certain that all of them cannot belong to both at once, as Altamura suggests. Nevertheless, a great part of the works ascribed to Jorz can, not without merit, be considered to have this Walleis as their author. Certainly, to him belong the *Heretical Articles* and the *Small Book on the Theory of Preaching* addressed to Theobald de Ursini, Archbishop of Palermo. Bale provides a fairly ample catalog of Thomas Walleis's works in Century 5, chapter 35, as does Pits for the 14th century, page 429.

<margin>1333.</margin>
<margin>* Familiar Letters, book 3, ep. 1.</margin>
**RICHARD OF BURY**, surnamed *Aungerville*, was English by nationality, from the county of Suffolk, born in Bury St. Edmunds, the son of Sir Richard Aungerville. Educated at Oxford University, he became so distinguished in learning that he was deemed worthy to be placed in charge of the education of Edward, Prince of Wales (afterwards King of England). Following his pupil to France after Edward was taken there by his mother Isabella, he served him as Treasurer in the regions of Gascony. Finally, after Edward took power in 1326, Richard obtained the highest dignities of the Court, being appointed first as Cofferer, then Treasurer of the Wardrobe, and soon Keeper of the Privy Seal; he was also twice sent as an ambassador to the Pope before the year 1333. At the beginning of 1333, he was named Dean of Wells, and by the end of the year, he was declared Bishop of Durham, consecrated on December 19th by Adam, Bishop of Winchester, at Chertsey. In the following year, he was made Lord Chancellor of England, and after two years, Lord Treasurer. He died at Auckland in the year 1345, on the 24th of April, at the age of 59. He was a clearly most learned man (Petrarch, who made distinguished mention of him *, calls him a man of "ardent genius"), most munificent, and most famous for the holiness of his character. He was especially noted for his immense zeal toward literature and the learned, whom he pursued with such love that he was deservedly considered the unique Maecenas <note>A famous Roman patron of the arts; here meaning a great financial supporter of scholars</note> of the educated of his century; he sent out from his own household the primary prelates and doctors of England. Having founded a most beautiful library at Oxford, he wrote in 1344 the *Philobiblon, or a Book on the Love of Books and the Institution of Libraries*, which was issued in print at *Speyer* in 1483; *Paris*, 1500, in quarto; edited by Thomas James at *Oxford*, 1599, in quarto; and with the Philological Letters edited by Goldast at *Frankfurt*, 1610, in octavo, page 400.

# The Century of Wyclif.

<note>original: "Sæculum Wicklevianum." Named after John Wyclif, a 14th-century reformer.</note>

...not having been found by reason of age, he founded it; but he corrupted it with the most foul fables which are interwoven almost everywhere, so that in the judgment of Isaac Casaubon <note>A famous classical scholar (1559–1614)</note>, it is not worth a single leaf of coltsfoot <note>original: "farfari." A common weed used here to imply the work is worthless</note>. That work consisted of twenty-three books, bringing the history from the birth of Christ down to the death of Leo the Philosopher in the year 911; it was dedicated to the Emperor Andronicus Palaeologus the Elder. Eighteen of these books survive today, which progress from the birth of Christ to the death of the Emperor Phocas in the year 610 of the Christian era. The only copy of this history remaining in the Christian world was snatched by a Turkish soldier from the library of King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary at Buda <note>Modern-day Budapest</note> and sold in the marketplace at Constantinople. Having been redeemed by a certain Christian, after many changes of fortune it came into the Imperial Library at Vienna, where it is now preserved. Joannes Langius prepared a Latin version of it, printed at Basel in 1553 and Antwerp in 1560 and 1562, with Langius’s notes added in 1573 and Frankfurt in 1588. It also appeared in Greek and Latin edited by Fronto le Duc <note>original: "Frontonis Ducæi"</note> in Paris, 1630, in two folio volumes. Furthermore, Philippe Labbe published **Nicephorus’s** *Metric Catalog of the Emperors of Constantinople and the Patriarchal See of Constantinople*, written more fully in prose, in his *Introduction to the Byzantine Writers*, Paris, 1648, page 34. There also appeared his *Synopsis of all Scripture arranged in Iambic Trimeters*, together with a prayer of intercession to God, in Greek, at Basel, 1536, in octavo.

**MATTHEW BLASTARES**, a Greek legal expert and Hieromonk <note>A monk who is also an ordained priest</note>, flourished in the year 1335, in which he compiled the *Alphabetic Arrangement of Canons* <note>original: "Alphabeticum Canonum Syntagma"</note>. This *Arrangement*, or *Alphabetic Synopsis of matters contained in the Holy Canons*, was published by the illustrious William Beveridge in Greek and Latin in the *Pandects of Canons*, Oxford, 1672, Volume 2, part 2, page 1. Likewise, his *Small Work on the Causes or Questions of Marriage* in Greek and Latin appears in Leunclavius’s *Greco-Roman Law*, book 8, page 478. A Greek version of the *Donation of Constantine the Great* <note>A famous (though later proven forged) document in which the Emperor Constantine supposedly gave authority over the Western Roman Empire to the Pope</note>, also prepared by him, appeared elsewhere in quarto along with the responses of Balsamon. J. B. Catumsyritus, an Italo-Greek, defended our Blastares against Arcudius in his book *On the Harmony of the Sacraments*, page 131. Before I leave this matter, let me note an error of the learned man Louis Ellies du Pin, who, in his *New Library of Ecclesiastical Writers* recently published in the French language, asserts that Blastares’s *Arrangement of Canons* has not yet been printed.

<margin>1335.</margin>
**BENEDICT XII**, formerly called *James Fournier*, was born at Saverdun on the Ariège river near the Pyrenees in the province of Toulouse. The son of a humble miller, he became a Doctor of Theology at Paris and professed the monastic life among the Cistercians at the Monastery of Bolbonne in the Diocese of Mirepoix. He was subsequently Abbot of Fontfroide <note>original: "Montis Frigidi"</note> in the Diocese of Narbonne, then Bishop of Pamiers, soon after Bishop of Mirepoix, and later created Cardinal-Priest with the title of Saint Prisca by his uncle John XXII in the year 1327. After his uncle's death, he was elected Roman Pontiff at Avignon on December 20, 1334, and inaugurated on January 8, 1335. At the beginning of his papacy, he condemned fifty-five "heresies," as he called them—articles regarding the poverty of Christ and the perfection of the monastic state and of Christ, which were being propagated by the Franciscans. In the year 1336, he defined that the souls of the blessed are admitted to the vision of God <note>The "Beatific Vision"—the belief that souls see God immediately after death</note> immediately after death, condemning the opinion of his predecessor John. In the year 1337, he excommunicated King John of Bohemia for violating ecclesiastical immunity. He not only denied absolution to the Emperor Louis the Bavarian, though he sought it often, but he also strengthened the censures of John XXII. Furthermore, he convinced the Visconti and other governors of cities and provinces appointed by the Emperors in Italy to cast off the Prince's yoke, seize their own provinces, and govern them henceforth under their own authority. Finally, he exhorted the Senate and People of Rome to administer the senatorial dignity—which they had hitherto held in the Emperor’s name and stead—under his own auspices and those of the Church. Provoked by so many injuries, the Emperor held a convention at Frankfurt in 1338 in the presence of Edward III, King of England, where, by the common counsel of princes and bishops, he issued a decree.

## SIMON FIDATUS OF CASCIA, an Italian by birth, took his surname from Cascia, a village in the territory of the Hernici where he was born. An Augustinian Hermit, he was distinguished for the holiness of his life and his eloquence in preaching. He flourished in the year 1335. Having built the Monastery of Saint Catherine for noble matrons and virgins—nuns of his own Order—at Mount Saint Caii in Florence five years earlier, he filled it and governed it until his death. He died on February 2, 1348. He was a man (in the judgment of the most learned Cardinal Bona <margin>* *Notes on Authors*, book on divine Psalmody, page 37.</margin>) remarkably pious and fervent; his notable work is *On the Deeds of the Lord Savior* <note>original: "de Gestis Domini Salvatoris"</note>, dedicated to Tommaso Corsini, a Florentine legal expert, published in *Cologne, 1540, in folio*. There is also a *Book on the Blessed Virgin, Basel, 1517*. He also wrote the aforementioned works. For there exist *fifteen Books of Interpretations of Evangelical Truth, or on the Deeds of the Lord Savior* dedicated to the Florentine legal expert Tommaso Corsini, published in *Cologne, 1540, in folio*. He also wrote a *Book on the Mirror of the Cross, a Book of Letters to various people, and other works in both the vernacular and the Latin language*; a list of these is provided by Joseph Pamphilus in the *Chronicle of the Augustinian Hermits*, page 51.

<margin>1336.</margin>
## GIOVANNI ANDREA <note>Latin: Joannes Andreas</note>, an Italian by nationality and a native of Mugello, was the son of John the Priest. Having been educated in letters by his father as well as by Bonifacio of Bergamo, he came to Bologna. There he applied himself so successfully to Papal Law <term>Canon Law</term> that he was considered the most celebrated legal expert <term>jurisconsult</term> of his century. He was a pupil of Martino de Sulmannis. He flourished in the year 1336. After teaching at Bologna for 45 years, he died of the plague in that same city on July 7, 1348. He had a son, Bonicontus, an excellent legal expert, who died before his father, having achieved great fame through several writings.

<margin>1336.</margin>
**GIOVANNI D’ANDREA**, an Italian by nation and a native of Mugello, was the son of John the Priest. Educated in letters by his father as well as by Bonifacio of Bergamo, he came to Bologna, where he devoted himself to Pontifical Law <note>Canon Law</note> with such success that he was considered the most celebrated of the <term>Jurisconsults</term> <note>legal experts</note> of his century. He was a disciple of Martino de Sulmani. He flourished in the year 1336. After teaching at Bologna for forty-five years, he died of the plague in that same city on the 7th day of July, 1348. He had a son, Bonicontus, an exceptional jurist, who died prematurely before his father after having gained a great reputation for himself through several writings.

### W R I T I N G S.

*The Novellae*, or Commentaries on the five books of the *Decretals* <note>original: "Decretalium," the papal decrees that formed the basis of medieval church law</note>. Published at Venice, 1581.
*Mercurial Glosses on the sixth book and the Clementines*, published in the same place, and at Lyon in 1572.
*Feudal Questions, as well as on Marriages, and Local Interdicts.* Venice, 1584.
*The Tree of Consanguinity, Affinity, and Cognation, both spiritual and legal.* Basel, 1517.
Additions to the *Speculum* <note>The "Mirror of Law"</note> of William Durand, Bishop of Mende, and a *Book on the Praises of St. Jerome* are attributed to him; these, in my opinion, have not yet been published.

<margin>1337.</margin>
**WILHELM VON BOLDENSELE**, a <term>Gilded Knight</term> <note>original: "Eques Auratus," a member of an order of knighthood, often the Order of the Golden Spur</note> of Jerusalem, flourished in the year 1337. At the request of Talleyrand, Count of Périgord and Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, he wrote a *History of the journey to the Holy Land undertaken by himself*. This *Travelogue* <note>original: "Hodoporicon"</note> survives, together with a *Letter* to Peter, Abbot of the Royal Court <note>Aula Regia</note> of the Cistercian Order in the Diocese of Prague, found in Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, Vol. 5, part 2, p. 96.

# The Century of Wyclif
<note>Named for the English reformer John Wyclif, this section covers the 14th-century figures whose work often prefigured the Reformation or debated the limits of papal power.</note>

<margin>
14th CENTURY
from the Year 1300.
1337.
</margin>
**ARNALDUS CESCOMES**, Archbishop of Tarragona, in the year 1337 wrote *Two Letters on driving the Saracens from Spain*; these are found in Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, Volume 2, page 267.

<margin>
1337.
</margin>
**WALTER BURLEY**, an Englishman, called the <term>Doctor Planus & Perspicuus</term> <note>original: "Plain and Clear Doctor," a Scholastic title reflecting his direct style of argumentation</note>, was a secular priest, though in the opinion of some he was a member of the Franciscan Order. An alumnus of Merton College at Oxford University, he later traveled to Paris, where he obtained the dignity of Master not without the highest praise for his learning. He heard John Duns Scotus teaching at both Oxford and Paris; however, upon returning to Oxford, he most sharply attacked Scotus's doctrine. He achieved a distinguished reputation for learning and served as a tutor to the most invincible Prince Edward III. He flourished, or as others say, died in the year 1337. Certainly, he was still occupied in writing books in that year at the age of 62. He wrote *Commentaries on the Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, and *innumerable philosophical works*; of these, several have seen the light of day, namely: *An Exposition on the eight books of Aristotle's Ethics*, Venice, 1521; *Questions on Aristotle’s Physics*, Venice, 1501; *On Porphyry’s Introduction, Gilbert de la Porrée, and the Old Art* <note>original: "Isagogen Porphyrii, Gilbertum Porretanum, & Artem veterem." The "Old Art" refers to the early logical works of Aristotle and Porphyry</note>, Venice, 1497, 1509; *On the Intension and Remission of Forms*, Venice, 1519; *Commentaries on Aristotle’s Posterior Analytics*, Oxford, 1517, in quarto, and Venice, 1552, 1504, 1537; *On State, Matter, and Form, and on Relatives*, Oxford, 1500, in quarto; and *On the Lives of the Philosophers*, 1472, in quarto. Bale (Century 5, chapter 42) and Pits (page 441) will provide the rest.

<margin>
1338.
</margin>
**JOHN OF JANDUN**, also known as John of Ghent from his birthplace, called the *Doctor of Perugia*, was a philosopher and theologian of no small renown. He strenuously defended the side of Emperor Louis against Pope John XXII, for which reason he was excommunicated by the Pope along with Marsilius of Padua. He died in the year 1338, in which he wrote the *Booklet for the Superiority of the Emperor*. This treatise exists as the *Instruction on Nullity: The Process of Pope John XXII against Emperor Louis regarding the Superiority of the Emperor in Temporal Matters*, found in Goldast’s *Monarchia*, Volume 1, page 18. His *Quodlibetal Questions* <note>Scholastic exercises where a teacher answered "whatever" questions posed by students</note> were published by Marsilio Ficino; and Goldast testifies <margin>* Preface to Volume 1.</margin> that he had read John's *Commentaries on the Books of the Sentences*. I, for my part, have been unable to find the place or time of that edition despite diligent search. Furthermore, many of his *Philosophical Works* exist, namely: *Questions on Aristotle’s Physics*, Venice, 1501, 1544, and Florence, 1485; *Commentaries on his Metaphysics*, Venice, 1525; *Questions on the three books On the Soul*, Vicenza, 1486, and Venice, 1497, 1561; *On the Heavens and the World*, and *On Averroes’ On the Substance of the Orb*, Venice, 1488, 1501; and perhaps others of lesser importance.

<margin>
1340.
</margin>
**BARLAAM**, a Calabrian by birth from the city of Seminara, was a monk of the Order of St. Basil and a man most highly refined in every branch of literature, <term>sharp in understanding and most capable at explaining what he understood, having mastered the depths of Euclid, Aristotle, and Plato; and most of all in these matters</term> <note>original Greek: "νοῆσαί τε ὀξὺς, καὶ νοηθέντα ἐξηγήσασθαι ἱκανώτατος, τή τε Εὐκλείδου καὶ Ἀριστοτέλους καὶ Πλάτωνος ἐκμελετήσας τὰ βάθη· τὸ δὲ μάλισθ' ὡς πρὸς ταῦτα ὧν"</note>, as Cantacuzenus says <margin>* History, book 2, chapter 39.</margin>. Having first been educated among the Latins, he agreed with the Latins against the Greeks. Later, crossing over to the camp of the Greeks, he strongly attacked the Latins in his writings; yet in the meantime, he gave cause for a most serious dispute among the Greeks. For having first arrived in Thessaloniki, he began to inquire into the customs, institutions, and doctrines of the Greek monks—especially those who called themselves <term>Hesychasts</term> <note>original Greek: "ἡσυχαστὰς," meaning those who seek "divine quiet" through contemplative prayer</note>. When he discovered that certain less-than-orthodox views were held by them, he hurried to Constantinople, where he was honorably received by John Cantacuzenus. He accused the monks of heresy before the Patriarch John and summoned Gregory Akindynos to be his <term>assistant</term>. The monks, having obtained Gregory Palamas as their leader, vigorously defended their cause and threw the charge of heresy back upon Barlaam. Meanwhile, Barlaam earned the favor of Emperor Andronicus by publishing many writings against the Latins and was appointed Abbot of the Monastery of the Holy Savior. A Synod was finally called around the year 1337, and both sides clashed with writings and arguments. Palamas contended that the light which surrounded Christ on Mount Tabor <note>A reference to the Transfiguration of Jesus</note> was something uncreated, natural, and a co-eternal light of God. Barlaam, on the other hand, asserted that the light neither emanated from the divine essence nor was the divine essence itself; and furthermore, that bodily eyes...

# The Century of Wyclif
<note>Named for the English reformer John Wyclif, this section documents the era's scholars and their debates over church authority and theology.</note>

Appendix *E*

<meta>catchword: WRITINGS.</meta>

...that no more divine power could be raised so high as to behold the deity.
<margin>14th CENTURY from the Year 1300.</margin>
The Synod defined nothing for either side; however, it censured the insolence and petulance of Barlaam in disputation with a sufficiently sharp rebuke. It imposed silence on Palamas <note>Gregory Palamas, the primary defender of Hesychasm, a mystical tradition of prayer in the Eastern Church</note> no less than on Barlaam. Barlaam cried out that an injustice had been done to him; and supported by the favor of the Emperor, he by no means ceased to attack his adversaries. In the year 1339, sent as a legate by the Emperor Alexios <note>The text likely refers to Emperor Andronikos III, though it notes "as it seems"</note>, he undertook a journey to Avignon. There, before Pope John <note>John XXII, though by 1339 Benedict XII was Pope; the text reflects the long-standing negotiations at the Avignon Papacy</note> in a <term>Consistory</term> <note>A formal meeting of the College of Cardinals presided over by the Pope</note> of Cardinals, he spoke at length to persuade them to call a General Synod to discuss the controversies on both sides. He sang to deaf ears. For the Pope did not wish for it unless the Greek Church would completely surrender. Therefore, having returned to Constantinople, Barlaam turned himself to his accustomed studies. He flourished in the year 1340. In the following year, after the death of Emperor Andronikos, the Palamites—who had drawn Cantacuzenus <note>John VI Kantakouzenos, a Byzantine statesman and later Emperor</note> to their side—acted entirely as they pleased. Barlaam secretly withdrew from Constantinople; after his departure, he was frequently condemned and excommunicated in many Synods. Meanwhile, having settled in the West, he defected to the side of the Latins and sharply attacked the dogmas of the Greeks in his writings. Shortly thereafter, he was appointed Bishop of Gerace in the Kingdom of Naples. It is not certain in which year he died. Those who, due to their ignorance of history, cannot reconcile the contradictory writings of Barlaam, talk nonsense when they split him into two different writers: one a Greek Monk and the other the Bishop of Gerace.

### W R I T I N G S.

*A Book against the Primacy of the Pope*, first edited in Greek and Latin by Johannes Luidus at *Oxford*, 1592, in quarto. It appeared with the notes of Salmasius <note>Claude Saumaise, a renowned French classical scholar</note>, then still a boy, at *Hanau*, 1608, in octavo. Finally, in his more advanced age, it was attached to the end of his books on the *Primacy of the Pope*, *Leiden*, 1645, in quarto.

*Logistica*, or *Algebraic Arithmetic* in six books. Greek and Latin, Strasbourg, 1572, in octavo; Paris, 1600, in quarto.

*Two Letters to friends residing in Greece regarding the Primacy of the Roman Church*. In Latin, found in Bzovius <note>Abraham Bzovius, a Dominican historian</note> at the year 1331, section 13.

*A Letter to Alexios Calothetus*, written on behalf of the Latins before his appointment as Bishop. Found in the same source at the year 1330, section 59.

*A Response to the Letter of Demetrius of Thessalonica on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. Found in the same source at the year 1332, section 5.

*A Proof through the Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son*. Found in the same source at the year 1333, section 2. <note>This "Procession" refers to the Filioque controversy, a central theological dispute between the Western and Eastern churches</note>

*Orations for the union of the Greeks with the Roman Church*, delivered to Pope Benedict XII at Avignon. Found in the same source at the year 1339, section 25.

*Ethics according to the Stoics* in two books. These appeared together with the aforementioned Letters and Orations, in Latin, in Canisius, Volume 6, page 4, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26.

Leo Allatius <note>A Greek scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note> testifies in *On Consent*, book 2, chapter 17, section 1, that he has read eighteen of Barlaam's treatises *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* against the Latins, two on the union of the Churches, and two on the Primacy of the Pope.

<margin>1340.</margin>
### MAXIMUS PLANUDES,
A Greek monk, a man learned in both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note> and cultivated in all branches of learning. He was especially dear to the elder Emperor Andronikos, by whom he was sent as a legate to Aquileia before the year 1327, along with Leo Orphanotrophos, to appease the Venetians who were angry with the Greeks. He flourished in the year 1340. He was still writing in the year 1353. Even his adversaries praise his doctrine and erudition. For thus Cardinal Bessarion <note>A famous 15th-century scholar-cardinal who sought to reconcile the Greek and Latin churches</note> addresses him long after his death:
> <note>original Greek: "Ου γὰρ ἂν ἐγὼ σὲ ἀνδρῶν..."</note> For I would not judge you poorly, O best and wisest of men, who were so practiced in every education, so advanced in philosophy and theory, having traveled through all the sciences and achieved fame in all, and who, in addition to Greek, had mastered the language of the Latins to the highest degree.

"For I would not think ill of you, O best and most wise man, who were occupied in every exercise of the disciplines," etc.

<margin>1340.</margin> GREGORY ACINDYNUS, a Greek monk and a follower of Barlaam. He was a most bitter enemy of Palamas and the Hesychast monks <note>Hesychasts were mystics who sought to see the "uncreated light" of God through silent prayer</note>, and indeed of the Latins. He flourished in the year 1340. About three years earlier, he had assisted Barlaam when he was acting against Palamas in the Synod of Constantinople, and together with him, he experienced the heavy censure of the Synod. Nevertheless, being a man of a restless nature, he did not hesitate to publicly accuse the Palamites of heresy. For this reason, he was called to judgment by Patriarch Joseph in the year 1341 in the Synod of Constantinople and ordered to observe silence under the penalty of anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note>. In the year 1347, when Cantacuzenos gained power and Isidore was elevated to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, he was condemned and excommunicated in frequent synods; thereafter he led an obscure and idle life. There exists an *Iambic Poem on the Heresies of Gregory Palamas*, in Greek, in Leo Allatius's *Orthodox Greece*, Volume 1, from pages 756 to 770. Two fragments in Greek and Latin are found in the same author's *On Consent*, book 2, chapter 16, section 3. There are also held in the Bavarian Library Greek manuscripts of Acindynus's two books (though mutilated) *On the Essence and Operation of God against Palamas, Gregoras, and Philotheus*. Jacob Gretser inserted summaries of these chapters into his notes on the *History of Cantacuzenos*, and from there Bzovius put them into his *Annals* for the year 1337, section 8. Finally, Gretser published the entire work at *Ingolstadt* in 1616.

# RICHARD ROLLE OF HAMPOLE, wrongly called *Pampolitanus* by some, but whose true surname was *Rolle*, was English by nation and a native of York. A Doctor of Theology and a hermit of the Order of Saint Augustine, he lived a hermit's life near the Hampole nunnery, situated four miles from Doncaster in the county of York. He flourished in the year 1340. He died in the year 1349 on the feast of Saint Michael <note>September 29</note> and was buried in the Monastery of Hampole. He seems to have obtained the title of "Saint" among his countrymen after his death. Indeed, a manuscript is held in the Cottonian Library <margin>* Under the shelfmark Tiberius A. 15.</margin> titled *The Office of Saint Richard, Hermit of Hampole*, which treats his life and miracles.

*The Prick of Conscience* <note>original: "Stimulus Conscientiæ"</note>, a work composed in English verse and divided into seven parts. I saw this manuscript in the Lambeth Library of the Archbishop of Canterbury, in quarto.
That he translated the Psalter into the English language, and that in his comments on that verse of David—"take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth"—he set forth his judgment on the necessity of vernacular Scriptures, is testified by the Most Reverend [James] Ussher in his manuscript *Specimen of the Dogmatic History of Controversies*, citing a certain manuscript codex.
Other works, which have not yet been published, are listed in a long line by [John] Bale and [John] Pits; the manuscripts are listed by [Thomas] James in *Eclogues*, part 2, page 35.

# ROBERT HOLCOT, English by nation and born in Northampton, was a monk of the Dominican Order and a Doctor and Professor of Theology at the University of Oxford. He flourished in the year 1340. **PHILIP OF MONCALIERI**, or of Genoa, born in the Subalpine region <note>Modern-day Piedmont, Italy</note>, a monk of the Order of Friars Minor [Franciscans], first professed in the Convent of Toulouse, then later Lecturer of the Convent of the Holy Place of Padua. **HENRY OF URIMARIA**, or Frimaria, German by nation and a native of Thuringia, an Augustinian Hermit, most devoted to Sacred Scripture and Aristotelian Philosophy, and a Doctor of Theology at the University of Paris. He flourished in the year 1340. Joseph Pamphilus <margin>* Chronicle of the Hermit Order, p. 40. † Apparatus Vol. 1, p. 733.</margin> and Possevinus, drawing from Jordan, honor his boundless benevolence toward the poor and his piety toward God with distinguished praise. They offer remarkable evidence of his charity, yet they depict his piety in such a way that we cannot help but suspect he was touched by a degree of "enthusiasm" <note>In this period, "enthusiasm" often referred to mystical ecstasies or claims of direct divine inspiration, which later historians sometimes viewed with skepticism</note>. Regardless, both authors attribute to him the glory of many miracles in life and in death. He died at a great age, after having endured immense pains of the kidneys and bladder for two years.

---
->W R I T I N G S.<-

*Additions to the Books of the Sentences*. Published together with the Commentaries of Giles of Rome, *Cologne, 1513.*
*Book on the Fourfold Impulse. Venice, 1498.* This was wrongly attributed to another Henry of the Dominican Order.
*Sermons on the Passion of the Lord and on the Saints. Hanau, 1513.* Also published with the preceding book, *Paris, 1514.*
*The Preceptorium*, which was frequently published under the name of Nicholas of Lyra, is attributed to him by some.
Many other of his manuscript works are listed by Joseph Pamphilus and, following him, Antonio Possevinus in the places cited.

<margin>1340.</margin>
**LUPOLD OF BEBENBURG**, or *Babenberg*, called Ludolph and Liutolf by some, German by nation, from the noble family of Bebenburche. A Professor of Both Laws <note>Civil and Canon Law</note> and a student of Johannes Andreae at the University of Bologna. Originally a Canon of Mainz, Würzburg, and Bamberg, he was made Bishop of Bamberg around the year 1340. So say Trithemius and Pantaleon. <margin>* On the Illustrious Men of Germany, part 2, p. 328.</margin> There are, however, some who deny the rank of Bishop to Lupold entirely. There exists his *Book to Rudolf, Duke of Saxony, On the Zeal of the Ancient Kings of Gaul toward the Princes of Germany*, in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26, page 88. Also his *Book on the Rights of the Kingdom and Empire* addressed to Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier, *Strasbourg, 1508, in quarto*. Both treatises were published together in *Paris, 1540; Cologne, 1564, in octavo; Basel, 1497, 1566; Strasbourg, 1603, 1609.*

# The Century of Wyclif
<note>This era is named after the English reformer John Wyclif (c. 1320–1384), whose influence defined the late 14th century.</note>

<margin>14th CENTURY from the Year 1300. — 1340.</margin>

## ALVARUS PELAGIUS,

or in reverse order Pelagius Alvarus, a Spaniard by nationality, a Galician by birth, born of a lineage not only of the lowest rank but even of shameful origin <note>This likely refers to being born out of wedlock, a common biographical detail in medieval clerical records</note>. He rose from being a cleric of the Diocese of Compostela and a Doctor of Canon Law <note>original: "Decretorum Doctore"</note> at Bologna to become a member of the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> in the year 1304, during the general Chapter held at Assisi. He then devoted himself to the study of Theology at Pisa; and having set out for Paris <note>original: "Lutetiam"</note>, he heard the teachings of John Duns Scotus <note>A hugely influential Franciscan philosopher-theologian known as the "Subtle Doctor"</note>. Around the year 1329, having defended the cause of Pope John XXII against Michael of Cesena <note>The Franciscan leader who broke with the Pope over the issue of apostolic poverty</note>, he was named an Apostolic Penitentiary. In the year 1332, on the 16th day before the Calends of July <note>June 16th</note>, he was appointed Bishop of Koroni in Achaia <note>In modern-day Greece</note>, and before the year 1340, Bishop of Silves in Lusitania <note>Modern-day Portugal</note>. It is not well established when he died. There exist two books *On the Lament of the Church* <note>original: "de Planetu Ecclesiæ"</note> dedicated to Peter Gomez, the Franciscan General, which Alvarus, having drafted them ten years earlier, corrected at Compostela in the year 1340. They were published at Ulm in 1474, at Lyon in 1517, and at Venice in 1560. He also wrote a *Summa of Theology*, Ulm 1474; the *Eye-Salve of Faith against Heresies* <note>original: "Collyrium Fidei"</note>, a manuscript in the Vatican and Colbertine libraries; and a lengthy sermon on the vision of souls delivered before Pope John XXII, in which he defends the Pope’s opinion. This is held in manuscript in the Library of Toledo. Other writings of his are mentioned by Wadding in the *Scriptores Ordinis Minorum* <note>Writers of the Order of Friars Minor</note>, page 15.

<margin>1342.</margin>

## JOHN KANTAKOUZENOS,

a native of Byzantium <note>Constantinople</note>, descended from the most illustrious Kantakouzenos family. His father was the Governor of the Peloponnese, whom he lost while still a boy when the father was only 21 years old. His mother was Theodora Palaeologina, a most distinguished woman, to whom the Emperor Michael I Palaeologus was a great-uncle. After he had been educated in literature and the science of military discipline to an uncommon degree in his youth, he was moved to the handling of the highest affairs of the Empire and began to shine in the court and the city. He married Irene, daughter of Andronicus Asan, the Grand Duke, and granddaughter of the elder Emperor Andronicus by his sister; by her, he had six children, three sons and as many daughters. Initially appointed Prefect of the Sacred Bedchamber <note>Grand Chamberlain</note> by the elder Emperor Andronicus, he lost the Emperor's favor around the year 1320 when he was found to be a partisan of the younger Andronicus, with whom he had cultivated a singular friendship from childhood. He was then appointed Grand Domestic <note>Commander-in-chief of the army</note> and Governor of Thrace by the younger Andronicus. Finally, when the younger Andronicus seized the reins of the Empire around the year 1328 and deposed his grandfather, he heaped honors and wealth upon Kantakouzenos, put him in command of the entire military, and desired him as a colleague in the Empire, though he did not obtain this because of Kantakouzenos's reluctance. The Emperor never did anything without his advice or against his will. Finally, dying in the year 1341, he committed to him both the guardianship of his son John Palaeologus, a boy of nine years, and the protection of the Empire. Kantakouzenos undertook the province entrusted to him no less vigorously than faithfully, until—due to the dissensions stirred up by the Empress Anna (mother of the Emperor John), John the Patriarch, and other nobles of Constantinople—he withdrew from the Court at the end of the same year into Macedonia, and was immediately declared a public enemy by Anna. A vast number of nobles and soldiers quickly flocked to Kantakouzenos; they compelled him, though he resisted for a long time, to don the imperial purple at Didymoticho. In the following year, on the 21st of May, he was crowned Emperor at Hadrianopolis <note>modern Edirne</note> with solemn pomp by Lazarus, the Patriarch of Jerusalem. After a war waged for five years, Kantakouzenos emerged victorious, and having captured Constantinople at the start of the year 1347, he gave John Palaeologus fair terms of peace: that both should retain the right to the Empire, though with unequal authority until John reached maturity, and thereafter with equal standing. On the 13th of May, he was crowned Emperor by Isidore, the Patriarch of Constantinople (whom he had substituted for John); and after a few days, he gave his daughter Helena in marriage to the Emperor John, to whom she had formerly been betrothed. Truly, the harmony between the imperial colleagues remained unshaken for only a short time. Suspicions having been sharpened into mutual hostilities, it came to arms again. The victorious John brought Constantinople under his power in the year 1355. Four days later, Kantakouzenos—who had long contemplated the abdication of the Empire and did not wish to prolong the civil war any further (even though his forces were not yet so worn down that he lacked the means to resist)—voluntarily and gladly shut himself away in the Monastery of Mangana near Constantinople. Changing his name from John to Joasaph or Josaphat, he cut his hair and put on the monastic habit; he detested war to such an extent that he joined his son Matthew, the Despot of the Peloponnese, with John Palaeologus by arms...

Having returned to the monastery, he gave himself entirely to the study of piety and letters, and having written a history of the things he had done, he cheered his unhappy old age. It is not clear for how many years he survived after laying down the purple <note>A phrase meaning to abdicate the imperial throne</note>; however, it is certain that he survived for many. There are those who maintain that he lived until the year 1374. At the urging of Nilus, and having taken for himself the fictitious name of Joasaph Stodulus <note>Joasaph of the Stoudios Monastery</note>, he wrote in an elegant no less than diffuse style a *History* of the deeds performed by the two Emperors named Andronicus and himself, from the year 1320 to 1360, in four books; this was preceded by a *Genealogy* of the preceding Andronicus Emperors from the year 1195 to 1320. Cardinal Bona <margin>* Note on the Author in the book on *Divine Psalmody*.</margin>, a most learned man, truly said of him: *“An exceptional historian, but extolling his own deeds too much.”* For he depicts his own deeds quite magnificently for the most part; and he is not ashamed to sometimes run off into his own praises. This *History* was published in Latin from the version by Jacob Pontanus along with his and Gretser’s notes at *Ingolstadt*, 1603, in folio; and in Greek and Latin with the notes of both at *Paris*, 1645, in 3 volumes, folio. There exist three *Orations* of the same man, and four *Apologies or Assertions for the Christian Faith against the Saracens and the Quran* <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> in Greek and Latin, edited by Rodolphus Gualtherus at *Basel*, 1543, folio, and with the Quran at *Basel*, 1555. His *Antirrhêtika* <note>Greek: ’Αντιῤῥητικά, meaning "Refutations"</note>, or *Contradictions against Prochorus Cydonius*, are also held in manuscript in the Vatican Library.

<margin>1342.</margin> **CLEMENT VI**, previously called Pierre Roger, a Frenchman by nationality, from the region of Limousin, originating from the town of Maumont, or as others say, Mont-Mal, the son of William. He was first a monk, then Abbot of the Monastery of Chaise-Dieu in Auvergne of the Benedictine Order; afterwards, having set out for Paris <note>original: "Lutetiam"</note> for the sake of theological studies, he became known to Pope John XXII, by whom he was successively made Prior of Saint-Baudile of Nîmes, Abbot of Fécamp in Normandy, Bishop of Arras <note>original: "Atrebatensis"</note>, Archbishop of Sens, and then in the year 1330 of Rouen. He was declared Cardinal Priest with the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus by Benedict XII in the year 1337. After the death of Benedict in the year 1342, on the 7th day of May, he was elected Roman Pontiff at Avignon, and crowned on the 19th day. At the beginning of his pontificate, in order to soothe the Romans who were irritated by the long absence of the Popes <note>This refers to the "Babylonian Captivity" of the Papacy in Avignon rather than Rome</note>, he reduced the Jubilee from every hundredth year to every fiftieth. He declared Emperor Louis [of Bavaria], who was bitterly pursuing his rights in Italy, to be a heretic and bound him with anathema <note>A formal ecclesiastical curse or excommunication</note>. When he was later asked more wisely by Louis for absolution, he refused to grant it by any other law than that Louis should hand over Occam <note>William of Ockham, the famous nominalist philosopher who fled to the Emperor's protection</note>, cancel his acts against the Popes, decree by edict that the Empire was a gift <note>original: "beneficium"</note> of the Roman See, confess that he himself had been a heretic, lay down the Empire, and not resume it except by the Pope's will. When Louis refused such unjust conditions, he bound him again with anathema in the year 1346; and he ordered the Electors to choose another Emperor for themselves shortly, who would prefer to have a king given to them by the Pope. In the year 1348, he bought the city of Avignon from Joanna, Queen of Naples and Sicily; and a little later he excommunicated her. He died at Avignon in the year 1352, on the 6th day of December. There exists an *Encyclical Letter against the Flagellant Heretics* <note>The Flagellants were a medieval religious sect that publicly whipped themselves as penance for sins</note> in the Councils, Volume 11, page 1876; another concerning the *Bishopric of Ossory* <note>original: "Offorensi"</note> in Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, Vol. 4, page 508; 10 others in Bzovius for the year 1342, etc.; 30 others in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors*, Vol. 3, for the years 1342 and 1343, folio 212; and in the same in the *Pontifical Register*, page 263. *17 others* in the same, Vol. 4, for the years 1351 and 1352; *39 others* in the same in the *Pontifical Register*, page 1. Several manuscript volumes of his *Letters and Decretals* exist in the Vatican Library. A *Proposal* made by him while he was still Archbishop of Rouen before the Pope and Cardinals in Consistory is in manuscript in the Pembroke Library at Cambridge, codex 89, number 1. The rest will be provided by Louis Jacob de Saint-Charles in his *Pontifical Library*, page 55.

He was active in the theological schools of Paris and Bologna, and bore a name among the most celebrated writers of his century. He flourished in the year 1343, at about which time he was appointed Bishop of Urbino by Pope Clement VI. For the sake of the Pontifical authority, which he [defended] in writing against the supporters of Emperor Louis...

# The Century of Wyclif
<note>This era is named after the English reformer John Wyclif (c. 1320–1384), whose influence defined the late 14th century.</note>

<header>The Wyclifite Century.</header>

<margin>14th CENTURY from the Year 1300.</margin>
...he championed [these causes], and as a most valiant fighter, he earned the greatest favor among the Roman Pontiffs. He died in the year 1350. A diligent reader of the works of Augustine and Ambrose, he excerpted their most notable opinions and, having arranged them in alphabetical order, gave them the name *Milleloquium* <note>original: "Milleloquium," meaning "A Thousand Sayings"—a massive theological encyclopedia or concordance</note>. *The Thousand Sayings of St. Augustine* appeared (begun indeed by his teacher Augustine <note>referring to Agostino Triumphus of Ancona</note> and completed by Bartholomew) at Lyon in 1555. *The Thousand Sayings of St. Ambrose* appeared at Lyon in 1556. His *Treatise against the errors that were found in the time of Duke Louis of Bavaria* is held in manuscript in the Augustinian Convent in Rome. I believe he noted [for] error [William of] Ockham, Marsilius [of Padua], and other assertors of the just supremacy of Princes in temporal matters. He also wrote a *Treatise on the four gifts*, two books *On spiritual warfare*, an *Exposition of the Lenten Gospels*, and a *Compendium of the book of Giles of Rome on the governance of princes*; which have not yet, as far as I know, emerged from the shadows <note>a metaphor for remaining unpublished or in manuscript form</note>.

<margin>1345.</margin>
**NICEPHORUS GREGORAS**, or rather the son of Gregoras, born in Byzantium <note>Constantinople</note> around the year 1295. While still a youth, he was very close with the Patriarch John Glykys and drew knowledge of eloquence from him. As he grew older, he cultivated the friendship of Theodore Metochites, learned astronomy from him, and was as dear to him as a son. At twenty-seven years old, he began to seek the favor of Emperor Andronicus; and having delivered a panegyric speech in his praise, he was appointed Ecclesiastical Chartophylax <note>a high-ranking official who kept the archives and records</note>. In 1325, sent by the Emperor as an envoy to the "Kral" <note>original: "Cralen," a Slavic title for King</note> of the Triballians or Serbians, having overcome many difficulties and dangers, he finally conducted the business successfully. In 1327, when the elder Andronicus was defeated by his grandson, Gregoras—who had remained constant to the grandfather's side—shared in his misfortune; he was present when the elder died five years later and delivered the funeral oration. He also praised Theodore Metochites, who died a few days later, in a funeral speech. After the elder's death, he lived in the court of the younger Andronicus. In 1334, when legates of Pope John XXII arrived at Constantinople seeking a dialogue on religion, Gregoras—who, because of his exceptional learning, was to be joined to the theological disputants—urged that the disputation should be avoided by all means, and he succeeded. Around 1338, he used his authority to oppose Barlaam <note>Barlaam of Calabria, a key figure in the Hesychast controversy regarding the nature of divine light</note>, who was sowing strife in the Greek Church. In 1341, he praised the deceased Emperor Andronicus the younger from the rostra <note>the public speaking platforms</note> during the funeral rites. He flourished around the year 1345, at which time he prepared himself to compose his *History*; and he bravely defended the side of Gregory Akindynos against Palamas <note>Gregory Palamas, the leader of the Hesychast movement which Gregoras opposed</note>. Thus, at a Synod held by Patriarch Callistratus, he was condemned along with the other Akindynists and forced into silence under penalty of excommunication. Indignant at the sentence, he withdrew to the Monastery of Christ <note>likely the Chora Monastery in Constantinople</note>; and having sent out insolent writings everywhere, he did not cease to accuse the Emperor and Patriarch of injustice, the Greek Church of corruption, and the monks of laziness, luxury, and heresy. Therefore, ordered by Emperor Kantakouzenos to remain in the Monastery of Christ, he was forbidden any kind of conversation or exchange of letters. In 1355, after Kantakouzenos abdicated the Empire, he subjected the theological controversies and Gregoras’s accusations to the judgment of a Synod; and he convicted the man, being present, of slander and lies. It is not clear how long Gregoras survived this struggle.

### W R I T I N G S.

<margin>* Politics, book 1, chapter 9, section 12.</margin>
**B**yzantine History in eleven books, from the capture of Constantinople by the Latins [1204] until the death of the younger Andronicus, or from the year 1204 to 1341. Regarding this, [Justus] Lipsius gives such a judgment *: *“He wrote a history equal to that of Nicetas Choniates, but by no means with equal refinement or diligence, and he was more affected by the vices of his age. He is superfluous or wanders off; and he mixes his own affairs and speeches unsuitably, even foolishly; nevertheless, his judgments are frequent and mostly correct: the causes of events are carefully placed: piety is instilled, and many things are appropriately traced back to that first cause, that is, to God. Surely no other writer asserts providence and fate more strongly.”* Kantakouzenos bitterly complains that a great injury was done to himself and to Emperor Andronicus the younger by Gregoras, and that the truth of the deeds performed was mostly obscured by lies and slanders.

<margin>1345.</margin>
**THOMAS OF STRASBOURG** <note>original: "Thomas de Argentina"; Argentina was the Latin name for Strasbourg</note>, German by nationality, from Strasbourg by birth (from which he took his name), a Parisian theologian of the Order of Hermits of St. Augustine, was prominent in the year 1345. In that year, he was elected Prior General of the Order for a three-year term, according to the usual custom, at the Convention held in Paris on the 11th of July <note>original: "V. Id. Julii"</note>. In the year 1348, at the Chapter of Pavia, and again in 1351 at Basel, his leadership was extended for other three-year terms, as it was also at the Convention of Perugia in 1354. He died in Vienna in 1357. His *Commentaries on the four books of the Master of Sentences* <note>referring to the standard theological textbook by Peter Lombard</note> are extant, published in Strasbourg 1490, Venice 1564, Genoa 1585, and elsewhere. Furthermore, this Thomas of Strasbourg is distinct from another Thomas of Strasbourg of the Order of Preachers <note>Dominicans</note>, who was prominent in the year 1491 and wrote *Sermons, Meditations, Letters, and Questions*; concerning whom Trithemius and Simler write. I believe those works have not yet been published.

---

<margin>1347.</margin>
**THEOPHANES**, Greek by nationality, Archbishop of Nicaea, was prominent in the year 1347, a contemporary of Gregory Akindynos. He wrote a distinguished *Work against the Jews* divided into two volumes, and a *Harmony of the Old and New Testaments* against the same; in which he constructs the truth of the Christian faith at length and proves unanswerably that the Messiah has already come long ago. Antonio Possevino provides an accurate as well as lengthy analysis of both works in the *Sacred Apparatus*, volume II, p. 470. They are held as manuscripts in the Roman College of the Society of Jesus, donated by Francisco Torres <note>original: "Fr. Turriano"</note>. Certain parts of his *Parallels* were translated into Latin by Gonsalvo Ponce and published in Rome, 1550, in quarto. A *Doctrinal letter to the Priests of his province*, showing what the duty and office of a priest is; and *another to the people of Nicaea concerning the duty of a Christian*, where he teaches that the company of the followers of Akindynos <note>original: "Acindynistarum"</note> as well as the Jews must be avoided, are preserved as manuscripts in the Vatican Library, as testified by Possevino in the *Appendix to the Sacred Apparatus*, p. 16.

# The Wyclifite Century
<note>This era is named after the English reformer John Wyclif (c. 1320–1384), whose influence defined the late 14th century.</note>

<header>The Wyclifite Century.</header>

<margin>14th CENTURY. Year 1300.</margin>
The Archbishop of Armagh <note>Richard FitzRalph, d. 1360</note> in Ireland was appointed by Pope Clement VI by the right of Provision <note>A "provision" was a direct papal appointment to a church office, bypassing local elections.</note>, and was consecrated at Exeter by Bishop John Grandisson on July 8. Both before and after he took up his Bishopric, there was a state of chief enmity between him and the **Mendicant Friars**; at Oxford, in his theological lectures, he used to mock their vain and proud poverty with false wit, but once he became a Bishop, he attacked them with a sharper pen. Indeed, crossing over to England in the year 1356, and having held sermons in London, he published nine conclusions against them. The Friars immediately accused him of heresy before the Pope and arranged for him to be summoned to Avignon. Having set out there, he remained for three years; and he died there in the year 1360 on November 16, before the lawsuit was finished.

# The Wyclifite Century
<note>This era is named after the English reformer John Wyclif (c. 1320–1384), whose influence defined the late 14th century. This page specifically tracks the lives of two giants of the era: the "Profound Doctor" Thomas Bradwardine and the father of Humanism, Petrarch.</note>

<header>The Wyclifite Century.</header>

<margin>
14th CENTURY
from the Year 1300.
</margin>

Educated at Merton College <note>A prestigious college at Oxford University founded in 1264</note>, where he served the office of Proctor in the year 1325, and was later distinguished with a Doctorate in Theology. Called to the royal court by John Stratford, the Archbishop of Canterbury, he was made the confessor of King Edward III, and was gifted a Canonry at Lincoln and the Chancellorship of St. Paul's Cathedral in London. Having been admitted to the royal confessions, he followed the King as he carried his victorious arms through France; he was so conspicuous everywhere for his holiness of life and authority that there were those who attributed Edward’s remarkable victories to this man’s prayers and piety rather than to the bravery of the soldiers or the skill of the leader. In the year 1348, upon the death of Archbishop Stratford, he was elected Archbishop of Canterbury by the Canterbury Chapter; however, with the King and the Pope preferring [John de] Ufford for the position, he lost the dignity at that time. But Ufford having died in the month of June before his consecration, Bradwardine was elected a second time by the Chapter, confirmed simultaneously by the King and the Pope, and consecrated by Cardinal Bertrand at Avignon. Returning to England, he survived only forty days after his consecration and died in London, having not yet been enthroned at Canterbury.

-> S C R I P T S <-

**On the Cause of God and the Truth of Causes against Pelagius**, in three books <note>original: "De Causa Dei... contra Pelagium". This was Bradwardine's masterpiece, a defense of divine grace against the "Pelagian" idea that humans can earn salvation through free will.</note>, which he organized while Chancellor of London from lectures held at Oxford at the request of his fellow Mertonians. They were published through the care of the celebrated Henry Savile in London, 1618, in folio.
**Theoretical Geometry**, Paris, 1530. **Theoretical Arithmetic**, Paris, 1502. Both published together, Paris, 1512.
**Treatise on Proportions**, Venice, 1505.
Bale (Century 5, chapter 87) and Altamura (*Dominican Library*, pages 133, 489) list many other unpublished works of Bradwardine—though Altamura dreams <note>The author implies Altamura is mistaken</note> that he was a Dominican.

---

<margin>1350.</margin>
**FRANCESCO PETRARCH**, an Italian by nation, was born on July 20, 1304, in Arezzo in Tuscany (though others say Ancisa in the Florentine territory, the seat of Petrarch’s ancestors), to an exiled Florentine father. He was educated in the liberal arts at Avignon and Carpentras in France, with Dante Alighieri as his teacher <note>While Petrarch was influenced by Dante, the claim that Dante was his personal tutor is likely an exaggeration or legend.</note>. He devoted himself to the study of Law for five years at Montpellier and for three years at Bologna. In the year 1327, after the death of his father—who had driven him into the study of law almost against his will—he returned from Bologna to Avignon. Taken into the household of Cardinal Giovanni Colonna, he traveled through France and Italy. Soon he chose a seat for his studies in a pleasant French valley which the inhabitants call Vaucluse <note>original: "Clausam", meaning "enclosed valley"</note>, located fourteen miles from Avignon.

Though growing old in a private home, he was by no means hidden from fame; he was the Prince of his century in genius, eloquence, poetic fluency, and in a Latin elegance unknown for so many centuries. He was no less pious than learned, and he lashed the loose morals of his age—especially those of the Roman court—with a sharp pen. Not yet thirty-six years old, he was invited to Rome and Paris on one and the same day to receive the laurel crown <note>The "poet laureate" crown, a revival of an ancient Roman tradition.</note>. Having set out for Rome in the year 1341, on Easter Sunday (the 15th of April), he was crowned with laurel on the Capitoline Hill by Senator Orso [dell'Anguillara], in the presence of the Senate and a huge crowd of Roman nobles and foreigners. About to return to Vaucluse, he received the Archdeaconry of the Church of Parma as a gift. 

Finally leaving his French retreat and wandering through various places, as an old man he served as a Canon in Padua. He would have even been created a Cardinal by Benedict XII, if he had not refused the Pope the debauchery of his sister, a most elegant virgin—though there are those who contend that Petrarch had no sister <note>This scandalous anecdote reflects the intense contemporary criticism of the Avignon Papacy's morality.</note>. He flourished in the year 1350, being very dear to the greatest Princes of the Christian world, who vied with each other to be celebrated by Petrarch’s eloquent Muse. He grew old at Arquà in the territory of Padua, and there finally died, seized by a stroke, in the year 1374 on July 14, just one day shy of seventy years old; he was carried out in a distinguished procession and buried in a magnificent tomb. I will add this single eulogy of him by Erasmus:
<margin>* from the book *Ciceronianus*</margin>
"The Prince of blossoming eloquence among the Italians," he says *, "seems to be Francesco Petrarch, famous and great in his own age; now he is hardly in anyone's hands."

**NICOLAUS CABASILAS**, the nephew of Nilus Cabasilas of Thessalonica and of two other Archbishops on his sister's side; first he was a Curator of the Sacristy. While performing this duty, he was sent by the Patriarch John of Constantinople <note>original: "CP."</note> around the year 1346 to the Emperor Cantacuzenus to persuade him to abdicate the empire. In the year 1347, he was sent as an envoy to the Empress Anna in the Palace by Cantacuzenus, who had recently captured Constantinople, to propose the peace terms offered to her by the victor. Finally, upon the death of his uncle Nilus, he succeeded him in the see of Thessalonica. He flourished in the year 1350. He was indeed a most learned writer, but a most bitter enemy of the Latins <note>original: "Latinorum verò hostis acerrimus" — Cabasilas was a staunch defender of Orthodox theology against Roman Catholic influence</note>. Authors are silent regarding the time of his death.

<margin>1350.</margin>
## ROGER OF CONWAY <note>original: "Rogerus Connovius"</note>, an Englishman by nation and a Welsh-Briton by birth, who took his origin and surname from the very ancient coastal town of Conway. While still a youth, he was admitted into the Franciscan family and was sent to the University of Oxford by his fellow <term>Friars Minor</term> <note>The "Friars Minor" is the formal name for the Franciscan Order.</note>. Having been thoroughly taught in Theology and Scholastic Philosophy, he received doctoral honors and a distinguished reputation for learning. On account of this, he was appointed by his peers as a primary professor of theology and eventually as the Provincial Minister of all England. He flourished in the year 1350. At that time, a great controversy was burning between the secular clergy and the <term>Mendicant Orders</term> <note>Mendicants were "begging" orders like the Franciscans and Dominicans who relied on charity rather than land ownership.</note> concerning the hearing of confessions and the performance of other pastoral duties, which the Mendicants had claimed for themselves everywhere, trampling upon the authority of the Church laws. Richard, the Archbishop of Armagh <note>Richard FitzRalph (c. 1295–1360), a major critic of the friars.</note>, pleaded the cause of the clergy. Our Roger entered the arena on behalf of the Mendicants and published *A book on the hearing of confessions by the Regulars, against the reports of Armagh*. This work appeared together with the work of the Archbishop of Armagh at *Paris in 1496 and 1511*, and in Goldast’s *Monarchy, Volume II, page 1392*. Three of his *Questions on the poverty of Christ and temporal lordship* exist in manuscript in the possession of Wadding. His remaining writings are listed by Bale (*Century VI, chapter 7*) and Wadding (*On the Writers of the Order of Friars Minor, page 312*). Furthermore, Roger died in London in the year 1360 and was buried in the monastery of the Friars Minor.

---

<margin>1352.</margin>
## INNOCENT VI, previously called *Stephen*, French by nation, from the region of Limoges, the son of Albert. A Doctor of both Civil and Canon Law, he was first an Auditor of cases in the Apostolic Palace, then Bishop of Noyon, later Bishop of Clermont, Major Penitentiary, and Cardinal Bishop of Ostia. Finally, in the year 1352, he was elected Roman Pontiff at Avignon on the 18th and crowned on the 30th of December. In the year 1355, he permitted the Emperor Charles IV, who had entered Italy with an army, to be crowned at Rome by the Cardinals, but only on the condition that he enter the City on foot and promise under oath that he would soon depart Italy and not return thereafter until summoned by the Pope. The weak-willed Emperor did not reject these conditions; he took the oath and submitted the majesty of the Empire to the Pope's ambition. In the year 1359, Innocent was the first of all the Popes to obtain from the Romans the right to appoint a Senator over them. He died at Avignon on the 12th of September, 1362, and was buried with the Carthusians at Villeneuve. There exist *Two Epistles on the celebration of the feasts of St. Augustine and St. Edward the King in England* (*Council Collection, Volume XI, page 1930*); twenty-three others in Bzovius under the year 1353, etc.; thirty others in Wadding's *Franciscan Annals* under 1353, etc.; and eighty others in the same work in the *Register of the Popes, page 27*. It is said that fifteen volumes of letters, or nineteen according to others, are preserved in manuscript in the Vatican Library.

He accused Barlaam of heresy and slander, while he himself was accused of being <unclear>a liar</unclear> <note>original Greek: ψευδέας (pseudeas)</note> by the other. The matter was brought before a Synod. Silence was imposed on both. Soon, however, the supreme authority having been handed to Cantacuzenus, Palamas—who was very familiar with him—obtained the condemnation of Barlaam in frequent Synods, though by no means were the sentences <insert>carried out</insert>. He successfully confirmed his own opinion concerning the Thaborite light <note>The "Thaborite light" refers to the light seen by the Apostles at the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor, which Palamas argued was uncreated divine energy.</note>. Around the year 1347, while war raged between the Emperors Cantacuzenus and Palaeologus, John the Patriarch <note>John XIV Kalekas</note>, suspecting Palamas of plotting against his throne, ordered him to be anathematized as a supporter of Cantacuzenus; when he refused to submit, the Patriarch cast him out of communion and shut him in prison. After Cantacuzenus took Constantinople, Palamas was released from prison by Empress Anna and sent as a legate to Victor <note>This likely refers to a Western or papal representative</note>, so that he might soften his anger against the family of the Palaeologi. After Patriarch John was ejected and immediately died, Palamas himself was designated Patriarch by Cantacuzenus; however, because the bishops preferred Isidore, he lost that dignity. At that time, it seems that the volume <term>Tomos</term> <note>A formal decree or volume of theological definitions.</note> which is read in Leo Allatius’s *On the Perpetual Agreement*, book 2, chapter 16, section 4 (Greek and Latin), was composed by certain clerics of Patriarch John, in which Isidore as well as Palamas are anathematized. Afterward, he was consecrated Archbishop of Thessalonica by Patriarch Isidore by order of Cantacuzenus, around the year (if I guess correctly) 1354; but not being admitted by the leaders of the city, he never obtained the seat. Therefore, he withdrew to Lemnos, where he enjoyed a comfortable leisure by the benefit of the Emperor. Shortly after, he was summoned from there by Patriarch Callistus to act against the Barlaamites and Akindynists in a Synod at Constantinople; he disputed strenuously and ensured that both were condemned by a synodal sentence. 

<margin>* History, Book 2, ch. 40.</margin>

It is not clear when he died. He was a man, according to the testimony of Cantacuzenus*, *distinguished not only in speech, but also most learned beyond others in the divine letters of Theology.* <note>original Greek: ἄλλων, ὃ λόγοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ τῆς Θεολογίας περὶ τὰς θείας ἐπικεκλημένας διαφέρων</note>

**GEORGE LECAPENUS**, a monk by vocation as it seems, lived in Thessaly and was an associate of Gregory Palamas; he flourished around the year 1354. At the start, it seems, of the year 1355, when he was asked by Emperor Cantacuzenus to invest his son Matthew with the imperial crown, he refused to comply and withdrew to the Monastery of Xamantis <note>Likely the Monastery of the Manganas in Constantinople</note>. Since he refused to return to his patriarchal duties, he was removed from the Patriarchate, and Philotheus was substituted in his place. Shortly after, when John Palaeologus took power, Callistus was restored to his see. In the following year, he was sent as an ambassador to Elizabeth, the widow of the Kral <note>original: "Cralis" — a Latinization of the South Slavic title 'Kral', meaning King</note> of Serbia, for the sake of confirming peace; there, at Pherae, the metropolis of the Serbians, he met his final day.

Whether that Homily belongs to this Callistus or the later one, the learned must decide; the same applies to the *Oration on the Dormition of the Mother of God* and another on the *Beheading of St. John the Baptist*, which exist as Greek manuscripts in the Imperial Library, according to Lambecius in his *Commentaries*, Book 4, page 62. The work *On the Monastic Life*, which is held as a Greek manuscript in the Barberini Library, seems to belong to the younger Callistus, according to Allatius in *On Consensus*, Book 2, Chapter 18, Section 13.

### PIERRE DE COLOMBIER

PIERRE DE COLOMBIER <note>Latin: Petrus de Columbario</note>, called by some *Pierre Bertrand the Younger*, was a Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. He flourished in the year 1355, when he was sent from Avignon to Rome by Pope Innocent VI to anoint and crown Emperor Charles IV; this he did on Easter Sunday of that same year. There exists a history of that journey and his return to Avignon, titled the *Roman Itinerary*, in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*, Volume 1, page 354.

1356.

### NICHOLAS EYMERIC

NICHOLAS EYMERIC, a Catalan by birth from Girona, was a member of the Dominican Order. He was appointed Inquisitor General of the faith throughout the entire jurisdiction of the King of Aragon by Pope Innocent VI in the year 1356. In 1371, he was made Chaplain and Chief Judge of cases by Gregory XI at Avignon. In 1375, he succeeded in having many of the teachings of Ramon Lull <note>A famous Majorcan philosopher and missionary whose mystical and logical works were controversial</note> condemned as heresy by the same Pope. He died in Girona at the Convent of St. Dominic on the 4th of January, 1399. His *Directory for Inquisitors* <note>Latin: "Directorium Inquisitorum," a famous manual for the interrogation and trial of heretics</note> exists, divided into three parts and published with the commentaries of Francisco Peña (Venice, 1595; Rome, 1578, 1587; and previously printed in Barcelona in 1503). Many other writings by Eymeric, still unpublished, are listed by Ambrogio de Altamura in the *Dominican Library*, page 142, and Oudin in his *Supplement*, page 667.

### DEMETRIUS CYDONES

DEMETRIUS CYDONES <note>Latin: Demetrius Cydonius</note>, or Cydo, a native of Byzantium (though Raphael Volaterranus calls him a Thessalonian), was a prominent courtier of Emperor Cantacuzenus and dear to him above others, serving as the Count of Private Affairs and a Secret Councilor. When Cantacuzenus, about two years before laying down the purple <note>The "purple" refers to the imperial office</note>, was contemplating retirement and the monastic life, Demetrius and Nicholas Cabasilas had the same intention in mind. Both were <note>original Greek: σοφίᾳ μὲν εἰς ἄκρον τῆς ἔξωθεν ἐπειλημμένοι, οὐχ ἧττον δὲ κᾀν ἔργοις φιλοσοφήσαντες, καὶ τὸν σώφρονα βίον, καὶ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ γάμου κακίαν ἀπηλλαγμένοι ᾑρημένοι</note> "attaining the very peak of worldly wisdom, and no less having lived as philosophers in their deeds, choosing a temperate life and remaining free from the distractions of marriage." Our subject flourished in the year 1357, entering the monastery alongside Emperor Cantacuzenus. Having left his homeland, he devoted himself to Latin literature and theology in Milan. Finally, having distributed his goods to the poor, he spent his life in a certain Cretan monastery and exchanged it for death.

**A** book *On the Accursed Dogmas of Gregory Palamas*, in which he recounts all the heresies of that man excerpted from his writings.
A book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, distributed into thirteen chapters. Both were published by Peter Arcadius among the *Golden Greek-Latin Works* with notes, printed in Rome, 1630.
A *Deliberative Oration to the Greeks on Not Returning Gallipoli*. Greek and Latin with notes, in Combefis, *New Addition*, Volume 2, page 1221.
