<margin>1357.</margin>
# RANULPH HIGDEN, or Hikeden, commonly called CESTRENSIS <note>Meaning "of Chester"</note>,

An Englishman by nationality, born in the Western region of the island, and a Benedictine Monk in the Monastery of Chester; he flourished in the year 1357. He died at a great age in the year 1363, in the sixty-fourth year of his life as a monk. When he had gathered a great store of materials from historians, especially English ones, he applied his mind to writing a history from the creation of the world. He composed this elegantly from the ancient historians, weaving in their complete and lengthy harmonies, yet always noting the names of the individuals from whom they were taken, and adding a marginal count of years from the time of Abraham. Indeed, he earned little more than the glory of a Compiler, except that in the final book he inserted much from his own store. Nevertheless, he performed the duty of a compiler so excellently that very few of our own historians can be compared with him in reliability, weight, and judgment. He gave the name *Polychronicon* <note>Greek for "The History of Many Ages"</note> to his work, and distributed the whole into seven books according to the number of the ages of the world and the days in which the world was created. The first book provides a topographical description of the world. The second proceeds from the creation of the world to the Babylonian Captivity of the Jews. The third from the Babylonian exile to the coming of Christ. The fourth from the birth of Christ to the arrival of the Saxons in England. The fifth from the Saxon landing to the arrival of the Danes. The sixth to the invasion of the Normans. The seventh down to his own times, specifically the year 1357. If some manuscripts carry the history further—as have occasionally fallen into my hands—it must be judged that this was added by another hand. For Ranulph himself, in the preface to the entire work, promises that he will bring the history down to that year; and at that point ends the English translation of the work made shortly after Ranulph’s death. Among the very many manuscript copies of this history that I have seen, by far the most beautiful is the one preserved in Gonville and Caius College (of which I myself was a student). 

By order of the noble Lord Thomas de Berkeley, John of Trevisa—a Cornish priest and Vicar of Berkeley—translated Ranulph’s *Polychronicon* into English; he was famous for many other writings, and especially for a complete English translation of both the Old and New Testaments. Into the translation of the *Polychronicon*, he wove several things of his own, though always with a distinguishing mark added, especially against the insolence and superstitions of the Monastic Orders, which he was accustomed to attack frequently. He brought the translation to an end, as appears from the note attached at the bottom, on April 18, 1387. Thus, [William] Caxton was clearly in error, either through carelessness or a typographical mistake, when he noted at the end of the version he printed that it was finished in the year 1357. For he [Caxton] updated the archaic style of the English language slightly and continued the history himself down to the year 1460, the first year of King Edward IV.

<margin>1357.</margin>
GREGORY OF RIMINI, an Italian by birth and from the city of Rimini, was a Doctor of Theology at Paris, an Augustinian Hermit, and, after the death of Thomas of Strasburg <note>Original: Thomas de Argentina</note>, the Prior General. He was elected at the assembly held at Montpellier on May 24, 1357. He died in Vienna the following year, sharing a tomb with Thomas of Strasburg. There exist his *Commentaries on the First and Second Books of the Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard medieval textbook for theology</note>, published in Valencia in 1500 and Venice in 1503. Also published were *Additions to his Writing on the Sentences* (Venice, 1522), *Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul and the Canonical Epistle of St. James*, and the *Book on Usury* (Rimini, 1522). Joseph Pamphilus, in his *Chronicle of the Order of Hermits* (page 58), mentions his *Book on Forms*, a *Treatise on the Customs of the Venetians*, and another *On the Conditions of the Florentines*. Simler and others also credit him with *Sermons for the Seasons and the Saints*.

---

<margin>1358.</margin>
ALPHONSUS VARGAS, Spanish by nation and from the city of Toledo, was an Augustinian Hermit. He taught Philosophy and Theology at the University of Paris for ten years and was made first Bishop of Badajoz <note>Original: Uffamensis/Pacensis</note> and finally Archbishop of Seville. He flourished in the year 1358. He died in Seville on October 13, 1359, or, as others maintain, on December 26, 1366. There exist his *Commentaries on the First Book of the Master of the Sentences* (dictated to his students at Paris in 1345), printed in Venice in 1490, and his *Questions on Aristotle’s Three Books on the Soul* (Vicenza, 1608; Venice, 1566).

---

<margin>1360.</margin>
NILUS, Metropolitan of Rhodes, a most bitter enemy of the Latins <note>Referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> and a follower of Gregory Palamas <note>A prominent Eastern Orthodox monk and theologian</note>, lived perhaps around the year 1360 (for I have not been able to trace his exact dates). If he was not a contemporary of Barlaam and Akindynos <note>Opponents of Palamas in the Hesychast controversy</note>, he was at least not much later than them; for he defines his positions in a Synod at Constantinople held by the Patriarch Isidore (which he calls the Ninth Synod), which condemned Barlaam. Whether this is the same Nilus who, according to Freher’s Chronology, became Patriarch of Constantinople in 1378, I cannot say. He stood on the side of those who condemned the Barlaamites as liars and in every way insane, and "more impious than other heretics" <note>Original Greek: κ’ ἀσεβέντας μᾶλλον τῶν ἄλλων αἱρετικῶν</note>, as he himself puts it. There exist in both Greek and Latin his *Brief Account of the Nine Holy and Ecumenical Synods*, published by the elder Justellus at the end of the *Nomocanon of Photius* (Paris, 1615, in 4to) and by the younger Justellus in the *Library of Canon Law* (ibid., 1661, folio, Vol. 2, page 1155). His *Oration on the Holy Matron from the Island of Chios* was published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius.

---

<margin>1360.</margin>
THOMAS STUBBS, or STOBAEUS, English by nation and from the city of York, was a Dominican monk and a Doctor of Sacred Theology. He flourished in the year 1360 and died after the year 1373. He wrote the *Lives or Chronicle of the Archbishops of York, from St. Paulinus to the death of John Thoresby*, or from the first founding of the see until the year 1373. That *Chronicle* exists among the *Ten Writers of England* published by the famous Twysden (London, 1652, folio, page 1685). Very many of his theological writings, still unpublished, are listed by Bale (Century 6, chapter 36), Pits (14th century, page 512), and Altamura in the *Dominican Library* (page 125).

<margin>1357.</margin>

**RANULPH HIGDEN**, or Hikeden, commonly called **OF CHESTER**, an Englishman by nation, born in the western region of the island, a Benedictine monk in the Abbey of Chester, flourished in the year 1357. He died an old man in the year 1363, in the sixty-fourth year of his monastic life. When he had gathered a great store of historians, especially English ones, he turned his mind to writing a history from the foundation of the world. He arranged it quite elegantly from those historians, weaving in their complete and lengthy accounts, yet attaching the names of each from whom they were taken, and adding a marginal calculation of years from the time of Abraham; thus he earned little glory other than that of a compiler, except that in the final book he inserted much from his own store. Nevertheless, he performed the duty of a compiler so excellently that very few of our own historians can be compared with him in reliability, gravity, and judgment. He gave his work the name *Polychronicon* <note>meaning "The History of Many Times"</note>; and distributed the whole into seven books, according to the number of the ages of the world and the days in which the world was created. The first book presents a topographical description of the world. The second proceeds from the foundation of the world to the Babylonian Captivity of the Jews. The third from the Babylonian migration to the coming of Christ. The fourth from the birth of Christ to the arrival of the Saxons in England. The fifth from the arrival of the Saxons to the arrival of the Danes. The sixth to the invasion of the Normans. The seventh to his own times, specifically the year 1357. If some copies carry the history further, such as have occasionally fallen into my hands, it must be considered that this was added by another hand; for Ranulph himself, in the preface of his work, promises that he will bring the history down to that year; and the English version of the work, finished shortly after Ranulph’s death, ends there. By far the most beautiful of the many manuscript copies of this history I have seen is the one kept in the College of Gonville and Caius (of which I myself was a student). At the order of the noble Lord Thomas of Berkeley, John of Trevisa, a Cornish priest and Vicar of Berkeley, translated Ranulph’s *Polychronicon* into English; he was also famous for many other writings, and especially for a complete English translation of both the Old and New Testaments. Into the translation of the *Polychronicon*, he wove some things of his own, always adding a mark of distinction, especially against the petulance and superstitions of the Monastic Orders, which he was accustomed to attack quite often. He brought the translation to an end in the year 1387, on the 18th day of April, as is clear from the note added at the conclusion: so that [William] Caxton was openly mistaken, whether by carelessness or a typographical error, who noted at the end of the version printed by him that it was finished in the year 1357. For he, having slightly changed the archaisms of the English language, continued the work himself until the year 1460, the first year of King Edward IV...

# The Wycliffite Century.

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY
from the Year 1300.
* Bale, Century 6, chapter 12.
† *The Corruption of the Fathers*, part 2, chapter 24.
</margin>
...published the printed version in London in 1482, in folio. This was William Caxton, who flourished under the king known as Edward <note>Edward IV</note> and was the first of all to bring the art of printing to England. John of Trevisa's translation itself, not yet polished by Caxton, survives in manuscript in the very well-furnished library of that most learned theologian of our nation, the Right Reverend Thomas Tenison. Furthermore, besides the aforementioned *Polychronicon*, Ranulph (whom others call Ralph) composed the *Distinctions of Theology*; the *Mirror of Curates*, which survives in manuscript in the library of Balliol College, Oxford, volume 69; a *Commentary on Job*; *On the Song of Songs*; *Sermons for the Year*; and certain other works which are listed by Bale.* To note this in passing: it is not unlikely that John of Trevisa's English translation of the Bible, which he completed by the command of his lord, Thomas de Berkeley, still survives in manuscript. Indeed, the illustrious Thomas James† reveals that three manuscript copies of a translation of the entire English Bible, completed long before Wycliffe, are preserved in the libraries of Oxford University.

<margin>1357.</margin>
**GREGORY OF RIMINI**, an Italian by birth and from the city of Rimini, was a Doctor of Theology at Paris and an Augustinian Hermit. After the death of Thomas of Strasbourg, he was elected Prior General at the assembly held in Montpellier on May 24, 1357. He died in Vienna the following year, sharing a tomb with Thomas of Strasbourg. His surviving works include: *Commentaries on the first and second books of the Sentences* <note>original: *Sententiarum*, the standard theological textbook by Peter Lombard</note>, published at Valencia in 1500 and Venice in 1503; *Additions to his Writings on the Sentences*, Venice, 1522; *Commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul* and the *Canonical Epistle of Saint James*; and a *Book on Usury*, Rimini, 1522. Joseph Pamphilus, in his *Chronicle of the Order of Hermits*, page 58, mentions his *Book on Forms*, a *Treatise on the Manners of the Venetians*, and another *On the Conditions of the Florentines*. Simler and others also attribute to him *Sermons for the Seasons* and *Sermons for the Saints*.

<margin>1358.</margin>
**ALPHONSUS VARGAS**, a Spaniard by nation and native of Toledo, was an Augustinian Hermit who taught philosophy and theology at the University of Paris for ten years. He was first made Bishop of Osma, then of Badajoz, and finally Archbishop of Seville. He flourished in the year 1358 and died in Seville on October 13, 1359, or, as others maintain, on December 26, 1366. His surviving works include: *Commentaries on the first book of the Master of the Sentences* (dictated to his students at Paris in 1345), printed at Venice in 1490; and *Questions on Aristotle's three books On the Soul*, published at Vicenza in 1608 and Venice in 1566.

<margin>1360.</margin>
**NILUS**, the Metropolitan of Rhodes and a bitter enemy of the Latins <note>the Western Church</note>, was a follower of Gregory Palamas. He lived perhaps around the year 1360 (as I have not been able to determine his exact age), being at least not much later than Barlaam and Akindynos, if not their contemporary. He defines the events in the Synod of Constantinople held by Patriarch Isidore (which he calls the Ninth Synod), which condemned Barlaam. I cannot say whether he is the same Nilus who, according to Freher’s Chronology, became Patriarch of Constantinople in 1378. He stood on the side of those who condemned the Barlaamites as liars, "mad in every way, and more impious than other heretics" <note>original Greek: κ’ ἀσεβόντας μᾶλλον ἢ ἄλλων αἱρετικῶν</note>, as he himself puts it. There exists, in both Greek and Latin, a *Brief Narration of the Nine Holy and Ecumenical Synods*, published by Justellus the elder at the end of Photius's *Nomocanon* <note>a collection of ecclesiastical law</note>, *Paris, 1615, in quarto*; and by Justellus the younger in the *Library of Canon Law, ibid. 1661, folio, Volume 2, page 1155*. An *Oration by the same author on Saint Matrona*, a native of the island of Chios, was published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius.

<margin>1360.</margin>
**THOMAS STUBBS**, or STOBÆUS, an Englishman by nation and native of York, was a Dominican monk and Doctor of Sacred Theology. He flourished in the year 1360 and died after the year 1373. He wrote the *Lives or Chronicle of the Archbishops of York*, from Saint Paulinus to the death of John Thoresby—that is, from the first foundation of the see until the year 1373. This Chronicle is found among the *Ten Writers of England* published by the illustrious Twysden in *London, 1652, folio, page 1685*. Many more of his theological writings, still unpublished, are listed by Bale in Century 6, chapter 36; Pits, age 14, page 512; and Altamura in the *Dominican Library*, page 125.

# The Century of Wycliffe.

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY.
From the Year 1300.
1360.
---
* On the Events of England, Book 5, page 2663.
† History, pages 305, 281, 256, 304.
---
See Huss’s *Reply against the Englishman John Stokes* among his Works, Volume 1, folios 109, 110.
</margin>

**JOHN WYCLIFFE**, an Englishman by birth, born in the northern parts, was educated at Oxford in Merton College, where he was first a Scholar and later a Fellow. He was eventually promoted to the headship of Canterbury College and Balliol College. A distinguished philosopher and a theologian most accomplished in every respect, he excelled no less in the sanctity of his life and the purity of his character than in his learning. He was perfectly instructed in Scholastic theology, being especially a studious reader of Ockham <note>William of Ockham, a famous English Franciscan philosopher</note>, the scholar of Cologne, and Armachanus <note>Richard FitzRalph, Archbishop of Armagh, known for his opposition to the friars</note>. After receiving the distinguished rank of Doctor, he publicly professed Theology at the University of Oxford until he was made Rector of the Church of Lutterworth in the Province of Leicestershire. Around the year 1360—at which time the superstitions of the age were worsening—he began to fiercely oppose, through both speech and writing, the terrible tyranny of the Roman Pontiff (which had already been deeply rooted for a long time), the erroneous dogmas widely accepted in the Schools, and the most shameful stain of vices admitted by all and even defended by many. In particular, he defended the rights of the Royal power and the Ecclesiastical Order with equal constancy and erudition against the terrible encroachments of the Roman Pontiff and the Mendicant Friars. For at that time, Papal arrogance had reached such a point of impudence that the King was left with no authority in ecclesiastical matters and only half-authority in secular ones; indeed, the Roman Court received more profit from England than did the King’s own court. Moreover, the troublesome swarm of Mendicant Friars <note>The four orders of friars: Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians</note> had utterly overturned the accepted discipline of the Church and all the rights of the Clergy; wandering about the churches, they forced themselves into the duties of the Parish Priests and refused to be subject to Episcopal rule or the ancient canons of the Church. Wycliffe, with the great eloquence he possessed, opposed such insane ambition and tyranny of the Pope and the Friars, teaching that both should be banished from the Church. In addition to this, he delivered the dogmas of the Christian faith to the common people, dressed in their native and unadorned simplicity. In place of the fables and trifles with which unlearned Christians had been baited for nearly the last several centuries, he preached the oracles of Holy Scripture everywhere and gave them to the people to read in their vernacular tongue <note>The English language</note>. It is no wonder, therefore, if he thereafter gained great favor among the good and envy among the wicked. Kings Edward III and Richard II of England held him very dear; the former sent Wycliffe as an ambassador to foreign regions, and the latter appointed him to his royal household. Both, however, called upon his doctrine and counsel for support in protecting the rights of the Royal power. Indeed, it was through Wycliffe's authority and favor among the highest nobles of the realm that more and harsher laws were enacted under these two Kings against the encroachments of the Roman Pontiff and the insolence of the Mendicant Friars than had been passed from the time of William the Norman until that final break with the Papal yoke under Henry VIII. Wycliffe was no less powerful among the common people than among the highest Orders of the Kingdom; so much so that Henry Knighton, a contemporary historian, complains: *“His disciples had multiplied excessively, and filled the whole world of the realm; indeed, they prevailed so much with their laborious dogmas that they gained half the people, or the greater part, to their sect.”*† Walsingham† pursues this at greater length, grieving that the villages, cities, and even the University of Oxford itself were infected by his doctrine. *“Far and wide,”* he says, *“through the regions, he expanded his preaching by staining the people, so that nearly all the greater men of the Provinces followed their error.”*—He seemed, by his teaching on absolution, to drown the Jordan <note>Likely a metaphor for the waters of baptism or grace</note> and all Christians in the Abyss. He spoke and preached publicly, with the Rectors of the churches being unable to stop him due to popular favor, since <unclear>th</unclear>ey heard him most gladly and preferred to expose themselves to danger rather than have him prohibited from preaching. Furthermore, Wycliffe himself, at the end of his *Confession on the Sacrament of the Altar*, records that more than a third of the Clergy were on his side and were prepared to defend his doctrine at the greatest risk to their lives. We pass over the high regard the University of Oxford held for Wycliffe, to the extent that his books were read in the public Schools and Colleges by common decree until the time of the Council of Constance <note>1414–1418, where Wycliffe's teachings were condemned</note>, and were handed over to each member of the University to be thoroughly studied according to the accepted custom. The Roman Pontiffs took it poorly that their authority in England was being undermined, grieving that their mask had been snatched away and their fictions exposed.

# The Century of Wycliffe.

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY.
From the Year 1300.
</margin>

The "little friars" <note>A dismissive term for the Mendicant orders, such as the Franciscans and Dominicans</note>, and indeed the very growth of piety and truth, stirred up envy in the wicked; so much so that it seems not at all surprising that countless evils were forged against Wycliffe’s head from every side. First, therefore, Simon Langham, Archbishop of Canterbury and Cardinal, around the year 1367, unjustly removed him from the leadership of Canterbury College at Oxford. Wycliffe had been duly elected Head of the College by the secular associates <note>Priests who were not members of a monastic order</note> according to the statutes given a few years earlier by Simon Islip, the Archbishop and founder. Certain meddlesome monks, who had recently forced their way into the College, took this poorly and strove with all their might to put one of their own companions into the leadership. Wycliffe and the secular associates expelled these insolent monks from the College. Langham took up the monks' cause and ordered Wycliffe to resign the leadership, substituting the monk Henry Woodhull in his place. When Wycliffe refused, the Archbishop seized the College's revenues. Wycliffe and his associates appealed to Pope Urban V. He committed the matter to Cardinal Andruynus to be judged. That man finally brought a sentence that only the monks should possess the College, excluding the seculars; Wycliffe and his associates were to be expelled, after first paying compensation to the monks for their "injuries." Pope Urban confirmed the Cardinal's sentence with a Bull <note>An official papal edict</note> given in the year 1370. The records of this legal process (as they call it) are preserved in the manuscript archives of the Archbishop's Library at Lambeth. Hitherto, his adversaries attacked Wycliffe through these hidden maneuvers. However, in the final years of King Edward <note>Edward III</note>, who was now weak with old age and nearly delirious, Simon Sudbury, the Archbishop of Canterbury, held a Synod in London in February of the year 1377, so that he might demand an account of Wycliffe’s doctrine, and perhaps exact punishment. Wycliffe was present and pleaded his cause fearlessly; through the support of John, Duke of Lancaster <note>John of Gaunt, a powerful prince and Wycliffe’s protector</note>, who was most devoted to his cause, and other nobles who stood by him, he escaped the blows and snares of the Bishops unharmed. After the death of Edward, when letters that Pope Gregory XI had sent to the Bishops against Wycliffe were brought to England, a new Synod was gathered at Lambeth in June of the same year; however, deterred by the threats of the nobles and the people, it did not dare to pass a final sentence against Wycliffe while he was present. He himself continued to defend the cause of truth in the courts, in the Universities, and in the Churches, through his voice, his writings, and his sermons.

<margin>* Book 5, page 2647.</margin>
Finally, however, with the affairs of the kingdom in turmoil and John of Lancaster withdrawing from the court, the Bishops—incited by frequent letters from Pope Gregory—attempted to uproot Wycliffe's doctrine under more favorable circumstances after they had drawn the weak King Richard II to their side. Thus, having held a Synod in London in the year 1382, they condemned the articles or dogmas defended by him: nine as <term>heresy</term> <note>Teachings contrary to established Church dogma</note> and fourteen as <term>error</term> <note>Minor theological mistakes, less severe than heresy</note>. They forced his followers either to make a <term>palinode</term> <note>A formal retraction or "singing back" of one's previous statements</note> or, having cast them into prison, punished them with the loss of their goods; finally, they decreed that even more severe measures should be taken against Wycliffe himself. For Wycliffe did not wish to present himself, having been warned by friends of the ambushes set for him by the prelates on his journey. Nevertheless, the Chancellor of Oxford University, both Proctors, and by far the greater part of the Senate pleaded the cause of the absent man; having sent a letter to the Synod secured with the public seal of the University, they rendered a magnificent eulogy of his learning, piety, and orthodox faith. After the sentence was passed by the Synod, Wycliffe still performed his usual duties of preaching and writing at Lutterworth, nor did he ever cease before his death; whether this was due to a revival of King Richard’s favor, or granted to the authority of the man’s fame and name, or finally because Wycliffe eluded the rage of his enemies with some kind of retraction of his dogma. For there is held in the works of Knighton * a brief "Declaration regarding the Sacrament of the Altar" in the common tongue <note>original: "vernaculo sermone" - Wycliffe wrote this in Middle English</note>, which the historian reports he offered to the Synod when driven by the fear of death. Yet that declaration is so far from actually favoring the dogma of <term>Transubstantiation</term> <note>The belief that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ</note> that it teaches the contrary opinion quite clearly. There are even those who claim that Wycliffe withdrew into Bohemia, and having found there an ample and fertile harvest of disciples, propagated his doctrine far and wide. But that is hardly certain. This, finally, is most certain: that Wycliffe died in peace at Lutterworth from a stroke <note>original: "paralysi"</note>, from which he had suffered for nearly two whole years, on the last day of December in the year 1387 <note>Historical records typically place his death in 1384; the author here cites 1387</note>, and was buried in his own Parish Church. He was a man such that the Christian world has not produced a greater in these latter ages; and who seems placed no less above praise than above envy. Every...

# The Century of Wycliffe.

...<note>original: multifariâ</note> was most highly instructed in a manifold knowledge of theological matters,
<margin>THE 14TH CENTURY. From the Year 1300.</margin> exceedingly skilled in the municipal laws <note>The common laws of England</note>, endowed with a rare gravity of character, and especially burning with zeal toward God and charity toward his neighbor. From this was born a desire to restore the church to its former purity; yet he did not allow this desire to exceed such limits that he would fail to hold the preservation of all ecclesiastical disciplinary laws as sacred. Even his worst adversaries never dared to call his exceptional piety into question; certainly many of them abundantly testify to his distinguished learning.
<margin>* Book 5, p. 2664.</margin> "He was powerful," says Knighton *, "and strong in disputations above all others, and in arguments he was believed second to none." The first to enter into scholastic combat with him was John Killingham, a Carmelite,
<margin>* Zizania bundle <note>referring to the Fasciculi Zizaniorum, a collection of documents regarding Wycliffite heresies</note> MS. in Bale, Century 6, chapter 4.</margin> who nevertheless acted with modesty (if Walden * is to be believed), admiring the excellence of his learning. Truly, in almost all his writings that exist today, Wycliffe displays an accurate knowledge of theology and a refined judgment. Everywhere he argues concisely and soundly, breathes an extraordinary piety, and is accustomed to interpreting Holy Scripture with the greatest clarity and skill. Nothing childish or idle (a common vice of writers of that age) can be found in him; everything is serious, well-considered, and polished. Finally, he is a man who lacked nothing for perfect erudition, except for a more fortunate age. However, it cannot be hidden that diverse and sometimes even contradictory doctrines can be found in his books. This does not detract from Wycliffe, but rather should result in his praise. For he did not attack the errors of the Roman Church driven by a certain overheated impulse of the mind, but led by mature judgment and reason; it is no wonder he did not uncover them all with a single blow. To say nothing of other articles, in his expositions of the Lord's Prayer, the Apostle's Creed, and the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, which I have read, he frequently admits the existence of Purgatory; (in the Manuscript *Treatise on Spiritual Prayer*, he teaches this clearly and at length). He advises that prayers be offered to the Saints so that they may intercede for us with God; he enumerates Seven Sacraments; and he preaches that souls placed in Purgatory are helped by the prayers of the Church Militant <note>The church on earth, as opposed to the 'Church Triumphant' in heaven</note>. It is certain, however, that he later renounced opinions of this kind.
<margin>* History of Bohemia.</margin> Certainly, Aeneas Sylvius * <note>Later Pope Pius II</note> testifies that the Wycliffites rejected the doctrine of the seven sacraments: for which reason he was also condemned by the Council of Constance. The same author relates that Purgatory was abolished by the Wycliffites, and prayers for the dead were held in mockery.
<margin>† Volume 3, p. 204.</margin> And Walden † records that Wycliffe forbade the invocation of saints—to say nothing of the many testimonies against purgatory and prayers for the dead brought forth from his writings by the illustrious James. Furthermore, that most learned man Thomas James, in a lengthy *Apology for Wycliffe* published in the English language at Oxford in 1608, fully demonstrated the accurate agreement of Wycliffe's doctrines with the current doctrine of the Church of England; he unconquerably washed away the calumnies of Parsons and others who, with the greatest injustice, heaped absurd opinions upon Wycliffe. After the death of this most famous Confessor, the Papists vented their rage against his holy remains with the greatest madness. At a Synod held in London in the year 1396, Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury, condemned 18 conclusions taken from Wycliffe's *Trialogus* <note>Wycliffe's major work on theology and philosophy</note> as heresy, and ordered all his books to be burned. Although there are arguments not to be despised that suggest this Synod should be dated to the year 1410. Especially important is the testimony of the Chancellor and the entire University of Oxford given to Wycliffe by a solemn decree in the year 1406, which is found at the end of the works of John Hus. After it had given him a distinguished eulogy of integrity and piety, and called him a champion of the faith who, through the sentences of Holy Scripture, catholically purged the individual mendicants <note>Friars who lived by begging</note> who blasphemed the religion of Christ with their voluntary beggary, it added the following:

> "Nor had the aforementioned Doctor been convicted of heretical depravity, nor delivered to the fires by our Prelates after his burial. Far be it from our prelates to have condemned a man of such integrity as a heretic; who, in matters logical, philosophical, theological, moral, and speculative, wrote without equal among all those of our University, as we believe."

The Council of Constance condemned 45 conclusions of the same man, partly as heresy and partly as error; it decreed that his books be burned in flames and his bones, removed from the tomb, be burned with fire. Richard Fleming, Bishop of Lincoln, executed the Council's decree by the command of Martin V in the year 1428. Sharp...

<margin>THE 14TH CENTURY.</margin>
...finally, the memory of Wycliffe was recently attacked by Varillas <note>Antoine Varillas (1624–1696), a French historiographer whose work was often criticized for its historical inaccuracies</note>, a French Historiographer; he revived ancient slanders and even devised new ones from the year 1300 onward, publishing both in his *History of Heresy*. Truly, that most lying historian slanders so absurdly for the most part, and so thoroughly disturbed the chronology of events, and admitted such gross and foolish errors, that he reveals himself everywhere as a most foul impostor, deserving to be met with laughter rather than refutation.

<margin>* History of Bohemia, chapter 35.</margin>
Wycliffe composed almost innumerable works in both the Latin and common tongues, filled with no ordinary learning; if we take as a witness Walden <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1375–1430), a leading English Carmelite theologian and opponent of the Wycliffites</note> himself, the most sworn enemy of Wycliffe: who, in a certain letter to Pope Martin V, professes that he was beyond measure astonished by the sharpness of Wycliffe’s assertions, the abundance of his authorities, and the force of his arguments. Aeneas Sylvius <note>Pope Pius II (1405–1464), author of the *History of Bohemia*</note> relates * that more than two hundred volumes of his works, most beautifully written and adorned with gold seals and precious bindings, were publicly burned by Subinco Lepus <note>Zbyněk Zajíc of Hasenburg (c. 1376–1411), the Archbishop of Prague, whose surname "Zajíc" means "hare" or "Lepus" in Latin</note>, the Archbishop of Prague, shortly before the Council of Constance. John Bale <note>A 16th-century English historian and former friar</note> lists a no less significant number of small works in his *Centuries*, Volume 6, Chapter 1, the vast majority of which he had seen with his own eyes. I would gladly believe that all of Wycliffe’s writings still lie hidden in England, and could be brought to light from our libraries, both public and private. I myself have seen many, partly printed and partly in manuscript; I shall next subjoin a brief list of them.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

***Four Books of Dialogues*** <note>Often referred to as the *Trialogus*</note>, *of which the first treats of Divinity and Ideas; the second encompasses the creation of all things; the third speaks most copiously of the Virtues and the vices contrary to them; the fourth touches upon the Sacraments of the Roman Church, its pestiferous endowment, the kingdom of the Antichrist, the fraudulent origin of the Friars and their hypocrisy, and various other things most worthy of being known in our age.* These Dialogues appeared under this title, printed in clear enough characters somewhere in Germany in the year 1525, in quarto, 175 leaves. A single copy is held in the Library of Trinity College at Cambridge.

***Wycliffe’s Wicket*** <note>original: *Ostiolum Wiclefi*</note>, *or an English Treatise on the Sacrament of the Altar,* in which he vigorously attacks Transubstantiation with arguments sought both from Philosophy and Scripture. Nuremberg 1546, octavo; Oxford 1612, quarto. However, whoever added to the title of the booklet that it was written in 1395 was hallucinating; for Wycliffe had died seven years prior.

***Two Treatises against the Mendicant Friars.*** *The first of these is a Petition to Richard II and the Estates of the Realm, that they might bring the little friars—who extol themselves beyond all law and right—back into order. The second attacks fifty errors and crimes of the little friars in as many chapters.* These appeared in English, edited by the celebrated Thomas James at Oxford, 1608, quarto.

***Wycliffite Aphorisms or Articles,*** published by John Foxe <note>Author of *Foxe's Book of Martyrs*</note> at Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentinae*</note> 1554, octavo. These indeed I have not yet seen.

***Nineteen Conclusions*** *extracted from his writings and condemned by Pope Gregory XI, found in the Councils, Volume 11, page 2041.* ***Twenty-four Conclusions*** *condemned in the Synod of London in the year 1382, in the same work, page 2053.* ***Eighteen Conclusions*** *taken from his Trialogus and condemned in the Synod of London in the year 1396, in the same work, page 2080.* ***Forty-five Articles*** *condemned in the Council of Constance in the year 1415, in the same work, page 45. All the aforesaid Conclusions and Articles are contained in the "Collection of Things to be Sought" <note>original: *Fasciculo Rerum Expetendarum*</note>, Cologne 1535, folio, pages 95, 133.*

***Prologue to the complete English version of the Bible*** *prepared by himself. In English, London 1550, octavo.*

***English version of the entire Holy Scripture,*** *which he composed from the Vulgate version of Jerome in the year 1383, as the manuscript codex preserved in Emmanuel College, Cambridge, has written on its front. For that manuscript version is held in the Library of the said College, most beautifully written, as it is also in the Cottonian Library under the image of Claudius E. 2, and in the Royal Library of our King James, as well as in the Lambeth Library and that of Sion College in London. A version of the New Testament <note>original: "Versio Novi Testamenti"</note> at the Cambridge University Library, by the same author, Class 3, number [blank], which is prefixed by a very long *Introduction on the authority and use of Holy Scripture*. Near the beginning of this, after listing the Canonical books of Scripture according to the opinion of the Jews and the Reformers, he declares all the rest to be *Apocryphal and lacking the authority of faith*.

*An Exposition on all the Sunday Epistles of the whole year*, in English, in which he most sharply attacks the dogmas and corruptions of the Papists. Manuscript in the same place [Cambridge], Class 10, Octavo.

*A Commentary on the Sunday Epistles and Gospels of the whole year*, though it is found mutilated at both the beginning and the end, in the College of St. John at Cambridge, C. 8.

*Various Treatises against the Clergy and other ranks*, in English. Manuscript in Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, Number 362, Quarto. In the margin of the volume, this note is inscribed: "In this volume are collected all those biting treatises concerning the errors and corruptions which John Wycliffe detected in his age, especially among the Clergy, the Monks, and the worldly orders." *Questions of the same author against the clergy* exist as English manuscripts in the Lambeth Library <note>The library of the Archbishop of Canterbury at Lambeth Palace</note> in Duodecimo.

*A Long Treatise on the actions of the soul*. Manuscript in the same place, among the Miscellaneous volumes, letter K, folio from page 47 to 88.

*A Formal Decision against John Kylengham the Carmelite* <note>original: "Determinatio contra Joannem Kylengham Carmelitam"</note>. Manuscript in the same place, from page 410 to 426.

*A Formal Decision against a certain Monk concerning Civil Lordship* <note>term: Civil Lordship (Dominion) — Wycliffe’s controversial theory that the right to rule and own property depends on being in a state of grace</note>, in Latin; in which he proves against the accused Monk that the resignation of the crown and the payment of tribute voluntarily made by King John of England to the Roman Pontiff in the past ought not to result in prejudice against the kingdom of England, nor bind the present king. Manuscript in the Lambeth Library in Octavo.

*A Commentary on the Psalms, and other Hymns of Holy Scripture and the Church Liturgy*. Manuscript in Trinity College, Cambridge, folio. *A Commentary on the first 75 Psalms* is held as a manuscript in the Lambeth Library.

*A Gospel Harmony* <note>original: "Harmonia Evangelica"</note>, by Clement, a Priest of Llanthony (who flourished in the year 1170 and wrote a long Commentary on the seven Canonical Epistles, preserved as a manuscript in the Lambeth Library), composed in the Latin language and *translated into English* by Wycliffe. A manuscript in the possession of Richard Chiswell, a London bookseller, Quarto.

*A Commentary on selected passages of Holy Scripture*, in English. Manuscript, Quarto, at the same place. *The Poor Rustic* <note>original: "Pauper Rusticus"</note>, or various miscellaneous Treatises in English, which teach the poor the whole Christian religion with the help of many books. Namely: *An Exposition of the Apostles' Creed, the Ten Commandments, and the Lord's Prayer; various Exhortations stirring men to the desire for heaven; The Counsel of Christ; On Good Patience; On Temptation; The Charter of Heaven; On the Spiritual Battle; On the name of Jesus; On the love of Jesus; On true Meekness; On the effect of the human will; On the active and contemplative life; The Mirror of Chastity*; which last, being filled with the most foul fables, seems especially unworthy of Wycliffe. This miscellaneous volume is held as a manuscript by the most learned man and my very dear friend Mr. John Laughton, Chief Librarian of Cambridge University, Duodecimo; and also in the Cambridge Public Library and in St. John’s College, where the manuscript volume bears the title *The Wycliffite Catechism*.

Another *Collection of Miscellanies*, namely: *An Exposition of the Ten Commandments*, much shorter than the previous one. *On the 7 deadly sins; On the 7 bodily senses and as many faculties of the soul; On the 7 spiritual virtues; On the 7 gifts of the Holy Spirit; On the 7 Sacraments; On the impediments to prayer; On the nature of faith; On the different degrees of charity; An Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer*, different from the preceding one and far more sharp in attacking Papal errors; *The Mirror of Sinners; The Charter of Heaven* (which is indeed the only work it has in common with the previous collection); *The Three Arrows*. This collection exists in Duodecimo in the possession of the Reverend Man, to be respected by me on many accounts, Thomas Tenison <note>Thomas Tenison (1636–1715), later Archbishop of Canterbury; a prominent theologian and bibliophile</note>, our theologian. Indeed, let us not wonder that many and diverse Treatises on the same subject are ascribed to Wycliffe; John Hus <note>The Bohemian reformer who was heavily influenced by Wycliffe’s writings</note>—who was most well-versed in Wycliffe’s writings—reveals * that he published several Expositions of the Ten Commandments and editions of Dialogues. I have seen yet a third Collection of Wycliffe's Miscellanies in...

* Reply against the Englishman John Stokes, among his works, Volume 1, folio 108.

# The Century of Wycliffe.

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1300.
</margin>

...in the Lambeth Library <note>The library of the Archbishop of Canterbury at Lambeth Palace</note>, in which, besides the Treatises mentioned above, there are held "Little Works," *on the desire for Jesus, on spiritual and carnal love, Knightly equipment and the armor of heaven.* Perhaps others are held elsewhere.

Besides these Manuscript Books which I myself have seen, James <note>Thomas James (c. 1572–1629), the first librarian of the Bodleian Library</note> frequently cites others seen by him in the *Apology for Wycliffe* praised above, namely: *A Book on the truth of Holy Scripture; another Treatise on the 7 mortal sins; a Miscellaneous Booklet; On Civil Dominion* (Manuscript in the public library at Oxford); *On Blasphemy; two Confessions on the Sacrament of the Altar, one in Latin, the other in English; three Sermons on the Lord's Sermon on the Mount; On the life of Priests; On the Rule of St. Francis; A Commentary on the Foundations of the Laws of England in the common tongue; finally a Latin Exposition of the Decalogue.* Bale <note>John Bale (1495–1563), an English historian</note> mentions that Wycliffe's *great Work on the ten commandments*, along with his *Trialogue*, and 23 other treatises, were left behind as he fled from Ireland. William Woodford provides many excerpts of the *Trialogue* in that *Refutation* which he carefully composed.

There are still Manuscripts held in the Cotton Library <note>The famous collection of Sir Robert Cotton, now in the British Library</note>: *Wycliffe's Postils <note term="postil">a marginal note or short commentary on a biblical text</note> on the Sunday and Weekday Gospels*, categorized under the bust of Claudius D. 8. Also *A Sermon on the Feast of All Saints, a Treatise on the manner of praying, and Another on virtues and vices*, all in English; categorized under the bust of Titus D. 19. numbers 16, 17, 18.

*A Treatise on the Incarnation of the Word* existed as a Manuscript in the Lumley Library, Book 297. *The Mirror of Secular Lords* is a Manuscript in the King’s Library at Westminster.

The *Work on the Abomination in the Holy Place* is preserved as a Manuscript in the Imperial Library of Vienna, according to Lambecius’s *Commentaries*, book 2, page 777.

---

<margin>1360.</margin>
**JOHN CALDERINUS**, a native of Bologna and a most celebrated legal expert, was adopted as a son by John Andreas after the death of Bonicontius; he flourished in the year 1360. He died at Bologna and is buried with the Dominicans. There exists a *Table containing the authorities and sentences of the Bible*, as they are cited in the Decretals <note>papal decrees forming part of Canon Law</note>, arranged in alphabetical order, published at *Speyer* in 1481. Also *Legal Advice or Responses, Venice* 1582, and mixed with the *Advice* of his son Gaspar, *Lyon* 1536. *Various Repetitions in Civil Law, Lyon* 1587. *A Treatise on the Ecclesiastical Interdict, Venice* 1584. Simler, in his *Library* page 350, lists his *Commentaries* on the books of Decretals, *Decisions*, and many other writings regarding both types of Law <note>Civil Law and Canon Law</note>.

<margin>1360.</margin>
**PETER BERCHORIUS** <note>Also known as Pierre Bersuire</note>, a Frenchman by birth and a native of Poitou, was a Monk of the Benedictine Order and Prior of the Monastery of St. Eligius in Paris; he flourished in the year 1360. He died in the year 1362 and was buried in his monastery. He wrote to John de Pratis, Bishop of Palestrina, a *Moral Biblical Dictionary*, arranged alphabetically, in which he treats the principal words in the manner of "commonplaces" and adapts them to moral lessons; likewise a *Moral Reduction of the Testament* in 14 books, in which almost the entire Scripture is explained tropologically <note term="tropology">an interpretation of scripture that seeks to find a moral or ethical meaning</note>, with Allegories frequently interspersed; finally, a *Moral Introduction*, divided into three parts. These three works appeared together at *Basel* 1515, *Paris* 1521 (4 folio volumes), *Venice* 1583 and 1589 (3 folio volumes), and *Cologne* 1620 (3 folio volumes).

<margin>1360.</margin>
**JOHN THE WISE, called CYPARISSIOTES** by surname, a Greek by nation, about whose age there is no firm agreement. However, it seems to me that he lived around the year 1360, as he was nearly contemporary with Gregory Palamas. There exists a *Material exposition of those things which are said about God by Theologians, distributed into 10 Decades*; in which indeed are contained the hidden mystical and symbolic mysteries of Theology, according to the opinion <margin>* Note from the Author.</margin> of Cardinal Bona †. It was published in Latin, edited by Francisco Torres at *Rome* 1581, in quarto, and in the *Library of the Fathers* Volume 21, page 377. Two of his *Sermons on the Palamite <note>Followers of Gregory Palamas, a prominent Eastern Orthodox theologian</note> Transgressions* are held in Greek and Latin in Combefis’s *Newest Supplement, Paris* 1672.

<margin>1360.</margin>
**MANUEL CALECA**, or Calecas, a Greek by nation and a Monk of the Dominican Order (as some maintain), flourished in the year 1360—not 1250 as many others claim—since he wrote against the Palamites. Therefore, Peter Galesinius <margin>\* Life of St. Bonaventure.</margin> deceives the reader when he places Caleca at the Second Council of Lyon in the year 1274.

->WRITINGS.<-

Four books *Against the errors of the Greeks regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit*: which Ambrogio Traversari <note>Original: "Ambrosius Camaldulensis"</note>, by order of Pope Martin V, translated into Latin. It was published by Petrus Stevartius with notes at Ingolstadt in 1608 and 1616 in quarto; thereafter it was reprinted in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26.

*A Book on the Essence and Operation of God against the Palamites* <note>Followers of Gregory Palamas, a Byzantine monk and theologian</note>, and their "false council" <note>Pseudo-synod</note> held under John Cantacuzenus.

*A Book on the Principles of the Christian Faith according to the tradition of Holy Scripture and Catholic Doctors*, divided into ten chapters. Fr. François Combefis published both small works in Greek and Latin in the *Latest Addition* <note>Auctuarium Novissimum</note>, Paris, 1672, folio.

Leo Allatius <note>A Greek scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note> testifies in his work *On Consent*, book 2, chapter 18, section 4, that he saw a very rich *Treatise on the Holy Trinity* by Calecas.

<margin>1360.</margin> **BARTHOLOMEW de GLANVILLE**, an *Englishman* called "of the Suffolk countryside" <note>Original: "Sudovolgiorum"</note>, born of the most illustrious blood of the Earls of Suffolk, and a monk of the Franciscan Order. He flourished in the year 1360. Being equipped with a distinguished knowledge of Theology and Philosophy—which he had cultivated with the greatest zeal at Oxford, Paris <note>Original: "Lutetia"</note>, and finally at Rome—he applied his mind to explaining the allegories and enigmas of Holy Scripture, which are for the most part veiled by the properties and figures of natural things. From roughly one hundred writers, whose names he lists after the preface, he composed the lengthy *Work on the Properties of Things* <note>Original: "Opus de proprietatibus rerum"</note>, divided into nineteen books. Of these, the first treats of God, the second of good and evil angels, the third of the rational soul, the fourth of bodily substance, and the remaining books treat of other created things. It was published in Strasbourg in 1488 and 1505 in quarto; in Nuremberg in 1492; and under the title *Of Allegories and Tropology in Both Testaments* in Paris, 1574. To these nineteen books, a twentieth is usually added *On the Accidents of Things*, namely: *On numbers, measures, weights, etc.*, and in the Paris edition of 1574, a *Book on the Properties of Bees*. A book of his *Sermons* was published in Strasbourg in 1491. John Pits <note>Original: "Pitseus"</note> mentions a manuscript *Book against Lorenzo Valla* in Balliol College, and a manuscript *Book of Practice* in the public library at Oxford, along with certain other works on page 495; and from him, Luke Wadding <note>Original: "Waddingus"</note> mentions them in *Writers of the Order of Minors*, page 50. John Bale <note>Original: "Baleus"</note> records in Century 6, chapter 15, that *Postils on the Scriptures* <note term="postil">a marginal note or short commentary on a biblical text</note> were composed by the same man. I myself saw in our King’s Library at Westminster manuscript Postils on the Gospels of St. Matthew and St. Mark in two volumes; one of these contained only the Postil on Matthew with the author's name attached, while the other contained Postils on both Gospels without the author's name. However, the fact that the Postil on Matthew found in both was the same demonstrated that both volumes are owed to the same author. Even though these might bear the name of a certain "John de Glanville," they could perhaps be deservedly ascribed to our Bartholomew. For as far as I know, no writer mentions a John de Glanville; and it is not entirely unusual for the names of authors to be incorrectly placed in manuscript volumes; not to mention that the age of the manuscript, as far as can be conjectured, agrees perfectly with Bartholomew’s era. Be that as it may, it will perhaps not be unpleasant to the reader to provide two snippets regarding the Eucharist which I transcribed from it. In the Postil on St. Matthew, therefore, at those words, *This is my body. This is my blood*, the author gave a gloss of this sort: *Mystically, "this" is referred to the body and "that" to the blood of Christ.* In the Postil on St. Mark, however, regarding the same words, he has these things: *Jesus took bread, namely figuring his body in the bread, which is the Church: And it is received as present in faith, blessed in number, broken in passions, given by examples, received in doctrines.*

<margin>1360.</margin> **JOHN RUYSBROECK**, a Belgian by nation, born in a village of the same name by the river Senne between Brussels and Halle; he was called the *Divine Doctor*, and was called "another Dionysius the Areopagite" by Dionysius the Carthusian...

# The Century of Wycliffe.

<margin>THE 14TH CENTURY. from the Year 1300.</margin>
...Priest of the Cathedral of Brussels and Vicar of the Church of St. Gudula; later, he was appointed at the age of sixty as the first Prior of the Monastery of Groenendaal <note>Original: "Viridis Vallis", meaning Green Valley</note> of the Order of Canons Regular of St. Augustine, which was newly founded in the Sonian Forest three miles <note>Original: "lapide", literally "stone", referring to milestones</note> from Brussels. He flourished in the year 1360. He died on the 2nd of December in the year 1381 at the age of 88. After his death, he was accused of heresy by Jean Gerson <note>A prominent French scholar and reformer</note> but was defended by Laurentius Surius <note>A Carthusian monk and hagiographer</note>. He wrote many short works in his mother tongue <note>Middle Dutch</note>, which are filled with piety and the love of God. He employed a mystical theology and a quite obscure style, emulating Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite in every respect. Laurentius Surius translated the most significant of these into Latin and oversaw their publication in the following order:

*A Summary of the Entire Spiritual Life.*
*The Mirror of Eternal Salvation.*
*Commentaries on the Tabernacle of Moses, and related matters, translated by Jordanus.*
*A Treatise on Certain Principal Virtues.*
*A Small Book on Faith and Judgment.*
*On the Four Temptations.*
*On the Seven Guards of the Spiritual School, or Wild Beasts.*
*On the Seven Steps of Love, translated by Gerard Groote.*
*On the Spiritual Espousals in three books, translated by Willem Jordaens.*
*On the Stone <note>Original: "calculo". Refers to "The Sparkling Stone"</note>, or, the Perfection of the Sons of God, translated by Willem Jordaens.*
*The Kingdom of the Lovers of God.*
*A Notable Work on True Contemplation.*
*Seven Very Useful Epistles.*
*Two Spiritual Songs.*
*Samuel, or, on High Contemplation.*
*A Brief Prayer.* All these short works were published in Cologne in 1552, folio, and in 1609, quarto.

<margin>1361.</margin>
## NICOLE ORESME, or OREM, French by birth and a Norman by country, was a leader <note>Original: "coryphæus"</note> among the theologians, philosophers, and mathematicians at the University of Paris. For this reason, he was chosen by King John of France to educate his son Charles—later called "The Wise"—in literature and good morals. After receiving his doctorate, he took over the governance of the College of Navarre <note>Original: "Navarrense Gymnasium"</note> in 1356, where he taught theology as part of his duties; by order of King Charles, he applied himself to a French translation of the Holy Bible. In the year 1361, when he was especially prominent, he was made Treasurer of the Royal Chapel and Dean of Rouen, and he resigned from his leadership of the College of Navarre. In 1363, he delivered a sharp speech before Urban V and the Cardinals at Avignon, in which he testified to his listeners and the entire clergy that destruction was looming not far off; he openly set forth the arguments for his prediction drawn from their own crimes. In 1370, following the commands of King Charles, he devoted his efforts to translating ancient writings into French; after about seven years, he received the Bishopric of Lisieux as his reward. He died around the year 1384.

->WRITINGS.<-

A Sermon on that passage of *Isaiah, "My salvation is near," etc.* delivered before Urban V and the Cardinals, edited by Flacius Illyricus and contained in the *Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth*, page 512; it was reprinted separately by Salomon Gesner at *Wittenberg* in 1604.
*A Book on the Alteration of Money.* <note>Considered one of the earliest and most significant medieval treatises on economics</note> It is found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26, page 226.
*A Treatise on the Sphere*, published in French at *Paris*, 1546.
*The Politics and Ethics of Aristotle, several books of Cicero, and Petrarch's book on the remedies of both fortunes*, translated by him into French and printed at *Paris* in 1486, 1488, and 1534; these hardly deserve to be included in the list <note>The author implies that translations are less significant than original works</note>.
Very many other writings by Oresme, and among these *115 Sermons* preserved in manuscript in the libraries of Navarre, the Vatican, and the Augustinians of Paris, are listed by Jean de Launoy in the *History of the College of Navarre*, Volume 2, page 458.

<margin>1362.</margin>
**URBAN V**, born with the name Guillaume de Grimoard <note>Latin: "Gulielmus Grisant"</note>, a Frenchman of the Limousin region, was a Doctor of Canon Law and a monk of the Benedictine Order. He served as the Abbot of the Monastery of St. Victor at Marseille and as a Legate of the Apostolic See in the kingdoms of Sicily and Naples. He was elected Roman Pontiff in 1362 while absent at Avignon on September 23rd; his election was confirmed on October 18th. He was enthroned at Avignon on the 31st of the same month, and consecrated and crowned on November 6th. At the beginning of his papacy, having excommunicated Bernabò Visconti, the Lord of Milan, he settled the troubled affairs of Italy as he saw fit. In the year 1363, he struck Peter, King of Castile <note>Known as Peter the Cruel</note>, with anathema and ordered him to be cast out of his kingdom; he commanded that Henry, Peter’s illegitimate brother, be considered the legitimate ruler and govern in Peter’s place. Soon, provoked by a slight offense, he cursed Peter, the King of Aragon, and decreed that he should be stripped of the kingdoms of Sardinia and Corsica. In the year 1367, he undertook a journey to Rome; having settled Italian affairs to his satisfaction, he entered in a triumphal procession. In 1368, he received the Emperor Charles IV in Rome after the Emperor had performed his festive duties for him. The following year, he summoned John Palaeologus, the Emperor of Constantinople, to Rome, having held out hope of obtaining aid against the Turks; he deemed him worthy of a sacred gift and dismissed him in 1370 after he swore to various formulas of obedience and faith. He died that same year, having first returned to Avignon, on December 19th. He was buried at St. Victor in Marseille. His *Letters* survive in *Councils*, Volume 11, pages 1957 and 2033. Also surviving is his *Constitution against the Plurality of Benefices* <note>A law against clergy holding multiple paid church offices simultaneously</note>, ibid. p. 1936; *eight other letters regarding the union of the Greek and Roman Churches* in Bzovius under the year 1365, etc.; *sixty others* in Wadding’s *Minor Annals*, Volume 4, under the year 1363, etc.; *fifty-seven others* in the same work in the *Papal Register*, p. 71; *Verses on the Lamb of God* <note>Latin: "Agno Dei"</note> in Victorellus’s additions to Ciacconius’s *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, 1630; and a *Volume of Letters* in manuscript in the Vatican Library. John Bale, while fleeing from Ireland, left behind his own manuscript of Urban's *Exposition on the Apocalypse*.

<margin>1362.</margin>
**HENRY**, a German by birth and a monk of Rebdorf, flourished in the year 1362. He wrote the *Annals of the deeds of the Emperors Adolf, Albert, Frederick III, Louis the Bavarian, and Charles IV*, from the year 1295 to the year 1363. Marquard Freher published these annals among the *Historians of Germany* at Frankfurt, 1600, Volume 1, p. 411.

<margin>1362.</margin>
**PHILOTHEUS**, a Greek by birth, cultivated the monastic life from his very cradle with the highest virtue and piety; he was later the Moderator <note>Abbot or Superior</note> of the Holy Lavra on Mount Athos, and before the year 1354, he was appointed Metropolitan of Heraclea. At the beginning of 1355, it seems, he was sent as an envoy to Didymoteicho by Kantakouzenos to negotiate peace between Kantakouzenos's son Matthew and his son-in-law Palaeologus. In the same year, after Callistus was deposed, Philotheus was elected Patriarch of Constantinople and promoted peace between Kantakouzenos and Palaeologus with great zeal. Soon after Palaeologus took possession of the city of Constantinople, Philotheus yielded the Patriarchate to Callistus and went into hiding for fear of the people. The following year, after Callistus was removed from the living, he was restored again to the See of Constantinople by Emperor John and was thereafter honored with the highest favor. He flourished in the year 1362. He died around the year 1371, after having administered the Patriarchate for fifteen years. He was a man who, in the judgment of Kantakouzenos <margin>*History book 4, chapter 32*</margin>, was "venerable for both his life and his speech to those who saw him" <note>Original Greek: κἀν βίῳ κἀν λόγῳ τοῖς ὁρῶσι ἀξιόχρεως ὤν πρὸς αἰδῶ</note>; venerable for his holiness of life and his eloquence.

*Liturgy and the Order for Ordaining a Deacon.* This survives in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26, p. 200.

*An Encomiastic Sermon on the Three Hierarchs: Basil, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom.* Found in Latin in the same work. The Greek and Latin version was edited by Jacob Pontanus together with the *Dioptra* of Philip the Solitary, published at Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto; and by Fronton du Duc in the *Supplement to the Fathers*, Paris, 1624, Volume 2, p. 313.

*Oration on the Cross.* Greek and Latin, in Gretser’s *On the Cross*, Volume 2, p. 1255.

# The Century of Wycliffe.
<note>This era is named after the English reformer John Wycliffe, reflecting the period's growing religious tensions and movements for reform.</note>

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1300.
</margin>

*Sermon for the third Sunday of the Fasts <note>original Latin: "Oratio in tertiam jejuniorum Dominicam"</note>. Greek and Latin, published in the same work, page 1477.*

*Refutation of the Anathemas written by Harmenopoulos. Exists in Greek and Latin in Leunclavius, Greco-Roman Law, book 4, page 288.*

*Fifteen books on the divine substance, operation, power, and the light on Mount Tabor, written in support of Gregory Palamas <note>Palamas was a monk and theologian who defended Hesychasm, a mystical tradition of prayer in the Eastern Orthodox Church</note> and against the ten books of Nicephorus Gregoras. These exist as manuscripts in the Bavarian and Vatican Libraries. A Latin fragment of them is presented by Bzovius under the year 1337; Leo Allatius provides two Greek fragments, one in his book on Purgatory (page 770) and the other in his book on Greek Ecclesiastical books (page 218).*

*Dogmatic sermons against the Barlaamites and Acindynists <note>Opponents of the Hesychast movement</note> are held as manuscripts in the Augsburg Library. The learned may decide whether these constitute the same work as the preceding entry.*

*Confession of Faith. Manuscript in the same location.*

*Homilies on the Gospels and the Saints for the entire year. Manuscripts in the Bavarian Library.*

*Homily on All Saints. Manuscript in the Imperial Library.*

*A Compendium on the economy of the man Christ <note>the "economy" refers to the divine plan for salvation through the Incarnation</note>, and a Eulogy of Saint Demetrius. Manuscripts in the Vatican Library.*

<margin>1362.</margin>
**BERNARD, THE STEWARD** <note>Latin: "Dapifer"</note>, a monk of Melk <note>Latin: "Molicensis"</note> in Austria, was distinguished in the year 1362. He wrote a *History of the Blessed Gothalmus, Cellarer of Saint Coloman*, which the celebrated Lambecius first brought to light in his *Commentary on the Vienna Library*, Volume 2, page 618.

<margin>1363.</margin>
**SAINT BRIGITTA** <note>Also known as Saint Bridget of Sweden</note>, of Swedish birth and royal blood, was the daughter of Birger and Sigrid and the wife of Ulf, Prince of Närke <note>Latin: "Wulfonis Nericiæ"</note>. From her earliest childhood <note>literally "from her fingernails"</note> she was nurtured in the study of piety and virtue; having been acquainted with divine visions from her very cradle (as it is said), she began to prefer the monastic life over marriage. Therefore, after she had persuaded her husband to go on a pilgrimage with her to Saint James <note>Santiago de Compostela in Spain</note> for the sake of religion, she first convinced him upon their return to vow perpetual continence, and then to enter a monastery. He agreed, though only after seven children had already been born to them; he joined the Cistercians and died not long after in the Monastery of Alvastra. Once freed from marriage, Brigitta devoted herself entirely to cultivating piety. She founded a new monastic order, which they call the Order of the Most Holy Savior, and became famous for frequent visions around the year 1363. After she had stayed for two years in the cells located near the Alvastra monastery, she was divinely warned that a shortcut to heaven could be found in Rome through the pardons and indulgences distributed by the Pope, which the Saints had earned. She undertook a journey there before the year 1350 and spent several years visiting holy sites. At last, after viewing the monuments of the Saints at Naples and Sicily, she was commanded by a divine vision to set out for Jerusalem. Returning after a year, she was seized by illness on the journey; having been brought back to Rome, she returned her soul to Heaven shortly after on July 23, 1373. She was first laid to rest at the Monastery of Saint Lawrence, and then in the following year, she was moved to the Abbey of Vadstena <note>Latin: "Wafthenæ"</note>. Boniface IX added her to the catalog of saints in the year 1391, and the Council of Constance confirmed her canonization in 1415.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

Eight books of **Revelations**. Matthias of Sweden, a Canon of Linköping—who is said to have composed excellent glosses on the entire Holy Scripture—provided a prologue for them. It is said that Bishop Alfonso of Jaén <note>Latin: "Gyennenis"</note> arranged the Revelations into order and distributed them into books at the command of Christ.
*The Rule of Saint Savior, given divinely from the mouth of Jesus Christ to his devoted bride, the Blessed Birgitta, comprised of 31 chapters.*
*The Angelic Sermon on the excellence of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which an Angel standing in her presence dictated to Birgitta.*
*Four Prayers divinely revealed.*
*Supplemental Revelations <note>Latin: "Revelationes Extravagantes"</note>, which Peter, the Prior of Alvastra, collected and arranged separately after they had been omitted from the first collection of Revelations.*

Furthermore, it should not be silenced that the author of her *Life* reveals in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk and hagiographer</note> that she saw to it that the Holy Scripture was translated for her into the Gothic tongue <note>The author refers here to Old Swedish, often called "Gothic" in early modern scholarship</note>, so that the ability to read the divine oracles in the common language would not be lacking.

<margin>
1367.
</margin>
SAINT CATHERINE, an Italian by nation, a native of Siena, daughter of Giacomo and <unclear>Lappa</unclear>, was born in 1347. Having entered her eighth year of age, she bound herself by a vow of perpetual virginity, dedicated herself entirely to Christ, and set her mind upon the Dominican religion; she was clothed in the habit of the Preachers shortly thereafter. I pass over those things which the most trifling monks babble regarding her many and frequent visions, her intimate communication of eyes and mouth, and her marriage entered into with Christ God, Best and Greatest. Indeed, whatever most dull-witted idlers might shamelessly and heartlessly load and infect the reputation of the most holy virgin with portentous absurdities—not to say blasphemies—she herself was certainly worthy of a better fate. She flourished around the year 1367, known for her sincere piety toward God, the purity of a chaste life, a burning charity toward the poor, and zeal for the Church. Having set out for Avignon before the year 1376, she appeased Pope Gregory XI, who was angry with the Florentines, through her prayers. Soon, at the command of the Pope—whom she had previously urged in frequent letters to finally desire to return to the City of Rome—she spoke so effectively in the assembly of Cardinals against the Roman Pontiff's absence from his Episcopal see that they all, with a crafty shout, judged that Avignon should be abandoned. Following Gregory XI into Italy in 1376, after his death she obstinately adhered to the party of Urban VI against Pope Clement. She died on the day before the Calends of May <note>April 29</note> in the year 1380, at the age of 33; she was recorded among the Saints by Pope Pius II in the year 1461.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Dialogues on the Providence of God* <note>original: "Dialogi de Providentiâ Dei"</note>, comprised of six treatises. Published in *Ingolstadt 1583, Cologne 1601, Venice 1611,* octavo.
364 Letters, weighty and full of piety, to various Popes, Cardinals, Kings, Princes, and others, written in the vernacular language <note>Italian</note>. Published in Italian at *Venice 1506,* folio; in French at *Paris 1644,* quarto.
*Prayer on the Annunciation of the Mother of God*, and many others, translated from the Italian into the Latin language by Raymond of Capua, of the Order of Preachers, Catherine’s confessor. They exist in *Ingolstadt 1583.*
*The Divine Doctrine* given through the Person of the Eternal Father to the intellect of the one speaking, divided into parts, treatises, and prayers: which the same Raymond translated into Latin, or perhaps wrote under Catherine’s name. Published in *Cologne 1553,* folio.

† April 30.

Furthermore, no one who has a sound mind would easily doubt that the famous *Revelations* of Catherine as well as Birgitta are nothing other than the delusions of a smoky brain. For however much the *Revelations* of Birgitta were approved by the Roman Cardinals (to whom Gregory XI in 1377 and Urban VI in 1379 had committed them for examination), and by Boniface IX in the Bull of Canonization prefixed to the *Works of Birgitta* (Rome 1557), and finally by the Council of Basel, and though they are affirmed to have proceeded from the Holy Spirit; and although Catherine’s prophetic gift and divine revelations are celebrated by Pius II in the Bull of her Canonization and by the Roman Church in the Breviary; yet the strange simplicity of the words, the noise of foolish opinions, the unpolished chatter, the absurd dogmas, and the worst style with which they everywhere teem—and their religious enthusiasm <note>Here used in the historical sense of "fanaticism" or "pretended inspiration"</note>—manifestly betray the fraud. What of the fact that they contradict each other? For the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin was revealed to Birgitta, but it was revealed as "maculate" <note>meaning Mary was conceived with original sin</note> to Catherine. Truly, we care little for the unrestrained intemperance of these little women. Let the Roman Church, to whose soil alone it pertains, see to it.

**PHILIP RIBOT**, a Spaniard by nation and a Catalan by birth, was a monk of the Carmelite Order in the Monastery of Girona. He eventually became the Provincial of his Order in Catalonia from the year 1300 <note>The text says 1300, though his flourish date of 1368 suggests a later decade of that century</note>, and flourished around the year 1368. He died at Peralada in his own monastery in the year 1391. He wrote the *Mirror of the Carmelites* <note>original: "Speculum Carmelitarum"</note>, or ten books on the institution, progress, privileges, and deeds of his Order. It was published in *Venice, 1507, folio* and *Antwerp, 1680, folio.* Possevinus <note>Antonio Possevino (1533–1611), a Jesuit diplomat and bibliographer</note> provides testimony that Ribot’s *Sermons and Letters* were once printed; however, I have been unable to find the years or locations of those editions.

<margin>
* Sacred Apparatus, Vol. 2, Page 280.
</margin>
A manuscript of Ribot’s *Mirror of the Carmelites* is held in the Lambeth Library in folio, which has attached to its end a complete and quite ancient English version. The most learned man John Battely, Archdeacon of Canterbury, demonstrated to me that this translation is owed to Thomas Scrope (also known as Bradley), the Bishop of Dromore (around the year 1434).

---

<margin>
1368.
</margin>
**L. COLUCCIO PIERO SALUTATI OF STIGNANO**, a Florentine by birth, was most highly refined in every branch of the humanities and was named Poet Laureate after Petrarch. He flourished in the year 1368. On account of his learning and prudence, he was summoned into the service of Popes Urban V and Gregory XI as a secretary; he was later called by the Republic of Florence to the same office and the dignity of the Chancellorship. He so strenuously resisted Gian Galeazzo, the Duke of Milan, who had brought war upon the Florentines, that Galeazzo acknowledged that the writings of Coluccio did him more harm than a thousand Florentine horsemen. Coluccio died at Florence on the 4th day before the Ides of May <note>May 12</note> in the year 1406. Two of his *Letters* are extant in Baluze’s *Miscellany*, Volume 4, page 510. Besides these, Coluccio wrote two books *On True Religion*, a *Disputation on the Preeminence of Jurisprudence over Medicine*, a *Book on Fortune and Fate* divided into five treatises, a *Book of Letters*, and a small work titled *The Night-Box* <note>original: "Loculus noctis"</note>. Michael Poccianti, in his *Catalog of Florentine Writers* (page 42), testifies that these are still preserved as manuscripts in the Florentine libraries. His letters are also held as manuscripts in the Cotton Library under the designation Caligula A. 16.

<margin>
1369.
</margin>
**PHILIP OF LEYDEN**, a Dutchman by birth, born of a knightly family in Leiden <note>original: "Lugduni Batavorum"</note>, received his doctoral laurel in both laws <note>term: "Juris utriusq;" - refers to both Canon (Church) law and Civil law</note> at Orléans. Around the year 1369, he publicly professed as a Canon at Paris, having been granted a Canonry of the Church of Saint Mary of Condé. Finally recalled to his fatherland by William of Bavaria, the Count of Holland, he was appointed to his private chapel and secret councils. Soon after, he was appointed Vicar to Arnold van Horn, the Bishop of Utrecht. Having undertaken a journey to Rome by order of his Prince, he received Canonries in Utrecht and Leiden from Pope Gregory XI, to whom he was very dear. He died at Utrecht on the 8th of June in the year 1386 and was buried in his native city. He wrote the *Treatise on the Republic and the Care and Lot of Rulers*, published by Joannes Severinus in *Leiden, 1516, folio*, and a *Lecture on the Third Book of the Decretals*. Franciscus Sweertius, in his *Belgian Athenaeum* (page 644), provides testimony that all of Philip’s *Works* were illustrated with a learned preface and brought to light by Jan Franconius; however, he indicates neither the year nor the place of the edition.

**GERARD THE GREAT**, called *Groote* in his native tongue, a Belgian by nation and from the city of Deventer, applied himself to theological studies at Paris with such success that he was promoted to a master’s degree at the age of eighteen. Having returned home, he was created a Canon of Utrecht and Aachen. Finally, having set out to visit and listen to Jan van Ruusbroec, the Prior of Groenendaal <note>original: "Viridis Vallis"</note>, he began to love the way of life of the Canons Regular living in that place. Therefore, having resigned both Canonries, he established the Clerics or Brethren of the Common Life <note>A significant Roman Catholic pietist community that emphasized education and simple living</note> at Deventer in his homeland, at Eemsteyn near Dordrecht, at Windesheim near Zwolle, and in many other places, so that they might instruct the youth in good literature and morals. He flourished in the year 1370. He died in the year 1384 on the 20th of August, in the 44th year of his age. Three *Small Works* <note>original: "Opuscula"</note> are extant, namely: *A Protestation regarding Truthful Preaching*; *Conclusions and Proposals*; and the *Treatise on the Study of the Sacred Books*; these are usually published with the works of Thomas à Kempis.
