## PHILOTHEUS ACHILLINUS,
a Frenchman by nation and a counselor to King Charles V, flourished in the year 1370. It remains uncertain who actually hides behind the assumed name of "Philotheus Achillinus." Led by a conjecture that is by no means empty, Goldast <note>Melchior Goldast (1578–1635), a Swiss jurist and historian</note> suspects it was Philippe de Mézières, a soldier who was first the Chancellor of the Kingdom of Cyprus, then a Chamberlain to Pope Gregory XI, and finally a member of the household of Charles V, King of the Franks, and his **most influential advisor** <note>original Greek: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan), meaning his "everything" or right-hand man</note>. Twenty-five years before his death, he left the court and retired to the Celestine Monastery in Paris, where he spent his life in a leisure that was both pious and scholarly; however, I believe he was still continually consulted on the most serious affairs of his kingdom. Whoever he may have been, Philotheus wrote a distinguished work against the unjust ambition and tyranny of the Roman Pontiff titled *The Dream of the Orchard* <note>original: "Somnium Viridarii"</note>, or *Books on Royal and Sacerdotal Power*, presented in the form of a dialogue between a Cleric and a Soldier. This work was published, though full of errors, in Paris in 1516; but a complete and corrected version appears in Goldast’s *Monarchia*, Volume 1, p. 58. Furthermore, that same Philippe de Mézières wrote the *Life of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Crete* (also known as Thomas de Thomasiis), who died at the beginning of the year 1366, in two books. This *Life* can be found in Bollandus <note>The *Acta Sanctorum*</note> under the date of January 29th.

## GALLUS,
a German by nation and Abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Königssaal <note>original: "Aulae Regiae," located near Prague, the capital of Bohemia</note>. Trithemius * praises him with distinguished acclaim for his skill in sacred literature, his extensive reading of the Ancients, his profound contemplation of divine matters, his sharp wit, and the holiness of his character; he flourished in the year 1370. For the instruction of his brothers, he wrote a quite lengthy work called *The Pomegranate* <note>original: "Malogranatum"</note>, in the form of a dialogue between a Father and a Son. The work is divided into three books, the first of which concerns the state of Beginners, the second the state of those Making Progress, and the third the state of the Perfect. It was published in Germany in 1481 in quarto, though the name of the place was omitted, and again in 1487 in folio. Furthermore, all authors who discuss him mention a book of *Sermons to the Brothers* written by him.

<margin>1370.</margin>

## GREGORY XI,
previously called Pierre Roger de Beaufort, a Frenchman by nation from the region of Limoges, was the son of Count William of Beaufort and the nephew of Clement VI through his sister Joanna Rogeria. At the age of 17, he was created Cardinal Deacon of the title of Santa Maria Nuova by his uncle and sent to Baldo <note>Baldo degli Ubaldi, a famous jurist</note>, who was then lecturing at Perugia, so that he might be instructed in the science of law. At age 35, in the year of Christ 1370, he was elected Roman Pontiff on December 30th, and consecrated and crowned on January 5th of the following year. In 1375, he struck Joanna, Queen of Sicily and Naples, with anathema because she had pardoned the crime of a certain traitor despite his intercession. The following year, he bound the Florentines, who were injurious to the liberty of the Church, with the highest kind of excommunication, or "anathema maranatha" <note>A severe form of excommunication</note>. Nevertheless, they made light of the Pope’s thunderbolts and forced the clergy to perform their ecclesiastical duties under penalty of death. In the same year, Gregory restored the Pontifical seat from Avignon back to Rome, where he was received by the Romans with incredible joy and triumph. He died in Rome in the year 1378, on March 27th. Five of his *Letters* are extant in the *Collections of the Councils*, Vol. 11, p. 2037; forty-two others in Bzovius under the year 1372, etc.; ninety-seven others in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors*, Vol. 4, under the year 1371, etc.; and 112 others in the same work in the *Pontifical Registry*, p. 103.

<margin>1372.</margin>

## BARTHOLOMEW ALBICIUS,
an Italian by race and a Pisan by birth, originating from Rivano in Tuscany, was a monk of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> and flourished in the year 1372. In the year 1399, having set out for the General Chapter of his Order held at Assisi, he presented his book *On the Conformities* <note>original: "de Conformitatibus," a famous work comparing the life of St. Francis to that of Jesus</note>, which he brought back having been approved by the unanimous vote of all. As a reward for his labor, he was gifted with the complete habit that Saint Francis himself once used. He died at a great age in the Convent of Pisa on December 10th, 1401. His *Conformities of Saint Francis* survives, along with his *Life*...

<margin>1373.</margin>
ISAAC ARGYRUS, a Greek monk, flourished in the year 1373. At that time, following Nicephorus Gregoras, he published his <term>Computus</term> <note>A mathematical and astronomical treatise used to calculate the date of Easter and other movable feasts</note>, dedicated to Andronicus, the governor of the city of Aenos. It was first published in Greek and Latin by Jacob Christmann at Heidelberg, 1611, in quarto. Later, Denis Pétau <note>Dionysius Petavius, a renowned Jesuit scholar of chronology</note> published it with his own version and illustrative notes in *On the Doctrine of Times*, Volume 3, page 359; however, he omitted the Epilogue, which is found in Christmann’s edition. Another *Computus*, which also seems to have belonged to the same Argyrus, was published by the same Pétau from the Library of the King of France, in the same volume, page 384.

<margin>
*Supplement, chapter 442. 
† Chronicle of the Order of Hermits, page 67.

BONAVENTURA BADUARIUS of PERAGA, Italian by nation and a citizen of Padua, born of an illustrious family. He was created a Doctor of Theology at the University of Paris after spending many years in study there. An <term>Augustinian Hermit</term> <note>A member of the Order of Saint Augustine</note>, he was elected Prior General of his Order at the assembly in Verona in the year 1377. He was declared a Cardinal-Priest with the title of St. Cecilia by Pope Urban VI in September 1378, and undertook various embassies on behalf of the Roman See. At length, while he was resisting the wicked attempts of Francesco da Carrara, the petty ruler of the Paduans, with as much mental constancy as he could muster, he was killed at Rome by assassins sent by him in the year 1386; or as others say, 1389; according to others 1396; and in the opinion of others 1399. There remain his *Mirror of the Blessed Mary*, Augsburg 1476; four volumes on the *Four Books of Sentences*, printed somewhere in Germany; and *Meditations on the Life of Christ*, likewise printed, according to the testimony of Aubert Miraeus* and Joseph Pamphilus†. Joseph Pamphilus, in the place cited, also records that Baduarius wrote commentaries on the Canonical Epistles of Saints James and John, as well as *Sermons for the Seasons*, *Sermons on the Saints*, and *Sermons to the Clergy*.

<margin>1377.</margin>
MATTHEW, commonly called "THE COLLECTOR" <note>original: "Florilegus," literally "The Flower-Gatherer," a name given to compilers of historical anthologies</note>, a Benedictine monk of Westminster, flourished in the year 1377. He wrote the *Flowers of Histories*, or Annals from the creation of the world to the year of Christ 1307, which were largely copied from Matthew Paris in the earlier part. These *Flowers* exist distributed into two books, published through the care of the Most Reverend Matthew Parker at London in 1567, and reprinted at Frankfurt in 1601. John Bale, in his *Centuries*, volume 6, chapter 31, provides evidence that this "Collector" extended these annals up to the year 1377, and indeed wove together chronicles of the monasteries of Westminster and St. Edmunds. However, that continuation, much less the chronicles, has not yet seen the light of day.

<margin>1378.</margin>
URBAN VI, previously called Bartholomew <note>Bartholomew Prignano</note>, Italian by nation, Neapolitan by homeland, and Archbishop of Bari. While he was diligently serving the Cardinals gathered in the Conclave after the death of Gregory XI and urging harmony, he was unexpectedly elected Roman Pontiff at Rome on the 8th day of April, 1378. He was crowned on the 18th, on the feast of Easter itself. However, the French Cardinals sharply disagreed; since they prevailed in number, they preferred a French Pope. Thus, withdrawing from Rome, they elected Cardinal Robert, Count of Geneva, as Pope at Fondi in the month of September, and bestowed upon him the name of Clement VII. From this was born a grave and long-lasting <term>schism</term> <note>The Great Western Schism, a period from 1378 to 1417 when there were rival claimants to the papacy</note> in the Christian world, which occupied the swords of soldiers in that age and the pens of writers even in ours. For there is no agreement among the Pontiff's own followers concerning the true Pope: but just as the government of the Western Churches was once divided between Urban and Clement and their successors, so even now, authors almost always following the partisan interests of their own people...

</margin>
...having followed [these leaders], they split into factions. Urban began to reside at Rome, and Clement at Avignon. Italy, Germany, and Pannonia <note>The Roman province covering modern-day Hungary and parts of Austria</note> adhered to the former; the rest of the Western World clung to the latter. Urban died after he had waged heavy wars against the Anti-pope Clement with both temporal and spiritual weapons for a full decade. He suffered captivity more than once and was tossed about by constant dangers; he died at Rome in the year 1389, on the 15th of October. There exist four *Letters* in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 11, page 2045. Also, *Constitutions on the Authors of Ecclesiastical Liberty* are found in Bzovius under the year 1383. *Other Letters* appear in Luke Wadding's *Annals of the Minors*, Volume 4, in the *Pontifical Registry*, pages 165, 166, 177, and 180, where twenty letters of Clement VII are also found. Richard Crackanthorpe published Urban's Bull regarding the preservation of the Orthodox faith from the Cottonian Library in his *Apology for the English Church against the Bishop of Spalato*. Furthermore, Urban's *Formulary* <note>A collection of official legal formulas and templates</note>, along with the Indulgences he granted, was published in the common language [Italian] at Messina in 1567. *Certain Ecclesiastical Constitutions* appear in a collection from Rome, 1572, in quarto. *Several Apostolic Letters or Bulls* are in Laertius Cherubini’s *Great Bullary*, Volume 1, 1617 and 1638.

---

<margin>1378.</margin>
ALBERT OF STRASBOURG <note>original: "Albertus de Argentina"; Strasbourg was known as Argentoratum or Argentina in Latin</note>, German by nation, a Master or Doctor of the city of Strasbourg, and perhaps a Priest. He was a close associate of the Bishop of Strasbourg, by whom he was sent as an envoy to Avignon to present himself to the Pope and to deliver the decree of Emperor Louis against Papal ambition. He flourished in the year 1378. He wrote a *Chronicle from the beginnings of Emperor Rudolph of Habsburg until the death of Charles IV*, or from the year of Christ 1270 to 1378. Cuspinianus published a mutilated [incomplete] version of it along with the *Roman Consuls* at Basel in 1553 and 1569 (which edition is specifically prohibited by name in the *Index of Prohibited Books*; indeed, the reading of Albert's entire *Chronicle* is forbidden until it is expurgated according to the judgment of the Inquisitors). Christian Urstisius published the complete version among the *German Writers* at Frankfurt in 1585 and 1670, Volume 2, page 97. Albert also wrote the *Life of Berthold of Buchegg*, Bishop of Strasbourg and Speyer from the year 1328 to 1353. Urstisius published this at the end of the history in the same place, page 167.

---

<margin>1380.</margin>
WILLIAM THORN, English by nation, a Benedictine Monk of the Monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury, flourished around the year 1380. He wrote the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Augustine of Canterbury*, from the arrival of Saint Augustine himself in Britain until the year 1397. He wrote with the highest faith and diligence, utilizing every available source; however, he borrowed the earlier part of the Chronicle up to the year 1272 from the History of Thomas Sprott, with a few parts revised. This Chronicle appeared among the *Ten Writers of English History* at London in 1652, folio, page 1757. Furthermore, William is said to have written certain other works, namely: *A History of the Kings of Kent, The Lives of Certain Saints, and Chronicles of the Counties, Bishoprics, and Abbeys throughout all England*, which have not yet been printed. The latter exists as a manuscript in the Library of Saint Benedict at Cambridge, codex 67.

---

<margin>1380.</margin>
BALDUS DE UBALDIS, Italian by nation, from the house of Perugia, born of the illustrious Ubaldi family. He was a student of Peter de Ubaldis (a Doctor of Perugia) in <term>Both Laws</term> <note>Civil Law and Canon Law</note>, and a pupil of Bartolus of Sassoferrato. First in the city of Perugia, and then summoned by Galeazzo Visconti of Milan, he taught both laws at Pavia <note>original: "Ticinum"</note> with a very large gathering and applause of students. He flourished in the year 1380, around which time he was consulted by the leading men of the Christian republic regarding the legal validity of the election of Popes Urban VI and Clement VII; he gave his legal opinion in favor of Urban. Finally, having been lightly bitten on the lip by his pet little dog, he contracted rabies four months later and died at the age of 72 in the year of Christ 1400, on the 28th of April (or, as others say, in the year 1423 in the month of September). Clad in the habit of Saint Francis (believing this would be most beneficial for the salvation of his soul), he wished to be buried. This took place at Pavia in the Convent of the Friars Minor.

# The Century of Wycliffe.

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY
from the year 1300.
</margin>

### W R I T I N G S.

Commentary on the books of the Decretals <note>original: "Decretalium"; these were collections of papal decrees that formed the basis of medieval Canon Law</note>. Venice, 1595.
Five volumes of Legal Opinions <note>original: "Consiliorum"</note>. Frankfurt, 1589; a sixth volume at Venice, 1600.
Commentary on the Code, the Fiefs, and the New and Old Digests <note>These are fundamental components of the Corpus Juris Civilis, the body of Roman Law</note>. Lyon, 1545.
Many other works by Baldus concerning Civil Law have appeared in print in almost countless locations. Jean-Jacques Boissard enumerates them all in a summary in *Portraits of Illustrious Men* <note>original: "Icones illustrium virorum"</note>, Part 1, page 102.

<margin>1381.</margin>
MICHAEL OF ANGRI <note>Also known as Michael Aignanus</note>, an Italian by birth and a native of Bologna—though there are those who wish to claim he originated from Lombardy—certainly entered the Carmelite Order at the monastery in Bologna. He was later distinguished with a doctorate in Theology from the University of Paris. He flourished in the year 1381, at which time he was appointed the nineteenth Prior General of his entire Order during the Chapter at Verona. Pope Urban VI had previously entrusted him with the duty of Vicar General. He administered the highest office of his Order for five years. He died in Bologna on the 1st of December in the year 1416; however, according to the calculation of Sixtus of Siena, he died in 1396. He was buried in the Carmelite Convent before the high altar. He wrote five books of *Commentaries on the Psalms*, in which he explains the entire Psalter using the Scholastic method <note>The rigorous, dialectical method of the medieval universities</note>, though not without success. This work was first published under the name of an Anonymous Author at Alcalá in 1524, and at Lyon in 1588 and 1602 in folio. It was finally restored to its true author in the editions of Venice, 1603, and Lyon, 1652 and 1673. Josias Simler, in his *Library* <note>original: "Bibliotheca"</note>, page 503, reports that Michael's commentary on the *Books of Sentences* <note>The standard theology textbook by Peter Lombard</note> was printed at Milan. Simler also lists many other writings by Michael, including a notable work on the *Most Pure Conception of the Virgin Mary*; others are listed by Antonio Alegre in his *Carmelite Paradise*, page 316.

<margin>1381.</margin>
RAYMOND JORDAN, who for a long time lay hidden under the pseudonym of "The Idiot" <note>original: "Idiota"; a name chosen to signify a simple, unlearned person to demonstrate humility</note> with his name suppressed, and who was thought to belong to the antiquity of the eighth or ninth century. He was a Canon Regular of the Augustinian Order, first serving as the Provost at Uzès in Gallia Narbonensis <note>Southern France</note>, and later as the Abbot of Celle in the Diocese of Bourges. He flourished from the year 1381.

### W O R K S.

Six books of *Contemplations*: *On the wretched course of this present life; on lost innocence; on conversion through the twelve months of the spiritual year, which produces the twelve fruits of the Spirit; on the constant conflict between the soul and the flesh; on the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit against the seven mortal sins; that the Holy Spirit is the helper of the soul, and on His various duties toward mankind; On the eight beatitudes; On Love; On True Patience; On Death; On the Blessed Virgin Mary.* These *Contemplations* were published at Paris in 1519, in quarto, and elsewhere.
*A Full Treatise on the Blessed Virgin.*
*Three books on the Religious State.*
A work on the *Spiritual Eye*, or the *Mystical Eye*. This appeared in a mutilated form under Raymond’s name, edited by Théophile Raynaud at Lyon in 1641. However, Luke Wadding demonstrated that it is actually the work of John of Wales. It had previously appeared in its entirety under the name of a certain Master P. Lacepiera at Venice in 1496, translated into Italian by Theophilus Romanus of the Augustinian Hermits.
*Rules Encompassing the Christian Life.*
*Paraphrase on Psalm 15*, which, along with the preceding small work, Philippe Labbe conjectures should be attributed to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.
All these works, which were usually held under the name of "The Idiot" in almost every edition of the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Bibliotheca Patrum"</note>, were claimed for Raymond by Théophile Raynaud, who saw to their publication with his own corrections at Paris in 1654, in quarto.

...having followed [different leaders], they split into factions. Urban remained at Rome, Clement at Avignon. To the former belonged Italy, Germany, and Hungary <note>original: "Pannonia"</note>; to the latter, the rest of the Western World. 

Urban died after he had waged heavy wars with the Antipope Clement, as much with physical arms as with spiritual ones, for a full decade. He suffered capture on more than one occasion and was tossed about by constant perils; he died at Rome in the year 1389, on the 15th of October. His *Four Letters* are found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 11, page 2045. His *Constitutions for the Protectors of Ecclesiastical Liberty* are found in Bzovius’s annals for the year 1383. *Another letter* is found in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minorites*, Volume 4, in the Papal Register, page 165, where twenty letters of Clement VII are also found. His *Bull on keeping faith with Heretics* <note>original: "Bullam ejus de fide Hæreticis servanda"</note> was published from the Cotton Library by Richard Crakanthorpe in his *Defense of the Anglican Church against de Dominis*. Furthermore, the *Forum of Urban*, along with the Indulgences granted by him, was published in the common tongue <note>Likely referring to a vernacular translation, possibly German or Italian</note> at Dilingen in 1567. *Certain Ecclesiastical Constitutions* appear in the Roman Collection of 1582. *Several Apostolic Letters or Bulls* are in Laertius Cherubini’s *Great Bullary*, printed in 1617 and 1638.

<margin>1378.</margin> ALBERT OF STRASBOURG <note>original: "Albertus de Argentina"</note>, German by birth and a citizen of Strasbourg, a Master or Doctor, and perhaps a Priest. He was an associate of the Bishop of Constance, by whom he was sent as an envoy to Avignon to present himself to the Pope and to deliver the decree of Emperor Louis against Papal ambition. He flourished in the year 1378. He wrote a *Chronicle* from the beginning of the reign of Emperor Rudolph of Habsburg until the death of Charles IV, or from the year of Christ 1270 to 1378. This work was published in a mutilated form by Cuspinian along with the *Roman Consuls*, Basel, 1553 and 1569 (which edition is specifically forbidden in the *Index of Prohibited Books*; indeed, the reading of the complete Chronicle of Albert is forbidden until it is purged according to the judgment of the Inquisitors). Christian Urstisius published the complete version among the *German Writers*, Frankfurt, 1585 and 1670, Volume 2, page 97. Albert also wrote the *Life of Berthold of Buchegg*, Bishop of Strasbourg and Speyer from the year 1328 to 1353. Urstisius published this at the end of the Chronicle in the same volume, page 167.

---

<margin>1380.</margin> WILLIAM THORN, English by nation, a Benedictine Monk of the Monastery of St. Augustine in Canterbury, flourished around the year 1380. He wrote a *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Abbots of St. Augustine in Canterbury*, from the entry of St. Augustine himself into Britain until the year 1397. He worked with the greatest loyalty and diligence; however, he borrowed the first part of the Chronicle up to the year 1272 from the History by Thomas Sprott, with a few things corrected. This Chronicle appeared among the *Ten Writers of English History*, London, 1652, folio page 1753. William is said to have written certain other things, namely: a *History of the Kings of Kent*, the *Lives of Certain Saints*, and *Chronicles of the Counties, Bishoprics, Orders, and Abbeys throughout all England*: these have not yet been printed. The last one exists as a manuscript in the Library of Corpus Christi College <note>original: "Bibliothecâ S. Benedicti"</note>, Cambridge, codex 67.

---

<margin>1380.</margin> BALDUS UBALDUS, Italian by birth, from a house in Perugia and descended from the noble Ubaldi family, son of Peter de Ubaldis, a Doctor of Perugia. He was a Doctor of Both Laws <note>meaning Civil Law and Canon Law</note> and a student of Bartolus of Sassoferrato. He taught both laws first in his home city, then was summoned by Galeazzo Visconti of Milan to Pavia <note>original: "Ticini"</note>, where he taught with a massive gathering and applause from his students. He flourished around the year 1380. At the time of the schismatic election of the Popes Urban VI and Clement VII, he was consulted by the highest men of the Christian republic and gave his legal opinion in favor of Urban. Finally, having been bitten slightly on the lip by his pet dog, which he was fond of, he contracted rabies <note>original: "rabiem concepit"</note> four months later and died in the year 1400, on the 28th of April, at the age of 76; or, as others say, in the year 1423 in the month of January. Clothed in the habit of St. Francis (believing it would contribute greatly to the salvation of his soul), he wished to be buried. This took place at Pavia in the Convent of the Friars Minor.

<margin>1381.</margin>
**MICHAEL ANGRIANUS**, or Aignanus, was an Italian by nation <note>original: "gente Italus"</note> and a native of Bologna, though there are some who wish to claim he originated from Lombardy. He certainly made his profession in the Carmelite Order at the monastery in Bologna, and was later distinguished with a doctorate in Theology from the University of Paris. He flourished in the year 1381, at which time he was appointed the nineteenth Prior General of his entire Order at the Chapter of Verona. Pope Urban VI had previously entrusted him with the duty of Vicar General. He administered the highest office of his Order for five years. He died at Bologna on the first of December in the year 1416, though according to the calculation of Sixtus of Siena, it was in 1396; he was buried in the Carmelite Convent before the high altar. He wrote *Commentaries on the Psalms in five books*, in which he explains the entire Psalter using the Scholastic method <note>a formal, academic approach to theology common in medieval universities</note>, yet not without success. That work appeared under the name of an *Unknown Author* at Alcalá <note>original: "Compluti"</note> in 1524, Lyon in 1588, and Lyon in 1602. It was finally restored to its true author in the editions of Venice, 1603, and Lyon, 1652 and 1673. Josias Simler, in his *Library* <note>original: "Biblioth."</note>, page 503, reports that his *Commentary on the Books of the Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" by Peter Lombard was the standard textbook for medieval theology students.</note> was printed at Milan; Simler also lists many other writings by Michael, including a notable *Work on the most pure Conception of the Virgin Mary*; others are listed by Antonio Alegre in his *Carmelite Paradise*, page 316.

<margin>1381.</margin>
**RAYMUNDUS JORDANUS**, who for a long time lay hidden under the name of **The Idiot** <note>original: "Idiota." This was a pseudonym used out of humility, meaning an unlearned or simple man.</note> with his true name suppressed, and who was once thought to belong to the antiquity of the eighth or ninth century. He was a Canon Regular of the Augustinian Order, first serving as the Provost of Uzès <note>original: "Uticensis"</note> in Gallia Narbonensis, and then as the Abbot of Selles-sur-Cher <note>original: "Cellensis"</note> in the Diocese of Bourges. He flourished from the year 1381.

### W O R K S.

*Six books of Contemplations: on the miserable course of this present life; on lost innocence; on conversion through the twelve months of the spiritual year producing the twelve fruits of the Spirit; on the constant conflict between the soul and the flesh; on the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit against the seven mortal sins; how the Holy Spirit is the helper of the soul, and on his various duties toward man; On the eight beatitudes; On Love; On true Patience; On Death; On the Blessed Virgin Mary.* These *Contemplations* were published at Paris, 1519, in quarto, and elsewhere.

*A full Treatise on the Blessed Virgin.*

*On the religious state, in three books.*

*Work on the Spiritual Eye: or the Mystic Eye.* It appeared, though in a mutilated form, under the name of Raymund, edited by Théophile Raynaud at Lyon in 1641. However, Luke Wadding demonstrated that this work should be attributed to John Gualensis <note>also known as John of Wales</note>. It had appeared previously in its entirety under the name of a certain Master P. Lacepiera at Venice in 1496, and was translated into Italian by Theophilus Romanus of the Augustinian Hermits.

*Rules embracing the Christian life.*

*Paraphrase on Psalm 15*, which, along with the preceding short work, Philippe Labbe conjectures should be attributed to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.

All these works, which were usually found under the name of "The Idiot" in almost every edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, were reclaimed for Raymund by Théophile Raynaud, who saw to their publication with his own corrections at Paris, 1654, in quarto.

# The Wycliffite Century.
<note>This century is named by the author after the English reformer John Wycliffe, who lived during this period.</note>

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY
from the year 1300.

<margin>1384.</margin>
**JOHN OF DAMBACH**, <note>original: "Joannes Tambacus"</note> a German by nation and a native of the Alsace region <note>original: "patriâ Argensis," likely referring to the diocese of Strasbourg/Argentinensis</note>, was a monk of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note> in the Monastery of Strasbourg. He served as the first Rector of the University of Prague and was eventually appointed Master of the Sacred Palace by Pope Urban <note>Urban VI</note> in the year 1366. He flourished in the year 1384. He died an octogenarian, though the exact year of his death is not certain. His surviving work includes the *Mirror of Patience, or fifteen books on the Consolation of Theology*, published in Paris (1493), Cologne (1502), Nuremberg (1509), and elsewhere. Another work of his, *On Guilt and Grace*, is held in manuscript by the Dominicans of the Great Convent in Paris. Many other writings of Dambach are listed in the *Library of the Preachers*, page 129, of which nothing certain is known.

<margin>1384.</margin>
**MARSILIUS OF INGHEN**, or Inghenius, was German by birth, though according to Trithemius and Bale he was English. He was a Doctor of the University of Paris, a Canon and Treasurer of the Church of Saint Andrew in Cologne, and the founder of the University <note>term: Gymnasium (here used in the classical sense of a place of higher learning or university)</note> of Heidelberg, as well as its first Doctor and Rector. He flourished in the year 1384. He died on the 20th of August <note>original: "xiii. Cal. Septembris"</note>, 1394, and was buried in the Church of Saint Peter in Heidelberg. He wrote *Commentaries on the four books of the Master of the Sentences* <note>The Sentences by Peter Lombard was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, which were printed in Strasbourg in 1501. Bale lists other writings of his in his fifth volume, which still remain hidden in obscurity.

<margin>1384.</margin>
**MANUEL II PALAEOLOGUS**, the legitimate <unclear>born</unclear> son of Emperor John V Palaeologus, earned the Empire through rare devotion toward his father. For when John, around the year 1380—having left his e<unclear>lder</unclear> son Andronicus in charge of Constantinople—traveled to the West to seek aid from Christian Princes ag<unclear>ainst</unclear> the growing power of the Turks, he was detained on his return by Venetian merchants because of unpaid debts. Andronicus, secure in his control of the Empire, laughed at his father's captivity; but Manuel, having scraped together money from his governorship in Thessalonica, hurried to Venice and redeemed his father by clearing the merchants' ledgers. Provoked by Andronicus's crime and liberated by Manuel’s piety, Emperor John disinherited him along with his son John, and designated Manuel as his successor after death; he even took him as a <unclear>co</unclear>-emperor while he was still living, around the year 1384. Andronicus, driven to rage by this disgr<unclear>ace</unclear>, fled to Bayezid, the King of the Turks; with the help of the Turk's auxiliary forces, he captured Constantinople, threw his father and brother into pr<unclear>ison</unclear>, and seized the Empire. After three years in prison, John <unclear>and</unclear> his son Manuel escaped, and by using the favor and aid of the tyrant Bayezid (who had become more h<unclear>ostile</unclear> toward Andronicus), they recovered the Empire; they handed Andron<unclear>icus</unclear> over to the Turks to be kept in perpetual imprisonment. In the year 1391, upon the death of his father John, Manuel began to reign alone. While he constantly defended the majesty of the Em<unclear>pire</unclear> against the ferocity of Bayezid, he fi<unclear>nally</unclear> suffered a siege of the Imperial City. Entrusting the defense of the City to John, the son of his brother Andronicus, he himself sailed to the West, following his father's ex<unclear>ample</unclear>, to obtain aid from the Latins; he was also <unclear>touched</unclear> by his father's misfortune. After he had tr<unclear>av</unclear>eled through Italy, France, England, Germany, and Hungary <note>original: "Pannoniam"</note>, he finally returned to Constantinople without having achieved his goal. When the people of Constantinople had almost despaired, salvation shone from elsewhere. For Tamerlane, <unclear>prince</unclear> of the Tatars, flew to Manuel's aid with a huge army, and Ba<unclear>jazet</unclear> broke the siege in the year 1401. In a battle joined with Tamerlane the following year, Bayezid was defeated and led away captive. After the tyrant was dead, Manuel entered into a l<unclear>ast</unclear>ing peace with Mehmet, Bayezid's son, and held the empire s<unclear>ecure</unclear>ly thereafter. He died, as they say, in the year 1418, but more correctly in 1425, after he—having become in<unclear>valid</unclear> and weak—had passed the torch of the Empire to his son John in the year 1419.

<margin>1385.</margin>
**JOHN DE BURGH** <note>original: "Joannes de Burgo"</note>, an Englishman by nation, Doctor of Theology, Chancellor of the University of Cambridge, and also Rector of the Church of Collingham in the county of Nottinghamshire, flourished in the year 1385, the year in which he compiled the *Pupilla Oculi* <note>The Pupil of the Eye</note>. For he wrote a book titled, *The Pupil of the Eye, highly necessary for all priests, both those with cures and those without; in which is treated the administration of the seven Sacraments, the ten precepts of the Decalogue, and the remaining ecclesiastical offices, which a rightly ordained priest ought not to be ignorant of.* It was published in *Paris*, 1510; *Strasbourg* <note>original: "Argentine"</note>, 1514; and *Rouen* <note>original: "Rothomagi"</note>, 1516, in quarto. How highly this book was once regarded is evident from the almost innumerable manuscript copies of it preserved in the public libraries at Cambridge; so much so that I cannot sufficiently marvel that so distinguished a writer completely escaped the diligence of Bale <note>John Bale (1495–1563), a famous English historian and bibliographer who chronicled British writers.</note>.

---

<margin>1389.</margin>
**MANUEL CHRYSOLORAS**, a Roman by origin <note>likely referring to his family's roots in the "Old Rome" before moving to the East</note>, a Byzantine by homeland, born of a most noble lineage, flourished in the year 1389. Around that time, he was sent to the West as an ambassador by the Emperor John Palaeologus the Elder <note>John V Palaeologus</note> to request aid against the Turks from Christian kings. After he had performed the duty entrusted to him before the King of England and other princes with the greatest diligence—though with unsuccessful results—he settled in Italy. There, he was the first of all to revive the study of Greek literature, which had been neglected in the West for more than seven hundred years and was indeed almost unknown. He taught first at Venice, soon at Florence, afterwards at Rome, and finally at Pavia <note>original: "Ticini"</note>. He had as students Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo, Francesco Barbaro, Philelphus, Poggio Bracciolini, Battista Guarino, and other leading men of the age. Around the year 1397, having been summoned from Florence by the Emperor Manuel [II] on his journey to the West, he went to Milan. After Manuel's departure, however, he returned to his usual teaching duties. In 1414, he went to Constance, being a keen observer of the General Council; there, in the following year on the 15th of April, he ended his life and was buried among the Dominicans of Constance. Aeneas Sylvius <note>The scholar-poet who later became Pope Pius II</note>, the Poet Laureate, placed an epitaph for him, which begins thus:

> I am he who taught the Latin lands to imitate the ancient arts,
> Having banished the circuitous mazes of speech; and I who
> Brought back to light the eloquence of the great Demosthenes and Cicero,
> Known by the name Chrysoloras,
> Here I lie after life, and rest in a foreign land, etc.

There exist *Three Letters on the Comparison of Old and New Rome* <note>New Rome is a traditional name for Constantinople</note>; the first is quite lengthy, addressed to Emperor John Palaeologus; the second to John Chrysoloras; and the third to Demetrius Chrysoloras, which are much shorter. They were published in Greek; the first also in Greek and Latin with the translation of Peter Lambeck, at the end of Codinus' *On the Antiquities of Constantinople*, *Paris*, 1655, in folio. His *Grammatical Questions* were published in Greek somewhere in octavo.

---

<margin>1389.</margin>
**BONIFACE IX**, previously called *Pietro Tomacelli* <note>original: "Petrus Tomacellus"</note>, a Neapolitan by birth. He was first appointed Acolyte and Apostolic Prothonotary by Urban VI, then Cardinal Deacon of Saint George in Velabro, and finally Cardinal Priest with the title of Saint Anastasia. After Urban’s death, he was elected Roman Pontiff in the year 1389, on the 2nd of November; consecrated on the 9th; and crowned on the

# The Wycliffite Century.
<note>This century (the 1300s) is named by the author after the English reformer John Wycliffe, whose challenges to church authority defined much of the era's theological debate.</note>

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY
from the Year 1300.
</margin>
on the 14th day of the same month, in the 34th year of his age—or, as others say, his 45th. In the year 1390, he confirmed the grant made to Charles, King of Sicily, and all his posterity, which had been urged by his predecessor Urban. In the year 1391, being a man most greedy for money (with which he enriched his relatives), he was the first to introduce the burden of **Annates** <term>Annates: a tax consisting of the first year's income of an ecclesiastical office, paid to the Papal treasury</term> upon the Church, decreeing that the first year's proceeds of ecclesiastical benefices should be paid to the Apostolic See, in imitation of the Jewish first-fruits. In the year 1394, after recent riots had been settled, he obtained the right to appoint magistrates at his pleasure, impose taxes, and organize the military. Thus, as Bzovius says <margin>* To the year 1394, number 1.</margin>, he was the first of all the Roman Pontiffs who appeared to have suppressed the entire power of the Roman people and to have obtained supreme command of the City. In the year 1400, having entered Rome from Assisi, where he had stayed for some years, he celebrated the Jubilee. He died in 1404, on the 1st of October. His *Letters and Constitutions* (four of them) are found in Bzovius for the years 1390, 1391, and 1403; another six are in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* for the years 1392, 1394, and 1399; and forty-two others are in the same work in the *Register of the Pontiffs*, page 177, with more in Volume IV.

---

<margin>1390.</margin>
**JOSEPH, CALLED ALSHAHER BILTABIB**, son of Al-marchum Al-mu-altagi, an Egyptian by nation and an Alexandrian by citizenship, was appointed Provost of the Catholic Church of the Blessed Virgin in the year 1390, having been ordained a Priest in 1348. This man interpreted almost all the Canons <note>Church laws and regulations</note> accepted in the Greek Church into the Arabic language in a paraphrastic manner. A complete manuscript version exists in the Bodleian Library. The famous Beveridge published the Canons of the first four General Councils, excerpted from this work in Arabic and Latin, in his *Pandects of Canons*, Oxford, 1672, Volume II, page 681.

---

<margin>1390.</margin>
<margin>* Library, page 558.</margin>
**PETER OF HERENTHALS** <note>original: "Petrus Herentalius"</note>, a Brabantine from the Belgian region, took his name from the town of Herenthals. A Canon and Prior of the Monastery of Floreffe of the Premonstratensian Order <note>A religious order of regular canons founded by St. Norbert</note>, he flourished in the year 1390. He died after the year 1436—provided that Simler * calculates correctly, who states that Peter's **Catena** <term>Catena: literally a "chain" of interpretations, a commentary made by linking together quotes from earlier Church Fathers</term> on the Psalms was composed around that year. Peter composed a lengthy exposition of the Psalms from various commentaries of the Fathers and Doctors, which was printed in Cologne, 1487; Reutlingen, 1498; Rouen, 1504; and Cologne, 1554. Oudin testifies in his *Supplement*, page 657, that he saw Peter's very extensive commentary on the four Gospels, as well as a *Chronicle* from the creation of the world to the year 1385, in manuscript in the Floreffe Library. The *Chronicle* is also held in the Colbertine Library, Codex 751. Certain other of his writings are listed by Fr. Sweertius in *Athenae Belgicae*, page 621.

---

<margin>1390.</margin>
**RALPH DE RIVO**, a Belgian by nation and Brabantine by homeland, called "of Breda," was the Dean of Tongeren. Most skilled in and tenacious of the ancient customs of the Church, he flourished in the year 1390. He died in Rome in the year 1401, on the 2nd of November, or according to others, in 1403, on the 10th of April. There exist his *Ecclesiastical Calendar*, or *Twenty-three Propositions on the Observance of the Canons*, published separately in Leuven, 1568, and reprinted in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXVI, page 289. Also, his *History of the Deeds of Three Bishops of Liège* <note>original: "Pontificum Leodiensium"</note>—Engelbert of Mark, John of Arkel, and Arnold of Horn—covering the years 1347 to 1386, which Jean Chapeaville first brought to light in *History of the Affairs of Liège*, Liège, 1616, quarto, Volume III, page 1.

---

<margin>1390.</margin>
**GERARD OF ZUTPHEN** <note>original: "Gerardus Zutphaniensis"</note>, named after his native city, was one of the first Regular Clerks of the Order of Saint Jerome, or the **Brothers of the Common Life** <note>A pietist community in the Netherlands that lived communally without taking formal vows</note>, instituted by Gerard Groote among the people of Deventer. Distinguished for his exceptional piety and rare learning, he flourished in the year 1390. He died on the 4th of December, 1398, at the age of 31. Two of his short ascetic works exist: one *On Interior Reformation, or the Powers of the Soul*; the other *On Spiritual Ascents*. These were published in Paris and Cologne in 1539, and appear frequently among the works of Thomas à Kempis and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXVI, page 234.

# The Wycliffite Century.
<note>The 14th century is labeled here as the "Wycliffite Century" because the theological challenges posed by the English reformer John Wycliffe dominated the intellectual and ecclesiastical discourse of the era.</note>

<margin>
THE 14TH CENTURY
from the Year 1300.
</margin>

<margin>1390.</margin>
<margin>*Annals of the Minors.</margin>
<margin>*Annals of the Minors, Volume IV, for the year 1395, section 2.</margin>
**WILLIAM WOODFORD**, also known as *Wilford*, an Englishman by birth, though Wadding* (to whom it is customary to count English writers among his own countrymen) claims he was Irish and from the city of Waterford. A monk of the Franciscan Order, he flourished in the year 1390. Six years later, at the Synod of London, he was chosen by Thomas Arundel, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the entire English Clergy to write a refutation of John Wycliffe’s *Trialogue* <note>original: "Trialogum"; Wycliffe's major work on theology and church reform</note>. He died, as is commonly reported, at Colchester in the year 1397. However, if it is true, as Wadding* maintains, that Woodford dedicated a *Short Work on Religion* <note>original: "Opusculum de Religione"</note> to Cardinal Julian in the year 1433, he must have lived a much longer life. His surviving works include: a book addressed to Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, against the *18 Articles* extracted from Wycliffe’s *Trialogue* and condemned (according to the general consensus of writers) at the Council of London in 1396; this is found in the *Collection of Desirable Things* <note>original: "Fasciculo Rerum expetendarum"</note>, Cologne, 1535, p. 96. Also, a *Determination against the Heresies of John Wycliffe*, which exists in manuscript at the Library of New College, Oxford (codex 87) and Merton College (codex 222). A *Defense against the Man of Armagh in the small book on the beggary of Christ* <note>original: "Defensorium contra Armachanum"; a refutation of Richard FitzRalph, the Archbishop of Armagh, who famously attacked the mendicant orders</note>, manuscript at Magdalen College, Oxford (codex 62). An *Extraction of the Errors of the Man of Armagh*, manuscript at New College, Oxford (codex 168). *On the Causes for the Condemnation of the Articles of John Wycliffe*, manuscript at Merton College (codex 210), which does not seem at all different from the first work mentioned. *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, manuscript at Exeter College, Oxford (codex 11). His *Summa on the Virtues*, which Prior Walter completed from the middle to the end, which I saw in manuscript at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. Many other works are listed by Bale in Century VII, chapter 3, and by Wadding in his *Writers of the Minor Order*, page 158.

---

<margin>1390.</margin>
**JOHN BROMYARD**, an Englishman of Hereford, was a monk of the Dominican Order <note>original: "Ordinis Prædicatorum"</note>, an eminent theologian and legal expert, a Doctor of Oxford, and finally a Professor of Sacred Theology at Cambridge. He fiercely opposed Wycliffe at the Synod of London in 1382. He flourished in the year 1390, although some mistakenly place him in the year 1290. He is said to have died after the year 1419. His *Summa for Preachers* <note>original: "Summa Prædicatorum"</note> survives, divided into two parts, in which he explains the principal topics and meanings of Church discipline in alphabetical order; printed in Nuremberg in 1485 and Venice in 1586. Other works include *Sayings on the Celebration of the Mass*, manuscripts at Merton College, Oxford (codex 210); *Exhortations*, manuscript in the public library at Cambridge (codex 208); and a *Treatise on Civil and Canon Law applied to a moral sense according to alphabetical order*, manuscripts at Pembroke College, Cambridge (codex 122), New College, Oxford (codex 140), and the Lambeth Library. Others are listed by Bale, Century VII, chapter 4, and Altamura in the *Library of Preachers*, page 63.

---

<margin>1394.</margin>
**BENEDICT XIII**, previously named Peter de Luna, was Spanish by birth, born of the highest nobility among the Aragonese. Created Cardinal-Deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin by Gregory XI, he sided with Clement VII after Gregory’s death and was sent as a legate to Spain by him in 1381. After Clement’s death, he was elected Roman Pontiff at Avignon on September 28, 1394, and was consecrated and crowned on October 11. He first took an oath that he would step down from the Papacy if Boniface IX also resigned. Although often appealed to by Christian princes and bishops to restore peace to the Church, he wove all kinds of intrigues and devised clever tricks to keep the Papacy for himself while deceiving others. Consequently, he was besieged at Avignon in 1398 by King Charles of France, captured, and placed in custody. Having escaped from prison in 1403, he returned to his usual arts of deception; though he never stopped professing he was ready to abdicate the Papacy, he nevertheless fought to retain it by hook or by crook <note>original: "per fas et nefas"</note>. On June 5, 1408, he was deposed by the Council of Pisa, fled to Catalonia, and in 1408 gathered a small council <note>original: "Conciliabulum"</note> of his followers at Perpignan. Soon after, established at Barcelona, he cursed his rival Popes, their followers, and the Fathers of the Council of Pisa with dire imprecations, and annulled the acts of the Council of Pisa. On July 26, 1417, he was removed from both the Papacy and the communion of the church by a decree of the Council of Constance. Nevertheless, though deserted by everyone, he held onto the title until his final breath...

</margin>...stubbornly held onto the title he had wrongly usurped. He died at Peñíscola, a fortress in the Kingdom of Valencia, on the 23rd day of May in the year 1423. His surviving works include: *Letters* (found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 11, pages 2086, 2113, 2157, 2268); a *Bull* in which he excommunicates all Kings and Princes who withdraw their obedience from him and decrees that they should be stripped of their domains (*Collection of Councils*, Volume 12, page 1812); a *Response to the Emperor Sigismund* (found in the works of Bzovius for the year 1415, number 19); an *Edict against the Jews* (ibid., number 35); and many other *Letters* found in the works of Dietrich von Nieheim. He also wrote a *Book on the Power of the Supreme Pontiff and the Council* (a manuscript in the Vatican Library) and a *Book of Consolations for Human Life against all Misfortunes*, which was published in Spanish.

<margin>1395.</margin> **HENRY KNIGHTON**, an Englishman by nationality and an Augustinian Canon <note>original: "Canonicus Regularis"</note> of the Monastery of Leicester, flourished around the year 1395. He was a distinguished historian; no one else pursued English history with greater faithfulness and diligence. He wrote a *Chronicle of Events in England in Five Books*, covering the period from roughly the year 950 to 1395. In the first book, he briefly runs through the deeds of the Saxon Kings up to the year 1066; the following three books, which reach the year 1377, he transcribed almost word-for-word from the *Polychronicon* of Ranulf Higden of Chester. Furthermore, he committed to writing a *History of the Deposition of King Richard II* of England, which took place in the year 1399. Both works are found among the *Ten Writers of English History* edited by the illustrious Twisden in London, 1652, pages 2311 and 2743.

<margin>1396.</margin> **PIERRE D'AILLY** <note>original: "Petrus de Alliaco"</note>, a Frenchman by nationality, was born in 1350 at Compiègne on the Oise River to parents of very humble means. Well-instructed in the liberal arts, he entered the College of Navarre at the University of Paris in 1372, being received among the company of theology candidates known as "bursars" <note>scholarship students</note>. In 1375, he began lecturing on the *Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard medieval theology textbook</note> in his college and preaching to the people in the church. Summoned to the Synod of Amiens while still a subdeacon, he delivered a sermon to the priests. On April 11th, 1380, he received his doctoral insignia. The following year, having delivered an oration before the Duke of Anjou, he declared on behalf of the University of Paris that a General Council was necessary to end the Schism <note>The Western Schism, where multiple popes claimed authority</note>; he was made a Canon of Noyon in that same year. In 1384, he was placed in charge of the College of Navarre, where he had Jean Gerson, Nicolas de Clémanges, and other most learned men as his students. Around the year 1387, before Pope Clement VII residing at Avignon, he argued the cause of the Paris Faculty of Theology against Jean de Monzon, a Dominican, whom they had recently condemned for publicly teaching his opinion regarding the "stained" Conception of the Blessed Virgin <note>A theological dispute over whether Mary was conceived with original sin; d'Ailly defended the idea of the Immaculate Conception</note>. In 1389, he was named Chancellor of the University of Paris and was employed by King Charles VI as his almoner and confessor. In 1394, he was appointed Treasurer of the Royal Chapel in Paris. In the same year, he was sent by King Charles to Benedict XIII (who had succeeded Clement VII) to consult on a means for ending the schism. In 1395, he was named Bishop of Le Puy, and in 1396, Bishop of Cambrai. In 1405 <note>The original text contains a printer's error "1305"</note>, while staying in Genoa, he delivered a sermon before Pope Benedict and persuaded him to decree that the Feast of the Trinity should be celebrated; this had previously been celebrated by only a few churches, but thereafter, under the leadership and authorship of the Bishop of Cambrai, it began to be observed everywhere. In 1409, he participated in the Council of Pisa. On June 7th, 1411, he was invited into the college of Cardinals by Pope John XXIII with the title of St. Chrysogonus, and three years later was sent as a legate to Germany. At the end of 1414 <note>The original text contains a printer's error "1314"</note>, he set out for the Council of Constance; he presided over its third session and was a major figure throughout the entire three-year period. At the end of 1417, when the Synod concluded, he delivered frequent sermons to the Fathers. He died in the year 1425 <note>The original text contains a printer's error "1325"</note> and was buried in the Cathedral Church of Cambrai; he was commonly called the *Eagle of France* and the *tireless hammer of those wandering from the truth*.

**ANTONIO DE BUTRIO**, an Italian by birth from Bologna, was a Doctor of Both Laws <term>Doctor utriusque iuris: a degree in both civil and church (canon) law</term>. He taught in the universities of Bologna and Ferrara and was the teacher of Johannes de Imola and Geminianus. He flourished in the year 1398. He died in Bologna on the 5th of October in 1408 (if Forster is to be believed) and was buried at St. Michael's. However, there is a manuscript codex in the Augsburg Library containing his *Lectures on the second part of the Decretals* <note>The Decretals are collections of papal decrees forming canon law.</note>, which claims the lecture was written in the year 1439. Yet, little trust should be placed in the inscriptions of these manuscript codices, as is evident from another codex in the same library which claims Zabarella’s *Lectures on the Clementines* was composed in 1436, even though it is certain the author died in 1417. Antonio’s *Commentary on the five books of Decretals* exists (Venice, 1578, in seven volumes), as does his *Commentary on the sixth book of Decretals* (Venice, 1575), his *Legal Counsels or Responses* (Venice, 1582), a *Treatise on the Right of Patronage* (Frankfurt, 1581), and two *Repertories*—one for Canon Law and one for Civil Law—published more than once, along with other works less relevant to this location.

1400.
* On the Writers of the Minorite Order, page 264.
</margin>

**NICHOLAS DE GORHAM**, whom some wish to claim was French, was more correctly English by nationality. He was born in the village of the same name in Hertfordshire, educated in the liberal arts at Merton College, Oxford, and honored with the degree of Master. Eventually, he joined the Dominicans <note>The Order of Preachers.</note> and, having moved to Paris, became famous for his learning and piety, serving as the Provincial of his Order in France. Wadding, however, numbers him among the Franciscans <note>The Order of Friars Minor.</note>. He lived perhaps at the end of this century, around the year 1400. Others place him around 1350, and some as early as 1296, claiming he served as a confessor to a certain King Philip of France.

*Commentaries on the four Evangelists*. Published in Cologne, 1537, in folio.
*Commentaries on the Acts of the Apostles*.

*Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles*. Frequently published under the name of Thomas Waleys.
*Commentaries on the Apocalypse*.
*Sermons for the Season and for the Saints* throughout the cycle of the entire year. Published with the *Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul* in Hagenau and Paris.
Johannes Keerberg collected all of Gorham's works and saw them published in two volumes in Antwerp, 1617 and 1620.
The *Commentaries of Thomas Waleys on Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy* are ascribed to Gorham in some manuscript codices.
The remaining unpublished works of Gorham are reviewed by Bale (Century 7, chapter 22), Altamura (*Library of the Dominicans*, page 71), and Simler (*Library of Zurich*, page 519).

<margin>1400.</margin>
**NILUS DAMYLA**, an Italian by birth and a priest-monk <term>Hieromonachus: a monk who is also an ordained priest in the Eastern Orthodox tradition</term> in the Monastery of Hierapetra of the Carcasini on the island of Crete, flourished in the year 1400. He was a most bitter enemy of the Latins <note>The Western/Catholic Church</note>. He wrote a *Work on the Order in the Divine Trinity* and *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, which remains in manuscript in the Vatican Library. Leo Allatius presents a fragment of it in Greek and Latin in his book against Hottinger (chapter 19, page 441). Furthermore, he composed a *Collection of Excerpts* addressed to Maximus the Monk, drawn from the sacred scriptures against those who argue that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father alone, but from the Father and the Son <note>This refers to the "Filioque" controversy, a major cause of the Great Schism between Eastern and Western Christianity</note>. He also wrote *Two Treatises*: one *On Pope Damasus and the faith of ancient Rome*, and another *On the two Photian Synods*. These are manuscripts in the Library of the King of France. From the latter treatise, Leo Allatius provides a Greek and Latin fragment in his book *On the Photian Synod* (chapter 9, page 179); another in the book *On Consent* (book 2, chapter 18, section 10); another from the second-to-last treatise in the *Addenda* (page 1375); and another from the second work in the same place (book 2, chapter 18, section 7). Other fragments can be seen in the same author's *On Consent* (book 2, chapter 9, section 5, and book 3, chapter 2, section 3).

<margin>1400.</margin>
**MAXIMUS**, a Greek Monk and a contemporary <term>σύγχρονος</term> of Damyla, whom Damyla attempted to influence through letters, though he found him to be an opponent of his views. He flourished around the year 1400. He wrote sharply in favor of the Latin <note>Western</note> dogma against the Greeks, sending *Epistles* on this matter to people everywhere, but especially to those in Constantinople. I believe his writings have not survived to this day.

**FRANCISCO XIMENIUS** <note>Francesc Eiximenis, c. 1330–1409</note>, Spanish by nation, Catalan by birth, from the house of Girona, Bishop of Elne and titular Patriarch of Jerusalem <note>original: "Pseudo-Patriarcha"</note>. <margin>1400.</margin>
**FRANCESCO ZABARELLA**, or de Zabarellis, an Italian by race, from the house of Padua, a Doctor of Both Laws <term>Doctor utriusque iuris: a scholar holding doctorates in both Civil and Canon (Church) law</term>. He taught at the university in his home city and at Florence, having learned from Johannes de Lignano, Baldus, and Saliceto; he was the teacher of Nicholas the Abbot of Palermo <note>Panormitanus</note>. He gained such great authority among his fellow citizens of Padua through the distinguished fame of his name and the integrity of his life that, when the Carrara family <note>The ruling dynasty of Padua</note> died out, they entrusted him with the duty of carrying the keys of his home city and making the surrender to the Venetians. Having long been the Archpriest of the Cathedral Church of Padua, he was finally elected Bishop by the Canons. However, honoring the will of his fellow citizens, he refused the offered dignity; in return, he received from them the very wealthy Abbey of Santa Maria di Praglia as a reward for his remarkable loyalty to his fatherland. He flourished in the year 1400. Though elected Bishop of Florence by the people, he lacked the actual dignity until the year 1411, when he was admitted into the college of Cardinals by Pope John XXIII with the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and also received confirmation of his see from him. Two years later, he was sent by the Pope to Emperor Sigismund to discuss the calling of a General Council and the ending of the schisms

<meta>This page transitions from the biography of Francesco Zabarella into a general overview of the 15th century, which the author labels the "Synodal Century" due to the prominence of Church Councils. <header>15TH CENTURY, from the Year 1400.</header>

# THE SYNODAL CENTURY.
<note>original: "Sæculum Synodale." This title refers to the 15th century's defining characteristic in Church history: the "Conciliar Movement," where massive councils (synods) attempted to reform the Church and settle the Great Schism.</note>

->Overview of the Century.<-

After the unrefined barbarism of so many centuries and such a long-lasting decay of letters, that long-awaited century finally arrived in which learning, having put to flight the shadows of ignorance, emerged as if from the underworld, and the study of the liberal arts and languages was restored to the Christian world. This should be credited to two primary causes: the capture of Constantinople by the Turks and the invention of the art of printing. Indeed, after the metropolis of the Greeks was conquered in the year 1453, the most learned men of that nation, driven by poverty and the harshness of the barbarian yoke, betook themselves to Western parts, especially to Italy. They brought with them to Latium <note>Latium refers here to the Latin-speaking Western world, specifically Italy.</note> a knowledge not only of the Greek language but of almost all better literature; at the very least, they served as an incentive for the Latins to strive for a wisdom beyond the knotty discipline of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval method of philosophy and theology which many humanists found overly technical and dry.</note>. Then, a few years earlier, the art of printing was discovered—whether the praise for this is owed to the Dutch or the Germans—which brought the ancient monuments of the learned into the light and published more recent works with marvelous speed. Such was the state of letters.

But if we look at ecclesiastical affairs, we shall find no century more fertile in Synods <note>Councils</note> from the fourth century onward. To say nothing of the councils and assemblies of lesser note, the Synod of Pisa was held in the year 1409 to remove the long-standing schism of the Roman Pontiffs from the midst; it decreed that Benedict XIII and Gregory XII should be removed from the Papacy and placed Alexander V over the Roman See. However, since this did not extinguish the schism so much as increase it—so that the Papal Triumvirate <note>A "Triumvirate" of three rival popes: Gregory XII (Rome), Benedict XIII (Avignon), and Alexander V (Pisa).</note> seemed intolerable to the Church—the Council of Constance was assembled in the year 1413 by the care of Emperor Sigismund. By its authority, since it could not be discerned which of the three was the true Pope, power was stripped from each of them, and Martin V was elevated to the Papacy in their place. For with the greatest constancy, the Fathers of that Council asserted the superiority of an Ecumenical Synod over the Pope—with the Roman Pontiffs who were present not even daring to mutter against it—and they confirmed this by a solemn decree as an indubitable article of faith. 

Yet the schism was not yet finished: Benedict XIII clung to the Papacy with his teeth until the very last act of his life. Of even weightier importance was the controversy which the Council of Constance had with the Hussites. These men, holding fast to the truth and the primitive faith, preached that the Eucharist ought to be administered to Christians under both kinds <note>original: "sub utraque specie," meaning both the bread and the wine, rather than the bread alone.</note>; at the very least, they demanded that both kinds be granted to them. The Fathers summoned Hus to Constance, having given him "public faith" <note>A "safe-conduct" or official guarantee of safety.</note>; yet when he arrived, they condemned him to the pyre, violating that faith. And so that they might close the mouths of the Hussites forever, they decreed in the 13th Session: *that although Christ instituted the venerable sacrament after supper and administered it to his disciples under both kinds, bread and wine, nevertheless, notwithstanding this, the Cup was to be withheld from the Laity.* 

The Ecumenical Synod of Basel, in the year 1431, strengthened and most powerfully asserted that superiority of the Council defined at Constance. Pope Eugenius IV had called it to comply with Emperor Sigismund; but as soon as he noticed the members at Basel asserting the Council's superiority over the Pope, he ordered the Synod to be dissolved and transferred to Bologna. The Fathers of the Council constantly resisted the Pope's audacity; they decreed that he should be removed from the Papacy unless he revoked his command. After innumerable evasions, Eugenius—fearing the example of the Popes deposed not long before by the Council of Constance—lowered his pride; obeying the orders of the Synod, he confirmed all its acts. However, once Emperor Sigismund (whose authority he most respected) was removed from the living, he returned to his usual arts of deception, and

...and [Pope Eugenius IV] celebrated the Council of Ferrara in the year 1438, which was moved to Florence the following year so that he might have something to oppose the decrees of the participants at Basel. To this place, lured by the vain hope of obtaining aid against the Turks, John, the Emperor of Constantinople, led a crowd of Greek Bishops. They disputed for some time regarding the "procession of the Holy Spirit" <note>The *Filioque* controversy: a debate over whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from both the Father and the Son.</note>, the Primacy of the Pope, Purgatory, and other articles of Religion; finally, a formula of Union was devised, which many of the Greeks signed, led either by the Emperor’s threats or corrupted by the Pope’s gold. Meanwhile, the Council of Basel extended its Sessions; and having deposed Eugenius, it granted the Papal dignity to Felix V. However, every one of the aforementioned Councils claimed for itself the title and authority of an **Ecumenical Council** <term>Ecumenical: Representing the whole of the Christian Church rather than a local branch.</term>; each deservedly received confirmation from the Roman see at various times, and they commanded that "undoubted faith" be given to their definitions by all Christians. Indeed, from the frequent and long-lasting sessions of Councils held in that century, and the very sharp controversy that followed regarding the authority of each, a certain result might not be poorly judged: that the infallibility of General Councils, previously accepted by only a few, obtained almost universal faith within the Roman Church. At the end of the Century, the Pragmatic Sanction of Saint Louis, which had been established in the year 1268, was recalled into use <note>The author is likely referring to the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges (1438), which asserted the "Gallican Liberties"—the independence of the French Church from certain papal controls—based on earlier precedents.</note>; by this, the Papal see suffered a heavy loss of power within Gaul [France]. For the Gallican Church took the decrees of the Councils of Constance and Basel to be religiously observed by itself, and did not allow Papal authority to wander beyond the limits set by the Ecclesiastical Canons. Meanwhile, the Council of Florence, which permitted everything to the whims of the Popes, prevailed in Italy and other parts of the West—yet in such a way that as the study of "good letters" <note>A term for the humanities and classical literature characteristic of the Renaissance.</note> and ancient Theology increased daily, the once-accepted opinion of "Apostolic fullness" <note>original: "Apostolicæ plenitudinis." This refers to the doctrine of absolute papal supremacy.</note> gradually vanished, and the mass of Papal omnipotence began to totter.

# WRITERS.
---

<margin>1401.</margin>
**JAN HUS**, a Bohemian by nation, born in the village named Husinec, was educated in "good letters" at the University of Prague, where he was made a Bachelor of Liberal Arts in the year 1393, a Master of Philosophy in 1395, and a Priest and Preacher of the Bethlehem Chapel in 1400. He became famous in the year 1401. A man, as even his adversaries admit, illustrious in doctrine and conspicuous in piety. While he pursued the study of sacred scripture and a "chaster" <note>original: "castioris." In this context, it means a purer theology based on original sources rather than medieval scholastic additions.</note> Theology—having set aside prejudices and with a sincere zeal for truth—he diligently read the writings of Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320–1384), the English "Morning Star of the Reformation."</note>, even if he did not hear his speeches in person. He easily recognized the most foul and no longer tolerable errors and corruptions of the Roman Church. Once recognized, he most strongly attacked them both through preaching and writing. He found a partner and assistant in his studies and labor in **JEROME OF PRAGUE**, likewise a Bohemian by nation, born in the city of Prague, nurtured in Theological studies at Paris and in the foremost Universities of France and Germany; he was most celebrated among his countrymen for a rare and clearly divine eloquence in preaching. The Bohemians received the doctrine of both men with eager ears; they crowded to their sermons in throngs; and they simultaneously recognized and hated the long-ingrained errors. Thus, as the trade in indulgences <term>Indulgences: Payments made to the Church in exchange for the remission of temporal punishment for sin.</term> grew cold among the Bohemians, the Papists cried out that religion was finished unless the daring of Jan and Jerome was quickly countered. Therefore, Zbyněk Zajíc <note>original: "Subinco Lepus." The author has translated the Czech name into Latin: *Zbyněk* as *Subinco* and *Zajíc* (meaning "hare") as *Lepus*.</note>, the Archbishop of Prague, rose up against both around the year 1408. He gathered a Synod, summoned the academics, condemned the dogmas and followers of Wycliffe, burned the books, and forbade Jan and Jerome the duty of preaching; he soon compelled them to leave the City. But after Zbyněk was removed from the living shortly thereafter, they returned to their accustomed duties of teaching. In the following years, Hus, having been reported for heresy to Popes Gregory XII and John XXIII, faced greater danger. The Popes [committed] the whole matter to Cardinal Colonna...

<margin>

from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...commit the matter to him. That man <note>The Pope or a high official</note> summoned Jan Hus to appear in Rome to be judged. Hus sent his representatives to prove his innocence with the strongest arguments; King Wenceslaus also sent ambassadors to protect Jan’s cause. The Cardinal admitted no defense; instead, he pronounced Jan to be an obstinate heretic. In the year 1413, as riots were increasing among the Bohemians due to religious causes, Hus was expelled from the city of Prague by King Wenceslaus. He began to preach among the villagers until the disturbances quieted down enough for him to be allowed to return. In the year 1414, once the Council of Constance had begun, Hus was provided with a letter of **safe conduct** <term>Safe Conduct: A document guaranteeing a traveler's safety through dangerous territory, issued here by the Emperor himself.</term> from Emperor Sigismund, which secured his safety through the "public faith of the Empire." This document was written in both German and Latin. Accompanied by several Bohemian nobles, Hus was led to Constance on the 3rd of November, having previously received letters from the Pope and the Council on his journey. However, the authority and reverence of a promise given with such solemn religious weight could not prevent Hus—despite the protests of Sigismund and the Germans—from being thrown into a most foul prison on the twenty-sixth day after his arrival. For six full months, he was driven through various prisons, suffering from starvation and torments; finally, he was condemned by the Council for heresy in his absence and without being heard, primarily because he administered the **Eucharist in both kinds** <note>original: "Eucharistiam in utrâq; specie" — This refers to giving both the bread and the wine to the laity, rather than just the bread, which was the Roman Catholic custom at the time.</note>. But when Emperor Sigismund took this injustice very poorly, Hus was granted the opportunity to debate and defend himself. Therefore, on the fifth and again on the seventh of June, he was brought forward and the contest began. However, everything was conducted with noise and shouting. Overwhelmed by insults and outcries, Hus was not permitted to say even a word unless he wished to **recant** <note>original: "palinodiam agere"</note>. He steadfastly refused, and was sent back to prison. On the 6th of July, he was brought out of prison again and stood before the Council; he was condemned for heresy, sentenced to the flames, stripped of his priestly garments, deprived of his academic degrees, and—crowned with a paper hat painted with evil demons—led to his execution. He met death with the greatest constancy and fortitude of soul, consumed by **burning alive** <note>original: "vivicomburio"</note> in an open meadow outside the city walls. In April of that same year, Jerome [of Prague] had come to Constance, having first received from the Council the power to arrive safely, though not to return (for the "good Fathers" had devised this pretext for their most wicked treachery). He was cast into prison and tortured with dire torments. After the death of Hus, he was forced by the terror of execution to recite a formula of abjuration from a written script. Nevertheless, having been sent back to prison, he began to be moved by repentance for his most shameful cowardice; shaking off his lethargy, he did not hesitate to profess the truth once more. Thus, on the 25th of May in the year 1416, he was brought into the Cathedral Church, where he spoke with such presence of mind and such invincible strength of argument that he reduced his adversaries to silence. Condemned therefore to the pyre on the 30th of May, he underwent a struggle equal to that of Hus, and won an equal triumph.
