<meta>This page continues from a list of the works of Jan Hus (the previous page ended with a partial title regarding the Great Schism) and transitions into a description of the "Golden Mirror" (*Speculum Aureum*) before beginning a detailed biography of the influential theologian Jean Gerson.</meta>

<header>The Synodal Century.</header>

<margin>15th CENTURY, from the Year 1400.</margin>
...depicts in the preface. First, I will uncover the most grave errors of the Roman Curia regarding the provision of benefices and the granting of indulgences; by eliminating these uncovered errors, I will condemn them along with the Simoniacs <note>Those who buy or sell church offices or sacred things.</note> and those who participate with them. Second, I will clearly reject as heretical certain writings of those who write in a less-than-Catholic manner, which seemed to provide the cause or occasion for such ecclesiastical destruction; there I will weaken the foundation of that destruction regarding things prohibited as Simoniacal, and the Simoniacal as prohibited—matters which seem to lead even many commonly skilled men into error. Third, I will declare the entire Roman Curia to be erroneous and struggling in a state of damnation, based on the truest foundations, as well as all those who have obtained ecclesiastical benefices from common law through exorbitant favors, by examining the fullness of the Pope's power. Accordingly, there will be three parts, which I advise the Reader to read through with all diligence. This *Golden Mirror* <note>Original: *Speculum Aureum*, a reformist text often attributed to Paulus Anglicus or Dietrich of Nieheim.</note> is available in Goldast's *Monarchy*, Volume 2, page 1527.

# JEAN CHARLIER DE GERSON

<margin>1404.</margin>
French by birth, originating from the village of the same name in the Diocese of Reims in Champagne, called the <term>Most Christian Doctor</term> <note>Latin: *Doctor Christianissimus*, a traditional title for Gerson reflecting his blending of mystical piety with academic theology.</note>, he was born in the year 1363 on December 14th <note>The 19th Kalends of January.</note>, the son of Arnulph and Elizabeth. Sent to Paris by his parents in 1377, he became a Fellow of the Arts at the College of Navarre. In 1382, he was received into the Society of Theologians, after having heard Pierre d'Ailly teaching for seven years and Gilles de Champs for three; he was designated Master of the College. A few years later, he obtained the office of Chancellor of Paris, which he performed with such prudence and honor that he is commonly called "The Chancellor" <term>par excellence</term> <note>Original Greek: *κατ’ ἐξοχὴν* (kat’ exochēn), meaning pre-eminently or above all others.</note> to this day. He was prominent in the year 1404. Those are clearly hallucinating who claim our John was a monk of the Celestine Order, and subsequently Prior of their monastery in Lyon; they have fallen into this error because our subject had two brothers, John and Nicholas, enrolled with the Celestines. 

In 1407, he opposed through sermons and writings the assertions of Jean Petit, who had affirmed that the murder of Louis, Duke of Orléans, was lawful; he caused Petit to be marked with a sharp censure by the Parisian Faculty. In 1408, at the Council of Paris—which King Charles had convened for the purpose of ending the Schism—he persuaded the King that obedience should be denied to both Popes, Benedict XIII and Gregory XII, until one yielded to the other. He pleaded with Benedict at Tarascon once and again, and a third time at Marseille in sermons, that he should lay down the papacy and give peace to the Church. In 1409, after Benedict and Gregory were deposed at the Council of Pisa and Alexander V was elected, since the schism was not ended but rather increased, Gerson wanted Alexander to enter into the same plan for peace he had previously urged upon Benedict. Truly, both men stubbornly held onto the Papacy once they had seized it. 

In 1413, when a grave sedition arose among the Parisians, Gerson went to meet the rioting populace and was sought for death or imprisonment. He looked to his own safety by flight and hid for several days among the upper vaults of the church of St. Mary <note>The Cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris.</note>; meanwhile, his house was plundered by the common people and his furniture snatched away. In 1414, he was sent as the Legate of the King of the French and the Province of Sens to the Council of Constance. There he left no stone unturned to remove the schism, that the peace and purity of the Church might be restored at once, errors corrected, and stains wiped away; in short, that the entire Christian world might be renewed in both its "Head and its members." When he discovered that the Popes stood in the way of the longed-for reformation, he wrote a commentary <term>On the Possibility of Removing the Pope from the Church</term> <note>Latin: *De Auferibilitate Papæ ab Ecclesiâ*. This was a key text of the Conciliar movement, arguing that the Church has the right to preserve itself even without a Pope.</note>, which was approved by the Fathers of the Council but by no means put into execution. 

Indeed, Gerson gained such authority for himself in the Synod through his exceptional reputation for learning and piety that he easily held primacy in all gatherings of learned men, and by the unanimous command of the Fathers, he composed the Decrees and Definitions of the Council. Furthermore, Cardinal Zabarella had nothing else to oppose the Hussites with except the authority of Gerson. *You say,* he said, *that the Chancellor of Paris is suspect to you; yet he is such a super-excellent Doctor that his equal can scarcely be found in all of Christendom.* While Gerson was diligently applying himself to the amendment of the Church, the Burgundians caused him great heartache. For they demanded from the Council that the censure of Jean Petit's assertions—issued eight years earlier by the Parisian Faculty, for which Gerson had strenuously fought—be subjected to examination once more. This was done, despite Gerson's resistance and...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Jean Charlier de Gerson, the Chancellor of the University of Paris. The previous page introduced his birth in Champagne and his title as the "Most Christian Doctor." This page details his exile following the Council of Constance and lists his major literary and theological contributions.</meta>

<header>The Synodal Century.</header>

<warning>The right margin of the text is partially obscured or cut off, resulting in incomplete words at the ends of several lines.</warning>

<margin>15th CENTURY, from the Year 1400.</margin> ...and others who stood on his side; the matter was sent to selected judges by the Council. They annulled the Parisian censure <note>This refers to the condemnation of the theologian Jean Petit, who had defended the Duke of Burgundy's assassination of the Duke of Orléans.</note>. Gerson appealed <note>original: *provocat*</note> to the Council. The Fathers confirmed the sentence of the judges. This turned out very badly for Gerson. For after the Council was dissolved in the year 1418, it was by no means free for him to return to Paris <note>original: *Lutetia*</note> to perform his duties as Chancellor. For the city had recently been occupied by Jean, Duke of Burgundy <note>Known as John the Fearless, he was Gerson's primary political adversary.</note>, who had previously arranged for the Duke of Orléans to be killed by assassins he had sent. Gerson, therefore, so that he might escape the madness of his adversaries, withdrew through the mountainous regions of Bavaria and various districts of Switzerland to Lyon <note>original: *Lugdunum*</note>. A refuge was prepared for him there with the Archbishop and his brother Jean, the Prior of the Celestines. He spent the remainder of his life there writing books and teaching the catechism to children <note>original: *parvulis*</note> in the Church of St. Paul. When he felt death was imminent, he brought his young disciples into the Church and ordered them to cry out to God for him daily in prayer:
> *My God, my Creator, have mercy on your most wretched servant Jean Gerson.*
The man, a prince of his century, died suddenly <note>original: *subito*</note> while praying, in the year 1429, on the 12th of July <note>original: *iv. Idus Julii*</note>. He was buried in the Basilica of St. Paul, where these words, *Repent and believe the Gospel*, most frequently used by him during his preaching, were inscribed as an epitaph on his tomb.

The Works of Gerson were produced through the care of Johann Geiler at *Strasbourg* in 1488 in 3 volumes, and in 1499 in 4 volumes; at *Cologne* in 1483 in 4 folio volumes; at *Basel* in 1518 in 4 volumes; and at *Paris* in 1521. An enlarged edition was published at *Paris* in 1606 in 4 volumes, which is the edition we have represented in its proper order in our index.

Furthermore, there are those who attribute the four books *On the Imitation of Christ* to our Gerson; but we shall say more concerning these matters below. <note>The authorship of this famous devotional work was a matter of intense debate between supporters of Jean Gerson and Thomas à Kempis.</note>

<margin>1406.</margin>
GREGORY XII, previously called Angelo Corraro, Titular Patriarch of Constantinople, and appointed Cardinal-Priest of the Title of St. Mark by Innocent VII, was elected Roman Pontiff at Rome in the year 1406 on the 30th day of November. He was crowned on the 5th of December at the age of 80. This election was made on the condition, however, that once he had attained the Papacy, he should invite the Antipope Benedict [XIII] by letter to a mutual abdication of the Papacy. He did indeed do this, nor did Benedict refuse the condition. Yet nothing was achieved by either side. One thing these "good" Pontiffs carry on their brow, another in their heart; and they play softly with one another. <note>original: "Aliud in fronte, aliud in corde gerunt... atq; alter alteri suaviter colludunt." The author is being sarcastic about the popes' political maneuvering.</note> Therefore, in a Council called at Pisa in 1409 by the Cardinals, both were deposed, and the elected Alexander V was placed in charge of the Roman see. Gregory, called to the Council, replied that it was not for the Cardinals but for himself to convene a Council; and thus he mocked and declined their judgment. Benedict did the same. Once Alexander was elected, the former fled to Rimini, the latter to Catalonia. Each created new Cardinals and contended to be held as the true Pontiff. Gregory, moreover, having gathered a Council at Friuli, struck the Pisan Fathers, Alexander, Benedict, and their followers with anathema <term>anathema: a formal curse by a church leader, excommunicating someone from the community</term>. Finally, in the year 1415, when he had long since become worthless in the eyes of all, he abdicated the Papacy himself at the Council of Constance through his proxy Carlo Malatesta on the 4th day of June. He was subsequently made Cardinal of Tusculum and perpetual Legate of Picenum. He died at Recanati in the year 1417 on the 4th day of July, and was buried in the Cathedral Church. There exists a *Letter to Peter de Luna, the Antipope* (Concil. Vol. xi. p. 2084), a *Response to the appeal of the Cardinals who had deserted him* (ibid. p. 2261), *Five other letters* (ibid. p. 2273, 2286), *Three other letters or Bulls* (Concil. Vol. xii. p. 105), *Other letters and responses* (found in Bzovius for the years 1406, 1408, 1409), and *many others* in Wadding's *Annals of the Minors* (Vol. V) and Dietrich von Nieheim (Books 2, 3, and 4).

<margin>1406.
*Cent.7.c.34.</margin>
JOHN LATHBURY (Bale calls him *Lathberium* less correctly), an Englishman by nation, a monk of the Franciscan Order in the Monastery at Reading, and educated in sacred letters at Oxford University, held a distinguished place among the theologians of that age. He flourished in the year 1406, in which he brought his *Commentary on the Lamentations* to completion. <note>original: "ad umbilicum perduxit" - literally "brought to the navel," an ancient idiom for finishing a book or scroll.</note> For he wrote a *Book of Morals on the Lamentations of Jeremiah*, very laborious and extensive, in 115 chapters. It was published in print in the year 1482 in folio. Bale lists other writings of his, namely: *Distinctions of Theology*, and a *Moral Alphabet*, manuscripts of which are in St. Peter's College, Cambridge; *Commentaries on Jeremiah, on the Acts of the Apostles, and on the Psalms, Lectures on the Scriptures, and various Sermons*; which indeed seem to have perished, or certainly have not yet come to light.

He had as his teacher Richard Courtenay, a cleric and kinsman of Henry, Prince of Wales. The Works of Gerson were published through the care of Johann Geiler at *Strasbourg* <note>original: "Argentinæ"</note> in 1488 (3 volumes) and 1499 (4 volumes); at *Cologne* in 1483 (4 volumes in folio); at *Basel* in 1518 (4 volumes); at *Paris* in 1521, and an enlarged edition at *Paris* in 1606 (4 volumes), which is the edition we have represented in order in our small Index.

Furthermore, there are those who would attribute the four books of the *Imitation of Christ* to our Gerson; but we shall say more concerning these matters below. <note>The *Imitation of Christ* is one of the most famous Christian devotional books; while often attributed to Thomas à Kempis, many in the 17th century argued it was written by Gerson.</note>

<margin>1406.</margin>
**GREGORY XII**, formerly called Angelo Corraro, titular Patriarch of Constantinople, and named Cardinal-Priest of the Title of St. Mark by Innocent VII, was elected Roman Pontiff at Rome in the year 1406, on the 30th day of November. He was crowned on the 5th day of December at the age of 80; however, he was elected on the condition that, having attained the Pontificate, he would invite the Antipope Benedict by letter to a mutual abdication of the Papacy. <note>This refers to the Great Western Schism, where two (and later three) men claimed to be the rightful Pope.</note> He did indeed do this, nor did Benedict refuse the condition. Nevertheless, nothing was actually achieved by either side. These "good" pontiffs carry one thing on their face and another in their heart; and they play a pleasant game with one another. Consequently, a Council having been called at Pisa by the Cardinals, both were deposed, and the elected Alexander V was placed in charge of the Roman See. Gregory, summoned to the Council, replied that it was his prerogative, and not the Cardinals', to convoke a Council; and thus he laughed at and declined their judgment. Benedict did the same. Once Alexander was elected, the former fled to Rimini, and the latter to Catalonia. Both created new Cardinals and contended to be held as the true Pontiff. Furthermore, Gregory, having assembled a Council at Cividale del Friuli <note>original: "Foro-julii"</note>, struck the Fathers at Pisa, Alexander, Benedict, and their followers with anathema [excommunication]. Finally, in the year 1415, when he had long since become worthless in the eyes of all, he abdicated the Papacy himself through his proxy Carlo Malatesta at the Council of Constance on the 4th day of June. He was thereafter made Cardinal of Tusculum and perpetual Legate of Picenum. He died at Recanati in the year 1417 on the 4th of July and was buried in the Cathedral Church. There exists his *Letter to the Antipope Pedro de Luna* (in the Councils, Vol. 11, p. 2084), a *Response to the appeal of the Cardinals who had deserted him* (ibid., p. 2261), *Five other Letters* (ibid., p. 2273, 2286), *Three other Letters or Bulls* (Councils, Vol. 12, p. 105), *Another Letter and Five Responses* in Bzovius for the years 1406, 1408, and 1409, and *many others* in Wadding’s *Annals of the Minors* (Vol. 5) and in Dietrich von Nieheim (Books 2, 3, and 4).

**JOHN LATHBURY** <note>original: "Joannes Latteburius"</note> (called somewhat incorrectly *Lathberium* by Bale), an Englishman by nationality, a monk of the *Franciscan* Order in the Convent at *Reading*, and educated in sacred letters at the University of *Oxford*, held an eminent place among the theologians of that age. He flourished in the year 1406, in which year he brought his *Commentary on the Lamentations* to completion. For he wrote a *Book of Morals on the Lamentations of Jeremiah*, a very laborious and lengthy work in 115 chapters. It was issued in print in the year 1482 in folio. Bale lists his other writings, namely: *Theological Distinctions* and a *Moral Alphabet*, which are manuscripts in St. Peter’s College, *Cambridge*; *Commentaries on Jeremiah*, on the *Acts of the Apostles*, and on the *Psalms*; *Scriptural Lectures*, and *Various Sermons*; these indeed seem to have perished, or certainly have not yet come to light.

He had as his teacher Richard Courtenay, a cleric and kinsman of Prince Henry of Wales. He was joined in the closest friendship with Robert Hallam, Bishop of *Salisbury* and Cardinal of the *Roman Church*. He flourished in the year 1408, in which year, having been provoked by Hallam

<meta>This page transitions from the biography of Pope Gregory XII to the life and works of Richard Ullerston, an English theologian at Oxford. # The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15th CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
</margin>

...who was called upon, published his *Treatise on the Reformation of the Church* at Oxford. For the weariness caused by the long-lasting Schism <note>The Great Western Schism (1378–1417), a period where there were two or even three rival claimants to the Papacy.</note> and the growing news of a General Council to be held as soon as possible had stirred many Prelates. These men were well aware of the most serious corruptions that had long prevailed in the Church and were most eager for reforms to finally be instituted; they sought to commit to writing the abuses and vices most deserving of reform so they could be proposed to the Council. Among these men, the Cardinal Robert <note>Robert Hallum, Bishop of Salisbury and a key figure at the Council of Constance.</note> shone forth; he was present at the Councils of Pisa and Constance, and being determined to promote the work of reformation so greatly desired, he gave this task to our Richard. He asked that Richard produce a well-labored commentary on the matter to note the abuses most in need of removal. Richard undertook the duty entrusted to him with the greatest faithfulness and wisdom, as he was uncommonly learned and touched by a great desire to restore ecclesiastical discipline once more. In composing this work, he followed the guidance of Robert of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), a famous English statesman and scientist-bishop known for his critiques of papal abuses.</note> above all others, whom he seems to have taken as his master of studies and Theology. Indeed, he was most well-versed in his writings and admired him so much that *he declared him to have been, in his own time, the light and lantern of this world*.

<margin>
Petitions regarding the Reform of the Church, Article 6.
</margin>

That Commentary exists under the title *Petitions regarding the Reformation of the Church Militant* <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the Christian church on earth, still struggling against sin and error, as opposed to the church in heaven.</note>; it is a manuscript in folio at Cambridge in the Library of Holy Trinity, and is most worthy to eventually see the light of day. This is especially true since, among so many treatises of that age regarding the corrupt state of the Church, none written by an English author has yet been published, except those which adversaries might claim were heretical. We, therefore, shall place here for the reader's favor the Prologue, in which a clear account of the whole work is given, and certain excerpts transcribed from the aforementioned manuscript.

->Here begins the Preface to the Treatise entitled, *The Petitions of Richard concerning the reformation of the Church Militant*.<-

To the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Robert, Bishop of Salisbury, his humble orator and servant, accepted into his friendship, Richard *Ullerston*, the least Professor of Sacred Scripture, offers the respects and honors due to such a father. Most Venerable Father, since for some time now I have been considering your zeal—not slackened but very great—for the unity of the church, and knowing again that it was your wish that my meager self should contribute some work among others striving for the unity of the church; so that, offering a poor man's small coin <note>original: "pauperculâ minutum," an allusion to the "Widow's Mite" in the Gospels.</note> to the world, I might receive praise for my devotion, seeing how much those more enriched in the Scriptures might be encouraged by my offerings to make progress in this matter. For this reason, I have set out to write certain things on this subject; which, if effectively carried out, I would certainly believe by the grace of God that the church, now wavering, would be reformed to a stable unity. For it seems to me that I should proceed under this figure: that in the manner of a preacher, in the person of the English Church, or rather the Universal Church, I should propose what seems to me necessary to be proposed, as if...

<margin>
Perhaps it should read "and as," and the word "me" should be deleted.
</margin>

...as if we were presenting ourselves as a province before the General Council. Therefore, I have set before myself sixteen articles to be touched upon by way of petitions directed to the General Synod. I subjoin the reasons why they ought to be fulfilled, strengthened, as I judge, by <term>canonical authority (laws of the church)</term>; so that, respect being had not to the petitioner but to the reasoning of the Church, whose persona I take on, they may obey reason. This reason rests upon the truth of Him who can neither deceive nor be deceived. May they busily demand the execution of what such a living reason has required, according to the wish of the writer, or rather according to the command of Him who impelled me to write: so that through this, the church now militant may be reformed to a solid unity. But because it is not certain what either the Universal Church or the English Church will define regarding the things to be requested by me; for this reason, if it please your Lordship, I have decided to name the present little work thus: *Richard's Petitions concerning the reformation of the Church Militant*. In these petitions I shall proceed as follows: namely, that the first Article will be about the orderly election of the Supreme Pontiff; the second will be about the avoidance of <term>Simony (the buying or selling of church offices)</term>; the third will be about the exaltation of the law of Christ. But the fourth will be against the abnormal <term>appropriation of churches (the practice of monasteries or bishops taking the income of a local parish)</term>. And the fifth for the perfection of suitable clergy. The sixth against exemptions. The seventh against <term>dispensations (legal exemptions from church law)</term>. The eighth against the <term>plurality of benefices (one person holding many church jobs at once)</term>. The ninth against appeals.

<summary>This page introduces Richard Ullerston and his influential "Petitions," a 16-point plan for church reform written at the request of Bishop Robert Hallum for the Council of Constance. The text highlights Ullerston's reliance on the earlier English reformer Robert Grosseteste and outlines the first nine areas targeted for reform, including simony and the mismanagement of church offices.</summary>

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15th CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...appeals. The tenth is against the abuse of privileges. The eleventh is against the apostasy of Clerics who involve themselves in secular business. The twelfth is against the special rights of Singers and Officials residing in the courts of Lords. The thirteenth is against extortions universally. The fourteenth shall be against the superfluous, overly expensive, and disordered finery in Clerics and their households. The fifteenth shall be for the more fruitful expansion of divine worship. And the sixteenth shall be for the procurement of peace between Christian kingdoms with the greatest effort.

At the end of the **Second Article**, he has this to say: "I say these things especially because no nation under heaven is so noted for such execrable and insatiable greed as is the Roman Curia <note>The administrative apparatus of the Holy See.</note>. So much so that everywhere on earth it has turned into a common proverb: namely, that 'The Roman Curia does not seek the sheep without the wool.'" <note>original: "Curia Romana non quærit ovem sine lanâ." A biting 15th-century critique meaning the church hierarchy only cares for the people if they can profit from them.</note>

**Article 3.** Thirdly, we ask that Christ's vicar here on earth <note>The Pope.</note> should esteem, exalt, and promote no other law as much as the law of Christ. The reasonableness of this petition is proven by the fact that otherwise he would not be a true vicar of Christ, nor would Christ be the best lawmaker—something which the ears of all Christians surely abhor to hear. For Christ did not complete his work so poorly that the authority of his Gospel should cease, or that he should establish a law of greater authority elsewhere, or that his Gospel should be held in less honor through any acts of his Successors than when it was first promulgated to them. From this it follows that by the Lord’s command, everyone should labor toward this end: that Christians should fear the transgression of His law more than any other ordinance or statute. Christians have experienced the opposite for so long that now, if we happen to speak of "laws," we immediately understand them to be human laws, and by no means the Gospel; which certainly is now esteemed no more in the Church than the verses of Cato <note>Dionysius Cato, a late-antique author of moral proverbs used in schools.</note> or the proverbs of Seneca; <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> except perhaps for that one saying to Peter and his Successors: "Whatever you bind on earth, etc." <note>Matthew 16:19, often cited to justify Papal authority.</note> Would that those who quote this word did not, through a total lack of understanding, allege it to the insult of the law of Christ. Thus matters have proceeded until we have reached the truth of the prophecy of Isaiah:
> This people glorifies me with its mouth and its lips; but its heart is far from me, and they have feared me by the mandate of men and by doctrines. <note>A paraphrase of Isaiah 29:13, also cited by Jesus in the Gospels.</note>

**Article 13.** Nor is it valid here to allege "custom" against good morals, especially since the longer an evil lasts, the worse it becomes. —— Otherwise, the entire heap of sins could easily be excused by saying, "this is how it is usually done," and "good men have done so," and again "such things have passed beyond human memory" without being challenged; and further "certain people who seemed to be someone of importance in the Church approved such things by both their writings and deeds." Far be it from us to suggest that all who do such things are in danger of perdition! But multiplying inconveniences is not the same as solving them. And as the Philosophers agree with Scripture: "Nothing violent is eternal." <note>original: "Nullum violentum æternum." A common medieval philosophical axiom.</note> Nothing remains for our salvation except that we amend for the better those things in which we have sinned, whether knowingly or unknowingly, in the matters previously mentioned.

<margin>* Cent. 7. c. 83.</margin>
In the same manuscript codex is found the same author's *Treatise on the Military Office*, written at the request of his teacher Richard Courtenay <note>Bishop of Norwich and Chancellor of Oxford.</note> and dedicated to Henry, Prince of Wales—afterward the most invincible King of England <note>Henry V.</note>. Bale <note>John Bale (1495–1563), a famous English historian and bibliographer.</note> enumerates other writings of Ullerston, namely: *A Defense of the Endowment of the Church* made by Constantine; *Commentaries on the Psalter*; *On the Canticles of the Church*; *Ordinary Lectures*; and a distinguished *Work on the Creed of the Church* produced in the year 1409. John Stanberry, the Bishop of Hereford, is said to have brought this last work back to light and illustrated it with commentaries in the year 1463.

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15th CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...from the year 1390, he was Bishop of Verden; after resigning that see a few years later, he was appointed Bishop of Cambrai by Pope Boniface IX. He flourished in the year 1410. *He wrote a History of the most grave schism <note>The Great Western Schism (1378–1417), a period when there were rival claimants to the papacy.</note> of his time between the Popes and Anti-popes in three books, covering the period from the death of Gregory XI to the election of Alexander V, or from the year of Christ 1378 to 1410, also weaving in a sufficiently clear history of civil affairs throughout.* This was published at Nuremberg in 1532 and Basel in 1560. To these three books, Theodoric added a fourth, divided into six tracts, to which he gave the title *The Grove of Union* <note>original: "Nemus Unionis"</note>. In this work, he discusses the methods attempted by Christian Kings to end the Schism, the tricks employed by Gregory XII and Benedict XIII to defeat all plans for peace, and the deposition of both at the Council of Pisa. He presents many records, letters, and Papal Bulls of the Popes, Cardinals, and others regarding the matters at hand, mixing them into his History. The complete four books were published at Basel in 1566, Nuremberg in 1592, and Strasbourg in 1608; they were also published with the commentaries of Francesco Zabarella and Jean Le Maire of Belgium regarding the same Schism in the same location in 1629. There also exists his *History of the Life of Pope John XXIII*, published under the name of Johannes Niemius by Heinrich Meibom at *Frankfurt in 1420. Also published were his works on the Privileges and rights of the Empire regarding the Investiture <note>The right of a monarch to appoint bishops and abbots, a major point of conflict between Popes and Emperors.</note> of Bishoprics and Abbeys as established by Popes and Roman Emperors, printed among other things at Basel in 1557 and Strasbourg in 1609 and 1618. Finally, there is his Exhortation to Rupert, King of the Romans, urging him to wake from his long sleep, extirpate the papal schism from the Church, and reform the rights of the Empire; found in Goldast’s "Monarchy," Volume 1, page 1381.*

---

<margin>1409.</margin>
THOMAS NETTER, called WALDENSIS after his place of birth, was English by nation, born in the village of Saffron Walden in the county of Essex. The son of John Netter and Matilda, he was educated in fine letters at Oxford and was granted the master’s cap <note>Awarded a Master of Arts degree.</note>. He entered the Carmelite order in London and flourished in the year 1409. He was also sent as an envoy by King Henry IV of England to the Council of Pisa, where he argued strenuously for the removal of the schism and disputed strongly against the factions of the Anti-popes Gregory and Benedict. Having returned home, he was made the twenty-third Provincial <note>The head of a religious order within a specific province or country.</note> of his Order in the year 1414. He fought against the Wycliffites <note>Followers of John Wycliffe, whose reformist views were condemned as heresy.</note> with the greatest fervor of spirit; indeed, he was so carried away by partisan zeal that he did not fear to sharply rebuke King Henry V in a public sermon for his sluggishness in punishing heretics. Because of this, he was seen as a unique champion of the faith and was appointed as the personal Confessor to King Henry; he was sent to the Council of Constance in 1415 to speak out against the Hussites <note>Followers of Jan Hus, a Czech reformer who was burned at the stake during the Council of Constance.</note>. In 1419, he was sent as an envoy to King Wladislaus of Poland and Michael, the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, for the sake of brokering peace. While fulfilling this embassy, he converted Vytautas, Duke of Lithuania—a man considered a most ferocious tyrant of the whole world—to the Christian faith. Later, following Henry V as he carried his victorious arms through France, Netter was present in the year 1422 to receive the final holy breaths of the Prince into his own bosom as he died. He was similarly appointed as Confessor and secretary to King Henry VI, and accompanied him to France so the King might take the crown of the realm at Paris. Netter died at Rouen in Normandy on the 3rd of November, 1430, and was honorably buried in the Convent of his fellow Carmelites. He wrote almost innumerable works, of which only one is found in print: *The Doctrinal of the Ancient Teachings of the Faith of the Catholic Church against the Wycliffites and Hussites*. This is a massive and lengthy work distributed into three volumes and dedicated to Pope Martin V. In the first volume, he treats of God, Christ, Peter, the Church, and the Religious orders; in the second, the Sacraments; and in the third, the Sacramentals. It was published by Badius Ascensius at Paris in 1532, then at Salamanca in 1556, and illustrated with brief explanations by Giovanni Battista Rossi at Venice in 1571 and elsewhere. Baleus reviews the rest of Waldensis's works in Century 7, chapter 84. A manuscript of his *Bundle of Tares* <note>original: "Fasciculus Zizaniorum," a collection of documents related to the Wycliffite heresy.</note> was in the possession of Bale, who presents some fragments from it in his work on English Writers. Another copy of the same was once held by the famous Ussher, as he himself testifies in his manuscript "Specimen of the Dogmatic History of Controversies."

15th CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
1410.
</margin>

SIMEON, a Greek by nation, who rose from a Monk to become the Archbishop of Thessalonica <note>Modern-day Thessaloniki, Greece</note>, rose to prominence in the year 1410. He was a contemporary of Callistus, the Patriarch of Constantinople, who held the throne around the year 1406. However, Possevino and Miræus, erring quite significantly, assert that he flourished six hundred years earlier. As a most fierce defender and champion of the Greek Church against the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>, and of the state against the Turks, he attacked the former with his writings and sustained the onslaughts of the latter with the greatest presence of mind. Indeed, when Thessalonica was besieged in the year 1428 by the tyrant Amurath <note>Sultan Murad II of the Ottoman Empire</note>, he could be induced by neither rewards nor threats to permit the Greeks to surrender to the Turks and expel the Latins. He died in September of the year 1429, six months before Thessalonica was once again captured by Amurath. Eugenius Nomophylax pursues his praises at length in the *Synodicon* usually recited on the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Church of Thessalonica: <note>original Greek: ὅς τῷ τῆς ἐκτός τε καὶ τῆς πνευματικῆς σοφίας πλήρει νόῳ ὑπερφυῶς γενομένῳ...</note> *who, being supernaturally filled in mind with the fullness of both external and spiritual wisdom, excelled in the Ascetic, or rather Angelic, way of life and conduct, and carried it out most perfectly with the highest virtue and praise, etc.* There exists his *Commentary on the Divine Temple, its Ministers, their Sacred Vestments, and the Most Holy Mystagogy or Mass*, written to certain pious Cretans; this was translated into Latin and published by Jacobus Pontanus at Ingolstadt in 1603, in quarto, and from there transferred into the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume XXII. But Pontanus, using a deception not infrequent among the Papists, had cut out many passages of the Commentary and mutilated more; thus, it is no wonder if he suppressed the Greek. Therefore, Jacobus Goar, a man of more candid soul, gave the Greek text joined with a more faithful Latin version in his *Greek Ritual* <note>original: "Euchologion"</note>, Paris, 1647, folio, page 212; he chastises the excessive "zeal," as he calls it, of Pontanus; and he does not deny that our Simeon, had he only been joined to the Roman Church, would be numbered among the ancient Fathers. Simeon also wrote an *Ecclesiastical Dialogue against all Heresies, concerning the sole faith of Our Lord Jesus Christ, the sacred Sacrifices, and all the mysteries of the Church*, collected from the Holy Scriptures and the fathers; this is held in Greek manuscript in the Vatican and Imperial Libraries; it is pious and learned, in the judgment of Allatius \*, and worthy to someday see the light \*, but "guided by a Catholic." Mark the man's caution. Would that they would grant it, however, provided that this Catholic does not possess the "zeal" of Pontanus.

From that work, Johannes Morinus extracted a notable Dissertation or *Dialogue on Penance*, and published it in Greek and Latin in the Appendix to his *Book on Penance*, page 125. Very many fragments of the same are held by Turrianus in his *Annotations on the Apostolic Constitutions*; by Petrus Arcudius in his *Book on the Concord of the Oriental and Occidental Churches*; and by Allatius in his work *On the Photian Synod* page 164, *Against Hottinger* pages 18, 110, 135, 278, and in his book *On Consent*, book 2, chapter 3, section 4. Furthermore, eighty-five of his *Responses to the Inquiries of Gabriel, Metropolitan of Pentapolis*, exist in manuscript in the Vatican Library. The same Allatius presents a notable fragment of them in Greek and Latin in his *Book against Hottinger*, page 78. Also: *A Book on the Priesthood to a certain Monk*. *A compendious Exposition of the Creed of our Orthodox and blameless Christian Faith.* *A necessary Exposition of the sentences of the Holy Creed, whence they were collected, and against whom they were dictated.* *Twelve Chapters which contain the sole faith of Christians or all the Articles of Faith, and that the Apostolic Creed contains them, and concerning the Virtues comprised therein.* *A little book on those things which the Latins have innovated.* These are manuscripts in the Vatican Library. I hear that a lengthy work of Simeon in Greek manuscript is preserved in the possession of the most learned man Henry Covel, Doctor of Divinity and Chancellor of the Church of York. The part of that work which was first mentioned, the *Commentary*, is quite small. Which other of the small works reviewed above might hold a place in the same, I have not yet learned.

He died at Bologna and was buried in the Church of St. Benedict, where the epitaph inscribed on his tomb includes, among other things, these two couplets:

->*Here lies the mirror of Canon Law and the anchor of Civil Law;*<-
->*A lofty mind now holds eternal dwellings.*<-

<note>Original Latin: "Canonis hic speculum, Civilis & Anchora Juris / Hic jacet: æternas mens tenet alta domos. / Quis superavit eum virtute micante? quis isto / Consiliis hominum clarior ante fuit?"</note>

His extant writings include *Commentaries on the Decretals and the Clementines*, published at Lyon in 1549 and 1553, and at Bologna in 1581; his *Consilia, or Legal Responses*, published at Venice in 1581, 1585, 1589, and 1599; and *Selected Questions of all the most Excellent Jurists*, arranged in three volumes, published at Frankfurt in 1581.

<margin>1410.</margin>
BOSTON OF BURY <note>Johannes Bostonus Buriensis</note>, English by nation, was a Benedictine monk in the Monastery of St. Edmund at Bury. An industrious as well as learned man, he flourished in the year 1410. To better promote the study of literature, he traveled through almost all the monasteries and colleges of England, searched through their libraries, sought out books, and arranged the writers in alphabetical order. He added their dates and biographies and noted in which libraries their monuments <note>In this context, "monuments" refers to their written works</note> could be found. This *Catalogue of Church Writers* (for so he wished his work to be called) existed as a manuscript once held by the celebrated Ussher <note>James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh</note>, and now by the most learned man Thomas Gale, Professor of Theology, who, we hope, will make it public in his own time; at the very least, he will illustrate our own Leland <note>John Leland, the 16th-century antiquarian</note> from it in his forthcoming edition. <margin>* Century 7, chapter 48.</margin> Bale <note>John Bale, a Protestant historian</note> is the authority for his having written, in addition, the *Mirror of Monastics* and a *Chronicle of his Monastery*, both of which seem to have perished.

<margin>1410.</margin>
JOHN XXIII, or as others number him, XXIV, previously called *Balthasar Cossa*, was a Neapolitan by birth. As a young man, he devoted himself to Civil and Canon Law at Bologna and was honored with a doctoral degree. Having then set out for Rome, he was admitted among the chamberlains by Boniface IX, soon becoming Archdeacon of Bologna, then Apostolic Protonotary, then Cardinal-Deacon of St. Eustace, and was appointed Legate of Flaminia; he brought Bologna and a large part of Flaminia back under the power of the Church. In the year 1409, he took part in the Council of Pisa. In the year 1410—poison having first been administered to his predecessor Alexander V <note>A common, though likely unfounded, rumor of the time</note>, and the Cardinals having been won over partly by bribes and partly by the terror of arms—he was elected Roman Pontiff at Bologna on May 17 and crowned on May 25. At the beginning of his pontificate, he anathematized King Ladislaus of Naples and ordered a Crusade to be preached against him, abundantly promising full remission of sins to all who fought for the Roman See. In the year 1413, compelled by fear of a threatened revolt by Emperor Sigismund, he proclaimed that a General Council should be held at Constance and promised that he would resign the Papacy, provided that the anti-popes Benedict and Gregory did the same. He himself entered Constance the following year on October 29 and opened the Council a few days later. However, when called upon by the Council Fathers to abdicate the Papacy, he sought delays; fearing worse outcomes, in March of the year 1415, he cast aside his papal insignia and fled secretly from the city of Constance by night, withdrawing to Schaffhausen, a town belonging to the Duke of Austria. Having been captured after his flight, he was brought to trial before the Council on forty charges, including heresy—specifically the denial of the immortality of the soul—atheism, simony <note>The buying or selling of church offices</note>, murder, poisoning, gambling, adultery, sodomy, and rape. Having been summoned several times to appear in vain, he was convicted and condemned; thus, on May 14, he was deposed from the Papacy by synodal decree. Soon, brought back from flight with the help of the Swiss and imprisoned at Mannheim, he was forced to abdicate the Papacy and confirm the acts of the Council. Therefore, after the document of his resignation was read in the Synod, the sentence of deposition was pronounced with greater solemnity on May 31 by the Bishop of Arras. John was then committed to the custody of Louis, Duke of Bavaria, and was held in prison for three years in the castle of Heidelberg. Finally released in the year 1418, he died at Florence the following year on December 22. There exists a Bull...

<margin>1411.</margin>
**JOHN GROSSI**, or *Grossus*, French by nation and from Toulouse by birth, was a monk of the Carmelite Order who flourished in the year 1411. In that year, he was elected the twenty-second Prior General of his Order during the Assembly at Bologna; in that capacity, he participated in the Council of Pisa <note>A council held in 1409 that attempted to end the Western Schism by deposing the two rival popes</note> in the same year. Twenty-two years earlier, he had been elected General of the same Order by those Carmelites who adhered to the Antipope Gregory VII <note>The text likely intends Gregory XII, as Gregory VII lived in the 11th century</note> at the Chapter of Perpignan. To restore the collapsed discipline of the Carmelites, he presided over three General Chapters of the Order: at Bagnols in 1416, Montpellier in 1420, and Pamiers in 1425. Finally, in the year 1424, being heavy with old age, he resigned his leadership after having increased the Order by ten monasteries and two provinces; he passed away that same year. He wrote *The Garden of the Carmelite Order* in three books, in which he describes at length the institution of his Order, its progress, and its men illustrious for either their learning or their piety. This work was published together with the *Mirror* of Philip Ribot and other writers on the same subject edited by Battista Cataneo (*Venice, 1507, folio*) and in the *Mirror of the Carmelites* which Daniel of the Virgin Mary, a Carmelite, saw to publication (*Antwerp, 1680, 4 volumes, folio*).

<margin>1412.</margin>
**JEROME OF SANTA FE**, apparently Spanish by nation, a convert from Judaism to Christianity and physician to Pope Benedict XIII, flourished in the year 1412. He wrote a book on refuting the errors of the Jews, and another against the Jewish Talmud. From the recitation of these works, more than five thousand Jews are said to have been converted to the Christian faith. Both appeared under the title *The Scourge of the Hebrews* <note>Original: "Hebræo-mastigis"</note> (*Frankfurt, 1602, octavo*) and are contained in the *Library of the Fathers*, Vol. 26, p. 528. The latter treatise had appeared previously at Zurich in 1552.

<margin>1414.</margin>
**VINCENT FERRER**, Spanish by nation from the Province of Valencia, was a monk of the Dominican Order, confessor to Benedict XIII, and Master of the Sacred Palace; he flourished in the year 1414. He was the most celebrated preacher of his age, who, having traveled through Spain, Italy, and France preaching for a span of thirty years, earned for himself a great reputation for eloquence and holiness, and produced the fruit of piety and penance in his listeners. The Dominicans and Papists—at least those with less judgment or modesty—tell miraculous stories about him: namely, that he restored sight to the blind, the ability to walk to the lame, and life to the dead; that he healed every kind of disease with a word; that he converted 35,000 Jews and 8,000 Saracens to the Christian faith; and that he led a hundred thousand lost souls back to a better life. Furthermore, they claim that even though he preached everywhere in his native Catalan tongue, he was understood by all listeners, of whatever nation they may have been <note>This refers to the "gift of tongues," a common miraculous attribute in hagiographies</note>. In the year 1418, he took part in the Council of Constance. When Martin V was elected by the Fathers of the Council, Vincent abandoned Benedict XIII, whose side he had supported until then, and thereafter attacked him sharply in his sermons. He died on the 5th of April, 1419, in the city of Vannes among the Bretons of Armorica, and was added to the catalog of Saints by Callixtus III in the year 1455.

<margin>1414.</margin>
**HERMANN OF LERBEKE**, a German by nationality, a member of the Order of Preachers <term>Order of Preachers: The Dominicans, a Catholic religious order focused on preaching and study</term> in the Monastery of St. Paul near Minden, flourished in the year 1414. He wrote the *History or Chronicle of the Counts of Schauenburg* from Adolf, the first of those counts, to the death of Otto of Schauenburg, covering the years 1006 to 1414. Heinrich Meibom was the first to bring this to light and publish it with notes at *Frankfurt* in 1620, in quarto.

<margin>1415.</margin>
**JOHN CAPREOLUS**, French by birth, originating from the town of Rodez <note>Latin: "Ratinen"</note> in the Diocese of Toulouse, a monk of the Order of Preachers and Professor of Theology at the University of Toulouse, a most fierce defender of the doctrine of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>. He flourished in the year 1415. He is said to have been present at the Council of Basel in the year 1431. When he died is uncertain. His *Commentaries on the four books of the Master of Sentences* <note>The standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages by Peter Lombard</note> are extant, *Venice*, 1484, 1514, 1588. Also, *Theological Defenses of Saint Thomas Aquinas*, ibid. 1483, in folio, if perhaps this is a different work from the preceding one. Ambrosius de Altamura provided a eulogy for him in the *Library of the Preachers*, page 158.

<margin>1315. <note>likely a printer's error for 1415</note></margin>
**PAUL OF BURGOS OF ST. MARY**, Spanish by nation, called *Burgensis* from his homeland, though others say he was born in the town of Santa Maria; a Jew by sect and easily the foremost among his people in nobility, learning, and wealth. Afterwards, however, he was converted to the Christian faith by reading the works of Saint Thomas. He was first Archdeacon of Treviño, then Bishop of Cartagena, and soon created Bishop of Burgos. He was placed in charge of the royal archives, made Arch-Chancellor of the Kingdoms of Castile and León, and finally appointed Patriarch of Aquileia. He flourished in the year 1415. Before accepting the faith, he had fathered three sons: Alfonso, Gonzalo, and Alvaro Garcia. He left the first as his successor in the see of Burgos, the second as Bishop of Plasencia, and the third as the propagator of his family. He is said to have died in the year 1435, on the 29th of August. There are extant: *Notable Additions to the Postils of Nicholas of Lyra on the whole of Scripture*, printed together with the *Lyra Postils* <term>Postils: Short commentaries or marginal notes on the Bible</term> at *Lyons* in 1590 and often elsewhere. *The Examination of the Scriptures* in two books, which he finished in the year of Christ 1434 at the age of 81. It was published at *Mantua*, 1474, in folio, and *Burgos*, 1591, in folio. *Twelve Questions on the Tetragrammaton Name* <note>The sacred four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, with notes by Johannes Drusius, *Franeker*, 1604, in octavo.

<margin>1416.</margin>
**NICHOLAS OF CLÉMANGES**, son of Nicholas, French by birth, born in the village of Clémanges in the province of Châlons-en-Champagne, called a Doctor of Theology by more recent writers. He had as an uncle Pierre de Clémanges, a very famous physician, and a brother Etienne, the provost of the College of Navarre. He himself was sent to Paris in the twelfth year of his age and was received into the College of Navarre, where he had as teachers Pierre de Nogent, Gerard Machet (later Bishop of Castres), and Jean Gerson. He thus made excellent progress in theology; however, he applied himself more than others to the study of eloquence and poetry. Around the year 1393, he was elected Rector by the University of Paris and was employed in writing letters. Having acquired a reputation through letters written in a most elegant style, he was summoned to the Avignon Court by Benedict XIII <note>The Avignon antipope during the Great Western Schism</note> and was [catchword: ordered] to assist him as secretary...

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15th CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...shortly after, he obtained the dignity of Treasurer of the Church of Langres <note>original: "Lingonensis"</note>. Around the year 1408, when Benedict XIII had placed an interdict <term>Interdict: An ecclesiastical censure that prohibits certain rites and services, such as the Mass, from being performed in a specific territory</term> on the Kingdom of France (which had recently withdrawn its obedience to him by royal edict), Clémanges undeservedly fell under suspicion of having drafted that interdict. In fact, he had left the Roman Court three months before the anathema was proclaimed and had retired to Genoa; nevertheless, he faced a great threat to his reputation and fortune. Therefore, withdrawing to the Carthusian Monastery of Val-profonde, and later to Fontaine-au-Bois, he found it necessary to plead for the Prince’s mercy and to clear himself of the charges by sending letters in every direction. Once the slanders were dispelled, he went to his people at Langres to fulfill his duties as Treasurer. In the year 1415, although he was requested by many on behalf of Benedict XIII to return to his court, he preferred his leisure and his little hut—where he was then hiding at Fontaine—to the honors of the Papal Court. Around that time, having resigned his position at Langres, he was appointed Cantor of the Church of Bayeux <note>original: "Baiocensis"</note>. Those are mistaken who claim he was the Archdeacon of Bayeux. He flourished in the year 1416, being close and dear to the greatest men of the age: Gerson <note>Jean Gerson, Chancellor of the University of Paris</note>, d'Ailly <note>Pierre d'Ailly, cardinal and theologian</note>, Ferrer <note>Vincent Ferrer</note>, and others. He died before the year 1440 and was buried in the Chapel of the College of Navarre <note>A prestigious college of the University of Paris</note> beneath a lamp hanging from the dome in front of the high altar; he has this short epitaph inscribed on his tomb: *He who was a lamp to the Church, lies beneath a lamp.* He was certainly a man endowed with sincere piety of soul, who used a style of writing more elegant than was common for his era. He was an intrepid critic and rebuker of wicked princes; with a sharp pen, he lashed the schisms, ambition, and vices of the Popes, the filth and greed of the clergy, the laziness, luxury, and lust of the monks—and finally, the loose morals of all ranks of society.

**JOSEPH**, a Greek by nation, Archbishop of Ephesus, and finally in 1416 elected Patriarch of Constantinople in a Synod of Constantinople. Some others, including Freher, maintain that the Patriarchate was undertaken by Joseph in the year 1424. However, Syropoulos <note>Sylvester Syropoulos was a high-ranking Greek official whose memoirs provide a critical eye-witness account of the Council of Florence</note> has placed the matter beyond doubt; he relates that Joseph died during the Council of Florence, having completed 23 years and 20 days in the Patriarchal office. Joseph obtained a difficult province, if ever there was one; he himself, whether you look at his natural disposition or the strength of his intellect, was far unequal to undertaking such a burden. For at that time, the affairs of the Greeks were so worn down by the Turks <note>The Ottoman Empire was aggressively expanding, leaving the Byzantine Empire in a desperate state</note> that it was necessary for them to seek the friendship and assistance of the Latins by any means, and to prioritize the safety of the State over the liberty of the Church. The union of the Greeks and Latins had been debated for a long time, and as the affairs of Constantinople daily grew worse, Emperor John <note>Emperor John VIII Palaiologos</note> pressed forward with the begun enterprise in haste. At first, Joseph consistently asserted the dignity of his Church and strongly disapproved of the journey to be undertaken by the Greek Bishops to a Western Council, predicting that it would result in the disgrace of the Greeks; he persuaded many that a Council should instead be summoned at Constantinople and the Latins called there. Later, however, overcome by the Emperor’s flatteries, he yielded; and having sent legates to the Council of Basel <term>Council of Basel: A major ecclesiastical council (1431–1449) intended to reform the church and end the schism with the Eastern Greeks</term> in 1435, he ratified the acts of that Synod. Again in 1437, having sent a leaden bull <note>A formal document sealed with a lead seal or "bulla"</note>, he declared himself ready to come to the West to restore the union between the Churches, and requested that the time and place for a General Council to be held for that purpose be defined. Two years later, when the authority of the Council of Basel had been diminished by the deceptions of Pope Eugenius <note>Pope Eugenius IV, who moved the council to Ferrara to maintain control</note>, the Greeks sided with Eugenius and decided to attend the Council summoned by him at Ferrara. Joseph presented himself as the leader of his race, though he was not so much concerned with defending the Greeks as with preserving the dignity of the Patriarchate of Constantinople. The man had devised countless vain ceremonies so that, in his first meeting with Pope Eugenius, he might show himself as an equal and by no means an inferior. But in vain. For both the misfortune of the Greeks and the arrogance of the Latins compelled the unhappy Patriarch to humble himself. Once a dispute over the doubtful articles of faith had begun on both sides, he judged that the union should be patched together by any law, and that they should even yield to the Latins—even if the truth stood with the Greeks—declaring without shame that they must obtain help against the Turks by any means.

> *But of the twenty-four heads of religion,* he said, *let us grant only one to the rank of the Latins; the remaining twenty-three will be sufficient to make up for the lack of that one.*

As matters neared an end, he lay down with a serious illness and wished to hear the opinions of the Fathers regarding the definition of affairs. Bessarion <note>A prominent Greek scholar and later a Cardinal who was a key advocate for the Union</note> read these to him secretly, but with the worst possible faith, having shortened them and changed them at his whim. Induced by such trickery as much as by an innate instability of mind, he subscribed to the dogmas of the Latins and urged other bishops to subscribe by his authority. But when he saw the Latins proceeding from articles of faith to nipping at the discipline of the Greek Church, he was moved by heavy repentance for the signature he had given; and after eight days, consumed by grief as well as illness, he died on the 10th day of June in the year 1439. There remain in Latin: *Letter to the Council of Basel*, Councils, Vol. 12, p. 545; and a *Leaden Bull to the same*, ibid., p. 571.

15th CENTURY

A Latin Oration to the Synod, dissuading the undertaking of a journey from Constantinople to the West, found in Syropoulos's *History of the Council of Florence* <note>original: "Hist. Concil. Florent."</note>, Section 2, chapter 18. Another Oration on the same subject, ibid. chapter 24. An exhortatory Oration to the Greek Bishops about to set out for Italy with him, that they might conduct themselves with constancy, ibid. Section 3, chapter 16.

<margin>1417.</margin>
**MARTIN V**, also known as the third <note>This likely refers to his place among the claimants or a specific counting of Martins in the Roman line</note>, formerly called Oddone Colonna, a Roman by birth, descended from the most illustrious blood of the Colonna family. He was educated in the study of Canon Law <note>original: "Juris Pontificii"</note> at Perugia. He was made a Referendary <note>A high-ranking official in the papal court</note> by Urban VI, and created Cardinal Deacon of San Giorgio in Velabro by Innocent VII. Having set out for the Council of Constance in the year 1414, he was among the foremost figures distinguished by his achievements. In the year 1417, after the three Antipopes had been deposed, the election of a new Pontiff was entrusted to the Cardinals present at the Council and to thirty delegates selected in equal numbers from five nations. He himself was elected Pope by the unanimous consent of all on the 11th day of November, a day sacred to the memory of Saint Martin. He was ordained a priest on the 12th, consecrated a Bishop on the 13th, and invested with the papal crown on the 21st. Having been created Pontiff, he considered nothing more important than dissolving the Council and evading the reformation of the Church, which had been promised so many times and demanded so earnestly by Emperor Sigismund and the Christian princes. He accomplished this by postponing the matter to a future Council, which he promised he would soon assemble. Therefore, despite the protests of the Emperor and the German bishops, he closed the Council the following year on the 22nd day of April. Citing the need to settle the disturbances in Italy by his presence, he departed from Constance on the 17th day before the Kalends of June <note>May 16</note>. In the year 1420, he declared a Crusade against the Bohemians, the followers of Hus <note>The Hussites</note>, granting full remission of sins to those who followed the banners of the sacred military. In the month of August 1423, he convened a General Council at Siena; however, when the mention of reforming the Church was introduced in the Synod, knowing well that he himself would be the target of these efforts <note>original: "eam in se fabam cudi probe sciens" - literally "knowing that the bean was being threshed on him," an idiom for bearing the brunt of a situation</note>, he hastily broke off the Council and deferred it for seven years to be held at Basel. In the year 1429, with the help of King Alfonso of Aragon, he compelled Gil Sánchez Muñoz <note>original: "Ægidium Munionis"</note>—who had been substituted five years earlier by the schismatic Cardinals under the title of Clement VIII following Benedict XIII—to abdicate the Papacy and forced his follower Cardinals to join his own side. Thus, at last, he finally put an end to the most grievous Schism which had raged in the Roman Church for 51 years. He died on the 20th day of February in the year 1431, at the age of 63. His Letters, Bulls, and Constitutions exist in the *Collection of Councils* <note>original: "Concil. Tom. xii. p. 252"</note>; other Letters and Constitutions appear in Bzovius under the year 1419; and many more in the *Great Bullary* of Laertius Cherubini, Volume 1. There is also a *Sermon on the Translation of Blessed Monica* (the mother of St. Augustine) from Ostia to Rome, in the *Augustinian History*, Toulouse 1641; the *Approbation of the Rule of the Hieronymite Monks*, among the works of Jerome, Volume 4; and *Laws for the Cardinals*, in the *Life* of him edited by Contelori.

---

<margin>1418.</margin>
**GOBELINUS PERSONA**, a German by nation, born in ancient Saxony (which is now called Westphalia) in the year 1358. After he had traveled through almost all of Italy and remained for a long time in the Roman Curia, he was initiated into the priesthood in the year 1386. Three years later, he was made Rector of the Chapel of the Holy Trinity in the city of Paderborn. However, because he did not hesitate to declaim in a public sermon against a certain edict issued by the city consuls, which was contrary to the Papal and Imperial factions, he lost his position and was appointed the Bishop's Vicar or Official. A little later, having experienced the envy of the monks of the Benedictine Order and having been endangered by poison, he left Paderborn and went to Bielefeld, where he was soon named Dean of the Cathedral Church. He flourished in the year 1418. Finally, weary of business, he donned the cowl <note>became a monk</note> and departed from the living when he was over sixty years old. He wrote a Chronicle from the creation of the world down to the year of Christ 1418, called the *Cosmodromium* <note>term: Cosmodromium; "The Course of the World"</note>, which he began before the year 1404 and finally finished in 1418. It was published with notes and an Appendix by Heinrich Meibom at Frankfurt in 1599, in folio. Molanus and Surius also attribute to him a *Life of Saint Meinulphus*, a Deacon of Paderborn and Confessor, whom Charlemagne took from the sacred font <note>meaning Charlemagne was his godfather</note>. Surius published it in an interpolated form and distorted by a changed style for October 5th; a genuine version, though omitting the heap of miracles, was published by Christoph Brower at Mainz in 1616.

### HENRY OF HESSE, or of Langenstein, German by nationality, Licentiate of Sacred Theology at the University of Paris, a Monk of the Carthusian Order <note>A strict, contemplative monastic order founded by St. Bruno</note>, and Prior of the Monastery of St. Mary in Gelderland near Arnhem; whom Trithemius rightly conjectures was a Canon of the Church of Worms, and was finally called to Vienna to lecture on Theology to the university students. He flourished in the year 1418. He died in the year 1428. He was an exceedingly prolific and industrious writer; although he spent thirty years explaining Genesis from his academic chair, he barely reached the fourth chapter of the book, yet filled as many volumes.

### JOSEPH BRYENNIOS, from Constantinople by homeland, a Monk by way of life, appointed to hold sermons for the People, flourished in the year 1420, which he himself indicates in the 8th Oration on the Trinity cited by Allatius. He wrote much against the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>: especially against their dogma on the Procession of the Holy Spirit <note>The "Filioque" controversy regarding whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son</note>. *Eighteen Orations* which he himself titled *On the Most-Divine Trinity* <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς ὑπερθέου τριάδος</note> are preserved as manuscripts in the Vatican Library. Leo Allatius, in *On Consent* book 2, chapter 18, section 14, lists their individual titles, arguments, beginnings, and the places where they were held, and he provides three fragments from them in Greek and Latin in the same place; others appear in chapter 5, section 3; chapter 15, section 7; and book 3, chapter 2, section 3; and in the book against Hottinger, pages 315, 318. Allatius also cites two of his orations on the future Judgment and eternal beatitude, and displays excerpts gathered here and there in Greek and Latin in the *Book on the Ecclesiastical Books of the Greeks*, pages 136, 146, 389, and in the *Book on Purgatory*, pages 79, 141, 713. By the same author are *Three Dialogues on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*—

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15th Century.
from the Year 1400.

A *Disputation on the Orthodox Church of the Holy Spirit*, and other works on Faith, are held as manuscripts in the Ambrosian Library.

### LEONARDO BRUNI OF AREZZO

<margin>1420.</margin>
LEONARDO BRUNI OF AREZZO, Italian by nationality, was born in the city of Arezzo, from which he took his surname. Nurtured in the study of "humane letters" <note>the Humanities, such as grammar, rhetoric, and history</note> from his very cradle, he won a great reputation among the most famous historians, orators, and philosophers of his century for the elegance of his Latin speech, the beauty of his style, and the sharpness of his intellect. Furthermore, he was the first among the Latins to elevate and restore the knowledge of the Greek language, which he had learned from Manuel Chrysoloras <note>a Byzantine scholar who brought Greek literature to Italy</note>. Having attained a massive reputation for learning among the Italians, he was summoned to the Roman court by Pope Innocent VII and appointed to the writing of apostolic epistles around the year 1404; he performed the same duty under the three following Popes: Gregory XII, Alexander V, and John XXIII. Finally recalled to Tuscany <note>Hetruria</note> by the Florentine Senate, he was appointed High Chancellor of the city by the unanimous vote of the Fathers <note>the city council</note>. He flourished in the year 1420. Blessed with a rich leisure, he applied his mind to writing histories and other scholarly works by which he served the world of literature excellently. Yet he was no less intent on amassing wealth, for which reason he is noted by historians for the most shameful greed and is soundly criticized. He died in Florence, full of days and glory, on March 9th <note>original: "vii. Id. Martii"</note> in the year 1443, at the age of 74. Buried in the Church of Santa Croce, he received a magnificent tomb and a no less glorious inscription, composed in these words:

> After Leonardo departed from life, History mourns, eloquence is mute; and it is said that the Muses, both Greek and Latin, could not hold back their tears.

Surely no one will easily deny Bruni the praise for eloquence and a most fertile intellect; indeed, Aeneas Sylvius <note>the future Pope Pius II</note> calls him that "splendor of Tuscany," <margin>* Epistle 51.</margin> than whom no one since Lactantius <note>a 4th-century Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero"</note> was closer to Cicero. Poggio Bracciolini <note>a famous humanist and contemporary</note> proclaims him to have been a most learned man and the most eloquent of all. <margin>† Invective against Philelphus, 2.</margin> Meanwhile, however, it cannot be hidden that he lacked many of the gifts of a perfect writer; and to use the words of Erasmus <margin>|| The Ciceronian.</margin> concerning him: "In ease of diction and clarity he approaches Cicero closely enough, but he lacks vigor and several other virtues; in some places he scarcely maintains the purity of the Roman tongue, though otherwise he is a man equally learned and upright." Add to this a stain than which none greater can be burned into a learned man: Bruni is held guilty of the crime of literary plagiarism. For he published the *Gothic History* of Procopius <note>a 6th-century Byzantine historian</note> translated into Latin, suppressing the true author's name and ascribing it to himself. This theft turned out very badly for Bruni. For a few years after his death, Cristoforo Persona vindicated the History back to Procopius; and having uncovered Bruni's shameful plagiarism, he offered up his fraud for the ridicule of the learned world.

---

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*A Small Book against Hypocrites.* Published in the *Collection of Things to be Sought*, Cologne, 1535.

*Twelve Books of Florentine History.* In these, while he narrates the foreign wars of the Florentines at length, he often remains silent regarding internal seditions for fear of offending his fellow citizens. Published by Sixtus Bruno at Strasbourg, 1610.

*Four Books on the Italian War against the Goths*, which he pilfered from Procopius. Basel 1531, Paris 1534, Bellovisius 1607.

*Three Books on the Punic War*, in which he professes to supply those parts of Livy that are missing due to the loss of the second Decade of his History. However, he took almost everything from Polybius; yet, in his ingratitude, he denies in the preface that he acted as a mere translator. Published at Augsburg, 1537, and under the name of Polybius by Badius Ascensius at Paris.

*Eight Books of Epistles.* Strasbourg 1521, Basel 1535.

*Dialogue on Morals.* Paris 1516.

*Translation of the ten books of Aristotle's Ethics.* Paris 1516. Bruni translates Greek quite successfully, for he not only employs a sufficiently clear style but also renders the sense of the Greek speech with great faithfulness, almost never using wordy paraphrases.

## GIAN FRANCESCO POGGIO, called BRANDOLINI

GIAN FRANCESCO POGGIO, called BRANDOLINI, Italian by nationality, was born in Terranuova, a town in the territory of Arezzo. He was thoroughly educated in the knowledge of languages and the humanities <note>the "studia humanitatis" including grammar, rhetoric, and history</note>, having been taught Greek by Manuel Chrysoloras. He served as Secretary to eight Roman Popes and was the senior Prefect; he flourished in the year 1420. He played a significant role in the Council of Constance, and there in 1417, he delivered a funeral oration praising the late Cardinal Zabarella. After the death of Pope Nicholas V in 1455—having served fifty years in the Roman Court and nearly forty in the office of Secretary—he was summoned back to Florence at the age of 72 to serve as the Secretary of the Republic. He died at a great age in 1459 and was buried in Florence. He was certainly a learned man, but if anyone ever possessed a quarrelsome and lewd character, it was he. <margin>* From "The Ciceronian."</margin> In the judgment of Erasmus, *nature was enough for him* <note>original: "Illi naturae satis fuisse"</note>, but art and erudition were not as plentiful; meanwhile, he used an "impure flow of speech," if we are to believe Lorenzo Valla <note>a rival humanist known for his strict standards of Latin purity</note>. Erasmus provides a much harsher judgment of Poggio <margin>* Letter 7 in Book 4.</margin> elsewhere; after rebuking Poggio's unbridled anger toward Lorenzo Valla (who was a hundred times more learned than Poggio himself), he adds this: *Poggio is a storyteller so unlearned that even if he were free of obscenity, he would still be unworthy of being read; however, he is so obscene that even if he had been the most learned of men, he ought to be rejected by all good people.*

<margin>1420.</margin>
**MACARIUS MACRES**, Greek by nationality, a Hieromonk <note>a monk who is also a priest</note> of Mount Athos, and a very close personal friend of George Phranzes. Through Phranzes’ efforts, he went to Constantinople and was appointed Hegumen <note>Abbot</note> of the Royal Monastery of the Pantocrator; he was later declared Great Protosyncellus <note>a high-ranking administrative deputy to a Patriarch</note>. He flourished in the year 1420. He was a most bitter enemy of the Latins <note>the Western Roman Catholic Church</note>, for which reason he was considered a heretic by the Patriarch of Constantinople (who agreed with the Latins at that time) and was hounded by many misfortunes. Before the year 1430, he was sent as an ambassador by Emperor John Palaeologus to Pope Martin V, alongside the Grand Duke Mark Jagros. He departed from the living on January 7, 1431, during his return journey. He was <term>a man most excellent in speech, virtue, and intelligence <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ ἄριστος κατάγε λόγον κὴ ἀρετὴν κὴ σύνεσιν</note></term>, if we are to believe Phranzes—*A man by far most outstanding in eloquence, strength of character, and understanding*. He wrote a *Work on the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son*, striving to prove that this doctrine *was not necessary, but was an innovation of the faith*. Leo Allatius mentions it in those exact words and reveals it was divided into ten chapters in *On Consensus*, book 2, chapter 18, section 10.

**NIKOLAUS VON DINKELSBÜHL**, German by nationality and a Swabian by birth, Rector of the University of Vienna, flourished in the year 1420. He was still active in 1431, when he was present at the Council of Basel as a delegate from the University of Vienna. His extant works include: *A Book on the Precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>; An Exposition on the Lord's Prayer; A Treatise on the Eight Beatitudes; A Manual for Confessors; A Book on the Three Parts of Penance; On the Eight Capital Vices; On Sins of the Tongue*; and others, published at Strasbourg in 1516. *A Treatise on the Gifts of the Holy Spirit, On the Five Senses, On Gratitude and Ingratitude, and On Sacramental Communion* exist as manuscripts in the Augsburg Library. Simler lists many more of Nicolaus’s writings in the *Zurich Library*, page 518, as does Possevinus (who usually copies Simler without credit) in the *Sacred Apparatus*, Volume 2, page 147.

## 15th CENTURY from the Year 1400.</header>

<margin>15th CENTURY from the Year 1400.</margin>
<margin>* On English Writers, p. 610.</margin>
...he found that the King <note>Henry V of England</note> had recently died at the Woods of Vincennes <note>original: "Saltum Vincennarum"; a royal residence near Paris</note>; and, compelled by his own spirit, he withdrew from the Court, returned to England, and prepared himself for writing. After the year 1434, he was made Bishop of St. Davids <note>original: "Episcopus Menevensis"</note>. He died in the year [unclear] and was buried among the Canons of the Church of St. Stephen at Westminster. As for what Pits <note>John Pits, the English biographer</note> claims*, that he departed from this life in the year 1423, I would suspect that a typographical error lies in the number. For besides the fact that Lyndwood himself asserts in his preface that he began this *Provinciale* <note>a foundational work on English canon law</note> of his and finally brought it to a conclusion in the year 1430, Pits himself proves this clearly enough when he notes that Lyndwood later entered into the favor of Henry VI, such that he was placed in charge of the see of St. Davids. He wrote the *Provinciale, or the Constitutions of England in Five Books* dedicated to Henry Chichele, his patron; in these he collected the Constitutions of fourteen Archbishops of Canterbury, from Stephen Langton to Henry Chichele, and provided them explained with very extensive commentaries. It was published in print by Badius Ascensius in *Paris*, 1505, in folio; then in *London*, 1557, in octavo; in *Oxford*, 1679, in folio; and, with the commentaries that related less to Canon Law having been trimmed away, it was edited by Robert Sharrock, Doctor of Laws, at *Oxford*, 1663, in octavo. Pits also attributes to him a *Catalog of certain Archbishops of Canterbury*, perhaps for no other reason than that it was published together with the *Provinciale* in *London*, 1557. Certainly, for no other reason is the reading of the *Constitutions of Otho and Ottoboni* <note>Papal legates to England in the 13th century</note> and the very full commentaries on them attributed to Lyndwood—which everyone knows are actually owed to John of Acton <note>original: "Joanni de Athonâ"</note>, who flourished at the end of the 13th Century—other than the fact that they are usually appended to the *Provinciale* in all editions. It is also said that Lyndwood wrote a *Summary of Cases* and a *Commentary on certain Psalms*, which have not yet been brought to light <note>published</note>. Furthermore, it should not be kept silent that Lyndwood, as an envoy to the Council of Basel from King Henry VI, offered to the Fathers of the Council, in the name of the King, a remarkable <insert>Appeal against the pride and arrogance of the Roman Pontiffs, proclaiming that no King on earth acknowledged a superior to himself in temporal matters.</insert> Thomas James, in his book *On the Corruption of the Fathers* (p. 201), complains that this Appeal has been omitted until now by all the editors of the Councils through the greatest fraud.

### **JOANNES CANANUS**, Greek by nationality, a Byzantine Historian,
flourished in the year 1422.
