<margin>1424.</margin>
### **GEORGIUS PHRANZA**, a native of Byzantium, was born in the year 1401
on August 30th, born of no ignoble family, as he was joined by kinship to Gregory Palaeologus Mamona, the Great Duke of Monemvasia. He lost both parents, who were carried off by the plague, in the year 1417. He himself was chosen by the Emperor Manuel in the following year, on March 17th, to be among the Chamberlains. He flourished in the year 1424; having been sent with two other envoys to Murad, the King of the Turks, for the sake of entering into peace, he managed the matter well. In the year 1425, he recorded the Last Will and Testament of the Emperor Manuel (to whom he had been employed for letters <note>as a secretary</note> two years prior) as he neared his fate, and he held a place among the executors; shortly afterward, he was highly commended by the dying Manuel to his son, the Emperor John. After the death of Manuel, he was taken in among the chamberlains and dearest friends by the Despot <note>a high Byzantine title</note> Constantine Palaeologus—with his brother, the Emperor John, granting this with difficulty—and he followed him to the governorship of the Peloponnese in the month of November. In the year 1428, after war had been stirred up between the Despot Constantine and the ruler Carlo <note>Carlo II Tocco</note>, Phranza was placed in charge of the military forces and captured the city of Glarentza. In the following year, while he was present as a counselor to Constantine as he attacked Patras, he shielded the prince's body with his own when he was endangered by a sudden breakout of the garrison; he was led away into a very harsh captivity by the people of Patras, but was soon liberated after a truce was agreed upon by both sides. When the war was revived, he again performed excellent service for Constantine, being brave in battle and prudent in counsel: he was often put in command of military troops, and often sent as an envoy to foreign princes, both barbarians <note>non-Greeks/Ottomans</note> and Christians alike; more than once he was captured by enemies and put up for sale. In the year 1431, after Patras was captured, he presided over it for Constantine.

<meta>This page continues the biography of the Byzantine historian George Sphrantzes (often called Phranza), which began on the previous page. It then introduces two major Western figures of the early 15th century: the legal scholar John of Imola and the influential diplomat Cardinal Julian Cesarini.</meta>

<header># The Synodal Century.
## 15th CENTURY from the Year 1400.</header>

<margin>
15th CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
</margin>

In 1432, he was sent to Emperor John <note>Emperor John VIII Palaiologos</note>. He held the dignity of Protovestiarius <note>original: "Protovestiarii"; a high-ranking Byzantine court official, originally in charge of the imperial wardrobe but later a major administrative role</note>. In the year 1436, he accompanied Constantine <note>the future Emperor Constantine XI</note>, who was withdrawing from the government of the Peloponnese, to the Imperial City <note>Constantinople</note>. In the year 1438, he took as his wife Helena, the daughter of Alexios Palaiologos, and was blessed with many children. In 1440, he joined Constantine as a companion when he returned to the Peloponnese; he was employed by him in matters of the greatest importance above others, granted the governorship of the city of Selymbria and the province of Sparta, and over the following eight years, he was distinguished by more than as many diplomatic missions. In 1448, after Constantine was elevated to the Empire following the death of his brother John, he began to be advanced to even greater dignity. For after he had served as an ambassador to Trebizond and Iberia <note>referring to Georgia in the Caucasus</note> and had betrothed the daughter of the King of Iberia to Emperor Constantine, he returned to Byzantium and was named Great Logothete <note>original: "Magnus Logotheta"; the chief minister or chancellor of the Byzantine Empire</note>. On May 29, 1453, when Constantinople was captured by the Turks, Phranza was dragged into slavery, sold, and taken away to Sparta in the Peloponnese; his wife and children were likewise sold and deported elsewhere. At the end of that year, having obtained his freedom, he withdrew to Thomas Palaiologos, the Despot <note>a title for a provincial ruler</note> of the Peloponnese and brother of Emperor Constantine; he was admitted among Thomas's household and granted the town of Certeza. In 1455, he ransomed his wife from slavery and undertook a mission to the Venetians. In 1460, as the resources of the Palaiologos brothers were worn down by internal war and the Turks were devastating the Peloponnese far and wide, Phranza followed the Despot Thomas as he fled to a certain monastery in Macedonia; stationed there, he awaited the outcome of events. After the Peloponnese was brought under Turkish power, he bid a long farewell to Greece in the year 1466. After traveling through Italy and visiting Viterbo, Rome, Ancona, and Venice, he settled in Corfu toward the end of the year. There, setting aside the name George and taking the name Gregory, he entered the monastic life and set himself to writing the history of his time. He finally finished it on March 29, 1477. It is not clear how long he lived after its completion. He wrote a *History of Byzantine Affairs* <note>original: "Historiam rerum Byzantinarum"</note> from the year 1260 to the year 1476 in four books, lightly touching upon events that occurred before he was born, but thereafter weaving the history with a grander narrative. Jacobus Pontanus translated it into Latin, contracted it into three books by removing frequent digressions, and published it with added notes alongside the works of Theophylact Simocatta at *Ingolstadt, 1604, in quarto*.

<margin>1425.</margin>

**JOHN OF IMOLA** <note>Joannes de Imola</note>, born in the territory of Bologna to parents who had moved to Bologna from Imola; he was a student of the elder Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis, one of the most famous jurists of the Middle Ages</note>. He was a celebrated Doctor of Both Laws <note>Civil and Canon Law</note> in his native city. He flourished in the year 1425. He died in Bologna on February 18, 1436, and was buried in the portico of the Church of St. Benedict. His extant works include *Commentaries on three books of the Decretals, on the sixth book of the Decretals, and on the Clementines* <note>these are the core texts of medieval Catholic Canon Law</note>, *published in Venice in 1575 in two volumes in folio*, which are well known to professors of Canon Law. Also a *Commentary on the first and second parts of the Infortiatum and the New Digest* <note>referring to divisions of the "Digest," a major part of Roman Civil Law</note>, *Bologna, 1580*; a volume of *Legal Counsels* <note>original: "Consiliorum"</note>, *Venice, 1581*; and others elsewhere.

<margin>1426.</margin>

**JULIAN CESARINI** <note>Julianus Cæsarinus</note>, born in Rome to an illustrious family, a Doctor of Both Laws and a professor in Italian universities; he made his way to the highest honors of the Roman Curia through the fame of his exceptional learning. He was appointed as an Apostolic Protonotary, a Referendary <note>an official who processed petitions to the Pope</note>, an Auditor of the Rota <note>a judge in the high church court</note>, and a Cleric of the Apostolic Chamber. Finally, he was named Cardinal Deacon with the title of Saint Angelus on May 24, 1426, or, as others hold, in 1430, by Martin V. Soon after, he was created Cardinal Priest with the title of Saint Sabina, and Bishop of Grosseto and Tusculum. Having attained the purple <note>the rank of Cardinal</note>, he was sent as a legate to Germany with an army to subdue the Hussites <note>followers of the reformer Jan Hus in Bohemia</note>. However, he was soundly beaten by the Hussites and put to flight, bringing back nothing but mockery. In 1431, he was sent to Basel by Eugenius IV, where he acted as the Pope's representative and presided over the General Council begun there. But when the Fathers of the Council strongly asserted the superiority of the Council over the Pope, Eugenius issued a letter to Julian at the end of the year, ordering him to dissolve the Council. Julian refused to do so, and in two letters written back to Eugenius, he rebuked him most sharply, attempting to draw him away from that plan with the weightiest arguments. He protested that the Pope would be the cause of a schism and of infinite evils unless he changed his mind. Furthermore, with the greatest constancy and the fame of his learning, he defended the authority of the Council and held the position of president until about the year 1438.

</margin>
...he changed course, and having made a transition to the side of Eugenius, he vigorously debated against Mark <note>Mark Eugenikos, Archbishop of Ephesus, the chief Eastern Orthodox opponent of the union</note> at the Council of Florence. When the Synod of Florence was dissolved, he was sent as a legate to Vladislaus, the King of Hungary and Poland. With the greatest treachery, he sought and obtained a violation of the peace that had recently been most solemnly established with Murad, the King of the Turks, and he absolved the King from the bond of his oath. That treachery ended most miserably for the Christian commonwealth. For in the battle joined at Varna in the year 1444, Vladislaus fell, and the Christian forces were destroyed; Julian himself, who went before the Christians into battle carrying the Cross, succumbed to his wounds and died in the 46th year of his age. There exist *Two Letters to Pope Eugenius*, in which he attempts to lead him away from the plan of dissolving the Synod of Basel, found in the *Collection of Matters to be Sought* <note>original: "Fasciculus Rerum Expetendarum", a famous collection of documents related to church reform published in Cologne, 1535</note>, page 27. A very lengthy *Speech delivered in the Council of Basel of the Catholic Church for the conversion of the Bohemians* <note>referring to the Hussites</note> is found in Volume 12, page 894, where many other speeches delivered in the same Council 
<margin>
Index of Manuscripts in the Library of Augsburg, p. 47.
</margin>
can be found scattered about. The records of the debate in the Council of Florence against the Greeks are found in the history of that Council. There was another Julian Cesarini, distinct from ours, of whom there exists a *Treatise on the Transfer of the Empire* in manuscript in the Augsburg Library; provided that what the title claims is true, that its author was a Legate of Pope Nicholas V.

<margin>1426.</margin>
**BERNARDINO,** called **OF SIENA** from his homeland, was born from the noble Albizeschi family. His father was a Sienese man in the town of Massa in Tuscany. He was born on September 8, 1380, the son of Tollo and Nera. He lost his mother at three years of age and his father at seven. In the year 1392, called to Siena by his relatives, he had Onuphrius as his teacher in Grammar and John of Spoleto in Philosophy. In the year 1396, he joined the Confraternity of the Disciplinarians of the Blessed Virgin Mary <note>original: "Confraternitati Disciplinatorum"; a lay penitent group known for public flagellation</note>, and he had a place in the Hospital of la Scala, which his cousin Tobia directed. He was distinguished above others for his frequent flagellations of the body, and for applying nettles and a hair shirt to his flesh as a remedy for lust. In the year 1400, while a most savage plague was raging through Italy, he prepared a distinguished reputation for piety and charity for himself by devoting diligent labor to nursing the sick, who flowed in crowds to the Hospital of la Scala. In the year 1404, he gave his name to the Franciscan religion <note>i.e., joined the Franciscan Order</note>; and after a short stay in the Sienese monastery, seeking peace, he betook himself to the Convent of Colombaio, situated far from the city in the middle of a grove. Having been initiated into the priesthood, he began to become quite famous for his sermons. Sent as the Guardian to the Holy Places by the General of his Order, he presided in the place of a protector; he also acted as the Commissary of the Holy Land. Returning to Italy, he traveled through the cities preaching with the highest reputation and popular applause. In his sermons, he acted with such practiced skill that he excited his listeners to an extraordinary reverence for the name of Jesus Christ. He was accustomed to carry about that most holy Name depicted in the center of a sun circumscribed by a circle; he often displayed it while preaching and exhorted the people to the adoration of the Name with many words. From then on, however, suspected of a desire for innovation, he was accused of heresy before Pope Martin V. Summoned to Rome, he indeed cleared himself of the crime, but he was ordered to abstain thereafter from the custom he had used. He was famous in the year 1426. He was designated as Bishop of Ferrara, Siena, and Urbino in succession by Pope Eugenius IV and was eagerly desired by the people, but he constantly refused the honors offered to him. But as the prefect of the Brothers of the Observance <note>original: "Fratribus de Observantiâ"; a reform movement within the Franciscans seeking a stricter adherence to the rule of St. Francis</note> (whom he himself had established around the year 1412) on this side of the mountains, he either restored more than three hundred collapsed monasteries or built them from the foundations. He died at L'Aquila in the Vestini region on May 20, 1444, at the age of 64. He was enrolled among the Saints by Nicholas V in the year 1450. The Papal storytellers spread clearly wonderful and innumerable things about him: that all kinds of diseases were blown away with a little word, that the dead were restored to life by the benefit of his relics, and they even claim for him a knowledge of the Greek language—though he was entirely unlearned in it—inspired divinely so that he dared to preach before the Greeks. They claim Christ and the Blessed Mother of God were often seen above the head of the preacher, and other portents of that kind; at which the fools are amazed, but the sane laugh.

# NICOLAUS TUDESCHUS,

<margin>1428.</margin>
Commonly called *Panormitanus* <note>meaning "the man from Palermo"</note>, a Sicilian by nation, born in Catania, a monk of the Benedictine Order, and Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Agatha (called the "Abbot of Manzano" by Trithemius and others); later Archbishop of Palermo, he flourished in the year 1428. He was by far the most celebrated legal expert of his century, so much so that on account of his extraordinary knowledge of both Civil and Canon Law, he was called by the common voice the "Lamp of the Law" <note>original: "Lucerna Juris"</note>. He was a disciple of Francesco Zabarella and Antonio Butrio. After he had taught Canon Law in the University of Siena, and from the year 1425 at Parma for some time, he was summoned to Rome and appointed an Auditor of the Rota <note>a high judicial court of the Roman Catholic Church</note>. In the year 1431, sent as an ambassador by the King of Aragon to the Council of Basel, he held the first place among all by his eloquence, the weight of his words, his profound knowledge of Canon Law, and the authority of his name. He most strongly defended the cause of the Council in a commentary published against Pope Eugenius; he established the Council's superiority over the Roman Pontiff with invincible arguments. However, when Eugenius rejected the authority of the Council and held a rival council at Ferrara, Tudeschus did not wish him to be condemned as a heretic on that account; indeed, he diverted the Fathers of the Council from their plan when they were preparing a common vote of excommunication against the Pope. Furthermore, he dashed the hopes of priests and abbots who were seeking not only places but also the right to give definitive votes in the Synod; he strongly asserted the ancient prerogative of the Bishops. Around the year 1440, he received the Cardinal’s purple from Pope Felix V <note>an "Antipope" elected by the Council of Basel</note> as a reward for his virtue and labors. He died, seized by the plague, in the year 1445, or as others hold, 1443.

->W O R K S.<-

*Very extensive Commentaries on the five books of the Decretals* <note>The *Decretals* were the primary collection of Papal laws used in the Middle Ages</note>. Published in Venice, 1492; Lyon, 1586; and on the first three books, ibid., 1524.
*Commentaries on the Clementines* <note>A later collection of Canon Law</note>, and their Glosses.
*Legal Opinions* <note>original: "Consilia"</note>, 118 in number.
*Seven most subtle Questions*. Published together with the *Legal Opinions* in Lyon, 1584, 1586.
*A Repetition on the chapter "Per tuas," regarding Arbitrators*.
*A Manual of Practice* usually observed in almost all courts.
*A Treasury of singular decisions in Canon Law*.

<margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 288.</margin>
*Treatise on the Superiority of a Council over the Pope*, or *A Defense of the Council of Basel against Pope Eugenius*. It seems hardly credible to Bellarmine* <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent Jesuit theologian who defended Papal authority</note> that such a book was written by Panormitanus; leaning on certain "straw arguments," he suggests the opposite and asserts that he sought the work in various editions of Panormitanus's Works in vain. But all this is said in spite of the truth, and perhaps in spite of his own conscience:

<margin>1429.</margin>
## ALEXANDER CARPENTARIUS
English by nationality, he was active around 1429, at which time he began to compose the *Destructorium vitiorum* <note>The Destroyer of Vices</note>. To him is owed that work which was published in *Venice*, 1582, in 4to; in *Nuremberg*, 1496; and elsewhere quite often, without the author’s surname, inscribed simply as "Alexander the Englishman." For it is found noted thus at the end of a manuscript codex in the library of Balliol College, Oxford: *“By dispelling the constraints of darkness, a certain son of a carpenter collected these noteworthy things mentioned above from the opinions of the Doctors and the documents of Holy Scripture; and he decided to present them to the honor of God for the utility of the Church,”* etc. The codex, however, bears the name of Alexander on the front. The celebrated James Ussher <note>An influential Irish Archbishop and historian</note> records these things as an eyewitness in his *Theological Library*. Furthermore, that *Destructorium* is also held in manuscript under Alexander’s name in the library of St. Peter’s, Cambridge, codex 115.

---

<margin>1430.</margin>
## RAYMUNDUS DE SABUNDE, or SEBEYDE
Spanish by birth, a Doctor of Arts and Medicine, and also distinguished in the faculties of Philosophy and Theology. He achieved great fame by teaching and writing in the Academy of Toulouse (which he eventually undertook to govern). He was active around 1430. There exists his *Natural Theology, regarding Man and Creatures, or the Treasury of Divine Considerations*, which he began at Toulouse in the year 1434 and completed toward the end of 1436; it was printed at *Daventry*, folio; *Strasbourg*, 1496; *Paris*, 1509; *Lyon*, 1540, 8vo; *Frankfurt*, 1631, 8vo; and *Venice*, 1581, 8vo. The Prologue is prohibited in the Roman Index <note>The Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the list of books banned by the Catholic Church</note> of Pope Clement VIII. This is not surprising, for he clearly teaches that all revealed truths are contained in Holy Scripture and are proposed by God to Christians by that single means. There is also a Dialogue of his titled *The Violet of the Soul*, which represents Raymond and Dominic "the Sower of Words" <note>original: "Dominicum Seminiverbium"</note> conversing about the nature of man, the knowledge of oneself, of God, and of neighbor, and regarding every debt by which we are bound to God and neighbor; this is essentially nothing other than the book on *Natural Theology* adapted into dialogue form by the author himself. This Dialogue was published in *Cologne*, 1501, 4to, and *Lyon*, 1568, 12mo.

* History of the Council of Florence, Section 3, Chapter 8.
</margin>
## DEMETRIUS CHRYSOLORAS
Greek by nationality, and from Thessaloniki, it seems; a supreme philosopher and astronomer, very dear to Emperor Manuel <note>Manuel II Palaiologos</note>. Having been asked by the Emperor one day while standing by him at dinner—as Sguropulus <note>Sylvester Syropoulos, a chronicler of the Council of Florence</note> relates—whether he could pronounce anything for certain regarding the future from the science of the stars, he replied that he had found from the convergence of the stars that the seventh Palaiologos <note>Referring to Emperor John VIII Palaiologos</note> would find a concord with the Latins and a union of the Churches that would be most ruinous and to be detested by all Christians. When the Emperor tried to deflect this onto his cousin John, Demetrius affirmed that his son John was the one destined by the stars. He was active around the year 1430. He wrote against the Latins a *Synoptic Oration* based on the arguments of Nilus of Thessaloniki; a *Dialogue on why it is not lawful for the Orthodox to accuse other Orthodox of any matter*; and finally a *Dialogue against the Oration which Demetrius Cydonius wrote against Nilus Cabasilas of Thessaloniki*. A fragment of this last Dialogue in Greek and Latin is provided by Leo Allatius <note>A Greek scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note> in his book against Hottinger, page 49. The individual short works of Demetrius are preserved in manuscript in the Vatican Library.

---

<margin>1430.</margin>
## MACARIUS
Likewise Greek by birth, Metropolitan of Ancyra <note>Modern-day Ankara</note>, he seems to have been active around the year 1430 or shortly before; he was a sharp critic of the Latins. There exists an unpublished work *Against the depraved opinions of the Latins*, and especially also against Barlaam, Akindynos, and their followers <note>Key figures in the 14th-century Hesychast controversy</note>, consisting of 100 chapters. Leo Allatius mentions it and criticizes it sharply in *On Consensus*, book 2, chapter 18, section 15.

1430.

ESAIAS, a native of Cyprus and a friend and follower of the Latins <note>The "Latins" refers to the Roman Catholic Church, as opposed to the Greek Orthodox Church</note>, flourished, if I guess correctly (for I have not yet been able to investigate his exact age with certainty), around the year 1430. He was certainly a contemporary of Nicolaus Sclengia, whose book on the *Procession of the Holy Spirit* against the Latins he attacked in a letter sent to him. In this letter, he accused Sclengia of silliness and impiety, and contended with many arguments to prove that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father <note>The "Filioque" controversy, a major theological divide between the Eastern and Western Churches</note>. That letter exists in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius’s *On Consent*, book 2, chapter 18, section 16, and in *The Orthodox Greeks*, volume 1, page 396.

<margin>
1430.
</margin>

JOHN ANAGNOSTA <note>His surname "Anagnosta" means "The Reader"</note> of Thessaloniki was present in his native city when it was captured by Murad II, the Prince of the Turks, in the year 1430; he was a participant in its labors and calamities. Recalled from flight by the promises of the victor, he continued to live in his former home in the city among other fellow citizens. However, when the tyrant returned two years later, John was stripped of his goods and regretted his decision to stay. He wrote a *Narrative of the Final Destruction of Thessaloniki* <note>original: *Narrationem de Extremo Excidio Thessalonicensi*</note>, to which he subjoined a *Monody or Prose Lamentation* <note>original: *Monodiam sive Threnum Prosaicum*</note>. Both were published in Greek and Latin by Allatius in his *Miscellanies*, part 2, pages 318 and 374.

<margin>
1430.
</margin>

PETER JEREMIAH, a Sicilian by nationality and from Palermo by home, was a Monk of the <term>Dominican Order</term> <note>Also known as the Order of Preachers</note> and a preacher of foremost eloquence; he flourished around the year 1430. First admitted among the Preachers at Bologna, he later returned to his native island and reformed several monasteries of his Order by his authority. Having finally returned to Bologna, he died (as is clear from his epitaph) in the year 1452, on the 5th day before the Nones of March <note>March 3rd</note>; though according to Altamura, it was in the year 1434.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*Sermons for the Seasons and for the Saints throughout the whole year.*
*Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer.*
*Exposition of the Ten Commandments.*
*Treatise on the Passion of the Lord.*
*Treatise on Faith.*

The Works of Peter Jeremiah just listed were published at Haguenau in 1514. Altamura, in his *Library of Preachers*, page 173, lists certain other works which do not yet seem to have been published.

<margin>
1430.
</margin>

NICHOLAS OF OSIMO, an Italian by race and from Picenum by birth, was a member of the <term>Order of Friars Minor</term> <note>The Franciscans</note> and an intimate friend of Bernardino of Siena; he flourished in the year 1430. He was a pious man and not unlearned. He performed many services for his Order and held various offices; in particular, he served as the Vicar of the province of Saint Angelus and as the Prefect of the sites in the Holy Land. Upon returning from Jerusalem, he died in the Monastery of the <term>Aracoeli</term> <note>The "Altar of Heaven" monastery in Rome</note>. He wrote a *Summa of Cases of Conscience* <note>original: *Summam Casuum Conscientiæ*</note>, printed at Venice in 1484; a *Supplement to the Pisanella Summa*, Milan 1444 <note>This date 1144 in the text is likely a typo for 1444</note> and Venice 1469 in 4to; an *Interrogatory for Confessors*, Venice 1489 in 8vo; *Commentaries on the Rule of the Friars Minor*; an *Epitome of Canon Law*; a *Book of Sermons*; and a *Lenten Cycle*; which Lucas Wadding reports in his *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*, page 263, were written by him but do not yet seem to have been published.

<margin>
1431.
</margin>

JOHN NIDER, German by nationality and Swabian by birth, was a supreme theologian of the Dominican Order, Prior of the Dominican House at Basel, <term>Inquisitor of Heretical Depravity</term>, and Rector of the University of Vienna. He flourished in the year 1431, at which time he was sent by the University of Vienna to the Council of Basel; he gained fame for himself through the disputations organized against the <term>Hussites</term> <note>Followers of the reformer Jan Hus, who sought church reforms in Bohemia</note>. At the beginning of the year 1432, he was sent as a legate from the Council to the Bohemians to invite them to the Synod with a guarantee of safety and hope for reformation, but his effort was in vain. For the memory of the burning of Hus and the perjury of the Council of Constance <note>The Council of Constance (1414-1418) had promised Jan Hus safe conduct but executed him anyway</note> had not yet faded from their minds. Nider died at Nuremberg in the year 1438.

<margin>1431.</margin> **EUGENIUS IV**, previously named *Gabriel Condulmer*, was born in Venice of illustrious blood, the nephew of Gregory XII through his sister, and the son of Angelo Condulmer. While still a youth, he joined the Canons of the Congregation of Saint George in Alga, wearing the habit of the Celestines. Having raised a reputation for holiness, he was called to Rome by his uncle and appointed Bishop of Siena, Clerk of the Chamber, Treasurer, and Cardinal Priest with the Title of Saint Clement. Under Martin V, he served as Legate first to Picenum and then to Bologna, managing affairs well in both places. After the death of Martin, he was elected Roman Pontiff on March 2, 1431, and crowned on the 11th day of the same month. At the beginning of his papacy, when <margin>* *Lives of the Pontiffs*, Basel, 1507.</margin> divine and human affairs were all in turmoil, says Johannes Stella*, he incited the Roman people to arms; a riot broke out, and the people compelled Eugenius to flee the city in a monk's cowl. They pursued him as he fled with darts and arrows; they removed the Papal magistrates from their positions, substituted their own, and asserted the liberty lost under Boniface. Driven from the City, Eugenius withdrew to Florence. At that time, the Council of Basel—which had been summoned by Martin V the previous year on July 23—was begun by Julian, Cardinal of Saint Angelus and legate of Eugenius. In its second session, held in March of the following year, the Council decreed that the Church must be reformed by the Council in both "Head and members" <note>A famous phrase in church history referring to the need to reform both the Papacy (the head) and the rest of the clergy and laity (the members)</note>, and that the Council could not be dissolved or transferred elsewhere without its own consent. Eugenius, unable to endure this, recalled his Legate and ordered the Council to be moved to Bologna. The Council strenuously vindicated its own authority, declaring the Pope's edict to be rash and a scandal to the Church; it ordered the Pope himself to appear before the Council within three months, unless he preferred to be disciplined by a decree of the Council. However, the Council frequently extended the deadline for him until the beginning of the year 1434. Eugenius, terrified by the threats of the Fathers <note>The "Fathers" refers to the high-ranking bishops and theologians attending the Council</note>, yielded to the Council, confirmed all its acts, revoked his own edicts, and sent Legates who were to comply with the Council in all things. After three years, however, when the Greeks were about to come to the West to establish union with the Latins, a dispute arose over the location of the meeting. Eugenius commanded the Council to be moved to Ferrara. The Fathers at Basel, on the contrary, accused Eugenius of simony, perjury, and other crimes, and ordered him to be judged at Basel. When he refused to obey, they declared him contumacious in the 28th session on October 1, 1437. In the following year, in the 31st session, they suspended him from Papal authority; and in 1439, in the 34th session, they completely deprived him of it. They decreed the acts of the Councils of Ferrara and Florence to be void and schismatic; and at the end of the year, on November 17, in the 39th session, they elected Amadeus, Count of Savoy...

# The Synodal Century

<margin>15th CENTURY from the Year 1400.</margin>

They chose for themselves a Pope by the title of **Felix V** <note>Amadeus VIII, Duke of Savoy, who was the last historical antipope</note>. Eugenius, meanwhile, thunders <note>original: *fulminat*, a term for issuing severe papal censures</note> not sparingly against the leaders of the Basel assembly; and having drawn the Greeks into Italy, he proceeds to celebrate his own Council. It was begun at Ferrara in the year 1438, and, due to an epidemic plague spreading there, was transferred to Florence toward the beginning of the following year. 

There was sharp disputation between the Greeks and the Latins for some time; at last, however, it was agreed upon by both sides. For the Emperor of Constantinople, John Palaiologos, having long since been reduced to desperate straits by the Turks, was present at the Council and bargained for aid to be brought to him against the barbarians. Little concerned for other matters regarding the faith or the liberty of his own Church, he compelled the Greek bishops by his own authority to yield to the side of the Latins. Thus, despite the protests of Mark of Ephesus <note>A prominent Greek theologian who famously refused to sign the union decree</note> and others who held fast to the ancient faith, it was defined by common vote that: Purgatory exists, the Pope is the head of the Church, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son <note>original: *Filioque*, the central theological dispute between East and West</note>, and unleavened bread <note>term: *azyma* — the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, a practice of the Western Church</note> can be used in celebrating the Eucharist. 

With the matter finished, the Council was dissolved. Emperor Palaiologos returned home with empty promises, and the Greek bishops returned laden with grief and disgrace. Eugenius, for his part, betook himself to Rome and thundered against Felix and those at Basel; nor did they less sharply hurl excommunications <note>original: *anathema*</note> back at Eugenius. The matter was conducted by both sides with insults, and indeed with arms, until at last in the year 1442, on the 16th of May <note>original: *xvii. Cal. Junii*</note>, the Fathers of Basel closed their Synod, having first announced a Council at Lyon to be held three years later. This closure was finally confirmed by Pope Nicholas V in the year 1449. Eugenius died on February 18, 1447, at the age of 64. 

There exist 24 of his **Letters** and **Bulls** in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 12, pages 469, 931, etc.; 33 **other Letters** (some of which are in Greek and Latin) in Volume 13, page 21, etc.; 10 **others** in Bzovius’s *Annals*, Volume 4; and many **others** in Waddington’s *Minor Annals*, Volume 5, and in the *Bullarium* of Laertius Cherubini, printed at Rome in 1617 and 1638.

<margin>1431.</margin>
## LAWRENCE JUSTINIAN, a Venetian by birth, a Patrician by rank, son of Bernard Justinian and Quirina, and a Canon Regular of the Order of Saint Augustine in the Congregation of Saint George in Alga.

After spending thirty years in the religious life, he was appointed Bishop of Venice by Eugenius IV around the year 1431, or as others have it, 1435; this was after he had employed every possible prayer and artifice to shake off the burden imposed upon him. He is a man rightly to be celebrated for his unfeigned piety toward God, his lavish charity toward the poor, and his immense zeal for religion. In the year 1450, he was raised to the title and dignity of Patriarch by Pope Nicholas V, and he was the first to bring the patriarchal peak <note>the rank of Patriarch</note> to his native city. He died on January 8, in the year of Christ 1455, at the age of 74. He was enrolled in the catalog of Saints by Clement VII in the year 1524.

### **ANDREW OF PETRA**, Archbishop of Colossae—or, as he is frequently called by Syropoulos <note>Sylvester Syropoulos, a Greek historian who wrote a famous account of the Council of Florence</note>, Archbishop of Rhodes. Born and educated among the Greeks and distinguished with the Episcopal dignity, he eventually went over to the Latins <note>meaning he converted from the Greek Orthodox to the Roman Catholic Church</note>. He flourished in the year 1432, at which time he was sent as a legate by Pope Eugenius to the Council of Basel. There, in a lengthy oration delivered on August 24, he attempted to persuade the Fathers to be compliant to Eugenius and to uproot the schism from the Church. Soon after, he was designated by the Council as a legate to the Greeks for the sake of entering into an agreement of concord. He had undertaken this duty once before; however, it is not entirely clear whether he actually traveled to the province newly entrusted to him. In the year 1438, at the Council of Ferrara, he argued strenuously against Mark of Ephesus and Bessarion regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit. His *Oration delivered in the Synod of Basel* is extant in the Collection of Councils, Volume 12, page 872, and in Bzovius under the year 1432, section 37. His *Assertions proposed in the Council of Ferrara against the Greeks* are found in the same source under the year 1438, section 8.

<margin>
1432.
</margin>
### **JOHN**, Archbishop of Taranto, flourished in the year 1432. He was likewise sent by Eugenius to the Council of Basel and spoke on behalf of the Pope in the Synod. In 1434, after peace was restored between Eugenius and the Council, he was again sent as a legate so that he might preside over the Council in the Pope's stead along with others. In 1438, having left the supporters of the Basel assembly, he went to Eugenius and took part in the Council of Ferrara. His *Oration delivered in the Synod of Basel* is extant in the Collection of Councils, Volume 12, page 884, and in Bzovius under the year 1432, section 51.

1433.
</margin>
### **GILLES CARLIER**, a Belgian by nationality and a native of Cambrai, was a fellow of the College of Navarre at the University of Paris and a Professor of Theology. After gaining no small reputation for himself through his lectures on the *Books of the Sentences* <note>term: *Sententiarum libros* — the "Sentences" of Peter Lombard, the standard textbook for medieval theology students</note> and his sermons to the people, he was created Dean of the Church of Cambrai on October 11, 1431. He flourished in the year 1433, when he was present at the Council of Basel and performed strenuous work in leading the Hussites <note>followers of the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus</note> back to the Church. Indeed, sent as a legate to Prague by the Council, he spared no labor to recall the Bohemians to the bosom of the Church, or at least to bring them to the Council. Having returned to Basel, he disputed in the Synod for four days against Nicholas the Taborite <note>Nicholas of Pelhřimov, a leading radical Hussite bishop</note>, the champion of the Hussites. He died at a great age on November 23, 1473.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*A Basket of Fragments* <note>original: *Sporta Fragmentorum*</note>, *in which are contained Treatises: On the preservation of the goods of the Church; A Defense of the Church; On the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Mary; Against the Iconoclasts; In favor of Celibacy, especially for the Clergy.*
*A Little Basket of Fragments* <note>original: *Sportula Fragmentorum*</note>, *which contains Treatises: On the election of Judas the betrayer; On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy; On life annuities; On Tithes; On Indulgences; On the integrity of Confession; On the non-eating of meat among the Benedictines; Against those who calculate the end of the world; On the cloistering of Religious women of the Order of St. Dominic.*
These two works, the *Basket* and the *Little Basket*, were published under the title *Consultations on Various Cases*, Brussels, 1478, in 2 volumes, folio.
*The Oration in which he responded for four days at the Council of Basel to the second article of the Bohemians, regarding the correction of public sins, which was proposed over two days by Nicholas the Taborite.* It is extant in the Collection of Councils, Volume 12, pages 1159 to 1248; in Bzovius under the year 1433, and 193; and in Canisius's *Ancient Readings*, Volume 3, page 289.
*Commentaries on the four books of the Sentences, 43 Sermons, and very many Treatises on various subjects*, are preserved as manuscripts in the Library of the College of Navarre. Launoy provides the titles and arguments of each in his *History of the Gymnasium of Navarre*, part 2, chapter 4, page 581.

**JOHN OF RAGUSA**, also known as *de Raguso*, a Dalmatian by nationality, a Monk of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, and a Procurator General. Under this title, he was sent as a legate to the Council of Basel at the beginning of the year 1433. For eight full days, he argued against Jan Rokycana, the advocate for the Hussites <note>a pre-Reformation Christian movement in Bohemia</note>. In the following year, he was sent by the Council to Constantinople to invite the Greeks to the Synod with the hope of peace and military aid. In the year 1438, having abandoned the side of the Basel Fathers, he went over to the camp of Pope Eugenius and was present at the Council of Ferrara. In the year 1440, having been granted the Bishopric of Strasbourg—or, as others have it, Argos—by the Pope two years prior, he was sent as a legate to Emperor John [VIII Palaiologos] in Constantinople. There are those who report that John of Ragusa was later co-opted into the number of Cardinals with the Title of St. Sixtus. His *Oration in which he responded over eight days at the Council of Basel to the first Article of the Bohemians, regarding Communion under both kinds, proposed by Jan Rokycana* survives; it is found in the Collection of Councils, Volume 12, page 1013 up to page 1159, in Bzovius under the year 1433, section 99, and in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume 3, part 2, page 1.

1433.

**GERARDO LANDRIANI**, Bishop of Lodi, flourished in the year 1433. At around that time, he was sent by the Council of Basel as a legate to Henry VI, King of England. In an assembly of the Estates of England <note>the Parliament</note>, he delivered an oration to the King; he requested with many pleas that, following the example of other kingdoms, ambassadors and bishops be sent from England to the Council, and that peace be granted to the afflicted state of French affairs. This *Oration* survives in the Collection of Councils, Volume 12, page 867.

He wrote a *Treatise for Pope Eugenius IV against the Council of Basel*, which Étienne Baluze first brought to light in the *Miscellanea*, Volume 3, page 303.

**HEINRICH KALTEISEN**, German by nationality, a native of Koblenz, commonly nicknamed *Cold Iron* <note>original: "Frigidum Ferrum", a literal Latin translation of his German surname Kalteisen</note>. Educated in his home city, he joined the Dominicans; having been distinguished with the laurel of a Doctorate at the University of Cologne, he took up the duty demanded of him by the Pope to preach the Crusade against the Bohemians. In the year 1433, at the Council of Basel, he disputed for three full days against Ulrich [of Znojmo], the patron of the Hussites. In the year 1440, he was created Master of the Sacred Palace and appointed Inquisitor of heretical depravity throughout all Germany, having previously been the Inquisitor of the faith among the people of Cologne. In the year 1452, on the third day before the Kalends of March <note>February 27th</note>, he was consecrated Archbishop of two provinces in Norway, Nidaros <note>modern Trondheim</note> and "Caesariensis," by Pope Nicholas V. He died in the year 1465, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October <note>September 26th</note>, and was buried in the Convent of Koblenz. His *Oration, in which he refuted the third Article of the Bohemians at the Council of Basel over three days—concerning the free preaching of the word of God—which had been proposed over two days by Ulrich, Priest of the Orphans* <note>the "Orphans" were a radical faction of the Hussites</note>, survives: Collection of Councils, Volume 12, page 1249 to page 1364; in Bzovius under the year 1433, section 254; and in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, Volume 4, part 2, page 1. His other writings, still unpublished, are reviewed by Trithemius on leaf 173 and Altamura on page 187.

**JUAN DE PALOMAR**, Archdeacon of Barcelona, Auditor of the Apostolic Palace, and Doctor of Canon Law at the University of Vienna. Sent ahead by Cardinal Giuliano [Cesarini] in the year 1431 to begin the Council of Basel, he thereafter conducted affairs with great distinction in the Synod. He became especially famous during the talks held in 1433 regarding the establishment of peace with the Hussites. For at the beginning of the year, sent as a legate by the Council to the Bohemians in Prague, he delivered frequent orations regarding peace before the Estates of the Kingdom; he persuaded them to send their own ambassadors and theologians to the Synod. Once the Hussites were brought to Basel and a disputation was entered into by both sides, he himself attacked the arguments of Peter Payne <note>an English Lollard who became a Hussite leader</note>, the last of all to speak for the Bohemians, in a three-day dissertation. Soon after, he returned to the Bohemians, who [left] Basel [fearing] treachery...

...had hastily departed out of fear, having been sent back, he established the long-desired peace of the Council and granted the Hussites <note>a reformist Christian movement in Bohemia following the teachings of Jan Hus</note> their demands. For it was agreed on both sides: that the Eucharist be given to the Laity under both kinds <note>original: "sub utrâq; specie"; meaning both the bread and the wine</note>; that enormous crimes be punished with sharp censure by the ecclesiastical authorities; that it be permitted for Priests to freely preach the word of God; and that priests should no longer involve themselves in the lordship of civil affairs. The *Oration* of Palemarius <note>Juan de Palomar</note>, in which he spent three days at the Council of Basel refuting the Bohemian article *regarding the civil lordship of the Clergy*—which had been proposed by the Englishman Peter Payne <note>original: "Petrus Rayne"</note>—can be found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 12, page 1364 up to 1432; in Bzovius under the year 1433, section 338; and in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, part 2, page 229. <margin>1434.</margin>
**ALFONSO TOSTADO**, Spanish by birth, was born in the town of Madrigal among the Vaccæi. In his early years, he devoted himself to the liberal arts at the University of Salamanca; later, having been admitted to the College of St. Bartholomew "at the Laurel" in Salamanca, he took holy orders in the Priesthood. Before he was even 22 years old, he had completed the entire course of literature, in all its breadth, with such a successful run that no subject of human knowledge seemed inaccessible to him. Later, supported by a triple public salary, he taught nearly all the liberal arts at the University of Salamanca. He flourished around the year 1434, at which time he is said to have participated in the Council of Basel. Eventually made Bishop of Avila <note>original: "Abulensis"</note>, he was employed by the King as a chaplain and counselor, and was created the Grand Referendary <note>a high-ranking judicial official</note> of the Spains. He died more full of glory than of days in the year of Christ 1454, not much older than forty, and was buried in the Church of Avila. He was honored by the Spaniards with an epitaph of this kind: *He is the wonder of the world, who examines everything that can be known.* <note>original: "Hic stupor est mundi, qui scibile discutit omne."</note> He was a man of truly stupendous memory, incredible diligence, and clearly rare judgment; he had not only penetrated the innermost shrines of Theology, but had also taken into his heart, so they say, the more hidden knowledge of foreign disciplines: Philosophy, Mathematics, Geography, History, and both Civil and Canon Law. Yet he was no less distinguished for piety and religion than for learning; he was so devoted to fasts, vigils, and prayers that the memory of the deceased is cherished with exceptional veneration among his countrymen. Regarding his diligence and tireless zeal for reading and writing, he was certainly the <term>polygraphōtatos</term> <note>Greek for "the most prolific writer"</note> not only of his own age, but of all centuries. In the space of 22 years, he wrote more than another person could carefully read through in almost an entire lifetime; in this, he is usually preferred even to the celebrated Didymus of Alexandria. He also matched Didymus in the admirable luck of his memory, so much so that he is said to have hardly ever forgotten anything he had read even once. Indeed, to say nothing of the immense volumes that are circulated in print, more than four hundred of his books are said to have perished in a shipwreck while they were being carried from Spain to Italy destined for the printing press. However, lest we think such great gifts were free from any flaw, some find in him a lack of chosen veneration toward the mystery of the Holy Trinity, many desire a greater reverence toward the Pope, and everyone wishes for more brilliance and elegance in his style. This is to say nothing of the accusations of Possevino, who complains that Tostado, carried away by too much zeal for defending his own opinions (which had been challenged by Cardinal Torquemada <note>original: "Turrecrematâ"</note> and noted by Pope Eugenius), had quite clearly attacked Papal authority itself.

*Fourteen Questions*, of which the first four represent almost the entire Holy Scripture in summary; the rest deal with the lineage and succession of the Gentile Gods. They were published printed in the Spanish idiom in *Antwerp, 1551.*
Furthermore, Tostado explained all the books of Holy Scripture with *Commentaries*; and he wrote countless *Short Works* on various subjects. As many of these as remain from being forgotten, Antonio Possevino presents their titles in the *Sacred Apparatus, Volume 1, page 47.*

<margin>1434.</margin>
**JOHN**, titular Patriarch of Antioch <note>he held the title honorarily, as the see was under non-Christian rule</note>, flourished in the year 1434. While stationed at Basel in that year, he composed a *Treatise on the Superiority of the Council over the Pope*; in which he specifically acts to support the superiority of the Council with arguments drawn from Canon Law. After he had publicly read his booklet in the Assembly of the Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>, he offered it to the fathers of the Council to be read. It is extant in the *Collection of Councils, Volume 12, page 912.*

---

<margin>1434.</margin>
**ISAIAH**, also himself a titular Patriarch of Jerusalem, was perhaps one of the Minorites <note>Franciscans</note> who at that time undertook missions in Eastern parts. To him was committed the care of reconciling the Armenian Church with the Roman Church, and this august title was conferred by the Pope. For neither the burden imposed on him, nor the submissive humility of the words with which he addresses the Pope, are characteristic of a true Patriarch. He flourished in the year 1434. Near the end of that year, in a very short Letter sent from the City of Constantinople, he promised that the union of the Armenians would be his concern. That *Letter is extant in the Collection of Councils, Volume 13, page 539.*

---

<margin>1436.</margin>
**MARK EUGENICUS**, a Greek by nation, first devoted his efforts to an open school for teaching boys and writing orations. Then, upon the departure of Emperor John [VIII Palaiologos] for the West, he was chosen on account of his rare learning and eloquence to be among the primary fighters for Greek dogmas against the Latins. He was granted the Archbishopric of Ephesus after the death of Metropolitan Joseph around the year 1436. In 1438, led by Emperor John to the Council of Ferrara, he held the first place among the Greeks after the Patriarch of Constantinople, both because of his fame for learning and because he took on the roles of the Patriarchs of Antioch and Jerusalem delegated to him. Near the beginning of the Council, he underwent the Emperor's most heavy wrath, because—requesting in a presented booklet that the word *Filioque* <note>the Latin phrase "and from the Son" added to the Nicene Creed, a major point of division between the Eastern and Western Churches</note> be removed from the Creed, and that *unleavened bread* <note>original: "azyma"</note> no longer be used in the Eucharist—he provoked <note>original: "exacerbavit", completed by the catchword "basset"</note> the mind of Pope Eugenius...

# The Synodal Century

<margin>
15TH CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...had [established]. By a common vote of everyone, the primary role was entrusted to Mark by the Greeks; his task was to draw up the line of battle, gather his forces, and both repel and return the blows of his adversaries. He carried out that assigned duty with an intrepid constancy of mind and immense fervor; acting as a sworn enemy to the Latins, he was driven by an unbridled zeal for the dignity of the Greek Church. In the first struggle, the sharp wit of Cardinal Julian [Cesarini], the leader of the Latins, fell far below the expectations people had of him; he was unaccustomed to the formal methods of disputation used in the Western Schools, and he lacked the truth of the cause he was pleading (for they were debating the "Procession of the Holy Spirit" <note>The *Filioque* controversy regarding whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, or from the Father and the Son</note>). But once Mark found Bessarion as his supporter, he spoke with such great flow of speech and such sharp logic in argument that he moved everyone to wonder. Meanwhile, because of his immoderate heat of spirit, the Latins—whom he did not hesitate to call Heretics—spread a false rumor among the common people that he was going mad. Regarding Bessarion himself, his companion in the work, Mark branded him with the title of "Evil Spirit" <note>original: "Cacodæmonis"</note>. As matters looked toward their conclusion, and with the Greek Bishops obeying the Pope and others being ordered by Emperor [John] Palaeologus to sign the decrees, Mark alone of all constantly refused; nor could he be led by any threats or promises to betray the liberty of the Greek Church. Therefore, after the council was dissolved and he returned to Constantinople, he was received by the people with almost divine honors. He continued to condemn the Latins in his writings, ensuring that the union, established with such great preparation and noise, fell away to nothing.

It survives in Greek and Latin along with the *Response* of Joseph of Methone, *Councils*, Volume 13, page 677.

1436.
</margin>
**BESSARION**, Greek by birth, a native of Trebizond, and a monk of the Order of Saint Basil. Around the year 1436, having been led out from his monastery after twenty-one years spent there, he was appointed Archbishop of Nicaea for the same reason for which Mark Eugenicus was chosen. In the year 1438, having set out for the Councils of Ferrara and Florence, he found a wide field for displaying his eloquence and learning. Given as a companion to Mark in the disputations, he conducted himself excellently; he sharply dissolved the arguments of the Latins, and [initially] defended the cause of the Greeks. Satisfied with the fame he acquired from that point (for the man sought nothing else), he subsequently stepped more softly toward the Latins; so that little by little he leaned toward their side and sought the favor of the Pope...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Bessarion of Nicaea, following the description of his shifting allegiances during the Council of Florence (1438–1439). While the previous page likely detailed his early cooperation with the anti-Latin party led by Mark of Ephesus, this page records his complete transition to the Roman Catholic cause and his subsequent career as a Prince of the Church and a humanist patron.</meta>

# The Synodal Century

<margin>
15TH CENTURY
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...[Bessarion's true leanings] were revealed by clear signs; he was sharply rebuked by Mark [of Ephesus] on that account and called a "Spurious" person and a traitor to his native Church. Near the end of the Council, having dropped the veil, he completely defected to the Latins; he vigorously promoted their cause and persuaded the dying Joseph, Patriarch of Constantinople, to confirm the definitions of the Council with his signature. After the Council was dissolved, having returned to Greece, he was designated Patriarch of Constantinople by Emperor John and the followers of the Latins. However, since the Greeks—at least those who had not "boiled away" their faith <note>original: "fidem non decoxerant," meaning those who had not compromised or bankrupted their religious integrity</note> at Florence—clung tenaciously to their ancestral religion and detested the friends of the Latins worse than a dog or a snake, he found it necessary to resign the Patriarchal dignity. 

Therefore, withdrawing to Italy, he was heaped with both riches and honors by Pope Eugenius and was co-opted into the College of Cardinals. By Nicholas V, the successor of Eugenius, he was appointed Bishop of Tusculum and Legate of Bologna; he administered that province with such great prudence for five years that he was designated as a perpetual Patron and Protector by both the Dominican and Franciscan orders. After the death of Nicholas in the year 1455, he was very nearly elected Supreme Pontiff by the Cardinals. After the year 1458, he was the advocate for Pope Pius II to undertake a war against the Turks; and having fulfilled a legation to Emperor Frederick, the princes of Germany, and the Republic of Venice, he incited everyone with most fervent prayers to the holy war. To the Germans, he "sang to the deaf" <note>an idiom meaning his pleas were ignored</note>, but to the Venetians, he added such spirit with his eloquent speech that they conscripted an army that was not to be despised. However, the sudden death of Pius scattered such great preparations for war. 

Around the year 1464, he was appointed by Pope Paul to the place of the deceased Cardinal Isidore, the titular Patriarch of Constantinople. After the death of Paul in the year 1471, he was sought for the Papacy by the votes of all, but he lost the dignity by a certain fatal chance. Sent as a legate to France by Pope Sixtus, upon his return he fell ill in Turin and met his death in Ravenna in the year 1472, at the age of 77. He was buried in Rome in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles. 

<margin>* Hist. l. 6.</margin>
He was a man who, in the judgment of Chalcocondyles <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles (c. 1430–1470), a Greek historian who chronicled the fall of the Byzantine Empire</note>, was "by far the most fortunate of the Greeks in natural intelligence, and in those things which are judged the most excellent, and in wisdom—both Greek and Roman—he was second to none" <note>original Greek: ξυνέσει τε τῆ ἀπὸ φύσεως... οὐδενὸς δεύτερος</note>. Indeed, he was not only most highly refined in every kind of literature but also the greatest patron of men of letters; so much so that his household seemed a "workshop of the liberal arts." He himself, having transported Greek books to Italy at great expense, established a most wealthy library in Venice; over which he placed Marcantonio Sabellico, summoned from Rome with a handsome salary; and at his death, he gave the library as a gift to the Republic of Venice.

## GEORGIUS SCHOLARIUS
A Greek by nation, "esteemed for wisdom among the Greeks" <note>original Greek: καὶ παρ’ Ἕλλησι τοῦ ἐν σοφίαν εὐδοκιμῶν</note>, as Chalcocondylas says \*; the most learned among the Greeks, the greatest follower and friend of Mark of Ephesus, and a most virulent enemy of the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>, he flourished in the year 1438. At last, embracing the monastic life and setting aside the name George, he assumed the name Gennadius and took up the leadership of a certain monastery on Mount Athos. Thus far, the facts are clear. In the remaining details, "the water is stuck" <note>original Latin idiom: "hæret aqua," meaning the historical record becomes murky or difficult to follow</note>. For at the same time in the East there flourished a certain Georgius Scholarius who, held as a close associate by Emperor John [VIII Palaeologus], attended the Council of Florence, and finally, after the capture of Constantinople, was raised to the Patriarchal throne of Constantinople while still a layman. After resigning this post five years later, he retired to a monastery under the name Gennadius and wrote many things in favor of the Latins. Whether this man was one and the same as the former, or what roles should be assigned to each, is not clear.

<margin>
* Preface to Volume 5 of the Council of Florence.
</margin>
Matthæus Caryophilus, Bishop of Iconium \*, is of the opinion that there were two Scholarii: one a friend of the Latins who attended the Council of Florence and died as a layman before the capture of Constantinople; the other an enemy of the same, who held the Patriarchate after the city was captured. However, that opinion is to be condemned on many grounds.

<margin>
† On the Agreement, book 3, chapters 5, 6; and Discourse on the Georges, p. 394.
</margin>
Leo Allatius † attacks that view at length and puts forward a version he constructed himself: namely, that George the friend of Mark [of Ephesus] was prevented by illness from attending the Council, and having died before the city was captured, cherished the cause of the Greeks to his very last breath; while George the Patriarch, by contrast, attended the Council and always agreed with the Latins. Allatius certainly piles up many arguments, which—if I may say so with all due respect to such a great man—by no means place the matter beyond all controversy. Caryophilus is indeed hallucinating; but what if we say only a single Scholarius flourished in that century, who, after first constantly defending his native Church, later defected to the Latins and ascended the Patriarchal throne?

<margin>
* History, book 2, chapter 19.
† Ecclesiastical History.
</margin>
Certainly, Phranza \* (a contemporary writer and very well-versed in the affairs of the Greek state, whose authority alone ought to outweigh a thousand arguments), Manuel Malaxus in his *Civil History of Constantinople* †, and others affirm this in plain words; to say nothing of the Latin writers. Indeed, those who know the "shifty" <note>original: "versipelle," meaning skin-changing or versatile</note> character of the Greeks are not so surprised that Scholarius changed his mind. Furthermore, Phranza and Rhacendyta (in Plusiadenus) record—to say nothing of Chalcocondylas for the moment—that whoever that Scholarius was who attended the Council of Florence, he was so far from joining the Latins that, as a rival to Mark of Ephesus, he most steadfastly refused to sign the decree. Be that as it may, we grant this much to the authority of the most learned Allatius and to at least some plausibility in his arguments: we shall "bisect" Scholarius <note>Treat him as two separate historical figures</note> and present the Patriarch in his own place below. Scholarius, the adversary of the Latins, wrote a *Syntagma* <note>A systematic collection or treatise</note> called the *Refuge of the Orthodox* <note>original Greek: Ὀρθοδόξος καταφύγιον</note> against the Synod of Florence, divided into eight parts or books. It was published in Greek in *London* in quarto, but without a printed date. Allatius cites several of his letters to Notaras (the Grand Duke and son-in-law of the Emperor) in manuscript, and provides fragments from them in *On the Agreement, book 3, chapter 5, section 8; Discourse on the Georges, pp. 397, 398;* and shows the beginnings of each on *p. 409.* The same author records that he read in manuscript an Oration *On the vain, irrational, and disorderly attempted innovation regarding the faith, by God's permission.*

# The Synodal Century

<margin>
15TH CENTURY
from the Year 1400. 1438.
</margin>

## JOANNES EUGENICUS
The <term>Nomophylax (Guardian of the Laws)</term> of the Great Patriarchal Church of Constantinople and the biological brother of Mark of Ephesus. He provided supporting aid to his brother in attacking the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note> while present at the Council of Florence in the year 1438. When he observed the Roman Pontiff <note>Pope Eugenius IV</note> weaving delays from day to day, and because he despised the somewhat timid spirit of his Emperor <note>John VIII Palaeologus</note>, he attempted to flee, drawing his brother Mark into the plan. However, he was brought back from his flight and paid for his attempted deed with his own shame. He wrote a *Refutation against the Synod of Florence* <note>original: "Antirrheticum adversùs Synodum Florentinam"</note>; certain fragments of which, in Greek and Latin, are presented by Leo Allatius in his book *On Purgatory*, pages 61, 220, 241, and 265.

---

<margin>1438.</margin>
## ISIDORE
Called "the Russian" <note>original: "Ruthenus"</note> from his Episcopal see, though Greek by race and, as it seems, a native of Thessalonica. He was a monk of the Order of Saint Basil and Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Demetrius in Constantinople. Around the year 1435, he was sent as an envoy by Emperor John to the Council of Basel along with Demetrius Palaeologus, the Great Duke. He agreed that his Emperor and the Greek bishops would attend the Council (rejecting Pope Eugenius), provided that the Fathers themselves kept the agreements; as a token of union, he celebrated the Mass in Basel. Shortly after his return, he was created Metropolitan of Kiev and Patriarch of all Russia. In the year 1438, acting as the representative for Patriarch Dorotheus of Antioch alongside Mark of Ephesus, he took part in the Council of Florence. For some time, he argued learnedly on behalf of the Greeks against the Latins. Afterward, however, he shifted his stance and went over to the Latin side heart and soul <note>original: "manibus pedibusque," literally "with hands and feet"</note>. This went so far that toward the end of the Council, having found a follower in Bessarion, he sharply (though in vain) contended that an excommunication should be struck against Mark of Ephesus by the Council for refusing to sign the decree. Therefore, Gemistus and Amyrutzius are mistaken in claiming that Isidore never consented to the decrees of the Synod of Florence. Once the Council was dissolved, he remained in Italy; and in the year 1439, he was declared a Cardinal-Priest by Pope Eugenius with the title of Saints Peter and Marcellinus. Returning soon to Russia, he was captured by the Russians, who detested the union entered into with the Roman Church. He was stripped of his property and cast into prison, but he finally escaped by flight with great difficulty. Later, he was honored with the titular Patriarchate of Constantinople by Nicholas V and sent as an envoy to the East. He was present at the fall of the most wretched Royal City <note>Constantinople</note> in the year 1453. Escaping from the hands of the Turks by a certain cleverness, he returned to Italy. Appointed Bishop of Sabina and Dean of the College of Cardinals, he finally died in Rome in the year 1463. He wrote a *Lamentable Letter on the Capture of Constantinople by the Turks*, sent from Pera in the year 1453 (not 1452, which is a numerical error); this is found among the *Turkish Letters* edited by Reusner, book 4, page 104.

---

<margin>1438.</margin>
<margin>* In Allatius, regarding the sons of Gemistus. On Agreement, book 3, chapter 3, section 6.</margin>
<margin>† In the place cited.</margin>
## GEORGIUS GEMISTUS
Surnamed **PLETHO** because of his love for Plato, as some believe. A native of Constantinople, though he spent most of his life in the Peloponnese, he was a most noble philosopher, frequently called "the wise" <note>original Greek: ὁ σοφὸς</note> by Sguropulus. "Greece has produced no one like him" <gloss>original Greek: οὐχ ἔφυσε ἡ Ἑλλάς</gloss> since the time of Plato and Aristotle—so much so that the soul of Plato seemed to have migrated into the body of Gemistus, as Cardinal Bessarion says in a letter \* to Demetrius and Andronicus, the sons of Gemistus. He was a sharp adversary of the Latins, to the point that when questioned by the Emperor around the year 1426 about his proposal to attend a Western Council, he entirely disapproved of it, prophesying that the matter would result in the disgrace and slavery of the Greek Church. Nevertheless, in 1438, he was brought to the Council of Florence by the Greeks so they might have someone to oppose the scholastic subtleties of the Latins. Indeed, he did not disappoint the high opinion held of him: he dissolved the knotty arguments of the Latins with singular sharpness and pleaded the cause of the Greeks with a balance of great verbal strength and eloquence. He acted with such zeal and invincible constancy of spirit that, setting aside the favor of the Emperor and the Latins, he never abandoned the cause he had undertaken, nor did he relax his fervor for debating until the very end of the Council. He died a centenarian upon returning to Greece, though it is not clear in which year. "That man was a great glory to all Greece," <gloss>original Greek: Μέγα κλέος Ἑλλάδι πάσῃ γέγονεν ἐκεῖνος ἀνήρ</gloss> says Bessarion †, "he will be a great ornament to her in the time to come." <gloss>original Greek: μέγας αὐτῇ κόσμος εἰς τὸν ἔπειτα χρόνον ἔσεῖται</gloss>. That man was a great glory to Greece: he will be a great ornament to her for posterity. He was greatly devoted to ancient philosophy, especially the Platonic, and held it in the highest...

15TH CENTURY
The Year 1400.
* Comparison of Plato & Aristotle, final chapter.

...he always cultivated with zeal, and he published many writings on its more hidden mysteries. Taking this opportunity, but moved more by envy of his reputation, George of Trebizond <note>A rival scholar and proponent of Aristotelianism</note> falsely accused him of having finally deserted the Christian faith for utter Paganism, and of offering prayers to the Sun in his extreme old age. However, George does not dare to deny Pletho's reputation for learning; he freely acknowledges that he was *not inferior in knowledge to Plato, though lesser in eloquence.*

*A Demonstration on the Procession of the Holy Spirit, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone* <note>original: "De Processione Spiritûs S. Demonstratio, Sp. S. ex Patre solo procedere"</note>, lest any absurdity follow from the contrary; in which he busies himself with demonstrating the opinion of the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox view, which rejects the "Filioque" clause added by the Western Church</note> using mostly philosophical arguments.

<margin>

</margin>
Another more extensive work on the same subject, and more abundant in arguments. Leo Allatius <note>A 17th-century scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note> reports in his book *On Consent* (Book 3, Chapter 3, Section 6) that both manuscripts were seen by him. There is also a manuscript held in the Library of Augsburg.

*Two Books on the deeds of the Greeks after the battle of Mantinea.* <note>original: "Libri ii. de gestis Græcorum post pugnam ad Mantineam"</note> These appeared in Latin from the version by Marc Antonio Antimaco in Basel, 1540; and in Greek at the end of Xenophon’s works in Venice, 1503, from the press of Aldus, and in Basel, 1557.

*On the Difference between the Philosophy of Aristotle and Plato.* Greek, Paris, 1541; Latin, Basel, 1574.

*Commentaries on the Oracles of Zoroaster.* <note>Zoroaster was the ancient Persian prophet; these 'oracles' were a collection of mystical Greek verses attributed to him</note> Greek and Latin, Paris, 1538, 1599. Leo Allatius, in his discourse on the various men named George and their writings (p. 385), lists a long series of unpublished works—primarily historical, rhetorical, and philosophical—which the curious reader may seek from him.

<margin>
Index of MSS. in the Library of Augsburg, p. 85, 90.
</margin>
A manuscript of his treatise *On Fate* exists in the Library of Augsburg. I have also seen a manuscript of his *Chorographic Description of Thessaly* <note>A detailed geographic mapping or description of the region</note> (which escaped Allatius's notice) in our Royal Library.

<margin>1438.</margin>
**SYLVESTER SGUROPULUS**, or as he signs himself in the Acts of the Council, *Syropoulos*, a Greek by birth, a Deacon of Constantinople, <term>Grand Ecclesiarch (Chief Overseer of the Church)</term>, and <term>Dicaeophylax (Guardian of the Laws)</term>. He was one of the five <term>Crucigeri (Cross-bearers)</term> of the Patriarch of Constantinople; these were men selected from all of Greece to be the Patriarch's more sacred advisors in ecclesiastical matters. They wore the figure of a cross fixed to their garments as a mark of honorary distinction. He flourished in the year 1438, when he followed his Patriarch to the Councils of Ferrara and Florence. He was either summoned to or involved himself in every transaction there. He was a supreme enemy of the Latins and a most fierce champion of Greek liberty. However, although he was chosen as one of the six champions to contend for Greek dogmas against the Latins, he refused to undergo the arduous task and obtained a disgraceful exemption from the number of disputants. Nevertheless, with such stubborn zeal, he sustained the wavering cause of his Church on every given occasion, such that he experienced the anger of the Emperor, the Patriarch, and Bessarion <note>A pro-union Greek cardinal</note>. At the conclusion of the Council, when ordered to sign the decree of union, he wove together innumerable delays and hesitated for a long time; eventually, terrified by the Emperor’s threats, he complied, though he first protested that he was forced by violence and signed against his will. Having returned home, when he realized he was hated by everyone on account of his signature at Florence, he resigned his office and, renouncing ecclesiastical business, turned to recording the events of the Council in writing. There exists his *History of the False Union between the Greeks and the Latins, or of the Council of Florence*, brought to light and edited with notes in Greek and Latin by the very learned Robert Creyghton (later Bishop of Bath and Wells), published at The Hague, 1660.

She was descended from the noble Vigri family; her father was John of Ferrara and her mother Benevenuta of Bologna. Having been admitted into the Order of Saint Clare, where she made her profession at Ferrara, she was transferred to Bologna so that she might lead the newly built...

# JUAN DE TORQUEMADA
<note>Latin: Joannes de Turrecremata. Not to be confused with his nephew, the Inquisitor General Tomás de Torquemada.</note>

Spanish by birth, taking his name from his native town called Torquemada in the common tongue, in the Diocese of Palencia; a monk of the Dominican Order in the Convent of St. Paul in Valladolid. Sent to the University of Paris, he earned the laurels of Theology and Canon Law, and taught both sciences for several years. Returning to Spain, he was placed in charge of the Monasteries of St. Paul in Valladolid and St. Peter in Toledo. Around the year 1431, he was summoned to the Roman Court by Pope Eugenius and granted the Mastership of the Sacred Palace, then sent to the Council of Basel: where he fought most strongly against the Hussites <note>A pre-Protestant Christian movement in Bohemia</note> and strenuously defended the interests of the Pope; he was also appointed by the Council to conduct a severe examination of the Revelations of St. Bridget. Around the year 1437, he was again sent as a legate to the people at Basel by the Pope; and soon recalled to the Council of Florence, he disputed learnedly against Mark of Ephesus. In 1439, he was created a Cardinal Priest with the title of St. Sixtus by Eugenius; and sent to France, he presided over the Synod of Bourges. He undertook many embassies to assert the authority of the Roman See; in all of which, if he did not achieve his desire, he at least gained fame, employing the highest prudence and learning, and distinguished by a rare holiness of life. In 1450, elevated to the Bishopric of Ourense in Galicia, he soon resigned it, being transferred by Pope Nicholas to Albano in Italy. In 1464, by the favor of Pius II, he exchanged the see of Albano for that of Sabina; and was distinguished by the Pope with the illustrious title of Defender and Protector of the Faith. He died an octogenarian in the year 1468, on September 26th. He was buried in Rome in the Monastery of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, which he himself had built during his life and had enriched with a hundred thousand gold coins at his death.

# JOHN LYDGATE

**JOHN LYDGATE**, English by birth, from the county of Suffolk, a Monk of the Benedictine Order in the Monastery of Bury [St. Edmunds]. After traveling through the Universities of foreign lands as well as those of his own country, he taught the humanities in his own monastery and devoted his efforts to instructing the children of the nobility. The prince of poets of his time in England, he composed many poems in his native tongue, and by translating many from the French and Italian languages, he acquired the greatest fame among his countrymen. His talent was exercised in various types of meters, and by paying close attention to the elegance of speech, he significantly refined the uncultivated English language, which formerly used to labor under barbarism. He flourished at the age of sixty in the year 1440. Having finally died at Bury, he was buried among his fellow monks.

His English books include: 9 Books on the *Falls of Illustrious Men* <note>original: "Casibus virorum illustrium"</note> from Adam up to John, King of France (who was captured by the English at Poitiers), or to the year of Christ 1364; these he translated from Giovanni Boccaccio and others, London 1527, 1554. The *Story of the Theban War* written in English verse, London, at the end of Chaucer’s Works, 1687, folio. A short poem on *Good Counsel*, in the same place, p. 569. Various minor works of his composed in English verse are held in the Lambeth Library <note>The historic library of the Archbishop of Canterbury</note>, namely: *How the Mass should be heard*, *Litanies*, *Good Counsel*, and a *Prayer to the Virgin*. Another prayer to God and the *Life of the Blessed Virgin Mary* in four books. *The Life of Saint Edmund, King and Martyr*, in English verse, a manuscript in the possession of the Most Reverend Primate, the Archbishop of Canterbury. *The Book of the Dance of Death* <note>original: "de saltu Machabræ," referring to the Danse Macabre</note>, London 1554. *The Life and Deeds of Hector*, London 1614. A metrical book in praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary; and several others printed in English types. He also wrote many things in Latin: historical, theological, and moral works. John Bale provides a list of all his minor works in both languages in his *Summary of British Writers* <note>Cent. 8, ch. 7</note>, as does the biographer John Pits <note>p. 632</note>.
