<margin>1440.</margin>

# GEORGE OF TREBIZOND

**GEORGE OF TREBIZOND**, of that origin indeed <note>His family was from Trebizond on the Black Sea</note>, but born on the island of Crete in the year 1396. After drinking in an excellent knowledge of literature at home, he set out for Rome; and having opened a school, he taught the knowledge of the Greek language and the liberal arts with the highest praise. Drawn by the fame of his singular learning, Pope Eugenius IV summoned him to the Court and appointed him as a Secretary. He flourished in the year 1440. After the death of Eugenius, King Alfonso invited him to Naples and honored him with a very generous salary. In the year 1465, while sailing from Crete to Constantinople, he heard from Byzantine sailors the account of the martyrdom of Andrew of Chios, who had recently been killed by the Turks for his confession of the Christian faith; he committed this to writing two years later upon returning to Rome.

As he reached old age, he was afflicted by a severe illness; after he recovered, he is said to have so forgotten all literature that he could neither write nor read. However, others write that this happened to him from deep mental anguish. For when he had offered the monuments of his genius—worked upon with the vigils of many years—to the Pope, thinking he would receive some grand reward, he received instead a wretched payment of only one hundred ducats. Consumed, therefore, by the pain of frustrated hope and indignation at the Pope's greed <note>literally "Papal avarice"</note>, Trebizond is said thereafter to have raved and to have thrown his money into the channel of the Tiber, adding the exclamation: *“Let the labors perish, and let the ungrateful money perish too!”* He died at the age of ninety in the year 1486. He left a son, Andreas Trapezuntius, who wrote a defense of his father against the scholar Theodore Gaza.

## GREGORY MELISSENUS, called *Mammas*, a Greek
monk-priest <note>original: "Hieromonachus"</note>, Penitentiary of the Church of Constantinople, and confessor to Emperor John. In the year 1438, he set out for the Council of Florence, acting on behalf of the Patriarch of Alexandria. At first, indeed, he so abhorred the Latins that he would not even pray to Christ the Lord in their churches. But afterward, corrupted by the gold of the Pope—which he himself did not conceal \*—he emerged as the greatest architect for forging the Union; he was announced as the *Protosyncellus* and *Primicerius* <note>These were high-ranking administrative titles in the Byzantine church hierarchy.</note> by the Emperor, with whom he enjoyed burning favor in the Council. In the year 1440, after the deposition of Metrophanes, the Patriarch of Constantinople—who had been substituted for Joseph the preceding year but had been anathematized by the Eastern Patriarchs in a gathered Synod for his subscription at Florence—Gregory was elevated to the patriarchal throne: after he had spent thirty years in the monastic life.

<margin>|| Robert Creyghton, Preface to Syropoulos.</margin>
<margin>* History, book 3.</margin>
It does not escape me that a man of no small learning || contends that Metrophanes was not moved from his seat before the city was captured, and that Gregory never obtained the Patriarchate. However, the authority of Phranzes \* <note>George Sphrantzes, a major Byzantine historian of the period.</note> prevails over a thousand conjectures in this matter; he records both the deposition of Metrophanes and the promotion of Gregory in clear words. Phranzes adds that after some years Gregory abdicated the patriarchate and died at Constantinople in the year 1451 like an exile. What drove him to this is not so clear. There are those who claim he sought Rome and eventually became famous there for miracles after his burial. Indeed, the letter of Pope Nicholas to Emperor Constantine suggests that Gregory was driven from the Patriarchate not so much by choice as by the Greeks, as a traitor to the Church at the Council of Florence; in it, the Pope instructs the petitioner to recall Gregory to his see, to ensure the people show him the reverence due to Pontifical authority, and not to permit him to be mocked as if he were an outcast priest. There exist writings by Gregory: An *Apology for the Synod of Florence* <note>original: "Apologia pro Synodo Florentinâ"</note> against the encyclical letter of Mark of Ephesus, and a *Refutation* of the same, in Greek and Latin, *Collection of Councils, Volume 13, p. 739*. An *Oration* or *Letter to Alexios Komnenos*, Emperor of Trebizond, *on the Procession of the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "de Processione Sp. S."</note> demonstrating that nothing was innovated by that addition to the Creed, "AND FROM THE SON" <note>The *Filioque* clause, a major point of theological dispute between East and West.</note>: in Greek and Latin in Leo Allatius’s *Orthodox Greece, Volume 1, p. 419*. Gregory mentions that he wrote other short works for the defense of the Synod of Florence, which have not yet come to light.

## THOMAS WALSINGHAM, an Englishman by nation, from the district of
Norfolk, born in a town of the same name not without fame, a monk of the Benedictine Order in the Monastery of St. Albans, where he held the office of Precentor. He flourished in the year 1440. He wrote two *Histories of English Affairs*, one shorter and the other more prolific. The former, taking its beginning from the year 1273, is carried forward until the year 1422. The latter, titled *The Standard of Normandy* <note>original: "Hypodigma Neustriæ"</note>, narrates the deeds in order from the Norman invasion in the year 1066 until the fifth year of King Henry V, the year of Christ 1417. Both were published by the famous Camden among the *Norman-English Writers*, London, 1574, folio; reprinted at Frankfurt, 1602, folio. Besides these, Walsingham wrote an *Addition to the Universal Chronicle of Ranulph Higden* <note>original: "Auctuarium Polychronici Ranulphi Higdeni"</note>;

<margin>* Century 7, Chapter 88.</margin>
which (if Bale \* is to be believed) contains the rarest *Histories*, and perhaps from no other source. That continuation takes its beginning from the year 1342 and proceeds to the year 1417. I have seen a single manuscript copy of it in the library of Gonville and Caius College, which however is mutilated at the end and does not progress beyond the year 1398. Finally, he is said to have committed to writing the *Deeds of Henry V, King of England*, in whose times he lived.

# JOHN OF CAPISTRANO, Italian by nationality, born in Abruzzo near L'Aquila <note>original: "Aquilam Marforum"</note>, of the noble Chiolorum family, was born in the year 1385.

He was a disciple and close associate of Bernardino of Siena; a member of the Franciscan Friars of the Regular Observance in the Florentine Convent, and twice served as the Vicar General of his Order in the "Cismontane" <note>This refers to the branches of the Franciscan order located on the "near side" of the Alps (Italy).</note> regions. He gained a very great reputation for his preaching and the distinguished holiness of his life, so much so that he was held in the highest favor by four Popes: Martin V, Eugenius IV, Nicholas V, and Calixtus III. He was at the height of his fame in the year 1440. As an Inquisitor of the faith and a Legate of the Apostolic See—sent first to Italy and then to Germany—he served the Papal cause with great distinction. Wandering through cities and towns like a traveling preacher <note>original: "agyrtæ," a term for a wandering beggar or street-preacher.</note>, he delivered sermons to the common people in marketplaces and at crossroads; by these, he persuaded many to take up the sacred military service <note>A reference to the Crusades.</note> against the enemies of the Roman See. Among the Germans and other foreign nations who were ignorant of the Italian language, he is said to have charmed the minds of his listeners in marvelous ways by using wild gestures in place of words. Having gathered an army of Crusaders (as they are called), he acted as their leader and set out to destroy heretics with fire and sword. In Campania, he burned eighty-six small towns belonging to the Fratricelli <note>A radical splinter group of Franciscans who were declared heretics for their extreme views on poverty.</note>. Then, passing into Germany, he waged a heavy war against the Hussites, and thanks to the unrestrained zeal of his followers, he generally carried the day. After the Bohemians were defeated, he then devoted his efforts to the common good of the Christian state. Enlisting more than one hundred thousand Crusaders, he brought relief in the year 1456 to Belgrade <note>original: "Tauruno," the Roman name for the area around modern Belgrade.</note>, a most fortified Hungarian city that was being besieged by Mehmed II, the Emperor of the Turks. There, he not only encouraged the soldiers with words and speeches, but he himself, carrying the Cross like a standard before the Christians, acted most bravely in the front line and inflicted a notable slaughter upon the Turks. He died at Villach <note>original: "Willaci"</note> in the Diocese of Pécs <note>original: "Quinqueecclesiensi"</note> on the 3rd of October in the year 1456, at the age of 71. He was added to the number of the Blessed by Gregory XV.

...he did not hesitate to criticize those devoted to foolish subtleties with a sharp pen. By this kind of freedom, he earned himself countless enemies, particularly <term>Poggio Bracciolini</term> <note>A famous Italian humanist known for rediscovering lost classical Latin manuscripts.</note>, with whom he engaged in a deadly war of writings. Leaving Rome either of his own accord or by the Pope's command around the year 1443, he betook himself to <term>Alfonso V, King of Aragon</term>, to whom he taught the elements of grammar. Yet, having found such a great patron, he could scarcely avoid being handed over to the Inquisitors as a defendant. Since he did not fear to condemn many Roman traditions as errors, he was called to the flames by the courtiers. Alfonso spared <unclear>Valla</unclear> from that punishment; however, he was forced to atone for his crime by being beaten with rods in the public square. Having returned again to Rome, and with the help of certain friends, he reconciled with the Pope. He was granted the power to teach and was further endowed with a generous salary. He died in the year 1465, on the Calends of August <note>August 1st</note>, at the age of 50. Regarding such a great critic,

<margin>* Book 7, Epistle 3.</margin>
<term>Erasmus</term> says: *“the most critical.”* <note>original Greek: "ὁ κριτικώτατος"</note> *“And who,”* he says, *“is of such a narrow mind, or confined by such great constraints of envy, that they would not praise Valla both magnificently and to the highest degree? With such great industry, such great zeal, and such great toil, he refuted the ignorance of others, rescued letters that were nearly buried from destruction, and restored Italy to its ancient splendor of eloquence. He even provided this service to the learned: that hereafter they might speak more circumspectly.”*

FLAVIUS BLONDUS <note>Also known as Biondo Flavio (1388–1463), a pioneering Renaissance humanist and historian often called the father of archaeology.</note>, or more correctly with the order reversed, *Blondus Flavius*, was Italian by birth, from the city of Forlì, and born in the year 1388. He devoted a successful effort to the study of the humanities, as was the fashion for the talents of Italians in that age. Having set out for Rome, he was summoned to the Papal court through the favor of certain Cardinals, and was appointed as a secretary to <term>Eugenius IV</term> <note>Pope from 1431 to 1447, known for the Council of Florence.</note>. Soon after, he was sent as an ambassador to the Venetians alongside the Bishop of Recanati. He flourished in the year 1440, serving as Secretary to the succeeding Popes up until <term>Pius II</term>. Under Pius II, he died at Rome in great poverty—as was fitting for a philosopher—on June 4th, 1463, at the age of 75. He left behind five sons of distinguished literary reputation, whom he had fathered with Margania, a woman of noble Roman blood. Joannes Gobelinus* <note>The pseudonym often used for the *Commentaries* of Pope Pius II.</note> offers the following judgment of him:

<margin>* Commentaries of Pope Pius II, Book 2.</margin>
> *Blondus was far removed from ancient eloquence; nor did he examine what he wrote with sufficient diligence: he was more concerned with how much he wrote rather than how true it was.*

### W R I T I N G S .

**T**hree Decades of Histories <note>original: *Historiarum Decades iii.*</note> (though the last of these contains eleven books), concerning events in the West from the decline of the Roman Empire until his own time, or from the year of Christ 410 to the year 1440. Pope Pius II reduced this history into an abridgment—an act that reflects no small praise upon Blondus. It was published separately along with the Abridgment of Pius at *Venice*, 1484, in folio.

*Three Books of Rome Restored* <note>original: *Romæ instauratæ libri iii.*</note>, dedicated to Pope Eugenius; in which he describes what Rome was like in his own time, restored after frequent devastations.

*Eight Books of Italy Illustrated* <note>original: *Italiæ illustratæ libri viii.*</note>, in which he commemorates the cities and regions of Italy (divided into eighteen provinces) and the most notable events of the later age.

*A Book on the Origin and Deeds of the Venetians* <note>original: *De Venetorum origine & gestis liber*</note>, from the laying of the foundations of the Republic until the capture of Ptolemais by the Saracens, or from the year of Christ 456 to 1291.

*Ten Books of Rome Triumphant* <note>original: *Romæ triumphantis libri x.*</note>, in which he treats the affairs of the ancient Romans: their religion, administration of the Republic, military service, customs, and triumphs.

The Complete Works of Blondus were published at *Basel*, 1559, in folio.

AMBROSIUS CAMALDULENSIS <note>Ambrogio Traversari (1386–1439), a monk and theologian who was a key figure in the attempted union of the Greek and Latin churches.</note>, Italian by birth, was from the town of Portico di Romagna, located not far from Florence. When he was fourteen years old, he was initiated into the Order of the <term>Camaldolese Monks</term> <note>A reformed branch of the Benedictines who live as hermits.</note>, who inhabited a certain hermitage among the Apennine mountains. He was a man most learned for the standards of his century, and—what few achieved in that age—skilled in both languages <note>meaning Latin and Greek</note>. He studied Greek under <term>Manuel Chrysoloras</term> <note>A pioneer in the introduction of Greek literature to Western Europe.</note> while he was teaching in Venice. He cultivated the knowledge of Greek letters with such great zeal that he was considered by Sguropulus† <note>Sylvester Syropoulos, a Greek historian of the Council of Florence.</note> to be "more knowledgeable in Greek education than all other Latins" <note>original Greek: "τῆς ἑλληνικῆς παιδείας εἰδημονέστερος"</note>. <margin>† History of the Council of Florence, Section 10, chapter 2.</margin> Having eventually been appointed Abbot General of his Order, he flourished in the year 1440. He was especially dear to the Supreme Pontiffs Eugenius IV and Nicholas V; he was often designated by them for the Cardinal's purple, but he missed out on that dignity either by his own choice or by some twist of fate. Sent as a legate by Eugenius to the <term>Council of Basel</term>, he defended the Pope's interests excellently. He worked no less diligently at the Councils of Ferrara and Florence, in which he argued sharply against the dogmas of the Greeks, and more than once delivered orations in Greek before the Emperor and the Greek Bishops. Sent from the Council of Ferrara to Florence by Eugenius, he obtained permission from the Florentine Republic to transfer the Council there. Furthermore, he was placed in charge of dispensing Papal alms, doling out small coins piece by piece to the starving Greeks at the Council. When a concord was finally struck between the Greeks and Latins, it was granted to the esteemed learning of Ambrose to compose the formula for entering the Union. <margin>|| Section 7, chapter 1.</margin> Sguropulus|| described him as: "A versatile and crafty man, a great pretender of piety, not uninitiated in the study of Greek discourse, and most faithful to the Pope" <note>original Greek: "ἀνὴρ ποικίλος τε καὶ πανουργος... τὰ δὲ πλεῖον εὐλαβείας, οὐκ ἀμύητος δὲ τῆς τῶν ἑλληνικῶν λόγων παιδείας, κὶ τῷ Πάπα πιστότατος."</note>. He died at a very great age, with a reputation for sanctity, in his Camaldolese Hermitage.

MEFFRETH, a German by nation and a Priest of the Church of Meissen, flourished in the year 1443, in which he testifies that he began his *Little Garden* <note>original: *Hortulus*</note>, while John, Bishop of the Diocese of Meissen, held the helm. He wrote *The Queen's Little Garden* <note>original: *Hortulum Reginæ*</note>, or Sermons on the Saints and for Sundays throughout the entire year, divided into Summer and Winter parts. These were published at Nuremberg, 1487, in folio; and at Basel, 1488, in 2 volumes, folio. I have inspected both editions in the Lambeth Library. However, Meffreth, following the ancient Doctors, dared to teach in his *Sermons on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin* that she was not immune from original sin. The editors of his work took this poorly; and thus, a short "Admonition from the Printer" is prefixed to the first edition, and in the later edition, a long "Premonition" by Friar Johannes de Lapide <note>Jean Heynlin (c. 1430–1496), a famous Carthusian theologian.</note>, a Carthusian and Doctor of Paris, is added to those sermons. In this, Meffreth's opinion and reasons are refuted and argued to be heresy. For the Carthusian does not deny that the opinion concerning the "stained" Conception of the Blessed Virgin prevailed in ancient times; but he contends strenuously that after the contrary definition was promulgated by the University of Paris, by the Council of Basel, and by Pope Sixtus IV, it is pure and simple heresy, to be rejected by all Catholics.

# REGINALD PECOCK

**REGINALD PECOCK** <note>original: *Reginaldus Pavo*—"Pavo" is the Latin word for "Peacock."</note>, an Englishman by nationality and a Welshman by birth, was educated at Oriel College, Oxford, where he eventually received the insignia of a Doctorate. He was a man distinguished for his supreme skill in theological matters and his upright character; on account of this, he easily came to the notice of that great patron <term>Maecenas: a Roman statesman whose name became a byword for a generous patron of the arts and letters</term> of piety and better literature, Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester. By the Duke's favor, he obtained the Bishopric of St. Asaph in the year 1444 and was moved to the see of Chichester in 1450. With great zeal of spirit, he devoted himself to bringing the *Wycliffites*—whom they commonly called *Lollards* <note>The Lollards were followers of John Wycliffe, who criticized the wealth and corruption of the Church and emphasized the authority of the Bible.</note>—back into the fold of the Roman Church. Intent upon this work until his old age, he published many books in both the common tongue <note>original: *vernaculo*; here meaning Middle English.</note> and in Latin. However, he was not so devoted to the Papal party that he failed to recognize and attack the very serious errors and superstitions then widely accepted in the Roman Church. Furthermore, he was so far from being hostile to the *Lollards* that he strongly disapproved of the burning at the stake <note>original: *vivicomburium*.</note> often inflicted upon them by the English Clergy, believing that the controversy should be settled by milder arguments and by reason alone. In his writings, he sharply attacked the infallibility of the "Representative Church"—whether in the person of the Pope or a General Council—an idea which, though neglected in that age, had begun to be hawked about in the Schools following the *Councils of Constance and Basel*. He contended that the Church, when defining Articles of Faith, could both err and indeed had quite often erred. This man, learned beyond the common lot of his century, had drawn other opinions from his excellent knowledge of antiquity; though these were little known at that time, they are now accepted by all, yet they provoked suspicions of heresy against him among the unlearned and his rival prelates. Consequently, after the death of Duke Humphrey, he was summoned to the Synod of Lambeth in the year 1457 by Thomas Bourchier, Archbishop of Canterbury. He was accused of heresy by the Bishops of Winchester, Lincoln, and Rochester, and by twenty-four theologians of the lower rank. He was ordered to renounce several errors, some collected from his writings and others fabricated by the deceit of his enemies. He performed a public recantation <note>original: *Palinodiam*.</note> at St. Paul’s Cathedral in London on December 4th of that same year. What happened to him after that is not entirely clear. Some record that he was removed by a secret death in prison; others that he was imprisoned in episcopal houses until his death; but many believe he retired to a certain monastery, having been given a very small stipend from the episcopal revenues. It is agreed by all that he survived his high office for only a short time. Truly, the Spanish authors of the recent *Index of Prohibited and Expurgated Books* deserve ridicule for calling our Pecock of Chichester a "False Bishop" <note>original: *Pseudo-episcopum*.</note> and dreaming that he was a "Lutheran" professor at Oxford. Certainly, no other writer of that age argued the cause of the Roman Church against the *Wycliffites* with greater sharpness and learning; regardless of this, he was a man who would not pretend that the worst corruptions of morals and discipline had not been introduced into the Church, and he disapproved of the rather crude superstitions that were then flourishing everywhere.

---

->W R I T I N G S .<-

**ON FAITH**, two books in the form of a dialogue between a Father and a Son, written in English. In the first book, he proves that faith rests only on probable arguments, not demonstrative ones; in the latter, he disputes quite acutely that Holy Scripture is the sole Rule of Faith. This latter book, together with some excerpts from the first and illustrated with a lengthy preface by the editor, was published in London, 1688, in quarto. The entire work survives in manuscript in Trinity College, Cambridge. Pecock composed this work only a few years before his death and his public recantation. Indeed, in it he mentions not only the *Repressor* (which he published in 1449) as having been written by him previously, but he also records many books as having been published long ago which he had only promised to write in the *Repressor*.

*The Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy*, a particularly lengthy work and, as it seems, polished with the greatest care. In this work, the author defends the accepted doctrines and rites of the Roman Church at length in the common tongue against the objections of the *Wycliffites*.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the detailed analysis of the writings of Reginald Pecock, specifically his defense of the Church against the Lollards while maintaining a scholarly and critical perspective on certain traditions.</meta>

<header>The Synodal Century.</header>
<meta>catchword: priest</meta>

<margin>15TH CENTURY. from the Year 1400.</margin>
he affirms. The whole work is divided into five parts; the first of which defends the rituals attacked by the Wycliffites through a general argument; the remaining parts defend them individually. In the first part, therefore, he addresses the "prize" objection of the Wycliffites, who would accept nothing—whether in doctrine or ceremonies—unless it was expressly approved by Holy Scripture. He takes it upon himself to prove primarily that Holy Scripture was not given to us to reveal those things which could be discerned by our natural talents; and thus, countless things must necessarily be done and believed by all Christians about which Holy Scripture has not a single word; indeed, he argues that the greater part of Christian faith and duty must be sought from natural reason. For he claims that the Christian religion (if you except the Sacraments) added almost nothing to the moral law; and therefore the whole of it (excluding the Sacraments) is founded not primarily in Holy Scripture, but in natural reason. From this it follows that the dictates of the law and natural reason must be obeyed, even if the Apostles of Christ had preached something contrary to them. However, he everywhere supposes that Holy Scripture is the rule and measure of revealed truths, as an undoubted dogma received by all; indeed, he clearly asserts this in nearly six hundred places.

In the second part, he defends the use of images and pilgrimages undertaken for the sake of religion; he does so quite sharply and not without learning, yet with such a lack of truth that he is frequently forced to defend absurd opinions. To pass over other examples: while explaining the origin and nature of the idolatry of the Jews and Gentiles, he claims that by the benefit of philosophy blossoming <note>original: *aufgefcentis*—a variant of *efflorescentis*</note> shortly before the birth of Christ, the ray of truth shone out so brightly 

<margin>* Part 2, chapter 17.</margin>
that all Gentiles born since the time of Christ (if you except a few of obscure name) have been entirely immune from the crime of idolatry. While arguing the cause of images, however, he by no means proves that worship should be offered to them; he contends only that it is permissible for images to be kept in churches as *commemorative* <note>meaning they remind the viewer of something</note> of God, His benefits, and the Saints, but by no means *representative* <note>meaning they do not stand in place of the divine or possess its essence</note>.

In the third part, he proves that it is lawful for Christian priests to possess lands and large estates; and against the Lollards, he asserts that the fault of a minister does not take away the honor due to his ministry, nor does it give the laity the power to withhold the tithes owed to him. Meanwhile, he attacks the "Donation of Constantine" <note>A famous forged document claiming Emperor Constantine gave supreme power over the Western Empire to the Pope; Pecock was one of the first to prove it a fake using historical analysis.</note>—which the cruder partisans of the Pope once fabricated was given to Pope Sylvester—using the most valid and powerful arguments.

<margin>† Part 3, chapters 12, 13.</margin>

In the fourth part, he demonstrates against the Lollards (who preferred the equality of all priests and wished for no orders to be admitted except Presbyters and Deacons) that various ranks of the priesthood must necessarily be admitted in the Church and were instituted by Christ. In the fourth chapter, he affirms the primacy of Peter and his successors, the Roman Pontiffs; and in the following sections, he disputes that laws concerning "indifferent things" <term>adiaphora: matters not essential to salvation but regulated for the sake of order</term> can be rightly established by the prelates of the Church, and that men can be lawfully compelled to keep them. Nevertheless, he does not unwillingly acknowledge that a vast hodgepodge <note>original: *farraginem*</note> of rites and ceremonies has long since been introduced into the Church; and he laments the countless evils that have arisen from them; indeed, he vows that he will write a book on that very subject, and prays that God may favor his vow.

<margin>|| Part 4, chapter 9.</margin>

In the final part, he defends the specific lifestyles of religious orders—which differ from the common Christian folk—their peculiar habits, magnificent buildings, and other customs. In the third chapter, he reviews the various heretical sects that vexed the ancient Church and their dogmas, placing the Waldensians and Wycliffites in the final spot. Thus far, he had defended six Church customs attacked by the Lollards. Five others remained to be defended in a similar manner, namely: 
1. Prayers offered to Saints and the "communication of merits" <note>the idea that the extra good deeds of saints could be sold or shared</note> commonly sold by priests and monks. 
2. The excessive multitude of precious vessels kept in churches, which could better be sold and distributed to the needy; and the honor given to images and relics of Saints. 
3. The constant use of the Sacraments, but especially the divine worship shown to the elements of the Eucharist. 
4. The use of oaths practiced by the clergy and imposed on others. 
5. The use of capital punishment and war approved by the Church. 

However, since these chapters were treated in other books, he did not wish to discuss them further in this place. I have leafed through the entire manuscript work in the Public Library at Cambridge, Class 4, fig. 3, in folio. From the many places that deserved to be noted, I have selected two above others: one concerning the Canonical books of Holy Scripture, and the other concerning the priesthood...

# The Synodal Century

...priests' marriages, another example, which I shall provide here, translated <note>The author of this Latin text is translating the original Middle English of Reginald Pecock into Latin; this present version renders it into English for the modern reader.</note> for the benefit of the readers.

<margin>15th CENTURY. From the year 1400.</margin>
*Part 1, chapter 19.* Furthermore, the adversaries ought not to produce the *History of Susanna* (*Daniel chapter 13*) in their defense. For that passage and story is not a portion of Holy Scripture, but is apocryphal. However, the true book of *Daniel*, in its entirety as Holy Scripture, ends at the twelfth chapter, as *Jerome* the translator <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who produced the Vulgate Bible translation.</note> testifies. And again in Part 2, chapter 17: when a heretic might object to the origin of the sentence on idolatry brought forward by him, citing the passage in *Wisdom 14*, he affirms that the author of that book was mistaken; and then he adds: "That passage of *Wisdom 14* is false; and I am entirely free to believe so. For the Book of *Wisdom* is not a book of Holy Scripture; and the bare assertion of the author or writer of that same book of *Wisdom*, whose name was *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher; though he did not write the Book of Wisdom, it was often attributed to him in the medieval period.</note>, by no means deserves equal faith, nor has it as much weight as Holy Scripture and the arguments I have brought forward on this matter above. And so, indeed, it seems to me that no faith should be given to the 14th chapter of *Wisdom* in this matter."

If it should seem a marvel to anyone of simpler mind that the said book of *Wisdom* holds such an exalted place in the Bibles of today, and is even placed in the Bibles with the same solemnity as other books of Holy Scripture, I answer him thus: In the beginnings of the Church, shortly after the passion of Christ, writings inciting men to holiness were very rare and few if compared to the books written on the same subject since that time. Later, when Christians were moved by a great zeal for pious books but were destitute of a sufficient supply, because of the devotion and eagerness with which men at that time received spiritual doctrines, they transcribed into their Bibles both the book of *Philo*, which is called *Wisdom*, and the book of *Jesus son of Sirach*, which is called *Ecclesiasticus*, and several others. This was due to the great devotion with which Christians were drawn to such books in a time of such scarcity of pious works; although they knew well enough that these said books were not from Holy Scripture. This is also testified more clearly by *Jerome* and others, that those books are not part of Holy Scripture. Indeed, that ancient devotion of placing said books in the Bibles has not ceased from the time when Bibles were commonly transcribed by private individuals even to this day. Nevertheless, the authority of those books is not raised any higher than it was of old; nor can it, for example, be expanded so far that they should be preferred over arguments greater than their own bare assertion.

*Part 3, chapter 15.* Whatever action any Apostle or his Scripture describes as being practiced in the moral life of a priest, it is not contrary to reason for that action to be practiced frequently by a priest. For otherwise, an Apostle and his Scripture would be describing something contrary to reason, which must by no means be granted. Now, the matter is such that Scripture sufficiently approves that all kinds of food, in sufficient quantity and with thanks given to God, may be taken by a priest or any other Christian, as is clear from *1 Timothy chapter 4*. In the same way, the action—that a priest may choose and take for himself a wife from among all virgins as he pleases (provided he does not enter into marriage immediately after the death of a first wife) <note>Pecock is referring to the prohibition of "digamy" or second marriages for clergy.</note>, and that he may beget children, hold possessions, have a household, nourish and educate children, and govern and provide for a wife, possessions, and children—that action, I say, is approved by Paul, and by the same argument by the other Apostles. Concerning Paul, the matter is clear from what is written in *1 Corinthians chapter 7* at the beginning, where he speaks to all the Christians of Corinth generally, and thus to priests no less than others. Also in *1 Timothy chapter 3* and *Titus chapter 1*, if they are taken in the sense in which they were understood in Paul's time, and from Paul's age until this day throughout all of *Greece* <note>Refers to the Eastern Orthodox tradition, which allows married priests.</note>, as the practice of that Church demonstrates; and even according to the understanding which the *Western Church* applied to those words from the days of *Peter and Paul* until the time of *Augustine*, as the custom of priests in the *Western Church* received in *Augustine's* age demonstrates; along with the *Tripartite History* <note>A widely used medieval history of the early Church compiled by Cassiodorus.</note> where it speaks of the *Council of Nicaea*; and *Augustine* himself, who made mention of the married priests of his own time. It cannot be denied, however, that *Paul* gave counsel to *Timothy* in *1 Timothy chapter 5* that he should keep himself chaste.

Furthermore, the time when this work was written can be most certainly determined from the work itself. In Part 5, chapter 6, he says several times that 34 years have passed since the beginning of the war between the *English and the French*; so it must necessarily have been written in the year 1449 <note>The "war" refers to the Lancastrian phase of the Hundred Years' War, often dated by 15th-century English writers from the 1415 campaign of Henry V.</note>.

# LEONARD OF UDINE,
otherwise called *of Belluno*, and by some *de Ma-*, an Italian by birth and a member of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>, a student and Professor at the University of Bologna, Chaplain and Preacher to Pope Eugenius IV, and Provincial of the Masters in Lombardy, flourished in the year 1444. *Flowery Sermons on the Sundays and Certain Feasts*, which he delivered in Florence in the year 1435 and in Venice. *Sermons on the Saints*, which appeared during the very infancy of the art of printing <note>The "incunabula" period of printing before 1501.</note> in the year 1446 without mention of a place; then in *Ulm* in 1475, *Speyer* in 1479, and Lyon in 1495, in quarto.
*A Treatise on the Commonplaces of Preachers*, Ulm, 1478.
*A Work on the Laws*, a volume of considerable bulk. It was published in *Venice* in 1473, in folio.

<header>The Synodal Century.</header>

<margin>15th CENTURY. from the year 1400.</margin>
While still a Friar <note>Latin: *Fraterculus*, literally "little brother," a humble term used for a member of a mendicant order, here referring to the Dominicans.</note>, he undertook embassies in the name of Florence to various princes, but especially to Popes Martin V and Eugenius. Eventually appointed Vicar General of the Neapolitan Congregation, he was finally, in the year 1446 on February 10th <note>Original Latin: *iv. Id. Februar.*, the fourth day before the Ides of February.</note>, named Archbishop of Naples by Pope Eugenius, though very much against his own will. In the year 1447 and again in 1455, he was sent as an envoy to Rome by the people of Naples to offer auspicious prayers to Nicholas V and Callistus III upon their elevation to the papacy. He died on May 2nd, 1459, at the age of 70, and was buried in the Church of St. Mark with great pomp. For Pope Pius II, who was then present in Florence, took upon himself the duty of overseeing the funeral; and after everyone had kissed the body before it was committed to the earth, he granted a plenary indulgence <term>indulgences: Remissions of temporal punishment for sins.</term> of seven years and as many "Forty-days" <note>Periods of penance or fasting equivalent to a Lent.</note>. For Antoninus did not pass away without a distinguished reputation for holiness; indeed, his biographers recount wonders concerning his piety, vigils, humility, and charity, though they accumulate miracles without end and without shame <note>Latin: *sine fronte*, literally "without a forehead," implying a lack of restraint or modesty in their claims.</note>. Indeed, even while still alive, Antoninus had excited such an opinion of his sanctity that Pope Nicholas V used to say that Antoninus deserved to be enrolled in the catalogue of saints no less while living than Bernardino of Siena did when dead. Pope Leo X finally intended to fulfill this wish, but being snatched away by death, he left the matter to be completed by his successor Hadrian, who entered Antoninus into the Calendar <note>Canonized him as a saint.</note> in the year 1523. It would certainly not be fair to deny Antoninus his reputation for piety; yet truth compels one to say that he was a writer of no judgment, who was accustomed to gather together old wives' tales and the most foul fables from every side.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Historical Summary*, or *Tripartite Chronicle*, compiled from many historians (whom he himself lists in the Preface) from the creation of the world until the year 1459. The first part runs from the creation of the world to Constantine the Great; the second from then to the year 1313; the third from then until his own times. Published in *Venice 1481*, *Nuremberg 1484*, *Basel 1491*, and with notes by P. Maturus at *Lyons 1586*, 3 volumes in folio.

*Theological Summary*, distributed in four parts. Published in *Memmingen 1483*, *Strasbourg 1496*, 4 volumes in folio, and *Venice 1591*.

*Confessional Summary*, published at *Strasbourg 1492, 1499*, quarto; *Paris 1516*, octavo; *Lyons 1564*, octavo; *Venice 1572*, sixteen-mo.

*Annotations on the Donation of Constantine the Great*. Held among other treatises by various authors, *Cologne 1535*.

*Trialogue on the Disciples at Emmaus*, together with a life of the author, printed in some places before the year 1500.

*Book on the Virtues*, *Nuremberg 1472*.

*Treatises on Excommunication, on the Ecclesiastical Interdict, on Irregularity, on Suspension, and on Usury*, found among the *Treatises on Law* published at *Venice 1584*.

The unpublished works of Antoninus are provided by Altamura in the *Library of Preachers* (p. 183) and Michael Poccianicius in the *Catalogue of Florentine Writers* (p. 13).

### NICHOLAS V.

<margin>1447.</margin>
NICHOLAS V, previously called *Tommaso of Sarzana* <note>Tommaso Parentucelli (1397–1455).</note>, born in a humble place, either Genoese by birth or, in the opinion of Platina, from Lucca. The son of Bartholomew the surgeon, he devoted himself to the study of liberal arts at Bologna through the kindness of Cardinal Niccolò Albergati. Then called to the Roman Curia, after he had won a reputation for learning and prudence in the debates held at Ferrara and Florence, he was sent as a legate to Germany by Pope Eugenius to recall Emperor Frederick and the Princes of the Empire from their siding with the Council of Basel back to obedience to the Roman See. Thomas accomplished this, and partly through eloquent speeches, partly through lavish promises of a reformation soon to follow, he swayed the minds of the Germans and brought an end to the schism. Returning to Rome in 1446, he received the Cardinal's hat and the Bishopric of Bologna as a reward for his labor. In the year 1447, following the death of Eugenius, he was elected Roman Pontiff on the 6th of March and crowned on the 19th. In 1449, using the power and arms of Emperor Frederick, he [removed] Felix <note>Felix V, the last historical Antipope.</note>, the Antipope, who had been substituted by the Council of Basel ten years prior after the deposition of Eugenius, from the Papacy...

<margin>1448.</margin>
NICHOLAS OF CUSA, named after his birthplace Kues, situated on the banks of the Moselle in the Diocese of Trier, was the son of a poor fisherman and a Doctor of Theology and Canon Law. At first, as some maintain according to Pennotus, he was a member of the Canons Regular and provost of the Monastery of Wotoberg; then Archdeacon of Liège and Dean of St. Florin in Konstanz.

In the year 1441, he was sent as an Apostolic Nuncio to the Imperial Diet at Mainz to draw the Emperor and the princes away from their obedience to the Council of Basel; he performed a similar legation to France not long after. On December 20, 1448, he obtained the dignity of Cardinal with the title of Saint Peter in Chains from Nicholas V; soon after, he was sent back to Germany to reform monasteries, to incite the princes of the Empire to undertake a war against the Turks, and to preach the Jubilee soon to be celebrated in Rome. <meta>This page continues the biography of the philosopher and theologian Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464) and provides a comprehensive list of his written works, followed by the start of an entry for the Florentine historian Matteo Palmieri.</meta>

<header>The Synodal Century.</header>

<margin>
15th CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
[Nicholas of Cusa], having been appointed Bishop of Brixen <note>The city of Brixen is located in the modern-day Italian province of South Tyrol.</note> in the County of Tyrol by [Pope] Nicholas [V], entered into a long-standing quarrel with Sigismund, Duke of Austria. For Sigismund did not wish for Cardinals to possess bishoprics in his territory by right of commendation <term>commendatio: A practice where a church office was granted to a person to hold "in trust," often allowing them to collect the revenues without necessarily fulfilling all local duties.</term>. Cusa appealed to Pope Callixtus III, who had succeeded Nicholas. The Pope excommunicated Sigismund and placed his region under an interdict <term>interdict: An ecclesiastical penalty that prohibits certain sacraments and religious services from being performed in a specific territory.</term>. Around the year 1459, Cusa set out for Brixen; there, he was besieged and captured by Sigismund. He eventually ransomed his freedom by paying a great weight of gold and surrendering the privileges of his church. Pope Pius II took revenge on Sigismund with a repeated excommunication; nevertheless, Cusa, deprived of his see, found it necessary to return to Italy. He died at Todi in Umbria on August 12, 1464, at the age of 63. His body was brought to Rome and laid to rest at the Church of St. Peter in Chains. In the opinion of Cardinal Bona, he was a man of *profound* <margin>* Prefatory note on the author in the book *On Divine Psalmody*.</margin> knowledge and of a refinement honed by the most subtle practice. Indeed, no one will easily deny his erudition; yet all find his constancy <note>In this context, "constancy" refers to his shifting political and theological allegiances, specifically his move from supporting the Conciliar movement to being a staunch defender of Papal supremacy.</note> to be lacking.

And since he would not revoke his errors, he paid for his boldness by being burned in the flames at the city of Corna <note>While the text claims he was burned at "Corna," historical records generally state that Palmieri died of natural causes in Florence, though his book *The City of Life* was posthumously condemned.</note>; though others say this happened at Florence. <margin>1450.</margin>
**JOHN CAPGRAVE**, an Englishman by nation, from the county of Kent. He was a Monk of the Augustinian Order in the Monastery of Canterbury and later, after receiving his Doctorate at Oxford, became the Provincial <term>provincial: A high-ranking superior who oversees all the monasteries of a particular religious order within a specific province or region.</term> of his order. He was the personal confessor and a very close friend to Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester. He flourished in the year 1450 and held a leading place among the English theologians of his age, being accustomed to thunder sharply against the loose morals of the clergy. He died at Lynn among the North-folk <note>Modern-day King's Lynn in Norfolk.</note> on the 12th day of August, in the year 1464, while Edward IV was in power, and he was buried among his fellow Augustinians. So indeed say Bale and Joseph Pamphilus. But Pits—whom Vossius and Miraeus follow—reports that he died only under Richard III, in the year 1484. He wrote the *Catalog or Legend of the Saints of England*, which was printed in *London, 1516, in folio*. Capgrave is said to have compiled this history from a very large and beautiful volume on the same subject which <margin>Under the Bust of Tiberius E. I.</margin> is preserved as a manuscript in the Cottonian Library <note>A famous collection of manuscripts formerly owned by Sir Robert Cotton, now part of the British Library; the volumes were famously organized by the busts of Roman Emperors atop the bookcases.</note>. He also left behind many other monuments of his talent, partly historical and partly theological, which are by no means to be despised. Most notably, he is said to have commented upon the entirety of Holy Scripture. Bale provides a large enough catalog of his writings in Century 8, chapter 1, and from him Pits on page 672, as well as Joseph Pamphilus in his *Chronicle of the Hermit Order*. Among these, there exist in manuscript: a *Commentary on Genesis* in the Oriel College Library, Oxford, Codex 20; *on the Acts of the Apostles* in the Balliol College Library, Oxford, Codex 171; *On [the same]* ibid., Codex 172; and a *History of all the Illustrious Henries*—including Kings, Emperors, Writers, and others—dedicated to King Henry VI of England, which I saw as a manuscript in the Library of the College of St. Benedict (or Corpus Christi), Cambridge, No. 296. I also saw the same work, though with Capgrave's name omitted, in the Cottonian Library under Tiberius A, vol. 8. There also exists there a manuscript under the bust of Vitellius D. 15, num. 7, the *Life of St. Gilbert, Founder of the Order of Sempringham*, written in English by Capgrave.

<margin>1450.</margin>
**THOMAS À KEMPIS**, surnamed *Hammerlein* or *Malleolus* <note>original: "Malleolus" is Latin for 'little hammer', a translation of his German name Hämmerlein.</note>, originating from the small town named Kempen in the Diocese of Cologne. He was the son of John and Gertrude, born around the year 1380. As a boy of thirteen, he was sent by his parents from his home for the sake of studies; there he had Florentius [Radewijns], the Prefect of the Brethren of the Common Life, as his teacher. After seven years, in the year 1400, he sought out the Monastery of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine of the Windesheim Congregation, located on Mount Saint Agnes near the city of Zwolle. There, having completed five years of novitiate under his brother John, the Prior of the Monastery, he took the habit in 1406, and after some years was made the Procurator and later the Sub-Prior of the Monastery. He flourished in the year 1450. He died at a great age in the year 1471, aged 92. He was a man, if ever there was one, pious and devoted; though some do not hide that in certain places, as if carried away by ecstasy, he acts as an enthusiast <term>enthusiast: In this era, the term often referred to those who claimed direct, personal divine inspiration, sometimes used critically to suggest a lack of rational or theological restraint.</term> and is almost raving. There is currently thought being given to enrolling him in the assembly of Saints in the Roman Church, according to <margin>* Chronological Endeavor on the Catalog of Popes, part 2, p. 83.</margin> Papebroch *, who mentions that his body was exhumed, not without miracles, in the year 1672 on the 11th day [of the month]...

->WORKS.<-

**30** Sermons to the Regular Novices.
9 Sermons to the Brothers.
*Most useful Sermons and Meditations or Prayers on the Passion of the Lord, 36 in number.*

<margin>
* On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 387.
</margin>
*Four Books on the Imitation of Christ.* A work great not so much in its size as in its usefulness and fame: many have praised its admirable yet charming zeal of expression, the weight of its sentiments, and its fiery sparks of piety. It will be enough for me to provide the notable eulogy of the Great Bellarmine *. "I have certainly," he says, "turned and re-turned this little work very often from my youth until my old age; and it always appeared new to me, and even now it tastes wonderfully to my heart." <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621) was a Jesuit Cardinal and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation. His endorsement was a mark of the highest prestige.</note> While no one fails to recognize the dignity of the book, writers slash at one another with deadly hatred regarding its author. I, for my part, do not involve myself in these disturbances, for it is not our place to settle such great disputes. However, I believe it will not be unwelcome to the reader to briefly note the opinions of others. Thus, the common consensus of both manuscripts and printers alike adjudges this work to our Thomas à Kempis. This received opinion is favored by a manuscript described by Thomas's own hand, which displays a note at the end as follows: *Finished and completed in the year of our Lord 1441, by the hands of Brother Thomas Kempis, at Mount St. Agnes near Zwolle.* <note>Mount Saint Agnes was a monastery of the Canons Regular of Mount St. Agnes in the Netherlands where Thomas spent most of his life.</note> To this is added the similarity of style and the well-known piety of Kempis.

But on the other hand, insurmountable difficulties militate against this. For besides the fact that the little note placed at the end of said manuscript argues that Thomas was not so much the Author as the scribe <note>original: "descriptorem."</note> of the work; and that Bonaventure ** <margin>** Collection 7, to the Brothers of Toulouse.</margin> cited a portion of the last chapter of the book word-for-word from this author, and said they were the words of a certain "devotional booklet on the Imitation of Christ": there is also a manuscript preserved in the Monastery of Gerardimonten <note>Geraardsbergen, in modern-day Belgium.</note> written without an author's name before the year 1400. Furthermore, there is another even older manuscript, to which the name of John of Gersen (or of Gessen), <margin>† On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 386. </margin> Abbot of Vercelli (who flourished from the year 1230 to 1245), is prefixed; this is said to be preserved in the Monastery of Arona, and is mentioned by Bellarmine †, who was otherwise inclined toward Kempis. Indeed, the editors of the Venice edition of 1501, since they prefixed the name of Abbot John, appealed to a manuscript written by the Abbot's own hand.

This latter difficulty (provided that manuscripts of this kind truly exist) can by no means be overcome. However, the followers of Kempis have weakened the former argument by contending that the aforementioned *Collections* are wrongly ascribed to Bonaventure, relying chiefly on the reason that Ubertino of Casale, who was younger than Bonaventure, is found cited in them. Hence, from the beginning of this century, a massive controversy arose between the Benedictines and the Canons Regular (on whose side stand the Jesuits). The former fight for John, the latter for Thomas; both sides fight as if "for their altars and hearths" <note>A Latin idiom (*pro aris et focis*) meaning to fight for what is most sacred or for one's very existence; here, it refers to the prestige of their respective religious orders.</note> to seize the merit of such a great work for their own Order. Constantino Gaetano entered the arena for the Benedictines; Heribert Rosweyde and Henricus Sommal for the Canons. These were followed on both sides by a huge number of "gladiators" who conducted the matter with Apologies, Defenses, and Refutations. Nor did the contest stay within the bounds of modesty; the business was conducted on both sides with insults and even fraud. Some complain of erased and altered titles in the manuscripts; others laugh at a "discovered" index of Thomas’s works.

Yet the lot of this fertile controversy did not fall out in such a way that it remains confined between Thomas à Kempis and John of Vercelli. For there were those who, since they knew little of John of Gersen (an obscure writer), and being deceived by the similarity of the name, adjudicated this little work to Jean Gerson, the Chancellor of Paris. But that opinion has long since been exiled by the learned. Recently, the author of a *Conjecture* published in Rome in 1667 took another path; having weighed the arguments on both sides, he is of the opinion that there was not one but several authors of this work. Thus, he leaves the glory of the Compiler to Thomas à Kempis, but ascribes the fourth book undoubtedly to Jean Gerson. Regarding the remaining three, however, he remains in doubt whether they should be ascribed to John of Vercelli, or to Ubertino of Casale, or to Pierre de Corbière.

### ANTONIUS DE ROSELLIS

ANTONIUS DE ROSELLIS, a Tuscan by nationality and a native of Arezzo, was a Doctor of Both Laws <note>Referring to Canon Law (church law) and Civil Law (secular law).</note> and a professor at the University of Padua. He was sent as the envoy of Pope Eugenius IV to the Council of Basel, and was afterwards a member of the secret council to Emperor Frederick III. He flourished in the year 1450. He died in vigorous old age at Padua in 1467. He wrote a distinguished work titled *The Monarchy* <note>original: "Monarchiam"</note>, concerning the power of the Emperor and the Pope. It is divided into five parts; it was composed under Pope Eugenius before the year 1440, and he expanded and revised it under Emperor Frederick after the year 1457. In this work, by bringing forth arguments from Holy Scripture, the writings of the Fathers, reason, and both branches of Law, he strives to prove that the Roman Pontiff does not preside over temporal matters; nor does he have any authority of the civil sword, nor indeed any superiority over the rest of the Bishops. This work was published at *Venice* in 1483 and 1587, and it is held in Goldast’s *Monarchia*, Volume 1, from page 252 to page 556. It is prohibited from being read in the Roman *Index Expurgatorius* <note>The official list of books the Catholic Church banned or required to be censored.</note>. There also exists his *Matrimonial Counsel* <note>original: "Consilium Matrimoniale"</note> among other legal treatises published at *Frankfurt*, 1580, page 121.

<margin>1450.</margin>

### DIONYSIUS à RICKEL

DIONYSIUS à RICKEL, surnamed "of Leeuwen," a Belgian by nationality, was born to honorable parents in the small town of Ryckel (which is a municipality of Hesbaye in the Diocese of Liège); he was called the *Ecstatic Doctor*. Educated in fine letters at the Academy of Cologne and created a Master of Arts, at the age of 21 he joined the Carthusian monks <note>A strict, contemplative monastic order founded by St. Bruno.</note> of the monastery at Roermond. He flourished in the year 1450, a friend and very close associate of Cardinal Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa, a famous German philosopher, theologian, and astronomer.</note>. He died in the year 1471 on the 12th of March, at the age of 69 (or, as others have it, 77). "A man most studious in the divine Scriptures," says <margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 173.</margin> Trithemius\*, "and skilled through constant practice; not ignorant of secular philosophy; subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech; singularly devoted in life and conversation; so much so that he was even held worthy of divine revelations... He wrote so many and such great things that, in the number of his small works, he has had no equal among the Latins except for Augustine."

<margin>15th CENTURY. from the Year 1400. 1450.</margin>
## ANTONY OF ROSELLIS
A Tuscan by nationality, born in Arezzo, a Doctor of both Laws <term>Doctor of both Laws: One who has attained the highest degree in both Canon (church) and Civil (secular) law.</term> and a lecturer at the University of Padua. He was sent as the envoy of Pope Eugenius IV to the Council of Basel, and was later a member of the secret council of Emperor Frederick III. He flourished in the year 1450. He died in vigorous old age at Padua in 1467. He wrote a distinguished work called *The Monarchy* <note>original: "Monarchiam"</note>, concerning the power of the Emperor and the Pope, divided into five parts; this was composed under Pope Eugenius before the year 1440, and expanded and revised under Emperor Frederick after the year 1457. In this work, bringing forth arguments from Holy Scripture, the writings of the Fathers, reason, and both Laws, he strives to prove that the Roman Pontiff does not preside over temporal matters; nor does he have any authority of the civil sword, nor even any superiority over the other Bishops. This work appeared at *Venice in 1483 and 1587*, and is contained in Goldast's *The Monarchy*, Volume 1, from page 252 to page 556; it is prohibited from being read in the *Roman Index of Forbidden Books*. His *Counsel on Marriage* <note>original: "Consilium Matrimoniale"</note> also exists among other *Legal Treatises, Frankfurt 1580, p. 121.*

<margin>1450.</margin>
## DENIS OF RYCKEL
Surnamed de Leeuwis, a Belgian by nationality, born to honorable parents in the small town of Ryckel, which is a municipality of Hesbaye in the Diocese of Liège; he was called the *Ecstatic Doctor* <term>Ecstatic Doctor: A title given to Denis because of his frequent mystical trances or "ecstasies."</term>. Educated in liberal arts at the University of Cologne and created a Master of Arts, at the age of 21 he joined the Carthusian monks of the monastery of Roermond. He flourished in the year 1450. He was a friend and very close associate of Cardinal Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a famous philosopher, theologian, and astronomer.</note>. He died in the year 1471 on the 12th day of March, at the age of 69, or as others have it, 77. <margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 173.</margin> *A man most studious in the divine Scriptures*, says Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and scholar.</note>, *and skilled through constant practice: also not ignorant of secular Philosophy; subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech; singularly devoted in life and conversation; so much so that he was even held worthy of divine revelations... He wrote so many and such great things that in the number of his short works, he had no equal among the Latins except Augustine.*

Thus far are the works of Denis the Carthusian that have come to our notice. Trithemius, in *Ecclesiastical Writers* <note>original: "de Script. Eccl."</note> p. 176, provides a sufficiently long catalog of his writings arranged by himself in a compendium. See also Simler in the *Zurich Library* <note>original: "Bibl. <margin>1450.</margin>
**JOANNES CANALES**, an Italian by birth and a Franciscan monk in the Monastery of Ferrara; a Doctor of Sacred Theology, distinguished by his knowledge of both sacred and secular literature, and especially by his refined understanding of the philosophy of Plato. He flourished in the year 1450. He was very well-regarded by Borso, the first Duke of Ferrara, by whom he was sent as an envoy to many Princes of Italy to conduct matters of great importance. He wrote books *On the Celestial Life; On the Nature of the Soul and its Immortality; On Paradise and the Happiness of the Soul; On Hell and the Torment of the Soul.* These appeared together at Venice in 1494, folio.

<margin>1450.</margin>
**GULIELMUS VORILONGUS** <note>Also known as William of Vaurouillon</note>, a Frenchman by nationality and a member of the Order of Friars Minor, a student of the Monastery of Dinan, flourished in the year 1450. He possessed such a reputation for erudition that when a very sharp controversy regarding the Blood of Christ <note>A theological dispute about whether the blood shed by Christ during the Passion remained united to his divinity during the three days he was in the tomb.</note> had long been active between the Franciscans and Dominicans, he was summoned to Rome to defend the position of his Order in the presence of Pope Pius II. He died at Rome in the year 1464 and was buried at the Ara Coeli. There exist writings by him, including a *Commentary on the four books of Sentences* <term>Sentences: The "Libri Quattuor Sententiarum" by Peter Lombard, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</term> (Lyon 1484, Paris 1503, Venice 1519), and the *Vade Mecum, or Repertory of propositions that are against Scotus, or a Collection of questions on the four books of Sentences,* Strasbourg 1501.

<margin>1450.</margin>
**JOANNES PLUSIADENUS**, known by that surname, a Chief Priest or Archpriest, flourished after the Council of Florence <note>A council (1438–1445) that attempted to reunite the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.</note>, around the year 1450, as it seems. Leo Allatius, in his book *On Consent* (Book 3, Chapter 3, Section 3), suspects that he is the same person as Joseph of Methone, because Joseph's booklet in favor of the Council of Florence against Mark of Ephesus bears the name of Joannes Plusiadenus on its frontispiece in a manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library. He asserts this almost as a certainty in his *Epilogue to Orthodox Greece*, Volume 1. Indeed, it was not at all uncommon for Greeks of a later age to change their name along with a change in their way of life; thus, the same man who was John during his priesthood could reasonably be thought to have become Joseph after receiving the miter <note>Becoming a bishop.</note>. However, if that passage we cited above from Sguropulus concerning the Bishop of Methone is to be understood as referring to Joseph (which indeed seems to be the case), then that man would be a Latin-supporter and quite distinct from our John. Plusiadenus wrote a *Dialogue or Disputation in favor of the Council of Florence*, which Leo Allatius published in Greek and Latin among the *Writers of Orthodox Greece*, Volume 1, p. 583.

<margin>1450.</margin>
**HILARIO**, a Greek monk and likewise a follower of the Latins, flourished around the year 1450. He wrote, after the Council of Florence, a *Dialectical Oration on the mystical bread of the Greeks and the unleavened bread of the Latins*: which Johannes Meursius published in Greek among various divine works at Leiden, 1619, 4to; and Leo Allatius published in Greek and Latin in *Orthodox Greece*, Volume 1, p. 655.

## JOHN CANALES,
An Italian by nationality, of the Franciscan Order, a monk in the Monastery of Ferrara, and a Doctor of Sacred Theology. He was distinguished for his knowledge of both sacred and secular <note>original: "profanarum"</note> letters, but especially for his refined understanding of Platonic Philosophy. ## WILLIAM VORILONG,
A Frenchman by nationality, a member of the Order of Minors <term>Order of Minors: The Franciscans.</term>, a student of the Monastery of Dinan, he flourished in the year 1450. He was of such great reputation for learning that when the very sharp controversy between the Franciscans and Dominicans regarding the Blood of Christ had long been active, he was summoned to Rome to defend the side of his order in the presence of Pope Pius II. He died in Rome in the year 1464 and was buried at the Altar of Heaven <note>original: "ad Aramcæli," referring to the Basilica of Santa Maria in Aracoeli</note>. There exist writings by him: *Commentary on the Four Books of Sentences* <term>Sentences: The "Libri Quattuor Sententiarum" by Peter Lombard, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</term> Lyon 1484, Paris 1503, Venice 1519; and the *Vade Mecum* <note>A handbook; literally "Go with me"</note>, a *Repertory of Propositions that are against Scotus, or a Collection of Questions on the Four Books of Sentences*, Strasbourg 1501.

## JOHN,
Surnamed PLUSIADENUS, a primary Priest or Archpriest, flourished after the Synod of Florence <note>The Council of Florence (1438-1445), which attempted to reunite the Catholic and Orthodox churches.</note>, around the year 1450, as it seems. Leo Allatius, in his book *On Consent* <note>original: "de Consensu"</note>, book 3, chapter 3, section 5, suspects him to be the same person as Joseph of Methone, because Joseph's small book in favor of the Synod of Florence against Mark of Ephesus bears the name of John Plusiadenus on its front in a manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library; and he holds this as almost certain in the *Epilogue to the Orthodox Greeks*, Volume 1. Indeed, it was not at all uncommon for Greeks of a later age to change their name upon changing their way of life <note>referring to taking monastic vows or receiving a high ecclesiastical office</note>; thus it can be considered not unfitting that the same man who was John before his episcopate was Joseph after receiving the mitre. But if that passage concerning the Bishop of Methone which we cited above from Syropoulos <note>original: "Sguro"</note> is to be understood as referring to Joseph (which indeed seems to be the case), then that man will be a Latin <note>a supporter of the Roman Church</note>, and quite different from our John. Plusiadenus wrote a *Dialogue or Disputation in favor of the Synod of Florence*, which Leo Allatius published in Greek and Latin among the *Orthodox Writers of Greece*, Volume 1, page 583.

* S
<meta>catchword: conscri-</meta>

## JOANNES ARGYROPULUS
<margin>15th CENTURY. from the Year 1400. 1450.</margin>
A native of Byzantium <note>original: "Byzantinus"</note>, he flourished in the year 1450 and thereafter. After Constantinople was captured by the Turks, he went into exile in Italy. Because of the rare erudition for which he was renowned, he was held in the highest honor by Cosimo de' Medici, the Prince of Florence—so much so that he was appointed tutor to Cosimo's son Peter and grandson Lorenzo, being treated as a father figure. He also lectured on Greek literature to the youth of Florence. Eventually, when a plague devastated Tuscany, he withdrew to Rome; there, by publicly lecturing on Aristotle, he earned a sufficiently large salary for himself. He died at the turn of the century in his seventies. He was a man who, besides his excessive gluttony and heavy drinking (for which he had a very bad reputation), was inflated with too high an opinion of himself and held the merits of others in contempt; he even dared to boast shamelessly <note>original: "illoto ore," literally "with unwashed mouth," an idiom meaning without reverence</note> that Cicero did not know Greek literature. Besides his *Latin versions and Commentaries on the books of Aristotle*, which have frequently been printed, he wrote for Duke Cosimo a *Book on the Procession of the Holy Spirit and the Decree of the Council of Florence*; this was published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius in *Orthodox Greece <note>original: "Græc. Orthod."</note>, Volume 1, page 400*. His *Monody on John, Emperor of Constantinople*, his *Consolation to the Emperor of Constantinople*, his *Book on Kingship*, and his *Comparison between the Princes of the Ancient and New Empires* survive in manuscript form in the Library of the King of the French.

## MATTHÆUS CAMARIOTA
<margin>1453.</margin>
A native of Constantinople (though others say Thessaloniki), he was the son of a certain Greek priest who died in the slaughter of Constantinople. An excellent philosopher and rhetorician, he flourished in Constantinople in the year 1453, where he was present for the capture of the city. A significant portion of a lengthy *Letter on the Capture of Constantinople* survives (transcribed by Theodorus Zygomalas into his own letter regarding the dangers and slaughters of the inhabitants of Constantinople), printed in Greek and Latin in Martin Kraus’s *Turco-Greece <note>original: "Turcogræciam"</note>, book 1, page 76*. Josias Simler, in the *Zurich Library* <note>original: "Bibliothec. Tigurin."</note> page 491, mentions that his *Epitome of Hermogenes* and a *Book on Rhetoric* survive as manuscripts. A *Synopsis of his Rhetoric* is held as a manuscript in the Augsburg Library. He also wrote *Commentaries on the Letters of Synesius* which were once in the possession of Johannes Zygomalas, according to Kraus in *Turco-Greece*, page 187. He wrote an *Encomium on the Three Hierarchs: Basil, Gregory, and Chrysostom*: this is held in Greek in the Library of the King of France, and perhaps elsewhere.
<margin>Index of Manuscript Books in the Augsburg Library, page 27.</margin>
Two treatises seem to be attributed to our Matthew which exist as Greek manuscripts in the Augsburg Library, distinguished by these titles: *Matthæus, Monk and Priest of Thessaloniki, on Divine Grace and Light, against those who called it a created thing*; and a *Treatise by the Same on those who teach spurious and foreign things in the Churches*. The former, and perhaps the latter, treatise attacked the Barlaamites <note>Followers of Barlaam of Calabria, who opposed the Hesychast practice of seeking to see the "Uncreated Light" of God.</note>, who denied that the Taboric Light <note>The light revealed at the Transfiguration of Jesus on Mount Tabor.</note> was something uncreated.

## DUCAS
<margin>1453.</margin>
Whose first name is unknown, a native of Byzantium, descended from the imperial family of the Ducas, and grandson of Michael Ducas, he flourished in the year 1453. After Constantinople was conquered by the Turks, he withdrew to the island of Lesbos and served in the court of Dorino Gattilusio, Prince of Lesbos, who was a Christian but a tributary of the Turks. In the year 1455, he was sent by Gattilusio to Hamza, the commander of the Turkish fleet, to deliver gifts, and he obtained peace and friendship from the Barbarian <note>A common historical term for the Ottoman forces in 15th-century Latin texts.</note> for the people of Lesbos. In the same year, he was sent as an envoy to Adrianople by Domenico Gattilusio, the successor of the recently deceased Dorino, to pay the tributes to Mehmed, the Emperor of the Turks. In the following years, he undertook two other embassies to the Turkish Tyrant; he survived the conquest of Lesbos by the Turks in 1462, which was taken through the greatest treachery. He wrote a *Byzantine History* concerning the final deeds of the Empire of Constantinople, from the death of Andronicus Palaeologus the Younger until the capture of the island of Lesbos by the Turks—that is, from the year of Christ 1341 to 1462—with summaries of the years from the creation of the world until the death of Andronicus prefixed to it. This History was published in Greek and Latin with the version and notes of Ismaël Boulliau, *Paris, 1649, folio.*

## GEORGIUS SCHOLARIUS
<margin>1453. * Note on the Author prefixed to the book "On Divine Psalmody."</margin>
Also known as GENNADIUS, a Greek by nation, perhaps a native of Constantinople, he was educated in every branch of literature in no common way. He was a disciple of Matthew Camariota, if one believes Maximos Margunios; a man (in the judgment of Cardinal Bona*) of polished tongue and sharp intellect. For many years before the Council of Florence, he was in the College of Teachers in Constantinople...

<margin>
15th CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
1450.
</margin>
**JOANNES ARGYROPULUS**, a Byzantine by birth, flourished in the year 1450 and thereafter. After Constantinople was captured by the Turks, he went to Italy as an exile from his homeland. On account of the rare erudition for which he was distinguished, he was held in the highest honor by Cosimo de' Medici, the Prince of Florence; so much so that, having been appointed tutor to Cosimo’s son Piero and his grandson Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo the Magnificent</note>, he was regarded as a father figure, and he interpreted Greek literature for the Florentine youth. Finally, when a plague devastated Tuscany, he withdrew to Rome; and by publicly lecturing on Aristotle, he earned a sufficiently ample salary for himself. He died as a septuagenarian as the century was drawing to a close. Aside from his immoderate gluttony and fondness for drink—for which he has a very bad reputation—he was a man puffed up with too high an opinion of himself and a despiser of others' merits; to such an extent that he dared to boast "with an unwashed mouth" <note>original: "illoto ore"; a Latin idiom meaning to speak disrespectfully or without due preparation</note> that Cicero did not know Greek literature. Besides his Latin translations and *Expositions of the books of Aristotle*, which have frequently been committed to the press, he wrote to Duke Cosimo a *Book on the Procession of the Holy Spirit and the Decree of the Council of Florence*, published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius in *Orthodox Greece, Volume 1, page 400*. By the same author, a *Funeral Lament for Emperor John of Constantinople*, a *Consolation to the Emperor of Constantinople*, a *Book on Kingship*, and a *Comparison between the Princes of the Ancient and New Empire* exist as manuscripts in the Library of the King of the French.

---

<margin>
1453.
Index of manuscript books in the Augsburg Library, p. 27.
</margin>
**MATTHÆUS CAMARIOTA**, a native of Constantinople (though others say Thessaloniki), was the son of a certain Greek priest who died in the slaughter of Constantinople. An outstanding philosopher and rhetorician, he flourished in Constantinople in the year 1453, where he was present for the capture of the city. A significant portion of a lengthy *Letter on the Capture of Constantinople* survives (transcribed by Theodorus Zygomalas into his own letter regarding the dangers and slaughters of the Constantinopolitans), in Greek and Latin in Martin Kraus’s *Turco-Græcia, book 1, page 76*. Josias Simler, in the *Zurich Library, page 491*, mentions that his *Epitome of Hermogenes* and a *Book of Rhetoric* exist as manuscripts. A *Synopsis of his Rhetoric* is held as a manuscript in the Augsburg Library. He also wrote *Commentaries on the Letters of Synesius* which were once in the possession of Johannes Zygomalas, according to Kraus in *Turco-Græcia, page 187*. An *Eulogy for the Three Hierarchs: Basil, Gregory, and Chrysostom* is held in Greek in the Library of the King of France, and perhaps elsewhere. Furthermore, two treatises appear to be owed to our Matthew which exist as Greek manuscripts in the Augsburg Library, distinguished by these titles: *Matthew the Monk and Priest of Thessaloniki on Divine Grace and Light against those who called it a creature*; and *The same author's Treatise on those who teach spurious and foreign things in the Churches*. The former, and perhaps the latter, treatise attacked the <term>Barlaamites</term> <note>Followers of Barlaam of Calabria, who opposed the Hesychast doctrine of the Uncreated Light</note>, who denied that the <term>Light of Tabor</term> <note>The light seen by the Apostles at the Transfiguration of Jesus on Mount Tabor</note> was something uncreated.

---

<margin>
1453.
</margin>
**DUCAS**, whose first name is hidden, was a Byzantine by birth, descended from the imperial family of the Ducases and the grandson of Michael Ducas. He flourished in the year 1453. After Constantinople was conquered by the Turks, he withdrew to the island of Lesbos and served in the court of Dorino Gattilusio, Prince of Lesbos, who was a Christian but a tributary of the Turks. In the year 1455, he was sent by Gattilusio to Hamza, the leader of the Turkish fleet, to deliver gifts, and he obtained peace and friendship from the barbarian for the Lesbians. In the same year, he was sent as an envoy to Adrianople by Domenico Gattilusio, the successor of the recently deceased Dorino, to pay the tributes to Mehmed, the Emperor of the Turks. In the following years, he undertook two other embassies to the Turkish tyrant; and he survived when Lesbos was conquered by the Turks in 1462 through the greatest treachery. He wrote a *Byzantine History* concerning the final deeds of the Empire of Constantinople, from the death of Andronicus Palæologus the Younger until the capture of the island of Lesbos by the Turks—that is, from the year of Christ 1341 to 1462—prefaced also by summaries of the years from the creation of the world until the death of Andronicus. That *History* was published in Greek and Latin with a translation and notes by Ismael Boulliau, *Paris, 1649, folio.*

---

<margin>
1453.
* Note on the Author prefixed to the book on Divine Psalmody.
</margin>
**GEORGIUS SCHOLARIUS**, who is also **GENNADIUS**, a Greek by nation and perhaps a Constantinopolitan by birth, was educated in every kind of literature in no common way; he was a disciple of Matthæus Camariota, if we trust Maximos Margunios. He was a man (in the judgment of Cardinal Bona*) of polished language and sharp wit. For many years before the Council of Florence, in the College of Teachers at Constantinople...
