<meta>This page continues the entry for George Scholarius (later known as Gennadius II), a pivotal Greek scholar and theologian during the fall of the Byzantine Empire. The previous page ended mid-word with "conscri-", referring to his works or records being written.</meta>

<header>The Synodal Century.</header>

<margin>
15th CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...written, he entered into no small favor with Emperor John <note>John VIII Palaiologos, reigned 1425–1448</note>; he was even admitted to the secret consultations of the Senate of Bishops. In the year 1438, having been led into Italy by the Emperor, it is not entirely clear what role he played in the Council of Florence <note>A council held to attempt the reunion of the Catholic and Orthodox churches</note>. Certainly, there are some Speeches circulated under his name addressed to the Synod of Florence; these not only favor the side of the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>, but even actively defend them. However, Rivetus and Creyghton contend that these were forged by some unsound mind
<margin>
* Rivet, *Sacred Criticism*, Book 4, ch. 19.
† Creyghton, *Preface to Sguropulus*.
|| Chalcocondylas, *History*, Book 6.
</margin>
and falsely attributed to the name of Gennadius. Truly, the excessive flattery of the Roman Church and the contempt for the Greeks with which those Speeches abound fall far below the noted prudence and gravity of Scholarius. Indeed, Allatius has refuted the somewhat weak authority of Chalcocondylas, which Rivetus used to support his argument. For Chalcocondylas states <note>original Greek: "|| Hist. l. 6."</note>: *Pope Eugenius (shortly after the Council of Florence was dissolved) sent certain learned men to Constantinople to enter into dialogue with the wise Greeks <note>original Greek: "εἰς διάλεξιν ἀφικομένους τοῖς τῶν Ἑλλήνων σοφοῖς"</note>, but they rejected the synod that had been held for them in Italy <note>original Greek: "οἱ ἢ προσείοντο τὴν γενομένην σφίσι ξύνοδον κατὰ τὴν Ἰταλίαν"</note>, with Mark of Ephesus <note>A staunch opponent of the church union</note>, the archbishop, taking the lead in opposing the doctrine of the Latins entirely <note>original Greek: "ὧδε τὴν ἀρχὴν τιθεμένῳ τῷ τῆς Λατίνων δόγματι τῷ παράπαν"</note>, as did the one then held in high esteem among the Greeks for wisdom <note>referring to Scholarius; original Greek: "καὶ τῷ τῷ τότε παρ' Ἕλλησι τὰ εἰς σοφίαν εὐδοκιμοῦντι"</note>, and nothing was accomplished by them,* etc. In this, I say, Rivetus was deceived by an error of the Latin translator, and wrongly understood those words—"opposing the doctrine of the Latins entirely"—as if they were said of Scholarius as much as of Mark. Nevertheless, even Rivetus would not deny that the earlier part of the passage regarding the "wise Greeks who rejected the synod held in Italy" must be applied to Scholarius no less than to Mark. Add to this the authority of Phranzes and Rhacendytes, who affirm that Scholarius by no means joined the Latins in the Synod of Florence; and the arguments that suggest there was only one George Scholarius. Certainly, we have the best reasons either to reject these Speeches or at least to doubt them. However that may be, it is more than sufficiently clear that Scholarius later agreed with the Latins. In the year 1453, after Constantinople was captured by the Turks, while still a layman, he was elevated to the vacant Patriarchal throne of the City by Emperor Mehmed <note>Sultan Mehmed II "the Conqueror"</note>; and he was showered with many unusual honors. At the start of his Patriarchate, the Tyrant <note>A common historical term for the Sultan</note> escorted him on foot from the Palace to the Patriarchal residence, and later listened not unwillingly as he discussed sacred matters. He presided over the See of Constantinople for five years, having changed his name from George to Gennadius; until, weary of governance—either because he grieved over the Greeks' perpetual hatred toward the Latins, or because he ceased to hope further for the conversion of Mehmed to the Christian faith—he laid down the burden, abdicated the Patriarchate, and retired to a monastery; dying around the year 1460.

### W R I T I N G S.

*An Epistle or hortatory Speech on entering into union with the Latins*, addressed to the Eastern Bishops in the Synod of Florence. At the very beginning of this work, evidence of forgery <note>original: "τῆς νοθείας"</note> is clear on the first reading. For the author prefaces his work by asking for pardon because he dares to involve himself in this business uninvited—whereas it is clearer than the sun from Sguropulus that Scholarius, even before leaving Constantinople, was very much involved in all the consultations of the Emperor and the Bishops regarding the forming of the union.

*Three other Speeches*, very lengthy, addressed to all the Fathers of the Synod of Florence. These four Speeches exist in Greek and Latin, translated by Matthew Caryophilus, at the end of the *Acts of the Council of Florence*, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 13, page 544.

*Exposition, or Apology for the holy and Ecumenical Synod of Florence, and a Defense of five Chapters defined in the Council against the Greeks*, namely: on the Procession of the Holy Spirit, the Sacrifice in Unleavened Bread, Purgatory, the Beatific Vision of the Saints, and the Primacy of the Pope. Peter Arcudius and Matthew Caryophilus—both most devoted to the Papal side—deny that this is a genuine work of Gennadius and confirm their opinion with many arguments. Leo Allatius, in *On the Consent*, book 3, chapter 6, section 2, attacks their reasoning and at great length claims the work for Gennadius. It was published in Latin at Dillingen, 1581, octavo; in Greek at Rome, 1577, octavo; and in the common language of the Greeks <note>Modern Greek</note> with a Latin version at Rome, 1628, quarto.

<meta>This page continues the bibliography of Gennadius Scholarius (George Scholarius), the first Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople under Ottoman rule. It also introduces biographical entries for Pope Callistus III and the philosopher Nicolaus de Orbellis.</meta>

<header>The Synodal Century.</header>

<sig>* S 2</sig>

<margin>15th CENTURY. from the Year 1400.</margin>
Oration to Emperor John <note>John VIII Palaiologos</note> in the Synod of Florence, when the Emperor sought his opinion on the union <note>The proposed union between the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches</note>. It is held in Greek and Latin in the *Councils*, Volume 13, page 478.

A very short oration made to the same Emperor at Constantinople, when he was consulted by him concerning the union. In Greek and Latin in Syropoulos, Section 3, chapter 6.

Confession, or Sermon held with Muhammad <note>Mehmed II, the Conqueror</note>, Emperor of the Turks, concerning the true faith of Christians: which Achmetes, the Governor of Beroea, translated into the Turco-Arabic language for the favor of Muhammad. It exists in Greek, Latin, and Turco-Arabic in Crusius’s *Turco-Graecia*, Book 2, page 110. Also in Greek and Latin in D. Chytraeus’s *Oration on the State of the Churches in Greece*, etc., Frankfurt 1583, octavo, page 173.

A small book on the Articles of Faith addressed to the same Muhammad, or a Dialogue on the way of human salvation, with the Turk questioning and the Patriarch responding. It is held in Greek and Latin in the *Haeresiologia* <note>A collection of writings on heresies</note>, Basel 1556, page 797, and published separately by Fuchtenius at Helmstedt, 1611, octavo.

A Treatise on Predestination addressed to Joseph, a monk of Thessaloniki. Published in Greek by D. Hoeschel at Augsburg, 1593, quarto. In Greek and Latin by Fred. Morel after the Appendix to the *Works of St. Basil*, Paris 1618. Finally illustrated with a new version and commentaries by Carolus Libertinus of the Society of Jesus, Greek and Latin, Wrocław 1681, quarto.

Oration on the one God in nature, and three in Persons <note>The Trinity</note>. Printed in Greek and Latin by Aldus Manutius together with the Hymns of [John] Damascene and others, Venice 1501, quarto.

All these works of Gennadius exist (except for the two Orations to Emperor John) in Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 26.

Exposition of the letters carved on the tomb of Constantine the Great concerning the destruction of the City of Constantinople and the empire of the Turks. It is held in Greek at the end of the *Chronicle* of Dorotheus, Metropolitan of Monemvasia, and the *Synopsis of Histories* by Matthew Cigala, both printed at Venice 1637, quarto.

Gennadius wrote besides this a Response to the arguments of Mark of Ephesus <note>Mark Eugenikos, a leading Orthodox opponent of the Union of Florence</note> concerning the Procession of the Holy Spirit, which, left incomplete by him as he was snatched away by death, someone else finished: (this was Cardinal Bessarion, if Caryophilus is to be believed); and a Response to the argument of the Greeks. Leo Allatius mentions that both works exist in manuscript in *On Consent*, Book 3, chapter 6, § 5. He also mentions other things written by Gennadius, still preserved in various libraries as manuscripts, in his *Discourse on the Georges*, page 400, etc.; for instance, a *Book on the Soul*; *On the empty, absurd, and disordered innovation of faith*; a *Canon* <note>A type of liturgical hymn</note> to Gregory Palamas, Archbishop of Thessaloniki, etc., to say nothing of the many things he translated from the Latin into the Greek language.

---

<margin>1455.</margin>
CALLISTUS III. Previously called Alfonso Borgia, of Spanish descent, a Catalan by birth, son of John. Educated in fine letters at the Academy of Lleida, he earned a Doctorate in both laws <note>Civil and Canon law</note>. Soon summoned as secretary and correspondent to Alfonso, King of Aragon; in the year 1429, he was created Bishop of Valencia by Pope Martin V, and by Eugenius IV he was created Cardinal with the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs around the year 1440. In the year 1455, he was elected Roman Pontiff on the 8th of April and crowned on the 20th, heavy now with decrepit age. Having entered the Pontificate, he immediately declared war on the Turks; having sent legates everywhere, he stirred up the Christian Princes and granted the most ample indulgences to the soldiers. And to encourage the Christians, he instituted and ordered the celebration of the Feast of the Transfiguration of Our Lord Jesus Christ. He himself, with thirteen armed galleys, devastated the coasts of the Turks; and at his death, he bequeathed one hundred and fifty thousand gold coins to be spent on the holy war. He died in the year 1458, on the 6th of August. Three letters exist in *Councils*, Volume 13, page 1391; nine others among the letters of Aeneas Sylvius <note>Pope Pius II</note>; and the *Office of the Transfiguration* among other Offices of the Roman Church.

---

<margin>1456.</margin>
NICOLAS D’ORBELLIS, or Dorbellus, French by nationality, of Angers by birth, a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note> of the Province of Tours, Professor of Scholastic Theology and Philosophy at the Academy of Poitiers. A most fierce champion of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a hugely influential medieval philosopher</note>, he flourished under Callistus III around the year 1456. Nothing is certain regarding his death.

A Commentary or Compendium on the four books of the *Sentences* <note>Peter Lombard's "Sentences" was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, according to the doctrine of Lord John Duns Scotus. *Haguenau 1503, quarto. Paris 1511, 1517, octavo. 1520.*
Sermons on all the Epistles of Lent <note>Quadragesima refers to the forty days of Lent</note>, *Lyon 1491.*

Eight books of Commentaries on Aristotle's *Physics*; two books *On the Heavens*; two books *On Generation and Corruption*; books on the *Meteorology*; twelve books on the *Metaphysics*; ten books on the *Ethics*. These appeared together with the preceding short work, *Basel 1503.*

<margin>1457.</margin> **GULIELMUS HOUPELANDUS** <note>William Houpeland</note>, a Frenchman by nation, born in Boulogne-sur-Mer, was granted a Master's degree in Theology at the University of Paris in 1457. Then he undertook the governance of the parish of Saint-Séverin as Archpriest in Paris, soon becoming a Canon of the Church of the Blessed Mary <note>Notre-Dame de Paris</note> and Archdeacon of Brie. Finally, as the Dean of the Faculty of Theology, he died in the year 1492 on the 2nd day of August. He wrote:
A Book on the Immortality of the Soul, and its state after death, most full of the various opinions of ancient Fathers, whether Philosophers, Poets, Catholic Doctors, or holy men. This appeared in *Paris, 1499, octavo.*

<margin>1457.</margin> **JACOBUS DE PARADISO** <note>James of Paradise, also known as Jacob of Jüterbog</note>, a German by nation, as it seems, a monk of the Carthusian Order, and a Doctor of Erfurt. He flourished in the year 1457. He wrote many things; of which the following appeared in print: *A Collection on the seven states of the Church mystically described in the Apocalypse, and on the authority of the Church, and on its reformation* in the *Antilogia Papae* <note>original: "Antilogia Papæ", a collection of writings critical of the papacy</note>, *Basel 1555, octavo, page 462;* found in Goldast's *Monarchia*, Volume 2, page 1567; and in the *Appendix to the Collection of Desired Matters, London 1688, folio.* Three Treatises, namely: *On the art of curing vices, On the lament of a sinner, and On the state and office of Ecclesiastical Persons, Amsterdam 1617. A Treatise on souls released from the body, Basel ———. quarto. A Book on telling or concealing the truth, Basel ——— folio*, as attested by Simler in the *Bibliotheca Tigurina, page 321.*

<margin>1458.</margin> **PIUS II.** Formerly called Aeneas Sylvius, an Italian by nation, born in Siena, originating from the illustrious Piccolomini family, the son of Sylvius and Victoria. He was born in Corsignano <note>modern Pienza</note> in the year 1405. In his native town, he learned grammar; however, he was so constrained by the narrowness of his family’s poverty that he was forced to perform all the duties of the countryside due to lack of means. In the year 1423, using the help of friends, he moved to the Gymnasium of Siena: where he primarily heard and read poets and orators; and in a short time, he published poems in both the Latin and Etruscan <note>Italian/Tuscan</note> languages. Then he applied himself to Civil Law. In the year 1431, however, he departed his homeland due to a serious war that arose among the citizens; and in the retinue of Cardinal Capranica, he set out for the Council of Basel. He was held in the highest honor by the Fathers for his rare learning; in turn, he strenuously defended the party of the Council for a whole decade with his voice and writings. Having been appointed Secretary of that Synod, Clerk of Ceremonies, Abbreviator of letters, and one of the Twelve Men (which was considered an illustrious magistrate there, almost censorial), he spoke seven times before the Council; he often presided over the Collators of Benefices; he undertook frequent embassies, sent once to Trent, a second time to Constance, once to Frankfurt, again to Savoy, and a third time to Strasbourg: where he admitted a crime <margin>* Book 1, Epistle 15.</margin> <note>This refers to his illegitimate child, a fact he famously detailed in a letter to his father</note> which he so little lamented that, in letters sent to his father, he almost boasted of it. Around the year 1437, while an open schism was burning between [Pope] Eugenius and the people of Basel, and the Pontiff was acting with "thunderbolts" <note>excommunications</note> and deprivations, while others slipped away secretly or defected openly, Aeneas remained constantly attached to the Synod.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, who would become Pope Pius II. It details his transition from a supporter of the Council of Basel and the antipope Felix V to a loyal servant of the Roman papacy and Emperor Frederick III, culminating in his own election to the papacy and his subsequent efforts to consolidate papal power and launch a crusade.</meta>

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15th CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
† Bull of Retraction.
</margin>
...he thought it necessary to do so. "We," he said †, "since we had nothing that could be taken from us, thought we should persevere, lest by abandoning the part which appeared truer to us, we should cause the loss of our soul." <note>Aeneas is explaining his earlier stubbornness in supporting the Council of Basel against the Pope</note> In the year 1439, he was admitted to the secrets of Pope Felix <note>Felix V was the antipope elected by the Council of Basel in opposition to Eugenius IV</note>; and shortly after, sent as a legate to Emperor Frederick, he earned the honor of being crowned poet laureate by the Emperor and deserved to be called among his friends. In 1442, summoned by Frederick from Basel, he moved to the Imperial court; having been made Prothonotary or Secretary of the Empire and co-opted into the Senatorial Order, he still did not yet dare to condemn the supporters of the Council of Basel; nor did he fully join the side of Pope Eugenius, but remained among the neutrals. Gradually, however, as Frederick moved to the side of Eugenius, Aeneas himself also changed his opinion step by step; and after he held the Imperial place at the Diet of Regensburg, where they discussed ending the Schism, and performed a double legation to Eugenius; at length, persuaded by Thomas of Sarzana <note>The Apostolic Legate in Germany who later became Pope Nicholas V</note>, he submitted his neck to Eugenius; and at the end of 1446 or the beginning of 1447, sent by Frederick to Rome, he brought the obedience of the German nation to the Apostolic See. After the death of Eugenius, he was chosen by the Cardinals to preside over the conclave during the interregnum. Gifted with the Bishopric of Trieste by Pope Nicholas, he returned to Germany; and chosen among the counselors by the Emperor, he managed the most serious affairs of the Empire. After four years, elevated to the Bishopric of Siena in the year 1452, he followed Frederick who had set out for Rome to receive the imperial crown, and was appointed Legate of Bohemia and all the regions of Austria during the return journey. Around the year 1456, sent to Italy by the Emperor to consult with the Pope and other Princes about waging war against the Turks, he received the Cardinal's purple from Callixtus III. After the death of Callixtus, in the year 1458, he was elected Roman Pontiff on the 19th of August and crowned on the 3rd of September. Great hope had been conceived of him, based on his learning and his most abundant promises that the Church would be reformed anew under his leadership. But he greatly disappointed that hope; having issued the *Bull of Retraction* <note>original: "Bulla Retractationis"</note>, he revoked those things which he had done in the Council against Pope Eugenius; and he openly declared that he would bring disobedient kings and princes back to the service of the Apostolic See by open force; he declared that a Council ought to be subject to the Pope; and having issued a Bull, he forbade anyone from appealing from a Pope to a Council under penalty of excommunication; and to use the words of Platina and Stella <note>Bartolomeo Platina and Johannes Stella, Renaissance historians</note> concerning him: *He did not cease to pursue with war, censures, interdicts, and curses any kings, dukes, peoples, or tyrants who sinned against him or any ecclesiastic, until he knew they had returned to health <note>original: "ad sanitatem rediisse," meaning a return to the "healthy" state of obedience to the Church</note>.* He spent almost the final times of his Pontificate preparing for a war against the Turks who were daily advancing to greater things; and when he had gathered a huge army of Crusaders and auxiliary soldiers, and had led them to be placed on the fleet at Ancona; seized by a slow fever there, he died in the year 1464 on the 14th of August. Carried back to Rome, he was buried in the Vatican.

### WORKS.

*The Bull of Retractions* of all things formerly done by him against Pope Eugenius in the Council of Basel. It stands in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 13, page 1407.

*Two books of Commentaries on the deeds of the Council of Basel.* They appeared in the *Collection of things to be sought* <note>original: "Fasciculo rerum expetendarum," a famous collection of texts on church reform</note>, Cologne 1535; separately at Basel 1577, octavo.

*A book on the Coronation of Felix V, Supreme Pontiff.*

*A book on the origin, region, and deeds of the Bohemians, or a Bohemian History from the first origin of the race up to the year 1458.* It appeared separately at Rome 1475, folio; Basel 1532, 1575; Hanau 1602, folio; Solingen 1528; Amberg 1593, quarto.

*Twenty books of Abbreviations of Flavio Biondo's Histories from the decline of the Empire up to the times of Pope John XXIII.* These are held together with Biondo's *History*, Venice 1484; separately at Basel 1533. <note>Flavio Biondo was a pioneering Renaissance historian; Aeneas condensed his massive work for easier reading</note>

*The first book of Cosmography, or Histories of the whole world, in which he treats of Asia Minor*, Paris 1534, octavo; Cologne 1573.

*Europe, or the second book of Cosmography, in which he embraces various histories of his own time.* Paris 1543, octavo; Cologne 1573, octavo; and in Freher’s *German Writers*, Hanau 1602, Volume 2, page 37.

*Commentaries* on the four books of the poet *Antonio Panormita* <note>original: "Antonii Panormitæ"</note> concerning the memorable sayings and deeds of *Alfonso, King of Aragon*. Published at Hanover, 1611, in quarto; Wittenberg, 1585, in quarto, with the commentaries of *Jakob Spiegel*; and at Rostock, 1590, in quarto, edited by *David Chytraeus*.

from the Year 1400.
1458.

# JOHANNES GOBELINUS, Vicar of Bonn, and Secretary to Pope Pius II.

He flourished in the year 1458. He was, as it seems, a veteran courtier of the Roman Curia; for he testifies that he saw Popes Martin V, Eugenius IV, Nicholas V, and Callistus III. He survived Pope Pius. There exist under his name *Twelve books of Commentaries on the deeds of Pope Pius II, or rather on all things done throughout Europe under the Pontificate of Pius from the year 1458 to 1464.* There is not sufficient agreement among the learned as to who the actual author of these was. Many lean toward the opinion that Pius himself published them under another's name. I have little doubt that Pius was indeed the author. However, the opinion seems more plausible to me that this history was left incomplete by Pius when he was snatched away by death, and was revised, supplemented, and made public by Johannes Gobelinus. For the historian Platina has these things to say about Pius:

> He also wrote twelve books of the deeds of his time in Italy, a work which he ended with his life before it was finished, and he forbade it to be published unless it were corrected.

Whoever the author finally was, he begins the work with the origin of the Piccolomini house <note>The noble family of Pope Pius II</note>; and he prefaces his reliability with these words:

> But you, who shall someday read these things, be so kind as to forgive nothing if I tell a lie.

This work was published through the care of Francesco Bandini Piccolomini, Archbishop of Siena, at Rome in 1584 in quarto; and in 1589 with the commentaries of Giacomo Piccolomini at Frankfurt, 1614, in folio.

# ALPHONSUS SPINA, Spanish by nation, a Christian converted from Judaism, a Monk of the Franciscan Order, and Rector of the University of Salamanca.

He flourished in the year 1459. He himself provides evidence of having held the office of Inquisitor of the Faith, since he records that Alfonso Debeiar, a priest of Valladolid, was reported by him for heresy to Peter, Bishop of Palencia, and forced to recant <note>original: "ad Palinodiam adactum"</note>; for no other reason, truly, than that he preached that confessions of sins should be made to the Parish priest rather than to the Mendicant religious <note>The Mendicants were friars, such as Franciscans and Dominicans, who often clashed with local clergy over the right to hear confessions and receive tithes.</note>. Finally, our Alfonso is said to have obtained the Bishopric of Thermopylae <note>original: "Orinopolitanum" — a titular see often associated with the name Thermopylae</note>. 

Published with the author's name suppressed was *The Fortress of Faith against Jews, Saracens, and other enemies of the Christian faith*, Nuremberg, 1494, in quarto; and by the care of Guillaume Totan, of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, at Lyon in 1511. The title of the Nuremberg edition declares it to have been written by a certain "distinguished Doctor of the Order of Minors" <note>The Franciscans</note> in the year 1459 in Western parts. But the Author himself relates † that he applied himself to composing the work in the town of Valladolid in the year 1458. 

Finally, the author's name was indicated by Juan de Mariana ||, who, narrating the execution of Álvaro de Luna, Constable of Castile, who was beheaded by the King of Castile in 1453, reports that Alphonsus Spina was present at his death:

> ...he who published the *Fortress of Faith*, a work of learned scholarship under a splendid title—though in a barbaric tongue <note>Mariana, writing in a more polished era, likely considered Spina's medieval Latin "barbaric" compared to classical standards</note>—and outstanding in its knowledge of divine matters.

Therefore, those who attribute this work to Thomas, Patriarch of Grado <note>original: "Barbariensi"</note> are mistaken; as are those who ascribe it to Guillaume Totan, supported perhaps by no other reason than that Totan took care to have it printed again. It is truly a work of such a kind, and so far from being unworthy of the general knowledge of the learned, that I believe it will not be unwelcome to the reader to provide a summary of its scope and subject matter. 

For it supplies a complete history of Religion as it then existed in the Roman Church; it teaches by what arguments heretics and Jews attacked the dogmas of the Church—whether the added Roman ones or the genuine Christian ones—and how the Inquisitors defended them. It indicates which dogmas were considered to hold a place among the necessary articles of faith; and it demonstrates what the "balance" of the Roman faith was before the coarser dogmas were disguised by the trickery of recent Methodists <note>The author uses "Methodists" to describe 17th-century Catholic controversialists who sought "short methods" to win debates, not the later Protestant denomination</note>. 

In the first book, therefore, he deals with the spiritual weapons of the Christian faithful, and especially of preachers; on the best method of preaching, for which he places the Holy Scriptures as the sole foundation (just as it is for the whole faith) *; on the nobility and excellence of the Catholic faith, which he proves at length to be older, nobler, and more useful than the Jewish law; and having brought forward the prophecies of the Old Testament concerning the future Messiah, he demonstrates that all things were fulfilled exactly in Christ. To other arguments which Christians are accustomed to bring, however, he mixes in the foulest nonsense, and from the name of Jesus itself—which he imagines to be that famous Tetragrammaton and to have been completely unknown to the Jews before the birth of Christ—he hammers out nearly a hundred arguments, truly straw-like and emptier than coltsfoot leaves <note>original: "farfari foliis"</note>; which he nevertheless boasts <meta>catchword: ctitat</meta>

### JOANNES GOBELINUS, Vicar of Bonn, and Secretary to Pope Pius II.

He flourished in the year 1458. He appears to have been a veteran courtier of the Roman Curia <note>The administrative apparatus of the Holy See</note>; for he testifies that he saw Popes Martin V, Eugenius IV, Nicholas V, and Callistus III. He survived Pope Pius. There exist under his name *Twelve books of Commentaries on the affairs of Pope Pius II, or rather on all things done throughout all Europe under the Pontificate of Pius from the year 1458 to 1464.* It is not sufficiently agreed upon among the learned who the actual author of these was. Many lean toward the opinion that Pius himself published them under another's name. I have little doubt that Pius was indeed the author. However, the more likely opinion seems to be that this History was left unfinished by Pius when he was snatched away by death, and was then supplemented, revised, and published by Joannes Gobelinus. For Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina, a famous Renaissance humanist and papal biographer</note> has this to say about Pius: *He also wrote twelve books of the things done in Italy during his own time; a work not yet completed when he finished his life, and which he forbade to be published unless it were corrected.* Whoever the author finally was, he takes his beginning from the origin of the House of Piccolomini; and he pledges his good faith with these words in the preface: *But you, who shall read these things at some time, consider them well, so that you forgive nothing to a liar.* It was published through the care of Francesco Bandini Piccolomini, Archbishop of Siena, at Rome in 1584 in quarto, and in 1589 with the Commentaries of Jakob Piccolomini at Frankfurt in 1614 in folio.

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.

...holiness. <note>original: "ctitat," likely "sanctitat."</note> Lest you think him a man of little substance, he testifies that he composed twenty-two *Sermons on the wondrous properties of the name of Jesus*. In the second book, he attacks heretics; and having prefaced much concerning the definition, nature, and origin of heresy, he enumerates and attacks in order the heresies finally springing up again in his own century. Of these, nearly the middle part is occupied with the matter of priestly Confession and Absolution. The tenth point teaches that the indulgences of Bishops are useless. The eleventh denies that prayers for the dead made by those living in mortal sin are of any benefit. The twelfth point abolishes Purgatory <note>The author is summarizing the arguments of the heretics that Alfonso intends to refute.</note>. Throughout the work, the arguments of the heretics are brought fully into the open; to these, Alfonso is accustomed to subjoin somewhat weak <note>original: "frigidiusculas," literally "chilly" or "feeble."</note> solutions. Speaking of the necessity of priestly Confession, he acknowledges that in the time of Ambrose it was not yet received in the Church; yet he attacks as a most grave heresy the opinion of those who judged that the duty of hearing confessions belonged to the Parish Clergy rather than to the Mendicant Orders <note>Mendicant Orders, such as the Franciscans and Dominicans, were friars who relied on alms and often clashed with local parish priests over ecclesiastical rights.</note>. Disputing about Purgatory, he strives to prove it from the example of Christ. He contends that Christ's soul, once released from the body, was imprisoned in Purgatory for three days until the Resurrection; and he teaches that it is a most certain article of faith that Purgatory is located beneath the earth, and that it tortures the souls held there with the "punishment of sense" <note>The "poena sensus" refers to physical torment, such as fire, as opposed to the "poena damni," the spiritual pain of being separated from God.</note>. In the final section, he deals with the punishment for heresy and the method of conducting an Inquisition; finally, he proposes this question: *Whether in any case Heretics are to be tolerated?* He decrees that in the punishment of heresy three things may be considered: the gravity of the crime, the charity of the correcting church, and the utility of the faithful. As to the first, heretics, as soon as they are caught, *ought rather to be put to death than arsonists or forgers.* As to the second, *they are not immediately handed over to extermination, but following the order of fraternal correction, they are admonished once or twice. If they reject the warnings, they are by no means to be tolerated any longer.* As to the third, *if the heretics defend their error openly and withdraw into secret meetings, then they are to be exterminated without delay or inquiry.* In the third book, he presents the arguments of the Jews against the Christian faith. Many of these oppose the genuine articles of the Christian religion, but the stronger ones militate against the specific doctrines of the Roman Church. Indeed, in the twenty-fourth argument, he strives to show the Jewish proof *that Christians are idolaters, because they adore the sacrament of the altar, and because of the veneration of images.* For the Jews say *that Christians are the worst idolaters, adoring Christ, a pure man, as God; and what is worse, they adore a host made and baked by them from wheat as if it were God, which is laughable; and afterward they eat it, which is horrible. They also adore images, the work of men's hands. That, however, is against the law of God, Deuteronomy 6, etc.* In the sixth reason, the Jew contends that many impossible things are taught in the Christian law. The tenth: *It is impossible that the true body of Christ is in the sacrament of the altar, since Christ spoke figuratively, and not really, saying: "This is my body."* 11th: *It is impossible that the body of Christ be in the sacrament of the altar by a miracle, since it does not appear to the eye.* 12th: *It is impossible that the body of Christ begins to be on the altar, because it does so neither by local motion nor by the conversion of another into itself.* 13th: *It is impossible that the body of Christ be whole, and that the flesh and blood remain in separate places under the species <note>The "species" are the outward appearances of bread and wine that remain after the substance has supposedly changed.</note> of bread and wine.* 14th: *It is impossible that the body of Christ be contained in so small a host, since the greater cannot be contained in the smaller.* 15th: *It is impossible that the single body of Christ be simultaneously on different altars, since one body cannot be in different places at once.* 16th: *It is impossible that the flesh and blood of Christ be under the species of bread and wine, since it is impossible for bodies to be in the same place at the same time; namely, the substance of the bread and wine with the flesh and blood of Christ; since those accidents, as they say, do not exist by themselves, nor in the air, nor in the flesh and blood of Christ, but subjectively in the substance of the bread and wine.* 17th: *It is impossible that the incorruptible body of Christ be in the sacrament of the altar, since it can rot and be eaten by mice.* 18th: *It is impossible that the body of Christ be in the sacrament, since when that is broken into parts, only a substance can be broken.* 19th: *It is impossible that this sacrament be consumed and yet not used up.* 20th: *It is impossible that he who eats a part of the host of this sacrament eats the whole Christ, since every part is smaller than the whole.* 21st: *It is impossible that it sometimes happens that one part of this sacrament remains on the altar, and another falls to the earth...*

...and is trampled underfoot. This, however, is impossible to say of God, since God cannot fall nor be trampled underfoot. XXII. It is impossible that if that Christ of yours, who is in the Sacrament, were God, he would not lift himself up when he falls to the ground, and would not allow himself to be handled by evil and unclean priests. XXIII. It is impossible that the true God is in that sacrament, <note>original: "sacram m̄ nō" — shorthand for "sacramento non"</note> for the reason that it descends into the stomach and to the places of digestion when it is consumed. XXIV. It is impossible that the true body of Christ is in that sacrament through a daily miracle. At great length, the Jewish interlocutor pursues these individual impossibilities through just as many chapters; to these, Alfonso usually attaches some "feeble" response <note>original: "ficulnam," literally "made of fig-wood," a Latin idiom for something weak or worthless.</note>. Not infrequently, however, he sets down the opposing arguments of Jews and Heretics to which he himself does not usually add even a single word. The remainder of this book deals with the "cruelty" and hatred of the Jews toward Christians, their various "follies," their misfortunes, the destruction of Jerusalem, the expulsion of Jews from Christian Provinces, their punishments, their future conversion, and the coming of the Antichrist. The fourth book depicts the origin, life, sect, and "trifling doctrine" of Muhammad; he attacks it with various arguments, and having established a comparison between the Christian and Islamic faiths, he demonstrates the points of agreement and discord between the two. In the "Eighth Consideration," a Saracen <note>A historical term for a Muslim.</note> is imagined to be disputing against the Christian faith: and among other things, he brings forward a new argument against the images that are kept in churches.

> For the Saracens, mocking us alongside the Jews, say that these things are not permitted to us, because we act against the divine commandment in Exodus 20, Deuteronomy 28, and Leviticus 26. They even mock Christians because they depict God in effigy, etc.

In the rest of the book, he has woven together a history of the wars between Muslims and Christians from the death of Muhammad down to his own times. The fifth book, having found a sufficiently frivolous subject, deals with the essence, order, difference, and governance of Demons, as well as their deadly hatred against the Christian faith, their illusions, power, habitation, and torments.

### JACOBUS PICCOLOMINÆUS
<note>Giacomo Piccolomini-Ammannati (1422–1479), a prominent Renaissance humanist and Cardinal.</note>

<margin>1460.</margin>
GIACOMO PICCOLOMINI, an Italian by birth from Lucca, was a student of Carlo and Leonardo Aretino <note>The Aretino brothers were famous humanist scholars from Arezzo.</note> in the study of poetry and eloquence. After he had properly cultivated his mind with literature, he came to Rome and served as secretary to the Cardinal of Fermo while Nicholas V held the Papal throne. After the death of Nicholas, he was secretary to Callixtus III; he performed the same duty for Pius II (his kinsman), to whom he was especially beloved and close. He flourished in the year 1460, in which he was created Bishop of Pavia by Pius; twenty months later, he was admitted into the number of Cardinals with the title of Saint Chrysogonus. In the year 1487, he ceased to be a Cardinal Priest and began to be called the Bishop of Tusculum. He died at the Laurentian Grottos of Lake Bolsena on the 11th of September, in the year 1489 <note>The text likely contains a dating error; other records place his death in 1479.</note>, at the age of 57. He was buried at the church of the Augustinians in Rome. He wrote *Seven Books of Commentaries on events performed throughout the whole world over a five-year period.* He begins them with the journey of Pius II to Ancona (who was about to set out against the Turks) and ends with the death of Juan Carvajal, Cardinal of Sant’Angelo; thus, he leads the narrative from the year 1464 to 1469. They were published together with the *Commentaries* of Gobelinus at Frankfurt in 1614. There also exist 782 of his *Epistles*, written from the year 1462 to 1489. These were published in Milan in 1521. Indeed, both works appeared together at Milan in 1506 and Frankfurt in 1614. From the sixth book of his commentaries, a *Historical narrative concerning the Hussites and George Podiebrad, King of Bohemia* was published at Hanau in 1602.

---

### ANDRÆAS BARBATIUS
<note>Andrea Barbazza (c. 1410–1479), a famous Sicilian jurist.</note>

<margin>1460.</margin>
ANDREA BARBAZZA, or Barbatias, otherwise known as *Andreas de Bartholomeo*, was a Sicilian from the city of Messina. He was a Professor of both Civil and Canon Law, a student of Johannes de Imola, and most celebrated in his art—so much so that he was everywhere called the "Monarch of the Laws." He flourished in the year 1460. In his declining years, he began to teach law at Bologna; there, since he was carried away by a provocative desire to tear apart accepted opinions, he earned the name "The Doting Old Man." <note>original: "Deliri Senis"</note> He died at Bologna and was buried at the church of Saint Petronius.

**GREGORY OF HEIMBURG**, a German by birth, was a Doctor of Both Laws <note>original: "Juris utriusque Doctor" — referring to both Civil (Roman) and Canon (Church) law.</note> and, by the judgment of Aeneas Sylvius, <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II.</note> was easily the first among Germans in the knowledge of law and judgment; he was a most fierce enemy of Papal authority, if ever there was one. Being present at the Council of Basel, he manfully opposed the primacy of the Pope, and formed a very close friendship with Aeneas Sylvius. Soon after, called upon by the citizens of Nuremberg, he performed the duties of the Syndicate <note>A legal and administrative office representing the city's interests.</note> for thirty years with the highest praise. In the year 1460, he undertook the role of Advocate for Sigismund, Duke of Austria, who had recently been excommunicated by the Pope; in the Duke's name, he appealed to the next general Council. Not content with these actions, he did not fear to tear up the Roman See from its foundations, calling it in his published pamphlets a "Synagogue," "Babylon," and the "Babylonian Harlot." Driven into a rage by this, Pope Pius II forgot their old friendship and, at the end of the year 1460, devoted Gregory to the curses of excommunication; writing a letter to the people of Nuremberg, he ordered that Gregory be cast out from the city and his goods confiscated. Gregory appealed from the Pope to a Council, and withdrawing into Bohemia, he laughed at the threats of Pius. Later, recalled to Germany by Diether, Archbishop of Mainz, he died in peace; he ordered that verse of Paul's <note>1 Corinthians 4:3.</note> to be inscribed on his tomb:

<margin>
* 1 Corinthians 4:3.
</margin>

> No human day shall judge me. <note>original: "Non judicabit me humana dies." This reflects his rejection of earthly/papal judgment in favor of God's.</note>

### WRITINGS.

An Admonition to the Emperor, Kings, and Christian Princes regarding the unjust usurpations of the Roman Popes; or, a Confutation of Papal Primacy. Found in Goldast's *Monarchy*, Volume 1, p. 557.

*An Invective against Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, the defender of Papal fullness of power.* Ibid. p. 1626.
These small works were published separately in *Frankfurt*, 1608, in quarto; the first three appeared in the *Apology for the Pope*, Basel, 1555, in octavo, and in the *Appendix to the Collection of Desirable Things*, London, 1688, folio, p. 114.

<margin>1460.</margin>
**HENRY OF GORKUM**, or *Gorichemius*, a Belgian by nation and Dutch by birth, took his surname from his native village. A distinguished theologian and philosopher, and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cologne, he flourished in the year 1460. His surviving works include the *Treatise on certain superstitious cases or ecclesiastical ceremonies*, published at Cologne in 1503 (quarto) and Lyon in 1621 (octavo). Also, the *Work on the celebration of Feasts*, published in the same place. Further, the *Conclusions and Concordances of the Bible and Canons in the books of the Master of the Sentences*, <note>The "Master of the Sentences" refers to Peter Lombard, whose work was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> with added summaries and the errors of the "Master" condemned in Paris and England. This was published in Cologne (1502), Basel (1513), and Venice (1506). He also wrote a *Commentary on Aristotle’s books "On the Heavens and the World"*, printed by Quentel in 1501, and *Metaphysical Questions on Being and Essence*, published by the same in 1502. Valerius Andreas, in his *Belgian Library* (page 353), and Franciscus Sweertius, in his *Belgian Athenaeum* (page 328), list many more of his unpublished short works. Finally, Gorkum saw to the publication of the "Sentences" of Peter Lombard and Thomas Aquinas, adding titles and conclusions, printed at Basel (1492, folio) and Strasbourg (1489).

<margin>1460.</margin>
**GEORGE**, also called **GREGORY, HERMONYMUS** or *Charitonymus*, a monk from Sparta, withdrew to France after the conquest of Constantinople. He taught Greek letters publicly at the University of Paris, receiving an annual salary for that purpose. He flourished in the year 1460, particularly under Pope Sixtus IV, with whom he was quite intimate. He was sent by the Pope as an envoy to England in 1476 to intercede with King Edward for the release of the Archbishop of York, who had been imprisoned. His surviving works include Gennadius Scholarius’s booklet *On the life of man's salvation*, which he translated into Latin (found in the *History of Heresies*, Basel, 1556, folio, page 797). He also rendered the *Life of Mohammed* into Latin, published with other works (Basel, 1541, octavo). His *Demonstration that Christ is the Son of God, and God*, was published in Greek and Latin alongside the works of Cyril, Damascene, and Psellus (Augsburg, 1608, octavo). A *Monody <note>A monody is a poem or song of lamentation for a deceased person.</note> on the death of George Gemistus* is preserved in manuscript in the Augsburg Library (see the *Index of Manuscript Codices of that Library*, page 90).

<margin>1460. * On the Offices of Constantinople, chapter 2. † Book on the Emperors of Constantinople.</margin>
**GEORGE CODINUS**, a Greek by nation, was called the "Curopalates"; <note>original: "Curopalates" — a high-ranking Byzantine court title, originally the official in charge of palace management.</note> however, it is entirely uncertain whether this was the name of his office or his family. His age is no less uncertain. Miraeus dates him to the year 1460—certainly a gross error—since Codinus * expressly mentions Andronicus Palaeologus the younger and Emperor John Cantacuzenus. <note>These figures lived in the 14th century, much earlier than 1460.</note> Gretser approached the truth more closely, making Codinus contemporary with Emperor Cantacuzenus in chapter 2; yet even he was off by at least a full century. For Codinus wrote after the conquest of Constantinople by the Turks, as he narrates that the City was captured under Emperor Constantine Palaeologus by the impious Agarenes <note>original: "Agarenis" — a medieval term for Muslims, referring to descendants of Hagar.</note> in the year of the World 6961 (that is, 1453 AD), and that the Emperor † perished in a glorious death. Therefore, he did not live before 1453, nor, it seems, much later; thus he may rightly be placed around the year 1460.

### WRITINGS.

<margin>Appendix.</margin>
*A book on the Offices and Officials of the Court and Church of Constantinople*. It appeared in Greek and Latin with a translation and notes by Franciscus Junius (who wished to hide his name under the Hebrew pseudonym "Nadabus Agmonius") at Frankfurt, 1588 (octavo). It was later published in an expanded edition by the same author at Heidelberg, 1596 (octavo). A Greek-Latin edition by the translator Gretser, with three books of observations and emendations, was published at Paris, 1625 (folio). Finally, it was published with those same notes and the very extensive notes of Jacques Goar at Paris, 1648 (folio).

*A book on the Origins of Constantinople*, excerpted from a certain ancient chronicle. George Douza first published it in Greek and Latin at Heidelberg, 1596 (octavo). It was reprinted with the notes of Johannes Meursius at Geneva, 1607 (octavo). Lucas Holstenius (Lambecius) saw to a new edition with an improved translation and very learned notes added at Paris, 1655 (folio).

### HENRY OF GORKUM,
or *Gorichemius*, a Belgian by nation and a Dutchman by birth, took his surname from his native village. A distinguished theologian and philosopher, he served as the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cologne and flourished in the year 1460. His surviving works include: *A Treatise on Certain Superstitious Cases or Ecclesiastical Ceremonies*, Cologne 1503 in quarto, Lyon 1621 in octavo; *A Work on the Celebration of Feasts*, published in the same location; and *Conclusions and Concordances of the Bible and the Canons for the books of the Master of the Sentences*, <note>The "Master of the Sentences" refers to Peter Lombard, whose 12th-century textbook was the standard for all medieval theological study.</note> with summaries added, including the "errors of the Master" condemned in Paris and England; published in Cologne 1502, Basel 1513, and Venice 1506. <margin>1460.</margin>
### GEORGE (otherwise GREGORY) HERMONYMUS,
or *Charytonimus*, a monk from Sparta, withdrew to France after the fall of Constantinople. He taught Greek literature publicly at the University of Paris, receiving an annual salary for that purpose. He flourished in the year 1460, but was especially prominent under Pope Sixtus IV, to whom he was very close. In 1476, the Pope sent him as an envoy to England to secure the release of the Archbishop of York from prison through his intercession with King Edward IV. There exists a small book by Gennadius Scholarius, *On the Life and Salvation of Men*, translated by him into Latin in the *Heresiology*, Basel 1556, folio page 797. He also translated the *Life of Muhammad* into Latin, published with other works in Basel, 1541, in octavo. His *Demonstration that Christ is the Son of God and God*, in Greek and Latin, was published with the short works of Cyril, Damascene, and Psellus in Augsburg, 1608. A *Monody on the Death of George Gemistus* <note>George Gemistos Plethon was a famous Neoplatonist philosopher who reintroduced Greek learning to the West.</note> is preserved as a manuscript in the Augsburg Library; see the Index of Manuscripts of that library, page 90.

### GEORGE CODINUS,
a Greek by nation, called *Curopalates*; <note>The "Curopalates" was originally a high-ranking Byzantine court title meaning "Head of the Palace."</note> it is entirely uncertain whether this was his official title or a family name. His dates are no less uncertain. Miræus places him around the year 1460, which is a significant error, since Codinus explicitly mentions the Emperors Andronicus Palaeologus the Younger and John Cantacuzenus. <note>These emperors reigned in the 14th century, much earlier than 1460.</note> Gretser came closer to the truth, making Codinus a contemporary of Emperor Cantacuzenus. However, he was still off by at least a full century. Indeed, Codinus wrote after the fall of Constantinople to the Turks, as he narrates † that the City was captured by the "impious Agarenes" <note>original: "Agarenis" — a medieval term for Muslims, referring to the descendants of Hagar.</note> in the year of the world 6961 (which is 1453 A.D.) under the Emperor Constantine Palaeologus, and that the Emperor met a glorious death. Therefore, he did not live before 1453; nor, it seems, much after it; thus, he may rightly be placed around the year 1460.

---

->W R I T I N G S.<-

<margin>Appendix.</margin>
*A book on the Offices and Officials of the Court and Church of Constantinople*. It appeared in Greek and Latin with the version and notes of Franciscus Junius (who wished to hide his name under the Hebrew-derived pseudonym "Nadab Agmonius") <note>The pseudonym "Agmonius" is a Greek-Latin pun on "Junius," both relating to reeds or rushes.</note> at Frankfurt, 1588; then an enlarged edition by the same author at Heidelberg, 1596. A Greek-Latin version by the translator Gretser, with three books of observations and emendations, Paris 1625; and finally with the same and the very extensive notes of Jacques Goar, Paris 1468.

*A book on the Origins of Constantinople*, excerpted from a certain ancient chronicle. Georgius Douza first published it in Greek and Latin at Heidelberg, 1596; it was reprinted with the notes of Johannes Meursius at Geneva, 1607. Lucas Holstenius (Lambecius) oversaw a new edition with a corrected translation and very learned notes added, Paris 1655.

from the Year 1400.

*A small book on the layout of the City of Constantinople.* <note>original: "De formâ Urbis Constantinopolitanæ libellus"</note> This was published in Greek and Latin together with the preceding short work, featuring the very learned observations of Peter Lambeck, *Paris, 1655, folio.*

*A book on the signs, statues, and other sights worth seeing in Constantinople.* <note>original: "Liber de signis, statuis, & aliis spectatu dignis Constantinopolis"</note> Published in Greek and Latin in a partial version by Jan Dousa with notes by Johannes Meursius, *Geneva, 1607, octavo.* The complete version with the translation and observations of Lambeck was published in *Paris, 1655, folio.*

*A book on the buildings of Constantinople.* <note>original: "Liber de ædificiis Constantinopolitanis"</note> This is available in Greek and Latin from the translation by Lambeck, illustrated with his notes, among the earlier short works, *Paris, 1655, folio.*

*A book on the construction of the Temple of Saint Sophia in Constantinople.* <note>original: "Liber de structurâ Templi S. Sophiæ CP."</note> Greek and Latin with notes by Meursius, *Leiden, 1607, octavo;* also with Lambeck’s observations, *Paris, 1655, folio.*

*A book on the Emperors of Constantinople, or on the years from the creation of the world to the Empire of Constantine the Great, and on those who reigned in that city until it was captured by the Turks.* <note>original: "Liber de Imperatoribus Constantinopolitanis..."</note> Published in Greek and Latin with the translation and notes of the celebrated Lambeck, *Paris, 1655, folio.* He also translated the *Dialogues* of Pope Gregory into the Greek language, <note>referred to here as the "Mass" or Liturgy in the original text</note> which was published in Greek by Morellus, *Paris, 1595, Greek and Latin;* and by François Du Jon in the *Supplement, Volume 2, page 125.* Leo Allatius, in his *Discourse on the Georges and their writings (page 362)*, notes that a much longer and more perfect version is held in the Barberini Library (Codex 75), though it is attributed there to Manuel Chrysoloras.

---

<margin>1464.</margin>

## PAUL II.
Formerly known as Peter Barbo, a Venetian by birth, the son of Nicholas and Polyxena, and the nephew of Pope Eugene IV through his sister. Though initially intent on a career in commerce, he dedicated himself to the study of letters after his uncle attained the Papal throne, using Giacomo Ricionio as his teacher. Soon after, he was called into the clergy by Eugene and was appointed Archdeacon of Bologna, Bishop of Cervia, Apostolic Protonotary, and created Cardinal with the title of Saint Mark. In the year 1464, he was elected Pope by the common vote of all on the 31st of August, and crowned on the 9th of September. Having undertaken the Papacy, he considered nothing more important than to repeal the acts of his predecessor, Pius II, and to treat his predecessor's friends with injury, while seeking to increase Papal authority through arms and intrigue. In 1466, in a Consistory, <note>A formal meeting of the Pope and Cardinals.</note> he condemned George of Poděbrady, King of Bohemia, who was a follower of the Hussites, <note>A pre-Protestant Christian movement following the teachings of Jan Hus.</note> with a sentence of heresy, struck him with an excommunication, and decreed he should be stripped of his kingdom. When Emperor Frederick turned down the offer of that realm, Paul granted it by Apostolic authority to Matthias, King of Hungary. Furthermore, through his legate to Bohemia, Lorenzo Roverella (the Bishop of Ferrara), he incited George’s subjects to rebellion. He was the first of all to make the use of the scarlet hat exclusive to Cardinals. He died of a sudden stroke in the year 1471 on the 26th of July, at the age of 53. Two of his *Letters* survive in the *Collection of Councils, Volume 13, page 811;* many others are in the Collection published in *Rome, 1579,* and in Cherubini’s *Bullarium, Rome, 1638.*

## RODRIGO SÁNCHEZ DE ARÉVALO
<margin>* Book on the Academies and learned men of Spain.</margin>
A Spaniard by nation, born in the diocese of Segovia. After he had labored for a decade in the study of Law at the University of Salamanca, he was made a Professor of Both Laws <note>Civil law and Canon law.</note> and the Arts. Later, he served as Chaplain, Auditor, and Counselor to King Henry IV of Castile, as well as Apostolic Referendary. He served first as Bishop of Oviedo, then of Palencia, and finally of Calahorra; he flourished in the year 1466. He was appointed Governor of the Castel Sant’Angelo in the city of Rome by Pope Paul II. At the command of King Henry, he wrote the *Spanish History in four books*, covering from the first origins of the people until the year 1469. Regarding him, along with Lucas of Tuy and Rodrigo Jiménez, Alfonso García Matamoros offers this judgment: *Since they wrote not for the pleasure of the ears, but for the memory and judgment of posterity, they stayed far away from charms, and just as far from foolishness and lies.* That *History* was published separately in Italy, and later in *Frankfurt among the "Illustrious Men of Spain," Volume 1, page 121.* Three of his treatises also exist: *On Appealing a Sentence of the Pope*, *On General Synods*, *On Remedies for the Afflicted Church*, and *On Remedies against the Turks.* These are in manuscript in Padua in the Library of Saint John in the Orchard, as indicated by Tomasini in his *Book on the Libraries of Padua, page 12.* Whether they have been printed, I do not know. Simler, in the *Zurich Library (page 605)*, also mentions a *Mournful yet Consolatory Letter on the capture of the island of Negroponte by the Turks* by the same author. Furthermore, his *Mirror of Human Life* <note>original: "Speculum vitæ humanæ"</note> was printed in *Rome (1468, folio), Paris (1475, folio), and Besançon (1488, octavo).*

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>15TH CENTURY. from the Year 1400.</margin>
The *Mirror of Human Life* <note>original: "Speculum Humanæ Vitæ"</note> by our Rodrigo was published, divided into two books. The first deals with every state of temporal life; the second with the spiritual, ecclesiastical, and regular <note>meaning life under a religious rule, like a monk or friar</note> state and life. The work is dedicated to Pope Paul II and is devoted to describing in detail the advantages and disadvantages of every rank and condition of life.

<margin>1467.</margin>
ALEXANDER OF IMOLA, also known by the surname TARTAGNUS, an Italian by birth born at Imola (formerly Forum Cornelii), was a most celebrated doctor of both laws <note>original: "Juris utriusq; consultus"; meaning he was an expert in both Civil and Canon law</note> and a disciple of Johannes of Imola and Johannes Ananiensis. He publicly taught the science of law at Pavia, Ferrara, and Bologna for nearly thirty years. He flourished in the year 1467, distinguished by such a great reputation for erudition that anyone who had not heard him teaching could hardly be counted among the learned Italian jurists of that age. He died in the year 1487 at the age of 54, in his 30th year of teaching, and was buried at the Church of Saint Dominic in Bologna. His surviving works include *Commentaries on the Sixth Book of the Decretals and the Clementines* <note>original: "Commentaria in sextum Decretalium, & Clementinas"; these are primary sources of Canon Law</note>, and *Seven Books of Legal Counsels*, published in Venice, 1571 and 1597, folio. Also, *Commentaries on the Old Digest, the Code, the New Digest, and the Infortiatum* <note>original: "Commentaria in Digestum vetus, Codicem, Digestum novum, & Infortiatum"; these are the constituent parts of the Corpus Juris Civilis, the body of Roman Law</note>, Lyons, 1558; and *Additions to Baldus de Ubaldis on the Code, Digest, and Infortiatum*, Lyons, 1545.

<margin>1468.</margin>
<margin>* Biographical note on the Author, placed before the book "On the Method of Divine Psalmody."</margin>
HENRICUS HARPHIUS <note>also known as Hendrik Herp</note>, a Belgian by nationality from the village of Erp (or De Herp) in the Brabant Campine, was a theologian and Provincial of the Franciscan Order of the Regular Observance, and finally the Guardian of the convent at Mechelen. He flourished in the year 1468. He died at Mechelen in the year 1478 and was buried in the middle of the choir among his fellow Franciscans; he was a *learned, methodical, and singular Master of Mystical Theology*, to use the words of Cardinal Bona.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

THREE BOOKS on mystical theology, both speculative and affective. The first is called the *Wedding Song* <note>original: "Epithalamium"</note>, the second the *Golden Directory for Contemplatives* <note>original: "Directorium aureum contemplativorum"</note>, and the third *Eden, or the Paradise of Contemplatives*. They were published in Cologne in 1538 and 1555. By order of the Apostolic See, they were purged of errors and "dregs" under the care of Peter Paul Philippi of the Dominican Order, at Rome in 1585, Brescia in 1601, and Cologne in 1611, in quarto. Indeed, the Roman Index <note>the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the list of prohibited books</note> warns that they should not be printed henceforth except according to the "adulterated" <note>the author likely means "corrected" or "expurgated"</note> Roman edition of 1585. The second part had been written by Harphius in German <note>meaning Dutch or Flemish, the vernacular of his region</note>. Therefore, Peter Blomovenna, a Carthusian of Leiden, translated it into Latin and illustrated it with an introductory preface.

*The Golden Mirror on the Ten Precepts of the Decalogue.* Nuremberg 1481, Basel 1496, Strasbourg 1520, quarto.

*The Mirror of Perfection.* Venice 1524.

*Three Conferences on the Perfection of Life, or a Compendium of the Directory.* Cologne 1536.

*Sermons for the Liturgical Seasons and the Saints.* Haguenau 1509, folio.

*A Book on the Three Parts of Penance*, published at the same place.

*A Treatise on the Threefold Coming of Christ*, also at the same place. Furthermore, Harphius composed almost all his works in the Belgian tongue <note>Flemish/Dutch</note>, which were later translated into Latin by others.

LAONICUS CHALCOCONDYLAS, or Chalcondylas (some call him Nicolaus instead of Laonicus, reversing the name), a Greek by nationality and an Athenian by birth, descended from an illustrious family. He flourished around the year 1468. He is said to have extended his life until the year 1490. He wrote *A History of the Origin and Deeds of the Turks in Ten Books* <note>original: "Historiam de origine & rebus gestis Turcarum libris x."</note>, covering the period from Osman, son of Ertuğrul, until the height of the reign of Mehmed II—that is, from the year of Christ 1300 to 1463. It was published in Latin from the version of Conrad Clauser, Paris 1550, Basel 1556, 1562; and in Greek and Latin at Geneva 1615, folio, and Paris 1650, folio.

**PAUL II.** Previously called Pietro Barbo, a Venetian by birth, the son of Niccolò and Polissena, and nephew of Eugene IV through his sister. **RODERICK BORGIA**, Cardinal of Valencia, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. He died in the year 1491 and was buried in the Church of St. Augustine. <note>original: "Roderici Borgiæ... Episcopi Portuensis & Canensis." This refers to the future Pope Alexander VI, who was the patron of Jacob Perez of Valencia; the works listed below belong to Jacob Perez.</note>

<margin>1470.</margin> **PETER NATALIS**, or de Natalibus, a Venetian by birth, from the parish of the Holy Apostles in the Diocese of Castello, Bishop of Equilio in the Province of Grado. He flourished in the year 1470. He was still living in the year 1482, when he put the finishing touches on his *Catalog*. He wrote the *History*, or *Catalog of Martyrs and Saints*, in which he narrates their lives, miracles, and passions; he was indeed more brief and more diligent concerning the truth than Jacob de Voragine, though he did not use much greater judgment. <note>Jacob de Voragine was the author of the famous "Golden Legend." The author here suggests Natalis is slightly more factual but still prone to legends.</note> For besides the fact that he is not free from the common vice of martyrologists—a lust for storytelling—he also numbered the heresiarch Priscillian and his follower Latrocinianus among the martyrs; not to mention others. This *Catalog* appeared in Strasbourg, 1502; Lyons, 1542. By the same author, the *Catalog of Saintly Senators and Their Deeds* appeared in Vicenza, 1493.

<margin>1471.</margin> **SIXTUS IV**, previously called **FRANCESCO DELLA ROVERE**, an Italian by nation, from the city of Savona, born of the most noble della Rovere family, son of Leonardo and Lucchina, born in the year 1414. Finally honored with the degree of Master at Padua, he lectured on Theology and Philosophy in the primary academies. Having acquired no ordinary reputation for erudition and eloquence, he was first appointed assistant to James Sarzuela, the Minister General of the Franciscan family, who was weighed down by old age; then Minister of the Province of Liguria, soon thereafter Procurator of his Order at the Roman court, and Vicar General of Italy; finally, upon the retirement of Sarzuela, he was appointed Minister General at the Chapter of Perugia. In the year 1467, he was named Cardinal Priest of the Title of St. Peter in Chains <note>original: "Sancti Petri ad Vincula"</note> by Paul II. After the death of Paul, he was elected Roman Pontiff on the 9th and crowned on the 25th of August. # The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...having confirmed the Confraternity of the Rosary, he granted an indulgence of 11,000 years to all those who addressed the Blessed Virgin with a certain short salutation. <note>original: "breviculâ quâdam Salutatione"</note> See the *Venetian Breviary* printed in 1522; and Hippolytus Maraccius, *Book on the Marian Pontiffs, Rome 1642, chapter 76.* In the year 1478, he excommunicated Lorenzo de' Medici and the Florentines and pursued them with arms because of Francesco Salviati, the Archbishop of Pisa, a most wicked rebel <note>Salviati was a key figure in the Pazzi Conspiracy against the Medici family; Sixtus IV supported the conspirators.</note> who had been punished with a well-deserved penalty. Shortly thereafter, resenting the growing power of the Venetians in Italy, he placed the entire Republic under a sacred interdict; and, having sent a sacred banner, he incited the Swiss to wage war against them, promising a plenary remission of sins to all who would fight under that banner. In the year 1483, he issued a Bull <note>The Bull *Grave Nimis*</note> regarding the controversy between the Franciscans and Dominicans over the conception of the Blessed Virgin; as they were branding each other with the mark of heresy, he commanded them under pain of anathema to abstain from such insults in the future. He died in the year 1484, on the 12th day of August. He was a man learned beyond the common lot of Popes, who established the Vatican Library by bringing in books from everywhere in Europe; however, he was infamous for the most foul morals and so enslaved to impure lusts that writers are ashamed to reveal them. Certainly, he was the first of all to grant access and license to public brothels in Rome, and he enriched the Apostolic treasury from the annual tax on prostitutes. <note>original: "scortorum vectigali"</note> There exist his *Decrees of the Third Council, Volume 13, page 1442*; sixteen other *Letters and Decrees* in Bzovius for the year 1472, etc.; the *Passage for the Expedition to the Holy Land*, <note>original: "Passagium pro Expeditione in Terram Sanctam"</note> in Freher’s *German Writers, Volume 2, page 161*; the *Letter to Charles of Burgundy*, in Baluze’s *Miscellany, Volume 4, page 527*; and very many *Bulls and Constitutions in the Roman Bullaries and Constitutions.* Furthermore, while he was still among the Cardinals, Sixtus wrote a *Book on the Blood of Christ* and *Commentaries on the Power of God against the errors of a certain Carmelite of Bologna, who affirmed that God by His omnipotence could not save a damned man.* Both treatises were published in *Rome, 1471.* His *Explanation of Nicholas Richard’s Treatise on the declaration of Indulgences granted for souls in Purgatory* was printed together with the said work of Nicholas in 1487. Lucas Wadding, in *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor, page 317*, and Ludovicus Jacob à Sancto Carolo, in *Library of the Pontiffs, page 203*, record that his *Treatise on Future Contingents* and his *Treatise on the Conception of the Most Blessed Virgin* are preserved in manuscript in Italian libraries.

<margin>1473.</margin>
## MARTIN THE MASTER
Known by the surname <term>Magister</term> <note>Latin for "The Master"; in French, Martin Le Maître.</note>, he was of the French nation, born in Tours of a very humble station, being the son of a certain butcher. Received into the College of Navarre, he earned his Bachelor’s degree in 1469 and the degree of Master with great praise in 1473. Afterward, retiring to the College of St. Barbara, he not only governed it but increased it with no small improvements; he lectured on Moral Philosophy with such renown that, shortly before his death, he was summoned to serve as the Confessor and Almoner to King Louis XI. He died at the age of fifty in the year 1482. His extant works include the *Book, or Moral Questions on Fortitude, Paris, 1489, folio*; the *Book on Temperance, Paris, 1490*; a *Very Useful and Necessary Exposition on Porphyry’s Book of Predicables, Paris, 1499* <note>Porphyry's *Isagoge*, a standard introductory text for medieval logic.</note>; the *Treatise on Consequences in the true and divine way of the Nominalists, Paris*, published by Denis Roce; and the *Question on Fate*, prefixed to *Albertus Magnus’s Compendium on the eight books of Physics, Paris*, published by Denis Roce.

<margin>1474.</margin>
## RUDOLPH AGRICOLA
A Frisian by birth, born in the village of Baflo near Groningen around the year 1442. After he had successfully laid the first foundations of literature at Groningen, he went to the University of Louvain, where he devoted himself to the study of philosophy and the liberal arts at the Falcon College. Having been granted the laurel of Philosophy, he withdrew to France so that he might bring his knowledge of "polite literature" <note>original: "politioris literaturæ," referring to the refined Latin and Greek of the Humanists.</note>—which he sought above all else—to the highest peak of perfection. Leaving France, he sought out Italy so that he might hear Theodore Gaza, who was then explaining Greek literature at Ferrara with great glory to his name. Having achieved his wish, he also added a knowledge of the Hebrew language, which was almost unknown in that century. Equipped with so many and such great gifts of mind, he returned to his homeland and [became] the Syndic <note>A legal representative or magistrate.</note> of the Republic of Groningen...

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...he spent some years. He flourished in the year 1474. Having been appointed as a legate by his fellow citizens to handle public business, he remained in the court of Emperor Maximilian for a period of six months; he successfully managed his homeland's cause, yet, by the common fate of great men, he experienced very little gratitude from his citizens. Having returned home, when he was requested by the people of Antwerp and others to direct their schools for a generous salary; he was summoned in the year 1482 by his intimate friend <note>original: "nectario suo," suggesting a very close or "sweet" companion</note>, Johann von Dalberg, the Bishop of Worms—to whom he had once read Greek literature—and he spent the rest of his life in Dalberg’s company, living sometimes in Worms and sometimes in Heidelberg. In both places, he publicly taught the humanities; indeed, he even held the rectorship of the Heidelberg Academy. This position had been conferred by Philip, Prince Palatine, who not only honored Agricola with a generous salary but also consulted him on matters of the greatest importance. Within three years, he held forth a torch for the study of better literature for the Academy of Heidelberg and all of Germany; he himself, besides his accurate knowledge of the three languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, the hallmark of a Renaissance scholar</note>, was most highly cultured in every kind of science: a supreme philosopher, an eloquent rhetorician, a distinguished theologian, and most devoted to music, painting, and other gentler arts. He died in Heidelberg, snatched away by an untimely death while he was occupied with translating the books of Dionysius the Areopagite into Latin, on October 28, in the year 1485, at the age of 42. He was buried among the Minorites in the Franciscan habit (for so he had wished). Ermolao Barbaro <note>A famous Italian humanist</note> placed a tomb for him; Johannes Reuchlin <note>A key figure in the German Renaissance and Hebrew studies</note> performed the funeral rites. Let Erasmus give his judgment on Agricola's style <margin>* Ciceronian.</margin>: "In a man of divine heart and hidden erudition," he said, "his style is by no means common; it is solid, vigorous, elaborate, and composed. However, it somewhat tastes of both Quintilian in its eloquence and Isocrates in its sentence structure, yet he is more sublime than either, and more expansive and clear than Quintilian. And yet, some other things stood in the way of his highest praise; especially the misfortune of his region and time. In Italy he could have been the greatest, had he not preferred Germany." I pass over that magnificent eulogy which Erasmus gave him in the Adage, *what has a dog to do with a bath!* <note>original: "quid cani cum balneo!"—a proverb used to describe someone out of place or unappreciated</note>; in that place, this greatest of men seems to have played the part of a flattering orator rather than a critical censor. He ranges widely there in praise of Agricola; he asserts that the world north of the Alps <note>original: "Cisalpinum orbem"</note> never produced anyone more perfect in all literary gifts. He proclaims his consummate eloquence, his widespread skill in languages, and his refined knowledge of philosophy; finally, he testifies that he was a supreme ornament to both Italy and Germany alike. The Papal Inquisitors of books took such a notable eulogy of Rudolph badly, so much so that it nowhere appears in the Aldine <note>original: "Manutianâ," referring to the publishing house of Aldus Manutius</note> edition of Erasmus's *Adages*. For it cannot be hidden that our Rudolph quite often and sharply attacked the manifest corruptions of the Roman Church in both his writings and his speeches.

**Bartholomew Platina**, called **Sacchi** by his father's name (others call him Baptist; but he is Bartholomew, according to Richard Fleming * who knew him well), was Italian by race and of Cremona by homeland, though some say of Verona; he took his surname from his home village <note>Platina is the Latin name for his birthplace, Piadena</note>. Born in a humble place and of obscure parents, he gave his youth to military service. Later in years, he applied himself to letters with no little success; he flourished in the year 1474. He came to the city <note>Rome</note> during the reign of Calixtus III and was admitted among the household staff by Cardinal Bessarion. Soon after, having been made an **Apostolic Abbreviator** <term>Abbreviator: a high-ranking papal official who drafted and condensed petitions and bulls into their final form</term> by Pope Pius II, he received priesthoods of no small value as a gift. 

After the death of Pius, he was removed from his position by Paul II and stripped of all his goods, for no other reason than that he had been held in honor under Pius. Platina took this very badly; besieging the Palace for twenty continuous days, and being by no means admitted to talk with the Pope, he sent a letter threatening to defect to kings and princes and urging them to call a Council <note>A General Council of the Church, which was often used as a political threat against the Pope's absolute authority</note> in which the Pope would be forced to give an account of his deeds. Paul punished Platina’s insolence with a very harsh prison and shackles. After four months in prison, he was freed by the prayers of Cardinal Gonzaga of Mantua and entered the Cardinal’s service. 

After three years, Paul ordered him to be arrested again, charged him with treason <note>original: "læsæ majestatis," literally 'injured majesty'</note>, and when he denied it, the Pope put him on the rack <note>original: "equuleo," a torture device</note> and tortured him with the heaviest torments. When indeed by no skill and no cruelty could he extort a confession of the crime, he accused the poor man of heresies; namely, because he used to dispute about the immortality of the soul and "wore out" <note>studied intensely</note> the writings of Plato and other philosophers. Finally, worn down by the prayers of Cardinals Bessarion and Gonzaga, the Pope led Platina out of prison after a year's stay; for the following two years, he enticed him with the vain hope of having his dignity restored. 

When Paul was removed from the living, he was succeeded by Sixtus IV, who, knowing well Platina’s innocence as well as his learning, chose him among his associates, enriched him with wealth, gave him a house on the Quirinal Hill, and put him in charge of the **Vatican Library**. He died in Rome, wiped out by the plague, in the year 1481, at the age of 60, and was buried in the Church of Saint Mary Major. He was a man indeed not unlearned, and one who, in the judgment of Erasmus *, would have been powerful in history if he had obtained a happier subject matter. In his *The Best Citizen* and his *Panegyric*, he approaches somewhat the image of Cicero, but at such a distance that he does not deserve this name by the calculations of the learned; otherwise a learned man, eloquent, and if I am not mistaken, good. Richard Fleming gave him an illustrious eulogy in his *Tibur Labors*, book 1. However, Cardinal Bona notes in the *Notice of Authors* prefixed to the book *On Divine Psalmody* that he is not very truthful in describing the lives of the Popes.
