<margin>1476.</margin>
**JEAN DE CIREY**, French by nation, from Dijon, a monk of the Cistercian Order; he was promoted from Abbot of Balerne to the leadership of Cîteaux <note>The mother house of the Cistercian Order</note> in the year 1476. He was exceedingly dear to Pope Innocent VIII on account of his singular gifts of mind. He disputed sharply against the **Commendatory system** <term>Commenda: a practice where the revenues of a monastery were given to a secular person or non-resident cleric, often leading to the decay of the abbey</term> of monasteries at the Synod of Orleans in 1477, at Tours in 1478, and in the Roman Curia before Pope Innocent, from whom he obtained many privileges for his Order. Weighted down by old age, he resigned his office and died at the end of that same year. There remain his **Compendium of Saints of the Cistercian Order** and a **Collection of Privileges** granted to the same Order by various Popes, Kings, and Princes, printed together at Dijon in 1491. This latter work appeared again at Antwerp in 1659. To it is joined an **Exhortation to the Monks of the Cistercian Order**, which Charles de Visch included in his *Library of Cistercian Writers, p. 201.*

<margin>1476.</margin>
**MASTER WESSEL GANSFORT**, also known as **BASILIUS**, a Frisian by birth and a citizen of Groningen; he was a countryman and most intimate friend of Rudolph Agricola. Because of his exceptional piety and learning, he was commonly called the **Light of the World** <note>original: "Lux mundi"</note>, and he was a most sworn adversary of papal authority and superstition. After drinking in the first foundations of letters at home, he betook himself to Paris and the most celebrated Academies of all Europe. By a native happiness of intellect and equally by immense diligence, he was seen to have climbed to the highest peak of letters: a distinguished rhetorician, poet, philosopher, and theologian, and skilled in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. He flourished in the year 1476. Distinguished by the laurel of Theology, he taught before a crowded audience at Paris, Cologne, Heidelberg, Rome, and especially at Basel (where he had Reuchlin as a student). He was by no means afraid to attack the authority of the Pope and the spurious traditions of the Roman Church in those places. What stung the leading theologians of that time no less was that he openly attacked the philosophical dogmas of Aristotle—which had long been received for use in the Church as much as in the schools—thinking that Platonic philosophy was truer and closer to the Christian faith. In disputing, he often placed the authority of St. Thomas [Aquinas] second, and preached that indubitable faith should be given to Scripture alone.
<margin>* Fol. 163.</margin>
Indeed, in the **Collection of Things to be Sought** <note>original: "Fasciculo Rerum Expetendarum," a famous collection of documents highlighting the need for Church reform</note> (first printed at Mainz in the year 1490), several of his dogmas are held which were then seen as **Paradoxes**; these were excerpted by certain Thomists <note>Followers of Thomas Aquinas</note> from his other works while he was preaching at Worms. In these, he denies that the Doctors of the Church have infallible authority in explaining Holy Scripture or handing down articles of faith; he calls into doubt the divine institution of feast days and fasts; he accuses those wandering to Rome on pilgrimage of folly; and he teaches that the commands of the Church do not bind a person under the penalty of sin—to say nothing of other articles of minor importance. The Inquisitors, Gerhard van Elten and Jakob Sprenger <note>Sprenger was the co-author of the *Malleus Maleficarum*, the famous manual on witch-hunting</note> of the Dominican Order, judged that such monstrous errors should be punished with a heavy penalty. At their persuasion, and almost by their compulsion, the Archbishop of Mainz, in a letter given to the Doctors of the Academies of Heidelberg and Cologne in the year 1479, ordered that Wessel's dogmas, suspected of heresy, should be excerpted from his books and subjected to examination. This was done with solemn preparation, and many errors excerpted from his writings were brought forward; concerning the rule of faith, for they wish that nothing is to be believed...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Wessel Gansfort, a Dutch theologian whose critiques of the medieval Church earned him the nickname "The Light of the World" among his supporters and "The Master of Contradictions" among his detractors. # The Synodal Century.

<margin>15TH CENTURY. from the Year 1400.</margin>
...he [refused to believe] <note>The Latin text begins mid-sentence with "luit," likely the end of "noluit" (did not wish/refused).</note> anything that is not held in Holy Scripture; regarding the Sacrament of the Eucharist, in which he believed the substance of the bread remains <note>This view, known as consubstantiation, was later a major point of debate during the Reformation</note>; regarding Indulgences, of which he hardly approved; regarding the authority of a General Council, which he taught was fallible; regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit, which he denied was owed to the Son as much as to the Father <note>This refers to the "Filioque" controversy between the Western and Eastern Churches</note>; and regarding very many other established opinions of Theology. Wessel first defended these views; however, when he felt the fire being threatened by the Inquisitors, he descended to a **Palinode** <term>Palinode: a formal retraction or recantation of a previous statement</term>. This greatly displeased certain Academic theologians of no obscure name, who grieved that such a great man had been acted upon so precipitously; they accused the Thomists <note>Followers of the scholastic system of Thomas Aquinas</note> of an excessively sharp and vain rivalry; indeed, they did not fear to assert that many of his articles **"and the greater Part could be sustained."** <margin>His examination near the end, in the *Fasciculus*, folio 166.</margin> As age weighed upon him, Wessel returned home and expounded the sacred scriptures in his native city, until, burdened by extreme old age, he retired to the Convent of Spiritual Virgins in Groningen <note>A community of the Sisters of the Common Life</note>, and thereafter devoted himself entirely to private leisure and prayer. He died over the age of seventy in the year 1489, and was buried among the Franciscans.

->W O R K S.<-

*   **A book on God’s providence.**
*   **Two books on the causes of the Incarnation, and on the magnitude and bitterness of the Lord's Passion.** Published at *Antwerp — 8vo.*
*   **A treatise on Ecclesiastical dignity, on true and right obedience, and to what extent the commands and statutes of Prelates obligate subjects.** It stands in Goldastus's *Monarchia*, Volume 1, page 563.
*   **On the Sacrament of Penance, and what are the keys of the Church.** <note>The "keys" refer to the power of the Church to forgive or retain sins.</note>
*   **On the power of binding and loosing.** <note>A reference to the authority given to the Apostles in the Gospel of Matthew.</note>
*   **What is the true communion of Saints.**
*   **Thirty-two Propositions on the treasure of the Church, and on its participation and distribution.** Found in Goldastus, ibid. page 573.
*   **On fraternities, etc.**
*   **On purgatory, and the state of souls after this life.**
*   **A treatise against the power of the Roman Pontiff regarding Indulgences.** Stands in Goldastus, ibid. page 576.
*   **Many Letters.**

All the small works of Wessel reviewed here were published under the title **A Medley of Theological Matters** <note>original: "Farraginis rerum Theologicarum"</note>, *Basel 1523, folio, and under the care of Martin Luther, Basel 1525, 4to.* An enlarged edition was prepared by Petrus Pappus at *Groningen in the year 1614.* Finally, by the care of Theodorus Strackius at *Marburg, 1617.*
*   **A book on the customs of ancient Heretics.** *Leipzig 1537.*
Wessel wrote certain other things, namely: **A book on hearing the Mass, A book on Justification through Christ**, etc., which I have not yet discovered whether they have been printed. Furthermore, all his writings are prohibited in the Roman Indexes <note>The *Index Librorum Prohibitorum*, the list of books banned by the Catholic Church</note>; and he himself is numbered among the condemned authors.

<margin>1477.</margin>
**ROBERT FLEMYNG**, an Englishman by nation, born of an illustrious family, a kinsman of Richard Flemyng, the Bishop of Lincoln. After the first foundations of literature were laid at Oxford in Lincoln College (which Bishop Richard had recently founded), he traveled to Italy and heard Baptista Guarino of Verona teaching at Ferrara; he was a student of the elegances of both languages <note>Latin and Greek</note>, and especially of poetry. Having come to Rome, he obtained the dignity of **Apostolic Protonotary** <term>Apostolic Protonotary: a high-ranking legal officer in the Roman Curia</term>. He was famous in the year 1477. At length returning to his fatherland, he was appointed Dean of the Church of Lincoln. He died at Lincoln and was buried in a chapel near his kinsman Richard. While he was still active in Italy, and staying in retreat at Tivoli in the year 1477, he wrote a magnificent **Encomium of Pope Sixtus IV** in two books of heroic verse, to which he gave the title **Tiburtine Midnight Labors** <note>original: "Lucubrationum Tiburtinarum"</note>. In the first book, he celebrates the lineage, life, achievements, and virtues of Sixtus; in the second, he washes away the slanders falsely attributed to him and places an illustrious eulogy upon his parentage; however, everywhere he uses shameful adulation and heaps immense praise upon an undeserving Pope; he is noted for scarcely any other reason. For [he was] not so fortunate... <insert>Append.</insert>

<margin>1479.</margin>
**JEAN RAULIN**, born in Toul, was the son of distinguished and noble parents. Educated in the study of the liberal arts at the College of Navarre in the University of Paris, he received his doctorate in Theology in 1479. In 1481, he succeeded Guillaume de Chateaufort in the governance of the College of Navarre, which he administered with the highest reputation for integrity and wisdom. Around 1497, having resigned his administrative post, he joined the Cluniac Monks <note>A reformed branch of the Benedictine order based at Cluny, France</note>; among them, he became as famous for his piety as he once was among the academics for his learning. In the year 1501, he undertook the task of reforming the Benedictine Order in the province, a duty committed to him by Cardinal d'Amboise, the Legate. He ceased to be among the living <note>A common euphemism for death</note> at Paris in the Cluny College on February 6, 1514, at the age of 71.

**S**ermons for the Advent of the Lord. Published in *Paris, 1516; ibid. 1519; Venice, 1584, in quarto.*
*Lenten Sermons*, distributed in two parts. *Paris, 1523; Venice, 1584.*
*Sermons on the Feast Days of the Saints for the whole year*, likewise in two parts. *Paris, 1524.*
*The Itinerary of Paradise*, or Sermons on Penance. *Paris, 1524.*
*Doctrinal on the Triple Death: Natural, of Guilt, and of Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. Paris, 1520.*
*The Itinerary of Paradise, Venice, 1585, in quarto.*
*Fourteen Sermons on the Eucharist. Paris, published by Jean Petit.*
*A Volume of 55 Letters*, to which are added a *Lecture on the Feast of St. Louis* on the theme: *Lord, the King shall rejoice in thy strength;* and a *Lecture held in the Cluniac College on the perfect Rule of St. Benedict. Paris, 1520, in quarto.*
*Oration on the Reformation of the Clergy to the General Chapter. Basel, 1498.*
The Theological Works of Raulin were published in *Antwerp, 1612, in 6 volumes, quarto.* The *Sermons* in *Paris, 1642, in 2 volumes, octavo.*
*Commentary on all the Logic books of Aristotle. Paris, 1500.*

<margin>1480.</margin>
**AGOSTINO PATRIZZI**, an Italian by nation, Canon of the Church of Siena and Secretary to Cardinal Francesco Piccolomini of Siena, flourished in the year 1480. Nine years earlier, he had accompanied the Cardinal of Siena, who was sent by Pope Paul II to the Assembly of the Germans at Ratisbon <note>Modern-day Regensburg</note> to request aid against the Turks; upon returning to Rome, he committed the history of the events of that Assembly to writing. He also wrote in that year, 1480, by the order of his master, a *History of the Councils of Basel and Florence*, specifically regarding the former, which he transcribed for the most part from the original manuscripts kept in the Church of Basel, as he himself reports. This *History of the Councils* is found in Volume 13, from page 1488 to page 1616. There also exists the *History of the Assembly of Ratisbon* among the German Writers published by Marquard Freher, *Frankfurt, 1602, Volume 2, page 143.*

<margin>1480.</margin>
**MATTHÄUS MARSCHALK VON PAPPENHEIM**, a German by nation, born of a most noble family, son of Ulrich Marschalk, Governor of the Duke of Bavaria, and Anna von Schwabsberg. He spent many years in the study of letters at foreign universities and earned a Doctorate in both Laws <note>Civil and Canon Law</note>. Having finally returned home, he was showered with a Canonry of the Church of Augsburg and other ecclesiastical benefits. He flourished in the year 1480. There exists the work called the *Southern Chronicle*, which runs through the events achieved in all of Europe very briefly according to the series of years from 852 to 1327, found in Freher’s *German Writers, Volume 1, page 311.* A fuller part of this *Chronicle*, which narrates events from the year 1276 to 1303 more abundantly, is found in the same work, page 327. Also the *Augsburg Chronicle* from the year 973 to 1104.

<margin>1480.</margin>
**GABRIEL BIEL**, a Swiss by birth, though others say he was from Speyer, known as *the Collector*, was a Doctor of Sacred Theology and a public professor at the University of Tübingen. He was summoned by Eberhard, Count of Württemberg—who founded that University in the year 1477—to teach Theology and Philosophy for a fixed salary. He flourished in the year 1480. He was very dear to Prince Eberhard and held in the highest esteem. After he had directed the chair at Tübingen for many years, he joined the order of the Brethren of the Common Life <note>original: *Clericorum Vitae communis*; a community of pious secular clergy and laymen focused on simple living and education</note> and, according to some, died in the year 1495; although there are those who maintain he lived until the year 1520. This seems less likely, however, since Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a famous 15th-century bibliographer</note> records that he was already of advanced age at Tübingen in the year 1494.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

**C**ommentaries on the four books of the *Master of the Sentences* <note>original: *Magistri Sententiarum*; referring to the standard theology textbook by Peter Lombard</note>. Published at *Basel, 1512; Brescia, 1574, in 3 volumes, quarto.*
*Exposition of the Canon of the Mass*, which in truth belongs to Eggeling of Brunswick, with a few things omitted by Biel and some added or changed; a fact which he himself quite honestly acknowledges at the end of the work. Published at *Lyons, 1542; Venice, 1576; Brescia, 1580; Bergamo, 1594.*
*Medicinal Sermons for the Seasons, the Mother of God, and the Saints throughout the year.* — 1499, folio. *Brescia, 1583, quarto; Basel, 1519.*
*Medicinal Sermons against the plague and the fear of death.*
*Defense of Obedience to the Pope, addressed to the Roman Church.*
*History of the Lord’s Passion.* Published together with the *Defense* and all the *Sermons* at *Hagenau, 1519.*

*Epitome of the writings of William of Ockham, and a Collection regarding the four books of the Sentences*, edited at the University of Tübingen. See the *Index of Manuscripts of the Augsburg Library, p. 102.*

<margin>1480.</margin>
**HERMOLAUS BARBARUS**, a Venetian Patrician, was born on the 21st day of May in the year 1454. He was the son of Franciscus Barbarus, a most learned man who held the highest rank in his home city. Hermolaus was a man born to revive the glory of fine literature in Italy, exceptionally learned in Greek and Latin, and most knowledgeable in the elegances of both languages. *A truly great and divine man*, says Erasmus, *who joined the purest morals to rare literacy; he shone no less for the innocence of his life than for the excellence of his learning.*
<margin>* The Ciceronian.</margin>
He flourished in the year 1480, having begun to write four years earlier. Sent as an ambassador from the Republic of Venice to the Roman Pontiff, he was appointed Patriarch of Aquileia by Innocent VIII in the year 1491 without the knowledge of the Venetian Senate. However, since the Ambassadors of the Republic who were conducting business at the Pope's court in Rome were forbidden by the laws of their country from accepting a priesthood or entering the Clergy without consulting the Senate, the Venetians took this defiance of the city's laws very seriously. They sent him letters commanding him to resign the Patriarchate without delay; otherwise, his father would be removed from office and his property would be confiscated by the treasury. Hermolaus stalled in vain, hoping the anger of the citizens might be softened by the delay. His father was stripped of his office and, after all attempts to resolve the matter failed, he died of a broken heart. Hermolaus himself was stripped of his goods, removed from the roll of citizens, and sentenced to perpetual exile. Crushed by such a blow of unhappy fortune—though certainly deserving of a better fate—this most learned man lived a life of poverty in Rome, sustained for some time by a meager allowance <note>original: *sportula*; originally a small basket of food given to clients in ancient Rome</note> from Pope Alexander; until he died in 1494, carried off by a common disease <note>original: *morbo plebeio*; likely referring to a plague or epidemic that struck the general population</note> at the age of 39, deprived even of the honor of a funeral. We have already heard Erasmus's judgment of him. But that praise is far too meager if compared to the eulogy by the same author which occurs elsewhere. For in the *Adages*, what...

"What does a dog have to do with a bath?" <note>original: *quid cani cum balneo?*; a proverb used to describe someone out of place, here likely referring to a critic of Hermolaus</note>—this is what is said of Hermolaus. He was a man who brought renown not only to his own Italy, but indeed to this entire century of ours: his authority among all the learned is such that it would be most impudent to disagree with him. His usefulness in restoring ancient literature was so distinguished that anyone who does not hold the memory of Hermolaus as sacred must be considered either a complete stranger to all learning or, at the very least, most ungrateful.

*Congratulatory Oration to Emperor Frederick*, Bruges 1486. Quarto, Basel, 1520.
*Compendium of Natural Science.* Lausanne 1579. Octavo.
*Corrections to Pliny* <note>original: *Castigationes Plinianae*; a massive work correcting thousands of errors in Pliny the Elder's Natural History</note> dedicated to Alexander VI. Rome 1492. Folio; and *Further Corrections*, ibid. 1493. Folio. Venice 1497.
*Orations, Lectures, etc.* Paris 1494. Quarto.
*Various Letters and Prefaces* among the letters of Angelo Poliziano. Basel. Books 1, 9, and 12.

*Corrections to Pomponius Mela; A Corollary to the first five books of Dioscorides on Medical Matters; Latin Versions of the books of Dioscorides, the paraphrases of Themistius*, and several small works by Plutarch, which appeared in various places and times.

<margin>* The Zürich Library, p. 288.</margin>
Furthermore, besides those works reviewed above, Hermolaus wrote two books *On Celibacy*, a book *Against the Barbarian Philosophers*, a poem *On Wifely Matters*, *Geometrical Squares*, *The Agreement of the Stars and Medicine*, *Rules for Writing History* addressed to M. Antonio Sabellico, numerous Orations and Letters, a book of 12,000 verses, a *Compendium of Galen*, and Latin versions of several Greek books, including the *Response of Gennadius, Patriarch of Constantinople, on the Catholic Faith to Mehmed, Emperor of the Turks*. <margin>1480.</margin>
**BAPTISTA SALVIS**, or *de Salis*, an Italian by nation and a Ligurian by birth. He was a member of the Franciscan Order and a student of the Province of Genoa. He flourished in the year 1480. He died after the year 1494. He wrote a *Summary of Cases of Conscience* <note>original: *Summam Casuum Conscientiae*; a practical manual for priests to use when hearing confessions</note>, which, taking its name from the author, is usually called the *Baptistiana*. It was published in Paris, 1499.

<margin>1480.</margin>
**PACIFICUS**, an Italian by race and a native of Novara, a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>. He flourished in the year 1480. He wrote a *Summary of Cases of Conscience*, called the *Pacifica* after the author's name: which Brother Tarvisinus, a Carmelite, translated into Italian and saw published in Venice, 1574 and 1580.

<margin>1480.</margin>
**ANGELUS DE CLAVASIO** <note>Angelo Carletti di Chivasso</note>, an Italian by nation and a Ligurian by birth, originating from the small town of that name <note>Chivasso</note>. He was a member of the Order of Friars Minor and Vicar General of the family of the Observants. A distinguished theologian and jurist, he flourished in the year 1480. He was most dear to Sixtus IV and other Roman Pontiffs, by whom he was honored with the title of Apostolic Nuncio and sent as a legate to collect money for the crusade against the Turks. He died at Cuneo in the Monastery of St. Mary of the Angels in the year 1495. He wrote a *Summary of Cases of Conscience*, commonly called the *Angelica*; which, after several famous editions, was printed in Venice in 1490 under the author's own care; more corrected editions appeared there in 1569, 1578, and 1582. Also Strasbourg 1513, Nuremberg 1488, 1492, and 1498, and Lyons 1534, 1588. Folio. He composed certain other things, namely: *A Treatise on Restitutions; A Treatise* entitled *The Ark of Faith*, etc., which were published at Alcalá in 1562. Quarto.

<margin>1480.</margin>
**BAPTISTA TROVAMALA**, called by others *Novamala*, an Italian Ligurian by birth and a monk of the Franciscan Order, flourished at Leuven from the year 1480. He wrote, *for the use of simple confessors, a Summary of Cases of Conscience*, which is usually called the *Rosella*, arranged according to the order of the alphabet. It appeared in Venice, 1499. Quarto. Paris, 1515. Octavo. Strasbourg, 1516. Folio.

**BERNARDINE OF L’AQUILA**, an Italian by birth, originating from the town of Fossa in the Abruzzo region <note>original: *Fossa Aprutii*</note>, was a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note> and a Procurator in the Roman Curia. He was highly skilled in both Civil and Canon Law <note>original: *Juris utriusque*</note> as well as in sacred literature; for this reason, he was called to the Roman Curia, where he performed the duties of a Preacher. He flourished in the year 1480. He died in the year 1503 in the Convent of St. Julian near the city of L’Aquila, at the age of 83. Finally, in the year 1515, his remains were moved from there to the Monastery of St. Angelus within Fossa and Ocra, where they are buried beneath the altar and are still honored with notable veneration today. His written works remain, including: *The Funeral Book* <note>original: *Funerale*</note>, Venice 1572; *Treatise on the Doctrine for those wishing to Marry*, among the *Venetian Legal Treatises*, 1584, Volume IX; *Admonitions for the Spiritual Life* (composed in 1491) in Italian, Venice 1572; *A Brief History of the Monasteries and Illustrious Men of the Province of St. Bernardine*; *A Scholastic Quodlibet*; *Lenten Sermons*; *A Century in Memory of the Passion of Christ*; *The Pilgrim*, or concerning Christ appearing in the form of a pilgrim to the disciples traveling to Emmaus; several books of *Sermons*; and the *Lives of St. Bernardine of Siena* and *St. Philip of L’Aquila* in Italian. Many of these are preserved as manuscripts in the aforementioned Monastery of St. Angelus, according to Wadding in *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*, page 54.

<margin>1480.</margin>
**ANTHONY OF BALOCCO**, called by others *Anthony of Vercelli*, was Italian by nation, born in the village of Balocco in the Diocese of Vercelli. He was a member of the Franciscan Order, from the family of the Regular Observance and the Province of Genoa. He flourished in the year 1480, being a most famous preacher throughout all of Italy. He wrote a *Lenten Cycle* on the twelve excellencies of the Christian faith, printed in Venice (1492) and Lyon (1504); a *Treatise on the Virtues*, Haguenau 1513, in quarto; and *Another Lenten Cycle on the eternal fruits of the Holy Spirit*, distributed into seventeen treatises. Luke Wadding, in *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*, page 29, lists the titles of each and reports that the entire work existed in his possession as a manuscript.

1480.
* Rosary, part 1, Sermon 3.
</margin>
**BERNARDINE TOMITANUS**, an Italian by nation from the city of Feltre, called by the nickname "The Small" <note>original: *Parvus*</note> because of his short stature. He was a member of the Order of Friars Minor and was very well-received by Popes Sixtus IV and Innocent VIII, for whom he performed service in managing the weightiest matters. He flourished in the year 1480. A man of rare purity of character and extraordinary eloquence in preaching, he was most celebrated among his countrymen. Later Franciscan historians have attributed almost innumerable miracles to him; indeed, his contemporary Bernardine de Bustis \* reports that when he was preaching at Vicenza, more angels were present in the air than men on the ground. But such tales are for the common folk <note>original: *ad popellum*</note>. A more certain sign of his piety is that, grieving for Christians afflicted by the intolerable usury of the Jews, he saw to it that the *Mount of Piety* <note>original: *Montem Pietatis*; a charitable institution that offered low-interest loans to the poor to counteract high-interest moneylenders</note> was established in many places, so that he might counter the tyranny of the circumcised moneylenders <note>original: *verporum nummulariorum*</note>. He died in Pavia <note>original: *Ticini*</note> on the 28th of September in the year 1494, and is still honored with the greatest veneration by the neighboring people. He wrote a *Small Treatise on the Method of Confessing*, published in Brescia, 1542, in duodecimo; and *Certain Italian Sermons on the Perfection of the Christian Life*, Venice 1532, in octavo.

<margin>1480.</margin>
**BERNARDINE DE BUSTIS**, Italian by birth, originating from the town of the same name <note>Busto Arsizio</note> in the Duchy of Milan, was a member of the Franciscan family. He was exceptionally well-instructed in the knowledge of Theology, Philosophy, and Jurisprudence for the standards of that age <note>original: *pro ratione ævi*</note>. A student of Michael de Carcano, he flourished in the year 1480, at which time he obtained from Pope Sixtus IV an Apostolic decree confirming the Office of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin, which he himself had composed. He was a man of illustrious fame for eloquence and outstanding skill in preaching, to be numbered among the primary leaders of his Order. So much so that, following the custom accepted in that age among the Italians—where the more distinguished Franciscan preachers were requested annually from the Minister General by a formal delegation from the more famous cities of Italy—Bernardine was destined almost every year from the time he first began to flourish to be sent to as many Princes or notable cities as requested him from the General. However, though he shone in whatever style of speaking he chose, he certainly possessed little strength of judgment, leaning toward empty super-

### W R I T I N G S.

*The Mariale*, or *Sermons on the Blessed Virgin Mary*, and her excellencies, not only for her individual feast days, but also for all the Sabbaths of the entire year. Published in Milan, 1494, in quarto; Strasbourg, 1496.
*Lenten Sermons* <note>original: *Quadragesimale*</note>. Strasbourg, 1496.
*The Rosary of Sermons* for Lent, and for all Sundays and feast days of the entire year; as well as on every preachably subject. Published distributed into two volumes at Haguenau, 1500; Lyon, 1507, 1525, in quarto; and with the *Mariale* at Brescia, 1588, in 3 volumes.
*Two Treatises for the Defense of the Mountains of Piety* <note>The *Montes Pietatis* were charitable institutions that offered low-interest loans to the poor to prevent usury</note>, written to Cardinal Bernardino de Carvajal in the year 1497. Milan, 1503, in folio.
*The Office of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin.*
*The Office of the Name of Jesus.* Both are recited by the Minorites <note>the Franciscans</note> to this day; the latter on the 14th of January, the former on the 8th of December.

<margin>1480.</margin>
**ROBERT CARACCIOLO**, an Italian by nation, born at Lecce in the Kingdom of Naples, and from there surnamed *Robert of Lecce*, was a member of the Order of Friars Minor, and finally a Bishop of Aquino, Lecce, and (as some wish) of L'Aquila in the province of the Marsi. He flourished in the year 1480. He flourished with the highest favor among many Popes and the entire Italian nation; having obtained great honor by a rare abundance and success in preaching, in which he was believed to excel so greatly that he was called by the common praise of everyone "The Second Paul." He was indeed an excellent preacher (considering those times), and a man clearly driven by zealous genius; he is said to have been able to draw tears from his audience at will; and he lashed the loose morals of the age with a sharp pen, especially the more-than-royal pomp of the Popes and Cardinals. He died in the year 1495, after he had performed the duty of a preacher for fifty years. He was buried in the Conventual Church of Lecce, and was praised by this sort of couplet carved in the middle of his tomb:

> This is that Robert of Christ; while he was leader,
> No prophet after Paul was more famous in the world.

*Lenten Sermons on Penance.* Venice, 1472, in quarto; Strasbourg, 1497, in folio.
*Sermons on the Annunciation of the Virgin Mary, on the Number of the Predestined and the Damned, on the Chains of Sinners, on Good Hope, and on the Judgment of the Plague.* These were published together with the preceding work in its second printing in the same place.

*Sermons for the Solemnities of the entire year, the Lord of Sabaoth, and the Most Blessed Virgin.* Venice, 1471, 1496.
*A book on the Formation of Man.* Nuremberg, 1470.

### MICHAEL OF MILAN,
Italian by nation, Milanese by birth, a distinguished Preacher of the Franciscan Order of the Regular Observance <note>The "Observants" were a branch of the Franciscans who sought to return to the strict, original poverty of St. Francis.</note>. He flourished in the year 1480. Wadding <note>Luke Wadding, the famous 17th-century Franciscan historian.</note> correctly conjectures that he was the same person as Michael de Carcano. <margin>* On the Writers of the Order of Minors, p. 261.</margin> Certainly, both had Milan as their homeland; both served in the Franciscan family; and almost the same Works are ascribed to both.

*The Confessional*, or a method for confessing. Venice, 1513, octavo.

*Sermons on the Saints*.

*Sermons on Penance for the days of Lent*.
*On Sins in general*.
*On the three principal sins: Pride, Avarice, and Lust*.
*On the four remaining capital sins, and their daughters* <note>In medieval theology, "daughter sins" were the specific vices that logically sprang from the seven root "capital" sins.</note>.
*A book on the Christian faith*.

### STEPHEN BRULIFER,
French by nation, Armorican <note>A native of Brittany.</note> by birth, from the house of Saint-Malo, of the Order of Minors [Franciscans], a Doctor of Paris, and a disciple of William Vorilong. He was a Professor of <term>Scholastic Theology</term> <note>A method of critical thought which dominated teaching in the medieval universities.</note> according to the opinion of <term>Scotus</term> <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan philosopher-theologian.</note> at Mainz and Metz. He flourished in the year 1480. He died in the Convent of Bernon in the Province of Brittany, apparently after the year 1500.

#### W R I T I N G S.

*Lecture Notes on the four books of the Sentences of St. Bonaventure* <note>The "Sentences" by Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook; scholars wrote "Reportata" or lecture notes based on their teaching of it.</note>. Published separately in Basel, 1501; Venice, 1504; Paris, 1507.
*A Book on the Most Holy Trinity, in which he sharply chastises Painters who depict the Holy Trinity with foolish images*.
*Sermons on the poverty of Christ and the Apostles*. Paris, 1500.
*An Apology against a certain Franciscan Bishop who condemned the Friars of the Regular Observance because they called themselves by a name other than that expressed in the Rule*.
*A Treatise on servile fear and the gifts of God*.
*A Treatise on Formalities according to the mind of Scotus*. These three Treatises were published in Venice, 1516, folio.
*A Declaration of the identities and distinctions of things according to Scotus*. Basel, 1507, octavo, at the end of the *Lecture Notes*.
*A Sermon on the value of Masses, delivered in the Synod of Mainz*.
The Works of Brulifer were published in Paris, 1499; and again there in 1500, octavo.

...deservedly to be celebrated. He flourished in the year 1480. Driven by an immense zeal for piety and the Christian cause, as he judged that the corrupted doctrine of the Roman Church and the even more corrupt morals of the clergy—especially those of Pope Sixtus—were not to be tolerated, he believed that applying a remedy to both evils would be for the benefit of Christendom. He acted through frequent prayers and exhortations with Sixtus privately and in the public assembly of the Cardinals, so that the long-delayed reformation might finally begin at last. Being received by the Pope and the Cardinals with mockery and ridicule, he turned elsewhere; and having received authority (as he claimed) from Emperor Frederick, he traveled to the city of Basel. In the Cathedral Church there, on March 25, 1482, he proclaimed a General Council to be convened in that place as soon as possible, *for the reformation of the Catholic faith (to use his own words), the correction of morals, the rooting out of crimes and vices, and the securing of universal peace among the Christian people.* Sixtus raged when he heard the news and sent letters to the people of Basel, demanding they send Andrew to him bound in chains. Andrew appealed from the Pope to a Council and repeated his call for the Council. Sixtus commanded his legate in Switzerland, Angelo, Bishop of Sessa, to hand Andrew over to the punishment of excommunication <term>Anathema: A formal curse by a pope or council of the Church, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine.</term>; he also threatened the reluctant people of Basel with dire curses. Since the Swiss cared little for the excommunication, the Pope sent Jodocus, the Bishop of Sion, to Emperor Frederick. After a long and very reluctant refusal, Jodocus finally persuaded the Emperor to command the people of Basel to hand Andrew over to custody under the penalty of high treason. This was done at the end of the year 1482, and after spending several months in prison, Andrew finally perished, strangled by a secret plot.

## GIROLAMO SAVONAROLA,
Italian by nation, born in Ferrara, though of Paduan origin, born of a noble family to parents Niccolò Savonarola <note>The text lists him as "Hieronymi," likely a slip by the author or printer, as his father was Niccolò and his grandfather was the famous physician Michele</note> and Elena Bonacolsi. He was born in the year 1452, on September 21 <note>original: *xi. Cal. Octob.*</note>. From his earliest childhood <note>literally: "from his tender little nails"</note>, he applied himself with the greatest diligence to the study of piety and the liberal arts, such that while still a youth he obtained a distinguished name among the learned. In the year 1474, having set out for Bologna without consulting his parents, he joined the Dominican family [order]; he undertook the duty assigned to him of teaching Philosophy and Metaphysics. Later, having been initiated into the sacred office [the priesthood], he began to thunder in frequent sermons to the people against the loose morals of the age; he employed such eloquence and had such happy success that he could bend the minds of his listeners to whatever persuasion he wished, and he struck a zeal for piety and religion into even the most abandoned of men.

<meta>This page concludes the account of Andrew, Archbishop of Krain, noting the massive crowds his preaching attracted, before transitioning into a detailed biography of the famous Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola. It documents Savonarola's rise in Florence, his conflict with Pope Alexander VI, his eventual execution, and the later rehabilitation of his writings.</meta>

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...he struck <note>This sentence completes a thought from the previous page regarding Andrew, Archbishop of Krain, who struck fear into the corrupt clergy</note> such fear into them, and was celebrated with such a great concourse of people everywhere, that even the largest churches could by no means contain the multitude of listeners. He flourished in the year 1480. He was a man born to promote religion, who, through the greatest austerity of life and unstained holiness of morals, drew the admiration of everyone to himself. By certain very sure predictions of future events <margin>* See Philippe de Commines, *History*, Book 8, Chapter 2.</margin> he won for himself the reputation of being almost a divine man. Equipped with such a reputation for piety and eloquence, it is truly a wonder how immense an authority he acquired among the Italians, so much so that all of Italy seemed to hang on the speaker's words. 

Holding frequent sermons from town to town, he devoted himself solely to chastising the deplorable malice of the age, restoring religion which had collapsed through the negligence of the Popes, and recalling piety, charity, and justice to the souls of Christians, while correcting the loose morals of all. Especially, however, he took care to expose the vices of the Popes, ecclesiastics, and princes of every kind, and to lash them with sharp satire. 

In the year 1489, he went to Florence, and in a short time, through his eloquent sermons, prophetic predictions, and the gravity of his morals, he gained such power that thereafter he directed everything in the Florentine Republic according to his will. In the year 1494, sent as an envoy by the Florentines to Charles [VIII], King of France, who was carrying victorious arms through Italy, he restrained the victor's anger with his authority and obtained peace for the citizens. 

By now, Girolamo <note>original: "Hieronymus" [Savonarola]</note> had begun to be hated by the Roman Curia and the entire ecclesiastical order, both because he shouted that the Church must be reformed and that one must depart from "Babylon" (hinting at Rome), and because he was in no way afraid to publicly note and bitterly criticize the vices of individuals. Especially, however, he drove Pope Alexander VI—that monster of vices and disgrace of the Christian religion—into a frenzy by exposing his crimes and magnifying them in his sermons. 

Therefore, in the year 1498, Alexander, having sent some Dominican friars to oppose Girolamo's sermons, drew some of the leading men to his side and saw to it that a hostile faction was stirred up. These men attacked Girolamo (who had previously been struck with an excommunication <term>Anathema: A formal curse by a pope or council of the Church, excommunicating a person.</term> by the Pope) with an armed force in the church, opening a way for themselves with sword and fire; they were, however, repelled by Girolamo’s followers after a sharp struggle. Soon, however, summoned by the Senate with a public guarantee of safety so that he might return unharmed to his monastery, he obeyed; and having left the church, he was handed over to prison with the greatest treachery. There, he was tortured with the most cruel torments to force him to confess that his prophecies were false. Girolamo yielded to the torments, and his mind being alienated by the excessive intensity of the pain, he complied with his captors. 

As soon as Pope Alexander knew that Girolamo had been led into chains, he demanded he be sent to Rome; when, however, he could not obtain this from the Florentines, he appointed two inquisitors of the faith as judges for him and sent them to Florence. These men prosecuted Girolamo, already half-dead from torture, as guilty of heresy, and after a hasty trial, they ordered his death for the following day. Girolamo met death with the greatest strength of spirit, strangled in the Florentine square and burned in the flames on May 23, 1498, at the age of 46. 

His followers honored the memory of the deceased with great honor and placed him among the martyrs. As for the crime certainly charged against him, his "heresy" was (to use the words of the Florentines' *letter to Alexander VI*) *to teach justice to all, to urge the citizens to use a certain equal right; to detect the traps of all against the Republic, nor to allow anyone to seize more for himself against the law of the city; to teach parents the best education and instruction of their children, so they might turn out worthy of the Christian name; to persuade women, having laid aside all finery, to follow Christ; that boys should know nothing more than the deeds of Christ and the Saints: and to do other things of this sort, which could easily move the love of the good and the hatred of the evil.*

Around the year 1556, under the pontificate of Pope Paul IV, there was a great struggle in the Roman Curia with much passion on both sides over the approval or prohibition of Girolamo's writings. The diligence of the Dominicans finally won out, and they obtained a judgment in favor of Girolamo; however, in such a way that a few books that had previously been placed on the Index <note>The Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the list of books banned by the Catholic Church.</note> were by no means removed from it: not indeed to be considered heretical or erroneous, but to be placed among the *suspended* (for so the judges wished to speak).

He flourished in the year 1480. A man born to promote religion, he drew the admiration of all to himself through the greatest austerity of life and the unblemished holiness of his character; and by certain very sure predictions of future events <note>Savonarola was famous for his "prophetic" warnings about the coming of the French King Charles VIII and the downfall of the Medici.</note>, he won for himself the reputation of being almost a divine man. Equipped with such a fame for piety and eloquence, it is truly a wonder what immense authority he gained among the Italians, so much so that all Italy seemed to hang upon the words of the speaker. Through frequent sermons held from town to town, he focused solely on this: to reproach the deplorable malice of the age, to restore the religion collapsed through the negligence of the Popes, to recall piety, charity, and justice into the souls of Christians, and to correct the loose morals of everyone. Above all, however, he made it his care to uncover the vices of the Popes, Ecclesiastics, and Princes of whatever kind, and to lash them with sharp satire.

In the year 1489, he went to Florence; and through his eloquent sermons, prophetic predictions, and the gravity of his character, he soon won such power for himself that he thereafter conducted everything in the Florentine Republic according to his will. In the year 1494, sent as an ambassador by the Florentines to Charles, King of France <note>Charles VIII, who invaded Italy in 1494.</note>, who was carrying his victorious arms through Italy, he restrained the victor’s anger by his own authority and obtained peace for the citizens.

And now Hieronymus <note>Girolamo Savonarola.</note> had begun to be hated by the Roman Curia <term>Curia: The administrative apparatus of the Holy See and the central body through which the Pope conducts the business of the entire Catholic Church.</term> and the entire order of Ecclesiastics, as much because he cried out that the Church must be reformed and that one must depart from Babylon (hinting at Rome) <note>He used the biblical "Babylon" as a metaphor for the corruption he saw in the Roman church.</note>, as because he did not fear in the least to openly note and bitterly criticize the vices of individuals. Especially, however, he had driven Pope Alexander VI—that monster of vices and the disgrace of the Christian religion—into a rage by uncovering his crimes and exaggerating them in his sermons.

Therefore, in the year 1498, Alexander, having sent some minor Dominican friars to oppose the sermons of Hieronymus, drew some of the leading men to his side and saw to it that a hostile faction was stirred up. These men, after Hieronymus had first been struck by an anathema from the Pope, invaded the temple with an armed hand and opened a way for themselves with sword and flame; they were, however, repelled by the followers of Hieronymus after a sharp struggle. But soon, summoned by the Senate with a public guarantee of safety so that he might return unharmed to the monastery, he obeyed; and having left the church, he was handed over to prison with the greatest treachery. He was tortured with the most savage torments so that he might be forced to confess that his prophecies were false. Hieronymus yielded to the torments, and his mind being alienated by the excessive violence of the pain, he complied.

As soon as Pope Alexander knew that Hieronymus had been led into chains, he demanded that he be sent to Rome; but when he could not obtain this from the Florentines, he appointed two Inquisitors of the faith as judges for him and sent them to Florence. These men put Hieronymus, already half-dead from torture, on trial for heresy; and after a tumultuous judgment, they declared his death for the following day. Hieronymus met it with the greatest fortitude of soul, being strangled and consumed by flames in the Florentine square on the 23rd day of May in the year 1498, at the age of 46. His followers cherished the memory of the deceased with great honor and placed him among the Martyrs.

As for the crime certainly charged against him; his "heresy" was (to use the words of the letter from the Florentines to Alexander VI) <note>The author is quoting a defense of Savonarola to show that his "heresy" was actually moral and political reform.</note>: *to teach everyone justice, to exhort citizens to use a certain equal right; to detect the traps of all against the Republic, and not to allow anyone to occupy more for himself against the law of the city; to tell parents the best education and instruction for their sons so that they might turn out worthy of the Christian name; to persuade women, having laid aside all finery, to follow Christ, and boys to know nothing more than the deeds of Christ and the Saints; and to do other things of this kind, which could easily move the love of the good and the hatred of the wicked.*

With a great heat of minds on both sides around the year 1556, under the pontificate of Paul IV, there was a struggle in the Roman Curia about approving or prohibiting the writings of Hieronymus. The diligence of the Dominicans finally won out and obtained a sentence in favor of Hieronymus; however, in such a way that a few books which had previously been placed on the Index <term>Index Librorum Prohibitorum: A list of publications deemed heretical or contrary to morality by the Catholic Church.</term> were by no means removed: not indeed to be held as heretical or erroneous, but to be placed among the *suspended* (for so the Judges wished to speak).

Written in the year 1497 and published in Florence, then Venice 1517, Paris 1524, in octavo <note>8° refers to octavo, a book size where the sheet is folded into eight leaves</note>; Venice 15...; Leiden 1633, in octavo. ### MARSILIO FICINO,

<margin>
1480.
</margin>
Italian by race, Florentine by homeland, son of Ficino the Surgeon, was born in the year 1433, on the 19th of October. Educated in letters at the expense of Lorenzo de' Medici, Prince of the Florentines, he had Luca Gymnianense and Commodus as teachers. After his literary studies were successfully completed, since he was considered most well-versed in every kind of Philosophy, a most celebrated Theologian and Physician, and indeed most skilled in Greek and Latin; he enjoyed the greatest favor with Lorenzo and Cosimo de' Medici; and by them he was presented with a respectable home, a Priesthood, a Canonry in the Cathedral Church of Florence, and annual stipends. Having obtained leisure through the favor of such great Patrons, he prepared himself to aid the cause of literature; and while others were eagerly translating the volumes of Aristotle, he himself undertook the translation of Plato's writings into Latin; he cultivated Platonic Philosophy 
<margin>
* Information from the Author in the book on the Divine Psalms, preface.
</margin>
with great zeal, and was the first of all to restore it in the West. "The Prince of Platonists," says Cardinal Bona *, "who alone among the Platonists can be traversed with an untroubled foot" <note>Meaning he is a safe guide who does not lead the reader into heresy</note>. He flourished in the year 1480. Being too devoted to philosophical matters...

<meta>This page concludes the biographical sketch of the philosopher Marsilio Ficino and begins a detailed bibliography of his works, focusing on his synthesis of Platonic philosophy and Christian theology.</meta>

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>

...he is said to have neglected the care of religion and piety; until, admiring the eloquence of Savonarola upon his arrival in Florence, he applied his mind to hearing his sermons. While he initially hungered for the "flowers of rhetoric" <note>ornate or stylish speech</note>, he received the small sparks of piety. He spent the remainder of his life in religious duties and wrote a most learned *Apology* on behalf of Savonarola. He died in the Villa di Careggi near Florence in the year 1499 and was buried in the Church of Saint Mary. Immediately after his death, he is said to have appeared to Michele Mercati of San Miniato, just as he had promised while alive; Baronius relates this near the end of his entry for the year 411, based on the faith of honest and most learned witnesses, stating that Ficino confirmed he had now experienced those things which he had previously argued concerning the immortality of souls.

## WERNER ROLEVINCK DE LAER, a Westphalian by birth,
originating from a small town in the Diocese of Münster; a <unclear>Carthusian</unclear> monk in the Monastery of Saint Barbara in Cologne. He flourished in the year 1480. He died in 1502, at the age of 77, and the 55th year of his conversion <note>Entering the monastic life</note>.

->WORKS.<-

<margin>
* On Latin History, book 3, chapter 6.
</margin>
*The Bundle of Times* <note>original: "Fasciculus Temporum"</note>, comprising all the Chronicles of the Ancients, arranged by Ages, from the creation of the world up to his own time. Werner produced a triple edition of <unclear>this work</unclear>. The first ended in the year 1470; a manuscript copy of it existed in the possession of [Gerard] Vossius. The second reached the year 1474; from that point, the Appendix or Continuation by Johann Linturius, pastor of Hosten in Vogtland, begins and proceeds up to the year 1514. That <unclear>edition</unclear> appeared in Louvain in 1476. The third edition is brought down to the year 1480, when Otranto was captured by the Turks; it appeared in Augsburg in 1481 and is found together with the Linturius Appendix among the *German Writers* of [Johannes] Pistorius, Frankfurt edition, volume 2, page 580.

Werner wrote several other things, namely: a *Calendar and Martyrology*, a <unclear>book</unclear> on the origin of the Frisians, a great work on all the Epistles of Saint Paul, seven books on the *Life of Saint Paul*, a book *On the governance of princes*, etc. A <unclear>list</unclear> of these, quite long and received from Werner himself, is presented by Trithemius in his book *On <unclear>Illustrious Men</unclear> of Germany*.

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>

[born in] Trittenheim. He was the son of Johann von Berg and Elisabeth von Longwy. Educated in the humanities at the Universities of Trier and Heidelberg, in the 22nd year of his age, on the day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin, he became a Benedictine monk in the monastery of St. Martin at Sponheim. While still a youth and a novice, he earned such great authority among his brethren through his rare erudition and exceptional piety—proving himself a distinguished philosopher, mathematician, poet, historian, and theologian—that in 1483, the second year of his conversion, he was elected Abbot by the common vote of the monks. He administered this office with the highest praise for twenty-two years; however, he was long and greatly harassed by a faction involving Nicolaus Remitius, his Prior (as they call the office), and certain other monks (whom he frequently traduces in his letters by the name <term>Cynonoti</term> <note>A term coined by Trithemius from the Greek for "dog-noted" or "shameless dogs," used to describe his rebellious subordinates</note>). Because he supported the interests of Prince Philip the Palatine against Count Hasso, he departed from his monastery on April 1, 1505. He stayed for a time with Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, who was then residing in Cologne, and later traveled with him into the Margraviate of Brandenburg, where he was received with clemency and great honor. After an interval of eighteen months, while the faction of monks was still active, he resigned his rule of Sponheim. Summoned by the letters of Lorenz, Bishop of Würzburg, he was appointed head of the monastery of St. James the Greater in the suburbs of Würzburg on October 15, 1506. There, enjoying abundant leisure and free from the cares of a wealthier and more turbulent monastery, he subsequently applied his whole mind to the pursuit of letters until his death, which occurred on December 13, 1518 (or as others say, 1519), at the age of 57. He was indeed a man of profound learning, who had few equals among the famous scholars of his century and scarcely any superior. He did not merely tread common paths, but unlocked the innermost shrines of more recondite learning, and perhaps scrutinized them too curiously; for this reason, as he himself complained <margin>* Book 2, Letter 42, p. 303.</margin>, he was commonly regarded as a **Magician**. There were those who loudly claimed he had raised the dead, summoned demons from the underworld, predicted the future, and bound thieves and robbers with incantations. Although these claims were fictitious and false, he did not deny that he had read most of the books of the magicians, as his work *Steganographia* <note>A famous work on cryptography and angel magic</note> abundantly testifies. Nor did he "sing only for himself and the Muses," but he also instructed many disciples in his monastery in better literature, so much so that not only from all over Germany did many very learned and respectable men flock to him, but also from Italy and all three parts of Gaul, as he himself informs us <margin>† Book 2, Letter 3, p. 195.</margin>. At great expense, he erected a truly remarkable library for the use and ornament of the Sponheim monastery, consisting of more than 2,000 manuscript codices of the better sort, in every faculty and in almost every language: Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Chaldean <note>Aramaic or Syriac</note>, Arabic, Indian, Ruthenian <note>Old East Slavic</note>, and Tartar (to say nothing of others). He discusses this library at length in several places, but especially in Book 1, Letter 32, and Book 2, Letter 46. Moreover, by his own labor, he wrote enough to fill a modest library by itself; we therefore present a catalog of those works here.

### W O R K S.

*Mystical Chronology of the Secondary Intelligences moving the spheres after God*, dedicated to Emperor Maximilian. *Cologne, 1567, octavo.*

*Compendium, or Abridgment, of the First Volume of the Chronicles on the origin of the race and Kings of the Franks*, covering 1,189 years from Marcomir (namely, the year 433 BC) down to King Pepin. A work that is primarily fabulous <note>meaning legendary or mythical</note> and collected from the most deceitful writers. Trithemius had also written two other volumes in which he wove the history of the Franks from Pepin to the 29th year of Emperor Maximilian, the year of Christ 1514. The *Compendium* of that first volume was published: *Paris, 1539, folio.*

*Book on the origin of the Frankish race*, patched together from the foulest fictions of the spurious Hunibald. It appeared together with the preceding work: *Basel, 1547*; and is contained in Schardius’s *German Affairs*, Volume 1, page 170.

*Chronicle of the succession of the Dukes of Bavaria and the Counts Palatine. Frankfurt, 1544, 1549, quarto.*

The works just enumerated, from the *Antipalus of Sorcerers* <note>original: "Antipalo maleficorum" — a work by Trithemius defending against charges of magic and discussing the occult.</note> inclusive, were published together under the title *Paralipomena of Trithemius* <note>original: "Paralipomenon Trithemii" — literally "things omitted" or a supplement.</note> by the same Busæus at Mainz in 1605 in octavo, and at Cologne in 1624 in octavo.

*Life of St. Maximin, Archbishop of Trier.* Found in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a famous hagiographer who compiled the lives of saints.</note> on the 16th day of November.

*Life of St. Maximus, Bishop of Mainz.* It appears in the same place on the 18th day of November.

*Letter to Peter, Abbot of Amerbach*, previously unpublished, found in Lambecius's *Commentary on the Library of Vienna*, Volume 3, Appendix, page 342.

*Six Books of Polygraphy, addressed to Emperor Maximilian, in which he accurately explains with wonderful subtlety infinite ways of writing and of safely expressing the secrets of our mind in almost any language.* <note>Polygraphy here refers to complex systems of cryptography and secret communication.</note> These appeared together with their key in 1518 in folio, and at Cologne in 1571 in octavo.

*Steganography, or the method of secret writing.* <note>The word "Steganography" was coined by Trithemius; it means "hidden writing."</note> Published with its key at Frankfurt in 1606 in quarto. It is a great and (as he himself calls it) excessively arduous work, which he set out to complete in eight books. He had already brought the first two to a conclusion by the year 1505; the rest he suppressed for a long time. Indeed, he himself tells us the reasons why he did so in his *Letters*, book 2, letter 43, page 303. Many openly condemn this book and accuse it of Magic. Others have defended it in their writings, among them Juan Caramuel Lobkowitz, who published a *Vindication of Trithemian Steganography* at Cologne in 1635 in quarto; and the Most Illustrious Prince, Augustus, Duke of Brunswick, who, in his *System of Cryptography* (which he published under the pseudonym Gustavus Selenus at Lüneburg in 1624 in folio), strives to purge that work from every stain of magical suspicion.

*Treatise on the Providence of God.* Altdorf, 1611, in octavo.

*History of the Bavarian War waged in the year 1504.* It appears in Freher’s *Collection of German Writers*, Volume 3, page 97.

*Chemical Treatise.* Published in 1611 in octavo, and at Strasbourg in 1613 in octavo. *Book on Poisoners* <note>original: "de Veneficis"</note>, printed in German at Ingolstadt in 1555 in quarto.

Many other works of Trithemius, not yet printed, are listed in a long enough line by Josias Simler in the *Library of Zurich*, page 421, and by Hieronymus Ghilinus in the *Theater of Learned Men*, page 13. Trithemius himself deals accurately with his own books—at what time and on what occasion they were written up to the end of the year 1506, and those which he meditated writing thereafter—in his *Letters*, book 2, letter 50.

AUGUSTINUS PATRICIUS, distinct from the Augustinus Patricius of Siena mentioned above; he was first Master of Ceremonies under Innocent VIII, then from the year 1483, Bishop of Pienza. He wrote to Bartholomew Paganuccius the *Life of Fabianus Bentius of Montepulciano, Professor of Holy Canons*, and a *Description of the arrival of Emperor Frederick III to Pope Paul II.* Jean Mabillon <note>A famous Benedictine monk and founder of the study of paleography.</note> was the first to extract and bring to light these two small works in the *Italian Museum*, Volume 1, part 2, page 251. He also testifies that he has in his possession another work by the same Augustine concerning the *Rites of the Roman Church*, which he promises to make public in the *Collection of Roman Rituals* that he is soon to publish.

<margin>1433.</margin>
JACOBUS GRUYTRODIUS, a German by nation, a monk of the Carthusian Order, and Prior of the Monastery of the Holy Apostles near Liège <note>original: "Leodium"</note>. *A man in the divine Scriptures*, says Trithemius, *studious and learned, devout in life and conversation, outstanding in talent, and sweet in eloquence.* He flourished in the year 1483. He died in the year 1492, on the 12th of February <note>original: "prid. Id. Februarias" — the day before the Ides of February.</note>. He wrote the *Fivefold Mirror: for Prelates, Subjects, Priests, Laymen, and the Elderly*: which was published falsely attributed to Dionysius the Carthusian. Trithemius enumerates many other small works of Gruytrodius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, page 179, and Simler lists even more in the *Library of Zurich*, page 316.

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>

<margin>1484.</margin>
## INNOCENT VIII.

Previously called *Giovanni Battista Cibo*, a Genoese by birth but of Greek origin, he was the son of Aaron, the viceroy of Naples. He was educated in the household of Kings Alfonso and Ferdinand of Naples, and under the companionship of Filippo Calandrini, the Cardinal of Bologna. He was first appointed Bishop of Savona by Pope Paul II, then Bishop of Melfi, later Datary <note>The Datary was a high-ranking official in the Roman Curia responsible for dating and processing papal documents and dispensations.</note>, and finally, in the year 1473, he was made Cardinal Priest with the title of St. Balbina. He was elected Roman Pontiff in the year 1484 on the 29th of August, and crowned on the 12th of September. In the year 1486, he absolved the Venetians—who had been excommunicated by his predecessor Sixtus—and received them back into the Church. In the year 1487, and again in 1489, he struck Ferdinand, King of Naples, with an excommunication because the King refused to return the tribute to the Church that had been waived by Pope Sixtus; he ordered the King deposed from his throne and released his subjects from their oath of obedience. In the year 1491, he granted an indulgence to the Norwegians so that they could celebrate the Holy Communion without wine <note>original: "sine vino sacram Synaxin celebrare possent" — This rare dispensation was granted because wine was extremely difficult to import and preserve in the harsh climate of Scandinavia.</note>. He died at the age of seventy in the year 1492, on the 25th of July. There exists a *Letter to Henry VII, King of England, concerning not dragging Clerics into secular courts.* (Council Collection, Volume 13, page 1431). There are *Eight Letters and Constitutions* found in Bzovius for the year 1484, etc., many others in the *Bullaria* <note>Collections of papal decrees or "Bulls."</note> and other collections of Pontifical Constitutions; some are among the letters of Angelo Poliziano. A *Volume of Letters* is in manuscript in the Imperial Library. *Others* exist in manuscript in the Library of the Celestines at Avignon.

<margin>1484.</margin>
## GIOVANNI PICO,

Prince of Mirandola and Concordia, called the *Phoenix* <note>Pico was nicknamed "The Phoenix" because of his unique and legendary intellectual talents, suggesting he was a once-in-a-generation marvel.</note>, Italian by nation and a native of Mirandola. He was the son of Giovanni Francesco Pico, Count of Mirandola, and Julia, born in the year 1463. While still a boy, he was adorned to a miraculous degree with the highest gifts of mind and body; even while still under the schoolmaster's rod, he held the first place among poets and orators. In the fourteenth year of his age, he went to Bologna for the purpose of learning Canon Law. When he had sampled this for two years, loathing the "squalor and trifles" of the Decretals <note>The Decretals were the primary textbooks of Church law; Pico, a budding humanist, found their medieval Latin style and legalistic focus unappealing.</note>, the young man, born for greater things, began to meditate on higher matters. He gave himself entirely to the contemplation of the most hidden things and to the study of both human and divine philosophy. Having traveled through the primary academies of France and Italy, he sought out the most learned professors of both philosophies everywhere; he read through the writings of almost all philosophers and pursued his work with such tireless mental zeal that he was considered a <term>Theologian</term> (a scholar of sacred scripture and doctrine) and a <term>Philosopher</term> (a scholar of logic and the natural world) perfect in every respect, while still a beardless youth. 

As for what pertains to more elegant literature, he was truly one who snatched the prize from all the men of his century for his elegance of speech, his wit, his grace, the power of his eloquence, the subtlety of his debating, and his knowledge of difficult languages. To an accurate knowledge of Greek and Latin, he had added the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Arabic dialects, which previously had not even been heard of by reputation in Italy. He rose to fame in the year 1484. Having spent seven years surveying the academies, and being eager for glory and fame, he proceeded to Rome: where he publicly proposed nine hundred questions for debate concerning Dialectical, Metaphysical, and Mathematical matters, sought from the hidden chests of the Latins and Greeks, from the very obscure Hebrew <term>Kabbalah</term> (a mystical Jewish tradition of scriptural interpretation), and from the most hidden mysteries of the ancient philosophers. He saw to it that these questions were posted in schools and at crossroads everywhere throughout all Europe, promising that he would pay the travel expenses of all learned men flying to Rome for the sake of debating. 

The envy of certain idle people stole the glory of such a great contest and triumph from the man of Mirandola; these people, taking it poorly that the universal mysteries of Theology and Philosophy were open to a young man and being debated among the common people, first attacked his questions with tricks and maneuvers: soon they accused thirteen of them as being errors and heresy. Mirandola, having immediately published an *Apology*, defended the truth of the questions and washed away the slanders of his adversaries. Pope Innocent, however, led by some unknown spite, forbade the reading of the little book of *Questions* and completely took away all hope of a debate. Having become more advanced in age, Mirandola began to hate that great "itch for debating": and having set aside the cultivation of philosophy and external arts, he settled entirely into a more chaste Theology; he diligently turned over the Sacred Books; he industriously compared the Latin and Greek versions with the Hebrew sources; he undertook to defend the truth of the Christian religion against the Jews and Muslims.

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15TH CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
...and especially he attacked and utterly defeated the impious as well as foolish tribe of Astrologers. In the year 1491, having resigned the government of the Principality of Mirandola and Concordia, he distributed the greatest part of his wealth to the poor; and retiring to a very pleasant villa in the territory of Ferrara, he devoted himself alone to God and the Muses <note>The "Muses" here refers to a life of scholarly and artistic study.</note>, becoming no less illustrious for his piety and boundless charity toward the needy than he had formerly been distinguished for his learning. Indeed, a little before his death, he was so inflamed with such a love for Christ and religion that he intended to distribute his remaining wealth to the poor and, protected only by a Crucifix, to wander the world with bare feet, preaching the Christian faith through cities, towns, and villages. He died at Florence (where he was accustomed to stay, delighting in the company of Marsilio Ficino and Angelo Poliziano) after being seized by a very severe fever, on the 17th of November <note>original: "xv. Cal. Decembr." — literally the 15th day before the Calends of December.</note>, in the year 1494, at the age of 32. He was buried in the Church of St. Mark in the habit of the Friars Preachers <note>The Dominican Order.</note>, which he had long ago vowed to take up and had put on. He was a man of plainly prodigious talent, and in the praise of his erudition for his age, he was second to none. Let us hear the Epitaph inscribed upon his tomb:

> ->Here lies Giovanni of Mirandola; the rest is known<-
> ->By the Tagus, the Ganges, and perhaps even the Antipodes.<-
<note>This famous epitaph suggests his fame reached the ends of the known world, from the rivers of Spain (Tagus) and India (Ganges) to the people on the opposite side of the globe (Antipodes).</note>

<margin>* In the style of Cicero.</margin>
His nature was plainly divine (says Erasmus * ) and his talent was suited to all things: but his style of speaking was also somewhat marred by his devotion to languages, Philosophy, and even Theology.

*Three books on Plato’s Symposium.*
*Elegy to Florence, in praise of Girolamo Benivieni.*
All the Works of Pico were published at Venice 1498; Strasbourg 1504; Basel 1573; Mirandola 1596; Basel 1601, folio.
Gianfrancesco Pico, Count of Mirandola, his nephew and heir, enumerates other writings of Pico in his *Life*, namely: *A book on the truth of Jerome’s translation against the slanders of the Jews. A defense of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, as far as the Psalms are concerned, against the same. A short book on the true calculation of time. Commentaries on the New Testament. A work against the seven enemies of the Church* (namely: Atheists, Pagans, Jews, Muslims, Christian heretics, impious but orthodox Christians, and Christians who are both impious and heretical). *Twelve books against divinatory Astrology. A translation and refutation of Ptolemy’s Centiloquium. Works against all Heretics, On the cure of diseases, On the harmony of Plato and Aristotle, Latin and Italian poems,* etc., which have not yet been brought to light.

CAROLUS FERNANDUS, or Phernandus, a Belgian by birth from the city of Bruges, blind from the very beginning of his life, yet learned beyond the ordinary; a distinguished Orator, Philosopher, Poet, and Preacher: a public Professor of the humanities at the University of Paris. He flourished in the year 1486.

**Æ**LIUS ANTONIUS NEBRISSENSIS, called *de Lebrixa* in his native tongue <note>Known in Spanish as Antonio de Nebrija</note>, was Spanish by nationality, born in the year 1444 in the town of the same name located on the marshes of the river Baetis <note>The Guadalquivir</note>. He was the son of Juan Martinez de Cala and Catharina de Xarana. After he had drunk in the elements of Grammar and Dialectics <note>Logic</note> in his homeland, he was sent to Salamanca, where for five years he studied Mathematics under Apollonius, Physics under Paschal de Aranda, and Ethics under Pedro of Osma. In the year 1463, having set out for Italy, he traversed almost all the Universities; he frequented the more distinguished Professors of the arts; and he attained a very rich knowledge of Theology, Civil and Canon Law, Medicine, and the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew languages. In the year 1473, recalled to his country by Alfonso Fonseca, Archbishop of Seville, he was the first of all to bring the science of polite literature <note>The Humanities</note> back to Spain by "right of recovery" <note>original: "postliminio" — a legal term used here to mean restoring something to its rightful place</note>; for nearly a thousand years, Spain, oppressed by the arms of the Vandals and Arabs, had lacked the splendor and elegance of the Latin tongue. Antonius, having been invited into the Archbishop's household, opened a grammar school in Seville and directed it for three years. Around the year 1476, after the death of his patron, he moved to Salamanca; and honored with a double salary, he undertook the management of two chairs (a thing which had happened to no one before): one for Grammar, the other for Poetics. In this literary pursuit, he devoted himself entirely to defeating the barbarism in which the minds of Spaniards had been neglected for so many centuries; he certainly took on a difficult task. For a love of their own faults had grown ingrained in the stubborn race of Scholastics <note>Traditional medieval scholars who resisted the new Humanist methods</note> along with the defects of their speech. They fought fiercely against Antonius, bringing charges of "innovation" against him, and almost accused him of heresy. These were the people whom Antonius—while he was scrubbing away the old filth of their speech—considered it a victory if he could merely persuade them to want to be cured. He flourished in the year 1488, when, invited by a generous salary, he moved into the household of Juan de Zúñiga, Grand Master of the Order of Alcántara. There, having found suitable leisure, he completed his Dictionary and other writings that served to illustrate Grammar. Meanwhile, the primary Professor at Salamanca having died, Antonius was appointed in the deceased man's place and returned to Salamanca. In the year 1504, he was summoned to court by King Ferdinand, who held him in the highest honor, so that he might record the history of the King's deeds in writing. Around the year 1508, he provided excellent assistance to Cardinal Ximenes, who was working on the trilingual edition of the Bible <note>The Complutensian Polyglot Bible, printed in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin</note>. In the year 1513, affected by some indignity or other from the ungrateful academics, he left Salamanca and gave himself to the patronage of Ximenes. Granted a lavish salary by him and made the first Professor of the University of Alcalá <note>The Complutense University</note>, he increased the cause of literature there through his writings and lectures with all his might. He died at Alcalá, taken by a stroke, on the 2nd of July, 1522, at the age of 77. He was the "Great Aristarchus of Spain" <note>A reference to the famous critic of Homer, meaning a supreme judge of letters</note>, a distinguished Orator, a man of much and varied reading, and a man of heavenly talent and eminent learning, the glory of the Roman toga: as Alfonso Matamoros calls him (*); who nevertheless elsewhere (†) acknowledges that the History which he wrote about the deeds of King Ferdinand was carried out by Antonius in a thin and even dejected style, with little diligence.

*Paraphrase of Sedulius’s Poem on the Miracles of Christ.* Published at Alcalá de Henares <note>original: "Compluti"</note> 1524, in quarto <note>a book size made by folding printed sheets twice to form four leaves</note>.

*Two books of Histories on the Navarrese War, waged by King Ferdinand against John, King of Navarre, in the year 1512.* Published everywhere at the end of the preceding History.
*Lexicon of Civil Law against certain notable errors of Accursius.* <note>Accursius was a 13th-century jurist whose glosses were the standard authority, often criticized by humanists like Nebrija for their medieval Latin</note>.
