<margin>1488.</margin>
**AURELIUS BRANDOLINUS**, nicknamed *Lippus* <note>The nickname "Lippus" translates to "bleary-eyed," referring to a chronic eye condition</note>, a Florentine by birth, was an eloquent theologian, highly skilled in music and rhetoric, and a most accomplished poet. He was so quick and effortless in composing verses that whatever he was about to say would tumble out in meter, even against his will. He flourished in the year 1488. Invited to Hungary by King Matthias Corvinus <note>Matthias Corvinus was one of the most powerful rulers in Central Europe and a great patron of the Renaissance</note>, he taught rhetoric at Buda and Esztergom <note>original: "Strigonii"</note> for several years. Upon returning to Italy, he joined the Order of Augustinian Hermits, taking the habit in a Florentine monastery. Eventually initiated into Holy Orders, he became known as one of the most celebrated preachers of his century. He died in Rome, having caught the plague, in the year 1498.

->W O R K S.<-

*Christian Paradoxes* in two books.
*On the Method of Writing* in three books. Cologne, 1573, in octavo.
*A Dialogue on the Condition of Human Life and Enduring Bodily Sickness*, addressed to Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary.
These three works were published together at Basel in 1498 and 1543.
*Poems on the death of Platina.* <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481) was a famous Renaissance humanist and the first librarian of the Vatican Library</note> These are found at the end of Platina’s own works.
The following have not yet emerged from the shadows: *All the Histories of the Old Testament rendered in a more elegant style*, *Many Histories of the Saints*, *Both Testaments narrated in verse*, *Commentaries on the Epistles of St. Paul*, and *Numerous Orations*; all of which Brandolinus is said to have written.

<margin>1488.</margin>
**PETRUS SCHOTTUS**, German by race and a native of Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratensis"</note>, was born to distinguished parents around the year 1459. Instructed in grammar and the first elements of literature by Johannes Müller, he traveled to Paris along with his teacher. Having stayed there for several years, he left nothing untried in every branch of knowledge. After gaining a great reputation there among all the learned and receiving his Bachelor’s degree, he returned home. Having briefly greeted his friends, he set out for Bologna; there he devoted himself to the study of poetry, rhetoric, and Greek literature, having Antonio of Brittany as his teacher in these subjects. He especially cultivated both Canon and Civil Law, earning a doctorate in both. He flourished in the year 1488. Upon returning to his homeland, he was appointed a Canon of the Church of St. Peter. He died in the middle of his life’s journey, snatched away by an untimely fate in 1491 at the age of 31, according to Trithemius <margin>* On Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 190.</margin>. His surviving works include: *The Lives of the Saints John the Baptist, John the Evangelist, and John Chrysostom*, in elegiac verse; and the *Praises of Jean Gerson*, likewise written in meter; also *Several Letters, and various Questions on matters pertaining to conscience.* Strasbourg, 1498.

<margin>1489.</margin>
**ARNOLDUS BOSTIUS**, or *Boschus*, a German by nationality and a monk of the Carmelite Order in the monastery of Ghent, flourished in the year 1489. He was very close friends with Trithemius, Ermolao Barbaro, Robert Gaguin, and other leaders of the Republic of Letters. He died at Ghent on the day before the Nones of April <note>April 4th</note> in the year 1499. His surviving works include *Two Books on the Illustrious Men of the Carthusian Order*, Cologne, 1609, in octavo. His other writings are listed by Trithemius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, page 204, including a *Third Book on the Illustrious Men of the Carmelite Order*, which Valerius Andreas <note>original: "Miræus"</note> reports is preserved as a manuscript at Mechelen. Certainly, it was once in the possession of John Bale, as was another work by the same author, *On the Patronage of Mary*.

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>15TH CENTURY. from the Year 1400. 1489.</margin>
**HEINRICH BEBEL** (Latinized: Henricus Bebelius), a German by birth, was born in Justingen in Swabia. Though born to parents of the lowest social rank, they were nonetheless honorable. He was a man exceptionally well-versed in every kind of fine literature; he was among the first to bring the study of more polished learning and the eloquence of the Latin language into Germany. He particularly cultivated the art of poetry, possessing such a fertile vein for verse that he was awarded the Poetic Laurel by Emperor Maximilian. He flourished in the year 1489. Called to the University of Tübingen in 1497, he undertook the public explanation of ancient poets, historians, and orators. He died after the year 1506.

*An Oration to Maximilian I, the Emperor, concerning the praises of himself and of Germany.* It is found among the *Writers of German Affairs* edited by Schardius, *Volume 1, page 95.*

*A Demonstration that the Germans are <term>αὐτόχθονας</term>* <note>original: "αὐτόχθονας", meaning "autochthonous" or indigenous—the claim that the Germans were original inhabitants of their land rather than migrants</note>. Ibid, p. 105.

*An Apology for the defense of the Roman Emperors, against Aeneas Sylvius and others, who belittle the name of the Emperors and mock their coronation.* <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, was a prolific humanist writer</note> Ibid, p. 109.

<margin>1489.</margin>
**DONATO BOSSI** (Latinized: Donatus Bossius), an Italian by race, from Milan by birth, was born in the year 1436. He flourished in the year 1489. He wrote a *Chronicle, or a History of human conditions and accounts* from the beginning of the world to his own time; likewise a *Chronicle of the Bishops and Archbishops of Milan* up to the year 1489. <margin>1490.</margin>
**MARCANTONIO COCCIO SABELLICO** (Latinized: Marcus Antonius Coccius Sabellicus), an Italian by nation, from the Aequi region by birth, or as others have it, born at the village of Varro on the Valerian Way. His father was a blacksmith. Well-cultivated in fine letters, he first opened a grammar school at Tivoli <note>Latin: Tiburtinos</note>; then, seeking higher things, he moved to Rome. Being received into the friendship and circle of Pomponio Leto, he drank more deeply of the knowledge of Latin eloquence; and having been crowned with the laurel wreath in a solemn ceremony on the Quirinal hill, he took the name "Sabellicus." He flourished in the year 1490. Leaving Rome, he taught noble boys in Udine near Aquileia. Soon, however, called by the people of Vicenza with double pay to lead the city's youth, he moved there. As his reputation for learning grew daily, he was summoned by the Venetian Senate to record the Republic's history and teach the liberal arts publicly. He was granted a salary of three hundred gold coins and appointed by Cardinal Bessarion as the prefect of the library founded by the Cardinal himself at St. Mark's. He died at age seventy in the year 1506, on the 7th day before the Kalends of May <note>April 25</note>, consumed by the "French Disease" <note>original: "lue Gallicâ," a common early name for syphilis</note> which the delirious old man <margin>* Erasmus, The Ciceronian, p. 374.</margin> had contracted from the love of an impure harlot. *A man eloquent by nature, and not lacking in art,* says Erasmus \*, *he sometimes declaims not unsuccessfully; he was quite splendidly engaged in history, but only in that which suits his own style of speaking.*

# The Synodal Century. 15th CENTURY. from the Year 1400.

12 Orations.
Various Poems.
All the works of Sabellico reviewed so far were published in Basel, 1560, in four volumes; all those listed from the books of *Examples* <note>Latin: Exemplorum libris</note> were published exclusively in Venice, 1505.
*Annotations on Horace*, Basel, 1580; on *Suetonius*, Venice, 1490 and Paris, 1610; on *Pliny*, Frankfurt, 1602 and Venice, 1508; on *Livy*, Venice and Paris, 1573. An *Oration on Livy regarding the praises of History*, also Paris. *Annotations on Valerius Maximus, Lucan, Papinius, Catullus, Cicero, and Valerius Flaccus*, printed together by Badius along with the *Annotations on Pliny, Livy, and Suetonius* in Paris.

<margin>1493.</margin>
**PONTICUS VIRUNNIUS** (or Virunnius), an Italian by birth from the city of Treviso, flourished around the year 1490. At approximately that time, to find favor with the Badoer family—a most distinguished Venetian family which claimed descent from the Britons—he reduced the first six books of Geoffrey of Monmouth's *History of British Affairs* <note>Latin: de rebus Anglicis Historiæ</note> into an epitome, removing the legendary fables. This *Epitome*, which narrates British history in six books from the time of Brutus to King Arthur (specifically the year of Christ 528), was published in Augsburg, 1534; London, 1585; and among the *Writers of British History* edited by Hieronymus Commelinus in Lyon, 1587, page 93. Ponticus also wrote *Commentaries on Virgil, Ovid's Metamorphoses, Statius's Achilleid, Claudian, and Johannes de Sacrobosco’s Sphere*; three books *On obscure passages of authors and corrupt names*; two books *On the misery of letters*; and a book of *Elegies and Epigrams*. I will not even list the Latin translations of various Greek writers and other small works enumerated by Simler on page 585.

<margin>1490.</margin>
**BONIFACIUS SIMONETA**, an Italian of the city of Milan, born of noble rank, was the paternal uncle of the historian Giovanni Simoneta. He was a monk of the Cistercian Order and eventually the Abbot of the Monastery of St. Stephen of Corno in the region of Piacenza. He flourished in the year 1490. He wrote to King Charles VIII of France his *Commentaries on Christian Persecutions and the History of the Popes from St. Peter up to Innocent VIII*. He did not weave these commentaries into a continuous narrative thread, but organized them using a completely new method into six books of letters. Several Orations are inserted into these; and in each of the 289 letters, he typically mixes in matters of anatomy, medicine, geography, astronomy, and mathematics. This work was published in Milan, 1492, and by the care of Hieronymus Emser in Basel, 1509.

**PETRUS APOLLONIUS COLLATIUS**, a priest of Novara, flourished—according to the opinion of Vossius * (which indeed seems more likely)—around the year 1490. However, by Bigne, Miræus, and others, he is assigned to the end of the seventh century. Vossius conjectures that he is the same person as the Apollonius Collatius who wrote the *Fasts*, whom Caesar Scaliger † lists among the authors of that declining age; Scaliger reveals him to have been a somewhat "chilly" poet, and even unfortunate when he departed from the elegiac meter. Our Apollonius wrote four books in heroic verse *On the Destruction of Jerusalem conquered by Titus*. These were published through the care of Jean Gagnée in Paris, 1516, and in a more corrected version by the study of Adriaan van der Burch in Antwerp at the workshop of Christophe Plantin, in Bigne’s *Appendix of Christian Poets*, page 731, and in the *Library of the Fathers*, Volume 12. There also exists a manuscript in the possession of the Reverend Father * Mabillon (which he had received as a gift from the celebrated Magliabechi, among other things) of our Apollonius’s *Heroic Poem on David and Goliath addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici*, from which it is clearer than light that he flourished at this very time.

# The Synodal Century. 15th CENTURY. from the Year 1400.

...indeed, he even enriched the leading Cardinals with the lands and castles of the Roman See. In ecclesiastical matters, he achieved nothing worthy of memory; he pursued entirely different goals, such that he scraped together money from every side by selling dispensations <note>A "dispensation" is a formal exemption from a church law or a vow, often granted by the Pope.</note> everywhere, showing no regard for law or decency. For this reason, in the year 1498, he granted Louis [XII] of France the power to divorce his wife Joan, for no other reason than that she was sterile and unattractive. His primary aim, pursued with every possible effort, was to acquire a secular principality for Caesar Borgia, his illegitimate son, through both lawful and unlawful means, and to convert the "Patrimony of Peter" <note>The lands and territories under the direct sovereign rule of the Pope.</note> into the Borgia family inheritance. Truly, neither father nor son lacked the ambition for this undertaking. The son, having drafted his father's army, expelled the petty rulers of Flaminia and Umbria from their cities with the greatest injustice; the father, by Apostolic authority, created his son Duke of both Provinces and Prince of the Ecclesiastical domain. However, the fates opposed these sacrilegious daring deeds. For Alexander died in the year 1503, on the 18th day of August, killed by poison through a fatal error of his cupbearer <note>Original: "fatali pincernæ errore." This refers to a famous (though debated) story that Alexander VI accidentally drank poisoned wine he had intended for his guests.</note>—poison which he himself had prepared for several of the wealthier Cardinals, whose riches he coveted, having invited them to dinner. The historians of that age, Guicciardini, Ciacconius, and others—to say nothing of more recent authors like Briet—extensively describe his most foul morals, his immense ambition, his most shameful greed, his detestable cruelty, his unspeakable lust, and his incestuous relations with his daughter Lucretia.

<margin>1492.</margin>
**BERNARDUS DE CARAVAIAL**, a Spaniard by birth, descended from an ancient and noble family from the city of Cáceres in the province of Extremadura. He was Bishop of Astorga <note>Latin: Africanis (likely a typo for Asturicensis)</note>, Badajoz, Cartagena, and Sigüenza, and served as the Ambassador of King Ferdinand of Spain to Innocent VIII. Eventually made a Cardinal by Alexander VI, he flourished in the year 1492. In the year 1511, when Pope Julius II most shamefully violated the promise formerly given to the Cardinals regarding the holding of an Ecumenical Council, Bernard, joined by several other Cardinals, declared a General Council to be held at Pisa, and celebrated it on the first of September. For this reason, he was deposed by Julius and lost his Cardinal's dignity. Restored by Leo X, he held the office of Dean in the Sacred College of Cardinals and obtained the Bishopric of Tusculum, having been honored previously with the title of Patriarch of Jerusalem. He died in Rome at the Monastery of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem on the 13th day of December, 1523. There exists an *Oration to the Cardinals delivered in the year 1492 concerning the election of the Supreme Pontiff*, printed in Rome in 1492. Nicolas Antonio mentions others in his *Spanish Library*, Volume 1, page 168: namely, an *Oration to Sixtus IV and the Cardinals on the day of the Lord's Circumcision in 1484*; a *Homily on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross* delivered before Emperor Maximilian at Mechelen in 1508; a *Sermon to the Cardinals in commemoration of the victory of Baza*; a *Consolatory Letter to King Ferdinand on the death of the Most Serene Prince John*; and an *Oration in the name of the Catholic Monarchs to Alexander VI*. Antonio confirms that each of these small works was published, though he indicates neither the place nor the time of publication.

<margin>1494.</margin>
## NICOLAUS BARIANUS,
an Italian by nation, from Piacenza by birth, a Monk of the Order of Augustinian Hermits, and most highly learned in Theology and Canon Law. He flourished in the year 1494. When a controversy arose between the Augustinians and the Minorites <note>The Minorites are the Franciscans (Order of Friars Minor).</note> regarding the right of precedence, he himself argued the cause of his associates with the greatest learning and obtained a ruling in their favor from the legal experts. He later committed his *Arguments* to writing and, under the title *The Vitalian Case on the Precedence of the Hermits and Minorites*, had them printed at *Cremona* in 1500. He also wrote a *Book on the Mount of Impiety* <note>Original: "Librum de monte impietatis." This likely refers to a critique of the "Monti di Pietà," charitable pawnbroking institutions, which some theologians argued were usurious.</note>, published at *Cremona* in 1496 and at the end of the book *On the Roman Mounts of Piety*, which appeared in *Leipzig* in the year 1670; and a *Lenten Quodlibet* <note>A "Quodlibet" was a formal academic debate on any subject proposed.</note> of 77 *Preachable Questions*, printed in *Bologna* in 1501 in quarto format.

<margin>1494.</margin>
## ROBERT GAGUIN,
a Belgian by birth, originating from the village of Calonne on the borders of Artois by the river Lys. While still at a young age, he entered the Monastery of Nieppe among the Morini and joined the Order of the Most Holy Trinity for the Redemption of Captives. He was later sent to Paris for the sake of his studies and stayed with his fellow members at the Monastery of St. Mathurin; he received a doctorate in both laws and was finally made General of his entire Order in the year 1473. He flourished in the year 1494. Distinguished no less for his prudence than for the fame of his learning, he undertook many embassies to Italy, Germany, and Britain on behalf of Kings Charles VIII and Louis XII of France. He was especially dear to the latter, by whom he was gifted a great sum of money and appointed Prefect of the Royal Library. He died in Paris in the year 1501, on the 11th day before the Calends of June <note>May 22nd.</note>, and was buried among his fellow Mathurins. He was a man not in the least unlearned, and uncommonly skilled in history, rhetoric, and poetry; yet everyone finds his reliability lacking in narrating domestic affairs and in praising his own people. Regarding his style, Erasmus <margin>* *The Ciceronian*.</margin> has this to say:
> *Robert Gaguin was held in great name not so long ago, though he was more marketable for his speech than for his writings; but that was in his own age; now he would scarcely be accepted among those who speak Latin correctly.*

*Poems on the Passion of St. Richard the Martyr, On the various Orders in the Church, On the misery of the human condition, A Dialogue against the idle and lazy. Paris*, 1598, with the book on the Conception of the Blessed Mary.

<margin>1494.</margin>
## JOHANN GEILER,
called "of Kaisersberg" <note>original: "Kayferbergius"</note> from his birthplace; for by nation he was an Alsatian, born in the imperial town of Kaisersberg on March 16, 1445; the son of Johann Geiler and Anna Zuber. After his first elementary studies, he was sent to the University of Freiburg and obtained the degree of Master. Soon initiated into sacred orders, he went to Basel to devote himself to the study of Theology. After five years had passed there, he obtained the insignia of the Doctorate. Having thus earned a distinguished reputation for his complete knowledge of theological matters, he was summoned first to Freiburg and soon after to Würzburg to undertake the duty of preaching. Finally, around the year 1478, invited by a larger salary and the persistent pleas of the citizens, he moved to Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratum"</note>; there, for thirty-three years in the Cathedral, he preached with the greatest eloquence to an equally large and applauding crowd of listeners. He flourished in the year 1494. Distinguished by his lavish liberality toward the needy, hospitality toward strangers, and an unconquerable zeal for piety, he won for himself the highest authority among the Germans. Furthermore, he was very dear to the Emperor Maximilian, by whom he was often summoned to court and held in the greatest honor. However, he was little liked by bishops and monks, whose shameful ignorance of learning and deplorable corruption of morals he sharply rebuked in his writings and sermons. He died on March 10, 1510, and was buried in Strasbourg in the great Cathedral near the pulpit.

### WRITINGS.

*Book of Sermons*, in which are mixed entire treatises: *On the Tree of Humanity*, *On the Tree of the Crucified*, *On the Twelve Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, *On the Death of Grace*, *On the Twenty-three Conditions of Death*, and *On the Preparation for a Happy Death*. Strasbourg, 1514, 1518.
*The Ship of Fools* <note>original: "Navicula fatuorum." Geiler adapted Sebastian Brant's famous social satire into a series of sermons.</note>, Strasbourg, 1510.

<margin>1494.</margin>
**JOHANNES REUCHLIN**, also called **CAPNIO** <note>Reuchlin’s name was Hellenized (translated into Greek) as "Capnio," which means "smoky," corresponding to the German "Rauch."</note>, a German by nationality and a Swabian by birth, was born at Pforzheim, a town in the Margraviate of Baden, in the year 1454, on the 5th day before the Kalends of January <note>December 28th.</note>. In his tender years, he was drawn to the boy choristers who served in the Church of his native town; as he possessed a very strong voice, he was summoned to the court of the Margrave of Baden. There, having been taught grammar, and far surpassing his adolescent peers in the strength of his talent and his excellent character, he was assigned as a companion to the young Count of Baden and sent with him to the University of Paris. In this place, besides the uncommon knowledge of the Latin language and Logic which he acquired, he learned Greek literature from George Hermonymus of Sparta. Under the same teacher, he also learned the art of painting letters beautifully; through this skill, he later earned a private income for himself and won the goodwill of many. In the year 1474, he went to Basel, where, having been granted the rank of Master of Philosophy, he began to teach both the Greek and Latin languages simultaneously. He commenced the study of Civil Law <note>original: "Juris Cæsarei," referring to Roman/Imperial law.</note> there and finally brought it to completion at Orleans, receiving the honors of a Doctorate in the year 1481. Returning to Germany, he was called to the court by Count Eberhard of Württemberg, and was first led to Rome in his retinue, and after his return, served as an ambassador to Emperor Frederick. While performing his embassy at the Court, a certain Jewish physician, Jehiel Loans, taught him the elements of the Hebrew language; Reuchlin <note>original: "Capnio"</note> later learned this language more accurately while serving as an ambassador in Rome from a certain Obadiah, to whom he gave one gold coin as a tuition fee <note>original: "Minerval"</note> for each hour. He had been sent to Rome by Philip, the Count Palatine, into whose court he had withdrawn after he had been forced into exile from Tübingen due to political disturbances in Württemberg. Once matters at home were settled, he returned to Tübingen, and having been chosen among the "Four Men" <note>A board of senior judges or magistrates.</note> of the Swabian Province, he dedicated his leisure to the promotion of the Hebrew language in the Christian world. He was especially famous from the year 1494, the year in which Trithemius wrote his *Catalog*. He was most skilled in both divine and human literature; equipped above all with a very accurate knowledge of the Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldean languages, he was the first in Germany to revive Hebrew and Greek literature and Latin elegance. This was done despite the roaring of the Monks and the <term>Scholastic Theologians</term> <note>Scholasticism was a medieval method of learning that focused on logic and dialectic, which the newer Humanists often found "barbaric" or overly complex.</note>, who easily predicted the ruin of their own knotted and barbaric theology from the revival of linguistic science and the study of elegance. Therefore, led by Johannes Hoogstraten <note>original: "Hocstrato"</note>, a member of the Dominican Order and Dean of the University of Cologne, they rose up against Reuchlin, accused him of heresy, burned his writings, and cried out that he favored the Jews more than was right; they treated his communication with "Pagan Poets" as if it were a capital crime. Nor did the injury stop within these bounds: they approached the Roman Pontiffs and demanded with persistent shouting that Reuchlin be cursed and his books be given to the flames, and that Hebrew letters be banished from the Christian commonwealth.

<summary>This page catalogs the diverse homiletic works of the Strasbourg preacher Johann Geiler von Kaisersberg and provides a detailed biography of Johannes Reuchlin, the pioneering German Humanist who revived the study of Greek and Hebrew in the face of intense opposition from conservative theologians.</summary>

--- Page 1132 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of Johannes Reuchlin (also known as Capnio), focusing on his intense conflict with the Inquisition over the preservation of Jewish literature and his subsequent academic career and death.</meta>

# The Synodal Century.

<margin>
15th CENTURY.
from the Year 1400.
</margin>
For the Inquisitors <note>Religious officials tasked with identifying and suppressing heresy.</note> bore it ill that Christians should cultivate the study of the Hebrew language. With great cunning, they had obtained an Edict from the Emperor decreeing that all Jewish books, except for the Holy Bible, should be committed to the flames. Their plan was surely to extort a large sum of money from the Jews, who would gladly pay to ransom their books. The Emperor consulted Reuchlin on the matter; he delivered a milder judgment, arguing that only those Jewish books which actively attacked the Christian faith should be burned, while the rest should be preserved. From this was born the bitter hatred of the Inquisitors and all the monks. Reuchlin avenged himself against the malice and insolence of this "hooded flock" <note>original: "Cucullati gregis," a disparaging reference to monks and their cowls.</note> with the sharpest satires—for such foolish dwellers in the dark deserved no more serious a style of refutation. He did this especially through the publication of the volume *Letters of Obscure Men* <note>original: "Obscurorum Virorum Epistolarum." This was a famous anonymous satire that mocked the bad Latin and ignorance of the Scholastic theologians.</note>, seasoned with admirable wit and humor, in which the crude and ridiculous style of the monks and Scholastics writing in Latin is mimicked to provoke laughter. This book was greedily received and circulated by all, and it is a wonder how deeply it stung the minds of the hooded ones. It so wounded Hoogstraten <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, a Dominican Inquisitor and Reuchlin’s primary antagonist.</note> that he died as if struck by a lethal grief. The remaining partners in the conspiracy finally obtained, through humble prayers to Pope Leo X, an Apostolic edict forbidding the reading or sale of those *Letters*. Reuchlin eluded the edict with a clever trick: he oversaw the production of a second volume of letters of the same sort—though far sharper than the first—as if it were not prohibited at all by the title of the decree. However, that quarrel was quite light compared to the capital controversy I mentioned above. That matter was first committed by the Pope to delegated judges; when they gave their verdict in favor of Reuchlin, the monks appealed to the Pope. Erasmus and Hutten <note>Ulrich von Hutten, a German knight and humanist scholar.</note> brought aid to Reuchlin; for this reason, the monks attacked them with various slanders, mocking pictures, and futile arguments. Finally, when the dispute between Luther and the preachers of Indulgences began in Germany, that contention gave way to a more serious one and gradually fell quiet. Relieved by these disturbances, Reuchlin taught both Greek and Hebrew letters at the University of Ingolstadt in his final years, until, overcome by jaundice <note>original: "morbo Icterico"</note>, he found it necessary to resign his care of literary matters.

<margin>
* On Ecclesiastical Writers, folio 201.
</margin>
He died at Stuttgart on the day before the Calends of August <note>July 31st</note> in the year 1521, at the age of 67. *Truly worthy,* says Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a Benedictine abbot and polymath.</note>, *of a man who should devote himself only to letters, and not also to the clamorous courts of the people. For not even Italy, nor our own century, could present us with a man equal to this great figure.*

*Three books on the Cabalistic Art* <note>original: "De Arte Cabalistica"</note>, dedicated to Leo X. Published separately at Hagenau, 1517; among the writers on the Cabalistic art at Basel, 1550; and with the *Catholic Truths* of Pietro Galatino, Frankfurt, 1612.
*Three books on the Miraculous Word* <note>original: "De Verbo mirifico"</note>, dedicated to Dalburg, Bishop of Worms and Chancellor; written in the form of a dialogue, in which the secrets of Greek, Hebrew, and Christian philosophy are related. *Venice 1486 (folio), Speyer 1494 (folio), Lyon 1552 (octavo)*, and with the preceding work, *Basel 1587.* Both works are prohibited in the Roman Indices <note>The Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the list of books banned by the Catholic Church.</note>.

<margin>1494.</margin>
**JACOB WIMPHELING**, likewise a German by nation, an Alsatian by birth, and a citizen of Sélestat, was born in the year 1449. Educated in the humanities at the local school in Sélestat, he proceeded in order to the Universities of Freiburg, Basel, Erfurt, and Heidelberg, so that he might drink from the fountain of knowledge in Theology and Canon Law; he was finally made a Licentiate <note>A degree ranking between a Bachelor and a Doctor</note> in both according to academic custom. Considered among the most eloquent preachers of that age, he was called to Speyer in the year 1494 to fulfill the office of Church Minister. He did this for several years, not without remarkable praise for his piety and erudition. Eventually weary of the secular world, he resigned his ecclesiastical dignity and, having set out for Heidelberg, took up the task of explaining the sacred authors—and among them Jerome—in the city's literary Gymnasium <note>An elite secondary school or academy</note>. To better serve the needs of the human race, he did not disdain to act as a schoolmaster; he shaped many adolescents of the highest promise—including Jacob Sturm of Strasbourg—in literature and good character.

Being himself instructed in superior literature, and finding it difficult to endure the ignorance and arrogance of the monks (whom he attacked with biting words), he was accused of heresy by the Augustinian monks before Pope Julius II. They claimed he had written somewhere that Saint Augustine was not a monk—or certainly not such a one as the Augustinians are now considered to be—nor did he wear the modern habit of the Order named after him. After hearing the case, the Pope acquitted Wimpheling by his own decree from the troublesome outcries of the monks and commanded silence upon his slanderers. After the Reformation begun by Luther, grieving at the schism brought upon the Church, he retired from the Heidelberg Gymnasium and thereafter lived a quiet life in Sélestat in the house of his sister Magdalena. He died nearly an octogenarian in the year 1528, on the 17th of November.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Epitome of the Emperors, and of deeds performed in Germany.* Basel, 1532. Together with the History by Widukind, and among the *German Writers* of Schardius, Volume 1, p. 170.
*Book on the life and character of the Bishops of Strasbourg, and of other Princes and prelates. Strasbourg 1512, 1661.*
*Adolescence.* <note>original: "Adolescentia"</note> A work written in the year 1500, in which precepts for the noble formation of character are handed down. *Strasbourg 1514.*
*Oration, or Counsel on waging war against the Turks.* Eisleben, 1603.
*On the grievances of the German nation against the Roman See and Curia, addressed to Emperor Maximilian.* Found in Freher’s *German Writers*, Volume 2, p. 373; however, it is not complete.
*Reply on the same argument against the Treatise of Aeneas Sylvius.* ibid. p. 381.
*Sermon to youths who are being initiated into sacred orders.* Printed at Basel by Herwagen.

*Rhetoric for boys.* Strasbourg, 1515.
*Philippics, or six Dialogues for the instruction of the sons of Philip, Elector Palatine.* Strasbourg, 1498.

**OLIVIER MAILLARD**, a native of Brittany <note>original: "Armoricus"</note> according to some, though others say Paris, was a Provincial of the Order of Friars Minor of the Regular Observance, and finally their Vicar General; he was a celebrated preacher at Paris and Nantes, and in the French and Burgundian courts. **MICHAEL FRANÇOIS**, of Gallo-Flemish descent and a native of Lille <note>original: "Infulensis"</note>, was a monk of the Dominican Order and a Doctor of Theology at Cologne. He served as the Confessor, Preacher, and Counselor to Philip of Austria <note>Philip the Handsome</note>, and was created Bishop of Selimbria <note>original: "Salubriensis," a titular see</note> shortly before his death. He flourished in the year 1494. He died in his homeland at Lille in the year 1502. He was a devotee of the Rosary of the Blessed Virgin, as superstitious as any other; in many writings, he proclaimed the merits of his Confraternity and extolled the majesty of the Most Blessed Virgin beyond what is right or divine law <note>original: "supra jus fasque"</note>.

**ANTONIO BONFINI**, an Italian by nationality, from the region of Apulia and the homes of Ascoli and Recanati, was highly educated in both Greek and Latin literature. He flourished in the year 1495. Held in the highest honor by Matthias Corvinus, the King of Hungary <note>Matthias Corvinus (reigned 1458–1490) was one of the most powerful rulers of his time and a great patron of the arts.</note>, he undertook the task of recording Hungarian history at the King’s encouragement. He did this using a style that was far from inelegant; having compiled the *History of Hungarian Affairs* <note>original: "Rerum Hungaricarum Historia"</note> in forty-five books—distributed into four and a half "Decades"—covering the period from the very origins of the nation down to the year 1495, he sent it as a gift to Ladislaus, King of Hungary, in that same year. The first three Decades were published through the care of Martin Brenner at *Basel, 1543*; the complete History, with additions and corrections by Joannes Sambucus, appeared in *Basel, 1568 (folio)*, *Frankfurt, 1581 (folio)*, and *Hanau, 1606 (folio)*. His *Symposium of Beatrice, or Three Dialogues on Virginity and Marital Fidelity* <note>original: "Symposium Beatricis, seu Dialogi III. de Virginitate & fide conjugali"</note> were published from the library of Sambucus at *Basel, 1572 (octavo)* and reprinted in *1621 (octavo)*. Furthermore, Josias Simler, in his *Zurich Library* (p. 48), lists the Greek books translated into Latin by Bonfini. Among these, *Hermogenes on Rhetoric* and the *Preliminary Exercises of Aphthonius the Sophist* <note>original: "Aphthonii Sophistæ Progymnasmata"</note> were printed at *Lyon in 1538*.

<margin>1495.</margin>
**GIOVANNI GIOVIANO PONTANO**, an Italian by birth, originated from the town of Cerreto in Umbria. His father, who was of no mean status, was murdered by rebellious citizens, and so as a young and destitute man, he fled to Naples. There, through the help of Antonio Panormitano <note>Antonio Beccadelli (1394–1471), a famous humanist known as "Il Panormitano."</note>, the Master of the Royal Archives, he was received into the court and favor of King Ferdinand. He was appointed tutor to Alfonso the Younger, the King's eldest son; eventually, upon the death of Panormitano, he was appointed to his position and took charge of the royal correspondence. He flourished in the year 1495. Though regarded as among the leading historians, poets, and orators of the century, he nevertheless provoked the hatred and envy of many due to his biting style and a certain arrogant air <note>original: "subagresti supercilio," literally "somewhat rustic or haughty eyebrow."</note>. From this, perhaps, arose the slander spread among the public while he was still alive: that he had published under his own name certain volumes of Cicero found in the ancient library of the Monastery of Monte Cassino, with only slight alterations. He died in the month of August, in the year 1503, at the age of 78. He was buried in Naples in the tomb he had built for himself, his wife, and his children. Regarding his style and talent, Erasmus has this to say in his *The Ciceronian*: <margin>* The Ciceronian.</margin> 
> *I am not so dull or so envious as to deny that Pontano was a supreme man, gifted with many outstanding natural talents. I, too, am swept away by the calm flow of his speech; the sweet ringing of his words, with their pleasant chime, charms my ears; and finally, the dignity and majesty of his oratory dazzles with a certain brilliance. Yet, he treats commonplaces in such a way that you can hardly distinguish whether he was a Christian or not. Without question, he must be numbered among the foremost men of letters.*

All these works, organized into three volumes, were sent to the press by Cratander of Basel in three volumes, octavo. <note>Andreas Cratander (ca. 1490–1540) was a prominent Swiss printer known for high-quality editions of humanistic texts.</note>

A *Dialogue on the extent to which Astrology should be believed* was published at Cologne in 1544.

<margin>1495.</margin>
## NICOLAUS SIMONIS, a Dutchman or Hollander by nationality, from Haarlem, was a monk of the Carmelite Order in the monastery at Haarlem. He eventually became the Provincial <note>A "Provincial" is a high-ranking official who governs a specific geographic district or "province" of a religious order.</note> in Lower Germany and the primary interpreter of Theology among his colleagues. He flourished in the year 1495 and died at a great age in Haarlem in the year 1511.

->WRITINGS.<-

*Sermons for the Seasons and the Saints*, which he titled *Vade Mecum* <note>literally "Go with me," a term for a handbook or guide carried on one's person</note>. I believe these were printed somewhere, but I have not yet discovered the place or year.
*Review Lectures and Disputations*, Venice, 1497. A single *Disputation* by which he became especially famous was published separately in the same place in 1487.
*Commentary on the second book of the Decretals* <note>The Decretals are letters of the Pope that formulate church law (canon law).</note>, Milan, 1505 and 1510.
*On the power of the Pope, the Emperor, and the Council* in four books, published at Milan at the end of the previous work.
Many other small works of his, both historical and theological, which have not yet been brought to light, are listed by Josias Simler in his *Zurich Library* (p. 525), Valerius Andreas in his *Belgian Library* (p. 582), and Antonio Alegrio in the *Carmelite Paradise* (16th Century, chapter 2, p. 350).

<margin>1495.</margin>
## JACOBUS SPRENGER, a German by nationality and seemingly from Cologne, was a monk of the Dominican Order and eventually a Provincial Prior. He flourished in the year 1495. After attaining the title of Master, he was appointed General Inquisitor of heretical depravity throughout Germany by Pope Innocent VIII (or, as others claim, Sixtus IV), alongside Heinrich Institor <note>Also known as Heinrich Kramer (c. 1430–1505).</note>, a theologian of the same Order. Assisted by his colleague, he wrote a famous work against female sorcerers, divided into three books, which he titled *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>The Hammer of Witches, first published in 1487. It became the most influential and widely used manual for the prosecution of witches.</note>. This appeared at Venice in 1576, Frankfurt in 1580, and Lyon in 1620, all octavo. However, the volume he composed *On the Institution, Approval, Miracles, and Indulgences of the Holy Rosary of the Blessed Virgin* seems to remain unpublished. Furthermore, the aforementioned Inquisitor Heinrich wrote a book *On the Power of the Pope against the Monarchy of Antonio Roselli* (a jurist of Padua), published at Venice in 1499, as well as several other works not yet made public, which are listed by Ambrose de Altamura in the *Library of Preachers* (p. 215).

<margin>1496.</margin>
## VINCENZO BANDELLO, an Italian by birth and a Lombard by region, originated from Castelnuovo in the Diocese of Tortona. He was a member of the Dominican Order and a professor of theology among them at the University of Bologna, often serving as the Regent of the academic school. He was eventually twice the Prior of his Order in Bologna and three times the Vicar General of the Congregation of Lombardy, or Prior of Milan. He flourished in the year 1496. Finally, in the general chapter held at Rome in 1501, he was elected General of the entire Order. He died at the age of seventy in the monastery of Monte Alto in Calabria in the year 1506 and was buried at the church of St. Dominic in Naples.

**JOANNES PALÆONYDORUS**, or *Veteraquinas* <note>Latinized form of "Oudewater," meaning "Old Water."</note>, a Dutchman by nationality, born in Oudewater, a town in the jurisdiction of Utrecht; a monk of the Carmelite Order in the Monastery of Mechelen, and Doctor of Sacred Theology. He flourished in the year 1496. He died in the year 1507 at the age of 74. We have his written works: *The Three-Part Bundle of Times* <note>original: "Fasciculus Temporum tripartitus"</note>, or the book, as he himself inscribed it, *The tripartite, anaphoric, panegyric book* <note>original: "trimereftus [trimerestus] anaphoricus panegyricus"</note> on the origin, state, and progress of his Carmelite Order, printed with Mainz types: *Manual of the same Order*, published at Mainz together with the *Bundle*: *The Bulwark of the Carmelites* <note>original: "Propugnaculum Carmelitarum"</note>, or a book on the antiquity and sanctity of the Hermits of Mount Carmel, printed at *Venice, 1570, in quarto*. His unpublished writings are reviewed by Simler in the *Zurich Library* <note>original: "Bibl. Tigurin."</note> p. 402; Fr. Sweertius in *Athenae Belgicae* p. 389; and Ant. de Alegre in *Carmelite Paradise* <note>original: "Paradis. Carmel."</note> p. 376. Many of his letters existed in the possession of Basilius.

<margin>1496.</margin>
**JOANNES BLÆRUS** <note>John Blair</note>, a Brabantian by people, from Diest by homeland, Prior of the Monastery of Saint James of the Benedictine Order within the walls of the City of Liège. He flourished in the year 1496. He wrote the *History of the Revelation of Blessed Juliana, a nun of Liège, made divinely in the year 1230, concerning the institution of the Feast of Corpus Christi.* <note>St. Juliana of Liège was the mystic whose visions led to the establishment of the Feast of Corpus Christi.</note> It appeared in the *Great Mirror of Examples* <note>original: "Magno Speculo Exemplorum"</note> at *Douai, 1603*, and is found in Bzovius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the year 1230, number 16.

<margin>1500.</margin>
**JOANNES NAUCLERUS**, or *Vergehaus*, a German by nationality, a Swabian by homeland, born of a noble place, son of Joannes Vergehaus (a man of knightly dignity and courtier to Count Louis of Württemberg); Doctor of both Laws <note>meaning both Civil and Canon Law</note>, and Professor of Canon Law in the Academy of Tübingen: of which he was appointed the first Rector by Count Everard of Württemberg, the founder, in the year 1477. He had once been the supervisor of the Count’s education in his youth, though he was hindered by the most wicked envy of unlearned courtiers from imbuing the Prince committed to his care with the elements of the Latin language. From the Court, Nauclerus retired to the Church, and having been appointed provost of the Collegiate Church at Stuttgart around the year 1460, he was sent as an ambassador by Count Ulrich of Württemberg to Duke Charles of Burgundy seven years later. After he had performed the supreme office of the Academy for some time, he also accepted the leadership of the Church of Tübingen. He flourished in the year 1500. He performed both duties with truly distinguished praise; and he sent forth many men of great name from the School of Tübingen, steeped in letters in no common way, including Johannes Reuchlin. <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a massive figure in German humanism and the study of Hebrew.</note> He wrote a *Universal Chronicle* <note>original: "Chronicon Universale"</note> succinctly encompassing the memorable affairs of all ages and nations from the Creation of the World up to the year 1500. It first appeared at *Tübingen in 1515*; then (enlarged and polished by Philipp Melanchthon <note>Melanchthon was a key leader of the Protestant Reformation and a famous Greek scholar.</note>) together with an Appendix by Nicolaus Baselius, a monk of Hirsau, up to the year 1514; and another by Conrad Tigermann and Bartholomaeus Laurent, briefly recording deeds from the year 1515 to 1544, at *Cologne, 1544, in folio*; then with the Appendix of Laurentius Surius from the year 1501 to 1564, at *Cologne, 1564, 3 volumes in folio*; and finally *in the same place, 1579, in folio*.

## AUGUSTINE, of the Italian nation, from the city of Pavia <note>original: "Ticinensi"</note>, at least a Canon Regular of Pavia, of the Lateran Congregation. He flourished in the year 1500. He died after the year 1520.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Life of the Blessed Monica*, mother of Saint Augustine.

*Clarification of Christian Religions*, or *of Religious Orders* <note>original: "Elucidarium Christianarum Religionum, sive Religiosorum Ordinum"</note>: in which he treats extensively of the Order of Augustinians, the life, character, and doctrine of Saint Augustine, and argues that the Augustinian Hermits are later in time than the Canons Regular. <note>This was a common point of historical dispute between the two branches of the Augustinians regarding which group could claim the most direct lineage from the saint.</note>

*Rule of the Most Holy Father Augustine*: in which is also contained the *Life of Saint Guarinus, Bishop of Palestrina and Cardinal*. This life, separated from the *Rule*, can be found in the works of Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a famous 16th-century hagiographer</note> under the date of February 6th.

These three works were published in Brescia in 1511.

Furthermore, our Augustine wrote a *Compendium of the Mirror of the Cross*, an *Exposition on Psalm 54* ("Save me, O God, by thy name"), and a *Treatise on Learned Ignorance* <note>original: "de doctâ ignorantiâ"</note>: whether these were indeed published in Brescia along with the aforementioned works, I do not sufficiently know. However it may be, they were published in print at Milan in 1603.

Moreover, a *Great Chronicle* composed by him remains hidden and as yet unpublished.

<margin>
1500.
* Ecclesiastical History.
</margin>

## MANUEL, a Greek by nation, a Peloponnesian by birth, a disciple of Matthias Kamariotes, and Rhetor <term>Rhetor: An official position in the Patriarchate of Constantinople, responsible for oratory and often acting as a legal or theological advisor.</term> of the Great Church of Constantinople; called "the most wise and most logical" <note>original Greek: "ὁ σοφώτατος καὶ λογικώτατος"</note> by Manuel Malaxos. He flourished in the year 1500, at which time he took up his pen against the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>. For he wrote an *Apology*, or *Refutation*, of the ten chapters of Friar Francis of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note> concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, unleavened bread <note>term: "Azymo," referring to the Greek-Latin dispute over using leavened vs. unleavened bread in the Eucharist.</note>, Purgatory, the primacy of the Pope, etc. Leo Allatius provides certain fragments from this work in his book *On Purgatory*, pages 82, 165, 772, and 939. The illustrious Stephanus le Moyne published almost the entire treatise (though a few parts are missing at the end) in Greek and Latin among his *Varia Sacra*, page 270. Manuel also wrote a *Book against Pletho's Work on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, in which he censures Pletho <note>Georgius Gemistus Pletho, a famous Neoplatonist philosopher</note> because he derived his arguments regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit not from theological principles but from the doctrine of the Pagans <note>original: "Gentilium"</note>. Leo Allatius presents a fragment in *On Consensus*, book 3, chapter 3, section 6; another appears in his *Dissertation on the Georges*, page 389.

# THE REFORMED CENTURY.

## Overview of the Century.

At the beginning of this century, Julius II—a man of a mind utterly abandoned to every form of wickedness <note>original: "vir projectissimi in omne scelus animi"</note>—was elevated to the Papacy. During the election, he had most solemnly pledged that he would convene a General Council within two years. Once he had obtained the Papacy, however, he cared little for fulfilling his word. He turned his mind only to recruiting military forces, crushing the liberties of the Italian cities, and expanding the borders of the Church's territory. He rejected with the greatest arrogance the petitions of the Cardinals who desired a Synod. Louis XII, King of France, finally checked the man’s intemperance; having been provoked to war by the Pope, the King ordered the Council of Tours to be held in the year 1510. That Synod dared to take several measures against Papal authority; among these, it decreed that a Vicar of Christ who acted with excessive ferocity could be rightfully opposed by arms, that the <term>Pragmatic Sanction</term> <note>A French decree from 1438 that limited the Pope's power over the French (Gallican) Church, particularly regarding appointments and taxes.</note> was to be restored to use, and that legates should be sent to Julius to compel him to announce a Council.

Julius stubbornly refused to announce a Council; accordingly, a great many Cardinals, supported by the patronage of King Louis and the Emperor Maximilian, celebrated a Council at Pisa in the year 1511. Once the Synod had begun, they ordered Julius to attend. They charged him with wicked treachery and breach of faith; they proclaimed that nothing worse or more ruinous could be expected in the Christian republic than this Vicar of Christ himself. After bringing to light a long and ridiculous list of Julian crimes, they decreed that he should be suspended from his dignity. Meanwhile, Julius, so as not to fail his own cause, arranged for an opposing Council to be celebrated in Rome at the Lateran Church in the year 1512; he ensured that the Pisan Fathers were condemned for heresy and devoted to the curses of the Church. As French arms met with little success in Italy, the Synod of Pisa was dissolved a short time later. This left a magnificent opportunity for triumph to Leo X, who had succeeded Julius in 1513 after the latter died during the fifth session of the Lateran Council. Leo prolonged that Council for a considerable time and conducted affairs according to his own pleasure; he saw to it that the Synod of Pisa was repeatedly anathematized, the Pragmatic Sanction abolished, the superiority of the Pope over a Council defined, and the opposing decrees of the Councils of Constance and Basel annulled.

As French fortunes took a turn for the worse, Francis I entered into the famous *Concordat* <note>The Concordat of Bologna (1515), which redefined the relationship between the French monarchy and the Papacy.</note> with Pope Leo in the year 1515. He compelled the Gallican Clergy <note>The French Catholic Church</note> to protest by solemn decree that they *renounced the Assembly of Pisa and adhered to the Lateran Council*; nevertheless, today the Gallican Church repudiates the Lateran Council and excludes it from the count of Ecumenical Councils. Indeed, scarcely sixty Bishops attended that Council, and even those were for the most part Italians—the most contemptible slaves of the Roman See. In the year 1517, Tetzel and other cronies of the Dominican Order traveled through Germany carrying Indulgences for sale; they were sent by Pope Leo to fleece the credulous common people of their money. Luther set himself against their audacity, and, having attacked the impious sermons of the Dominicans, he gradually moved against the more significant errors of the Roman Church. Thus, he successfully inaugurated the Reformation—so long desired and so often attempted in vain. It was received with the greatest eagerness and applause by the greatest men of the age, and within a short time, it spread through the better part of the Western Church, while the lower regions <note>original: "inferis," likely referring to the Roman hierarchy or "the powers of hell" in a rhetorical sense</note> raged in fruitlessly and the Roman See gnashed its teeth.

<summary>This page provides an overview of the early 16th century, detailing the conflicts between Pope Julius II and the French monarchy, the rival Councils of Pisa and the Lateran, and the eventual spark of the Protestant Reformation by Martin Luther in 1517.</summary>
<keywords>Julius II, Leo X, Council of Pisa, Lateran Council, Pragmatic Sanction, Louis XII, Francis I, Martin Luther, Indulgences, Tetzel, Reformation, Gallican Church</keywords>

# W R I T E R S.

<margin>1501.</margin>
**JUAN LUIS VIVES**, Spanish by ancestry and a native of Valencia; he applied himself to Grammar at home and to Logic in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note>. This early education was so unfortunate—having encountered teachers who were hopelessly devoted to the trifles of the <term>Sophists</term> and <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Medieval philosophers and theologians whose complex, abstract methods were often criticized by Renaissance humanists for being disconnected from reality and written in "barbaric" Latin.</note> and to an uncultivated barbarism—that far from absorbing the more refined humanities, he even attacked them in his writings. Indeed, when the study of more polished literature was introduced to Spain by Antonio de Nebrija <note>The author of the first grammar of the Spanish language and a key figure in Spanish humanism.</note>, and the Scholastic teachers (who delighted in that crude squalor of speech) opposed such a laudable undertaking with all their might <note>original: "manibus pedibusque," literally "with hands and feet."</note>, our Luis is said to have lent a hand to a certain Valencian theologian who was attacking Antonio. 

Eventually, however, having become learned in Greek and Latin literature far beyond the common lot at the University of Leuven, he emerged from the mud. The further he had strayed from the true path of erudition, the more sharply he exerted himself in restoring the elegances of both languages. He flourished in the year 1501 <note>Vives was born in 1492; 1501 here likely marks his placement within the chronological registry of the century rather than his primary period of activity.</note>. At the University of Leuven, he was employed (apparently on a public salary) to lecture on the liberal sciences to the academic youth; there, he had as a pupil the most noble young man William de Croÿ, who was shortly thereafter elevated to the see of Toledo. During that time, the great restorer of learning and ancient theology, **Erasmus**, having dared a magnificent thing, had undertaken to shake the writings of the ancient Latin Fathers out of their long-standing neglect, cleansing them of errors and filth to bring them into the light. Vives was called into partnership in this counsel by Erasmus and took up the task of revising and elucidating with commentaries the most celebrated work of St. Augustine, *The City of God* <note>original: "De Civitate Dei"</note>. 

With what great success he performed this is known to all who care for good literature. Having finished his work in the year 1522, he dedicated it in a letter sent from Leuven to **Henry VIII**, King of England. Being most welcome to the King for that reason, he was soon summoned to the English Court to oversee the education of Princess Mary, the King’s only daughter. Having performed that duty for several years, he was eventually forced to leave the court and the kingdom because he disapproved of Henry’s divorce; indeed, he even experienced the royal wrath, being held in "free custody" <note>A form of house arrest or detention where the prisoner is not in a dungeon but restricted in movement.</note> for six months, and was only released with difficulty. From there, he withdrew to Belgium and settled in Bruges; having taken a wife, he devoted his efforts to raising a family and writing books. He died in Bruges in the year 1537, or as others say, 1541. *A man most practiced in every kind of discipline*, says Paolo Giovio <note>original: "Jovius," an Italian physician and historian.</note>, *and most deserving of praise regarding good literature—at whose passing no one more learned remained in Spain.* 

Erasmus says: *Indeed, I find in him neither a lack of wit* <margin>* The Ciceronian.</margin> *nor of erudition, nor of memory. He possesses a ready abundance of thoughts and words; and though he was somewhat harsh at the beginning, his eloquence matures in him more and more every day. If neither life nor study fails him, there is great hope that he will be numbered among the <term>Ciceronians</term>.* <note>Humanists who aimed to write Latin in the exact style and vocabulary of Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>

BATTISTA MANTOVANO, called by the surname Spagnolo or Hispaniolus, of Italian stock, a native of Mantua, born to a Spanish Celtiberian father and an Italian mother. He was born—if Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), a famous historian and biographer</note> is to be believed—from a secret union on April 17, 1448. He was a monk of the Carmelite Order in the Mantuan Convent, an exceptional poet, and a theologian of no small renown; indeed, he had added a knowledge of Hebrew letters to a deeper understanding of the Latin language, and he considered it a sin to spend his poetic vein on trivial or profane matters. He was at his peak in the year 1501. After having been elected Vicar General by his Congregation six times, he was finally appointed General of the entire Order at a very crowded Chapter of the Carmelites in Rome in 1513. However, after three years, feeling himself unequal to such a great burden, he voluntarily resigned his dignity so that he might more easily devote himself to God and sacred studies. Truly, this opportunity lasted him but a short time. He died in Mantua on April 11, 1516, at the age of 68. Upon his death, Federico, Prince of Mantua, placed a marble statue of him, crowned with laurel, on a triumphal arch next to the image of Virgil Maro. He was certainly a man of great talent and eloquence; he might have been considered the best poet, had he not lived in those times when there was no place for mediocre poets. In the number of his poems, he is second to none, as he left behind more than fifty-five thousand verses written by himself. Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a highly influential and often harsh literary critic</note> judges these with a somewhat harsh criticism to be "Scabrous" 
<margin>

</margin>
and so "born in the countryside" that they taste of nothing refined. Lilio Giraldi <note>Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus (1479–1552), a humanist scholar</note> is a little more lenient. He says: *As a young man, he was a more praiseworthy poet. But when that youthful heat and fervor subsided, he could not be restrained, flowing out messily like a river without a dam beyond its banks. For we can scarcely read those poems which he wrote later in life. Indeed, Mantuan had the misfortune that, at the very end of his life, he was forced to repel the blows of critics stabbing at his writings by publishing a defense.*

1501.

**BAPTISTA MANTUANUS** <note>Battista Spagnoli, known as the "Christian Virgil."</note>, surnamed Spagnoli or Hispaniolus, Italian by nation and Mantuan by homeland, was born on April 17, 1448, to a Spanish father from the Celtiberian region and an Italian mother, from an illicit union—if Jovius <note>The historian Paolo Giovio</note> is to be believed. He was a monk of the Carmelite Order in the Convent of Mantua. He was an exceptional poet and a quite famous theologian; indeed, he had added the study of Hebrew letters to his deep knowledge of the Latin language. He considered it a sin <note>original: *piaculum*</note> to spend his poetic talent on lewd or profane matters. He flourished in the year 1501. After being elected Vicar General of his congregation six times, he was finally appointed General of the entire Order in a crowded Carmelite Chapter in Rome in 1513. After three years, however, feeling unequal to such a great burden, he voluntarily resigned his dignity so that he might more easily devote himself to God and sacred studies. Truly, that opportunity lasted only a short time. He died at Mantua on March 22 <note>original: "the 11th day before the Kalends of April"</note>, 1516, at the age of 68. After his death, Federico, Prince of Mantua, placed a marble statue crowned with laurel in a triumphal arch next to the image of Virgil Maro. He was certainly a man powerful in both talent and abundance of speech; he could have been considered the best poet, had he not lived in those times when there was no room for mediocre poets. In the number of his poems, however, he was inferior to none, as he left behind more than fifty-five thousand verses written by himself. Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a notoriously harsh Renaissance critic</note> judges these with a rather harsh censure to be "scabby" <note>original: *Scabiosos*</note> 
<margin>
† Poetics, book 6.
|| Dialogue on the Poets of his century.
</margin>
and so rural in origin that they taste of nothing refined <note>original: *urbanum*</note>. Lilias Gyraldus <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi</note> softens this a little. "As a young man," he says, "he was a more praiseworthy poet. But when that youthful heat and fervor settled, like a river without a dam flowing filthily outside its banks, he could not be restrained. For we can hardly read the poems he wrote later in life." Indeed, Mantuan had the misfortune that near the very end of his life, he was forced to repel the blows of critics stabbing at his writings by publishing a defense.

# The Century of Reform.

<margin>16th CENTURY from the Year 1500.</margin>
<margin>* On the deeds of Francisco Ximénez, book 1.</margin>
...the first; in which, in the judgment of Gomez <note>original: "Gomecio," referring to Álvar Gómez de Castro, the biographer of Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros</note>*, he excellently compensates for the roughness of his style with the reliability of the matters he reports.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

*On the navigation of the Ocean, or on the Islands recently discovered by Christopher Columbus*, 30 books, written in the year 1502. Published separately in Paris, 1587, in octavo <note>8°</note>.

*On his Babylonian Embassy*, 3 books. Published together with the preceding work in Basel, 1533, and Cologne, 1574, in octavo <note>8°</note>.

*Thirty-eight books of Letters*, in which almost the entire history of events in Europe over as many years (specifically from 1488 to 1525) is presented, contained in 823 letters. This work appeared in Alcalá de Henares <note>original: "Compluti"</note> in 1530 and Amsterdam in 1670, in folio <note>f.</note>.

<margin>1501.</margin>
**FRANCESCO GIORGIO**, a Venetian by birth, a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>; deeply devoted to Platonic philosophy and Talmudic commentaries, he wandered into many errors, which he held mostly in common with Origen <note>An early Christian theologian whose speculative views on the soul were controversial in the 16th century</note>. Among these, his opinion on the terrestrial Paradise especially deserves to be noted; following Philo and Origen, he twists its entire history into an allegorical sense. He flourished in the year 1501. He died in the year 1510. He wrote six volumes of *Problems on Holy Scripture*, published in Venice, 1536, and Paris, 1574, in quarto <note>4°</note>: and *Three Songs on the Harmony of the World, printed in Venice, 1525, and Paris, 1545, in folio <note>f.</note>.*

<margin>1501.</margin>
<margin>* On the Writers of the Order of Friars Minor, p. 38.</margin>
**ANTONIO TROMBETTA**, called *Tubeta* by some, Italian by nation, born in Padua, of the Order of Friars Minor, Minister of the Province of Saint Anthony, and professor of Metaphysics in the Academy of Padua, a distinguished follower of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher whose complex system was known as "Scotism"</note>. He held that provincial office for 22 years. He flourished in the year 1501. While teaching Metaphysics at Padua, he was granted the monastery of Saint Leonard of Mathemaura of the Order of Saint Benedict, under the title of a Commendam <note>a practice where a benefice or its income was granted to a person without the usual duties</note>, by Pope Julius II. Through his great diligence in teaching, writing, and debating, he obtained the favor and friendship of almost the entire Roman Curia, especially of the most learned Cardinal Pietro Bembo. Finally made titular Archbishop of Athens, and then Bishop of Urbino, he was summoned by Julius II to the Lateran Council. He died in his native city in the year 1518 at the age of 82, and was buried in the church of Saint Anthony. He wrote *Expositions on the Introductory Formalities to the Theology of Scotus*; which Antonio Syrrectus, a fellow Franciscan, had published shortly before. *Syrrectus’s Formalities* appeared in Paris, 1588 and 1605; *Trombetta’s Exposition* was printed at the end of these in *Venice, 1518.* Otherwise, *Questions on Metaphysics, and a Treatise on Future Contingencies*: which Wadding <note>Luke Wadding, the primary historian of the Franciscan order</note>* reports that Trombetta wrote, have not yet, I believe, left the press. However, his *Treatise against the Averroists on the Purification of Human Souls* was printed in *Venice, 1498, in folio.*

<margin>1501.</margin>
**BONIFACE DE CEVA**, Italian by nation, born in Liguria, son of the Marquis of Ceva, kinsman to the Dukes of Saxony, Doctor of Both Laws <note>Civil and Canon Law</note>. After applying himself for a long time to the Law Courts, he joined the Franciscan Order and took the habit in the Convent of Red Mountain <note>original: "Rubei Montis"</note> in the Province of Saint Bonaventure. He flourished in the year 1501. Because of his remarkable prudence and skill in managing affairs, he was employed more than once as a mediator of peace <note>original: "pacis Sequester"</note> among the rioting princes of France. Made Minister and Commissary of the Province of France by his fellow members, and Reformer of the provinces of Tours and Saint Bonaventure, as well as the great Convent of Paris, he restored each to better discipline through new Constitutions published by himself. He died in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note> on April 12th, 1512. He wrote, besides the aforementioned Constitutions, well known to the Friars Minor, a work of no small labor, which he titled, *Travel Excursions on the Various Vices of Men, addressed to John, Bishop of Turin.* It appeared in *Paris, 1518. A Treatise on Christian Perfection. Paris, 1517. Lenten and Easter Sermons, in the same place. A Treatise on*

16th CENTURY

<margin>1501.</margin>
**ANTONIO BONITO**, an Italian by nationality from Cucchari, a member of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note> and Prefect of the Province of Terra di Lavoro, flourished in the year 1501. He provided long-term service in governing the Royal Chapel for Queen Joanna the mother and Joanna the daughter of Aragon. Later appointed as almoner to King Ferdinand, he undertook the governance of the Church of Montemarano and was eventually transferred to Acerno. He showed such great benevolence toward the needy everywhere that he was commonly called the "Father of the Poor." He died around the year 1510. There exists his *Elucidation on the Immaculate Conception of the Glorious Virgin* <note>original: "Elucidarium de Conceptione immaculatâ..."</note>, printed in Naples, 1507. However, the *Manual* which he wrote, containing almost all definitions and disputes regarding cases of conscience, does not yet seem to have been published by the printing press.

<margin>1501.</margin>
**JUAN DE ARGAMANES**, a Spaniard by birth, of the Franciscan Order, from the Province of St. James. He flourished in the year 1501. He wrote the *Mirror of the Friars Minor*, in which he explains the most serious difficulties that could be found in the Franciscan Rule. It appeared in the *Handbook or Manual of the Friars Minor* in the year 1535; an Italian edition was published in Treviso in 1593. His *Treatise on the Value of Indulgences* was printed in Seville in 1548 and 1622. His *Shield of the Holy Nuns* <note>original: "Clypeus sacrarum Monialium"</note> is found in the *Handbook of the Friars Minor*.

<margin>1501.</margin>
**PELBART OSVALD**, a Hungarian by nationality from the city of Temesvár, an exceptional preacher of the Franciscan Order. He flourished in the year 1501. He wrote a quite thick volume to which he gave the title *The Golden Rosary of Sacred Theology*, divided into four parts according to the four books of the *Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>; it was based on the teachings of the Subtle Doctor <note>A title for Duns Scotus</note>, St. Bonaventure, and other holy Doctors. Since Pelbart was snatched away by death before finishing the fourth of these four books, it was completed by Oswald de Lasko, Pelbart's disciple. The complete work was published in Haguenau in 1504 and 1508 in two folio volumes; in Venice in 1586 and 1589 in four volumes; and in Brescia in 1594. Additionally, there are other works written by him: *Sermons for the Sundays of the Year* and *On the Saints*, published in Paris by François Regnault; a *Triple Lenten Cycle* <note>original: "Quadragesimale triplex"</note>, namely on penance, vices, and the precepts of the Decalogue; and the *Stellarium of the Blessed Virgin*. A single work is usually compiled from these three, titled *The Orchard of Sermons* <note>original: "Pomærium Sermonum"</note>, which appeared in Haguenau in 1475 and 1498, and Venice in 1586 in quarto. Furthermore, his *Stellarium of the Crown of the Most Glorious Virgin* was printed in Venice in 1587, and his *Commentaries on the Psalms* in Haguenau in 1504.

<margin>1501.</margin>
**JOHANN MEDER**, a German by nationality, a theologian of the Franciscan Order of the Regular Observance, and a noted preacher among the people of Basel. He flourished in the year 1501. He wrote *The Parable of the Prodigal Son*, or a complete volume of sermons for the entire year based on that same parable, in which he explains at length the origin, progress, and effects of Penance. It was published in Basel in 1510 and Paris in 1511 in octavo.

<margin>1501.</margin>
**MAURICE DE PORTU** (known as **O'FIHELY** in his native language), an Irishman, commonly called the "Flower of the World" <note>original: "Flos Mundi"</note>, a member of the Franciscan Order. He lived among the Conventual Friars in Italy from his early youth, staying for about forty years. He flourished in the year 1501. Having been called to the University of Padua, he lectured on theology for a long time. Finally, however, having been named Archbishop of Tuam by Pope Julius II, he took part in the Lateran Council in the year 1512 and signed the first two sessions. Upon returning to his homeland, he was received with the greatest veneration by his countrymen, not only for his immense reputation for learning and piety, but also for the faculty of granting plenary indulgences, which he had obtained from the Pope and brought with him to Ireland. He died in Galway before his fiftieth year on the 8th day before the Calends of June <note>May 25</note> in the year 1513, or as others maintain, 1514. He was a man most highly skilled in theological and philosophical matters according to the doctrine of Scotus, more than almost anyone else; he spent nearly his entire life cultivating these studies.

*The revised Reportata* <note>Student lecture notes</note> *of the same author.* Paris, 1518.
*Abridgments on the Formalities of Scotus.* Paris, octavo.
*Notes and Brief Commentaries on nearly all the works of Scotus.* Found in the latest Lyons edition of Scotus's *Works*.
*Dictionary of Holy Scripture:* which indeed does not progress beyond the letter E. Published in Venice, 1603.
*Handbook of the Faith.* Venice, 1591, in quarto.
*Book of Distinctions*, Manuscript in the libraries of the Conventual Friars of Ravenna and Assisi.
Luke Wadding <note>The primary historian of the Franciscan order</note> reviews several other works of the same author in *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*, page 256.

<margin>1501.</margin>
**NICOLAS DIONYSII**, called by others **de Nyse**, a Frenchman by nationality and a theologian of no small reputation in the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>. He was the Provost of the Rouen Convent, Vicar of the Province of France, and soon after, the Provincial Minister. He flourished in the year 1501. He died at Rouen on the 18th of May, 1509, and was buried in the Chapter House before the altar.

->WORKS.<-

*The Resolution of Theologians, or Commentaries on the four books of the Sentences.* Venice, 1568, 1574.
*The Summary, or Gem of Preachers, or several Sermons.* Published in Basel, 1508, and Brescia, 1585.
*Summer and Winter Sermons.*
*Double Sermons for Advent.*
*Sermons for Lent.* All these last-listed sermons were published in Rouen, 1508, and Strasbourg, 1510.
*Sermons on the Season from the second Sunday after Easter until Advent.* Paris, 1510.
*The Mirror of Mortals, or on the Four Last Things* <note>The "Four Last Things" are Death, Judgment, Heaven, and Hell</note>. Paris, 1518.

<margin>1502.</margin>
**JACQUES ALMAIN**, a Frenchman by race, from the region of Sens, a theologian of great renown among the Scholastics. He was most devoted to the teachings of Scotus, Ockham, and Biel <note>Three of the most influential late-medieval philosophers</note>. He was a student of the College of Navarre at the University of Paris and a pupil of John Mair <note>original: "Ioannis Majoris", a famous Scottish philosopher and historian teaching in Paris</note>. He flourished in the year 1502. As soon as he had received his Master of Arts, he taught Logic and Natural Philosophy publicly, and he published his reflections on both disciplines between the years 1505 and 1508. In the year 1508, he obtained a place in the Theological Fellowship of Navarre, and finally, in 1511, he received his doctoral laurel in theology. The following year, he lectured on the *Sentences* in his college and illustrated them with commentaries. Around the same time, he was chosen by the Faculty of Theology to refute the book by Thomas Cajetan <note>A prominent Italian Dominican cardinal and philosopher</note> regarding the authority of the Pope over a Council; this book had been sent from the Council of Pisa to the Parisians. He performed this task with the greatest sharpness and learning. Having recited his book in a very crowded assembly of all the theologians, he saw it approved by the votes of everyone. He died in the year 1515, snatched away by an untimely death.
