### WORKS.

**Moral Philosophy** <note>original: "Moralia"</note>, which contains four treatises, namely: *On the essence of acts and habits and their impediments; on the three Theological virtues, Faith, Hope, and Charity; on the human virtues; and on the opposites of those same virtues.* These were published together in *Paris, 1510 and 1512.*

*Disputed Question held during the Vesperies* <note>The "Vesperies" was a formal academic debate held the evening before a doctoral candidate received their degree</note> *regarding natural, civil, and ecclesiastical Lordship.* This is found in the same place as above, and among the *Works of Gerson*, Volume 1, page 688.

*Incomplete Lecture on the Fourth Book of the Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard textbook for medieval theology students</note>, *concerning Penance and Marriage*, from distinction 14 to 37. It is found in the same place.

*Complete Lecture on the Third Book of the Sentences.* Published in the same place, and separately in *Lyons, 1527, in octavo.*

*Exposition on the Questions or Decisions of William of Ockham regarding Ecclesiastical and Secular Power.* This is held in Goldast's *Monarchia*, Volume 1, page 588; among the *Works of Gerson*, Volume 1, page 751; and separately in *Paris, 1526, in octavo*, and with the aforementioned books in the same city, *1512.*

*Book on the Authority of the Church and the Councils against Thomas de Vio Cajetan* <note>Cajetan was a leading defender of Papal authority against the conciliarists</note>. It is found in Gerson, Volume 1, page 705, and separately in *Cologne, 1514.*

*Dictations on the Sentences of Master Robert Holkot regarding acts of faith and the intellect, acts of faith, and the freedom of the will. Paris, 1512, and 1526, in octavo.*

*Physical Morsels* <note>original: "Embammata Physicalia." "Embammata" usually refers to dipping-sauces or appetizers, here used metaphorically for brief scholarly points or "tastes" of natural philosophy</note>. *Paris, 1505.*

*Treatise on the Five Consequences. Paris, 1508.*

The *Works of Almain* were published (though I do not know if they were all included) in *Paris, 1516.*

---

<margin>1503.</margin>
**FINUS HADRIANUS** <note>Fino Adriani</note>, an Italian by nationality from a family of Ferrara, and a Master of the Ducal Treasury of Scriptures <note>a financial or legal officer in the court of the Duke of Ferrara</note>; he was living as an old man in the year 1503, as he himself testifies in the Preface to his work. He wrote *The Scourge against the Jews* <note>original: "Flagellum adversus Judæos"</note>, divided into nine books: which was issued from the printing presses in *Venice, 1538, in quarto.*

<margin>1504.</margin>
**ALBERT KRANTZ** <note>original: "Albertus Crantzius"</note>, a German by birth, born of an honorable family in Hamburg, a Doctor of Canon Law and Theology, created around the year 1490 after he had visited many Universities. In 1482, having been made Rector of the University of Rostock, he taught Theology and Canon Law there for some time. Later, returning to his home city, he was made a Canon <note>a member of the clergy serving a cathedral</note> of the Church of Hamburg; and having been honored with the duty of Professor of Theology, he eventually emerged as the Dean of the College of Canons. He flourished in the year 1504. He certainly prayed with his deepest vows for the reformation of the Church and for its ancient purity: however, when Luther was beginning his desired work, Krantz—almost as if despairing—was accustomed to say: *Brother, brother, go to your cell and say: "God have mercy on me."* <note>original: "Frater, frater, abi in cellam, & dicito; Miserere mei Deus." This famous anecdote suggests Krantz agreed with the need for reform but feared Luther's efforts were futile or dangerous.</note> He died in Hamburg in the year 1517, on the 7th day before the Ides of December <note>December 7th</note>, and was buried in the cemetery of the main church.

### W R I T I N G S.

**Metropolis**, or the Ecclesiastical History of the Churches in Germany, especially those in Saxony, founded or restored in the age of Charlemagne, from the year of Christ 780 up to the year 1504, comprised in twelve books. Published in *Basel, 1548; Cologne, 1574, in octavo; Frankfurt, 1576 and 1590.*

*Saxon History, in thirteen books. Cologne, 1520; Frankfurt, 1575.*

*Vandal History, in fourteen books. Frankfurt, 1575.*

*Chronicle of other Northern nations, namely: Denmark, Sweden, and Norway. Strasbourg, 1546*; and with an addition by J. Wolf, *Frankfurt, 1575.* Krantz begins each of these Histories from the age of Charlemagne and finishes them in the year 1504. The Roman Indexes <note>The Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the list of books banned by the Catholic Church</note> forbid the reading of all these works of Krantz until they have been expurgated.

*A booklet on the Office of the Mass, printed at Rostock, 1505.*

### JOHN STELLA

**JOHN STELLA**, a citizen of Venice and a priest of the Church of Saint Mary the Beautiful <note>original: "D. Mariæ formosæ," referring to the Santa Maria Formosa church in Venice</note>, wrote in the year 1505. It is not well established when he died. He wrote, using an old-fashioned and simple style, a *Commentary on the Lives and Manners of the Roman Pontiffs* from Saint Peter down to the second year of Julius II, which was the year of Christ 1505. Meanwhile, he himself does not deny in a letter to Antonio Suriano, the Patriarch of Venice, that he omitted many things—especially from the most recent times—which could not be safely committed to writing. Indeed, even if he remained silent on the matter, anyone would easily recognize that he shamefully flatters the most recent Popes; among these were Alexander VI and Julius II, who were the worst not only of all Popes but of all men. This work appeared in *Venice, 1507*; then in *Basel, 1570*; and finally in 1650 in 24mo format. Stella also wrote a book titled *Augustalis* concerning the Roman Emperors. This appeared in *Venice, 1503.*

---

<margin>1506.</margin>

### DAMIAN CRASSUS

**DAMIAN CRASSUS**, an Italian by nationality, hailing from Rivoli, a town located in the sub-alpine region above Turin; he was a monk of the Dominican Order, and eventually became the Provincial <note>A "Provincial" is a high-ranking superior who oversees a specific geographic "province" of a religious order</note> in Lombardy; meanwhile, as a Master of Sacred Theology, he was appointed Regent of the College of Saint Thomas in the University of Pavia <note>original: "Academiâ Ticinensi"</note>. He flourished in the year 1506. He died in the year 1516. He wrote a fairly lengthy commentary on *Job*; and in the year 1506, he saw to its publication along with several other treatises, among which is the *Book of Questions regarding Saint John the Evangelist*. For while Damian was head of the College of Saint Thomas, he asserted in debate the proposition that Saint John was a "Blood Relative of Christ" and a "Blood Relative of God," along with many other claims, against John of Cassivis of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note>. He later published these arguments, organized into a book.

---

<margin>1506.</margin>

### FRANCISCO JIMÉNEZ

**FRANCISCO JIMÉNEZ**, <note>Commonly known as Cardinal Cisneros (1436–1517)</note> of Spanish stock, born in Cisneros, a notable town in the Kingdom of León, was descended from the most illustrious Cisneros family. His father was Alfonso Jiménez de Cisneros and his mother was Maria. Originally named Gonzalo at the sacred font, he later took the name Francisco when he donned the monk's cowl. Destined for the priesthood from his earliest years, he was educated in letters with the greatest care. He studied grammar at Alcalá de Henares <note>original: "Compluti"</note>, and Philosophy, Theology, and "Both Laws" <note>term: Both Laws — "Jus utrumque" refers to the study of both Civil and Canon (Church) Law</note> at Salamanca. From there he set out for Rome to practice law, but upon hearing of his father's death, he returned to his homeland, armed with what are called "expectative letters" <note>note: These were papal documents that granted the holder a right to the next church position or "benefice" that became vacant</note> from the Pope. Relying on these, he took possession of the Archpriestship of the town of Uceda, which happened to be vacant at the time; for this reason, he was seized by Alfonso Carrillo, the Archbishop of Toledo, and held in chains for a long time. At last set free, he traded his Archpriestship for a "Chaplaincy" (as they call it), the largest in the Church of Sigüenza. While stationed at Sigüenza, he took a Hebrew teacher and drank in the elements of the Hebrew and Chaldean <note>term: Chaldean — In this period, this usually referred to Aramaic or Syriac</note> languages; he was also the advisor to Juan López of Medina for the founding of an academy. Moved by the man's excellent reputation, Cardinal Pedro González de Mendoza, the Bishop of Sigüenza, entrusted him with the administration of the entire diocese as Vicar and enriched him with wealthy priestly offices. A short time later, weary of worldly affairs and meditating on a retreat, he resigned his offices and dignities and joined the Franciscan monks in the monastery at Toledo. Disturbed by the fame of that place, he considered an even more secret retreat; and with earnest prayers, he obtained permission to be sent away to a tiny, narrow house for a very few companions called Castañar; shortly after, he was placed in charge of a similar small monastery at Salzeda. In the year 1492, he was appointed as Confessor to Queen Isabella; and he was made the Provincial of his order for both Castiles. In the year 1495, he was appointed successor to Cardinal Mendoza as Archbishop of Toledo; and thus, by the right of his see, he emerged as the Primate and Archchancellor of all Spain. In the year 1500, he laid the foundations of the University of Alcalá <note>original: "Academiæ Complutensis"</note>. He flourished in the year 1506. Four years earlier, he had begun that famous work, an accurate edition of the Holy Bible prepared in three languages at Alcalá <note>note: This is the famous "Complutensian Polyglot Bible," the first printed polyglot of the entire Bible</note>: having summoned from everywhere at the greatest expense—especially from the Vatican Library—the most corrected manuscript codices, and having hired at a huge salary the most learned men, Alfonso de Zamora, Alfonso the physician of Alcalá, and Pablo Coronel, regarding Hebrew mat- <meta>catchword: -ters</meta>

...most skilled in these matters: Demetrius of Crete, Antonio of Nebrija, Lopez de Zúñiga, and Ferdinand of Pinto <note>original: "Pintiano," referring to Hernán Núñez de Toledo, a professor at Salamanca</note>, who were most expert in Greek and Latin literature. The labor devoted to this extraordinary undertaking lasted roughly fifteen years; so much so that the edition reached its completion almost at the same time as the death of Jiménez, after it had cost him fifty thousand gold coins and more. Around the same time, he restored the Mozarabic Liturgy <note>The Mozarabic Rite is an ancient form of Christian worship practiced by Christians living under Muslim rule in Spain</note> to six churches in Toledo. This liturgy had been used throughout the entire Church of Toledo since the time of Isidore, and after the conquest of Toledo by the Moors, it continued in the six churches the barbarians had permitted to the Christians. However, after the city was recovered by Alfonso VI toward the end of the eleventh century, it had gradually fallen into disuse. Jiménez brought it back to those six churches through a legal restoration; and in the year 1504, he gave it to Melchior Gurrizio of Genoa to be printed in Toledo. In the year 1506, during the political disturbances in Castile following the death of Queen Isabella, Jiménez was elected by the unanimous vote of the Castilian nobles as the Guardian of Queen Joanna (who was then suffering from mental illness) and as the Protector of the boy Charles <note>The future Holy Roman Emperor Charles V</note>. In the year 1507, he was granted the dignity of Cardinal by Pope Julius II, and soon after was appointed Inquisitor General of the Faith throughout the entire kingdom of Castile. Finally, after the death of King Ferdinand, from the year 1515, he governed all of Spain with vicarious authority for two years while Charles was absent. This truly great man, born to advance the cause of letters, died at Roa <note>original: "Pintiæ"</note> on the 6th of the Ides of November <note>November 8th</note> in the year 1517, at about 80 years of age. He was buried in the Primary Church of Toledo. As we mentioned above, he caused a magnificent edition of the Holy Bible to be prepared by the most learned men, at his own expense and even according to his own direction. In this work, the books of the Old Testament are arranged in three columns on each page. The first of these displays the Hebrew text, the second the common Latin <note>The Vulgate</note>, and the third the Greek of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note>, illustrated with an added interlinear Latin translation. To these, in the books of the Pentateuch, the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> is added in the lower margin, to which is also attached a Latin translation <term>word-for-word</term> <note>original: "κατὰ πόδας," literally "at the feet"</note>. In the non-canonical books (for Jiménez established the Canon of Scriptures according to the view of the Hebrews), besides the Greek version of <term>the Seventy</term> <note>original: "τῶν ὁ."</note>, there are two Latin versions: one the common Vulgate, and the other an interlinear word-for-word translation. In the books of the New Testament, besides the most emended Greek text, there is only the common Latin version. Added in the final volume was a most extensive dictionary <note>original: "Onomasticon"</note> of Hebrew, Chaldean, and Greek words. This most beautiful work appeared, dedicated to Pope Leo X, printed at Alcalá de Henares <note>original: "Compluti"</note> in six volumes in folio, the last of which came off the press in the year 1515. Furthermore, Alvaro Gomez <note>original: "Alvarus Gomecius"</note> records that a volume of *Letters* written by Jiménez exists in manuscript in the archives of the Church of Toledo; he even presents a few in his biography of the man.

* Concerning the life of Jiménez, book 4.
1506.
</margin>
**ALPHONSUS ZAMORA**, a Spaniard by nationality but Jewish by birth, was born to Jewish parents in the city of Zamora. He was most learned in Hebrew literature and mysteries, and had governed public schools among the Jews before he embraced the Christian faith. Finally initiated by baptism, he became famous in the year 1506. On account of his remarkable skill in Hebrew matters, he was invited by Cardinal Jiménez with a very generous salary, and he spent nearly fifteen years of labor on the preparation of that most noble Complutensian edition of the Bible.

->W R I T I N G S.<-

> *A Chaldean and Hebrew Vocabulary of the Old Testament.*
*Interpretations of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Greek names of both Testaments.*
*A Catalog of those things in both Testaments which were written differently due to the fault of scribes than they are in the Hebrew and Greek, and in certain ancient Bibles.*
*Introductions to the Art of Hebrew Grammar.*

These works make up the final volume of the Complutensian Bible; in the writing of these, our Alphonfus played the leading part, and in the following ones, he acted alone.

<margin>1507.</margin> ANTONIO DE BURGOS, a Spaniard from the city of Salamanca; a Doctor of Both Laws <term>Juris utriusque Doctor; a scholar who has earned degrees in both Civil and Canon Law</term> at Bologna, and a member of the Spanish College of St. Clement, founded by Cardinal Gil Albornoz. He taught Pontifical <note>Canon</note> Law at the University of Bologna for twenty years under quite honorable conditions. He was famous in the year 1507. Having achieved an exceptional reputation for learning and integrity, he was summoned to the Roman Curia by Pope Leo X and made a Referendary of Both Signatures <note>A high-ranking legal official in the Vatican administration</note>. From then on, he devoted his efforts to managing the most serious affairs for the Roman Pontiffs until his death. He passed away in Rome in his seventies on the [blank] day of December, 1525. His surviving works include: *A Commentary on the useful and daily Title "On Buying and Selling" in the Decretals* <note>The Decretals are a primary collection of Papal laws</note>. *Pavia 1511, Parma 1574, Venice 1575, Lyon 1575, in folio. Commentaries on two other Titles of the Decretals, namely "On Constitutions" and "On Rescripts," printed with the former; and Various Repetitions in Civil Law, published in Venice, 1587.*

---

<margin>1507.</margin> BERNARD BASIN, a Spaniard and Doctor of Theology of Paris, and Canon of the Church of Zaragoza, was famous in the year 1507. He was well known from the year 1491, when he delivered an oration with the highest praise before nineteen Cardinals in the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome on the feast day of St. Thomas Aquinas. He wrote a *Book on the Magic Arts and the Evils of Sorcerers, which was printed in Paris in 1506 in octavo; Frankfurt 1580 in octavo; and in the first part of Volume 11 at Lyon, 1620, in octavo.*

---

<margin>1508.</margin> FILIPPO DECIO, Italian by nation and a native of Milan, son of Tristano de Desio. At the age of seventeen, he was sent to Pavia, where he heard his brother Lancelotto, Giasone del Maino, and Giovanni dal Pozzo teaching Both Laws. Later, following his brother Lancelotto when he was called to Pisa by the Florentines, he gave himself as a student to Baldo Novello, Filippo Corneo, and Girolamo Zanettini. At age 22, he earned the insignia of a doctorate and accepted a lectureship on the *Institutes* <note>The foundational textbook of Roman Law</note> assigned to him by the Pisans. He was famous in the year 1508. He adorned his professorial office with such sharp insight, eloquence, and richness of speech that he drew listeners to his chair in crowds, exciting the envy of other professors. Because of this, Bartolomeo Soccini, a Professor of Imperial <note>Civil</note> Law in the same school, grieving that he was deprived of students, requested either that he himself or Filippo be dismissed from his duties. The Pisans therefore assigned Filippo the teaching of Pontifical Law and made him a colleague to Felino Sandeo. This gave Filippo material for an even greater triumph. For Felino, immediately indignant that his own chair was stripped of its crowd of listeners and feeling himself unequal to the partnership with Filippo, went to Rome; through slanders, he brought it about that Filippo was forced to resign his teaching post. Filippo, having left Pisa, offered his services to the Sienese, by whom he was most gladly received. A little later, when the Sienese state was in turmoil, he was recalled to Pisa and taught Canon Law. Then he moved to Pavia, invited with a rich salary by the French governor. While he held the Chair at Siena, he was asked for an opinion by the Council of Pisa in 1511 regarding the right to summon a Synod (which Pope Julius contended belonged solely to the Roman See); he wrote in favor of the Council's authority against the Pope. Therefore, when the French were driven out of Pavia, Cardinal Matthäus Schiner of Sion gave up Filippo’s house alone to be plundered by the soldiers. He withdrew to France, where he taught Pontifical Law at Bourges for nearly two years...

### W R I T I N G S.

*Legal Opinion for the authority of the Church over the Pope in the matter of the Synod of Pisa held in the year 1511.* <note>original: "Consilium pro Ecclesiæ authoritate supra Papam..."</note> It is found in Goldast’s *Monarchy*, Volume 2, page 1667.

*Legal Opinions in Two Volumes,* purged <note>meaning edited or corrected for errors</note> by N. Antonio Gravatio. Venice 1581.

<margin>1510.</margin>
**THOMAS RADINUS**, called **TODISCHUS** <note>Tommaso Radini Tedeschi (c. 1488–1527)</note>, an Italian by birth from the city of Piacenza, a most subtle Dominican theologian, poet, philosopher, and distinguished orator; what is even more remarkable is that he attained so many great branches of knowledge without the help of a teacher. He was prominent in the year 1510. He wrote to Emperor Maximilian *A Book on the Beauty of the Soul*, which he named *Callipsychia* <note>From the Greek words for "beautiful soul"</note>, published in Milan in 1511. Another titled *The Sidereal Abyss*, Paris 1514, quarto. *An Oration against Luther*, Leipzig 1520, quarto, and *another against Melanchthon*, Rome 1522, quarto.

<margin>1511.</margin>
**CYPRIANUS BENETUS**, or *Benedictus* <note>Cyprian Benet</note>, Spanish by race and Aragonese by birth, a member of the Dominican Order and a Doctor of Theology of Paris. He was prominent in the year 1511, distinguished as much for his learning as for his piety. He died after the year 1522.

### W R I T I N G S.

*Treatise on the primary seat of the World.*
*On the Council.*
*On Ecclesiastical power.*
*On the authority of the Supreme Pontiff.*
These four Treatises, dedicated to Popes Julius II and Leo X, were published in Rome in 1512, in quarto.
*A Dialogue on the excellence and utility of Theology.*
*On the preeminence, mercy, etc., of Charles, King of the Spains.* <note>Referring to the future Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V</note> Published with the preceding Dialogue in Rome in 1518, quarto.
*A powerful Hortatory Oration to Pope Hadrian VI to hasten his journey.* Published somewhere in quarto.
*A Treatise on not changing Easter* published under the name of Cyprianus Venetus, Doctor; mentioned by Simler in the *Bibliotheca Tigurina*, page 152, who also suggests, perhaps not wrongly, that this "Venetian" was the same as our Benetus.

<margin>1512.</margin>
**MARCUS VIGERIUS** <note>Marco Vigerio della Rovere (1445–1516)</note>, an Italian by birth from the region of Liguria and the house of Savona, a monk of the Order of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>. He had as his teacher Francesco della Rovere, his fellow citizen and brother monk, who was later elevated to the Pontifical seat under the name of Sixtus IV. After he had long lectured on Theology at Padua and in the Gymnasium of Roman Wisdom <note>the University of Rome, "La Sapienza"</note>, he was made Bishop of Senigallia, then enrolled among the Cardinals of the Roman Church and granted the Bishopric of Palestrina <note>original: "Prænestino"</note>. He was prominent in the year 1512, in which year he took part in the Lateran Council, having been summoned by Pope Julius II.

His extant writings include the *Christian Decachord on the Principal Mysteries of the Incarnate Word* <note>original: "Decachordum Christianum..." — a 'decachord' refers to a ten-stringed instrument, used here as a metaphor for a ten-part musical or literary harmony</note>, published in Fano in 1507 and Antwerp in 1616. Also, *A Meditation on the Excellence of the Instruments of the Lord’s Passion* <note>original: "Lucubratio de excellentia Instrumentorum..."</note>, Rome 1512. <margin>1512.</margin>
JOHANNES AVENTINUS, known by the surname Turmaier, a Bavarian by birth, hailed from Abensberg <note>An ancient town in Lower Bavaria, referred to here by its Latin name Abusina</note>, a small town in Upper Bavaria. He was born in 1466 to his father Johannes Turmaier, the local innkeeper <note>original: "Pandocheum"</note>. After finishing his early education, his parents sent him to Ingolstadt to study philosophy and the liberal arts. He then moved to Paris <note>original: "Lutetiam"</note>, where he attained the degree of Master of Arts after several years of rigorous study across all disciplines. He rose to prominence in the year 1512 as an eminent philologist, mathematician, and historian. Returning to Germany, he went to Vienna, where he lectured on oratory and poetry to a select audience for a long time. Then, traveling to Krakow, he publicly taught Greek literature. Soon recalled to his homeland in 1509, he began to explain Cicero's *Dream of Scipio* and *Rhetoric for Herennius* at Ingolstadt with the highest praise. In 1512, he was called to Munich and appointed as tutor to Princes Ludwig and Ernst of Bavaria; a few years later, he accompanied Ernst on a journey to Italy. Having completed his duties as a tutor, he set himself to writing the *Annals of the Bavarians* <note>original: "Annalibus Boiorum" — the 'Boii' were the ancient Celtic people from whom the name Bavaria is derived</note>, with the Princes of Bavaria providing funding with the greatest generosity. After surveying all the libraries of the entire province and the archives of the monasteries—sometimes in his hometown, sometimes in Regensburg <note>original: "Ratisponæ"</note> with his most upright friend Erasmus Brimfius—he settled down and worked diligently on the project. In 1533, three years after marrying, he established his home in Ingolstadt, invited by the most noble Leonard von Eck to instruct his son Oswald in literature. Toward the end of the year, while traveling by carriage from Ingolstadt to Regensburg, he was seized by a very serious illness and took to his bed in Regensburg. As the disease worsened daily, he passed away on the 5th Ides of January [January 9th], 1534, at the age of 68. He was buried in Regensburg in the Church of St. Emmeram.

<margin>1513.</margin>
**LEO X**, previously named Giovanni de' Medici, was a Florentine by birth, originating from the most noble Medici family. He was the son of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Known as Lorenzo the Magnificent</note> and Clarice Orsini. Having been tutored by Angelo Poliziano and Bernardo Michelozzi, he was educated in both Greek and Latin literature. While he was still almost an infant, King Louis XI of France—as a favor to his father Lorenzo—granted him a distinguished Archbishopric. When he was a boy of thirteen, Pope Innocent VIII co-opted him into the college of Cardinals with the title of Saint Mary in Dominica. After the Medici were suppressed by King Charles VIII of France and cast down from the leadership of Florentine affairs, he himself was driven from Rome and lived for a long time in exile among foreign nations. Around the year 1503, having returned to Rome, he entered into great favor with Pope Julius; and having been appointed Legate of Bologna, he was captured by the French in the year 1512 at the Battle of Ravenna. Led to Milan, he disturbed and weakened the Council of Pisa (which had been moved there by the Cardinals) through his mere presence and steadfastness. Soon after, having escaped the hands of the French by a certain cunning, he withdrew to his own province. In the year 1513, at the age of 37, he was elected Roman Pontiff by the younger Cardinals on the 11th of March, and crowned on the 19th of March. He continued the Lateran Council, which had been begun by his predecessor Julius the year before, for a full four years; this was done so that he might have a counter-measure to oppose the Council of Pisa, and a means to deceive <note>original: "fucum faceret" — literally "to apply dye," meaning to present a false or painted-over appearance</note> the Christian world, which was longing for reform with the most burning prayers. Everything here was conducted at the Pontiff's whim: the decrees of the Synods of Basel and Constance were revoked, the majesty of Councils was utterly prostrated, and the Pontifical See was raised to the supreme peak of authority. Most notably, in the 11th Session held in the year 1516, the **Pragmatic Sanction** <note>A French decree limiting papal power over the French church</note>—originally established by Saint Louis, King of France—was condemned and abolished by the votes of the entire Council as schismatic, nefarious, and an injury to Papal authority; this was done despite the fact that the Fathers themselves acknowledged, in so many words, that the Sanction and all its contents had been approved by the Council of Basel. In the same Bull revoking the Sanction, it was defined that no one can be in the Church who deserts the chair of the Roman Pontiff; that Christ established the successors of Saint Peter as his vicars in such a way that whoever does not obey them "shall die the death" <note>A biblical expression for certain execution</note>; and what was of the greatest importance: that the Roman Pontiff for the time being, as one holding authority over all Councils, has full right and power for summoning, transferring, and dissolving Councils. It was claimed that this is clearly established by the testimony of Holy Scripture, the sayings of the Holy Fathers, the decrees of the Canons, and the explicit confession of the Councils themselves. Furthermore, Leo was a pure and simple atheist—if ever there was one—for whom the only religion was to live life pleasurably. At the beginning of his pontificate, after he noticed that the war against King Louis XII of France (who had been excommunicated by his predecessor) was not succeeding well, he broke his treaty with Emperor Maximilian and the Swiss with the utmost treachery and went over to the side of the French; to them, he gave the Empire of Constantinople as a gift by Apostolic authority <note>This refers to the titular title, as Constantinople was then the capital of the Ottoman Empire</note>. Around the year 1515, he sent **Tetzel**, a Dominican monk, into Germany (and others elsewhere) to scrape together an immense amount of money from the sale of indulgences. This was done with the highest impiety and impudence; for the shameless salesmen of Indulgences (as a contemporary Catholic Bishop testifies *) preached everywhere that both the living and the dead 
<margin>* *The Burden of the Church*, Cologne, 1531, chapter 15.</margin>
were released through plenary indulgences from all punishments and guilt alike, without any distinction, and were immediately saved; ——— *to such an extent that if a sinner who had obtained full pardons happened to die, he would immediately fly to heaven without any other temporal or purgatorial satisfaction.* Leo died, not without suspicion of poison, in the year 1521 on the 1st of December. There are 33 extant Letters and Constitutions in the *Councils*, Vol. 14, p. 129, etc.; another 58 in Bzovius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the year 1513, etc. (44 of which are found in Bembus); many more in Laertius Cherubini’s *Great Bullary*; and finally, sixteen books of Letters written in his name by **Pietro Bembo** (who served as his secretary), published in Basel, 1566.

**SIMON BENIGNIUS** <note>Also known as Šimun Kožičić Benja</note>, Bishop of Modruš in Croatia, was prominent in the year 1513. In that year, he addressed the Fathers of the Lateran Council who were to celebrate the sixth session on the 27th of April; he spoke concerning the schisms of the previous century, the promised reformation of the whole Church (to use his own words), and the waging of war against the Turks. This sermon is extant, along with a dedicatory letter to Bernardino dei Frangepani, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 14, page 144.

<margin>1513.</margin>
**BALTHASAR DEL RIO**, a Spaniard by birth from the city of Palencia, was a <term>Scholastic</term> <note>A teacher or cathedral official</note> at Mondoñedo in Galicia, Archdeacon of Cesena, Chamberlain to Leo X, Apostolic <term>Protonotary</term> <note>A high-ranking papal legal official</note>, and Secretary to Cardinal Albornoz; he was prominent in the year 1513. In that year, he inaugurated the seventh session of the Lateran Council on the 17th of June by delivering a sermon on the undertaking of an expedition against the Turks, based on the text from Matthew 17:20: *Nothing will be impossible for you* <note>original: "Nihil impossibile erit vobis"</note>. That sermon is preserved with a dedicatory preface to King Ferdinand of Spain in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 14, page 165, and was printed separately in Rome in 1513, in quarto.

<margin>1513.</margin>
**JOANNES BAPTISTA GARGHA**, an Italian from the city of Siena and a Knight of Jerusalem <note>A member of the Knights Hospitaller</note>, was prominent in the year 1513. At that time, he spoke from the sacred pulpit to the Fathers of the Lateran Synod who were to hold the eighth session on the 17th of December, regarding the undertaking of war against the Turks and bringing aid to the island of Rhodes. This oration is extant, preceded by a letter to Fabrizio del Carretto, Grand Master of the Order of Jerusalem, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 14, page 195.

<margin>1514.</margin>
**ANTONIUS PUCCIUS** <note>Antonio Pucci</note>, a Roman by birth and a Clerk of the Apostolic Chamber (succeeding his father in that office), was prominent in the year 1514. At the command of Leo X, he provided the prelude to the ninth session of the Lateran Council, held on the 5th of May, with a sermon on the majesty and privileges of the Church, and the restoration of peace and piety to the Christian commonwealth. However, he flattered Pope Leo (who was present at the Synod) most foully; he did not blush to attribute to the Pope the words of Psalm 72:11: *All kings of the earth shall adore him, and serve him* <note>original: "Omnes reges terræ adorabunt eum, & servient ei"</note>. That sermon is extant, with a letter to Pope Leo, in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 14, page 231.

<margin>1515.</margin>
**STEPHANUS** <note>Stefano Taleazzi</note>, Bishop of Torcello in the Venetian territory and Archbishop of Patras, was prominent in the year 1515. In that year, at the age of seventy, he preached before the Pope and the Bishops who were to hold the tenth session of the Lateran Council on the 4th of May, speaking on the necessary and much-desired reformation of the whole Church and the authority of the Apostolic See. He employed truly monstrous flattery toward the Pope, proclaiming that "all power in heaven and on earth" had been given to him, so that he himself might command the whole world and obey God alone; and that he should require as much obedience from his subjects as he himself rendered to God. That sermon is found in the *Collection of Councils*, Volume 14, page 261.

**PETRUS GALATINUS** <note>Pietro Colonna Galatino</note>, an Italian by birth as it seems (at least he lived in the Convent of Bari in the province of Apulia), was a Christian converted from Judaism, a monk of the Franciscan Order, and a Doctor of Arts and Theology. He was a close associate of L. Pucci, Cardinal of the Four Crowned Saints, and eventually an Apostolic Penitentiary. He was prominent in the year 1516. He died after the year 1532. Being quite skilled in Hebrew matters, at the urging of Emperor Maximilian and Pope Leo, he sought to demonstrate the "Talmudic and Kabbalistic follies" of the Jews and the truth of the Christian faith, as well as to defend the reputation of Johannes Reuchlin which had been attacked by Scholastic theologians. He composed a work in the form of a dialogue between Galatinus, Capnio <note>Reuchlin's Greek name</note>, and Hochstraten entitled *Work on the Secrets of Catholic Truth* <note>original: "Opus de Arcanis Catholicæ Veritatis"</note>, organized into twelve books. Indeed, through a "monstrous plagiarism" (as it is deservedly called by Jean Morin <note>A 17th-century French biblical scholar</note>), he compiled almost the entire work from Raymond Martini’s *Dagger of Faith* <note>original: "Pugione"</note>, or at least from Porchetus Salvaticus’s *Victory*, adding very little of his own. He preserved almost the same words, sentences, translations, examples, and citations of authors throughout; yet he did not name Porchetus—from whom he had transcribed with a full hand—even once. The work was first published at *Ortona a Mare* <note>original: "Orthone-maris"</note> in 1518 (though it had been begun many years before this); then at *Basel* in 1550, in folio; in the same place in 1561; at *Paris* in 1602; and at *Frankfurt* in 1612 and 1672, both in folio. Galatinus wrote other works as well, namely a *Summa of Theology* <note>original: "Summam Theologiæ"</note>; a very extensive *Commentary on the Apocalypse*; and a *Treatise on the Correct Interpretation of Holy Scripture*. Also a singular work *On the Church Established, Abandoned, and Restored* <note>original: "de Ecclesiâ institutâ, destitutâ & restitutâ"</note>; a *Treatise on the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist*; *On the Intellectual Soul*; *On Man*; *On the Seven Times and States of the Church*; *On Recognizing Pestilential Men*; *On the Angelic Pastor*; an exposition of a certain obscure Roman prophecy; *On the Prophecies of Methodius, St. Cataldus, and Blessed Cyril*; and *On the Diadem of the Best Prince*. Wadding <margin>* Concerning the Writers of the Order of Friars Minor, page 280.</margin> testifies that these works, transcribed from the Vatican original, remained in his possession; he promised that he would bring them to light, but he never fulfilled the promise he had given.

**MARTIN LUTHER**, a German by nationality and a Saxon by birth, was born in Eisleben <margin>1517.</margin>, a town in the territory of Mansfeld, on the 10th day of November, 1483. His father was Hans Luther, who at one time held a magistracy in Mansfeld, and his mother was Margaret Lindemann. In his fourteenth year he was sent to Magdeburg, and in the following year to Eisenach, so that he might build upon the rudiments of letters learned at home with deeper knowledge. Having spent four years at Eisenach, he went to the University of Erfurt in the year 1501; there, honored with the degree of Master of Philosophy in 1503, he began to teach philosophy. Soon, however, by the advice of his parents, he turned his mind—which was suited for all subjects—to the study of Jurisprudence <note>The study of Law</note>. In 1504, terrified by the violent death of a certain fellow student, he joined the Monks of the Augustinian Order in the Monastery at Erfurt without the knowledge of his friends. There he applied himself diligently to the reading of Holy Scripture (for here, in a certain obscure corner of the library, he happened to see Latin codices of the Bible for the first time) and to thoroughly studying the writings of St. Augustine and the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine</note>. In 1507, he took the habit <note>original: "cucullum induit," literally "put on the cowl"</note>; and having been initiated into sacred orders, he began to sing Mass. In 1508, he was transferred from Erfurt to the University of Wittenberg by Johann von Staupitz, where he explained the logic and physics of Aristotle for three years. In 1512, sent to Rome as a legate in the name of his convent, he saw and lamented the corrupt morals of the Roman court. Having returned to Wittenberg, he was created a Doctor of Theology in 1513, with Frederick, Duke of Saxony—who was greatly delighted by his sermons—providing the expenses. Having obtained his laurel <note>A metaphor for his doctoral degree</note>, he gave himself to the study of the Greek and Hebrew languages; and undertaking to lecture on the Epistle to the Romans from his chair, he refuted the dogma of justification that was commonly accepted in the schools and sermons. He became famous in the year 1517, when, by God’s favor, he presented himself as the leader and standard-bearer for reforming religion. For at that time, offended by the monstrous audacity of Tetzel <note>original: "Tecelii"</note> and his associates who were carrying venal <term>indulgences</term> <note>Certificates sold by the Church to reduce temporal punishment for sins</note> throughout Germany, and by their impious doctrines, he posted his propositions against the Pontifical Indulgences on the Church at Wittenberg. Tetzel and his swindling associates raged; they condemned Luther for heresy and called for him to be burned. From this arose the opportunity for Luther to treat the controversy more fully and accurately. Yet he did this with such modesty that he promised silence at the same time, provided that it was also required of his adversaries; and he submitted his writings to the judgment of the Bishop and his provincial, and even to that of Pope Leo; nor did he ask for anything else than that a different form of preaching be imposed on the heralds of Indulgences. Meanwhile, a thick line of enemies rose up against Luther: Johann Eck, Sylvester Prierias, Jakob van Hoogstraten, and others who tore him apart with insults and slanders, exhorting the Pope to punish him with flames. Luther, a man of more fervent spirit and not at all born to endure insults, took this very poorly; having dared greater things, he did not hesitate to attack the Papal seat itself. For, being daily better taught as a man most studious of Holy Scripture and the Holy Fathers, he recognized the errors of the Roman Church more and more, and once recognized, he did not cease to refute them in published writings. In 1518, summoned by his Augustinians to the Chapter of Heidelberg, he traveled there; and having held a disputation, he demonstrated the truth of his dogmas. At the end of the year, he went to Augsburg to plead his case before the legate Cajetan, to whom the Pope had committed the matter for judgment. Cajetan ordered him to recant his opinion. Luther asked to be taught better things from Holy Scripture, and stated that he would not stubbornly assert anything, and would stand by the judgment of the Church in all things...

Galatinus wrote several other works as well: namely, a *Summary of Theology*; a very extensive *Commentary on the Book of Revelation*; a *Treatise on the Correct Interpretation of Holy Scripture*; a singular work *On the Church Instituted, Abandoned, and Restored*; a *Treatise on the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist*; *On the Intellective Soul*; *On Man*; *On the Seven Times and States of the Church*; *On Identifying Pestilential Men*; *On the Angelic Shepherd*; an *Exposition of a Certain Obscure Roman Prophecy*; *On the Prophecies of Methodius, Saint Cataldus, and Blessed Cyril*; and *On the Crown of the Best Prince*. Wadding <note>Luke Wadding, the famous Franciscan historian</note> testifies that these works, transcribed from the original manuscripts in the Vatican, were in his possession; he promised to publish them, but never fulfilled the pledge he gave.

## MARTIN LUTHER

A German by nationality and a Saxon by birth, Luther was born in Eisleben, a town in the district of Mansfeld, on the 10th of November in the year 1483. His father was Johannes Luther, who at one time held a magisterial office in Mansfeld, and his mother was Margaret Lindemann. In his fourteenth year, he was sent to Magdeburg, and in the following year to Eisenach, so that the basic literary training he received at home might be crowned with deeper knowledge. After spending four years at Eisenach, he moved to the University of Erfurt in 1501; there, having been honored with the degree of Master of Philosophy in 1503, he began to teach philosophy. Soon, however, following the advice of his parents, he turned his mind—which was suited for all pursuits—to the study of Jurisprudence <note>The study of Law</note>. 

In 1504, terrified by the violent death of a certain classmate, he joined the Monks of the Augustinian Order in the monastery at Erfurt without the knowledge of his friends. There, he applied himself diligently to the reading of Holy Scripture (for it was in this place, in an obscure corner of the library, that he happened to see a Latin codex of the Bible for the first time) and to the thorough study of the writings of Saint Augustine and the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine</note>. In 1507, he took the cowl <note>Entered the priesthood</note>; and having been initiated into holy orders, he began to sing the Mass. In 1508, he was transferred from Erfurt to the University of Wittenberg by Johann von Staupitz, where for three years he explained the Logic and Physics of Aristotle. 

In 1512, acting as a legate to Rome on behalf of his monastery, he saw and lamented the corrupt morals of the Roman court. Returning to Wittenberg, he was created a Doctor of Theology in 1513, with Frederick, Duke of Saxony—who was greatly delighted by Luther's sermons—providing the funds. Having obtained his degree, he devoted himself to the study of the Greek and Hebrew languages; and undertaking the task of lecturing on the *Epistle to the Romans* from his chair, he refuted the dogma of justification that was then commonly accepted in the schools and sermons. 

He became famous in the year 1517, when, by the favor of divine power, he presented himself as the leader and standard-bearer for the reform of religion. It was then that he was first offended by the monstrous audacity of Tetzel and his associates, who were carrying <term>Indulgences</term> <note>Certificates sold by the Church to reduce the temporal punishment for sins</note> for sale throughout Germany, and by their impious doctrines; he posted his propositions against Papal Indulgences on the Church at Wittenberg. Tetzel and his swindling associates grew furious; they condemned Luther for heresy and called for him to be burned. This gave Luther the opportunity to treat the controversy more fully and accurately. Yet he did so with such modesty that he promised silence, provided it was also enjoined upon his adversaries; he submitted his writings to the judgment of the Bishop and his provincial superior, and even to Pope Leo; he asked for nothing more than that a different form of preaching be imposed upon the heralds of Indulgences. 

Meanwhile, a dense line of enemies rose up against Luther—Johannes Eck, Sylvester Prierias, Jacobus Hochstraten, and others—who tore into him with insults and calumnies, exhorting the Pope to punish him with flames. Luther, a man of a more fiery spirit and not at all born to endure insults, took this very poorly; having dared greater things, he did not hesitate to attack the Papal see itself. For, being a man most studious of Holy Scripture and the Holy Fathers, and being daily taught more certain truths, he recognized the errors of the Roman Church more and more, and once recognized, he did not cease to refute them in published writings. In 1518, summoned by his fellow Augustinians to the Chapter of Heidelberg, he traveled there; having held a disputation, he demonstrated the truth of his doctrines. At the end of the year, he went to Augsburg to plead his case before the legate Cajetan, to whom the Pope had entrusted the matter for judgment. Cajetan ordered him to recant his opinion. Luther asked to be taught better things from Holy Scripture, and declared that he asserted nothing stubbornly, and was...

# The Century of Reform.

<header>The Century of Reform.</header>

<margin>
16th CENTURY
from the Year 1500.
</margin>
Having professed himself ready, he appealed to the Pope. Having returned home, so as not to stir up troubles in the Church or the state, he considered withdrawing and planned a departure to France. However, after his plan was discovered, he was ordered by Prince Frederick to remain at Wittenberg; and he appealed from the Pope to a General Council. In the year 1518, having set out for Leipzig, he held a lengthy disputation with Johann Eck <note>Johannes Eckius, a prominent defender of Catholicism against the Reformation</note> concerning the authority of the Pope, Purgatory, and Indulgences. In the year 1520, having been condemned and struck with anathema <note>excommunication</note> by Pope Leo, he declared a war to the death from that time against the Papal authority, immediately and publicly burning the Canon Law and Leo's bull at Wittenberg. In the year 1521, summoned by Emperor Charles to the Diet of Worms <term>Diet: a formal deliberative assembly of the Holy Roman Empire</term> under public safe-conduct, he confessed the faith he had previously set forth in writing with invincible constancy of soul; nor could he be led by any threats to condemn his books. Soon outlawed by the Emperor, he lay hidden for almost an entire year in the Wartburg Castle by the order of Prince Frederick. In the year 1522, having emerged from his hiding place, he went to Wittenberg without Frederick's knowledge; and thereafter he openly pleaded the cause of religion. In the year 1524, he laid aside his monastic cowl; and he succeeded in having the Mass abolished in the cathedral church of Wittenberg. In the year 1525, he married Catherine von Bora, a noble maiden and formerly a nun; a marriage perhaps not entirely timely, which nevertheless the Divine Power ratified with manifold offspring. In the year 1529, through the efforts of Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, he held a colloquy at Marburg with the theologians who were followers of Zwingli and Karlstadt <note>Huldrych Zwingli and Andreas Karlstadt, leaders of other branches of the Reformation</note> concerning the establishment of peace. But the excessive stubbornness of the theologians on both sides stood in the way of the Prince's laudable wish. In the year 1534, he committed to the press the Holy Bible translated into German by himself previously in parts and published, finally finished and joined into one volume. He died—a truly great man—at Eisleben, his birthplace, where he had come having been summoned by the Counts of Mansfeld for the sake of settling a dispute, in the year 1546, on the 18th day of February, in the climacteric year <note>A "climacteric" year was historically considered a critical turning point in life, usually multiples of 7 or 9; Luther was 62 turning 63</note> of his age; he was buried with honors at Wittenberg. He possessed by nature a sagacious, sharp, and very fervent intellect, made for undertaking any great tasks; a man, if ever there was one, of an invincible and undaunted spirit. Whenever the cause of truth was at stake, he cared for neither the love nor the hatred of anyone; he disregarded the Pope’s thunderbolts and the Emperor’s edicts no less than the insults of the common people, and bravely despised them. Meanwhile, I would not deny that Luther indulged his passions more freely than was proper, and even drew his pen against the princes of the greater nations with an unrestrained spirit. Truly, *each of us suffers his own spirit* <note>original: "quisque suos patimur manes" — a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, suggesting everyone must face their own destiny or consequences</note>. In the field of literature, he labored not idly: he himself, as those times allowed, was not moderately learned. He placed his zeal especially in searching out the meanings of Holy Scripture, and he explained a very large part of it in commentaries. He restored theology, which had been corrupted for many centuries past, to its original integrity to the best of his ability. In which matter, if he perhaps seems less than orthodox in some places, the fault is to be turned not so much toward himself as toward the condition of the time in which he lived; nor is it a wonder if he contracted certain stains, he who set out to cleanse the Augean stable <note>An allusion to the Greek myth of cleaning a monumental amount of filth in a single day; here referring to Church corruption</note>. He kept the standard of primitive antiquity before his eyes, and certainly (as Erasmus once correctly noted in a *letter* <margin>* Book 12, Letter 10.</margin> to Cardinal Albert), many things are condemned in Luther’s books as heretical which are read in the books of Bernard and Augustine as orthodox, or even as pious; and he adds that Luther wrote many things more imprudently than impiously. Nor should it be passed over what Melchior Adam <margin>† Page 115.</margin> reports in his *Life of Luther*, that Erasmus, when the Pope’s orators were inciting him to attack Luther, replied, "*Luther is too great for me to write against; indeed, he is so great that from reading a single small page of Luther, I learn more than from all of Thomas [Aquinas].*" He used a style that was certainly somewhat harsh, for rare as yet were the likes of Erasmus, Poliziano, Longolius, Bembo, and Sadoleto, who were intimately familiar with Cicero, Livy, and Terence. However unpolished and unrefined it may be, Luther’s vivid diction certainly breathes genuine piety and immense zeal everywhere, and seems to pour forth not so much words as the things themselves. Luther wrote many things on various subjects; these, published in different years and printed at Wittenberg, were arranged into seven volumes. We shall present a small index of these to the reader shortly.

<meta>This page concludes the bibliographic listing of Martin Luther's Latin works, specifically addressing the various editions (Wittenberg and Jena) and acknowledging the sources used for chronology. It marks the conclusion of the primary text before moving to the index.</meta>

# The Reformed Century

<header>THE REFORMED CENTURY</header>
<sig>Dd 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: INDEX</meta>

<margin>
16th CENTURY
from the Year 1500
</margin>

Justus Jonas prepared that Wittenberg edition: another appeared at *Jena* in 1564 in 4 volumes in folio, <note>A "folio" is a large book format where the paper sheets are folded only once.</note> and *in the same place* in 1612 in 7 volumes in folio. Moreover, Simler enumerates many more of Luther's writings in the *Bibliotheca Tigurina* <note>original: "Biblioth. Tigurin."; this refers to the "Zurich Library" catalog by Josias Simler, published in 1574.</note> on page 484, as does his usual copyist Boissard in *Icones illustrium virorum* <note>original: "Icon. illustr. vir."; this is "Portraits of Illustrious Men," a biographical work featuring engravings and short lives.</note> part III, page 210. Both of these authors review the individual small works of Luther according to the chronological order in which they were written or published; however, both are somewhat inaccurate. Therefore, we have for the most part applied more certain chronological markers from other sources. Finally, Luther published almost innumerable works in German, which appeared collected together with the vernacular translations of his Latin works at *Wittenberg* in 1551 in 12 volumes in folio. We have deemed it advisable to omit those writings here, as they pertain very little to our current subject <note>The author is focusing on the scholarly Latin record rather than the popular German publications.</note>.

<sig>B 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Hono-</meta>

# INDEX OF SUBJECTS
### Of noteworthy things contained in this work.

---

->The reader is advised that in this index (omitting things<-
->properly belonging to individual writers), only those things<-
->are included which, noted in passing as it were, might not be<-
->so easily found in their places at first glance.<-

->Pr. denotes the Prolegomena [Introductory Remarks], A. denotes the Appendix.<-
->Where several numbers together refer to the Appendix, they are included in brackets.<-

---

Abercius Marcellus, 51.
*Abexas* [original: *Ἀβέξας*], what it meant to the followers of Basilides, 29, 30. <note>Basilides was a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher; "Abexas" or "Abraxas" was a mystical name for the supreme deity in his system.</note>
The Letter of Abgar to Christ, and Christ's Replies; their authenticity is asserted, 2. Arguments to the contrary are refuted, ibid. <note>Abgar V was a legendary King of Edessa who supposedly corresponded with Jesus through letters.</note>
The Acoemetae [Sleepless] Monks, why and from where they were so called, 28. They favored the Nestorians, ibid. <note>The Acoemetae were a Byzantine monastic order who maintained 24-hour continuous prayer in shifts.</note>
Governors of Provinces used to transmit records of their deeds to Rome, 24.
The *Acts of Pilate* concerning Christ, what they were, ibid. <note>An apocryphal text also known as the Gospel of Nicodemus.</note>
Acts of the Holy Martyrs, 64.
Famous Academies and Schools flourishing under Charlemagne, 503.

Adimantus the Manichaean, 100.
Albigensians, see Waldensians.
Andreas of Trebizond [original: *Trapezuntius*], 118. A.
The English distinguished by their study of ecclesiastical antiquity, Pr. 33.
The power of ordaining English Bishops unjustly claimed by the Pope, 448.
Anglo-Saxons converted to the faith of Christ, 382.

The neglect of ecclesiastical antiquity falsely charged against Protestants, Pr. 33.
The study of ecclesiastical antiquity commended, Pr. 34.

# INDEX OF SUBJECTS.

---

->W.<-

The origin, progress, and persecutions of the **Waldensians**, 632. <note>The Waldensians were a medieval Christian movement originating in the 12th century that emphasized poverty and lay preaching; they were frequently targeted by the Inquisition.</note>
Their innocent customs and dogmas, according to the testimony of their very adversaries, ibid.

<column-break/>

->Z.<-

**Zosimus’s** slander regarding Pope Innocent, 289. <note>Zosimus (5th century AD) was a pagan historian whose "New History" was often critical of Christian figures.</note>
The defense of Zosimus by **Leunclavius**, more clever than prudent and solid, 380. <note>Johannes Leunclavius was a 16th-century German scholar who translated Zosimus into Latin.</note>

---

->THE END.<-

->Available for sale at the shop of Richard Chiswell.<-
<note>Richard Chiswell (1639–1711) was one of the most prominent booksellers and publishers in London during this period.</note>

*Three Books on the Ritual Laws of the Hebrews and Their Reasons*, by **John Spencer**, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Folio. <note>original: "De Legibus Hebræorum ritualibus"; this was a foundational work in the comparative study of religion.</note>

*Two Books on Sacrifices*. In the first, all the sacrifices of the Jews and some of those of the pagan nations are explained. In the second, the Sacrifice of Christ. In both, the opinion of the Catholic Church on these matters is defended against **Faustus Socinus** and his followers. By **William Outram**, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Quarto. <note>Socinus was the founder of Socinianism, which denied the Trinity and the orthodox view of the atonement.</note>

*Nine Books of the Histories of Herodotus of Halicarnassus*. Including his account of the *Life of Homer*, excerpts from Ctesias's books on *Persian and Jewish Matters*, in Greek and Latin. Also **Henri Estienne’s** *Apology for Herodotus*. Added to this edition are a chronology of the history and geographical tables of Herodotus; likewise variant readings and notes collected from many manuscripts and ancient writers, together with an index in Greek and Latin. Folio.

*The Norfolk Library*, or a Catalogue of manuscript and printed books in every art and language, which **Henry, Duke of Norfolk**, gave to the **Royal Society of London** for the promotion of natural science. Quarto.

**Willem ten Rhijne**, Doctor of Medicine: *Dissertations on Arthritis*, a *Schematic Appendix*, and on *Acupuncture*. Also three orations on the antiquity and dignity of chemistry and botany; on physiognomy, and on monsters, illustrated with figures and the author's notes. Octavo. <note>Ten Rhijne was a Dutch physician who provided one of the first detailed Western descriptions of acupuncture.</note>

*Critical Disquisitions* on various editions of the **Bible** through different places and times. To which are added the corrections of a certain Parisian theologian to the short work of **Isaac Vossius** on the *Sibylline Oracles*, and his response to the objections of recent Sacred Criticism. Quarto.

The remedies of the *Pharmacopoeia of the Royal College of London*, described succinctly and arranged in alphabetical order so that each may be found more quickly at first glance. Second edition. At the end is attached a *Catalogue of Simples*. Edited by **James Shipton**, London Pharmacist. <note>"Simples" refers to medicinal herbs or plants used as individual ingredients in medicine.</note>
